title: Accidents at work statistics
text:
EU statistics on fatal and non-fatal accidents at work, as well as standardised rates per 100 000 employed people. Data extracted in September 2025 Planned article update: 25 September 2026 There were 3 367 fatal accidents at work in the EU in 2024, an increase of 69 deaths compared with the year before. In 2024, close to a quarter (23.0%) of all fatal accidents at work in the EU took place in the construction sector. In 2024, around three quarters (75.9%) of all accidents at work in the EU caused wounds, superficial injuries, dislocations, sprains, strains, concussions or internal injuries. |alt=A dynamic column chart showing the incidence rate per hundred thousand inhabitants of fatal accidents at work. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. This article presents a set of main statistical findings in relation to indicators concerning [[Glossary:Non-fatal accident at work|non-fatal]] and [[Glossary:Fatal accident at work|fatal accidents at work]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]; the statistics presented were collected as part of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/methodology#Health%20and%20safety%20at%20work European statistics on accidents at work (ESAW)] administrative data collection exercise. This article is included in a set of statistical articles concerning specific health conditions in the EU which forms part of an online publication on [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] An accident at work is defined in ESAW methodology as a discrete occurrence during the course of work which leads to physical or mental harm. Fatal accidents at work are those that lead to the death of the victim within 1 year of the accident taking place. Non-fatal accidents at work are defined as those that cause at least 4 full calendar days of absence from work (they are sometimes also called ‘serious accidents at work’). Non-fatal accidents at work may result in a considerable number of working days being lost and often involve considerable harm for the workers concerned and their families. They have the potential to force people, for example, to live with a permanent disability, to leave the labour market, or to change jobs. ===Number of accidents=== In 2024, there were 2.78 million non-fatal accidents at work that resulted in at least 4 calendar days of absence from work and 3 367 fatal accidents at work in the [[Glossary:EU_enlargements|EU]] (see Table 1), a ratio of 826 non-fatal accidents for every fatal accident. Compared with the year before, non-fatal accidents decreased by 43 742 (down 1.5%) and fatal accidents increased by 69 (up 2.1%). Men were considerably more likely than women to have an accident at work. In 2024, around 2 out of every 3 (67.2%) non-fatal accidents at work in the EU involved men. Factors that influence these statistics include the proportion of men and women who are in employment; the different types of work that men and women carry out; and the activities in which they work. For example, there are far more accidents in the mining, manufacturing or construction sectors, which tend to be male dominated. It is generally the case that men tend to work on a full-time basis, whereas women are more likely to work on a part-time basis; as such, women spend a shorter period of time (on average) in the workplace, and this may also decrease their likelihood of having an accident at work. Between 2023 and 2024, the number of non-fatal accidents at work in the EU that involved men decreased (down 41 154), while there was a decrease (down 1 923) in the number of non-fatal accidents that involved women. [[Image:Number of non-fatal and fatal accidents at work, 2024 (people).png |thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Number of non-fatal and fatal accidents at work, 2024

''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hsw_n2_01}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=hsw_n2_02}}|alt=A table showing the number of non-fatal accidents at work as a total, for men and for women, and the total number of fatal accidents at work. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Incidence rates=== An alternative way to analyse the information on accidents at work is to express the number of accidents in relation to the number of employed people; this produces a ratio referred to as an incidence rate. In Figures 1 and 2, simple incidence rates are shown relating the number of accidents to the overall number of employed people. For any given country, these statistics give an indication of the likelihood that an employed person had an accident. Across the whole of the EU, there were 1.65 fatal accidents per 100 000 employed people in 2024. Fatal accidents at work are relatively rare events and so their number and incidence can vary greatly from year to year, particularly in smaller EU countries. In 2024, the number of fatal accidents per 100 000 employed people ranged from fewer than 1.00 in the Netherlands, Germany and Sweden to at least 3.00 fatal accidents per 100 000 employed people in Bulgaria and France (see Figure 1). The highest incidence rate among EU countries was recorded in France, with 3.61 fatal accidents per 100 000 employed people. However, France has a specific system for notification and recognition of accidents at work centred on reporting work-related events. This system does not usually differentiate between the accidents where the main cause is the work and the accidents occurring at work. The latter cases should be excluded only if other work-related causal elements are ruled out. This might lead to a higher number of work accidents reported in France in comparison with other countries, including those with similar accident notification systems. The main characteristics differentiating the French system from other systems are listed in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/Annexes/hsw_acc_work_esms_an_4.pdf annex] attached to ESAW metadata. [[Image:Fatal accidents at work, 2024 (incidence rates per 100 000 employed people).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Fatal accidents at work, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hsw_n2_02}}|alt=A column chart showing fatal accidents at work as incidence rates per hundred thousand employed people. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Across the EU, there were 1 359 non-fatal accidents per 100 000 employed people in 2024. The range for incidence rates among EU countries was from fewer than 100 non-fatal accidents per 100 000 employed people in Romania and Bulgaria to more than 2 000 per 100 000 employed people in Spain, Portugal and France (see Figure 2). Particularly low incidence rates for non-fatal accidents may reflect under-reporting, for example, linked to poorly established reporting systems, little financial incentive for victims to report such accidents, or non-binding legal obligations for employers. In the same way, well-established reporting/recognition systems may often explain high incidence rates in some countries. While the phenomenon of low non-fatal incidence rates can in part be considered to reflect under-reporting, the situation for incidence rates of fatal accidents is different as it is much more difficult to avoid reporting a fatal accident. [[Image:Non-fatal_accidents_at_work,_2024_(incidence_rates_per_100_000_employed_people).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Non-fatal accidents at work, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hsw_n2_01}}|alt=A column chart showing non-fatal accidents at work as incidence rates per hundred thousand employed people. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Standardised incidence rates=== When comparing data between countries, incidence rates can be difficult to interpret, for example, when comparing the effectiveness of measures to prevent accidents at work. This is because the likelihood of having an accident is, among other factors, related to the economic activity in which a person works; the relative importance (weight) of different economic activities varies between countries according to the structure of each domestic economy. To account for this, standardised incidence rates are calculated and data for these are shown in Figures 3 and 4. Such rates assume that the relative sizes of economic activities within each national economy are the same as within the EU as a whole. As such, these standardised incidence rates give a more neutral comparison of the health and safety situation across countries. Note that these standardised incidence rates have a slightly narrower activity coverage than the simple incidence rates, as they exclude the mining and quarrying sector as well as some service activities. Standardised incidence rates only cover [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE Rev. 2]] Sections A and C to N, thus excluding Sections B and O to U. On this basis, across the EU there was an average of 2.10 fatal accidents per 100 000 employed people in 2024 (see Figure 3), while there were 1 464 non-fatal accidents per 100 000 employed people (see Figure 4). In 2024, the highest standardised incidence of fatal accidents at work was recorded in France (4.48 deaths per 100 000 employed people), followed by Bulgaria (3.92 deaths per 100 000 employed people) and Latvia (3.74 deaths per 100 000 employed people). At the other end of the range, the Netherlands and Luxembourg recorded the lowest standardised incidence rates among EU countries, with fewer than 1.00 fatal accidents per 100 000 employed people in 2024. [[Image:Fatal accidents at work, 2024_(standardised incidence rates per 100 000 employed people).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Fatal accidents at work, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hsw_mi01}}|alt=A column chart showing fatal accidents at work as standardised incidence rates per hundred thousand employed people. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 4 shows that the standardised incidence rate of non-fatal accidents at work in 2024 was generally higher in some of the EU countries with insurance-based accident reporting systems: Portugal reported 2 951 non-fatal accidents per 100 000 employed people, followed by Spain and France with rates of 2 641 and 2 550 per 100 000 employed people, respectively. Insurance-based accident reporting systems offer a significant financial compensation for the victim when an accident is reported, as opposed to legal obligation systems in which victims are covered by the general social security system. Among the eastern or [[Glossary:Baltic_Member_States|Baltic]] EU countries, which mostly have legal obligation systems, Slovenia (1 536 per 100 000) and Estonia (913 per 100 000) were the only ones to report an incidence rate of more than 700 non-fatal accidents per 100 000 employed people. By far the lowest standardised incidence rates were reported in Romania and Bulgaria, at 64 and 92 non-fatal work accidents per 100 000 employed people, respectively; again, it should be noted that these values may reflect a relatively high degree of under-reporting. [[Image:Non-fatal accidents at work, 2024_(standardised incidence rates per 100 000 employed people).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Non-fatal accidents at work, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hsw_mi01}}|alt=A column chart showing non-fatal accidents at work as standardised incidence rates per hundred thousand employed people. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Analysis by activity=== As noted above, the incidence of accidents may – in part – be higher for men (than for women) due to the economic activities where they are more likely to work. Indeed, the number of accidents at work varies greatly depending upon the economic activity in question (see Figure 5) and is positively skewed in relation to male-dominated activities. Within the EU, the construction, transportation and storage, manufacturing, and agriculture, forestry and fishing sectors together accounted for 65.0% of all fatal accidents at work in 2023 and 44.4% of all non-fatal accidents at work. Close to a quarter (23.0%) of all fatal accidents at work in the EU took place within the construction sector, while transportation and storage (15.9%) had the next highest share. Manufacturing (13.8%) and agriculture, forestry and fishing (12.1%) were the only other NACE sections for which double-digit shares of the total number of fatal accidents were recorded. Non-fatal accidents were relatively common in 2023 within EU manufacturing (18.3% of the total), construction (12.7%), distributive trades (12.4%) and human health and social work activities (12.3%); these 4 were the only NACE sections for which double-digit shares of the total number of non-fatal accidents were recorded. [[Image:Fatal and non-fatal accidents at work by NACE section, EU, 2024 (% of fatal and non-fatal accidents).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Fatal and non-fatal accidents at work by NACE section, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hsw_n2_01}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=hsw_n2_02}}|alt=A double bar chart showing the share of accidents at work in each NACE section. For each NACE section, data are shown for non-fatal accidents and for fatal accidents. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Analysis by type of injury=== Figure 6 presents an analysis of data according to the type of injury sustained when people were involved in accidents. In the EU, there were 3 types of particularly common injuries in 2024, namely, wounds and superficial injuries (29.3% of the total), dislocations, sprains and strains (26.3%) and concussions and internal injuries (20.3%). These were followed by 1 other relatively common type, bone fractures (11.6%). None of the other types of injuries accounted for a double-digit share of the total number of accidents in the EU, with the next highest share for shocks (4.0%). Although not shown in this article, the data collected in the context of ESAW also include an analysis of which body parts were injured in accidents (such as the head, neck, back, torso and organs, arms and hands, and legs and feet) as well as information on the causes and circumstances of accidents. [[Image:Fatal and non-fatal accidents at work by type of injury, EU, 2024 (% of accidents).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Fatal and non-fatal accidents at work by type of injury, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hsw_n2_07}}|alt=A bar chart showing the share of various types of injuries among all accidents at work. Data are analysed for 14 different types of injury. Data are shown for the EU for 2024. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Accidents at work_Health2026.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== In December 2008, the [[Glossary:European Parliament (EP)|European Parliament]] and the [[Glossary:Council of the European Union|Council]] adopted {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R1338:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1338/2008}} on Community statistics on public health and health and safety at work. The regulation is designed to ensure that health statistics provide adequate information for all EU countries to monitor Community actions in the field of public health and health and safety at work. In April 2011, {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0349:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) No 349/2011}} on statistics on accidents at work was adopted specifying in detail the variables, breakdowns and metadata that EU countries are required to deliver – this legislation is being implemented in a number of phases. Note also that {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011D0231:EN:NOT|title=Commission Decision No 2011/231/EU}} from April 2011 granted derogations to certain EU countries with respect to the transmission of statistics on accidents at work. European statistics on accidents at work (ESAW) is the main data source for EU statistics relating to health and safety at work issues. ESAW includes data on occupational accidents that result in at least 4 calendar days of absence from work, including fatal accidents. The phrase ‘during the course of work’ means while engaged in an occupational activity or during the time spent at work. This generally includes cases of road traffic accidents in the course of work but excludes accidents during the journey between home and the workplace. The statistics presented for accidents at work refer to declarations made either to public (social security administrations) or private insurance schemes, or to other relevant national authorities (for example, those controlling labour or workplace inspections). Indicators on accidents at work may be presented as absolute values, as percentage distributions, as incidence rates in relation to every 100 000 employed people (the denominator being provided by the authorities that are responsible for ESAW data collection in EU countries or by the EU’s [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|labour force survey (EU-LFS)]]) or as standardised incidence rates. The data generally relate to all economic activities, unless otherwise specified. For example, the analyses in Figures 3 and 4 cover NACE Sections A and C to N. Because the frequency of accidents at work varies between NACE activities – high risk activities include agriculture, forestry and fishing, manufacturing, construction, distributive trades, and transportation and storage – a standardisation procedure is performed to facilitate the comparison of national data. A direct standardisation method is used with weights calculated for the European reference population: the weights represent the proportion of the reference (working) population in each NACE activity. National incidence rates are calculated for each NACE activity, and these are combined using the fixed set of EU weights to produce an overall standardised incidence rate for the EU country concerned. More details are available in a [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/Annexes/hsw_acc_work_esms_an_2.docx methodological note]. Statistics on accidents at work may reflect under-coverage or under-reporting. Under-coverage exists when the relevant population is not covered by the data source for accidents, for example when a certain economic activity or employment type is excluded. Under-reporting relates to the situation where an accident occurs but is not reported although the related economic activity is included. The extent of under-coverage of ESAW data can be analysed partially by comparing the reference population (of workers) in ESAW with data derived from the LFS. Under-reporting is more difficult to analyse and establish but some comparisons are available. Comparing results from the reporting systems used for the legal obligation to report an accident with systems based on insurance reports is 1 possible method; this may indicate under-reporting in the system for the legal obligation of accidents or over-reporting in insurance-based systems. Another method is to compare (geographically or over time) the ratio of fatal to non-fatal accidents, as the reporting of fatal accidents can be expected to be accurate due to their severe nature. Comparisons can also be made with data from household surveys, for example from the EU-LFS (which includes periodic modules on accidents at work and work-related health problems). In addition, changes in the way data are collected and processed in EU countries may have an influence on the number and incidence of accidents at work in a particular year. For example, on 30 June 2016 a number of derogations from provisions in the EU regulation governing ESAW ended for several EU countries. This had a significant effect on the data concerning accidents at work for the reference year 2014. For example, for the first time French data included full coverage of all employees in economic activities covered by NACE Sections A to S. This led to a substantial increase in the number of accidents recorded in France (compared with 2013). In a similar vein, the 2014 data for Belgium included information pertaining to accidents in the public sector for the first time and this also resulted in an increase in the reported number of accidents. In 2016, some correction factors were removed from Greek data by the national statistical authority due to methodological issues which caused a considerable decrease in the number of accidents reported for reference year 2014 (compared with 2013). Finally, Dutch and Norwegian data (the latter are not included in the EU total) for the 2014 reference year for non-fatal accidents decreased significantly due to methodological issues. ===Context=== A safe, healthy working environment is a crucial factor in an individual’s quality of life and is also a collective concern. Governments in EU countries recognise the social and economic benefits of better health and safety at work. Reliable, comparable, up-to-date statistical information is vital for setting policy objectives and adopting suitable policy measures and preventative actions. The [[Glossary:Treaties of Rome|Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union]] (Article 153) states that ‘[...] the Union shall support and complement the activities of the EU Member States in the following fields: (a) improvement in particular of the working environment to protect workers’ health and safety; [...]’. The main principles governing the protection of workers’ health and safety are laid down in a 1989 framework {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31989L0391:EN:NOT|title=Directive (89/391/EEC)}}, the basic objective of which is to encourage improvements in occupational health and safety. All sectors of activity, both public and private, are covered by this legislation, which establishes the principle that the employer has a duty to ensure workers’ health and safety in all aspects relating to work, while the worker has an obligation to follow the employer’s health and safety instructions and report potential dangers. Within this field, the European Commission’s policy agenda for the period 2021 to 2027 was set out in the Communication '''[https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=151&langId=en EU strategic framework on health and safety at work 2021–27]''' ({{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52021DC0323:EN:NOT|title=COM(2021) 323 final}}). It aims to ensure that the EU continues to play a leading role in the promotion of high standards for working conditions within the EU as well as further afield. The communication outlined 3 major challenges *anticipating and managing change in the new world of work brought about by the green, digital and demographic transitions *improving prevention of workplace accidents and illnesses *increasing preparedness for any potential future health crises. The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the crucial importance of health policy, including health and safety at work. The European Commission is working towards providing strategic policy orientations that aim to contribute to the improvement of the health and safety of workers across the EU. This is particularly important with respect to a new set of risks, such as those resulting from new ways of working, new technologies and digitalisation, or the impact of pandemics and associated containment measures, alongside more traditional risks of accidents at work, such as exposure to dangerous substances. At the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, preventive measures were put in place with the aim of limiting the spread of the Coronavirus and to combat the pandemic. Among these, some economic activities were either completely stopped or restricted by many governments or employers. In some cases, working remotely or from home became more common. This had a direct impact on all economic activities. For those sectors where the activity was stopped or reduced, the number of accidents decreased. Inactivity or reduced activity in certain sectors resulted in a lower number of workers and/or hours worked, and therefore showed an unusually large decrease in reported accidents at work. By contrast, in some sectors the COVID-19 pandemic generated an increase in activity. For example, this was the case for human health activities, residential care activities or social work activities without accommodation. These activities were generally characterised by higher numbers of reported accidents at work during the pandemic, especially when COVID-19 cases of occupational origin were included (following national practices and legislation). Public services that deal with receipt of notifications as well as the reporting, investigation and recognition of accidents at work may have functioned with limited capacities during parts of the crisis. The combined impact of the issues described above led to an overall decrease in the reported number of accidents at work for reference year 2020, while there was a partial rebound across most EU countries and many economic activities during 2021 and 2022. In 2023, the number of occupational COVID-19 cases recognised as accidents at work reduced considerably also as the effect of administrative decisions related to ceasing recognition in several countries. ===Other articles=== *[[Accidents and injuries statistics]] *[[Accidents at work - statistics by economic activity|Accidents at work - statistics by economic activity]] *[[Accidents at work - statistics on causes and circumstances|Accidents at work - statistics on causes and circumstances]] *[[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] - online publication *[[Health statistics introduced]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/database Health], see :Health and safety at work (hsw) ::Accidents at work (ESAW, 2008 onwards) (hsw_acc_work) :::Main indicators (hsw_mi) :::Details by NACE Rev. 2 activity (2008 onwards) (hsw_n2) :::Causes and circumstances of accidents at work (ESAW phase III) (hsw_ph3) ::Accidents at work (ESAW) - until 2007 (hsw_acc7_work) ::Accidents at work and other work-related health problems (source LFS) (hsw_apex) ::Work related health problems and accidental injuries - LFS 1999 (hsw_inj_pb) ::Occupational diseases (EODS; 2013 onwards) - experimental statistics (hsw_occ) ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/overview Health] ===Methodology=== '''''ESMS metadata files''''' *{{Template:Esms|code=hsw_acc_work_esms|title=Accidents at work (ESAW, 2008 onwards)}} (ESMS metadata file – hsw_acc_work_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=lfso_20_esms|title=2020. Accidents at work and other work-related health problems}} (ESMS metadata file – lfso_20_esms) '''''Publication''''' *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-RA-12-102|title=European statistics on accidents at work (ESAW) – Summary methodology – 2013 edition}} ===External links=== *[https://osha.europa.eu/en European Agency for Safety and Health at Work] *[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/rights-work/health-and-safety-work_en European Commission – Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion – Health and safety at work], see **[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/rights-work/health-and-safety-work/strategic-policy-documents_en EU strategic framework (2021–27)] *[https://www.eurofound.europa.eu/en/topics/health-and-well-being European Foundation for the Improvement of Living and Working Conditions (EUROFOUND) – Health and well-being] *[https://www.ilo.org/topics-and-sectors/safety-and-health-work International Labour Organization (ILO) – Safety and health at work] {{Unit|topic=X_Health}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Accidents at work statistics]] [[Category:Health|Accidents at work statistics]] [[Category:Accidents at work|Accidents at work statistics]] [[Category:Labour market (incl. labour force survey) |Accidents at work statistics]] [[Category:Health and safety|Accidents at work statistics]] [[Category:Statistical article|Accidents at work statistics]] [[Category:September2026|Accidents at work statistics]]

title: Adult Education Survey (AES) methodology
text:
This article describes the methodology of the [[Glossary:Adult_education_survey_(AES)|adult education survey (AES)]], a [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] harmonised survey on adult participation in learning activities. The AES along with the following two other data collections, the [[Glossary:Continuing_vocational_training_survey_(CVTS)|continuing vocational training survey (CVTS)]] and the [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)| EU labour force survey (EU-LFS)]] provide EU statistics on [[Glossary:Lifelong_learning (LLL)|lifelong learning]]. ===Introduction=== The AES provides an overview of the participation of individuals in education and training (i.e. formal and non-formal education and training as well as informal learning). The reference period for the participation in the learning activities is the twelve months prior to the interview. A pilot survey took place around the year 2007, followed by an AES in 2011, 2016 and 2022, underpinned by European legislation. Up to 2016, the survey focused on people aged 25-64. Due to changes in the legislation, the most recent AES covered people aged 18-69. The following information is available from the AES: *Participation in formal education, non-formal education and training and informal learning (respectively labelled FE, NFE and INF); *Access to information on learning possibilities; *Time spent on education and training; *Characteristics of the learning activities; *Reasons for not participating; *Obstacles to participation; *Employer financing and costs of learning; *Self-reported language skills. Comparable data from 2007, 2011, 2016 and 2022 AES can be found in the following folders of the database: *Participation in education and training (last 12 months) (trng_aes_12m0); *Participation in informal learning (last 12 months) (trng_aes_12m4); *Access to information on education and training (last 12 months) (trng_aes_12m1); *Time spent on education and training (last 12 months) (trng_aes_12m2); *Obstacles to participation in education and training (last 12 months) (trng_aes_12m3); *Self-reported language skills (educ_lang_00). ===Coverage and mandate=== Four waves of the AES have been implemented so far. The first AES (2007 AES) was a pilot survey conducted in 26 EU Member States (Ireland and Luxembourg did not participate), as well as in Norway, Switzerland and Tukey. This first wave was carried out based on a gentlemen’s agreement between 2005 and 2008 (depending on the country). The second wave (2011 AES) was conducted in 27 EU Member States (Croatia did not participate), Norway, Switzerland as well as in Serbia and Turkey between July 2011 and June 2012. This statistical operation was for the first time conducted under the institutional mandate set in {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R0452:EN:NOT|title=Regulation 452/2008}}, and implemented by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32010R0823:EN:NOT|title=Regulation 823/2010}}. This legal basis establishes the collection of data on the participation of adults (aged 25–64) in learning activities every five years. The third wave (2016 AES) was conducted in the 28 EU Member States, Norway, Switzerland as well as in Serbia, Turkey, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina and North Macedonia between July 2016 and March 2017. {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32014R1175:EN:NOT|title=Regulation 1175/2014}} provided the implementation details of this wave. The fourth wave (2022 AES) was conducted in the 27 EU Member States, Iceland, Norway, Switzerland as well as in Serbia, Turkey, Albania, and North Macedonia between July 2022 and March 2023. Data collection is based on {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32021R0861:EN:NOT|title=Regulation 861/2021}}. Further information on each wave is available in the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/trng_aes_12m0_esms.htm reference metadata] and in the [http://circabc.europa.eu/w/browse/ac6f3889-ab25-4f75-9c7a-de997f65e2db implementation manuals]. ===Basic concepts=== '''Lifelong learning''' encompasses all learning activities undertaken throughout life with the aim of improving knowledge, skills and competences, within personal, civic, social or employment-related perspectives. The intention or aim to learn is the critical point that distinguishes these activities from non-learning activities, such as cultural or sporting activities. '''Adult learning''' means the participation of adults in lifelong learning. Adult learning usually refers to learning activities after the end of [[Glossary:Initial_education|initial education]]. The main indicator of adult learning is the '''participation rate in education and training''' of those aged 25-64 and covers participation in both formal and non-formal education and training. '''Learning activities''' are any activities of an individual organised with the intention to improve their knowledge, skills, and competences. There are two fundamental criteria that distinguish learning activities from non-learning activities: they must be intentional and organised. '''Intentional''' learning (as opposed to random learning) is defined as a deliberate search for knowledge, skills or competences or attitudes of lasting value. '''Organised''' learning is defined as learning planned in a pattern or sequence with explicit or implicit aims. The learning activities are defined within a classification named {{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-15-011|title=classification of learning activities (CLA)}}. The current version of the CLA (2016 edition) is aligned with [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|ISCED 2011]]. The 2016 edition of the CLA applies to the 2016 and 2022 AES. 2007 and 2011 AES refer to the 2006 edition of the CLA; however, data between the waves are overall comparable. The CLA defines three main types of learning activities as follows: [[Image:Classification_of_learning_activities.png|thumb|centre|500px|Table 1: Classification of learning activities
''Source:'' Eurostat, Classification of learning activities manual (2016)]] *'''Formal education and training''' is defined as “education that is institutionalised, intentional and planned through public organisations and recognised private bodies, and - in their totality - constitute the formal education system of a country. Formal education programmes are thus recognised as such by the relevant national education or equivalent authorities, e.g. any other institution in cooperation with the national or sub-national education authorities. Formal education consists mostly of initial education [...]. Vocational education, special needs education and some parts of adult education are often recognised as being part of the formal education system. Qualifications from formal education are by definition recognised and, therefore, are within the scope of ISCED. Institutionalised education occurs when an organisation provides structured educational arrangements, such as student-teacher relationships and/or interactions, that are specially designed for education and learning”.Source ISCED 2011. *'''Non-formal education and training''' is defined as “education that is institutionalised, intentional and planned by an education provider. The defining characteristic of non-formal education is that it is an addition, alternative and/or complement to formal education within the process of lifelong learning of individuals. It is often provided in order to guarantee the right of access to education for all. It caters to people of all ages but does not necessarily apply a continuous pathway structure; it may be short in duration and/or low-intensity; and it is typically provided in the form of short courses, workshops or seminars. Non-formal education mostly leads to qualifications that are not recognised as formal or equivalent to formal qualifications by the relevant national or sub-national education authorities or to no qualifications at all. Nevertheless, formal, recognised qualifications may be obtained through exclusive participation in specific non-formal education programmes; this often happens when the non-formal programme completes the competencies obtained in another context”.Source ISCED 2011. *'''Informal learning''' is “intentional, but it is less organised and less structured ... and may include for example learning events (activities) that occur in the family, in the workplace, and in the daily life of every person, on a self-directed, family-directed or socially-directed basis.”Source CLA 2016. '''Job-related non-formal education and training''': the respondent takes part in the non-formal education and training activity in order to obtain knowledge and/or learn new skills needed for a current or future job, to increase earnings, to improve job and/or career opportunities in a current or another field and generally to improve his/her opportunities for advancement and promotion. '''Employer-sponsored job-related non-formal education and training''': all job-related non-formal education and training activities paid at least partially by the employer and/or done during paid working hours. ===Usual breakdowns and classifications=== '''Educational attainment level''' The educational attainment level is the highest level of education successfully completed by an individual. Educational attainment is classified according to the [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|International standard classification of education (ISCED)]]. This classification allows for international comparability between the different national education systems, introducing criteria to categorise the education levels into a common nomenclature. It therefore facilitates comparisons across countries based on uniform and internationally agreed definitions. The successful completion of an education programme must be validated by a recognised qualification, i.e. a qualification officially recognised by the relevant national education authorities. In cases where there is no certification, successful completion must be associated with full attendance. When determining the highest level, both general and vocational education should be taken into consideration. 2016 and 2022 AES were classified according to ISCED 2011; 2007 and 2011 AES were classified under ISCED 1997. The AES data dissemination considers the following broad levels of aggregation: *Less than primary, primary and lower secondary education: this aggregate refers to levels 0, 1 and 2 of the ISCED 2011 (online code ED0-2). Data up to 2011 refer to ISCED 1997 levels 0, 1 and 2 but also include level 3C short (educational attainment from ISCED level 3 programmes of less than two years); *Upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education: this aggregate corresponds to ISCED 2011 levels 3 and 4 (online code ED3_4). ISCED 2011 level 3 programmes of partial level completion are considered within ISCED level 3. Data up to 2011 refer to ISCED 1997 levels 3C long, 3A, 3B and 4; :*Upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education - general: this aggregate corresponds to ISCED 2011 levels 34 and 44 (online code ED3_4GEN). Data are available from 2022 onwards; :*Upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education - vocational: this aggregate corresponds to ISCED 2011 levels 35 and 45 (online code ED3_4VOC). Data are available from 2022 onwards; *Tertiary education: this aggregate covers ISCED 2011 levels 5, 6, 7 and 8 (short-cycle tertiary education, bachelor's or equivalent level, master's or equivalent level, doctoral or equivalent level, online code ED5-8 ‘tertiary education’). Data up to 2011 refer to ISCED 1997 levels 5 and 6. '''Occupation''' Occupation is defined as the task and duties undertaken by each worker in their job. The [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_occupations_(ISCO)|International standard classification of occupations (ISCO)]] organises jobs into a clearly defined set of groups. AES as from 2011 were classified according to ISCO-08; 2007 AES was classified under ISCO-COM 88. Data are directly comparable for the categories shown online. Four categories of employee occupations are distinguished in the online tables on occupation: *Managers, professionals, technicians and associate professionals; *Clerical support workers, service and sales workers; *Skilled manual workers; and *Elementary occupations. '''Foreign languages - level of self-reported knowledge''' The knowledge of foreign languages is self-reported by the respondents and is categorised in four levels in the AES questionnaire (except in 2011 where the category ‘hardly any language skills’ was not included). *Hardly any language skills; *Beginner (basic user); *Intermediate (independent user); and *Advanced (proficient user). In the online tables of the domain educ_lang_00, only the categories ‘basic’, ‘good’ and ‘proficient’ are displayed; the category ‘hardly any language skills’ is included in the category ‘basic’. '''Degree of urbanisation''' Three types of areas are defined based on population density: *'''cities''': at least 50% of the population lives in urban centres; *'''towns and suburbs''': at least 50% of the population lives in urban clusters and less than 50% of the population lives in urban centres; *'''rural areas''': at least 50% of the population lives in rural grid cells. ===Questionnaire=== The 2022 AES European standard questionnaire has the following structure: 1.0 - General information 1.1 - Information on the household 1.2 - Information on the individual :1.2.1 Demographic background :1.2.2 Educational attainment :1.2.3 Not completed formal education :1.2.4 Main activity status :1.2.5 Characteristics of the main job :1.2.6 Parental education and country of birth 1.3 - Access to information about learning possibilities and guidance 1.4 - Participation in education and training :1.4.1 Formal education :1.4.2 Non-formal education and training ::1.4.2.1 Details on activities 1.5 - Obstacles to participation in education and training 1.6 - Informal learning 1.7 - Languages 1.8 - Self-perceived health 1.9 - Income of the household ===Quality reports=== National quality reports for the 2022 AES are gradually being published via the reference metadata. For the 2016 AES, national quality reports are available on [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/d14c857a-601d-438a-b878-4b4cebd0e10f/library/cef44c0d-b1cb-456a-a32f-bba65028b51a?p=1&n=10&sort=name_ASC Circabc]. Summary tables for the EU are available on [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/d14c857a-601d-438a-b878-4b4cebd0e10f/library/769a4f77-2258-4c87-9136-ab195e7c4d74?p=1&n=10&sort=name_ASC Circabc]. For the 2011 AES, national quality reports as well as an EU quality report featuring metadata and methodological aspects of the survey are available on [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/d14c857a-601d-438a-b878-4b4cebd0e10f/library/60d3e326-f5d2-417c-816d-63f824bf685b?p=1&n=10&sort=name_ASC Circabc]. For the 2007 AES, an evaluation of the national quality reports is available on [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/d14c857a-601d-438a-b878-4b4cebd0e10f/library/18ff522e-0d08-416c-86f7-5c6a3543356f/details Circabc]. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:AES_methodology_SE.xlsx|Tables and figures]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Context=== [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publishes data on education and training which can be found on Eurostat's [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/education-and-training/data/database database] and cover the following features: *participation in education and training; *learning mobility; *education personnel; *education finance; *education and training outcomes; *languages. These statistics are based on four main data sources: *Education systems – joint UNESCO-OECD-Eurostat (UOE) data collection; *Adult education survey (AES); *Continuing vocational training survey (CVTS); and *Labour force survey (EU-LFS). Statistics on adult learning – which can be found under the folder 'adult learning' in the 'participation in education and training' section of Eurostat's database on education and training – are based on the AES, the LFS and the CVTS. The adult education survey and the labour force survey both provide data on participation in adult learning from the individuals' perspective while the CVTS covers the theme of adult learning through the enterprises (continuing vocational training). The LFS also provides data on the participation in formal and non-formal education and training on a more frequent basis than the AES. Main differences in the data on education and training in the LFS and in the data on education and training in the AES are the reference period (4 weeks and – from 2022 – 12 months in the LFS, 12 months in the AES), the coverage of non-formal education (the LFS does not cover guided on-the-job training) and the overall aim and design of the surveys (AES is as survey dedicated to learning activities, LFS is about labour market participation, and also especially the fact that proxies are possible when collecting the LFS data while they are not recommended and almost never used in most countries when collecting the AES data). On the other hand, the information found in the AES is richer than that of the LFS in the sense that the AES describes the learning activities in depth and also offers information on the command of foreign languages. ===Other articles=== *[[Education and training in the EU - facts and figures]] ===Database=== [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/education-and-training/database Education and training (educ)] For adult participation in learning, see: : Participation in education and training (educ_part) :: Adult learning (trng) ::: Participation in education and training (last 12 months) (trng_aes_12m0) ::: Participation in informal learning (last 12 months) (trng_aes_12m4) ::: Access to information on education and training (last 12 months) (trng_aes_12m1) ::: Time spent on education and training (last 12 months) (trng_aes_12m2) ::: Obstacles to participation in education and training (last 12 months) (trng_aes_12m3) For self-reported language skills, see: : Languages (educ_lang) :: Self-reported language skills (educ_lang_00) ===Dedicated section=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/education-and-training/overview Education and training] ===Publications=== *[[Adult learning statistics]] *[[Adult learning statistics - characteristics of education and training]] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/microdata/adult-education-survey Access to microdata] ===Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/trng_aes_12m_esms.htm Adult Education Survey (reference metadata)] *[https://circabc.europa.eu/w/browse/ac6f3889-ab25-4f75-9c7a-de997f65e2db AES – EU implementation manuals and further methodological information] ===External links=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/education/policies/eu-policy-in-the-field-of-adult-learning_en EU policy in the field of adult learning] *[http://www.unesco.org/uil/ UNESCO Institute for Lifelong Learning] === Notes === ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Article_name'' {{Unit|topic=X_Education_surveys}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Adult Education Survey (AES) statistics methodology]] [[Category:Education and training|Adult Education Survey (AES) statistics methodology]] [[Category:Background article|Adult Education Survey (AES) statistics methodology]]

title: Actual and usual hours of work
text:
EU statistics are provided on the main results of the Labour force survey (LFS) for the European Union (EU) and Member States. Data extracted in May 2026 Planned article update: May 2027 In 2025, the average working week at EU level lasted 35.9 hours. This varied across the EU, from 31.9 actual hours of work in the Netherlands to 39.6 in Greece. Among full-time employed people in the EU, men worked on average 39.4 hours per week compared with 37.6 hours for women, with differences exceeding 3 hours in Ireland, the Netherlands and Greece. Belgium had the largest difference in usual weekly working hours between employees (35.2 hours) and own-account workers (43.2 hours). This article highlights the main aspects of working hours for different groups of workers (e.g. men and women, part-time and full-time workers, employees and self-employed people) and across various economic activities and occupations. More specifically, it focuses on the average number of weekly actual and usual hours of work which employed people spent in their main job in 2025. The statistics in this article are based on the [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)|EU labour force survey (EU-LFS)]]. === Working hours vary across EU countries === In 2025, the actual weekly hours of work of [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] full-time and part-time workers aged 20-64 in their main job averaged 35.9 hours. This number refers to the hours people worked in their main job in the reference week (see [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser-backend/api/public/explanatory-notes/get/Info_note_LFSQ_20240604.pdf methodological notes for the difference between actual and usual hours of work]). The average actual working hours per week differ between EU countries (see Map 1). The longest average weeks were recorded in Greece (39.6 hours), followed by Poland and Bulgaria (38.7 hours), Lithuania (38.4 hours), and Slovenia (38.3 hours). By contrast, the shortest weeks were in the Netherlands (31.9 hours), with Germany and Denmark (33.9 hours each) and Austria (34.0 hours). [[Image:Map_actual_and_usual_hours_of_work_2025.png|thumb|center|600px|Map 1: Average number of actual weekly hours of work in main job, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfsa_ewhan2}}|alt= Map showing average number of actual weekly hours of work in the main job of the age group 20 to 64 years in the EU countries, EFTA countries and candidate countries. Each country is colour coded based on a range of hours per week for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Employed people by the average actual working hours in a week === In the EU, in 2025, employed people reported the following average weekly working hours in their main job (see Figure 1) * 9.9% did not work in their main job during the reference week * 7.2% worked between 0.5 and 19.5 hours * 6.6% worked between 20 and 24.5 hours * 3.4% worked between 25 and 29.5 hours * 9.2% worked between 30 and 34.5 hours * 16.4% worked between 35 and 39.5 hours * 37.6% worked between 40 and 44.5 hours * 4.0% worked between 45 and 49.5 hours * 5.8% worked 50 hours or more per week The range of 40.0–44.5 actual working hours per week represented the largest share of employed people in most countries, with the highest proportions recorded in Bulgaria (82.8%), Latvia (77.1%) and Romania (75.5%). Exceptions were observed in Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France and Ireland, where the largest share of employed people worked on average between 35.0 and 39.5 hours per week. Figure 1 In general, there is a strong consistency between actual and usual hours of work, although actual working hours tend to be lower than usual working hours. This difference can be explained by the fact that usual working hours are not affected by absences from work, whereas actual working hours in the reference week are affected by holidays, sick leaves or other kinds of absences. A comparison of the distribution of actual and usual working hours in the main job by status in employment shows that self-employed people were more strongly represented in the higher working-hour categories (i.e. 40.0–44.5 hours and 45.0 hours or more) than employees (see Figure 2). Among employees, the largest share worked between 40.0 and 44.5 hours per week (38.4%), while only 6.4% worked 45.0 hours or more. By contrast, among self-employed people, equal shares (32.2%) were recorded for both the 40.0–44.5 hours category and the 45.0 hours or more category. Figure 2
=== Patterns in average actual working week: by full-time and part-time workers and sex === Average weekly working hours for full-time employed people in the EU differed between men and women in 2025: men worked 39.4 hours per week on average, while women worked 37.6 hours (see Figure 3). For women, the longest working week was recorded in Slovenia (39.2 hours), followed by Lithuania (39.1 hours) and Latvia and Poland (both 38.9 hours). The shortest average working weeks for women were observed in the Netherlands (35.0 hours), Finland (35.6 hours), Ireland (35.9 hours) and Belgium (36.4 hours). For men, only four EU countries recorded an average working week of 40 hours or more in 2025: Greece (41.8 hours), Poland (40.6 hours), Slovenia (40.2 hours) and Cyprus (40.0 hours). Men in full-time employment worked the fewest hours per week in Finland and the Netherlands (both 38.4 hours), followed by Hungary and Sweden (both 38.5 hours). The largest differences between men and women (3 hours or more per week) were observed in Ireland, where men worked 39.9 hours per week compared with 35.9 hours for women, the Netherlands (38.4 hours for men and 35.0 hours for women), and Greece (41.8 hours for men and 38.8 hours for women). By contrast, the smallest differences between men and women, of less than 0.5 hours per week, were recorded in Latvia and Bulgaria. Figure 3 The pattern of weekly working hours by sex differed for part-time workers. At EU level, men and women employed part time worked a similar number of hours per week on average (21.7 hours for men and 21.9 hours for women). However, in many EU countries, women working part time recorded longer average working weeks than men in the same category. Denmark showed the largest difference between women and men employed part time, with women working on average 21.3 hours per week compared with 18.0 hours for men. By contrast, Latvia was one of the few countries where men employed part-time worked longer hours than women, averaging 21.3 hours per week compared with 20.7 hours for women.
=== Average actual weekly working hours by economic activity and occupation === The average length of the working week, measured in actual hours worked, varied across economic activities ([[Glossary:NACE|NACE Rev. 2]]) in 2025 (see Figure 4). The longest average working weeks were recorded in '''Agriculture, forestry and fishing''' (41.2 hours), followed by '''Mining and quarrying''' (38.9 hours) and '''Construction''' (38.6 hours). By contrast, the shortest average working weeks were observed in '''Activities of households''' as employers (27.1 hours), '''Education''' (31.8 hours) and '''Arts, entertainment and recreation''' (32.7 hours). Figure 4 Across occupational groups classified according [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_occupations_(ISCO)|ISCO-08]]), '''Skilled agricultural, forestry and fishery workers''' recorded the longest average working week in the EU in 2025, with 42.0 actual working hours per week, followed by '''Managers''' (40.6 hours) and '''Armed forces occupations''' (39.4 hours) (see Figure 5). By contrast, the shortest average working weeks were observed among workers in '''Elementary occupations''' (31.8 hours), '''Clerical support workers''' (34.0 hours) and '''Service and sales workers''' (34.5 hours). Figure 5
=== Usual average working week of employees and self-employed people === At EU level, in 2025, self-employed people with employees (i.e. employers) recorded the longest average usual working week in their main job, at 46.4 hours, followed by self-employed people without employees (also known as ‘own-account workers’) with 39.7 hours. By comparison, employees worked an average of 36.6 usual hours per week (see Figure 6). The longest average working weeks for employers were recorded in France (50.0 hours), Belgium (49.8 hours) and Greece (49.2 hours). Belgium also showed the largest difference in usual weekly working hours between employees (35.2 hours) and own-account workers (43.2 hours). In many EU countries, own-account workers worked more usual hours per week than employees in 2025. However, the opposite pattern was observed in Cyprus, Latvia, Estonia, Lithuania and Romania, where employees worked notably more hours than own-account workers. The largest differences were recorded in Cyprus and Latvia, where employees worked on average 5.5 and 4.5 hours per week more, respectively, than own-account workers. Among all EU countries, the longest average working weeks for own-account workers were recorded in Greece (46.3 usual hours per week), Belgium (43.2 hours), Spain (43.1 hours) and Poland (43.0 hours). For employees, the longest average working weeks were observed in Cyprus and Romania (both 40.1 hours per week). In all other EU countries, employees worked on average fewer than 40 usual hours per week. The shortest average working weeks for employees were recorded in the Netherlands (32.1 hours), Denmark (34.1 hours) and Germany (34.6 hours). Figure 6
=== Data sources === '''Source:''' The European Union Labour force survey (EU-LFS) is the largest European household sample survey providing quarterly and annual results on labour participation among people aged 15 years and over, and on people outside the labour force. It covers residents in private households. Conscripts in military or community service are not included in the results. The EU-LFS is based on the same target populations and uses the same definitions in all countries, which means that the results are comparable between countries. The EU-LFS is an important source of information about the situation and trends in national and EU labour markets. Each quarter around 1.2 million interviews are conducted throughout the participating countries to obtain statistical information for some 100 variables. Due to the diversity of information and the large sample size, the EU-LFS is also an important source for other European statistics like education statistics or regional statistics. '''Reference period:''' Yearly results are obtained by calculating the average of the four quarters in the year. '''Coverage:''' The results from the survey currently cover all [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union]] countries, the [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] countries (Iceland, Norway and Switzerland), as well as the [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]] (Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Serbia and Türkiye). For Cyprus, the survey covers only the areas of Cyprus controlled by the Government of the Republic of Cyprus. '''European aggregates:''' EU refers to all 27 EU Member States. If data are unavailable for a country, EU aggregates are calculated using the data for the most recent period available for the country in question. Such cases are indicated. '''Country notes: ''' '''The Netherlands''' collects EU-LFS data using a rolling reference week instead of a fixed reference week, i.e. interviewees are asked about the situation in the week before the interview rather than a pre-selected week. '''Definitions and main concepts''' EU-LFS concepts and definitions adhere the resolutions of the International Conference of Labour Statisticians held every 5 years, organised by the [[Glossary:International Labour Organization (ILO)|International Labour Organization (ILO)]]. Key employment characteristics, as per the EU Labour Force Survey, include * [[Glossary:Employee - LFS|Employees]] are those working for a public or private employer and who receive compensation in the form of wages, salaries, payment by results, or payment in kind; this category includes non-conscript armed forces members * [[Glossary:Self-employed|Self-employed persons]] work in their businesses, farm or professional practice. They are considered working during the reference week if they meet criteria such as working for profit; spending time on business operations; or establishing a business * Full-time and part-time work distinction is usually based on respondents’ spontaneous responses, except in the Netherlands and Iceland, where a 35-hour limit is applied, Sweden where a limit is applied to the self-employed, and Norway where those working between 32 and 36 hours are asked whether they have a full- or part-time position * Actual hours worked in the reference week are the hours the person spends in work activities during the reference week. they provide measurement of direct labour input. Working hours are collected in time intervals based on a half-hour scale (i.e. 0-0.5 hours, 0.5-1.0 hours, 1.0-1.5 hours, etc..). Specifically, average actual weekly hours are the number of hours actually worked per week in the main job, in the reference week, namely the hours spent in work activities including unpaid overtime. Periods of absence from work, such as sick leave, holidays and commuting time, account for 0 hours of work. * Usual hours worked are the number of hours per week usually worked in the main job. They are the modal value of the actual hours worked per week over a long reference period, excluding weeks when an absence from work occurs (e.g. holidays, leaves, strikes). They provide measurement of the organisation of working time. Working hours are collected in time intervals based on a half-hour scale (i.e. 0-0.5 hours, 0.5-1.0 hours, 1.0-1.5 hours, etc..). Specifically, average usual weekly hours are the number of hours usually worked per week in the main job that comprises all hours including extra hours, either paid or unpaid, which the person normally works. It excludes the travelling time between home and workplace, the time for the main meal break, education and non-job-related training. It includes production activities, ancillary activities (travel between different places of work, personnel management), education and training necessary for carrying out the work. * Economic activity refers to that of the economic unit where the work is performed. For reference, please consult the [[Glossary:NACE|classification NACE]]. In the EU-LFS, the sector ‘activities of households as employers’ excludes ‘undifferentiated goods and services producing activities of households for own use’. * Occupation: for reference, please consult the [[Glossary:ISCO|classification ISCO]]. '''Additional methodological information''' More information on the EU-LFS can be found via the online publication [[EU_labour_force_survey|EU Labour Force Survey]], which includes eight articles on the technical and methodological aspects of the survey. The EU-LFS methodology in force from the 2021 data collection onwards is described in [[EU_Labour_Force_Survey_-_new_methodology_from_2021_onwards|EU Labour Force Survey - new methodology from 2021 onwards]]. Detailed information on coding lists, explanatory notes and classifications used over time can be found under [[EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation|EU labour force survey - documentation]]. For more information on the background definitions on hours of work, please consult Topic 6 "Working conditions including working hours" from [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/1978984/6037342/EU-LFS+Explanatory+notes+from+Q1+2021+onwards.pdf/51353dd0-06de-2857-799a-dc1a92d70da8?t=1619349110590 EU Labour Force Survey Explanatory Notes]. ===Context=== Employment statistics serve various analyses, including macroeconomic (labour as a production factor), [[Glossary:Labour productivity|productivity]] or [[Glossary:Competitiveness|competitiveness]] studies. They can also be used to study a range of social and behavioural aspects related to an person's employment situation, such as the social integration of minorities, or employment as [[Glossary:Household - social statistics|household]] income. Employment is both a structural and a short-term indicator. As a structural indicator, it may shed light labour markets and economic systems’ structures, measured through labour supply and demand balance, or the quality of employment. As a short-term indicator, employment follows the [[Glossary:Business cycle|business cycle]]but has limitations, as employment is often seen as a [[Glossary:Lagging indicator|lagging indicator]]. Statistics on the hours of work measure working conditions as one of the dimensions of employment. The "average number of usual weekly hours of work in the main job" is an indicator providing a perspective to the organisation of working time. ===Other articles=== *[[Labour market (incl. labour force survey)|All articles on the labour market]] *[[Employment - title: Accidents at work - statistics on causes and circumstances
text:
EU statistics on fatal and non-fatal accidents at work, analysed by causes and circumstances. Data extracted in November 2025 Planned update: November 2026 During 2023, 3 in 10 (32.0%) non-fatal accidents at work in the EU took place on industrial sites. During 2023, more than a quarter (27.1%) of fatal accidents at work in the EU resulted from losing control of a machine, tool or transport/handling equipment. During 2023, the most common types of non-fatal accidents at work in the EU resulted from physical or mental stress (24.7%) or impact with a stationary object (24.0%). This article presents a set of main statistical findings in relation to indicators concerning [[Glossary:Non-fatal accident at work|non-fatal]] and [[Glossary:Fatal accident at work|fatal accidents]] at work in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]; the statistics presented have been collected as part of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/methodology European statistics on accidents at work (ESAW)] administrative data collection exercise. The particular focus of this article is an analysis of these statistics according to the worker’s location at the time of the accident, the type of working process and physical activity being undertaken at the time of the accident, and the cause of the accident. The data are presented for the total economy (all activities) and for 5 selected [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE Rev. 2]] sections: agriculture, forestry and fishing (NACE Section A), manufacturing (Section C), construction (Section F), distributive trades (Section G), and transportation and storage (Section H). This article is included in a set of statistical articles concerning specific health conditions in the EU which forms part of an online publication on [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]].
'''''Underestimation because of incomplete information''''' While all EU countries provided information for the total number of fatal and non-fatal accidents at work with a breakdown by economic activity (NACE), it should be noted that not all of them provided data according to all the categories of the variables on causes and circumstances presented in this article. The accidents for EU countries that did not provide data for a particular analysis are included within the ‘no information’ heading and the countries for which this applies are indicated in footnotes to the tables and figures included here. Thus, the total number of accidents is correct for individual EU countries as well as for the EU as a whole. However, for several of the analyses, notably by workstation (location), by working process and by specific physical activity, the proportion of accidents within the EU for which no information is available is relatively high. As such, when analysing the EU data, the number of accidents for the various categories that are specified (and the share of these categories in the total) should be regarded as a lower limit: these numbers (and shares) are likely to be underestimated.

'''''When combining several classifications, fatal accidents at work can be rare events''''' The absolute number of fatal accidents at work can be relatively small when looking at detailed data. This is the case, for example, when focusing on particular economic activities for individual EU countries (especially for the smaller ones) and/or when crossed with the various other classifications used in this article. An example can be seen in the final figure of this article (Figure 8), where all of the fatal accidents at work that took place within Cyprus’s construction sector resulted from an impact with a stationary object. However, there were only 4 fatal accidents at work in the Cypriot construction sector in 2023. As such, particularly high shares may reflect rare events, rather than a more general concentration of accidents in a combination of the categories studied.
===Workstation accidents=== '''''Non-fatal accidents''''' In 2023, close to two thirds (65.4%) of the 2.82 million non-fatal accidents that took place at work in the EU occurred when a person was at their usual workstation or within the usual local unit of work (see Table 1). These accidents relate to fixed workstations in a workshop, shop, office and more generally, premises of the local unit of the employer. Just under a fifth (19.8%) of the total number of non-fatal accidents at work took place at an occasional or mobile workstation or during a journey made on behalf of an employer (these statistics exclude trips made to/from work). Examples of employees with mobile workstations include lorry drivers, construction workers or refuse collectors. Examples of employees with occasional workstations include people making occasional journeys on behalf of their employer, people making specific interventions for their employer outside their usual local unit (for example, on the premises of a client for a meeting, or to install or repair something). A relatively small share (2.0%) of all non-fatal accidents at work took place in other locations/workstations. Note that information on the location of accidents at work was not available for about 1 in 8 (12.9%) of all non-fatal accidents at work in the EU in 2023. In 2023, the likelihood of a non-fatal accident at work taking place in the EU at a person’s usual workstation was higher for people working in manufacturing (80.9% of all non-fatal accidents at work) and in distributive trades (78.5%). As might be expected given the nature of the work, for people working in construction (48.2% of all non-fatal accidents at work in construction) or in transportation and storage (38.3%), accidents at an occasional or mobile workstation or during a journey on behalf of their employer were considerably more likely than for the other activities shown in Table 1. The share of non-fatal accidents at work which took place in other workstations did not rise above 2.0% for most of the NACE sections presented, the only exception being agriculture, forestry and fishing (11.4%). [[Image:Non-fatal and fatal accidents at work by workstation and economic activity, EU, 2023_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Non-fatal and fatal accidents at work by workstation and economic activity, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7db12bdf-a43f-41b6-9a8d-78dbddfe2ea0?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-14T10:47:22Z hsw_ph3_01]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_01__custom_7682908/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=68baec7c-d589-4f55-a5b9-a75da965bef9&c=1696504184384 hsw_ph3_01])|alt=A table showing the number of non-fatal and fatal accidents at work. Data are analysed by the type of workstation at which the accident occurred and by 5 economic activities at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 1 presents a similar analysis to that shown in Table 1 but with information presented by sex. In the EU, among people who had experienced a non-fatal accident at work in 2023 this was more likely to have occurred at their usual workstation or within the usual local unit of work for women than it was for men. For all activities together, this location accounted for 73.1% of all non-fatal accidents at work among women whereas among men the share was 61.6%. A similar pattern was observed for construction (48.9% for women and 39.1% for men), distributive trades (83.0% for women and 76.1% for men), transportation and storage (54.4% for women and 49.8% for men) and manufacturing (81.8% for women and 80.7% for men). Within agriculture, forestry and fishing, a slightly larger proportion of non-fatal accidents at work occurred at their usual workstation or within the usual local unit of work among men (46.6%) rather than women (42.2%). Some of these differences may be linked to structural differences in the occupations that are carried out by men and women within an economic activity. For example, in construction a higher proportion of men (48.5%) than women (36.9%) experienced a non-fatal accident at work in occasional or mobile workstations or during a journey made on behalf of an employer in 2023, suggesting that men in the EU were more likely to work on external construction sites or to drive vehicles and that women were more likely to work in administrative or supporting roles within the local unit of work. [[Image:Non-fatal accidents at work by workstation, sex and economic activity, EU, 2023_(%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Non-fatal accidents at work by workstation, sex and economic activity, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_01__custom_3227324/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=a3899ceb-2dbb-4a0c-9689-512c185aaf8c&c=1660923381910 hsw_ph3_01])|alt=A stacked bar chart showing the shares of non-fatal accidents at various workstations. The analysis of type of workstation includes usual workstation, occasional workstation, other workstation and no information. Bars are shown separately for men and for women, for the total and 5 economic activities at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Fatal accidents''''' In 2023, there were 3 298 fatal accidents at work in the EU (see Table 1). Among the fatal accidents at work for which the location of the accident was specified, the vast majority either took place in occasional or mobile workstations or during a journey made on behalf of an employer (43.0% of the total) or in the usual workstation or local work unit (40.8%). As with non-fatal accidents at work, a relatively small share (2.8%) of fatal accidents at work took place at other workstations. For 13.5% of fatal accidents at work, there was no information available for the location of the accident. Across the EU, fatal accidents at work were, in 2023, more likely than average to occur in occasional or mobile workstations or during a journey made on behalf of an employer within transportation and storage (63.0%), construction (51.9%) and distributive trades (50.2%). Fatal accidents at work within manufacturing were most common (61.3%) in the usual workstation or local work unit. Within agriculture, forestry and fishing, 6.1% of fatal accidents at work took place at other workstations, by far the highest share among the economic activities shown in Table 1. ===Working environment=== '''''Non-fatal accidents''''' The analysis of accidents at work presented in Table 2 provides information concerning the type of working environment where accidents took place. In 2023, the highest share of non-fatal accidents at work in the EU occurred at industrial sites (32.0%), followed by tertiary sites (17.8%) such as offices. Close to a tenth of all non-fatal accidents at work were in 2 other working environments: public areas (10.2%) and construction sites, opencast quarries or mines (also 10.2%). As might be expected, non-fatal accidents at work for certain activities were concentrated in particular working environments, such as industrial sites for manufacturing (79.3% of the total for this activity), construction sites, opencast quarries or mines within construction (60.2%) and farming, fish farming or forest zones for agriculture, forestry and fishing (72.3%). [[Image:Non-fatal and fatal accidents at work by working environment and economic activity, EU, 2023_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Non-fatal and fatal accidents at work by working environment and economic activity, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hsw_ph3_02__custom_18403291/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=2bd7cfeb-2189-4c2c-b72d-63b213b81335&c=1760438854000 hsw_ph3_02]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_02__custom_7683160/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=3d767dc6-18c1-427b-90c8-f6ccb194ad11&c=1696505038855 hsw_ph3_02])|alt=A table showing the number of non-fatal and fatal accidents at work, analysed by the working environment where the accident occurred and by 5 economic activities at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 2 provides a similar analysis for non-fatal accidents at work in the EU, with additional information by age. It shows that in 2023 a higher proportion of non-fatal accidents at work involving young people (defined here as those aged less than 25 years) were on industrial sites, or on construction sites, opencast quarries or mines. By contrast, among older people (defined here as those aged 55 years and over) non-fatal accidents at work were more likely (than for younger workers) to occur at tertiary sites, in public areas, or in farming, fish farming or forest zones. These figures are influenced, at least to some degree, by the relative size of each age group within the total workforce for different activities: for example, a relatively high number of older people work in agriculture, forestry and fishing.
