[[Image:Non-fatal accidents at work by working environment, age and economic activity, EU, 2023_(%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Non-fatal accidents at work by working environment, age and economic activity, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_02__custom_3560496/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=eb8e87e2-9a43-4597-ac85-f2731861c104&c=1665502588486 hsw_ph3_02])|alt=A stacked bar chart showing the shares of non-fatal accidents in various working environments. The analysis of working environment includes industrial site; tertiary; construction site quarry or mine; public area; farming; and other. Bars are shown separately for 3 age groups, for the total and 5 economic activities at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Fatal accidents''''' Turning to fatal accidents at work, as shown in Table 2, the highest share across the EU in 2023 was in public areas (25.0%), followed by industrial sites (19.8%), construction sites, opencast quarries or mines (16.9%) and farming, fish farming and forest zones (10.6%). Looking at the selected NACE sections, the proportion of fatal accidents at work that took place in public areas was higher than the share of non-fatal accidents at work in public areas for each of the 5 activities shown. A particularly high share of fatal accidents at work within transportation and storage took place in public areas (58.5%). By contrast, compared with non-fatal accidents at work, the share of fatal accidents at work was particularly low at tertiary sites (6.8% compared with 17.8% for non-fatal accidents at work) and at industrial sites (19.8% compared with 32.0%). ===Working process accidents=== The information presented in Table 3 is related to the main type of work performed by the victims of accidents. In 2023, the most common working processes in which a non-fatal accident at work took place in the EU included production, manufacturing, processing or storing (12.2% of all non-fatal accidents at work) and the provision of services to enterprises and/or the general public, including intellectual activities (7.7%). Note that for more than two thirds (69.0%) of non-fatal accidents at work in the EU, information on the working process was not available or was from a minor category (these 2 categories are combined in Table 3). As may be expected, certain working processes were more common as causes of non-fatal accidents at work in particular activities across the EU in 2023. For example: *within agriculture, forestry and fishing, there was a relatively high proportion of non-fatal accidents at work that were linked to agricultural work, forestry, horticulture, fish farming or work with live animals (35.2% of non-fatal accidents at work in this sector) *within manufacturing, 29.8% of non-fatal accidents at work occurred while involved in production, manufacturing, processing or storing *within construction, 19.5% of non-fatal accidents at work were linked to excavation, construction, repair or demolition work *within transportation and storage, 12.5% of non-fatal accidents at work were related to movement, sport or an artistic activity. These 4 combinations of economic activities and working processes also recorded the highest numbers of fatal accidents at work in the EU, ranging from 70 deaths in manufacturing related to production, manufacturing, processing or storing up to 233 deaths in construction related to excavation, construction, repair and demolition. [[Image:Non-fatal and fatal accidents at work by working process and economic activity, EU, 2023_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Non-fatal and fatal accidents at work by working process and economic activity, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/edb75a76-a88a-452c-b453-e87d5eccaf9b?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-14T10:47:50Z hsw_ph3_03]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_03__custom_7683412/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=0322c233-2f7c-4ead-886a-a6a3eea021b6&c=1696505777795 hsw_ph3_03])|alt=A table showing the number of non-fatal and fatal accidents at work, analysed by the working process during which the accident occurred and by 5 economic activities at the NACE section. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Specific physical activity=== Data relating to accidents at work by specific physical activity concern what the victim was doing at the exact time of an accident in contrast to the information by working process (as shown above) which describes the main task being performed over a more substantial period. Almost a fifth (19.7%) of the non-fatal accidents at work that took place in the EU in 2023 could be associated with the physical activity of movement (see Figure 3), while around 1 in 8 (12.4%) were linked to the handling of objects, and close to a tenth (9.2%) to carrying something by hand. The situation was somewhat different concerning fatal accidents at work in the EU, insofar as the largest share of all fatal accidents at work in 2023 took place while people were driving or aboard transport or handling equipment (17.9%), although the next highest share was associated with movement (17.3%). [[Image:Accidents at work by specific physical activity and economic activity, EU, 2023_(%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Accidents at work by specific physical activity and economic activity, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_04__custom_3560699/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=4163e75b-1dec-4f45-8fcd-36eab71076e9&c=1665503705938 hsw_ph3_04]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_04__custom_7683570/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=477c0043-b77a-407a-9ee8-0efbcc8dd067&c=1696506151579 hsw_ph3_04])|alt=A stacked bar chart showing the shares of accidents during various physical activities. The analysis of physical activities includes movement; handling of objects; carrying by hand; working with hand-held tools; driving/being on board transport or handling equipment; operating a machine; presence; other or no information. Bars are shown separately for fatal and non-fatal accidents, for the total and 5 economic activities. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Considering that the highest share of fatal accidents at work in 2023 was linked to the specific physical activity of driving or being on board transport or handling equipment, Figure 4 shows more detailed information for this specific physical activity solely for the transportation and storage sector. Across the EU, 11.3% of all non-fatal accidents at work in the transportation and storage sector could be attributed to driving or being on board transport or handling equipment. More than a quarter of non-fatal accidents at work in the Dutch, Romanian and Slovenian transportation and storage sectors in 2023 were linked to driving or being on board transport or handling equipment; shares of at least 1 in 5 were also recorded in Spain, Croatia, Latvia and Bulgaria. By contrast, in Finland and Luxembourg fewer than 1 in 10 non-fatal accidents at work in the transportation and storage sector resulted from driving or being on board transport or handling equipment, while in Lithuania there were almost no non-fatal accidents at work in the transportation and storage sector from this activity. Figure 4 also shows that there were 11 EU countries (among the 18 for which data are available) where at least half of all fatal accidents at work within the transportation and storage sector in 2023 could be attributed to the specific physical activity of driving or being on board transport or handling equipment; among these, the share was 100.0% in Croatia and 80.0% in Finland. By contrast, a quarter (25.0%) of fatal accidents at work within the transportation and storage sector in Luxembourg were attributed to driving or being on board transport or handling equipment, the lowest share among EU countries. [[Image:Accidents at work within the transportation and storage sector – share from driving_being on board a means of transport or handling equipment, 2023_(%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Accidents at work within the transportation and storage sector – share from driving/being on board a means of transport or handling equipment, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_04__custom_3227451/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=62f1e554-0896-43f7-b794-e83f2240baea&c=1660924993925 hsw_ph3_04])|alt=A double column chart showing the percentage share of accidents at work within the transportation and storage sector resulting from driving/being on board a means of transport or handling equipment. Data are shown for non-fatal and for fatal accidents. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Cause of accident=== The cause of an accident is defined in terms of the last event differing from the norm that resulted in an accident. In 2023, the most common causes that triggered non-fatal accidents at work in the EU included losing control of machines, tools or transport and handling equipment (21.7% of the total), slipping, stumbling or falling (20.0%) and body movement under or with physical stress (19.7%). The share of non-fatal accidents at work in the EU in 2023 for which no information on the cause is available was relatively small (10.7%). Losing control of machines, tools or transport and handling equipment was also the most common cause of fatal accidents at work, accounting for 27.1% of the total number of workplace deaths in the EU in 2023, while slipping, stumbling or falling (15.4%), and breakage, bursting or collapse of material agents (12.3%) were the only other causes that accounted for double-digit shares of the total number of such accidents. The share of fatal accidents at work in the EU in 2023 for which no information on the cause is available was close to a fifth (18.5%). [[Image:Accidents at work by cause and economic activity, EU, 2023_(%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Accidents at work by cause and economic activity, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_06__custom_3227390/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=dc99b46e-711f-46e6-bc90-99cf81f00426&c=1660924613321 hsw_ph3_06]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_06__custom_7685754/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=c5e5504e-81af-4b45-af51-7aa1009f0929&c=1696511418308 hsw_ph3_06])|alt=A stacked bar chart showing the shares of accidents analysed by cause, distinguishing lost control; slipping, stumbling, falling; body movement; body movement without physical stress; breakage of a material agent; shock fright, violence, threat or presence; overflow leak, vaporisation or emission; electrical problem, explosion or fire; other deviations; and no information. Bars are shown separately for fatal and non-fatal accidents, for the total and 5 economic activities at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Considering that the highest numbers of non-fatal and fatal accidents at work in 2023 were caused by losing control of machines, tools or transport and handling equipment, Figure 6 shows more detailed information for this cause of accidents within the distributive trades sector. Some 27.0% of all non-fatal accidents at work in the EU’s distributive trades sector in 2023 could be attributed to losing control of machines, tools or transport and handling equipment; the share was somewhat higher for fatal accidents at work (37.8%). An analysis of the 2023 data for EU countries reveals that more than two fifths of all non-fatal accidents at work in the distributive trades sectors of Cyprus, Germany, Slovenia and Austria were caused by losing control of machines, tools or transport and handling equipment. A similar analysis reveals that all fatal accidents at work in the Cypriot and Lithuanian distributive trades sectors could be attributed to losing control of machines, tools or transport and handling equipment, while the share was also at least half in Hungary, Spain, Germany, Austria, Italy, Slovenia, Portugal and Sweden. A total of 9 EU countries reported no fatal accidents at work in the distributive trades sector that could be attributed to losing control of machines, tools or transport and handling equipment. [[Image:Accidents at work within the distributive trades sector – share from losing control of machines, tools, or transport and handling equipment, 2023_(%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Accidents at work within the distributive trades sector – share from losing control of machines, tools, or transport and handling equipment, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_06__custom_3227445/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=f3c97e49-a234-45ee-ae70-0f5fe40a655c&c=1660924935362 hsw_ph3_06])|alt=A double column chart showing the percentage share of accidents at work within the distributive trades sector resulting from losing control of machines, tools or transport and handling equipment. Data are shown for non-fatal and for fatal accidents. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Contact mode of injury=== Data on accidents at work by contact mode of injury relate to how the victim of an accident was hurt by the material agent that caused their injury. If there are several modes of injury identified, then the mode causing the most serious injury should be recorded. In 2023, the most common contact modes for non-fatal accidents at work across the EU included physical or mental stress (24.7% of all non-fatal accidents at work), impact with a stationary object (in other words, the victim was in motion; 24.0%), contact with a sharp/pointed or rough/coarse agent (14.5%), and being struck by an object in motion/a collision (13.0%). Note that there was no contact or no information on the contact mode for 9.6% of non-fatal accidents at work. A similar analysis for fatal accidents at work reveals that the most common contact mode of injury was being struck by an object in motion/a collision (23.8% of all fatal accidents at work in the EU), followed by impact with a stationary object (21.4%) and being trapped or crushed (13.8%). For 15.1% of fatal accidents at work, there was no contact or information on the contact mode is not available. Within the transportation and storage sector, being struck by an object in motion accounted for 37.3% of all fatal accidents at work in the EU in 2023, while 33.0% of fatal accidents at work within distributive trades were attributed to the same mode. By contrast, within the construction sector the most common mode of injury in a fatal accident at work was an impact with a stationary object (victim in motion), which accounted for approximately a quarter (25.6%) of all non-fatal accidents at work and more than a third (34.0%) of all fatal accidents at work in this sector. [[Image:Accidents at work by contact mode of injury and economic activity, EU, 2023_(%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Accidents at work by contact mode of injury and economic activity, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_08__custom_3227437/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=e5d79b4f-566e-4dee-84a2-a98f440e5a57&c=1665504724298 hsw_ph3_08]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_08__custom_7685928/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=a3a7a43f-256b-4da1-a148-309499c8b081&c=1696512030519 hsw_ph3_08])|alt= A stacked bar chart showing the shares of accidents analysed by contact mode of injury, distinguishing physical or mental stress; impact with a stationary object; contact with sharp, pointed, rough or coarse agent; struck by an object in motion/collision; trapped or crushed; animal or human bite or kick; electrical voltage, temperature, hazardous substances; drowned, buried or enveloped; other; and no contact or information. Bars are shown separately for fatal and non-fatal accidents, for the total and 5 economic activities at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This information is developed further in Figure 8 which presents a more detailed analysis of accidents in the construction sector resulting from an impact with a stationary object. This contact mode of injury accounted for more than half of all non-fatal accidents at work in the construction sectors of Greece (60.0%) and Bulgaria (51.9%) in 2023, whereas the share was lowest in France (19.3%). A similar analysis reveals that all (100.0%) fatal accidents at work in the Cypriot construction sector could be attributed to an impact with a stationary object, as could at least half of all fatal accidents at work in the construction sectors of Ireland, the Netherlands, Austria, Spain and Bulgaria. No such fatal accidents at work were reported from this mode of contact in 2023 in the construction sectors of Denmark, Luxembourg, Malta and Finland. Note that for relatively small EU countries, the absolute number of fatal accidents at work in this sector may be very small; for example, the construction sectors of Luxembourg, Malta and Finland each had 2 fatal accidents at work in 2023, while there were 4 such fatalities in Denmark. [[Image:Accidents at work within the construction sector – share from impact with a stationary object (victim in motion), 2023_(%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Accidents at work within the construction sector – share from impact with a stationary object (victim in motion), 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_PH3_08__custom_3227440/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=5c327650-a69f-44de-9887-24e553b5317a&c=1660924886639 hsw_ph3_08])|alt=A double column chart showing the percentage share of accidents at work within the construction sector resulting from impact with a stationary object (victim in motion). Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=Accidents at work causes and circumstances Health2025 V2.xlsx|title=Accidents at work by causes and circumstances: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== In December 2008, the [[Glossary:European Parliament (EP)|European Parliament]] and the [[Glossary:Council of the European Union|Council]] adopted {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R1338:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1338/2008}} on Community statistics on public health and health and safety at work. The regulation is designed to ensure that health statistics provide adequate information for all EU countries to monitor Community actions in the field of public health and health and safety at work. In April 2011, a [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0349:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 349/2011}} on statistics on accidents at work was adopted specifying in detail the variables, breakdowns and metadata that EU countries are required to deliver – this legislation is being implemented in a number of phases. Note also that a {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011D0231:EN:NOT|title=Commission Decision No 2011/231/EU}} from April 2011 granted derogations to certain EU countries with respect to the transmission of statistics on accidents at work. European statistics on accidents at work (ESAW) is the main data source for EU statistics relating to health and safety at work issues. ESAW includes data on occupational accidents that result in at least 4 calendar days of absence from work, including fatal accidents. The phrase ‘during the course of work’ means while engaged in an occupational activity or during the time spent at work. This generally includes cases of traffic accidents (road or other means of transport) for journeys that are made during the course of work but excludes accidents that take place during a journey between home and the workplace. There are 9 variables related to causes and circumstances of accidents at work within the ESAW data collection. According to the ESAW Regulation, countries are free to choose at least 3 out of these 9 variables on causes and circumstances and should report data for these (they may provide information on more than 3 variables if they choose to do so). As such, while the total coverage of the EU is complete for each individual variable, the proportion of information that is not specified (included within the heading ''no information'' in tables and figures in this article) can vary greatly depending on how many and which EU countries have provided detailed information. The complete list of 9 variables covers: workstation, working environment, working process, specific physical activity, material agent associated with the specific physical activity, deviation, material agent associated with the deviation, contact – mode of injury, material agent associated with the contact – mode of injury. An accident at work is defined in ESAW methodology as a discrete occurrence during the course of work which leads to physical or mental harm. Fatal accidents at work are those that lead to the death of the victim within 1 year of the accident taking place. Non-fatal accidents at work are defined as those that imply at least 4 full calendar days of absence from work (they are sometimes also called ‘serious accidents at work’). Non-fatal accidents at work often involve considerable harm for the workers concerned and their families and they have the potential to force people, for example, to live with a permanent disability, to leave the labour market, or to change job. Indeed, they may result in a considerable number of working days being lost within the EU’s economy. The statistics presented for accidents at work refer to declarations made to either public (social security administrations) or private insurance schemes, or to other relevant national authorities (for example, those controlling labour or workplace inspections). Indicators on accidents at work may be presented as absolute values, as percentage distributions, as incidence rates in relation to every 100 000 employed people (the denominator being provided by the authorities that are responsible for ESAW data collection in EU countries or by the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|EU labour force survey (EU-LFS)]]) or as standardised incidence rates. For more information on ESAW data please refer to the main article on [[Accidents_at_work_statistics|accidents at work statistics]]. ===Context=== A safe, healthy working environment is a crucial factor in an individual’s quality of life and is also a collective interest. Governments across the EU recognise the social and economic benefits of better health and safety at work. Reliable, comparable, up-to-date statistical information is vital for setting policy objectives and adopting suitable policy measures and preventing actions. For more information on health and safety at work policy, please refer to the main article on [[Accidents_at_work_statistics|accidents at work statistics]]. ===Other articles=== *[[Accidents at work statistics]] *[[Accidents at work - statistics by economic activity|Accidents at work – statistics by economic activity]] *[[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] – online publication *[[Health statistics introduced]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/database Health], see: :Health and safety at work (hsw) ::Accidents at work (ESAW, 2008 onwards) (hsw_acc_work) :::Causes and circumstances of accidents at work (ESAW Phase III) (hsw_ph3) ::::Accidents at work by sex, age, severity, NACE Rev. 2 activity and workstation (hsw_ph3_01) ::::Accidents at work by sex, age, severity, NACE Rev. 2 activity and working environment (hsw_ph3_02) ::::Accidents at work by sex, age, severity, NACE Rev. 2 activity and working process (hsw_ph3_03) ::::Accidents at work by sex, age, severity, NACE Rev. 2 activity and specific physical activity (hsw_ph3_04) ::::Accidents at work by sex, age, severity, NACE Rev. 2 activity and material agent of specific physical activity (hsw_ph3_05) ::::Accidents at work by sex, age, severity, NACE Rev. 2 activity and deviation (hsw_ph3_06) ::::Accidents at work by sex, age, severity, NACE Rev. 2 activity and material agent of deviation (hsw_ph3_07) ::::Accidents at work by sex, age, severity, NACE Rev. 2 activity and contact mode of injury (hsw_ph3_08) ::::Accidents at work by sex, age, severity, NACE Rev. 2 activity and material agent of contact mode injury (hsw_ph3_09) ===Thematic section=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/overview Health] ===Methodology=== '''''ESMS metadata file''''' *{{Template:Esms|code=hsw_acc_work_esms|title=Accidents at work (ESAW, 2008 onwards)}} (ESMS metadata file – hsw_acc_work_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=lfso_20_esms|title=2020. Accidents at work and other work-related health problems}} (ESMS metadata file – lfso_20_esms) '''''Publication''''' *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-RA-12-102|title=European statistics on accidents at work (ESAW) – Summary methodology – 2013 edition}} ===External links=== *[https://osha.europa.eu/en European Agency for Safety and Health at Work] *[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/rights-work/health-and-safety-work_en European Commission – Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion – Health and safety at work], see: **[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/rights-work/health-and-safety-work/strategic-policy-documents_en EU strategic framework (2021–27)] *[https://www.eurofound.europa.eu/en/topics/health-and-well-being European Foundation for the Improvement of Living and Working Conditions (EUROFOUND) – Health and well-being] *[https://www.ilo.org/topics-and-sectors/safety-and-health-work International Labour Organization (ILO) – Safety and health at work] ''View this article online at {{fullurl:{{PAGENAME}}}}'' {{Unit|topic=X_Health}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Accidents at work – statistics on causes and circumstances]] [[Category:Health|Accidents at work – statistics on causes and circumstances]] [[Category:Accidents at work|Accidents at work – statistics on causes and circumstances]] [[Category:Health and safety|Accidents at work – statistics on causes and circumstances]] [[Category:Labour market (incl. labour force survey) |Accidents at work – statistics on causes and circumstances]] [[Category:Statistical article|Accidents at work – statistics on causes and circumstances]] [[Category:November2026|Accidents at work – statistics on causes and circumstances]]

title: Accidents at work - statistics by economic activity
text:
EU statistics on fatal and non-fatal accidents at work, analysed by economic activity (industry). Data extracted in August 2026 Planned update: September 2027 In 2024, the highest incidence of non-fatal accidents at work in the EU was observed in construction, with 2 783 such accidents per 100 000 employed people. In 2024, the highest incidence of fatal accidents at work in the EU was observed in mining and quarrying, with 8.7 such accidents per 100 000 employed people. This article presents a set of main statistical findings in relation to indicators concerning [[Glossary:Non-fatal accident at work|non-fatal]] and [[Glossary:Fatal accident at work|fatal accidents]] at work in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. The statistics presented have been collected as part of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/methodology European statistics on accidents at work (ESAW)] administrative data collection exercise. This article analyses these statistics according to the type of economic activity in which accidents occur, focusing on selected activities: agriculture, forestry and fishing ([[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE Rev. 2]] Section A); mining and quarrying (NACE Section B); manufacturing (NACE Section C); construction (NACE Section F); distributive trades (comprising wholesale, retail and motor trades, NACE Section G); transport and storage (NACE Section H); accommodation and food service activities (NACE Section I); administrative and support service activities (NACE Section N); public administration and defence (NACE Section O); and human health and social work activities (NACE Section Q). This article is included in a set of statistical articles concerning specific health conditions in the EU which forms part of an online publication on [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]]. ===Developments over time=== '''''Non-fatal accidents''''' In 2024, there were 2.781 million non-fatal accidents that resulted in at least 4 calendar days of absence from work in the EU (see Table 1). The total number of non-fatal accidents at work in the EU rose between 2014 and 2019, up some 204 000 (equivalent to an overall increase of 7.0%). To some extent, this increase may reflect methodological changes in data collection/compilation in some EU countries. For more information, please refer to the [[Accidents_at_work_statistics#Data sources|data sources]] section of the main article on [[Accidents_at_work_statistics|accidents at work statistics]]. In 2020, this upward trend was interrupted, as the number of non-fatal accidents fell by 399 000, down 12.7%. This change reflects, at least in part, the impact of the COVID-19 crisis on EU labour markets and working conditions. There was a partial rebound in the number of non-fatal accidents, up 151 000 (equivalent to an increase of 5.5%) in 2021 and 81 000 (2.8%) in 2022. However, the number of non-fatal accidents fell again in 2023, down 44 000 (a fall of 2.0%). In absolute terms, non-fatal accidents in 2024, in the EU were most common in: *manufacturing – 510 000 (18.3% of the total) *construction – 353 000 (12.7%) *distributive trades – 345 000 (12.2%) *human health and social work activities – 341 000 (12.3%). Given that the workforces of these activities vary greatly in size, the incidence rate (the number of non-fatal accidents at work for every 100 000 employed people) gives a clearer impression of where workers were more likely to encounter non-fatal accidents. In 2024, the highest incidence of non-fatal accidents at work in the EU was observed in construction, with 2 783 such accidents per 100 000 employed people. Transport and storage (2 320 per 100 000) and administrative and support service activities (1 958 per 100 000) were the only other NACE sections with incidence rates above 2 000 per 100 000 employed people. The lowest incidence rate among the selected activities was for public administration and defence (1 080 per 100 000 employed people), as shown in Table 1. There was an overall decrease in the EU’s incidence rate of non-fatal accidents between 2013 and 2019 (down 4.2%), reflecting faster growth in the number of employed people than in the number of non-fatal accidents. Among the selected activities, incidence rates for non-fatal accidents at work were generally lower in 2019 than in 2013. This situation was observed for 7 out of the 10 NACE sections for which data are shown. Between 2013 and 2019, there was a notable increase in incidence rates for non-fatal accidents for human health and social work activities (up 9.3%) and smaller increases for agriculture, forestry and fishing (up 2.7%) and public administration and defence (up 0.9%). Note that the changes observed for the EU in some activities may be linked to changes in the coverage of specific activities for some EU countries, for example because of the end of derogations or voluntary data collection. Focusing just on the latest annual change, the incidence rate of non-fatal accidents fell 2.4% between 2023 and 2024. Among the 10 NACE sections for which information is presented in Table 1, the only increase in 2023 was observed for mining and quarrying (up 0.6%). The largest decreases in the incidence rate of non-fatal accidents in 2024 were recorded for accommodation and food service activities and administrative and support service activities (both down 4.2%). [[Image:Non-fatal accidents at work by economic activity, EU, 2013–24 Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Non-fatal accidents at work by economic activity, EU, 2013–24
'' Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_N2_01__custom_3227054/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=775a8b09-7f57-4cff-a54d-f5ba83611b4a&c=1660920042852 (hsw_n2_01)] |alt=A table showing the number and incidence rate of non-fatal accidents at work. Data are analysed by economic activity at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2013 to 2024 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Fatal accidents''''' In 2024, there were 3 367 fatal accidents at work in the EU (see Table 2), resulting in a ratio of 826 non-fatal accidents for every fatal accident. The total number of fatal accidents at work in the EU was the same in 2019 as it had been in 2013. A quite stable development was also observed in the next 4 years: there were 50 fewer deaths in 2020 (note that there is a break in series), 31 more in 2021, 103 fewer in 2022, 12 more in 2023 and 69 more in 2024. In absolute terms, fatal accidents in the EU were most common in 2024 in: *construction, 776 (23.0% of the total) *transport and storage, 537 (15.9%) *manufacturing, 466 (13.8%) *agriculture, forestry and fishing, 408 (12.1%) *distributive trades, 275 (8.2%) *administrative and support service activities, 236 (7.0%). In 2024, the highest incidence rate of fatal accidents at work (the number of fatal accidents at work for every 100 000 employed people) in the EU among the economic activities shown in Table 2 was observed in mining and quarrying with 8.7 fatal accidents per 100 000 employed people. Construction (6.1 per 100 000 employed people), agriculture forestry and fishing (5.5 per 100 000) and transport and storage (4.8 per 100 000) were the only other NACE sections with incidence rates above 1.7 per 100 000 employed people. The lowest incidence rate was for human health and social work activities (0.4 per 100 000). Across the EU, the decrease in the incidence rate of fatal accidents at work between 2013 and 2019 (down by 10.7%) alongside a stable number of fatal accidents reflected growth in the number of employed people. During the period from 2013 to 2019, there was a larger decrease in the incidence of fatal accidents at work than of non-fatal accidents. While incidence rates for fatal accidents at work – as for non-fatal accidents – were generally lower in 2019 than in 2013 for most activities, increases were observed in the incidence rates of fatal accidents for human health and social work activities (up 25.9%), accommodation and food service activities (up 14.3%) and agriculture, forestry and fishing (up 7.8%). Focusing on the latest annual change, the incidence rate of fatal accidents in the EU increased 1.2% between 2023 and 2024. The decrease in the incidence rate was in contrast to the 2.1% increase in the number of such accidents, as the number of employed people increased in 2024. Relatively large increases in the incidence rate were observed for accommodation and food service activities (up 32.2%), administrative and support service activities (up 11.7%), public administration and defence (up 11.5%), distributive trades (up 10.3%) and manufacturing (up 5.6%). Decreases were observed for mining and quarrying (down 18.9), agriculture, forestry and fishing (down 7.9%), construction (down 2.5%) and transport and storage (down 0.8%). [[Image:Fatal accidents at work by economic activity, EU, 2013–24 Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Fatal accidents at work, by economic activity, EU, 2013–24
'' Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hsw_n2_02__custom_13639169/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=774e6ad8-0600-44fa-b3ca-33ac25079ec4&c=1730887199004 (hsw_n2_02)]|alt=A table showing the number and incidence rate of fatal accidents at work. Data are analysed by economic activity at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2013 to 2024 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Analysis of non-fatal accidents by sex and age=== Men are generally more likely than women to be involved in an accident at work. In 2024, 2 out of every 3 (67.1%) non-fatal accidents at work in the EU involved men (excluding cases where the sex of the victim experiencing the accident was not reported). To some extent, this reflects the fact that more men than women work; this difference is particularly strong in several activities with high incidence rates. Another factor that influences differences is the different types of work that men and women carry out, even within a particular activity. The difference in incidence rates for men and women in construction was particularly large, with the rate for non-fatal accidents at work 6.2 times as high for men as for women in 2024. Similarly, the incidence rate for men was 5.1 times as high as for women in mining and quarrying. The only activity with a higher incidence rate for women than for men was human health and social work activities (1.1 times as high for men). [[Image:Non-fatal accidents at work by economic activity and sex, EU, 2024 Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Non-fatal accidents at work by economic activity and sex, EU, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_N2_01__custom_3227082/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=09f7d2e2-061c-421f-b048-ed12e9b273f6&c=1660920454008 (hsw_n2_01)]|alt=A table showing the number and incidence rate of non-fatal accidents at work. Data are analysed by economic activity at the NACE section level and by sex. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Focusing on the 10 activities presented in Table 3, the 4 highest incidence rates for non-fatal accidents at work among women in the EU in 2024 were for transport and storage, human health and social work activities, administrative and support service activities, and accommodation and food service activities. For men, construction, transport and storage, administrative and support service activities and mining and quarrying had the 4 highest rates (see Table 4). [[Image:Highest incidence rates of non-fatal accidents by economic sector and sex, EU, 2024 Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 4: Highest incidence rates of non-fatal accidents by economic sector and sex, EU, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/HSW_N2_01__custom_3561248/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=b4f2fd6d-3ce0-4e7d-b0b0-1374033bddeb&c=1665507554608 (hsw_n2_01)]|alt=A table showing the 4 NACE sections with the highest incidence rates of non-fatal accidents for each sex. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 1 helps to identify the activities where workers of a particular age range make up a greater or lesser share of those having suffered a non-fatal accident at work. It should be kept in mind that the age profile of the workforce may vary between economic activities. Younger workers (those aged less than 25 years) accounted for 12.4% of all non-fatal accidents at work in the EU in 2024. Higher than average (for all economic activities) shares of non-fatal accidents among young workers were recorded in the following sectors: *administrative and support service activities (13.4%) *construction (14.2%) *distributive trades (16.6%) *accommodation and food service activities (22.6%). Older workers (those aged 55 years and over) accounted for 21.2% of all non-fatal accidents at work in the EU in 2024. Higher than average shares of non-fatal accidents among older workers were recorded for: *transport and storage (22.3%) *human health and social work activities (25.6%) *public administration and defence (28.3%) *agriculture, forestry and fishing (28.6%). [[Image:Non-fatal accidents at work by age and economic activity,_EU, 2024_(% of non-fatal accidents for each activity).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Non-fatal accidents at work by age and economic activity, EU, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/be630415-2495-4ec6-b239-fa99455bce62?lang=enh (sw_n2_03)]|alt=A stacked bar chart showing non-fatal accidents at work. The stacks show the shares for the age groups starting at less than 18 years and 18 to 24 years, through 10-year age groups from 25 to 34 up to 55 to 64 years, finishing at 65 years or over. Bars are shown for economic activities at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Severity of accidents=== The data presented in Figure 2 include information for non-fatal and fatal accidents. This analysis identifies the number of calendar days or months (grouped into several classes) during which the victim was unfit for work, excluding the day of the accident itself, or whether there was a permanent incapacity or death (within 1 year of the accident) as a result of the accident at work. In the EU, a considerable majority (84.1%) of all accidents at work in 2024 involved the victim being unfit for work for less than 3 months, while some 11.7% were for longer periods (or resulted in permanent incapacity) and 0.1% were fatal accidents. For the remaining 4.0% of cases, the severity (in terms of duration of being unfit for work) was unknown. Accidents at work resulting in the victim being unfit for work for less than 3 months made up a relatively large proportion of accidents at work in the EU in 2024 in accommodation and food service activities (88.8%), manufacturing (87.6%) and distributive trades (87.1%). By contrast, the share of workplace accidents in the EU in 2024 that were non-fatal but resulted in the victim being unfit for work for 3 months or more made up a particularly large share of all workplace accidents for mining and quarrying (21.4%). Fatal accidents accounted for 0.1% of all workplace accidents in the EU in 2024. Among the selected activities, transport and storage (0.2%), construction (also 0.2%), agriculture, forestry and fishing (0.4%), and mining and quarrying (0.5%) had higher shares. [[Image: Accidents at work by severity and economic activity, EU, 2024_(% of accidents for each activity).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Accidents at work by severity and economic activity, EU, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fd18cbcd-eb9b-4b96-a93b-ad6ddf14b19a?lang=en (hsw_n2_04)]|alt=A stacked bar chart showing the severity of accidents at work. The stacks show the severity from 4 to 6 days through to fatal. Bars are shown for economic activities at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Analysis by injured body part=== The description of an accident at work includes information on the injured body part. The following options are available for recording the body part injured in an accident at work: *head *neck *back *torso and organs *upper extremities *lower extremities *whole body and multiple sites *other parts of body injured *not specified. Figures 3 and 4 present an analysis of the type of body part injured in non-fatal and fatal accidents. '''''Non-fatal accidents at work''''' For all activities combined, the most common body parts injured in non-fatal workplace accidents in the EU in 2024 were: *the upper extremities (shoulders, arms and hands), with 39.6% of the total number of non-fatal accidents at work *the lower extremities (hips, legs and feet) with 34.2%. The only other type of body part with a share that was more than a tenth of the EU total was the back, accounting for 10.5% of all injuries in 2023. [[Image:Economic activities with the highest and lowest shares of injury (in non-fatal accidents) to commonly injured body parts, EU, 2023_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 5: Economic activities with the highest and lowest shares of injury (in non-fatal accidents) to commonly injured body parts, EU, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/78aff2a9-4687-4143-86e5-0bbcbcba0c8b?lang=en (hsw_n2_06)]|alt=A table showing the 4 economic activities with the 2 highest and 2 lowest shares of injury (in non-fatal accidents) for 3 commonly injured body parts: upper extremities, lower extremities and back. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Looking more closely at data for injured body parts for the individual economic activities analysed in this article (see Figure 3 and Table 5), in 2024 non-fatal accidents at work that resulted in injuries of the upper extremities were particularly common in the EU within manufacturing (52.2% of all accidents in manufacturing) and the accommodation and food service activities (49.3%), but were less common in public administration and defence (29.9%) and transport and storage (27.7%). For injuries of the lower extremities, there was less variation by activity, with the highest shares for transport and storage (35.3%) and agriculture, forestry and fishing (34.2%), while the lowest shares were for accommodation and food service activities (26.6%) and manufacturing (24.9%). Back injuries were relatively common within human health and social work activities (16.4%) and public administration and defence (12.6%), while agriculture, forestry and fishing (7.2%) and mining and quarrying (6.8%) were the activities with the lowest shares. [[Image:Non-fatal accidents at work by part of body injured and economic activity.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Non-fatal accidents at work by part of body injured and economic activity, EU, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d6dd3b47-cc51-409a-b96f-d0f939d16ae3?lang=en (hsw_n2_06)]|alt=A stacked bar chart showing non-fatal accidents at work. The stacks show the shares for the various injured body parts. Bars are shown for economic activities at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Fatal accidents at work''''' Turning to fatal accidents at work, the distribution by the body part that was injured was very different. For all activities combined, 1 in 3 fatal accidents in the EU in 2024 related to injuries of the whole body or multiple sites (32.2%), while just over a fifth (20.4%) were head injuries and just over a tenth (12.1%) were injuries to the torso and organs – see Figure 4. The most common category of injuries in fatal accidents at work in the EU in 2024 concerned the whole body and multiple sites; this was observed for 8 of the 10 economic activities shown (when excluding the residual category of not specified); the exceptions were accommodation and food service activities as well as agriculture, forestry and fishing, for which head injuries were more common. The highest share of fatal accidents at work concerning the whole body and multiple sites was recorded for mining and quarrying (59.1%), while the lowest were human health and social work activities (12.4%) and accommodation and food service activities (14.2%). Looking at the less common body parts injured in fatal accidents at work in the EU in 2024, activities with relatively high shares included: *manufacturing, transport and storage, agriculture, forestry and fishing and construction activities for upper extremities injuries *public administration, human health and social work, and agriculture, forestry and fishing activities for neck injuries *public administration and defence as well as mining and quarrying for injuries of the lower extremities *mining and quarrying,public administration and defence and agriculture, forestry and fishing for back injuries. [[Image:Fatal accidents at work by part of body injured and economic activity.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Fatal accidents at work by part of body injured and economic activity, EU, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/defebd0a-9d6b-41ad-9235-35b76fb02347?lang=en (hsw_n2_06)]|alt=A stacked bar chart showing fatal accidents at work. The stacks show the shares for the various injured body parts. Bars are shown for economic activities at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Analysis by type of injury=== Figures 5 and 6 show (for non-fatal and fatal accidents, respectively) analyses of data according to the type of injury sustained when people were involved in accidents. Note that the selected types of injury are similar but not identical in the 2 figures. '''''Non-fatal accidents at work''''' In 2024, the most common injuries in the EU resulting from non-fatal accidents were wounds and superficial injuries (26.3% of the total), dislocations, sprains and strains (26.9%), concussion and internal injuries (20.3%) and bone fractures (11.6%). Wounds and superficial injuries had the highest share of non-fatal accidents across 7 of the 10 economic activities shown in Figure 5: *dislocations, sprains and strains accounted for a higher share for public administration and defence *dislocations, sprains and strains, and concussion and internal injuries accounted for higher shares for transport and storage as well as for human health and social work activities. Looking at the less common types of injuries resulting from non-fatal workplace accidents in the EU in 2024, some were quite common in particular activities. *Bone fractures were relatively common in mining and quarrying (18.9% of all non-fatal accidents in this activity) as well as agriculture, forestry and fishing (18.6%) compared with the average for all activities (11.6%). *The loss of body parts (amputations) was also relatively common in mining and quarrying (1.4%) as well as agriculture, forestry and fishing and manufacturing (both 0.9%) compared with the overall average (0.4%). *Burns, scalds and frostbite were 3.7 times as common in accommodation and food service activities (6.4%) as the average for all activities (1.7%). *Poisoning and infections were particularly common in human health and social work activities, manufacturing and in agriculture, forestry and fishing (0.6% in the three activities). [[Image:Non-fatal accidents at work by type of injury and economic activity, EU, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Non-fatal accidents at work by type of injury and economic activity, EU, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e8f977d8-dd81-4bc3-b43f-589650c5ecf5?lang=en (hsw_n2_07)]|alt=A stacked bar chart showing non-fatal accidents at work. The stacks show the shares for the various types of injuries. Bars are shown for economic activities at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Fatal accidents at work''''' For fatal accidents at work in 2024, the most commonly observed injury types across the EU (when excluding the residual categories of other and not specified) were multiple injuries (22.4% of fatal accidents) and concussion and internal injuries (19.6%), followed by bone fractures (9.3%). *Concussion and internal injuries were the most common type of injury in 2024 for 5 of the 10 economic activities shown in Figure 6: agriculture, forestry and fishing, manufacturing, human health and social work activities, administrative and support service activities and accommodation and food service activities *Multiple injuries were the most common type of injury for mining and quarrying, transport and storage, construction, distributive trades and public administration and defence. *Although having only the third highest share, bone fractures were relatively common for agriculture, forestry and fishing (15.0%) and accommodation and food service activities (14.4%). Less common types of injuries resulting from fatal workplace accidents in the EU in 2024 included the following: *wounds and superficial injuries – these were somewhat more common within agriculture, forestry and fishing (7.9%) and manufacturing (6.7%) than on average across all activities (5.7%) *poisoning and infections – these were relatively common types of injuries resulting from fatal workplace accidents for administrative and support service activities (2.1%) agriculture, forestry and fishing (1.0%) and manufacturing (0.9%) well above the average for all activities (0.6%) *accidents involving drowning and asphyxiation – these were much more common in agriculture, forestry and fishing (7.4%) and in accommodation and food service activities (5.9%) than the overall average (3.3%) *burns, scalds and frostbite – these were much more common in manufacturing (3.7%) and administrative and support service activities (2.1%) than they were across all activities (1.5%). [[Image: Fatal accidents at work by type of injury and economic activity, _EU, 2024_(% of fatal accidents for each activity).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Fatal accidents at work by type of injury and economic activity, EU, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/dbf8cc3d-ff8c-4da6-8aad-c609594826cb?lang=en (hsw_n2_07)]|alt=A stacked bar chart showing fatal accidents at work. The stacks show the shares for the various types of injuries. Bars are shown for economic activities at the NACE section level. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=Accidents at work by economic activity Health11 2025.xlsx|title=Accidents at work by economic activity: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== In December 2008, the [[Glossary:European Parliament (EP)|European Parliament]] and the [[Glossary:Council of the European Union|Council]] adopted {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R1338:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1338/2008}} on Community statistics on public health and health and safety at work. The regulation is designed to ensure that health statistics provide adequate information for all EU countries to monitor Community actions in the field of public health and health and safety at work. In April 2011, a [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0349:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 349/2011}} on statistics on accidents at work was adopted specifying in detail the variables, breakdowns and metadata that EU countries are required to deliver – this legislation is being implemented in a number of phases. Note also that a {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011D0231:EN:NOT|title=Commission Decision No 2011/231/EU}} from April 2011 granted derogations to certain EU countries with respect to the transmission of statistics on accidents at work. European statistics on accidents at work (ESAW) is the main data source for EU statistics relating to health and safety at work issues. ESAW includes data on occupational accidents that result in at least 4 calendar days of absence from work, including fatal accidents. The phrase ‘during the course of work’ means while engaged in an occupational activity or during the time spent at work. This generally includes cases of road traffic accidents in the course of work but excludes accidents during the journey between home and the workplace. An accident at work is defined in ESAW methodology as a discrete occurrence during the course of work which leads to physical or mental harm. Fatal accidents at work are those that lead to the death of the victim within 1 year of the accident taking place. Non-fatal accidents at work are defined as those that imply at least 4 full calendar days of absence from work (they are sometimes also called ‘serious accidents at work’). Non-fatal accidents at work often involve considerable harm for the workers concerned and their families and they have the potential to force people, for example, to live with a permanent disability, to leave the labour market, or to change job. Indeed, they may result in a considerable number of working days being lost within the EU’s economy. The statistics presented for accidents at work refer to declarations made to either public (social security administrations) or private insurance schemes, or to other relevant national authorities (for example, those controlling labour or workplace inspections). Indicators on accidents at work may be presented as absolute values, as percentage distributions, as incidence rates in relation to every 100 000 employed people (the denominator being provided by the authorities that are responsible for ESAW data collection in EU countries or by the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|EU labour force survey (EU-LFS)]]) or as standardised incidence rates. For more information on ESAW data please refer to the main article on [[Accidents_at_work_statistics|accidents at work statistics]]. ===Context=== A safe, healthy working environment is a crucial factor in an individual’s quality of life and is also a collective interest. Governments across the EU recognise the social and economic benefits of better health and safety at work. Reliable, comparable, up-to-date statistical information is vital for setting policy objectives and adopting suitable policy measures and preventative actions. At the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, preventive measures were put in place with the aim of limiting the spread of the Coronavirus and to combat the pandemic. Among these, some economic activities were either completely stopped or restricted by many governments or employers. In some cases, working remotely or from home became more common. This had a direct impact on all economic sectors. For the economic sectors where the activity was stopped or reduced, the number of accidents decreased. Inactivity or reduced activity in certain sectors resulted in a lower number of workers and/or hours worked, and therefore showed an unusual decrease in reported accidents at work. By contrast, in some sectors the COVID-19 pandemic generated an increase in activity. For example, this was the case for human health activities, residential care activities or social work activities without accommodation. Therefore, the increased activity resulted in generally higher numbers of reported accidents at work, especially when the cases of COVID-19 of occupational origin were included depending on national practice and legislation. Public services that deal with receipt of notifications, as well as the reporting, investigation and recognition of accidents at work may have functioned with limited capacities during parts of the crisis. The combined impact of the issues described above led to a decrease in the reported number of accidents at work in the data collection for the reference year 2020 compared with the previous year for the majority of reporting countries. In 2021 and 2022, the number of non-fatal accidents in the EU partially rebounded, before falling again in 2023 (remaining below the level of 2019); the number of fatal accidents also partially rebounded in 2021 but fell slightly in 2022 and increased marginally in 2023 (remaining below the level of 2019). For more information on health and safety at work policy, please refer to the main article on [[Accidents_at_work_statistics|accidents at work statistics]]. ===Other articles=== *[[Accidents at work statistics]] *[[Accidents at work - statistics on causes and circumstances|Accidents at work – statistics on causes and circumstances]] *[[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] – online publication *[[Health statistics introduced]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/database Health], see: :Health and safety at work (hsw) ::Accidents at work (ESAW, 2008 onwards) (hsw_acc_work) :::Details by NACE Rev. 2 activity (2008 onwards) (hsw_n2) ::::Non-fatal accidents at work by NACE Rev. 2 activity and sex (hsw_n2_01) ::::Fatal accidents at work by NACE Rev. 2 activity (hsw_n2_02) ::::Non-fatal accidents at work by NACE Rev. 2 activity and age (hsw_n2_03) ::::Accidents at work by days lost and NACE Rev. 2 activity (hsw_n2_04) ::::Accidents at work by NACE Rev. 2 activity and size of enterprise (hsw_n2_05) ::::Accidents at work by NACE Rev. 2 activity and part of body injured (hsw_n2_06) ::::Accidents at work by NACE Rev. 2 activity and type of injury (hsw_n2_07) ===Thematic section=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/overview Health] ===Methodology=== '''ESMS metadata files''' *{{Template:Esms|code=hsw_acc_work_esms|title=Accidents at work (ESAW, 2008 onwards)}} (ESMS metadata file – hsw_acc_work_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=lfso_20_esms|title=2020. Accidents at work and other work-related health problems}} (ESMS metadata file – lfso_20_esms) '''Publication''' *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-RA-12-102|title=European statistics on accidents at work (ESAW) – Summary methodology – 2013 edition}} ===External links=== *[https://osha.europa.eu/en European Agency for Safety and Health at Work] *[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/rights-work/health-and-safety-work_en European Commission – Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion – Health and safety at work], see: **[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/rights-work/health-and-safety-work/strategic-policy-documents_en EU strategic framework (2021–27)] *[https://www.eurofound.europa.eu/en/topics/health-and-well-being European Foundation for the Improvement of Living and Working Conditions (EUROFOUND) – Health and well-being] *[https://www.ilo.org/topics-and-sectors/safety-and-health-work International Labour Organization (ILO) – Safety and health at work] ''View this article online at {{fullurl:{{PAGENAME}}}}'' {{Unit|topic=X_Health}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Accidents at work – statistics by economic activity]] [[Category:Health|Accidents at work – statistics by economic activity]] [[Category:Health and safety|Accidents at work – statistics by economic activity]] [[Category:Accidents at work|Accidents at work – statistics by economic activity]] [[Category:Labour market (incl. labour force survey)|Accidents at work – statistics by economic activity]] [[Category:Statistical article|Accidents at work – statistics by economic activity]] [[Category:November2026|Accidents at work – statistics by economic activity]]

title: Acquisition of citizenship statistics
text:
This article presents recent statistics on the acquisition of citizenship in the European Union (EU) Data extracted 17 March 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 In 2024, EU countries granted citizenship to close to 1.2 million people who had their usual residence on EU territory, an increase of 12% compared with 2023. Most of the new citizenships were granted by Germany (288 700; 24.5% of the EU total), Spain (252 500; 21.4% of the EU total), Italy (217 400; 18.5%), France (103 700; 8.8%) and Sweden (63 000; 5.4%). In 2024, Syrians, Moroccans and Albanians remained in the top 3 recipients of EU country citizenship. This article presents recent statistics on the acquisition of [[Glossary:Citizenship|citizenship]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Citizenship is the legal bond between an individual and a state, acquired by birth, naturalisation, or other means according to national legislation. Naturalisation is the process by which a state grants its citizenship through a formal act on application of the individual concerned. Other ways of granting citizenship may include spouses of nationals, minors adopted by nationals and descendants of nationals born abroad returning to the country of origin of their ancestors. Naturalisation rate is the ratio of the number of persons who acquired the citizenship of a country during a calendar year over the total number of non-national residents in the same country at the beginning of the year. ===Main trends in the acquisition of citizenship=== In 2024, 1 177 232 people obtained citizenship of the EU country of their usual residence, an increase of 11.6% compared with 2023 (Figure 1). This was mainly the result of increases in absolute terms in Germany (88 900 more residents were granted German citizenship than in 2023), followed by Spain (12 300 more) and France (6 400 more) (Table 1). By contrast, the largest decreases in absolute terms compared with 2023 were observed in Romania (down by 8 500) and by Sweden (down by 4 800). Figure 1
[[Image:2026-03-12_Visual_SE_ACQ_table_1.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Total number of acquisitions of citizenship (in thousands), 2014-2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_acq__custom_20724159/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=670658b8-8b45-4e12-b273-cfd822db4dd5&c=1774528651000 migr_acq])|alt=Table showing the total number of acquisitions of citizenship for each year from 2014 to 2024 for the EU, the EU Member States and the EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In relative terms, the largest increases occurred in Denmark (86.4%), Slovakia (59.2%), Germany (44.5%) and Malta (38.8%), while the largest decreases occurred in Romania (-67.9%), Estonia (-29.7%) and Hungary (-28.3%) (Figure 2). Figure 2
Figure 3 ===Acquisition of citizenship in relation to the total population and naturalisation rate=== In relation to the total population on 1 January 2024, the highest number of citizenships were granted by Luxembourg (8.8 per 1 000 persons), followed by Sweden (6.0), Spain (5.2), Belgium (5.1) and Ireland (4.5) (Figure 4). Figure 4 An indicator commonly used to measure the effect of national policies on citizenship is the "[[Glossary:Naturalisation rate|naturalisation rate]]" or ratio of the total number of citizenships granted over the stock of [[Glossary:Non-nationals|non-national]] population in a country at the beginning of the year. It is important to note that changes in naturalisation rates can also be attributed to changes in the non-national population and in the way the non-national population is measured (see [[#Data sources|Data sources]]). In 2024, in the EU as a whole, 2.7 usual residents per 100 resident non-national citizens were granted citizenship. The country with the highest naturalisation rate was Sweden (7.5), followed by Italy (4.1) and Spain and the Netherlands (each 3.9), while Lithuania (0.1), Bulgaria and Estonia (each 0.3) had the lowest rates (Figure 5). Figure 5 ===Acquisition of citizenship by group of previous citizenship=== The majority (88.0%) of people granted an EU citizenship in 2024 were previously citizens of a non-EU country. Citizens of another EU country than the country of residence accounted for 10.6%. People without (or with unknown) citizenship represented 1.8% of the total (Table 2). In Hungary and Luxembourg, the majority of new citizenships (60.5% and 59.7% respectively) concerned citizens of another EU country (Table 2). In Luxembourg, Portuguese citizens accounted for the largest share (35.5%), followed by French (21.4%), Italian (8.8%) and Belgian citizens (8.3%). In Hungary, most new citizenships were for Romanians (71.4%) followed by Slovaks (20.0%) (Table 4). [[Image:Acquisitions of citizenship by group of previous citizenship, 2024 v3.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 2: Acquisitions of citizenship by group of previous citizenship, 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_acq__custom_20724019/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=8ccd032d-f316-4981-a265-be0a7c9ff570&c=1774528344000 migr_acq])|alt=Table showing the acquisitions of citizenship by group of previous citizenship in 2024 for the EU, EU Member States and EFTA countries. The table displays both the absolute numbers and the percentages of the total number of newly acquired citizenships in the EU. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] For the EU as a whole, the largest groups in terms of previous citizenship in 2024 were Syrians (110 100 persons, 9.3% of all acquisitions of citizenship), Moroccans (97 100, 8.2%), Albanians (48 000, 4.1%), Turks (41 300, 3.5%) and Romanians (39 900, 3.4%) (Table 3). [[Image:2026-03-12_Visual SE ACQ_table_3.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 3: Ten main countries of previous citizenship of the new citizens, 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_acq__custom_20724390/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=009dd231-8c4b-4fa3-887f-d1013a9fb93d&c=1774529111000 migr_acq])|alt=Table showing the ten main countries of previous citizenship of the new citizens in 2024, showing for each country the total acquisitions in the EU and the main EU country granting citizenship. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The main EU countries granting citizenship to each of the top 5 nationalities were, respectively (Table 3): * Syrians: Germany (75.6%), the Netherlands (8.7%), and Sweden (6.9%) * Moroccans: Spain (44.2%), Italy (28.5%), and France (14.9%) * Albanians: Italy (65.9%) and Greece (22.3%) * Turks: Germany (54.6%), Netherlands (15.7%) and France (11.7%) * Romanians: Italy (37.0%) and Germany (21.7%). [[Image:2026-03-12_Visual SE ACQ_table_4.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 4: Main countries of former EU and non-EU citizenship, 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_acq}}|alt=Table showing the main five countries of previous EU and non-EU citizenships of persons acquiring citizenship in 2024 for each EU Member state and EFTA country. The values are displayed for each country in absolute numbers and as a percentage of the total EU and non-EU previous citizenships of persons acquiring citizenship. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Acquisition of citizenship by age and sex=== The distribution by sex shows a slight predominance of women (50.9%, compared with 49.1% men), especially for the age groups above 30 years (55.4% women in the age group 60-64 years) (Table 5). In 2024, acquisitions of citizenship by women outnumbered acquisitions by men in all but 10 EU countries (Bulgaria, Germany, Italy, Lithuania, Hungary, Austria, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Sweden). The highest proportion of citizenship acquisitions by women was recorded in Croatia (63.6%), while the country with the highest share of acquisitions by men was Lithuania (58.9%). [[Image:Age and sex distribution of persons acquiring citizenship, 2024 v2.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 5: Age and sex distribution of persons acquiring citizenship, 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_acq}}|alt=Table showing the age and sex distribution of persons acquiring citizenship in the EU, the EU countries and the EFTA countries in 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, the [[Glossary:Median_age|median age]] of persons acquiring citizenship in the whole of the EU was 31.7 years. The EU country with the lowest median age was Greece: half of its new citizens were younger than 19.7 years. The highest median age was in Cyprus (43.9 years). Age distribution varied from one EU country to another due to differences in citizenship legislation and age structure of the non-national population (see [[#Data sources|Data sources]]). However, the common feature uniting all was that most new citizenships were acquired by younger people, and that the numbers declined with age. In 2024, 37.4% of persons granted citizenship of an EU country were younger than 25 years; another 43.0% were aged 25-44 years, while those aged 45 years and over accounted for 19.6% (Table 5 and Figure 6). Children below the age of 15 years represented 23.7% of persons granted citizenship of an EU country; the highest proportions of children were observed in France (34.3%), Greece (31.3%), Austria (29.4%) and Slovenia (28.4%). The countries with the lowest proportion of citizenship acquisitions by children were Lithuania (1.6%), Croatia (3.9%), Ireland (7.8%) and Luxembourg (8.8%). Across all EU countries, 7.3% of those who were granted citizenship were at least 55 years of age. Cyprus (30.7%), Lithuania (21.0%) and Latvia (20.3%) had the highest shares of citizenships granted to persons aged 55 years and over. The countries with the lowest shares of citizenships granted to persons aged 55 years and over were Austria (2.9%) and Slovenia (4.2%). Figure 6 === Source data for tables === {{Template:Excel|filename=Tables - SE - Acquisition of citizenship statistics 2024 v4.xlsx|title=Acquisition of citizenship statistics - tables}} ===Data sources=== [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] produces statistics on a range of issues related to acquisitions of citizenship, international migration flows and migrant population stocks. Data are collected on an annual basis and are supplied to Eurostat by the national statistical authorities of the EU Member States. Data for Germany ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_acq/default/table?lang=en migr_acq] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_acq1ctz/default/table?lang=en migr_acq1ctz]) are rounded to the nearest multiple of 5 starting from reference year 2018. The break in time series for Romania in 2017 relates to the introduction of improved administrative data sources that give more complete breakdowns for country of previous citizenship. Data in this article are rounded to the nearest hundred. '''Definitions''' This article concerns the '''acquisition of citizenship''' by the '''usually resident population''' of Member States. Usual residence means the place where a person normally spends the daily period of rest, regardless of temporary absences for purposes of recreation, holidays, visits to friends and relatives, business, medical treatment or religious pilgrimage. '''Citizenship''' is the legal bond between an individual and a state, acquired by birth, naturalisation, or other means according to national legislation. Naturalisation is the process by which a state grants its citizenship through a formal act on application of the individual concerned. Other ways of granting citizenship may include spouses of nationals, minors adopted by nationals and descendants of nationals born abroad returning to the country of origin of their ancestors. The '''naturalisation rate''' is the ratio of the number of persons who acquired the citizenship of a country during a calendar year over the stock of non-national residents in the same country at the beginning of the year. The naturalisation rate should be used with caution, however, as the numerator includes all means of acquisition and not just naturalisation of eligible residing non-nationals and the denominator includes all non-nationals and not just the relevant population, i.e. those non-nationals who are eligible for naturalisation. There are 2 ways of recording '''age''': ''Age reached'': number of complete years lived at the end of the calendar year in question. Under this age concept, a person born in 1951 will be 52 on each day of the calendar year 2003, irrespective of his or her birthday. ''Age completed'': number of completed years lived at most recent birthday. Detailed information on the different modes of acquisition of citizenship in force in different countries can be found at the [http://globalcit.eu/ GLOBALCIT website]. The category [[Glossary:Recognised non-citizen|recognised non-citizen]] is particularly relevant in the Baltic States. ===Context=== Within the European Commission, the Directorate-General for Migration and Home Affairs is responsible for European migration policy. In September 2020, the European Commission presented the [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en New Pact on Migration and Asylum] which was adopted by the European Parliament in April 2024 and by the Council in May 2024. This pact provides a comprehensive approach that delivers a common European response to migration. It allows the EU to manage migration in a fair and sustainable way, ensuring solidarity between countries while also providing certainty and clarity for people arriving in the EU and protecting their fundamental rights.
