title: Agri-environmental indicator - cropping patterns
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the agri-environmental indicator - cropping patterns. Data from August 2026 Planned update: October 2028 (with data from the Farm Structure Survey 2026) Of the 156.2 million hectares (ha) of land in the EU used for agricultural production in 2023, 97.7 million ha were farmed as arable land, 47.2 million ha as permanent grassland, 11.1 million ha as permanent crops, with the remainder as kitchen gardens. The amount of land used in the EU for agricultural production in 2023 was 2.7 million hectares less than in 2010 (equivalent to -1.7 %), underpinned by 2.8 million fewer hectares (-5.6 %) of permanent grassland. Source:[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistical-atlas/?mids=Roads,EURONYM,BORDERS,AGRIAREA2&o=1,1,0.7,1&ch=CH_CENSUS_POP¢er=52.15635,14.70353,4.349410035507113&tab=Legend&lcis=AGRIAREA2&style=gridviz/farm-statistics/agricultural-area/share-of-arable-land&bl=true&mpc=1& Statistical Atlas] This article provides data on the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] [[Glossary:Agri-environmental indicator (AEI)|agri-environmental indicator]] '''cropping patterns'''. It consists of an overview of data, complemented by information needed to interpret these data. The indicator on cropping patterns is part of a [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators set of indicators], providing a comprehensive picture of the integration of environmental concerns into the [[Glossary:Common_agricultural_policy_(CAP)|Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)]]. === Analysis of cropping patterns at EU level === '''Cropping patterns in 2023: arable land accounted for a majority of the EU's UAA''' The area used for agricultural production, known as the total [[Glossary:Utilised_agricultural_area_(UAA)|utilised agricultural area (UAA)]], was 156.2 million hectares in 2023 across the [[Glossary:EU|EU]] as a whole. In 2023, [[Glossary:Arable_land|arable land]] covered 97.7 million hectares in the EU, accounting for a large majority of the utilised agricultural area (equivalent to 62.5% - see Figure 1). [[Glossary:Permanent_grassland|Permanent grassland]] covered a further 47.2 million hectares (30.2%), with [[Glossary:Permanent_crops|permanent crops]] (including orchards, citrus and olive groves and vines) covering 11.1 million hectares (7.2%), and [[Glossary:Kitchen_gardens|kitchen gardens]] about 0.2 million hectares (0.1%).
[[Image:F1 Type of agricultural land cover.png|thumb|centre|640px|Figure 1: Type of agricultural land cover
(% share of utilised agricultural area, EU, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/78ee5ebb-7527-46ca-bc2c-4016d84b370d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-06T12:25:18Z ef_fsi_lus])|alt=a doughnut chart showing the type of agricultural land cover as a percentage share of utilised agricultural area in the EU in the year 2023. The segments show permanent crops, kitchen gardens, arable land, permanent grassland. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''Trend in cropping patterns towards less permanent grassland and more permanent crops''' Between 2010 and 2023, there was an overall reduction in utilised agricultural area in the EU of 2.7 million hectares (equivalent to -1.7%). This was underpinned by a decline of 2.8 million hectares in the area of permanent grassland (-5.6%). The area of arable land was relatively unchanged, with a modest decline of 0.3 million hectares (-0.3%). By contrast, there was a modest increase of 0.5 million hectares (+4.9%) in the area of land used for permanent crops. '''Arable land ''' Although for the EU as a whole the area covered by arable land fell only slightly between 2010 and 2023 (-0.3% to 97.7 million hectares), there were considerable differences in developments between EU countries (see Figure 2). There were 4 countries for which the area of arable land increased by more than 10%: Ireland (+32.4%), Latvia (+21.2%), Cyprus (+16.2%) and Estonia (+10.5%). By contrast, there were 3 countries for which the area of arable land decreased by more than 20%: Portugal (-27.6%), Greece (-21.1%) and Malta (-20.2%). In Portugal, whilst there was a decline in arable land, there was a corresponding rise in the area of permanent grassland. In Greece, the decline in arable land was part of a general decrease in its utilised agricultural area. In Ireland, the growth in arable land is explained by a rise in temporary grassland.
[[Image:F2 Developments in arable land area (% change, 2010 - 2023).png|thumb|centre|640px|Figure 2: Developments in arable land area
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/06316174-bc7d-4b99-8f8c-0e307bbaddc0?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-07T08:09:16Z ef_fsi_lus])| alt=a bar chart showing the increase/decrease of arable land area as a percentage change in the EU and in each EU country between the years 2010 and 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Analysis of cropping patterns at country level === '''Largest shares of EU agricultural land are in France and Spain''' In 2023, about two-thirds (68.4%) of the EU's UAA was farmed across 6 countries: France (27.2 million ha, the equivalent of 17.4% of the EU total), Spain (23.5 million ha or 15.0%), Germany (16.6 million ha, or 10.6%), Poland (14.6 million ha, or 9.3%), Romania (12.6 million ha, or 8.0%) and Italy (12.4 million ha, or 7.9%). No other EU country had more than 6.0 million ha of UAA (see Figure 3). [[Image:F3 Utilised Agricultural Area (UAA).png|thumb|centre|640px|Figure 3: Utilised agricultural area
(% share of EU total, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/78ee5ebb-7527-46ca-bc2c-4016d84b370d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-06T12:25:18Z ef_fsi_lus])|alt=a doughnut chart showing the percentage share of the EU's utilised agricultural area in EU countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''France had more hectares of arable land and permanent grassland than other EU countries, Spain more hectares of permanent crops''' France had 17.0 million ha of arable land in 2023, the equivalent of 17.4% of the EU's total arable land. Germany had 11.7 million ha (12.0%) of arable land, while Spain had 11.5 million ha (11.8%) and Poland 11.2 million ha (11.4%). These 4 EU countries accounted for just over one half (52.6%) of the EU's arable land. France also had 9.2 million ha of permanent grassland in 2023, the equivalent of 19.5% of the EU's total permanent grassland area. Spain had 7.3 million ha (15.5%) of permanent grassland, Germany 4.7 million ha (10.0%), Ireland had 3.7 million ha (7.9%) and Romania had 3.6 million ha (7.7%). These 5 EU countries accounted for about 60% of the EU total area of permanent grassland. Spain had 4.6 million ha of permanent crops in 2023, the equivalent of 41.1% of the EU total. Italy had 2.3 million ha (20.8%) of permanent crops, France 1.0 million ha (9.1%), Portugal and Greece 0.9 million ha each. Together, the 5 countries accounted for 86.6% of the EU's permanent crops area. '''UAA in Finland and Denmark dominated by arable land and in Ireland by permanent grassland''' How much land countries dedicate to arable land, permanent grassland and permanent crops varies considerably and can be influenced, among other things, by climatic, topographic and agronomic factors. In 2023, 8 EU countries used three-quarters or more of their respective UAA as arable land, with the highest values recorded for Finland and Denmark (99.2% and 89.8% of their UAA respectively). The lowest share of arable land (22.0% of the UAA) was in Portugal (see Figure 4). [[Image:F4 Type of agricultural land use (% share of utilised agricultural area, EU countries, 2023).png|thumb|centre|640px|Figure 4: Type of agricultural land use
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/78ee5ebb-7527-46ca-bc2c-4016d84b370d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-06T12:25:18Z ef_fsi_lus])|alt=a horizontal stacked bar chart showing the type of agricultural land use as a percentage share of utilised agricultural area in EU countries in the year 2023. The stacks show arable land, permanent grassland, permanent crops and kitchen gardens. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Several EU countries with low shares of arable land reported high shares of permanent grassland. By far the highest share was in Ireland (73.5%). Other countries where permanent grassland covered more than half of the UAA included Slovenia (58.3%), Portugal (54.4%) and Luxembourg (52.4%). By contrast, less than 2% of the UAA was occupied by permanent grassland in Malta, Finland and Cyprus. Mediterranean countries tended to have higher proportions of UAA as permanent crops; the shares ranged from 11.7% of UAA in Malta to 23.3% in Portugal, with Italy, Spain, Greece and Cyprus in between. The share of permanent crops in UAA was less than 2% in 12 EU countries.
===Crop diversity of arable land in the EU=== '''Majority of agricultural holdings with arable land grow more than one type of arable land crops''' Crop diversity is an important characteristic of agricultural production systems, as it can contribute to the resilience of farming, support biodiversity and influence the sustainable use of natural resources. The analysis presented here focuses on crop diversity within arable land, based on crops considered at a detailed level of classification. In 2023, slightly more than one half (55.6%) of the EU's holdings with arable land crops, grew two or more different crops. Of the 5.9 million holdings with arable land, 2.6 million (44.4%) grew only 1 crop, 1.3 million (22.2%) grew 2 crops, 0.8 million (14.0%) grew 3 crops, and 1.2 million (19.5%) grew more than 3 crops. Luxembourg (70.7%) Austria (62.0%) and Germany (59.8%) were the three countries where the share of holdings with arable land growing more than 3 crops was highest. By contrast, Cyprus (5.0%), Malta (3.9%) and Ireland (2.9%) were the three countries where this share was lowest (see Figure 5). [[Image:F5r Crop diversity, 2023 (% share of holdings with arable crops according to .png|thumb|centre|640px|Figure 5: Crop diversity
(% share of number of crops, EU countries, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/48167168-c36c-47ce-a2f8-30ae40dd9825?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-17T10:54:11Z ef_fsi_cdiv])|alt=a horizontal stacked bar chart showing the share of agricultural holdings with arable crops according to the number of different arable crops grown in 2023; the stacks show the share of 1 crop holdings, the share of 2 crop holdings, the share of 3 crop holdings and the share of holdings with more than 3 crops. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=Cropping patterns 2023 SE v.03 20260826.xlsx|title=Download Excel file}} ===Data sources=== '''Indicator definition''' Cropping patterns are defined as trends in the share of the [[Glossary:Utilised_agricultural_area_(UAA)|utilised agricultural area (UAA)]] occupied by the main agricultural land cover types ([[Glossary:Arable_land|arable land]], [[Glossary:Permanent_grassland_and_meadow|permanent grassland]], [[Glossary:Permanent_crops|permanent crops]] and [[Glossary:Kitchen_gardens|kitchen gardens]]), and they are measured by the following indicators: '''Main indicator''' * Share (%) of main agricultural land cover types (arable land, permanent grassland, land under permanent crops and kitchen gardens) in total UAA. '''Supporting indicator''' * Areas (in hectares) occupied by arable crops, permanent grassland, permanent crops and kitchen gardens. '''Links with other indicators''' This indicator has links to a number of other [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators AEI indicators] that describe developments in some of the main contributory factors. '''Data used''' In this article, cropping patterns are described on the basis of [[Glossary:Farm_structure_survey_(FSS)|farm structure]] data. Farm structure data are collected from agricultural censuses every ten years and from sample surveys every 3 or 4 years in between. These surveys are conducted consistently throughout the EU under the provisions of [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2018/1091/oj/eng Regulation (EU) 2018/1091] on Integrated Farm Statistics, providing comparable and representative statistics on livestock and land use across countries and time, at regional level. The unit underlying the farm structure data collections is the [[Glossary:Agricultural_holding|agricultural holding]], a technical-economic unit under single management engaged in agricultural production. A range of different physical thresholds have been used to define the coverage of farm structure surveys, with an impact on the comparability of data across time. More information about the thresholds and their impact on comparability can be found in the background article [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Integrated_farm_statistics_-_impact_of_changes_in_coverage Farm structure survey – impact of changes in coverage]. The implementation of the Integrated Farm Statistics (IFS) in 2020 introduced a division of the target population into two components: the ‘main frame’ includes agricultural holdings above physical thresholds defined in the legislation, while the ‘frame extension’ covers smaller holdings below these thresholds. In the legislative framework, data collection requirements for below-threshold units vary across time. This variability leads to gaps in data availability for the entire population of agricultural holdings and poses challenges for the comparability of results. To address this issue, an estimation procedure based on imputation techniques applied at the level of microdata has been developed to produce consistent estimates for below-threshold units where data are missing, which have been published in the Eurobase datasets under Farm structural indicators [ef_fsi]. More information about the estimation of missing data in IFS can be found in the article [[Farm_structure_-_estimation_of_missing_data|Farm structure - estimation of missing data]]. '''Methodology''' The utilised agricultural area (UAA) is the total area taken up by arable land (including temporary grassland and fallow land), permanent grassland, permanent crops and [[Glossary:Kitchen_gardens|kitchen gardens]]. It should be noted that common land is included in farm structure data collections in some countries and this has an [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Integrated_farm_statistics_-_impact_of_changes_in_coverage impact on data on land cover]. [[Glossary:Arable_land|Arable land]] in agricultural statistics is land worked (ploughed or tilled) regularly, generally under a system of crop rotation. [[Glossary:Permanent_grassland|Permanent grassland]] is land used permanently (for several consecutive years, usually 5 or more years) to grow herbaceous forage crops and not included in the crop rotation scheme on the agricultural holding. Permanent grassland can be used for grazing by livestock or mown for hay, silage (stocking in a silo) or used for renewable energy production. [[Glossary:Permanent_crops|Permanent crops]] are ligneous crops, meaning trees or shrubs, not grown in rotation, but occupying the soil and yielding harvests for several (usually more than five) consecutive years. Permanent crops mainly consist of fruit and berry trees, bushes, vines and olive trees. Permanent crops are usually intended for human consumption and generally yield a higher added value per hectare than annual crops. They also play an important role in shaping the rural landscape (through orchards, citrus groves, vineyards and olive tree plantations) and helping to balance agriculture within the environment. ===Context=== '''Introduction''' Cropping patterns provide insights into the relationship between the environmental conditions and farming systems across the EU. They reflect how agricultural land is allocated among different crop types and land cover, including arable crops (such as cereals, oilseeds, protein crops and fodder crops), permanent crops (including fruit plantations, olive groves and vineyards) and permanent grassland. Cropping patterns vary considerably across the EU as a result of differences in climate, soils, topography, water availability, farm structure and market conditions. They also evolve over time in response to technological developments, policy measures and changing economic and environmental conditions. Monitoring changes in cropping patterns helps assess the sustainability and resilience of agricultural systems and supports the evaluation of agricultural, environmental and climate policies. '''Policy relevance''' Cropping patterns are influenced by a wide range of interacting drivers, including policy measures. The [Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)] remains one of the principal policy frameworks influencing cropping patterns in the EU. Under the CAP 2023–2027, Member States implement CAP Strategic Plans that combine EU-wide objectives with interventions tailored to national and regional conditions. Consequently, the influence of the CAP on cropping patterns varies across Member States. Several CAP instruments directly or indirectly affect cropping patterns. These include enhanced conditionality requirements and eco-schemes, which encourage farming practices that comply high EU standards for public, plant, and animal health and welfare and that contribute to EU climate targets, as well as support to [[Glossary:Organic farming|organic farming]] and to areas with natural constraints ([[Glossary:Areas_facing_natural_constraints|ANC]]). Other EU policies also influence cropping patterns. The [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/water/water-framework-directive_en Water Framework Directive] and the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/water/nitrates_en Nitrates Directive] should be noted, including requirements such as growing catch crops in designated areas. Legislation underpinning the Natura 2000 network of protected areas (the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/nature-and-biodiversity/birds-directive_en Birds Directive] and the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/nature-and-biodiversity/habitats-directive_en Habitats Directive]) limit human activities to ensure that the sites are managed in a manner compatible with the conservation objectives of protected habitats and species. Changes in cropping patterns also have an impact on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Greenhouse_gas_(GHG) greenhouse gas (GHG)] emissions. As such, they are relevant for achieving the climate-neutrality objectives set into the [https://climate.ec.europa.eu/areas-action/european-climate-law_en European Climate Law] and the carbon-removal targets of the revised [https://climate.ec.europa.eu/areas-action/land-use-sector_en#what-is-the-land-use-land-use-change-and-forestry-regulation-lulucf Regulation on land use, land use change and forestry (LULUCF)]. Land management decisions, particularly regarding permanent grasslands and cropland management, influence greenhouse gas emissions and carbon removals. More broadly, cropping patterns contribute to the objectives of the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/biodiversity-strategy-2030_en EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030], the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/soil-health/soil-strategy-2030_en EU Soil Strategy for 2030] and wider efforts to increase the resilience and sustainability of European food production. '''Agri-environmental context''' Cropping patterns are strongly linked to the way natural resources (soil, water, air, biodiversity) are managed and impacted by management practices. Many of the current land cover/use patterns have developed over centuries and still shape agricultural landscapes today. In general, agriculture is more sustainable when dominance of one or a few crops (mono-cropping) is avoided, since this can be associated with a reduction of the supply of eco-system services.Grab, H., Danforth, B., Poveda, K., & Loeb, G. (2018). Landscape simplification reduces classical biological control and crop yield. Ecological Applications, 28(2), 348-355Connelly, H., Poveda, K., & Loeb, G. (2015). Landscape simplification decreases wild bee pollination services to strawberry. Agriculture, Ecosystems and Environment, 211, 51-56Dainese, M., Isaac, N. J. B., Powney, G. D., Bommarco, R., Öckinger, E., Kuussaari, M., Pöyry J., Tim G. Benton T. G., Gabriel D., Hodgson J. A., Kunin W. A., Lindborg R., Sait S. M., Marini, L. (2017). Landscape simplification weakens the association between terrestrial producer and consumer diversity in Europe. Global Change Biology, 23(8), 3040-3051 Mosaic landscapes often have high landscape and biodiversity values. Crop diversification can increase resilience of agricultural systemsLin, B. B. (2011). Resilience in agriculture through crop diversification: Adaptive management for environmental change. Bioscience, 61(3), 183-193. and support beneficial insects providing biological control, thus reducing the dependence on insecticidesRedlich, S., Martin, E. A., & Steffan-Dewenter, I. (2018). Landscape-level crop diversity benefits biological pest control. Journal of Applied Ecology, 55(5), 2419-2428. .Adopting crop rotations leads to positive environmental impacts and at the same time global improvement of soil productivity in the long term, which increases yieldsMudgal S., Lavelle P., Cachia F., Somogyi D., Majewski E., Fontaine L., Bechini L., Debaeke P. (2010) [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/363884907_Environmental_impacts_of_crop_rotations_in_the_EU Environmental impacts of different crop rotations in the European Union,] Final Report for the European Commission (DG Environment).. Permanent grassland has high recognition, due to the substantial role it plays in landscape and nature conservation Osterman, O. P. (1998) The need for management of nature conservation sites under Natura 2000. Journal of Applied Ecology 35: 968-973Bignal, E.M., D.I. McCracken (2000). The nature conservation value of European traditional farming systems. Environmental Reviews 8: 149-171Beaufoy et al., 1994. Beaufoy, G., D. Baldock and J. Clark, (1994). The Nature of Farming: Low intensity farming systems in nine European countries. London, Institute for European Environmental Policy. 66. Semi-natural grasslands are among the areas with the richest biodiversity in the EU (e.g. wooded meadows of Estonia). However, in the most intensive permanent pastures farmers re-seed with selectively bred cultivars of grass and other fodder species and may use [[Glossary:Fertiliser|mineral fertilisers]] and herbicides. This allows farmers to achieve high yields, but with little associated biodiversity value. There are negative impacts on [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/cap-my-country/sustainability/environmental-sustainability/climate-change_en climate change] of this type of intensive grassland, when compared to more extensive permanent grassland. Under CAP’s conditionality requirements, farmers must maintain permanent grasslands, and in environmentally sensitive zones, converting and ploughing these lands is prohibited, recognising their importance for biodiversity conservation and climate mitigation. === Other articles === * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agriculture,_forestry_and_fishery_statistics Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics] * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agri-environmental_indicators Agri-environmental indicators] * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Farm_structure_survey_(FSS) Farm structure survey (FSS)] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database Agriculture (agr)], see: :Farm structure (ef) :Farm structural indicators (ef_fsi) :Main farm land use (ef_fsi_lus) :Crop diversity (ef_fsi_cdiv)

title: Agri-environmental indicator - irrigation
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the agri-environmental indicator - irrigation. Data from IFS 2023 No planned update date In 2023, about one tenth (9.6%, or 14.9 million hectares) of the EU’s utilised agricultural area (UAA) was considered irrigable. The area of land actually irrigated was 10.0 million hectares (equivalent to 6.5% of UAA). In 2023, Italy, Spain and France together accounted for about two-thirds of the irrigable area of the EU (66.4%) and of the irrigated area (64.7%). The share of irrigable and irrigated areas in the EU’s UAA remained largely unchanged in 2023 from that in 2010. [[Image:Headline r Share of irrigable and irrigated areas in EU total (%, 2023).png|thumb|center|500px|Share of irrigable and irrigated areas in EU total
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/02f49407-971e-44b2-a600-fa94494fd81e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-25T13:23:55Z ef_fsi_irri])|alt= Horizontal bar chart showing the shares of individual EU Member States in the EU total areas of irrigable and irrigated areas. Each country has two bars representing irrigable areas and irrigated areas for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article provides a fact sheet of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] [[Glossary:Agri-environmental indicator (AEI)|agri-environmental indicator]] '''irrigation'''. It consists of an overview of data, complemented by information needed to interpret these data. This article on irrigation in the EU is part of a [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators set of similar fact sheets], providing a comprehensive picture of the integration of environmental concerns into the [[Glossary:Common_agricultural_policy_(CAP)|Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)]]. Disclaimer: For irrigated area, Regulation 2018/1091 exempted countries from carrying out the 'Irrigation' module in 2023 if irrigable area represented less than 2% of the UAA and where there were no NUTS 2 level regions with irrigable area corresponding to at least 5% of the UAA. Exempted countries: Czechia, Estonia, Ireland, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg and Slovenia. === Analysis at EU and country level === '''In 2023, two-thirds of the EU’s irrigable agricultural land was actively irrigated''' The total agricultural area in the EU equipped for irrigation ([[Glossary:Irrigable area|irrigable area]]) was 14.9 million ha in 2023 (Table 1). However, the area actually irrigated ([[Glossary:Irrigated area|irrigated area]]) was 10.0 million hectares (ha), equivalent to two-thirds of irrigable area capacity. Malta was the only EU country that used all its irrigable area capacity in 2023. [[Image:T1 Irrigable and irrigated areas (2010 and 2023).png|thumb|center|500px|Table 1: Irrigable and irrigated areas (2010 and 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5f8edece-ec28-45d0-bb76-afc8bf2d3910?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-25T13:33:55Z ef_fsi_irri]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/329f3a07-cfb3-4a57-9541-556e846b7222?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-25T13:34:43Z ef_fsi_lus])|alt= a table showing the irrigable and irrigated areas in the EU and Member States in the years 2010 and 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] It should be underlined that the irrigated area itself does not indicate information about the actual quantity of water applied. In addition, this fact sheet does not explore water efficiency in irrigation, nor groundwater depletion in irrigated areas. Whether or not agricultural land is irrigated reflects a variety of factors, including water availability, soil type, climate and the type of crop being produced. Italy, Spain and France together accounted for about two-thirds of the irrigable area of the EU (66.4%) and of the irrigated area (64.7%). Italy had 3.6 million hectares of irrigable area and 2.2 million hectares of irrigated area in 2023 (see Figure 1), using about 61% of its irrigable area capacity. Spain had 3.5 million hectares of irrigable area and 2.7 million hectares of irrigated area (equivalent to 78% of irrigable area capacity). France had 2.8 million hectares of irrigable area and 1.5 million hectares of irrigated area (equivalent to 54% of irrigable area capacity). [[Image:F1 Share of irrigable and irrigated areas in EU total (%, 2023).png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 1: Share of irrigable and irrigated areas in EU total
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/02f49407-971e-44b2-a600-fa94494fd81e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-25T13:23:55Z ef_fsi_irri])|alt= Horizontal bar chart showing the shares of individual EU Member States in the EU total areas of irrigable and irrigated areas. Each country has two bars representing irrigable areas and irrigated areas for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Mediterranean countries generally had the highest shares of irrigable and irrigated areas relative to their ([[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|utilised agricultural area (UAA)]]) (see Table 1 and Figure 2). Malta (32.1%) and Italy (29.1%) had the highest shares of irrigable UAA in 2023. Malta (32.1%) and Greece (20.3%) had the highest shares of UAA actually irrigated. Beyond the Mediterranean region, irrigation is often used on a supplementary basis to improve crop production in dry summers. The choice of crops to produce also has an impact, even in more northerly countries. A little more than one quarter (27.0%) of the UAA in the Netherlands is irrigable area and almost one fifth (19.0%) was actually used for irrigation in 2023. Horticulture, fruit and vegetables production are key sectors in the Netherlands. [[Image:F2 Share of irrigable and irrigated areas in UAA (%, 2023).png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 2: Share of irrigable and irrigated areas in UAA
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b1d1a79e-3b1b-4919-bc36-abee03f35e64?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-25T14:00:03Z ef_fsi_irri]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/329f3a07-cfb3-4a57-9541-556e846b7222?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-11T07:36:33Z ef_fsi_lus])|alt=a double vertical bar chart showing the shares of irrigable and irrigated areas in UAA for the EU and individual Member States for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''The share of irrigable and irrigated areas in the EU’s UAA little changed''' The share of irrigable and irrigated areas in the EU’s UAA remained largely unchanged in 2023 from that in 2010 (see Figure 3). Among EU countries, however, there were some where there was an expansion in areas equipped for irrigation: the sharpest increases between 2010 and 2023 were in Malta (4.6 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]]), followed by Austria (3.8 pp). There were others where there was a sharp contraction: Greece (-13.7 pp), Cyprus (-7.7 pp) and Denmark (-5.7 pp). The contrasts between countries were arguably even more prominent in terms of the actual areas irrigated. There were considerable increases in the share of irrigated area in the Netherlands (11.7 pp) and Malta (7.4 pp) but sharp contractions in Greece (-9.4 pp) and Denmark (-5.3 pp). Greece, Denmark, Cyprus, as well as Sweden, Spain and Bulgaria, were the only countries with lower shares in 2023 of both areas equipped for irrigation and areas actually irrigated than in 2010. [[Image:F3 Change in share of irrigable and irrigated areas in UAA (percentage points, 2010-2023).png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 3: Change in share of irrigable and irrigated areas in UAA
''Source:'' ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5f8edece-ec28-45d0-bb76-afc8bf2d3910?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-25T13:33:55Z ef_fsi_irri]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/329f3a07-cfb3-4a57-9541-556e846b7222?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-25T13:34:43Z ef_fsi_lus])|alt=a double horizontal bar chart showing the change in share of irrigable and irrigated areas in UAA in the EU and Member States between the year 2010 and the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Agri-environmental indicator Irrigation SE article v3.0 20260629.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === '''Indicator definition''' The indicator assesses the trend of the [[Glossary:Irrigable area|irrigable]] and [[Glossary:Irrigated area|irrigated]] areas and their share of the total [[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|utilised agricultural area (UAA)]]. The '''irrigable area''' is the area which is equipped for irrigation. This area does not show so much variation from year to year as it is costly for the farmer to invest in irrigation equipment. The '''irrigated area''' measures the actual amount of land irrigated and can vary significantly from year to year due to, for instance, meteorological conditions or the choice of crops.. '''Main indicator''' *Share of irrigable area in utilised agricultural area (UAA) (and its trend) '''Supporting indicators''' *Irrigable area *Irrigated area *Share of irrigated area in total UAA '''Links with other indicators''' This indicator has links to a number of other [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators AEI indicators] that describe developments in some of the main contributory factors. The link to AEI 20 "Water abstraction" is especially important as the relative and total area irrigated do not provide enough information to estimate the environmental implications of irrigation on depletion of water resources and thus the sustainability of the cropping systems. The link to AEI 12 "Intensification/Extensification" is relevant as [[Glossary:Intensification|intensification]] processes in cropping systems usually go together with an increase in inputs such as water use, while [[Glossary:Extensification|extensification]] usually has the opposite effect. So this indicator tells something about the driving forces behind the changes in irrigable area. '''Data used and methodology''' The indicator is considered fully operational. Proposals to improve this indicator include: *collecting data on water metering to be able to monitor and evaluate this practice. Water metering is an important practice to improve the efficiency of water use by irrigation. *analysing data at [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/water/participation/map_mc/map.htm river basin] scale. As the EU water policy is mainly built on it, it would be relevant for the information to be aggregated to this scale at some point. *improve link with the AEI 20 indicator. The effects of irrigation on the environment depend also on the current state of water management in the area. Negative effects can for instance occur in water stressed areas. To be able to assess the effects of irrigation on the environment it would be necessary to link the data to water abstraction and state of water in the area. Data on irrigable areas and irrigated areas are collected in the Integrated Farm Statistics (IFS). The available time series starts in 2005 for most EU countries. Farm structure data are collected from agricultural censuses every ten years and from sample surveys every 3 or 4 years in between. The main tables from the 2023 survey are gradually being published and are used in this analysis. '''Explanatory note''' The implementation of the Integrated Farm Statistics (IFS) introduced a division of the target population into two components: the ‘main frame’ includes agricultural holdings above physical thresholds defined in the legislation, while the ‘frame extension’ covers smaller holdings below these thresholds. In the legislative framework, data collection requirements for below-threshold units vary across time. This variability leads to gaps in data availability for the entire population of agricultural holdings and poses challenges for the comparability of results. To address this issue, an estimation procedure based on imputation techniques applied at the level of microdata has been developed to produce consistent estimates for below-threshold units where data are missing, which have been published in the Eurobase datasets under Farm structural indicators [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/explore/all/agric?sort=category&lang=en&subtheme=agr.ef.ef_fsi&display=list ef_fsi]. === Context === The primary objective of irrigation is to provide plants with sufficient water to obtain optimum yields and a high-quality harvested crop. Irrigation is essential in dry climates where precipitation is not sufficient for plant growth. Supplemental irrigation is also vital to produce high levels of quality and yield of crops on croplands in semi-arid and sub-humid climates during dry seasonal periods and drought spells where otherwise farming would not be economically viable. Irrigation increases yield and therefore contributes significantly to agricultural output and food supply. Irrigation water use is a major driving force behind [[Glossary:Water_abstraction|water abstraction]] globally. In the EU, the agricultural sector accounts for 31 % of the total water use in average for the 2020-2023 period, the majority of which for irrigation European Environment Agency, [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/water-abstraction-by-source-and Water abstraction by source and economic sector in Europe, 2025.].. Water abstraction at unsustainable rates occurs when the demand for water exceeds the amount available during a certain period. In the coming years, climatic conditions like a decrease in precipitation together with the lengthening of the thermal growing season may lead to a slight increase in water requirement for irrigation. Rates of agricultural water use depend on various factors: the crop species chosen (e.g. water-intensive crops such as potatoes in northern Europe or cotton, grain maize, and rice in southern Europe), the share of irrigated area, the irrigation technology in use (e.g. drip versus furrow irrigation), the irrigation strategy of the farmer (e.g. full versus complementary irrigation), the presence of legal restrictions, water prices and pumping costs, and certainly the weather conditions. Because of the inter-annual variability of the given factors affecting irrigation requirements, irrigated areas may change year to year, while irrigable areas (defined as the total area equipped for irrigation) are less variable in time. For this reason, irrigable areas are used to present trends in irrigation. '''Policy relevance and context''' The need for a sustainable and integrated approach to managing water resources in Europe is reflected in water-related policy and legislation. The [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/water/water-framework-directive_en Water Framework Directive (WFD)], as the EU’s principal legal framework for water management, promotes sustainable water use by setting out the rules for the protection of available water resources. A balance between abstraction and recharge of groundwater must be ensured, with the aim of achieving good quantitative status with respect to groundwater. The WFD also requires that water pricing policies are implemented that provide adequate incentives for the efficient use of water resourcesEuropean Commission, [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=COM:2010:0228:FIN:EN:PDF Report from the Commission to the Council and the European Parliament – Second Follow-up Report to the Communication on water scarcity and droughts in the European Union COM (2007) 414 final, Brussels, 2010 .] . Stemming from the WFD, the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52025DC0280&qid=1750857768458 2025 European Water Resilience Strategy] sets the current political roadmap, investment priorities and main actions to strengthen the implementation of the Directive and to adapt EU’s water policy to emerging pressures from climate change and increasing water demand, in line with the [https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/e6cd4328-673c-4e7a-8683-f63ffb2cf648_en 2024-2029 Political Guidelines]European Commission, [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52025DC0280&qid=1750857768458 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions European Water Resilience Strategy, Brussels, 2025.] . According to the Report from the Commission to the Council and the European Parliament on the implementation of the Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC) and the Floods Directive (2007/60/EC) (Third River Basin Management Plans and Second Flood Risk Management Plans) [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM%3A2025%3A2%3AFIN&qid=1738746144581 (7th Implementation Report, 2024]), water abstraction for agriculture had increased in the 2010-2019 period by 8%, due to the increasing demand for irrigation specifically in southern Europe, where water scarcity is exacerbated by climate change. Changing crops to those more adapted to region-specific hydrological conditions, improving soil management and increasing the uptake of water reuse are mentioned as key adaptations to curb water abstraction in agriculture in this reportEuropean Commission, [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM%3A2025%3A2%3AFIN&qid=1738746144581 Report from the Commission to the Council and the European Parliament on the implementation of the Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC) and the Floods Directive (2007/60/EC) Third river basin management plans Second flood risk management plans, Brussels, 2025.] . In line with these objectives, the [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy_en Common Agricultural Policy 2023-2027] is supporting efforts to increase water resilience in agriculture, with a strengthening of conditionality and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Good_agricultural_and_environmental_conditions_(GAEC) GAEC] standards, including controls on abstraction, as well as significant support for practices to improve soil health, with positive effects on water storage capacity. Rural development measures can also support investments in improving the efficiency of irrigation installations, the use of recycled water for irrigation and rainwater harvesting
'''Agri-environmental context''' Within Europe, there is a great variability in the availability of water resources and, therefore, a marked spatial variability in agricultural water management practices and consumption. Climate is the main factor that determines agricultural water consumption; there are regions where irrigation is the only source of water for crop cultivation (this is the case during summer in some Mediterranean areas), while in other regions, irrigation is used as a supplement to rain-fed agriculture. Irrigation technology is also a major factor influencing the level of agricultural water consumption. The number of Member States that experience seasonal or long-term droughts has increased over the years. Agricultural water use is a serious concern especially in southern parts of Europe, where water is scarce and highly variable from year to year. In dry periods of the year or in generally dry regions it is necessary to irrigate certain crops to obtain reasonable yields. If not properly applied, irrigation can lead to over-abstraction of groundwater supplies, secondary [https://esdac.jrc.ec.europa.eu/themes/soil-salinization salinisation ](by salt-rich irrigation water and/or insufficient drainage), and to pollution of water by nutrients, pesticides, and other farm inputs. [https://esdac.jrc.ec.europa.eu/themes/erosion Soil erosion] can arise from intensive irrigation on slopes. While increasing agricultural production on the land, irrigation can also lead to the destruction of former high nature value habitats including [[Glossary:Arable land|arable ]]dry land and low density [[Glossary:Permanent grassland|pastures]]. If irrigation over-abstracts the sustainably available water resources, desiccation of former wetlands and the reduction of sensitive aquatic environments can occur. The environmental impact of irrigation, however, depends on the water abstraction rate and the water availability at local level. The water sources used for irrigation also matter, e.g. surface water can be replenished much faster than groundwater. Irrigation can also have environmental benefits. Traditional irrigation systems create diverse and intricate landscapes, which support a variety of wildlife and have important cultural and historic value. In the same way, the creation and management of rice fields often provide important feeding and over-wintering opportunities for some bird species. Moreover, through redistribution of water resources, new irrigation projects can contribute to improvement of aquifer recharge and habitat conservation in the areas receiving the new water. This may be the case, for instance, for irrigation projects that entail the creation of wetland areas, which may provide new feeding and/or breeding opportunities for wildlife. Investment in modern irrigation equipment can reduce water consumption and increase the crop water productivity, enabling sustainable agricultural production in rural areas and fighting land abandonment. === Other articles === *[[Water statistics]] ===Database=== *[{{Template:Database|dedicated_section=agriculture}} Agriculture (agr)], see: ::Farm structure (ef) :::Farm structural indicators (ef_fsi) ::::Irrigable and irrigated area (ef_fsi_irri) ::::Main farm land use (ef_fsi_lus) === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators Agri-Environmental Indicators] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/overview Agriculture - Overview] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-049|title=Key Figures on the European food chain — 2025 edition}} ===Methodology=== *Farm structure ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/ef_sims.htm ef]) ===Legislation=== *[http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:52006DC0508 Commission Communication COM(2006)508 final] - Development of agri-environmental indicators for monitoring the integration of environmental concerns into the common agricultural policy *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32018R1091 • Regulation 2018/1091] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 July 2018 on integrated farm statistics === Footnotes === {{Unit|topic=X_Agriculture}} [[Category:Agriculture, fisheries, and forestry|Agri-environmental indicator - irrigation]] [[Category:Agriculture|Agri-environmental indicator - irrigation]] [[Category:Environment and agriculture|Agri-environmental indicator - irrigation]] [[Category:Environment|Agri-environmental indicator - irrigation]] [[Category:Statistical_article|Agri-environmental indicator - irrigation]] [[Category:Water|Agri-environmental indicator - irrigation]] [[Category:no update|Agri-environmental indicator - irrigation]]

title: Agri-environmental indicator - livestock patterns
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the agri-environmental indicator - livestock patterns. Data from August 2026 Planned update: October 2028 (with data from the Farm Structure Survey 2026) In 2023, the EU’s average livestock density was 0.7 livestock units (LSUs) per hectare (ha) of utilised agricultural area. Among EU countries, the density ranged from 0.2 LSU/ha in Latvia and Bulgaria to 3.3 LSU/ha in the Netherlands and Malta. Between 2010 to 2023, livestock densities in most EU countries decreased. The sharpest rate of decline was in Croatia (-40%). The main exceptions were in Ireland (+13%), Cyprus (+9%), and Greece (+7%). In 2023, nearly half of the EU’s livestock (measured in livestock units) were cattle, 27% were pigs, and 18% were poultry. The share of the EU's farms that had livestock declined from 54% in 2010 to 46% in 2023. Livestock density index, 2020
''Source'': Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistical-atlas/?mids=Roads,EURONYM,BORDERS,LIVESTOCK2&o=1,1,0.7,1&ch=CH_CENSUS_POP,LIVESTOCK¢er=52.13099,14.73974,4.349410035507113&tab=LayerControl&style=gridviz/farm-statistics/livestock/livestock-density-index&bl=true&mpc=1&lcis=LIVESTOCK2& Statistical Atlas] This article provides data on the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] [[Glossary:Agri-environmental indicator (AEI)|agri-environmental indicator]] '''[[Glossary:Livestock_pattern|livestock patterns]]'''. It consists of an overview of data, complemented by information needed to interpret these data. The indicator on livestock patterns is part of a [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators set of indicators] providing a comprehensive picture of the integration of environmental concerns into the [[Glossary:Common_agricultural_policy_(CAP)|Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)]]. Livestock patterns are defined as trends in the share of major livestock types ([[Glossary:Cattle|cattle]], [[Glossary:Sheep|sheep]], [[Glossary:Goat|goats]], [[Glossary:Pig|pigs]], and [[Glossary:Poultry|poultry]]) and in the density of [[Glossary:Livestock_unit_(LSU)|livestock units (LSU)]] on [[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|utilised agricultural area (UAA)]]. === Livestock density at EU level in 2023=== The total [[Glossary:Livestock_density_index|livestock density index]] gives an indication of the pressure that livestock farming places on the environment. In 2023, the total livestock density in the EU was 0.7 livestock units (LSU) per hectare of UAA. This was lower than the corresponding ratio from the Agricultural Census of 2010 (0.8 LSU/ha). The [[Glossary:Grazing_livestock_density_index|grazing livestock density index]] gives an indication of the environmental pressure of livestock grazing on [[Glossary:Fodder_area|fodder area]], which consists of fodder crops grown on [[Glossary:Arable_land|arable land]] and of [[Glossary:Permanent_grassland|permanent grassland]]. The livestock counted as grazing animals are cattle, sheep, and goats. For the EU as a whole, the grazing livestock density in 2023 was 1.2 LSU of grazing livestock per hectare of fodder area (Figure 1).
[[Image:F1 Total livestock density and grazing livestock density (livestock units per hectare, 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Livestock density and grazing livestock density, 2023
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_lskds__custom_22397357/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=35730997-c0aa-42a6-8997-66087e89ce89&c=1786951732000 ef_fsi_lskds]), and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_grds__custom_22397355/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=17a56606-2bd4-481c-ba8b-0daf10bec60c&c=1786951764000 ef_fsi_grds])|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing the total livestock density and grazing livestock density as livestock units per hectare in 2023, for the EU, EU countries and Norway. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Livestock density at country level in 2023 === '''The Netherlands and Malta had the highest livestock densities among EU countries''' Three countries had much higher total livestock densities than any others (see Figure 1). The highest total livestock densities among EU countries in 2023 were in the Netherlands and Malta (both 3.3 LSU/ha), followed by Belgium (2.5 LSU/ha). No other EU country had a total livestock density above 2.0 LSU/ha in 2023. The lowest total livestock densities among the EU countries in 2023 were in Latvia (0.5 LSU/ha), followed by Slovakia and Portugal (both 0.6 LSU/ha). Between 2010 and 2023, there was a general trend of reduced total livestock density (see Figure 2). Across the EU as whole, the total livestock density fell by 7%. A majority of EU countries recorded lower total densities, with the sharpest falls being recorded for Croatia (-40%) and Hungary, Denmark, and Lithuania (all below -20%). However, there were higher total densities in a few EU countries during this period, with the sharpest rises being noted for Ireland (+13%), Cyprus (+9%), and Greece (+7%). [[Image:F2 Developments in total livestock density (% change, 2010-2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Developments in livestock density, 2010-2023
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_lskds__custom_22397480/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=679b1b95-2742-4a1a-b383-aa3b6185278c&c=1786952598000 ef_fsi_lskds])|alt= a vertical bar chart showing the developments in livestock density as % change from 2010 to 2023, in the EU, EU countries and Norway. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Grazing livestock density was higher than total livestock density in the majority of EU countries''' Taking into account [[Glossary:Agricultural_holding|agricultural holdings]] with grazing livestock and fodder area simultaneously, Malta had the highest density of grazing livestock in 2023 (6.9 LSU/ha), followed by Cyprus (3.4 LSU/ha). The Netherlands and Belgium were the only other EU countries with grazing livestock densities of above 2.5 LSU/ha (2.7 LSU/ha and 2.6 LSU/ha respectively). In the majority of EU countries, the grazing livestock density was higher than total livestock density, with the Netherlands and Ireland being the exceptions. The grazing livestock density was significantly higher that total livestock density in Malta, Greece, Cyprus, and Poland.
=== Livestock population structure in 2023 === '''The total number of livestock units in the EU declined by 9.7 million between 2010 and 2023, although the relative structure of the livestock population was broadly unchanged''' In 2023, there were roughly 110 million livestock units (LSU) in the EU. About half (49%) were cattle, 27% were pigs, and 18% were poultry. Despite the decline in livestock units from 119 million in 2010 (adjusted to exclude [[Glossary:Equidae|equidae]] like live horses and donkeys), the relative structure of the EU livestock population in 2023 was broadly the same as in 2010. The highest numbers of LSU in the EU were recorded in France(19.6 million LSU), Spain (15.4 million LSU), Germany (15.0 million LSU), and Poland (9.6 million LSU). These countries together represented more than half (54%) of the entire livestock population in the EU measured in LSU (Figure 3). [[Image:F3 Share of livestock units (% of total EU, 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Share of livestock units, 2023
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c9e2cf75-1816-45e2-996c-db2b28704697?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-17T11:30:13Z ef_fsi_lsk])|alt= a horizontal bar chart showing each EU country's share in the EU's total livestock units for 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Almost half of the livestock population in the EU in 2023, as measured by livestock units, were cattle''' There were more cattle (in terms of LSU) than any other type of livestock in the vast majority of EU countries and they accounted for an absolute majority of total LSU in 13 EU countries. Indeed, national livestock populations were dominated by cattle in Luxembourg (87% of total LSU), Ireland (82%), as well as in Lithuania, Slovenia, Estonia, and Latvia (all about two-thirds of their respective LSUs). By contrast, less than one-quarter of the livestock population in Greece was accounted for by cattle (23%) (see Figure 4). Pigs accounted for roughly two-thirds (65%) of the livestock population in Denmark in 2023 and a little under half (44%) of the livestock population in Spain. Pigs also accounted for more than one-third of the livestock populations of Belgium (38%), the Netherlands (35%), and Germany (34%). As well as in Denmark and Spain, pigs were also the largest livestock category in Cyprus (32% of total LSUs). By contrast, pigs accounted for less than or 10% of total livestock in Greece (10%) and Ireland (7%). '''Poultry accounted for the third largest share of the livestock population in most EU countries, and sheep accounted for the largest share in Greece''' Poultry was the third most numerous category of livestock in a majority of the EU countries. The highest share of poultry within a national livestock population was in Hungary (30%). There were two other countries where poultry represented more than one-fourth of the national livestock population: Malta (28%) and Poland (27%). In 17 EU countries, the share of sheep in the total livestock population was less than 5%. Greece was the only country where sheep constituted the largest category of livestock (40% of the total). The next highest shares were found in Romania (23%) and Cyprus (14%). When looking at [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA countries]], Norway also had a significant sheep population (19% of total LSU). Goats were a relatively small part of the overall livestock population of most EU countries. Only in Greece (14%), Cyprus (10%), and Romania (3%) were the shares above or equal to 3% of total LSUs in 2023. [[Image:F4r Livestock population (% of total livestock units, 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Livestock population, 2023
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_lsk__custom_22397734/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=0653bb04-2386-4dac-bb7f-ed7333975e4b&c=1786953636000 ef_fsi_lsk])|alt= a stacked vertical bar chart showing the livestock populations of cattle, pigs, sheep, goats and poultry as % of total livestock units in 2023, for the EU and EU countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Agricultural holdings with livestock in 2023 === '''About 46% of agricultural holdings in the EU kept livestock''' There were 4.0 million agricultural holdings with livestock in the EU in 2023 out of a total of 8.8 million farms, the equivalent of 46% of all farms. This share was much lower than in 2010 (54%), reflecting a sharper rate of decline (-39%) from the loss of 2.6 million livestock farms than the rate of decline (-27%) from the overall loss of 3.3 million farms (see Figure 5). '''In Ireland, about nine in ten farms kept livestock in 2023''' As many as nine in ten farms (92%) in Ireland kept livestock in 2023, which was a substantially higher share than that of any other EU country. The next highest share was recorded in Austria (72%). These two countries were two of only three countries where the share of livestock farms in total agricultural holdings increased from 2010 to 2023. Luxembourg (71%), Romania (69%), and Slovenia (68%) complete the list of EU countries where at least two in every three agricultural holdings raised livestock in 2023. By contrast, less than 20% of farms kept livestock in some Mediterranean countries, such as Spain (19%), Italy (15%), and Malta (14%). [[Image:F5 Agricultural holdings with livestock (% of total number of agricultural holdings, 2010 and 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Agricultural holdings with livestock, 2010 and 2023
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_farms__custom_22397984/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=5e1e34c2-5f54-452e-8237-385c93b7b9a4&c=1786954763000 ef_fsi_farms]), and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_lsk__custom_22397868/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=dfae7920-69aa-4333-8793-5d7b0fcaf62a&c=1786955067000 ef_fsi_lsk])|alt= a double bar chart showing agricultural holdings with livestock as a % of total number of farm holdings in 2010 and 2023 in the EU, EU countries and Norway.]] '''The number of agricultural holdings as a whole and those with livestock fell sharply between 2010 and 2023 in most EU countries''' In almost all EU countries, the total number of farms and the number of farms with livestock declined between 2010 and 2023. The exceptions were Czechia, where numbers of both variables increased, and Italy, where the number of livestock farms increased. The rate of decline in farms with livestock was faster than the rate for all farms in most EU countries. This was clearest in Latvia, where the rate of decline in farms with livestock between 2010 and 2023 (-65%) was roughly twice as fast as the rate for all farms (-32%). The sharpest declines in the number of farms with livestock were calculated for Bulgaria (-83%) and Hungary (-81%), with the number also more than halving in another 8 countries. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:SE article Livestock patterns v0.1 20260826.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] == Data sources == '''Indicator definition''' Livestock patterns are defined as trends in the share of major livestock types (cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, poultry and rabbits, breeding females) and density of livestock units (LSU) on agricultural land. '''Main indicator''' * [[Glossary:Livestock_density_index|Total livestock density]] ([[Glossary:Livestock_unit_(LSU)|livestock units]]/hectare of [[Glossary:Utilised_agricultural_area_(UAA)|utilised agricultural area (UAA)]]) '''Supporting indicators''' * Number of animals ([[Glossary:Cattle|cattle]], [[Glossary:Sheep|sheep]], [[Glossary:Goat|goats]], [[Glossary:Pig|pigs]], [[Glossary:Poultry|poultry]] and rabbits, breeding females), expressed in LSU * Share (%) of major livestock types (cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, poultry and rabbits) in total livestock population (measured in LSU) * [[Glossary:Grazing_livestock_density_index|Grazing livestock density]] (grazing livestock units/hectares of [[Glossary:Fodder_area|fodder area]]) '''Links with other indicators''' This indicator has links to a number of other [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators AEI indicators] that describe developments in some of the main contributory factors. '''Data used''' Livestock patterns are described on the basis of [[Glossary:Farm_structure_survey_(FSS)|farm structure data]]. Farm structure data are collected from agricultural censuses every ten years and from sample surveys every 3 or 4 years in between. These surveys are conducted consistently throughout the EU under the provisions of [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2018/1091/oj/eng Regulation (EU) 2018/109 on Integrated Farm Statistics], providing comparable and representative statistics on livestock and land use across countries and time, at regional level. The unit underlying the FSS is the [[Glossary:Agricultural_holding|agricultural holding]], a technical-economic unit under single management engaged in agricultural production. A range of different physical thresholds have been used to define the coverage of farm structure surveys, with an impact on the comparability of data across time. More information about the thresholds and their impact on comparability can be found in the background article [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Integrated_farm_statistics_-_impact_of_changes_in_coverage Farm structure survey – impact of changes in coverage]. The implementation of the Integrated Farm Statistics (IFS) introduced a division of the target population into two components: the ‘main frame’ includes agricultural holdings above physical thresholds defined in the legislation, while the ‘frame extension’ covers smaller holdings below these thresholds. In the legislative framework, data collection requirements for below-threshold units vary across time. This variability leads to gaps in data availability for the entire population of agricultural holdings and poses challenges for the comparability of results. To address this issue, an estimation procedure based on imputation techniques applied at the level of microdata has been developed to produce consistent estimates for below-threshold units where data are missing, which have been published in the Eurobase datasets under Farm structural indicators [{{Template:Publication|code=ef_fsi|title=ef_fsi}}]. More information about the estimation of missing data in IFS can be found in the article [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Farm_structure_-_estimation_of_missing_data Farm structure - estimation of missing data]. '''Methodology''' In this article, holdings are counted as [[Glossary:Holding_with_livestock|holdings with livestock]] when they have cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, poultry or rabbits (breeding females). The total number of livestock units (LSU) is calculated as the sum of the LSU of cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, poultry and rabbits (breeding females). In this article, holdings with livestock exclude holdings with zero LSU. The livestock density measures the stock of animals (cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, poultry and rabbits, breeding females) expressed in LSU per hectare of utilised agricultural area. Livestock numbers are converted into livestock units using [[Glossary:Livestock unit (LSU)|specific coefficients]], where one LSU is the grazing equivalent of one adult dairy cow. A livestock unit (LSU) is a reference unit which facilitates the aggregation of livestock from various species and ages. Livestock units are not calculated for bees and other livestock. The utilised agricultural area (UAA) is the total area taken up by [[Glossary:Arable_land|arable land]] (including temporary grassland and fallow land), [[Glossary:Permanent grassland|permanent grassland]], [[Glossary:Permanent crops|permanent crops]] and [[Glossary:Kitchen gardens|kitchen gardens]]. It should be noted that common land is included in FSS in some countries and this has an impact on the comparability of data on land use. More information on this can be found in the background article on [[Farm structure survey – common land]]. The grazing livestock density measures the stock of grazing animals (cattle, sheep and goats) expressed in livestock units (LSU) per hectare of fodder area. Fodder area includes plants harvested green, permanent pastures, meadows and rough grazings, and other root crops n.e.c. === Context === '''Introduction''' Livestock patterns help to interpret the relationship between agricultural livestock production and the environment by describing the types and numbers of animals raised in an area. This article uses livestock density as an indicator of the pressure of livestock farming on the environment. The environmental impacts of livestock farming vary depending on the intensity of farming. Extensive grazing regions support biodiversity, maintain semi-natural habitats and deliver important ecosystem services, whereas livestock production that exceeds the carrying capacity of local land resources may contribute to nutrient losses, air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. Total livestock density, defined as the ratio of total livestock (including battery (indoor) animals such as pigs and poultry) to the total utilised agricultural area (UAA) of a farm, region, or country, provides a proxy measure of the intensity of livestock production. Livestock units standardise different animal species according to their feed requirements, allowing comparisons across production systems. The relationship between livestock and land differs between farming systems. Herbivorous livestock (bovines, sheep and goat) depend to different degrees on grassland and forage resources and are suited to extensive production systems. In 'zero hectare' farms Farms with livestock but no utilised agricultural area., animals (generally pigs and poultry) are kept indoors and fed with specific feedstuffs. '''Policy relevance and context''' The [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy_en Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)] influences livestock systems through a range of instruments that support viable farm incomes while contributing to environmental and climate objectives. Under the CAP 2023–2027, Member States implement interventions through their CAP Strategic Plans, including measures promoting sustainable grassland management, animal welfare, nutrient management and climate mitigation. Livestock density measured by the ratio between livestock units and hectare of utilised agricultural area (LSU/ha) remains an important contextual indicator within the [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy/cap-overview/pmef_en Performance Monitoring and Evaluation Framework (PMEF)], supporting the assessment of structural developments in agriculture and the environmental context in which CAP interventions are implemented. Livestock patterns are also relevant for a range of European Union policies addressing climate change, biodiversity, water and air quality, and sustainable food systems. They provide context for assessing progress towards the environmental objectives of the Commission, including the implementation of environmental legislation such as the long-standing [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/water/nitrates_en Nitrates Directive]. More recently, the Commission's initiatives under the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/water/nitrates_en Vision for Agriculture and Food], including work on the [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/overview-vision-agriculture-food/eu-livestock-strategy_en Livestock Strategy] and the [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/farming/crop-productions-and-plant-based-products/cereals/reducing-plant-protein-deficit-eu_en#protein-action-plan Action Plan], aim to strengthen the long-term sustainability and resilience of livestock production, improve nutrient circularity, reduce environmental impacts and increase the production and use of sustainably produced protein sources within the EU. Data on livestock patterns provide important contextual information for monitoring these. '''Agri-environmental context''' Grazing by livestock has created the landscape and habitat diversity of pastoral farming systems, which remain particularly important in the mountainous regions of EuropeBignal, E.M., McCracken, D.I., 'The nature conservation value of European traditional farming systems'. ''Environmental Reviews'', No 8, 2000, pp. 149-171.. Without grazing by livestock, especially cattle and sheep, most of these valued agricultural landscapes would disappear. Extensively managed permanent grassland with low grazing livestock densities provide habitats for many specialised plant and animal speciesBrak, B.H., Hilarides, L., Elbersen, B.S., van Wingerden, W., ''Extensive livestock systems and biodiversity: The case of Islay''. Alterra Report 1100, Wageningen, 2004.Beaufoy, G., Baldock, D., Clark, J., ''The Nature of Farming: Low intensity farming systems in nine European countries''. London, Institute for European Environmental Policy, 66, 1994.. But low total and grazing livestock densities could also indicate a risk of land abandonment which may result in the loss of environmental diversity, while high grazing livestock densities could indicate overgrazing with increased risks of soil erosion and nutrient surpluses. The total livestock density reflects the pressure on the environment from manure. Exports of manure and manure processing to reduce nutrients are non-significant in most countries and storage capacity of manure is limited Eurostat, [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agriculture_-_manure_storage_statistics ‘Agriculture - manure storage statistics’], 2025 , so increases in livestock units per hectare of UAA lead to increased manure-spreading on the area concerned. Excessive manure-spreading could increase nutrient surpluses. Intensive livestock systems, especially pig and poultry production, are one of the main sources of potential nutrient surpluses, with associated environmental impacts on air and water. A high number of animals per ha could also lead to [[Glossary:Intensification|intensification]] of fodder production and imports of animal feedstuffs to meet the feed requirements of the animals. Such imports are an external source of nutrients and therefore leads to additional emissions of NH3 and nutrient surplus of soils. High total livestock densities are therefore associated with pressure on the environment in general and air and water quality in particular. Low total livestock densities could indicate high specialisation on crop production and insufficient provision of manure, which could increase the need for industrial [[Glossary:Fertiliser|fertilisers]] which contribute to GHG emissions through its production. Storage, management and application of manure also leads to emissions of air pollutants such as NOx and NH3 and emission of fine particles with a diameter of 2.5 μm or less (so-called PM2.5). Release of ammonia from animal husbandry and fertiliser use is a leading cause of air pollution, especially in large parts of Europe Andrea Pozzer et al. , 'Impact of agricultural emission reductions on fine-particulate matter and public health', ''Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics'', 2017. ([http://dx.doi.org/10.5194/acp-17-12813-2017 DOI: 10.5194/acp-17-12813-2017]) Livestock production generates the largest share of food-related [[Glossary:Greenhouse_gas_(GHG)|greenhouse gas (GHG)]] emissionsGerber P. J. et al., ''Tackling climate change through livestock: a global assessment of emission and mitigation opportunities'', Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN, 2013. both directly through enteric fermentation in ruminants and through emission related to manure. Livestock farming is a food production process with relatively low calories or proteins produced per area (as compared with vegetal protein crops such as cereals or pulses). On the other hand, ruminants are able to convert for humans inedible biomass into high quality food on land that otherwise not always could be brought into agricultural production Parodi, A., Leip, A., De Boer, I.J.M., Slegers, P.M., Ziegler, F., Temme, E.H.M., Herrero, M., Tuomisto, H., Valin, H., Van Middelaar, C.E., Van Loon, J.J.A., Van Zanten, H.H.E., ''Future foods: towards a sustainable and healthy diet for a growing population'', Nature Sustainability (in print), 2018.. === Other articles === *[[Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics]] *[[Agri-environmental indicators]]
