title: Agri-environmental indicator - farm specialisation
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the agri-environmental indicator - specialisation. Data from April 2026. Planned update: April 2029. Against a background of falling farm numbers in the EU, the share of remaining farms that are specialised in crops has increased sharply, principally at the expense of mixed farms. 58.9% of EU farms in 2023 were specialised in crop production, 20.6% were specialised in livestock production and 20.0% were mixed farms. The average size of almost all types of farm increased between 2005 and 2023 as farms merged or were taken over. [[Image:Figure_1_Farm_specialisations_(share_of_all_EU_farms,_%,_2023).png |thumb|center|700px|Farm specialisations (share of all EU farms, %, 2023)
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ce5f7141-77e5-4980-aaca-4d011496368c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-01T09:28:24Z ef_fsi_ecsz])|alt= Doughnut chart showing farm specialisations as percentage share of all EU farms for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article provides a fact sheet of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] [[Glossary:Agri-environmental indicator (AEI)|agri-environmental indicator]] farm '''specialisation'''. It consists of an overview of data, complemented by all information on [[#Methodology|definitions,]] [[#Methodology|measurement methods]] and [[#Context|context]] needed to interpret them correctly. The specialisation article is part of a [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agri-environmental_indicators_-_fact_sheets set of similar fact sheets] providing a complete picture of the state of the agri-environmental indicators in the EU. === Assessment === '''Number of farms in sharp decline''' There were 8.8 million agricultural holdings (hereafter named ‘farms’) in the EU in 2023. This was an estimated 5.6 million fewer farms than in 2005, equivalent to an estimated decline of about 39% (see the Statistics Explained article on Farms and Farmland in the European Union for more analysis). Farms can be classified according to the activities that dominate farm income, as measured by [[Glossary:Standard output (SO)|standard output (SO)]]. Some farms earn income from diverse activities (mixed farming), while others specialise in crops or livestock. Farm specialisation describes the dominant activity in farm income: an agricultural holding is said to be specialised when a particular activity provides at least two-thirds of the standard output of an agricultural holding. 58.9% of all farms in 2023 were categorised as specialist crops farms (see Figure 1): 35.0% were specialised in field cropping, 21.6% in permanent crops and a small share (2.4%) in horticulture. 20.6% of the EU’s farms were specialist livestock farms, with specialisation in dairying being the most common type (4.7% of all farms), followed by cattle-rearing and fattening (4.2%), poultry (3.7%) and sheep, goats and other grazing livestock (3.5%).
[[Image:Figure_1_Farm_specialisations_(share_of_all_EU_farms,_%,_2023).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Farm specialisations
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ce5f7141-77e5-4980-aaca-4d011496368c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-01T09:28:24Z ef_fsi_ecsz])|alt= Doughnut chart showing farm specialisations as percentage share of all EU farms for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Mixed farms, comprising farms with crops and livestock or various types of crops or various types of livestock where no one activity provides at least two-thirds of standard output, accounted for a further 20.0% of all farms in the EU in 2023. Some farms (0.5% of the total) could not be classified because they are subsistence in nature or because they produce goods for which no standard output was calculated. '''Number of mixed farms and livestock farms in EU down particularly sharply: specialisation in crops rising''' Between 2005 and 2023, the number of specialist and mixed-type farms across the EU declined. However, the rate of reduction varied considerably. There were 2.6 million fewer ‘mixed farms’ in the EU between 2005 and 2023, equivalent to a decline of 59.5%. There were 1.8 million fewer livestock specialist farms, equivalent to a decline of 49.5%, and there were 1.0 million fewer crop specialist farms, equivalent to a decline of 16.7%. These developments have reshaped the EU’s farm stock. Of the remaining 8.8 million EU farms in 2023, crop specialists now dominate (58.9% of all farms compared with 43.2% in 2005). Conversely, livestock specialist farms (20.6% compared to 24.9%) and mixed farms (20.0% compared with 30.1%) are less common (see Figure 2). [[Image:Figure_2_Change_in_farm_specialisations_(%_share_of_all_farms,_2005_and_2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Change in farm specialisations
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7734c6ee-3caf-4eec-844a-5367020a3a8b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-14T14:47:14Z ef_fsi_ecsz]), and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/88d244c7-b18d-445e-a786-b7f1619c58c6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-14T14:49:30Z ef_fsi_ecsz])|alt= Three separate bar charts with scatter plot showing farm specialisations as percentage share of all farms in individual EU Member States. The columns represent the year 2023 and the scatter plots 2005 in the charts for crop specialists, livestock specialists, mixed farming and non-classified farms. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The loss of mixed farms in the EU between 2005 and 2023 was underpinned by the declines in Romania (0.9 million fewer mixed farms) and Poland (0.7 million fewer mixed farms), although there were declines in every EU country. In 2023, the share of mixed farms in all farms was lower than in 2005 in all EU countries, except for the Netherlands where rates of decline in other specialist farm types were even stronger. Mixed farms represented 41.1% of all farms in Latvia in 2023, the highest share among EU countries and relatively similar to the share in 2005 (44.0%). In some EU countries, the number of mixed farms declined particularly sharply between 2005 and 2023: Slovakia (-91.8%), Bulgaria (-90.9%), Hungary (-82.2%), Lithuania (-75.7%) and Poland (-72.2%). In some of these countries, the rate of decline in mixed farm numbers was far sharper than specialist farms, resulting in a much smaller share of all farms in 2023. In terms of [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage point]] (p.p.) declines, the sharpest falls in mixed farm shares between 2005 and 2023 were in Lithuania (-30.2 p.p.), Bulgaria (-26.4 p.p.) and Slovakia (-25.7 p.p.). The overall loss in specialist livestock farms in the EU from 2005 to 2023 included combined losses of 1.0 million holdings in Romania, Poland and Hungary, although there were declines in every EU country. The share of livestock specialist farms in all farms was lower in 2023 than in 2005 in a majority of EU countries. Specialist livestock farms represented 88.8% of all farms in Ireland in 2023, the highest share among EU countries but down slightly from 92.2% in 2005. The sharpest percentage point (p.p.) declines in the share of livestock specialist farms were in Hungary (-31.8 p.p.), Finland (-18.1 p.p.) and Sweden (-16.8 p.p.). The decline in the number of crop specialist farms in the EU between 2005 and 2023 was less sharp than livestock specialist farms and mixed farms. In part, this reflected growing numbers of crop specialist farms in some EU countries like Croatia, Lithuania, Portugal and Slovenia, suggesting that some farms that had previously been either livestock specialist or mixed farms had changed to specialise in crops. In 2023, Greece had the highest proportion of crop specialist farms among EU countries (80.8% compared with 75.7% in 2005). By contrast, Ireland had the lowest share with only one in every ten farms (9.9%), although this share of crop specialist farms was almost twice as much as in 2005. Within the lower stock of farms, the share of crop specialist farms rose in almost every EU country, the sharpest percentage point (p.p.) increases between 2005 and 2023 being in Hungary (+40.8 p.p.), Lithuania (+39.6 p.p.) and Slovakia (+37.2 p.p.). Only in Italy, Latvia, Austria and Cyprus were the shares almost unchanged, the rate of decline in crop specialist farms mirroring the rate for all farms. '''Farms in 2023 generally larger than in 2005''' Despite the sharp decline in the number of farms between 2005 and 2023, the amount of land used for agricultural production in the EU remained almost unchanged (-0.6%). The average (mean) size of farms in the EU grew from 10.9 ha in 2005 to 17.8 ha in 2023. The average size of almost all specialist farms increased during this period (see Figure 3). [[Image:Figure_3_Average_size_of_specialist_farms_(ha_per_holding,_EU,_2005_and_2023).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Average size of specialist farms
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4562616c-31f1-44aa-9c67-900867281a34?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-15T07:40:57Z ef_fsi_ecsz]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/48554037-93c3-4e46-a2fb-24b35eed9937?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-15T07:43:21Z ef_fsi_ecsz]), and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8d7edb9a-aefd-41be-971c-03ab5cd5990c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-15T07:47:08Z ef_fsi_ecsz])|alt= Three separate bar charts showing average size of specialist farms in the EU in hectares per holding. The charts for crop specialists, livestock specialists and mixed farms have various categories each with two bars comparing the year 2023 with 2005. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among crop specialist farms in the EU, specialist cereals, oilseed and protein crop farms had the highest average size in 2023 (29.8 ha), and this was much higher than in 2005 (20.5 ha). Specialist permanent crop farms (including specialist vineyards, specialist fruit and citrus fruit, specialist olives and various permanent crops combined) and specialist horticulture farms in the EU also tended to be larger in 2023 than in 2005, though average sizes generally remained under 10 ha. Among livestock specialist farms in the EU, specialist cattle-rearing and fattening farms had the highest average size in 2023 (44.5 ha) in 2023, which was about 11 ha higher on average than in 2005. The average size of almost all types of specialist livestock farm in the EU was higher in 2023 than in 2005. Among farm types, field crops-grazing livestock (combined) farms in the EU had the highest average size in 2023 (54.1 ha). The average size of these kinds of farms more than doubled between 2005 and 2023 (up from 21.7 ha). With little change in the area used for agricultural production but falling numbers of farms, the rise in the average size of the EU’s 8.8 million farms in 2023 reflects the consolidation and acquisition of farms. '''Fewer specialist livestock farms in 2023 but with more livestock''' Livestock of various species and age can be aggregated together using the concept of the [[Glossary:Livestock unit (LSU)|livestock unit (LSU)]]. Although the number of specialist livestock farms in the EU declined sharply, the number of livestock units that the remaining farms held increased sharply. This trend was noted for all types of specialist livestock farm (see Figure 4). In 2023, the average specialist pig farm in the EU held 223 LSUs. This was considerably higher than the average of 84 LSUs in 2005. The increases in average LSUs on specialist dairying farms and specialist poultry farms were also particularly sharp. In 2023, the average specialist dairying farm in the EU held 63 LSU, up from 29 LSU in 2005. Likewise, the average specialist poultry farm in the EU held 52 LSU in 2023, up sharply from 19 LSU in 2005. [[Image:Figure 4 Average size of specialist livestock farms (LSU per holding, EU, 2005 and 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Average size of specialist livestock farms
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d8c33e2f-39f0-4bc0-a6d3-c8b765078e7d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-17T10:24:05Z ef_fsi_lsk])|alt= A bar chart showing average size of specialist livestock farms in the EU in livestock units per holding, with two bars comparing the year 2023 with 2005. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''One half of the EU's utilised agricultural area (UAA) was on crop specialist farms''' In 2023, 83.6 million hectares in the EU were on crop specialist farms, 53.5% of the EU’s total utilised agricultural area (UAA). A further 49.4 million hectares were on the EU’s livestock specialist farms, equivalent to 31.6% of the total UAA, with most of the rest on mixed farms (23.1 million hectares, equivalent to 14.8%). At country-level, the share of UAA managed by each specialisation type (see Figure 5) strongly mirrored the number of holdings by type of specialisation. Bulgaria had the highest share of the UAA managed by crop specialist farms in the EU (75.2%). By contrast, Ireland had the highest share (87.6%) of UAA managed by livestock specialist farms. In no EU country was a majority of UAA managed by mixed farms, the highest national share being in Czechia (34.4%). [[Image:Figure 5 Utilised agricultural area (% share of total, by farming type, 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Utilised agricultural area
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4562616c-31f1-44aa-9c67-900867281a34?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-15T07:40:57Z ef_fsi_ecsz])|alt= Queued horizontal bar chart showing utilised agricultural area as percentage share of total by farming type in the EU and individual EU Member States. Totalling 100 percent, each country bar has four queues representing crop specialist farms, livestock specialist farms, mixed farms and non-classifiable farms for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In broad terms, crop specialist farms were particularly common in many countries from Eastern Europe and the Mediterranean (such as Greece, Malta, and Croatia), reflecting conditions suitable for growing particular kinds of cereals, fruit and / or olives. By contrast, specialist livestock holdings were more common in several countries in north-west Europe (such as Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Belgium) as well as Alpine countries like Austria and Slovenia. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:210426 Specialisation statistics 2023SE..xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === '''Indicator definition''' [[Glossary:Agricultural holding|Agricultural holdings]] can be classified according to the activities that dominate farm income, as measured by standard output. Some farms earn income from diverse activities (mixed farming), while others specialise (crop specialist, livestock-specialist). Farm specialisation describes the dominant activity in farm income: an agricultural holding is said to be specialised when a particular activity provides at least two-thirds of the standard output of the agricultural holding. '''Main indicator''' Share of the [[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|utilised agricultural area (UAA)]] managed by specialised farming. '''Supporting indicator''' Number and share of specialised holdings. '''Links with other indicators''' This indicator has links to a number of other [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators AEI indicators] that describe developments in some of the main contributory factors. '''Data used and methodology''' Specialisation is described on the basis of data from the [[Glossary:Farm_structure_survey_(FSS)|farm structure]]. Agricultural holdings are subject to the EU's typology on farming systems. Before 2010 such classification was based on the determination of the [[Glossary:Standard gross margin (SGM)|standard gross margin (SGM)]] of each holding (i.e. its [[Glossary:Economic size|economic size]]). From 2010 onwards the farm typology has been based on standard output (SO). The principle of both concepts (SO and SGM) is the same, only the way they are calculated differs. Data calculated with SO are therefore not directly comparable with data calculated with SGM. For survey years 2005 and 2007 results have been recalculated in SO to allow analysis of key characteristics by farm type or by economic size of the holding across time. The Union typology for holdings is defined in the Council Regulation (EC) No 1217/2009 and further specified in the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2746. This article presents data with the farm typology based on SO. === Explanatory note=== The implementation of the Integrated Farm Statistics (IFS) introduced a division of the target population into two components: the ‘main frame’ includes agricultural holdings above physical thresholds defined in the legislation, while the ‘frame extension’ covers smaller holdings below these thresholds. In the legislative framework, data collection requirements for below-threshold units vary across time. This variability leads to gaps in data availability for the entire population of agricultural holdings and poses challenges for the comparability of results. To address this issue, an estimation procedure based on imputation techniques applied at the level of microdata has been developed to produce consistent estimates for below-threshold units where data are missing, which have been published in the Eurobase datasets under Farm structural indicators [[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/explore/all/agric?sort=category&lang=en&subtheme=agr.ef.ef_fsi&display=list ef_fsi]]. === Context === '''Introduction''' Information on specialisation shows the diversity of types of agricultural production systems and structures. Farm specialisation occurs when a single type of farming dominates farm income. An agricultural holding is said to be specialised when a particular activity provides at least two thirds of the production or the business size of the farm. This can be described on different levels of details; a "Specialist field crop" farm can be a specialist of "cereals, oilseeds and protein crops" or of "general field cropping" For more information on the classification of agricultural holdings by type of farming see the Basic Act, {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009R1217:EN:NOT|title=Council Regulation (EC) No 1217/2009 of 30 November 2009}} that set up a network for the collection of accountancy data on the incomes and business operation of agricultural holdings in the European Community. This is supplemented by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32014R1198:EN:NOT|title=Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 1198/2014 of 1 August 2014}}. The Basic Act is supported by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32015R0220:EN:NOT|title=Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/220 of 3 February 2015}} and by the amending {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R1975:EN:NOT|title=Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1975 of 31 October 2019}} . These two sub-categories can then be broken down further into specialist on e.g. "rice" or "root crops". This article uses the classification of more general types of farming i.e. farms focusing on arable crops, permanent crops, livestock (incl. grazing livestock) or mixed farms. '''Policy relevance''' During the last 20 years average farm size has grown while the number of farms has continued to decrease. This is a structural adjustment which has been driven by the subsidies of [[Glossary:Common agricultural policy (CAP)|Common Agriculture Policy (CAP)]] (proportional to farmed areas), and economic considerations. Specialisation can lead to a higher efficiency in production, supporting an increase in the level of production per production unit (e.g. unit of land, livestock unit, agricultural work unit or capital unit). An indicator of specialisation is the trend in the share of the agricultural area managed by specialised types of farm. It shows whether farming overall is becoming more specialised and which specialised farm types are becoming more important. '''Agri-environmental context''' Farm specialisation towards crops or livestock has an impact on the [[Glossary:Gross nitrogen balance|nutrient balance]] of a holding. [[Glossary:Fertiliser|Fertilisers]] and manure contain large amounts of nutrients which crops use to grow. However, the amount of nutrients a crop can take up is limited, and the excess can leak into water, soil and air, causing a range of environmental problems. The EU has indeed adopted different pieces of legislation which aim at reducing and preventing pollution from, inter alia, nutrients (Water Framework Directive, Nitrates Directive, Air Quality Directive). On the one hand, specialised livestock holdings with little or no crop area or pasture are likely to have a nutrient surplus, as it is not possible to spread all of the manure produced on the farm on crop area or pastures belonging to the agricultural holding without severe risks to the environment. This can be mitigated if the farm is able to [[Glossary:Extensification|extensify]] its production, to export excess manure to neighbouring farms with large crop areas or to process the manure. However, when a whole region is specialised in livestock breeding, manure disposal can be very problematic, as high transport costs may make the transport of manure to other regions prohibitively expensive. Thus manure processing and mitigation measures which act at the source of the pollution can be effective. Specialist crop holdings, on the other hand, may face a nutrient deficit and have to import nutrients. Due to the low availability of manure, regions specialised in cropping tend to rely on mineral fertilisers which are produced with high amounts of energy and contribute to greenhouse gases. If not applied correctly, this mineral fertilisation can also lead to water pollution. Specialisation of individual farms is associated with the intensification of the production and the increased use of chemical inputs (per unit area), the mechanisation and the simplification of landscape. As a result, the specialisation of individual farms considerably increases the pressure on biodiversity, soil, water and air quality. Such negative effects on the environment can be mitigated in regions which have a mix of farms. However, when farm specialisation occurs at the regional level, land use is changed towards less diverse cropping and/or livestock patterns due to more concentration on a limited number of products. The introduction of conditionality requirements under the CAP requires farmers to preserve the soil potential and enhance soil fertility to ensure long-term productivity, by setting minimum requirements with regard to the diversity over time and space in the growing of different crops. In intensive areas, a less diverse cropping/livestock pattern already can cause a loss of diversity in farmland habitats, as well as in associated flora and fauna, crop varieties and livestock breeds, leading to an overall reduction in genetic diversity. However, some specialised systems have positive impacts on the environment if they are able to produce environmental benefits. For instance, extensive cattle and sheep grazing in mountainous regions. The environmental effects of mixed farming are less obvious, but as above, they are mitigated if the farming is extensive. Diversification can improve income security and thus the viability of a farm, by spreading risks over several activities. Diversification could potentially prevent land abandonment in such areas. If one activity fails, say, because of animal or crop disease, other activities may still render income. A specialised holding, on the contrary, mainly depends on a single activity. If this fails, the viability of the entire holding may be at stake. When farmers cease activities in marginal areas agricultural habitats are lost and the risk of soil erosion may increase. [[Glossary:Organic farming|Organic farms]] are more focused on integrated use of livestock and land resources. Through [[Glossary:Crop rotation|crop rotation]], crop diversity and use of livestock manure, natural resources are managed in a more sustainable way than in specialised and intensive farms. The holistic approach of organic farming requires a livestock production related to the land, where the produced manure is used to nourish the crop production. === Other articles === *[[Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics]] *[[Agri-environmental indicators]] *[[Glossary:Farm structure survey (FSS)|Farm structure survey (FSS)]] ===Publications=== title: Agri-environmental indicator - soil cover
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the agri-environmental indicator - soil cover. Data extracted in June 2020 Planned update: 18 December 2026 In 2016, 23 % of arable land in the EU was left as bare soil without any vegetation cover during winter. Soil cover limits the risk of soil erosion, nutrient and pesticide run-off. During winter, almost half of the arable land (46 %) was covered by normal winter crops in the EU in 2016; in the warm regions Cyprus and Malta, the majority of arable land is covered during winter. The share of permanent grassland, a year-round soil cover, increased strongly in Ireland (11.6 percentage points) and Lithuania (6.7 p.p.) between 2013 and 2016. [[Image:Image1_Example_soil_cover_on_arable_land_in_winter.jpg|thumb|center|500px|Example of soil cover on arable land in the winter (multi-annual crops in the front, normal winter crops sown in the back)
''Source:'' Eurostat (Germany/Wassenach, January 2018)|alt= an image showing example of soil cover on arable land in the winter, multi-annual crops in the front, normal winter crops sown in the back. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article provides a fact sheet of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] [[Glossary:Agri-environmental indicator (AEI)|agri-environmental indicator]] '''soil cover'''. It consists of an overview of data, complemented by information needed to interpret these data. This article on soil cover in the EU is part of a [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/agri-environmental-indicators set of similar fact sheets], providing a comprehensive picture of the integration of environmental concerns into the [[Glossary:Common_agricultural_policy_(CAP)|Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)]]. This article reports on [[Glossary:Soil cover|soil cover]] during winter, i.e. to keep agricultural land with a cover of winter crops, crop residues or catch/cover crops. This is important for preventing nutrient and [[Glossary:Pesticide|pesticide]] run-off, and soil erosion. Keeping agricultural land covered may improve soil fertility and help mitigate the effects of climate change through the preservation and increased sequestration of soil organic carbon. === Analysis at EU and country level === '''In 2016, 23% of arable land in EU-27 was left bare during winter''' [[Glossary:Soil cover|Soil cover]] refers to the vegetation cover of the soil surface (in this context, on [[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|utilised agricultural area]]). Different soil cover measures can be used in agriculture to prevent soil degradation. Maintaining a crop cover during winter is one such practice. Normal winter crops, e.g. winter wheat, serve this purpose, as do cover crops that are not planted as [[Glossary:Cash crops |cash crops]] but to reduce nutrient leakage and soil erosion and to provide other environmental benefits. Farmers can also leave plant residues on the field after harvest. Multi-annual plants, which are sown and then cultivated over several years, like temporary [[Glossary:Grassland|grassland]], contribute to a permanent soil cover, as does [[Glossary:Fallow land|fallow land]]. Figure 1 shows the different types of winter cover on arable land for the European Union and the United Kingdom in 2016 as a share of [[Glossary:Arable land|arable land]].In 2016, 23 % of arable land in [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU-27]] was left as bare soil without any vegetation cover in winter. Almost half of the arable land (46 %) was covered by normal winter crops. Cover or intermediate crops, plant residues and multi-annual plants occupy shares of 8 %, 7 % and 8 % respectively in arable land. The [[Glossary:Soil cover|soil cover]] on arable land during winter varies among countries. In Cyprus and Malta, the climate is less harsh during winter and the majority of the arable area is covered by normal winter crops. In Finland, on the other hand, the winters are cold and hardly any of the arable area is covered by normal winter crops. The highest shares of arable land covered with cover or intermediate crops are found in Belgium and Austria, while the highest shares left under plant residues are reported in Estonia, Portugal and Finland. Estonia and Latvia have the highest shares of cover by multi-annual plants. In most of the aastern European countries (Bulgaria, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Slovakia) more than a third of the arable area was left bare in winter. Soil cover was not reported for all of the [[Glossary:Arable land|arable area]] which limits the comparability of the data across countries, for more information see the section methodology under [[#Data sources | data sources]].
[[Image:Figure1_Share_of_soil_cover_in_arable_land_during_winter_EU27_UK_2016.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 1: Share of soil cover during winter in arable land, EU-27 and UK, 2016
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_mp_soil}} for soil cover and {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_lus_main}} for arable land|alt= a horizontal stacked bar chart showing the share of soil cover during winter in arable land, in the EU-27 and the UK for the year 2016. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''The share of permanent grassland in UAA increased strongly in Ireland and Lithuania''' [[Glossary:Permanent grassland|Permanent grasslands]] offer year-round soil cover and therefore reduce the risk of soil erosion. One quarter of the Member States have a share of permanent grassland and meadows in [[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|utilised agricultural area (UAA)]] higher than 40 %, with the highest shares found in Ireland, Slovenia, Portugal, Luxembourg, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, in descending order (for more information see fact sheet [[Agri-environmental indicator - cropping patterns|AEI 10.1 - Cropping patterns]]). The share of permanent grassland in UAA remained almost stable in [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU-27]] between 2013 and 2016 (+0.2 %). In Ireland, however, the share increased by 11.6 percentage points (from 79.0 % to 90.6 %). Also Lithuania, the country with the highest decline in permanent grassland between 2005 and 2010, saw a strong increase in the share of permanent grassland between 2013 and 2016 by 6.7 percentage points. The highest decrease was reported by Estonia with 3.3 percentage points (Figure 2).
[[Image:Figure2_Change_in_share_of_permanent_grassland_in_UAA_EU27_UK_2013-2016.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 2: Change in share of permanent grassland in UAA, EU-27 and UK, 2013-2016
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_lus_pegrass}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_m_farmleg}}|alt= a vertical bar chart showing the change in share of permanent grassland in UAA in the EU-27 and the UK from the year 2013 to the year 2016. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Analysis at regional level === '''The share of maize in arable land remained either stable or decreased between 2013 and 2016 in most EU-27 regions''' Maize has a short growing period and thus a short soil coverage period. In addition, maize is grown in rows with large distances, resulting in a high risk of surface run-off and soil erosion. After harvest in the autumn, the soil is more or less completely bare until sowing maize again or, more rarely, another crop next spring.
Map 1 shows the share of green and grain maize in total [[Glossary:Arable land|arable land]] for [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU-27]] countries at [[Glossary:Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)|NUTS]] 2 level (Germany at NUTS 0Germany is only available on [[Glossary:Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)|NUTS]] 0 level for the moment, but will be updated on NUTS 2 level when data becomes available.) in 2016. The region Provincia Autonoma di Trento in northern Italy had the highest share of maize in arable land (68 %) in 2016, but at the same time a low share of arable land in total land cover. Other regions with high shares of maize (> 50 %) are Alsace in France and Provincie Antwerpen in Belgium. Focusing on regions with large arable land areas (> 500 000 ha), Aquitaine in France and Lombardia in Italy have shares of maize over 40 %. High shares of maize can generally be identified especially in central and eastern Europe, northern parts of Spain and Portugal and the Portuguese Açores. The most northern and southern regions generally have a small share of maize, less than 5 %.
Map 2 compares the change in share of maize between 2013 and 2016. In 108 regions, i.e. more than half of the EU-27 regions, the share of the [[Glossary:Arable land|arable area]] covered by green and grain maize remained stable (between -1 and 1 percentage point difference). More regions (74) reported a decrease in the share of maize than an increase; only 16 regions reported an increase by more than 2 percentage points. The largest decline of more than 10 percentage points occurred in the regions Valle d'Aosta, Veneto and Friuli-Venezia Giulia (Italy), the Azorean islands (Portugal) and Ipeiros (Greece). The largest increase of 5 percentage points was in Centru (Romania).
[[Image:Map1_Share_of_maize_EU27_UK_2016.png|thumb|center|500px|Map 1: Share of (green and grain) maize in arable land by NUTS 2 regions, EU-27 and UK, 2016
(% of total arable land)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_lus_allcrops}}|alt= a map showing the share of green and grain maize in arable land by NUTS 2 regions in the EU-27 and UK in the year 2016. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:Map2_Change_in_share_of_maize_EU27_UK_2013-2016.png|thumb|center|500px|Map 2: Change in share of (green and grain) maize in arable land by NUTS 2 regions, EU-27 and UK, 2013-2016
(Difference in percentage points)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_lus_allcrops}}|alt= a map showing the change in share of green and grain maize in arable land by NUTS 2 regions in the EU-27 and the UK from the year 2013 until the year 2016. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Soil_cover_statistics_2016.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === '''Indicator definition''' [[Glossary:Soil cover|Soil cover]], i.e. when soil is covered by crops, including catch/cover crops, is important for preventing nutrient and [[Glossary:Pesticide|pesticide]] run-off. In addition, soil cover may improve soil fertility and reduce the risk of soil erosion. '''Main indicator''' *Share of the year when the [[Glossary:Arable land|arable area]] is covered by plants or plant residues. '''Supporting indicators''' *Share of arable area covered by the following soil cover types: **winter crops, such as winter [[Glossary:Cereal|cereals]], winter rape, or grass. **cover or intermediate crops, such as lucerne, clover, legumes or grass. These are not planted for the purpose of harvest or grazing, but provide benefits such as reduced nutrient leakage and soil erosion. **plant residues, e.g. stubbles that are left on the field after the harvest. **multi-annual plants, such as temporary grassland or hops, cultivated during several years, or [[Glossary:Fallow land|fallow land]]. **bare soil. *Share of [[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|utilised agricultural area (UAA)]] covered by [[Glossary:Permanent grassland|Permanent grassland]]. *Share of arable area covered with (green and grain) maize. '''Links with other indicators''' This indicator has links to a number of other [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/agri-environmental-indicators AEI indicators] (especially [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Agri-environmental_indicator_-_soil_erosion soil erosion] that describe developments in some of the main contributory factors. '''Data used''' All data (data on soil cover types, [[Glossary:Permanent grassland|permanent grassland]], maize, [[Glossary:Arable land|arable area]] and utilised agricultural area) are available from the [[Glossary:Farm structure survey (FSS)|Farm Structure Surveys (FSS)]]. Countries did not report soil cover for areas under glass or protective cover. Data sources in Eurobase: *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/ef_mp_soil?lang=en ef_mp_soil] for soil cover types, *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_lus_pegrass/default/table?lang=en ef_lus_pegrass] for [[Glossary:Permanent grassland|permanent grassland]], *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_lus_allcrops/default/table?lang=en ef_lus_allcrops] for green and grain maize, *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_lus_main/default/table?lang=en ef_lus_main] for [[Glossary:Arable land|arable land]] , *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_m_farmleg/default/table?lang=en ef_m_farmleg] for [[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|utilised agricultural area (UAA)]]. The legal basis for the FSS from 2010 onwards is {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R1166:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1166/2008}} of 19 November 2008 on farm structure surveys and the survey on agricultural production methods, which repealed Council Regulation (EEC) No 571/1988. The FSS are conducted consistently throughout the EU with a common methodology at a regular base and provide therefore comparable and representative statistics across countries and time, at regional levels (down to [[Glossary:Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)|NUTS]] 3 level). Every 3 or 4 years the FSS is carried out as a sample survey, and once in the ten years as a census. The basic unit underlying the FSS is the agricultural holding. The FSS covers all agricultural holdings with [[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|UAA]] of at least one hectare (ha) and also those holdings with UAA of less than 1 ha where their market production exceeds certain natural thresholds. Although the thresholds for defining an agricultural holding can be different between countries (as high as five hectares of UAA in some cases), it has been ensured that the survey covers 98 % of the UAA and the livestock of each country. For more information see the metadata file [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/ef_esms.htm ef_esms]. '''Indicator methodology''' Ideally the soil cover indicator provides an estimate of the number of days in a year when agricultural land is covered by plants or plant residues. The greater the cumulative soil cover, the less surface run-off is generated, and thus the erosion of soil and the transport of soil, nutrients, pesticides and faecal microbes to waterways are reduced. The degree of soil cover provided by each crop depends on its growth period, its leaf area and how quickly cover is established after seeding. The equal distribution of crops or residues is the determining factor to measure the erosion risk. Summarising the impact of any crop, management system or protective cover depends on how much protection is available at a given period during the year, relative to the amount of erosive rainfall that falls during that period. The report from the research project Diredate [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/agri-environmental-indicators/projects] (a project on identifying data needs to establish [[Glossary:Agri-environmental indicator (AEI)|AEI]]) pointed out that seeding and harvest dates and number of days from sowing until crop is established is very dependent on local soil management and climatic conditions. However, using the precise number of days of soil cover will in general not improve the indicator very significantly. To evaluate the risk of nutrient leaching and soil erosion in combination with soil cover detailed geo-referenced data on soil quality and management are needed. Earth-Observation data also offer a great potential to assess areas with bare soil. Soil cover was not reported for all of the arable area. For example, for areas under glass or protective cover, it was not necessary to report soil cover. Countries however included and excluded different areas of [[Glossary:Land use|land use]] for which soil cover needed to be reported. Also non-response and other issues may limit the comparability of the data across countries. === Context === '''Introduction''' Soil cover, i.e. periods of the year when soil is covered by crops, including catch/cover crops, is important for preventing nutrient and [[Glossary:Pesticide|pesticide]] run-off. In addition, soil cover may improve soil fertility and reduce the risk of [http://eusoils.jrc.ec.europa.eu/library/themes/erosion/ soil erosion]. *'''Cover crops '''are crops grown mainly to reduce soil erosion by covering the ground with living vegetation and living roots that hold the soil. *'''Green manure crops '''are crops grown to help maintain soil organic matter and fertility. *'''Catch crops '''are crops grown to retrieve remaining nutrients in the soil following a [[Glossary:Cash crops |cash crop]] , preventing nutrient loss over the winter. Statutory catch crops, i.e. under sown grass or crucifers sown just before or after harvest and ploughed before sowing the next crop, are included in the legislation in some countries to reduce nitrate leaching during autumn and winter. The monitoring of soil cover: *gives valuable information about trends towards good farming practices, *contributes information about likely soil fertility and organic carbon sequestration, *provides significant information about the risks of nitrate leaching and run-off, *provides significant information about erodibility of soils, *could be improved by information about intercropping and tillage systems. '''Policy relevance and context''' In 2019, the European Commission adopted its communication on [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52019DC0640 The European Green Deal]. It announced a [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/fs_19_6729 Zero pollution action plan for water, air and soil] and a targeted [https://ec.europa.eu/info/horizon-europe-next-research-and-innovation-framework-programme/mission-area-soil-health-and-food_en research mission on soil] under the under the Horizon Europe programme. In February 2020, the [https://ec.europa.eu/info/news/healthy-agricultural-soils-24-eu-countries-coordinate-unprecedented-research-programme-2020-feb-26_en Commission announced] that 24 European countries joined a European Joint Programme on Soil which will be closely aligned with future work under this mission. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0381 Farm to Fork] and [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0380 Biodiversity strategy 2030] develop further on policy actions planned to support soil health and the sustainability of soil and the use of agricultural soils. Among other actions, the Commission will update its [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52006DC0231 Soil Thematic Strategy] in 2021. According to the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Land_use_statistics Lucas Survey] of 2015, 41 % of the EU's total area is used by agriculture. This fact alone highlights the importance of cultivation methods for the protection of the soil resource. Sustainable soil management is an important policy target, because soil is essentially a non-renewable resource with potentially rapid degradation rates and extremely slow formation and regeneration processes. Furthermore, soil available for food production per person is limited. Soil degradation processes such as erosion, decline in [https://esdac.jrc.ec.europa.eu/themes/soil-organic-carbon-content soil organic matter], [https://esdac.jrc.ec.europa.eu/themes/soil-contamination soil contamination], [https://esdac.jrc.ec.europa.eu/themes/soil-sealing soil sealing], [https://esdac.jrc.ec.europa.eu/themes/soil-compaction soil compaction], decline in [https://esdac.jrc.ec.europa.eu/themes/soil-biodiversity soil biodiversity] and [https://esdac.jrc.ec.europa.eu/themes/soil-salinization salinisation] can cause soil to lose its capacity to carry out its main functions. Such degradation processes can result from inappropriate farming practices e.g. low soil cover over winter, unbalanced fertilisation, use of heavy machinery, or overgrazing. Soil degradation may also result from [[Glossary:Farmland abandonment|abandonment]] of certain farming practices, for example traditional [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/agriculture/pdf/BIO_crop_rotations%20final%20report_rev%20executive%20summary_.pdf crop rotation] systems or fertilising with leguminous crops, practices which contribute to the maintenance and restoration of soil organic matter content. In most Member States codes of good agricultural practice aim to improve soil management by farmers. The following policies do not specifically require data on soil cover, but relate to this indicator: *The [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/water/water-nitrates/index_en.html Nitrates Directive] aims to protect water quality across Europe by preventing nitrates from agricultural sources polluting ground and surface waters and by promoting the use of good farming practices (including closed periods of fertilisers application, crop rotations, soil winter cover, and catch crops, in order to limit leaching during the wet seasons). *[http://ec.europa.eu/food/plant/pesticides/sustainable_use_pesticides/index_en.htm Framework Directive for the Sustainable Use of Pesticides]: {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0128:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/128}} encourages a rational and precise pesticide use, as well as appropriate crop and soil management practices . *The [[Glossary:Common agricultural policy (CAP)|Common Agricultural Policy]] (CAP) contributes to preventing and mitigating soil degradation processes. In particular, [https://ec.europa.eu/info/food-farming-fisheries/sustainability-and-natural-resources/agriculture-and-environment/cap-and-environment/agri-environment-measures_en agri-environment measures] offer opportunities for: **favouring the build-up of soil organic matter; **the enhancement of soil biodiversity; **the reduction of soil erosion, contamination and compaction. In addition, the provisions of [https://ec.europa.eu/info/food-farming-fisheries/key-policies/common-agricultural-policy/income-support/cross-compliance_en cross-compliance], notably with respect to the obligation to keeping agricultural land in good agricultural and environmental condition, can play an important role for soil protection. *[http://unfccc.int/2860.php United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)]: Conservation tillage can have beneficial impacts on combating global warming as it can reduce soil carbon losses. '''Agri-environmental context''' Soil is a hugely important non-renewable resource, vital for human and economic health, as well as the production of food. Farmers play a vital role in preserving agricultural soils and can influence its properties through their agricultural practices. Processes like desertification, erosion, the decline in organic matter in soil, soil contamination (e.g. by heavy metals), soil compaction and salinity can reduce the ecological state and, thereby, the productive capacity of soil. There is therefore a close link between soil sustainability, our food production and the livelihood of farmers. Serious soil degradation, which threatens the productivity of the different soils, is widespread in Europe. The soil cover of arable lands with plants and crop residues provides many environmental benefits as it protects soils from erosion risk, reduce run-off of nutrients and pesticides and thus their pressure on water, and contribute to maintenance of biodiversity. The efficiency of different soil cover types in terms of preventing nutrient and pesticide run-off etc. may differ as well as their suitability for various farming practices. Many alternative farming systems, such as low-impact farming and permaculture farming aims to integrate agriculture and natural ecosystems. There are farming practices that boost sustainability, such as precision agriculture, agro-ecology (including [https://ec.europa.eu/info/food-farming-fisheries/farming/organic-farming_en organic farming]), carbon farming and agro-forestry. The Common Agricultural Policy supports agri-environmental-climate measures through [https://ec.europa.eu/info/food-farming-fisheries/key-policies/common-agricultural-policy/rural-development_en Rural Development Programmes] and [https://ec.europa.eu/info/food-farming-fisheries/key-policies/common-agricultural-policy/income-support/greening_en greening]. In the future, support for [[Glossary:Eco-schemes |'eco-schemes']] will also continue. === Other articles === * [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/agri-environmental-indicators Agri-environmental indicators - fact sheets] ===Database=== *[{{Template:Database|dedicated_section=agriculture}} Agriculture (agr)], see: ::*Farm structure (ef) :::*Main farm indicators by NUTS 2 regions (ef_mainfarm) ::::*Farm indicators by agricultural area, type of farm, standard output, legal form and NUTS 2 regions ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_m_farmleg|title=ef_m_farmleg}}) :::*Farm land use by NUTS 2 regions (ef_landuse) ::::*Main farm land use by NUTS 2 regions ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_lus_main|title=ef_lus_main}}) ::::*Crops by classes of UAA in number of farms and hectare by NUTS 2 regions ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_lus_allcrops|title=ef_lus_allcrops}}) ::::*Permanent grassland by NUTS 2 regions ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_lus_pegrass|title=ef_lus_pegrass}}) :::*Management and practices (ef_mp) ::::*Soil cover by NUTS2 regions ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_mp_soil|title=ef_mp_soil}}) === Thematic section === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/agri-environmental-indicators Agri-Environmental Indicators] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/overview Agriculture - title: Agri-environmental indicator - mineral fertiliser consumption
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the agri-environmental indicator - mineral fertiliser consumption. Data extracted in June 2026 Planned update: June 2027 In 2024, farmers across the EU used 8.9 million tonnes of nitrogen fertiliser. This represented a strong increase (+5.8%) compared with 2023. The agricultural sector used 0.9 million tonnes of phosphorus fertilisers in 2024, representing a sharp increase (+7.7%) on 2023. [[Image:NI_Mineral_fertiliser_consumption_in_agriculture_20260617.png|thumb|center|700px|
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4407a328-6777-448a-873b-f18a2c642e95?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-19T12:18:47Z aei_fm_usefert])|alt=Area chart showing mineral fertiliser consumption in agriculture as million tonnes in the EU from 2014 to 2024. The years with the highest and lowest consumption are indicated. For more details see link to dataset below.]] This article provides a fact sheet of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] [[Glossary:Agri-environmental indicator (AEI)|agri-environmental indicator]] '''mineral fertiliser consumption'''. It consists of an overview of data, complemented by information needed to interpret these data. This article on mineral fertiliser consumption in the EU is part of a [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators set of similar fact sheets], providing a comprehensive picture of the integration of environmental concerns into the [[Glossary:Common_agricultural_policy_(CAP)|Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)]].
=== Analysis at EU level ===
'''Mineral fertiliser consumption in agriculture rebounded in 2024''' In 2024, farmers across the EU used 9.8 million tonnes of mineral fertilisers - nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) – for agricultural production (see Figure 1). This represented a 6.0% year-on-year increase, though consumption remained 15.8% below the relative peak in 2017. Please note that throughout the rest of this article, the term ‘consumption’ refers to the use of mineral fertilisers in agriculture. Nitrogenous fertilisers (ammonia, urea, ammonium nitrate) are produced using energy from natural gas, which is closely tied to oil prices. The EU's nitrogen-based fertiliser industry has long relied on natural gas imports from Russia. Phosphates are mainly mined outside of the EU and, therefore, incur high transportation costs. Russia and Belarus are key global producers of rock-based fertilisers (phosphates and particularly potassium). Russia’s military aggression against Ukraine and the resulting sanctions on Russian exports led to sharply [https://agridata.ec.europa.eu/extensions/DashboardFertiliser/FertiliserPrices.html higher fertiliser prices] throughout 2022. This likely contributed to the decrease in fertiliser consumption in the EU that year ([https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52022DC0590(01) Communication on ensuring availability and affordability of fertilisers, European Commission, 2022]). While prices dropped sharply in 2023, they remained above pre-2022 levels. Prices then stabilised in 2024. After 2 years of contraction, the consumption of mineral fertilisers in agriculture rebounded strongly in 2024. [[Image:F01_Mineral_fertiliser_consumption_in_agriculture_20260609.png|thumb|center|700px| Figure 1: Mineral fertiliser consumption in agriculture
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4407a328-6777-448a-873b-f18a2c642e95?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-19T12:18:47Z aei_fm_usefert])|alt=Area chart showing mineral fertiliser consumption in agriculture as million tonnes in the EU from 2014 to 2024. The years with the highest and lowest consumption are indicated. For more details see link to dataset below.]] In 2024, the EUs agricultural sector used an estimated 8.9 million tonnes of nitrogen fertiliser, representing a strong increase (5.8%) from 2023. This rise bucked the downward trend noted since 2017 (see Figure 2). Earlier declines in nitrogenous fertiliser consumption during the 1990s and into the 2000s were driven by key policy changes. These included the introduction of the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/water/nitrates_en Nitrates Directive] (ND) in 1991, the implementation of national action programmes for designated nitrate vulnerable zones (NVZs), and reforms to the [[Glossary:Common_agricultural_policy_(CAP)| CAP]] that decoupled payments from production levels ([https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2019-07/market-brief-fertilisers_june2019_en_0.pdf Fertilisers in the EU - Prices, trade and use, DG AGRI, 2019]). [[Image:F02_Nitrogen_fertiliser_consumption_in_agriculture_20260609.png|thumb|center|700px| Figure 2: Nitrogen fertiliser consumption in agriculture
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5d4596ad-cbd4-4461-9d59-62e6be704bb2?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-19T12:21:49Z aei_fm_usefert])|alt=a vertical bar chart with one line showing the Nitrogen fertiliser consumption in agriculture in million tonnes in the EU from 2014 to 2024. The bars show annual consumption and the lines shows 3 year moving average. For more details see link to dataset below.]] In 2024, the EU’s agricultural sector also used 0.9 million tonnes of phosphorus fertiliser, representing a sharp rise (7.7%) compared to the level in 2023 (see Figure 3). [[Image:F03_Phosphorus_fertiliser_consumption_in_agriculture_20260609.png|thumb|center|700px| Figure 3: Phosphorus fertiliser consumption in agriculture
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ef6b510c-8dca-4b93-a1f3-372b0f13a584?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-19T12:23:03Z aei_fm_usefert])|alt= a vertical bar chart with one line showing the phosphorus fertiliser consumption in agriculture in million tonnes in the EU from 2014 to 2024. The bars show annual consumption and the lines shows 3 year moving average. For more details see link to dataset below.]] === Analysis at country level ===
Note: Mineral fertiliser consumption in agriculture is also influenced by weather and climate conditions. For example, during prolonged and severe droughts – like those in 2012 and 2019 – farmers may have reduced their application of fertilisers in anticipation of lower crop yields. To smooth out these short-term fluctuations and better identify longer-term trends, this article uses 3-year moving averages. When these averages are shown, the year is presented in quotation marks (e.g. "2014" refers to the average over the period 2013-2015). Countries with the highest agricultural production levels and largest utilised agricultural areas in the EU typically use the most nitrogen fertiliser (see Table 1): in 2024, these included France (1.8 million tonnes) and Germany (1.1 million tonnes). [[Image:Nitrogen fertiliser consumption in agriculture (1000 tonnes, 2014-2024).png|thumb|center|700px| Table 1: Nitrogen fertiliser consumption in agriculture
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5d4596ad-cbd4-4461-9d59-62e6be704bb2?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-19T12:21:49Z aei_fm_usefert])|alt=a table showing Nitrogen fertiliser consumption in agriculture per 1000 tonnes from 2014 to 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries and some candidate countries. For more details see link to dataset below.]] Between "2014" and "2023" there was growth in agriculture’s nitrogen fertiliser consumption in nine EU countries (see Figure 4). The sharpest rate of increase was in Romania, though this largely reflects starting from a relatively low absolute level compared with the EU average ([https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2019-07/market-brief-fertilisers_june2019_en_0.pdf Fertilisers in the EU - Prices, trade and use, DG AGRI, 2019]). These increases were offset by the reductions in the other 18 EU countries, including some of the largest agricultural producers. In particular, Germany recorded the sharpest rate of decline in the nitrogen fertiliser consumption (-39.3%). Among other EU countries, the rates of decline in France and Spain were also sharper than the EU average. [[Image:F04_Overall_change_in_nitrogen_fertiliser_consumption_in_agriculture_20260609.png|thumb|center|700px| Figure 4: Overall change in nitrogen fertiliser consumption in agriculture
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5d4596ad-cbd4-4461-9d59-62e6be704bb2?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-19T12:21:49Z aei_fm_usefert])|alt=a A vertical bar chart showing Overall change in nitrogen fertiliser consumption in agriculture as a percentage change from 2014 to 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries, and Türkiye. For more details see link to dataset below.]] The highest levels of phosphorus consumption in agriculture were also for the EU's largest agricultural producers (see Table 2): these included Spain (138 300 tonnes in 2024), Poland (124 200 tonnes in 2023), France (122 700 tonnes in 2024) and Italy (98 700 tonnes in 2024). [[Image:Phosphorus fertiliser consumption in agriculture (1000 tonnes, 2014-2024).png|thumb|center|700px| Table 2: Phosphorus fertiliser consumption in agriculture
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ef6b510c-8dca-4b93-a1f3-372b0f13a584?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-19T12:23:03Z aei_fm_usefert])|alt=a table showing Phosphorus fertiliser consumption in agriculture per 1000 tonnes from 2014 to 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries and some candidate countries. For more details see link to dataset below.]] Between "2014" and "2023", phosphorus fertiliser consumption in agriculture declined in 19 EU countries. The sharpest rates of decline were in Germany, Luxembourg and Austria. By contrast, there was particularly sharp growth in Romania and Bulgaria. [[Image:F05_Overall_change_in_phosphorus_fertiliser_consumption_in_agriculture_20260609.png|thumb|center|700px| Figure 5: Overall change in phosphorus fertiliser consumption in agriculture
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ef6b510c-8dca-4b93-a1f3-372b0f13a584?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-19T12:23:03Z aei_fm_usefert])|alt=A vertical bar chart showing the percentage change in phosphorus fertiliser consumption in agriculture for the average between 2013 and 2015 compared with the average between 2022 and 2024 for the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries, Türkiye and Albania. For more details see link to dataset below.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:20260609 Mineral Fertiliser Consumption 2024 Charts and tables v2.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]]
=== Data sources ===
'''Indicator definition''' Mineral fertiliser consumption refers to the quantity of nutrients - nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) - in mineral fertilisers used in agriculture over a calendar year. '''Main indicator:''' * Absolute volumes (tonnes) of N and P '''Links with other indicators''' The consumptions of nitrogen and phosphorus fertilisers are linked to the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/aei_pr_gnb/default/table?lang=en gross nutrient balances], as nutrient inputs to the soil, as well as other [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators agri-environmental indicators]. '''Data used''' Eurostat publishes data on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/aei_fm_usefert/default/table?lang=en consumption of inorganic fertilisers in agriculture (aei_fm_usefert)]. '''Methodology''' The data source used in the assessment of this indicator is national data. Tonnes of N and P inorganic fertiliser consumption for year t are transmitted annually each t + 1, at NUTS 0 level and (for 11 countries) at NUTS 2 level. It has to be noted that data sources on fertiliser consumption are not harmonised in the Member States (i.e. countries use different sources such as farm surveys, production/trade statistics, sales statistics or administrative records). Therefore, in some countries, official statistics on mineral fertiliser use as such are estimated based on different types of available data. The reference period is the calendar year, however, in some cases countries report data based on the crop year. In such cases, no corrections are currently made. '''Limitations of data''' The comparability of the data is weakened by the lack of harmonization of data sources and (in some cases) of the reference year. Data from production/sales statistics may also overestimate the use of mineral fertilisers due to the inclusion of intermediary goods and of non-agricultural use of fertilisers. Eurostat is working together with Member States to improve the data collection on mineral fertiliser used in agriculture.
=== Context ===
Nutrients, such as nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P), are absorbed from the soil by plants, for their growth. They mainly come in the form of mineral – inorganic – fertilisers, which are widely used in agriculture to optimise production, and organic fertilisers such as manure. Nitrogen and phosphorus fertilisers greatly enhance crop production, but excessive use may lead to losses of these nutrients to the environment, contributing to environmental pollution. N and P behave differently in terms of their availability for loss from the agricultural system. N is highly soluble with limited build-up in the soils, and research shows a positive relationship between application rate and nitrate loss from the soil root zone. P losses from land occur due to [https://esdac.jrc.ec.europa.eu/themes/erosion soil erosion] and agricultural run-off. Historic over-fertilisation of P can build up soil P saturation, in which case even negligible new fertiliser inputs may increase pollution. The intensity of fertiliser use has implications for agricultural production and the potential environmental impacts of nutrient run-off from farmland. Agricultural research shows that nutrient requirements (and hence consumption) vary for different crop types and yield expectations and are influenced by previous land management, soil type and climatic factors. Food production has become highly dependent on mineral P fertilisers. For example, some 80% of phosphorus use is in agriculture. The main source of P in the world is phosphate rock - a non-renewable resource. The majority of phosphate rock reserves in the world are concentrated in a few countries, none of them EU Member States, making the EU highly dependent on imports. Phosphate rock is on the list of [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52014DC0297 critical raw materials] for the EU. It means that phosphate rock is a high supply-risk and of a high economic importance. Increasing the effectiveness of organic fertiliser use will contribute to decreased use of mineral fertiliser since [[Glossary: Organic_farming | organic farmers]] do not apply synthetic mineral fertilisers. Organic fertilisers may consist of manure, composts and [[Glossary:Sewage sludge|sewage sludge]]. These organic fertilisers are important sources of N and P, especially on livestock farms and farms near urban areas. This indicator is strongly linked to the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators agri-environmental indicators]: Gross nitrogen balance, risk of phosphorus pollution, ammonia emissions, GHG emissions and water quality - nitrate pollution.
'''Recent global developments''' It should be acknowledged that the period under review in this article does not consider recent market turmoil. The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, as part of the wider Middle East conflict, has had a direct impact on the fertiliser market. Significant amounts of fertiliser (about one third of global maritime trade), urea, ammonia and phosphates typically pass through the strait ([https://knowledge4policy.ec.europa.eu/node/85089_ga Strait of Hormuz Disruptions - Implications for Global Trade and Development, European Commission, 2026]). This Statistics Explained article therefore sets in place a solid backdrop against which the impact of the conflict on fertiliser use will later be assessed.
'''Policy relevance and context''' Application of fertilisers is a major factor contributing to losses of nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate from agricultural soils into ground and surface water bodies. This loss can occur via run-off along the soil surface or as sub-surface loss via leaching and drainflow. Consequently, legislative initiatives through the [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/water/water-nitrates/index_en.html Nitrates Directive] and the [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/water/water-framework/index_en.html Water Framework Directive] have sought to limit nutrient losses to water bodies through more careful management of agricultural land. The Nitrates Directive included the designation of nitrate vulnerable zones (NVZs), establishment of Code(s) of Good Agricultural Practice to be implemented by farmers on a voluntary basis, establishment of Action Programs to be implemented by farmers within NVZs on a compulsory basis, and national monitoring and reporting. In the Water Framework Directive, an indicative list of pollutants includes organophosphorus compounds and substances that contribute to eutrophication (in particular nitrates and phosphates). Measures suggested in this context aim at reducing the influx of nutrients, such as nitrogen and phosphorus to the groundwater and surface waters and include the reduction of nutrient application, the modification of cultivation techniques, proper handling of fertilisers, and the prevention of soil erosion through erosion minimising soil cultivation. Other agri-environmental policies and initiatives that affect the consumption of nitrogen and phosphorus fertilisers: *In its [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A52020DC0380 Biodiversity strategy], the Commission pledged to act to reduce nutrient losses by 50% and to reduce the use of fertilisers by at least 20% by 2030. This is to be achieved, among other actions, through implementing in full the environmental and climate legislation and through developing with the Member States an integrated nutrient management action plan. *United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change ([http://unfccc.int/2860.php UNFCCC]). Countries report on their progress in limiting greenhouse-gas emissions by submitting annual emission inventories and national reports. The application of mineral nitrogen fertilisers by agriculture is one of the items to be reported. *National Emissions Ceiling Directive ([http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2016.344.01.0001.01.ENG&toc=OJ:L:2016:344:TOC| NEC Directive]). This Directive sets national reduction commitments for the five pollutants (sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, volatile organic compounds, ammonia and fine particulate matter) responsible for acidification, eutrophication and ground-level ozone pollution which leads to significant negative impacts on human health and the environment. Targets are set for the years 2020 and 2030. Each EU Member State is required to produce a National Air Pollution Control Programme by 31 March 2019 setting out the measures it will take to ensure compliance with the 2020 and 2030 reduction commitments. The inventory data can be viewed in the [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/topics/in-depth/air-pollution/national-air-pollutant-emissions-data-viewer-2005-2023 EEA National Emission Ceilings Directive emissions data viewer]. *UNECE Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution [http://www.unece.org/env/lrtap/multi_h1.html Gothenburg protocol]. For the EU Member States, the emission ceilings in the protocol are transposed into the NEC Directive (see above). *Common Agricultural Policy ([http://ec.europa.eu/info/food-farming-fisheries/key-policies/common-agricultural-policy_en CAP]). The EUs agriculture policy encourages environmentally friendly farming practices through greening, rural development payments, and cross-compliance. * Natura 2000, the [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/nature/legislation/birdsdirective/index_en.htm Birds Directive] and the [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/nature/legislation/habitatsdirective/index_en.htm Habitats Directive]. The main purpose of the Habitats Directive is to ensure biological diversity through the conservation of natural habitats and of wild flora and fauna within the European territory, while taking into account economic, social, cultural and regional requirements. Depending on the specific conditions of a certain area, these include measures to reduce the use of pesticides and fertilisers, measures to mitigate the effects of soil compaction, e.g. limitations on the use of machinery or the setting of stocking limits, or measures aiming to regulate the irrigation of agricultural land. Farmers who have agricultural land in Natura 2000 sites and face restrictions due to the requirements of the Habitat-Directive are eligible to receive payments for the management of these sites by the Rural Development Regulation, which helps promote environmental-friendly farming. === Other articles === * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators Agri-environmental indicators - Factsheets] * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agri-environmental_indicators Agri-environmental indicators - overview of articles in Statistics Explained] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture Agriculture (agr)], see: ::Agriculture and environment (aei) :::Consumption of inorganic fertilisers ({{Template:Publication|code=aei_fm_usefert|title=aei_fm_usefert}}) ::Farm structure (ef) :::Main farm indicators by NUTS 2 regions (ef_mainfarm) ::::Farm indicators by agricultural area, type of farm, standard output, legal form and NUTS 2 regions [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/EF_M_FARMLEG/default/table?lang=en (ef_m_farmleg)] ::Farm structure (ef) :::Farm land use by NUTS 2 regions (ef_landuse) ::::Farms and hectares by type of crops, utilised agricultural area, economic size and NUTS 2 region ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_lus_allcrops|title=ef_lus_allcrops}}) ::Farm structure (ef) :::Farm land use by NUTS 2 regions (ef_landuse) ::::Permanent grassland by NUTS 2 regions ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_lus_pegrass|title=ef_lus_pegrass}}) ::Organic farming (org) :::Organic crop area by agricultural production methods and crops (from 2012 onwards) ({{Template:Publication|code=org_cropar|title=org_cropar}}) === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators Agri-Environmental Indicators] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/overview Agriculture - Overview] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-FK-20-001|title=Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics}} - 2020 edition ===Methodology=== *Consumption of inorganic fertilisers ([http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/aei_fm_usefert_esms.htm aei_fm_usefert_esms]) *Farm structure ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/ef_sims.htm ef_sims]) *Crop production ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/org_esms.htm org_cropar_esms]) ===Legislation=== *[http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:52006DC0508 Commission Communication COM(2006)508 final] -
