title: Agri-environmental indicator - soil erosion
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the agri-environmental indicator - soil erosion. Data extracted in June 2026 No planned update Soil erosion by water is a major environmental challenge in the EU, threatening agricultural productivity and water quality. 5.1% of the EU’s non-artificial erodible areas were at risk of severe soil erosion by water in 2023. Mediterranean and Alpine countries remain the most vulnerable, while northern European and Baltic countries generally face lower erosion risks by water. [[Image:Image1_Example_of_soil_water_erosion_on_arable_land.JPG|thumb|center|500px|Example of soil water erosion on arable land
Source: Eurostat|alt= an image showing an example of soil water erosion on arable land. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article provides information on the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] [[Glossary:Agri-environmental indicator (AEI)|agri-environmental indicator]] '''soil erosion by water'''. It is part of a [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators set of similar fact sheets], providing a comprehensive picture of the integration of environmental concerns into the [[Glossary:Common_agricultural_policy_(CAP)|Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)]]. === Introduction === '''What is soil erosion?''' Soil erosion means the detachment, transport, and deposition of soil particles by erosive agents, mainly water, tillage and wind. Soil erosion by water is the most widespread form of soil degradation in Europe. It is understood as the removal of soil by rain fall and can take different forms: rain splash, sheet erosion (uniform removal of a thin layer of soil), rill erosion (formation of small channels) or gully erosion (development of larger, permanent channels). Soil erosion by water occurs mainly in areas with a high rainfall intensity, steep topography and limited land cover. Among the main consequences are a loss of cultivable, fertile soil, the pollution of surface water and possibly a destruction of infrastructure. A loss of soil is irreversible. The area at risk of soil erosion by water is derived from a model that estimates soil loss caused by raindrop impact, sheet wash and rill erosion. The modified version of the [https://web.jrc.ec.europa.eu/policy-model-inventory/explore/models/model-rusle2015/ Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) model] is based on input data on rainfall erosivity, soil erodibility, land cover management, slope length and slope steepness. === Analysis at EU and country level === '''Soil erosion by water in the EU: an overview'''
The EU area estimated to be at risk of severe soil erosion by water reduced from 197 000 km² in 2016 to 190 000 km² in 2023, a decrease of 3.4%. This represents a considerable slowdown compared with the period 2000 to 2016, when the respective area shrunk by 13.4%. The share of total non-artificial erodible land that was at risk of severe soil erosion by water has been slowly decreasing over the last decades from 6.1% in 2000 to 5.3% in 2016 and 5.1% in 2023.
[[Image:soil_erosion_figure_1.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Area at risk of severe soil erosion by water
''Source:'' Joint Research Centre, Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sdg_15_50/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=6c610421-4f4f-4a8f-a350-c1be2399f853&c=1782825967000 (sdg_15_50)]|alt= a vertical bar chart showing square kilometer of area affected by severe soil water erosion for the year 2023 in the EU-27. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
According to recent research, the economic impact of soil erosion remains significant: the cost of lost agricultural productivity is estimated at around EUR 1.3 billion annuallyPanagos at al. (2024),[https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2023.140183 Understanding the cost of soil erosion: An assessment of the sediment removal costs from the reservoirs of the European Union], Journal of Cleaner Production, Volume 434, 2024, 140183, ISSN 0959-6526.. '''The risk of soil erosion in countries differs'''
The risk of soil erosion by water varies substantially across Member States, reflecting differences in precipitation patterns, topography and land cover. A higher risk is observed in areas with high rainfall erosivity, steep slopes and reduced vegetation density. [[Image:soil_erosion_figure__2.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 1: Area at risk of severe soil erosion by water
''Source:'' Joint Research Centre, Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sdg_15_50/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=6c610421-4f4f-4a8f-a350-c1be2399f853&c=1782825967000 (sdg_15_50)]|alt= a map of the EU showing the soil water erosion rate by country for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
In 2023, the highest shares of land at risk of severe water erosion were in Italy (24.4%), Slovenia (19.0%), and Austria (15.3%). In contrast, the lowest shares, close to 0.0%, were estimated for Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and the Netherlands. In absolute numbers, the largest areas at risk of severe soil erosion by water were in Italy (67 000 km2), Spain (40 000 km2), and Romania (16 000 km2). [[Image:Area at risk of severe soil erosion by water (% of the non-artificial erodible area, 2016 and 2023) V1.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Area at risk of severe soil erosion by water
''Source:'' Joint Research Centre, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_15_50}}|alt= bar chart showing the shares of land area at risk by severe soil erosion by water for the EU-27 and Member states for the years 2016 and 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Between 2016 and 2023 decreases were observed above all in Slovakia (from 4.6% to 3.6%), Spain (9.0% to 8.2%), and Hungary (2.5% to 1.8%). Five EU countries saw increases, most notably Croatia (5.1 to 7.3%), Cyprus (6.5% to 7.0%), and Portugal (4.1% to 4.4%).
Projections indicate that soil loss from water erosion could increase by 13.0%–22.5% by 2050 compared to current levels, primarily driven by climate change and increasing rainfall erosivityPanagos et al. (2021), [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1462901121001970 Projections of soil loss by water erosion in Europe by 2050], Environmental Science and Policy, 124: 380–392.. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Soil erosion statistics explained 30 06 2026.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === The numbers are estimated by the Joint Research Centre (JRC) using a soil erosion susceptibility model (the [https://web.jrc.ec.europa.eu/policy-model-inventory/explore/models/model-rusle2015/ modified version of the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) model]). Input data are taken from the JRC’s European Soil Erosion Modeling platform.
Eurostat data that are used in this model are available in [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c32d0d1b-cebc-4772-b681-7475eb559daf?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-24T09:25:14Z Soil management practices by arable land area, farmtype, crop rotation and NUTS 2 region (ef_mp_prac)] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a2ea8354-51ce-4440-9eae-58c133ec6739?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-24T09:25:39Z Soil cover by arable land area, farmtype, crop rotation and NUTS 2 region (ef_mp_soil)]. '''Indicator definition''' The indicator estimates the area at risk of severe erosion by water such as rain splash, sheet-wash and rills (soil loss greater than 10 tonnes per hectare and year). The area is expressed in square kilometres (km2) and as a percentage of the total non-artificial, erodible area in the country.
The land area includes the following [https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/corine-land-cover CORINE Land Cover (CLC)] classes: Agricultural areas, forest and semi natural areas excluding beaches, dunes, sand plains, bare rock, glaciers and perpetual snow. Generally, artificial, sandy, rocky and icy surfaces as well as wetlands and water bodies are not included. '''Methodology''' The data are based on the [https://web.jrc.ec.europa.eu/policy-model-inventory/explore/models/model-rusle2015/ modified version of the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) model]. They do not represent measurements but estimates of the risk of soil erosion by water. The model considers only soil erosion from rain splash, sheet wash and rill formation.
The model considers six main factors controlling soil erosion: the erosivity of the eroding agents (water), the erodibility of the soil (including stoniness), the slope steepness and the slope length of the land, the land cover and management, and the human practices designed to control erosion. The model estimates erosion by means of an empirical equation: Er = R K L S C P Where: Er = (annual) soil loss (tonne per hectare per year)
R = rainfall erosivity factor (MJ mm ha-1 h-1 yr-1)
K = soil erodibility factor (t ha h ha-1 MJ-1 mm-1)
L = slope length factor (dimensionless)
S = slope steepness factor (dimensionless)
C = cover management factor (dimensionless)
P = human practices aimed at erosion control (dimensionless)
For further description of the data, see the following metadata: *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/sdg_15_50_esmsip2.htm Area at risk of severe soil erosion by water (sdg_15_50)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/aei_pr_soiler_esms.htm Estimated soil erosion by water, by erosion level, land cover and NUTS 3 region (aei_pr_soiler)] === Context === Healthy soils play a crucial role in supporting agricultural productivity and food security, but also provide key ecosystem services like storage, filtration and transformation of water, carbon and nitrogen. Maintaining soil health is therefore critical to ensure the continued provision of these functions. Agriculture is negatively affected by soil erosion, but also contributing to it, as land use and land management can be driving forces of soil erosionBorrelli, P., Panagos , P. 2026. [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352340925011035 A data-driven indicator for assessing the evolving impact of the EU Common Agricultural Policy on soil erosion mitigation]. Data in Brief, 112390, DOI: 10.1016/j.dib.2025.112390. The risk can be reduced through good agricultural practices, for example reduced tillage, preserving plant residues, planting winter crops, stone walls, grass margins and contour farming. Soil erosion by water is one of the most widespread forms of soil degradation in Europe. It occurs through water run-off, rain splash, sheet wash and rill formation that remove the soil. Other types of erosion causing significant soil loss are tillage erosion (36.0% of total soil displacement), wind erosion (10.0%) and crop harvesting (2.7%)Borrelli et al. (2023), [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41893-022-00988-4 Policy implications of multiple concurrent soil erosion processes in European farmland], Nature Sustainability, Volume 6, January 2023, 103–112.. These processes often occur almost unnoticed without leaving substantial geomorphic evidence but may act as a trigger and enhance soil degradation. The loss of soil leads to a decline in organic matter and nutrient content and may damage the soil structure. As a consequence, the soil is less fertile, and agricultural productivity is likely to decrease. Less profound soils also mean a reduction of their water storage capacity, which may enhance the risk of flooding and landslides in adjacent areas. Soil loss is almost always irreversible. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52021DC0699 EU Soil Strategy for 2030] sets out a framework and concrete measures to protect, restore and sustainably use soils. Building on this approach, the new [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/soil-health/soil-monitoring-law_en Soil Monitoring Law] establishes a common framework for the systematic monitoring and assessment of soil health across EU Member States, aligning soil protection with that of water, air and the marine environment. ===Other articles=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agri-environmental_indicators_-_fact_sheets Agri-environmental indicators - fact sheets] *[https://esdac.jrc.ec.europa.eu/content/soil-erosion-water-rusle2015 Joint Research Centre (JRC) - Soil erosion by water (RUSLE2015)] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sdg_15_50/default/table?lang=en&category=sdg.sdg_15 sdg_15_50 - Area at risk of severe soil erosion by water] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/aei_pr_soiler/default/table?lang=en aei_pr_soiler - Estimated soil erosion by water, by erosion level, land cover and NUTS 3 region] ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database/agri-environmental-indicators Agri-Environmental Indicators] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/overview Agriculture - Overview] ===Methodology=== *Metadata of Area at risk of severe soil erosion by water ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/sdg_15_50_esmsip2.htm sdg_15_50]) *Metadata of Estimated soil erosion by water, by erosion level, land cover and NUTS 3 region ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/aei_pr_soiler_esms.htm aei_pr_soiler]) ===Legislation=== *[https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/soil-health/soil-monitoring-law_en Soil Monitoring Law] - The EU's Soil Monitoring Law in force since December 2025 protects and restores soils, ensuring that they are used sustainably. *[http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:52006DC0508 Commission Communication COM(2006)508 final] - title: Agri-environmental indicator - tillage practices
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the agri-environmental indicator - tillage practices Data extracted in July 2020. Planned update: 18 December 2026 Conventional tillage was the most wide-spread tillage practice in EU-27 in 2016, applied on two-thirds of the total arable area, implying intensive ploughing and harrowing which can have negative impacts on the environment. In 2016, Portugal reported the highest decline in the share of conventional tillage practices in tillable area, Romania in absolute terms, compared with 2010. The majority of tillable area in Cyprus and Portugal was under conservation tillage in 2016. [[Image:Tractor_ploughing.jpg|thumb|center|500px|Tillage practice on arable land
''Source:'' [https://pixabay.com/en/service/terms/#usage Pixabay]|alt= an image of a tractor ploughing. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article provides a fact sheet of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] [[Glossary:Agri-environmental indicator (AEI)|agri-environmental indicator]] '''tillage practices'''. It consists of an overview of data, complemented by information needed to interpret these data. This article on tillage practices in the EU is part of a [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/agri-environmental-indicators set of similar fact sheets], providing a comprehensive picture of the integration of environmental concerns into the [[Glossary:Common_agricultural_policy_(CAP)|Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)]].
[[Glossary:Tillage practices | Tillage practices]] refer to the soil treatment of [[Glossary:Arable land | arable land]] carried out between the harvest and the following sowing/cultivation operation. Intensive ploughing and harrowing can have negative environmental impacts, like [[Glossary:Pesticide | pesticide]] and nutrient runoff, soil erosion, soil compaction and loss of organic matters. In order to prevent erosion and degradation and to preserve soil biodiversity, it is important to reduce soil disturbance through reduced or no tillage. === Analysis at EU level === '''Conventional tillage was the most wide-spread tillage practice in the EU in 2016''' [[Glossary:Tillage practices | Tillage practices]] can be distinguished in three methods: [[Glossary:Conventional tillage | conventional tillage]], [[Glossary:Conservational tillage | conservation tillage]] and [[Glossary:Zero tillage | zero tillage]]. Conventional tillage involves intensive ploughing and harrowing with a tractor, which leads to a total inversion of the soil. Conservation tillage, on the other hand, tries to minimise soil disturbance and leave most of the crop residues on the surface. Zero tillage means that the soil is not tilled at all.
Figure 1 shows the share of the three tillage practices in the [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU-27]] in 2016. Conventional tillage was the most wide-spread tillage practice in the EU. Two-thirds of the arable area was tilled with conventional tillage practices, while almost a fifth was tilled with conservation practices, and zero tillage was rarely applied (left pie chart). A similar picture emerges focusing only on tillable area (right pie chart). [[Image:Figure1_Share_of_tillage_practices_in_the_EU27_2016.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 1: Share of tillage practices in the EU-27, 2016
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_mp_prac}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_lus_main}}|alt= two pie charts showing the share of tillage practices in the EU-27 for the year 2016, the first pie chart shows in arable area and the second pie chart shows tin tillable area. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''Conservation and zero tillage was practised mainly on large farms in the EU in 2016''' The size of the holding seems to influence the tillage practices applied on the land (Figure 2)The following data of some countries and categories is not available or confidential and therefore not included: Bulgaria: 10-99.9 ha farms of 'zero tillage'; Denmark: <2 ha farms of 'zero tillage'; Germany: 0 ha farms of 'conservation tillage'; Ireland: 0 ha farms of all categories and 2-4.9 ha farms of 'zero tillage'; Cyprus: 10-19.9 ha farms of 'zero tillage'; Luxembourg: <2 ha farms of all categories and 2-19.9 ha farms of 'zero tillage'; Malta: medium-sized farms and large farms; Slovenia: large farms.. More than half of the arable land, 54.0 %, belongs to large farms (≥100 ha) and a proportionally larger share (72.3 %) of the area on which conservation or zero tillage is applied is found on these farms. Small farms (<20 ha) managed 16.8 % of the arable land (Figure 2). These farms counted a slightly larger share of the area conventionally tilled (20.1 %), and a smaller share under conservation/zero tillage (6.4 %). Lastly, 21.3 % of the land under conservation or zero tillage was found on medium-sized farms, which manage 29.2 % of the arable land. Of the land managed with conventional tillage, 31 % was found on medium-sized farms.
[[Image:Figure2_Share_of_tillage_practices_by_size_of_holding_EU-27_2016.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 2: Share of tillage practices by size of holding in the EU-27, 2016)
(Size refers to the arable area of the holding)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_mp_prac}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_lus_main}}|alt=a donut chart with three levels showing the share of tillage practices by size of holding in the EU-27in the year 2016, the layers show conventional tillage, conservation and zero tillage and arable area for small farms, medium sized farms and large farms. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Analysis at country level === '''In Cyprus, conservation tillage practices covered half of the arable land in 2016''' Figure 3 shows the share of total [[Glossary:Arable land | arable area]] tilled with [[Glossary:Conventional tillage | conventional]], [[Glossary:Conservational tillage | conservation]] and [[Glossary:Zero tillage | zero tillage]] for the [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU-27]] in 2016 on country level. In addition, it contains the arable area for which tillage practices are not recorded, eg for multi-annual plants. This applies especially to countries with high shares of temporary grassland (eg Ireland, Latvia, the Netherlands, Finland and Sweden)For comparison, figures on temporary grassland can be found in the data set [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/EF_LUS_ALLCROPS__custom_3709235/default/table?lang=en ef_lus_allcrops] in Eurostat's database Eurobase.. In Malta, all arable land under tillage was tilled with conventional tillage practices, while in Cyprus more than half of the arable land was tilled by conservation practices. Estonia had the highest share of zero tillage in arable land (11 %).
[[Image:Figure3_Share_of_tillage_practices_in_arable_area_EU27_UK_2016.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 3: Share of tillage practices in arable area, EU-27 and UK, 2016
''Source:'' Eurostat ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_mp_prac}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_lus_main}}|alt= a horizontal stacked bar graph showing the share of tillage practices in arable area in the EU-27 and the UK for the year 2016. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''The highest shares of conventional practices in tillable area in 2016 were in Malta, Poland, Croatia, Italy and Latvia''' Figure 4 refers only to the tillable area of [[Glossary:Arable land | arable area]]. In 2016, the highest shares of [[Glossary:Conventional tillage | conventional tillage]] of more than 90 % were in Malta, Poland, Croatia, Italy and Latvia. The only countries where the majority of tillable area was under conservation tillage were Cyprus (54 %) and Portugal (51 %). High shares of conservation tillage practices were also reported for Bulgaria (43 %) and Germany (42 %). [[Glossary:Zero tillage | Zero tillage]] practices were generally very low ranging from 0 to 13 % with the highest shares of ≥ 10 % in Estonia, Romania, Belgium and Finland. [[Image:Figure4_Share_of_tillage_practices_in_tillable_area_EU27_UK_2016.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 4: Share of tillage practices in tillable area, EU-27 and UK, 2016
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_mp_prac}}|alt= a horizontal stacked bar graph showing the share of tillage practices in tillable area in the EU-27 and the UK for the year 2016. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''Portugal reported the highest decline in the share of conventional tillage, Romania in absolute terms''' Comparing the change in share of [[Glossary:Tillage practices | tillage practices]] in tillable area in the EU between 2010 and 2016, it turns out that it remained rather stable at EU-level, whereas large differences can be identified at country level (Figure 5). Portugal performed a large-scale conversion of conventional tillage to conservation tillage with a significant increase of +31.8 p.p. in conservation tillage practices. However, in absolute terms, Germany and France reported the highest increase in conservation tillage by more than 1 million hectares each. Romania reported the highest decline in conventional tillage of almost 1 million hectares. On the other side, in some countries conventional tillage practices increased since 2010. This applies on a larger scale to Bulgaria (+15.2 p.p.), Poland (+14.5 p.p.) and Greece (+8.3 p.p.). In absolute terms, Poland revealed by far the highest increase in conventional tillage with more than 6 million hectares. The most significant change in shares regarding zero tillage occurred in Belgium (+9.6 p.p.) and in absolute terms in France (increase of >400 000 ha). [[Image:Figure5_Change_in_share_of_tillage_practices_in_tillable_area_EU27_UK_2010-2016.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 5: Change in share of tillage practices in tillable area, EU-27 and UK, 2010-2016
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_mp_prac}}|alt= a horizontal stacked bar chart showing change in share of tillage practices in tillable area in the EU-27 and the UK from the year 2010 to the year 2016.]]
=== Analysis at regional level === '''Alentejo in southern Portugal reported the highest share of conservation tillage in tillable area in 2016''' In almost half of the regions at [[Glossary:Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)|NUTS]] 2 level, [[Glossary:Conventional tillage | conventional tillage]] was applied on more than 80 % of the tillable area in 2016 (Map 1). Considering only regions with large arable areas of ≥800 000 ha, the regions with the highest shares (90 %) of conventional tillage could be found in Croatia (Kontinentalna Hrvatska), Italy (Emilia-Romagna), Latvia, Hungary (Észak-Alföld and Dél-Alföld), Poland (Mazowieckie, Lubelskie, Kujawsko-Pomorskie and Wielkopolskie) and Romania (Észak-Alföld). [[Image:Map1_Share_of_conventional_tillage_in_tillable_area_EU27_UK_2016.png|thumb|center|500px|Map 1: Share of conventional tillage in tillable area by NUTS 2 regions, EU-27 and UK, 2016
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_mp_prac}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_lus_main}}|alt= a map showing the share of conventional tillage in tillable area by NUTS 2 regions in the EU-27 and the UK for the year 2016. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
The shares of tillable area on which conservation tillage was applied in 2016 varied from 0 % in Malta and Italy (Valle d'Aosta, Liguria, Provincias Autonomas di Bolzano and Trento) to 76 %. The highest shares ≥65 % were reported in eastern Germany (Thüringen, Chemnitz and Sachsen-Anhalt) and Portugal (Alentejo and the island Madeira) (Map2). [[Image:Map2_Share_of_conservation_tillage_in_tillable_area_EU27_UK_2016.png|thumb|center|500px|Map 2: Share of conservation tillage in tillable area by NUTS 2 regions, EU-27 and UK, 2016
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_mp_prac}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_lus_main}}|alt= a map showing the share of conservation tillage in tillable area by NUTS 2 regions in the EU-27 and the UK for the year 2016. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
The share of [[Glossary:Zero tillage | zero tillage]] practices ranged only from 0-28 %. Highest shares of ≥20 % were observed in the [[Glossary:Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)|NUTS]] 2 regions Province Luxembourg in Belgium, Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano in Italy and Helsinki-Uusimaa in Finland (Map 3). [[Image:Map3_Share_of_zero_tillage_in_tillable_area_EU27_UK_2016.png|thumb|center|500px|Map 3: Share of zero tillage in tillable area by NUTS 2 regions, EU-27 and UK, 2016
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_mp_prac}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_lus_main}}|alt= a map showing the share of zero tillage in tillable area by NUTS 2 regions in the EU-27 and the UK for the year 2016. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Tillage_practice_statistics_2016.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === '''Indicator definition''' [[Glossary:Tillage practices | Tillage practices]] refer to the soil treatment of [[Glossary:Arable land | arable land]] carried out between the harvest and following sowing/cultivation operation. Three tillage methods can be distinguished: [[Glossary:Conventional tillage | conventional tillage]], [[Glossary:Conservational tillage | conservation tillage]] and [[Glossary:Zero tillage | zero tillage]]. '''Main indicator''' *Arable areas under [[Glossary:Conventional tillage | conventional tillage]], [[Glossary:Conservational tillage | conservation tillage]] and [[Glossary:Zero tillage | zero tillage]]. '''Supporting indicator''' *Share of arable areas under conventional, conservation and zero tillage. *Share of tillable area under conventional, conservation and zero tillage. Special aspect: *Share of arable area under conventional and conservation and zero tillage by size of holding. '''Links with other indicators''' This indicator has links to a number of other [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/agri-environmental-indicators AEI indicators] that describe developments in some of the main contributory factors: '''Data used''' Data about tillage practices and [[Glossary:Arable land|arable area]] are available from the [[Glossary:Farm structure survey (FSS)|Farm Structure Surveys (FSS)]] on [[Glossary:Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)|NUTS]] 0 and NUTS 2 level. They are not regularly collected. Data sources in Eurobase: *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_mp_prac/default/table?lang=en] for tillage practices, partially for arable area and for size of holding, *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_lus_main/default/table?lang=en] for arable area. The legal basis for the FSS from 2010 onwards is {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R1166:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1166/2008}} of 19 November 2008 on farm structure surveys and the survey on agricultural production methods, which repealed Council Regulation (EEC) No 571/1988. The FSS are conducted consistently throughout the EU with a common methodology at a regular base and provide therefore comparable and representative statistics across countries and time, at regional levels (down to [[Glossary:Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)|NUTS]] 3 level). Every 3 or 4 years the FSS is carried out as a sample survey, and once in the ten years as a census. The basic unit underlying the FSS is the agricultural holding. The FSS covers all agricultural holdings with [[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|UAA]] of at least one hectare (ha) and also those holdings with UAA of less than 1 ha where their market production exceeds certain natural thresholds. Although the thresholds for defining an agricultural holding can be different between countries (as high as five hectares of UAA in some cases), it has been ensured that the survey covers 98 % of the UAA and the livestock of each country. For more information see the metadata file [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/ef_esms.htm ef_esms]. '''Methodology''' The indicator is mature and no conceptual or modelling development is needed. Tillage practices refer to the tillage operations carried out between the harvest and following sowing/cultivation operation. Data on tillage practices were collected for the arable area sown/cultivated during the reference year. The article refers to the area as 'tillable area'. Only the area of main crops is included. Multi-annual plants like temporary [[Glossary:Grassland|grassland]], leguminous plants, industrial crops (hops or aromatic plants) etc. were excluded from the survey and covered separately in the category 'not recorded' (see e.g. Figure 1 and 3), which covers about 10 % of the total arable area. In addition, also kitchen gardens and area under glass or other (accessible) protective cover are excluded, as well as [[Glossary:Permanent grassland|permanent grassland]] and permanent crops that do not belong to arable areas. The sum is composed as follows: ∑ (conventional tillage + conservation tillage + zero tillage) = arable land – arable land not sown/cultivated during the reference year. === Context === [http://eusoils.jrc.ec.europa.eu/projects/SOCO/FactSheets/ENFactSheet-05.pdf Conservation agriculture] encompasses a set of complementary agricultural practices which minimise alteration of the composition and structure of the soil, safeguarding it against erosion and degradation, and preserving soil biodiversityJRC, 'Sustainable agriculture and soil conservation' (SoCo) project, [http://eusoils.jrc.ec.europa.eu/projects/SOCO/FactSheets/ENFactSheet-05.pdf Fact sheet 5 Conservation Agriculture]: *permanent [[Glossary:Soil cover|soil cover]] (cover crops, residues and mulches) to protect the soil and contribute to the suppression of weeds; *minimal soil disturbance (through reduced or no-tillage) in order to preserve soil structure, soil fauna and [http://eusoils.jrc.ec.europa.eu/ESDB_Archive/octop/octop_download.html organic matter]; *diversified [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/agriculture/pdf/BIO_crop_rotations%20final%20report_rev%20executive%20summary_.pdf crop rotations] and crop combinations, which promote soil micro-organisms and disrupt plant pests, weeds and diseases. Conservation agriculture is commonly called conservation tillage. Some specific practices of conservation tillage include direct sowing (also called direct drilling or no-tillage), reduced tillage (also called mulch tillage or minimum tillage), zone, strip or row tillage, surface incorporation of crop residues and cover crops. These are tillage methods that leave most of the crop residues (plant material remaining after harvest) on the surface, which may be also covered by spontaneous vegetation or by sowing appropriate species. The main difference between conventional cultivation methods (conventional tillage) and simplified cultivation techniques is in the lack of inversion ploughing. Furthermore, fragmentation and disturbance are greatly reduced in simplified cultivation techniques. Soil fragmentation decreases from deep reduced tillage to direct sowing (Table 3)Louwagie G.et all, 2009. Addressing soil degradation in EU agriculture. Relevant processes, practices and policies. Report on the project ‘Sustainable Agriculture and Soil Conservation (SoCo)’. Available [http://eusoils.jrc.ec.europa.eu/ESDB_Archive/eusoils_docs/other/EUR23767_Final.pdf here].. The information about tillage practices helps assess other indicators as such on soil cover, risks of nitrate leaching, and organic matter of soils. Any disturbance of soils may enhance turnover of nutrients and thereby increase the potential risk of loss of, for example, nitrogenous compounds and phosphorus through surface runoff and soil erosion. In particular, tillage in the autumn may increase the potential risk of losses during the following winter period. On the other hand, reduced tillage may in the short term lead to increased use of [[Glossary:Herbicide|herbicides]] in order to compensate for the reduced mechanical weed control. Further, reduced tillage may contribute to carbon sequestration in soil and thereby may alter the emissions of [[Glossary:Greenhouse gas (GHG)|greenhouse gases (GHG)]], especially CO2 and N2Oe.g. Six, J., Ogle, S.M., Breidt, F.J., Conant, R.T., Mosier, A.R., Paustian, K. 2004. The potential to mitigate global warming with no-tillage management is only realized when practised in the long term. Global Change Biology, 10, 155–160. Reduced tillage and no-tillage can potentially reduce the need for labour hours by 30-40 and 50-75 % respectively, depending on the geographical location (northern or southern Europe). Similarly, consumption of fuel can realistically drop by 10-20 % (up to 50 %) and 25-35 % (up to 60 %) for reduced tillage and no-tillage respectively. Nevertheless, switching to conservation agriculture might require significant capital investment (for example, in sowing equipment) and greater attention in the use of chemicals (that is for weeding). Furthermore, conservation agriculture is a complex, site-specific farming system, requiring training of farmers and adaptation to local circumstances before maximum economic benefits can be obtained. The practices forming the basis for conservation agriculture are also (individually) used in other farming systems (e.g. conventional, organic)Louwagie G., et al., 2009. Final report on the project ‘Sustainable Agriculture and Soil Conservation (SoCo). Available [http://eusoils.jrc.ec.europa.eu/ESDB_Archive/eusoils_docs/other/EUR23820.pdf here].. '''Policy relevance and context, including Agri-environmental context''' Tillage, crop rotation and soil cover are practices related to pesticide and nutrient runoff, soil erosion, soil compaction etc. The same policies relevant for soil cover are relevant in the context of tillage practices, see the description in the article for [[Agri-environmental indicator - soil cover]]. === Other articles === *[[Agri-environmental indicators]] - online publication * [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/agri-environmental-indicators Agri-environmental indicators - fact sheets] ===Database=== *[{{Template:Database|dedicated_section=agriculture}} Agriculture (agr)], see: ::*Farm structure (ef) :::*Farm land use by NUTS 2 regions (ef_landuse) ::::*Main farm land use by NUTS 2 regions ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_lus_main|title=ef_lus_main}}) :::*Management and practices (ef_mp) ::::*Agricultural practices ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_mp_prac|title=ef_mp_prac}}) === Thematic section === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/agri-environmental-indicators Agri-Environmental Indicators] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/overview Agriculture - Overview] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-FK-18-001|title=Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics}} - 2018 edition *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-FK-19-001|title=Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics}} - 2019 edition ===Methodology=== *Farm structure survey metadata: [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/ef_esms.htm ef_esms] ===Legislation=== *[http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:52006DC0508 Commission Communication COM(2006)508 final] - Development of agri-environmental indicators for monitoring the integration of environmental concerns into the common agricultural policy *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/2393397/2518883/itro_COMMISSION+STAFF+WORKING+DOCUMENT/47021509-d163-4572-aad7-e4bd0aad14ef Commission Staff working document] accompanying COM(2006)508 final ===External links=== *European Commission - [http://ec.europa.eu/agriculture/cap-overview_en Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)] *DG Agriculture and Rural Development: [http://ec.europa.eu/agriculture/envir/soil/index_en.htm Agriculture and soil protection] *DG Environment: [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/soil/three_en.htm Soil] *Joint Research Centre (JRC): [http://eusoils.jrc.ec.europa.eu/ EUROSOILS - European Soil Portal] === Footnotes === <'''footnote text will be automatically inserted if reference tags are used in article content text (use reference icon on ribbon)'''> {{Unit|topic=X_Agriculture}} [[Category:Agriculture, fisheries, and forestry|Agri-environmental indicator - title: Agri-environmental indicators - fact sheets
text:
<highlight>
This article is part of an [[Agri-environmental indicators|online publication]] providing the current state of play of [[Glossary:Agri-environmental indicator (AEI)|agri-environmental indicators]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. It presents the policy background and provides additional information on the setting-up of the agri-environmental indicators. It also contains an overview table showing the 28 agri-environmental indicators within the so-called 'DPSIR' (Driving force — Pressure — State — Impact — Response) framework and provides links to the fact sheets for each  indicator. 
</highlight>

<articlecontent>
<sesection>
=== Policy background  ===

*Since the entry into force of the [[Glossary:Treaty on European Union|Treaty on European Union]] in 1993, there has been a legal obligation for the European Union to take account of environmental protection requirements when drawing up and implementing EU policies.

*In the early 2000s, the Commission issued a communication [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:52000DC0020:EN:NOT COM final 0020/2000], which defined the objectives for monitoring the integration of environmental concerns in the agriculture policy and identified a set of 35 agri-environmental indicators. It was followed a year later by [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52001DC0144&rid=1 COM final 0144/2001], which identified concepts and potential data sources and described further necessary work.

*Agriculture is a fully  European policy area where the instruments of the [[Glossary:Common agricultural policy (CAP)|common agricultural policy (CAP)]] are decided by the [[Glossary:Council of the European Union|Council of the European Union]] and the [[Glossary:European Parliament (EP) | European Parliament (EP)]]. Sustainable management of natural resources is one of the three priorities of the CAP 2014-2020.
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Establishing agri-environmental indicators  ===

The IRENA operation (Indicator Reporting on the Integration of Environmental Concerns into Agriculture Policy) was launched in 2002 to further develop agri-environmental indicators for monitoring the integration of environmental concerns into the common agricultural policy (CAP). It was a joint exercise between DG Agriculture and Rural Development, DG Environment, Eurostat and DG Joint Research Centre, and the [[Glossary:European Environment Agency (EEA)|European Environment Agency (EEA)]]. The purpose of the IRENA operation was to develop and compile for [[Glossary:EU-15|EU-15]] the set of [https://circabc.europa.eu/faces/jsp/extension/wai/navigation/container.jsp?FormPrincipal:_idcl=FormPrincipal:_id1&FormPrincipal_SUBMIT=1&id=bb6b7ed6-1616-4a81-9c8b-8c9212ed9b50&javax.faces.ViewState=j1IuGCuyQwK6b%2BLErF463ISaZW6VCoTG6ptwpa0yApaiOWEKyKg9Clm%2BVf3a8q8Iq%2FC6VZ9pF1HRsG8ynit9T0ap%2F7%2Bs5fGJqeYzLLveopV59OK%2B3%2FefFzKf98s8HPCNmKf5l8jR%2Fcw6SvKP69y%2Fp8aQBn8ezC9rRCryZA%3D%3D 35 indicators] defined in [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:52000DC0020:EN:NOT COM final 0020/2000] and [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52001DC0144&rid=1 COM final 0144/2001] at the appropriate geographical levels and, as far as possible, on the basis of existing data sources. 

The [http://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/eea_report_2005_6 final report] presented agri-environmental relationships using the Driving force — Pressure — State — Impact — Response (DPSIR) model. Interlinkages were shown in agri-environmental storylines in relation to major agri-environmental themes: water, land use and soil, climate change and air quality, and biodiversity and landscape. At the centre of the DPSIR framework is the current '''state''' of the agricultural environment and how this has changed over time. State indicators bring to the fore any undesirable changes which need to be combated, (for example, nitrate or pesticide concentrations in water) as well as particularly desirable states which should be preserved (for example, many agricultural landscapes or valuable habitats). The second step is to identify the '''pressures''' which have brought about undesirable change and environmental benefits resulting from farming which have helped to preserve or enhance the environment. These have, respectively, a negative and positive '''impact''' on the environment.The third step is to link these pressures and processes to the '''driving forces '''in the economy (farmers' activities, which are themselves driven by market forces), as it is these driving forces that are directly influenced by agricultural policy, and it is here where the integration process is applied. Finally, it is necessary to monitor how society's '''response''' to these issues is working. Are agri-environmental measures having the desired effect, are they responding quickly enough, or are they producing unforeseen problems? This framework allows the relevant questions to be posed, and the information needed to answer these questions, i.e. the indicators, to be identified. The IRENA operation led to substantial progress in the development of agri-environmental indicators at EU-15 level, and particularly regarding concepts, identification of data sources and compilation of data sets. 

Commission Communication [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:52006DC0508:EN:NOT COM final 0508/2006] addressed outstanding issues and identified 28 agri-environmental indicators (AEI) to monitor the integration of environmental concerns into the common agricultural policy. To aid the Commission in setting up a permanent and stable arrangement for the indicator system a project called "DireDate" was financed, followed by other [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agri-environmental-indicators/links projects ]  both at Member State and EU-level.  

Despite efforts over the last >10 years, several limitations remain in a number of indicators: 

*deficiencies in the data sets related to certain indicators, in terms of harmonisation (e.g. farm management), or [[Glossary:Geographical_coverage|geographical coverage]] (e.g. water quality)
*data availability (e.g. genetic diversity or pesticide risk)
*some indicators still require further conceptual improvement (e.g. high nature value farmland areas).


These limitations do not invalidate the usefulness of the indicators for agri-environmental analysis. Rather, they suggest that further work is needed on these indicators to improve the concepts and methodological approaches, improve data collection methods, develop new data sets where necessary, and improve/validate existing modelling tools.
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Fact sheets  ===

The fact sheets for the 28 AEI as listed in [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:52006DC0508:EN:NOT COM final 0508/2006]. The table below shows the 28 AEI within the DPSIR framework and provides a link to a fact sheets for each of these indicators.

title: Agricultural land prices and rents - statistics
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of agricultural land prices and rents between EU countries,. Data extracted in January 2026 Planned article update: January 2027 In 2024, the average price of one hectare of arable land in the EU was €15 224 In 2024, renting one hectare of arable land or permanent grassland was most expensive in the Netherlands (an average of €941) Each factor of production used in agriculture typically earns a type of income; labour receives a wage, entrepreneurs profit, capital earns interest and land generates rental income. Understanding land prices and rents is also a key element in understanding the future prospects of agriculture. The level of land prices depends on a number of factors; these include national factors (such as laws), regional factors (such as climate and proximity to networks) and localised productivity factors (such as soil quality, slope or drainage). The market forces of supply and demand, including the influence of foreign ownership rules, can also influence the price of agricultural land. Competition for land comes not only from farmers but also from others planning to use land for purposes other than agriculture. As such, it is interesting to see prices at a point in time and note the developments in prices for regions over time. This article analyses the differences in agricultural land prices and rents between EU countries. It presents data from the most recent data collection. === Agricultural land prices in the EU === In 2024, the average price of one hectare of [[Glossary:Arable land|arable land]] in the EU was €15 224. This average price was 38 times more than the average annual rental price of €403 per hectare of arable land. Among the 23 EU countries for which 2024 data are available, the price of one hectare of arable land varied from a low of €4 825 on average in Latvia to €201 263 on average in Malta. Data for Malta reflect the limited availability of agricultural land and the pressure for alternative uses, resulting in prices higher than in other EU countries (see Figure 1). At regional level, the highest prices for arable land were in the Dutch region of Flevoland (an average €187 109 per hectare). By contrast, the lowest was in the Swedish region of Övre Norrland (an average €1 933 per hectare). [[Image:Average prices of arable land in the EU, 2024 (€ per hectare) V2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Average prices of arable land in the EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/apri_lprc__custom_19818122/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=dab6725d-b55d-4c23-81f7-412707aae7bc&c=1769509105532 (apri_lprc)]|alt=Scatter chart showing average prices of arable land as euros per hectare in individual EU countries. Each country has three scatter plots representing highest regional price, national average and lowest regional price for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Buying arable land was usually more expensive than buying [[Glossary:Permanent grassland|permanent grassland]]. The average price of one hectare of arable land in the EU was €15 224 whereas the average price of one hectare of permanent grassland in 2024 was €11 753. Arable land was more expensive than permanent grassland in all countries, except Luxembourg, and almost all regions. Permanent grassland was cheapest in Bulgaria at €1 877 per hectare in 2024, about 4.5 times less than the equivalent cost of one hectare of arable land (at €8 679). The percentage difference between the price of permanent grassland and arable land was widest in the region of Voreio Aigaio in Greece (twenty-fold difference between €1 775 per hectare of permanent grassland and €36 968 per hectare of arable land). In terms of absolute value, it was widest in Wien (the difference between €56 700 per hectare of permanent grassland and the average €180 000 per hectare of arable land). === Agricultural land rental prices === Not all land is owned by the farmer working it. Many farmers rent their land, as either a short or long-term business decision. The cost of renting land is another factor that farmers have to absorb in their business. Mirroring the variation in agricultural land prices, annual rental prices of one hectare of agricultural land (average of arable land and permanent grassland) also vary starkly between countries and regions within countries. As with agricultural land prices, there were also considerable variations in land rents between countries and regions. Within the EU, the average rental price of arable land and / or permanent grassland was €295 per hectare in 2024. Renting one hectare of arable land and/or permanent grassland in 2024 was most expensive in the Netherlands (€941 on average), followed by Denmark (€580) and Greece (€509). It was lowest in Slovakia (€69 on average), Croatia (€76) and Malta (€92), the latter reflecting a government-imposed cap under the ''Agricultural Leases (Reletting) Act''. Among the EU's regions, renting one hectare of arable land and/or permanent grassland in 2024 was most expensive in the Spanish region of Canarias (€2 785 on average), followed by Flevoland (€1 825) and North Brabant (€1 098) in the Netherlands. By contrast, rental prices were lowest in Mellersta Norrland and Övre Norrland in Sweden (both €36 per hectare on average in 2024), followed by Stredné Slovensko (€43 per hectare) and Východné Slovensko (€44 per hectare) in Slovakia. Permanent grasslands are the main agricultural land use in those regions. Among the EU countries that reported separate rental prices for arable land and permanent grassland, renting permanent grassland was always cheaper than renting arable land. The rent of one hectare of permanent grassland in 2024 ranged from a low of €38 on average in Slovakia to €407 on average in Ireland. The equivalent range for arable land was from €82 on average in Slovakia to €540 on average in Ireland. [[Image:Average rental prices of arable land and permanent grassland in the EU, 2024 (€ per hectare)V1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Average rental prices of arable land and permanent grassland in the EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/apri_lrnt__custom_19817574/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=7a30c227-8ff7-4d87-b862-afdf14228e8c&c=1769507786924 (apri_lrnt)]|alt= Scatter chart showing average rental prices of arable land or permanent grassland in the EU as euros per hectare in individual EU countries. Each country has three scatter plots representing highest regional price, national average and lowest regional price for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Data sources === Agricultural land prices and rents are now being collected on an annual basis and a common methodology has been developed as a basis for comparable statistics. These datasets were made available publicly in 2018. '''Key indicators and concepts''' Agricultural land prices refer to the price of one hectare of free agricultural land without buildings or plantations during the reference period (a calendar year). Depending on the EU country, these prices can be collected from the owner of the agricultural land who is selling (selling prices) or from the physical person/legal person/legal entity who is purchasing the land for agricultural purposes (purchase prices). Agricultural land rents refer to the price of renting one hectare of agricultural land without buildings or plantations for 1 year. The renting price should be collected from the agricultural holdings renting the land for agricultural purposes (renting price paid). The reference period is the calendar year. The prices and rents expressed in national currency are converted into euro by using the corresponding annual exchange rate, to allow comparisons among EU countries. Eurostat has estimated the EU average land price and rent as weighted averages based solely on data from the 24 EU countries, for which data are available. Weighting was based on land areas from the 2023 Integrated Farm Structure Survey. Until 2024, data collection was conducted on a voluntary basis, which accounts for the partial coverage across EU countries. In the context of the SAIO Regulation, Eurostat adapted the methodology used to calculate EU aggregates, in particular in the estimations of the weighting values. To avoid a break in the time series, EU aggregates were subsequently recalculated for the entire period using this new methodology. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Land prices and rents 01 2026..xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Context=== '''''Agricultural land values and rents''''' Policymakers follow developments in the land market to evaluate the impact of policies on it. Statistics on land prices and rents, expressed as absolute prices, facilitate an insight into various key issues (sales versus rental markets, effect of new users, CAP changes, environmental pressures, etc.). In addition, absolute prices help to properly assess how the farmland value relates to agricultural income and hence whether farms remain viable given changes in agricultural land prices and rents. Furthermore, regional data enable the identification of the situations where land prices are a driving factor in terms of structural change. These policy requirements have driven the need for reliable and comparable data on agricultural land prices and rents. === Other articles === *[[Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database Agriculture (agri)], see: :Land prices and rents (apri_lpr) ::Agricultural land renting prices for one year by region (apri_lrnt) ::Agricultural land prices by region (apri_lprc) ::Agricultural land renting prices for one year by region - historical data (until 2009) (apri_lrnt_h) ::Agricultural land prices by region - historical data (until 2009) (apri_lprc_h) ===Dedicated section=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/overview Agriculture] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-049|title=Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics — 2025 edition}} (Statistical book) ===Methodology=== *[[Media:Apri lpr esms an4.pdf|Handbook on statistics on agricultural land prices and rents, 2020 edition]] ===Legislation=== EU agricultural land price and rent statistics are based on an [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/749240/9456301/ESSC_2018-38-09-LandPricesRents.pdf/5f196760-b1c6-481b-bfc4-9b24610a0860 ESS agreement of October 2018] between Eurostat and the Member States. {{Unit|topic=X_Agriculture}} [[Category:Agriculture, fisheries, and forestry|Agricultural land prices and rents - statistics]] [[Category:Agriculture|Agricultural land prices and rents - statistics]] [[Category:Farm structure|Agricultural land prices and rents - statistics]] [[Category:Statistical article|Agricultural land prices and rents - statistics]] [[Category:January2027|Agricultural land prices and rents - statistics]]
