title: Agriculture statistics - family farming in the EU
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of agriculture statistics of family farming in the EU Data extracted in October 2023 Planned article update: June 2029 Family farms accounted for about 9 in every 10 of the EU’s 8.8 million farms in 2023. Family farms were much smaller on average than non-family farms in 2023 (about 11 hectares of utilised agricultural area compared with about 89 hectares). Family farms worked a majority of the EU’s utilised agricultural area (about 56% of the 156.2 million hectares used) and accounted for a majority of the total agricultural labour force (about 69%). [[Image:Farms in the EU, 2023 (by family, non-family type) v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/613d4272-3ef0-4d48-8ed2-0521955555e4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T14:17:08Z ef_lf_fam])|alt= Horizontal queued bar chart showing the number of farms in individual EU Member States. Each country has three queues representing farms with only family workers, farms where family workers make up more than 50 percent and non-family farms for the year 2023. Note should taken that data for Bulgaria, Greece, Italy and Poland relate to 2020 instead of 2023. Data are not shown for Spain, Lithuania and Slovenia because they are not comparable with other EU countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The term 'family farm' in this article is based on the United Nations' [[Glossary:Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) |Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO)]] [https://www.fao.org/world-agriculture-watch/tools-and-methodologies/definitions-and-operational-perspectives/family-farms/en/ definition ]as any farm under family ownership where 50 % or more of the agricultural labour force was provided by [[Glossary:Farm labour force - family labour |family workers]]. In other words, a family farm is managed and operated by a household where the labour is largely supplied by that household. A more detailed division of family farms is made in this article, between those farms where labour was provided exclusively by the family (farms with only family workers) and those where 50% or more (but not 100%) of the labour force was family workers. This article analyses the importance of family farming in the EU and the prevalence of family farms in the different EU countries. It presents data from the most recent [[Glossary:Farm structure survey (FSS)|farm structure survey (FSS)]]. ===Structural profile of farms at EU level === '''''Family farms account for slightly more than 9 in every 10 farms in the EU ''''' There were 8.8 million farms in the EU in 2023, the vast majority of which (an estimated 91%) can be classified as family farms that operate as family-run businesses in which the farm is passed down through the generations. Indeed, family farms dominate the structure of EU agriculture in terms of their numbers, their contribution to agricultural employment and, to a lesser degree, the area of land that they cultivate and the value of the [[Glossary:Standard output|output]] they generate. Just over one half of farms (an estimated 51%) in the EU were farmed completely by the holder and family members in 2023. In addition, about another 40% of all EU farms were farmed by family labour that accounted for at least one half of all labour. Non-family farms accounted for only about 9% of all farms in the EU in 2023 (see Figure 1). [[File:F1 Family farming in the EU, 2023 (% shares of EU totals).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Family farming in the EU, 2023
''Source:'' ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/613d4272-3ef0-4d48-8ed2-0521955555e4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T14:17:08Z ef_lf_fam])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing estimated EU percentage shares of family farming. Five columns represent agricultural holdings, utilised agricultural area, total labour force, livestock units and standard output. Totalling 100 percent, each column contains three stacks representing farms with only family workers, farms where family workers make up more than 50 percent and non-family farms for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The characterisation of agriculture in the EU as still being founded on family farms is further supported by their shares of a number of key land, labour, capital and economic variables; they accounted for a majority of the [[Glossary:utilised agricultural area (UAA)|utilised agricultural area (UAA)]] in 2023 (about 56% of the 156.2 million hectares used), and a majority of the total agricultural labour force (about 69%), as well as almost one half of [[Glossary:Livestock unit|livestock units]] and standard output. '''''Non-family farms account for disproportionately high share of land, labour, capital and economic output''''' Even though non-family farms only accounted for about 9% of all farms in the EU in 2023, they accounted for much higher shares of the amount of land used for agricultural production (about 44%), of the total labour force (about 31%), of livestock units (about 51%) and of standard output (about 53%). '''''Family farms: many but relatively small''''' Although family farms were common in the EU, they were consistently smaller than non-family farms. Non-family farms tended to be larger than family farms in terms of the average amount of land used for agricultural production and, as a result, the average amount of livestock held per farm, the average size of the labour force and the economic size of the farm. In 2023, the average (mean) size of a farm in the EU was 17.8 hectares (ha) in 2023. However, this figure masks considerable differences between family (about an average 11 ha) and non-family farms (about an average 89 ha). Underlining this apparent dichotomy in the structure of farming in the EU, non-family farms had many more livestock units (an estimated 67 more units) than family farms, used the equivalent of many more people full-time on average (an estimated two and a half people more) and had an economic output that was multiple times higher (an estimated 12 times) than family farms (see Figure 2). [[Image:Average size of farms in the EU, by type of farm labour, 2023.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Average size of farms in the EU, by type of farm labour, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat (Agricultural Census, 2020)|alt= Four separate horizonal bar charts showing average size of farms in the EU by type of farm labour. Chart 1, average utilised agricultural area per holding in hectares. Chart 2, average labour force per holding in annual work units. Chart 3, average number of livestock units per holding in livestock units. Chart 4, average standard output per holding in euros. Each chart has three bars representing farms with only family workers, farms where family workers make up more than 50 percent and non-family farms for the year 2020. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Family farms: sharp decline in numbers but changing composition''''' The number of farms in the EU has been in sharp decline for a number of years: between 2005 and 2023, the EU lost 5.6 million farms, almost all of which were family farms (see article [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Farms_and_farmland_in_the_European_Union_-_statistics Farms and farmland in the European Union]). Of the remaining family farms, there has been an apparent shift away from farms with only family workers towards farms where family workers make up more than 50% (but not 100%) of the labour; the share of farms with only family workers decreased by about 11 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] between 2010 and 2023, whereas those where family workers make up 50% or more (but not 100%) of the labour increased by about 11 percentage points. So whilst family farms still dominate the working landscape of farming in the EU, the number of family farms that rely solely on family workers has declined particularly fast. ===Structural profile of farms - analysis of EU countries === '''''Majority of farms are family farms in all EU countries''''' Of the 8.8 million farms in the EU in 2023, just under one third (32.6%) were in Romania (see Figure 2 of the article on (see Figure 2 of the article on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Farms_and_farmland_in_the_European_Union_-_statistics Farms and farmland in the European Union]), with the next highest shares being in Italy (14.3%) and Poland (14.0%). In 2023, family farms accounted for at least 75% of all farms in all but 3 EU countries for which comparable data are available (see Figure 3); the exceptions were Denmark (about 69%), Estonia (about 60%) and France (about 51%), where the share of non-family farms in all farms was sharply higher than in 2010. [[Image:Distribution of farms, 2023 (% of farm holdings) v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Distribution of farms, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/613d4272-3ef0-4d48-8ed2-0521955555e4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T14:17:08Z ef_lf_fam])|alt= Horizontal queued bar chart showing distribution of farms as percentage of farm holdings in individual EU Member States. Totalling 100 percent, each country bar has two queues representing family farms and non-family farms for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Average size of family farms much smaller than non-family farms in most EU countries''''' Family farms were typically much smaller than non-family farms in terms of their utilised agricultural area (see Figure 4). Among the countries for which comparable data are available, the exceptions were Belgium and the Netherlands where there were minimal differences. The disparities were most pronounced in Czechia, Slovakia and Latvia. [[Image:Average (mean) size of farms in EU countries, 2023 (hectares, for family and non-family farms) v2.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Average (mean) size of farms in EU countries, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/681537b5-1882-4095-9ac5-84587cfda95b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-15T06:14:50Z ef_lf_fam])|alt= Horizontal bar chart showing average (mean) size of farms in individual EU Member States in hectares. Each country has two bars representing family farms and non-family farms for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Family farms were also much smaller than non-family farms in economic terms (see Figure 5) among the countries for which comparable data are available. For example, the average economic output of a family farm in Romania was approximately €3 500 in 2023 compared to an average of about €63 000 for non-family farms, highlighting the very small nature of most family farms in Romania. [[Image:Average economic size of farms in EU countries, 2023 (EUR, for family and non-family farms) v2.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Average economic size of farms in EU countries, 2023
''Source:'' ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f6c5b967-1daf-4c0b-acaf-527e4b151b5b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-15T06:19:15Z ef_lf_fam])|alt= Horizontal bar chart showing average economic size of farms in individual EU Member States in euros. Each country has two bars representing family farms and non-family farms for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Average use of labour on family farms much less than non-family farms''''' In all EU countries for which comparable data are available, the average amount of labour used for agricultural activities on non-family farms far exceeded the average on family farms (see Figure 6). By way of example, in Czechia the average volume of labour (measured in Annual Work Units or full-time labour equivalents) was 11.4 AWUs on non-family farms compared to 1.0 AWU on family farms. The gap was narrowest in Ireland with an average 1.8 AWU per on-family farm compared to 1.3 AWU per family farm. [[Image:Average labour input on farms, 2023 (AWU, for family farms and non-family farms) v2.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Average labour input on farms, 2023
''Source:'' ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/66588337-05d2-4bf8-8f20-5593f8e7abf4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-15T06:25:46Z ef_lf_fam])|alt= Horizontal bar chart showing average agricultural labour input on farms in individual EU Member States. Each country has two bars representing family farms and non-family farms for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Split between those countries where a majority of livestock were found on family farms and those where a majority were found on non-family farms''''' In half of the EU countries for which comparable data are available, family farms reared a majority of livestock. The highest majorities of over 80% were in Austria, Greece, Malta and Luxembourg (see Figure 7). In stark contrast, 15% or less of livestock were reared on family farms in Estonia, Slovakia, Czechia and Denmark. [[Image:Distribution of farm livestock by type of farm, 2023 (% of all livestock units) v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Distribution of farm livestock by type of farm, 2023
''Source:'' ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b0dad0ce-fc1b-4289-b436-62dc4dad0d95?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-15T06:30:07Z ef_lf_fam])|alt= Horizontal queued bar chart showing the percentage distribution of farm livestock by type of farm in individual EU Member States. Totalling 100 percent, each country bar has three queues representing farms with only family workers, farms where family workers make up more than 50 percent, and non-family farms for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Split between those countries where a majority of economic output was generated on family farms and those where a majority was generated on non-family farms ''''' In half of the EU countries for which comparable data are available, family farms accounted for a majority of the value of agricultural output produced by the agricultural sector (the EU average being about 47%). Indeed, family farms generated more than 75% of the standard output from agriculture in Malta, Greece, Austria, Poland and Luxembourg (see Figure 8). However, family farms generated only 20% or less of the standard output from agriculture in Slovakia, Estonia, Czechia and France. [[Image:Distribution of standard output by type of farm, 2023 (% of total standard output) v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Distribution of standard output by type of farm, 2023
''Source:'' ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ebf3820e-206b-4054-8241-232c790d8c30?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-15T06:34:15Z ef_lf_fam])|alt= Horizontal queued bar chart showing the percentage distribution of standard output by type of farm in individual EU Member States. Totalling 100 percent, each country bar has three queues representing farms with only family workers, farms where family workers make up more than 50 percent, and non-family farms for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:SE Data Family farming in the EU v3.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== The statistics used in this article come from the Integrated Farm Statistics (IFS) results of 2023 and, where these are unavailable, from the Agricultural Census of 2020. ===Explanatory note=== The implementation of the Integrated Farm Statistics (IFS) introduced a division of the target population into two components: the ‘main frame’ includes agricultural holdings above physical thresholds defined in the legislation, while the ‘frame extension’ covers smaller holdings below these thresholds. In the legislative framework, data collection requirements for below-threshold units vary across time. This variability leads to gaps in data availability for the entire population of agricultural holdings and poses challenges for the comparability of results. For many variables, an estimation procedure based on imputation techniques applied at the level of microdata has been developed to produce consistent estimates for below-threshold units where data are missing, which have been published in the Eurobase datasets under Farm structural indicators [ef_fsi]. This is not the case for family farm statistics. EU estimates in this article are built on the complete coverage provided by most countries, supplemented by the above threshold data from the others. When data are shown by country, only those countries that provided data from the full coverage are shown, although for Bulgaria, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg (where confidentiality issues arose) and Poland this referred to 2020 data. ===Key indicators and concepts=== Using data from the IFS, and applying the FAO definition for family farms at an operational level, it is possible to analyse farms on the basis of their labour input. Family farms may be defined as: *farms with exclusively family labour; *farms that have predominately family labour (at least 50% of the agricultural labour force). By contrast, non-family farms are defined as: *farms with predominantly non-family labour (less than 50% of the agricultural labour force); *farms without any family labour. Labour force data are provided in terms of a simple count of the number of persons as well as being converted into annual work units. Due to the high share of seasonal and part-time work in agriculture, it is generally considered appropriate to assess labour input using data presented in [[Glossary:Annual work unit (AWU) |annual work units]]. One annual work unit corresponds to the work performed by one person who is occupied on a farm on a full-time basis for a full year [[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|Utilised agricultural area]] is the total area taken by arable land, permanent grassland, permanent crops and kitchen gardens used by the holding, regardless of the type of tenure or of whether it is used as a part of common land. A [[Glossary:livestock unit (LSU)|livestock unit]] is a reference unit which facilitates the aggregation of livestock from various species and age, through the use of specific coefficients established initially on the basis of the nutritional or feed requirement of each type of animal. The [[Glossary:Standard output (SO)|standard output]] of an agricultural product (crop or livestock) is the average monetary value of the agricultural output at farm-gate price, in euro per hectare or per head of livestock. The standard output is used to classify [[Glossary:agricultural holding|agricultural holdings]] by type of farming and by economic size. The data for 2023 that are detailed in this article are based on farms under the main frame and the frame extension of the IFS 2023. Note that in 2023 not all countries provided frame extension data (namely Bulgaria, Greece, Spain, Italy, Poland, Slovenia and Lithuania). This is in line with current regulation but limits the comparability across years and countries. For country comparisons, the data available for 2020 were used for Bulgaria, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg (where confidentiality issues arose) and Poland. Please refer to the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-reports/w/ks-01-26-029-en-n Principal quality characteristics of EU countries' farm data collections for 2023] for further information on the coverage and limitations in comparability. ===Context=== '''''Family farming''''' The [https://www.fao.org/family-farming-decade/home/en/ United Nations Decade of Family Farming (2019-2028)] continues to provide the main global policy framework for supporting family farming. It promotes actions to strengthen the economic, social and environmental sustainability of family farms through a Global Action Plan with seven interconnected pillars of work containing measures on local and global levels. At EU level, family farms continue to be supported through the [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy_en common agricultural policy (CAP)] for 2023–2027. The policy aims to foster a smart, competitive, resilient and diversified agricultural sector while contributing to environmental and climate objectives and supporting rural areas. Under the architecture of the current policy cycle, the CAP Strategic Plans implemented by Member States based on local needs ensure that small and medium-sized farmers and young farmers continue to receive targeted support, while following stricter environmental standards (conditionality). The CAP also funds rural development initiatives aimed at improving supply chain positioning, increasing producer cooperation, and investing in farm modernization to keep rural communities vibrant, which in turn promote the sustainability of family farming. '''''Benefits of family farming''''' [https://www.fao.org/family-farming/background/en/ According to the FAO], more than 90% of the 570 million farms worldwide are managed by an individual or a family and rely primarily on family labour and they produce 80% of the world’s food in value terms. The role of family farming is key for global food security and for preserving traditional food products, contributing to a balanced diet and safeguarding the world’s agro-biodiversity and the sustainable use of natural resources. At the same time, it boosts local economies, especially when combined with specific policies aimed at the social protection and well-being of communities. '''''Challenges for family farmers''''' The main challenges facing family farms often reflect issues that are common for all types of small business: access to resources (such as land and capital) or access to markets (particularly in relation to the bargaining power of small farms in the food chain). Demographics provide a social challenge for family farms, as inter-generational succession issues may impact upon the sustainability of family farming and influence trends in land consolidation/fragmentation. Family farms face additional sectoral challenges related to climate change adaptation, increasing production costs, labour availability and investment needs associated with the digital and environmental transitions. === Other articles === *[[Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics]] *[[Agri-environmental indicators]] *[[Glossary:Farm structure survey (FSS)|Farm structure survey (FSS)]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database Agriculture (agr)], see: :Farm structure (ef) ::Farm labour force (ef_lf) :::Agricultural family labour force by age, title: Agriculture statistics - machinery and digitalisation
text:
Insert short description for search engines Data extracted in May 2026 Planned article update: December 2032 Over 40% of EU farms have access to the internet. Nearly 1 in 5 EU farms with utilised agricultural area (UAA) apply some form of precision farming technology or technique. Larger farms in both physical and economic size exhibit higher adoption rates of digital technologies and automated systems than smaller farms. Tractors are the most common conventional machinery type among EU farms, with a prevalence rate of nearly 80%. Digital technologies, automated systems, and machinery play a pivotal role in modernising agriculture by enhancing efficiency and sustainability at the farm level, reducing labour requirements, and optimising agricultural inputs.
The digitalisation of the sector—defined as the adoption and integration of digital technologies such as sensor systems, variable rate technologies, GPS/GNSS, big data, artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and the [[Glossary:Internet_of_Things_(IoT)|Internet of Things]] (IoT)—has the potential to transform agriculture. It can address key sectoral challenges while boosting competitiveness.
This article draws on the results of the 2023 [[Glossary:Farm_structure_survey|Farm Structure Survey]] to examine how digital tools, automated systems, and machinery are being adopted across EU farms, and how farm structure is associated with technology uptake.
This analysis includes only agricultural holdings above the physical thresholds set by [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2018/1091/oj Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 on integrated farm statistics], which represent an estimated 98% of the [[Glossary:Utilised_agricultural_area_(UAA)|utilised agricultural area]] (UAA) and 99% of the [[Glossary:Livestock_unit_(LSU)|livestock units]] (LSU) of all farms in the EU in 2023. Any mention to UAA, LSU or EU farms refers only to this subset, which is used as the denominator in the calculation of percentages. Very small agricultural holdings are excluded. === Digital technology adoption on EU farms varies by country and farm structure === ===== Internet access and digital tools ===== The adoption of digital technologies in agriculture begins with basic infrastructure, particularly internet access. In 2023, about 43% of EU farms reported having internet access, with some Northern and Central European countries (Denmark, Germany, Slovakia, Latvia, Czechia, and Austria) recording rates above 90% (Figure 1). One in ten farms in the EU used farm management information systems in 2023. France had the highest adoption rate (about 60%) among EU countries. By contrast, robotics adoption—defined as machines capable of autonomous operation without direct human intervention—remained relatively low, covering about 7% of all farms. The adoption rate was highest in the Netherlands (about 35%). [[Image:Farms with access to internet, farm management information systems and robotics (%, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Farms with access to internet, farm management information systems and robotics (%, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/db526f69-938a-48e5-8e9b-5f6a5e344a71?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-13T13:18:19Z (ef_mp_digi)]|alt=A chart showing the share of farms with access to internet, farm management information systems and robotics.]] Access to the internet and digital tool adoption rates not only vary considerably between EU countries, but also between farms of different economic sizes within the same country; adoption rates are in fact positively correlated with the economic size of farms. About three-quarters (74%) of all EU farms with a total standard output of €100 000 or over reported internet access (Figure 2), compared to only one-fifth (about 21%) of those with a total standard output of less than €2 000. The same pattern was noted for the use of farm management information systems (about 44% compared to 2%, respectively) and robotics (about 31% compared to about 1%, respectively). [[Image:Farms with internet access and digital tools according to economic size of farm (%, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Farms with access to internet, farm management information systems and robotics according to economic size of farm (%, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/db526f69-938a-48e5-8e9b-5f6a5e344a71?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-13T13:18:19Z (ef_mp_digi)]|alt=A chart showing farms with access to internet, farm management information systems and robotics according to economic size of farm. ]] ===== Precision farming ===== Precision farming refers to the application of modern information technology to gather, process and analyse data of high spatial and temporal resolution for decision-making and operations in crop production. Just under 18% of farms with utilised agricultural area (UAA) applied some kind of precision farming technology or practice in 2023, including robotics for plant protection products, band spraying of plant protection products, variable rate techniques, precision monitoring of crops and soil analysis (Figure 3). Soil analysis was by far the most widespread practice, with about 11% of farms taking it up, followed by variable rate techniques (about 5%) and band spraying of plant protection products (about 4%). [[Image:Farms with precision farming (%, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Farms with precision farming (%, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d9df1618-a92b-4751-8d91-e044705fdb41?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-13T13:08:51Z (ef_mp_digicr)]|alt=A chart showing the share of farms with precision farming.]] Only a minority of EU farms with UAA used precision farming technologies or techniques, regardless of size class or the type of technology and practice (Figure 4). However, adoption rates were progressively higher among larger farms, most notably in the use of robotics for plant protection products. In farms with 100 ha or more of UAA, adoption rates varied between about 8% for band spraying of plant protection products and 46% for soil analysis. In stark contrast, precision crop monitoring and the use of robotics for plant protection products were used by less than 1% of farms with less than 5 ha of UAA. [[Image:Farms with precision farming according to size of farm (%, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Farms with precision farming according to size of farm (%, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d9df1618-a92b-4751-8d91-e044705fdb41?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-13T13:08:51Z (ef_mp_digicr)]|alt=A chart showing the share of farms with precision farming according to the size of the farm]] Although only about 18% of EU farms with UAA adopted precision farming technologies or practices, these farms managed about 44% of the EU’s total UAA (see Figure 5). In some EU countries the share of UAA managed by farms using precision farming technologies or techniques was considerably higher than the EU average; in Luxembourg, Finland and Estonia at least three-quarters (75%) of the national UAA was managed in this way. This contrasted with Greece and Cyprus where the share was below 10%. [[Image:Utilised agricultural area of farms with precision farming (%, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Utilised agricultural area of farms with precision farming (%, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/77d417bd-4507-4522-81ab-250b78c543f0?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-13T13:10:02Z (ef_mp_digicr)]|alt=A chart showing the utilised agricultural area of farms with precision farming,by EU country.]] ===== Livestock farming technologies ===== Livestock farms use specialised machinery and automated systems to reduce labour, increase productivity, and improve product quality. In 2023, about one quarter (25%) of all farms with livestock used some type of machinery for livestock management, including technologies for the welfare and health monitoring of animals, grinder mixer for animal feeding, automatic feeding systems, technologies for the automatic regulation of barn climate and milking robots (Figure 6). The use of grinder mixer for animal feeding (about 15%) or animal welfare and health monitoring systems (about 11%) were the most prevalent types of machinery or automated systems. [[Image:Farms with machinery for livestock management (%, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Farms with machinery for livestock management (%, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f27b4bba-463c-4f9a-bd62-1b1cbd0ad8e6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-10T09:39:45Z (ef_mp_digilsk)]|alt=A chart showing farms with machinery for livestock management]] Adoption rates of precision livestock technologies varied significantly by farm size, measured in livestock units (LSU) (see Figure 7). For most types of livestock machinery, adoption rates increased with farm size. The exceptions were grinder mixers for animal feeding and milking robots for which the adoption rates were higher for mid-to-large-sized farms (100 and 499.9 LSU) than for the largest farms (≥500 LSU). This pattern mirrors the structure of dairy farms, which tend to be smaller in terms of LSU on average than extensive cattle-rearing and fattening farms and intensive granivore farms. The use of technologies for the automatic regulation of barn climate was simultaneously the most widespread type of machinery for livestock management among the largest farms with livestock (about 71%) and the least widespread among the smallest (less than 5 LSU; under 1%). [[Image:Farms with machinery for livestock management according to size class of LSU (%, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Farms with machinery for livestock management according to size class of LSU (%, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f27b4bba-463c-4f9a-bd62-1b1cbd0ad8e6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-10T09:39:45Z (ef_mp_digilsk)]|alt=A chart showing farms with machinery for livestock management according to size class of LSU]] EU farms using machinery for livestock management covered the equivalent of about 71% of all LSU on EU farms (Figure 8). Among EU countries, shares were highest in Denmark and the Netherlands (about 90%) and lowest in Greece (about 20%). [[Image:Livestock units of farms with machinery for livestock management (%, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Livestock units of farms with machinery for livestock management (%, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/83c6f4ac-e32b-45a4-ad02-51361b83afc3?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-10T09:42:40Z (ef_mp_digilsk)]|alt=A chart showing livestock units of farms with machinery for livestock management, by EU country]] === Use of conventional farm machinery in the EU is widespread === In 2023, about 84% of EU farms used conventional machinery (Figure 9), including tractors and machinery for tillage, planting, fertilisation, application of plant protection products and harvesting activities. Of these, tractors were the most common (about 79% of all farms), closely followed by tillage machinery, seeders and planters, spreaders, pulverisators or sprayers for fertilisers, and equipment for application of plant protection products (about 65%). [[Image:Farms using conventional machinery (%, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: Farms using conventional machinery (%, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e39651cf-d5db-4c6b-b25e-5ae4495db582?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-13T15:43:23Z ef_mp_mach]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e574067d-f48c-4654-a8cb-2938df25f479?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-13T15:45:28Z ef_mp_digi])|alt=A chart showing farms using conventional machinery.]] In 2023, almost all farms in Poland and Finland used conventional farm machinery (see Figure 10). In Slovakia and Greece, about two-thirds (68% and 65%, respectively) of farms used conventional farm machinery, the lowest shares among EU countries. The most common machinery ownership model in the EU was sole ownership; just over one third (about 35%) of EU farms owned solely all their conventional machinery. A little over one quarter (about 27 %) of farms used a combination of their own machinery and machinery that was used or owned by several other holdings. This includes shared and rented machinery. Farms that did not own their machinery and only rented or shared from others represented a further one-fifth of farms (about 21%). Outright (sole) ownership of conventional machinery was particularly common in Ireland and Slovenia (both about 83% of farms). By contrast, farms that relied on sharing and renting conventional machinery from other holdings was typical in Romania and the most common model in Greece and Hungary. The use of machinery of the mixed ownership model was the most common form in Germany, Austria, Denmark and Luxembourg, with this practice being reported in at least 60% of all farms. [[Image:Farms using conventional machinery according to ownership status (%, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 10: Farms using conventional machinery according to ownership status (%, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e39651cf-d5db-4c6b-b25e-5ae4495db582?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-13T15:43:23Z ef_mp_mach]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e574067d-f48c-4654-a8cb-2938df25f479?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-13T15:45:28Z ef_mp_digi])|alt=A chart showing farms using conventional machinery according to ownership status, by EU country.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Machinery Digitalisation SE v2.0 20260616.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === Farm structure data are collected from agricultural censuses every 10 years and from sample surveys every 3 or 4 years in between. Results from the 2023 survey are being published gradually. This analysis includes only agricultural holdings above the physical thresholds set by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R1091:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 1091/2018}} on integrated farm statistics. === Context === Digitalisation is at the centre of the European Commission’s priorities and embedded in the framework of the [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/overview-vision-agriculture-food/digitalisation_en Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)], with digital technologies acting as key enablers of innovation, economic performance, resilience, and sustainability at the farm level. The national CAP Strategic Plans support farmers through training, financial incentives, and infrastructure development to bridge the digital divide and shape the future of the sector. Such priorities are also highlighted in the Commission’s [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/overview-vision-agriculture-food/vision-agriculture-and-food_en Vision for Agriculture and Food], which proposes the launch of an EU-wide digital strategy on agriculture. Digital technologies in agriculture—such as precision farming, robotics, and farm management systems—are key to improving competitiveness, reducing environmental impact, and addressing labour shortages, but their adoption remains uneven across the EU, according to the Joint Research Centre’s (JRC) report [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC141259 The state of digitalisation in EU agriculture: insights from farm surveys (JRC, 2025)]. According to the report, national and regional differences in the adoption of digital technologies across the EU are shaped by a combination of factors, including the specific structure of the agricultural sector, economic conditions, access to capital and financial support, the quality of infrastructure and the availability of technology. High upfront costs and limited digital skills are considered the primary barriers to wider adoption, with most farmers relying on their own financial resources to invest in new technologies. Digital technologies for livestock production are generally considered the most expensive, followed by crop-specific technologies. Age also plays a role in the adoption of digital technologies, with younger farmers described as more likely to pursue it than older farmers, although the relationship can vary by technology type, digital literacy rate and region. Specialised and targeted digital training is mentioned as a necessary tool to overcome adoption barriers. ===Other articles=== *[[Agriculture|All Statistics Explained articles on agriculture]] === Database === *'''Detailed datasets''' :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database Agriculture (agr)], see: ::Farm structure (ef) ::Management and practices (ef_mp) ::Internet facilities, robotics, precision farming and machinery for livestock management in farms by economic size of farm, farm type and NUTS 2 region ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_mp_digi/default/table?lang=en&category=agr.ef.ef_mp ef_mp_digi]) ::Precision farming by age and training of manager, size of farm and NUTS 2 region ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_mp_digicr/default/table?lang=en&category=agr.ef.ef_mp ef_mp_digicr]) ::Machinery for livestock management by age and training of manager, size classes of livestock and NUTS 2 region ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_mp_digilsk/default/table?lang=en&category=agr.ef.ef_mp ef_mp_digilsk]) ::Machinery used by agricultural holdings by type of ownership, farm size, farm type and NUTS 2 region ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_mp_mach/default/table?lang=en&category=agr.ef.ef_mp ef_mp_mach]) === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/overview Agriculture] === Publications === *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-049|title=Key figures on the European food chain - title: Agriculture - manure storage statistics
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of EU Agriculture manure storage Data extracted in January 2025. Planned article update December 2028. 4 in every 10 holdings had manure storage facilities in 2020. Greater likelihood of manure storage facilities on holdings with higher livestock numbers. Decline in the share of EU holdings with liquid manure storage facilities without cover: down 5 percentage points between 2010 and 2020. |alt= Map showing the change in liquid manure storage facilities without cover between 2010 and 2020. Seven classes in percentage point ranging from the highest 3 to the lowest -50. Positive percentage points indicate an negative outcome, while negative values shows a positive outcome. Note that these figures need to be interpreted with caution as the trend is likely to be affected by changes in the methodology of data collection. This article presents statistics on [[Glossary:Manure|manure]] storage facilities in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] by focusing on shares rather than absolute values (see section [[Agriculture_-_manure_storage_statistics#Methodology|methodology]] below). These facilities are found on [[Glossary:Agricultural holding|agricultural holdings]] used to store manure before its application on the land to improve its nutrient content. From an environmental perspective, storage facilities represent a potential source for emissions of pollutants, such as [[Glossary:Ammonia_(NH3)|ammonia]] (NH3), nitrous oxide (N2O) and [[Glossary:Methane_emissions|methane]] (CH4), as well as for the leaching and run-off of nitrate (NO3-) and phosphorus pentoxide (P2O5). A reduction in these adverse environmental factors can be achieved by using adequate storage facilities. Note that a separate SE article on manure management will provide information on different [[Glossary:Type_of_manure_application|types of manure application]] to reduce the environmental impact of incorporating solid, slurry and liquid manure on fields. This topic is not covered in this article. === Agricultural holdings with manure storage facilities in 2020 === '''4 in every 10 holdings had manure storage facilities.''' In 2020, about 40% of the EU’s agricultural holdings had manure storage facilities. For a majority of EU countries, more than one half of holdings either stored solid and/or liquid manure on the holding in facilities or stored solid dung on the field, covered or not (see Figure 1). The highest proportions of holdings with manure storage facilities were in Slovenia (99.9%), Latvia (98.8%) and Estonia (92.3%). [[File:Share_manure_storage_facilities.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 1: Share of agricultural holdings with manure storage facilities (%, 2020)
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_mp_ms|title=ef_mp_ms}})|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing the percentage distribution of manure storage facilities on holdings by countries. Each have two bars representing holdings with and without manure storage facilities in 2020. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] By contrast, less than 1 in 10 holdings in Cyprus (6.8%) had manure storage facilities, with particularly low shares also in Greece (11.1%) and Italy (17.8%). It is important to consider the overall structure of agriculture in each of the EU countries when analysing the proportion of holdings with and without manure storage facilities. For example, almost 1 in 5 of the EU’s holdings in 2020 was in Romania. However, in relation to the total number of holdings in Romania, the proportion of holdings with manure storage facilities was below the EU average (40%). '''Storage facilities for solid dung were found on a majority of holdings in the EU.''' Given the importance of assessing emissions of nitrous oxide (N2O) in agriculture, a distinction is made between solid and liquid manure storage systems. Solid dung can be stored in unconfined piles, stacked in heaps, as dry lots in open confinement areas without vegetative cover or in compost piles which are aerated. Another practice is the deep litter method that allows the manure and bedding material to accumulate and decompose inside the stable. Liquid manure can be stored in pits below animal confinement that have slatted floors or kept either uncovered or covered in tanks or ponds at the farm. Note that some agricultural holdings can store manure in more than one of these different types of facility. Each type of storage facility has its own characteristics that a farmer must take into consideration: among others, these concern differences in storage volume, odour level, potential run-off, retention of nutrient content, potential gas dangers and emissions levels, site requirements and suitability. To compare the different types of manure storage facilities between countries, relative percentages are used (see Figure 2). Across the EU, 57% of holdings with manure storage facilities had facilities for storage of solid dung in 2020, 16% had covered facilities for liquid manure, 10% had deep litter systems, 6% had pits below animal confinement, 5% had liquid manure without cover and another 6% had other manure facilities. The use of different types of manure storage facility on farms varied considerably among EU countries. Nevertheless, storage facilities for solid dung were the most common form of storage in almost all EU countries in 2020. The exceptions were in Ireland (just 36% compared to 47% for covered liquid manure facilities) and the Netherlands (30% for both solid dung and covered liquid manure facilities). Indeed, storage facilities for solid dung represented above 60% of all types of farm storage facility in 13 EU countries: there were shares above 90% in Cyprus, Bulgaria, and Greece. Storage facilities for liquid manure with permeable or impermeable covers were found in relatively high numbers in Ireland, Switzerland (44% of all storage facilities), Austria (35% of all storage facilities), Slovenia (34%), the Netherlands (30%) and Germany (29%). By contrast, there were almost no liquid manure storage facilities with covers in Bulgaria, Greece, or Romania. There were generally relatively few holdings in the EU with uncovered liquid manure facilities. Nevertheless, they accounted for just over 1 in every 5 storage facilities on holdings in Finland (22%), and 1 in 10 storage facilities on farms in France (13%) and Spain (11%). Manure storage with deep litter, manure stored in pits below animal confinement and other facilities were much less common in most EU countries. The most notable exceptions were in Portugal (where together they accounted for 66% of all storage facilities), Denmark (45%) and Hungary (40%). [[File:Types_manure_storage_facilities.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 2: Types of manure storage facilities on agricultural holdings (%, 2020)
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_mp_ms|title=ef_mp_ms}})|alt=Vertical bar chart showing the relative percentage distribution of different types of manure storage facilities on holdings by countries. Six classes varying in types of manure storage facilities, each country has one column representing the relative share of the different types of storage facilities in 2020. Malta, confidential data for liquid manure without coverage and manure storage in other facilities excluded. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ''' Greater likelihood of manure storage facility on holdings with higher livestock numbers.''' Holdings with more livestock, as measured by [[Glossary:Livestock_unit_(LSU)|livestock units (LSU)]], were more likely to have manure storage facilities. Almost 90% of holdings between 100 and 500 LSU had manure storage facilities. This proportion declined with each smaller size class: about one quarter (25%) of farms with 0 to 5 LSU had manure storage facilities. There were very few EU holdings with manure storage facilities that had no livestock (see Figure 3). [[File:Share_manure_LSU.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 3: Share of agricultural holdings that have or do not have manure storage facilities by size in terms of livestock unit (%, EU, 2020)
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_mp_ms|title=ef_mp_ms}})|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing the percentage distribution of holdings that have or do not have manure storage facilities according to the size in terms of livestock units. Bars on the left-hand side indicate holdings with manure storage facilities and those on the right-hand show holdings without storage facilities according to size classes of livestock units in 2020. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] About two-thirds of farms (67%) without UAA (zero ha) had manure storage facilities but only about one third (30%) of small farms with less than 5 ha of UAA had. This reflects the fact that many farms specialising in pig or poultry production had no UAA (for example the animals are housed rather than free-range), but did have manure storage facilities. [[File:Share_manure_UAA.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 4: Share of agricultural holdings that have or do not have manure storage facilities by size in terms of utilised agricultural area (%, EU, 2020)
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_mp_ms|title=ef_mp_ms}})|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing the percentage distribution of holdings that have or do not have manure storage facilities according to the size in terms of utilised agricultural area. Bars on the left-hand side indicate holdings with manure storage facilities and those on the right-hand show holdings without storage facilites according to size classes of utilised agricultural area in 2020. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Change in holdings with manure storage facilities between 2010 and 2020 === '''Decline in the share of EU holdings with liquid manure storage facilities without cover: down 5 percentage points between 2010 and 2020''' Liquid manure storage without cover, such as uncovered anaerobic lagoons, tanks, or ponds, present an environmental risk with regards to [[Glossary:Ammonia_(NH3)|ammonia (NH3)]] emissions and nutrient leaching or run-off into surface and ground waters. There was a decline (5 percentage points) in the share of EU holdings with liquid manure storage facilities without cover between 2010 and 2020. Indeed, there were no longer any holdings in the Netherlands and Malta, as well as Iceland, that had these facilities in 2020. In many others, like Belgium, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Norway and Switzerland, the proportion of holdings with uncovered liquid manure storage facilities decreased by more than 30 percentage points. However, in a handful of EU countries, such as Spain (+5pp), Estonia (+3pp), Czechia (+0.4 pp), Bulgaria (+0.2 pp) and Italy (+0.1 pp), the use of uncovered liquid manure storage facilities became more common. |alt= Map showing the change in liquid manure storage facilities without cover between 2010 and 2020. Seven classes in percentage point ranging from the highest 3 to the lowest -50. Positive percentage points indicate an negative outcome, while negative values shows a positive outcome. Note that these figures need to be interpreted with caution as the trend is likely to be affected by changes in the methodology of data collection. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. Map 1: Change of liquid manure storage facilities without cover (percentage points, 2010-2020)
Source: Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_mp_ms|title=ef_mp_ms}}) === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:SE_Manure_Storage_Data_Graphs_20250122.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === Integrated Farm Statistics Survey (IFS) data are collected from agricultural censuses every ten years and from sample surveys every 3 or 4 years in between. Manure storage indicator is derived from data collected in the 2010 survey on agricultural production methods and the animal housing and manure management module of the 2020 agricultural census. === Context === Manure storage is one of 28 [[Glossary:Agri-environmental_indicator_(AEI)|agri-environmental indicators]] established by the European Commission to monitor the integration of environmental concerns into the [[Glossary:Common_agricultural_policy_(CAP)|Common agricultural policy (CAP)]]. Through its resource use, agriculture changes rural landscapes and contributes to resource depletion and degradation. Via substance emissions into the wider environment, agriculture may contribute to a complex series of ecological impacts, including human health effects, biodiversity loss and climate change. Policy responses to environmental and climate concerns have included the introduction of: resource use constraints and limits; emission and concentration limits; best available techniques, methods and practices. Nature conservation policies have also been implemented that set various agricultural constraints. [[Glossary:Agri-environmental_indicator_(AEI)|Agri-environmental indicators]] can be used to analyse over time the effects of agriculture on the environment and the interaction between the two, as well as the effectiveness and efficiency of agricultural and environmental policy measures. To reduce ammonia and greenhouse gas emissions and nutrient leaching and run-off to ground and surface waters, EU policies address manure storage facilities. The most important policies include the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31991L0676:EN:NOT|title=Nitrates Directive 0676/1991}}, the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32000L0060:EN:NOT|title=Water Framework Directive 0060/2000}} and {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32016L2284:EN:NOT|title=Emission Directive 2284/2016}}, which aim to protect water quality across Europe by preventing nitrates from agricultural sources polluting ground and surface waters. Farmers are also encouraged to install new manure storage facilities with adequate coverage preventing leaching run-off of nitrates and phosphorus as well as reducing ammonia emissions. === Other articles === *[[Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics]] *[[Agri-environmental indicators]] *[[Glossary:Farm structure survey (FSS)|Farm structure survey (FSS)]] *[[Glossary:Survey_on_agricultural_production_methods_(SAPM)|Survey on agricultural production methods (SAPM)]] === Selected datasets === *[{{Template:Main tables|dedicated_section=agriculture}} Agriculture (t_agri)] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database Agriculture (agr)], see: :Farm structure (ef) ::Management and practices (ef_mp) :::Manure storage facilities by utilised agricultural area, size class of livestock, farm type and NUTS 2 region ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_mp_ms|title=ef_mp_ms}}) :::Utilised agricultural area fertilised by manure application technique, farm type and NUTS 2 region ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_mp_ma|title=ef_mp_ma}}) :::Import and export of manure by farm type and NUTS 2 region ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_mp_mne|title=ef_mp_mne}}) ===Dedicated section=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/overview Agriculture] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-24-000|title=Key figures on the European food chain — 2024 edition}} === Methodology === The table {{Template:Publication|code=ef_mp_ms|title=ef_mp_ms}} contains the population covered by the module animal housing and manure management sent to Eurostat in 2020 detailed in item 3.6.3 in the metadata file for each country. Virtual entities (common land units without a farm manager) are excluded from the table as they are not agricultural holdings according to the definition set in Art 2(a) of the Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 July 2018. The dimension STATINFO refers to the thresholds laid down in Annex II of the Regulation (EU) 2018/1091. ABVTH (above threshold) corresponds to the agricultural holdings that meet at least one of the physical thresholds listed in Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 with regards to the size of agricultural land or the number of livestock units. BLWTH (below threshold) corresponds to the agricultural holdings that fall below all physical thresholds listed in Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 with regards to the size of agricultural land or the number of livestock units. TOTAL corresponds to all agricultural holdings. For a few countries (namely Spain, Slovenia, and Lithuania), the data of this table do not cover the agricultural holdings accounting for at least 98% of the total utilised agricultural area (without kitchen gardens) and at least 98% of the total livestock units of the country and the data cover only the ABVTH (above threshold) category. While this complies with Regulation (EU) 2018/1091, it limits the comparability across all countries in 2020. For this reason, the figures in this article are only presented for the coverage above threshold (ABVTH). Further details about the coverage and limitations in the comparability of the data across and within years can be found in the latest [https://wikis.ec.europa.eu/display/IFS/9.7+How+to+interpret+the+figures+from+Eurobase+tables IFS handbook in Section 9.7]. ===Legislation === '''Main legislation''' {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R1116:EN:NOT|title=Regulation 1116/2008}} of the European Parliament and of the Council on farm structure surveys and the survey on agricultural production methods (farm structure survey from 2010 to 2016). {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R1091:EN:NOT|title=Regulation 1091/2018}} of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 July 2018 on integrated farm statistics and repealing Regulations (EC) No 1166/2008 and (EU) No 1337/2011. '''Implementing legislation''' {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009R1200:EN:NOT|title=Implementing Regulation 1200/2009}} on farm structure surveys and the survey on agricultural production methods (farm structure survey from 2010 to 2016). {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R1874:EN:NOT|title=Implementing Regulation 1874/2018}} of 29 November 2018 on the data to be provided for 2020 under Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 of the European Parliament and of the Council on integrated farm statistics and repealing Regulations (EC) No 1166/2008 and (EU) No 1337/2011, as regards the list of variables and their description. ===External links=== *[https://agridata.ec.europa.eu/extensions/DataPortal/home.html Agri-food data portal] {{Unit|topic=X_Agriculture}} [[Category:Agriculture, fisheries, and forestry|Agriculture - manure storage statistics]] [[Category:Agriculture|Agriculture - manure storage statistics]] [[Category:Statistical article|Agriculture - manure storage statistics]] [[Category:December2028|Agriculture - manure storage statistics]]

title: Air freight transport statistics
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the air freight transport. Data extracted in December 2025 Planned article update: 7 December 2026 Air freight and mail transport in the EU increased by 8.7% between 2023 and 2024 In 2024, 14.3 million tonnes of freight and mail were transported by air in the EU. In 2024, Frankfurt Main was the main EU airport for freight and mail, with 2.0 million tonnes. [[Image: Air freight and mail transport by type of transport, EU, 2024_(%, based on total freight and mail transported).png|thumb|center|400px|Air freight and mail transport by type of transport, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/avia_gooc__custom_18929801/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=9cdad51a-d110-4f62-8716-c4cc92fac8d9&c=1763385727000 avia_gooc])|alt= Pie chart showing air freight and mail transport by type of transport in percentages based on total freight and mail transported. Three sections represent extra-EU, intra-EU and national for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article analyses recent freight and mail data on air transport in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA]] countries and 4 of the [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries]], Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia and Türkiye. The role of air transport in freight transport is less significant than in passenger transport, as aircraft are an expensive [[Glossary:Transport mode|transport mode]] in terms of [[Glossary:Tonne-kilometre|tonne-kilometres]] and only competitive for longer distances and relatively light high-value or perishable goods. The article distinguishes between national (domestic), [[Glossary:Intra-EU|intra-]] and [[Glossary:Extra-EU|extra-EU]] transport, then examines the significance and ranking of airports. === Air freight and mail transport in the EU increased by 8.7% between 2023 and 2024 === Total freight and mail transport in the EU increased by 8.7% in 2024 compared with 2023 (Table 1), reaching 14.3 million tonnes. This increase was mainly due to intra -EU transport which grew by 9.1%, while extra-EU was relatively stable (+0.1%). In contrast, national transport decreased by 4.3%. Between 2023 and 2024, freight and mail transport by air increased in all EU countries, except Poland (-3.6%) and Latvia (-2.7%). Among the EFTA and candidate countries, only Iceland recorded a decrease (-2.3%). The highest increase was registered by Hungary (+65.9%), followed by Czechia (+43.7%), Greece (+36.7%) and Cyprus (+20.1%). Among the remaining EU countries, 11 recorded a growth between 10% an 15%. Noticeable increases were also recorded in the EFTA countries Norway (+27.5%) and Switzerland (+14.6%) as well as in all candidate countries, North Macedonia showing the highest, with +92.3%. In 2024, the highest volume of freight and mail was loaded and unloaded at German airports, with 4.7 million tonnes. Belgium, Spain, France, Italy, the Netherlands and the candidate country Türkiye were the other countries with more than 1 million tonnes of freight and mail loaded and unloaded in 2024. [[Image: Air freight and mail transport by type of transport, 2024.png|thumb|center|800px|Table 1: Air freight and mail transport by type of transport, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/avia_gooc__custom_18929801/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=9cdad51a-d110-4f62-8716-c4cc92fac8d9&c=1763385727000 avia_gooc])|alt= Table showing air freight and mail transport by type of transport in tonnes for the EU and individual EU countries for the year 2024. The change compared to 2023 is also presented. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 1 indicates that the extra-EU transport represented 83.3% of the total air freight and mail transport. It was the main origin/destination far ahead of intra-EU transport (13.9%) and national transport (2.9%). Compared with 2023, intra-EU and national transport lost 1.2 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] and 0.4 pp in 2024, respectively, to the benefit of extra-EU. [[Image: Air freight and mail transport by type of transport, EU, 2024_(%, based on total freight and mail transported).png|thumb|center|800px|Figure 1: Air freight and mail transport by type of transport, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/avia_gooc__custom_18929801/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=9cdad51a-d110-4f62-8716-c4cc92fac8d9&c=1763385727000 avia_gooc])|alt= Pie chart showing air freight and mail transport by type of transport in percentages based on total freight and mail transported. Three sections represent extra-EU, intra-EU and national for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Map 1 gives a picture of the extra-EU market. Eastern Asia was the main origin/destination of freight and mail transported by air in 2024, with 25.4% of the total extra-EU transport, followed by North America (21.5%). The lowest share was observed for Australasia, S. Sea Is. & Antarctica (0.03%). Decreases were observed in transport with Central America and Caribbean (-6.4%), rest of Africa (Africa without Eastern Africa) (-0.9%) and Northern America (-0.4%). By contrast, transport with the other world regions increased between 2023 and 2024. In relative terms, the highest growths were recorded for transport with Central Asia (+47.5%), Western Asia (+24.4%), Oceania and southern polar regions (+18.5%), South eastern Asia (+13.4%) and Eastern Asia (+12.8%). [[Image: Extra-EU air freight and mail transport, EU, 2024.png|thumb|center|800px|Map 1: Extra-EU air freight and mail transport, EU, 2024
''Source:'' ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/avia_goexcc__custom_18555344/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=290fc9ec-2e1d-44cd-a10c-3e0fec5d0b96&c=1763385480000 avia_goexcc])|alt= Map showing extra-EU air transport of freight and mail from the EU in 2024 to various parts of the world as percentage of world region and its share in extra-EU air transport, thousand tonnes loaded and unloaded, and the percentage change between 2024 and 2023. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, Frankfurt Main was the main EU airport in terms of tonnes of freight and mail loaded/unloaded, with 2.0 million tonnes, closely followed by Paris Charles de Gaulle, with 1.9 million tonnes (Table 2). Amsterdam Schiphol, Leipzig Halle and Liege were the other EU airports with more than 1 million tonnes in 2024. When looking at the number of flights, the ranking was slightly different. Leipzig Halle was first with 49 948 flights, followed by Paris Charles de Gaulle (38 071 flights), Köln Bonn (34 706 flights), Liege (24 334 flights), Frankfurt Main (23 743 flights) and Milano Malpensa (22 975 flights). These were the only airports with more than 20 000 flights. Among the top 20 airports, 18 registered a growth between 2023 and 2024 in terms of total freight and mail loaded/unloaded. Budapest Liszt Ferenc International recorded the highest increase (+65.7%), followed by Roma Fiumicino (+44.4%), Zaragoza (+39.6%) and Liege (+20.4%). In addition, 6 airports recorded a growth between 10% and 20%. By contrast, Köln Bonn (-3.5%) and Leipzig Halle (-0.6%) recorded a decrease between 2023 and 2024. [[Image: Top EU airports for freight and mail transport, 2024.png|thumb|center|800px|Table 2: Top EU airports for freight and mail transport, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/avia_gooa__custom_18934738/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=fc182e13-78c6-481f-a220-018ab37b13d0&c=1763397145000 avia_gooa])|alt= Table showing top airports for freight and mail transport in the EU for the year 2024 by tonnes carried and percentage change between 2024 and 2023. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === For long distances over 2 000 km, 99% of the total transport was extra-EU in the period 2022-2023=== Figure 2 presents freight and mail transport by type of transport and distance class. For long distances over 2 000 km, 99% of the total transport was extra-EU in 2024, 2023 and 2022. For distances between 1 500 and 1 999 km, extra-EU transport represented 58% of the total in 2024 and 2022. In 2023, this share was 55%. Intra-EU transport of freight and mail was predominant in distances inferior to 1 500 km. In 2024, it represented 73% of total transport in the 1 000–1 499 km distance class, 69% in 500–999 km class and 51% in 300–499 km class. When looking at distances lower than 300 km, intra-EU transport represented 53%, while national claimed 39% of the total freight and mail on board. [[Image:Air freight and mail transport by type of transport and distance class, EU, 2022, 2023 and 2024_(%, based on freight and mail on board).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Air freight and mail transport by type of transport and distance class, EU, 2022, 2023 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1403a9bf-4e09-4890-bd26-5d9abdf7daae?lang=en&createdAt=2025-11-17T13:15:33Z avia_goodis])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing air freight and mail transport by type of transport and six distance classes in the EU. These classes each have three columns representing the years 2022, 2023 and 2024. Totalling 100 per cent, each column contains three stacks representing national, intra-EU and extra-EU. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media: Air freight transport statistics_2025-12.xlsx|Air freight and mail transport statistics]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== More recent freight and mail data are available in the Eurostat database for several countries. Eurostat encourages reporting countries to provide statistics on air transport in advance of the regulatory deadline. For certain countries, the data are available already up to 3 months after the end of a reference month. '''Main definitions''' The definitions used for air transport statistics are included in {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32003R1358:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1358/2003}} of 31 July 2003 implementing {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32003R0437:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 437/2003}} of 27 February 2003 on statistical returns in respect of the carriage of passengers, freight and mail by air. The main definitions are the following: *On Flight Origin and Destination (OFOD): Traffic on a commercial air service identified by a unique flight number subdivided by airport pairs in accordance with the point of embarkation and point of disembarkation on that flight. This is linked to the definition of passengers carried. *Freight and mail loaded/unloaded: All freight and mail loaded onto or unloaded from an aircraft. This excludes direct transit freight and mail. In principle, information provided in this article is based on On Flight Origin/Destination (OFOD) data. Only when OFOD data have not been reported have airport declarations been used. *Airport coverage: In principle, this article covers air transport to and from any airports in the reporting countries with more than 150 000 passengers annually. '''Double counting: ''' the national aggregates and total intra-EU aggregates exclude any double counting. It includes all the departures figures reported plus ‘a part of’ arrivals declarations, ‘a part of’ including those arrivals for which the corresponding partner airport departure declarations are missing. '''Map 1:''' the component countries comprising the world regions as defined for this map are based on the [[Glossary:Geonomenclature_(GEONOM)|geonomenclature]] used by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] for external trade statistics. The components of each world region can be extracted from the aviation domain in the Eurostat online database or obtained upon request. Care should be taken when drawing any conclusions regarding world regional shares, as passengers who either stop over or change planes en route are allocated to the country where they made their connections, rather than the country of first origin or final destination. '''In this article''' *":" means "not available" *"-" means "not applicable" *"0n" means "less than half the unit used" *"0" means real zero ===Context=== All figures presented in this article have been extracted from the Eurostat aviation database. The database is available online from the Eurostat web page. ===Other articles=== *[[Air passenger transport statistics]] *[[Air passenger transport - data by month]] *[[Transport statistics at regional level#Air transport|Transport statistics at regional level – air transport]] ===Selected Datasets=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/database Transport], see selected datasets: :Air transport (t_avia) ::Air transport of passengers (ttr00012) ::Air transport of goods (ttr00011) ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/database Transport], see detailed datasets: :Air transport (avia) ::Air transport measurement – passengers (avia_pa) :::Detailed air passenger transport by reporting country and routes (avia_par) ::Air transport measurement – freight and mail (avia_go) ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=transport}} Transport] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code= KS-01-24-021 |title=Key figures on European transport – 2024 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code= KS-01-25-003 |title=Key figures on Europe – 2025 edition }} ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=avia_pa_esms|title=Passenger and freight transport by air/Traffic data/Air transport at regional level}} (ESMS metadata file -
