title: Agriculture statistics at regional level
text:
Eurostat regional yearbook; 2026 edition; flagship publication; EU; regional statistics; NUTS; agriculture; farm structure; precision farming; farm size; large farms; young farm managers; female farm managers; robotics; variable rate techniques; precision monitoring Data extracted in March 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 This article forms part of the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026]'', an annual [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications flagship publication]. It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the [[Glossary:EU|EU]], [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate]] countries. A [[Regional_yearbook_introduction#A_short_reading_guide|short reading guide]] is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps. In 2023, young farmers under 40 accounted for about 1 in every 9 of all farm managers in the EU; the highest regional share was recorded in the eastern French region of Franche-Comté, at 28%. In the EU, some 2% of all agricultural holdings made use of autonomous or robotic machinery for crop protection tasks in 2023; this share rose to more than a quarter of all holdings in the French regions of Picardie, Ile-de-France, Centre — Val de Loire and Nord-Pas de Calais. [[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH13_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2225e30a-0555-4bb3-be37-bd825beb2306?lang=en ef_m_farmang)]|alt=A bar chart showing EU regions with the highest shares of young farm managers, in percent. Data are shown for 2023, for selected NUTS level 2 regions and for the EU average. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:Infographics-CH13_RYB2026.png|thumb|right|380px|Which EU regions had the highest shares of young farm managers?]] Agriculture remains a key sector in the EU, shaping not only food and feed supply but also rural landscapes, regional economies and territorial identity. In recent years, farmers have increasingly been encouraged to balance their primary role of food production with the provision of wider public goods. These include the maintenance of countryside landscapes, the preservation of biodiversity, and contributions to environmental sustainability and climate objectives. As a result, agricultural activity is increasingly understood in a broader regional development context, where farming practices interact with environmental management, land use planning and rural development. Farms in the EU play a crucial role in ensuring the availability of safe, high-quality and affordable food for consumers, while also sustaining a diverse range of regional agricultural products. The food produced by EU farmers is closely linked, through tradition and heritage, to Europe’s cultural and territorial diversity. Variations in climate, soil conditions, topography and farming techniques contribute to a wide range of agricultural practices, from intensive arable to extensive pastoral farming, resulting in a diverse range of output and landscapes.
'''More about the data: farm structure survey''' This article draws on the results of the 2023 [[Glossary:Farm_structure_survey_(FSS)|farm structure survey]]. The analyses include only agricultural holdings above the physical thresholds set by ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2018/1091/oj Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 on integrated farm statistics]'', which represented an estimated 98% of the [[Glossary:Utilised_agricultural_area_(UAA)|utilised agricultural area (UAA)]], 99% of the [[Glossary:Livestock_unit_(LSU)|livestock units (LSUs)]] and 99% of the [[Glossary:Standard_output_(SO)|standard output]] of all farms in the EU. Any references to the UAA, LSUs, standard output, or EU farms relate exclusively to this subset, which is used as the denominator for calculating percentages. Very small agricultural holdings are excluded to ensure comparability.
This final chapter of the ''Eurostat regional yearbook'' presents agricultural statistics, focusing on 2 principal areas: *farm structure – with information on the average size of farms, the relative importance of large farms, the share of young farmers and the share of female farm managers *a focus on precision farming – innovative agricultural techniques that rely on technology to improve productivity (for example, the use of automated machinery to apply pesticides or adjust fertiliser application across different parts of a field, or the use of sensors and drones to monitor crop growth). In 2023, farm managers aged under 40 – ‘young farmers’ – accounted for 11.8% of all EU farm managers of holdings above the Regulation physical thresholds (see the '''infographic''' and explanation above in the shaded box). The highest regional share was recorded in the eastern French region of Franche-Comté (28.3%). There were 7 other NUTS level 2 regions where at least a quarter of all farm managers were aged under 40: the Austrian regions of Oberösterreich, Vorarlberg, Kärnten and Tirol, the Finnish archipelago of Åland, the French region of Bourgogne and the Czech capital region of Praha. ===Farm structure === Farm structure statistics provide essential insights into the organisation and characteristics of [[Glossary:Agricultural_holding|agricultural holdings]] across the EU. They describe key aspects such as farm size, land use, labour input and the demographic profile of farm managers, offering a basis for analysing structural differences within and between regions. The data may be used, among other purposes, to monitor trends in farm consolidation and generational renewal. Note that, to ensure comparability throughout this chapter, the data exclude very small farms/holdings. According to the latest available data for 2023, there were 6.1 million farm holdings in the EU above the Regulation physical thresholds, collectively managing 1.51 million km² of agricultural land; this corresponded to 36.9% of the total land area. These figures underline the continued importance of agriculture in shaping land use patterns and regional development in the EU. '''''Farm sizes show limited regional variation across many EU countries''''' '''Map 1''' shows, for each NUTS level 2 region, the farm size category – based on 4 size categories – that accounted for the largest share of the utilised agricultural area. In 2023, there was little regional variation within many EU countries. For example, large farms of at least 100.0 hectares (ha) were the dominant category in terms of utilised agricultural area across all regions of Bulgaria, Czechia, Denmark, Hungary, Slovakia and Sweden, as well as in Cyprus, Luxembourg and the Baltic EU countries; this was also the case in all but 1 of the regions across (mainland) France, Romania and Finland. By contrast, farms with between 30.0 and 100.0 hectares accounted for the largest share of utilised agricultural area in the regions of Ireland, much of Belgium and the Netherlands, in a cluster of regions covering southern Germany, most of Austria and northern Italy, as well as in several regions of northern Spain. At the other end of the spectrum, the smallest farms (with fewer than 30.0 hectares of agricultural area) accounted for the largest share of utilised agricultural area across many of the regions located in the southern EU countries (principally in Greece and Italy), but also in both regions of Slovenia, as well as much of Croatia and Poland. In some regions, the relative importance of large farms (with at least 100.0 hectares of agricultural area) was particularly marked, as they accounted for more than 90.0% of the region’s total agricultural area: *5 regions from eastern Germany – Sachsen-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Brandenburg, Thüringen and Leipzig *2 regions in western Slovakia – Bratislavský kraj and Západné Slovensko. A similar analysis for small farms (with fewer than 5.0 hectares of agricultural area) indicates that their relative importance was particularly marked in other regions, where they accounted for more than a third of the region’s agricultural area: *Attiki (2020 data), Peloponnisos and Kriti in Greece *Canarias in Spain *Guadeloupe in France (2020 data) *Liguria, Calabria and Campania in Italy. Map 1: Dominant farm size
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e1a1f02a-46bf-4d91-a69a-8ed908a1f332?lang=en ef_m_farmang]) [[Image:Dominant farm size (based on % share of utilised agricultural area, by NUTS 2 regions, 2023)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Dominant farm size
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e1a1f02a-46bf-4d91-a69a-8ed908a1f332?lang=en ef_m_farmang])]] Since 2010, the average farm size across the EU has generally increased, reflecting ongoing structural change within agriculture. Smaller holdings have declined in number, while larger, more commercially oriented farms have expanded due to consolidation, mechanisation and productivity pressures. This pattern was particularly evident in eastern EU countries such as Bulgaria, Poland and Romania, where a relatively high number of very small semi-subsistence farms consolidated into larger units, as farming shifted towards more market-oriented systems. This process has been reinforced by rural depopulation, with younger people migrating to cities and/or abroad in search of better-paid employment, while older farmers retire without successors. '''''Across the EU, average farm size grew from 19.7 hectares in 2010 to 24.7 hectares in 2023''''' '''Map 2''' shows changes in average farm size – measured in hectares per holding – across 3 reference periods. In the EU, the average of holdings above the Regulation threshold increased from 19.7 hectares in 2010 to 21.5 hectares in 2016, before rising more sharply to 24.7 hectares in 2023. Across NUTS level 2 regions, there were 123 regions (out of 216 for which data are available) where average farm size increased in both periods (from 2010 to 2016 and again from 2016 to 2023). Overall, comparing 2010 and 2023, average farm size increased in 178 of the 216 regions, indicating a widespread pattern of farm consolidation across the EU. The most marked increases in average farm size were recorded in several regions across Bulgaria. For example, average farm size almost doubled in each period in the north-western region of Severozapaden, rising from 34.6 hectares in 2010 to 62.1 hectares in 2016, before reaching 115.9 hectares in 2023. Substantial increases were also observed in the neighbouring northern Bulgarian regions of Severoiztochen and Severen tsentralen, as average farm size increased by more than 50.0 hectares in both of these regions between 2010 and 2023. Outside Bulgaria, the largest absolute increases were observed in the French regions of Centre — Val de Loire and Franche-Comté, where average farm size grew by 31.3 and 31.2 hectares, respectively. '''''In 2023, average farm size peaked at 284.1 hectares in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, compared with just 0.8 hectares in Região Autónoma da Madeira''''' In 2023, the largest average farm size was recorded in the northern-eastern German region of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, at 284.1 hectares; this was 11.5 times higher than the EU average. There were 4 other regions in eastern Germany where the average size of farms exceeded 190.0 hectares: Sachsen-Anhalt, Brandenburg, Thüringen and Leipzig. The next largest average farm sizes were recorded in the French capital region of Ile-de-France (141.3 hectares) and in the Czech region of Severozápad (138.7 hectares). At the other end of the range, there were 17 regions within the EU where the average farm size was smaller than 6.5 hectares in 2023 (as shown by the lightest shade in '''Map 2'''). These 17 regions were concentrated in: *7 regions of Greece – including the capital region of Attiki, Peloponnisos, Ipeiros, Kriti, Sterea Elláda, Notio Aigaio and Voreio Aigaio *4 regions of Italy – Liguria, Calabria, Campania and Provincia Autonoma di Trento. However, Região Autónoma da Madeira (Portugal) had the smallest average farm size in 2023, at 0.8 hectares. This reflects, among other factors, the island’s steep terrain with agriculture carried out on narrow terraces, as well as the historical division of land among families, resulting in fragmented plots suited to growing high-value crops such as bananas, sugarcane and grapes.

Together, these large farms managed 80.6 million hectares of agricultural land (around 806 000 km²). In economic terms, large farms generated a standard output of €137.7 billion, accounting for just over a third (around 35%) of the total output of all agricultural holdings. '''Figure 1''' presents the 20 NUTS level 2 regions in the EU where large farms recorded the highest shares of all agricultural holdings, total utilised agricultural area and standard output in 2023. A comparison reveals that 8 regions featured prominently for each of these 3 indicators, namely, the eastern German regions of Brandenburg, Leipzig, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Sachsen-Anhalt and Thüringen; the French regions of Ile-de-France and Lorraine; and the Czech region of Severozápad. In the French capital region of Ile-de-France, the presence of large farms was particularly pronounced, with such holdings accounting for 62.5% of all agricultural holdings in 2023. There were 2 further French regions that recorded majority shares: Centre — Val de Loire (56.6%) and Lorraine (55.4%). There were 4 regions with shares just below half, including Picardie and Bourgogne (also in France), and Sachsen-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (in eastern Germany). The standard output of agricultural holdings measures the monetary value of agricultural output at farm-gate prices. In regions characterised by economies of scale, specialised high-value production and efficient production systems, large farms tend to account for a relatively high share of standard output. In 2023, this pattern was particularly evident in German, Czech and Slovak regions, as well as in Estonia, where large farms commonly accounted for more than three quarters of agricultural standard output. At the upper end of the distribution, large farms in the German region of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern generated 86.3% of standard output in agriculture, with a similar share recorded in the French region of Lorraine (86.1%). For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Across the EU, young farmers accounted for about 1 in 9 of all farm managers in 2023; this share peaked at 28.3% in the eastern French region of Franche-Comté''''' Farm managers are the people responsible for the normal daily financial and production routines of running a farm, such as decisions on what and how much to plant or rear, and what labour, materials and equipment to employ. Often, the farm manager is also the owner (the ‘holder’) of the agricultural holding; however, this is not always the case, particularly where the farm has a separate legal identity. Note that, as with the remainder of this chapter, the information presented below excludes very small farms/holdings that fall below the Regulation physical thresholds. Differences in the structure of agricultural holdings within the EU are often reflected in patterns of ownership and management: smaller farms are typically family-run, while larger farms are more commonly managed by professional managers employed by agricultural enterprises. Many farm managers in the EU continue to work well beyond what is typically considered retirement age in other sectors of the economy. This slow pace of generational renewal may pose challenges for the long-term sustainability of agriculture, potentially limiting innovation and productivity due to a lack of a more dynamic and diverse farm workforce. In 2023, there were 723 000 farm managers of EU holdings above the Regulation physical thresholds under the age of 40. By contrast, there were 2.0 million farmers aged 65 or over. Younger farmers are more likely to manage medium-sized or large farms, which may reflect their higher levels of agricultural training, as well as their exposure to modern and innovative practices. Conversely, older farm managers predominantly work on smaller farms, which often yield relatively low levels of agricultural income. In 2023, young farm managers accounted for 11.8% of all EU farm managers of holdings above the Regulation physical thresholds. Their share was noticeably higher in a broad area extending from France, through the Alps into Czechia, Slovakia and Poland. This pattern may reflect targeted policy support aimed at encouraging more young people into agriculture, including initiatives such as start-up grants, low interest loans, reduced land prices, support with land access, income support, training programmes, and opportunities to foster innovation and diversification. By contrast, the lowest shares of young farm managers were concentrated in southern EU countries, Romania and Slovenia. In some regions, this may be linked to challenges in generational transition, such as financial barriers, limited access to land, capital and knowledge, declining rural fertility rates and the appeal of alternative career prospects. The share of young farm managers was also relatively low in several regions across Ireland and the Netherlands, where the consolidation of farming may have created significant barriers to young people wishing to enter the industry. '''Map 3''' highlights the regional distribution of young farm managers in 2023. There were 36 NUTS level 2 regions where the share of young farm managers was at least 20.0% (as shown by the darkest shade). This group included: *7 out of 9 regions in Austria (with the capital region of Wien and the easternmost region of Burgenland just below this share) *15 regions in France *8 regions in Poland *3 regions in Czechia *a single region from each of Slovakia and Finland *Luxembourg. In 2023, Franche-Comté in eastern France (28.3%) and Oberösterreich in northern Austria (27.2%) had the highest shares of young farm managers. Young farm managers were particularly scarce in southern EU countries. There were 25 regions where they accounted for fewer than 7.0% of all farm managers, concentrated in the southern EU countries of Greece (8 regions), Portugal (6 regions), Italy (4 regions) and Spain (3 regions); Cyprus also recorded a very low share. Outside southern Europe, low shares of young farm managers were observed in the Romanian capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov and in the French outermost regions of Mayotte and Martinique. The year is designed to highlight the essential role women play across the farm to fork chain, seeking to raise awareness and promote actions that will close gender gaps and improve women’s livelihoods. Compared with their male counterparts, female farm managers are generally underrepresented in the EU’s agricultural sector. In 2023, fewer than a fifth (17.2%) of all EU farm managers of holdings above the Regulation physical thresholds were female. Where women do manage farms, they are more likely to operate relatively small holdings, although generational renewal may gradually increase women’s participation in larger and more commercially oriented farming systems. Women accounted for fewer than half of all farm managers across all NUTS level 2 regions. In 2023, the highest regional shares were clustered in northern Spain, southern Italy and much of Austria, with relatively high shares also observed in Poland and certain regions of Greece. By contrast, the lowest shares of female farm managers were concentrated in the Netherlands in particular, alongside Denmark, Czechia, Germany, Ireland and the Nordic countries; low shares were also recorded in Cyprus and Malta. These differences may reflect a range of structural factors, including variations in farm size, inheritance practices, labour market structures and the prevalence of family farming, all of which can influence the likelihood of women having farm management roles. The distribution of female farm managers was broadly balanced around the EU average: in 2023, there were 134 out of 241 regions (55.6% of all regions for which data are available) with a share of female farm managers that was below the EU average. At the lower end of the distribution, the Dutch region of Friesland recorded the lowest share (2.7%; with around 6 000 female farm managers), while the highest share was observed in the northern Austrian region of Oberösterreich (42.5%; with 211 600 female farm managers). In 2023, there were 25 NUTS level 2 regions where the share of female farm managers was at least 28.5% (as shown by the darkest shade in '''Map 4'''). Relatively high shares of female farm managers were concentrated in Italy (11 regions, including Molise which recorded the highest share in Italy), Greece (4 regions, including Voreio Aigaio), Austria (4 regions, including Oberösterreich) and Spain (3 regions, including Principado de Asturias). At the lower end of the distribution, there were 12 regions in the EU where the share of female farm managers was below 5.0% in 2023. This group included 10 out of the 12 regions from the Netherlands; the exceptions being Zeeland (where the share was 5.0%; 2020 data) and Utrecht (no information available). The other 2 regions with relatively low shares were Åland in Finland (3.6%) and Syddanmark in Denmark (4.9%). Map 4: Female farm managers

It aims to improve the efficiency, productivity and environmental sustainability of farming by tailoring inputs – such as water, fertilisers and plant protection products – to the specific conditions and needs of crops and soils. As with the remainder of this chapter, the information presented below excludes very small farms/holdings that fall below the Regulation physical thresholds. As a result, the reported uptake may be somewhat overstated, as the data do not capture management practices and agricultural techniques in very small farms/holdings, where these technologies are generally less likely to be used. '''In 2023, almost a third of all farms in Picardie (northern France) used robotics for plant protection''' Within the context of the EU’s farm structure survey, the use of robotics for plant protection refers to the deployment of automated or semi-automated machines that carry out plant protection tasks, for example, the application of crop protection products (such as herbicides, fungicides or insecticides) with minimal human intervention. In 2023, 1.8% of all agricultural holdings in the EU above the Regulation physical thresholds used robotics to apply plant protection products. The distribution of shares across NUTS level 2 regions was asymmetric and slightly skewed in a positive direction: more than half (53.3%) of all regions for which data are available had shares below the EU average, while a smaller number exhibited substantially higher shares, resulting in a pronounced right tail to the distribution. '''Map 5''' shows that there were a number of clusters which displayed a particularly high uptake of robotics for applying plant protection products in 2023, with double-digit shares recorded in: *all regions of Denmark and Finland *all regions in the northern half of France. The highest regional share was observed in the northern French region of Picardie, where 32.1% of agricultural holdings reported the use of robotics for plant protection applications. The next highest shares were also recorded in northern France: Ile-de-France (29.8%) and Centre — Val de Loire (29.2%). At the other end of the distribution, there were 84 regions across the EU where fewer than 0.5% of all agricultural holdings used robotics for plant protection products in 2023. They were principally concentrated in southern and eastern regions of the EU, including: *all regions of Croatia, Lithuania and Romania *all regions of Greece and Italy (among those for which data are available) *all but 1 region in Austria (among those for which data are available) *14 of the 17 regions in Poland. Within this group of 84 regions, there were 18 where no or virtually no use of robotics for plant protection products was recorded; most of these were located in Greece or Italy.

The strategy aims to: *efficiently produce statistics which meet users’ needs *not significantly increase the burden on respondents and on statistical systems, while making more statistics available *improve the coherence between the agricultural statistics sub-domains *clarify and streamline concepts and definitions *improve the quality of agricultural statistics *improve integration between agricultural, forestry, land use and environmental statistics *increase the flexibility and reaction speed of the statistical system allowing easier introduction of adaptations to new needs, statistics and methodological approaches for supporting better policy-making and decision processes *develop a responsive and responsible governance structure for agricultural statistics. '''Integrated farm statistics''' Integrated farm statistics (IFS) collect data that describe the structure of agricultural holdings, offering an insight into the general characteristics of farms and farmers. This information is complemented by, among other datasets, detailed data on land use, livestock, labour, production methods, rural development measures and agro-environmental aspects of farming. Within a policy context, Eurostat’s structural farm statistics play a key role in monitoring and analysing developments across the sector, informing decision-making under the common agricultural policy (CAP) and other EU policies (such as those related to rural development or environmental sustainability). Structural agricultural statistics are collected through a combination of: *agricultural censuses carried out once every 10 years and aligned with recommendations of the [https://www.fao.org/world-census-agriculture/en Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations] (the latest census was conducted in 2020) and *intermediate sample-based farm structure surveys that are conducted twice between censuses (the latest survey was conducted in 2023; the next survey is due to take place in 2026). The latest agricultural census covered approximately 300 variables spanning a broad range of topics, including general characteristics of farms and farm managers, land use and livestock, the agricultural labour force, animal housing and manure management, and support measures for rural development. Data from the census may help frame policy debates, answering questions such as: *who will farm in the future given the large share of older farm managers? *how many women are farming? *is agriculture becoming dominated by big business? *is organic farming expanding? The collection of structural agricultural statistics within the EU is governed by a common legal framework ensuring harmonised data. Since the 2020 agricultural census, this framework has been the IFS system. The legal basis for the IFS is ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2018/1091/oj Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 on integrated farm statistics]''. It defines a set of core variables alongside provisions for collecting additional variables through modules. For the reference year 2023, the list of variables and their descriptions is specified in ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2021/2286/oj/eng Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/2286]''. Similar implementing provisions apply for other reference years (2020 and 2026). Each country is allowed, in line with the legislation, to set up thresholds that may exclude very small agricultural holdings, as long as the conditions for minimum coverage of 98% of the utilised agricultural area (excluding kitchen gardens) and 98% of the livestock units of the country are guaranteed. The standard threshold for the utilised agricultural area is 5 hectares, while that for livestock is 1.7 livestock units; other more detailed physical thresholds also apply. The 2023 farm structure survey included a module on machinery and equipment that provided information on precision farming through a dedicated set of variables. This data collection provides a new source of information about the adoption of digital and technology-based approaches, with particular attention on practices that may improve resource efficiency and reduce environmental pressure. They include: *the use of robotics and automated machinery (such as autonomous tractors or robotic milking systems) *variable rate application techniques (where inputs are applied at differing rates within a field based on spatial variability) *tools for precision crop monitoring (including satellite-based observation, drone imagery or GPS-guided equipment). In addition to survey data, EU countries increasingly make use of administrative data sources. This growing integration of administrative data has been facilitated by advances in information technology (IT) systems and improved coordination between government authorities. As a result, the system has resulted in a reduction in response burden for farmers. For more information: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-25-058 Integrated farm statistics manual, 2023 survey – 2026 edition] ====Indicator definitions ==== '''Agricultural holding''' An agricultural holding (or farm) is a single unit, both technically and economically, operating under a single management, which undertakes economic activities in agriculture, either as its primary or secondary activity. The holding may also provide other supplementary (non-agricultural) products and services. '''Farm manager''' A farm manager is the natural person responsible for the normal daily financial and production routines of running an agricultural holding. Agricultural holdings normally have only 1 manager, but it is possible for there to be co-managers, for example if the holder shares the management with a spouse or other family member. The manager undertakes the day-to-day management of the holding without assumption of economic and legal responsibility for it (as these are the responsibilities of the holder). In sole-holder holdings, the manager and the holder are usually the same person. Young farm managers are defined as farm managers under the age of 40 years. '''Precision farming''' The use of precision farming refers to the application of modern IT to gather, process and analyse multisource data of high spatial and temporal resolution for decision making and operations in the management of crop production. It involves, among other techniques: *robotics *variable rate technology (GPS system or Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)) *the use of precision monitoring through sensor technologies (LiDAR, Ph sensors, GPS sensors, accelerometer sensors, electromagnetic sensors) *big data and artificial intelligence. '''Robotics''' refers to machines with enhanced levels of intelligence that enable them to perform autonomous agricultural tasks without direct human intervention. These tasks may relate to crop or livestock production and include, for example, soil preparation, seeding, transplanting, weeding, pest and disease control, harvesting, automatic feeding, milking or manure removal. Within this broad category, robotics for plant protection products refers specifically to robotic systems used for the application of plant protection products in crop production. These systems may operate autonomously or in a semi-autonomous mode and are often integrated with monitoring technologies such as sensors, scanners or cameras to detect pests and diseases. Applications include mobile or wireless pesticide spraying robots, band sprayers, semi-automatic spraying systems in greenhouses and unmanned aerial systems such as drones or helicopters used for the targeted application of plant protection products. '''Variable rate techniques''' are precision agriculture technologies that enable the automated and spatially differentiated application of agricultural inputs, such as seeds, fertilisers, plant protection products or water. Application rates are adjusted according to intra-field variability, based on data from sources such as sensors, satellite imagery, geographic positioning systems (GPS) or other digital monitoring systems. These techniques aim to optimise input use by improving efficiency and productivity while reducing the consumption of conventional agricultural inputs. They are an integral part of precision farming systems and may incorporate enabling technologies such as drones or artificial intelligence. Variable rate techniques include map-based or sensor-based variable rate application systems; variable rate seeding systems; variable rate fertiliser application systems; planters and seed drills equipped with variable rate technology; map-based weed control systems; and pneumatic spreaders with variable discharge control. '''Precision monitoring of crops''' refers to the use of integrated technologies, devices, protocols and computational methods to observe, measure and analyse crop conditions in a spatially and temporally detailed manner. It supports improved agricultural management by providing timely and high-resolution information on crop development and field variability, thereby serving as a decision-support framework for precision agriculture that enables more targeted and efficient management of inputs and interventions. The precision monitoring of crops combines multiple data sources and monitoring systems, including weather stations, digital mapping of soil properties, yield mapping, vegetation indices, soil scanning technologies and crop health monitoring systems. Data are typically collected through in-field sensors, remote sensing platforms (such as satellites or drones) and geospatial information systems; they are subsequently processed using analytical or algorithmic tools. Applications include the assessment of soil variability, monitoring of crop growth and stress conditions, detection of nutrient deficiencies or the identification of pest/disease outbreaks. '''Standard output''' The standard output is defined as the average monetary value of agricultural output at farm-gate price (crops and livestock), providing a measure of the overall economic size of farms, expressed in euro (€). The standard output may be used to classify agricultural holdings by type of farming and/or by economic size. '''Utilised agricultural area''' The utilised agricultural area refers to the total area of land used by an agricultural holding for agricultural production. It comprises arable land, permanent grassland, permanent crops and kitchen gardens, regardless of land tenure or legal form of occupation. It also includes areas of common land where these are actively utilised by the holding. The utilised agricultural area excludes non-agricultural land such as woodland, farmyards, buildings and other land not used for agricultural production. ===Context=== '''Common agricultural policy (CAP)''' The [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy_en common agricultural policy CAP] is among the EU’s oldest policies (it was launched in 1962), supporting agriculture and contributing to Europe’s food security. It aims to: *support farms and improve agricultural productivity so that consumers have a stable supply of affordable food *ensure that EU farmers can make a reasonable living *help tackle climate change and the sustainable management of natural resources *maintain rural areas and landscapes across the EU *keep the rural economy alive, promoting jobs in farming, agri-food industries and associated sectors. At the end of 2021, a political agreement was reached on a common agricultural policy for the period 2023 to 2027. It entered into force on 1 January 2023, aiming to establish a fairer, greener and more performance-based CAP. ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/2116/oj Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 on the financing, management and monitoring of the common agricultural policy]'' is designed to make the CAP more responsive to future challenges, while continuing to support EU farms for a sustainable and competitive agricultural sector. This modernised agricultural policy is built around 10 specific objectives that are focused on social, environmental and economic goals: *to ensure a fair income for farms *to increase competitiveness *to improve the position of farms in the food chain *climate change action *environmental care *to preserve landscapes and biodiversity *to support generational renewal *vibrant rural areas *to protect food and health quality *to foster knowledge and innovation. After 2027, the CAP will have a central place within the EU’s budget to deliver on the strategic orientations provided by the EU’s [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/overview-vision-agriculture-food/vision-agriculture-and-food_en vision for agriculture and food]. The CAP funding framework will be delivered through National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRP Plans), designed to result in a better use of synergies across the various funding instruments to address the needs of EU farmers, agriculture and rural areas. For example, income support for farmers will be simplified by moving from the current system of land-linked ‘entitlements’ to payments based on eligible hectares and lump sums. The EU has budgeted €387 billion of funding for the CAP as part of its long-term budget, the multiannual financial framework (2021 to 2027). This comes from 2 different funds: €291 billion from the European agricultural guarantee fund (EAGF) and €96 billion from the European agricultural fund for rural development (EAFRD), the latter including €8 billion allocated as part of the European Recovery Instrument (also known as NextGenerationEU). This funding is intended to encourage farmers to help deliver a green transition in agriculture and rural areas, while providing support for reforms considered essential to Europe’s ambitious environmental targets. The CAP includes several interventions specifically targeting young farmers. They are tailored to the national conditions of each EU country and developed within their [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/cap-my-country/cap-strategic-plans_en strategic plans]. At least 3% of each country’s budget for direct payments must go to support for young farmers. Young farmers may benefit from a combination of several actions including: *complementary income support for young farmers *support for the establishment of young farmers, new farmers and rural business start-ups. '''European Green Deal''' ''[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en The European green deal]'' is the EU’s strategy for sustainable growth; it aims to turn climatic and environmental challenges into opportunities for a broad range of policy areas. The CAP plays a part in this transition, as approximately 40% of its budget is climate relevant. The European agriculture and food system, supported by the CAP, is already a global benchmark in terms of safety, security of supply, nutrition and quality. New policy developments are designed to ensure that the EU’s agriculture sector remains a leader in sustainability, delivering environmental, health and social benefits by encouraging farm managers to contribute towards its climatic and environmental ambitions. The EU’s goals include: *ensuring food security in the face of climate change and biodiversity loss *reducing the environmental and climate footprint of the EU’s food system *strengthening the resilience of the EU’s food system *leading a global transition towards competitive sustainability from farm to fork. '''Farm to fork strategy''' ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0381 A Farm to Fork Strategy for a fair, healthy and environmentally friendly food system]'' (COM(2020) 381 final) lies at the heart of the European green deal. It has several wide-ranging aims, including to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and the consumption of natural resources; protect the environment and reverse biodiversity loss; promote fairer economic returns for those in the supply chain (particularly primary producers); and increase the level of organic farming. With this in mind, the strategy includes a number of targets designed to transform food systems across the EU by 2030. For example, it aims to increase the share of agricultural land in the EU used for organic farming to at least 25%, reduce by at least 50% the use of chemicals and more hazardous pesticides, and reduce by at least 20% the use of fertilisers. By making food systems environmentally friendlier, fairer, healthier and more sustainable, the EU’s farm to fork strategy seeks to accelerate the EU’s green transition. '''Biodiversity strategy''' The ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52020DC0380 EU Biodiversity strategy for 2030 – Bringing nature back into our lives]'' (COM(2020) 380 final) is a comprehensive and long-term plan to protect nature and reverse the degradation of ecosystems (in particular, those with the most potential to capture and store carbon and to prevent/reduce the impact of natural disasters). It seeks to put Europe’s biodiversity on a path to recovery by 2030, while building resilience to future threats such as the impacts of climate change, forest fires, food insecurity and disease outbreaks. As part of the strategy: *the EU will expand [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/nature-and-biodiversity/natura-2000_en Natura 2000 sites] to protect areas with high biodiversity and climate value *the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/nature-and-biodiversity/nature-restoration-regulation_en Nature Restoration Law] sets binding targets for recovering habitats and species across the EU; it also focuses on unlocking biodiversity funding, strengthening governance and integrating nature into public and business decisions. '''A vision for agriculture and food''' In February 2025, the European Commission unveiled a ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0075 Vision for Agriculture and Food – Shaping the future of farming and the agri-food sector for future generations in Europe]'' (COM(2025) 75 final). This seeks to foster trust and dialogue across the entire value chain through close engagement with relevant institutions, farmers, food chain operators and civil society. The vision aims to create a sustainable, resilient and competitive agri-food sector that supports farmers, while protecting the environment. Key objectives include promoting innovation and digitalisation, ensuring fair incomes for farmers and strengthening food security. It also seeks to eliminate unfair trading practices and to propose a fairer, simpler and more targeted CAP. By fostering collaboration, research and policy support, the EU aims to balance productivity with sustainability, ensuring the agriculture sector can meet future challenges and provide safe, affordable food for all Europeans. Within the context of the vision, the EU has, among other initiatives: *delivered a [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/overview-vision-agriculture-food/generational-renewal_en generational renewal strategy] *promoted women’s participation in farming and the rural economy, for example through the establishment of the [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/overview-vision-agriculture-food/women-farmers_en Women in farming platform] *presented a [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/bioeconomy-strategy_en bioeconomy strategy]. ===Other articles=== *[[Agricultural_production_-_crops|Agricultural production – crops]] *[[Agricultural_production_-_livestock and meat|Agricultural production – livestock and meat]] title: Air safety statistics in the EU
text:
Data show a good safety record for commercial air transport in recent years, particularly for EU-registered operators Data from September 2025 Planned article update: 16 Septmber 2026 In 2024, 91.2% of all fatalities in aviation accidents on EU territory occurred in non-commercial operations involving EU-registered aircraft (83 out of 91 fatalities). In 2024, aeroplanes accounted for the highest share of fatalities in aviation accidents within EU territory involving world-registered aircraft (76.4%). 2024 recorded the highest number of persons seriously injured in commercial air transport accidents within EU territory involving EU-registered aircraft over the past decade (27 persons). [[Image: Persons killed in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft by aircraft category, EU, 2023 and 2024_(number).png|thumb|center|750px|''Source:'' Eurostat, {{Stable link|title=|code=tran_sf_aviavi}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the number of persons killed in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft on EU territory. Five categories of aircraft each have two columns representing the years 2023 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Detailed data from the [https://easa.europa.eu/ European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA)] show a good safety record for commercial air transport in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union]] over the past years. However, a single major accident, such as the one in July 2023, can seriously affect this generally positive image. Most fatalities are recorded in non-commercial operations. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) is a European Union agency, governed by European public law. EASA has created standard requirements for regulating safety and promoting environmental sustainability in civil aviation. It collects detailed data on aviation incidents and accidents and performs in-depth safety-relevant analyses. === Most of the aviation accident fatalities concerned non-commercial operations === In its Annual Safety Review 2018, the EASA highlighted that 2017 was an exceptional year for global airline safety, with fewer fatalities than at any time in the industry's history (155 deaths). In the Annual Safety Review 2019, EASA reminded us that there is no room for complacency, following an increase observed in 2018: 189 persons in total died in aviation accidents on EU territory in 2018, involving EU-registered aircraft. As highlighted in EASA's Annual Safety Review 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic brought new challenges to every aspect of life and industry on earth. In particular, the air transport industry was severely impacted as a consequence of the restrictive measures taken by countries around the world to prevent the spread of the pandemic. The Annual Safety Review 2022 pointed out the risk to safety due to the reduced flying time of pilots over an extended period, the traffic in Europe in 2021 being back around 85% of 2019 levels. The Annual Safety Review 2023 confirmed this trend for 2022, with traffic levels at around 93% of the pre-pandemic levels, with the share rising to 95.5% in 2023, according to the Annual Safety Review 2024. The Annual Safety Review 2025 confirmed again this trend with the number of fatal accidents rising again to the level of the pre-COVID-19 pandemic in 2024. In 2024, 91 fatalities were recorded in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft and within the EU territory. However, fewer fatalities were recorded in 2024 compared with the previous year, as shown on Figure 1. In both 2023 and 2024, most fatalities were linked to accidents involving aeroplanes (83.5% of the total number of fatalities in 2023 and 81.3% in 2024). The accidents which occurred in 2024 included crashes of aeroplanes conducting non-commercial operations in France (18 victims), Spain (15 victims) and Italy (13 victims). All accidents in 2024 involving sailplanes occurred during non-commercial operations. The accident with the highest fatalities involved German-registered aircraft, in which 7 persons lost their lives. Half of the fatalities in helicopter accidents (in total operations) occurred in Spain (4 fatalities), involving a helicopter registered in that country. [[Image: Persons killed in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft by aircraft category, EU, 2023 and 2024_(number).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Persons killed in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft by aircraft category, EU, 2023 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, {{Stable link|title=|code=tran_sf_aviavi}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the number of persons killed in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft on EU territory. Five categories of aircraft each have two columns representing the years 2023 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, 91.2% of the fatalities recorded were related to non-commercial operations (see Figure 2). In all the previous years, this category also accounted for the majority of the fatalities, with the exception of 2015. In that year, crashes involving commercial air transport accounted for 58.7% of the fatalities, due to the accident of a German-registered aircraft in France (150 fatalities). Together with 2014 (when 82 persons were killed in non-commercial operations accidents), 2024 recorded the lowest number of fatalities with 83 persons losing their lives in non-commercial operations on EU territory. [[Image: Persons killed in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft by aviation category, EU, 2024_(%)_up.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Persons killed in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft by aviation category, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, {{Stable link|title=|code=tran_sf_aviavi}}|alt= Pie chart showing the percentage of persons killed in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft by aviation category in the EU for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, the second category with the highest number of fatalities was specialised operations, which accounted for 5.5% of all fatalities in aviation accidents (5 persons killed). In comparison, there were 7 fatalities in 2023, 5 in 2022 and 11 in 2021. Specialised operations include activities such as agriculture, aerial advertisement, photography, and similar tasks. To complete the picture, fatalities in commercial air transport accounted for 3.3% of all fatalities in aviation accidents (3 persons killed), an increase compared with 2023, when no fatalities were recorded in this category. === No major accidents involving EU-registered aircraft were recorded in commercial air transport over the last 9 years === Figure 3 shows the number of persons killed in commercial air transport accidents involving EU-registered aircraft for the period 2014-2024. Information on whether the accident took place on EU territory or elsewhere in the world is also presented in the chart. From 2016 to 2024, no major accidents were recorded in commercial air transport. However, 2015 was marked by the German aircraft crash mentioned above and the accident on the Sinai Peninsula (Egypt) involving an Irish-registered aircraft on a charter flight (224 fatalities). In July 2014, an aircraft registered in Spain, but leased to an Algerian operator, crashed in Mali (116 fatalities). [[Image: Persons killed worldwide in commercial air transport involving EU-registered aircraft, by area of occurrence, 2014-2024_(number).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Persons killed worldwide in commercial air transport involving EU-registered aircraft, by area of occurrence, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, {{Stable link|title=|code=tran_sf_aviavi}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the number of persons killed in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft on EU territory. Each reference year from 2014 to 2024 have two columns representing the EU territory and the rest of the world. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In addition to accidents involving EU-registered aircraft, there were also other fatal air transport accidents in EU airspace involving aircraft that were not registered in the EU. Figure 4 presents the number of fatalities in commercial air transport accidents since 2014 on EU territory, regardless of whether the aircraft involved were registered in an EU country or in another country. Thus, the information shown in Figure 4 includes the accident in France mentioned earlier. No other major accidents occurred on EU territory involving world-registered aircraft. [[Image: Persons killed in commercial air transport involving world-registered aircraft, EU, 2014-2024_(number).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Persons killed in commercial air transport involving world-registered aircraft, EU, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, {{Stable link|title=|code=tran_sf_aviavi}}|alt= Line chart showing the number of persons killed in commercial air transport involving world-registered aircraft in the EU over the period from 2014 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === There were 685 fatalities in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft over the period 2020-2024 === Table 1 presents the cumulated number of persons killed in aviation accidents over the period 2020-2024, by country of registration, area of occurrence (worldwide or in EU territory) and aircraft category. Worldwide, there were 635 fatalities in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft, of which 525 occurred in aeroplane accidents. Over the same period, 85 persons were killed in sailplane accidents, 68 in helicopter accidents and 7 in balloon accidents involving EU-registered aircraft. Of all those killed worldwide, 495 fatalities from aeroplane accidents, 82 from sailplane accidents, 64 from helicopter accidents and 6 from balloon accidents occurred within EU territory. No fatalities were recorded in Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) accidents over the period 2020-2024. However, it should be noted that data on UAS accidents have been collected only since 2023. [[Image: Persons killed in aviation accidents by country of registration, area of occurrence and aircraft category, 2020-2024 (number).png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Persons killed in aviation accidents by country of registration, area of occurrence and aircraft category, 2020-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, {{Stable link|title=|code=tran_sf_aviavi}}|alt= Table showing the number of persons killed in aviation accidents by country of registration, area of occurrence and aircraft category in the EU, individual EU Member States and EFTA countries over the period 2020 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] During the period 2020-2024, no fatalities were recorded in accidents involving aircraft registered in Estonia, Ireland, Croatia, Luxembourg and Malta. Over the same period, less than 10 fatalities occurred in accidents involving aircraft registered in 12 other EU countries. The number of fatalities ranged between 10 and 50 in accidents involving aircraft registered in a further 7 countries. Most fatalities in aviation accidents during this period occurred in connection with aircraft registered in France and Germany (217 and 162 persons killed, respectively), followed by Italy with 73 fatalities. Among the EFTA countries, there were 40 fatalities in accidents involving aircraft registered in Switzerland and 12 involving aircraft registered in Norway. Table 2 presents the cumulated number of persons killed in aviation accidents over the period 2020-2024, by country of occurrence and aircraft category, for all aircraft regardless of their country of registration. Overall, 681 fatalities were recorded in air transport accidents that occurred within EU territory. Among these, 520 involved aeroplanes, 84 sailplanes, 70 helicopters, 6 balloons and 1 UAS. For helicopters, sailplanes, balloons and UAS, accidents often occur in the country where the aircraft is registered, as they mainly concern domestic flights. However, for aeroplanes, differences between the country of registration and the country of occurrence of the accident can be higher. [[Image: Persons killed in aviation accidents involving world-registered aircraft by country of occurrence and aircraft category, 2020-2024 (number).png|thumb|center|700px|Table 2: Persons killed in aviation accidents involving world-registered aircraft by country of occurrence and aircraft category, 2020-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, {{Stable link|title=|code=tran_sf_aviavi}}|alt= Table showing the number of persons killed in aviation accidents involving world-registered aircraft by country of occurrence and aircraft category in the EU, individual EU Member States and EFTA countries over the period 2020 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In the period 2020-2024, no fatalities were recorded in Estonia, Latvia, Luxembourg and Malta. Over the same period, there were less than 10 fatalities in 10 other EU Member States. The number of fatalities ranged between 10 and 50 in 9 additional Member States. Most fatalities in aviation accidents occurred in France and Germany (205 and 113 fatalities, respectively) between 2020 and 2024. When looking at aeroplanes, France registered the highest number of fatalities over the same period (175 persons killed). === The number of persons seriously injured in commercial air transport accidents doubled in 2024 === While fatalities highlight the most severe outcomes of aviation accidents, injuries (whether serious or slight) provide additional insight into the broader aviation safety picture. In 2024, the aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft resulted in 214 persons being seriously or slightly injured, representing a slight decrease compared with 2023 (229 persons) as shown in Figure 5. By aircraft category, the number of persons seriously or slightly injured in accidents involving EU-registered sailplanes almost doubled between 2023 and 2024 (23 and 41 injuries, respectively). Accidents involving EU-registered aeroplanes accounted for 60.3% of all persons injured in 2024 (129 persons injured), making this the category with the highest number of injuries. No persons were reported seriously or slightly injured in EU-registered UAS accidents in either 2023 or 2024. [[Image: Persons injured in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft by aircraft category, EU, 2023 and 2024_(number).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Persons injured in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft by aircraft category, EU, 2023 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, {{Stable link|title=|code=tran_sf_aviavi}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the number of persons injured in aviation accidents involving EU-registered aircraft by aircraft category within EU territory. Five categories of aircraft each have two columns representing the years 2023 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When focusing on commercial air transport accidents over the period 2014-2024 (see Figure 6), the total number of persons injured has been increasing since 2019 (from 19 in 2019 to 63 in 2024). This rise is mainly due to the growing number of persons slightly injured, which went up from 2 in 2020 to 37 in 2023 and 36 in 2024. These high figures for slight injuries are due to an accident in Spain in 2023, which resulted in 27 persons being slightly injured, and to accidents in Spain (10 persons slightly injured) and Italy (12 persons slightly injured) in 2024. Despite these increases, the number of persons seriously injured decreased to 12 in 2023, but rose again to 27 in 2024, mainly due to an accident in Lithuania in which 10 persons were seriously injured. [[Image: Persons seriously injured and slightly injured in commercial air transport involving EU-registered aircraft, EU, 2014-2024_(number).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Persons seriously injured and slightly injured in commercial air transport involving EU-registered aircraft, EU, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, {{Stable link|title=|code=tran_sf_aviavi}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing the number of persons seriously injured and slightly injured in commercial air transport accidents involving EU-registered aircraft within EU territory. Each column representing the years 2014 to 2024 contains two stacks representing persons seriously injured and persons slightly injured. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Aeroplanes were the aircraft type most frequently involved in accidents in 2024 === Table 3 presents the number of accidents involving world-registered aircraft by country of occurrence and aircraft category in 2024. In total, 533 air transport accidents were reported in the EU, with aeroplanes accounting for the largest share (321), ahead of sailplanes (127) and helicopters (64). In 2024, 14 balloon accidents and 7 UAS accidents were also recorded. [[Image: Accidents involving world-registered aircraft by country of occurrence and aircraft category, 2024 (number).png|thumb|center|750px|Table 3: Accidents involving world-registered aircraft by country of occurrence and aircraft category, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, {{Stable link|title=|code=tran_sf_aviaac}}|alt= Table showing the number of accidents involving world-registered aircraft by aircraft category in the EU, individual EU Member States and EFTA countries in 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, no aviation accidents were recorded in Cyprus, Latvia, Luxembourg and Malta. Less than 10 accidents occurred in 10 other EU countries, while in another 10 EU countries the number of accidents ranged between 10 and 50. Most accidents involving aircraft registered worldwide took place in France, Germany, and Spain, with 124, 113, and 59 accidents, respectively. Among aeroplanes specifically, France recorded the highest number of accidents, with 100 accidents. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Air_safety_statistics_2025-10_up.xlsx|title=Air safety statistics}} ===Data sources=== In May 2025, an updated administrative arrangement between Eurostat and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) was signed regarding the technical cooperation in the field of air transport safety statistics. The data presented in this article stem from the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA). The EASA is an agency of the European Union that is governed by European public law and establishes common requirements for the regulation of safety and environmental sustainability in civil aviation. EASA was set up by a [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2002/1592/oj/eng Council and Parliament Regulation (EC) 1592/2002] repealed by [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32018R1139 Regulation (EU) 2018/1139]. The EASA collects detailed data on aviation incidents and accidents and performs detailed safety-relevant analyses as far as possible. The agreement between EASA and Eurostat allows for the dissemination of selected statistical data through Eurostat's dissemination database. All data displayed in this article are annual, with available time series going back to 2014. Data for 2022, 2023 and 2024 should be considered provisional, as accident investigations may still be ongoing. The conclusions of the final investigation reports might therefore slightly alter the data. Data are collected by EASA under the frame of the [https://www.easa.europa.eu/en/document-library/regulations/commission-regulation-eu-no-9652012/ Commission Regulation (EU) No 965/2012]. The so-called 'Air Ops Regulation' contains provisions for the following types of air operations with aeroplanes and helicopters: * commercial air transport (CAT) operations, * non-commercial operations with complex motor-powered aircraft (NCC), * non-commercial operations with other-than complex motor-powered aircraft (NCO), and * specialised operations (e.g. aerial work), both commercial and non-commercial (SPO). The Air Ops Regulation is applicable to all the EU Member States and to all operators of aeroplanes and helicopters which have their principal place of business, are established or reside in an EU Member State. More information about [https://www.easa.europa.eu/en/domains/air-operations/air-operations-general Air Operations] are available on EASA website. Accidents are defined as follow in [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02010R0996-20240519&qid=1760021584682 Regulation (EU) No 996/2010]: an occurrence associated with the operation of an aircraft which, in the case of a manned aircraft, takes place between the time any person boards the aircraft with the intention of flight until such time as all such persons have disembarked, or in the case of an unmanned aircraft, takes place between the time the aircraft is ready to move with the purpose of flight until such time it comes to rest at the end of the flight and the primary propulsion system is shut down, in which: * a person is fatally or seriously injured as a result of: ** being in the aircraft, or, ** direct contact with any part of the aircraft, including parts which have become detached from the aircraft, or, ** direct exposure to jet blast except when the injuries are from natural causes, self-inflicted or inflicted by other persons, or when the injuries are to stowaways hiding outside the areas normally available to the passengers and crew; or * the aircraft sustains damage or structural failure which adversely affects the structural strength, performance or flight characteristics of the aircraft, and would normally require major repair or replacement of the affected component, except for engine failure or damage, when the damage is limited to a single engine, (including its cowlings or accessories), to propellers, wing tips, antennas, probes, vanes, tires, brakes, wheels, fairings, panels, landing gear doors, windscreens, the aircraft skin (such as small dents or puncture holes) or minor damages to main rotor blades, tail rotor blades, landing gear, and those resulting from hail or bird strike, (including holes in the radome); or * the aircraft is missing or is completely inaccessible. ===Context=== The implementation of the [https://www.europarl.europa.eu/factsheets/en/sheet/133/air-transport-single-european-sky Single European Sky] (various legislative packages, 2004-2024) resulted in a considerable increase in air traffic and the number of air carriers. Aviation safety in the European Union is based on close cooperation between the European Commission, the EASA, [https://www.eurocontrol.int/ Eurocontrol] and the national civil aviation authorities, but also with aircraft manufacturers, airlines, and, considering the inherently international nature of air transport, the [http://www.icao.int/ International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO)]. The backbone of this cooperation is a set of common safety rules, directly applicable in a uniform manner across the EU. Safety checks are performed at European airports on a random basis, but with particular attention to companies which have previously shown safety deficiencies. This can lead to restrictions or even the banning of non-compliant air carriers from flying to Europe. ===Other articles=== *[[Air passenger transport statistics|Air passenger transport statistics]] title: Applying the degree of urbanisation manual
text:
__notoc__ ONLINE PUBLICATION
Applying the degree of urbanisation manual
 ''Applying the Degree of Urbanisation – A methodological manual to define cities, towns and rural areas for international comparisons'' is an online publication, also available to [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-02-20-499 download in PDF format]. It was produced in close collaboration by 6 organisations – the [[Glossary:European_Commission_(EC)|European Commission]], the [https://www.fao.org/home/en Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)], the [https://unhabitat.org/ United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat)], the [[Glossary:International_Labour_Organization_(ILO)|International Labour Organization (ILO)]], the [[Glossary:Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development_(OECD)|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)]] and [[Glossary:World_Bank|The World Bank]]. This manual develops a harmonised methodology to facilitate international statistical comparisons and to classify the entire territory of a country along an urban-rural continuum. The degree of urbanisation classification defines cities, towns and semi-dense areas, and rural areas. This first level of the classification may be complemented by a range of more detailed concepts, such as: metropolitan areas, commuting zones, dense towns, semi-dense towns, suburban or peri-urban areas, villages, dispersed rural areas and mostly uninhabited areas. This manual is intended to complement and not replace the definitions used by national statistical offices (NSOs) and ministries. It has been designed principally as a guide for data producers, suppliers and statisticians so that they have the necessary information to implement the methodology and ensure coherency within their data collections. It may also be of interest to users of subnational statistics so they may better understand, interpret and use official subnational statistics for taking informed decisions and policymaking.
