title: Aquaculture statistics
text:
This article presents information on aquaculture activities in the EU. Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: April 2027 Aquaculture farming in the EU yielded about 1.0 million tonnes of aquatic organisms in 2024, worth €4.6 billion. Spain, France, Greece and Italy together produced two-thirds (64.6%) of the EU's aquaculture output volume in 2024. EU aquaculture production is mainly focused on finfish species and molluscs. [[Image:Total production of fishery products (million tonnes of live weight, EU, 2000-2024_v2).png|thumb|center|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=fish_ca_main}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=fish_aq_q}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=fish_aq2a}}|alt= an image of the total production of fishery products]] This article gives an overview of recent statistics relating to [[Glossary:Aquaculture|aquaculture]] production in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]].
The current common fisheries policy (CFP) of the EUSee, [http://ec.europa.eu/fisheries/cfp/index_en.htm http://ec.europa.eu/fisheries/cfp/index_en.htm]. aims at an environmentally, economically and socially sustainable use of the common resource including aquaculture production. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. == EU Aquaculture == '''Aquaculture: in 2024, about 1.0 million tonnes of aquatic organisms yielded in the EU, worth €4.6 billion''' Aquaculture is the production of fish and other aquatic organisms like molluscs and crustaceans under controlled conditions; it is an alternative to catching wild fish and takes place both inland and in marine areas. Aquaculture is a key component of both the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) and the Blue Growth For more information, see the [https://ec.europa.eu/maritimeaffairs/policy/blue_growth_en maritime affairs] section on the European Commission's website. agenda to support sustainable growth in this sector. Aquaculture farming in the EU yielded an estimated 1.0 million tonnes of aquatic organisms in 2024, corresponding to one-quarter of the output of European fisheries as a whole. This share was well below the global average in 2022 (about 49% ''The state of world fisheries and aquaculture, 2024'' — FAO, available at [https://openknowledge.fao.org/handle/20.500.14283/cd0683en].), underlining the growth potential in the EU. In terms of output, the EU's aquaculture sector was the thirteenth largest worldwide, a little0 more than Thailand, with a 0.9% share of the volume of global output in 2022. The value of aquaculture production in the EU was an estimated €4.6 billion in 2024, representing just over two-fifths of the total value of the EU's total production of fishery products (landings and aquaculture). '''Four countries produced about two-thirds of the EU's aquaculture output volume and its value''' Four EU countries were responsible for about two-thirds (64.6%) of the EU's total output in tonnes live weight of farmed aquatic organisms in 2024 (see Figure 1); Spain produced a little less than one-quarter (an estimated 24.3%) of the total, followed by France (17.9%), Greece (12.6%) and Italy (9.7%). Different aquatic organisms fetch different prices. For instance, the average first sale prices for mussels were about €1.3 per kg, for seabass around €7.3 per kg, and for tuna were about €12.6 per kg. Among EU countries, France had the highest value of aquaculture output in 2024 (an estimated €857 million), representing 18.5% of the EU total. The value of output was next highest in Spain (€856 million), then in Greece (€689 million) and Italy (€384 million). To put the EU's aquaculture industry in some perspective, the value of aquaculture output in Norway exceeded that of the whole of the EU; Norway produced 1.6 million tonnes of aquatic organisms (almost exclusively salmon), worth €9.5 billion in 2024. Norway was the world's sixth largest producer in aquaculture fish production in 2022, with a 1.8% global share. It was also the world's second largest exporter of aquatic organisms, after China. [[Image:Figure 1 Aquaculture production (tonnes of live weight, 2024_v3).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Aquaculture production
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/fish_aq2a__custom_21026882/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=6907c361-784d-4409-8351-44ea706d44dc&c=1776341035000 fish_aq2a])|alt= a vertical bar chart showing the aquaculture production in 2023 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] All fisheries production in the EU's landlocked countries (Czechia, Hungary, Austria and Slovakia) comes from aquaculture. Note that Luxembourg has no market production. In general, aquaculture plays a major role in the countries around the Mediterranean Sea and the Black Sea. In Malta, aquaculture accounted for 91.4% of total fisheries production in tonnes live weight in 2023, a similar proportion as in Slovenia. Aquaculture also accounted for a majority of total fisheries production in Cyprus (89.0%), Romania (79.9%), Greece (69.8%) and Bulgaria (62.8%). == Aquaculture species and specialisation == '''EU aquaculture production focused on finfish species and molluscs''' Finfish (particularly trout, seabream, seabass, carp, tuna and salmon) and molluscs (particularly mussels, oysters and clams) together accounted for almost all of aquaculture production by weight in the EU in 2024. Rainbow trout was the most valuable species farmed in the EU in 2023, accounting for 17.9% of all aquaculture production. The farmed production of seabass, seabream and oysters were the next most valuable (see Figure 2). [[Image:Main_species_in_aquaculture_production_(%,_EU,_2024).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Main species of aquaculture production
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/FISH_AQ2A__custom_10881832/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=97b87b3f-29dd-4a01-8d91-125c51a2b251&c=1713171993577 fish_aq2a]) and Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/FISH_AQ2A__custom_3504224/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=e59c73ca-5418-41fb-b181-a738d557c700&c=1664892047700 fish_aq2a])|alt= two horizontal bar charts showing the main species in aquaculture production, one chart shows the weight in tonnes and one chart shows the values in euros. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The production of algae and seaweed is an emerging sector of the blue economy. In addition to catches at sea, principally in the Atlantic, Northeast area, there is an increasing, albeit small, amount from aquaculture. These algae and seaweeds (including brown, red and green seaweeds) are used for example in food, feed production, industrial and pharmaceutical products. Although the volume of production of aquatic plants from aquaculture is small compared with catches and landings of aquatic plants (about 1%), the value of production is relatively high. France was the main EU producer of farmed aquatic plants in 2024, which had an average price of about €20 per kg (wet weight). There is considerable specialisation in the market, with some EU countries like Spain and Portugal also targeting high value added cultivated species. '''A high degree of country specialisation within the EU''' The aquaculture sector is highly specialised within the EU. Spain produced nearly 3 in every 4 tonnes of the EU's farmed Mediterranean mussels (''Mytilus galloprovincialis'') in 2024, largely due to its rafts in the estuaries of northern Spain using the 'off bottom' method. Blue mussels (''Mytilus edulis'') were farmed in the Atlantic, Northeast area by the France (about half of the EU total in 2024), followed by the Netherlands and Ireland. Both 'off bottom' (preferred in Ireland) and 'on-bottom' methods (preferred in the Netherlands) were used. Atlantic bluefin tuna (''Thunnus thynnus'') were farmed in cages in only four EU countries: Malta accounted for about 53% of EU farmed production of bluefin tuna, Spain about 31%, Croatia about 14%, with a small amount (around 1%) also being produced in Portugal. Greece produced more than half of the EU's farmed production of gilthead seabream (''Sparus aurata'') and more than half of European seabass (''Dicentrarchus labrax'') in 2024. Poland and Czechia were the leading EU producers of common carp (''Cyprinus carpio''), together producing about half of the EU total. At world level, common carp was the fifth most farmed finfish species. Ireland was the only EU country farming salmon in the EU in 2024, producing about of 13 400 tonnes. However, this quantity was far below the 1.5 million tonnes farmed in Norway. At world level, Atlantic salmon (''Salmo salar'') was the eighth most produced finfish species. Within the EU, Pacific cupped oysters (''Magallana gigas'') were produced mainly in France. Worldwide, about 33% of all molluscs produced in 2022 were cupped oysters. Italy produced nearly 3 in every 4 tonnes in 2024 of the EU’s farmed Japanese carpet shell (''Ruditapes philippinarum''). At world level, it was the second most produced species among the molluscs (23% of the total in 2022). The production of farmed rainbow trout (''Oncorhynchus mykis'') in the EU is something of an exception to the general observation about country specialisation; rainbow trout were farmed in 25 EU countries. About 50% of the farmed live-weight of rainbow production in the EU in 2024 came from the combined output of France, Italy and Denmark. ==EU aquaculture volume and value== '''Steady level of EU aquaculture production volume but rising value''' Between 2010 and 2024, the volume of EU aquaculture production remained relatively stable (see Figure 3). However, the value of this production increased sharply (up 72%) due to higher prices, particularly in 2021 and 2022. [[Image:Aquaculture_production_and_value_(2010=100,_EU_and_Norway,_2010-2024).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Aquaculture production and value
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/fish_aq2a__custom_21026882/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=6907c361-784d-4409-8351-44ea706d44dc&c=1776341035000 fish_aq2a])|alt= a line chart with four lines showing the aquaculture production and value in the EU and Norway from 2010 to 2024. the lines show Norway in Euro, Norway in tonnes, the EU in Euro and the EU in tonnes. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Over this same period, there was a sharp increase in both the volume and value of Norwegian aquaculture production. In 2024, the volume of aquaculture production in Norway was 64% higher than in 2010. Despite a slight decrease of 0.7% between 2022 and 2023, output rebounded with an increase of approximately 1.0% in 2024. The value of output in 2024 was slightly less than two and half times more than in 2010, with sharp rises in 2021 and 2022 building on more gradual growth in many other years throughout the period. == Organic Aquaculture == '''Organic aquaculture production on the rise in the EU''' A number of EU countries farm aquaculture products according to organic criteria. In Ireland, almost half (about 46%) of aquaculture production (mainly salmon) was farmed organically in 2024. The next highest shares among EU countries were in the Netherlands (about 45% in 2024), Germany (about 35% in 2024) and Lithuania (about 29% in 2024). These shares contrasted sharply with other EU countries, including the three with the highest level of aquaculture production in 2024; the share of organic aquaculture production in total aquaculture production was less than 2% in France, Romania, Spain, Poland, Slovakia and Czechia. Organic aquaculture production grew rapidly across several EU countries between 2015 and 2024, in some cases from scratch. There was almost no organic production in the Netherlands and Germany in 2014. By 2024, organic aquaculture production was 13 000 tonnes in Germany and about 15 000 tonnes in the Netherlands. Organic aquaculture was already established in Italy but it expanded by a further 6 000 tonnes by 2024. By contrast, organic aquaculture production saw notable contractions in some regions; Ireland's output fell by almost 15 000 tonnes between 2015 and 2024, while Romania saw a decrease of 6 000 tonnes over the same period. [[Image:Organic_aquaculture_production_(%_share_of_total_aquaculture_production,_selected_Member_States,_2024_v2).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Organic aquaculture production
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/74f4fe89-3d9f-4f7e-a02b-9bd23ee42ee6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-15T13:01:33Z org_aqtspec])|alt= a vertical bar chart showing the Organic aquaculture production as a percentage share of the total aquaculture production in selected Member States. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] == Aquaculture production per capita == '''Only one country producing more aquaculture products per capita than the global average''' In 2024, the European Union (EU-27) produced an average of 2.25 kg of aquaculture products per capita. This average masks substantial variation among EU countries, as production is often concentrated in countries with extensive coastlines and favorable marine environments. Notable 2024 production levels include: Malta: 33.9 kg per capita, Greece: 12.2 kg per capita, Cyprus: 9.4 kg per capita and Croatia: 7.6 kg per capita. In contrast, landlocked countries and those with smaller sectors, such as Belgium (0.02 kg per capita) and Germany (0.4 kg per capita), contribute far less to the per capita average. [[Image:Map1 Aquaculture production per capita(in kg per capita, 2024_v5).png|thumb|center|700px|Map 1: Aquaculture production per capita
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=fish_aq2a}},([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_gind__custom_21049233/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=444c4a13-89d1-4e1e-a1f9-b2e4bbb4989c&c=1776429308000 demo_gind])|alt= a map showing the aquaculture production in 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The EU's per capita production is modest when compared to neighboring EEA countries that specialize in high-volume finfish farming, particularly Atlantic salmon. Based on 2024 data: Iceland produced 147.3 kg per capita, and Norway reached 300.9 kg per capita. Furthermore, the EU's production level is also significantly lower than the global average of approximately 16.4 kg per capita, which is based on a record world aquaculture production of 130.9 million tonnes reached in 2022 and a global population of roughly 8 billion people. While EU aquaculture volumes have remained relatively stable between 2010 and 2024, global production has followed a strong growth trajectory, increasing at nearly twice the rate of world population growth since 1961. The gap between the EU’s 2.25 kg per capita and the global average of 16.4 kg per capita highlights the significant "growth potential" for the sector within the Union. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=SE_AQ_2024_Tables_Graphs_v3.xlsx|title= Aquaculture: figures}} === Data sources === Fisheries statistics are collected by Eurostat from official national sources for the EU countries and members of the European Economic Area (EEA). The statistics are collected using internationally agreed concepts and definitions developed by the Coordinating Working Party (CWP), comprising Eurostat and several other international organisations with responsibilities in fisheries statistics. Aquaculture production refers to the farming of aquatic (freshwater or saltwater) organisms, under controlled conditions. Aquaculture implies some form of intervention in the natural rearing process such as regular stocking, feeding and protection from predators. Farming also implies individual or corporate ownership of the stock being cultivated. The legal basis for aquaculture statistics is [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32008R0762 Regulation (EC) No 762/2008] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 July 2008. The legal basis for organic aquaculture is [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2007/834/oj Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007] of 28 June 2007 on organic production and labelling of organic products and [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32008R0889&qid=1665674618269 Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008] of 5 September 2008 laying down detailed rules for its implementation. '''Symbols''' In order to improve readability, only the most significant meta-information has been included under the tables and figures. The following symbols are used, where necessary: *''Italic'' data value is forecasted, provisional or estimated and is likely to change *'''':'''' not available or confidential *''''-'''' not applicable === Context === [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52019DC0640&qid=1754146316522 The European Green Deal] and the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52021DC0236 EC Communication on aquaculture] for the period 2021 to 2030 underline the contribution of aquaculture to sustainable food systems and to the green transition. In this context, the sector is relevant to the Union’s objectives of achieving climate neutrality under the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32021R1119 European Climate Law], protecting nature under the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A52020DC0380 EU Biodiversity Strategy] for 2030, and advancing the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A52021DC0400 Zero Pollution Action Plan]. Practical guidance in this area was further developed in 2025 through the [https://aquaculture.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2025-10/code%20of%20good%20practices%20on%20fish%20welfare%20and%20fish%20welfare-HZ0125147ENN.pdf Code of good practices on fish welfare and fish welfare indicators], published under the EU aquaculture support framework. Support for these objectives is provided through the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/1139/oj/eng European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF)] for 2021–2027. With a budget of €6.1 billion, the EMFAF co-finances national programs to promote sustainable fishing and aquaculture. In April 2026, the Commission activated emergency funding under EMFAF to shield the fisheries and aquaculture sectors from the impacts of the Middle East crisis and to enable compensation for the resulting economic disruption. === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/fisheries/database Fisheries (fish)] :Catches by fishing area (fish_ca) :Aquaculture production (fish_aq) :Landings of fishery products (fish_ld) :Fishing fleet (fish_fleet) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/fisheries/database Fisheries (t_fish)] :Catches in all fishing regions (tag00076) :Catches in the title: Asylum decisions - quarterly statistics
text:
<metadescription>EU quarterly statistics provide an analysis of the asylum decisions.</metadescription>

<newarticle pic="Vanja Stokic Shutterstock 2137169587 RV.jpg"> </newarticle>
<updatedata>
Data extracted on 8 June 2026

Planned article update: 16 September 2026

</updatedata>

<highlight>

<highlight-message>
In Q1 2026, EU countries granted protection status at first instance to 84 925 asylum seekers, up 27.6% compared with the same quarter of 2025 and down 18.0% compared with Q4 2025.
</highlight-message>

<highlight-message>
Among persons granted protection status at first instance in the EU in Q1 2026, 53.4% received refugee status, 24.1% subsidiary protection, and 22.5% humanitarian status.
</highlight-message>

<highlight-message>
Afghans and Venezuelans were the main beneficiaries of protection status in the EU in Q1 2026.
</highlight-message>

[[Image:SE F0 Map.pdf|thumb|centre|700px|Source: Eurostat - [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e4b62e1c-99cb-4bc4-b0d5-1547900c90dc?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T13:29:01Z migr_asydcfstq]|alt= Map showing the number of asylum applicants granted protection status in reporting countries in Q1 2026. Each country is classified based on a range in numbers of positive first instance decisions. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

This article describes recent developments in relation to the [[Glossary:Asylum decision|first instance decisions on applications]] for international protection in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. It looks at the main trends, including positive and negative decisions, and focuses on the 3 types of positive outcomes: [[Glossary:Asylum_decision|refugee status, subsidiary protection and humanitarian status]]. It also provides information on the first instance decisions for unaccompanied minors and the number of decisions withdrawing protection status granted at first instance.

</highlight>

<articlecontent>

<sesection>
=== Main trends in the number of asylum decisions ===

In Q1 2026, 205 945 first instance decisions were issued in the EU, down 10.5% compared with the previous quarter (230 035) and up 3.7% compared with Q1 2025 (198 560). Out of these first instance decisions, 41.2% were positive (84 925) and 58.8% were negative (121 025).

EU countries granted protection status at first instance to 84 925 persons in Q1 2026, which is 18.0% less than in the previous quarter (103 580) and 27.6% more than in Q1 2025 (66 575).

Among these persons, 53.4% received refugee status (45 345 persons), 24.1% were granted subsidiary protection (20 460), and 22.5% received humanitarian status (19 120) (Figure 1). Compared to the previous quarter, the number of granted refugee statuses decreased by 21.7%, the number of humanitarian statuses decreased by 19.9%, and the number of subsidiary protections decreased by 6.2%. While refugee status and subsidiary protection are defined by EU law, humanitarian status is specific to national legislation and does not apply in some EU countries.

<vistool>
   <script type="application/json">{
    "utility": "wcloud",
    "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202606/90b0ae80-60dd-11f1-b429-d99b4afa80b1/uec.json"
}</script>
<caption>Figure 1</caption>
</vistool>

</sesection>


<sesection>
=== First instance decisions by country of decision ===

The highest number of asylum seekers who received protection status at first instance in Q1 2026 was reported by Germany (27 860, 32.8% of the EU total), ahead of Spain (16 820, 19.8%), and France (15 210, 17.9%) (Figure 2). Altogether, these 3 countries granted 70.5% of the protection statuses at first instance in the EU in Q1 2026. Compared to the previous quarter, there was a 27.5% decrease in Spain, 20.3% decrease in Germany and 12.8% decrease in France.

<vistool>
   <script type="application/json">{
    "utility": "wcloud",
    "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202606/9d267720-60dd-11f1-92e3-c3704e35a829/uec.json"
}</script>
<caption>Figure 2</caption>
</vistool>

The distribution of first instance decisions by outcome (refugee status, subsidiary protection, humanitarian status and rejected) in Q1 2026 varied by country (Figure 3). The percentage of positive decisions was highest in Estonia (98.6%), Austria (72.5%) and Spain (59.3%). By contrast, the lowest share of positive decisions at first instance was recorded in Croatia (3.1%), Cyprus (5.6%) and Czechia (14.7%). Hungary issued fewer than 30 first instance decisions, therefore no share was computed.

<vistool>
  <script type="application/json">{
    "utility": "wcloud",
    "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202606/a6881d30-60dd-11f1-92cd-bf5832d223c6/uec.json"
}</script>
<caption>Figure 3</caption>
</vistool>

</sesection>


<sesection>
=== First instance decisions by citizenship of asylum seekers ===

In Q1 2026, Afghans received the largest number of protection statuses in the EU (29.4% of all persons granted protection status at first instance in the EU, 24 960 persons). They were followed by Venezuelans (12.3%, 10 435), Syrians (7.7%, 6 505), and Malians (5.2%, 4 390) (Figure 4).

<vistool>
    <script type="application/json">{
    "utility": "wcloud",
    "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202606/af660240-60dd-11f1-976d-ed9b9fb73afd/uec.json"
}</script>
<caption>Figure 4</caption>
</vistool>

Among the top 10 citizenships that received the highest number of decisions in the EU in Q1 2026, Venezuelans had the highest [[Glossary:Recognition_rate|recognition rate]] (93.4%), followed by Afghans (77.8%) and Ukrainians (64.6%) (Figure 5).

<vistool>
   <script type="application/json">{
    "utility": "wcloud",
    "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202606/b82e05c0-60dd-11f1-9080-3f97f49f329b/uec.json"
}</script>
<caption>Figure 5</caption>
</vistool>

</sesection>


<sesection>
=== Decisions on asylum applications for unaccompanied minors ===

In Q1 2026, for the 26 EU countries that reported data, 3 500 first instance decisions on asylum applications lodged by unaccompanied minors were made in the EU, which is 0.1% less than in the previous quarter (3 505).

These decisions resulted in 1 535 unaccompanied minors granted protection status, down 10.5% compared with the previous quarter (1 715). The recognition rate for unaccompanied minors was 43.9% in Q1 2026.

Germany issued the highest number of positive decisions on applications lodged by unaccompanied minors (590 persons, 38.4% of the EU total) (Figure 6), followed by Italy (215, 14.0% of the EU total) and Spain (175, 11.4% of the EU total). Compared to the previous period, 42.2% more positive decisions were issued in Germany (415 persons in Q4 2025), 8.5% less  positive decisions in Italy (235) and 43.5% less in Spain (310).


<vistool>
    <script type="application/json">{
    "utility": "wcloud",
    "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202606/c132ed20-60dd-11f1-9467-091b08d22d8b/uec.json"
}</script>
<caption>Figure 6</caption>
</vistool>

The main beneficiaries of protection status among unaccompanied minors seeking asylum in the EU were Somalis (290 persons, 18.9% of the EU total), Afghans (255, 16.6%) and Syrians (230, 15.0%). Somalis unaccompanied minors had a recognition rate of 76.3%, Afghans 60.0% and Syrians 31.7%.

</sesection>


<sesection>
=== Decisions withdrawing protection status ===

EU countries may decide to withdraw protection status when new elements or findings arise indicating that there are reasons to reconsider the validity of protection.

In Q1 2026, EU countries took 5 300 decisions to withdraw protection status granted at first instance, up 15.2% compared with the previous quarter (4 600).

The highest number of decisions withdrawing protection status granted at first instance was reported by Austria (1 760, 33.2% of the EU total), followed by Germany (1 730, 32.6%) and the Netherlands (375, 7.1%). Compared to the previous quarter, there was a 71.3% increase in Germany (1 010 persons in Q4 2025), a 38.6% increase in Austria (1 270) and a 45.3% decrease in the Netherlands (685) (Figure 7).

</sesection>

<datadetails>

=== Data sources ===

[[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] produces statistics on a range of issues relating to international migration under the provisions of Article 4 of [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32007R0862 Regulation (EC) No 862/2007].

Data are provided to Eurostat with a monthly frequency (for asylum application statistics, including applications by unaccompanied minors), quarterly frequency (for first instance decisions) and annual frequency (for final decisions based on appeal or review and resettlement). The statistics are based on administrative sources and are provided to Eurostat by statistical authorities, ministries of the interior or related immigration agencies in the EU Member States.

Two different categories should be taken into account when analysing asylum statistics. The first includes asylum seekers who have lodged a claim (asylum application) and whose claim is under consideration by the relevant authority. The second is composed of persons who have been recognised, after consideration, as [[Glossary:Refugee|refugees]], or have been granted another kind of international protection ([[Glossary:Asylum decision|subsidiary protection]]), or were granted protection on the basis of the national law related to international protection ([[Glossary:Asylum decision|authorisations to stay for humanitarian reasons]]), or were rejected from having any form of protection.

Statistics on asylum decisions are available for different stages of the asylum procedure. [[Glossary:Asylum decision|First instance decisions]] are decisions granted by the respective authority acting as a first instance of the administrative or judicial asylum procedure in the receiving country. By contrast, [[Glossary:Asylum decision|final decisions on appeal or review]] relate to decisions granted at the final instance of administrative or judicial asylum procedure and which result from an appeal lodged by an asylum seeker rejected in the preceding stage. 

Limitations on data availability affecting the information presented in this article:
* Data for humanitarian status is specific to national legislation and does not apply in some EU countries. They are not applicable for Belgium, Bulgaria, France, Croatia, Cyprus, Latvia, Luxembourg, Portugal and Slovenia. 
* Data for unaccompanied minor asylum applicants granted protection status at first instance, are missing for Cyprus from Q1 2021 to Q4 2023 (derogation), for Poland from Q1 2021 to Q4 2023 (derogation) and from Q1 2024 (not provided), and for Switzerland from Q1 2021 (not provided). EU aggregates have been computed based on available data.
* Data for Spain from Q1 2025 are provisional.
* Data for Switzerland are missing for first instance decisions for Q1 2026 and for withdrawals of first instance decisions for Q4 2025.

The article presents statistical information on third-country nationals, meaning non-EU citizens (including stateless persons), seeking asylum in the EU and other European countries.

Data presented in this publication is rounded to the nearest five.
Calculations were made with rounded numbers, so the sum of percentages or values ​​may not equal 100 or the total value.

Distribution of asylum decisions by outcome (Figure 3) and recognition rates (Figure 5) are calculated from unrounded numbers and only for a total number of first instance decisions equal to or greater than 30.

</datadetails>


<context>
=== Context ===

The 1951 Geneva Convention relating to the status of refugees (as amended by the 1967 New York Protocol) has, for over 70 years, defined who is a refugee, and laid down a common approach towards refugees, which has been one of the cornerstones for the development of a common asylum system within the EU. Since 1999, the EU has been working towards creating a common European asylum regime in accordance with the Geneva Convention and other applicable international instruments. The [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/index_en Directorate-General Migration and Home Affairs (DG HOME)] is responsible for developing EU policies on asylum.

The [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/promoting-our-european-way-life/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en Pact on Migration and Asylum] entered into force on 11 June 2024 and applies from 12 June 2026. This Pact provides a common European response to migration. It allows the EU to manage migration in a fair and sustainable way, ensuring solidarity between countries while also providing certainty and clarity for people arriving in the EU and protecting their fundamental rights. The Pact on Migration and Asylum will ensure that countries share the effort responsibly, showing solidarity with the ones that protect our external borders and with those facing particular migratory pressure, while preventing irregular migration to the EU. The Pact also gives the EU and its countries the tools to react rapidly in situations of crisis, when countries are faced with large numbers of arrivals or when a third-country or non-State entity tries to instrumentalise migrants in order to destabilise the Union.

The main legal instruments on asylum are:

* [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1351 Asylum and Migration Management Regulation (EU) 2024/1351] (AMMR) of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on asylum and migration management, amending Regulations (EU) 2021/1147 and (EU) 2021/1060 and repealing [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02013R0604-20130629 Regulation (EU) No 604/2013];

* [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1348 Asylum Procedure Regulation (EU) 2024/1348] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 establishing a common procedure for international protection in the Union and repealing [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32013L0032 Directive 2013/32/EU];

*[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ%3AL_202401359 Crisis and Force Majeure Regulation (EU) 2024/1359] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 addressing situations of crisis and force majeure in the field of migration and asylum and amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1147;

* [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1358 Eurodac Regulation (EU) 2024/1358] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on the establishment of ‘Eurodac’ for the comparison of biometric data in order to effectively apply Regulations (EU) 2024/1351 and (EU) 2024/1350 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Council Directive 2001/55/EC and to identify illegally staying third-country nationals and stateless persons and on requests for the comparison with Eurodac data by EU countries’ law enforcement authorities and Europol for law enforcement purposes, amending Regulations (EU) 2018/1240 and (EU) 2019/818 of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32013R0603 Regulation (EU) No 603/2013] of the European Parliament and of the Council;

* [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1356 Screening Regulation (EU) 2024/1356] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 introducing the screening of third-country nationals at the external borders and amending Regulations (EC) No 767/2008, (EU) 2017/2226, (EU) 2018/1240 and (EU) 2019/817;

* [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1347 Qualification Regulation (EU) 2024/1347] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on standards for the qualification of third-country nationals or stateless persons as beneficiaries of international protection, for a uniform status for refugees or for persons eligible for subsidiary protection and for the content of the protection granted, amending Council Directive 2003/109/EC and repealing [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32011L0095 Directive 2011/95/EU] of the European Parliament and of the Council;

* [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ%3AL_202401346 Reception Conditions Directive (EU) 2024/1346] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 laying down standards for the reception of applicants for international protection;

* [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1350 Union Resettlement and Humanitarian Admission Framework Regulation (EU) 2024/1350] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 establishing a Union Resettlement and Humanitarian Admission Framework and amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1147.

The respective annual, quarterly, and monthly datasets are available in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/asylum/database Eurostat database].

These data are usually compiled and transmitted to Eurostat by statistical authorities, ministries of the interior, or related immigration agencies.

</context>


</articlecontent>

title: Asylum applications - annual statistics
text:
The latest statistics on asylum applicants in the EU are presented. Data extracted on 16 March 2026. Planned article update: March 2027. In 2025, 669 365 first-time asylum applicants (non-EU citizens) applied for international protection in EU countries, down by 27% compared with 2024. Venezuelan, Afghan and Syrian were the top citizenships of asylum seekers in the EU in 2025. Spain, Italy, France and Germany were the main countries of destination for first-time asylum applicants in the EU in 2025. [[Image:Asylum annual timeserie 2025.jpg|thumb|center|700px|First-time asylum applicants in EU countries, 2008–2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5e881ce8-bb01-4f83-91ad-88ec1ef4d922?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:22:45Z migr_asyappctza])|alt=a line chart with one line showing the number of first-time asylum applicants of non-EU citizens in the EU from 2008 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article outlines recent developments in relation to the number of [[Glossary:Asylum applicant|asylum applicants]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Asylum is a form of international protection given by a state on its territory. It is granted to a person who is unable to seek protection in their country of citizenship and/or residence, in particular for fear of being persecuted for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion. ===Main trends in the number of asylum applicants=== In 2025, 669 365 first-time asylum applicants (non-EU citizens) applied for international protection in EU countries, down by 26.6% compared with 2024 (912 425) (Figure 1). First-time asylum applicants accounted for a large majority (83.9%) of the total number of asylum applicants in the EU (797 760) recorded in 2025. Additionally, there were 127 340 subsequent asylum applicants recorded across the EU countries in 2025, up 51.3% when compared with 2024 (84 160). Figure 1 In 2025, more males than females sought asylum in EU countries (Figure 2). Men aged 18-34 years accounted for 36.2% of the total number of first-time applicants. The proportions of boys and girls aged less than 14 years were similar (respectively 50.9% and 49.1%). By contrast, there were more boys (69.5%) than girls (30.5%) for children aged 14-17 years. Figure 2
===Where do asylum seekers make their application?=== With 141 035 first-time asylum applicants registered in 2025, Spain was the EU country with the highest number of applicants, accounting for 21.1% of all first-time applicants in the EU. Italy came second (126 635, 18.9%), followed by France (116 370, 17.4%), Germany (113 170, 16.9%), and Greece (55 380, 8.3%). These 5 EU countries together accounted for 82.6% of all first-time asylum applicants in the EU last year. Compared with 2024, the number of first-time asylum applicants decreased in 24 EU countries, with the 3 largest absolute decreases observed in Germany (-116 525 applicants, or 50.7% less), Italy (-24 485 applicants, or 16.2% less) and Spain (-24 400 applicants, or 14.7% less). Among the 3 EU countries that registered increases, the highest increase was observed in Latvia (+490 applicants, or 61.3% more). Figure 3 Compared with the population of each EU country (as of 1 January 2025), the highest number of registered first-time asylum applicants in 2025 was recorded in Greece (5.3 first-time applicants per 1 000 people), followed by Cyprus and Spain (each 2.9), Luxembourg (2.6) and Ireland (2.4). In 2025, there were 1.5 first-time asylum applicants per 1 000 people in the EU. [[Image:SE A M1 ratio per 1000 people v2.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 1: First-time asylum applicants per 1 000 people, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5db0db0e-c074-44cf-9319-646c15ff60f4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:05:08Z migr_asyapp1mp])|alt=a map showing the number of first-time asylum applicants per 1 000 population in 2025, in the EU, EU countries and EFTA countries.]]
===Where do asylum seekers come from?=== In 2025, Venezuela overtook Syria, which was the main country of citizenship of asylum seekers in the EU since 2013. Venezuelans lodged 89 455 first-time applications (13.4% of the total number of first-time applications in the EU), followed by Afghanistan with 63 830 applications (9.5% of the EU total). Syria ranked third with 39 985 applications (6.0%), followed by applicants from Bangladesh (5.3%, 35 300 applications), and Türkiye (3.6%, 24 205 applications). Among the 15 most common citizenships of first-time asylum applicants in the EU in 2025, the number of asylum seekers increased for 4 of them. The largest absolute increase compared with 2024 was observed for Venezuelans (+16 525, or 22.7% more). In contrast, the number of asylum seekers decreased the most for citizens of Syria (-108 175, or 73.0% less), Colombia (-29 480, or 58.6% less) and Türkiye (-22 625, or 48.3% less). Figure 4 In 2025, Syrian was the main citizenship of asylum seekers in 6 EU countries (Table 1). The citizens of Ukraine and Afghanistan were the main group of asylum seekers in 4 EU countries. The largest number of Venezuelans was registered in Spain (94.2% of all Venezuelan asylum seekers in the EU). For Bangladeshis, the vast majority was registered in Italy (77.8%). The largest numbers of Syrians and Afghans were registered in Germany (58.2% and 37.6% respectively). [[Image:Five main citizenships of first-time asylum applicants, 2025v1.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Five main citizenships of first-time asylum applicants, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/00a7b5e7-1878-4b1b-a97a-235716fa6da7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:10:22Z migr_asyappctza])|alt=a table showing five main citizenships of first-time asylum applicants of non-EU citizens in 2025. The table shows the five main citizenships for the EU, EU countries and EFTA countries]] For more information on first-time asylum applicants, by country of citizenship and by receiving countries, explore our interactive visualisation ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/visualisations/asylum-applicants/ First-time asylum applicants]).
===Applications by unaccompanied minors=== In 2025, 21 125 [[Glossary:Unaccompanied_minor|unaccompanied minors]] applied for asylum for the first time in the EU, a decrease of 38.9% compared to 2024 (34 595) (Figure 5). The EU countries that received the highest number of asylum applications from unaccompanied minors were Germany (4 925, 23.3% of the total), the Netherlands (3 615, 17.1%), Spain (3 210, 15.2%), Greece (3 030, 14.3%) and Belgium (1 615, 7.6%). Compared with 2024, the number of unaccompanied minors decreased in 18 EU countries, with the 3 largest absolute decreases observed in Germany (-8 420 applicants, or 63.1% less), Bulgaria (-2 030 applicants, or 78.1% less) and Greece (-1 640 applicants, or 35.1% less). Among the 5 EU countries that registered increases, the highest increase was observed in Spain (+21 300 applicants, or 252.7% more). Figure 5 In 2025, Afghans were the largest group of unaccompanied minors seeking asylum in the EU (2 690 applicants, 12.7% of the total number). They were followed by Eritreans (2 345, 11.1%), ahead of applicants from Syria (2 330, 11.0%), Egypt (2 295, 10.9%) and Somalia (2 290, 10.8%) (Figure 6). Figure 6
===Applications under the accelerated procedure=== In 2025, there were 124 150 asylum [[Glossary:Application_under_the_accelerated_procedure|applications under the accelerated procedure]] in EU countries, an increase of 21.1% compared with 2024 (102 535) (Figure 7). The largest number of asylum applications under an accelerated procedure in 2025 was recorded in France (56 790), followed by Italy (43 755) and, at a distance, Greece (13 200). Figure 7
===Applicants receiving material reception conditions at the end of the year=== According to the latest available data, there were 573 890 [[Glossary:Applicant_receiving_material_reception_conditions|applicants receiving material reception conditions]] at the end of 2024 in the EU. Among the EU countries, the largest number of applicants receiving material reception conditions was registered in France (137 445) and Italy (129 635) (Figure 8). Figure 8
===Pending applications at the end of the year=== At the end of December 2025, 1 219 390 applications for international protection in EU countries were under consideration by national authorities, a decrease of 2.2% compared to December 2024 (1 247 100) (Figure 9). Germany continued to have the highest number of [[Glossary:Pending_asylum_application|pending applications]] (306 590, or 25.1% of the EU total), ahead of Spain (248 740, or 20.4%), Italy (234 165, or 19.2%) and France (153 090, or 12.6%). These 4 EU countries together accounted for 77.3% of all pending applications in the EU at the end of 2025. Figure 9
===Withdrawn asylum applications=== In 2025, 103 595 asylum applications were withdrawn across the EU countries (Figure 10). The largest number of [[Glossary:Asylum_application_withdrawn|withdrawals]] was registered in Germany (20 175), followed by Spain (17 590) and Croatia (17 330). A distinction is made between explicit withdrawal, when the applicant formally withdraws their application and informs the authorities, and implicit withdrawal, when the authorities close the case because the application is considered abandoned. In most EU countries, the majority of withdrawals were implicit, with the highest shares observed in Austria and Hungary (each 100.0%), Spain (99.1%), Croatia (98.5%), Slovenia (97.6%) and Greece (94.2%). In contrast, most explicit withdrawals were observed in Estonia (100.0%), Ireland (90.5%) and France (87.0%). Figure 10 === Source data for tables === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Table1 asylum top5 citizenships 2025v1.xlsx|title=Asylum applications - annual statistics: Table 1}} ===Data sources=== [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] produces statistics on a range of issues relating to international migration. Between 1986 and 2007, data on asylum was collected on the basis of a gentlemen’s agreement. Since 2008 data have been provided to Eurostat under the provisions of Article 4 of [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:32007R0862:EN:NOT Regulation (EC) No 862/2007]. Data for statistics on asylum applications, including applications by unaccompanied minors are provided to Eurostat with a monthly frequency. The statistics are based on administrative sources and are provided to Eurostat by statistical authorities, ministries of the interior or related immigration agencies in the EU countries. Asylum applicants mean asylum seekers who have lodged a claim (asylum application) and whose claim is under consideration by the relevant authority. Annual aggregated data on asylum applicants are computed from monthly data. Annual aggregated data on first-time unaccompanied minor asylum applicants are computed from monthly data and refer to minors according to the age claimed by applicant at the time of application. This number is different from the statistics on asylum applicants considered to be unaccompanied minors after the age assessment procedure has been completed. Limitations on data availability affecting the information presented in this article: *2021 to 2023 data on subsequent applicants for Cyprus not available due to derogations. *2025 data on first-time and subsequent asylum applicants are provisional for Spain and not available for Iceland. *2024 and 2025 data on unaccompanied minors are not available for Poland and Switzerland and provisional for Spain. *2025 data on asylum applications under the accelerated procedure are provisional for Spain and not available for Iceland. *2023 data on asylum applicants having benefited from material reception conditions at the end of the reference year are not available for Germany and Romania not available due to derogations. 2023 and 2024 data are of low reliability for Switzerland. 2024 data not available for Germany and are provisional for Spain. *2025 data on pending applications are provisional for Spain, of low reliability for Italy and not available for Iceland. *2025 data on asylum applications withdrawn by type of withdrawal are provisional for Spain and not available for Iceland. The article presents statistical information on third-country nationals, meaning non-EU citizens (including stateless persons), seeking asylum in the EU and other European countries. Data presented in this publication are rounded to the nearest five. Calculations were performed using rounded numbers. ===Context=== The 1951 Geneva Convention relating to the status of refugees (as amended by the 1967 New York Protocol) has, for over 70 years, defined who is a refugee, and laid down a common approach towards refugees, which has been one of the cornerstones for the development of a common asylum system within the EU. Since 1999, the EU has worked towards creating a common European asylum regime in accordance with the Geneva Convention and other applicable international instruments. The [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/index_en Directorate-General Migration and Home Affairs (DG HOME)] is responsible for developing EU policies on asylum. The [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en Pact on Migration and Asylum] was adopted by the European Parliament in April 2024 and by the Council in May 2024. This Pact provides a comprehensive approach that delivers a common European response to migration. It allows the EU to manage migration in a fair and sustainable way, ensuring solidarity between countries while also providing certainty and clarity for people arriving in the EU and protecting their fundamental rights. The Pact on Migration and Asylum will ensure that countries share the effort responsibly, showing solidarity with the ones that protect our external borders and with those facing particular migratory pressure, while preventing irregular migration to the EU. The Pact also gives the EU and its countries the tools to react rapidly in situations of crisis, when countries are faced with large numbers of arrivals or when a third-country or non-State entity tries to instrumentalise migrants in order to destabilise our Union. The main legal instruments on asylum are: * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1351 Asylum and Migration Management Regulation (EU) 2024/1351] (AMMR) of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on asylum and migration management, amending Regulations (EU) 2021/1147 and (EU) 2021/1060 and repealing [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02013R0604-20130629 Regulation (EU) No 604/2013]; * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1348 Asylum Procedure Regulation (EU) 2024/1348] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 establishing a common procedure for international protection in the Union and repealing [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32013L0032 Directive 2013/32/EU]; *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ%3AL_202401359 Crisis and Force Majeure Regulation (EU) 2024/1359] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 addressing situations of crisis and force majeure in the field of migration and asylum and amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1147; * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1358 Eurodac Regulation (EU) 2024/1358] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on the establishment of ‘Eurodac’ for the comparison of biometric data in order to effectively apply Regulations (EU) 2024/1351 and (EU) 2024/1350 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Council Directive 2001/55/EC and to identify illegally staying third-country nationals and stateless persons and on requests for the comparison with Eurodac data by EU countries’ law enforcement authorities and Europol for law enforcement purposes, amending Regulations (EU) 2018/1240 and (EU) 2019/818 of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32013R0603 Regulation (EU) No 603/2013] of the European Parliament and of the Council; * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1356 Screening Regulation (EU) 2024/1356] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 introducing the screening of third-country nationals at the external borders and amending Regulations (EC) No 767/2008, (EU) 2017/2226, (EU) 2018/1240 and (EU) 2019/817; * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1347 Qualification Regulation (EU) 2024/1347] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on standards for the qualification of third-country nationals or stateless persons as beneficiaries of international protection, for a uniform status for refugees or for persons eligible for subsidiary protection and for the content of the protection granted, amending Council Directive 2003/109/EC and repealing [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32011L0095 Directive 2011/95/EU] of the European Parliament and of the Council; * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ%3AL_202401346 Reception Conditions Directive (EU) 2024/1346] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 laying down standards for the reception of applicants for international protection; * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1350 Union Resettlement and Humanitarian Admission Framework Regulation (EU) 2024/1350] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 establishing a Union Resettlement and Humanitarian Admission Framework, and amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1147. In May 2010, the European Commission presented an [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:52010DC0213:EN:NOT action plan for unaccompanied minors] (COM(2010) 213 final), who are regarded as the most exposed and vulnerable victims of migration. This plan aims to set up a coordinated approach and commits all EU countries to grant high standards of reception, protection and integration for unaccompanied minors. In December 2011, the European Commission adopted a Communication on '[http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:52011DC0835:EN:NOT Enhanced intra-EU solidarity in the field of asylum]' (COM(2011) 835 final). This provided proposals to reinforce practical, technical and financial cooperation, moving towards a better allocation of responsibilities and improved governance of the asylum system in the EU, namely through: * introducing an evaluation and early warning mechanism to detect and address emerging problems; * making the supporting role of the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) more effective; * increasing the amount of funds available and making these more flexible, taking into account significant fluctuations in the number of asylum seekers; * developing and encouraging the relocation of beneficiaries of international protection between different EU countries. ===Other articles=== *[[Asylum applications - monthly statistics]] *[[Temporary protection for persons fleeing Ukraine - monthly statistics]] *[[Statistics on countries responsible for asylum applications (Dublin Regulation) ]] *[[Enforcement of immigration legislation statistics]] *[[Residence permits - title: Asylum decisions - annual statistics
text:
This article outlines recent developments in relation to the decisions on applications lodged by asylum applicants in the European Union. Data extracted on 17 April 2026 Planned article update: 23 April 2027 In 2025, EU countries granted protection status to 361 325 asylum seekers, down 17.5% compared with 2024 (437 735). Among persons granted protection status in the EU in 2025, 51.0% received refugee status, 25.3% humanitarian status, and 23.7% subsidiary protection. Afghans, Venezuelans, Syrians and Ukrainians were the main beneficiaries of protection status in the EU in 2025. This article describes recent developments in relation to the [[Glossary:Asylum decision|first instance and final decisions]] on applications lodged by [[Glossary:Asylum applicant|asylum applicants]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. It looks at the main trends, including positive and negative decisions, and focuses on the 3 types of positive outcomes: refugee status, subsidiary protection and humanitarian status. It also provides information on the first instance and final decisions for unaccompanied minors and the number of decisions withdrawing protection status granted at first instance and final decisions. The article further describes the development of the number of people resettled in the EU. === Main trends in the number of asylum decisions === In 2025, 1 002 535 decisions on asylum applications were issued in the EU, of which 832 360 were first instance decisions and 170 175 were final decisions following an appeal or review. Decisions made at first instance resulted in 325 765 people being granted protection status, while another 35 565 people received protection status after an appeal or review. Overall, EU countries granted protection status to 361 325 asylum seekers in 2025, down 17.5% compared with 2024 (437 735). Among the asylum seekers granted positive decisions at first and final instance in 2025 (Figure 1), 51.0% received refugee status (184 455 persons), 25.3% received humanitarian status (91 355) and 23.7% were granted subsidiary protection (85 515). Compared with 2024, the number of refugee statuses granted decreased by 0.5%, humanitarian status increased by 10.7%, and subsidiary protection decreased by 49.7%. While refugee status and subsidiary protection are defined by EU law, humanitarian status is specific to national legislation and does not apply in some EU countries. Figure 1 The highest number of people who received protection status in 2025 was reported by Germany (103 360, 28.6% of the EU total), ahead of Spain (76 210, 21.1%) and France (72 930, 20.2%) (Figure 2). All together, these 3 countries granted 70% of the protection statuses at EU level. Figure 2 In 2025, Afghans received the largest number of protection statuses in the EU (27.2% of all persons granted protection status in the EU, 98 175 persons) (Figure 3). They were followed by Venezuelans (16.4%, 59 285), Syrians (4.8%, 17 420), Ukrainians (4.7%, 17 140), Somalis (3.8%, 13 665), Malians (3.4%, 12 455), Turks (3.0%, 10 920), Haitians (2.8%, 10 000) and Eritreans (2.7%, 9 680). Figure 3 === First instance decisions on asylum applications === In 2025, 325 765 asylum seekers were granted positive outcomes of first instance decisions: 166 820 were granted refugee status (20.0% of total first instance decisions), 86 410 were granted humanitarian status (10.4%) and 72 535 were granted subsidiary protection (8.7%) (Figure 4). The recognition rate at the EU level, i.e. the share of all positive decisions among the total number of decisions, was 39.1% for the first instance decisions. More than 90% of first instance decisions were positive in Estonia in 2025. 60 to 70% of positive decisions were in Hungary, Ireland and Austria. On the contrary, 20 to 30% of positive decisions were made in Italy, Belgium, Latvia, Sweden, Bulgaria and Czechia. Less than 10% of positive first instance decisions were issued in Croatia and Cyprus. Figure 4 The largest group of asylum seekers who obtained protection status via first instance decisions in the EU in 2025 were Afghans (94 580, 29.0% of positive first instance decisions). They were followed by Venezuelans (58 685, 18.0%) and Ukrainians (16 815, 5.2%). Afghans (62.3%) were granted protection status in first instance decisions mainly in Germany, while nearly all Venezuelans (97.1%) received protection status in Spain, and the majority of Ukrainians (77.9%) were granted protection status in France. Among the top 10 citizenships that received the highest number of first instance decisions in the EU in 2025, Venezuelans (92.1%), Ukrainians (73.3%) and Afghans (73.3%) had the highest recognition rates (Figure 5). Figure 5 === Final decisions taken on appeal or review === In 2025, 35 565 asylum seekers were granted positive outcomes at final instance following an appeal or review; 17 635 were granted refugee status (10.4% of total final decisions), 12 980 were granted subsidiary protection (7.6%) and 4 950 were granted humanitarian status (2.9%) (Figure 6). The recognition rate at EU level was 20.9% for final decisions in appeal or review. The highest shares of positive final decisions in appeal or review were recorded in the Netherlands (46.0%), Lithuania (43.1%) and Austria (34.6%). Less than 5% of positive final decisions were issued in Latvia, Czechia, Greece, Malta, Spain, Croatia, Cyprus, Poland and Slovenia. No positive final decisions were issued in Luxembourg and Portugal, while no final decisions on asylum applications were issued in Hungary. Slovakia issued fewer than 30 final decision, so no share was computed. Figure 6 The largest group who obtained protection status on appeal or review in the EU in 2025 were Syrians (6 645 persons, 18.7% of positive final decisions). They were followed by Afghans (3 595, 10.1%) and Turks (2 445, 6.9%). Nearly all Syrians (90.3%) were granted protection status in final decisions in Germany. The majority of Afghans received protection status on appeal or review, primarily in France (35.7%) and Germany (33.8%), while most Turks were granted protection status in Germany (58.1%) and France (30.5%). Among the top 10 citizenships that received the highest number of final decisions after an appeal or review in the EU in 2025, Syrians (67.3%), Afghans (36.3%) and citizens of Democratic Republic of the Congo (20.2%) had the highest recognition rates (Figure 7). Figure 7
 === Decisions on asylum applications from unaccompanied minors === In 2025, for the 26 EU countries that reported data, 11 990 first instance decisions on asylum applications lodged by unaccompanied minors were made in the EU, and a further 620 final decisions following an appeal or review. A total of 12 610 asylum decisions on unaccompanied minors were issued. That was 30.0% less than in 2024 (18 025). Decisions made at first instance resulted in 6 800 unaccompanied minors being granted protection status, while another 240 received protection status after an appeal or review. Overall, in 2025, EU countries granted protection status to 7 040 unaccompanied minors seeking asylum, down 52.4% compared with the 2024 (14 780). Across the EU countries, Germany issued the most positive decisions on applications lodged by unaccompanied minors (2 525 persons, 35.9% of positive decisions lodged by unaccompanied minors), followed by Italy (945, 13.4%) and the Netherlands (850, 12.1%) (Figure 8). Figure 8
 The main beneficiaries of protection status among unaccompanied minors seeking asylum in the EU were Afghans (2 275 persons, 32.3% of positive decisions lodged by unaccompanied minors), Somalis (1 160, 16.5%), Eritreans (725, 10.3%) and Malians (705, 10.0%). === Decisions withdrawing protection status === EU countries may decide to withdraw protection status when new elements or findings arise indicating that there are reasons to reconsider the validity of protection. Decisions are taken by the competent administrative or judicial bodies either at first instance or on appeal (final decision). In 2025, EU countries took 16 110 decisions to withdraw protection status granted at first instance and a further 4 690 decisions withdrawing protection status granted at final instance. Compared with the previous year, withdrawals of first-instance decisions rose by 58.7%, while final decisions increased by 16.1%. The highest number of decisions withdrawing protection status granted at first and final instance was reported by Germany (4 005), the Netherlands (3 470) and Austria (3 370) in 2025 (Figure 9). Compared to the previous year, the number of withdrawals increased in Austria by 129.3% (1 470 persons in 2024) and in Germany by 25.7% (3 185), while the Netherlands saw a decrease of 5.4% (3 370). Figure 9 === Resettled persons === [[Glossary:Resettlement|Resettlement]] to the European Union, on request by [https://www.unhcr.org/ UNHCR], is the transfer of vulnerable persons from third countries to EU countries, where they are admitted and granted the right to stay and any other rights comparable to those granted to beneficiaries of international protection. In 2025, 10 220 persons were resettled in EU countries, marking a 25.9% decrease from 2024 (13 790). Adults accounted for just over half (52%), while minors under 18 made up 48% (4 835 persons). Of these minors, 99.3% were accompanied by their parents, with only 0.7% (35 persons) being unaccompanied. The highest number of resettled persons was reported by France (3 055, 29.9% of the EU total) followed by Germany (2 230, 21.8%), Italy (915, 9.0%), Sweden (900, 8.8%) and Spain (860, 8.4%). These 5 countries accounted for 78% of all resettled refugees in the EU countries in 2025 (Figure 10). Compared with the previous year, resettlement figures rose by 28.9% in France (2 370 persons in 2024) and by 16.2% in Spain (740). Conversely, numbers fell by 0.6% in Sweden (905), 47.3% in Italy (1 735) and 61.0% in Germany (5 720). Figure 10 In 2025, Afghans formed the largest group of resettled persons (2 640 persons, 25.8% of all persons resettled in the EU), followed by Syrians (1 795, 17.6%), citizens of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (1 485, 14.5%) and Sudanese (1 150, 11.2%). The main countries of previous residence of resettled persons in 2025 were Pakistan (1 395 persons, 13.6% of all resettled persons in the EU), Türkiye (1 305, 12.8%), Rwanda (1 025, 10.0%), Egypt (890, 8.7%) and Lebanon (735, 7.2%). The vulnerable persons were resettled in the EU territory based on a decision on refugee status (6 385 persons, 62.5% of all persons resettled in the EU), on subsidiary protection (535, 5.2%) and other positive decisions (2 580, 25.3%). Additionally, 7% of resettled persons in the EU countries were still awaiting a decision on their protection status (715 persons). In 2025, most persons were resettled through the European Union resettlement schemes or framework (58.4%). A further 21.9% were resettled under national resettlement frameworks, 18.2% through the European Union humanitarian admission scheme, and 1.5% via national humanitarian admission frameworks. === Source data for graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Annual decisions data 2025.xlsx|title=Annual data on asylum decisions}} === Data sources === [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] produces statistics on a range of issues relating to international migration under the provisions of Article 4 of [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32007R0862 Regulation (EC) No 862/2007]. Data are provided to Eurostat with a monthly frequency (for asylum application statistics, including applications by unaccompanied minors), quarterly frequency (for first instance decisions) and annual frequency (for final decisions based on appeal or review and resettlement). The statistics are based on administrative sources and are provided to Eurostat by statistical authorities, ministries of the interior or related immigration agencies in the EU Member States. Two different categories should be taken into account when analysing asylum statistics. The first includes asylum seekers who have lodged a claim (asylum application) and whose claim is under consideration by the relevant authority. The second is composed of persons who have been recognised, after consideration, as [[Glossary:Refugee|refugees]], or have been granted another kind of international protection ([[Glossary:Asylum decision|subsidiary protection]]), or were granted protection on the basis of the national law related to international protection ([[Glossary:Asylum decision|authorisations to stay for humanitarian reasons]]), or were rejected from having any form of protection. Statistics on asylum decisions are available for different stages of the asylum procedure. [[Glossary:Asylum decision|First instance decisions]] are decisions granted by the respective authority acting as a first instance of the administrative or judicial asylum procedure in the receiving country. By contrast, [[Glossary:Asylum decision|final decisions on appeal or review]] relate to decisions granted at the final instance of administrative or judicial asylum procedure and which result from an appeal lodged by an asylum seeker rejected in the preceding stage. [[Glossary:Resettlement|Resettlement]] data relate to resettled persons who have actually arrived on to the territory of the Member State and not to selected persons who remain in the third country waiting for a transfer to the Member States or to persons covered by future resettlement commitments. Only resettled persons arriving into a Member State from a third country are counted. Transfers between Member State of asylum-seekers, refugees or persons enjoying subsidiary protection status are not included in this category. Limitations on data availability affecting the information presented in this article: * Data for humanitarian status is specific to national legislation and does not apply in some EU countries. They are not applicable for Belgium, Bulgaria, France, Croatia, Cyprus (since 2015), Latvia, Luxembourg, Portugal and Slovenia. * Data for first instance decisions and final decisions are missing for Croatia for 2008 - 2011, for Cyprus for 2008 and for Iceland for 2025. EU aggregates for 2008 - 2011 were computed based on available data. * Data for first instance decisions and final decisions are provisional for Spain for 2025. EU aggregates for 2025 were computed based on available data. * Data for final decisions in appeal or review are missing for Italy for 2025. EU aggregates for 2025 were computed based on available data. * Data for unaccompanied minor asylum applicants granted protection status at first and final instance, are missing for Cyprus for 2021 - 2023, for Poland from 2021 and for Switzerland from 2021. EU aggregates were computed based on available data. * Data for decisions withdrawing protection status are missing for Denmark for 2008 - 2010 and 2015, Spain for 2008 - 2012, France for 2008, 2010, 2011, Croatia for 2008 - 2011, Cyprus for 2008, Lithuania for 2008 and 2015, Luxembourg for 2008, Hungary for 2011 - 2014, the Netherlands for 2008 - 2013, Portugal for 2010, Romania for 2010, Slovakia for 2010 and 2012, Finland for 2008 - 2011, Iceland for 2010 and 2013, Liechtenstein for 2008, 2011, 2012, 2014, Norway for 2008. Data for decisions withdrawing protection status are not applicable for Ireland. * Data for resettled persons are missing for Czechia for 2008 - 2009, Croatia for 2008 - 2011, and Iceland for 2025. EU aggregates for 2008 - 2011 were computed based on available data. * Data for resettled persons by country of previous residence are missing for France for 2021 - 2023, for Iceland for 2022 - 2024 and for Switzerland for 2021 - 2025. * Data for resettled persons by resettlement framework are missing for France for 2021 - 2023. The article presents statistical information on third-country nationals, meaning non-EU citizens (including stateless persons), seeking asylum in the EU and other European countries. Data presented in this publication is rounded to the nearest five. Calculations were made with rounded numbers, so the sum of percentages or values may not equal 100 or the total value. Distribution of asylum decisions by outcome (Figure 4 and Figure 6) and recognition rates (Figure 5 and Figure 7) are calculated from unrounded numbers and only for a total number of first instance decisions equal to or greater than 30. === Context === The 1951 Geneva Convention relating to the status of refugees (as amended by the 1967 New York Protocol) has, for over 70 years, defined who is a refugee, and laid down a common approach towards refugees, which has been one of the cornerstones for the development of a common asylum system within the EU. Since 1999, the EU has been working towards creating a common European asylum regime in accordance with the Geneva Convention and other applicable international instruments. The [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/index_en Directorate-General Migration and Home Affairs (DG HOME)] is responsible for developing EU policies on asylum. The [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/promoting-our-european-way-life/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en Pact on Migration and Asylum], presented by the Commission in September 2020, was adopted by the European Parliament in April 2024 and by the Council in May 2024. This Pact provides a common European response to migration. It allows the EU to manage migration in a fair and sustainable way, ensuring solidarity between countries while also providing certainty and clarity for people arriving in the EU and protecting their fundamental rights. The Pact on Migration and Asylum will ensure that countries share the effort responsibly, showing solidarity with the ones that protect our external borders and with those facing particular migratory pressure, while preventing irregular migration to the EU. The Pact also gives the EU and its countries the tools to react rapidly in situations of crisis, when countries are faced with large numbers of arrivals or when a third-country or non-State entity tries to instrumentalise migrants in order to destabilise the Union. The main legal instruments on asylum are: * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1351 Asylum and Migration Management Regulation (EU) 2024/1351] (AMMR) of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on asylum and migration management, amending Regulations (EU) 2021/1147 and (EU) 2021/1060 and repealing [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02013R0604-20130629 Regulation (EU) No 604/2013]; * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1348 Asylum Procedure Regulation (EU) 2024/1348] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 establishing a common procedure for international protection in the Union and repealing [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32013L0032 Directive 2013/32/EU]; *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ%3AL_202401359 Crisis and Force Majeure Regulation (EU) 2024/1359] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 addressing situations of crisis and force majeure in the field of migration and asylum and amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1147; * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1358 Eurodac Regulation (EU) 2024/1358] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 on the establishment of ‘Eurodac’ for the comparison of biometric data in order to effectively apply Regulations (EU) 2024/1351 and (EU) 2024/1350 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Council Directive 2001/55/EC and to identify illegally staying third-country nationals and stateless persons and on requests for the comparison with Eurodac data by EU countries’ law enforcement authorities and Europol for law enforcement purposes, amending Regulations (EU) 2018/1240 and (EU) 2019/818 of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32013R0603 Regulation (EU) No 603/2013] of the European Parliament and of the Council; * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32024R1356 Screening Regulation (EU) 2024/1356] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 introducing the screening of third-country nationals at the external borders and amending Regulations (EC) No 767/2008, (EU) 2017/2226, (EU) 2018/1240 and (EU) 2019/817;
