title: Business - statistics on profits and investment
text:
EU statistics on non-financial corporations' profits, investments, saving, and net lending and borrowing. Data extracted in November 2025 Planned article update: December 2026 In 2024, non-financial corporations in the EU had a profit share of 40.1% and an investment rate of 22.1%. In 2024, profit shares of non-financial corporations varied among EU countries from 32.2% in France to 74.9% in Ireland. In 2024, the investment rate of non-financial corporations varied among EU countries from 15.9% in Luxembourg to 28.5% in Hungary. ''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/NASA_10_NF_TR__custom_18795158/default/table (nasa_10 _nf_tr)] ===Overview=== This article focuses on the distribution of profit, [[Glossary:Investment_-_NA|investment]] and their components among EU non-financial corporations (businesses whose main economic activity is non-financial). Economic developments in production, income generation and (re)distribution, consumption and investment may be better understood when analysed by [[Glossary:Institutional_sector|institutional sector]]. The [[Glossary:Non-financial_corporations_sector|non-financial corporations sector]] comprises all private and public corporate enterprises that produce goods or provide non-financial services to the market. This article presents [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] statistics derived from [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sector-accounts European sector accounts], which form part of the [[Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)|European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)]]. Data are provided for the EU and the euro area. Most indicators are presented in relation to gross value added. This standardisation helps make spatial comparisons between countries of different sizes. ===Profit shares: distribution of value added=== Value added is the value generated by the [[Glossary:Production_account|production account]]. Figure 1 shows that most of the value added of non-financial corporations is used to compensate the supply of labour and capital, referred to as the [[Glossary:Compensation_of_employees|compensation of employees]] and [[Glossary:Gross_operating_surplus_-_NA|gross operating surplus]] in [[Glossary:National_accounts_(NA)|national accounts]]. Gross operating surplus is a measure of profit (before taxes on income and wealth) and may include the remuneration of self-employed people in countries that include them in the non-financial corporations sector (rather than the household sector). A small part of value added is used to pay [[Glossary:Taxes_on_production_and_imports|taxes on production]] (less [[Glossary:Subsidies|subsidies]]). The [[Glossary:Profit_share_of_non-financial_corporations|profit share]] of non-financial corporations is the gross operating surplus divided by gross value added. This indicator shows the proportion of non-financial corporations’ value added during the production process that remunerates the supply of capital (or pays income and wealth taxes). Different profit shares in different economies can be explained by a number of factors, such as the relative importance of labour or capital-intensive industries, labour productivity and labour costs. Figure 1 In 2024, profit shares were slightly higher in the EU (40.1%) than in the euro area (39.7%). Among the EU’s 4 largest economies, Italy (43.8%) had the highest profit share for non-financial corporations in 2024, the only one above the EU average. The profit shares in Spain (39.0%), Germany (37.2%) and France (32.2%) were all relatively low. In fact, the profit share in France was the lowest recorded among all EU countries. In 2 EU countries, the gross operating surplus of non-financial corporations represented more than half of the gross value added during the production process: 74.9% in Ireland and 56.5% in Malta. Ireland's high share can be attributed to large foreign-owned multinational companies located in the country that have a high capital intensity. ===Profit shares between 2014 and 2024=== Figure 2 Between 2014 and 2024, the profit share of non-financial corporations in the EU remained stable, hovering around 40%. From 2014 to 2018, in the EU’s 4 largest countries, there were minor declines in Germany and Spain, while France remained stable, and Italy reported comparatively high levels. In 2019 and 2020, the profit share of non-financial corporations in Spain decreased, France remained broadly stable, and Italy continued to record high levels. During the post-pandemic period (2021-2023), both the EU and the 4 largest countries experienced temporary increases, followed by a decline in 2024, with the largest reductions observed in Germany and Italy. ===From gross operating surplus to net lending/borrowing === The gross operating surplus of non-financial corporations is mainly used to pay taxes on income and wealth and to remunerate capital, for example, in the form of [[Glossary:Interest|interest]] or [[Glossary:Dividends|dividends]] paid to shareholders. In addition, non-financial corporations receive interest and other [[Glossary:Property_income|property income]] from their financial investments, for example, in the form of dividends or reinvested earnings. After accounting for these payments and income as well as other miscellaneous current transfers, the remaining gross operating surplus becomes the savings of non-financial corporations. These savings may be used, for example, for investments, other capital transactions, or loans; if the investment and other capital transactions exceed savings, the corporations may need to borrow. Figure 3 shows non-financial corporations’ gross operating surplus, how it is distributed, and the resulting net lending (for a positive surplus) or net borrowing (for a negative surplus). In 2024, total net distributive transactions (taxes, interest, other property income/expenditure, other current transactions and capital transactions) in the EU represented -37.7% of value added. [[Image:2024_From_gross_operating_surplus_to_net_lending_borrowing.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3 From gross operating surplus to net lending/ borrowing 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e8557068-5851-4952-92da-c9fcb68ce2aa?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-02T11:47:23Z (nasa_10_nf_tr)]]] Among EU countries, the share of total net distributive transactions by non-financial corporations in 2024 was largest in Ireland (-61.1%) and lowest in Romania (-32.0%). Aside from capital transactions, when looking at different types of current distributive transactions, the largest share for non-financial corporations in 2024 was generally net property income. In the EU, net property income was equivalent to -11.0% of value added, accounting for nearly two thirds of all net current distributions (taxes on income and wealth, net property income and other current transactions). Taxes on income and wealth were equivalent to -4.9% of non-financial corporations’ value added in the EU. Cyprus recorded the largest ratio of taxes on income and wealth to value added among all of the EU countries, at -14.0%, followed by Greece (-10.4%). The ratio of taxes on income and wealth to value added was smaller than -3.5% of value added in the 3 [[Glossary:Baltic_countries|Baltic countries]] and Hungary. Non-financial corporations’ savings and net borrowing (or lending) are used to finance gross capital formation, other capital transfers and acquisitions less disposals of non-financial non-produced assets. Gross capital formation includes [[Glossary:Gross_fixed_capital_formation|gross fixed capital formation]] (referred to elsewhere in this article as investment), changes in inventories, and acquisitions less disposals of valuables. [[Glossary:Non-financial_non-produced_assets|Non-financial non-produced assets]] include land, mineral reserves or radio spectra. The difference between savings and all capital transactions is called [[Glossary:Net_lending_net_borrowing|net lending net borrowing]], depending on whether it is positive or negative. If non-financial corporations are net lenders, it means that they have an excess of savings over investment and other capital transactions that they can lend to other sectors of the national economy or to [[Glossary:Non-resident|non residents]]. Conversely, they are net borrowers when they need to borrow money from other sectors to supplement their savings in order to finance their investments and other capital transactions. In 2024, non-financial corporations in the EU were net lenders, with their net lending valued at 2.4% of the gross value added. Non-financial corporations of the 4 EU’s largest economies were also net lenders in 2024, above the EU average: Italy at 3.6%, Spain at 3.1%, Germany at 3.1% and France at 2.5%. ===Investment rates=== Investment is the largest part of capital transactions. The [[Glossary:Business_investment_rate|investment rate]] of non-financial corporations presented in Figures 4 shows investments in [[Glossary:Fixed_assets|fixed assets]] (mainly machinery, equipment, buildings and intellectual property rights) as a percentage of value added in the production process. In 2024, the investment rate was higher in the EU (22.1%) than in the euro area (21.5%). Figure 4 Hungary reported the highest rate (28.5%) among all EU countries. Rates below 20.0% were reported in 7 EU countries, with the lowest rate in Luxembourg (15.9%). Although Ireland’s investment rate was relatively low in 2024, it is usually very volatile and quite high (greatly influencing the overall EU rate). It peaked at 67.1% in 2019, due to the very large number of multinational companies in the country. In that same year, Ireland accounted for 9% of the total non-financial corporations gross fixed capital formation in the EU, even though it has just 1% of the EU population and 3% of GDP. ===Investment rates between 2014 and 2024=== Although annual investments may be volatile for individual corporations, cyclical trends can be observed at national level. Figure 6 shows investment rates from 2014-2024 in the EU and its 4 largest economies. Figure 5 From 2014 to 2018, gross investment rates of non-financial corporations increased in the EU and in its 4 largest economies, except in Spain and France in 2015. Since 2019, the investment rate has risen in Spain and Germany, while France and Italy have recorded modest declines. Currently, among the 4 economies, the rate is highest in Spain (24.2%) and lowest in Germany (18.8%). France and Italy have rates of 21.7% and 22.1%, respectively. ===Source data for tables and graphs=== {{Template:Excel|filename=Business - statistics on profits and investment NA2025.xlsx|title=Business - statistics on profits and investment}} ===Data sources=== The compilation of sector accounts follows the [[Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)|European system of accounts (ESA 2010)]]. '''''The non-financial accounts''''' Non-financial accounts provide a systematic description of the different stages of the economic process: production, generation and distribution, use and accumulation of income. Each of the accounts ends with a balancing item: value added, operating surplus, primary income, disposable income, saving. For non-financial corporations, some of these can be seen as profit measures. The data presented in this article do not take account of profits/losses caused by changes in the price levels of assets or by extraordinary events (such as catastrophic losses). Profit measures may be calculated either gross or net of depreciation (called [[Glossary:Consumption_of_fixed_capital_(CFC)|consumption of fixed capital]] in national accounts): in this article all indicators are presented gross of the consumption of fixed capital. '''''The non-financial corporations sector''''' [[Glossary:Institutional_sector|Institutional sectors]] in national accounts bring together economic units with broadly similar characteristics and behaviour. The non-financial corporations sector is 1 of 5 sectors that make up the domestic economy. The other sectors are financial corporations, general government, households and non-profit institutions serving households. The non-financial corporations sector consists of institutional units that are independent legal entities and market producers whose principal activity is the production of goods and non-financial services. '''''Indicator definitions''''' The profit share of non-financial corporations is the gross operating surplus divided by gross value added. This profitability indicator shows the share of the value added created during the production process that is used to remunerate capital. The gross investment rate of non-financial corporations measures investment in fixed assets (such as buildings, machinery, software and major improvements to fixed assets) to the value added created during the production process. The investment rate for the total economy and for individual institutional sectors is a key indicator for economic analysis and EU policymaking, in particular in the context of monitoring EU countries' economies under the European Semester, for example, [https://commission.europa.eu/content/eu-economic-governance-monitoring-prevention-correction/european-semester/european-semester-timeline/spring-package_en country specific recommendations / European Commission recommendations]. The investment rate is also part of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/euro-indicators principal European economic indicators] (PEEIs). ===Other articles=== *[[Households - statistics on income, saving and investment|Households – statistics on income, saving and investment]] *[[Households_-_statistics_on_financial_assets_and_liabilities|Households – statistics on financial assets and liabilities]] *[[Non-financial_corporations_-_statistics_on_financial_assets_and_liabilities|Non-financial corporations – statistics on financial assets and liabilities]] ===Main tables=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sector-accounts/database Annual sector accounts (ESA 2010) (t_nasa_10)] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sector-accounts/database Annual sector accounts (ESA 2010) (nasa_10)], see ::Key indicators - annual data (nasa_10_ki) ::Non-financial transactions - annual data (nasa_10_nf_tr) ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sector-accounts/overview Institutional sector accounts] ===Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/KS-02-13-269 European system of accounts – ESA 2010] *{{Template:Esms|code=nasa_10_nf_tr_esms|title=Non-financial transactions – annual data (nasa_10_nf_tr)}} *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sector-accounts/methodology/member-states-accounts Sector accounts in countries] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sector-accounts/legislation Key legal documents for institutional sector accounts] ===External links=== *[https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/macroeconomic_and_sectoral/sector_accounts/html/index.en.html European Central Bank (ECB) – Sector accounts] {{Unit|topic=X_National_accounts}} [[Category:Economy and finance|Business – statistics on profits and investment]] [[Category:National accounts (incl. title: Businesses in human services
text:
Insert short description for search engines Data extracted in June 2026 Planned article update: January 2027 In 2023, 'Education' accounted for 1.5% of people employed within the business economy, while ‘Human health and social work activities' for 8.3%, and ‘Arts, entertainment and recreation’ for 1.4%. Altogether, businesses in the human services sector accounted for 3.7% of EU business economy's net turnover, generating around €1.4 trillion.

This article presents an overview of statistics for 3 economic activities within the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union's (EU)]] services economy: education; human health and social work activities and arts, entertainment and recreation as covered by [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] Rev. 2 Section  P, Q and R. It belongs to a [[Business economy by sector - NACE Rev. 2|set of statistical articles]] on 'Business economy by sector'. === Structural profile === In 2023, 3.0% of all [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]] in the [[Glossary:EU|EU]]'s [[Glossary:Business economy|business economy]] (Sections B to N and P to R, as well as Divisions S95 and S96) were classified as ‘Education'(Section P) and also ‘Arts, entertainment and recreation '(Section R), a total of close to 1 million enterprises each, while ‘Health and social work activities'(Section Q) accounted for 2.4 million enterprises corresponding to 7.3% of all enterprises. In terms of economic contribution, ‘Education' (Section P) generated €77.5 billion in value added, ‘Health and social work activities' (Section Q) accounted for a significantly higher €628.9 billion, and ‘Arts, entertainment and recreation' (Section R) contributed €117.9 billion. Altogether these services represents 7.9% of the EU’s business economy value added. [[File:Table_1_Key_indicators_Businesses_in_human_services,_(NACE_Sections_P,_Q_and_R),_EU,_2023.png |thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Key indicators - Businesses in human services (NACE Sections P, Q and R), EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/be6d3314-e179-4df9-bbdf-0fdc68352a5c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-17T14:04:12Z (sbs_ovw_act)]|alt=A table showing an overview of key indicators in human services (NACE Sections P, Q and R), in the EU in 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023 the [[Glossary:Gross operating rate - SBS|gross operating rate]] (the relation between the [[Glossary:Gross operating surplus - SBS|gross operating surplus]] and [[Glossary:Turnover - SBS|turnover]]) for the EU's education was 17.2%, for health and social work activities it was 17.3% and for arts, entertainment and recreation it was 19.9%. ===Sectoral analysis=== The 3 human services (P, Q, R) display disparity. At the NACE division level education counts only 1 division; health and social work activities is composed of 3 divisions; arts, entertainment and recreation of 4 divisions. For more information and comparisons between the divisions please refer to Data browser, see [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/93e3cec9-0e2d-4032-81ef-df938479330b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-17T14:16:10Z Enterprises by detailed NACE Rev. 2 activity and special aggregates (sbs_ovw_act)].
Figure 1a|alt=An interactive chart showing the sectoral breakdown of key indicators, absolute values, for NACE Sections P, Q and R in the EU in 2023, comparing education; human health and social work activities and arts, entertainment and recreation. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

Figure 1b|alt=An interactive chart showing the sectoral breakdown of key indicators, ratios, for NACE Sections P, Q and R in the EU in 2023, comparing education; human health and social work activities and arts, entertainment and recreation. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

===Country overview=== Human services play different roles at country level in the national business economy: in education, the highest shares of employment were found in Spain (3.4%), Cyprus (3.3%) and Greece (3.2%), while the highest shares of value added were recorded in Cyprus (2.1%), Spain (1.7%) and Sweden (1.3%). In human health and social work activities, the highest shares of employment were found in the Netherlands (18.6%), Belgium (15.0%) and Germany (14.6%), while for value added the highest shares were recorded in the Netherlands (12.1%), Germany (9.6%) and Belgium (8.5%). In arts, entertainment and recreation, Malta (5.4%), Sweden (2.7%) and Spain (2.4%) recorded the highest employment shares, whereas Malta (10.8%), Slovakia (4.1%) and Hungary (2.5%) had the highest in value added.
Figure 2
Figure 3a: Businesses in human services: Key indicators, EU, 2023 |alt=An interactive chart showing key indicators, absolute values, for human services by EU countries in 2023, including metrics such as turnover, value added and employment for NACE Sections P, Q and R. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Figure 3b For average employee benefits expense within businesses in the human services in 2023, please consult the data available on this bookmark, where you will also find information on the wage-adjusted labour productivity ratio, which accounts for the different levels of pay and social charges between EU countries and activities, see [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3b14a582-e5f8-4e33-9ad3-f403c67fc364?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-18T11:22:53Z Enterprises by detailed NACE Rev. 2 activity and special aggregates (sbs_ovw_act)].
===Size class analysis=== Human services (NACE Sections P, Q, and R) exhibit varying concentrations of economic activity within [[Glossary:SMEs|small and medium size enterprises]] ( 0 to 249 persons). SMEs account for the vast majority of businesses in these sectors and play a pivotal role in driving sectoral output, also within human services. In particular, education, and arts, entertainment, and recreation are dominated by SMEs: they contributed over 81% of employment in both sectors and generated 74% of value added in education and 60% in arts, entertainment, and recreation. By contrast, [[Glossary:Large enterprises|large enterprises]] (250+ persons) had a more pronounced role in human health and social work activities, where they accounted for more than 47% of employment and over 48% of value added. For further information on number of people employed, value added and number of enterprises according to enterprise size class, please refer to the Eurostat database; see [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7926aa6c-c110-4a66-a4f5-6cbedd4e7586?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-18T12:48:52Z Enterprise statistics by size class and NACE Rev. 2 activity (sbs_sc_ovw)]. [[File:Table_2_Key_size_class_indicators,_Businesses_in_human_services,_(NACE_Sections_P,_Q_and_R),_EU,_2023.png |thumb|center|700px|Table 2: Key size class indicators - Businesses in human services sectors (NACE Sections P, Q and R),EU, 2023
''Source:''Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/53e5ad70-03fb-4542-ba9c-5890552b77f6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-18T12:10:22Z (sbs_sc_ovw)]|alt=A table showing key size class indicators for human services sectors (NACE Sections P, Q and R) in the EU in 2023, broken down by enterprise size class including micro, small, medium and large enterprises. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
You can also browse variables in human services - [[Glossary:Enterprise_-_SBS|number of enterprises]], [[Glossary:Number_of_employees_and_self-employed persons_-_EBS|number of persons employed]], [[Glossary:Net_turnover_-_EBS|net turnover]], [[Glossary:Value_added_-_EBS|value added]],[[Glossary:Value_of_output_-_EBS|value of output]], [[Glossary:Total_purchases_of_goods_and_services_-_EBS|purchases of goods and services]], [[Glossary:Employee_benefits_expense_-_EBS|employee benefit expenses]], [[Glossary:Hours_worked_by_employees_-_EBS|hours worked by employees]], social security costs - by enterprise size class in the interactive visualisation below.
===Regional data: human services === For regional data on education; human health and social work activities and arts, entertainment and recreation, such as number of [[Glossary:Local_unit_-_SBS|local units]] or [[Glossary:Wages_and_salaries_-_EBS|wages and salaries]] please refer to the 2 interactive regional maps below.
Map 1: Businesses in human services, by region, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https: to be included sbs_r_nuts2021])
Map 2: Businesses in human services sectors, by region, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https:to be included sbs_r_nuts2021]) === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= H services Masterfile REV.xlsx|title=Businesses Human services - 2023 data}} ===Data sources=== Eurostat's structural business statistics (SBS) describe the structure, conduct and performance of economic activities, down to a detailed activity level (several hundred sectors). Without this structural information, short-term data on the economic cycle would lack context and would be more difficult to interpret. '''Coverage''': Structural business statistics cover the 'business economy', which includes industry, construction and many services (NACE Rev. 2 sections B to N, P to R as well as division S95 and S96). Structural business statistics do not cover agriculture, forestry and fishing, nor public administration. Structural business statistics describe the business economy through the observation of units engaged in an economic activity; the unit in structural business statistics is generally the enterprise. An enterprise carries out one or more activities, at one or more locations, and it may comprise one or more legal units. Enterprises that are active in more than one economic activity (plus the value added and turnover they generate, the people they employ, and so on) are classified under the NACE heading corresponding to their principal activity; this is normally the one which generates the largest amount of value added. '''Data sources''': The analysis presented in this article is based on the main dataset for [[Glossary:Structural business statistics (SBS)|structural business statistics (SBS)]], size class data and regional data, all of which are published annually. The main series provides information for each EU country as well as a number of non-EU countries at a detailed level according to the activity classification NACE. Data are available for a wide range of variables. In structural business statistics, size classes are generally defined by the number of persons employed. A limited set of the standard structural business statistics variables (for example, the number of enterprises, turnover, persons employed and value added) are analysed by size class, mostly down to the three-digit (group) level of NACE. The main size classes used in this article for presenting the results are: *small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs): with 1 to 249 persons employed, further divided into; **micro enterprises: with less than 10 persons employed; **small enterprises: with 10 to 49 persons employed; **medium-sized enterprises: with 50 to 249 persons employed; *large enterprises: with 250 or more persons employed. As seen in the figures above, structural business statistics also include regional data. Regional SBS data are available at NUTS levels 1 and 2 for most of the EU countries, Iceland and Norway, mostly down to the two-digit (division) level of NACE. The main variable analysed in this article is the number of persons employed. The type of statistical unit used for regional SBS data is normally the local unit, which is an enterprise or part of an enterprise situated in a geographically identified place. Local units are classified into sectors (by NACE) normally according to their own main activity, but in some EU countries the activity code is assigned on the basis of the principal activity of the enterprise to which the local unit belongs. The main SBS data series are presented at national level only, and for this national data the statistical unit is the enterprise. It is possible for the principal activity of a local unit to differ from that of the enterprise to which it belongs. Hence, national SBS data from the main series are not necessarily directly comparable with national aggregates compiled from regional SBS. ===Context=== European enterprise policy is conducted by the [https://commission.europa.eu/about-european-commission/departments-and-executive-agencies/internal-market-industry-entrepreneurship-and-smes_en Directorate-General (DG) for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs (GROW)] The [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]]'s enterprise policies aim to create a favourable environment for business to thrive within the EU, creating higher productivity, economic growth, jobs and wealth. Policies are aimed at reducing administrative burden, stimulating innovation, encouraging sustainable production, and ensuring the smooth functioning of the EU's internal market. ===Other articles=== *[[Businesses in the manufacturing sector]] *[[Structural business statistics – overview article]] *[[Structural business statistics at regional level]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database?node_code=sbs Structural business statistics (sbs)] ===Dedicated section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/overview Structural business statistics webpage] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/publications Recent Eurostat publications on SBS] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-key-figures/w/KS-01-25-003 Key figures on Europe – 2025 edition] – see subchapter on Business *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/KS-01-25-037 Eurostat’s Regional Yearbook] – see chapter 8. Business *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20241205-1 News Article] – 2022 final data===Methodology=== ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=sbs_esms|title=Structural business statistics}} – SBS metadata file *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-25-016 European business statistics methodological manual for business demography statistics – 2025 edition] ===Legislation=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/legislation Details on SBS Legislation] *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32019R2152 European Business Statistics Regulation] ===External links=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/competition/index_en.html European Commission – Competition], see:
*[http://ec.europa.eu/competition/sectors/consumer_goods/overview_en.html Competition Policy]
*[http://ec.europa.eu/growth/about-us/index_en.htm European Commission — Directorate-General (DG) for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs (GROWTH)], see:
*[https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/services_en Single market for services]
*[https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/smes_en Entrepreneurship and SMEs]
*[http://ec.europa.eu/environment/index_en.htm European Commission — Environment], see:
*[http://ec.europa.eu/environment/eussd/ Sustainable development]

title: Businesses in financial and insurance activities sector
text:
EU statistics present an overview of the European Union's (EU) Financial and insurance activities sector. Data extracted in June 2026 Planned article update: January 2027 In 2023, businesses in the financial and insurance activities sector generated €0.9 trillion of value added. There were almost 5 million people employed in businesses in the financial and insurance activities sector in 2023. This article presents an overview of statistics for the European Union's (EU) Financial and insurance activities sector, as covered by [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] Rev. 2 Section K. It belongs to a [[Business economy by sector - NACE Rev. 2|set of statistical articles]] on 'Business economy by sector'. Eurostat's [[Glossary: Structural business statistics (SBS)|structural business statistics (SBS)]] report about enterprises active in the financial and insurance sector under market conditions ('[[Glossary:Market producer|market producers]]') since reference year 2021.

===Structural profile=== In 2023, the [[Glossary:EU-27|EU]]'s financial and insurance activities sector (Section K) comprised a total of around 883 000 [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]]. These enterprises [[Glossary:Persons employed - SBS|employed]] almost 5 million people and accumulated a [[Glossary:Turnover_-_SBS|net turnover]] of €2.4 trillion. It generated around €0.9 trillion in [[Glossary:Value added|value added]].
[[File:Table 1 Key indicators Financial and insurance activities (NACE Section K), EU, 2023.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Key indicators: Financial and insurance activities (NACE Section K), EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6f369c44-b6b4-44a6-a2db-92725b4794c2?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-07T12:55:14Z (sbs_ovw_act)]|alt= Table showing the value of key indicators in Financial and insurance activities in the EU for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, the EU's financial and insurance activities sector recorded the second highest value for [[Glossary:Apparent labour productivity - SBS|apparent labour productivity]] and the highest for [[Glossary:Average personnel costs - SBS|average employee benefits expense]] among all the NACE sections within the business economy. Combining these 2 ratios into the [[Glossary:Wage-adjusted labour productivity ratio|wage-adjusted labour productivity ratio]] shows the extent to which value added per person employed covers average personnel costs per employee. In 2023, the financial and insurance activities sector had a wage-adjusted labor productivity ratio of 245.0%, reflecting the sector's high productivity. This was the second highest ratio across all NACE sections within the business economy.
The [[Glossary:Gross operating rate - SBS|gross operating rate]] stood at 24.8% for the EU's financial and insurance activities sector in 2023. This figure surpassed the 13.1% average of gross operating rate for the business economy, ranking second among the NACE sections. The gross operating rate indicates the share of [[Glossary:Turnover - SBS|turnover]] remaining after paying for purchased goods and services as well as employee benefits expense (in other words, the [[Glossary:Gross operating surplus - SBS|gross operating surplus]]). ===Sectoral analysis=== The financial and insurance activities sector is organised into 3 NACE divisions at 2-digit level: * financial service activities, except insurance and pension funding (Division 64), * insurance, reinsurance and pension funding, except compulsory social security (Division 65), * activities auxiliary to financial services and insurance activities (Division 66).
In 2023, more than half of the EU's employment in the financial and insurance activities sector was allocated to the subsector of 'Financial service activities, except insurance and pension funding' (Division 64), which encompasses activities of obtaining and redistributing funds other than for the purpose of insurance or pension funding or compulsory social security. It includes, among others, monetary intermediation done by banks and central banks, activities of holding companies, as well as trusts, funds and similar financial entities — see Figure 1a.
Figure 1a|alt=An interactive chart showing the sectoral breakdown of key indicators, absolute values, for NACE Section K in the EU in 2023]]
Figure 1b|alt=An interactive chart showing the sectoral breakdown of key indicators, ratios, for NACE Section K in the EU in 2023]]
The highest number of enterprises, although on a smaller scale, was recorded in the subsector of activities auxiliary to financial services and insurance activities (Division 66). This division includes the provision of services involved in or closely related to financial service activities, but not themselves providing financial services, like stock exchanges and management of mutual or pension funds. This subsector employed 1.5 million persons, as seen in Table 2a. [[File: Table_2a_.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 2a: Sectoral analysis of key indicators, Financial and insurance activities (NACE Section K), EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fb693c86-aa90-4637-8b26-82b872ca9e66?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-13T09:43:59Z (sbs_ovw_act)]|alt= Table showing sectoral analysis of key indicators of Financial and insurance activities in the EU for the year 2023 based on number of enterprises, number of persons employed, net turnover, value added and employee benefits expense. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[File: Table_2b_.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 2b: Sectoral analysis of key indicators, Financial and insurance activities (NACE Section K), EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/94c2da33-4181-4007-8ecc-2d2d9e20b821?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-13T09:46:37Z (sbs_ovw_act)]|alt= Table showing sectoral analysis of key indicators of Financial and insurance activities in the EU for the year 2023 based on number of enterprises, number of persons employed, net turnover, value added and employee benefits expense. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Country overview=== In 2023, Luxembourg recorded the highest relative importance of the financial and insurance sector within its total business economy, with financial activities accounting for around 38% of value added and 12% of employment relative to the business economy total. Ireland, Malta, Estonia, Cyprus also showed above-average shares relative to their business economies, both in terms of employment and value added particularly in value added, where financial activities represented between 9.6% and 14.6% of total business economy value added. Figure 2 illustrates the diverse financial and insurance activities sector's contributions to the business economy among countries.
Figure 2|alt=An interactive chart showing the relative importance of businesses in the commercial and consumer services sectors across EU member states in 2023, covering NACE Section K. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among the 5 largest EU countries, Germany created 220 668 million of euro of value added in market activities in the financial and insurance sector in 2023. France recorded the next highest share, counting 137 330 million of euro of value added. The contribution of the top 5 countries in the financial and insurance activities sector accounted for 562 067 million of euro of value added and employed 3 305 414 persons. In terms of employment, the financial and insurance activities sector in Germany had the highest share in the whole business economy followed by France, Italy, Spain and Poland— see Figure 3a.
Figure 3a |alt=An interactive chart showing key indicators, absolute values, for commercial and consumer services sectors by EU countries in 2023, including metrics such as turnover, value added and employment for NACE Section K. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Figure 3b|alt=An interactive chart showing additional key indicators, ratios, for financial and insurance sectors by EU countries in 2023, complementing Figure 3a with further breakdowns across NACE Section K. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

=== Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Businesses in financial and insurance services sector 30-06-2026 v2 REV.xlsx|title=Businesses in financial and insurance activities sector - 2023 data}} ===Data sources and availability=== '''Coverage''' The financial and insurance activities sector includes financial service activities, including insurance, reinsurance and pension funding activities and activities to support financial services. It covers, as well, the activities of holding assets, such as activities of holding companies and the activities of trusts, funds and similar financial entities.
The activities covered by the financial and insurance activities sector are categorized as follows: *financial service activities, except insurance and pension funding (Division 64) **monetary intermediation (Division 641) **activities of holding companies (Division 642) **trusts, funds and similar financial entities (Division 643) ** Other financial service activities, except insurance and pension funding (Division 649) This division encompasses activities of obtaining and redistributing funds other than for the purpose of insurance or pension funding or compulsory social security. It includes, among others, monetary intermediation done by banks and central banks, activities of holding companies, as well as trusts, funds and similar financial entities *insurance, reinsurance and pension funding, except compulsory social security (Division 65) **insurance (Division 651) **reinsurance (Division 652) **pension funding (Division 653) This division includes the underwriting annuities and insurance policies and investing premiums to build up a portfolio of financial assets to be used against future claims. Provision of direct insurance and reinsurance are included. *activities auxiliary to financial services and insurance activities (Division 66) **activities auxiliary to financial services, except insurance and pension funding (Division 661) **activities auxiliary to insurance and pension funding (Division 662) **fund management activities (Division 663) This division includes the provision of services involved in or closely related to financial service activities, but not themselves providing financial services, like stock exchanges and management of mutual or pension funds. The primary breakdown of this division is according to the type of financial transaction or funding served. ''Data sources'' Structural business statistics cover the 'business economy', which includes industry, construction and many services (NACE Rev. 2 sections B to N, P to R as well as division S95 and S96). Structural business statistics do not cover agriculture, forestry and fishing, nor public administration.
Structural business statistics describe the business economy through the observation of units engaged in an economic activity; the unit in structural business statistics is generally the enterprise. An enterprise carries out one or more activities, at one or more locations, and it may comprise one or more legal units. Enterprises that are active in more than one economic activity (plus the value added and turnover they generate, the people they employ, and so on) are classified under the NACE heading corresponding to their principal activity; this is normally the one which generates the largest amount of value added.
The analysis presented in this article is based on the main dataset for [[Glossary:Structural business statistics (SBS)|structural business statistics (SBS)]], size class data and regional data, all of which are published annually. SBS only cover the activities of market producers, meaning those acting under market conditions. Contrary to most activities covered by SBS, non-market producers represent a significant part of the Financial and insurance activities sector. The main series provides information for each EU countries as well as a number of non-EU countries at a detailed level according to the activity classification NACE. Data are available for a wide range of variables.
In structural business statistics, size classes are generally defined by the number of persons employed. A limited set of the standard structural business statistics variables (for example, the number of enterprises, turnover, persons employed and value added) are analysed by size class, mostly down to the three-digit (group) level of NACE. The main size classes used in this article for presenting the results are: *small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs): with 1 to 249 persons employed, further divided into **micro enterprises: with less than 10 persons employed; **small enterprises: with 10 to 49 persons employed; **medium-sized enterprises: with 50 to 249 persons employed; *large enterprises: with 250 or more persons employed. Structural business statistics also include regional data. Regional SBS data are available at NUTS levels 1 and 2 for most of the EU countries, Iceland and Norway, mostly down to the two-digit (division) level of NACE. The main variable analysed in this article is the number of persons employed. The type of statistical unit used for regional SBS data is normally the local unit, which is an enterprise or part of an enterprise situated in a geographically identified place. Local units are classified into sectors (by NACE) normally according to their own main activity, but in some EU countries the activity code is assigned on the basis of the principal activity of the enterprise to which the local unit belongs. The main SBS data series are presented at national level only, and for this national data the statistical unit is the enterprise. It is possible for the principal activity of a local unit to differ from that of the enterprise to which it belongs. Hence, national SBS data from the main series are not necessarily directly comparable with national aggregates compiled from regional SBS. ===Context=== European enterprise policy is conducted by the [https://commission.europa.eu/about-european-commission/departments-and-executive-agencies/internal-market-industry-entrepreneurship-and-smes_en Directorate-General (DG) for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs (GROW)] The [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]]'s enterprise policies aim to create a favourable environment for business to thrive within the EU, creating higher productivity, economic growth, jobs and wealth. Policies are aimed at reducing administrative burden, stimulating innovation, encouraging sustainable production, and ensuring the smooth functioning of the EU's internal market. ===Other articles=== *[[Business economy by sector - NACE Rev. 2|Other analyses of the business economy by NACE Rev. 2 sections]] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Structural_business_statistics_overview Structural business statistics – overview article] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/database Structural business statistics (sbs)] ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/overview Structural business statistics webpage] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/publications Recent Eurostat publications on SBS] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-key-figures/w/KS-01-25-003 Key figures on Europe – 2025 edition] – see subchapter on Business *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/KS-01-25-037 Eurostat’s Regional Yearbook] – see chapter 8. Business *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20241205-1 News Article] – 2022 final data===Methodology=== ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=sbs_esms|title=Structural business statistics}} – SBS metadata file *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-25-016 European business statistics methodological manual for business demography statistics – 2025 edition] ===Legislation=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/legislation Details on SBS Legislation] *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32019R2152 European Business Statistics Regulation] ===External links=== *[https://finance.ec.europa.eu/banking_en European Commission on Banking, banking union, insurance & pensions] *[https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/index_en Directorate-General Economic and Financial Affairs] *[https://www.eiopa.europa.eu/tools-and-data/insurance-statistics_en European Insurance and Occupational Pension Authority – insurance statistics] *[https://www.eiopa.europa.eu/tools-and-data/occupational-pensions-statistics_en European Insurance and Occupational Pension Authority – occupational pensions statistics] {{Unit|topic=X_Structural_business_statistics}} [[Category:Industry, trade, and services|Businesses in the Financial and insurance activities sector]] [[Category:Structural business statistics (SBS)|Businesses in the Financial and insurance activities sector]] [[Category:Services|Businesses in the Financial and insurance activities sector]] [[Category:Vistool|Businesses in the Financial and insurance activities sector]] [[Category:Statistical article|Businesses in the Financial and insurance activities sector]] [[Category:July2027|Businesses in the Financial and insurance activities sector]]

title: Businesses in non-manufacturing industries
text:
EU statistics present an overview of the European Union's (EU) businesses in the non-manufacturing industries. Data extracted in January 2026 Planned article update: January 2027 In 2023, 'Mining and quarrying' accounted for 0.2% of persons employed within the business economy, while 'Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply' represented 0.9%. 'Water supply, sewerage, waste management and remediation activities' around 1%. Altogether, the businesses in non-manufacturing industries accounted for 8.1% of EU business economy's net turnover, generating around €3.1 trillion.

This article presents an overview of statistics for 3 economic activities within the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union's (EU)]] industrial economy: mining and quarrying; electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply; and water supply, sewerage, waste management and remediation activities, as covered by [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] Rev. 2 Section B; D and E. It belongs to a [[Business economy by sector - NACE Rev. 2|set of statistical articles]] on 'Business economy by sector'. ===Structural profile=== In 2023, only 0.1 % of all [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]] in the [[Glossary:EU|EU]]'s [[Glossary:Business economy|business economy]] (Sections B to N and P to R, as well as Divisions S95 and S96) were classified as 'Mining and quarrying'; (Section B), a total of around 16 900 enterprises. 'Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply'; (Section D) accounted for 203 500 enterprises, and for 'Water supply, sewerage, waste management and remediation activities' (Section E) this figure was 82 100 enterprises, corresponding to 0.6% and 0.2 % of all enterprises, respectively. In terms of economic contribution, 'Mining and quarrying' (Section B) generated €41.1 billion in value added. The 'Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply' (Section D) sector contributed a significantly higher €393.5 billion, while 'Water supply, sewerage, waste management and remediation activities' (Section E) accounted for €113.8 billion. Despite these substantial sums, these industries remain among the smaller NACE sections within the EU's business economy when measured by their overall share of total value added. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The [[Glossary:Gross operating rate - SBS|gross operating rate]] (the relation between the [[Glossary:Gross operating surplus - SBS|gross operating surplus]] and [[Glossary:Turnover - SBS|turnover]]) for the EU's Mining and quarrying sector was 16.9 %; for the electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply sector it was 11.4 %, and for the water supply, sewerage, waste management and remediation activities sector it was 15.3 % in 2023. ===Sectoral analysis=== The 3 non-manufacturing sectors (B,D,E) display disparity. At the NACE division level the mining and quarrying sector is composed of 5 divisions, Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply of 1 division and water supply, sewerage, waste management and remediation activities of 4 divisions. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]]

title: Businesses in distributive trade sector
text:
EU statistics present an overview of the European Union's (EU) businesses in the distributive trade sector. Data extracted in June 2026 Planned article update: January 2027 In 2023, the distributive trade sector accounted for 18.4% of persons employed within the EU's business economy and 17.6% of all enterprises. The distributive trade sector generated €1 576 billion of value added in the EU in 2023, representing 15.1% of the business economy total.
Figure 1a|alt=An interactive chart showing the sectoral breakdown of key indicators, absolute values for NACE Section G in the EU in 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
This article presents an overview of statistics for the distributive trade sector within the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union's (EU)]] economy, as covered by [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] Rev. 2 Section G. It belongs to a [[Business economy by sector - NACE Rev. 2|set of statistical articles]] on 'Business economy by sector'. The distributive trade sector covers wholesale and retail trade and the repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles. It acts as the link between producers and consumers, and is one of the largest sectors of the EU's business economy in terms of both the number of enterprises and the number of people employed. Activity in the sector is closely tied to household consumption and consumer confidence. ===Structural profile=== In 2023, 17.6% of all [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]] in the [[Glossary:EU|EU]]'s [[Glossary:Business economy|business economy]] (Sections B to N and P to R, as well as Divisions S95 and S96) were classified as 'Distributive trade' (Section G), a total of about 5.8 million enterprises. These enterprises [[Glossary:Persons employed - SBS|employed]] 29.8 million people, accounting for 18.4% of business economy employment. In terms of economic contribution, the distributive trade sector generated €1 576.0 billion in value added in 2023, corresponding to 15.1% of the business economy total. Net turnover reached €11.4 trillion, while gross operating surplus stood at €653.2 billion. Employee benefits expense across the sector amounted to €923.0 billion. [[File: Table_1_distributive_trade_.png |thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Key indicators, Distributive trade (NACE Section G), EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_ovw_act__custom_21816973/default/table?lang=en sbs_ovw_act]|alt=A table showing an overview of key indicators in the distributive trade sector (NACE Section G) in the EU in 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The [[Glossary:Apparent labour productivity - SBS|apparent labour productivity]] of the EU's distributive trade sector in 2023 was €52 900 per person employed. The sector recorded a [[Glossary:Wage-adjusted labour productivity ratio|wage-adjusted labour productivity ratio]] of 144.6% and a [[Glossary:Gross operating rate - SBS|gross operating rate]] (the relation between the [[Glossary:Gross operating surplus - SBS|gross operating surplus]] and [[Glossary:Turnover - SBS|turnover]]) of 5.8%. ===Sectoral analysis=== The distributive trade sector (NACE Section G) is composed of 3 divisions: wholesale and retail trade and repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles (Division 45), wholesale trade except of motor vehicles and motorcycles (Division 46) and retail trade except of motor vehicles and motorcycles (Division 47). For more information and comparisons between the divisions please refer to the Data browser, see [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_ovw_act/default/table Enterprises by detailed NACE Rev. 2 activity and special aggregates (sbs_ovw_act)].
Figure 1a|alt=An interactive chart showing the sectoral breakdown of key indicators, absolute values for NACE Section G in the EU in 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

Figure 1b|alt=An interactive chart showing the sectoral breakdown of key indicators, absolute values for NACE Section G in the EU in 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Country overview=== In 2023, the relative importance of the distributive trade sector within national business economies was highest in Greece, where the sector accounted for around 24% of employment and 20% of value added — the highest share on both measures. Bulgaria and Denmark also stood out in employment terms, at around 23% and 22% respectively, while Latvia and Romania recorded high value added shares of around 19%.
Figure 2|alt=An interactive chart showing the relative importance of the distributive trade industry in 2023, covering NACE Section G. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
In 2023, Germany was the largest EU country for the distributive trade sector in value added terms, generating around €405 billion. The top 5 was completed by France, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands.
Figure 3a |alt=An interactive chart showing key indicators, absolute values, for the distributive trade industry by EU member state in 2023, including metrics such as turnover, value added and employment for NACE Section G. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Figure 3b|alt=An interactive chart showing additional key indicators, ratios, for the distributive trade industry in 2023, complementing Figure 3a with further breakdowns across NACE Section G. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] For average employee benefits expense within the businesses in the distributive trade industry in 2023, please consult the data available on this bookmark, where you will also find information on the wage-adjusted labour productivity ratio, which accounts for the different levels of pay and social charges between EU countries and activities, [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_ovw_act__custom_21559546/default/table Enterprises by detailed NACE Rev. 2 activity and special aggregates (sbs_ovw_act)]
===Size class analysis=== The distributive trade sector is characterised by a strong presence of micro and small enterprises. In 2023, of the roughly 5.8 million enterprises in the sector, 5.46 million (93.7%) were micro enterprises employing fewer than 10 persons. Despite this fragmentation, [[Glossary:Large enterprises|large enterprises]] (employing 250 or more persons) play a significant role in sectoral output: they employed 9.8 million people and generated €600 billion of value added in 2023. Large enterprises also recorded a high apparent labour productivity (around €61,200 per head), above the sectoral average of around €52,900. For further information on number of persons employed, value added and number of enterprises according to enterprise size class, please refer to the Eurostat database; see [link] [sbs_ovw_act] [[File: Table_2_distributive_trade_.png |thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Key size class indicators, Distributive trade (NACE Section G), EU, 2023

The main series provides information for each EU country as well as a number of non-EU member countries at a detailed level according to the activity classification NACE. Data are available for a wide range of variables. In structural business statistics, size classes are generally defined by the number of persons employed. A limited set of the standard structural business statistics variables (for example, the number of enterprises, turnover, persons employed and value added) are analysed by size class, mostly down to the three-digit (group) level of NACE. The main size classes used in this article for presenting the results are: *small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs): with 1 to 249 persons employed, further divided into; **micro enterprises: with less than 10 persons employed; **small enterprises: with 10 to 49 persons employed; **medium-sized enterprises: with 50 to 249 persons employed; *large enterprises: with 250 or more persons employed. As seen in the figures above, structural business statistics also include regional data. Regional SBS data are available at NUTS levels 1 and 2 for most of the EU countries, Iceland and Norway, mostly down to the two-digit (division) level of NACE. The main variable analysed in this article is the number of persons employed. The type of statistical unit used for regional SBS data is normally the local unit, which is an enterprise or part of an enterprise situated in a geographically identified place. Local units are classified into sectors (by NACE) normally according to their own main activity, but in some EU countries the activity code is assigned on the basis of the principal activity of the enterprise to which the local unit belongs. The main SBS data series are presented at national level only, and for this national data the statistical unit is the enterprise. It is possible for the principal activity of a local unit to differ from that of the enterprise to which it belongs. Hence, national SBS data from the main series are not necessarily directly comparable with national aggregates compiled from regional SBS. ===Context=== This article presents an overview of statistics for the Distributive trade sector in the EU, as covered by NACE section G. ===Other articles=== *[[Business economy by sector - NACE Rev. 2|Other analyses of the business economy by NACE Rev. 2 sections]] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Structural_business_statistics_overview Structural business statistics – overview article] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/database Structural business statistics (sbs)] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/publications Recent Eurostat publications on SBS] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-key-figures/w/KS-01-25-003 Key figures on Europe – 2025 edition] – see subchapter on Business *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/KS-01-25-037 Eurostat’s Regional Yearbook] – see chapter 8. Business *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20241205-1 News Release SBS] ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=sbs_esms|title=Structural business statistics}} – SBS metadata file ===Legislation=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/legislation Details on SBS Legislation] *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32019R2152 European Business Statistics Regulation] ===External links=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/dgs/jrc/index.cfm Joint Research Centre - EU Science Hub], see: :*[http://eurocodes.jrc.ec.europa.eu/ Eurocodes] {{Unit|topic=X_Structural_business_statistics}} [[Category:Industry, trade, and services|Businesses in the distributive trade sector]] [[Category:Structural business statistics (SBS)|Businesses in the distributive trade sector]] [[Category:Statistical article|Businesses in the distributive trade sector]] [[Category:Vistool|Businesses in the distributive trade sector]] [[Category:January2027|Businesses in the distributive trade sector]]

title: Businesses in the commercial and consumer services sectors
text:
Insert short description for search engines Data extracted in May 2026 Planned article update: January 2027 In 2023, ‘Transportation and storage' accounted for 6.4% of persons employed within the business economy; ‘Accommodation and food service activities' for 7.0%; ‘Information and communication' for 4.5%; 'Real estate activities' for 1.7%; ‘Professional, scientific and technical activities’ for 7.6% and ‘Administrative and support service activities’ for 8.7%. Businesses in the commercial and consumer services sectors accounted for 20.4% of the EU business economy's net turnover in 2023, generating around €7.8 trillion.
Sectoral analysis of businesses in the commercial and consumer services (NACE Sections H, I, J, L, M and N), EU, 2023|alt=An interactive chart showing the sectoral breakdown of key indicators, absolute values, for NACE Sections H, I, J, L, M and N in the EU in 2023, comparing transportation and storage; accommodation and food service activities; information and communication; real estate; professional, scientific and technical activities and administrative and support service activities. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
This article presents an overview of statistics for 6 economic activities, as covered by [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] Rev. 2 Section H; I; J; L; M and N, within the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union's (EU)]] services economy: * transportation and storage * accommodation and food service activities * information and communication * real estate * professional, scientific and technical activities * administrative and support service activities It belongs to a [[Business economy by sector - NACE Rev. 2|set of statistical articles]] on 'Business economy by sector'. === Structural profile === In 2023, 4.4% of all [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]] in the [[Glossary:EU|EU]]'s [[Glossary:Business economy|business economy]] (Sections B to N and P to R, as well as Divisions S95 and S96) were classified as ‘Transportation and storage ' (Section H) and also ‘Information and communication ' (Section J), each with a total of close to 1.461 million enterprises. The ‘Accommodation and food service activities ' (Section I) accounted for 1.988 million enterprises, corresponding to 6.0% of all enterprises. For ' Real estate activities ' (Section L) this figure was 1.589 million enterprises, equivalent to 4.8%. A further 15.6% were classified as ‘Professional, scientific and technical activities’ (Section M), and 5.9% as ‘Administrative and support service activities’ (Section N), with a total of 5.172 and 1.937 million enterprises, respectively. In terms of economic contribution, ’Transportation and storage’ generated €597.8 billion in value added. The ‘Accommodation and food service activities ' accounted for €320.4 billion, ‘Information and communication ' contributed significantly higher with €716.1 billion, ‘Real estate activities ' reported the lowest amount within the 6 economic activities at €268.6 billion, while ‘Professional, scientific and technical activities’ created the highest at €779.3 billion; ‘Administrative and support service activities’ contributed at €607.1 billion. These services play a key role in the EU’s business economy, representing 31.4% of total value added. [[File:Table 1 Key indicators Businesses in the commercial and consumer services sectors, (NACE Sections H, I, J, L, M and N), EU, 2023.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Key indicators: Businesses in the commercial and consumer services sectors (NACE Sections H, I, J, L, M and N), EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d72b561e-6078-4776-b357-63f696c680cb?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T12:00:54Z (sbs_ovw_act)]|alt=A table showing an overview of key indicators in the commercial and consumer services sectors (NACE Sections H, I, J, L, M and N), in the EU in 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, the [[Glossary:Gross operating rate - SBS|gross operating rate]] (the relation between the [[Glossary:Gross operating surplus - SBS|gross operating surplus]] and [[Glossary:Turnover - SBS|turnover]]) was 12.7% for the EU's transportation and storage sector, 14.1% for accommodation and food service activities, 16.5% for information and communication, 35.5% for real estate, 17.3% for professional, scientific and technical activities, and 12.6% for administrative and support service activities. ===Sectoral analysis=== The 6 commercial and consumer services sectors (H, I, J, L, M, N) display disparity. At the NACE division level transportation and storage section is composed of 5 divisions; accommodation and food service of 2 divisions; information and communication of 6 divisions; real estate of 1 division; professional, scientific and technical activities of 7 divisions and administrative and support service activities of 6 divisions. For more information and comparisons between the divisions please refer to Data browser, see [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fd5b1024-b941-41a8-abd7-900c1d2a407d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-21T08:57:47Z Enterprises by detailed NACE Rev. 2 activity and special aggregates (sbs_ovw_act)].
Figure 1a|alt=An interactive chart showing the sectoral breakdown of key indicators, absolute values, for NACE Sections H, I, J, L, M and N in the EU in 2023, comparing transportation and storage; accommodation and food service activities; information and communication; real estate; professional, scientific and technical activities and administrative and support service activities. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

Figure 1b|alt=An interactive chart showing the sectoral breakdown of key indicators, ratios, for NACE Sections H, I, J, L, M and N in the EU in 2023, comparing transportation and storage; accommodation and food service activities; information and communication; real estate; professional, scientific and technical activities and administrative and support service activities. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

===Country overview=== Commercial and consumer services sectors play different roles at country level in the national business economy. In 2023, the highest shares of business economy value added were recorded in Lithuania (15.1%), Denmark (9.8%) and Latvia (8.1%) for the transportation and storage sector; in Greece (8.6%), Cyprus (8.4%) and Croatia (7.0%) for the accommodation and food service sector; in Ireland (19.1%), Cyprus (15.9%) and Malta (14.6%) for the information and communication services sector; in Sweden (5.7%), Latvia (5.5%) and Estonia (5.0%) for the real estate sector; in Luxembourg (13.7%), Malta (10.8%) and the Netherlands (10.1%) for the professional, scientific and technical activities sector; and in the Netherlands (9.3%), Malta (8.3%) and Belgium (7.2%) for the administrative and support service activities sector.
Figure 2|alt=An interactive chart showing the relative importance of businesses in the commercial and consumer services sectors across EU member states in 2023, covering NACE Sections H, I, J, L, M and N. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Figure 3a |alt=An interactive chart showing key indicators, absolute values, for commercial and consumer services sectors by EU countries in 2023, including metrics such as turnover, value added and employment for NACE Sections H, I, J, L, M and N. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Figure 3b|alt=An interactive chart showing additional key indicators, ratios, for commercial and consumer services sectors by EU countries in 2023, complementing Figure 3a with further breakdowns across NACE Sections H, I, J, L, M and N. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] For average employee benefits expense within the businesses in the commercial and consumer services sectors in 2023, please consult the data available on this bookmark, where you will also find information on the wage-adjusted labour productivity ratio, which accounts for the different levels of pay and social charges between EU countries and activities, [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7f3897be-1c81-421d-af12-d94fa97c486b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-21T10:09:05Z Enterprises by detailed NACE Rev. 2 activity and special aggregates (sbs_ovw_act)].
===Size class analysis=== The commercial and consumer services sectors (NACE Sections H, I, J, L, M and N) are characterised by different concentration of economic activity within [[Glossary:Large enterprises|Large enterprises]] (250+ persons). Despite representing a small fraction of the total businesses, these firms are the primary drivers of sectoral output, accounting for almost 45% of employment and around 55% of value added in the information and communication and in the transportation and storage sectors. In contrast, SMEs are the main contributors to sectoral performances in the other 4 sectors. For further information on number of persons employed, value added and number of enterprises according to enterprise size class, please refer to the Eurostat database, see [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/31e50d53-742d-4519-8c3a-e61c7c651771?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-21T10:18:00Z Enterprise statistics by size class and NACE Rev. 2 activity (sbs_sc_ovw)]. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
You can also browse variables in the commercial and consumer services sectors - such as [[Glossary:Value_of_output_-_EBS|value of output]], [[Glossary:Total_purchases_of_goods_and_services|purchases of goods and services]], or [[Glossary:Hours_worked_by_employees_-_EBS|hours worked by employees]], - by enterprise size class in the interactive visualisation below.

''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f8fe4a8d-13d3-4df0-beb0-b36881095d84?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T12:31:55Z sbs_r_nuts2021])

''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/536a18ee-a6cc-4fa1-8833-919b2c35423c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T12:32:44Z sbs_r_nuts2021]) === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= Copy_of_CC_services_Masterfile_REV_1.1.xlsx |title=Businesses in the commercial and consumer services sectors - 2023 data}} ===Data sources=== Eurostat's structural business statistics (SBS) describe the structure, conduct and performance of economic activities, down to a detailed activity level (several hundred sectors). Without this structural information, short-term data on the economic cycle would lack context and would be more difficult to interpret. '''Coverage''': Structural business statistics cover the 'business economy', which includes industry, construction and many services (NACE Rev. 2 sections B to N, P to R as well as division S95 and S96). Structural business statistics do not cover agriculture, forestry and fishing, or public administration. Structural business statistics describe the business economy through the observation of units engaged in an economic activity; the unit in structural business statistics is generally the enterprise. An enterprise carries out one or more activities, at one or more locations, and it may comprise one or more legal units. Enterprises that are active in more than one economic activity (plus the value added and turnover they generate, the people they employ, and so on) are classified under the NACE heading corresponding to their principal activity; this is normally the one which generates the largest amount of value added. '''Data sources''': The analysis presented in this article is based on the main dataset for [[Glossary:Structural business statistics (SBS)|structural business statistics (SBS)]], size class data and regional data, all of which are published annually. The main series provides information for each EU country as well as a number of non-EU member countries at a detailed level according to the activity classification NACE. Data are available for a wide range of variables. In structural business statistics, size classes are generally defined by the number of persons employed. A limited set of the standard structural business statistics variables (for example, the number of enterprises, turnover, persons employed and value added) are analysed by size class, mostly down to the 3-digit (group) level of NACE. The main size classes used in this article for presenting the results are: *small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs): with 1 to 249 persons employed, further divided into; **micro enterprises: with less than 10 persons employed; **small enterprises: with 10 to 49 persons employed; **medium-sized enterprises: with 50 to 249 persons employed; *large enterprises: with 250 or more persons employed. As seen in the figures above, structural business statistics also include regional data. Regional SBS data are available at NUTS levels 1 and 2 for most of the EU countries, Iceland and Norway, mostly down to the 2-digit (division) level of NACE. The main variable analysed in this article is the number of persons employed. The type of statistical unit used for regional SBS data is normally the local unit, which is an enterprise or part of an enterprise situated in a geographically identified place. Local units are classified into sectors (by NACE) normally according to their own main activity, but in some EU countries the activity code is assigned on the basis of the principal activity of the enterprise to which the local unit belongs. The main SBS data series are presented at national level only, and for this national data the statistical unit is the enterprise. It is possible for the principal activity of a local unit to differ from that of the enterprise to which it belongs. Hence, national SBS data from the main series are not necessarily directly comparable with national aggregates compiled from regional SBS. ===Context=== European enterprise policy is conducted by the [https://commission.europa.eu/about-european-commission/departments-and-executive-agencies/internal-market-industry-entrepreneurship-and-smes_en Directorate-General (DG) for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs (GROW)] The [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]]'s enterprise policies aim to create a favourable environment for business to thrive within the EU, creating higher productivity, economic growth, jobs and wealth. Policies are aimed at reducing administrative burden, stimulating innovation, encouraging sustainable production, and ensuring the smooth functioning of the EU's internal market. ===Other articles=== *[[Businesses in the manufacturing sector]] *[[Structural business statistics overview]] *[[Structural business statistics at regional level]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database?node_code=sbs Structural business statistics (sbs)] ===Dedicated section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/overview Structural business statistics webpage] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/publications Recent Eurostat publications on SBS] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-key-figures/w/KS-01-25-003 Key figures on Europe – 2025 edition] – see subchapter on Business *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/KS-01-25-037 Eurostat’s Regional Yearbook] – see chapter 8. Business *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20241205-1 News Article] – 2022 final data===Methodology=== ===ESMS metadata files=== *{{Template:Esms|code=sbs_esms|title=Structural business statistics}} – SBS metadata file ===Legislation=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/legislation Details on SBS Legislation] *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32019R2152 European Business Statistics Regulation] ===External links=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/competition/index_en.html European Commission – Competition], see:
