title: Characteristics of micro high-growth enterprises
text:
EXPERIMENTAL
 Statistics on high-growth enterprises (HGEs) and their prominent and proven role in employment creation and economic growth in European countries. Data extracted in December 2020 No update planned for this article. Approximately 25-30 % of micro high-growth enterprises are young enterprises up to 5 years old. In the information and communication sector, on average 37 % of micro high-growth enterprises were young enterprises up to 5 years old. [[Image:High growth enterprises - visual.png|centre|500px]] Economic growth and job creation have been key issues on the European political agenda for years. At enterprise level, high-growth enterprises (HGEs) have a prominent and proven role in employment creation and economic growth in European countries. The regular collection of data on HGEs currently covers enterprises recording average annualised employment growth of 10 % or more over a three-year period. In addition, the enterprises have at least 10 employees when they start growing. For many years now, high-growth enterprises have been an established and regulated part of the Business Demography data collection. The methodology for assessing micro high-growth enterprises was developed and tested as part of the pilot action. The approach adopted is largely in line with the methodology currently used for identifying and measuring HGEs with 10 or more employees. This article is based on the experimental statistical results of a recent pilot action assessing the characteristics of micro high-growth enterprises, including their size, age, legal form and group status. A total of 10 [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU Member States]] (Bulgaria, Denmark, Estonia, Lithuania, Croatia, the Netherlands, Austria, Portugal, Finland and Sweden) and 2 [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA ]] countries (Iceland and Norway) participated in the development project on micro high-growth enterprises. It is the first time this kind of data on micro high-growth enterprises has been collected as part of an EU project. Due to the pilot nature of this project and the limited number and size of participating countries, the results should be interpreted with caution. === Size class === Micro high-growth enterprises are defined as enterprises employing less than 10 employees when starting their high growth period. This group of [[Glossary:Micro_enterprises|micro enterprises]] is not included in the statistics for traditional high-growth enterprises; these statistics only include enterprises with 10 or more employees at the beginning of the growth period. In the following analysis, micro enterprises are broken down into two size classes: 1-4 employees and 5-9 employees. Typically, there are more micro HGEs in the size class of 5-9 employees than in the size class of 1-4 employee. The frequency of being an HGE in both size classes was the highest in Bulgaria, Denmark, Norway and the Netherlands, where around 15 % of enterprises with 5-9 employees were classified as high growth. In the smaller size class of 1-4 employees, typically 5 % or less of the enterprises were high-growth enterprises, except for Bulgaria, where more than 20 % of enterprises with 1-4 employees were classified as HGEs. It should be noted that the criterion for being classified as an HGE was to have a minimum increase of 3.3 employees in the enterprise over a period of three years, which is obviously more easy to obtain in larger enterprises (5-9 employees) than in smaller ones (1-4 employees) (see methodological note as well). [[Image:Percentage of micro high-growth enterprises by size class in 2017_(%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 1: Percentage of micro high-growth enterprises by size class in 2017 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat, high-growth enterprises development project| alt= A bar chart showing the percentage of micro high-growth enterprises by size class (1-4 employees and 5-9 employees) in 2017 in some EU countries and some EFTA countries. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at the employee shares of micro HGEs, the difference between size classes of 1-4 employees and 5-9 employees is not substantial (see Figure 2). High-growth enterprises account for a larger share of employees in the 5-9 size class, typically around 15-25 %. In the smaller size class of 1-4 employees, the contribution of HGEs to employment is considerable, though somewhat smaller than in the 5-9 employee size class. The highest employee shares - well above 20 % in both size classes - were recorded for Denmark, the Netherlands and Norway. By contrast, the lowest HGE employee shares of 1-4 employee size class were observed in Austria, Portugal, Finland and Croatia, accounting for around 11-13 % of employees in this size class. The lowest HGE employee shares in the 5-9 employee size class were in Austria, Finland and Lithuania, at roughly 15 %. [[Image:Percentage of high-growth enterprises in employees by size class in 2017_(%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 2: Percentage of high-growth enterprises in employees by size class in 2017 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat, high-growth enterprises development project| alt= A bar chart showing the percentage of high-growth enterprises in employees by size class (1-4 employees and 5-9 employees) in 2017 in some EU countries and some EFTA countries. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Legal form=== Business demography statistics include the legal form of the enterprise as one of the variables. When dealing with high-growth enterprises, it is often the case that the potential for high growth is best realised in the legal form of a limited liability company. Such a company generally has better access to finance, risk capital and skilled employees – all critical conditions for high growth - as compared to other legal forms of sole proprietorships or partnerships. The limited liability company is a dominant legal form in micro enterprises with 1-10 employees across the participating countries (see Figure 3). On average, almost 70 % of these enterprises were limited liability companies, while they were even more frequent among micro HGEs, accounting for more than 80 % of these enterprises. The pattern appears to be relatively stable across participating countries. In five countries (Estonia, Portugal, Sweden, Lithuania and Iceland), more than 90 % of micro HGEs were limited liability companies, whereas the lowest shares were observed in Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands, around 60 %. In all countries, the limited liability companies were more frequent in micro HGEs compared to all micro enterprises. In conclusion, the average frequency of limited liability companies among HGEs is higher than that for all micro enterprises. This implies that the potential for high growth in relation to the legal form structure seems favourable in micro HGEs, given the favourable conditions that limited liability companies have for accessing critical resources such as finance, risk capital and skills. [[Image:Share of limited liability companies of micro HGEs and all micro enterprises in 2017_(%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 3: Share of limited liability companies of micro HGEs and all micro enterprises in 2017 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat, high-growth enterprises development project| alt= A bar chart showing the share of limited liability companies of micro HGEs and all micro enterprises (micro high-growth enterprises and all micro enterprises) in 2017 in some EU countries and some EFTA countries. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Group status === Group status reflects the independence of the enterprise, i.e. whether an enterprise belongs to an [[Glossary:Enterprise_group|enterprise group]] or not. If an enterprise belongs to an enterprise group, it may have less decision-making power than genuinely independent enterprises. On the other hand, enterprises within the group may have better access to multiple resources, such as skilled employees, research and innovation, marketing, technology and finance. Therefore, in the context of high-growth enterprises it is important to understand the role of group structure as a facilitator for growth. In earlier Eurostat pilot projects, group status has been included and analysed with some quite interesting results[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Statistics_on_small_and_medium-sized_enterprises#General_overview Statistics on small and medium-sized enterprises]. Considerable differences in the share of dependent vs. independent enterprises are also typical across countries. Figure 4 shows that there are four countries – Austria, Sweden, Norway and Iceland - where around 40 % of all HGEs are dependent micro HGEs, which is a prominent proportion. At the other end, less than 10 % of enterprises were dependent enterprises in Bulgaria, the Netherlands, Portugal, Croatia and Finland, implying that a great majority of the micro HGEs in these countries - more than 90 % - have an independent status. However, when measuring the volume of employees or value added, dependent enterprises have a more pronounced role in this. Dependent micro HGEs had higher shares of employment and value added compared to their share of enterprises in all countries. Furthermore, dependent micro HGEs had higher value added shares than shares of employment in all countries, thus emphasising their economic importance. Dependent micro HGEs with the highest shares of employment and value added were recorded for Austria, Sweden, Norway and Iceland, i.e. also the same countries with the highest shares with enterprises. [[Image:Share of dependent enterprises of all micro high-growth enterprises in 2017_(%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 4: Share of dependent enterprises of all micro high-growth enterprises in 2017 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat, high-growth enterprises development project| alt= A bar chart showing the share of dependent enterprises of all micro high-growth enterprises (enterprises, employees and value added) in 2017 in some EU countries and some EFTA countries. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Looking at the group status of micro enterprises by size class, broken down into 1-4 and 5-9 employees (see Figure 5), shows a consistent pattern in all countries, with the frequency of dependent HGEs somewhat higher in the 5-9 employee size class compared to the 1-4 employee size class. The largest differences between size classes were observed in the same countries that had the highest shares of dependent micro HGEs, i.e. Sweden, Austria, Iceland and Norway. [[Image:Share of dependent enterprises of all micro high-growth enterprises by size class in 2017_(%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 5: Share of dependent enterprises of all micro high-growth enterprises by size class in 2017 (%).png
''Source:'' Eurostat, high-growth enterprises development project| alt= A bar chart showing the share of dependent enterprises of all micro high-growth enterprises by size class (1-4 employees and 5-9 employees) in 2017 in some EU countries and some EFTA countries. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Age of an enterprise === The age of an enterprise is an interesting factor to follow in the context of high-growth enterprises. Traditionally young, meaning less than 5 years old, high-growth enterprises have been a population of special attention, since they form the core of the most dynamic enterprises in our economies. Even if the number of enterprises in this group is not that large, it includes enterprises with high potential for rapid growth and expansion. It is worth noting that the definition for age is not always explicit nor is it always fully comparable across countries. The age of the enterprises was broken down into three age groups: 5 years old or less (young enterprises), 5-10 years old and more than 10 years old. Figure 6 shows the employees by different enterprise age groups in micro HGEs and all micro enterprises. It is clear that young micro HGEs and micro HGEs that are 5-10 years old have a higher share of employees than all micro enterprises, while the opposite is true for enterprises 10 or more years old. While some 45 % of the employees of micro HGEs were in enterprises 10 years or older, more than 60 % of the employees of all micro enterprises belonged to this age class. [[Image:Employees broken down by age of enterprise in micro high-growth enterprises and micro enterprises in 2017, unweighted average of 10 countries (%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 6: Employees broken down by age of enterprise in micro high-growth enterprises and micro enterprises in 2017, unweighted average of 10 countries_(%)
''Source:'' Eurostat, high-growth enterprises development project| alt= A bar chart showing the employees broken down by age of enterprise in micro high-growth enterprises and micro enterprises (1-4 employees and 5-9 employees) in 2017 as unweighted average of 10 countries. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the age of enterprises. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 7 shows the share of young micro HGEs out of all HGEs and the share of young enterprises out of all micro enterprises, broken down by NACE section. In all sectors, the share of young high-growth enterprises is much higher than that of micro enterprises on average, suggesting that the micro HGEs tend also to be young enterprises. This interesting result may also have some obvious policy implications when roughly 25-30 % of micro HGEs are maximum 5 years old while a much smaller share - some 15-20 % - of all micro enterprises qualify as falling into the age group of young enterprises. Obviously, in certain sectors - such as information and communication, accommodation and food services – the density of young high-growth enterprises is higher than in other sectors of the economy. For example in information and communication, on average almost 37 % of micro high-growth enterprises were maximum 5 years old, while about 27 % of all micro high-growth enterprises in the business economy were 5 years old or younger. [[Image:Share of enterprises of 5 years or younger, by sector, unweighted average 2017_(%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 7: Share of enterprises of 5 years or younger, by sector, unweighted average 2017 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat, high-growth enterprises development project| alt= A horizontal bar chart showing the share of enterprises of 5 years or younger, by sector, unweighted average (micro high growth enterprises and all micro enterprises) in 2017. The vertical axis displays the categories, while the horizontal axis displays the types of enterprises. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Looking at the employment shares of young micro HGEs and all micro enterprises by sector, the outcome appears much the same. It is clear that the employment share of young HGEs is also roughly 10 percentage points higher than the employment share of all micro enterprises in each sector. The youngest profile of enterprises is in information and communication, accommodation and food services and administrative services; in all these activities young enterprises accounted for 30 % or more of both enterprises and employees. The enterprises least young were recorded in the traditional sectors of trade, other services and professional and technical services, which were largely business services. [[Image:Employment share of 5 years or younger enterprises, by sector, unweighted average in 2017_(%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 8: Employment share of 5 years or younger enterprises, by sector, unweighted average in 2017 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat, high-growth enterprises development project| alt= A horizontal bar chart showing the employment share of 5 years or younger enterprises, by sector, unweighted average (micro high growth enterprises and all micro enterprises) in 2017. The vertical axis displays the categories, while the horizontal axis displays the types of enterprises. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 9 shows the share of young micro HGEs out of all micro HGEs across countries in the business economy. It should be noted that the country comparison is made with reservations, since measuring or identifying the age of an enterprise is not a straightforward task and country practices may differ. As a result, Sweden, Austria, Norway and Denmark appear to have the lowest share of young enterprises in the business economy, roughly 20 %. This applies to both the share of enterprises and their employees. By contrast, the largest share of young HGEs appears to be in Bulgaria, Estonia, Lithuania and the Netherlands. In these countries some 35-40 % of micro HGEs were young, which is almost double the frequency compared to the lowest ranking countries. In the business economy, the shares of micro HGEs and their employees closely follow each other. [[Image:Business Economy, share of 5 years or younger high-growth enterprises in 2017_(%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 9: Business Economy, share of 5 years or younger high-growth enterprises in 2017 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat, high-growth enterprises development project| alt= A bar chart showing the Business Economy, share of 5 years or younger high-growth enterprises (enterprises and employees) in 2017 in some EU countries and some EFTA countries. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The role of young high-growth enterprises in the information and communication sector in different countries is shown in Figure 10. It appears that the age structure of enterprises in this sector varies a lot across countries. The highest share of young enterprises was observed in Estonia and Bulgaria followed by Lithuania and Iceland where more than 40 % of the micro HGEs in information and communication were 5 years old or younger. At the other end, in Sweden and Norway slightly over 20 % of HGEs were young while the average of the countries was 37 %. Figure 10 also shows that the share of young HGEs and the share of employees in these enterprises follow each other very closely in the information and communication sector. [[Image:Information and Communication, share of 5 years or younger high-growth enterprises in 2017_(%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 10: Information and Communication, share of 5 years or younger high-growth enterprises in 2017 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat, high-growth enterprises development project| alt= A bar chart showing the Information and Communication, share of 5 years or younger high-growth enterprises (enterprises and employees) in 2017 in some EU countries and some EFTA countries. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Type of growth === The definition of high growth traditionally includes only organic growth, meaning it excludes growth due to mergers, acquisitions and takeovers. In this pilot project, the focus was also to assess the role of organic vs. gross growth, including also growth due to mergers, acquisitions and takeovers. As the countries have different tools and practices for tracing organic vs. gross growth, the results should be interpreted with caution. In addition, the data was available only for a limited number of countries. Looking at Figure 11, two groups of countries clearly stand out. In the majority of countries, organic growth applies to some 90 % or more of all micro HGEs observed. For these countries, the same levels apply also for employees and value added. The data for Sweden, Finland and partly the Netherlands suggest that if taken into account, mergers, acquisitions and takeovers would considerably increase the number of high-growth enterprises, their employees and value added. In these countries, roughly two thirds of growth can be considered organic while one third is due to mergers, takeovers or acquisitions. In other countries where the data is available, close to 100 % is due to organic growth. The results may be explained by the fact that there are different tools and capabilities in countries to trace growth that is not organic. [[Image:Organic growth as share of total (i_e_ gross growth) in micro high-growth enterprises in 2017_(%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 11: Organic growth as share of total (i_e_ gross growth) in micro high-growth enterprises in 2017 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat, high-growth enterprises development project| alt= A bar chart showing the organic growth as share of total (i_e_ gross growth) in micro high-growth enterprises (enterprises, employees and value added) in 2017 in some EU countries and some EFTA countries. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Conclusions=== The proportion of micro HGEs is higher in the size class of 5-9 employees compared to the size class of 1-4 employees. The HGE frequencies in both size classes were the highest in Bulgaria, Denmark, Norway and the Netherlands, where around 15 % of enterprises with 5-9 employees were classified as high growth. Group status reflects the independence of the enterprise i.e. whether the enterprise belongs to an enterprise group or not. If an enterprise belongs to an enterprise group, it may have less decision-making power than genuinely independent enterprises. On the other hand, enterprises within the group may have better access to multiple resources, such as skilled employees, research and innovation, marketing, technology and finance. Therefore, in the context of high-growth enterprises it is important to understand the role of group structure as a facilitator for growth. There are four countries – Austria, Sweden, Norway and Iceland - where dependent micro HGEs account for a prominent share of all HGEs at around 40 %. At the other end, dependent enterprises accounted for less than 10 % of enterprises in Bulgaria, the Netherlands, Portugal, Croatia and Finland. This implies that a great majority, more than 90 %, of the micro HGEs in these countries have independent status. When measuring the volume of employees or value added, dependent enterprises have a more pronounced role in this. Traditionally young, i.e. less than 5 years old, high-growth enterprises have been a population of special attention since they comprise the core of the most dynamic enterprises in our economies. Even if this group is not that large in terms of the number of enterprises, it includes enterprises with a high potential for rapid growth and expansion. In all sectors, the share of young high-growth enterprises is much higher than the share of micro enterprises on average, suggesting that the micro HGEs tend also to be young enterprises. Approximately 25-30 % of micro HGEs are maximum 5 years old, while a much smaller share - some 15-20 % - of all micro enterprises qualify as falling into the age group of young enterprises. Looking at the employment shares of young micro HGEs and all micro enterprises by sector, the outcome appears much the same. It is clear that the employment share of young HGEs is also roughly 10 percentage points higher than the employment share of all micro enterprises in each sector. The youngest profile of enterprises is in information and communication, accommodation and food services and administrative services; in all these activities, young enterprises accounted for 30 % or more of both enterprises and employees. The enterprises least young were recorded in the traditional sectors of trade, other services and professional and technical services, which were largely business services. ===Feedback=== To help Eurostat improve these experimental statistics, users and researchers are kindly invited to give us their [mailto:ESTAT-BUSINESS-DEMOGRAPHY@ec.europa.eu?subject=Feedback_on_experimental_statistics feedback by email] === Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=P1 FIGURES 8.3 update V2.xlsx|title=High-growth enterprises - tables and figures}} === Data sources === '''The methodology applied for defining micro high-growth enterprises''' The methodology applied requires that the minimum growth in absolute numbers for a micro HGE is 3.31 employees in 3 years. This threshold is drawn from current HGE methodology where an enterprise with exactly 10 employees in the beginning of growth, having average annualised growth of 10% in the number of employees over a three-year period, would have the number of employees in year t at least 1.331 times higher than in year t-3. For reasons of consistency, the scope of the micro enterprises is limited only to the size class of 1-9 employees in the year of the beginning of growth and consequently omits the 0-employee size class. In this project, the same absolute number of growth (3.31 employees) is applied to enterprises with 1 to 9 employees at the starting year of the growth (t-3). As a result, the population of micro high-growth enterprises needs to grow by at least 3.31 employees in 3 years. The methodology applied should, in principle, follow the same as in the OECD-Eurostat manual on BD, and in particular the relevant parts dealing with high-growth enterprises. This harmonised methodology would make it possible to compare and benchmark the standard HGE data with our new micro HGE data. It is also important to emphasize the issue of head count versus full-time equivalent (FTE), as country practices may differ. Also, the number and share of part time workers may influence the figures across sectors and countries. === Context === Economic growth and job creation have been key issues on the European political agenda for many years. At enterprise level, high-growth enterprises (HGEs) have a prominent and proven role in employment creation and economic growth in European countries. The current definition for high-growth enterprises excludes all enterprises having 1 to 9 employees in the beginning of the growth period (i.e. 3 years before the reference year); therefore these enterprises do not belong to the current business demography data collection on HGEs. The results are based on the experimental statistical results of a recent pilot action assessing the role of micro high-growth enterprises in economic growth and job creation. A total of 10 EU Member States (Bulgaria, Denmark, Estonia, Lithuania, Croatia, the Netherlands, Austria, Portugal, Finland and Sweden) and 2 EFTA countries (Iceland and Norway) participated in the development project on micro high-growth enterprises. It is the first time this kind of data on micro high-growth enterprises has been collected as part of an EU project. Due to the pilot nature of this project and the limited number and size of participating countries, the results should be interpreted with caution. === Other articles === *[[Business demography statistics]] === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/micro-high-growth-enterprises Experimental statistics - micro high-growth enterprises] === Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/7894008/12445868/Methodological-note.pdf/16fa1088-4a0c-4a1c-5b18-601ca61bb2a8?t=1613487055280 Methodological note: New statistics on High Growth Enterprises] === Footnotes === {{Unit|topic=X_Structural_business_statistics}} [[Category:Industry, trade, and services|Characteristics of micro high-growth enterprises]] [[Category:Structural business statistics (SBS)|Characteristics of micro high-growth enterprises]] [[Category:Business demography|Characteristics of micro high-growth enterprises]] [[Category:Statistical article|Characteristics of micro high-growth enterprises]] [[Category:Experimental statistics|Characteristics of micro high-growth enterprises]] [[Category:No update|Characteristics of micro high-growth enterprises]]

title: Causes of death statistics by age group
text:
EU statistics are presented on the major causes of death analysed by age group. Data extracted in March 2026 Planned article update: April 2027 Among older people (aged 65 years or over) in 2023, the standardised death rate of circulatory diseases – the most common cause of death in the EU – was higher for men than for women in every EU country. In 2023, the lowest standardised death rate of circulatory diseases among people aged 65 years or over was reported in France and the highest in Bulgaria. In the population aged less than 65 years, the highest standardised death rate in the EU in 2023 was for cancer, ahead of circulatory diseases and external causes. |alt=A dynamic double column chart showing standardised death rates for deaths from circulatory diseases for two age groups. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. This article uses the most recent statistics on [[Glossary:Cause of death|causes of death]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. It is important to identify and record the underlying reasons for [[Glossary:Death|deaths]] and make this information available to policymakers, health services and the public. With these data, it is possible to describe and understand the rate and trends in causes of death. The data also serve to provide information on changing epidemiological circumstances. Most causes of death vary significantly by age and by sex. This article gives an overview of [[Glossary:Standardised death rate (SDR)|standardised death rates]] for the EU as a whole and for EU countries with analyses by cause, age and sex of the deceased. The use of standardised death rates facilitates comparisons both over time and between countries, independently of different population age structures. This article is included in a set of statistical articles concerning health status in the EU which forms part of the online publication ''[[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]]''. ===Most frequent causes of death in the EU in 2023=== In the EU, there were 4.8 million deaths of residents in 2023. Among these, 4.1 million deaths (85.2% of the total) occurred among people aged 65 years or over (hereafter referred to as elderly people); the remaining 715 000 deaths were among people aged less than 65 years. The principal causes of death and their related death rates differ between these age groups. Just over a third (35.0%) of all deaths in the EU’s resident elderly population in 2023 were caused by diseases of the circulatory system (see Table 1). Nearly 1 in 3 of these (or 10.9% of all deaths) were caused by ischaemic heart disease. The second most frequent cause of death among elderly people was cancer, accounting for just over a fifth (22.2%) of all deaths. The third most common cause of death among elderly people was respiratory diseases, accounting for 8.4% of all deaths among elderly people. Among residents of the EU aged less than 65 years, the 2 leading causes of mortality were reversed: cancer was the most frequent cause of death, accounting for slightly more than 1 in 3 (33.9%) deaths in this age group; diseases of the circulatory system were the second most frequent cause of death (20.2% of the total). They were followed by external causes of death with a share of 12.4% (of which more than half were accidents). [[Image:Three main causes of death by age group, EU, 2023_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Three main causes of death by age group, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bcb2e4db-c52a-4a18-939f-95209056264e?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4552d84a-c385-4a83-a7f5-b77700fb9f17?lang=en hlth_cd_aro])|alt=A table showing the three main causes of death. Data are analysed by age group: people aged 65 years or over and those aged less than 65 years. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Analyses by sex and age of the most frequent causes of death in the EU in 2023 === In the EU, circulatory diseases were a more frequent cause of death among resident elderly women than among elderly men. These diseases accounted for 37.2% of all deaths among elderly women in 2023 and 32.6% of all deaths among elderly men – see Figure 1. The reverse situation was observed for the next 2 leading causes of death. Cancer accounted for 18.8% of all deaths among elderly women and 26.0% among elderly men. Respiratory diseases Data on respiratory diseases do not include COVID-19. accounted for 7.7% of all deaths among elderly women and 9.1% among elderly men. The fourth most frequent cause of death among elderly people differed between the sexes; among elderly women it was mental and behavioural disorders (5.8% of all deaths among women aged 65 and over) and among elderly men it was diseases of the nervous system (4.1% of all deaths among men aged 65 and over). Among EU residents aged less than 65 years who died in 2023, cancer was the principal cause of death; 45.2% of all females in this age group and 28.2% of all males (see Figure 1). The second, third and fourth most common causes of death among people aged less than 65 years were also the same for males and females: circulatory diseases accounted for 15.0% of all deaths among females aged less than 65 years compared with 22.8% among males; external causes accounted for 7.9% of all deaths among females aged less than 65 years, compared with 14.6% among males; digestive diseases accounted for 6.2% of all deaths among females aged less than 65 years and 8.3% among males. [[Image:Frequency of major causes of death analysed by age group and sex, EU, 2023 (%)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Frequency of major causes of death analysed by age group and sex, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/44bb72b4-34a7-403a-8981-fe118da1549c?lang=en hlth_cd_aro])|alt=A set of four pie charts showing the shares for major causes of death. Data are analysed by age group and sex. The four pie charts show the shares for males aged 65 years or over, females aged 65 years or over, males ages less than 65 years and females aged less than 65 years. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Standardised death rates higher among elderly people for most causes of death''' Figure 2 shows standardised death rates beyond the 4 most common causes of death among elderly people (circulatory diseases, cancer, respiratory diseases and mental and behavioural disorders as presented in Figure 1). For these other leading causes of death, rates for the EU are shown in Figure 2 for the whole population, people aged 65 years or over and people aged less than 65 years. Based on standardised death rates, a common cause of death was symptoms, signs and abnormal clinical and laboratory findings, not elsewhere classified. This residual category includes cases when a definitive diagnosis has not been established or when a condition is described by its symptoms (such as fever or respiratory arrest) or other abnormal findings. In 2023, the standardised death rate of this condition was 16 times as high for elderly people as for people aged less than 65 years. Conditions with particularly large relative age gaps included diseases of the genitourinary system (where the rate for elderly people was 73 times as high as that for younger people) and COVID-19 (69 times as high). By contrast, the age gap was narrower for diseases of the digestive system (the rate for elderly people was 11 times as high as that for younger people) and external causes of morbidity and mortality (6 times as high). [[Image:Other causes of death in people aged 65 years or over analysed by age group, EU, 2023 (standardised death rate per 100 000 inhabitants in the age group)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Other causes of death in people aged 65 years or over analysed by age group, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7a9227cc-2c2b-4d7e-bc2c-e0ebba09671c?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A triple bar chart showing causes of death other than for the four most common causes. Data are analysed by age group with information for people aged 65 years or over, people aged less than 65 years and the total population. Data are shown for standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants within each age group. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Standardised death rates in 2023 were higher among elderly residents in the EU than among younger residents for nearly all other causes of death. ===Standardised death rates by country=== The standardised death rate of circulatory diseases in 2023 was higher among elderly men than elderly women across all EU countries (see Figure 3). The highest standardised death rates from circulatory diseases among elderly men and elderly women were reported in Bulgaria, followed by Romania. France was the only EU country to report a standardised death rate of circulatory diseases among elderly men below 1 000 deaths per 100 000 male inhabitants in 2023, while rates below this level were reported for elderly women by 10 EU countries. In 2023, the lowest standardised death rates from circulatory diseases within the elderly population were reported by France, 946 deaths per 100 000 male inhabitants and 612 deaths per 100 000 female inhabitants. [[Image:Deaths from circulatory diseases among people aged 65 years or over, 2023 (standardised death rate per 100 000 male_female inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Deaths from circulatory diseases among people aged 65 years or over, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9ba95be9-9012-42c1-839e-11a478b4d920?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A double column chart showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants from circulatory diseases among people aged 65 years or over. Data are analysed by sex for elderly male and female inhabitants. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, the standardised death rate of cancer among people aged 65 years or over was higher among men than women across all EU countries (see Figure 4). Croatia, Latvia, Slovenia and Hungary recorded the highest standardised death rates from cancer among elderly men, with over 1 600 deaths per 100 000 male inhabitants. Cyprus recorded the lowest rate, 1 011 deaths from cancer per 100 000 men aged 65 years or over. Among elderly women, Denmark and Hungary recorded over 900 deaths from cancer per 100 000 female inhabitants aged 65 years or over. There were 4 countries – Cyprus, Bulgaria, Spain and Portugal – which reported fewer than 600 deaths from cancer per 100 000 elderly female inhabitants. [[Image:Deaths from cancer among people aged 65 years or over, 2023 (standardised death rate per 100 000 male_female inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Deaths from cancer among people aged 65 years or over, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/397d4e69-941e-46ba-908e-5707a4f3edaa?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A double column chart showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants from cancer among people aged 65 years or over. Data are analysed by sex for elderly male and female inhabitants. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, the standardised death rate of respiratory diseases among people aged 65 years or over was higher among men than women across all EU countries (see Figure 5). The highest standardised death rate of respiratory diseases among elderly men in the EU was recorded in Malta, with 793 deaths per 100 000 elderly male inhabitants. Among elderly women, the highest rates were recorded in Malta, Denmark and Ireland, all with 450 or more deaths per 100 000 elderly female inhabitants. The lowest death rates from respiratory diseases among elderly men were recorded in Finland (223 per 100 000 elderly male inhabitants), Slovenia (237 per 100 000 elderly male inhabitants) and Lithuania (261 per 100 000 elderly male inhabitants). The lowest death rate of respiratory diseases among elderly women was recorded in Lithuania (84 per 100 000 elderly female inhabitants), with rates also below 140 per 100 000 elderly female inhabitants in Finland, Latvia, Estonia and Slovenia. [[Image:Deaths from respiratory diseases among people aged 65 years or over, 2023 (standardised death rate per 100 000 male_female inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Deaths from respiratory diseases among people aged 65 years or over, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/79f9ecd8-2786-4d99-a711-3f8b3914d73c?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A double column chart showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants from respiratory diseases among people aged 65 years or over. Data are analysed by sex for elderly male and female inhabitants. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among people aged 65 years or over, the highest standardised death rates from mental and behavioural disorders in 2023 among the EU countries were recorded in the Netherlands, Malta, Germany, Denmark and Ireland, both for men and for women (see Figure 6). Equally, the lowest rate both for elderly men and for elderly women was observed in Bulgaria, with particularly low rates, of less than 10 per 100 000 elderly male/female inhabitants, also observed in Romania and Slovakia. In a small majority of EU countries (14), the standardised death rate of mental and behavioural disorders was higher in 2023 among elderly women than among elderly men. The widest gap with a higher rate for elderly women was in Cyprus, while the widest gap with a higher rate for elderly men was in Slovenia. [[Image:Deaths from mental and behavioural disorders among people aged 65 years or over, 2023 (standardised death rate per 100 000 male_female inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Deaths from mental and behavioural disorders among people aged 65 years or over, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8d560aab-7b73-49e6-9989-873460703411?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A double column chart showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants from mental and behavioural disorders among people aged 65 years or over. Data are analysed by sex for elderly male and female inhabitants. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Developments over time=== '''Men aged 65 years or over''' Figure 7 shows standardised death rates for selected major causes of death among elderly men in the EU between 2013 and 2023. The EU standardised death rate of cerebrovascular diseases among elderly men decreased by close to a third (down 30%). A decrease of around a quarter was observed for death rates from ischaemic heart disease (down 23%) and decreases around a fifth for colorectal cancer (down 17%) and lung cancer (down 17%). Among the 5 causes of death shown in Figure 7 which recorded overall declines, the smallest decrease in the standardised death rate was for prostate cancer (down 10%). By contrast, the EU standardised death rate of dementia among elderly men increased by over a quarter (up 26%) between 2013 and 2023. The death rate of accidents among elderly men increased by 21%, largely due to a 16% increase between 2020 and 2022. An increase of 3% was observed for the death rate of diabetes mellitus among elderly men. [[Image:Causes of death among men aged 65 years or over, EU, 2013–23_(index based on standardised death rate per 100 000 male inhabitants, 2013 = 100)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Causes of death among men aged 65 years or over, EU, 2013–23
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/249a86d9-8834-41b8-9805-f5485a6d83c5?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A line chart with eight lines showing indices for causes of death among men aged 65 years or over, based on standardised death rates per hundred thousand male inhabitants. The lines show prostate cancer, colorectal cancer, lung cancer, ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular diseases, accidents, dementia and diabetes mellitus. The index value is equal to 100 for 2013. Data are shown for 2013 to 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Women aged 65 years or over''' Figure 8 shows standardised death rates for selected major causes of death among elderly women in the EU between 2013 and 2023. The largest decrease was observed for cerebrovascular disease, which fell by 33% across the EU, similar to the fall observed among elderly men. The death rate of ischaemic heart disease among elderly women decreased by 29%, a larger decrease than that observed for elderly men. The rate of colorectal cancer was down 15% for elderly women, also similar to the fall observed for elderly men. A decrease of 9% was observed for diabetes mellitus, reflecting falls in the 3 most recent years after an increase in 2020 which had more than reversed the decreases accumulated since 2013. For breast cancer, the overall decrease was relatively small, down 4%. The EU standardised death rate of accidents among elderly women increased 19% between 2013 and 2023, similar to the rise observed among elderly men. Also similar to the situation observed among elderly men, was the increase observed among elderly women in deaths from dementia (up 27%). In contrast to the situation observed among elderly men, the standardised death rate of lung cancer increased every year among elderly women; the overall increase was 28%. [[Image:Causes of death among women aged 65 years or over, EU, 2013–23_(index based on standardised death rate per 100 000 female inhabitants, 2013 = 100)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Causes of death among women aged 65 years or over, EU, 2013–23
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1ff818b3-96da-402d-aad4-13bffb85c8e3?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A line chart with eight lines showing indices for causes of death among women aged 65 years or over, based on standardised death rates per hundred thousand female inhabitants. The lines show lung cancer, breast cancer, colorectal cancer, ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular diseases, accidents, dementia and diabetes mellitus. The index value is equal to 100 for 2013. Data are shown for 2013 to 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''People aged less than 65 years''' Across the EU, the standardised death rate for people aged less than 65 years fell by 14.1% between 2013 and 2023 (see Table 2). Larger than average decreases were noted for 2 of the 3 main causes of death. The standardised death rate of cancer fell 23.6%, that for circulatory diseases by 22.5% and that for external causes by 11.9%. [[Image:Standardised death rate for residents aged less than 65 years, EU, 2013–23 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Standardised death rate for residents aged less than 65 years, EU, 2013–23
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9f5c6f4d-b715-46b4-9d82-e65f439a37fe?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A table showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for residents aged less than 65 years. Data are analysed by cause of death, showing all causes of death, cancer, circulatory diseases and accidents. Data are shown for 2013 to 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Causes of death by age group_Health2026.xlsx|title=Causes of death by age group – tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== Statistics on the underlying causes of death provide information on [[Glossary:Mortality|mortality]] patterns. This source is documented in more detail in a background article on the [[Causes_of_death_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of causes of death statistics]] which provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. '''Legal basis for the data collection''' Since the 2011 reference year, reporting countries have submitted data to Eurostat based on the requirements of [http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2008/1338/oj Regulation (EC) No 1338/2008] on Community statistics on public health and health and safety at work, and [http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/328/oj Regulation (EU) No 328/2011] on Community statistics on public health and health and safety at work, as regards statistics on causes of death. For data before the 2011 reference year, countries submitted data to Eurostat based on a gentlemen’s agreement established within the context of Eurostat’s Working Group on Public Health Statistics. There are currently 33 countries submitting data on the causes of death to Eurostat: *all 27 [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU countries]] *all 4 [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA countries]] *4 [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]] (Georgia, Moldova, Serbia and Türkiye). National and regional (NUTS level 2) data are collected. '''Classification of the causes of death''' Statistics on the causes of death are based on [[Glossary:Medical certification|medical information provided in death certificates]]. Causes of death are classified by the 86 causes in the [[Glossary:European_shortlist_of_causes_of_death|European shortlist]] which is based on the [[Glossary:International classification of diseases (ICD)|International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems]]. When the COVID-19 pandemic started, the [[Glossary:WHO|World Health Organization (WHO)]] introduced emergency codes in the ICD version 10 (ICD-10) that countries could use to report deaths from COVID-19. In Eurostat’s dissemination database, the codes are available as follows: *U071 – COVID-19, virus identified (deaths where COVID-19 has been confirmed by laboratory testing) *U072 – COVID-19, virus not identified (COVID-19 virus not identified) *U_COV19_OTH – COVID-19 other (COVID-19 death not elsewhere defined). The data for COVID-19 reported in this article were calculated by adding the data for these 3 codes, however the data disseminated in Eurostat’s dissemination database are for each separate code. More information about ICD-10 codes used for COVID-19 can be found on the [https://icd.who.int/browse10/2019/en#/U07.1 WHO’s website]. '''Standardised death rate''' The number of deaths from a particular cause of death can be expressed relative to the size of the population. A [[Glossary:Standardised death rate (SDR)|standardised death rate]] is adjusted to a standard age distribution. This facilitates comparisons of rates over time and between countries. The population used for the standardisation of crude rates is based on the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-RA-13-028&language=en European standard population] in use since summer 2013. ===Context=== Statistics on causes of death are among the oldest medical statistics available. They provide information on developments over time and differences between countries in causes of death. These statistics play a key role in the general information system relating to the state of health in the EU. They may be used to determine which preventive and medical-curative measures or which investments in research might increase the life expectancy of the population. Statistics concerning causes of death among people aged 65 years or over (referred to in this article as elderly people) are of increasing interest. A dramatic change in the nature and delivery of [[Glossary:Healthcare|healthcare]] over the past century has resulted in much longer life spans and a greater prevalence of chronic illnesses. In turn, this has led to increased demand on healthcare systems, particularly for long-term care. Public health programmes throughout the EU are often targeted at reducing mortality among people aged less than 65 years through preventive measures, for example, the promotion of healthier lifestyles through improved nutrition, lower tobacco and alcohol consumption, an increase in physical activity or a reduction of workplace risk. According to Eurostat’s 2023 baseline year projections, the share of the population aged 65 years or over in the EU is [[Glossary:Projection|projected]] to increase relatively rapidly to 27.1% of the total population by 2040 and then to 30.4% by 2060 before increasing more slowly to 33.6% by 2100; in 2026, the share was 22.3%. ===Other articles=== '''Online publications''' *[[Health in the European Union - facts and figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] *[[Disability statistics]] '''Causes of death''' *[[Causes of death statistics]] *[[Causes of death - monthly title: Chemicals production and consumption statistics
text:
EU indicators cover the production and consumption of industrial chemicals, focusing on hazardous substances for humans and the environment Data extracted in December 2025. Planned article update: 10 December 2026. Consumption of '''hazardous chemicals''' has fallen substantially, decreasing by 47 million tonnes since 2014. Since 2014, there has been an 18 million tonnes reduction in the consumption of the '''most harmful substances''', dropping from 48 million to 30 million tonnes, indicating targeted efforts to reduce these chemicals. In 2024, the '''production''' of chemicals hazardous to human health in the EU was 172 million tonnes, while the '''consumption''' of chemicals hazardous to health was 170 million tonnes. This article presents an analysis of indicators that have been developed and compiled by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], covering the production and consumption of industrial chemicals in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] with a particular focus on substances being hazardous to human health or hazardous to the environment. The indicators represent the volume (in tonnes) of production and consumption and not the actual risks associated with the use of chemicals, i.e. production and consumption data do not describe the exposure to hazardous [[Glossary:Hazardous_chemicals|hazardous chemicals]]. ===Total production of chemicals=== Figure 1 shows the development of chemicals production in the EU since 2004 (index 2004 = 100), covering the total production of chemicals, including hazardous and non-hazardous categories, chemicals hazardous to the environment and chemicals hazardous to health. It should be noted that a substance can be classified both as hazardous to health and hazardous to the environment The total production of industrial chemicals in the EU peaked at 301 million tonnes in 2007. During the financial and economic crisis, production fell and reached its so far lowest level in 2009. After a rebound in 2010, the production of chemicals in the EU decreased again and remained relatively stable during the period 2011-2015. In 2017, for the first time since 2010, there was a noticeable increase of more than 10 million tonnes. However, starting in 2018, total production began to decline once more. By 2024, the production of chemicals was equal to 224 million tonnes, reflecting a slight increase from 2023 but still significantly lower than levels recorded in 2009. [[Image:Production_of_chemicals,_EU,_2004–24_(2004_%3D_100).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Production of chemicals, EU, 2004-2024
(Index 2004 = 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2a6d3359-c483-4569-a8ea-7ef51912c3bd?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-15T10:05:38Z (env_chmhaz)]|alt= Line chart showing production of chemicals in the EU. Three lines represent hazardous to the environment, hazardous to health, and the total of hazardous and non-hazardous over the years 2004 to 2023. The year 2004 is indexed at 100. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Production of chemicals hazardous to health=== The total EU production of chemicals hazardous to health shows a notable downward trend over the 20-year period from 2004, decreasing from 236 million tonnes to 172 million tonnes (Figure 2). ''These chemicals are divided into 3 groups:'' * '''Most harmful substances for human health''' are those that can cause cancer, genetic mutations in germ cells, reproductive harm, disrupt endocrine functions, or lead to organ damage with repeated exposure at low levels or respiratory sensitisation. * '''Substances of concern for human health''' are those suspected of causing cancer, genetic mutations in germ cells, reproductive harm or endocrine disruption, or those that can cause organ damage following acute exposure or repeated exposure at moderate levels) or skin sensitisation. * '''Hazardous substances for human health''' include chemicals that pose acute risks via skin, inhalation, or dermal exposure, can cause skin and eye irritation/corrosion, or present aspiration hazards. [[Image:Production_of_chemicals_hazardous_to_health,_EU,_2004-24_(million_tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Production of chemicals hazardous to health, by toxicity, EU, 2004-2024
(million tonnes)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cffda51e-abbc-4619-8210-0ed1515cb441?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-15T10:08:22Z (env_chmhaz)]|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing production of chemicals hazardous to health by toxicity in the EU over the years 2004 to 2024. Each year column has five stacks representing five levels of toxicity in million tonnes. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The production of the '''most harmful substances for human health''' has steadily decreased from 55 million tonnes in 2004 to 45 million tonnes by 2024. The '''substances of concern''' saw a reduction from 27 million tonnes to 19 million tonnes over the same period. Particularly notable is the significant decrease in '''other hazardous substances''', dropping from 154 million tonnes to 109 million tonnes, which reflects broader efforts across diverse chemical types to reduce hazardous production. While overall chemical production has also declined, these trends are consistent with a significant industry shift, supported by EU regulatory and legislative initiatives, including the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/chemicals-strategy_en chemicals strategy for sustainability], that aim to promote the production of non-hazardous alternatives over hazardous substances. This indicates the EU's ongoing commitment to advancing safer and more sustainable chemical practices while safeguarding public health and the environment. ===Effective changes in the production of chemicals hazardous to health=== Figure 3 illustrates the shifts in EU chemical production from 2004 to 2024, distinguishing between chemicals hazardous to health and those that are not. The data indicates a sustained decrease in the production of hazardous to health chemicals, alongside a significant rise in the production of non-hazardous chemicals. These changes reflect a positive shift towards safer chemical compositions, driven by more than just economic fluctuations. The decline in hazardous chemical production may be attributed to regulatory measures aimed at replacing these substances with safer alternatives. While broader trends in chemical production and consumption could also play a role, the overall decrease in production volumes highlighted in Figure 2 is indicative of a strategic move towards less harmful production. [[Image:Effective_changes_in_the_production_of_chemicals_hazardous_to_health,_EU,_2004_–_2024_(%25_point)_.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Effective changes relative to 2004 in the production of chemicals hazardous to health and of chemicals not hazardous to health, EU, 2004-2024
(percentage points)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d3dc1541-f36b-478d-bc77-3a638c535e84?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-15T10:11:56Z (env_chmhaz)]|alt= Vertical bar chart showing effective changes compared with the year 2004 in the production of chemicals as percentage points in the EU. Each year 2005 to 2023, has two columns representing hazardous to health and not hazardous to health. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The share of chemicals not hazardous to human health in total chemical production has increased since 2004, while the share of chemicals hazardous to human health are decreasing. Despite yearly fluctuations, the figures show a consistent trend over time. ===Production of chemicals hazardous to the environment=== Figure 4 presents the development of the production of chemicals that are hazardous to the environment, shown as an index in Figure 1, analysed in more detail according to 3 classes of environmental hazard. ''These chemicals are divided into 3 groups'': * '''Most harmful substances for the environment''' include chemicals that are persistent, bioaccumulative (or mobile) and toxic, have endocrine-disrupting effects, or pose hazards to the ozone layer * '''Substances of concern for the environment''' are chemical substances that pose a threat to ecosystems, including those that are chronically toxic to aquatic life and suspected endocrine disruptors. * '''Hazardous substances for the environment''' are chemical substances that cause acute harm to aquatic organisms. The production volume of the most harmful chemicals for the environment is relatively small (below 2 million tonnes). The aggregated production of these 3 classes in the EU experienced an increase from 2004 to 2007, reaching a peak total volume of 83 million tonnes. Following the peak of 2007, the production of chemicals hazardous to the environment fell by approximately 10 million tonnes over the next 2 years. There was a notable rebound in the production of chemicals hazardous to the environment in 2010. This rebound mirrored an overall recovery in chemical production post-economic downturn. However, during the period from 2010 to 2015, production volumes across these classes decreased again. Starting in 2016, production began to rise again, reaching a new peak in 2017, followed by fluctuations in production levels until 2021. In 2022, a significant decrease occurred, and by 2023, production further declined, marking an absolute minimum for the entire reporting period at 64 million tonnes. In 2024, production saw a slight increase to 66 million tonnes. [[Image:Production of chemicals hazardous to the environment, EU, 2004-2024.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Production of chemicals hazardous to the environment, EU, 2004-2024
(million tonnes)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a4eae6a5-f577-47e4-af6a-a79cd0257fb7?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-15T10:13:35Z (env_chmhaz)]|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing production of chemicals hazardous to the environment by toxicity in the EU over the years 2004 to 2024. Each year column has five stacks representing five levels of toxicity in million tonnes. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In the EU, the share of chemicals hazardous to the environment in the total chemicals production was relatively stable over the period 2004-2024, fluctuating between 28% and 30%. Overall, the production of chemicals hazardous to the environment declined by approximately 17 million tonnes from 2004 to 2024, with considerable variations among the different hazard classes. The largest overall decrease in EU production during this period was recorded for substances of concern for the environment. The production volume fell by about 12 million tonnes, representing a 17% decrease. In contrast, other classes showed much smaller changes. ===Total consumption of chemicals === The consumption indicators build on the results of the production indicators. Consumption volumes result by adding the net import to the production volumes of the chemicals. While the production figures of the individual chemicals remain relatively constant over time, the import / export figures vary considerably. Figure 5 shows the development of EU chemicals consumption since 2004 as indices of the total consumption (including hazardous and non-hazardous), of chemicals hazardous to the environment, and chemicals hazardous to health. The total consumption of chemicals in the EU – similar to the total production in Figure 1 – increased between 2004 and 2007, peaking at 322 million tonnes in 2007. During the financial and economic crisis, consumption fell in 2008 and 2009. The rebound in activity in 2010 was as much as the decrease reported in 2009. In 2011, the consumption of chemicals in the EU decreased and then remained relatively stable until 2019. In 2020, the year of the COVID-19 pandemic, consumption declined to 270 million tonnes. After a slight recovery in 2021, there has been a significant decline in consumption with an all-time low of the reporting period at 220 million tonnes in 2023. In 2024 the consumption of chemicals rose to 232 million tonnes. [[Image:Consumption_of_chemicals,_EU,_2004–24_(2004_%3D_100).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Consumption of chemicals, EU, 2004-2024
(Index 2004 = 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bb1addfb-5701-49c8-8b35-5b2a462d04ed?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-15T10:14:57Z (env_chmhaz)]|alt= Line chart showing consumption of chemicals in the EU. Three lines represent hazardous to the environment, hazardous to health, and the total of hazardous and non-hazardous over the years 2004 to 2024. The year 2004 is indexed at 100. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Consumption of chemicals hazardous to health=== Figure 6 shows the consumption of chemicals hazardous to health, from 2004 to 2024. The differences between the consumption and production are relatively small. Net trade added between 3% and 6% (between 5 million tonnes and 13 million tonnes; except in the years 2017, 2023 and 2024) to the sum of the production of the 3 classes of chemicals hazardous to health. In 3 years, the net trade was negative. In 2017, there was an export surplus of about 1 million tonnes. While the export surplus in 2023 was negligible, it increased to 2 million tonnes in 2024. The consumption indicator shows similar trends as indicator on the production of chemicals hazardous to health, see Figure 2. In general, the production of chemicals within the EU is the most important contribution for the consumption figures (compared with the export and import of chemicals). [[Image:Consumption_of_chemicals_hazardous_to_health,_EU,_2004–24_(million_tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Consumption of chemicals hazardous to health, by toxicity, EU, 2004-2024
(million tonnes)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e29d2cd0-20e2-4de9-b12f-d46362782c11?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-15T10:16:14Z (env_chmhaz)]|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing consumption of chemicals hazardous to health by toxicity in the EU over the years 2004 to 2023. Each year column has five stacks representing five levels of toxicity in million tonnes. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Consumption of chemicals hazardous to the environment=== Figure 7 shows the consumption of chemicals hazardous to the environment, by toxicity, during 2004-2024. Initially, between 2004 to 2015, the EU experienced a net import surplus, with consumption consistently outstripping production up to 3%. Over time, however, this dynamic shifted dramatically. The comparison with Figure 4 highlights that the consumption indicator closely mirrored production figures for most of the period. However, notable differences occured in 2017, 2018, and again in 2022 to 2024, as the EU transitioned to a net exporter for environmentally hazardous chemicals. This shift represents a significant trend in the EU’s trade dynamics. In 2017, net exports accounted for approximately 10 million tonnes or 13% of the overall production of the 3 classes of chemicals hazardous to the environment. By 2023, this figure increased to 11 million tonnes, reaching 13 million tonnes in 2024, equivalent to 17% and 20% of the production volume, respectively. [[Image:Consumption_of_chemicals_hazardous_to_the_environment,_EU,_2004–24_(million_tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 7: Consumption of chemicals hazardous to the environment, by toxicity, EU, 2004-2024
(million tonnes)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9fcc41e9-a898-4e81-a870-defba9d6d6f9?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-15T10:17:20Z (env_chmhaz)]|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing consumption of chemicals hazardous to the environment by toxicity in the EU over the years 2004 to 2023. Each year column has five stacks representing five levels of toxicity in million tonnes. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Chemicals prod-cons statistics ref2024-final.xlsx|title=Chemicals production and consumption statistics: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The production indicators presented in this article are derived from annual statistics on the production of manufactured goods ([[Glossary:PRODCOM|Prodcom]]). In addition, the consumption indicators integrate data on imports and exports from [[Glossary:COMEXT|COMEXT]] (EUROSTAT's reference database for international trade). The evaluation of both (PRODCOM and COMEXT) is based on publicly available data. The evaluation is based on publicly available data. The data for building the indicators was extracted on 24 11 2025 (PRODCOM data (including import export data)). The consumption is calculated according to the equation: :::::'''Consumption = production + imports – exports''' Data for the EU aggregate are only available from reference year 2004 onward. The information presented on the production and consumption of chemicals hazardous to the environment and of chemicals hazardous to health has been compiled from detailed production statistics and import/export statistics. As well as the total figures, each of these aggregates is available with a division into 3 hazard classes: these classes of aquatic toxicity and toxicity to human health are based on classifications according to the CLP Regulation (Regulation (EC) 1272/2008 on classification, labelling and packaging of substances and mixtures) and the criteria for the identification of chemicals as ‘most harmful substances” (in Commission Communication C/2024/1995) and ‘substances of concern’ (in the Eco-design and Sustainable Products Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1781)). It should be noted that the indicators do not describe the actual risks associated with the use of chemicals, but instead their level of production in quantity terms. Indeed, production and consumption are not synonymous with exposure, as some chemicals are handled in closed systems, or as intermediate goods in controlled supply chains. For the indicator on chemicals hazardous to the environment, chemicals are divided into 3 classes based on their hazard on the aquatic environment, see Figure 4. An analysis of the production and consumption of chemicals hazardous to the environment can be used to monitor any developments in shifting from more harmful to less harmful chemicals. Chemicals hazardous to health are divided into 3 toxicity classes, see Figure 2. An analysis of the production and consumption of chemicals hazardous to human health can be used to monitor any developments in shifting production from more hazardous chemicals to less hazardous chemicals and thereby address an important objective of the EU Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability: to reduce risks through the substitution of hazardous by less hazardous substances. ===Context=== [http://bookshop.europa.eu/en/general-union-environment-action-programme-to-2020-pbKH0113833/downloads/KH-01-13-833-EN-C/KH0113833ENC_002.pdf?FileName=KH0113833ENC_002.pdf&SKU=KH0113833ENC_PDF&CatalogueNumber=KH-01-13-833-EN-C The General Union Environment Action Programme to 2020 — also referred to as the 7th Environment Action Programme] (7th EAP) — guides the EU's environment policy up to 2020. It contains proposals for further actions that promote the implementation of REACH and aims to develop — by 2018 — a 'Union strategy for a non-toxic environment' that is conducive to innovation and the development of sustainable substitutes including non-chemical solutions, building on cross-cutting measures to be undertaken by 2015 to ensure: *the safety of manufactured nanomaterials and materials with similar properties; *the minimisation of exposure to endocrine disruptors; *appropriate regulatory approaches to address combination effects of chemicals; and *the minimisation of exposure to chemicals in products, including inter alia imported products, with a view to promoting non-toxic material cycles and reducing indoor exposure to harmful substances. The Rio+20 United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development decided to launch a process to develop a set of [http://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/focussdgs.html Sustainable Development Goals] (SDGs). In June 2014, an Open Working Group of the General Assembly issued a proposal including 17 goals and 169 targets, for adoption by the UN General Assembly on 25-27 September 2015. Three targets in the proposal call for action in areas related to the production and consumption of chemicals. These are target 3.9: "By 2030, substantially reduce the number of deaths and illnesses from hazardous chemicals and air, water and soil pollution and contamination", under Goal 3 "Ensure healthy lives and promote well-being across all ages"; target 6.3 "By 2030, improve water quality by reducing pollution, eliminating dumping and minimizing release of hazardous chemicals and materials, halving the proportion of untreated wastewater and increasing recycling and safe reuse by [x] per cent globally" (where the 'x' is to be defined at a later stage), under Goal 6 "Ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all"; and target 12.4 "By 2020, achieve the environmentally sound management of chemicals and all wastes throughout their life cycle, in accordance with agreed international frameworks, and significantly reduce their release to air, water and soil in order to minimize their adverse impacts on human health and the environment", under Goal 12 "Ensure sustainable consumption and production patterns". The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development was agreed in 2015 and is a "plan of action for people, planet and prosperity", according to its preamble. It provides a window of opportunity to drive transformative changes in the chemicals and waste sector to move towards sustainable development. Within these processes, intense discussions and clarifications are taking place about the question of what contributions can be made by the chemical industry to support the Sustainable Development Goals. The strong limitations of non-sustainable chemistry are clearly visible now. The recent challenges require a new way of thinking about chemicals and a new way to handle them. A holistic approach is necessary to realise the benefits of chemicals for societies in reaching the SDGs – and to prevent the negative impacts of chemicals along their life cycle. This holistic approach is called "sustainable chemistry" (Blum et al. 2017; UNEP 2018). Such an approach should take into account the 3 dimensions of sustainable development, preventive measures, and the entire life cycle of a chemical (design, production, use and disposal). ===Other
