title: Cardiovascular diseases statistics
text:
Statistics on cardiovascular diseases show that they are the leading cause of death in the EU, mainly concerning heart attacks and strokes. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 In 2023, the standardised death rate for diseases of the circulatory system in Bulgaria was 5.7 times as high as that in France. Across the EU, in-patients with diseases of the circulatory system spent a total of 77 million days in hospital in 2023. The number of heart bypasses per 100 000 inhabitants decreased between 2018 and 2023 in all but 4 of the 25 EU countries for which data are available. This article presents an overview of [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] statistics related to cardiovascular diseases and focuses on cardiovascular mortality, healthcare activities, operations and procedures. Cardiovascular diseases are the leading [[Glossary:Cause of death|cause of death]] in the EU. They cover a broad group of medical problems that affect the circulatory system (the heart and blood vessels), often resulting from atherosclerosis, the abnormal build-up of plaque (made of, among other constituents, cholesterol or fatty substances) deposited on the inside walls of a person’s arteries. Some of the most common diseases that affect the circulatory system include ischaemic heart disease (which includes heart attacks) and cerebrovascular diseases (which includes strokes). This article is included in a set of statistical articles concerning healthcare activities in the EU which forms part of the online publication [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union – facts and figures]]. ===Deaths from cardiovascular diseases=== '''''There were 1.59 million deaths in the EU from diseases of the circulatory system''''' Diseases of the circulatory system place a considerable burden on healthcare systems and government budgets. In 2023, there were 1.59 million deaths in the EU resulting from diseases of the circulatory system, which was equivalent to 32.8% of all deaths. This percentage was considerably higher than the second most prevalent cause of death, [[Cancer_statistics|cancer]] (malignant neoplasms; 23.9% of all deaths). An article on [[Causes_of_death_statistics|causes of death statistics]] looks in more detail at the leading causes of death in the EU. [[Image:Causes of death – diseases of the circulatory system, residents, 2023_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Causes of death – diseases of the circulatory system, residents, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2dd09e65-b190-4a1f-9dca-c3206a7425a6?lang=en hlth_cd_aro] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6a320044-a9dd-4836-a08e-4336dc19968f?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A table showing deaths from diseases of the circulatory system of residents, in number, as a share of all deaths and as standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Diseases of the circulatory system are among the main causes of mortality in each of the EU countries (as shown in Table 1): in 2023, they accounted for more than half of all deaths in Bulgaria, Romania, Lithuania and Latvia. By contrast, fewer than a quarter of all deaths in Belgium, Cyprus, the Netherlands, France and Denmark were caused by diseases of the circulatory system, with Denmark recording the lowest share at 21.1%. The largest gaps between the sexes in relation to the share of people dying from diseases of the circulatory system were recorded in the 3 [[Glossary:Baltic Member States|Baltic countries]] as well as Slovenia and Romania. In these EU countries, the proportions of females dying from diseases of the circulatory system in 2023 were between 10.7 and 12.6 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points]] higher than those for males; these were the only EU countries to report an imbalance in excess of 10.0 percentage points. There were 5 EU countries where a higher proportion of males than females died from diseases of the circulatory system: in Denmark, Finland and Ireland, the shares of male deaths were, respectively, 1.9, 1.7 and 1.3 percentage points higher than those for females; smaller differences were observed in Sweden and the Netherlands. '''''Cyprus recorded the narrowest difference in standardised death rates for diseases of the circulatory system between males and females''''' [[Glossary:Standardised death rate (SDR)|Standardised death rates]] are calculated as a weighted average of age-specific death rates and therefore improve comparability both over time and between countries. The EU’s standardised death rate for diseases of the circulatory system was 313.0 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2023, with the rate for males some 1.4 times as high as that for females. In the same year, the standardised death rate for cancer in the EU was 233.1 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants. Standardised death rates for diseases of the circulatory system were systematically higher for males than for females in 2023 across all of the EU countries, although the differences between the sexes were relatively small compared with many other causes of death. The smallest absolute difference between males and females for standardised death rates for diseases of the circulatory system was recorded in Cyprus, at 54 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants; the next smallest differences (between 60 and 80 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants) were reported in Luxembourg, Malta, Portugal, the Netherlands and Belgium. The largest differences were recorded in Latvia (386 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants), Bulgaria (376 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants) and Lithuania (316 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants); these were the only countries to record a difference (between the rates for males and females) of more than 300 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants. Table 1 shows that deaths from diseases of the circulatory system become more common at advanced ages. While this is true for the vast majority of causes of death, the standardised death rate for diseases of the circulatory system among those aged 65 years and over in the EU in 2023 was 39 times as high as the standardised death rate for people aged less than 65 years; this can be compared with the same ratio for all causes of death, where the standardised death rate for those aged 65 years and over was 22 times as high as for people aged less than 65 years. For more information, see the article on [[Causes_of_death_statistics_by_age_group|causes of death statistics by age group]]. Note that the risk of females dying from diseases of the circulatory system before the age of 65 years was particularly low. '''''Within the EU as a whole, standardised death rates for males were consistently higher than those for females for all forms of diseases of the circulatory system''''' A more detailed analysis of causes of death for diseases of the circulatory system is presented in Table 2. EU standardised death rates for males in 2023 were higher than those for females for each of the 6 causes of death presented. For ischaemic heart diseases (International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision (ICD-10) codes I20 to I25), the standardised death rate for males in the EU was 1.9 times as high as the corresponding rate for females. The difference between the sexes was less marked for other heart diseases (ICD-10 codes I30 to I51), cerebrovascular diseases (ICD-10 codes I60 to I69) and other diseases of the circulatory system (the remainder of ICD-10 codes I00 to I99, not elsewhere covered). [[Image:Standardised death rates – diseases of the circulatory system, residents, 2023 (per 100 000 male_female inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Standardised death rates – diseases of the circulatory system, residents, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0c27a9fd-e778-49c3-8d88-f49fb952b6d8?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A table showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for diseases of the circulatory system. Data are analysed by sex and for 6 types of diseases of the circulatory system. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Some of the highest standardised death rates for ischaemic heart diseases were recorded in 2 of the Baltic countries: Lithuania had the highest rate in 2023 for males (529.7 per 100 000 male inhabitants) and for females (315.7 per 100 000 female inhabitants), followed by Latvia, Hungary, Slovakia and Romania for males, and Slovakia, Hungary, Latvia and Romania for females. The lowest standardised death rates for males for ischaemic heart diseases were recorded in France, followed by the Netherlands, Portugal, Luxembourg and Belgium. For females, the lowest standardised rates were also recorded in France, in this case followed by Spain, Belgium, Cyprus, Luxembourg, Portugal and the Netherlands. '''''The standardised death rate for cerebrovascular diseases in Bulgaria was 7.2 times as high as the rate in France''''' In 2023, the highest standardised death rates for cerebrovascular diseases were recorded in Bulgaria, Latvia, Romania and Lithuania. The lowest rate was recorded in France. As for all diseases of the circulatory system, there were large variations across the EU countries in 2023, with the standardised death rate in Bulgaria (where the highest rate was recorded) 7.2 times as high as that in France (where the lowest rate was registered). The EU standardised death rate for cerebrovascular diseases was 1.3 times as high among males as among females; this pattern was observed across all EU countries with the exception of Cyprus where the rate for females (42.5 per 100 000 female inhabitants) was marginally higher than the rate for males (42.3 per 100 000 male inhabitants). The largest sex difference was observed in Estonia, where the rate was 1.7 times as high among males as among females. ===Cardiovascular healthcare=== Changes in the number of deaths associated with diseases of the circulatory system may occur for a variety of reasons, including preventive measures such as, among others, lifestyle changes in the population (for example, a reduction in the number of smokers), the improvement of screening for risk factors, as well as new surgical procedures and forms of medication. '''''The number of resident in-patients with diseases of the circulatory system discharged from hospitals across the EU was 9.5 million in 2023''''' [[Glossary:Hospital_discharges|Hospital discharges]] of resident [[Glossary:In-patient|in-patients]] treated for diseases of the circulatory system show a very large variation across EU countries. While absolute figures for discharges are clearly linked to the number of residents of each country, the level of discharges may, among other influences, also reflect the incidence of each disease and differences in healthcare systems (for example, the balance between day care and in-patient treatment, as well as the availability of surgeons, hospital beds, emergency interventions and care facilities). In 2023, 9.5 million resident in-patients with diseases of the circulatory system were discharged from hospitals across the EU. '''''Bulgaria recorded the highest ratio per inhabitant of hospital discharges for resident in-patients with diseases of the circulatory system''''' In 2023, Bulgaria recorded the highest ratio per inhabitant of hospital discharges for resident in-patients with diseases of the circulatory system, with 4 200 in-patient discharges per 100 000 inhabitants. Lithuania, Germany and Latvia were the only other EU countries to record more than 3 000 resident in-patient discharges per 100 000 inhabitants (see Figure 1). Portugal (900 in-patient discharges per 100 000 inhabitants) recorded the lowest ratio and was the only EU country with fewer than 1 000 discharges per 100 000 inhabitants; relatively low ratios were also recorded in Ireland, the Netherlands, Denmark and Luxembourg (each recording fewer than 1 200 discharges per 100 000 inhabitants). [[Image:Hospital discharge rates for resident in-patients with diseases of the circulatory system, 2023 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Hospital discharge rates for resident in-patients with diseases of the circulatory system, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/039e9fdc-59d8-4e34-a1e0-03db5c297a38?lang=en hlth_rinpat2])|alt=A column chart showing hospital discharge rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for resident in-patients with diseases of the circulatory system. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Across the EU, in-patients with diseases of the circulatory system (ICD-10 codes I00 to I99) spent a total of 77 million days in hospital in 2023. By far the highest share – almost a third of the total (32.1%) – was accounted for by in-patients in Germany, while Italy and France (both 11.7%) were the only other EU countries recording double-digit shares. '''''In Lithuania, resident in-patients with diseases of the circulatory system spent an average of 14.8 days in hospital per stay''''' When patients are treated for a disease of the circulatory system they tend to spend a relatively lengthy period of time in hospital, reflecting the seriousness of some of these conditions. Table 3 presents an analysis of the average length of hospital stays for resident in-patients treated for a disease of the circulatory system in 2022 and 2023. The average length of stay in 2023 ranged from 4.1 days in Bulgaria up to 14.8 days in Lithuania. Average stays in hospital for resident in-patients treated for diseases of the circulatory system of close to or more than 10.0 days were also recorded in Hungary, Austria, Estonia, Portugal and Czechia. [[Image:Average length of hospital stay for resident in-patients with diseases of the circulatory diseases, 2022 and 2023 (days)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Average length of hospital stay for resident in-patients with diseases of the circulatory system, 2022 and 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/50c0cf37-efc3-4a2e-8894-b6b03db6377a?lang=en hlth_ralos1])|alt=A table showing the average length of stay in days for resident in-patients with selected diseases of the circulatory system. Data are presented for 5 types of respiratory diseases. Data are shown for 2022 and 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In half of the 22 EU countries for which data are available (see Table 3), there was a fall in the average length of hospital stays between 2022 and 2023 for resident in-patients treated for a disease of the circulatory system. The largest decreases – 0.3 fewer days in hospital – were recorded in Luxembourg and Romania. By contrast, the average length of a hospital stay for resident in-patients who were treated for a disease of the circulatory system rose by 5.4 days in Lithuania, 1.3 days in Hungary, 0.7 days in Cyprus and 0.6 days in France. Table 3 also provides a more detailed analysis of the average length of hospital stays for resident in-patients treated for 4 different types of circulatory disease. On average, in both 2022 and 2023, resident in-patients with cerebrovascular diseases (ICD-10 codes I60 to I69) spent the highest number of days in hospital, followed by those treated for heart failure (ICD-10 code I50) and then those with atherosclerosis (ICD-10 code I70). By comparison, the average length of stay for acute myocardial infarctions (not shown in Table 3), also known as heart attacks (ICD-10 codes I21-I22), ranged in 2023 from 10.0 in Lithuania to 3.8 in Sweden. On average, patients with acute myocardial infarction spend fewer days in hospital than for the circulatory diseases presented in Table 3. Changes in the number of deaths associated with diseases of the circulatory system may occur for a variety of reasons. These include preventive measures, such as lifestyle changes in the population (for example, a reduction in the number of smokers), the improvement of screening for risk factors, as well as developments in treatment such as new surgical procedures or forms of medication. '''''Transluminal coronary angioplasty was a common form of intervention for patients treated for cardiovascular diseases''''' Table 4 provides an overview of the rates (number of surgical operations and procedures conducted, both for in-patients and day cases, in hospitals per 100 000 inhabitants) for 2 procedures related to cardiovascular diseases. [[Image:Surgical operations and procedures performed related to diseases of the circulatory system, 2018 and 2023 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 4: Surgical operations and procedures performed related to diseases of the circulatory system, 2018 and 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e1b9f578-da45-4405-8bf3-50e77f94a7e9?lang=en hlth_co_proc3])|alt=A table showing the number of coronary artery bypass grafts and transluminal coronary angioplasties per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2018 and 2023 for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] A relatively common operation for patients treated for cardiovascular diseases was a bypass anastomosis for heart revascularisation – also referred to as a coronary artery bypass graft or heart bypass. This is a surgical procedure whereby arteries to the heart are replaced by blood vessels from another part of the body. In 2023, there were 145 500 heart bypass operations conducted across the EU, approximately 17 000 operations fewer than in 2018 (comparison excluding Greece and Latvia, for which 2018 data are not available). The number of heart bypasses per 100 000 inhabitants decreased in all but 4 EU countries between 2018 and 2023: Cyprus, Ireland, Luxembourg (note all 3 have a break in series) and Romania. Germany recorded the highest number of heart bypass operations (38 000) and had the sixth highest frequency when taking account of population size (45.7 operations per 100 000 inhabitants), behind Cyprus (68.8 times per 100 000 inhabitants), Croatia (63.9 times per 100 000 inhabitants), Belgium (55.5 times per 100 000 inhabitants), Lithuania (51.9 times per 100 000 inhabitants) and Greece (48.2 times per 100 000 inhabitants). This procedure was least common in Spain, where it was performed on average 15.5 times per 100 000 inhabitants; Malta (15.9 times per 100 000 inhabitants) was the only other EU country to record fewer than 20 procedures per 100 000 inhabitants. '''''326 500 coronary angioplasties were conducted in Germany in 2023''''' The more common of the 2 procedures shown in Table 4 was transluminal coronary angioplasty. This is a non-surgical procedure used to treat coronary arteries that have narrowed; a deflated balloon is fed through blood vessels until it reaches the site of the blockage before inflating the balloon to open up the artery (allowing blood to flow normally). Across the EU, there were 1.11 million transluminal coronary angioplasty procedures conducted in 2023; this was approximately 50 000 procedures more than in 2018 (comparison excluding Greece, Latvia and Slovakia, for which 2018 data are not available). The number of transluminal coronary angioplasty procedures per 100 000 inhabitants increased in 13 EU countries. Aside from Cyprus (which has a break in series), the biggest increase was recorded in Bulgaria, where the number of transluminal coronary angioplasty procedures increased by 186.4 procedures per 100 000 inhabitants between 2018 and 2023. Aside from Denmark (which has a break in series), the biggest decrease was recorded in Lithuania, down 38.1 procedures per 100 000 inhabitants. With 326 500 coronary angioplasties performed in 2023, Germany accounted for 29.3% of the total number of procedures carried out in the EU, considerably more than in any other EU country; France (205 000) and Italy (137 000) were the only other EU countries to report more than 100 000 procedures. The highest rate per 100 000 inhabitants (see Table 4) was 545.0 in Croatia, followed by 432.0 in Bulgaria and 392.1 in Germany. This procedure was least common in Greece where it was conducted 69.5 times per 100 000 inhabitants, while relatively low rates were also recorded in Portugal and Spain, both under 130 per 100 000 inhabitants. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Cardiovascular_diseases_Health2026.xlsx|title=Cardiovascular diseases: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''Key concepts''' An [[Glossary:In-patient|in-patient]] is a patient who is formally admitted (or ‘hospitalised’) to an institution for treatment and/or care and stays for a minimum of 1 night or more than 24 hours in the hospital or other institution providing in-patient care. An in-patient or day care patient is discharged from hospital when formally released after a procedure or course of treatment (episode of care). A discharge may occur because of the finalisation of treatment, signing out against medical advice, transfer to another healthcare institution, or because of death. A day case refers to a patient who receives planned medical and paramedical services delivered in a healthcare facility and who is formally admitted for diagnosis, treatment or other types of healthcare and is discharged on the same day. Day care is the care of a day case. An in-patient or day care patient is discharged from hospital when formally released after a procedure or course of treatment (episode of care). A discharge may occur because of the finalisation of treatment, signing out against medical advice, transfer to another healthcare institution, or because of death. The number of deaths from a particular cause of death can be expressed relative to the size of the population. A standardised (rather than crude) death rate can be compiled which is independent of the age and sex structure of a population. This is done as most causes of death vary significantly by age and by sex; the standardisation facilitates comparisons of rates over time and between countries Standard population report: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-ra-13-028.. For country-specific notes on causes of death, please refer to the national metadata reports, which can be accessed through the links at the beginning of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/hlth_cdeath_sims.htm European metadata report]. '''Healthcare resources and activities''' Statistics on healthcare resources (such as personnel and medical equipment) and healthcare activities (such as information on surgical operations and procedures and hospital discharges) are documented in a background article on the [[Healthcare_non-expenditure_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of healthcare non-expenditure statistics]]. This provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. For hospital discharges and the length of stay in hospitals, the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/Annexes/hlth_res_esms_an_2.pdf International Shortlist for Hospital Morbidity Tabulation (ISHMT)] is used to classify data from 2000 onwards; Chapter IX covers diseases of the circulatory system: *hypertensive diseases (0901) *angina pectoris (0902) *acute myocardial infarction (0903) *other ischaemic heart disease (0904) *pulmonary heart disease and diseases of pulmonary circulation (0905) *conduction disorders and cardiac arrhythmias (0906) *heart failure (0907) *cerebrovascular diseases (0908) *atherosclerosis (0909) *varicose veins of lower extremities (0910) *other diseases of the circulatory system (0911). For surgical operations and procedures, the [http://icd9cm.chrisendres.com/ International Classification of Diseases – clinical modification] (ICD-9-CM) is used: *operations on the cardiovascular system (35 to 39) *transluminal coronary angioplasty (36.01, 36.02 and 36.05) *bypass anastomosis for heart revascularisation (36.1). For country-specific notes, please refer to the annexes at the end of the national metadata reports, which can be accessed through the links at the beginning of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/hlth_res_esms.htm European metadata report]. The Eurostat {{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-028|title=Healthcare non-expenditure statistics manual}} provides an overview of the classifications, both for mandatory variables and variables provided on a voluntary basis. '''Causes of death''' Statistics on causes of death provide information on [[Glossary:Mortality|mortality]] patterns, supplying information on developments over time in the underlying causes of death. This source is documented in more detail in a background article on the [[Causes_of_death_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of causes of death statistics]]. This provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. Under Commission {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0328:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 0328/2011}}, countries provide causes of death data to Eurostat within 24 months (T+24) after the end of the reference year. Causes of death are currently classified according to the 86 causes in the [[Glossary:European_shortlist_of_causes_of_death|European shortlist]], which is based on the [[Glossary:International classification of diseases (ICD)|International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD)]]. Chapter IX of the ICD covers diseases of the circulatory system: *acute rheumatic fever (I00 to I02) *chronic rheumatic heart diseases (I05 to I09) *hypertensive diseases (I10 to I15) *ischaemic heart diseases (I20 to I25) *pulmonary heart disease and diseases of pulmonary circulation (I26 to I28) *other forms of heart disease (I30 to I52) *cerebrovascular diseases (I60 to I69) *diseases of arteries, arterioles and capillaries (I70 to I79) *diseases of veins, lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes, not elsewhere classified (I80 to I89) *other and unspecified disorders of the circulatory system (I95 to I99). '''Symbols''' In tables, a colon ':' is used to show where data are not available. Data in italics are estimates or provisional. ===Context=== Statistics concerning cardiovascular diseases are of particular significance because these diseases are the principal cause of death within the EU. Increased prevention, especially for heart disease and strokes, has resulted in decreases across most EU countries concerning the number of people who face disability, reduced quality of life and premature death. Nevertheless, cardiovascular diseases continue to touch the lives of millions of Europeans each year. According to the [https://world-heart-federation.org/ World Heart Federation], modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular diseases include hypertension, diabetes, obesity, hypercholesterolemia, tobacco and related products use, stress, sleep disorders, sedentary lifestyle, harmful alcohol consumption and unhealthy eating. Cardiovascular diseases are included as 1 of the 5 main strands covered by the European Commission’s [https://health.ec.europa.eu/non-communicable-diseases/healthier-together-eu-non-communicable-diseases-initiative_en Healthier together – EU non-communicable diseases (NCD) initiative]. The initiative was launched in December 2021 and aims to support EU countries in identifying and implementing effective policies and actions to reduce the burden of major NCDs and improve citizens’ title: Characteristics of the railway network in Europe
text:
Statistics on the characteristics of the railway network in Europe and its development since 1990, covering the EU Member States, the EFTA countries, the candidate countries and one potential candidate. Data extracted in February 2026 Planned article update: February 2027 The total length of the railway network in the EU shrunk by 7.9% between 1990 and 2024. In contrast, it increased by 12.2% in Spain, mainly due to the construction of dedicated high-speed lines. Relatively large expansions were also noted in Estonia (+14.1%; +145 km) and the Netherlands (+9.5%; +263 km) over this period. In 2024, the densest railway networks in the EU were reported in Czechia (123.2 metres of railway line per square kilometre of land area) and Belgium (118.7); Greece (14.0) and Finland (19.4) had the lowest network densities. In 2024, Luxembourg had the highest share of electrified railway lines in the EU, with 96.7%, followed by Belgium (88.0%) and Sweden (75.1%), all well above the EU average of 57.6%. In 2024, there were 8 554 km of dedicated high-speed railway lines in the EU, with Spain and France together accounting for close to 70% of the total EU high-speed network. The high-speed network in the EU has increased by more than 80% since 2008. [[Image:Map 5 Railway lines by type of track gauge, 2025 rev.png|thumb|center|700px|''Source:'' Register of Infrastructure managed by the European Union Agency for Railways, data of 31-12-2025.|alt= Map showing the railway lines with different (narrow, standard, large) track gauge in the EU Member States, the EFTA countries, in 2025. Each type of track gauge is presented with different colour.]] An efficient, secure and interoperable railway infrastructure is essential for sustainable transport of persons and freight across Europe, ensuring reliable and low-emission production chains and mobility. The railway infrastructure is an important component of the Fit-for-55 package's sector policies on transport, aimed at meeting the transport sector's targets as part of the European Green Deal. This article presents data on different characteristics of the [[Glossary:Railway_network|railway network]] in Europe. The data generally cover the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU) countries]], the [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA countries]], the [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries and the potential candidate]]. The article includes data on the development of the length of the railway network in Europe and on its density. It provides information on the development in electrification of the network, as well as in its capacity through increases and decreases in the length of [[Glossary:Railway_line|lines]] with 2 or more parallel tracks. Information on tracks with different track gauges is also provided. A special section is dedicated to the development of high-speed railway lines. Finally, the article looks into railway lines [[Glossary:Level_crossing_accidents|level crossings]], and lines equipped with the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS), both important issues for [[Railway_safety_statistics_in_the_EU|railway safety]]. These 2 last aspects are limited to the EU countries and EFTA countries, as the data come from the European Union Agency for Railways (ERA). Metro, tram and light rail urban lines are not included in these 'heavy' railway statistics.According to the latest NACE revision (NACE rev 2.1), ’49.1 Passenger rail transport’ distinguishes between ’49.11 Passenger heavy rail transport’ and ’49.12 Other passenger rail transport’ which corresponds mainly to metro, tram and light rail urban transport (previously classified under '49.3 Other land transport’). The rail statistics presented here correspond to ‘Passenger heavy rail transport’ and ‘Freight rail transport’. ===Developments in the extent and density of the national railway networks=== In 1990, the [[Glossary:Railway_network|railway network]] in the EU still amounted to 220 420 km. By 2024, it had decreased to 201 314 km, corresponding to a decline of 8.7%. However, the situation in the individual EU countries differs considerably (see Figure 1). Among the EU countries, Spain recorded by far the largest expansion of its railway network between 1990 and 2024 in actual length (+1 757 km; +12.2%). Relatively large expansions were also noted in Estonia (+14.1%; +145 km) and the Netherlands (+9.5%; +263 km) over this period. In contrast, the national rail networks were considerably reduced between 1990 and 2024 in Poland (-25.2%; -6 600 km) and Latvia (-23.6%; -570 km). The same negative development was registered in the 2 countries with the largest national railway networks in the EU, France (-19.9%, -6 800 km) and Germany (-11.8%, -5 200 km). Considerable differences were also noted among the candidate countries over the same period: while Türkiye showed a strong increase in its railway network (+35.4%; +2 990 km), stimulated notably by the building of new high-speed lines, Albania saw the length of its network reduced by 62.5% (-420 km). [[Image:Figure 1 Railway network length in selected countries, 1990-2024 (index 1990=100)V1.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Railway network length in selected countries, 1990-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/212ba546-3700-4f7f-ba68-43ab8d28b3d1?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T07:41:08Z (rail_if_line_tr)]|alt= Line chart showing the development in the length of national railway lines in countries over the period 1990-2024, presented as an index 1990=100. In addition to the EU total, the chart shows the development for the EU Member States Germany, Estonia, Spain, France, Latvia, the Netherlands and Poland, as well as for Türkiye. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Railway and other transport networks tend to be the densest in metropolitan areas with large population concentrations and economic activities, while there are fewer railway lines in areas with low population and limited industry. Thus, the density of the railway network, measured in metres of railway line per km2 of land area, overall tends to be lower in countries with large less-populated regions. Map 1 provides a picture of the railway network density in Europe. Within the EU, the countries with the highest density of railway network can be found in the centre of northern Europe, reflecting both their high population density and relatively high volumes of freight transport. In 2024, Czechia had the highest railway network density with 123.2 metres of railway lines per km2 of land area. Other EU countries with high density were Belgium (118.7 m/km2), Germany (110 m/km2) and Luxembourg (104.8 m/km2), far above the EU average of 49.1 m/km2. Lower densities are reported for EU countries on the outskirts of the EU. Greece, with its many islands, had the lowest railway network density, with 14.0 m/km2. Low values were also recorded in the [[Glossary:Nordic_countries|Nordic countries]] (Finland 19.4 m/km2; Sweden 26.8 m/km2), the [[Glossary:Baltic_countries|Baltic countries]] (Estonia 27.2 m/km2, Latvia 28.9 m/km2, Lithuania 30.7 m/km2), the Iberian peninsula (Portugal 27.8 m/km2, Spain 32.3 m/km2) and Ireland (29.8 m/km2). There are stark contrasts between the EFTA countries: Norway had a lower network density than any of the EU countries, at 10.9 m/km2 in 2024, explained essentially by a very uneven population distribution. In Switzerland, the density stood at 133.1 m/km2, higher than in any country in the EU. Generally, low density values are shown for the candidate countries and the potential candidate; ranging from 9.0 m/km2 in Albania and 14.9 m/km2 in Türkiye to 43.7 in Serbia and 32.7 in Ukraine (2023 data). Map 1: Density of national railway networks, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4db39eb6-dc2e-4359-a985-ecafa50b704d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T07:41:57Z (rail_if_line_tr)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a2815d08-0652-462f-a303-bbeffe75b7bf?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T08:33:07Z (reg_area3)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7153742f-629f-4498-a340-02b957ec1a9a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T08:33:56Z (enpe_reg_area3)] [[Image:M1_Density of the railway networks, 2024_v2.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 1: Density of national railway networks, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4db39eb6-dc2e-4359-a985-ecafa50b704d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T07:41:57Z (rail_if_line_tr)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a2815d08-0652-462f-a303-bbeffe75b7bf?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T08:33:07Z (reg_area3)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7153742f-629f-4498-a340-02b957ec1a9a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T08:33:56Z (enpe_reg_area3)], national data|alt= Map showing the density of national railway networks in the EU Member States, the EFTA countries, the candidate countries and one potential candidate in 2024. Each country is shaded based on the metres of railway line per square kilometre of land area. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Development in the share of electrified lines=== Electrification is a key element of the modernisation of railway networks, further reducing the negative environmental impact of railway transport compared with road transport and other transport modes, most heavily dependent on fossil fuels. Non-electrified railway lines are mainly used by diesel-powered locomotives and railcars. Figure 2 shows the development in the electrification of the railway network in the EU and for selected countries with notable electrification levels or developments. Between 1990 and 2024, there was a considerable increase in the electrification of the lines of the European railway network: whereas 39.9% of all railway lines in the EU were electrified in 1990, this share increased to 57.6% by 2024. The strongest increase occurred in Portugal, where the electrification rate rose from 14.7% to 70.9%, an increase of 56.2 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]]. Other EU countries that progressed considerably over this period were Greece (+37.3 pp, between 1997 and 2024), Finland (+33.0 pp), Denmark (+27.3 pp), France (+24.6 pp), Luxembourg (+24.0 pp), as well as Belgium (+22.1 pp). Ireland had the lowest share of electrified lines in 2024, with just 2.6%, only slightly higher than the 1.9% it featured in 1990. Among the candidate countries, Türkiye showed a considerable increase: from 7.2 % in 1990 to 57.5 % in 2024 (+50.4 pp). [[Image:F2_Electrified railway lines in selected countries, 1990-2024_v2.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Electrified railway lines in selected countries, 1990-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7b761f62-cdac-4026-8d6d-5290c26010bb?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T07:44:26Z (rail_if_line_tr)]
|alt= Line chart showing the development in the share of electrified railway lines in selected EU Member States over the period 1990-2024, presented as the percentage of electrified lines in the total length of railway lines. In addition to the EU total, the chart shows the development for the EU Member States Belgium, Denmark, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Luxembourg, Portugal and Finland, as well as for Serbia. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] As shown in Map 2, Luxembourg has by far the highest level of electrification within the EU, with 96.7% in 2024. Belgium also has a high degree of electrification, with 88.0% of the network in 2024. Other EU countries with high electrification rates are Sweden (75.1%), Bulgaria (74.6%) and the Netherlands (74.4%). Only 53 kilometres of the Irish railway lines were electrified by 2024, corresponding to 2.6% of the national network. In the Baltic countries too, the electrification rate is generally low, with 8.1% in Lithuania, 12.0% in Estonia and 13.7% in Latvia. As an EFTA country, Switzerland stands out with an almost complete electrification of its national railway network (99.8% in 2024). Among the candidate countries and the potential candidate, Georgia (98.4%) and Montenegro (90.5%) both have a high degree of electrification, whereas Albania, Moldova and Kosovo** This designation is without prejudice to positions on status, and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo Declaration of Independence. reported no electrified railway lines. Map 2: Electrified railway lines, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f1907b23-bc8b-4ef5-9302-dc1fde17f3fb?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T07:45:18Z (rail_if_line_tr)] [[Image:M2_Electrified railway lines, 2024_v1.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 2: Electrified railway lines, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f1907b23-bc8b-4ef5-9302-dc1fde17f3fb?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T07:45:18Z (rail_if_line_tr)]|alt= Map showing the share of electrified railway lines in the EU Member States, EFTA countries, the candidate countries and one potential candidate in 2024. Each country is shaded based on its share of electrified lines in the total length of railway lines. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Electrified railway lines by type of current=== A railway network can be electrified according to various types of electric current characteristics. In Europe, the following main types of electric current are in use: Alternating Current (AC) 50 Hz / 25 000 Volts, AC 16 2/3 Hz / 15 000 Volts, Direct Current (DC) 3 000 Volts and DC 1 500 Volts. In the European Union, the share of the first 3 above-mentioned types of current is about 30% each (32.0%, 28.3% and 31.3%, respectively) while the share of DC 1 500 V is about 7.5% (Table 1). Due to these different systems, modern European electric locomotives are often designed to be multi-system, to be able to operate cross-border. [[Image:T1_Length of electrified railway lines by type of current, 2024_v1.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Length of electrified railway lines by type of current, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/35bca454-9349-4de2-9a32-80dd642d0dd8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T07:49:15Z (rail_if_electri)]
|alt= Table showing the length of electrified railway lines by type of current in the EU, EU Member States, EFTA countries, the candidate countries and one potential candidate in 2024. The columns show the type of current. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Alternating current is predominantly used in Bulgaria, Greece, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Romania, Finland and Sweden (in these countries, all electrified railway lines are operated with AC), Croatia (99.7% of the electrified railway lines), Portugal (98.6%), Germany and Hungary (both 96.6%) and Austria (94.7%) (Map 3). The share of AC is also significant in Denmark (80.3%) and in France (65.4%). In contrast, in Estonia, Ireland, Latvia and Poland, AC is not used at all; in those countries direct current is used exclusively. The use of AC is also insignificant in Slovenia (1.5% of total electrified railways lines operates with AC) and in Italy (6%), while it is quite small in the Netherlands (12.7%) and Belgium (16.4%). Map 3: Electrified railway lines with alternating current, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9cddcd91-4e94-49d7-ae0d-eab3a3705101?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T07:50:33Z (rail_if_electri)] [[Image:M3_Electrified railway lines with alternating current, 2024_v1.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 3: Electrified railway lines with alternating current, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9cddcd91-4e94-49d7-ae0d-eab3a3705101?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T07:50:33Z (rail_if_electri)]|alt= Map showing the share of electrified railway lines with alternating current in the EU Member States, EFTA countries, the candidate countries and one potential candidate in 2024. Each country is shaded based on its share of electrified lines with alternating current in the total length of railway lines. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Increased capacity and safety through expansion of lines with 2 or more tracks=== In addition to the length of the railway lines, an important aspect of the capacity of national railway networks is the share of lines with 2 or more parallel tracks. Multiple parallel tracks enable more efficient, safer and denser traffic on railway lines, increasing flexibility and reducing the effects of any disturbances. Figure 3 highlights the development in lines with 2 or more parallel tracks in the EU and in selected countries that stand out. Over the last decades, the capacity of the EU railway network has constantly improved, with the share of lines with 2 or more parallel tracks growing from 31.8% in 1990 to 40.8% in 2024, an increase of 9 pp. This represented an additional 12 194 km of railway lines equipped with 2 or more tracks over the period. In Greece, the share of lines with multiple tracks expanded strongly, from 9.9% in 1990 to 35.5% in 2024 (+25.6 pp; +400 km). This share also increased considerably in Spain (+19.8 pp) and France (+16.2 pp). In absolute numbers, the lines with 2 or more parallel tracks grew most in Spain (+3 550 km), Italy (+2 040 km), Germany (+1 990 km) and France (+1 280 km). In contrast, between 1990 and 2024, the share of the railway lines equipped with 2 or more tracks declined slightly in 4 EU countries: Ireland (-4.0 pp), Lithuania (-3.4 pp), Slovenia (-0.9 pp) and Estonia (-0.2 pp). [[Image:F3_Railway lines with 2 or more tracks in selected countries, 1990-2024_v2.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Railway lines with 2 or more tracks in selected countries, 1990-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1ff7a940-7d5f-4181-9095-5dc69ac0b04e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T07:47:15Z (rail_if_line_tr)]
|alt= Line chart showing the development in the share of railway lines with 2 or more tracks in selected countries over the period 1990-2024, presented as the percentage of lines with 2 or more tracks in the total length of railway lines. In addition to the EU total, the chart shows the development for the EU Member States Germany, Greece, Spain, France and Italy, as well as for Türkiye. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] A certain pattern with respect to the share of railway lines with 2 or more parallel tracks can be recognised between countries in the north, east and furthest west of the EU and countries in the middle and south (see Map 4). The highest shares of railway lines with multiple tracks are found in Belgium (81.2%) and the Netherlands (70.5%). Both countries feature a relatively small land area, high population density and high levels of freight transport to and from important seaports (Rotterdam and Amsterdam in the Netherlands; Antwerp in Belgium). France (62.8%), Luxembourg (59.0%), Germany (48.6%) and Italy (46.0%) also have national networks with a high share of lines with multiple tracks. The lowest shares of railway lines with multiple tracks are found in Estonia (9.4%) and Croatia (10.5%). Low shares are also found in the Nordic countries: Finland (12.1%) and Sweden (19.1%) and in eastern countries such as Hungary (17.9%) and Latvia (20.1%). Among non-EU countries, Norway is similar to its Nordic neighbours Finland and Sweden in this aspect. Its share of 8.0% of railway lines equipped with multiple tracks is lower than in any of the EU countries. Even lower rates are found in some of the candidate countries and the potential candidate. Moreover, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Albania and Kosovo* are not reporting any railway lines with multiple tracks, while the highest shares were reported in Ukraine (34.3%, 2023 data), followed by Georgia (26.3%), Türkiye (16.8%) and Serbia (10.4%). For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Track gauge: an important feature for interoperability of railway networks=== One important feature of a railway network with respect to connectivity and interoperability is the width of the tracks, known as ''track gauge''. The track gauge is the smallest distance between a pair of rails, measured between the inside of the rail heads. Generally, one distinguishes between 'large gauge' railway tracks (more than 1 435 mm width), 'standard gauge' (1 435 mm) and 'narrow gauge' (less than 1 435 mm). Lines with narrow track gauge play only a marginal role in the EU railway network, with a share of only 1.6% in the total length of the network in 2024. However, narrow gauge lines are still of some importance in some countries or regions. The most striking development over the period 1990-2024 took place in Greece, where the share of lines with narrow track gauge decreased from 35.9% in 1990 to 5.5% in 2024 (-30.4 pp), mainly through sharp declines in 1998, 2014 and 2022. Portugal also recorded a considerable slimming-down of its narrow track gauge network over this period, from 12.7% of its national network in 1990 to 3.8% in 2024 (-8.9 pp). Austria retained one of the highest shares of narrow-gauge lines with 6.6% of the total network in 2024, compared with 6.3% in 1990, a slight increase of 0.3 pp. However, within this period, the share ranged between 5.3% and 5.6% from 2001 to 2018. The share of narrow track lines declined by 3.8 pp to 0% in Romania and by 2.6 pp to 3.1% in Bulgaria over this period. Among other European countries, Switzerland stands out with a number of narrow-gauge lines in its mountain regions. These narrow-gauge lines make up slightly over a quarter of the Swiss railway network, remaining relatively stable over the period. Only a slight decrease has been recorded, down 1.0 pp from 26.9% in 1990 to 25.9% in 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Generally, few railway lines with narrow track gauge still exist, most of them in mountainous regions. Indeed, these offer significant advantages in difficult terrain due to lower construction costs, tighter curve radii, and smaller spatial footprints. Some become heritage lines being operated as museum or touristic lines or local tramway networks (both out of the scope of the ‘heavy’ railway statistics). In the railway network considered by the EU railway interoperability and safety directivesEU directives 2016/797 on interoperability of the rail system within the EU and 2016/798 on railway safety (95.4% of the whole railway network in EU and EFTA countries), their share is only 0.7% (Map 5). It is worth to notice that, for instance, the Swiss narrow gauge networks are out of this scope. Large track gauge is also still in use in some EU countries: it is predominantly used in Estonia, Ireland and Finland (in all 3 countries the complete network is large track gauge), Latvia (98.2% of the railway lines), Portugal (96.2%) and Lithuania (93.3%). The large gauge in the Baltic countries and Finland corresponds to the “Russian gauge” (between 1520 and 1524 mm), legacy of their initial development during the XIXth century. The share of large track gauge is also significant in Spain (70.7%), with same characteristics as in Portugal (“Iberian gauge”: 1668 mm). In Romania, Hungary, Slovakia and Poland, large track gauge can also be found but their share in total railway lines ranges between 0.6% and 3.0% - they are all “Russian gauge” established near the border with ex-Soviet Union, facilitating interoperability with their neighbour countries (Moldova, Ukraine, Belarus, Lithuania). Conversely, Lithuania has settled 96 km of standard gauge near its border with Poland. In the EFTA countries, large track gauge is not used at all. In the candidate countries and potential candidate, large track gauge is used only in Georgia (all railway lines), Moldova (93.2% of total railway lines) and Ukraine (98.1%, 2023 data) – still the “Russian gauge”. Each type of track gauge is presented with different colour.]] ===European high-speed rail network gradually expanding=== An important target of European policies is to reduce the environmental impact of the transport sector and its emissions of [[Glossary:Transport_greenhouse_gases|greenhouse gases]]. In this context, the steady expansion of the interconnected [[Glossary:High-speed_rail|high-speed]] railway network across Europe is a vital contribution towards strengthening rail travel as an alternative to road and air, which cause substantially higher CO2 and greenhouse gas emissions per [[Glossary:Passenger-kilometre|passenger-kilometre]]. Dedicated high-speed railway lines are railway lines specifically built to allow traffic at speeds of 250 km/h or higher on their main segments. Figure 5 shows how, over the 16 years from 2008 to 2024, the network of dedicated high-speed railway lines in the EU has expanded by 3 820 km (+80.7%), from roughly 4 700 km to just over 8 500 km. This high-speed network is interoperable across the EU, with connections operating across national borders. This rapid progress is mainly attributable to the expansion of the dedicated high-speed lines in Spain and France, which together make up close to 70% of the high-speed network in the EU (Spain 37.3%; France 32.1%). From 2008 to 2024, the high-speed network in Spain increased from 1 244 km to 3 192 km (+1 948 km; +156.6%), becoming the most important network in Europe, while in France it expanded from 1 865 km to 2 748 km (+883 km; +47.3%). The dedicated high-speed network in Germany grew from 864 km to 1 159 km over the same period (+295 km; +34.1%), while that in Italy increased from 532 km to 1 097 km (+565 km; +106.2%). For the other EU countries with dedicated high-speed lines, there were only limited changes: the network in Belgium increased from 139 to 211 km, while in the Netherlands it remained unchanged, at 90 km. Denmark opened its first 57 km of dedicated high-speed lines in 2019. Among the candidate countries, Türkiye was the only one with specifically built high-speed railway lines: whereas there were no high-speed lines in 2008, the country reported 2 182 km in 2024. [[Image:F5_Dedicated high-speed railway lines with a maximum speed of 250 km_h or more, 2008-2024_v1.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Dedicated high-speed railway lines with a maximum speed of 250 km/h or more, 2008-2024

For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] As mentioned, Spain, France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Denmark are the only EU countries with dedicated high-speed railway lines. Although these networks are vital to strengthening rail travel as an environment- and climate-friendly alternative primarily to road and air travel, the shares of the dedicated high-speed lines within the national railway networks are more limited. The share in Spain was 19.7% of the total length of the national railway network in 2024. In France, the share stood at 10.0%. In the other EU countries with dedicated high-speed lines, the shares ranged between 6.5% in Italy to 2.3% in Denmark. Progress was substantial in Türkiye, as the dedicated high-speed lines made up 19.1% of its national railway network in 2024. ===Level crossings on railway tracks remain an important safety issue=== An intersection where a road is crossing a railway track, at 'street level', is called a ''level crossing''. There are two types of level crossings: ''active level'' crossings and ''passive'' level crossings. An active level crossing is equipped with devices that are activated when it is unsafe to cross the railway tracks. These devices include physical protections such as barriers and gates, as well as warning signals such as lights, bells, horns, etc. Passive level crossings are rail track crossing points without any active devices to protect or warn users. A main challenge for [[Railway_safety_statistics_in_the_EU|railway safety]] is to reduce the number of level crossings, as cars, cyclists and pedestrians may come into direct contact with trains and other rolling stock. Indeed, [[Glossary:Level_crossing_accidents|accidents at level crossings]] is one of the main categories of railway accidents, both with respect to the number of persons killed and the number of accidents. The main strategies for reducing the risk of accidents between road users and railway rolling stock is to build underpasses or tunnels for the roads or the rail tracks in order to eliminate level crossings (also beneficial for the fluidity of road traffic and reduced emissions), as well as converting passive level crossings into active ones through the installation of active devices to protect and warn. Information on the number of level crossings, as well as of the number of level crossings equipped with the different types of active safety devices, are part of the [https://www.era.europa.eu/domains/common-safety-methods/common-safety-targets-csm_en Common Safety Indicators (CSI)] compiled by the European Union Agency for Railways (ERA). Data on railway safety and accidents, sourced from the ERA, are available in Eurostat's online database, under: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database Transport] (see 'Transport safety (trans_sf)') and then 'Rail transport safety (tran_sf_rail)'. Between 2010 and 2024, the total number of level crossings in the EU decreased by 19.3% (from 114 464 to 92 387). The number of level crossings were significantly reduced over this period in Greece (-48.4%), the Nordic countries Sweden (-41.5%), Denmark (-39.6%) and Finland (-37.7%), as well as in Austria (-39.1%). In absolute number of level crossings, the numbers fell most in Sweden (-4 717, -41.5%), followed by France (-4 171; -22.7%), Germany (-3 948, -22.7%) and Poland (-2 153; -15.2%). Still, the number of level crossings are typically more prevalent on railway lines in regions with lower population densities and thus less road traffic crossing the railway lines. Closures of certain railway sections in such regions may have had a certain impact on the overall reduction of the number of level crossings. From a safety perspective, it makes sense to analyse the number of level crossings, and passive level crossings in particular, relative to the length of railway lines operated. Figure 6 shows the development from 2010 to 2024 in the number of rail track crossings per 100 kilometres of railway lines in the EU, in the individual EU countries and in the EFTA countries. In 2024, there were on average 45.9 level crossings per 100 km of railway lines in the EU, down from 56.1 in 2010 (-18.3%). Most level crossings were found in Czechia (82.6 per 100 km of railway lines), followed by Hungary (81.2) and the Netherlands (71.6). Between 2010 and 2024, the number of level crossings relative to the length of the network was reduced by 40.1% in Sweden, from 101.9 level crossings per 100 km of lines in 2010 to 61.0 in 2024. Other EU countries that were able to substantially reduce the relative number of level crossings over this period were Finland (-37.7%, to 40.4 level crossings per 100 km of lines in 2024), Austria (-36.9%, to 55.7 in 2024) and Denmark (-35.7%, to 35.7 in 2024). Norway had a higher number of level crossings per 100 km of railway lines than any of the EU countries, with 79.0 in 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Railway lines equipped with a traffic management system (ERTMS)=== The installation of Train Protection Systems (TPS) is widely considered as one of the most effective safety measures for reducing train collision risks. However, national TPS are non-interoperable, the main reason why a European standard was developed in the second half of the 1990s: the ETCS (European Train Control System), through track-based (ETCS level 1) or radio-signal (ETCS level 2). The full European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) is made of European or international components for train protection (ETCS), but also radio communication (Global System for Mobile Communications – Railway - GSM-R). GSM-R is, among others, a necessary complement to ETCS level 2. The policy of the Trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T) states that ERTMS shall be deployed in full on the TEN-T railway network by 2030. Out of the 18 EU countries for which data on ETCS deployment are available for 2025, the use of ETCS level 1 (track-based) signalling system was the unique choice in Bulgaria, Croatia, Luxembourg and Slovenia, the predominant choice in Belgium, Spain, Romania, Slovakia and Switzerland (Table 2). Spain offers the particularity that more than 800 km of lines are equipped with both track-based and radio-signal ETCS systems. By contrast, the use of ETCS Level 2 (radio-signal) was the unique choice in Denmark, Sweden and Norway, and dominant in Czechia, Germany, France, Italy, Hungary, the Netherlands, Austria and Poland. In the 20 EU countries for which 2025 data on GSM-R deployment are available, GSM-R is much more developed than ETCS, with Romania as the only apparent exception. Most of these figures have been extracted from the Register of Infrastructure (RINF) managed by ERA, on 31 December 2025. Table 2 also incorporates additional information provided by Infrastructure Managers as part of the data quality assessment. Each type of signalling system is presented with different colour.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Characteristics of the railway network in Europe updated 06Mar2026_v2.xlsx|title=Characteristics of national railway networks in Europe 1990-2025}} === Data sources === '''Data collection''' Statistics on railway infrastructure are mainly collected on a voluntary basis through the [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] / [[Glossary:UNECE|United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE)]] / [https://www.itf-oecd.org/ International Transport Forum (ITF)] Common Questionnaire for Inland Transport Statistics. The Common Questionnaire is based on a goodwill agreement with the participating countries. Eurostat, UNECE and ITF cooperate on coordinating and streamlining data collection at international level to reduce the administrative burden on national administrations, as many of the about 50 reporting countries are members of more than one of the organisations. Data is generally provided by the [[Glossary:European_statistical_system_(ESS)|national statistical institutes or responsible transport administrations]]. However, methodologies are not harmonised at EU level, apart from the illustrated {{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-048|title=Eurostat/UNECE/ITF Glossary for Transport Statistics}} which harmonises definitions, thus comparability across countries may be restricted for certain topics or indicators. As data provision is voluntary, data may not be available for all EU Member States for each indicator. Thus, EU aggregates may be estimated or missing. Eurostat cooperates closely with the [https://www.era.europa.eu/ European Union Agency for Railways (ERA)] with respect to statistics on the European railway network. Eurostat publishes data provided by ERA on railway lines equipped with the [[Glossary:European_rail_traffic_management_system_(ERTMS)|ERTMS railway traffic management system]] issued from the Register of Infrastructure (RINF) and on level crossings, provided through ERA's [https://www.era.europa.eu/domains/common-safety-methods/common-safety-targets-csm_en Common Safety Indicators]. An in-depth exchange of data with geographical coordinates has also been implemented between the Register of Infrastructure (RINF) managed by ERA and the technical characteristics of the railway network segments collected every 5 years through Regulation (EU) 2018/643, Annex V. This comparison of maps also has an impact on national aggregates. Some additional data, filling in missing information for certain indicators (old time series, or in relation to high-speed lines), have been provided by the [https://uic.org/ International Union of Railways (Union Internationale des Chemins de Fer: UIC)], with which Eurostat exchange certain data and cooperate closely regarding definitions. '''Coverage''' The data in this article covers the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|EU Member States]], the [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA countries]] and the [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries and one potential candidate]]. There are no railways in Cyprus, Malta and Iceland. There is only a minor railway network in Liechtenstein. '''Definitions''' All definitions of the indicators are taken from the illustrated {{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-048|title=Eurostat/UNECE/ITF Glossary for Transport Statistics}}, currently in its 6th edition (2026). This glossary can be found on Eurostat’s website. For the specific definitions related to railway infrastructure, see chapter A. ''Railway transport'', sub-chapter A.I ''Infrastructure'' of the Glossary for transport statistics. ===Context === The EU is committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2050, delivering on its commitments under the Paris Agreement. The [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en European Green Deal] aims to transform the EU into a fair and prosperous society with a modern and competitive economy. It is a package of policy initiatives, which includes initiatives covering the climate, environment, energy, transport, industry, agriculture and sustainable finance – all of which are strongly interlinked. The transport sector currently accounts for a quarter of the EU's [[Glossary:Transport_greenhouse_gases|greenhouse gas emissions]], of which [https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/transport_en 70% come from road transport]. Investing in transport infrastructure, particularly in railways and inland waterways transport, contributes to the decarbonisation of transport. The [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal/transport-and-green-deal_en European Green Deal sets a clear objective of reducing emissions from transport] by 90%, compared with 1990 levels, by 2050. The European Commission's {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX%3A52020DC0789:EN:NOT|title=Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy}} and its action plan sets out 82 initiatives to reach this target. Efficient transport services and infrastructure are vital to exploiting the economic strengths of the European Union, supporting the internal market and growth, and enabling economic and social cohesion. They also influence trade competitiveness, as the availability, price, and quality of transport services have strong implications on production processes and the choice of trading partners. National rail networks have different technical specifications for infrastructure, which makes it more difficult and costly to run a train from one country to another. EU policies aim to overcome such differences. Creating an integrated European railway area thus requires better technical compatibility – 'interoperability' – of infrastructure, rolling stock, signalling and other characteristics of the rail system. Procedures for authorising the use of rolling stock across the EU's [[Glossary:Railway_network|rail network]] also need to be simplified. Eurostat's transport statistics are vital for monitoring EU transport policies and targets, providing key information in a coherent and reliable manner. Data are generally provided in accordance with the respective legal acts on statistics for the different transport. However, some important information is not covered by these legal acts, including information on the characteristics of the transport infrastructure. Comparable international data on railway infrastructure is instead collected on a voluntary basis through the Eurostat/UNECE/ITF Common Questionnaire on Inland Transport Statistics. === Other articles
