title: Children - material deprivation
text:
Children - material deprivation Data extracted in May 2025 Planned article update: June 2027 In 2024, 39.1% of children with parents who had a low level of education were materially deprived. In 2024, 5.6% of children with parents who had a high level of education were materially deprived. In 2024, in the EU, 13.6% of children aged less than 16 were materially deprived. [[Image:Child-material-deprivation-2024.jpg |thumb|centre|700px|
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code= ilc_chmd03}}|alt=Vertical bar chart showing child material deprivation as percentages in the EU and individual EU countries for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article presents statistical data on the situation of children (aged less than 16 years) in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] who were materially deprived in 2024. [[Glossary:Material_deprivation|Material deprivation]] is defined as an enforced lack of at least three items from a set of 17 items (12 child-specific and 5 household-specific). The analysis compares children of different age groups and examines the impact of their parents' educational level. All figures are based on EU statistics on income and living conditions ([[Glossary:EU-SILC|EU-SILC]]) available from [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat’s]] online database. EU-SILC data are available for all [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU Member States]]. === Key findings === In 2024, 13.6% of children (aged less than 16 years) in the EU were materially deprived. The highest rate was recorded for children aged 12-15 years old (14.7%) compared with 12.8% for children aged 5 years old or less. The highest rates of [[Glossary:Child_deprivation|child material deprivation]] for children aged 16 or less were observed in Greece (33.6%), Romania (31.8%) and Bulgaria (30.4%). On the other hand, the lowest values were observed in Croatia (2.7%), Slovenia (3.8%) and Sweden (5.6%). [[Image:Fig1_Child material deprivation, 2024_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Child material deprivation, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code= ilc_chmd01}}|alt=a vertical bar chart showing child material deprivation in 2024 in the EU and EU Member States. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Child material deprivation by age groups === In 2024, at EU level, the child material deprivation rate was highest in the age group 12-15 years and lowest among children aged 5 years or less (14.7% as compared with 12.8%). This pattern was repeated in 20 out of the 27 EU countries, with the highest differences recorded in Austria (7.4 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]]), Cyprus (6.1 pp) and Ireland (6.0 pp) (see Figure 2). Italy and Germany showed very similar values across all the four age groups. Slovakia, the Netherlands, Portugal, Finland, and Hungary recorded their lowest child material deprivation rate value in the age group 12-15 years. [[Image:Fig2_Child material deprivation, by age group, 2024_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Child material deprivation, by age group, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code= ilc_chmd01}}|alt=a vertical bar chart with four bars showing Child material deprivation, by age group in 2024 in the EU and the EU Member States. The bars show ages, five years or less, six to eleven years, twelve to fifteen years, and less than sixteen years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Level of education of the parents === One of the factors that affects material deprivation of children (further to the reducing effect that targeted social transfers can have) is the level of education of their parents, which is largely linked to their [[Glossary:Labour_market|labour market]] situation. '''Children whose parents attained a lower educational level are more likely to experience material deprivation compared with children whose parents attained a higher education level.''' An adult’s education level affects the type of job an individual can access. Generally, the lower the level, the higher the risk is for the individual and for the household, including children, to experience material deprivation compared with those with a higher educational level. In 2024, 39.1% of children in the EU living in a household whose parents had a low level of education of at most lower secondary ([[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|ISCED]] levels 0-2), were experiencing material deprivation. On the other hand, the respective rate for children living in households whose parents had a high level of education (tertiary education, ISCED levels 5-8), was 5.6% (see Figure 3). The child material deprivation gap for children based on the parents’ level of education was therefore 33.5 pp. The gap among the EU countries ranged from 5.0 pp in Luxembourg to 87.0 pp in Slovakia. In 7 out of the 27 EU countries, the gap was above 50.0 pp. [[Image:Fig3_Child material deprivation, by the highest level of education attained by their parents, 2024_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Child material deprivation, by the highest level of education attained by their parents, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code= ilc_chmd03}}|alt=a vertical bar chart with two bars showing child material deprivation, by the highest level of education attained by their parents in 2024 in the EU. The bars show at most lower secondary education and tertiary education. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Child_material_deprivation_tables_figures.xlsx|Children - material deprivation: tables and figures]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === The data used in this article are derived from [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions]] (EU-SILC). EU-SILC data are compiled annually and are the main source of statistics that measure income and living conditions in Europe; it is also the main source of information used to link different aspects relating to the quality of life of [[Glossary:Household|households]] and individuals. Information on material deprivation specific to children was collected in 2024 as a part of the three-yearly variables on Children based on Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2242. The reference population for the information presented in this article is all private households and their current members residing in the territory of an EU Member State (or non-member country) at the time of data collection; persons living in collective households and in institutions are excluded from the target population. The data for the EU are population-weighted averages of national data. === Context === '''The child specific deprivation rate''' is the percentage of children below 16 who suffer from the enforced lack of at least three items out of the following 17 (unweighted) items: # Child: Some new clothes # Child: Two pairs of shoes # Child: Fresh fruits and vegetables daily # Child: Meat, chicken, fish daily # Child: Suitable books # Child: Outdoor leisure equipment # Child: Indoor games # Child: Leisure activities # Child: Celebrations # Child: Invite friends # Child: School trips # Child: Holiday # Household: Replace worn-out furniture # Household: Arrears # Adults in the household: InternetIf at least half of the adults in the household are deprived of this item, the child is considered deprived of the item. # Household: Home adequately warm # Household: Car Only children lacking an item for affordability reasons (and not by choice or due to any other reasons) are considered deprived of this item. Those lacking the item “for other reasons” are treated, together with those who have the item, as not deprived. '''Educational attainment level''' is classified according to [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|ISCED]] — the international standard classification of education. The (latest) 2011 version has the following levels: Low level of education: • ISCED level 0 — early childhood • ISCED level 1 — primary education • ISCED level 2 — lower secondary education Medium level of education: • ISCED level 3 — (upper) secondary education • ISCED level 4 — post-secondary non-tertiary education - medium level of education; High level of education: • ISCED level 5 — short-cycle tertiary education; • ISCED level 6 — bachelor’s or equivalent level; • ISCED level 7 — master’s or equivalent level; • ISCED level 8 — doctoral or equivalent level. The educational level of children’s parents is defined for this article as the highest level of education attained by one of the parents. For example, if father has a low level of education of at most lower secondary (ISCED "levels 0-2"), and mother has a medium level of education (upper-secondary education) (ISCED "levels 3-4") it is considered that the child’s parents have a medium level of education. === Other articles === '''Statistical articles''' *[[Material deprivation statistics - early results ]] *[[Children at risk of poverty or social exclusion]] *[[Living conditions in Europe - income distribution and income inequality]] *[[Living conditions in Europe]] — online publication *[[Migrant integration statistics - poverty and social exclusion]] *[[Quality_of_life_indicators_-_material_living_conditions|Quality of life indicators — material living conditions]] '''Methodological articles''' *[[EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)_methodology|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) methodology]] **[[EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)_methodology_-_material_deprivation_by_dimension|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) methodology — material deprivation by dimension]] **[[EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)_methodology_-_economic_strain|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) methodology — economic strain]] '''Glossary item''' * [[Glossary:Child deprivation]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/database Income and living conditions (ilc)], see: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=ilc_chmd Child-specific material deprivation; EU-SILC 3-yearly module] === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/overview Income and living conditions] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-DZ-18-001|title=Living conditions in Europe — 2018 edition}} ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=ilc_esms|title=Income and living conditions}} (ESMS metadata file — ilc_esms) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/data Income and living conditions — information on data] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/methodology Income and living conditions — methodology] === Legislation === {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R2242:EN:NOT|title=Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2242}} === Footnotes === {{Unit|topic=X_Living_conditions}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Children - material deprivation]] [[Category: Income and living conditions|Children - material deprivation]] [[Category:Poverty and social exclusion|Children - material deprivation]] [[Category:Statistical article|Children - material deprivation]] [[Category:June2027|Children - material deprivation]]

title: Children at risk of poverty or social exclusion
text:
Data for children at risk of poverty and exclusion are analysed and compared with data for adults and for the elderly. Living conditions for children are examined according to their parents’ level of education and country of birth. Data extracted on 7 May 2025 Planned article update: October 2026 Between 2023 and 2024, the percentage of children at risk of poverty or social exclusion in the EU slightly decreased from 24.8% to 24.2%. In 2024, 24.2% of children aged less than 18 in the EU were at risk of poverty or social exclusion compared with 20.3% of people aged 18 years and over. In 2024, in the EU, 11.0% of children aged less than 18 whose parents’ level of education was high were at risk of poverty or social exclusion, compared with 61.2% of children whose parents’ level of education was low. [[Image:Children AROPE, 2024.png|thumb|center|700px|
Children at risk of poverty or social exclusion, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_peps01n}}|alt= an infographic showing children at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2024, in the EU, EU Member States. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article presents statistical data on the situation of children (aged less than 18 years) in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] who were [[Glossary:At_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_(AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)]] in 2024. The analysis compares children with people aged 18 years and over and displays the impact of the parents’ educational attainment on the children AROPE levels.
The percentage of people who are at risk of poverty or social exclusion encompasses people who are in at least one of these three situations: * people who are [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|at risk of poverty]]: those with an equivalised disposable income that is below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold; * people who suffer from [[Glossary:Severe_material_and_social_deprivation_rate_(SMSD)|severe material and social deprivation]]: those who cannot afford at least seven out of thirteen deprivation items (six related to the individual and seven related to the household) that are considered by most people to be desirable or even necessary to lead an adequate quality of life; * people (aged less than 65 years) [[Glossary:Persons_living_in_households_with_very_low_work_intensity|living in a household with very low work intensity]]: those living in households where adults worked equal to or less than 20% of their total combined work-time potential during the previous twelve months.
===Children at risk of poverty or social exclusion=== In 2024, the proportion of children at risk of poverty or social exclusion in the EU was 24.2%. At national level, the highest rates were observed in Bulgaria (35.1%), Spain (34.6%) and Romania (33.8%). On the other side, the lowest rates were recorded in Slovenia (11.8%), Cyprus (14.8%) and Czechia (15.4%). '''The percentage of children at risk of poverty or social exclusion slightly decreased between 2023 and 2024''' At the EU level, between 2023 and 2024, the percentage of children at risk of poverty or social exclusion decreased by 0.6 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]], from 24.8% to 24.2% (Figure 1). At the national level, Finland recorded the highest rise, with an increase of 3.5 pp, followed by Croatia (+2 pp), Belgium and Bulgaria (+1.2 pp each). In contrast, large decreases were observed in Romania (-5.2 pp), Ireland (-3.7 pp) and Hungary (-3.3 pp). Italy was the only EU country that did not experience any change, remaining steady at 27.1%. [[Image: Fig1_Children AROPE, 2023 and 2024_(% of population in respective age group).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Children aged less than 18 years at risk of poverty or social exclusion, 2023 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_peps01n}}|alt=a vertical bar chart with a marker showing the percentage of children aged less than 18 years at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2023 and 2024. The bar shows 2024 and the marker shows 2023 in the EU and EU Member States. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''In 2024, the risk of poverty or social exclusion was higher for children than for people aged 18 years and over''' In 2024, children aged less than 18 in the EU were at a higher risk of poverty or social exclusion (24.2%) compared with people aged 18 and over (20.3%), resulting in a difference of 3.9 pp (Figure 2). Across the EU countries, 20 of them experienced a higher risk among children aged less than 18, with the largest differences recorded in Spain (10.5 pp), Malta and Romania (both 7.3 pp) and France (7.2 pp). Among the countries where people aged 18 years and over faced a higher risk of poverty or social exclusion than children, the largest differences were observed in Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania, with people aged 18 years and over exceeding children’s risk by 8.0, 7.1 and 3.6 pp, respectively. [[Image:Fig2_People AROPE, by age group, 2024_(% of population in respective age group).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: People at risk of poverty or social exclusion, by age group, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_peps01n}}|alt=a double vertical bar chart showing the share of persons at risk of poverty or social exclusion, by age group, 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''In 2024, children whose parents attained a higher education level were less likely to be at risk of poverty or social exclusion''' In 2024, 61.2% of children in the EU living with parents who had at most lower secondary education ([[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|ISCED]] levels 0-2) were at risk of poverty or social exclusion. For those with parents who attained tertiary education ([[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|ISCED]] levels 5-8), the proportion was 11.0% (Figure 3). This resulted in a risk gap of 50.2 pp based on parents' education levels. At the national level, the gap was above 50.0 pp in 16 EU countries. The lowest gaps were observed in Denmark (29.3 pp), Portugal (29.5 pp) and Estonia (35.5 pp), while the largest differences were recorded in Romania (69.9 pp), Czechia (70.4 pp) and Bulgaria (71.5 pp). [[Image: Fig3_Children AROPE, by educational attainment level of their parents, 2024_(% of population aged less than 18 years).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Children at risk of poverty or social exclusion, by the educational attainment level of their parents, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_peps60n}}|alt=a double vertical bar chart showing the share of children aged less than 18 years at risk of poverty or social exclusion, analysed by the educational attainment level of their parents, 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Children_in_AROPE_2024_tables_and_figures_rev.xlsx|title=Children_at_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data used in this article are derived from the [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU Statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]]. EU-SILC data are compiled annually and are the main source of statistics that measure income and living conditions in Europe; it is also the main source of information used to link different aspects relating to the quality of life of [[Glossary:Household|households]] and individuals. The reference population for the information presented in this article is all private households and their current members residing in the territory of an EU Member State (or non-member country) at the time of data collection; persons living in collective households and in institutions are excluded from the target population. The data for the EU are population-weighted averages of national data. The reference period for individuals' characteristics is 2023. The data is available for the 27 Member States as well as Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Serbia, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Albania and Türkiye. [[Glossary:At_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_(AROPE)|At-risk-of-poverty or social exclusion rate (AROPE)]] is the headline indicator to monitor [[Glossary:The_European_Pillar_of_Social_Rights_Action_Plan_(EU_2030_targets)|the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan (EU 2030 targets)]] poverty target. It reflects the share of the population which is either [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|at risk of poverty]], and/or [[Glossary:Severe_material_and_social_deprivation_rate_(SMSD)|severely materially and socially deprived]] and/or lives in a household with [[Glossary:Persons_living_in_households_with_very_low_work_intensity|very low work intensity]]. '''Educational attainment level''' is classified according to [[Glossary: International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|ISCED]] — the international standard classification of education. The (latest) 2011 version defines the following levels: *ISCED level 0 — early childhood education; *ISCED level 1 — primary education; *ISCED level 2 — lower secondary education; *ISCED level 3 — (upper) secondary education; *ISCED level 4 — post-secondary non-tertiary education; *ISCED level 5 — short-cycle tertiary education; *ISCED level 6 — bachelor’s or equivalent level; *ISCED level 7 — master’s or equivalent level; *ISCED level 8 — doctoral or equivalent level. The analysis presented in this article focuses on the following aggregations of ISCED levels: *ISCED levels 0-2: less than primary, primary and lower secondary education; *ISCED levels 5-8: tertiary education. ===Other articles=== *[[Living conditions in Europe| All articles from Living conditions in Europe]] *{{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-24-001|title=Key figures on European living conditions – 2024 edition}} *[[EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)_methodology_-_people_at_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) methodology - people at risk of poverty or social exclusion]] *[[Living conditions in Europe - poverty and social exclusion|Living conditions in Europe — poverty and social exclusion]] title: Children in migration - asylum applicants
text:
Children in migration - asylum applicants Data extracted 22 April 2026 Planned article update: April 2027 158 400 first-time asylum applicants were aged less than 18 years old, representing 23.7% of the total number of first-time asylum applicants recorded in the EU in 2025. Afghans (16.9%), Syrians (13.0%) and Venezuelans (10.7%) were by far the most represented citizenships of first-time asylum applicants aged less than 18 years old in the EU in 2025. In 2025, unaccompanied minors accounted for 13.3% of the total number of first-time asylum applicants aged less than 18 years old. The percentage of positive decisions on asylum applications was higher for minors than for adults over the period from 2014 to 2025. Among all migrants, minors are a particularly vulnerable group requiring special care. Based on available [[Glossary:Asylum|asylum]] data, this article focuses on developments over the period from 2014 to 2025 of one of the main components of the [[Glossary:Immigration|immigration]] of minors in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union]] (EU) and in [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] countries: the number of first-time asylum applicants aged less than 18 years old. === Main trends in 2025 === In 2025, the total number of first-time asylum applicants aged less than 18 years old in the EU was 158 400 persons (Figure 1). When comparing this figure with the total EU population aged less than 18, it corresponds to 2.0 minor first-time asylum applicants per 1 000 minor residents in the EU. Figure 1 also shows that overall 119 435 minors received protection status at first and final instances in 2025 while the asylum applications of 20 970 minors were rejected in the final instance. At the end of 2025, 254 625 minors were awaiting a decision on their asylum application in the EU. Figure 1 Figure 2 provides some insights into the characteristics of minor first-time asylum applicants for the year 2025: persons aged less than 18 years old accounted for 23.7% of the total number of first-time asylum applicants in the EU, the majority were male (55.4%) and 13.3% of them were unaccompanied minors. Figure 2 === Development from 2014 to 2025 === Figure 3 shows that the number of first-time asylum applicants aged less than 18 years old rose until the peak of the “migration crisis” in 2016 (377 090). From 2016 onwards, a downward trend was observed with a minimum value of 128 320 in 2020 (the drop observed in 2020 may be mostly explained by the COVID-19 outbreak and the related introduction of movement restrictions and border closures). Numbers increased again from 2021 to 2023, reaching 254 725 in 2023, before falling slightly to 234 825 in 2024. In 2025, the figure decreased further to 158 400 - the lowest level since 2020. Over the period from 2014 to 2026, nearly 2.6 million minors lodged an asylum application in the EU. Figure 3 When looking at the breakdown by [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU countries]] (Figure 4), the main destination in the EU for first-time asylum applicants aged less than 18 years old over the period from 2014 to 2025 was Germany (43.9%) followed by France (12.0%) and Spain (6.9%). In 2025, Germany (32.1%), France (20.5%) and Spain (15.7%) remained the 3 main destinations for minor first-time asylum applicants, followed by Greece at a distance (7.5%). The comparison of the breakdowns by EU country observed over the period from 2014 to 2025 and in 2025 shows marked increase in the shares recorded in Spain and France, and notable decline in Hungary, and, even more so, in Germany. Figure 4 Figure 5 shows the number of minor first-time asylum applicants relative to the population aged less than 18 years old. The circle markers depict the highest (maximum) value of the ratio of the number of first-time asylum applicants aged less than 18 relative to the population aged less than 18 years for any year from 2014 to 2025; the lowest (minimum) value is indicated by the cross markers. The distance between these 2 markers (portrayed by the vertical line) indicates the range observed over the whole period. The differences between the maximum and minimum values recorded between 2014 and 2025 were largest in Sweden, Hungary, Austria, Germany, Greece and Cyprus. Figure 5 Figure 5 also includes a square for the average from 2014 to 2025. The highest average ratios, at least 2 times higher than the EU average (2.7 per 1 000 persons), were recorded in Austria, Greece, Germany, Cyprus and Sweden. By contrast, the lowest average ratios were observed in Estonia, Portugal, Czechia and Slovakia; in all of these, the national average was less than one tenth of the EU average. === Citizenship of minor first-time asylum applicants === In 2025, Afghans, Syrians and Venezuelans were the most represented citizenships of minor first-time asylum applicants in the EU (Figure 6). They were followed by citizens of Türkiye and Somalia. The share of these 5 citizenships represented nearly half of the total of first-time asylum applicants aged less than 18 years in 2025. Figure 6 Figure 7 illustrates the development of the number of first-time asylum applicants aged less than 18 by main geographical area. The peaks recorded for Asia in 2015 and 2016 illustrate the “migration crisis”. In 2015, the maximum number of first-time asylum seekers with European (non-EU) citizenship was also observed. After these peaks, the Asian and European curves were characterised by a downward trend until 2020, an increase between 2021 and 2023, and again a decrease in 2024 and 2025. As for Africa, a regular upward trend was visible until 2017, before starting to fluctuate over the next 4 years. The numbers rose again from 2021 to 2024, before declining in 2025. Finally, the number of minor first-time asylum seekers who were citizens of an American country increased significantly between 2016 and 2019, followed by a decline in 2020 and 2021. This was followed by renewed growth between 2022 and 2024, and a decrease in 2025. Figure 7 === Minor first-time asylum applicants by sex === Figure 8 presents the development of the share of males in the total number of first-time applicants aged less than 18. Over the whole period, the share of males for minor first-time applicants was significantly higher than 50%, with a minimum of 54.1% observed in 2019 and a maximum of 64.2% in 2015, whereas the average value over the period from 2014 to 2025 was equal to 57.8%. Figure 8 === Share of minors in the total number of first-time applicants === As seen in Figure 9, the share of minors in the total number of first-time asylum applicants was not stable over time, ranging between 23.7% in 2025 and 32.3% in 2016. One of the main features is that the share of minors increased during the “migration crisis” and remained over 30% through 2021. After 2021, the proportion declined sharply, dropping to 25.0% in 2022 and reaching its lowest point of 23.7% in 2025. Figure 9 Figure 10 shows the share of minors in the total number of first-time asylum applicants by EU country in 2025. In 13 countries the share was above the EU average, with the highest values observed in Austria (57.3%), Germany (44.9%) and Finland (31.2%). In contrast, in 14 countries the share was below the EU average, with the lowest values observed in Italy (3.8%), Slovenia (5.3%), Czechia (7.5%) and Estonia (9.0%). Figure 10 === Unaccompanied minor first-time asylum applicants === At EU level, the share of unaccompanied minor first-time asylum applicants in the total number of first-time asylum applicants aged less than 18 years old was on average 15.3% over the period from 2014 to 2025, with a maximum value of 24.5% recorded in 2015 and a minimum value of 7.5% in 2019 (Figure 11). Once again, the highest value was recorded during the “migration crisis”, but the share of unaccompanied minors dropped quickly just after this period, before increasing up to 22.1% in 2022. Figure 11 When looking at the share of unaccompanied minors in the EU countries in 2025, the highest values can be found in Slovenia (78.6%), Latvia (72.9%), Bulgaria (56.2%), the Netherlands (49.8%) and Lithuania (47.1%). Figure 12 Figure 13 presents the 10 main countries of citizenship with the highest number of unaccompanied minors applying for asylum for the first time in one of the EU countries in 2025. The most represented citizenships of unaccompanied minor first-time asylum applicants in the EU in 2025 were Afghans, Eritreans and Syrians. Figure 13 === Decisions on asylum application for minors === Figure 14 shows that the ratio between the total number of positive decisions and the total number of decisions either at first instance or after appeal was higher over the period 2014 to 2025 for minor first-time asylum applicants than for adult first-time asylum applicants. This difference was more significant for first instance decisions than for decisions taken in appeal. It means that the first instance acceptance rate for minors was 1.5 times higher than for adults, while for the final decisions on appeal, the acceptance rate for minors was 1.2 times higher than for adults. Figure 14 Figure 15 indicates that the asylum procedure is processed faster for minors than for adults, since the share of minors in the total number of pending applications is always lower than the share of minors in the total number of first-time asylum applicants. Between 2014 and 2025, the difference between the 2 shares was not constant, and it reached its lowest in 2015 at the beginning of the migration crisis, reflecting the pressure at that time on the asylum systems in the EU. Figure 15 ===Decisions granting temporary protection to minors fleeing Ukraine=== On 4 March 2022, the European Council unanimously adopted an implementing decision introducing [[Glossary:Temporary_protection|temporary protection]] for people fleeing Ukraine as a consequence of Russia's invasion.
On 31 December 2025, based on available data, about 1.3 million minors (non-EU citizens), who had fled Ukraine as a consequence of the Russian invasion in 2022, were under temporary protection in the EU. Poland reported a total of 447 180 minors who benefitted from decisions granting temporary protection. Germany (328 410 beneficiaries) and Czechia (89 335) were the other EU countries with the highest total numbers of minor beneficiaries of temporary protection (Figure 16). Poland (46.1%) recorded the highest share of minors in the total number of non-EU citizens benefitting from decisions granting temporary protection on 31 December 2025, followed by Hungary (32.5%) and Belgium (30.4%). At EU level, the share was 30.2%. Figure 16 Detailed analysis of temporary protection statistics can be consulted in the more comprehensive monthly [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Temporary_protection_for_persons_fleeing_Ukraine_-_monthly_statistics Statistics Explained article]. === Data sources === '''Asylum statistics''' Since 2008 data have been provided to Eurostat under the provisions of Article 4 of the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?qid=1414508297956&uri=CELEX:32007R0862 Regulation (EC) No 862/2007]; most of the statistics presented in this article were collected within this regulatory framework. Data are provided to Eurostat with a monthly, quarterly or annual frequency, and are based on administrative sources. They are supplied to Eurostat by statistical authorities, home office ministries/ministries of the interior or related immigration agencies in the EU countries. '''Methodological notes''' 1) Limitations on data availability affecting the information presented in this article: * 2025 data not available for Iceland. * 2014 and 2015: data on first-time asylum applicants not available for Liechtenstein. * 2014-2020: total number of asylum applicants considered to be unaccompanied minors was used in the calculations. * 2021-2025: data refer to unaccompanied minor first-time asylum applicants, the complete data are not available for Italy, France, Cyprus and Poland. * 2025: data on final decisions not available for Italy. ''Data on temporary protection'' * France: In most cases, minors can stay in France without a permit. Therefore, minors are generally not included in statistics on temporary protection. 2) Member State data refer to the number of persons applying for asylum for the first time in that Member State. Persons may however apply for international protection in more than one Member State in a given reference year. Consequently, the EU total may include such multiple applications. Values are rounded to the nearest 5. === Context === In recent years, the number of minors arriving in the European Union, many of whom are unaccompanied, has increased substantially, particularly in 2015 and 2016. Protecting minors is first and foremost about upholding European values of respect for human rights, dignity and solidarity, regardless of status and at all stages of migration. The European Union, together with its Member States and with the support of the relevant EU agencies (European Border and Coast Guard Agency; European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) and the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights (FRA)), has been active on this front for many years. The existing EU policies and legislation provide a solid framework for the protection of the rights of the minors who migrate, covering all aspects including reception conditions, the treatment of their applications and integration. The European Union is fully committed to implement the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which calls for a world in which every child grows up free from violence and exploitation, has his/her rights protected and access to quality education and healthcare. The 2015 Valletta Summit [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/media/21839/action_plan_en.pdf 2015 Valletta Summit action plan] political declaration and its Action Plan calls for the prevention of and fight against irregular migration, migrant smuggling and trafficking in human beings (with a specific focus on women and minors). The [https://www.eeas.europa.eu/sites/default/files/10_hr_guidelines_protection_en.pdf EU Guidelines on the Promotion and Protection of the Rights of the Child] renew the EU's commitment to promote and protect the indivisibility of the rights of the child in its relations with third countries, including countries of origin or transit. In this context, the Council reaffirmed the need to protect all refugee and minor migrants, regardless of their status, and give primary consideration at all times to the best interests of the child, including unaccompanied minors and those separated from their families, in full compliance with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and its Optional Protocols. Within the [[Glossary:European_Commission_(EC)|European Commission]], the [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/index_en Directorate-General Migration and Home Affairs] is responsible for immigration policy, whereas the [https://ec.europa.eu/info/departments/justice-and-consumers_en Directorate-General for Justice and Consumers] is in charge of [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/rights-child/eu-strategy-rights-child-and-european-child-guarantee_en child policy]. All relevant legal acts and information regarding the EU’s immigration policy can be accessed on the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/summary/chapter/23.html European Commission’s website]. Readers interested in the recent development of the global immigration policy in the European Union are also invited to consult the [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en pact on migration and asylum] that entered into force in June 2024 and will enter into application in June 2026. This Pact provides a comprehensive approach that delivers a common European response to migration. It allows the EU to manage migration in a fair and sustainable way, ensuring solidarity between countries while also providing certainty and clarity for people arriving in the EU and protecting their fundamental rights. ===Other articles=== [[:Category:Migration and asylum|All articles on migration and asylum]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/children-migration/database Children in migration] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/asylum/database Asylum] ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/children-migration Children in migration] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/asylum Asylum] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/asylum/publications All publications on asylum] ===External links=== *[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/promoting-our-european-way-life/migration-and-asylum_en European_Commission — Migration and asylum] *[https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/legal-migration-and-resettlement_en DG Migration and Home Affairs — Legal migration and resettlement] *[https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies_en DG Migration and Home Affairs — Policies] *[https://ec.europa.eu/info/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights_en DG Justice and Consumers — Policies] === Footnotes === ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Article_name'' {{Unit|topic=X_Population}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Children in migration - asylum applicants]] [[Category:Migration and asylum|Children in migration - asylum applicants]] [[Category:Children in migration|Children in migration - asylum applicants]] [[Category:Statistical article|Children in migration - asylum applicants]] [[Category:Vistool|Children in migration - asylum applicants]] [[Category:April2027|Children in migration - asylum applicants]]

Children in migration - facts and figures
 '''Children in migration – facts and figures''' is an online [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publication providing recent statistics on migrant children in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] based on demography, international migration, acquisition of citizenship, asylum and residence permits statistics. This publication consists of individual articles that get updated according to their respective data release date.

title: Children in migration - demography and migration
text:
Children in migration - demography and migration Data extracted on 20 May 2026 Planned article update: May 2027 On 1 January 2025, around 7.8 million people aged less than 18 years did not have the citizenship of their country of residence in the EU. In 2024, 523 000 non-EU citizen and stateless minors aged less than 15 years immigrated to one of the EU countries, which is 9% less than in 2023 (574 000). In 2024, 15% of newborns (517 000 births) in the EU had a mother who was not an EU citizen. [[Image:Children in migration demography and migration edition2026 v2.png|thumb|centre|700px| '' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6f10beb8-748e-41af-bda5-5f83f9da2e30?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-26T07:06:09Z migr_pop2ctz])|alt= Map showing share of the non-national children in the child population of the country of residence as percentages for the EU countries and surrounding countries. Each country is classified based on the percentage range as of 1 January 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
This article presents European statistics on minors in migration based on international migration flows, the number of national and non-national residents in the population (stocks) as well as data relating to live births by citizenship of mother and the acquisition of citizenship. It focuses mainly on minors arriving in or residing in an EU country different from their country of citizenship, encompassing both intra-EU migration and immigration from non-EU countries. Migration of minors depends mainly on the migration of their parents or relatives, although it also includes unaccompanied minors. The main explanatory factors of migration can be found in the combination of economic, environmental, political and social factors: either in a migrant's country of origin (push factors) or in the country of destination (pull factors). This article forms part of the online publication [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Children_in_migration_-_facts_and_figures Children in migration - facts and figures] that also provides a range of complementary statistics on asylum applicants under the age of 18 and residence permits for family reasons issued to minors. === Total number of non-national minors in the EU: main indicators in 2025 === On 1 January 2025, around 7.8 million people aged less than 18 years did not have the citizenship of their country of residence in the EU, accounting for 9.8% of the total number of minors living in the EU and 17.4% of the total number of non-national residents (Figure 1). Looking at the distribution by main age groups, the highest share was observed for the 5-9 years age group (29.6%). Figure 1 As shown in Figure 2, Germany (27.3%), France (18.1%), Spain (14.2%) and Italy (13.1%) were the main EU countries hosting non-national minors – almost three out of four minors without the citizenship of their country of residence were residing in 1 of those 4 EU countries. Figure 2 In relative terms, the highest shares of non-national minors in the total minors' population were observed in Luxembourg (45.1%), Austria (22.5%), Malta (20.6%) and Cyprus (18.6%) (Figure 3). The shares were also higher or equal to 10% in Germany, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Denmark, Ireland and France. The lowest shares were observed in Slovakia (0.4%) and Poland (0.8%). Figure 3 The share of non-national minors in the total non-national population (Figure 4) depends on the number of factors including past migration flows, the number of births of non-national children on the territory of the host country and on policies regarding the acquisition of citizenship. This share was equal or higher than the EU average (17.4%) in 7 EU countries, with the highest value in France (21.8%), and the lowest in Latvia (4.1%) and Slovakia (6.7%). Figure 4 Looking at the shares of non-national resident population by different age groups of minors, it varies from one EU country to another (Table 1). For example, the share of minors aged less than 5 years was higher than 30% in Malta and Sweden, and lower than 20% in Bulgaria, Latvia, Lithuania and Hungary. [[Image:T1_Non-national_resident_population_aged_less_than_18_by_age_groups,_EU_and_EFTA_countries,_1_January_2025_v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Non-national resident population aged less than 18 by age groups, EU and EFTA countries, 1 January 2025
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6f10beb8-748e-41af-bda5-5f83f9da2e30?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-26T07:06:09Z migr_pop2ctz])|alt= Table showing children aged less than 18 years resident in EU and EFTA countries without having citizenship in their country of residence for the EU; individual EU and EFTA countries as of 1 January 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Non-national minors in the EU: development from 2020 to 2025 === Figure 5 shows the contribution of non-national minors on the development of the total minors' population in the EU. This dynamic is influenced by several factors: emigration and immigration flows, acquisition of citizenship, birth of non-national children, and the fact that each year, some minors become adults. Between 1 January 2020 and 1 January 2025, the population of non-national minors increased by 20.1% (an additional 1.3 million). This only partially offset the 4.1% decrease in the population of national minors (3.1 million less). As a result, the total population of minors declined by 2.2% (1.8 million less). Figure 5 These opposing trends in the populations of non-national and national minors led to an increase in the share of the population of non-national minors in the total minors' population in the EU, from 8.0% in 2020 to 9.8% in 2025 (Figure 6). Figure 6 === Number of minors aged less than 15 years in the EU by main groups of citizenship === Figure 7 presents the development in the minors' population aged less than 15 years in the EU having either an EU citizenship different from the EU country where they reside or a non-EU citizenship (including stateless). In both cases, an upward trend was visible from 2020 to 2025, but the total growth of minors being non-EU citizens (+25.3%) was notably higher than for minors being EU citizens (+2.7%). On 1 January 2025, the number of non-EU citizen minors was more than twice (2.6) the number of EU citizen minors. Figure 7 On 1 January 2025, 71.8% non-national minors aged less than 15 years were non-EU citizens or stateless. Table 2, which provides a breakdown of the non-national resident population aged less than 15 by the main groups of citizenship for EU and EFTA countries, shows that this structure can vary greatly from one country to another. In Belgium and Luxembourg, the majority of non-national minors were having a citizenship of another EU country. In Cyprus, the Netherlands, Austria and Slovakia, the share of minors with another EU country citizenship in the total number of non-national minors was higher than 40%. In eight countries (Bulgaria, Estonia, Greece, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania and Slovenia) this share was lower than 10%. [[Image:T2_Non-national_resident_population_aged_less_than_15_by_main_groups_of_citizenship,_EU,_1_January_2025_v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Non-national resident population aged less than 15 by main groups of citizenship, EU, 1 January 2025
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1750c654-6206-4836-af4c-444b1b0a93dd?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-26T07:09:10Z migr_pop1ctz])|alt= Table showing breakdown by main group of citizenship of children aged less than 15 years and who do not have citizenship of their country of residence in EU, individual EU and EFTA countries as of 1 January 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 8 presents the corresponding share of minors aged less than 15 years in the total population by main groups of citizenship on 1 January 2025. At EU level, 14.4% of the national residents were aged less than 15 years, whereas 14.5% of non-national residents were aged less than 15 years. Concerning the share of minors in the non-national populations, 12.7% were EU citizens, 15.3% non-EU citizens, 15.9% stateless and 54.3% with an unknown citizenship. The share of minors in the national population was higher than in non-national population in 21 EU countries (in particular in Latvia, Slovakia, Estonia and Ireland), while the share of minors in the non-national population with EU citizenship was higher than that for non-EU citizen minors in only 3 EU countries (Latvia, Cyprus and Malta). Figure 8 Table 3 provides some indicators on the trend in the resident population of non-national minors aged less than 15 years in the EU and EFTA countries over the period 2020-2025. Among the 11 EU countries where the share of non-nationals in the population aged less than 15 years is higher than 10%, this share increased the most in Malta (+5.0 pp), Cyprus (+4.2 pp) and Ireland (+4.0 pp). In all 3 countries, this increasing share of non-national minors was mainly explained by the increasing share of minor non-EU citizens. At the EU level, the annual average growth rates show opposing trends between national and non-national minors, with a decrease of 1.6% for national minors and an increase of 3.4% for non-national minors. The difference in growth rates between EU and non-EU minors is 4.1 pp, with EU minors growing by 0.5% and non-EU minors by 4.6%. [[Image:T3_Share_of_non-national_resident_population_aged_less_than_15_in_the_total_resident_population_aged_less_than_15_v3.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Share of non-national resident population aged less than 15 in the total resident population aged less than 15 as of 1 January 2025, and average growth rate by main groups of citizenship, 2020-2025
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/426a1b35-aa33-4783-9516-6ab9a0250a55?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-26T07:10:25Z migr_pop1ctz])|alt= Table showing share in the resident population of children aged less than 15 years as of 1 January 2025 and average growth rate by main group of citizenship over the years 2020 to 2025 for the EU, individual EU countries and EFTA countries. For more details, see the link to the dataset below. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Immigration of minors aged less than 15 years by main groups of citizenship === Immigration of minors is one of the factors that influence the total number of non-national minors in the total population. In addition to EU-citizen minors living in an EU country different from their country of citizenship and non-EU-citizen (including stateless) minors, immigration statistics include national minors having returned to their country of citizenship. Figure 9 shows the trend from 2020 to 2024 in the immigration of minors in the EU for those three main groups of citizenship. It should be noted that the aggregate EU figures presented here do not represent the immigration flows to the EU from non-EU countries, as they also include flows between different EU countries. The sharp increase in 2022 was mainly driven by non-EU citizens and stateless persons, whose numbers jumped from 291 352 in 2021 to 927 379 in 2022. This group then declined in 2023 and 2024, but remained the largest category in 2024 (523 153). By contrast, nationals and EU citizens showed much smaller changes: both increased slightly up to 2022 and then fell in 2023 and 2024. Figure 9 Table 4 provides the breakdown by main groups of citizenship for available EU and EFTA countries in 2024. At EU level, most immigrant minors in the EU were non-EU citizens (66.4% of all immigrant minors in 2024). In Germany, Spain, France and Italy the level of immigration of minors was higher than 50 000. In all those countries, the share of non-EU-citizen and stateless immigrant minors was over 50%, with the highest value recorded for Germany (75.8%). By contrast, a share of nationals higher than 50% of the total minors' immigration was observed in Latvia, Lithuania, Romania and Slovakia. [[Image:T4_Immigrants_aged_less_than_15_by_main_groups_of_citizenship,_2024_v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 4: Immigrants aged less than 15 by main groups of citizenship, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/aad32c81-6bd1-45c5-8379-ac133d0e0138?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-26T07:12:32Z migr_imm1ctz])|alt= Table showing immigration of children aged less than 15 years in 2024 as the total number and percentages broken down by main groups of citizenship for the EU, individual EU countries and EFTA countries. For more details, see the link to the dataset below. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 10 illustrates the proportion of minors under 15 within the total immigration figures in the EU, categorised by citizenship group. In 2024, at the EU level, the share of immigrant minors was highest among nationals (15.4% of all immigrant nationals), compared to non-EU citizens (14.2% of all non-EU immigrants), and lowest among EU citizen minors moving to a different EU country (10.8% of all EU citizen immigrants).
Figure 10 === Live births by mother's citizenship === The number of births of non-national children is another factor influencing the share of non-national children in the total population of resident children. Table 5, which gives the number of live births by citizenship of mother in 2024, provides an indicator to measure this phenomenon. In absolute terms, 147 953 children were born from a mother with an EU citizenship living in an EU country different from her country of citizenship and 517 383 were born from a non-EU citizen mother, including stateless mothers. Even if not all new-born children automatically receive their mother's citizenship, this data highlights the importance of considering births in the analysis of child migration. Table 5 shows that at EU level, the yearly average growth rate of the total number of births (-3.3%) was negative between 2020 and 2024. The rate was negative for the number of live births recorded for mothers with national citizenship (-4.1%) and for mothers with another EU citizenship (-5.0%) whereas it was positive for mothers with a non-EU citizenship (+2.0%). [[Image:T5_Live_births_by_mother’s_main_groups_of_citizenship_in_2024_v3.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 5: Live births by mother’s main groups of citizenship in 2024, and average growth rate by main groups of citizenship, 2020-2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/dc167bf6-0eb3-421a-aa8d-cf680aee7662?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-26T07:14:40Z demo_faczc])|alt= Table showing live births by mother’s citizenship as total number in 2024 and average growth rate over the years 2020-2024 for the EU, individual EU countries and EFTA countries. For more details, see the link to the dataset below. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Acquisition of citizenship === Figure 11 shows the shares of minors aged less than 15 years who acquired a citizenship of an EU country in the total number of acquisitions of citizenships, disaggregated by the previous country of citizenship. In 2024, this share was equal to 19.6% for minors previously citizens of another EU country and 23.8% for minors previously citizens of a non-EU country. Figure 11 The share of minors who acquired EU citizenship varies greatly from one EU country to another. In 2024, the share of minors previously citizens of another EU country who acquired an EU citizenship in the total of acquisitions of citizenship was higher than the EU average in 7 EU countries, with the highest share observed for Latvia (80.4%). The share of minors previously citizens of a non-EU country was equal or higher than the EU average in 7 EU countries, with 2 highest shares recorded in France (35.6%) and Greece (31.4%). === Source data for tables === *[[Media:Children_in_migration_tables_edition2026_v4.xlsx|Children in migration - tables]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === This article presents European statistics on minors in migration based on international migration flows, the number of national and non-national residents in the population (stocks) as well as data relating to live births by citizenship of mother and acquisitions of citizenship. It focuses mainly on flows and stocks of foreign and stateless minors broken down by EU and non-EU citizens. Data are collected on an annual basis and are supplied to [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] by the national statistical authorities of the EU and EFTA countries. Information on data reliability, series breaks, differing definitions and flags can be consulted in the online datasets. '''Legal sources''' Since 2008, migration and international protection data have been collected based on [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32007R0862 Regulation (EC) No 862/2007]. The analysis and composition of the EU, EFTA and candidate countries as of 1 January of the reference year are given in [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32010R0351 Commission Regulation (EC) No 351/2010]. This defines a core set of statistics on international migration flows, population stocks of foreigners, the acquisition of citizenship, residence permits, asylum and measures against illegal entry and stay. Although EU countries may continue to use any appropriate data sources according to national availability and practice, the statistics collected under the Regulation (EC) No 862/2007 must be based on common definitions and concepts. Most EU countries base their statistics on [[Glossary:administrative data|administrative data]] sources such as population registers, registers of foreigners, registers of residence or work permits, health insurance registers and tax registers. Some countries use mirror statistics, sample surveys or estimation methods to produce migration statistics. The implementation of the Regulation is expected to result in increased availability and comparability of migration statistics.
As stated in Article 2.1(a), (b) and (c) of Regulation (EC) No 862/2007, immigrants who have been residing (or who are expected to reside) in the territory of an EU country for '''a period of at least 12 months''' are counted in immigration statistics. Whereas emigrants living abroad for more than 12 months are counted in emigration statistics. Data collected by Eurostat concern migration for a period of 12 months or longer. Therefore, migrants include people who have migrated to the country for a period of one year or more as well as persons who have migrated on a permanent basis. Eurostat collects data on acquisitions of citizenship under the provisions of Article 3.1(d) of Regulation (EC) No 862/2007, which states that 'Member States shall supply to the Commission (Eurostat) statistics on the numbers of (…) '''persons having their usual residence in the territory of the Member State''' and having acquired during the reference year the citizenship of the Member State (…) disaggregated by (…) the former citizenship of the persons concerned and by whether the person was formerly stateless'.
'''Definitions:''' '''Non-national category''' includes the following categories: EU citizens (excluding the reporting country), non-EU citizens, stateless and unknown. '''Age:''' There are 2 ways of recording age: ''Age reached'': number of complete years lived at the end of the calendar year in question. Under this age concept, a person born in 1951 will be 52 on each day of the calendar year 2003, irrespective of his or her birthday. ''Age completed'': number of completed years lived at most recent birthday.
'''Methodological notes:''' For migration flows, data presented in this article refer to age reached for all EU countries with the exception of Germany (2020-2023 data), Estonia (2022 data), Ireland, Greece, Spain (2022 and 2023 data), Lithuania (2023 and 2024 data), Malta, Austria, Romania and Slovenia. In these countries data is by age completed. For acquisitions of citizenship, data presented in this article refer to age reached for all EU countries with the exception of Germany, Ireland, Greece, France, Lithuania, Malta, Austria, Romania and Slovenia. In these countries, data is by age completed. '''Portugal did not transmit population data by country of citizenship for 1 January 2025 and immigration data for 2024. The EU aggregates were estimated using Portugal’s corresponding data from 1 January 2024 for population data and corresponding data from 2023 for immigration data.''' [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/14916382/15042455/Guidance+on+the+inclusion+of+refugees+from+Ukraine+who+benefit+from+temporary+protection+in+the+EU+in+the+usually+resident+population.pdf/6582f6ec-02af-1d40-06b2-d32ff4bf7d9b?t=1674548136616 Guidance on the inclusion of refugees from Ukraine who benefit from temporary protection in the EU in the usually resident population]: persons from Ukraine granted [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52022PC0091&qid=1646384923837 temporary protection] should be counted as part of the usually resident population. Based on this, those who arrived from Ukraine and were granted temporary protection during the year – and who are believed to still be present at the end of the year – should be counted as immigrants during the year and as part of the migrant stock at the end of the reference period. For the reference year 2024, Poland and Slovakia did not include refugees from Ukraine who benefit from temporary protection in their population and migration statistics. For the reference year 2023, Poland, Slovakia, Sweden and Liechtenstein did not include refugees from Ukraine who benefit from temporary protection in their population and migration statistics. For the reference year 2022, Bulgaria, Poland, Slovakia, Finland, Sweden, Liechtenstein and Switzerland did not include refugees from Ukraine who benefit from temporary protection in their population and migration statistics. There are some limitations in data comparability, as definitions and coverage can vary across countries. Namely, the recommended population definition is the usually resident population; however, in default, registered or legal population definitions may also be used. Immigration is defined as the action by which a person establishes his or her usual residence in a country for a period that is or is expected to be of at least 12 months, having previously been resident in another country. Coverage of asylum seekers and refugees from Ukraine who benefit from temporary protection, as well as hard-to-reach groups or immigrants who have not registered their arrival, may also differ between countries. Data sources can also vary between countries, and estimation methods may be employed. For more detailed information, please refer to the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/migr_immi_esms.htm Eurostat International Migration Statistics Metadata] and the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/demo_pop_esms.htm Eurostat Population Metadata]. === Context: EU migration policy === In recent years, the number of children in migration arriving in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union]], many of whom are unaccompanied, has increased in a dramatic way, particularly due to migration crisis in 2015-2016, and recently in 2022 due to the war in Ukraine.
Protecting minors is first and foremost about upholding European values of respect for human rights, dignity and solidarity. This is why protecting all children in migration, regardless of status and at all stages of migration, is a priority. The European Union, together with its Member States and with the support of the relevant EU agencies (European Border and Coast Guard Agency; European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) and the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights (FRA)), has been active on this front for many years. The existing EU policies and legislation provide a solid framework for the protection of the rights of the child in migration covering all aspects including reception conditions, the treatment of their applications and integration.
The protection of children in migration starts by addressing the root causes which lead so many of them to embark on perilous journeys to Europe. This means addressing the persistence of violent and often protracted conflicts, forced displacement, inequalities in living standards, limited economic opportunities and access to basic services by making sustained efforts to eradicate poverty and deprivation and develop integrated child protection systems in non-EU countries. The European Union and its Member States have stepped up their efforts to establish a comprehensive external policy framework to reinforce cooperation with partner countries in mainstreaming child protection at the global, regional and bilateral level. The European Union is fully committed to implement the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which calls for a world in which every child grows up free from violence and exploitation, has his/her rights protected and access to quality education and healthcare. The 2015 Valletta Summithttps://www.consilium.europa.eu/media/21839/action_plan_en.pdf political declaration and its Action Plan calls for the prevention of and fight against irregular migration, migrant smuggling and trafficking in human beings (with a specific focus on women and children).
The [https://www.eeas.europa.eu/sites/default/files/10_hr_guidelines_protection_en.pdf EU Guidelines on the Promotion and Protection of the Rights of the Child] renew the EU's commitment to promote and protect the indivisibility of the rights of the child in its relations with non-EU countries, including countries of origin or transit. In this context, the Council reaffirmed the need to protect all refugee and migrant children, regardless of their status, and give primary consideration at all times to the best interests of the child, including unaccompanied children and those separated from their families, in full compliance with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and its Optional Protocols.
Within the [[Glossary:European_Commission_(EC)|European Commission]], the [https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/migration-and-home-affairs_en Directorate-General for Migration and Home Affairs] is responsible for immigration policy, whereas the [https://ec.europa.eu/info/departments/justice-and-consumers_en Directorate-General for Justice and Consumers] is in charge of child policy. All relevant legal acts and information regarding the EU's immigration policy can be accessed on the [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/new-pact-migration-and-asylum_en European Commission's website]. Readers interested in the recent development of the global immigration policy in the European Union are also invited to consult the [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en pact on migration and asylum] that entered into force in June 2024 and will enter into application in June 2026. The Pact on Migration and Asylum underlines that the EU asylum and migration management system needs to provide for the special needs of vulnerable groups, including children. In particular, the reform of EU rules on asylum and return is an opportunity to strengthen safeguards and protection standards under EU law for migrant children with the following goals: * The right for the child to be heard in the context of asylum and migration proceedings. * Unaccompanied minors should be appointed a guardian within 15 working days. * Unaccompanied minors and families with children under 12 years to be exempted from the mandatory border procedure. * Develop effective alternatives to detention for children and their families. * Rules on evidence required for family reunification simplified. * The right to adequate accommodation and assistance, prompt and non-discriminatory access to education, and early access to integration services, will be reinforced.
