title: City statistics – nomenclature of territorial units
text:
<pdftheme>1</pdftheme>

<updatedata>
Planned article update: 5 November 2024
</updatedata>

<highlight>

The aim of this chapter is to provide information on the new coding and labelling system for city statistics, which will replace the current one in the Eurostat's database in 2020.

In 2017, the Regulation (EC) No 1059/2003 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 May 2003 on the establishment of a common nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS) was amended to include a number of territorial typologies: including cities and Functional Urban Areas (FUAs) (the city plus its commuting zone). The {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R1130:EN:NOT|title=Commission Implementing Regulation (Tercet) (EU) 1130/2019}} of 2 July 2019 is providing the uniform conditions for the harmonised application of territorial typologies pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 1059/2003 of the European Parliament and of the Council (NUTS). 

The new principles for coding and labelling of the spatial units used for city data collection are designed to facilitate the data collection at city level using the legally recognised territorial typologies.

This article forms part of [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]’s [[City_statistics_manual|City statistics manual]].

</highlight>


<articlecontent>

<sesection>
=== General principles  ===

* The statistical unit to be classified are the urban territories built up from Local Administrative Units (LAUs) following the TERCET Regulation, namely: Functional Urban Areas and Cities.
* In some cases, the urban centre stretches far beyond the boundaries of the central municipality and 'Greater cities' are defined. This shall be transparent from the labelling. The 'Greater cities' will be the default city level. Cities that are components of greater cities will be no longer part of the data collection as “stand alone” cities.
* The classification and coding shall allow to group areas that are characterised by certain common properties: all cities in a country; all capital cities.
* The classification and coding shall allow the running of certain algorithms. These algorithms shall be able to process information summarised in the code to produce relevant information.
* It shall be possible to easily calculate the population of all cities within a country without double counting.
* The classification and coding shall provide the opportunity to implement changes (adding, modifying or removing a city). 
* The classification and coding shall be defined in a way that favours stability. Preferably, code changes shall be an exception. In the case of a modification of the underlying territorial entity (city or FUA), codes will persist but data will be flagged with ‘break in time series’.

These new principles allow for the grouping of all cities in a country without double-counting and also for all capital cities in Europe. It will be transparent from the labelling that Madrid (greater city) is not identical to the municipality of Madrid. Further improvement is that the concepts of cities and FUAs will be reflected in the coding in a consistent way. The new classification and coding provide the opportunity to implement changes (adding, modifying or removing a city. 

</sesection>

<sesection>
=== New coding  ===

* CCxxxF		Functional Urban Area (FUA)
* CCxxxC		City/Greater City

Where:

* CC is the country code
* xxx is a running number;
* The same running number (xxx) indicates that the City is included in the FUA. However, a FUA can include multiple Cities so not all Cities within a FUA will have the same running number; all Cities shall have a FUA. If a city has no commuting zone than the FUA is identical to the city.
* All capitals will be coded as xxx=001;
* Cities which are bigger than the municipality will be labelled as 'greater';

</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Main changes  ===

* The FUAs will receive 'F' instead of 'L' in order to avoid unnecessary reference to the old Larger Urban Zone concept;  
* 'K' will be no longer used in the coding (K indicated Kernel; this concept is no longer used); 
* The numbering will be updated to remove holes and the 500 codes; 
* Cities which are components of greater cities will be no longer part of the data collection; 
* Codes will remain stable. Changes will be stored in an attribute table, which might for instance be joined with the LAU list. In case of changes to the city boundaries with more than 1 % population moving, data will be flagged with "break in series (b)"; 
* The version code will be dropped. 

</sesection>


<sesection>
=== Examples of new and old codes in the classification:  ===

[[Image:Table 1 Examples of new and old codes in the classification.png |thumb|centre|500px]]

</sesection>

<sesection>
=== History of the coding  ===

The collection of statistics for cities - the so-called “Urban Audit” - started two decades ago. The ultimate goal was to contribute to improving the quality of urban life by: 

* supporting the exchange of information between cities; 
* helping to identify best practices; 
* facilitating benchmarking across the EU; 
* providing information on the dynamics within the cities and between cities and their surrounding areas. 

Within the Urban Audit, cities were previously referred to as ‘core cities’ and ‘kernels’ - now called cities and Greater cities, while FUAs were previously referred to as ‘larger urban zones’. In the past, the coding was adjusted and extended according to the changing scope and needs of the data collection and it became partly inconsistent and non-transparent to users. For instance: 

* Most capitals have the 'running number' 001, but not all (for example NL002C2 Greater Amsterdam). 
* Some cities were taken over from the former 'Large City Audit' list. The Large City Audit was executed between 2007 and 2011. It included all, at that time, 'non Urban Audit' cities with more than 100 000 inhabitants. For these cities, the running number of the code starts with 5. DE502C1 Mannheim is an example.
* The version numbers (the last digit of the city and FUA code) indicate very well that changes occurred in the boundaries; however, they do not give information on the time when the change happened. This hinders the swift production of map layers since the information on LAU boundaries of which year are to be used to build the City/FUA is missing.
* Kernels have been suppressed; however, some codes still use the letter 'K'.
* The Greater Cities are used together with the Cities, which can lead to double counting. For instance, data on the municipality of Barcelona and the Greater city of Barcelona are in the same dataset.
* The former 'Larger Urban Zones' have been redefined and renamed and are now called 'Functional Urban Areas'.  However, their code still uses the letter 'L'.

</sesection>


</articlecontent>

title: City statistics – social conditions
text:
1EU city statistics for living conditions; Subchapter 2.4 of Eurostat’s manual on city statistics. Last updated: 5 November 2024. This subchapter on living conditions is 1 of 9 thematic subchapters that provide a comprehensive glossary of variable definitions used within city statistics. The glossary is designed to ensure a clear understanding and interpretation of data disseminated by Eurostat, thereby improving the clarity of data requirements for the providers of these statistics in national statistical offices, while supporting the standardisation of statistical concepts across Europe. This subchapter forms part of Eurostat’s ''[[City_statistics_manual|City statistics manual]]''. ===Private households by composition=== [[Image:Private households by composition_CSM2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 10: Private households by composition|alt=A table showing variables from the city statistics data collection. Variables are presented for the composition of private households, identifying the number and types of private households and the size of the population living in them. The table shows a list of variable codes, their labels and measurement units. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32017R0543 Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/543 on population and housing censuses regarding the technical specifications of the topics and their breakdowns] provides 2 different definitions for the count of the '''number of private households (excluding institutional households) (DE3001V)''' *under the '''housekeeping concept''', a private household is defined as either **a '''1-person household''' – this refers to a person who lives alone in a separate housing unit or who occupies, as a lodger, a separate room (or rooms) in a housing unit but doesn’t join with any other occupants to form a multiperson household **a '''multiperson household''' – this refers to a group of 2 or more people who share the whole or part of a housing unit and provide themselves with food and possibly other essentials for living; the members of a group may pool their incomes to varying extents *under the '''household-dwelling concept''', all the people living in a housing unit are considered members of the same household; therefore, the number of occupied housing units is equal to the number of households, and their locations are identical. According to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/543, whenever possible, the ‘housekeeping concept’ should be preferred for identifying private households. This is because it provides a more detailed and nuanced understanding of household composition by considering actual living arrangements and resource-sharing practices among individuals. This method allows for a clearer distinction between 1-person households and multiperson households based on their living and economic arrangements, which can be crucial for certain types of socio-economic analysis. In city statistics, the household-dwelling concept is preferred. This is due to a reliance on administrative data for the production of statistics on cities and functional urban areas. Administrative records, such as those from housing registers, often list all occupants of a housing unit collectively, making it more straightforward to apply the household-dwelling concept. Data are collected for the following types of private household. *The '''number of 1-person households (DE3002V)'''. *The '''number of lone parent private households (with children aged less than 18 years) (DE3005V)''' – a 1-family household with only 1 adult and at least 1 child aged less than 18 years; the adult isn’t necessarily a biological parent, rather they are an adult of the family nucleus. *The '''number of lone pensioner (above retirement age) households (DE3008V)''' – a single-person household where that person has retired from work and has typically reached the national retirement age; as the national retirement age varies across EU countries, the emphasis is on the fact that these people won’t work anymore. Only people who have worked earlier are included, so people who never worked, for example, due to a handicap, and/or those receiving unemployment benefits aren’t included. People who supplement their pension with earnings from other sources (short-term tasks or others) should be included within this category. *The '''number of households with children aged less than 18 years (DE3011V)''' – a private household (either a 1-family household or a household with 2 or more families) with 1 or more adults (aged over 18 years) and at least 1 child (aged less than 18 years). *The '''number of people living in private households (excluding institutional households) (DE3017V)''' – a count of the number of individuals who reside in a private housing unit. ===Housing=== [[Image:Housing_CSM2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 11: Housing|alt=A table showing variables from the city statistics data collection. Variables are presented for housing, identifying the number of and different types of dwellings, their average area and average price. The table shows a list of variable codes, their labels and measurement units. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] The '''number of conventional dwellings (SA1001V)''' is a count of the number of structurally separate and independent dwellings at fixed locations designed for permanent human habitation. At the reference date, these conventional dwellings may be used as a residence, vacant, or reserved for seasonal or secondary use. ‘Separate’ means the premises are surrounded by walls and covered by a roof or ceiling, allowing 1 or more persons to isolate themselves. ’Independent’ means having direct access from a street, staircase, passage, gallery or grounds. Occupied conventional dwellings are those which are the usual residence of 1 or more persons at the time of the census. The '''number of empty conventional dwellings (SA1025V)''' refers to conventional dwellings that aren’t the usual residence of any person at the time of the census. These include dwellings reserved for seasonal or secondary use, vacant dwellings and conventional dwellings with people present but not included in the census. Dwellings may be classified by type of building where they are placed. Different types of buildings/housing and their characteristics are defined by the ''[https://unece.org/DAM/stats/publications/2015/ECECES41_EN.pdf Conference of European Statisticians – Recommendations for the 2020 Censuses of Population and Housing]'' (New York and Geneva, 2015). A building is any independent structure containing 1 or more dwellings, rooms, or spaces, covered by a roof and enclosed by external or dividing walls extending from the foundations to the roof. Buildings may serve various purposes, such as residential, agricultural, commercial, industrial, cultural or service-oriented. Examples include detached houses, apartment buildings, factories, shops, warehouses, garages and barns. Residential buildings are categorised as follows. *The '''number of houses (SA1004V)''', disaggregated into **detached houses – a standalone house not attached to any other buildings **detached houses with 1 dwelling – a single dwelling unit **detached houses with 2 dwellings – 2 separate units, 1 above the other **semi-detached houses – 2 attached dwellings **row (or terraced) houses – at least 3 attached or connected dwellings, each with separate access to the outside. *The '''number of apartment buildings (SA1005V)''', which may be located in **apartment buildings with 3–9 dwellings **apartment buildings with 10 or more dwellings. An apartment is defined as a dwelling within an apartment building. Note: if a house contains more than 1 dwelling, these units shouldn’t be classified as apartments. As noted above, in the context of social statistics a '''household''' is defined as a housekeeping unit or, operationally, as a social unit *having common arrangements *sharing household expenses or daily needs *in a shared common residence. As such, a household includes either 1 person living alone or a group of people, not necessarily related, living at the same address with common housekeeping. In other words, sharing at least 1 meal per day or sharing a living/sitting room. By contrast, collective households or institutional households include, for example, hospitals, old people’s homes, residential homes, prisons, military barracks, religious institutions, boarding houses, workers’ hostels and so on. There are 4 specific indicators in the data collection that cover households *the '''number of households living in houses (SA1007V)''' – a count of private households residing in houses *the '''number of households living in apartments (SA1008V)''' – a count of private households residing in apartments *the '''number of households owning their own dwelling (SA1011V) ''' – a count of private households that own the dwelling in which they reside *the '''number of households living in private rented dwellings (SA1013V)''' – a count of private households that live in dwellings which are rented. The '''average area of living accommodation (SA1022V)''' is measured as the interior floor space within the outer walls of occupied dwellings, expressed in square metres per person (m²/person). It excludes non-habitable areas like cellars and attics, as well as shared spaces in multi-unit buildings. Alternatively, data providers may choose to measure the total area of rooms inside a dwelling. A ’room’ is defined as an enclosed space within the dwelling, with walls reaching from the floor to the ceiling (or roof) and must be at least 2 metres high (over most of its area). A room must also be large enough to fit a bed for an adult, with a minimum size of 4 square metres. Rooms that meet these criteria include bedrooms, dining rooms, living rooms, habitable cellars or attics, servant’s quarters and kitchens. However, smaller kitchens (less than 4 square metres), verandas, utility rooms (like boiler or laundry rooms), lobbies, bathrooms and toilets aren’t counted as rooms. Additionally, rooms without windows, such as some cellars are typically excluded, unless they are used for domestic purposes (for example, large lobbies with functional use or windowless internal bedrooms). The '''average annual rent for housing (SA1049V)''' is defined within the ''[https://unstats.un.org/unsd/classifications/unsdclassifications/COICOP_2018_-_pre-edited_white_cover_version_-_2018-12-26.pdf classification of individual consumption according to purpose (COICOP)]'' as Group 04.1, ‘actual rentals for housing’, as paid by tenants during the reference year. This amount, expressed in euro per square metre (€/m²) includes the amount paid to the landlord, irrespective of any social benefits the tenant receives from public authorities, even if such payments go directly to the landlord at the tenant’s discretion. Rentals typically cover *the use of the land on which the property stands *the dwelling occupied *fixtures and fittings for heating, plumbing, lighting, and so on *furniture, in the case of a furnished dwelling *the use of a garage for parking in connection with the dwelling (the garage doesn’t need to be physically attached to the dwelling, nor leased from the same landlord). Rentals don’t include *payment for garages or parking spaces not used in connection with the dwelling (COICOP Class 07.2.4). *charges for water supply (04.4.1), refuse collection (04.4.2) and sewerage collection (04.4.3) *co-proprietor charges in multi-occupied buildings for services like caretaking, gardening, stairwell cleaning, heating, lighting, maintenance of lifts and refuse disposal chutes (04.4.4) *charges for electricity (04.5.1) and gas (04.5.2) *charges for heating and hot water supplied by district heating plants (04.5.5). The average price for buying a house is defined as the average buying price for all houses sold during the reference year, in euros (€). This includes both new and existing houses, be they terraced, semi-detached or detached houses. Prices for new houses should include VAT, while for existing houses transfer taxes should be excluded. Real estate agency fees are excluded in all cases. Since most houses come with attached parcels of land (often in the form of a garden), and the separation of land price isn’t typically recorded, any land involved in transactions for buying a house should be included in the average price. The '''average price for buying a house (SA1050V)''' concerns the overall price for the property in euro (€), while the '''average price for buying a house relative to its area (SA1052V)''' provides a measure of average property costs relative to their size, expressed in euro per square metre (€/m²). The average price for buying an apartment is defined as the average buying price for all apartments sold during the reference year, in euros (€). This includes both new and existing apartments. Prices for new apartments should include VAT, while for existing apartments, transfer taxes should be excluded. Real estate agency fees are excluded in all cases. If newly built apartments are sold with a parcel of land (often in the form of a garden), any land involved in transactions for buying an apartment should be included in the average price. The '''average price for buying an apartment (SA0151V)''' concerns the overall price for the dwelling in euro (€), while the '''average price for buying an apartment relative to its area (SA1053V)''' provides a measure of average property costs relative to their size, expressed in euro per square metre (€/m²). Note: there are 2 ways to collect house/apartment prices *the average price for transacted dwellings (houses/apartments) during the reference year (which is generally easier), or *the average price for the stock of dwellings.
'''Legislation in force and other documents''' *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32008R0763 Regulation (EC) No 763/2008 on population and housing censuses] *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32017R0543 Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/543 on population and housing censuses as regards the technical specifications of the topics and of their breakdowns]

title: Climate-related taxes
text:
Insert short description for search engines Data extracted in October 2025 Planned article update: 17 September 2026 Revenue from carbon dioxide related taxes, including from the EU Emissions Trading Scheme, has increased strongly in the EU in recent years, reaching more than €50 billion in 2023. The revenue from energy taxes in the EU amounted to €261 billion in 2023 or 1.5% of the EU gross domestic product (GDP). However, this represented the lowest share of GDP since 2008. [[Image:Revenue from carbon dioxide (CO2) related taxes, EU, 2017-2023 (billion €, current prices).png|Revenue from carbon dioxide (CO2) related taxes, EU, 2017-2023 (billion €, current prices)|800px]]
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/716d6be7-a5b8-4c84-86d9-0ecdd3da51f7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-23T14:01:59Z env_ac_taxind2]
[[Glossary:Climate-related_taxes|Climate-related taxes]] are an important policy instrument used by the EU and its Member States to meet the Union’s long-term targets for reducing [[Glossary:Greenhouse_gas_(GHG)|greenhouse gas (GHG)]] emissions and limiting global warming in line with the Paris Agreement. These taxes, by placing levies on goods and services whose production or use generate greenhouse gas emissions, aim to make polluting activities more expensive and therefore encourage businesses and consumers to reduce their carbon footprints. They can be applied directly to emissions or the carbon content of [[Glossary:Fossil_fuel|fossil fuels]], or indirectly through taxes on energy products or motor vehicles. This article is a part of the Eurostat online publication [[Statistics_on_climate_change_mitigation|Statistics on climate change mitigation]]. It presents an overview of climate-related taxes in the EU by focusing on 2 types of taxes reported as part of Eurostat’s data collection on [[Glossary:Environmental_tax|environmental taxes]] – energy and transport taxes. These two types of taxes account for the bulk of environmental tax revenue in the EU, contributing to about 95% of total environmental tax revenue in 2023, with energy taxes alone accounting for more than 75%. === What are climate-related taxes? === Mitigating climate change and limiting global warming in line with the Paris Agreement requires significant reductions in [[Glossary:Greenhouse_gas_(GHG)|greenhouse gas (GHG)]] emissions. To this end, the EU has committed to cut net GHG emissions by at least 55% compared with emissions produced in 1990, and to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050. To meet these targets, EU governments can use a range of policy instruments to steer the necessary emission reductions and support [[Glossary:Climate_change_mitigation|mitigating climate change]]. Mitigation policies can take the form of market-based (fiscal) instruments and non-market-based instruments (such as regulation or information) that incentivise behavioural change and drive significant transformations in carbon-intensive sectors: *Market-based (fiscal) instruments refer to direct monetary transactions that make environmentally undesirable behaviour more expensive, for example through taxes or emissions trading, or that promote environmentally desirable behaviour, for example through environmentally beneficial tax incentives, subsidies or [[Investments_in_climate_change_mitigation|investment]]. *Non-market-based instruments seek to guide production or consumption decisions towards low-carbon alternatives through legal obligations (i.e. regulation), non-monetary incentives, enhanced information or enabling conditions (for example, public transport infrastructure). Figure 1 provides an overview of the policy instruments for mitigating climate change. [[Image:Overview of climate change mitigation policy instruments.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Overview of climate change mitigation policy instruments
''Source:'' Adapted from [https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2778/343194 European Commission, Directorate-General for Taxation and Customs Union and ECORYS (2021), Taxation in support of green transition – An overview and assessment of existing tax practices to reduce greenhouse gas emissions – Final report, Luxembourg: Publications Office of the European Union]|alt=A hierarchical chart showing an overview of the policy instruments available related to climate change mitigation. For more details please use the link below the image.]] Environmental taxes are an important price-based instrument and have already been promoted for several decades as a key instrument of environmental policy. By increasing the cost of individual environmentally harmful activities, environmental taxes aim to internalise negative impacts stemming from individual consumption behaviour and production activities. Governments consequently use these taxes to cope with negative externalities that are not reflected in market prices. A [[Glossary:Climate-related_taxes|climate-related tax]] is an environmental tax on activities, goods or services that negatively contribute to climate change. Such a tax is specifically designed to encourage behaviours that reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. In this article, the tax categories considered as climate-related include the following: *'''Energy taxes''' are taxes on energy production and on energy products used for both transport and stationary purposes. They include '''carbon dioxide (CO2) taxes''', which are levied on the carbon content of fossil fuels. Government revenues from the auctioning of emissions permits under the '''EU Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS)''' are included as a subset of CO2 taxes. *'''Transport taxes''' include taxes related to the ownership and use of motor vehicles as well as taxes on other transport equipment and related transport services. The data reported here refer to environmental tax revenue collected by governments and payable by the different economic agents. While climate-related taxes such as energy taxes, carbon taxes or emissions trading systems can generate substantial revenues in the short and medium term, these revenue streams are expected to decline in the long term as the transition to a low-carbon economy progresses and emissions decrease. '''Climate-related taxes account for around 95% of environmental tax revenue in most economic activities''' Energy and transport taxes account for the bulk of [[Glossary:Environmental_tax|environmental tax]] revenue in the EU. In 2023, these climate-related taxes contributed to about 95% of total environmental tax revenue, with energy taxes alone accounting for more than 75%. In comparison, taxes on pollution and resources play a relatively minor role. This pattern holds true when looking at environmental tax revenue from different [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|economic activities]] and from [[Glossary:Household_sector|households]] (see Figure 2). Resource taxes play a certain role in mining and quarrying, while pollution taxes made up about 20% of environmental tax revenue in water supply and sewerage in 2023. In all other economic sectors and for households, climate-related taxes (energy and transport) accounted for about 95%. In electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply (hereinafter referred to as ‘electricity and gas supply’), almost all environmental taxes are energy taxes. The share of transport taxes is highest for households and in the services sector, accounting for more than 20% of all environmental tax revenue. Notably, the share of transport taxes was just above 10% in the transportation and storage sector. This is because taxes on fuels (such as petrol and diesel) are counted under energy taxes rather than under transport taxes (see the sections on ‘Energy taxes’ and on ‘Transport taxes’ below for an overview of the respective tax bases). Figure 2 The remainder of this article focuses on energy and transport taxes as climate-related taxes. For an analysis of all environmental tax data collected by Eurostat (including pollution and resource taxes), see the article on [[Environmental_tax_statistics|Environmental tax statistics]]. === Energy taxes === Energy taxes are the primary source of environmental tax revenue in the EU, accounting for about three-quarters of total environmental tax revenue. Energy taxes are levied on energy products for both transport and stationary purposes. They also include taxes levied on the carbon content of fossil fuels (CO2 related taxes) and proceeds from the auctioning of emission allowances under the EU Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS). In 2023, the revenue from energy taxes in the EU amounted to €261 billion. However, putting this figure in relation to other economic data reveals that it only represented 1.5% of the EU gross domestic product (GDP) and 3.8% of the EU total government revenue from taxes and social contributions in 2023. These values are the lowest shares recorded since 2008 and show that in recent years energy tax revenue has been growing more slowly than GDP and the revenue from other taxes. In 2023, corporations contributed slightly more than half (53%) of energy taxes, while households contributed 44%. Within economic producers, companies from the service sector (including wholesale and retail trade) contributed most (15% of total tax revenue), followed by companies from the manufacturing and the transportation and storage sectors (12% each). Figure 3 shows the breakdown of energy tax revenue by payer for the EU; data for individual countries can be selected via the respective drop-down option. Figure 3 In most EU countries corporations contributed more than half of energy taxes in 2023. There were only 3 countries (France, Slovenia and Denmark) where households contributed more than 50%. In a further 3 countries (Luxembourg, Malta and Austria), non-residents contributed a relatively large share of energy taxes. In Luxembourg, non-residents contributed even more than 50% in 2023, likely due to cross-border fuel sales. '''Energy tax revenue relative to gross value added''' In 2023, corporations paid €139 billion in energy taxes in the EU, which corresponded to 0.9% of the [[Glossary:Gross_value_added|gross value added]] (GVA) generated by them. The share of energy taxes in GVA is highest for electricity and gas supply and transportation and storage (see Figure 4). The tax-to-GVA ratio has increased strongly for electricity and gas supply in recent years, peaking at almost 8% of GVA in 2022 before falling back to 5% in 2023. For transportation and storage, the share had remained at around 5% between 2008 and 2021, only to fall to around 4% in 2022 and 2023. In other sectors, the tax share was below 3% of GVA in 2022 and 2023. Despite being the sector contributing most to energy tax revenue, the services sector had the lowest tax share, at 0.4% of GVA in 2023. This is due to the sector’s large GVA, which in 2023 was twice as high as all other sectors combined. Figure 4 === Carbon dioxide related taxes === Carbon dioxide (CO2) related taxes or carbon taxes are levied on the carbon content of fossil fuels. While overall energy taxes increase the price of energy products, CO2 taxes must have a clear tax base linked to the carbon content, which makes this type of tax distinct compared with other energy taxes. A CO2 tax consequently provides an incentive to use a fuel with a lower carbon content. CO2 taxes are regarded as a borderline case between energy and pollution taxes. However, given that they are levied on energy products and have usually been introduced as a substitute for other energy taxes, they are recorded as energy taxes in EU statistics. Several countries have already introduced a carbon tax, which ranges from less than €1 per tonne of carbon in Poland to more than €110 in Sweden, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland (for details, see the World Bank’s ‘[https://carbonpricingdashboard.worldbank.org/ State and Trends of Carbon Pricing Dashboard]’). Apart from country-specific levies, EU CO2 taxes also cover government revenue from the auction of emission permits under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), which is recorded by all EU countries. Between 2017 and 2023, the revenue from CO2 related taxes increased strongly in the EU, growing from €15 billion in 2017 to more than €50 billion in 2023 (see Figure 5). This means that while CO2 related taxes accounted for only 6% of energy taxes in 2017, their share increased to almost 20% in 2023. During the same period, the EU’s [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fb299379-1540-400d-b19c-94168a251c93?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-27T14:07:12Z carbon emissions from economic producers and households] fell by 18.6%, from 3.4 billion tonnes in 2017 to 2.7 billion tonnes in 2023. This highlights the increasing importance of this kind of tax and also reflects the increasing revenue from the EU ETS. For an analysis of ETS revenue, see the article on [[Environmental_tax_statistics|Environmental tax statistics]]. Figure 5 === Estimating effective carbon rates === [[Glossary:Climate-related_taxes|Climate-related taxes]] ultimately aim to reduce carbon emissions by making environmentally undesirable behaviour more expensive. Putting taxes (measured in euro) in relation to emissions (measured in tonnes) allows to monitor how expensive emissions actually are. It also sheds light on the converse tax reliefs that governments may grant to certain economic actors or products (e.g. some types of fossil fuel). The [[Glossary:effective carbon rate|effective carbon rate]] (ECR) is a prominent metric in this regard, measuring the price on carbon emissions arising from the sum of taxes and tradeable permits, expressed per tonne of carbon dioxide (CO2). The ECR is also good for comparing carbon prices across countries and sectors. Eurostat – in close cooperation with national statistical institutes – is exploring the centralised production of comparable ECR data for European countries.A preliminary proxy of ECR can be derived by dividing energy taxes from Eurostat’s data on environmental taxes by economic activity by carbon dioxide emissions from Eurostat’s air emissions accounts. Some further adjustments are necessary (please see ECR methodology under ‘data sources’). The preliminary analysis of EU ECR focuses on households and the most relevant economic sectors – manufacturing, electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply, transportation and storage, and road transport. These activities represent roughly 60% of taxes paid and more than 80% of emissions by corporations in previous years. Data on all producers and total economy are also provided. Figure 6 shows the range of EU ECR values in the period 2019 to 2023. Overall, ECR values are higher for households than for corporations. Among corporations, ECR seem much lower for manufacturing and energy supply compared to transportation sector. Figure 6 There is no consensus on the ‘appropriate’ carbon price that should be attained in the EU or elsewhere. From an environmental perspective, and in application of the ‘[https://environment.ec.europa.eu/economy-and-finance/ensuring-polluters-pay_en polluter pays principle]’, higher carbon prices appear more appropriate, as they would disincentivise emissions or use of high-carbon fuels. From an economic perspective, however, high carbon prices may be detrimental to economic growth and investment and affect private consumption due to higher inflation (the European Central Bank has published a number of assessments of the macroeconomic implications of higher carbon prices; see the ‘External links’ section at the end of this article).
In the absence of clear carbon price objectives, indicative benchmarks can help to put ECR figures in perspective. Scenarios for modelling climate change mitigation pathways (such as those published in [https://www.nature.com/articles/nclimate2572 academic journals] and by the [https://www.ipcc.ch/sr15/chapter/chapter-2/ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]) suggest that limiting the global temperature increase to 1.5°C – as aimed for in the Paris Agreement – requires reaching net zero carbon emissions by around 2050. The World Bank’s [https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/f1439afb-82a8-5a92-b95f-0f224da85169 High-Level Commission on Carbon Pricing and Competitiveness] concluded that to meet this aim, carbon prices would need to reach between $50 and $100 per tonne of CO2 equivalent by 2030. Academic studies on carbon prices, such as a [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-020-0880-3 study on a net zero scenario for the United States], came to a similar conclusion. The [[Glossary:OECD|OECD]] refers to these 2030 benchmarks in its [https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/serials/oecd-series-on-carbon-pricing-and-energy-taxation_6f88e167.html reports on effective carbon rates], suggesting that carbon prices should be in the range of €60 and €120 per tonne of CO2 by 2030 (converted to real 2023 EUR and rounded).

Further indicative ECR benchmarks for the EU can be derived from the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) [https://www.iea.org/reports/world-energy-outlook-2022 Net Zero Emissions (NZE) by 2050 scenario], which assumes carbon prices in advanced economies rising to $250 per tonne of CO2 by 2050. Referring to the IEA’s NZE scenario, the European Central Bank (ECB) in [https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/economic-bulletin/articles/2023/html/ecb.ebart202305_01~a6ff071a65.en.html#toc6 its own assessments] assumes the average ECR in the euro area to increase to €140 per tonne of CO2 in 2030. While these indicative benchmarks can help to better gauge the magnitude of national ECR figures, their adequacy and accuracy cannot be easily assessed and depend on the year taken as a reference and the year in which the benchmark should apply.
 === Transport taxes === Transport taxes are the second-largest source of environmental tax revenue in the EU, accounting for just below 20% of the total. Transport taxes primarily consist of levies related to motor vehicle ownership and usage. In 2023, the revenue from transport taxes in the EU amounted to €64 billion, which corresponds to 0.4% of the EU’s GDP and 0.9% of the EU total government revenue from taxes and social contributions. In 2023, households paid two-thirds (67%) of transport taxes, while corporations paid 32%. Within economic producers, companies from the service sector (including wholesale and retail trade) paid the most (17% of total transport tax revenue), followed by companies from the transportation and storage sector (6%) and the manufacturing sector (5%). Figure 7 shows the breakdown of energy tax revenue by payer for the EU; data for individual countries can be selected via the respective drop-down option. Figure 7 In most EU countries households contributed more than half of transport taxes in 2023, reflecting the strong link between transport taxes and private vehicle ownership and use. Corporations shouldered more than half of transport tax revenue in only 5 countries. In 3 of them (Czechia, Estonia and Slovakia), corporations (mainly from the services sector) contributed more than two-thirds of transport tax revenue. === Data sources === The data presented in this article re collected as part of the [[Glossary:European_Environmental_Economic_Accounts|European environmental-economic accounts]]. An environmental tax is a tax whose tax base is a physical unit (or a proxy of it) of something that has a proven, specific negative impact on the environment and which is defined in the [[Glossary:European_system_of_national_and_regional_accounts|European system of accounts]] (ESA 2010) as a tax. The data presented in this article refer to [[Glossary:Environmental_taxes_by_economic_activity_(ETEA)|environmental tax revenue]] from corporations (referring to economic activities according to the [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE classification]]) and from [[Glossary:Household_sector|households]]. Eurostat collects data on environmental taxes at a detailed level, by economic activity, under [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02011R0691-20250624 Regulation (EU) 691/2011 on European environmental economic accounts]. Environmental tax revenue can be allocated according to the different economic activities paying the taxes. Eurostat collects data on environmental taxes using a categorisation by economic activity (based on the [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE Rev. 2 classification]], supplemented by information for households, non-residents and a residual category for taxes that could not be allocated). See the classification of economic activities below. Increasing revenue from environmental taxes should be interpreted with caution. The increases may be caused by the introduction of new taxes or an increase in tax rates. Alternatively, they may be linked to an increase in the tax base caused, for instance, by a higher consumption of energy products. '''Classification of economic activities''' In environmental accounts, the data are organised by economic activity, using the [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE classification]]. This arrangement makes it possible to supplement national accounts with an integrated environmental-economic analysis. The scope encompasses production by all businesses resident in a country, including those operating ships, aircraft and other transportation equipment in other countries. The NACE Rev. 2 groups used in this article are: *Agriculture, forestry and fishing — NACE Rev. 2 Section A *Mining and quarrying — NACE Rev. 2 Section B *Manufacturing — NACE Rev. 2 Section C *Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply — NACE Rev. 2 Section D *Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities — NACE Rev. 2 Section E *Construction — NACE Rev. 2 Section F *Wholesale and retail trade; repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles — NACE Rev. 2 Section G *Transportation and storage — NACE Rev. 2 Section H *Services (except wholesale and retail trade, transportation and storage) — NACE Rev. 2 Sections I to U *Total — all NACE activities More detailed data on individual economic activities such as the manufacture of chemicals (C20) or of basic metals (C24) can be accessed through the data tables specified below each graph. Environmental tax statistics also include the [[Glossary:Institutional_sector|institutional sector]] of [[Glossary:Household_sector|households]] as consumers and non-residents. An additional ‘not allocated’ category is used when it is not possible to allocate taxes to one of the categories mentioned before. '''Effective Carbon Rates – methodology''' The data used for the calculation of EU ECR stem from the European environmental accounts based on [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02011R0691-20250624 Regulation (EU) 691/2011 on European environmental economic accounts], in particular environmental taxes and air emissions (greenhouse gases). Eurostat adjusted these data to produce the ECR indicator reported in this article. The relevant taxes comprise (1) carbon-specific taxes, where the tax base relates to the carbon content of the fuel; (2) excise taxes on fossil fuels and similar (including transport fuels); and (3) payments associated with the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). The CO2 emissions are those associated with fuel combustion (but excluding emissions from biomass used as fuel). Some adjustments to the data are necessary. Taxes related to electricity and taxes on the maintenance of strategic reserves are removed. While taxes are collected by applying the [[Glossary:Territorial_principle|territorial principle]], air emissions accounts are collected based on the [[Glossary:Residence_principle|residence principle]]. The different methodologies may affect results, in particular in relation to the transportation sector. Therefore, CO2 emission data must be adjusted to the territorial principle, using information bridging the two principles to ensure consistency with taxes data. These adjustments can be done with the help of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_aibrid_r2/default/table?lang=en&category=env.env_air.env_air_aa air emissions accounts totals bridging to emission inventory totals]. This dataset includes so-called bridging items showing the differences between the national totals as derived from two internationally established approaches/methods: * Production perspective (accounts) – include air emissions emitted by economic actors and households residing in the EU. They also include emissions from international transport operated by economic actors established in the EU. * Territorial perspective (inventories) – include air emissions occurring within the borders of the EU members. They are aligned with the definition of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change UNFCCC. Below, an example of the adjustment via the bridging items, focussing on air transport: {| style="background-color: #f5faff; vertical-align: top" class="wikitable" |- | (i) || Air transport (AEA) = (iv) + (ii) - (iii) || 100 |- | (ii) || Air emissions by resident units released from use of fuel purchased abroad - air transport || 10 |- | (iii) || Air emissions by non-resident units released from use of fuel purchased on the territory - air transport || 20 |- | (iv) || Air transport (territorial) = (i) + (iii) - (ii) || 110 |} Note: Bridging items are available also for total economy, land transport, water transport (and fishing vessels). The calculation of the ECR is a key component of the broader workstream on harmful subsidies. The methodology has been developed through extensive multilateral collaboration. Progress is also advancing on the centralised computation of national ECRs. Preliminary analyses show promising results: the carbon rates derived from tax and emission data are consistent with the ones reported by countries. Further adjustments might be needed, in particular for countries heavily affected by the switch from resident to territorial emissions. === Context === In the European Union, [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02011R0691-20250624 Regulation (EU) 691/2011 on European environmental economic accounts] (including its amendments in 2014 and 2022) has established a common framework for the collection, compilation, transmission and evaluation of [[Glossary:European_Environmental_Economic_Accounts|European environmental economic accounts]], for the purpose of setting up environmental economic accounts as satellite accounts to the European System of Accounts (ESA). The environmental economic accounts in the Regulation are grouped in the following 6 modules: * [[Glossary:Air_emissions_accounts_(AEA)|Air emissions accounts]] * [[Glossary:Economy-wide_material_flow_accounts_(EW-MFA)|Economy-wide material flow accounts]] * [[Glossary:Environmental_tax|Environmental taxes]] * [[Glossary:Classification_of_environmental_protection_activities_(CEPA)|Environmental protection expenditure]] accounts * [[Glossary:Environmental_goods_and_services_sector_(EGSS)|Environmental goods and services sector (EGSS)]] accounts * [[Glossary:Physical_energy_flow_accounts_(PEFA)|Physical energy flow accounts]] More information on these modules can be found through [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/environment/overview Eurostat’s dedicated section on environment]. The most recent amendment of the Regulation - through [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202403024 Regulation (EU) 2024/3024] - introduced 3 further modules: * Forest accounts * Environmental subsidies and similar transfers accounts * Ecosystem accounts Preparing the implementation of these new modules is one of the key objectives of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/1798247/6191525/European+Strategy+for+Environmental+Accounts/ European Strategy for environmental accounts (ESEA)] for the period 2024-2028. In line with the EU’s commitment to tackling environmental challenges and becoming climate-neutral, the environmental accounts are vital for providing better information for supporting Europe's [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/competitiveness_en sustainable prosperity and competitiveness] and its [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/quality-life_en quality of life as] well as for implementing the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/environment-action-programme-2030_en 8th Environmental Action Programme] and the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/sustainable-development-goals_en Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)]. === Other articles === *[[Greenhouse_gas_emission_accounts|Greenhouse gas emission accounts]] *[[Energy_accounts|Energy accounts]] *[[Greenhouse_gas_emission_footprints|Greenhouse gas emission footprints]] *[[Investments_in_climate_change_mitigation|Investments in climate change mitigation]] *[[Environmental_tax_statistics|Environmental tax statistics]] *[[Tax_revenue_statistics|Tax revenue statistics]] *[[Environmental_accounts_-_establishing_the_links_between_the_environment_and_the_economy|Environmental accounts - establishing the links between the environment and the economy]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/explore/all/envir?lang=en&subtheme=env.env_eta&display=list&sort=category Environmental taxes] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_taxind2/default/table?lang=en Environmental taxes by economic activity (NACE Rev. 2) (env_ac_taxind2)] === Thematic section === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=environment}} Environment] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/climate-change/overview Climate change] === Publications === *{{Template:Publication|code=ks-gq-23-016|title=Environmental taxes – A statistical guide – 2024 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=ks-ra-07-015|title=NACE Rev. 2 - Statistical classification of economic activities}} === Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/environment/methodology#Environmental%20taxes%20and%20subsidies Environmental taxes and subsidies] *{{Template:Esms|code=env_ac_taxind2_esms|title=Environmental taxes by economic activity (NACE Rev. 2)}} (ESMS metadata file — env_ac_taxind2_esms) === Legislation === *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02011R0691-20250624 Regulation (EU) 691/2011 on European environmental economic accounts] === Data visualisations === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/dashboard/environmental-accounts/ Environmental accounts dashboard] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/egd-statistics/ Statistics for the European Green Deal] === External links === *[https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/serials/oecd-series-on-carbon-pricing-and-energy-taxation_6f88e167.html OECD Series on Carbon Pricing and Energy Taxation] *Analyses by the European Central Bank (ECB) on carbon prices: **[https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/economic-bulletin/focus/2024/html/ecb.ebbox202401_04~92ad3c032a.en.html Assessing the macroeconomic effects of climate change transition policies] **[https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/blog/date/2023/html/ecb.blog.230525~4a51965f26.en.html How will higher carbon prices affect growth and inflation?] **[https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/economic-bulletin/articles/2023/html/ecb.ebart202305_01~a6ff071a65.en.html The macroeconomic implications of the transition to a low-carbon economy] ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Article_name'' {{Unit|topic=X_Sustainable_development_indicators}} [[Category:Environment and energy|Climate-related taxes]] [[Category:Environment|Climate-related taxes]] [[Category:Environment -
