museums, libraries and cultural sites; photographic and other services, ECOICOP 2: 09.6)]; * [https://showvoc.op.europa.eu/#/datasets/ESTAT_European_Classification_of_Individual_Consumption_according_to_Purpose_version_2_%28ECOICOP_2%29/data?resId=http:%2F%2Fdata.europa.eu%2Fed1%2Fecoicop2%2F0971 'books' (ECOICOP 2: 09.7.1)]; * [https://showvoc.op.europa.eu/#/datasets/ESTAT_European_Classification_of_Individual_Consumption_according_to_Purpose_version_2_%28ECOICOP_2%29/data?resId=http:%2F%2Fdata.europa.eu%2Fed1%2Fecoicop2%2F1321 'jewellery and watches' (ECOICOP 2: 13.2.1)]. === HICP for cultural goods and services – trends at EU level === In 2025, among the selected cultural goods and services analysed, the HICP sub-indices showed annual price increases above the 'all-items HICP' (2.5% year-on-year) for 'jewellery and watches' (8.8%), 'newspapers and periodicals' (5.0%), 'subscriptions to audiovisual streaming services and rental of audiovisual content' (4.2%) and 'cultural services' (3.6%). Annual increases below the 'all-items HICP' were recorded for 'books' (2.2%) and 'video game computers, consoles, game applications and software' (1.1%). By contrast, the sub-indices decreased for 'cultural goods' (-0.1%) and 'equipment for the reception, recording and reproduction of sound and vision' (-5.7%). For the EU aggregate, which refers to the current composition of the EU, HICP sub-indices for the selected cultural goods and services showed distinct patterns over the period 2015–2025. The sub-indices for 'jewellery and watches' and 'newspapers and periodicals' recorded the strongest increases among the categories presented. The sub-indices for 'cultural services' and 'books' also rose steadily, with stronger growth from 2021 onwards. The opposite pattern was observed for 'equipment for the reception, recording and reproduction of sound and vision', where the sub-index followed a long-term downward trend, despite some short-term fluctuations. The detailed developments are presented in Figure 1.

[[Image:Figure_1_-_The_total_HICP_and_HICPs_for_selected_cultural_goods_and_services,_EU27,_2015-2025_(%,_annual_rate_of_change).png|thumb|centre|700px||Figure 1: The HICP all-items and HICPs for selected cultural goods and services, EU-27, 2015-2025

''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c605e821-0212-48fa-b6fd-3bae4a1f395e?lang=en prc_hicp_ainr)]|alt=a line chart with nine lines showing the harmonised indices of consumer prices for selected cultural goods and services in the EU from 2015 to 2025 as a percentage, annual rate of change. The lines show the following nine categories, HICP all-items, equipment for the reception, recording and reproduction of sound and vision, television and radio licences and fees, subscriptions to audiovisual streaming services and rental of audiovisual content, video game computers, consoles, game applications and software, hire of game software and subscription to online games, cultural goods, cultural services, books, newspapers and periodicals, jewellery and watches. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''EU data show varied price developments across selected cultural goods and services''' To analyse the evolution of prices of the selected cultural goods and services in the medium term, the 5-year [[Glossary:Annual_average_growth_rate_(AAGR)| 'annual average growth rates' (AAGR)]] are presented in Figure 2. The indices show that in the EU countries, HICP sub-indices for 'jewellery and watches' and 'newspapers and periodicals' increased faster than the 'all-items HICP' between 2020 and 2025. For this period, their average annual growth rates were 5.6% and 5.5%, respectively, compared with 4.7% for the 'all-items HICP'. Positive growth rates were also recorded for 'cultural services', 'subscriptions to audiovisual streaming services and rental of audiovisual content', 'books' and 'cultural goods', although these remained below the 'all-items HICP'. By contrast, the HICP sub-indices for 'equipment for the reception, recording and reproduction of sound and vision' and for 'video game computers, consoles, game applications and software' declined over the same period, by 3.2% and 0.6% per year on average, respectively. The lighter bars show the 2024-2025 'annual average rates of change', providing a short-term perspective on these developments. For 'jewellery and watches' and 'subscriptions to audiovisual streaming services and rental of audiovisual content', the annual increases in 2025 exceeded their respective average annual rates observed over 2020–2025, pointing to a recent acceleration in price growth. A change in direction was observed for 'video game computers, consoles, game applications and software', for which the sub-index increased in 2025 after declining over the 5-year period. The opposite pattern was observed for 'cultural goods', which recorded a slight year-on-year decline after positive average annual growth over 2020–2025. For 'equipment for the reception, recording and reproduction of sound and vision', the annual decline in 2025 was stronger than the average annual decrease recorded over the 5-year period. For the remaining sub-indices (all with positive rates of change), the annual increase observed between 2024 and 2025 was lower than the 5-year average annual growth recorded over 2020–2025 period. This points to a recent moderation in price growth compared with the 5-year average (see Figure 2).

[[Image:Figure 2 - Harmonised indices of consumer prices for selected cultural goods and services, EU27, annual average rates of change 2020-2025 and 2024-2025 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Harmonised indices of consumer prices for selected cultural goods and services, EU-27, annual average rates of change 2020-2025 and 2024-2025
(%)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cf47a7e3-0467-4b13-bff4-76e54e529333?lang=en prc_hicp_ainr)]|alt=a horizontal bar chart showing the harmonised indices of consumer prices for selected cultural goods and services in the EU for annual average rates of change from 2020 to 2025 and 2024 to 2025. The bars show the following, HICP all-items, equipment for the reception, recording and reproduction of sound and vision, television and radio licences and fees, subscriptions to audiovisual streaming services and rental of audiovisual content, video game computers, consoles, game applications and software, hire of game software and subscription to online games, cultural goods, cultural services, books, newspapers and periodicals, jewellery and watches. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== HICP for cultural goods and services – focus on countries ===
'''Strong price-index growth for 'jewellery and watches' and 'newspapers and periodicals'''' Between 2020 and 2025, the HICP sub-index for 'jewellery and watches' increased faster than the 'all-items HICP' in 22 EU countries (see Table 1). The highest 5-year annual average growth rate, exceeding 10%, were recorded in Bulgaria, Hungary and Estonia. Ireland was the only EU country where this sub-index decreased over this period, with an average annual rate of -10.3%. From 2024 to 2025, the HICP sub-index for 'jewellery and watches' increased by at least 10% in 15 EU countries. In most EU countries, the annual rates of change observed in 2024–2025 were higher than the 5-year average annual rates recorded over 2020–2025. Croatia was the only country where the short-term increase was lower than the 5-year average, while Ireland continued to record a decline, though less pronounced than over the longer period.
'Newspapers and periodicals' also showed sustained growth above the 'all-items HICP'. Between 2020 and 2025, the sub-index in this category increased faster than the 'all-items HICP' in 20 EU countries. The highest 5-year average annual rates of change for this sub-index were recorded in Romania (15.1%) and Hungary (13.5%). These two countries also recorded the largest gaps between the average annual rate for 'newspapers and periodicals' and the 'all-items HICP'. From 2024 to 2025, increases in the HICP sub-index for 'newspapers and periodicals' remained widespread, although the short-term picture was more varied; the sub-index increased by more than 10% in 5 EU countries: Romania, Hungary, Slovenia, Latvia and Estonia. Spain was the only EU country where this sub-index did not increase. In 12 EU countries, the 2024–2025 annual rate of change was higher than the 2020–2025 average. At the same time, for the EU countries, the latest annual increase was slightly lower than the 5-year average, pointing to a modest moderation in price growth for this category.
Between 2020 and 2025, the HICP sub-index for 'cultural services' increased in all EU countries, but its 5-year annual average growth rate remained below the 'all-items HICP' in 15 of them. The fastest increases were recorded in Hungary (10.5%) and Czechia (10.3%). From 2024 to 2025, this sub-index increased faster than the 'all-items HICP' in 21 EU countries. The highest annual increases were recorded in Croatia (10.1%), followed by Estonia (9.8%), Hungary (9.5%) and Slovakia (9.4%).
'''Audiovisual content subscriptions and rentals: 2024-2025 annual increase exceeded the 5-year average in most EU countries''' The HICP sub-index for 'subscriptions to audiovisual streaming services and rental of audiovisual content' showed stronger growth in the short term than over the 5-year average. Between 2020 and 2025, this sub-index increased in 21 of the 24 EU countries for which data were available. However, the increase exceeded the headline HICP in only two countries: Denmark (by 1.7 percentage points), and Finland, (by 0.7 percentage points). Negative 5-year average annual rates were recorded in Croatia (-0.2%) and Slovakia (-10.4%), while the sub-index remained unchanged in Luxembourg. From 2024 to 2025, the sub-index for audiovisual content subscriptions and rentals increased in 23 of the 25 EU countries for which data were available and rose faster than the 'all-items HICP' in 19 of them. Annual increases of more than 5% were recorded in 13 EU countries, with the highest rates observed in Romania (20.3%), Portugal (15.1%) and Greece (12.8%). By contrast, the sub-index remained unchanged in Bulgaria and decreased in Czechia (-2.1%).
In 2025, the annual average price index for 'books' was lower than in 2020 in two EU countries. The decline in book prices between these years was most noticeable in Ireland, where the index recorded an average decrease of 4.1% per year. Over that 5-year period, average book price rates rose faster than the headline inflation rate in 3 EU countries – Croatia, Malta and Sweden. From 2024 to 2025, average book price rate grew faster than the headline inflation rate in 12 EU countries, increased at a slower pace than inflation in 12 EU countries, and declined in 3 EU countries (Ireland: -6.7%, the Netherlands: -4.9% and Bulgaria: -4.7%).
Between 2020 and 2025, the HICP sub-index for 'cultural goods' increased in 20 of the 24 EU countries for which data were available, but in almost all of them its average annual rate of change remained below the 'all-items HICP'. Ireland was the only EU country where this sub-index increased faster than the 'all-items HICP'. The highest 5-year average annual increases were recorded in Hungary (8.1%), Ireland (5.7%) and Poland (5.0%), while decreases were observed in France (-0.2%), Belgium (-0.4%), Greece (-0.5%), and Finland (-1.1%). From 2024 to 2025, developments became more mixed, with the sub-index increasing in 15 of the 24 EU countries and decreasing in nine, resulting in a slight decline at EU countries' aggregate level (-0.1%). The strongest annual increases were observed in Ireland (14.7%) and Sweden (9.6%), while the largest decreases were recorded in Poland and Finland (both -3.4%), followed by France (-2.8%).
The HICP sub-index for 'video game computers, consoles, game applications and software' increased in 15 of the 26 EU countries for which data were available over the period 2020–2025, and in 17 EU countries from 2024 to 2025. In both periods, Czechia recorded the highest increase (20.4% on average per year over 2020–2025 and 17.0% from 2024 to 2025). Among the remaining EU countries, the highest increases were much lower: 5.1% in Poland over 2020–2025 and 7.7% in the Netherlands from 2024 to 2025. The only two-digit annual decline was observed in Ireland (-11.6%) in the short-term comparison from 2024 to 2025.
'''Price indices for sound and vision equipment declined in most EU countries''' Country-level developments for the HICP sub-index for 'equipment for the reception, recording and reproduction of sound and vision' were consistent with the downward pattern observed at EU countries' aggregate level. Over the period 2020–2025, average annual increases were recorded only in Czechia (3.5%), Romania (1.9%), Finland (1.8%) and Austria (1.0%), while the sub-index remained unchanged in Hungary and the Netherlands. Declines were recorded in the remaining 21 EU countries, with the strongest 5-year average annual decreases observed in Belgium (-11.8%), Bulgaria (-9.9%), Luxembourg (-8.6%) and Italy (-7.7%). From 2024 to 2025, decreases became even more widespread, with the sub-index falling in 24 EU countries. The only increases were recorded in Finland (3.8%), Malta (2.8%) and Romania (1.1%). Two-digit annual declines were observed in Bulgaria (-13.5%) and Belgium (-14.7%).

=== Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Consumer prices of cultural goods and services 2026 - tables and figures.xlsx|title=HICP - Price developments for cultural goods and services: tables and figures}} === Coverage and data sources === Eurostat disseminates data on price developments using the [[Glossary:Harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)|harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)]]. The HICP provides a comparable measure of inflation for EU Member States and across different goods and services. It measures changes over time in the prices of consumer goods and services acquired by households. In other words, they are consumer price indices calculated according to a harmonised methodology and common definitions laid down in EU law. The HICP index reference period has been updated to 2025 = 100. This means that index values are expressed relative to 2025, while annual rates of change describe price developments between consecutive periods. '''The HICP under ECOICOP version 2''' For the classification of goods and services, the HICP is based on the European Classification of Individual Consumption by Purpose (ECOICOP). From 2026 onwards, HICP data are compiled and disseminated according to the new version of this classification, ECOICOP version 2, which is aligned with the Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose 2018 (COICOP 2018) developed by the United Nations Statistics Division. HICP series under ECOICOP version 2 are available and cover the period from 1996 to 2025. It also contributes to well-being, social cohesion and inclusion. The cultural and creative sectors provide a stimulus for economic growth, job creation and international trade. The EU has initiated the [https://culture.ec.europa.eu/creative-europe Creative Europe programme] aalongside several policy actions within the EU Work Plan for Culture 2023-2026. The work plan, adopted by EU culture ministers in December 2022, sets out 4 main priorities for European cooperation in cultural policymaking: * Artists and cultural professionals: empowering the cultural and creative sectors. * Culture for the people: enhancing cultural participation and the role of culture in society. * Culture for the planet: unleashing the power of culture. * Culture for co-creative partnerships: strengthening the cultural dimension of EU external relations. Producing reliable, comparable and up-to-date cultural statistics, which provide a basis for sound cultural policymaking, is a cross-sectoral priority for the European Commission. Eurostat compiles culture statistics from various data collections to provide policymakers and other users of statistics with information on the main developments in culture, covering areas like title: Consumer prices of recreational and sporting goods and services
text:
Data on EU price developments for sports goods and services Data extracted in May 2026 Planned article update: May 2027 After years of moderate price increases, the annual average rate of change for prices of ‘recreational and sporting services’ in the EU rose by 5% in 2022, accelerating further by 6.5% in 2023 and 4.8% in 2024, still remaining high at 4.1% in 2025. The harmonised index of consumer prices for ‘sporting, camping and open-air recreation equipment’ was negative in 2025 at EU level (-0.7%) for the first time since 2019. This article gives an overview of how prices of recreational and sporting goods and services have changed based on the [[Glossary:Harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)|harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)]].
In addition to the headline inflation aggerate, the 'all-items HICP', there are around 400 sub-indices for different goods and services. The article focuses on two categories and four sub-categories which are directly related to sport: *[https://showvoc.op.europa.eu/#/datasets/ESTAT_European_Classification_of_Individual_Consumption_according_to_Purpose_version_2_%28ECOICOP_2%29/data?resId=http:%2F%2Fdata.europa.eu%2Fed1%2Fecoicop2%2F0922 Sporting, camping and open-air recreation equipment (ECOICOP 2 09.2.2)]; **[https://showvoc.op.europa.eu/#/datasets/ESTAT_European_Classification_of_Individual_Consumption_according_to_Purpose_version_2_%28ECOICOP_2%29/data?resId=http:%2F%2Fdata.europa.eu%2Fed1%2Fecoicop2%2F09221 sporting equipment (ECOICOP 2 09.2.2.1)]; **[https://showvoc.op.europa.eu/#/datasets/ESTAT_European_Classification_of_Individual_Consumption_according_to_Purpose_version_2_%28ECOICOP_2%29/data?resId=http:%2F%2Fdata.europa.eu%2Fed1%2Fecoicop2%2F09222 camping and open-air recreation equipment (ECOICOP 2 09.2.2.2)]; *[https://showvoc.op.europa.eu/#/datasets/ESTAT_European_Classification_of_Individual_Consumption_according_to_Purpose_version_2_%28ECOICOP_2%29/data?resId=http:%2F%2Fdata.europa.eu%2Fed1%2Fecoicop2%2F0946 recreational and sporting services (ECOICOP 2 09.4.6)]; **[https://showvoc.op.europa.eu/#/datasets/ESTAT_European_Classification_of_Individual_Consumption_according_to_Purpose_version_2_%28ECOICOP_2%29/data?resId=http:%2F%2Fdata.europa.eu%2Fed1%2Fecoicop2%2F09462 services associated with the practice of sports (ECOICOP 2 09.4.6.2)]; **[https://showvoc.op.europa.eu/#/datasets/ESTAT_European_Classification_of_Individual_Consumption_according_to_Purpose_version_2_%28ECOICOP_2%29/data?resId=http:%2F%2Fdata.europa.eu%2Fed1%2Fecoicop2%2F09463 services associated with attendance at sporting events (ECOICOP 2 09.4.6.3)].
===HICP for sporting goods and services – trends at EU level=== In 2025, the annual average rate of change for the HICP sub-index for ’recreational and sporting services’ in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] was 4.1%, which was 1.6 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] higher than for the all-items HICP (2.5%). If before 2022 this sub-index had values around 2% at European level, starting from that year higher values were recorded: 5% in 2022, a peak of 6.5% in 2023 and 4.8% in 2024 (see Figure 1).
The sub-index for ‘sporting, camping and open-air recreation equipment’ was -0.7% in 2025. Similarly to the ‘recreational and sporting services’, this index increased at a much faster pace from 2022 onwards, peaking at 3.8% in 2022 and remaining at 3.5% in 2023. In 2024, however, the annual average rate of change for this class returned to its previous values, dropping to 1% in 2024.
[[Image:Figure 1 - The all-items HICP and the HICPs for sporting goods and services, EU-27, 2015-2025_(%, annual rate of change)_.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: The all-item HICP and the HICPs for sporting goods and services, EU-27, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/prc_hicp_ainr__custom_19969820/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=c02c127f-4532-42e5-bf9f-fdcff0a1b5bb&c=1770193555805 prc_hicp_ainr])|alt=line chart with three lines showing the harmonised indices of consumer prices for selected sporting goods and services in the EU from 2015 to 2025 as a percentage of annual rate of change. The lines show equipment for sport, camping and open air recreational, all items HICP, and recreational and sporting services. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
In the mid-term perspective, the [[Glossary:Annual_average_growth_rate_(AAGR)|annual average growth rate]] shows that prices for ‘services associated with the practice of sports’ and ‘services associated with attendance at sporting events’ rose on average from 2020 to 2025 by 4.5% and 4.8%, respectively, in the EU. The indices for the same period were lower for ‘camping and open-air recreation equipment’ and ‘sporting equipment’, 3% and 1.5%, respectively (see Figure 2). Prices increased faster between 2024 and 2025 than they did on average between 2020 and 2025 for 'services associated with attendance at sporting events’ (5.3%). The rate of change for 2025 compared to 2024 was slower for ‘services associated with the practice of sports’ (3.7% compared to 4.5% of the 2020-2025 period). Conversely, the 2024-2025 annual average rate of change was negative for ‘camping and open-air recreation equipment’ and ‘sporting equipment’ (-0.2% and -0.8%, respectively).
[[Image:Harmonised indices of consumer prices for selected sporting goods and services, EU-27, annual average rates of change 2020-2025 and 2024-2025 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Harmonised indices of consumer prices for selected sporting goods and services, EU-27, annual average rates of change 2020-2025 and 2024-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/prc_hicp_ainr__custom_19970310/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=a9ce38f6-c7be-44b2-8f83-20d7c48edc29&c=1770195085273 prc_hicp_ainr])|alt=a double horizontal bar chart showing harmonised indices of consumer prices for selected sporting goods and services in the EU. The bars show annual average rates of change from 2020 to 2025 and from 2024 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===HICP for sporting goods and services – focus on countries=== All EU countries recorded an increase in the all-items HICP in 2025 compared to 2020. In 15 EU countries, the 2020-2025 HICP annual average growth rate was below the EU average of 4.7%, with the smallest increase seen in Finland (3.3%), Denmark, France and Malta (3.4%). Between 2024 and 2025, the rate of change of the all-items HICP was 2.5% in the EU, with 10 countries experiencing lower inflation rates during this period.
Between 2020 and 2025, the annual average growth rate for ’sporting equipment’ was positive but lower than the all-items HICP in 16 countries and stable at 0% in Greece. During this period the sub-index fell in 5 EU countries, with a negative peak in Portugal (-5.7%). An increase in the period 2020 to 2025 for ’camping and open-air recreation equipment’ was observed in 18 EU countries (data were not available for 6 countries). In the same period, average prices for this category rose faster than the all-items HICP only in Romania. From 2024 to 2025 the price index for this category of goods decreased in 12 EU countries for which data are available.
Between 2024 and 2025, prices for ‘services associated with the practice of sports’ and ‘services associated with attendance at sporting events’ increased in all EU countries where data were available, with the exception of Slovenia (-0.2% for ‘services associated with the practice of sports’). The biggest increases were recorded in Bulgaria (11.2%) for ‘services associated with the practice of sports’ and in Croatia (37.7%) for ’services associated with attendance at sporting events’.
[[Image:Table 1 - The all-items HICP and the HICPs for sporting goods and services, annual average rates of change 2020-2025 and 2024-2025 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: The all-items HICP and the HICPs for sporting goods and services, annual average rates of change 2020-2025 and 2024-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/prc_hicp_ainr__custom_19986843/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=ea01369a-d851-4dc7-b673-5c1ff15d725d&c=1770278175402 prc_hicp_ainr]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/prc_hicp_ainr__custom_19986861/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=458d5804-1515-4045-91df-eb279833e0c3&c=1770278268397 prc_hicp_ainr])|alt=a harmonised indices of consumer prices for selected sporting goods and services, annual average rates of change from 2020 to 2025 and from 2024 to 2025 in EU Member States, some EFTA countries, some candidate countries and one potential candidate. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=HICP - Price development for sporting goods and services 2026.xlsx|title=HICP - Price development for sporting goods and services: tables and figures}}
=== Coverage and data sources === Eurostat disseminates data on price developments using the [[Glossary:Harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)|harmonised indices of consumer prices (HICPs)]]. The HICP provides a comparable measure of inflation for EU Member States and across different goods and services. It measures changes over time in the prices of consumer goods and services acquired by households. In other words, they are consumer price indices calculated according to a harmonised methodology and common definitions laid down in EU law. The HICP index reference period has been updated to 2025 = 100. This means that index values are expressed relative to 2025, while annual rates of change describe price developments between consecutive periods. '''The HICP under ECOICOP version 2''' For the classification of goods and services, the HICP is based on the European Classification of Individual Consumption by Purpose (ECOICOP). From 2026 onwards, HICP data are compiled and disseminated according to the new version of this classification, ECOICOP version 2, which is aligned with the Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose 2018 (COICOP 2018) developed by the United Nations Statistics Division. HICP series under ECOICOP version 2 are available and cover the period from 1996 to 2025. '''ECOICOP 2 codes relevant for sport statistics''' Goods and services related to sport, present in the ECOICP 2 classification, include: *'''sporting equipment:''': ** gymnastic, physical education and sporting equipment, such as balls, shuttlecocks, nets, rackets, bats, skis, golf clubs, discuses and javelins; ** parachutes, paragliders and other skydiving equipment; ** firearms and ammunition, other weapons, and body armour for hunting, sport and personal protection ** fishing rods and other fishing equipment; ** skateboards, kickboards, smart balance wheels and hover boards * walking sticks and canes for recreational purposes (e.g., hiking and tracking); ** game-specific footwear (ski boots, football boots, golfing shoes and other such footwear fitted with ice skates, rollers, spikes, studs, etc.); ** game-specific sportswear (ski suits, etc.); ** protective sports headgear; ** other protective sports gear, such as life jackets, boxing gloves, sport gloves, body padding, shin guards, goggles, belts, supports. *'''Camping and open-air recreation equipment:''': ** equipment for beach and open-air games, such as bowls, croquet, flying disc games, and volleyball and inflatable boats, rafts and swimming pools; ** tents, sleeping bags, backpacks for camping, air mattresses, inflating pumps, camping stoves and gas, barbecues and other camping accessories; ** Global Positioning System (GPS) (satellite-based radionavigation positioning) equipment for boating and hiking. *'''Services associated with the practice of sports:''': ** recreational and sporting services provided at skating rinks, swimming pools, golf courses, gymnasiums, fitness centres, tennis courts, squash courts, bowling alleys and shooting ranges; ** ski slopes, ski lifts and the like; ** cable-car and chairlift transport at ski resorts and holiday centres; ** out-of-school lessons, as provided to individuals and groups, in aerobics, skating, skiing, swimming and other sports; ** sports club and fitness centre memberships fees; ** boating-related navigational aid services; ** sports competition participation fees; ** fees for sports title and sports category certificatesfees for sports title and sports category certificates; ** hunting and fishing licences; ** paid fishing; ** fees for membership in fishermen’s and hunters’ clubs. *'''Services associated with attendance at sporting events''': **– admission tickets to live sporting events, such as football games, hockey games, ice-skating competitions, ski competitions, soccer games, tennis matches, horse-racing, motor-racing, track cycling (at velodromes) and so on. ===Context=== The multiannual work programme ([https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-9771-2024-INIT/en/pdf EU Work plan for Sport for 2024-2027]), agreed by the EU Council, sets the priorities and principles for cooperation on sport between the European Commission and the Member States. Several expert groups have been set up to achieve concrete results. Among them, the Expert Group on the Economic Dimension of Sport (XG ECO) and the Expert Group on Health-Enhancing Physical Activity (XG HEPA) play a key role in implementing evidence-based policies in the sports sector. XG ECO, for example, has developed an economic definition of sport ('[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/6921402/0/Vilnius+Definition+Sport+CPA2008+official+2013_09_19.pdf Vilnius definition]'), and made progress towards developing Sport [[Glossary:Satellite account|Satellite Accounts]] in some EU countries. XG HEPA is working on implementing the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52013PC0603&from=EN Council recommendations on physical activity] adopted in 2013. These include a monitoring framework with indicators both for the level of physical activity and for policies to promote physical activity in EU countries. Eurostat comparable data on international trade, employment in sport, participation in sporting activities, etc. make a valuable contribution to the monitoring and development of the EU's policies in this area. ===Other articles=== *[[Employment in sport]] *[[International trade in sporting goods]] *[[Enterprises in the sports sector]] *[[Household expenditure on sporting goods and services]] *[[Sport participation - practicing sport and physical activity]] *[[Sport participation - attending live sporting events]] *[[HICP methodology]] (background article) *[[Culture]] (all Statistics title: Contingent liabilities and non-performing loans - statistics
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of contingent liabilities and non-performing loans - statistics for the EU and the member states. Data extracted in January 2026 Next planned article update: January 2027 In 2024, the Netherlands, Finland, and Italy recorded the highest rates of government guarantees in the EU. In 2024, EU countries with largest liabilities of public corporations outside general government were Germany, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. [[Image: Government guarantees in the EU 2024_v2.jpg|centre|thumb|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/10f11bdd-6919-4548-847a-7909fac0ef2c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-30T09:53:09Z (gov_cl_guar)]|alt= The vertical bar chart shows government guarantees as percentage of GDP in individual EU Member States for the year 2024. Each country column has three stacks representing central government, state government and local government. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article presents data on [[Glossary:government|government]] [[Glossary:guarantees|guarantees]], [[Glossary:Liability|liabilities ]] of government-controlled entities (public corporations) classified outside general government, and liabilities related to off-balance public-private partnerships (PPPs). Similarly, the article also includes data on government non-performing loans (NPLs, assets), which could imply a loss for governments if these loans are not repaid. The dataset constitutes contingent liabilities which are only potential liabilities, that may become actual government liabilities under certain conditions. These data add further transparency to the public finances in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union]] by providing a more comprehensive picture of potential impacts on [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|Member States]]' financial positions. === Overview of contingent liabilities === Contingent liabilities data include 4 main indicators which are typically measured as percent of GDP: # government guarantees, the most common type of contingent liabilities # liabilities of government-controlled entities (public corporations) classified outside general government # liabilities related to off-balance public-private partnerships (PPPs), where off-balance means that these liabilities are not recorded on the government balance sheets # government non-performing loans (NPLs, assets). Furthermore, government guarantees could be split into one-off ad-hoc guarantees and standardised guarantees. Standardised guarantees are those guarantees that provide coverage for similar types of credit risk in a large number of typically smaller size contracts. For standardised guarantees, it is generally not possible to precisely estimate the default risk of each individual guaranteed claim. However, it is feasible to predict the number of defaults among a large pool of such loans. Moreover, public corporations classified outside the government are divided into non-financial and financial public corporations. '''These 4 indicators are independent of each other and may overlap'''. For example, the debt of a public corporation classified outside of government may be guaranteed by the government. In this case, the same amount will appear under both indicators (i) government guarantees, and (ii) liabilities of public corporations classified outside government. The table below presents a summary of contingent liabilities data reported to Eurostat: [[Image:Total_general_government_contingent_liabilities_new.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Total general government contingent liabilities and non-performing loans in the EU Member States, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/10f11bdd-6919-4548-847a-7909fac0ef2c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-30T09:53:09Z (gov_cl_guar)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1588d3fd-f5fd-4570-9409-7a5e3267a390?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-30T10:10:11Z (gov_cl_ppp)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6bf8a463-407b-45c3-9a46-a2593dfbe131?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-30T09:56:46Z (gov_cl_liab)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ddd0ef4e-ae37-4bc1-ae65-fc769bd712a0?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-30T09:57:39Z (gov_cl_npl)]|alt= Table showing total general government contingent liabilities and non-performing loans as percentage of GDP in individual EU Member States for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In several countries, a significant portion of [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0a5599f7-0406-4863-8c26-7b01770efa2b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-23T09:15:55Z guarantees is provided to financial institutions] – particularly in Finland, Greece, Luxembourg, Hungary, France and Belgium. These guarantees were often granted in the context of either the COVID-19 crisis or the 2008-09 financial crisis. During the COVID-19 crisis, many of these guarantees were issued through standardized guarantee programs, which involved a large number of similar, relatively small-scale guarantees, such as those for loans to small and medium-sized enterprises. Further explanations can be found in the [https://s-circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/ca7c9cc4-b473-4abc-8e95-263dcd57d79d/library/848dd989-d79a-49d4-9136-0cae1428f92f/details country-specific notes] on guarantees section below. === The highest rates of government guarantees in the EU were recorded in the Netherlands, Finland and Italy === The most common form of contingent liabilities in the EU countries is government guarantees on the liabilities, and occasionally, on the assets of third parties. In 2021, these guarantees saw a significant increase across the EU, driven by the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, as seen in the graph below. In 2022, the level of government guarantees was further influenced by the ensuing energy crisis, following the Russian aggression against Ukraine. In 2024, there was a decrease of guarantees in most of the EU countries. The highest rates of government guarantees were recorded in the Netherlands (31.0% of [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|GDP]]), Finland (17.0%), Italy (14.6%), Germany (13.6%) and Hungary (13.0%). On the lower end of the scale, rates of less than 1% of GDP were recorded in Ireland, Czechia and Bulgaria. [[Image: Government guarantees, total from 2021 to 2024_upd.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Government guarantees, total from 2021 to 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/10f11bdd-6919-4548-847a-7909fac0ef2c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-30T09:53:09Z (gov_cl_guar)]|alt= Vertical bar chart showing government guarantees total as percentage of GDP in individual EU countries. Each country has four columns representing the years 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
In most EU countries, the central government is the predominant guarantor. A notable level of local government guarantees can be seen in Finland, Sweden, France and Denmark. ===Liabilities of public corporations were the highest in Germany=== In 2024, liabilities of public corporations were highest in Germany. The level of liabilities of public corporations classified outside general government varied widely among the EU countries. Significant amounts of liabilities were recorded in Germany (84.4%), ahead of the Netherlands (73.1%), Luxembourg (65%) and France (61.9%). By contrast, small amounts of public corporation liabilities were recorded in Slovakia (3.4%), Spain (4.3%), Cyprus (7.3%) and Romania (8.7%). The high level of liabilities in certain EU countries is primarily due to the data including liabilities of public banks controlled by government. Most of these liabilities consist of deposits held by households or by other private or public entities. Generally, financial institutions have significantly higher debt liabilities compared with non-financial corporations. At the same time, these institutions have also significant amounts of financial assets, which are not captured in this data collection. [[Image:Figure 2 Liabilities of public corporations outside general government, 2024 % of GDP.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Liabilities of public corporations outside general government, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6bf8a463-407b-45c3-9a46-a2593dfbe131?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-30T09:56:46Z (gov_cl_liab)]|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing liabilities of public corporations outside general government as percentage of GDP in individual EU countries Each country column has two stacks representing liabilities of units involved in financial activities and liabilities of units involved in other activities for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Highest level of non-performing loans in Cyprus=== In 2024, Cyprus remained the country with the highest stock of non-performing loans (assets) of the general government, at 9.0% of GDP, followed by Croatia and Greece, reporting a share of 0.8% and 0.6% respectively. Eurostat recommends the 'unlikely-to-pay' (UTP) loans to be considered within the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/esa2010/chapter/view/7/#h388 ESA 2010 7.101(c) definition of NPLs] and reported accordingly. Implementation of this recommendation by EU countries is still ongoing. A few EU countries are also reporting accounting provisions instead of NPLs at a nominal value, or at a 'reset' value, in case government transfers have been booked against NPL assets. Progress will continue towards harmonization of NPL reporting among EU countries. === Off-balance public-private partnerships liabilities: highest in Portugal === In 2024, liabilities related to off-balance public-private partnerships (PPPs), long-term construction contracts where assets that are recorded outside government accounts, were below 2% of GDP in all EU countries. Nine EU countries had no such liabilities. Portugal had the highest share (1.2% of GDP), followed by Slovakia (1.0%) and Latvia (0.6%). These PPP liabilities are predominantly due to motorway projects. In many EU countries, off-balance PPPs were observed at both the central and local government levels. In addition, a few federal countries, like Belgium, Spain and Austria, also had off-balance PPPs related to state governments. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Contingent liabilities and non-performing loans - tables and figures 01 2026.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === Implementation guidance is provided in the [https://s-circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/ca7c9cc4-b473-4abc-8e95-263dcd57d79d/library/76ab3116-fc1f-4606-8ffb-521c81633162/details Eurostat decision of 22 July 2013] on Supplement on contingent liabilities and potential obligations to the EDP related questionnaire. Annex 1 to the Decision contains 2 questionnaire forms, the supplement to the EDP related questionnaire on contingent liabilities and potential obligations and the questionnaire on government-controlled units classified outside general government. The questionnaires need to be completed by EU Member States' statistical authorities and transmitted to Eurostat annually before 31 December (T+12 months), whereas this publication is being made 1 month after Member State data are transmitted to Eurostat (i.e. T+13 months). The metadata clarifying the completeness, definitions, use of estimations or timeliness of the data are to be provided to Eurostat alongside the above questionnaire forms. '''Main data indicators:''' '''Guarantees''' are arrangements whereby the guarantor undertakes to a lender that if a borrower defaults, the guarantor will make good the loss the lender would otherwise suffer. A '''one-off guarantee''' is defined as individual, and guarantors are not able to make a reliable estimate of the risk of calls. One-off guarantees are linked to debt instruments (e.g. loans, bonds). Data refer to the total stock of debt guaranteed by government units. '''Standardised guarantees''' are guarantees that are issued in large numbers, usually for relatively smaller amounts, along identical lines. It is not possible to estimate precisely the risk of each loan being in default but it is possible to estimate how many, out of a large number of such loans, will default. Examples are mortgage loan guarantees, student loan guarantees, etc. Data refer to the total stock of assets covered by the standardised guarantees. While the provisions for standardised guarantees are considered an actual liability, the total stock of assets covered by standardised guarantee is regarded as a contingent liability. '''Non-performing loans (NPLs, government assets)''': a loan is non-performing when payments of interest or principal are past due by 90 days or more, or interest payments equal to 90 days or more have been capitalised, refinanced, or delayed by agreement, or payments are less than 90 days overdue, but there are other good reasons (such as a debtor filing for bankruptcy) to doubt that payments will be made in full. NPL data are not exhaustive for some Member States. Further methodological guidance is being implemented in order to ensure that NPL definitions, used by different EU Member States, are aligned with the definitions of [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/esa2010/chapter/view/7/#h388 ESA 2010 7.101(c) definition of NPLs].'' '''Public-private partnerships (PPPs)''' are long-term contracts between 2 units, 1 of which is normally a corporation (or a group of corporations, private or public) called the operator or partner, and the other normally a government unit called the grantor. PPPs involve a significant capital expenditure to create or renovate fixed assets by the corporation, which then operates and manages the assets to produce and deliver services either to the government unit or to the general public on behalf of the government unit. Public-private partnership recorded off-balance sheet of government means that the assets are not considered as economically owned by government and the gross-fixed capital formation is not recorded as an expenditure of government at the moment it is incurred. '''Total outstanding liabilities related to PPPs recorded off-balance sheet of government''' are expressed as the adjusted capital value. This is an initial contractual capital value that is progressively reduced over time by the amount of "economic depreciation" which is calculated on the basis of estimates or actual data. The adjusted capital value reflects the current value of the asset at the time of reporting. The amount is deemed to reflect the gross fixed capital formation and debt impact in the case that government would have to take over the assets during the life of the contract. It is to be underlined that the above indicators have a heterogeneous nature and represent different types of potential impact on public finance. Additionally, in some cases, the same fiscal risk might be reflected by 2 or more indicators. For instance, when a government guarantees the liability of a government-controlled entity classified outside general government, the potential risks are covered both by data presented for 'Guarantees' and 'Liabilities of government-controlled entities classified outside general government'. Therefore, evaluating the total risk for public finance by summing up the indicators could overestimate the potential impact. '''Liabilities of government-controlled entities (public corporations) classified outside general government''' are defined as the stock of liabilities at the end of the year, based on the business accounts of corporations and reported either as business liabilities or as Maastricht liabilities by the Member States. These government-controlled entities are classified outside general government due to their behaviour as market units. For a better picture of the extent of liabilities depending on the sector activities, these liabilities are split into liabilities of entities involved in financial activities and entities involved in other activities. Entities involved in financial activities include units classified according to NACE Rev 2 Division 64: "Financial service activities, except insurance and pension funding", but excluding sub-division 6411 "National Bank"; Division 65: "Insurance, reinsurance and pension funding, except compulsory social security"; and Division 66: "Activities auxiliary to financial services and insurance activities". Entities involved in other activities refer to units performing all other activities. '''''Country-specific notes''''' Further explanations can be found in the [https://s-circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/ca7c9cc4-b473-4abc-8e95-263dcd57d79d/library/848dd989-d79a-49d4-9136-0cae1428f92f/details country-specific notes]. '''Data availability and data quality''' Regarding the data availability and data quality, 3 aspects should be taken into account: data coverage, data completeness and data comparability. '''''Data coverage and consolidation''''' The data coverage depends on the respective indicator: Data for '''government guarantees''' relate only to the guarantees provided by government to the units classified outside general government. Data for '''government guarantees''' are consolidated, except for 2 Member States (Finland and Sweden), where there might be double-counting of some guarantees. Data on guarantees do not include: 1) Government guarantees issued within the guarantee mechanism under the Framework Agreement of the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF) and the European Stability Mechanism (ESM); 2) Derivative-type guarantees meeting the ESA2010 definition of a financial derivative; 3) Deposit insurance guarantees and comparable schemes; 4) Government guarantees issued on events which occurrence is very difficult to cover via commercial insurance (earthquakes, large scale flooding, etc.). Data for '''non-performing loans''' refer to the non-performing loans provided by units included into general government (including all the institutional units which are part of the central, state and local government and social security funds) towards other units which are classified outside general government. Data for '''non-performing loans''' are consolidated for the general government. Data provided for particular sub-sectors of the general government might be not consolidated. For '''off-balance sheet PPPs''' data refer to the Private-Public Partnerships projects which are not included in the government accounts. The consolidation is not applicable for this indicator. Off-balance sheet PPPs data do not include data on off-balance sheet concession contracts, as defined in Chapter 2 of [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/ea7c19f7-9146-11e8-8bc1-01aa75ed71a1/language-en the Guide to the Statistical Treatment of PPPs]. For '''liabilities of public corporations''', data covers public corporations classified in the sectors of non-financial corporations (S.11), financial corporations (S.12), non-profit institutions serving households (S.15) and the rest of world (S.2) but which are controlled by the general government sector and with liabilities exceeding 0.01% of GDP. The data refer only to public corporations classified outside general government. The liabilities of public corporations classified inside general government are fully reflected in the government accounts. It should be noted that the data reported for liabilities of public corporations classified outside general government is not consolidated at group level, which means that part of the debt of these units could be towards entities in the same company group, which could imply that some liabilities are reported twice. However, the debt between units in the same group is not identifiable from the data reported due to the fact that, as agreed with the Member States in the framework of the 2012 Task Force, the data should be provided to Eurostat for each individual unit and not for accounts at the level of the consolidated group. In the context of the first publication of data on liabilities of government-controlled entities in February 2015, some concerns were raised regarding a possible overestimation of the liabilities due to non-consolidation. Therefore, Eurostat launched a pilot project in order to investigate the availability of consolidated data between public parent companies and their subsidiaries (intragroup consolidation) in individual Member States. Eurostat invited Member States to provide to Eurostat, on a voluntary basis, consolidated group accounts in order to assess the impact of consolidation on the figures published. Several countries are providing intragroup consolidated figures, in addition to the non-consolidated data. These consolidated data can be extracted from the same database using the dimension "gov_cl_liab" CO_NCO (Consolidated-non-consolidated). The analyses of the 2 sets of data (consolidated versus unconsolidated) corresponding to the same reference year show that for some of the countries there is no substantial impact due to non-consolidation while for some other countries there is a clear overestimation of the liabilities at non-consolidated level. '''''Data completeness''''' A lot of progress was achieved in the last years with regard to data completeness. The data is mostly exhaustive for all the indicators and all the Member States. For the Member States for which data is not fully exhaustive, e.g. data for local government is not available or some small units are not included, detailed information is included in the [https://s-circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/ca7c9cc4-b473-4abc-8e95-263dcd57d79d/library/848dd989-d79a-49d4-9136-0cae1428f92f/details country specific footnotes] which are available on Eurostat's website. The country specific footnotes provide information on the exhaustiveness of all 4 indicators. '''''Data comparability''''' Data are country specific and closely linked to the economic, financial and legal structure of the country. In some countries, governments provide more guarantees to units outside general government, while in others, this is not the case. In some Member States there are Private-Public Partnerships projects which are not included in the government accounts, while in some other countries such PPP projects do not exist at all. With regard to the liabilities of public corporations, it should be mentioned that the data collection only refers to liabilities without balancing them with the assets. This aspect is very important in the case of financial institutions, which normally have both significant amounts of assets and debt liabilities. Some Member States have more entities controlled by general government and involved in financial services than others, and therefore they report higher liabilities than those where such entities do not exist at all, or are few. Additionally, for some of the Member States, a large part of the liabilities reported by financial institutions concern deposits held by households or other public or private entities in government-controlled banks. With regard to the comparability of data for liabilities of public corporations, it should be also mentioned that, when compiling the liabilities of public corporations, the Member States could choose which concept to use for the reporting of liabilities, either business accounts or national accounts concepts. When reporting the data following the business accounts definitions, the countries included all the liabilities from the financial statements of the company, including also liabilities related to the item [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/esa2010/chapter/view/7/#h383 other accounts payable (F.8)]. A majority of countries reported the data for public corporations following the business accounts definitions. Nevertheless, a few countries (e.g. Spain, Belgium, the Netherlands and Slovakia), reported Maastricht liabilities, notably data on liabilities for items (as defined in ESA 2010): currency and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/esa2010/chapter/view/7/#h377 deposits (AF.2)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/esa2010/chapter/view/7/#h378 debt securities (AF.3)], and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/esa2010/chapter/view/7/#h379 loans (AF.4)] and excluding the item other accounts payables (AF8). Due to the above-mentioned reporting, some additional comparability limits should be also taken into account. '''Revision and timetable''' Revised data for past years are available in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/government-finance-statistics/database?node_code=gov_cl Eurostat database], along with explanatory information on revisions and/or major changes. === Context === The data on contingent liabilities and potential obligations of government are collected in the framework of the Enhanced Economic Governance package (the "six-pack") adopted in 2011. The economic governance package describes a set of European legislative measures meant to reform the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stability_and_Growth_Pact Stability and Growth Pact] and to introduce greater macroeconomic surveillance in the European Member States, in response to the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_debt_crisis European debt crisis] of 2009. In this context, the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011L0085:EN:NOT|title=Council Directive 2011/85}} amended by new {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32024L1265:EN:NOT|title=Council Directive 2024/1265}} requires the Member States to publish relevant information on contingent liabilities which could have potentially large impacts on public budgets. The data collection on contingent liabilities represents a step towards more transparency of public finances in the EU by giving a more comprehensive picture of EU Member States' financial positions. In this sense, the data on contingent liabilities includes data on the following indicators: government guarantees, liabilities related to public-private partnerships recorded off-balance sheet of government, liabilities of units controlled by government but classified outside general government (public corporations) and non-performing loans (government assets). It is to be underlined that contingent liabilities are not part of the general government (Maastricht) debt as defined in the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009R0479:EN:NOT|title=Council Regulation (EC) No 479/2009}} of 25 May 2009 on the application of the Protocol on the excessive deficit procedure annexed to the Treaty establishing the European Community. Nevertheless, the collection of data on the indicators such as government guarantees, liabilities related to public-private partnerships recorded off-balance sheet of government, liabilities of government-controlled entities classified outside general government (public corporations) and non-performing loans (government assets) gives the possibility to capture the so-called government "contingent" liabilities. Contingent liabilities are only potential liabilities and not actual liabilities of government. They can nevertheless materialise and become actual government liabilities only if certain specific conditions prevail. For example, non-performing loans show a bigger risk of non-repayment as normal loans. A significant amount of non-performing loans of government could imply a higher government exposure and a potential loss for government if these loans were not repaid by their original debtor. The collection and publication of data on the above-mentioned indicators was agreed with the EU Member States in the framework of the Task Force on the implications of the Directive on the collection and dissemination of fiscal data. In addition, the [https://s-circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/ca7c9cc4-b473-4abc-8e95-263dcd57d79d/library/76ab3116-fc1f-4606-8ffb-521c81633162/details Eurostat Decision of 22 July 2013] on the "Supplement on contingent liabilities and potential obligations to the EDP related questionnaire" provides further details on this data collection and the indicators. ===Other articles=== *[[Government finance statistics - quarterly data]] *[[Structure of government debt]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/government-finance-statistics/database Government finance statistics and EDP statistics], see: :'''Government contingent liabilities and potential obligations (gov_cl)''' ::Government guarantees (gov_cl_guar) ::Liabilities related to private-public partnerships (PPPs) recorded off-balance sheet of government (gov_cl_ppp) ::Liabilities of government-controlled entities classified outside general government (gov_cl_liab) ::Non-performing loans of government (gov_cl_npl) === Dedicated section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/government-finance-statistics/methodology/contingent-liabilities-non-performing-loans Government finance statistics - contingent liabilities] === Publications === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/DDN-20260130-1 News Item - Data on contingent liabilities and non-performing loans in the EU Member States (January 2026)] *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/ALL/?uri=CELEX:52019DC0081 The Commission Report on implicit liabilities with potential impact on public budgets (February 2019)] *[https://s-circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/ca7c9cc4-b473-4abc-8e95-263dcd57d79d/library/41ede383-f7e2-4fe6-893f-c5c8f53a99ab/details Publication of data related to the Articles 3(2) and 14(3) of the Directive 2011/85 at national level] === Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/gov_cl_esms.htm ESMS metadata file - Government contingent liabilities and potential obligations (gov_cl)] === Legislation === *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011L0085:EN:NOT|title=Council Directive 2011/85}} of 8 November 2011 on requirements for budgetary frameworks of the Member States. *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32024L1265:EN:NOT|title=Council Directive 2024/1265}} of 29 April 2024 amending Directive 2011/85/EU on requirements for budgetary frameworks of the Member States. *[https://s-circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/ca7c9cc4-b473-4abc-8e95-263dcd57d79d/library/76ab3116-fc1f-4606-8ffb-521c81633162/details Supplement on contingent liabilities and potential obligations to the EDP related questionnaire (July 2013)] {{Unit|topic=X_Excessive_deficit_procedure}} [[Category:Economy and finance|Contingent liabilities and non-performing loans - title: Continuing Vocational Training Survey (CVTS) methodology
text:
3 This article describes the methodology of the [[Glossary:Continuing_vocational_training_survey_(CVTS)|continuing vocational training survey (CVTS)]] — the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] harmonised survey on continuing [[Glossary:Vocational_training|vocational training]]. The CVTS provides comparable data on vocational training within the EU [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]] with at least 10 or more employed persons and belonging to a certain group of economic activities. The CVTS along with the following two other data collections, the [[Glossary:Adult_education_survey_(AES)|adult education survey (AES)]] and the [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)|EU labour force survey (EU-LFS)]] provide EU statistics on [[Glossary:Lifelong_learning (LLL)|lifelong learning]]. Lifelong learning is defined as an intentional search for knowledge throughout life (after the end of initial education in particular). It is aimed at improving a person’s skills and competences for personal or professional reasons. The CVTS is an EU-wide data collection on continuing vocational training carried out in enterprises. It refers to education and training activities financed totally or partially by the enterprise for their persons employed. The use of work-time and the acquisition of training equipment is also considered as financing. The following topics are covered in the CVTS data: * provision of CVT courses and other forms of CVT (training/non-training enterprises); * CVT strategies; * participants in CVT courses; * costs of CVT courses; * time spent in CVT courses; * characteristics of CVT courses; * assessment of CVT activities. On top of these topics, some information on initial vocational training is also collected through the CVTS. ===Coverage and mandate=== Six waves of the CVTS have been carried out until now with the reference years 1993, 1999, 2005, 2010, 2015 and 2020. '''CVTS 1993''' The 1993 CVTS was carried out as a pilot survey with a sample of 50 000 enterprises in all [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU Member States]] (at the time [[Glossary:EU-12|EU-12]]). The [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)]] was used to classify the business sectors covered by the survey. Agriculture, fishing, public administration, education, health and social work, activities of households and extra-territorial organisations and bodies were not included (see Table 1). The 1993 survey had limited comparability with the following rounds. Its results were disseminated through the [https://circabc.europa.eu/sd/a/93d76039-ea54-4d78-b71d-47f34872131d/CVTS1_results.pdf 1993 CVTS results] publication. '''CVTS 1999''' The following round of the CVTS took place in 1999 and covered 24 of the current [[Glossary:EU-28|EU-28]] Member States (Croatia, Cyprus, Malta and Slovakia not included and only the region of Pomorskie was surveyed in Poland). This wave of the survey was conducted based on a gentlemen’s agreement, and used the same coverage of the business sectors as the 1993 CVTS. Detailed information on this round of CVTS can be found in the [https://circabc.europa.eu/sd/a/628cacca-301b-4f0c-b1b7-e33dca9f1628/CVTS2_EUmanual.pdf 1999 CVTS Manual]. The 1999 CVTS data are available in Eurostat's online database in the tables of the ‘[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=trng_cvts trng_cvts2]’ series. Despite the guidelines of the gentlemen’s agreement, the 1999 edition of the CVTS also had limited comparability with the other rounds. '''CVTS 2005''' The 2005 CVTS covered the [[Glossary:EU-27|EU-27]] of that time and Norway. {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32005R1552:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1552/2005}} of the European Parliament and of the Council established ‘a common framework for the production of European statistics on vocational training in enterprises’, and was the legal basis for the 2005 survey. This legislation was complemented by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32006R0198:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation No 198/2006}} which sets out the specific details of the variables, sample size, transmission of the data and quality aspects of the CVTS. This third round of the survey continues to use the NACE Rev.1.1 classification for describing the economic sector of the enterprises. '''CVTS 2010''' Further legal arrangements (namely {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32010R0822:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) No 822/2010}}, amending {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32006R0198:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 198/2006}}) were the framework for the fourth round of CVTS carried out for the reference year 2010. The changes were aimed at the simplification of variables, reducing the burden on respondents, adjusting the sampling and adapting it to the NACE Rev.2 classification. The geographical coverage included 27 EU Member States (excluding Ireland) and Norway. [[Image:Continuing_vocational_training_survey_metadata_2022.png|thumb|centre|500px|Table 1: Continuing vocational training survey metadata
''Source:'' Metadata file [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/trng_cvt_esms.htm trng_cvt_esms]]] '''CVTS 2015 and 2020''' CVTS 5 was carried out in 2016 for CVT activities that took place in 2015. {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32014R1153:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) No 1153/2014}} (amending Regulation (EC) No 198/2006) provides the implementation details for CVTS 5. While the majority of variables remained unchanged compared to CVTS 4, some variables were simplified or removed in order to further reducing the burden of CVTS to the extent possible. For details see the CVTS 5 implementation manual. CVTS 6 was carried out in 2021, for the reference year 2020 and following the same requirements as CVTS 5. Detailed information on each round of the CVTS can be found in the [https://circabc.europa.eu/sd/a/a58c12f7-4370-460c-b4e3-caa92e9c06f8/LLL_Metadata_HomePage.htm complementary methodological information.] ===Basic concepts=== Continuing vocational training (CVT) consists in training measures or activities which have as their primary objectives the acquisition of new competences or the development and improvement of existing ones and which must be financed at least partly by the enterprises for their persons employed who either have a working contract or who benefit directly from their work for the enterprise such as unpaid family workers and casual workers. Persons employed holding an apprenticeship or training contract should not be taken into consideration for CVT. The training measures or activities must be planned in advance and must be organised or supported with the special goal of learning. CVT can take place on-site, online or both (blended/hybrid learning). Random learning and initial vocational training (IVT) are explicitly excluded. CVT measures and activities cover both CVT courses and other forms of CVT. '''CVT courses''' CVT courses are usually separated from the active workplace (learning takes place in locations specially assigned for learning, like a class room or training centre). They show a high degree of organisation (time, space and content) by a trainer or a training institution. The content is designed for a group of learners (e.g. a curriculum exists). Two distinct types of CVT courses are identified: internal (managed by the enterprise itself) and external CVT courses (managed by third-party organisations). '''Other forms of CVT''' Other forms of CVT are typically connected to the active work and the active workplace, but they can also include participation (instruction) in conferences, trade fairs, etc. for the purpose of learning. These other forms of CVT are often characterised by a degree of self-organisation (time, space and content) by the individual learner or by a group of learners. The content is often tailored according to the learners’ individual needs in the workplace. The following types of other forms of CVT are identified: * planned training through guided on-the-job training; * planned training through job rotation, exchanges, secondments or study visits; * planned training through participation (instruction received) in conferences, workshops, trade fairs and lectures; * planned training through participation in learning or quality circles; and * planned training through self-directed learning/e-learning. '''Training enterprises''' Training enterprises are enterprises that provided either CVT courses or other forms of CVT for their persons employed during the reference year. '''Participant in CVT courses''' A participant in CVT courses is a person who has taken part in one or more CVT courses during the reference year. Each person should be counted only once, irrespective of the number of CVT courses they have participated in (e.g. if a person employed has participated in two externally managed courses and one internally managed course, they should be counted as one participant). '''Costs of CVT courses''' The costs of CVT courses cover: * fees and payments for CVT courses; * travel and subsistence payments related to CVT courses; * the labour costs of internal trainers for CVT courses (direct and indirect costs); and * the costs for training centre, training rooms and teaching materials. CVT course costs also include the cost of contributions made by the enterprise to collective funding arrangements through government and intermediary organisations but exclude receipts from collective funding arrangements, subsidies and financial assistance from government and other sources. '''Time spent on CVT courses''' Time spent on CVT courses refers to paid working time (in hours) spent on CVT courses, i.e. the time that all participants have spent in total during the reference year. This should only cover the actual training time, and only the time spent during the paid working time. '''Initial vocational training''' Since 2005, the CVTS contains some variables on initial vocational training (IVT). IVT within enterprises is defined as a formal education programme (or a component of it) where working time alternates between periods of practical training (workplace) and general/theoretical education (educational institution/training centre). The definition of IVT differs between CVTS waves, for details see the implementation manuals for each wave, available in [https://circabc.europa.eu/w/browse/309a34ff-5bb5-4bce-9dc9-fc5a64ab1fc2 CIRCABC]. '''Number of persons employed''' The number of persons employed is defined as the total number of persons who work in the observation unit excluding persons employed holding an apprenticeship or training contract (i.e. the definition of persons employed in CVTS deviates from the one used for structural business statistics as regards the treatment of persons employed holding an apprenticeship or training contract). For additional definitions used in CVTS and further information see the CVTS implementation manuals available in [https://circabc.europa.eu/w/browse/309a34ff-5bb5-4bce-9dc9-fc5a64ab1fc2 CIRCABC]. ===Usual breakdowns and classifications=== '''Principal economic activity of the enterprise''' The [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|classification of economic activities (NACE)]] is used in the CVTS to describe the economic sector of the enterprises. NACE is a four-digit classification providing the framework for collecting and presenting a large range of statistical data according to economic activity in various statistical data sets. Several versions have been developed since 1970. NACE Rev.1.1 was used for the first three rounds of CVTS and NACE Rev.2 for the 2010 and 2015 rounds. '''Size class''' A threshold of 10 persons employed is applied as the minimum for the coverage of enterprises. The classification of the size of the enterprises uses the following classes: * Small — from 10 to 49 persons employed * Medium — from 50 to 249 persons employed * Large — 250 persons employed and more === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:CVTS_methodology_v010.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Context=== '''Education statistics in the EU''' [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publishes data on education and training which can be found on Eurostat's [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/education-and-training/data/database database] and cover the following features: *participation in education and training; *learning mobility; *education personnel; *education finance; *education and training outcomes; *languages. These statistics are based on four main data sources: *Education systems – joint UNESCO-OECD-Eurostat (UOE) data collection; *Adult education survey (AES); *Continuing vocational training survey (CVTS); and *Labour force survey (EU-LFS). Statistics on lifelong learning – which can be found under the folders 'adult learning' and 'continuing vocational training in enterprises' in the 'participation in education and training' section of Eurostat's database on education and training – are based on the AES, the LFS and the CVTS. The adult education survey and the labour force survey both provide data on participation in lifelong learning from the individuals' perspective while the CVTS covers the theme of lifelong learning through the enterprises' viewpoint (continuing vocational training). ===Other articles=== *[[Education_and_training_in_the_EU_-_facts_and_figures|Education and training in the EU – facts and figures]] *All pages on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Category:Education_and_training education and training] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Adult_learning_statistics Adult learning statistics] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/education-and-training/database Education and training (educ)], see: ::Participation in education and training (educ_part) :::Continuing vocational training in enterprises (trng_cvt) ===Dedicated section=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/education-and-training/overview Education and training] ===Methodology=== '''Metadata''' *{{Template:Esms|code=trng_cvt_esms|title=Continuing vocational training in enterprises}} (ESMS metadata file – trng_cvt_esms) '''Manuals and other methodological information''' vocational training] *[https://ec.europa.eu/education/policies/eu-policy-in-the-field-of-adult-learning_en European Commission – Education and training – Adult learning]
