title: Crime statistics
text:
<newarticle pic="Karanik yimpat Shutterstock 626843165 RV.jpg"> </newarticle>

<metadescription>EU statistics on crime. </metadescription>

<updatedata>
Data extracted in April 2026

Planned article update: April 2027
</updatedata>

<highlight>

<highlight-message>The number of intentional homicides in the EU increased by 1.4% in 2024, compared with 2023.
</highlight-message>

<highlight-message> In the EU, 3.9 per 1 million women were victims of intentional homicide, nearly double the rate for man in 2024.
</highlight-message>

<highlight-message>
In 2024, the number of sexual violence offences, including the rape, continued to rise in the EU.
</highlight-message>

<highlight-message>Police-recorded crimes against property in the EU decreased in 2024: thefts went down by 2.0%, robberies by 4.0% and burglaries by 2.6% compared with the previous year.
</highlight-message>

<vistool>
<script type="application/json">{
  "utility": "wcloud",
  "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202604/00e80ac0-3970-11f1-93aa-97f4949d42ef/uec.json"
}</script>
</vistool>


The statistics presented in this article are based on official figures for police-recorded offences (criminal acts) in Europe between 2008 and 2024.  The number of police-recorded crimes varies widely across the EU, even relative to population size. This can be due to different laws, different police recording practices and different reporting rates to the police, which can affect comparison.

</highlight>

<articlecontent>


<sesection>
=== 3 953 intentional homicides in the EU in 2024 ===
<newarticle>In 2024, police has recorded 3 953 [[Glossary:Intentional_homicide|intentional homicides]] in the EU, compared with the previous year, the figure increased 1.4% (Figure 1). An increase was observed in 16 out of the 27 EU countries, and the biggest upward changes in absolute numbers were occurring in Germany and Finland.</newarticle> 
<vistool>
<script type="application/json">{
  "utility": "wcloud",
  "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202604/00e80ac0-3970-11f1-93aa-97f4949d42ef/uec.json"
}</script>
<caption>Figure 1</caption>
</vistool>
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Number of women killed by family members is nearly double than for men===
The number of female victims of intentional homicide killed by family members or intimate partners in 2024 were 3.9 per 1 million women, that is nearly double than the rate for male victims reached 2.3 per million men.

Women are more frequently victims of intentional homicide by family members or intimate partners – the EU rate per 1 million women fluctuated between 3.9 and 4.3 from 2015 to 2024, peaking in 2022 (Figure 2). In 2024, the rate decreased to 3.9.

By contrast the EU rate of intentional homicide male victims killed by family members or intimate partners remained notably lower than those for women. Over the same period, it ranged from 1.9 to 2.3 per one million men with the lowest values in 2016, 2021 and 2022. In 2024, the rate increased from 2.2 in 2023 to 2.3 male victims per one million men.

These figures highlight the persistent gender disparity in domestic and intimate partner homicides across the EU.
<vistool>
<script type="application/json">{
  "utility": "wcloud",
  "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202604/9f026b60-3a31-11f1-8319-4d27f99e8e7f/uec.json"
}</script>
<caption>Figure 2</caption>
</vistool>
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== The number of sexual violence offences increased during 2014-2024 ===
From 2014 to 2024 the number of [[Glossary:Sexual_violence|sexual violence]] offences, including [[Glossary:Rape|rape]], as recorded by police in the EU, has shown a steady increase, reaching a 94.2% increase in 2024 as compared to 2014. The number of rape offences, as part of sexual violence offences, increased by 150.4% during this period (Figure 3). In 2024, 256 302 sexual violence offences (including 98 190 rape offences) were registered, showing a 5.0% increase (including a 6.8% increase in rape) compared to 2023.

The increased number of police-recorded sexual violence offences are closely connected to raising awareness in the society and might impact reporting rates.
<vistool>
<script type="application/json">{
  "utility": "wcloud",
  "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202604/9efb36e0-3a3a-11f1-bb24-3f849c28a50f/uec.json"
}</script>
<caption>Figure 3</caption>
</vistool>
</sesection>


<sesection>
=== Number of property related offences have increased after the pandemic === 
During the pandemic (2020-2021), police-recorded [[Glossary:Theft|theft]] offences in the EU had their lowest dip in 2021 – a decrease of 20.1% compared with 2019 (Figure 4). In 2024, there were 5 261 267 registered thefts, a 21.4% increase compared to 2021, and a 2.0% decrease compared with 2023.

In 2024, the number of police-registered [[Glossary:Burglary|burglary]] offences was 1 197 932. After steady decrease from 2010 to 2021, the number of police-recorded burglary offences showed a 9.0% increase compared to 2021 and a 2.6% decrease compared with 2023.

[[Glossary:Robbery|Robbery]] is less prevalent, however, the most serious property related crime of the 3. In 2024, in the EU, the number of police-recorded robbery offences was 251 162, an increase of 8.7% compared to 2021 and a 4.0% decrease compared with 2023.
<vistool>
<script type="application/json">{
  "utility": "wcloud",
  "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202604/04ce8bf0-3a34-11f1-95f9-f72ee472958d/uec.json"
}</script>
<caption>Figure 4</caption>
</vistool>
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Corruption offences slightly increased in 2024 === 
In 2024, there were 82 947 [[Glossary:Corruption|corruption]] offences as registered by police, including 9 207 [[Glossary:Bribery|bribery]] offences, which was a respective 9.8% and 0.4% increase compared to 2023 (Figure 5). The number of corruption offences has reached the highest figure in 2024 since 2017. The highest number (18 464) of bribery offences was registered in 2018.

<vistool>
<script type="application/json">{
  "utility": "wcloud",
  "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202604/9801af80-3a3f-11f1-b335-875da044bdf3/uec.json"
}</script>
<caption>Figure 5</caption>
</vistool>
</sesection>

<excel>
=== Source data for tables and graphs ===
{{Template:Excel|filename=Crime statistics 2026v2.xlsx|title=Source data for graphs}}

</excel>

<datadetails>

===Data sources===
==== Statistics on crime and criminal justice systems in general ====
Data sources include police and other law enforcement agencies, public prosecutors, law courts, prisons, relevant ministries, and statistical offices. The national authorities are responsible for official figures that are sent to Eurostat and to the United Nations
[https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/data-and-analysis/United-Nations-Surveys-on-Crime-Trends-and-the-Operations-of-Criminal-Justice-Systems.html (UN Survey on Crime Trends and Operations of Criminal Justice Systems)]. The crimes are classified according to the [http://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/data-and-analysis/statistics/iccs.html ICCS (International Classification of Crime for Statistical Purposes)]. [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/18846431/KS-GQ-24-010-EN-N.pdf/ef737587-085e-6018-8038-e41f59222020?version=3.0&t=1712826948630 Counting methodologies for offences and persons] should be applied. Countries' compliance with the classification of crimes and counting methodologies is explained in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/crim_sims.htm crime metadata].
====The data of this article====
This article presents results based on official figures for police-recorded offences (criminal acts) from 2008 onwards. The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/crime/database web database] contains figures as reported (no adjustment). 
==== Particular crimes ====
Additional data on intentional homicide, rape, and sexual assault:
*[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/47bdbc68-2521-4ca8-b4b1-ff4dcd257ace?lang=en Victims, suspects, prosecutions, convictions]
*[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/614006d2-0663-45a0-9857-e47cdeb87be7?lang=en Prisoners]
*[https://dataunodc.un.org/dp-intentional-homicide-victims Worldwide homicide statistics]
==== Earlier data ====
*[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/20a8d3da-68f3-4f91-87b5-c9ccdb29e133?lang=en Police-recorded crimes 1950-1992 (total)]
*[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/93ecbcfb-64a0-4863-8fe0-065fe8b0c045?lang=en Police-recorded crimes 1993-2007 (by crime)]


</datadetails>

<context>
===Context===
Crime statistics are used by EU institutions, national authorities, media, politicians, organisations, and the general public. Each state establishes its criminal laws, define crimes, legal proceedings and justice reactions, as well as specifications for official crime statistics (except for crimes that are covered by international or EU law). Typically, comparing crime statistics between countries is challenging due to different national criminal laws and different criminal justice systems.

However, it could also be argued that there are many similarities between European countries. This, combined with public and political interest, was the background for developing EU-wide crime statistics. Over the last decade, EU institutions, national authorities, and the UN have cooperated to improve European crime statistics. A major quality improvement is to use a [http://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/data-and-analysis/statistics/iccs.html common classification of crimes.]

Official crime statistics mainly reflect how the authorities register and handle cases. The figures are provided by national authorities such as the police, prosecution, courts, and prisons. Of those, police figures give the broadest picture, as they include recorded offences, whether or not they led to prosecution. Still, the police records do not measure the total occurrence of crime. Simply put, the total occurrence would be the reported plus the unreported, minus the incorrectly reported. It is fair to assume that the reporting rate is high when a police record is required to support an insurance claim (e.g. car theft and burglary).

</context>

</articlecontent>

title: Culture statistics - cultural employment
text:
EU cultural employment hit 8.9M jobs in 2025, up 1.3%, with a record-low gender gap across the EU labour market. Data extracted in June 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 In 2025, 8.9 million people were in cultural employment across the EU, representing 4.3% of total employment. In 2025, cultural employment in the EU grew by 1.3% compared with 2024. In 2025, the gender gap in cultural employment was the smallest on record, with 4.48 million men and 4.41 million women employed in the sector.

|alt=Dynamic map showing Cultural employment in 2025 in the EU, EU Member States, and some of the EFTA and candidate countries. This article, which forms part of the '''[[Culture_statistics|"Culture statistics" online publication]]''', provides an overview of developments in cultural [[Glossary:Employment|employment]] and information on cultural employment’s share of total employment in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Data on cultural employment come from the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|European Union Labour Force Survey (EU-LFS)]]. The analysis looks at cultural employment by age, sex, [[Glossary:Educational_attainment_level|level of educational attainment]], professional status, and full-time or part-time employment. It also examines the employment characteristics of creative and performing artists, authors, journalists, and linguists. The statistics follow the methodology set out in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-26-001 Guide to Eurostat culture statistics]. Cultural employment includes all people working in [[Glossary:Economic_activity|economic activities]] classified as cultural, whether or not they are employed in a specifically cultural occupation. It also covers people in cultural occupations, whether or not they are employed in a cultural economic activity. The concept of cultural employment, together with the full list of economic activities and occupations included in its scope, is described in the [[#Data_sources|Data sources]] section.
===Cultural employment – current situation and recent developments=== In 2025, cultural employment represented 4.3% of total employment in the EU, equal to 8.9 million people, with national shares ranging from 1.8% in Romania to 5.7% in the Netherlands. Overall, cultural employment accounted for a larger share of total employment in western and northern EU countries than in eastern and southern EU countries (see Map 1).
[[Image:Map 1 - Cultural_employment_2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Cultural employment 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d41940b9-6df3-4836-b7c3-c5b241bdc332?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-03T15:26:20Z cult_emp_sex])|alt= a map showing cultural employment in 2025 in the EU, EU countries, and some of the EFTA and candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''Cultural employment over recent years''' At EU level, cultural employment increased by 1.3% between 2024 and 2025. It rose in 21 EU countries, with the largest increases in Bulgaria (+10.6%), Cyprus (+10.1%), and Greece (+9.2%). It declined in 6 countries, most notably in Luxembourg (−11.6%), Denmark (−4.2%), and Estonia (−3.1%); see Figure 1. Looking beyond the most recent annual change, patterns over the 3 years from 2022 to 2025 varied between countries. Since 2022, cultural employment has increased overall in 19 EU countries. In 5 countries – Belgium, Germany, Greece, Finland, and Sweden – the increase in 2025 followed 2 consecutive annual declines. In Denmark and Estonia, the increase between 2022 and 2023 was followed by declines in both subsequent years. In Italy and Austria, 2 consecutive annual increases were followed by a decline in 2025.

[[Image:Figure 1 - Cultural employment ‒ annual rates of change, 2023-2025_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Cultural employment ‒ annual rates of change, 2023-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7c628692-9985-4068-9117-a04f506f1cf9?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-03T15:26:55Z cult_emp_sex])|alt= a vertical bar chart showing the annual rates of change in cultural employment from 2023-2025 in the EU, EU countries, and some of the EFTA and candidate countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Table 1 complements Figure 1 by presenting the number of people in cultural employment and the share of cultural employment in total employment at EU and national levels. Between 2024 and 2025, France (+20 800 people) and Spain (+19 400) recorded the largest increases in the number of people in cultural employment. Italy (−7 300 people), Denmark (−6 300), and Austria (−5 200) recorded the largest decreases. Over the same period, the share of cultural employment in total employment increased in 14 EU countries, declined in 4, and stayed unchanged in 9. Bulgaria recorded the largest increase (0.3 [[Glossary:percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]], while Luxembourg recorded the largest decrease (−0.7 pp).

[[Image:Table 1 - Cultural employment, 2022 to 2025_v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Cultural employment, 2022 to 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fedaff97-2a70-4efc-a0c7-d47c58799777?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-03T15:27:59Z cult_emp_sex])|alt= a table showing cultural employment from 2022 to 2025 in terms of number of people and share of total employment, and the changes in shares for both from 2024 to 2025. The data presents the EU, EU countries, and some of the EFTA and candidate countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''Trends in employment across cultural sectors''' Figure 2 shows employment trends at EU level from 2014 to 2025 in 9 selected cultural sectors, defined using NACE Rev. 2. Together, these sectors employed 5.5 million people, or 62% of all people in cultural employment, in 2025. The main patterns are as follows: :* Employment in creative, arts, and entertainment activities (NACE R90) declined substantially in 2020 and 2021. It recovered strongly in 2022 and, after a slight decline in 2023, rose again in 2024 and 2025, reaching 1.1 million people, the highest level over the period shown. :* Employment in design, photographic, translation, and interpretation activities (NACE M74.1, M74.2, M74.3) increased in 2025, continuing the overall upward trend observed since 2020. :* Employment in advertising agency and media representation activities (NACE M73.1) increased overall between 2014 and 2024, but decreased slightly in 2025. :* Employment in cultural heritage activities (NACE R91) was below its 2024 peak, but still higher than in any year before 2024. :* Employment in audio-visual production, sound recording, and music publishing activities (NACE J59) continued to increase, reaching nearly 0.5 million people in 2025. :* The long-term decline in employment in selected publishing activities (part of NACE J58) continued in 2025. In contrast, employment in printing and reproduction of recorded media (NACE C18) rose moderately, interrupting the earlier downward trend. :* Employment in programming and broadcasting activities (NACE J60) declined between 2021 and 2023, but increased in both 2024 and 2025, reaching almost 0.3 million people. :* Employment in other selected manufacturing activities, including jewellery and musical instruments (NACE C32.1 and C32.2), remained broadly stable over the period. A temporary increase in 2022 was followed by a return to lower levels in 2023 and 2024, before a modest rise in 2025.
[[Image:Figure 2 - Evolution of cultural employment by selected NACE Rev_ 2 activities, EU, 2014-2025_(thousands)_v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Evolution of cultural employment by selected NACE Rev. 2 activities, EU, 2014-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/309384ea-2ec1-4ea6-825e-5461e8f07e03?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-16T12:18:49Z cult_emp_n2])|alt= a line chart with 9 lines showing the evolution of cultural employment by selected NACE Rev. 2 activities in the EU from 2014 to 2025. The lines show the selected NACE Rev. 2 activities. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Characteristics of cultural employment in 2025===
'''Cultural employment by sex, age and educational attainment''' In 2025, the socio-demographic profile of cultural employment in the EU was broadly similar to that of total employment, when broken down by sex and age. Differences were more marked when looking at educational attainment. Women’s share in cultural employment was higher than their share of total employment (49.6% versus 46.5%). By age, cultural employment had higher shares of people aged 30-39 years (24.8% in cultural employment versus 22.4% in total employment), those aged 65 years and over (4.8% versus 3.4% in total employment), and those aged 15-29 years (17.9% versus 17.1%). In contrast, the shares were lower for those aged 50-64 years (28.8% versus 32.3%) and 40-49 years (23.7% versus 24.9%). The structure by educational attainment differed more markedly between cultural and total employment. In 2025, cultural employment was characterised by a generally higher level of education, with 61.9% of people having [[Glossary:Tertiary_education|tertiary education (ISCED 5-8)]], 31.3% having upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education, and 6.7% having the lowest levels of educational attainment (ISCED 0-2). In total employment, the corresponding shares were 39.5%, 45.3%, and 15.1%, respectively (see Figure 3).

[[Image:Figure 3 - Cultural and total employment by sex, age and educational attainment, EU, 2025_v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Cultural and total employment by sex, age, and educational attainment, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/665c90f2-a445-4416-bd95-1a3cad54f66d?lang=en cult_emp_sex]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/32beaac6-c544-45dd-bc73-01d6a5b3cf2f?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-03T15:36:32Z lfsa_egan2]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1fe17b95-2f28-412b-a941-25b64d614ed1?lang=en cult_emp_age]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b5f1f4b2-0556-4450-8d8f-e8d73fdd962d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-03T15:35:19Z lfsa_egan]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1646ce19-31ee-433b-8765-ff71be07ac5f?lang=en cult_emp_edu]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6ced626a-cef6-4e11-83c6-a32b7a52cbba?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-03T15:36:15Z lfsa_egaed])|alt=A stacked bar graph showing the cultural and total employment by sex, age, and educational attainment in the EU in 2025. For each category there are two bars: one shows total employment and one shows cultural employment. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

'''The share of women in cultural employment''' Between 2014 and 2025, the number of women in cultural employment in the EU increased every year except in 2020. In 2025, it rose by about 1.4% compared with 2024, slightly faster than the increase among men (1.2%). As a result, the difference between the shares of men and women in cultural employment remained below 1 pp, at 50.4% for men and 49.6% for women (see Figure 4).

[[Image:Figure 4 - Evolution of cultural employment in the EU by sex, 2014-2025_(thousands)_v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Evolution of cultural employment in the EU by sex, 2014-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e0b27850-c4ce-4d3a-9201-146c01373add?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-03T15:38:42Z cult_emp_sex])|alt=a line chart with two lines showing the evolution of cultural employment in the EU by sex from 2014 to 2025. The lines show men and women. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Although the shares of men and women in cultural employment at EU level in 2025 were almost equal, national patterns differed considerably. In 17 EU countries, women accounted for more than half of cultural employment. Estonia recorded the highest share of women in cultural employment (62.3%), followed by Latvia (60.5%), Lithuania (59.4%), and Luxembourg (59.2%). Italy (44.4%) and Belgium (44.6%) had the lowest shares. For more detailed data on cultural and total employment by sex, age and educational attainment, please refer to the {{Template:Excel|filename=Culture statistics - cultural employment (2026)_v2.xlsx|title=Cultural employment: tables and figures}}.

===Some other characteristics of cultural employment===
The EU-LFS also provides information on additional socioeconomic characteristics that allow a more detailed analysis of cultural employment, including [[Glossary:Self-employed|self-employment]], working patterns (full-time and part-time), type of employment contract (permanent or temporary), and whether people have only 1 job.

'''Self-employment''' Alongside the high share of people with tertiary education, cultural employment has a relatively high proportion of self-employed people. This reflects the independent and specialised nature of many cultural occupations, such as authors, performing artists, musicians, painters, sculptors, and craftspeople. In 2025, almost a third (31.6%) of people in cultural employment across the EU were self-employed, compared with an average of 13.7% in the whole economy. Italy (47.7%) and the Netherlands (44.2%) recorded the highest shares of self-employed people in cultural employment. Shares above the EU average were also observed in Czechia, Ireland, Austria, Slovakia, Greece, France, Finland, and Spain. Fewer than 20% of people in cultural employment were self-employed in Denmark (19.0%) and Romania (15.8%). In all 26 EU countries with available data, self-employment was more common in cultural employment than in total employment.

'''Full-time work''' At EU level, the share of full-time work was lower in cultural employment than in total employment (76.6% compared with 81.2%). The same pattern appeared in almost all EU countries, except for the Netherlands, Romania, and Belgium, where the shares were almost identical. The lower share of full-time work in cultural employment, observed in most EU countries, may partly reflect more flexible or project-based forms of work in some cultural activities, including self-employment and freelance work. Full-time employment in the cultural field varied considerably across countries, from 61.3% in the Netherlands to 98.3% in Romania. The Netherlands and Romania illustrate 2 distinct labour market contexts: in the Netherlands, full-time work was relatively uncommon in both cultural and total employment, whereas in Romania it was almost universal in both. These examples show that cross-country differences in the share of full-time work in cultural employment need to be interpreted in relation to each country’s labour market structure.

'''Permanent jobs and people with only 1 job''' Differences between cultural and total employment were smaller for permanent jobs and for people with only 1 job. In 2025, 83.5% of employees in cultural employment had a permanent job, compared with 87.3% of employees in total employment. The lowest shares of permanent jobs in cultural employment were in the Netherlands (72.4%) and France (72.7%), while the highest were in Romania (99.5%), Bulgaria and Lithuania (both 98.9%), and Hungary, Latvia, and Estonia (all above 95%). Having only 1 job was also slightly less common in cultural employment than in total employment. At EU level, 93.1% of people in cultural employment had only 1 job, 2.8 pp below the share in total employment (95.9%). The difference was small in Bulgaria, Romania, Croatia, Malta, Poland, and Italy, where the share in cultural employment was no more than 1 pp lower than in total employment. The largest gaps were in Denmark, Estonia, and Austria, where the share was more than 5 pp lower. In Denmark, 82.3% of people in cultural employment had only 1 job, 7.9 pp below the share in total employment and the lowest share among EU countries (see Table 2).

[[Image:Table 2 - Selected labour market characteristics of cultural employment and total employment, 2025 (%)_v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Selected labour market characteristics of cultural employment and total employment, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/344e1e92-489a-4aa6-b677-392711d6be74?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-02T09:42:08Z cult_emp_wsta])|alt= a table showing the selected labour market characteristics of cultural employment and total employment in the EU in 2025 in the EU, EU countries, and some of the EFTA and candidate countries. These labour characteristics include self-employment, full-time jobs, permanent jobs, and people with only one job. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Focus on artists, authors, journalists, and linguists===
This final section presents data on the employment characteristics of 2 groups of cultural occupations, as defined in ISCO-08 groups 264 and 265: creative and performing artists (including visual artists, musicians, dancers, actors, film directors, etc.) and authors, journalists, and linguists. In this article, these occupations are referred to collectively as ’artists and writers’. In 2025, the EU had almost 1.8 million artists and writers, accounting for 20.0% of cultural employment. Of these, 46.3% were self-employed, a much higher share than in total employment (13.7%) and in cultural employment overall (31.6%). In Germany and Cyprus, the share of self-employed artists and writers was about 5 times higher than the share of self-employed people in total employment. Self-employment shares of at least 50% among artists and writers were observed in Italy (65.5%), the Netherlands (64.0%), Czechia (58.1%), Portugal (57.8%), Ireland (55.6%), and Finland (51.2%). In 2025, 71.4% of artists and writers in the EU worked full-time, around 5 pp below the share in cultural employment (76.6%) and nearly 10 pp below the share in total employment (81.2%). Latvia and Cyprus recorded the largest gaps, where the shares of artists and writers working full-time were around 25 pp and 24 pp below the shares in total employment (65.8% versus 90.8% and 67.1% versus 91.1%, respectively). In contrast, the share of artists and writers working full-time was higher than in total employment in the Netherlands (by 8 pp) and in Luxembourg (by over 3 pp). Artists and writers were also less likely than employees in total employment to have a permanent job. In 2025, 74.0% of employees working as artists and writers in the EU had a permanent job, compared with 87.3% of employees in total employment. In most EU countries, artists and writers had a lower share of permanent jobs, with Malta, Croatia, Lithuania, Romania, Slovakia and Hungary as exceptions. France showed the largest difference: 54.3% of employees working as artists and writers had a permanent job, around 30 pp below the share in total employment. In 2025, 90.4% of artists and writers across the EU had only 1 job, compared with 95.9% of people in total employment. The share of people with only 1 job was lower among artists and writers in all EU countries except Luxembourg and Romania. In Sweden, Denmark, Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania, the share of artists and writers with only 1 job was at least 10 pp below share in total employment. Denmark recorded the lowest share, with 78.2% of artists and writers having only 1 job, meaning that around 1 in 5 had multiple jobs (see Table 3).

[[Image:Table 3 - Characteristics of persons working as creative and performing artists, authors, journalists and linguists, 2025 (thousands, %)_v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Characteristics of persons working as creative and performing artists, authors, journalists, and linguists, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/77a0328b-0aec-4f92-8796-fff1b32925e5?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-03T15:46:44Z cult_emp_art]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/16756bb3-630e-48b1-989d-f187bdbe4996?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-03T16:00:34Z cult_emp_artpc])|alt= a table showing the characteristics of people working as creative and performing artists, authors, journalists, and linguists in 2025 in the EU, EU Member States, and some of the EFTA and candidate countries. These labour characteristics include self-employment, full-time jobs, permanent jobs, and people with only one job. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

=== Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Culture statistics - cultural employment (2026)_v2.xlsx|title=Cultural employment: tables and figures}}


===Data sources=== The statistical concept of cultural employment follows the methodology described in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-26-001 Guide to Eurostat culture statistics]. Cultural employment is defined by combining economic activities (classified using [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE Rev. 2]]) with a set of occupations (classified using [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_occupations_(ISCO)|ISCO-08]]).

'''Defining cultural employment''' Cultural employment covers 3 situations (see Figure 5): * a person holds a cultural occupation and works in the cultural sector (for example, a ballet dancer employed by a ballet company or a journalist working for a daily newspaper) * a person holds a cultural occupation outside the cultural sector (for example, a designer who works in the motor vehicles industry) * a person holds a non-cultural occupation in the cultural sector (for example, an accountant working in a publishing house).
[[Image:Figure 5 - Definition of the scope of cultural employment - examples (2026).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Definition of the scope of cultural employment - examples
''Source:'' [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-26-001 Guide to Eurostat culture statistics — 2026]|alt= A diagram showing examples of the definition of the scope of cultural employment. For more details please use the link to the Guide to Eurostat culture statistics below the image.]]
[[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat’s]] statistics on cultural employment are based on the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|EU-LFS]], which covers people aged 15 years and over. Eurostat compiles data on cultural employment crossing the economic activity in which a person works with their occupation, using a matrix to produce an aggregate for cultural employment. The data can be analysed in more detail, for example by sex, age, or level of educational attainment.

The 2 lists below set out the economic activities (NACE Rev. 2) and occupations (ISCO-08) used to calculate cultural employment aggregated from the EU-LFS.

In 2025, the Expert Group on Culture Statistics revised the set of economic activities and occupations included in the cultural scope, adding further codes; '''these are shown in bold''' in the lists below. The corresponding cultural employment aggregates and breakdowns were subsequently recalculated from the 2011 reference year onwards to ensure that the revised scope was applied consistently over time.

The EU-LFS requires data to be provided for NACE divisions (2-digit level) and for ISCO minor groups (3-digit level). Most countries voluntarily provide more granular data. For countries without information at NACE 3-digit level and/or ISCO 4-digit level, estimates are produced using coefficients derived from countries that provide the highest level of detail.

'''Estimating cultural employment''' When estimating cultural employment, it is difficult to determine how much of some economic activities and occupations is genuinely cultural. For this reason, activities and occupations that are only partly cultural are excluded from the estimates. For example, the ISCO code 1431 (Sports, recreation, and cultural centre managers) has a cultural component, but it is not possible to identify the share relating specifically to culture within this occupational group. A cautious approach was therefore adopted, and this occupation (and similar cases) was excluded from the cultural employment aggregate. In addition, the EU-LFS collects sufficiently detailed information on the economic activity and occupation only of the respondent’s main job and does not cover secondary jobs (for example, in the cultural field). These secondary jobs are therefore excluded from the cultural employment aggregate. Given these limitations and the approach used, the data on cultural employment are likely to underestimate the actual extent of employment in this field.
==== Time series ==== [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32019R1700 Regulation (EU) 2019/1700] entered into force on 1 January 2021 and caused a break in the EU-LFS time series for several EU countries. To continue monitoring employment and unemployment despite this break, countries assessed its impact in their country and calculated impact factors or break-corrected data for a set of indicators. Break-corrected data are published for the main EU-LFS indicators. More information on the EU-LFS is available in the [[EU_labour_force_survey|online publication]], which includes 8 articles on the survey’s technical and methodological aspects. The used methodology is described in [[EU_Labour_Force_Survey_-_new_methodology_from_2021_onwards|methodology from 2021 onwards]] article. Detailed information on coding lists, explanatory notes and classifications used over time is provided under [[EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation|documentation]]. The ‘definition differs’ flag for France and Spain is related to methodological changes introduced with the new EU Labour Force Survey methodology from 2021 onwards.
===Context=== Culture is one of Europe’s key assets: it underpins values and identity and fosters a sense of belonging. It also supports well-being, social cohesion, and inclusion. The cultural and creative sectors drive economic growth, job creation, and international trade. To support cultural activities, the EU has launched the [https://culture.ec.europa.eu/creative-europe Creative Europe programme] and introduced several policy measures under the [https://www.europeanheritagehub.eu/document/eu-work-plan-for-culture-2023-2026/ 2023-2026 EU Work Plan for Culture]. The work plan, adopted by EU culture ministers in December 2022, sets 4 main priorities for European cooperation in cultural policy: * artists and cultural professionals: empowering the cultural and creative sectors * culture for the people: enhancing cultural participation and the role of culture in society * culture for the planet: unleashing the power of culture * culture for co-creative partnerships: strengthening the cultural dimension of EU external relations. One of the European Commission’s priorities across all sectors is to produce reliable, comparable and up-to-date cultural statistics to support sound cultural policymaking. Eurostat compiles culture statistics from several data collections to track cultural trends in areas such as education, employment, business, international trade, and cultural participation and consumption.

title: Culture statistics - cultural participation
text:
Data on cultural participation EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) covering the population aged 16 years or more. Data extracted in March 2026 Planned update: October 2029 In 2022, women participated in cultural activities at higher rates than men – this pattern was also observed in 2015. In 2022, the participation rate in cultural activities among people with the highest incomes was at least twice that of those with the lowest incomes in 17 EU countries. In 2022, more than half of people with disabilities in Denmark, Luxembourg, Finland, and the Netherlands participated in cultural activities. This article, part of the online publication ''[[Culture_statistics|Culture statistics]]'', presents key findings on people’s participation in cultural activities and people’s practice of artistic activities. These findings are from [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/microdata/european-union-statistics-on-income-and-living-conditions EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)], conducted in [[Glossary:EU|EU]], [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]], and [[Glossary:candidate countries|candidate countries]]. In 2022, in addition to annual data, EU-SILC collected 3-yearly data on health and 6-yearly data on quality of life, from which the data presented in the article are extracted. Participation in cultural activities includes going to the cinema, attending live performances (plays, concerts, operas, ballet and dance performances, etc.) and visiting cultural sites (historical monuments, museums, art galleries or archaeological sites). The practice of artistic activity includes activities such as playing an instrument, composing music, singing, dancing, acting, photography, etc. The overall scope of the data collection covered various aspects of participation and non-participation in cultural activities during the 12 months preceding the interview, among individuals aged 16 and over. Detailed breakdowns are available, including sex, age, educational attainment level, degree of urbanisation, income level, and more. Additionally, in 2022, data on cultural participation among people reporting some level of disability became available. It is important to note that although the data were collected in 2022, respondents were asked about their cultural participation (such as going to the cinema, attending live concerts, or visiting certain types of art galleries and museums) during the previous 12 months (often covering most of 2021). Consequently, the data may show lower levels of participation compared to 2015 results due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Moreover, restrictions in place during the pandemic varied from country to country, and this should be considered when comparing 2022 data among EU Member States.


===Cultural participation – general findings===
'''''In 15 EU countries, over half of residents participated in cultural activities''''' In 2022, in most EU countries (15 out of 26; data for Germany are not available due to high item non-response rate) over half of residents aged 16 or older participated in cultural activities in the previous year. Compared with 2015, reported cultural participation declined across all EU countries except Spain, where cultural participation remained stable at 58.5%. The most noticeable decreases were observed in France, Slovakia, Latvia, and Sweden, where the share of the population participating in cultural activities fell by more than 20 [[Glossary:percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]]. In 2022, the highest levels of cultural participation were primarily recorded in western and [[Glossary:Nordic Member States|Nordic Member States]], at 77.7% in Luxembourg and 77.3% in Denmark, followed by the Netherlands, Finland, Sweden, Ireland, and Estonia (all five countries on at least 60%). At the other end of the range, less than a quarter of the adult population in Romania (22.2%) and Bulgaria (19.7%) reported participating at least once within the last 12 months in any of the listed cultural activities (see Table 1).

'''Cultural participation by type of activity''' According to Table 1, among the three types of cultural activities analysed – going to the cinema, attending live performances and visiting cultural sites – the decline reported in 2022 was most pronounced in the attendance of live performances. While in 2015, this activity was the most popular in 13 countries, in 2022 it was the most popular in only 4 countries. In 2015, going to the cinema and visiting cultural sites were the most common activities in 9 and 5 EU countries respectively, while in 2022 these two activities recorded the highest rates of cultural participation of any cultural activity in 11 different EU countries each. In 2022, Denmark had the highest rate of cinema attendance of any country in the sample (52.4%). And in 2022, Luxembourg recorded the highest rates for attending live performances and visiting cultural sites of any country in the sample (48.5% and 63.3%, respectively). In contrast, Bulgaria had the lowest percentage of participants in cinema attendance of any country in the same and Bulgaria and Romania had the lowest rates for attending live performances and visiting cultural sites.

'''Cultural participation by sex''' '''''In 2022, women participated in cultural activities at higher rates than men in most countries''''' In most EU countries, the percentage of women participating in the selected cultural activities slightly exceeded the shares reported for men. This pattern was observed in 18 out of 27 countries in 2015 and 17 out of 26 countries in 2022 (see Figure 1). In 2022, Denmark showed the highest participation rate in cultural activities for women of any country in the sample (79.6%), while Luxembourg recorded the highest percentage for men (77.5%), The lowest participation rates of any country in the sample for both sexes were observed in Bulgaria (20.5% women and 18.7% men). The differences between the shares of men and women in cultural participation were generally small, not exceeding 2 pp in 15 countries in 2015 and in 17 countries in 2022. In 2015, differences above 4 pp were noted in three countries: Slovakia (6 pp difference in favour of women), Ireland (5 pp difference in favour of women), and Romania (4 pp difference in favour of men). In 2022, only one country showed a difference greater than 4 pp (Denmark, 5 pp difference in favour of women). In 2022, the countries with the closest gender parity in cultural participation were Malta, Slovenia, Greece, Spain, Luxembourg and Belgium, with differences not exceeding 0.3 pp. However, comparing 2022 with 2015, the decrease in the percentage of women participating in cultural activities was larger than that observed for men in 14 countries. The most significant changes in cultural participation by sex occurred among women in Slovakia (a decrease of 25 pp, from 62.3% in 2015 to 36.9% in 2022) and among men in France (a decrease of 23 pp, from 76.6% to 53.6% over the same period). The smallest changes were recorded in Spain (+0.1 pp for men, from 58.5% to 58.6%, and -0.2 pp for women, from 58.5% to 58.3%).

'''Cultural participation by age''' Despite the decrease in 2022 compared with 2015, the overall structure of cultural participation by age remained unchanged: participation in cultural activities decreases with age. This pattern was consistently observed in 2015 and 2022 across all EU countries. In 2015, the percentage of cultural participants aged 16-29 was at least double that of those aged 65 and over in 15 countries; in 2022, it was at least double in 20 countries. In 2022, the highest percentages of cultural participation among individuals aged 16-29 were recorded in Luxembourg (89%) and the Netherlands (86.9%). For the remaining age groups, the highest rates were observed in Denmark (81% for those aged 30-54, 74.7% for those aged 55-64, and 65.8% for those aged 65 or over) and in Luxembourg (78% for those aged 30-54, 72.4% for those aged 55-64, and 69.5% for those aged 65 or over). The lowest percentages of cultural participation across all age groups were recorded in Bulgaria and Romania. Comparing 2022 with 2015, cultural participation decreased by at least 10 pp in the age groups 16-29 and 65 and over in 13 EU countries and by at least 10 pp among those aged 30-54 in 15 countries and among those aged 55-64 in 14 countries. The largest declines in cultural participation were recorded for individuals aged 16-29 and 30-54 in Latvia (25 and 23 pp, respectively), for those aged 55-64 in Sweden (29 pp) and for those aged 65 or over in France and Sweden (25 pp). The smallest decrease in cultural participation for people aged 16 to 29 was observed in Spain (1 pp). In other age groups, slight increases in some countries were also observed between 2015 and 2022. For those aged 30-54, the cultural participation rate increased by 2 pp in Poland; for those aged 55-64, by 2 pp in Spain and 1 pp in Poland; and for those aged 65 or over, by 4 pp in Spain and 3 pp in Luxembourg (see Table 2).

'''Frequency of cultural participation''' '''''Countries with high rates of cultural participation also saw more individuals participating more frequently in cultural activities during the year ''''' In 2022, residents of EU Member States mostly participated in cultural activities between one and three times during the year preceding the interview, with the highest rates for participation between one and three times in the year seen in Luxembourg (51.7%) and Finland (46.6%). Participation in cultural activities more than three times a year was noticeably lower across all EU countries. However, countries with a generally high rate of cultural participation also showed higher percentages of individuals participating in cultural activities at least four times a year, particularly in Denmark (33.6%), the Netherlands (30.1%), Luxembourg (25.9%), and Estonia (25.3%). By contrast, Bulgaria (80.3%), Romania (77.8%), and Croatia (67.6%) were the three EU countries where over two thirds of the population did not participate in any cultural activity during the previous 12 months. A significant change between 2015 and 2022 was related to more frequent cultural participation (’at least four times a year’). In 2015, eight EU countries recorded a higher percentage of their adult population participating in cultural activities at least four times a year compared with the percentage of their population participating one to three times a year. But in 2022, in all EU countries, the share of adults participating in cultural activities one to three times a year exceeded that of those participating at least four times a year (see Table 3). This was due in particular to developments in 15 EU countries where the share of adults participating in cultural activities at least four times a year declined by more than 10 pp between 2015 and 2022. Among those participating in cultural activities at least four times a year, the largest declines were noted in Sweden (-25 pp between 2015 and 2022), Finland, France, and Luxembourg (-22 pp each between 2015 and 2022). Less frequent cultural participation (up to three times during the year) increased in 13 EU Member States between 2015 and 2022. Luxembourg saw the largest increase for this frequency (20 pp over this period), followed by Belgium (8 pp) and Slovenia (6 pp). Conversely, Greece, Slovakia, and Latvia recorded the largest decreases (10 pp each). It is important to note that COVID-19 restrictions continued to affect cultural participation patterns across several EU Member States in 2022.

===The structure of cultural participation in 2022 – additional socio-economic indicators===
'''Cultural participation by educational attainment''' Cultural participation shows higher rates among individuals with higher levels of educational attainment. As Figure 2 clearly shows, in 2022 this pattern was observed across all EU countries. In 15 countries, at least two thirds of individuals with a tertiary education participated in cultural activities. The highest cultural participation rate among tertiary-educated people was seen in Luxembourg (88.7%), followed by Denmark, Portugal, and the Netherlands. Bulgaria recorded the lowest percentage of individuals with a tertiary education who participated in cultural activities (39.5%). It was the only country where the rate of cultural participation among people with tertiary educational attainment was lower than 50%. In Portugal, Poland, Romania, France, Belgium, Hungary and Ireland, cultural participation among those with a tertiary education was at least 40 pp higher than the level recorded for people with lower secondary education or less.

'''''In 19 EU countries, the participation rate in cultural activities for individuals with a tertiary education was at least twice that of those with only a lower secondary education''''' Among the population with a lower secondary education or less, there were only two countries in which more than half of individuals participated in cultural activities in 2022: Denmark (63.2%) and Luxembourg (54.3%). In Romania and Bulgaria, countries that were at the other end of the range, this rate was below 10%. In 19 out of 26 countries, cultural participation among individuals with a tertiary education was twice as high as among those with the lowest level of education. Moreover, with the exceptions of Denmark (23 pp), Estonia (28 pp), and Sweden (29 pp), all EU countries recorded differences of at least 30 pp between the cultural participation rates of people with a lower secondary education or less and those with a tertiary education. The greatest differences were recorded in France, Romania, Poland, and Portugal (Portugal had the greatest difference of all at 51 pp). The most varied cultural participation rates across countries were observed for people with upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education. These rates were below the participation level observed for the whole population in 20 out of 26 EU countries. In four countries (Lithuania, Slovakia, Czechia, and Latvia), participation rates were no more than 10 pp higher for individuals with upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education than for those with the lowest level of education. Conversely, only in Malta was the difference between the percentage of individuals with upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education participating in culture and those with tertiary education participating in culture less than 10 pp (see Figure 2).

'''Cultural participation by degree of urbanisation''' Breaking down the population by the degree of urbanisation of area of residence showed a slightly higher percentage of cultural participation in 2022 among people living in cities, compared with residents of towns and suburbs and rural areas. In 2022, this pattern was recorded in 23 EU countries (except Belgium, Ireland, and Malta). Overall, in most EU countries (17 out of the 26 with available data), the difference between the areas with the highest and lowest cultural participation rates did not exceed 15 pp. The smallest difference was seen in Malta and Belgium (5 pp each), followed by the Netherlands (6 pp each). This shows that in these countries, the degree of urbanisation of a person’s area of residence did not play a major role in influencing their cultural participation. By contrast, the largest differences in participation rates between people living in cities and those living in rural areas were found in Bulgaria (22 pp), Poland (21 pp) and Hungary (20 pp). In 16 EU countries, more than half of city residents participated in the analysed cultural activities at least once in the previous year, with the highest rate in Luxembourg (86.1%) and the lowest in Bulgaria (29.7%). Similarly, in 15 EU countries, over half of the residents in towns and suburbs spent some time on cultural activities at least once within 12 months, with Denmark having the highest participation rate (76.4%) and Bulgaria having the lowest (16.9%). And in rural areas, more than half of residents participated in cultural activities in 12 EU countries, with the highest participation rate in Luxembourg (76.6%) and the lowest in Bulgaria (8.0%) (see Figure 3).

'''Cultural participation by income''' Across the EU, the rate of cultural participation was higher among the highest income group (fifth quintile, the top 20%) than the lowest income group (first quintile, the bottom 20%). In 2022, the highest levels of cultural participation among those from the fifth quintile of income were recorded in Luxembourg (90.1% of whom participated in a cultural activity at least once in the previous year), Denmark (87.9%), and the Netherlands (83.1%). In contrast, in Slovakia, Croatia, Romania, and Bulgaria, fewer than half of the people with the highest incomes participated in any of the cultural activities. Among people from the first quintile of income, the highest levels of cultural participation were recorded in Denmark (69.4%), Luxembourg (64.7%), Finland (53.3%), and the Netherlands (50.2%). Cultural participation rates below 20% among people with the lowest incomes were recorded in Cyprus, Croatia, Romania, and Bulgaria. The 2022 participation rate in cultural activities for the highest income group was at least twice that of the lowest income group in 17 EU Member States. Differences in cultural participation rates between people in the uppermost and lowermost income quintiles were relatively small in the Nordic Member States and Luxembourg, where the ratio was at most 1.5. Conversely, in Bulgaria, people with the highest incomes were 6.5 times more likely to participate in cultural activities than their fellow citizens with the lowest incomes (see Figure 4).

===Cultural participation of people with disabilities===
Cultural participation is more difficult for people with disabilities. In 2022, data were made available on cultural participation among people reporting at least some level of activity limitation. The results showed a lower rate of cultural participation among people with disabilities compared with the overall population aged 16 and over across all EU countries. In general, in countries with higher overall cultural participation rates, the participation rate among people with disabilities was also higher. In the EU in 2022, cultural participation rates greater than 50% among people with disabilities were observed in Denmark (68.3%), Luxembourg (67.9%), Finland (55.4%), and the Netherlands (55.4%). At the other end of the scale were Bulgaria (6.1%), Romania (7.1%), Croatia (11.3%), and Cyprus (14.1%) (see Table 4).

'''Cultural participation of people with disabilities by type of activity and sex''' '''''Of the three activities analysed, visiting cultural sites was most frequently practiced by people with disabilities'''''
As shown in Table 4, among people with disabilities, the most popular cultural activity differs according to the Member State: * in 19 EU Member States it was ‘visiting cultural sites’, with the highest rate observed in Luxembourg (55.5%); * in 5 EU Member States it was ‘attending live performances’; * in 3 EU Member States it was ‘going to the cinema’’ (in Ireland ‘visiting cultural sites’ and ‘going to the cinema’ had the same participation rate). Additionally, ‘going to the cinema’ was the cultural activity with the lowest participation rate among people with disabilities in 16 EU countries, while ‘attending live performances’ had the lowest participation rate among people with disabilities in 10 countries. The highest percentages of people with disabilities participating in the specified activities were recorded in Denmark and Luxembourg. In Luxembourg, in the year before the survey, 55.5% of all individuals with disabilities visited a cultural site at least once, 39.3% attended live performances, and 36.7% went to the cinema. In Denmark, 46.5% of people with disabilities visited a cultural site at least once, 43.0% went to the cinema at least once, and 37.5% attended live performances at least once. In 18 EU countries, the percentage of women with disabilities participating in cultural activities was higher than that of men. In Hungary, the shares were the same for women and men (17.1%). The opposite trends (where men with disabilities were more likely to participate in cultural activities than women with disabilities) were observed in only a few southern EU countries (Greece, Spain, Italy, Malta, and Slovenia), as well as in Luxembourg and Sweden. In 13 out of 26 EU countries with available data, the difference in cultural participation rates between women and men did not exceed 2 pp, indicating that sex was not a key variable in influencing cultural participation among people with a disability. Looking at the cultural activity engaged in more detail, ‘visiting cultural sites’ was the cultural activity with the highest participation rate among women with disabilities in 17 countries (and was the cultural activity with the highest participation rate among men with disabilities in 19 countries). ‘Attending live performances’ was the cultural activity with the highest participation rate among women with disabilities in 7 countries (in Croatia ‘visiting cultural sites’ and ‘attending live performances’ had the same participation rate among women with disabilities) and it was the cultural activity with the highest participation rate among men with disabilities in 5 countries. ‘Going to the cinema’ was the cultural activity with the highest participation rate among women with disabilities in 3 countries and among men with disabilities in 2 countries.

===Cultural participation – practising artistic activities===
'''Participation in artistic activities''' As part of the EU-SILC Quality of Life module on social and cultural participation in 2022, respondents were not only asked about their participation in cultural events. They were also asked about their practice of artistic activities, such as playing a musical instrument, composing music, singing, dancing, acting, photography/filmmaking, drawing, painting, sculpting, engaging in other visual arts/handcrafts, writing poems/short stories/fiction, etc. In 2022, nearly two thirds of the adult population (aged 16 or older) in Finland (65.8%) reported having practised an artistic activity at least once during the 12 months prior to the data collection, the highest rate among EU countries. More than half of adults in Denmark, Austria, and Slovakia also reported having practised an artistic activity in the previous 12 months. At the other end of the range, less than 20% of residents in France, Luxembourg, Romania, Croatia, and Italy engaged in artistic activities, with the lowest share observed in Italy (17.3%). It must be stressed that, for artistic practices, in particular those conducted outside a person’s home, the COVID-19 restrictions still in place in 2021 might have had an impact on these figures. By way of reference, in 2015 at EU level, 65.5% of residents said they had not practised any artistic activity in the previous 12 months, ranging from 29.8% in Finland to 87.0% in Romania. In 2022, EU citizens saying they had not practised any artistic activity in the previous 12 months ranged from 34.2% in Finland to 82.7% in Italy. Weekly – or even more frequent – participation in artistic activities was most common among residents of Finland (37.8%), the Netherlands (30.9%), Ireland (28.6%), Austria (26.9%) and Denmark (25.6%). In contrast, weekly – or more frequent – participation in artistic activities engaged fewer than 10% of residents in Portugal, Hungary, Bulgaria, Croatia, Poland, and Romania (see Figure 5).

'''Practising artistic activities by sex and age''' Among European adults who practised artistic activities at least once in the 12 months prior to the survey, women generally participated more frequently than men, (except in Italy where men had a 3 pp higher participation rate). The difference reached up to 21 pp in Finland, where over three quarters of women (76.5%) but only half of men (55.1%) pursued artistic activities in the previous 12 months. Significant differences were also noted in Lithuania (17 pp difference in favour of women) and in Denmark and Sweden (16 pp difference in favour of women). In 12 countries, this difference was less than 5 pp, with the most balanced proportions observed in Malta, where 41.6% of women and 41.0% of men practised artistic activities. Just as is the case with cultural participation, practising artistic activities decreases with age. In 2022, among individuals aged 16 to 29, more than a quarter of women practised artistic activities in 25 EU countries (except Italy) and more than a quarter of men did so in 20 countries (except Poland, Italy, Portugal, Belgium, Luxembourg, and France). However, among those aged 65 or older, more than a quarter of women practised artistic activities in only 13 EU countries, and more than a quarter of men did so in only 11 EU countries. The decline in the percentage of the population practising artistic activities with age was observed for both women and men in almost all EU countries. An inverse trend was only seen in the Netherlands, where the percentage of men practising artistic activities consistently increased with age. In the Netherlands, 39.0% of men aged 16-29 engaged in artistic activities, compared with 48.3% of men aged 65 and over (see Table 5).

=== Data sources=== Statistical concepts and definitions for [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions income and living conditions domain (EU-SILC)] are specified in [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32019R1700&from=en Regulation (EU) 2019/1700], [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32019R2181&from=EN Regulation (EU) 2019/2181] and [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32019R2242&from=EN Regulation (EU) 2019/2242]. Countries must follow the annex of Regulation (EU) 2019/2242, where the list of variables is set out, including their methods, flags, units and reference periods. A more detailed description of the list of variables as well as information on their implementation are available in the [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/853b48e6-a00f-4d22-87db-c40bafd0161d/library/8db0fafd-a762-4427-bd03-ec0ad72e2914/details methodological guidelines]. In 2022, in addition to annual data, the EU-SILC contained a module on [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2020.386.01.0009.01.ENG health] (with data collected every 3 years) and a module on [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2020.386.01.0009.01.ENG quality of life] (with data collected every 6 years). The data were collected in all 27 EU Member States, in 3 of the EFTA countries (Iceland, Norway and Switzerland), as well as in Montenegro, Serbia and Türkiye. The target population was people aged 16 years or more, while the reference period was 12 months prior to the interview. The questionnaire of the 2022 module on quality of life covered the following cultural activities: *going to the cinema (in other words, film screenings at motion-picture theatres); *attending live performances by professionals or amateurs (for example theatre, dance, music); *visiting cultural sites (trips to historical monuments, museums, art galleries or archaeological sites); *practising of artistic activities (for example, playing an instrument, composing music, singing, dancing, acting, photography/filmmaking, drawing, painting, sculpting, engaging in other visual arts/handcrafts, writing poems/short stories/fiction, and so on); *reading books (having read books – including eBooks and audiobooks in the 12 months preceding the data collection). This module also included questions related to the reasons for non-participation in cultural activities, and Eurostat disseminated several indicators that were broken down by sex, age, degree of urbanisation, poverty or social-exclusion situation, disability and more. In the ‘Income and Living Conditions’ section, you will find more information about the definitions of the main indicators and concepts used [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Category:Living_conditions_glossary (Living conditions glossary)].
=== Context === Culture is one of Europe’s greatest assets: it is a source of values and identity and provides a sense of belonging. It also contributes to well-being, social cohesion and inclusion. The cultural and creative sectors provide a stimulus for economic growth, job creation and international trade. The EU has initiated the [https://culture.ec.europa.eu/creative-europe Creative Europe programme] alongside several policy actions within the EU Work Plan for Culture 2023-2026. The work plan, adopted by EU culture ministers in December 2022, sets out 4 main priorities for European cooperation in cultural policymaking: * Artists and cultural professionals: empowering the cultural and creative sectors. * Culture for the people: enhancing cultural participation and the role of culture in society. * Culture for the planet: unleashing the power of culture. * Culture for co-creative partnerships: strengthening the cultural dimension of EU external relations. Producing reliable, comparable and up-to-date cultural statistics, which provide a basis for sound cultural policymaking, is a cross-sectoral priority for the European Commission. Eurostat compiles culture statistics from various data collections to provide policymakers and other users of statistics with information on the main developments in culture, covering areas like education, employment, business, international trade, participation patterns and consumption patterns. ===Other articles=== *Cultural participation (cult_pcs): **[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Culture_statistics_-_use_of_ICT_for_cultural_purposes Culture statistics – use of ICT for cultural purposes] **[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Culture_statistics_-_household_expenditure_on_culture Culture statistics – household expenditure on culture] *[[Culture]] (all Statistics Explained articles on culture) === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/culture/database Culture (cult)], see: **Cultural participation ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database?node_code=cult_pcs cult_pcs]) ::: • Participation in cultural activities - EU-SILC, Quality of Life module ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database?node_code=cult_pcs_ilc cult_pcs_ilc]) :::: • Persons participating in cultural or sport activities in the last 12 months by sex, age, educational attainment, activity type and frequency (ilc_scp03) :::: • Persons participating in in cultural or sport activities in the last 12 months by income quintile, household composition, degree of urbanisation, activity type and frequency (ilc_scp04) :::: • Persons not participating in cultural or sport activities in the last 12 months by sex, age, educational attainment, activity type and reasons (ilc_scp05) :::: • Persons practicing artistic activities by sex, age, educational attainment and frequency (ilc_scp07) :::: • Persons reading books in the last 12 months by sex, age, educational attainment and number of books (ilc_scp27) :::: • Persons participating in cultural or sport activities by sex, age, level of disability (activity limitation), activity type and frequency (ilc_scp37) ===Thematic section=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/culture/overview Culture] ===Publications=== * [[Culture_statistics|Culture statistics — online publication]] *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-18-011|title=Guide to Eurostat culture statistics — 2018 edition}} ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-18-011|title=Guide to Eurostat culture statistics — 2018 edition}} *[https://ec.europa.eu/assets/eac/culture/library/reports/ess-net-report_en.pdf European statistical system network on culture (ESSnet-Culture final report (2012))] *{{Template:Esms|code=cult_pcs_esms|title=Cultural participation}} (ESMS metadata file — cult_pcs_esms)
