title: Culture statistics - cultural enterprises
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of culture enterprises. Data extracted in December 2025 Planned article update: January 2027 In 2023, 2.1 million cultural enterprises in the EU generated around €202 billion value added, 1.9% of the total business economy. The cultural sector’s [[Glossary:Net_turnover_-_EBS|net turnover]] was around €524 billion, 1.4% of the total net turnover generated within the EU’s business economy in 2023. In 2023, small and medium-sized enterprises generated most of the EU cultural sector’s value added. This article presents 2023 statistics concerning enterprises in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7bb7c598-a254-428d-a9b8-f08792d86152?lang=en cultural sector]. It is part of the online publication ''[[Culture_statistics|Culture statistics]]''. [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] compiles these figures from two primary sources: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/overview Structural Business Statistics] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/business-demography business demography statistics]. ===Key indicators for cultural enterprises in the EU=== In 2023, there were about 2.1 million cultural enterprises in the EU, representing 6.4% of all businesses within the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Business_economy business economy]. Over a quarter of these enterprises were involved in 'Creative, arts and entertainment activities' (28.6%), while 'Printing and reproduction of recorded media; manufacture of musical instruments and jewellery' represented the largest share of the total value added by the EU’s cultural sector (15.1%). Table 1 highlights the cultural sector’s importance by illustrating its share within the business economy. In terms of the number of businesses, the Netherlands (11.0%) and Sweden (10.9%) had notably high shares. Conversely, cultural enterprises formed less than 5% of the total business economy in 6 EU countries, with Bulgaria (3.2%) and Slovakia (3.1%) having the smallest shares. Cyprus had the highest share of value added generated by cultural enterprises relative to its national business economy (5.4%), followed by Finland and Malta (both at 2.6%). Cyprus also recorded the highest turnover share for cultural enterprises (5.0%), followed by France (1.8%), Sweden and Finland (both at 1.7%).

[[Image:Table 1 - Key indicators for cultural enterprises, 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Key indicators for cultural enterprises, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a4c114a4-34dc-47ef-9707-6d61a5260284?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-09T09:43:05Z sbs_ovw_act)]|alt= Table showing main indicators for cultural enterprises in the EU, individual EU countries, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries for the year 2026. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
In 2023, just over half of all cultural enterprises in the EU (51.8%) were located in 4 EU countries: France (18.0%), Italy (12.6%), the Netherlands (12.1%) and Spain (9.2%). Germany contributed the largest share of value added by cultural enterprises in the EU (25.5% of the EU total), followed by France (18.7%) and Italy (11.7%). Combined, these 3 countries made up 55.9% of the total value added. They also accounted for 54.5% of the EU cultural sector’s turnover.

[[Image:Figure 1 - EU Member States' shares in the EU total for main indicators concerning the cultural sector, 2023_(%, share of EU total).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: EU Countries' shares in the EU total for main indicators concerning the cultural sector, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2c408ec8-4493-40d6-af17-5e92a0be20ef?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-09T09:47:35Z sbs_ovw_act)]|alt= Scatter chart showing EU countries' shares in the EU total for main indictors concerning the cultural sector as a percentage share of the EU total in the year 2023. Each EU country has three scatter plots representing the number of enterprises, value added at factor cost and turnover. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Number of enterprises and value added by product category === The various economic activities collectively form the total cultural aggregate, providing a statistical snapshot of enterprises within the cultural sector. These activities are grouped under the following broad headings: :*'Printing and reproduction of recorded media; manufacture of musical instruments and jewellery' :*'Retail sale of cultural goods in specialised stores' :*'Publishing' :*'Motion picture and television, sound recording and music publishing; renting of video tapes and discs' :*'Programming and broadcasting; news agency activities' :*'Architectural activities' :*'Specialised design activities' :*'Photographic activities' :*'Translation and interpretation activities' :*'Cultural education' :*'Creative, arts and entertainment activities' :*'Libraries, archives, museums and other cultural activities' The economic activities listed under each broad heading are presented in Table 3 of the ''Coverage and data sources'' section.
'''In 2023, the majority of cultural enterprises were involved in 'Creative, arts and entertainment activities'.''' Among all cultural enterprises operating in the EU in 2023, the largest number was engaged in 'Creative, arts and entertainment activities' (28.6%). Additionally, two other broad headings had a double-digit share of the total number of cultural enterprises (see Figure 2): 'Architectural activities' (15.8%) and 'Specialised design activities' (14.3%).

[[Image:Figure 2 - Number of cultural enterprises, by broad heading, EU, 2023(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Number of cultural enterprises, by broad heading, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4c047a31-ce90-41ed-9e6d-2102a641c230?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-09T09:48:29Z sbs_ovw_act)]|alt= Doughnut chart showing number of cultural enterprises by broad heading as a percentage share of total in the EU for the year 2023. The chart consists of seven broad headings, a group of other activities, and a group of unspecified cultural sector activities, totalling one hundred percent. Additionally the stack column shows detailed values of broad headings grouped as other activities. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Although 'Creative, arts, and entertainment activities' represented the largest area in terms of the number of enterprises, Figure 3 shows that in 2023, at least half of value added generated by cultural enterprises came from the following groups of activities: :*'Printing and reproduction of recorded media; manufacture of musical instruments and jewellery' (15.1%) :*'Motion picture and television, sound recording and music publishing; renting of video tapes and discs' (14.9%) :*'Architectural activities' (14.9%) :*'Publishing' (14.1%).
[[Image:Figure 3 - Value added for the cultural sector, by broad heading, EU, 2023(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Value added for the cultural sector, by broad heading, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bd07acfb-9c1f-4e5a-be41-74bf66131979?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-09T09:55:26Z sbs_ovw_act)]|alt= Doughnut chart showing value added at factor cost for the cultural sector by broad heading as a percentage share of total in the EU for the year 2023. The chart consists of seven broad headings, a group of other activities, and a group of unspecified cultural sector activities, totalling one hundred percent. Additionally the stack column shows detailed values of broad headings grouped as other activities. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Among all types of cultural activities, 'Programming and broadcasting; news agency activities' stood out for the economic value relative to the number of enterprises. With just 0.7% of the total number of cultural enterprises, these activities generated 8.0% of the sector's total value added in the EU (€16.0 billion). Conversely, activities related to 'Cultural education', which accounted for 3.9% of enterprises in the sector, generated 0.8% of the cultural sector’s total value added (€1.7 billion). Country-level data reveal that in 2023, 'Creative, arts and entertainment activities' had the largest share of cultural enterprises in 17 EU countries, led by Sweden, where 45.6% of all cultural enterprises were active in that field. 'Architectural activities' formed the largest group of business activities in the cultural sector in 7 EU countries, led by Belgium, where they accounted for 31.6% of all cultural enterprises. Cultural enterprises involved in 'Specialised design activities' were most numerous in Croatia (23.3%) and Denmark (21.8%), see Figure 4.

[[Image:Figure 4 - Number of cultural enterprises, by broad heading, 2023_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Number of cultural enterprises, by broad heading, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c43ab2e2-b0a8-4eeb-9c77-c2448909f02f?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-09T10:18:33Z sbs_ovw_act)]|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing number of cultural enterprises by broad heading as a percentage for the EU, individual EU countries, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries in the year 2023. Each country column totals one hundred percent and contains ten stacks that represent the broad headings. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Figure 5 provides a similar national breakdown by broad headings based on value added generated. In 2023, in 13 EU countries, manufacturing-related cultural activities accounted for the largest share of value added ('Printing and reproduction of recorded media; manufacture of musical instruments and jewellery'). The share was highest at 41.6% in Malta. In 4 EU countries, led by Cyprus (76.8%), the highest value added within the cultural sector was generated by 'Publishing' activities (including books; newspapers; journals and periodicals; computer games). In France (21.2%), Spain (18.2%) and Belgium (17.3%) the largest share was attributed to 'Motion picture and television, sound recording and music publishing; renting of video tapes and discs'. In Luxembourg (37.4%), Austria (25.1%) and Germany (19.7%), 'Architectural activities' accounted for the highest shares of value added; while in the Netherlands (22.4%) Denmark (18.3%) and Portugal (16.6%) the largest contributions came from 'Creative, arts and entertainment activities'.

[[Image:Figure 5 - Value added of the cultural sector, by broad heading, 2023_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Value added of the cultural sector, by broad heading, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e9836013-37fc-4756-a7ae-800355c3103f?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-09T11:18:29Z sbs_ovw_act)]|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing value added at factor cost for the cultural sector by broad heading as a percentage for the EU, individual EU countries, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries in the year 2023. Each country column totals one hundred percent and contains ten stacks that represent the broad headings. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===How big are the enterprises in the cultural sector?=== Businesses employing fewer than 250 people, referred to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), are essential to the EU economy and they tend to dominate in several branches of the EU’s cultural sector. Table 2 shows indicators presented above further broken down by business size (defined by the number of people employed). In 2023, SMEs employed the majority of the EU’s workers across the various economic activities related to culture. The only exception was in 'Programming and broadcasting activities', where two-thirds of people (68.7%) were employed by large companies. Additionally, most EU workers in 'Photographic activities' (91.8%), 'Specialised design activities' (82.4%), and 'Translation and interpretation activities' (75.2%) were employed by micro enterprises (employing fewer than 10 people). Moreover, in 2023 SMEs generated most of the EU cultural sector’s value added. This is true for all branches for which data were available, except 'Programming and broadcasting activities'.

[[Image:Table 2 - Key indicators for selected cultural activities, by enterprise size class, EU, 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Key indicators for selected cultural activities, by enterprise size class, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7068fe26-a859-4d89-b717-ddfe70dea81b?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-09T11:19:12Z sbs_sc_ovw)]|alt= Table showing key indicators for selected cultural activities by enterprises size class in the EU for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Which cultural sectors experience the most business start-ups (and closures)?=== Business demography statistics include indicators such as business birth and death rates. This information is used to analyse demographic trends, reflecting the dynamism with which economic structures adapt to changing market conditions (definitions of the indicators analysed are available below in the ''Coverage and data sources'' section of the article). For analysing cultural activities, business demography statistics are compiled for a limited subset of activities within the service sector (see Table 3 for a complete list).

'''In specialised design activities, approximately 1 in 6 enterprises were newly established in 2023.''' Figure 6 provides a summary of enterprise birth and death rates for a selection of cultural activities, along with their corresponding employment shares. In 2023, the EU enterprise birth rate for services within the business economy was 10.7% (NACE Sections G to S, excluding Section O: public administration and defence; compulsory social security and Division 94: activities of membership organisations), indicating that for every 100 active enterprises, approximately 11 were newly established during the reference period. Out of 7 listed cultural activities, 4 reported an enterprise birth rate higher than the average for all services in the business economy. The highest enterprise birth rate was observed in 'Specialised design activities' (15.9%). Meanwhile, the EU enterprise death rate for services in the business economy was 8.6%, 2.1 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] lower than the enterprise birth rate. Furthermore, 4 of the 7 listed cultural activities reported enterprise death rates higher than the average for services in the business economy. Within the cultural sector, 'Specialised design activities' recorded the highest death rate (10.9%), and 'Programming and broadcasting activities' the lowest (5.7%). In 2023, start-ups (newly established enterprises) employed 10.6% of all people in 'Specialised design activities', which was more than 4 times the average employment share of new enterprises across the entire service sector in the EU (2.7%). Other culture-related activities where start-ups had notably high employment shares included 'Photographic activities' (10.4%), and 'Translation and interpretation activities' (6.7%). However, economic activities with a high share of people employed in new enterprises also tended to have a high share of people employed in businesses that ceased operations. In 2023, at least 6% of people employed in each of the 3 cultural fields mentioned above were working in enterprises that closed. Overall, the ratio of employment in start-ups to employment in businesses that ceased operations was highest for 'Motion picture, video and television programme production, sound recording and music publishing activities', where 5.4% of people were employed in newly established enterprises, compared with 3.5% of people in businesses that closed. Conversely, in 'Programming and broadcasting activities' and 'Translation and interpretation activities', shares of employment in businesses that started operations were only slightly higher than in those that closed, while for 'Libraries, archives, museums, and other cultural activities', the share of employment in newly established enterprises was lower than in those that closed.

[[Image:Figure 6 - Enterprise birth and death rates and employment shares for _selected cultural activities, EU, 2023_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Enterprise birth and death rates alongside employment shares for selected cultural activities, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/53d1198c-b7d8-4889-833e-faba4b348226?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-09T11:19:31Z bd_size)]|alt= Combined vertical bar chart illustrating enterprise birth and death rates and corresponding employment shares for selected cultural activities in the European Union in 2023. The chart features eight categories, each divided into two columns: one representing the birth rate and employment share of enterprise births and the other showing the death rate and employment share of enterprise closures. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
In 2023, the employment share of start-ups in specialised design activities was at least twice as high as the average for all services in the business economy in each EU country where such a comparison could be made (i.e. excluding Finland and Portugal). This relationship was most pronounced in France, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, where this share was more than 6 times higher than the average for all services in the business economy. The highest employment share in start-ups for specialised design activities was recorded in Malta (17.7%), while the lowest was observed in Austria (4.2%). The employment share for new enterprises in 'Creative, arts and entertainment activities' was at least twice as high as the average for services in the business economy in every EU country for which the complete set of data is available (i.e. excluding Ireland and Portugal). Within this field of activity, Malta also recorded the highest employment share among newly created businesses (30.5%), while the lowest was observed in Finland (4.2%, see Figure 7).

[[Image:Figure 7 - Employment share of newly born enterprises for selected cultural activities, 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Employment share of newly born enterprises for selected cultural activities, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bb9d78ab-97a5-4e1b-8acb-22c0cfeab278?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-09T11:21:00Z bd_size)]|alt= Combined vertical bar chart and scatter chart showing employment share of newly born enterprises for selected cultural activities as a percentage share of total employment for each activity in the EU, individual EU countries, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries for the year 2023. Each country has two columns representing specialised design activities and creative arts and entertainment activities. The scatter plot line across the two columns represents services in the business economy. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=Culture statistics - cultural enterprises 2025 figures (2023 data) adj v3.xlsx|title=Cultural enterprises: tables and figures}}
===Coverage and data sources=== Full details of the NACE codes in this article are given in Table 3.
[[Image:Table 3 - Cultural activities covered by the EU's structural business statistics and business demography statistics.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Cultural activities covered by the EU's Structural Business Statistics and business demography statistics
''Source:'' Eurostat, [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/KS-GQ-18-011 Guide to Eurostat culture statistics, 2018 edition]|alt= Table showing cultural activities covered by the EU’s structural business statistics and business demography statistics sourced from the Guide to Eurostat culture statistics, 2018 edition. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Eurostat compiles data on cultural enterprises from 2 distinct sources: :*[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/overview Structural Business Statistics] :*[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/business-demography Business demography statistics] Both statistics are restricted to market-oriented activities.


'''Structural Business Statistics''' Structural Business Statistics cover industry, construction, trade and market services, as defined by the [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|statistical classification of economic activities (NACE)]]. This classification enables a detailed sectoral breakdown of business activities. The information is available for a broad range of structural indicators (including data for the number of enterprises, the number of people employed, turnover and value added) and can also be broken down by business size. The version of NACE currently used in the European Statistical System is NACE Rev. 2, implemented since 2008. Structural Business Statistics describe the structure, conduct and performance of enterprises within the non-financial business economy (NACE Sections B to S, except public administration and defence, compulsory social security, and activities of membership organisations). Starting with the reference year 2021, Structural Business Statistics are compiled under [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/2152/oj Regulation (EU) 2019/2152] and its implementing act, [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2020/1197/oj Regulation (EU) 2020/1197]. The data presented for the cultural sector cover various economic activities classified under NACE Rev. 2 – see Table 3 for the composition of the total cultural sector aggregate and other aggregates describing the cultural sector in the main series of Structural Business Statistics. Regulation (EU) 2019/2152 extended the statistical coverage of business statistics, making available for the first time from reference year 2021 the following cultural activities: :*Division 90 (Creative, arts, and entertainment activities) :*Division 91 (Libraries, archives, museums, and other cultural activities) :*Class 85.52 (Cultural education) Historical data remain accessible to users at Eurostat’s database under code [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/culture/database?node_code=cult_ent_h '''cult_ent_h''']. Within the context of Structural Business Statistics, the following definitions apply: *The '''enterprise''' as defined in [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/1993/696/oj/eng Council Regulation (EEC) No 696/93] is the smallest combination of legal units that form an organisational unit producing goods or services, which benefits from a certain degree of autonomy when making decisions, especially those on allocating its current resources. An enterprise carries out one or more activities at one or more locations. It may be a sole legal unit. The term enterprise is used in this article to refer to the number of active enterprises. *'''The number of active enterprises''' is the number of all statistical units which at any time during the reference period were enterprises, as defined in Council Regulation (EEC) No 696/93, and active during the same reference period. A statistical unit is considered to have been active during the reference period, if during that period it # had a positive net turnover # produced outputs # had employees or # carried out investments. *'''The number of employees and self-employed persons (the number of persons employed)''' is the sum of the number of employees and number of self-employed persons. The number of employees represents the average number of people who were, at some time during the reference period, employees of the statistical unit. The number of self-employed persons is the average number of people who were at some time during the reference period the sole owners or joint owners of the statistical unit in which they work. Family workers and outworkers (people who work away from their employer’s premises) whose income is a function of the value of the outputs of the statistical unit are also included. *'''Net turnover''' consists of all income arising during the reference period during ordinary activities of the statistical unit, and is presented net of all price reductions, discounts and rebates granted by it. :Excluded from net turnover are: ::- all taxes, duties or levies linked directly to revenue ::– any amounts collected on behalf of any principal, if the statistical unit is acting as an agent in its relationship with this principal ::- all income not arising in the course of ordinary activities that the statistical unit carries out. Usually, these types of income are classified as Other (operating) income, Financial income, Extra-ordinary income or under a similar heading, depending on the respective set of generally accepted accounting standards used to prepare the financial statements. *'''Value added''' is a composite indicator of net operating income, adjusted for depreciation, amortisation and employee benefits, all components recognised as such by the statistical unit during the reference period. Its value is given by the formula: ::- net turnover (+) ::- income from product- or turnover-related subsidies (+) ::- capitalized output (+) ::- change in stock of goods (±) ::- total purchases of goods and services (-) :Alternatively, it can be calculated from the gross operating surplus by adding personnel costs. Structural Business Statistics may be broken down by the following business size classes for analytical purposes. *'''Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)''' employing 1 to 249 people, composed of: **micro enterprises with fewer than 10 people employed **small enterprises with 10 to 49 people employed **medium-sized enterprises with 50 to 249 people employed. They should also have an annual turnover of up to €50 million, or a balance sheet total of no more than €43 million. *'''Large enterprises''' with 250 or more people employed.
'''Business demography statistics''' Business demography statistics cover information for business births and deaths, as well as indicators relating to survival rates or the impact newly founded enterprises have on employment. These statistics are usually drawn from business registers, although some EU Member States seek to increase data availability by integrating alternative sources. Within the context of business demography statistics, the following definitions are applied: *An '''active enterprise''' – an enterprise is considered to have been active if, in the period concerned, it # had a positive net turnover # produced outputs # had employees # carried out investments. *An '''enterprise birth''' refers to a count of newly established enterprises registered in the relevant population in the business register, adjusted for errors. An enterprise birth amounts to the creation of a combination of production factors with the restriction that no other enterprises are involved in the event. These births do not include entries into the population due to mergers, break-ups, split offs or the restructuring of a set of enterprises. It does not include entries into a sub-population that result only from a change of activity. *The '''enterprise birth rate''' for a given reference period (usually one calendar year) is defined as the number of enterprise births, expressed as a percentage of the total number of active enterprises. *An '''enterprise death''' refers to a count of the number of deaths of enterprises registered in the population concerned in the business register corrected for errors. An enterprise death amounts to the dissolution of a combination of production factors with the restriction that no other enterprises are involved in the event. These deaths do not include exits from the population due to mergers, takeovers, break-ups or the restructuring of a set of enterprises. It does not include exits from a sub-population that result only from a change of activity. *The '''enterprise death rate''' for a given reference period (usually one calendar year) is defined as the number of enterprise deaths, expressed as a percentage of the total number of active enterprises.


'''Note on data coverage and confidentiality''' When aggregates are based on incomplete coverage, estimates may be published. In such cases, data are flagged with the symbol 'e' to indicate an estimated value. This estimation is applied when the relative difference between the rounded and actual value — calculated as (rounded value – real value) / real value × 100 — is less than or equal to 5%. The estimate of '''2 100 000 cultural enterprises''' in the EU, used exclusively for this article, is based on data for EU countries available at the most detailed, NACE 4-digit level. Due to confidentiality, certain NACE codes were excluded from the calculations: :* number of cultural enterprises: 32.12 ('Manufacture of jewellery and related articles') – France; 32.20 ('Manufacture of musical instruments') – Cyprus :* value added: 32.20 – Cyprus; 47.61 ('Retail sale of books in specialised stores') – Romania; 58.13 ('Publishing of newspapers') – Italy; 58.20 ('Publishing of computer games') – the Netherlands :* turnover: 32.20 – Cyprus; 58.13 – Italy; 58.20 – the Netherlands. Estimated, provisional and incomplete data are indicated in the footnotes to the published tables and figures. ===Context=== Culture is one of Europe's greatest assets: it is a source of values, identity and a sense of belonging. It also contributes to well-being, social cohesion and inclusion. The cultural and creative sectors provide a stimulus for economic growth, job creation and international trade. The EU has initiated the [https://culture.ec.europa.eu/creative-europe Creative Europe programme] alongside several policy actions within the EU Work Plan for Culture 2023-2026. The work plan, adopted by EU culture ministers in December 2022, sets out 4 main priorities for European cooperation in cultural policymaking: :*Artists and cultural professionals: empowering the cultural and creative sectors. :*Culture for the people: enhancing cultural participation and the role of culture in society. :*Culture for the planet: unleashing the power of culture. :*Culture for co-creative partnerships: strengthening the cultural dimension of EU external relations. Producing reliable, comparable and up-to-date cultural statistics, which provide a basis for sound cultural policymaking, is a cross-sectoral priority for the European Commission. Eurostat compiles culture statistics from various data collections to provide policymakers and other users of statistics with information on the main developments in culture, covering areas like education, employment, business, international trade, participation patterns and consumption patterns.

title: Culture statistics - culture-related education
text:
Data on culture-related education are largely derived from a joint data collection exercise based on administrative data that is run by UNESCO, the OECD and Eurostat; there are also data presented from the EU's latest adult education survey. Data extracted in June 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 In 2024, 13.7% of tertiary students in the EU were studying in culture-related fields. Between 2019 and 2024, among all students pursuing culture-related fields of education, the number of students in arts increased the most. Women accounted for close to two thirds of all tertiary students in culture-related fields.
This article forms part of the '''[[Culture_statistics|Culture statistics]]''' online publication. It describes two areas that link education with culture: *tertiary students who are studying culture-related fields; *the role played by education in facilitating cultural exchanges, for example by learning foreign languages. The definition of culture-related education used in these statistics is provided in the [[#Data_sources|Data sources]] section.
===Tertiary students in culture-related fields of education=== '''Tertiary students – around 2.6 million studying in culture-related fields across the EU in 2024'''

In 2024 there were around 2.6 million students in the EU studying in culture-related fields. This represented 13.7% of all tertiary students in the EU (see Figure 1). The share of students in culture-related fields was higher than the EU average in 6 EU countries. The largest share was in Italy at 19.7%, followed by Sweden (17.1%), Estonia (15.9%), Greece (14.9%), France (14.5%) and Germany (14.2%). The smallest shares of tertiary students in culture-related fields were in Malta (9.5%), Luxembourg (8.4%), Slovenia (8.2%), Cyprus (8.0%) and the Netherlands (7.0%).

[[Image:Figure 1 - Tertiary students in culture-related fields of education, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Tertiary students in culture-related fields of education, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/educ_uoe_enrt03__custom_16423054/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=a6f68b00-5cc3-435c-a1dd-ea4bb59c3dcb&c=1745834428409 (educ_uoe_enrt03)]|alt= Vertical bar chart showing percentage share of tertiary students in culture-related fields of education in the EU, individual EU Member States, EFTA countries, Türkiye, Serbia, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Albania and Bosnia and Herzegovina for the year 2024.]]
'''Between 2019 and 2024, the number of people studying arts increased the most among all those pursuing culture-related fields of education'''

Table 1 compares the number of students in 2024 with those in 2019 at national level. It shows that in this timeframe, 14 of the 27 EU countries with available data saw an increase in the number of students in culture-related fields. An increase in the total number of tertiary students was seen in 19 EU countries. The highest increases in the number of students in culture-related fields were recorded in Sweden (21.0%), Hungary (19.0%) and Italy (17.0%). An increase in the number of students in culture-related fields of education was also observed in 11 other EU countries. Conversely, Denmark (-18.0%), Lithuania (-15.0%), Luxembourg and Slovenia (both -13.0%) and Poland (-11.0%) recorded the largest decreases. In Denmark and Bulgaria the number of students decreased in all culture-related fields of education. The highest increase in the number of students was observed in arts. This growth concerned 21 out of 26 EU countries with available data. Malta, Greece and Croatia saw the most significant growth in arts students, with 41.0%, 30.0% and 23.0% respectively. 'Architecture and town planning' saw an increase in 16 EU countries, 'journalism and information' in 10 countries and 'humanities and languages' in 9 countries. The most significant decreases among all culture-related fields of education were seen in 'architecture and town planning', dropping by 51.0% in Lithuania and by 47.0% in Malta between 2019 and 2024.

[[Image:Table 1 - Number of students in culture-related fields of education, 2019 and 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Number of students in culture-related fields of education, 2019 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/EDUC_UOE_ENRT03__custom_22067670/default/table (educ_uoe_enrt03)]|alt= Table showing the number in thousands and percentage change of students in culture related fields of education in the EU, individual EU Member States, EFTA countries, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Albania, Serbia and Türkiye for the years 2019 and 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''In most EU countries, the highest number of students in culture-related tertiary education were enrolled in humanities and languages''''

Figure 2 provides a breakdown of culture-related fields that tertiary students studied in 2024. 'Humanities and languages' was the most common field of study in the EU (more than 1.2 million tertiary students), representing almost half (45.9%) of all tertiary students in culture-related disciplines. Otherwise, 28.0% of the EU students in culture-related fields in 2024 were enrolled in arts, while 9.6% were studying journalism and information studies, 8.9% were studying architecture and town planning and 7.1% were studying in other fields related to arts and humanities (the latter include arts and humanities not further defined, together with interdisciplinary programmes and qualifications involving arts and humanities). Humanities and languages account for the greatest share of tertiary students in culture-related fields. In 2024, this was observed in 19 of the 26 EU countries with available data, with the greatest share recorded in Luxembourg (78.1%), followed by Romania (59.1%) and Sweden (54.3%). In the remaining 7 countries (where humanities and languages were not the most common subjects), arts had the greatest share of tertiary students in culture-related fields. Ireland and Malta were the only EU countries where 'arts' was chosen by more than half (59.9% and 50.6% respectively) of all students in culture-related fields. The largest shares of tertiary students in journalism and information studies were reported in Slovakia (24.1%), followed by Lithuania (22.4%) and Croatia (16.9%), while the largest shares for town planning and architecture were reported in Austria (18.8%) and Belgium (18.4%).

[[Image:Figure 2 Distribution of tertiary students in culture-related fields of education, 2024 (%, share of all tertiary students in culture-related fields).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Distribution of tertiary students in culture-related fields of education, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/EDUC_UOE_ENRT03__custom_22067724/default/table (code=educ_uoe_enrt03)]|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage share distribution of tertiary students in culture-related fields of education in the EU, individual EU Member States, EFTA countries, Türkiye, North Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Albania, Montenegro and Serbia for the year 2024. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has at most five stacks representing culture-related fields. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''Women accounted for most tertiary students in each of the culture-related fields of study'''

In 2024, there were more female than male tertiary education students in the EU studying culture-related fields, with women accounting for 64.8% of the total (see Figure 3). The share of women was slightly greater among those studying journalism and information studies (69.3%) and humanities and languages (66.8%), while the gap between the sexes was much less pronounced for those studying architecture and town planning, where women accounted for 57.2% of all students.

[[Image:Figure 3 Tertiary students in culture-related fields of education, by sex, EU, 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Tertiary students in culture-related fields of education, by sex, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/EDUC_UOE_ENRT03__custom_22069054/default/table (educ_uoe_enrt03)]|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage tertiary students in culture-related fields of education by sex in the EU. Five sections represent all fields and four specific fields. Totalling 100 percent, each section column has two stacks representing women and men for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Foreign languages===
'''In 2024, lower secondary school pupils in Luxembourg, Finland, Malta and the Netherlands were taught at least 2 foreign languages on average'''
* In 2024, the average number of foreign languages learnt by pupils in lower secondary education (ISCED level 2) was higher than 2 in Luxembourg (2.2), Finland (2.2), Malta and the Netherlands (2.1). Ireland (0.8) recorded the lowest average number of foreign languages at ISCED level 2. * The average number of foreign languages studied by pupils in upper secondary general education (ISCED level 3) peaked at 2.5 in Luxembourg. It was higher than 2 in Finland, in the Flemish community of Belgium and in Slovakia. By contrast, Portuguese and Irish pupils in upper secondary general education were studying just 0.8 foreign languages on average. Generally, there was less focus on teaching foreign languages in vocational compared with upper secondary general education. Poland, Italy, Cyprus, Portugal and Romania did not show significant differences regarding the number of foreign languages between these 2 educational paths. The average number of foreign languages studied by pupils enrolled in upper secondary vocational education in Estonia, Portugal, the Netherlands, Greece, Lithuania, Germany, Spain and Denmark was less than 1.0 (see Figure 4).

[[Image:Figure 4 - Average number of foreign languages studied per pupil in secondary education, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Average number of foreign languages studied per pupil in secondary education, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/EDUC_UOE_LANG03__custom_22069869/default/table (educ_uoe_lang03)]|alt= Scatter chart showing average number of foreign languages studied per pupil in secondary education in the EU, individual EU Member States, Iceland, Norway, North Macedonia, Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina for the year 2024. Each country has three scatter plots representing lower secondary, upper secondary general and upper secondary vocational. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''English is the most common foreign language taught to upper secondary pupils in the EU'''

Table 2 shows that English was by far the most taught foreign language in upper secondary general education in the EU. The next most taught foreign languages were Spanish, German and French. In 2024, across most EU countries, 96.0% of upper secondary general education pupils were learning English as a foreign language. In 11 countries, this figure reached 100%, meaning that all pupils were studying English. The exceptions, where fewer than 90.0% of pupils learnt English as a foreign language, were Hungary (89.0%), Bulgaria (88.0%), Luxembourg (83.0%), Denmark (79.0%) and Portugal (67.0%). In addition to English, looking at the next most frequently studied foreign language in upper secondary general education in each of the EU countries, German and French appear 8 times and Spanish 6 times. Close geographic and historical ties also influence which foreign languages pupils learn. In 2024, the second most frequently taught foreign language in the [[Glossary:Baltic_Member_States|Baltic countries]] was Russian, in Malta it was Italian, and in Finland Swedish.

[[Image:Table 2 - Four most-learnt foreign languages in upper secondary general education, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Four most-learnt foreign languages in upper secondary general education, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/EDUC_UOE_LANG01__custom_22070276/default/table (educ_uoe_lang01)]|alt= Table showing percentage share of pupils learning each of the 4 most learnt foreign languages in upper secondary general education in the EU, individual EU Member States, Norway, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia and Serbia for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Culture_statistics - culture-related education (2026).xlsx|title=Culture-related education: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The education statistics presented in this article draw principally on a joint exercise run by [[Glossary:United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)|UNESCO]], the [[Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)|OECD]] and [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] known as the [[UNESCO_OECD_Eurostat_(UOE)_joint_data_collection_–_methodology|UOE data collection]]. It provides annual statistics on the participation in and the completion of education programmes by pupils and students, as well as data on education staff and education spending.

'''Tertiary students in culture-related fields of education''' The [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|international standard classification of education (ISCED)]] is the reference classification for organising educational programmes and related qualifications by levels and fields. ISCED 2011 took into account a range of changes to education systems (for example, those relating to the [https://ec.europa.eu/education/policies/higher-education/bologna-process-and-european-higher-education-area_en Bologna process] in tertiary education, or the expansion of education programmes for very young children). Levels of education are classified by ISCED 2011 as follows
*ISCED 0: early childhood education *ISCED 1: primary education *ISCED 2: lower secondary education *ISCED 3: upper secondary education *ISCED 4: post-secondary non-tertiary education *ISCED 5: short-cycle tertiary education *ISCED 6: bachelor's or equivalent level *ISCED 7: master's or equivalent level *ISCED 8: doctoral or equivalent level
ISCED also classifies fields of education and training ([http://uis.unesco.org/sites/default/files/documents/international-standard-classification-of-education-fields-of-education-and-training-2013-detailed-field-descriptions-2015-en.pdf ISCED-F 2013]). Within this classification, the following fields have been identified as being related to culture: * ISCED-F 02: Arts and Humanities (fine arts, music and performing arts, audio-visual techniques and media production, design, craft skills, religion, history and archaeology, philosophy and ethics, language acquisition, literature and linguistics, etc.); * ISCED-F032: journalism and information (journalism and reporting, library, information, archiving); * ISCED-F0522: natural environments and wildlife; * ISCED-F 0731: architecture and town planning.
'''Foreign languages'''
Within the UOE data collection, Eurostat gathers information on foreign language teaching in primary and secondary educational programmes. The educational curriculum drawn up in each country defines the languages considered as foreign languages. Regional languages are included if they are considered as alternatives to foreign languages. Non-nationals studying their native language in special classes or those studying the language(s) of the host country are excluded. Foreign languages learnt in formal education include all modern languages taught as foreign languages; ancient Greek, Latin, Esperanto and sign languages are excluded. Only foreign languages studied as compulsory subjects or as compulsory curriculum options are included.

===Context=== Culture is one of Europe’s greatest assets: it is a source of values, identity and a sense of belonging. It also contributes to well-being, social cohesion and inclusion. The cultural and creative sectors provide a stimulus for economic growth, job creation and international trade. In accordance with Article 167 of the Treaty of Lisbon, the EU is obliged to contribute to the flowering of the cultures of the Member States, while respecting their national and regional diversity and at the same time bringing the common heritage to the fore. The EU supports these objectives through the [https://culture.ec.europa.eu/creative-europe Creative Europe programme] and a number of policy actions included in the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32022G1207%2801%29&qid=1671635488811 work plan for culture (2023-2026)]. The work plan, adopted by EU culture ministers in December 2022, sets out 4 main priorities for European cooperation in cultural policymaking * Artists and cultural professionals: empowering the cultural and creative sectors * Culture for the people: enhancing cultural participation and the role of culture in society * Culture for the planet: unleashing the power of culture * Culture for co-creative partnerships: strengthening the cultural dimension of EU external relations Producing reliable, comparable and up-to-date cultural statistics, which provide a basis for sound cultural policymaking, is a cross-sectoral priority for the European Commission. Eurostat compiles culture statistics from several different data collections to provide policymakers and other users of statistics with information on the main developments in the field of culture, covering issues such as education, employment, business, international trade, participation patterns and consumption patterns.

title: Culture statistics - gender equality
text:
Culture statistics in the EU, focusing on gender differences, cultural employment and women's presence in managerial roles, gender pay gaps and disparities in cultural participation and purchasing habits. (Sensitivity level: CU) GPT@EC AI generated content – please use with caution. Data extracted in May 2025 Planned article update: 24 September 2026 In 2024 at EU level, 50.4% of cultural workers were men and 49.6% women, representing the lowest gender gap in cultural employment in the last 10 years. In 2022, men’s gross hourly earnings in cultural employment were on average 13.5% above those of women in the EU. This article from the online publication [[Culture_statistics|Culture statistics]] examines cultural data across the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]], focusing on gender differences. It covers employment, the gender pay gap, cultural activity participation, and online purchases of cultural goods. It notes a narrowing gender gap in cultural employment and women's significant presence in managerial roles. However, a gender pay gap persists, with more women in low-wage positions. The article also highlights gender differences in cultural participation, including among people with disabilities, and reading and purchasing habits. It provides a comprehensive view of gender-related statistics in the EU's cultural sector, noting progress and ongoing challenges in gender equality. === Employment of men and women in the cultural sector === This section analyses cultural employment by sex, showing how the gender employment gap has changed over time, and presents data on women employed in managerial positions in cultural economic activities. '''In 2024, the EU’s cultural sector recorded the smallest gender employment gap in 10 years''' Figure 1 shows the share of women and men employed in the cultural sector in the EU between 2015 and 2024. At the beginning of this period, the share of women employed in the sector was 46.8% compared with 53.2% of men. This relatively small difference has decreased over the years. After a period of stability between 2016 and 2018, the gender employment gap gradually narrowed to reach the smallest difference of 0.8 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp) in 2024 (50.4% of men vs 49.6% of women).

Figure 1

Cultural employment by sex varied significantly across the EU countries in 2024, as shown in Figure 2. In 16 EU countries, the share of women in cultural employment was higher than that of men. Among these, Latvia and Estonia had the biggest differences, with 32.6 pp and 24.2 pp, respectively, in favour of women. By contrast, in 11 EU countries the share of cultural employment was higher for men than women; the highest shares being in Spain and Italy where they were around 10 pp higher for men. Greece, Romania and Austria had an almost perfect gender employment balance in the cultural sector.

Figure 2

Figure 3 illustrates the annual rate of change both in cultural employment and in total employment for women and men at EU level from 2015 to 2024. Except for 2018, throughout the whole time series the annual rate of change for women in cultural employment was higher than that of men. Compared with total employment, cultural employment showed stronger fluctuations during the past 10 years. In particular, the rate of change for men in cultural employment turned negative in 2015, 2020 and 2023, whereas in total employment this only happened in 2020, a year that was impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic.

Figure 3

'''Cultural employment by sex and labour market characteristic''' As shown in Figure 4, in 2024 notable differences were observed particularly for what concerned self-employment and full-time employment. Around 27.7% of women in cultural employment were self-employed compared with 35.6% of men. The proportion of self-employed workers in cultural employment was more than double that of total employment for both male and female workers. On full-time employment, differences were also noted between men and women. In 2024, for total employment 90.3% of men were engaged in full-time work, while for cultural employment this figure was 81.9%. The share of women engaged in full-time work was significantly lower than that of men, standing at around 70% for both total and cultural employment. For men, a low level of full-time employment is characteristic of the cultural field, while for women, this is not the case; women show low levels of full-time employment both in cultural and total employment. This indicates that the inequalities between male and female workers in full-time employment are not specific to the cultural sector but are a general characteristic of the labour market.

Figure 4

'''Women in managerial positions''' Figure 5 shows the percentage of female workers aged 15 and over employed in managerial positions, in both total and cultural employment, over the last 10 years. This indicator shows the unbalanced distribution of decision-making positions between men and women. Throughout the time series, the percentage of women occupying managerial positions was always below 50%. Despite this clear sign of inequality, since 2015 the share of women employed in managerial positions in both total employment and cultural employment has increased. This was particularly evident in the cultural sector, where in 2024 43.9% of female workers were employed as managers compared with 35.2% in total employment.

Figure 5

=== Gender pay gap and low-wage earners in culture === '''In 2022, women’s gross hourly earnings in cultural employment were on average 13.5% lower than those of men in the EU''' This section analyses the results of the 4-yearly [[Glossary:Structure_of_earnings_survey_(SES)|structure of earnings survey]], which provides comparable data at EU level on [[Glossary:Earnings|earnings]]. The gender pay gap refers to the difference in average hourly earnings between men and women. The unadjusted [[Glossary:Gender_pay_gap_(GPG)|gender pay gap]] is calculated as the difference between the average gross hourly earnings of male and female paid employees as a percentage of the average gross hourly earnings of male paid employees.
Figure 6 presents the unadjusted gender pay gap in 2022 for 5 selected cultural economic activities: * Creative, arts and entertainment activities * Libraries, archives, museums and other cultural activities * Motion picture, video and television programme production, sound recording and music publishing activities * Printing and reproduction of recorded media * Programming and broadcasting activities The gender pay gap ranged between -1% in Slovenia, indicating slightly lower earnings for men in the cultural sectors, and 23.2% in Latvia, indicating more than one fifth higher average hourly earnings for men than women. At EU level, this indicator showed that men earned on average 13.5% more per hour than women. A total of 15 EU countries were below this average and 12 above. In 26 of the 27 EU countries, men earned more than women. Besides Slovenia, where women in the selected cultural sectors earned more than men, in Luxembourg the gender pay gap was below 5%, indicating a fairly high degree of parity between the earnings of men and women. The differences in the average characteristics can result from many factors, including the prevailing employment of one sex in certain economic activities or the dominating employment of one sex in some occupations. For an analysis of the gender pay gap drivers, please see the article [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Gender_pay_gap_statistics Gender Pay Gap statistics].

Figure 6

Figure 7 shows the proportion of low-wage earners by sex in the selected cultural sectors across the EU. Low-wage earners are defined as employees earning two thirds or less of the national median gross hourly earnings, with the threshold varying for each EU country. In 2022 at EU level, 16.1% of the female employees in the selected cultural activities were found to be low-wage earners, compared to 11.2% of male employees. These figures were broadly in line with those for total employment, but differences emerged when breaking down the indicator by specific cultural activity. The ‘printing and reproduction of recorded media’ sector stood out as the most unequal sector, with 25.9% of women with low wages compared with 12.4% of men, followed by ‘Motion picture, video and television programme production, sound recording and music publishing activities’, with 23.0% of women with low wages compared with 15.1% of men. The percentage of women with low wages was not lower than that for men in any of the 5 selected cultural activities.

Figure 7

=== Gender equality in cultural participation === '''In 2022, women participated in cultural activities more than men in 17 EU countries''' This section presents data on cultural participation in the EU, including going to the cinema, attending live performances, visiting cultural sites and reading books. In 2022, women’s participation rates exceeded those of men in 17 of the 26 EU countries with available data. In 14 countries, more than half of men and women reported participating in cultural activities at least once during the 12 months preceding the interview (see Figure 8). Denmark had the highest participation rate for women (79.6%), while Luxembourg had the highest rate for men (77.5%). Denmark recorded the largest difference (4.6 pp) in the participation rate between women (79.6%) and men (75.0%). This indicates that despite the slight prevalence of women participating in cultural activities in most EU countries, strong inequalities in this area are not observed. The country with the lowest participation rate in cultural activities for both women and men was Bulgaria, with rates of 20.5% for women and 18.7% for men, followed by Romania (21.8% for women and 22.7% for men) and Croatia (33.6% for women and 31.1% for men).

Figure 8

Breaking down the data by type of cultural activity, in 2022 there were no noticeable differences between men and women in terms of going to the cinema or visiting cultural sites. By contrast, in 24 of the 26 countries with available data, women systematically reported more frequently having attended live events than men. The highest difference was reported in Czechia, where 38% of women declared that they had attended a live cultural event at least once in the preceding 12 months compared with 28% of men (see Figure 9).

Figure 9

'''Women participated in cultural activities more than men in all age groups except for 65 and over in 2022''' In half of the countries, the percentage of men aged 65 and over who reported participating in cultural activities surpassed that of women (see Table 1). In all the EU countries with available data except for Hungary, women aged 16-29 participated in cultural activities more than men. Women in this age group in Luxembourg recorded the highest participation rate in the EU at 90.4%, with the Netherlands following closely with 87.3%. Denmark had the smallest difference in participation rates between men and women (0.1 pp), showing almost parity in this area. On cultural habits among people aged 55-64, noticeable differences in participation rates between men and women were recorded in Estonia, with 45.4% of men and 60.8% of women, and in Lithuania where the rate was 32.4% for men and 47.0% for women.

[[Image:Table_1_-_People_participating_in_cultural_activities_in_the_last_12_months_by_sex_and_age_group_2022.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1 - People participating in cultural activities in the last 12 months by sex and age group 2022
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_scp03}}|alt=A table showing the share of people in the EU participating in cultural activities in the last 12 months by sex and age group for the year 2022. Data are shown as percentage for the EU Member States, some of the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image]]

'''In 2022, ‘no interest’ was reported as the main reason for not reading books by both men and women''' Figure 10 presents 2022 EU data on the reading of books, by sex and number of books read. Books read include e-books or audio books during the last 12 months but exclude podcasts. All types of books are counted (historical, scientific, poetry, novels, etc.) except schoolbooks or manuals for work. Higher reading rates were reported for women. The percentage of men who reported not having read a single book was significantly higher than that of women (55.5% against 39.5%). Moreover, as the number of books read increased, the difference between women and men widened. While the rate of reading fewer than 5 books per year was 4.0 pp higher for women (28.8% versus 24.8%), this difference increased to 4.5 pp for 5-9 books and to 7.5 pp for 10 books or more.

Figure 10

Figure 11 gives some interesting insights into the reasons given for not reading books. In 2022, lack of interest was reported as the primary reason by both women and men across the EU. More than half of men (56.5%) mentioned lack of interest, but the rate was 12.1 pp lower for women. Financial difficulties, lack of time, difficulties, and other reasons were mentioned more often among women.

Figure 11

Table 2 shows the participation of individuals in cultural activities categorised by level of disability ([[Glossary:Activity_limitation|activity limitation]]), broken down by sex and country in 2022. The EU-SILC ‘quality of life’ variables provide, amongst others, the breakdown by disability level (activity limitation). In 19 EU countries, the cultural participation rate of women with some or severe activity limitations exceeded that of men. Notably, in Denmark, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Finland more than half of both women and men with activity limitations participated in cultural activities. In Denmark the participation rate of women with a disability reached 71.4%, and in Luxembourg the rate for men stood at 69.1%.

[[Image:People_participating_in_cultural_activities_by_sex_and_level_of_disability,_2022.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: People participating in cultural activities by sex and level of disability, 2022
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_scp37}}|alt=A table showing the share of people in the EU participating in cultural activities by sex and level of disability for the year 2022. Data are shown as percentage for the EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image]]
'''In 2024, women bought printed and electronic books more than men, while men used the internet to buy films or series to stream or download, and for gaming more than women''' The [[Glossary:information and communication technology (ICT)|information and communication technologies (ICTs)]] have become the most common way of accessing culture for large parts of the society throughout the EU. This section presents data on the purchase of cultural goods and services by individuals aged 16-74 who used the internet in the 3 months preceding the data collection. The following cultural goods and services bought online are covered: *printed books, magazines or newspapers *e-books or audio books as downloads *subscriptions to films, series or sports streaming services *subscriptions to music streaming services *subscriptions to online news sites, online newspapers or online magazines *subscriptions to gaming streaming services *games as downloads *tickets to cultural or other events This section presents data on the purchase of cultural goods and services by individuals aged 16-74 who used the internet in the 3 months preceding the data collection. As shown in Figure 12, there are differences between men and women in this respect. In 2024, 31.4% of men had a paid subscription to films, series or sports streaming services. This was the category most frequently reported by male internet users, followed by the purchase of tickets to events (24.2%). For women, similarly to men, video streaming services (28.0%) and events tickets (25.4%) were the most common categories of cultural products purchased online. At EU level, women were keener to use the internet to purchase both printed and digital publications, while men surpassed women in purchasing video contents, music and videogames online. For what concerns the online purchase of tickets to events, the difference between women and men was quite minimal (1.2 p.p. difference in favour of women), showing a fairly similar access to this type of product.

Figure 12

=== Source data for tables === {{Template:Excel|filename=Culture statistics - gender equality Tables.xlsx|title=Culture statistics - gender equality tables}} === Data sources=== Eurostat’s statistics on cultural employment are sourced from the EU [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(EU-LFS)|Labour Force Survey]], which collects data from people aged 15 and over. Eurostat compiles the data by area of economic activity in which the employed person works and their occupation, using a matrix to create an aggregate for all cultural employment. For details on the estimation methods used by Eurostat in the area of cultural employment refer to the article [[Culture_statistics_-_cultural_employment|Culture statistics - cultural employment]]. The data on earnings presented in this article are the result of a special ad hoc extraction from the 4-yearly [[Glossary:Structure_of_earnings_survey_(SES)|structure of earnings survey (SES)]], conducted in the EU Member States, EFTA countries as well as candidate and potential candidate countries. The SES provides comparable information at EU level on the relationship between the level of earnings, individual characteristics of employees (sex, age, occupation, length of service, educational level) and their employer (economic activity, size of the enterprise, etc.) for the reference years 2002, 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018 and 2022. Statistics on cultural participation are from the [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions]]. The EU-SILC is the EU reference source for comparative statistics on income distribution and social inclusion at European level. In 2022, in addition to annual data, the EU-SILC included variables on health (with data collected every 3 years) and variables on quality of life (with data collected every 6 years). The data were collected in all 27 EU Member States, in 3 of the EFTA countries (Iceland, Norway and Switzerland), as well as in Montenegro, Serbia and Türkiye. The target population was people aged 16 years and over, while the reference period was 12 months prior to the interview. The COVID-19 pandemic restrictions were still in force in some countries at the time of data collection. Due to the high non-response rate, 2022 data for Germany is not available. A detailed description of the list of variables as well as information on their implementation are available in the methodological guidelines. The data on online purchase of cultural goods and services are derived from the EU survey on the use of ICT in households and by individuals. The survey is conducted every year as from 2002. The aim of the ICT survey is to provide relevant statistics on areas such as access to and use of ICTs, use of the internet, use of e-commerce and ICT skills. Data are broken down by many variables including age, sex and level of educational attainment. The target population is people aged 16-74 living in private households. See [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/digital-economy-and-society/legislation digital economy and society legislation]. === Context === Culture is one of Europe’s greatest assets: it is a source of values, identity and a sense of belonging. It also contributes to wellbeing, social cohesion and inclusion. The cultural and creative sectors provide a stimulus for economic growth, job creation and international trade. In accordance with Article 167 of the Treaty of Lisbon, the EU is obliged to ‘contribute to the flowering of the cultures of the Member States, while respecting their national and regional diversity and at the same time bringing the common heritage to the fore’. The EU supports these objectives through the [https://culture.ec.europa.eu/creative-europe Creative Europe programme], as well as through a number of policy actions set out in the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32022G1207%2801%29&qid=1671635488811 work plan for culture] (2023-2026). The work plan, adopted by EU culture ministers in December 2022, sets out 4 main priorities for European cooperation in cultural policymaking: * artists and cultural professionals: empowering the cultural and creative sectors * culture for the people: enhancing cultural participation and the role of culture in society * culture for the planet: unleashing the power of culture * culture for co-creative partnerships: strengthening the cultural dimension of EU external relations The production of reliable, comparable and up-to-date cultural statistics, which provide a basis for sound cultural policymaking, is a cross-sectoral priority for the Commission. Eurostat compiles culture statistics from several different data collections to provide policymakers and other users of statistics with information on the main developments in the area of culture, covering issues such as education, employment, business, international trade, participation patterns and consumption patterns. ===Other articles=== **[[Culture_statistics_-_cultural_participation|cultural participation]] **[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Culture_statistics_-_use_of_ICT_for_cultural_purposes Culture statistics – use of ICT for cultural purposes] **[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Culture_statistics_-_household_expenditure_on_culture Culture statistics – household expenditure on culture] *[[Culture]] (all Statistics Explained articles on culture) === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/culture/database Culture (cult)], see: ::Cultural employment [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database?node_code=cult_emp (cult_emp)]
