title: Culture statistics - household expenditure on culture
text:
Data on household consumption expenditure on culture derived from the EU's household budget survey (HBS) covering individual private households. Data extracted in May 2023 and March 2025 Planned article update: February 2028 In 2020, 2.7% of total consumption expenditure by EU households went to culture-related goods and services. In 2020, households in the EU spent 27.0% of their total cultural expenditure on audio-video and information processing equipment and 25.1% on books and newspapers. This article forms part of the online publication ''[[Culture_statistics|Culture statistics]]''. It provides an overview of key figures on household consumption expenditure on culture-related goods and services. The data are collected through the [[Glossary:Household budget survey (HBS)|household budget survey (HBS)]], a national survey carried out by EU countries collecting data primarily on households’ consumption expenditure on goods and services.
===Household expenditure on cultural goods and services – scope and level===
Within household expenditure, the aggregate covering cultural goods and services is based on the [[Glossary:classification_of_individual_consumption_by_purpose_(COICOP)|classification of individual consumption by purpose (COICOP)]] and comprises 14 different items grouped into the following 5 broad categories of cultural expenditure: * equipment (portable devices, information processing equipment and equipment for the reception, reproduction and recording of vision, sound and recording media (CDs, DVDs, Blu-ray disks, vinyl records, etc.); * books and newspapers; * fees and subscriptions (broadcasters’ fees and subscriptions, including TV on demand, cable and paid TV, as well as various streaming services that enable the reception of audio and video content; this also includes hiring prices for equipment and accessories for cultural purposes); * attendance and entertainment (cinemas, theatres, museums, libraries, concerts and services of photographers and performing artists); * articles for artistic expression and creation (including cameras, video cameras, musical instruments, stationery and drawing materials).

'''''2.7% of total household consumption expenditure in the EU was spent on cultural goods and services''''' According to the latest HBS data, in 2020 private households in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] spent, on average, an estimated 2.7% of their total expenditure on cultural goods and services (see Figure 1). The share of culture-related expenditure in total household consumption expenditure varied considerably across the EU countries. Several factors might impact this share, including household income, price levels, the ease of access to cultural venues, national cultural policies, and habits. In 2020, 8 countries recorded a share of cultural expenditure in total household budgets above the average among the 24 EU countries with available data. The highest percentage of the household budget spent on cultural purposes was in Denmark (3.9%). By contrast, in 16 countries the share was below the EU average, with the smallest share in Greece (1.3%).

Figure 1 also shows the average level of household expenditure on cultural goods and services, expressed in [[Glossary:Purchasing power standard (PPS)|purchasing power standards (PPS)]]. The PPS is an artificial currency unit, which makes it possible to produce meaningful indicators required for cross-country comparisons, truly reflecting the differences in the purchasing power of households. In 2020, Austria, Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands had the highest levels of expenditure on cultural goods and services, on average, more than 1 000 PPS yearly. Lowest shares with less than 300 PPS were recorded in Greece, Slovakia, Lithuania and Bulgaria.
[[Image:Figure 1 - Mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, 2020)_(v2025).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cult_pcs_hbs}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services in the EU, individual EU Member States, Serbia and Montenegro for the year 2020. Using the left axis, the country columns represent percentage share of total household expenditure. Using the right axis, scatter plots show PPS per country. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''''All countries that spent more than 50% of total expenditure on food and housing, spent less than 2.5% on culture''''' For comparison, at EU level in 2020, 2.7% of household expenditure was spent on culture, while 48.6% went on food and housing. In Figure 2, the vertical axis represents cultural expenses as a percentage of the total households expenditure, while the horizontal axis represents the percentage spent on food and housing, showing an inverse relationship between expenditure in essential goods, such as food and housing, and culture expenditure. In all countries where food and housing accounted for more than 50% of the total, less than 2.5% was spent on culture. Furthermore, in Figure 2, the size of the circles represents the ratio between the 2 categories of expenditure: the bigger the circle, the larger the gap between cultural expenditure and food and housing. At EU level, the spending on food and housing was about 18 times higher than on culture, with considerable differences between countries. Notably, in Malta, Austria and Germany, food and housing spending was 9 to 11 times cultural spending; while in Greece, Bulgaria and Hungary households spent over 40 times as much on food and housing as on culture.

[[Image:Figure 2 - Mean household expenditure on food and housing and _mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, 2020_(v2025).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Ratio between mean household expenditure on food and housing and mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, 2020
(% and ratio)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hbs_exp_t121}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=cult_pcs_hbs}}|alt= Bubble chart showing ratio between percentage mean household expenditure on food and housing on the horizontal axis and percentage mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services on the vertical axis in the EU, individual EU Member States, Serbia and Montenegro for the year 2020. The different sizes of the country bubbles represent the ratio. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Structure of household expenditure for culture-related purposes===
'''''On average, EU households allocated about a quarter of their cultural expenditure to information processing and audio-video equipment and another quarter to books and newspapers''''' In 2020, on average 27.0% of EU household cultural expenditure went on information processing, audio-video equipment and recording media, 25.1% on books and newspapers, 20.9% on broadcasters’ fees and hiring of equipment and accessories for culture and 13.6% on attendance and entertainment, leaving the remaining 13.4% for articles of artistic expression and creation. Figure 3 shows the structure of household expenditure on culture from the 2015 and 2020 HBSs. Expenditure shares for books and newspapers, and attendance and entertainment remained relatively stable between the 2 surveys. Compared with the 2015 survey, in 2020 a higher share of expenditure went to articles for artistic expression and creation as well as to equipment, while a smaller portion was spent on fees and subscriptions. The 2020 round of the HBS took place during the COVID-19 pandemic for many countries. Due to the specific circumstances related to the crisis, the fieldwork was altered and changes had to be made to the usual methods of data collection, and thus caution is needed when comparing 2015 with 2020 figures. For more details, please refer to the ’Data sources and methodology’ section of this article.

[[Image:Figure 3 - Distribution of mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, by expenditure purpose, EU, 2020 and 2015_(v2025).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Distribution of mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, by expenditure purpose, EU, 2020 and 2015
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cult_pcs_hbs}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, by expenditure purpose as percentage share of all household cultural expenditure in the EU. Five sections represent the five broad expenditure purposes. Each section has two columns comparing the household budget survey of the year 2020 with 2015. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
The structure of household expenditure across the 5 categories showed in Figure 3 at EU level varied significantly between countries. Figure 4 shows the diverse nature of cultural spending across the EU countries for the 5 aggregates.
* '''Information processing equipment, audio-video equipment and recorded media''' accounted for the largest part of the households’ cultural spending in 14 EU countries. The highest percentage was in Lithuania (45.2%) and Spain (44.7%), while the lowest was in Slovenia (17.8%). * Household expenditure on '''books and newspapers''' ranged from 16.4% in Slovakia to 36.6% in Italy. In Italy and Germany, these products represented the largest part of total culture-related expenditure. * In 8 countries '''fees and subscriptions''' represented the largest part of expenditure on cultural goods and services. The lowest share for fees and subscriptions was observed in Spain (2.6%), while the highest was in Bulgaria (40.7%). * '''Attendance and entertainment''' accounted for more than a fifth of household cultural budgets in Latvia (30.3%), Estonia (23.6%), and Cyprus (20.9%). This category had the lowest impact on household culture-related expenditure in Hungary (6.6%) and Poland (5.3%). * Expenditure on '''articles for artistic expression and creation''' accounted for approximately one fifth of households’ cultural budgets in Belgium (19.1%). The smallest share of culture-related household budgets was allocated for this purpose in Denmark (3.7%).

[[Image:Figure 4 - Mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, by broad expenditure purpose, 2020_(v2025).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, by broad expenditure purpose, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cult_pcs_hbs}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, by broad expenditure purpose as percentage share of all household cultural expenditure in the EU, individual EU Member States, Serbia and Montenegro. Totalling 100 percent, each country column contains five stacks representing the five broad expenditure purposes for the year 2020. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Table 1 analyses the structure of cultural expenditure in the EU, providing information about all 14 cultural items that comprise mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services. This level of granularity shows that in 2020 the largest proportion of EU households’ expenditure on cultural goods and services went on television and radio broadcasting fees, hiring fees for equipment and accessories for culture (20.9%), followed by newspapers and magazines and information processing equipment (12.6% each), and books (12.4%). Conversely, the smallest shares of household expenditure on cultural goods and services were for photographic and cinematographic equipment (1.7%) and the repair of audiovisual, photographic, and information processing equipment (0.6%). In 2020, the shares of the different expenditure categories varied greatly across the EU countries. Broadcasters’ fees and subscriptions, hire of equipment and accessories for culture ranged from 2.6% of households’ cultural budget in Spain to 40.7% in Bulgaria. Books ranged from 5.2% in Slovakia to 24.8% in Italy. Equipment for the reception, recording, and reproduction of sound, vision, and picture ranged from 5.4% in Slovenia to 15.6% in Cyprus.

[[Image:Table 1 - Distribution of mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, by expenditure purpose, 2020_(v2025).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Distribution of mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, by expenditure purpose, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cult_pcs_hbs}}|alt= Table showing distribution of mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services by expenditure purpose as PPS and percentage of all household cultural expenditure in the EU, individual EU Member States, Serbia and Montenegro for the year 2020. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Household cultural expenditure - impact of household income ===
'''''EU mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services was greatly influenced by income levels''''' In 2020, household expenditure on cultural goods and services varied significantly across the income distribution, showing a strong income dependency.

As shown in Figure 5, increases in spending on culture-related purposes were the most pronounced between households in the fourth and fifth income quintile. In 11 out of 22 EU countries with available data, households belonging to the fifth quintile spent at least 1.5 times as much as households from the fourth quintile.

The highest to lowest quintile ratio measures the difference in culture-related expenditure between income groups. With the exception of 3 EU countries, the mean consumption expenditure for households in the fifth quintile was at least 3 times higher that of households in the first income quintile, indicating sharp inequalities in cultural spending due to income.

The most notable disparities in household expenditure on cultural goods and services across different income quintiles were observed in Cyprus. As shown by the highest-to-lowest income quintile ratio, for households in the fifth quintile, culture-related expenditure was 9 times higher than that in the first quintile (1 226 PPS vs 133 PPS). Significant disparities in culture-related expenditure based on household income were also present in Spain and Latvia, where households in the highest income group spent around 5 times as much on culture as those in the lowest income group.

By contrast, the least variation in household cultural expenditure between different income quintiles was observed in Slovakia, where spending on culture-related purposes was nearly equal between income quintiles, and where households with the highest income spent for culture-related purposes only twice as much as households with the lowest income (375 PPS vs 178 PPS).

[[Image:Figure 5 - Mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, by income quintile, 2020_(v2025).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services, by income quintile, 2020
(in PPS – left axis; highest to lowest quintile ratio – right axis)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cult_pcs_qnt}}|alt= Scatter chart showing mean household expenditure on cultural goods and services by income quintile in the EU, individual EU Member States, Serbia and Montenegro for the year 2020. Using the left axis as PPS, each country has five scatter plots representing the first, second, third, fourth and fifth quintiles. Using the right axis, each country has a scatter plot representing the highest to lowest income quintile ratio. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Culture statistics - Household expenditure on culture 2020 (v2025).xlsx|title=Household expenditure on culture: tables and figures}}
=== Data sources and methodology ===
Eurostat compiles data on cultural expenditure from the [[Glossary:Household_budget_survey_(HBS)|household budget survey (HBS)]]. Household consumption expenditure on cultural goods and services reflects the level of cultural participation and may be influenced by a range of factors, including household composition, age, wealth/income, the availability of cultural facilities and price structures. Data on household consumption expenditure are available in national currencies, euro and PPS; the latter are used to eliminate price-level differences between countries. The use of data in PPS terms ensures that information is valued at a uniform price level and therefore reflects only volume differences in the economy, as opposed to price-level differences. As an example of the order of magnitude of the PPS, data [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hbs_exp_t111/default/table?lang=en on mean consumption expenditure per household and per adult equivalent], are available in different units of measure, including PPS, national currency and euro, which can be compared by country. Data are collected using national surveys in each participating country. The collection involves a combination of one or more interviews and diaries or logs maintained by households and/or individuals, generally on a daily basis (recording their consumption over time). The HBS is carried out most often every 5 years, the most recent referring to 2020. The fieldwork for the 2020 HBS data collection took place between 2018 and 2022 for the majority of EU Member States, with the exceptions of Cyprus, Malta and France, where data were collected between 2015 and 2017. Data for these countries have been produced by converting 2015 to 2020 reference year prices using the 2020 HICP coefficient. For Sweden, data for the 2020 wave were not available at the time of writing. For Portugal and Romania, data for the categories on cultural goods and services were not available. For Czechia and Italy, the data by income quintile were not available. The data collection and expenditure patterns of households in some EU Member States could have been affected by the COVID-19 pandemic and related restrictions. Data on household expenditure can be used to analyse expenditure patterns of specific types of household or expenditure patterns for particular groups of goods and services (such as cultural items, as covered in this article). This information is mainly used at EU level in connection with consumer protection policy. HBS statistics have also been used in conjunction with information on [[Consumer_prices_of_cultural_goods_and_services|Consumer prices of cultural goods and services]] to develop a consumer market scoreboard that tracks how markets in various sectors of the economy have been performing from a consumer’s perspective. HBS statistics are based on the ECOICOP classification. Developed by the [https://unstats.un.org/home/ United Nations Statistics Division] the [[Glossary:Classification_of_individual_consumption_by_purpose_(COICOP)|classification of individual consumption by purpose (COICOP)]] provides a framework to classify and analyse individual consumption expenditure by households, non-profit institutions serving households, and general government. The European version — ECOICOP — extends the classification to five digits to better meet the need for more detailed data on household budgets and consumer price indices. Culture-related goods and services within ECOICOP cover cultural goods such as books and newspapers, the manufacture of various articles that enable artistic creation (for example, musical instruments, photo and video cameras or drawing materials) or the equipment for the consumption of various forms of culture (TV and stereo equipment, [[Glossary:Information and communication technology (ICT)|information and communication technologies]], as well as the actual media on which some cultural products can be delivered (CDs, DVDs or Blu-ray). In an [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/341465/3199631/essnet-culture.pdf/a6518128-69b3-4d89-82b8-060a3ad0d1d5 ESSnet-Culture final report] (2012), the following COICOP items were identified as relating to culture (for the consumption expenditure of households): *books; *newspapers and periodicals; *cinemas, theatres and concerts; *museum, libraries and zoological gardens; *musical instruments; *cameras and accessories for photographic and cinematographic equipment; *stationery and drawing materials; *services of photographers and performing artists; *television and radio fees, hire of equipment and accessories for culture; *information processing equipment; *reception, recording and reproduction of sound and vision; *recording media; *reception, recording and reproduction of sound; *repair of audiovisual, photographic and information processing equipment. For the purpose of this article, the concept of household expenditure on cultural goods and services comprises the ECOICOP categories listed in Table 2.
[[Image:Table 2 - Household expenditure on cultural good and services by broad categories and ECOICOP codes involved.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Household expenditure on cultural good and services by broad categories and ECOICOP codes involved
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/KS-GQ-18-011 (Guide to Eurostat culture statistics – 2018 edition)]]]
=== Context ===
Culture is one of Europe's greatest assets: it is a source of values, identity and a sense of belonging. It also contributes to well-being, social cohesion and inclusion. The cultural and creative sectors provide a stimulus for economic growth, job creation and international trade. The EU supports these objectives through the [https://culture.ec.europa.eu/creative-europe Creative Europe programme] and several policy actions included in the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32022G1207%2801%29&qid=1671635488811 work plan for culture (2023-2026)]. The work plan, adopted by EU culture ministers in December 2022, sets out 4 main priorities for European cooperation in cultural policymaking: * Artists and cultural professionals: empowering the cultural and creative sectors. * Culture for the people: enhancing cultural participation and the role of culture in society. * Culture for the planet: unleashing the power of culture. * Culture for co-creative partnerships: strengthening the cultural dimension of EU external relations. The production of reliable, comparable and up-to-date cultural statistics, which provide a basis for sound cultural policymaking, is a cross-sectoral priority for the European Commission. Eurostat compiles culture statistics from several different data collections to provide policymakers and other users of statistics with information on the main developments in the field of culture, covering issues such as education, employment, business, international trade, participation patterns and consumption patterns. === Other articles === *[[Culture|Culture (all Statistics Explained articles on culture)]] *[[Consumer_prices_of_cultural_goods_and_services|Consumer prices of cultural goods and services]] *[[Household_budget_survey_-_statistics_on_consumption_expenditure|Household budget survey - title: Culture statistics - use of ICT for cultural purposes
text:
Data extracted in April 2026. Planned article update: June 2027. In 2025, men were more likely than women to access cultural content online. Paid subscriptions to audiovisual content and event tickets were the top online cultural purchases. Across all EU countries, people mainly used generative AI tools for private purposes.



This article is part of an online publication '''[[Culture_statistics|Culture statistics]]'''. The way we access culture has changed. For many people in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], using [[Glossary:Information and communication technology (ICT)|information and communication technologies (ICTs)]] is a common way of getting cultural content. Eurostat (the EU’s statistical office) looked into these trends in its annual [[Glossary:EU survey on the use of ICT in households and by individuals|survey on ICT usage in households and by individuals]]. It focused on 3 culture-related online activities, cross-refencing them with key socio-economic characteristics (see [[Culture_statistics_-_use_of_ICT_for_cultural_purposes#Data_sources|Data sources]]). The activities were: * '''using the internet for certain cultural activities''' (e.g. TV, news, music, games) * '''using generative artificial intelligence tools for various purposes''' * '''buying certain cultural goods and services online''' (e.g. subscriptions, event tickets, physical and digital cultural content) Here, the term '''internet users''' refers to all individuals in the EU aged 16 to 74 who had actively used the internet in the 3 months before the survey.
===Accessing culture online=== '''''Most popular activities were watching and reading content, followed by listening to music and gaming'''''

In 2025, over 9 out of 10 (94%) people in the EU aged 16 to 74 had used the internet at least once in the previous 3 months. The highest shares of users were recorded in Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands and Luxembourg with over 99% of individuals having done so. By contrast, in 6 other EU countries, fewer than 90% of people used the internet, with the lowest use seen in Bulgaria (87%) and Croatia (86%) See[[Digital_economy_and_society_statistics_-_households_and_individuals#Internet_usage| Digital economy and society statistics - households and individuals]]. Internet users increasingly prefer audiovisual content, as shown in the dynamic chart above. In the EU, the most popular online cultural activity was streaming TV or videos (79% of internet users, 2024 data). Next came reading online news sites, newspapers or news magazines (71%, 2025 data), listening to or downloading music (65%, 2024 data), and playing or downloading games (34%, 2024 data). At national level, these were usually the top activities too (see Figure 1). At least 75% of internet users in 21 EU countries streamed video content, and this activity ranked first in 17 EU countries. The Netherlands reported the highest use at 96%. Meanwhile, at least 75% of users in 16 countries read online news content. This activity came first in 10 countries, with the highest figure in Czechia (92%). In 7 countries, at least 75% of users had listened to or downloaded music, with the highest share in Ireland (82%). The least favourite activity in all EU countries was playing or downloading games, but Denmark (52%) and the Netherlands (50%) recorded the highest shares.

[[Image:Figure 1 - Use of the internet for selected cultural purposes, 2024-2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Use of the internet for selected cultural purposes, 2024-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/66261f89-f618-4a8b-a303-002a697731a9?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T08:21:45Z isoc_ci_ac_i])|alt= a chart showing the use of the internet for selected cultural purposes in 2024 and 2025 in the EU, EU Member States, selected EFTA and candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''Access to online cultural content by socio-economic characteristics''' Various socio-economic factors influence whether people use the internet to access cultural content. In this section we look at age, sex, level of education, degree of urbanisation and employment status (see Table 1). The use of the internet for cultural purposes varied by age. Over 80% of younger people (age groups 16-24 and 25-34) streamed TV or videos and listened to music online, and these figures dropped with age. For listening to music online, the drop was even bigger. Playing or downloading games peaked among the youngest age group and declined steadily with age. By contrast, people aged 16-24 were the least likely to read online news content (62%, 9 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] lower than the total population). However, the figure then increased with age, peaking for people aged 35-44 (76%), before declining slightly. Men reported consuming slightly more cultural content online than women, with gaps ranging from 3 pp for streaming TV or videos (80% vs 77%) to 7 pp for playing or downloading games (37% vs 30%). Generally, people with higher levels of education attained were more likely to access cultural content online than people with lower levels of education or no formal education. The biggest differences were for reading online news (83% vs 53%), listening to music (74% vs 59%) and watching videos (86% vs 73%). The one exception was playing or downloading games, where the pattern was reversed (32% vs 38%). As for degree of urbanisation, city dwellers were more likely to use the internet for cultural purposes than people living elsewhere. Employment status is also an influencing factor (i.e. whether a person is employed, unemployed, a student or economically inactive but not a student). Students accessed cultural content online more than other groups. Almost all internet-using students watched online TV or videos (93%) and listened to or downloaded music (89%), and more than half played or downloaded games (64%). However, employed people were the group most likely to read news online (75%).

[[Image:Table 1 - Use of the internet for selected cultural purposes, by socio-economic characteristic, EU, 2024-2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Use of the internet for selected cultural purposes, by socio-economic characteristic, EU, 2024-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c41614ac-e1f2-41ab-90ee-8630682d2c1a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T08:21:59Z isoc_ci_ac_i])|alt= a table showing the use of the internet for selected cultural purposes, by socioeconomic characteristic in 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Using generative artificial intelligence tools=== '''''Private use the most common reason, but patterns vary'''''

Cultural activities now increasingly involve digital creation and interaction. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools support these activities, allowing people to produce and transform text, images, audio and video. In 2025, more than one third of internet users in the EU (35%) reported using generative AI tools in the previous 3 months. People mostly used generative AI for private purposes (27%), followed by professional (16%) and then formal education purposes (10%). There were big variations between countries, ranging from just under one quarter to nearly half of respondents. The highest figures for AI use were in Greece, Estonia and Denmark (all 49%), followed by Malta (48%), Finland (47%) and Cyprus (47%), but the lowest were in Italy (22%) and Romania (19%). In all EU countries, people mostly used generative AI tools for private purposes, with Cyprus and Greece coming top (both 46%) followed by Estonia (40%). Meanwhile, using AI for professional purposes was most common in Malta (31%), Denmark and the Netherlands (both 27%). For formal education purposes, Sweden and Malta (both 21%) came first, followed by Denmark (18%). In EU countries above the EU average (35%), the balance between private and professional use varied (see Figure 2). In Greece and Cyprus, people mostly used AI for private purposes, but relatively little for work purposes. However, in the Netherlands, the gap between the 2 was minimal (28% and 27%, respectively). The differences were also relatively small in Finland, Denmark, Ireland and Malta.

[[Image:Figure 2 - Use of generative AI tools for various purposes, 2025 (% of individuals who used internet in the last 3 months).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Use of generative AI tools for various purposes, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f24d974d-f7b4-45fc-ad47-bc58cebcbac6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T08:22:14Z isoc_ai_iaiu])|alt= a chart showing the percentage of internet users who used generative AI tools for private, professional, or formal education purposes in 2025, broken down by the EU, EU countries, EFTA countries, and candidate countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''Use of generative AI by socio-economic characteristics''' Various socio-economic factors influence the use of generative AI tools (see Figure 3). Younger internet users were more likely to use these tools than older people. Nearly two thirds (65%) of people aged 16-24 had interacted with these tools in the previous 3 months against just 8% of users aged 65-74. Overall use declined steadily with age. However, patterns differed depending on why people used the tools. Using AI for formal education was considerably more popular in the youngest age group (16-24), at 40%. This is expected, as most of the people in the 16-24 age group are still in formal education. Professional use was highest among individuals aged 25-34 (27%), declining with age. As for sex, men used AI more than women for private and professional purposes, though there was no difference for formal education-related use. Education is also a major factor. Almost half (49%) of people with a high level of formal education had used AI against around one quarter of people with a medium level of education (27%) or little or no formal education (26%). This difference was even bigger for professional use (31% vs 5%). Also, city dwellers used generative AI tools (42%) more than people in towns and suburbs (33%) or rural areas (27%). Looking at employment status, students were most likely to use generative AI tools. In 2025, 72% of students used these tools, especially for formal education (52%) and private purposes (48%). Economically inactive people (13%) were least likely to use AI.

[[Image:Figure 3 - Use of generative AI tools for various purposes, by socio-economic characteristic, EU, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Use of generative AI tools for various purposes, by socio-economic characteristic, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e2bc65c2-7aab-4743-ac7f-d042dfc6dfe1?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T08:22:26Z isoc_ai_iaiu])|alt= a chart showing the use of generative AI tools for private, professional, or formal education purposes in the EU in 2025, broken down by socio-economic characteristic as a percentage among people who used the internet in the previous 3 months. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Buying cultural goods and services online=== '''''Paid subscriptions to audiovisual content and event tickets were the top online purchases'''''

In 2025, 39% of internet users in the EU purchased cultural services online, which corresponds to 37% of the total EU population. For paid online subscriptions, the shares of both internet users and the total population increased by more than 3 pp in 2025. As shown in Figure 4, buying subscriptions to film, series or sports streaming services were the most popular use (33% of internet users). Buying tickets online for cultural or other events came next (29%), followed by subscriptions to music streaming services (23%). Subscriptions to gaming streaming services came last (6%). Patterns of accessing cultural content (purchase vs subscription) differed depending on the type of content. In 2025, 12% of internet users purchased digital copies of video games for personal use, while 6% subscribed to gaming streaming services. Physical media – such as CDs, vinyl records, DVDs or Blu-ray discs – were purchased by 6% of internet users (2024 data). If digital products were more commonly purchased than physical ones for audiovisual content, the opposite was for books: while 9% of internet users had purchased e-books or audiobooks, this figure was nearly double for printed books, at 16% (2024 data).

[[Image:Figure 4 - Use of the internet for buying cultural services and goods in the last three months, EU, 2024-2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Use of the internet for buying cultural goods and services in the last three months, EU, 2024-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d475082a-2f6e-41f0-a484-b2d690d19001?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T08:22:41Z isoc_ec_ibgs])|alt= a horizontal bar chart showing the use of the internet for buying cultural goods and services in the EU in 2024 and 2025 as a percentage among people who used the internet in the previous 3 months. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''Online purchase of cultural goods and services by socio-economic characteristics''' '''''Age, education and living in a city: the biggest factors'''''

People aged 25-34 were generally most likely to purchase cultural services online, with the share declining gradually with age (see Table 2). However, online gaming (including downloads and subscriptions) was most common among people aged 16-24. And for subscriptions to online news sites, digital newspapers or magazines, the share was similar (around 8%) for most age groups but lower among those aged 16-24 (4%). Educational background is also a factor: higher levels of education were associated with higher shares of internet users purchasing cultural goods and services online. The biggest differences were for reading-related content: 16% of internet users who had completed tertiary education had purchased e-books or audiobooks online, more than twice the figure for people with a medium level of formal education (7%) and about 4 times the figure for people with little or no formal education (4%). However, for gaming-related content, there was less of a difference. For example, 7% of people who had completed tertiary education had a paid subscription to a gaming streaming service, against 6% of people with a medium level of education and 5% of people with little or no formal education. Where people live (degree of urbanisation) also influences purchasing behaviour. City dwellers were more likely to buy cultural goods and services online than people living elsewhere. In 2025, this gap was biggest for buying event tickets (34% in cities vs 23% in rural areas) and for subscriptions to a music streaming service (27% vs 18%). This partly reflects better access to cultural activities and high-speed internet in urban areas. For most cultural products, men were more likely than women to make online purchases. This trend was clear for purchasing games as downloads (17% of men vs 8% of women), software as downloads (17% vs 10%), and subscriptions to gaming streaming services (9% vs 3%). However, women were more likely to buy event tickets and e-books or audiobooks online (but the difference was less than 3 pp for both). Looking at self-defined employment status, students and employed people were most likely to purchase cultural goods and services online. Students’ top purchases were tickets to events (36%), followed by subscriptions to music streaming services (30%) and games as downloads (22%). For employed people, the top purchases were subscriptions to video streaming services (40%), followed by e-books or audiobooks as downloads (11%) and subscriptions to news content (9%). By contrast, economically inactive people (other than students) were generally the least likely to buy cultural goods and services online, although they came second for paid subscriptions to online news content (6%) after employed people.

[[Image:Table 2 - Use of the internet for buying cultural goods and services, by socioeconomic characteristic, EU, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Use of the internet for buying cultural goods and services, by socio-economic characteristic, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5b8ed0b9-3e18-46b7-be4e-32f27d0c67e9?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T08:22:53Z isoc_ec_ibgs])|alt= a table showing the use of the internet for buying cultural goods and services, by socioeconomic characteristic in the EU in 2025 as a percentage among people who used the internet in the previous 3 months. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''''Online purchases of cultural goods and services were most popular in Ireland, the Netherlands and Denmark'''''

Figure 5 shows how online purchases varied across the EU for the 5 most popular cultural goods and services analysed in this article. Ireland, Denmark and the Netherlands came top in most categories, while Romania and Bulgaria had the lowest shares. More than half of internet users in Ireland (64%), Denmark (61%), the Netherlands (59%) and Sweden (54%) had bought subscriptions to film, series or sports streaming services, and this figure was over 20% in 19 other EU countries. For event tickets, Ireland (52%), the Netherlands and Denmark (48% in both countries) came top again. In 8 other EU countries, over one third of internet users had made this type of purchase (Finland, Greece, Czechia, Estonia, Cyprus, Sweden, Luxembourg and Germany). Subscribing to a music streaming service came 3rd overall, with at least one quarter of internet users making this type of purchase in 9 EU countries. The cultural services next in the ranking – software as downloads (4th), games as downloads (5th) and e-books or audiobooks as downloads (6th) – were less popular across all EU countries. But, in certain countries, the rates were still relatively high. For example, over a quarter of internet users in Ireland (28%) and Estonia (26%) had purchased software as a download. Games as downloads were purchased by 23% of internet users in Denmark and 21% in Sweden. And a quarter of users in Ireland had purchased e-books or audiobooks as downloads, along with 21% of users in Croatia.

[[Image:Figure 5 - Five from those selected types of cultural goods and services bought most frequent by internet in the last three months, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Five from those selected types of cultural goods and services bought most frequent by internet in the last 3 months, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ba2f3894-04a9-413f-8e6a-44ec478b4e95?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T08:23:07Z isoc_ec_ibgs])|alt= a chart showing the percentage of internet users who purchased five selected types of cultural goods and services online in 2025, broken down by EU, EU-countries, EFTA countries, candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=Culture_statistics_-_Use_of_ICT_for_cultural_purposes_2026.xlsx|title=Use of ICT in cultural participation: tables and figures}} === Footnotes === ===Data sources=== All the data in this article are taken from the annual [[Glossary:EU survey on the use of ICT in households and by individuals|EU survey on ICT usage in households and by individuals]]. The survey started in 2002 and aims to collect statistics on aspects such as accessing and using ICT, internet use, use of e-commerce and digital skills. The data can be broken down according to many variables, such as age, sex and level of educational attainment. The target population is people aged 16 to 74 living in private households. See [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/digital-economy-and-society/legislation digital economy and society legislation]. When analysing internet use for cultural purposes, 3 groups of indicators were used. '''Use of the internet for selected cultural activities'''
''Indicators are sourced from Eurostat table isoc_ci_ac_i and include the following activities:'' * reading online news sites, newspapers or news magazines (I_IUNW1) * watching internet-streamed TV or videos (I_IUSTVV) * listening to music (e.g. web radio or music streaming) or downloading music (I_IUMUSS1) * playing or downloading games (I_IUPDG) '''Use of generative artificial intelligence tools'''
''Indicators are sourced from Eurostat table isoc_ai_iaiu and include the following activities:'' * use of generative AI tools: in the last 3 months (I_IUAI) * use of generative AI tools: for private purposes (I_IUAIPR) * use of generative AI tools: for professional (work) purposes (I_IUAIWP) * use of generative AI tools: for formal education (I_IUAIFE) '''Use of the internet for purchasing selected cultural goods and services'''
''Indicators are sourced from Eurostat table isoc_ec_ibgs, and include:'' * an aggregated indicator covering online purchases of cultural services (I_BCS2) * individuals having a paid subscription to a films, series or sports streaming service (I_BFLMS2) * individuals having a paid subscription to a music streaming service (I_BMUSS2) * individuals having a paid subscription to online news sites, online newspapers (e-papers) or online magazines (I_BBOOKNLS2) * individuals having a paid subscription to a gaming streaming service (I_BGAMSS) * online purchasing of tickets to events (I_BTICK2) * online purchasing of printed books, magazines or newspapers (I_BBOOKNLG) * online purchasing of music as CDs, vinyls, films or series as DVDs, Blu-ray, etc. (I_BMUFL) * software as downloads (I_BSOFT2) * games as downloads (I_BGAMES2) * e-books or audio books as downloads (I_BBOOK2) '''The most recent available data are from 2024 for the following indicators:''' * watching internet-streamed TV or videos (I_IUSTVV) * listening to music (e.g. web radio or music streaming) or downloading music (I_IUMUSS1) * playing or downloading games (I_IUPDG) * online purchasing of printed books, magazines or newspapers (I_BBOOKNLG) * online purchasing of music as CDs, vinyls, films or series as DVDs, Blu-ray, etc. (I_BMUFL) ===Context=== Culture is one of Europe’s greatest assets: it is a source of values and identity and provides a sense of belonging. It also contributes to well-being, social cohesion and inclusion. The cultural and creative sectors stimulate economic growth, job creation and international trade. To boost cultural activities, the EU has launched the [https://culture.ec.europa.eu/creative-europe Creative Europe programme] alongside several policy measures under the 2023-2026 EU work plan for culture. The work plan, adopted by EU culture ministers in December 2022, sets out 4 main priorities for European cooperation in cultural policymaking * artists and cultural professionals: empowering the cultural and creative sectors * culture for the people: enhancing cultural participation and the role of culture in society * culture for the planet: unleashing the power of culture * culture for co-creative partnerships: strengthening the cultural dimension of EU external relations. One of the European Commission’s priorities across all sectors is producing reliable, comparable and up-to-date cultural statistics as a basis for sound cultural policymaking. Eurostat compiles culture statistics from various data collections to track cultural trends in areas like education, employment, business, international trade and participation and consumption patterns. ===Other articles=== *[[Culture|Culture (all Statistics Explained articles on culture)]] *[[Digital_economy_and_society|Digital economy and society (all Statistics Explained articles on the digital economy and society)]] *[[Digital_economy_and_society_statistics_-_households_and_individuals|Digital economy and society statistics - households and individuals]] *[[E-commerce_statistics_for_individuals|E-commerce statistics for individuals]] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Category:Sport Sport] (articles on sport statistics) ===Database=== * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/culture/database Culture (cult)], see: ** use of ICT for cultural purposes [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/culture/database?node_code=cult_pcs_ict (cult_pcs_ict)]

title: Degree of urbanisation classification - 2011 revision
text:
This background article presents the degree of urbanisation typology for [[Glossary:LAU2|Local Administrative Units level 2]] (LAU2). It describes the methodology developed in 2011 to classify LAU2s into thinly, intermediate and densely populated areas. These three types of area have been identified and defined using a criterion of geographical contiguity in combination with a minimum population threshold based on population grid square cells of 1 km2. This methodology has been jointly developed by DG AGRI and DG REGIO of the [[Glossary:European_Commission_(EC)|European Commission]] with the support of the Joint Research Center (JRC) and [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]. The article also describes the original degree of urbanisation classification based on population size and density of LAU2s. === Degree of urbanisation classification === The Degree of urbanisation (DEGURBA) is a classification that indicates the character of an area. Based on the share of local population living in urban clusters and in urban centres, it classifies local administrative units level 2 ([[Glossary:LAU2|LAU2]]) into three types of area: ''[[Glossary:Thinly-populated_area|thinly populated area]]'' (rural area); ''[[Glossary:Town or suburb |intermediate density area]]'' (towns and suburbs/small urban area), and [[Glossary:Densely_populated_area|''densely populated area'' ]](cities/large urban area). [[Image:Degree of Urbanisation 2011 - V2.png|thumb|centre|450px|Map 1: Degree of urbanisation 2011
''Source:'' EFGS, JRC, Eurostat, LandScan, REGIO-GIS]] '''Methodology''' The classification of local administrative units (LAU2) in the mentioned areas uses as a criterion the geographical contiguity in combination with the share of local population living in the different type of clusters. In a first step, the typology of clusters starts by classifing grid cells of 1 km2 to one of the three folowing clusters, according to their population size and density: *[[Glossary:Urban centre|High-density cluster]]/urban centre: contiguous grid cells of 1 km2 with a density of at least 1 500 inhabitants per km2 and a minimum population of 50 000; *[[Glossary:Urban_cluster|Urban cluster]]: cluster of contiguous grid cells of 1 km2 with a density of at least 300 inhabitants per km2 and a minimum population of 5 000; *[[Glossary:Rural_grid_cell|Rural grid cell]]: grid cell outside high-density clusters and urban clusters. In a second step, local administrative units (LAU2) are then classified to one of three type of areas: *'''Densely populated area''' (alternative names: cities or large urban area): at least 50 % lives in high-density clusters; in addition, each high-density cluster should have at least 75 % of its population in densely-populated LAU2s; this also ensures that all high-density clusters are represented by at least one densely-populated LAU2, even when this cluster represents less than 50 % of the population of that LAU2; *'''Intermediate density area''' (alternative name: towns and suburbs or small urban area): less than 50 % of the population lives in rural grid cells and less than 50 % live in high-density clusters; *'''Thinly-populated area''' (alternative name: rural area): more than 50 % of the population lives in rural grid cells. Figure 1 shows the degree of urbanisation classification by grid cells and LAU2 units, and the set of images in Figure 2 provides an example of the type of cluster and degree of urbanisation of the city of Cork, Ireland. [[Image:Degree of urbanisation - Grid cells and LAU2 units approaches.png|thumb|centre|450px|Figure 1: Degree of urbanisation- Grid cells and LAU2 units
''Source:'' Eurostat]]
[[Image:Cork, Ireland - Type of cluster and degree of urbanisation.png|thumb|centre|450px|Figure 2: Cork, Ireland: Type of cluster and degree of urbanisation
''Source:'' Eurostat]] === Revision of the degree of urbanisation === The original degree of urbanisation defined the three types of areas based on the population size and density and contiguity of local administrative units level 2 (LAU2). As LAU2s vary considerably in area size, the results were distorted, reducing the comparability between countries with large LAU2s and small LAU2s. For this reason, the classification of the degree of urbanisation has recently been revised and modified. After the revision, the above-mentioned types of area have been identified and defined using a criterion of geographical contiguity in combination with a minimum population threshold based on population grid square cells of 1 km2. These grid cells all have the same shape and surface, which avoids distortions caused by using units varying in size. The new methodology, that replaces the methodology used in the [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)|Labour Force Survey]] (LFS), has been agreed by the Directorates-General (DGs) for Regional and Urban Policy, Agriculture and Rural Development and Eurostat, and it is implemented from reference year 2012 onwards in all surveys concerned. === Advantages of the population grid approach === The two main advantages of the new methodology based on population grid cells are greater comparability and a harmonisation of spatial concepts. '''Greater comparability and less distortion''' The problem with the original degree of urbanisation is that it relied on the population size of LAU2s as one of the main criteria. If a LAU2 was large enough, even the presence of a large city would lead to it being classified as thinly populated. For example, the original degree of urbanisation classified the LAU2 of Uppsala (SE), Aalborg (DK) and Badajoz (ES) as thinly populated despite the presence of cities with more than 100 000 inhabitants. As a result, the degree of urbanisation of countries with large LAU2s was underestimated compared to countries with small LAU2s. This new approach also uses the criterion of [[Glossary:Population_density|population density]] but applied to units of analysis of the same size: 1km2 grid cells. As a result, it can look inside the large LAU2s and detect the presence of towns or cities within a LAU2. Therefore, the results are less distorted and more comparable between countries. '''Harmonising four spatial concepts''' Prior to the new degree of urbanisation, four similar but not identical urban-rural spatial concepts were used: rural areas (according to the [[Glossary:Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development_(OECD)|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development]] (OECD), thinly populated area, densely populated area, and [[Glossary:City data collection|Urban Audit City]] (see Figure 3). [[Image:Four conflicting spatial concepts.png|thumb|centre|450px|Figure 3: Four conflicting spatial concepts
''Source:'' Eurostat]] The OECD method classifies all LAU2 with a population density below 150 inhabitants per km2 as rural. This is different from the original degree of urbanisation method which also took into account population size and contiguity. This OECD method will also classify large LAU2s within a city as rural due to low population density. The Urban Audit covered a large sample of cities with at least 50 000 inhabitants. These cities were not selected in a harmonised manner and not all cities were included. The Urban Audit was not compatible with the densely populated areas identified by the original [[Glossary:LFS|LFS]] method. The new degree of urbanisation ensures that rural areas equal thinly populated areas. This also means that rural regions are identified using the same approach (share of population in rural grids). The high-density clusters were used to identify all cities with an urban centre with at least 50 000 inhabitants. As a result the Urban Audit now covers all those cities and the densely populated areas are identical to the Urban Audit cities (see Figure 4). [[Image:Harmonised spatial concepts.png|thumb|centre|450px|Figure 4: Harmonised spatial concepts
''Source:'' Eurostat]] === Adjustments required by the population grid approach === In order to classify properly LAU2s based on the grid cell approach described, a few additional correction rules must be provided: *If the LAU2s do not have a raster equivalent, they are classified according to the share of territory in rural grid cells and high-density clusters; *Thinly populated LAU2s may be classified as intermediate or densely populated due to border effects if rural grid cells cover most of the territory. For that reason, LAU2s with a population below 5 000 inhabitants and 90 % of its area in rural grid cells are reclassified as rural area; *Very small densely populated LAU2s may be classified as thinly populated due to the coarse resolution of the population grid. For that reason, LAU2s with an area less than 5 km2 but with a share of surface outside rural grid cells higher than 30 % are reclassified as intermediate density or densely populated according to the share of the correspondent cluster. As LAU2s vary considerably in area, this methodology will lead to a closer match between a high-density cluster and densely populated LAU2s in countries with small LAU2s than in those with large LAU2s. To take this difference into account, the classification can be adjusted as following: *A densely populated LAU2 can be classified intermediate as long as 75 % of its high-density cluster population remains in densely populated LAU2s; *A thinly populated or intermediate density LAU2 can be classified as densely populated if it belongs to a group of LAU2s with a political function and if the majority of population of this group of LAU2s lives in a high-density cluster. ===Other articles=== *[[Population grids]] (background article) *[[Regions and cities ]] *[[Territorial typologies]] ===Tables=== *[{{Template:Main tables|dedicated_section=population}} Population (t_populat)], see: :Demography (t_pop) ::Demography - Regional data (t_demoreg) ===Database=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/cities/data/database Urban audit] ===Dedicated section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=degree_urbanisation}} Degree of urbanisation] *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=region_cities}} Regions and cities], see: :City statistics - Urban Audit *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=rural_development}} Rural development] ===External links=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/dgs/jrc/index.cfm?id= European Commission - Joint Research Centre] *[http://www.eea.europa.eu/data-and-maps/data/population-density-disaggregated-with-corine-land-cover-2000-2 European Environment Agency - Population density disaggregated with Corine land cover 2000] *[http://www.efgs.info/ European Forum for GeoStatistics] *[http://www.oecd.org/gov/regional-policy/OECD_regional_typology_Nov2012.pdf OECD REGIONAL TYPOLOGY] (pdf file, 1.93 Mb) *[http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docgener/work/2014_01_new_urban.pdf DG REGIO working paper on the new degree of urbanisation - 2014] {{Unit|topic=X_Regions}} [[Category:General and regional statistics|Degree of urbanisation classification - 2011 revision]] [[Category:Regions and cities|Degree of urbanisation classification - 2011 revision]] [[Category:Background article|Degree of urbanisation classification - 2011 revision]] [[Category:Regions and cities - background articles|Degree of urbanisation classification - 2011 revision]]

title: Culture statistics - international trade in cultural goods
text:
Data on international trade in cultural goods are derived from Eurostat's international trade statistics. Data extracted in July 2025. Planned article update: October 2026. In 2024, cultural goods valued at €31.5 billion were exported outside the EU. In 2024, compared with 2019, 'Antiques' stood out as the category of cultural goods with the highest increase in Extra-EU exports, rising by +75.9%. In 2024, in most EU countries (22), at least half of the value of cultural goods exports was directed to other EU countries.
[[Image:Figure 7 - Value of extra-EU exports of cultural goods by main partner and by category, EU, 2024_(€ million).png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source: ''Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cult_trd_prt}}|alt=Sankey flow diagram showing the value in euro millions of extra-EU exports of cultural goods by main partner and by category in the EU in 2024.]]
This article is part of the ''[[Culture_statistics|Culture statistics]]'' online publication. Trade statistics for cultural goods provide information on the value of international exchanges of these goods (based on current prices when data were captured) and show the proportion of cultural trade relative to all [[Glossary:EU_enlargements|EU]] international trade. The analysis looks mainly at data from 2024 and presents
*[[Glossary:Export|export]] and [[Glossary:Import|import]] values in absolute and relative terms (in euro million and as a share of total trade respectively) *[[Glossary:Extra-EU_and_intra-EU|extra-EU and intra-EU]] trade *the type of goods traded *the EU's main trading partners; and *a 5-year comparison to account for mid-term tendencies in the sector Statistics on international trade in cultural goods are based on data extracted from [[Glossary:COMEXT|COMEXT]], Eurostat's database on international trade in goods.
=== Cultural trade in 2024 at EU and national level === This article analyses statistics on international trade in cultural goods for the [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU]], 5 [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]] (Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia and Türkiye) and 1 potential candidate (Kosovo*). ''*This designation is without prejudice to positions on status, and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo Declaration of Independence.''

'''Trade partners for the EU and EU countries'''

The aggregated data for the EU concern extra-EU trade, presenting the EU as a single entity and excluding intra-EU trade (between the EU countries). By contrast, trade data at national level for individual EU countries concern both intra-EU and extra-EU trade. Cultural goods in international trade, are those using 'creation' or 'artistic expression' in the production process, the purpose of which is to transmit aesthetic, symbolic or artistic values, or which are considered to enable artistic expression or can be recognised as designed primarily to provide access to cultural content. Goods meeting those criteria are identified in 12 groups of cultural products – 'Antiques', 'Works of art', 'Craft articles', 'Jewellery', 'Books', 'Newspapers, journals and periodicals', 'Maps', 'Architectural plans and drawings', 'Photographic plates and films', 'Recorded media', 'Video game consoles', and 'Musical instruments' (see Figure 9). These groups are very diverse; some contain products for mass consumption ('Books', 'Newspapers') and others only specialised items ('Architectural plans and drawings', 'Photographic plates and films'). The statistics do not cover the large-scale manufactured products that partially give access to cultural content (for example, TV sets, cameras, smartphones, or tablets).

'''Extra-EU trade in cultural goods – 2019 and 2024 overview'''

When comparing 2024 with 2019, the value of extra-EU exports of cultural goods increased by 42.3% (from €22.1 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] in 2019 to €31.5 billion in 2024), and the value of extra-EU imports increased by 6.4% (from €18.5 billion in 2019 to €19.6 billion in 2024). The [[Glossary:Trade_balance|trade balance]] for cultural goods increased from €3.7 billion in 2019 to €11.9 billion in 2024. The ratio of exports to imports – the 'cover ratio' – rose from 1.20 in 2019 to 1.60 in 2024 (see Table 1). 'Jewellery' (54.6%), 'Works of art' (10.7%), 'Books' and 'Recorded media' (8.9% each) accounted for the largest shares of extra-EU cultural goods exports in 2019. In 2024, 'Jewellery' represented almost two-thirds of such exports (65.0%), followed by 'Works of art' (10.6%) and 'Books' (5.6%). Concerning extra-EU imports of cultural goods, in 2019, the largest shares were recorded for 'Jewellery' (41.0%), 'Video games consoles' (20.6%), 'Books' (9.2%) and 'Works of art' (8.2%). In 2024, the largest shares were for 'Jewellery' (34.6%), 'Video games consoles' (18.7%), 'and 'Works of art' (15.8%) categories. The increase in the total value of cultural goods exports between 2019 and 2024 was driven mainly by the category 'Jewellery' (+€8.4 billion), whose value was largely influenced by high Jewellery exports from Italy to Türkiye, reaching a historical maximum of €5.3 billion. Additionally, 'Works of art' (+€1.0 billion) and 'Antiques' (+€0.5 billion) contributed smaller but notable shares to this growth. This increase was partly counterbalanced by declines observed in Other cultural categories, notably 'Recorded media' (-€0.4 billion) and 'Books' (-€0.2 billion), reflecting lower export values in media-related products. Regarding imports, the main contributors to the increase in the total value of cultural goods were 'Works of art' (+€1.6 billion), while 'Jewellery' recorded the highest decrease (-€0.8 billion).

'''International trade in cultural goods developments'''

Figure 1 illustrates the evolution of extra-EU trade in cultural goods (solid lines) in a broader time perspective and in relation to the overall trends in total extra-EU trade. The stable growth in the value of cultural goods trade observed between 2015 and 2019 collapsed in 2020, reflecting the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on international trade flows. Exports and imports of cultural goods followed different patterns in that year: exports of cultural goods showed a sharper decline compared with total exports, while imports were less affected. The values of cultural exports and imports rebounded in 2021 and continued to increase in 2022 and 2023. In 2024, extra-EU exports of cultural goods recorded a significant year-on-year increase of 21.2%. This sharp rise contrasts with the relatively stable trend in total extra-EU exports, which grew only marginally over the same period (+1.1%). By contrast, imports of cultural goods fell by 20.4% from their 2023 peak, interrupting the upward trajectory observed in the 3 preceding years. As for total extra-EU imports, they decreased by 3.4%, following a sharper contraction already recorded in the previous year. On average between 2011 and 2024, the value of cultural goods exports accounted for about 1.0% of total extra-EU exports, while imports represented around 0.9% of total extra-EU imports. In 2024, cultural goods corresponded to 1.2% of total extra-EU exports and 0.8% of total extra-EU imports.

'''International trade in cultural goods in the EU countries'''

As shown in Table 2, the value of cultural goods exports increased in 20 of the 27 EU countries between 2019 and 2024. The highest increase was registered in Ireland, with a value in 2024 that was 2.7 times higher than 5 years before. The absolute value of exports increased the most in Italy (+€8.5 billion), the Netherlands (+€2.7 billion), and Ireland (+€1.1 billion). It decreased the most in Poland (-€1.1 billion) and Germany (-€0.7 billion). Compared with 2019, the value of cultural goods imports increased in 18 EU countries. The largest increases in absolute terms were recorded in the Netherlands (+€1.6 billion) and Ireland (+€1.1 billion). Decreases in the value of cultural goods imports were observed mainly in Poland (-€0.7 billion), France and Germany (-€0.4 billion each). In 2024, 12 EU countries had a positive trade balance in cultural goods. The largest positive trade balance in cultural goods was in Italy (+€13.1 billion), followed by France (+€1.8 billion) and the Netherlands (+€1.3 billion). Italy was the trade balance leader in both years. By contrast, in 2024, the largest trade deficit in cultural goods was recorded in Austria (-€1.0 billion).

'''Contribution of cultural trade to overall exports'''

Looking at the 5-year perspective between 2019 and 2024, the share of cultural goods in total exports increased by at least 0.1 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] in 6 EU countries, with the largest relative rise in Italy (up from 1.8% to 2.7%). In 19 EU countries, the share of cultural goods in total exports decreased, with the largest decline in Poland (down from 1.4% to 0.7%, see Figure 2). In 2024, cultural products accounted for more than 1% of the total value of national exports of goods (including extra-EU and intra-EU trade) in Italy (2.7%) and France (1.8%). By contrast, the shares of cultural goods in national exports were relatively small in Cyprus, Luxembourg, Slovenia, Bulgaria and Hungary (0.2% each), as well as in Finland (0.1%).

'''Contribution of cultural trade to overall imports'''

As shown in Figure 3, imports of cultural goods in 2024 represented more than 1% of total national imports in Ireland, France (both 1.3%) and Austria (1.1%). In contrast, the lowest shares were recorded in Lithuania, Slovenia and Hungary (0.2% each). In 7 EU countries, this share was higher in 2024 than in 2019. The most notable increase was observed in Ireland (up from 0.7% to 1.3%), while the sharpest decrease was in Poland (from 1.1% to 0.5%).

===Intra-EU and extra-EU trade===
For most EU countries, trade with other EU countries accounted for more than half of both exports and imports of cultural goods (see Figure 4). Notable exceptions include the Netherlands and Ireland, reflecting their specific role linked to [[Glossary:Quasi-transit|quasi-transit]] trade.The high share recorded in the Netherlands may be attributed in part to the impact of quasi-transit of goods, in other words, the so-called ’Rotterdam effect’ (see the Data sources section for more details). In 2024, EU countries exported cultural goods worth €56.0 billion, of which 43.7% went to other EU countries and 56.3% to non-EU countries. The highest intra-EU exports shares were recorded in Poland (86.2%) and Romania (85.8%), while the lowest were in Ireland (11.7%), Italy (21.5%) and France (27.5%). Sweden, Spain and Denmark showed a more balanced pattern, with cultural goods exports split almost equally between intra-EU and extra-EU destinations. Imports of cultural goods totalled €41.7 billion, with 52.9% coming from intra-EU partners. The share of intra-EU imports was particularly high in Slovakia (91.9%) and Austria (85.9%), while the lowest shares were observed in the Netherlands (23.8%), Ireland (42.0%) and France (43.8%). Countries with a balanced distribution of cultural goods imports between intra- and extra-EU destinations were Malta, Belgium, Germany and Italy.

=== Trade in cultural goods by product === '''Exports of cultural goods by categories'''

In 2024, 'Jewellery' made of precious metals and stones dominated the extra-EU exports of cultural goods in terms of value (65.0%). Together with 'Works of art' (10.6%) and 'Books' (5.6%), the 3 categories accounted for more than 80% of the total value of extra-EU cultural goods exports (see Table 3). The level of trade in cultural goods is affected by many factors, including the characteristics of cultural products that make them mass-market or niche products, technological innovations driving new consumption patterns, abilities among countries in producing and processing these goods, etc. The categories of cultural products and the EU countries where these categories are the leading domains of the total export of cultural goods are listed below. * 'Jewellery' accounted for more than half of the total value of cultural goods exports in Italy (87.9%), Cyprus (79.8%), France (64.7%) and Ireland (64.5%). In other 9 EU countries (Romania, Malta, Portugal, Luxembourg, Belgium, Spain, Denmark, Greece and Germany), 'Jewellery' remained the main category of cultural goods but did not exceed 50% of total cultural goods exports value. * 'Works of art' represented the highest share of cultural goods exports in Luxembourg (35.2%), equal to that of the 'Jewellery' category. * 'Books' were the main cultural goods exported by 7 EU countries – accounting for more than half of total exports value from Latvia (69.3%), Lithuania (58.0%) and Slovenia (53.7%) – followed by Hungary, Poland, Estonia and Croatia. * the 'Recorded media' category amounted to the highest share of total cultural goods export value in 3 EU countries – Finland (46.1%), Czechia (42.6%) and Austria (36.8%). * the 'Video game consoles' category had high shares in 4 EU countries – the Netherlands (46.4%), Bulgaria (45.2%), Slovakia (33.9%) and Sweden (32.9%).

'''Imports of cultural goods by categories'''

In 2024, 4 categories together accounted for over three-quarters of the total import value of cultural goods into the EU from non-EU countries: 'Jewellery' (34.6%), 'Video game consoles' (18.7%), 'Works of art' (15.8%) and 'Books' (9.4%) – see Table 4. Looking at imports in individual EU countries (and therefore taking account of both intra-EU imports and extra-EU imports) * in 14 countries, 'Jewellery' had the highest share in the total value of cultural goods imports, exceeding half of the total value of cultural goods imports in Italy (53.5%) and Romania (53.0%) * 'Video game consoles' recorded the highest share in 8 countries – the most in the Netherlands (49.6%), followed by Slovakia, Poland, Sweden, Croatia, Spain, Finland and Hungary * 'Works of art' was the leading category of cultural imports in Belgium (23.6%) * 'Books' represented the highest share in Slovenia (33.0%) and Luxembourg (28.8%) * 'Craft' accounted for the highest share in terms of value in Bulgaria (31.4%), while 'Recorded media' were predominant in Czechia (26.6%)

===The EU's main partners for trade in cultural goods=== '''Leading destinations for EU exports of cultural goods'''

In 2024, the EU's main export markets for cultural goods were Switzerland (18.7% of extra-EU exports by value, €5.9 billion), Türkiye (18.1%, €5.7 billion) and the United States (15.7%, €4.9 billion). Together, they accounted for over half of all exports of cultural goods, while exports to each of the EU's other trading partners were below 10% (see Figure 5). The share of the EU's 10 main export partners in cultural goods trade rose from 80.0% in 2019 to 82.4% in 2024. Over the period considered, the largest absolute increases were recorded for exports to Türkiye (+€5.3 billion) and to the United States (+€1.9 billion). By contrast, the steepest decline was observed in exports to the United Kingdom (-€2.0 billion).

'''Leading countries for cultural goods imported into the EU''' In 2024, more than a quarter of the EU imports of cultural goods (26.1%) were from China. Together with Switzerland (16.4%), and the United States (13.8%) these 3 countries accounted for more than half of all cultural goods imports into the EU (see Figure 6). The share of the EU's 10 main import partners in cultural goods trade fell from 92.6% in 2019 to 90.0% in 2024. Between 2019 and 2024, the largest increase was recorded for imports from China (from €4.4 billion in 2019 to €5.1 billion in 2024), while the largest decrease was observed for imports from the United Kingdom (from €3.8 billion to €2.6 billion).

===Extra-EU cultural goods' trade flows by category of product=== '''Exports'''

As shown in Figure 7, in 2024, 'Jewellery', with a value of more than €20.5 billion, was the most exported cultural goods category outside the EU. Switzerland was the main destination to which Jewellery products were directed, followed by Türkiye and the United States. 'Works of art' exported outside the EU, with a total value of €3.3 billion, were mainly directed to the United States, the United Kingdom and Switzerland. Furthermore, extra-EU trade of cultural products such as 'Books', 'Recorded media' and 'Crafts' were more widely distributed across partner countries. These categories also recorded notable export shares to destinations outside the EU's 10 main trading partners for cultural goods.
[[Image:Figure 7 - Value of extra-EU exports of cultural goods by main partner and by category, EU, 2024_(€ million).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Value of extra-EU exports of cultural goods by main partner and by category, EU, 2024

'''Imports''' Figure 8 shows the trade relations with the top 10 extra-EU partners by category of imported cultural goods. In 2024, more than one-third of all cultural goods imported into the EU were 'Jewellery'. Switzerland was the main origin of these imports, accounting for 33.8% of the EU's overall Jewellery imports, followed by China (10.4%). 'Video game consoles' and 'Works of art' together accounted for a similar share to that of 'Jewellery'. Imports of 'Video game consoles' were dominated by China, representing 74.7% of the import value in this category, while imports of 'Works of art' were mainly shared between the United Kingdom (33.7%), the United States (27.4%) and Switzerland (21.5%). In addition to 'Video game consoles' imports, China was a leading partner for the EU's imports of Craft articles and Musical instruments, accounting for 47.8% and 38.1% of the import values in these categories, respectively. Other main partners for cultural goods can be identified in categories where at least one-third of the import value came from a single country. These include the United States for 'Photographic plates and films' (91.7%), Switzerland for 'Jewellery' (33.8%), and the United Kingdom for 'Books' (33.3%). For 'Antiques' two leading partners were observed: the United States (36.8%) and the United Kingdom (34.7%). Several trade partners were strongly associated with specific cultural goods. 'Jewellery' accounted for more than half of all cultural goods imports from Thailand (97.1%), Türkiye (78.6%), Hong Kong (78.4%), India (78.3%) and Switzerland (71.2%), while 'Video game consoles' dominated imports from Malaysia (81.5%), Japan (56.7%) and China (53.5%).
