These skills can help overcome geographical and social barriers; for example, they can help people living in remote regions or from socially disadvantaged groups to make effective use of online services. The [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/digital-decade-policy-programme digital decade] policy programme provides a framework for Europe’s digital transformation, setting common objectives and targets. It reflects the EU’s broader ambition to achieve digital sovereignty in an open and interconnected world, supporting an inclusive, sustainable and competitive digital future. The programme sets a number of key objectives, including that at least 80% of the population should have basic digital skills by 2030. While basic digital skills are essential for all, older adults, people with low levels of education and people outside the labour market face higher risks of digital exclusion. By contrast, advanced ICT skills are increasingly important, both for competitiveness and technological sovereignty.
'''More about the data: defining digital skills''' The digital skills of individuals may be measured through a digital skills indicator. This is a composite indicator covering activities in 5 areas of digital competence. *Information and data literacy: articulating information needs; locating and retrieving digital data, information and content; judging the relevance of a source and its content; storing, managing, organising digital data, information and content. *Communication and collaboration: interacting, communicating and collaborating through digital technologies while being aware of cultural and generational diversity; participating in society through public and private digital services and participatory citizenship; managing one’s digital identity and reputation. *Digital content creation: creating and editing digital content; improving and integrating information and content into an existing body of knowledge while understanding how copyright and licences are to be applied; knowing how to give understandable instructions for a computer system. *Problem-solving: identifying needs and problems, and resolving conceptual problems and problem situations in digital environments; using digital tools to innovate processes and products; keeping up-to-date with the digital evolution. *Safety skills: protecting devices, content, personal data and privacy in digital environments; protecting physical and psychological health, and being aware of digital technologies for social well-being and social inclusion; being aware of the environmental impact of digital technologies and their use. To achieve at least a basic overall level of digital skills, individuals must have performed at least 1 activity in each of these 5 areas of competence. For example, within digital content creation, they should have carried out at least 1 of the following: using word processing software; using spreadsheets; editing photos, video or audio files; copying or moving files between folders, devices or cloud storage; creating files combining elements such as text, images, tables, charts, animation or sound; using advanced spreadsheet functions (such as formulas, macros and other developer tools) to organise, analyse or modify data; writing code in a programming language.
'''''In 2025, West-Nederland recorded the highest regional share of people with at least basic digital skills, at 85.2%''''' In 2025, 60.4% of people aged 16 to 74 in the EU had at least basic digital skills; this figure was 19.6 percentage points below the policy target for 2030. '''Map 4''' shows the regional distribution across NUTS level 1 regions; this is relatively homogeneous within individual EU countries, while more pronounced differences could be observed between countries. Across the EU, the regional distribution was slightly skewed, as 49 regions (out of the 87 for which data are available) recorded shares above the EU average, while 38 were below it. The highest regional shares of people with at least basic digital skills – already at or above the policy target of 80.0% – were recorded in Denmark, Ireland, the Netherlands and Finland. By contrast, the lowest shares were observed in eastern EU countries, in particular Bulgaria and Romania. Looking in more detail, the Dutch regions of West-Nederland (85.2%) and Oost-Nederland (84.2%) had the highest regional shares, while 5 other regions also recorded shares above the policy target of 80.0%: Ireland (82.8%), Denmark (81.5%), the 2 remaining Dutch regions of Noord-Nederland (81.0%) and Zuid-Nederland (80.6%), and Finland (81.0%). There was a notable gap to the next highest share, recorded in the Spanish capital region of Comunidad de Madrid (71.9%). At the other end of the distribution, the lowest shares of people with at least basic digital skills were concentrated in eastern EU countries. In 2025, there were 5 regions where fewer than 40.0% of people had these skills: all 4 regions from Romania – including Macroregiunea Patru, which recorded the lowest share in the EU (27.1%) – and Severna i Yugoiztochna Bulgaria.

These policy priorities are expected to have a significant impact on ICT usage in enterprises by accelerating the availability and adoption of advanced digital infrastructures and services. In particular, they are likely to facilitate greater integration of high-performance computing and AI-driven applications into business processes, thereby supporting increased digitalisation, efficiency gains and innovation capacity across enterprises in the EU.
'''More about the data: ICT usage in enterprises''' The information presented in this section is based on results of an [[Glossary:EU_survey_on_ICT_usage_and_e-commerce_in_enterprises|EU survey on ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises]]. Regional ICT statistics are presented for NUTS level 2 regions. They cover enterprises with 10 or more people employed in NACE Sections C to N (excluding K) and Group 95.1, hereafter referred to as the ‘non-financial business economy’. Exceptions include Belgium (where the data refer to NUTS level 1 regions) and Germany, Ireland, Greece, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Finland, Albania, Serbia and Türkiye (where national data are presented). Data for Romania relate to reference year 2023 instead of 2025.
'''''More than half of all enterprises in the EU’s non-financial business economy made use of business software in 2025''''' In 2025, some 53.5% of all enterprises in the EU’s non-financial business economy used business software (defined here as software for enterprise resource planning (ERP), customer relationship management (CRM) or business intelligence (BI)). '''Figure 2''' highlights that a relatively high proportion of enterprises in Denmark, Finland, Belgium and the Netherlands used business software. By contrast, the share of enterprises using business software was relatively low in several eastern EU countries – in particular, Bulgaria and Romania. The share of enterprises using business software varied considerably across the EU. In 2025, there were 74 regions (out of a total of 115 for which data are available) that reported shares below the EU average, while 40 regions were above it; the Swedish capital region of Stockholm had an identical share to the EU average. This apparent imbalance is partly due to the use of national data for several EU countries with many regions: for example, France, the Netherlands and Finland are each represented as a single region, and all had shares that were considerably above the EU average. By contrast, Germany – for which only national data are available – had a share that was slightly below the EU average. At the top end of the distribution, the Danish region of Sjælland recorded the highest share (75.6% of enterprises making use of business software). Several other regions also reported shares of at least 70.0%, including: the Spanish regions of La Rioja, País Vasco, Cataluña and Aragón; the Danish regions of Midtjylland, Syddanmark and Hovedstaden; the Belgian region of Vlaams Gewest; and Finland. In several multi-regional eastern EU countries, capital regions typically recorded the highest share of enterprises making use of business software reflecting a concentration of knowledge-intensive service enterprises and administrative headquarters; this pattern was also evident in Sweden and Lithuania. In 2025, 8 regions across the EU reported less than a quarter of enterprises using business software. This group comprised 6 regions in Romania (all based on 2023 data) and 2 regions in Bulgaria. Sud-Est (Romania) recorded the lowest share across EU regions with 9.9% of enterprises using business software. There were 2 other Romanian regions that had shares below 20.0%, namely Sud-Vest Oltenia (11.1%) and Sud-Muntenia (13.7%), while Severen tsentralen (20.1%) had the lowest share in Bulgaria. There were considerable variations in the share of enterprises using business software across many parts of the EU, with particularly pronounced differences in Spain and Romania. In Spain, regional shares ranged from a high of 72.8% in La Rioja down to 33.0% in Ciudad de Melilla. Romania (2023 data) also had a wide range, albeit at generally lower levels, with a peak of 43.6% in București-Ilfov and a low of 9.9% in Sud-Est.

''''' Midtjylland in Denmark was the only region in the EU where more than half of enterprises made use of artificial intelligence in 2025 ''''' In 2025, 20.0% of enterprises with 10 or more people employed in the EU’s non-financial business economy used [[Glossary:Artificial_intelligence_(AI)|artificial intelligence (AI)]]. This share increased considerably in recent years (see below for more details).
'''More about the data: artificial intelligence''' AI refers to the ability of machines or computers to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence. The statistics presented below concern enterprises making use of at least 1 of the following AI technologies generating pictures, videos, sound/audio: *performing analysis of written language *converting spoken language into machine-readable format *generating written or spoken language or programming code *identifying objects or persons based on images *using machine learning *automating different workflows or assisting in decision-making *enabling physical movement of machines via autonomous decisions based on observation of surroundings. As with the previous section on enterprise use of business software, the statistics below are presented for an aggregate covering the non-financial business economy – as defined by NACE Sections C to N (excluding K) and Group 95.1.
In 2025, the Danish region of Midtjylland (50.8%) recorded the highest share of enterprises using at least 1 AI technology (see '''Map 5'''). There were 7 other regions in the EU with shares of at least 35.0%, including: *Stockholm, the capital region of Sweden (44.8%), and Västsverige (37.1%) *Sjælland in Denmark (42.7%) *the Belgian capital region of Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest (42.3%; NUTS level 1) *Finland (37.8%; national data) *Wien, the capital region of Austria (37.4%), and Vorarlberg (36.4%). The share of enterprises using AI technologies was particularly low in regions characterised by limited internet use/access. This suggests that structural factors – such as the composition of regional economies or infrastructure gaps – may help explain some of the observed differences. In 2025, the lowest enterprise adoption rates for AI were generally recorded in eastern EU countries. Overall, there were 9 EU regions that reported fewer than 5.5% of enterprises using AI, including: *Severozapaden (1.8%), Yugoiztochen (4.5%), Yuzhen tsentralen (4.6%) and Severen tsentralen (4.8%) in Bulgaria *Mazowiecki regionalny (2.9%), which surrounds the capital region of Warszawski stołeczny (where a much higher share was recorded, at 16.0%), Warmińsko-mazurskie (4.5%) and Świętokrzyskie (5.3%) in Poland *Ciudad de Melilla (3.5%) in Spain *Romania (5.2%). There were considerable inter-regional variations in the share of enterprises making use of AI. In 2025, the largest absolute differences were observed in: *Denmark, from a high of 50.8% in Midtjylland to a low of 32.1% in the neighbouring region of Nordjylland (a difference of 18.7 percentage points) *Spain, from a high of 27.4% in the capital region of Comunidad de Madrid to a low of 3.5% in Ciudad de Melilla (a difference of 23.9 points) *Austria, from a high of 37.4% in the capital region of Wien to a low of 18.3% for the easternmost region of Burgenland (a difference of 19.1 points). There were also considerable differences in relative terms, for example: *in Spain, the highest share was recorded in Comunidad de Madrid (27.4%); this was 7.8 times as high as the lowest share in Ciudad de Melilla (3.5%) *in Bulgaria, the highest share was in the capital region of Yugozapaden (13.3%); this was 7.4 times as high as the lowest share in Severozapaden (1.8%).

Across the EU, the share of enterprises within the non-financial business economy using AI increased from 8.1% in 2023 to 20.0% by 2025, representing a gain of 11.9 percentage points. A closer look at developments across EU regions indicates that there was a relatively rapid uptake of AI in absolute terms. The most pronounced growth was recorded in Denmark, where the share of enterprises using AI grew from 15.2% in 2023 to 42.0% in 2025 (up 26.8 percentage points). Marked increases were also observed in the Belgian Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest (up 25.6 points), Sweden (up 24.7 points) and in the westernmost Austrian region of Vorarlberg (up 24.2 points). The proportion of EU enterprises using AI in 2025 was 2.5 times as high as in 2023. In relative terms, the strongest growth across regions was recorded in the easternmost Austrian region of Burgenland, where enterprise use of AI was 6.2 times as high (rising from 2.9% in 2023 to 18.3% in 2025). Substantial increases were also observed in Estonia (4.5 times as high; rising from 5.2% to 23.4%) and in the northern Hungarian region of Észak-Magyarország (also 4.5 times as high; rising from 1.4% to 6.3%). While the share of enterprises using AI increased in recent years for the vast majority of regions, a small number recorded annual declines. Falls were more frequently observed between 2023 and 2024 than between 2024 and 2025, with no region recording a decline for both periods. Between 2023 and 2024, the largest decreases were observed in the Spanish regions of La Rioja (where enterprise use of AI fell from 10.8% to 6.1%), Ciudad de Melilla (from 4.5% to 1.5%) and Principado de Asturias (from 12.7% to 10.0%). The largest decrease between 2024 and 2025 was recorded in Greece, as the share fell from 9.8% to 8.9%.

===Source data for figures and maps=== {{Template:Excel|filename=RYB2026 CH06 Digital society.xlsx|title=Regional digital society statistics}} ===Data sources=== Rapid technological changes in areas related to the internet and other new applications of ICTs pose challenges for statistics. As such, statistical tools are adapted to satisfy new demands for data and the ICT survey is reassessed on an annual basis. European ICT surveys provide timely statistics on individuals, households and enterprises relating to their use of ICTs. Many of these statistics are/were used in the benchmarking frameworks associated with the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission’s]] 6 priorities for the period 2019 to 2024: ''[https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/priorities-2019-2024/europe-fit-digital-age_en A Europe fit for the digital age]'' and the EU’s ''[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/europe-fit-digital-age/europes-digital-decade-digital-targets-2030_en digital decade targets for 2030]'' that are based on 4 points: skills, digital transformation of businesses, secure and sustainable digital infrastructures, and the digitalisation of public services. '''''ICT in households and by individuals''''' A majority of the data in this chapter are based on an annual [[Glossary:EU survey on the use of ICT in households and by individuals|survey on the use of ICT in households and by individuals]]. The legal basis for the 2025 survey is ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.LI.2019.261.01.0001.01.ENG Regulation (EU) 2019/1700 of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing a common framework for European statistics relating to persons and households, based on data at individual level collected from samples]''. This framework is implemented through a series of annual regulations that specify the detailed information to be collected, making it possible for the survey to be tailored to technological developments so that policymakers can have access to data that measure the impact of new technologies and services. For 2025, the survey was implemented by ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32024R2182 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU)  2024/2182]'' and supplemented by ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32024R2515 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU)  2024/2515]''. The population of households consists of all households having members in the age group of 16 to 74. The population of individuals consists of all people aged 16 to 74. The question on access to the internet is addressed to households, while questions on the use of ICTs are answered by individuals within a household. The information presented (and the underlying database) are organised according to survey years; the results presented refer to individuals’ experiences generally during the 3 months (but sometimes during the 12 months) prior to a survey. Regional statistics on ICT are generally available for NUTS level 2 regions. However, the latest data for Germany and Greece are only provided for NUTS level 1 regions; a similar situation exists for Türkiye. The latest information for Croatia concerns national data; a similar situation exists for Norway and Albania. For reference year 2025, regional statistics are presented according to NUTS 2024. For some EU countries, no information was available for earlier reference periods when preparing this publication. As such, comparisons over time are impacted by the change in classification with a coherent time series only available for NUTS level 1 regions in Poland and for national data in Portugal. '''''ICT use in enterprises''''' The data shown at the end of this chapter are based on an annual EU survey on ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises. The statistics were obtained from surveys conducted by national statistical authorities. The results of these annual surveys are used to benchmark ICT-driven developments, both by following developments for core variables over time and by looking in greater depth at other aspects at a specific point in time. The legal basis for the 2025 survey is ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32019R2152 Regulation (EU) 2019/2152 of the European Parliament and of the Council on European business statistics]''. In this fast-changing environment, this framework is implemented through a series of annual regulations. For reference year 2025, the survey was implemented by ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32024R1883 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/1883]''. The statistical unit for the regional data concerning the use of business software and artificial intelligence is the enterprise. The population consists of all enterprises with 10 or more people employed. The data are presented for an aggregate covering the non-financial business economy – as defined by NACE Sections C to N (excluding K) and Group 95.1. ==== Indicator definitions ==== '''Daily internet users''' Internet users, in the context of ICT statistics in the EU, are defined as people aged 16 to 74 making use of the internet in whatever way: *whether at home, at work or from anywhere else *whether for private or professional purposes *regardless of the device or type of connection used. Eurostat collects data on the frequency of internet access among individuals. This chapter presents information on the share of individuals who used the internet on average at least once a day. '''Digital skills''' The data presented on digital skills are collected every 2 years (biennial). The digital skills indicator is a composite measure based on selected internet and software-related activities performed by individuals aged 16 to 74 across 5 different areas: information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, problem-solving, and safety skills. The digital skills indicator is based upon the assumption that individuals who report having carried out specific activities possess the corresponding skills (in other words, the indicator serves as a proxy for actual digital competence). Skills are assessed for each of the 5 areas using 2 categories: ‘basic’ and ‘above basic’. The results presented combine these measures and therefore refer to individuals with ‘at least basic skills’. To achieve a level of at least basic overall digital skills, individuals must have performed at least 1 activity related to each of the 5 different areas. '''Internet activities''' People participating in social networks are people creating user profiles and posting messages or other contributions to websites and applications such as Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok or X (formerly Twitter). People using internet banking are people using online banking services either through a website or an app (application). The indicator relating to people using the internet to interact with public authorities concerns the interaction of individuals with public administrations through ICT. It can consist of obtaining information, downloading forms, returning filled-in forms or going through an administrative procedure completely electronically. '''Enterprise use of ICTs''' Enterprise use of business software refers to the use of software systems that support core business processes such as administration, production, logistics, customer management and decision-making. Enterprises with 10 or more people employed were asked whether they used specific types of business software. The data presented refer to enterprises that made use of at least 1 of the following: *enterprise resource planning (ERP) software to manage resources by sharing information among different functional areas such as accounting, planning, production or marketing *customer relationship management (CRM) software for managing information about customers such as relations or transactions *business intelligence (BI) software for accessing and analysing data, presenting analytical findings to provide detailed insights for decision-making and strategic planning. Enterprise use of AI refers to systems that use specific technologies to gather and/or use data to predict, recommend or decide. Enterprises with 10 or more people employed were asked whether they made use of a range of specific technologies. The data presented refer to enterprises that made use of at least 1 of the following AI technologies generating pictures, videos, sound/audio: *AI for performing analysis of written language *AI for machine learning *AI for automating different workflows or assisting in decision-making *AI for converting spoken language into machine-readable format *AI for identifying objects or persons based on images *AI for generating written or spoken language or programming code *AI enabling physical movement of machines via autonomous decisions based on the observation of surroundings. ===Context=== Digital technologies and ICT innovations are rapidly reshaping economies and societies, opening new business opportunities and transforming public and private life. Emerging technologies such as the internet of things and AI are increasingly enabling automation across key areas, including health, security, climate action, transport, energy and public administration. At the same time, digitalisation is changing how people learn, work, communicate and pursue personal goals, extending opportunities beyond traditional geographic and social boundaries. However, these changes also bring important challenges. The EU is seeking to strengthen its technological autonomy and develop frameworks to protect citizens from risks such as disinformation. Many individuals report concerns surrounding the use and protection of their personal data. Cyber threats can endanger both personal safety and critical infrastructure, while the rapid development of AI also raises increasing regulatory, ethical and security concerns. '''European Commission priorities''' In February 2020, the European Commission adopted an overarching presentation of ideas and actions for ''[https://commission.europa.eu/publications/communication-shaping-europes-digital-future_en Shaping Europe’s Digital Future]'', as well as specific proposals in relation to: *''{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52020DC0066:EN:NOT|title=A European strategy for data}}'' (COM(2020) 66 final), which seeks to promote the EU as a leading role model for a society empowered by data to make better decisions – in business and the public sector *a ''{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52020DC0065:EN:NOT|title=White Paper on Artificial Intelligence – A European approach to excellence and trust}}'' (COM(2020) 65 final). The ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32022R0868 Data Governance Act]'' (Regulation (EU) 2022/868) entered into force in June 2022. Its design supports the development of common European data spaces in strategic domains, involving both private and public players. Examples include health, the environment, energy, agriculture, mobility, finance, manufacturing, public administration and skills. This initiative aims to make more data available and facilitate data sharing across sectors and EU countries to leverage the potential of data for the benefit of citizens and businesses. For example: *good data management and data sharing may enable industries to develop innovative products and services *with more data available, the public sector may develop better policies, leading to more transparent governance and more efficient public services. The ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32022R1925 Digital Markets Act]'' (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925) entered into force in November 2022. It establishes a set of objective criteria for qualifying large online platforms as ‘gatekeepers’ (characterised by their strong economic or intermediation position). The Act aims to ensure that these platforms behave in a fair way, for example: *gatekeepers can no longer engage in self-preferencing on their platforms *users can delete pre-installed software from their devices and can download apps from alternative app stores *businesses can get free access to advertising data and can agree contracts outside of a gatekeeper platform *developers can use alternative payment or identification systems. The ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng Digital Services Act]'' (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065) sets out new standards for the accountability of online platforms regarding illegal content, disinformation and other societal risks. It aims to empower and protect users by requiring online platforms to tackle illegal content and to increase accountability and transparency. The general obligations of the act apply to all online platforms since February 2024. Very large online platforms or search engines reaching more than 45 million users a month are subject to more stringent rules. Designed as a single, uniform set of rules, the act (among other conditions): *creates stronger public oversight of online platforms (in particular, those that reach more than 10% of the EU’s population) *is designed to increase the mechanisms for the removal of illegal content and for the effective protection of users’ fundamental rights *provides measures to counter illegal goods, services or content online *introduces new obligations on the traceability of business users in online marketplaces *provides safeguards for users, including the possibility to challenge platforms’ content moderation decisions *bans certain type of targeted adverts *increases obligations for very large platforms and search engines to prevent the misuse of their systems. In January 2024, the ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32023R2854 Data Act]'' (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on harmonised rules on fair access to and use of data) entered into force. Its design promotes a fair distribution of the value of data by establishing clear and fair rules for accessing and using data in the European economy – a necessity heightened by the growing prevalence of the internet of things. As a result, the design and manufacture of connected products should empower users (businesses or consumers) to access, use and share any generated data both easily and securely. '''Digital Decade''' Digital skills are central to the EU’s digital strategy, supporting technological sovereignty, reducing the digital divide and fostering a human-centred digital environment. ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dec/2022/2481/oj Decision (EU) 2022/2481 establishing the Digital decade policy programme]'' defines 4 key pillars for Europe’s digital transformation: *a digitally skilled population and highly skilled professionals *secure and sustainable digital infrastructures *digital transformation of businesses *digitalisation of public services. The programme includes 2 core targets for individuals by 2030: *at least 80% of people aged 16 to 74 should have basic digital skills *there should be at least 20 million ICT specialists. Concerning the digital transformation of businesses, the programme sets the following targets for 2030: *at least 75% of EU enterprises should take up 1 or more of the following **cloud computing services **big data **artificial intelligence *more than 90% of SMEs in the EU reach at least a basic level of digital intensity. The programme also aims to ensure an inclusive and secure digital transition by promoting participation, fair competition for SMEs, access to data, adoption of technologies (such as cloud, data analytics and AI), deployment of innovative infrastructures, online public services, cybersecurity uptake, and research on sustainable digital innovation. Implementation is supported by an annual cooperation cycle between the European Commission and EU countries, including a shared monitoring system for tracking progress, an annual report with recommendations, national strategic roadmaps and support for multi-country projects. In 2025, the European Commission released its third report on the ''[https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/state-digital-decade-2025-report State of the Digital Decade]''. While the report identified progress in areas such as fifth generation (5G) coverage, it also highlighted gaps in AI deployment, semiconductor capacity, digital skills and the protection of vulnerable groups. In late 2024, European Commission President – Ursula von der Leyen – set out new ''[https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029_en Political guidelines]'' for the next mandate period (2024 to 2029). These guidelines define 7 key priorities, including a focus on sustainable prosperity and competitiveness in Europe. A central objective under this priority is to increase productivity by accelerating the spread and uptake of digital technologies across the EU economy. ===Other articles=== '''General articles''' title: Disability statistics - financial situation
text:
This article looks at the financial situation of people in the EU with disabilities (activity limitation) compared with people without a disability. Data extracted in: June 2025 Planned article update: October 2026 In 2024, 38.8% of people in the EU with a disability could not afford to go away for a 1-week annual holiday. In 2024, 12.8% of people in the EU with a disability could not afford to eat meat, fish or a vegetarian equivalent at least every other day. In 2024, 38.0% of people in the EU with a disability could not meet unexpected financial expenses. :[[Glossary:Country_codes|Country codes]] This article presents various aspects of the financial situation of people with a [[Glossary:Disability|disability]] ([[Glossary:Activity_limitation|activity limitation]]). The findings presented in this article are based on the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union’s]] (EU’s) [[Glossary:EU-SILC|statistics on income and living conditions]] (EU-SILC) and relate to the 2024 reference year; they cover people aged 16 years or over. This article is one of a set of articles on disability which forms part of the online publication [[Disability statistics|Disability statistics]]. ===Struggling to make ends meet === '''''People with a disability are more likely to struggle to make ends meet'''''
'''Financial difficulties''': [[Glossary:Household|households]] are asked, for example, whether they struggle to make ends meet, whether they can afford to go away for a 1-week holiday once a year, whether they can afford to eat meat or fish (or a vegetarian equivalent) regularly, or whether they have fallen behind with payments (for a mortgage or rent, utility bills or hire purchases).
In 2024, 22.8% of people aged 16 years or over with a disability (having some or severe activity limitations) in the EU lived in households that reported having difficulties in making ends meet; in other words, their financial resources did not cover their usual necessary expenses. For comparison, the share was 15.0% among people without a disability (no activity limitations) – see Figure 1. In all EU countries, people with a disability were more likely to have difficulties in making ends meet in 2024 than people without a disability. The share of people with a disability living in a household that reported suffering such financial difficulties was *lowest in Luxembourg (8.0%; 2022 data), Germany (11.0%), the Netherlands (11.2%) and Finland (13.2%) *highest in Greece (75.5%) and Bulgaria (52.0%). [[Image:Share of people aged 16 years or over living in households that reported having difficulties in making ends meet, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024 (%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Share of people aged 16 years or over living in households that reported having difficulties in making ends meet, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dm060}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the share of people aged 16 years or over living in households that reported having difficulties in making ends meet. Data are shown for people with or without a disability (activity limitation). Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU and the euro area as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===1-week annual holiday=== '''''38.8% of people with a disability could not afford to go away for a 1-week annual holiday''''' A consequence of difficult financial circumstances may be the inability to go on holiday. This is measured as someone being unable to afford a 1-week holiday once a year – see Figure 2. In the EU in 2024, people aged 16 years or over with a disability were more likely to find themselves in this position (38.8%) compared with people (of the same age) without a disability (23.4%). [[Image:Share of people aged 16 years or over living in households unable to afford a 1-week annual holiday, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024_(%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Share of people aged 16 years or over living in households unable to afford a 1-week annual holiday, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dm020}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the share of people aged 16 years or over living in households unable to afford a 1-week annual holiday. Data are shown for people with or without a disability (activity limitation). Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU and the euro area as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In all EU countries, the share of people living in households unable to afford a 1-week annual holiday was higher among those with a disability than those without a disability. In 2024, the share of people with a disability who lived in a household unable to afford a 1-week annual holiday was above half in 7 EU countries: 79.4% in Romania, 66.3% in Bulgaria, 61.0% in Greece, 60.2% in Hungary, 58.1% in Lithuania (provisional data), 57.0% in Croatia and 51.9% in Portugal. The lowest values among the EU countries were observed in Luxembourg (11.6%; 2022 data), and Finland (20.9%), Sweden (22.3%) and the Netherlands (22.8%). === Meat, fish or a vegetarian equivalent at least every other day=== '''''12.8% of people with a disability were unable to afford to eat meat, fish or a vegetarian equivalent at least every other day''''' The financial difficulties faced by people with a disability in the EU can also be seen by the fact that, in 2024, 12.8% lived in households that were unable to afford to eat meat, fish or a vegetarian equivalent at least every other day. The share of people without a disability in a similar situation was notably lower, at 7.4%. In all EU countries, people with a disability were more likely than people without a disability to live in a household that was unable to afford to eat meat, fish or a vegetarian equivalent at least every other day. In 2024, the percentage of people with a disability living in a household unable to afford to eat meat, fish or a vegetarian equivalent at least every other day varied greatly between EU countries, ranging from 1.5% in Cyprus to upwards of 20.0% in Slovakia, Romania, Hungary and Bulgaria (where the highest share was recorded, at 29.9%). [[Image:Share of people aged 16 years or over living in households unable to afford to eat meat, fish or a vegetarian equivalent at least every other day, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Share of people aged 16 years or over living in households unable to afford to eat meat, fish or a vegetarian equivalent at least every other day, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dm030}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the share of people aged 16 years or over living in households unable to afford to eat meat, fish or a vegetarian equivalent at least every other day. Data are shown for people with or without a disability (activity limitation). Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU and the euro area, as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Unexpected financial expenses=== '''''38.0% of people with a disability would be unable to meet unexpected financial expenses''''' In 2024, 38.0% of people with a disability in the EU lived in households which would be unable to meet unexpected financial expenses, compared with 26.5% among people without a disability.
'''Being unable to meet unexpected financial expenses''' means that a household would be unable to cover an unexpected essential expense from its own resources, that is, without asking for help: for example, borrowing money from friends or family, going overdrawn on a bank account, or worsening its situation with regard to potential debts. Examples of essential expenses are having surgery, paying for a funeral, having major repairs carried out in the house or replacing durable goods (such as a washing machine or a car).
[[Image:Share of people aged 16 years or over living in households that would be unable to meet unexpected financial expenses, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024 (%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Share of people aged 16 years or over living in households that would be unable to meet unexpected financial expenses, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dm040}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the share of people aged 16 years or over living in households that would be unable to meet unexpected financial expenses. Data are shown for people with or without a disability (activity limitation). Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU and the euro area, as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In all EU countries, people with a disability were more likely to be unable to meet an unexpected financial expense in 2024 than people without a disability. There was substantial variation between EU countries in the share of people with a disability living in households that would be unable to meet an unexpected financial expense. The highest share was 64.3% in Lithuania (provisional data) and the lowest was 24.0% in Luxembourg (2022 data) and the Netherlands – see Figure 4. === Falling behind with payments === '''''Financial difficulties may leave households unable to service their debts or to pay their usual expenses such as utility bills''''' In 2024, people with a disability in the EU were somewhat more likely to live in a household that had fallen behind with payments (for a mortgage or rent, utility bills or hire purchases) during the previous 12 months than people without a disability: this share was 10.2% for people with a disability compared with 8.0% of people without a disability. In 2024, people with a disability were more likely to live in a household that had fallen behind with payments during the previous 12 months than people without a disability; this pattern was observed in all EU countries. The percentage of people with a disability in such households was highest in Greece (44.5%) and Bulgaria (23.0%) – the only EU countries with shares above 20.0%. By contrast, the lowest shares were recorded in Czechia (3.4%) and the Netherlands (4.6%) – the only EU countries with shares that were less than 5.0%. Focusing on older people in the EU, specifically those aged 65 years or over, in 2024 some 5.8% of older people with a disability lived in a household that had fallen behind with payments during the previous 12 months, compared with 3.8% of older people without a disability. In all EU countries, older people with a disability were more likely to live in a household that had fallen behind with payments during the previous 12 months than older people without a disability. In 2024, the percentage of older people with a disability in such households was highest in Greece (40.4%), Bulgaria (18.9%) and Romania (16.4%). The lowest shares were recorded in the Netherlands (0.8%) and Czechia (1.4%). [[Image:Share of people living in a household that had fallen behind with payments (for a mortgage or rent, utility bills or hire purchases) during the previous 12 months, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024 (%) Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Share of people living in a household that had fallen behind with payments (for a mortgage or rent, utility bills or hire purchases) during the previous 12 months, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dm050}}|alt=A table showing the share of people living in a household that had been behind with payments (for a mortgage or rent, utility bills or hire purchases) during the previous 12 months. Data are shown for people aged 16 years or over and for people aged 65 years or over, with a disaggregation between people with or without a disability (activity limitation). Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU and the euro area, as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== {{Template:Excel|filename=Disability statistics - financial situation Health2025 upd.xlsx|title=Disability statistics – financial situation: tables and figures}} === Data sources=== EU-SILC is the source of comparative statistics on income distribution and social inclusion in the EU. It provides annual data for the EU countries as well as most [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate countries|enlargement]] countries on income, poverty, social exclusion and other aspects of living conditions. The reference population for EU-SILC is limited to private households and their current members residing in the territory of the surveying country at the time of data collection. People living in collective households and institutions are generally excluded from the reference population; this constitutes a limitation for disability statistics. All household members are surveyed, but only those aged 16 years or over are interviewed. The source is documented in more detail in this [[Health_variables_in_SILC_-_methodology|background article]], which provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. In EU-SILC, disability is approximated according to the concept of [[Glossary:Activity_limitation|global activity limitation]], which is defined as a limitation – because of health problems – in carrying out usual activities (for at least the previous 6 months). This is considered to be an adequate proxy for disability, both by the scientific community and organisations representing people with disabilities. This definition is also in line with the concept of disability as set out in the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=LEGISSUM%3Aem0047 European disability strategy 2010–2020] and its successor, the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030_en Strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities 2021–2030]. === Context === Disability statistics are used to measure the impact and effectiveness of EU policy aimed at ensuring equal rights for people with disabilities. The EU has adopted several strategies aimed at improving the lives of people with disabilities *by reducing discrimination and inequalities *by providing support to enjoy fully their human rights, fundamental freedoms and EU rights on an equal basis with others. In light of this, the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030_en 2021-2030 EU Strategy for the rights of people with disabilities] sets EU objectives and priority actions in several areas, such as accessibility, citizens’ rights, the quality of life, equal access and non-discrimination, and the promotion of the rights of people with disabilities. To find out more, please visit the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030/monitoring-framework_en webpage on the monitoring framework for the objectives and actions of this strategy]. To ensure sound monitoring and reporting of this topic, the European Commission is reinforcing the collection of data on the situation of people with disabilities in areas where knowledge gaps have been identified, for example in relation to access to the labour market. The EU is also a signatory of the [[Glossary:United Nations (UN)|United Nations]] (UN) [https://social.desa.un.org/issues/disability/crpd/convention-on-the-rights-of-persons-with-disabilities-crpd Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities] (CRPD). === Other articles=== '''Online publications''' *[[Disability statistics]] *[[Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] title: Disability statistics - elderly needs for help or assistance
text:
The European Health Interview Survey aims at measuring on a harmonised basis and with a high degree of comparability among Member States the health status (including disability), health determinants (including environment) and use and limitations in access to health care services of the EU citizens. Data extracted in August 2022. Planned article update: November 2027. In 2019, almost half of the EU elderly population (people aged 65 and over) reported difficulties with at least one personal care or household activity. In 2019, 46.6 % of the EU elderly population with a severe difficulty in personal care or household activities reported a lack of assistance with those activities. Almost 30 % of the EU elderly population with a difficulty in personal care or household activities used home care services for personal needs. [[Image:Disability-elderly 17-08-2022.png |thumb|center|700px|]]
This article provides an overview of the assistance used or required by elderly people in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] to overcome personal care or household activity limitations (such as difficulty in showering, using toilets, doing housework or shopping). It is one of a set of statistical articles concerning disability statistics in the EU and accompanies a number of methodological articles which make up an [[Disability_statistics|online publication on disability statistics]]. With rising life expectancy, more people now reach an age where declining physical and mental health make them dependent on help from others. This has an impact on long-term care expenditure, which is rising faster than expenditure on health and pensions. The data presented in this article come from the third wave of the [[Glossary:European_health_interview_survey_(EHIS)|European Health Interview Survey (EHIS)]], conducted in 2019. EHIS covers people aged 15 and over, while the data presented in this article refer to those aged 65 and above, in other words, the elderly population. === Difficulties in personal care or household activities === '''Almost half of the EU elderly population (people aged 65 and over), reported difficulties with at least one personal care or household activity''' Regarding personal care and household activities, Figure 1.1 shows that, on average, 49.7 % of the EU elderly population reported having moderate or severe difficulties (represented by the category ‘Limited’), while 50.3 % reported not having any difficulties (‘Not limited’). In almost half of the EU Member States (13), as well as in Serbia and Turkey, a higher share of people reported moderate or severe difficulties with at least one personal care or household activity, while in 14 countries, the trend was the opposite i.e. there was a higher share of people with no difficulties in those activities (see Figure 1.1). This was also the case in Iceland and Norway. Among the EU Member States, the highest rates for persons with difficulties in personal care or household activities were recorded in Romania (80.1 %) followed by Lithuania (67.4 %), Slovakia (66.2 %) and Latvia (65.5 %). [[Image:Persons limited in personal care or household activities, 2019 (% share of the population aged 65 and above).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1.1: Persons limited in personal care or household activities, 2019
(% share of the population aged 65 and above)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_ehis_tae}}|alt=A figure showing the percentage of persons aged 65 years and above limited in personal care or household activities for 2019 for the EU countries as well as for some EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Women were more likely than men to report difficulties with personal care or household activities''' An analysis by sex indicates that the proportion of women that reported limitations (moderate or severe) in personal or household activities was higher than that of men (57.1 % versus 39.9 %, for EU); this was the case for all EU Member States (see Figure 1.2). The highest gender gaps were found in Portugal (30.8 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]]), Cyprus (27.2 pp) and Spain (23.0 pp). A higher difference was found in Turkey (31.0 pp). [[Image:Persons limited in personal care or household activities by sex, 2019 (% share of the population aged 65 and above).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1.2: Persons limited in personal care or household activities by sex, 2019
(% share of the population aged 65 and above)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_ehis_tae}}|alt=A figure showing the percentage of persons aged 65 years and above limited in personal care or household activities by sex for 2019 for the EU countries as well as for some EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Difficulties with personal care or household activities more prevalent among those with lower educational attainment''' Among the EU Member States, difficulties with personal care or household activities for the elderly were more prevalent among those with less than primary, primary and lower secondary educations (56.2 %) compared to those with upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary educations (46.4 %) or tertiary educations (35.3 %) (see Figure 2). [[Image:Persons limited in personal care or household activities by educational attainment level, 2019 (% share of the population aged 65 and above).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Persons limited in personal care or household activities by educational attainment level, 2019
(% share of the population aged 65 and above)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_ehis_tae}}|alt=A figure showing the percentage of persons aged 65 years and above limited in personal care or household activities by educational attainment level for 2019 for the EU countries as well as for some EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Across educational levels and EU Member States, there was a considerable educational gap between the elderly with upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education and tertiary educational level who reported having difficulties with personal care or household activities. The highest differences were observed in Slovakia (17.1 pp) and Belgium (15.8 pp), while in the case of Spain and Finland, the educational gap was considerably smaller (i.e. 1 pp or less). In contrast, in Portugal, more persons with tertiary educations considered that they have difficulties (33.7 %) compared to those with upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary educations (28.7 %). '''More than one quarter of the elderly population with less than primary, primary and lower secondary education reported difficulties with personal care activities''' When looking only to the personal care activities (also known as activities of daily living), the trend was similar; at EU level, 28.4 % of elderly persons with less than primary, primary and lower secondary educations reported difficulties in personal care activities compared with 20.5 % of people with an upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education and 14.5 % with a higher educational level (see Figure 3). [[Image:Persons limited in personal care activities by educational attainment level, 2019 (% share of the population aged 65 and above).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Persons limited in personal care activities by educational attainment level, 2019
(% share of the population aged 65 and above)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_ehis_pc1e}}|alt=A figure showing the percentage of persons aged 65 years and above limited in personal care activities by educational attainment level in 2019 for the EU countries as well as for some EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The same pattern is observed across all Member States, except in Greece, Spain and Portugal where the lowest share of elderly persons reporting difficulties with the daily activities was found among those having completed upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (see Figure 3). '''Almost a quarter of the EU elderly population was limited in at least one daily life activity''' In the EU, the share of people aged 65 and over limited in at least one of the five measured daily life activities (namely, feeding oneself, getting in and out of bed or chair, dressing and undressing, using toilets, bathing or showering) was 23.6 % in 2019. Among the EU Member States, eight of them reported more than 25.0 % of elderly persons having difficulties with those activities, while in Ireland, Denmark and Malta, that share was less than 12 % (see Figure 4). [[Image:Persons limited in personal care activities by activity where the limitation is encountered, 2019 (% share of the population aged 65 and above).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Persons limited in personal care activities by activity where the limitation is encountered, 2019
(% share of the population aged 65 and above)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_ehis_pc1e}}|alt=A figure showing the percentage of persons aged 65 years and above limited in personal care activities by activity where the limitation is encountered in 2019 for the EU countries as well as for some EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The activities with which the elderly had the most difficulties were ‘Getting in and out of a bed or chair' (17.2 %) and ‘Bathing or showering’ (16.5 %). This pattern holds for the majority (18) of the EU Member States with the exception of Belgium, Estonia, Greece, Spain, Croatia, Cyrus, Italy, Lithuania and Hungary, where ‘Bathing or showering’ was the most common activity where difficulties were encountered among the elderly. The daily activity ‘’Feeding oneself’ was the least problematic, as less than 10 % of the elderly in almost all EU countries encountered difficulties with it, except for Romania, Poland and Lithuania, where the rate was slightly above 10 %. [[Image:Persons limited in household activities by educational attainment level, 2019 (% share of the population aged 65 and above).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Persons limited in household activities by educational attainment level, 2019
(% share of the population aged 65 and above)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_ehis_ha1e}}|alt=A figure showing the percentage of persons aged 65 years and above limited in household activities by educational attainment level in 2019 for the EU countries as well as for some EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In all EU Member States, the share of elderly persons reporting difficulties with household activities (namely, preparing meals, using the telephone, shopping, managing medication, doing light housework, doing occasional heavy housework, taking care of finances and everyday administrative tasks) was also highest among those with less than primary, primary and lower secondary educational level (54.0 %), compared to those with upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education (44.2 %) or tertiary education (32.9 %) (see Figure 5). An exception to this pattern was Portugal, where the share of persons with tertiary educations was above the one for persons with upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary educations. As observed in Figure 5, there was a considerable gap between the less than primary, primary and lower secondary education and tertiary educational level among the elderly persons reporting difficulties with household activities. The largest gaps were recorded in Slovakia (35.8 pp), Austria (34.7 pp) and Croatia (33.1 pp), while for Malta and Sweden, the educational gap was considerably smaller (10.6 pp and 11.5 pp, respectively). [[Image:Persons limited in household activities by activity where the limitation is encountered, 2019 v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Persons limited in household activities by activity where the limitation is encountered, 2019
(% share of the population aged 65 and above)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_ehis_ha1e}}|alt=A table showing the percentage of persons aged 65 years and above limited in household activities by activity where the limitation is encountered in 2019 for the EU countries as well as for some EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 1 provides information on the share of people having difficulties with different household activities. In total, 47.4 % of the elderly in the EU encountered difficulties in at least one or more activity in 2019. Most difficulties were experienced with ‘Occasional heavy housework’ (44.9 %), ‘Shopping’ (22.6 %) and ‘Light housework’ (20.6 %). This pattern holds for most EU Member States with the exception of Belgium, Denmark, Spain, Cyprus, Latvia, Malta, Romania and Slovenia, where the second most common activity, with which the elderly reported to have difficulties, was ‘Light housework’. This was also the case in Iceland, Serbia and Turkey. The activities “Using the telephone’’ and ‘’Managing medication” were reported the least problematic by the elderly population (about 9 %). The only exception was found in Malta where the share of the elderly having difficulties "Preparing meals" was slightly lower than the share for "Managing medication" (8.7 % and 9.0 %, respectively). === Need for help with personal care or household activities === People having difficulties with personal care or household activities (in particular, those having a severe difficulty) are likely to seek for help or assistance with those problematic activities. Whether the elderly persons who struggle with everyday activities (that is, those with severe difficulties) receive or need (more) help is next presented. '''Almost half of the elderly population with a severe difficulty in personal care or household activities reported a lack of assistance with those activities''' In EU, 46.6 % of elderly persons with a difficulty in personal care or household activities reported a lack of assistance in 2019, while 40.1 % reported they ‘Get enough assistance’ and 13.3 % stated they had ‘No need for assistance’. The latter category might indicate people who do not want any help, wishing to remain entirely independent. Across EU Member States, the share of those lacking assistance ranged from 74.6 % in Luxembourg, to 23.4 % in Malta (Figure 6). [[Image:Persons limited in personal care activities by need for assistance, 2019 (% share of the population aged 65 and above).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Persons severely limited in personal care or household activities by need for assistance, 2019
(% share of the population aged 65 and above)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code= hlth_ehis_tadlh}}|alt=A table showing the percentage of persons severely limited in personal care or household activities by need for assistance in 2019 for the EU countries as well as for some EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The countries with the highest proportions of the elderly with severe difficulties stating that they receive enough assistance were Latvia (60.9 %) and Austria (60.4 %), while the countries with the lowest proportions were Finland (16.0 %) and Malta (16.9 %). === Self-reported use of home care services === '''Almost 30 % of the EU elderly with severe difficulties in personal care or household activities used home care services for personal needs''' At the EU level, in 2019, the share of elderly persons with severe difficulties in activities and who self-reported the use of home care services for personal needs was 28.6 %, compared to 6.9 % of those having a moderate difficulty and 2.6 % for those with no difficulty. Across the EU Member States, there was a difference in the usage of the home care by the elderly with severe difficulties. The share ranged from more than 50 % in Belgium, Denmark and the Netherlands to less than 5% in Romania. [[Image:Self-reported use of home care services by level of difficulty with personal care or household activities, 2019 (% share of the population aged 65 and above).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Self-reported use of home care services by level of difficulty with personal care or household activities, 2019
(% share of the population aged 65 and above)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code= hlth_ehis_am7ta}}|alt=A figure showing the percentage of self-reported use of home care services by level of difficulty with personal care or household activities in 2019 by the population aged 65 and above for the EU countries as well as for some EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Elderly needs for help or assistance 2022.xls|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === The third wave of the [[Glossary:European health interview survey (EHIS)|European health interview survey (EHIS)]] is the source of information for the data presented in this article. The general coverage of the EHIS is the population aged 15 years and over living in private households residing in the national territory. This source is documented in more detail in this [[European_health_interview_survey_-_methodology|background article]] which provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. The third wave of the EHIS was conducted in all 27 EU Member States, as well as in Iceland, Norway, Serbia and Turkey. The data collection period was generally 2019. However, it was 2018 for Belgium, 2018–2019 for Austria, and 2019–2020 for Germany and Malta. '''''According to the current legal framework, EHIS is to be conducted every five years. EHIS wave 4 is planned to be conducted in 2025 under the new Regulation (EU) 2019/1700 of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing a common framework for European statistics relating to persons and households, based on data at individual level collected from samples (this regulation foresees the periodicity of EHIS to change to 6 years).''''' More details about EHIS are available in this [[European_health_interview_survey_-_methodology|background article]] which provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. Limitations in personal care activities show the level of difficulty in at least one personal care activity covering feeding, getting in and out of a bed or a chair, dressing and undressing, using a toilet, bathing or showering based on the self-reports of the population aged 65 and over. Respondents evaluated the extent of their difficulties on the following scale: no difficulty (in this article referred to as not limited), some difficulty, a lot of difficulty and cannot do at all (all of them composing the category limited). Limitations in household activities show the level of difficulty in at least one household activity covering preparing meals, using the telephone, shopping, managing medication, carrying out light housework, carrying out occasional heavy housework, taking care of finances and everyday administrative tasks based on the self-reports of the population aged 65 and over. It should be noted that there may be other than health reasons behind difficulties doing household activities. Respondents evaluated the extent of their difficulties on the following scale: no difficulty (in this article referred to as not limited), some difficulty, a lot of difficulty and cannot do at all (all of them composing the category limited). The indicator on home care services shows the use of any type of home (health and social) care services. It includes only formal care services provided by professional health or social workers (not by family members or friends) and refers to the past 12 months prior to the interview. '''Limitations of the data''' All of the indicators presented in this article are derived from self-reported data so they are, to a certain extent, affected by respondents’ subjective perception as well as by their social and cultural background. EHIS does not cover the institutionalised population, for example, people living in health and social care institutions who are more likely to face limitations than the population living in private households. It is therefore likely that, to some degree, EHIS under-estimates the share of the population facing limitations. Finally, despite substantial and continuous efforts for harmonisation, the implementation of EHIS is organised nationally, which may impact on the results presented, for example, due to differences in the formulation of questions or their precise coverage. === Context === In March 2021, the European Commission presented a new [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=738&langId=en&pubId=8376&furtherPubs=yes Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2021-2030] aiming to tackle the diverse challenges that persons with disabilities face. The Strategy aims to progress on all areas of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, both at EU and Member State level. The goal is to ensure that persons with disabilities in Europe, regardless of their sex, racial or ethnic origin, religion or belief, age or sexual orientation: * enjoy their human rights, * have equal opportunities, * have equal access to participate in society and economy, * are able to decide where, how and with whom they live, * can move freely in the EU regardless of their support needs, * no longer experience discrimination. This new and strengthened Strategy takes account of the diversity of disability comprising long-term physical, mental, intellectual or sensory impairments (in line with Article 1 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities). It contains an ambitious set of actions and flagship initiatives in various domains. Persons with disabilities are still at a higher risk of poverty and social exclusion than persons without disabilities. Access to healthcare, lifelong learning, employment, and leisure remains difficult, participation in political life is limited, and persons with disabilities are still discriminated against. Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated existing inequalities. One of the major inequalities is about labour market: "only 50 % of persons with disabilities has a job, compared to 75% of persons without disabilities. The Commission calls on Member States to unlock the potential of persons with disabilities and improve their position on the labour market"[https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/qanda_21_813 Questions and Answers: Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2021 - 2030]. Already in 2023, the European Commission will issue guidance on the participation of persons with disabilities in the electoral process. It will also support inclusive democratic participation, including for persons with a disability, through the new Citizenship, Equalities, Rights and Values program. Indicators on activity limitations and use of home care services are used for monitoring long-term care systems.
