title: Disability statistics - housing conditions
text:
This article looks at the housing conditions of people in the EU with a disability (activity limitation) compared with people without a disability. Data extracted in: June 2025 Planned article update: October 2026 In 2024, 66.5% of people in the EU aged 16 years or over with a disability lived in a household that owned their own home, while 33.5% lived in rented accommodation. In 2024, the housing cost overburden rate for people in the EU aged 16 years or over with a disability was 10.4%, ranging from 2.0% in Cyprus to 21.2% in Denmark and 33.0% in Greece. :[[Glossary:Country_codes|Country codes]] This article presents various aspects of the housing conditions faced by people with a [[Glossary:Disability|disability]] ([[Glossary:Activity limitation|activity limitation]]). The data come from the [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]] and relate to the 2024 reference year; they cover people aged 16 years or over. This article is one of a set of articles on disability which forms part of the online publication [[Disability statistics|Disability statistics]]. ===Tenure status=== '''''In the EU as a whole, there was no major difference between people with or without a disability in terms of home ownership, but people with a disability were much less likely to have an outstanding loan or mortgage''''' In 2024, 66.5% of people aged 16 years or over with a disability (some or severe activity limitation) in the EU lived in a [[Glossary:Household|household]] that owned their own home – see Table 1. Among people with a disability, 15.4% were owners who still had a mortgage or loan to pay off and 51.1% had no outstanding mortgage or housing loan. For comparison, 70.0% of people aged 16 years or over with no disability lived in a household that owned their own home, 3.5 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points]] higher than the share for people with a disability. Among people with no disability, 23.7% still had a mortgage or loan to pay off, 8.3 pp higher than the share for people with a disability. Therefore, the share of people with no disability who had no outstanding mortgage (46.3%) was lower than the share for people with a disability. At least in part, these differences may reflect different age structures of the subpopulations of people with or without a disability which in turn impacts on the likelihood that people are at a stage of their lives when they have paid off any mortgages or house loans. [[Image:Distribution of people aged 16 years or over, by tenure status and by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024 (%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Distribution of people aged 16 years or over, by tenure status and by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dhc010}}|alt=A table showing the share of people aged 16 years or over by tenure status. Data are shown for people with or without a disability (activity limitation), disaggregated for owners and for tenants. Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU and the euro area as well as for the EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Therefore, 33.5% of people with a disability in the EU lived in rented accommodation in 2024: 20.4% paid rent at the market rate and the remaining 13.1% paid a reduced rent or no rent at all. For people without a disability, 30.0% lived in rented accommodation: 20.9% paid rent at the market rate and 9.1% paid a reduced rent or no rent. *the share of people without a disability paying a market price rent was 0.5 pp higher than the equivalent share for people with a disability *the share of people with a disability paying a reduced rent or no rent at all was 4.0 pp higher than the equivalent share for people without a disability With 2 exceptions – Germany and Austria – the EU countries generally reported that over half of all people with a disability lived in owner-occupied dwellings in 2024 – see Table 1. In 15 EU countries, the share of people living in owner-occupied dwellings was lower in 2024 among people with a disability than it was among people without a disability. The largest difference was in Sweden (where 53.2% of people with a disability lived in owner-occupied dwellings, 14.1 pp lower than the equivalent share among people without a disability); shares more than 10.0 pp lower among people with a disability were also observed in the Netherlands and Belgium. ===Accommodation quality=== '''''People with a disability more often living in sub-standard accommodation''''' Across the EU, people with a disability were more likely to experience problems associated with housing deprivation – see Figure 1. For 3 types of surveyed issues related to the area where people live, the issues were more common in 2023 among people with a disability. *22.5% of people with a disability reported noise from neighbours or from the street, compared with 16.9% of those without a disability *15.0% of people with a disability reported pollution, grime or other environmental problems in the area where they lived, compared with 11.2% among people without a disability *13.0% of people with a disability were aware of crime, violence or vandalism in the area where they lived, compared with 9.1% among people without a disability Equally, all 3 issues related to the accommodation itself were more common among people with a disability. *18.9% of people with a disability said they had a leaking roof, damp walls, floors or foundation, or rot in the window frames or floor in their home in 2023; among people without a disability the share was 13.8% *13.2% of people with a disability reported that they were unable to keep their home adequately warm in 2024, compared with 8.0% among people without a disability *8.3% of people with a disability complained of living in a dwelling considered too dark in 2023, compared with 6.1% among people without a disability [[Image:Share of people aged 16 years or over affected by sub-standard accommodation conditions, by level of disability (activity limitation), EU, 2023or 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Share of people aged 16 years or over affected by sub-standard accommodation conditions, by level of disability (activity limitation), EU, 2023 or 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dhc070}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dhc100}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dhc110}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dhc120}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dhc130}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dhc140}}|alt=A double bar chart showing the share of people aged 16 years or over affected by sub-standard accommodation conditions. Data are shown for people with or without a disability (activity limitation), disaggregated down into issues related to the area where people live and issues related to the accommodation itself. Data are shown in percent, for 2023 or 2024, for the EU. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Overcrowding=== '''''People aged 16 years or over with a disability were less likely to live in an overcrowded household''''' Another indicator of housing quality is the number of people living in the same dwelling. The [[Glossary:Overcrowding_rate|overcrowding rate]] is defined as the share of people living in an overcrowded household. [[Image:Overcrowding rate for people aged 16 years or over, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024 (%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Overcrowding rate for people aged 16 years or over, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dhc040}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the overcrowding rate for people aged 16 years or over. Data are shown for people with or without a disability (activity limitation). Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU and the euro area as well as for the EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In the EU, the overcrowding rate in 2024 was lower for people with a disability than it was for people without a disability, the shares being 11.0% and 16.1%, respectively – see Figure 2. This situation was also observed in 25 of the EU countries. The largest difference was recorded in Romania, where 23.1% of people with a disability experienced overcrowding, 16.7 pp lower than the share among people without a disability (39.8%). There were 2 EU countries – Sweden and Finland – where the overcrowding rate was higher for people with a disability; in both cases, the differences in the rates for people with or without a disability were small, 1.9 and 1.1 pp, respectively. Among the EU countries, the overcrowding rate in 2024 for people with a disability ranged from 1.3% in Malta, 1.7% in Cyprus, 2.2% in Ireland and 2.8% in the Netherlands to 30.1% in Poland and 34.2% in Latvia. '''''People aged 65 years or over with a disability more likely to experience overcrowding''''' A different pattern was observed among people aged 65 years or over – see Figure 3. In 2024, the overcrowding rate in the EU was higher for people with a disability (6.9%) than for people without a disability (5.4%). This situation was also observed in 24 of the EU countries. The largest difference was recorded in Latvia, where 27.0% of people aged 65 years or over with a disability experienced overcrowding, 8.8 pp higher than the share among people aged 65 years or over without a disability (18.2%). In Italy, there was no difference in the overcrowding rate for people aged 65 years or more between those with or without a disability. In the 2 EU countries – Croatia and Malta – where the overcrowding rate was lower for people aged 65 years or over with a disability, the differences in the rates for people aged 65 years or over with or without a disability were small, 0.3 and 0.1 pp, respectively. In 2024, the overcrowding rate for people aged 65 years or over with a disability ranged in the EU countries from 0.0% in Malta to 22.8% in Poland and 27.0% in Latvia. [[Image:Overcrowding rate for people aged 65 years or over, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024 (%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Overcrowding rate for people aged 65 years or over, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dhc040}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the overcrowding rate for people aged 65 years or over. Data are shown for people with or without a disability (activity limitation). Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU and the euro area as well as for the EU, EFTA and enlargement countries.]] ===Housing costs=== '''''People with a disability more likely to be overburdened by housing costs''''' Housing costs as a share of disposable income indicate people’s ability to afford the costs associated with their housing. Households with a higher income may find it easier to cope with a high share of housing costs in relation to their disposable income. Nevertheless, if housing costs are greater than or equal to 40% of disposable income, this is deemed an overburden: the share of people whose housing costs meet this criterion is referred to as the [[Glossary:Housing cost overburden rate|housing cost overburden rate]]. [[Image:Housing cost overburden rate for people aged 16 years or over, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024 (%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Housing cost overburden rate for people aged 16 years or over, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dhc060}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the housing cost overburden rate for people aged 16 years or over. Data are shown for people with or without a disability (activity limitation). Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU and the euro area as well as for the EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In the EU, the housing cost overburden rate was 10.4% in 2024 for people aged 16 years or over with a disability compared with 7.8% for people without a disability. In 21 EU countries, the housing cost overburden rate was higher among people with a disability than for people without a disability – see Figure 4. The widest gaps were recorded in Sweden (7.5 pp), Denmark (6.6 pp) and Belgium (6.3 pp). Among the EU countries, the housing cost overburden rate for people with a disability ranged in 2024 from 2.0% in Cyprus and 3.0% in Ireland to 21.2% in Denmark and 33.0% in Greece. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Disability_statistics_-_housing_conditions_Health2025_upd3.xlsx|title=Disability statistics – housing conditions: tables and figures}} === Data sources=== EU-SILC is the source for comparative statistics on income distribution and social inclusion in the EU. It provides annual data for the EU countries as well as most [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate countries|enlargement]] countries on income, poverty, social exclusion and other aspects of living conditions. The reference population for EU-SILC is limited to private households and their current members residing in the territory of the surveying country at the time of data collection. People living in collective households and institutions are generally excluded from the reference population; this constitutes a limitation for disability statistics. All household members are surveyed, but only those aged 16 years or over are interviewed. The source is documented in more detail in this [[Health_variables_in_SILC_-_methodology|background article]], which provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. In EU-SILC, disability is approximated according to the concept of [[Glossary:Activity_limitation|global activity limitation]], which is defined as a limitation – because of health problems – in carrying out usual activities (for at least the previous 6 months). This is considered to be an adequate proxy for disability, both by the scientific community and organisations representing people with disabilities. This definition is also in line with the concept of disability as set out in the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=LEGISSUM%3Aem0047 European disability strategy 2010–2020] and its successor, the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030_en Strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities 2021–2030]. === Context === Disability statistics are used to measure the impact and effectiveness of EU policy aimed at ensuring equal rights for people with disabilities. The EU has adopted several strategies aimed at improving the lives of people with disabilities *by reducing discrimination and inequalities *by providing support to enjoy fully their human rights, fundamental freedoms and EU rights on an equal basis with others. In light of this, the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030_en 2021-2030 EU Strategy for the rights of people with disabilities] sets EU objectives and priority actions in several areas, such as accessibility, citizens’ rights, the quality of life, equal access and non-discrimination, and the promotion of the rights of people with disabilities. To find out more, please visit the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030/monitoring-framework_en webpage on the monitoring framework for the objectives and actions of this strategy]. To ensure sound monitoring and reporting of this topic, the European Commission is reinforcing the collection of data on the situation of people with disabilities in areas where knowledge gaps have been identified, for example in relation to access to the labour market. The EU is also a signatory of the [[Glossary:United Nations (UN)|United Nations]] (UN) [https://social.desa.un.org/issues/disability/crpd/convention-on-the-rights-of-persons-with-disabilities-crpd Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities] (CRPD). Housing policy in EU countries is a national policy, rather than an EU policy. === Other articles === '''Online publications''' *[[Disability statistics]] *[[Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] '''Related articles''' *[[Self-perceived health statistics]] *[[Living conditions in Europe - housing|Living conditions in Europe – housing]] *[[Living conditions in Europe - self-perceived discrimination|Living conditions in Europe – self-perceived discrimination]] *[[Living conditions in Europe - poverty and social exclusion|Living conditions in Europe – poverty and social exclusion]] title: Disability statistics - population with difficulties in basic activities
text:
This article compares people in the EU reporting difficulties in basic activities. Data are analysed by type of difficulty, severity of difficulty, sex, age, education level, poverty status and income. Data extracted in: November 2024. Planned article update: May 2027. In 2022, more than 1 in 3 (37.0%) people aged 16 years or over in the EU reported difficulties in one or more basic activities. The most common difficulties were in seeing (20.3%), walking (18.5%) and remembering/concentrating (14.8%). [[Image:Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting difficulties in basic activities, EU, 2022 (%).png|thumb|centre|800px|Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting difficulties in basic activities, EU, 2022
(%)
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_hch17}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_hch16}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_hch19}}|alt=A stacked column chart showing the share of people aged 16 years or over reporting difficulties in basic activities. Data are shown for the share of people with severe, moderate or no difficulties, analysed by sex, age, educational attainment, poverty status, income and type of difficulty. Data are shown in percent, for 2022, for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Disability can be measured in various ways. This article uses a measure of disability that is based on the level of difficulty in basic activities (such as seeing, hearing or self-care), rather than the one related to an [[Glossary:Activity_limitation|activity limitation]] (for instance, difficulty reading or listening to radio, jogging), which is more commonly used by Eurostat. The findings presented in this article are based on the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union’s (EU’s)]] [[Glossary:EU-SILC|statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]]. This article is part of a [[Disability statistics|set of articles]] on [[Glossary:Disability|disability]] which presents various aspects of the life of people with a disability. === Share of people reporting difficulties in basic activities === [[Image:Share_of_people_aged_16_years_or_over_reporting_difficulties_in_basic_activities,_2022_(%).png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 1: Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting difficulties in basic activities, 2022
(%)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_hch17}}|alt=A bullet chart showing the share of people aged 16 years or over reporting difficulties in basic activities. Data are shown for people with severe, moderate or no difficulties. Data are shown in percent, for 2022, for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2022, more than 1 in 3 (37.0%) people aged 16 years or over in the EU reported moderate or severe difficulties in one or more basic activities (see Figure 1). Among the EU countries, more than half of the population aged 16 years or over in Denmark, Finland and the Netherlands reported a moderate or severe difficulty for at least one basic activity. By contrast, less than a quarter of the population reported such difficulties in Ireland, Malta, Cyprus and Greece. In the EU, most people aged 16 years or over who reported one or more difficulties in basic activities in 2022 had moderate rather than severe difficulties. Whereas 9.7% of all people aged 16 years or over reported severe difficulties, this share was 2.8 times as high (at 27.3%) for moderate difficulties. In other words, among the subpopulation of people who reported difficulties in one or more basic activities, just over 1 in 4 reported severe difficulties. Among the EU countries, Luxembourg and Romania had the largest relative differences between the share of people aged 16 years or over reporting moderate difficulties and those reporting severe difficulties: in 2022, 1 in 5 people reporting difficulties in these countries reported severe difficulties. By contrast, the share of people reporting severe difficulties among all people reporting difficulties was close to 1 in 3 in Portugal and France. === Types of difficulties === '''''Seeing and walking were the most common types of difficulties''''' In the EU, the most common types of difficulties in basic activities in 2022 were in seeing (20.3% of people aged 16 years or over) and in walking (18.5%); the least common difficulties among the 6 types of basic activity that were surveyed were in communicating (4.7%) and in self care (6.7%). It should be noted that it was common for some people to have a difficulty in more than one of these basic activities: the shares of people with difficulties in each of the 6 types of basic activities sum to 76.8%, compared with the 37.0% share of people with difficulties in at least one basic activity. As such, people reporting difficulty in one or more basic activities had a difficulty in an average of 2.1 types of activities. [[Image:Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting difficulties in basic activities, 2022T (%)_Health2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting difficulties in basic activities, 2022
(%)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_hch19}}|alt=A table showing the share of people aged 16 years or over reporting difficulties in 6 distinct basic activities. Data are shown for people with difficulties and people without difficulties in terms of seeing, hearing, walking, remembering or concentrating, communicating and self care. Data are shown in percent, for 2022, for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among the EU countries (data not available for Germany) *13 countries recorded 'seeing' as the most common basic activity with which people reported a difficulty, *difficulty in 'walking' was recorded as the most common difficulty in Belgium, Bulgaria, Ireland, Greece, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta and Austria, *difficulty in 'remembering or concentrating' was the most common difficulty in Estonia, the Netherlands, Finland and Sweden, *22 countries recorded 'communicating' as the least common basic activity with which people reported a difficulty, *'self-care' was the least common difficulty in the Netherlands, Austria, Slovenia and Sweden. [[Image:Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting difficulties in basic activities, by basic activity and sex, EU, 2022 (%)_Health2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 2: Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting difficulties in basic activities, by basic activity and sex, EU, 2022
(%)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_hch19}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the share of people aged 16 years or over reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, analysed by basic activity and sex. Data are shown for men and women with moderate or severe difficulties in terms of seeing, hearing, walking, remembering or concentrating, communicating and self care. Data are shown in percent, for 2022, for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2022 in the EU, for 5 of the 6 types of basic activities, women were more likely than men to report moderate difficulties; the exception being hearing, for which men were marginally more likely than women to report moderate difficulties. Women were also more likely to report severe difficulties for 4 of the 6 types of basic activities: for hearing, the shares of people reporting severe difficulties were the same for women and for men; for communicating, men were marginally more likely than women to report severe difficulties. === Analyses of severe difficulties by sex, age, educational attainment, poverty status and income === '''''Women were more likely than men to report difficulties''''' In 2022, women were more likely than men to report one or more severe difficulties in basic activities; see Figure 3. In the EU, 11.0% of women aged 16 years or over reported severe difficulties with basic activities, compared with 8.2% of men. This pattern was repeated in all of the EU countries. *The widest gender health gaps were recorded in Estonia (5.3 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points]], pp), Latvia (5.1 pp), the Netherlands (4.8 pp) and Finland (4.5 pp). *Ireland (0.3 pp) and Cyprus (0.9 pp) had the smallest differences between the sexes. In this context, it should be noted that the data are not age-standardised and that a greater share of women than men are in older age groups where difficulties in basic activities are more common. [[Image:Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, by sex, 2022 (%)_Health2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 3: Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, by sex, 2022
(%)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_hch17}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the share of people reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, analysed by sex. Data are shown for men and women. Data are shown in percent, for 2022, for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Older people were more likely than younger people to report severe difficulties''''' The share of people reporting one or more severe difficulties with basic activities has a distinct age pattern, as people in higher age groups are more likely than people in lower age groups to report severe difficulties in basic activities (see Figure 4). In 2022, the share of people aged 16 to 44 years who reported severe difficulties was 3.4% in the EU; the highest share was recorded among people aged 65 years or over, at 22.7%. An age gap concerning difficulties in basic activities could be observed for all countries in 2022. *With one exception, the smallest share of people reporting severe difficulties was observed among people aged 16 to 44 years. The exception was Sweden, where this share was the lowest among people aged 45 to 64 years. *In all countries, the highest share reporting severe difficulties was recorded for persons aged 65 years or over. *The widest gaps between the shares reporting severe difficulties among people aged 65 years or over and among people aged 16 to 44 years were observed in Estonia, Slovenia, Latvia, Spain and Portugal, all with gaps of at least 24.5 pp. *The narrowest age gaps concerning severe difficulties in basic activities were observed in Denmark (9.9 pp), Luxembourg (10.3 pp) and Sweden (10.5 pp). [[Image:Share of people reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, by age, 2022 (%)_Health2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 4: Share of people reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, by age, 2022
(%)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_hch17}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the share of people reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, analysed by age. Data are shown for people aged 16 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 years or over. Data are shown in percent, for 2022, for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''People with a low level of educational attainment were more likely to report severe difficulties''''' There are also clear differences when looking at the relationship between severe difficulties in basic activities and [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|educational attainment levels]] (see Figure 5). In the EU, 16.7% of people aged 16 years or over having completed, at most, lower secondary education reported severe difficulties in basic activities in 2022. This can be compared with 7.9% among people having completed upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education and 5.0% among people with a tertiary level of educational attainment. This gap between educational attainment levels was apparent in all EU countries. The pattern observed for the EU was repeated in all but one EU countries. The one exception was Italy, where the share was slightly higher for people with a tertiary level of educational attainment than for those having completed upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education. The widest gap in the share of people reporting severe difficulties in basic activities between people with the highest and the lowest educational attainment levels was observed in Slovenia (20.4 pp), followed by Finland (17.9 pp) and Lithuania (17.3 pp). The narrowest educational gaps among the EU countries were observed in Italy and Malta (both with gaps close to 7.0 pp). [[Image:Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, by level of educational attainment, 2022 (%)_Health2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 5: Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, by level of educational attainment, 2022
(%)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_hch16}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the share of people reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, analysed by educational attainment. Data are shown for people with low, medium or high levels of educational attainment. Data are shown in percent, for 2022, for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''People not at risk of poverty were less likely to report severe difficulties''''' There is also a clear pattern when looking at the relationship between severe difficulties in basic activities and [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|poverty status]] (see Figure 6). In the EU, 8.8% of people aged 16 years or over who were not at risk of poverty reported difficulties in basic activities in 2022, compared with 13.8% among people who were at risk of poverty. This poverty gap was apparent in all EU countries, although it varied in size considerably, with all countries reporting a higher share among people at risk of poverty. The widest gaps in the share of people reporting severe difficulties in basic activities between people at risk or not at risk of poverty were observed in Estonia (18.7 pp), Latvia (15.4 pp) and Slovenia (13.1 pp). The narrowest gaps among the EU countries were observed in Greece, Luxembourg (both 0.9 pp), Slovakia (1.0 pp), Italy (1.2 pp) and Romania (1.9 pp). [[Image:Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, by poverty status, 2022 (%)_Health2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 6: Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, by poverty status, 2022
(%)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_hch19}}|alt= A high-low chart showing the share of people reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, analysed by poverty status. Data are shown for people at risk of poverty or not at risk of poverty. Data are shown in percent, for 2022, for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''People with lower income levels were more likely to report severe difficulties''''' In the EU, 14.5% of people aged 16 years or over in the 1st [[Glossary:Income quintile group|income quintile]] (the 20% of people with the lowest income) reported severe difficulties in basic activities in 2022. This share could be compared with 12.4% for the 2nd quintile, 9.3% for the 3rd (middle) quintile, 7.3% for the 4th quintile and 5.1% for the 5th (top) income quintile (the 20% of people with the highest income). In other words, the prevalence of self-reported severe difficulties in basic activities was highest in the bottom income quintile and was progressively lower in higher income quintiles with the lowest share among the top income quintile. Figure 7 shows the share of people who reported severe difficulties in basic activities and its relation to income; for reasons of readability, the figure only shows the shares for the bottom, middle and top income quintiles. In 2022, most EU countries showed a similar pattern to that observed for the EU: higher shares of people who reported severe difficulties in basic activities were recorded for the 1st (bottom) income quintile and lower shares for the 5th (top) income quintile, while the shares for the 3rd (middle) income quintile were between these 2 values (see Figure 7). The only exception among the EU countries was Greece, where a higher share of people reported severe difficulties in basic activities within the middle income quintile than within the bottom income quintile. The largest differences in the share of people with severe difficulties in basic activities between people in the bottom and top income quintiles in 2022 were observed in Estonia (22.8 pp) and Latvia (20.3 pp). By contrast, there was relatively minor difference observed between the shares for the bottom and top income quintiles in Italy (2.4 pp), Greece (3.0 pp), Luxembourg (3.6 pp) and Romania (3.9 pp). [[Image:Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, by income quintile, 2022 (%)_Health2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 7: Share of people aged 16 years or over reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, by income quintile, 2022
(%)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_hch17}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the share of people reporting severe difficulties in basic activities, analysed by income quintile. Data are shown for people in the 1st, 3rd and 5th income quintiles. Data are shown in percent, for 2022, for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=Disability statistics - population with difficulties in basic activities Health2025.xlsx|title=Disability statistics – population with difficulties in basic activities: tables and figures}} === Data sources and availability === The EU-SILC is the source of comparative statistics on income distribution and social inclusion in the EU. It provides annual data for the EU countries as well as most [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate countries|enlargement]] countries on income, poverty, social exclusion and other aspects of living conditions. The reference population for the EU-SILC is limited to private [[Glossary:Household|households]] and their current members residing in the territory of the surveying country at the time of data collection. People living in collective households and institutions are excluded from the reference population; this constitutes a limitation for disability statistics. All household members are surveyed, but only those aged 16 years or over are interviewed. The source is documented in more detail in this [[Health_variables_in_SILC_-_methodology|background article]], which provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. In EU statistics, disability is usually approximated according to the concept of global activity limitation, which is defined as a limitation – because of health problems – in carrying out usual activities (for at least the previous 6 months). However, this article concerns people reporting difficulties in basic activities as defined by the Washington Group short set of questions on functioning. '''Washington Group Short Set of questions on Functioning (WG-SS)''' The [https://www.washingtongroup-disability.com/ Washington Group on Disability Statistics] promotes and coordinates international cooperation in the area of health statistics focusing on the development of disability measures suitable for statistics. In particular, the focus is on developing methodology which can be used in a valid, reliable and internationally/cross-culturally comparable manner. A short set of functioning questions provide the basis for the data presented in this article. The 6 basic activities covered are seeing, hearing, walking, remembering or concentrating, communicating and self-care. The short set on functioning identifies 6 commonly occurring limitations which aim to represent the majority of (but not all) people with limitations in basic activities. They aim to identify people with similar types and degrees of limitations in basic actions regardless of nationality or culture. The questions are the following: *Do you have difficulty seeing even if wearing glasses? *Do you have difficulty hearing even if using a hearing aid? *Do you have difficulty walking or climbing steps? *Do you have difficulty remembering or concentrating? *Do you have difficulty with (self-care such as) washing all over or dressing? *Using your usual language, do you have difficulty communicating (for example understanding or being understood by others)? Response categories are 'no difficulty', 'some difficulty', 'a lot of difficulty' or 'cannot do at all'. For the statistics published in this article, the responses ''a lot of difficulty'' and ''cannot do at all'' have been aggregated as 'severe difficulties'. '''Educational levels – ISCED''' Educational attainment is an important factor for individuals, in society as a whole, and in the labour market. Higher levels of education usually lead to higher rates of employment, higher productivity and higher lifetime earnings for individuals, alongside greater life satisfaction. In this article, 3 aggregated levels of educational attainment are presented *less than primary, primary or lower secondary level of education ([[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|ISCED]] 2011 levels 0 to 2; referred to as a low level of education) *upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (ISCED 2011 levels 3 and 4; referred to as a medium level of education) *tertiary education (ISCED 2011 levels 5 to 8; referred to as a high level of education). '''Poverty status''' People who are at risk of poverty have an [[Glossary:Equivalised disposable income|equivalised disposable income]] after [[Glossary:Social transfers|social transfers]] which is below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold. The latter is set at 60% of the national [[Glossary:Median|median]] equivalised disposable income after social transfers. === Context === Disability statistics are used to measure the impact and effectiveness of EU policy aimed at ensuring equal rights for people with disabilities. The EU has adopted several strategies aimed at improving the lives of people with disabilities *by reducing discrimination and inequalities, and *by providing support to enjoy fully their human rights, fundamental freedoms and EU rights on an equal basis with others. In light of this, the [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1484&langId=en 2021–2030 EU Strategy for the rights of people with disabilities] sets EU objectives and priority actions in several areas, such as accessibility, citizens’ rights, the quality of life, equal access and non-discrimination, and the promotion of the rights of persons with disabilities. To find out more, please visit the [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1552&langId=en webpage on the monitoring framework for the objectives and actions of this strategy]. To ensure sound monitoring and reporting of this topic, the European Commission is reinforcing the collection of data on the situation of people with disabilities in areas where knowledge gaps have been identified, for example in relation to access to the labour market. The EU is also a signatory of the [[Glossary:United Nations (UN)|United Nations]] (UN) [https://social.desa.un.org/issues/disability/crpd/convention-on-the-rights-of-persons-with-disabilities-crpd Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities] (CRPD). ===Other articles=== '''Online publications''' *[[Disability statistics]] *[[Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] title: Disability statistics - poverty and income inequalities
text:
This article looks at the risk of poverty or social exclusion for people in the EU with a disability (activity limitation) compared with people without a disability. Data extracted in: July 2025. Planned article update: December 2026. In 2024 in the EU, 28.8% of people with a disability were at risk of poverty or social exclusion, compared with 17.9% among people with no limitations. In 2024 in the EU, 68.2% of people with a disability would have been at risk of poverty, but after taking account of social transfers (such as benefits and allowances) the share was 20.7%. [[Image:Number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, by type of risk, EU, 2024 (millions)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, by type of risk, EU, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_pees01n}}|alt=A Venn diagram showing the number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion. Data are shown for people at risk of poverty, for people living in a household with very low work intensity, and for severely materially and socially deprived people. Data are shown in millions, for 2024, for the EU. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. ]] This article presents various aspects of the income, social and employment situation of people with a [[Glossary:Disability|disability]] ([[Glossary:Activity_limitation|activity limitation]]). The data come from [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union’s]] (EU’s) [[Glossary:EU-SILC|statistics on income and living conditions]] (EU-SILC) and relate to the 2024 reference year; they cover people aged 16 years or over. This article is one of a set of articles on disability which forms part of the online publication [[Disability statistics|Disability statistics]]. === At risk of poverty or social exclusion === '''''Higher rate of being at risk of poverty or social exclusion among people with a disability''''' The [[Glossary:At_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_(AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion]] indicator measures the number or percentage of people who are *[[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|at risk of poverty]] and/or *[[Glossary:Severe material and social deprivation rate (SMSD)|severely materially and socially deprived]] and/or *[[Glossary:Persons living in households with very low work intensity|living in a household with a very low work intensity]]. The number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion is a headline indicator to monitor the [[Glossary:The_European_Pillar_of_Social_Rights_Action_Plan_(EU_2030_targets)|European pillar of social rights (EU 2030 targets)]]; it is presented in this article both in its aggregated form and for its constituent parts. [[Image:Share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024 (%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dpe010}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dpe020}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dm010}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dpe040}}|alt=A table showing the share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion. Data are shown for people aged 16 years or over for people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, for people at risk of poverty, for people facing severe material or social deprivation, and for people aged less than 65 years living in households with very low work intensity. These data are shown for people with or without a disability (activity limitation). Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU and the euro area, as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, 28.8% of people in the EU aged 16 years or over with a disability (activity limitation) were at risk of poverty or social exclusion, compared with 17.9% of people with no disability. Similar results were observed for the at-risk-of-poverty rate (20.7% compared with 14.2%), severe material and social deprivation rate (10.4% compared with 4.7%) and the share of individuals aged less than 65 years who lived in [[Glossary:Household|households]] with [[Glossary:Persons living in households with very low work intensity|very low work intensity]] (18.4% compared with 5.5%). The last of these comparisons reflects, at least in part, the more difficult access to labour markets faced by people with a disability. The share of people with a disability (activity limitation) who were at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2024 ranged, among the EU countries, from 15.6% in Czechia to 43.8% in Bulgaria and 45.8% in Lithuania. '''''People with a disability were most likely to be at risk of poverty in the Baltic countries and Croatia''''' The at-risk-of-poverty rate among people aged 16 years or over with a disability (activity limitation) was highest in 2024 in the [[Glossary:Baltic Member States|Baltic countries]] and Croatia: 38.2% in Lithuania, 37.8% in Croatia, 35.5% in Estonia and 34.8% in Lativa. The lowest rates among people with a disability were in Czechia (11.6%), Slovakia (12.6%), the Netherlands (13.7%) and Belgium (13.8%). As such, the rate was 3.3 times as high in Lithuania as in Czechia. With regard to the share of people at risk of poverty, the absolute gap between people with or without a disability was also wide in 2024 in Croatia and the Baltic countries, all in the range of 18.9 to 23.2 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points]]). By contrast, Slovakia recorded at-risk-of-poverty rates that were slightly lower for people with a disability than for those without (a gap of 1.2 pp). '''''People with a disability were most likely to experience severe material and social deprivation in Bulgaria and Romania''''' In 2024, all EU countries recorded a higher share of people experiencing severe material or social deprivation among people with a disability than among those without. Among people aged 16 years or over with a disability, severe material and social deprivation was most common in 2024 in Bulgaria (27.1%) and Romania (26.7%). These 2 shares were notably higher than in the other EU countries, as the next highest share was 18.5% in Greece. In 15 EU countries, fewer than 10.0% of people with a disability experienced severe material and social deprivation. The lowest share was 3.3% in Cyprus. As such, the share was 8.2 times as high in Bulgaria as in Cyprus. In absolute terms, the widest gap between persons with a disability and those with no disability was in Romania, a difference of 13.0 pp, while double-digit differences were also recorded in Bulgaria (12.1 pp) and Hungary (11.4 pp). '''''People with a disability were most likely to live in a household with very low work intensity in Lithuania''''' The final indicator in Table 1 concerns people aged less than 65 years; it shows the share living in a household with very low work intensity. Among people with a disability, this share was highest in 2024 in Lithuania (31.6% - provisional data). At the other end of the range, Luxembourg (6.8%; 2022 data) had the lowest share among the EU countries. As such, the share was 4.6 times as high in Lithuania as in Luxembourg. In 2024, all EU countries recorded a larger share of people aged less than 65 years living in a household with very low work intensity among people with a disability than among those without. In absolute terms, the widest gaps were in Lithuania (25.2 pp) and Belgium (22.0 pp), while the narrowest gap was in Luxembourg (4.4 pp; 2022 data). === Impact of social transfers on the at-risk-of-poverty rate === '''''The at-risk-of-poverty rate among people with a disability was lowered greatly by social transfers''''' In 2024, 68.2% of people in the EU aged 16 years or over with a disability would have been at risk of poverty if social transfers (social benefits and allowances) had not taken place; this is the [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate_before_social_transfers|at-risk-of-poverty rate before social transfers]]. By contrast, slightly more than a fifth (20.7%) of the same people were at risk of poverty after taking social transfers into account – see Figure 1. For people with a disability, the at-risk-of-poverty rate before social transfers in 2024 ranged among the EU countries from 80.2% in Greece to 54.7% in Luxembourg (2022 data). In all EU countries, the at-risk-of-poverty rate after social transfers in 2024 for people with a disability was lower than the rate before transfers. The difference in these 2 rates was generally large, ranging from 58.4 pp in Greece (80.2% before social transfers compared with 21.8% after social transfers) to 27.2 pp in Latvia (62.0% compared with 34.8%). [[Image:At-risk-of-poverty rate for people aged 16 years or over with a disability (activity limitation), before and after social transfers, 2024 (%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: At-risk-of-poverty rate for people aged 16 years or over with a disability (activity limitation), before and after social transfers, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dpe030}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dpe020}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the at-risk-of-poverty rate for people aged 16 years or over with a disability (activity limitation). Data are shown for the rates before and after social transfers. Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU and the euro area as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. ]] ===In-work poverty=== '''''People with a disability were more likely to face in-work poverty than people with no disability''''' Regardless of whether people have a disability or not, being in employment generally reduces the risk of poverty. In 2024, 8.2% of employed people in the EU aged 18 years or over were at-risk-of-poverty, while the share was 15.5% for all people of the same age group. As such, employment reduces the risk of poverty but does not make it disappear. The [[EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)_methodology_-_in-work_poverty|in-work at-risk-of-poverty rate]], in other words the risk of poverty among employed people, is a key indicator of labour market integration, in particular for people having a disability. In the EU, 9.7% of employed people with a disability were at risk of-poverty in 2024, while this rate was 8.0% among employed people with no disability – see Figure 2. In 2024, the highest in-work at-risk-of-poverty rate among people with a disability was observed in Romania (21.8%), notably higher than the next highest rate among the EU countries, 16.9% in Luxembourg (2022 data). The lowest rate was recorded in Finland (3.0%). In Slovakia, Bulgaria and Slovenia, the in-work at-risk-of-poverty rate was higher among people without a disability than among those with a disability: the gap between the two rates was highest in Slovakia (3.9 pp). In the remaining 24 EU countries, the in-work at-risk-of-poverty rate was lower among people without a disability than among those with a disability. The widest gaps between the rates were in Romania (11.3 pp) and Hungary (8.2 pp). [[Image:In-work at-risk-of-poverty rate for people aged 18 years or over, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024 (%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 2: In-work at-risk-of-poverty rate for people aged 18 years or over, by level of disability (activity limitation), 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_dpe050}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the in-work at-risk-of-poverty rate for people aged 18 years or over. Data are shown for people with or without a disability (activity limitation). Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU and the euro area as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. ]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Disability statistics - poverty and income inequalities_Health2025.xlsx|title=Disability statistics – poverty and income inequalities: tables and figures}} === Data sources and availability === EU-SILC is the source of comparative statistics on income distribution and social inclusion in the EU. It provides annual data for the EU countries as well as most [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate countries|enlargement]] countries on income, poverty, social exclusion and other aspects of living conditions. The reference population for EU-SILC is limited to private households and their current members residing in the territory of the surveying country at the time of data collection. People living in collective households and institutions are generally excluded from the reference population; this constitutes a limitation for disability statistics. All household members are surveyed, but only those aged 16 years or over are interviewed. The source is documented in more detail in this [[Health_variables_in_SILC_-_methodology|background article]], which provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. In EU-SILC, disability is approximated according to the concept of global activity limitation, which is defined as a limitation – because of health problems – in carrying out usual activities (for at least the previous 6 months). This is considered to be an adequate proxy for disability, both by the scientific community and organisations representing people with disabilities. This definition is also in line with the concept of disability as set out in the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=LEGISSUM%3Aem0047 European disability strategy 2010–2020] and its successor, the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030_en Strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities 2021–2030]. === Context === Disability statistics are used to measure the impact and effectiveness of EU policy aimed at ensuring equal rights for people with disabilities. The EU has adopted several strategies aimed at improving the lives of people with disabilities *by reducing discrimination and inequalities *by providing support to enjoy fully their human rights, fundamental freedoms and EU rights on an equal basis with others. In light of this, the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030_en 2021-2030 EU Strategy for the rights of people with disabilities] sets EU objectives and priority actions in several areas, such as accessibility, citizens’ rights, the quality of life, equal access and non-discrimination, and the promotion of the rights of people with disabilities. To find out more, please visit the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030/monitoring-framework_en webpage on the monitoring framework for the objectives and actions of this strategy]. To ensure sound monitoring and reporting of this topic, the European Commission is reinforcing the collection of data on the situation of people with disabilities in areas where knowledge gaps have been identified, for example in relation to access to the labour market. The EU is also a signatory of the [[Glossary:United Nations (UN)|United Nations]] (UN) [https://social.desa.un.org/issues/disability/crpd/convention-on-the-rights-of-persons-with-disabilities-crpd Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities] (CRPD). The financial situation of households has become a key area of concern during the cost-of-living crisis. A growing share of people in the EU – particularly those in vulnerable situations – face difficulties paying their energy bills and paying for food. The links between poverty and ill-health suggest that the cost-of-living crisis may worsen health inequalities across the EU. ===Other articles=== '''Online publications''' *[[Disability statistics]]
