title: Disability statistics - unemployment and people outside the labour force
text:
This article provides information about people in the EU with a disability (activity limitation) in terms of their access to the labour market, specifically in terms of unemployment or being outside the labour market; it covers people who are impacted by long-standing limitations in their usual activities due to health problems. The article provides information on the unemployment rate, the share of unemployed people who are long-term unemployed and the share of people outside the labour force. Data extracted in: October 2025 Planned article update: September 2027 In 2024, the unemployment rate among people aged 15 to 64 years in the EU with a severe disability was 11.6%, compared with 5.9% for people without a disability. In 2024, 45.0% of people aged 15 to 64 years in the EU with a severe disability who were unemployed had been unemployed for at least 12 months, compared with 31.1% for people without a disability. In 2024, 67.7% of people aged 15 to 64 years in the EU with a severe disability were outside the labour force (neither employed nor unemployed), compared with 21.8% for people without a disability. [[Image:Unemployment rate of people aged 15–64 years, by level of disability, 2024_(% of the labour force)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Unemployment rate of people aged 15–64 years, by level of disability, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfsa_urgaeddl}}|alt=A bullet chart showing the unemployment rate of people aged 15 to 64 years. Data are shown for people with or without a disability. Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] This article provides recent statistics on some aspects of the [[Glossary:Labour force|labour force]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] relating to people with disabilities. It focuses on the [[Glossary:Unemployment|unemployment rate]], the share of unemployed people who are [[Glossary:Long-term_unemployment|long-term unemployed]] and the share of [[Glossary:People_outside_the_labour_force|people outside the labour force]]. The data come from the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (EU-LFS)|EU labour force survey (EU LFS)]] and relate to the 2024 reference year; the focus of this article is on people aged 15 to 64 years. This article is one of a set of statistical articles on disability which forms part of the online publication [[Disability_statistics|Disability statistics]]. [[Glossary:Disability|Disability]] is approximated according to the concept of global [[Glossary:Activity_limitation|activity limitation]], which is defined as self-assessment of own level of limitation – because of health problems – in carrying out usual activities, for at least the previous 6 months (that is, being limited or severely limited in an everyday activity that people usually do). ===Unemployment rate === '''In 2024, the unemployment rate for people aged 15 to 64 years in the EU with a severe disability was 11.6%''' Across the EU in 2024, the unemployment rate for people aged 15 to 64 years without a long-standing limitation in usual activities due to health problems (hereafter referred to as a disability) was 5.9%. This rate was higher for people with some disability (9.1%) and higher still for people with a severe disability (11.6%) – see Figure 1. The pattern of a lower unemployment rate for people without a disability and a higher rate for people with a severe disability was observed in the EU both for men and for women. In 2024, the gap between the unemployment rate for people without a disability and people with some disability was larger for men (3.9 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points]]) than for women (2.4 percentage points). For people without a disability, the unemployment rate was higher for women than for men, whereas for people with some disability and for people with a severe disability the rate was higher for men. The gender gap was largest among people with a severe disability, as the unemployment rate was 2.6 percentage points higher for men (12.9%) than for women (10.3%). In 2024, the pattern of the lowest unemployment rate for people without a disability and the highest unemployment rate for people with a severe disability was observed for younger people (aged 15 to 24 years), for people aged 25 to 54 years and for older people (aged 55 to 64 years). Within the EU, the gap between the unemployment rate for people without a disability and people with some disability was 4.4 and 4.3 percentage points, respectively, for younger people and for people aged 25 to 54 years; this gap was narrower (2.8 percentage points) for older people. Regardless of the level of disability, unemployment rates were higher for younger people and lower for older people. Across the EU in 2024, the difference in rates for people with no disability (11.6 percentage points between the unemployment rates for younger and older people) and with some disability (13.2 percentage points) were similar, but the gap was notably larger for people with a severe disability (20.6 percentage points). In 2024, the pattern of the lowest unemployment rate for people without a disability and the highest unemployment rate for people with a severe disability was observed in the EU for people with medium and high levels of educational attainment. For people with a low level of educational attainment, the unemployment rate was slightly lower for people with a severe disability than for people with some disability. Regardless of the level of disability, the unemployment rate was highest for people with a low level of educational attainment and lowest for people with a high level of educational attainment. [[Image:Unemployment rate of people aged 15–64 years, by level of disability, EU, 2024 (% of the labour force) v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Unemployment rate of people aged 15–64 years, by level of disability, EU, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfsa_urgaeddl}}|alt=A grouped column chart showing the unemployment rate of people aged 15 to 64 years. Data are shown for people with a severe disability, with some disability and without a disability; for each of these levels of disability, data are analysed by sex, age group and education level. Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] Among people aged 15 to 64 years with a disability, the highest unemployment rate in 2024 was in Lithuania (20.0%), where it was more than double the EU average (9.5%) – see Figure 2. The lowest unemployment rates among people with a disability were observed in the Netherlands (5.5%) and Germany (5.7%). The disability gap for the unemployment rate was 3.6 percentage points in the EU (rates of 5.9% for people without a disability and 9.5% for people with a disability). This gap ranged from 0.4 percentage points in Luxembourg to 9.5 percentage points in Hungary and 13.3 percentage points in Lithuania. [[Image:Unemployment rate of people aged 15–64 years, by level of disability, 2024_(% of the labour force)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Unemployment rate of people aged 15–64 years, by level of disability, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfsa_urgaeddl}}|alt=A bullet chart showing the unemployment rate of people aged 15 to 64 years. Data are shown for people with or without a disability. Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] ===Share of long-term unemployment === '''In 2024, 45.0% of unemployed people aged 15 to 64 years in the EU with a severe disability were long-term unemployed''' In the EU, 31.1% of unemployed people aged 15 to 64 years without a disability were long-term unemployed. This share was higher for people with some disability (39.5%) and higher still for people with a severe disability (45.0%) – see Figure 3. The pattern of the lowest share of long-term unemployment among people without a disability and the highest share among people with a severe disability was observed, across the EU, both for men and for women. In 2024, the gap between the share of long-term unemployment for people without a disability and people with some disability was more than twice as high for men (11.7 percentage points) than for women (5.0 percentage points). Whereas the share of long-term unemployment was higher among women than among men for people without a disability, the reverse was observed for people with some or with a severe disability. In 2024, the pattern of the lowest share of long-term unemployment for unemployed people without a disability and the highest share for unemployed people with a severe disability was observed, across the EU, for people aged 25 to 54 years and for older people (aged 55 to 64 years); data are incomplete for younger people (aged 15 to 24 years). Regardless of the level of disability, the share of long-term unemployment was higher for older unemployed people and lower for unemployed people aged 25 to 54 years. [[Image:People aged 15–64 years in long-term unemployment, by level of disability, EU, 2024 (% of unemployed people) Disab2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: People aged 15–64 years in long-term unemployment, by level of disability, EU, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfsa_upgadl}}|alt=A grouped column chart showing the share of long-term unemployed people within all unemployed people, for people aged 15 to 64 years. Data are shown for people with a severe disability, with some disability and without a disability; for each of these levels of disability, data are analysed by sex and age group. Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] Among unemployed people with a disability, by far the highest shares of long-term unemployment in 2024 were in Slovakia (67.1%) and Greece (66.2%), both of which had shares that were more than 1.5 times as high as the EU average (40.6%) – see Figure 4. The lowest share of long-term unemployment among unemployed people with a disability was observed in Denmark (18.5%). The disability gap for the share of long-term unemployment ranged from 2.5 percentage points in Slovakia to 22.4 percentage points in Latvia, 23.0 percentage points in Lithuania and 24.2 percentage points in Czechia. [[Image:People aged 15–64 years in long-term unemployment, by level of disability, 2024_(% of unemployed people)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: People aged 15–64 years in long-term unemployment, by level of disability, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfsa_upgadl}}|alt=A bullet chart showing the share of long-term unemployed people within all unemployed people, for people aged 15 to 64 years. Data are shown for people with or without a disability. Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] ===People outside the labour force=== '''In 2024, 67.7% of people aged 15 to 64 years in the EU with a severe disability were outside the labour force''' In the EU, 21.8% of people aged 15 to 64 years without a disability were outside the labour force in 2024. This share was higher for people with some disability (35.0%) and much higher still for people with a severe disability (67.7%) – see Figure 5. The pattern of a lower share of people who were outside the labour force for people without a disability and a higher share for people with a severe disability was observed both for men and for women across the EU. In 2024, the gap between the shares for people without a disability and people with some disability was larger for men (14.7 percentage points) than for women (11.0 percentage points). For people without a disability or with some disability, women were more likely than men to be outside the labour force. For people with a severe disability the reverse was observed, with higher shares for men. In 2024, the pattern of the lowest share of people who were outside the labour force for people without a disability and the highest share for people with a severe disability was observed across the EU for 2 of the 3 age groups: people aged 25 to 54 years and older people (aged 55 to 64 years). For younger people (aged 15 to 24 years), the share of people who were outside the labour force was lowest for people with some limitations. Regardless of the level of disability, people aged 15 to 24 years were more likely to be outside the labour force than people aged 25 to 54 years. In this context, it should be noted that the share of people who were outside the labour force is particularly high in the younger age group, regardless of the level of disability, reflecting the fact that many people in this age group are still at school or in tertiary education. In 2024, the pattern of the lowest share of people outside the labour force for people without a disability and the highest rate for people with a severe disability was observed, across the EU, for people with low, medium and high levels of educational attainment. Regardless of the level of disability, the share of people outside the labour force was highest for people with a low level of educational attainment and lowest for people with a high level of educational attainment. The gap was narrowest for people with a severe disability (31.8 percentage points between the shares of people outside the labour force for people with low or high levels of educational attainment) and widest for people with no disability (35.9 percentage points). [[Image:Share of people aged 15–64 years outside the labour force, by level of disability, EU, 2024 (% of the population) v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Share of people aged 15–64 years outside the labour force, by level of disability, EU, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfsa_ipgaeddl}}|alt=A grouped column chart showing the share of people aged 15 to 64 years outside the labour force. Data are shown for people with a severe disability, with some disability and without a disability; for each of these levels of disability, data are analysed by sex, age and education level. Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] Among people with a disability, by far the highest shares of people who were outside the labour force in 2024 were in Bulgaria (88.7%), Greece (75.7%) and Romania (70.9%), all of which had shares that were at least 1.5 times as high as the EU average (44.5%) – see Figure 6. The lowest shares of people who were outside the labour force among people with a disability were observed in Finland (28.0%), Estonia (30.1%) and Sweden (30.5%). The disability gap for the share of people who were outside the labour force ranged from 10.7 percentage points in Luxembourg to 64.8 percentage points in Bulgaria. [[Image:Share of people aged 15–64 years outside the labour force, by level of disability, 2024_(% of the population)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Share of people aged 15–64 years outside the labour force, by level of disability, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfsa_argaeddl}}|alt=A bullet chart showing the share of people aged 15 to 64 years who were outside the labour force. Data are shown for people with or without a disability. Data are shown in percent, for 2024, for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Disability statistics – unemployment and people outside the labour force Health20251201.xlsx|title=Disability statistics – unemployment and people outside the labour force: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The European Union labour force survey (EU LFS) is the largest European household sample survey providing quarterly and annual results on labour participation among people aged 15 and over and on people outside the labour force. It covers residents in private households. Although focused on the labour market, the EU LFS also provides statistics on education and disability. The EU-LFS is documented in this [[EU_labour_force_survey|background article]] which provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. Disability is measured with a variable assessing the limitations people have experienced – because of health problems – in carrying out usual activities (for at least the previous 6 months); the resulting measure is called the global activity limitation indicator (GALI). '''Classification of education levels''' The [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|International standard classification of education (ISCED)]] is the basis for international education statistics, describing different levels of education; it was first developed in 1976 by [[Glossary:UNESCO|UNESCO]] and revised in 1997 and again in 2011. [https://www.uis.unesco.org/en/methods-and-tools/isced ISCED 2011] differentiates 9 levels of education: early childhood education (level 0); primary education (level 1); lower secondary education (level 2); upper secondary education (level 3); post-secondary non-tertiary education (level 4); short-cycle tertiary education (level 5); bachelor’s or equivalent level (level 6); master’s or equivalent level (level 7); doctoral or equivalent level (level 8). '''People outside the labour force''' A person is outside the labour force, according to the definitions set up by the [https://ilostat.ilo.org/about/standards/icls/ International Conference of Labour Statisticians (ICLS)], organised by the [[Glossary:International_Labour_Organization_(ILO)|International Labour Organisation (ILO)]], if they are not part of the [[Glossary:Labour_force|labour force]], meaning they are neither [[Glossary:Employed_person_-_LFS|employed]] nor [[Glossary:Unemployed|unemployed]]. The set of people outside the labour force was previously also known as the (economically) inactive population. '''Unemployment''' An unemployed person is defined by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], according to the definitions set up by the [https://ilostat.ilo.org/about/standards/icls/ International Conference of Labour Statisticians (ICLS)], organised by the [[Glossary:International_Labour_Organization_(ILO)|International Labour Organisation (ILO)]], as a person meeting all of the following conditions: *aged 15 to 74 years, *not employed during the reference week according to the definition of [[Glossary:Employment|employment]], *currently available for work, in other words, available for paid employment or [[Glossary:Self-employed|self-employment]] before the end of the 2 weeks following the [[Glossary:Reference period|reference week]], *actively seeking work, in other words, had either carried out activities in the 4-week period ending with the reference week to seek paid employment or self-employment or found a job to start within a period of at most 3 months from the end of the reference week. The unemployment rate is the number of people unemployed as a percentage of the labour force. '''Long-term unemployment''' Long-term unemployment refers to people who have been unemployed for at least 12 months (a year). The unemployment period is defined as the duration of a job search, or as the length of time since the last job was held (if shorter than the time spent on a job search). '''Educational attainment''' Educational attainment is a term commonly used to refer to the highest level of education that an individual has successfully completed. In this article, data on educational attainment are presented for 3 aggregates of educational attainment: *low – less than primary, primary and lower secondary education (ISCED levels 0 to 2) *medium – upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education (ISCED levels 3 and 4) *high – tertiary education (ISCED levels 5 to 8). ===Context=== Disability statistics are used to measure the impact and effectiveness of EU policy aimed at ensuring equal rights for people with disabilities. The EU has adopted several strategies aimed at improving the lives of people with disabilities: *by reducing discrimination and inequalities *by providing support to enjoy fully their human rights, fundamental freedoms and EU rights on an equal basis with others. In light of this, the [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1484&langId=en 2021–30 EU Strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities] sets EU objectives and priority actions in several areas, such as accessibility, citizens’ rights, quality of life, equal access and non-discrimination, and the promotion of the rights of people with disabilities. To find out more, please visit the [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1552&langId=en webpage on the monitoring framework for the objectives and actions of this strategy]. To ensure sound monitoring and reporting of this topic, the European Commission is reinforcing the collection of data on the situation of people with disabilities in areas where knowledge gaps have been identified. Within the [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/european-pillar-social-rights-building-fairer-and-more-inclusive-european-union/european-pillar-social-rights-action-plan_en European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan], one of the [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_22_3782 EU 2030 social targets] concerns employment. Its goal is for the share of adults aged 20 to 64 years to be in employment to reach at least 78% by 2030. The EU is also a signatory of the [[Glossary:United Nations (UN)|United Nations (UN)]] [https://social.desa.un.org/issues/disability/crpd/convention-on-the-rights-of-persons-with-disabilities-crpd Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD)]. Given the broad nature of the UN Convention and the EU’s disability strategy, policy issues related to disability concern the social integration of people with disabilities in all aspects of life. The functional status of people needs to be taken into account in many policy areas, such as health, social protection, housing, transport, culture, education and employment. Policy development in these areas can benefit from reliable data on the functional status of the population. Being unemployed may impact a person’s financial situation as well as that of their family. It can also impact on mental health, induce a sense of a loss of self-esteem and contribute to social exclusion, affecting not just the unemployed person but also other family members. Unemployment may have wider consequences for governments (such as expenditure on social benefits combined with lower tax income), society (with unemployment associated with crime and other pressures on communities) and the economy (through a relatively low level of purchasing power). ===Other articles=== '''Online publications''' *[[Disability_statistics|Disability statistics]] *[[EU labour force survey statistics|EU labour force survey statistics]] *[[EU labour force survey|EU labour force survey]] – methodological publication ===Database=== title: Disability statistics background - European health and social integration survey
text:
3 Latest update of text: November 2015 This background article explains the data from the European Health and Social Integration Survey (EHSIS), a population [[Glossary:Survey|survey]] that provides information relating to a biopsychosocial model of [[Glossary:Disability|disability]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Starting from this model, people with disabilities are those who face barriers to participation associated with a [[Glossary:Longstanding health problem or disease|long-standing health problem]] and/or a [[Glossary:Basic activity difficulty|basic activity difficulty]]. The EHSIS not only presents information on barriers to participation that are related to disability, but also looks at a range of other barriers to participation, such as finance and convenience. The article provides information on the main features of the disability data derived from the EHSIS, their historical development, some main methodological features and information concerning data quality. This article is one of a set of background articles concerning the [[Disability_statistics#10. Methodological annex|methodology]] for the production of disability statistics in the EU and accompanies a number of statistical articles which make up an online publication on [[Disability_statistics|disability statistics]]. ===Main features=== '''Statistical objectives''' The EHSIS aims to provide statistical data — on a harmonised basis and with a high degree of comparability between the EU Member States — applying the concept of disability used by the [[Glossary:World Health Organization (WHO)|World Health Organisation]]’s [http://www.who.int/classifications/icf/en/ International classification of functioning, disability and health (ICF)], based on a biopsychosocial model.  
'''Disabled people are those facing barriers to participation in any life area, owing to a long-standing health problem and/or a basic activity difficulty.'''
For more information on disability models, please refer to an [[Disability_statistics_introduced|introductory article on disability statistics]]. '''Scope of the data''' The EHSIS includes questions in three sections: #socio-economic background; #a health component to identify long-standing health problems and activity difficulties; #a list of 10 life areas that enable an individual to be a fully functional and integrated member of society, used to measure social integration in general and identify disability in particular. The general coverage of the survey is the population aged 15 or over living in [[Glossary:Private household|private households]] residing in the territory of the country. ===Development and legal basis=== '''Development and history''' The European disability and social integration module (EDSIM) was initially conceived as a module for the [[Glossary:European health interview survey (EHIS)|European health interview survey (EHIS)]]. However, before being integrated into the EHIS it was decided to extend the planned module and to implement it as an independent disability survey, which then became known as the EHSIS. The EHSIS was a one-off survey launched by Eurostat and conducted in 2012 or 2013 through calls for tenders. Only five national statistical authorities (Denmark, Spain, Latvia, Hungary and Slovenia) were partly or fully involved in the exercise; elsewhere it was implemented by private enterprises. As well as data for the EU Member States, data were also collected for Iceland and Norway. Data were not collected for Ireland (as the contract for the Irish survey was cancelled) nor for Croatia as it was not an EU Member State at the time of launching the call for tenders. In November 2013, Eurostat and representatives of the national statistical authorities agreed to discontinue this survey and instead to consider including a disability module into the future waves of the European health interview survey (EHIS). '''Legal basis''' The EHSIS was conducted on the basis of calls for tenders and contracts, in other words, without a legal obligation. ===Methodology=== '''Main sources''' The EHSIS was implemented in each participating EU Member State or non-member country based on a model questionnaire with instructions for interviewers. The contracting authorities were asked to translate it according to a standard translation protocol. No deviation was allowed except those resulting from cultural differences and the data collection method used: adaptations were needed in case of telephone or web-based interviews. '''Geographical coverage''' Data were collected for all of the EU Member States except for Ireland and Croatia, and also for Iceland and Norway. Aggregates were calculated for the [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU-27]] as a whole and for the [[Glossary:European Economic Area (EEA)|European economic area]]. Note that these aggregates exclude data for Ireland and the aggregate for the European economic area also excludes data for Liechtenstein; for these reasons these aggregates are disseminated as estimates. '''Statistical units''' The [[Glossary:Statistical unit|statistical unit]] is the individual. '''Main concepts and definitions''' A summary is given below of the topics surveyed in the EHSIS. Links to more detailed information are presented below under the heading [[#Further methodological information|further methodological information]]. '''''Socio-economic background''''' This section of the survey includes background classificatory questions, such as: *where the person is living, country of birth, nationality; *sex, age; *marital status, household composition, income; *education level; *labour status, occupation. '''''Health status''''' The health component includes: *the [[Glossary:Minimum European Health Module (MEHM)|minimum European health module (MEHM)]] comprising questions about **a person’s general health condition ([[Glossary:Self-perceived health|self-perceived health]]) **the self-reported existence of long-standing illnesses or long-standing health problems ([[Glossary:Chronic morbidity|chronic morbidity]]) and **the severity of limitations in usual activities due to a health problem ([[Glossary:Activity limitation|activity limitation]]); *questions about the existence of one or more long-standing health problems from a list of 18 groups; *questions about basic activity difficulties (such as seeing, hearing, walking and communicating); *questions about activities of daily living/personal care activities (such as bathing, dressing and feeding oneself); *questions about instrumental activities of daily living/household activities (such as preparing meals, using the telephone, going shopping and doing housework). A '''long-standing health problem''' is an illness, disease, injury or other health condition which has lasted or is likely to last for at least six months. The main characteristics of a long-standing health problem are that it is permanent and may be expected to require a long period of supervision, observation or care. Acute (temporary) health problems, such as a sprained ankle or a respiratory tract infection are not considered as being long-standing. For the various types of activities — basic activities, personal care activities and household activities — respondents were asked to rate the '''level of difficulty''' between: *no difficulty; *some difficulty; *a lot of difficulty; *cannot do at all/unable to do. '''''Barriers to life areas''''' The final section of the survey concerns a list of 10 areas (also referred to as domains) concerning important aspects of life that relate to an individual’s ability to be a fully functional and integrated member of society. These areas were identified as being the most relevant from the ICF. The areas are: *mobility, *transport, *accessibility to buildings, *education and training, *employment, *internet use, *social contact and support, *leisure pursuits, *economic life, *attitudes and behaviour. For each of these areas respondents were asked whether: *there were barriers restricting their participation in specified area and what those barriers were; *a lack of aids or equipment prevented participation; *a lack of personal help or assistance prevented participation. Note that these questions concerning participation in life areas and restrictions to participation were asked to all respondents, not just those with a long-standing health problem or a basic activity difficulty. '''''People with disabilities and the severity of their disability''''' Based on the information participation in the 10 life areas and the re asons for barriers to participation, respondents were classified as disabled or not. '''People with disabilities''' are those who face barriers to participation in any (in other words, at least one) of the 10 life areas, where the barrier is associated with a long-standing health problem and/or a basic activity limitation. A person identifying a long-standing health problem and/or basic activity limitation as barrier in any life domain was categorised as disabled. Important note: not all people who have a long-standing health problem and/or basic activity limitation are disabled as it may be that these problems or limitations were not barriers to any of the 10 selected life areas. The '''severity of disability''' was calculated by adding up the number of life areas where a respondent encounters a barrier associated with a long-standing health problem and/or a basic activity limitation. For the purposes of data presentation three levels of severity were compiled, for those facing disability barriers in: one life area, two or three life areas, and four or more life areas. '''Reference period''' The EHSIS data refer to the situation of the population at the time of the survey. For long-standing health problems it concerns problems that had lasted or were likely to last for at least six months. '''Main classifications''' EHSIS makes use of the following international classifications: *the international classification of functioning, disability and health (ICF); *educational attainment is compiled according to the 1997 version of the [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|international standard classification of education (ISCED 1997)]]; *occupation in employment uses the 2008 version of the [[Glossary:International standard classification of occupations (ISCO)|international standard classification of occupations (ISCO-08)]]; *the economic sector in employment is collected according to an aggregation — into 10 headings — of the section level (one letter) of the 2008 version of the [[Glossary:Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)|statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE Rev. 2)]]. '''Further methodological information''' A model questionnaire and detailed information on the questions asked are available in the [https://circabc.europa.eu/w/browse/3d77833d-9d3d-4311-ab4c-9393cd076a73 EHSIS questionnaire interviewer instructions.] Metadata concerning the results of the EHSIS are available from [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/hlth_dsb_prve_esms.htm European health and social integration survey (EHSIS)] (ESMS metadata file — hlth_dsb_prve_esms). ===Data quality=== The data collection methods for this survey were prepared taking into account issues of comparability and harmonisation between EU Member States. As a basis for a high degree of comparability, a common questionnaire covering the three sections was prepared. No deviation was allowed except those resulting from cultural differences and the data collection method used (adaptations were needed in case of telephone or web-based interviews). Eurostat checked the consistency and integrity of the microdata so that a minimum output quality standard was reached. In addition, data were accompanied by national quality reports stating the accuracy and reliability of the data. The coverage of the EHSIS limits its completeness in a number of ways, most notably in that it excludes children (under the age of 15) and people living in collective households and in institutions. As such it does not provide information on disabled children, and the data for persons aged 15 and over are biased in so far as the prevalence of disability in collective households and in institutions is different from that in private households. '''Coverage errors''' A failure to include all members from the target population in the sampling frame is likely to yield a coverage error. A variety of sampling frames were employed across countries. Population registers were used in 11 countries, random digit dialling (RDD) and list-assisted RDD was used in 10 countries, and area probability samples were drawn in the remaining seven countries. In 18 countries, the sampling frame was updated during the year of the survey data collection (2012); in seven countries (the Czech Republic, Estonia, Spain, Italy, Cyprus, Lithuania and Malta) the frame was a year older. Older frames were used in Greece and Portugal (both 2001), as well as in Romania (2004). '''Use of proxy interviews''' Since many of the questions in the EHSIS interview are subjective and rely on respondent’s own assessment of their situation, proxy interviews — in other words, when someone else answers on behalf of the interviewee — were permissible only when the sampled person was severely impaired. '''Unit response rates''' Traditionally, face-to-face surveys yield the highest response rates, followed by telephone surveys, mail and web surveys. One caveat in the calculation of response rates for EHSIS is that they do not account for cases with unknown eligibility. As such, in telephone surveys for example, ‘ring-no-answer’ cases are probably included in the denominator (number of eligible units), even though it is unknown whether these are business lines, or numbers that not working for other reasons. This might explain the remarkably low response rates for telephone surveys, in particular when using the ‘random digit dialling’ method for selecting the sample (in such cases, the response rates were below 20 %). In most countries, the main reason for non-response was refusal to take part in the interview. In only 10 Member States (Belgium, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Portugal, Romania, Finland and Sweden), the main reason for non-response was failure to contact the selected sampled person. The extent to which refusals and non-contacts are systematically different from those interviewed in the EHSIS on disability-related measures may introduce bias in the estimates reported by country. Most countries used post-stratification to adjust for non-response. ===Data dissemination=== '''Published data''' Statistical data from the EHSIS are available in two formats. [[Disability_statistics_background_-_European_health_and_social_integration_survey#See also|Statistics Explained articles]] provide data and analysis, while Eurobase provides a set of multi-dimensional [[Disability_statistics_background_-_European_health_and_social_integration_survey#Database|databases]]. Disseminated EHSIS data are normally analysed by age and/or sex and often by other dimensions, including: labour status, educational attainment level, income quintile and household type. Most of the published EHSIS data are focused on disabled people. However, some of the data are concerned with people reporting a long-standing health problem or limitations in basic activities, personal care activities or household activities, regardless of whether they are disabled or not. '''Time coverage''' The data available from the EHSIS refer to 2012. '''Units''' All indicators are published in Eurostat’s databases as the number of people, while the Statistics Explained articles concerning EHSIS data also present data as percentages, for example the percentage of disabled people in the population, or the percentage of disabled people with specific socio-demographic characteristics. '''Timing of data release''' The data from the EHSIS were disseminated in May 2015. ===See also=== '''Online publications''' *[[Disability_statistics|Disability statistics]] *[[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] '''Other background articles related to the methodology of disability statistics''' *[[European_health_interview_survey_-_methodology|European health interview survey - methodology]] *[[Health_variables_in_SILC_-_methodology|Health variables in SILC - methodology]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/database Health (hlth)], see: : Disability (hlth_dsb) ===Dedicated section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/overview Health] ===Methodology / Metadata=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/hlth_dsb_prve_esms.htm European health and social integration survey (EHSIS)] (ESMS metadata file — hlth_dsb_prve_esms) *The [https://circabc.europa.eu/w/browse/3d77833d-9d3d-4311-ab4c-9393cd076a73 EHSIS questionnaire interviewer instructions] contain a model questionnaire *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/disability/data List of data sources] ===External links=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=756&langId=en&moreDocuments=yes European Commission — Directorate-General for Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion — Social protection and social inclusion — EU social indicators] *[http://ec.europa.eu/health/indicators/echi/list/ European Commission — Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety — Public health — ECHI — European Core Health Indicators] *[http://ec.europa.eu/health/indicators/policy/index_en.htm European Commission — Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety — Public health — Indicators — Policy] *[http://www.who.int/classifications/icf/en/ International classification of functioning, disability and health (ICF)] ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Disability_statistics_background_-_European_health_and_social_integration_survey'' {{Unit|topic=X_Disability}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Disability statistics background -
