title: EU international trade in transport services
text:
The EU International trade in services shows the transactions between residents and non-residents. Data extracted in February 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 Sea transport was the biggest contributor to EU international trade in transport services between 2010 and 2024, accounting for about half of the total transport services, for both exports and imports. The United States was the EU's main trading partner in transport services in 2024, accounting for about 17.8% of EU exports and 16.0% of EU imports. The role of trade in services in [[Glossary:EU-27|(EU)]] has increased steadily over the past decade and continues to gain importance in an increasingly interconnected and globalised economy. Services account for a growing share of the EU’s external trade, reflecting the structural transformation of advanced economies towards knowledge and network based activities. [[EU international trade in transport services#Context|International trade in services]] statistics record transactions between residents and non-residents, in accordance with the Extended Balance of Payments Services Classification ([https://web-archive.oecd.org/2014-06-16/308081-EBOPS-2010.pdf EBOPS 2010]), which distinguishes 12 main service categories. In 2024, ‘Transport services’ remained one of the largest components of the EU’s [[Glossary:Extra-EU|extra-EU]] trade in services. It accounted for 16.5% of total extra-EU services [[Glossary:Export|exports]] and 16.2% of total extra-EU services [[Glossary:Import|imports]], confirming its position among the top three service categories. The largest category continued to be ‘Other business services’, which is analysed separately. This article examines the structure and recent developments of the EU’s extra-EU trade in transport services. Transport services are subdivided into 4 main components as defined by the [http://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/bop/2007/bopman6.htm Balance of Payments Manual 6 (BPM6) par. 10.74]: ‘Sea transport’, ‘Air transport’, ‘Other modes of transport’ (including rail, road and inland waterways), and ‘Postal and courier services’. In 2024, sea transport continued to represent the largest share of EU transport services exports, reflecting the EU’s central role in global maritime logistics and container shipping. Air transport showed further recovery and stabilisation following the strong rebound observed in 2022 and 2023, supported by the normalisation of passenger traffic and sustained demand for air cargo. Trade in other modes of transport expanded more moderately, in line with developments in cross-border land transport and regional value chains. Postal and courier services maintained steady growth, underpinned by the continued expansion of e-commerce and digital trade. Overall, the performance of transport services in 2024 points to a stabilisation phase after the volatility experienced during the pandemic and the subsequent energy and supply chain shocks. The EU maintained a broadly balanced position in extra-EU transport services trade, with exports and imports evolving at similar rates. The sustained importance of transport services in the EU’s external trade highlights their strategic relevance for economic competitiveness, resilience and connectivity. Looking ahead, the outlook for EU transport services trade will depend on global economic conditions, geopolitical developments and progress in the green and digital transitions. Continued monitoring of structural trends and policy coordination at EU level will be key to ensuring that transport services remain a competitive and resilient pillar of the EU’s external trade. === General overview === Figure 1 presents the time series for the EU’s extra-EU trade in transport services over the period 2010–2024. Throughout the entire period, exports of transport services exceeded imports, resulting in a continuous surplus for the European Union. Between 2010 and 2019, exports of transport services showed an overall upward trend, with only two annual declines: in 2013 (-3.0% compared with the previous year) and in 2016 (-5.2%). From 2017 to 2019, exports increased each year. In 2020, exports fell sharply by 16.6%, reflecting the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and the associated containment measures, which severely disrupted international passenger and freight transport. A strong rebound was observed in 2021 (+38.5%), followed by a further substantial increase in 2022 (+42.1%), when exports reached a peak of approximately €313.7 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] — the highest level recorded over the observed period. In 2023, exports declined by 20.4%, mainly due to lower receipts from sea transport services, yet remained at the third highest level in period 2010-2024. In 2024, exports stabilised and recorded a moderate increase compared with 2023, supported by a partial recovery in maritime freight rates and continued growth in air transport services. Despite remaining below the 2022 peak, export values stayed well above pre-pandemic levels. Imports followed a broadly similar pattern. In 2020, imports decreased by 11.8%, a smaller contraction than that observed for exports. In 2021 and 2022, imports rebounded strongly (+34.2% and +38.6%, respectively), reaching a peak of around €241 billion in 2022. In 2023, imports declined by 11.8%, largely driven by lower sea transport payments, but still recorded the third highest value during the observed period 2010-2024. 2024 data indicate a moderate increase in imports compared with 2023, reflecting improved trade flows and stabilising transport prices. As in previous years, imports remained below exports, maintaining the EU’s surplus in transport services trade. Overall, the sharp contraction in 2020 and the strong rebound in 2021–2022 underline the sensitivity of transport services to global shocks and price developments, particularly in maritime shipping. The correction observed in 2023 and the stabilisation in 2024 suggest a gradual normalisation of market conditions after the exceptional volatility linked to the pandemic and subsequent supply chain disruptions. The persistent surplus in transport services highlights the EU’s structural strength in international transport activities, notably in maritime and air transport. However, the pronounced cyclical fluctuations observed since 2020 demonstrate the sector’s exposure to global demand conditions, freight rate volatility and geopolitical developments. [[Image:F01-ITSS_TR-data_2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: EU trade in transport services with extra EU, 2010-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3a7a6e3e-5a1d-44f2-9273-87c607d97e2e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T08:37:16Z bop_its6_det])|alt=line graph with three lines on EU trade in transport services with extra from 2010 to 2024 in euro billion. The lines show exports, imports and balance.]] Figures 2 and 3 present the breakdown of extra-EU trade in transport services by main sub-category over the period 2010–2024. The four sub-categories considered are sea transport, air transport, other modes of transport (rail, road and inland waterways) and postal and courier services. Throughout the entire period, sea transport accounted for the largest share of both exports and imports, reaching the highest shares in 2021 for exports 62.1% and for imports 51.6%. In 2023, sea transport represented 50.8% of total extra-EU transport services exports and 44.3% of imports. In 2024, its share increased slightly for both flows, reflecting the continued normalisation of maritime freight rates compared with the exceptionally high levels recorded in 2021 and 2022. Nevertheless, sea transport remained the dominant component of EU transport services trade. Air transport constituted the second largest sub-category. In 2023 and 2024, it accounted for 27.7% of exports and 28.8% (in 2023) and 29.7% (in 2024) of imports. In 2024, the relative importance of air transport increased marginally, supported by further recovery in international passenger traffic and sustained demand for air cargo services. Other modes of transport represented 16.5% of exports and 22.7% of imports in 2023. In 2024, their shares recorded slight decline. Postal and courier services accounted for the smallest share of transport services trade, with 5.0% of exports and 4.2% of imports in 2023. In 2024, their contribution declined marginally, although the continued growth in e-commerce and cross-border parcel deliveries, the postal and courier services overall weight in total transport services trade remained limited. Overall, the structure of EU transport services trade remained relatively stable over time, with sea and air transport jointly accounting for more than 75% of total exports and imports for the observed period 2010-2024. However, the period 2020–2024 highlighted the sensitivity of sea transport to global price cycles and demand fluctuations, while air transport showed a gradual recovery following the pandemic-related collapse in passenger traffic. The persistent dominance of sea and air transport underlines the EU’s strong integration into global maritime and aviation networks. At the same time, the concentration of trade in these two sub-sectors increases exposure to global shocks, freight rate volatility and geopolitical tensions affecting major shipping routes and air corridors. [[Image:F02-ITSS_TR-data_2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Contribution of sea, air, other modes of transport and postal and courier services to EU exports to non-member countries, 2010-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9f1970a3-1ef9-4e8a-9a16-3c8f358182f5?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T08:50:18Z bop_its6_det])|alt=A stacked bar chart on the contribution of sea, air, other modes of transport and postal and courier services to EU exports to non-member countries from 2010 to 2024 in euro billion. The bars show sea transport, air transport, other modes of transport and postal and courier services]]
[[Image:F03-ITSS_TR-data_2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Contribution of sea, air, other modes of transport and postal and courier services to EU imports from non-member countries, 2010-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/da44da19-8119-4ffc-a74e-c69924831de3?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T08:53:03Z bop_its6_det])|alt=a stacked bar chart on the contribution of sea, air, other modes of transport and postal and courier services to EU imports from non-member countries, from 2010 to 2024 in euro billion. The bars show sea transport, air transport, other modes of transport and postal and courier services.]] Figure 4 shows the main extra-EU partners of the European Union in trade in transport services in 2024. In 2024, the United States was the EU’s largest partner for exports of transport services, accounting for 17.8% of total extra-EU exports. It was followed by the United Kingdom (13.7%) and Switzerland (8.3%). Together, these three partners represented about 40% of the EU’s extra-EU transport services exports. Overall, the geographical structure of exports show limited changes over time, confirming the strong transatlantic and European orientation of EU transport services trade. With regard to imports, the United States also ranked first in 2024, accounting for 16.0% of total extra-EU imports of transport services. The United Kingdom followed with 10.8%, while China (except Hong Kong) ranked third with 7.6%. Overall, the EU’s trade in transport services remains concentrated among a limited number of major partners, reflecting the scale of transatlantic trade, the proximity and economic integration with the United Kingdom and Switzerland, and the importance of China in global shipping and supply chains. The prominence of the United States and the United Kingdom in both exports and imports highlights the strategic importance of stable and predictable trade relations with these partners. At the same time, the role of China underlines the EU’s exposure to developments in global maritime transport and Asian supply chains. [[Image:F04-ITSS_TR-data_2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Main trading partners' share of EU exports and imports of transport services, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/85c126e8-419f-45c3-a414-615a368dd081?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T08:58:02Z bop_its6_det])|alt=two pie charts on the main trading partners' share of EU exports and imports of transport services in 2024. One pie chart shows exports and one pie chart shows imports]] === Sea transport === Sea transportAccording to [https://unstats.un.org/unsd/publication/Seriesm/seriesM_86Rev1e.pdf MSITS] par. 3.83 covers international freight and passenger transport services provided by seagoing vessels. Cruise fares are excluded (recorded under travel), as is transport through underwater pipelines (included under pipeline transport). Figure 5 illustrates the development of the EU’s extra-EU trade in sea transport services over the period 2010–2024. Throughout the entire period, exports exceeded imports, resulting in a persistent trade surplus for the European Union. Over the longer term, sea transport displayed marked cyclical movements. In 2016, both exports and imports declined significantly (by 11.1% and 6.0%, respectively). Between 2017 and 2019, both flows increased continuously. In 2020, exports fell by 6.7% and imports by 5.7%, reflecting the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on global trade and shipping activity. A pronounced rebound followed in 2021 and 2022. In 2021, exports rose by 55.7% and imports by 41.3%. Growth continued in 2022, when exports increased by 41.5% and imports by 34.1%, reaching historically high levels. This surge was closely linked to exceptional increases in global freight rates and supply chain disruptions. In 2023, both exports and imports decreased sharply (by 34.6% and 21.9%, respectively), as maritime freight rates normalised and global trade growth slowed. Transaction values returned to levels close to those recorded in 2021, though remaining above pre-pandemic levels. 2024 data indicate a stabilisation of sea transport trade. Exports recorded a moderate increase compared with 2023, while imports rose slightly, reflecting more stable freight rates and a gradual recovery in trade volumes. Despite remaining below the 2022 peak, sea transport continued to account for the largest share of the EU’s transport services trade and to generate a substantial surplus. The evolution of sea transport services over the period 2020–2024 highlights the strong sensitivity of the sector to global economic conditions, freight rate volatility and disruptions in supply chains. The exceptional peak in 2022, followed by a correction in 2023 and stabilisation in 2024, underlines the cyclical nature of maritime markets. [[Image:F05-ITSS_TR-data_2024.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Evolution of sea transport services trade for the EU, 2010-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/770263ef-792e-49a2-b092-5fc1c5ffbe0d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T09:00:09Z bop_its6_det])|alt= a triple line graph on the evolution of sea transport services trade for the EU from 2010 to 2024 in euro billion. The lines show exports, imports and balance.]] Figure 6 presents the main extra-EU partners of the European Union in sea transport services trade for 2024. In 2024, the United States was again the EU’s largest partner for sea transport services. It accounted for 16.3% of total extra-EU exports and 13.1% of total extra-EU imports. For exports, China (except Hong Kong) ranked second, with a share of 10.8%, followed by Singapore (6.9%). For imports, China was the second largest partner (8.8%), slightly ahead of Singapore (7.7%). This distribution reflects the importance of transpacific trade routes and major global shipping hubs in Asia for EU maritime services. Overall, the geographical structure of the EU’s sea transport services trade remains concentrated among a limited number of large economies and global shipping hubs. This concentration mirrors the structure of global merchandise trade and the strategic importance of major maritime routes. The strong role of the United States, China and Singapore in the EU’s sea transport services trade underlines the EU’s deep integration into global maritime networks. At the same time, this concentration exposes the sector to developments affecting key trade corridors and international shipping markets. [[Image:F06-ITSS_TR-data_2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Main trading partners' share of EU exports and imports of sea transport services, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/44362a87-179d-4228-94c2-374ac8198559?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T09:01:33Z bop_its6_det])|alt=two pie charts on the main trading partners' share of EU exports and imports of sea transport services in 2024. One pie chart shows exports and one pie chart shows imports.]] === Air transport === Air transportAccording to [https://unstats.un.org/unsd/publication/Seriesm/seriesM_86Rev1e.pdf MSITS] par. 3.84 covers all international freight and passenger transport services provided by aircraft. Over the period 2010–2024, exports of air transport services from the European Union consistently exceeded imports, resulting in a positive trade balance throughout the entire time series (Figure 7). Between 2010 and 2019, exports followed a generally upward trend. In contrast, imports showed moderate year-to-year fluctuations but remained broadly stable up to 2019. In 2020, both flows contracted sharply because of the COVID-19 pandemic and the associated travel restrictions. Exports declined by 49.0%, while imports fell by 36.2%. The values recorded in 2020 were the lowest observed over the period 2010–2024. In 2021, a partial recovery took place, with exports increasing by 19.5% and imports by 17.5%. However, both flows remained well below their pre-pandemic levels. A strong rebound followed in 2022: exports rose by 75.3% and imports by 70.4%, surpassing their 2019 levels, driven by the resumption of international passenger traffic and sustained air cargo demand. In 2023, air transport was the only sub-category of transport services to continue expanding, with exports increasing by 6.3% and imports by 9.4%, reflecting the ongoing recovery of long-haul travel and further normalisation of global mobility. 2024 data indicate continued, albeit more moderate, growth in both exports and imports of air transport services. Passenger volumes approached or exceeded pre-pandemic levels on most major routes, while air freight activity stabilised. As a result, trade values reached new highs in nominal terms, consolidating the EU’s surplus in air transport services. The evolution of air transport services over the past decade illustrates both the sector’s vulnerability to global mobility restrictions and its capacity for rapid recovery once conditions normalise. The sharp contraction in 2020, followed by a strong rebound in 2022 and sustained growth in 2023 and 2024, highlights the cyclical and demand-sensitive nature of aviation. [[Image:F07-ITSS_TR-data_2024.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Evolution of air transport services trade for EU, 2010-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2f806aef-6a82-4c4a-81a4-23a46e76856b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T09:02:28Z bop_its6_det])|alt= a triple line graph on the evolution of air transport services trade for EU, from 2010 to 2024 in euro billion. The lines show exports, imports and balance.]] Figure 8 shows the main extra-EU partners of the European Union in air transport services trade for 2024. In 2024, the United States remained the EU’s largest partner for air transport services, accounting for 27.8% of total extra-EU exports and 18.1% of total extra-EU imports. The prominence of the United States reflects the scale of transatlantic passenger and cargo flows. The United Kingdom ranked second, with 18.9% of exports and 11.4% of imports. Despite its status as a non-EU country, the United Kingdom continues to play a central role in European air connectivity. Among other partners, Switzerland was the third largest destination for EU exports of air transport services (4.4%), while China (except Hong Kong) ranked third for imports (6.6%), underlining the importance of long-haul intercontinental routes and the progressive recovery of passenger services on Asian routes. Overall, the geographical structure of EU air transport services trade remains highly concentrated, with the United States and the United Kingdom jointly accounting for nearly half of exports and a substantial share of imports. The strong concentration of air transport services trade with a limited number of partners highlights the strategic importance of stable and predictable aviation relations, particularly across the Atlantic and with neighbouring European countries. [[Image:F08-ITSS_TR-data_2024.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Main trading partners' share of EU exports and imports of air transport services, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/75ffb32a-2f0b-4bec-a1bd-f99f1d3e92e2?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T09:03:25Z bop_its6_det])|alt=two pie charts on the main trading partners' share of EU exports and imports of air transport services in 2024. One pie chart shows exports and one pie chart shows imports.]] === Other modes of transport === Other modes of transport services comprise all transport services other than sea and air. They include space transport, rail transport, road transport, inland waterway transport, pipeline transport, electricity transmission and other supporting and auxiliary transport services (i.e. services that cannot be allocated to sea or air transport). Figure 9 presents the development of extra-EU trade in other modes of transport over the period 2010–2024. During the observed period, exports and imports fluctuated, with imports exceeding exports in several years. A negative balance was recorded in 2010 and again from 2018 onwards, indicating a structural deficit in this sub-category in recent years. Compared with sea and air transport, the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 was more limited. Exports increased by 8.4% and imports by 4.0%, reflecting the essential role of road, rail and pipeline transport in maintaining cross-border supply chains within Europe and with neighbouring countries. In 2021 and 2022, trade expanded markedly. Imports recorded their highest annual increase in 2021 (+40.3%), while exports grew most strongly in 2022 (+20.7%). These developments were partly linked to higher energy prices, increased pipeline and electricity transmission transactions, and the recovery of land-based freight transport. In 2023, exports decreased slightly (-1.1%) and imports more substantially (-12.8%), yet both flows remained at the second highest levels observed over the period 2010–2024. 2024 data indicate broadly stable developments. Exports and imports recorded a decrease compared with 2023 (-4.3% and -0.2%). Despite this stabilisation, imports continued to exceed exports, maintaining a negative balance in this category. The relatively moderate volatility observed in other modes of transport highlights their stabilising role within overall transport services trade. In particular, road, rail and pipeline transport proved more resilient during the pandemic than sea and air transport. At the same time, the persistent deficit since 2018 points to structural dependencies, notably in energy-related transport services. [[Image:Evolution of other modes of transport services trade for EU, 2010-2024 (€ billion) Version 9.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: Evolution of other modes of transport services trade for EU, 2010-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4786bf8a-2611-46e7-b647-4c93960453d9?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T09:04:31Z bop_its6_det])|alt= a triple line graph on the evolution of other modes of transport services trade for EU, from 2010 to 2024 in euro billion. The lines show in euro 1000 million exports, in euro 1000 million imports and in euro 1000 million balance.]] Figure 10 presents the main extra-EU partners of the European Union in trade in other modes of transport services for 2024. In 2024, the United Kingdom was the EU’s largest partner in this sub-category, accounting for 30.2% of extra-EU exports and 21.1% of imports. The strong position of the United Kingdom reflects the high intensity of cross-Channel road and rail transport, as well as energy-related flows. Switzerland ranked second, with 23.0% of exports and 13.5% of imports. Its prominent role is linked to its geographical proximity and its integration in European land transport networks. The United States was the third largest partner, accounting for 7.9% of exports and 13.2% of imports. Trade with the United States in this category mainly relates to pipeline transport, electricity transmission and auxiliary transport services. Overall, the geographical structure of trade in other modes of transport services is more concentrated in neighbouring European countries than in the case of sea and air transport, reflecting the regional nature of land-based and energy transport networks. The predominance of the United Kingdom and Switzerland underlines the importance of close regulatory cooperation and efficient border management for land transport services. [[Image:F10-ITSS_TR-data_2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 10: Main trading partners' share of EU exports and imports of other modes of transport services, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/11d75763-18ea-4171-a707-265da536078f?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T09:05:32Z bop_its6_det])|alt= two pie charts on the main trading partners' share of EU exports and imports of other modes of transport services in 2024. One pie chart shows exports and one pie chart shows imports.]] === Postal and courier services === Postal and courier servicesAccording to the [http://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/bop/2007/bopman6.htm Balance of Payments Manual 6 (BPM6) par. 10.82] cover the collection, transport and delivery of letters, newspapers, periodicals, brochures, other printed matter, parcels and packages, including post office courier and mailbox rental services. Figure 11 presents the evolution of extra-EU postal and courier services trade over the period 2010–2024. Between 2010 and 2013, both exports and imports were largely stable. In 2014, trade recorded a sharp increase, with exports rising by 188% and imports by 89.8%, reflecting the rapid expansion of cross-border e-commerce and parcel delivery services. Between 2015 and 2019, export and import transactions remained relatively stable. From 2020 to 2022, postal and courier services experienced significant growth, driven by increased demand for e-commerce deliveries during the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent recovery period. In 2023, values decreased slightly, by 3.5% for exports and by 4.2% for imports, reflecting a modest normalisation after the pandemic-related surge. The balance of postal and courier services trade was negative until 2013 but has remained positive since 2014, indicating that EU providers have maintained a competitive position in the global market for postal and courier services. 2024 data suggest a modest continued increase in imports and slight decrease in exports, supported by sustained cross-border e-commerce activity and improved logistics services. Overall, the sub-category remains the smallest contributor to total transport services but continues to exhibit steady growth and resilience. The evolution of postal and courier services highlights the growing importance of e-commerce and logistics in the EU’s external trade. Despite being the smallest sub-category of transport services, it demonstrates strong potential for further expansion. [[Image:Evolution of postal and courier transport services trade for EU, 2010-2024 (€ billion) version 1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 11: Evolution of postal and courier services trade for EU, 2010-2024 (€ billion)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b99ab096-50e3-4eba-b03b-5f59483bc0c5?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T09:06:44Z bop_its6_det]) |alt=a triple line graph on the evolution of postal and courier services trade for EU from 2010 to 2024 in euro billion. The lines show exports, imports and balance.]] Figure 12 presents the main extra-EU partners of the European Union in postal and courier services trade for 2024. In 2024, the United Kingdom was the EU’s largest export partner, accounting for 15.5% of total extra-EU exports of postal and courier services. It was followed by Hong Kong with 13.9%. and China (except Hong Kong) with 13.5%. These shares highlight the importance of both European and Asian trade hubs in supporting EU providers’ international deliveries. For imports, the United States was the dominant partner, accounting for 48.1% of total extra-EU imports. The United Kingdom followed with 14.4%, and Switzerland ranked third with 4.8%. The prominence of the United States reflects the scale of e-commerce and parcel delivery flows from North America to the EU. Trade in postal and courier services is strongly shaped by cross-border e-commerce and global parcel flows. The concentration of exports in the United Kingdom and Asia, and of imports in the United States, underscores the importance of major trade hubs and established logistics networks. Targeted investment and regulatory support in postal and courier services will help the EU capitalise on the growth of global e-commerce while maintaining efficiency, sustainability, and resilience in international logistics. [[Image:F12-ITSS_TR-data_2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 12: Main trading partners' share of EU exports and imports of postal and courier services, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/90fd78be-c18f-4650-a229-fe387aea65ef?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T09:07:39Z bop_its6_det])|alt=two pie charts on the main trading partners' share of EU exports and imports of postal and courier services in 2024. One pie chart shows exports and one pie chart shows imports.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=EU international trade in transport services_2024.xlsx|title=EU international trade in transport services - graphs and tables}} === Data sources=== EU statistics on transport services trade are drawn from the Eurostat reference database on international trade in services. The data are compiled in accordance with the sixth edition of the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (BPM6), the current international methodology for balance of payments statistics. Data are updated annually and are available from 2010 onwards for EU aggregates, all EU Member States, and non-EU countries, ([[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]], [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]], and other trading partners. Pre-2010 data are also available in the Eurostat reference database, and are prepared according to the previous BPM5 methodology. Statistics on extra-EU trade are calculated as the sum of transactions conducted by the 27 EU Member States and the EU institutions (excluding the [[Glossary:European_Central_Bank_(ECB)|European Central Bank]] and the European Stability Mechanism) with countries outside the EU. Intra-EU flows are not included. ===Definition and classification of transport services=== TransportAs defined by the [http://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/bop/2007/bopman6.htm Balance of Payments Manual 6 (BPM6) par. 10.74] refer to the carriage of people and goods from one location to another, including related supporting and auxiliary services. Transport can be classified according to: # [[Glossary:Mode_of_transport|mode of transport]] and # What is carried. The transport services category can be further divided into 4 sub-categoriesAs defined by the [http://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/bop/2007/bopman6.htm Balance of Payments Manual 6 (BPM6) par. 10.74] , namely: * Sea transport * Air transport * Other modes of transport (including rail, road, inland waterways, space transport, pipeline transport, electricity transmission, and other supporting services) * Postal and courier services. In the case of passenger transport, international trade in transport services covers all services provided by resident carriers to [[Glossary:non-resident|non-residents]] and by non-resident carriers to residents. However, the transport of travellers (non-residents) themselves is classified under travel services in international trade statistics, not under transport. In the case of freight, transport services include all international transport of a country’s exports and imports of goods. This comprises: * Freight services provided by resident operators on the compiling economy’s exports within the customs frontier of the exporting economy (recorded as exports of freight services), and * Freight services provided by non-resident operators within the compiling economy on its exports (recorded as imports of freight services). This methodology ensures that trade in transport services captures the full scope of economic activity associated with the international carriage of goods and passengers, while remaining consistent with international statistical standards. === Context === International trade in services forms a key component of the current account of the balance of payments and records transactions between residents and non-residents of a country over a given period. These statistics are compiled in accordance with the sixth edition of the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (BPM6), which distinguishes 12 main service categories, including transport services. Over the period 2010–2024, European Union trade in services with non-EU countries showed a sustained upward trend for both exports and imports. This reflects the increasing integration of the EU economy into global markets and the growing importance of services in international trade. The continued expansion in trade in services, particularly in transport, underscores the strategic role of connectivity, logistics, and mobility in supporting the EU’s external economic relations and overall competitiveness. Some implications: * The long-term growth trend highlights the importance of monitoring structural changes in service trade, including shifts between transport, travel, and other service sub-sectors. * Reliable, harmonised data are essential for assessing the EU’s balance of payments, identifying trade surpluses or deficits, and informing policy decisions aimed at enhancing competitiveness and resilience. * The increasing role of services trade supports the need for policies that facilitate digitalisation, sustainability, and efficient cross-border service provision. ===Conclusions and policy considerations=== The availability of harmonised, annual transport services data since 2010 provides a reliable basis for monitoring the EU’s external connectivity and trade performance. Key policy considerations include: * Supporting data-driven policy-making, using harmonised statistics to identify trends, trade imbalances, and structural dependencies across transport sub-sectors. * Strengthening the resilience of transport networks, informed by trends in sea, air, land, and postal services trade. * Aligning transport and trade policies with sustainability objectives, using detailed statistics to guide the green transition in international transport services. * Enhancing international cooperation and regulatory alignment, leveraging robust trade data to negotiate agreements and facilitate interoperability across borders. Accurate and consistent transport services statistics are essential for assessing the EU’s position in global trade, designing effective transport, e-commerce and digitalisation policies, and supporting strategic decision-making at both EU and Member State levels. === Other articles === *[[:Category:Balance_of_payments|All articles on balance of payments]] *[[Balance of payments and international investment position manual (BPM6)]] *[[Measuring international trade in services - from BPM5 to BPM6]] *[[Services trade by enterprise characteristics - STEC]] *[[EU international trade in other business services]] *[[International trade in services]] *[[Services trade statistics by modes of supply]] *[[International Trade in Services statistics - background]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-services/database International trade in services, geographical breakdown (bop_its6)] === Thematic section === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-services/overview International trade in services - Overview] *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=balance_of_payments}} Balance of payments] === Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=bop_6_esms|title=Balance of payments - International transactions (BPM6)}} (ESMS metadata file — bop_6_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=bop_its6_esms|title=International trade in services, geographical breakdown (BPM6)}} (ESMS metadata file — bop_its6_esms) === Legislation === *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32005R0184:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 184/2005}} of 12 January 2005 on Community statistics concerning balance of payments, international trade in services and foreign direct investment. ([https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/LSU/?uri=CELEX:32005R0184 Summary]) *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012R0555:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 555/2012}} of 22 June 2012 amending Regulation (EC) No 184/2005 on Community statistics concerning balance of payments, international trade in services and foreign direct investment, as regards the update of data requirements and definitions. *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32016R1013:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 2016/1013}} of 8 June 2016 amending Regulation (EC) No 184/2005 on Community statistics concerning balance of payments, international trade in services and foreign direct investment. ===Visualisations === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=international_trade_in_services}} International trade in services - Statistics Illustrated] === External links === *[http://ec.europa.eu/trade/ European Commission — Trade] *[http://www.imf.org/external/np/sta/itserv/methdev.htm International Monetary Fund (IMF) — International Trade in Services: Recent Methodological Developments] *[http://unstats.un.org/unsd/tradeserv/TFSITS/newsletter.htm Newsletter of the Interagency Task Force on Statistics of International Trade in Services] *[http://www.oecd.org/trade/services-trade/ OECD — Services trade] *[http://unstats.un.org/unsd/tradeserv/TFSITS/manual.htm United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) — Manual on Statistics of International Trade in Services 2010 (MSITS 2010)] === Footnotes === <'''footnote text will be automatically inserted if reference tags are used in article content text (use reference icon on ribbon)'''> {{Unit|topic=X_International_trade_services}} [[Category:International trade|EU international trade in transport services]] [[Category:International trade in services|EU international trade in transport services]] [[Category:International trade in services by type of service|EU international trade in transport services]] [[Category:Statistical article|EU international trade in transport services]] [[Category:March2027|EU international trade in transport services]]

title: EU labour force survey - methodology
text:
<pdftheme>3</pdftheme>
<articlecontent>
<sesection>
=== Introduction ===
This [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] article describes the methodology of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union]] [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|labour force survey (EU-LFS)]] applicable until the 2020 data collection. It gives specific information on the concept of the labour force status and the definitions of the variables used until that year. 

The new methodology in force from the EU-LFS 2021 data collection onwards is described in the article  [[EU Labour Force Survey - new methodology from 2021 onwards]] 

Both articles are part of a '''[[EU labour force survey|set of online articles]]''' on the EU-LFS. 
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== EU-LFS concept of labour force status  ===

'''Definition of the labour force status'''

Labour force status is the cornerstone concept for labour market statistics. Accordingly, individuals are classified in three categories as [[Glossary:Employed person - LFS|employed]], [[Glossary:Unemployment|unemployed]] or [[Glossary:People_outside_the_labour_force|outside the labour force]]. These definitions are explained below. The definitions used in the EU-LFS follow the Resolution of the 13th International Conference of Labour Statisticians, convened in 1982 by the [[Glossary:ILO|International Labour Organisation]] (hereafter referred as the ‘ILO guidelines’). To further improve comparability within the EU, while remaining fully compatible with the ILO guidelines, {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32000R1897:EN:NOT|title=Regulation 1897/2000}}, gives a more precise definition of unemployment. 

'''''Employment (persons in employment):''''' 

Employed persons comprise persons aged 15 years and more who were in one of the following categories: 

*(a) persons who during the reference week worked for at least one hour for pay or profit or family gain.

*(b) persons who were not at work during the reference week but had a job or business from which they were temporarily absent. 

This definition is applicable to [[Glossary:Employee - LFS|employees]], self-employed persons and family workers. 
Pay includes cash payments or 'payment in kind'(payment in goods or services rather than money), whether payment was received in the week the work was done or not.  

Exceptions to the standard age group 15 years and more are: 16 years and more in Spain, Italy, Sweden (until 2001) and United Kingdom; 15 to 74 years in Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Hungary, Finland, Sweden (2001 onwards) and Norway (2006 onwards); 16-74 in Iceland and Norway (until 2005).

For further details and treatment of borderline cases (like seasonal workers, lay-offs, unpaid family workers, employment in activities for own-consumption, vocational training, absences, etc.) see variable WSTATOR in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide].

'''''Unemployment:''''' 

Unemployed persons comprise persons aged 15 to 74 years who were:

*(1) not employed according to the definition of employment above;

*(2) currently available for work, i.e. were available for paid employment or self-employment before the end of the two weeks following the reference week;

*(3) actively seeking work, i.e. had taken specific steps in the four week period ending with the reference week to seek paid employment or self-employment or who found a job to start later, i.e. within a period of at most three months from the end of the reference week.

For the purposes of point (3), the following are considered as specific steps:

:*a) having been in contact with a public employment office to find work, whoever took the initiative (renewing registration for administrative reasons only is not an active step),

:*b) having been in contact with a private agency (temporary work agency, firm specialising in recruitment, etc.) to find work,

:*c) applying to employers directly,

:*d) asking among friends, relatives, unions, etc., to find work,

:*e) placing or answering job advertisements,

:*f) studying job advertisements,

:*g) taking a recruitment test or examination or being interviewed,

:*h) looking for land, premises or equipment,

:*i) applying for permits, licenses or financial resources.

Education and training are considered as ways of improving employability but not as methods of seeking work. 

*Persons without work and in education or training will only be classified as unemployed if they are ‘currently available for work’ and ‘seeking work’, as defined in points (2) and (3). 

*During the off-season, seasonal workers cannot be considered as having a formal attachment to their high-season job because they do not continue to receive a wage or salary from their employer although they may have an assurance of return to work. If they are not at work during the off-season, they are classified as unemployed only if they are ‘currently available for work’ and ‘seeking work’, as defined in points (2) and (3).

Exceptions to the standard age group 15 to 74 are: 16 to 74 years in Spain, Italy, Sweden (until 2000), United Kingdom, Norway (until 2005) and Iceland.

Before 2001 unemployment results used to refer to persons aged 15 years and more. 

For further details, see variables WSTATOR, SEEKWORK, AVAILBLE and METHODA to METHODM in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS user guide and the EU-LFS explanatory notes].

'''''Labour force:''''' 

The labour force, formerly called active population, is the population employed or unemployed.

'''''People outside the labour force:''''' 

People outside the labour force, formerly called economically inactive persons, are those who are neither employed nor unemployed.

'''''Derivation of the labour force status in the European Union labour force survey:''''' 

Given the complexity of the definitions of employment and unemployment above, and in order to achieve a measurement as objective as possible, EU-LFS respondents are not asked directly if they are employed, unemployed or outside the labour force. Instead, they are asked about their labour market behaviour in a certain reference week and then their labour status is derived according to the following derivation chart: 

[[Image:EU_LFS_CH3_METH.png|thumb|center|650px|Labour force classification in the EU-LFS]] 

For further details see derivation of the variable ILOSTAT in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide].

'''Indicators to supplement the unemployment rate''' 

In addition to the three labour statuses explained above (employment, unemployment, economic inactivity), there are three other important indicators of the labour situation:

*'''[[Glossary:Underemployed part-time worker|Underemployed part-time workers]]''' are persons aged 15-74 working part-time who wish to work additional hours and are available to do so. Part-time work is recorded as self-reported by individuals.

*'''[[Glossary:Person available to work but not seeking|Persons available to work but not seeking]]''' are persons aged 15-74 neither employed nor unemployed who want to work, are available for work in the next 2 weeks but are not seeking work. 

*'''[[Glossary:Person seeking work but not immediately available|Persons seeking work but not immediately available]]''' are the sum of persons aged 15-74 neither employed nor unemployed who: (1) are actively seeking work during the last 4 weeks but not available for work in the next 2 weeks; (2) found a job to start in less than 3 months and are not available for work in the next 2 weeks; (3) found a job to start in 3 months or more; (4) are passively seeking work during the last 4 weeks and are available for work in the next 2 weeks.
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Other concepts and definitions ===

The following list gives a short overview of other important concepts and definitions besides the labour force status used in the EU-LFS.
The reference document for the definitions of these variables is the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide]. They contain detailed information on the definition of each variable. 

'''Socio-demographic and geographic characteristics''' 

*'''Nationality:''' Nationality is interpreted as citizenship. Citizenship is defined according to national legislation of each country. For the reference definition, please consult the variable NATIONAL in [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide].

*'''Country of birth:''' For the purpose of this variable, current national boundaries should be considered rather than the boundaries at the time of the respondent's birth. For the reference definition, please consult the variable COUNTRYB [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide].

*'''Marital status:''' Marital status is the conjugal status of each individual in relation to the marriage laws of the country (i.e. de jure status). For the reference definition, please consult the variable MARSTAT in [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide].

*'''Dependent child:''' A child is defined as a household member aged less than 25 years and in full social and economic dependence from other household member/-s (parents/ adults). All household members aged below 15 are by default considered dependent, and hence 'children', whereas an additional check on the social and economic dependence is required for the household members aged between 15 and 24. For details, please consult the variable HHCOMP in [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide].

*'''Recent immigrants:'''Foreign born persons or persons with a nationality different to the country of residence who have been resident five years or less in the reporting country. For details, please consult the variable YEARESID in [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide].

*'''Degree of urbanisation:''' This is to classify the place of residence by 3 types of area: densely-populated, intermediate and thinly-populated. For reference, please consult the variable DEGURBA in [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide].

'''Educational attainment and participation in education and training'''

* The '''educational attainment level''' of an individual is the highest [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|ISCED (International standard classification of education)]] level successfully completed, the successful completion of an education programme being validated by a recognised qualification, i.e. a qualification officially recognised by the relevant national education authorities or recognised as equivalent to another qualification of formal education. In countries where education programmes, in particular those belonging to ISCED levels 1 and 2, do not lead to a qualification the criterion of full attendance of the programme and normally gaining access to a higher level of education may have to be used instead. When determining the highest level, both general and vocational education should be taken into consideration. For more detailed information see the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide] for the variables HATLEVEL, HATFIELD, HATYEAR.

* '''Participation in education and training''' covers participation in formal and non-formal education and training. The reference period for the participation in education and training is the four weeks prior to the interview. For more detailed information see the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide] for the variables EDUCSTAT and COURATT as well as the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Classifications classifications ISCED and CLA].

'''Employment - principal activities and professional status'''

*'''Economic activity:''' This is the economic activity of the estiblishment where the work is performed. For reference, please consult the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Classifications classification NACE].

*'''Occupation:''' For reference, please consult the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Classifications classification ISCO].

*'''Professional status:''' This is the classification of employed persons into employees, self-employed and unpaid family workers. For the reference definitions, please consult the variable STAPRO in [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide] as well as the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Classifications classification ICSE].

*'''Employees with fixed-term contracts:''' The concept of fixed-term contract is only applicable to employees, not to self-employed. In most of the [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU Member States]], a majority of jobs are based on written labour contracts. In some countries, however, contracts of this type are settled only in specific cases e.g. for public-sector jobs, apprentices or other trainees within an enterprise. Given these institutional discrepancies, the concepts of ‘temporary employment’ and ‘work contract of limited duration’ (or ‘permanent employment’ and ‘work contract of unlimited duration’) describe situations which, in different institutional contexts, may be considered similar. For the reference definitions, please consult the variable TEMP [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide] as well as the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Classifications classification ICSE].

'''Employment - Working time''' 

*'''Working time:''' The EU-LFS collects data on "number of hours usually worked per week" and "number of hours actually worked during the reference week". The number of hours usually worked per week comprises all hours including extra hours, either paid or unpaid, which the person normally works, but excludes the travelling time between home and workplace and the time taken for the main meal break (usually at lunchtime) are excluded. The number of hours actually worked during the reference week covers all hours including extra hours regardless of whether they were paid or not. For the reference definitions, please consult the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide] for the variables HWUSUAL and HWACTUAL.

*'''Atypical working time:''' The atypical work distinguishes between "evening or night work, "Saturday or Sunday working" and "shift work".

:*Evening and night work: Since the definitions of evening and night differ widely, it is not easy to establish a strictly uniform basis for all Member States. In general, however, ‘evening work’ is considered to be work done after usual working hours but before the usual hours of sleep in the Member State concerned. It implies the opportunity to sleep at normal times. ‘Night work’ is generally be regarded as work done during usual sleeping hours and implies abnormal sleeping times.

:*Saturday and Sunday working: This concept is interpreted strictly on the basis of formal agreements concluded with the employer.

:*Shift-work: The question of shift work applies only to employees. Shift work is a regular work schedule during which an enterprise is operational or provides services beyond the normal working hours from 8 am to 6 pm on weekdays (evening closing hours may be later in the case of a longer break at noon in some Member states).

:For the reference definitions, please consult the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide] for the variables SHIFTWK, EVENWK, NIGHTWK, SATWK and SUNWK.

*'''Full-time/part-time:''' This variable refers to the main job. The distinction between full-time and part-time work is generally based on a spontaneous response by the respondent. The main exceptions are the Netherlands and Iceland where a 35 hours threshold is applied, Sweden where a threshold is applied to the self-employed, and Norway where persons working between 32 and 36 hours are asked whether this is a full- or part-time position. 

*'''Involuntary part-time employment:''' This is when respondents report that they work part-time because they are unable to find full-time work. For the reference defintions, please consult the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide] for the variables FTPT and FTPTREAS.

*'''Total duration of temporary job or work contract of limited duration:''' This refers to the total of the time already elapsed plus the time remaining until the end of the contract. For the reference definitions, please consult the variable TEMPDUR in [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey_-_documentation&stable=0&redirect=no#Explanatory_notes_and_user_guide_for_the_core_variables EU-LFS explanatory notes and EU-LFS user guide].

'''Unemployment'''

*'''Long-term unemployment''' consists of unemployed persons aged 15-74 who are looking for a job for one year or more.
</sesection>

</articlecontent>

title: EU labour force survey - modules

=== Introduction === This [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] article describes the modules of the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|European Union Labour Force Survey (EU-LFS)]]. The aim of a module is to provide users with statistics on a specific topic concerning the [[Glossary:Labour_market|labour market]] by adding a set of variables to supplement the core EU-LFS. This article is part of a '''[[EU labour force survey|set of online articles]]''' on the EU-LFS. === Overview of the modules === Since 1999 an inherent part of the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|European Union Labour Force Survey (EU-LFS)]] are the modules. These were called "ad hoc modules" until 2020. From 2021 onwards they are named either "regular modules", when the variables have an 8 yearly periodicity, or "modules on an ad hoc subject" for variables not included in the regular data sets. The {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31998R0577:EN:NOT|title=Regulation 0577/1998}} of 9 March 1998 on the organisation of a labour force sample survey in the Community, in force until 2020, specified that a further set of variables may be added to supplement the information from the core questionnaire of the EU-LFS. The ad hoc modules were set by Commission regulation by group of 3 years. For details on the regulations for the ad hoc modules and their topics and description, please consult the article [[EU labour force survey – main features and legal basis | EU Labour Force Survey – Main features and legal basis]]. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.LI.2019.261.01.0001.01.ENG Regulation (EU) 2019/1700], also called the Integrated European Social Statistics Framework Regulation (IESS FR), and its [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2019.336.01.0059.01.ENG Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2240] for the labour force domain, which apply from 1 January 2021, define the regular data sets and the ad hoc subjects. Moreover, the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32020R0256&from=EN Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/256] establishing a multiannual rolling planning lists the topics to be collected from 2021 to 2028 for the 8 yearly variables and ad hoc subjects. For general information on the availability of microdata for researchers and information on publication guidelines for the module variables, please consult the article [[EU labour force survey – data
