title: Economic development in enlargement countries
text:
This article presents information from national accounts, as well as information on labour force and employment for the EU [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries and potential candidate]]. It covers Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Albania, Serbia, Türkiye and Kosovo and Ukraine. Data extracted in May 2026 Planned article update July 2027 Türkiye's economy remained by far the largest among the enlargement countries. Its GDP at current market prices was €1.4 trillion in 2025, corresponding to 7.5% of that of the EU. Ukraine had the second largest economy, with a GDP of €176.3 billion in 2024 (2025 data not available). Labour market conditions improved substantially across most enlargement countries between 2014 and 2024. Despite a temporary interruption during the COVID-19 pandemic, unemployment more than halved in North Macedonia and Serbia, while Türkiye's unemployment rate dropped to 8.8% in 2024 after peaking at 13.7% in 2019. Türkiye posted the highest FDI inflows among the enlargement countries, peaking at €7.8 billion in 2018. Serbia also strengthened its position, with inflows rising from €1.2 billion in 2014 to €4.3 billion in 2022, while North Macedonia exceeded €1 billion in 2024. [[image: CPC_unemployment rate_2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/02c71e84-9107-43ce-97a0-a4f8a0b0df5d?lang=en lfsa_urgan])|alt=Infographic showing the unemployment rates in the EU and the EU enlargement countries in 2024. Data for Moldova, Georgia, Albania, Ukraine and Kosovo are not available. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article is part of an [[Enlargement_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]] and provides information on a range of economic statistics for the [[Glossary:Candidate countries|enlargement countries]], compared with the corresponding data for the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. The data used in this article have all been submitted to and validated by Eurostat's subject matter units, following the same process as for the EU countries. For Georgia, data on the indicators presented in this article are not yet transmitted according to this process and are therefore not yet available. However, data on Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are also presented in the [[European_Neighbourhood_Policy_countries_-_statistical_overview|Statistics Explained articles for European Neighbourhood Policy - East]] countries; these articles are based on annual indicators supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country. The data managed by the National Bureau of Statistics of Moldova does not include data from the Transnistrian region over which the government of Moldova does not exercise control. Since 2014, data for Ukraine generally exclude the illegally annexed Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the City of Sevastopol and the territories which are not under control of the Ukrainian government. For Ukraine official statistics for 2022-2025 were not fully produced due to the martial law. It will gradually be produced and disseminated as defined by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine, taking into account the specific conditions of producing statistics during Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. This article presents key economic indicators for the period 2014–2025. Where a table or graph refers to a single reference year (for example, 2025), or where annual data are unavailable for certain countries, the most recent available data within the preceding five years are used. Especially when the end years are intended to be shown but the corresponding data series are not available, data from the closest possible years are presented instead (for example 2022–2024 instead of 2025). The analyses cover [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]] in euros and euros per capita at current market prices, along with growth in real GDP and the evolution of [[Glossary:Unemployment|unemployment statistics]]. It also includes data on [[Glossary:Gross fixed capital formation (GFCF)|gross fixed capital formation (GFCF)]], as well as [[Glossary:Foreign_direct_investment_(FDI)|foreign direct investments (FDI)]] flows from the balance of payments. ==Gross domestic product at current market prices== [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|Gross domestic product (GDP)]] is an aggregate measure of the size of an economy, based on its total final output. It is the standard measure of the value added created through the production of goods and services in a country during a certain period. GDP includes consumer spending, government spending, net exports, and total investments. GDP at current market prices can be used to compare the size of different economies when expressed in the same currency (for example, the Euro). However, comparisons should consider population size, differences in the cost of living and the effects of inflation. Gross domestic product at current market prices (nominal GDP) in 2025 places the European Union at 18 801.8 billion €, reflecting its substantially larger economic scale compared with the enlargement countries (Figure 1). Among the enlargement countries, Türkiye records the highest nominal GDP, at 1 406.2 billion €, followed by Ukraine with 176.3 billion € (2024 data), and Serbia with an estimated 88.7 billion €. Bosnia and Herzegovina reports 27.5 billion € (2024 data), ahead of Albania with 25.0 billion € (2024 provisional data) and Moldova with 18.0 billion € (provisional data), while North Macedonia reaches an estimated 16.9 billion €. KosovoThis designation is without prejudice to positions on status and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo Declaration of Independence. and Montenegro record the lowest levels, at 11.0 billion € and 8.2 billion € respectively, both based on provisional data. The distribution highlights the considerable differences in aggregate economic size between the EU and the enlargement countries, as well as the variation within the enlargement region itself. Türkiye accounts for by far the largest economy among the enlargement countries, while Bosnia and Herzegovina, Albania, Moldova, North Macedonia, Kosovo and Montenegro remain comparatively small in nominal terms. The presence of estimates, provisional figures and 2024 data as the most recent available for some countries should also be considered when comparing the latest available values. [[Image: CPC26_Gross domestic product at current market prices, 2025 (euro billion)_up.png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 1: Gross domestic product at current market prices, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a3e83e65-1e36-42d4-be76-431577061dda?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-26T06:39:36Z nama_10_gdp])|alt=Bar chart showing GDP at market prices in euro billions in the EU and the enlargement countries Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, Türkiye and Ukraine. Data not available for Georgia. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] == Gross domestic product per capita at current market prices== Analysis of nominal GDP per capita (per person) removes the effect of population size, facilitating comparisons between countries. Although GDP per capita at current market prices is influenced by price level changes (inflation), it provides a broad economic indicator that can be used for a basic assessment of living standards. Figure 2 shows substantial disparities in GDP per capita between the EU and enlargement countries in 2025. In 2025, the European Union records a GDP per capita of 41 620 €, substantially higher than the levels observed in the enlargement countries for which data are available. Among the enlargement countries, Türkiye reports the highest GDP per capita, at 14 140 € (2024 data), followed closely by Serbia with an estimated 13 540 € and Montenegro with 13 110 € (provisional data). North Macedonia records 8 590 € (2024 estimated data), while Bosnia and Herzegovina reaches 8 050 € (2024 data). Albania reports the lowest value among the available countries, at 6 500 €, based on 2022 data instead of 2025. No data are available for Ukraine and Kosovo. Overall, the data point to notable disparities in income levels across the enlargement countries, with Türkiye, Serbia and Montenegro at the higher end of the available range. Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and North Macedonia remain at comparatively lower levels. [[Image:CPC26_Gross domestic product per capita at current market prices, 2025_(€ per capita).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Gross domestic product per capita at current market prices, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ba7fc62a-16d7-4f98-8de9-cad337c2de60?lang=en nama_10_pc])|alt= line chart showing gross domestic product per capita at current market prices for the enlargement countries and the EU for the year 2025. Data for Georgia, Moldova, Ukraine and Kosovo are not available. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] == Growth in real gross domestic product == Real GDP, also called GDP at constant prices, measures the volume of output without considering changes in prices. Its annual growth rate shows the real change in economic activity and allows comparison of the dynamics of economic development over time and across countries. Figure 3 shows the real annual growth rates of GDP year-on-year, in other words the changes in constant price GDP compared with the year before, in the enlargement countries and in the EU for the years from 2021 to 2025. The enlargement countries generally recorded stronger real GDP growth than the EU over the 2021-2025 period, reflecting a more dynamic post-pandemic recovery path. While growth in the EU moderated from 6.4% in 2021 to 0.4% in 2023 before recovering slightly to 1.5% in 2025, most enlargement countries maintained comparatively higher growth rates throughout the period. Following the strong rebound in 2021, when Montenegro (13.0%), Türkiye (11.8%), Kosovo (10.7%) (provisional data), Albania (9.0%), Serbia (7.9%) and Bosnia and Herzegovina (7.4%) recorded strong growth rates, economic growth gradually moderated across most enlargement countries. Nevertheless, growth generally remained above the EU average. In 2022 and 2023, Montenegro recorded the strongest growth rates among the enlargement countries, at 7.7% and 6.5% respectively. Türkiye also continued to record relatively strong growth (5.4% and 5.0% respectively). Kosovo maintained robust performance (4.3% and 4.1%). Ukraine recorded a sharp contraction in 2022 (-28.8%), reflecting the impact of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, followed by a strong recovery in 2023 (5.5%) and continued to show growth in 2024 (3.2%). In 2024, growth rates across the enlargement countries ranged from 3.0% in North Macedonia (provisional data) to 4.6% in Kosovo, remaining above the EU growth rate of 1.1%. Albania maintained stable growth at 4.0% (provisional data) and Serbia recorded 3.9% (provisional data). Türkiye’s growth moderated further to 3.3%, while Montenegro slowed to 3.2%, although both continued to outperform the EU average. For 2025, available data point to continued economic expansion across the enlargement countries. Türkiye and Kosovo both recorded growth of 3.6%, followed closely by North Macedonia at an estimated 3.5%. Montenegro reported provisional growth of 2.7%, and Serbia an estimated 2.0%, all remaining above the EU growth rate of 1.5%. No 2025 data are available for Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Ukraine. [[Image: CPC26_Growth in real gross domestic product, 2021-2025_(chain linked volumes, % change compared with previous year).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Growth in real gross domestic product, 2021-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3bbcc7be-facf-4b37-8bf6-8aa5c1e139d6?lang=en nama_10_gdp])|alt= vertical bar chart showing growth in real gross domestic product for the EU enlargement countries and the EU for the years 2021 to 2025. Data for Georgia and Moldova are not available. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Unemployment rates === [[Glossary:Unemployment|Unemployment rates]] are key indicators of economic performance, reflecting labour market conditions, household income capacity and social stability across countries and regions. Analysing unemployment trends helps to identify differences in economic resilience and adjustment across countries. Figure 4 presents the evolution of unemployment rates in the enlargement countries compared with those in the EU. Among the enlargement countries, unemployment rates generally declined over the period 2014–2024, reflecting overall improvements in labour market conditions prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. In several economies, though, this downward trend was temporarily interrupted during the pandemic period, with unemployment rates increasing in 2020 and/or 2021. Nevertheless, most countries resumed a declining trend thereafter. It should be noted that, for all participating countries, there was a break in the time series for unemployment rates in connection with the introduction of a [[EU_Labour_Force_Survey_-_new_methodology_from_2021_onwards|new methodology for the EU Labour Force Survey]] from reference year 2021 on. North Macedonia recorded a particularly strong and continuous reduction in unemployment throughout the entire period, including during the pandemic years, with the rate declining from 28.0% in 2014 to 17.3% in 2019 and further to 12.3% in 2024, representing an overall decrease of 15.7 percentage points. Montenegro also experienced relatively high unemployment rates, overall with a moderately falling trend between 2014 (18.0%) and 2019 (15.2%). However, in 2020 there was a sharp increase in the unemployment rate, rising to 17.9%. More recent data are not available for Montenegro. Serbia also experienced sustained improvements in unemployment throughout the period, despite a temporary increase to 11.2% in 2021 (break in time series in 2021). Overall, the unemployment rate declined from 19.4% in 2014 to 10.5% in 2019 and further to 8.6% in 2024, corresponding to a total reduction of 10.8 percentage points. In Türkiye, unemployment significantly increased from 10.9% in 2018 to 13.7% in 2019 and remained elevated in 2020–2021 (break in time series in 2021), before declining steadily to 8.8% in 2024. For Bosnia and Herzegovina, data are available only from 2021 onwards. Over the 2021–2024 period, the unemployment rate decreased steadily from 17.4% to 12.6%, a reduction of 4.8 percentage points. Comparable data for Albania, Kosovo and Ukraine are not available in the dataset. Despite these improvements, unemployment rates in most enlargement countries remained above the EU average in 2024. The EU recorded a sustained improvement in labour market conditions over the period 2014–2024, with the unemployment rate declining from 10.9% in 2014 to 6.7% in 2019 and further to 5.9% in 2024, despite a temporary and small increase during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020–2021 (break in time series in 2021). [[Image:CPC26_Unemployment, 2014-2024_(% of labour force, ages 15-74).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Unemployment rates, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/02c71e84-9107-43ce-97a0-a4f8a0b0df5d?lang=en lfsa_urgan])|alt= combined line charts showing the unemployment rates in the EU and enlargement countries during 2014 – 2024, expressed as the share of population aged 15-74 years in total labour force. Data for Albania, Georgia, Moldova, Ukraine and Kosovo are not available. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Gross fixed capital formation=== [[Glossary:Gross fixed capital formation (GFCF)|Gross fixed capital formation (GFCF)]] indicates how much of the [[Glossary:Gross value added|value added]] in an economy is invested rather than consumed. It is considered an indicator of future business activity. In general, GFCF tends to increase in times of economic growth and business confidence. Conversely, it tends to decrease in case of economic uncertainty or recession. GFCF as a percentage of GDP at current market prices in the period 2015 to 2025 is presented in Figure 5 for the enlargement countries, compared with the EU. Across the enlargement countries, Türkiye and Kosovo registered the highest levels of gross fixed capital formation, peaking at 32.9% in both Türkiye (2023) and Kosovo (2021). In 2025, both maintained elevated investment levels of 30.6% and 32.4%, respectively, well above the EU average. Montenegro experienced pronounced fluctuations, increasing sharply from 20.7% in 2015 to 29.8% in 2018, before declining to 20.4% in 2023 and recovering moderately to 22.3% in 2025 (2025 provisional). North Macedonia showed comparatively stable investment dynamics, declining from 23.8% in 2015 to 20.0% in 2018, followed by a gradual recovery to 24.7% in 2023 and 24.0% in 2025 (2024 provisional; 2025 estimated). Serbia recorded a sustained increase in investment from 16.8% in 2015 to 23.9% in 2022, before stabilising around 23% thereafter (2023–2024 provisional; 2025 estimated). Albania displayed moderate fluctuations, with investment declining from 26.1% in 2015 to 24.3% in 2023 before recovering slightly to 24.4% in 2024 (2024 provisional; 2025 not available). Bosnia and Herzegovina showed a generally upward trend, increasing from 21.4% in 2015 to 24.4% in 2024, although data for 2025 are not available. Moldova showed moderate fluctuations in gross fixed capital formation over the period. Investment peaked at 24.9% of GDP in 2020 before declining to 19.4% in 2023. It recovered to 22.0% in 2025 (provisional data), although it remained below the level recorded in 2015. Ukraine had shown the lowest investment levels among the countries presented and the greatest volatility over the period. Gross fixed capital formation increased from 13.5% of GDP in 2015 to 17.6% in 2018–2019, before declining sharply to 11.9% in 2022 and partially recovering to 18.5% in 2024. The EU gross fixed capital formation remained relatively stable over the period 2015–2025, fluctuating within a narrow range between 20.0% and 22.1% of GDP. Following a gradual increase from 20.0% in 2015 to 22.0% in 2019, investment levels remained broadly resilient during the pandemic period, standing at 21.9% in 2020 and 21.8% in 2021, before reaching 22.1% in 2023 and moderating slightly to 21.3% in 2025. [[Image: CPC26_Gross fixed capital formation, 2015-2025_(% of GDP at current market prices)_up.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Gross fixed capital formation, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a3e83e65-1e36-42d4-be76-431577061dda?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-26T06:39:36Z nama_10_gdp])|alt= line chart showing gross fixed capital formation as share of GDP at current market prices in percent, for the enlargement countries and the EU for the years 2015 to 2025. Data for Georgia and Moldova are not available. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Foreign direct investment balance=== [[Glossary:Foreign_direct_investment_(FDI)|Foreign direct investments (FDI)]] arises when a unit resident in one economy makes an investment that gives control or a significant degree of influence over the management of a company that is resident in another economy. FDI tends to promote stable economic links between economies through direct access for direct investors in home economies to production units in host economies. Within a proper policy framework, FDI assists host economies in developing local companies, promotes international trade through access to markets, and contributes to the transfer of technology and know-how. The coverage of FDI for analytical purposes includes income flows and financial transactions recorded in the direct investment functional category in the [[Glossary:Balance_of_payments|balance of payments]]. As FDI may reflect large investments in specific projects within a limited time frame, values can vary greatly from one year to another. One way of analysing FDI is to consider it according to the direction of the investment (inward – direct investment in the reporting economy; outward – direct investment made abroad by resident entities). This approach provides a clear understanding of an economy’s position as both a host and an investor. Figure 6 presents the net FDI, calculated as the balance between net inward and net outward direct investment cross-border transactions. Over the period 2014–2023 (2024 data not available), the EU recorded predominantly net FDI outflows, with particularly large outflows observed in 2015 (-€178.2 billion), 2021 (-€407.6 billion) and 2022 (-€223.4 billion). Net inflows were recorded in 2020 (€151.2 billion), likely reflecting the exceptional economic conditions during the COVID-19 pandemic. Overall, the scale of FDI transactions in the EU remained substantially larger than in the enlargement countries, underlining the EU’s role as a major global investor and host economy. Among the enlargement countries, Türkiye recorded the highest net FDI inflows in absolute terms, reaching €7.8 billion in 2018 before declining to €5.6 billion in 2019 and dropping sharply to €422.0 million in 2020 during the pandemic period. Net inflows recovered thereafter to €3.1 billion in 2022 before moderating to €936.0 million in 2023 (2014–2017 and 2024 data not available; 2022–2023 Eurostat estimates). Serbia also recorded comparatively high net FDI inflows, increasing from €1.2 billion in 2014 to €1.9 billion in 2016 and reaching €4.3 billion in 2022, indicating a substantial strengthening in foreign investment over the period (2017–2021 and 2023–2024 data not available). Albania maintained positive net inflows throughout the available period, rising from €862.3 million in 2020 to €1.4 billion in 2023 (2014–2019 and 2024 data not available). North Macedonia displayed more moderate but increasing FDI inflows, rising from €154.7 million in 2020 to €1.0 billion in 2024, despite fluctuations in earlier years (2014–2015 and 2018–2019 data not available). Kosovo also recorded positive FDI inflows, increasing from €286.6 million in 2020 to €556.8 million in 2022 (2014, 2017–2019 and 2023–2024 data not available). Montenegro recorded net FDI inflows of €468.0 million in 2020, although comparable data for the remaining years are not available (2014–2019 and 2021–2024 data not available). Comparable data for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Ukraine are not available. [[Image: CPC26_Foreign direct investment balance, 2014-2024_(€ million).png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 6: Foreign direct investment balance, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4a450e71-feb3-4e22-919f-eb1c545f87d9?lang=en bop_fdi6_flow])|alt=line chart showing the net balance of foreign direct investment flows in euro millions in the EU and the enlargement countries Albania, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia and Türkiye from 2014 to 2024. Data not available for Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Moldova, Ukraine. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= CPC26_Economic_developments_v5.xlsx|title= Economic developments in the enlargement countries: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== All economic statistics in this article presented as monetary values are based on current price series, i.e. nominal values without adjustments for price changes, unless otherwise stated. Data for the EU and the enlargement countries are compiled under European system of national and regional accounts [[Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)|(ESA 2010)]], the EU accounting framework for a systematic and detailed description of an economy. The structure of ESA 2010 is consistent with the international guidelines on national accounting as outlined in the [[Glossary:United Nations (UN)|United Nations]]' [[Glossary:System of national accounts (SNA)|system of national accounts]] (the 2008 SNA). Eurostat issues manuals, handbooks, and other methodological guidance to support a harmonised implementation of ESA 2010. The legal basis for ESA 2010 is [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2013/549/oj/eng Regulation (EU) No 549/2013 on the European system of national and regional accounts in the European Union], which defines a methodology (on common standards, definitions, classifications and accounting rules that shall be used for compiling accounts and tables on comparable bases and a programme of data transmission setting out the time limits for the EU countries to transmit to Eurostat the accounts and tables. It was amended by [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32023R0734 Regulation (EU) 2023/734]]. So far, Eurostat published data on GDP and main components for 9 of the enlargement countries: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, Türkiye and Ukraine. Balance of payments (BoP) statistics are the central source for data on balance of trade in goods and services and on Foreign direct investment (FDI) transactions. BoP statistics are internationally compiled based on the methodology recommended by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Manuals on Balance of Payments and International Investment Position. For the reference period the methodological framework prevailed in external sector statistics was set up in the IMF’s Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual Sixth Edition (BPM6). The IMF Statistics Department published the updated version of the Manual (BPM7) in March 2025. The BPM6 update is being coordinated with the updated version of the System of National Accounts (2025 SNA). At the moment it is foreseen that the new manuals will be implemented in the EU in 2029 or 2030. The definitions of unemployment and the labour market used are based on international recommendations by the [[Glossary:International_Labour_Organization_(ILO)|International Labour Organization (ILO)]]. The concepts and definitions used in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey European Union labour force survey (EU-LFS)] follow the resolutions of the International Conference of Labour Statisticians (ICLS) organised every 5 years by the International Labour Organisation (ILO). The unemployment rate is an important indicator with both social and economic dimensions. Increasing unemployment results in a loss of income for individuals, increased pressure with respect to government spending on social benefits and a reduction in tax revenue. From an economic perspective, unemployment may be viewed as unused labour capacity. The main source for European labour force statistics is the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (EU-LFS)|European Union labour force survey (EU LFS)]]. This [[Glossary:Household|household]] survey is carried out in all EU countries in accordance with European legislation and provides figures at least every quarter. Among the enlargement countries, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia and Türkiye have implemented the EU-LFS instrument and conduct the labour force survey according to the same guidelines, methodology and standards as the EU countries. ===Context=== National accounts provide an internationally agreed standard for compiling measures of economic activity through a coherent, consistent and integrated set of macroeconomic accounts. These accounts record how economic activity is distributed among businesses, consumers, government and foreign countries, detailing key items such as production, consumption, savings and investment. The use of internationally accepted concepts and definitions permits an analysis of different economies, such as the interdependencies between the economies of the EU countries, or a comparison between the EU and non-EU countries. Within the EU, multilateral economic surveillance was introduced through the [[Glossary:Stability and growth pact (SGP)|stability and growth pact]], which provides for the coordination of fiscal policies. The reformed Stability and Growth Pact (SGP), which entered into force in April 2024 through Regulation (EU) 2024/1263 and related legislative acts, shifted EU fiscal surveillance towards a more country-specific framework focused on debt sustainability. Under the new rules, member states are required to submit medium-term fiscal-structural plans setting out expenditure paths and reforms aimed at placing public debt on a plausible downward trajectory. Economic statistics is one of the cornerstones of global, regional and national governance, for example, to analyse national economies during global financial and economic crisis or to put in place EU initiatives such as the [https://ec.europa.eu/info/business-economy-euro/economic-and-fiscal-policy-coordination/eu-economic-governance-monitoring-prevention-correction/european-semester_en European semester] or [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/macroeconomic-imbalances-procedure macroeconomic imbalance procedures (MIP)]. While basic principles and institutional frameworks for producing statistics are already in place, the enlargement countries are expected to increase the volume and quality of their data progressively, and to transmit these data to Eurostat in the context of the EU enlargement process. EU standards in the field of statistics require the existence of a statistical infrastructure based on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/quality/european-quality-standards/european-statistics-code-of-practice principles] such as professional independence, impartiality, relevance, confidentiality of individual data and easy access to official statistics; they cover methodology, classifications and standards for production. Eurostat assesses and supports the alignment of statistical production in the enlargement countries with the EU acquis in the field of statistics. Eurostat supports the national statistical offices and other producers of official statistics through a range of initiatives, such as statistical projects, training courses, traineeships, study visits, workshops and seminars, and participation in meetings within the European Statistical System (ESS). Additional information on statistical cooperation with the enlargement countries is provided in the Statistics explained background article [[Enlargement policy and statistical cooperation]]. ===Other articles=== *[[Enlargement_countries_-_statistical_overview|Enlargement countries — statistical overview]] — online publication *[[International_statistical_cooperation|International statistical cooperation]] — online publication *[[National_accounts_and_GDP|National accounts and GDP]] — online publication ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=nama_10 Annual national accounts (nama10)], see: ::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=nama_10_ma Main GDP aggregates (nama_10_ma)] :::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=nama_10_gdp GDP and main components (output, expenditure and income) (nama_10_gdp)] :::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=nama_10_a10 Gross value added and income by A*10 industry breakdowns (nama_10_a10)]] :::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=nama_10_pc Main GDP aggregates per capita (nama_10_pc)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=labour Labour market (labour)], see: :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=employ Employment and unemployment (employ)] ::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=lfsa LFS series – detailed annual survey results (lfsa)] :::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=lfsa_unemp Unemployment – LFS series (lfsa_unemp)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code= bop Balance of payments - International transactions (bop)], see: :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=bop_fdi European Union direct investments (bop_fdi)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code bop_q6 Balance of payments statistics and international investment positions (BPM6) (bop_q6)] :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=bop_fdi6 European Union direct investments (BPM6) (bop_fdi6)] ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-cooperation/regional-cooperation/enlargement Enlargement countries] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/national-accounts/overview National Accounts] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/labour-market Labour market] *'''Factsheets''' :{{Template:Publication|code=KS-04-23-313|title=Basic figures on the candidate countries and potential candidate – Factsheets}} – 2023 edition :{{Template:Publication|code=KS-05-22-089|title=Basic figures on Western Balkans and Turkey – Factsheets}} – 2022 edition :{{Template:Publication|code=KS-08-21-097|title=Basic figures on enlargement countries – Factsheets}} – 2021 edition *'''Leaflets''' :{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-20-273|title=Basic figures on enlargement countries}} – 2020 edition ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=na10_esms|title=National accounts (ESA 2010) (na10)}} (ESMS metadata file — na10_esms) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/lfsa_esms.htm LFS series - detailed annual survey results (lfsa)] (ESME metadata file — lfsa) ===External links=== *European Commission: [https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/economic-and-financial-affairs_en Economic and Financial Affairs (DG ECFIN)] *European Commission: [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/index_en Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood] *European Commission: [https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/enlargement-and-eastern-neighbourhood_en Directorate-General for Enlargement and the Eastern Neighbourhood (DG ENEST)] === Footnotes === <'''footnote text will be automatically inserted if reference tags are used in article content text (use reference icon on ribbon)'''> {{Unit|topic=X_International_statistical_cooperation}} [[Category:General and regional statistics|Economic developments in enlargement countries]] [[Category:International cooperation|Economic developments in enlargement countries]] [[Category:EU enlargement countries|Economic developments in enlargement countries]] [[Category:Non-EU_countries|Economic developments in enlargement countries]] [[Category:Statistical_article|Economic developments in enlargement countries]] [[Category:July2027|Economic developments in enlargement countries]]

title: Economic developments in European Neighbourhood East countries
text:
This article is part of an online Eurostat publication that provides a statistical overview over the European Neighbourhood Policy-East (ENP-East) countries. The article presents statistics on the economic developments for Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine and compares these with the EU. Data extracted in January 2026. Planned article update: March 2027. Growth in real GDP in 2024 by the ENP-East countries was uneven across the region. Georgia noted the highest increase at 9.7%, followed by Armenia with 5.9% and Azerbaijan with 4.1%. Growth in Moldova was almost flat at 0.1%. In 2023, Moldova had the lowest economic activity rate among the European Neighbourhood East countries, with only 58.4% of the population aged 20 to 64 employed or actively seeking work. Azerbaijan recorded the highest rate, 80.6%, slightly higher than the EU rate (80.0%). Unemployment in the ENP-East countries showed diverse developments between 2014 and 2024. Georgia and Armenia recorded high rates with pandemic spikes, Azerbaijan and Moldova remained low. Ukraine’s unemployment rate averaged 9% over the period with available data (to 2021). In comparison, EU unemployment decreased steadily from 10.9% to 5.9% over the period. Unlike the other ENP-East countries, which were net importers of both goods and services relative to GDP (based on available data), Azerbaijan stood out as net exporter of goods and a net importer of services. Goods amounted to 17.7% of GDP in 2019 and 11.9% in 2024, with services totalled -5.4% and -2.8%. [[File: ENPE26_Unemployment rates.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/26f347f6-e9cd-45ee-b25b-00c33f8de9bc?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:16:48 lfsa_urgan]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6e09bc9e-dbfe-4730-864e-9e2cd230848a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:15:36Z enpe_lfsa_urgan])|alt= Infographic showing the unemployment rates in the EU, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Moldova, Georgia and Ukraine in 2024. The data are represented as horizontal line, sorted by value. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article is part of an [[European_Neighbourhood_Policy_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]]. It presents statistics on recent economic developments for 5 [[Glossary:European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP)|European Neighbourhood Policy-East (ENP-East)]] countries, namely, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine. Information on these 5 countries is compared with developments in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are also [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]]. The European Council granted Moldova and Ukraine candidate status on 23 June 2022 and Georgia on 14 December 2023. This article does not contain any data on Belarus, as statistical cooperation with Belarus has been suspended as of March 2022. Data shown for Georgia exclude the regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia over which the government of Georgia does not exercise control. The data managed by the National Bureau of Statistics of Moldova does not include data from the Transnistrian region over which the government of Moldova does not exercise control. Since 2014, data for Ukraine generally exclude the illegally annexed Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the City of Sevastopol and the territories which are not under control of the Ukrainian government. For Ukraine official statistics for 2022-2025 were not fully produced due to the martial law. It will gradually be produced and disseminated as defined by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine, taking into account the specific conditions of producing statistics during Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. This article presents key economic indicators for the period 2014-2024. Where a table or graph refers to a single reference year (for example, 2024), or where annual data are unavailable for certain countries, the most recent available data within the preceding five years are used. Where both the start and end years are intended to be shown but the corresponding data series are not available, data from the closest possible years are presented instead (for example, 2023 data instead of 2024). The analyses cover gross domestic product (GDP) in euros and euros per capita at current market prices, along with real GDP growth and the evolution of [[Glossary:Unemployment|unemployment_statistics]]. It also includes data on [[Glossary:Gross_fixed_capital_formation_(GFCF)|gross fixed capital formation]], [[Glossary:Trade_balance|trade balance]] in goods and services with the rest of the world, as well as [[Glossary:Foreign direct investment (FDI)|foreign direct investments (FDI) flows]] flows from the balance of payments. ===Gross domestic product (GDP)=== [[Glossary:GDP|Gross domestic product (GDP)]] is an aggregate measure of the size of an economy, based on its total final output. It is the standard measure of the value added created through the production of goods and services in a country during a certain period. GDP includes consumer spending, government spending, net exports, and total investments. This indicator is based on nominal GDP (also called GDP at current prices or GDP in value). It reflects economic output in value terms. GDP at current market prices can be used to compare the size of different economies when expressed in the same currency (for example, the euro). However, comparisons should consider population size, differences in the cost of living and the effects of inflation. Notably, more robust comparisons over time can be made using real GDP growth or PPP-adjusted indicators. The ENP-East countries totalled a nominal GDP of €309 billion in 2024, an overall increase of 2.7.% compared with 2023. Their combined GDP accounted for to 1.7% of the EU’s GDP (€18.0 trillion) in 2024, the same share as in 2023. As shown in Figure 1, in 2024, Ukraine remained the largest economy among the European Neighbourhood East countries, with its GDP at current market prices estimated at €168 billion (based on 2023 data). Azerbaijan continued to rank as the second largest economy in the region, with a GDP of €69 billion, followed by Georgia (€32 billion), Armenia (€24 billion) and Moldova (€17 billion, provisional). [[Image: ENPE26_Gross domestic product at current market prices, 2024 (euro billion)_v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Gross domestic product at current market prices, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7fff3517-d52b-4aa8-b8ec-1a8f7fcadf70?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:30:40Z nama_10_gdp]), and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9968b74b-3569-4daf-bb0c-62c0727e0c2a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:29:54Z enpe_nama_10_gdp])|alt= Line chart showing GDP at current market prices in euro billions in the European Neighbourhood Policy-East countries Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine from 2014 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Gross domestic product per capita at current market prices=== Analysis of nominal GDP per capita (per person) removes the effect of the population size, facilitating comparisons between countries. Although GDP per capita at current market prices is influenced by price level changes (inflation), it provides a broad economic indicator that can be used for a basic assessment of living standards. While Ukraine is the largest economy in the ENP-East countries, measuring GDP per capita at current market prices places the country further down the ranking, in fifth position (€4 077, based on 2021 data, in Figure 2). In 2024, Georgia had the highest GDP per capita (€8 541), followed by Armenia (€7 908), Moldova (€7 001, provisional) and Azerbaijan (€6 730). The EU average (€39 940) remains substantially higher than in the ENP-East countries, emphasising the contrast between total economic size and per -capita economic output (see Figure 2). Global developments, including the ongoing effects of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and fluctuations in world market prices, have continued to influence inflation and exchange rates across the ENP-East countries. These factors influenced GDP expressed in euro, contributing to differences in per capita values across the region. In the case of Ukraine, where the available data are based on 2021 figures, such factors may partly explain why GDP per capita remains lower relative to the other ENP-East countries despite the country’s overall economic size. [[Image: ENPE26_Gross domestic product per capita at current market prices, 2024_(euro per capita)_v2 .png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 2: Gross domestic product per capita at current market prices, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cbfe46d2-1193-4cb5-8267-35ac5e79f349?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:23:05Z nama_10_pc]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/efaff938-5ff0-46b2-bee5-e7333b6a9b4c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:19:25Z enpe_nama_10_gdp])|alt= Bar chart showing GDP in euro per capita at current market prices, in the EU, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine for 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Growth in real gross domestic product=== Real GDP, also called GDP at constant prices, measures the volume of output without considering changes in prices. Its annual growth rate shows the real change in economic activity and allows comparison of the dynamics of economic development over time and across countries. By focusing on real output rather than total value in euro, it complements per capita measures, which account for population size. Data on annual change in real GDP are shown in Figure 3 for the period 2020-2024. The year 2020 marked the start of the COVID-19 pandemic with the associated impact on economies worldwide. The period 2020-2024 was marked by pronounced volatility in real GDP across the EU and ENP-East countries. The COVID-19 pandemic led to a widespread contraction in 2020, largest in Moldova (-8.3%), Armenia (-7.2%) and Georgia (-6.3%), exceeding the EU average decline (-5.6%). A strong post-pandemic rebound occurred in 2021, notably in Moldova (+13.9%) and Georgia (+10.6%), reflecting a rapid recovery in these economies. The onset of Russia’s war of aggression in 2022 led to a sharp decline in Ukraine’s GDP (-28.8%), while Armenia (+12.6%) and Georgia (+11.0%) continued to record robust growth. In the subsequent years, Georgia and Armenia sustained high growth rates, with Georgia reaching +9.7% in 2024. Moldova’s growth remained minimal (a provisional +0.1 in 2024). EU real GDP contracted sharply by 5.6% in 2020, reflecting the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. This was followed by a strong rebound of 6.4% in 2021 and continued growth of 3.5% in 2022. Economic expansion slowed markedly to 0.4% in 2023, before increasing slightly to 1.1% in 2024. Overall, the period was characterised by a sharp contraction, a robust recovery, and subsequent moderation in growth. Compared with the ENP-East countries, the EU showed a more moderate and stabilised growth path following the post-pandemic rebound. [[Image: ENPE26_Growth in real gross domestic product, 2020-2024_(chain linked volumes, % change on previous year)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Growth in real gross domestic product, 2020-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/42cccdb9-a900-4644-93ce-c3652f65eab9?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:32:02Z nama_10_gdp]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/43136d85-a419-4459-8d04-162f6d8eae13?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:31:22Z enpe_nama_10_gdp])|alt= bar chart showing the year-on-year growth in real GDP, measured in percent change compared with the previous year, for the EU, Moldova, Georgia, Ukraine, Armenia and Azerbaijan for 2020 to 2024. The bars represent the real GDP growth of a country for each year, with the bars coloured according to year. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Unemployment rates=== [[Glossary:Unemployment|Unemployment_rates]] rates are key indicators of economic performance, reflecting labour market conditions, household income capacity and social stability across countries and regions. Analysing unemployment trends helps to identify differences in economic resilience and adjustment across countries. Figure 4 presents the evolution of unemployment rates in the ENP-East countries compared with those in the EU. Between 2014 and 2019, the EU unemployment rate decreased steadily from 10.9% to 6.7%, a decline of 4.2 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp). This was followed by a slight increase to 7.1% in 2020-2021 during the pandemic (break in the time series in 2021), and a further decrease to 5.9% in 2024. Overall, it marked a total reduction of 5.0 percentage points between 2014 and 2024. Across the ENP-East region, trends in unemployment rates show a combination of high pre-pandemic levels, sharp increases during the COVID-19 pandemic, and differing patterns of post-pandemic recovery. Georgia experienced a marked increase in unemployment from 11.6% in 2019 to 18.5% in 2020, peaking at 20.6% in 2021, before declining to 13.9% in 2024 (2018 series break). Armenia’s rate remained elevated between 18.2% and 19.0% in 2018-2020, before gradually declining to 13.4% by 2024. Azerbaijan maintained low unemployment near 5% until a rise to 7.2% in 2020 (+2.2 pp), reverting to 5.3% in 2024 (2019 series break). Moldova’s unemployment remained stable at low levels, rising at 5.1% in 2019 and ending at 4.0% in 2024 (2019 series break). Ukraine’s rates remained largely stable at 9% until 2019, then rising to 9.8% in 2021 (2020 series break; 2022-2024 data unavailable). Overall, the ENP-East countries illustrate considerable differences in unemployment levels, pandemic impact, and post-pandemic adjustment across the region. [[Image: ENPE26_Unemployment rates, 2014-2024_(% of population 15-74 years old)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Unemployment rates, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3408d571-9e78-428c-b8fa-52b18ddbefab?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-13T13:38:21Z lfsa_urgan]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8283e337-b0f9-4f6d-b598-1b3b46f2b776?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-13T13:36:52Z enpe_lfsa_urgan])|alt= Line chart showing in Unemployment rates in the EU, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine for the years 2014 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Gross fixed capital formation === [[Glossary:Gross_fixed_capital_formation_(GFCF)|Gross fixed capital formation (GFCF)]] indicates how much of the value added in an economy is invested rather than consumed. It is considered an indicator of future business activity. In general, GFCF tends to increase in times of economic growth and business confidence. Conversely, it tends to decrease in case of economic uncertainty or recession. GFCF as a share of GDP shows notable differences across the EU and ENP-East countries. In the EU, GFCF increased steadily from 19.6% in 2014 to 22.0% in 2019, remaining around this level until a slight decline to 21.2% in 2024. Among the ENP-East countries, Armenia’s GFCF declined from 20.6% in 2015 to 15.8% in 2019, followed by a rebound to 21.3% in 2024. Georgia’s GFCF peaked at 26.0% in 2016, then declined to 19.8% in 2022 before recovering to 21.3% in 2024. Moldova’s GFCF decreased from 26.0% of GDP in 2014 to 22.2% in 2016, fluctuated up to 24.9% by 2021, and declined to 20.0% in 2024. Ukraine’s GFCF rose from 14.2% in 2014 to 17.6% in 2019, dropped to 11.9% in 2022, and rebounded sharply to 20.0% in 2023 (2024 data are not available). Azerbaijan displayed substantial volatility in GFCF, from 27.4% in 2014 down to 16.8% in 2024. Overall, GFCF in ENP-East countries remained above the EU level for much of the period, though this gap narrowed or reversed in 2022-2024. It exhibited larger fluctuations over time, with declines during the pandemic period and subsequent recoveries in the following years. This may reflect changes in fixed capital investments or fluctuations in GDP, while particularly high investment in some years can be linked to larger projects or programmes. [[Image: ENPE26_Gross fixed capital formation, 2014-2024_(% of GDP)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Gross fixed capital formation, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/72ad4149-d179-4d3d-9f1d-a0bb500f086a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:33:35Z nama_10_gdp]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2d37c91a-bcab-437c-af4d-378879bde076?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:32:50Z enpe_nama_10_gdp_ea])|alt= Line chart showing the evolution of gross fixed capital formation in the EU, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine for the years 2014 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === External balance of goods and services === The external [[Glossary:Trade_balance|trade balance]] is the difference between exports and imports of goods and services. This balance is important for sustainable GDP growth. Measured as a share of GDP, it is also an expression of the openness of the economy and its dependence on international trade. Figure 6 presents the external balance of goods and services in the ENP-East countries for the years 2019 and 2024. Data for Ukraine are not available. In 2024, Moldova, Georgia and Armenia’s international trade in goods resulted in deficits (net goods imports). The ratios of these deficits relative to GDP amounted to -30.9% for Moldova, -38.4% for Georgia and -8.4% for Armenia. However, for services, these same countries recorded net exports, i.e., the value of exports of services was higher than that of imports: 5.1% in Moldova, 22.8% in Georgia and 5.6% in Armenia. Nevertheless, the surpluses in trade of services did not offset the deficits in the trade of goods, leading to overall deficits in the total trade balance of goods and services for each of these countries. Azerbaijan’s international trade in goods and services showed the opposite structure, with net exports of goods in both 2019 (17.7%) and 2024 (11.9%) but net imports of services of -5.4% in 2019 and -2.8% in 2024, respectively. In total, Azerbaijan maintained a positive balance of trade in goods and services for both years. In the EU, the trade balances relative to GDP remained slightly positive for both goods and services in 2024, at 2.1% and 1.1%, respectively, remaining broadly similar to 2019 (2.1% and 0.6%). [[Image: ENPE26_External balance of goods and services, 2019 and 2024_(% of GDP)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: External balance of goods and services, 2019 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2400d5ad-018f-4730-b85b-fc6071e5675b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:26:50Z bop_gdp6_q]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4aa3bb57-b22c-46e3-b563-f16e893e9b3e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:26:03Z enpe_nama_gdp_ext])|alt=Bar chart showing the external balance of goods and services, with bars separately identifying goods from services. Data for 2019 and 2024 are presented for the EU, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Foreign direct investment balance=== [[Glossary:FDI|Foreign direct investment (FDI)]] arises when a unit resident in one economy makes an investment that gives control or a significant degree of influence over the management of a company that is resident in another economy. FDI tends to promote stable economic links between economies through direct access for direct investors in home economies to production units in host economies. Within a proper policy framework, FDI assists host economies in developing local companies, promotes international trade through access to markets, and contributes to the transfer of technology and know-how. The coverage of FDI for analytical purposes includes income flows and financial transactions recorded in the direct investment functional category in the [[Glossary:Balance of payments|balance of payments]]. As FDI may reflect large investments in specific projects within a limited time frame, values can vary greatly from one year to another. One way of analysing FDI is to consider it according to the direction of the investment (inward – direct investment in the reporting economy; outward – direct investment made abroad by resident entities). This approach provides a clear understanding of an economy’s position as both a host and an investor. The figure 7 presents the net FDI, calculated as the balance between net inward and net outward direct investment cross-border transactions. Over the period 2014-2024, Ukraine was by far the ENP-East country that attracted the highest net inflows of FDI. High net FDI inflows were recorded in 2021 at €6 391.6 million and 2019 at €4 629.7 million. Low net FDI outflows were recorded in 2015 at -€160.9 million and in 2020 at -€68.6 million. The 2020 value should be seen in context of the high inflows the previous and the following year, as well as the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. Ukraine’s net FDI dropped sharply to EUR 249.9 million in 2022, before rebounding to EUR 4 102.8 million in 2023 and easing to EUR 3 436.1 million in 2024. The trend corresponds to the economic disruptions observed in 2022, including damage to infrastructure, reduced household consumption, and increased uncertainty. The rebound in FDI in 2023 is in line with the assessment that, despite Russia’s ongoing war of aggression, Ukraine’s macroeconomic indicators have been stronger than expected, contributing to an upward revision of the country’s growth outlook. Until 2017, Azerbaijan experienced positive net FDI inflows, with highs of €1 670.9 million in 2014 and €1 740.8 million in 2016. From 2018 on, net direct investments in the country were negative, reaching -€4 407.9 million in 2022. FDI outflows continued in 2023, though at a reduced scale of -€1 500.3 million, and further eased to -€895.2 million in 2024. Georgia recorded high net FDI inflows in 2022 (€1 809.0 million) and 2023 (€1 515.7 million) before decreasing to €1 058.7 million in 2024. Armenia’s inflows surged in 2022 (€875.4 million) but declined sharply to €69.1 million by 2024, returning close to pre-2022 levels. Moldova maintained positive but more moderate inflows, peaking at €514.0 million in 2022 and remaining above €320 million in 2023-2024. Over the period 2014-2023 (2024 data not available), the EU recorded predominantly FDI outflows, with particularly sharp outflows observed in 2015 (-€178.2 billion) and 2021 (-€407.6 billion). Net inflows were limited, notably in 2020 (€151.2 billion). Overall, the scale of net FDI transactions in the EU was substantially larger than in the ENP-East countries, highlighting the EU’s position as a major global investor and host economy. [[Image: ENPE26_Foreign direct investment balance, net flows, 2014-2024 (euro million)_v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Foreign direct investment balance, net flows, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f8237284-413f-47f9-b26e-9b0a8e2bb788?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:28:34Z bop_fdi6_flow]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/38ba6071-7a63-4972-91d0-349b519c0411?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:27:51Z enpe_bop_fdi6])|alt= Line chart showing the evolution of the FDI, net flows in Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine during 2014-2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=02_ENPE26_Economic Developments_Infographic_V3.xlsx|title=European Neighbourhood Policy — East countries — Economic developments: infographics}} *{{Template:Excel|filename=02_ENPE26_Economic_Developments_V6.xlsx|title=European Neighbourhood Policy — East countries — Economic developments: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data for ENP-East countries are supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country on a voluntary basis. The data result from an annual data collection cycle that has been established by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]. These statistics are available free-of-charge on Eurostat’s website, together with a range of additional indicators for ENP-East countries covering most socio-economic topics. Data for the EU are compiled under European system of national and regional accounts [[Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)|European system of national and regional accounts (ESA)]] the EU accounting framework for a systematic and detailed description of an economy. The structure of ESA 2010 is consistent with the international guidelines on national accounting as outlined in the international guidelines on national accounting as outlined in the United Nation’s [[Glossary:System_of_national_accounts_(SNA)|System of national accounts (SNA)]] standard. The structure of ESA 2010 is consistent with the international guidelines on national accounting set out in 2008 SNA. Eurostat issues manuals, handbooks, and other methodological guidance to support a harmonised implementation of ESA 2010. GDP is the central measure of national accounts, which summarises the economic position of a country (or region). It can be calculated using different approaches: the [[Glossary:Output approach|output approach]]; the [[Glossary:Expenditure approach|expenditure approach]]; and the [[Glossary:Income approach|income approach]]. The main aggregates of national accounts are compiled from institutional units, namely non-financial or financial corporations, [[Glossary:General government sector|general government]], households, and [[Glossary:Non-profit institutions serving households (NPISH)|non-profit institutions serving households (NPISH)]]. [[Glossary:Balance_of_payments|Balance of payments]] (BoP) statistics is the central source for data on [[Glossary: Trade_balance|balance of trade in goods and services]] and on [[Glossary:FDI|Foreign direct investment (FDI)]] transactions. BoP statistics are internationally compiled based on the methodology recommended by the [[Glossary: International_Monetary_Fund_(IMF)| International Monetary Fund (IMF)]] in Manuals on Balance of Payments and International Investment Position. For the reference period the methodological framework prevailed in external sector statistics was set up in the IMF’s Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual Sixth Edition (BPM6). The definitions of unemployment and the labour market used are based on international recommendations by the [[Glossary:International_Labour_Organization_(ILO)|International Labour Organization (ILO)]]. The concepts and definitions used in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey European Union labour force survey (EU-LFS)] follow the resolutions of the International Conference of Labour Statisticians (ICLS) organised every 5 years by the International Labour Organization (ILO). The unemployment rate is an important indicator with both social and economic dimensions. Increasing unemployment results in a loss of income for individuals, increased pressure with respect to government spending on social benefits and a reduction in tax revenue. From an economic perspective, unemployment may be viewed as unused labour capacity. Time series for unemployment are used by the European Commission, other public institutions, and the media as an economic indicator, while banks may use the data for business cycle analysis. The public is also interested in information concerning unemployment. ===Context=== Indicators derived from national accounts provide a picture of the economic situation; they are widely used for analysis and [[Glossary:Forecasting|forecasting]], as well as policymaking. The 2008-2009 global financial and economic crisis underscored the need to develop more robust macroeconomic statistics. Such statistics enhance the surveillance and monitoring of financial systems, support sustainable governance, and provide valuable information on recovery measures. The use of internationally accepted concepts and definitions enables meaningful comparisons across economies. This includes analysing interdependencies between EU Member States and comparing the EU with non-member countries. On 2 July 2021, the European Commission and the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy presented the [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/IP_21_3367 Eastern Partnership: a Renewed Agenda] for cooperation with the EU's Eastern partners. This agenda is based on the five long-term objectives, with resilience at its core, as defined for the future of the [https://neighbourhood-enlargement.ec.europa.eu/european-neighbourhood-policy/eastern-partnership_en Eastern Partnership (EaP)] in the Joint Communication [https://eeas.europa.eu/headquarters/headquarters-homepage/76166/joint-communication-eastern-partnership-policy-beyond-2020-reinforcing-resilience-%25E2%2580%2593-eastern_en Eastern Partnership policy beyond 2020: Reinforcing Resilience – an Eastern Partnership that delivers for all] in March 2020. The Eastern Partnership’s agenda for recovery, resilience and reform is underpinned by an 'Economic and Investment Plan for the Eastern Partnership (EaP): Investing in resilient and competitive economies and societies' (Annex I of the Joint Staff Working Document). More detailed overviews are given in a [https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/document/download/94735c00-2cfa-4ef7-92a6-41515b8b466d_en Factsheet on the Eastern Partnership Joint Communication], presenting the policy objectives and the specific priorities, as well as in a [https://neighbourhood-enlargement.ec.europa.eu/document/download/d675e1d6-fd68-45fa-a671-80a69a117f1f Factsheet on EU-Eastern Neighbourhood flagship projects 2023-2024]. The [https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/news/eastern-partnership-summit-joint-declaration-2021-12-15_en Joint Declaration of the Eastern Partnership Summit 'Recovery, Resilience and Reform'] of 15 December 2021 reaffirmed the strong commitment to a strategic, ambitious and forward-looking Eastern Partnership. At the [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/meetings/international-ministerial-meetings/2023/12/11/ Eastern Partnership Foreign Affairs Ministerial meeting of 11 December 2023], the EU, member states and partners declared that they will step up their efforts to implement the Eastern Partnership’s agenda for recovery, resilience and reform, as well as tackling challenges related to the ongoing consequences of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine for the entire region. On 14-15 December 2023, the European Council decided to [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2023/12/14/european-council-conclusions-on-ukraine-enlargement-and-reforms/ open accession negotiations] with Moldova and Ukraine, and granted the status of candidate country to Georgia. In cooperation with its ENP partners, Eurostat has the responsibility to promote and implement the use of European and internationally recognised standards and methodology for the production of statistics, necessary for designing and monitoring policies in various areas. Eurostat manages and coordinates EU efforts to increase the capacity of the ENP countries to develop, produce and disseminate good quality data according to European and international standards. Additional information on the policy context of the ENP is provided on the website of [https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/index_en Directorate-General Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood (ENEST)]. A regional statistical cooperation programme, STAT-East, is in place since January 2026 to strengthen partner countries’ statistical capacity to develop, produce and disseminate high-quality statistics and to reinforce the independence and institutional capacity of national statistical systems. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Non-EU_countries|All articles on non-EU countries]]
