title: Education and training statistics at regional level
text:
Eurostat regional yearbook; 2026 edition; flagship publication; EU; regional statistics; NUTS; education and training; enrolments; educational attainment; transition from education to work; early leavers Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 This article forms part of the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026]'', an annual [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications flagship publication]. It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the [[Glossary:EU|EU]], [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate]] countries. A [[Regional_yearbook_introduction#A_short_reading_guide|short reading guide]] is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps. In 2025, there were 4 regions across the EU where at least 70% of people aged 25 to 34 had attained a tertiary level of education. All 4 were capital regions: Sostinės regionas (Lithuania), Ile-de-France (France), Eastern and Midland (Ireland) and Warszawski stołeczny (Poland). Within the EU, almost two thirds of vocational graduates aged 20 to 34 with upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education had been exposed to at least 1 month of work-based learning in 2025; the highest regional shares were recorded in the Spanish regions of Noroeste and Noreste.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:SDG wheel icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:Compet and SDG wheel icons RYB2026_small.png|left]]
[[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH03_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2403bb4b-d4fa-4d76-8435-737489034d17?lang=en edat_lfse_04])|alt=An infographic showing the ten EU regions with the highest shares of people aged 25 to 34 with tertiary educational attainment. Data are shown in percent for 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Alongside the provision of health care, public spending on education is widely regarded as one of the most important investments in human capital. Education can play a key role in advancing socio-economic progress, especially in an increasingly globalised world where a highly skilled workforce has the potential to strengthen productivity, foster innovation and enhance competitiveness. This chapter presents data following the common progression of pupils and students through different levels of the education system (according to the [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|International standard classification of education (ISCED)]]; see box below for more details), before looking at educational attainment levels and the transition from education into work. Administrative data on the participation of pupils and students in various levels of education generally refer to 2024, while the latest information from other datasets (surveys) generally concerns 2025. The infographic above presents data for the 10 NUTS level 2 regions across the EU with the highest shares of people aged 25 to 34 with a tertiary level of educational attainment. In 2025, several of these were capital regions. For example, the share reached 77.4% in Sostinės regionas (Lithuania), 72.7% in Ile-de-France (France), 70.4% in Eastern and Midland (Ireland) and 69.6% in Warszawski stołeczny (Poland).
'''European Education Area''' Education and training play a vital role in the economic and social strategies of the EU. In February 2021, a ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32021G0226(01) Council Resolution on a strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training towards the European Education Area and beyond (2021-2030)]'' (2021/C 66/01) was adopted. It sets out 7 policy targets for the [https://education.ec.europa.eu/ European Education Area] that are designed to remove barriers to learning and improve access to quality education for all. The first targets were established for 2025, namely, that: *at least 60% of recent graduates from [[Glossary:Vocational_education_and_training_(VET)|vocational education and training (VET)]] should have participated in work-based learning during their studies *at least 47% of adults aged 25 to 64 should have participated in learning during the previous 12 months. The second set of targets refer to 2030: *less than 15% of pupils aged 15 should be low-achievers in reading, mathematics and science *less than 15% of pupils in the eighth grade (aged 14 or 15) should be low-achievers in computer and information literacy *at least 96% of children between the age of 3 and the starting age for compulsory primary education should participate in early childhood education and care *less than 9% of young people (aged 18 to 24) should leave education and training early *at least 45% of people aged 25 to 34 should have a higher education qualification. Several of these targets are referred to within this chapter.
===Enrolments === In 2024, there were an estimated 94.7 million pupils and students enrolled across the EU in all levels of education from pre-primary to tertiary (as covered by ISCED levels 02 to 8).
'''More about the data: classifying education levels''' As national education systems vary in terms of structure and curricular content, statistics on education and training are compiled according to the international standard classification of education (ISCED). This is the reference classification for organising formal education programmes and related qualifications by education levels and fields into internationally agreed categories. The most recent version of the ISCED classification – ''[https://www.uis.unesco.org/en/methods-and-tools/isced ISCED 2011]'' – was adopted by the UNESCO General Conference in November 2011 and identifies the following levels of education: *early childhood education – ISCED level 0 **early childhood educational development – ISCED code 010 **pre-primary education – ISCED code 020 *primary education – ISCED level 1 *lower secondary education – ISCED level 2 *upper secondary education – ISCED level 3 *post-secondary non-tertiary education – ISCED level 4 *tertiary education – ISCED levels 5 to 8 **short-cycle tertiary education – ISCED level 5 **bachelor’s or equivalent level – ISCED level 6 **master’s or equivalent level – ISCED level 7 **doctoral (PhD) or equivalent level – ISCED level 8. Across all EU countries, school attendance is compulsory – at least for primary and lower secondary education. Young people who have successfully completed lower secondary education may enter upper secondary education (ISCED level 3), when they generally have to choose certain subjects or specialisations to study, alongside their future education and/or career paths. Upper secondary (or intermediate) education typically ends in the EU when students are aged 17 or 18. These programmes are designed primarily to prepare students so that they may continue their studies at a tertiary level (general programmes), or to provide them with skills and competencies that are relevant for a specific occupation or trade (vocational programmes). Tertiary education (ISCED levels 5 to 8) builds on secondary education, providing learning activities at a higher level of complexity. This level of higher education – provided by universities and other tertiary educational institutions – can play an important role in society, fostering innovation, while increasing economic development and growth.
'''Participation rates in early childhood education''' Research has shown that early experiences of children often play a critical role in long-term development. Early childhood education and care programmes, which are intentionally designed to support children’s cognitive, language, physical and socio-emotional development, are considered educational in the ISCED classification (ISCED level 0, early childhood education) At this age, learning activities are very different to the traditional methods adopted within the context of compulsory schooling, and – most of the time – take place alongside / as part of caring activities (in other words, supervision, nutrition and health). According to ISCED, programmes providing only childcare – without a sufficient set of purposeful learning activities – are not classified as early childhood education.. Early childhood education programmes are typically designed to introduce young children to organised instruction outside of the family context. Programmes have an intentional education component and target children below the age of entry into primary education (ISCED level 1). Early childhood education programmes constitute the first level of education and training systems and play a key role in redressing ‘unequal’ life chances, tackling inequalities by preventing the formation of early skills gaps.
'''More about the data: statistics on early childhood education and care''' Within the strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training towards the European Education Area and beyond, a key policy target concerns the share of young children – between the age of 3 and the starting age of compulsory primary education – who participate in early childhood education and care. Eurostat data on early childhood education (ISCED level 0) are used to measure progress towards the goal of having at least 96% of children in this age group participating in early childhood education and care by 2030 It should be noted that the wording of the EU target is for participation in ‘early childhood education and care’ and not ‘early childhood education’. Early childhood education and care refers to any regulated arrangement for children from birth to compulsory primary school age, regardless of the programme content, whereas early childhood education refers specifically to ISCED programmes. The former encompasses not only early childhood education but also programmes which do not meet the minimum requirements to be classified as such (for example, childcare only programmes). Although the EU target is for participation in early childhood education and care, the Regulation stipulates that Eurostat’s data on participation rates in early childhood education will be used to measure progress towards this target. This means that, in practice, the EU target for participation in early childhood education and care programmes concerns only those programmes which meet criteria to be classified as early childhood education. For more details on the difference between these 2 terms, please consult an article on [[Early_childhood_education_statistics|early childhood education statistics]].. Within this section, regional statistics presented for Germany relate to NUTS level 1 regions, while national data are presented for the Netherlands.
Based on the latest available data, there were an estimated 15.6 million children (of any age) enrolled in early childhood education across the EU in 2024 (data for Belgium, Greece, Italy and Malta only cover pre-primary education). '''Map 1''' shows a more detailed picture for 198 NUTS level 2 regions, it covers pupils between the age of 3 and the starting age of compulsory education at primary level. While the participation rate in early childhood education averaged 94.4% across the whole of the EU, there were considerable differences in regional rates. The highest rates were generally recorded in western regions of the EU and lower rates across several eastern regions. Capital regions had higher participation rates than their respective national averages in several EU countries, including Belgium, Germany, Croatia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia. By contrast, capital regions in countries such as Czechia, Italy, Portugal or Romania recorded below-average rates. '''''In 2024, there were 20 regions across the EU where practically every child (100.0%) between the age of 3 and the age for starting compulsory primary education participated in early childhood education''''' By 2024, the share of children between the age of 3 and the starting age for compulsory primary education participating in early childhood education had already reached the EU’s strategic target of 96.0% in exactly half of all EU regions for which data are available (99 out of 198 regions) – see '''Map 1'''. These 99 regions, which had already met or exceeded the 2030 target were mainly concentrated in Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Spain, France, Lithuania, Hungary, Poland, Portugal and Sweden (for each of these countries, more than half of all regions had reached this level); Luxembourg had also achieved the policy target of 96.0%. At the upper end of the distribution, 20 EU regions recorded participation rates of 100.0% in early childhood education. Almost half of these were located in France (9 regions), while a further five were in neighbouring Belgium. Across the EU, there were 5 capital regions with universal enrolment of young children in early childhood education, namely Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest (Belgium), Ile-de-France (France), Grad Zagreb (Croatia), Budapest (Hungary) and Warszawski stołeczny (Poland). As such, it is interesting to note that while some of the lowest participation rates were observed in eastern EU countries, 3 of the 5 capital regions with universal enrolment were also located in the same group of countries. In 2024, the share of young children participating in early childhood education was below 85.0% in 17 of the 198 regions for which data are available. These regions with relatively low participation rates were mainly concentrated in eastern EU countries, including all 8 regions of Romania, 2 regions from each of Czechia and Slovakia, as well as a single region from Croatia. This group also included the French island regions of Mayotte and Corse, as well as a single region from each of Austria and Portugal. At the lower end of the distribution, there were 5 EU regions where the participation rate in early childhood education was below 75.0%: *4 of these were located in Romania – Nord-Est recorded the lowest share in the EU (70.6%), while the remaining regions included the capital of Bucureşti-Ilfov, Sud-Muntenia and Sud-Est *the only other region below this level was Východné Slovensko in Slovakia.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:SDG wheel icon RYB2026.png|50px]]
Map 1: Participation rates in early childhood education
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a6c42125-c30a-4ce1-ac87-e2f7b0c12b4a?lang=en educ_uoe_enra22]) [[Image:Compet and SDG wheel icons RYB2026_small.png|left]] [[Image:Participation rates in early childhood education (%, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Participation rates in early childhood education
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a6c42125-c30a-4ce1-ac87-e2f7b0c12b4a?lang=en educ_uoe_enra22])]] '''Participation in tertiary education''' The number of people enrolling in tertiary education across the EU has risen in recent decades, reflecting several factors, such as: *demographic patterns *changes in labour force participation (particularly for women) *increased demand from employers for tertiary education qualifications (for jobs that previously required a secondary level of education) *an increased awareness of the benefits of tertiary education *access to student finance, scholarships and other benefits *different patterns of learning mobility (within and from outside of the EU) *an increased demand for longer tertiary education (such as the extension from a bachelor’s degree to master’s or doctoral (PhD) studies) *an increasing share of adults participating in [[Glossary:Lifelong_learning (LLL)|lifelong learning]]. Looking ahead, developments in artificial intelligence (AI) may also influence enrolment patterns across tertiary education. On the one hand, AI is likely to increase demand for advanced digital, analytical and interdisciplinary skills, which could encourage higher participation in tertiary studies. On the other hand, as AI automates a growing share of routine tasks, employers may place less emphasis on traditional degree-based qualifications for some roles, instead prioritising specific, verifiable skills and competencies. '''''In 2024, there were 19.1 million tertiary education students enrolled across the EU''''' There were approximately 19.1 million students enrolled in the EU’s tertiary education institutions in 2024. As such, tertiary students accounted for 1 in 5 (20.1%) of the total number of pupils and students enrolled within the EU’s education system. A majority of the students enrolled in the tertiary education sector were female (54.9% of the total). In 2024, 11.2 million EU students were enrolled in bachelor’s programmes. This figure was approximately twice as high as the count of students enrolled in master’s programmes (5.6 million). The other 2 types of tertiary programmes had fewer students: 1.5 million enrolled in short-cycle programmes (either academic or vocational) and 0.7 million in doctoral programmes. As noted above, females made up the majority of students enrolled in tertiary education. This gender gap was particularly apparent among students studying for a master’s degree (where 58.6% were female) and somewhat smaller among students studying for a bachelor’s degree (where 54.3% were female). By contrast, males accounted for a small majority of the students pursuing a short-cycle tertiary education qualification (51.5%) and a doctoral degree (50.3%). The highest absolute numbers of tertiary students were recorded in predominantly urban regions from some of the most populous EU countries. In 2024, the French capital region of Ile-de-France (791 400 students) and the German region of Nordrhein-Westfalen (772 100 students; NUTS level 1) were the only regions within the EU to record more than 0.5 million tertiary students enrolled. A further 13 regions had between 250 000 and 500 000 tertiary students enrolled: *4 regions in Spain – the capital region of Comunidad de Madrid, Cataluña, Andalucía and Comunitat Valenciana *3 regions in Germany – Bayern, Baden-Württemberg and Hessen (all NUTS level 1) *3 regions in Italy – the capital region of Lazio, Lombardia and Campania *the capital regions of Warszawski stołeczny (Poland) and Attiki (Greece) *the French region of Rhône-Alpes. '''Map 2''' shows the proportion of all tertiary students enrolled in bachelor’s, master’s or doctoral degrees (note that short-cycle tertiary education has been omitted due to partial coverage for some regions). Each national education system has its own specific characteristics, with a particular offer of fields or levels of education. This may explain why some regions have no students enrolled for short-cycle tertiary education qualifications or for a master’s or doctoral (PhD) degree, as these educational levels are not offered. In such cases, the shares of students enrolled in other types of tertiary education may be higher than elsewhere. For example, in the Finnish archipelago of Åland, a bachelor’s degree was the only form of tertiary education available and therefore accounted for 100.0% of all tertiary enrolments. '''''In 2024, the most populous German region – Nordrhein-Westfalen – recorded the highest number of students enrolled in bachelor’s programmes''''' In 2024, there were 11.2 million students across the EU enrolled in bachelor’s programmes. Across NUTS level 2 regions, there were 8 regions where more than 90.0% of tertiary students followed a bachelor’s programme: the Finnish region of Åland, as noted above, had the highest share (100.0%), while the others in this group included: *3 regions in Greece – Sterea Elláda, Ipeiros and Kriti *2 regions in Belgium – Prov. West-Vlaanderen and Prov. Luxembourg *2 regions in Spain – the autonomous Ciudades de Ceuta y Melilla. In absolute terms, the highest numbers of tertiary students studying for a bachelor’s degree in 2024 were concentrated in Nordrhein-Westfalen (467 200; NUTS level 1), followed by the French, Spanish, Greek and Italian capital regions of Ile-de-France (334 700), Comunidad de Madrid (261 700), Attiki (258 900) and Lazio (251 900). '''''The French capital region of Ile-de-France recorded the highest number of master’s students in 2024''''' There were 5.6 million students enrolled to study for a master’s education across the EU in 2024. There were 4 NUTS level 2 regions where more than half of all tertiary students (excluding short-cycle tertiary education) followed a master’s programme: Burgenland (80.6%) and Niederösterreich (58.5%) in eastern Austria, La Rioja in northern Spain (55.2%) and Cyprus (51.0%). In absolute terms, the highest number of students studying for a master’s degree in 2024 was observed in the French capital region of Ile-de-France (323 000 students; just 11 700 fewer than were studying for a bachelor’s degree). There were also relatively high counts in 2 German regions (both NUTS level 1) and 2 Italian regions – Nordrhein-Westfalen (263 500 students), Bayern (176 400 students), Lazio (146 900 students) and Lombardia (145 100 students). '''''In 2024, the German region of Nordrhein-Westfalen had the highest number of students enrolled in doctoral (PhD) programmes''''' In 2024, there were 726 700 doctoral or equivalent students enrolled in the EU. Luxembourg (14.0%) and the eastern German region of Sachsen (10.2%; NUTS level 1) were the only regions in the EU to report double-digit shares of tertiary students (excluding short-cycle tertiary education) enrolled in a doctoral programme. The next highest shares were recorded in the German regions of Baden-Württemberg (8.3%), Saarland (8.2%), Bayern and Berlin (both 7.5%), as well as the Portuguese region of Centro (8.2%) and the Finnish capital region of Helsinki-Uusimaa (8.0%). The highest numbers of doctoral students in 2024 were recorded in 3 German regions (all NUTS level 1): Nordrhein-Westfalen (41 400 students), Bayern (33 700 students) and Baden-Württemberg (32 800 students). Outside Germany, the next highest count was observed in the French capital region of Ile-de-France (26 500 students).

'''Participation in short-cycle tertiary education''' Across the EU, short-cycle tertiary education accounted for a single-digit share of tertiary students for both men and women in 2024. '''Participation in bachelor’s programmes''' Within the EU, a majority of the tertiary students following a bachelor’s programme in 2024 were female; 6.1 million compared with 5.1 million male students. There were 3 other regions – all located in Greece – where at least 90.0% of male tertiary education students were enrolled in bachelor’s programmes. In 2024, there were 121 out of 211 NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available, where the share of male tertiary education students enrolled in bachelor’s programmes was higher than the corresponding share among female students. The widest gender gaps were observed in the south-eastern Polish region of Podkarpackie (76.4% for men compared with 58.7% for women) and in the western Greek region of Dytiki Elláda (80.0% for men compared with 62.9% for women). '''Participation in master’s programmes''' Across the EU, there were 3.3 million female and 2.3 million male students enrolled in master’s programmes in 2024. This corresponded to 31.3% of all female tertiary education students, compared with 27.1% of male tertiary education students. The share of female tertiary education students enrolled in master’s programmes was higher than the corresponding share for males in 164 out of the 211 NUTS level 2 regions for which 2024 data are available. The widest gender gap in favour of men was recorded in the easternmost Austrian region of Burgenland – which also had the highest overall share of master’s students – with 68.3% of male tertiary education students enrolled in master’s programmes compared with 59.4% of female tertiary education students. ===Educational attainment=== A basic level of education is desirable for all, as it provides the opportunity to participate in economic and social life. Nevertheless, people with higher levels of educational attainment generally tend to experience a wider range of job opportunities, higher levels of income and tend to be more satisfied with life, while they usually have a lower likelihood of being unemployed.
'''More about the data: educational attainment''' Educational attainment is measured as the highest level of education successfully completed, based on the ISCED classification. These statistics refer to the education level reached prior to the survey interview. Note that some people in the target age range might: *still be studying (for a higher level of education) *have completed their highest level of education in a different region from where they were living at the time of the survey.
'''People with an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education qualification''' In 2025, 41.7% of people in the EU aged 25 to 34 had attained an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary level of education (ISCED levels 3 and 4). This represented a decrease of 0.3 percentage points compared with 2024 and continued a downward trend observed over the past 2 decades, from a peak of 52.9% in 2002 (when the time series began). During this period, the share of people with an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary level of educational attainment fell each year, consistent with rising participation in tertiary education (see below), with the largest annual decrease observed in 2023 (down 1.0 percentage points). '''Map 3''' shows regional variations in the share of people aged 25 to 34 who had attained an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary level of education in 2025. At the top end of the distribution, there were 16 NUTS level 2 regions where at least 60.0% of people had attained an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary level of education (shown by the darkest shade in the map). These regions were predominantly located in eastern EU countries, reflecting a greater prevalence of the vocational education and training pathway into skilled employment. This group of 16 was composed of: *5 regions in Czechia *4 regions in Hungary *2 regions in each of Croatia and Romania *1 region in Slovakia *as well as single regions in Greece and Italy. In 2025, the highest proportion of people aged 25 to 34 with an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education qualification was recorded in the Greek island region of Voreio Aigaio (70.0%). High shares were also observed in the Hungarian regions of Nyugat-Dunántúl (68.3%) and Dél-Alföld (66.6%), as well as the Romanian region of Vest (67.7%). At the other end of the range, 17 NUTS level 2 regions reported that less than a quarter of all people aged 25 to 34 had an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary level of educational attainment in 2025 (as shown by the lightest shade in '''Map 3'''). Spain accounted for 14 of these 17 regions, with shares below 20.0% in: *Ciudad de Ceuta (12.5%) *Cataluña (18.5%) *País Vasco (19.1%) *Comunitat Valenciana (19.9%). The only Spanish regions with shares of 25.0% or above were the island regions of Illes Balears and Canarias, the north-western regions of Principado de Asturias and Galicia, and Ciudad de Melilla. Outside Spain, there were 2 capital regions where less than a quarter of all people aged 25 to 34 had attained an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education qualification in 2025: *Ile-de-France in France (20.4%) *Sostinės regionas in Lithuania (21.5%).

These include a lack of relevant work experience, insufficient skills, limited job opportunities in the region where they reside or high unemployment levels during an economic downturn. The final section of this chapter provides an insight into the situation of young people aged 18 to 24 as they seek to move from education into work, while it also highlights the exposure of vocational education graduates to work-based learning. '''Early leavers from education and training''' Within the EU, education policy seeks to ensure that everyone (irrespective of age) has the skills, knowledge and capabilities to develop their careers. The transition from education into work may prove particularly difficult for people with low levels of literacy and numeracy, those who leave education at an early age, and people coming from disadvantaged backgrounds. A particular area of concern is the proportion of [[Glossary:Early leaver from education and training|early leavers from education and training]]. These people are defined here as individuals aged 18 to 24 who have at most a lower secondary level of educational attainment (ISCED levels 0 to 2) and who were not engaged in any further education and training (during the 4 weeks preceding the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|labour force survey (EU-LFS)]]). The proportion of early leavers is 1 of 7 key targets outlined in the strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training towards the European Education Area and beyond; the EU has set a goal to reduce the proportion of early leavers to less than 9.0% by 2030. '''''Within the EU, the share of young people who were early leavers from education and training was 9.1% in 2025''''' Over the past 2 decades, the proportion of early leavers from education and training among people aged 18 to 24 has steadily declined across the EU. Starting at 16.9% in 2002 (the first year of the time series), the share fell continuously until 2017, when it reached 10.5%. It then remained stable in 2018 before resuming its downward path. After another brief pause (no change in 2023), the rate declined further and stood at 9.1% by 2025. As such, the latest rate for the EU is within 0.2 percentage points of the 2030 policy target for early leavers from education and training. Within the EU, the number and share of early leavers from education and training is influenced by a range of factors, including geography and sex. *Spatially, the share of early leavers tends to be higher in sparsely populated regions and former industrial heartlands. This may be linked, among other reasons, to limited educational opportunities and weak local labour markets, which discourage young people from staying (longer) in education and training, while acting as a ‘push factor’ encouraging those with higher levels of educational attainment to seek opportunities elsewhere. *Gender differences also play a considerable role, with young men generally more likely to leave education and training earlier than young women. This reflects the pattern observed above, whereby young women were more likely than young men to have a tertiary level of educational attainment (see '''Figure 2''' below). '''''More than half of all regions had attained the EU’s policy target for early leavers''''' In 2025, more than half (100 out of 196) of the NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available had a share of early leavers from education and training below the 9.0% policy target (see '''Map 5'''). These 100 regions were spread across much of the EU. Subject to data availability – with data for some countries available only at NUTS level 1 and others having partial coverage, all due to relatively low data reliability – they included: *every region of Greece, Croatia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovenia and Sweden *all but 1 region in Czechia *as well as Ireland, Latvia, Luxembourg and Slovakia. The lowest share of early leavers from education and training was recorded in the Czech capital region of Praha (1.3% in 2024). The next lowest shares, in 2025, were recorded in the Croatian regions of Jadranska Hrvatska (2.0%) and Sjeverna Hrvatska (2.3%), the Greek regions of Voreia Elláda (2.1%) and the capital of Attiki (2.4%), as well as the Lithuanian capital region of Sostinės regionas (2.3%). At the other end of the range, 20 NUTS level 2 regions had a share of early leavers from education and training of at least 15.5% in 2025. This group was located primarily in Germany (5 regions), Spain, France and Romania (all 4 regions), although it also included single regions from each of Bulgaria, Hungary and Portugal. Many of these regions were characterised as sparsely populated, island and/or peripheral regions, but with some notable exceptions; it is likely that a disproportionately high share of students from island and/or peripheral regions have to leave home if they wish to follow a particular course or programme, leaving behind a higher concentration of early leavers. Berlin was the only capital region in this group, with a 15.7% share of early leavers. The share of early leavers from education and training exceeded 20.0% in 6 disparate regions: *the French outermost regions of Mayotte (38.9%) and Guyane (25.5%) *the Romanian region of Sud-Est (25.1%) *the French island region of Corse (21.5%; 2023 data) *the Portuguese island region of Região Autónoma dos Açores (21.1%) *the southern Spanish Región de Murcia (20.6%).

'''Exposure of VET graduates to work-based learning''' EU policymakers place considerable emphasis on work-based learning as a key component of vocational education and training (VET), recognising its role in easing the transition from education to employment and strengthening labour market relevance. Through a range of initiatives, they seek to ensure that VET systems combine classroom instruction with practical experience in real work environments, thereby improving a graduates’ employability and skills. These efforts focus on expanding apprenticeship schemes, strengthening cooperation between education providers and employers, and improving the quality and availability of work-based training opportunities. Work-based learning is widely acknowledged as a central feature of high-performing VET systems, as it allows learners to develop job-specific competences alongside transversal skills such as problem-solving, communication and teamwork. Exposure to real work environments during training also helps VET graduates make more informed career choices and facilitates smoother school-to-work transitions.
'''More about the data: exposure of VET graduates to work-based training''' A ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32020H1202(01) Council Recommendation of 24 November 2020 on vocational education and training (VET) and the European Education Area]'' set a policy objective that, by 2025, at least 60% of recent VET graduates in the EU should have experienced work-based learning for at least 1 month. The indicator used to monitor this target captures exposure to work-based learning as part of VET programmes, including apprenticeships, traineeships and other structured workplace training that forms an integral part of the curriculum. The indicator is derived from the EU’s labour force survey: *the denominator covers graduates aged 20 to 34 with upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary vocational educational attainment (ISCED code 35 and ISCED code 45) who completed their studies during the previous 3 years *the numerator includes those who reported at least 1 month of work experience while studying in a workplace (a company, government or non-profit organisation).
'''''In 2025, almost two thirds of vocational graduates in the EU had been exposed to work-based training''''' Within the EU, 66.0% of vocational graduates aged 20 to 34 from upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education (ISCED 35 and 45) had been exposed to at least 1 month of work-based learning in 2025; this was 6.0 percentage points higher than the EU target of 60.0%. At NUTS level 1, the vast majority of regions (51 out of 72 for which data are available) also recorded shares above the 60.0% target in 2025. Subject to data availability, this was the case in all regions of Germany, Spain, France, the Netherlands, Austria and Sweden. Shares above the target were also observed for Denmark, Estonia, Lithuania, mainland Portugal, Slovenia and Finland (excluding Åland). At the upper end of the distribution, 14 regions recorded shares of at least 95.0%. This group included 5 regions in France, and 3 regions in each of Germany, Spain and the Netherlands. The highest regional shares were observed in the Spanish regions of Noroeste and Noreste, at 98.9% and 98.0%, respectively. By contrast, all of the regions in Belgium, Italy and Hungary recorded shares below 60.0%; this was also the case for Czechia, Ireland, Greece, Croatia, Cyprus, Luxembourg (2023 data), Malta, Romania and Slovakia as well as in 1 Polish region. At the lower end of the distribution, 9 regions had shares below 30.0%, including: *Romania, which had the lowest share in the EU, at 9.1% *Italy, where 4 out of 5 regions had shares below 30.0%, including Sud which was the only other region in the EU to record a single-digit share (9.6%); the exception was Nord-Est (33.9%) *Czechia, Cyprus, Greece and Ireland.

'' Source:'' Eurostat (labour force survey and online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/694c52b7-1330-4033-9413-fd5fa6fbd9e6?lang=en edat_lfse_9919])]] === Source data for figures and maps === {{Template:Excel|filename=RYB2026 CH03 Education and training.xlsx|title=Regional education and training statistics}} ===Data sources=== As the structure of education systems varies between EU countries, a framework for assembling, compiling and presenting regional, national and international education statistics is a prerequisite for the comparability of data – this is provided by the international standard classification of education (ISCED). ISCED 2011 was adopted by the UNESCO General Conference in November 2011 and is used as the basis for the statistics presented here. Most EU education statistics are collected as part of a jointly administered exercise that involves the [[Glossary:United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)|UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UNESCO-UIS)]], the [[Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)]] and Eurostat, referred to as the UOE data collection exercise. This exercise is based on administrative sources, with data compiled by education ministries or national statistical offices. Reference periods are the calendar year for data on expenditure and the school/academic year (classified to the calendar year in which the school/academic year finishes) for all non-financial data. Eurostat collects data for regional enrolments separately. These statistics include information on the numbers of pupils/students enrolled by age, sex and ISCED level, at NUTS level 2. Their legal basis, from school year 2012/13, is ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32013R0912 Commission Regulation (EU) No 912/2013 concerning the production and development of statistics on education and lifelong learning, as regards statistics on education and training systems]''. The EU’s labour force survey (EU-LFS) provides regional education statistics about the population’s level of educational attainment, the number of early leavers from education and training, the employment rates of recent young graduates, the exposure of VET graduates to work-based learning, as well as adult participation in education and training. It covers the population of individuals aged 15 or over living in private households; information for each new reference year is made available in the spring of the following year. EU-LFS data up to 2013 are based on ISCED 1997, while data from 2014 onwards are based on ISCED 2011. Data are generally comparable over this time period, although there are breaks in series for Estonia and Austria due to level shifts resulting from the reclassification of programmes spanning different ISCED levels. ==== Indicator definitions ==== '''Participation in early childhood education''' For the purpose of this publication, the participation rate in early childhood education is defined as the share of children between the age of 3 and the age when compulsory education at the primary level starts; more detailed information on the starting ages for compulsory education and for compulsory primary education is provided in this [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/Annexes/educ_uoe_enr_esms_an_6.xlsx annex]. The starting age of primary education is before the age of compulsory education in some countries, while in other countries compulsory education starts at the pre-primary level (in other words, it may be compulsory to attend early childhood programmes for a year or more before the start of primary education). '''Students enrolled in tertiary education''' Tertiary education is defined as ISCED levels 5 to 8. It builds on secondary education, providing learning activities in specialised fields of study. Tertiary education comprises short-cycle tertiary education (ISCED level 5), bachelor’s or equivalent (ISCED level 6), master’s or equivalent (ISCED level 7) and doctoral (PhD) or equivalent (ISCED level 8) education. For the first 3 of these, students generally need to have successfully completed an upper secondary programme, while those wishing to study for a doctorate generally need to have completed a master’s programme. The number of students in tertiary education may reflect capacities and policies for the development of particular educational levels, but is also linked to qualification requirements, subject choice and/or job opportunities. As students grow older and education becomes more specialised, student mobility generally increases. As such, international flows of students may have a considerable impact on the share/number of students enrolled. '''Educational attainment''' Educational attainment is a term commonly used to refer to the highest level of education that an individual has successfully completed. The strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training towards the European Education Area and beyond (2021 to 2030) introduced 2 targets. *The share of early leavers from education and training (defined as people aged 18 to 24 with no more than a lower secondary education and no longer in education or training) should be less than 9% by 2030. This target is supplemented by a complementary indicator, namely, that the share of people aged 20 to 24 with at least an upper secondary (or intermediate) level of educational attainment should be at least 90% by 2030. *The share of people aged 25 to 34 with a tertiary level of educational attainment should be at least 45% by 2030. The data presented above for educational attainment cover 2 different levels of education: *upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education (as defined by ISCED levels 3 and 4) *tertiary education (as defined by ISCED levels 5 to 8). '''Early leavers from education and training''' The indicator of early leavers from education and training is derived from the EU labour force survey. It is defined as the share of the population aged 18 to 24 with no more than a lower secondary level of educational attainment who are no longer in education or training. The strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training towards the European Education Area and beyond (2021 to 2030) introduced a target for the share of early leavers from education and training, whereby this should be less than 9% in the EU by 2030. '''Exposure of VET graduates to work-based learning''' This indicator is derived from the EU labour force survey. It is defined as the share of recent graduates from vocational education and training (VET) benefitting from exposure to work-based learning during their vocational education and training. The denominator covers people aged 20 to 34 with an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary educational attainment of vocational orientation who had successfully completed their highest level of education in the 3 years prior to the survey. The numerator covers people among the denominator who indicated they had undertaken work experience of at least 1 month while studying (for example, work experience in a company, government institution or non-profit organisation), as part of the curriculum of the formal programme they were following. ===Context=== Each of the EU countries is responsible for its own education and training policy. However, the EU supports national actions and helps address common education and training challenges through what is known as the [[Glossary:Open method of coordination (OMC)|open method of coordination]]. Indeed, the EU provides a policy forum for discussing topical issues (for example, ageing societies, the skills deficit or global competition) and also provides EU countries with an opportunity to exchange best practices. Within this context, the European Commission has presented a wide range of initiatives for developing education and training in the EU, such as improving key competences (for example, literacy, language skills, digital skills and entrepreneurship), making better use of digital technology for teaching and learning, and developing mutual recognition of diplomas. The EU is in the process of building a [https://education.ec.europa.eu/ European Education Area], designed to provide quality and inclusive education, training and lifelong learning for all, as enshrined within the [[Glossary:The_European_Pillar_of_Social_Rights_Action_Plan_(EU_2030_targets)|European Pillar of Social Rights]]. In February 2021, a strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training towards the European Education Area and beyond (2021 to 2030) was adopted. As a means of monitoring progress, a series of reference levels (or benchmarks) for EU performance in education and training have been agreed. These 7 targets for the EU as a whole are intended to support monitoring strategic education and training priorities during the period 2021 to 2030. A mid-term review of the European Education Area was conducted during 2023, providing an opportunity to assess progress and identify ongoing and emerging challenges. This process involved consultation, dialogue and shared reflection with a range of stakeholders and concluded that the priority areas for future work include: *implementing initiatives across Europe as well as nationally and locally *improving [https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/improving-quality quality and equity] across all sectors of education and training *strengthening education for active citizenship, including [https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/BRIE/2023/747459/EPRS_BRI(2023)747459_EN.pdf European citizenship education] *supporting the [https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/teachers-trainers-and-school-leaders/teaching-professions teaching profession] by addressing teacher shortages as well as promoting professional development and mobility opportunities *expanding access to [https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/action-plan digital education and skills development for all] *removing the remaining barriers to the [https://education.ec.europa.eu/education-levels/higher-education/inclusive-and-connected-higher-education/automatic-recognition-of-qualifications automatic recognition of qualifications] *providing a [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52024DC0144 blueprint for a European degree]. The European Commission officially launched the Erasmus programme on 1 July 1987 (39 years ago, as of summer 2026). At the end of 2020, political leaders agreed on the [https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/ Erasmus+ programme] for 2021 to 2027. The programme supports education and training in the EU by offering mobility and cooperation opportunities in higher education, vocational education and training, school education, adult education, youth and sport. It has a budget of €26.2 billion and prioritises social inclusion, the green and digital transitions, and young people’s participation in democratic life. Altogether, the Erasmus and Erasmus+ programmes have enabled more than 16 million people to study, work or volunteer abroad. === Footnotes === ===Other articles=== title: Ecosystem accounts - measuring the contribution of nature to the economy and human wellbeing
text:
<pdftheme>8</pdftheme>
<metadescription>How nature and its various ecosystems contribute to the wellbeing of society and the economy.</metadescription>

<highlight>

Do you wonder how nature and its various ecosystems contribute to the wellbeing of society and the economy? Would you like to know how these benefits can actually be captured and presented in a statistical system? Over the past few years, many different actors such as the European Commission including Eurostat, the United Nations, national statistical offices and the research community have been working together to shed some light on these questions. Initial results for the EU were published in June 2021 in the report [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-FT-20-002 Accounting for ecosystems and their services in the European Union (INCA)]. 

This article provides an overview of work on ecosystem accounts at EU-level and in a number of European countries. The last section highlights the policy context of ecosystem accounts and their uses for policy-making.

</highlight>


<articlecontent>

<sesection>
== Introduction to ecosystem and ecosystem services accounting  ==

Ecosystem accounting is a statistical framework for organising data, tracking changes in the extent and the condition of ecosystems, measuring ecosystem services and linking this information to economic and other human activity. It aims to illustrate the benefits society receives from ecosystems and their services.

More concretely, ecosystem accounts can answer questions such as: 
* What is the extent of wetlands at country or at EU-level? How have their extent and condition changed over time?
* How is the condition of farmland soil changing? How much carbon does it retain?  How much agricultural soil is lost due to urbanisation, and in particular where do these losses take place?
* Where and by which sector are ecosystem services, such as water purification used? Where is investment in water purification measures needed?
*What is the value of nature-based recreation in the EU? How has it changed over time? 



== The international System of Environmental-Economic Accounting  ==

The System of Environmental Economic Accounting (SEEA) is an internationally agreed statistical system that brings together environmental and economic information into one common framework. It comprises several areas of interest covered by different SEEA handbooks, including: 
* the [https://seea.un.org/sites/seea.un.org/files/seea_cf_final_en.pdf SEEA Central Framework (SEEA CF)]
* the [https://seea.un.org/ecosystem-accounting SEEA Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA EA)]
* the [https://seea.un.org/sites/seea.un.org/files/ae_final_en.pdf SEEA Applications and Extensions]

The SEEA EA (SEEA Ecosystem Accounting) provides conceptual guidance for developing ecosystem extent, ecosystem condition and ecosystem services accounts. It complements the SEEA CF by moving beyond the assessment of individual environmental resources (e.g. 'land' or 'forest') to an ecosystem perspective where ecosystems and the services they provide interact as part of a natural process within a specific spatial area.

The SEEA EA was adopted by the UN Statistical Commission in March 2021 as:
* the first international statistical standard on ecosystem accounting (chapters 1-7 on the accounting framework and physical accounts)
* as internationally recognized statistical principles and recommendations (chapters 8-11 on monetary accounts and valuation)


== Developing ecosystem accounts in the EU  ==
=== '''Ecosystem accounts at EU level''' ===

INCA (Integrated Natural Capital and ecosystem services Accounting) was a joint project of Eurostat, DG Environment (DG ENV), DG Research and Innovation (DG RTD), the Joint Research Centre of the European Commission (JRC) and the European Environment Agency (EEA), running from 2015 to 2021. The project was developed to address key policy objectives of the [https://ec.europa.eu/environment/action-programme/ EU’s Environment Action Programme] and the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/biodiversity-strategy-2030_en EU Biodiversity Strategy,].
Its first objective was to  pilot ecosystem accounts at EU level by integrating existing EU data sources, paving the way for for a regular production of ecosystem accounts in the EU in a comparable and coordinated manner. In addition to developing and employing biophysical models for building ecosystem services accounts, INCA integrated geospatial information with statistical datasets, as well as administrative data. 

==== Ecosystem services accounts developed under INCA ====

Within INCA, the JRC published ecosystem services accounts for crop provision, timber provision, global climate regulation, flood control (access the full report [https://ec.europa.eu/jrc/en/publication/ecosystem-services-accounting-part-ii-pilot-accounts-crop-and-timber-provision-global-climate here]), water purification (access the publication [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2212041616304545 here]), crop pollination and nature-based recreation (access the full report [https://ec.europa.eu/jrc/en/publication/ecosystem-services-accounting-part-i-outdoor-recreation-and-crop-pollination here]). Due to the varying and sometimes long data update cycles of the different input data sets, the current latest data point is 2021. A GIS-plug-in tool (so called 'INCA tool') was developed to speed up the production of ecosystem services accounts - a prerequisite for a regular data production. All results on INCA ecosystem services accounts, including accounting tables and maps, the INCA tool as well as a catalogue of output datasets and links to input data are available on the [https://ecosystem-accounts.jrc.ec.europa.eu/ INCA website].

==== Extent accounts developed under the INCA project ====

Ecosystem extent accounts are about delineating ecosystem types and showing how they change over time. The EEA published first results in their [https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/natural-capital-accounting-in-support natural capital accounting report] in May 2019. Currently, these extent accounts cover nine ecosystem types. In the future, the plan is to develop a wider list of ecosystem types linked to the habitat classification of the [https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/ EU nature information system]. This would enable providing more detail on the development of the extent and spatial distribution of ecosystems in the EU.

=== '''Experimental ecosystem accounts in European countries''' ===

Several European countries started experimenting in ecosystem accounting. Some of this work was supported by grants from Eurostat for National Statistical Institutes to develop ecosystem accounts. 

*Bulgaria: The National Statistical Institute of Bulgaria developed ecosystem extent accounts for MAES ecosystem types and for Natura 2000 sites in Bulgaria for the years 1990, 2000, 2006 and 2012. In addition, the use of data such as cadastre data and statistical surveys was tested. Access the full report [https://circabc.europa.eu/sd/a/521ef181-ad94-4e05-8ab5-34a160693cb6/BG-2017-Ecosystem%20accounts.pdf here].

*Denmark: The Danish Statistical Office developed experimental ecosystem services supply and use tables for a number of services such as crop, timber, fish, wild terrestrial animals, groundwater for drinking and outdoor recreation. Access the full report [https://circabc.europa.eu/sd/a/d0ba3da6-4009-4ced-ab5d-bb3a64e9304b/DK-2017-Ecosystem%20services%20accounts.pdf here].

*Estonia: In 2019, Statistics Estonia developed the first national level ecosystem extent accounts, linking these to economic sectors. Furthermore, they produced accounts for a large number of ecosystem services, including provisioning, regulating and cultural, and exploring a range of validation techniques and some policy uses, for grassland ecosystem type.

*Finland: In 2018, the Finnish Environment Institute (SYKE) together with the Natural Resources Institute Finland (LUKE) test piloted a monetary ecosystem asset account for commercial marine fish, developed supply and use tables for forest carbon related ecosystem services and pilot accounts for outdoor recreation. Access the full report [https://circabc.europa.eu/sd/a/2403d31e-e57f-44f3-85b6-892d89986d7a/FI-2017-Ecosystem%20accounts.pdf here]. Furthermore, in 2019 the same institutions developed ecosystem accounts for the marine environment, using data reported for the [https://ec.europa.eu/environment/marine/eu-coast-and-marine-policy/marine-strategy-framework-directive/index_en.htm Marine Strategy Framework Directive], accounts for outdoor recreation in Finish lakes and explored some methodological question (valuation using simulated exchange values and the links between ecosystem condition and services). Access the full report [https://webgate.ec.testa.eu/sygma/reporting/;jsessionid=NMIElnnjjQk_o0VdrekLubC1maR7JHImy9FncVwg6UHxk-dYMGAp!-143590178?projectNo=831232&ticket=ST-30001072-sMhvTcmHM93otUej7MKb7iKU7WLZxVYyyNSx9o4J0IrQKL7r1iLsA7hIvBwmWbE7dP2qzkfcWm0qpOfFWewEoK-rS0vSrmBGYCi1lTRY9UPUi-i1vBDETHk3lP5La8cizwwv0yPTzcEc0sorxEcYLcJw5YRv2YqFuB434XzGGiDVtLn7u1HpFUwubNnQNbDFszblO here].

*Italy: The Italian Institute for Environmental Protection and Research (ISPRA), together with the Basque Centre for Climate Change and the Italian National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT) developed supply and use tables for outdoor recreation, crop pollination, flood regulation and water provision for regions in Italy. Access the full report [https://circabc.europa.eu/sd/a/592b5cea-c859-4229-a7da-bf38a1543c97/IT-2017-Ecosystem%20accounting(0).docx here].

*The Netherlands: In 2018, Statistics Netherlands developed carbon accounts for the Netherlands. Access the full report, further information on the project and additional ecosystem accounting work [https://www.cbs.nl/en-gb/background/2017/45/the-seea-eea-carbon-account-for-the-netherlands here]. In 2019, their project under Eurostat´s grant focus on pollinators and the use of remote sensing to identify their habitat and its quality. The report can be accessed [https://webgate.ec.testa.eu/sygma/reporting/?projectNo=831057&ticket=ST-30018661-yTPvSWyFYqR8Tf5V16cTStce02NGFfJ0L2zaBfN5rHLXQLZbNRlVlAXqzrvcm1IYyeq2K9eG61MDLuX1aZX2Op-rS0vSrmBGYCi1lTRY9UPUi-jLS5F6ohxroacV3ZIn1gJ0zqbPldH26LoxzhKsMzx2LyVSSaYrXm8u7tIzTfQ4pJuD1Mq7PGMyM6y1zttRIpm5d here].

*The United Kingdom: The UK is at the forefront of developing ecosystem accounts in Europe. With Eurostat´s support, the UK Office for National Statistics (ONS) conducted a project assessing the restoration potential of ecosystems considering the expected future flow of ecosystem services, in physical and monetary terms, from restored ecosystems. The conceptual framework was then tested in a pilot study for peatlands. On overview of the work on ecosystem accounting by the UK ONS can be accessed [https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/environmentalaccounts/bulletins/uknaturalcapitalaccounts/2019 here].

== Policy context  ==
In December 2024, the first EU legislation ([https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202403024 Annex IX of amended Regulation(EU) 691/2011 on the European environmental-economic accounts] entered into force. It specifies reporting requirements on ecosystem accounts for EU Member States. Starting from 2026, Member States will be reporting to Eurostat data on ecosystem extent accounts, seven ecosystem services accounts and ecosystem condition accounts for five types of ecosystem and using nine indicators, using common definitions - as specified in the legal text - and common methods - as developed by the Task force on ecosystem accounting and published at [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/environment/methodology Eurostat's methodological website on the environment, under tab 'Ecosystem accounts'].

</sesection>
