title: Education and training statistics introduced
text:
<metadescription>Background policy information related to the collection of EU statistics for education and training.</metadescription>
<updatedata>
Latest update of text: September 2024.
</updatedata>

<highlight title=false>
<newarticle>Alongside the provision of health care, public expenditure on [[Glossary:Education|education]] is often considered as 1 of the most important investments that can be made in people. Education has the potential to drive socioeconomic development forward: this is particularly the case in a globalised world, where a highly skilled workforce can be an advantage in terms of productivity, innovation and competitiveness.</newarticle>

Education, [[Glossary:Vocational education and training (VET)|vocational training (VET)]] and more generally [[Glossary:Lifelong learning (LLL)|lifelong learning]] play a vital role in both an economic and social context. The opportunities which the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] offers its citizens for living, studying and working in other countries make a major contribution to cross-cultural understanding and personal development.

The consolidated versions of the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ%3AC%3A2016%3A202%3ATOC Treaty on European Union] and of the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A12006E%2FTXT Treaty establishing the European Community] acknowledge the importance of education and training by stating that ‘the Community shall contribute to the development of quality education by encouraging cooperation between EU countries and, if necessary, by supporting and supplementing their action ... The Community shall implement a vocational training policy which shall support and supplement the action of the EU countries’. As such, the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] follows up on policy cooperation and works with EU countries, while funding various programmes.

This article starts by explaining several EU education-related policy issues and concludes by introducing Eurostat’s statistics on education and training.
</highlight>

<articlecontent>
<sesection>
===European Education Area===

A [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32021G0226(01) Council Resolution on a strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training towards the European Education Area and beyond] (2021/C 66/01) was adopted by the [[Glossary:Council of the European Union|Council]] in February 2021. It seeks to remove barriers to learning and improve access to quality education for all people through 5 strategic priorities during the period 2021 to 2030
*improving quality, equity, inclusion and success for all in education and training
*making lifelong learning and mobility a reality for all
*enhancing competences and motivation in the education profession
*reinforcing European higher education
*supporting the green and digital transitions in and through education and training.

In order to monitor progress, 7 EU-wide targets have been introduced. They define benchmarks against which the EU’s performance across education and training may be judged, including
*the share of low-achieving 15-year-olds in basic skills – reading, mathematics and science – should be less than 15%, by 2030
*the share of low-achieving 8th graders (generally 13-year-olds) in digital skills – computer and information literacy – should be less than 15%, by 2030
*at least 96% of children between the age of 3 and the age for starting compulsory [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|primary education]] should participate in early childhood education and care, by 2030
*the share of [[Glossary:Early_leaver_from_education_and_training|early leavers (aged 18 to 24) from education and training]] should be less than 9%, by 2030
*the share of people aged 25 to 34 with [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|tertiary educational]] attainment should be at least 45%, by 2030
*the share of recent graduates from vocational education and training (VET) benefiting from exposure to work-based learning during their VET should be at least 60%, by 2025
*at least 47% of people aged 25 to 64 should have participated in adult learning during the previous 12 months, by 2025.

The latest EU data for these 7 targets are available on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/education-and-training/information-data/policy-context Eurostat’s website – Education and training – Policy context].

The European Education Area’s strategic framework promotes collaboration between EU countries and key stakeholders and allows the monitoring of progress towards the achievement of their collective vision. It does so by
*strengthening means of policy cooperation
*enhancing synergies with other relevant initiatives, including the [https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/strategy/strategy-2020-2024/our-digital-future/european-research-area_en European Research Area] and the [https://education.ec.europa.eu/education-levels/higher-education/inclusive-and-connected-higher-education/bologna-process Bologna Process]
*identifying targets and indicators to guide work and monitor progress
*fostering the integration of education and training into the [https://commission.europa.eu/business-economy-euro/economic-and-fiscal-policy-coordination/european-semester_en European Semester] process.
</sesection>

<sesection>
===European Year of Skills===

The European Commission designated the period from 9 May 2023 to 8 May 2024 as the ‘[https://year-of-skills.europa.eu/index_en European Year of Skills]’.

The European Year of Skills was designed to ‘promote reskilling and upskilling, helping people to get the right skills for quality jobs’. It aimed to provide fresh impetus to help the EU reach 2 of its social targets that form part of the [https://op.europa.eu/webpub/empl/european-pillar-of-social-rights/en/ European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan] (see below).

Embedded within the European Year of Skills, the [https://vocational-skills.ec.europa.eu/index_en European Vocational Skills Week] (23 to 27 October 2023) outlined how vocational education and training is key for people of all ages to upskill and reskill for their personal development and careers.
</sesection>

<sesection>
===European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan===

The [https://op.europa.eu/webpub/empl/european-pillar-of-social-rights/en/ European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan] sets out 20 key principles that are considered essential for fair and well-functioning labour markets and social protection systems. It lays out 3 headline targets for the EU to reach by 2030, with 2 of these linked to education and training, namely that, by 2030
*at least 60% of all adults should participate in training every year
*at least 78% of the population aged 20 to 64 should be in employment.

In the context of recovery from the COVID-19 crisis and the digital and green transitions, the desire to see adult participation in training rise to 60% is considered paramount if the EU is to improve employability, boost innovation, ensure social fairness and close the digital skills gap. A key factor of success will be to ensure that adults are able to engage in upskilling and reskilling later in life. To do so, the EU has announced a number of related targets that seek to strengthen and increase adult participation in training; 1 of these seeks to ensure that, by 2030, at least 80% of people aged 16 to 74 have basic digital skills (a precondition for inclusion and participation in the labour market and society in a digitally transformed Europe).
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Early childhood education and care ===

Early childhood education and care (ECEC) includes centre-provided and family day care, privately- and publicly-funded, pre-school and pre-primary provision. It has the potential to lay the foundations for later success in life in terms of education, well-being, employability and social integration and is, as such, an efficient and effective investment in education and training.

ECEC is particularly important for children from disadvantaged backgrounds. Indeed, every child in the EU should have the right to affordable and high-quality ECEC, as outlined in the European Pillar of Social Rights. Through achieving this goal, educational attainment in the EU should be decoupled from social, economic and cultural status.

The European Commission supports EU countries and facilitates cooperation between them by providing data and analysis on developments and issues concerning ECEC, identified as a priority area for cooperation under the European Education Area initiative for the period 2021–30. In May 2019, the Council adopted a [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32019H0605(01) Recommendation on High-Quality Early Childhood Education and Care Systems]. A European Commission working group supports peer-based learning, sharing knowledge and best practices for monitoring and evaluating the quality of ECEC provision. It also supports EU countries in their efforts to improve access to and the quality of early childhood education and care. As part of this work, the working group has published
*a [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/4c526047-6f3c-11eb-aeb5-01aa75ed71a1/language-en toolkit] for inclusive ECEC
*[https://op.europa.eu/fr/publication-detail/-/publication/47ba3c3a-6789-11eb-aeb5-01aa75ed71a1/language-en guidelines] on how to recruit, train and motivate well-qualified ECEC staff.

The European Commission is also working on a European Child Guarantee to ensure that every child in the EU at risk of poverty or social exclusion has access to the most basic rights, including healthcare and education.

As part of the European Education Area initiative, the EU has agreed a target for 2030
*to have at least 96% of children between 3 years old and the starting age for compulsory primary education participating in early childhood education and care.
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== School education ===

Schools are a focus area for cooperation to ensure that the European Education Area becomes a reality. The European Commission’s vision is based on 5 dimensions
*quality and equity in education and training – work on key competences, tackling early school leaving, fostering multilingualism and language awareness in schools, promoting supportive learning environments, addressing well-being and mental health at school
*school teachers and school leaders – guidance and work on supporting teachers’ and school leaders’ careers and professional development, promoting teachers’ learning mobility
*digital education – digital competences and skills are considered essential to give every individual an equal chance to thrive in life, find employment and to be an engaged citizen (more information is provided below in the section on the [[#Digital Education Action Plan|Digital Education Action Plan]])
*green education – whereby education and training systems/institutions can act as catalysts to support a shift to a more sustainable society (more information is provided below in the section on [[#Green education|Green education]])
*the EEA in the world – EU instruments for quality and inclusive, digital and green education are widely used across educational communities of non-EU countries, with the EU contributing towards a holistic approach to education and training.

As part of the European Education Area strategic framework, a working group on schools was established by the European Commission. It is composed of representatives from national educational authorities and stakeholder organisations active in the field education. The working group offers opportunities for peer learning, sharing of best practices and information, networking and collaboration on topics related to school success, and education for environmental sustainability.

As part of the European Education Area initiative, the EU has agreed 3 specific targets concerning school education for 2030
*the share of low-achieving 15-year-olds in basic skills – reading, mathematics and science – should be less than 15%
*the share of low-achieving 8th graders (generally 13-year-olds) in digital skills – computer and information literacy – should be less than 15%
*the share of early leavers (aged 18 to 24) from education and training should be less than 9%.
</sesection>

<sesection>
===Higher education===

Higher education occupies a unique position – serving society and the economy – as it sits at the crossroads of education, research and innovation. There are a broad range of higher education institutions across the EU, from universities, research and technology institutes to vocational education and training institutions, or schools of art/design.

In May 2017, the European Commission adopted a Communication on [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52017DC0247 a renewed EU agenda for higher education] (COM(2017) 247 final), focusing on 4 priority activities
*tackling future skills mismatches and promoting excellence in skills development
*building inclusive and connected higher education systems
*ensuring higher education institutions contribute to innovation
*supporting effective and efficient higher education systems.

The Communication also proposed to streamline EU support for higher education by
*creating a knowledge hub to enhance data quality, comparability, data collection and indicators and draw lessons from the implementation of EU higher education data tools to date
*strengthening the work of the [https://eacea.ec.europa.eu/national-policies/eurydice/ Eurydice network] and cooperation with the [[Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)|OECD]] to avoid a duplication of efforts
*simplifying student mobility by building on existing [https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/ Erasmus+] projects for the electronic exchange of student data and exploring the feasibility of establishing an electronic student identification system
*initiating a discussion on efficient support to students, staff, institutions and higher education systems.

The European Commission has a number of other [https://education.ec.europa.eu/education-levels/higher-education/about-higher-education higher education initiatives] that are intended to enable the higher education sector to adapt and thrive; they are based on shared values, such as excellence and inclusion. The following list provides a summary of some recent initiatives.
*Micro-credentials certify the learning outcomes of short-term learning experiences: they offer a flexible, targeted way to help people develop the knowledge, skills and competences they need for their personal and professional development. The EU has put in place a set of [https://education.ec.europa.eu/education-levels/higher-education/micro-credentials recommendations] to support the development, implementation and recognition of micro-credentials across institutions, businesses, sectors and borders, promoting lifelong learning through shorter forms of learning opportunities, to ensure that everyone has the knowledge, skills and competences they need to thrive in their personal and professional lives.
*A [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2022:16:FIN Communication on a European strategy for universities] (COM(2022) 16 final) outlined plans to develop ‘European universities’ – transnational alliances of higher education institutions based on long-term structural and strategic cooperation – as a key pillar of the European Education Area. With an announcement in mid-2024 concerning additional funding, the initiative was providing support for the establishment of 64 European universities – designed to enable Europeans to cooperate across languages, borders and disciplines – bringing together more than 560 higher education institutions.
*The [https://education.ec.europa.eu/education-levels/higher-education/european-student-card-initiative European Student Card Initiative (ESCI)] is designed to promote student mobility across Europe, through a European student card (for students to benefit from a range of services), an Erasmus+ App (to assist with practical administrative steps), and a range of digital solutions to connect higher education institutions (so they may better manage Erasmus+ mobile students).
</sesection>

<sesection>
===Erasmus+===

The [[Glossary:Erasmus programme|Erasmus programme]] was 1 of the most well-known European programmes and ran for just over a quarter of a century; in 2014 it was superseded by the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32021R0817 EU’s programme for education and training, youth and sport], referred to as Erasmus+. The programme’s current funding period runs from 2021 to 2027. It has an estimated budget of €26.2 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] (which is nearly double the funding of the 1st funding period (2014–20)).

The Erasmus+ programme supports priorities and activities set out in the European Education Area, Digital Education Action Plan and the European Skills Agenda. It also
*supports the European Pillar of Social Rights
*implements the [https://europa.eu/youth/strategy_en EU Youth Strategy 2019–27] which seeks to engage young people so they become active citizens participating in democracy and society
*develops the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=LEGISSUM:ef0025 European dimension in sport] (COM(2011) 12 final).

Erasmus+ offers mobility and cooperation opportunities in school education (including early childhood education and care), higher education, vocational education and training, adult education and sport. The programme has 4 overarching priorities – inclusion, digital, green, democratic participation. It is designed so that Europeans from all backgrounds may benefit from the opportunities offered, which provide real life-changing experiences, with positive effects on professional, social, educational and personal development. The programme aims at being more inclusive by improving participation rates among vulnerable and under-represented groups. Through developing digital skills and competences in areas such as combating climate change, clean energy, artificial intelligence, robotics or big data analysis, it may
*contribute to sustainable growth and ensure equity, prosperity and social inclusion
*support and facilitate transnational and international cooperation in the fields of education, training and sport to strengthen European identity and the participation of young people in democratic processes.

Erasmus+ supports 3 key actions
*learning mobility for individuals, both within the EU and beyond, for example through study and training, traineeships, and teaching and professional development
*cooperation among organisations and institutions – for innovation and the exchange of good practices – between educational institutions, or between educational institutions and organisations for young people, businesses, local and regional authorities and non-governmental organisations (NGOs)
*support for policy development and cooperation – designed to promote the active participation of young people in democratic life.

The latest information available concerning the reach and impact of Erasmus+ concerns 2022. Participation in Erasmus+ rebounded to a level that was above that recorded before the COVID-19 pandemic. There were 1.2 million students or staff members who studied, trained or volunteered abroad in 2022 thanks to Erasmus+, with 13.3% of all participants having a low level of opportunity (special needs, from disadvantaged backgrounds, or from outermost regions of the EU). Erasmus+ provided funds to 26 000 projects that were spread over 73 000 organisations, with a budget of €4.0 billion.
</sesection>

<sesection>
===Vocational education and training (VET)===

VET prepares people for work (to qualify them for the labour market) and develops skills so that they remain employable and respond to the needs of the economy. It provides learners with essential skills that enhance their employability and support their personal development. In a broader context, VET may boost enterprise performance, competitiveness, research and innovation.

Initial vocational education and training (I-VET) is usually carried out at upper secondary level and post-secondary level before students begin their working life. It takes place either in a school-based environment (mainly in the classroom) or in a work-based setting (such as training centres and companies). On average, 50% of young Europeans aged 15 to 19 participate in I-VET at upper secondary level. However, this average figure masks significant geographical differences across EU countries, as participation rates range from 15% to upwards of 70%.

Continuing VET (C-VET) usually takes place after initial education and training or after beginning working life. It aims to upgrade knowledge, to help people acquire new skills and to retrain and further their personal and professional development; it is largely work based.

European cooperation on VET dates back to 2002 and the [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/MEMO_04_293 Copenhagen process], when plans were put in place to enhance European cooperation, matching what had previously been done for higher education – the [https://education.ec.europa.eu/education-levels/higher-education/inclusive-and-connected-higher-education/bologna-process Bologna process] – with a similar process for VET. The principal objectives of the Copenhagen declaration included to
*develop a framework for the transparency of qualifications and competences
*cooperate in quality assurance
*establish a credit transfer system for VET
*strengthen policies, systems and practices for lifelong guidance
*support the development of qualifications and competences at sectoral level
*give attention to the learning needs of teachers and trainers.

Policy developments in relation to VET were subsequently enhanced, for example through the [https://education.ec.europa.eu/document/riga-conclusions Riga conclusions (2015)], which provided a new set of medium-term (2015–20) deliverables in the field of VET.

Subsequently, VET was identified as a focus area for cooperation under the European Education Area initiative. On 24 November 2020, the Council of the EU adopted a [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32020H1202(01) Recommendation on vocational education and training (VET) for sustainable competitiveness, social fairness and resilience] (2020/C 417/01). It defines key principles for ensuring that vocational education and training in the EU adapts swiftly to labour market needs and provides quality learning opportunities for young people and adults alike. It places a strong focus on the increased flexibility of vocational education and training, reinforced opportunities for work-based learning, apprenticeships and improved quality assurance.

On 30 November 2020, ministers in charge of vocational education and training from EU countries, European social partners and the European Commission endorsed the ''[https://www.cedefop.europa.eu/files/osnabrueck_declaration_eu2020.pdf Osnabrück Declaration on vocational education and training as an enabler of recovery and just transitions to digital and green economies]''. It sets out new policy actions for the period of 2021 to 2025 to complement the Council Recommendation on vocational education and training for sustainable competitiveness, social fairness and resilience, namely to
*promote resilience and excellence through quality, inclusive and flexible VET
*establish a new lifelong learning culture emphasising the relevance of C-VET and digitalisation
*foster the sustainability of VET
*develop a European education and training area and international VET.
</sesection>

<sesection>
===Adult learning activities===

Adult learning refers to a range of formal and informal learning activities, both general and vocational, undertaken by adults after leaving initial education and training. Individuals may pursue adult learning for a variety of reasons, for example, to
*enhance their employment prospects
*develop personally or professionally
*obtain transferrable skills, such as critical thinking.

The right to education, training and lifelong learning is enshrined in the European Pillar of Social Rights (principle 1). Furthermore, 1 of the headline targets in the Pillar of Social Rights is to have, by 2030, 60% of all adults participating in training every year.

A [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32021G1214(01) Council Resolution on a new European agenda for adult learning 2021-2030] (2021/C 504/02) adopted on 29 November 2021 highlights the need to increase adult participation significantly in formal, non-formal and informal learning. It focuses on 5 priority areas
*governance of adult learning
*supply and take-up of lifelong learning opportunities with sustainable funding
*accessibility and flexibility – to adapt to the needs of adults
*quality, equity, inclusion and success in adult learning – emphasising the professional development of adult learning staff, the mobility of both learners and staff, quality assurance and active support to disadvantaged groups
*green and digital transitions and related skill needs.
</sesection>

<sesection>
===Digital Education Action Plan===

The [https://ec.europa.eu/education/education-in-the-eu/digital-education-action-plan_en Digital Education Action Plan (2021–27)] (COM(2020) 624 final) is a renewed EU policy initiative to support the sustainable and effective adaptation of education and training systems to the digital age. It was adopted in September 2020 and contributes towards achieving a number of the European Commission’s priorities
*[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/europe-fit-digital-age_en A Europe fit for the digital age]
*[https://next-generation-eu.europa.eu/index_en NextGenerationEU], which aims to create a greener, more digital, healthy, strong and equal EU
*[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0625 the European Education Area] by 2025
*the [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1223&langId=en European Skills Agenda] by 2025
*the [https://op.europa.eu/webpub/empl/european-pillar-of-social-rights/en/ European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan], which includes 3 key social policy targets by 2030
*the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/europe-fit-digital-age/europes-digital-decade-digital-targets-2030_en Digital Decade], which has a number of specific targets and objectives to guide the EU’s digital transformation through to 2030.

The Digital Education Action Plan sets out 2 strategic priorities.
:1. Fostering the development of a high-performing digital education system, including
:*infrastructure, connectivity and digital equipment
:*effective digital capacity planning and development, including up-to-date organisational capabilities
:*digitally competent and confident teachers and education and training staff
:*high-quality learning content, user-friendly tools and secure platforms which respect e-privacy rules and ethical standards.
:2. Enhancing digital skills and competences for the digital transformation, requiring
:*basic digital skills and competences from an early age
:*digital literacy, including tackling disinformation
:*computing education
:*good knowledge and understanding of data-intensive technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI)
:*advanced digital skills, which produce more digital specialists
:*ensuring that girls and young women are equally represented in digital studies and careers.
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Green education ===

A wide range of initiatives and actions on the environment and sustainability are taking place in education and training across the EU. Indeed, education and training systems have the potential to provide a catalyst in the shift to a more sustainable society. However, a socially just transformation requires people to have the knowledge, skills and attitudes to shape and cope with these potentially profound changes.

The European Commission’s work in this field is designed to ensure that sustainability becomes a systemic feature of education policy and practice in the EU, for example
*a [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32022H0627(01) Council Recommendation on learning for the green transition and sustainable development] (2022/C 243/01) supports EU countries to embed sustainability into education and training programmes
*the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC128040 European sustainability competence framework] sets out the knowledge, skills and attitudes learners of all ages need to acquire for the green transition, as presented in the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en European Green Deal]
*[https://education.ec.europa.eu/about-eea/working-groups?#Environmental working groups on the green transition and sustainability] have been set up for school education and for vocational education and training, adult learning and higher education
*[https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/programme-guide/part-a/priorities-of-the-erasmus-programme Erasmus+] supports a range of initiatives related to sustainability in education and training
*the EU’s [https://learning-corner.learning.europa.eu/index_en Learning Corner] includes [https://learning-corner.learning.europa.eu/learning-materials_en?f%5B0%5D=topics_topics%3A11 teaching and learning materials on sustainability] and the climate crisis for primary and secondary schools.
</sesection>

<sesection>
===Education and training statistics===

The measurement of progress towards the objectives described above requires a broad range of comparable statistics. Eurostat’s education and training statistics describe education and training systems in the EU, alongside their outcomes, including data for
*participation in education and training (including adult learning)
*learning mobility
*education personnel
*education finance
*education and training outcomes
*language learning and self-reported language skills.

The standards for international statistics on education are set by 3 international organisations
*the [[Glossary:United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)|United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)]] Institute for Statistics (UIS)
*the [[Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)]]
*[[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], the statistical office of the EU.

The main source of data is a [[Glossary:UOE data collection|joint UNESCO/OECD/Eurostat (UOE) data collection]] on education statistics. This is the basis for the core components of Eurostat’s database on education statistics. In combination with the joint data collection, Eurostat also collects data on regional enrolments and foreign language learning. Education statistics for educational attainment and adult learning are principally provided through household surveys, in particular the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|EU labour force survey (EU-LFS)]], which is complemented by an [[Glossary:Adult education survey (AES)|adult education survey (AES)]] and the [[Glossary:Continuing vocational training survey (CVTS)|continuing vocational training survey (CVTS)]].

The UOE data collection exercise is based on administrative sources, with the data compiled by education ministries or national statistical authorities. Reference periods are the calendar year for data on expenditure and the school/academic year (classified to the calendar year in which the school/academic year finishes) for all other non-financial data.

The [https://uis.unesco.org/en/topic/international-standard-classification-education-isced international standard classification of education (ISCED)] is the basis for international education statistics, describing 9 different [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|levels of education]].

More information about the joint data collection is available in an article on the [[UNESCO_OECD_Eurostat_(UOE)_joint_data_collection_%E2%80%93_methodology|UOE methodology]].

Annual reports and country factsheets with key statistics pertaining to the EU’s programme supporting education, training, young people and sport – Erasmus+ – are available on the [https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/resources-and-tools/statistics-and-factsheets European Commission’s website].

title: Economy at regional level
text:
Eurostat regional yearbook; 2026 edition; flagship publication; EU; regional statistics; NUTS; economy; GDP; gross value added; income; net disposable income; employee compensation; hours worked; real labour productivity Data extracted in March 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 This article forms part of the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026]'', an annual [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications flagship publication]. It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the [[Glossary:EU|EU]], [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate]] countries. A [[Regional_yearbook_introduction#A_short_reading_guide|short reading guide]] is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps. Among EU regions, the French capital region of Ile-de-France had the highest share of the EU’s GDP (4.8% of the total in 2024). At the other end of the scale, the Finnish archipelago of Åland had the smallest share (0.009%). In 2024, 3 EU regions recorded GDP per inhabitant more than twice the EU average: the Irish regions of Eastern and Midland (2.68 times the average) and Southern (2.17 times), as well as Luxembourg (2.45 times).
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:Compet_icon_RYB2026_small.png|left]]
[[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH07_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ab669015-7d88-400c-8fae-ad324b467aa4?lang=en nama_10r_2gdp])|alt=An infographic based on a treemap showing the twenty EU regions with the largest shares of the EU’s GDP, in percent. Data are shown for NUTS level 2 regions for 2024. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:Infographics-CH07_RYB2026.png|thumb|right|380px|Which EU regions had the highest shares of GDP?]] Between 2008 and 2024, the EU economy grew overall by 18.2% in real terms, despite a series of atypical shocks, including the global financial and economic crisis, the European sovereign debt crisis, Brexit, the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. Such events have added to structural challenges – including climate change, ageing populations, weak productivity growth, inequality, and territorial disparities – while also exacerbating policy-driven issues such as energy security/supply and defence spending, as well as cyclical pressures like the cost-of-living crisis. The EU’s [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]] has fluctuated widely in recent years, reflecting the impact of these atypical shocks, with economic activity contracting in 2009 (down 4.3%), 2012 (down 0.8%) and 2020 (down 5.6%). By contrast, there were strong rebounds in 2021 (up 6.4%) and 2022 (up 3.5%), followed by modest rates of growth in 2023 (up 0.4%) and 2024 (up 1.1%). The French capital region of Ile-de-France had the largest share of the EU’s GDP (4.8%) in 2024, nearly twice that of Lombardia in northern Italy (2.8%). There were 17 other regions that accounted for more than 1.0% of the EU’s GDP, including 6 from Germany, 3 from each of Spain and Italy, and 2 from each of France and the Netherlands. Among these 19 regions with the highest shares, 6 were capital regions – namely, those of France, Ireland, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands and Germany. These 19 regions with the highest shares of the EU’s GDP collectively accounted for 32.2% of economic output. By comparison, the 170 regions across the EU with the lowest levels of GDP together contributed a similar share (32.3%). ===Regional gross domestic product (GDP) and gross value added=== The EU’s GDP at market prices was €18.0 trillion in 2024, equivalent to an average of €39 900 per inhabitant. However, behind these aggregate figures, the performance of individual regions varied considerably. Patterns of regional economic development are explored in more detail below. '''Largest regional economies in the EU''' In 2024, 10 NUTS level 2 regions within the EU had GDP exceeding €250 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]]. The French capital region, Ile-de-France, had by far the largest regional economy (€866 billion), followed by Lombardia in northern Italy (€505 billion) and Oberbayern in southern Germany (€359 billion). Three other regions had GDP above €300 billion: Eastern and Midland (the capital region of Ireland), Comunidad de Madrid (Spain’s capital region) and Cataluña (also Spain). The remaining regions within the top 10 had GDP between €250 and €300 billion: Rhône-Alpes (France) and Stuttgart, Düsseldorf and Darmstadt (all Germany).
'''More about the data: measuring the size of an economy''' The central measure of national accounts, GDP, summarises the economic position of a country or a region. This well-known balance has traditionally been divided by the total number of inhabitants to create the derived indicator of GDP per inhabitant. While GDP continues to be used for monitoring economic developments, playing an important role in economic decision-making, it is complemented by other indicators to inform policy debates on, for example, social and environmental issues. This is because GDP does not take account of externalities such as environmental sustainability or other issues, like income distribution or social inclusion. These are increasingly seen as important drivers for [[Glossary:Sustainable development|sustainable development]] and the overall quality of life. In order to compensate for price level differences between countries, GDP can be converted using conversion factors known as [[Glossary:Purchasing power parities (PPPs)|purchasing power parities (PPPs)]]. The use of PPPs, rather than market [[Glossary:Exchange rate|exchange rates]], results in data being denominated in an artificial common currency unit called a [[Glossary:Purchasing power standard (PPS)|purchasing power standard (PPS)]]. In contrast to euro-based (€) series, a series denominated in PPS tends to have a levelling effect, as countries and regions with very high GDP per inhabitant in euro terms also tend to have relatively high price levels. For example, the cost of living in Luxembourg is generally much higher than the cost of living in Bulgaria. Regional economic statistics are usually reported in current price (or ‘nominal’) terms; in other words, their current value during the particular reference year in question. To make comparisons over time, it is usually more revealing to use a volume series, where values are adjusted to take account of price changes; in other words, they have been deflated. During periods of high inflation – such as the recent cost-of-living crisis – a time series presented in current price terms will show faster growth than a volume series. For example, suppose GDP rose from €100.0 billion to €110.0 billion, while inflation was 8.0%. In volume terms using the prices of the first year, GDP in the second year would be €101.85 billion, implying real growth of 1.85%, compared with a 10.0% increase in nominal terms.
'''''In 2024, GDP per inhabitant in the capital region of Ireland – Eastern and Midland – was 2.7 times as high as the EU average''''' '''Map 1''' is based on regional GDP per inhabitant, adjusted for purchasing power and expressed as an index relative to the EU average. It is an important measure, reflecting regional wealth and living standards. Furthermore, the EU’s cohesion policy uses this ratio to identify less-developed regions, targeting funding at those below 75% or 100% of the EU average, thereby aiming to reduce regional disparities and promote convergence. In 2024, the distribution of GDP per inhabitant was relatively skewed: 37% of NUTS level 2 regions – 90 out of 244 for which data are available – recorded levels at or above the EU average. In 2024, the highest levels of GDP per inhabitant in PPS were largely found in: *a band of regions stretching from the [[Glossary:Benelux|Benelux]] countries, down through Germany, into Austria and northern Italy *several of the EU’s capital regions, as well as another region in Ireland. There were 19 NUTS level 2 regions across the EU where GDP per inhabitant was at least 50% above the EU average in 2024. This group included: *11 capital regions, namely those of Ireland, Czechia, Belgium, Romania, Denmark, the Netherlands, Hungary, France, Poland, Slovakia and Sweden *Luxembourg *the Irish region of Southern *the German regions of Hamburg, Oberbayern and Stuttgart *the Dutch region of Utrecht *the northern Italian region of Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen *the Belgian region of Prov. Brabant wallon. Among these relatively ‘wealthy’ regions, the Irish capital region of Eastern and Midland had the highest level of regional GDP per inhabitant; its ratio was 2.7 times as high as the EU average in 2024. There were 2 other regions where GDP per inhabitant was more than 2.0 times as high as the EU average: Luxembourg (2.5) and another Irish region, Southern (2.2).
'''More about the data: comparing GDP per inhabitant across EU regions''' Some of the economic differences between regions may reflect the (sometimes artificial) administrative boundaries that are used to delineate regions. It is often the case that part of the income generated in ‘wealthy‘ regions may be attributed to labour input from commuters who live in surrounding regions where, among other possible advantages, housing and other costs may be lower. In addition, some regions with high levels of GDP are characterised by a strong presence of multinational enterprises. This may distort their levels of economic activity, especially if assets (for example, technology patents) are domiciled in a region. For example, the Southern region of Ireland hosts several of the world’s top technology and pharmaceutical businesses.
Across the vast majority of EU countries, capital regions had the highest level of GDP per inhabitant. In 2024, there were 3 exceptions: *Germany, where Hamburg, Oberbayern, Stuttgart, Darmstadt, Bremen and Braunschweig recorded higher levels than the capital region of Berlin *Italy, where Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen, Lombardia, Valle d’Aosta/Vallée d’Aoste, Provincia Autonoma di Trento and Emilia-Romagna recorded higher levels than the capital region of Lazio *Austria, where Salzburg recorded a higher level than the capital region of Wien. '''Map 1''' also shows that many regions with relatively low levels of GDP per inhabitant were concentrated in south-east Europe or the EU’s outermost regions. In 2024, 12 NUTS level 2 regions had GDP per inhabitant below 50% of the EU average: * 2 French regions, with Mayotte (30%) and Guyane (41%) recording the lowest values across the EU * 5 Greek regions * 3 Bulgarian regions *single regions from Hungary and Romania.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]]
Map 1: GDP per inhabitant
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ab669015-7d88-400c-8fae-ad324b467aa4?lang=en nama_10r_2gdp]) [[Image:Compet_icon_RYB2026_small.png|left]] [[Image:GDP per inhabitant (index relative to EU average = 100, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: GDP per inhabitant
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ab669015-7d88-400c-8fae-ad324b467aa4?lang=en nama_10r_2gdp])]] '''Map 2''' shows the overall change in GDP across EU regions between 2019 and 2024. It illustrates developments by comparing the last pre-COVID reference year with the most recent available data, highlighting regions that have returned to – or remain below – their pre-pandemic levels of economic activity. Between 2019 and 2024, the EU’s GDP grew overall by 5.6% in real terms. Developments across the 244 NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available varied considerably. A total of 197 regions recorded positive growth, with higher levels of economic activity in 2024 than in 2019. By contrast, GDP fell across 46 regions, and remained unchanged in a single region. The most robust GDP growth was recorded in the Irish capital region of Eastern and Midland – which also had the highest GDP per inhabitant – as GDP rose 38.0% between 2019 and 2024. The other 2 Irish regions also saw very high increases: Northern and Western up 36.4% (the second highest in the EU) and Southern up 26.0% (sixth highest). Outside of Ireland, the highest growth rates were in: *the Romanian capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov (up 33.0%) *Malta (up 32.9%) *the French outermost region of Mayotte (up 32.1%). Almost all of the EU’s capital regions recorded an expansion in economic activity during the period under consideration, with Helsinki-Uusimaa (Finland) the only exception; its GDP fell 1.9% in real terms. The largest contraction in economic activity between 2019 and 2024 was registered in the Bulgarian region of Yugoiztochen, where GDP fell 20.5%, reflecting, among other factors, structural economic challenges, weak investment, low productivity and demographic pressures. There were 4 other regions that recorded double-digit contractions: *Dytiki Makedonia (Greece) *Groningen (the Netherlands), where natural gas extraction from the main gas field was phased-out in 2024 *Sud-Muntenia and Sud-Vest Oltenia (both Romania).
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]]
Map 2: Change in GDP
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ae67be32-0ec7-4846-8841-38798a69f4e1?lang=en nama_10r_2gvagr]) [[Image:Compet_icon_RYB2026_small.png|left]] [[Image:Change in GDP (% in real terms, by NUTS 2 regions, 2019–24)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 2: Change in GDP
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ae67be32-0ec7-4846-8841-38798a69f4e1?lang=en nama_10r_2gvagr])]] ===Income=== '''Net disposable income''' Having analysed GDP from the [[Glossary:Output approach|output side]], this section examines income. The focus is on [[Glossary:Household_disposable_income|net disposable income]], which includes earnings from wages and salaries, self-employment and income from investments such as interest, dividends and rents. Net disposable income represents the total amount of money households have available for spending and saving, after deducting taxes and mandatory social contributions, and including any transfers or benefits they receive from the government. In 2023, net disposable income across the EU was €9 461 billion, which was €703 billion higher than in 2022, representing an increase of 8.0%; note that during this period, both wages and salaries and the general cost of living were rising relatively quickly. When expressed in relation to the total population, net disposable income in the EU averaged €21 000 per inhabitant in 2023. This monetary average was slightly skewed, as 130 out of 244 NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available (53.3% of all regions) had net disposable income per inhabitant higher than the EU average. '''Map 3''' shows that some of the highest levels of net disposable income per inhabitant were concentrated in the Benelux countries, Denmark, Germany, Ireland and Austria. Across NUTS level 2 regions, Luxembourg recorded the highest average, as net disposable income per inhabitant stood at €39 700 in 2023. This was followed, at some distance, by Oberbayern in Germany (€34 700) and the Belgian region of Prov. Vlaams-Brabant (€31 700). There were 8 other regions where net disposable income was at least €30 000 per inhabitant, 5 of which were in Germany (concentrated in the south) and 3 in Belgium (in the north and centre). At the other end of the range, there were 18 NUTS level 2 regions where net disposable income was less than €10 000 per inhabitant in 2023: *a majority were concentrated in Romania (7 regions), Bulgaria (5 regions) and Hungary (4 regions) *while there were also single regions from France and Poland. In 2023, the lowest level of net disposable income among NUTS level 2 regions was recorded in the Bulgarian region of Severozapaden (€6 100 per inhabitant). As such, net disposable income per inhabitant in Luxembourg was 6.5 times as high as in Severozapaden. Note that these figures are expressed in euro terms and do not account for differences in local price levels. Regions with high euro-denominated incomes tend to also have a higher cost of living – for example, prices in Luxembourg are generally higher than those in Bulgaria. Map 3: Net disposable income
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4619613e-e763-42db-8c92-745eff186c84?lang=en nama_10r_2hhinc]) [[Image:Net disposable income (EUR per inhabitant, by NUTS 2 regions, 2023)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 3: Net disposable income
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4619613e-e763-42db-8c92-745eff186c84?lang=en nama_10r_2hhinc])]] '''Net disposable income per inhabitant relative to GDP per inhabitant'''
'''More about the data: analysing regional statistics for net disposable income''' Economic hubs across the EU tend to drive wealth creation. Part of the output generated in these regions, however, comes from commuters who live in surrounding regions (or even other countries). In regional accounts, GDP is recorded where it is generated (the place of work), whereas income is recorded where people live (their place of residence). Consequently, the ratio of net disposable income per inhabitant to GDP per inhabitant is generally lower in regions that concentrate economic activity – for example, capital regions and other major urban centres – and higher in surrounding regions where a significant part of the workforce commutes to work elsewhere. For example, the regional economy of the Czech capital region of Praha benefits from inflows of commuters from the surrounding region of Střední Čechy. In a similar vein, the relatively high level of GDP per inhabitant recorded in Luxembourg may, at least in part, be attributed to the impact of cross-border commuters from the neighbouring regions of Prov. Luxembourg (Belgium), Trier (Germany) and Lorraine (France). The types of economic activities located within individual regions also affect the relationship between net disposable income and GDP. In regions specialised in activities characterised by higher levels of productivity (such as pharmaceutical manufacturing or information and communication technology), average wages and salaries tend to be relatively high, while remuneration often represents a smaller share of value added. By contrast, average wages and salaries tend to be lower in regions specialised in less-productive activities, such as agriculture or tourism-related activities.
In 2023, net disposable income averaged €21 000 per inhabitant across the EU, while GDP per inhabitant was €38 400. As such, net disposable income per inhabitant accounted for 55% of GDP per inhabitant. Looking back to 2019, the share of net disposable income in GDP was also 55%, suggesting that disposable incomes have grown at a similar pace to GDP in recent years. '''Map 4''' presents the latest developments in net disposable income per inhabitant relative to GDP per inhabitant; the data are expressed as an index with 2019 set equal to 100.0. This indicator reflects changes in residents’ purchasing power relative to regional economic output. Values above 100.0 indicate that disposable incomes grew faster (or declined slower) than GDP between 2019 and 2023, while values below 100.0 indicate slower income growth. Across NUTS level 2 regions, there were few clear patterns to the development of net disposable income relative to GDP between 2019 and 2023. Lower indices were generally observed in peripheral regions of the EU. By contrast, higher indices were often concentrated along a west–east corridor, starting in France, extending through Belgium and the Netherlands, continuing across Germany and Austria, and reaching into Czechia, Hungary and eastern Poland. The fastest income growth was concentrated in Czechia, where net disposable incomes rose more than 10% faster than GDP in a majority of regions. The only exceptions were Severovýchod, Praha and Jihovýchod, where incomes still grew faster than economic output. Outside Czechia, only 2 other regions saw income growth exceed GDP growth by more than 10%: Dytiki Makedonia in northern Greece (which recorded the fastest relative growth across the EU) and the westernmost region of Hungary, Nyugat-Dunántúl. In Dytiki Makedonia, there was almost no change in GDP per inhabitant between 2019 and 2023, up from €15 200 to €15 500 (an increase of 2.0%), while net disposable income per inhabitant grew from €10 700 to €13 200 (an increase of 23.4%). Between 2019 and 2023, there were 118 NUTS level 2 regions across the EU where GDP grew faster (or declined more slowly) than net disposable income. There were 4 regions that recorded indices in 2023 that were below 90.0, as rapid economic growth outpaced income growth: *Severozapaden and Yugoiztochen in Bulgaria *Northern and Western in Ireland *Cyprus. Map 4: Net disposable income per inhabitant as a share of GDP per inhabitant
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes:[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/26dc5f09-0d0d-4c50-bef9-8a35cfae55ef?lang=en nama_10r_2hhinc] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/152bae28-dd06-487c-a169-ac0071892837?lang=en nama_10r_2gdp]) [[Image:Net disposable income per inhabitant (index relative to 2019 = 100.0, by NUTS 2 regions, 2023)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 4: Net disposable income per inhabitant as a share of GDP per inhabitant
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes:[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/26dc5f09-0d0d-4c50-bef9-8a35cfae55ef?lang=en nama_10r_2hhinc] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/152bae28-dd06-487c-a169-ac0071892837?lang=en nama_10r_2gdp])]] [[Glossary:Compensation of employees|Employee compensation]] is defined (within national accounts) as remuneration, in cash or in kind (such as a company car or vouchers for meals), payable by an employer to an employee in return for work done; it also includes payments linked to social contributions (such as health or pension contributions). In 2023, the compensation of employees across the EU was valued at €8.12 billion, compared with €9.46 billion for net disposable income; as such, employee compensation accounted for 85.9% of net disposable income. Across NUTS level 2 regions, this share ranged from a low of 39.9% in the Greek island region of Ionia Nisia to a high of 125.1% in the Danish capital region of Hovedstaden. The high share in Hovedstaden may reflect, among other factors: *a substantial proportion of compensation being paid in taxes and social contributions *households acting as net contributors, paying more in taxes and contributions than they receive in benefits (a common feature for ‘wealthier’ regions) *high housing costs and borrowing (which can result in negative net property income and reduced levels of disposable income) *commuting effects (which increase compensation recorded in capital regions). Alongside the Danish capital region, similar patterns – with shares exceeding 100.0% – were also observed in the capital regions of Ireland, Sweden, Finland, the Netherlands, Croatia and France; this was also the case in Luxembourg. These observations underline that employee compensation can represent a relatively high share of net disposable income in (capital) regions with high wages and salaries, significant taxation and substantial income redistribution, especially if a large proportion of the workforce earning wages and salaries resides outside the region. '''Map 5''' presents information on the compensation of employees as a share of net disposable income. This indicator can be used to analyse the structure of household income and the relative importance of wages and salaries compared with other sources of income, such as investments or social transfers. A higher share suggests that income is primarily driven by wages and salaries, while a lower share indicates that non-labour sources may contribute more substantially to households’ net disposable income. It should be noted that employee compensation is recorded before deductions for income taxes and social contributions, whereas net disposable income is measured after these deductions. '''Map 5''' presents regional data for NUTS level 2 regions in 2023, expressed as an index with the national average set equal to 100.0. Values above this level indicate that employee compensation accounts for a larger share of household income than the national average (this is often the case in regions with higher wages and salaries, significant taxation and extensive redistribution). Lower values tend to be found in regions characterised by lower wages and salaries or where non-labour sources (such as property or investment income) make up a larger portion of households’ net disposable income. High indices were particularly evident in several capital regions. The Romanian capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov recorded the highest value across NUTS level 2 regions in 2023, as employee compensation was equal to 96.4% of net disposable income, which was 132.5% of the national average (72.7%). Relatively high index values were also observed in 3 other eastern capital regions: Bratislavský kraj in Slovakia (122.9% of the national average), Grad Zagreb in Croatia (119.1%) and Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (117.2%). There were 3 other regions that recorded indices of at least 115.0%: the northern Italian region of Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen (116.6%), as well as the capital regions of France (115.6%) and Spain (115.0%). At the other end of the range, there were 16 NUTS level 2 regions where the share of employee compensation in net disposable income was lower than 85.0% of the national average in 2023. This group was composed of: *3 regions from each of Italy and Romania *2 regions from each of Bulgaria and Greece *single regions from Germany, Spain, France, Poland, Portugal and Slovakia. Some of the lowest regional shares were recorded in relatively rural areas that are well known as tourist destinations, including the Greek island regions of Ionia Nisia and Notio Aigaio, the southern Italian regions of Calabria and Sicilia, the Algarve in southern Portugal, and Principado de Asturias in northern Spain. In these regions that are popular with tourists, the share of employee compensation in net disposable income is often relatively low because a substantial portion of household income comes from non-labour sources. High-value property or capital ownership can generate significant non-wage income through rentals or business profits, while the compensation of employees is often seasonal, part-time and relatively low. Map 5: Employee compensation as a share of net disposable income
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c983160f-4143-426b-a3a4-5ca36c965ad2?lang=en nama_10r_2hhinc]) [[Image:Employee compensation as a share of net disposable income (index relative to national average = 100.0, by NUTS 2 regions, 2023)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 5: Employee compensation as a share of net disposable income
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c983160f-4143-426b-a3a4-5ca36c965ad2?lang=en nama_10r_2hhinc])]] === Productivity indicators === '''Hours worked per employee in industry''' The final section of this chapter presents information on productivity indicators. It includes measures for hours worked per employee (which can reveal differences in work patterns) and employment and real labour productivity which capture the output generated by workers. Together, these indicators highlight regional variations in labour market structure, labour utilisation and efficiency, providing an insight into differences in regional economic performance. The data shown in '''Map 6''' relate to the industrial economy, as defined by [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] Rev. 2 Sections B to E. In 2023, the EU’s industrial economy had 31.6 million employees. Together, they worked a total of 52.2 billion hours, equivalent to 1 651 hours per employee, or an average of 31.7 hours per week. Note that this figure is a simple calculation based on the absolute values for hours worked and employees, and it does not account for time off – including holidays or sickness – which would likely increase the average number of hours worked by each employee. Equally, it does not take account of part-time or seasonal work. In 2023, there were 18 NUTS level 2 regions where industrial employees worked an average of at least 2 000 hours. These regions were concentrated in just three EU countries: 10 from Poland, 6 from Greece and 2 from Croatia. The highest average was recorded in the Croatian capital region of Grad Zagreb, at 2 575 hours per employee. Across the EU, the average number of hours worked by industrial employees fell modestly between 2019 and 2023, from 1 670 to 1 651 hours per employee; equivalent to a decrease of almost 20 hours per employee. Expressed as an index with 2019 set equal to 100.0, the EU index for hours worked per industrial employee stood at 98.8 in 2023. In '''Map 6''', values below 100.0 indicate that average hours worked per industrial employee declined. This may reflect factors such as more part-time or seasonal work, reduced or shared working hours, organisational changes or temporary labour market disruptions. Most decreases were modest. The largest declines – more than 10.0% – were recorded in the Croatian region of Sjeverna Hrvatska, the Spanish region of Ciudad de Ceuta, the Greek region of Dytiki Makedonia and the Irish region of Northern and Western. By contrast, values above 100.0 indicate that average hours worked per industrial employee rose, because the total number of hours worked increased faster (or decreased more slowly) than the number of employees. Increases were generally modest – less than 5.0% – although there were several regions in southern and eastern EU countries that reported higher increases: *Grad Zagreb and Jadranska Hrvatska in Croatia (note that both have a break in series) *Calabria, Valle d’Aosta/Vallée d’Aoste, Basilicata and Puglia in Italy *Peloponnisos in Greece. Map 6: Hours worked per employee in industry
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c983160f-4143-426b-a3a4-5ca36c965ad2?lang=en nama_10r_3empers] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ae6ccbb9-2835-4a01-8d7e-995cf1441a37?lang=en nama_10r_2emhrw]) [[Image:Hours worked per employee in industry (index relative to 2019 = 100.0, by NUTS 2 regions, 2023)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 6: Hours worked per employee in industry
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c983160f-4143-426b-a3a4-5ca36c965ad2?lang=en nama_10r_3empers] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ae6ccbb9-2835-4a01-8d7e-995cf1441a37?lang=en nama_10r_2emhrw])]] '''Employment and real labour productivity'''
'''More about the data: analysing regional statistics for labour productivity''' Labour productivity can be defined as GDP (or gross value added) divided by a measure of labour input, typically the number of people employed or the total number of hours worked. The information presented in '''Map 7''' is based on labour productivity per hour worked, which should not be influenced by changes in the structure of the employment market. For instance, the ratio is not impacted if there is a shift from full-time to part-time work, or if working hours are curtailed (for example, due to labour market restrictions). High labour productivity may be linked to the efficient use of labour and/or reflect the skills and experience of the labour force. These in turn may result from the specific mix of activities present in each regional economy as some activities, for example, knowledge-intensive industrial activities and business or financial services tend to be characterised by higher levels of labour productivity (as well as higher levels of employee compensation).
In 2019, the number of people employed across the EU stood at 209.9 million. By 2023, this had increased by 7.8 million (3.7%), reaching 217.7 million. In 2023, each person working in the EU generated an average of €49.3 of value per hour worked. When expressed in constant (2020) prices, this figure can be used to construct indices that measure real productivity changes adjusted for inflation. '''Map 7''' shows the development of employment and real labour productivity between 2019 and 2023 for NUTS level 2 regions. Values above 100.0 indicate that a region experienced an increase in employment and/or real productivity during this period. The vast majority of EU regions saw employment growth between 2019 and 2023, up in 202 out of 232 regions for which a complete set of information are available. While the EU-wide average increase was 3.7%, several regions recorded double-digit employment growth: *Sjeverna Hrvatska in Croatia, which had the largest expansion, at 29.8% (note there is a break in series) *4 of the French outermost regions (all except Mayotte) *all 3 Irish regions *Pest in Hungary *Luxembourg and Malta. A majority of NUTS level 2 regions across the EU also reported an increase in real labour productivity between 2019 and 2023, with 147 out of 232 regions reporting growth. Real labour productivity in the EU rose by 2.2%, while 24 regions recorded double-digit increases. These regions were predominantly located in eastern EU countries, with the highest counts in Croatia (all 4 regions), Bulgaria, Romania and Slovakia (3 regions each), Poland (2 regions) and a single region from Hungary. The remainder of this group included all 3 regions of Ireland, 2 regions from Austria, the French outermost region of Mayotte, the Lithuanian capital region of Sostinės regionas, and Malta. Between 2019 and 2023, 6 regions recorded at least 10.0% growth for both employment and real labour productivity. This group comprised: *all 3 Irish regions *Sjeverna Hrvatska in Croatia *Pest in Hungary *Malta. By contrast, there was only 1 region in the EU that experienced declines of at least 5.0% for both employment and real labour productivity between 2019 and 2023. In the Romanian region of Sud-Muntenia, employment decreased 9.5%, while real labour productivity fell 7.7%. Any declines in employment and real labour productivity may reflect a combination of factors, including the sectoral composition of regional economies – where activity is concentrated in vulnerable industries such as agriculture or traditional manufacturing – outflows of labour to other regions or abroad, and structural challenges such as low levels of investment.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]]
Map 7: Employment and real labour productivity
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e5473bd5-c5d5-4869-8e27-7cf97de42b8a?lang=en nama_10r_3empers], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/671e4667-6b47-4ef6-b7dc-ecb1d69847b9?lang=en nama_10r_2rlp], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f4de0626-3589-4f7c-b714-2c62d15ad791?lang=en nama_10_pe] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b8b32a3b-dc80-4974-8364-be3e82b71282?lang=en nama_10_lp_ulc]) [[Image:Compet_icon_RYB2026_small.png|left]] [[Image:Employment and real labour productivity (index relative to 2019 = 100.0, by NUTS 2 regions, 2023)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 7: Employment and real labour productivity
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e5473bd5-c5d5-4869-8e27-7cf97de42b8a?lang=en nama_10r_3empers], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/671e4667-6b47-4ef6-b7dc-ecb1d69847b9?lang=en nama_10r_2rlp], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f4de0626-3589-4f7c-b714-2c62d15ad791?lang=en nama_10_pe] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b8b32a3b-dc80-4974-8364-be3e82b71282?lang=en nama_10_lp_ulc])]] ===Source data for figures and maps=== {{Template:Excel|filename=RYB2026 CH07Economy.xlsx|title=Regional economic statistics}} ===Data sources=== '''European system of national and regional accounts''' The [[Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)|European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)]] is the latest internationally compatible accounting framework for a systematic and detailed description of the EU economy. [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-2010/overview ESA 2010] has been implemented since September 2014 and is consistent with worldwide guidelines on national accounting, as set out in the [[Glossary:System of national accounts (SNA)|system of national accounts (2008 SNA)]]. ESA 2010 provides a framework for consistent, comparable, reliable and up-to-date economic statistics for EU countries. The legal basis for these statistics is ''{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32013R0549:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 549/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 May 2013 on the European system of national and regional accounts in the European Union}}''. ESA 2010 is not restricted to annual national accounting, as it also applies to regional accounts and to quarterly and shorter period accounts. It is harmonised with the concepts and classifications used in many other social and economic statistics (for example, statistics on employment, business or international trade) and as such serves as a central reference for socio-economic statistics. '''Regional data''' Statistics from regional economic accounts are presented here for NUTS level 2 regions (more detailed/granular information at NUTS level 3 is available for GDP, gross value added at basic prices and employment). The data for statistical regions in the EFTA and candidate countries are sometimes unavailable and have been replaced (where appropriate) by national aggregates. Data for non-EU countries are sometimes only available for earlier reference periods when compared with those presented for EU regions; all discrepancies are footnoted under maps and figures. '''Indicator definitions''' '''''Gross domestic product and value added''''': gross domestic product (GDP) is a measure of the overall size of an economy. As an aggregate measure of production, GDP is equal to the sum of the gross value added of all resident institutional units engaged in production, plus any taxes on products and minus any subsidies on products. '''''Income''''': the distribution and redistribution of income results in balancing items, namely [[Glossary:Allocation of primary income account|primary income]] and [[Glossary:Household_disposable_income|disposable income]]. In regional accounts, these income measures are limited to households. '''''Compensation of employees and labour productivity''''': in national accounts, the compensation of employees is defined as the total remuneration, in cash or in kind, payable by an employer to an employee in return for work done by the latter during an accounting period. It consists of wages and salaries in cash or in kind and employer’s actual and imputed social contributions. Labour productivity reflects the (average) amount of goods and services produced relative to a measure of labour input; it can be measured in a variety of ways. For example, GDP relative to the number of employed people or relative to the total number of hours worked. In both cases, the resulting ratio for a country or a region can subsequently be expressed as an index (relative to the EU average, the national average, or a specific reference year). ===Context=== With the arrival of a new European Commission, [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029_en 7 priorities for 2024 to 2029] were identified, including 3 with a direct impact on the economy: *[https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/competitiveness_en a new plan for Europe’s sustainable prosperity and competitiveness] *[https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/european-social-fairness_en supporting people, strengthening our societies and our social model] *[https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/global-europe_en a global Europe: leveraging our power and partnerships]. In December 2020, the [https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/eu-budget/long-term-eu-budget/2021-2027_en multiannual financial framework covering the period 2021 to 2027] was adopted. This provided resources to kick-start the European economy, through boosting the green and digital transitions, and making it fairer, more resilient and more sustainable for future generations. An emergency European Recovery Instrument (also known as [https://next-generation-eu.europa.eu/index_en Next Generation EU]) reinforced the framework, providing a plan that was designed to ensure the EU could emerge stronger from the COVID-19 crisis. The plan seeks to transform economies and societies so they work for everyone, setting a blueprint for a new growth model based on a clean, innovative and inclusive economy and digital and tech sovereignty. The framework for [https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/policy/what/investment-policy_en EU cohesion policy] dates back to 1986 and the ''Single European Act''. This sought to enhance regional policies by ensuring balanced development, as well as social, economic and territorial cohesion. The intent of regional policies is not the transfer of economic wealth from relatively affluent to less affluent regions, but rather support for programmes that aim to resolve regional issues. Cohesion policy is an active form of solidarity that includes measures designed – through strategic investment – to boost economic growth, jobs, the quality of life, as well as green and digital transitions. It plays a role in 5 key areas: *'''a smarter Europe''' – for example, through innovation and digitisation, economic transformation and support for SMEs *'''a greener, low carbon transition to zero carbon economy''' – investing in energy transition, renewables and the fight against climate change, and providing support to those territories most affected by the socio-economic impact of the transition to climate neutrality *'''a better connected Europe''' – enhancing mobility and highlighting strategic transport and digital networks, for example, investing in the digital transition to expand very-high-speed internet access, boost digital skills, and investing in information technology equipment *'''a more social and inclusive Europe''' – supporting quality employment, education, skills, social inclusion and equal access to healthcare *'''a Europe closer to its citizens''' – promoting locally led development by fostering sustainable and integrated development across all types of territories. To reach these goals, the EU has set aside €392 billion for economic, social and territorial cohesion during the period 2021 to 2027. This support is principally delivered through 4 key instruments, namely the [https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/funding/erdf_en European Regional Development Fund], the [https://european-social-fund-plus.ec.europa.eu/en European Social Fund+], the [https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/funding/cohesion-fund_en Cohesion Fund] and the [https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/funding/just-transition-fund_en Just Transition Fund]. Regional accounts are important in this context, as they are used, among other purposes, to decide upon the regional allocation of cohesion policy expenditure. As of 2021, the rules for allocating funding became simpler: they were tailored to locally led development strategies that continue to take account of GDP per inhabitant, alongside information on the socio-economic and environmental situation (for example, youth unemployment rates, low levels of educational attainment, the reception and integration of migrants, or climate change). ===Other
