title: Educational attainment statistics
text:
This article provides statistics on levels of education by country, age group and sex of the population of the European Union, EFTA and candidate countries Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: May 2027 In 2025, 45% of 25-34-year-olds in the EU had completed tertiary education. In 2025, 86% of 20-24-year-olds in the EU had completed at least an upper secondary education. [[Image:Population aged 25-74 by educational attainment level, EU, 2015-2025_(% of the population aged 25-74).png|thumb|center|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a8ef3d0b-e022-4133-bc71-76617d510694?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-17T11:05:21Z edat_lfs_9903])|alt= Line chart showing population aged 25 to 74 years by educational attainment level as a percentage of the total population aged 25 to 74 years in the EU. Three lines represent ISCED levels zero to two, levels three and four, and levels five to eight over the years 2015 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article provides recent statistics on [[Glossary:Education|education]] levels by country, age group and sex of the population in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]], [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate]] countries. The article forms part of the online publication [[Education_and_training_in_the_EU_-_facts_and_figures|Education and training in the EU - facts and figures]]. Educational attainment plays a major role in the labour market, in the lives of individuals and in society in general. Higher levels of education usually lead to higher rates of employment, higher productivity and higher lifetime earnings for individuals and greater life satisfaction. More generally, having at least an upper secondary education is often considered as the minimum level needed to fully participate in society and lead a fulfilling life. This article looks at 3 main levels of educational attainment # low (lower than primary, primary and lower secondary education) # medium (upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education) # high (tertiary education, i.e. education provided by universities and other higher education institutions) Relevant [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/education-and-training/information-data/policy-context EU level targets] related to educational attainment are also presented. ===Distribution of the EU population by educational attainment in 2025=== * 21.2% of people aged 25-74 in the EU had a low educational attainment level * 44.4% had a medium educational attainment level (9.5% had a general qualification and 34.9% a vocational qualification) * 34.3% had a high educational attainment level, i.e. tertiary education [[Image:Distribution of the population aged 25-74 by educational attainment level, 2025_(% of the population aged 25-74).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Distribution of the population aged 25-74 years by educational attainment level, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a845cce2-030c-4d2c-bbd9-965e118f2983?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-17T10:53:37Z edat_lfs_9903])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing the distribution of the population aged 25 to 74 years by educational attainment level as a percentage of the total population aged 25 to 74 years in the EU, the EU Member States, the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries. Totaling 100 percent, each country column has four stacks representing low, medium general orientation, medium vocational orientation and high levels of education for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''Educational attainment levels''' Figure 1 shows the distribution of the population aged 25-74 years by educational attainment level and how it varies among EU countries. The 3 different levels of educational attainment are * less than primary, primary or lower secondary level of education (International Standard Classification of Education ([[Glossary:ISCED|ISCED]]) 2011 levels 0–2) – referred to as a low educational attainment level or low level of education * upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (ISCED 2011 levels 3 and 4) – referred to as a medium educational attainment level or medium level of education; this level has information on whether the programme had a general or vocational orientation * tertiary education (ISCED 2011 levels 5–8) – referred to as a high educational attainment level or high level of education
The share of people with a low level of education ranged from 4.4% in Lithuania to 42.6% in Portugal. Lithuania, Poland, Czechia, Slovakia and Latvia had the lowest shares of people with a low level of education (all less than 10%), while Malta, Italy, Spain and Portugal had the highest (all above 35%). Ireland, Luxembourg, Sweden, Cyprus and Lithuania reported the highest shares of people with tertiary education (over 45%), while Romania and Italy reported the lowest shares (below 21%). Overall, the share of people with a high level of education ranged from 17.3% in Romania to 55.0% in Ireland. For the medium level of education, Spain, Portugal and Luxembourg had the lowest shares (below 30%), while Slovakia and Czechia had the highest (above 65%). For this educational level, a distinction between general and vocational qualifications is made, with vocational qualifications considered to be more relevant for the labour market because they are more job oriented. Looking at this distinction, the share of people that had a vocational qualification was higher than the one with a general qualification in almost all countries. The only exceptions were Cyprus, Greece, Portugal, Ireland, Spain and Malta. The extent to which these qualifications prevail in a country reflects both national education systems and labour markets. ===Development of educational attainment levels over the last 10 years=== Trends in educational attainment levels from 2015 to 2025 are illustrated in Figure 2 * the share of people aged 25-74 with tertiary education increased from 26.7% in 2015 to 34.3% in 2025 * the share of the population with a low level of education decreased from 27.3% in 2015 to 21.2% in 2025 * the share of people with a medium level of education slightly decreased from 46.1% in 2015 to 44.5% in 2025 The proportion of people with a low level of education was surpassed by those with tertiary education in 2016. Since then, the gap between these 2 groups has increased, with 13.1 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp) more people having tertiary education than a low level of education in 2025. [[Image:Population aged 25-74 by educational attainment level, EU, 2015-2025_(% of the population aged 25-74).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Population aged 25-74 years by educational attainment level, EU, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a8ef3d0b-e022-4133-bc71-76617d510694?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-17T11:05:21Z edat_lfs_9903])|alt= Line chart showing population aged 25 to 74 years by educational attainment level as a percentage of the total population aged 25 to 74 years in the EU. Three lines represent ISCED levels zero to two, levels three and four, and levels five to eight over the years 2015 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Educational attainment levels vary between age groups=== Just like the overall development of educational attainment levels over time, the patterns of educational attainment levels across the EU population have also changed significantly. * On average, younger people attain higher levels of education than older people. In 2025, 83.4% of people aged 25-54 in the EU had attained at least an upper secondary level of education, compared with 71.7% of those aged 55-74 * Younger people (25-54 years) are less likely to have a low educational attainment level: 16.6% compared with 28.3% for the older age group (55-74 years). Those with a tertiary level of education amounted to 40.7% of the group aged 25-54 and 24.6% of the group aged 55-74 * The share of those with a medium level of education was 47.1% for the group aged 55-74 and thus somewhat higher than for the age group 25-54 where it was 42.8% (see Figures 3 and 4) Among the people in the EU with a medium level of educational attainment, the share of those with a vocational qualification was relatively similar for the 2 age groups: 76.9% for those aged 25-54 years and 80.9% for those aged 55-74 years. However, these shares varied a lot between countries. In Romania, vocational qualifications were common in both age groups: 95.1% for the younger age group and 96.5% for the older. For the older age group, an even higher share was reported for Germany (97.2%). By contrast, the lowest shares were in Cyprus (33.1% for those aged 25-54) and Portugal (12.0% for those aged 55-74). Moreover, significant differences between the age groups can be observed in countries with low shares of vocational qualifications. In Portugal, the share of vocational qualifications was more than three times higher for the younger age group (37.0% vs 12.0%). In Greece the share of the younger group outnumbered that of the older one by a factor of 1.7 (40.9% vs 24.6%). Similar but less pronounced patterns can be observed in Ireland, Spain and Cyprus. Reforms in the national education systems in favour of vocational training as well as labour market demand could explain these trends. [[Image:Distribution of the population aged 25-54 by educational attainment level, 2025_(% of the population aged 25-54).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Distribution of the population aged 25-54 by educational attainment level, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a40fe945-1940-46f2-98ee-e571a6bb6550?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-17T11:08:30Z edat_lfs_9903])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing the distribution of the population aged 25 to 54 years by educational attainment level as a percentage of the total population aged 25 to 54 years in the EU, the EU Member States, the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries. Totaling 100 percent, each country column has four stacks representing low, medium general orientation, medium vocational orientation and high levels of education for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] [[Image:Distribution of the population aged 55-74 by educational attainment level, 2025_(% of the population aged 55-74).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Distribution of the population aged 55-74 by educational attainment level, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fc596390-8cf0-4d2a-9994-75e2c92135b3?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-17T11:27:09Z edat_lfs_9903])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing the distribution of the population aged 55 to 74 years by educational attainment level as a percentage of the total population aged 55 to 74 years in the EU, the EU Member States, the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries. Totaling 100 percent, each country column has four stacks representing low, medium general orientation, medium vocational orientation and high levels of education for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Policy indicators for educational attainment=== As part of the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32021G0226(01):EN:NOT|title=strategic framework for the European Education Area}} several strategic priorities for 2021-2030 have been set and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/education-and-training/information-data/policy-context 7 EU level targets] have been agreed upon. Two indicators for educational attainment are used for policy monitoring * an EU-level target indicator for tertiary attainment * a complementary indicator for the share of people with at least an upper secondary education '''''Tertiary education is becoming increasingly important''''' Successfully completing tertiary education is becoming more important due to the increased demand for highly skilled individuals in the EU’s labour market. Higher education plays an essential role in society by fostering innovation, increasing economic development and growth, and improving more generally the population’s well-being. For more detailed information see the [[Tertiary_education_statistics|statistics explained article on tertiary education]]. In February 2021, the Council approved the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32021G0226(01):EN:NOT|title=Resolution on a strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training towards the European Education Area and beyond (2021-2030)}}. This resolution sets an EU-level target that the share of people aged 25-34 with a tertiary level of education should be at least 45% by 2030. Figure 5 shows the share of the population aged 25-34 with tertiary education in 2025. In the EU, this share amounted to 44.8%. Almost half the EU countries have already reached the target for 2030. The highest shares were in Ireland, Luxembourg, Lithuania and Cyprus, at 60% or more. By contrast, the lowest share of people with tertiary educational attainment was in Romania, where it was below 25%. [[Image:Population aged 25-34 with tertiary educational attainment (ISCED 5-8), 2025_(% of the population aged 25-34).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Population aged 25-34 years with tertiary educational attainment (ISCED 5-8), 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9029ec50-ddb2-48ef-8491-adb42ba900c6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-17T11:32:48Z edat_lfse_03])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing population aged 25 to 34 years with tertiary educational attainment ISCED levels five to eight as a percentage of population aged 25 to 34 years in the EU, the EU Member States, the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries for the year 2025. A line across all country columns represents the year 2030's EU level target. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''More women than men have a tertiary level of education''''' Across the EU, women had already reached the 2030 EU-level target in 2019: 45.1% of women aged 25-34 had completed tertiary education. In 2025, this share rose to 50.6%. The share of tertiary educational attainment for men in the same age group stood at 39.3% in 2025. The proportion of men with tertiary education has increased over the last 10 years but at a slower pace than for women. This has led to a slightly wider gender gap over time: 11.3 pp in 2025 vs 10.6 pp in 2015 (see Figure 6). [[Image:Population aged 25-34 with tertiary educational attainment (ISCED 5-8), by sex, EU, 2015-2025_(% of the population aged 25-34) .png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Population aged 25-34 years with tertiary educational attainment (ISCED 5-8), by sex, EU, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fdf0c398-ba3a-4183-b29c-ce17002da164?lang=en edat_lfse_03])|alt= Line chart showing population aged 25 to 34 years by sex with tertiary educational attainment ISCED levels five to eight as a percentage of population aged 25 to 34 years in the EU over the years 2015 to 2025. Four lines represent the total, males, females and the year 2030's EU level target. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Completion of upper secondary education is also of interest for policymakers''''' The share of people aged 20-24 with at least an upper secondary qualification has been agreed as a supplementary indicator to the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32021G0226(01):EN:NOT|title=EU level target}} for [[Early_leavers_from_education_and_training|early leavers from education and training]]. The skills and competences gained through upper secondary education are increasingly seen as the minimum requirements for a successful move into the labour market and the foundation for further learning and a fulfilling life. Figure 7 shows that, in 2025, the average share of people aged 20-24 in the EU with at least an upper secondary education was 85.7%. The EU countries with the lowest shares were in Luxembourg, Denmark and Germany, all below 80%. The highest shares were in Croatia, Greece and Ireland where it stood above 95%. Compared with 2015, this share increased in all countries except Cyprus, Finland, Austria, Slovenia, Czechia, Slovakia and Latvia. Portugal and Spain reported the largest increases, up 12.7 pp and 11.9 pp, respectively. [[Image:Population aged 20-24 with at least an upper secondary education (ISCED 3-8), 2015 and 2025_(% of the population aged 20-24).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 7: Population aged 20-24 years with at least an upper secondary education (ISCED 3-8), 2015 and 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b2482383-ee1b-4a86-87c7-901dccb83069?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-17T11:41:49Z edat_lfse_03])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing population aged 20 to 24 years with at least an upper secondary education ISCED levels three to eight as a percentage of the population aged 20 to 24 years in the EU, the EU Member States, the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries. Each country has two columns comparing the year 2015 with 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''More women than men have completed at least an upper secondary level of education''''' A higher proportion of women reached this level of education compared with men: 87.9% for women aged 20-24 and 83.6% for men in the same age group (see Figure 8). The share for women was higher than for men in all EU countries except in Romania, Bulgaria and Lithuania. In Slovakia, the shares were about the same for women and men. In Spain and Latvia, the differences between men and women were the largest, with 8.8 pp or more in favour of women. [[Image:Population aged 20-24 with at least an upper secondary education (ISCED 3-8) by sex, 2025_(% of the population aged 20-24).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 8: Population aged 20-24 years with at least an upper secondary education (ISCED 3-8) by sex, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bff6388f-8d7b-4164-854c-2fd45158fb39?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-17T11:46:25Z edat_lfse_03])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing population aged 20 to 24 years by sex with at least an upper secondary education ISCED levels three to eight as a percentage of the population aged 20 to 24 years in the EU, the EU Member States, the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries. Each country has two columns comparing men with women for the year 2025. A scatter plot over both columns highlights the total of each country. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Educational attainment 2026.xlsx |title=Educational attainment: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The EU [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)|Labour Force Survey (LFS)]] provides statistics on educational attainment. The EU-LFS is documented in this [[EU_labour_force_survey|background article]], which provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, and related concepts and definitions. Data on educational attainment are calculated as annual averages of quarterly data. For data on educational attainment based on the EU-LFS, the International Standard Classification of Education 2011 ([https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000219109.locale=en ISCED 2011]) has been applied since 2014. Up to 2013 [https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000111387 ISCED 1997] is used. Eurostat's online database presents data on educational attainment for four aggregates * less than primary, primary and lower secondary education (ISCED levels 0-2) * upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education (ISCED levels 3 and 4) * at least upper secondary education, i.e. upper secondary, post-secondary non-tertiary and tertiary education (ISCED 2011 levels 3-8, ISCED 1997 levels 3-6) * tertiary education (ISCED 2011 levels 5-8, ISCED 1997 levels 5 and 6) At this level of aggregation, data are comparable over time for all available countries except Austria and Estonia (see the reference metadata [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/edat1_esms.htm Educational attainment level and transition from education to work (based on EU-LFS]). As from 2021, for ISCED levels 3 and 4, a breakdown by general and vocational qualifications is available for all age groups. Up to 2020, this breakdown is only available for those aged 15-34. ===Context=== Educational attainment is the visible output of education systems and forms a measure of their success. For individuals, attainment levels have a major impact on the quality of life and job opportunities. The level of educational attainment people reach is measured according to the [[International_Standard_Classification_of_Education_(ISCED)|International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED)]]. The February 2021 {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32021G0226(01):EN:NOT|title=Council resolution on a strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training towards the European education area and beyond (2021-2030)}} builds on the previous frameworks for European cooperation in education and training (ET), namely the ET2010 and ET2020 frameworks. It fixes 5 strategic priorities: (i) improving quality, equity, inclusion and success for all; (ii) making lifelong learning and mobility a reality for all; (iii) enhancing competences and motivation among teaching professionals; (iv) reinforcing European higher education; and (v) supporting the green and digital transitions. The document also sets out [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/education-and-training/information-data/policy-context 7 EU level targets], the first 5 of which are to be achieved by 2030. The EU-level target for tertiary level attainment is that the share of persons aged 25-34 with tertiary educational attainment should be at least 45%. One supplementary indicator complementing the EU-level target on [[Glossary:Early_leaver_from_education_and_training|early leavers from education and training]] is the share of people aged 20-24 with at least an upper secondary qualification. For more information, see the [[Early_leavers_from_education_and_training|statistical explain article on the subject]]. Indicators for educational attainment – among others – are also used to reflect the principles of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/european-pillar-of-social-rights European Pillar of Social Rights] and to monitor the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/overview Sustainable Development Goals]. ===Other articles=== *[[EU_labour_force_survey_statistics|EU labour force survey statistics — online publication]] *[[Education_and_training_in_the_EU_-_facts_and_figures|Education and training in the EU — facts and figures]] ===Database=== title: Education statistics - STEM fields
text:
Insert short description for search engines Data extracted in Month YYYY Planned article update: Month YYYY This article presents statistics on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) education in the European Union (EU), focusing on three key indicators aligned with the Council Resolution on a strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training towards the European Education Area (2021-2030), approved by the Council (EPSCO) on 29 June 2026. To strengthen Europe’s competitiveness, innovation capacity, and gender equality, the EU proposes new 2030 targets for STEM enrolment at vocational (VET), tertiary, and doctoral (PhD) levels. It focuses on six closely related indicators: the share of students enrolled in STEM fields at tertiary level and in initial medium-level vocational education and training (VET), the distribution of these STEM students by sex, the share of students enrolled in ICT PhD programmes and the female share within these programmes. Using data from 2015 to 2024, it highlights how countries compare to EU-level benchmarks on the share of students enrolled in STEM and ICT, and how female participation has evolved over time. At upper-secondary vocational level, STEM enrolment stood at 34.1 % in the EU, up slightly since 2015, with Iceland reporting by far the highest share (60.9 %) and Luxemburg the lowest (26.8 %). In 2024, around one-third of tertiary students in the EU were enrolled in STEM fields, slightly below the policy benchmark of 32 % across the EU. Female participation in tertiary STEM reached roughly 32 %, meaning just under 2 out of every 5 STEM students were women. ICT PhD programmes remained a niche pathway: only 3.9 % of EU doctoral students were in ICT in 2024, with Luxembourg a clear outlier at more than 23 %, and women making up about one-quarter of ICT PhD students across the EU.
=== STEM in upper-secondary vocational education: modest EU growth, large national gaps === At initial upper-secondary VET level, STEM fields constitute a substantial share of enrolments. In the EU, the total share of students enrolled in STEM in this stream was 33.1 % in 2015 and increased slightly to 34.1 % in 2024, an absolute rise of 0.99 percentage points.[1] Enrolment peaked in 2021 (35.4), likely reflecting pre-pandemic stability in vocational training demand, before dropping to its lowest point in 2016 (33.1). In 2024, Iceland recorded the highest share of STEM students in initial upper-secondary VET, at 60.9 %. This was followed by Cyprus (60.3%) and Bulgaria (50.3%), which were almost double the EU average. At the other end of the spectrum, lowest shares were observed in Luxembourg (26.8%), Belgium (27.2) and Spain (29.0%). The gap between these two extremes was nearly 34 percentage points, illustrating how strongly national education systems differ in their emphasis on STEM in vocational pathways. Female participation in STEM at upper-secondary VET level has improved. The EU female share rose from 14.1 % in 2015 to about 16.1 % in 2024, an increase of just over 2 percentage points. Still, women remain under-represented, and country differences are again substantial. Romania stands out with the highest female share in STEM VET in 2024 (around 36.5 %), while Iceland shows one of the lowest female shares (about 8.9 %). This nearly 28-point range indicates that encouraging girls and young women into STEM vocational programmes remains a major challenge in many education systems. Over the past decade (2015–2025), the share of STEM programmes in vocational education and training (VET) increased by 0.99 percentage points across the EU as a whole. The highest increases occurred in Iceland (18.1 pp), Lithuania (11.9 pp) and Sweden (9.9 pp), whereas the highest decreases occurred in Greece (23.7 pp), Malta (8.5 pp) and Romania (7.8 pp).The female share of STEM VET in the EU increased by an average of 0.2 percentage points per annum between 2015 and 2025, rising from 14.1 to 16.1 percentage points. This increase was recorded in almost all EU countries; the highest increases were seen in Belgium (7.9 pp), Finland (5.9 pp) and Sweden (5.1 pp). However, it decreased in Greece, Portugal, Denmark and Iceland by 8.3 pp, 3.1%, 1.5 pp and 1.2 pp respectively. (Figure 2). === Tertiary STEM enrolment: close to the benchmark, but not consistently above it === At tertiary level, the EU benchmark foresees that at least 32 % of students should be enrolled in STEM fields.[2] In practice, the EU average has been close to, but slightly below, this target. Between 2016 and 2024, the EU share of tertiary STEM students fluctuated around 27–28 %. In 2016, it stood at 27.2 %, and by 2024 it was 27.1 %, a small decrease of 0.13 percentage points. Some countries are well above the EU average. In 2024, Ireland reported the highest share of tertiary STEM enrolment among the countries covered, at 37.4 %, clearly surpassing the EU benchmark. By contrast, Malta recorded the lowest share, at 13.2 %, less than half the target level. The distance between these two countries was over 24 percentage points, underlining the diverse role and attractiveness of STEM in different higher education systems. EU figures also show relative stability over time in many countries, rather than strong upward or downward trends. For example, Germany’s share of tertiary STEM students remained around 36–37 % across the period, consistently above the EU average but without major change. In some countries, such as Luxembourg, the share increased considerably, reflecting a growing focus on STEM in newly developed or expanded tertiary programmes. === Women in tertiary STEM: rising, but still below “two in five” === The benchmark for gender in tertiary STEM envisages that at least 2 out of every 5 STEM students should be female, corresponding to a share of 40 %.[2] EU data show that progress has been positive, but the target is not yet reached. The female share of tertiary STEM enrolment in the EU rose from about 31.0 % in 2016 to 32.2 % in 2024, an increase of roughly 1.3 percentage points. At country level, the picture is mixed. In 2024, Iceland recorded one of the highest female shares in tertiary STEM (around 40.7 %), clearly above the “two in five” benchmark. In contrast, Hungary posted a female share of about 24.9 %, nearly 7 percentage points below the EU average and far from the benchmark. Across countries with data, the range between the highest and lowest female shares in 2024 was about 16 percentage points. This variation suggests that some education systems have been more successful than others in making STEM fields attractive and accessible to women. === The share of students enrolled in ICT PhD programmes === ICT PhD programmes represent the most specialised level considered in this article. The policy guideline states that at least 5 % of doctoral students should be enrolled in ICT programmes.[3] EU-level data show that this target has not yet been met. In 2015, about 3.4 % of EU doctoral students were in ICT; by 2024 this had risen to 3.9 %, a modest increase of 0.52 percentage points. As with STEM more broadly, there are large national differences. In 2024, Luxembourg was a clear outlier, with more than 23.2 % of doctoral students enrolled in ICT, far exceeding the 5 % benchmark. By contrast, Denmark reported 0 %, meaning that no ICT PhD enrolments were recorded in the data for that year. The difference between these two countries was over 23 percentage points. Several other countries, including Estonia and Finland, also reported shares well above the EU average, while many remained closer to or below 5 %. === Women in ICT PhD programmes: under-represented but gaining ground === For ICT PhD programmes, the benchmark specifies that at least 1 out of every 3 students should be female, equivalent to a 33 % share.[3] The EU data show that female participation in ICT doctoral studies is still below this target but has improved over time. For the EU as a whole, the female share rose from 20.5 % in 2015 to 24.4 % in 2024, an increase of 3.9 percentage points. Country patterns again vary widely. Malta stands out with the highest female share in ICT PhD programmes in 2024 (45.5 %), well above the one-third benchmark. At the lower end of the range, Slovakia reported a female share of 18.3 %, substantially below both the EU average and the benchmark. The range between these extremes was over 27 percentage points. Other countries, such as Estonia and Ireland, have seen strong increases in female participation over the decade, moving closer to or above the benchmark. However, the overall EU picture indicates that women still represent a minority in ICT PhD programmes. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= Education statistics - STEM fields.xlsx |title= Education statistics - STEM fields: tables}} === Data sources === '''Source''' The standards for international statistics on education are set by 3 international organisations *the [[Glossary:United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)|United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)]] institute for statistics (UIS) *the [[Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)]] *[[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], the statistical office of the EU. The source of data used in this article is a [[Glossary:UOE data collection|joint UNESCO/OECD/Eurostat (UOE) data collection]] on education statistics, and this is the basis for the core components of Eurostat’s database on education statistics. In combination with the joint data collection, Eurostat also collects data on regional enrolments, foreign language learning and tertiary graduates with credit mobility. More information about the joint data collection is available in an article on the [[UNESCO_OECD_Eurostat_(UOE)_joint_data_collection_%E2%80%93_methodology|UOE methodology]]. '''Classification''' The [https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000219109 international standard classification of education (ISCED)] is the basis for international education statistics, describing 9 different [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|levels of education]]. Eurostat data by fields of education are classified according to the [https://www.uis.unesco.org/sites/default/files/medias/fichiers/2025/04/international-standard-classification-of-education-fields-of-education-and-training-2013-detailed-field-descriptions-2015-en.pdf ISCED-F 2013] classification. The fields of education – as classified by ISCED-F 2013 – are broad domains, branches or areas of content covered by an education programme or qualification. The classification has a 3-level hierarchy based on broad fields (the highest level), narrow fields (the second level) and detailed fields (the third level) of education. === Context === '''Tertiary education builds on secondary education by providing learning activities in specialised fields. It includes not only academic education, as commonly understood, but also advanced vocational and professional education. On 29 June 2026, the Council (EPSCO) approved a STEM Education Strategic Plan. The plan focuses on three key indicators aligned with the Council Resolution on a strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training towards the European Education Area (2021–2030). Although education and training systems have already taken steps to raise awareness and support action to improve STEM skills, a stronger focus on STEM education and training is needed to sustain competitiveness, preparedness and technological leadership. The three key indicators are as follows: * at least 45% of students in initial medium-level VET should be enrolled in STEM fields, and at least one in five of these students should be female; * at least 32% of tertiary-level students should be enrolled in STEM fields, and at least two in five of these students should be female; * at least 5% of students should be enrolled in ICT PhD programmes, and at least one in three of these students should be female. ''' === Other articles === *[[Name of related Statistics Explained articles or online publication]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/education-and-training/database Education and training (educ)], see: ::Participation in education and training (educ_part) :::Pupils and students - enrolments (educ_uoe_enr) === Thematic section === === Publications === *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-RA-07-002|title=Title of the publication}} ''Publications in Statistics Explained (either online publications or Statistical articles) should be in 'See also' above'' Classification of Education (ISCED) 2011] *[https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000232343 ISCED 2011 Operational Manual – Guidelines for classifying national education programmes and related qualifications] ISCED-F 2013] – fields of education *[https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/d14c857a-601d-438a-b878-4b4cebd0e10f/library/626093fd-6f18-4e18-83e8-722031c1f824/details UOE data collection on formal education – Manual on concepts, definitions and classifications] – 2025 edition *[[UNESCO_OECD_Eurostat_(UOE)_joint_data_collection_–_methodology|UNESCO OECD Eurostat (UOE) joint data collection – methodology]] === Legislation === *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R0452:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 452/2008}} of 23 April 2008 concerning the production and development of statistics on title: Educational expenditure statistics
text:
Statistics on EU educational expenditure cover the sources of funding from pre-primary to tertiary levels of education. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: August 2027 In 2023, public spending on education relative to gross domestic product (GDP) was highest in Sweden (6.8%), while it was lowest in Romania (3.0%). In 2023, financial aid from governments to households and students for tertiary education ranged from less than €20 per student in Latvia and Greece, to €8 204 in Denmark. This article presents education expenditure statistics in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] based on the [[Glossary:UOE data collection|joint UNESCO/OECD/Eurostat (UOE) data collection]] and forms part of an online publication titled [[Education_and_training_in_the_EU_-_facts_and_figures|Education and training in the EU – facts and figures]]. Expenditure on education may help foster economic growth, enhance [[Glossary:Productivity|productivity]], contribute to people’s personal and social development, and help reduce social inequalities. This article presents different sources of funding (such as by the government or by households), as well as education expenditure by educational institutions. It covers [[Glossary:Pre-primary_education|pre-primary]] to [[Glossary:Tertiary_education|tertiary]] levels of education, in other words expenditure on all levels of education except for [[Glossary:Participation_in_early_childhood_education|early childhood educational development]] (the latter defined by the [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|International standard classification of education (ISCED)]] level 0, category 010). ===Overall education expenditure=== [[Image:Expenditure on education (excluding early childhood educational development), by source of funds and type of transaction, 2023_(EUR million)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Expenditure on education (excluding early childhood educational development), by source of funds and type of transaction, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6fb1961b-289b-414b-bf63-740d720afd52?lang=en educ_uoe_fine01]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9c13c67f-fdbd-4d54-9e5a-125330b1147e?lang=en educ_uoe_fine02]), and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3b39a281-e785-487d-994a-e077b6e627ec?lang=en educ_uoe_fine03])|alt=A table showing expenditure on education (excluding early childhood educational development), by source of funds and type of transaction. Data are shown in millions of euro for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among EU countries, the funding of education mainly comes from government, with a smaller role for private sources (including households, enterprises, [[Glossary:Non-profit institution (NPI)|non-profit organisations]] and religious institutions), and an even smaller role for non-domestic sources (including international organisations such as the [[Glossary:United Nations (UN)|United Nations]] or the [[Glossary:World Bank|World Bank]]). *In 2023, the share of total education spending coming from governments among the EU countries ranged from 64.0% in Greece to 94.8% in Luxembourg. It should be noted that some government expenditure relates to payments and transfers for education to the non-educational private sector – this includes subsidies to households and students, as well as payments to other non-educational private entities. As such, this part is counted twice, once in government expenditure and a second time in the expenditure of households and other non-educational private entities. *The share of non-educational private sources (households and other private entities) was relatively high in some countries, between a fifth and a quarter in Portugal, Malta, and Spain, and above a quarter in Cyprus (27.1%) and Greece (28.3%). *The share of expenditure on education that came from non-domestic sources was 10.1% in Greece, 8.7% in Slovakia, 8.3% in Estonia, and 7.7% in Croatia (2022 data); elsewhere its share was at most 6.7%, and often 1.5% or lower. The highest overall levels of government expenditure on educational institutions were unsurprisingly recorded in the most populous EU countries: in 2023, expenditure peaked at €185.6 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] in Germany, followed by €142.7 billion in France. Figure 2 provides more information on [[Glossary:Public expenditure on education|public expenditure on education]], while Table 2 as well as Figures 3 and 4 provide more information on expenditure on educational institutions, not just from governments, but also from other sources. [[Image:Distribution of expenditure on education (excluding early childhood educational development) by level of education, 2023 (% of expenditure on education)A_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Distribution of expenditure on education (excluding early childhood educational development) by level of education, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/330713bc-b270-4be7-8ada-bdd1b816fd9c?lang=en educ_uoe_fine01])|alt=A stacked column chart showing the distribution of expenditure on education (excluding early childhood educational development) by level of education. Each column has four stacks representing different levels of education (pre-primary, primary and lower secondary, upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary, and tertiary). Data are shown in percent for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, the highest share of total expenditure on education in the EU (excluding Estonia, Ireland, and Croatia) was allocated to primary and lower secondary education, around two fifths (40.5%). The second largest share was for tertiary education, which accounted for over a quarter (26.3%) of total expenditure on education. The third largest share was for upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education, which accounted for over a fifth (21.2%) of the total. The smallest share of total expenditure on education was recorded for pre-primary education, at over a tenth (12.0%). In 2023, primary and lower secondary education accounted for the largest share of total expenditure on education in all the EU countries for which data are available – see Figure 1. This share ranged from 30.8% in Bulgaria to 52.4% in Luxembourg (the only EU country to record an absolute majority of its expenditure dedicated to primary and lower secondary education). In 2023, expenditure on tertiary education generally accounted for the second-highest share within EU countries, although there were 4 countries where the second-highest share was recorded for upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education: Belgium, Czechia, and Italy, as well as Luxembourg (where tertiary education had the smallest share among those education levels shown in Figure 1). Tertiary education accounted for around a fifth to a third of total education expenditure in nearly all of the EU countries for which data are available, with the exceptions being Luxembourg (11.0%) and Czechia (19.4%) below this range, and Austria (34.1%) and Denmark (38.1%) above it. Across the EU countries, upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education typically accounted for 16.4% to 23.6% of total education expenditure in 2023; lower shares were recorded in Lithuania (12.1%) and Denmark (13.5%), while higher shares were recorded in Italy (26.9%) and Belgium (25.4%). The share for pre-primary education ranged from 5.7% in Cyprus – and less than 10.0% in the Netherlands, Greece, Denmark, Malta, Portugal, and Spain – to around a fifth of total education expenditure in Latvia (18.5%), Lithuania (20.3%), and Bulgaria (20.7%). Pre-primary education did not account for the lowest share of education expenditure in 4 EU countries: *in Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden, spending on upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education was lower than on pre-primary education *in Luxembourg, expenditure on tertiary education was lower than on pre-primary education. ===Public expenditure=== [[Image:Public expenditure on education (excluding early childhood educational development) relative to GDP, 2023 (%)A_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Public expenditure on education (excluding early childhood educational development) relative to GDP, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e2e9b9b1-c840-4bd9-84bb-4f799e046b77?lang=en educ_uoe_fine06])|alt=A column chart showing public expenditure on education (excluding early childhood educational development) relative to GDP. Data are shown in percent for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA, and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, the highest level of public expenditure on education relative to [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]] among the EU countries was observed in Sweden (6.8%), followed by Finland (6.3%), Belgium (6.2%), and Denmark (6.1%) – see Figure 2. Among the remaining EU countries, ratios of public expenditure on education relative to GDP generally ranged between 3.9% and 5.3%, with Romania (3.0%), Croatia (3.1%; 2022 data), Greece (3.3%), Malta (3.4%), and Hungary (3.6%) below this range. ===Expenditure of educational institutions=== [[Image:Expenditure on educational institutions (excluding early childhood educational development), 2023_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Expenditure on educational institutions (excluding early childhood educational development), 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/61423098-c4c4-48d9-97d1-d917c22e0ed3?lang=en educ_uoe_fini01])|alt=A table showing expenditure on educational institutions (excluding early childhood educational development). Data are shown in millions of euro for the total and as a percentage share of the total for various types of capital and current expenditure. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA, and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 2 presents a 2023 analysis of expenditure on educational institutions (either expenditure made directly by the institutions themselves or made by governments on behalf of institutions); no data are available for Ireland. *In Greece, Hungary, the Netherlands, Slovakia, Poland, Estonia (excluding pre-primary education), and Luxembourg, [[Glossary:Capital_expenditure|capital expenditure]] was at least 10.0% of total capital and current expenditure on educational institutions; in Germany, the share was almost at this level (9.7%). *By contrast, capital expenditure accounted for less than 5.0% of total capital and current expenditure in Romania and Belgium. In more than half of the EU countries for which data are available (9 out of 16), the majority of expenditure on educational institutions in 2023 was on teachers’ pay. However, this pay accounted for a lower share (40% to 50% of expenditure) in Slovakia, France, Lithuania, Czechia, and Finland, while Estonia (37.6%; excluding pre-primary education) and Malta (36.9%) were just below this range. [[Image:Expenditure on educational institutions (excluding early childhood educational development) per pupil_student, by sector, 2023 (EUR per pupil_student in full-time equivalents)A_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Expenditure on educational institutions (excluding early childhood educational development) per pupil/student, by sector, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/adf2fda5-1b8a-4cbf-93b1-dca3a0afdc3b?lang=en educ_uoe_fini04]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/19c101f7-e6a4-4426-986d-f7f617f9fae7?lang=en educ_uoe_fini01]), and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e0372348-511f-4327-a80f-1d7acea3efe1?lang=en educ_uoe_fine10])|alt=A bullet chart (in other words, a column and marker chart) showing expenditure on educational institutions (excluding early childhood educational development). Data are shown in euro per pupil/student in full-time equivalents for all institutions and for public institutions. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Declining [[Glossary:Birth|birth rates]] and shifts in population structures have resulted in smaller school age populations in many EU countries, and this development is projected to continue. In turn, this may well have an impact on ratios such as the average educational expenditure per pupil (for example if expenditure is held constant). This ratio may also be impacted by other factors, such as the participation rate of young children in education. For most EU countries, [[Glossary:Average|average]] annual expenditure (from public and private sources) on all educational institutions per pupil/student ranged from €3 754 in Bulgaria to €15 323 in Denmark (see Figure 3). Outside this range were: *Luxembourg, which had a considerably higher average educational expenditure per pupil/student at €27 531 *Romania at €2 775, which had a lower average. In a majority of the EU countries for which comparable data are available, average expenditure per pupil/student was higher in public institutions than in all other institutions (in 20 out of 26 countries). [[Image:Expenditure on educational institutions (excluding early childhood educational development) per pupil_student, by level of education, 2023_(EUR)A_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Expenditure on educational institutions (excluding early childhood educational development) per pupil/student, by level of education, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ccdccc28-de64-4d56-ad06-5e0d4f10de65?lang=en educ_uoe_fini04])|alt=A high-low chart showing expenditure on educational institutions (excluding early childhood educational development). Data are shown in euro per pupil/student in full-time equivalents for four different levels of education (pre-primary, primary and lower secondary, upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary, and tertiary). Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] With the exceptions of Greece, Cyprus, Italy, Lithuania, and Portugal, expenditure on educational institutions per pupil/student was highest among tertiary education institutions (no data available for Ireland). There was a general pattern observed, insofar as expenditure per pupil/student often increased from the lowest to the highest level of education – see Figure 4: *just over half of the EU countries for which data are available reported that their lowest average expenditure per pupil was for pre-primary education (no data available for Estonia, Ireland, or Croatia) *the lowest average expenditure per pupil was recorded for primary and lower secondary education in Bulgaria, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, and Slovakia *the lowest average expenditure per pupil was recorded for upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education in Denmark, Estonia (among the 3 education levels for which Estonian data are available), Poland, Slovenia, Finland, and Sweden *Greece was an exception in that its lowest average expenditure per pupil/student was for tertiary education. ===Financial aid to households and students=== [[Image:Financial aid from government to households and students, 2023 (EUR per pupil_student)A_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Financial aid from government to households and students, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e037cacd-3625-463e-a46e-fcdcddc03f23?lang=en educ_uoe_fine02]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ae5889ef-f7c6-4bb4-a2ed-231f45101d8d?lang=en educ_uoe_fine10])|alt=A high-low chart showing financial aid from government to households and students. Data are shown for tertiary education and for upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education. Data are shown in euro per pupil/student for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Financial assistance for education to households or students may take a variety of different forms contingent on a student’s status, including scholarships, public loans, and allowances. The relative importance of financial support may also depend on the education level being analysed, as compulsory education is generally free to all pupils/students, while tertiary education may or may not be free. Figure 5 shows information related to the financial aid given to households and students. Note that these data reflect, to some degree, the national organisation of education systems. They also reflect the various methods that are used to fund education systems and to provide welfare support and other forms of financial aid to encourage students to remain within the education system. As primary and lower secondary education are largely compulsory and tend to be provided free of charge, these levels are excluded from the information presented. With the exceptions of Czechia and Latvia, the level of financial aid to households and students in 2023 was higher for tertiary education than for upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education. Note that, in some countries, the capacity of the tertiary education sector is relatively low; this may lead to support being provided to students so that they can study abroad. Financial support for outward degree mobility is not covered by the data shown. The level of financial aid for upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education averaged €562 per pupil across the EU (excluding Ireland, Greece, and Croatia) in 2023. Among the EU countries, it peaked at €1 684 per pupil in Ireland (2022 data) and also exceeded €1 500 per pupil in Denmark, Sweden, and the Netherlands. For this level of education, the lowest average financial aid per pupil was recorded in Croatia, at €7 per pupil (2022 data). For tertiary education, the level of financial aid averaged €1 801 per student across the EU in 2023 (excluding Ireland and Croatia). The highest averages were observed in Ireland (€8 300 per student; 2022 data) and Denmark (€8 204 per student), while averages above €3 000 per student were also observed in Sweden, the Netherlands, and Germany. For this level of education, the lowest average financial aid per student was recorded in Latvia, at €9 per student. [[Image:Financial aid from government to households and students as a share of total public expenditure on education, 2023 (%)A_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Financial aid from government to households and students as a share of total public expenditure on education, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/aa446952-c941-4993-b4a6-8ce84cbdd6d6?lang=en educ_uoe_fina01])|alt=A high-low chart showing financial aid from government to households and students as a share of total public expenditure on education. Data are shown for three different levels of education (primary and lower secondary, upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary, and tertiary). Data are shown in percent for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] *In 2023, the share of public expenditure on tertiary education used for financial aid to households and students exceeded 20.0% in the Netherlands, Denmark, and Sweden, was close to a third in Italy (31.7%), and peaked at 47.9% in Ireland (2022 data) – see Figure 6. *For upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education, shares of more than 10.0% were reported for Denmark, the Netherlands, Sweden, Ireland (2022 data) and Slovenia, where a peak of 17.2% was recorded. *For primary and lower secondary education, shares were below 1.0% in the majority of EU countries. Bulgaria reported the highest share at 14.2%, double the next highest share (7.1% in Romania). [[Image:Distribution of financial aid from government to households and students in tertiary education by type of expenditure, 2023 (%)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Distribution of financial aid from government to households and students in tertiary education by type of expenditure, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6de702b2-107a-4cf4-bf34-1b5e6940aefa?lang=en educ_uoe_fine02])|alt=A stacked column chart showing the distribution of financial aid from government to households and students in tertiary education by type of expenditure. Each column has stacks for student grants and for student loans. Data are shown in percent for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Student fees and financial support can play an important role in impeding or facilitating access to tertiary education. While fees may impose a financial burden, various support measures may be used to alleviate obstacles to study. Figure 7 focuses on direct financial support to students in the form of grants and loans; note that indirect support may be available to students (and their families) through allowances or tax incentives. Almost all of the EU countries offer at least 1 type of direct financial aid (a grant or a loan) to students in tertiary education. In some of the EU countries, grants and loans both exist; as such, students may have to apply through separate procedures to receive 1 or both forms of aid. Figure 7 shows the distribution of financial aid to households and students in tertiary education; note that there were 18 EU countries (no data for Croatia) where student loans either did not exist or where student loans accounted for a very small share of the total financial aid provided (less than 1.0%). Therefore, there were only 8 EU countries (detailed below) where the division in aid between student grants and student loans was not almost entirely weighted in favour of student grants: *in Poland, Slovakia, Denmark, Cyprus, and Germany, between 84.7% and 98.7% of the financial aid from government to tertiary students was provided in the form of student grants *by contrast, in Hungary, the Netherlands, and Sweden a majority of the financial aid for tertiary students was provided in the form of student loans. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Educational expenditure ET2026.xlsx|title=Educational expenditure statistics: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''Source''' The source of data used in this article is a [[Glossary:UOE data collection|joint UNESCO/OECD/Eurostat (UOE) data collection]] on education statistics and this is the basis for the core components of [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]’s database on education statistics; in combination with the joint data collection, Eurostat also collects data on regional enrolments and foreign language learning. More information about the joint data collection is available in an article on the [[UNESCO_OECD_Eurostat_(UOE)_joint_data_collection_%E2%80%93_methodology|UOE methodology]]. '''Classification''' The [http://uis.unesco.org/en/topic/international-standard-classification-education-isced international standard classification of education (ISCED)] is the basis for international education statistics, describing 9 different [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|levels of education]]. '''Key concepts''' Education expenditure refer to the financial year of the country, as defined nationally (for year ''t''). Note that in the following concepts the expression ‘expenditure by or on (…) institutions’ is used for *'''expenditure by the institutions themselves''' – for example, salaries paid by a fiscally autonomous university *'''expenditure by governments on, or on behalf of, the institutions''' – for example, salaries paid by a national education ministry directly to individual teachers/lecturers who are employed in public or private schools/universities and other educational institutions. '''Expenditure for all levels of education combined''' encompasses the expenditure for all education programmes from pre-primary (ISCED level 0, category 020) to a doctoral or equivalent level of tertiary education (ISCED level 8). '''Total expenditure''' comprises current and capital expenditure. Current expenditure comprises personnel expenditure and other current expenditure; the latter includes, for example, services provided by outside providers (such as maintenance of school buildings), as well as purchases of teaching materials, electricity and telecommunications. '''Total public expenditure on education''' includes: *direct public funding for educational institutions *transfers to [[Glossary:Household|households]] and [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]] (including non-profit organisations). Generally, the public sector funds education either by: *bearing directly the current and capital expenses of educational institutions – direct expenditure for educational institutions *supporting students and their families with scholarships and public loans, as well as by transferring public subsidies for educational activities to private enterprises or non-profit organisations (transfers to private households and enterprises). '''Expenditure on institutions''' is not limited to that made on instructional services, but also includes expenditure on ancillary services for students and families, where these services are provided through educational institutions. At the tertiary education level, spending on research and development can be significant and this is included in the data presented to the extent that any such research is performed by educational institutions. As such, expenditure on educational institutions includes expenditure on: *core educational goods and services, such as teaching staff, school buildings, or schoolbooks and teaching materials *peripheral educational goods and services such as ancillary services, general administration and other activities. Education expenditure on institutions covers all types of public or private schools/universities and other educational institutions that are involved in delivering or supporting educational services. '''Expenditure on educational institutions from public sources''' corresponds to direct expenditure on educational institutions from public sources. It may take 1 of 2 forms: *direct purchases by government of educational resources to be used by educational institutions (such as the payment of teachers’ salaries by a central or regional education ministry) *payments made by government agencies to educational institutions that have responsibility for purchasing educational resources themselves (for example, a government appropriation or block grant to a university, which the university then uses to compensate staff and/or to purchase other resources). Direct expenditure by a government agency excludes tuition payments to an institution that have been received from students (or their families) enrolled in public schools under that agency’s jurisdiction, even if such tuition payments flow, initially, to the government agency rather than to the institution in question. '''Expenditure on educational institutions from private sources''' comprises the following: school fees; materials (such as textbooks and teaching equipment); transport to school (if organised by the school); meals (if provided by the school); boarding fees; expenditure by employers on initial [[Glossary:Vocational education and training (VET)|vocational training]]. '''Public financial aid''' to students refers to direct public assistance to pupils/students in the form of scholarships, public loans and family allowances contingent on student status. This is not a full measure of the level of assistance students may receive as, for instance, students (or their families) may also get financial support indirectly, for example through ancillary services (in other words, student welfare services such as meals, transportation, healthcare or dormitories) or tax reductions. '''Accounting conventions''' Data on educational expenditure are compiled on a cash accounting rather than an [[Glossary:Accrual recording|accrual]] accounting basis. As such, expenditure is recorded in the year in which the payments occurred. This means in particular that: *capital acquisitions are counted fully in the year in which the expenditure occurs *depreciation of capital assets is not recorded as expenditure, though expenditure on repair and maintenance is recorded in the year it occurs. Expenditure on student loans is recorded as the gross loan outlays in the year in which the loans are made, without netting-off repayments from existing borrowers. ===Context=== Education accounts for a significant proportion of total public expenditure in all EU countries. The largest education budget item is usually expenditure for staff. The cost of teaching usually increases substantially as a young person moves through the education system, with expenditure per pupil/student considerably higher in tertiary educational institutions than in primary schools. Although tertiary education generally costs more per pupil/student, the highest share of total education spending is normally allocated to secondary education, as this level teaches a larger share of the total number of pupils/students. There is a policy debate in many EU countries regarding how to increase or maintain funding for education, improve efficiency and promote equity. This challenge became harder in the context of the global financial and economic crisis, subsequent sovereign debt crises, COVID-19 pandemic and cost-of-living crisis. The debate is not purely about the levels and sources of finance, but also concerns proposals for reforms of education policies and systems and raises questions as to the development of labour force skills for the future, for the benefit of individuals and society. Possible approaches to funding include tuition fees, administrative or examination charges. Another potential fundraising source is partnerships between business and higher educational establishments. Education costs may be balanced by needs-based or merit-based support: *merit-based support includes support awarded on the basis of academic performance *needs-based support includes income-contingent grants, loans or other support to try to stimulate enrolment rates in higher education, in particular among the less well-off and disadvantaged members of society, thereby promoting equal opportunities as well as social mobility and inclusion. An analysis of national student fees and support systems in European higher education is available in a [https://eurydice.eacea.ec.europa.eu/data-and-visuals/national-student-fees report] produced by the [[Glossary:European_Commission_(EC)|European Commission]], the [https://www.eacea.ec.europa.eu/index_en European Education and Culture Executive Agency] and [https://eurydice.eacea.ec.europa.eu/ Eurydice]. ===Other articles=== *[[Education_and_training_in_the_EU_-_facts_and_figures|Education and training in the EU – facts and figures]] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-BF-05-002&language=en A guide to educational expenditure statistics] – 2005 edition ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/education-and-training/database Education and training (educ)], see ::Education finance (educ_uoe_fin) ===Thematic section===
