title: Employment and employee benefits expenses in EU businesses
text:
Insert short description for search engines Data extracted in October 2025 Planned article update: June 2027 For each hour worked by their employees in 2023, businesses had to disburse between €40 and €50 in 7 EU countries (Denmark, Luxembourg, Belgium, Ireland, Austria, Netherlands, Finland), contrasting with values around €10 in 6 EU countries (Latvia, Hungary, Croatia, Greece, Bulgaria, Romania). On average in the EU for 2023, each euro that businesses spent on employment contributed to the generation of €1.5 of value added, ranging from around €1.3 (Austria, France) to around €2 or more (Ireland: €2.5, Malta: €2.0, Luxembourg: €1.9). The cost of employment per hour worked in the EU’s manufacturing sector in 2023 was €21 for firms with fewer than 50 employees, while it was €38 for firms with over 250 employees. Consistently across EU countries, the cost of employment is relatively high in sectors such as finance, ICT, and energy, and relatively low in hospitality and retail. In the [[Glossary:EU|European Union]] (EU) there are about 33 million businesses, employing more than 162 million people. This article analyses employment cost by comparing [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU countries]] across 3 critical indicatorsThese indicators are derived from the components of employee benefits (forms of consideration given by the unit in exchange for service rendered by employees or for the termination of employment.) : '''1. Cost structure:''' What is the share of social security cost (versus wages and salaries) in total employment-related expenses? '''2. Hourly cost:''' How much employment-related expense occurs for 1 hour worked by an employee? '''3. Effectiveness:''' How much value is added to the enterprise output per euro in employment-related expenses? There is a substantial geographical disparity in the average hourly cost of labour. Moreover, the capacity of business enterprises to transform labour costs into value added varied strongly geographically, across different economic activities and enterprise size classes. [[Image:Table_1_Employee_benefits_overview,_2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Employee benefits overview (2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a05f1ab8-6bc5-4902-b8bc-bb3f76883c5a?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-26T10:17:55Z (sbs_sc_ovw)]|alt=A table showing an overview of employee benefits in the EU by NACE sector for the year 2023. Data are shown in absolute numbers or in euro million for the EU, the EU Member States, some of the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 1 shows a business landscape across the EU. Together, the firms in Europe paid out nearly €4.7 trillion in wages and salaries, and when adding social security contributions and other costs, the total employee benefits expense reached close to €6 trillion. These figures underline both the scale of European business activity and the significant role of labour costs in the economy. The data also show how broad the EU’s business landscape is: a substantial share of employment and wages comes from a large base of smaller enterprises rather than a few large ones. Please note that the analysis in this article does not consider national differences in relative price levels. === What is the share of social security cost in total employment-related expense? === [[Glossary:Structural_business_statistics|Structural business statistics]] (SBS) data show how wages, social contributions and other employee benefits together determine total labour costs in EU businesses. While wages are the most visible measure of employment conditions, the broader category of employee benefits gives a fuller picture of the financial commitment firms make to their workforce. The ratio between wages and total employee benefits demonstrates that in Europe’s social protection systems, non-wage labour costs are a major component of total employment expenditure and closely linked to the different social and regulatory systems in the EU Member States.
An example of how relatively high labour costs and a strong social protection framework translate into volume is Germany. The business economy of this country employed over 38 million people, more than one-fifth of the EU total. Its wage and salaries exceeded €1.4 trillion, and total employee benefits reached almost €1.8 trillion. Social contributions paid by the German business economy amounted to around €323 billion.
[[Image:G1_Employer's_social_charges_as_a_percentage_of_employee_benefits_expense-percentage_updated.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Employer’s social charges as a percentage of employee benefits expense - percentage (2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f76af41d-295d-4ae8-812c-e36c339347f2?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-29T13:19:05Z (sbs_sc_ovw)]|alt=A horizontal bar chart showing the share of employer social charges in the EU for the year 2023. Data are shown as percentage of employee benefits expense for the EU, the EU Member States, some of the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 1 illustrates how employers’ social charges contributed to the overall cost of employee benefits across EU countries. Social charges are driven by the diverse national social protection models across Europe. On average, social charges represented around 21% of total employee benefits in the EU, but this share varied widely between countries. It ranged from around 3% in some eastern EU countries to around 30% in parts of northern and western Europe. In the northern and western parts of the EU, some countries maintained high employers' contributions, while others such as Denmark, Luxembourg, Ireland and Finland recorded well below-average shares. Southern economies like Italy, Spain and Portugal reported above-average charges. Overall, the data confirm that the EU average does not capture the significant variation between EU countries. While all economies balance wages and social contributions as part of total employment expenses, the degree to which employers directly fund social protection remains one of the key structural differences across Europe’s labour markets. === What is the amount of employment-related expense per hour worked by an employee? === [[Image:Table 2 Employment benefits expense per hour worked by employees, by sector, 2023 (euro per hour) 22-01-2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Employment benefits expense per hour worked by employees, by sector (€/h) (2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9847a9ae-31eb-4228-bf96-d0a73c69082c?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-27T10:13:28Z (sbs_sc_ovw)]|alt=A table showing the employment benefits expense per hour worked by NACE sector for the year 2023. Data are shown as euro per hour for EU, the EU Member States, one of the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 2 provides a broad view of how much employment-related expense occurred per hour worked across different sectors in European countries. The figures capture total labour costs per hour covering wages, salaries, and social contributions. At EU level, the average cost per hour worked was around €28–€31 in most sectors, with higher values in capital-intensive industries such as electricity, gas, and air conditioning supply (€43), information and communication (€40), and financial and insurance activities (€57). Labour-intensive service sectors, like accommodation and food services (€17) and retail (€24), remained at the lower end. This general hierarchy holds true across nearly all EU countries, highlighting how sectoral composition drives overall labour cost differentials. Typically, northern and western European economies (such as Denmark, Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Germany) reported the highest hourly employment costs, frequently above €50 per hour in advanced sectors and often more than double the EU average. These figures reflect high wage levels, stronger collective bargaining systems, and significant employers' social contributions. In contrast, southern and eastern European countries (including Bulgaria, Romania, and Balkan countries) recorded far lower costs, often below €10–€15 per hour in most sectors. These lower figures indicate both smaller wage bases and lighter employers' contribution burdens. The data also underline strong sectoral consistency across regions: regardless of country, activities such as finance, ICT, and energy remained among the most expensive, while hospitality and retail are universally less costly. This suggests that while total levels differ, the relative cost ranking between industries is notably stable across Europe. [[Image:Figure_2_Employee_benefits_expense_per_hour_worked_by_employees,_2023_(euro_per_hour).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Employment benefits expense per hour worked by employees (€/h) for the total Business economy, by countries (2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2fc9bc57-a964-410c-a9fb-f3d3e6f51ecf?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-02T12:53:56Z (sbs_sc_ovw)]|alt=A vertical bar chart showing employee benefits expense per hour worked by employess in the EU by sector for the year 2023. Data are shoen in euro per hour for the EU, the EU Member States, some of the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Map 1: Employee benefits expense per hour worked by employees, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_ovw_act/default/table?lang=en (sbs_ovw_act)]
Figure 2 and Map 1 show different angles of the average employment-related cost per hour worked in 2023, reflecting both wage levels and employers' social contributions. While Figure 2 reveals the high degree of disparity between counties, Map 1 reveals the regional pattern behind it. At EU level, the average cost per hour stood at around €29, but the spread across countries was substantial, ranging from just over €9 in Romania to almost €49 in Denmark. A geographical divide confirms that northern and western European countries recorded the highest hourly employment costs (typically €40 or more), reflecting well-developed economies with strong collective bargaining and high average wages. In contrast, southern and eastern European countries reported much lower costs, often below €12 per hour. These figures align with lower wage levels and less extensive social protection system. Overall, the dataset highlights a north–south and west–east cost gradient, confirming the labour cost differences in the European labour market. [[Image:Figure_3_Employee_benefits_expense_per_hour_worked_by_employees,_by_NACE_sector,_EU,_2023_(euro_per_hour).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Employment benefits expense per hour worked by employees (€/h), by NACE sector (EU, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b440afb7-f6e5-423a-9701-b2457ffc3921?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-22T12:39:12Z (sbs_sc_ovw)]|alt=A horizontal bar chart showing employment benefits expense per hour worked by employees in the EU by NACE sector for the year 2023. Data are shown in euro per hour. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 3 provides an overview of average employment-related expenses per hour worked across NACE sectors in the EU. At EU level, the data reveals a 'hierarchy' of labour costs by sector: • Top end: ‘Financial and insurance activities’ (around €57 per hour) were highest, followed by ‘Electricity, gas, steam, and air conditioning supply’ (€43) and ‘Information and communication’ (€40). • Mid-range: Manufacturing (€31), and human health and social work (€32) showed moderate but substantial labour costs. • Lower end: Service-oriented and labour-intensive sectors, including ‘Accommodation and food services’ and ‘Other personal services’ (both around €17), reported significantly smaller employment costs. Overall, the dataset highlights that the relative cost ranking between industries was notably stable across Europe, regardless of national cost levels. [[Image:Figure_4_Employee_benefits_expense_per_hours_worked_by_employees,_manufacturing_sector,_EU,_2023_(euro_per_hour).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Employment benefits expense per hour worked by employees (€)/h, manufacturing sector, by size class (EU, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1a0dcabd-a47e-42c5-9d69-6a6ff6dbcef9?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-22T12:47:22Z (sbs_sc_ovw)]|alt=A vertical bar chart showing employee benefits expense per hour worked by employees for the manufacturing sector in the EU for the year 2023. Data are shown in euro per hour. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 4 reveals the cost structure in the EU manufacturing sector by size class in the EU. What stands out is the clear relationship between firm size and labour costs. Small enterprises (fewer than 50 employees) reported an average cost of around €21 per hour, while medium-sized firms (50–249 employees) paid around €26, and large enterprises (250 or more employees) reached over €38 per hour. This steady progression suggests that larger firms can offer more comprehensive benefit packages. This pattern also highlights structural characteristics of the EU manufacturing landscape: smaller firms, which make up the vast majority of enterprises, tend to compete on flexibility and cost efficiency, while larger manufacturers are more capital- and technology-intensive, often integrated into international supply chains and operated under collective agreements. Overall, the figures illustrate that labour costs in EU manufacturing scaled with enterprise size, reflecting differences in productivity, job quality, and employment conditions. [[Image:Table_3_Employment_benefits_expense_per_hour_worked_by_employees,_manufacturing_sector,_by_size_class,_2023_(euro_per_hour).png |thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Employment benefits expense per hour worked by employees (€/h), manufacturing sector, by country and size class (2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a5928878-4631-4f24-8e28-f6bc2021808b?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-22T14:39:36Z (sbs_sc_ovw)]|alt=A table showing employment benefits expense per hour worked by employees for the manufacturing sector by size class for the year 2023. Data are shown in euro per hour for the EU, the EU Member States, one of the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 3 focuses on the manufacturing sector across the EU by size class. At EU level, the average cost of employing a worker in manufacturing was €31 per hour, placing it among the most expensive but still industrially competitive sectors of the European economy. However, this headline number hides strong contrasts: costs ranged from under €10 per hour in the eastern part of Europe to over €50 per hour in countries such as Belgium, Denmark, and the Netherlands. Another striking feature is the consistent increase in labour costs with enterprise size. Across nearly all EU countries, large manufacturers (250+ employees) paid significantly more per hour than small firms. === How much value is added per euro of employment related expense? === Companies rely on their employees to create products for the market. Nonetheless, value creation depends on far more than just employment. Capital intensity plays a major role, as industries reliant on advanced equipment or infrastructure can generate higher value from each euro of labour spending. Know-how and workforce capacity, including education, technical skills, and management efficiency, further shape productivity outcomes. Other elements such as market size and competitiveness, the firm's capacity to innovate and adopt new technology, access to finance, the regulatory or tax environment, the impact of multi-national actors, and the sectoral composition of the economy also influence performance. As a result, the capacity of businesses to transform labour costs into economic output vary strongly between [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU countries]] and different economic activities, as shown in Table 4. [[Image:Table_4_Value_added_per_employment_benefits_expense,_2023_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Table 4: Value added per employment benefits expense (%), by NACE Sections (2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d14154f1-6225-4001-8c72-1fffa126a015?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-27T10:35:41Z (sbs_sc_ovw)]|alt=A table showing the share of value added per employment benefits expense in the EU for the year 2023. Data are shown in percentage for the EU, the EU Member States, dome of the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] At EU level, the highest ratios were seen in ‘Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply’ (387%), ‘Mining and quarrying’ (230%), and ‘Financial and insurance activities’ (245%). These sectors are typically capital-intensive, meaning much of their productivity comes from machinery, infrastructure, or advanced systems rather than direct labour input. The high ratios in these industries indicate that each euro spent on employees generated a comparatively large amount of value added. Similarly, ‘Real estate activities’ (242%) and ‘Information and communication’ (148%) also performed strongly, driven by technology, tangible and intangible assets, and high-skilled labour. In contrast, labour-intensive sectors such as ‘Accommodation and food services’ (128%), ‘Arts, entertainment and recreation’ (145%), and ‘Other personal service activities’ (93%) depend heavily on human work with limited opportunities for automation or scalability. The manufacturing sector (162%) sat around the EU average, reflecting its mix of capital investment, technological input, and human labour. It demonstrated high productivity but varied widely across countries. [[Image:Table_5_Value_added_per_employment_benefits_expense,_by_NACE_group_of_business_services,_2023_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Table 5: Value added per employment benefits expense (%), by NACE group of business services (2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/639e55a2-30f3-43cb-99b0-ec04b3135f2d?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-22T14:05:24Z (sbs_ovw_act)]|alt=A table showing the share of value added per employment benefits expense in the EU by NACE group of business services for the year 2023. Data are shown in percentage for the EU, the EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The data on the wage-adjusted labour productivity for European specialised services in 2023 reveals 2 opposing trends in cost efficiency. While the EU average for high-value sectors like ‘Legal Activities’ (115%) and ‘Computer Programming’ (117%) comfortably exceeded the 100% threshold (meaning value added exceeds personnel costs), national results varied greatly. The most striking results were very high values in some activities, sometimes recording ratios exceeding 400%. This often signifies success in attracting large multinationals or exploiting wage arbitrage rather than purely local labour output. For instance, Cyprus ‘Software publishing’ (433%), Malta ‘Computer programming’ (408%), and Ireland ‘Management consultancy’ (280%) might have been partly due to the heavy influence of multinational enterprises (MNEs) and strategic fiscal optimisation. In the emerging market sphere, Romania’s 402% in ‘Legal activities’ might be partly the result of successful wage arbitrage, where specialised firms generate value priced at international standards with low local personnel costs. Conversely, figures below the 100% mark (meaning personnel cost exceeds value added) reveal a cost pressure in some high-wage economies. Service sector competitiveness is increasingly driven by the successful separation of revenue generation from local cost structure. [[Image:Figure_5_Value_added_per_employment_benefits_expense,_for_the_total_business_economy,_2023_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Value added per employment benefits expense (%), for the total Business economy (EU, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f86ed80c-c18e-41a9-813c-3cc5abc5efaa?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-02T13:15:46Z (sbs_sc_ovw)]|alt=A vertical bar chart showing the share of value added per employment benefits expense for the total business economy in the EU for the year 2023. Data are shown in percentage for the EU, the EU Member States, some of the EFTA countries and some of the candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 5 shows the efficiency with which EU countries transform labour costs into economic output. For the EU as a whole, each euro spent on employment contributed to the generation of €1.48 of value added, but this average does not capture the wide national differences driven by structural factors. At the top of the scale, Ireland (250%), Malta (203%), and Luxembourg (191%) stand out as outliers. These high figures are partly driven by strong foreign investment, capital-intensive industries, and the influence of multinational enterprises (MNEs). Among central and eastern European countries, several economies, including Romania (181%), Croatia (180%), and Bulgaria (173%), performed notably well due to lower labour costs combined with growing industrial capacity, reflecting ongoing catch-up dynamics. Conversely, larger western European economies such as France (126%) and Austria (135%) fell below the EU average, generally reflecting more labour-intensive production structures and higher relative labour costs. In essence, value creation depends on far more than just employment expenses; factors such as capital intensity, sectoral structure, and technological sophistication play decisive roles in determining productivity across Europe. [[Image:Figure_6_Value_added_per_employment_benefits_expense,_by_NACE_Section,_EU,_2023_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Value added per employment benefits expense (%), by NACE Sections (EU, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/37d1ad0d-fd60-4f32-ae72-a1be78022c85?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T09:29:15Z (sbs_sc_act)]|alt=A vertical bar chart showing the share of value added per employment benefits expense in the EU by NACE section for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The data on value added per euro of employment benefit expenses provides a view of how effectively EU industries translate labour costs into economic output. At the top of the scale, sectors like ‘Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply’ (387%), ‘Financial and insurance activities’ (245%), and ‘Real estate activities’ (242%) recorded the highest ratios. These sectors are typically capital and technology-intensive, relying heavily on infrastructure and intangible assets rather than large labour inputs. High value-added figures here indicate that labour costs represent only a small fraction of total production costs. In contrast, labour-intensive sectors such as ‘Accommodation and food service activities’ (128%) displayed much lower ratios. These industries depend heavily on direct human labour, face limited possibilities for automation, and generate less value per euro spent on employees. Sectors such as ‘Manufacturing’ (162%) and Information and communication (148%) sat around the middle. The data underscores that high value-added ratios are associated with industries that leverage advanced technology, capital assets, and expertise, while sectors dependent on manual or interpersonal work remain constrained by their human labour intensity. [[Image:Figure_7_Value_added_per_employment_benefits_expense_in_business_services,_by_NACE_sector-groups,_EU,_2023_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Value added per employment benefits expense in business services, by NACE sector-groups (EU, 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5440bc22-39eb-48b1-8fcc-e5c04d893022?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T09:34:41Z (sbs_sc_act)]|alt=A horizontal bar chart showing the share of value added per employent benefits expense in business services in the EU by NACE sector groups for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The EU average for wage-adjusted labour productivity in specialised service sectors generally showed a homogenous economic structure, with the vast majority of activities surpassing the critical 100% threshold (where value added covers personnel costs). Leading the list were highly technical and compliance-focused fields: ‘Technical testing and analysis’ (119%), ‘Computer programming’ (117%), and ‘Accounting activities’ (117%). Core knowledge-based services also demonstrated high profitability, though with slightly lower margins. ‘Architectural and engineering activities’ (115%) and ‘Advertising’ (113%) showed strong results, while Management consultancy (108%) operated on tighter margins. The only specialised service activity to fall well below the 100% sustainability threshold was the Employment activities (N78) sector, which recorded a significantly lower average of 81%. Overall, high-skill services maintained structural profitability, while labour-intensive, high-volume sectors like employment agencies faced systemic competitive pressure that limits their capacity for high-margin operation. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Employment_and_employee_benefits_expenses_in_EU_businesses_Rev_Final.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === ==== Coverage, units and classifications ==== Eurostat’s [[Glossary:Structural_business_statistics|structural business statistics]] (SBS) provide the data that allow an in-depth analysis of labour costs, their composition and relationship to other economic indicators. SBS depicts the related indicators for different economic activities (detailed [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] segments) and size classes of businesses in the [[Glossary:EU|EU]]. It can relate labour input to economic output and performance of enterprises and thereby enable analysis of the interdependency of different factors, including those mentioned above, at a detailed levelSBS data are an important input to related statistics from National Accounts that are available only at an aggregated level.. This article provides examples for such a study, but can of course not spell out all possible angles. The goal of this article is to compare enterprise conditions across different EU Member States and economic activities (NACE). The comparison focuses specifically on indicators related to employment, including wages and salaries, and employers’ contributions to social security. The analysis relies on structural business statistics (SBS) data, see article [[Structural_business_statistics_overview|Structural business statistics overview]]. It is important to note that SBS provides information only for market-producing enterprises (the business economy), not the entire economy of a country. SBS employs definitions that are closely aligned with those relevant for running businesses, such as variables used in business accounting. This alignment ensures the data's direct relevance for the management of companies, particularly those interested in comparing employment costs across different EU Member States and economic sectors. Structural business statistics cover the ’business economy’, which includes industry, construction and many services (NACE Rev. 2 sections B to N, P to R as well as division S95 and S96). Structural business statistics do not cover agriculture, forestry and fishing, nor public administration. Structural business statistics describe the business economy through the observation of units engaged in an economic activity; the unit in structural business statistics is generally the enterprise. An enterprise carries out one or more activities, at one or more locations, and it may comprise one or more legal units. Enterprises that are active in more than one economic activity (plus the value added and turnover they generate, the people they employ, and so on) are classified under the NACE heading corresponding to their principal activity; this is normally the one which generates the largest amount of value added. NACE Rev. 2 was adopted at the end of 2006, and implemented in structural business statistics from the 2008 reference year. Compared with NACE Rev. 1.1, this has enabled a broader and more detailed set of information to be compiled on services, while also updating the classification to identify new areas of activity better. Starting with the reference year 2021, structural business statistics are compiled under the legal basis of {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R2152:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2152/2019}} on European business statistics and its implementing act, {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32020R1197:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 1197/2020}} on technical specifications and arrangements. ==== Size class and regional analysis ==== Structural business statistics are also available with an analysis by region or by enterprise size class. In structural business statistics, size classes are defined by the number of persons employed, except for specific data series within retail trade activities where turnover size classes are also used. A limited set of the standard structural business statistics variables (for example, the number of enterprises, turnover, value added and persons employed) is analysed by size class, mostly down to the 3-digit (group) level of NACE. For statistical purposes, SMEs are generally defined as those enterprises employing fewer than 250 persons. The number of size classes available varies according to the activity under consideration. However, the main groups used in this article are: • small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs): with less than 250 persons employed, further divided into; • micro enterprises: with less than 10 persons employed; • small enterprises: with 10 to 49 persons employed; • medium-sized enterprises: with 50 to 249 persons employed; • large enterprises: with 250 or more persons employed. Structural business statistics contain a comprehensive set of basic variables describing business demographics and employment characteristics, as well as monetary variables (mainly concerning operating income and expenditure, or investment). In addition, a set of derived indicators has been compiled: for example, ratios of monetary characteristics or per head values. === Context === [https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/document/download/e566634a-29cf-4adf-a98d-1e708c873af8_en?filename=COM_2025_26_F1_COMMUNICATION_FROM_COMMISSION_TO_INST_EN_V10_P1_3877708.PDF The 2025 Annual Single Market and Competitiveness Report] ===Other articles=== *[[Business economy by sector - NACE Rev. 2|Other analyses of the business economy by NACE Rev. 2 sections]] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Structural_business_statistics_overview Structural business statistics – overview article] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Structural_business_statistics_at_regional_level Structural business statistics at regional level] ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/overview Structural business statistics] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/database Structural business statistics (sbs)], see: :Enterprise statistics on the whole business population (sbs_ovw) ::Enterprise statistics by size class and NACE Rev. 2 activity (from 2021 onwards) (sbs_sc_ovw) ::Enterprises by detailed NACE Rev. 2 activity and special aggregates (sbs_ovw_act) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database?node_code=sbs Structural business statistics (sbs)] data navigation tree === Publications === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/KS-01-24-007 European Business Statistics Methodological Manual for Structural Business Statistics (2024 edition)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/publications Recent Eurostat publications on SBS] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-key-figures/w/KS-01-25-003 Key figures on Europe – 2025 edition] – see subchapter on Business *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/KS-01-25-037 Eurostat Regional Yearbook – 2025 edition] – see chapter 8. Business *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20241205-1 News Release SBS] – 2022 final data *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/business-demography/publications Recent Eurostat publications on BD] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20241025-2 News Release BD2022 final data] === Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/sbs_esms.htm Reference metadata (ESMS) - Structural business statistics] • Business registers — Recommendations Manual • Glossary of business statistics • Handbook on the design and implementation of business surveys • Use of administrative sources for business statistics purposes • Information on the structure of labour cost are also available from the Labour Cost Survey (LCS). [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Labour_cost_structural_statistics_-_levels Labour cost structural statistics - levels] The two data collections are complementary: The LCS provides more detailed information about the structure of labour cost (including of non-wage cost), as well as about cost for part-time versus full-time employment. In contrast, SBS can relate labour cost to economic indicators like value added (which LCS cannot), and is available for every reference year while the LCS is only conducted every four years. The most recent LCS data are available for reference year 2020; the update with 2024 data is planned for September 2026. === Data visualisations === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/dashboard/european-statistical-monitor/ European statistical monitor] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/visualisations/ Data Visualisation - Key Indicators: Structural Business Statistics] === External links === *[http://ec.europa.eu/competition/index_en.html European Commission – Competition], see: *[http://ec.europa.eu/environment/index_en.htm European Commission – Environment], see: :*[http://ec.europa.eu/environment/waste/packaging/index_en.htm Waste: packaging] *[http://ec.europa.eu/growth/index_en.htm European Commission – Internal market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs], see: :*[https://ec.europa.eu/growth/single-market/goods_en Single market for goods] :*[https://ec.europa.eu/growth/single-market/single-market-services_en Single market for services] === Legislation=== *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R2152:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2152/2019}} on European business statistics and its implementing act *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32020R1197:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 1197/2020}} on technical specifications and arrangements === Footnotes === {{Unit|topic=X_Structural_business_statistics}} [[Category:Industry, trade, and services|Employment and employee benefits expenses in EU businesses]] [[Category:Structural business statistics (SBS)|Employment and employee benefits expenses in EU businesses]] [[Category:Statistical article|Employment and employee benefits expenses in EU businesses]] [[Category:June2027|Employment and employee benefits expenses in EU businesses]]

title: Employment and value added - an analysis with FIGARO data
text:
FIGARO tables – full international and global accounts for research in input-output analysis. Official inter-country supply, use and input-output data for the EU. A tool for analysing the social, economic and environmental effects of globalisation in the EU. A study on value added and employment. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 In 2024, EU exports to non-EU countries generated €2 905 billion of gross value added, corresponding to 17.9% of the EU total gross value added (€16 200 billion). In the EU, the employment of 32.9 million people was supported by exports to non-EU countries in 2024; the share of employed people supported by EU exports increased from 12.1% in 2010 to 15.0% in 2024. Between 2010 and 2024, value added generated by EU exports to non-EU countries increased most in Ireland (€49.0 to €280.8 billion), Malta (€1.7 to €6.4 billion), Bulgaria (€5.2 to €18.6 billion), and Romania (€12.8 to €45.2 billion). Value added generated in each EU country by exports of all EU countries to non-EU countries, 2010-2024 The production of goods and services requires inputs, which may be sourced domestically or globally. The final value of a product may well reflect value that has been added in many different stages of the production chain through the combination of factors of production, including [[Glossary:Employment|employment]]. [[Glossary:Gross_value_added|Gross value added]] may have been generated and employment input may have been located in many different countries. This fact is not always visible in conventional trade statistics, which generally reflect the total value of a product when traded. An analysis of the gross value added and employment in [[Glossary:Export|exports]] and final use of goods and services can offer a more profound understanding of international trade relations. This article aims to provide deeper insights into gross value added and employment in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] associated to [[Glossary:Global_value_chains_(GVC)|global value chains]], using the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-supply-use-input-tables/overview FIGARO tables]. === Trends for the EU as a whole === In 2024, EU exports to non-EU countries generated €2 905 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] of gross value added in the EU; this represented 17.9% of the EU total gross value added (€16 200 billion) (see Figure 1). Compared to 2023, the share increased by 0.2 [[Glossary:percentage point|percentage points (pp)]] (from 17.7%). A comparison with 2010 shows a rise of 3.9 pp (from 14.0%). In 2024, in terms of employment, 32.9 million people in the EU were supported by exports to non-EU countries. These employed people accounted for 15.0% of the total EU employment. Between 2023 and 2024, the share rose by 0.2 pp (from 14.8%). From 2010 to 2023, it increased by 2.9 pp (from 12.1%). Figure 1 shows that the shares of value added (references to value added should be understood as [[Glossary:Gross_value_added|gross value added (GVA)]] throughout this article) and employment embedded in EU exports to non-EU countries follow a similar trend between 2010 and 2024. The sharpest drop for both was due to the COVID-crisis (between 2019 and 2020). By contrast, the biggest annual increase was registered between 2011 and 2012 (+1.3 pp for each indicator). [[Image: Domestic value added and employment embodied in EU exports, EU, 2010-2024_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Share of value added and employment embedded in EU exports, EU, 2010-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a7c72b7c-619d-4c6a-9688-c9a1f8b0eb04?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-08T07:05:02Z naio_10_fgde]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/20a277e6-245f-4702-938b-1599620a43b3?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-08T07:12:30Z naio_10_fgdee]) |alt=Line chart showing the evolution from 2010 to 2024, for the EU as a whole, of the share of value added generated by EU exports to the total value added and of the share of employment supported by EU exports to the total employment. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Another way to study the impact of globalisation is to analyse the EU value added and employment contained in the final use of goods and services by non-EU countries (rather than those contained in EU exports of goods and services). In 2024, the final use of products in non-EU economies generated €2 788 billion of gross value added in the EU, corresponding to 17.2% of the EU total gross value added, and supported the employment of 31.6 million people, corresponding to 14.4% of the total EU employment (see Figure 2). [[Image: Domestic value added and employment embodied in foreign final use, EU, 2010-2024_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Share of value added and employment embedded in foreign final use, EU, 2010-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://intragate.ec.europa.eu/eurostat/staging/databrowser/bookmark/10249911-2160-4b42-9414-20efcd743cdf?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-08T07:32:59Z naio_10_fgdfi]) and ([https://intragate.ec.europa.eu/eurostat/staging/databrowser/bookmark/4e63d7d2-6fcc-4add-9b73-9fc5bbf42433?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-08T07:44:56Z naio_10_fgdfef]) |alt=Line chart showing the evolution from 2010 to 2024, for the EU as a whole, of the share of value added generated by foreign final use to the total value added and of the share of employment supported by foreign final use to the total employment. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Shares and levels by EU country === Among EU countries, Germany generated the most value added from EU exports in its domestic economy: in 2024, €675.8 billion of German value added was due to exports from the EU, including from Germany itself. The level of export-generated value added in Germany was higher than in France (€389.3 billion) and Ireland (€280.8 billion) combined, who had the next highest levels. However, it should be noted that Germany’s economy is also the largest among EU countries. Italy (€271.0 billion) and the Netherlands (€231.6 billion) followed. Between 2010 and 2024, value added generated by EU exports to non-EU countries increased most, in relative terms, in Ireland (€49.0 to €280.8 billion, +474%), Malta (€1.7 to €6.4 billion, +288%), Bulgaria (€5.2 to €18.6 billion, +259%), and Romania (€12.8 to €45.2 billion, +253%). All countries saw their domestic value added from EU exports grow during this time period. Countries with the smallest relative increases were Finland (from €28.9 to €42.4 billion, +47%), Greece (from €17.1 to €25.2 billion, +47%), and Sweden (from €63.4 to €100.8 billion, +59%). Figure 3 Besides the estimation of the value added embedded in each EU country as a result of EU exports to non-EU countries, the FIGARO macroeconomic globalisation indicators can also provide insight into the value added generated in the EU as a whole by the exports from a particular EU country to non-EU countries. Figure 4 presents the value added created in the EU by the exports of each EU country to non-EU countries between 2010 and 2024. In 2024, Germany (€631.6 billion), France (€389.8 billion), Ireland (€316.9 billion), Italy (€275.8 billion), and the Netherlands (€227.3 billion) were also the countries generating the highest value added by their exports across the EU. The countries with the largest relative increases in the EU value added between 2010 and 2024 thanks to their exports to non-EU countries were Ireland (from €52.0 to €316.9 billion, +509%) and Malta (from €2.0 to €8.7 billion, +335%). Those corresponding to the smallest relative increases were Finland (from €31.2 to €45.5 billion, +46%), Greece (from €16.6 to €24.9 billion, +50%), Sweden (from €65.3 to €105.2 billion, +61%), the same as for the value added generated in each EU country by EU exports. Figure 4 Comparing Figure 3 (value added generated in each EU country by exports of all EU countries) with Figure 4 (value added generated in the EU by exports of each EU country), in 2024 the value added generated in Germany due to all EU exports (including from Germany) to non-EU countries was higher than the value added generated in the EU (including Germany) by German exports to non-EU countries. The difference between the 2 indicators amounted to €44.2 billion (€675.8 billion versus €631.6 billion). Consequently, Germany received larger benefits (in value added terms) from the exports of other EU countries than the benefits it provides in other EU countries through its own exports. Other beneficiaries from cross-border spillover effects were Spain (€196.0 billion versus €178.3 billion, +€17.7 billion) and Poland (€131.5 billion versus €115.7 billion, +€15.8 billion). Conversely, Denmark received smaller benefits from the exports of the other EU countries than the benefits they provide in the other EU countries through their own exports. In Denmark, €87.3 billion of domestic value added was generated by exports from all EU countries (including from Denmark), whereas €96.9 billion of value added across the EU (some of which in Denmark) was generated by Danish exports to non-EU countries. The difference – with Denmark being a net contributor to the value added in the other EU countries – was €9.6 billion. Similarly, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Hungary, as well as Czechia, Estonia, France, Italy, Cyprus, Malta, Austria, Portugal, Slovakia, Finland, and Sweden, were net contributors of cross-border spillover effects. === Domestic and spillover effects === The EU value added generated (EU employment supported respectively) by the exports of each EU country to non-EU countries can be divided up into 2 parts: the domestic effect and the spillover effect. The '''domestic''' effect reflects the value added (employment resp.) in a given EU country that is generated (supported resp.) by '''its own exports''' to non-EU countries while the '''spillover''' effect reflects the value added (employment resp.) in a given EU country that is generated (supported resp.) by '''the exports of other EU countries''' to non-EU countries, for example for the production of intermediate inputs to be used in other EU countries' exports to non-EU countries. Results for the value added related to these 2 effects are presented in Figure 5 for the year 2024. At EU level, out of €2 905 billion of value added generated by EU exports in 2024, €2 394 billion were generated in the exporting EU countries, and therefore related to domestic effect; this corresponds to 82.4%. Consequently, €510.3 billion, or 17.6%, were due to cross-border spillover effects (value added generated in a EU country due to the exports of other EU countries to non-EU countries). Among the EU countries, the smallest shares of domestic effect were reached by Slovakia (72.0%) and Czechia (73.0%). Poland (73.9%), Austria (74.5%), Latvia (74.6%), and Estonia (74.7%) closely followed. In these countries, the share of spillover effects in the domestic value added linked to EU exports was consequently the highest among EU countries (all above 25%). By contrast, Ireland (7.9%), Malta (8.8%), and Cyprus (9.0%) recorded the lowest shares of cross-border spillover effects (all 3 below 10%). [[Image: Value added generated in each EU country by exports of all EU countries to non-EU countries, domestic and spillover effect, 2024_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Value added generated in each EU country by exports of all EU countries to non-EU countries, domestic and spillover effect, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/adaa5d77-b65a-438c-ad75-68587fb4baea?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-11T10:29:40Z naio_10_fgde])|alt=Vertical bar chart presenting the value added in the EU generated by exports of each EU Member State for the year 2024. The bar of each EU Member State is broken down by domestic (lower part) and spillover (upper part) effects. EU Member States are ranked by decreasing order of spillover effect. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Global value chain participation === The indicators "value added in exports" are also used to measure the participation in global value chains (GVCs) and make comparison between countries, allowing a better understanding of the economic interdependencies and vulnerabilities. The forward participation in GVCs refers to the value added generated in an economy by its exports to serve other economies to produce goods and services for export. For a EU economy, the indicator is presented as the share of domestic value added generated by foreign exports in the total exports of this EU economy. By symmetry, the backward participation in GVCs of a EU economy is defined as the share of foreign value added in exports in the total exports of this EU economy. The sum of backward and forward participation is called the global value chain participation. Figure 6 presents the evolution between 2010 and 2024 for the 3 indicators (i.e. forward participation, backward participation, and global value chain participation) for each EU country and for the EU as a whole. At EU level, the global value chain participation reached 34.5% in 2024, resulting from the sum of 20.2% of backward participation and 14.2% of forward participation. Since 2010, the EU backward participation increased by 1.9 percentage points (from 18.3%) and the EU forward participation slightly decreased by 0.3 pp (from 14.5%). The rise in the EU backward participation since 2010 reflects greater integration, higher connectedness, and larger capacity of the EU to harness the benefits of globalisation, but this may also increase the risk of supply chain disruptions and vulnerabilities. Among the EU countries, the highest value chain participation in 2024 was reported by Greece, with 53.7%, induced by a high backward participation of 42.2%. Luxembourg (47.2%) and Cyprus (46.7%) followed, similarly due to high backward participation (35.4% and 36.2% respectively). By contrast, Croatia (27.7%), Romania (28.2%), and Latvia (28.6%) recorded the lowest shares of value chain participation. Figure 6 === Value added and employment in foreign final use by country === The following section examines the repartition by non-EU country of the EU value added and employment in foreign final use. As seen above, in 2024, the final use of goods and services by non-EU countries generated €2 788 billion of EU value added and supported the employment of 31.6 million EU workers. Figure 7 presents the breakdown of these 2 indicators by country of final use. In 2024, trade with the United States had the highest impact on EU value added and employment in foreign final use, with the US purchase of goods and services for final consumption or investment purposes generating €585.8 billion EU value added and supporting the employment of 6.0 million EU workers. These figures correspond to 21.0% of the €2 788 billion EU value added and 19.1% of the 31.6 million EU workers, respectively, due the total final use of goods and services by non-EU countries. For EU value added, China followed with €289.8 billion (10.4%), ahead of the United Kingdom with €276.0 billion (9.9%), induced by their purchase of goods and services for final consumption or investment purposes. In contrast, for EU employment, the United Kingdom was the next highest with 3.4 million (10.6%) EU workers due to their final use, ahead of China with 3.1 million (9.8%). Switzerland followed at some distance for both EU value added and employment, generating €126.6 billion (4.5%) and supporting 1.5 million workers (4.7%) respectively, thanks to their final use of goods and services in 2024. [[Image: EU value added and employment in foreign final use, by country of final use, 2010-2024 (% on all non-EU countries).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: EU value added and employment in foreign final use, by country of final use, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c8862d8e-c9ea-4bac-acc6-dcec84c95a3d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-11T20:32:11Z naio_10_fgdf]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6e16d540-35a2-4088-a699-190123be3f49?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-11T20:39:43Z naio_10_fgdfe]) |alt=Vertical bar chart presenting the value added generated and the employment supported in the EU by the final use of goods and services in the main non-EU economies for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== *[[Media: SE_article_VAEMPL_2026ed.xlsx |Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== '''''Concepts and definitions''''' Macroeconomic globalisation indicators presented in this article are computed using the FIGARO tables ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-supply-use-input-tables/information-data#figaro Full International and Global Accounts for Research in Input-Output Analysis]), through the application of the Leontief quantity model ([https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/inputoutput-analysis/431D85A5E459AB078479852169EA77D7 Miller and Blair, 2022]). This model relies on the interdependencies between industries and countries, represented mathematically in the form of technical coefficient matrices. The Leontief inverse matrix is derived, which captures the total direct and indirect effects of changes in final use across countries and industries. The FIGARO tables are a statistical product of the integrated global accounts for economic modelling. They are constructed by combining multiple data sources, including National Accounts Main Aggregates (NAMA), Supply and Use Tables (SUTs), Balance of Payments (BoP), and trade statistics for goods and services. Meeting standards from the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-2010/overview European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)], the methodology ensures alignment with national accounts concepts, and integrates adjustments for trade asymmetries and valuation differences. The FIGARO tables link national accounts and data on business, trade and employment for the 27 EU Member States (Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Croatia, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary, Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland, and Sweden), 2 EFTA countries (Norway and Switzerland), 5 EU candidate countries (Albania, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, and Türkiye), and 15 main EU trading partners (Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, Mexico, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, South Korea, the United Kingdom, and the United States). A 'rest of the world' region completes the FIGARO tables. The FIGARO tables present the relationship between economies at a detailed level of 64 industries and 64 products, following the NACE and CPA classifications, as defined in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/KS-01-13-429-3A-C ESA 2010 national accounts transmission programme]. Key steps in the FIGARO process involve harmonising classifications, estimating trade margins, and balancing bilateral trade flows between countries, aligned with national accounts. This process generates inter-country supply, use and input-output tables that detail the flows of goods and services across industries and countries, enabling comprehensive analysis of global value chains, production, and environmental impacts. The following main applications are produced based on the FIGARO tables: *macroeconomic globalisation indicators, *greenhouse gas footprints linked to final consumption and investment in the EU. '''''Macroeconomic globalisation indicators''''' Macroeconomic globalisation indicators are designed to capture the direct and indirect economic effects across both industries and countries (spillovers), providing a nuanced understanding of the EU’s economic interdependencies and vulnerabilities. The EU value added (employment resp.) embedded in EU exports includes not only value added (employment resp.) by enterprises that are directly exporting, but also by those supplying goods and/or services for the production of exported goods and services; in other words, it also includes value added (employment resp.) by upstream enterprises. This may concern value added (employment resp.) by enterprises in the same industry as the exporter or in a different one (depending, in part, how detailed an activity classification is used). Equally, exports by enterprises in one EU Member State may support value added (employment resp.) in the same exporting Member State or in a different one. This article analyses the following macroeconomic globalisation indicators: *'''Domestic value added in exports - EU perspective''' = the gross value added generated, in the origin EU economy, by the exports of the exporting EU economy to non-EU economies. The indicator corresponds to the value added created, along the value chain, by the direct and indirect production of goods and services for extra-EU exports. It is measured in thousand euro, and as percentage of extra-EU exports. *'''Domestic employment in exports - EU perspective''' = the employment, in the origin EU economy, supported by the exports of the exporting EU economy to non-EU economies. The indicator corresponds to the employment created, along the value chain, by the direct and indirect production of goods and services for extra-EU exports. It is measured in number of persons, and as percentage of total employment. *'''Domestic value added in foreign final use''' = the gross value added generated, in the selected EU economy, along the value chain, by the production of goods and services that are purchased by users abroad (in the other EU and non-EU economies) for final consumption or investment purposes. The indicator is measured in thousand euro, and as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and percentage of gross value added. *'''Domestic employment in foreign final use''' = the employment, in the selected EU economy, supported, along the value chain, by the production of goods and services that are purchased by users abroad (in the other EU and non-EU economies) for final consumption or investment purposes. The indicator is measured in number of persons and as a percentage of total employment. *'''Exports by industry''' = the total (intra- and extra-EU) exports of goods and services of EU countries for intermediate and final uses. The values are measured in basic prices and follow national accounts concepts; they differ from international trade statistics (measured in FOB values). The indicator is measured in million euro, and as a percentage of total exports. *'''Global value chain participation - EU perspective''' = the sum of backward and forward participation. The backward participation with the EU perspective is calculated as a share of foreign (non-EU) value added in EU exports. The forward participation with the EU perspective is calculated as a share of value added generated in the EU by non-EU economies’ exports. These 3 indicators are measured in percentage of total EU exports. See [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/naio_10_fg_esms.htm Metadata on all available macroeconomic economic globalisation indicators] for further details. Detailed information on the indicators, their definition and use can be found in the Statistical Working Paper [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-01-24-017 Macroeconomic globalisation indicators based on FIGARO. Insights into the measurement of value added and employment in the EU]. It is worth mentioning that the macroeconomic globalisation indicators provide results in values (not differentiating between prices and volumes). Hence, results and conclusions about dependence in global value chains must be carefully considered. Additionally, throughout this article, all references to value added should be understood as [[Glossary:Gross_value_added|gross value added (GVA)]]. '''''What are domestic and spillover effects?''''' The '''domestic effect''' reflects the value added (employment respectively) in a given EU country that is '''generated (supported resp.) by its own exports''' to non-EU countries. This value added (employment resp.) may be in the same industry as the one that exports the goods or services (direct domestic effect) or in another industry (indirect domestic effect). As such, the indirect domestic effect is effectively an ''industry spillover effect'' within a single EU country – it is the value added (employment resp.) in a particular industry that is generated (supported resp.) by the exports of a different industry (within the same EU country). This article does not present the split of the domestic effect into direct and indirect effect but this one can be computed using the Eurostat dissemination datasets {{Stable link|title=|code=naio_10_fgde}} for the value added and {{Stable link|title=|code=naio_10_fgdee}} for the employment and dividing the economy into the different industries (according to the [[Glossary:Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)|NACE]] activity classification). By contrast, the '''spillover effect''' reflects the value added (employment resp.) in a given EU country that is '''generated (supported resp.) by the exports of other EU countries''' to non-EU countries. For example, it includes value added (employment resp.) in a country engaged in the production of intermediate inputs to be used in other EU countries' exports to non-EU countries. '''''Frequency and availability''''' The FIGARO tables and applications, including the macroeconomic globalisation indicators, are produced and updated annually (generally in summer). In July 2026, the time series '''from 2010 to 2024''' has been published (period ''T''-24 months, ''T'' being the year of release). The time series is in line with the latest macroeconomic aggregates. '''''More information''''' For more information, please refer to the thematic section for the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-supply-use-input-tables/overview supply, use, input-output and FIGARO tables]. ===Context=== '''''Purpose''''' The FIGARO tables offer the first official set of inter-country supply, use, and input-output data for the EU, serving as a crucial analytical tool. They enable comprehensive analyses of the social, economic, and environmental effects of globalisation, particularly relevant for studies on competitiveness, growth, productivity, employment, environmental impact, international trade, and global value chains. Used to evaluate EU policies, these tables also assess the economic interdependencies within the EU (or euro area or individual member countries) in the context of an increasingly globalised world. '''''Partners''''' The FIGARO tables are the result of a long-term collaboration between Eurostat and the European Commission's [https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/projects-and-activities/trade-and-industrial-policy-analysis_en Joint Research Centre]. Both partners also collaborate within the GIANT initiative (Global Input-Output Accounts), which is an global inter-agency network comprising the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the International Labour Organisation (ILO), the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (UN-ECLAC), the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UN-ECA), and the World Trade Organisation (WTO), which aims to explore synergies and common action among the various initiatives on the compilation of multi-country (extended) supply, use, and input-output tables. ===Other articles=== *[[Employment and value added using FIGARO data - automotive industry]] *[[Employment and value added using FIGARO data - pharmaceuticals]] *[[Economic globalisation indicators]] *[[Supply and use tables for the European Union and the euro area]] *[[Supply and use tables for individual countries]] *[[Building the System of National Accounts - supply and use tables|Building the System of National Accounts – supply and use tables]] *[[National accounts and GDP]] *[[Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment]] - online publication ===Database=== *Data can be accessed through the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-supply-use-input-tables/database thematic section] and are stored in [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/cec66924-a924-4f91-a0ef-600a0531e3ba/library/460a20fc-5956-44f9-8633-2821eb48dd62?p=1 Circabc]. Files containing the macroeconomic globalisation indicators are released in Excel format (for summary tables) and parquet file format (for detailed tables). *Data are also available from the Eurostat dissemination database in the folder "Macroeconomic globalisation indicators based on FIGARO (naio_10_fg)". ===Dedicated section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-supply-use-input-tables/overview Supply, use and input-output tables (SUIOTs) and FIGARO tables] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-01-24-017 Macroeconomic globalisation indicators based on FIGARO. Insights into the measurement of value added and employment in the EU] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-books/-/ks-gp-19-001 EURONA 1/2019 – The employment content of EU exports: an application of FIGARO tables] – see Chapter 3 *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-working-papers/-/KS-TC-19-002 EU inter-country supply, use and input-output tables – Full international and global accounts for research in input-output analysis (FIGARO)] ===Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-01-24-017 Macroeconomic globalisation indicators based on FIGARO. Insights into the measurement of value added and employment in the EU] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-books/-/ks-gp-19-001 EURONA 1/2019 – The employment content of EU exports: an application of FIGARO tables] – see Chapter 3 *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-working-papers/-/KS-TC-19-002 EU inter-country supply, use and input-output tables – Full international and global accounts for research in input-output analysis (FIGARO)] === Visualisations === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/dashboard/globalisation/ Eurostat globalisation dashboard] ===External links=== *[https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/projects-and-activities/trade-and-industrial-policy-analysis_en European Commission's Joint Research Centre - Trade and industrial policy analysis] *[https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/publications_en?f%5B0%5D=oe_publication_subject%3Ahttp%3A//data.europa.eu/uxp/2616&f%5B1%5D=oe_publication_type%3Ahttp%3A//publications.europa.eu/resource/authority/resource-type/FORECAST European Commission's Directorate-General for Economic and Financial Affairs - European Economic Forecasts] *[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/strategic-foresight/2020-strategic-foresight-report/resilience-dashboards_en European Commission - Resilience Dashboards] *[https://iri.jrc.ec.europa.eu/index.php/scoreboard/2023-eu-industrial-rd-investment-scoreboard The 2023 EU Industrial R&D Investment Scoreboard] *[https://www.oecd.org/sti/ind/measuring-trade-in-value-added.htm OECD – Trade in value added] {{Unit|topic=X_Input_output}} [[Category:Economy and finance|Employment and value added -
