title: Employment and value added using FIGARO data - automotive industry
text:
FIGARO tables – full international and global accounts for research in input-output analysis. Official inter-country supply, use and input-output data for the EU. A tool for analysing the social, economic and environmental effects of globalisation in the EU. A study on value added and employment for the automotive sector. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 At EU level, exports from the car industry generated less domestic value added in 2024 (€185.5 billion) than in 2023 (€190.1 billion), marking a reversal after growth since 2020. EU purchase of Chinese automotive products for final consumption or investment generated €4.2 billion of gross value added in China in 2024, up from €1.3 billion in 2010. In 2024, the EU automotive industry’s trade exposure towards the United States, the United Kingdom, and China amounted to €18.3, €16.0, and €11.7 billion, respectively. Exposure of the EU towards its main trading partners, 2010-2024 (thousand euro) This article delves into [[Glossary:Gross_value_added|gross value added (GVA)]] and [[Glossary:Employment|employment]] in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] associated with the [[Glossary:Global_value_chains_(GVC)|global value chains (GVCs)]] in the automotive industry that serves as a classic example of GVCs in Europe. It analyses macroeconomic globalisation indicators derived from the FIGARO tables (Full International and Global Accounts for Research in Input-Output Analysis) using the Leontief quantity model ([https://www.cambridge.org/us/universitypress/subjects/economics/econometrics-statistics-and-mathematical-economics/input-output-analysis-foundations-and-extensions-3rd-edition?format=PB&isbn=9781108723534 Miller and Blair, 2022]). GVCs are often not immediately visible in conventional trade statistics, which typically report the total value of a product at the point of trade. The automotive sector is important for the EU, as demonstrated in the [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/strengthening-european-competitiveness/eu-competitiveness-looking-ahead_en#paragraph_47059 Draghi Report], which dedicates a comprehensive chapter to the history, relevance, current status, and challenges faced by the EU in this arena. The data analysis focuses on [https://ec.europa.eu/competition/mergers/cases/index/nace_all.html NACE industry C29], encompassing motor vehicles, trailers, and semi-trailers (hereafter referred to as motor vehicles). For simplicity, the terms “vehicles”, "cars", and “automotive,” as well as “industry” and “sector,” are used interchangeably throughout. More information on the methodology used in the article can be found in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Employment_and_value_added_using_FIGARO_data_-_automotive_industry#Data_sources Data sources] section. === Value added in trade === The EU value added (references to value added should be understood as [[Glossary:Gross_value_added|gross value added (GVA)]] throughout this article), of the automotive industry is around €270 billion in 2024, accounting for 1.7% of the EU total GVA (€16.2 trillion). Germany was the largest contributor, with GVA of €152.1 billion (3.9% of the country's total GVA), followed by Italy (€18.3 billion, 0.9%), Spain (€15.8 billion, 1.1%), Sweden (€14.5 billion, 2.9%), France (€13.8 billion, 0.5%), Czechia (€13.6 billion, 4.6%), and Poland (€9.9 billion, 1.3%). EU exports of automotive products to non-EU countries reached €235.0 billion in 2024, representing 6.2% of the EU total exports of goods and services (€3.8 trillion). Meanwhile, EU imports of automotive products from non-EU countries amounted to €107.2 billion (3.4% of €3.1 trillion of EU total imports), resulting in a [[Glossary:Trade_surplus|trade surplus]] of €127.8 billion. A more detailed analysis of gross value added in trade reveals that EU exports of automotive products to non-EU countries contained €185.5 billion of '''domestic''' value added in 2024 (see Figure 1). This indicator, calculated from an EU perspective, represents the GVA generated in the EU economy by its exports of automotive products to non-EU economies, and includes value added from different EU countries and industries (spillover effects) within the EU, reflecting the industry’s complex supply chains. In contrast, '''foreign''' value added in EU automotive exports to non-EU countries (i.e. GVA generated outside of the EU by the exports of the EU economy to non-EU economies) generated €43.9 billion of GVA outside the EU in 2024. Between 2020 and 2022, the EU automotive industry relied increasingly on foreign suppliers for materials, parts, and intermediate goods. This trend, known as vertical specialisation or backward GVC linkage, may be driven by increases in prices, volumes, or both. However, between 2022 and 2024, the foreign value added in EU exports decreased (from €45.2 to €43.9 billion), indicating a pause in the previously growing trend. [[Image: Domestic and foreign value added embodied in EU automotive exports, EU, 2010-2024_(€ billion).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Domestic and foreign value added embedded in EU automotive exports, EU, 2010-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c0831fb6-33fe-49c0-b9de-b6b23aff4e65?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-06T12:40:26Z naio_10_fgde]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bd49e403-de9e-4740-90cd-16f08c4cfb8b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-06T12:47:27Z naio_10_fgfeie]) |alt=Line chart showing the evolution from 2010 to 2024, for the EU as a whole, of the domestic and foreign value added in exports of the EU automotive industry. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figures 2 and 3 illustrate the involvement of the EU main trading partners in EU vehicle exports over time. In 2024, the United Kingdom was the country whose imports of automotive products generated the highest value added '''in the EU''' (€36.7 billion, corresponding to 19.8% of the total EU value added generated by EU automotive exports), followed by the United States (€30.5 billion, 16.4%) and China (€21.6 billion, 11.6%)(see Figure 2). The EU value added from EU automotive exports to China rose sharply from €9.0 billion in 2010 to €27.4 billion in 2022, then fell to €24.8 billion in 2023 and €21.6 billion in 2024. In contrast, the importance of EU automotive exports to the United Kingdom and the United States, in terms of EU GVA, increased from 2010 to 2015, declined until 2020–2021, and then rose again in recent years. In 2024, Türkiye and Switzerland were also significant contributors to the EU value added generated by EU vehicles exports, with €13.8 and €10.0 billion, respectively. In 2024, the United Kingdom was also the largest player in terms of GVA generated '''outside the EU''' by EU vehicle exports, accounting for €9.5 billion, equivalent to 21.7% of the total value added in non-EU countries from EU automotive exports (see Figure 3). The United States was the next-largest contributor to foreign value added in EU automotive exports with €6.6 billion (15.1%). For these 2 importing countries, the value added generated in their economy follows the same trend as the value added generated in the EU (i.e. a rise from 2010 to 2015, followed by a decrease until 2020-2021, and an increase in recent years). The United States was followed by China, with €4.6 billion (10.6%), displaying a similar pattern as for the EU value added (i.e. an increase from 2010 to 2022, and a decrease in 2023 and 2024). In this case also, Türkiye and Switzerland came next, with €3.6 and €2.2 billion in 2024, respectively. Analysing the domestic (Figure 2) and foreign (Figure 3) value added in EU automotive exports reveals that the United Kingdom, the United States, and China are the key players in the automotive industry, not only as significant importers of EU vehicles but also as crucial suppliers of inputs required by the EU automotive sector for its exports. Figure 2 Figure 3 === Value added in final use === This section explores the contribution of the EU automotive industry to the value added embedded in the final use of goods and services in non-EU countries (domestic value added). It also analyses how much value added is generated in the automotive industries of non-EU countries (foreign value added) as a result of the EU final use of goods and services. In doing so, it considers the value added contribution of the automotive industry arising from the final use of products from all industries. This approach differs from that presented in the previous section, which examined the GVA contribution of the entire EU economy (across all industries) in the EU exports of the automotive industry to non-EU countries. Figure 4 illustrates the changes in the EU '''domestic''' automotive industry value added due to non-EU final use from 2010 to 2024. This indicator shows an upward trend, increasing from €51.7 billion in 2010 to €83.6 billion in 2017, before declining to €62.1 billion in 2020, and then rising again to €86.8 billion in 2024. The '''foreign''' automotive industry value added from EU final use displays a slightly different trend. It rose from €14.2 billion in 2010 to €28.0 billion in 2019, experienced a brief dip to €23.7 billion in 2020, and then climbed again to €32.6 billion in 2024. [[Image: Domestic and foreign value added in final use, EU, 2010-2024_(€ billion).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Domestic and foreign value added in final use, EU, 2010-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/866cbea1-6c1f-45e3-a106-c365d404ad35?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-06T14:43:44Z naio_10_fgdf]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/26303e45-d946-4a94-b72f-547dc9e7ffb5?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-06T14:47:16Z naio_10_fgfd]) |alt=Line chart showing the evolution from 2010 to 2024, for the EU as a whole, of the domestic and foreign value added generated in the automotive industry by final use. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] A detailed evolution of the '''domestic''' value added of the EU automotive industry resulting from non-EU final use, broken by partner country, is provided in the interactive Figure 5. In 2024, the United States accounted for €17.5 billion, representing 20.2% of the total EU automotive industry value added ending up in the final use of non-EU consumers, making it the largest contributor to the EU value added. The United Kingdom and China were the next-largest contributors, with €14.1 and €10.6 billion, representing 16.2% and 12.2% of the EU's domestic value added generated for non-EU final use, respectively. Türkiye and Switzerland followed, with €5.0 billion (5.7%) and €4.1 billion (4.7%), making them important markets for the EU automotive industry as well. Together, the United States, China, the United Kingdom, Türkiye, and Switzerland accounted for nearly 60% of the value added generated in the EU automotive industry due to the foreign final use of goods and services in 2024. The '''foreign''' value added generated in non-EU automotive industries by EU final use reached €32.6 billion in 2024. This reflects an increase in nominal terms of 130% since 2010 (€14.2 billion), but a slight decrease compared with 2023 (€32.8 billion). Figure 6 illustrates the role of EU final use as a driver of non-EU value added generation, highlighting the contribution from each non-EU country for the period 2010 to 2024. In 2024, Türkiye (being one of the largest vehicle manufacturers), with €4.4 billion, accounted for the largest share of value added in the non-EU automotive industry due to EU final use (13.4%). China followed with €4.2 billion (13.0%), after having peaked at €5.0 billion in 2022. Japanese automotive producers ranked next in 2024 in terms of foreign value added generated by EU final use, with €3.6 billion (11.0%). Other important countries include the United Kingdom, the United States, South Korea, and Mexico, with shares of 9.9%, 7.2%, 7.1%, and 6.0%, respectively. Collectively, Türkiye, China, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States accounted for around 55% of the total foreign automotive value added due to EU final use in 2024. Figure 5 Figure 6 === Exposure to trade disruptions === The EU automotive industry has strong bilateral relationships with the United Kingdom, the United States, China, and Türkiye. Two angles have been addressed previously: the value added in trade (EU value added in automotive exports), and the value added in final use (EU value added in automotive industry in total foreign final use). When appropriately combined, these 2 approaches become an indication of the overall exposure to trade disruptions. This exposure indicator provides a comprehensive view of all linkages between the EU and a target country. For instance, in 2024, the EU exposure towards the United States in the automotive industry reached €18.3 billion (see Figure 7). This figure represents the sum of the EU value added in various categories, including: # final automotive exports # intermediate exports of automotive products to the United States ending up in its final use, or in a third country’s final use # intermediate exports of automotive products to a third country ending up in the United States. The EU exposure to the United Kingdom in the same year was €16.0 billion, making the United Kingdom the next most important partner in the car industry. Relations with China have strengthened over the past decade, increasing the EU trade exposure from €4.7 billion in 2010 to €11.7 billion in 2024. In 2020 and 2021, the EU exposure to China was very similar to its exposure to the United States and the United Kingdom. The EU exposure towards Türkiye increased in recent years, reaching €6.0 billion in 2024. EU relationships with the United States, the United Kingdom, China, and Türkiye in the automotive sector are primarily characterised by greater exposure of the EU to these countries than of their exposure to the EU (see Figure 8). However, the car industry of Türkiye and the United States has become more exposed to the EU final use of goods and services in recent years, increasing to €4.9 and €2.7 billion, respectively, in 2024. This growth reflects the deeper integration of the automotive sector of these 2 countries not only into EU final use but also into third-country final use through EU production and into third-country production for EU final use. The exposure of China towards the EU also increased over the last decade, though with a slight drop in the last two years, rising from €1.5 billion in 2010 to €5.7 billion in 2022, then declining to €4.8 billion in 2024. Figure 7 Figure 8 === EU employment in final use === Examining EU employment triggered by domestic and foreign final use provides another lens through which to understand the impact of GVCs on European lives. In 2024, 6.6 million people were employed in the whole EU (across all industries) to meet final demand for products from the automotive industry. Among them, 4.0 million supported the final demand of EU consumers (domestic final use) and 2.6 million supported the final demand of non-EU consumers (foreign final use)(see Figure 9). EU employment in all industries linked to domestic final use of automotive products reached its peak in 2019, with 4.6 million workers, while EU employment in all industries linked to foreign final use of automotive products was highest in 2015, with 2.9 million workers. [[Image: EU employment in all industries generated by final use of products in the automotive industry, by group of countries of final use, 2010-2024_(thousand of persons).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: EU employment in all industries generated by final use of products in the automotive industry, by group of countries of final use, 2010-2024 (million of people)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://intragate.ec.europa.eu/eurostat/staging/databrowser/bookmark/5760f523-a3aa-40f7-83ad-06588cdfd945?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-07T15:42:52Z naio_10_fgdfef]) |alt=Bar chart showing the evolution, from 2010 to 2024, of the EU employment in all industries generated by final use of products in the automotive industry, for EU and non-EU final consumers. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 10 presents the number of employed people for each country of final use. In 2024, Germany was by far the country generating the highest employment in the EU (all countries and all industries together) through its final use of automotive products, with 1.6 million workers. The following EU countries were France, Italy, and Spain, supporting 466, 392, and 318 thousand workers, respectively, with their automotive final use. Non-EU economies with the highest impact on EU employment through their final demand of automotive products were the United States, the United Kingdom, and China, with 566, 405, and 315 thousand workers supported in the EU. [[Image: EU employment in all industries generated by final use of products in the automotive industry, by country of final use, 2024_(thousand of persons).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 10: EU employment in all industries generated by final use of products in the automotive industry, by country of final use, 2024 (thousand of people)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://intragate.ec.europa.eu/eurostat/staging/databrowser/bookmark/5760f523-a3aa-40f7-83ad-06588cdfd945?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-07T15:42:52Z naio_10_fgdfef]) |alt=Horizontal bar chart showing the EU employment in all industries generated by final use of products in the automotive industry by country of final use for the reference year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:SE article EMPL&VA automotive sector 2026ed.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === '''''Concept and definitions''''' Macroeconomic globalisation indicators presented in this article are computed using the FIGARO tables ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-supply-use-input-tables/information-data#figaro Full International and Global Accounts for Research in Input-Output Analysis]), through the application of the Leontief quantity model ([https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/inputoutput-analysis/431D85A5E459AB078479852169EA77D7 Miller and Blair, 2022]). This model relies on the interdependencies between industries and countries, represented mathematically in the form of technical coefficient matrices. The Leontief inverse matrix is derived, which captures the total direct and indirect effects of changes in final use across countries and industries. The FIGARO tables are a statistical product of the integrated global accounts for economic modelling. They are constructed by combining multiple data sources, including National Accounts Main Aggregates (NAMA), Supply and Use Tables (SUTs), Balance of Payments (BoP), and trade statistics for goods and services. Meeting standards from the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-2010/overview European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)], the methodology ensures alignment with national accounts concepts, and integrates adjustments for trade asymmetries and valuation differences. The FIGARO tables link national accounts and data on business, trade and employment for the 27 EU Member States (Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Croatia, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary, Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland, and Sweden), 2 EFTA countries (Norway and Switzerland), 5 EU candidate countries (Albania, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, and Türkiye), and 15 main EU trading partners (Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, Mexico, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, South Korea, the United Kingdom, and the United States). A 'rest of the world' region completes the FIGARO tables. The FIGARO tables present the relationship between economies at a detailed level of 64 industries and 64 products, following the NACE and CPA classifications, as defined in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/KS-01-13-429-3A-C ESA 2010 national accounts transmission programme]. Key steps in the FIGARO process involve harmonising classifications, estimating trade margins, and balancing bilateral trade flows between countries, aligned with national accounts. This process generates inter-country supply, use and input-output tables that detail the flows of goods and services across industries and countries, enabling comprehensive analysis of global value chains, production, and environmental impacts. The following main applications are produced based on the FIGARO tables: *macroeconomic globalisation indicators, *[[Glossary:Greenhouse_gas_(GHG)|greenhouse gas]] footprints linked to final consumption and investment in the EU. What are Global Value Chains (GVCs)? The production of goods and services relies on inputs, which can be sourced locally or globally. The final value of a product reflects the value that has been added in the different stages of the production chain, through the combination of factors of production, including employment. GVA may be generated, and employment may be located, in multiple countries. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as GVCs, which have significantly transformed international trade over the past few decades. GVCs have driven economic growth, innovation, and shaped global production networks, fostering a complex and interconnected world. By fragmenting production across borders, GVCs have capitalised on lower transportation costs and digital infrastructure. However, recent geopolitical events have disrupted the value chains, reshaping the global landscape. In response, countries are adopting policy measures, such as tariffs and export controls, to safeguard their economic security. Under the [https://commission.europa.eu/about-european-commission/towards-new-commission-2024-2029_en political guidelines 2024-2029 of the European Commission's President von der Leyen], resilient and strategically managed GVCs will become increasingly crucial for navigating global trade and maintaining economic stability. '''''Indicators''''' This article analyses the following macroeconomic globalisation indicators: *'''Imports by industry''' = the total ([[Glossary:Extra-EU_and_intra-EU|intra- and extra-EU]]) imports of goods and services of EU countries for intermediate and final uses. The values are measured in basic prices and follow national accounts concepts; they differ from international trade statistics (measured in [[Glossary:Cost,_insurance_and_freight_(CIF)|cost, insurance, and freight]] values, i.e. CIF). The indicator is broken down by exporting industry, classified according to NACE Rev. 2. It is measured in million euro, and as a percentage of total imports. *'''Exports by industry''' = the total (intra- and extra-EU) exports of goods and services of EU countries for intermediate and final uses. The values are measured in basic prices and follow national accounts concepts; they differ from international trade statistics (measured in [[Glossary:Free_on_board_(FOB)|free-on-board]] values, i.e. FOB). The indicator is broken down by exporting industry, classified according to NACE Rev. 2. It is measured in million euro, and as a percentage of total exports. *'''Domestic value added in exports - EU perspective''' = the gross value added generated in a EU economy (origin) by the exports of a EU economy (exporting) to non-EU economies. It corresponds to the value added created, along the value chain, by the direct and indirect production of goods and services for extra-EU exports. The indicator is broken down by exporting industry, classified according to NACE Rev. 2. It is measured in thousand euro, and as percentage of extra-EU exports. *'''Foreign value added in exports - EU perspective''' = the gross value added generated in a non-EU economy (origin) by the exports of a EU economy (exporting) to non-EU economies. It refers to the value added generated by the imports of goods and services used by the EU economy to produce other goods and services for extra-EU export. The indicator is broken down by exporting industry, classified according to NACE Rev. 2. It is measured in thousand euro, and as percentage of extra-EU exports. *'''Domestic value added in foreign final use''' = the gross value added generated, in the selected EU economy, along the value chain, by the production of goods and services that are purchased by users abroad (in the other EU and non-EU economies) for final consumption or investment purposes. The indicator is measured in thousand euro, and as a percentage of [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|Gross Domestic Product (GDP)]] and percentage of gross value added. *'''Foreign value added in domestic final use''' = the gross value added generated abroad, along the value chain, by the production of goods and services that are purchased by users from the selected EU economy for final consumption or investment purposes. This indicator highlights how industries abroad are connected to EU final consumers and investors. It is broken down by industry of origin, classified according to NACE Rev. 2. It is measured in thousand euro, and as a percentage of domestic final use. *'''Trading partner exposure''' = the domestic gross value added generated by the exports of an economy to a trade partner directly and indirectly through third countries. This indicator is built up on domestic value added in exports and domestic value added in foreign final use, and enables a more comprehensive assessment of the dependencies and potential vulnerabilities between the EU and its trade partners. It is measured in thousand euros. Metadata on all available macroeconomic economic globalisation indicators is available via this [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/naio_10_fg_esms.htm link]. Detailed information on the indicators, their definition and use can be found in the Statistical Working Paper [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-01-24-017 Macroeconomic globalisation indicators based on FIGARO. Insights into the measurement of value added and employment in the EU]. It is worth mentioning that the macroeconomic globalisation indicators provide results in values (not differentiating between prices and volumes). Hence, results and conclusions about dependence in GVCs must be carefully considered. Additionally, throughout this article, all references to value added should be understood as [[Glossary:Gross_value_added|gross value added (GVA)]]. '''''Frequency and availability''''' The FIGARO tables and applications, including the macroeconomic globalisation indicators, are produced and updated annually (generally in summer). In July 2026, the time series '''from 2010 to 2024''' has been published (period ''T''-24 months, ''T'' being the year of release). The time series is in line with the latest macroeconomic aggregates. '''''More information''''' For more information, please refer to the thematic section for the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-supply-use-input-tables/overview supply, use, input-output and FIGARO tables]. === Context === '''''Purpose''''' The FIGARO tables offer the first official set of inter-country supply, use, and input-output data for the EU, serving as a crucial analytical tool. They enable comprehensive analyses of the social, economic, and environmental effects of globalisation, particularly relevant for studies on competitiveness, growth, productivity, employment, environmental impact, international trade, and global value chains. Used to evaluate EU policies, these tables also assess the economic interdependencies within the EU (or euro area or individual member countries) in the context of an increasingly globalised world. '''''Partners''''' The FIGARO tables are the result of a long-term collaboration between Eurostat and the European Commission's [https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/projects-and-activities/trade-and-industrial-policy-analysis_en Joint Research Centre]. Both partners also collaborate within the GIANT initiative (Global Input-Output Accounts), which is an global inter-agency network comprising the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the International Labour Organisation (ILO), the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (UN-ECLAC), the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UN-ECA), and the World Trade Organisation (WTO), which aims to explore synergies and common action among the various initiatives on the compilation of multi-country (extended) supply, use, and input-output tables. === Other articles === *[[Employment and value added - an analysis with FIGARO data]] *[[Employment and value added using FIGARO data - pharmaceuticals]] *[[Economic globalisation indicators]] *[[Supply and use tables for the European Union and the euro area]] *[[Supply and use tables for individual countries]] *[[Building the System of National Accounts - supply and use tables|Building the System of National Accounts – supply and use tables]] *[[National accounts and GDP]] *[[Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment]] - online publication ===Database=== *Data can be accessed through the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-supply-use-input-tables/database thematic section] and are stored in [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/cec66924-a924-4f91-a0ef-600a0531e3ba/library/460a20fc-5956-44f9-8633-2821eb48dd62?p=1 Circabc]. Files containing the macroeconomic globalisation indicators are released in Excel format (for summary tables) and parquet file format (for detailed tables). *Data are also available from the Eurostat dissemination database in the folder "Macroeconomic globalisation indicators based on FIGARO (naio_10_fg)". ===Dedicated section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-supply-use-input-tables/overview Supply, use and input-output tables (SUIOTs) and FIGARO tables] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-01-24-017 Macroeconomic globalisation indicators based on FIGARO. Insights into the measurement of value added and employment in the EU] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-books/-/ks-gp-19-001 EURONA 1/2019 – The employment content of EU exports: an application of FIGARO tables] – see Chapter 3 *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-working-papers/-/KS-TC-19-002 EU inter-country supply, use and input-output tables – Full international and global accounts for research in input-output analysis (FIGARO)] ===Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-01-24-017 Macroeconomic globalisation indicators based on FIGARO. Insights into the measurement of value added and employment in the EU] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-books/-/ks-gp-19-001 EURONA 1/2019 – The employment content of EU exports: an application of FIGARO tables] – see Chapter 3 *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-working-papers/-/KS-TC-19-002 EU inter-country supply, use and input-output tables – Full international and global accounts for research in input-output analysis (FIGARO)] === Visualisations === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/dashboard/globalisation/ Eurostat globalisation dashboard] ===External links=== *[https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/projects-and-activities/trade-and-industrial-policy-analysis_en European Commission's Joint Research Centre - Trade and industrial policy analysis] *[https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/publications_en?f%5B0%5D=oe_publication_subject%3Ahttp%3A//data.europa.eu/uxp/2616&f%5B1%5D=oe_publication_type%3Ahttp%3A//publications.europa.eu/resource/authority/resource-type/FORECAST European Commission's Directorate-General for Economic and Financial Affairs - European Economic Forecasts] *[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/strategic-foresight/2020-strategic-foresight-report/resilience-dashboards_en European Commission - Resilience Dashboards] *[https://iri.jrc.ec.europa.eu/index.php/scoreboard/2023-eu-industrial-rd-investment-scoreboard The 2023 EU Industrial R&D Investment Scoreboard] *[https://www.oecd.org/sti/ind/measuring-trade-in-value-added.htm OECD – Trade in value added] {{Unit|topic=X_Input_output}} [[Category:Economy and finance|Employment and value added using FIGARO data - title: Employment in large-scale multinational enterprise groups
text:
EU statistics on employment in large-scale multinational enterprise groups. Data extracted: April 2026 Planned article update: April 2027
EXPERIMENTAL
 In 2024, more than 35 million people were working in large-scale multinational enterprise groups operating in EU and EFTA countries, according to the EuroGroups Register. Figure 1 This article gives an overview of the employment and control of the large-scale [[Glossary:Multinational_enterprise_(MNE)|multinational enterprise]] groups operating in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|EU]] and [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|European Free Trade Association (EFTA)]] countries in 2024, according to the data available in the European statistical register on multinational enterprise groups ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/statistical-business-registers/overview EuroGroups Register (EGR)]). A large-scale multinational enterprise group is a multinational enterprise group [[Glossary:Number_of_employees_and_self-employed_persons_-_EBS|employing]] at least 1 000 people in EU and EFTA countries and having at least 150 people employed in at least 2 EU and EFTA countries.The definition of a large-scale multinational enterprise group is as described in ''Article 2'' of {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0038:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/38/EC}}. In 2024, according to the EGR: * More than 35 million people were working in large-scale multinational enterprise groups operating in EU and EFTA countries; these represent an increase of around 5% with respect to the previous year. From the {{Template:Publication|code=egr_emp|title=persons employed in multinational enterprise groups}}, more than 2 out of 3 of them were working in a large-scale one.Without the second condition to have more than 150 people employed in at least two EU and EFTA countries, the number of MNE groups with at least 1 000 employees was around {{Template:Publication|code=egr_mne_n2sc|title=8 800}} and employed about {{Template:Publication|code=egr_emp|title=43 million}} people in the EU and EFTA countries in 2024 * The vast majority of the people employed in large-scale multinational enterprise groups were working in a group controlled by an EU or EFTA country, with only 20% of them controlled from abroad. * Almost half of these groups were active mainly in the manufacturing sector, with a large concentration (33.5%) of the people employed in large-scale multinational enterprise groups. Check the [[structure of multinational enterprise groups in the EU]] for more information about the entire population of MNE groups in the EU and EFTA countries according to the EGR. ===Employment in large-scale multinational enterprise groups operating in the EU and EFTA countries=== The source used in this article is the EGR, the European statistical business register for multinational enterprise groups. The scope of the EGR defines a multinational enterprise group as an enterprise group that operates in at least 2 countries, with one of these being in the EU or EFTA. Among them, large-scale multinational enterprise groups are the groups employing at least 1 000 people in the EU and EFTA countries and having at least 150 people employed in each of 2 of these countries. These groups are important for those Directorates General of the European Commission having responsibilities on the implementation of policy in the employment area. In 2024, according to the EGR: * Among the more than 51 million people working in a multinational enterprise group in EU and EFTA countries, over 35 million were working in a large-scale multinational enterprise group. This represents an increase of around 5% with respect to the previous year. * Around 4 100 (representing a 3% increase with respect to the previous year) large-scale multinational groups were present in the EU and EFTA countries, accounting for 2.7% of the multinational enterprise groups operating in the territory. ===Which countries control the large-scale multinational enterprise groups that operate in the EU and EFTA countries?=== Most of the large-scale multinational enterprise groups that operate in the EU and EFTA countries are controlled by an EU or EFTA country (3 out of 4): Figure 2 Since 2018, the number of large-scale multinational enterprise groups have been steadily increasing. Since 2018, an increase of around 20%; while in the last year alone, the number of large-scale multinational enterprise groups increased by almost 3%. Together with the fact that employment in the EU and EFTA countries in these groups increased, in the last year alone, around 5%, depicts that not only more large-scale multinational enterprise groups are present in the EU and EFTA countries, but also, they are getting larger in terms of employment. When looking at the distribution of groups between the EU and EFTA countries, it is rather stable, and some countries control most of these large-scale multinational enterprise groups. In 2024, the distribution looked like this: [[Image:Map_(number_groups)_-_EU-EFTA_2024.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 1: Large-scale MNE groups operating in EU and EFTA countries by controlling country, 2024
''Source'': EuroGroups Register {{Stable link|title=|code=egr_mne}}|alt=A map showing the number of large-scale multinational enterprise groups controlled by EU or EFTA countries for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Within the EU territory, most groups are controlled by Germany, with more than 650 of them; followed by France, the Netherlands, Italy and Sweden, controlling more than 200 groups each. In the EFTA territory, the country controlling the most groups is Switzerland, with more than 200 groups. There are also some small countries which control a large number of groups given their size, this is the case, for example, of Luxembourg, controlling more than 50 of these groups, even though the country represents only 0.1% of the {{Template:Publication|code=demo_gind|title=EU's population}}. From outside, the countries controlling the most large-scale multinational enterprise groups operating in the EU and EFTA countries are the United States and the United Kingdom, followed by Japan: [[Image:Map_(number_groups)_-_World_2024.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 2: Large-scale MNE groups operating in EU and EFTA countries by controlling country, 2024
''Source'': EuroGroups Register {{Stable link|title=|code=egr_mne}}|alt=A map chart showing the number of large-scale multinational enterprise groups by country of control for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===How much large-scale multinational enterprise groups impact the national employment?=== Workers of large-scale multinational enterprise groups are spread across the different EU and EFTA countries. According to {{Template:Publication|code=sbs_sc_ovw|title=structural business statistics (SBS)}}, almost 170 million people were working in EU and EFTA countries; out of those, more than 20% (around 35 million) of them worked in a large-scale multinational enterprise group. However, the distribution of these workers was very heterogeneous across the different countries: [[Image:Map_(share_employment)_-_EU-EFTA_2024.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 3: Percentage of people employed by large-scale multinational enterprise groups, 2024
''Source'': EuroGroups Register {{Stable link|title=|code=egr_emp}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=sbs_sc_ovw}}|alt=A map chart showing the share of total employment in large-scale multinational enterprise groups by country, 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In Greece, Cyprus and Iceland the impact of large-scale multinational enterprise groups in the national employment was limited, with less than 7.5% of the workforce being employed at a large-scale multinational enterprise group. On the contrary, in other countries, such as Luxembourg, Sweden, Czechia or Switzerland more than 30% of the workforce was being employed by a large-scale multinational enterprise group. ===In which sectors do large-scale multinational enterprise groups operate?=== In 2024, the EGR large-scale multinational enterprise groups operating in the EU and EFTA countries carried out a variety of economic activities, covering more than 20 [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE]] sections and almost 90 NACE divisions. These groups were mainly active in the manufacturing sector, covering around 45% of them. However, in terms of employment, although the manufacturing sector is still the most prevalent, it accounts for a lower share, with 33.5% of the employment (or about 12 million people) in large-scale multinational enterprise groups. This indicates that groups operating mainly in the manufacturing sector tend to be smaller in terms of employment when compared to other sector groups active in other sectors, like it can be, for instance, the financial or insurance services: Figure 3 ===Feedback=== To help Eurostat improve these experimental statistics, users and researchers are kindly invited to give us their [mailto:ESTAT-EGR@ec.europa.eu?subject=Feedback_on_experimental_statistics feedback by email] ===Data sources=== The EGR database is the source of the above-mentioned large-scale MNE groups data. The EGR is the statistical business register of the EU Member States and EFTA countries for MNE groups. It produces data in yearly cycles and covers microdata on the groups and their enterprises and legal units. The EGR aims to register all MNE groups that have enterprises in EU Member States or EFTA countries, including European and non-European groups. The EGR does not cover all-resident enterprise groups – those with enterprises only in one country, and independent enterprises. The EGR microdata help explore the structure and impact of MNE groups in Europe. One can analyse group size, complexity, and employment patterns in European countries, together with their European influence. The EGR makes it possible to present results from two sides: from the MNE group perspective, based on the country of control of the group, and from the national perspective of the country in which the group is located, irrespective of where the control unit is located. The EGR is a statistical business register that serves statistical purposes only. Access to EGR data is restricted to national statistical institutes and national central banks that produce official statistics in the EU Member States and EFTA countries. ===Context=== Globalisation and the increasing complexity of multinational enterprise group activities means it is difficult to produce business statistics and macroeconomic statistics and correctly and consistently reflect MNE group activities in European statistics. To better analyse cross-border transactions of large-scale multinational enterprise groups and correctly record them in statistical business registers, statisticians in the [[Glossary:European statistical system (ESS)| European Statistical System (ESS)]] and [[Glossary:European_System_of_Central_Banks|European System of Central Banks (ESCB)]] need to be able to observe the complete and correct economic structures of MNE groups. ===Other articles=== * [[Structure of multinational enterprise groups in the EU]] * [[EuroGroups_Register_and_industry_concentration|EuroGroups Register and title: Employment in foreign-controlled multinational enterprise transport groups
text:
EXPERIMENTAL
 Multinational enterprise groups active in transport and its employment distirbution Data extracted in October 2025 No planned article update Between 2018 and 2023, the number of people employed in transport and storage enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled multinational enterprise groups increased by 30%, reaching around 1.3 million in 2023. [[Image:M1_Weight_of_foreign_controlled_MNE_groups_in_transport_employment,_2023.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 1: Weight of transport enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups, EU, 2023
''Source:'' EuroGroups Register and SBS data]] This article is based on experimental statistics provided by the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/statistical-business-registers/overview EuroGroups Register (EGR)]. [[Glossary:Multinational_enterprise_(MNE)|Multinational enterprise (MNE) groups]] play a major role in the EU economy. This article examines the share of employment in the transport and storage sector ([[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE]] section H) enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups. The data refer mainly to the reference year 2023. From 2018 to 2023, foreign-controlled MNE groups increased their workforce in transport and storage by 30%, reaching 1.3 million employees, or 12% of sector employment. Predominantly, these were [[Glossary:EU|EU]] or [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] enterprises focused on transport support, road freight, and postal services. Highest employment rates were found in [[Glossary:Benelux|Benelux]], [[Glossary:Scandinavian_countries|Scandinavia]], Poland, Czechia, and Slovakia, with France having the lowest in the EU. Globally, Germany and France were top employers abroad, while outside the EU-EFTA territory, the United States and the United Kingdom emerged as key players in the transport sector. === About 1.3 million people employed in enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups=== The number of people employed in transport and storage enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups increased by 30% between 2018 and 2023. It exceeded one million in 2019 and reached nearly 1.3 million in 2023. Two thirds of these people worked for companies belonging to MNE groups controlled by EU or EFTA countries. This broad region of control was more dynamic (+33% between 2018 and 2023) than the rest of the world (+25%). Figure 1 === Of which more than half in support activities for transport === The overall share of people employed in transport and storage enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups stood at 12.0% in 2023. Support activities for transport at 25.3%, water transport (NACE division H50) at 25.0%, and air transport (NACE division H51) at 20.8% had the highest proportions of people employed in companies belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups. This high concentration in support activities for transport explains why this sector accounted for 24% of total employment, but 51% of employment in companies belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups (and even 59% of employment in companies belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups by non-EU non-EFTA countries). In absolute terms, road freight transport ranked second, with 210 000 people employed. They accounted for only 6% of total employment in this activity, half of the overall average share for the transport and storage sector (NACE section H). Postal and courier services ranked third with 138 000 people employed, just before other land transport (NACE groups H49.3 and H49.5) with 126 000 people employed. Rail transport (NACE groups H49.1 and H49.2) was proportionally the least affected, with 5.6% of total employment. [[Image:Table_1_Employment_in_transport_enterprises_belonging_to_foreign-controlled_MNE_groups_by_main_activity,_EU,_2023_(persons_employed,_in_thousands_and_%_of_total_employment).png |thumb|center|725px|Table 1: Employment in transport enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups by main activity, EU, 2023
''Source:'' EuroGroups Register and SBS data]] === Employment in MNE groups by EU country === In absolute terms, based on employment in enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups, Germany ranked first among EU and EFTA countries (191 000 people), followed by Poland (167 000), Spain (126 000), Italy (120 000) and the Netherlands (113 000). Together these 5 countries accounted for 56% of total employment in transport businesses belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups within the EU. [[Image:Table_2_Employment_in_transport_enterprises_belonging_to_foreign-controlled_MNE_groups,_by_country_of_the_enterprise,_2023_(persons_employed,_in_thousands).png|thumb|center|725px|Table 2: Employment in transport enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups, by country of the enterprise, 2023
''Source:'' EuroGroups Register and SBS data]] In relative terms, several countries had the shares of employment in enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups above 18%: the Benelux and Scandinavian countries, as well as Slovakia, Cyprus, Malta and Czechia. Luxembourg topped the list with 33.4%, followed by Sweden (27.5%) and the Netherlands (25.9%). On the opposite end of the scale, France is the least affected among the EU, with 5.9%, followed by Lithuania (6.4%) and several South-Eastern European countries. [[Image:M1_Weight_of_foreign_controlled_MNE_groups_in_transport_employment,_2023.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 1: Weight of transport enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups, EU, 2023
''Source:'' EuroGroups Register and SBS data]] === Enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups by country and activity === The detailed analysis of activities by country is limited by the small number of reporting units or by the dominance of a few large companies belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups. This is especially the case in air transport and water transport, where the situation across countries is highly contrasted. Table 3 presents the percentages of employment in enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups, where data is not affected by statistical confidentiality. This is generally the case for support activities for transport, road freight transport and postal and courier services. Among these 3 sectors of activity, employment in companies belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups in Czechia presented a particularly high share in support activities for transport (55.6%), followed by Belgium (51.5%). In road freight transport such businesses were most prominent in Luxembourg (30.3% of total employment), Slovakia (15.8%) and Poland (10.9%). In postal and courier services Denmark (31.7%), Sweden (23.8%) and Estonia (22.3%) recorded the highest proportions. [[Image:Table_3_Employment_in_selected_activities_of_transport_enterprises_belonging_to_foreign-controlled_MNE_groups,_by_country_of_the_enterprise,_2023_(%_of_total_employment).png |thumb|center|725px|Table 3: Employment in selected activities of transport enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled MNE groups, by country of the enterprise, 2023
''Source:'' EuroGroups Register and SBS data]] === EU and EFTA controlling countries in absolute terms and in relative shares === Statistics can also be compiled by EU and EFTA countries of control, showing the employment in enterprises abroad controlled by domestic MNE groups. The enterprises in Table 3 are limited to EU countries, for consistency with Figure 2. Germany (232 000 people employed by German MNE groups in other EU countries) and France (176 000) were by far the most significant controlling countries, followed by the Netherlands (72 000) and the EFTA country Switzerland (69 000). Figure 2 German and French controlled MNE groups together accounted for nearly half of all people employed by enterprises belonging to foreign-controlled EU and EFTA MNE groups in the transport and storage sector across the EU. Their share was particularly high in postal and courier services (74% combined), air transport (over 65%), other land transport (60%) and support activities for transport (44%). The Netherlands had high shares in road freight and in water transport, Denmark in water transport and in support activities for transport, Luxembourg in other land transport, Italy in water transport, Austria in rail transport, Ireland in air transport, Estonia in water transport, and Switzerland in support activities for transport . Water transport in overall was less concentrated. Figure 3 In relative terms (when the number of people employed abroad by domestic MNE groups is compared to the total domestic transport employment), Luxembourg, Denmark, Switzerland, Cyprus, the Netherlands, Ireland, Austria and Estonia surpassed France and Germany. The EGR covers the EU countries in both dimensions: country of enterprise (i.e. enterprise resident in the country) and country of control (i.e. country of the unit ultimately controlling the MNE group to which the enterprise belongs). Each country can consider which phenomenon is the more important in its national case. In order to assess the impact of MNE groups on national economies, we have calculated the “net employment abroad” indicator which is defined as the balance between the employment abroad controlled by domestic MNE (Figure 2) and the domestic employment controlled by foreign MNE (Table 2). A positive “net employer abroad” is then a country where the domestically-controlled MNE groups employ more people abroad than foreign-controlled MNE groups employ domestically.” Figure 4 Germany and France were the most prominent ''“net employers abroad”'' in the transport sector among EU countries, with similar figures (138 000 and 127 000 people employed, respectively), followed by Luxembourg (34 000) and Denmark (28 000). At the opposite end of the scale, Poland (-109 000 people employed) recorded the most negative value for this indicator (indicating that it was more controlled by foreign EU MNE groups than it controlled itself), followed by Spain (-37 000), Czechia (-33 000) and Sweden (-32 000). In relative terms, Luxembourg (137% of its total domestic employment), Denmark and Cyprus (both 18%) surpassed France (8%). [[Image:M2_Net_transport_employment_abroad_EU_MNE_groups,_2023.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 2: Net transport employment abroad by EU controlled MNE groups (domestically vs foreign-controlled MNE groups), 2023
''Source:'' EuroGroups Register and SBS data]] === The most significant controlling countries outside of the EU and EFTA === Most of the statistical information presented can be determined for countries outside the EU and EFTA territory when they act as country of control. However, this is not possible when they are considered as countries of enterprise (i.e. enterprise resident in countries outside the EU and EFTA territory). In line with the statistical trends observed for the overall EU-EFTA territory and its Member States, the United States emerges as the most significant controlling country outside of the EU and EFTA, significantly ahead of the United Kingdom. China, including Hong Kong, follows closely, slightly ahead of Japan and the United Arab Emirates. Figure 5 === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Foreign-controlled multinational enterprise groups in transport employment - article REV.xlsx|Employment in foreign-controlled multinational enterprise transport groups: figures and tables]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === This micro data linking exercise focused on linking the available statistical information from following data sources: * Structural business statistics (SBS); * the National Statistical Business Registers (NSBR); * the EuroGroups Register (EGR) The '''Structural Business Statistics''' describe the detailed structure, economic activity, and performance of businesses over time. The SBS data collection has very good coverage in terms of size class of enterprises and their economic activity. Thus, this source provides the most comprehensive picture of the European economy, both at country and EU level. The '''National Statistical Business Registers''' are the registers of businesses at national level, of which a common core is harmonised pursuant to {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R2152:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2019/2152}} as a basis for the preparation and coordination of surveys and as a source of information for the statistical analysis of the business population and its demography, for the use of administrative data, and for the identification and construction of statistical units. The '''EuroGroups register''' is the source of the MNE groups data. It produces data in yearly cycles and covers microdata on the MNE groups and their consisting enterprises and legal units. It serves statistical purposes only. Access to EGR data is restricted to national statistical institutes and national central banks that produce official statistics in the EU Member States and EFTA countries. The EGR aims to register all MNE groups that have enterprises in EU Member States or EFTA countries, including European and non-European MNE groups. The data in this article covers the [[Glossary:EU-27|EU countries]] and the [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA countries]]. === Context === Globalisation and the increasing complexity of multinational enterprise group activities means it is difficult to produce business statistics and macroeconomic statistics and correctly and consistently reflect MNE group activities in European statistics. To better analyse cross-border transactions of multinational enterprise groups and correctly record them in statistical business registers, statisticians in the [[Glossary:European_statistical_system_(ESS)|European Statistical System (ESS)]] and [[Glossary:European_System_of_Central_Banks|European System of Central Banks (ESCB)]] need to be able to observe the complete and correct economic structures of multinational enterprise groups. === Other articles === * [[Structure of multinational enterprise groups in the EU]] * [[Employment_in_large-scale_multinational_enterprise_groups|Employment in large-scale multinational enterprise groups]] * [[Economic_indicators_of_enterprises_belonging_to_multinational_enterprise_groups|Economic indicators of enterprises belonging to multinational enterprise groups]] * title: Employment and value added using FIGARO data - pharmaceuticals
text:
Insert short description for search engines Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 In 2024, EU exports from the pharmaceutical industry supported employment for one million people in the EU, corresponding to 0.46% of total EU employment. EU employment linked to pharmaceutical exports to the United States more than doubled between 2010 and 2024 (from 116 000 to 297 000 workers). In 2024, the exposure of the EU pharmaceutical industry to potential trade disruptions towards the United States, Switzerland, and China reached €58.6, €16.4 and €13.3 billion, respectively, in terms of EU gross value added. Employment (in all industries) supported by exports of the pharmaceutical industry, by importing country, EU, 2010-2024

The pharmaceutical sector is a significant contributor to the economy of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], as highlighted in the [https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/ec1409c1-d4b4-4882-8bdd-3519f86bbb92_en?filename=The%20future%20of%20European%20competitiveness_%20In-depth%20analysis%20and%20recommendations_0.pdf Draghi Report]. Combining cutting-edge research with strategic manufacturing to develop vital medications and therapies, this sector is one of the most dynamic in Europe. The European pharmaceutical industry is crucial for economic growth, contributing significantly to job creation and export revenues. However, it faces several challenges, including global competition and market fragmentation. To provide more insights into this sector, this article analyses the [[Glossary:Gross_value_added|gross value added]] and [[Glossary:Employment|employment]] associated with its [[Glossary:Global_value_chains_(GVC)|global value chains (GVCs)]]. Analysing the GVCs can offer a deeper understanding of international trade relations than conventional trade statistics, which typically report the total value of a product at the point of trade. The article focuses on [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] industry C21, which includes the manufacture of basic pharmaceutical products and pharmaceutical preparations. For simplicity, the terms "pharmaceutical industry" and "pharmaceutical sector" are used interchangeably. === EU employment linked to foreign final use === In 2024, total employment in the EU manufacturing industry, which includes the pharmaceutical industry, reached 30 million people. Although [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU ]]manufacturing employment fell between 1995 and 2014, it rose by 3.28% between 2010 (the first year of the FIGARO data) and 2024. Employment in the EU pharmaceutical industry supported by the final use of goods and services in non-EU countries has also increased since 2010, but much more sharply, by 101.03%. In 2024, the final use of products by consumers outside the EU supported the employment of 351 730 people in the EU pharmaceutical industry, twice the number recorded in 2010 (174 962 workers) (see Figure 1a). The share of EU pharmaceutical employment linked to foreign final use of products in total EU manufacturing employment was 0.60% in 2010 and reached 1.17% in 2024 (see Figure 1b). This means that the foreign-final-use component of the EU pharmaceutical employment grew much faster than overall EU manufacturing employment during this period. Consequently, employment in the EU pharmaceutical industry supported by final consumption outside the EU rose sharply and steadily between 2010 and 2024, showing both the expansion of the EU pharmaceutical workforce and its growing dependence on external demand. Figure 4 === Direct and indirect effects of EU exports on employment === The employment supported by the EU exports from the pharmaceutical industry, discussed in the previous section, can arise either within the pharmaceutical industry itself or in other industries. The former represents the direct effect of EU exports on employment, while the latter reflects the indirect effect, effectively an industry spillover within the EU. This indirect effect captures employment in one industry that is sustained by exports from another industry in the EU. Figure 5 compares the direct and indirect employment effects of pharmaceutical exports within the EU. It shows both the employment within the pharmaceutical industry supported by exports from all industries and the employment in other industries supported by exports from the pharmaceutical industry. Please note that the industries are presented according to the NACE Rev. 2 activity classification. The data reveal that the direct effect is by far more significant than the indirect effect. In 2024, 341 400 people were employed in the EU pharmaceutical industry thanks to its own exports to non-EU countries. By contrast, EU exports from all other industries supported employment for only 27 400 people in the pharmaceutical sector. Meanwhile, EU pharmaceutical exports sustained 663 600 workers across other industries, confirming the role of the pharmaceutical industry as a net contributor to broader EU employment through its exports to non-EU countries. In terms of percentages, the spillover effects from the EU exports of the pharmaceutical industry accounted for 66.0% (663 600 / 1 005 000) of the EU employment supported by pharmaceutical exports, whereas the spillover effects from the EU exports from other industries only contributed to 7.44% (27 400 / 368 800) of employment in the pharmaceutical sector linked to EU exports. Consequently, the indirect effect of EU exports on employment is strongly asymmetric for the pharmaceutical industry: its employment depends primarily on its own exports rather than on exports from other sectors, while it acts through its exports as a generator of employment across the wider EU economy. === Exposure to trade disruptions === As demonstrated in the previous sections, the EU pharmaceutical industry maintains strong bilateral trade relationships with the United States, China, and Switzerland, as well as with Japan, and the United Kingdom. The analysis examined 2 key perspectives: first, EU employment in the pharmaceuticals industry linked to foreign final use and second, EU employment supported by pharmaceutical exports. A similar analytical framework can be applied to value added (references to value added should be understood as [[Glossary:Gross_value_added|gross value added (GVA)]] throughout this article), distinguishing between: EU value added in the pharmaceutical industry incorporated into foreign final use, and EU value added embedded in pharmaceutical exports. When combined, these 2 indicators provide a comprehensive measure of the overall exposure to potential trade disruptions. The exposure indicator offers an exhaustive view of all linkages between the EU and a target partner country. For instance, in 2024, the EU exposure of the pharmaceutical industry towards the United States reached €58.6 billion (see interactive Figure 6). This number represents the sum of the EU value added in various categories, including: # final pharmaceutical exports # intermediate exports of pharmaceutical products to the United States ending up in its final use, or in a third country’s final use # intermediate exports of pharmaceutical products to a third country ending up in the United States. Figure 6 The United States remained the dominant EU pharmaceutical trade partner throughout 2010–2024, with the EU exposure rising sharply from €11.6 billion in 2010 to €58.6 billion in 2024. This growth was particularly pronounced in 2 distinct phases: first, a steep increase from €11.6 billion in 2014 to €17.2 billion in 2015, followed by a second surge from €33.0 billion in 2021 to €44.4 billion in 2022. Overall, the United States accounted for the highest absolute growth, with increase becoming especially marked after 2014. Meanwhile, China emerged as the fastest-growing trade partner in relative terms, with EU exposure expanding tenfold from €1.3 billion in 2010 to €13.3 billion in 2024. By 2019, it had overtaken both the United Kingdom and Japan. However, the EU trade exposure to China constantly remained below that of Switzerland, which is characterised by a stable upward trend from €4.3 billion in 2010 to €16.4 billion in 2024. This growth was consistent and free of major fluctuations, reflecting the role of Switzerland as a reliable and expanding trade partner. Switzerland and China established themselves as the second- and third-largest EU pharmaceutical trade partners by 2024. However, the EU exposure to these 2 countries remained far below that of the United States. For the United Kingdom, the EU trade exposure rose gradually from €3.8 billion in 2010 to €6.1 billion in 2016. This rise stalled in subsequent years, leaving the figure at just €6.3 billion by 2021, but rose again subsequently to €8.8 billion in 2024. By contrast, Japan demonstrated near-linear growth from €1.8 billion in 2010 to €5.6 billion in 2022, followed by a decrease to €5.1 billion in 2024. Figure 7 The exposure indicator can also be analysed from the perspective of the pharmaceutical industry of the EU trade partners. Interactive Figure 7 illustrates how trade exposure of key EU partners to the EU evolved between 2010 and 2024 for the pharmaceutical industry. During this period, the United States and Switzerland recorded the highest exposure levels, which gradually grew. The United Kingdom, India and China also experienced steady growth, but starting from significantly lower baselines. A comparison of Figures 6 and 7 reveals asymmetries in exposure levels. For instance, in 2024, the exposure of the United States to the EU stood at €15.5 billion, which is far below the EU exposure to the United States (€58.6 billion). A similar imbalance existed for China (€1.1 billion versus €13.3 billion) as well as for the United Kingdom, although less pronounced (€6.1 billion versus €8.8 billion). Conversely, Switzerland displayed greater exposure to the EU than the EU did to them: €18.1 billion versus €16.4 billion. However, the 2 exposure levels are similar for India for 2024: €1.6 billion. The rising exposure of the United States and Switzerland (as well as the United Kingdom, India and China) to the EU reflects the deepening integration of their pharmaceutical industries into the final exports to EU consumers, but also the intermediate exports to third countries ending up in the EU, and the intermediate exports to the EU for further processing and re-export to third-country markets. Likewise, the high and increasing level of EU exposure to the United States, Switzerland and China underscores the growing embeddedness of the EU pharmaceutical sector in multiple dimensions. This includes not only direct and indirect supply chains serving US, Swiss, and Chinese consumers, but also supply-chain dynamics with third-country final use where US, Swiss, and Chinese production incorporates EU pharmaceutical inputs.
