title: Enlargement policy and statistical cooperation
text:
<updatedata>Article last updated: February 2026</updatedata>

<introarticle>
This article is part of a series of [[International_statistical_cooperation|background articles]] that present the international statistical cooperation activities of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] with non-member countries (also known as non-EU countries or third countries), and focuses on [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/enlargement-policy_en enlargement policy], which is part of the [[Glossary:Treaty on European Union|Treaty on European Union]]. 
Eurostat’s priorities concerning the enlargement process include supporting the enlargement countries in the development of their statistical systems, monitoring progress on economic, social and institutional reforms and integrating the statistical data of enlargement countries in the Eurostat database. 
</introarticle>
<articlecontent>
<sesection>
==EU enlargement policy==
Accession negotiations assess a [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate country’s]] ability to meet the obligations of EU membership. They focus on how and when countries will comply with '''the EU ''acquis'''''. The [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/eu-enlargement_en '''EU Enlargement Policy'''] remains a key driver of democratic, social, and economic reform in the enlargement countries. It has strengthened governance and created new opportunities for trade and growth across an expanded internal market. As reaffirmed in the [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029_en '''EU Commission’s 2024-2029'''] priorities, enlargement is a strategic objective that supports stability, resilience, and competitiveness in Europe’s changing geopolitical environment.

The EU’s enlargement and neighbourhood engagement are supported by the [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/funding-technical-assistance/overview-instrument-pre-accession-assistance_en '''Instrument for Pre-Accession'''] (IPA) and the  [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/funding-technical-assistance/neighbourhood-development-and-international-cooperation-instrument-global-europe-ndici-global-europe_en '''Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument – Global Europe (NDICI–Global Europe)''']. Since 2007, IPA provides financial and technical assistance to enlargement countries, helping build institutional capacities and support reforms throughout the accession process, fostering progressive developments in the region.  Currently at its third edition, IPA III (2021–2027) is closely aligned with EU flagship initiatives and strategies for the Western Balkans, supporting targeted investments and reforms in the region. NDICI–Global Europe is the EU’s significant external financing tool for 2021–2027, promoting stability, sustainable development, and international partnerships. It merges several previous instruments to provide more flexible and coordinated support for partner countries, particularly those most in need. The instrument contributes to achieving the [https://sdgs.un.org/2030agenda '''UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development'''] and the [https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-paris-agreement?utm_source=chatgpt.com '''Paris Agreement on climate change'''], while reinforcing the EU’s role as a global partner in resilience and sustainable growth.

The EU Member States have granted the perspective of membership to several [https://www.europarl.europa.eu/topics/en/article/20180126STO94113/enlargement-how-do-countries-join-the-eu#:~:text=Which%20countries%20want%20to%20join,is%20a%20potential%20candidate%20country '''neighbouring countries'''], which are at different stages of the enlargement process. The [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/enlargement-policy/enhanced-eu-engagement-western-balkans_en '''EU’s enlargement policy for the Western Balkans'''], aims to promote stability, regional cooperation, and alignment with EU values and standards. It supports gradual integration into the EU single market and advances reforms in governance, the rule of law, and the economy. The [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/funding-technical-assistance/reform-and-growth-facility-western-balkans_en '''Reform and Growth Facility'''], complementing the [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/enlargement-policy/overview-instrument-pre-accession-assistance_en '''Instrument of Pre-accession Assistance (IPA III)'''], provides financial and technical support to sustain reforms and strengthen resilience in neighbouring countries. It underpins key initiatives such as the [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/funding-technical-assistance/growth-plan-moldova_en '''EU–Moldova Reform and Growth Plan  (2025)'''], [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-approves-reform-agendas-albania-kosovo-montenegro-north-macedonia-and-serbia-paving-way-2024-10-23_en '''reform agendas'''] for '''Albania''', '''Kosovo'''<ref>This designation is without prejudice to positions on status, and is in line with UNSCR 1244 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo Declaration of Independence.</ref>, '''Montenegro''', '''North Macedonia''', and '''Serbia (2024) ''', '''Bosnia and Herzegovina (2025)''' and the [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/eu-solidarity-ukraine/eu-assistance-ukraine/ukraine-facility_en '''Ukraine Facility (2024)'''].
</sesection>
<sesection>
==The role of official statistics in the enlargement process==
Official statistics play a double role in the enlargement process: 
*the EU ''acquis'' in the field of statistics ([https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/enlargement-policy/conditions-membership/chapters-acquis_en Chapter] 18 of 35, on the negotiation process) defines the harmonisation of statistics with EU standards and rules, which has to be achieved in the pre-accession period;
*they serve other EU policy areas by providing data for monitoring progress and assessing the impact of policies.
</sesection>
<sesection>
==The EU ''acquis'' in the field of statistics==
The EU ''acquis'' is divided into '''six thematic clusters''', with '''official statistics forming Chapter 18''', under ''Cluster 1: Fundamentals''. Statistics also play a key role in other chapters, as they enable '''screening and monitoring''' of progress towards meeting the '''accession criteria'''.

The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-25-009 '''Statistical Requirements Compendium (SRC)'''] outlines the legal basis, methodologies and data requirements of the EU ''acquis'' in statistics. Since 2024, it has been organised according to the ''Classification of Statistical Activities (CSA) Rev. 2.0 (2023)'', covering six areas:
[[Image:ES3.png|thumb|centre|590px|'''CSA Rev. 2.0: Six Statistical Activity Domains''']]

Before negotiations begin, the '''screening process''' helps the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:European_Commission_(EC) '''European Commission'''] and each candidate country assess the level of preparedness for adopting EU rules. The Commission '''monitors reform progress''' in candidate countries and in potential candidates and reports annually to the [[Glossary:Council_of_the_European_Union|'''Council''']] and [[Glossary:European_Parliament_(EP)|'''European Parliament''']] through the [https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/enlargement-policy/strategy-and-reports_en '''Enlargement Package country reports''']. The first reports covering '''Moldova''', '''Georgia''', and '''Ukraine''' were published in '''2023'''.

The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02009R0223-20241226&qid=1745846927785 '''Law'''] on European statistics - Regulation (EC) No 223/2009, as amended and revised by the Regulation (EU) 2024/3018 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2024 defines the legal framework for developing, producing and disseminating European statistics. It sets out the '''principles''', '''procedures''' and '''responsibilities''' of national and EU statistical authorities, with [[Glossary:Eurostat|'''Eurostat''']] serving as the EU’s statistical authority.

Quality and trust in statistics are ensured through the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-catalogues/-/KS-02-18-142 '''European Statistics Code of Practice'''] (ESCoP), which sets '''16 principles''' governing the production and dissemination of official statistics. It is aligned with the [[Glossary:United Nations (UN)|'''United Nations''']]’ [http://unstats.un.org/unsd/dnss/gp/fundprinciples.aspx '''Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics'''] and the [[Glossary:United Nations (UN)|'''United Nations''']]’ [http://unstats.un.org/unsd/methods/statorg/Principles_stat_activities/principles_stat_activities.htm '''Principles governing international statistical activities''']. The ESCoP adjusts the principles to the EU context and contains indicators to measure their implementation.

The '''EU ''acquis'' in statistics''' requires enlargement countries to build '''robust statistical systems''' capable of producing official statistics aligned with evolving EU standards. [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] supports this process by:
*'''Monitoring alignment''' with the EU acquis in statistics (Chapter 18);
*'''Providing technical assistance''' through training, study visits, management programmes, statistical projects and participation in European Statistical System (ESS) meetings;
*'''Implementing cooperation programmes''', both '''multi-country''' and '''bilateral''', to strengthen national statistical capacities and ensure the production of '''harmonised''', '''high-quality data''' that are compliant with the EU ''acquis''.

In addition, Eurostat conducts [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-cooperation/regional-cooperation/assessments#Sector%20review peer reviews and sector reviews]. Peer reviews are assessments of how a country's statistical system adheres to the European Statistics Code of Practice. Sector reviews analyse in detail the statistical production processes in specific sectors. They are specifically tailored to the needs of selected partner countries. Countries request a detailed review of a statistical sector to receive recommendations on how to align this sector of statistics with European requirements.
</sesection>
<sesection>
==Eurostat’s IPA strategy with the enlargement countries for the period 2021 – 2027==
Statistical cooperation with the enlargement countries is aimed at supporting them in their efforts to become compliant with the EU acquis in statistics. The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/12944781/19585138/Eurostat_IPA_strategy_2021-27.pdf/0b07657a-a72c-a840-559e-bc381ad920a2?t=1720678988144 '''IPA strategy 2021–2027'''] targets priority areas for improvement and strives to make the achieved results sustainable. This strategy covers the Western Balkans and Türkiye, but not the three newest enlargement countries: Moldova, Georgia, and Ukraine. Its timeframe aligns with the [https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/eu-budget/long-term-eu-budget/2021-2027_en '''EU multi-annual financial framework'''] and IPA III, the unified EU pre-accession funding instrument. The objectives of the strategy are to:
*increase the production and dissemination of high-quality statistical data;
*implement the European Statistics Code of Practice;
*strengthen the administrative and management capacity of national statistical systems;
*enhance regional statistical cooperation.
</sesection>
==Data sources and publications==
Enlargement countries - Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, Türkiye, Ukraine,<ref>On 14-15 December 2023, the European Council decided to open accession negotiations with Moldova and Ukraine and granted the status of candidate country to Georgia. These three countries are also ENP-East countries.</ref> and Kosovo - progressively increase the production and dissemination of statistics, which are aligned to EU standards, to support the EU accession process. Most countries already submit data to Eurostat that are disseminated through:
*[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database '''Eurobase'''] – Eurostat’s free reference database, where statistics validated from enlargement countries are published alongside EU Member States;
*[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Enlargement_countries_-_statistical_overview '''Statistics Explained'''] – articles covering specific statistical domains;
*Eurostat publications, such as the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat Regional Yearbook], that include harmonised data from enlargement countries  when data are available.
Georgia, Moldova, and Ukraine also provide some data, but much of it is still being validated and not yet disseminated in the Eurobase tables along with the data from EU Member States.   To fill these gaps, selected annual indicators from these countries are collected in an additional, simplified data collection and disseminated in Eurobase via the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/explore/all/general?lang=en&subtheme=noneu.enpe&display=list&sort=category ENP-East domain] and in [[International_cooperation|Statistics Explained articles]]. These data are supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authority. They are not validated by Eurostat and without assurance as regards their quality and adherence to EU statistical methodology. The dissemination of validated data in the regular Eurobase tables is expected to expand in the coming years.
</articlecontent>

title: Enterprises - access to finance and public funding for innovation purposes
text:
Insert short description for search engines Data extracted in September 2025 Planned article update: September 2027 In 2020-2022, EU businesses used around half of their equity finance fully or partly for innovation projects, compared with less than a quarter of their debt finance. The share of EU businesses that used equity financing was more than twice as high in large companies (13%) than in small companies (5%) in 2020-2022. [[Image:3_Enterprises_that_tried_to_obtain_private_funding_through_equity_or_debt,_by_wh.png|Enterprises that tried to obtain private funding through debt or equity, by whether their attempt was successful or not, and by use for innovation (incl. R&D), EU, 2020-2022
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4d8986d4-83f8-451a-b455-5aac275ade48?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:00:11Z inn_cis13_fin] ; [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6ae3313a-4e6e-4a99-a07c-e4a5c81e532a?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:02:20Z inn_cis13_finrd] ; [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/17a4f515-f9cd-4a82-94d3-a2bebf053957?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:04:04Z inn_cis13_bas])|thumb|centre|700px|alt=A stacked bar chart showing the share of enterpises in the EU that tried to obtain private funding through debt or equity, by whether their attempt was successful or not, and by use for innovation, for the period from 2020 to 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Financing innovation activities: a crucial ingredient for enterprises’ success === The facility (or difficulty) with which enterprises can obtain finance matters for their capacity to grow and adapt to new market conditions, in short: to their survival and success. It also matters for their capacity to innovate because innovation activity requires investment. The proceeds from innovation activity flow back into the enterprises as benefits (turnover for innovative products; increased efficiency of processes) only after the innovation effort – the amount of the investments can be high, and the time-lag long. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) deserve a particular focus because they might find it harder than large companies to obtain the finance that they would need for their innovation projects. There are many sizable EU funding schemes targeted towards SMEs. Eurostat’s statistics on business innovation, obtained with the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Glossary:Community_innovation_survey_(CIS) Community Innovation Survey (CIS)], provide information on the access to finance. This data has features that many other data sources lack: they can report along employment size classes of enterprises (enabling SME related analysis); they can be related to innovation activity in the enterprises; they are available for different economic NACE activities. This article reports on: • the financing options used by enterprises: '''private financing''' (through debt or equity); '''public financial support''' (direct or indirect). • the usage of the financing for '''innovation''' activities. • the '''size''' of the companies (number of employed people). The figures presented are from the 2022 round of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Glossary:Community_innovation_survey_(CIS) Community Innovation Survey (CIS)] which covers the period from 2020 to 2022. The article refers only to the whole business economy and does not distinguish different economic activities (e.g. industry versus services). Moreover, the article presents results only for the whole EU and not for individual EU countries. However, such data is available in Eurostat's public database (Eurobase) and enable deeper analysis. === Enterprises’ access to private finance at a glance === During 2020-2022, around 6% of EU enterprises used debt for financing innovation activities, while 3% raised equity (finance provided in exchange for a share in the ownership of the enterprise) for this purpose, see Figure 1. Debt was the most widely used form of financing in general; 27% of EU companies obtained debt financing, while 6% raised equity. However, among the companies that financed themselves through equity, a proportionally larger share used this type of financing for innovation activities. Around half of firms that raised equity used it fully or partly to fund their innovations, compared with less than a quarter of firms that incurred debt. Investment in an innovation project is widely seen as riskier than other types of investment. In equity financing, part of that risk is borne by the shareholders, making equity more convenient for financing enterprises’ innovation activities than debt. [[Image:1_Debt_&_Equity_total.png|Figure 1: Enterprises that obtained private funding through debt or equity, by use for innovation (incl. R&D), EU, 2020-2022
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4d8986d4-83f8-451a-b455-5aac275ade48?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:00:11Z inn_cis13_fin] ; [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6ae3313a-4e6e-4a99-a07c-e4a5c81e532a?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:02:20Z inn_cis13_finrd] ; [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/17a4f515-f9cd-4a82-94d3-a2bebf053957?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:04:04Z inn_cis13_bas])|thumb|centre|700px|alt=A stacked bar chart showing the share of enterpises in the EU that tried to obtain private funding through debt or equity, by use for innovation, for the period from 2020 to 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Enterprises’ access to public financial support at a glance === More than a quarter (28%) of all enterprises received financial support from the public sector, e.g. the EU, national or regional government during 2020-2022. This support includes grants, subsidised loans, and loan guarantees, sourced from local, national, or EU entities. The majority of companies that received public funding, 18% of the total number of enterprises, reported using this support exclusively for purposes other than innovation. This may include operational support, infrastructure development, or other business activities. The remaining 10% of enterprises received public funding dedicated to their innovation activities, including research and development (R&D). This allocation pattern indicates that while public funding is accessible to some enterprises, it is not predominantly channelled towards innovation activities. The interpretation of these figures should recognise that they cover public financial support via grants, subsidised loans, and loan guarantees, rather than indirect public support e.g. through tax incentives or tax breaks that were used in some countries during the COVID-19 pandemic. Additionally, the figures vary strongly between countries (from 6% of all enterprises receiving such public funding in Romania, 7% in Latvia, to 40% in Finland and 41% in Belgium). [[Image:2_Enterprises_by_whether_they_received_public_funding,_by_use_for_innovation.png|Figure 2: Enterprises by whether they received public funding, by use for innovation (incl. R&D), EU, 2020-2022
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ff6feefc-c421-4d36-9f3c-edb509734b57?lang=en inn_cis13_pub] ; [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/07941500-0309-4f62-a8f9-f4ab89f6fce8?lang=en&createdAt=2025-08-27T16:29:08Z inn_cis13_bas]).|thumb|centre|700px|alt=Enterprises by whether they received public funding, by use for innovation (incl. R&D), EU, 2020-2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Detailed analysis by size class === Analysing the data by the size of companies ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Enterprise_size enterprise size] class) provides evidence that is required for the formulation and monitoring of SME related policies in the EU. ‘SMEs’ cover enterprises with fewer than 250 persons employed. These companies are compared to ‘large’ enterprises (250 and more persons employed). The SME category is usually subdivided into: • Micro enterprises (0-9 persons employed) • Small enterprises (10-49 persons employed) • Medium-sized enterprises (50 to 249 persons employed) This article compares small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to large enterprises with 250 or more employees. However, it should be noted that the CIS does not cover micro enterprises with a view to limiting the overall burden to responding companies. ====Private funding==== The breakdown by firm size shows a clear trend, see Figure 3. The larger the company, the easier it could access financing. This is particularly true of equity financing, which was more common as company size increased. About 13% of companies with 250 or more employees obtained equity funding, compared with 5% of companies with between 10 and 49 employees. Looking at the purpose of funding, a proportionally larger number of companies that financed themselves through equity used these funds for investments in innovation, although debt was the most widely used form of financing. Less than a quarter of firms that incurred debt did so to fund their innovations, compared with around half of firms that financed themselves through equity. These proportions remained fairly similar regardless of the size class considered. This highlights the challenges that companies of all sizes faced in financing innovation projects through debt. Altogether, investment through equity was more often synonymous with investment in innovation, and equity was more accessible to larger companies. This was reflected in the fact that a mere 2% of small companies with 10 to 49 employees financed their innovation activities through equity, compared with 6% of larger companies with 250 or more employees. Investment in an innovation project is inherently riskier than other types of investment. Equity financing effectively allows part of the risk incurred to be transferred to shareholders. As a result, access to equity appears to be more suitable for financing innovation investments than debt. The rightmost section of each bar in Figure 3 highlights the proportion of firms that were unsuccessful in securing these funds, which was approximately 2% for debt financing and 1% for equity financing. [[Image:3_Enterprises_that_tried_to_obtain_private_funding_through_equity_or_debt,_by_wh.png|Figure 3: Enterprises that tried to obtain private funding through debt or equity, by whether their attempt was successful or not, and by use for innovation (incl. R&D), EU, 2020-2022
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4d8986d4-83f8-451a-b455-5aac275ade48?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:00:11Z inn_cis13_fin] ; [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6ae3313a-4e6e-4a99-a07c-e4a5c81e532a?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:02:20Z inn_cis13_finrd] ; [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/17a4f515-f9cd-4a82-94d3-a2bebf053957?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:04:04Z inn_cis13_bas])|thumb|centre|700px|alt=A stacked bar chart showing the share of enterpises in the EU that tried to obtain private funding through equity, by innovation status and size class, for the period from 2020 to 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 4 further elaborates on how companies used debt depending on their behaviour in terms of innovation. Innovation-active companies incurred more debt than non-innovation-active companies. Among innovation-active firms, the additional proportion of firms using debt corresponds to firms that use these funds in whole or in part to invest in innovation activities. Indeed, the proportion of innovation-active companies that took on debt for non-innovation-related investments was nearly equal to that of non-innovation-active companies, whose investments were, by definition, not linked to innovation. This pattern appears to be fairly similar regardless of the size class considered. As can be seen in the rightmost section of each bar in Figure 4, the proportion of companies that tried to obtain debt financing but were unsuccessful was slightly higher for the innovation-active companies than the other (approximately 2% versus 1%). This underscores the challenges innovative companies faced in obtaining credit; as they were more likely to apply for debt that might be intended for innovation projects, that are often comparatively risky, they were also more likely to be denied. These difficulties are particularly evident among small businesses with fewer than 249 employees. Interestingly, this pattern did not hold for larger businesses with 250 or more employees. These larger firms are nearly equally likely to fail in securing debt financing whether they are innovation-active or not. [[Image:4_Enterprises_that_tried_to_obtain_private_funding_through_debt.png|Figure 4: : Enterprises that tried to obtain private funding through debt, by innovation status and size class,EU, 2020-2022
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4d8986d4-83f8-451a-b455-5aac275ade48?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:00:11Z inn_cis13_fin] ; [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6ae3313a-4e6e-4a99-a07c-e4a5c81e532a?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:02:20Z inn_cis13_finrd] ; [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/07941500-0309-4f62-a8f9-f4ab89f6fce8?lang=en&createdAt=2025-08-27T16:29:08Z inn_cis13_bas])|thumb|centre|700px|alt=A pie chart showing the share of enterpises in the EU by whether they received private funding, by use for innovation, for the period from 2020 to 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] As can be derived from Figure 5, attempts to obtain financing through equity was much more prevalent for innovation-active companies than for those that are not. In total, about 11% of innovation-active firms tried to obtain equity financing, against 4% of non-innovation-active firms. Not only did innovation-active firms utilise more equity to fund their innovations, but they also made more use of equity for other investment purposes. This highlights a key characteristic of innovation-active companies: they manage to get shareholders more involved in their investment projects. The largest companies made the most use of equity, regardless of the objective pursued. Around 16% of large innovation-active enterprises obtained equity funding; of those firms, about half utilised these funds entirely or partially for innovation purposes. [[Image:5_Firms_that_tried_to_obtain_private_funding_through_equity.png|Figure 5: : Enterprises that tried to obtain private funding through equity, by innovation status and size class,EU, 2020-2022
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4d8986d4-83f8-451a-b455-5aac275ade48?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:00:11Z inn_cis13_fin] ; [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6ae3313a-4e6e-4a99-a07c-e4a5c81e532a?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:02:20Z inn_cis13_finrd] ; [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/07941500-0309-4f62-a8f9-f4ab89f6fce8?lang=en&createdAt=2025-08-27T16:29:08Z inn_cis13_bas])|thumb|centre|700px|alt=A stacked bar chart showing the share of enterpises in the EU that received private funding through debt, by use for innovation, by innovation status and size class, for the period from 2020 to 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ====Public financial support==== Figure 6 depicts the proportion of companies that received public financial support, distinguishing between innovation-active companies and those that are not. Innovation-active companies were proportionally twice as numerous as others to receive public support. This difference can be explained by the subsidies obtained to finance innovation. Indeed, the gap between innovation-active and non-innovation-active companies corresponds almost exactly to the proportion of companies that have obtained this funding to support their innovation efforts. [[Image:6_Enterprises_that_received_public_funding,_by_use_for_innovation.png|Figure 6: Enterprises that received public funding, by use for innovation (incl. R&D), by innovation status and size class, EU, 2020-2022
Source:Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ff6feefc-c421-4d36-9f3c-edb509734b57?lang=en inn_cis13_pub] ; [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/17a4f515-f9cd-4a82-94d3-a2bebf053957?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:04:04Z inn_cis13_bas])|thumb|centre|700px|alt=A Enterprises that received public funding, by_use for innovation]] When examining the breakdown by size category, one standout observation is the extent to which large enterprises with 250 or more employees were able to obtain public funding, especially to support their innovation efforts. Large innovation-active enterprises received a significant 27% of public funding for innovation activities, which is notably higher than other size classes. Larger firms are more able to channel public resources into innovation, reflecting their strategic focus and capability to leverage such funding effectively. In contrast, proportionately fewer smaller innovative enterprises were subsidised for their innovation activities. This was particularly true for the innovation-active firms with 10 to 49 employees, only 17% of which received public funding for their innovation activities. As mentioned above, innovation projects are typically costly, time-consuming and risky. These difficulties are naturally more challenging for smaller organisations, which typically have more limited financial resources. Data suggests potential barriers that hinder their access to public funding. These include a pressing need to focus on survival and operational needs, limiting their ability to seek public support for innovation purposes. These findings highlight the opportunity for public authorities to tailor public funding policies to the specific needs and capacities of different enterprise sizes, particularly ensuring that smaller firms can effectively access funding towards innovation. This tailored approach could help maximise the impact of public funding across all enterprise sizes. In addition to the direct support discussed above, countries also offer indirect aid through tax incentives, which are intended to reduce a company’s tax burden. Many countries offer programmes specifically designed to support innovation efforts, including R&D. Figure 7 shows how tax incentives of any kind were used differently by innovation-active and non-innovation-active enterprises across the 12 EU countries for which this data is available. A distinction is made between programmes dedicated to innovation and those that are not. [[Image:7_Enterprises_that_received_tax_incentives_by_use_for_innovation.png|Figure 7: Enterprises that received tax incentives by use for innovation (incl. R&D), by innovation status and size class, EU, 2020-2022
Source:Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1948c877-3b55-4278-8715-f024737c3dc0?lang=en inn_cis13_txal] ; [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/17a4f515-f9cd-4a82-94d3-a2bebf053957?lang=en&createdAt=2025-09-09T16:04:04Z inn_cis13_bas])|thumb|centre|700px|alt=A Enterprises that received tax incentives, by_use for innovation]] When examining solely tax incentives received for purposes other than innovation, innovative companies significantly outperformed their counterparts in obtaining them; about 14% of them received these tax incentives compared with just 6% of non-innovative firms. This discrepancy suggests that enterprises committed to innovation are more likely to invest in understanding and applying for tax incentives regardless of the purpose, viewing them as integral components of their growth strategy. Alongside their extensive use of tax incentives that do not target innovation, a significant proportion of innovative companies (14%) also managed to mobilise extra tax incentives specifically targeting their innovation activities. Notably, the data show that larger enterprises were more likely to benefit from tax incentives. This was true for tax incentives for purposes other than innovation. It was even more the case for tax incentives aimed at innovation. Indeed, 33% of large innovative companies (with 250 employees or more) made use of them, compared with 9% of small innovative companies (with 10 to 49 employees). A factor contributing to this trend might be a disparity in awareness and capability for navigating tax schemes of any kind, e.g. where smaller enterprises are led by technically skilled individuals rather than formally trained business administrators. In addition, many small businesses might operate with a comparatively short-term focus due to cash flow constraints, which can make the process of applying for and managing tax incentives seem administratively burdensome. Consequently, they may be less aware of, and therefore under-utilise, available tax allowances and incentives. In contrast, larger enterprises benefit from more sophisticated financial departments equipped with the expertise to navigate complex tax schemes effectively. This expertise allows them to capitalise on the broader range of tax advantages available to them, facilitating a more strategic approach to innovation and R&D investment. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Enterp_access to_finance_public_funding_for_inno_FOR UPLOAD in the SE tool V5.xlsx|Download Excel file]] ===Data sources === The '''Community Innovation Survey''', abbreviated as '''CIS''', is conducted in every [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] Member State to collect data on [[Glossary:Innovation|innovation]] in businesses, i.e. on [[Glossary:Product innovation|product innovation]] (goods or services) and [[Glossary:Business process innovation|business process innovation]] (e.g. production methods; logistics; information processing and communication; accounting and administrative operations; organisational, management and marketing aspects). The legal basis for CIS is Commission Implementing {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32022R1092:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2022/1092}} of 30 June 2022 laying down technical specifications of data requirements for the topic ‘Innovation’ pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2019/2152. ===Context=== The European Commission and other EU institutions maintain policies and many financial support schemes to facilitate the access to appropriate financing for enterprises. The European Commission supports access to finance for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) through various initiatives, including working with financial institutions like the European Investment Bank, and promoting a range of funding options such as loans and venture capital. [https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities_en An overview of EU funding programmes] and the [https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/access-finance_en ‘access to finance’ portal] confirm the attention that the EU gives to funding research and innovation. For example, [https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe_en Horizon Europe] is the EU's research and innovation programme for 2021-2027 with a budget of €95.5 billion. Horizon Europe and many other European funding programmes promote competitiveness of enterprises in the EU, optimises investment impact, facilitate collaboration and strengthen the impact of research and innovation and within a strengthened [https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/strategy/strategy-research-and-innovation/our-digital-future/european-research-area_en European Research Area]. They help to create jobs, new knowhow, and technologies. A dual focus is put on SMEs and on innovation. Eurostat’s data on financing in the context business innovation, with the capacity to link this to characteristics of the enterprise, provides an important element in the reporting ‘drawing board’ that is available to observe the situation. It is also helpful to provide structure to monetary data obtained through other sources. The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Glossary:Community_innovation_survey_(CIS) Community Innovation Survey (CIS)] offers insights into company achievements relating to innovations of products and business processes. It also enables valuable cross-referencing of this innovation performance with other aspects of company behaviour. Among these factors, access to finance emerges as a crucial driver, empowering innovative companies to obtain the financial means for the development of their innovations. Emphasising funding for innovation is critical because developing innovations typically involves longer timeframes and higher risks compared to other investments. The main concept defined in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-01-18-852 Oslo Manual] to characterise companies engaged in innovation is that of ’innovation-active’ firms. A firm is considered to be ’innovation-active’ if it either introduced an innovation (product or business process innovation) during the observation period, or has been involved in any ongoing, abandoned, suspended, or completed innovation activity that has not (yet) led to the introduction of an innovation. Innovation activities cover a wide range of activities undertaken by firms to develop product or business process innovations. These may include research and development (R&D), but also other business development activities (financial, commercial, etc.), provided that they are aimed at developing an innovation. These activities may or may not ultimately result in an innovation being implemented by the company. === Other Articles === *[[Community Innovation Survey 2022 - key indicators]] *[[Innovation profiles of enterprises - results]] *[[Innovation profiles of enterprises - methodology]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/science-technology-innovation/database Science and technology (scitech)], see: :Community innovation survey (inn) ::Results of the community innovation survey 2022 (CIS2022) (inn_cis13) === Thematic section === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=science_technology_innovation}} Science, technology and innovation] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/website/cis/library.html Community Innovation Survey (CIS): Questionnaire library] === Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-24-008 EBS methodological manual on statistics on business innovation] *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-18-852|title=Oslo Manual}} *{{Template:Esms|code=inn_cis13_esms|title=Community innovation survey 2022 (CIS2022) (inn_cis13)}} === Legislation === *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32022R1092:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 2019/2152}} *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012R0995:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 2020/1197}} *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R2152:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 2022/1092}} === External links === *[https://projects.research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/en/statistics/performance-indicators/european-innovation-scoreboard/eis-2024#/ European Innovation Scoreboard (EIS) 2024 and Regional Innovation Scoreboard (RIS) 2023] *[http://www.oecd.org/innovation/ OECD — Innovation] {{Unit|topic=X_Structural_business_statistics }} [[Category:Science, technology, and digital society|Enterprises - title: Entrepreneurship - statistical indicators
text:
EU statistics on business demography present data on the number of enterprises, their birth rates, death rates and survival rates. Data from June 2026 Planned update: May 2027 In 2023, 5 years old enterprises in the EU had an average annual employment growth rate of over 16% in the first 5 years of their operations. In 2023, the contribution of newly born enterprises to employment in the business economy was below 2% in Finland, Germany, Denmark, Luxembourg, Austria, Sweden and the Netherlands, but above 5% in Greece, Estonia and Portugal. This article presents results about * '''newly created enterprises''' in the year 2023 as well as '''young enterprises''' that were established 1 to 5 years before the reference year 2023 and have survived until then. The article highlights their '''contribution to employment growth''' in the business economy. * '''young high-growth enterprises ('Gazelles')'''. [[Glossary:Gazelle|Gazelles]] are a specific sub-population of [[Glossary:High-growth enterprise|high-growth enterprises]] defined by their age of a maximum of 5 years. These companies have shown their potential for high growth already in the early years after start-up. * the '''innovation activity of enterprises in years 2020-2022''', e.g. by the age of the company or its belonging to an enterprise group. ===Why are young enterprises important for the economy ?=== The creation of an enterprise offers opportunities, not least the possibility to make the dream come true of becoming independent and self-employed. Often, there is a strong relationship between a new enterprise and the owner behind – the entrepreneur. '''‘Entrepreneurship’''' matters: it adds to the dynamism, agility, openness, and diversity of the society.
Moreover, new enterprises are of key importance for '''generating new jobs and economic growth'''. Most new companies start up without or with only very few employees. However, even where the job creation by young enterprises might be limited in the first years, they lay the groundwork for later growth.
To provide information on the evolution of entrepreneurial activity and the dynamics within the business economy, '''Statistics on Business Demography''' document important events in the life cycle of an enterprise from creation to dissolution, thereby offering insights into enterprise survival or discontinuity. Important statistical indicators of business demography statistics are data on * births of enterprises * survivals of newly created enterprises * (young) High Growth Enterprises * deaths of enterprises In the policy discourse, the term ‘startups’ is mostly associated with enterprises which do not only exhibit high growth rates, but also above average innovation. The Community Innovation Survey (CIS) is a '''survey on business innovation''' that reports for example about how many enterprises translate inventions into innovation that result in the introduction of new business processes in the firm or new products in the market, and translate these innovations into commercial success. These results also show the innovation activity of companies in relation to its age or group status (belonging to an enterprise group).
=== Birth of enterprises and their contribution to job creation===
Figure 1
Figure 1 shows enterprise birth rates in 2023 across different sectors, reflecting the number of new enterprises relative to all active ones. While some sectors thrive as breeding grounds for new enterprises, others seem to face inherent hurdles that impact enterprise creation. In 2023, the ‘Administrative and support service activities’ sector stood out with a high birth rate of 16.5%, indicating a dynamic and accessible sector for new businesses. Tech-enabled infrastructure like 'Transport and storage', digitally driven sectors ‘Information and communication’ and ‘Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply’, as well as socially relevant sectors like ‘Education’ or ‘Arts, entertainment and recreation’, also demonstrated strong birth rates.
This contrasts with ‘Mining and quarrying’ which showed a low birth rate of 6.0%, likely due to high economies of scale and entry barriers, and regulatory challenges. Low birth rates were also observed in ‘Water supply; sewage and waste management’ (6.1%) followed by ‘Manufacturing’ and ‘Wholesale and retail trade’ with birth rates close to 8%. [[Image: F2_New_enterprises_by_size_class_and_economic_activity,_EU,_2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: New enterprises by size class and economic activity, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=bd_size__custom_17177540}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage structure of active enterprises by sector of business economy in the EU and individual EU Member States. Totalling 100 percent, each country column contains three stacks representing services, construction and industry for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image]] When an enterprise is born, a new economic entity is created. Figure 2 shows the proportion of enterprise births by number of employees in 2023. Newly created enterprises were very small: for the total economy (industry, construction, market services) * 83.4% of new businesses consisted solely of self-employed individuals; * 15.4% launched with 1 to 4 employees; * 0.8% of all born enterprises had 5 to 9 employees; * 0.4% 10 or more employees. This highlights the prevalence of solo entrepreneurs or owner-driven ventures, especially in industries like ‘Education’, ‘Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply’, ‘Arts, entertainment and recreation’ and 'Professional, scientific and technical activities' where the percentage of businesses starting without any employees (i.e. consisting solely of self-employed individuals) was above 90%. ‘Education’ saw as much as 93% due to the prevalence of independent educators, freelance tutors, and online course creators who can operate as sole proprietors with low start-up costs and flexible business model.
Conversely, ‘Accommodation and food service activities’ stood out, as 39% of new enterprises started with 1 to 4 employees, indicating an immediate need for personnel. Also industries such as ‘Mining and quarrying’ and ‘Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities’ had a relatively higher percentage of new enterprises starting with 5 to 9 employees, indicating that those sectors often require larger initial teams due to the collective nature of the tasks. Finally, sectors like ‘Real estate activities’, ‘Education’, ‘Professional, scientific, and technical activities’ and ‘Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply’ showed very few new enterprises with 10 or more employees, what coincides also with the lowest share of 5 to 9 employees for those sectors, underscoring the cautious approach new entrants take given the complexities or resource constraints.
Figure 3
Figure 3 shows the share of new jobs created in total jobs available (represented by columns and percentage on the left axis) as well as average size of enterprises in terms of persons employed (presented by dots and number on the right axis).
In 2023, newly born enterprises in Portugal accounted for a significant 5.9% of employment in the business economy. However Greece had the highest average of 2.2 persons employed per created enterprise. In the EU, the average size of newborn enterprise was 1.1 persons. High numbers of jobs per enterprise might reflect a cultural inclination towards slightly larger business setups, or perhaps a business environment where starting a business requires a small team to handle early operational demands; it might also reflect below average labour costs.
Estonia accounted for the second-largest share of new jobs at 5.1%, followed closely by Greece, Slovakia, and Malta, each with a similar rate of around 4.5%. With the exception of Greece, these countries also had comparable average sizes for newly established enterprises, ranging from 1.1 to 1.2 persons per business.
At the lower end of the scale, Finland, Luxembourg, Germany, and Denmark recorded the smallest shares of new jobs, between 0.9% and 1.2%. Among these, Germany had the third-highest average size for newborn enterprises (1.5 persons), trailing only Ireland (1.6 persons). In contrast, Finland reported the smallest average size - 0.4 person per enterprise - which may partly reflect the inclusion of ventures with no employees (e.g., holding companies), delayed hiring later in the year, or limitations in the data sources used. Meanwhile, the Netherlands and France recorded an average of 0.6 persons per new enterprise. Such differences could be partly attributed to local economic conditions, regulatory and fiscal environments, societal attitudes towards entrepreneurship or prevalence of NACE sectors in the respective countries.
===Young enterprises' share in the business economy=== [[Image:F4-Young_up_to_5_years_old_enterprises_by_economic_activity,_EU,_2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Young (up to 5 years old) enterprises by economic activity, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=bd_size__custom_15263052}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage structure of active enterprises by sector of business economy in the EU and individual EU Member States. Totalling 100 percent, each country column contains three stacks representing services, construction and industry for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image]] In 2023, the landscape of young enterprises - those aged 1 to 5 years - across the EU showed varying levels of employment contributions within different sectors (see Figure 4)Survived (young) enterprises by activity are compared with active enterprises in the reference year, however for survived enterprises activity is taken from the year of birth, but for active enterprises from the reference year. Data are analysed at section level; in practice it can be assumed that within 1 to 5 years activity would not change from one section to the other. . These are young enterprises that were established 1 to 5 years ago and survived until 2023. These emerging enterprises are vital to several economic activities, though their impacts differ significantly by industry.
Within the real estate sector, young enterprises accounted for 19.9% of employment, provided by 0.4 million new enterprises, indicating significant growth potential and adaptability. A very similar pattern was also observed in ‘Arts, entertainment, and recreation’ with a high share of employment in new enterprises (18.8%) and a relatively low number of new enterprises (0.3 million).
The construction sector also showed strong engagement, with young enterprises making up 18.0% of employment and totalling 1.3 million enterprises, which is one of the highest numbers of young enterprises among the sectors, exceeded only by ‘Professional, scientific and technical activities’ and ‘Wholesale and retail trade; repair of motor vehicles’, accounting respectively for 1.6 million and 1.4 million new enterprises in 2023.
Service-oriented sectors, such as ‘Professional, scientific, and technical activities’, ‘Education’ and ‘Accommodation and food services’, exhibited substantial employment shares from young enterprises accounting for 17% to 18%, probably driven by evolving market needs and innovation. Though the number of young enterprises in those sectors varied greatly, the first had one of the highest numbers among sectors, and the latter 2 accounted for 0.4 million and 0.5 million, respectively.
In the ‘Information and communication’ sector, young enterprises contributed 13.1% to employment, while in ‘Administrative and support services’, they accounted for 12.7%. These figures demonstrate a moderate but significant presence of young businesses in these industries.
Traditional sectors like ‘Transportation and storage’ and ‘Wholesale and retail trade’ saw young enterprises contributing of respectively 10.9% and 9.6% to employment, while in ‘Human health and social work activities’ and ‘Financial and insurance activities’ they accounted for 8.5% and 7.9% respectively.
Conversely, in capital-intensive sectors such as ‘Manufacturing’ (4.6%), ‘Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply’ (4.2%), ‘Water supply; sewerage, waste management’ (3.9%),and ‘Mining and quarrying’ (2.2%), young enterprises had lower employment contributions as very few new enterprises were present in these sectors, with the last 3 sectors accounting for only 0.7% of all new enterprises in 2023. These figures reflect high economies of scale and complexity of these industries.
Figure 5
Figure 5 illustrates the resilience of 5-year-old enterprises - those founded in 2018 and still active in 2023 - across the EU, along with their employment contributions.
Poland had the highest share of 5-year-old enterprises, representing 5.3% of all active businesses, suggesting a robust environment for long-term business survival. It was followed by the Netherlands and Slovakia (both 5.2%), Malta (5.1%), and France (5.0%). Beyond shares of enterprises, Malta also stood out for its employment impact, with five-year-old enterprises accounting for 3.5% of total employment - the highest share in the EU. Greece matched this figure, also recording a 3.5% employment share from employment in active enterprises.
At the lower end, Austria had a modest 2.4% share of surviving 5-year-old enterprises, though its employment impact (2.4%) aligned with the EU average. Germany recorded the lowest employment contribution from this cohort (1.2%), while Denmark had one of the lowest share of 5-years-old enterprises (3.0%) and an employment share of just 1.5%. Overall, resilience in business survival did not always translate to an equivalent employment impact, underscoring the complex interplay between survival strategies, economic conditions, different degrees of capital intensity and automation of production, and employment dynamics.
===Employment growth in young enterprises=== [[Image: Growth in employment of young enterprises by survival years and economic activity, EU, 2023 (%) v2.png |thumb|centre|700px| Figure 6: Growth in employment of young enterprises by survival years and economic activity sectors in EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=bd_size__custom_17237708}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage structure of active enterprises by sector of business economy in the EU and individual EU Member States. Totalling 100 percent, each country column contains three stacks representing services, construction and industry for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image]] Employment growth is a fundamental objective of economic policy, and young enterprises significantly contribute by creating new jobs. The survival of these businesses is equally important, as it sustains employment and fuels innovation, driving economic vitality. In 2023, the analysis of employment growth among young enterprises across various EU sectors presented intriguing insights (Figure 6). Here employment in young enterprises in 2023 was compared to the annual average employment in the year of birth of the same enterprises. This can significantly magnify the impact of small absolute changes for enterprises with fewer starting employees.
The total business economy observed a rapid increase in employment of new enterprises, particularly in the first 2 years of their activity. Employment in 1-year-old enterprises increased by 32.7% compared to the year of birth. Enterprises that were born in 2021 reached 51.9% employment growth by their second year and 69.1% growth was observed for 3-year-old enterprises, slowing down growth for enterprises founded in 2019 reaching 70.8% by the fourth year; those born in 2018 showed an increase of 82.6% by the fifth year.
Sectoral disparities in employment growth may partly reflect differences in baseline workforce sizes for enterprise birth - small numerical increases can translate into large percentage gains for smaller enterprises.
The industry sector consistently outperformed construction and services, with enterprises peaking at 85.6% by their fifth year for enterprises born in 2018. The enterprises born in 2022 and survived to 2023, had 41.7% growth in employment - by 9 percent points more than in average for total economy, 2-years-old enterprises showed even higher growth in employment of 64.3% exceeding average by 12.4 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]], followed by growth of 75.5% for 3-years-old enterprises and 84.3% for 4-years-old enterprises.
The services sector mirrored the overarching business economy trend, as most new enterprises were in the services sector, with measured growth from 30.8% in 1-year-old enterprises to 82.5% in 5-year-old surviving enterprises.
Construction had the most consistent growth over years, starting at 39.5% after 1 year and soaring to 82.9% for enterprises that survived 5 years.
===Young high-growth enterprises===
Figure 7
Figure 7 illustrates data on young high-growth enterprises, known as "Gazelles", a specific subset of high-growth enterprises that are 4 and 5 years old. These enterprises have demonstrated significant potential for rapid expansion in terms of employees early in their development.
The available data reveal that the ‘Accommodation and food service’ sector had the highest number of young high-growth enterprises (2.5 thousands), followed by ‘Construction’ (2.0 thousands). The strong performance in these sectors can largely be attributed to a post-pandemic rebound in tourism, travel, and hospitality, which significantly boosted demand. Additionally, high demand for both public and private infrastructure projects has driven growth in construction. The inherently labour intensive nature of these industries further supports their expansion, as they require substantial workforces to meet rising needs.
Close behind were ‘Administrative and support services’ (1.9 thousand), followed by ‘Wholesale and retail trade (including motor vehicle repairs)’ and ‘Manufacturing’, each with around 1.5 thousand enterprises. These sectors thrive in employment growth due to their adaptability to market demands, labour-intensive operations, and structural tailwinds - such as outsourcing trends in administrative services, e-commerce expansion in retail, and reshoring coupled with green transitions in manufacturing.
In contrast, sector ‘Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply’ showed far weaker growth in employment and had 15 young high-growth firms (gazelles), followed by ‘Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities’ with 87 firms. The low number of young high-growth firms in these sectors indicates that few enterprises that started 4 or 5 years ago had at least 10 employees in the beginning of growth and achieved annualised employment growth exceeding 10% over a three-year period. These normally are small or inherently stable but slow-growing companies. EU data for sectors ‘Mining and quarrying’ and ‘Real estate activities’ were confidential for year 2023. === Enterprises and innovation === Innovation is a critical driver for enterprises seeking to gain a competitive advantage in today’s dynamic market landscape. The ability to innovate enhances businesses’ adaptability and growth potential. The Community Innovation Survey (CIS) reports about enterprises with 10 or more employees. [[Image:Enterprises which are part of enterprise groups by innovation status, 2020-2022 (%) v2.png |thumb|centre|700px| Figure 8: Enterprises which are part of enterprise groups by innovation status, 2020-2022
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=inn_cis13_bas}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage structure of active enterprises by sector of business economy in the EU and individual EU Member States. Totalling 100 percent, each country column contains three stacks representing services, construction and industry for the year 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image]] When exploring the life cycle of young enterprises and the factors contributing to their success, it is important to recognise that some young enterprises gain a head start by being part of an enterprise group. This might provide them with easier access to capital, knowledge, and organisational support.
Figure 8 presents 2022 data from the CIS. There were 18 EU countries that reported voluntarily on the group status of enterprises, revealing a distinct difference in innovation activities between young enterprises that are part of an enterprise group and those operating independently. Among enterprises affiliated with an enterprise group, 68% are identified as innovation active, compared to only 45% of independent enterprises. This disparity highlights the advantages of being part of a group, including easier access to finance, knowledge transfer, and structured environments conducive to innovation. Some group-affiliated young enterprises serve as experimental hubs for larger organisations, exploring new technologies or business models with reduced financial exposure. Additionally, group membership often facilitates market access and stronger networks, essential for scaling innovative solutions. In contrast, independent enterprises might struggle with limited resources and higher operational pressures, prioritising immediate concerns over long-term innovation investments. Overall, the data illustrate that being part of an enterprise group offers fertile ground for innovation.
Due to their group affiliations, enterprises belonging to an enterprise group may not fit perfectly to the idea of an SME. However, they are a minority, as on average, 95.1% of SMEs operate independently of any enterprise group (see Table 1). [[Image: T 1 Share of independent dependent enterprises by size, EU, 2022.png |thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: New enterprises by size class and economic activity, EU, 2022
''Source:'' EuroGroups Register and SBS data Eurostat|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage structure of active enterprises by sector of business economy in the EU and individual EU Member States. Totalling 100 percent, each country column contains three stacks representing services, construction and industry for the year 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image]]
[[Image:Breakdown_of_enterprise_total_turnover_by_innovation_status,_2022_(%)_08-07-2025.png |thumb|centre|700px| Figure 9: Breakdown of enterprise total turnover by innovation status, 2022
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=inn_cis13_bas_ip}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage structure of active enterprises by sector of business economy in the EU and individual EU Member States. Totalling 100 percent, each country column contains three stacks representing services, construction and industry for the year 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image]]
Similarly, Figure 9 covers all EU countries and further illustrates the importance of innovation in driving enterprise success, particularly how it correlates with turnover generation across different enterprise sizes. The dataset reflects figures from 2022 and indicates that 80% of turnover is generated by innovation-active businesses. This underscores the critical impact of business innovation on revenue generation, and vice versa.
There is a progression: as businesses scale, so does their capacity to invest in and benefit from innovation. With greater resources and R&D expenditure, bigger firms are strategically better positioned to prioritise innovation, and effectively translate it into turnover. The share of turnover coming from innovation-active firms was * 54% in small enterprises (those with 10 to 49 employees), * 70% in medium-sized enterprises (50 to 249 employees), * 89% in the largest enterprises (250 or more employees). [[Image: Breakdown of enterprises by innovation status, by age class, 2020-2022 (%) v2.png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 10: Breakdown of enterprises by innovation status, by age class, 2022
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=inn_cis13_yreg_ip}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage structure of active enterprises by sector of business economy in the EU and individual EU Member States. Totalling 100 percent, each country column contains three stacks representing services, construction and industry for the year 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image]] Figure 10 provides another perspective on innovation activities based on the age of businesses. In 2022, enterprises established in 2013 or earlier showed a balanced approach to innovation, with 51% identified as innovation active. Similarly, those founded between 2014 and 2017 maintained the same proportion, while for enterprises established between 2018 and 2019, or in 2020 and after, there was only a slight decline. Overall, the data across various age classes reveal only minor differences in innovation engagement, suggesting that while newer businesses face unique challenges, the role of innovation remains significant across all enterprise ages. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Website SE Entrepreneurship--2026 MASTERFILE draft v2.xlsx|title=Entrepreneurship – statistical indicators: tables and figures}} === Data sources === Eurostat's '''Business demography statistics''' (BD) provide information on the dynamics of the business economy. They capture how the composition of the enterprise population changes over time. They also show how the economic contribution of the business economy in terms of employment develops across a number of enterprise characteristics. Business demography statistics cover, amongst other things, the birth, survival (followed up to 5 years after birth) and death of enterprises within the business population. They report changes in the stock of enterprises within the business economy from one year to the next, reflecting among other things the level of competition, entrepreneurial spirit and the business environment.
Business demography statistics reflect the employment dynamics within the business economy by measuring growth in terms of employment. European business demography statistics are compiled for 2 different enterprise populations: :A) All enterprises, whether they have employees or not :B) Only enterprises that have employees.
This article focuses only on one option, i.e. on all enterprises, independent from the presence of employees.
Business demography data are also available at regional level. These statistics are becoming increasingly important as many economic phenomena in the single European market are present across national borders. Regional level business demography data show regional hot spots of innovation and technological development within the countries, or sometimes stretching across national borders. Furthermore, the regional concentration of selected activities as well as job creation can be traced from regional data for policy purposes. This article does not present any regional data.
Statistical business registers are the main source for BD statistics. Data come from the national statistical business registers in the EU, EFTA, and enlargement countries. In practice, most of these national statistical business registers are based on a combination of administrative and statistical sources.
The '''Community Innovation Survey''' (CIS) is designed to provide information on the innovativeness of business economy sectors, to enable the analysis of innovation drivers or barriers or to assess innovation outcomes. The survey focuses, among others, on the following aspects: * product innovation (new to firm; new to the market) * business process innovation * innovation development * innovation activities * innovation expenditure * turnover from innovative products * incentives for the implementation of innovation * innovation cooperation * source of financing for innovation * sources of information on innovation * barriers to innovation * others The CIS provides various innovation indicators by 3 main breakdown variables: type of innovator, economic activity, and size class of enterprise.

'''Coverage, units and classifications''' Business demography covers the [[Glossary:Business economy|business economy]], which includes industry, construction and many services (([[Glossary:Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)|NACE Rev.2]])sections B to N, P to R as well as division S95 and S96). Business demography statistics do not cover agriculture, forestry and fishing, or public administration. Starting with the reference year 2021, business demography statistics are compiled under the legal basis of the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32019R2152 EU Regulation 2019/2152] on European business statistics and its implementing act, [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32020R1197 EU Regulation 2020/1197] on technical specifications and arrangements. The information from the CIS covers the business sectors (B-C-D-E-46-H-J-K-71-72-73) for enterprises with 10 or more persons employed. === Context=== Business demography is an important subject for policy-maker discussions about increasing the level of employment, since it is one of the main priorities of the EU growth strategy. Enterprise demography reflects, to some degree, the dynamism of the EU economy through the adaptation of economic structures to changing market conditions. The potential contribution that enterprise creation can make to employment is also one of the most important aspects drawing the attention of policy makers to the subject of enterprise demography. In this context, enterprise creation can be seen as an indicator of [[Glossary:Competitiveness|competitiveness]], as a factor of economic growth and as a vital means of creating jobs. Business demography provides information for births, deaths and survival rates of enterprises, as well as information on related employment data. The 2 main measures used for employment are the number of [[Glossary:Persons employed - SBS|persons employed]] and the number of employees. The demography of the business population is represented by data on: *the [[Glossary:Active enterprise|active population of enterprises]]; *their [[Glossary:Birth of enterprise|birth]]; *their [[Glossary:Enterprise survival|survival]] (followed up to 5 years after birth); *their [[Glossary:Enterprise death rate|death]]. Particular attention is paid to the impact that these demographic events have on employment levels. Business demography data can be used to analyse the dynamics and innovation of different markets, such as: *entrepreneurship in terms of the propensity to start a new business, such as analysed in the joint OECD/Eurostat Entrepreneurship Indicators Programme; *how newly-born enterprises can contribute to the creation of jobs. === Other articles=== *[[High-growth enterprises - statistics]] – background article on high-growth enterprises and young high-growth enterprises (gazelles) *[[Structural business statistics overview]] - see chapter "Business demography" *[[Structural business statistics (SBS)]] - theme entry page *[[Structural business statistics at regional level]] see chapter 'Enterprise demography: births, deaths and survival' *[[Quarterly registrations of new businesses and declarations of bankruptcies - statistics]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/database Business demoghraphy (bd)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database?node_code=bd Business demography (bd)] === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/business-demography/overview Business demography] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/overview Structural business statistics] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/business-demography/publications Recent Eurostat publications on BD] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/publications Recent Eurostat publications on SBS] === Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/bd_sims.htm Business demography metadata] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-25-016 European business statistics methodological manual for business demography statistics – 2025 edition] *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-RA-07-010|title=Eurostat-OECD Manual on Business Demography Statistics}} === External links=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/growth/smes_en European Commission -
