title: Environmental accounts - establishing the links between the environment and the economy
text:
Environmental accounts are a statistical system bringing together economic and environmental information in a common framework to measure the contribution of the environment to the economy and the impact of the economy on the environment. They offer a means of monitoring the pressures exerted by the economy on the environment and of exploring how these might be abated. Environmental accounts organise environmental data from many domains using the same concepts and terminology as the national accounts, and thus they show the interaction between economic, household and environmental factors and consequently are more informative than national accounts alone. Environmental accounts can be used to answer questions such as: Which industry is emitting most greenhouse gases? How do patterns of consumption and production affect the environment? What is the effect of economic policy measures, such as an environmental tax on the generation of waste or air emissions? How fast is the environmental economy growing and how does it compare with the rest of the economy? European environmental accounts are used for EU policy making e.g., [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi SDGs], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/circular-economy circular economy], the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/environment-action-programme-2030_en 8th Environment Action Programme], etc. === Introduction to environmental accounting === Environmental accounts are a multipurpose data system encompassing a conceptual framework and tables which describes the interrelations between the economy and the environment in a way that is consistent with the national accounts. For instance, they shed light on the amount of pollution produced by industries and households and allow a comparison with the employment and value of output produced by these sectors, or with the expenditure made by these sectors to avoid pollution. Politicians can use this information to decide where it is most efficient to act. [[Image:Environment-economy 1.png|thumb|centre|500px]] Environmental accounts provide an integrated framework for data, indicators and analysis. Integrating environment-related data with the [[Glossary:National_accounts_(NA)|national accounts]] framework makes the resulting indicators more consistent among themselves and permits aligning also with the social aspects of sustainable development and the employment aspects of green growth. The accounts allow bringing together, in a single accounting framework, information on a range of natural resources (for example water, minerals, energy, timber, fish, oil, land and ecosystems) and human activities (e.g., pollution and waste, production, consumption and accumulation). The European environmental accounts do not yet cover all these aspects, because the international standards from the [http://unstats.un.org/unsd/envaccounting/seea.asp System of Environmental-Economic Accounting 2012] are being implemented gradually (see next section about present developments). Environmental accounts integrate existing data and provide coherence. The structure of the accounts enables a wide range of source information to be compared and contrasted to provide better estimates. The accounting system enables the organization of information into tables and accounts in an integrated and conceptually coherent manner. This information can be used to create coherent aggregates, indicators and trends across a broad spectrum of environmental and economic issues. From the viewpoint of compilation of estimates, one advantage of the environmental accounts is that they are (mostly) compiled by reorganising already existing data. [[Image:Pyramid information 1.png|thumb|centre|500px]] One of the most important features of the environmental accounts is their capacity to organise and present coherently information in both physical terms (often for the environment) and monetary terms (often for the economy). A key focus of measurement is the use of physical units to record flows of materials and energy that enter and leave the economy and flows of materials and energy within the economy itself. These are called physical flows. Environmental accounts apply the accounting concepts, structures, rules, classifications and principles of the national accounts to environmental information. Particularly important is the alignment to the national accounts' production boundary and residence principle, i.e. adopting a scope based not on territory but on residence of the producer units, the scope used for [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|Gross Domestic Product]]. This makes environmental accounts consistent, in general, with [[Glossary:National_accounts_(NA)|national accounts]], and allows joint analysis. In practice, the basic framework includes physical and monetary supply and use tables (which report what flows go in and what come out), functional accounts and asset accounts for natural resources (which report how the opening stock plus changes give the closing stock). The measurement of physical flows is structured around the flows of natural inputs from the environment to the economy, flows of products within the economy and flows from the economy to the environment i.e., residuals. The range of applications of environmental accounts includes resource efficiency and [[Glossary:Resource_productivity|productivity]], decomposition analysis, analysis of net wealth and depletion, sustainable production and consumption. The accounts also provide an information base for the development of models e.g. input-output analysis and general equilibrium modelling. The international standard is the [http://unstats.un.org/unsd/envaccounting/seea.asp System of Environmental-Economic Accounting 2012 – Central Framework (SEEA 2012 CF)]. It was produced and released under the auspices of the [[Glossary:United_Nations|United Nations]] Statistics Division, the European Commission (Eurostat), the Food and Agriculture Organisation of the UN, the [[Glossary:OECD|OECD]], the [[Glossary:International Monetary Fund|International Monetary Fund]] and the [[Glossary:World Bank|World Bank]] group. It was endorsed as an international standard by the United Nations Statistical Commission in 2012. The SEEA 2012 CF builds on the previous versions, SEEA 2003 and 1993. [[Image:SEEA CF 2012.png|thumb|centre|500px]] === European environmental accounts === The European environmental accounts are established in {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02011R0691-20250101:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 691/2011}}. The Regulation provides a legal framework for a harmonised collection of comparable data from all EU Member States and EFTA countries. The European environmental accounts are consistent with the SEEA 2012 CF and are structured in modules. Only some parts of the SEAA 2012 CF are presently implemented. The Regulation includes six modules. Links to Statistics Explained articles reporting results of those accounts can be found at the bottom of this article. The following are the present modules: '''1) Air emissions accounts (AEA)''' record the emissions to the atmosphere of six [[Glossary:Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gases]] including CO2 and seven air pollutants. AEA offer breakdowns by 64 emitting industries plus households and a coverage consistent with the residency principle of national accounts. These features are not available from national emission inventories under the international conventions [http://www.unece.org/env/treaties/welcome.html CLRTAP] and [http://newsroom.unfccc.int UNFCCC], making AEA suitable for integrated modelling, e.g. of greenhouse gas footprints and climate-change modelling scenarios. See figure 1. Furthermore, Eurostat also produces quarterly estimates of greenhouse gas emissions using models building on (annual) air emissions accounts and statistical predictors.
Figure 1
'''2) Economy-wide material flow accounts (EW-MFA)''' report the amounts of physical inputs into the economy, material accumulation in the economy and outputs to other economies or back to nature. Physical inputs are classified in 50 material categories of biomass, metal ores, non-metallic minerals and fossil energy materials. EW-MFA are used to estimate, among other things, resource extractions by the economies, material consumption, [[Glossary:Resource_productivity|resource productivity]], material footprints and the [[Glossary:Decoupling|decoupling]] between economic growth and extraction of natural resources. See figure 2. [[Image:Development of resource productivity in comparison with GDP and DMC-2023-Figure1.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Resource productivity in comparison to GDP and DMC, EU, 2000-2023
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_10_gdp}} {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_mfa}} {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_rp}}|alt= a line chart with three lines showing resource productivity in comparison to GDP and DMC in the EU from 2000 to 2023.]] '''3) Physical energy flow accounts (PEFA)''' report flows of energy (including natural inputs used to manufacture energy products and energy residuals) from the environment into the economy, within the economy and from the economy to the environment. Energy flows are reported with a breakdown by type of natural inputs, products and residuals as well as by supplier and user (64 industries plus households). PEFA can be used for energy productivity, analyses, modelling, etc. [[Image:Net domestic energy use and gross value added by 64 production activities (NACE).png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 3: Net domestic energy use and gross value added by 64 production activities (NACE)
European Union (EU), 2022
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_pefa04}}, estimations based on {{Stable link|title=|code=naio_10_cp1610}}
For list of NACE Rev 2 codes see [[Media:NACE sections - codes.xls|here]]]] '''4) Environmental taxes''' report environmental taxes (in four broad groups: energy, transport, pollution and resources) with a breakdown by 64 paying industries plus households. All tax figures are consistent with [[Glossary:National_accounts_(NA)|national accounts]] and can be compared with GDP, total taxes and [[Glossary:Social_contributions|social contributions]], and other economic aggregates. See figure 4. [[File:ETEA24S-F02-v03-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_category_as_percent_of_TSC_and_GDP.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Environmental tax revenue by category as % of TSC and GDP, 2022
(%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_tax}}|alt= Combined vertical stacked bar chart and scatter chart showing environmental tax revenue by category as percentage of TSC and GDP in the EU, individual EU Member States, Iceland, Switzerland and Norway for the year 2021. Each country column has three stacks representing the categories of energy, transport and pollution and resources. The scatter plots for each country represent percentage of GDP.]] '''5) Environmental goods and services sector (EGSS) accounts''' report information on the production of goods and services that have been specifically designed and produced for the purpose of environmental protection or resource management. The EGSS accounts cover the following characteristics: [[Glossary:Output|output]], [[Glossary:Export|exports]] of the produced products, related [[Glossary:Gross value added|gross value added]] and [[Glossary:Employment|employment]]. The accounts have a breakdown by 21 industries and by functional classifications of environmental protection and resource management (CEPA and CReMA). EGSS can be used to monitor the growth of the environmental economy, green jobs, etc. See figure 5. [[Image:Development_of_key_indicators_for_the_environmental_economy_and_the_overall_economy,_EU,_2000–2022_(Index_with_base_year_2000_=_100)_v2.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 5: Development of key indicators for the environmental economy and the overall economy, EU, 2000–2022
(2000 = 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_egss1}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_egss2}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_10_gdp}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_10_a10_e}}|alt=A line chart showing the development of key indicators for the environmental economy and the overall economy of the EU, from 2000 to 2022. ]] '''6) Environmental protection expenditure accounts (EPEA)''' report mostly from a demand perspective the expenditures undertaken by economic units for environmental protection purposes. EPEA collects [[Glossary:Output|output]], [[Glossary:Intermediate_consumption|intermediate consumption]], [[Glossary:Import|imports]] & [[Glossary:Export|exports]], [[Glossary:Gross_fixed_capital_formation_(GFCF)|investment (gross fixed capital formation)]] and transfers with a breakdown by four sectors and by functional classifications of environmental protection (CEPA). See figure 6. [[Image:Fig4_Investments_for_environmental_protection_by_environmental_domain,_EU,_2024_(%_of_total_environmental_protection_investments).png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 6: Investments for environmental protection by environmental domains, EU, 2024
(% of total environmental protection investments)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_epigg1}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_epissp1}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_epiap1}}|alt= a pie chart showing the Investments for environmental protection by environmental domains in the EU, 2024. The segments show, air, waste water, waste, soil and groundwater, noise, biodiversity, Radiation, R&D and other.]] In addition to the existing mandatory 6 modules, Eurostat will start collecting forest accounts as well as environmental subsidies and similar transfers in 2025 and ecosystem accounts in 2026. '''Forest accounts''' cover, in principle, natural assets (wooded land, timber); economic aspects (value added, output and products of the forestry and logging industry) and environmental aspects (wood balances, carbon capture, residuals and defoliation). In practice, because the collection is still voluntary, data are only complete or close to complete for the economic aspects. [[Image:Employment per area of forest, 2000 and 2022_(persons employed _ 1 000 ha).png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 7: Employment per area of forest, 2000 and 2022
(persons employed / 1 000 ha)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_10_a64_e}}, and {{Stable link|title=|code=for_area_efa}}]] '''Ecosystem accounts''' based on the standard [https://seea.un.org/sites/seea.un.org/files/documents/EA/seea_ea_white_cover_final.pdf SEEA Ecosystem Accounting], which was adopted internationally in 2021. These accounts are compiled using spatially explicit data and information about the extent of ecosystem assets, their condition and the ecosystem services they produce. There are three categories of ecosystem accounts, namely: (1) ecosystem extent accounts record the total area of ecosystems, classified by type within a specified area (ecosystem accounting area); (2) ecosystem condition accounts record the condition of ecosystems using selected characteristics at specific points in time. Over time, they record the changes to their condition and thus provide valuable information on the health of ecosystems; (3) ecosystem services accounts record the supply of ecosystem services by ecosystem assets and the use of those services by economic units, including households. Examples are global climate regulation, pollination, crops provision and ecosystem-based tourism. A separate [[Ecosystem_accounts_-_measuring_the_contribution_of_nature_to_the_economy_and_human_wellbeing|article]] provides an introduction to ecosystem accounts. '''Environmental subsidies and similar transfers accounts''' record subsidies and other forms of Government support measures that help to protect the environment such as tax rebates, tax exemptions, tax credits, tax deferrals, etc. Measures that lower prices and stimulate consumption that can lead to an increase in congestion and air pollution are called potentially environmentally damaging subsidies. The accounts distinguish between current transfers (including subsidies), capital transfers and tax abatements. Data are broken down by receiving institutional sector and functional classifications of environmental protection and resource management (classifications CEPA and CReMA). For now this is a voluntary, annual data collection. [[Image:Environmental transfers paid to each institutional sector by the general government (as percentage out of total), 2022.png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 8: Environmental transfers received by corporations broken down by economic activities (%), 2022
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_esst_ggcp}}|alt=A vertical stacked bar chart showing the share of environmental transfers paid to each institutional sector by general government for the year 2022. Data are shown as percentage for the participating EU Member States and EFTA countries, as well as the sum of all reporting countries.]] As can be seen, these modules and accounts are at different stages of maturity. The development of European environmental accounts is set out in the multi-annual [https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&rct=j&q=&esrc=s&source=web&cd=4&ved=2ahUKEwi8v5DU0bvkAhXGC-wKHTIuB_AQFjADegQIAhAC&url=https%3A%2F%2Fec.europa.eu%2Feurostat%2Fdocuments%2F1798247%2F6191525%2FEuropean%2BStrategy%2Bfor%2BEnvironmental%2BAccounts%2F&usg=AOvVaw3VEUtkQwfmAByvUjphQ8q6 European Strategy for Environmental Accounts], the latest of which covers the period 2024-2028. Eurostat also produces environmental statistics, such as [[Waste statistics]], [[Municipal waste statistics]], [[Water statistics]] and [[Forests, forestry and logging|Forestry statistics]]. === Policy relevance and uses of environmental account === The effect of human activity on the environment has emerged as an important policy issue. On the one hand, there is growing concern about the effect of economic activity upon the local and global environment. On the other hand, continued economic growth and human welfare are dependent upon the benefits obtained from the environment. In recent years European policies focused more and more on how the European economy can be developed in a [[Glossary:Sustainable_development|sustainable]] direction, with a particular focus on (mitigation of and adaptation to) [[Glossary:Climate change|climate change]]. Environmental accounts are well placed to support coherent analytical and policy frameworks to inform debates and guide policy related to the interrelationship between the economy and the environment. As an accounting system, they enable the organisation of information into tables and accounts in an integrated and conceptually coherent manner. This information can be used to create coherent indicators to be used to inform decision-making and to generate accounts and aggregates for a wide range of purposes. Given their multidisciplinary scope, the environmental accounts are designed to be coherent with and complementary to other international standards, recommendations and classifications such as National Accounts (ESA 2010), the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position, NACE, CPA, etc. Environmental accounts can be used for policy development and evaluation as well as decision-making in a number of ways. Firstly, the summary information (provided in the form of aggregates and indicators) can be applied to issues and areas of the environment which are the focus of decision makers. Secondly, the detailed information, which covers some of the key drivers of change in the environment, can be used to provide a richer understanding of the policy issues. Thirdly, environmental accounts data can be used in models and scenarios designed to assess the national and international economic and environmental effects of different policy scenarios within a country, between countries and at a global level. The European environmental accounts are used for a growing number of EU policies. Indicators derived from the accounts are used for: * monitoring EU progress towards the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi sustainable development goals]. Eurostat is called to regularly monitor progress towards the SDGs in an EU context. For this purpose it coordinated the development of the EU SDG indicator set and keeps it up to date. It also produces regular monitoring reports on progress towards the SDGs in an EU context. Some of the indicators in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/information-data indicator set] are based on environmental accounts. * The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/circular-economy circular economy]. A circular economy aims to maintain the value of products, materials and resources for as long as possible by returning them into the product cycle at the end of their use, while minimising the generation of waste. Indicators based on environmental accounts are part of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/circular-economy/monitoring-framework monitoring framework for the circular economy]. * The [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/environment-action-programme-2030_en 8th Environment Action Programme] reiterates the EU’s long-term vision to 2050 of living well, within planetary boundaries. It sets out priority objectives for 2030 and the conditions needed to achieve these. The action programme aims to speed up the transition to a climate-neutral, resource-efficient economy, recognising that human wellbeing and prosperity depend on healthy ecosystems. Monitoring progress towards the EU’s environment and climate goals is particularly important. * [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/integration/green_semester/expert_group_en.htm Greening the European Semester] is about ensuring that macroeconomic policies are sustainable - economically, socially and environmentally. Furthermore, there is policy demand for potential additional applications in the areas named above as well as in green growth and green jobs, climate change and energy union, natural capital, biodiversity, environmental taxation, transport policies, sustainable financing and bio-economy. === See also === *[[Greenhouse gas emission accounts]] *[[Air pollution statistics - title: Environment statistics at regional level
text:
Eurostat regional yearbook; 2026 edition; flagship publication; EU; regional statistics; NUTS; environment; climate change mitigation; climate change impacts; air quality; landscape features; greenhouse gas emissions; drought impact on ecosystems; fine particulate matter [[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH12 RYB2026.png |thumb|centre|380px|''Source:'' EDGAR_GHG_NUTS2_v3.0. GHG emissions at subnational level, European Commission (JRC), see [https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2025_nuts2 https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2025_nuts2]]] Data extracted in March 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 This article forms part of the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026]'', an annual [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications flagship publication]. It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the [[Glossary:EU|EU]], [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate]] countries. A [[Regional_yearbook_introduction#A_short_reading_guide|short reading guide]] is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps. Between 1990 and 2024, greenhouse gas emissions in the EU fell by just over a third. Across EU regions, the largest decreases were recorded in Dytiki Makedonia (Greece; down 79.8%), Sostinės regionas (Lithuania; down 74.6%) and Região Autónoma da Madeira (Portugal; down 73.1%). In 2024, approximately 25% of assessed regions in the EU showed evidence of lasting drought impacts, with persistent drought-related reductions in vegetation productivity. In 2023, around three quarters of EU regions had already met the 2030 target to cut premature deaths from fine particulate matter by 55% compared with 2005.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:SDG wheel icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:Compet and SDG wheel icons RYB2026_small.png|left]]
[[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH12_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|650px|''Source:'' EDGAR_2025_GHGs_NUTS2. GHG emissions at subnational level, European Commission (JRC), see [https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2025_nuts2 https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2025_nuts2]|alt=A bar chart showing EU regions with the largest falls in greenhouse gas emissions, based on the quantity of tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalents, relative to 1990. Data are shown for 2024, for selected NUTS level 2 regions and for the EU average, with the information detailing the overall change, in percent.]]
Climate change and environmental degradation are among the most pressing global threats, affecting ecosystems, human health and the economy. These challenges are interconnected: while climate change harms biodiversity and alters ecosystems, intact and healthy ecosystems can help mitigate its effects (for example through carbon storage) and support adaptation (by regulating water, reducing floods and heat, preventing desertification and improving air quality). The [[Glossary:United Nations (UN)|United Nations (UN’s)]] [https://sdgs.un.org/2030agenda 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development] is a long-term strategy that seeks to achieve a range of social, economic, environmental and institutional objectives. The objectives are divided into a set of 17 [https://sdgs.un.org/goals Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)], with 1 of its core principles being to ‘leave no one behind’. Within the EU, [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/database specific indicators] are used to measure progress towards achieving the SDGs in a European context. For example, SDG 13, ‘take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts’ underscores the risks of global warming and extreme weather. Indeed, 2024 was the hottest year on record globally, leading to record temperatures, widespread displacement of people, as well as economic and social disruption. Despite ongoing international efforts and commitments under the [https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-paris-agreement Paris Agreement], it is becoming increasingly challenging to limit long-term warming to 1.5°C. The infographic above highlights that EU greenhouse gas emissions fell by 34.9% between 1990 and 2024, with much larger reductions in greenhouse gas emissions in regions such as Dytiki Makedonia (Greece), Sostinės regionas (Lithuania) and Região Autónoma da Madeira (Portugal). ===Climate change mitigation=== SDG 13 is designed to strengthen resilience and adaptive capacity to climate-related hazards and natural disasters, integrating climate change measures into national policies, while improving education and raising awareness and institutional capacity on climate change mitigation, adaptation, impact reduction and early warning. EU countries are legally committed to fighting climate change by shifting to a climate-neutral economy with net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/1119 Regulation (EU) 2021/1119 establishing the framework for achieving climate neutrality]'' – hereafter referred to as the European Climate Law – seeks to create a cleaner and healthier EU by transforming the way enterprises and people behave, both in terms of production and consumption patterns. This legal act provides the EU’s contribution to the Paris Agreement, which set an ambitious global goal ‘to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels’. Alongside a package of policy initiatives, the European Climate Law makes the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en European Green Deal’s] goal of climate neutrality by 2050 legally binding. It also sets an intermediate target: to decrease EU greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030 (compared with 1990 levels). Such decreases will require profound and transformative changes, for example, to energy and transport systems, industrial processes and agriculture, as well as increased carbon removal by ecosystems. '''Map 1''' shows progress towards these targets, with greenhouse gas emissions across the EU having fallen by 34.9% between 1990 and 2024. Note: data exclude international shipping and aviation – although both form part of the overall targets – as these items are excluded from the regional datasets presented in this chapter. '''''Greenhouse gas emissions fell in approximately 85% of EU regions between 1990 and 2024''''' Between 1990 and 2024, greenhouse gas emissions fell in 204 of the 241 NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available, while 37 regions experienced an increase. All regions in Bulgaria, Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Lithuania, Hungary, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland and Sweden recorded a decrease in greenhouse gas emissions during the period under consideration; this was the case in Estonia, Latvia, Luxembourg and Malta too. *Emissions generally declined strongly in eastern and Baltic EU countries. *Most regions in western and Nordic EU countries experienced modest decreases in greenhouse gas emissions between 1990 and 2024. *Developments in southern EU countries were more varied, with several regions – including Cyprus – recording sharp increases, while others registered sizeable decreases in emissions; this mixed pattern was observed across all multi-regional countries. Between 1990 and 2024, greenhouse gas emissions fell by more than 55% in 27 regions. '''Map 1''' highlights these regions that have already exceeded the EU’s 2030 emissions reduction target: *7 regions across Germany (including the capital region) *4 regions in Romania (including the capital region) *3 regions in Italy *2 regions in Denmark (including the capital region) *2 regions in Hungary *the capital regions of Bulgaria and Lithuania *single regions in Czechia, Greece, Spain, Poland and Portugal *the neighbouring Baltic countries of Estonia and Latvia. While greenhouse gas emissions across the EU declined by more than a third (34.9%) between 1990 and 2024, several regions recorded considerably larger decreases. Dytiki Makedonia in Greece (down 79.8%) registered the largest decline, partly reflecting the phasing-out of lignite-based electricity generation. The next biggest decreases were in Sostinės regionas, the capital region of Lithuania (down 74.6%), and Região Autónoma da Madeira in Portugal (down 73.1%). In contrast to the general pattern of emissions declining across most eastern and Baltic EU countries, the Croatian capital region and 3 Polish regions recorded increases. Between 1990 and 2024, greenhouse gas emissions rose in most regions across Ireland and Spain, as well as in Cyprus. Some of the highest increases occurred in regions that are popular with tourists, such as Spain’s eastern Mediterranean coast and Portugal’s Algarve. At the upper end of the distribution, the largest increases were recorded in the autonomous Spanish cities and the French outermost regions. Elsewhere: *emissions almost doubled in Región de Murcia (southern Spain; up 97.9%) and also rose at a rapid pace in La Rioja (northern Spain; up 75.7%) *the next largest increase was observed in Cyprus (where emissions rose 67.1%) *the Croatian capital region, Grad Zagreb, was the only other region in the EU to report its emissions growing by more than half (up 58.4%).
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:SDG wheel icon RYB2026.png|50px]]
Map 1: Greenhouse gas emissions
'' Source:'' EDGAR_2025_GHGs_NUTS2. GHG emissions at subnational level, European Commission (JRC), see [https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2025_nuts2 https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2024_nuts2] [[Image:Compet and SDG wheel icons RYB2026_small.png|left]] [[Image:Greenhouse gas emissions (index relative to 1990 = 100.0, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Greenhouse gas emissions
'' Source:'' EDGAR_2025_GHGs_NUTS2. GHG emissions at subnational level, European Commission (JRC), see [https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2025_nuts2 https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2025_nuts2]]] '''Figure 1''' shows the NUTS level 2 regions with the highest and lowest changes in greenhouse gas emissions between 1990 and 2024. It highlights a wide variation of developments among the regions of Spain, Greece, France and Portugal, in contrast to relatively narrow variations observed across the regions of Slovenia, Slovakia, Austria, Ireland, Bulgaria and Finland. *In Spain, greenhouse gas emissions in Ciudad de Ceuta more than quadrupled compared with 1990 levels. By contrast, emissions in the north-western region of Principado de Asturias fell sharply, registering a fall of 63.2% over the same period. In 2024, the index for Ciudad de Ceuta was 11.1 times as high as the index for Principado de Asturias (representing the largest regional variation across EU countries). *In Greece, the central mainland region of Sterea Elláda experienced the fastest growth in greenhouse gas emissions, rising by 43.8% between 1990 and 2024. This contrasts sharply with developments in the northern region of Dytiki Makedonia, where emissions fell by 79.8% (representing the largest decrease between 1990 and 2024 across EU regions). *In France, greenhouse gas emissions in Mayotte were approximately 3.5 times as high in 2024 as in 1990, while the northern region of Haute-Normandie witnessed a near-halving of its emissions over the same period, down 49.5%. *In Portugal, the southern region of Algarve experienced a 43.1% increase in greenhouse gas emissions between 1990 and 2024, whereas Região Autónoma da Madeira registered a considerable decrease (down 73.1%) during the same period.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:SDG wheel icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:Compet and SDG wheel icons RYB2026_small.png|left]]
[[Image:Greenhouse gas emissions (index relative to 1990 = 100, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Greenhouse gas emissions
'' Source:'' EDGAR_2025_GHGs_NUTS2. GHG emissions at subnational level, European Commission (JRC), see [https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2025_nuts2 https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2025_nuts2]|alt=High low plot showing greenhouse gas emissions. Data are presented as an index relative to 1990 set equal to 100 and are based on the overall change in tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalents between 1990 and 2024. Data are shown for the region with the highest and the region with the lowest change in each country, as well as the national average. Data are presented for 2024. Data are shown for level 2 regions in EU, EFTA and candidate countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Between 1990 and 2024, greenhouse gas emissions across the EU generally followed a moderate downward path, reflecting steady progress in reducing carbon intensity. Most years saw annual decreases in emissions, although there were intermittent periods with increases (often linked to phases of rapid economic growth), such as in 1995–96, 2000–01, 2003–04 and 2015–16. The most striking falls in EU emissions occurred in 2020 and 2023, with decreases of 7.8% and 7.5%, respectively. The fall in 2020 was largely the result of the COVID-19 pandemic, as an abrupt slowdown in economic activity, linked to widespread lockdowns, sharply curtailed transport, industrial and energy demand. By contrast, the decline in 2023 was linked more to decreases in consumer demand in the face of high prices, structural changes as fossil fuels were replaced by renewable energy (in the face of continued volatility in global energy markets, exacerbated by Russia’s war against Ukraine), and improvements in energy efficiency. The steady progress over time observed across the EU as a whole masks substantial differences in regional developments. '''Figure 2''' provides a more detailed picture of the development of greenhouse gas emissions in the NUTS level 2 regions with the highest/lowest changes between 1990 and 2024; note that a threshold of at least 3 000 tonnes of CO2-equivalents was used when selecting the regions. *During the period under consideration, Región de Murcia in southern Spain recorded the largest increase in greenhouse gas emissions. The region experienced a particularly sharp rise in emissions between 2005 and 2006, which may be attributed, at least in part, to an expansion of its electricity generation facilities. Emissions fluctuated thereafter but generally followed a downward trend, falling overall by 19.4% between 2006 and 2024. *Having peaked in 2008 (77.0% higher than in 1990), greenhouse gas emissions in Cyprus fell for 5 consecutive years before resuming a generally upward trend. By 2024, emissions were 67.1% above their 1990 level and just 5.5% below the peak of 2008. The relatively high and growing level of emissions in Cyprus may be linked to continued reliance on fossil fuels, high emissions linked to energy use, transport, waste and household consumption, as well as economic growth outpacing decreases in carbon intensity. *By 2012, greenhouse gas emissions in the northern Greek region of Dytiki Makedonia were 12.5% higher than their 1990 level. However, a period of rapid change, driven by economic restructuring and the increasing deployment of clean energy sources, led to an overall decline of 82.0% in emissions between 2012 and 2024. The most pronounced annual decreases occurred in 2019 and 2020, when emissions fell by 26.2% and 40.6%, respectively. *The development of greenhouse gas emissions in the Lithuanian capital region of Sostinės regionas followed a different path (from that observed in Dytiki Makedonia). Emissions fell sharply in the early 1990s, likely linked to post-Soviet economic restructuring. Thereafter, with cleaner energy and efficiency improvements, emissions continued to decline, albeit at a slower pace. Over the most recent decade, emissions in Sostinės regionas generally fell, although annual increases were recorded in 2020 and 2021, as well as a modest increase in 2024 (up 0.3%).
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:SDG wheel icon RYB2026.png|50px]]
[[Image:Change in greenhouse gas emissions (index relative to 1990 = 100, selected NUTS 2 regions, 1990–2024)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|650px|Figure 2: Change in greenhouse gas emissions
''Source:'' EDGAR_2025_GHGs_NUTS2. GHG emissions at subnational level, European Commission (JRC), see [https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2025_nuts2 https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2025_nuts2]|alt=Line chart showing greenhouse gas emissions.]]
[[Image:Compet and SDG wheel icons RYB2026_small.png|left]] [[Image:Change in greenhouse gas emissions (index relative to 1990 = 100, selected NUTS 2 regions, 1990–2024)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Change in greenhouse gas emissions
''Source:'' EDGAR_2025_GHGs_NUTS2. GHG emissions at subnational level, European Commission (JRC), see [https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2025_nuts2 https://edgar.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset_ghg2025_nuts2]|alt=Line chart showing greenhouse gas emissions.]] ===Climate change impacts=== '''Drought impact''' SDG 15 ‘life on land’ aims to protect, restore and promote the sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems; sustainably manage forests; combat desertification; halt and reverse land degradation; and halt biodiversity loss. Its objectives are embedded within the European Commission’s priorities for 2024 to 2029 under the heading of ‘[https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/quality-life_en Sustaining our quality of life: food security, water and nature]’. Droughts and water scarcity are becoming increasingly frequent and severe across the EU ([https://climate.copernicus.eu/esotc/2025 ESOTC, 2025]). These events reduce water availability, lower agricultural output, accelerate soil erosion and release carbon stored in soils. They also threaten biodiversity, hinder habitat restoration, disrupt species migration and promote the spread of invasive alien species, as highlighted in the EU’s ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32024R1991 Nature Restoration Regulation]'' ((EU) 2024/1991), a key element of the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/biodiversity-strategy-2030_en EU biodiversity strategy for 2030]. Drought undermines nature’s ability to provide environmental, social and economic benefits. It reduces carbon sequestration, jeopardises climate mitigation, and affects adaptation, biodiversity restoration and soil management. Droughts also impede progress towards [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy/cap-overview/cap-glance/key-policy-objectives-cap-2023-27_en common agricultural policy (CAP) objectives] and the goals of the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en European green deal], as well as biodiversity and soil initiatives. As such, the EU seeks to reduce drought impacts and strengthen resilience through measures addressing water scarcity, sustainable water management and climate adaptation. Water scarcity is a major climate change risk that arises when available water resources are insufficient to meet the needs of society, economic sectors and ecosystems. It can compromise water availability for households, agriculture, industry, energy generation and the environment. Meteorological droughts – defined as prolonged periods of below-average precipitation relative to long-term climatic conditions – can provide an early indication of emerging water scarcity. The indicator presented below focuses on meteorological drought impacts, capturing drought-related declines in vegetation productivity. This differs from hydrological droughts, which affect surface and groundwater resources, such as rivers, reservoirs and aquifers, and typically develop after more prolonged precipitation deficits. Drought exposure refers to the degree to which an area experiences drought conditions, such as precipitation deficits or soil moisture shortages. Drought impact, by contrast, describes the actual consequences of those conditions on environmental, social or economic systems. In the context of agricultural drought, drought exposure reflects the occurrence of soil moisture deficits, whereas drought impact is observed through reductions in vegetation productivity resulting from those deficits. As a result, areas with similar levels of drought exposure may experience different impacts depending on factors such as vegetation type, land management practices, irrigation and ecosystem resilience. The [[Glossary:European_Environment_Agency_(EEA)|European Environment Agency (EEA)]] monitors drought exposure as a key climate indicator, defined as the area experiencing significant soil moisture deficits relative to the 2000 to 2020 baseline. The drought impact indicator presented in this section tracks reductions in vegetation productivity caused by soil moisture deficits during the growing season. Based on remote-sensing data, it identifies areas where soil moisture falls below the long-term average for the 2000 to 2020 reference period. Drought impact is quantified as the share of a region’s area where vegetation productivity does not recover to its baseline (2000 to 2020) conditions because of drought. As a result, the indicator captures areas experiencing above-average drought impacts relative to the long-term record, rather than representing the total area exposed to or affected by drought ([https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/drought-impact-on-ecosystems-in-europe?activeAccordion=546a7c35-9188-4d23-94ee-005d97c26f2b EEA, 2025]). Projections indicate that drought conditions in Europe will become more frequent, longer-lasting and more intense under climate change. In 2024, drought exposure covered 601 000 km2 (14% of the EU), below the exceptional peak observed in 2022, but slightly above 2023. The overall extent of intense drought impacts in the EU has been gradually increasing. Between 2000 and 2024, as the area of drought impact followed an upward development due to low precipitation, high evaporation and intermittent heatwaves. Notably high levels were recorded in 2003, 2012, 2018 and particularly 2022, when the EU experienced its hottest summer to date and its second warmest year on record; approximately 558 000 km2 of land were impacted by drought with vegetation productivity well below the baseline conditions. Pressure on EU ecosystems eased in 2023 and 2024, with broadly similar areas affected. In 2024, 156 700 km2, or 3.7% of the EU’s total area, was impacted by drought. The largest areas affected were cropland (55.9% of the impacted area), woodland and forest (21.4%) and grassland (9.1%). Approximately 30% of the EU regions assessed showed evidence of lasting drought impacts in 2024, indicating that vegetation productivity in parts of their territory had not recovered to baseline (2000 to 2020) conditions following drought-related reductions.
[[Image:SDG wheel icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:SDG_wheel_icon_RYB2026_small.png|left]]
[[Image:Area of drought impact on ecosystems (1 000 km, EU, 2000–24)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Area of drought impact on ecosystems
'' Source:'' [https://sdi.eea.europa.eu/datashare/s/zQL57mZeF6Qs2Xc/download European Environment Agency (EEA)] and Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a031623e-5e1f-4499-a916-cd39e99c8416?lang=en sdg_15_42])|alt=Stacked column chart showing the area of drought impact on ecosystems as measured by the share of land area where vegetation productivity did not recover to 2000 to 2020 baseline conditions. Stacks are shown for cropland, woodland and forest, grassland, heathland and scrub, urban, sparsely vegetated land, inland wetlands. Data are presented for 2000 to 2024. Data are shown for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''''Drought impact was particularly prevalent across south-eastern regions of the EU in 2024''''' '''Map 2''' shows the share of each region’s area exposed to a severe soil moisture deficit in 2024, where – due to drought – vegetation productivity did not recover to baseline (2000 to 2020) conditions. There were 870 regions across the EU where the area impacted by drought remained lower than or equal to the average drought impact recorded for the years 2000 to 2020 (as shown by the lightest shade in the map). This was the case for a band of regions stretching from Portugal and Ireland in the west, through much of Spain, France and the Benelux countries into Germany, Austria and several eastern EU countries. The pattern was more mixed in several of the Nordic and Baltic countries, where some regions experienced higher-than-average drought impacts. Along the easternmost and southernmost edges of the EU, a relatively large number of regions experienced a higher-than-average share of land affected by drought. In 2024, Malta was the only EU country where drought impact on ecosystems accounted for more than half (57.5%) of its total area. There were 5 other countries in the EU that recorded double-digit shares: Bulgaria (20.1%), Romania (17.5%), Cyprus (13.0%), Greece (11.4%) and Italy (10.7%). In 2024, the distribution of drought impacts was highly skewed: one quarter (290 out of the 1 160) of the NUTS level 3 regions across the EU for which data are available experienced lasting drought impacts, while three quarters had no lasting impact. These 290 affected regions that were impacted by drought, included: *every region of Bulgaria, Malta and Romania *all but 3 regions of Greece (the exceptions being Chios, Larisa and Kerkyra) *more than half the regions of Poland *and Cyprus. Among the 290 regions that experienced some impact from drought during 2024, the regions with the largest areas of land affected – in absolute terms – were: *Lovech, in northern Bulgaria (998 km2) *Lleida, in north-eastern Spain (989 km2) *Caraş-Severin, in western Romania (977 km2). The regions with the highest shares of land impacted by drought were all situated on the Italian island of Sicilia, namely: *Enna (95.2%) *Caltanissetta (89.0%) *Siracusa (87.3%). More generally, there were 19 regions where more than half of the total area was impacted by drought in 2024. This group included: *Voreios Tomeas Athinon in Greece *Eivissa y Formentera, Mallorca, Murcia and Alicante/Alacant in Spain *8 regions on Sicilia, 1 on Sardegna and the south-eastern region of Matera in Italy *both regions in Malta *Galaţi and Botoşani in Romania.

A key aspect of this goal is to reduce the environmental impact of urban areas, in particular through improving air quality and enhancing the management of municipal and other forms of waste. Air quality can deteriorate considerably due to human activities such as industrial processes, the burning of solid fuels, transport, agriculture and the generation or treatment of waste. In addition, natural sources of air pollution include volcanic eruptions, desert dust and sea salt. Air pollution remains a major cause of premature death and disease across the EU, with fine particulate matter (PM2.5) identified as having the most serious human health impacts. Some of the most common causes of both illness and premature death attributed to air pollution include heart disease, stroke, lung disease, lung cancer and asthma; these illnesses also have an associated economic cost through lost working days and healthcare expenditure. To address this, the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/zero-pollution-action-plan_en EU’s zero pollution action plan] has set a target to reduce premature deaths caused by fine particulate matter by at least 55% by 2030 (relative to 2005 levels). More broadly, the plan aims to bring air, water and soil pollution down to levels no longer considered harmful to human health and natural ecosystems by 2050.
'''More about the data: air quality guidelines, commitments and targets''' Premature deaths are deaths that occur before a person reaches an expected age. This expected age is typically the life expectancy of a country, stratified by sex and age. In this context, premature deaths are considered preventable if their cause can be eliminated. Fine particulate matter refers to particles with a diameter of 2.5 micrometres or less (otherwise referred to as PM2.5). In September 2021, the [[Glossary:World_Health_Organization_(WHO)|World Health Organization (WHO)]] issued new global air quality guidelines, emphasising the need to safeguard public health: the long-term guideline level was set as an annual average of 5 µg/m3 for PM2.5. These guidelines reflect growing scientific evidence that even low concentrations of air pollution may pose significant risks to human health. As part of its goal to eliminate pollution by 2050, the European Commission has outlined key targets and initiatives. Among these, an intermediate goal to reduce premature deaths resulting from exposure to air pollution by at least 55% between 2005 and 2030. In December 2024, a revised ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202402881 Directive on ambient air quality and cleaner air for Europe]'' (Directive (EU) 2024/2881) came into force. Under this directive, the European Commission will review the latest scientific evidence on air pollution and its health impacts by the end of 2030 and every 5 years thereafter – or more often if new findings warrant it – to ensure the EU’s air quality standards continue to be appropriate. The directive sets a new annual limit value for the EU of 10 µg/m3 for PM2.5, to be met by 1 January 2030. The revised directive also aims to strengthen air quality plans and roadmaps for territorial units where pollution exceeds EU standards. It updates air quality limits for 12 pollutants, including fine particulate matter. In addition, it also provides an opportunity for individuals to seek compensation if their health is harmed due to violations of EU air quality rules.
The penultimate section of this chapter presents statistics on the health impacts of air pollution associated with exposure to fine particulate matter. The EEA estimates that fine particulate matter resulted in 182 400 premature deaths across the EU in 2023 (down 23.5% compared with 2022). Note that all the information in this section on premature deaths attributable to fine particulate matter concerns a cohort of people aged 30 years or more – sometimes referred to as the ‘affected population’ – as this is the age range generally considered in epidemiological studies. '''''In 2023, there were 3 478 premature deaths attributed to fine particulate matter in the northern Italian region of Milano''''' The highest numbers of premature deaths among people aged 30 years or more were primarily estimated to have occurred in southern and eastern EU countries, particularly in predominantly urban regions. The northern Italian region of Milano had the highest estimated number (3 478 premature deaths in 2023), followed by the Spanish region of Barcelona (2 883 deaths) and the Italian capital region of Roma (2 743 deaths). There were 3 additional regions in Italy and Spain that were also estimated to have more than 2 000 premature deaths: the Italian regions of Torino and Napoli, and the Spanish capital region of Madrid. At the other end of the distribution, very low levels were recorded across several parts of northern Europe. In 2023, 17 EU regions had no premature deaths attributed to fine particulate matter among the affected population. The vast majority of these (14 regions) were located in Sweden, primarily in the northern part of the country. The remaining 3 regions were composed of the predominantly rural regions of Arr. Bastogne in southern Belgium, Kesk-Eesti in central Estonia and Lungau in Austria. Finland likewise had a very low estimated value, based on its national data. While the absolute number of premature deaths attributed to exposure to fine particulate matter was generally high in some of the most populous regions of the EU, the most significant impacts of air pollution in terms of premature deaths per 100 000 inhabitants were generally observed in industrialised and urbanised regions, particularly across eastern EU countries. These regions are typically characterised by high concentrations of industrial activity in traditional sectors such as coal mining, steel production, cement manufacture and chemical industries. In addition, some also have a relatively high share of households burning coal or wood for heating, and/or suffer from traffic congestion – other factors that may exacerbate air pollution. '''''Between 2005 and 2023, the number of premature deaths attributed to fine particulate matter in the EU fell by 56.9%''''' Between 2005 and 2023, the number of premature deaths attributed to fine particulate matter among people aged 30 years or more fell from 423 600 to 182 400 within the EU, a decrease of 56.9%. The regional distribution of changes in premature deaths was skewed: in 754 out of 1 055 regions for which data are available (71.5% of all regions), the number of premature deaths fell faster than the EU average between 2005 and 2023. Note that this relates to the relative change in the rate of premature deaths attributed to fine particulate matter during the period under consideration; it does not reveal whether the initial or final rates were comparatively high or low (for example, relative to the total population). Rather, it reflects the direction and magnitude of change from the initial level. In relation to the 2030 target of reducing the number of premature deaths in the EU among the affected population by at least 55%, 792 regions had already achieved this level of reduction by 2023 (however, it should be noted that the target applies to the EU as a whole rather than to individual regions). This group included: *every region of Belgium, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Lithuania and Sweden *as well as Latvia, the Netherlands, Portugal and Finland (for which only national data are available). At the other end of the distribution, the north-western Greek region of Ioannina was the only region in the EU where the estimated number of premature deaths among people aged 30 years or more attributed to fine particulate matter was higher in 2023 than in 2005. This region lies in a mountain basin where atmospheric conditions – particularly in winter – can trap air pollutants and limit their dispersion. More generally, there were clusters of regions in mainland Greece, northern Italy and central Poland with relatively small decreases in the estimated number of premature deaths attributed to fine particulate matter among the affected population between 2005 and 2023. The use of solid fuel for domestic heating and an ageing population structure may be linked to increased exposure and vulnerability to air pollution in some of these. Furthermore, as with Ioannina, geographical conditions may also play a role. For example, some of the most persistent air pollution issues in Italy are concentrated in the densely populated plains of the Po valley, where topography hinders air circulation and traps pollutants from agriculture, industry and transport.

===Landscape features=== Landscape features have historically been an integral component of agricultural land, closely associated with farming practices and providing a range of environmental and agronomic benefits. However, as farming has grown more intensive, many landscape features have disappeared from agricultural areas or have been left neglected and unmanaged. Landscape features contribute to biodiversity and the provision of ecosystem services, including habitat support, pollination, soil erosion control, water quality protection and climate change mitigation. In addition to environmental benefits, landscape features can also enhance field-level productivity by improving soil fertility, supporting natural pest regulation and increasing water availability. Across much of the EU, traditional farming systems integrate landscape features, which serve functional roles such as delineating field boundaries, providing shelter for livestock and maintaining ecological connectivity. These landscape features also possess cultural and historical significance, as illustrated by the ‘bocage’ (hedgerow-dominated) landscapes of north-west France or the dry-stone walls that segment agricultural land in countries such as Ireland and Malta. Within [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/2115/oj/eng Regulation (EU) 2021/2115], Annex I established Indicator I.21 – ''Enhancing provision of ecosystem services: share of agricultural land covered with landscape features''. This indicator is recognised across several EU policy frameworks, including the [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy/cap-overview/cap-glance_en common agricultural policy (CAP)] and the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/biodiversity-strategy-2030_en EU biodiversity strategy for 2030], and is referenced in legislation such as the ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32024R1991 Nature Restoration Regulation]'' ((EU) 2024/1991). Previously, no EU-wide database on landscape features existed. To address this gap, the [https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/index_en Joint Research Centre (JRC)], at the request of the [https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/agriculture-and-rural-development_en Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development], developed a harmonised monitoring system. Building on the existing [[Glossary:Land_use_-_cover_area_frame_survey_(LUCAS)|land use and cover area frame survey (LUCAS)]], a dedicated landscape features module was introduced to collect detailed information in support of environmental and agricultural monitoring. This has provided consistent data on the distribution and types of landscape features across EU countries and NUTS level 2 regions. It also establishes a long-term, repeatable framework, enabling policymakers to track changes over time and assess the impact of agricultural and environmental policies. The LUCAS landscape features module only considers such features in an agricultural context. These features are defined as small fragments of non-productive and typically, but not only, semi-natural vegetation present in, or adjacent to, agricultural land, providing ecosystem services and support for biodiversity. To ensure consistency, the module defines minimum and maximum sizes for landscape features: *linear features have a width greater than 1 metre and smaller than 20 metres *patchy features have an area between 1 square metre and 5 000 square metres (or 0.5 hectares). The different landscape features are subsequently grouped into 4 main categories: *grassy features – comprising field margins, buffer strips and grassed thalwegs (grassed waterways, natural or constructed channels, typically seeded with grass or low-growing vegetation, located along the deepest, most concave line of a valley or slope, used to manage surface run-off, reduce soil erosion and prevent the formation of rills and gullies) *stony features – covering stone walls, terraces, cairns and rocky outcrops *wet features – encompassing ditches, ponds, seepage areas and small wetlands *woody features – including hedges, wooded strips, isolated trees, trees in line and grouped trees.

Images provided for grassy features, stony features, wet features and woody features.]] It is important to note that these landscape features should be located in or adjacent to agricultural land. More specifically, this includes all elements that are lying: *within an agricultural field (typically within arable land, grassland or permanent crops) *between agricultural fields *between an agricultural field and linear infrastructure (a farm track, road or railway) *between an agricultural field and detached buildings (such as individual farmyards, or agricultural buildings) *between an agricultural field and water bodies (for examples, rivers, lakes or reservoirs). Within the LUCAS landscape features module, the principal indicator for analysis is the ratio between the area covered by landscape features and the area covered by agricultural land, expressed in percent. Estimates of the share of landscape features in agricultural land based on the LUCAS 2022 module results were provided by the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC135966 JRC]. '''The LUCAS landscape features module'''
To obtain an unbiased estimation of the share of landscape features in agricultural lands, the LUCAS 2022 module was conducted on a subset of the points observed in the field during the LUCAS survey. The primary observation unit in the module is a 1 hectare quadrat (100 metres by 100 metres), with the LUCAS sample point at its centre. Within each quadrat, landscape features are assessed at 41 locations arranged in an offset grid. [[File:p_44863108.jpg|700px]]
Background imagery © Google; Imagery © Maxar Technologies

'''Example of the 41 point sampling grid used in the LUCAS landscape features module. The left panel shows the arrangement of the sampling locations, with the central point corresponding to the original LUCAS sample point. The right panel shows the same sampling grid overlaid on an aerial photo.'''
[[Image:41 point sampling grid_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px]] The methodology uses a two-step approach:
*at first, an office-based photo-interpretation is conducted using very high resolution images to look for the presence and type of landscape features
*subsequently, a field survey of the same observation units is used to confirm or revise the photo interpretation. Photos are taken of the central point and in the 4 cardinal directions at each point (these are [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/lucas/database/primary-data#lucasphotos freely available] on the Eurostat website).
During the 2022 survey, 92 633 quadrats were surveyed (which encompasses almost 3.8 million data points), providing a comprehensive and accurate assessment of landscape features across the EU. For more information: JRC Publications – ''[https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC135966 Estimation of the share of Landscape Features in agricultural land based on the LUCAS 2022 survey]'' For more information: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistical-atlas/?config=LUCAS Eurostat Statistical Atlas – LUCAS 2022]
'''''Approximately 5.6% of the EU’s agricultural land was covered by landscape features in 2022''''' The abundance of landscape features is often considered as an important metric for analysing agricultural biodiversity. Based on the LUCAS survey data, the JRC estimates that landscape features covered 5.6% of the EU’s agricultural land in 2022, with the largest share attributed to woody features (3.2%), followed by grassy (1.9%), wet (0.4%) and stony (0.2%) features. '''Map 4''' provides information on the distribution of landscape features across NUTS level 2 regions. While there was a very mixed pattern across EU regions, landscape features broadly accounted for a high share of the agricultural land in a band of regions running from southern Bulgaria and Greece, through Croatia and Italy, into France, northern Spain and Ireland. By contrast, relatively low shares were recorded across many regions in the eastern EU countries, as well as in southern Germany and Austria. There were 23 regions across the EU where the share of landscape features in agricultural land was equal to or above 10.0%. This group of regions was widely distributed among EU counties, including: *6 regions stretching along the whole of Italy *3 regions in northern Sweden *2 predominantly urban regions in Germany (where the overall area given over to agricultural land was small in absolute terms) *2 regions in northern Spain *2 regions in southern France *a single region from each of Bulgaria, Greece, Croatia, Hungary, Austria and Portugal *Cyprus and Malta. In 2022, the highest regional shares for landscape features in agricultural areas were recorded in the northern Italian region of Valle d’Aosta/Vallée d’Aoste (33.3%; low reliability, likely over-estimated), Malta (30.0%), the northern Swedish region of Mellersta Norrland (23.0%) and Cyprus (21.1%). Within these regions, relatively low levels of large-scale, industrialised agriculture have helped preserve traditional land structures. As a result, landscape features – whether natural (like tree lines and streams) or man-made (like terraces and stone walls) – remain a prominent characteristic of agricultural areas. Their high shares likely reflect a mix of geographic, climatic and historical factors, for example: *in mountainous regions such as Valle d’Aosta/Vallée d’Aoste, agriculture is constrained by steep slopes, altitude and fragmented terrain, leading to irregular-shaped fields interspersed with features like terraces, hedgerows, stone walls and patches of woodland (often essential for soil stabilisation and water management)
