title: Enterprises in the sports sector
text:
Data on EU enterprises active in the NACE sectors 93.1 'Sports activities', 85.51 'Sports and recreation education' and 32.3 'Manufacture of sports goods' Data extracted in October 2025. Planned article update: December 2026. In 2023, businesses within the EU’s sports sector generated value added of approximately €33 billion, marking a 13.8% rise from 2022. In 2023, enterprises focused on sports and recreational education made up one fifth of all educational enterprises within the EU. In 2023, 99.9% of EU sports activities enterprises were classified as small and medium-sized, responsible for 60.8% of the sector’s total value added. This article provides indicators concerning sports sector enterprises in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]], based on the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/overview structural business statistics (SBS)]. === What constitutes the sports sector? ===
For the context of this article, the sector encompasses: *sporting '''activities''' *sports '''education''' *sports goods '''manufacturing'''. The SBS cover the core sporting activities, defined by the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/6921402/0/Vilnius+Definition+Sport+CPA2008+official+2013_09_19.pdf/30838d11-01ea-431f-8112-50786e187c1c Vilnius Definition of sport] under [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] Rev.2 group 93.1 — Sports activities. Table 1 shows the details of this NACE group and its classes at 4 digits level. [[Image:T1Sports activities covered by the EU's structural business statistics from 2021.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: Sports activities covered by the EU's structural business statistics from 2021
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-ra-07-015 NACE Rev. 2 - Statistical classification of economic activities])|alt= Table showing sports activities covered by the EU's structural business statistics sourced from NACE Rev. 2 - Statistical classification of economic activities. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Moreover, to provide a comprehensive overview of the broad definition of sport, alongside NACE group 93.1, this article presents data related to: *NACE class 85.51 — '''Sports and recreation education''' *NACE group 32.3 — '''Manufacturing of sports goods'''. === Sports activities enterprises in the EU: main indicators ===
'''Enterprises in the sports sector in 2023 generated around €33 billion in value added'''
In 2023, in the EU approximately '''200 000 enterprises''' operated within the sports sector, constituting 0.6% of all businesses in industry, construction and market services. These enterprises generated €33 [[Glossary:billion|billion]] in [[Glossary:Value_added_-_EBS|value added]], while their [[Glossary:Net_turnover_-_EBS|turnover]] (the total value of market sales of goods and services) reached around €70 billion. These figures correspond to 0.3% of value added and 0.2% of turnover for all businesses across industry, construction and market services (see Table 2). At national level, the share of enterprises in the sports sector relative to businesses in industry, construction and market services exceeded 1% in Finland (1.6%), Slovenia (1.3%) and Latvia (1.2%), while Poland recorded the lowest share at 0.3%. Spain registered the highest figures for value added and turnover, accounting for 0.8% and 0.4% of the total national economy, respectively. [[Image:T2Main indicators for enterprises in sports sector, 2023.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 2: Main indicators for enterprises in sports sector, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_ovw_act__custom_18637490/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=bebd1797-d351-4248-8508-5dca05ab4909&c=1761637410074 sbs_ovw_act])|alt= Table showing main indicators for enterprises in sports sector in the EU, individual EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries for the year 2023. Presented are the number of enterprises and value added and turnover for each country, in euro millions and as a share of total in industry, construction and market service. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, Spain, France, Germany, and Italy collectively represented 45% of all enterprises in the EU sports sector, with Spain holding the largest share at 17% (see Figure 1). Combined, these 4 countries accounted for around 70% of the total value added by the EU sporting sector, where Germany recorded the highest proportion at 25.2% followed by Spain at 21.0%. Furthermore, Germany and Spain led in turnover, together contributing 43.5% of the overall turnover generated by EU sporting enterprises. [[Image:F1EU Member States' shares in the EU total for main indicators concerning the sports sector, 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: EU Member States' shares in the EU total for main indicators concerning the sports sector, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_ovw_act__custom_18460245/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=9742dca7-9551-43ca-88b1-0fc0b21e8992&c=1760709499002 sbs_ovw_act])|alt= Scatter plot chart showing EU Member States' shares in the EU total for main indicators concerning the sports sector in percentage share of EU total in individual EU Member States for the year 2023. Each country has three scatter plots representing the number of enterprises, value added and turnover. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''In 2023, enterprises in the sports sector achieved a more pronounced increase in value added and turnover than those in industry, construction and market services in total''' Table 3 illustrates the rate of change from 2022 to 2023 for the 3 indicators analysed thus far (number of enterprises, value added and turnover) within the sports sector and the non-financial business economy. At EU level, each of these indicators showed a significant rise in the sports sector, surpassing the growth seen in industry, construction and market services in total. This was especially evident in turnover within the sports sector, which rose by 16.7% in 2023, while the non-financial business economy remained relatively stable with a modest increase of 0.6%. Examining the rate of change in 2023 for the 3 indicators in individual EU countries: *The number of enterprises increased in 21 of the 26 EU countries for which data was available, with the most notable rises reaching double-digit percentages in Croatia (+21.6%), Malta (+21.5%), Estonia (+18.3%), Portugal (+11.8%), and Slovakia (+10.4%); *Malta (+66.5%) and Croatia (+65.9%) saw the most substantial growth in value added within the sports sector compared to the previous year; *All EU countries with available data experienced a rise in turnover within the sports sector, with the highest increases in Malta (+38.8%) and Latvia (+36.1%). [[Image:T3Change in the number of enterprises, value added and turnover, 2022-2023.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 3: Change in the number of enterprises, value added and turnover, 2022-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_ovw_act__custom_18460756/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=a1ba43d5-83ee-4942-9497-52b664a8ce80&c=1760711022748 sbs_ovw_act])|alt= Table showing change in the number of enterprises, value added and turnover as a percentage annual rate of change for the EU, individual EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''In 2023, fitness facilities constituted more than half of the businesses in the sports sector in Cyprus and Greece, whereas in the Netherlands nearly half of the sector’s businesses were linked to sports club activities.''' Examining the specific activities within the sport businesses, ’other sports activities’ held the largest share of enterprises in the sports sector at the national level in 19 EU countries, with Slovenia leading at 89.3% of all enterprises in this sector. ’Other sports activities’ includes activities such as sport event producers and promoters, self-employed sportsmen and athletes, referees, judges, timekeepers and activities by sports leagues and regulatory bodies. ’Fitness facilities’ formed the largest category of business activities in the sports sector in 5 EU countries, with more than half of the enterprises in the sports sector in Cyprus (63.6%) and Greece (59.1%). Moreover, businesses involved in ’activities of sport clubs’ were most prevalent in the Netherlands (46.1%) and Belgium (37.5%) (see Figure 2). [[Image:F2Number of enterprises in the sports sector, by NACE class, 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Number of enterprises in the sports sector, by NACE class, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_ovw_act__custom_18480170/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=7a540925-3731-4e8e-8892-df7fc581c6a6&c=1760951619692 sbs_ovw_act])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing number of enterprises in the sports sector as a percentage for the EU, individual EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries in the year 2023. Each country column totals one hundred percent and contains five stacks that represent the NACE classes. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''In 2023, sport clubs were responsible for the majority of value added by businesses in the sports industry across 9 EU countries''' In 2023, Sport club activities contributed the most to the value added by enterprises in the sports sector in 9 EU countries, with Italy (65.0%), Lithuania (64.5%), and Spain (51.9%) having the highest shares. Conversely, as shown by Figure 3, Czechia, Slovakia and Luxembourg recorded negative figures for value added by sport club activities in the same year. 7 EU countries, notably Slovakia at 90.1%, reported the highest share of value added in the sports sector from ’operation of sports facilities’. Romania (55.9%), Malta (54.7%), and Luxembourg (46.9%) demonstrated significant shares in 'fitness facilities’. Meanwhile, the remaining 7 EU countries (excluding Ireland due to unavailable data) recorded their greatest contributions in 'other sports activities', with Slovenia leading at 73.4%. [[Image:F3Value added for enterprises in the sports sector, by NACE class, 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Value added for enterprises in the sports sector, by NACE class, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_ovw_act__custom_18480170/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=6c555cad-961d-415a-951b-e8d37b6ed5e6&c=1760952012846 sbs_ovw_act])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing value added enterprises in the sports sector as a percentage for the EU, individual EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries in the year 2023. Each country column totals one hundred percent and contains five stacks that represent the NACE classes. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===What is the size of enterprises in the sports sector?===
Small and medium-sized enterprises (‘SMEs’) are crucial to the EU’s economy. They drive job creation and economic growth. Like other industries, SMEs, defined as businesses with less than 250 employees, form the majority of EU enterprises in the sports sector. Table 4 presents key indicators for enterprises in the sports sector, categorised by business size class, which is determined by the number of employees. In 2023, SMEs constituted the largest share of EU enterprises in the sports sector (99.9%), a figure consistent with their presence in industry, construction and market services (99.8%). Large enterprises, employing 250 people or more within the sports sector, comprised less than a fifth of the workforce (18.2%), which is lower than their proportion in industry, construction and market services (36.5%). Further analysis reveals that SMEs generated 60.8% of the value added by the EU’s enterprises in the sports sector in 2023. This percentage was significantly higher than that of all enterprises in industry, construction and market services (50.9%), underscoring the importance of SMEs in this sector. [[Image:T4Main indicators for enterprises in the sports sector, by enterprise size class, EU, 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 4: Main indicators for enterprises in the sports sector, by enterprise size class, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_sc_ovw__custom_18480492/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=242cf9f4-3e4d-47cf-b789-af574e95dd72&c=1760952303556 sbs_sc_ovw])|alt= Table showing main indicators for enterprises in the sports sector by enterprise size class in the EU for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Sports education enterprises in the EU===
Sports education involves providing instruction in athletic activities to groups, such as through camps and schools (e.g. team sports, swimming, yoga lessons). Sport holds significant importance in educational businesses: in 2023, the EU had an estimated 200 000 enterprises for sports and recreation education. France registered approximately 67 000 of these enterprises, followed by the Netherlands with nearly 33 000 businesses; together these 2 countries comprised half of the sports and recreation education enterprises in the EU (see Table 5). In 2023, France also led in value added by enterprises for sports and recreation education in the EU, achieving €1.2 billion. Germany followed with €902 million from about 12 200 enterprises, and the Netherlands with €736 million. These 3 EU countries were the only ones to exceed €1 billion in turnover from sports and recreation education enterprises in 2023, representing more than half of the EU’s turnover in this sector. France stood out with over €2 billion, followed by Germany (€1.6 billion) and the Netherlands (€1.2 billion). [[Image:T5Main indicators for sports and recreation education enterprises, 2023.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 5: Main indicators for sports and recreation education enterprises, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_ovw_act__custom_18481273/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=f47dd04c-8657-48a5-bfe1-e80ecd8ce95b&c=1760954335325 sbs_ovw_act])|alt= Table showing main indicators for sports and recreation education enterprises in the EU, individual EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries for the year 2023. Presented are the number of enterprises and value added and turnover for each country, in euro millions and as a share of total in industry, construction and market service. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, within the EU, enterprises on sports and recreation education constituted one fifth of all private businesses in the education sectors (in NACE class 85.51 over NACE division 85, excluding public education institutions). These enterprises also contributed to 6.5% of the overall value added in the education sector. 4 EU countries had over a third of their education enterprises dedicated to sports and recreation: Slovenia (42.6%), Malta (37.0%), Sweden (33.4%) and Finland (33.2%). Conversely, this proportion fell below 5% in Czechia (4.1%), Slovakia (3.9%), and Spain (3.1%). Slovenia maintained its leading position in the EU for sports and recreation enterprises in terms of value added, with 29.9% of the total value added in education coming from these enterprises. This figure is nearly double that of the next countries, Austria (16.2%), Finland (15.9%) and Denmark (14.7%, despite having only 19.7% of its education companies dedicated to sports and recreation education). In contrast, 3 EU countries had less than 2% value added from sports and recreation education, with Greece and Slovakia reporting the lowest figures at 1.5% (see Figure 4). [[Image:F4Share of number of enterprises and value added for sports and recreation education in total education, 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Share of number of enterprises and value added for sports and recreation education in total education, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_ovw_act__custom_18484960/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=7bfc827f-d879-4f81-a707-07d8cd98be0e&c=1760963274486 sbs_ovw_act])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the share of number of enterprises and value added for sports and recreation education in total education in the EU, individual EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries for the year 2023. Each country has two columns representing the share of number of enterprises and the share of value added. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Who manufactures sporting goods in the EU?===
In 2023, approximately 5 400 enterprises across the EU were involved in manufacturing of sporting goods (under NACE group 32.3), generating €2.5 billion in value added, with a turnover reaching around €8 billion (see Table 6). France and Czechia together made up over a quarter of all enterprises manufacturing sporting goods in the EU, each holding a share of at least 10% of the total EU enterprises in this category. For 5 countries–Latvia, Slovakia, Belgium, Estonia and Luxembourg–the percentage was below 1%, while Malta did not report any data on enterprises in this sector. In 2023, Germany and Italy led the way, generating €524 and €523 million respectively, contributing over 20% to the total EU value added by enterprises manufacturing sporting goods. Alongside Austria and France, these countries accounted for over two-thirds of the total EU value added. When comparing value added with the number of enterprises, these countries do not always excel in both indicators. For example, Austria had one of the highest shares of total EU value added (14%) but had a relatively low share of enterprises (2.7%). Conversely, Poland held the fourth-highest share of enterprises in the EU (9.1%) yet had a relatively low share of the value added (2.6%). Regarding turnover generated by sports goods manufacturers, more than a quarter of the EU total was recorded in Italy (26.5%). The other significant shares were attributed to the same EU countries as for value added – Austria (15.8%), Germany (15.7%), and France (12.5%). [[Image:T6Main indicators for enterprises manufacturing sporting goods, 2023.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 6: Main indicators for enterprises manufacturing sporting goods, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_ovw_act__custom_18485409/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=4b493350-e9b3-4b86-b15a-bb195a21a401&c=1760964260029 sbs_ovw_act])|alt= Table showing main indicators for enterprises manufacturing sporting goods in the EU, individual EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries for the year 2023. Presented are the number of enterprises and value added and turnover for each country in euro millions. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] SMEs significantly contributed to the manufacturing of sporting goods. In 2023, nearly 70% of people employed in sports manufacturing were in SMEs, with 17.3% employed in micro enterprises (which have fewer than 10 employees). Additionally, Figure 5 shows that SMEs were responsible for 61.9% of the value added and 59.9% of the turnover within EU sports manufacturing in 2023. [[Image:F5Main indicators for enterprises manufacturing sporting goods, by enterprise size class, EU, 2023.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 5: Main indicators for enterprises manufacturing sporting goods, by enterprise size class, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sbs_sc_ovw__custom_18638443/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=5074432f-a0df-42c0-8cb5-302de83ced4d&c=1761641089577 sbs_sc_ovw])|alt= Three separate doughnut charts showing persons employed, value added and net turnover by enterprise size class in the EU for the year 2023. Each chart has four segments representing each size class for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Enterprises in sports sector 2025.xlsx|title=Enterprises in sports sector: tables and figures}} === Data sources === The list of sporting goods is identified based on several key sources: *the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/6921402/0/Vilnius+Definition+Sport+CPA2008+official+2013_09_19.pdf/30838d11-01ea-431f-8112-50786e187c1c Vilnius Definition] of Sport agreed by the EU Working Group on Sport and Economics in 2007 *the [https://ec.europa.eu/assets/eac/sport/library/studies/study-contribution-spors-economic-growth-final-rpt.pdf Study on the Contribution of Sport to Economic Growth and Employment in the EU] *the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-statistical-working-papers/w/ks-01-25-041 EU Sport Satellite Account: Research into estimating the economic value of sport in the EU – 2025 edition] *the [https://www.uis.unesco.org/en/methods-and-tools/framework-cultural-statistics UNESCO Framework for Culture statistics], which considers sport as a cultural domain, updated in 2009 and 2025 by the UNESCO Institute for Statistics. Eurostat gathers data on sport-related enterprises from the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/overview Structural business statistics (SBS)]. '''Structural business statistics''' The Structural Business Statistics (SBS) cover industry, construction, trade and market services, as defined by the [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)]]. This classification allows for a detailed sectoral breakdown of business activities. It provides information on a wide array of structural indicators, including data on the number of businesses, employees, turnover, and value added, which can be further broken down by the size of the business. The version of NACE currently used within the European Statistical System is NACE Rev. 2, implemented since 2008. The SBS describe the structure, conduct and performance of businesses within the non-financial business economy (NACE sections B to S, excluding public administration and defence, compulsory social security, and membership organisations). From the reference year 2021, the SBS are compiled under [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32019R2152 EU regulation 2019/2152] and [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32020R1197 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1197]. Within the SBS, the following definitions are applicable: *An '''enterprise''' as defined in Council Regulation (EEC) No 696/93 is the smallest combination of legal units that forms an organisational unit producing goods or services. It benefits from a certain degree of autonomy in decision-making, especially regarding resource allocation, and may carry out one or more activities at one or more locations. An enterprise can be a sole legal entity. *The '''Number of active enterprises''' refers to all statistical units that were ’enterprises’ during the reference period, as defined in Council Regulation (EEC) No 696/93, and were active during that period. A statistical unit is deemed active if it realised positive net turnover, produced outputs, employed individuals, or made investments during the reference period. *The '''Number of employees and self-employed persons (the number of persons employed)''' is the sum of the number of employees and number of self-employed persons. The ’number of employees’ is the average of persons who were employees at any time during the reference period. The ’number of self-employed persons’ is the average of persons who were sole owners or joint owners of the statistical unit where they work. Family workers and outworkers whose income depends on the value of the unit’s outputs are also included. *'''Net turnover''' includes all income generated during the reference period through regular activities of the unit, presented after deducting price reductions, discounts, and rebates. Excluded from net turnover are: **all taxes, duties or levies directly linked to revenue; **amounts collected on behalf of a principal, if the unit is acting as an agent for the principal; **income not arising from ordinary activities, typically classified as ’Other (operating) income’, ’Financial income’, ’Extra-ordinary income’ or similar, depending on the accounting standards used for financial statements. *'''Value added''' is a composite indicator of net operating income, adjusted for depreciation, amortisation and employee benefits, all recognised by the unit during the reference period. Its value is calculated as: **net turnover (+) **income from product- or turnover-related subsidies (+) **capitalised output (+) **change in stock of goods (±) **total purchases of goods and services (-). Alternatively, it can be derived from the gross operating surplus by adding personnel costs. The SBS may be broken down by business size-class for analytical purposes, as follows: *'''Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)''' employing 1 to 249 people, comprising: **micro enterprises with fewer than 10 employees; **small enterprises with 10 to 49 employees; **medium-sized enterprises with 50 to 249 employees. They should also have an annual turnover of up to €50 million, or a balance sheet total not exceeding €43 million. *'''Large enterprises''' with 250 or more employees. When EU aggregates are not based on a full coverage, estimates may be published, flagged as ‘Estimated value’ (Estimation error from ±1 % to ±5 %). For further details, refer to metadata on {{Template:Esms|code=sbs_esms|title=Structural business statistics (sbs)}}.
===Context===
The multiannual work programme [https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-9771-2024-INIT/en/pdf (EU work plan for Sport for 2024-2027]) agreed by the [[Glossary:EU_Council|EU Council]], establishes priorities and principles for cooperation on sport between the European Commission and the Member States. Several expert groups have been set up to achieve tangible results. Notably, the Expert Group on the Economic Dimension of Sport (XG ECO) and the Expert Group on Health-Enhancing Physical Activity (XG HEPA) are pivotal in implementing evidence-based policies in the sports sector. XG ECO has developed an economic definition of sport ('[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/6921402/0/Vilnius+Definition+Sport+CPA2008+official+2013_09_19.pdf Vilnius definition]'), and progressed towards developing Sport [[Glossary:Satellite account|Satellite Accounts]] in some EU countries. XG HEPA is working on implementing the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52013PC0603&from=EN Council recommendations on physical activity] adopted in 2013, including a monitoring framework with indicators for physical activity levels and policies promoting physical activity in EU countries. Eurostat’s comparable data on enterprises, international trade, employment in sport, participation in sporting activities, and more, contribute significantly to the monitoring and development of EU title: Environmental subsidies and similar transfers statistics
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the environmental subsidies and similar transfers. Data extracted in March 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 In 2023, EU environmental transfers represented 1.1% of GDP, ranging from 0.2% of GDP in Denmark and Finland to 3.8% of GDP in Italy. In 2023, general government remained the primary source of environmental transfers at EU level. In 2023, most environmental transfers were dedicated to energy (renewables and savings) and air and climate protection. |alt=A vertical bar chart showing the share of total environmental transfers received by the national economy for the year 2023. Data are shown as percentage of GDP for the participating EU countries and EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. This article provides an overview of data on environmental subsidies and similar transfers (ESST) in the EU. ESST are subsidies and other current transfers as well as capital transfers to activities protecting the environment (waste and waste water management for example) and managing natural resources (renewable energy production and materials recovery for example). Since 2025, the data collection is mandatory according to Regulation 691/2011. Data are available for 26 EU Countries, with Cyprus having a derogation to transmit data on ESST until end of 2027, and 2 EFTA countries. The data describe transfers paid either by the general government or non-resident institutional units (the Rest of the World) and received by national recipients of corporations, households, general government and non-profit institutions serving households (NPISH) institutional sectors and by the Rest of the World. === National environmental transfers ranged between 3.8% and 0.2% of GDP in 2023 === In 2023, environmental transfers in the EU amounted to 1.1.% of GDP, with considerable variation acrossEU countries. Italy recorded the highest ratio at 3.8% of GDP, followed by Czechia (2.5%), Latvia (1.3%), Germany (1.2%) and Greece (1.2%). At the lower end of the distribution, Denmark and Finland both reported 0.2%, while Luxembourg (0.3%), Spain (0.3%) and Ireland (0.3%) also remained among the EU countries with the smallest relative levels of environmental transfers (see Figure 1). [[Image:F1_Total_environmental_transfers_received_by_the_national_economy_as_percentage_of_GDP,_2023_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Total environmental transfers received by the national economy as percentage of GDP (%), 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_esst_cepgg}},{{Stable link|title=|code=env_esst_ceprw}}|alt=A vertical bar chart showing the share of total environmental transfers received by the national economy for the year 2023. Data are shown as percentage of GDP for the participating EU countries and EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Environmental transfers increased slightly in several EU countries between 2022 and 2023 === Between 2022 to 2023, environmental transfers as a share of GDP rose in the EU from 1.0% to 1.1%. At country level, the largest increases were recorded in Czechia from 1.7% to 2.5% of GDP, and in Italy from 3.1% to 3.8%. From 2022 to 2023, some countries reported declines, notably Austria (from 1.3% to 0.8%), Bulgaria (from 0.7% to 0.4%) and Romania (from 0.9% to 0.6%)(see Figure 2) . [[Image:F2_Total_environmental_transfers_received_by_the_national_economy_as_percentage_of_GDP,_years_2022-2023_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Total environmental transfers received by the national economy as percentage of GDP (%), years 2022-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_esst_cepgg}},{{Stable link|title=|code=env_esst_ceprw}}|alt=A vertical multi bar chart showing the share of total environmental transfers received by the national economy for the years 2022 to 2023. Data are shown as percentage of GDP for the participating EU countries and EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Environmental transfers are mainly paid by general government === In 2023, general government remained the primary source of environmental transfers at EU level and in most reporting countries. Austria and Sweden reported that all environmental transfers were funded by general government, while Luxembourg also recorded shares exceeding 99%. In contrast, only 4 countries reported significant inflows of environmental transfers from abroad, including EU funds. In Lithuania, 73% of environmental transfers originated from foreign sources, while Bulgaria and Romania reported shares of 66% and 64% respectively. Estonia also received over 60% of its environmental transfers from abroad (see Figure 3). [[Image:F3_Distribution_of_environmental_transfers_received_by_the_national_economy_from_the_general_government_and_abroad,_2023_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Distribution of environmental transfers received by the national economy from the general government and abroad (%), 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_esst_cepgg}},{{Stable link|title=|code=env_esst_ceprw}}|alt=A vertical stacked bar chart showing the distribution of environmental transfers received by the national economy from general government and abroad for the year 2023. Data are shown as percentages for the participating EU countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Corporations, general government and households are the main recipients === There are clear differences across European countries in the way governments distribute environmental transfers among institutional sectors. On average in the EU, a substantial share of ESST went to households and corporations. By contrast, direct transfers within the general government sector or to non-profit institutions remained relatively limited in most countries. However, national patterns varied widely. In Italy, Austria and Finland, households received a dominant share of environmental transfers (83.2%, 48.4% and 43.7% respectively). In contrast, Portugal, Croatia and Spain allocated a much larger proportion of ESST to corporations (84.5%, 82.6% and 65.1% respectively). In Slovakia, the Netherlands and Malta the share was higher for intra-governmental transfers (86.2%, 51.8% and 51.2% respectively). Finally, Luxembourg and Denmark showed notable shares of transfers sent abroad, reflecting international environmental financing or cross-border mechanisms (see Figure 4) [[Image:F4_Environmental_transfers_paid_to_each_institutional_sector_by_the_general_government,_2023_(as_percentage_of_total).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4:Environmental transfers paid to each institutional sector by the general government (as percentage out of total), 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_esst_cepgg}}|alt=A vertical stacked bar chart showing the share of environmental transfers paid to each institutional sector by general government for the year 2023. Data are shown as percentage for the participating EU countries and EFTA countries, as well as the sum of all reporting countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Most transfers to corporations are paid to a limited number of economic activities === Environmental transfers to corporations are highly concentrated in a few key economic activities, with the energy sector (electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply) consistently receiving the largest share in many countries. Another major recipient of ESST is 'water supply, sewerage, waste management and remediation activities', which accounts for a substantial portion of transfers in many countries. In several countries, manufacturing and agriculture, forestry and fishing also receive notable shares. Corporations operating in the energy sector received more than 80% of transfers paid to corporations in Portugal, Spain, Czechia and Greece. Corporations operating in ’water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities’ received more than 50% of transfers paid to corporations in Bulgaria, Croatia and Slovakia. 'Agriculture, forestry and fishing' activities received more than 50% of transfers paid to corporations in Ireland, Latvia and Sweden. 'Manufacturing' activities were paid a significant (more than 30%) share of corporations’ ESST in Denmark Luxembourg and Austria. Overall, the distribution reflects a mix of structural economic differences and policy priorities (see Figure 5) [[Image:F5_Environmental_transfers_received_by_corporations_broken_down_by_economic_activities,_2023_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Environmental transfers received by corporations broken down by economic activities (%), 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_esst_cepggcp}}|alt=A vertical stacked bar chart showing the share of environmental transfers received by corporations broken down by economic activities for the year 2023. Data are shown as percentages for the participating EU countries and EFTA countries, as well as the sum of the reporting countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Most environmental transfers are dedicated to energy (renewables and energy savings) and air and climate protection === Environmental transfers received by the national economy can also be analysed according to their environmental purpose. In 2023, transfers were mainly concentrated in a few key purposes, notably energy from renewable sources, energy savings and management, and air and climate protection, although the relative importance of each category varied considerably across countries. Support for energy from renewable sources accounted for a very large share of transfers in several countries, reaching very high levels in Spain (around 70%) and Denmark (around 65%). Energy savings and management dominated in countries such as Italy (around 90%) and Greece (around 45%), and also represented a substantial share in France (around 30%) and Ireland (around 20%). Meanwhile, air and climate measures were particularly prominent in Sweden (over 50%) and Luxembourg (around 45%). Other environmental purposes also played a significant role in specific countries. Wastewater and water resources accounted for a large share in Bulgaria (around 35%) and Slovenia (around 35-40%), while waste, materials recovery and savings were especially important in Malta (around 40%) and Slovakia (around 30%), see Figure 6. [[Image:F6_Distribution_of_environmental_transfers_received_by_the_national_economy,_classified_by_environmental_purposes,_2023_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Distribution of environmental transfers received by the national economy, classified by environmental objectives (%), 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_esst_cepgg}},{{Stable link|title=|code=env_esst_ceprw}}|alt=A vertical stacked bar chart showing the distribution of environmental transfers received by the national economy classified by environmental objectives for the year 2023. Data are shown as percentages for the participating EU countries and EFTA countries, as well as the sum of the reporting countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=Environmental subsidies and similar transfers 2023-2026-03-23 SE rev.xlsx|title=Environmental subsidies and similar transfers — figures and tables}} === Data sources === With environmental transfers, governments finance either measures to reduce the market price of certain products ('subsidy on product') or other types of measures to support economic activity or consumption ('current transfer') or finance environmental investments ('capital transfer'). Eurostat collects data on ‘environmental subsidies and similar transfers’ accounts (ESST) on a voluntary basis since 2017. Since 2025, ESST is a part of the Regulation (EU) 691/2011 and require data reporting on an annual basis. ESST are based on the Environmental-Economic Accounting 2012 Central Framework (SEEA-CF 2012) and the European System of National and Regional Accounts (ESA 2010). The concept of 'subsidies and similar transfers' refers to 'transfers' as covered in SEEA-CF 2012 § 4.136: “transactions in which one institutional unit (in this case, the government) provides a good, service or asset to another unit without receiving from the latter any good, service or asset in return as a direct counterpart”. These transfers may be classified depending on certain characteristics in: Subsidies (D.3) – SEA 2010 §4.30; Social contributions and benefits (D.6) – SEA 2010 §4.83; Other current transfers (D.7) – ESA 2010 §4.112 and Capital transfers (D.9) – SEA 2010 §4.145 and §4.146. Therefore, subsidies in this terminology are one specific type of transfers. Sometimes, term ‘subsidy’ is used as a synonym of ‘transfers’ or ‘subsidies and similar transfers’ (See SEEA-CF 2012 §4.137). Transfers that are part of the scope of ESST are those mentioned above that are “intended to support activities that protect the environment or reduce the use and extraction of natural resources” (SEEA-CF 2012 §4.138). The set of activities that are considered as ‘environmental’, thus included in the scope, are delineated by the classification of environmental purposes. ''Note: The SEEA-CF 2012 is currently under revision by the UN Statistical Commission expected in the coming years.'' ''Note: ESA 2010 is also under revision following the adoption of the 2025 SNA.'' The Classification of environmental purposes (CEP) has been adopted as an international classification in 2024, The CEP classification is built on the two functional classifications used in the current SEEA-CF monetary environmental accounting , CEPA 2000 mad CreMA 2008. Environmental subsidies and similar transfers are paid by general government (S.13 as in ESA 2010 §2.111) and the rest of the world (S.2 as in ESA 2010 §2.131). Those transfers are received by institutional sectors within the economy (general government; corporations – S.11 and 12 in ESA 2010 §2.45 and 2.55; households – S.14 in ESA 2010 §2.118; and non-profit institutions serving households – S.15 in ESA 2010 §2.129) and granted to the rest of the world. In order to ease comprehension by the reader, rest of the world is also named 'Other countries' when referring to transfers received from abroad and ‘sent to other countries’ when referring to transfers paid to them by general government. Environmental subsidies and similar transfers paid by general government to corporations are further broken down according to activities using the NACE Rev 2 classification. === Context === The environmental subsidies and similar transfers accounts are part of the European environmental economic accounts framework. ESST data reporting is required through Regulation 691/2011, annex VIII. === Other Articles === *[[Environmental protection - spending and investments]] === Database === * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/environment/database Environment (env)], see: :Environmental subsidies and similar transfers (env_esst_cep) ::Environmental subsidies and similar transfers from general government, by environmental activity, sector of recipient and ESA category of transfer (ENV_ESST_CEPGG) ::Environmental subsidies and similar transfers from general government to corporations, by environmental activity, ESA category of transfer and NACE Rev. 2 activity of recipient (ENV_ESST_CEPGGCP) ::Environmental subsidies and similar transfers from the Rest of the World to the domestic economy, by environmental activity and ESA category of transfer (ENV_ESST_CEPRW) ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=environmental_accounts}} Environment] === Methodology=== * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-25-061 Environmental subsidies and similar transfers - Guidelines, 2025 edition] *{{Template:Esms|code=env_esst_esms|title=Environmental subsidies and similar transfers}} (ESMS metadata file — env_esst_esms) === Legislation === *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0691:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 691/2011}} on European environmental economic accounts *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32024R3024:EN:NOT|title=Regulation 3024/2024}} ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Article_name'' {{Unit|topic=X_Environmental_accounts }} [[Category:Environment and energy|Environmental subsidies and similar transfers statistics]] [[Category:Environment|Environmental subsidies and similar transfers statistics]] [[Category:Environment - economic issues|Environmental subsidies and similar transfers statistics]] [[Category:Statistical article|Environmental subsidies and similar transfers statistics]] [[Category:March2027|Environmental subsidies and similar transfers statistics]]

title: Environmental tax statistics
text:
EU environmental tax revenue reached €371.9bn in 2024, equal to 2.1% of GDP, with energy taxes making up over three-quarters of the total. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 In 2024, total environmental tax revenue in the EU amounted to €371.9 billion, representing 2.1% of EU gross domestic product (GDP) and 5.1% of total EU government revenue from taxes and social contributions (TSC). Taxes on energy in the EU accounted for more than three-quarters of the total revenues from environmental taxes (77.2% of the total) in 2024, well ahead of taxes on transport (18.0%) and pollution and resources (4.8%). [[Image:Environmental_tax_revenues_2014-2024_in_the_EU.jpg|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_taxind2}}|alt= Vertical stacked bar chart showing environmental tax revenue by type in euro billions for the EU. Each year column contains three stacks representing energy taxes, transport taxes, and pollution and resources taxes, all in euro billions. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article provides an updated overview of [[Glossary:Environmental_tax|environmental tax]] data in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]], incorporating the latest figures up to 2024. According to {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02011R0691-20140616:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) N° 691/2011 on European environmental economic accounts}}, an environmental tax is a tax whose tax base is a physical unit (or a proxy of it) of something that has a proven, specific negative impact on the environment and which is defined in the [[Glossary:European_system_of_national_and_regional_accounts_(ESA_2010)|European system of accounts]] (ESA 2010) as a tax. The article highlights recent trends in environmental tax revenue statistics and identifies the main contributors to these changes. It also serves as a complement to the existing Eurostat publication on environmentally related taxes '{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-23-016|title=Environmental Taxes – A Statistical Guide, 2024 edition}}'. ===Environmental taxes in the EU=== The €371.9 billion in environmental taxes recorded for the EU in 2024 represents a 6.1% increase compared with 2023, following a 3.8% increase between 2022 and 2023. Despite these increases, the share of environmental taxes in [[Glossary:Tax_revenue|total tax]] and [[Glossary:Social_contributions|social contribution]] revenues, excluding [[Glossary:Imputed_social_contributions|imputed social contributions]], declined from 6.1% in 2021 to 5.2% in 2024, a decrease of 0.9 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] (see Figure 1 below). This indicates that, although environmental tax revenues continued to increase in absolute terms, they grew more slowly than overall tax and social contribution revenues. [[Image:SE-ETEA26-Fig02-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_type.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Environmental tax revenue by type and total environmental taxes as share of TSC (total government revenue from taxes and social contributions) and GDP (gross domestic product), EU 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_taxind2}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_10_gdp}}|alt=Combined vertical stacked bar and line chart showing environmental tax revenue by type and total environmental taxes as a share of TSC and GDP in the EU from 2014 to 2024. Energy taxes are the largest component of environmental tax revenue throughout the period. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, environmental taxes accounted for 5.2% of total revenues from taxes and social contributions in the EU, continuing the slight decline observed since 2021 (6.1%). Considerable differences remained across countries. Bulgaria (9.7%) and Greece (9.4%) recorded the highest shares, although both experienced substantial decreases over the three-year period. Other countries with relatively high shares included the Netherlands (7.7%), Slovenia (7.3%), Latvia (7.2%), and Poland (7.0%). At the other end of the scale, Luxembourg recorded the lowest share (2.9%), followed by Sweden (3.9%) and Norway (4.0%). While most countries showed only modest year-to-year changes, notable increases were observed in Italy, where the share rose from 5.5% in 2022 to 6.5% in 2024, and in Hungary from 5.2% in 2022 to 5.8% in 2024. Overall, the data indicate that, despite relatively stable levels in many countries, the contribution of environmental taxes to total tax revenues declined slightly at EU level and continued to vary markedly across Europe. [[Image:SE-ETEA26-Fig01-Environmental_taxes-22-23-24.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Environmental taxes, as percentage of total taxes and social contributions (but excluding [[Glossary:Imputed_social_contributions|imputed social contributions]]) for 2022, 2023, and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_taxind2}}|alt=Vertical bar chart showing Environmental taxes for 2022, 2023, and 2024 as a percentage of total revenues from taxes and social contributions. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Environmental tax categories=== '''Environmental energy taxes remain the main source of revenues in most countries''' Environmental tax revenue is divided into four main categories: energy taxes, transport taxes, pollution taxes, and resource taxes. Given the relatively small share of pollution and resource taxes in total environmental tax revenue, along with difficulties in classifying some minor national taxes, this article combines these two categories when presenting the breakdown of environmental taxes. In 2024, total environmental tax revenue across the EU amounted to approximately €371.9 billion, with energy taxes constituting the largest share at €287.0 billion, followed by transport taxes at €67.0 billion, and pollution and resource taxes combined accounting for €17.9 billion. [[Image:SE-ETEA26-Table1.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Total environmental tax revenue by type of tax (including and excluding [[Glossary:Imputed_social_contributions|imputed social contributions]]) and tax payer, EU 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_taxind2}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_10_gdp}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_taxag}}|alt=Table showing total environmental tax revenue by type of tax and tax payer as percentages and euro millions in the EU for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, environmental tax revenue in the EU was composed mainly of energy taxes, which accounted for more than 77.2% of the EU’s environmental tax revenue (totalling approximately €287.0 billion). This category encompasses [[Glossary:Levies|levies]] on energy products such as coal, oil products, natural gas, and [[Glossary:Electricity|electricity]] used for both stationary and transport purposes. By convention, CO₂ taxes are also included within this group. Transport taxes formed the second-largest category, generating approximately €67.0 billion, representing around 18.0% of the EU’s total environmental tax revenue. These taxes primarily consist of levies related to motor vehicle ownership and usage. Meanwhile, pollution and resources taxes made up the smallest share, generating approximately €17.9 billion and accounting for about 4.8% of the EU’s total environmental tax revenue. Pollution and resource taxes include various types of taxes on [[Glossary:Raw_material|raw material]] extraction, air and water emissions, noise, and waste management.
Figure 3 shows environmental tax revenues in 2024 as a percentage of [[Glossary:GDP|GDP]] and of total government revenue from taxes and social contributions, excluding imputed social contributions. The latter is further broken down into energy, transport, and pollution and resource taxes. Comparable data are also available for three EFTA countries. In the EU, energy taxes accounted for the largest share of total government revenue from taxes and social contributions (4.04%), followed by transport taxes (0.94%), and pollution and resource taxes (0.25%). Among the Member States, the contribution of energy taxes ranged from 2.35% in Malta to 8.89% in Bulgaria, while transport taxes ranged from 0.06% in Czechia to 2.04% in the Netherlands. Pollution and resource taxes generally represented only a small proportion of total government revenue, although relatively high values were observed in Croatia (1.58%) and the Netherlands (1.10%). Overall environmental tax revenues amounted to 2.06% of GDP in the EU, ranging from 0.97% in Ireland to 3.76% in Greece. Among the [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] countries, Switzerland recorded the highest contribution from transport taxes (2.24%), while Iceland stood out for its comparatively low contribution from energy taxes (1.55%) and relatively high contribution from pollution and resource taxes (1.07%). Environmental tax revenues amounted to 1.44% of GDP in Switzerland, 1.58% in Norway, and 1.56% in Iceland. [[Image:SE-ETEA26-Fig03-Environmental_tax_revenue_by_category_as_share_of_TSC_and_GDP.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Environmental tax revenue by category as % of TSC (total government revenue from taxes and social contributions) and GDP, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_taxind2}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_10_gdp}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_taxag}}|alt=Stacked vertical bar chart showing environmental tax revenue in 2024 for EU countries and Switzerland, Norway, and Iceland as a percentage of total government revenue from taxes and social contributions (TSC), with a circle marker on each bar indicating the same revenue as a percentage of GDP. Each country’s bar is split into three categories: energy taxes, transport taxes, and pollution and resource taxes. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Environmental tax revenue by payer and NACE''' In 2024, the 6.1% growth in environmental tax revenues (see Figure 4) differed considerably across institutional sectors and countries, with the largest variations observed for corporations. At EU level, the contribution of corporations to the growth of environmental tax revenues was 2.8%. Several countries recorded a particularly strong contribution from corporations to tax revenues growth, notably Romania (+19.2%), Hungary (+14.8%), Latvia (+13.2%), Poland (+10.6%) and Lithuania (+8.2%). In contrast, corporations made a negative contribution to the growth of environmental tax revenues in Sweden (-18.5%), Luxembourg (-6.8%), Greece (-4.5%), Bulgaria (-3.9%), Germany and Slovakia (both -2.0%), and Finland (-1.1%). Contributions to the growth of tax revenues by households were generally more moderate, with a positive contribution in most countries and with a negative contribution in a limited number of Member States. Contributions to growth by non-residents remained close to zero in almost all countries and had little impact on overall developments. Overall, the results indicate that changes in environmental tax revenues in 2024 were driven primarily by developments in the corporate sector rather than by households.
  [[Image:SE-ETEA26-Fig01b-Growth_of_environmental_taxes.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Growth in environmental taxes 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_taxind2}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_10_gdp}}|alt=Stacked column chart showing the growth of environmental tax revenues from 2023 to 2024 for the EU Member States, Norway, Switzerland and Iceland, and candidate countries, decomposed into contributions from households, corporations, and non-residents. EU environmental tax revenues increased by around 6%, mainly due to corporations. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
To succeed in the [https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/climate-strategies-targets/2050-long-term-strategy_en EU's climate neutrality objective by 2050], taxation systems are a key policy tool. Well-designed tax reforms can stimulate economic growth, reduce [[Glossary:Greenhouse_gas_(GHG)|greenhouse gas]] emissions through effective carbon pricing, and support an equitable transition. In 2024, total environmental tax revenues are almost evenly split between households and the corporations sector. The donut chart below (Figure 5) shows the distribution of environmental tax revenues in the EU for the year 2024, categorised by payer type: Households, Non-Residents, and Corporations (classified under [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]], which is the classification used for economic activities). Environmental taxes paid by households accounted for 47.5% of total environmental tax revenues, while corporations contributed 50.5% to total environmental taxes. Among corporations, those active in manufacturing activities (NACE C) contributed the most, accounting for 11.6% of total environmental taxes; corporations in transport and storage activities (NACE H) followed, contributing 10.1%. Non-residents paid 2.0% of total environmental taxes. [[Image:SE-ETEA26-Fig05-Environmental_tax_revenue_EU_2024.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Contributions to environmental tax revenue 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_taxind2}}|alt=Doughnut chart showing the breakdown of environmental tax revenue in the EU in 2024 by payer. Industries (NACE) account for 50.5% of total environmental tax revenue, households for 47.5%, and non-residents for 2.0%.]] Although in 2024 environmental tax revenues in the EU were nearly evenly split between households and corporations, national patterns vary significantly (see Figure 6 below). Some countries like Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, and France rely heavily on household contributions (over 55%), while Romania, Estonia, Czechia, and Bulgaria show a strong industrial tax contribution. Luxembourg stands out with more than one third (35.8%) of its environmental tax revenue coming from non-residents, likely due to cross-border fuel sales. In contrast, countries such as Germany, Cyprus, and Sweden display a more balanced distribution across payer groups. These variations reflect national economic structures, energy use, and policy choices affecting environmental taxation. [[Image:SE-ETEA26-Fig06-Breakdown_of_Environmental_taxes.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Environmental taxes by economic activity, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_taxind2}}|alt=Stacked vertical bar chart showing environmental taxes by economic activity as percentage of environmental tax revenue in the EU for individual EU Member States, Iceland, Switzerland, and Norway, and candidate countries. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has five stacks representing five economic activities for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Environmental tax revenues fall while labour taxes remain stable''' The [https://www.europarl.europa.eu/thinktank/en/document/LDM_BRI(2012)120306 Roadmap to a Resource Efficient Europe] included the following milestone: a shift from the taxation of labour towards environmental taxation, which would lead to a substantial increase in the share of environmental taxes in government revenue, in line with best practice in EU countries. Figure 7 shows developments in environmental taxes and labour taxes as a result. [[Image:SE-ETEA26-Fig04-Taxes_on_labour_and_environmental_taxes_as_share_of_total_taxation.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 7: Taxes on labour and environmental taxes as share of total taxation
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_taxind2}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_taxag}}|alt=Line chart showing labour taxes and environmental taxes as a share of total taxation in the EU from 2014 to 2024 (index 2014 = 100). Labour taxes remain broadly stable around the 2014 level, whereas environmental taxes decrease markedly after 2021 and remain significantly below their 2014 level in 2022–2024.]] Between 2014 and 2024, labour tax revenues in the EU remained relatively stable, fluctuating narrowly around the base [[Glossary:Index_number|index value]] of 100, with minor variations between 98.8 and 101.9 until 2020. From 2019 onwards, environmental tax revenues experienced a marked decline, dropping sharply to an index value of 82.8 in 2023 and increasing slightly to an index value of 83.2 in 2024. This represents a 16.8% decrease compared to 2014 levels, highlighting a significant reduction in environmental tax revenues relative to the base year.
===Energy taxes=== '''Energy taxes: corporations surpass households as primary contributors''' Energy taxes are the primary source of environmental tax revenues in the EU, which is a trend that continued in 2024 for all different payer groups. In the EU, households contributed an average of 43.3% to energy taxes, underlining their key role in final energy consumption (see Figure 8). [[Image:SE-ETEA26-Fig07-Breakdown_of_Energy.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 8: Energy taxes by economic activity, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_taxind2}}|alt=Stacked vertical bar chart showing energy taxes by economic activity as percentage of energy tax revenue in the EU in individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Iceland, and Norway, and candidate countries. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has five stacks representing five economic activities for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''Emission permits''' EU Member States generate substantial revenue through emission permits, which allow holders to release a specific amount of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. Under the European [[Glossary:Emissions_trading_system_(ETS)|Emissions Trading System (ETS)]], these permits are classified as taxes according to ESA 2010, the standard used for compiling macroeconomic statistics, including National Accounts. Governments are increasingly using cap-and-trade schemes like the EU ETS to regulate CO2 emissions. Launched in 2005, the EU ETS initially allocated emission allowances for free. Since 2013, however, auctioning has become the primary method for distributing these permits. In the third phase of the ETS (2013–2020), over 70% of allowances were auctioned, and this figure has continued to rise, with phase 4 (2021–2030) introducing a gradual reduction in the total number of emission permits. This phase focuses on protecting sectors at risk of relocating production outside the EU by providing 100% free permits, while free allocations for less exposed sectors will be phased out after 2026. Revenue from ETS auctions is recorded as "other taxes on production" (D.29) under ESA 2010. This means the revenue is recognised in the year the permits are used for emissions, rather than when they are auctioned.
In 2024, EU countries reported €31.3 billion in revenues from EU emissions trading system (ETS) allowances (see Figure 9), representing a 3.5% decrease compared with 2023. Between 2014 and 2024, the marked growth, particularly after 2017, reflects strengthening carbon pricing and the expanding role of emissions trading. In 2024, Poland (€5.7 billion) and Germany (€5.5 billion) were the largest contributors, while Spain and Italy each reported revenues exceeding €3 billion. Although revenues from ETS allowances declined in Hungary and Luxembourg, most Member States recorded increases. In total the EU aggregate increased by 3.5% in 2024. Overall, the data underline the continued importance of the EU ETS as a key instrument for carbon pricing across the European Union. [[Image:SE-ETEA26-Fig08-Total_EU_tax_revenue_from_ETS.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 9: Total EU tax revenue from [[Glossary:ETS|ETS]], 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_taxind2}}|alt=Combined bar and line chart showing total EU tax revenue from the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and its annual growth rate from 2014 to 2024. ETS tax revenue increases strongly over the period, while the growth rate peaks in 2019 before slowing and turning slightly negative in 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Transport taxes=== '''Transport taxes: households shoulder the majority of the burden''' This category covers taxes on energy production and on energy products used for both transportation and stationary applications. Key transport fuels include petrol and diesel, while energy sources for stationary use comprise fuel oils, natural gas, coal, and electricity. Taxes on [[Glossary:Biofuels|biofuels]] and other [[Glossary:Renewable_energy_sources|renewable energy sources]] are also included, as well as taxes on energy product stockpiles. Transport taxes, typically applied to vehicle purchases and road usage, have tended to fluctuate in line with vehicle sales. In 2024, transport tax revenues in the EU amounted to €67.0 billion, of which €44.6 billion (66.6%) were paid by households, €21.7 billion (32.4%) by industries, and €0.7 billion (1.1%) by non-residents (see Figure 10). Compared with 2023, transport tax revenue increased for all payer groups, with the largest relative increase recorded in taxes paid by non-residents (+13.9%), although these represented only a small share of total transport tax revenue. Households remained the principal contributors to transport tax revenues throughout the EU. [[Image:SE-ETEA26-Fig09-Breakdown_of_Transport_taxes.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 10: Transport taxes by paying economic activities, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_taxind2}}|alt=Stacked vertical bar chart showing transport taxes by economic activity as percentage of transport tax revenue in the EU for individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Norway, and Iceland, and candidate countries. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has five stacks representing five economic activities for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, households were by far the main contributors to transport tax revenues in the EU, accounting for 66.6% on average. This reflects the strong link between transport taxes and private vehicle ownership and use. Transport taxes include, in particular, vehicle registration taxes and other related taxes. The services sector followed with 23.1%, while industry (8.2%), agriculture (1.1%), and non-residents (1.1%) made up smaller shares. National patterns vary widely: Ireland (80.4%), Malta (78.7%), and Finland (76.2%) show particularly high household shares, indicating a tax structure focused on private vehicle users. In contrast, Slovakia (11.4%) and Czechia (11.5%) report much lower household shares, with the bulk of transport taxes paid by businesses, especially in the services sector, which contributes over 55% in both countries. These differences reflect national transport habits, tax policies, and vehicle ownership trends across Europe. === Pollution and resource taxes === '''Pollution and resource taxes: data indicate a diverse approach across the EU''' For 2024, pollution and resource taxes remain the smallest category with a consistent upward trend (see Figure 11). Starting at about €10 billion in 2008, they increased to around €17.9 billion in 2024. This reflects a growing recognition of the need to address broader environmental issues, not just energy and transportation, but the more extensive impact of resource use and pollution. [[Image:SE-ETEA26-Fig10-Breakdown_of_Taxes_on_PollutionRes.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 11: Pollution and resource taxes by paying economic activities, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_taxind2}}|alt=Stacked vertical bar chart showing transport taxes by economic activity as percentage of pollution and resource tax revenue in the EU for individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Norway, and Iceland, and candidate countries. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has five stacks representing five economic activities for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, pollution and resource tax revenues in the EU were mainly paid by households (44.1%), followed by industries (31.5%), and the services sector (18.8%). The share from agriculture remained relatively small, averaging 2.8%, while non-residents contributed 2.0%. The distribution of these taxes reflects the varying ways countries apply environmental taxes and levies, with some focusing more on household-level waste and pollution charges, and others on industrial emissions or resource use. Overall, the data indicates a diverse approach across the EU to taxing environmental impacts beyond energy and transport. === Conclusion === Environmental taxes should not be interpreted independently of other environmental accounts—they are embedded within the broader framework of monetary environmental accounts and closely linked to related statistical areas such as Environmental Protection Expenditure Accounts (EPEA), Environmental Subsidies and Similar Transfers (ESST), and potentially environmentally damaging subsidies (PEDS). At the same time, analysing environmental tax revenues alongside other datasets—such as [[Glossary:Air_emissions_accounts_(AEA)|air emission accounts]] or energy balances—provides valuable insights into the interactions between economic instruments and environmental pressures. This integrated perspective supports more comprehensive and effective policy analysis and decision-making. === Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=SE26-ETEA-v3.xlsx |title=Environmental tax statistics — figures and tables}} ===Data sources=== Eurostat collects data on environmental taxes at a detailed level, by economic activity, under [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2011/691/oj/eng Regulation (EU) N° 691/2011] on European environmental economic accounts. The Eurostat publication titled '{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-23-016|title=Environmental taxes — a statistical guide}}' constitutes the methodological basis for this data collection. In addition, using 'National Tax Lists', a supporting dataset to Table 9 from the ESA transmission programme, Eurostat gathers data on environmental taxes for 3 categories: energy, transport, and pollution/resource taxes. The data are then validated and published. Data relating to environmental taxes can be used to analyse the revenue stream from such taxes and to provide a relative measure of the importance of these taxes through the calculation of ratios relative to GDP or to the total revenue from all taxes and social contributions. In the first case (ratio relative to GDP), the comparison helps to provide an understanding of the tax burden. In the second case, the comparison helps to assess whether or not the tax burden is shifting from other tax bases (for example, labour income) towards environmental taxes. It has to be noted that the total revenue of taxes and social contributions used to compute the ratio does not include imputed social contributions. For further information concerning various tax aggregates, see [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/974dcfe2-4a39-4870-b8a3-70d58f56ff79?lang=en 'Main national accounts tax aggregates']. Environmental tax revenue can also be allocated according to the different economic activities paying the taxes. Eurostat collects data on environmental taxes using a categorisation by economic activity (based on the [[Glossary:Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)|NACE Rev. 2]] classification supplemented by information for households, non-residents, and a residual category for taxes that could not be allocated). Increasing revenue from environmental taxes should be interpreted with caution. The increases may be caused by the introduction of new taxes or an increase in tax rates, or alternatively may be linked to an increase in the tax base caused, for instance, by a higher consumption of energy products. ===Context=== In today’s economy, production and consumption decisions have a significant impact on the environment. Environmental policies, in particular fiscal policies through taxes, seek to balance economic growth with ecological sustainability. These environmentally related taxes are based on the ‘polluter-pays’ principle, encouraging more sustainable behaviour while generating revenue to address environmental damage. Environmental taxes are an important policy instrument in the EU’s strategic agenda, aimed at strengthening its competitiveness and ensuring the success of the climate neutrality objective. Economic instruments for pollution control and natural resource management are an important part of environmental policy in the EU Member States. The range of instruments that are available includes, among others, environmental taxes, fees and charges, tradeable permits, deposit-refund systems, and [[Glossary:Subsidies|subsidies]]. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52019DC0640 European Green Deal] creates the context for well-designed tax reforms which boost economic growth and resilience to climate shocks and help contribute to a fairer society and to a just transition. Environmental taxes play a direct role by sending the right price signals and providing the right incentives for sustainable behaviour by producers, users, and consumers. The use of economic tools for the benefit of the environment is also promoted in Goal 17 of the [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/sustainable-development/SDGs/implementation/index_en.htm EU sustainable development goals]. === Other articles=== *[[Tax revenue statistics]] === Selected Datasets === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/environment/database Environment (t_env)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/environment/information-data/environmental-taxes-subsidies Environmental taxes (t_env_eta)], see: :Environmental tax revenues (ten00141) :Energy taxes (ten00139) :Implicit tax rate on energy (ten00120) === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/environment/database Environment (env)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/environment/information-data/environmental-taxes-subsidies Environmental taxes (env_eta)], see: :{{Template:Publication|code=env_ac_tax|title=Environmental tax revenues (env_ac_tax)}} :{{Template:Publication|code=env_ac_taxind2|title=Environmental taxes by economic activity (NACE Rev. 2) (env_ac_taxind2)}} :{{Template:Publication|code=gov_10a_taxag|title=Main national accounts tax aggregates (gov_10a_taxag)}} === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/environment/overview Environment] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/environment/information-data/environmental-taxes-subsidies Environmental taxes and subsidies] === Publications === *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-EI-23-001|title=Key figures on Europe — Statistics Illustrated - 2023 edition}} — Statistical book, 2023 *[https://ec.europa.eu/taxation_customs/business/economic-analysis-taxation/taxation-trends-eu-union_en Taxation trends in the European Union - Data for the EU Member States, Iceland and Norway, 2020] === Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=env_ac_tax_esms|title=Environmental tax revenues}} (ESMS metadata file — env_ac_tax_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=env_ac_taxind2_esms|title=Environmental taxes by economic activity (NACE Rev. 2 )}} (ESMS metadata file — env_ac_taxind2_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=ten00120_esmsip2|title=Implicit tax rate on energy (ITR)}} (ESMS metadata file — ten00120_esmsip) === Legislation === *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0691:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 691/2011}} of 6 July 2011 on European environmental economic accounts *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/LSU/?uri=CELEX:32011R0691 Summaries of EU legislation: European environmental economic accounts] === External links === *[http://ec.europa.eu/environment/index_en.htm European Commission — Environment — Policies] *[https://ec.europa.eu/energy/topics/energy-strategy-and-energy-union_en European Commission — Energy Strategy] *[http://ec.europa.eu/taxation_customs/index_en.htm European Commission — Taxation and Customs Union] *[https://ec.europa.eu/taxation_customs/economic-analysis-taxation/taxes-europe-database-tedb_en European Commission - Taxes in Europe database] === Footnotes ===
