'''Malta''' 

In Malta, no physical or economic threshold applies to FSS surveys.  However, it should be noted that the coverage in 2013 is different from the coverage in 2010 and earlier years. Compared to 2010 and earlier years, the 2013 coverage excluded those holdings which were type 9 holdings in 2010 (holdings with only fallow land or kitchen gardens and with no standard output in 2010). Still, Malta covered these holdings in the national FSS 2013 dissemination, with the values of the characteristics from FSS 2010. These holdings are not covered and disseminated by Eurostat in the FSS 2013.

Apparently, the number of holdings decreased by 25 % between 2010 and 2013. However:
*If we remove the type 9 holdings from both 2010 and 2013 populations, the actual decrease is only by 12 %. However, this approach is not optimal, as unlike in 2010, the 2013 population is under-covered (holdings which were type 9 in 2010 and type different from 9 in 2013 are not, and cannot possibly be included in 2013, as they were not surveyed in 2013).   Table 14 shows  the impact of the coverage change on key characteristics of all survey years by comparing them first in the survey populations, and then in the populations obtained after removing type 9 holdings from all years. This approach, as mentioned above, has the disadvantage of under-coverage in 2013. Table 14 shows that, if we compare only the populations without type 9 holdings over the years 2003-2013, on average there would be a loss of 18.0 % holdings, 5.0 % UAA, 6.7 % labour force, 2.6 % arable land and 32.6 % kitchen gardens. There would be no loss of permanent crops, livestock and standard output. This is obvious as it is expected that type 9 holdings have fallow land (part of arable land, which is part of UAA), kitchen gardens, labour force, but do not have permanent crops, livestock and standard output.
*If we remove the type 9 holdings only from the 2010 population (which are no longer covered in 2013), the actual decrease is only by 1 %. However, this approach is also not optimal, for example because the structure of holdings by typology over time is affected: while the 2010 data will not include any type 9 holdings, the 2013 data will include those type 9 holdings which acquired this status between 2010 and 2013. Moreover, this approach cannot be sustained long term as it would mean following a panel in future surveys (always removing the holdings which had type 9 in 2010).   Table 14 also illustrates the impact of the coverage change on key characteristics over 2010-2013 by comparing them first in the survey populations, and then in the populations obtained after removing the type 9 holdings only from 2010. The impact is negligible on permanent crops, livestock, all livestock main categories and standard output and (very) significant on number of holdings, UAA, arable land, kitchen gardens and labour force.

[[Image:Table 14. Evolution of main characteristics for Malta, 2003-2013.png|Table 14: Key characteristics, relative changes in the surveyed and comparable populations (without type 9 holdings), 2003-2013, Malta|thumb|centre|500px]]

We can conclude that there is no optimal approach to show actual trends over time. There is always under-coverage of 2013 population concerning holdings that were of type 9 in 2010 and of a type different from 9 in 2013, which cannot be dealt with. 

For more information, see the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/national-methodology-reports national methodological reports].

'''Poland'''  

Poland increased the survey thresholds in the 2010 agricultural census, which led to the decrease of survey coverage between 2007 and 2010.
Table 15 shows  the impact of this change on key characteristics of survey years by comparing the key characteristics, first in the survey populations and then in the comparable populations obtained after applying all years' thresholds to the data of each year.

[[Image:Table 15. Evolution of main characteristics for Poland, 2003-2013.png|Table 15: Key characteristics, relative changes in the surveyed and comparable populations (above all years' thresholds), 2003-2013, Poland |thumb|centre|500px]]

While apparently, between 2007 and 2010, the number of holdings decreased by 37 %, the total UAA by 7 %, of which the biggest drop was for the area of kitchen gardens (by 59 %), the total LSU decreased by 7 %, of which the biggest drop has been recorded for the goats (by 26 %), the labour force directly employed by the holdings decreased by 16 % and the SO increased by 11 %, in reality, the number of holdings decreased only by 16 %, the kitchen gardens by 31 %, the goats by 7 %, the labour force by 10 % and the SO increased by 13 % over comparable populations. If all thresholds (basically 2010 thresholds) are applied to the previous surveys (FSSs 2003, 2005 and 2007), on average over 2003-2007, 26.5 % fewer holdings and 7.7 % less labour force directly employed by the holdings would be covered. Although the impact on the total LSU, the total UAA and the standard gross margin is negligible, the impact can be very significant for specific livestock and land use categories. The thresholds would decrease the number of goats counted in the FSS between 2003 and 2007 on average by 20.2 %, sheep by 3.6 %, laying hens by 4.9 %, kitchen gardens by 28.8 % and permanent crops by 4.4 %. The impact on cattle, pigs, arable land and permanent grassland would remain negligible. The change of thresholds in 2010 as compared to 2007 therefore does not affect UAA, LSU and standard output/standard gross margin key characteristics, but mainly affects trends of number of holdings, labour force, indicators related to holding characteristics such as legal personality of the holdings, characteristics related to the holders and farm managers of the holdings and other gainful activities, and specific livestock and crop categories (goats, sheep, laying hens, kitchen gardens and permanent crops). Trends of these characteristics cannot, therefore, be directly interpreted from survey data disseminated on Eurostat's website. To interpret trends for these characteristics, a correction should be made to the survey data, to exclude from the analysis holdings falling under all years' thresholds (basically 2010 thresholds being enough), see Table 15.

Poland introduced in the FSS 2013 new physical thresholds for natural persons (mushrooms area, number of rabbits, wild animals kept for slaughter and beehives, as well as covering all organic farming holdings regardless of thresholds). Furthermore, concerning the legal persons, all such holdings were included in 2010, while in 2013 only the ones with specific agricultural activities were included and, in addition, regardless of the agricultural activities, the ones with agricultural land of at least 1 hectare and the ones which run livestock production. Although the thresholds in 2013 include wild animals, holdings with only fur animals (other than rabbits) were not sent to Eurostat. Moreover, fur animals are not counted in 'other livestock' in the dataset, but the rearing of fur animals is counted among the other gainful activities. It is not possible to analyse the change of coverage completely accurately based on the information available in Eurostat, because not all the thresholds applied used characteristics as defined in Eurostat's database. Using some approximations, Eurostat made however an analysis. As Table 15 shows, the change of thresholds between 2010 and 2013 can be considered negligible with regards to all analysed key characteristics. The 2013 NMR also mentions that 2010 and 2013 data are comparable.

For more information, see the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/national-methodology-reports national methodological reports].

'''United Kingdom'''  

The FSS thresholds, and hence the survey coverage, have been modified several times in the United Kingdom since the 2000 survey. Moreover, the various UK countries used slightly different thresholds. For example, compared to the threshold of 6 hectares of total area and other physical thresholds applied in 2000, between 2003 and 2007 England and Wales covered all active farms, i.e. all holdings thought to have some form of agricultural activity at the time of the survey according to the Farm Register. However, this threshold has again been modified following the entry into force of Regulation (EC) No 1166/2008 and from 2010 onwards the threshold of 5 hectares of UAA, together with additional physical thresholds, applies. While apparently, between 2007 and 2010, the number of holdings decreased by 18 %, the labour force directly employed by the holdings by 13 % and the number of goats (in LSU) increased by 8 %, in reality, the number of holdings decreased only by 7 %, the labour force by 10 % and goats increased by 12 % over comparable populations. If the 2013/2010 thresholds are applied to the previous surveys (FSSs 2000-2007), on average 22.9 % fewer holdings, 8.1 % less labour force and 13.6 % fewer goats would be covered. The impact on the total LSU, UAA, SO and other analysed characteristics is negligible.

The change of thresholds in 2010, therefore, affects trends of number of holdings, goats, labour force, holding characteristics such as legal personality of the holdings, characteristics related to the holders and farm managers of the holdings and other gainful activities. Trends of these characteristics cannot, therefore, be directly interpreted from survey data disseminated on Eurostat's website. To interpret trends, a correction has to be made to previous survey years, to include in the analysis only holdings above 2013/2010 thresholds, see Table 19. On the other hand, the time series data is comparable on the total UAA, LSU, SO as well as arable land, permanent grassland, permanent crops, cattle, sheep, pigs and laying hens.

[[Image:Table 19. Evolution of main characteristics for United Kingdom, 2000-2013.png |Table 19: Key characteristics, percentage in the surveyed and comparable population (above 2013 thresholds), 2000-2013, United Kingdom|thumb|centre|500px]]

It is also important to note that there are differences between the coverage of data disseminated by Eurostat and by the United Kingdom (though not by much in the majority of cases) because Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland use slightly different thresholds in their national surveys:
*for Northern Ireland, the thresholds include all active farm businesses with at least 1 hectare of farmed land, or with any cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, significant poultry or horticultural activity.
*for Wales, the thresholds include all holdings with a SGM greater than zero.
*for Scotland, the thresholds include all holdings with at least 0.5 hectares of farmed land or with any crops (including temporary grass) or with more than 1 livestock unit or at least 1 worker, with deer or at least 20 poultry.


For more information, see the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/national-methodology-reports national methodological reports].
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Conclusions  ===

Where national survey coverage has been modified following EU legislation and national decisions, some trends in disseminated data likely mislead users. Users could get information on survey coverage changes from Eurostat metadata and the national methodological reports, but such action is less probable for data extracted for a large number of countries. Besides, the metadata information on the impact of the coverage change on the main indicators does not clarify the impact on specific indicators that users might use. Therefore, countries and Eurostat are now discussing approaches to disseminate more comparable FSS results on a specific place on Eurostat's website.
</sesection>

title: Farmers and the agricultural labour force - statistics
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of farmers and the agricultural labour force Data extracted in May 2026 Planned article update: May 2029 Agriculture remains a big employer within the EU; 8.4 million people worked in agriculture in 2023. There are few young farmers; only 10.7% of EU farm managers were under the age of 40 years old in 2023. Farming is a male dominated profession, only 31.5% of farmers being women in 2023. [[Image:F2 Age classes of farm managers, by gender (% of all farm managers, EU, 2023).png|thumb|centre|500px|Age classes of farm managers, by gender

''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7af5fbdc-2a3b-4c31-ab78-f5b80d63c2a8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-18T12:29:04Z ef_fsi_agesex])|alt= an image of a horizontal bar chart showing the age classes of farm managers, by gender expressed as a percentage of all farm managers in the EU in the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Knowing how many people are employed in agriculture is not as straightforward as it might seem and certainly not as easy as other sectors of the economy. This is explained by the fact that many farmers and farm workers pursue agriculture as a part-time activity, that many farms are family-run with family members providing help on the farm at different times of the year, and that there are seasonal peaks in labour (particularly when it comes to harvesting). In this analysis, 4 distinctions are made: (i) agricultural employment (ii) the regular agricultural labour force (iii) the volume of agricultural work carried out and (iv) farm managers. Each of these sheds a light on a different aspect of those working in agriculture which can be important for policy purposes. Employment data covers employees and self-employed persons but excludes many part-time farmers and help from family members; it is a measure that allows comparisons to be made across different sectors of the economy. The regular agricultural labour force measured by farm structure statistics is the broadest category that includes even those that work part-time and provide free labour, which is common for many family members of the farmer. The amount of labour actually provided can be converted into full-time labour equivalents (called Annual Work Units) to get an idea of the volume of work carried out in agricultural activities. Farm managers can be thought of as decision-making farmers; there is one farm manager per agricultural holding. ==== Agriculture remains a big employer in the EU; about 8.4 million people work in agriculture ==== People working in agriculture (crop and animal production, hunting and related service activities) accounted for about 3.9% of total employment in the EU in 2023 (see Figure 1), corresponding to an estimated 8.4 million persons. Agriculture is a particularly big employer in Romania, accounting for about one in every five persons (20.7%) employed in the country in 2023, as well as in Bulgaria (14.1% of total employment), Greece (9.5%) and Poland (7.8%). [[Image:F1 Employment in agriculture (% of total employment, 2010 and 2023).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 1: Employment in agriculture
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/973fa2b7-3530-4818-81e0-bd83d8c2df4a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-19T07:03:03Z nama_10_a64_e])|alt=a double vertical bar chart showing employment in agriculture expressed as a percentage of total employment for the year 2010 and the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Nevertheless, many more people help out on farms without being employed by them. This helps explain why the EU's regular agricultural labour force is much higher, at 16.6 million people in 2023; for many of these people, farm work only represented a minor activity. Indeed, when converted into Annual Work Units (AWUs) that measure the volume of work carried out in terms of full-time labour equivalents, the agricultural labour force provided work that was equivalent to 7.8 million full-time workers, similar to the total number of people employed in agriculture. It is this measure of the volume of work that is used as the labour factor in partial labour productivity measures. ==== Farming remains a predominantly family activity ==== In 2023, about 85% of the EU’s regular agricultural workforce employed directly by farms were either the sole holder (farmer) or members of his/her family. Nevertheless, there were 3 EU countries in which a majority of the regular agricultural labour force were non-family members; Slovakia (59% of the regular workforce), Czechia (58%) and France (58%). ==== Farm managers are typically male and relatively old ==== Farm managers are those responsible for the normal daily financial and production routines of running a farm. As such, they can be thought of as farmers; they make the decisions on what to plant or how many livestock to rear, just as much as when to buy materials and sell stock. Only one person per farm can be identified as a farm manager. Often the farm manager is also the owner of the farm but this need not be the case especially when the farm has a legal form. Slightly more than two thirds (68.5%) of farm managers on the EU's 8.8 million holdings were male in 2023. A majority (61.0%) of farm managers (both sexes combined) were at least 55 years of age. Only 10.7% of farm managers (both sexes combined) were young farmers (see Figure 2) - defined here as those under the age of 40 years. [[Image:F2 Age classes of farm managers, by gender (% of all farm managers, EU, 2023).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 2: Age classes of farm managers, by gender
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7af5fbdc-2a3b-4c31-ab78-f5b80d63c2a8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-18T12:29:04Z ef_fsi_agesex])|alt=a horizontal bar chart showing the age classes of farm managers, by gender expressed as a percentage of all farm managers in the EU in the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Young farmers were particularly scarce in Cyprus (4.0% of all farm managers) and Portugal (4.9%). They were more common in Austria (24.1%), France (20.7%) and Luxembourg (19.7%), the highest shares among EU countries. By contrast, there was a relatively high proportion of farmers of 65 years of age or more in many countries; in Cyprus (52.3%) and Portugal (51.9%) they represented a small majority of all farmers, and also represented two-fifths or more of farmers in Italy (45.6%), Malta (43.4%), Romania (41.7%) and Spain (39.7%). These top heavy age structures underline the policy interest in farm succession and the need to encourage a new generation of farmers. The gender imbalance among farmers was particularly strong in the Netherlands; only about one in every sixteen farmers (6.2%) was female in 2023. Female farmers were also relatively uncommon in Finland (9.8% of all farmers), Ireland (10.1%), Denmark (10.9%) and Germany (11.2%), among others. There was a closer gender balance in Latvia and Lithuania (with 43.5% and 43.3% shares respectively of farmers that were female), but nowhere in the EU was there a majority of female farmers. Older farm managers tend to work on the smallest farms (when measured in economic terms or in relation to their agricultural area), which are characterised by subsistence households and low levels of agricultural income. Three-quarters (75.1%) of the EU's farm managers that were 65 years of age or older worked on either semi-subsistence farms or very small farms in 2023 (see Figure 3). [[Image:F3 Farm managers, by age class and economic size of farm (%, EU, 2023).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 3: Farm managers, by age class and economic size of farm
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_fsi_ecsz}}|alt= a vertical stacked bar chart with five bars showing the farm managers, by age class and economic size of farm expressed as a percentage in the EU for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] A higher share of young farmers managed medium and large-sized farms (36.6%) than was the case in other age classes. Indeed, the share was progressively lower through each older class of farm manager, with only 10.2% of farmers aged 65 years and older managing medium and large-sized farms. In part, this distinction might be explained by the fact that young farmers had higher levels of educational attainment in terms of full agricultural training (20.1% vs 4.1% for over 65-year-olds) and had followed up-to-date professional training courses including those on new and innovative farming practices. ==== Very few farm managers in the EU have full agricultural training ==== Most farm managers in the EU only have [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Farmers_training_level practical experience]; this was the case for seven in every ten (71.4%) of them in 2023. Only one in ten (9.7%) of farm managers had [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Farmers_training_level full agricultural training], and the rest (18.8%) had [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Farmers_training_level basic agricultural training] (see Figure 4). In some EU countries, the level of agricultural training among farm managers was particularly low; in Greece, Cyprus and Malta only around 0.7 % of farm managers had full agricultural training and in Romania only 1.0%, the overwhelming majority of which had only practical experience. Only a few countries had relatively high proportions of farm managers with full agricultural training; these were the Netherlands (63.1%), Luxembourg (50.0%), Czechia (36.8%), Estonia (35.3%) and Belgium (30.3%). [[Image:F4 Level of agricultural training of EU farm managers (%, by type of training, 2023).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 4: Level of agricultural training of EU farm managers
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1c9401ce-0811-418f-b5b7-61b9de827b8a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-20T13:10:46Z ef_fsi_training])|alt= a horizontal stacked bar chart comparing the level of agricultural training of farm managers in the EU and each Member State in 2023. For each country, the proportions of managers with only basic training, with practical experience only, and with full agricultural training are shown. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ==== Fewer farms, fewer farmers ==== As the number of farms in the EU has declined, so has the number of farmers and those employed in agriculture; the share of people employed in agriculture fell from 5.6 % of total EU employment in 2010 to 3.9% in 2023 (as shown in Figure 1). Between 2010 and 2023, the volume of work carried out by the EU's labour force in agricultural activities declined by 1.8 million AWUs, a reduction of almost one fifth (-19.1%). The biggest losses were in Poland (about 0.6 million AWUs, equivalent to a decline of 30.6%), Romania (about 0.2 million AWUs; -17.6%), Bulgaria (about 0.2 million AWUs;-59.3% decline) and France (also about 0.2 million AWUs; -22.8%). The impact of this decline in labour on agricultural output is reviewed within the article on [[Performance of the agricultural sector#Agricultural_productivity|agricultural productivity]] in the article on the [[Performance of the agricultural sector|performance of the agricultural sector]]. ==== Young farmers remain scarce: female farmers continue to be in the minority but share increasing ==== Young farmers remain scarce in the EU; in 2010, 7.5% of farm managers in the EU were under the age of 35 years old (a ceiling taken in order to enable comparisons) but this share had fallen to 5.6% in 2023. Against the backdrop of a sharp decline in the overall number of farmers, the share of farm managers that are women increased from 28.3% in 2010 to 31.5% in 2023 (see Figure 5). [[Image:F5 Female farm managers (% of all farm managers, by age class, EU, 2010 - 2023).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 5: Female farm managers
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/74467532-6837-49f8-abb6-cfaff4117dbb?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-18T12:43:36Z ef_fsi_agesex])|alt=a horizontal stacked bar chart showing female farm managers expressed as a percentage of all farm managers, by age class in the EU from the year 2010 to the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Farmers and the agricultural labour force 180526.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== Farm structure data are collected from agricultural censuses every ten years and from sample surveys every 3 or 4 years in between. The main tables from the 2023 survey are gradually being published and are used in this analysis. Additional information comes from National Accounts employment data by industry and agricultural labour input statistics gathered for the Economic Accounts for Agriculture. ===Explanatory note=== The implementation of the Integrated Farm Statistics (IFS) introduced a division of the target population into two components: the ‘main frame’ includes agricultural holdings above physical thresholds defined in the legislation, while the ‘frame extension’ covers smaller holdings below these thresholds. In the legislative framework, data collection requirements for below-threshold units vary across time. This variability leads to gaps in data availability for the entire population of agricultural holdings and poses challenges for the comparability of results. To address this issue, an estimation procedure based on imputation techniques applied at the level of microdata has been developed to produce consistent estimates for below-threshold units where data are missing, which have been published in the Eurobase datasets under Farm structural indicators [ef_fsi]. ===Context=== Farming is an activity that is about growing crops and raising livestock. It is the business of providing key primary ingredients for the food that we eat and much of what we drink. Farming draws on a set of resources to produce these agricultural goods, as well as agricultural services. These resources or 'factors of production' can be broadly categorised as land, labour, knowledge, capital and entrepreneurship. Within the EU, the farming sector operates under the common agricultural policy (CAP), which has been reformed a number of times over the years. The common agricultural policy plays a pivotal role in shaping the EU’s agricultural industry. Recent reforms have encouraged greener practices by allocating more funds to conservation and biodiversity. The common agricultural policy also supports farmers’ livelihoods, ensures food supply and security by stabilising agricultural markets, while contributing to EU trade negotiations by maintaining high quality and safety standards for agricultural products. The EU’s new Vision for Agriculture and Food is central to building a sustainable food system and protecting biodiversity, while securing rural livelihoods and enhancing the stability of the food chain, alongside ambitions to achieve climate neutrality. Key priorities include: strengthening the role of farmers in the food value chain; promoting sustainable farming practices and empowering consumers to choose balanced, eco-friendly diets; encouraging generational renewal and gender equality; making knowledge, training and skills more accessible; improving resilience by helping the food system adapt to shocks, such as climate change, market volatility or systemic crises. === Other articles === *[[Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics]] *[[Agri-environmental indicators]] *[[Glossary:Farm structure survey (FSS)|Farm structure survey title: Farms and farmland in the European Union - statistics
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of farms and farmland in the European Union Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: April 2029 There were 8.8 million agricultural holdings in the EU in 2023, about 3 in 5 (62.8%) of which were less than 5 ha in size. EU farms used 156 million hectares (ha) of land for agricultural production in 2023, 38.1% of the total land area of the EU. The number of farms in the EU has been in steep decline, but the amount of land used for production has changed relatively little. [[Image:F1 Distribution of EU farms and utilised agricultural area.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_physz__custom_20806739/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=961a602b-680e-478c-b7d4-064bf55e5cb0&c=1775034917000 ef_fsi_physz]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_physz__custom_20805372/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=76766134-f7fd-4240-880b-d98875d76aab&c=1775031707000 ef_fsi_physz])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing percentage distribution of EU farms and utilised agricultural area according to farm size. Eight size ranges in hectares, each have two columns representing farms and UAA for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. ]] The EU's farms are numerous and varied; they are of all sizes, varied in terms of what is grown or animals that are reared, run under different management structures and found in areas that have different geologies, topographies and climates. ===Farms in 2023=== '''There were 8.8 million agricultural holdings in the EU in 2023 ''' In 2023, there were 8.8 million agricultural holdings in the EU, of which 2.9 million holdings (the equivalent of 32.6%) were in Romania. There were more than twice the number of farms in Romania as the next EU country; there were 1.3 million farms in Italy (the equivalent of 14.3% of the EU total), with 1.2 million farms in Poland (14.0%) and 0.8 million in Spain (9.1%). Together, these 4 countries accounted for 70.1% of all farms in the EU. '''The vast majority of the EU's farms are family farms''' The overwhelming majority [[Media:Data Family farming in the EU.xlsx|(about 93% in 2020)]] of the EU's farms are classed as being family farms, defined as being farms on which 50% or more of the agricultural labour force is provided by family members. Family farms were the dominant farm type in all EU countries. '''Most of the EU's farms are small in nature''' Almost two-thirds (a provisional 62.8%) of the EU's farms were less than 5 hectares (ha) in size in 2023 (see Figure 1). These small farms can play an important role in reducing the risk of rural poverty, providing additional income and food. At the other end of the production scale, 7.6% of the EU's farms were of 50 ha or more in size and worked two-thirds (68.3%) of the EU's utilised agricultural area (UAA). Although the average mean size of an agricultural holding in the EU was 17.8 ha in 2023, only about 17% of farms were this size or larger. [[Image:F1 Distribution of EU farms and utilised agricultural area.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Distribution of EU farms and utilised agricultural area according to farm size
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_physz__custom_20806739/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=961a602b-680e-478c-b7d4-064bf55e5cb0&c=1775034917000 ef_fsi_physz]), and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_physz__custom_20805372/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=76766134-f7fd-4240-880b-d98875d76aab&c=1775031707000 ef_fsi_physz]))|alt= Vertical bar chart showing percentage distribution of EU farms and utilised agricultural area according to farm size. Eight size ranges in hectares, each have two columns representing farms and UAA for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This distribution pattern was particularly clear in Romania, the EU country with the highest number of farms; 9 in every 10 farms (90.2% or 2.6 million farms) were smaller than 5 ha, but the 1.0% of all farms that were of 50 ha or more in size farmed a little over one half (53.1%) of all the UAA in the country. Small farms of under 5 ha represented a majority of all farms in Malta (97.0% of the total), Cyprus (88.0%), Greece (73.%), Portugal (71.1%), Croatia (70.1%), Bulgaria (61.3%), Italy (60.6%), Slovenia (57.6%), Hungary (55.0%), and Poland (50.7%). The number of small farms in certain EU countries and regions reflects a mixture of crop specialisation (such as small olive groves and vineyards), of wide land ownership, and geological and topographical constraints. Larger farms (of 50 hectares or more) were relatively common in Luxembourg (53.0% of all farms), France (48.4%), Finland (35.1%), Denmark (33.6%), and Germany (32.0%). In most EU countries, a majority of UAA was concentrated on the largest farms (50 ha or more in size). Indeed, the largest farms in Czechia (27.2% of the total) and in Slovakia (20.9% of the total) accounted for as much as 92% of their respective utilised agricultural areas, the highest proportions among EU countries. '''EU farms can be characterised in three distinct size groups''' Broadly-speaking, there are 3 distinct groups of farms in the EU: (i) semi-subsistence farms, where the focus is on growing a high proportion of food to feed farmers and their families (ii) small and medium-sized farms that are generally family-run businesses and (ii) large agricultural enterprises which are more likely to have a legal form or be cooperatives. These distinctions are made clearer by analysing farms in terms of their economic size. Of the EU's 8.8 million farms, one third (2.9 million holdings) had a standard output below €2 000 per year and were responsible for generating only 1% of the EU's total agricultural economic output. These very small farms are at the (semi-) subsistence end of the farming scale. A further 2.5 million farms had an economic output within the range of €2 000 - €8 000 per year. Together these very small and small farms accounted for approaching two-thirds (62.2%) of all farms in the EU in 2023 but were responsible for only 3.4% of the EU’s total agricultural economic output. In contrast, 330 000 farms (3.8% of the EU total) each produced a standard output of €250 000 per year or more in 2023 and were responsible for a majority (60.1%) of the EU's total agricultural economic output; these farms can be characterised as being large agricultural enterprises. A majority (57.0%) of the standard output generated by agriculture across the EU was from the combined farms in France (17.7%), Italy (14.9%), Germany (12.8%), and Spain (11.6%) in 2023. Although Romania accounted for about one third of the EU's farms, it accounted for only 3.7% of the EU's standard output (see Figure 2). [[Image:F2r Farms and standard output, 2023 (share of EU total, %).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Farms and standard output, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_ecsz__custom_20806626/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=0e215672-c221-4d4d-b7b0-80114635d8ba&c=1775034651000 ef_fsi_ecsz])|alt= Horizontal bar chart showing percentage share of EU total farms and standard output in individual EU Member States. Each country has two bars representing farms and standard output for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''EU farms remain diverse in terms of what they grow or rear''' The diversity of farm types can be shown according to what is grown or reared, based on whether there is a single dominant activity or not. A farm is specialised when a particular activity provides at least two-thirds of the production or the business size of an agricultural holding. Others have a mix of activities in which no one activity dominates. Some farms are specialised in crop production, whether that be where field crop activities are the dominant activity, or where permanent crops (like apples, grapes and olives) dominate, or indeed horticultural activities. Some farms are specialised in animal production and animal products, whether that be where grazing livestock or granivores (such as pigs and poultry) dominate. Other farms have a mix of crops, mix of livestock, or mix of crops and livestock. Almost 6 in every 10 farms (58.9%) in the EU could be categorised as being crop specialist farms in 2023. About one third (35.0%) of all farms were specialised in field cropping, about one fifth (21.6%) were specialised in permanent crops, with the remainder (2.4%) being specialist horticultural farms. In this grouping of crop specialists, specialist cereals, oilseeds and protein crop farms were the most numerous in 2023 (18.3% of all EU farms – see Figure 3). This was closely followed by general field cropping farms that specialised in root crops (such as potatoes and sugar beet), in field vegetables and field crops (16.7% of all EU farms). Another one fifth (20.6%) of the EU's farms were specialist livestock farms, with specialist dairy farms (4.7%) and specialist cattle-rearing and fattening (4.2%) the most numerous within this group. Mixed farms accounted for another one fifth (20.0%) of the EU’s farms in 2023, with a small percentage of farms not being classifiable. [[Image:Fig 3 Farms by type of specialisation (share of all EU farms, %, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Farms by type of specialisation
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_ecsz__custom_20807076/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=ce5f7141-77e5-4980-aaca-4d011496368c&c=1775035704000 ef_fsi_ecsz])|alt= Two layer doughnut chart showing percentage share of all EU farms by type of specialisation. The inner layer has three sections representing crop specialists, livestock specialists and mixed faming. The outer layer further breaks down the three specialisations by specific plants and animal specialisations for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In many Mediterranean countries (Greece, Cyprus, Spain, Italy, Greece and Malta), as well as Finland and Hungary, specialist cropping was the dominant farm type (with a share of more than 70% of all farms), while in parts of north-west Europe (Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands), as well as Austria, specialist livestock farming was the dominant activity (with a share of more than 50% of all farms). Between 30% and 41% of farms were mixed holdings in Latvia, Lithuania, Croatia, and Romania in 2023. '''Farms managed a little less than one half (45.6%) of the total land area of the EU in 2023''' Farms in the EU managed 156.2 million hectares as UAA in 2023, corresponding to 38.1% of the total land area of the EU, and an additional 31.2 million hectares as either un-utilised agricultural areas, wooded areas or other areas on farms. Agricultural landscapes dominated the countryside in a few EU countries; about 73.6% of Ireland’s land area was used as agricultural land in 2023 and the share was also particularly high in Denmark (62.6%). In Hungary, Romania, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, slightly more than one half of the total land area was used as agricultural land. This was in starkest contrast to Finland and Sweden where forests dominated the landscape. In these 2 Nordic countries, agricultural land use only represented the equivalent of 7.4% and 7.3% of their respective total land areas. Indeed, they were the only EU countries where woodland belonging to agricultural holdings accounted for a higher share of the land area than that used for agricultural purposes (see Figure 4). [[Image:F4r Land belonging to farms by type of land (% share of total land area, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Land belonging to farms by type of land
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_lus__custom_20811523/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=4edd6acc-3d35-4c5c-b370-8a5bee94c904&c=1775046827000 ef_fsi_lus]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/reg_area3__custom_20811827/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=f16418b9-1b1b-4503-becf-136719ea6f33&c=1775047584000 reg_area3])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage share of total land area land belonging to farms by type of land in the EU, individual EU Member States. Each country column contains two stacks representing utilised and unitilised agricultural areas on farms. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] France (27.2 million ha) and Spain (23.5 million ha) had the largest utilised agricultural areas in the EU in 2023, 17.4% and 15.0%, respectively, of the EU total. There were also more than 10 million hectares of UAA in Germany (16.6 million ha, equivalent to 10.6% of the EU total), Poland (14.6 million ha, or 9.3% of the EU total), Romania (12.6 million ha, or 8.0%) and Italy (12.4 million ha, or 7.9%). In 2023, a majority (56.2%) of the total land area of Denmark was dedicated to arable land, by far the highest share of any EU country – see Figure 5. In Ireland, a majority (54.0%) of the total land area was dedicated to permanent grassland, double the share of any other EU country. In Portugal, a tenth (9.9%) of the total land area was dedicated to permanent crops like vineyards, olive groves and citrus fruit orchards, with a similar proportion in Spain (9.1%). [[Image:F5r Land belonging to farms by type of land (% share of total land area, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Land belonging to farms by type of land
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_lus__custom_20811523/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=4edd6acc-3d35-4c5c-b370-8a5bee94c904&c=1775046827000 ef_fsi_lus]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/reg_area3__custom_20811827/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=f16418b9-1b1b-4503-becf-136719ea6f33&c=1775047584000 reg_area3])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage share of total land area land belonging to farms by type of land in the EU, individual EU Member States. Each country column contains four stacks representing unitilised agricultural areas, permanent crops, permanent grassland and arable areas on farms. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===The evolution of farms and farmland between 2005 and 2023=== '''The number of farms has been in steep decline''' The number of farms in the EU has been in decline for a long time. In the relatively short period between 2005 and 2023, there was a loss of 5.6 million farms across EU countries, equivalent to an estimated decline of 39%. Over this period, there were fewer farms in every EU country. The largest reductions were recorded in Romania (a loss of 1.4 million farms, equivalent to a decline of -33%), Poland (an indicative loss of 1.2 million farms, or -50%), Hungary (a loss of 0.5 million farms, or -74%), Italy (an indicative loss of 0.5 million farms, or -27%), and Bulgaria (an indicative loss of 0.4 million farms, or -80%). '''Most farms lost in the smallest size classes: remaining farms getting larger''' The decline in the overall number of farms in the EU largely reflected the sharp decline in the number of the very smallest farms; between 2005 and 2023, the EU had 4.9 million fewer farms under 5 ha. Nevertheless, there were also lower EU farm numbers in each size up to 100 ha. Through consolidation and acquisition, there was an increase of 75 000 farms in the EU that were of a size greater than 100 ha. This pattern of restructuring (see Figure 6) was reflected in most EU countries, though the farm size at which numbers started increasing was sometimes considerably lower than the over 100 ha classes. For example, in Italy farm numbers grew in each size class between 5 ha and 249.9 ha. In Bulgaria, farm numbers rose in each size class over 10 ha and in Romania in each class over 20 ha. An interesting dichotomy appeared in Denmark, with growth in the number of the very smallest (each size class under 5 ha) and very largest farms (over 250 ha). A similar development was noted in Ireland, for holdings under 2 ha and those over 100 ha. This seems to reflect a development in some countries for farms with no or little UAA but with animals kept in farm buildings, contributing to the overall increase in the economic size of farms. [[Image:F6r Overall change in the number of farms and .png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Development in the number of farms and utilised agricultural area by size class
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_physz__custom_20955453/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=51664834-396c-473d-9be1-cbc1173ef104&c=1776065354000 ef_fsi_physz]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/39915836-df2e-4077-b7de-f56d21c63e1b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-13T07:33:04Z ef_fsi_physz]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/dd2dc703-9711-4487-a81d-de1ecf748360?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-13T07:35:45Z ef_fsi_physz])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing percentage development in the number of farms and utilised agricultural area by size class in the EU. The total and eight size ranges in hectares, each have two columns representing number of farms and UAA from the year 2005 to 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''The amount of land used in the EU for agricultural production changed little''' The amount of land that was used for agricultural production changed little between 2005 and 2023 (down 0.6% between these two survey years), despite the sharp reduction in farm numbers. At the EU-level, this consolidation of agricultural land was reflected in the growth in the average size of farms, from about 11 ha in 2005 to 18 ha in 2023. '''Legal form of holdings growing''' There were about 407 000 farms in the EU that had a legal basis in 2023, the equivalent of 4.6% of all farms. This represented an increase of 90 000 farms taking this form in the period between 2005 and 2023, and increases were noted in every farm size category. The equivalent share of all EU farms that had a legal basis in 2005 was 2.2%. About 45% of all EU farms over 100 ha had a legal basis in 2023, a similar proportion that in 2005 (43%). This share was as high as 58% of all EU farms over 250 ha in 2023. Farms with no UAA accounted for the sharpest percentage point increase in farms with a legal basis: from 4.1% of all EU farms with no UAA in 2005 to 13.1% in 2023. Most of these farms raise or finish animals indoors with no utilised agricultural area. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Farms-Farmland 0170426.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== Farm structure data are collected from agricultural censuses every ten years and from sample surveys every 3 or 4 years in between. The main tables from the 2023 survey are gradually being published and are used in this analysis. ===Explanatory note=== The implementation of the Integrated Farm Statistics (IFS) introduced a division of the target population into two components: the ‘main frame’ includes agricultural holdings above physical thresholds defined in the legislation, while the ‘frame extension’ covers smaller holdings below these thresholds. In the legislative framework, data collection requirements for below-threshold units vary across time. This variability leads to gaps in data availability for the entire population of agricultural holdings and poses challenges for the comparability of results. To address this issue, an estimation procedure based on imputation techniques applied at the level of microdata has been developed to produce consistent estimates for below-threshold units where data are missing, which have been published in the Eurobase datasets under Farm structural indicators [[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database ef_fsi]]. ===Context=== Farming is an activity that is about growing crops and raising livestock. It is the business of providing key primary ingredients for the food that we eat and much of what we drink. Farming draws on a set of resources to produce these agricultural goods, as well as agricultural services. These resources or 'factors of production' can be broadly categorised as land, labour, knowledge, capital and entrepreneurship. Within the EU, the farming sector operates under the common agricultural policy (CAP), which has been reformed a number of times over the years. The common agricultural policy plays a pivotal role in shaping the EU’s agricultural industry. Recent reforms have encouraged greener practices by allocating more funds to conservation and biodiversity. The common agricultural policy also supports farmers’ livelihoods, ensures food supply and security by stabilising agricultural markets, while contributing to EU trade negotiations by maintaining high quality and safety standards for agricultural products. The EU’s new Vision for Agriculture and Food is central to building a sustainable food system and protecting biodiversity, while securing rural livelihoods and enhancing the stability of the food chain, alongside ambitions to achieve climate neutrality. Key priorities include: strengthening the role of farmers in the food value chain; promoting sustainable farming practices and empowering consumers to choose balanced, eco-friendly diets; encouraging generational renewal and gender equality; making knowledge, training and skills more accessible; improving resilience by helping the food system adapt to shocks, such as climate change, market volatility or systemic crises. === Other articles === *[[Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics]] *[[Agri-environmental indicators]] *[[Glossary:Farm structure survey (FSS)|Farm structure survey (FSS)]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database Agriculture (agr)], see: :Farm structure (ef) ::Farm structural indicators (ef_fsi) :::Physical size of farms by utilised agricultural area and legal form ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/ef_fsi_physz?category=agr.ef.ef_fsi ef_fsi_physz]) :::Average economic size of farms by standard output, farm type and age of farm manager ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_ecsz/default/table?lang=en&category=agr.ef.ef_fsi ef_fsi_ecsz]) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database General and regional statistics], see: :Regional statistics by NUTS classification (reg) ::Area by NUTS 3 region ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/reg_area3?category=reg reg_area3]) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database Agriculture (t_agr)] ===Thematic section=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-24-024|title=A look at European farms – agricultural census results}} ===Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/ef_sims.htm Farm structure (ef)] ===Legislation=== '''Main legislation''' *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R1091:EN:NOT|title=Regulation 2018/1091}} of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 July 2018 on integrated
