title: Fertility statistics
text:
EU statistics provide an overview of fertility evolution: decline in the mid-1960s, followed by a rise in the early 2000s and another decline in 2013 followed by a slight increase up to 2016 and another decrease until 2020. Data extracted on 19 February 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 3.55 million babies were born in the EU in 2024. The total fertility rate stood at 1.34 live births per woman in the EU in 2024, ranging from 1.01 in Malta to 1.72 in Bulgaria. 29.9 years was the average age of women at the birth of their first child in the EU in 2024, ranging from 26.9 in Bulgaria to 31.9 in Italy. :::''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_find__custom_20166283/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=d581b4b1-bde2-4513-a9ce-4e703c1e04a2&c=1771427420000 demo_find]) [[Image:Map01 Config Total fertility rate 2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: Total fertility rate, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_find__custom_20166283/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=d581b4b1-bde2-4513-a9ce-4e703c1e04a2&c=1771427420000 demo_find])|alt= an interactive map showing total fertility rate for the EU Member States and surrounding countries. Each country is colour-coded based on live births per woman. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article looks at the developments observed for a range of indicators concerning the number of [[Glossary:Birth|births]] and [[Glossary:Fertility|fertility]] across the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Fertility rates have steadily declined from the mid-1960s through to the turn of the century in the EU countries. However, at the beginning of the 2000s, the [[Glossary:Fertility|total fertility rate]] in the EU showed signs of rising again. This development stopped in 2010 (when the total fertility rate in the EU was 1.57) and a subsequent decline was observed to a relative low in 2013 (1.51), followed by a slight increase in 2016 (1.57) and another decrease until 2020 (1.51). After an increase in 2021 (1.53), the total fertility rate decreases again in the following years reaching its historic low in 2024 with 1.34 live births per woman. ===Almost 2 times fewer children born in the EU in 2024 than 6 decades ago=== In 2024, 3.55 million children were born in the EU, corresponding to a [[Glossary:Birth|crude birth rate]] (the number of live births per 1 000 persons) of 7.9. For comparison, the EU crude birth rate was 10.5 in 2000, 12.8 in 1985 and 16.4 in 1970. During the period 1961-2024, the highest annual total for the number of live [[Glossary:Birth|births]] in the EU was recorded in 1964, at 6.8 million children. From this comparative high until the beginning of the 21st century, the number of live births in the EU declined at a relatively steady pace, reaching a low of 4.36 million in 2002 (see Figure 1). This was followed by a modest recovery in the number of live births, with a high of 4.68 million children born in the EU in 2008, which in turn was followed by a general downward trend, although with modest increases in 2014 and 2016. Live births in the EU firstly declined to 4.07 (in 2020), then slightly increased to 4.09 million in 2021 and since 2022 again started decreasing. In 2024, total number of live births in the EU was 3.55 million children. Figure 1 ====1.34 live births per woman in the EU in 2024==== In recent decades, Europeans have generally been having fewer children, and this pattern partly explains the slowdown in the EU's population growth (see [[Population_and_population_change_statistics|Population and population change statistics]]). The most widely used indicator of fertility is the [[Glossary:Fertility|total fertility rate]]: this is the mean number of children that would be born alive to a woman during her lifetime if she were to pass through her childbearing years conforming to the age-specific fertility rates of a given year. A total fertility rate of around 2.1 live births per woman is considered to be the replacement level in developed countries: in other words, the average number of live births per woman required to keep the population size constant in the absence of [[Glossary:Migration|migration]]. A total fertility rate below 1.3 live births per woman is often referred to as 'lowest-low fertility'. The total fertility rate is comparable across countries since it takes into account changes in the size and structure of the population. In 2024, the total fertility rate in the EU was 1.34 live births per woman (Figure 2). The EU's total fertility rate rose from a low of 1.43 in 2001 and 2002 to a relative high of 1.57 in 2008 and 2010; this was subsequently followed by a slight decrease to 1.51 in 2013 before modest rebounds until 2017, when the indicator started to decrease again. The EU fertility rate declined to 1.51 (in 2020) live births per woman, slightly increased to 1.53 (in 2021) and since 2022 has been decreasing again, from 1.46 (in 2022) to a new low of 1.34 in 2024 . Figure 2 ====Bulgaria with the highest and Malta with the lowest total fertility rate in 2024==== Among the EU countries, Bulgaria reported the highest total fertility rate in 2024, with 1.72 live births per woman, followed by France (1.61) and Slovenia (1.52). By contrast, the lowest total fertility rates in 2024 were recorded in Malta (1.01 live births per woman), Spain (1.10) and Lithuania (1.11). Between 2023 and 2024, the total fertility rate decreased in 24 EU countries, remained stable in 2 (Luxembourg and the Netherlands) and increased only in Slovenia (from 1.51 in 2023 to 1.52 in 2024), while the highest decrease was recorded in Romania (from 1.54 in 2023 to 1.39 in 2024). In the majority of the EU countries, the total fertility rate declined considerably between 1980 and 2000-2003: by 2000, values had fallen below 1.30 in Bulgaria, Czechia, Greece, Spain, Italy, Latvia and Slovenia. After reaching a low point between 2000 and 2003, the total fertility rate increased in many of the EU countries and by 2024, all of them except Estonia, Greece, Spain, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Poland and Finland reported total fertility rates that were above 1.30 (Table 1). In the past 50 years, total fertility rates in the EU countries have, in general, been converging: in 1970, the disparity between the highest rates (recorded in Ireland) and the lowest rates (recorded in Finland) was around 2.0 live births per woman. By 1990 this difference – between a high in Cyprus and a low in Italy – had decreased to 1.1 live births per woman. By 2010, the difference had fallen again to 0.8 live births per woman with a high in Ireland and a low in Hungary. By 2024 the difference narrowed to 0.7 when the highest total fertility rate was recorded in Bulgaria and the lowest rate was recorded in Malta'''. [[Image:Total fertility rate, 1970-2024 (live births per woman) v2.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: Total fertility rate, 1970-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5b648a0c-4b73-4a73-8b4c-e2f12bcf9d90?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-18T15:08:21Z (demo_find)]|alt= Table showing total fertility rate as live births per woman for the EU, individual EU Member States, EFTA countries and some candidate countries for the years 1970, 1980, 1990, 2004, 2014, 2023 and 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Women in the EU are becoming mothers later in life=== Figure 3 shows that the mean age of women at childbirth in the EU continued to rise between 2001 and 2024, from an average of 29.0 to 31.3 years. The same trend is observed for the mean age of women at birth of the first child during the same period, from a value of 28.8 in the EU in 2013 (the first year for which the EU value is available) to a value of 29.9 in 2024. Figure 3 Indeed, women in the EU appear to be having fewer children while they are young, and more children later in life (see, for example, data for 2024 in Figure 4 at ages higher than 30 years). While the fertility rates for women aged less than 30 years in the EU have declined since 2004, those for women aged 30 years and over have risen. In 2004, the fertility rate for women aged 25-29 years was the highest among all age groups. In 2024, the fertility rate for women aged 30-34 years became the highest. The fertility rate for women aged 35 years and over is also on the increase. Figure 4 ===Total fertility rate and age of women at birth of first child=== Figure 5 shows a plot of the total fertility rate against the mean age of women at the birth of their first child in 2024. Some of the countries with the highest total fertility rates also had a relatively high mean age of women at the birth of their first child.
Four different groups of EU countries can be broadly identified based on their position with respect to the EU averages (as identified by the quadrants defined by the yellow lines).
The first group (top right quadrant) is composed of Denmark, Germany, Ireland, Cyprus, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden where both the total fertility rate and the mean age of women at the birth of their first child were above the EU average.
A second group (bottom left quadrant) is made up of Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta and Poland: both their total fertility rates and mean ages of women at the birth of their first child were below the EU averages.
A third group (bottom right quadrant) composed of Greece, Spain, Italy, Luxembourg, Austria and Finland recorded a higher than average mean age of women at the birth of their first child but a lower total fertility rate than the EU average.
The final group (top left quadrant) was composed of Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia, France, Croatia, Hungary, Romania, Slovenia and Slovakia; in each of these, the total fertility rate was higher than the EU average but the mean age of women at the birth of their first child was below the EU average. Figure 5
====In 2024, women in the EU who gave birth to their first child were on average aged 29.9 years==== As can be seen in Map 1, on average in the EU, women who gave birth to their first child in 2024 were aged 29.9 years. The lowest mean age at birth of a first child can be found in Bulgaria (26.9 years) and Romania (27.2 years); the highest values can be observed in Italy (31.9 years) and Luxembourg (31.6 years). [[Image:Map02_Mean_age_of_women_at_birth_of_first_child_2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Mean age of women at birth of first child, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f70cc500-aca6-4dcd-9ba6-fe52110cab4f?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-18T15:13:47Z (demo_find)]|alt= Map showing mean age of women in years at birth of first child for the EU Member States and surrounding countries. Each country is colour-coded based on five specific age groups, namely less than 27 years, between 27 and 28 years, between 28 and 29 years, between 29 and 30 years and aged 30 years and over for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Almost half of children born in the EU in 2024 were born to first-time mothers=== Close to half (46.6%) of the children born in the EU in 2024 were first-born children, with this share exceeding half in Portugal (54.6%), Luxembourg and Malta (both 53.9%), and 50.7% in Spain (see Figure 6). By contrast, the lowest shares of first-born children were recorded in Latvia (39.9%) and Slovakia and Estonia (both 41.2%). In the EU, more than one-third (35.1%) of all live births in 2024 were of second-born children, around one-eighth (12.1%) were third-born children, and the remaining 6.2% were of fourth-born or subsequent children. Across the EU countries, the highest share of the total number of live births of fourth or subsequent children was recorded in Slovakia (9.9%), followed by Finland (9.4%) and Romania (9.2%). Figure 6 ===In 2024, the share of children born to foreign-born mothers stood at 24%=== The foreign-born mothers shown in the Figure 7 concern mothers who were not born in the reporting country, but in another EU country or outside the EU. 68% of the children born in Luxembourg in 2024 were from foreign-born mothers. The second highest share of births to foreign-born mothers was in Cyprus with 42%. In Malta, Austria, Belgium, Spain, Portugal and Germany at least one-third of children were born to foreign-born mothers and two-thirds were born to native-born mothers. Conversely, 97% of live births in 2024 in Bulgaria, Romania and Slovakia were born to native-born mothers. Compared with 2013 (the first year for which data are available for all EU countries), most of the EU countries in 2024 showed an increase in live births from foreign-born mothers. Malta recorded the highest increase in live births from foreign-born mothers (27 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] from 11% in 2013 to 38% in 2024) followed by Portugal (17 pp from 16% to 33%), and Spain, Slovenia, Cyprus and Czechia for which increases of around 9 pp were recorded. Figure 7 === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Fertility statistics YB2026 SE 03 26 v2.xlsx|title=Fertility statistics, main figures: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] compiles information for a large range of demographic data, including statistics on the number of live births by sex (of newborns), by the mother's age, citizenship, country of birth, level of educational attainment and marital status. Fertility statistics are also collected in relation to the number of births and by birth order (in other words, the rank of the child – first, second, third child and so on). A series of fertility indicators is produced from the information collected, including the total fertility rate and fertility rates according to the mother's age, the mean age of women at childbirth, the crude birth rate or the relative proportion of births outside of marriage. ===Context=== The EU's social policy does not include a specific strand for family issues. Policymaking in this area remains the exclusive responsibility of EU Member States, reflecting different family structures, historical developments, social attitudes and traditions from one Member State to another. Nevertheless, policymakers may well evaluate fertility statistics as a background for family policymaking. Furthermore, a number of common demographic themes are apparent across the whole of the EU, such as a reduction in the average number of children being born per woman and the increasing mean age of mothers at childbirth. The EU has been going through a period of demographic and societal change. On 17 January 2023, the European Commission published the Staff Working Document on [https://commission.europa.eu/system/files/2023-01/the_impact_of_demographic_change_in_a_changing_environment_2023.PDF The impact of demographic change – in a changing environment] which provides further analysis of the demographic changes. In response to the June 2023 European Council conclusions, on 11 October 2023, the Commission put forward a toolbox to support Member States in addressing demographic challenges and their impact on Europe's competitive edge. More information on the work of the European Commission to tackle the impact of demographic change in Europe can be found in the [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029_en European Commission dedicated pages.] ===Other articles=== *[[Marriage and divorce statistics]] *[[Mortality and life expectancy statistics]] *[[Population and population change statistics]] *[[Population structure and ageing]] *[[EU population diversity by citizenship and country of birth]] *[[Migration to and from the EU]] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/demography-population-stock-balance/publications All publications on demography, population stock and balance] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/interactive-publications/demography-2025 Demography of Europe - 2025 edition] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-key-figures/w/ks-01-25-003 Key figures on Europe - 2025 edition] *[https://commission.europa.eu/system/files/2023-01/Demography_report_2022_0.pdf The impact of demographic change in a changing environment] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/ks-01-25-037 Eurostat Regional Yearbook - 2025 edition] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/interactive-publications/regions-2025 Regions in Europe - 2025 edition] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/demography-population-stock-balance/database Demography, population stock and balance] ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/demography-population-stock-balance Demography, population stock and balance] ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=demo_fer_esms|title=Fertility}} (ESMS metadata file — demo_fer_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=demo_pop_esms|title=Population}} (ESMS metadata file — demo_pop_esms) ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Fertility_statistics'' {{Unit|topic=X_Population}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Fertility statistics]] [[Category:Population and demography|Fertility statistics]] [[Category:Vistool|Fertility statistics]] [[Category:Fertility and births|Fertility statistics]] [[Category:Statistical article|Fertility statistics]] [[Category:March2027|Fertility statistics]]

title: Farm tenure
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of farm tenure in the EU. Data from April 2024 Planned article update: December 2028 In 2023, almost as much rented farmland as own-farmed land in the EU. Almost 30% of the EU’s utilised agricultural area found on very large tenant farms over 100 hectares with a further 19% on very large own-farmed holdings in 2023. Between 2010 and 2023, an additional 1.2 million hectares were tenant farmed, contrasting starkly with a decline of 6.1 million hectares that were own-farmed. [[Image:F1 Share of utilised agricultural area by type of farm tenure (% share, EU and countries, 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_tenure__custom_22339042/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=a14eb649-c62b-4105-9841-8a49820e0b95&c=1786094122000 ef_fsi_tenure])|alt= 100% stacked bar chart showing how the utilised agricultural area in the EU, EU countries and Norway is distributed by farm tenure, for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article provides information about farm tenure in the [[Glossary:EU|European Union (EU)]]. It consists of an overview of data, complemented by all information on definitions,measurement methods and [[#Context|context]] needed to interpret them correctly. There were 8.8 million agricultural holdings (hereafter named ‘farms’) in the EU in 2023 ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_fsi_farms|title=ef_fsi_farms}}). On the vast majority of these farms, the land is either owned by the holder or rented (as tenant farms). Nevertheless, many farms include a mix of part-owned and part-rented land. As a result, the analysis in this article is limited to the tenure of the area used for farming, to avoid double counting the number of farms or the number of farm managers. ===Almost as much rented farmland as own‑farmed land in the EU=== The EU’s farmland is worked by farms under different [[Glossary:Type of tenure|types of tenure]]. In 2023, [[Glossary:Type of tenure|land owned and farmed by holders]] accounted for 47.4% of the EU’s [[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|utilised agricultural area]], a slightly higher share than was farmed as rented land by tenant farmers (45.3%). Together, these two forms of tenure cover the vast majority of agricultural land in the EU, with common land (3.5%) and share farming and other tenure modes (3.8%) being much less common – see Figure 1. The distribution of farmland by tenure among EU countries was mixed. In 10 EU countries, own-farmed land accounted for a majority of utilised agricultural area, with the highest shares in Poland (75.5%), Portugal and Slovenia (both 69%). In a further 10 EU countries, tenant-land (rented) accounted for a majority of utilised agricultural area, with the highest shares being in Bulgaria (76.7%), Slovakia (74.9%) and Malta (73.9%).
[[Image:F1 Share of utilised agricultural area by type of farm tenure (% share, EU and countries, 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Share of utilised agricultural area by type of farm tenure (% share, EU and countries, 2023)
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_tenure__custom_22339042/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=a14eb649-c62b-4105-9841-8a49820e0b95&c=1786094122000 ef_fsi_tenure])|alt= 100% stacked bar chart showing how the utilised agricultural area in the EU, EU countries and Norway is distributed by farm tenure, for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Forms of tenure other than own-land and rented land were notable in some EU countries. In Greece, common land accounted for 29.5% of utilised agricultural area, the highest share among EU countries. In the Netherlands, shared land or other tenure modes accounted for 13.8% of utilised agricultural area, slightly more than the shares in the Romania (12.4%) and Italy (10.9%). ===Almost two-thirds of rented land on farms over 100 hectares in size=== In 2023, slightly more than one half (53.0%) of the EU’s utilised agricultural area (UAA) was found on very large farms with at least 100 hectares; almost 30% was on very large tenant farms and 19.0% on very large own-farmed holdings, the rest being on common land and shared or other tenure models (see Figure 2). Despite their considerable number, small farms (with fewer than 5 hectares of land) represented only a small share of the EU’s agricultural area: 4.8% of the total on owned farmland and 0.5% on rented farmland. [[Image:F2 Distribution of utilised agricultural area .png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Distribution of utilised agricultural area by farm size and type of tenure (% share of total, EU, 2023)
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_tenure__custom_22011529/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=a2d5ad3b-a39f-4830-90ee-22700ce343f8&c=1786095273000 ef_fsi_tenure])|alt= clustered bar chart showing the distribution of utilised agricultural area by farm size and type of tenure - owner or tenant - as a percentage share of the total, for the EU in 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, about two-thirds (65.6%) of all rented land for agricultural production (UAA) was on very large farms of over 100 hectares. By comparison, only 40.1% of all own-farmed UAA was on very large farms. ===Small growth in rented farmland=== Although the amount of utilised agricultural area in the EU declined by an estimated 2.9 million hectares between 2010 and 2023 to 156.2 million hectares, the amount of land that was rented increased by an estimated 1.2 million hectares. This contrasted with a sharp decline of 6.1 million hectares in the amount of own-farmed land, although some of this may be due to a reclassification as common land. In some EU countries, there were notable changes in farm tenure between 2010 and 2023 (see Figure 3). There was greater own-farmed utilised agricultural area in Slovakia (up 13 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]], albeit from a relatively low level) and France (up 12 pp). By contrast, there was greater tenant-farmed utilised agricultural area in a number of other EU countries; the increase was between 10 to 15 percentage points in Estonia, Austria, Ireland, Romania, Italy, and Denmark. [[Image:F3 Changing shares of utilised agricultural area by type of farm tenure.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Changing shares of utilised agricultural area by type of farm tenure (%, EU and countries, 2010 and 2023)
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/14b8779e-4301-4882-8701-9a2de53ce52a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-07T10:20:38Z ef_fsi_tenure])|alt=A double graph showing the changes in the shares of utilised agricultural area by type of farm tenure in the EU for the years 2010 and 2023. Data are shown as percentage share of all utilised agricultural area for the EU, EU countries and Norway. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:310826 Farm tenure.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === The table {{Template:Publication|code=ef_fsi_tenure|title=ef_fsi_tenure}} describes owner- and tenant-farmed agricultural areas. The data collections are organised in line with the EU legislation. For 2020 (the agricultural census), 2023 and 2026, they are organised in line with the Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 and have a new structure, consisting of a core data set and several modules. The data are as comparable and coherent as possible across European countries. '''Indicator definition''' Type of tenure refers to the ownership of the land parcels and depends on the situation on a reference day of the year of the survey. It includes: * Farming on own land (OWN_UAA) - utilised agricultural area farmed by the agricultural holding and held by the holder as a property or farmed by the holder acting as a usufructuary or heritable long-term leaseholder or under some other equivalent type of tenure. * Farming on rented land (RENT_UAA) - utilised agricultural area rented by the agricultural holding in return for a fixed rent agreed in advance (in cash, kind or otherwise), and for which there is a (written or oral) tenancy agreement. The utilised agricultural area is allocated to only one agricultural holding. If the utilised agricultural area is rented out to more than one agricultural holding during the reference year, it is normally allocated to the agricultural holding with which it is associated on the survey reference day or which used it for the longest period during the reference year. * Farming on common land (CMNL_UAA) - utilised agricultural area used by the agricultural holding but not belonging directly to it, i.e. on which common rights apply. * Share farming or other tenure modes (SHROTH_UAA) - utilised agricultural area which is: ** shared, meaning farmed in partnership by the landlord and the share cropper under a written or oral share-farming contract. The output (either economic or physical) of the share cropped area is shared between the two parties on an agreed basis. ** under other modes of tenure not covered elsewhere under the previous items. === Context === Both family-owned and tenant-run farms are a cornerstone of the agricultural sector in the EU, reflecting circumstances under which a tenure mode is better suited to particular economic and social conditions. When farmland tenure is secure, there is greater confidence in making investment decisions for economic growth. Insecurity and instability in farmland tenure can lead to conflict and exclusion, particularly of poorer farmers. An added dimension in the EU has been the transition to liberalised land markets through the process of accession to the EU and the slow pace of land restitution in some of the EU countries. Access to financial capital, escalating land prices and the lack of access to land are some of the barriers to entry in farming. At a time when a majority (61.0% in 2023 and climbing) of farm managers are over the age of 55 years ({{Template:Publication|code=ef_fsi_agesex|title=ef_fsi_agesex}}), looking at supporting the move of younger people into farming is increasingly important for the EU’s food security and the longer-term sustainability of the sector. Only 10.7% of EU farm mangers were under 40 years old in 2023 (ef_fsi_agesex). Tenure security is also highlighted as an enabler of more local, inclusive and sustainable food chainsSee [https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/8bf3c43c-51c7-4a76-aa33-6d950d9fbd09 Land tenure and sustainable agri-food systems (2021), ILC, FAO and GLTN.]. === Other articles === *[[Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics]] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agri-environmental_indicators_-_fact_sheets Agri-environmental indicators] *[[Glossary:Farm structure survey (FSS)|Farm structure survey (FSS)]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database Agriculture (agr)], see: :Farm structure (ef) ::Farm structural indicators (ef_fsi) :::Tenure of utilised agricultural area ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ef_fsi_tenure/default/table?lang=en&category=agr.ef.ef_fsi ef_fsi_tenure]) === Thematic section === title: Final energy consumption in services - detailed statistics
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the final energy consumption in services. Data extracted in June 2026 Planned article update: June 2027 In 2024, the services sector accounted for 13.5% of final energy consumption in the EU. Within the services sector, the largest energy consumers in the EU in 2024 were wholesale and retail trade activities, human health and social work activities, accommodation and food services activities, and professional, scientific and technical activities. In 2024, electricity (52.0%) and natural gas (25.4%) together accounted for more than three quarters of the final energy consumption of the EU’s services sector. With a consumption of 4 971 petajoules (PJ)Petajoule is a unit of energy equal to 1015 joules. in 2024 and a share of 13.5% of final energy consumption in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], the services sector has a far smaller energy consumption than transport activities (32.3%), households (26.0%) and the industry sector (24.5%), only exceeding agriculture, forestry and fishing (3.6%). However, behind its relatively small size, the services sector hides an impressive diversity of activities, from hospitals to hotels and from schools to stadiums. This article presents data on [[Glossary:Final energy consumption|final energy consumption]] in services in the EU, broken down by activities and specific energy products, for the year 2024.Data for 2024 are available for all EU Member States except Cyprus, which was granted a full derogation for the collection on disaggregated final energy consumption in services. Belgium and Greece were granted a partial derogation: for Belgium, only data on electricity and natural gas are available; for Greece, only data on solid fossil fuels are available. Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/2199 of 17 October 2023 granted derogations for the entire collection to Cyprus for reference years 2022, 2023 and 2024. The Implemented Regulation also granted partial derogations to Belgium and Greece for several families of fuels for reference years 2022, 2023 and 2024. The term energy product refers to primary and secondary fuels or fuel groups such as natural gas, electricity, renewables, etc.For the full list of energy products, please refer to Annex A of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008 on energy statistics. Primary fuels/products transformed into electricity, heat or any other secondary product are not accounted in their respective fuel group, but directly as the energy product that is finally consumed. For example, wind power transformed into electricity or biogas transformed into heat are not accounted as renewables and biofuels, but as electricity and heat, respectively. === Energy products used in the services sector === Electricity (52.0%) and natural gas (25.4%) accounted together for more than three-quarters of the final energy consumption in the EU’s services sector in 2024. Following these two main fuels, [[Glossary:Renewable energy sources|renewable energy sources]] accounted for 8.7% of consumption, followed by heat at 7.7%, and then oil and [[Glossary:Petroleum products|petroleum products]] at 5.6%. The remaining 0.6% were taken by other energy products such as coal or waste (see Figure 1). [[File:Final energy consumption in the services sector by energy product, EU, 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Final energy consumption in the services sector by energy product, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/793a1ef2-4484-426c-98e1-5a5c951df894 nrg_bal_s])|alt= a pie chart with six segments showing the Final energy consumption in the services sector by energy product, in the EU in 2024. The segments show electricity, natural gas, renewables energies, heat, oil and petroleum products and other fuels. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Over the entire period from 1990 to 2024, total final energy consumption in services rose by 25%, from 3 969 PJ in 1990 to 4 971 PJ in 2024. Hovering around 4 000 PJ in the first half of the 1990s, consumption then rose steadily from 1996, reaching a consumption peak of 5 860 PJ in 2010. Afterwards, consumption remained between 5 000 and 5 600 PJ, with low points in 2014 and 2020. In 2023 and 2024, the energy consumption of the services sector dipped below the 5 000 PJ boundary for the first time since 2002. Figure 2 shows the evolution of different energy products used for energy purposes in the services sector in the EU. Electricity remained the largest energy source for services and rose in significance during the same period. From 1 344 PJ in 1990, the consumption of electricity in the services sector increased continuously until 2010, before stabilising at around 2 600 PJ. Electricity went from supplying a third of consumption in services in 1990 (33.9%) to a half in 2024 (52.0%). In contrast, from 1990 to 2006, the consumption of oil and petroleum products by services hovered around 1 000 PJ, with the sector’s share decreasing from 25.3% to 16.0%; but after 2006, consumption declined, reaching 279 PJ in 2024. Natural gas overtook oil and petroleum products as the second largest energy source for services in 1993: consumption rose from 856 PJ in 1990 to 1 642 PJ in 2006, hovered around 1 500 PJ, with a share between 25% and 30%, before decreasing from 2022 onwards. Services’ consumption of renewables steadily increased, with a notable jump in 2017: between 1990 and 2024, the consumption of renewables by services had multiplied by 18. Finally, solid fossil fuels, the fourth largest source of energy for services in 1990, saw consumption fall drastically in the 1990s, remaining low from then on. [[File:Figure 2 Evolution of final energy consumption in the services sector by energy product, EU, 1990-2024 (PJ).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Evolution of final energy consumption in the services sector by energy product, EU, 1990-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c2e6c3e2-91cb-451d-b008-0c8126ed97b4 nrg_bal_s])|alt= A line chart with seven lines showing the Evolution of final energy consumption in the services sector by energy product in the EU from 1990 to 2024. The lines show electricity, natural gas, renewable energies, heat, oil and petroleum products, solid fossil fuels and other fuels. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Largest energy consumers in services=== In 2024, half of the energy consumption of services in the EU was taken up by just four sub-sectors. Wholesale and retail trade consumed 1 021 PJ of energy, making up more than a fifth of energy consumption (21.2%) of all services. Human health and social work activities (506 PJ) and accommodation and food service activities (503 PJ) rounded up the podium with an almost equal consumption and a share of 10.5% of energy consumption for each sector. Professional, scientific and technical activities, also including minor other types of services, closed this quatuor with 10.2% of the consumption (492 PJ). [[File:Final energy consumption by sub-sector of the services sector, EU, 2024 (PJ).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Final energy consumption by sub-sector of the services sector, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e1eb78a0-e95e-492b-b87e-e46cd34676dc nrg_d_serq_n])|alt= A horizontal bar chart showing the total final energy consumption by sub-sector of the services sector in 25 countries of the EU in 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The article will now focus on these four main sub-sectors. It will present the composition of their energy consumption and compare it to the shares of energy products in the services sector as a whole. We see similarities in energy product use among sub-sectors and compared to the overall energy mix of the sector, but also some striking differences. Wholesale and retail trade made up the largest part of final energy consumption in the services sector in the EU. Its shares of energy products were similar to the services sector as a whole, with electricity and natural gas accounting for 54.6% and 22.9%. However, compared with other activities, the share of heat consumption of wholesale and retail trade was smaller (5.0% in 2024). The largest portion of this sub-sector was taken up by retail trade, with a consumption of 644 PJ in 2024, a consumption larger than both the second or the third largest sub-sectors of services (human health and social activities and accommodation and food service activities). Retail trade followed the same order in shares of energy products as the services sector itself, but emphasised electricity (59.5%) over both natural gas (20.0%) and heat (4.1%). In contrast, the smaller wholesale trade activities (306 PJ in 2024) consumed a lot less electricity (46.5%) and a lot more oil and petroleum products (12.0%) compared with other service activities; it also had a higher consumption of natural gas (26.9%) and heat (5.8%). [[File:Figure 4 Final energy consumption in wholesale and retail trade by energy product, EU, 2024 (PJ).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Final energy consumption in wholesale and retail trade by energy product, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c2013d05-aa3f-4869-b071-71ea95c5f68b nrg_d_serq_n])|alt= three vertical stacked bar charts showing total final energy consumption in wholesale and retail trade by energy product in 25 countries of the EU in 2024. One bar shows wholesale and retail trade as a whole, and the two others show respectively wholesale trade and retail trade. The stacks show the different products - electricity, natural gas, renewable energies, heat, oil and petroleum products and other fuels. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Human health and social work activities, including hospitals and residential care activities, consumed 506 PJ of energy in 2024. They also stood out by consuming more natural gas than electricity, with shares of 42.2% for natural gas and 35.0% for electricity. With a consumption of 72 PJ, heat made up 14.2% of the energy consumption of this sub-sector, an unusually high share among the services sector. Accommodation and food services activities, including hotels and restaurants, stood out with their large consumption of renewable energies; with 82 PJ of the 503 PJ total consumption in 2024, renewable energies made up 16.3% of the sub-sector’s energy consumption. Most of these renewables were consumed by accommodation activities, where they represented almost a quarter of the consumption. In contrast, almost two-thirds of the consumption of food and beverage service activities was taken up by electricity alone. Overall, in 2024, the energy consumption of accommodation activities was higher than the one of food and beverage service activities (respectively 278 and 226 PJ). Comprising various activities such as legal, consultancy, architectural, engineering, research and development, advertising, veterinary or membership organisations activities, the “Professional, scientific and technical activities and Other service activities” sub-sector consumed 492 PJ of energy in 2024. This sub-sector displayed a relatively large share of electricity (58.9%) in its energy consumption compared to other sub-sectors. [[File:Final energy consumption in selected sub-sectors of the services sector by energy product, EU, 2024 (PJ).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Final energy consumption in selected sub-sectors of the services sector by energy product, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7fefec78-4750-401d-b01c-d2a8682aca14 nrg_d_serq_n])|alt= three vertical stacked bar charts showing total final energy consumption in selected sectors of services by energy product in 25 countries of the EU in 2024. The three bars show professional, scientific and technical activities and other services, human health and social work activities, and accommodation and food services activities. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=SE Services 2024.xlsx|title=Final energy consumption in services - tables and figures}}[[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources and availability === The statistics presented in this article are based on the annual data submitted to Eurostat in line with Regulation (EC) 1099/2008 on energy statistics. Complete disaggregated data on final energy consumption in services are available for 2024 for all but three EU Member States. In line with the derogations granted to them, Cyprus did not report disaggregated data on final energy consumption in services for 2024, and Belgium and Greece reported this data only partially. As of reference year 2022, the reporting is mandatory with a deadline of 31 March of the second year following the reference year. For several countries, the data are also available for the period 2020-2021, during which the reporting was voluntary. The methodology is harmonised for all reporting countries, resulting in a high level of comparability across countries.
'''Methodological notes''' In this article, the “services sector” includes the energy consumed by businesses and offices in the public and private sectors, according to its definition in {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R1099:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008}} on energy statistics. The “disaggregated data on final energy consumption in services” includes 48 Divisions from the Statistical Classification of Economic Activities (NACE) defined in Annex A Article 2.6.3.1. of Regulation (EC) 1099/2008 and defined as “sub-sectors” in this article. These Divisions are: * All the Divisions from NACE Sections E, G, I, J, K, L, M, N, O, P, Q, R, S and U * Divisions C33, H52 and H53 Out of these 48 Divisions, one NACE Class is excluded (NACE 84.22 – defence activities). The services sector as defined in energy statistics excludes the energy consumed by transport activities, transformation activities and activities of the energy sector. Transport activities are reported under their own collection ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Final_energy_consumption_in_transport_-_detailed_statistics Final energy consumption in transport]). Transformation activities and activities of the energy sector are reported under their own categories in the energy balances. For this reason, differences with other data sources, such as energy flow accounts, are expected. In some Member States, the energy consumption of a commercial tenant is filed to the name of the landlord, and therefore under the category “real estate activities”, instead of the real activity of the commercial tenant. This means many sub-sectors of services may be slightly underestimated, whereas the “Financial and insurance activities; real estate activities” sub-sector may be overestimated. With both Eurostat and Member States aware of this issue, Eurostat expects the quality of the data to improve in future years. Per Article 2(g) of {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32023R0137:EN:NOT|title=Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/137}} on the revision of NACE and the transition from NACE Revision 2 to NACE Revision 2.1, the latest revision of NACE will apply to this collection and to energy statistics as a whole from reference year 2027 onwards, with disaggregated data on final energy consumption in services applying the new revision expected in the first half of 2029. === Context === Disaggregation of statistics on final energy consumption is crucial for policy makers to monitor and further develop energy policies. Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008 on energy statistics put in place four collections to gather detailed data on final energy consumption. Mandatory reporting of final energy consumption started in 2017 (reference year 2015) for the residential sector (households), in 2022 (reference year 2020) for the industry sector, and in 2024 (reference year 2022) for both the services sector and transport activities. === Other Articles === *[[Energy|All articles on energy]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/energy/database Energy - detailed datasets (t_nrg)], see: :Energy statistics - quantities, annual data (nrg_quanta) ::Disaggregated final energy consumption (nrg_d) :::*[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nrg_d_serq_n/default/table?lang=en Disaggregated final energy consumption in services - quantities by NACE Rev. 2 activity (nrg_d_serq_n)] :::*[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nrg_d_sercv/default/table?lang=en Disaggregated final energy consumption in services - calorific values (nrg_d_sercv)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/energy/database Energy - selected datasets (t_nrg)], see: :Energy statistics - main indicators (t_nrg_indic) :Sustainable Development indicators Goal 7 - Affordable and clean energy (t_nrg_sdg_07) === Thematic section === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=energy}} Energy] === Publications === *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-064|title=Sustainable development in the European Union — 2026 edition }} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-26-007|title=Energy in Europe — 2026 interactive edition}} === Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=nrg_bal_esms|title=Energy balances}} (ESMS metadata file — nrg_bal_esms) * {{Template:Esms|code=nrg_quant_esms|title=Energy statistics - quantities}} (European and national ESMS metadata file — nrg_quant_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=nrg_cb_esms|title=Supply, transformation and consumption — commodity balances}} (ESMS metadata file — nrg_cb_esms) === Legislation === *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R1099:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) 1099/2008 on energy statistics}} === Visualisations === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/infographs/energy_portal/enviz.html Interactive energy visualisations] -
