title: Financial corporations - statistics on financial assets and liabilities
text:
Statistics that focus on the annual stock of financial assets and liabilities for financial corporations in the EU and the euro area. Data extracted on 24 October 2025 Planned article update: 30 October 2026 In 2024, 5 EU countries – Germany, France, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Ireland – collectively accounted for approximately 72% of the financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations in the EU. The total financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations in the EU increased almost continuously between 2014 and 2024; they only decreased in 2022. [[Image:Annual rate of change for total financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations, 2024 (%, change over previous year)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Annual rate of change for total financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_f_bs}}|alt=A grouped column chart showing the annual rate of change for total financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations. Data are shown in percentages for 2024 for the EU and the euro area and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article focuses on the annual stock of [[Glossary:Financial assets and liabilities|financial assets and liabilities]] for [[Glossary:Financial corporations sector|financial corporations]]. Note that there are complementary articles that provide similar information on [[Households_-_statistics_on_financial_assets_and_liabilities|households]] and [[Non-financial_corporations_-_statistics_on_financial_assets_and_liabilities|non-financial corporations]]. A comparison between these sectors (excluding general government) is available in the article on non-financial corporations. The [[Glossary:Financial corporations sector|financial corporations sector]] consists of institutional units which are independent legal entities and market producers, and whose principal activity is the production of financial services. Such institutional units comprise all corporations and quasi-corporations, which are principally engaged in: *financial intermediation (financial intermediaries) and/or *auxiliary financial activities (financial auxiliaries). Also included are institutional units providing financial services where most of either their assets or their liabilities are not transacted on open markets. Across the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], the financial assets of financial corporations mainly comprise loans, equity and investment fund shares, and debt securities. The financial liabilities of financial corporations mainly comprise equity and investment fund shares, currency and deposits, insurance reserves, pension entitlements and standardised guarantees. The data presented in this article relate to a detailed set of [[Glossary:Consolidated financial account|consolidated]] financial [[Glossary:Financial accounts and balance sheets|balance sheets]] for the financial corporations sector, as released by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]. Note that statistics detailing the [[Glossary:Financial accounts and balance sheets|financial accounts]] may be consolidated or non-consolidated; the latter record not only transactions and positions between sectors (in other words, financial corporations with other actors in the economy) but also transactions and positions within the same sector (in other words, between financial corporations). This article provides an analysis of financial assets and liabilities in the EU and the [[Glossary:Euro area|euro area (EA)]], as well as for individual EU countries, 1 of the [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA]] countries (Norway) and 2 of the [[Glossary:Candidate countries|enlargement countries]] (North Macedonia and Türkiye). Data are generally available for 2024; the latest data available for North Macedonia are for 2023. Some indicators are presented in relation to [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]], which is beneficial for making cross-country comparisons, especially between countries of different size. ===Assets and liabilities=== '''''Financial assets of EU financial corporations valued in 2024 at 5.1 times GDP''''' Total financial assets of financial corporations in the EU were valued at €91 895 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] in 2024; this was slightly higher than the value of their financial liabilities, which stood at €91 254 billion, a difference of €641 billion (or 0.7%). This difference was marginally smaller than that recorded in 2023, when it was €701 billion (or 0.8%). The annual rate of change for total financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations between 2023 and 2024 is illustrated in '''Figure 1'''. The EU recorded increases of 6.3% and 6.4% for assets and liabilities, respectively. It should be noted that rates of change are calculated in national currencies. Among EU countries, the highest annual growth rates were observed in Lithuania, up 18.6% for assets and 19.0% for liabilities. The next fastest growth rates were recorded for Ireland (17.4% for assets and 17.2% for liabilities), Romania (13.6% for assets and 13.0% for liabilities) and for Czechia (13.4% for assets and 12.1% for liabilities). Cyprus, Hungary and Finland were the only EU countries which had negative annual rates of change, down, respectively, 8.9%, 2.1% and 1.8% for assets and 8.5%, 3.0% and 1.3% for liabilities. [[Image:Annual rate of change for total financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations, 2024 (%, change over previous year)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Annual rate of change for total financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_f_bs}}|alt=A grouped column chart showing the annual rate of change for total financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations. Data are shown in percentages for 2024 for the EU and the euro area and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The share of each EU country in the EU’s total financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations in 2024 is presented in '''Figure 2'''. Germany held just over a fifth of the financial assets (21.7%) and liabilities (21.5%) of financial corporations in the EU, followed by France (15.4% for assets and 15.9% for liabilities), Luxembourg (14.0% for assets and 14.1% for liabilities), the Netherlands (11.0% for assets and 10.9% for liabilities) and Ireland (9.8% for assets and 9.7% for liabilities). These 5 EU countries collectively accounted for 71.8% of the financial assets and 72.1% of the financial liabilities of financial corporations in the EU. Apart from Italy and Spain, the other EU countries held shares of less than 3.0% each. Some of the smaller EU countries accounted for relatively high shares of the financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations in the EU in 2024. This was clearly the case for Luxembourg, which had the third highest shares (after Germany and France), as well as for Ireland, which had the fifth highest share. This reflects the large international activity of the financial sector in both of these EU countries. A comparison between the shares of financial assets and financial liabilities for each EU country reveals that these were generally similar. France and Italy had the largest difference, as financial corporations in France held a 0.5 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points (points)]] higher share of the EU’s financial liabilities than their share of the EU’s financial assets, while the reverse situation was observed in Italy. [[Image:Share of the EU's total financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations, 2024 (%)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Share of the EU’s total financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_f_bs}}|alt=A grouped column chart showing EU countries’ shares of the EU’s total financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations. Data are shown in percentages for 2024 for EU countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Figure 3''' presents the financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations as a percentage of GDP. In 2024, these assets were valued in the EU at 510% of GDP, while these liabilities were valued at 507%, resulting in net financial assets equivalent to 3.6% of GDP. The financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations in Luxembourg were both valued in 2024 at 14 900% of GDP, in other words 149 times the level of GDP. Luxembourg’s financial assets and liabilities as a percentage of GDP were 29 times the EU average. In Malta, financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations were valued around 30 to 31 times the level of GDP, while in Cyprus, Ireland and the Netherlands the values were 9 to 16 times the level of GDP. Apart from Denmark (where these assets and liabilities were valued, respectively, at 5.6 and 5.5 times the level of GDP), this ratio was 5.0 or lower in all other EU countries. Romania was the only EU country where the value of the financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations in 2024 was below that of GDP. The data shown in Figure 3 demonstrate the importance of financial corporations in several small and medium-sized EU countries: Luxembourg clearly stands out, while financial corporations also play a substantial role in the economies of Malta, Ireland, Cyprus and the Netherlands. [[Image:Financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations as a percentage of GDP, 2024 (%)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations as a percentage of GDP, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_f_bs}}|alt=A grouped column chart showing the financial assets and liabilities of financial corporations as a percentage of GDP. Data are shown in percentages for 2024 for the EU and the euro area and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Structure of assets and liabilities=== '''''The largest shares of financial corporations’ financial assets were equity and investment fund shares, loans and debt securities''''' There are 4 prominent types of instruments of assets and liabilities of financial corporations in the EU: currency and deposits; debt securities; loans; equity and investment fund shares. There were 4 other types of assets and liabilities which accounted for smaller shares (from 0.2% to 5.9% each) of total financial assets of EU financial corporations in 2024: monetary gold and special drawing rights (SDRs); insurance, pensions and standardised guarantees; financial derivatives and employee stock options; other accounts receivable/payable. In this article, these smaller types of instruments are grouped together as ‘other instruments’ – see '''Figure 4''' for assets and '''Figure 5''' for liabilities. The category of equity and investment fund shares accounted for the largest share (30.4%) of financial assets of EU financial corporations in 2024. This type of instrument was followed by loans (26.6%) and debt securities (22.7%). Currency and deposits and other instruments accounted for 10.6% and 9.6%, respectively. A majority of EU countries had debt securities, loans, and equity and investment fund shares as the 3 largest types of assets held by financial corporations in 2024. *There were 8 EU countries which had equity and investment fund shares as their principal instrument: Luxembourg (52.7% of assets), Cyprus (47.7%), Denmark (44.1%), Malta (43.4%), Sweden (43.3%), the Netherlands (41.3%), Ireland (36.6%) and Germany (27.0%). *The largest share of assets in Greece (54.7%), Poland (40.2%), Romania (40.0%), Slovenia (38.2%), Italy (35.9%) and Latvia (28.8%) was in debt securities. *In all other EU countries, the principal instrument was loans, as was also the case in Norway, North Macedonia (2023 data) and Türkiye. Aside from these 3 main instruments, the share of assets in currency and deposits was relatively large (over 15.0%) in Croatia, Bulgaria, Slovenia, Latvia, Lithuania and Germany. More than 10.0% of assets were in other instruments in France, Germany and Poland, mainly financial derivatives and employee stock options and/or other accounts receivable/payable. [[Image:Share of type of assets of financial corporations, 2024 (% share of total financial assets of financial corporations)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Share of type of assets of financial corporations, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_f_bs}}|alt=A stacked column chart showing the shares of each type of asset within financial corporations’ total financial assets. The analysis of assets shows equity and investment fund shares, currency and deposits, debt securities, loans and other instruments. Data are shown in percentages for 2024 for the EU and the euro area and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Financial corporations’ financial liabilities were mainly equity and investment fund shares as well as currency and deposits''''' The largest shares of total financial liabilities of the EU’s financial corporations in 2024 were equity and investment fund shares (34.2%) and currency and deposits (30.2%). Among other instruments (20.9%), a substantial share of liabilities was due to the contribution of insurance, pensions and standardised guarantees (which had a 12.0% share of the total value of liabilities). A comparison of the structure of financial assets and liabilities for the EU’s financial corporations in 2024 shows that loans and debt securities made up larger shares (26.6% and 22.7% respectively) of assets compared with much smaller shares (6.1% and 8.6%) of liabilities. By contrast, currency and deposits accounted for 10.6% of assets compared with 30.2% of liabilities. Insurance, pensions and standardised guarantees also made up a relatively high share of liabilities (12.0%) compared with a small share of assets (0.2%). Among EU countries, currency and deposits, equity and investment fund shares, and other instruments generally accounted for the largest shares of the financial liabilities held by financial corporations in 2024. *Currency and deposits represented 79.0% of liabilities in Greece, 65.6% in Slovenia, 65.0% in Poland, 64.0% in Romania and 63.7% in Bulgaria. Currency and deposits also accounted for more than half of the total in a further 8 EU countries as well as in North Macedonia (2023 data) and Türkiye. In a further 6 EU countries, currency and deposits accounted for the largest share of liabilities, although this share was below 50.0%; this was also the case in Norway. *More than half of the total liabilities were equity and investment fund shares in Luxembourg (70.8%), Malta (69.5%) and Ireland (60.5%). In Cyprus, Hungary, the Netherlands and Denmark, equity and investment fund shares also accounted for the largest share of liabilities, although this share was below 50.0%. *Sweden (33.7%) was the only EU country where the largest share of liabilities was held as other instruments, mainly insurance, pensions and standardised guarantees. Among the smaller instruments, loans were relatively important in 2024 in Cyprus (27.8% of total financial liabilities) and in Hungary (22.6%), while debt securities accounted for 20.6% of liabilities in Finland. [[Image:Share of type of liabilities of financial corporations, 2024 (% share of total financial liabilities of financial corporations)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Share of type of liabilities of financial corporations, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_f_bs}}|alt=A stacked column chart showing the shares of each type of liability within financial corporations’ total financial liabilities. The analysis of liabilities shows equity and investment fund shares, currency and deposits, debt securities, loans and other instruments. Data are shown in percentages for 2024 for the EU and the euro area and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Developments=== '''''The value of financial assets of financial corporations as a percentage of GDP increased in 2024 in most EU countries''''' Growth in the total financial assets of EU financial corporations was uninterrupted during the period 2014-21. By 2021, the total value of assets had increased by 41.3%, from €60 103 billion in 2014 to €84 930 billion in 2021. A similar development was observed for total financial liabilities over the same period. These increased by 41.6% from €59 473 billion in 2014 to €84 230 billion in 2021. This upward development for financial assets and financial liabilities was reversed in 2022. The value of assets and of liabilities fell 1.0% and 0.9%, respectively. Growth returned in 2023 and 2024, as the value of assets increased (compared with 2022) 9.3% to reach €91 895 billion, while the value of liabilities also increased 9.3% to reach €91 254 billion, equivalent to 52.9% and 53.4%, respectively, above their 2014 values. The value of financial assets of financial corporations as a percentage of GDP was 9.2 points higher in 2024 than in 2023 in the EU, a relative increase of 1.8%. This ratio decreased in 2024 in 10 EU countries (see '''Figure 6'''). The largest relative decrease observed among EU countries was for Cyprus (down 15.0%), followed at some distance by Hungary (down 9.5%). Among the 17 EU countries which recorded an increase, the fastest growth in relative terms was in Lithuania, as this ratio increased 11.7%. [[Image:Total financial assets of financial corporations as a percentage of GDP, 2023 and 2024 (%)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Total financial assets of financial corporations as a percentage of GDP, 2023 and 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_f_bs}}|alt=A grouped column chart showing the financial assets of financial corporations as a percentage of GDP. Data are shown in percentages for 2023 and 2024 for the EU and the euro area and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Shares in assets and liabilities per type of financial corporation === '''''The contributions of each subsector of financial corporations were similar for assets and for liabilities''''' The contributions in 2024 from each subsector of financial corporations across the EU were similar for assets and for liabilities. The specialisation within certain subsectors is illustrated in '''Figures 7 and 8'''. The largest subsector within financial corporations in the EU was monetary financial institutions other than the central bank, with a 38.7% share both for assets and for liabilities. This was followed by other financial intermediaries (except insurance corporations and pension funds (ICPFs)), financial auxiliaries, captive financial institutions (CFIs) and money lenders, with a 22.5% share of assets and a 22.4% share of liabilities. The third largest shares were for non-money market fund (non-MMFs) investment funds (17.8% of assets and 18.4% of liabilities), followed by insurance corporations and pension funds (12.9% of assets and 12.4% of liabilities) and central banks (8.1% of assets and 8.0% of liabilities). For 21 EU countries (as well as Norway, North Macedonia (2023 data) and Türkiye), monetary financial institutions other than the central bank held the largest shares of assets and liabilities. *In Cyprus, Malta, Hungary and the Netherlands, the highest shares of assets and liabilities were in other financial intermediaries (except ICPFs), financial auxiliaries, CFIs and money lenders. *In Ireland and Luxembourg, the highest shares of assets and liabilities were in non-MMF investment funds. For monetary financial institutions other than the central bank, the highest shares of assets were recorded in France, Poland, Finland and Spain, all within the range of 55% to 58%. For central banks, shares of 36.5%, 29.5% and 29.1% were recorded in Greece, Slovenia and Latvia, respectively. For other financial intermediaries (except ICPFs), financial auxiliaries, CFIs and money lenders, shares above 75% were observed in Malta and Cyprus, while the share was below 50% in all other EU countries. For non-MMF investment funds, Ireland and Luxembourg reported shares that were more than double those in any other EU country, 48.5% and 45.3%, respectively. The highest shares for insurance corporations and pension funds were in Sweden and Denmark, at 28.0% and 25.9%, respectively. Looking at the combined contributions of the central bank and other monetary financial institutions, the shares were relatively low in several EU countries that have a large financial corporations sector, namely Malta, Luxembourg, Cyprus, Ireland and the Netherlands. [[Image:Financial assets of financial corporations analysed by subsector, 2024 (% share of total financial assets of financial corporations)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Financial assets of financial corporations analysed by subsector, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_f_bs}}|alt=A stacked column chart showing the shares of subsectors within the financial assets of financial corporations. The analysis of subsectors shows monetary financial institutions other than the central bank, other financial intermediaries (except ICPFs), financial auxiliaries, CFIs and money lenders, non-MMF investment funds, and insurance corporations and pension funds. Data are shown in percentages for 2024, for the EU and the euro area and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] [[Image:Financial liabilities of financial corporations analysed by subsector, 2024 (% share of total financial liabilities of financial corporations)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Financial liabilities of financial corporations analysed by subsector, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_f_bs}}|alt= A stacked column chart showing the shares of subsectors within the financial liabilities of financial corporations. The analysis of subsectors shows monetary financial institutions other than the central bank, the central bank, other financial intermediaries (except ICPFs), financial auxiliaries, CFIs and money lenders, non-MMF investment funds, and insurance corporations and pension funds. Data are shown in percentages for 2024, for the EU and the euro area and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Financial corporations - statistics on financial assets and liabilities NA2025.xlsx|title=Financial corporations – financial assets and liabilities: figures}} *{{Template:Excel|filename=Financial corporations - statistics on financial assets and liabilities-Annex NA2025.xlsx|title=Financial corporations – financial assets and liabilities: annex (detailed tables)}} ===Data sources=== The compilation of financial accounts follows the [[Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)|European System of Accounts 2010 (ESA 2010)]]. '''The financial account and balance sheet''' Eurostat’s website includes detailed [[Glossary:Financial accounts and balance sheets|financial accounts]] by country. Financial accounts are published in [[Glossary:Consolidated financial account|consolidated and non-consolidated]] forms; within this article the former are presented. As a rule, the accounting entries in ESA 2010 are non-consolidated, as a consolidated financial account requires information on the counterpart grouping of institutional units. Note that data for the EU and EA aggregates are calculated as a sum of data for EU and EA countries; no adjustment is made for flows between countries and EU institutions. ===Context=== Financial accounts form part of the [[Glossary:National accounts (NA)|national accounting]] framework and are compiled in the EU in accordance with ESA 2010. They are a significant tool for analysing financial developments and policy decisions, and provide key statistical information on financial transactions, other financial flows and financial balance sheets by [[Glossary:Institutional sector|institutional sector]], including financial corporations. Particular issues relating to the financial corporations sector include its capacity to withstand shocks. Indeed, since the global financial and economic crisis financial accounts for financial corporations have been integrated into an enlarged set of policy indicators – the EU’s macroeconomic imbalance procedure (MIP) surveillance mechanism – that are used to identify potential macroeconomic risks early on, prevent the emergence of harmful macroeconomic imbalances and correct the imbalances that are already in place. The types of assets and liabilities that financial corporations hold carry different levels of risk and can be used to assess financial risk. ===Other articles=== *[[Households_-_statistics_on_financial_assets_and_liabilities|Households – statistics on financial assets and liabilities]] *[[Non-financial_corporations_-_statistics_on_financial_assets_and_liabilities|Non-financial corporations – statistics on financial assets and liabilities]] ===Selected datasets=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sector-accounts/database Annual sector accounts (ESA 2010) (t_nasa_10)] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sector-accounts/database Annual sector accounts (ESA 2010) (nasa_10)], see: :Financial flows and stocks (nasa_10_f) ::Financial balance sheets - annual data (nasa_10_f_bs) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/macroeconomic-imbalances-procedure/database Macroeconomic imbalance procedure scoreboard] ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sector-accounts/overview Institutional sector accounts] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/macroeconomic-imbalances-procedure/overview Macroeconomic imbalance procedure (MIP)] ===Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/KS-02-13-269 European system of accounts – ESA 2010] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/nasa_10_f_esms.htm Financial flows and stocks (Eurostat metadata)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/macroeconomic-imbalances-procedure/methodology Methodology for the macroeconomic imbalance procedure scoreboard] ===Legislation=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sector-accounts/legislation Key legal documents for institutional sector accounts] ===External links=== *[https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/economic-and-fiscal-governance/macroeconomic-imbalances-procedure_en European Commission – macroeconomic imbalance procedure (MIP)] ''View this article online at {{fullurl:{{PAGENAME}}}}'' {{Unit|topic=X_National_accounts_methods}} [[Category:Economy and finance|Financial corporations – statistics on financial assets and liabilities]] [[Category:National accounts (incl.
