title: Flash estimates of income inequalities
text:
Flash estimates on the evolution of income inequalities and poverty in 2023. Data extracted in July 2023 No planned article update
EXPERIMENTAL
 Eurostat’s income flash estimates show that the at risk of poverty rate in the EU is likely to have decreased slightly (-0.2 pp), with a stronger decrease for child poverty (-0.8 pp) from 2022 to 2023 (income year). Flash estimates indicate that in 2023 (income year) the EU median disposable household income increased by 6.0 % in nominal terms while remaining stable in real terms. [[Image:Median_income,_nominal_versus_real_terms,_EU,_2019-2023_(income_year).png |thumb|centre|700px|alt= a line chart with two lines showing the change in median equivalised disposable income, by income quintile in the EU in the EU and EU Member States]] This article presents experimental statistics ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators flash estimates]) on income inequality and poverty indicators for 2023, produced by Eurostat using microsimulation and nowcasting techniques. Flash estimates refer to the year-on-year change from 2022 to 2023 for '''income-based indicators''' and complement the 2022 income data from the European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC) collected in 2023. The flash estimates aim to give preliminary information on income trends until the corresponding data from the EU-SILC become available (2024). The methodology considers both the effect of the labour market trends on employment income and changes made to social protection schemes by national governments in 2023. For the latter, Eurostat uses the [https://euromod-web.jrc.ec.europa.eu/overview/what-is-euromod EUROMOD] microsimulation modelSocial benefits and taxes are simulated via the EUROMOD tax benefit model. This is maintained, developed and managed by the Joint Research Centre of the European Commission, in collaboration with Eurostat and national authorities from the EU countries., which provides the effects of direct taxes, social security contributions and benefits on households income. Throughout the remainder of the article, income year is used as the reference period for the flash estimates. ===Key findings=== Flash estimates for 2023 show a significant overall increase of 6.0 % from the previous year in median [[Glossary:Equivalised_disposable_income|equivalised disposable income]] at EU level, with positive changes estimated for all countries. Estimates of the at risk of poverty rate (AROP) suggest it remained stable at EU level, with a slight, not statistically significant decrease of 0.2 percentage points (pp). Most countries show a stable AROP, or not significant changes. Estimates show a significant decrease in 6 countries (the Netherlands, Germany, Estonia, Spain, Portugal and Finland), and an increase in 4 countries (Greece, France, Luxembourg, and Austria). At EU level, a similar trend is estimated in the AROP for individuals aged 18 to 64 years, while the AROP rate for children (less than 18 years old) is expected to have declined by 0.8 pp. It should be noted that these indicators are based on nominal disposable income and do not incorporate changes in the cost of living and purchasing power. In real terms, the nowcasted median disposable income for 2023 is estimated to have increased in 16 countries, decreased in 5 and remained stable in 6. At the EU level, the median income in real terms shows a slight increase of 0.2 % in 2023 compared to 2022. This diversity reflects the heterogeneous impact of inflation across countries. At the EU level, 2023 still sees rising prices for food and non-alcoholic beverages (12.6 %), while prices for electricity, gas, and other fuels show a moderate annual average rate of change (1.4 %), following the significant increases in 2022 (42.4 %).
Produced by Eurostat as experimental statistics, flash estimates aim to provide preliminary information for the latest income year until the corresponding data from the EU-SILC becomes available. To reflect the inherent uncertainty of model-based estimates, flash estimates are released as Rounded Uncertainty Intervals (RUI) rather than point estimates. They indicate the direction and magnitude of change throughout the article. A number of caveats and assumptionsIncomplete information and model errors for the estimation of employment income; over-simulation and assumptions of full take-up of benefits; lack of information on the informal economy and workers who fell outside the safety net of the tax-benefit system. should be considered when interpreting the flash estimates. For more details, see the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/7894008/8256843/flash-estimates-methodological-note-2023.pdf/6f25bba0-07c5-7126-3571-19b58e47514a?t=1718682336317 methodological note].
=== At risk of poverty rate === Eurostat produced flash estimates on income in 2023 to predict the change in the AROP (overall and breakdowns) for the upcoming 2024 EU-SILC. As shown in Figure 1, the flash estimates show a very slight, not statistically significant drop in AROP overall, based on 2023 income estimates at EU level. A similar trend is estimated in the AROP for individuals aged 18 to 64 years, which shows slightly lower levels. On the other hand, the AROP rate for children (less than 18 years old) exhibits the strongest estimated annual decrease from 2022 to 2023, declining by 0.8 pp. [[Image:At_risk_of_poverty_rate,_EU,_2019-2023_(income_year)_%_of_population.png |thumb|centre|600px|Figure 1: At risk of poverty rate, EU, 2019-2023 (income year), % of population
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_li02}} and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Experimental statistics: Flash estimates on Income inequality and poverty indicators]|alt= A line chart showing the risk of poverty rate (income year), EU, 2019-2023 between 2019 and 2023 in the EU, in percentage of population. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The two figures below (2a and 2b) depict the time series for AROP at country level between 2019 and 2023 (income years). They include EU-SILC values for 2019-2022 and 2023 income flash estimates as intervals. For visualisation purposes, EU countries have been clustered into two groups by AROP for 2022 income. Figure 2a includes 15 countries where the value for the 2022 AROP income year is below the EU average. Within this group: * for 2019-2022 (income years), the largest decreases are in Belgium and Germany (-1.8 pp and -1.7 pp respectively) and the largest increases are in Slovakia and the Netherlands (2.9 pp and 1.6 pp respectively); * for 2023 (income year), flash estimates show a significant decrease for Germany, Finland, and the Netherlands (highlighted in green), and a significant increase for Austria and France (highlighted in red). [[Image:Arop_all_underEU_v1.jpg |thumb|centre|600px|Figure 2a: At risk of poverty rate, 2019-2023 (income year). Countries with a 2022 AROP (income year) below the EU average
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_li02}} and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Experimental statistics: Flash estimates on Income inequality and poverty indicators]|alt= A list of line charts showing the risk of poverty rate (income year) between 2019 and 2023 in multiple EU countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 2b includes 12 countries where the value for the AROP in 2022 is above the EU average. Within this group: * in the 2019-2022 period (income years), the largest falls are in Bulgaria (-3.2 pp) and Romania (-2.3 pp), while the largest increase is in Estonia (1.8 pp); * for 2023, flash estimates show a significant decrease for Spain, Portugal, and Estonia (highlighted in green), and a significant increase for Greece, and Luxembourg (highlighted in red). [[Image:Arop_all_aboveEU_v1.jpg |thumb|centre|600px|Figure 2b: At risk of poverty rate, 2019-2023 (income year). Countries with a 2022 AROP (income year) above the EU average
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_li02}} and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Experimental statistics: Flash estimates on Income inequality and poverty indicators]|alt= A list of line charts showing the risk of poverty rate between 2019 and 2023 in multiple EU countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] At the aggregate EU level, the AROP breakdown for the working-age population (18-64) is estimated to have decreased slightly by 0.3 pp in 2023. As shown in Figure 3, a statistically significant increase is estimated for Luxembourg, Czechia, Greece, and France (in descending order), while a statistically significant decrease is estimated for Spain, Estonia, Slovenia, Finland, Germany, Lithuania, Malta, and Portugal (in descending order). [[Image:Titleyes_At_risk_of_poverty_rate_18-64_.jpg|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 3: At risk of poverty [18-64]: year on year change (pp), 2023 vs 2022, Flash estimates (FE) as rounded uncertainty levels (RUI)
''Source:'' Eurostat: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Experimental statistics: Flash estimates on Income inequality and poverty indicators]|alt= A bar chart showing the population at risk of poverty rate, 2023 vs 2022, flash estimates as rounded uncertainty intervals, by the age group of 18-64. The vertical axis presents the year-on-year percentage points change, while the horizontal axis presents the list of countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Improvements in employment income sustain the overall estimated growth in disposable income === Total employment income (including wages and self-employment income) across income quintiles (based on the ranking of people in terms of their employment income) is estimated to have increased. Flash estimates show slightly higher increases for workers with lower earnings. [[Image:Total_employment_income_in_the_EU,_2023,_%_change_compared_to_2022,_by_quintile.png |thumb|centre|600px|Figure 4: Total employment income in the EU, 2023, % change compared to 2022, by quintile
''Source:'' Eurostat: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Experimental statistics: Flash estimates on Income inequality and poverty indicators]|alt= A bar chart showing the total employment income in the EU, 2023, % change compared to 2022 in the EU. The vertical axis presents the percentage, while the horizontal axis presents the quintile. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 5 provides a comprehensive overview of nominal median income ([[Glossary:Equivalised_disposable_income|equivalised disposable income]]) across different income quintiles in the EU from 2019 to 2023 (income year). For 2023, the flash estimates indicate consistent and similar year-on-year growth for all the income quintiles: first and second quintiles are estimated to have grown by 6.3 % compared to the previous year, the third (median) and forth quintile by 6.0 %, and the fifth quintile by 6.1 %. [[Image:Median_income_in_nominal_terms_by_quintile,_EU,_2019-2023_(income_year)_.png |thumb|centre|600px|Figure 5: Median income in nominal terms by quintile, EU, 2019-2023 (income year)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_di01}} and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Experimental statistics: Flash estimates on Income inequality and poverty indicators]|alt= A line chart showing the median income between 2019 and 2023 in the EU. The vertical axis presents the nominal terms, while the horizontal axis presents the income year. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Median income is estimated to have increased significantly at EU level and across all countries === Figure 6 presents the expected change in median disposable income in nominal terms by country. In all countries, a statistically significant increase is estimated for 2023 compared with 2022 (income year). For the EU as a whole, median disposable income is estimated to have risen by 6.0 % in 2023, with 20 countries registering increases above 5 % (in green). [[Image:Titleyes_Median_income.jpg|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 6: Median income: year-on-year % change, 2023 vs 2022
''Source:'' Eurostat: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Experimental statistics: Flash estimates on Income inequality and poverty indicators]|alt= A bar chart showing the median income between in 2023 vs 2022 in EU countries. The vertical axis presents the year-on-year percentage change, while the horizontal axis presents the countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''EU median income in real terms nowcasted to remain stable in 2023''' The estimated 6.0 % nominal rise in median income across the EU translates into stable median income in real terms, estimated to have risen by 0.2 % in 2023 (see Figure 7). At EU level in 2023, prices were still rising for food and non-alcoholic beverages (12.6 %), while prices for electricity, gas, and other fuels showed more moderate annual average rate of change (1.4 %) following the significant increases in 2022 (42.4 %). [[Image:Median_income,_nominal_versus_real_terms,_EU,_2019-2023_(income_year).png |thumb|centre|600px|Figure 7: Median income, nominal versus real terms, EU, 2019-2023 (income year)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_li01}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_di18}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=ert_bil_eur_a}} and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Experimental statistics: Flash estimates on Income inequality and poverty indicators]|alt= A line chart showing the median income between 2019 and 2023 in the EU. The vertical axis presents the income in euro, while the horizontal axis presents the income year. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Map 1 compares the estimated values for median equivalised disposable income for 2023 in real terms at country level. As seen previously, though nominal estimates indicate positive changes for all countries, the real-term analysis reveals a more varied picture. Specifically, median disposable income is estimated to have increased in 16 countries and decreased in 5 (Czechia, Germany, France, Italy and Hungary). In 6 countries (Denmark, Cyprus, Latvia, Malta, Austria and Sweden), the real median income is thought to have remained stable. This diversity underscores the variable impact of inflation across the EU. [[Image:europe-ch (1).png|thumb|centre|500px| Map 1: Median income in real terms: year-on-year % change, 2023 vs 2022
''Source:'' Eurostat: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Experimental statistics: Flash estimates on Income inequality and poverty indicators]|alt= A map showing the median income in real terms in 2023 vs 2022 in the EU. The dark green colour presents the statistically significant increase, while the yellow and brown colour presents the statistically significant decreases. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''''Support measures to cope with rising inflation and the cost of living''''' In the standard methodology for flash estimates produced by Eurostat, policies and income support measures for households are simulated via EUROMOD. A comprehensive tax-benefit microsimulation model for the EU, EUROMOD simulates direct taxes and social insurance contributions, as well as most cash social benefits. An assessment of the impact of tax-benefit systems on income distribution and labour incentives within the EU can be found in the [https://euromod-web.jrc.ec.europa.eu/resources/other-reports EUROMOD baseline report 2023], a Joint Research Centre report that provides baseline results from EUROMOD version I6.0+, focusing on income poverty, inequality and work incentive indicators. For 2023, EUROMOD simulates the income support measures implemented at national level to shield consumers from rising and volatile energy prices. Anti-inflationary measures include indexation, lump sum benefits/transfers, social assistance benefits, housing benefits, child/family allowances, tax credits for electricity and adjustments to income tax brackets. These measures often target minimum living standards. This is the case for increases in unemployment benefits and minimum income levels, which support vulnerable sub-groups and low-income households. In particular, EUROMOD indicates a general positive impact for simulated family and child allowances in most EU countries in 2023. More information on these measures and on the policies simulated in EUROMOD in different countries can be found in the [https://euromod-web.jrc.ec.europa.eu/resources/country-reports EUROMOD Country Reports]. Note that standard income and poverty indicators in nominal terms do not account for changes in the cost of living. By contrast, inflation-adjusted indicators, such as median income in real terms at least partly reflect the impact of rising prices and related compensation measures (e.g. VAT cuts, social tariffs and price caps).
=== Inflation continues to increase in 2023 === Figure 8 illustrates the [[Glossary:Harmonised_index_of_consumer_prices_(HICP)|Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices]] (HICP) annual average rate of change for its main components in the EU in 2022 and 2023. The data highlights significant inflationary trends, with notable increases across several categories. In 2023, the overall HICP saw a substantial rise, reflecting broader inflationary pressures across the EU. Among the 12 main headings, the biggest rise in consumer prices in 2023 was for food and non-alcoholic beverages – up 12.6 % on average and continuing the upward trend in 2022. Restaurants and hotels followed, with an average increase of 8.4 %, while alcoholic beverages and tobacco rose by an average of 7.8 %. Housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels also saw a substantial but more moderate rises (3.4 % on average), following the dramatic price hikes in 2022 (18 %). [[Image:HICP,_Annual_average_rate_of_change,_EU,_2022_and_2023.png|thumb|centre|600px| Figure 8: HICP, annual average rate of change, EU, 2022 and 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=prc_hicp_aind}}|alt= A horizontal bar chart showing the HICP, annual average rate of change between 2022 and 2023 in the EU. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 9 illustrates the annual average rate of change in 2023 compared to 2022 for the overall HICP (red dots), and the two main contributing headings for the last 2 years: ’Food and non-alcoholic beverages’ (blue bars), and ’Housing, water, electricity, gas, and other fuels’ (gold bars). The chart reveals a very heterogeneous situation across the EU, with the overall HICP ranging from 17 % in Hungary down to 2.3 % in Belgium. Among the HICP main headings, the EU annual average rate of change is particularly high (12.6 %) for ‘food and non-alcoholic beverages’, with all countries experiencing significant increases. This rise was especially pronounced in Hungary (23.8 %), Slovakia (17.3 %), Poland (15.9 %), and Estonia (15.6 %). Housing and utility costs also increased considerably in 20 countries, but went down in 7 countries (Belgium, Denmark, Greece, Spain, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden) despite the overall inflationary trend. The impact of these headings on the HICP overall varies across countries due to their different weights, which means the contribution of each component to the overall HICP can differ from one country to another. [[Image:HICP_Annual_average_rate_of_change_2023_versus_2022_%.png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 9: HICP, Annual average rate of change, 2023 versus 2022, %
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=prc_hicp_aind}}|alt= A stacked bar chart showing the HICP, Annual average rate of change in 2023 vs 2022 in the EU. The vertical axis presents the percentage, while the horizontal axis presents the following categories: food and non-alcoholic beverages, housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels and HICP- Overall. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 10 illustrates the median share of disposable income spent on specific essential items by households within the EU across different income quintiles, based on the latest Eurostat figures from the 2020 wave of the joint income, consumption and wealth experimental datasetAvailable for 22 countries.. Households in the lowest income quintile spent more than the 80 % of their disposable income on ‘Food and non-alcoholic beverages’ (blue bars) and ‘Housing, water, electricity, gas, and other fuels’ (gold bars). There is a clear inverse relationship between income level and the share of income spent on essential services. As income increases, the percentage of income spent on essential items decreases. This trend highlights the greater financial burden faced by lower-income households in meeting basic needs, compared to their higher-income counterparts. Recent price rises are thus more likely to affect the material wellbeing of low-income households, as they spend a larger portion of their income on these essential items. [[Image:Median_income_spent_on_essential_items_by_income_quintile,_EU,_%,_2020.png|thumb|centre|600px| Figure 10: Median income spent on essential items by income quintile, EU, %, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=icw_aff_01}}|alt= A stacked bar chart showing the median income spent on essential items in 2020 in the EU. The vertical axis presents the percentage, while the horizontal axis presents income quintile for 2 categories: food and non-alcoholic beverages and housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Feedback=== To help Eurostat improve these experimental statistics, users and researchers are kindly invited to give us their [mailto:ESTAT-FLASH-EST-INCOME@ec.europa.eu?subject=Feedback_on_experimental_statistics feedback by email]. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=SE_Flash_estimates_income_inequalities_v3a.xlsx |title=Flash estimates of income inequalities during the 2023 income data: tables and figures}} === Data sources === The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/overview EU-SILC] indicators provide insights into the economic wellbeing and other living conditions on EU residents based on data collected during a specific year, denoted as N. This data encompasses both the characteristics of households for that year (N) and the income from the preceding year, N 1. The income for year N-1 is an estimate for income of year N within the EU-SILC. To consider differences in household size and composition and thus enable comparisons of income levels, the concept of equivalised disposable income is used. It is based on the total net (also referred to as disposable) household income divided by the number of 'equivalent adults', using a standard (equivalence) scale. [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Eurostat flash estimates] complement structural and detailed indicators from the EU-SILC to capture the latest income changes. They offer early indicative results for income year N, supporting the EU's policy agenda until the EU-SILC data become available. Flash estimates are based on modelling and microsimulation techniquesThe flash estimates for Romania are based on current income information collected through the Household Budget Survey ([[Glossary:HBS|HBS]] – Romania) and for Sweden on the national microsimulation model. that consider the complex interaction between labour market developments, economic and monetary policies, and the implementation of social reforms. In terms of data sources, Eurostat uses the latest information on labour from the 2023 [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/lfs Employment and unemployment (Labour Force Survey)] together with the [https://euromod-web.jrc.ec.europa.eu/overview/what-is-euromod EUROMOD] microsimulation model, which provides the effects of direct taxes, social security contributions and benefits on household income. The section of the article on inflation is based on the [[Glossary:HICP|HICP]], which is an index for measuring the change in prices of consumer goods and services acquired by households in monetary transactions. See [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Consumer_prices_-_inflation#Inflation:_price_changes_over_time_in_the_European_Union Consumer prices - inflation] for more information on this topic. === Context === Indicators on poverty and income inequality are based on EU statistics on income and living conditions ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/overview EU-SILC]). The [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|AROP]] is part of the at risk of poverty or social-exclusion rate defined in connection with the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:The_European_Pillar_of_Social_Rights_Action_Plan_(EU_2030_targets) EU 2030 target on poverty and social exclusion] [[Glossary:At_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_(AROPE)|(AROPE)]]. Providing timelier social statistics – especially indicators on income poverty and inequality – is a priority for the Commission and the [[Glossary:European_statistical_system_(ESS) |European Statistical System]]. To better monitor the effectiveness of social policies at EU level, [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators flash estimates] offer early indicative results for income year N, until EU SILC data become available. These estimates, which are part of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics experimental statistics] produced by Eurostat, have a release date appreciably earlier than the survey data: i.e. flash estimates for the 2023 income year are published in June 2024, complementing the EU SILC 2023 data which refers to the 2022 income year. These estimates can be used in preliminary discussions and analysis until the final EU-SILC 2024 data for 2023 income are available in 2025. While the standard nowcasting methodology focuses on nominal data, additional analysis in the article reflects the estimated impact of inflation in 2023. For 2023, EUROMOD includes the simulation of income measures to shield consumers from rising energy prices in several countries. These measures encompass indexation, lump sum benefits/transfers, social assistance benefits, housing benefits, children/family allowances, tax credits for electricity, and increased income tax brackets often related to minimum living standards (increase in unemployment benefits, minimum income, etc.). However, flash estimates based on EUROMOD do not account for changes in indirect taxes or household expenditures and do not capture the effects of a complete range of price-related measures, such as VAT changes, social tariffs and price caps. It should be noted that most of the policies implemented to counter inflation in 2022 were not continued in 2023 in countries such as Belgium, Bulgaria, Denmark, Estonia, Spain, Hungary, Ireland, Lithuania, Latvia, the Netherlands and Slovakia. More information on the specific policy measures simulated in EUROMOD in different countries can be found in the [https://euromod-web.jrc.ec.europa.eu/resources/country-reports EUROMOD country reports]. === Other Articles === * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Latest_developments_in_income_dynamics_and_poverty&stable=0 Latest developments in income dynamics and poverty] === Selected Datasets === * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/7894008/8256843/main-results-2023.xlsx/680d1fa4-bdeb-6c3e-38f7-9ec6d5c5332e?t=1718699388937 Data in 2023 income estimates] === Thematic section === [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Experimental statistics on income inequality and poverty indicators] === Methodology === [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/7894008/8256843/flash-estimates-methodological-note-2023.pdf/6f25bba0-07c5-7126-3571-19b58e47514a?t=1718682336317 Methodological note FE 2023]. === External links === [https://euromod-web.jrc.ec.europa.eu/ EUROMOD Tax-benefit microsimulation model for the European Union] === Footnotes === {{Unit|topic=X_Social_statistics}} [[category:Population and social conditions|Flash estimates of income inequalities]] [[Category:Living conditions|Flash estimates of income inequalities]] [[Category:Household income, expenditure and debt|Flash estimates of income inequalities]] [[Category:Experimental statistics|Flash estimates of income inequalities]] [[Category:Statistical article|Flash estimates of income inequalities]] [[Category:No update|Flash estimates of income inequalities]]

title: Foreign-controlled enterprises statistics - inward FATS
text:
EU statistics on foreign affiliates measuring the importance of enterprises resident in one country which are controlled by a unit resident in another. Data extracted in November 2025 Planned article update: 8 October 2026 In 2023, foreign-controlled enterprises accounted for 1.1% of enterprises that were active within the EU's business market producers. In 2023, approximately one quarter of the total value added in the business market producers of the EU was generated by foreign-controlled enterprises. In 2023, the United States accounted for the largest share of the EU workforce employed by foreign affiliates in the EU that were ultimately controlled by residents from outside the EU. [[Image: Share_ENT_EMPL_AV_2023v3.jpg|thumb|centre|600px|''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=fats_activ}}|alt= Scatter chart showing percentage of total foreign controlled enterprises in the EU, individual EU countries and candidate countries. Each country has three scatter plots representing value added, employees and self-employed persons, and number of enterprises for the year 2023.]] [[Glossary:Structural business statistics (SBS)|Structural business statistics]] on inward [[Glossary:Foreign_affiliates_statistics_(FATS)|foreign affiliates]] provide information that may be used to measure the impact of globalisation, for example, through indicators covering [[Glossary:Net turnover - EBS|net turnover]], [[Glossary:Number of employees and self-employed persons - EBS|employment]], productivity or innovation performance. The statistics presented in this article concern activities within the business [[Glossary:Market producer|market producers]], as defined by [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] Sections B-S (except Section O and Division 94).
'''Statistics on foreign affiliates''' For statistical purposes, foreign affiliates are considered to be enterprises resident in one country and controlled by a unit resident in another. There are two distinct sources of information: so-called inward FATS which cover the activities of enterprises within the EU that are under foreign control, and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Foreign-controlled_enterprises_statistics_-_outward_FATS outward FATS ] which cover the activities of EU affiliates abroad. The globalised economy is increasingly characterised by intricate business networks. As a result, it can be difficult to untangle these complicated and often blurred chains of control. To do so, statistics on foreign affiliates are compiled according to the ultimate controlling institutional unit (UCI) — determined by proceeding up a foreign affiliate's chain of control until there is no further controlling interest; by doing so, potential double-counting of the same affiliates (by several countries) can be avoided. In this context, control refers to the ownership of a controlling share of the shareholders' voting power and the ability to determine the general policy of an enterprise, for example by choosing appropriate directors. In this way, an enterprise is said to be controlled by an institutional unit when the latter (a single investor or a group of investors acting together) owns — directly or indirectly — more than half of the voting shares in the enterprise.
===Foreign-controlled enterprises in the EU=== '''''One of the most striking aspects concerning foreign-controlled enterprises is their very small absolute number''''' In 2023, foreign-controlled enterprises accounted for just 1.1% of enterprises that were active within the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|EU's]] business market producers. Over 60% of foreign-controlled enterprises were ultimately controlled by a unit from one of the other EU countries compared with enterprises ultimately controlled by a unit from non-EU countries. As such, geographical proximity would appear to be an important determining factor when foreign investors consider their options — perhaps reflecting some caution to first invest in nearby markets (which may also be culturally and/or linguistically close) before considering investments further afield (both geographically or culturally). Indeed, the attractiveness of different countries can often be linked to proximity, historical, cultural or linguistic ties with, for example, a high proportion of the foreign-controlled enterprises in Ireland are ultimately controlled by units from the United Kingdom and the United States. The contribution of foreign-controlled enterprises to economic performance was much greater, both in terms of employment and, in particular, [[Glossary:Value added - EBS|value added]], than in terms of the number of enterprises. This may be explained, at least in part, by foreign-controlled enterprises generally being much larger in size than domestic (or nationally controlled) enterprises. In 2023, foreign-controlled enterprises provided work to almost one in seven (15.5%) persons that were employed within the EU's business market producers; their share of total value added was considerably higher, as foreign-controlled enterprises contributed 24.0% of the EU total. '''''In 2023, non-EU countries controlled almost three-quarters of the foreign-controlled enterprises in Ireland ''''' In 2023, nearly a third (27.9%) of all enterprises in the business market producers in Luxembourg were foreign-controlled; this share was considerably higher than in any of the other EU countries, as the next highest share was in Estonia (10.9%). At the other end of the range, the share of foreign-controlled enterprises in the total enterprise population was less than 1.0% in Belgium, Cyprus, France, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden. The lowest share were recorded in France, Italy and Poland (0.1%). In 2023, a significant majority of foreign-controlled enterprises in Slovakia (80.6%) and Greece (78.3%) were ultimately under the control of a unit from another EU country. At the other end of the range, almost three-quarters of the foreign-controlled enterprises in Ireland (73.2%) and a bit over half of the foreign-controlled enterprises in Malta (57.9%) were controlled by institutional units resident outside the EU. '''''In 2023, over two-fifths of the business market producers workforce of Luxembourg were employed by foreign-controlled enterprises ''''' As seen for the number of enterprises, Luxembourg recorded the highest share in 2023 — among the EU countries — of its business market producers workforce employed by foreign-controlled enterprises (44.5%); note also that there is a sizeable financial services sector in Luxembourg and that this too is characterised by a strong international presence. Slovakia also had a high share (28.0%) of its business market producers workforce employed by foreign-controlled enterprises (see Figure 1). [[Image: Share_ENT_EMPL_AV_2023v3.jpg|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Share of foreign-controlled enterprises, business market producers, 2023 (% of total)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=fats_activ}}|alt= Scatter chart showing percentage of total foreign controlled enterprises in the EU, individual EU countries and candidate countries. Each country has three scatter plots representing value added, employees and self-employed persons, and number of enterprises for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In addition to Luxembourg and Slovakia, 3 other EU countries had a significant presence of foreign-controlled enterprises in their business economy workforce in 2023 — Czechia (27.5%), Ireland (27.3%) and Romania (26.9%) — many characterised by relatively low [[Wages_and_labour_costs|wage costs]] and high numbers of people working for foreign-controlled enterprises in the manufacturing sector, often controlled by units from other EU countries. In a few countries, a majority of those working for foreign-controlled enterprises in 2023 were employed by an enterprise that was controlled from outside the EU, the largest share by far was employed in Ireland (79.0%). '''''Foreign-controlled enterprises generated more than two-thirds of the value added for the Irish business market producers in 2023''''' In 2023, at least one-seventh of the total value added in the business market producers economies of each of the EU countries was generated by foreign-controlled enterprises. Among the countries with relatively low shares were France (15.4%), Italy (17.4%), Greece (17.7%), and Germany (18.2%). Meanwhile, eleven EU countries saw shares within the 20-30% range. Additionally, another eleven EU countries experienced shares between 30-60% and in Ireland foreign-controlled enterprises accounted for more than two-thirds (71.3%) of total value added in the Irish business market producers' 2023. ===Foreign-controlled enterprises by economic activity=== '''''The United States accounted for the largest share of the EU workforce employed by foreign affiliates in the EU that were ultimately controlled by residents from outside the EU''''' Table 1 presents an analysis for some of the activities where foreign affiliates were most prominent. In 2023, among the foreign-controlled enterprises whose ultimate control was located outside the EU, the highest share of the workforce in these activities was almost exclusively accounted for by enterprises that were ultimately controlled by units from the United States. The two exceptions were manufacture of electrical equipment and manufacture of coke and refined petroleum products where a higher share of the workforce was employed by enterprises ultimately controlled by units respectively from Switzerland the United Kingdom, followed by the United States in second place. For most of these activities with a high contribution of value added from foreign affiliates, Switzerland and the United Kingdom were often the second or third most common location of control outside of the EU. Japan and China also figured in the top 3, taking second and third place for the manufacture of motor vehicles and Japan being third in Manufacture of electrical equipment. [[Image:T1Share of employment among extra-EU foreign-controlled enterprises for selected economic activities, EU, 2023v2.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: Share of employment among extra-EU foreign-controlled enterprises for selected economic activities, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=fats_activ}}|alt= Table showing share of employment among extra-EU foreign-controlled enterprises for selected economic activities in the EU. Each activity has three named countries as having the highest, second highest and third highest share for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Foreign-controlled enterprises: intra-mural R & D expenditure=== '''''Over one fifth of the expenditure on intra-mural R & D that took place within the EU's industry and construction sectors in 2023 was accounted for by foreign-controlled enterprises''''' Although corporate [[Glossary:Research and development (R %26 D)|research and development (R & D)]] activities often remain highly concentrated close to headquarters of [[Glossary:Multinational enterprise (MNE)|multinational enterprises]], there is some evidence to suggest that foreign-controlled enterprises in the EU may be more R & D intensive than their nationally-owned competitors. Indeed, foreign-controlled enterprises are seen as an integral part of some national innovation systems, as the research activities of large multinationals can potentially benefit host nations by promoting knowledge and technology transfers. In 2023, foreign-controlled enterprises accounted for over one-quarter (25.0%) of intra-mural R & D expenditure within the industrial and construction sectors (NACE Sections B-F) of 18 EU Member States (see Figure 2 for data availability), and a slightly higher share (25.2%) of the total number of [[Glossary:Research and development (R %26 D) personnel and researchers|R & D personnel]] (16 Member States; see Figure 3). [[Image: IM RND EXPN B-F by CTL of ENT 2023v3.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Intra-mural R & D expenditure in industry and construction, by control of enterprise, 2023
(% of total)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=fats_activ_rd}}|alt= Queued horizontal bar chart showing intra-mural R&D expenditure in industry and construction by control of enterprise as percentage of total in the EU, individual EU Member States. Each country bar has three queues representing reporting EU Member States, intra-EU and extra-EU for the year 2023.]] In Czechia, Ireland, Hungary, Luxembourg, Romania, Slovakia, Spain and Sweden more than half of the expenditure on intra-mural R & D that took place in industry and construction in 2023 was accounted for by foreign-controlled enterprises, as well as the majority of R & D personnel in those countries (except Spain) worked for a foreign-controlled enterprise. [[Image:RND PER B-F by CTL of ENT 2023v3.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: R & D personnel in industry and construction, by control of enterprise, 2023
(% of total)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=fats_activ_rd}}|alt= Queued horizontal bar chart showing R&D personnel in industry and construction by control of enterprise as percentage of total in the EU, individual EU Member States. Each country bar has three queues representing reporting EU Member States, intra-EU and extra-EU for the year 2023.]] === Source data for tables and figures (MS Excel) === *{{Template:Excel|filename=IFATS 2023v3.xlsx|title=Inward foreign affiliates statistics: tables and figures}} === Other articles === *[[Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/globalisation-businesses/database] , see: ::Foreign controlled EU enterprises - inward FATS (fats) === Thematic section ==== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/globalisation-businesses/overview] === Methodology === '''Metadata''' *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/fats_sims.htm Foreign controlled EU enterprises - inward FATS (fats) (ESMS metadata file — fats_esms)] '''Further methodological information''' *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/globalisation-businesses/methodology] === Legislation === *[http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2017:240:FIN European Commission — reflection paper on harnessing globalisation (COM(2017) 240)] {{Unit|topic=X_Globalisation}} [[Category:Industry, trade, and services|Inward foreign affiliates statistics]] [[Category:Globalisation of businesses|Inward foreign affiliates statistics]] [[Category:Foreign controlled enterprises|Inward foreign affiliates statistics]] [[Category:Statistical article|Inward foreign affiliates statistics]] [[Category:October2026|Inward foreign affiliates statistics]]

title: Foreign direct investment - stocks
text:
EU statistics on foreign direct investment (FDI) stocks measuring the total value of direct investment at a given point in time. Data by partner, by economic activity and the share of EU countries in the EU total. Data extracted in January 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 At the end of 2024, the United States and the United Kingdom were the principal locations for stocks of EU outward investment; they were also the principal inward investors in the EU, along with offshore financial centres. [[Image:Extra-EU foreign direct investment positions, by partner, EU, 2024 (% of extra-EU total)_GL2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Extra-EU foreign direct investment positions, by partner, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6264323e-f7e8-4c9d-9fc3-fe9f8d658b57?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-05T17:19:50Z bop_fdi6_pos])|alt=A double bar chart showing the EU’s foreign direct investment positions with a selection of non-EU countries. For each partner, bars are shown presenting the share of extra-EU investment abroad and the share of direct investment in the EU. Data are presented for the EU for 2024. Data are shown in percent. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ''[[Globalisation_patterns_in_EU_trade_and_investment|Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment]]'' is an online [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publication presenting a summary of recent [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] statistics on economic aspects of globalisation, focusing on patterns of EU trade and investment. In a globalised economy, enterprises can make investments abroad to establish a commercial/territorial presence in foreign markets, for example, by founding hotel or retail chains. Within the [https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/26-gats.pdf General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS)], this type of trade in services is referred to as mode 3 (the supply of international services). [[Glossary:Foreign direct investment (FDI)|Foreign direct investment (FDI)]] stocks (or positions) measure the total value of direct investment at a given point in time; the statistics presented in this article focus on stocks as measured at the end of the year. === EU’s inward and outward investment by partner=== '''''At the end of 2024, the United States and the United Kingdom were the principal locations for the EU’s outward FDI stocks …''''' Comparing the EU’s positions for inward with outward investment, inward investment appears to be somewhat more concentrated in the hands of a relatively small number of developed economies; the EU’s outward stock of FDI was somewhat more widely distributed, for example including several developed and emerging economies (see Figure 1). At the end of 2024, the shares of the EU’s outward stocks of FDI located in Brazil, the United Kingdom, Mexico, China and India were all more than 1.0 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage point (pp)]] higher than the respective shares of FDI held in the EU by these countries. For example, while Brazil accounted for a -0.2% share of inward FDI positions in the EU economy, 3.0% of the EU’s outward stocks of FDI were held in Brazil. At the end of 2024, the United States had the biggest share (28.7%) of the EU’s FDI stocks abroad, valued at €2 673 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]]; the second largest partner was the United Kingdom (19.5%), with offshore financial centres (excluding Hong Kong and Singapore) having the third largest share (8.8%) and Switzerland the fourth largest (8.4%). Among the selected partner countries, Asian economies together accounted for 12.2% of the EU total (principally Singapore, China, India, the United Arab Emirates and Hong Kong). '''''… and were also among the largest inward investors in the EU, together with offshore financial centres''''' At the end of 2024, the United States held close to a third (31.0%) of the inward investment in the EU from the rest of the world; as such, the United States was the major holder of FDI stocks in the EU, valued at €2 243 billion. Offshore financial centres (17.9%) and the United Kingdom (17.5%) were the next largest holders of FDI in the EU. A majority of the stocks held by offshore financial centres were registered in the Cayman Islands, Bermuda, the British Virgin Islands and Jersey (as well as Singapore and Hong Kong for which data are presented separately). [[Image:Extra-EU foreign direct investment positions, by partner, EU, 2024 (% of extra-EU total)_GL2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Extra-EU foreign direct investment positions, by partner, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6264323e-f7e8-4c9d-9fc3-fe9f8d658b57?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-05T17:19:50Z bop_fdi6_pos])|alt=A double bar chart showing the EU’s foreign direct investment positions with selected non-EU countries. For each partner, bars are shown for the share of direct investment abroad and direct investment in the EU. Data are presented for the EU. Data are shown for 2024 and are expressed in percent (as a share of the extra-EU total). The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === EU’s inward and outward investment by activity=== '''''FDI stocks were concentrated in the services sector''''' An analysis of the EU’s international investment position at the end of 2023 reveals that the services sector – defined here as financial and insurance activities, distributive trades, professional, scientific and technical activities, information and communication, administrative and support service activities, real estate activities, transportation and storage, accommodation and food service activities, arts, entertainment and recreation, human health and social work activities, other service activities, education and public administration – accounted for 79.5% of the EU’s outward investment positions (direct investment abroad). '''''Inward FDI positions held in the EU at the end of 2023 for financial and insurance activities were valued at €4 394 billion''''' The activity structure of the EU’s FDI positions was dominated by financial and insurance activities and by manufacturing. At the end of 2023, both of these activities recorded a positive balance, with higher stocks of outward rather than inward investment. Most other activities (services and non-services) also registered positive balances, with higher stocks of EU investment abroad. The EU’s outward stocks of investment in financial and insurance activities were valued at €5 221 billion (see Figure 2), which was more than half (58.4%) of the total for all outward positions. The EU’s inward position for financial and insurance activities was valued at €4 394 billion (62.7% of the total). Manufacturing was the second largest activity by these measures, with the EU’s outward position valued at €1 406 billion and the inward position valued at €866 billion. [[Image:Extra-EU foreign direct investment positions, by economic activity, EU, 2023 (EUR billion)_GL2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Extra-EU foreign direct investment positions, by economic activity, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5c72eedf-fda9-400c-b6eb-f67900b6d9e4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-05T17:21:54Z bop_fdi6_pos])|alt=A double bar chart showing the EU’s foreign direct investment positions by economic activity. For each economic activity, bars are shown for the share of direct investment abroad and direct investment in the EU. Data are presented for the EU. Data are shown for 2023 and are expressed in billions of euro. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 3 presents a more detailed analysis of the EU’s FDI positions abroad within manufacturing. It shows that, at the end of 2023, a majority of the EU’s outward stocks of FDI within manufacturing were held in the following activities: chemicals, food, beverages and tobacco, transport equipment and pharmaceuticals. Each of these activities recorded a double-digit share of the EU’s outward stock of FDI in manufacturing, with a peak of 15.9% for chemicals. By contrast, textiles and wearing apparel accounted for one of the lowest shares of the EU’s outward stock of FDI in manufacturing activities (2.2% of the manufacturing total); this may suggest that enterprises involved in the manufacture of these goods made use of alternative forms of industrial organisation (for example, outsourcing or subcontracting). [[Image:Extra-EU foreign direct investment positions abroad, by manufacturing activity, EU, 2023 (% of manufacturing total)_GL2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Extra-EU foreign direct investment positions abroad, by manufacturing activity, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/243f72a8-b582-4a6d-a83a-eaa320f81349?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-05T17:22:33Z bop_fdi6_pos])|alt=A bar chart showing the EU’s direct investment positions abroad for detailed manufacturing activities. Data for each activity are presented as a share of the manufacturing total. Data are shown for 2023 and are expressed in percent. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===FDI positions in EU countries=== '''''The Netherlands and Luxembourg together held almost half of all the EU’s FDI outward stocks at the end of 2024''''' Figure 4 presents the inward and outward FDI positions of EU countries; note the information presented includes not only stocks of FDI held in non-EU countries but also stocks in other EU countries. At the end of 2024, the Netherlands and Luxemburg both accounted for high shares of the total inward and outward investment positions of EU countries. Indeed, the Netherlands (24.9%) and Luxembourg (21.8%) together held nearly half (46.7%) of the outward stock of FDI; note that for both of these countries (especially Luxembourg), [[Glossary:Special-purpose_entity_(SPE)|special purpose entities (SPEs)]] continue to play a significant role. The pattern for inward investment positions was quite similar, as the Netherlands (24.2%) and Luxembourg (18.5%) again held the highest shares among EU countries at the end of 2024; the next highest share was 8.2% in Germany. Note that while Germany had an 8.2% share of the EU’s inward investment positions, its share of the EU’s outward FDI positions was higher, at 12.2% at the end of 2024. A similar pattern was observed for France, which held 8.6% of the EU’s outward positions, some 2.2 pp higher than its share of inward investment (6.4%). Based on the value of FDI stocks (rather than shares of the EU total), the EU countries which were net investors – with a higher value of stocks abroad at the end of 2024 – included Luxembourg, Germany, the Netherlands, France, Belgium, Italy, Sweden, Ireland, Denmark, Austria and Finland. [[Image:Foreign direct investment positions, 2024 (% of EU total)_GL2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Foreign direct investment positions, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=bop_fdi6_pos}}|alt=A high-low chart showing EU countries’ shares of the EU direct investment. The high-low markers compare the shares for direct investment abroad with direct investment in the reporting economy. Data are shown for 2024 and are expressed in percent. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Foreign direct investment - stocks GL2026.xlsx|title=Foreign direct investment - stocks: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The various analyses presented in this article – by partner country, by activity and for EU countries – are based on the latest data available: for the analysis by partner country and for EU countries, the most recent reference period is 2024; for the analysis by activity, the latest period is 2023. The analyses by partner country and by activity are presented in relation to the EU’s FDI stocks with non-EU countries (also referred to as extra-EU stocks). The analyses for EU countries include not only extra-EU stocks but also stocks of FDI between EU countries (also referred to as intra-EU stocks). Analyses of FDI stocks are based on a fixed list of countries: Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, Chile, China, Egypt, Hong Kong, India, Israel, Japan, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Mexico, Norway, Qatar, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, South Korea, Switzerland, Taiwan, Türkiye, Ukraine, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the United States and Uruguay; note also that an additional aggregate has been included with these partners, namely, offshore financial centres. The analyses of EU investment by partner are based on a fixed list of countries: Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, Egypt, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Israel, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, Morocco, Nigeria, Norway, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, South Korea, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, Türkiye, Ukraine, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States, as well as offshore financial centres. Note that information for Hong Kong and Singapore is shown separately and hence these 2 countries are excluded from the offshore financial centres aggregate (to avoid double-counting). ===Other title: Foreign direct investment - flows
text:
EU statistics on foreign direct investment (FDI) flows measuring the value of direct investment for the most recent year; data by partner; data by economic activity. Data extracted in January 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 In 2024, the United Kingdom and the United States dominated the EU’s outward investment flows, while Gibraltar was the largest source of inward investment flows. In 2023, distributive trades accounted for the highest value of FDI flows into EU countries (€59.0 billion) and the highest value of FDI flows abroad from EU countries (€59.1 billion). [[Image:Top 10 partners for flows of extra-EU foreign direct investment, EU, 2024 (EUR billion)_GL2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Top 10 partners for flows of extra-EU foreign direct investment, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bd2ec29b-f8c5-4fc2-bc8b-d9360a27bbb2?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-05T18:03:15Z bop_fdi6_geo])|alt=Two column charts showing the value of flows of foreign direct investment for the year 2024. Data are shown for the EU’s top 10 partners. One chart shows EU flows abroad and the other chart shows flows into the EU. Data are presented in billions of euro. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ''[[Globalisation_patterns_in_EU_trade_and_investment|Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment]]'' is an online [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publication presenting a summary of recent [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] statistics on economic aspects of globalisation, focusing on patterns of EU trade and investment. As with domestic investment, flows of [[Glossary:Foreign direct investment (FDI)|foreign direct investment (FDI)]] can exhibit a very high degree of volatility from one year to the next. These changes may be linked to global economic events, sector-specific developments or the individual situations of enterprises considering foreign investments. The information presented in this article examines flows of FDI between the EU and non-EU countries. ===Recent developments in EU FDI flows === The time series available for the EU’s FDI flows (based on the latest methodology) begins in 2013, several years after the global financial and economic crisis. By 2014, inward and outward flows of FDI had started to recover from that crisis. Nevertheless, investment flows followed a fluctuating pattern between 2014 and 2024 (see the article on [[World direct investment patterns|world direct investment patterns]]), suggesting there was a sustained period of uncertainty among investors. *Between 2014 and 2017, the development for the value of flows – both outward and inward – remained positive with fluctuations from one year to the next. *The situation changed in 2018, when there was a marked fall in investment levels, both for inward and outward flows; indeed, the value of EU direct investment abroad (-€149.3 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]]) and the value of direct investment into the EU (-€231.1 billion) turned negative (indicating reverse investment or disinvestment in both directions). *In 2019 and 2020, the EU’s FDI flows returned to positive – although relatively low – values. *In 2021, the direction of change diverged, as the first of 4 consecutive negative values was recorded for direct investment into the EU, while the EU’s investment abroad remained positive (increasing compared with 2020). *In 2022 and 2023, negative values were recorded for both flows (more marked in 2023 than 2022). *In 2024, the value of inward investment into the EU remained negative (-€205.0 billion), while the EU’s investment abroad returned to a positive value (€58.8 billion). ===The EU’s FDI investment partners=== In 2024, a sizeable proportion of the EU’s outward flows of FDI were destined for the United Kingdom (€57.8 billion) or the United States (€30.2 billion). The next largest outward flow was €16.9 billion to Brazil. None of the remaining destinations recorded investments from the EU that exceeded €10.0 billion, although the value of EU outward investment flows to India and Mexico were only slightly lower than this level (see Figure 1). There were 5 countries (3 of which were offshore financial centres) for which the EU recorded negative outward investment flows that were larger than -€10.0 billion: the United Arab Emirates (-€64.7 billion), Jersey (-€24.6 billion), Canada (-€16.8 billion), Bermuda (-€14.4 billion) and the Dominican Republic (-€10.9 billion). In 2024, Gibraltar – also an offshore financial centre – was the biggest origin of inward investment flows into the EU, providing €48.1 billion of FDI, considerably higher than any other partner. The next largest flows of FDI into the EU were from Australia (€12.1 billion) and China (€10.6 billion). None of the remaining partners provided investments into the EU that exceeded €10.0 billion, with the next highest levels from 2 more offshore financial centres, namely, Jersey (€6.1 billion) and Liechtenstein (€3.5 billion). There were 9 countries for which the EU recorded negative inward investment flows larger than -€10.0 billion in 2024. The largest of these values were recorded for the United States (-€63.4 billion) and Hong Kong (-€49.2 billion). The EU was a net recipient of FDI from 8 out of the 10 largest investors in the EU in 2024, the exceptions being South Korea and Türkiye. The EU was a net investor in all of the top 10 destinations for its outward investment flows. [[Image:Top 10 partners for flows of extra-EU foreign direct investment, EU, 2024 (EUR billion)_GL2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Top 10 partners for flows of extra-EU foreign direct investment, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bd2ec29b-f8c5-4fc2-bc8b-d9360a27bbb2?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-05T18:03:15Z bop_fdi6_geo])|alt=Two column charts showing the value of flows of foreign direct investment. Data are shown for the EU’s top 10 partners. One chart shows EU direct investment flows abroad and the other shows flows of direct investment in the EU. Data are presented in billions of euro. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===EU FDI flows by activity=== '''''In 2023, distributive trades accounted for the highest value of EU inward and outward flows of FDI''''' In 2023, the largest flows of outward FDI (calculated as the sum of FDI flows between EU countries and FDI flows to non-EU countries) were recorded for distributive trades (€59.1 billion), electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply (€27.6 billion) and information and communication (€20.5 billion) – see Figure 2. Distributive trades also recorded the highest value of inward investment flows (calculated as the sum of FDI flows between EU countries and FDI flows from non-EU countries), at €59.0 billion in 2023, followed by professional, scientific and technical activities (€27.8 billion) and administrative and support service activities (€24.4 billion). By far, the largest negative values (reverse investment or disinvestment) were recorded for financial and insurance activities, at -€441.6 billion for outward FDI and -€503.0 billion for inward FDI. [[Image:Foreign direct investment flows, by economic activity, EU, 2023 (EUR billion)_GL2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Foreign direct investment flows, by economic activity, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a4870383-b991-48a2-aa1d-2b6ab0e79fc2?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-05T18:01:44Z bop_fdi6_flow])|alt=A double bar chart showing the value of foreign direct investment flows by economic activity. Each economic activity has bars representing EU direct investment flows abroad and direct investment flows into the EU. Data are presented for 2023 and are expressed in billions of euro. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Foreign direct investment - flows GL2026.xlsx|title=Foreign direct investment - flows: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The 2 analyses presented in this article – by partner country and by economic activity – are based on the latest data available: for the analysis by partner country, the most recent reference period is 2024; for the analysis by activity, the latest reference period is 2023. The overall level of inward and outward FDI flows were considerably different in 2024 from those in 2023. In 2023, both flows were negative (indicating reverse investment or disinvestment in both directions), whereas in 2024 flows of direct investment into the EU remained negative, while flows of EU direct investment abroad turned positive. Note the analysis by partner country is for the EU’s FDI flows with non-EU countries (also referred to as extra-EU flows). The analysis by activity includes not only extra-EU flows but also FDI flows between EU countries (also referred to as intra-EU flows). === Other articles === *[[Globalisation patterns in EU trade and
