title: Gender pay gap statistics
text:
EU statistics on gender pay gap show the inequalities between wages of men and women, by working profile, economic activity, age, and public/private sector. Data extracted in February 2026 Planned article update: February 2027 In 2024, the average unadjusted gender pay gap in the EU was 11.1%. In 2024, in the EU, Estonia and Luxembourg recorded the highest (18.8%) and lowest (-0.8%) gender pay gaps respectively, before accounting for factors that affect final pay. |alt= Interactive vertical bar chart showing the unadjusted gender pay gap as percentages of male gross earnings for the EU, euro area, individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Norway and Iceland for the year 2024. This article provides a brief overview of gender pay gap [[Glossary:Gender pay gap|(GPG)]] statistics, including the unadjusted gender pay gap used to monitor imbalances in earnings between men and women. The unadjusted gender pay gap is defined as the difference between the average gross hourly earnings of male and female employees expressed as a percentage of the average gross hourly earnings of male employees. It is calculated for enterprises with 10 or more employees. === Gender pay gap levels vary significantly across EU === For the economy as a wholeHere defined as industry, construction and services except public administration and defence and compulsory social security: [[Glossary:Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)|NACE]] Rev. 2 Sections B to S with the exception of Section O., in 2024, women's gross hourly earnings were on average 11.1% less than those of men in the European Union ([[Glossary:EU-27|EU]]) ; 11.4% in the [[Glossary:Euro area|euro area]]. Across EU countries, the gender pay gap varied by 19.6 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]], ranging from -0.8% in Luxembourg to 18.8% in Estonia (Figure 1). This means that, without correcting for differences in individual and job characteristics of employed men and women, Luxembourg is the only EU country where, on average, men earned less than women, in 2024. [[Image:Figure 1 The unadjusted gender pay gap, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: The unadjusted gender pay gap, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sdg_05_20__custom_20276997/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=d667ba1a-56a5-4735-8be6-1cf4cdf820fb&c=1772183977000 sdg_05_20])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the unadjusted gender pay gap as percentages of male gross earnings for the EU, euro area, individual EU Member States and some EFTA countries for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Part-time versus full-time employment === Pay gaps can also be analysed from the perspective of part-time or full-time employment (Figure 2). However, information at this level of detail is not available for all EU countries. In 2024, the gender pay gap for part-time workers varied from -8.3% in Bulgaria to 23.8% in Slovenia. A negative unadjusted gender pay gap means that, on average, women's gross hourly earnings are higher than those of men. These negative gaps should be analysed in the context of the characteristics of employees and the labour market: women engaging in the labour market may have comparatively higher skills and education levels than men. For full-time workers, pay gaps varied also widely across the EU countries in 2024, ranging from -8.1% in Belgium to 19.9% in Latvia. [[Image:The unadjusted gender pay gap by working time, 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: The unadjusted gender pay gap by working time, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/earn_gr_gpgr2wt__custom_20277083/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=d8a29b16-6ca0-460a-8fb4-eb9389cb281e&c=1772185465000 earn_gr_gpgr2wt]); see [[Glossary:Country codes|Country codes]]|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the unadjusted gender pay gap by working time as percentages for individual EU Member States and EFTA countries. Each country has two columns representing part-time and full-time work for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Gender pay gap much lower for young employees=== The gender pay gap is generally much lower for new entrants into the labour market and it tends to widen with age. However, those differences over age groups can have different patterns across the EU countries and across age groups within the same country (Table 1). In the age group < 25 years, Estonia and Lithuania showed the greatest values for gender pay gaps in 2024 (18.8% and 12.8% respectively), meaning that, on average, men’s gross hourly earnings are higher than those of women. The gender pay gap might increase with age as a result of the career interruptions women may experience during their working life more often than men. Information at this level of detail is not available, however, for all EU countries. [[Image:The unadjusted gender pay gap by age, 2024 v3.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: The unadjusted gender pay gap by age, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/earn_gr_gpgr2ag__custom_20277998/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=6dbbc320-199c-490b-9852-bf56781b769b&c=1772185549000 earn_gr_gpgr2ag]); see [[Glossary:Country codes|Country codes]]|alt= Table showing the unadjusted gender pay gap by age group as percentages for individual EU Member States and EFTA countries for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Highest gender pay gap in financial and insurance activities === A breakdown for the different sectors of the economy also reveals interesting patterns (Table 2). However, information at this level of detail is not available for all EU countries. In the EU countries where data is available, except Spain, the gender pay gap in financial and insurance activities ([[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE]] Rev. 2 section K) is higher than in the business economy as a whole (NACE Rev. 2 aggregate B to N). In 2024, the gender pay gap in financial and insurance activities varied from 12.2% in Spain to 40.3% in Hungary. Within the business economy as a whole, the lowest gender pay gap was recorded in Malta (4.5%) and the highest in Estonia (22.6%). [[Image:The unadjusted gender pay gap by economic activity, 2024 v3.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 2: The unadjusted gender pay gap by economic activity, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/earn_gr_gpgr2__custom_20296409/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=4e660551-e5a8-44df-a748-578aa81865e9&c=1772187910000 earn_gr_gpgr2]); see [[Glossary:Country codes|Country codes]]|alt= Table showing the unadjusted gender pay gap by economic activity as percentages for individual EU Member States and EFTA countries for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] It is also interesting to highlight the economic activities for which a significant number of EU countries recorded negative gender gaps in 2024. In particular, 13 EU countries recorded negative gender pay gaps in the water supply, sewerage, waste management and remediation activities (NACE Rev. 2 section E) and 14 in the construction sector (NACE Rev. 2 section F). ===Gender pay gap higher in the private sector=== In 2024, all EU countries (for which data are available), except Slovenia, recorded a higher gender pay gap (in absolute terms) in the private sector than in the public sector (Table 3). This might be due to the fact that, in most EU countries, pay in the public sector is determined by transparent wage grids that apply equally to men and women. The gender pay gap varied in the private sector from 6.1% in Belgium to 21.8% in Portugal, and in the public sector from -3.5% in Cyprus to 17.4% in Czechia. [[Image:The unadjusted gender pay gap by economic control, 2024 v4.png|thumb|centre|500px|Table 3: The unadjusted gender pay gap by economic control, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/earn_gr_gpgr2__custom_20296409/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=4e660551-e5a8-44df-a748-578aa81865e9&c=1772195491000 earn_gr_gpgr2ct]); see [[Glossary:Country codes|Country codes]]|alt= Table showing the unadjusted gender pay gap by economic control, that is public and private as percentages for individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Norway and Iceland for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Possible causes of the unadjusted gender pay gap === As an unadjusted indicator, the gender pay gap gives an overall picture of the differences between men and women in terms of earnings and measures – a concept which is broader than discrimination in the sense of "equal pay for work of equal value". Indeed, parts of the difference in earnings of men and women can be explained by (1) differences in the average characteristics of male and female employees and (2) differences in the financial returns for the same characteristics. In the methodological study: {{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-035|title=Gender pay gaps in the European Union – 2025 edition}}, both drivers of the unadjusted gender pay gap are analysed based on the 2022 edition of the four-yearly Structure of Earnings Survey (SES). ===Data sources=== From reference year 2006 onwards, the unadjusted gender pay gap is based on the methodology of the [[Glossary:Structure of earnings survey (SES)|Structure of earnings survey (SES)]] according to {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31999R0530:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 530/1999}}. The SES is carried out with a four-yearly periodicity. The most recent reference years available for the SES are 2018 and 2022. Eurostat computed the gender pay gap for these years on this basis. For the intermediate years, EU Member States provide Eurostat gender pay gap estimates benchmarked on the SES results. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Gender pay gap statistics March-2026v5.xlsx|Gender pay gap statistics - tables and figures]] [[Image:Microsoft Excel 2010 Logo.png|20px|link=]] *[[Media:Gender pay gap statistics analytical tables.xlsx|Gender pay gap statistics - analytical tables]] [[Image:Microsoft Excel 2010 Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Context=== Reducing the gender pay gap is one of the key priorities of gender policies at both EU and national levels. At EU level, the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] prioritised "reducing the gender pay, earnings and pension gaps and thus fighting poverty among women" as one of the key areas in the framework of the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52020DC0152 A Union of Equality: Gender Equality Strategy 2020-2025]. The unadjusted gender pay gap indicator is used to monitor imbalances in earnings between men and women. The Pay Transparency Directive [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/970/oj (Directive (EU) 2023/970)] is currently being transposed into national law, and it aims at enhancing the application of the principle of equal pay for equal work or work of equal value between men and women through pay transparency standards and enforcement mechanisms. ===Other articles=== *[[Gender statistics]] *[[Earnings statistics]] *[[Minimum wage statistics]] *[[Wages and labour costs]] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-TC-18-003|title=A decomposition of the unadjusted gender pay gap using Structure of Earnings Survey data}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-FW-22-004|title=The life of women and men in Europe - A statistical portrait}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-035|title=Gender pay gaps in the European Union – 2025 edition}} ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/labour-market/database Labour market (including Labour Force Survey], see: :Earnings ::Gender pay gap in unadjusted form (earn_grgpg) :::Gender pay gap in unadjusted form - Nace rev.2 (earn_grgpg2) :::Gender pay gap in unadjusted form - Nace rev.1.1 (earn_grgpg1) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/labour-market/database Labour market (including Labour Force Survey], see: ::Gender pay gap in unadjusted form (sdg_05_20) ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=labour_market}} Labour market (including Labour Force Survey], see: :Earnings *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/equality-non-discrimination/overview], see: :Gender equality ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=earn_grgpg2_esms|title=Gender pay gap in unadjusted form - Nace Rev. 2}} (ESMS metadata file - earn_grgpg2_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=earn_ses_main_esms|title=Structure of earnings survey}} (ESMS metadata file - main indicators) *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-TC-18-003|title=A decomposition of the unadjusted gender pay gap using Structure of Earnings Survey data}} (Collection: Statistical working papers) ===Legislation=== *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31999R0530:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 530/1999}} * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/LSU/?uri=CELEX:31999R0530 Summaries of EU Legislation: Statistics on earnings and labour costs] ===External links=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/justice/gender-equality/gender-pay-gap/index_en.htm Equal Pay] - the gender pay gap in the EU, how the EU fights pay discrimination, actions for improving pay equality. *[http://ec.europa.eu/justice/gender-equality/index_en.htm European Commission - Justice] *[http://eurofound.europa.eu/ Eurofound] *[http://www.eige.europa.eu/ European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE)] === Footnotes === {{Unit|topic=X_Labour_market}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Gender pay gap statistics]] [[Category:Labour market (incl. labour force survey)|Gender pay gap statistics]] [[Category:Gender|Gender pay gap statistics]] [[Category:Wages and earnings|Gender pay gap statistics]] [[Category:Statistical_article|Gender pay gap statistics]] [[Category:February2027|Gender pay gap statistics]]

title: Global value chain disruptions and enterprise responses in the EU
text:
test test test Data extracted in December 2025 Planned article update: December 2028 Around 80% of enterprises experienced global value chain (GVC) constraints between 2021 and 2023. Among enterprises experiencing GVC constraints, 76% reported a moderate level of impact, and 58% reported a high level. The most frequently reported GVC constraints were rising input costs related to energy (62% of enterprises), limitations related to COVID-19 (56%), and increases in other input costs (56%). The 3 most common strategies to mitigate GVC constraints were boosting digitalisation (32% of enterprises), prioritising trusted suppliers (30%), and nearshoring within the EU (29%). This article explores how recent events, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical tensions and the energy crisis, have affected the organisation and resilience of GVCs within the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Enterprises reported the following [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Global_value_chain_disruptions_and_enterprise_responses_in_the_EU&stable=0#Constraints_and_transformation_drivers_affecting_GVCs_in_the_EU key constraints and transformation drivers]: * Increased costs of raw materials related to energy * Increased costs of raw materials (except energy and transportation) * Problems with transportation capacity, time, and costs * Supply shortages in existing supply chains * Constraints related to COVID-19 * Transformation drivers related to environmental policies * EU sanctions on Russia Enterprises adopted [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Global_value_chain_disruptions_and_enterprise_responses_in_the_EU&stable=0#Reorganisation_of_GVCs_in_response_to_business_constraints several strategies] as a response to the encountered GVC constraints and limitations: * Digitalisation: increasing the digitalisation of the processes within GVCs * Resilience over cost: focusing on reliable suppliers and expanding the size of inventories * Regionalisation: nearshoringNearshoring refers to the practice of relocating business functions or sourcing partners to nearby or neighbouring countries, typically within the same region. and farshoringFarshoring involves sourcing or relocating business functions or sourcing partners to distant countries, often outside the region. business functions * Expansion: expanding existing supplier networks * Backsourcing: returning business functions from abroad to the home economy The results in this article present the outcomes of one module of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/globalisation-businesses/information-data GVC survey 2021-23] conducted across 23These are 22 EU countries (except CY, EE, HR, LU, and SI) and Norway. European countries, covering enterprises with more than 50 employees in [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] sections B–N. The survey period spans 2021 to 2023. === Overview === Besides the main points already mentioned above, the businesses reported the following issues affecting their supply chains: * The COVID-19 pandemic was a frequently reported constraint (56%), primarily affecting GVC operations in 2021 and 2022. * The European energy crisis drove sharp input-cost inflation: 62% of enterprises reported high impact on costs related to energy, while 56% faced elevated costs for inputs other than energy and transport. * Supply shortages of raw materials, intermediate, and final goods were reported by 49% of enterprises, peaking at 66% in Austria and 64% in Portugal. * Transportation constraints (capacity, time, or cost) affected 47% of enterprises, with peripheral countries and those depending heavily on manufacturing most exposed. * Changes in environmental regulations acted as transformation drivers, affecting the GVCs of 38% of EU enterprises. * Around 27% of enterprises reported that their GVCs were affected by the EU sanctions on Russia. * Enterprises favoured resilience over cost-efficiency: 32% increased digitalisation, and 30% focused on buying from the most reliable suppliers. * Nearshoring within the EU (29%) outpaced farshoring (18%), with the highest rate observed in Portugal (51%) and the lowest in Sweden (15%). * Supplier consolidation was prevalent, with 30% of firms reducing their supplier base versus 17% expanding it, highlighting a shift towards trusted partners. === Impact of GVC constraints and reorganisation of GVCs === Between 2021 and 2023, enterprises in the EU were affected by a combination of external shocks that disrupted GVCs and structural drivers that prompted their transformation. The COVID-19 pandemic triggered lockdowns and transport bottlenecks, leading to a 9.4% decline in exports and an 11.6% drop in imports in 2020 – the deepest slump since 2000 (source article [[International trade in goods]]). This shock was followed by an energy crisis triggered by Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine: gross available energy in the EU fell by 4.5% and natural gas consumption by 13.3% in 2022, amid an import dependency rate of 62.5% and record-high prices for non-household consumers (source article [[Natural gas price statistics]]). Concurrently, economic sanctions on Russia eliminated its coal exports to the EU by Q4 2022 and reduced its share of liquefied natural gas EU imports between 2022 and 2024 (source article [[EU imports of energy products - latest_developments]]). Quantitatively, the magnitude of these shocks is striking; 80.0% of enterprises reported that one or more constraints or limitations impacted their GVCs or that they reorganised their GVCs during 2021-2023, with 49% experiencing supply shortages of raw materials, intermediate, and final goods. The rise of energy-related costs impacted 62% of enterprises, while 56% faced higher expenses for other inputs. Transportation constraints (capacity, time or cost) affected 47% of enterprises. On the policy front, 56% of enterprises reported COVID-19 measures and 27% of enterprises reported that EU sanctions on Russia affected their GVCs. Finally, over half of all enterprises (58%) reported either a high impact of GVC constraints or that they had significantly reorganised some parts of their GVCs to respond to these constraintsEach responding enterprise was required to assess the level of impact separately for each of the 7 constraints analysed in this article. Since enterprises could attribute different levels of impact across multiple constraints, the shares of enterprises reporting a moderate or high impact are independent and therefore do not add up to a common total.. Figure 1 presents the percentages of enterprises whose GVCs were impacted by constraints or underwent reorganisation, by country, for the period 2021-2023. A moderate level of impact or extent was reported by 75.9% of enterprises, while 58.5% reported a high level of impact or extent. EU countries with large manufacturing sectors and high energy import dependency, such as Portugal (90.5%), France (89.6%) and Austria (88.3%), reported the highest shares of affected enterprises. In contrast, Poland (51.3%) and Bulgaria (59.7%) reported the lowest shares, indicating comparatively greater resilience. [[Image:Figure_1_Percentage_of_enterprises_whose_global_value_chains_were_impacted_by_constraints_or_reorganisation,_by_country.png |thumb|center|725px|Figure 1: Percentage of enterprises whose global value chains were impacted by constraints or reorganisation, by country, 2021-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/gvc_effgvc?category=gbs.iss_gvc.gvc.gvc_mot (gvc_effgvc)]|alt= A bar chart showing the percentage of enterprises reporting moderate or high impact from seven types of GVC constraints. Increase of input costs and COVID-19-related restrictions were the most frequently reported by EU enterprises. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] These findings highlight the widespread challenges EU enterprises faced in maintaining their GVCs between 2021 and 2023. While the scale of disruption varied by country, the data point to a clear need for continued investment in resilience, adaptability and strategic planning to prepare for future shocks. === Constraints and transformation drivers affecting GVCs in the EU === GVCs in the EU have been subject to varied constraints, including supply shocks, cost inflation, transport disruptions and regulatory measures, all of which have tested the resilience of companies. The constraints covered by the data in this article include increased energy-related input costs, higher non-energy input costs, COVID-19-related limitations, transport capacity and cost issues, supply shortages of key inputs, and EU sanctions on Russia. In addition, the data includes transformation drivers linked to environmental policy measures. This section presents the share of enterprises affected by these constraints. Energy price volatility was the greatest constraint in the EU, with 61.9% of enterprises reporting higher energy-related input costs (Figure 2)For Figures 2 and 8, the percentages shown represent the share of enterprises reporting a moderate or high impact for each individual constraint. In this case, enterprises were required to select only 1 level of impact per constraint – either ‘Not applicable’, ‘No impact’, ‘Moderate impact’ or ‘High impact’. The figures display the sum of the shares for moderate and high impact. These shares do not add up to 100%, as they exclude responses indicating ‘Not applicable’ or ‘No impact’. If all 4 response categories were shown, their combined total would reach 100% for each constraint.. Elevated costs for non-energy inputs affected 55.6% of enterprises, while 55.9% reported COVID-19-related limitations, echoing a 9.4% slump in EU goods exports in 2020 (source article [[International trade in goods]]). Transport bottlenecks impacted 46.7% of enterprises, while 49.1% reported supply shortages in existing chains. Transformation drivers linked to environmental policies affected 37.6% of EU enterprises, adding further layers of complexity to the disruptions already facing GVCs. The fewest enterprises reported sanctions on Russia (8.0%) and environmental policy changes as highly impactful (8.4%). [[Image:Figure_2_Constraints_affecting_global_value_chains_in_the_EU.png|thumb|center|725px|Figure 2: Constraints affecting global value chains in the EU, 2021-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/gvc_effgvc?category=gbs.iss_gvc.gvc.gvc_mot (gvc_effgvc)]|alt= A bar chart illustrating the percentage of enterprises reporting different GVC effects. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] One of the most widespread and immediate GVC and supply chain constraints reported by enterprises was the shortage of key inputs across supply chains. Data on supply shortages capture the share of enterprises reporting difficulties in procuring essential inputs, such as raw materials, intermediate goods, and final goods, which lead to logistical bottlenecks and policy-induced disruptions. In Austria, 65.7% of enterprises reported supply chain shortages, followed by Portugal at 63.4% and Germany at 56.1%, while Bulgaria (32.6%) and Latvia (36.7%) had the lowest shares. On average, 49.1% of enterprises across the surveyed countries faced shortages of raw materials, intermediate, and final goods, underlining widespread strains on EU supply chains (Figure 3). The wide variation between manufacturing-heavy economies and more service-oriented ones highlights how sectoral composition and energy dependence shape vulnerability to input shortages. [[Image:Figure_3_Supply_shortages_of_raw_materials,_intermediate_and_final_goods_and_services,_by_country.png|thumb|center|725px|Figure 3: Supply shortages of raw materials, intermediate and final goods and services, by country, 2021-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/gvc_effgvc?category=gbs.iss_gvc.gvc.gvc_mot (gvc_effgvc)]|alt= A bar chart showing the share of enterprises by country reporting supply shortages of raw materials. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Raw material cost pressures are broken down into energy-related and non-energy input increases across EU countries, illustrating how enterprises navigated volatile markets in 2021-23. Portuguese enterprises most frequently reported increased energy-related input costs as a constraint, with 79.7% indicating this issue, and 74.9% citing increased costs for other inputs. In contrast, Romanian enterprises reported the lowest shares for both categories, at 39.6% for energy-related input costs and 40.1% for other input costs. On average, 61.9% of enterprises reported higher energy-related input costs, and 55.6% reported elevated costs for other inputs (Figure 4). These pronounced cost constraints, driven by surging energy prices and supply-chain bottlenecks, underscore the need for enterprises to diversify energy sources and secure critical raw materials, which is in line with Eurostat’s findings on [[Industrial_producer_price_index_overview|industrial producer price volatility]]. [[Image:Figure_4_Increased_costs_of_raw_materials,_by_country.png|thumb|center|725px|Figure 4: Increased costs of raw materials, by country, 2021-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/gvc_effgvc?category=gbs.iss_gvc.gvc.gvc_mot (gvc_effgvc)]|alt= an image of a bar chart showing the share of enterprises by country reporting increased raw material input costs. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Efficient [[Transport_statistics_introduced|transport connectivity]] is essential for company operations. Bottlenecks in capacity, timing and cost can severely disrupt the movement of goods within the [[Glossary:Single_market|single market]]. Problems with transport capacity, time or cost were reported by 63.0% of enterprises in Portugal (the highest share), while just 36.3% of Lithuanian enterprises reported such issues; the EU average stood at 46.7% (Figure 5). Countries with heavy manufacturing activity and long supply routes, such as Italy (60.9%) and Austria (60.0%), also faced pronounced transport challenges, whereas service-oriented economies like Lithuania and Latvia (37.6%) exhibited greater resilience. The high impact of transport-related constraints highlights the need for targeted EU transport policy measures to enhance multimodal infrastructure and improve cross-border logistics. [[Image:Figure_5_Problems_with_transportation_capacity,_extended_transport_time_or_transport_costs_from_already_existing_locations_to_markets,_by_country.png|thumb|center|725px|Figure 5: Problems with transportation capacity, extended transport time or transport costs from already existing locations to markets, by country, 2021-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/gvc_effgvc?category=gbs.iss_gvc.gvc.gvc_mot (gvc_effgvc)]|alt= A bar chart showing the share of enterprises by country reporting transport-related constraints in their GVCs. The highest shares were in Portugal, Italy and Austria, with Latvia and Lithuania reporting the lowest. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Environmental policy-related measures act as drivers of transformation in GVCs. Designed to align trade and production with the EU’s climate and environmental objectives, these measures are reshaping sourcing strategies and supplier relationships. According to the GVC survey data, 37.6% of EU enterprises reported having to adapt their GVCs in response to such measures, with the highest share observed in France (49.5%) and the lowest in Bulgaria (28.1%). Policy-related factors contributed to the complexity of managing global supply chains for EU firms during the period. Some of these measures had short-term effects on firm operations, as they were introduced in response to urgent public health, and geopolitical priorities and are expected to support more resilient, sustainable, and secure supply chains in the long term. COVID-19-related limitations affected an average of 55.6% of enterprises, peaking in Austria at 69.3% and dipping to 33.1% in Poland (Figure 6), while 27.4% of enterprises reported that their GVCs were affected by EU sanctions on Russia, the most in Portugal (39.4%), and the lowest perceived impact in France (19.5%). However, it is worth noting that sanctions on Russia took effect around March 2022, covering slightly more than half of the observed period. [[Image:Figure_6_Global_value_chains_affected_by_policy_constraints_and_limitations,_by_country.png
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/gvc_effgvc?category=gbs.iss_gvc.gvc.gvc_mot (gvc_effgvc)]|alt= A bar chart showing the percentage of enterprises by country reporting COVID-19 restrictions, environmental policies, and EU sanctions on Russia as GVC constraints. COVID-19 restrictions were most frequently reported, the most in Austria, Germany, and France. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] With sanctions on Russia identified as a significant source of GVC disruption, Figure 7 examines the spectrum of their direct impact on EU enterprises’ GVCs. In this context, 44.5% of enterprises reported that sanctions did not apply to their operations, while 28.1% reported no impact. A further 19.4% experienced a moderate impact, and 8.0% experienced a very high impact, meaning that just over 1 in 4 enterprises faced at least moderate disruption related to EU sanctions on Russia. This distribution aligns with the observed 62% decline in EU exports to Russia and an 85% drop in imports between Q1 2022 and Q4 2024 following successive sanction packages. It highlights the disparate nature of sanction risk across sectors. [[Image:Figure_7_Impact_of_EU_sanctions_on_Russia_on_global_value_chains.png|thumb|center|725px|Figure 7: Impact of sanctions on Russia on global value chains, 2021-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/gvc_effgvc?category=gbs.iss_gvc.gvc.gvc_mot (gvc_effgvc)]|alt= A pie chart showing the percentage of enterprises reporting GVC-related impacts from EU sanctions on Russia. 72.5% of enterprises reported no impact or not applicable, 19% reported moderate impact and 8% reported high impact. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] These findings highlight the complex and multifaceted nature of the constraints that disrupted GVCs between 2021 and 2023. They also underscore the importance of resilience-building measures, as businesses had to navigate cost pressures, logistical challenges, and evolving policy environments. === Reorganisation of GVCs in response to business constraints === As previous figures illustrated, most EU businesses reported diverse constraints, ranging from supply shortages of raw materials and goods to rising energy and non-energy input costs and transport capacity bottlenecks and policy measures, including COVID-19 restrictions and Russia sanctions. To mitigate these challenges, companies adopted various reorganisation strategies between 2021 and 2023. They accelerated the digitalisation of GVC processes, forged new nearshore partnerships within the EU, prioritised their most reliable suppliers and built buffer inventories. Others explored farshoring and broader supplier network diversification, reflecting a multi-pronged approach to bolster resilience and maintain operational continuity. Digitalisation emerged as the leading reorganisation strategy among EU enterprises, with 32.3% of them reporting an increase in digitalisation of GVC processes between 2021 and 2023, closely followed by a focus on the most reliable suppliers at 30.1% and nearshoring within the EU at 29.2% (Figure 8). Strategies of increased inventories were reported by 27.6% of enterprises, while 18.0% of enterprises engaged in farshoring outside the EU. Expanding existing supplier networks was the least common GVC reorganisation strategy at 16.9%. These figures underscore enterprises’ prioritisation of technology-driven and proximity-based strategies. Most strategies were implemented to a moderate extent rather than a high extent. For example, 24.2% of enterprises increased digitalisation moderately, and 8.1% to a high extent. Nearshoring was implemented to a moderate extent by 24.4% of enterprises, compared with 4.8% to a high extent. On the other hand, farshoring (15.2% moderate, 2.8% high) and expanding supplier networks (14.7% moderate, 2.2% high) were the least common strategies. The data suggest that while a significant share of enterprises took steps to reorganise their GVCs in response to constraints encountered, most did so cautiously and at a moderate scale. This indicates a general tendency towards incremental adaptation rather than comprehensive restructuring, reflecting both uncertainty in the global environment and the practical limits of rapid operational change. [[Image:Figure_8_Reorganisation_of_global_value_chains_in_response_to_business_constraints.png|thumb|center|725px|Figure 8: Reorganisation of global value chains in response to business constraints, 2021-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/gvc_effgvc?category=gbs.iss_gvc.gvc.gvc_mot (gvc_effgvc)]|alt= A bar chart showing the share of enterprises adopting specific GVC reorganisation strategies in response to business constraints. Increased digitalisation, nearshoring within the EU, and prioritising reliable suppliers were the most commonly reported strategies. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] As part of the GVC reorganisation efforts, many enterprises adjusted the geographic distribution of their suppliers to reduce exposure to external constraints. Enterprises moved to secure their supply routes and reduce exposure to distant constraints; 29.2% reported engaging in nearshoring, compared with 18.0% pursuing farshoring (Figure 9). Portugal (50.9%) and Latvia (48.6%) recorded the highest shares of enterprises moving closer to the EU market, while Sweden (14.6%) reported the lowest share. In every country, nearshoring rates exceeded farshoring rates, reflecting a clear trend towards regionalisation of supply chains. The gap between nearshoring and farshoring was particularly pronounced in Slovakia, Portugal and Latvia, suggesting that enterprises in these countries were especially motivated to reduce geopolitical and logistical risks by sourcing closer to home. [[Image:Figure_9_Enterprises_engaging_in_nearshoring_and_farshoring,_by_country.png|thumb|center|725px|Figure 9: Enterprises engaging in nearshoring and farshoring, by country, 2021-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/gvc_effgvc?category=gbs.iss_gvc.gvc.gvc_mot (gvc_effgvc)]|alt= A bar chart comparing the share of enterprises engaging in nearshoring and farshoring by country. The number of enterprises reporting nearshoring exceeded farshoring in every country, with the highest shares reported in Portugal, Latvia, and Malta. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Following the sourcing shifts shown in Figure 9, enterprises have also rebalanced their supplier networks, with consolidation emerging as the dominant approach. In Portugal, 50.5% of enterprises reported reducing their supplier base, compared with 33.7% that expanded networks; Latvia (41.4% vs 27.3%) and Italy (40.0% vs 20.4%) mirrored this trend, while Belgium reported the lowest rates (17.2% reduction vs 7.4% expansion). On average, 30.1% of enterprises reduced the number of suppliers by focusing on the most reliable ones, against 16.9% seeking new partnerships, indicating a strategic focus on trusted supplier relationships. Notably, the Netherlands recorded nearly balanced figures (23.3% reduction and 20.7% expansion), suggesting a dual approach to managing risk and opportunity (Figure 10). [[Image:Figure_10_Consolidation_of_supplier_base,_by_country.png|thumb|center|725px|Figure 10: Consolidation of supplier base, by country, 2021-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/gvc_effgvc?category=gbs.iss_gvc.gvc.gvc_mot (gvc_effgvc)]|alt= A bar chart comparing the share of enterprises in each country that responded to GVC constraints by either focusing on the most reliable suppliers or expanding their supplier networks. Portugal and Latvia reported the highest shares for both strategies. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] On the other hand, backsourcing remained rare, with an average of only 2.0% of enterprises returning functions to their own operations and 2.2% to another domestic enterprise between 2021 and 2023 (Figure 11). Malta (5.9% returned in-house; 6.8% to domestic partners) and Lithuania (5.7%; 5.0%) led this trend, followed by Ireland (5.6%; 4.8%) and Greece (4.1%; 3.3%). In most EU countries, fewer than 3% of enterprises reported returning business functions from abroad, with the Netherlands (0.2%; 0.6%) and France (0.2%; 0.6%) at the lower end. These low rates reflect the complexity, cost and strategic considerations of relocating specialised functions. [[Image:Figure_11_Enterprises_backsourcing_business_functions,_by_country.png|thumb|center|725px|Figure 11: Enterprises backsourcing business functions, by country, 2021-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/gvc_effgvc?category=gbs.iss_gvc.gvc.gvc_mot (gvc_effgvc)]|alt= A bar chart showing the share of enterprises in each country that responded to GVC constraints by returning business functions from abroad to their domestic operations or to another domestic enterprise. Malta and Lithuania reported the highest shares, while Latvia and the Netherlands reported the lowest. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In parallel with reshoring and supplier adjustments, companies also overhauled internal processes to cushion against GVC or supply chain constraints. Across the EU, 34.1% of companies increased the digitalisation of their value-chain processes, while 27.6% boosted stocks and inventories to buffer against supply-chain disruptions (Figure 12). Portugal led these efforts, with 51.7% of enterprises reporting an increase in the digitalisation of their GVC operations and 39.8% of enterprises raising inventory levels, followed by Czechia (46.8%; 31.9%) and Austria (45.0%; 35.5%). Conversely, Poland (13.0%; 17.7%) and Bulgaria (15.2%; 16.2%) reported the lowest uptake, reflecting their service-oriented profiles and shorter supply chains. Although digitalisation was the preferred strategy overall, only 6 countries relied more heavily on traditional inventory-building, highlighting how sectoral and national factors shape resilience choices. This combination of technology investment and buffer-stock strategies emphasises a complementary approach: digital tools enhance visibility and agility, while higher inventories provide a safety net against unexpected disruptions. [[Image:Figure_12_Enterprises_changing_business_processes_to_overcome_global_value_chains_constraints,_by_country.png|thumb|center|725px|Figure 12: Enterprises changing business processes to overcome global value chains constraints, by country, 2021-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/product/view/gvc_effgvc?category=gbs.iss_gvc.gvc.gvc_mot (gvc_effgvc)]|alt= A bar chart showing the share of enterprises in each country that responded to GVC constraints by either increasing the digitalisation of processes within global value chains or by increasing stocks or inventory. On average, the strategy of increasing digitalisation was more commonly implemented. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The data in this article demonstrate that EU enterprises faced a broad spectrum of supply-chain constraints between 2021 and 2023, ranging from pandemic lockdowns and energy-market shocks to transport bottlenecks and evolving policy measures. These constraints highlight the complex nature of disruptions in GVCs. Country-level variations reveal how sectoral structure, energy dependency, and geographic position can shape enterprise vulnerability, with manufacturing-intensive economies generally more exposed than service-oriented ones. Enterprises responded to GVC constraints with a mix of resilience-driven reorganisation strategies, most notably accelerating the digitalisation of GVC processes, forging partnerships within the single market and consolidating supplier bases while building buffer inventories. The concurrent adoption of multiple approaches underscores that no single strategy is sufficient; digital tools, regional sourcing, and trusted supplier relationships form a robust defence against future shocks. === The way forward === The next data release is planned for late 2028Five EU countries have a derogation from collecting GVC data, since their total number of enterprises with 50 or more persons employed in sectors B-N is less than 1% of the EU total. These are Cyprus, Croatia, Estonia, Luxembourg, and Slovenia., providing a comprehensive picture of the impacts of GVC constraints and reorganisation strategies. Eurostat will continue to improve GVC statistics in subsequent survey rounds by incorporating emerging constraints, enterprise responses, and enhanced microdata-linkage methodologies to deliver more granular insights. The next GVC survey will cover the period 2024-2026. It is set to introduce new topics, such as the impacts of digital transition, sustainability and circular-economy metrics, and resilience to geopolitical shocks (e.g. introduction of import tariffs), to reflect the latest developments shaping value-chain organisation. It is important to strengthen policy-monitoring frameworks to assess the effectiveness of resilience and diversification measures, ensuring that future GVC statistics remain a cornerstone for evidence-based economic policymaking and a robust single market. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:SE article-ready table 2025 GVC shocks final.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Context === To stay competitive, enterprises increasingly organise their production globally in GVCs by breaking up their value chains into smaller parts supplied by a growing number of providers located worldwide. These GVCs comprise the full range of activities required to bring a product or service from conception through the different phases of production, delivery to final consumers and disposal after use. GVC statistics can help measure organisational and spatial patterns in global and regional value chains and monitor their effects on employment, wages, value added, innovation, skills, enterprise survival and turnover. The GVC data are in high demand from statisticians, researchers and policymakers. From an EU policy perspective, such analysis provides crucial data on the movement of EU jobs to non-EU countries, dependency on foreign parts of the chain, and the EU’s integration into GVCs. Moreover, in the post-COVID-19 world, there are reports of a shortening of GVCs and a de-globalisation trend resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic. Therefore, statistics on GVC are necessary to support policies on trade, job sustainability and economic development. To monitor evolving GVC patterns and enterprise responses to shocks, the GVC survey 2021-23 was launched under the triennial framework of the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R2152:EN:NOT|title=European Business Statistics Regulation 2019/2152}} and the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32022R0918:EN:NOT|title=GVC Implementing Regulation 2022/918}}, covering enterprises across 22 EU countries. In the survey, respondents assessed their experiences by selecting one of 4 response options: not applicable, no impact or extent, moderate impact or extent, or high impact or extent. Most of the the figures shown reflect only those enterprises that reported a moderate or high impact or extent (also referred to as any impact or extent). === Other articles === title: Geospatial analysis at Eurostat
text:
Data from April 2015 This article presents spatial analysis, a set of techniques and tools to study spatio-temporal relationships inherent in data. The article further sets out the possibilities for its usage and gives some examples where spatial analysis has been conducted with statistical data of the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]]. [[Glossary:GISCO|GISCO]], the team managing the '[[Glossary:Geographical_information_system_of_the_Commission_(GISCO)|Geographical information system of the Commission]]', is a centre of excellence of spatial analysis within the [[Glossary:European_Commission_(EC)|European Commission]]. === What is spatial analysis? === The term spatial analysis defines a set of techniques used to visualise, process or analyse data with spatial attributes. This definition implies a very wide-reaching field for the spatial analysis, as much data are inherently spatial, being referenced to locations in two- or three-dimensional space. Collecting the spatial attributes (geographic location) of statistical or other data is what creates the spatial data and hence allows the spatial analysis. The term spatial analysis is often used in different contexts: * A map or a time sequence of maps may be considered as spatial analysis when visualising the spatial aspects of datasets according to chosen criteria (see Map 2). * Processing and analysing spatial data using the set of functions provided by many [[Glossary:Geographical_information_system_(GIS)|geographical information system (GIS)]] software packages such as overlaying, buffering, filtering, distance computations, etc. Descriptive statistics — calculating maxima, minima, means, variances and others — are also referred to as ‘spatial analysis’ (see Map 1). * A more advanced usage of the term refers to the combining of spatial and statistical techniques to analyse spatial and temporal data in a number of scientific fields such as environmental, agricultural, medical, social, economic and political sciences, as well as urban planning, engineering and other sciences. This type of spatial analysis typically requires access to comprehensive stack of geospatial, statistical and other thematic data sources and is normally not conducted by statistical offices. Map 1, for example, shows the number of airports the resident population around the airport of Burgos in Spain can reach within a 2-hour journey. This analysis was an element in a recent performance audit carried out by the European Court of Auditors (ECA) which investigated the return-on-investment of public spending on airport infrastructures. [[Image:Number_of_airports_overlapping_with_the_audited_airport_Burgos,_Spain_(LEBG).png|thumb|centre|450px|Map 1: Number of airports overlapping with the audited airport Burgos, Spain (LEBG)
''Source:'' Eurostat Population (2006) and Tourism data (2006/2010)]] === Spatial analysis for statistical purposes === Statisticians seldom discuss spatial analysis, although spatial analysis techniques are widely used to create the reference for the collection of statistical data and are involved in much of the collection, dissemination and analysis of statistical data. The following examples will illustrate how spatial statistics and spatial analysis are used in official European statistics. '''Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics''' Large amounts of European Union (EU) regional statistical data are collected, harmonised but also (geo)spatially located using the [[Glossary:Nomenclature_of_territorial_units_for_statistics_(NUTS)|nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)]] and [[Glossary:Local_administrative_unit_(LAU)|local administrative units (LAUs)]] as references. The collected data are used for the socio-economic analysis of the regions, applying spatial analysis techniques and references to EU regional policies. The NUTS and LAU classifications and geospatial statistical datasets are therefore the starting point for any EU-wide spatial analysis. The maintenance of this hierarchical system of administrative units and the respective geographical information (GI) datasets is a complex undertaking involving demographic and economic indicators to outline the boundaries of the statistical units. '''Regional statistics''' Regional statistics are a helpful tool to understand the regional diversity. Considering national figures alone does not reveal the full picture of what is happening in the European Union; indeed, there are often significant differences between regions of the same country when one looks at smaller geographical areas. Regional statistics are based on a harmonised convention in the definition of regions which is contained in the NUTS. Identifying, mapping and analysing regional differences, using NUTS and LAU classified statistical data, provide an opportunity for interesting insights based on (geo)spatial variation of diverse statistical indicators. The [[Eurostat_regional_yearbook|Eurostat regional yearbook]] provides an overview of official, regional statistics that are available within Europe. See [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Regional_yearbook_foreword Regional Yearbook foreword]. [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistical-atlas/gis/viewer/ The Eurostat Statistical Atlas] is an online application for the dynamic visualisation of the maps from the Eurostat regional yearbook. Regional data may be easily compared against other statistical data for the same administrative unit, against the data for the adjacent units, displaying infrastructure and geographical features. [[Image:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)_per_inhabitant,_in_purchasing_power_standard_(PPS),_by_NUTS_2_regions,_2011.png|thumb|centre|450px|Map 2: Gross domestic product (GDP) per inhabitant, in purchasing power standard (PPS), by NUTS 2 regions, 2011 (1)
(% of the EU-28 average, EU-28 = 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_r_e2gdp}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_r_e3popgdp}}]] '''What is the boundary of a city?''' The need for spatial analysis becomes evident when the question ‘[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/cities/spatial-units What is a city?]’ is asked. Any analysis of the spatial dimension of EU cities starts with this question, which then leads to others, focusing on the spatial characteristics of the cities. What is actually the ‘core city’ and what is its area? What is the boundary of ‘the [[Glossary:Functional_urban_area|functional urban area]]’ (FUA) and how can these boundaries be identified? How can the city be divided into ‘sub-city districts’ (SCD) applying population criteria? The [[Glossary:City data collection|City data collection]] system provides information on different aspects of the quality of urban life in a cross-section of Europe’s cities’. The collected data is used for analysis of the spatial dimensions of the European cities, focusing on development of the city infrastructure and socio-economic dynamics. Regional and city development is observed from the perspective of urban-rural connectivity, administrative and political boundaries, interactions of the city with its surroundings and other phenomena with spatial dimensions. [[Image:Urban_audit,_Madrid,_2011.png|thumb|centre|450px|Map 3: Urban audit, Madrid, 2011
''Source:'' Eurostat]] '''Degree of urbanisation classification (DEGURBA)''' The [[Degree of urbanisation classification - 2011 revision|degree of urbanisation (DEGURBA)]] is a classification of LAU2s created using spatial analysis techniques. The classification was developed jointly by DG AGRI and DG REGIO with the support of the [https://ec.europa.eu/jrc/en Joint Research Centre (JRC)] and Eurostat. Local administrative units level 2 (LAU2) are classified into three types of area based on the share of local population living in urban clusters and in urban centres: * densely populated area (cities/large urban area); * intermediate density area (towns and suburbs/small urban area); and * thinly populated area (rural area). Urban, suburban and rural areas are concepts used by policymakers, researchers, national administrations and international organisations. In the [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU Member States]] and the [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|European Free Trade Association (EFTA)]] countries, the degree of urbanisation helps to structure data according to this classification from a wide range of surveys, including the [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)|Labour Force Survey (LFS)]] and the Survey on Income and Living Conditions [[Glossary:EU-SILC|(SILC)]]. See also [http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docgener/work/2014_01_new_urban.pdf Working Paper on 'Harmonised definition of cities and rural areas']] Data by degree of urbanisation is presently available for the following statistical domains: * labour market; * education and living conditions; and * [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/degree-of-urbanisation/overview welfare and tourism]. [[Image:Degree_of_urbanisation_for_local_administrative_units_level_2_(LAU2)_,_2013.png|thumb|centre|450px|Map 4: Degree of urbanisation for local administrative units level 2 (LAU2) , 2013(1)
''Source:'' Eurostat, JRC, EFGS, REGIO-GIS]] ===Other articles=== *[[Population grids]] (background article) *[[Geographical information system of the Commission (GISCO)]] *[[:Category:Regions_and_cities_typologies|All background articles on regional typologies]] ===Database=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/gisco/geodata Geodata, for downloadable geodata files] ===Dedicated section=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/gisco/overview GISCO: Geographical Information and maps] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/nuts/overview NUTS – Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/regions/overview Regions] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/cities/overview Cities (City data collection)] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/degree-of-urbanisation/overview Degree of Urbanisation] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/metropolitan-regions/overview Metropolitan regions] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/lucas/overview Land cover/use statistics (LUCAS)] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/maritime-policy-indicators/overview Maritime policy indicators] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/rural-development/overview Rural development] ===Publications=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/publications/regional-yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook (online publication)] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/4031688/6917606/KS-04-14-908-EN-N.pdf/ GISCO compact guide] *[http://www.eca.europa.eu/en/Pages/NewsItem.aspx?nid=5510 EU-funded airport infrastructures: poor value for money] ===Visualisations=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistical-atlas/gis/viewer/ Statistical Atlas] - select statistical domain 'Population' (top right) *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RSI/ Regional Statistics Illustrated] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RSI/#?vis=city.statistics&lang=en City Statistics Illustrated] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RSI/#?vis=typologies.urb_typology&lang=en Typologies Illustrated] ===External links=== *[http://www.efgs.info/ EFGS – European Forum for Geography and Statistics] *[http://inspire.jrc.ec.europa.eu/ INSPIRE – Infrastructure for Spatial Information in the European Community] *[https://ec.europa.eu/jrc/en JRC – Joint Research Centre of the European Commission] *[http://ec.europa.eu/dgs/agriculture/index_en.htm European Commission DG Agriculture and Rural Development] *[http://ec.europa.eu/dgs/regional_policy/index_en.htm European Commission DG Regional and Urban Policy] *[http://www.espon.eu/ ESPON – European Spatial Planning Observatory Network] ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Geospatial_analysis_at_Eurostat'' {{Unit|topic=X_GIS}} [[Category:General and regional statistics|Geospatial analysis at Eurostat]] [[Category:Regions and cities|Geospatial analysis at Eurostat]] [[Category:Background article|Geospatial analysis at Eurostat]] [[Category:Regions and cities - title: Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment
text:

Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment
 '''Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment''' is an online [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publication presenting a summary of recent [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] statistics on economic aspects of globalisation, focusing on global value chains, patterns of EU trade and investment. It complements the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/dashboard/globalisation/ Globalisation dashboard] which provides an overview of main globalisation data. The articles in this publication look at the data and developments in more detail, providing background and explanation on global value chains, trade partnerships and investments. This publication consists of individual articles that get updated according to their respective data release date.
