title: Government expenditure on cultural, broadcasting and publishing services
text:
EU statistics on government expenditure for cultural services, broadcasting and publishing services are presented according to the classification of the functions of government (COFOG). Data extracted on 20 August 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 In 2024, general government expenditure across the EU on cultural services amounted to €87.8 billion or 1.0% of all general government expenditure. [[Image:General government expenditure on cultural services, broadcasting and publishing services, 2024 (% of total expenditure) .png|thumb|centre|600px|''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A vertical double bar chart showing general government expenditure on cultural services, broadcasting and publishing services for the year 2024. Data are presented as a percentage of total expenditure. The EU, the euro area 20, the euro area 21, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries are represented in the graph, each with one bar for cultural services and another for broadcasting and publishing services. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article focuses on [[Glossary:Government revenue and expenditure|government expenditure]] on cultural services as well as on broadcasting publishing services. It is based on data gathered by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] as part of the data collection exercise on government expenditure by the [[Glossary:Classification of the functions of government (COFOG)|classification of functions of government (COFOG)]]. It is part of a [[Government expenditure by function|set of statistical articles]] based on general government expenditure by function. '''General government expenditure on cultural services, broadcasting and publishing services''' In the [[Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)|European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)]], the [[Glossary:General government sector|general government sector]] is defined as consisting of institutional units which are non-market producers whose output is intended for individual and collective consumption, and are financed by compulsory payments made by units belonging to other sectors, and institutional units principally engaged in the redistribution of national income and wealth. The general government sector comprises central government, state government, local government and social security funds. The main functions of general government units include organising and redirecting flows of money, goods and services or other assets among corporations, among households, and between corporations and households (examples include the redistribution of national income and wealth), or the production of goods and services to satisfy households’ needs (for example, the provision of state health care or culture to the whole community). The data presented here concern two COFOG groups (see ''Data sources'' section for more details): *cultural services (08.2); and *broadcasting and publishing services (08.3). ===General government expenditure on cultural services, broadcasting and publishing services=== In 2024, across the [[Glossary:EU-27|EU]], approximately 1.0% of total general government expenditure was allocated to '''cultural services''' and around 0.4% of total general government expenditure was devoted to '''broadcasting and publishing services'''. [[Image:General government expenditure on cultural services, broadcasting and publishing services, 2024 (% of total expenditure) .png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 1: General government expenditure on cultural services, broadcasting and publishing services, 2024 (% of total expenditure)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A vertical double bar chart showing general government expenditure on cultural services, broadcasting and publishing services for the year 2024. Data are presented as a percentage of total expenditure. The EU, the euro area 20, the euro area 21, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries are represented in the graph, each with one bar for cultural services and another for broadcasting and publishing services. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This percentage remained relatively stable over time within the [[Glossary:EU-27|EU]], although there were considerable differences when analysing the results for individual countries (see Figure 1). ===Highest share of expenditure on cultural services in Malta, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Hungary === In 2024, the highest shares of expenditure on cultural services in total expenditure were recorded in Malta (2.5%), Estonia (2.2%), Latvia (2.0%), Lithuania and Hungary (each 1.9%), and among EFTA countries in Iceland (2.2%). The lowest shares were observed in Greece (0.4%), Cyprus (0.5%), Italy, Romania and Portugal (all 0.7%). In absolute terms, EU general government expenditure on cultural services was €87.8 billion in 2024, increasing from €81.7 billion in 2023 by around 8%. EU general government expenditure on cultural services as a share of GDP stood at 0.5% in 2024, with this ratio remaining stable at EU level throughout the reported time series from 2010. Between 2023 and 2024, the ratio also remained stable in the majority of the Member States, increased in Bulgaria and Poland and decreased for Hungary. Table 1 shows general government expenditure on cultural services in 2023 and 2024, while Table 2 shows similar information for broadcasting and publishing services (data are shown in absolute values and as a share of all general government expenditure for both reference years). [[Image:General government expenditure on cultural services, 2023 and 2024.png|thumb|centre|600px|Table 1: General government expenditure on cultural services, 2023 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=Table showing general government expenditure on cultural services for the years 2023 and 2024. Data are presented in euro millions and as percentage of GDP for the EU, the euro area 20, the euro area 21, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

===Highest share of expenditure on broadcasting and publishing services in Hungary === In 2024, the highest shares of expenditure on broadcasting and publishing services in total expenditure were recorded in Hungary (0.7%), Croatia, Germany, Ireland, Slovenia, Austria and Denmark (all 0.5%), as well as Switzerland among EFTA countries (0.6%). The lowest share was observed in Malta (0.1%). In absolute terms, EU general government total expenditure on broadcasting and publishing services in 2024 stood at €36.6 billion, an increase of around 6% from €34.6 billion in 2023. EU general government expenditure on broadcasting and publishing services as a share of GDP stood at 0.2% in 2024, unchanged throughout the reported time series. Between 2023 and 2024, the ratio remained unchanged for most Member States. [[Image:General government expenditure on broadcasting and publishing services, 2023 and 2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 2: General government expenditure on broadcasting and publishing services, 2023 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=Table showing general government expenditure on broadcasting and publishing services for the years 2023 and 2024. Data are presented in euro millions and as percentage of GDP for the EU, the euro area, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

=== Source data for tables and graphs ===
'''''The detailed tables [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] are available [[Media:SE Cofog web 2026 08 20.xlsx |here]].'''''
===Data sources=== '''Reporting of data to Eurostat''' Annual government finance statistics (GFS) data are collected by Eurostat on the basis of the European System of Accounts (ESA 2010) transmission programme. Member States are requested to transmit, among other tables, table 1100, 'Expenditure of general government by function' eleven months after the end of the reference period. Table 1100 provides information about expenditure of the general government sector divided into main COFOG functions and ESA 2010 categories. The transmission of the COFOG I level breakdown (divisions) is compulsory for general government and its subsectors for the years from 1995 onwards, whereas information on the COFOG II level (COFOG groups) is provided on a compulsory basis for general government for the reference years from 2001 onwards. The main reference year used in this publication is 2024 as the latest year available at EU level. Data was extracted on 20 August 2026. '''Provisional data''' While a significant effort was undertaken to harmonise the recording of government measures to alleviate the impact of increasing energy prices, a full harmonisation of data for the reference year 2024 was not yet achieved. Data for the EU and euro area aggregates (2024), Belgium (2024), Germany (2022-2024), Spain (2024), France (2023-2024), Portugal (2024) and Slovakia (all years) is provisional. '''Classification of government expenditure by function''' General government expenditure by classification of the functions of government (COFOG) is collected at two levels of detail. At its most aggregate level it classifies government expenditure into 10 main functions (divisions or COFOG level I breakdowns): general public services; defence; public order and safety; economic affairs; environmental protection; housing and community affairs; health; '''recreation, culture and religion'''; education; social protection. These divisions are further broken down into groups (COFOG level II). COFOG division 08 for recreation, culture and religion consists of the following COFOG groups: * 08.1: recreational and sporting services; * 08.2: cultural services; * 08.3: broadcasting and publishing services; * 08.4: religious and other community services; * 08.5: R&D related to recreation, culture and religion; * 08.6: recreation, culture and religion not elsewhere classified. Among these six groups, cultural services and broadcasting and publishing services are those which account for a majority of culture-related government expenditure in the EU. Culture-related items cannot be distinguished in data for Groups 08.5 and 08.6. '''Cultural services''' covered by COFOG Group 08.2 include: * the provision of cultural services; * administration of cultural affairs; * supervision and regulation of cultural facilities; * operation or support of facilities for cultural pursuits (libraries, museums, art galleries, theatres, exhibition halls, monuments, historic houses and sites, zoological and botanical gardens, aquaria, arboreta, etc.); * production, operation or support of cultural events (concerts, stage and film productions, art shows, etc.); * grants, loans or subsidies to support individual artists, writers, designers, composers and others working in the arts or to organisations engaged in promoting cultural activities; * national, regional or local celebrations provided they are not intended chiefly to attract tourists. '''Broadcasting and publishing services''' covered by COFOG Group 08.3 include: * administration of broadcasting and publishing affairs; * supervision and regulation of broadcasting and publishing services; * operation or support of broadcasting and publishing services; * grants, loans or subsidies to support the construction or acquisition of facilities for television or radio broadcasting; * the construction or acquisition of plant, equipment or materials for newspaper, magazine or book publishing; * the production of material for broadcasting and its presentation; * the gathering of news or other information; * the distribution of published works. Further information is available in Eurostat’s {{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-19-010|title=manual on sources and methods for the compilation of COFOG statistics — 2019 edition}}. '''Definition of general government total expenditure ''' Government total expenditure is defined in ESA 2010, paragraph 8.100 by using as reference a list of ESA 2010 categories. Government total expenditure comprises the following categories: *P.2, 'intermediate consumption': the purchase of goods and services by government; *P.5, 'gross capital formation' consists of: (a) gross fixed capital formation (P.51g); (b) changes in inventories (P.52); (c) acquisitions less disposals of valuables (P.53); where *P.51g, 'gross fixed capital formation': consists of acquisitions, less disposals, of fixed assets during a given period plus certain additions to the value of non-produced assets realised by the productive activity of producer or institutional units. Fixed assets are tangible or intangible assets produced as outputs from processes of production that are themselves used repeatedly, or continuously, in processes of production for more than one year; *D.1, 'compensation of employees': the wages of government employees plus non-wage costs such as social contributions; *D.29, 'other taxes on production, payable', *D.3, 'subsidies, payable', *D.4, 'property income, payable', consists of : (a) 'interest, payable' (D.41) and (b) 'other property income, payable' (D.42+D.43+D.44+D.45), where *D.41, 'interest': excludes settlements under swaps and forward rate arrangements, as these are treated as financial transactions in the ESA 2010; *D.5, 'current taxes on income, wealth, etc., payable'; *D.62, social payments: cover social benefits and pensions paid in cash; *D.632, 'social transfers in kind - purchased market production'; *D.7, 'other current transfers, payable'; *D.8, 'adjustments for the change in pension entitlements'; *D.9, 'capital transfers payable'; *NP, 'acquisitions less disposals of non-financial non-produced assets': public investment spending. Non-financial non-produced assets consist of land and other tangible non-produced assets that may be used in the production of goods and services, and intangible non-produced assets. *Capital investments includes P.5 and NP. *Other current expenditure includes D.29, D.5 and D.8. '''Gross Domestic Product''' Throughout this publication, the nominal GDP, i.e. GDP at current prices is used. In principle, the latest GDP available at time of publication is used. Please also refer to metadata files linked below. ===Context=== Culture is one of Europe’s greatest assets: it is a source of values, identity and a sense of belonging; it also contributes towards well-being, social cohesion and inclusion. The cultural and creative sectors may also provide a stimulus for economic growth, job creation and international trade. That is why culture is becoming increasingly important within the EU. In accordance with Article 167 of the Lisbon Treaty, the EU ''shall contribute to the flowering of the cultures of the Member States, while respecting their national and regional diversity and at the same time bringing the common heritage to the fore''. The EU supports these objectives through the [https://culture.ec.europa.eu/creative-europe Creative Europe] programme, as well as a number of policy actions set out in the [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52014XG1223(02)&from=EN Work Plan for Culture (2015-2018)] and the [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52018XG1221(01)&from=EN Work Plan for Culture (2019-2022)]. The latter, adopted by EU culture ministers in November 2018, sets out the main priorities for European cooperation in cultural policymaking: sustainability in cultural heritage; cohesion and well-being; an ecosystem supporting artists, cultural and creative professionals and European content; gender equality; and international cultural relations. The production of reliable, comparable and up-to-date cultural statistics, which provide a basis for sound cultural policymaking, is a cross-sectorial priority in the latest work plan. title: Government expenditure on defence
text:
EU statistics analyse general government expenditure on defence. Data extracted on 20 August 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 General government expenditure in the EU on defence amounted to 1.5% of GDP in 2024. [[Image:General government total expenditure on defence, 2024, % of GDP, overview.png|centre|700px|General government total expenditure on defence, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A vertical bar chart showing the total general government expenditure on defence for the year 2024. Data is presented as percentage of GDP for the EU, the euro area 20, the euro area 21, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries.]] This article analyses data on [[Glossary:Total_general_government_expenditure|general government expenditure]] on 'defence' (according to the [[Glossary:Classification_of_the_functions_of_government_(COFOG)|Classification of the Functions of Government - COFOG).]] It is part of a [[Government expenditure by function|set of statistical articles]] based on general government expenditure by function. [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] collects data on general government expenditure by economic function according to the international Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG) in the framework of the [[Glossary:ESA_2010|European System of National Accounts (ESA 2010).]] === Expenditure on 'defence' === In 2024, 'defence' expenditure amounted to 1.5% of [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]] for the [[Glossary:EU|EU]] and 1.4% of GDP for the [[Glossary:euro area|euro area]]. As a share of total expenditure, in 2024, defence expenditure amounted to 3.0% in the EU and 2.8% in the euro area. [[Image:Government_expenditure_by_function_in_the_EU_in_2024_(€_billion).png|centre|700px|Figure 1: EU government expenditure by function, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A graphic image showing general government expenditure by function in the EU for the year 2024. Data are expressed in euro billions for each function.]] In 2024, as a percentage of GDP, the highest levels of total expenditure on defence in the EU countries were observed in: *Estonia (3.7% of GDP) *Poland (2.9% of GDP) *Latvia (2.7% of GDP) *Lithuania (2.6% of GDP) *Greece (2.2% of GDP) *Hungary and Sweden (both 2.0% of GDP), as well as *France, Denmark, and Cyprus (all 1.8% of GDP). Among the [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA countries]], Norway reported defence expenditure of 2.1% of GDP. By contrast, Ireland (0.1% of GDP), Malta (0.5% of GDP), and Luxembourg and Austria (both 0.7% of GDP) had comparatively low expenditure on defence in the EU when measured as as percentage of GDP. Among the EFTA countries, Iceland reported the lowest level of expenditure on defence, as it does not have a standing army (0.2% of GDP). [[Image:General government total expenditure on defence, 2024, % of GDP.png|centre|700px|Table 1: General government total expenditure on defence, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}, see [[Glossary:Country codes|country codes]]|alt=A table showing the total general government expenditure on defence for the year 2024, expressed as a percentage of GDP and divided into each defence category. Data is shown for the EU, the euro area, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries.]] At the level of the EU, the major part of 'defence' expenditure is concentrated in the COFOG group 'military defence' (1.3% of GDP in 2024). 'Civil defence', 'R&D defence' and 'defence expenditure not elsewhere classified' together amounted to less than 0.1% of GDP at the level of the EU, while 'foreign military aid' accounted for 0.2% of GDP in 2024. Research and development on defence made up a small part of government expenditure in all countries except France (0.1% of GDP). 'Foreign military aid' amounted to 0.2% of GDP for the EU, with notable amounts in: *Denmark (0.5% of GDP) *the Netherlands and Germany (both at 0.3% of GDP) *Latvia, Sweden, Luxembourg, Finland, Bulgaria and Belgium, as well as Norway among the EFTA countries (all at 0.2% of GDP) *Spain, Lithuania, Greece, Portugal, Romania, Italy, France, Croatia, and Cyprus (all at 0.1% of GDP). It should be noted that the reporting of military aid in response to Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine is not yet fully harmonised for all countries, so that donations of equipment in kind may not yet be fully reflected in the total expenditure for 'foreign military aid' for all countries - see also metadata notes. Such omissions do not effect the level of total expenditure and total expenditure on defence. [[Image:General government total expenditure on defence, 2024_% of GDP.png|centre|700px|Figure 2: General government total expenditure on defence, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A stacked vertical bar chart showing the total general government expenditure on defence for the year 2024. Each bar is divided into the separate categories related to defence with the data presented as percentage of GDP for the EU, the euro area, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries.]] === Expenditure on 'defence' by type of transaction === At the level of the EU, nearly two-fifths (39.0%) of total expenditure on defence in 2024 was devoted to '[[Glossary:Compensation_of_employees|compensation of employees]]', that is wages and salaries as well as employers' actual or imputed [[Glossary:Social_contributions|social contributions]]. Some 28.2% was devoted to '[[Glossary:Intermediate_consumption|intermediate consumption]]', consisting of government purchases of goods and services, except where these are regarded as capital formation. [[Glossary:Gross_capital_formation|Gross capital formation]] (net purchases of fixed assets - "investments" - and inventories) amounted to 23.4% of defence expenditure in 2024, such as the purchase of new equipment and infrastructure as well as net additions to inventories. (Other) [[Glossary:Current_transfers|current]] and capital transfers, for example for military aid, made up 8.4% of total expenditure at the level of the EU according to the data reported. [[Image:General government expenditure on defence by transaction, EU, 2024_ _€ billion.png|centre|700px|Figure 3: General government expenditure on defence by transaction, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A pie chart showing the EU defence expenditure by detailed categories for 2024.]] === Evolution of 'defence' expenditure from 2010-2024 === At the level of the EU, increases in 'defence' expenditure as a percentage of GDP were noted from 2010-2024 (from 1.4% of GDP in 2010 to 1.5% of GDP in 2024). Compared with 2023, the level of defence expenditure in the EU also increased as a percentage of GDP (from 1.3% of GDP in 2023 to 1.5% of GDP in 2024). At the EU level, the share of defence expenditure in total expenditure increased from 2.7% in 2010 to 3.0% in 2024. The share of defence expenditure in total expenditure in 2024 also increased for third consecutive year, from 2.4% in 2021, 2.6% in 2022, and 2.7% in 2023, to 3.0% of GDP in 2024. [[Image:Detailed evolution of EU general government total expenditure on defence, 2020-2024__€ billion.png|centre|700px|Figure 4: Detailed evolution of EU general government total expenditure on defence, 2020-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A pie chart showing composition of defence expenditure for the EU by type of transaction.]] In absolute terms, in 2024, EU defence expenditure increased to €266 billion, up from €232 billion in 2023, €207 billion in 2022, €185 billion in 2021, and €176 billion in 2020. The 15% increase in defence expenditure between 2023 and 2024 represents the strongest relative increase among the broad government expenditure functions. Between 2020 and 2024, expenditure on 'military defence' at the level of the EU increased from €158 billion to €227 billion and 'foreign military aid' increased from €9 billion to €28 billion. === Source data for tables and graphs ===
'''''The detailed tables [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] are available [[Media:SE Cofog web 2026 08 20.xlsx |here]].'''''
=== Data sources and availability === '''Reporting of data to Eurostat ''' Annual government finance statistics (GFS) data are collected by Eurostat on the basis of the European System of Accounts (ESA 2010) transmission programme. Member States are requested to transmit, among other tables, table 1100, 'Expenditure of general government by function' 11 months after the end of the reference period. Table 1100 provides information about expenditure of the general government sector divided into main COFOG functions and ESA 2010 categories. The transmission of the COFOG I level breakdown (divisions) is compulsory for the years 1995 onwards, whereas information on the COFOG II level (COFOG groups) at general government level is provided on a compulsory basis for the reference years 2001 onwards. The main reference year used in this publication is 2024 as the latest year available at EU level. Data was extracted on 20 August 2026. '''Provisional data''' Data for the EU and euro area aggregates (2024), Belgium (2024), Germany (2022-2024), Spain (2024), France (2023-2024) and Portugal (2024), Slovakia (all years) is provisional. Please also refer to the detailed metadata notes: *{{Template:Esms|code=gov_10a_exp_esms|title=General government expenditure by function (COFOG) }} (ESMS metadata file — gov_10a_exp_esms) '''Definition of general government and its subsectors ''' The data relate to the general government sector of the economy, as defined in ESA 2010, paragraph 2.111: 'The general government sector (S.13) consists of institutional units which are non-market producers whose output is intended for individual and collective consumption, and are financed by compulsory payments made by units belonging to other sectors, and institutional units principally engaged in the redistribution of national income and wealth'. '''Classification of functional expenditure of government ''' The Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG) classifies government expenditure into 10 main categories (divisions known as the 'COFOG I level' breakdown): general public services; defence; public order and safety; economic affairs; environmental protection; housing and community affairs; health; recreation, culture and religion; education; social protection. These divisions are further broken down into 'groups' (COFOG II level). For 'defence', the groups are *'military defence', *'civil defence', *'foreign military aid', *'R&D defence', *'defence n.e.c.'. Further information is available in the Eurostat {{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-19-010|title=Manual on sources and methods for the compilation of COFOG Statistics.}} '''Satellite accounts''' Administrative expenditure data is additionally collected in so-called satellite accounts. In general, the amount of expenditure recorded in satellite accounts is expected to exceed the expenditure recorded under the respective COFOG division. More details on the comparability of COFOG data with satellite accounts data can be found in the COFOG manual. In particular, as regards defence expenditure, COFOG division 'defence' cannot be easily compared with NATO measures of defence expenditure. The main reasons are: COFOG is a classification by main purpose implying that some expenditure within COFOG 'public order and safety' might be counted under NATO methodology; the treatment of pensions in COFOG is within division 'social protection' and the COFOG treatment of employers' social contributions follows ESA 2010 and the time of recording may be different. '''Definition of general government total expenditure ''' Government total expenditure is defined in ESA 2010, paragraph 8.100 by using as reference a list of ESA 2010 categories. More detail is provided in the overview article on [[Government expenditure by function – COFOG]]. '''Gross Domestic Product''' Throughout this publication, the nominal GDP, i.e. GDP at current prices is used. In principle, the latest GDP available at time of publication is used. please also refer to metadata linked below. '''Time of recording & symbols used''' In the ESA 2010 system, recording is on an accrual basis, that is, when 'economic value is created, transformed or extinguished, or when claims and obligations arise, are transformed or are cancelled.' ":" not available "pp" percentage points '''More data and information ''' For more country-specific notes, e.g. on missing data, please refer to the metadata published on Eurobase. The authors can be contacted at ESTAT-GFS@ec.europa.eu === Context=== In the framework of the European System of National Accounts (ESA 2010), Eurostat collects data on general government expenditure by economic function according to the international Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG) – see methodological note. ===Other articles === *[[Government expenditure by function]] - online publication *[[Government expenditure by function – COFOG]] - overview article *[[Government finance statistics]] *[[Government finance statistics - quarterly data]] *[[Structure of government debt]] *[[Tax revenue statistics]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/government-finance-statistics/database Government finance statistics and EDP statistics], see: :Government statistics (gov) ::Government finance statistics (EDP and ESA2010) (gov_gfs10) :::Annual government finance statistics (gov_10a) ::::Government revenue, expenditure and main aggregates (gov_10a_main) ::::General government expenditure by function (COFOG) (gov_10a_exp) ::::Main national accounts tax aggregates (gov_10a_tax_ag) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/government-finance-statistics/database Government finance statistics and EDP statistics], see: :Government statistics (t_gov) ::Annual government finance statistics (t_gov_10a) === Dedicated section === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=government_finance_statistics}} Government finance statistics] === Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=gov_10a_main_esms|title=Government revenue, expenditure and main aggregates}} (ESMS metadata file — gov_10a_main_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=gov_10a_exp_esms|title=General government expenditure by function (COFOG) }} (ESMS metadata file — gov_10a_exp_esms) *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-19-010|title=Manual on sources and methods for the compilation of COFOG statistics - Classifications of the Functions of Government - 2019 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-23-002|title=Manual on government deficit and debt — implementation of ESA 2010}} — 2022 edition === Legislation=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-02-13-269|title=European system of accounts - ESA 2010}} {{Unit|topic=X_Government_accounts}} [[Category:Economy and finance|Government expenditure on defence]] [[Category:Government finance and excessive deficit procedure (EDP)|Government expenditure on defence]] [[Category:Government expenditure by function|Government expenditure on defence]] [[Category:Government finance statistics|Government expenditure on defence]] [[Category:Statistical article|Government expenditure on defence]] [[Category:March2027|Government expenditure on defence]]

title: Government expenditure on economic affairs
text:
EU statistics analyse general government expenditure on economic affairs. Data extracted on 20 August 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 General government expenditure in the EU on economic affairs amounted to €954 billion or 5.3% of GDP in 2024. [[Image:General government total expenditure on economic affairs, 2024 .png|thumb|centre|700px|General government total expenditure on economic affairs, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A stacked vertical bar chart showing the total general government expenditure on economic affairs for the year 2024. Each bar is divided into the separate economic categories with the data presented as percentage of GDP for the EU, the euro area 20 and the euro area 21, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries.]] This article analyses data on [[Glossary:Total_general_government_expenditure|general government expenditure]] on 'economic affairs' (according to the [[Glossary:Classification_of_the_functions_of_government_(COFOG)|Classification of the Functions of Government - COFOG).]] It is part of a [[Government_expenditure_by_function|set of statistical articles]] based on general government expenditure by function. [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] collects data on general government expenditure by economic function according to the international Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG) in the framework of the [[Glossary:ESA_2010|European System of National Accounts (ESA 2010).]] === Expenditure on 'economic affairs' === Government expenditure on 'economic affairs' at the level of the reporting countries exhibits considerable variability over time as recorded amounts may be influenced by operations of an extraordinary nature, such as disposal of [[Glossary:Non-financial_non-produced_assets|non-financial non-produced assets]] (recorded as negative expenditure) and capital injections recorded as capital transfers. Such capital injections are notably benefitting financial institutions and public corporations. Other extraordinary capital transfers comprise [[Glossary:Guarantees|guarantee]] calls. Furthermore, the majority of [[Glossary:Subsidies|subsidies]] granted to producers are recorded in this division.
In 2024, in the [[Glossary:EU-27|EU]], total expenditure of general government on 'economic affairs' represented 5.3% of [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]], a decrease compared with 2023 (-0.5 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]]). The decrease in the ratio compared with the previous year (5.8%) was a consequence of increases in GDP and a decrease in 'economic affairs' expenditure by -€44 billion. For the years 2020 and 2021, this division was highly impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic as governments introduced measures to mitigate its effects, most notably by furlough schemes recorded as subsidies to the employer, other subsidies introduced in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, and capital injections recorded as capital transfers. In 2022, this division was still influenced by the government measures to mitigate the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, although to a lesser extent than in 2020 and 2021. However, government measures to mitigate the impact of increasing energy prices (for example, caps on energy prices) strongly influenced the level of expenditure in this division in 2022 and 2023. Besides variability over time, there are also considerable variations at the level of the EU countries. Within the division 'economic affairs', at the level of the EU in 2024, the highest ratio to GDP represented expenditure related to 'transport' (2.5% of GDP), followed by expenditure on 'general economic, commercial and labour affairs' (1.0% of GDP), and by 'fuel and energy' (0.6% of GDP). Expenditure on 'research and development related to economic affairs' accounted for 0.4% of GDP. 'Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting' made up 0.3% of GDP. Economic affairs related to 'other industries' and 'mining, manufacturing and construction' both made up 0.2% of GDP. Expenditure not elsewhere classified (n.e.c.) and 'communication' both accounted for 0.1% of GDP. [[Image:Government_expenditure_by_function_in_the_EU_in_2024_(€_billion).png|centre|700px|thumb|Figure 1: EU government expenditure by function, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A graphic image showing general government expenditure by function in the EU for the year 2024. Data are expressed in euro billions for each function.]] In the EU, a large part of expenditure on 'agriculture, forestry and fishing and hunting' falls within the competency of the EU. As a consequence, expenditure of national governments of EU countries in this group tends to be smaller in comparison with [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] and other countries. Capital injections into financial institutions recorded as capital transfers explain the relatively high figures for some countries over the time period. Such expenditure is recorded in COFOG group 'general economic, commercial and labour affairs'. === In 2024, government expenditure reported by countries on 'economic affairs' ranged between 2.1% of GDP in Ireland and 7.7% of GDP in Hungary=== [[Image:General government total expenditure on economic affairs, 2024, % of GDP.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: General government total expenditure on economic affairs, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A table showing the total general government expenditure on economic affairs for the year 2024, expressed as a percentage of GDP and divided into each economic category. Data is shown for the EU, the euro area, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries.]] In 2024, Hungary reported the highest amount for 'economic affairs' expressed as ratio to GDP (7.7%), followed by Malta (7.6%), and Austria (7.1%). The lowest amounts of government expenditure were recorded in Ireland (2.1%), Cyprus (2.9%), Denmark (3.1%), and Lithuania (3.2%). The importance of the 'economic affairs' division is also highly dependent on the amount of subsidies given to public or private transportation companies as well as expenditure on public roads. Expenditure of transport companies (including those responsible for transport infrastructure) that are classified within the general government sector are even more important contributors to this functional group. Capital investments (gross capital formation, e.g. into transport infrastructure such as roads or railways) is an important part of expenditure in this group. In 2024, the highest expenditure to GDP ratios for 'transport' were recorded in Latvia (4.2%), Hungary (3.8%), Czechia (3.6%), Luxembourg and Sweden (both 3.5%). By contrast, the lowest levels of expenditure in 'transport' in relation to GDP were observed in Cyprus (0.8%) and in Ireland (1.2%). In 2024, the highest amounts recorded for 'general economic, commercial and labour affairs' were recorded in Belgium (3.0% of GDP), Malta (1.6% of GDP), and France and Austria (both 1.5% of GDP). In 2020 and 2021, and to a lesser extent in 2022, this functional group included labour-market measures to reduce the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, such as furlough schemes. It also covered other subsidies granted regardless of the industry concerned. For example, in 2022 and 2023, it included general subsidies to help businesses that use energy as an input in production. ===Annual decrease in 2024 for expenditure on 'economic affairs' after the strong increases in 2020 and 2021=== Overall, EU general government expenditure grew from €8 442 billion in 2023 to €8 855 billion in 2024, with increases observed across all the main functions of expenditure, except for 'housing and community amenities' and 'economic affairs'. In 2024, expenditure on 'economic affairs' stood at €954 billion, a decrease compared with 2023 (€998 billion), but remaining high in comparison with the pre-COVID-19 pandemic level. In 2020 and in 2021, the relative increases observed compared with 2019 were mostly due to government measures taken to counterbalance the negative economic effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, for example by providing subsidies to businesses affected by the pandemic, capital injections (e.g. for transport companies), and furlough schemes (insofar as these are recorded as subsidies, that is, considered to primarily provide general support to the labour market; some furlough schemes are recorded in social protection if they are deemed to primarily support the affected employees). In 2022, this division was still influenced by the government measures to mitigate the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, although to a lesser extent than in 2020 and 2021. However, government measures to mitigate the impact of increasing energy prices strongly influenced the level of expenditure in this division in 2022 and 2023. At the level of the EU, expenditure on 'economic affairs' decreased by €44 billion between 2023 and 2024 (€954 billion in 2024 and €998 billion in 2023). The share of 'economic affairs' expenditure in total expenditure decreased from 11.8% in 2023 to 10.8% in 2024. Despite the decrease in 2024, the share of 'economic affairs' expenditure in total expenditure was still relatively high compared with the 2010-2020 period, after peaking in 2021 (12.8%). [[Image:Detailed evolution of EU general government total expenditure on economic affairs, 2020-2024_€ billion.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Detailed evolution of EU general government total expenditure on economic affairs, 2020-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A vertical bar chart showing the total general government expenditure in the EU by detailed function for the years 2020 to 2024.]] Looking at the detail of functions within 'economic affairs', at EU level, the evolution in these detailed functions is strongly influenced by support measures to mitigate the impact of high energy prices. The strongest increase between 2023 and 2024 can be observed in the group 'transport' (€449 billion in 2024 compared with €426 billion in 2023). The strongest decrease is observed in 'fuel and energy' (€103 billion in 2024 compared with €160 billion in 2023), reflecting a lower impact of support measures to mitigate the impact of high energy prices, although the level in 2024 remains above the level of the year 2021. A stronger decrease is also observed in 'general economic, commercial and labour affairs' (€181 billion in 2024 compared with €193 billion in 2023), reflecting the lower impact of measures to mitigate the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2024, even if the level remains above the year 2019. ===Capital investments are the most important form of expenditure within 'economic affairs'=== In 2024, at the level of the EU, capital investments were the most important part of expenditure on economic affairs, with a share of 24% of total expenditure on economic affairs. They were followed by: * subsidies (23%) *[[Glossary:Intermediate_consumption|intermediate consumption]] (21%) *[[Glossary:Compensation_of_employees|compensation of employees]] (wages, salaries and employers' [[Glossary:Social_contributions|social contributions]]) (15%) and *[[Glossary:Capital_transfers|capital transfers]] (14%). === Source data for tables and graphs ===
'''''The detailed tables [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] are available [[Media:SE Cofog web 2026 08 20.xlsx |here]].'''''
=== Data sources and availability === '''Reporting of data to Eurostat ''' Annual government finance statistics (GFS) data are collected by Eurostat on the basis of the European System of Accounts (ESA 2010) transmission programme. Member States are requested to transmit, among other tables, table 1100, 'Expenditure of general government by function' 11 months after the end of the reference period. Table 1100 provides information about expenditure of the general government sector divided into main COFOG functions and ESA 2010 categories. The transmission of the COFOG I level breakdown (divisions) for the general government sector and its subsectors is compulsory for the years 1995 onwards, whereas information on the COFOG II level (COFOG groups) is provided on a compulsory basis for the general government sector from the reference years 2001 onwards. The main reference year used in this publication is 2024 as the latest year available at EU level. Data was extracted on 20 August 2026. '''Provisional data''' While a significant effort was undertaken to harmonise the recording of government measures to alleviate the impact of increasing energy prices, a full harmonisation was not yet achieved, please refer to country notes. Data for the EU and [[Glossary:Euro-area|euro area]] aggregates (2024), Belgium (2024), Germany (2022-2024), Spain (2024), France (2023-2024) and Portugal (2024), Slovakia (all years) is provisional. '''Definition of general government and its subsectors ''' The data relate to the general government sector of the economy, as defined in ESA 2010, paragraph 2.111: 'The general government sector (S.13) consists of institutional units which are non-market producers whose output is intended for individual and collective consumption, and are financed by compulsory payments made by units belonging to other sectors, and institutional units principally engaged in the redistribution of national income and wealth’. In general, the amount of expenditure recorded in satellite accounts is expected to exceed the expenditure recorded under the respective COFOG division. More details on the comparability of COFOG data with satellite accounts data can be found in the COFOG manual. '''Definition of general government total expenditure ''' Government total expenditure is defined in ESA 2010, paragraph 8.100 by using as reference a list of ESA 2010 categories. More detail is provided in the overview article on [[Government expenditure by function – COFOG]]. '''Gross Domestic Product''' Throughout this publication, the nominal GDP, i.e. GDP at current prices is used. In principle, the latest GDP available at time of publication is used. Please also refer to metadata files linked below. title: Government expenditure on education
text:
EU statistics on government expenditure on education are presented according to the Classification of the functions of government. Data extracted оn 20 August 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 General government expenditure in the EU on education amounted to €860 billion or 4.8% of GDP in 2024. [[Image:General government total expenditure on education, 2024 .png|thumb|centre|700px|General government total expenditure on education, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A stacked vertical bar chart showing the total general government expenditure on education for the year 2024. Each bar is divided into the separate education categories with the data presented as percentage of GDP for the EU, the euro area 20, the euro area 21, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries.]] This article analyses data on [[Glossary:Total_general_government_expenditure|general government expenditure]] on 'education' (according to the [[Glossary:Classification_of_the_functions_of_government_(COFOG)|Classification of the Functions of Government - COFOG).]] It is part of a [[Government expenditure by function|set of statistical articles]] based on general government expenditure by function. [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] collects data on general government expenditure by economic function according to the international
Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG) in the framework of the [[Glossary:ESA_2010|European System of National Accounts (ESA 2010).]] === Expenditure on 'education' === In the COFOG classification in use in this publication, expenditure on 'education' is divided into groups based on the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=International_Standard_Classification_of_Education_(ISCED) ISCED 1997 classification]. The following COFOG groups form the education division: *'pre-primary and primary education' *'secondary education' *'post-secondary non-tertiary education' *'tertiary education' *'education not definable by level' *'subsidiary services to education' (e.g. expenditure on providing school buses) *'R&D education' (i.e. related to education, not all R&D undertaken for example in universities) and *'education not elsewhere classified’ (n.e.c). [[Image:General government total expenditure on education, 2024, % of GDP.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: General government total expenditure on education, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A table showing the total general government expenditure on education for the year 2024, expressed as a percentage of GDP and divided into each education category. Data is shown for the EU, the euro area 20, the euro area 21, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries.]] In 2024, general government expenditure on 'education' in the EU amounted to €860 billion or 4.8% of [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]]. Of this, both 'pre-primary and primary education' as well as 'secondary education' accounted for 1.7% of GDP. For 'tertiary education', expenditure amounting to 0.8% of GDP was reported in the EU, while 'subsidiary services to education' (e.g. school transport) amounted to 0.3% of GDP. === Large differences between countries in the importance of expenditure on education === As a percentage of GDP, in the EU, the highest ratios were reported by: *Sweden (at 7.3% of GDP) *followed by Belgium, Finland, and Estonia (all 3 at 6.3% of GDP) *Latvia (6.1% of GDP) and *Poland and Denmark (both 5.6% of GDP). Among the [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA countries]], Iceland reported the highest ratio (7.0% of GDP). By contrast, the lowest ratios were reported by: *Ireland (2.7% of GDP) *Greece (3.9% of GDP) *Romania and Italy (both 4.0% of GDP) and *Spain (4.1% of GDP). As a share of total expenditure at the level of the EU, general government expenditure on ‘education’ amounted to 9.7% in 2024. At country level, ‘education’ expenditure accounted for relatively high shares of general government total expenditure in 2024 in these countries: *Sweden (14.4%) *Estonia (14.2%) *Lithuania (13.9%) *Latvia (13.4%) *Cyprus (13.2%) *Malta (12.6%) *Ireland (12.0%), as well as *Switzerland (16.3%) and Iceland (14.9%) among the EFTA countries. The lowest shares of ‘education’ expenditure in total expenditure were observed for Italy (8.0%), Greece (8.2%), France (8.9%), and as well as Spain and Germany (both at 9.1%). At the level of COFOG groups related to education in 2024, the highest shares in total expenditure for 'pre-primary and primary education' were observed for Sweden (9.2% of total expenditure) and Ireland (8.5%). For 'secondary education', the highest shares in total expenditure in 2024 were observed for Bulgaria (5.9%) and Lithuania (5.4%), while for 'tertiary education', the highest shares in total expenditure were observed in Denmark (3.1%), the Netherlands, Finland and Hungary (all 3.0%), as well as in Switzerland and Iceland (both 3.1%) among the EFTA countries. === Expenditure on 'education' by type of transaction === In 2024, at level of the EU, expenditure on education was divided into transactions as follows: *around 62.7% was in the form of '[[Glossary:Compensation_of_employees|compensation of employees]]' (meaning wages, salaries and employers' [[Glossary:Social_contributions|social contributions]], e.g. for teachers) *13.9% was in the form of '[[Glossary:Intermediate_consumption|intermediate consumption]]' (meaning purchases of goods and services) *6.0% was in the form of ‘[[Glossary:Social_benefits|social benefits]] other than [[Glossary:Social_transfers|social transfers]] in kind and social transfers in kind’ (purchased market production, for example school transport) and *5.9% was in the form of ‘other [[Glossary:Current_transfers|current transfers]]’. This latter category contains, for example, payments to private schools. ‘Capital investments’ ([[Glossary:Gross_capital_formation|gross capital formation]]), for example on school buildings, accounted for around 8.3% of education expenditure. === Evolution of 'education' expenditure from 2010-2024 === At the level of the EU, government expenditure on 'education' as a ratio to GDP ranged between 5.0% of GDP (2010) and 4.6% of GDP (2017, 2018, and 2022) in the period 2010-2024. In 2024, it stood at 4.8% of GDP. In 2010, government expenditure on education at the level of the EU stood at 5.0% of GDP and then gradually decreased to 4.6% of GDP in 2017. An increase up to 4.9% of GDP in 2020 was largely a result of the decrease in GDP during the COVID-19 pandemic. Between 2020 and 2024, EU general government expenditure on education as a ratio to GDP decreased from 4.9% of GDP in 2020 to 4.6% in 2022, and then reversed to reach 4.8% of GDP in 2024. At the level of the EU, the share of expenditure on education in total expenditure stood at 9.9% of total expenditure in 2010 and increased slightly to 10.0% of expenditure in 2019. As 'education' expenditure is less impacted by government measures in response to the COVID-19 pandemic as well as rising energy prices compared with other functions of government expenditure, in comparison with 2019, the relative share of education in total government expenditure has decreased to 9.7% of total expenditure in 2024. Compared with 2023, a slight increase is observed - from 9.6% of total expenditure in 2023 to 9.7% of total expenditure in 2024. [[Image:Government_expenditure_by_function_in_the_EU_in_2024_(€_billion).png|centre|700px|thumb|Figure 1: EU government expenditure by function, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A graphic image showing general government expenditure by function in the EU for the year 2024. Data are expressed in euro billions for each function.]] === Source data for tables and graphs ===

title: Government expenditure on public order and safety
text:

Data is shown for the EU, the euro area 20, the euro area 21, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries.]] At the level of the [[Glossary:EU|EU]], general government total expenditure on 'public order and safety' in 2024 stood at 1.7% of [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]]. Within this COFOG division, the equivalent of 0.9% of GDP was spent on 'police services', as the most significant COFOG group in this division by expenditure. Around 0.3% of GDP was accounted for by expenditure on 'law courts' and 0.2% of GDP each on 'fire protection services' (including civil protection operations such as dealing with flooding, mountain rescue, beach surveillance) and 'prisons'. In 2024, the level of expenditure on 'public order and safety' as a percentage of GDP was the highest in the following countries: *Latvia (3.2% of GDP) *Romania and Bulgaria (both 2.8% of GDP) *Croatia and Poland (both 2.4% of GDP) and *Slovakia (2.3% of GDP). It was the lowest in: *Ireland (0.7% of GDP) *Denmark (1.0% of GDP) *Luxembourg and Finland (both 1.3% of GDP) *Malta, Austria, and Slovenia (all 1.5% of GDP), as well as *Norway among the EFTA countries (1.0% of GDP). As a ratio to GDP, Latvia and Romania (both 1.7% of GDP) spent the highest amount on 'police services', followed by Croatia (1.5% of GDP), Bulgaria (1.4% of GDP), Cyprus (1.3% of GDP), and Greece (1.2% of GDP). This group comprises also expenditure on the operation of border and coast guards. Expenditure on 'fire protection services' ranged between 0.1% and 0.4% of GDP in 2024, with the highest ratios reported by Greece (0.4% of GDP), then Latvia, Germany, Estonia, Finland, Romania, France, Bulgaria, Czechia, and Poland (all 0.3% of GDP). Expenditure on 'law courts' in the EU, which comprises expenditure on the operation of courts and the justice system, was highest in Bulgaria (0.7% of GDP), followed by Poland, Latvia, and Croatia (all 0.5% of GDP). For the rest of the reporting countries the ratio ranged between 0.1% and 0.4% of GDP in 2024. Expenditure on 'prisons' ranged between 0.04% and 0.2% of GDP in all countries except Latvia (0.4% of GDP), the Netherlands, Sweden, and Hungary (all 0.3% of GDP) in 2024. === Expenditure on public order and safety by type of transaction === At the level of the EU, by far the largest part of expenditure on 'public order and safety' in 2024 was on '[[Glossary:Compensation_of_employees|compensation of employees]]' (69% of total expenditure), i.e. wages, salaries and employers' [[Glossary:Social_contributions|social contributions]] for staff working in this field, for example, police, judges, firemen, and prison guards. '[[Glossary:Intermediate_consumption|Intermediate consumption]]' (including expenditure on outsourcing services) made up about 20% of total expenditure, and capital investments about 8%. [[Image:Government_expenditure_by_function_in_the_EU_in_2024_(€_billion).png|centre|700px|thumb|Figure 1: EU government expenditure by function, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A graphic image showing general government expenditure by function in the EU for the year 2024. Data are expressed in euro billions for each function.]] === Source data for tables and graphs ===

title: Government expenditure on general public services
text:
EU statistics analyse general government expenditure on public services. Data extracted on 20 August 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 General government expenditure in the EU on general public services amounted to €1 096 billion or 6.1% of GDP in 2024. [[Image:General government total expenditure on general public services, 2024_% of GDP.png|thumb|centre|700px|General government total expenditure on general public services, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A stacked vertical bar chart showing the total general government expenditure on general public services for the year 2024. Each bar is divided into the separate general public service categories with the data presented as percentage of GDP for the EU, the euro area 20, the euro area 21, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article analyses data on [[Glossary:Total_general_government_expenditure|general government expenditure]] on 'general public services' (according to the [[Glossary:Classification_of_the_functions_of_government_(COFOG)|Classification of the Functions of Government - COFOG).]] It is part of a [[Government expenditure by function|set of statistical articles]] based on general government expenditure by function. [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] collects data on general government expenditure by economic function according to the international Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG) in the framework of the [[Glossary:ESA_2010|European System of National Accounts (ESA 2010).]] === Expenditure on 'general public services' === At the level of the [[Glossary:EU|EU]], expenditure on general public services made up 6.1% of [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]] in 2024. Among the more detailed functions (COFOG groups), in 2024, at the level of the EU: *'executive and legislative organs made up 1.9% of GDP *'foreign economic aid' made up 0.3% of GDP *'general services' made up 1.2% of GDP *'basic research' made up 0.7% of GDP *'general public services not elsewhere classified' (n.e.c) made up 0.1% of GDP and *'[[Glossary:Public_debt|public debt]] transactions' made up 1.9% of GDP. The functions 'R&D general public services' and 'transfers of a general nature between different levels of government' made up a very small part of expenditure. (For the latter group, no amounts are expected to be reported at general government level.) [[Image:General government total expenditure on general public services, 2024, % of GDP.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: General government total expenditure on general public services, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A table showing the total general government expenditure on general public services for the year 2024, expressed as a percentage of GDP and divided into each general public service category. Data is shown for the EU, the euro area, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Expenditure related to 'general public services' was higher in the below countries than in the other reporting countries: *Hungary (10.0% of GDP) *Greece (8.3% of GDP) *Italy (7.7% of GDP) *Belgium and Finland (both 7.1% of GDP), as well as *Iceland (7.6% of GDP) among the EFTA countries. Ireland (2.0% of GDP), Bulgaria (2.9% of GDP), Lithuania (3.6% of GDP), the Netherlands (4.1% of GDP), and Estonia (4.3% of GDP) were the countries reporting the lowest levels for 2024. This was partially due to the relatively low level of general [[Glossary:Government_gross_debt|government gross debt]] in Bulgaria, Latvia, and Lithuania, as well as generally low levels of total expenditure in these countries. Within the division 'general public services', expenditure related to the COFOG group 'public debt transactions' amounted to 1.9% of GDP for the EU in 2024. At the level of the reporting countries in 2024, expenditure in this COFOG group amounted to 5.0% in Hungary, 4.0% in Italy, 3.6% in Greece, followed by Spain and Romania, both at 2.5% of GDP. Among the [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA countries]], Iceland reported the highest ratio (4.8% of GDP). The relatively high amount for Iceland is partly explained by the inclusion in government accounts of units engaged in providing loans. At the other end of the scale, total expenditure in 'public debt transactions' amounted to 0.4% of GDP in Luxembourg, 0.5% of GDP in Bulgaria, and 0.6% of GDP in Estonia and Ireland, as well as 0.3% of GDP in Switzerland among the EFTA countries. This COFOG group contains almost exclusively interest payments to service government gross debt as well as indirectly measured financial intermediation service charges (FISIM). After the group 'executive and legislative organs', the group 'public debt transactions' represents the largest share of expenditure within the COFOG division 'general public services' at EU level. In 2024, at the level of the EU, expenditure on 'foreign economic aid' made up 0.3%. Sweden and Denmark reported the highest 'foreign economic aid' as a ratio to GDP (both 0.7%), followed by Luxembourg and Germany (both 0.5%), and the Netherlands (0.4% of GDP). Among the EFTA countries, Norway reported 0.9% of GDP in 2024 - the highest level among all reporting countries. The group 'executive and legislative organs' contains, among other expenditure items, some of the so-called EU own resource payments (notably [[Glossary:Value_added_tax|VAT]]- and [[Glossary:GNI|GNI]]-based contributions, as well as the own resource based on non-recycled plastic waste packaging). This partially explains the higher level of expenditure of EU countries in this group compared to other countries. At the level of the EU, total expenditure on 'executive and legislative organs' amounted to 1.9% of GDP in 2024. The highest level of expenditure in 'executive and legislative organs' in 2024 was reported by Croatia (3.4% of GDP), Hungary (3.2% of GDP), as well as Slovakia and Portugal (both 3.0% of GDP). Meanwhile, the lowest value in the EU was reported by Ireland (0.9% of GDP), and among the EFTA countries, Switzerland (0.8% of GDP). In 2024, as a ratio to GDP, expenditure on 'basic research' was highest in Sweden (1.5% of GDP) and Denmark (1.3% of GDP), as well as in Switzerland among the EFTA countries (1.7% of GDP). === Expenditure on general public services by transaction === In 2024, at the level of the EU, around 31% of the expenditure on general public services was in the form of '[[Glossary:Property_income|property income]], payable'. This almost entirely concerned [[Glossary:Interest|interest]] on general government debt instruments and was allocated to the COFOG group '[[Glossary:Public_debt|public debt transactions]]'. Around 23% of expenditure in the 'general public services' function was in the form of '[[Glossary:Compensation_of_employees|compensation of employees]]', around 16% of expenditure was in the form of other [[Glossary:Current_transfers|current transfers]] (e.g. for EU own resources allocated to group 'executive and legislative organs', grants in the context of foreign economic aid) and around 15% of total expenditure was in the form of '[[Glossary:Intermediate_consumption|intermediate consumption]]'. Capital investments account for around 10% of total expenditure in this function. === Evolution of expenditure on general public services from 2010-2024=== At the level of the EU, expenditure on general public services decreased from 7.1% of GDP in 2010 to 6.1% of GDP in 2024, although since 2017, a relatively stable ratio can be observed. Total expenditure of general government in the EU, expressed as a ratio to GDP, was 50.7% of GDP in 2010 compared to 49.1% of GDP in 2024. Among the major functions of government, general public services decreased the most between 2010 and 2024 measured as a ratio to GDP or percentage of total expenditure. The share of general public services at EU level decreased from 13.9% of total expenditure in 2010 to 12.3% of total expenditure in 2019 and 11.3% of total expenditure in 2020. From 2021 onwards the ratio follows an upward trend, from 11.4% of total expenditure in 2021, 11.9% of total expenditure in 2022, and 12.0% of total expenditure in 2023, to 12.4% of total expenditure in 2024. The share in total expenditure between 2020 and 2022 was affected by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, which mainly led to increases in expenditure on economic affairs and health. [[Image:Government_expenditure_by_function_in_the_EU_in_2024_(€_billion).png|centre|700px|thumb|Figure 1: EU government expenditure by function, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A graphic image showing general government expenditure by function in the EU for the year 2024. Data are expressed in euro billions for each function.]] === Source data for tables and graphs ===
'''''The detailed tables [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] are available [[Media:SE Cofog web 2026 08 20.xlsx |here]].'''''
=== Data sources and availability === '''Reporting of data to Eurostat ''' Annual government finance statistics (GFS) data are collected by Eurostat on the basis of the European System of Accounts (ESA 2010) transmission programme. Member States are requested to transmit, among other tables, table 1100, 'Expenditure of general government by function' eleven months after the end of the reference period. Table 1100 provides information about expenditure of the general government sector divided into main COFOG functions and ESA 2010 categories. The transmission of the COFOG I level breakdown (divisions) is compulsory for the years 1995 onwards, whereas information on the COFOG II level (COFOG groups) is provided on a compulsory basis for the general government sector for the reference years 2001 onwards. The main reference year used in this publication is 2024 as the latest year available at EU level. Data was extracted on 20 August 2026. '''Provisional data''' While a significant effort was undertaken to harmonise the recording of government measures to alleviate the impact of increasing energy prices, a full harmonisation was not yet achieved. Data for the EU and [[Glossary:Euro-area|euro area]] aggregates (2024), Belgium (2024), Germany (2022-2024), Spain (2024), France (2023-2024), Portugal (2024), and Slovakia (all years) is provisional. '''Definition of general government and its subsectors ''' The data relate to the general government sector of the economy, as defined in ESA 2010, paragraph 2.111: 'The general government sector (S.13) consists of institutional units which are non-market producers whose output is intended for individual and collective consumption, and are financed by compulsory payments made by units belonging to other sectors, and institutional units principally engaged in the redistribution of national income and wealth’. '''Classification of functional expenditure of government ''' The Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG) classifies government expenditure into ten main categories (divisions known as the 'COFOG I level' breakdown): general public services; defence; public order and safety; economic affairs; environmental protection; housing and community affairs; health; recreation, culture and religion; education; social protection. These divisions are further broken down into 'groups' (COFOG II level). For 'general public services', the groups are *'executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs', *'foreign economic aid', *'general services', *'basic research', *'R&D General public services', *'general public services n.e.c.', *'public debt transactions', *'transfers of a general character between different levels of government'. Further information is available in the Eurostat {{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-19-010|title=Manual on sources and methods for the compilation of COFOG Statistics.}} '''Satellite accounts''' Administrative expenditure data is additionally collected in so-called satellite accounts. In general, the amount of expenditure recorded in satellite accounts is expected to exceed the expenditure recorded under the respective COFOG division. More details on the comparability of COFOG data with satellite accounts data can be found in the COFOG manual. '''Definition of general government total expenditure''' Government total expenditure is defined in ESA 2010, paragraph 8.100 by using as reference a list of ESA 2010 categories. More detail is provided in the overview article on [[Government expenditure by function – COFOG]]. '''Gross Domestic Product''' Throughout this publication, the nominal GDP, i.e. GDP at current prices is used. In principle, the latest GDP available at time of publication is used. Please also refer to metadata files linked below. '''Time of recording & symbols used''' In the ESA 2010 system, recording is on an accrual basis, that is, when ‘economic value is created, transformed or extinguished, or when claims and obligations arise, are transformed or are cancelled.' ":" not available "pp" percentage points '''More data and information ''' For more country-specific notes, e.g. on missing data, please refer to the metadata published on Eurobase. The authors can be contacted at ESTAT-GFS@ec.europa.eu === Context=== In the framework of the European System of National Accounts (ESA 2010), Eurostat collects data on general government expenditure by economic function according to the international Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG) – see methodological note. ===Other articles === *[[Government expenditure by function]] - title: Government expenditure on recreation, culture and religion
text:
EU statistics on government expenditure for recreation, culture and religion are presented according to the Classification of the functions of government. Data extracted on 20 August 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 General government expenditure in the EU on recreation, culture and religion amounted to €213 billion or 1.2% of GDP in 2024.

[[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] collects data on general government expenditure by economic function according to the international
Classification of the Functions of Government (COFOG) in the framework of the [[Glossary:ESA_2010|European System of National Accounts (ESA 2010).]] === Expenditure on 'recreation, culture and religion' === In 2024, Hungary (2.5% of GDP), Estonia (1.9% of GDP), Croatia and Finland (both 1.7% of GDP), followed by Denmark, Slovenia, France and Malta (all 1.5% of GDP) as well as Iceland (3.0% of GDP) and Norway (1.5% of GDP) among EFTA countries registered the largest ratios to GDP of government expenditure in the 'recreation, culture and religion' function compared with 1.2% of GDP in the [[Glossary:EU-27|EU]] and 1.1% of GDP in the [[Glossary:EA-20|euro area (euro area 20)]]. Ireland registered the lowest ratio (0.4% of GDP) in 2024 devoted to 'recreation, culture and religion', followed by Cyprus (0.5% of GDP), Bulgaria (0.7% of GDP) and Portugal (0.8% of GDP). [[Image:General government total expenditure on recreation, culture and religion, 2024, % of GDP.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: General government total expenditure on recreation, culture and religion, 2024 (% of GDP)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A table showing the total general government expenditure on recreation, culture and religion for the year 2024, expressed as a percentage of GDP and divided into each recreation, culture and religion category. Data is shown for the EU, the euro area 20, the euro area 21, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The majority of expenditure on 'recreation, culture and religion' at EU level in 2024 was devoted to 'cultural services' (0.5% of GDP), followed by 'recreational and sporting services' (0.4% of GDP), 'broadcasting and publishing services' (0.2% of GDP) and 'religious and other community services' (0.1% of GDP). ===Evolution of general government expenditure on 'recreation, culture and religion'=== Over the period 2010-2024, the share of government expenditure on 'recreation, culture and religion' ranged between 1.3% and 1.1% of total expenditure, with peak in 2010 and lower points in 2015-2017 as well as in 2022. As expenditure on 'recreation, culture and religion' was less impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic and the impact of high energy prices compared to other functions of government expenditure, the relative share of 'recreation, culture and religion' in total government expenditure decreased by 0.1 percentage points in 2020-2024 compared to 2019. In absolute terms, at the level of the EU, expenditure on 'recreation, culture and religion' decreased in 2020 (by €0.3 billion) and increased by around €8.7 billion in 2021, €12.0 billion in 2022 and €15.3 billion in 2023 and €12.5 billion in 2024 to stand at €213.1 billion in 2024. [[Image:Government_expenditure_by_function_in_the_EU_in_2024_(€_billion).png|centre|700px|thumb|''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10a_exp}}|alt=A graphic image showing general government expenditure by function in the EU for the year 2024. Data are expressed in euro billions for each function. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs ===
