title: Healthcare expenditure statistics - overview
text:
An overview of EU statistics on healthcare systems across EU countries. Data extracted in October 2025 Planned article update: November 2026 Current healthcare expenditure in the EU was €1 720 billion in 2023. This was equivalent to 10.0% of gross domestic product (GDP). Among EU countries, Germany (11.7%), France (11.5%), Austria and Sweden (both 11.2%) had the highest current healthcare expenditure relative to GDP in 2023. Among EU countries, the largest expansions (in percentage terms) in current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant between 2014 and 2023 were recorded in Romania, Bulgaria, Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Czechia, Estonia and Croatia, where expenditure more than doubled. :[[Glossary:Country_codes|Country codes]] This article presents key statistics on expenditure aspects of [[Glossary:Healthcare|healthcare]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. More detailed information is available – with analyses by functions, providers and financing schemes – in [[Healthcare_expenditure_statistics_by_function,_provider_and_financing_scheme|a separate article]]. Healthcare systems are organised and financed in various ways across EU countries, but universal access to quality healthcare, at an affordable cost to both individuals and society at large, is widely regarded as a basic right in the EU. Statistics on healthcare expenditure and financing may be used to evaluate how a healthcare system responds to the challenge of universal access to quality healthcare, through measuring financial resources available for the healthcare sector and the allocation of these resources between healthcare activities (for example, preventive and curative care) or groups of healthcare providers (for example, [[Glossary:Hospital|hospitals]] and ambulatory centres). This article forms part of an online publication on [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]]. It should be noted that the latest data presented in this article are for 2023. Therefore, the data in this article show the situation after the COVID-19 pandemic. For this reason, particular attention should be paid when comparing 2022 and 2023 data with data for 2020 to 2021 and when comparing data for 2020 and 2021 with earlier years. ===Healthcare expenditure=== '''Germany, France, Austria and Sweden had the highest current healthcare expenditure relative to GDP in 2023''' Current healthcare expenditure in the EU was €1 720 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] in 2023. Germany had the highest level of current healthcare expenditure among EU countries, valued at €492 billion in 2023. France recorded the second highest level of current healthcare expenditure (€325 billion), followed by Italy (€179 billion) and Spain (€138 billion). In 2023, current healthcare expenditure in the EU was equivalent to 10.0% of [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]]. Among the EU countries, Germany recorded the highest ratio, which was equivalent to 11.7% of GDP; the next highest ratios were in France (11.5%), Austria and Sweden (both 11.2%) – see Table 1. By contrast, current healthcare expenditure accounted for less than 7.0% of GDP in 4 EU countries: Luxembourg, Romania (both 5.7%), Hungary (6.4%) and Ireland (6.6%). [[Image:Table 1 Current healthcare expenditure, 2023V1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Current healthcare expenditure, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hf}}|alt=A table showing current healthcare expenditure. Data are presented in million euro, euro per inhabitant, purchasing power standards per inhabitant and as a ratio relative to GDP in percent. Data are shown for 2023, for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Relative to population size and in euro terms, current healthcare expenditure in 2023 was highest among EU countries in Luxembourg (€6 888 per inhabitant). It is interesting to note that Luxembourg had the highest ratio per inhabitant despite having the lowest ratio of healthcare expenditure to GDP, reflecting the high level of GDP in Luxembourg. A significant proportion of workers in Luxembourg are cross-border workers and live outside the country and, as non-residents, the expenditure on their healthcare is not included in Luxembourg’s health accounts while their economic activity contributes to Luxembourg’s GDP. Following on from Luxembourg, the next highest ratios in 2023 were observed in Ireland, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Sweden, all above €5 700 per inhabitant. In turn, these were followed by Belgium, Finland and France with ratios between €4 700 and €5 500 per inhabitant. There was then a relatively large gap to Malta, Italy, Spain, Slovenia, Cyprus, Portugal and Czechia with ratios above €2 400 but below €3 300 per inhabitant. All of the remaining 10 EU countries recorded average expenditure below €2 100 per inhabitant; 1 of these, Romania, recorded an average spend on healthcare below €1 000 per inhabitant. The ratio between the highest (Luxembourg) and lowest (Romania) levels of expenditure per inhabitant was 7.1 : 1. [[Image:Current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant, 2023_HCE2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hf}}|alt=A grouped column chart showing current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant in euro and in purchasing power standards. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The disparities in current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant are less apparent when expenditure is expressed in [[Glossary:Purchasing power standard (PPS)|purchasing power standards (PPS)]]. This measure adjusts for differences in price levels between EU countries. Germany (5 413 PPS per inhabitant), Austria (4 900 PPS per inhabitant) and the Netherlands (4 848 PPS per inhabitant) recorded the highest ratios of healthcare expenditure per inhabitant in PPS terms. Romania (1 776 PPS per inhabitant) had the lowest ratio. As such, by taking account of price level differences, the ratio between the highest (Germany) and lowest (Romania) levels of healthcare expenditure per inhabitant was considerably smaller than the equivalent ratio in euro terms mentioned above, as it was 3.0 : 1. === Developments over time === Table 2 and Figures 2 and 3 highlight developments in the level of healthcare expenditure and the level of healthcare expenditure relative to GDP in recent years, focusing on a comparison between 2014 and 2023. Note that the analyses in Table 2 and Figure 2 are presented in current price terms and so reflect price changes (inflation and deflation) as well as changes in real expenditure. Based on the data shown in Table 2, all EU countries recorded higher healthcare expenditure in 2023 than in 2014. The largest overall increases were observed in Romania, Lithuania, Malta, Bulgaria, Estonia, Czechia, Latvia, Cyprus and Poland, where expenditure in 2023 was more than double that in 2014. The highest increase, in Romania, was 144.7%, equivalent to a compound annual average increase of 10.5%. The smallest increases between 2014 and 2023 were observed in Italy (up 23.6% overall) and Sweden (25.1%). [[Image:Current healthcare expenditure, 2014–23_HCE2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Current healthcare expenditure, 2014–23
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hf}}|alt=A table showing current healthcare expenditure. Data are presented in million euro for 2014 to 2023 and for the overall change between 2014 and 2023 in percent. Data are shown for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] As well as being affected by price changes, comparisons of healthcare expenditure over time can also be influenced by demographic changes. Figure 2 shows the average healthcare expenditure per inhabitant in 2014 and 2023. All EU countries recorded a higher level of expenditure per inhabitant in 2023 than in 2014. As with the rate of change based on overall expenditure, Romania recorded the largest increase, with average expenditure per inhabitant increasing by 155.6%; in Bulgaria, Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Czechia, Estonia and Croatia, this ratio also at least doubled. The smallest increase was observed in Sweden, up 15.2%. [[Image:Current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant, 2014 and 2023 (EUR)_HCE2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant, 2014 and 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hf}}|alt=A grouped column chart showing current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant. Data are presented in euro per inhabitant for 2014 and for 2023. Data are shown for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 3 provides another analysis of the change in overall healthcare expenditure between 2014 and 2023, focusing on the ratio between this expenditure and GDP. Healthcare expenditure and GDP are both influenced by price changes and so, when combining the 2 indicators in a ratio, the impact of inflation may cancel out to some degree: this depends on the extent to which the price changes related to healthcare expenditure are similar to those experienced in the economy as a whole. There were 7 EU countries that reported a lower ratio of healthcare expenditure to GDP in 2023 than in 2014. Ireland recorded the largest decrease, down 2.7 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points]], its share falling from 9.2% in 2014 to 6.6% in 2023, in part reflecting a large increase in Irish GDP between these years. The 6 other decreases were smaller than 1.0 points. In EU countries where the ratio was higher in 2023 than it had been in 2014, the increase was not more than 1.2 percentage points in most cases. A larger increase was observed in Latvia, up 1.6 points. [[Image:Current healthcare expenditure relative to GDP, 2014 and 2023 (%)_HCE2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Current healthcare expenditure relative to GDP, 2014 and 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hf}}|alt=A grouped column chart showing current healthcare expenditure relative to GDP in percent. Data are shown for 2014 and for 2023, for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=Healthcare expenditure statistics - overview HCE11 2025.xlsx|title=Healthcare expenditure statistics – overview: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The 2023 data for the EU, Malta and Finland are provisional, as are the 2022 data for Norway. '''Tables in this article use the following notation''' *A colon ':' is used to show where data are not available. '''Current healthcare expenditure''' Current healthcare expenditure quantifies the economic resources dedicated to health functions, excluding capital investment. Current healthcare expenditure is primarily concerned with healthcare goods and services that are consumed by resident units, irrespective of where that consumption takes place (it may be in the rest of the world) or who is paying for it. As such, exports of healthcare goods and services (to non-resident units) are excluded, whereas imports of healthcare goods and services for final use are included. '''System of health accounts – methodology''' [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], the [[Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)]] and the [[Glossary:World Health Organization (WHO)|World Health Organization (WHO)]] established a common framework for a joint healthcare data collection exercise. The data collected relates to healthcare expenditure following the methodology of the [[Glossary:System of health accounts (SHA)|system of health accounts (SHA)]]. The SHA shares the goals of the [[Glossary:System of national accounts (SNA)|system of national accounts (SNA)]]: to constitute an integrated system of comprehensive, internally consistent and internationally comparable accounts, which should as far as possible be compatible with other aggregated economic and social statistical systems. Health accounts provide a description of the monetary flows related to final consumption expenditure on healthcare goods and services. Health accounts are used in 2 main ways: internationally, where the emphasis is on a selection of comparable expenditure data; nationally, with more detailed analyses of healthcare spending and a greater emphasis on comparisons over time. For more details on health accounts, see [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf/60aa44b0-2738-4c4d-be4b-48b6590be1b0 A system of health accounts, 2011 – revised edition]. The core set of SHA tables addresses 3 basic questions: i) what kinds of healthcare goods and services are consumed, ii) which healthcare providers deliver them and, iii) which financing schemes are used to finance the expenditure? '''Healthcare expenditure – legal basis''' [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2021.387.01.0110.01.ENG Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/1901 of 29 October 2021 as regards statistics on health care expenditure and financing] is the legal basis for data collection according to SHA 2011 methodology for healthcare expenditure. {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32015R0359:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/359 of 4 March 2015 implementing Regulation (EC) No 1338/2008 as regards statistics on healthcare expenditure and financing}} applied to data from reference year 2014 to 2020. Statistics on healthcare expenditure are documented in a [[Healthcare_expenditure_statistics_-_methodology|background article]] which provides more information on the scope of the data, the legal framework, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. ===Context=== Health systems across the globe are developing in response to a multitude of factors, including new medical technology and improvements in knowledge providing new health services and a greater access to them; changes in health policies to address specific diseases and demographic developments; new organisational structures and more complex financing mechanisms. However, access to healthcare and greater patient choice is increasingly being considered against a background of financial sustainability. Within the European Commission, the [https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/health-and-food-safety_en Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety] and the [https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/employment-social-affairs-and-inclusion_en Directorate-General for Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion] are responsible for policy actions on health. ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2021.107.01.0001.01.ENG Regulation (EU) 2021/522 establishing a Programme for the Union’s action in the field of health (‘EU4health programme’) for the period 2021 to 2027]'' provides funding to EU countries, health organisations and non-governmental organisations (NGOs). In May 2024, the European Commission summarised work done and progress made within the health domain through a communication ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52024DC0206 The European Health Union: acting together for people’s health]'' (COM(2024) 206 final). It highlights a range of actions designed to make people’s lives safer and healthier. The Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety has constituted a list of 88 [https://health.ec.europa.eu/indicators-and-data/european-core-health-indicators-echi_en European core health indicators (ECHIs)] for monitoring progress in relation to health policy and broader objectives. Among these, it specifically recommends following developments on: *[https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/dyna/echi/?indlist=77a expenditure on healthcare as a percentage of GDP] *[https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/dyna/echi/?indlist=77b expenditures on healthcare in purchasing power standards (PPS)]. ===Other articles=== '''Online publication''' *[[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] '''Methodology''' *[[Healthcare_expenditure_statistics_-_methodology|Healthcare expenditure]] title: Healthcare expenditure statistics by function, provider and financing scheme
text:
Statistics on healthcare systems across the EU countries. There are 3 analyses provided: the sources of financing, the healthcare functions that are financed and the providers of healthcare. Data extracted in October 2025 Planned article update: November 2026 In 2023, 52.3% of current healthcare expenditure in the EU was financed by compulsory schemes and savings accounts and 28.2% by government schemes. The remaining 19.5% was financed by other financing agents. In 2023, 52.7% of current healthcare expenditure in the EU was for curative and rehabilitative care and 17.8% for medical goods. The remaining 29.5% was for other functions. In 2023, 36.8% of current healthcare expenditure in the EU related to provision by hospitals, 25.6% by providers of ambulatory care and 16.2% by retailers and other providers of medical goods. The remaining 21.3% was supplied by other providers. :[[Glossary:Country_codes|Country codes]] This article presents detailed statistics on expenditure and financing aspects of [[Glossary:Healthcare|healthcare]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], with analyses by financing scheme, function and provider. An overview of healthcare expenditure statistics is available in [[Healthcare_expenditure_statistics_-_overview|a separate article]]. Healthcare systems are financed and organised in different ways across the EU countries, but universal access to quality healthcare, at an affordable cost to both individuals and society at large, is widely regarded as a basic right in the EU. Statistics on healthcare expenditure and financing can be used to evaluate how a healthcare system responds to the challenge of universal access to quality healthcare, through measuring financial resources available to the healthcare sector and the allocation of these resources between healthcare activities (for example, preventive and curative care) or groups of healthcare providers (for example, [[Glossary:Hospital|hospitals]] and ambulatory centres). This article forms part of an online publication on [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]]. It should be noted that the latest data presented in this article are for 2023. Therefore, the data in this article show the situation after the COVID-19 pandemic. For this reason, particular attention should be paid when comparing 2022 and 2023 data with data for 2020 to 2021 and when comparing data for 2020 and 2021 with earlier years. ===Key data and overview of healthcare financing, functions and providers=== Current healthcare expenditure in the EU was €1 720 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] in 2023. This was equivalent to 10.0% of [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]]. Relative to population size and in euro terms, current healthcare expenditure in 2023 was €3 835 per inhabitant. Healthcare expenditure can be analysed from 3 perspectives: the sources of financing, the healthcare functions that are financed and the providers of healthcare. Table 1 identifies the largest sources of financing, functions and providers. *In the EU, compulsory contributory health insurance schemes and compulsory medical savings accounts (which are generally part of the social security system and are hereafter referred to as compulsory schemes/accounts) had a 52.3% share of all financing in 2023. Government schemes accounted for 28.2%. *More than half (52.7%) of healthcare expenditure in the EU in 2023 was for curative and rehabilitative care, while nearly a fifth (17.8%) was for medical goods. *Hospitals were the largest providers of healthcare in expenditure terms, accounting for more than a third (36.8%) of all expenditure in the EU in 2023. Providers of ambulatory health care (25.6%) and retailers and other providers of medical goods (16.2%) were the second and third largest providers of healthcare in expenditure terms. [[Image:Analysis of current healthcare expenditure, 2023 (%)_HCE2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Analysis of current healthcare expenditure, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hf}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hp}}|alt=A table showing an analysis of current healthcare expenditure. Data are presented as a share of current healthcare expenditure in percent. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. Detailed information is presented for financing, functions and providers of healthcare. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] While Table 1 presents an overview of the 3 areas (sources of financing, functions and providers), the remainder of this article looks at each of these areas in more detail. ===Healthcare expenditure by financing scheme=== '''Government and compulsory schemes/accounts together financed 80.6% of healthcare expenditure in the EU in 2023''' Figure 1 provides a simplified analysis of healthcare expenditure by financing scheme, distinguishing government schemes, compulsory schemes/accounts, as well as all other financing agents. The combined share of government schemes and compulsory schemes/accounts in total current healthcare expenditure was 80.6% across the EU. This combined share was 81.0% or higher in 9 EU countries, peaking at 86.1% in Sweden. Elsewhere in the EU, this combined share was 79.0% or lower, with shares below 70.0% in 6 countries; Latvia had the lowest share (59.6%). In most of the EU countries, either government schemes or compulsory schemes/accounts dominated. *In 9 EU countries, government schemes accounted for more than half of all expenditure. *In 15 EU countries, compulsory schemes/accounts accounted for more than half of all expenditure. *In Bulgaria and Austria, compulsory schemes/accounts registered a larger share than government schemes or other sources, but less than half of the total. *In Greece, other sources provided a greater share of financing than either government schemes or compulsory schemes/accounts. Compulsory schemes/accounts accounted for close to or in excess of three quarters of overall spending on healthcare in France (80.0%), Luxembourg (78.7%), Germany (78.0%), Croatia (77.4%), Slovakia (75.0%) and the Netherlands (74.6%) in 2023, but less than 5.0% in Spain, Portugal, Ireland, Italy and Malta. It should be noted that compulsory schemes/accounts do not exist in Denmark, Latvia and Sweden. By contrast, Sweden (86.1%) and Denmark (83.3%) reported that government schemes accounted for more than four fifths of their expenditure on healthcare, while shares around three quarters were registered in Ireland (76.0%) and Italy (72.9%). [[Image:Major sources of financing of current healthcare expenditure, 2023 (% of current healthcare expenditure)_HCE2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Major sources of financing of current healthcare expenditure, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hf}}|alt=A stacked column chart showing major sources of financing of current healthcare expenditure as share of all current healthcare expenditure in percent. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The stacks for each country sum to 100% and present the shares for government schemes, compulsory contributory health insurance schemes and compulsory medical savings accounts, and other financing agents. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 2 provides a similar analysis of healthcare expenditure by financing scheme, but with more detail concerning other financing schemes. The third largest source of healthcare funding in the EU was household out-of-pocket payments, with a 14.9% share in 2023. This was the highest share in Greece, the third highest share in Cyprus and Austria, and the second highest in all other EU countries. This source accounted for a third or more of total healthcare expenditure in Bulgaria (35.5%), Latvia (35.1%) and Greece (34.3%). Luxembourg, France and Croatia were the only EU countries where household out-of-pocket payments accounted for less than a tenth of healthcare expenditure, with shares ranging from 8.8% to 9.4%. [[Image:Current healthcare expenditure, analysed by source of financing, 2023 (% of current healthcare expenditure)_HCE2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Current healthcare expenditure, analysed by source of financing, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hf}}|alt= Table showing current healthcare expenditure analysed by source of financing as percentage of current healthcare expenditure. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. Detailed information is presented for seven different sources of financing. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Voluntary health insurance schemes generally represented a small share of healthcare financing in the EU in 2023. Their share peaked at 13.3% in Slovenia, followed by 10.6% in Ireland; the next highest share was 8.2% in Portugal. There were 5 EU countries where voluntary health insurance schemes provided less than 1.0% of the finance for healthcare expenditure in 2023, with the lowest share recorded in Czechia (0.2%). The final analysis concerning financing (see Figure 2), shows the same sources of financing as in Table 2, but presented as values per inhabitant in [[Glossary:Purchasing power standard (PPS)|purchasing power standards (PPS)]] rather than as a share of all healthcare expenditure. When expenditure is expressed in PPS, the expenditure data account for differences in price levels between countries. This analysis shows how much is spent on average per inhabitant from each of the different sources. The total for all sources (the overall height of each stacked column) shows the average expenditure per inhabitant. To put this in perspective, the EU, EFTA and enlargement countries have been ranked based on their overall level of current healthcare expenditure relative to GDP. [[Image:Current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant, analysed by source of financing, 2023 (PPS per inhabitant)_HCE2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant, analysed by source of financing, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hf}}|alt=A stacked column chart showing current healthcare expenditure per inhabitant, analysed by source of financing. Data are presented in PPS per inhabitant. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. Each country has seven stacks representing different financing sources. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Healthcare expenditure by function=== '''Curative and rehabilitative care services accounted for more than half of current healthcare expenditure in 2023 in all but 2 of the EU countries''' The functional patterns of healthcare expenditure presented in Figure 3 and Table 3 show that curative and rehabilitative care services accounted for more than 50.0% of current healthcare expenditure in 2023 in the vast majority of EU countries. The exceptions were Germany and Malta, with shares of 46.5% and 47.1%, respectively. The average for the EU was 52.7%. By contrast, at the upper end of the range, close to two thirds of current healthcare expenditure in 2023 was spent on curative and rehabilitative care services in Cyprus, Portugal (both 65.3%) and Poland (64.2%). [[Image:Major functions of healthcare expenditure, 2023 (% of current healthcare expenditure)_HCE2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Major functions of healthcare expenditure, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hc}}|alt=A stacked column chart showing major functions of healthcare expenditure as a share of all current healthcare expenditure in percent. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The stacks for each country sum to 100% and present the shares for curative care and rehabilitative care, medical goods, and other functions. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Medical goods accounted for 17.8% of healthcare expenditure in 2023''' Medical goods (non-specified by function) were the second largest function in the EU in 2023, with a 17.8% share of current healthcare expenditure. There was a substantial variation between the EU countries in terms of the share of expenditure on medical goods. The lowest shares were recorded for the Netherlands (9.8%), Denmark (11.6%) and Ireland (11.8%). By contrast, the highest share – where medical goods accounted for close to a third of current healthcare expenditure – was recorded for Bulgaria (32.5%). [[Image:Healthcare expenditure, analysed by function, 2023 (% of current healthcare expenditure)_HCE2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Healthcare expenditure, analysed by function, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hc}}|alt=A table showing healthcare expenditure analysed by function, as a share of all current healthcare expenditure in percent. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. Detailed information is presented for seven different functions. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The proportion of healthcare expenditure for long-term healthcare was 17.1% in the EU in 2023: more information about this function is provided below. *The fourth largest function was expenditure for ancillary services (such as laboratory testing or the transportation of patients), which averaged 5.0% of current healthcare expenditure in 2023 in the EU. Among the EU countries, this share ranged from 0.0% in Denmark and 1.0% in the Netherlands to 11.7% in Estonia. *The next largest function was preventive care, which accounted for 3.7% of healthcare expenditure in the EU in 2023. The share of this care was highest in the Netherlands (5.2%) and lowest in Malta (0.9%). *Expenditure related to governance and health system and financing administration was only slightly smaller, with a 3.6% share in the EU in 2023. This expenditure ranged from 0.8% in Finland to 5.0% in France. '''Long-term healthcare expenditure accounted for more than a quarter of current healthcare expenditure in 2023 in the Netherlands and Sweden''' As noted above, services related to long-term healthcare accounted for 17.1% of current healthcare expenditure in the EU in 2023. This share was below 10.0% in 11 of the EU countries (see Figure 4). Relatively low shares could be due to the main burden of long-term healthcare residing with family members, with no payment being made for providing these services. On the other hand, more than a fifth of healthcare expenditure was attributed to long-term healthcare in Finland, Germany, Denmark, Malta, Ireland and Belgium, with this share exceeding a quarter in Sweden (27.5%) and the Netherlands (29.1%). It should be noted that it can be difficult to separate the medical/health and social components of expenditure for long-term care, leading to an inevitable impact on cross-country comparisons. [[Image:Long-term healthcare as a share of current healthcare expenditure, 2023 (%)_HCE2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Long-term healthcare as a share of current healthcare expenditure, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hc}}|alt=A column chart showing long-term healthcare as a share of current healthcare expenditure in percent. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Healthcare expenditure by provider=== '''In expenditure terms, hospitals were the main providers of healthcare in most EU countries in 2023''' An analysis of current healthcare expenditure by provider is shown in Figure 5 and Table 4. It should be borne in mind that healthcare providers classified under the same group do not necessarily perform the same set of activities. For example, hospitals may offer day care, out-patient, ancillary or other types of services, in addition to in-patient services. Hospitals accounted for the highest proportion (36.8%) of healthcare expenditure in 2023 in the EU. Among the EU countries, the share of current healthcare expenditure related to hospitals ranged from 27.2% of the total in Germany to 50.5% in Croatia. Only in Germany was the share of healthcare expenditure of hospitals lower than that of ambulatory health care providers. [[Image:Healthcare expenditure by major providers, 2023 (% of current healthcare expenditure)_HCE2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Healthcare expenditure by major providers, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hp}}|alt=A stacked column chart showing healthcare expenditure by major providers as a share of all current healthcare expenditure in percent. Data are shown for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The stacks for each country sum to 100% and present the shares for hospitals, providers of ambulatory healthcare, retailers and other providers of medical goods, and other providers. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The second largest healthcare provider (in expenditure terms) was generally that of ambulatory health care providers. Their share of current healthcare expenditure in 2023 averaged 25.6% in the EU and ranged from 15.9% in Bulgaria to 33.8% in Belgium. The share of current healthcare expenditure accounted for by retailers and other providers of medical goods averaged 16.2% in the EU in 2023. However, their share varied greatly between the EU countries, from 7.6% in the Netherlands and 9.6% in Belgium to 27.5% in Romania, 30.0% in Slovakia, 30.1% in Greece and 32.3% in Bulgaria. Table 4 gives information on the relative size of the providers shown in Figure 5 as well as more detailed information on the shares of other providers. By far the largest of the other providers was residential long-term care facilities. Among the EU countries, the share of residential long-term care facilities within current healthcare expenditure varied from 0.1% in Slovakia, 0.4% in Bulgaria and 0.6% in Croatia to 21.1% in Malta, with the share in the Netherlands above this range at 28.0%. [[Image:Healthcare expenditure, analysed by provider, 2023 (% of current healthcare expenditure)_HCE2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 4: Healthcare expenditure, analysed by provider, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_sha11_hp}}|alt=A table showing healthcare expenditure analysed by provider as a share of all current healthcare expenditure in percent. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. Detailed information is presented for 10 different providers. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename= Healthcare expenditure statistics by function provider and financing scheme HCE2025.xlsx|title=Healthcare expenditure statistics by function, provider and financing scheme: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The 2023 data for the EU, Malta and Finland are provisional as are the 2022 data for Norway. '''Tables in this article use the following notation''' *A colon ':' is used to show where data are not available. '''Key concepts''' Current '''healthcare expenditure''' quantifies the economic resources allocated to health functions, excluding capital investment. Healthcare current expenditure is primarily concerned with healthcare goods and services that are consumed by resident units, irrespective of where that consumption takes place (it may be in the rest of the world) or who is paying for it. As such, exports of healthcare goods and services (to non-resident units) are excluded, whereas imports of healthcare goods and services for final use are included. '''Medical goods''' are split into i) pharmaceuticals and other medical non-durable goods and ii) therapeutic appliances and other medical durables. This category aims to include all consumption of medical goods where the function and mode of provision is not specified. It includes medical goods acquired by the beneficiary either as a result of prescription following a health system contact or as a result of self-prescription. It excludes medical goods consumed or delivered during a health care contact that are prescribed by a healthcare professional. '''Long-term healthcare''' consists of a range of medical and personal care services that are consumed with the primary goal of alleviating pain and suffering and reducing or managing the deterioration in health status in patients with a degree of long-term dependency. The aim of '''long-term social care''' is to provide services and support, by formal and informal care givers, to individuals who, for reasons of disability, illness or other dependency, need help to live as normal a life as possible. Social care covers a wide range of services, including professional advice and support, accommodation, various types of assistance in carrying out daily tasks, home visits, home help services, provision of meals, special equipment, house adaptation for disabled people, as well as assessment and care management services. There may be a mixed economy of health and social care provision and this mix of services can make it difficult to separate expenditure between health and social components. For the purpose of this article, the analysis of '''long-term healthcare''' (as shown in Figure 4) is composed solely of the health component. '''System of health accounts – methodology''' [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], the [[Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)|Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD)]] and the [[Glossary:World Health Organization (WHO)|World Health Organization (WHO)]] established a common framework for a joint healthcare data collection exercise. The data collected relates to healthcare expenditure following the methodology of the [[Glossary:System of health accounts (SHA)|system of health accounts (SHA)]]. The SHA shares the goals of the system of national accounts (SNA): to constitute an integrated system of comprehensive, internally consistent and internationally comparable accounts, which should as far as possible be compatible with other aggregated economic and social statistical systems. Health accounts provide a description of the monetary flows related to the final consumption expenditure on healthcare goods and services. Health accounts are used in 2 main ways: internationally, where the emphasis is on a selection of comparable expenditure data; nationally, with more detailed analyses of healthcare spending and a greater emphasis on comparisons over time. For more detail on health accounts, see [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf/60aa44b0-2738-4c4d-be4b-48b6590be1b0 A system of health accounts, 2011 – revised edition]. The core set of SHA tables addresses 3 basic questions i) what kinds of healthcare goods and services are consumed ii) which healthcare providers deliver them and iii) which financing schemes are used to finance the expenditure? Healthcare expenditure is recorded in relation to the [[Glossary:International classification for health accounts (ICHA)|international classification for health accounts (ICHA)]], defining: *healthcare expenditure by financing schemes (ICHA-HF) – classifies the types of financing arrangements through which people obtain health services; healthcare financing schemes include direct payments by households for services and goods and third-party financing arrangements *healthcare expenditure by function (ICHA-HC) – details the split in healthcare expenditure following the purpose of healthcare activities – such as, curative care, rehabilitative care, long-term care (health), or preventive care *healthcare expenditure by provider (ICHA-HP) – classifies units contributing to the provision of healthcare goods and services – such as hospitals, residential facilities, ambulatory health care services, ancillary services or retailers of medical goods. '''Healthcare expenditure – legal basis''' [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2021.387.01.0110.01.ENG Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/1901 of 29 October 2021 as regards statistics on health care expenditure and financing] is the legal basis for data collection according to SHA 2011 methodology for healthcare expenditure. The regulation applies to data from reference year 2021. {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32015R0359:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/359 of 4 March 2015 implementing Regulation (EC) No 1338/2008 as regards statistics on healthcare expenditure and financing}} applies to data from reference year 2014 to 2020. Statistics on healthcare expenditure are documented in a [[Healthcare_expenditure_statistics_-_methodology|background article]] which provides more information on the scope of the data, the legal framework, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. ===Context=== Health systems across the globe are developing in response to a multitude of factors, including new medical technology and improvements in knowledge; new health services and greater access to them; changes in health policies to address specific diseases and demographic developments; new organisational structures and more complex financing mechanisms. However, access to healthcare and greater patient choice is increasingly being considered against a background of financial sustainability. Within the European Commission, the [https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/health-and-food-safety_en Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety] and the [https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/employment-social-affairs-and-inclusion_en Directorate-General for Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion] are responsible for policy actions on health. ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2021.107.01.0001.01.ENG Regulation (EU) 2021/522 establishing a Programme for the Union’s action in the field of health (‘EU4health programme’) for the period 2021 to 2027]'' provides funding to EU countries, health organisations and non-governmental organisations (NGOs). In May 2024, the European Commission summarised work done and progress made within the health domain through a communication ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52024DC0206 The European Health Union: acting together for people’s health]'' (COM(2024) 206 final). It highlights a range of actions designed to make people’s lives safer and healthier. The Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety has constituted a list of 88 [https://health.ec.europa.eu/indicators-and-data/european-core-health-indicators-echi_en European core health indicators (ECHIs)] for monitoring progress in relation to health policy and broader objectives. Among these, it recommends specifically following developments for: *[https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/dyna/echi/?indlist=77a expenditure on healthcare as a percentage of GDP] *[https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/dyna/echi/?indlist=77b expenditures on healthcare in purchasing power standards (PPS)]. ===Other articles=== '''Online publication''' title: Healthcare personnel statistics - dentists, pharmacists and physiotherapists
text:
EU statistics are provided on dentists, pharmacists and physiotherapists. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 Among the EU countries, Greece, Cyprus, Bulgaria, Luxembourg, Lithuania and Romania all reported at least 110 practising dentists for every 100 000 inhabitants in 2024, while Portugal reported a similar ratio for dentists licensed to practice. Among the EU countries, Malta had 159 practising pharmacists for every 100 000 inhabitants in 2024 (the highest ratio), while the Netherlands had 23 practising pharmacists for every 100 000 inhabitants (the lowest ratio). Among the EU countries, Luxembourg, Germany and Belgium had at least 200 practising physiotherapists for every 100 000 inhabitants in 2024. In the EU in 2024, there were around 14 600 dentistry graduates and around 20 100 pharmacy graduates. |alt=A dynamic column chart showing the number of dentist graduates per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. This article presents an overview of [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] statistics on dentists, pharmacists and physiotherapists. It provides information on these specialist healthcare personnel, as well as data relating to dentistry and pharmacy graduates. This article is included in a set of statistical articles concerning healthcare activities in the EU which forms part of an online publication on [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union – facts and figures]]. ===Healthcare personnel=== For [[Glossary:Dentists|dentists]] and [[Glossary:Pharmacists|pharmacists]], Eurostat collects data for 3 concepts: *‘practising’ – health care professionals providing services directly to patients *‘professionally active’ – ‘practising’ professionals plus health care professionals for whom their medical education is a prerequisite for the execution of their job *‘licensed’ – health care professionals who are registered and entitled to practise as health care professionals. In this article, preference is given to the concept of ‘practising’ health care professionals. For some EU countries, data are not available for this concept and therefore data are presented for an alternative concept instead; footnotes indicate these exceptions in each table and figure. Comments on data on health care professionals licensed to practise or professionally active are not included in the text when referring to numbers relative to population size (per 100 000 inhabitants). Table 1 provides an overview for 2024 of the number of practising dentists, pharmacists and physiotherapists. Based on the sum of available data (see Table 1 for more details of the coverage and on concepts used by different EU countries), there were around 375 000 practising dentists and around 428 000 practising pharmacists in the EU countries, while there were an estimated 661 000 physiotherapists across the EU. As such, the combined number of practising dentists, pharmacists and physiotherapists (around 1.5 million) was below the total number of practising [[Glossary:Physician|physicians]] (2.0 million); more information on physicians can be found in the statistical article on [[Healthcare_personnel_statistics_-_physicians|physicians]]. [[Image:Practising dentists, pharmacists and physiotherapists, 2024_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Practising dentists, pharmacists and physiotherapists, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/85862ec2-b696-4600-8ba3-1e47aa7c920d?lang=en hlth_rs_prs2])|alt=A table showing the number and ratio per hundred thousand inhabitants of practising dentists, pharmacists and physiotherapists. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the table are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, Germany reported the highest number of dentists with 71 983 practising dentists, followed by Italy (51 680) and France (48 413). Poland and Spain were the only other EU countries to record more than 30 000 dentists. There were 6 EU countries that reported fewer than 2 000 practising dentists: Slovenia (1 633), Estonia (1 434), Latvia (1 340), Cyprus (1 270), Luxembourg (808) and Malta (295). For pharmacists, the highest number in 2024 was reported in Italy, with 83 158. France (63 111), Spain (60 233) and Germany (56 460) followed. The lowest numbers of pharmacists were reported in Luxembourg, Malta and Estonia, which each reported fewer than 1 000 pharmacists. As for dentists, Germany reported the highest number of physiotherapists in 2024, with 205 000. France was the only other EU country to report more than 100 000 physiotherapists, with 108 030. In the majority of the remaining EU countries, the number of physiotherapists ranged from 71 263 in Italy to 1 109 in Latvia; Malta and Estonia were below this range. '''''Greece and Cyprus had the highest numbers of dentists relative to population size in 2024''''' In relation to population size, Greece and Cyprus reported, respectively, 133 and 130 practising dentists per 100 000 inhabitants. Bulgaria, Luxembourg, Lithuania and Romania were the other EU countries where there were at least 110 practising dentists per 100 000 inhabitants in 2024. Among the remaining EU countries, the number of practising dentists per 100 000 inhabitants was generally within the range of 52 in Malta to 104 in Estonia; only Ireland was below this range, with 47 practising dentists per 100 000 inhabitants – see Figure 1. [[Image:Practising dentists, 2014 and 2024_(per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Practising dentists, 2014 and 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3e702b8c-3090-4ec2-bab6-86bd2802e93c?lang=en hlth_rs_prs2])|alt=A double column chart showing the number of practising dentists per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2014 and 2024 for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Between 2014 and 2024, the number of practising dentists increased in 23 out of the 25 countries for which data are available. The biggest increases were recorded in Poland, Romania, Luxembourg and Cyprus; all of which recorded an increase of more than 30 dentists per 100 000 inhabitants (note there is a break in series in Poland and in Romania). Finland and Sweden recorded the only decreases, down 3 and 1 dentists per 100 000 inhabitants, respectively. '''''Malta had the highest number of pharmacists per 100 000 inhabitants in 2024''''' Taking into account the population of each EU country, Malta recorded the highest number of practising pharmacists in 2024, at 159 per 100 000 inhabitants – see Figure 2 for information concerning differences in data coverage for individual EU countries. There were also relatively high ratios of pharmacists in Italy (141 per 100 000 inhabitants) and Belgium (134 per 100 000 inhabitants). The majority of the other EU countries reported between 61 pharmacists per 100 000 inhabitants in Denmark and 123 in Spain, although the Netherlands (23 per 100 000 inhabitants) reported a ratio that was considerably lower. [[Image:Practising pharmacists, 2014 and 2024_(per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Practising pharmacists, 2014 and 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ed44d06c-7873-44c4-9fa1-588c5562665b?lang=en hlth_rs_prs2])|alt=A double column chart showing the number of practising pharmacists per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2014 and 2024 for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Between 2014 and 2024, the number of practising pharmacists increased in nearly all the countries for which data are available; France was an exception, as there was a small decrease (2 fewer practising pharmacist per 100 000 inhabitants). Excluding the countries that reported a break in series (notably Cyprus, Bulgaria and Ireland), the largest increase was recorded in Malta, where the number of practising pharmacists increased by 46 per 100 000 inhabitants; elsewhere this increase was between 1 (the Netherlands) and 25 (Romania) pharmacists per 100 000 inhabitants. '''''Luxembourg had the highest number of physiotherapists per 100 000 inhabitants in 2024''''' In 2024, the relative distribution of physiotherapists across the individual EU countries was more diverse than for dentists or pharmacists, ranging from 356 per 100 000 inhabitants in Luxembourg and more than 200 per 100 000 inhabitants in Germany and Belgium down to 18 per 100 000 inhabitants in Romania – see Figure 3. [[Image:Practising physiotherapists, 2014 and 2024_(per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Practising physiotherapists, 2014 and 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ed551e7a-8fca-4ce9-8b0b-a000b415150f?lang=en hlth_rs_prs2])|alt=A double column chart showing the number of practising physiotherapists per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2014 and 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Between 2014 and 2024, none of the EU countries for which data are available for both years recorded a decrease in the number of physiotherapists. The smallest increase was in Sweden, up from 133 to 134 per 100 000 inhabitants. The increase in physiotherapists exceeded exceeded 100 per 100 000 inhabitants in Luxembourg (up 129 psychotherapists per 100 000 inhabitants); the increase also exceeded 100 extra physiotherapists per 100 000 inhabitants in in Poland and Austria, although they both had a break in series. ===Health graduates=== Table 2 presents data on the number of dentists and pharmacists graduating in EU countries. In 2024, there were around 14 600 dentistry graduates and around 20 100 pharmacy graduates across the EU. [[Image:Graduates – dentists and pharmacists, 2014, 2019 and 2024_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Graduates – dentists and pharmacists, 2014, 2019 and 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/98349291-ebc4-45e8-8817-8d986ec54766?lang=en hlth_rs_grd2])|alt=A table showing the head count number and ratio per hundred thousand inhabitants of graduate dentists and pharmacists. Data are shown for 2014, 2019 and 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the table are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The EU’s most populous country, Germany, had the highest number of dentistry graduates (2 448) in 2024, while there were 2 030 dentistry graduates in Romania, 1 928 in Spain, 1 446 in France, 1 112 in Poland and 1 043 in Portugal; none of the other EU countries had more than 1 000 graduates. There were 6 EU countries where there were fewer than 100 dentistry graduates: Ireland (95), Latvia (68), Cyprus (58), Slovenia (44), Estonia (30) and Malta (16). Note that Luxembourg does not offer full training in dentistry, therefore there were no graduates. By contrast, the highest numbers of pharmacy graduates were recorded in Italy (4 108), France (3 479), Spain (2 550) and Germany (2 259). There were also around 1 000 pharmacy graduates in Poland, Portugal and Romania. At the other end of the range, there were fewer than 100 pharmacy graduates in Lithuania (96), Estonia (55), Latvia (49) and Malta (29). As for dentistry, Luxembourg does not offer full training in pharmacy, therefore there were no graduates. Relative to the total number of inhabitants, Romania recorded the highest number of dentistry graduates in 2024 at 11 graduates per 100 000 inhabitants (see Figure 4 for more information on the data coverage for each EU country). Portugal (10 graduates per 100 000 inhabitants) and Bulgaria (9 graduates per 100 000 inhabitants) recorded the next highest ratios. All other EU countries for which data are available reported between 2 and 6 dentistry graduates per 100 000 inhabitants. [[Image:Graduates – dentists, 2014 and 2024 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Graduates – dentists, 2014 and 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bac8ba58-8fc0-497b-a65d-f8222995afb2?lang=en hlth_rs_grd2])|alt=A double column chart showing the number of dentist graduates per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2014 and 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among the countries for which data are available for both years, the number of dentistry graduates increased or remained the same between 2014 and 2024 in all but 2 EU countries: it fell in Czechia by 0.8 dentistry graduates per 100 000 inhabitants and in Lithuania by 0.5 dentistry graduates per 100 000 inhabitants. Excluding Cyprus, where there were no dentistry graduates prior to 2022, the largest increase was seen in Bulgaria (note that is a break in series), where this ratio increased by 4.7 dentistry graduates per 100 000 inhabitants. Portugal, Romania and Croatia reported increases of 2.9 to 3.6 graduates per 100 000 inhabitants. In the remaining countries, this increase was no more than 1.9 graduates per 100 000 inhabitants. Cyprus recorded, by far, the highest ratio of pharmacy graduates in relation to its total population, at 15 graduates per 100 000 inhabitants in 2024 (see Figure 5 for more information on the data coverage for each EU country). The next highest ratio was recorded in Portugal (10 graduates per 100 000 inhabitants). The majority of the other EU countries for which data are available reported between 3 and 7 pharmacy graduates per 100 000 inhabitants, with relatively few pharmacy graduates in the Netherlands (1 graduate per 100 000 inhabitants). Note that Luxembourg does not offer full training in pharmacy, therefore there were no graduates. [[Image:Graduates – pharmacists, 2014 and 2024 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Graduates – pharmacists, 2014 and 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/dcfa00f6-b3b5-4d79-b87a-2170ec350d90?lang=en hlth_rs_grd2])|alt=A double column chart showing the number of pharmacist graduates per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2014 and 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] There were more varied changes observed between 2014 and 2024 for pharmacy graduates than for dentistry graduates. The number of pharmacy graduates per 100 000 inhabitants increased in 9 countries. Excluding Cyprus, where there were no pharmacy graduates prior to 2017, the largest increase was observed in Bulgaria, where the number of pharmacy graduates increased from 4 to 7 per 100 000 inhabitants. Denmark, Finland and Croatia were the only other countries to report an increase of at least 1.0 pharmacy graduates per 100 000 inhabitants. A decrease was observed in 13 countries, with the largest decreases in Malta, Slovakia, Portugal and Romania, all down 2 to 3 graduates per 100 000 inhabitants. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Healthcare personnel statistics - dentists, pharmacists and physiotherapists Health2026.xlsx|title=Dentists, pharmacists and physiotherapists: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''Key concepts''' Dentists diagnose, treat and prevent diseases, injuries and abnormalities of the teeth, mouth, jaws and associated tissues. They use a broad range of specialised diagnostic, surgical and other techniques to promote and restore oral health. Pharmacists store, preserve, compound, dispense and sell medicinal products – irrespective of where they provide these services. They may also provide advice on the proper use and adverse effects of drugs and medicines following prescriptions issued by medical doctors and other health professionals. Physiotherapists assess, plan and implement rehabilitative programmes that improve or restore human motor functions, maximise movement ability, relieve pain syndromes, and treat or prevent physical challenges associated with injuries, diseases and other impairments. They apply a broad range of physical therapies and techniques such as movement, ultrasound, heating, laser and other techniques. Practising dentists and pharmacists provide services directly to patients. Dentists and pharmacists have completed university studies in their respective domains and all 3 professions need to be licensed to practise. Dentists and pharmacists who are working in administration, research or other posts that exclude direct contact with patients and clients are excluded from the definition of those who are practising, whereas they are included in the definition for those who are professionally active (as long as their job requires an education in dentistry/pharmacy). The broader definition of dentists and pharmacists who are licensed to practise additionally includes those for whom their dentistry/pharmacy education is not a prerequisite for the execution of the job, as well as those who are unemployed, retired or working abroad. Data on dental and pharmacy graduates cover the number of students who have obtained a recognised qualification in dentistry or pharmacy in a given year; a minimum of 3 years of training is required to practise as a physiotherapist. '''Healthcare resources''' Statistics on healthcare resources (such as personnel and medical equipment) are documented in a background article on the [[Healthcare_non-expenditure_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of healthcare non-expenditure statistics]]. This provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis and the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. Two more statistical articles on health professionals are available, for [[Healthcare_personnel_statistics_-_physicians|physicians]] and for [[Healthcare_personnel_statistics_-_nursing_and_caring_professionals|nurses and caring professionals]]. For country specific notes on these data collections, please refer to the annexes at the end of the national metadata reports accessible from links at the beginning of the {{Template:Esms|code=hlth_res_esms|title=European metadata report}}. Common definitions have been agreed between [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], the [[Glossary:OECD|OECD]] and the [[Glossary:World Health Organization (WHO)|World Health Organization (WHO)]] with respect to the employment of various health care professionals. There are 3 main concepts which are used to present these data. In this article preference is given to the concept of ‘practising’ dentists and pharmacists: *‘practising’ – health care professionals providing services directly to patients *‘professionally active’ – ‘practising’ professionals plus health care professionals for whom their medical education is a prerequisite for the execution of their job *‘licensed’ – health care professionals who are registered and entitled to practise as health care professionals. The {{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-028|title=Healthcare non-expenditure statistics manual}} provides an overview of the classifications, both for mandatory variables and variables provided on a voluntary basis. '''Symbols''' In tables, a colon ‘:’ is used to show where data are not available. Data in italics are estimates or provisional. ===Context=== According to [[Glossary:EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]], an estimated 2.8% of the EU’s population (aged 16 years and over) reported they had unmet needs for dental examination due to financial reasons in 2025; this figure was nearly 3 times as high as the corresponding share of the population reporting they had finance-related unmet needs for medical examination (1.0%). This difference may, at least in part, be due to national social security systems covering fewer people or a lower proportion of the total cost of dental care, resulting in some individuals having to pay a relatively large share of their dental expenses out of their own pockets (or through private health insurance). ‘Dental tourism’ is an area that has seen particularly rapid growth in several EU countries in recent years, for example, in Bulgaria, Spain or Hungary. Relatively low prices, increased patient mobility, lower prices for air travel, and greater consumer confidence and awareness have led some to consider the option of having dental treatment abroad. This pattern may be expected to develop in the coming years: {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011L0024:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2011/24/EU}} of the [[Glossary:European Parliament (EP)|European Parliament]] and of the [[Glossary:Council of the European Union|Council]] on the application of patients’ rights in cross-border healthcare was implemented in 2013 and provides patients with increased rights and promotes cooperation between health systems. Some health professionals seek jobs in other EU countries. Aside from the expected benefits for the individuals concerned, their movement can impact labour markets. {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32005L0036R(03):EN:NOT|title=Directive 2005/36/EC}} on the recognition of professional qualifications provides a Europe-wide legal framework enabling EU countries to recognise each other’s qualifications. A range of health professionals – including dentists, pharmacists and physiotherapists – enjoy automatic recognition. In other words, if someone is a certified practitioner in their home EU country then they are automatically entitled to practise anywhere else in the EU. The directive also provides a set of minimum requirements for each professional activity, including the need for a compulsory university degree in order to be a dental practitioner or a pharmacist, and a minimum study/training period of 4 years for dental practitioners, 5 years for pharmacists and 3 years for physiotherapists. ===Other articles=== '''Online publications''' *[[Health in the
