title: Heavy fuel oil - production, trade and use
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the heavy fuel oil - production, trade and use. Data extracted in September 2021 No planned update In 2019, 5 EU Member States accounted for nearly 75% of intra and extra EU imports of fuel oil. Most fuel oil in the EU is used to power ships engaged in international navigation; in 2019 this amounted to 35 000 kt. [[Image:Heavy fuel 2 final 12-10-2021.jpeg|centre|600px| alt= An image showing the evolution of output from refineries in EU countries producing a minimum of 1 000 kt of fuel oil between 1990 and 2020.]] This article gives an overview of a specific oil product known as fuel oil. Due to its weight it is also addressed as heavy fuel oil. Energy statistics on this product are available for all 27 [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU Member States]] for the period 1990 to 2019. The refinery processes split crude oil into a light fraction (diesel, naphtha and petrol) and heavy residues (fuel oil and bitumen). Due to its viscosity and sulphur content, fuel oil is difficult to use and refineries generally try to reduce its production. Most ships are using fuel oil, and most of the sulphur contained in fuel oil ends up in the atmosphere when combusted in the ship’s engine (source : [https://www.imo.org/en/MediaCentre/HotTopics/Pages/Sulphur-2020.aspx IMO]). Due to growing concerns over the environmental impact, more ambitious efforts to limit pollution from ship transport are on envisaged (see at the end of this article). ''Authors: Audrey Errard, Cristina Martello and Michael Goll'' === What is fuel oil ? === [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/ramon/nomenclatures/index.cfm?TargetUrl=DSP_GLOSSARY_NOM_DTL_VIEW&StrNom=CODED2&StrLanguageCode=EN&IntKey=33013161&RdoSearch=CONTAIN&TxtSearch=fuel%20oil&CboTheme=36940303 Fuel oil] covers all residual fuel oils, including those obtained by blending. It is divided into two categories depending on its sulphur content: * "low sulphur fuel oil" where the sulphur content is lower than 1 %. * "high sulphur fuel oil" where the sulphur content is 1 % m/m or higher. === Fuel oil production has decreased over the last thirty years === The production of fuel oil has decreased over the last decades (see Figure 1). In 2020, 21 Member States were still producing fuel oil, of which thirteen produced more than 1 000 kt (see Figure 1). Luxembourg, Latvia, Malta and Estonia have never had any refineries, while Cyprus stopped producing fuel oil in 2004, and Slovenia in 2000. Changed processing techniques in refineries limited the production of fuel oils during the last decades. This means that the percentage (weight) of fuel oil per ton of crude oil intake in refineries diminished. [[Image:Evolution of output from refineries in EU-Member States producing a minimum of 1000 kt of fuel oil in 2019, 1990-2020_.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 1: Evolution of output from refineries in EU-Member States producing a minimum of 1000 kt of fuel oil in 2019, 1990-2020
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nrg_cb_oil}}| alt= A line chart showing the evolution of output from refineries in EU-Member States producing a minimum of 1000 kt of fuel oil between 1990 and 2020. The vertical axis displays the output, while the horizontal axis displays the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The most significant decreases in output over the 1990-2020 period were observed in Italy and Spain. Italy was the main producer in the EU until 2011. Nowadays, the Netherlands is the main producer with 9 000 kt in 2020. In 1990, Italy produced 24 000 kt compared with 5 400 kt in 2020. Spain produced just under 15 000 kt in 1990 and 2 400 in 2020. In 2020, five Member States accounted for about 60 % of the fuel oil production in the EU, namely the Netherlands (19 % with 9 000 kt), Germany (13 % with 6 200 kt), Italy (11 % with 5 400 kt), France (9 % with 4 400 kt) and Sweden (8 % with 3 900 kt). In seven countries, high sulphur fuel oil (> 1 % sulphur) represents more than 50 % of total fuel oil production (Figure 2). [[Image:Share of fuel oil by sulphur content in EU-Member States in 2019 (%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 2: Share of fuel oil by sulphur content in EU-Member States in 2019 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nrg_cb_oil}}| alt= A bar chart showing the share of fuel oil by sulphur content in EU-Member States in 2019. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The production of fuel oil (as a proportion of the amount of crude oil refinery intake) varies in the Member States, with a maximum of 29 % for Ireland and a minimum of 1 % for Romania in 2020 (see Figure 3). These figures can be partially explained by the fact that each refinery is “tuned” to the crude oil type it treats (crude oil quality changes depending on the source country and field), and can be very specialised (e.g. for kerosene). Many Member States have only one refinery, while some, the Netherlands for example, have several refineries with different specialisations. [[Image:Percentage of fuel oil output in relation to crude oil refinery intake _ evolution over time, lowest and highest value in the EU, 1990-2020_.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 3: Percentage of fuel oil output in relation to crude oil refinery intake _ evolution over time, lowest and highest value in the EU, 1990-2020
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nrg_cb_oil}}| alt= A line chart showing the percentage of fuel oil output in relation to crude oil refinery intake _ evolution over time, lowest and highest value in the EU between 1990 and 2020. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Trade of fuel oil in the EU and with third countries === Intra EU fuel oil trade (imports and exports each around 25 000 kt), is bigger in volume than extra EU trade (imports 15 000 kt, exports 20 000 kt). In 2019, EU Member States imported about 40 000 kt of fuel oil, of which almost 25 000 kt were coming from other EU countries and around 15 000 kt were imported from countries outside the EU (40.4 % from Russia, 16.3 % from the United Kingdom and 11.5 % from Norway). In 2019, Member States exported about 45 000 kt of which 25 000 kt were sent to other EU countries and 20 000 kt were exported to countries outside the EU (19.8 % to the US, 16.7 % to the United Kingdom and 16.6 % to Saudi Arabia ; see Figure 4). [[Image:Evolution of imports, exports, use in international maritime bunkers and production (refinery output) of fuel oil in the EU, 1990-2019 (kt).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 4: Evolution of imports, exports, use in international maritime bunkers and production (refinery output) of fuel oil in the EU, 1990-2019 (kt)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nrg_bal_c}}| alt= A line chart showing the evolution of imports, exports, use in international maritime bunkers and production (refinery output) of fuel oil in the EU between 1990 and 2020. The vertical axis displays the numbers, while the horizontal axis displays the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Five Member States accounted for nearly 75 % of the imports of the EU, namely the Netherlands (29 % with 11 500 kt), Spain (17 % with, 6 600 kt), Belgium (14 % with 5 500 kt), France (7 % with 2 800 kt) and Denmark (6 % with 2400 kt) (see Figure 5). [[Image:Imports of fuel oil in largest EU-importers since 1990 (kt).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 5: Imports of fuel oil in largest EU-importers since 1990 (kt)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nrg_bal_c}}| alt= A line chart showing the imports of fuel oil in largest EU-importers since 1990 (kt) since 1990. The vertical axis displays the numbers, while the horizontal axis displays the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Five Member States accounted for 55 % of total EU exports including intra EU trade, namely the Netherlands (22 % with 9 500 kt), Belgium (9 % with 4 100 kt), France (8 % with 3 700 kt), Italy (8 % with 3 600 kt) and Sweden (7 % wih 3 100 kt) (see Figure 6). [[Image:Exports of fuel oil in largest EU-exporters since 1990 (kt).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 6: Exports of fuel oil in largest EU-importers since 1990 (kt)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nrg_bal_c}}| alt= A line chart showing the exports of fuel oil in largest EU-importers since 1990 (kt) since 1990. The vertical axis displays the numbers, while the horizontal axis displays the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] As previously mentioned, production in Italy, France and Germany (Figure 1) has decreased continuously over the last decades but has remained stable in the Netherlands. In contrast, imports and exports drastically decreased in the Netherlands since 2015, while trade in the other EU countries changed to a lesser extent (see Figures 1, 4, 5 and 6). === Use of fuel oil in the EU === Fuel oil is either used in industry (3 450 kt in 2019) for processing heat generation etc. but also in the transformation sector (5 700 kt in 2019 for power plants) to generate electricity and heat and in the transport sector for domestic navigation (coastal shipping, inland waterways etc.; 1 500 kt in 2019). However, by far the biggest amount of fuel oil is used to power ships engaged in international navigation (international shipping). Fuel oil used for this purpose is stored in international maritime bunkers and amounted to 35 000 kt in 2019. Figure 7 shows that since 2006, fuel oil is mainly used in international navigation. [[Image:Share of international navigation in total use of fuel oil in the EU, 1990-2019 (%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 7: Share of international navigation in total use of fuel oil in the EU, 1990-2019 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nrg_cb_oil}}| alt= A bar chart showing the share of international navigation in total use of fuel oil in the EU between 1990 and 2020. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2019, fuel oil was used mainly for international navigation, and in some countries almost exclusively, such as Slovenia, the Netherlands, Malta and Belgium, and in many of the countries bordering the Baltic sea, such as Latvia, Lithuania (both over 90 %), Denmark, Sweden (both over 80 %), and to a lesser extent Estonia (74 %), Finland, Poland and Germany (25-50 %) (see Figure 8). [[Image:Share of international navigation in total use of fuel oil in 2019 (%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 8: Share of international navigation in total use of fuel oil in 2019 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nrg_cb_oil}}| alt= A bar chart showing the share of international navigation in total use of fuel oil in 2019. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the EU-27 and EU countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Not all Member States used fuel oil in equal amounts. In 2019, five Member States accounted for over 75 % of the fuel oil used for international navigation in the EU, namely the Netherlands (27 % with 9 200 kt), Belgium (21 % with 7 000 kt), Spain (16 % with 5 500 kt), Greece and Italy (6 % with 2 100 kt each) (see Figure 9). [[Image:Largest users of fuel oil in international navigation in the EU in 2019 and evolution since 1990 (kt).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 9: Largest users of fuel oil in international navigation in the EU in 2019 and evolution since 1990 (kt)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nrg_bal_c}}| alt= A line chart showing the largest users of fuel oil in international navigation in the EU in 2019 and evolution since 1990 (kt). The vertical axis displays the number, while the horizontal axis displays the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === About international navigation and international regulations === Due to growing concerns over the environmental impact of pollution due to the use of fuel oil, the International Maritime Organization of the United Nations (IMO) organised the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships ([https://www.imo.org/en/About/Conventions/Pages/International-Convention-for-the-Prevention-of-Pollution-from-Ships-(MARPOL).aspx MARPOL]) in the 1970s. In 1997, the MARPOL Protocol was adopted to amend the Convention and one of its annexes limits the sulphur content in fuel oil used for navigation/shipping. Decisions taken at international level (UN) are always transposed to EU law. As a consequence, in the EU, the sulphur content in fuel oil is regulated to limit marine pollution from ships. This means that ships must use fuel oil with a limited sulphur content to prevent the emission of ozone-depleting substances, such as sulphur oxides (SOx) ([https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/76a4e627-1ede-11e6-86d0-01aa75ed71a1/language-en Directive (EU) 2016/802 of the European Parliament and of the Council]). This limit has been revised several times over the last decades. Since their introduction in 2015, the regulations to lower sulphur oxide (SOx) emissions at sea seemed to have a certain but rather limited impact on the trade and the production of fuel oil. However, the amount of fuel oil used in international navigation has remained more or less constant in the EU during the last twenty years. Apart from the Netherlands, since 2015 no clear reduction regarding the use of fuel oil in international navigation in the EU is visible. Nowadays, most of the fuel oil produced in the EU is used for international navigation to satisfy the increased need for this transport fuel which has grown in the last years due to increased international trade e.g. with Southeast Asia. On 1 January 2020, “[https://www.imo.org/en/MediaCentre/HotTopics/Pages/Sulphur-2020.aspx IMO 2020]” came into force. The goal is to pursue efforts in improving air quality, preserving the environment and protecting human health. * Outside of Emission Control Areas (ECAS), the sulphur content in the fuel oil used by ships is set to 0.5 % m/m at the most. * Inside of ECAS the limit is set to 0.10 % m/m as a maximum. The four ECAS are: the Baltic Sea area, the North Sea area, the North American area, and the United States Caribbean Sea area. Given the new limit (0.5 % m/m outside ECAS, 0.1 % inside ECAS), it is expected that this will affect the production and the use of fuel oil in the future in Members States further. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:SE-Fuel-oil 2021 final-online oct2021-2.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === Energy statistics are available for all 27 Member States. Data are available for the period 1990 to 2019 (nrg_bal_c) and 2020 (nrg_cb_oil; provisional data) and are based on the annual oil questionnaire. === Context === The Energy statistics {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32088R1099:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008}} is the legal basis for the reporting of annual energy questionnaires. ===Other articles=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Energy Energy sources and other topics] ===Selected Datasets=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/energy/database Energy - Observed gross inland deliveries = Fuel oil used inside the boundaries of a given country in the transformation-, energy-, transport-, industry- and other sectors. ===Legislation=== *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R1099:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008}} of 22 October 2008 on energy statistics {{Unit|topic=X_Energy}} *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52010DC2020:EN:NOT|title= EUROPE 2020: A strategy for smart, sustainable and inclusive growth}} *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/LSU/?uri=CELEX:52010DC2020 Summaries of EU legislation: Europe 2020: the European Union strategy for growth and employment] *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/LSU/?uri=CELEX:32008R1099 Summaries of EU legislation:] Common system for the production of energy statistics ===External links=== *[https://www.imo.org/en IMO - International Maritime Organization of the United Nations] *[https://www.imo.org/en/MediaCentre/HotTopics/Pages/Sulphur-2020.aspx IMO 2020 - cutting sulphur oxide emissions] *[https://www.imo.org/en/About/Conventions/Pages/International-Convention-for-the-Prevention-of-Pollution-from-Ships-(MARPOL).aspx International convention for the prevention of pollution from ships (MARPOL)] ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Article_name'' {{Unit|topic=X_Energy}} [[Category:Environment and energy|Heavy fuel oil - production, trade and use]] [[Category:Energy|Heavy fuel oil - production, trade and use]] [[Category:Oil|Heavy fuel oil - production, trade and use]] [[Category:No update|Heavy fuel oil - production, trade and use]] [[Category:Statistical article|Heavy fuel oil - production, trade and use]] [[Category:Authored article|Heavy fuel oil - production, trade and use]]

title: Healthy life years statistics
text:
EU statistics are provided on healthy life years. Data extracted in July 2025 Planned article update: October 2026 In the EU, the number of healthy life years at birth in 2023 was 63.3 years for women and 62.8 years for men. This represented approximately 3 quarters (75.4%) and 4 fifths (79.8%) of the total life expectancy for women and men, respectively. Whether extra years of life gained through increased longevity are spent in good or bad health is a crucial question. Since [[Glossary:Life expectancy|life expectancy at birth]] is not able to fully answer this question, indicators of health expectancies, such as [[Glossary:Healthy life years (HLY)|healthy life years]] (also called [[Glossary:Healthy life years (HLY)|disability-free life expectancy]]) have been developed. These focus on the quality of life spent in a healthy state, rather than the quantity of life, as measured by life expectancy. As such, healthy life years are an important measure of the relative health of people in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union]] (EU). This article is one of a set of statistical articles concerning [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|health status]] in the EU which forms part of the online publication [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]]. ===Healthy life years at birth=== In the EU, the number of healthy life years at birth in 2023 was 63.3 years for women and 62.8 years for men, a [[Glossary:Gender gap|gender gap]] of 0.5 years. Life expectancy in 2023 was 84.0 years for women and 78.7 years for men, a gap of 5.3 years. As the gender gap was considerably smaller in terms of healthy life years than it was for overall life expectancy, most of the additional years of life expectancy for women tend to be lived with activity limitations. Therefore, men tended to spend a greater share (79.8%) of their somewhat shorter lives free from activity limitations than women (75.4%) did. Across the EU countries, life expectancy at birth for women in 2023 ranged between 79.7 years in Bulgaria and 86.7 years in Spain; a difference of 7.0 years. A similar comparison for men shows that the lowest life expectancy in 2023 was recorded in Latvia at 70.5 years and the highest in Sweden 81.7 years; a range of 11.2 years. The corresponding ranges for healthy life years at birth were *between 54.3 years in Latvia and 71.1 years in Malta (a range of 16.8 years) for women (see '''Figure 1''') *between 51.2 years in Latvia and 71.7 years in Malta (a range of 20.5 years) for men (see '''Figure 2'''). [[Image:Healthy life years at birth, women, 2015 and 2023 (years)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Healthy life years at birth, women, 2015 and 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_hlye}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the number of healthy life years at birth for women. Data are shown for 2015 and 2023 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]]
[[Image:Healthy life years at birth, men, 2015 and 2023 (years)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Healthy life years at birth, men, 2015 and 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_hlye}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the number of healthy life years at birth for men. Data are shown for 2015 and 2023 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] The expected number of healthy life years at birth was higher for women than for men in 17 of the EU countries (see '''Table 1'''). The difference between the sexes was generally relatively small: there were 5 EU countries where the gap rose to more than 3.0 years in favour of women (Bulgaria, Slovenia, Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia) and 1 where the gap rose to more than 3.0 years in favour of men (the Netherlands). [[Image:Healthy life years, 2023 (years)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Healthy life years, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_hlye}}|alt=A table showing the number of healthy life years for men and women at birth and at age 65 years. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] As such, there were considerably wider differences between EU countries in terms of the quality of life (health wise) that people may expect to live, when compared with the overall differences in life expectancy. In 2023, women in Denmark could expect to live 66.2% of their lives free from any activity limitation, compared with 89.0% for women in Bulgaria. In 2023, men in Denmark could expect to live 71.4% of their lives free from any activity limitation, compared with 92.0% for men in Bulgaria. ===Healthy life years at age 65 years=== An analysis comparing healthy life years between the sexes at age 65 years in 2023 shows that there were 20 EU countries where women could expect more healthy life years than men and 7 where men could expect more healthy life years than women. *Women aged 65 years could expect to live between 1.2 and 1.8 years longer free from disability than men in Slovenia, Bulgaria, France and Estonia. *Men aged 65 years could expect to live between 1.1 and 1.3 years longer free from disability than women in Portugal and Malta. [[Image:Healthy life years at age 65 years, women, 2015 and 2023 (years)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Healthy life years at age 65 years, women, 2015 and 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_hlye}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the number of healthy life years at age 65 years for women. Data are shown for 2015 and 2023 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]]
[[Image:Healthy life years at age 65 years, men, 2015 and 2023 (years)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Healthy life years at age 65 years, men, 2015 and 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_hlye}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the number of healthy life years at age 65 years for men. Data are shown for 2015 and 2023 for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] === Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename= Healthy life years statistics_Health2025.xlsx|title=Healthy life years statistics: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] calculates information relating to healthy life years for 3 ages: at birth, at age 50 years and at age 65 years. This information is calculated using [[Glossary:Death|mortality]] statistics and [[Glossary:Data|data]] on [[Glossary:Activity limitation|self-perceived long-standing activity limitations]]. Mortality data come from Eurostat’s demographic database, while self-perceived long-standing activity limitations data come from a [[Glossary:Minimum European Health Module (MEHM)|European health module]] that is integrated within the data collection for [[Glossary:EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions]] (EU-SILC). '''Self-perceived long-standing limitations in usual activities due to health problems''' EU-SILC is documented in more detail in this [[Health_variables_in_SILC_-_methodology|background article]] which provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed for health-related variables, as well as related concepts and definitions. The general coverage of EU-SILC is all private households and their members (who are residents at the time of data collection); it therefore excludes people living in collective households. The relevant EU-SILC questions concerning long-standing activity limitation are the following. *Are you limited because of a health problem in activities people usually do: severely limited, limited but not severely or not limited at all? *If the answer is ‘severely limited’ or ‘limited but not severely’, have you been limited for at least the past 6 months: yes or no? '''Limitations of the data''' The indicator presented in this article is derived from self-reported data. As such, it reflects – to a certain extent – respondents’ subjective perceptions, as well as their social and cultural background. EU-SILC does not cover the institutionalised population, for example, people living in health and social care institutions who are more likely to face activity limitations than people living in private households. It is therefore likely that, to some degree, this data source under-estimates the share of people facing such limitations. Furthermore, the implementation of EU-SILC is organised nationally, which may impact the results presented, for example, due to differences in the formulation of questions or changing the related questions in a specific year. ===Context=== The health status of people is difficult to measure because it is hard to define consistently between individuals, populations, cultures, or even across time periods. The demographic measure of life expectancy has often been used as a proxy for the state of a nation’s health, partly because it is based on a characteristic that is simple and easy to understand – namely, that of death. Indeed, life expectancy at birth remains among the most frequently quoted indicators of health status and economic development. Life expectancy at birth rose rapidly in the last century due to a range of factors, including decreases in infant mortality, rising living standards, improved lifestyles and better education, as well as advances in [[Glossary:Healthcare|healthcare]] and medicine. While most people are aware that successive generations are living longer, less is known about the health of the EU’s ageing population. Indicators on healthy life years are based on the concept of the quality of life, by focusing on those years that may be enjoyed by individuals free from the limitations of illness or disability. Chronic disease, frailty, mental disorders and physical disability tend to become more prevalent in older age and may result in a lower quality of life for those who suffer from such conditions, while the burden of these conditions may also impact on healthcare and pension provisions. Healthy life years also monitor health as a productive or economic factor. An increase in healthy life years is one of the main goals of the EU’s health policy, given that this would not only improve the situation of individuals (as good health and a long life are fundamental objectives of human activity) but also lead to lower public healthcare expenditure and likely increase the possibility that people continue to work later into life. If healthy life years increase more rapidly than life expectancy, then not only are people living longer, but they are also living a greater share of their lives free from health problems. In March 2021, the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] adopted a [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030_en Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2021–2030] that aims to ensure that people with disabilities can experience full social and economic inclusion on an equal basis with others and live free from discrimination. The strategy focuses on implementing the [https://www.un.org/development/desa/disabilities/convention-on-the-rights-of-persons-with-disabilities/convention-on-the-rights-of-persons-with-disabilities-2.html United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities] and consolidating the EU’s body of law in this field. In recent years, active and healthy ageing innovation and policy actions have been supported through joint efforts of the European Commission and EU countries, such as the [https://www.aal-europe.eu/ Active and Assisted Living Programme] (AAL), the [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/eip-aha European Innovation Partnership on Active and Healthy Ageing] (EIP-AHA), the [https://jp-demographic.eu/ Joint Programming Initiative – More Years, Better Lives] and the [https://innovation4ageing.tehnopol.ee/ Innovation Network for Scaling Active and Healthy Ageing] (IN-4-AHA). The Commission has also awarded grants to hundreds of research and innovation projects through [https://wayback.archive-it.org/12090/20220124130848/https://ec.europa.eu/programmes/horizon2020/en/h2020-section/health-demographic-change-and-wellbeing Horizon 2020 Societal Challenge 1 – Health, Demographic change and Wellbeing] (archived webpage), promoting the development and uptake of digital health innovations for the benefit of older adults’ health and well-being. The Commission’s [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/communication-enabling-digital-transformation-health-and-care-digital-single-market-empowering Communication on enabling the digital transformation of health and care in the digital single market] invited, among other things, the promotion of empowering people and citizens, of all ages, to manage their health and well-being actively with the help of digital technologies. ===Other articles=== '''Online publications''' *[[Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] *[[Disability statistics]] '''Health status title: High-growth enterprises in the EU
text:
Statistics on high-growth enterprises in the EU, as well as the results for high-growth micro enterprises from countries that report these data on a voluntary basis Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: February 2027 In 2023, the EU's 'Information and communication' sector had the highest share of high-growth enterprises, representing 16.5% of firms with 10 or more employees, while ‘Mining and quarrying’ had the lowest - less than half that figure. In 2023, the strongest employment footprint of high-growth enterprises was in 'Accommodation and food services', providing 22.6% of all jobs in that sector. High-growth micro enterprise shares of businesses with at least one employee ranged from 5.7% in Portugal to just 1.1% in Poland; the highest share was in the ‘Accommodation and food service’ sector at 4.9% share. Preliminary 2024 data show that the EU's 'Arts, entertainment and recreation' sector saw the largest rise in high-growth enterprises: up by more than 33% compared with 2023. In 2023, [[Glossary:High-growth_enterprise|high-growth enterprises]] accounted for 10.5% of all active EU businesses with 10 or more employees, yet they provided 12.9% of jobs. Gazelles – five and four years old high-growth enterprises made up 8% of all high-growth firms, representing 0.9% of the EU’s active businesses with 10 or more employees. Countries showed significant variation in both the shares of high-growth enterprises and the share of employees working in them, where gaps were even wider than for enterprise shares. Preliminary 2024 figures revealed that the number of high-growth enterprises in the EU remained nearly unchanged from the previous year, suggesting overall stability - though significant variations were observed between countries. The ‘Arts, entertainment, and recreation’ sector led in growth, while ‘Water supply; sewerage; waste management; and remediation activities’ saw a decline, with employment trends mirroring these shifts. This article presents the most recent data on high-growth enterprises in the EU, as well as the results for high-growth micro enterprises from countries that report these data on a voluntary basis. High-growth enterprises are vital drivers of economic dynamism, contributing disproportionately to job creation, innovation, and productivity growth. Access to their data is essential for policymakers and businesses looking to identify growth trends and competitive advantages. ===Change in number of high-growth enterprises=== [[File:Fig 1 Change in number of high-growth enterprises in 2024 (preliminary data) compared to 2023 (final data) (%).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Change in number of high-growth enterprises in 2024 (preliminary data) compared to 2023 (final data), %
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bd_hg__custom_20814499/default/table?lang=en (bd_hg)]|alt=A bar chart showing the percentage growth of high-growth enterprises in 2024 (preliminary data) compared to 2023 across EU Member States and EFTA countries.]]]
Preliminary results for 2024 show that the number of high-growth enterprises in the EU decreased by 0.1% compared with final 2023 data (Figure 1). The total number of employees fell by 2.5%. The highest growth in the number of high-growth enterprises was recorded in Latvia, where the number of high-growth enterprises rose by 23.6%. It was followed by Spain, Malta, and Portugal, which all saw increases ranging between 12.2% and 14.4%. On the other hand, several countries experienced a contraction in their high-growth business population. The notable declines were observed in Greece (-18.4%) and Cyprus (-18.3%), followed by Luxembourg, Italy, Hungary, Ireland, and Poland, where the decreases ranged from -14.2% to -10.5%. The development of the number of high-growth enterprises varied by economic activity (Figure 2). [[File:Fig 2 Change in number of high-growth enterprises by sector in 2024 (preliminary data) compared to 2023 (final data), EU (%).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Change in number of high-growth enterprises by sector in 2024 (preliminary data) compared to 2023 (final data), EU, %
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bd_hg__custom_19873410/default/table?lang=en (bd_hg)]|alt= A horizontal bar chart comparing the growth rates of high-growth enterprises by NACE sector in the EU, showing the performance variance between service-oriented activities and industrial sectors.]]]
The largest increase in number of high-growth enterprises was observed in 'Arts, entertainment and recreation' (+33.4%), followed by 'Accommodation and food service activities' (+17.3%) and 'Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply' (+11.0%). Employment in high-growth enterprises saw significant variation across sectors. The ‘Arts, entertainment and recreation’ sector experienced the highest growth, with a 39.5% increase, while the ‘Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply’ sector followed closely at 38.3% - a rate proportionally 3 times higher than that of enterprises. Meanwhile, ‘Accommodation and food service activities’ also recorded a notable of 15.9%. The steepest declines in number of high-growth enterprises occurred in ‘Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities’ (-12.8%), ‘Manufacturing’ (-11.3%), and ‘Construction’ (-8.7%). Employment reductions in these sectors mirrored their respective high-growth enterprise rates. A notable disparity emerged between the growth in ‘Administrative and support service activities’, the number of high-growth enterprises rose by just 1.1%, yet employment fell sharply by 9.9%. Similarly, in ‘Human health and social work activities’, the number of such enterprises declined slightly (-0.3%), while employment dropped by 10.2%. === High-growth enterprises: employment and sectors === In 2023, the EU had 180 000 high-growth enterprises employing over 14 million people. About 15 000 of these were young enterprises (4 or 5 years old). On average, a high-growth enterprise employed around 79 people, while young ones averaged 56 employees. Overall, high-growth enterprises accounted for 10.5% of all active enterprises with 10 or more employees, with young high-growth enterprises representing 0.9% of the total (Figure 3). Despite their smaller share of the business population, these enterprises contributed a significant 12.9% to total employment, while young high-growth enterprises provided 0.7%. [[File:Fig_3_Share_of_high-growth_enterprises_in_all_enterprises_and_employment_share,_2023_(%).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Share of high-growth enterprises in all enterprises and employment share, 2023, %
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bd_hg__custom_20806741/default/table?lang=en (bd_hg)]|alt= A vertical bar chart showing, by country, the share of high-growth enterprises among active enterprises with at least 10 employees and the share of employees working in those enterprises.]]]
Among EU countries, Ireland recorded the highest share of high-growth enterprises among active businesses with 10 or more employees (21.1%). It also had the highest proportion of employees working in these enterprises (30.0%). Greece followed, with the second-highest rates in both categories: 17.1% of enterprises and 28.4% of employees. Finland, Denmark, and Malta each had shares of around 16% for high-growth enterprises, along with relatively high proportions of employees in these firms. At the lower end of the scale, Cyprus had the smallest share of high-growth enterprises (2.8%), though a significantly high share of employees in them (6.4%). Belgium and France had slightly higher enterprise shares (7.3% and 8.6%, respectively), but their employee proportions were much lower. When considering young high-growth enterprises (as a share of all high-growth enterprises), at least 1 enterprise out of 10 high-growth enterprises was young in Lithuania, Latvia, Bulgaria, and Croatia. Conversely, Hungary and Belgium had the lowest proportions, having less than 0.4 gazelles per high-growth enterprise. [[File:Fig_4_Share_of_high-growth_enterprises_by_sector,_EU,_2023_(%).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Share of high-growth enterprises by sector, EU, 2023, %
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bd_hg__custom_20807815/default/table?lang=en (bd_hg)]|alt=A sectoral bar chart displaying the concentration of high-growth enterprises across different economic activities in the EU.]]]
Figure 4 shows the concentration of high-growth enterprises across the EU by NACE sector. The 'Information and communication' sector had the highest at 16.5%, followed by 'Arts, entertainment and recreation' and 'Accommodation and food service activities'. 'Administrative and support services' stood out for having the highest proportion of young high-growth firms. Overall, growth was concentrated in service and technology sectors, while more traditional industries like 'Mining', 'Real estate', and 'Manufacturing' had the lowest shares of high-growth enterprises. [[File:Fig_5_Employment_share_of_high-growth_enterprises_by_sector,_EU,_2023_(%).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Employment share of high-growth enterprises by sector, EU, 2023, %
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bd_hg__custom_20807815/default/table?lang=en (bd_hg)]|alt=A dual-indicator chart comparing the proportion of high-growth enterprises to their respective share of total sectoral employment.]]]
Figure 5 shows that high-growth enterprises provided a high share of jobs. Often, the share of jobs in high-growth enterprises exceeds their share of active enterprises – though this is not always the case. The largest gap appears in 'Accommodation and food service activities'. In this sector, high-growth enterprises accounted for 13.7% of firms but a much higher 22.6% of jobs. This shows that high-growth enterprises in service-oriented fields are major job creators. In contrast, in capital-intensive industries rapid enterprise growth does not always lead to a matching increase in the workforce share. Young high-growth enterprises had the highest employment share in 'Administrative and support services', accounting for 1.5% of jobs in active enterprises with 10 or more employees. The 'Accommodation and food services' sector, along with 'Information and communication', also recorded high shares of employment, 1.5% and 1.3% respectively. However, their overall proportion of employment in all high-growth enterprises was lower than in administrative and support services. === High-growth micro enterprises === Data on high-growth micro enterprises in 2023 are provided on a voluntary basis by 10 countries (Figure 6). Portugal and Greece recorded the highest shares of these enterprises in their employer business populations, at 5.7% and 5.6% respectively. The Netherlands followed at 4.2%, while Slovakia, Italy, Romania, Iceland reported shares of around 3%. At the lower end of the scale, Poland had the smallest share (1.1%), followed by France (2.3%) and Croatia (2.4%). [[File:Fig_6_Share_of_high-growth_micro_enterprises_in_employer_business_population,_2023_(%).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Share of high-growth micro enterprises in employer business population, 2023, %
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bd_hg_micro__custom_20727952/default/table?lang=en (bd_hg_micro)]|alt=A bar chart illustrating the share of high-growth micro-enterprises (1 to 9 employees) within the employer business population for a selection of reporting countries.]]]
[[File:Fig_7_Share_of_high-growth_micro_enterprises_in_employer_business_population_by_sectors,_2023_(%).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 7: Share of high-growth micro enterprises in employer business population by sector, 2023, %
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bd_hg_micro__custom_20727952/default/table?lang=en (bd_hg_micro)]|alt=A sectoral bar chart showing the share of high-growth micro-enterprises across various industries, based on the aggregate data of ten reporting countries.]]]
Across the 10 reporting countries, the distribution of high-growth micro enterprises varied significantly by sector in 2023 (Figure 7). 'Accommodation and food service activities' had the highest concentration, with high-growth micro enterprises accounting for 4.9% of businesses having at least one employee. 'Mining and quarrying' and 'Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation' followed, each at 4.3%. On the other hand, the share of high-growth micro enterprises remained below 1.5% in 'Financial and insurance activities' and 'Real estate activities'. In these sectors, small firms tend to expand their output through productivity gains, technology, and outsourcing rather than through additional hiring, so growth is less likely to be captured by an employment-based measure. === Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=SE Masterfile BD HGE final.xlsx|title=SE high-growth enterprises}} ===Data sources=== High-growth enterprises are those that had at least 10 employees at the beginning of a 3-year period and recorded annual growth in the number of employees above 10% over that period. For example, an enterprise with 10 employees in year t-3 qualifies as high-growth if its average workforce exceeds 13.31 employees by year t. This threshold reflects annualised growth of over 10% based on annual average headcounts. High-growth micro enterprises are small firms that start with 1 to 9 employees and expand by more than 3.31 employees over a three-year period. '''Coverage, units and classifications''' Business demography covers the [[Glossary:Business economy|business economy]], which includes industry, construction and many services (([[Glossary:Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)|NACE Rev.2]])sections B to N, P to R as well as division S95 and S96). Business demography statistics do not cover agriculture, forestry and fishing, nor public administration. Starting with the reference year 2021, business demography statistics are compiled under the legal basis of the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32019R2152 EU regulation 2019/2152] on European business statistics and its implementing act, [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32020R1197 EU regulation 2020/1197] on technical specifications and arrangements. ===Context=== High-growth enterprises (HGEs) play an important role in job creation and innovation in the EU's single market. As drivers of employment, industrial renewal and sectoral productivity, they are at the heart of [[Entrepreneurship_-_statistical_indicators|European entrepreneurship]] and economic growth. Statistical information about high-growth enterprises can support several European initiatives. In policy discourse, terms like 'startups' and 'scale-ups' are often associated with enterprises which exhibit high growth rates. Policies and projects under the Commission's [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/startup-europe Startup Europe] initiative, [https://eic.ec.europa.eu/eic-funding-opportunities/eic-accelerator-0_en funding by the European Innovation Council (EIC)] or initiatives within the [https://eismea.ec.europa.eu/programmes/single-market-programme_en Single Market Programme] are designed to support (highly innovative) companies in scaling their growth. They aim at boosting competitiveness, in particular for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), whose central role as the backbone of Europe's economy is reflected in the European Commission's [https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/smes/sme-strategy_en SME strategy]. Intended to improve business conditions for 'startups' and 'scale-ups', such policies range from easing access to finance to reducing administrative burdens, in particular for SMEs. In the context of the EU's twin green and digital transitions, there are also sector- and technology-specific accelerator programmes for 'start-ups' and 'scale-ups', for example by the [https://eit.europa.eu/tags/accelerator European Institute of Innovation and Technology (EIT)] or the [https://startupprize.eu/ European Startup prize]. The [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/activities/digital-programme Digital Europe Programme] provides funding for key areas of the digital economy, including super-computing, artificial intelligence and cyber-security. A network of [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/activities/edihs European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs)] provides a support infrastructure of knowledge hubs to aide companies with challenges arising from the digital transformation. Their roll-out across different regions of the EU aims to embed innovation at a regional level. Similarly, the [https://cor.europa.eu/en/plenaries-events/awards/european-entrepreneurial-region-eer/ European Entrepreneurial Region (EER)] as well as the [https://startupregions.eu/ Startup Europe regions network] highlight the importance of supporting entrepreneurial activity, in particular of 'start-ups' and 'scale-ups', as an investment in regional competitiveness. === Other articles === *[[Business demography statistics]] *[[European Business Statistics]] *[[High-growth enterprises - statistics]] *[[Entrepreneurship - statistical indicators]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/business-demography/database Business demoghraphy (bd)]
=== Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/business-demography/overview Business demography] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/overview Structural business statistics] === Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/bd_sims.htm Business demography metadata] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-25-016 European business statistics methodological manual for business demography statistics – 2025 edition] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-ra-07-010 Eurostat-OECD Manual on Business Demography Statistics - 2007 edition] === External links === *[http://ec.europa.eu/growth/smes_en European Commission - Enterprise and Industry - Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) - Promoting Entrepreneurship] ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Article_name'' {{Unit|topic=X_Structural_business_statistics}} [[Category:Industry, trade, and services|High-growth enterprises in the EU]] [[Category:Business demography|High-growth enterprises in the EU]] [[Category:Statistical article|High-growth enterprises in the EU]] [[Category:February2027|High-growth enterprises in the EU]]

title: High-growth enterprises - statistics
text:
<newarticle pic="Rawpixel.com Shutterstock 451168228 RV.jpg"></newarticle>

<metadescription> Official statistics on high-growth enterprises (HGEs)</metadescription>

<highlight>
Data on the growth of firms can offer many interesting insights: 
*What can we learn from observing the growth trajectories of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)? 
*How does growth change with enterprise age? 
*Do firms form particularly strong growth clusters in specific regions or sectors? 

Official statistics on high-growth enterprises (HGEs) can help to answer such questions by informing about their economic and sectoral characteristics. As such, this type of data is [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/c32b9be3-5460-11ea-aece-01aa75ed71a1/language-en/format-PDF/source-277746143 a key guidepost for many policy areas], from cohesion to employment and social policy, or from industrial to innovation policy. 

After introducing these policy areas, this article gives an overview of the data on high-growth enterprises available at Eurostat, also referring to news items, explanatory articles, glossary entries and databases on this topic. By presenting relevant statistical definitions embedded in broader statistical domains and policy areas, the article aims to guide the reader through Eurostat's broad range of data about HGEs.
</highlight>
<articlecontent>
<sesection>
=== High-growth enterprises in the context of European policymaking ===
High-growth enterprises (HGEs) play an important role in job creation and innovation in the EU's single market. As drivers of employment, industrial renewal and sectoral productivity, they are at the heart of [[Entrepreneurship_-_statistical_indicators|European entrepreneurship]] and economic growth. 
Statistical information about high-growth enterprises can support several European initiatives. In policy discourse, terms like 'startups' and 'scale-ups' are often associated with enterprises which exhibit high growth rates. Policies and projects under the Commission's [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/startup-europe Startup Europe] initiative, [https://eic.ec.europa.eu/eic-funding-opportunities/eic-accelerator-0_en funding by the European Innovation Council (EIC)] or initiatives within the [https://eismea.ec.europa.eu/programmes/single-market-programme_en Single Market Programme] are designed to support (highly innovative) companies in scaling their growth. They aim at boosting competitiveness, in particular for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), whose central role as the backbone of Europe's economy is reflected in the European Commission's [https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/smes/sme-strategy_en SME strategy]. Intended to improve business conditions for 'startups' and 'scale-ups', such policies range from easing access to finance to reducing administrative burdens, in particular for SMEs. 

In the context of the EU's twin green and digital transitions, there are also sector- and technology-specific accelerator programmes for 'start-ups' and 'scale-ups', for example by the [https://eit.europa.eu/tags/accelerator European Institute of Innovation and Technology (EIT)] or the [https://startupprize.eu/ European Startup prize]. The [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/activities/digital-programme Digital Europe Programme] provides funding for key areas of the digital economy, including super-computing, artificial intelligence and cyber-security. A network of [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/activities/edihs European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs)] provides a support infrastructure of knowledge hubs to aide companies with challenges arising from the digital transformation. Their roll-out across different regions of the EU aims to embed innovation at a regional level. Similarly, the [https://cor.europa.eu/en/plenaries-events/awards/european-entrepreneurial-region-eer/ European Entrepreneurial Region (EER)] as well as the [https://startupregions.eu/ Startup Europe regions network] highlight the importance of supporting entrepreneurial activity, in particular of 'start-ups' and 'scale-ups', as an investment in regional competitiveness. </sesection>
<sesection>
===Indicators available at Eurostat at a glance ===
To describe high-growth enterprises, Eurostat's statistics on the structure and dynamics of European businesses, in particular in the domain of [[Business_demography_statistics|business demography]], offer relevant indicators. Unlike some of the terms used synonymously for 'high-growth enterprises' in popular and policy discourse, the term [[Glossary:High-growth_enterprise|'high-growth enterprise']] in official statistics has a clear definition specified in the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32020R1197:EN:NOT|title=Implementing Regulation}} of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/legislation European Business Statistics Regulation]<ref>Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1197 laying down technical specifications and arrangements pursuant to the Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council (EU) 2019/2152 on European business statistics ('EBS Regulation').</ref>: 'a high-growth enterprise is an [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprise]] with an average annualised growth in employees that is greater than 10% over a 3 year period, whereby the enterprise must have at least 10 employees at the beginning of said growth period'. 

Based on this '''employment-based definition''' laid down in the Regulation, Eurostat publishes the following indicators, for which data collection is mandatory in all EU countries:
* number of high-growth enterprises and number of young high-growth enterprises
* number of employees in high-growth enterprises and number of employees in young high-growth enterprises
* average size of high-growth enterprises
* share of high-growth enterprises in the population of [[Glossary:Active_enterprise|active enterprises with 10 employees and over]] 
* employment share of high-growth enterprises in the population of [[Glossary:Active_enterprise| active enterprises with 10 employees and over]]. 
The data collection according to the definition based on employment covers all EU countries.

An alternative to the employment-based definition presented above relies on turnover to distinguish high-growth enterprises. According to this definition, a high-growth enterprise is an [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprise]] with an average annualised growth in turnover that is greater than 10% over a 3 year period, whereby the enterprise must have at least 10 employees at the beginning of said growth period. Based on this '''turnover-based definition''', 2 indicators are available:
* number of high-growth enterprises 
* share of high-growth enterprises in the population of [[Glossary:Active_enterprise| active enterprises with 10 employees and over]]. 
As the data collection according to the definition based on turnover is voluntary, country coverage of these variables is incomplete, with data available for less than half of the EU countries. 

Additional business demography indicators, such as death and survival rates are not available for high-growth enterprises.
For further details about calculations and coverage, the methodological section of this article offers more in-depth explanations.
The table below shows links to databases, which contain one or more of these indicators:
[[Image: List of tables.png|thumb|centre|900px|Table 1: Table showing links to available databases [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bd_hg/default/table?lang=en&category=bsd.bd bd_hg], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bd_hg_micro/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=b59167a8-969f-4054-8ef6-11086220bf78 bd_hg_micro], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bd_hgnace_r/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=054c3078-94f0-4fd9-86dc-6fe3d18d867e bd_hgnace_r], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/urt_bd_hgn__custom_13617713/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=1f81eda9-eeb0-4c4c-a4b5-e8398cf83ea2 urt_bd_hgn], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/met_bd_hgn/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=e872a37f-5fc9-4612-b230-2747e3678068 met_bd_hgn]
|alt= Table showing links to available databases on high-growth enterprises. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
</sesection>
<sesection>
=== Gazelles: Young high-growth enterprises ===
In the context of enterprise maturity, it is possible to distinguish sub-populations amongst high-growth enterprises based on their age. The EBS Regulation defines young high-growth enterprises ('gazelles') as 5 and 4 year old enterprises with at least 10 employees at the beginning of their growth period (for the full statistical definition, see methodological section of this article). Some of the indicators listed above are also available for the gazelle subpopulation, based on both the employment and the turnover definition of high-growth enterprises:
* number of young high-growth enterprises (gazelles)
* share of young high-growth enterprise (gazelles) in the population of [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Active_enterprise active enterprises with 10 employees and over].
The data collection for employment-based gazelles is mandatory. So full data coverage by countries is available. Some countries provide voluntarily also turnover-based data on gazelles. For the relevant database, please consider the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=High-growth_enterprises_-_statistics#Indicators_available_at_Eurostat_at_a_glance overview table] above.
Additional business demography indicators, such as death and survival rates are not available for gazelles.
From reference year 2021 onwards, the data collection on the gazelle sub-population according to the employment-based definition is compulsory. Available indicators are:
* number of gazelles 
* number of employees in gazelles
* average size of gazelles
* share of gazelles in the population of [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Active_enterprise active enterprises with 10 employees and over] 
* employment share of gazelles in the population of [[Glossary:Active_enterprise| active enterprises with 10 employees and over]].
</sesection>
<sesection>
=== A geographical perspective: High-growth enterprises by regional and territorial units ===
To explore the spatial distribution of high-growth enterprises, Eurostat also offers a geographical breakdown for some of the variables, which are collected as part of the compulsory data collection. This breakdown is available at different levels of granularity, from the national level down to small regions, defined at the [[Glossary:Nomenclature_of_territorial_units_for_statistics_(NUTS)|NUTS 3 level]]. The relevant database is listed in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=High-growth_enterprises_-_statistics#Indicators_available_at_Eurostat_at_a_glance overview table] above. 

A complement to this is a breakdown by territories, i.e. a classification of geographical units by their territorial nature rather than their location alone. This typology distinguishes between urban and rural regions as well as between coastal and mountainous regions, allowing for a closer analysis of high-growth enterprises by territory. Like the geographical breakdown, only some of the compulsory, employment-based variables are available at this granularity. The relevant database is listed in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=High-growth_enterprises_-_statistics#Indicators_available_at_Eurostat_at_a_glance overview table] above.

Finally, high-growth enterprises can be analysed from a spatial economy perspective in a breakdown by metropolitan regions. For this breakdown, 2 variables from the employment-based compulsory collection are available: i) the number of high-growth enterprises and ii) the share of high-growth enterprises in the population of active enterprises with at least 10 employees. The relevant database is listed in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=High-growth_enterprises_-_statistics#Indicators_available_at_Eurostat_at_a_glance overview table] above. 
</sesection>
<sesection>
=== A sectoral perspective: High-growth enterprises by economic activity ===
For sector-specific analysis, high-growth enterprises can be broken down by economic activity, a perspective particularly relevant for guiding sector-specific policy measures.
The indicators presented above are available for different economic activities as recorded by NACE Rev. 2, at different levels of granularity, from the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=NACE_background#Structure_and_coding_of_NACE first level (sections)] to the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=NACE_background#Structure_and_coding_of_NACE third level (groups)]. Not all indicators have coverage of all economic activities at the highest level of granularity. For ratio-based indicators in particular, coverage is determined by the coverage of the denominator. For further information, the [[High-growth_enterprises_-_statistics#Statistical_definitions_and_Methodological_notes|Statistical definitions and methodological notes]] offers a more in-depth explanation. 
While it is possible to combine the sectoral and the geographical perspective, economic breakdowns of geographical units beyond the country are available at section level only. 
</sesection>
<sesection>
=== High-growth micro enterprises ===
Currently, statistics on high-growth enterprises cover enterprises with 10 and over employees at the beginning of growth. To extend the data collection to enterprises that are very small at the beginning of their growth (for the full statistical definition, see methodological section of this article), a pilot project was created to cover micro enterprises with 1 to 9 employees based on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/7894008/12445868/Methodological-note.pdf/16fa1088-4a0c-4a1c-5b18-601ca61bb2a8?t=1613487055280 similar methodological principles] as the data collection on high-growth enterprises. 

Most importantly, its growth criterion to distinguish high-growth micro enterprises was derived from the high-growth enterprise population with at least 10 employees. For these, annualised growth of more than 10% over a 3 year period entails an employee count of more than 13.31 employees after 3 years. Analogously, micro enterprises with 1 to 9 employees at the beginning of growth need to grow by more than 3.31 employees over 3 years to be called high-growth micro enterprises.

On these high-growth micro enterprises, 12 countries submitted data to Eurostat as part of the pilot project<ref>The reference year, for which the pilot study collected data, was 2017. The countries which participated in the pilot study are Austria, Bulgaria, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Lithuania, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal and Sweden.</ref>. The following variables were collected: number of enterprises, employees, persons employed, turnover and finally gross value added. Additionally, a breakdown into 2 size classes is available, distinguishing between enterprises with 1 to 4 employees and those with 5 to 9 employees. Due to the non-mature nature of these statistics, the data collected in this study is published under the category [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/micro-high-growth-enterprises experimental statistics]. A thematic deep dive into high-growth micro enterprises based on the data collected in the pilot study can be found in this [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Characteristics_of_micro_high-growth_enterprises Statistics Explained article]. 

After the conclusion of the pilot project, a new data collection on high-growth micro enterprises was launched in which EU countries can transmit data to Eurostat on a voluntary basis. The relevant database is listed in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=High-growth_enterprises_-_statistics#Indicators_available_at_Eurostat_at_a_glance overview table] above. 
</sesection>
<sesection>
=== Statistical definitions and methodological notes ===
As described above, the statistical definition of high-growth enterprises is laid down in the EBS legislative framework <ref>Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1197 laying down technical specifications and arrangements pursuant to the Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council (EU) 2019/2152 on European business statistics ('EBS Regulation').</ref>. Specifically, Variable 210103, defining the number of high-growth enterprises includes the statistical definition of high-growth enterprises: "[…] enterprises, having at least 10 employees in t – 3, with average annualised growth in number of employees greater than 10% per annum, over a 3 year period (t – 3 to t). It does not include enterprises, as defined in variable 210201 'enterprise births', in t – 3."<ref>[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32020R1197&from=EN Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020] of 30 July 2020 laying down technical specifications and arrangements pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2019/2152 of the European Parliament and of the Council on European business statistics repealing 10 legal acts in the field of business statistics (europa.eu).</ref> 

In other words, for a given reference year, the definition of high-growth enterprises includes all enterprises which were a) active but b) not born 3 years before the reference year, c) had at least 10 employees 3 years before the reference year and d) exhibit an average annualised growth in employees which is greater than 10% in the 3 year period leading up to the reference year. EU countries are legally obliged to use this definition in their compulsory annual data collections in this area. An alternative definition, based on which additional data can be submitted to Eurostat on a voluntary basis, refers to the turnover rather than employment to measure growth. By this definition, high-growth enterprises are those with an average annualised growth in turnover that is greater than 10% over a 3 year period, with the size threshold of 10 and over employees still applicable. As such, high-growth enterprises according to the turnover-based definition must also have at least 10 employees in t – 3, and those which are born in t – 3 are excluded from the high-growth population of t, even if they satisfy all the other conditions.

The rationale for excluding enterprises, which were born in t – 3, in both the employment-based and the turnover-based definition, is to make sure that all enterprises in the population have the same average period of activity for each year considered for the growth period. For new-born enterprises, the average period of activity in the first year of operation varies, depending on the month in which they were founded.

For more detailed methodological notes, the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-ra-07-010 2007 Eurostat-OECD Manual on Business Demography Statistics] as well as the [https://unece.org/statistics/publications/guidelines-use-statistical-business-registers-business-demography-and UN guidelines on the use of statistical business registers for business demography and entrepreneurship statistics] provide more in-depth explanations. 
It is important to note that the Eurostat-OECD Manual uses a different growth threshold for high-growth enterprises, namely 20%. This threshold has since been reduced to 10% for international data reporting, based on results from pilot studies. The UN guidelines also recommend 10%. For Eurostat data, the 10% threshold is a legal requirement laid down in the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32020R1197:EN:NOT|title=Implementing Regulation}} of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/legislation European Business Statistics Regulation]. 

Regarding data coverage, it is important to note that not all indicators cover all economic activities at the highest level of granularity. For ratio-based indicators in particular, coverage is determined by the lower granularity component of the fraction. Since count variables for high-growth enterprises are available down to the NACE group level, this lower granularity component is usually the denominator, which depends on the active enterprise population of enterprises with 10 employees and over. 
</sesection>
