title: Hourly labour costs
text:
EU statistics on average hourly labour costs. Data extracted on 31 March 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 Hourly labour costs ranged from €12.0 in Bulgaria to €56.8 in Luxembourg in 2025. In 2025, non-wage labour costs were highest in France (32.3% of total labour costs) and Sweden (31.7%). [[Image:Hourly labour costs, 2025 (€), map.png |thumb|center|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lc_lci_lev__custom_20776181/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=76bf5785-9c0c-4477-b427-f553e2790a22&c=1774880004000 lc_lci_lev])|alt=a map showing the estimated hourly labour costs for 2025 in euros. In the EU Member States and EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article provides recent statistics on [[Glossary:Average hourly labour cost|hourly labour costs]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. In 2025, average hourly labour costs were estimated at €34.9 in the [[Glossary:EU|EU]] and at €38.2 in the [[Glossary:Euro area|euro area]]. However, this average masks sizeable gaps between EU countries, with hourly labour costs ranging from €12.0 in Bulgaria to €56.8 in Luxembourg. When comparing labour cost estimates in euro over time, it should be noted that the data for the EU countries outside the euro area are influenced by the [[Glossary:Exchange rate|exchange rate]] movements. ===Hourly labour costs ranged from €12.0 to €56.8 in 2025=== In 2025, average hourly labour costs in the whole economy (see paragraph 'Data sources') were estimated to be €34.9 in the EU and €38.2 in the euro area (EA21). However, this average masks sizeable differences between EU countries, with the lowest hourly labour costs recorded in Bulgaria (€12.0), Romania (€13.6) and Hungary (€15.2) while the highest were in Luxembourg (€56.8), Denmark (€51.7) and the Netherlands (€47.9). Figure 1 shows the labour costs across EU countries. [[Image:Estimated hourly labour costs, 2025 (€).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Estimated hourly labour costs, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lc_lci_lev__custom_20772058/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=6cace959-bdea-4106-92bc-fabdfba08688&c=1774871897000 lc_lci_lev])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing estimated hourly labour costs in euros in the EU, euro area, individual EU Member States and some EFTA countries. Each country has two stacks representing wages and salaries and other labour costs for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:Hourly labour costs in € 2025.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Hourly labour costs in euro
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lc_lci_lev__custom_20768188/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=c29d3a2d-e454-4fc2-a6fb-f280216adaec&c=1774862376000 lc_lci_lev])|alt= Table showing hourly labour costs in euros in the EU, euro area, individual EU Member States snd some EFTA countries for the years 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. The percentage of total 2025 non-wage costs and percentage change between 2025 and 2024 are also shown. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:Hourly labour costs in national currency for non-euro area countries.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 2: Hourly labour costs in national currency for non-euro area countries
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lc_lci_lev__custom_20768332/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=1e200fe2-48f7-44e0-b74a-8b85bbe3c056&c=1774862637000 lc_lci_lev])|alt= Table showing hourly labour costs in national currency for non-euro area countries for the whole economy of enterprises with 10 or more employees for the years 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. The percentage change between 2025 and 2024 is also shown. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Share of non-wage costs highest in France and Sweden=== The 2 main components of labour costs are wages & salaries and non-wage costs such as employers' social contributions. The share of non-wage costs in the whole economy was 24.8% in the EU and 25.6% in the euro area (see Table 1 and Figure 2). [[Image:Non-wage costs, 2025 (% of total).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Non-wage costs, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lc_lci_lev__custom_20772280/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=b933b50f-0bef-4494-8ed1-158f8d0fff03&c=1774872034000 lc_lci_lev])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing non-wage costs as percentage of total in individual EU Member States and some EFTA countries for the year 2025. Two lines across all country columns compare them with the EU and euro area. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] These estimates for 2025, published by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], cover [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]] with 10 or more [[Glossary:Employee - SBS|employees]] and are based on the 2020 [[Glossary:Labour cost survey (LCS)|Labour Cost Survey (LCS2020)]], except for Malta (based on LCS2016). They are extrapolated with the corresponding annual growth rates from [[Glossary:Labour_cost_index_(LCI)|Labour cost index (LCI)]]. ===Labour costs per hour lowest in the construction sector=== In the EU, labour costs per hour were the highest in the mainly non-business economy excluding public administration (€35.5) and the lowest in the construction sector (€31.5). Gaps were larger in the euro area, with industry being the highest paying sector (€40.3 per hour) and construction the lowest (€34.4 per hour) (see Table 3). [[Image:Hourly labour costs in €, breakdown by economic activity in 2025.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 3: Hourly labour costs in euro, breakdown by economic activity in 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lc_lci_lev__custom_20768476/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=b13eb483-e4f6-45d5-97ce-2efb241e3ce5&c=1774862950000 lc_lci_lev])|alt= Table showing hourly labour costs in euro as breakdown by economic activity in enterprises with 10 or more employees in the EU and some EFTA countries in the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:Hourly labour costs in NAC for non EA countries, breakdown by econ activity in 2025.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 4: Hourly labour costs in national currency for non-euro area countries, breakdown by economic activity in 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lc_lci_lev__custom_20768556/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=5af5046b-4ffd-4117-8d04-f0be27c73129&c=1774863084000 lc_lci_lev])|alt= Table showing hourly labour costs in national currency for non-euro area countries as breakdown by economic activity in the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Hourly labour costs increased most in Bulgaria and Croatia=== Between 2024 and 2025, hourly labour costs in the whole economy (in euro) rose by 4.1% in the EU and by 3.8% in the euro area (see Figure 3). Within the euro area, hourly labour costs increased in all EU countries, except Malta (-0.5%). The largest increases were recorded in Bulgaria (+13.1%), Croatia (+11.6%), Slovenia (+9.3%) and Lithuania (+9.2%) and the lowest in France (+2.0%) and Italy (+3.2%) followed by Spain, Cyprus and Luxembourg (all +3.5%). For EU countries outside the euro area, the hourly labour costs expressed in national currency also increased in all countries, with the largest variations recorded in Romania (+10.6%), Hungary (+8.9%) and Poland (+8.8%). They increased the least in Denmark (+3.0%). [[Image:Relative change in hourly labour costs,2025_2024,whole economy,in %_rev1.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Relative change in hourly labour costs 2025/2024 for the whole economy
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lc_lci_lev}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage relative change in hourly labour costs between the year 2025 and 2024 for the whole economy in the EU, euro area, individual EU Member States, Iceland and Norway. Each country column has two stacks representing in national currency and exchange rate effect. Each column has a scatter line marking the percentage change in euro. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Hourly_labour_costs_2025_-_update_March_2026_rev4.xlsx|Hourly labour costs - tables and figures, 2025]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== '''Labour cost survey''' The labour cost survey (LCS) provides structural information on labour costs. The survey is conducted every four years and the most recent LCS refers to the year 2020. The LCS covers [[Glossary:Observation unit|observation units]] with 10 or more [[Glossary:Employee - LFS|employees]] and all economic activities except NACE Rev. 2 sections : 'A - Agriculture, forestry and fishing', 'O - Public administration and defence; compulsory social security', 'T - Activities of households as employers; undifferentiated goods - and services - producing activities of households for own use' and 'U - Activities of extraterritorial organisations and bodies'. The labour cost per hour from the LCS is calculated as: Compensation of employees + [[Glossary:Vocational training|Vocational training]] costs + Other expenditure + Taxes – Subsidies. For the EU the weight of each variable in the labour cost per hour in 2020 was: {| border="1" cellspacing="1" cellpadding="1" width="280" |- | Compensation of employees | 98.98% |- | Vocational training costs | 0.57% |- | Other expenditure | 0.46% |- | Taxes | 0.73% |- | Subsidies | 0.74% |} '''Labour cost index''' The labour cost index (LCI) is a short-term indicator showing the development of hourly labour costs incurred by employers. It is calculated by dividing the labour costs by the number of hours worked. Total labour costs consist of costs for wages and salaries, plus non-wage costs (such as employer's social contributions). These do not include vocational training costs or other expenditures (such as recruitment costs, spending on work clothes, etc.). The LCI covers all business units irrespective of the number of employees and all economic activities except agriculture, forestry and fishing, private households and extra-territorial organisations. The index equals 100 in 2020 and is available 70 days after the reference quarter. The labour cost per hour from the LCI is calculated as: Compensation of employees + Taxes – Subsidies From the table above it can be concluded that for the EU, the LCI labour cost concept covers approximately 99.0% of the LCS labour concept. This percentage varies from country to country. The lowest percentages are observed in Ireland and the Netherlands where the LCI concept represents 96.9% of the LCS labour cost concept. See {{Stable link|title=|code=lc_nstruc_r2}}. In this publication, the whole economy includes NACE Rev. 2 sections B to N and P to S, and can be subdivided into the following economic activities: The '''mainly non-business economy''' (excluding public administration), which includes NACE Rev. 2 sections P to S (Education; Human health & social work activities; Arts, entertainment & recreation and Other service activities); for the EU this accounts for about 25% of the labour costs of the whole economy. The '''business economy''', which includes NACE Rev. 2 sections B to N; for the EU this accounts for about 75% of the total labour costs of the whole economy. It can be further broken down into: '''Industry''', which includes NACE Rev. 2 sections B to E (Mining and quarrying; Manufacturing; Electricity, gas, steam & air conditioning supply; and Water supply, sewerage, waste management & remediation activities). Industry accounts for around 23% of the whole economy in the EU. '''Construction'''; NACE Rev. 2 section F, which accounts for 5% of the whole economy in the EU. '''Services''', which include NACE Rev. 2 sections G to N (Wholesale and retail trade, repair of motor vehicles & motorcycles; Transportation & storage; Accommodation & food service activities; Information & communication; Financial & insurance activities; Real estate activities; Professional, scientific & technical activities; Administrative & support service activities). They account for around 47% of the whole economy in the EU. Excluded are NACE Rev. 2 sections : 'A - Agriculture, forestry and fishing', 'O - Public administration and defence; compulsory social security', ' T - Activities of households as employers; undifferentiated goods - and services - producing activities of households for own use' and 'U - Activities of extraterritorial organisations and bodies'. '''Country notes''' Spain and Finland: data for 2024 are taken from national sources. Austria and Iceland: data for 2025 are taken from national sources. Malta: data for 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 are benchmarked on Labour Cost Survey data 2016 (LCS2016) instead of LCS2020, pending further analysis. Belgium: data for 2025 are not being released due to the unavailability of LCI data. '''Estimation method''' Estimates for the years after 2020 are obtained by extrapolating the hourly labour costs, derived from the latest Labour Cost Survey (LCS2020) except for Malta where LCS2016 is used, with the Labour Cost Index (LCI). LCI data are not adjusted for calendar effects except in the case of Denmark, Sweden, Norway and Iceland where only calendar-adjusted data are available. '''Caveats''' Using the LCI to extrapolate the LCS values means assuming the following hypothesis: *the labour cost per hour of all business units behaves in the same way as the labour cost per hour of business units with 10 or more employees; *'Vocational training costs' and 'Other expenditure' behave similarly to 'Compensation of employees', 'Taxes' and 'Subsidies'. These assumptions, especially the first one, can lead to a small over or under-estimation of the annual labour cost per hour. '''Conversion to euro''' LCI data used to extrapolate labour cost levels are calculated in national currencies. To compile European aggregates, the results for non euro area countries are first converted into euros using the average exchange rates recorded for year 2025. '''Geographical information''' Although data in this news article refer to 2025, the euro area is calculated in its current composition (including Bulgaria). The euro area (EA21) included Belgium, Bulgaria, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Croatia, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, Portugal, Slovenia, Slovakia and Finland. The European Union (EU27) includes Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Croatia, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary, Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland and Sweden. ===Context=== The collection of labour costs is an essential part of the range of statistics that are relevant for an understanding of the [[Glossary:Inflation|inflationary or deflationary]] process and the cost dynamics in the economy. Information on labour costs is required for economic and monetary policies, wage bargaining and economic analyses. Labour costs are an important potential source of [[Glossary:Inflation|inflation]] since they account for a large proportion of the total costs borne by private businesses, which may pass on higher labour costs, in particular if not reflected in higher productivity, to consumers via higher end prices, thus fueling inflation. Equally, low or negative growth in hourly labour costs may signal [[Glossary:Inflation|deflation]] risks. A timely publication of labour cost levels is therefore of the utmost importance for the [[Glossary:European_Central_Bank_(ECB)|European Central Bank (ECB)]] in order for it to be able to monitor inflation in the euro area. ===Other articles=== *[[Earnings statistics]] *[[Labour cost index - recent trends]] *[[Labour cost structural statistics - levels]] *[[Labour markets at regional level#Earnings at a regional level|Labour markets at regional level - Earnings at a regional level]] *[[Wages and labour costs]] ===Publications=== '''Previous publications''' title: Healthcare personnel statistics - nursing and caring professionals
text:
Statistics on nursing and caring professionals with information on specialist healthcare personnel, as well as data pertaining to nursing and midwifery graduates. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 Luxembourg and Ireland reported that, respectively, 1.5% and 1.4% of its inhabitants were nurses (1 472 and 1 419 per 100 000 inhabitants in 2024); there were 7 other EU countries where this ratio was in excess of 1 000 per 100 000 inhabitants. Among EU countries, Ireland recorded the highest number of midwives relative to population size, 81 per 100 000 inhabitants in 2024. The next highest ratios were in Sweden, Poland and Belgium (79, 79 and 74 per 100 000 inhabitants, respectively). In 2024, Belgium recorded the highest number of midwifery graduates relative to population size among the EU countries, 6 per 100 000 inhabitants. The highest number of nursing graduates relative to population size was recorded in Finland, 81 per 100 000 inhabitants. |alt=A dynamic column chart showing the number of graduates of nursing professionals per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2024, for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. This article presents an overview of [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] statistics on nursing and caring professionals. It provides information on specialist [[Glossary:Healthcare|healthcare personnel]], as well as data relating to nursing and midwifery graduates. Nursing and caring professionals provide services directly to patients in [[Glossary:Hospital|hospitals]], as ambulatory care and in patients’ homes. Among others, these professionals include: *qualified [[Glossary:Nurse|nurses]] The data on nurses published by Eurostat constitute the number of professional nurses who fulfil the requirements of [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2005/36/oj/eng Directive 0036/2005/EC] on the recognition of professional qualifications. *[[Glossary:Midwife|midwives]] *caring personnel (personal care workers in health services, working in hospitals, private homes and independent residential settings). This article is included in a set of statistical articles concerning healthcare resources in the EU which forms part of the online publication [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union – facts and figures]]. ===Healthcare personnel=== For healthcare personnel, Eurostat collects data for 3 concepts (the last of these is not collected for caring personnel): *‘practising’ – health care professionals providing services directly to patients (variable 1.4, see illustration below) *‘professionally active’ – ‘practising’ professionals plus health care professionals for whom their medical education is a prerequisite for the execution of their job *‘licensed’ – health care professionals who are registered and entitled to practise as health care professionals, including those for whom their nursing education is not a prerequisite for the execution of their job and those who are economically inactive (for example, unemployed or retired). In this article, preference is given to the concept of ‘practising’ health care professionals. [[Image:Practising nurses and caring personnel, 2024_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Practising nurses and caring personnel, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/544e6884-6d46-4b95-a2bc-b2a3a5949ddb?lang=en hlth_rs_prs2])|alt=A table showing the number and ratio per hundred thousand inhabitants of practising nurses, midwives and caring personnel. Data are shown for 2024 for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the table are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Based on a sum of the available data (see Table 1 for more information concerning the data coverage for individual EU countries), in 2024 there were approximately 3.7 million practising nurses and 175 000 practising midwives in the EU. There were more than 2.8 million practising caring personnel (no data for France, Cyprus, Luxembourg, Portugal and Sweden). ==== Practising nurses ==== Nursing professionals assume responsibility for the planning and management of patient care, including the supervision of other healthcare workers, working autonomously or in teams with medical doctors and others in the application of preventive and curative care. Although nurses have traditionally provided care to patients under the guidance of a [[Glossary:Physician|physician]], they are increasingly permitted in many EU countries to practise independently as professionals. This however depends to some extent on their qualifications and level of training. Nursing professionals in the EU are required to complete a university course of at least 3 years. [[Image:Variables collected by Eurostat related to nurses_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Illustration: Variables collected by Eurostat related to nurses|alt=Illustration displaying the categories of nurses, coded according to whether they are mandatory or not. The categories are practising nurses, professionally active nurses and nurses licensed to practice. The variable practising nurses is variable 1.4 and is mandatory. The variables for professionally active and licensed to practice are voluntary.]] The number of nurses may vary between EU countries according to differences in healthcare systems and how nurses are classified. Equally, the number of nurses compared with other personnel (such as physicians) also varies between different providers of healthcare, for example between hospitals and long-term nursing care facilities. In 2024, Germany had the highest number of practising nurses among EU countries, at 1.05 million; this was considerably higher than the second highest count, recorded in France (608 000; 2023 data); see Table 1. In turn, the number of nurses in France was considerably higher than the next highest value, 408 000 recorded in Italy, while Spain (280 000) was the only other EU country to report more than 250 000 nurses. Malta and Cyprus recorded the smallest number of nurses, both around 5 000. '''''Luxembourg and Ireland had the highest numbers of nurses per inhabitant in the EU''''' Luxembourg had 1 472 practising nurses per 100 000 inhabitants and Ireland 1 419 per 100 000 inhabitants; the value for Ireland includes midwives who also have a nursing qualification. Ireland was followed by Finland with 1 290 nurses per 100 000 inhabitants and Germany with 1 251 per 100 000 inhabitants. Belgium (2022 data), the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark and Austria all recorded more than 1 000 practising nurses per 100 000 inhabitants. In other words, there were 9 EU countries where at least 1.0% of the population were nurses. [[Image:Practising nurses, 2019 and 2024 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Practising nurses, 2019 and 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6714b500-2175-4416-a196-0c0e42690303?lang=en hlth_rs_prs2])|alt=A double column chart showing the number of practising nurses per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2019 and 2024 for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Elsewhere, the number of practising nurses was generally within the range of 400 to 900 per 100 000 inhabitants in 2024. Croatia (265 per 100 000 inhabitants) and Greece (248 per 100 000 inhabitants; incomplete coverage) recorded somewhat lower ratios, while the lowest ratio was in Romania, at 106 per 100 000 inhabitants. A comparison of the latest data shows that there were 14 times as many nurses per 100 000 inhabitants in Luxembourg as in Romania in 2024. Expressed in a different way, each practising nurse in Luxembourg covered an average of 68 inhabitants, while in Romania the same ratio was 943 inhabitants per nurse. Among the EU countries for which data are available for 2019 and 2024 (alternative reference years for some countries, see Figure 1 for more details), the number of practising nurses relative to population size fell in 7 countries during the period under consideration. The biggest decreases were reported in Bulgaria, Austria and Spain (change in coverage), where the number of practising nurses fell by 21, 15 and 14 per 100 000 inhabitants, respectively. There were smaller decreases recorded for Belgium, Czechia (note the break in series), Latvia and Cyprus. The number of nurses per 100 000 inhabitants increased in 20 EU countries. The largest increases were recorded in Ireland (2021 to 2024), Slovenia and Luxembourg, where the ratio increased, respectively, by 165, 138 and 121 nurses per 100 000 inhabitants. ==== Practising nurses by age and sex ==== '''''Lithuania had the largest share of practising nurses aged 55 years or over''''' In 2024, almost half (48.0%) of all practising nurses in Lithuania were aged 55 years or over; the next highest share was recorded in Latvia (41.6%). These were the only EU countries (out of the 21 for which data are available – see Figure 2 for more details) where the share of nurses aged 55 years or over was above 30.0%; Denmark recorded the third highest share, at 29.5%. By contrast, 17 out of 26 EU countries recorded a share over 30.0% for practising doctors aged 55 years or older (see the article on [[Healthcare_personnel_statistics_-_physicians|physicians]] for more information). In 7 EU countries, the share of older nurses was less than 20.0%, with the lowest share in Slovenia (13.2%). The highest shares of younger nurses (under 35 years) were recorded in Croatia (37.0%), the Netherlands (36.7%), Malta (35.0%), Spain (34.1%) and Slovenia (33.3%); these were the only countries with a share of younger nurses of a third or more. [[Image:Practising nurses, by age, 2024 (%)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Practising nurses, by age, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ac1ad9ed-3688-4f82-8ba4-664fddcc2678?lang=en hlth_rs_nurse])|alt=A stacked column chart showing the share of nurses by age. The age groups are for people less than 35 years, 35 to 44 years, 45 to 54 years, 55 to 64 years and people aged 65 years or over. Data are for 2024 for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''In all EU countries for which data are available, more than 70% of all practising nurses were women''''' The analysis presented in Figure 3 shows that, in 2024, more than 70% of practising nurses were women in every EU country for which data are available. Around half of the EU countries (9 out of 21) for which data are available reported that more than 90.0% of nurses were women. The highest share was in Latvia, where 99.5% of nurses were women. The highest shares of male nurses were recorded in Malta and Italy, at 26.9% and 23.8%, respectively. For comparison, the share of female practising physicians in 2024 ranged from 41% to 75%. [[Image:Practising nurses, by sex, 2024 (%)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Practising nurses, by sex, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7024bd8f-33fa-43de-9c27-7d343c4691b8?lang=en hlth_rs_nurse])|alt=A HiLo chart showing the distribution by sex of nurses. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ====Midwives==== As with nurses, practising midwives plan, manage, provide and evaluate care services. Midwives do so before, during and after pregnancy and childbirth, providing delivery care for reducing health risks to women and new-born children; they may work autonomously or in teams with other healthcare providers. The distribution of midwives across the EU countries was somewhat different to that for nurses: the highest number of practising midwives in 2024 was recorded in Poland (28 800), followed by Germany (28 000) and France (25 700), with the lowest number (fewer than 300) recorded in Malta. Among the EU countries, Ireland had the highest ratio of midwives relative to its population size, 81 per 100 000 inhabitants in 2024 – see Figure 4 for more information concerning the data coverage for individual EU countries. Sweden, Poland (both 79 per 100 000) and Belgium (74 per 100 000; 2022 data) had the next highest ratios, followed at some distance by Malta (52 practising midwives per 100 000 inhabitants). At the other end of the range, the lowest ratio of the number of midwives to population was recorded in Romania, where there were, on average, 15 practising midwives per 100 000 inhabitants in 2024. The highest ratio (in Ireland) was 5.6 times as high as the lowest ratio (in Romania). [[Image:Practising midwives, 2019 and 2024 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Practising midwives, 2019 and 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ae4991a6-2e3c-4bd6-9f09-8190215044ba?lang=en hlth_rs_prs2])|alt=A double column chart showing the number of practising midwives per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2019 and 2024 for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Caring personnel === Caring personnel include health care assistants and home-based personal care workers. *Health care assistants in institutions provide direct personal care and assistance with activities of daily living to patients and residents in a variety of health care settings such as hospitals, clinics and residential nursing care facilities. They generally work under the direct supervision of medical, nursing or other health professionals or associate professionals. *Home-based personal care workers provide routine personal care and assistance with activities of daily living to people who need such care due to the effects of ageing, illness, injury, or other physical or mental conditions and are living in private homes and other independent residential settings. Subject to data availability (see Table 1 for more information concerning the data coverage for individual EU countries), Germany (688 000), Italy (646 000) and Spain (608 000) had the highest number of caring personnel in 2024, followed at some distance by the Netherlands (266 000); note that recent data are not available for France, for which older data show that France used to have the largest caring personnel workforce. The smallest numbers were recorded in Croatia (836) and Bulgaria (1 047). '''''The number of caring personnel per 100 000 inhabitants in Finland was considerably higher than in the other EU countries''''' Finland had 2 406 caring personnel per 100 000 inhabitants in 2024, which was by far the highest ratio among the EU countries (see Table 1 for more information concerning the data coverage for individual EU countries). Denmark (1 508 per 100 000 inhabitants in 2023) and the Netherlands (1 478 per 100 000 inhabitants) were the only other EU countries to record more than 1 250 caring personnel per 100 000 inhabitants. In 4 EU countries, this ratio was below 100 per 100 000 inhabitants in 2024: Greece (62 per 100 000 inhabitants; incomplete coverage), Poland (34 per 100 000 inhabitants; 2022 data), Croatia (22 per 100 000 inhabitants) and Bulgaria (16 per 100 000 inhabitants). ===Employment in hospitals=== Table 2 focuses on nurses, midwives and health care assistants employed in hospitals. This coverage of healthcare personnel differs from Table 1 in that it includes the narrower concept of health care assistants Number of healthcare assistants (ISCO-08 code: 5321) employed by a hospital. rather than caring personal. Among the EU countries, Germany recorded the highest absolute number of nurses and midwives employed in hospitals (581 000), while France (395 000) and Italy (287 000) were the only other EU countries (for which recent data are available) to record more than 200 000 nurses and midwives in hospitals in 2024. A similar analysis for health care assistants working in hospitals reveals the highest counts were in France (253 000) and Spain (155 000); none of the other EU countries for which there are recent data recorded more than 80 000 health care assistants working in hospitals. The availability of data converted into [[Glossary:Full-time equivalent (FTE)|full-time equivalent]] units indicates that employment in hospitals was generally close to full-time. For nurses and midwives, the number in full-time equivalents was equal to at least 80.0% of the number in head counts for 9 of the 13 EU countries for which data are available. Falling just below this range were Estonia (79.8%), Austria (79.5%), the Netherlands (78.5%) and Germany (73.8%). For health care assistants, both measures are available for 12 EU countries, 9 of which recorded ratios between full-time equivalents and head counts of at least 80.0%. By contrast, in Germany (77.2%), Denmark (68.9%) and the Netherlands (65.9%), a smaller proportion of health care assistants employed in hospitals appeared to work on a full-time basis. [[Image:Nurses and caring professionals employed in hospitals, 2024_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Nurses and caring professionals employed in hospitals, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6c84eff2-f2e9-43a5-b720-6fe12ff29969?lang=en hlth_rs_prshp2])|alt=A table showing the number of nurses and caring professionals employed in hospitals as a head count, in full-time equivalents and as a ratio per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2024 for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the table are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Relative to population size, among the 15 EU countries for which recent data are available, the number of nurses and midwives (in full-time equivalents) employed in hospitals generally ranged from 240 per 100 000 inhabitants in Hungary to 644 per 100 000 inhabitants in Denmark, with Romania (80 per 100 000 inhabitants) well below this range. Data in full-time equivalents are available for 14 EU countries in relation to the number of health care assistants employed in hospitals. In 2024, there were fewer than 100 health care assistants in hospitals per 100 000 inhabitants in the Netherlands (which had the lowest number at 55 per 100 000 inhabitants), Belgium, Germany and Austria, while the majority of the remaining EU countries reported ratios between 107 and 255 health care assistants in hospitals per 100 000 inhabitants. Above this range, Malta and France reported, respectively, 374 and 342 health care assistants in full-time equivalents in hospitals per 100 000 inhabitants. ===Health graduates=== Table 3 focuses on graduates for the 2 most qualified occupations covered by this article, namely nurses and midwives. Among the EU countries, there were 143 000 nurses who graduated in 2024 – see Table 3 for more information concerning the data coverage for individual EU countries. When expressed relative to population size, there were 32 nursing graduates per 100 000 inhabitants in the EU in 2024. Relative to population size, the number of nurses graduating in 2024 peaked in Finland (81 per 100 000 inhabitants) and the Netherlands (65 per 100 000 inhabitants). The lowest ratios of nurses graduating per 100 000 inhabitants were recorded in Romania, Bulgaria (both 8 per 100 000 inhabitants), Cyprus (9 per 100 000 inhabitants) and Luxembourg (10 per 100 000 inhabitants). Between 2014 and 2024, there was a mixed development in the number of nurses graduating in EU countries (see Table 3 for more information concerning the data coverage): 12 out of the 25 countries for which data are available recorded increases. Bulgaria (note the break in series), the Netherlands, Croatia and Lithuania recorded particularly high growth rates, as their numbers of graduates were, respectively, 1.9, 1.8, 1.7 and 1.5 times as high in 2024 as in 2014. By contrast, the largest decline in the number of nursing professional graduates was recorded in Cyprus (down by approximately three quarters). [[Image:Graduates – nurses and midwives, 2014 and 2024_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Graduates – nurses and midwives, 2014 and 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4ded0a36-d160-4a17-966c-4cd502daab4e?lang=en hlth_rs_grd2])|alt=A table showing the number and ratio per hundred thousand inhabitants of nurses and midwife graduates. Data are shown for 2014 and 2024 for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the table are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, there were considerably fewer midwifery graduates than nursing graduates in the EU: approximately 6 900. When expressed per 100 000 inhabitants, the number of midwifery graduates in 2024 was highest in Belgium at 6.3 per 100 000 inhabitants, while the lowest ratio was 0.2 per 100 000 inhabitants in Romania. Between 2014 and 2024, there were 16 EU countries which recorded an increase in the number of midwifery graduates and 9 countries recorded a decrease; incomplete data for Cyprus and Slovenia. Leaving aside Luxembourg, which had 0 midwife graduates in 2014, the largest increases in relative terms were recorded in Austria, Portugal and Greece, where the number of graduates in 2024 was more than twice as high as in 2014. At the other end of the range, the biggest relative decreases in midwifery graduates between 2014 and 2024 were recorded in Germany, Croatia and Romania, all down by at least 30%. ===Workforce migration – nurses=== Cross-border migration of health workers is a long-standing and growing phenomenon within the EU and globally. Many healthcare staff within the EU may have been trained in a country different to where they work; this includes people who trained in 1 EU country and moved to work in another EU country as well as people who trained outside the EU and moved to an EU country. An analysis of the place of training of nurses is available for most EU countries (see Table 4 for more details); this analysis distinguishes domestically trained and foreign-trained nurses. Among the EU countries for which recent data are available, the largest numbers of foreign-trained nurses in 2024 were recorded in Germany (119 000), Ireland (41 000), Italy (23 000), Austria (15 000) and Belgium (11 000). Elsewhere, the number of foreign-trained nurses was below 5 000, with the lowest number recorded in Estonia (37). In 16 of the countries for which data are available, at least 95.0% of nurses in 2024 had been domestically trained, with this share peaking at 99.9% in Romania. Somewhat lower shares were recorded in Germany (88.6%) and Austria (86.3%), while the share in Ireland was clearly lower, at approximately half (46.0%). As well as information on the stock of foreign-trained nurses, data are also available for the annual inflow of foreign-trained nurses. In 2024, 32 500 foreign-trained nurses started working in Germany, while 4 600 started in Ireland and 1 500 in Spain. In each of the 15 other EU countries for which data are available, the number of foreign-trained nurses was below 1 000, with Latvia, Romania, Bulgaria, Estonia and Lithuania recording fewer than 20. The annual inflow of foreign-trained nurses in 2024 was equivalent to 6.1% of the whole stock of nurses in Ireland, which was a much higher ratio than in any other EU country. The second highest ratio was 3.1% in Germany, followed by 0.8% in Austria; the 13 other EU countries for which data are available recorded ratios of at most 0.4%. The annual inflow of foreign-trained nurses in 2024 was equivalent to 27.3% of the stock of foreign-trained nurses in Germany and 20.8% in Poland, which were much higher shares than in other EU countries. The next highest shares were 12.8% in Denmark, 12.2% in Czechia (2023 data) and 11.2% in Ireland, with shares below 10.0% in the 11 other EU countries for which data are available. [[Image:Migration of nurses, 2024_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 4: Migration of nurses, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/27946bfd-2f43-4fd0-bd80-3704f5bf51af?lang=en hlth_rs_wkmg2])|alt=A table showing the number of nurses and whether they were trained domestically or abroad as well as the annual inflow of nurses trained abroad. Data are shown for 2024 for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the table are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= Healthcare_personnel_statistics_-_nursing_and_caring_professionals_Health2026.xlsx|title=Healthcare personnel statistics – nursing and caring professionals: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''Key concepts''' Practising nurses, midwives and caring personnel provide services directly to patients. They include professional nurses and midwives, health care assistants and home-based personal care workers. Data on associate professional nurses (ISCO 08 code 3221) are not included (see below for the full list of relevant ISCO codes). Employment data cover the number of health care staff (head counts) and the number of people in full-time equivalents directly employed in hospitals (both general and specialised hospitals); self-employed people working in hospitals are also included, for example, those working with service contracts as health professionals. Data on graduates for any given year cover the number of students who have graduated in either nursing or midwifery, so they may become a professional or associate professional nurse or midwife; the data for associate professional nurses are not shown in this article. The data exclude those who have graduated in other fields of studies which do not provide a recognised foundation for the practice of nursing or midwifery. Within the EU, {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32005L0036:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2005/36/EC}} of the [[Glossary:European Parliament (EP)|European Parliament]] and of the [[Glossary:Council of the European Union|Council]] defines the training of nurses responsible for general care as comprising at least 3 years of study or 4 600 hours of theoretical and clinical training. Data on workforce migration cover the stock of domestically and foreign-trained nurses, as well as the annual inflow of foreign-trained nurses. Data on the stock of nurses is broken down into domestically trained and foreign-trained people; the latter also include people who are native-born but foreign-trained (by country of first qualification). Data on the annual inflow of nurses cover the nurses who have obtained a recognised qualification in nursing in another country and who in a given year are receiving a new authorisation to practice in the receiving country. '''Healthcare resources''' Statistics on healthcare resources (such as personnel and medical equipment) are documented in a background article on the [[Healthcare_non-expenditure_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of healthcare non-expenditure statistics]]. This provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis and the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. Common definitions have been agreed between [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], the [[Glossary:OECD|OECD]] and the [[Glossary:World Health Organization (WHO)|World Health Organization (WHO)]] with respect to the employment of various health care professionals. There are 3 main concepts which are used to present these data. Eurostat gives preference to the concept of ‘practising’ nurses, midwives and caring personnel: *‘practising’ – health care professionals providing services directly to patients *‘professionally active’ – ‘practising’ professionals plus health care professionals for whom their medical education is a prerequisite for the execution of their job *‘licensed’ – health care professionals who are registered and entitled to practise as health care professionals. Data on nurses, midwives and caring personnel are classified according to the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO); they are defined under ISCO 08 as codes 222, 322 and 532: *222 nursing and midwifery professionals **2221 nursing professionals **2222 midwifery professionals *322 nursing and midwifery associate professionals **3221 nursing associate professionals **3222 midwifery associate professionals *532 personal care workers in health services **5321 health care assistants **5322 home-based personal care workers **5329 personal care workers in health services not elsewhere classified. For country specific notes on these data collections, please refer to the annexes at the end of the national metadata reports accessible from links at the beginning of the {{Template:Esms|code=hlth_res_esms|title=European metadata report}}. In particular, note that: *data for Cyprus assume that all private sector nurses are practicing *data for personnel employed in hospitals in Lithuania are in full-time equivalents compiled relative to the number of contractual hours; some personnel may work 1.25 or 1.5 times the contractual hours and consequently the data in full-time equivalents may exceed data based on head counts *data for graduates for Poland count graduates at each level of ISCED *data for nurses for Portugal include nurses who hold a post/job for which a nursing education is not required. '''Symbols''' In tables, a colon ‘:’ is used to show where data are not available. Data in italics are estimates or provisional. ===Context=== There are concerns about a shortage of nursing and caring professionals in the EU. These may become exacerbated as the population continues to age and nurses and caring professionals move from employment into retirement or leave for other reasons. A consequence of future demographic developments is that the number of elderly people (aged 65 years or more) in the EU is forecast to increase by 31% between 2025 and 2050 ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/population-projections Eurostat baseline projections 2025]); during this period, the share of the elderly in the total population is projected to increase from 21.9% in 2025 to 29.1% by 2050. This ageing of the EU’s population is likely to result in considerable demands for a range of care services, as an increasing proportion of the population becomes frail and suffers from declining physical and mental health. European healthcare systems will therefore need to anticipate future skills requirements for health professionals – in particular, nurses and caring professionals – so these may be matched against the demands of an increasingly aged society, for example, a likely shift away from care in hospitals towards care in the home. On 7 September 2022, the European Commission proposed a [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?langId=en&catId=89&furtherNews=yes&newsId=10382#navItem-relatedDocuments European care strategy]. The Commission proposed actions to support EU countries in improving working conditions and work-life balance for carers and to ensure quality, affordable and accessible care services across the European Union. === Footnotes === ===Other articles=== '''Online publications''' *[[Health in the European Union - facts and figures|Health in the European Union – facts and figures]]
