title: ICT in enterprises and the environment
text:
EU statistics on ICT in enterprises and the environment. Data extracted in June 2026 Planned article update: June 2028 In 2025, 24.9% of EU enterprises used ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption. In 2025, 17.4% of EU enterprises used ICT systems or solutions to reduce the materials used or to enhance the use of recycled materials. In 2025, 28.9% of EU enterprises reported that they sell, return to a leasing enterprise, or donate their ICT equipment when it is no longer used. For decades, the adoption of digital technologies by enterprises has influenced not only their performance but also environmental aspects. As the [[Glossary:EU|EU]] has a plan to become the first climate-neutral continent, it is important that enterprises take steps to reduce their environmental impact. They can help to reduce their environmental footprint by considering environmental aspects when dealing with the digital transformation, namely when selecting, using or disposing of their [[Glossary:Information_and_communication_technology_(ICT)|ICT]] equipment and services. This article presents recent statistical data on some environmentally friendly practices that enterprises are implementing when taking decisions on their activities, among other things, to reduce their environmental impact. === Using ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption and/or material use === Digitalisation can speed up the transition towards a climate-neutral, circular and more resilient economy. Enterprises play an important role in this transition by implementing environmentally friendly practices, which have additional advantages (reducing costs for example). Figure 1 shows the share of enterprises with at least 10 employees or self-employed persons using ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption and/or material use (or enhance the use of recycled materials). According to data for 2025, 24.9% of EU enterprises used ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption. Adoption rates varied significantly across EU countries, ranging from 41.1% in Croatia to 10% in Bulgaria. Other countries with high adoption rates were Denmark (32.6%), France (31.2%), Belgium (31.1%) and Malta (30.6%). Conversely, as in Bulgaria, Latvia (13.9%) and Hungary (13.6%) fewer than 15% of enterprises implemented these measures. In 2025, 17.4% of EU enterprises used ICT systems or solutions to reduce material use or to enhance the use of recycled materials, which is fewer than 1 in 5 enterprises. The highest share of enterprises with such ICT systems or solutions was observed in Malta (28.8%), followed by Lithuania (25.8%), Belgium (25.6%) and Denmark (23.2%). At the other end of the scale, adoption was the lowest in Bulgaria and Austria (both 7.6%), Hungary (8.1%), Czechia (8.7%) and Slovakia (9.9%), where less than 10% of enterprises used such solutions (Figure 1). [[Image:Enterprises using ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption and or material use, 2025 (% of enterprises).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Enterprises using ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption and/or material use, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/242f6883-9313-4849-846f-a469fc38fa6b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-18T14:51:17Z (isoc_e_envs)]|alt=A line with markers chart showing the percentage of enterprises using ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption and/or material use. Data are shown as percentage of enterprises. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] With regard to the size of enterprises, Figure 2 shows that large enterprises are more likely to use ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption or material use compared to small and medium-sized enterprises. In 2025, nearly 3 in 5 large enterprises (58%) used ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption, compared with 36.4% of medium-sized enterprises and 21.8% of small enterprises. The disparity narrows slightly in the case of the use of ICT systems and solutions to reduce material use or enhance the use of recycled materials. Nearly half of large enterprises (46%) used such ICT systems or solutions, alongside over 1 in 4 medium-sized enterprises (26.7%) and fewer than 1 in 6 small enterprises (15%) (Figure 2). [[Image:Enterprises using ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption and or material use, by size class, EU, 2025 v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Enterprises using ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption and/or material use, by size class, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/242f6883-9313-4849-846f-a469fc38fa6b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-18T14:51:17Z (isoc_e_envs)]|alt=A horizontal bar chart showing the percentage of enterprises using ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption and/or material use, by size class. Data are shown as percentage of enterprises for the EU. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The use of ICT systems or solutions for reducing energy consumption or material use (including enhancing the use of recycled materials) varied across different economic sectors. In terms of reducing energy consumption, the adoption rates in 2025 ranged from 46.4% to 17.8%. The highest share of enterprises using such systems or solutions was observed in electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply, followed by manufacturing (30.2%) and information and communication (29.4%). The lowest adoption rates were recorded in administrative and supportive service activities (17.8%), the only sector where less than 20% of enterprises used such ICT systems or solutions (Figure 3). A similar pattern emerged for enterprises using ICT systems or solutions to reduce material use or to enhance recycled materials. The highest adoption rates were recorded in electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply (28.6%), manufacturing (25%) and water supply, sewerage, waste management and remediation activities (21.5%). On the other hand, administrative and support service activities (13.1%), the transportation and storage sector (13.8%) and accommodation and food service activities (13.8%) recorded the lowest adoption rate (Figure 3). [[Image:Enterprises using ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption and or material use, by economic activity, EU, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Enterprises using ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption and/or material use, by economic activity, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c0ed737b-c006-4999-bdb3-41f2d9c52739?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-18T14:58:20Z (isoc_e_envn2)]|alt=A horizontal bar chart showing the percentage of enterprises in the EU using ICT systems or solutions to reduce energy consumption and/or material use, by economic activity for the year 2025. Data are shown as percentage of enterprises for the EU. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Disposing of unused ICT equipment === Enterprises have different ways of disposing of unused ICT equipment (e.g. computers, monitors, mobile phones), some of which contribute to a more circular economy. Unused equipment may be disposed of through electronic waste collection/recycling (by the enterprise itself or through a retailer), retained in the enterprise (to be used as spare parts, for example, or to prevent sensitive information being disclosed), sold, returned to the leasing enterprise, or donated, to be re-used in another organisation (second life-cycle). As Figure 4 shows, 77% of EU enterprises with 10 or more employees and self-employed persons reported disposing of ICT equipment through electronic waste collection or recycling, and 49.3% kept unused ICT equipment in the enterprise, while 28.9% of enterprises sell, return to a leasing enterprise, or donate ICT equipment when it is no longer used. Concerning the size class of an enterprise and the way unused ICT equipment is disposed of, the most significant difference between large and small enterprises (30 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]]) was observed for enterprises that sell, return to a leasing enterprise, or donate ICT equipment when no longer used (Figure 4). [[Image:Enterprises disposing of ICT equipment when it is no longer used, by method of disposing and size class, EU, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Enterprises disposing of ICT equipment when it is no longer used, by method of disposing and size class, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c05c376b-ffe3-4652-a2c4-ba16e8a583c0?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-18T15:01:36Z (isoc_e_envs)]|alt=A vertical multi-bar chart showing the percentage of enterprises in the EU that dispose of ICT equipment when it is no longer used for the year 2025, by method of disposing and size class. Data are shown as percentage of enterprises. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2025, the share of enterprises reporting that they disposed of their ICT equipment through electronic waste collection/recycling when it was no longer used did not differ significantly across the different economic activities. The share ranged from 85.5% in the electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply sector to 71.9% in transportation and storage and 71.8% in accommodation and food service activities (Figure 5). As Figure 5 shows, a more pronounced difference emerged among enterprises that kept their ICT equipment in the enterprise when it is no longer used. Here the share varied significantly, from 39.3% in accommodation and food service activities to 60.7% in information and communication. For enterprises that sell, return to a leasing enterprise, or donate their ICT equipment when it is no longer used in the different economic activities, the highest shares were recorded in the information and communication sector (50.0%), followed by electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply activities (47.4%) and professional, scientific and technical activities (39.4%). Conversely, the lowest shares were recorded in water supply, sewerage, waste management and remediation activities (23.3%) and construction (23.9%) (Figure 5). [[Image:Enterprises disposing of ICT equipment when it is no longer used, by method of disposing and economic activity, EU, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Enterprises disposing of ICT equipment when it is no longer used, by method of disposing and economic activity, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e26b5855-edf9-4b6f-b34c-48cdd50cd39a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-18T15:04:56Z (isoc_e_envn2)]|alt=A horizontal bar chart showing the percentage of enterprises in the EU that are disposing of ICT equipment when it is no longer used in 2025 by method of disposing and economic activity . Data are shown as percentage of enterprises. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 6 shows a closer look at the cross-country comparison and highlights significant variation in how enterprises dispose of their ICT equipment when it is no longer used. In 2025, the share of the enterprises reporting that they disposed of their ICT equipment through electronic waste collection/recycling ranged from 90.9% in Finland to 44.6% in Bulgaria, while the share of enterprises that kept their ICT equipment in the enterprise ranged from 65.1% in Germany to 22.5% in Greece. The share of enterprises that sell, return to a leasing enterprise, or donate their ICT equipment when it is no longer used shows similar disparity. The share ranged from 46.4% to 17.6%. At the higher end of the scale was Croatia (46.4%), followed by the Netherlands (44.8%) and Finland (43%), while at the lower end of the scale, Greece (17.6%) and Bulgaria (19.7%) reported the fewest enterprises engaging in these practices (Figure 6). [[Image:Enterprises disposing of ICT equipment when it is no longer used, by method of disposing, 2025 (% of enterprises).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Enterprises disposing of ICT equipment when it is no longer used, by method of disposing, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e3e8a419-1ada-4bc6-ad61-9b729f4a1524?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-18T15:08:52Z (isoc_e_envs)]|alt=A vertical bar chart showing the percentage of enterprises in the EU that are disposing of ICT equipment when it is no longer used for the year 2025, by method of disposing. Data are shown as percentage of enterprises for the EU, the EU Member States, one EFTA country and one of the candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:2025 ICT and the environment - data and graphs v2.xlsx|ICT and the environment - data and graphs]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === '''Source:''' Data presented in this article are based on the results of the 2025 [[Glossary:EU_survey_on_ICT_usage_and_e-commerce_in_enterprises|EU survey on ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises]]. Statistics were obtained from surveys in enterprises conducted by national statistical authorities in the first months of 2025. Source data shown as ':' refer to data that are unavailable, unreliable, confidential or not applicable. Unreliable data are included in the calculation of European aggregates. Data presented in this article may differ from the data in the database on account of updates made after the data extractions used for this article. Data in the database are organised according to the survey year. '''Sample:''' In 2025, 157 000 of the 1.53 million enterprises in the EU were surveyed. Of the 1.53 million enterprises, approximately 83% were small enterprises (with 10-49 employees or self-employed persons), 14% medium-sized (50-249 employees or self-employed persons) and 3% large enterprises (250 or more employees or self-employed persons). '''Main concepts:''' The observation statistical unit is the enterprise, as defined in the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31993R0696:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EEC) No 696/1993}} of 15 March 1993. The survey covered enterprises with at least 10 employees or self-employed persons. Economic activities correspond to the [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE Revision 2]] classification . The sectors covered are manufacturing, electricity, gas and steam, water supply, construction, wholesale and retail trade, repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles, transportation and storage, accommodation and food service activities, information and communication, real estate, professional, scientific and technical activities, administrative and support activities and repair of computers and communication equipment. === Context === Digital transformation can have a positive impact on the environment and on environmental sustainability by applying environmentally friendly procedures. Digital transformation is high on the European policy agenda, with making [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/europe-fit-digital-age_en Europe fit for the digital age] and empowering its citizens and businesses with a new generation of technologies being one of the main political priorities of the European Commission for the coming years. In 2021, the [https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/digital-compass Digital Compass for the EU's Digital Decade] (COM(2021)118 final), set the EU’s digital targets for 2030, evolving around four cardinal points: skills, digital transformation of businesses, secure and sustainable digital infrastructures, and digitalisation of public services. The relevant statistics are related to the Commission priority [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en A European Green Deal], which is the roadmap for making the EU's economy sustainable. The policy priority is for the moment to focus on three dimensions of the positive impact of ICT in the environment (green ICT, ICT for sustainability): enterprises' environmentally friendly procedures, home office and virtual meetings. === Other Articles === *[[Digital economy and society statistics - enterprises]] *[[Use of artificial intelligence in enterprises]] *[[Use of Internet of title: ICT security in enterprises
text:
Recent statistical data are provided on information and communication technologies (ICT) security in the European Union (EU). Data from December 2024 Planned article update: December 2026 In 2024, 92.76% of EU enterprises used at least one ICT security measure. In 2023, 21.54% of enterprises in the EU suffered various consequences due to ICT related security incidents. [[Image:ICT security in enterprises, EU, 2024 (% of enterprises).png |thumb|centre|500px|ICT security in enterprises, EU, 2024 (% of enterprises)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=isoc_cisce_ra}} and {{Stable link|title=|code= isoc_cisce_ic}}|alt= a vertical bar chart showing ICT security in enterprises in the EU in the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article analyses recent statistical data on [[Glossary:Information and communication technology (ICT)|information and communication technologies (ICT)]] security in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Results were obtained through a specific set of questions in the 2024 questionnaire of the [[Glossary:EU survey on ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises|EU survey on ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises]]. In this context, ICT security refers to relevant incidents as well as measures, controls and procedures applied by [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]] in order to ensure integrity, confidentiality and availability of their data and ICT systems. ===ICT security in EU enterprises=== [[Image: ICT security in enterprises, 2024 (% of enterprises).png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: ICT security in enterprises, 2024 (% of enterprises)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=isoc_cisce_ra}} and {{Stable link|title=|code= isoc_cisce_ic}}|alt=a table showing ICT security in enterprises in the year 2024, in the EU, EU countries, Norway and some candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, 92.76% of EU enterprises with 10 or more employees or self-employed persons used at least one measure in order to ensure integrity, availability and confidentiality of data and ICT systems. More than 1 in 3 enterprises (35.50%) reported having documents putting in place measures, practices or procedures on ICT security. In a fifth of enterprises (21.82%) these documents were defined or reviewed in the last 12 months. 59.97% of EU enterprises made their staff aware of their obligations in ICT security related issues. Finally, 1 in 5 enterprises (21.54%) experienced consequences due to ICT related security incidents in 2023 (Figure 1). [[Image: ICT security in enterprises, EU, 2024 (% of enterprises).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: ICT security in enterprises, EU, 2024 (% of enterprises)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=isoc_cisce_ra}} and {{Stable link|title=|code= isoc_cisce_ic}}|alt=a vertical bar chart showing ICT security in enterprises in the EU in the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === ICT security measures === In 2024, 92.76% of EU enterprises used at least one of the ICT security measures presented in Figure 2. The most common measure used was the strong password authentication (83.69%), followed by data backup to a separate location or cloud (79.23%) and network access control (65.43%). Less than half of enterprises reported using Virtual Private Networks (VPN) (49.64%) or maintaining log files for analysis after security incidents (45.16%). Enterprises less frequently used a combination of 2 or more authentication mechanisms (39.84%), encryption techniques for data, documents or e-mails (39.72%), ICT security tests (34.64%), ICT risk assessments (34.10%), or authentication via biometric methods (18.27%) (Figure 2). [[Image: ICT security measures used by enterprises, EU, 2024 (% of enterprises).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: ICT security measures used by enterprises, EU, 2024
(% of enterprises)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=isoc_cisce_ra}}|alt= a horizontal bar chart showing ICT security measures used by enterprises in the EU in the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 3 provides a closer look at the most and least used ICT security measures according to the enterprise size. The ICT security measure ''strong password authentication'' was used by almost all large enterprises (96.78%), by 90.66% of medium-sized ones and more than 8 in 10 small enterprises (82.03%). Similar figures were reported for the second most popular ICT security measure – the ''data backup to a separate location'', which was used by 94.95% of the large enterprises, 88.48% of the medium size enterprises and 77.09% of small enterprises. Larger differences related to the enterprise size were observed in the share of enterprises using the less common ICT security measures. The ''ICT risk assessment'' was used by 75.62% of large enterprises, while the share of small enterprises using this particular measure was more than 2 times less (29.35%). Regardless of the enterprise size, the ''authentication via biometric methods'' was the least used ICT security measure, although the share of large enterprises using this measure (38.55%) was significantly higher than the figure recorded for small enterprises (16.44%). [[Image: Most and least used ICT security measures, by size class, EU, 2024 (% of enterprises).png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 3: Most and least used ICT security measures, by size class, EU, 2024
(% of enterprises)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=isoc_cisce_ra}}|alt= a vertical bar chart with four bars showing the most and least used ICT security measures, by size of the enterprise, in the EU in the year 2024, the bars show the different sizes of enterprises for the different ICT security measures. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Documents on measures, practices or procedures on ICT security === In 2024, 35.50% of EU enterprises had documents which put in place measures, practices or procedures on ICT security. Shares higher than 50% were registered in Finland (59.41%), Denmark (59.11%) and Portugal (54.29%). On the other hand, less than 20% of the enterprises had documents on measures, practices or procedures on ICT security in Greece (18.28%), Hungary (13.75%) and Bulgaria (13.67%) (Figure 4). [[Image: Enterprises with documents on measures, practices or procedures on ICT security, 2024 (% of enterprises).png |thumb|centre|700px| Figure 4: Enterprises with documents on measures, practices or procedures on ICT security, 2024
(% of enterprises)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=isoc_cisce_ra}}|alt=a vertical bar chart showing enterprises with documents on measures, practices or procedures on ICT security in the year 2024, in the EU, EU countries, Norway and some candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] More than one-fifth of the enterprises in the EU (21.82%) have defined or reviewed their documents on measures, practices or procedures on ICT security during the last 12 months. For 7.58% this was the case between 12 and 24 months ago and for another 4.58% more than 24 months ago. More than half of large enterprises (57.87%) reported having defined or reviewed their documents on ICT security within the last 12 months, while for medium-sized and small enterprises this share was significantly lower with 35.72% and 17.98% respectively (Figure 5). [[Image: Enterprises having defined or reviewed their document(s) on measures, practices or procedures on ICT security, by size class, EU, 2024 (% of enterprises).png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 5: Enterprises having defined or reviewed their document(s) on measures, practices or procedures on ICT security, by size class, EU, 2024
(% of enterprises)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=isoc_cisce_ra}}|alt= a vertical bar chart with four bars showing enterprises having defined or reviewed their document(s) on measures, practices or procedures on ICT security, by size in the EU in the year 2024, the bars show the different sizes of enterprises for the 3 different time periods. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Enterprises make persons employed aware of their obligations in ICT security related issues=== In 2024, almost 3 out of 5 EU enterprises (59.97%) made their employees aware of their obligations in ICT security related issues. Voluntary training or internally available information for instance on the intranet was the most common form used (42.59% of enterprises), followed by contracts such as employment contracts (34.25%) and by compulsory training courses or viewing compulsory material (24.51%). The share of enterprises making persons employed aware of their obligations in ICT security by any of the measures presented in Figure 6, was particularly high for large (92.34%) and medium-sized enterprises (76.45%). Nevertheless, also more than half of small enterprises (55.99%) reported making persons employed aware of their obligations in ICT security (Figure 6). [[Image: Enterprises making persons employed aware of their obligations in ICT security related issues, by size class, EU, 2024 (% of enterprises).png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 6: Enterprises making persons employed aware of their obligations in ICT security related issues, by size class, EU, 2024
(% of enterprises)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=isoc_cisce_ra}}|alt=a vertical bar chart with four bars showing enterprises making persons employed aware of their obligations in ICT security related issues, by size in the EU in the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among all EU countries, the percentage of enterprises making persons employed aware of their obligation in ICT security ranged from 77.47% in Czechia, followed by Finland (74.81%), Denmark (70.07%) and Ireland (69.16%) to 38.96% in Croatia and 31.68% in Greece. In 21 EU countries, the share of enterprises, which reported making persons employed aware of their obligations in ICT security related issues was higher than 50% (Figure 7). [[Image:Enterprises making persons employed aware of their obligations in ICT security related issues, 2024 (% of enterprises).png |thumb|centre|700px| Figure 7: Enterprises making persons employed aware of their obligations in ICT security related issues, 2024
(% of enterprises)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=isoc_cisce_ra}}|alt= a vertical bar chart showing enterprises making persons employed aware of their obligations in ICT security related issues by any measure in the year 2024 in the EU, EU countries, Norway and some candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Consequences of ICT related security incidents === In 2023, more than 1 in 5 EU enterprises (21.54%) experienced ICT related security incidents leading to consequences such as the unavailability of ICT services, destruction or corruption of data or disclosure of confidential data (Figure 1). The ICT security incidents can be caused by malicious attacks from outside or inside the enterprise, or by non-malicious causes, such as hardware or software failures or unintentional action by own employees. In 2023, enterprises more often reported damages to enterprises' ICT services or data being caused by non-malicious incidents. The most commonly reported consequence caused by ICT security incidents was the unavailability of ICT services due to hardware or software failures (17.97% of enterprises). In comparison, unavailability of ICT services due to attack from outside (e.g. ransomware attacks, Denial of Service attacks) was reported by 3.43% of enterprises. Destruction or corruption of data resulting from hardware or software failure was reported by 3.87% of enterprises, while infection with malicious software or unauthorised intrusion led to destruction or corruption of data in 1.89% of enterprises. Least frequently, enterprises reported disclosure of confidential data due to intrusion, pharming or phishing attack or intentional actions of own employees (1.57%) or due to unintentional actions of own employees (1.15%) (Figure 8). [[Image: Enterprises experienced ICT related security incidents leading to consequences, EU, 2023 (% of enterprises).png |thumb|centre|700px| Figure 8: Enterprises experienced ICT related security incidents leading to consequences, EU, 2023 (% of enterprises)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=isoc_cisce_ic}}|alt= a vertical bar chart showing enterprises experienced ICT related security incidents leading to consequences in the EU in the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Considering the economic activity breakdown, during 2023, more than one-fourth of the enterprises in information and communication, professional, scientific and technical activities, electricity, gas, steam, air conditioning and water supply and real estate activities experienced ICT security incidents leading to unavailability of ICT services, destruction or corruption of data or disclosure of confidential data. In construction and transport and storage this was the case for less than 1 in 5 enterprises (Figure 9). [[Image:Enterprises experienced ICT related security incidents leading to consequences, by economic activity, EU, 2023 (% of enterprises).png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 9: Enterprises experienced ICT related security incidents leading to consequences, by economic activity, EU, 2023
(% of enterprises)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=isoc_cisce_icn2}}|alt=a horizontal bar chart showing enterprises experienced ICT related security incidents leading to consequences in the EU in the year 2023, the bars show all the different economic activities. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:2024 ENT ICT security tables and graphs.xlsx|ICT security statistics - graphs and tables]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources=== '''Source: ''' Data presented in this article are based on the results of the 2024 EU survey on 'ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises'. Statistics were obtained from surveys in enterprises conducted by National Statistical Authorities in the first months of 2024. '''Sample:''' In 2024, some 157 000 enterprises, with 10 or more employees or self-employed persons, out of 1.54 million in EU were surveyed. Out of these 1.54 million enterprises, approximately 83% were small enterprises (with 10-49 employees or self-employed persons), 14% medium (50-249 employees) and 3% large enterprises (250 or more employees). '''Main concepts:''' The observation statistical unit is the enterprise, as defined in the [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:31993R0696:EN:NOT Regulation 696/1993] of 15 March 1993. The survey covered enterprises with at least 10 persons employed. Economic activities correspond to the classification [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] Revision 2. The sectors covered are manufacturing, electricity, gas and steam, water supply, construction, wholesale and retail trades, repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles, transportation and storage, accommodation and food service activities, information and communication, real estate, professional, scientific and technical activities, administrative and support activities and repair of computers and communication equipment. === Context=== In the context of the survey on enterprises, ICT security refers prominently to measures, controls and procedures applied by enterprises in order to ensure integrity, confidentiality and availability of data and ICT systems. The relevant statistics would be used in the context of the [https://ec.europa.eu/digital-single-market/en/cyber-security European Strategy for Cyber Security] that provides the overall strategic framework for the EU initiatives on cybersecurity and cybercrime. Trust and security are an important element of [https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/priorities-2019-2024/europe-fit-digital-age_en Europe fit for digital age]. From the legislative point of view, on 7th December 2015, the European Parliament and the Council reached an agreement on the Commission's proposed measures to increase online security in the EU. The [https://ec.europa.eu/digital-single-market/en/network-and-information-security-nis-directive Network and Information Security (NIS) Directive] is the first piece of European legislation on cybersecurity that was adopted by the European Parliament on 6 July 2016 and entered into force in August 2016. NIS includes common provisions across the Union, addressing national capabilities and preparedness, EU-level cooperation, take up of risk management practices and an information sharing culture in NIS and notification of IT incidents. Moreover, on 13th September 2017 the Commission adopted a cybersecurity package. The [https://ec.europa.eu/digital-single-market/en/cyber-security Cybersecurity Act], which has now entered into force, lies at the core of the package. ===Other articles=== *[[Digital economy and title: ICT education - a statistical overview
text:
EU statistics detailing developments within the information and communication technology (ICT) sector in relation to persons with an ICT education, with analyses by sex, educational attainment and age. Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: May 2027 In the EU, more than 9 out of 10 ICT-educated people are employed. In 2025, women accounted for 16.6% of the total number of employed people in the EU with an ICT education, up slightly by 0.6 percentage points from 2016. In 2025, 74.8% of those employed in the EU with an ICT education had attained a tertiary level of education, representing an annual average increase of 5.2% since 2016. This article provides an overview of recent developments in relation to digital skills within the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. More specifically, it presents a range of statistics that describe the composition of the EU [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|labour force]] in possession of an [[Glossary:Information and communication technology (ICT)|information and communication technology (ICT)]] education. This is defined as those having achieved formal qualifications at least at upper secondary level within the fields of computer use, computer science, database and network design and administration, or software and applications development and analysis. Many countries now regard understanding ICT and mastering the basic skills and concepts of ICT as part of core education, alongside reading, writing and numeracy, while prosperous countries, businesses and individuals are often characterised by developing advanced ICT skills as a key factor of their success. Digitalisation and automation have transformed society and the economy with an ever-deepening impact on everyday life. With the increased application of digital technologies into a broad range of economic sectors such as manufacturing, energy, retail, transport, finance, education and healthcare, as well as the ICT sector itself, there has been rapid growth in the demand for [[ICT_specialists_in_employment|ICT specialists]]. This had a profound impact on the skillset that are sought by employers across the EU, while policymakers have become increasingly concerned by digital skills shortages, which may result in less innovation, lower levels of productivity or slower overall economic growth. ===General perspectives about the labour force for persons with an ICT education === The [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU]] labour force is composed of people who are in employment and those who are unemployed. In 2016, the EU labour force (or the total number of economically active people) that were in possession of an ICT education numbered over 2.5 million people; by 2025, this number rose to 3.6 million (see Figure 1). Of these, 3.3 million people aged 15-74 years in the EU were employed and in possession of an ICT education in 2025. In contrast, there were 269 700 people with an ICT education who were unemployed. [[Image:Employed and unemployed persons with an ICT education, EU, 2016-2025 (in thousand persons)V2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Employed and unemployed persons with an ICT education, EU, 2016-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3b870fda-bea7-43f3-8d84-04fae7a121b7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-21T15:18:10Z (isoc_ski_itemp)]|alt= Stacked area chart showing developments in thousands of persons with an ICT education in the EU. Two stacks represent employed and unemployed persons over the years 2016 to 2025.]] During the period 2016-2025, the proportion of people with an ICT education who were unemployed decreased from 8.8% in 2016 to 7.5% in 2025 with the lowest point of 5.9% in 2022. In more recent years, the share has increased, while still remaining below its 2016 level. In 2025, it rose by 1.0 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] compared with the previous year. Over the same period, the labour market for people with an ICT education consistently expanded, with 2 peaks in 2018 and in 2022. The first peak in 2018 saw an increase of 6.6% in the number of [[Glossary:Employed person - LFS|employed people]] with an ICT education compared with the previous year. In the following years, growth slowed, with rates ranging from 3.1% to 4.1%. However, in 2022, the growth rate picked up again, reaching 7.1% compared with 2021. In the subsequent years, the active population with an ICT education continued to grow, but at a slower pace. In 2025, it increased by 5.1% compared with 2024. [[Image:Distribution_of_employed_persons_with_an_ICT_education_by_sex,_educational_attainment_level_and_age,_2016_and_2025v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Distribution of employed persons with an ICT education by sex, educational attainment level and age, 2016 and 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/isoc_ski_itsex__custom_21560071/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=7af6b49a-a809-4696-b2e9-1a648869dc3e&c=1779376495000 (isoc_ski_itsex)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/isoc_ski_itedu__custom_21560118/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=fb72526f-bbfa-4867-a656-ec9ad0ff8123&c=1779376599000 (isoc_ski_itedu)] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/isoc_ski_itage__custom_21560134/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=3b870fda-bea7-43f3-8d84-04fae7a121b7&c=1779376690000 (isoc_ski_itage)]|alt= Table showing percentage distribution of employed persons with an ICT education by sex, educational attainment level and age in the EU, individual EU Member States, Iceland, Norway, Switzerland, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia and Türkiye for the years 2016 and 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''While employment rates among people with an ICT education remained stable at EU level, considerable differences were observed across countries''''' While there was an overall increase between 2016 and 2025 in the size of the EU labour force with an ICT educational background, there were various patterns of development across EU countries. In 2025, 92.5% of people in the labour force with an ICT education were employed in the EU. A majority of countries (17) displayed equal or higher values, the highest rates being observed in Bulgaria and Czechia (both 97.9%), followed by Lithuania, Malta, Croatia and Slovakia (all above 96%). By comparison, the highest shares of people with an ICT education who were unemployed in 2025 were recorded in Finland (12.0%), Italy (11.8%) and France (10.9%). [[Image: Share of the labour force with an ICT education by labour status, 2025_(in %).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Share of the labour force with an ICT education by labour status, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3b870fda-bea7-43f3-8d84-04fae7a121b7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-21T15:18:10Z (isoc_ski_itemp)]|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage share of the labour force with an ICT education by labour status in the EU, individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Norway, Serbia and North Macedonia. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has two stacks representing employed and unemployed for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] A comparison between 2016 and 2025, based on the share of the labour force with an ICT education who were in employment, reveals there was little overall change at EU level. In 2016, 91.2% of the EU labour force with an ICT education were employed, while nine years later this share was 1.3 pp higher, at 92.5% in 2025. Between 2016 and 2025, the share of people in the labour force with an ICT education who were employed rose by 20.3 pp in Greece (to 89.9%), by 13.4 pp in Croatia (to 96.4% ), by 10.7 pp in Slovenia (to 95.1%), and by 10.3 pp in Portugal (to 92.4%) – see Figure 3. By comparison, reductions were recorded in France, where the share of those employed fell by 6.2 pp (to 89.1%), in Estonia (down 5.9 pp, to 90.2%), in Latvia (down 4.8 pp, to 89.8%), and in Sweden (down 4.7 pp, to 89.4%), among others. Among the non-EU countries for which data are available, the most notable increases between 2016 and 2025 were observed in North Macedonia (up 12.8 pp) and Serbia (up 6.7 pp). [[Image: Share of persons with an ICT education who are employed in the labour force, 2016 and 2025_(in %).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Share of persons with an ICT education who are employed in the labour force, 2016 and 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3b870fda-bea7-43f3-8d84-04fae7a121b7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-21T15:18:10Z (isoc_ski_itemp)]|alt= Scatter chart showing percentage share of employed persons in the labour force with an ICT education in the EU, individual EU Member States, Norway, Switzerland, Iceland, Serbia, North Macedonia, Türkiye and Montenegro. Each country has two scatter plots representing the years 2016 and 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Employed people with an ICT education by sex=== '''''Men accounted for more than four-fifths (80%) of the total number of employed people with an ICT education in the EU ''''' In 2025, men accounted for an 83.4% share of the 3.3 million people in the EU who were employed and had an ICT education (see Figure 4), while women accounted for the remaining 16.6%. This gender gap was observed in all EU countries. The highest shares of men among employed people with an ICT education were recorded in Czechia (92.9%), followed by Slovenia and Latvia (89.1% and 89.0%, respectively). In the remaining EU countries, the share of men ranged between approximately 70.0% and 90.0%, with the lowest share observed in Denmark (70.0%). Women accounted for more than one-quarter (25%) of the employed people with an ICT education in Croatia, Bulgaria, Romania, Sweden, and Denmark, where the highest share (30.0%) was recorded. [[Image: Share of employed persons with an ICT education by sex, 2025_(in %).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Share of employed persons with an ICT education by sex, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/isoc_ski_itsex__custom_21560071/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=7af6b49a-a809-4696-b2e9-1a648869dc3e&c=1779376495000 (isoc_ski_itsex)]|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage employed persons with an ICT education by sex in the EU, individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Norway, Serbia and North Macedonia. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has two stacks representing men and women for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Between 2016 and 2025, the number of employed women with an ICT education in the EU increased. On average, this number rose by 5.1% per annum during the period, while the number of men who were employed and had an ICT education increased by an average of 4.5% per annum (see Figure 5). These developments for the EU confirm the fact that between 2016 and 2025, the number of employed people with an ICT education increased on average for both men and women in 18 out of the 22 EU countries for which data are complete. Among the remaining countries, two patterns can be observed. In Cyprus, Greece and Finland, the number of employed women decreased, while the number of employed men and the total number of employed people with an ICT education increased. A different pattern was observed in Hungary, where the number of employed women increased, while both the number of employed men and the total number of employed people with an ICT education decreased. Over the same period, the largest average annual increases in the number of employed women with an ICT education were recorded in Croatia, Ireland and Austria, with respectively 24.6%, 17.8% and 13.5% per annum. Among non-EU countries with available data, Serbia observed an increase in the number of employed women with an ICT educational background of 6.3% over the period followed by Norway and North Macedonia (5.0% and 4.3%, respectively). By contrast, Switzerland displayed an overall decrease (-2.2%) in the number of employed people in possession of an ICT education for both men (-1.7%) and women (-5.7%). [[Image: Average annual rate of change for the number of employed persons with an ICT education by sex, 2016 - 2025_(in %).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Average annual rate of change for the number of employed persons with an ICT education by sex, 2016-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/isoc_ski_itsex__custom_21560071/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=7af6b49a-a809-4696-b2e9-1a648869dc3e&c=1779376495000 (isoc_ski_itsex)]|alt= Scatter chart showing percentage average annual rate of change for the number of persons employed with an ICT education by sex in the EU, individual EU Member States, Norway, Switzerland, North Macedonia and Serbia. Each country has two scatter plots representing men and women from the year 2016 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Employed people with an ICT education by level of educational attainment=== '''''More tertiary graduates in ICT employed over time''''' In 2025, more than 7 out of 10 (74.8%) employed people in the EU with an ICT education had a [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|tertiary level]] of educational attainment (see Figure 6). This was 3.3 pp higher than in 2016, when the corresponding share was 71.5%. There were, however, considerable differences between the EU countries with regard to levels of educational attainment. In 2025, more than 9 out of 10 employed persons with an ICT education in Denmark (97.7%), France (96.6%), Cyprus (96.4%), Ireland (92.3%), Bulgaria (91.1%) and Croatia (90.9%), had completed a tertiary level of education. By comparison, a majority of those employed with an ICT education in Portugal (58.8%) and Italy (69.2%) did not have a tertiary level of education. Among most EFTA and candidate countries with available data – Norway, Switzerland, Serbia– higher or comparable shares of employed people with a tertiary level of education in ICT were recorded compared with the EU average. North Macedonia also showed a higher share (67.7%), although lower than in the other countries. [[Image: Share of employed persons with an ICT education by educational attainment level, 2025_(in %).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Share of employed persons with an ICT education by educational attainment level, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/isoc_ski_itedu__custom_21560118/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=fb72526f-bbfa-4867-a656-ec9ad0ff8123&c=1779376599000 (isoc_ski_itedu)]|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage share of employed persons with an ICT education by educational attainment level the EU, individual EU Member States, Norway, Switzerland, Serbia and North Macedonia. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has two stacks representing non-tertiary education and tertiary education for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Between 2016 and 2025, the number of employed people in the EU with an ICT education at tertiary level increased, on average, by 5.2% per annum. The corresponding rate of change for employed people with an upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary level of educational attainment was lower, at 3.0% per annum (see Figure 7). The highest average annual growth rates for the number of employed people with an ICT education at tertiary level were recorded in Ireland (21.3% per annum), Luxembourg (20.0% per annum), Portugal (14.2% per annum) and Croatia (11.5% per annum). Hungary (-1.2% per annum) was the only EU country to report an overall decline in the number of employed people with an ICT education during the period 2016-2025. Similarly, there were some countries where the number of employed people with a level below tertiary education decreased. Most notably in Croatia, where it did so by 14.4% per annum, but also in Finland (-2.9% per annum), Hungary (-1.8% per annum) and Romania (-0.1% per annum). By contrast, in Greece, the share that declined was the number of people with tertiary education, by 0.8% per annum. Among candidate and EFTA countries with available data over the period, Norway and North Macedonia recorded higher growth rates in the number of employed people with an ICT education than the EU average (6.4% and 5.8% per annum, respectively). Serbia also experienced an increase, although more moderate (4.5% per annum). By contrast, Switzerland recorded a decline (-2.2% per annum), driven by the decrease in employment for people in possession of a tertiary level of educational attainment (-3.2% per annum over the period). [[Image: Average annual rate of change for the number of employed persons with an ICT education by educational attainment level, 2016-2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Average annual rate of change for the number of employed persons with an ICT education by educational attainment level, 2016-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/isoc_ski_itedu__custom_21560118/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=fb72526f-bbfa-4867-a656-ec9ad0ff8123&c=1779376599000 (isoc_ski_itedu)]|alt= Scatter chart showing percentage average annual rate of change for the number of employed persons with an ICT education by educational attainment level in the EU, individual EU Member States, Norway, Switzerland, North Macedonia and Serbia. Each country has two scatter plots representing non-tertiary education and tertiary education from the year 2016 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Employed people with an ICT education by age=== ''''' More than two-thirds (66.67%) of the total number of employed people in the EU with an ICT education were aged 15-34 years''''' In 2024, slightly more than 2 out of every 3 (68.2%) employed people in the EU with an ICT education were aged 15-34 years. Moreover, young people in this age group accounted for the majority of employed people in possession of an ICT education in all the EU countries. The share of young people in the total number of employed people with an ICT education in 2025 was relatively low in Finland (58.7%) and Ireland (51.6%). By comparison, this young group aged 15-34 years accounted for more than three-quarters of the total number of employed people with an ICT education in Italy (79.6%), Latvia (76.8%), Poland (76.8%) and Slovenia (75.3%). In addition to these, 10 other countries – Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Czechia, Malta, Hungary, Greece, France, the Netherlands and Belgium – also recorded shares of young people employed with ICT education above or equal to the EU average. [[Image: Share of employed persons with an ICT education by age, 2025_(in %).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Share of employed persons with an ICT education by age, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=isoc_ski_itage}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage share of employed persons with an ICT education by age in the EU, individual EU Member States, Norway, Switzerland, North Macedonia and Serbia. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has two stacks representing 15 to 34 years and 35 to 74 years for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Between 2016 and 2025, both age groups showed a similar average annual increase in the number of employed people with ICT education, with growth rates of 4.8% per annum for people aged 15-34 years and 4.1% per annum for people aged 35-74 years. In absolute terms, over the same period, the number of young employed people with an ICT education increased by about 717 300, while the number of older employed people rose only by 294 600. This was accompanied by an increase in the share of young people aged 15-34 years in the total number of employed people with an ICT education in the EU from 67.0% to 68.2%. At country level, the highest growth rates for young ICT-educated people were observed for Ireland (with 18.8% per annum on average) followed by Luxembourg and Portugal. In most EU countries (23) with available data for both age groups, the number of employed people with an ICT educational background increased in parallel across the 2 age categories. However, Greece recorded a decline in the number of people employed with ICT education belonging to the younger age group (-1.0% per annum); and Finland saw this decline in the older age group (2.6% per annum). In Hungary, a general decrease was observed across both age groups. Among the non-EU countries with available data, developments were mixed. In Norway, a slight decline was experienced in the older age group, while in Switzerland, employment of people with an ICT education decreased across both age groups. By contrast, North Macedonia and Serbia recorded increases across both age groups, with a more notable rise among older people in both cases. [[Image: Average annual rate of change for the number of employed persons with an ICT education by age, 2016-2025_(in %).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: Average annual rate of change for the number of employed persons with an ICT education by age, 2016-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/isoc_ski_itage__custom_21560134/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=3b870fda-bea7-43f3-8d84-04fae7a121b7&c=1779376690000 (isoc_ski_itage)]|alt= Scatter chart showing percentage average annual rate of change for the number of employed persons with an ICT education by age in the EU, individual EU Member States, Norway, Switzerland, North Macedonia and Serbia. Each country has two scatter plots representing 15 to 34 years and 35 to 74 years from the year 2016 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=ICT_Education_ICT2026v2.xlsx|title=Persons with an ICT education: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data used in this article are derived from the EU [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|Labour Force Survey (LFS)]]. The information presented is based on microdata from the LFS and covers the population aged 15-74 years in order to be aligned with a range of other indicators relating to digital skills which are collected as part of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/digital-economy-and-society/information-data EU survey on the use of ICT in households and by individuals]. Within the LFS, the labour force — or economically active population — is defined as the population employed or unemployed. It, therefore, excludes people who are economically inactive, such as students, people choosing not to work, and the retired. Employment covers people aged 15-74 years living in private households, who during the reference week, worked for at least 1 hour, for pay, profit or family gain, or were not at work but had a job or business from which they were temporarily absent, for example because of illness, holidays, industrial dispute or education and training. As such, the total number of employed people includes employees, self-employed people and family workers. The collection of statistics on employed people with an ICT education is carried out across the whole economy and no information is collected on the principal economic activity in which each person works. Likewise, the data collection exercise does not provide information in relation to the occupations/tasks that are carried out. In other words, it is possible that some employed people with an ICT education made little or no use of their studies in their work. Unemployed people are defined by Eurostat, according to the guidelines of the International Labour Organisation, as people aged 15 to 74 years without work during the reference week who are available to start work within the next 2 weeks and who have actively sought employment at some time during the last 4 weeks. ICT education is defined in terms of the International Standard Classification of Education fields of education (ISCED-F 2013) and covers computer use, database and network design and administration, software and applications development and analysis, inter-disciplinary programmes and qualifications. The following codes identifying ICT education background are: 061 "Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs)"; 068 "Inter-disciplinary programmes and qualifications involving Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs)". Indeed, ISCED-F 2013 further clarifies that "Inter-disciplinary or broad programmes and qualifications are those which combine several detailed fields of education and training where no single detailed field dominates. Many inter-disciplinary programmes and qualifications cover several narrow or even broad fields. In this classification, the 'leading subject rule' is used to determine the broad field into which the inter-disciplinary study should be classified. That is, the leading subject or subjects determines the (broad) field." The introduction of ISCED-F 2013 together with the implementation of IESS regulation in 2021 (for more details consult the link to legislation) have impacted ICT education data series. As an exact transcoding was not possible for all variables and all past years, comparable times series are now only available from 2016 onwards. Levels of education refer to the educational attainment level of a person, in other words, to the highest level of education successfully completed. The levels are defined in terms of the ISCED 2011 classification, with tertiary education comprising ISCED levels 5-8 and non-tertiary education comprising ISCED levels 3 and 4 (upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education). In most of the countries, diplomas in the field of ICT are not delivered in lower secondary education levels (ISCED levels 1 and 2). For data on educational attainment based on the EU-LFS, ISCED 2011 is applied. Data is broken down into 2 educational attainment level groups, (1) upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education (ISCED levels 3 and 4) and (2) tertiary education (ISCED levels 5 to 8). Data introduce an age filter for the variable that describes the field of education: the field of education is reported only for respondents who completed their highest level of educational attainment either before they reached 34 years of age or within the 15 years preceding the survey year. While this change has a marginal effect on most ICT education data, it does affect the age breakdown in the specific dataset on employed people with an ICT education by age (isoc_ski_itage). ===Context=== Digitalisation and automation can generate new business opportunities through the development of new production processes, products and markets. This may drive the demand for new skills in the workplace, leading to changes in education systems which may have to adapt to technological changes in order to provide students with up-to-date training and education that meets the requirements of prospective employers. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the impact of digitalisation on education and training was much more limited. The pandemic demonstrated that having an education and training system that is fit for the digital age, is essential. Many people have since needed to acquire new skills, change sectors, or upskill to maintain employment in a rapidly evolving environment. The EUs digital ambitions for 2030 are translated into specific targets and milestones, delineated by the https://commission.europa.eu/system/files/2021-09/communication-digital-compass-2030_en.pdf Digital Compass Communication]. There is a crucial need to keep investing in the skills of the people in Europe, both to help them prosper and to ensure the competitivity of the European economy on the global scale. The Digital Decade policy programme 2030 sets up a monitoring and cooperation mechanism to achieve the common objectives and targets for Europe's digital transformation. In 2023, skills were at the heart of European priorities with [https://year-of-skills.europa.eu/index_en the European Year of Skills], which started on 9 May 2023 and ran for 12 months, aiming at gathering all relevant forces to work together to promote skills development, and thereby improving professional and life opportunities for people. The European Year of Skills aimed at helping to address the skills gaps in the European Union and boost the EU skills strategy, helping to reskill people with the focus on digital and green technology skills. The [https://education.ec.europa.eu/kk/focus-topics/digital-education/action-plan Digital Education Plan] and the [https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/industry/strategy_en Industrial Strategy] for Europe made clear that the pathways to the recovery will be supporting the creation of a greener, more digital and resilient European Union in which the skills of the labour force are adapted to cope with a fast changing labour market. The European Year of Skills also contributed to the [https://commission.europa.eu/document/41514677-9598-4d89-a572-abe21cb037f4_en Green Deal Industrial Plan], to enhance the competitiveness of Europe's net-zero industry and support climate neutrality. ===Other articles=== *[[ICT_specialists_in_employment|ICT specialists in employment]] *[[ICT_specialists_-_statistics_on_hard-to-fill_vacancies_in_enterprises|ICT specialists - statistics on hard-to-fill vacancies in enterprises]] *[[Skills for the digital age|Skills for the digital age]] *[[Young people - digital world|Young people - digital world]] *[[Towards Digital Decade targets for Europe|Towards Digital Decade targets for Europe]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/digital-economy-and-society/database Digital economy and society (isoc)], see: :Science, technology, digital society ::Digital economy and society (isoc) :::Digital skills (isoc_sk) ::::ICT training (isoc_skt) :::::Persons with ICT education by labour status (isoc_ski_itemp) :::::Employed persons with ICT education by sex (isoc_ski_itsex) :::::Employed persons with ICT education by educational attainment level (isoc_ski_itedu) :::::Employed persons with ICT education by age (isoc_ski_itage) ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=digital_economy_and_society}} Digital economy and society] ===Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Category:Digital_economy_and_society_glossary Digital economy and society glossary] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/isoc_ski_itemp_esms.htm Persons with ICT education by labour status (isoc_ski_itemp)] (ESMS metadata file — isoc_ski_itemp_esms) *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/employ_esms.htm Employment and unemployment (labour force survey)] (ESMS metadata file — employ_esms) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/lfsa_esms.htm LFS series - detailed annual survey results (lfsa)] ((ESMS metadata file — lfsa_esms) ===Legislation=== *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52016DC0381:EN:NOT|title=A New Skills Agenda for Europe - Working together to strengthen human capital, employability and competitiveness (COM(2016 381 final)}} update forthcoming in May 2025 *[https://pact-for-skills.ec.europa.eu/community-resources/publications-and-documents/european-skills-agenda-sustainable-competitiveness-social-fairness-and-resilience_en European Skills Agenda for Sustainable Competitiveness, Social Fairness and Resilience (1 July 2020)] *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32019R1700&from=EN Framework regulation on Integrated European Social Statistics (from 2021 onwards)] ===External links=== *[https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/europes-digital-decade Europe's Digital Decade | Shaping Europe’s digital future] *[https://ec.europa.eu/education/education-in-the-eu/digital-education-action-plan_en Digital Education Action Plan] *[https://commission.europa.eu/document/41514677-9598-4d89-a572-abe21cb037f4_en Green Deal Industrial Plan] *[https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC144121 The Digital Competence Framework] *[https://digital-skills-jobs.europa.eu/en Digital Skills and Jobs Platform] *[https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1223&langId=en European Skills Agenda] *[https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1517&langId=en The Pact for Skills] *[https://ec.europa.eu/growth/industry/policy/skills_en Skills for Industry] *[https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-skills-outlook-2023_27452f29-en.html OECD Skills Outlook 2023 - title: ICT sector - value added, employment and R&D
text:
EU statistics are presented for economic developments in the information and communication technology (ICT) sector, including information on value added, employment, labour input ratios and research and development (R & D). Data extracted in April 2025 Planned article update: March 2027 In 2023, value added by the EU’s ICT sector was equivalent to 5.2% of gross value added (GVA). The EU’s ICT sector employed more than 7.36 million people in 2023, which marks 3.4% of the total employment. At EU level, nearly 18% of total business enterprise R&D expenditures can be attributed to the ICT sector. Developments in the [[Glossary:Information and communication technology (ICT)|information and communication technology (ICT)]] sector have led to significant changes in the methods of production and patterns of employment across the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. This article provides an overview of economic developments within the EU’s ICT sector; the primary sources of information that are used for this article are [[Glossary:Structural business statistics (SBS)|structural business statistics (SBS)]], [[Glossary:National accounts (NA)|national accounts]] and [[Glossary:Research and development (R %26 D)|research and development (R & D)]] statistics. ===The weight of the ICT sector in the economy=== The [[Glossary:Value added - EBS|value added]] of the ICT sector in the EU was over €816 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] in 2023, 5.24% of the EU’s [[Glossary:Gross value added|gross value added]]. This includes over €697 billion (4.47% of the EU’s gross value added) coming from ICT services, and nearly €120 billion (0.77% of the EU’s gross value added) coming from ICT manufacturing. The evolution of the ICT sector, measured as its weight relative to gross value added, shows (Figure 1) a steady annual growth of around 6% until 2021, followed by a stabilisation in 2022, and then a decline in 2023 (4%); even though the volume of the ICT sector’s value added (in absolute monetary terms) grew 3%, from over €792 billion in 2022, its share in the economy dropped 0.22 percentage points (pp.) in 2023. [[Image:Evolution_of_the_percentage_of_the_ICT_sector_in_Gross_value_added,_EU,_2019-2023_(in_%,_relative_to_gross_value_added)_.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Evolution of the percentage of the ICT sector in gross value added, EU, 2019-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e5978f82-f9cb-42e3-90cb-5af8a269e0c2?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-24T06:15:21Z isoc_bde15ag]|alt=Line chart showing the share of the ICT sector in gross value added in the EU from 2019 to 2023. The percentage increases from 4.86% in 2019 to 5.19% in 2020, then rises further to 5.46% in 2021. It remains stable at 5.46% in 2022 before declining slightly to 5.24% in 2023. Overall, the trend is upward from 2019 to 2022, followed by a modest decrease in 2023. A note indicates a break in the time series in 2021. ]] ==== Distribution of the percentage of ICT across EU countries ==== The distribution of the share of the ICT sector in the gross value added across European countries in 2023 renders important differences among them (Figure 2). Ireland stood out the most, with ICT sector contributing 30.9% of its gross value added. Along with Ireland, Malta (11.7%), Bulgaria (8.1%), and Latvia (6.6%) were among the EU countries with relatively high ICT sector contributions, each exceeding the EU average. On the other side were find Italy (3.1% ) and Greece (3.2%) with the lowest shares. [[Image:Percentage_of_the_ICT_sector_in_Gross_value_added.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Percentage of the ICT sector in gross value added, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e73b1a7a-b4e1-4ba7-ac78-6c27848d5153?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-24T06:18:55Z isoc_bde15ag] | alt= choropleth map of Europe showing the percentage of the ICT sector in gross value added by country in 2023. Values vary widely across countries, with an EU average of 5.24%. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The ICT sector is also different in terms of the ICT breakdowns. The distribution of the share of ICT services in gross value added across European countries in 2023 shows, once again, Ireland as the country with the highest value (17.4%). Among the rest of the EU countries, Cyprus (11.2%), Malta (11%), and Bulgaria (7.9%) followed, also reporting comparatively high shares. (Figure 3A) Compared with ICT services, the contribution of ICT manufacturing remains relatively limited in most countries, accounting for only a small proportion of gross value added. Ireland (13.6%) stood out as a clear outlier, with a substantially higher share than all other countries. Other high shares were observed in Hungary (1.1%), Malta (0.7%), and Austria (0.6%), although these remained well below the level observed in Ireland. (Figure 3B) [[Image:Percentage_of_ICT_services_and_manufacturing_in_Gross_value_added.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Percentage of the ICT subsectors in gross value added, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6e12c191-d59f-40a0-8e22-7e863f503ee7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-24T06:20:13Z isoc_bde15ag] | alt= two side-by-side choropleth maps of Europe. One (on the left) is showing the percentage of the ICT services in gross value added, and the other (on the right) is showing the percentage of the ICT manufacturing in gross value added. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ==== Composition of the ICT sector ==== The ICT services sector consists of 6 economic activities under NACE Rev. 2. These are: * wholesale of information and communication equipment, * software publishing, * telecommunications, * computer programming, consultancy and related activities, * data processing, hosting and related activities; web portals, * repair of computers and communication equipment. “Computer programming, consultancy and related activities” accounted for by far the largest share, representing 52% of total ICT services1. “Telecommunications” followed, with a contribution of 21%, while “Software publishing”” would be estimated by a further 11%. The remaining activities accounted for less than 20% of gross value added from ICT services (Figure 4). [[Image:Components_of_ICT_services,_EU,_2023_(relative_to_gross_value_added).png|thumb|right|700px|Figure 4: Components of ICT services, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9271911b-10df-4fb8-8210-cc38848f27dc?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-24T06:29:23Z sbs_ovw_act]|alt=a pie chart showing the shares of six components of ICT services. The volume of each component is in relation to gross value added. Those shares are as follow: Computer programming, consultancy and related activities: 52% (estimated value); Telecommunications: 21%; Software publishing: 11% (estimated value); Wholesale of information and communication equipment: 8%; Data processing, hosting and related activities, web portals: 8% (estimated value); Repair of computers and communication equipment: 1% (estimated value). For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The “Telecommunications” sector was the second most important component of ICT– the first one being “Computer programming, consultancy and related activities”. The value added for “Telecommunication”, increased visibly with enterprise size. Large enterprises (250 and more persons employed) accounted for the largest values with more than €120 billion of value added in 2023. Medium-sized enterprises (50–249 persons employed) also made a substantial contribution with €10.7 million, whereas small and micro enterprises (fewer than 50 persons employed) together generated nearly the same value, at €11.7 million. [[Image:Telecommunications_sector_by_the_size_of_the_enterprises,_EU,_2023_(in_value_added_-_million_euro).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Telecommunications sector by the size of the enterprises, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8cb7ed9e-2173-48bf-a0c1-bed88da7520e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-24T07:10:40Z sbs_sc_ovw]| alt=a bar chart showing value added of telecommunications sector in EU in 2023 by the size of the enterprises. The far biggest share with over 120 billion euros of value added comes from the enterprises with 250 and more persons employed. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. ]] ===ICT Employment === The EU’s ICT sector employed more than 7.36 million people in 2023, which marks 3.38% of the total employment. This included more than 0.5 million people employed in ICT manufacturing and over 6.8 million people employed in ICT services. The share of ICT employment in total employment within the EU has grown 0.39 pp. since 2019 as highlighted in Figure 6. This rise is entirely due to the growth in the share of the employment in ICT services, which has grown 0.41 pp. since 2019. In the same period, the share of ICT manufacturing employment dropped by 0.02 pp. [[Image:Evolution_of_the_share_of_ICT_sector_employment_in_total_employment,_EU,_2019-2023_(in_%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Evolution of the share of ICT sector employment in total employment, EU, 2019-2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f3229429-af5d-4297-8945-a26a603a5288?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-24T07:12:39Z isoc_bde15ap]|alt= line chart showing the evolution of the share of ICT sector employment in total employment in EU over the years 2019-2023. For the whole ICT sector in the EU in 2023 it equalled nearly €111 000 per person employed. This is a rise of 3.4% since 2021, when the apparent labour productivity amounted to just under €107 300 per person employed (Figure 10). It is worth noting that there are significant differences between the subsectors. Specifically, the apparent labour productivity in EU in 2023 in ICT services was around €102 400 per person employed, meanwhile in ICT manufacturing it reached as high as around €215 770 per person employed. A preliminary analysis of the data in 2023 from the share of the ICT sector in total business enterprise expenditure on research and development (R&D) showed that the sector plays a significant role in business-driven research and development activity in the EU, where nearly 18% of total business enterprise R&D expenditures can be attributed to the ICT sector.
