title: Industrial producer price index overview
text:
EU statistics on the industrial producer price index refer to the gross monthly change in the trading price of industrial products. Data extracted in February 2026 Planned article update: February 2027 [[Image:Figure 1 EU, EA-21, Industrial producer prices, total, domestic and non-domestic market, 2015 - 2025.png|thumb|center|600px|EU, EA-21 Industrial producer prices, total, domestic and non-domestic market, 2015 - 2025, unadjusted data (2021 = 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c723f765-43d8-4a6e-b0f2-cd2480082b34?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-05T10:57:39Z (sts_inpp_m)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9a3e5c77-00f1-434f-a84d-4cc020a54687?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-04T10:32:26Z (sts_inppd_m)] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/47d46162-f4d1-40ae-978e-5b05bbd0dadf?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-05T11:07:21Z (sts_inppnd_m)] |alt= Line chart showing industrial producer prices as unadjusted data with the year 2021 indexed at 100 for the EU and EA (euro area). Six lines represent EU total market, EA total market, EU domestic market, EA domestic market, EU non-domestic market and EA non-domestic market over the years 2015 to 2025.]] This article provides a general overview of the (industrial) [[Glossary:Producer price index (PPI)|producer price index (PPI)]], sometimes also called output price index, as it is calculated and used at the level of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] and its Member States. ''Please also see the monthly [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-euro-indicators/w/4-05082026-ap Eurostat News Release from 5 August 2026].'' Please note that the news release focusses on domestic producer prices while this article also presents industrial producer prices for the total market (domestic and non-domestic). === Role of the industrial producer price index=== The industrial producer price index measures the gross monthly change in the trading price of industrial products (there are also producer price indices for [[Construction producer price and construction cost indices overview|construction]] and for [[Services producer price index overview|services]]). The industrial producer price index (PPI) measures price changes from the point of view of the producers/manufacturers of a product (it is thus an output price). In this it differs from consumer price indices, which measure the prices from the point of view of consumers/buyers (see below). The PPI reflects basic prices, which exclude [[Glossary:Value added tax (VAT)|VAT]] and similar deductible taxes directly linked to [[Glossary:Turnover - SBS|turnover.]] By contrast, any subsidies on products received by the producer should be added. In order to show the true development of price movements, actual transaction prices - instead of list prices - are collected. === Industrial producer price index - sub-indices=== There are 2 sub-indices for the industrial producer price index, one for the domestic market and one for the non-domestic market (Figure 1). When combined, the sub-indices give the change in the PPI for a given industry. For producer prices on the non-domestic market, the prices are calculated at national frontiers, FOB (free on board); this means that the seller pays for transportation of the goods to the port of shipment, plus loading costs, and the buyer pays freight, insurance, unloading costs and transportation from the port of destination to their factory. All characteristics that determine the price of the products have to be taken into account. This includes quantity of units sold, transport provided, rebates, service conditions, guarantee conditions and destination. [[Image:Figure 1 EU, EA-21, Industrial producer prices, total, domestic and non-domestic market, 2015 - 2025.png|thumb|center|600px|EU, EA-21 Industrial producer prices, total, domestic and non-domestic market, 2015 - 2025, unadjusted data (2021 = 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c723f765-43d8-4a6e-b0f2-cd2480082b34?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-05T10:57:39Z (sts_inpp_m)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9a3e5c77-00f1-434f-a84d-4cc020a54687?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-04T10:32:26Z (sts_inppd_m)] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/47d46162-f4d1-40ae-978e-5b05bbd0dadf?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-05T11:07:21Z (sts_inppnd_m)] |alt= Line chart showing industrial producer prices as unadjusted data with the year 2021 indexed at 100 for the EU and EA (euro area). Six lines represent EU total market, EA total market, EU domestic market, EA domestic market, EU non-domestic market and EA non-domestic market over the years 2015 to 2025.]] The index for the non-domestic market is further divided into an index for the euro area and one for the non-euro area (Figure 2). These sub-indices are only provided for countries in the euro area. As Figures 1 and 2 illustrate, the various sub-indices for the [[Glossary:EU-27|EU]], the [[Glossary:Euro_area|euro area]] and for domestic and non-domestic market all moved in a relatively similar fashion even those the index levels are somewhat different. [[Image:Figure 2 EU, Industrial producer prices non-domestic market, 2015 - 2025.png|thumb|center|600px|Figure 2:EU, Industrial producer prices non-domestic market, 2015 - 2025, unadjusted data (2021 = 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/47d46162-f4d1-40ae-978e-5b05bbd0dadf?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-05T11:07:21Z (sts_inppnd_m)] |alt= Line chart showing industrial producer prices as unadjusted data with the year 2021 indexed at 100 for the EA (euro area). Three lines represent total non-domestic market, EA non-domestic market and non-EA non-domestic market over the years 2015 to 2025.]]
[[Image:Figure 3 EU, Domestic industrial producer prices - total and main industrial groupings (MIG) 2020 - 2025).png |thumb|center|600px|Figure 3: EU, domestic industrial producer prices - total and main industrial groupings (MIG) 2020 - 2025, unadjusted data (2021 = 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d93d3c0f-09af-48f7-bbcb-085d2b77fe32?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-04T10:14:38Z (sts_inppd_m)] |alt= Line chart showing domestic industrial producer prices of total and main industrial groupings as unadjusted data with the year 2021 indexed at 100 for the EU. Six lines represent total industry, intermediate goods, energy, capital goods, durable consumer goods and non-durable consumer goods over the years 2020 to 2025.]] ===Industrial producer prices - development since 2015=== Following the financial and economic crisis in 2008/2009 producer prices regained their pre-crisis level in late 2010/early 2011. In the years following 2015 industrial producer prices remained relatively stable. In 2020, industrial producer prices on the domestic market rapidly decreased by around 3.9% during the first wave of the COVID-19 crisis. The fall was remarkable since it occurred in a short period of just three months (February to May). The size of the reduction was, however, smaller than during the financial crisis. As of June 2020, industrial producer prices started to increase again. The development was quite dynamic and even accelerated during the last months of 2021 and the first half of 2022. Between May 2020 and September 2022, the domestic industrial producer price index increased by almost two thirds. Between September 2022 and July 2023, industrial producer prices fell again – almost as dynamically as they had increased in the months before. Since then prices have remained relatively stable (compared with the turbulent development in the preceding months) and are still at a historically high level. Figure 3 shows the (annual) aggregated price data on the domestic market for the [[Glossary:Main industrial grouping (MIG)|Main industrial groupings (MIG)]]. For most areas, prices developed in a relatively stable manner. Producer prices for energy are, however, very volatile and react much stronger in times of crisis. Figure 3 also shows that the unprecedented increase in producer prices between May 2020 and September 2022 was to a large extent the result of an increase in energy prices. [[Image: Figure 4 EU, Domestic output prices for energy 2021 - 2025, unadjusted data .png|thumb|center|600px|Figure 4: EU, domestic output prices for energy 2021 - 2025, unadjusted data (2021 = 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/826f644c-e8f6-4949-825b-8f8ddbf10ef6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-04T10:24:04Z (sts_inppd_m)] |alt= Line chart showing domestic output prices for energy as unadjusted data with the year 2021 indexed at 100 for the EU. Five lines represent, mining coal and lignite, coke and refined petroleum products, total energy, extraction crude petroleum and natural gas and electricity, gas, steam, air conditioning over the years 2021 to 2025.]] Figure 4 shows in greater detail how the recent developments of producer prices were influenced by energy prices. Between January 2021 and September 2022 (the peak of the price development), domestic industrial producer prices increased by 55.2%. During the same period, producer prices for energy increased by an average of almost 5.0% per month, which amounted to a total increase of 147.6%. Since September 2022, energy prices dropped by 32.8%. Particularly strong were the variations for the extraction of crude petroleum and natural gas (8.4% on average per month between January 2021 and September 2022 and -2.6% on average per month between September 2022 and December 2025). [[Image:Table 1 Industrial producer prices, total, annual rates of change 2020-2025, unadjusted data.png|thumb|center|600px|Table 1: Industrial producer prices, total market, annual rates of change 2020 - 2025, unadjusted data
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a7460499-e19a-4463-94e0-f64eda79a82a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-05T12:30:18Z (sts_inppd_a)] |alt= Table showing industrial producer prices total market annual rates of change as unadjusted data for the EU, EA, individual EU Member States, Norway, Switzerland, North Macedonia, Albania, Serbia and Ukraine for the years 2020 to 2025.]] Table 1 shows the annual rates of change for the EU, the euro area and the individual [[Glossary:EU_enlargements|EU countries]] and some other countries (total market). In 2020, the total industrial producer price dropped in a large majority of countries and the magnitude of the decreases sometimes reached the levels that were witnessed during the economic and financial crisis in 2008/2009. In 2021, almost all countries witnessed massive increases in industrial producer prices, often with annual rates of change of two digits. Despite the fact that prices started to fall again in the later months of 2022, the annual rates for this year were exceptionally high for all countries. In 2023, the consolidation of price levels that had already started in the second half of 2022 continued. Around one third of the countries even showed a negative rate of change for total industrial output prices. In 2024 this development further accelerated resulting in an average decrease of domestic producer prices for total industry of 2.5% in the EU. In almost all countries a significant reduction in prices was recorded. In 2025 the general level of producer prices remained relatively stable. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=STS industrial producer prices 2026.xlsx|title=Industrial producer price index overview - tables and figures}} === Data sources === '''Coverage''' The data collection at European level is based on {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R2152:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 2019/2152}} (European Business Statistics Regulation) of 27 November 2019 and {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32020R1197:EN:NOT|title=Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 2020/1197}} of 30 July 2020. In addition to the regulations there is also a methodological guide to ensure consistent data collection in all countries which was developed by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] with the help of Member States. All Member States are obliged to transmit data at 2-digit level of the [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] classification (an EU standard classification of economic activities) for: *Mining and quarrying (Section B); *Manufacturing (Section C); *Electricity, gas and water supply (Section D and division E36). The industrial producer price index is published monthly. Countries send data to [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] no later than one month and 5 days after the end of the [[Glossary:Reference period|reference period]]. Eurostat publishes the European price index 1 month and 5 days after the reference period. '''Data collection''' The PPI data are based on selling prices reported by establishments of all sizes selected as being representative of the whole population. Regular collection of prices data normally flows from a sample of units and a sample of their products. Data are increasingly collected by electronic means. The basic sampling method used varies from one national statistical authority to another (cut-off sampling or sampling proportional to size are applied) and depends on the market that is being studied – i.e. domestic or non-domestic. On the domestic market, the sample of enterprises is normally drawn from the Statistical Business Register. The observation units for the PPI for the non-domestic market are very often selected from external trade data. Samples for the PPI for the non-domestic market are generally much smaller than those for the domestic market. One key issue in the production of PPIs is to measure the price of the same product over time. In many industrial sectors, the products evolve rather quickly. Therefore methods to deal with the change of product and quality [[Glossary:Adjustment|adjustment]] are important. The aim is to measure accurately which part of the price development comes from a quality change and which part is a real price change. Especially for tailor made industrial products (e.g. railway locomotives) rather sophisticated methods are needed to identify price changes in a correct manner. Weights for the [[Glossary:Aggregation|aggregation]] of prices into indices are based on turnover information from the Structural Business Statistics database or on information coming directly from Member States. Weights and base years are generally revised every five years. The data in this article were calculated with 2021 as the [[Short-term business statistics - base year 2021|base year]] (=100). === Context === PPI data are widely used by both the business community and government, and enable monthly monitoring of prices at different stages of the manufacturing process. There are three major uses of PPIs. *As an [[Glossary:Economic_indicator|economic indicator]] – PPIs capture price movements prior to the retail level. Therefore, they may foreshadow subsequent price changes for businesses and consumers. They can be an early indicator of inflationary pressures in the economy. These data are used in formulating fiscal and monetary policies. *As a [[Glossary:Deflator|deflator]] of other economic series – PPIs are used to adjust other economic time series for price changes. *As the basis for contract price adjustments (escalation) – PPI data are used in escalating purchase and sales contracts. These contracts typically specify amounts of money to be paid at some point in the future. It is often desirable to include an escalation clause that takes account of increases in input prices. In many countries, there is a big demand for PPIs from the business and trade organisations. As these indices have already been in existence for decades, they are part of economic life for national accountants and businesses. For these uses they need to be maintained by the national statistical institutes at a detailed level. Many medium-sized and small countries calculate detailed PPIs beyond the requirements of the EU Regulation in order to satisfy a national demand. [[Image:Figure 5 EU, Industrial producer price and consumer price for food products and beverages, 2015-2025, unadjusted data (2021 = 100).png |thumb|center|600px|Figure 5: EU, Industrial producer price and consumer price for food products, 2015-2025, unadjusted data (2021 = 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/623893f9-f8cd-4664-9ca9-7f830871ca87?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-04T10:06:03Z (sts_inppd_m)] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2d28d5c4-1a25-46db-a8c2-8f5bf57f4151?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-04T09:20:20Z (prc_hicp_midx)]|alt= Line chart showing industrial producer price and consumer price for food products and beverages as unadjusted data with the year 2021 indexed at 100 for the EU. Two lines represent consumer price and producer price over the years 2015 to 2025.]] To some extent the direction and magnitude of changes in the PPI for finished goods prefigures a similar change in the [[Glossary:Consumer price index (CPI)|consumer price index (CPI)]] for all items (Figure 5). This relation is however not general. Both the PPI and CPI measure price change over time for a fixed set of goods. A primary use of the PPI is to [[Glossary:Deflated|deflate]] revenue streams in order to measure real growth in output. A primary use of the CPI is to adjust income and expenditure streams for changes in the cost of living. The different uses cause various conceptual differences that can be described as follows: *The definition of prices – The price collected for an item included in the PPIs is the revenue received by its producer. Sales and excise taxes are not included in the price because they do not represent revenue to the producer. The price collected for an item included in the CPI is the expenditure by a consumer for the item. Sales and excise taxes are included in the price because they are necessary expenditures by the consumer for the item. *The composition of the set of commodities and services – The target set of goods and services included in the PPIs is the entire marketed output of the producers. The set includes both goods and services purchased by other producers as inputs to their operations or as capital investment, and goods and services purchased by consumers either directly from the service producer or indirectly from a retailer. Because the PPI target is the output of the producers, imports are excluded. The target set of items included in the CPI is the set of goods and services purchased for consumption purposes by the households. This set includes imports. ===Other articles === *[[Industrial production (volume) index overview]] *[[Industrial import price index overview]] *[[Construction producer price and construction cost indices overview]] *[[Services producer price index overview]] === Publications === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/short-term-business-statistics/publications All News Releases] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/short-term-business-statistics/database Short-term business statistics (sts)], see: :Industry (NACE Rev.2) (sts_ind) ::Producer prices in industry (sts_ind_pric) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/short-term-business-statistics/database Short-term business statistics (t_sts)], see: :Industry (NACE Rev.2) (t_sts_ind) ::Producer prices in industry (PPI) (t_sts_ind_pric) === Thematic Section === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=short_term_business_statistics}} Short-term business statistics] === Methodology === *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-21-001|title=European Business Statistics Manual – 2021 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-21-018|title=European business statistics manual for short-term business statistics – 2021 edition}} *{{Template:Esms|code=sts_esms|title=Short-term business statistics - Metadata in SDMX format}} (ESMS metadata file — sts_esms) *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/metadata More information on Metadata in Eurostat] {{Unit|topic=X_Short-term_statistics}} [[Category:Industry, trade, and services|Industrial producer price index overview]] [[Category:Short-term business statistics (STS)|Industrial producer price index overview]] [[Category:Industry short-term statistics|Industrial producer price index overview]] [[Category:Prices|Industrial producer price index overview]] [[Category:Statistical article|Industrial producer price index overview]] [[Category:February2027|Industrial producer price index overview]]

title: Industrial turnover index overview
text:
EU statistics an overview of development of the industrial turnover indicator is given for the European Union, the euro area and the EU Member states. Data extracted in August 2026. Planned article update: August 2027. This article provides an overview of the development of the industrial turnover indicator in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], the [[Glossary:Euro area|euro area]] and the EU [[Glossary:EU Member States|countries]] over recent years, and describes how it is compiled. The index of industrial turnover is a [[Glossary:Business cycle|business cycle]] indicator which measures the monthly development of turnover in the European industry. The data presented in this article are taken from European [[Short-term business statistics introduced|short-term statistics (STS)]] which are collected under the [[Short-term business statistics - legal base|European business statistics regulation]]. Industry turnover as presented in this article covers turnover in mining and quarrying and in manufacturing ([[NACE background|NACE Rev. 2]] sections B and C). ===Overview=== Industrial turnover data published by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] distinguish between domestic turnover, i.e. turnover generated with sales to units in the same country and non-domestic turnover for sales from a business in one country to someone in another country (the non-domestic turnover data are further divided according to whether the buyer of the industrial goods has its seat in a euro area country or not). As Figure 1 indicates, the overall developments of domestic and non-domestic turnover data is slightly different in level but the general patterns of domestic and non-domestic turnover are very similar. Figure 1 Industrial turnover in the [[Glossary:EU-27|EU]] increased steadily but relatively slowly since 2013. In February 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic set in and industrial turnover decreased by more than 30% in just 2 months. The following months from May to July saw a rapid but partial recovery to an index of about 90% of the pre-crisis level. In the following years, between July 2020 and October 2022, industrial turnover remained on a dynamic growth path – to a large extent as a result of increasing prices. After October 2022 industrial turnover somewhat decreased. March 2026 saw another dynamic increase of industrial turnover by around 4%. Table 1 shows the annual rates of change of industrial turnover (mining and quarrying and manufacturing) in the European Union, the euro area, the EU countries and some other countries for which data are available (calendar adjusted data). [[Image:Industrial turnover, 2015-2025 (annual % change), calendar adjusted data Table 1.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Industrial turnover, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ad3d1d52-d694-470f-9480-ca24908eaa02?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-04T10:07:29Z sts_intv_a])|alt= a table showing the industrial Turnover, annual percentage change from 2015 to 2024 using calendar adjusted data, in the EU, euro area, EU Member States, the EFTA countries and candidate countries.]] The 2020 data are clearly influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic. In the EU, turnover in industry decreased by 9.5%, in the euro area even by 10.2%. There were, however, noticeable differences between countries. The drop in turnover was particularly strong in Luxembourg (-13.4%), France (-13.1%), Belgium and Greece (both -12.1%), and in Spain (-12.0%) while in Ireland (4.0%) and Latvia (2.2%) industrial turnover still increased. As a result of the recovery after the COVID-19 pandemic, and also as a consequence of increasing prices, industrial turnover increased quite dynamically in 2021 (EU 15.6%, euro area 15.5%). All countries for which data are available recorded positive rates of change, which were particularly high in Belgium (30.9%), Lithuania (29.2%), and Greece (25.3%). In 2022, industrial turnover continued its dynamic growth not least as a result of rapidly increasing prices levels. The EU total industrial turnover increased by 19.9%, in the euro area the rate of change was 19.6%. The highest rates of change were recorded in Bulgaria (36.1%), Poland (30.9%), Lithuania (30.5%), and Greece (30.3%). In 2023, industrial turnover decreased in the EU (-1.4%) and in the euro area (-1.9%). Particularly strong decreases were recorded in Finland (-9.2%), Lithuania (-8.8%), and Ireland (-8.2%). Some countries however still maintained positive rates of change, e.g. Malta (9.5%) and Cyprus (8.2%). In 2024 the decline in industrial turnover continued. For the EU the annual rate of change was -2.4%, for the euro area -2.6%. The strongest decreases were recorded in Hungary (-5.2%), and in Poland (-5.1%). The highest increases were found in Denmark (7.6%) and in Malta (5.4%). In 2025 industrial turnover in the EU and the euro area slightly increased. The highest increases were recorded in Ireland (15.9%) and in Cyprus (9.0%). The strongest decreases were found in Hungary (-2.8%) and Malta (-1.7%).
=== Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=STS industrial turnover 08 2026.xlsx|title=Industrial turnover index overview: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The definition of turnover is rather straightforward. It comprises basically what is invoiced by the seller. Rebates and price deductions are taken into account as well as special charges that the customer might have to pay. Turnover does not include [[Glossary:Value added tax (VAT)|VAT]] or similar deductible taxes. Information on industrial turnover is often collected by business surveys. However, quite a number of National Statistical Institutes rely on administrative sources, i.e. VAT declarations, to obtain the data. According to the [[Short-term business statistics - legal base|European business statistics regulation and the Implementing regulation]] data on service turnover have to be made available by the National Statistical Institutes on a monthly basis. European aggregates are calculated by summing up weighted national indices. The weights correspond to the share of the countries in the turnover of industrial activities in the base year. The data in this article were calculated with the [[Short-term business statistics - base year 2021|base year 2021]]. All results for the indicator of turnover in industries are published on the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/short-term-business-statistics/database Eurostat website.] ===Context=== The turnover indicator in industry represents the development of sales in industry. It is therefore a value indicator that is influenced by two factors: changes in prices of the traded industrial goods and changes of the traded volumes of goods. Apart from the influence of price changes which constitute a differences between turnover and production volumes there are also some other methodological differences, e.g. production figures include stocked good which are not yet sold. [[Image:Monthly turnover and production in industry, EU, 2000-2026 (2021=100), seasonally adjusted data V1.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Monthly turnover and production in industry, EU, 2000-2026
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5c7fc8e0-7918-49e1-b971-b7f1d842c928?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-04T10:12:04Z sts_intv_m]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2ec0061c-3a44-49b7-92bb-201a050dbf66?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-04T10:16:52Z sts_inpr_m])|alt= a line chart with two lines showing the EU Monthly turnover and production in industry from 2000 to 2026 using seasonally adjusted data. The lines show turnover industry and production industry. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In general the connection between both indicators was relatively close as is indicated by Figure 2 which represents the [[Short-term business statistics - seasonal adjustment methods|seasonally adjusted]] monthly indicator values for turnover and production in industry for the years 2000-26. Figure 2 also shows that since early 2021 industrial production more or less stagnated while industrial turnover increased quite dynamically. As a consequence the index of industrial turnover is now considerable higher than the index for industrial production. ===Other articles=== *[[Industrial production (volume) index overview]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/short-term-business-statistics/database Short-term business statistics (sts)], see: :Industry (sts_ind) ::Turnover in industry (sts_ind_tovt) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/short-term-business-statistics/database Short-term business statistics (t_sts)], see: :Industry (NACE Rev.2) (t_sts_ind) ::Turnover in industry (NACE Rev.2) (t_sts_ind_tovt) ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=short_term_business_statistics}} Short-term business statistics] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-SF-07-058|title=Focus on the link between new orders, turnover and production for industrial activities}} - Statistics in focus 58/2007 ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-21-001|title=European Business Statistics Manual – 2021 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-21-018|title=European business statistics manual for short-term business statistics – 2021 edition}} *{{Template:Esms|code=sts_esms|title=Short-term business statistics - Metadata in SDMX format}} (ESMS metadata file — sts_esms) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/metadata More information on Metadata in Eurostat] {{Unit|topic=X_Short-term_statistics}} [[Category:Industry, trade, and services|Industrial turnover index overview]] [[Category:Short-term business statistics (STS)|Industrial turnover index overview]] [[Category:Industry short-term statistics|Industrial turnover index overview]] [[Category:Statistical article|Industrial turnover index overview]] [[Category:August2027|Industrial turnover index overview]]

title: Inequality in Southern Mediterranean countries
text:
This article is part of an online Eurostat publication that provides a statistical overview of the Southern Mediterranean countries. The article presents statistics on gender inequalities and inequalities between age groups for Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Palestine and Tunisia and compares these with the EU. Data extracted in March 2026 Planned article update: June 2027 In 2024, women lived longer than men in all Southern Mediterranean countries. The gap in life expectancy ranged from 4.6 years in Tunisia (2022) to 2.2 years in Palestine. In the EU, the gap was 5.2 years. Economic activity is much higher for men than for women in most Southern Mediterranean countries. In 2024, the difference was 57.7 percentage points in Palestine and 55.8 pp higher in Egypt, compared with 9.3 pp in the EU. Among the Southern Mediterranean countries, Egypt had the widest unemployment gender gap in 2024, with unemployment for women 10.1 percentage points higher than for men. In the EU, the gap was just 0.6 pp. This article is part of an [[European_Neighbourhood_Policy_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]]. It presents information on 9 [[Glossary:European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP)|Southern Mediterranean]] countries, namely, Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Palestine ''This designation shall not be construed as recognition of a State of Palestine and is without prejudice to the individual positions of the Member States on this issue.'' and Tunisia. Information on these countries is compared with developments in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]]. This article does not contain any data on Syria, as cooperation with Syria was suspended from 2011 until recently, and no data are collected yet. Lebanon data does not account for Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon. Data for Libya are not available. This article presents statistics on inequality with respect to [[Glossary:Life expectancy|life expectancy]], [[Glossary:Activity rate|economic activity]] and [[Glossary:Unemployment|unemployment]] between men and women; unemployment between people with [[Glossary:Educational attainment level|different education levels]]; [[Glossary:Long-term unemployment|long-term unemployment]] between men and women; and unemployment between youths and adults. The differences between groups are expressed in [[Glossary:percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] for the indicators measured in shares of the population, and in years for life expectancy. ===Differences in life expectancy === [[Glossary:Life expectancy|Life expectancy]] at birth is the average number of years a newborn child can expect to live if the current [[Glossary: Cause of death|mortality conditions]] do not change during the rest of their life. Differences in life expectancy between women and men may reflect disparities with respect to living conditions, access to health services, etc. The gender gap for life expectancy at birth is defined as the number of years that a newborn girl can expect to live minus the number of years a newborn boy can expect to live. Over the period from 2014 to 2024, gender gaps for life expectancy in the Southern Mediterranean countries were consistently tighter than in the EU. In the most recent year available, Tunisia recorded the highest life expectancy gender gap among Southern Mediterranean countries, with women expected to live 4.6 years (2022 data) longer than men. Israel had the second highest gender gap, with a difference of 4.1 years (2024 data) between women and men. In contrast, Palestine (2.2 years; 2024 data) and Egypt (2.4 years; 2019 data) noted the lowest gender gaps in life expectancy. Across the Southern Mediterranean, the gender gaps for life expectancy fluctuated throughout the period 2014-2024 with all countries experiencing increased gender gaps in some years. Notable year-on-year increases occurred in Algeria and Jordan in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, with the gender gaps widening by 2.2 and 1.4 years, respectively. Data for Lebanon and Libya are not available. In the EU, the life expectancy gender gap decreased slightly over the period, from 5.8 years in 2014 to 5.2 years in 2024, with slight increases only in 2016 and 2020. However, several breaks in the time series limit the comparability of the EU data over time. [[Image: ENPS26_Life expectancy gender gap, 2014-2024_(difference in years).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Life expectancy gender gap, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_mlexpec__custom_19753811/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=ce7bfc7e-d7eb-48a9-914c-514c4a6ed877&c=1769003134529 demo_mlexpec]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/enps_demo_mlexpec__custom_19753799/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=ec86ab50-0530-411b-8b38-6911d5ff7289&c=1769003102442 enps_demo_mlexpec])|alt= line chart showing the difference in life expectancy at birth between male and female, measured in years, in the EU and the European Neighbourhood Policy-South countries Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Morocco, Palestine and Tunisia from 2014 to 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Economic activity gender gap=== The economic activity gender gap is calculated as the activity rate of men minus the activity rate of women. The economic activity rate is the percentage of active persons, including both employed and unemployed persons, in relation to the population. Figure 2 shows the differences in economic activity rate between men and women in the Southern Mediterranean countries and in the EU over the period 2014-2024. Except for Israel, the economic activity gender gaps in the Southern Mediterranean countries were far wider than in the EU throughout this period. The widest gap in 2024 was recorded in Palestine, where the activity rate of men was 57.7 [[Glossary:percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] higher than for women. The activity rate gender gap exceeded 50 pp also in Egypt (55.8 pp), Algeria (53.5 pp; 2019 data) and Morocco (53.4 pp). There were wide gender gaps also in Lebanon (47.7 pp; 2022 data), Tunisia (41.3 pp) and Jordan (39.2 pp; 2023 data). Israel stood out with an activity rate for men only 3.1 pp higher than that of women in 2024, significantly lower than in the other Southern Mediterranean countries and in the EU. From 2014 to 2024, the gender gap shrunk notably in Jordan (-11.4 pp; 2014-2023), Tunisia (-6.1 pp; 2015-2024) and Israel (-4.6 pp). Over the same period, the gender gap widened in Egypt (+6.6 pp) and Palestine (+4.2 pp). In the EU, the activity rate of men was 9.3 pp higher than that of women in 2024. Compared with 2014, the gender gap had shrunk by -2.4 pp, falling slightly each year of the period except 2018 when it remained stable. [[Image: ENPS26_Economic activity gender gap, 2014-2024_(percentage points difference in activity rate by sex).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Economic activity gender gap, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfsa_argan__custom_19753781/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=1901135c-40b7-494a-b5ad-44628c29f57e&c=1769003064688 lfsa_argan]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/enps_lfsa_argaed__custom_19753769/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=4a22d9d5-1364-4206-b950-7af272b1b94c&c=1769003028135 enps_lfsa_argaed])|alt= line chart showing the economic activity, measured in percentage points difference in activity rate by sex. The colour coded lines show the respective developments in the EU and the European Neighbourhood Policy-South countries Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Morocco, Palestine and Tunisia from 2014 to 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Unemployment gender gap=== The [[Glossary:Unemployment|unemployment]] rate is the percentage of persons in the [[Glossary:Labour_force|labour force]] that are currently unemployed but actively seeking work. The current section focuses on the difference in unemployment of men and women in the adult population aged 25-74. The gender gap is calculated as the unemployment rate for women minus the corresponding rate for men. A higher unemployment rate for one sex compared to the other may reflect gender-specific disparities in labour market access and opportunities. Across the Southern Mediterranean countries, trends in the unemployment gender gap reveal varied dynamics between countries, with some countries experiencing persistently wide disparities and others showing either narrowing gaps or consistently low differences. Israel displayed consistently small and even negative unemployment gender gaps throughout the period 2014-2024, indicating slightly higher unemployment rates for men than for women in most years. The gaps ranged between -0.6 pp and 0.2 pp, with the most recent figure -0.4 pp in 2024. Among the other Southern Mediterranean countries, the unemployment rate for women was generally higher than that for men, with the unemployment gender gap ranging from 3.6 pp in Lebanon (2022 data) to 10.1 pp in Egypt in 2024. Palestine was an exception, recording dramatic shifts in the unemployment gender gap: after surging at 20.0 percentage points (pp) in 2021, the gap slightly narrowed to 19.7 pp in 2022, before falling sharply to 5.6 pp in 2023 and -5.2 pp in 2024. However, the 2023 and 2024 data cover the West Bank only, data are unavailable for Gaza, limiting comparability with previous years. Between 2014 and 2024, the unemployment gender gap widened most for Algeria (+4.6 pp; 2014-2019) and Morocco (+4.5 pp). Apart from Palestine, the gender gap decreased most in Egypt (-3.1 pp). The European Union, reported a stable and modest gender gap 2014-2024, fluctuating between 0.5 pp and 0.8 pp throughout the period, standing at 0.6 pp in 2024. [[Image: ENPS26_Unemployment gender gap, 2014-2024_(percentage points difference in unemployment rate).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Unemployment gender gap, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfsa_urgan__custom_19753761/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=ffbc7ffd-3c05-4156-9c93-ab200af2e2ad&c=1769002993942 lfsa_urgan]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/enps_lfsa_gap__custom_19753745/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=ecc28711-09de-4363-bc46-6b4441709191&c=1769002957661 enps_lfsa_gap])|alt= line chart showing the difference in unemployment rate between women and men, measured in percentage points, with the unemployment rates calculated as shares of the respective economically active population aged 25-74. The colour coded lines show the respective developments over the period 2014 to 2024 for the EU and the European Neighbourhood Policy-South countries Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Morocco, Palestine and Tunisia. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Unemployment rate by education level === The unemployment rate with respect to the [[Glossary: Educational attainment level|highest level of education completed]] is analysed in Figure 4, presenting data for 2014 and 2024. The levels of education are defined by the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=International_Standard_Classification_of_Education_(ISCED) International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED)]: low (having completed ‘less than primary’, primary or at most lower secondary education), medium (upper secondary and post-secondary non tertiary) and high (tertiary) level of education. In 2024, Palestine experienced the highest unemployment rates among the Southern Mediterranean countries for people with low (34.6%) and medium education (28.5%), and the second highest for people with high education 21.1%). The 2024 data for Palestine cover the West Bank only, data are unavailable for Gaza. For low and medium education, this was substantially higher than it had been in 2014 but significantly lower for high education. Lebanon (2022 data) had the highest unemployment rate for high education with 25.1%, which was higher than for medium education (24.1%) but lower than for low education (27.1%). In Morocco, Egypt and Israel, the highest unemployment rates were noted for people with medium education, with 21.1%, 15.3% and 3.2%, respectively. Whereas unemployment had fallen since 2014 for all education levels in Egypt, in Morocco unemployment rates had risen for both medium and high education between 2014 and 2024. In Israel, education rates had also fallen over the decade for all education levels, and at 3.0% for low, 3.2% for medium and 2.5% for high education remained lower than in the EU. In the EU, unemployment rates almost halved for all three main levels of education between 2014 and 2024. For low education, unemployment fell from 18.4% in 2014 to 10.5% in 2024, for medium education from 8.5% to 4.7%, and for high education from 6.3% to 3.5%. [[Image: ENPS26_Unemployment rate by education level, 2014 and 2024_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Unemployment rate by education level, 2014 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfsa_urgaed__custom_20236029/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=2eab7aed-a29e-44d1-96a7-178011ccc77b&c=1771925455398 lfsa_urgaed]) and Eurostat data collection|alt= bar chart showing the percentage of unemployed people within the labour force for each education attainment group. The colour coded bars show the respective developments over the period 2014 to 2024 for the EU and the European Neighbourhood Policy-South countries Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Morocco, Palestine and Tunisia. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Long-term unemployment gender gap === [[Glossary:Long-term unemployment|Long-term unemployment]] refers to unemployed persons who have been actively seeking employment for one year or more. Long-term unemployment data is an important indicator for structural problems in the labour market. The gender gap is calculated as the long-term unemployment rate for women minus that for men. In 2024, Tunisia recorded the highest gender gap for long-term unemployment among the Southern Mediterranean countries, with the rate for women 9.2 pp higher than the rate for men. Wide gaps were also recorded in Algeria with 7.6 pp (2019 data) and Morocco with 7.1 pp. Palestine experienced much higher long-term unemployment for women than for men in the period 2014-2022, with the gender gap peaking at 19.7 pp in 2021. From 2022 to 2023, the gap halved to 9.7 pp, and fell further to 4.4 pp in 2024. However, it should be noted that the 2023 and 2024 data cover the West Bank only, data are unavailable for Gaza. Egypt also experienced high long-term unemployment gender gaps between 2016 and 2019, in the range 10.9 to 13.3 pp, following a steep rise from 2015 to 2016 (+11.6 pp). The gap decreased in the following years, reaching 5.9 pp in 2021. In Israel, there were only marginal differences in the long-term unemployment rates of women and men, with gender gaps of 0.0 pp or -0.1 pp throughout the period 2014-2024. Between 2014 and 2024, the long-term unemployment rates for men and women were not vastly different in the EU, with the gender gaps ranging between 0.0 pp and -0.3 pp. [[Image: ENPS26_Long-term unemployment gender gap, 2014-2024_(percentage points difference in long-term unemployment rate).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Long-term unemployment gender gap, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/une_ltu_a__custom_19753725/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=1a302386-8b46-40a4-889a-9b33ea96f0d4&c=1769002900712 une_ltu_a]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/enps_lfsa_gaplg__custom_19753715/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=228cd97b-a06f-478e-819b-a1635da7c916&c=1769002867615 enps_lfsa_gaplg])|alt= line chart showing the difference in long-term unemployment rate between women and men, measured in percentage points, with the unemployment rates calculated as shares of the respective economically active population aged 15-74. The colour coded lines show the respective developments over the period 2014 to 2024 for the EU and the European Neighbourhood Policy-South countries Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Lebanon, Morocco, Palestine and Tunisia. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Unemployment gap between young adults === The unemployment gap between economically active young people (‘youths’), aged 15-24, and the rest of the active population (‘adults’), aged 25-74, is calculated as the unemployment rate of youths minus the rate of adults. Between 2014 and 2024, the unemployment rate of youths was consistently higher than that of adults in both the Southern Mediterranean countries and in the EU, highlighting ‘youth unemployment’ as a specific concern. Over this period, the gap between youths and adults with respect to unemployment fluctuated in each of the Southern Mediterranean countries. In the countries with the widest gaps in the recent years, Jordan with 29.3 pp (2023 data) and Tunisia with 27.9 pp (2024 data), experienced only minor increases in the gaps over the available periods. Despite year-on-year fluctuations, the difference in unemployment between youths and adults widened by just +0.6 pp in Jordan (2014-2023) and +1.1 pp (2019-2024) in Tunisia. In comparison, in Morocco the gap between youth unemployment and adult unemployment increased strongly (+14.1 pp) 2014-2024, reaching 26.2 pp in 2024. The same applied to Lebanon, where the gap increased by +7.5 pp from 2018 to 2022, reaching 22.2 pp. In Palestine, the gap fluctuated between 18.9 pp and 22.4 pp 2014-2021, before falling to a lower level at 14.4 pp to 14.8 pp in the period 2022-2024. Israel generally recorded only moderate differences in unemployment rates between youth and adults between 2014 and 2024, with the trend corresponding to an overall decrease from 5.6 pp in 2014 to 1.9 pp in 2024 despite minor fluctuations. Between 2014 and 2017, the EU experienced a steady reduction in this gap, which subsequently remained stable between 10.8 pp and 9.2 pp through 2024. In 2024, youth unemployment rate was 9.8 pp higher than that of adults in the EU. [[Image: ENPS26_Unemployment gap between youths and adults, 2014-2024_(percentage points difference in unemployment rate).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Unemployment gap between young adults and the rest of the economically active population, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfsa_urgan__custom_19753700/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=b672344b-2a37-4ee7-91c2-c0e55a24f0d4&c=1769002830648 lfsa_urgan]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/enps_lfsa_urgan__custom_19753684/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=7a0cab5f-7498-48e5-9f69-a8ac29a0c090&c=1769002784153 enps_lfsa_urgan]).|alt= line chart showing the unemployment gap as the difference in unemployment rate between young adults, aged 15-24, and the rest of the economically active population, aged 25-74, measured in percentage points. The unemployment rates are calculated as the percentage of unemployed persons in these two groups of the economically active population. The colour coded lines show the respective developments over the period 2014 to 2024 for the EU and the European Neighbourhood Policy-South countries Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Morocco, Palestine and Tunisia. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=ENPS26 Inequality 2026.xlsx|title=Inequality in European Neighbourhood South countries: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data for Southern Mediterranean countries are supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country on a voluntary basis. The data result from an annual data collection cycle that has been established by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]. These statistics are available on Eurostat's website, together with a range of additional indicators covering most socio-economic areas. In the dedicated data collection for Southern Mediterranean, the unemployment and labour market indicators are defined in line with the recommendations and standards published by the International Labour Organisation (ILO). The unemployment figures are based on the ILO standard definition of unemployment, which counts people without a job who have been actively seeking work in the last 4 weeks and are available to start. For the EU, the definitions used in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/lfs European Union labour force survey (EU-LFS)] are based on the ILO recommendations and standards. ===Context=== EU cooperation with the Southern Mediterranean countries is guided by the [https://north-africa-middle-east-gulf.ec.europa.eu/what-we-do/pact-mediterranean_en Pact for the Mediterranean ‘One Sea, One Pact, One Future’]. The Pact reflects the EU’s commitment to strengthening its partnership with the southern Mediterranean countries and to building a common Mediterranean space that is connected, prosperous, resilient and secure, based on shared interests and joint responsibility. The Pact for the Mediterranean ‘One Sea, One Pact, One Future’ sets out a long-term vision to foster shared prosperity, stability, and sustainable development across the Euro-Mediterranean region. It establishes a strategic framework for cooperation, built around three interlinked thematic “pillars”: I. People: driving force for change, connections and innovation; II. Stronger, more sustainable and integrated economies, and III. Security, preparedness and migration management. Its core objectives include strengthening economic integration through enhanced trade, investment, and digital connectivity; accelerating the green and just transition by aligning climate action, renewable energy cooperation, and water security; and promoting human development via education, youth employment, and social cohesion initiatives. The Pact also aims to deepen political dialogue to address common security challenges, like migration, while reinforcing democratic governance. The Pact for the Mediterranean was endorsed by the EU and southern Mediterranean partners in November 2025 on the occasion of the 30th anniversary of the Barcelona process, with the European Council welcoming the Pact in its conclusions 20 November 2025. The [https://www.eeas.europa.eu/sites/default/files/joint_staff_working_document_renewed_partnership_southern_neighbourhood.pdf Economic and Investment Plan for the Southern Neighbours] complements this agenda. In cooperation with its Southern Mediterranean partners, Eurostat has the responsibility to promote and implement the use of European and internationally recognised standards and methodology for the production of statistics, necessary for designing and monitoring policies in various areas. Eurostat manages and coordinates EU efforts to increase the capacity of the Southern Mediterranean countries to [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-catalogues/-/KS-32-11-955?inheritRedirect=true&redirect=%2Feurostat%2Fen%2Fpublications%2Fleaflets develop, produce and disseminate good quality data] according to European and international standards. Additional information on the policy context of the Southern Mediterranean region is provided on the website of [https://north-africa-middle-east-gulf.ec.europa.eu/index_en Directorate-General for Middle East, North Africa and the Gulf (DG MENA)]. The EU has been supporting statistical capacity building in the region for a number of years, among others by providing technical assistance to national statistical authorities and by sharing best practice and transferring know-how. A key tool for this statistical cooperation is the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Statistical_cooperation_-_European_Neighbourhood_Policy-South_(ENP-S) MEDSTAT programme], a multiannual regional cooperation programme for statistics addressing common issues and requirements. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Non-EU_countries|All articles on non-EU countries]] title: Inflation in the euro area
text:
EU statistics on inflation show the most recent annual rates of change for the euro area inflation and its main components. Data from August 2026. Extracted on 01 September 2026 Planned update: 17 September 2026 Euro area annual inflation is expected to be 3.3% in August 2026, up compared to July 2026. [[Image:Euro area annual inflation and its main components 10 years.png|thumb|centre|700px|Source: Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/906676dc-06bc-4076-a95a-1f14304670f6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-16T08:13:44Z (prc_hicp_minr)]|alt=Line chart with five lines showing the development of euro area annual inflation and its four main components monthly during the last ten years until August 2026. The four components are: food, alcohol and tobacco, energy, non-energy industrial goods, and services. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The figures presented in this article are based on euro area Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) available on 1 September 2026. They refer to the evolving composition of the euro area. Thus, data for months up to December 2025 represent the euro area with 20 countries, while data for January 2026 onwards represent the euro area with 21 countries. ===Euro area annual inflation rate and its main components=== [[Glossary: Euro area|Euro area]] annual inflation is expected to be 3.3% in August 2026, up from 2.9% in July 2026. Looking at the main components of euro area inflation, energy had the highest annual rate in August 2026 (14.3%, compared with 10.3% in July), followed by services (3.0%, compared with 3.3% in July), non-energy industrial goods (1.2%, compared with 0.9% in July) and food, alcohol & tobacco (1.2%, stable compared with July). [[Image:Euro area annual inflation and its main components table.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Euro area annual inflation and its main components: weights for 2026 and rates for August 2025 and March 2026-August 2026 (estimated)
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/aa461f7d-8941-4117-bb11-cc0a3aab7893?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-31T09:00:47Z prc_hicp_iw]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/37487c30-0847-4b98-bdc1-ac550684693d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-01T09:35:30Z prc_hicp_minr])|alt=Table on the euro area annual inflation and its main components. The ten rows show the following items: 1) all-items, 2) all-items excluding energy, 3) all-items excluding energy and unprocessed food, 4) all-items excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, 5) food, alcohol and tobacco, 6) processed food, alcohol and tobacco, 7) unprocessed food, 8) energy, 9) non-energy industrial goods, and 10) services. Data is shown in eight columns: first, the item group's weight in 2026 in per mil, followed by the euro area annual inflation in the month of August 2025 and finally one column per month for the six months from March 2026 to August 2026. For more details, please use the links to the source datasets codes below the image.]]
[[Image:Euro area annual inflation and its main components 10 years.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Euro area annual inflation and its main components, August 2016-August 2026 (estimated)
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/906676dc-06bc-4076-a95a-1f14304670f6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-16T08:13:44Z prc_hicp_minr])|alt=Line chart with five lines showing the development of euro area annual inflation and its four main components monthly during the last ten years until August 2026. The four components are: 1) food, alcohol and tobacco, 2) energy, 3) non-energy industrial goods, and 4) services. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:Euro area annual inflation and its main components 2 years.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Euro area annual inflation and its main components, August 2024-August 2026 (estimated)
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3791b86c-7db3-4cf4-a143-fb6600ac6bcc?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-04T10:30:23Z prc_hicp_minr])|alt=Line chart with five lines showing the development of euro area annual inflation and its four main components monthly during the last two years until August 2026. The four components are: 1) food, alcohol and tobacco, 2) energy, 3) non-energy industrial goods, and 4) services. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Main components of inflation === Each of the main components contributes in varying degrees to the headline inflation in the euro area. In terms of weights for 2026, 100% for the headline HICP, services is the largest component, accounting for around 46.8% of household final monetary consumption expenditure in the euro area. It is followed by non-energy industrial goods with around 25.2%. Food, alcohol & tobacco and energy account for around 18.9% and 9.0%, respectively. Together, they comprise less than one third of euro area expenditure, but they can have significant impacts on the headline inflation as their prices tend to fluctuate significantly more than the other components. The weights of the main components of the euro area for 2026 are presented in Figure 3. Table 2 shows their relative weights for 2026. title: Influenza statistics
text:
EU statistics are presented on influenza. Data extracted in October 2025 Planned article update: 2 November 2026 In 2023, almost half (47.1%) of the people aged 65 years or over in the EU were vaccinated against influenza. Denmark had the highest vaccination rate in the EU in 2023, with 77.5% of people aged 65 years or over vaccinated against influenza. There were 7 589 deaths of EU residents from influenza in 2022. Influenza vaccination rate, people aged 65 years or over, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hlth_ps_immu__custom_18269725/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=77753344-cc1b-4031-9981-bb32b0a090ae&c=1759496908000 hlth_ps_immu])


This article presents an overview of [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] statistics related to influenza. It includes the following data: *influenza vaccination rates among people aged 65 years or over, for 2009 to 2023 For most countries, the year corresponds to the influenza season which ended in the year mentioned; alternatively it corresponds to the calendar year. Hence, the year 2023 corresponds to the influenza season 2022/23 or calendar year 2023. See the section on data sources for more information. *standardised death rates from influenza, by age group, for 2022. Data on influenza vaccination for 2020-2022 may have been impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic and its related restrictions. For this reason, particular attention should be paid when comparing data across time. In some EU countries, healthcare resources were placed under intense pressure (particularly at the start of the pandemic) from an influx of patients with COVID-19. The pandemic also resulted in a range of knock-on effects including, among others, some services being curtailed/postponed due to the number of COVID-19 patients, staff shortages within hospitals and day care centres due to infection/quarantine procedures, and patients being hindered access to medical services due to their own infection/quarantine as well as lockdown or travel restrictions. The COVID-19 vaccination programmes may also have increased awareness of other preventive measures, such as vaccination for influenza. This article is included in a set of statistical articles concerning specific health conditions in the EU which forms part of an online publication on [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]]. ===Influenza vaccination rates – based on vaccination programme data=== '''''The rate of vaccination increased during pandemics''''' In the EU, just under half (47.1%) of people aged 65 years or over were vaccinated against seasonal influenza in 2023. As can be seen from Figure 1, between 2009 and 2023 (data not available for 2012 and 2013), the rate of vaccination against influenza in the EU fluctuated. The rate was highest at the beginning of this time series, 52.4% in 2009. It then fell to its lowest level in 2015 (39.9%) and remained around this level for 2 years. In 2018, 2019 and 2020, the rate increased by 1 or 2 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points]] each year. The largest increase (during the time series available) was recorded in 2021, with the vaccination rate increasing from 43.5% in 2020 to 50.7% in 2021. The rate fell back somewhat in 2022 and again in 2023 but remained relatively high, at 47.1%. In general, the influenza seasons with the highest vaccination rates occurred during the same periods as [[Glossary:World Health Organization (WHO)|World Health Organisation (WHO)]] declared pandemics. An outbreak of [https://www.who.int/emergencies/situations/influenza-a-(h1n1)-outbreak swine flu] occurred in 2009 and 2010, and the influenza seasons 2020, 2021 and 2022 occurred during the [https://www.who.int/europe/emergencies/situations/covid-19 COVID-19 pandemic]. [[Image:Influenza vaccination rate, people aged 65 years or over, EU, 2009–23 (%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Influenza vaccination rate, people aged 65 years or over, EU, 2009-2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hlth_ps_immu__custom_10178918/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=1bba35dd-e12e-4122-800f-4c3543caee86&c=1759496937000 hlth_ps_immu])|alt=A column chart showing the influenza vaccination rate of people aged 65 years or over. Data are shown for 2009 to 2011 and 2014 to 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Vaccination rates vary between EU countries''''' Among the EU countries, there are various policies to make influenza vaccines available to the general public. Often these vaccines are targeted at older age groups or other people who have a higher risk of poor health outcomes if they catch influenza (such as people who are immunocompromised). Figure 2 shows considerable differences between EU countries in relation to the overall uptake of influenza vaccinations among people aged 65 years or over in 2013 and 2023. More than three quarters of people aged 65 years or over in Denmark (77.5%) and in Ireland (75.7%) were vaccinated against influenza in 2023, as were 71.8% in Portugal. By contrast, less than a fifth of older people were vaccinated in Slovenia (17.6%), Latvia (15.8%), Bulgaria (15.2%), Slovakia (11.7%) and Poland (9.6%), the latter recording the lowest rate across the EU. In 19 of the EU countries, the share of older people vaccinated against influenza was higher in 2023 than it had been in 2013 (see Figure 2 for more information on the different coverage and reference years used in some countries).The proportion of the population aged 65 years or over vaccinated against influenza was more than 25.0 pp higher in 2023 than in 2013 in Denmark (up 32.5 pp), Estonia (up 27.4 pp) and Portugal (up 26.9 pp). By contrast, the biggest declines were recorded in Malta (down 10.6 pp), Hungary (down 8.5 pp) and the Netherlands (down 5.7 pp). [[Image:Influenza vaccination rate, people aged 65 years or over, 2013 and 2023 (%)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Influenza vaccination rate, people aged 65 years or over, 2013 and 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hlth_ps_immu__custom_3241944/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=37009a53-fac3-43d2-baa8-50ec0cf39d37&c=1762425832000 hlth_ps_immu])|alt=A double column chart showing the influenza vaccination rate of people aged 65 years or over. Data are shown for 2013 and 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Deaths from influenza=== There were 7 589 deaths of EU residents from influenza in 2022, equivalent to 1.52 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants. Among these, 6 886 deaths occurred in people aged 65 years or over, equivalent to 7.01 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants of the same age. Note that the number of deaths from influenza can vary greatly between years. For example, in 2018 there were 12 705 deaths from influenza, 35 times more than in 2021. This large fall may reflect, at least in part, the impact of measures introduced against COVID-19, as some of these (such as social distancing, a greater focus on hand washing and the use of masks) also reduced the spread of influenza (see the [[#Data sources|Data sources]] section for information on influenza mortality). Among EU countries, the highest [[Glossary:Standardised_death_rate|standardised death rate]] for influenza in 2022 was reported in Austria, with 3.73 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants. The Netherlands (with 3.56 deaths from influenza per 100 000 inhabitants) and Belgium (with 3.07 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants) were the only other EU countries to report standardised death rates over 3.00. By contrast, there were 4 EU countries which reported fewer than 0.20 deaths from influenza per 100 000 inhabitants: Hungary (0.13), Slovakia (0.12), Romania (0.11) and Cyprus (where the lowest rate was recorded, at 0.10 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants). The standardised death rate for influenza was considerably higher among people aged 65 years or over than people aged less than 65 years. Among EU residents, the rate for older people was 7.01 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2022, compared with 0.19 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants among people aged less than 65 years. As for the population as a whole, Austria and the Netherlands reported the highest standardised death rates for influenza among those aged 65 years or over with, respectively, 18.00 and 16.41 deaths per 100 000 people aged 65 years or over. There were also double-digit standardised death rates for this age group in Belgium (14.43 deaths), France (11.53), Estonia (10.90) and Denmark (10.74). The lowest standardised death rates were recorded for people aged 65 years or over in Cyprus (0.00 deaths)Eurostat uses confidentiality rules when there are very few deaths in a group, to ensure that disseminated data are confidential. These data are noted with ':' and a 'c' indicator. Consequently, when expressed as standardised death rates, certain causes of death are reported as 0.0 per 100,000 people, even if there are a few cases, to ensure individuals can't be identified., Hungary (0.39), Romania (0.51) and Slovakia (0.62). In 2022, the standardised death rate from influenza among people aged less than 65 years was highest in the Netherlands (0.45), France (0.37), Estonia (0.36) and Belgium (0.32). There were no deaths from influenza among this younger age group in Malta or Slovakia. [[Image:Standardised death rate from influenza, 2022 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Standardised death rate from influenza, 2022
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hlth_cd_asdr2}}|alt=A high-low chart showing the standardised death rate per hundred thousand inhabitants from influenza. Data are analysed by age groups: the total, people aged less than 65 years and people aged 65 years or over. Data are shown for 2022 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=Influenza statistics_Health2025.xlsx|title=Influenza statistics: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''Key concepts''' The number of deaths from a particular cause of death can be expressed relative to the size of the population. A [[Glossary:Standardised_death_rate|standardised (rather than crude) death rate]] can be compiled which is independent of the age and sex structure of a population: this is done as most causes of death vary significantly by age and according to sex and the standardisation facilitates comparisons of rates over time and between countries. '''Influenza vaccinations''' This article presents data on influenza vaccinations, largely derived from administrative sources that are linked to vaccination programmes (see further information in the background article on the [[Healthcare_non-expenditure_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of healthcare non-expenditure statistics]]). For country specific notes on these data collections, please refer to the annexes at the end of the national metadata reports, which are accessible from links at the beginning of the {{Template:Esms|code=hlth_res_esms|title=European metadata report}}. The {{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-028|title=Healthcare non-expenditure statistics manual}} provides an overview of the classifications, both for mandatory variables and variables provided on a voluntary basis. '''''Vaccination programme data''''' The extent of influenza vaccinations is based on the percentage of people aged 65 years or over who have been immunised against influenza during the reference period (defined as 1 July to 30 June, which ended in the reference period). The vaccination rate is calculated by influenza season or by calendar year. Some countries may use European health interview (EHIS) survey data to calculate the vaccination rate for influenza; the last round of the EHIS was in 2019. Please see the table below for more information on sources. [[Image:Data sources for immunisation against influenza (among population aged 65 years or over), 2023_Health2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Data sources for immunisation against influenza (among population aged 65 years or over), 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat|alt=A table summarising the source, reference period and age range for data on influenza vaccinations. Information is shown for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Data for the EU are calculated using the reference year data for each EU country. If data are not available for a particular reference year, the most recent available data from the previous 5 reference years is used. The EU data are population-weighted averages. '''Causes of death''' This article also includes statistics on causes of death. These are documented in more detail in a background article on the [[Causes_of_death_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of causes of death statistics]]. This provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. The Eurostat causes of death data collection is based on confirmed death certificates established by medical experts assessing the underlying cause of death. There is a difference in the coding of cases of influenza deaths: these concern cases where influenza was the established underlying cause of death or where death occurred in someone who had influenza at or close to the time of death. There may be differences in how countries determined the underlying cause of death, particularly in cases where the deceased had multiple morbidities, or coinfections with other respiratory diseases (for example, COVID-19 or pneumonia); see the article on [[Respiratory_diseases_statistics|respiratory diseases statistics]] for more information. The significant decrease in influenza deaths in 2021 and increase in 2022 could be attributed, at least in part, to a combination of public health measures in 2021, such as enhanced vaccination strategies, social distancing, mask mandates and enhanced hygiene practices enacted to tackle the COVID-19 pandemic. It should also be taken into account that at the beginning of the pandemic, [https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/classification/icd/covid-19/guidelines-cause-of-death-covid-19-20200420-en.pdf?sfvrsn=35fdd864_2&download=true WHO guidelines] recommended the use of ICD-10 codes for COVID-19 for all deaths from clinically compatible illnesses and where COVID-19 contributed to the death; this may play a part in the underreporting of influenza deaths. For country-specific notes, please refer to the national metadata reports, which can be accessed through the links at the beginning of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/hlth_cdeath_sims.htm European metadata report]. ===Context=== Vaccination is vital for primary prevention and offers the most cost-effective, long-term strategy for reducing the burden of diseases across the EU. Immunisation through vaccination is the best available defence against serious, preventable, and sometimes deadly, contagious diseases. Thanks to widespread vaccination, smallpox has been eradicated, Europe made polio-free and many other diseases almost eliminated. That said, vaccination rates for various diseases are showing signs of decline across many EU countries, including for childhood vaccinations. Influenza is an annual, seasonal virus that affects Europe in the winter. The majority of people who die from influenza are aged 65 years or over, many of whom face other complications/illnesses, such as heart disease or chronic lung disease. During an influenza epidemic, there may be significant costs for health services (associated with caring for those who fall sick) and for businesses in general (lost production as a result of time taken off work). To help countries prepare their response to a likely increase of COVID-19 and influenza in the autumn and winter 2022/23, the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] published a [https://health.ec.europa.eu/publications/covid-19-preparing-autumn-winter-2023_en Communication] on preparing for this period, including recommendations to combine COVID-19 and influenza vaccination campaigns where possible. Integrating population-based surveillance systems for influenza, SARS-CoV-2 (the virus that causes the COVID-19 illness) and other respiratory viruses to monitor the spread and intensity of respiratory viruses is a key recommendation published by [https://www.who.int/europe/home WHO/Europe] in its [https://www.who.int/europe/news/item/19-07-2022-rapidly-escalating-covid-19-cases-amid-reduced-virus-surveillance-forecasts-a-challenging-autumn-and-winter-in-the-who-european-region strategy recommendations] to protect the most vulnerable. [https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC)] was set up to help strengthen Europe’s defences against infectious diseases, such as influenza, SARS, COVID-19 and HIV/AIDS. The ECDC works in partnership with national health protection bodies in Europe to develop continent-wide disease surveillance and early warning systems. [https://vaccination-info.eu/en The European Vaccination Information Portal (EVIP)] was developed by the ECDC, in partnership with the European Commission and the [https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/homepage European Medicines Agency (EMA)] and includes information of influenza vaccination. === Footnotes === ===Other articles=== '''Online publications''' *[[Health in
