title: Inland waterway freight transport - quarterly and annual data
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the inland waterway freight transport - quarterly and annual data. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 EU inland waterway freight transport fell by 3.0% in 2025 compared with 2024. Germany and the Netherlands dominated EU inland waterway transport in 2025 with 71.9% of the total. Self-propelled vessels dominated transport performance. ‘Metal ores’ was the largest goods category transported by inland waterways in 2025. This article presents the main annual and quarterly statistics on [[Glossary:Inland_waterway|inland waterway]] freight transport in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] and the [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate country]] Serbia. It includes quarterly and annual data for total transport and [[Glossary:Container|container]] transport, as well as annual data for transport by type of goods, type of transport, type of vessel, and type of dangerous goods. For more detailed statistics on inland waterway transport by type of goods, please refer to the Statistics Explained article [[Inland waterway freight transport statistics by type of goods]]. For more detailed statistics on inland waterway transport of containers, please refer to the Statistics Explained article [[Inland waterways - statistics on container transport]]. For more detailed statistics on inland waterway freight transport at regional level, please refer to the Statistics Explained article [[Inland waterway freight transport at regional level]]. === Inland waterway freight transport performance decreased by 3.0% in 2025 compared with 2024 === Activity in inland waterway transport was volatile during the period 2015-2025. Measured in [[Glossary:Tonne-kilometre|tonne-kilometres]], activity slightly decreased between 2015 and 2016 (-0.2%). A slight increase was observed in 2017 (+0.5%) followed by a sharp fall in 2018 (-10.9%) and an immediate rebound in 2019 (+6.6%) (Figure 1). In 2020, a decrease (-5.9%) was observed, while in 2021, a new rebound was registered with a 3.6% increase. In 2022, a sharp decline was recorded with a drop of 9.8%. In 2023, inland waterway freight transport performance reached the lowest point since data have been available for the EU (i.e. 2005). After the rebound observed in 2024 (+4.5%), a fall by 3.0% was observed in 2025, equivalent to a 3.7 billion tonne-kilometre reduction. When examining inland waterway transport activity measured in tonnes, a similar drop was recorded in 2025 (-3.1%), corresponding to a 14.9 million tonne reduction (Figure 5). Figure 1 At a quarterly level, movement was more erratic and no clear seasonal pattern can be identified (Figure 2). Some noticeable changes were observed over the period 2015-2025 when comparing with the same quarter of the previous year. In particular, the year 2018 showed a particularly sharp decline in Q4 (-25.3%), which was the highest registered during the period from 2015 to 2025. In contrast, Q4 2019 showed the highest increase in the period from 2015 to 2025 when compared with the same quarter of the previous year (+18.4%). In 2022, the decline in Q3 (-25.0%) was the second-largest recorded during the period from 2015 to 2025. It coincided with the lowest level of freight transport performance on EU inland waterways since Q1 2006, when quarterly EU data first became available. In 2025, decreases were observed in the first three quarters, while Q4 remained stable compared to the same quarter in 2024. The largest decrease in 2025 was observed in Q2 (-6.8%). Figure 2 The main contributors by far to EU inland waterway transport (in tonne-kilometres) in 2025 were Germany and the Netherlands. Transport on inland waterways in these 2 countries accounted for 71.9% of EU inland waterway transport (Figure 3). In 2025, transport on inland waterways (in tonne-kilometres) decreased in 12 out of the 16 EU countries for which data are available, compared with 2024. The highest decrease was recorded in Sweden (-50.8% or -91 million tonne-kilometres), followed by Austria (-20.4% or -266 million tonne-kilometres), Romania (-13.0% or -1.6 billion tonne-kilometres), Slovakia (-11.9% or -84 million tonne-kilometres), and Hungary (-10.2% or -157 million tonne-kilometres). In contrast, the largest increase compared with 2024 was recorded in Lithuania (+74.5%, or +5 million tonne-kilometres), followed by Czechia (+29.7%, or +4 million tonne-kilometres), Poland (+18.5%, or +5 million tonne-kilometres), and Finland (+5.8%, or +12 million tonne-kilometres). However, the large changes in percentage observed for these 4 countries should be interpreted within the context of their initially low values. [[Image:Inland waterway freight transport, 2015, 2024, and 2025 (billion tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|center|750px|Figure 3: Inland waterway freight transport, 2015, 2024, and 2025
''Source'': Eurostat - {{Stable link|title=|code=iww_go_atygo}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=iww_go_qnave}}|alt= A vertical bar chart showing inland waterway freight transport in 2015, 2024, and 2025 in some of the EU Member States and a candidate country. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at the type of transport at EU level, international transport accounted for more than half of the total transport in 2025 (54.7%) when expressed in tonne-kilometres (Figure 4). National transport accounted for 24.9% and transit transport for 20.4%. For 6 EU countries and the candidate country Serbia, international transport represented the highest share of transport. Austria (74.0%) and Germany (64.1%) had the highest shares of international transport in 2025. In Italy (2024 data), Lithuania, Finland, and Sweden, there was only national transport. In Czechia, Poland, and France, national transport was predominant (97.4%, 82.2%, and 60.2%, respectively). The 5 remaining countries had higher shares of transit transport, mainly due to their geographical position. Croatia recorded the highest share (97.2%), followed by Bulgaria (92.8%), Luxembourg (87.9%), Slovakia (83.0%), and Hungary (60.1%). Figure 4 When looking at the transport of freight in tonnes, the picture is quite similar to the one for tonne-kilometres, although there are some noticeable differences (Figure 5). All countries recorded decreases in 2025 compared with 2024, except for Lithuania (+60.5%), Czechia (+7.8%), Poland (+5.2%), Bulgaria (+0.5%), and the Netherlands (+0.1%). However, the large changes in percentages for Lithuania, Poland, and Czechia should be interpreted within the context of their low initial values. It should be noted that while Bulgaria and the Netherlands registered an increase in the transport of goods measured in tonnes (+0.5% and +0.1%, respectively), a decrease was observed in the transport of goods measured in tonne-kilometres (-5.7% and -0.3%, respectively). The largest relative drops in the number of tonnes transported were registered for Sweden (-52.2%), Romania (-12.3%), Slovakia (-11.9%), and Austria (-11.6%). However, the large changes in percentage for Sweden should be interpreted within the context of its low initial values. It should be noted that while Finland registered a decrease in the transport of goods measured in tonnes (-2.7%), an increase was observed in the transport of goods measured in tonne-kilometres (+5.8%). [[Image:Inland waterway freight transport, 2015, 2024, and 2025 (million tonnes).png|thumb|center|750px|Figure 5: Inland waterway freight transport, 2015, 2024, and 2025
''Source'': Eurostat - {{Stable link|title=|code=iww_go_atygo}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=iww_go_qnave}}|alt= A vertical bar chart with 3 bars showing inland waterway freight transport in 2015, 2024, and 2025 in million tonnes in the EU, some EU Member States, and a candidate country. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] At the EU level, the amount of freight transported on inland waterways was 1.0 tonnes [[Glossary:Per-capita|per inhabitant]] in 2025 (Figure 6). The Netherlands had the highest amount with 18.4 tonnes of freight transported per inhabitant, followed by Belgium (13.1), and Luxembourg (7.3). All other countries registered less than 2.6 tonnes of freight transported per inhabitant in 2025. [[Image:Inland waterway freight transport, 2015, 2024, and 2025 (tonnes per inhabitant).png|thumb|center|750px|Figure 6: Inland waterway freight transport, 2015, 2024, and 2025
''Source'': Eurostat - {{Stable link|title=|code=iww_go_atygo}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=iww_go_qnave}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_gind}}|alt= A vertical bar chart with 3 bars showing inland waterway freight transport in 2015, 2024, and 2025 in tonnes per inhabitant in the EU, some EU member States, and a candidate country. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === ‘Metal ores’ was the largest goods category transported by inland waterways === At EU level, the main types of goods (according to [[Glossary: NST_2007|NST_2007]] classification) transported in 2025 were ‘[[Glossary:Metal_ores|metal ores]]’, ‘coke and refined [[Glossary:Petroleum_products|petroleum products]]’, ‘chemicals, rubber and plastic, nuclear fuel’, and ‘products of agriculture’. These 4 categories accounted for 64.0% of all goods transport (in tonne-kilometres) on EU inland waterways (Figure 7). Compared with 2024, the largest changes in the share of the different goods types in total transport performance were recorded for ‘products of agriculture’ (which decreased by 2.3 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]], or pp) and ‘coal and crude petroleum’ (which increased by 1.3 pp). Figure 7 Transport performance (in tonne-kilometres) decreased substantially in 2025 compared with 2024 for ‘products of agriculture’ (-19.6%) (Figure 8). In contrast, the largest transport performance increase was observed for ‘coal and crude petroleum’ (+21.3%). Figure 8 === Self-propelled barges accounted for more than half of the total EU transport performance === In 2025, the vessel type ‘self-propelled barge’ was predominantly used for goods transport on EU inland waterways, accounting for more than half (51.6%) of the total EU transport performance based on tonne-kilometres (Figure 9). The transport performance using ‘self-propelled barges’ increased by 0.8% compared with 2024. The second- and third-most-used types of vessel were the ‘self-propelled tanker barge’ (24.5%), which decreased by 3.9%, and the ‘barge not self-propelled’ (20.5%), which decreased by 5.1%. Transport performance involving ‘other goods carrying vessel’ and ‘seagoing vessel’ decreased substantially by 39.0% and 21.0%, respectively, whereas transport performance involving ‘tanker barge not self-propelled’ increased by 8.8%. Figure 9 The vessel types ‘self-propelled barge’ and ‘barge not self-propelled’ accounted for the largest amount of goods transported in 2025 in all countries except Slovakia and Sweden (Figure 10). Together with ‘self-propelled tanker barges’, they accounted for between 94.8% and 100% of total transport in 12 out of the 15 EU countries for which data are available. Sweden was an exception, reporting only ‘seagoing vessels’. The other exceptions were Finland, where ‘seagoing vessels’ accounted for 45.6%, and Slovakia, where ‘other goods carrying vessels’ represented 74.2% Figure 10 === German-flagged vessels ranked among the top 3 nationalities in 6 out of 15 EU countries=== In 2025, vessels registered in Germany were among the 3 most common nationalities of freight transport vessels in 6 of the 15 EU countries for which data are available (Table 1). Although they did not rank first in any country, they placed second in Czechia, Germany and Austria, and third in Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Slovakia. Vessels registered in the Netherlands and Slovakia also appeared frequently, each ranking among the top 3 in 5 countries. Vessels registered in the Netherlands ranked first in Belgium, Germany, Luxembourg, and the Netherlands. Vessels registered in Belgium, Austria, and Romania each appeared among the top 3 in 4 countries, while vessels registered in France appeared in 2 countries. Finally, 4 other nationalities (vessels registered in Czechia, Poland, Finland, and Sweden) each appeared once. In 7 countries (Czechia, France, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Finland, and Sweden), the most common nationality of freight transport vessels was the country’s own. In Poland and Finland, all vessels performing freight transport were registered in their own country. By contrast, in Bulgaria, Croatia, Luxembourg, and Hungary, no vessels registered in their own country were among the top 3. In all countries, the cumulative share of the top 3 vessel nationalities was at least 59%; in 7 EU countries, it exceeded 88%, and in 6 EU countries, it exceeded 90%. [[Image:Top 3 vessel nationalities performing inland waterway freight transport in each Member State, 2025 (%, based on tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|center|750px|Table 1: Top 3 vessel nationalities performing inland waterway freight transport in each Member State, 2025
''Source'': Eurostat - {{Stable link|title=|code=iww_go_anave}}|alt= a table showing the top 3 vessel nationalities performing inland waterway freight transport in some EU member States and a candidate country, as a percentage based on tonne-kilometres. For each Member State, it shows the first, second, and third share of other Member States freight. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Container transport performance fell in 2025 by 1.3% compared with 2024 === The inland waterway transport of freight [[Glossary:Freight container|containers]] in the EU, measured in [[Glossary:Twenty-foot_equivalent_unit_(TEU)|20-foot equivalent unit-kilometre (TEU-kilometres)]], was relatively stable between 2015 and 2016 (-0.3%) (Figure 11). An increase was observed in 2017, reaching a new peak in container transport. In 2018, 2019, and 2020, 3 declines were recorded (-8.6%, -3.1%, and -4.9% compared with the previous year, respectively). In 2021, a rebound was observed with a 4.2% increase. In 2022, a substantial downturn was observed, by 8.2%. The downwards trend continued in 2023, with a 6.6% decrease. This led to the lowest volume (1 279 million TEU-kilometres) in container transport performance since 2009 (1 132 million TEU-kilometres). In 2024, a rebound was observed with a 3.7% increase, immediately followed by a decrease of 1.3% in 2025. Figure 11 Regarding the quarterly inland waterway transport of containers, an overall upward trend was visible from 2015 to mid-2018 (Figure 12). Strong increases were recorded in 2017, leading to a new peak in Q3 2017 (453 million TEU-kilometres). In 2018, considerable decreases were observed in Q3 and Q4 compared with the same quarters in 2017 (-12.2% and -30.4%, respectively). This led to a new low point in Q4 2018 (304 million TEU-kilometres). The year 2019 also started with sharp declines but ended with a strong increase in Q4 (+18.7%). In 2021, increases were observed in the first 2 quarters compared with the same quarters of 2020 (+3.5% and +19.6%, respectively), whereas there were declines in Q3 and Q4 2021 (-3.8% and -0.2%, respectively). In 2022, substantial decreases were recorded in all quarters, even if more moderate in Q2 (-2.9%): -6.6% in Q1, -12.5% in Q3, and -10.7% in Q4. In 2023, decreases were recorded in Q1, Q2, and Q4 when compared with the same quarters of the previous year (-2.3%, -12.6%, and -11.3%, respectively), while a slight increase was observed in Q3 (+0.6%). In 2025, increases were recorded in the first 2 quarters compared with the same quarters of the previous year (+4.6% and +0.7%, respectively), while decreases were recorded in the last 2 quarters (-4.7% and -5.4%, respectively). Figure 12 In 2024, the largest contribution to the transport of containers (in TEU-kilometres) came from the Netherlands, followed by Germany (Figure 13). Together, the 2 countries accounted for 88% of all EU container transport. It should be noted that 2 countries reported no transport of containers in 2015, 2024, and 2025: Czechia and Finland. In addition, Poland and Slovakia reported no transport of containers in both 2024 and 2025. Out of the 11 countries reporting container transport in 2025, 5 recorded growth compared with 2024. The highest increase was recorded in Austria (+587.3%), followed by Croatia (+473.3%), Bulgaria (+215.9%), and Hungary (+94.7%). In contrast, the highest decrease in container transport performance in 2025 was recorded by Romania (-77.7%), followed by Luxembourg (-61.6%), France (-11.8%), and Sweden (-10.1%). However, these large changes in percentages should be considered in relation to the low initial values for most of these countries. [[Image:Inland waterway transport of containers, 2015, 2024, and 2025_(million TEU-kilometres).png|thumb|center|750px|Figure 13: Inland waterway transport of containers, 2015, 2024, and 2025
''Source'': Eurostat - {{Stable link|title=|code=iww_go_actygo}}|alt= a vertical bar chart with 3 bars showing the inland waterway transport of containers in 2015, 2024, and 2025, in million TEU-kilometres, for some of the EU Member States. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at the loading status of containers (Figure 14), EU transport of loaded containers in 2025 accounted for more than two-thirds of total EU container transport (69.6%). Sweden was the country with the highest share of transport of loaded containers with 99.1%, followed by France (76.5%), Belgium (74.0%), Germany (71.1%), and the Netherlands (67.1%). Bulgaria, Croatia, and Austria recorded only transport of empty containers in 2025. The 3 remaining countries transported more empty containers than loaded ones: Hungary (99.9% of empty containers); Luxembourg (88.6%) and Romania (57.0%). Figure 14 === ‘Flammable liquids’ is the most transported dangerous goods category in EU inland waterways === The transport of dangerous goods is a voluntary data collection. In 2025, data on the transport of dangerous goods was reported by 7 out of 17 countries (Table 2). While it is still difficult to identify the types of dangerous goods transported at EU level due to lack of data for all EU countries, it can be observed that ‘flammable liquids’ was the main category in all the countries reporting such data. Overall, 'flammable liquids' accounted for 72.1% of the total tonnage of transported dangerous goods. Czechia reported no transport of dangerous goods in 2025. [[Image:Inland waterway transport of dangerous goods by type of dangerous goods, 2025 (thousand tonnes).png|thumb|center|750px|Table 2: Inland waterway transport of dangerous goods by type of dangerous goods, 2025
''Source'': Eurostat - {{Stable link|title=|code=iww_go_adago}}|alt= a table showing the inland waterway transport of dangerous goods by type of dangerous goods, in 2025, in thousand tonnes. The columns show 14 types of dangerous goods for some of the Member States. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=SE_Article_IWW_Quarterly-Annual_2026-07.xlsx|title=Inland waterway freight transport - quarterly and annual data: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== All figures presented in this article have been extracted from the [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] online inland waterways transport database. The related datasets are collected according to {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R0974:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 2018/974}} of the [[Glossary:European_Parliament_(EP)|European Parliament]] and of the Council on statistics of goods transport by inland waterways. Regulation (EU) No 2018/974 consolidated the initial {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32006R1365:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1365/2006}} on statistics of goods transport by inland waterways and all its implementing and amending legal acts: {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32007R0425:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EC) No 425/2007}} (implementing regulation), {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32007R1304:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EC) No 1304/2007}} (amending regulation) and {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32016R1954:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 2016/1954}} (amending regulation). Regulation (EU) 2018/974 states that data must be supplied by all Member States for which the total volume of goods transported annually by inland waterways exceeds 1 million tonnes. Currently, 17 Member States provide data on a mandatory or voluntary basis: Belgium (BE), Bulgaria (BG), Czechia (CZ), Germany (DE), France (FR), Croatia (HR), Italy (IT), Lithuania (LT), Luxembourg (LU), Hungary (HU), the Netherlands (NL), Austria (AT), Poland (PL), Romania (RO), Slovakia (SK), Finland (FI), and Sweden (SE). The legal act requires only the provision of a reduced annual dataset for countries exceeding the 1-million-tonne threshold but where no international or transit traffic exists. '''Definitions''' '''National inland waterway transport''': Inland waterway transport between 2 ports of a national territory irrespective of the nationality of vessel. '''International inland waterway transport''': Inland waterway transport between 2 ports located in different national territories. '''Transit inland waterway transport''': Inland waterway transport through a national territory between 2 ports both located in another national territory or national territories provided that in the total journey within the national territory there is no [[Glossary:Transshipment|transshipment]]. '''Calculation of EU aggregates''': In Figures 5 and 6, the EU international and total goods transport in tonnes is calculated excluding double counting. To achieve that, the EU total international transport is calculated by adding the international unloadings declared by the EU countries plus the international loading for which the unloading country is not in the EU. Then, the EU total transport is calculated by adding the national transport and the total international transport. For transit transport measured in tonnes, an EU aggregate equal to the sum of the country figures is not valid because volumes of freight transported are reported by all transit countries through which the transport takes place before reaching the unloading destination. Therefore, the same volume may be reported 2, 3, or more times without the possibility to eliminate multiple counting. At the same time, figures for transit transport are included in the EU national or international transport as they are reported not only by the transit countries but also by the loading and unloading countries. So, for the EU total volume of freight, it is enough to sum the total national and international figures. '''Annual changes in the EU aggregate''' In some instances, the calculation of annual changes for the EU in tonne-kilometres and/or tonnes and/or TEU-kilometres excludes data for countries where data were unavailable for one of the reference years, to ensure comparability over time. Occurrences include: *the calculation of the percentage change between 2015 and 2016, which excluded data reported by Sweden because data for 2015 were not available *the calculation of the percentage change between 2016 and 2017, which excluded data reported by Finland because data for 2017 were not available *the calculation of the percentage change between 2018 and 2019, which excluded data reported by Finland because data for 2018 were not available *the calculation of the percentage change between 2024 and 2025, which excluded data reported by Italy because data for 2025 were not available *the calculation of the percentage change in inland waterway transport of containers between 2021 and 2022, which excluded data reported by Sweden because data for 2021 were not available *the calculation of the percentage change in quarterly inland waterway transport of containers between 2024 and 2025, which excluded data reported by Croatia because transit data for 2024 were not available. '''Country-specific notes''' *Belgium: A break in time series can be observed in 2018 due to an improvement of the data collection system. However, the break in time series for Belgium has only a minor impact on the overall EU aggregate. *Bulgaria: Transit data supplied include Romanian national inland waterway transport data equivalent to Bulgarian transit transport. *Croatia: Quarterly transit transport data are not available until Q4 2024. *Italy: No data available for 2025. Data are delivered on a voluntary basis. Only a simplified annual dataset is provided. *Lithuania: Data are delivered on a voluntary basis. Only a simplified annual dataset is provided. *Hungary: Due to a methodological change, transit data are underestimated for Q3 2013 and are not comparable with the other quarters. *Romania: Transit data supplied include Bulgarian national inland waterway transport data equivalent to Romanian transit transport. *Finland: No data available for 2017 and 2018. Data are delivered on a voluntary basis. Only a simplified annual dataset was provided until 2016. *Sweden: Data were delivered on a voluntary basis until 2021. Only a simplified annual dataset was provided until 2021. *Serbia: Only quarterly data are currently available. Data available since 2018. '''Breakdown by group of goods''' The NST 2007 classification is available on the [[Glossary:Standard goods classification for transport statistics (NST)|Statistics Explained Glossary]]. '''Symbols''' *":" not available *"-" not applicable *"0" real zero ===Context=== The content of this statistical article is based on data collected within the framework of {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R0974:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 2018/974}} of the European Parliament and of the Council on statistics of goods transport by inland waterways. ===Other articles=== *[[Inland waterway freight transport statistics by type of goods]] *[[Inland waterways - title: Inequality in enlargement countries
text:
This article presents statistics on inequalities by gender and by education level, as well as income inequalities, in the EU and enlargement countries. It presents data for Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Kosovo, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, Türkiye and Ukraine, and compares these with the corresponding data for the EU. Data from April 2026 Planned article update July 2027 In 2025, the economic activity rate in Türkiye was 36.9 percentage points (pp) higher for men than for women, mainly due to the particularly low rate for women. This gender gap was about four times higher than in the EU (9.0 pp). Unemployment for men was higher than for women in North Macedonia 2020-2025. In 2025, the gender gap was -1.1 pp. Among the other enlargement countries, the highest gap was recorded in Bosnia and Herzegovina with 7.5 pp. Youth unemployment (age 15-24) was higher than among adults (age 25-74) in all enlargement countries in 2025. Bosnia and Herzegovina had the highest difference with 21.6 pp, Türkiye the lowest with 8.3 pp. This article is part of an [[Enlargement_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]]. It provides information on the [[Glossary:Candidate countries|enlargement countries]] and compares this information with the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. The data used in this article have all been submitted to and validated by Eurostat's subject matter units, following the same process as for the EU countries. For Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine, data on the indicators presented in this article are not yet transmitted according to this process and are therefore not yet available, except for data on life expectancy. However, data on Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are also presented in the [[European Neighbourhood Policy countries - statistical_overview|Statistics Explained articles for European Neighbourhood Policy – East]] countries; these articles are based on annual indicators supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country. Data shown for Georgia exclude the regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia over which the government of Georgia does not exercise control. The data managed by the National Bureau of Statistics of Moldova does not include data from the Transnistrian region over which the government of Moldova does not exercise control. Since 2014, data for Ukraine generally exclude the illegally annexed Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the City of Sevastopol and the territories which are not under control of the Ukrainian government. For Ukraine official statistics for 2022-2025 were not fully produced due to the martial law. It will gradually be produced and disseminated as defined by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine, taking into account the specific conditions of producing statistics during Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. This article presents statistics on differences between men and women, between people with different education levels and between youth and adults. It presents data on inequality with respect to: [[Glossary:Life expectancy|life expectancy]], [[Glossary:Activity rate|economic activity]] and [[Glossary:Unemployment|unemployment]] between men and women; unemployment between people with [[Glossary:Educational_attainment_level|different education levels]]; [[Glossary:Long-term_unemployment|long-term unemployment]] between men and women; and unemployment between youths and adults. The differences between groups are expressed in [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] for the indicators measured in shares of the population, and in years for life expectancy. In addition, [[Glossary:Income quintile share ratio|inequalities of the income distribution]] is analysed by comparing the highest household incomes with the lowest ones. Where a table or graph refers to a single reference year (for example, 2024), or where annual data are unavailable for certain countries, the most recent available data within the preceding five years are used. Where both the start and end years are intended to be shown but the corresponding data series are not available, data from the closest possible years are presented instead (for example, 2023 data instead of 2024). ===Life expectancy gender gap=== [[Glossary:Life expectancy|Life expectancy]] at birth is the average number of years a newborn child can expect to live if the current [[Glossary:Cause_of_death|mortality conditions]] do not change during the rest of their life. Differences in life expectancy between women and men may reflect disparities with respect to living conditions, access to health services, etc. The gender gap for life expectancy at birth is defined as the number of years that a newborn girl can expect to live minus the number of years a newborn boy can expect to live. Figure 1 presents the life expectancy gender gap for the enlargement countries and the EU over the period 2014-2024. In general, both the EU and all enlargement countries saw a drop in life expectancy at birth during 2020 and 2021 as a result of the Covid pandemic. In 2020, the decline was generally greater among men than among women, slightly widening the gender gap in all countries for which 2020 data are available. However, in 2021 the decreases for women were larger than for men in several countries, thus reversing this development somewhat. It should be noted that there was a break in the time series in 2024 for all enlargement countries for which 2024 data are available, as well as for the EU. In addition, there were breaks in the series for Serbia also in 2022 and 2023, and for North Macedonia in 2021. For the EU aggregate, there were breaks in the time series in most of the years of the period, reflecting corresponding breaks in one or more of the EU countries. The gap in life expectancy between women and men was greater in Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia than in the EU in the most recent years with available data. Women were expected to live 9.9 years longer than men in Ukraine (2019), 8.9 years in Moldova (2023) and 8.8 years in Georgia (2024). In Kosovo''This designation is without prejudice to positions on status, and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo Declaration of Independence.'', the gender gap was 5.7 years in 2016, the only data point available in the period. In comparison, women in the EU were expected to live 5.2 years longer than their male counterparts in 2024. In Türkiye, the life expectancy gender gap was almost equivalent to that of the EU, standing at 5.3 years, despite the overall life expectancy being 2.4 years less than in the EU for women and 2.5 years less for men. Albania had overall life expectancies for women and men even closer to those in the EU, but the gender gap was significantly lower, at 4.0 years in 2024. The other enlargement countries also recorded somewhat lower gaps than the EU. In 2024, the life expectancy gender gap was 4.9 years in Montenegro, 4.4 years in North Macedonia (2021) and 4.6 years in Serbia. From 2014 to 2024, the life expectancy gender gap fell from 5.8 to 5.2 years in the EU, despite slight increases in 2016 and during the Covid pandemic in 2020/2021. In the enlargement countries, the gender gap in life expectancy evolved unevenly over the period analysed, with some fluctuations across the time series. Between 2014 and 2024, the gap narrowed overall in Türkiye (from 5.5 to 5.3 years) and Serbia (from 5.2 to 4.6 years), despite some variation in-between. By contrast, the gap widened overall in Georgia (from 8.3 to 8.8 years), Albania (from 3.7 to 4.0 years) and Montenegro (from 4.8 to 4.9 years), although developments were not uniform over time. Data for Moldova and Kosovo are available for only one reference year each. [[Image:CPC26_Life expectancy gender gap, 2014-2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Life expectancy gender gap, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0b719900-596a-454b-be9f-58fdd240c108?lang=en demo_mlexpec])|alt= line chart showing the difference in life expectancy at birth between women and men, measured in years, in the EU and the enlargement countries from 2014 to 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Economic activity gender gap=== The economic activity gender gap is calculated as the [[Glossary:Activity rate|activity rate]] of men minus the activity rate of women. The economic activity rate is the percentage of active persons, including both employed and unemployed persons, in relation to the total population. Figure 2 shows the differences in economic activity rate between men and women in the enlargement countries and in the EU over the period 2015-2025. In all the enlargement countries for which these data are available, the economic activity gender gap was wider than in the EU. However, in the countries for which data are available for the whole period, the gap decreased, albeit with fluctuations around the main trend. It should be noted that, for all participating countries, there was a break in the time series in connection with the introduction of a [[EU_Labour_Force_Survey_-_new_methodology_from_2021_onwards|new methodology for the EU Labour Force Survey]] from reference year 2021 on. Data for Albania, Georgia, Kosovo, Moldova and Ukraine are not available. In 2025, men's activity rates in the enlargement countries were relatively close to the rate in the EU, at between 1.4 and 5.0 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] lower. Women's activity rates in the enlargement countries were much lower than for men in 2025, despite having risen from 2015. Throughout the period 2015-2025, Türkiye's gender gap was about four times greater than that of the EU, primarily attributable to the particularly low female activity rate. However, Türkiye achieved the largest decrease in the activity rate gender gap among the enlargement countries, with its activity rate gap dropping from 42.1 pp in 2015 to 36.9 pp in 2025, despite a minor uptick in 2020. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the gender gap was 24.7 pp in 2021 (the oldest data available), rising slightly to 24.9 pp in 2025. In North Macedonia, it fell from 25.5 pp in 2015 to 20.5 pp in 2025, despite fluctuations that reached a peak at 27.0 pp in 2016. In Serbia, the gender gap was relatively modest compared with the other enlargement countries, with the difference in activity rate decreasing from 16.0 pp in 2015 to 11.4 pp in 2025. A relatively moderate gender gap was recorded also in Montenegro, increasing from 11.4 pp in 2015 to 13.6 pp in 2020 (more recent data not available), with a peak at 15.1 pp in 2018. In comparison, in the EU the gender gap in economic activity rate decreased gradually from 11.6 pp in 2015 to 9.0 pp in 2025. [[Image:CPC26_Economic activity gender gap, 2015-2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Economic activity gender gap, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ca272ee8-a98a-4b04-bc58-045b58324022?lang=en lfsa_argan])|alt= line chart showing the difference in economic activity rate between men and women, measured in percentage points, in the EU and the enlargement countries from 2015 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Unemployment gender gap === The [[Glossary:Unemployment|unemployment]] rate is the percentage of persons in the [[Glossary:Labour_force|labour force]] that are currently unemployed but actively seeking work. The current section focuses on the difference in unemployment of men and women in the adult population aged 25-74. The gender gap is calculated as the unemployment rate for women minus the corresponding rate for men. Figure 3 presents the gender gap between the unemployment rates of men and women for the enlargement countries and the EU over the period 2015-2025. In the enlargement countries, as well as in the EU, unemployment was lower in 2025 than it had been in 2015, both for men and women. Overall, the difference between men and women fluctuated more in the enlargement countries than in the EU. For all participating countries, there was a break in the time series for unemployment from 2020 to 2021 in connection with the introduction of a new methodology for the EU Labour Force Survey from reference year 2021 on. North Macedonia stood out among the enlargement countries by having negative gender gaps throughout most of the period. The unemployment rate for women consistently remained below that of men from 2015 to 2025, except in 2019 when the unemployment rate for women exceeded that for men by 1.7 pp. Bosnia and Herzegovina recorded by far the highest unemployment gender gap among the enlargement countries throughout 2021–2025, i.e. according to the new EU-LFS methodology. Data prior to 2021 are not available for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Whereas the unemployment rates for both women and men more than halved between 2015 and 2025 in North Macedonia and Serbia, Türkiye recorded the lowest declines for both women and men among the enlargement countries. Türkiye’s unemployment gender gap fluctuated throughout the period, overall rising from 2.5 pp in 2015 to 3.3 pp in 2025. In Serbia, the unemployment gap experienced a short period of narrowing before a modest increase; however, the overall trajectory has been one of steady reduction, culminating in its lowest recorded levels (0.8 pp) in 2024 and 2025. Between 2015 and 2020, the gender gap in unemployment in Montenegro was moderate, but fluctuated somewhat between -1.0 pp (2016) and 1.6 pp (2017). In the most recent year available, 2020, the unemployment gender gap stood at 0.8 pp. The EU reported a relatively stable and modest gender gap, fluctuating between 0.5 pp and 0.8 pp throughout the period, with the most recent value at 0.5 pp in 2025. [[Image:CPC26_Unemployment gender gap, 2015-2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Unemployment gender gap, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5e33c619-3f21-47e6-adfe-fa21d80d7973?lang=en lfsa_urgan])|alt= line chart showing the difference in unemployment rate between men and women, measured in percentage points, in the EU and the enlargement countries from 2015 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Unemployment rate by education level === The unemployment rate with respect to the [[Glossary:Educational_attainment_level|highest level of education completed]] is analysed in Figure 4, presenting data for 2015 and 2025. The levels of education are defined by the [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|International standard classification of education (ISCED)]]: low (having completed ‘less than primary’, primary or lower secondary education), medium (upper secondary and post-secondary non tertiary) and high (tertiary) level of education. For all participating countries, there was a break in the time series for unemployment from 2020 to 2021, in connection with the introduction of a new methodology for the EU Labour Force Survey from reference year 2021 on. In general, the chart shows, with few exceptions, that the higher the level of education, the lower the unemployment. In 2025, Bosnia and Herzegovina recorded an unemployment rate of 21.4% among persons with low education, the highest rate among the enlargement countries. This figure was nearly twice that of persons with medium education (10.9%) and three times higher than for persons with high education (7.1%). Data for Bosnia and Herzegovina are not available for 2015. In North Macedonia, there was a significant drop (roughly 50%) in the unemployment rates for all three levels of education between 2015 and 2025: from 29.9% to 15.6% for persons with low education, from 23.7% to 10% for persons with medium education and from 18.9% to 7.3% for persons with a high education. Serbia observed similar decreases in the unemployment rates, except for people with low education, starting from already relatively low levels in 2015. Between 2015 and 2025, the rates fell from 15.8% to 13.6% for persons with low education, from 17.1% to 8.1% for persons with medium education and from 14.3% to 5.8% for persons with high education. Türkiye had the lowest unemployment rates among the enlargement countries in 2015: 8.9% for persons with low education, 9.1% for medium education and 8.3% for high education. The rates were slightly lower in 2025, with rates of 7.0% (low education), 8.0% (medium education) and 7.1% (high education). It is notable that in Türkiye, there were no significant differences in unemployment rates with respect to education level. In Montenegro, the unemployment rates in 2015 were 28.7% for low education, 16.8% for medium education and 9.4% for high education. However, data are not available for 2025. Between 2015 and 2025, unemployment rates in the EU decreased from moderate to lower levels. For persons with low education, the rate dropped from 17.4% to 10.8%. Those with medium education saw rates fall from 7.9% to 4.8%, while for individuals with high education, unemployment declined from 5.8% to 3.6%. In 2025, the unemployment rates for persons with medium and high education were lower in the EU than in any of the enlargement countries with available data. For persons with low educational attainment, however, the EU unemployment rate remained higher than in Türkiye. [[Image:CPC26_ Unemployment rate by education level, 2015 and 2025_.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Unemployment rate by education level, 2015 and 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a9e0677f-b048-4155-b8b5-0ac76ba094c0?lang=en lfsa_urgaed])|alt= bar chart showing the unemployment rate by education level of persons aged 24-65, in the EU and the enlargement countries in 2015 and in 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Long-term unemployment gender gap === [[Glossary:Long-term_unemployment|Long-term unemployment]] refers to unemployed persons who have been actively seeking employment for one year or more. Long-term unemployment data is an important indicator for structural problems in the labour market. The gender gap is calculated as the long-term unemployment rate for women minus that for men. Figure 5 shows the development in the gender gap in long-term unemployment in the enlargement countries and the EU over the period 2015-2025. Long-term unemployment declined more in the enlargement countries than in the EU, for both men and women, but stayed higher overall. The exception was Türkiye, where long-term unemployment was lower than in the EU during most of the period 2015-2025, at least for men. Gender differences in long-term unemployment varied across the enlargement countries but remained nearly zero in the EU. For all participating countries, there was a break in the time series for unemployment from 2020 to 2021, in connection with the introduction of a new methodology for the EU Labour Force Survey from reference year 2021 on. Long-term unemployment in Bosnia and Herzegovina fell from 2021 to 2025; data before 2021 are not available. However, long-term unemployment among women was significantly higher than for men in Bosnia and Herzegovina during this period, thus the gender gap remained significantly higher than in any of the other enlargement countries. The long-term unemployment gender gap ranged between 5.4 pp in 2023 and 7.0 pp in 2025. In Türkiye, where long-term unemployment rates remained notably low, the gap fluctuated, reaching its lowest point at 1.6 pp in 2025 and peaking at 2.8 pp in 2019. Long-term unemployment in Serbia dropped significantly, especially among women, reducing the gender gap from 3.0 pp in 2015 to just 0.6 pp by 2025. There was a substantial reduction in long-term unemployment in North Macedonia. Nonetheless, the rate of long-term unemployment among men exceeded that of women throughout the period, except in 2019 when the rates were equal. This resulted in generally negative gender gaps, with the widest gap at -3.0 pp in 2021. Between 2015 and 2020, the gender gap in long-term unemployment in Montenegro fluctuated, ranging from -1.0 pp in 2016 to 1.2 pp in 2020. More recent data are not available for Montenegro. From 2015 to 2025, long-term unemployment rates for both men and women dropped nearly simultaneously in the EU, going from 4.9% for both genders in 2015 to 2.0% for women and 1.8% for men in 2025. The difference between the genders fluctuated slightly, staying between 0.0 pp (2015) and 0.3 pp (2021). [[Image:CPC26_Long-term unemployment gender gap, 2015-2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Long-term unemployment gender gap, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e2bea94c-3629-434d-932d-ebdb48ac1694?lang=en une_ltu_a])|alt= line chart showing the difference in long-term unemployment rate between men and women, measured in percentage points, in the EU and the enlargement countries from 2015 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Inequality of the income distribution === The [[Glossary:income quintile share ratio|income quintile share ratio]], also known as the S80/S20 ratio, measures income inequality by comparing the total income of the top 20% of earners (the top [[Glossary:quintile|quintile]]) to that of the bottom 20% of earners (the bottom quintile). Figure 6 presents the trend in the S80/S20 ratio in the enlargement countries and the EU over the period 2015-2025. Overall, income inequality decreased in both the enlargement countries and the EU. However, the ratio declined from a higher starting point and at a faster rate in the enlargement countries. In the EU, the income inequality ratio fell more slowly, with only minor fluctuations, from an already low level of 5.2 in 2015 to 4.7 in 2024 (2025 data not available). Kosovo reported by far the highest S80/S20 ratio observed, at 15.6 in 2018; this is the only available data point for Kosovo. In Türkiye, this income inequality indicator rose over the period, but with notable fluctuations. Overall, the inequality ratio increased from 8.6 in 2015 to 8.9 in 2025. Except for Kosovo’s single observation, Türkiye consistently had the highest S80/S20 ratio among the enlargement countries since 2018. From 2015 to 2017, Serbia had the highest S80/S20 ratio. However, its income distribution inequality ratio experienced a significant decline, dropping from its peak of 11.0 in 2016 — the highest recorded among the enlargement countries, except for Kosovo in 2018 — to below 6.0 in the most recent years. In 2024, the ratio stood at 5.6. Income inequality in Montenegro declined over the period, with the S80/S20 ratio decreasing from 7.5 in 2015 to 5.6 in 2022, the most recent data available. North Macedonia also experienced a reduction in income inequality, with the S80/S20 ratio falling from 6.6 in 2015 to 5.6 in 2023 (the most recent data available). There was a break in the time series for North Macedonia in 2021. For Albania, data on income inequality is available only for the period from 2017 to 2023, showing a significant decrease, with the S80/S20 ratio reduced from 7.5 to 4.9. [[Image:CPC26_Inequality of income distribution, 2015-2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Inequality of income distribution, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/873c145b-0001-43c3-b470-e940aff8f4b0?lang=en ilc_di11])|alt= line chart showing inequality of the income distribution, measured through the income quantile share ratio S80/S20, in the EU and the enlargement countries from 2015 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Unemployment gap between youths and adults === The unemployment gap between economically active young people (‘youths’), aged 15-24, and the rest of the active population (‘adults’), aged 25-74, is calculated as the unemployment rate of youths minus the rate of adults. The development in the gap between the unemployment rates of youths and adults over the period 2015-2025 is presented in Figure 7. From 2015 to 2025, young and adult unemployment rates were generally higher in enlargement countries — excluding Türkiye — than in the EU. During this period, unemployment for both groups declined across all enlargement countries and within the EU. Between 2015 and 2025, the unemployment rate of young people was consistently higher than that of adults in both the enlargement countries and in the EU, highlighting ‘youth unemployment’ as a specific concern. Serbia experienced a significant reduction in the unemployment gap between youths and adults, which fell from 27.5 pp in 2015 to 15.7 percentage points by 2025, with the most notable decrease occurring between 2015 and 2016. North Macedonia also saw an overall decline, moving from 23.5 pp in 2015 to 19.5 pp in 2025, although this trend was marked by frequent fluctuations. A major shift occurred between 2018 and 2019, with the unemployment age gap falling by -7.0 pp. In Türkiye, unemployment rates for both young and adult populations rose during the early part of the period, then later decreased. The gap between these groups shifted from 9.9 pp in 2015 to 14.0 pp in 2020, before dropping to 8.3 pp by 2025. In Montenegro, the unemployment age gap decreased from 22.2 pp in 2015 to 11.3 pp in 2019. However, it rose to 20.1 pp in 2020, primarily due to a significant increase in youth unemployment. Data for the years 2021 to 2025 are not available. The EU experienced a steady reduction in the unemployment age gap, with the difference in unemployment rates between young people and adults decreasing from 12.9 pp in 2015 to 10.1 pp by 2025. [[Image:CPC26_Unemployment gap between youths and adults, 2015-2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Unemployment gap between youths and adults, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1f57ed3f-484f-416a-9ad7-14f426ee65a2?lang=en lfsa_urgan])|alt= line chart showing the difference in unemployment rate between youths aged 15-24 and adults aged 25-74, measured in percentage points, in the EU and the enlargement countries from 2015 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== {{Template:Excel|filename=CPC26_Inequality_V2b_.xlsx|title=Enlargement countries - Inequality: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data in income disparities used in this article are mainly derived from [[Glossary:EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]], which is the main source of statistics that measure income and living conditions in Europe. Among the enlargement countries, Türkiye started the full implementation of EU-SILC in 2006, while North Macedonia launched it in 2010, Montenegro and Serbia in 2013, Albania in 2017, Kosovo in 2018 and Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2022. The main source for European labour force statistics is the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|European Union labour force survey (EU LFS)]]. This [[Glossary:Household|household]] survey is carried out in all EU Member States in accordance with European legislation and provides figures at least every quarter. It should be noted that, for all participating countries, there is a break in the EU-LFS time series in connection with the introduction of a [[EU_Labour_Force_Survey_-_new_methodology_from_2021_onwards|new methodology for the EU Labour Force Survey]] from reference year 2021. Among the enlargement countries, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia and Türkiye have implemented the EU-LFS instrument and conduct the labour force survey according to the same guidelines, methodology and standards as the EU countries. While basic principles and institutional frameworks for producing statistics are already in place, the enlargement countries are expected to increase the volume and quality of their data progressively, and to transmit these data to Eurostat in the context of the EU enlargement process. EU standards in the field of statistics require the existence of a statistical infrastructure based on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/quality/european-quality-standards/european-statistics-code-of-practice principles] such as professional independence, impartiality, relevance, confidentiality of individual data and easy access to official statistics; they cover methodology, classifications and standards for production. Eurostat assesses and supports the alignment of statistical production in the enlargement countries with the EU acquis in the field of statistics. Eurostat supports the national statistical offices and other producers of official statistics through a range of initiatives, such as statistical projects, training courses, traineeships, study visits, workshops and seminars, and participation in meetings within the [[Glossary:European statistical system (ESS)|European Statistical System (ESS)]]. The ultimate goal is the provision of harmonised, high-quality data that conforms to European and international standards. ===Context=== This article presents a selection of indicators relevant to analysing inequalities between different sections of society, based on the policy relevance of the indicators as well as the availability of data. The indicators presented highlight in particular differences in the situation between women and men (i.e. [[Gender statistics|gender gaps]]) with respect to life expectancy and opportunities in the labour market, as well as inequalities between persons with different education levels with respect to unemployment and inequalities in the distribution of income within the enlargement counties and the EU. The [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/european-pillar-social-rights-building-fairer-and-more-inclusive-european-union_en European Pillar of Social Rights] lays down the key principles and rights essential for fair and well-functioning labour markets and social protection systems. The [[Glossary:Open method of coordination (OMC)|open method of coordination (Social OMC)]] for social protection and social inclusion aims to promote social cohesion and equality through adequate, accessible and financially sustainable social protection systems and social inclusion policies. Additional information on statistical cooperation with the enlargement countries is provided in the Statistics explained background article [[Enlargement policy and statistical cooperation]]. ===
