title: Inland transport infrastructure at regional level
text:
EU statistics are provided on the inland transport network of the EU, EFTA and Candidate Countries: motorways, railways and inland waterways. Data extracted in March 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 Between 2014 and 2024, 3 Spanish regions, 1 Slovakian, 2 Czechian, 1 Irish, 1 Italian and 1 Bulgarian region had the largest expansion of motorways in the EU. In 2024, the highest motorway densities were found in regions of Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium, as well as in the capital regions of Hungary, Spain, Czechia, Croatia and Austria. In 2024, 2 German regions had the highest railway line density (above 600 km/1 000 km²), while 3 regions of Greece had the lowest (below 10 km/1 000 km²). In 2024, the 20 EU regions with the highest inland waterway density included 12 regions in the Netherlands. [[Image: Motorway density, by regions, 2024_v4.png|thumb|center|600px|''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8428e45b-bd1f-4c67-a434-a331240dd8da?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-09T13:44:10Z tran_r_net])|alt= Map showing motorway density by regions in the EU Member States and available EFTA and enlargement countries. Each country is labelled based on the range of kilometres of motorways per thousand square kilometres for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article presents recent data on the inland transport network of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|Candidate Countries]], covering [[Glossary:Motorway|motorways]], [[Glossary:Railway|railways]] and [[Glossary:Inland waterway|inland waterways]]. The evolution of the transport network is closely linked to the general development of the economy. This is particularly true for goods transport and, to a lesser extent, for passenger transport. === The densest motorway networks are located around capitals and key economic hubs === The EU has one of the densest transport networks in the world. This reflects a number of factors, including population density and transport demand. Transport demand is particularly high in urban and other densely populated areas, industrial areas and main seaports. In 2024, the highest motorway densities were found in regions of Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium as well as in the capital region of Hungary, Austria, Spain, Czechia and Croatia. (see Table 1). [[Image: Motorway density, the 20 regions with the highest density, NUTS 2 regions, 2024.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Motorway density, the 20 regions with the highest density, 2024 (EU, ''EFTA and Candidate Countries'')
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/07d743f8-923f-455f-8798-cfb47aa05978?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-10T15:20:45Z tran_r_net])|alt= Table showing motorway density as kilometres of motorways per thousand square kilometres in the 20 NUTS 2 regions of the EU Member States, EFTA and Candidate Countries with the highest density for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Linking the length of motorways to the area of the regions gives a good picture of the motorway infrastructure and density within the EU (see Map 1). The highest motorway densities are found around European capitals and other big cities, in large industrial conurbations and around major seaports. Most European capitals and large cities are surrounded by a ring of motorways in order to meet the high demand for road transport in metropolitan areas. In 2024, dense motorway networks could be found in regions around capitals: Budapest (120 km/1 000 km2), Wien (109 km/1 000 km2), Madrid (92 km/1 000 km2), Berlin (86 km/1 000 km2), Praha (82 km/1 000 km2) and Zagreb (76 km/1 000 km2). Region sizes vary across the EU with some capitals being designated as [[Glossary:Nomenclature_of_territorial_units_for_statistics_(NUTS)|NUTS 2]] regions themselves, such as Wien, whereas other capitals are parts of a larger NUTS 2 region, such as Paris being part of the Île-de-France region. As a consequence, small capital regions might have higher motorway densities compared with larger regions that include a capital. For example, the motorway density of the small Wien region is higher than the density of the large Île-de-France region, even though Paris has a larger motorway network than Wien. In 2024, other densely populated regions with high motorway density included Zuid-Holland (134 km/1 000 km2) and Utrecht (124 km/1 000 km2), 2 regions in the western part of the Netherlands of high economic importance. High motorway densities were also found around major seaports of northern Europe: the motorway densities of the NUTS 2 regions of Bremen (169 km/1 000 km2) with the port of Bremerhaven, of Zuid-Holland with the port of Rotterdam (134 km/1 000 km2) and of Hamburg (104 km/1 000 km2) were among the highest of all European regions. Another reason for the high density of the motorway network in some central Europe countries (such as Germany) is the proportionately high volume of transit freight traffic. The density of motorways on islands is generally low, as islands cannot be reached directly by road. Instead, they rely on sea or air transport. Even so, the motorway density of the region of Canarias appeared relatively high at 39 km/1 000 km2 in 2024. [[Image: Motorway density, by regions, 2024_v4.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 1: Motorway density, by regions, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8428e45b-bd1f-4c67-a434-a331240dd8da?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-09T13:44:10Z tran_r_net])|alt= Map showing motorway density by regions in the EU Member States and available EFTA and enlargement countries. Each country is labelled based on the range of kilometres of motorways per thousand square kilometres for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In terms of motorway expansion, between 2014 and 2024 the most significant expansion took place in certain regions of Spain: extensive motorway segments (between 131 and 242 kilometres) were built in the south and north of Spain, reflecting still the results of Spain's ambitious road building programme that started in the 1990s. Slovakian, Turkish, Czech, Irish, Bulgarian and Italian regions also show significant network expansions (see Figure 1). [[Image: Motorway expansion between 2014 and 2024, the 15 regions with the highest expansion, NUTS 2 regions_(km of motorways).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Motorway expansion between 2014 and 2024, the 15 regions with the highest expansion, NUTS 2 regions (EU, EFTA and Candidate Countries)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/80404eed-4703-437d-9447-9909a4be8f32?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-09T13:25:38Z tran_r_net])|alt= Horizontal bar chart showing motorway expansion between the years 2014 and 2024 as kilometres of motorways in the 15 regions of the EU Member States, EFTA and Candidate Countries with the highest expansion. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In more detail, the most significant motorway expansion between 2014 and 2024 took place in Andalucia in south Spain (242 km), closely followed by the region of Istanbul in Türkiye (240 km). At the third place, the Slovakian region of Stredné Slovensko had motorway expansion of 214 km. Castilla y León (191 km) and Galicia (131 km), 2 Spanish northwest regions also appeared in the top 15 for motorway expansion (see Figure 1), as well as 2 regions in Czechia (Střední Čechy and Střední Morava). The Eastern and Midland region of Ireland, as well as the regions of in Bulgaria and of Veneto in Italy were also among the top 15 the noticeable increases in many regions of eastern EU countries could be explained by the very limited motorway networks in these regions at the beginning of the century and the considerable investments that followed, often co-funded by the European Regional Development Fund and Cohesion Fund. Apart from the aforementioned region of Istanbul, the Candidate Country Türkiye was listed in the top 15 with 5 other regions, with expansions ranging between 134 km (Izmir) and 195 km (Kocaeli, Sakarya, Düzce, Bolu, Yalova). ===Highest railway line density often in capital regions and around transport hubs === Railway line density is especially high in the regions of Germany, Czechia and Hungary (see Map 2). Unsurprisingly, high rail density ratios were observed in capital regions, such as Berlin, Budapest, Praha, Bucuresti-Ilfov and Île-de-France (which includes Paris) where network nodes have developed. Regional rail density is also driven by the presence of economic activities such as heavy industries or seaport infrastructures. In 2024, the density of railway lines was high in western and central parts of Europe and lower in the peripheral areas. The highest network densities, above 300 km/1 000 km2, could be found in 3 regions in Germany, 1 in Hungary and 1 in Czechia, followed by 28 other EU regions in Belgium (data at NUTS 0 level), Czechia, Poland, Germany, Romania, France, Croatia, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovakia, and Luxembourg (above 100 km/1 000 km2). Looking at individual regions, the densest railway networks in 2024 were observed in 2 German regions: Berlin (764 km/1 000 km2) and Hamburg (639 km/1 000 km2). These regions were followed by Budapest (484 km/1 000 km2), Praha (433 km/1 000 km2) and Bremen (389 km/1 000 km2). Hamburg and Bremen are 2 smaller NUTS 2 regions where extensive freight lines to and from seaports contribute to a high density. Freight transport railway lines also played a leading role in several regions where coal and steel industries have long remained predominant, such as the Saarland region in western Germany (136 km/1 000 km2) and Śląskie in southern Poland (156 km/1 000 km2). [[Image: Railway line density, by regions, 2024_v2.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 2: Railway line density, by regions, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4d4610dc-4871-4b8b-aae7-8d84da97ac82?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-09T13:48:37Z tran_r_net])|alt= Map showing the railway line density by regions in the EU Member States and available EFTA and enlargement countries. Each country is labelled based on the range of kilometres of railway lines per thousand kilometres for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Focusing on railway infrastructure at country level, there are significant differences among countries with respect to the share of the network that were electrified in 2024 (see Figure 2). Luxembourg (97%), Belgium (88%), Sweden and Bulgaria (75%), the Netherlands and Austria (74%), Italy (73%), and Portugal (71%) registered the highest shares, while Ireland, and the [[Glossary:Baltic_states|Baltic States]] were the only EU countries where less than 20% of the network was electrified in 2024. [[Image: Share of electrified lines in total railway network length, 2024_(%).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Share of electrified lines in total railway network length, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cee3a0fa-72f4-4c62-9284-bbc1e0954cb9?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-09T13:54:21Z tran_r_net])|alt= Horizontal bar chart showing share of electrified lines in total railway network length as percentages for individual EU Member States some EFTA and Candidate Countries for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Very high density of inland waterways in the Netherlands === Inland waterway transport concerns mainly goods transport. This network is unequally spread over the EU, with some regions completely lacking navigable inland waterways and others having a very long waterway system, such as the regions of the Netherlands. In the Netherlands, while the Rhine delta constitutes a natural feature for inland navigation, for most regions man-made canals constitute the main share of navigable inland waterways. A very high density of more than 200 km/1 000 km2 was observed in 7 regions of the Netherlands: Zuid-Holland (318 km/1 000 km2), Zeeland (304 km/1 000 km2), Friesland (300 km/1 000 km2), Utrecht (282 km/1 000 km2), Noord-Holland (281 km/1 000 km2), Groningen (268 km/1 000 km2) and Flevoland (238 km/1 000 km2) (see Table 2). The lowest density in the Netherlands was registered in the Drenthe region (75 km/1 000 km2), which still ranked 12th amongst all regions for which data were available. A part of this dense inland waterway network plays a strategic role for freight transport between both the ports of Rotterdam (located in the Zuid-Holland region) and Amsterdam (Noord-Holland) and regions in Germany and Belgium. [[Image: Inland waterway density (navigable canals, rivers and lakes), the 20 EU regions with the highest density, NUTS 2 regions, 2024_v3.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 2: Inland waterway density (navigable canals, rivers and lakes), the 20 EU regions with the highest density, NUTS 2 regions, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/91459ba4-aa4a-48a4-a2dc-4217599375aa?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-09T14:12:09Z tran_r_net]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/11df8361-271d-4c12-a609-ebbb2b9951d8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-09T14:17:14Z reg_area3])|alt= Table showing inland waterway density in navigable canals, rivers and lakes as kilometres of inland waterways per thousand square kilometres in the 20 NUTS 2 regions of the EU Member States, with the highest density for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Out of the top 20 regions with the highest density, 4 belonged to France: Nord-Pas-de-Calais (55 km/1 000 km2 - essentially composed of canals and rivers), Île-de-France (53 km/1 000 km2 – dominated by rivers), Alsace (41 km/1 000 km2 – largely composed of rivers and canals), and Picardie (34 km/1 000 km2). The network in most French regions is a mix between rivers and canals, except for Champagne-Ardenne, Picardie, Haute-Normandie, Basse-Normandie, Centre — Val de Loire, Midi-Pyrénées, Auvergne and Lorraine where canals take a 100% share, in contrast to Poitou-Charentes where the inland waterways are entirely composed of rivers. Other regions with a dense inland waterway network were found in Czechia (Praha: 65 km/1 000 km2), Hungary (Budapest: 57 km/1 000 km2), Croatia (Panonska Hrvatska: 40 km/1 000 km2) and Finland (Länsi-Suomi: 35 km/1 000 km2). [[Image: Inland waterway density (navigable canals, rivers and lakes), EU NUTS 2 regions, 2024_v2.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 3: Inland waterway density (navigable canals, rivers and lakes), EU NUTS 2 regions, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/91459ba4-aa4a-48a4-a2dc-4217599375aa?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-09T14:12:09Z tran_r_net]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/11df8361-271d-4c12-a609-ebbb2b9951d8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-09T14:17:14Z reg_area3])|alt= Table showing inland waterway density in navigable canals, rivers and lakes as kilometres of inland waterways per thousand square kilometres by NUTS 2 region of the EU Member States for the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= Inland_transp_infra_at_regional_level_2026_v4.xlsx |title=Inland transport infrastructure at regional level - graphs and tables}} === Data sources === [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] collects regional statistics on the infrastructure of road, railways and inland waterways, as well as vehicle stocks and road accidents. The data are provided on a voluntary basis by the EU Member States, [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] countries and some [[Glossary:Candidate countries|Candidate Countries]]. The data are collected at NUTS 0, NUTS 1 and NUTS 2 levels. ''Density calculation'' The reference area for the calculation of motorway and railway line density is the land area of the regions (e.g. excluding lakes and rivers): this is the area where such infrastructure can be built; the reference area for the calculation of inland waterway density is the total area of the regions (e.g. area including lakes and rivers). Land area data for several regions in Norway, as well as for Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia are not available in the dataset: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/reg_area3/default/table?lang=en Area by NUTS 3 region]. As a result, indicators expressed per thousand square kilometres (such as the densities in Table 1, Map 1, Figure 1, Map 2, Table2 and Table 3) are not available for these 2 countries and some regions. ''Rankings in figures and tables'' As the data collection is performed on a voluntary basis, data are not available for some countries; consequently, the rankings presented are based on the available data and they should be analysed with caution. ''Country coverage'' *Motorways: 2024 data on the length of the motorway network are not available for Bosnia and Herzegovina, Albania, and Serbia. In certain cases, 2023 data have been used, as mentioned in the footnotes. A certain number of countries do not feature a motorway network: Malta, Latvia, Iceland and Liechtenstein. *Railways: Data for NUTS2 regions in Denmark, Germany, Lithuania, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia are not available. A certain number of countries do not feature a rail network: Cyprus, Malta and Iceland. Albania and Kosovo* have no electrified railways. *Inland waterways: 2024 data on the length of the network (navigable rivers and lakes, navigable canals) are not available for: Belgium, Germany, Italy and Poland. Data for several NUTS 2 regions in Sweden are not available. Some countries do not have navigable inland waterways at all; others may have a network, but it does not meet the minimum requirements in terms of minimum carrying capacity according to the 1992 UNECE/ECMT Classification of European Inland Waterways, canals, navigable rivers. *Data for the Candidate Countries have been compiled on the basis of available data. *Available 2023 data have been used if 2024 data were not reported. ''* This designation is without prejudice to positions on status, and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo Declaration of Independence.'' ''Country-specific notes'' *Estonia: data on motorways refer to 1st class roads. *Italy: data for motorways and railway lines declared for Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen (ITH1) include the network for the Provincia Autonoma di Trento (ITH2). For the purpose of the maps, the total area of the 2 regions has been considered and the density figures have been equally spread between these 2 regions. *Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Serbia have reported transport infrastructure data. The network density indicators could however not be calculated as the area information (land area for motorways and rail, total area for inland waterways) was not available at the time of publishing. The same occurred for several regions in Norway. *The Netherlands: Since the waterways define the borders between regions, the lengths that were reported for all NUTS 1 and NUTS 2 regions were attributed to both bordering regions. *Ireland: reported data for inland waterways exclude lakes. ''Regional breakdown'' The Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics (NUTS) was established by Eurostat around 50 years ago in order to provide a single uniform breakdown of territorial units for the production of regional statistics for the Community. Since then, it has been updated regularly. Five smaller EU Member States (Estonia, Cyprus, Latvia, Luxembourg and Malta) are not sub-divided into NUTS regions. Very similar to the EU-specific NUTS classification, a statistical regions breakdown also exists for the EFTA countries and the Candidate Countries. Here too, the smaller countries Liechtenstein, Iceland and North Macedonia are not sub-divided into regions. ===Context === Efficient transport services and infrastructure are vital to exploiting the economic strengths of all regions of the European Union, to supporting the internal market and growth, and enabling economic and social cohesion. They also influence trade competitiveness, as the availability, price, and quality of transport services have strong implications on production processes and the choice of trading partners. Transport investments enable economic growth and job creation. Investing in transport infrastructure, particularly in railways and inland waterway navigation, also contributes to the decarbonisation of transport. The sector currently accounts for around one quarter of the EU’s greenhouse gas emissions, with road transport responsible for about 73% of transport emissions in recent years (see: [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/greenhouse-gas-emissions-from-transport Greenhouse gas emissions from transport in Europe]). Transport, however, faces a wide range of challenges across the EU: underinvestment, lack of suitable financing solutions, continuous growth of urban populations, and various regulatory and administrative barriers. The European Commission is addressing these issues, paving the way for the competitive and sustainable EU transport system of tomorrow. The [https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/mobility-strategy_en Strategy for Sustainable and Smart Mobility] sets the actions needed in each transport mode for delivering on the [https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal/transport-and-green-deal_en European Green Deal], enabling in this way smoother connectivity and a more resilient Single European Transport Area. Efficient connectivity for all EU citizens is a critical aspect of social inclusion and an important determinant of well-being. It stimulates economic growth, territorial cohesion and helps reduce our impact to the environment. Transport is the only economic sector in which greenhouse gas emissions are higher than in 1990, despite the mitigation efforts undertaken. The European Green Deal has therefore set the key objective to deliver a 90% reduction in transport-related greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Building missing links at borders between EU Member States and along key European routes, as well as removing bottlenecks or interconnecting transport modes in terminals, is vital for the Single Market and for connecting Europe with external markets and trade partners. The smooth functioning of the European network requires integration and interconnection of all modes of transport. The adaptation of infrastructure to new mobility patterns and the deployment of infrastructure for clean energy sources pose additional challenges that require new investments and a different approach to the design of networks. === Other articles === *[[Freight transport statistics - modal split]] *[[Railway freight transport statistics]] *[[Characteristics of the railway network in Europe]] *[[Road freight transport statistics]] *[[Inland waterway freight transport - quarterly and annual data]] *[[Transport statistics at regional level]] *[[Stock of vehicles at regional level]] === Publications === *{{Template:Publication|code= KS-01-25-037|title= Regional yearbook 2025}} - Chapter 11, Transport *{{Template:Publication|code= KS-01-25-048|title=Glossary for Transport Statistics}} *{{Template:Publication|code= KS-01-25-057|title= Key figures on European transport - 2025 edition}} === Database === *Transport, see: ::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=tran_r Regional transport statistics (tran_r)] :::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=tran_r_net Road, rail and navigable inland waterways networks by NUTS 2 regions (tran_r_net)] *Area, see: ::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=reg Regional statistics by NUTS classification (reg)] :::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=reg_area3 Area by NUTS 3 region (reg_area3)] === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/overview Transport statistics] ===Data visualisations=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RCI/#?vis=nuts2.transport&lang=en Regional Statistics Illustrated] === External links === *[https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/infrastructure-and-investment_en European Commission - title: Inland waterway freight transport statistics by type of goods
text:
Statistics on inland waterway goods transport are presented for the EU and other countries connected to the EU inland waterways network, focusing on the main type of goods transported. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 In 2025, freight transport on EU inland waterways, measured in tonne-kilometres, decreased by 3.0% compared with 2024. 'Metal ores and other mining and quarrying products' was the main type of goods transported on EU inland waterways in 2025, accounting for 22.2% of the total tonne-kilometres performed for all types of goods and 26.7% of the total tonnes transported. In 2025, inland waterway transport of 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products' and 'coke and refined petroleum products' continued to be led by the Netherlands and Germany. This article presents inland waterway goods transport in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] and other countries connected to the EU inland waterway network. It focuses on the main types of goods transported, based on annual data for 2025 and comparisons with 2024. For an overview of the annual and quarterly inland waterway transport, please refer to the Statistics Explained article [[Inland waterway freight transport - quarterly and annual data]]. In 2025, the total volume of goods transported on EU inland waterways was 458 million tonnes, a decrease of 3.1% compared with the previous year. The total transport performed reached 118 billion tonne-kilometres, down by 3.0% from 2024 (Table 1). Measured in total transport performance (tonne-kilometres), 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium' (NST2007 division 03) and 'coke and refined petroleum products' (NST2007 division 07) were the 2 most transported types of goods. By contrast, when measured by the volume of goods transported in tonnes, 'coke and refined petroleum products' ranked third, slightly behind 'unidentifiable goods: goods which for any reason cannot be identified and therefore cannot be assigned to groups 01-16' (NST2007 division 19). Germany and the Netherlands were the 2 leading EU countries in terms of inland waterway transport of both 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products' and of 'coke and refined petroleum products'. === 'Metal ores and other mining and quarrying products' – top type of goods transported === 'Metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium' (NST2007 division 03) was the main type of goods transported on EU inland waterways in 2025, both in terms of tonne-kilometres (Table 1) and tonnes (Table 2). It accounted for nearly a quarter of total tonne-kilometres (22.2%) and slightly more than a quarter of total tonnes transported (26.7%). Transport of this type of goods, measured in tonnes, continued to decline, falling by 4.0% in 2025 following a drop of 2.7% in 2024. By contrast, transport performance, measured in tonne-kilometres, reversed course, falling by 7.1% in 2025, after increasing by 2.3% in 2024. When analysed by type of transport, 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium' (NST2007 division 03) recorded the largest decline in tonne-kilometres in transit transport (-15.0%), followed by international transport (-6.7%) and national transport (-2.4%). In terms of tonnes transported, international transport of this type of goods declined by 6.3% in 2025, while national transport fell by 2.0%. In 2025, international transport continued to account for the largest share of tonne-kilometres (53.9%), while national journeys made up 28.7%. [[Image: Inland waterway transport by type of goods and type of transport, EU, 2024-2025 (million tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Inland waterway transport by type of goods and type of transport, EU, 2024-2025
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ac7f143f-83b4-4499-8e7b-2441ac97cf8a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-30T14:51:42Z iww_go_atygo])|alt= a table showing the inland waterway transport by type of goods and type of transport in the EU from 2024 to 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] 'Coke and refined petroleum products' (NST2007 division 07) constituted the second most significant type of goods transported on EU inland waterways in 2025 in terms of tonne-kilometres, and the third in terms of tonnes. It represented 16.2% of the tonne-kilometres performed and 15.9% of the total tonnes transported. The transported volume in terms of tonnes transported of this type of goods was 40.3% less than the one of 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium'. Compared with 2024, transport of 'coke and refined petroleum products' decreased for both tonnes (-4.5%) and tonne-kilometres (-3.6%). When analysed by type of transport, 'coke and refined petroleum products ' (NST2007 division 07) recorded the largest decline in tonne-kilometres in transit transport (-8.7%), followed by national transport (-4.4%) and international transport (-1.7%). In terms of tonnes transported, national transport of this type of goods declined by 5.1% in 2025, while international transport fell by 3.9%. In 2025, international transport continued to account for the largest share of tonne-kilometres (59.3%), while national journeys made up 24.4%. 'Chemicals, chemical products, and man-made fibres; rubber and plastic products; nuclear fuel' (NST2007 division 08) remained the third largest type of goods in terms of tonne-kilometres, reaching 16.9 million tonne-kilometres in 2025, representing a decrease of 0.6% compared with 2024. In terms of tonnes transported, this type of goods ranked fourth in 2025, at 55.0 million tonnes, representing an increase of 0.2% compared with 2024. [[Image: Inland waterway transport by type of goods and type of transport, EU, 2024-2025 (thousand tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Inland waterway transport by type of goods and type of transport, EU, 2024-2025
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ac7f143f-83b4-4499-8e7b-2441ac97cf8a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-30T14:51:42Z iww_go_atygo])|alt= a table showing the inland waterway transport by type of goods and type of transport in the EU from 2024 to 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] 'Mail, parcels' (NST2007 division 15) recorded the strongest increase between 2024 and 2025, with a growth of 117.7% for tonne-kilometres performed and 765.0% for tonnes transported. However, it is important to note that the large changes in percentage observed for this type of goods should be interpreted within the context of their initially low values. 'Coal and lignite; crude petroleum and natural gas' (NST2007 division 02) also recorded a strong increase between 2024 and 2025, with a growth of 21.3% for tonne-kilometres performed and 8.0% for tonnes transported. The transport of 'machinery and equipment n.e.c. office machinery and computers; electrical machinery and apparatus n.e.c. radio, television and communication equipment and apparatus; medical, precision and optical instruments; watches and clocks' (NST2007 division 11) also expanded, up by 20.6% in tonne-kilometres and 12.8% in tonnes. Transport by 'textiles and textile products; leather and leather products' (NST2007 division 05) rose substantially by 19.2% in tonne-kilometres whereas it decreased by 2.0% in tonnes. In addition, 'other non-metallic mineral products' (NST2007 division 09) recorded a notable increase in tonne-kilometres performed, at +16.6% in 2025 compared with 2024, while tonnes transported increased only slightly by 2.3%. Moreover, 'grouped goods: a mixture of types of goods which are transported together' (NST2007 division 18) recorded a notable increase of tonne-kilometres performed, at 15.5% in 2025 compared with 2024. However, the transported volume for this type of goods saw a decrease in tonnes of 6.2%. Meanwhile, 'other goods n.e.c.' (NST2007 division 20) recorded an increase in tonnes transported, at +14.0%, but the tonne-kilometres performed decreased by 12.0%. The largest reductions were observed for 'goods moved in the course of household and office removals; baggage and articles accompanying travellers; motor vehicles being moved for repair; other non-market goods n.e.c.' (NST2007 division 17), down by 33.3% for tonne-kilometres and 14.2% for tonnes. This was followed by 'products of agriculture, hunting and forestry; fish and other fishing products' (NST2007 division 01), down by 19.7% for tonne-kilometres and 12.3% for tonnes. The type of goods 'furniture; other manufactured goods n.e.c.' (NST2007 division 13) also decreased substantially by 18.6 % for tonne-kilometres whereas tonnes transported increased by 6.0%. The type of goods 'wood and products of wood and cork (except furniture); articles of straw and plaiting materials; pulp, paper and paper products; printed matter and recorded media' (NST2007 division 06) also recorded large decreases, at -9.1% for tonne-kilometres and -13.6% for tonnes transported. Overall, these declines mainly occurred in type of goods with a relatively low to moderate transport volume, although some, such as 'products of agriculture, hunting, and forestry; fish and other fishing products', still represent substantial absolute volumes. ===The Netherlands and Germany dominated transport of 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products'=== In 2025, the main country involved in the EU inland waterway transport of 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products' was the Netherlands, which alone accounted for 43.7% of the tonnes transported and 38.3% of the tonne-kilometres performed (Figure 1). Germany secured second position in both metrics, scoring 22.3% of the tonnes transported and 31.1% of the tonne-kilometres performed. This distribution remained broadly unchanged compared with the previous year and reflects the extensive inland waterway networks in the Netherlands and Germany, which play a significant role in their transport systems. These networks are also connected to major ports such as Rotterdam and Hamburg, which are key hubs for imports to and exports from the EU. Figure 1 Regarding the inland waterway transport of 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products', the next 3 countries in the top 5 were Belgium, France, and Romania. However, the ranking of these 3 countries was different when looking at tonnes or tonne-kilometres. In terms of tonnes of 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products' transported, Belgium came third with a share of 16.7%, followed by France (9.2%) and Romania (3.0%). In terms of tonne-kilometres performed, Romania was in third place with a share of 8.6%, followed by Belgium (7.9%) and France (6.8%) (Figure 1). The main international route for inland waterway transport of 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products', in terms of tonne-kilometres performed, was between the Netherlands and Germany, accounting for more than two-fifths (42.9%) of the EU total (Table 3). The main route was the one from the Netherlands to Germany (31.1%), while the same route in the opposite direction, from Germany to the Netherlands, was in second place (11.8%). The Netherlands was present in 4 of the top 5 flows and in 5 of the top 10 flows overall. Germany was the loading or unloading country in 3 of the top 10 flows related to the transport of this type of goods, as well as Belgium and Serbia. Romania and Ukraine appeared twice in the top 10 flows. France and Austria got 1 appearance in the top 10 flows. Four flows involved non-EU countries. The flow from Romania to Serbia ranked fifth, followed by the flow from Ukraine to Serbia in sixth place, the flow from Ukraine to Austria in ninth place, and the flow from Serbia to Romania in 10th place. [[Image: Top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of metal ores, 2025 (million tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium, 2025
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/075c2a9e-349d-4b9c-ae51-74e412af708d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-30T14:57:36Z iww_go_atygofl])|alt= a table showing the top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium in 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at volumes in tonnes of the inland waterway transport of 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products', the main route observed was also between the Netherlands and Germany, accounting for almost half (48.9%) of the EU total (Table 4). The main country-to-country flow was the one from the Netherlands to Germany (38.0%) while the same route in the opposite direction, from Germany to the Netherlands, was in fourth place only (11.0%). The top 10 flows in terms of tonnes were dominated by 6 countries: the Netherlands (with 5 appearances), Belgium and Germany (with 4 appearances each), France (with 3 appearances), followed by Austria, Romania, Slovakia, and Serbia (1 appearance each). The flow from Romania to Serbia, the sole EU/non-EU route among the top flows, ranked eighth. [[Image: Top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of metal ores, 2025 (thousand tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 4: Top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium, 2025
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/557cfed0-6142-4f29-9030-95c103a57cb4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-30T14:57:57Z iww_go_atygofl])|alt= a table showing the top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium in 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===The Netherlands and Germany were the top transporters of 'coke and refined petroleum products' === In 2025, the main countries involved in the EU inland waterway transport of 'coke and refined petroleum products' were, as in previous years, the Netherlands and Germany (Figure 2). The Netherlands ranked first, with 55.3% of the total tonnes transported and 42.2% of the tonne-kilometres performed. Germany ranks second, with 28.0% of the total tonnes transported and 41.7% of tonne-kilometres performed. These shares reflect the longer distances performed by vessels passing through German inland waterways. In terms of tonnes transported, Belgium ranked third, with a share of 5.5%, followed by France (3.8%) and Romania (2.5%). In terms of tonne-kilometres performed, Romania, with a share of 5.6%, ranked third, followed by France (2.8%) and Belgium (2.6%). Figure 2 In terms of tonne-kilometres performed for 'coke and refined petroleum products', the flows between the Netherlands, Germany, and Belgium occupied the first 5 positions of the top 10 country-to-country flows, as well as the seventh flow, and together accounted for 69.3% of total tonne-kilometres performed on inland waterways in Europe (Table 5). The main flow is from the Netherlands to Germany, accounting for 18.9% of the total tonne-kilometres performed. France and Switzerland also ranked among the top 10 unloading countries, with France receiving goods from the Netherlands and Germany, and Switzerland receiving goods from Germany. Completing the overview, the flow from Romania to Serbia, the sole EU/non-EU route among the top flows, ranked ninth. [[Image: Top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of coke and refined petroleum products, 2025 (million tonne-kilometres).png |thumb|centre|700px|Table 5: Top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of coke and refined petroleum products, 2025
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2e959427-ea2c-40d1-a683-416a2d46a8f6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-30T14:58:38Z iww_go_atygofl])|alt= a table showing the top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of coke and refined petroleum products in 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at volumes of 'coke and refined petroleum products' transported in tonnes, the pattern is broadly similar to that observed for tonne-kilometres (Table 6). The top 10 flows are mainly dominated by the Netherlands and Germany (5 appearances), whereas Belgium, appeared 3 times, while France appeared twice. The main flow is from the Netherlands to Belgium, accounting for 42.5% of the total tonnes transported. This flow was third in terms of tonne-kilometres (12.9%), indicating shorter journey lengths between the 2 countries. The flow from Austria to Hungary ranked ninth among the top 10. Completing the overview, the flows from Germany to Switzerland, and from Romania to Ukraine, the EU/non-EU routes among the top flows, ranked fifth and sixth, respectively. [[Image: Top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of coke and refined petroleum products, 2025 (thousand tonnes).png |thumb|centre|700px|Table 6: Top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of coke and refined petroleum products, 2025
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/58c4966d-8ada-4ff7-9fd0-b3d225e1e906?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-30T14:58:21Z iww_go_atygofl])|alt= a table showing the top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of coke and refined petroleum products in 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and figures (MS Excel)=== {{Template:Excel|filename=SE_article_Goods_2026-09.xlsx|title=Inland waterway transport statistics by type of goods}} === Data sources=== All figures presented in this article have been extracted from the [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] online inland waterways transport database. The related datasets are collected according to {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R0974:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2018/974}} of the European Parliament and of the Council on statistics of goods transport by inland waterways. Regulation (EU) 2018/974 states that data must be supplied by all Member States for which the total volume of goods transported annually by inland waterways exceeds 1 million tonnes. Currently, 17 EU countries provide data on mandatory or voluntary basis: Belgium (BE), Bulgaria (BG), Czechia (CZ), Germany (DE), France (FR), Croatia (HR), Italy (IT), Lithuania (LT), Luxembourg (LU), Hungary (HU), the Netherlands (NL), Austria (AT), Poland (PL), Romania (RO), Slovakia (SK), Finland (FI), and Sweden (SE). The legal act requires only the provision of a reduced annual dataset for countries exceeding the 1 million tonnes threshold but where no international or transit traffic exists. '''Definitions''' '''National inland waterway transport''': Inland waterway transport between two places (a port or place of loading and a port or place of unloading) within a national territory irrespective of the country in which the vessel is registered. It may involve transit through a second country, although for this country this transport must be reported as transit. '''International inland waterway transport''': Inland waterway transport between two places (a port or place of loading and a port or place of unloading) located in different countries. It may involve transit through one or more countries. For the latter countries, this transport must be reported as transit. '''Inland waterway transit transport''': Inland waterway transport through a national territory between two places (a port or place of loading and a port or place of unloading) both located in another national territory or national territories, provided that in the total journey within the national territory, there is no loading and unloading operation. '''EU''' includes data for all Member States providing data. '''Calculation of EU aggregates''': In Table 2, EU international and total goods transport in tonnes is calculated by addressing the issue of double counting. This issue arises because both the country of loading (Country A) and the country of unloading (Country B) report tonnes for the same transport activity. Therefore, simply summing the values reported by individual EU countries is not feasible, as the same transport would be counted twice leading to inflated totals. More precisely, to avoid the issue of double counting, the calculation of EU aggregates for tonnes is currently performed as follows: * EU aggregate for national transport: Total reported for national transport by all reporting EU countries (no risk of double counting); * EU aggregate for international transport: Total reported by the reporting EU country, when it is the unloading country. If the unloading country does not report data, then the data from the loading country is used instead. For example, if goods are transported from Germany (loading country) to Switzerland (unloading country), only the data reported by Germany would be considered in the calculation, as Switzerland does not provide any data. * EU aggregate for total transport: National transport + International transport (Transit transport is not considered). For transit transport measured in tonnes, an EU aggregate equal to the sum of the country figures is not valid, because volumes of freight transported are reported by all transit countries through which the transport takes place, before reaching the unloading destination. Therefore, the same volume may be reported 2, 3, or more times without the possibility of eliminating multiple counting. At the same time, figures for transit transport are included in the EU national or international transport as they are reported not only by the transit countries but also by the loading and unloading countries. Therefore, for the EU total volume of freight, it is enough to sum the total national and international figures. '''Calculation of country flows''': In Tables 3 and 5, presenting the tonne-kilometres results, international and transit transport reported by the EU countries are taken into account. In Tables 4 and 6, presenting the results in tonnes, only international transport reported by the EU countries is taken into account in order to avoid double counting. In addition, the loading country in these two tables also corresponds to the reporting country. Data from Italy and Lithuania are not available in these tables. '''Country-specific notes''' '''Bulgaria''': Transit data supplied include Romanian national IWW transport data equivalent to Bulgarian transit transport. '''Italy''': No data available for 2025. Data are delivered on a voluntary basis. Only a simplified annual dataset is provided, covering tonnes and tonne-kilometres by type of transport and type of goods. The breakdown by country/region of loading and unloading is not collected. '''Lithuania''': Data are delivered on a voluntary basis. Only a simplified annual dataset is provided, covering tonnes and tonne-kilometres by type of transport and type of goods. The breakdown by country/region of loading and unloading is not collected. '''Romania''': Transit data supplied include Bulgarian national IWW transport data equivalent to Romanian transit transport. '''Sweden''': No traffic was conducted by Swedish registered vessels certified for inland waterway traffic in Sweden since no certificates have been issued at the Swedish Transport Agency. '''Breakdown by group of goods''' The NST 2007 classification is available on [https://showvoc.op.europa.eu/#/datasets/ESTAT_Standard_goods_classification_for_transport_statistics__NST_2007/unknown/data ShowVoc]. The abbreviation 'n.e.c.' stands for 'not elsewhere classified'. '''Symbols''' *":" not available *"-" not applicable or real zero *"0" less than half of the unit used and thus rounded to zero === Context=== The content of this statistical article is based on data collected within the framework of {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R0974:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2018/974}} of the European Parliament and of the Council on statistics of goods transport by inland waterways. === Other articles === *[[Freight transport statistics - title: Innovation profiles of enterprises - methodology
text:
Eurostat presents a new tool to report on innovation in European businesses: the Innovation Profiles. Last update: February 2025 === Why Innovation Profiles of enterprises? === Innovation in businesses is a complex process. It requires multiple capabilities and involves various activities that can result in several outcomes. The [[Glossary:Community_innovation_survey_(CIS)|Community Innovation Survey]] (CIS) is the established tool for reporting on business [[Glossary:Innovation|innovation]] in Europe. The measurement of innovation in businesses, and the interpretation of results, thrives on a solid conceptual and methodological foundation: the OECD/Eurostat [https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2018/10/oslo-manual-2018_g1g9373b.html Oslo Manual 'Guidelines for collecting and using data on innovation'] (latest edition from 2018) The 2018 review of the [https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2018/10/oslo-manual-2018_g1g9373b.html Oslo Manual 'Guidelines for collecting and using data on innovation'] led to a redesign of the CIS survey starting with its 2018 wave (see the background article [[Community Innovation Survey - design improvement in 2018|Community Innovation Survey]]). The redesign improved the information balance between innovators and low- or non-innovators because most variables are now available for all enterprises.. The concepts of the Oslo Manual are acknowledged to reflect the reality in businesses best in view of their innovation. In turn, the CIS is acknowledged to implement these concepts in surveys on business innovation as well as possible. The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/website/cis/library.html CIS survey questions] related to business innovation have been developed over many years, stood the test of time, and are today copied by many other innovation surveys worldwide. Since 2022, the CIS is conducted in all EU Member States within the framework of European Business Statistics (EBS)Starting with the CIS 2022 round, the CIS was integrated into the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/european-business-statistics framework of European Business Statistics] (EBS). This means that the data are produced and transmitted to Eurostat according to Regulation (EU) [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32019R2152 2019/2152] ('EBS Regulation') and the General Implementing Act to this regulation, Regulation (EU) [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32020R1197 2020/1197] ('EBS GIA'). These 2 Regulations are common to other domains, for example [[Glossary:Structural_business_statistics|Structural Business Statistics]] (SBS) and [[Glossary:Business_demography|Business Demography Statistics]] (BD). Specifically for the Community Innovation Survey (CIS), Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2022/1092/oj 2022/1092] applies. This framework ensures that CIS data are compatible with the output of all other European data collections on enterprises and the economy. It enables comparisons between data for different countries and from different data collections., and the data collection is guided by the '[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-24-008 EBS methodological manual on statistics on business innovation]'. CIS results are thus comparable between the countries, as well as coherent with other business statistics. The data collections within EBS have different user groups. They range from researchers with the capacity to understand complex concepts and interpret the data in all facets, to expert users of tabulated data, and to users who want to have a quick at-the-glance overview of business innovation. The data output of the statistical offices serves all those interests. More than other EBS data collections, surveys on business innovation have researchers, academia, and professional users as a focus groupThis is e.g. reflected by the fact that the CIS is the only EBS data collection for which anonymised microdata are made available to researchers. See section 7.4 'Transmission of CIS microdata' in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-gq-20-006 EBS Methodological Manual on Business Innovation].. They are mostly acquainted with the concepts and can dexterously interpret CIS data. The CIS offers researchers a myriad of possibilities to classify enterprises about their innovation – and indeed researchers have used CIS data in many ways, depending on the focus of their analysis. The CIS reports on innovation activities and shows if an enterprise has innovation capabilities, i.e. can create innovation itself. It identifies if an enterprise has 'implemented' the innovation (sold on the market or brought to use in the firm) as well as the degree of novelty of an innovation. It reports on the presence and level of [[Glossary:Research_and_development_(R_&_D)|research and development (R&D) activities]], the presence of ongoing or abandoned innovation efforts, and the innovative potential for companies that have not introduced innovations. Admittedly, it takes some knowledge to fully understand and disentangle the concepts of the Oslo Manual, e.g. 'innovation' in general, 'business innovation', different kinds of 'innovation implementation', 'new-to-market' versus 'new-to-the-firm product innovation’, ‘innovation activities', 'innovation capabilities', etc. The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database standard tabulation of aggregated CIS results], together with the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/inn_cis12_esms.htm metadata], methodological [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/science-technology-innovation/publications Statistics Explained articles] and the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-24-008 EBS methodological manual on business innovation] achieve this to a good extent. However, there was still no at-the-glance overview of innovation in businesses before 2023. This is why Eurostat and the Statistical Offices of EU Member States developed 7 easy-to-understand Innovation Profiles. They are based on the established concepts of business innovation and account for all relevant aspects in parallel. The Innovation Profiles capture the complete picture of innovation in European businesses and provide better information to analysts and policy-makers than 1-dimensional standard indicators. The Innovation Profiles have many advantages. They make it possible to present the various survey results (e.g. on innovation capabilities and outcomes) in terms of simple proportions of the population, which increases the possibilities for charts and visualisations. For the same reason, they facilitate the development of indicators that allow results to be compared along concepts related to business innovation. Finally, they are very useful in the design of Microdata Linking (MDL) exercises, as they allow innovation data to be linked directly to other databases, so that aggregates from other data sources can be calculated for each of these watertight groups of enterprises. From the CIS 2022 onwards, the Innovation Profiles are universally used to demonstrate the impact of innovation on business activities and their outcomes. Many CIS variables are broken down by Innovation Profiles. Eurostat publishes Statistics Explained articles on CIS results broken down by Innovation Profiles. This article explains the motivation and methodology behind the Innovation Profiles. === Underlying principles === Two key principles guided the construction of the Innovation Profiles: * Mutual exclusivity: there must be no overlap between 2 profiles. * Exhaustivity: the entire target population of the CIS must be covered. In summary, each enterprise covered by the CIS is allocated to exactly 1 Innovation Profile. The Innovation Profiles were carefully designed and tested to ensure that these 2 principles are respected in practice. === Seven Innovation Profiles === Innovation profiling takes an intuitive, pragmatic and relevant approach in choosing a hierarchy. Seven basic Innovation Profiles were developed around the lines of analysis shown below (Figure 1 presents a tabular representation of the Innovation Profiles). The CIS reports on the enterprise as the 'generator' of innovation (enterprise as the 'subject'), rather than on the innovation itself (resulting innovation as the 'object'). This logic is in line with policy purposes: the question is not "How many innovations were reported for a country and how successful were they?" The mere number of innovations is not a good indicator for a successful outcome innovation activity, and producing statistics on the success of all innovations in a country is not feasible. Instead, the question is rather: "What do enterprises do to have innovation, what conditions do they face, which conditions are favourable for innovation, and what can be done to create favourable conditions and thereby increase the competitiveness of an economy?" This logic is, therefore, also the logic of the innovation profiling. [[Image:F1_Combining_the_core_CIS_variables_Innovation_Profiles.png|Figure 1: Combining the core CIS variables: Innovation Profiles
''Source:'' Eurostat|thumb|centre|700px|alt= Table showing the combined core CIS variables as Innovation Profiles.]] Innovation profiling uses established concepts of measuring business innovation, and puts them into a hierarchy according to their inherent relevance for describing enterprises in view of their innovative behaviour. # At the very top level, the structure distinguishes between firms with and without innovation activities. The Oslo Manual defines innovation activities as "all developmental, financial and commercial activities undertaken by a firm that are intended to result in an innovation for the firm" ([https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2018/10/oslo-manual-2018_g1g9373b.html Oslo Manual, OECD, 2018], p.68). Innovation activities are the starting point for a firm to engage in innovation. These activities characterise the firms that have either introduced at least 1 type of innovation (product or business process) or that have been involved in any ongoing or abandoned activities in pursuit of an innovation. # At the 2nd level, the structure distinguishes enterprises that have implemented an innovation during the reference period from those that have not. The implementation of an innovation is mostly the desired outcome of innovation activity, and it is therefore again intuitively logical to place it at the second level of the innovation profiling. The concept of 'implementation' is essential to the definition of innovation in the Oslo Manual. For business enterprises, it means that their product has been introduced into the market, or that a new business process has been brought into use by the firm. # The 3rd level refers to the innovation capabilities of enterprises. The Oslo Manual dedicates great attention to the measurement of business capabilities for innovation because it is "of critical importance for the analysis of the drivers and impacts of innovation (why some firms have innovation and others do not)" ([https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2018/10/oslo-manual-2018_g1g9373b.html Oslo Manual, OECD, 2018], p.35). The innovation profiling identifies innovators with their own substantial innovation capabilities. These firms develop their product or business process innovations themselves or together with other enterprises or organisations, or they co-operate on any of their innovation activities with other enterprises or organisations. # The 4th level of analysis refers to the innovation itself. The profiles take a market perspective, and answer the basic questions: Has the enterprise introduced a product innovation not previously offered by competitors? If not: Has it improved its assortment (this includes only products that are identical or very similar to those already offered by competitors)? If not: Has it implemented any business process innovation (with a potential indirect effect on the market)? # At the 5th level, the structure systematically distinguishes according to the possible presence of R&D (R&D performers versus non-R&D-performers) within the resulting Innovation Profiles. R&D can be an important input to innovation. Hence, its presence allows for better disentangling of the profiles of both enterprises that introduced product or business process innovations (Profiles I to IV), and those enterprises that worked on innovations but did not implement them (Profile V). Enterprises without innovation activities (Profiles VI and VII) are not subject to this ultimate alternative because, by definition, these firms do not carry out any R&D (which is considered an innovation activity); they are all considered as non-R&D-performers. The resulting Innovation Profiles are: '''PROFILE I: In-house product innovators with market novelties''' This group includes enterprises that introduced a product innovation that was developed by the enterprise and that was not previously offered by competitors (new-to-market product innovation). Profile I comes closest to the intuitive idea of a breakthrough innovator who creates radically new products and pioneers them to the market. They have innovation capability and use this to compete in the existing marketplace, or even to create new markets. '''PROFILE II: In-house product innovators without market novelties''' This group includes enterprises that introduced a product innovation that was developed by the enterprise but that is identical or very similar to products already offered by competitors (new-to-firm product innovation). Profile II enterprises are actively trying to stay abreast with competitors by renewing or enlarging their assortment. '''PROFILE III: In-house business process innovators without in-house developed product innovations''' Until the CIS2022 round, firms with product innovations that were not developed in-house were not checked further for their possible business process innovations developed in-house. Such companies were classified under Profile IV despite their innovation capabilities. This was improved from the CIS2024 onwards: now all firms that either had no product innovation or had a product innovation but not developed in-house, but that on the other hand had in-house developed business process innovations are included in Profile III. This allows Profile III to belong unambiguously to the overarching group of those companies ''WITH'' innovation capabilities. On the other side of the border, Profile IV then includes firms that have not developed any of their innovations in-house, regardless of whether they are product or business process innovations. This clearly places Profile IV within the overarching group of those firms ''WITHOUT'' innovation capabilities. This change in methodology was analysed in depth and tested by the CIS Task Force. The impact on the results is expected to be very limited. It consists exclusively of a slight shift of firms from Profile IV to Profile III, allowing the necessary shift from the group of firms without innovation capabilities to that with innovation capabilities. This group includes enterprises that have not introduced any in-house developed product innovation (Profiles I and II), but that have introduced a business process innovation that was developed in-house. Profile III firms aim at becoming more efficient. They actively work to become more competitive by introducing better business processes. The impact of their innovation activity on the market is indirect, e.g. by being able to offer lower prices or better non-monetary conditions to their customers, or by attempting to reach new customers for their established products. '''PROFILE IV: Innovators that do not develop innovations themselves''' This group includes enterprises that have introduced an innovation, either a product or a business process, but none of which was developed in-house. Profile IV companies strive to be competitive in their markets by introducing better products or business processes. However, they choose not to build up innovation capabilities themselves. The improvement of their products or business processes is a result of buying in innovation from other firms and implementing it in the own firm. '''PROFILE V: Non-innovators with innovation activity''' This group includes enterprises that have not introduced any innovation recently, but have either ongoing or abandoned innovation activities. Enterprises from Profile V have not introduced any innovation during the 3-year reference period, but are not estranged to the idea of innovation either. They have worked on innovations in the last 3 years but have not (yet) brought them to completion and implementation (i.e. they did not sell any innovative product on the market or brought any process innovation into use within the firm); or they have simply abandoned these projects. '''PROFILE VI: Non-innovators without innovation activity but with potential to innovate''' This group includes enterprises that did not introduce any innovation, and had no ongoing or abandoned innovation activities, but were considering innovating. Profile VI enterprises have not introduced or worked on any innovation during the 3-year reference period, but they are not completely estranged to the idea of innovation either. '''PROFILE VII: Non-innovators without innovation activity and without potential to innovate''' This group includes all other enterprises. They have no innovation, they have no ongoing or abandoned innovation activities, and they have not considered innovation. They prefer to continue with business as usual and can be said to have no inclination to innovate. === See also === *[[Community Innovation Survey - design improvement in 2018]] *[[Community Innovation Survey 2022 - key indicators]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database Science and technology] (scitech), see: :Community innovation survey (inn) ::Results of the community innovation survey 2022 (CIS2022) (inn_cis13) === Dedicated section === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=science_technology_innovation}} Science, technology and innovation] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/website/cis/library.html Community Innovation Survey (CIS): Questionnaire library] === Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-24-008 EBS methodological manual on statistics on business innovation] *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-18-852|title=Oslo Manual}} *{{Template:Esms|code=inn_cis12_esms|title=Community innovation survey 2020 (CIS2020) (inn_cis12)}} (ESMS metadata file — inn_cis12) === Legislation === *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32022R1092:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 2019/2152}} *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012R0995:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 2020/1197}} *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R2152:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 2022/1092}} === External links === *[https://projects.research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/en/statistics/performance-indicators/european-innovation-scoreboard/eis-2024#/ European Innovation Scoreboard (EIS) 2024 and Regional Innovation Scoreboard (RIS) 2023] *[http://www.oecd.org/innovation/ OECD — Innovation] === Notes === {{Unit|topic=X_Structural_business_statistics }} [[Category:Science, technology, and digital society|Innovation profiles of enterprises -
