title: Inland waterway freight transport at regional level
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of inland waterway freight transport at regional level. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 Zuid-Holland (NL36) was the region that handled the highest tonnage of freight transported by inland waterways in 2025, accounting for 17.9% of the total inland waterway freight handled in the EU. The top 20 NUTS 2 regions for handling freight transported by inland waterways represented more than three-quarters of the total inland waterway freight handled in the EU in 2025. [[Image:Inland waterway freight handled by NUTS 2 region, 2025.png|thumb|center|700px|''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f369c6d4-c78a-46e7-a149-a665df0512db?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-10T13:14:21Z iww_go_atygofl])|alt=A map showing inland waterway freight handled in the EU by NUTS 2 region in 2025 in million tonnes loaded and unloaded. The volume of goods is represented by bubbles in each NUTS 2 region. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article presents regional statistics on inland waterway freight transport in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] and non-EU countries connected to the EU inland waterway network. It focuses on regional data for total transport and container transport. For an overview of annual and quarterly inland waterway transport, please refer to the Statistics Explained article [[Inland waterway freight transport - quarterly and annual data]]. === Inland waterway freight handled in Zuid-Holland (NL36) represented 17.9% of the EU total in 2025 === In 2025, 903.4 million tonnes of freight were handled, i.e. loaded and unloaded, in the EU by inland waterways. Map 1 presents the inland waterway freight handled by NUTS 2 region in 2025. Data are available for 93 EU NUTS 2 regions. Zuid-Holland (NL36) ranked first in 2025 with 161.7 million tonnes, accounting for 17.9% of the total inland waterway freight handled in the EU. Prov. Antwerpen (BE21) followed with 92.7 million tonnes (or 10.3%), ahead of Noord-Holland (NL32) with 70.1 million tonnes (or 7.8%), Düsseldorf (DEA1) with 63.4 million tonnes (or 7.0%) and Zeeland (NL34) with 46.6 million tonnes (or 5.2%). Completing the picture with Noord-Brabant (NL41) at 32.3 million tonnes (or 3.6%), the cumulative share crossed the halfway mark. The top 20 NUTS 2 regions for inland waterway freight handled accounted for more than three-quarters (75.6%) of the total inland waterway freight handled in the EU in 2025, slightly lower than in 2024 when it was 76.1% (-0.5 percentage points). [[Image:Inland waterway freight handled by NUTS 2 region, 2025.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 1: Inland waterway freight handled by NUTS 2 region, 2025
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f369c6d4-c78a-46e7-a149-a665df0512db?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-10T13:14:21Z iww_go_atygofl])|alt=A map showing inland waterway freight in the EU handled by NUTS 2 region in 2025 in million tonnes loaded and unloaded. The volume of goods is represented by bubbles in each NUTS 2 region. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The map shows a heavy concentration of handled freight in a few key regions, mainly located in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany. This is not surprising, as these 3 countries have extensive inland waterway networks that play a major role in their national transport systems. These networks are also connected to major ports such as Rotterdam, Antwerp-Bruges and Hamburg, which are key hubs for imports to and exports from the EU. Figure 1 shows the freight handled in the top 20 NUTS 2 regions in 2025, alongside the freight handled in these regions in 2024. Among the top 20 regions, 12 experienced a decrease from 2024 to 2025. The largest drops were recorded in Prov. Hainaut (BE32) (-16.4%), Sud-Est (RO22) (-15.6%), Prov. Antwerpen (BE21) (-10.0%), Prov. Oost-Vlaanderen (BE23) (-7.1%), Limburg (NL42) (-4.3%), and Düsseldorf (DEA1) (-4.0%). By contrast, 7 regions recorded an increase. The most significant one was for Prov. Limburg (BE) (BE22) (+4.7%), followed by Weser-Ems (DE94) (+2.4%), and Gelderland (NL22) (+2.1%). Köln (DEA2) remained the same in 2025 compared with 2024, at 13.4 million tonnes. Figure 1 In 2025, 4 regions were ranked lower in the list of the top 20 and 4 regions were ranked higher, compared with 2024. The other regions remained in the same position. Prov. Limburg (BE) (BE22) entered the top 20 at the expense of Darmstadt (DE71) which was no longer in the top 20 in 2025. Figure 2 presents the distribution between loaded and unloaded inland waterway freight across the top 20 NUTS regions in 2025, highlighting the diverse dynamics of freight movement. Figure 2 Zuid-Holland (NL36) and Zeeland (NL34) had a clear emphasis on loaded freight, with 67.1% and 64.6% of their handled freight being loaded in 2025, respectively. Among the other regions of the top 20, Prov. Hainaut (BE32), Sud-Est (RO22), Karlsruhe (DE12), Limburg (NL42), Prov. Antwerpen (BE21), and Noord-Holland (NL32) also leaned slightly more towards loaded freight in 2025. This could suggest that these regions are significant producers or transit points for goods heading elsewhere. By contrast, Düsseldorf (DEA1) and Overijssel (NL21) primarily served as a destination for goods, with their unloaded freight accounting for 72.0% and 71.0% in 2025, respectively. Among the other regions in the top 20, 10 had higher shares for unloaded freight, ranging from 51.3% in Münster (DEA3) to 64.3% in Noord-Brabant (NL41), implying they might be key recipients of goods or transit points. === 'Metal ores' largest type of goods handled in most of the top 20 NUTS 2 regions in 2025=== Table 1 presents the top 3 type of goods handled in the top 20 NUTS 2 regions for inland waterway transport in 2025. It should be noted that the data presented in this table may be influenced by the tonnage of unidentifiable goods reported, in particular when analysing the shares of each type of goods. Unidentifiable goods are goods which for any reason cannot be identified and therefore cannot be assigned to the other [https://showvoc.op.europa.eu/#/datasets/ESTAT_Standard_goods_classification_for_transport_statistics_%28NST_2007%29/data NST2007 divisions]. The tonnage of unidentifiable goods was particularly high for some regions, such as Prov. Oost-Vlaanderen (BE23) (69.1%) and Prov. Antwerpen (BE21) (58.7%). Unidentifiable goods have not been considered as one of the top 3 type of goods. However, if they would, this would make that category appear in the top 3 types of goods for both the Prov. Antwerpen (BE21), Noord-Brabant (NL41), the Prov. Oost-Vlaanderen (BE23), Overijssel (NL21), and Limburg (NL42). [[Image: Top 3 type of goods handled in the top 20 NUTS 2 regions for inland waterway transport, 2025 (%, based on tonnes loaded and unloaded).png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Top 3 type of goods handled in the top 20 NUTS 2 regions for inland waterway transport, 2025
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f369c6d4-c78a-46e7-a149-a665df0512db?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-10T13:14:21Z iww_go_atygofl])|alt=A table presenting the top 3 goods categories handled in the top 20 EU NUTS 2 region for inland waterway transport in 2025. The percentage of the goods category on the total tonnes loaded and unloaded in each region is presented. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] 'Metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium' (NST2007 division 03) appeared to be the leading type of goods in 2025, representing the primary type of goods for 12 regions of the top 20, being second in 2 regions and third in 5 additional regions. The only region not having this type of goods in the top 3 was Münster (DEA3). When looking at the shares of this type of goods in total inland waterway freight transport in each region, it was particularly high in Prov. Limburg (BE) (BE22), at 58.0%, and Gelderland (NL22), at 56.8%. 'Coke and refined petroleum products' (NST2007 division 07) also emerged as a prominent category, being the top type of goods handled in 6 regions, second in 2 and third in 5 regions. The highest shares for this product were observed in Köln (DEA2) at 56.2%, and Münster (DEA3), at 45.9%. 'Chemicals, chemical products, and man-made fibers; rubber and plastic products; nuclear fuel' (NST2007 division 08) also held a notable presence, ranking first in 1 region, second in 9 regions and third in 2 regions. Rheinhessen-Pfalz (DEB3) and Zeeland (NL34) had the highest shares for this product category, at 31.5% and 27.1%, respectively. One of the 3 above-mentioned types of goods was in first place in all regions of the top 20, except in Sud-Est (RO22) where 'products of agriculture, hunting, and forestry; fish and other fishing products' (NST2007 division 01) came first, with a share of 41.8% on total inland waterway freight tonnage in this region. To complete the picture, 5 further types of goods appeared in the top 3 places for the top 20 regions. These 5 types of goods were: 'basic metals; fabricated metal products, except machinery and equipment' (NST2007 division 10) – once in second place and 4 times in third place; 'food products, beverages, and tobacco' (NST2007 division 04) – twice in second place and twice in third place; 'coal and lignite; crude petroleum and natural gas' (NST2007 division 02) – twice in second place and once in third place; 'other non-metallic mineral products' (NST2007 division 09) – once in second place and once in third place; and ‘wood and products of wood and cork (except furniture)’ – once in second place. When looking at the cumulated share of the top 3 types of goods, Köln (DEA2) topped the list with 89.9%. Close followers included Münster (DEA3) at 83.9%, and Zeeland (NL34) at 80.8%. The cumulated share of the top 3 types of goods represented more than 50% in all the top 20 regions, with the exception of Prov. Oost-Vlaanderen (BE23) with 20.0%, Prov. Antwerpen (BE21) with 26.9% and Noord-Brabant (NL41) with 49.3%. However, the share for these 3 regions is largely influenced by the high level of unidentifiable goods reported (69.1%, 58.7% and 16.0%, respectively). === Zuid-Holland (NL36) pivotal hub in the inland waterway transport network === Table 2 presents the top 20 regional flows for inland waterway freight transport in 2025. It shows that the transport of freight involving Zuid-Holland (NL36) as either the region of loading or the region of unloading accounted for 22.8% of the total tonnage transported in the EU in 2025. Zuid-Holland (NL36) appeared in 12 of the top 20 regional flows in 2025. In particular, this region appeared as the loading NUTS2 region in all the top 3 flows and as the unloading NUTS2 region in the flows ranked fourth to sixth. In terms of freight volume transported between Zuid-Holland (NL36) and Düsseldorf (DEA1), 30.7 million tonnes (or 6.7% of total inland waterway freight transported in the EU) were loaded in Zuid-Holland (NL36) and unloaded in Düsseldorf (DEA1). Conversely, 4.2 million tonnes (or 0.9%) were loaded in Düsseldorf (DEA1) and unloaded in Zuid-Holland (NL36). [[Image: Top 20 NUTS 2-NUTS 2 region flows for inland waterway freight transport, 2025.png|thumb|center|750px|Table 2: Top 20 NUTS 2-NUTS 2 region flows for inland waterway freight transport, 2025
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f369c6d4-c78a-46e7-a149-a665df0512db?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-10T13:14:21Z iww_go_atygofl])|alt=A table presenting the top 20 EU NUTS 2-NUTS 2 region flows for inland waterway freight transport in 2025. The tonnes transported and the shares of the region flows on total tonnes are presented. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Other regions well-represented in the top 20 regional flows for inland waterway freight transport were Prov. Antwerpen (BE21), which appeared in 6 of the top 20 flows in 2025, Zeeland (NL34) in 5 flows, Noord-Holland (NL32) in 4 flows, and Düsseldorf (DEA1) in 3 flows. To complete the picture, Noord-Brabant (NL41) appeared in 2 flows while Prov. Oost-Vlaanderen (BE23), Rheinhessen-Pfalz (DEB3), and Sud-Est (RO22) appeared in 1 flow each. Freight transported within solely Zuid-Holland (NL36) in 2025 represented 1.4% of total freight transported in the EU (or 6.6 million tonnes). Four other regions witnessed significant internal freight transport: tonnage transported within Prov. Antwerpen (BE21) accounted for 5.9 million tonnes in 2025, representing 1.3% of total inland waterway freight transported in the EU. Zeeland (NL34), Sud-Est (RO22) and Noord-Holland (NL32) also showed strong internal flows, contributing 0.9%, 0.7% and 0.7%, respectively, to the total transport share, with 4.0 million, 3.3 million and 3.2 million tonnes transported, respectively. Despite the prominence of these top 20 routes, the largest share of tonnage transport was distributed across a wide network of 2 607 remaining routes, including regional flows reported by France, with 319.5 million tonnes transported in 2025, accounting for 69.8% of total inland waterway freight transported in the EU. This underscores the vast and varied connectivity of the inland waterway transport network, suggesting that while certain routes are undoubtedly significant, the overall system thrives on a dense web of diverse transport routes. === Zuid-Holland (NL36) and Prov. Antwerpen (BE21) accounted for almost half of the total inland waterway freight in containers handled in the EU in 2025 === Map 2 presents the volume of inland waterway freight in containers handled, expressed in [[Glossary:Twenty-foot_equivalent_unit_(TEU)|Twenty-foot Equivalent Units (TEUs)]], by NUTS 2 region in 2025. Data are available for 51 EU NUTS 2 regions. Zuid-Holland (NL36) ranked first in 2025 with 3.7 million TEUs, accounting for 32.5% of the total inland waterway freight in containers handled in the EU. Prov. Antwerpen (BE21) followed with 1.8 million TEUs (or 15.7%). Summing up these 2 regions, they accounted for almost half (48.2%) of the total inland waterway freight in containers handled in the EU. Noord-Brabant (NL41) followed with 0.9 million TEUs (or 7.6%). [[Image: Inland waterway freight in containers handled by NUTS 2 region, 2025.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 2: Inland waterway freight in containers handled by NUTS 2 region, 2025
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/94439e7a-8ad9-4789-8fc6-188f82905f46?lang=en&createdAt=2025-10-02T09:54:48Z iww_go_actygofl])|alt=A map showing inland waterway freight in containers handled by EU NUTS 2 region in 2025 in thousand TEUs loaded and unloaded. The volume of containers is represented by bubbles in each NUTS 2 region. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The map shows a heavy concentration of inland waterway freight transported in containers in a few key regions, mainly located in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany. These three countries have extensive inland waterway networks that play a major role in their national transport systems. These networks are also connected to major ports, such as Rotterdam, Antwerp-Bruges and Hamburg, which are major ports for container transport. Figure 3 presents the top 20 NUTS 2 regions for handling containers for inland waterway transport in 2025, as well as the containers that had been handled in the same regions in 2024. While most regions of the top 20 experienced an increase between 2024 and 2025, 8 regions recorded a decrease. Zeeland (NL34) decreased by 15.7%, Prov. Limburg (BE22) by 13.6%, Karlsruhe (DE12) by 12.2%, Prov. Antwerpen (BE21) by 8.7%, Köln (DEA2) by 8.4%, Rheinhessen-Pfalz (DEB3) by 7.2%, Friesland (NL12) by 7.1%, and Prov. Liège (BE33) by 3.7%. By contrast, Braunschweig (DE91) experienced a significant growth from 54 854 TEUs in 2024 to 70 563 TEUs in 2025, the most substantial increase among the top 20 regions (+28.6%). Overijssel (NL21) (+15.3%), Hamburg (DE60) (+14.6%), Noord-Brabant (NL41) (+12.5%) and Drenthe (NL13) (+9.8%) also recorded substantial increases. Figure 3 In 2025, 3 regions were ranked lower in the list of the top 20, and 4 regions were ranked higher compared with 2024. The other regions remained in the same position, including the 9 first regions of the top 20. Braunschweig (DE91) entered the top 20 at the expense of Freiburg (DE13) which is no longer in the top 20 in 2025. Figure 4 presents the distribution between loading and unloading containers for inland waterway transport across the top 20 NUTS regions in 2025. Among the top 20 NUTS 2 regions, 15 regions loading and unloading activities of containers were broadly balanced, with no split exceeding 53/47%. Zeeland (NL34) and Prov. Antwerpen (BE21) emerged predominantly as destinations for freight in containers, with 67.2% and 58.0% of containers, respectively, being unloaded there in 2025. Braunschweig (DE91) also had higher container unloading activity than loading, with a 46.0%-54.0% distribution in 2025. Figure 4 By contrast, Karlsruhe (DE12) leaned slightly more towards containers being loaded, with a 56.4% share in 2025 being loaded there. Köln (DEA2) also had higher container loading activity than unloading, with a 55.2%-44.8% distribution in 2025. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=SE-Article-IWW-Regional-2026-09.xlsx|title=Inland waterway freight transport at regional level: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== All figures presented in this article have been extracted from the [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] online database on inland waterway transport. The related datasets are collected according to {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R0974:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2018/974}} of the European Parliament and of the Council on statistics of goods transport by inland waterways. Regulation (EU) 2018/974 states that data must be supplied by all Member States for which the total volume of goods transported annually by inland waterways exceeds 1 million tonnes. Currently, 17 Member States provide data on a mandatory or voluntary basis: Belgium (BE), Bulgaria (BG), Czechia (CZ), Germany (DE), France (FR), Croatia (HR), Italy (IT), Lithuania (LT), Luxembourg (LU), Hungary (HU), the Netherlands (NL), Austria (AT), Poland (PL), Romania (RO), Slovakia (SK), Finland (FI) and Sweden (SE). The legal act requires only the provision of a reduced annual dataset for countries exceeding the threshold of 1 million tonnes but where no international or transit traffic exists. '''Definitions''' '''Tonnes handled:''' this corresponds to the tonnes of goods loaded and unloaded. '''Tonnes transported:''' this corresponds to the tonnes of goods transported between two loading/unloading points. '''Table 2:''' Other routes also include tonnes reported by the loading country when the unloading country does not report data (e.g. Switzerland, Serbia, etc.). '''Country specific notes''' France: data at regional level for years 2024 and 2025 are not available for publication. Italy: data are delivered on a voluntary basis. Only a simplified annual dataset is provided, covering tonnes and tonne-kilometres by type of transport and type of goods. The breakdown by country/region of loading and unloading is not collected. title: Innovations with environmental benefits

<highlight>

<highlight-message>
Between 2020 and 2022, EU industry innovated to clean up production processes: about 10% of industrial firms reduced their energy consumption or CO2 footprint; 8% focused on recycling waste, water, or materials; 7% switched to renewable energy sources.
</highlight-message>

<highlight-message>
Between 2020 and 2022, innovations helped EU industrial products become more sustainable: 8% reduced their energy consumption or CO2 footprint; 7% facilitated recycling; 6% extended the products’ lifecycle.
</highlight-message>
</highlight>

<articlecontent>
<sesection>
=== Innovations with impact on the natural environment: overview===
 
Innovations that have a positive impact on the natural environment are a main driver for economies and societies to become more sustainable, resource-efficient, and competitive. Companies innovate in 2 ways – they can improve the environmental sustainability of production and internal processes or of the consumer products. The [[Glossary:Community innovation survey (CIS)|Community Innovation Survey (CIS)]] looks into the benefits obtained directly within the company and those obtained indirectly when the new product is consumed.

Some main findings of the survey for the period 2020-2022:
* Most common benefit is reduced energy consumption or carbon footprint
* Recycling improvements are also frequent
* The majority of improvements are focused on internal processes, fewer on the final products
* Industrial companies innovate more for environmental impact than service companies
* Larger companies more often have environmental innovations
* Country performance varies due to company practices and sectoral economic structures

This article refers to all business enterprises covered by the CIS for the 24 [[Glossary:EU Member States|EU countries]] for which data are comparable and complete, with the exception of Bulgaria, the Netherlands and Sweden.




== What is the share of European companies that introduce innovations benefiting the environment? ==


<vistool> <script>{ "utility": "wcloud", "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202512/18ece2d0-df23-11f0-bd20-45c5158ac7ea/uec.json"}</script> <caption>Figure 1</caption> </vistool>

A major contribution companies can make to protect the natural environment is to innovate with a view to having more sustainable internal processes, e.g. for production or logistics. The most frequently observed environmental impact of innovation within companies was the reduction of their energy consumption and CO2 emissions, noted in 8% of the European companies surveyed. Following closely, 6% of companies have implemented innovative measures for recycling waste, water, or materials. Approximately 5% of companies have focused on replacing fossil fuels and reducing pollution. Lastly, 4% of companies reported innovation initiatives to decrease material and water usage or substitute them with less polluting alternatives, making these efforts slightly less prevalent.



<vistool> <script>{ "utility": "wcloud", "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202601/e8da9050-ebc8-11f0-abb4-4586a049192c/uec.json"}</script> <caption>Figure 2</caption> </vistool>



Companies can also innovate to create products that have a less harmful impact on the natural environment when used by the consumers. When considering the indirect environmental impact of product innovations that offer ecological benefits at the point of consumption by the end user, there was a prevalence of energy reduction and CO2 footprint reduction, which concerned around 8% of companies. Next followed recycling (5%), extended product life (5%) and pollution reduction (5%).


== Cleaner production and processes within the company ==

The CIS informs about enterprises that have introduced one or more innovations that, during the production and processing, resulted in:

* reducing material or water use per unit of output
* reducing energy use or CO2 ‘footprint’ (i.e. reduced total CO2 emission)
* reducing soil, light, noise, water or air pollution
* replacing a share of materials with less polluting or hazardous substitutes
* replacing a share of fossil energy with renewable energy sources
* recycling waste, water, or materials for own use or sale


==== Industry compared to services ====

<vistool> <script>{ "utility": "wcloud", "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202511/6b8334c0-c939-11f0-a05d-3f3d9a6fef76/uec.json"}</script> <caption>Figure 3</caption> </vistool>

When examining the environmental impacts achieved through process improvements, industrial companies demonstrated greater efforts to improve their environmental impact than service companies, possibly because industrial production causes more emissions than providing services. This is particularly the case for reducing energy consumption and carbon footprint, which was achieved in 10% of industrial companies compared to 7% of service companies. Other environmental improvements are also more prevalent in industry than in services.

==== Comparison of companies by their size ====

<vistool> <script>{ "utility": "wcloud", "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202511/885bbd70-c939-11f0-b92f-b960a7f230bb/uec.json"}</script> <caption>Figure 4</caption> </vistool>

The largest companies are those that achieve the most environmental innovations. In particular, reducing energy consumption or carbon footprints concerned 23% of companies with 250 employees or more. This was also the case for other environmental benefits, which were all more prevalent among larger companies. In this context, it should be mentioned that larger companies have generally higher innovation rates than smaller ones (78% of all large companies in the EU are innovation active; versus 47% of all [[Glossary:Small_and_medium-sized_enterprises_(SMEs)|SMEs]], read more in the [[Innovation profiles of enterprises - results|article on innovation profiles of companies]]).

==== Comparison by country ====

<vistool> <script>{ "utility": "wcloud", "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202511/a93b5210-c939-11f0-8c23-0f5b43b3920d/uec.json"}</script> <caption>Figure 5</caption> </vistool>

EU countries show very different results as to their performance in terms of environmental improvements to their processes. For example, 16% of Estonian and Slovenian companies reduced their energy consumption and carbon footprint with their process innovations, compared with only around 1.5% of Romanian and Cypriot companies. Differences in the composition of the countries’ economies as regards the share of different economic activities (NACE) influence these shares.


== Cleaner consumption by the end user of the company’s products ==

Enterprises are increasingly aware of the impact their products have when used by consumers. This is driven not only by an environmental awareness inside the company, but also by customers who want to use products with a limited negative ecological impact. The CIS presents data on enterprises that sold innovative products that, during the usage by the consumer:

* reduced energy use or CO2 ‘footprint’ (8% of all companies)
* reduced air, water, soil, light or noise pollution (5% of all companies)
* facilitated recycling of product after use (5% of all companies)
* extended product life through longer-lasting, more durable, or easier-to-repair products (5% of all companies)


==== Industry compared to services ====

<vistool> <script>{ "utility": "wcloud", "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202511/0297d6e0-c93a-11f0-a1f0-6dedc914cabd/uec.json"}</script> <caption>Figure 6</caption> </vistool>

Environmental innovations related to products (goods or services) are more common in industry than in services. Again, the emissions during the consumption of industrial products were generally higher than during the consumption of services, explaining in part the greater effort made by industrial companies to reduce the negative environmental impact than service providers.


==== Comparison of companies by their size ====

<vistool> <script>{ "utility": "wcloud", "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202511/2013efc0-c93a-11f0-93d3-254bdc91beb6/uec.json"}</script> <caption>Figure 7</caption> </vistool>


Larger enterprises led the way in implementing innovations with environmental benefits linked to product consumption. For example, among enterprises with 250 or more employees, 18% offered products focused on reducing energy consumption and carbon footprint, whereas this figure stood at just 6% for smaller companies with 10 to 49 employees.

==== Comparison by country====


<vistool> <script>{ "utility": "wcloud", "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202601/7d344fa0-f13a-11f0-b06f-01233e279522/uec.json"}</script> <caption>Figure 8</caption> </vistool>

The comparison by country shows significant variations. For instance, when considering the most prevalent environmental benefit, i.e. reduction in energy consumption or carbon footprint, Estonia led the way, with 16% of its companies having implemented such innovations. Conversely, Cyprus ranked lowest, with only 1% of its firms implementing them. Again, these figures have to be seen against the background of a different composition of the economy in regard to different economic activities (NACE).

<datadetails>
=== Data sources ===

The [[Glossary:Community_innovation_survey_(CIS)|Community Innovation Survey]], abbreviated as CIS, is conducted in every [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] Member State to collect data on [[Glossary:Innovation|innovation]] in businesses, i.e. on [[Glossary:Product innovation|product innovation]] (goods or services) and [[Glossary:Business process innovation|business process innovation]] (e.g. production methods; logistics; information processing and communication; accounting and administrative operations; organisational, management and marketing aspects).

The legal basis for CIS is Commission Implementing [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32022R1092 Regulation (EU) 2022/1092] of 30 June 2022 laying down technical specifications of data requirements for the topic ’Innovation’ pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2019/2152.
</datadetails>

<context>
=== Context ===
The [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/clean-industrial-deal_en Clean Industrial Deal], launched in February 2025 and following up on the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en European Green Deal], helps the economies in the EU become more sustainable and resource-efficient. It outlines concrete actions to turn decarbonisation into a driver of growth for European industries. The Clean Industrial Deal focuses e.g. on the clean-tech sector which is at the heart of future competitiveness and necessary for industrial transformation, circularity, and decarbonisation. It invests in the 'clean transition' of manufacturing and stimulates research and innovation. Much of this innovation happens in the business sector.

The [[Glossary:Community_innovation_survey_(CIS)|Community Innovation Survey]] offers insights into company achievements relating to innovations of products and business processes that impact on the natural environment. Eurostat’s data on enterprises that have such innovations, with the capacity to link this to characteristics of the enterprise, provide an important element in the reporting ‘drawing board’ that is available to observe the situation. The CIS enables valuable cross-referencing of this innovation performance with other aspects of company behaviour. A dual focus is put on SMEs and on innovation. The data from the CIS is also helpful to provide structure to related data obtained through other sources.

The main concepts of the CIS are defined in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-01-18-852 Oslo Manual] (4th edition) to characterise companies engaged in innovation, or ‘innovation-active’ firms. A firm is considered to be ’innovation-active’ if it either introduced an innovation (product or business process innovation) during the observation period, or has been involved in any ongoing, abandoned, suspended, or completed innovation activity that has not (yet) led to the introduction of an innovation. Innovation activities cover a wide range of activities undertaken by firms to develop product or business process innovations. These may include research and development (R&D), but also other business development activities (financial, commercial, etc.), provided that they are aimed at developing an innovation. These activities may or may not ultimately result in an innovation being implemented by the company.

An innovation with environmental benefits is a new or improved product or process of an enterprise that generates lower environmental impacts, compared to the enterprise’s previous products or processes, and that has been made available to potential users or brought into use. The environmental benefit can be the primary objective of the innovation or a by-product of other objectives. 
The environmental benefits of an innovation can occur during the production of a good or service, or during its consumption or use by the end user of a product. The end user can be an individual, another enterprise, the government, etc.


This article presents data on the number of enterprises with such innovation, distinguishing:

*the type of impact (e.g. reduced CO2 footprint; better recycling options; reduced material or water use; reduced pollution of the soil, water, and air; etc.)
*economic sectors of the companies (e.g. industry; services; more detailed segments of the NACE)
*size of the companies (e.g. small; medium-sized; large)
*geographical location of the companies (countries of the EU and EFTA)

The CIS can link this data to many more characteristics of the enterprise and enables valuable cross-referencing of this innovation performance with other aspects of company behaviour. This data, even though not presented in this article, is available on Eurostat’s database ’Eurobase’.


The data presented in this article for:

*the ‘Industry’ cover NACE Rev 2.0 Sections B, C, D, E, and thus exclude construction;
*for ‘Services’ cover NACE Rev 2.0 Sections H, J, K, and Divisions 46, 71, 72 or 73;
*for the ‘Total’ cover NACE Rev 2.0 Sections B, C, D, E, H, J, K, and Divisions 46, 71, 72 or 73, and thus exclude construction;

The scope of the CIS is limited to enterprises with 10 or more persons employed. The number of persons employed is the sum of employees and self-employed persons. Eurostat provides information for the following firm size classes:

*10 to 49 persons employed (small enterprises);
*50 to 249 persons employed (medium-sized enterprises);
*250 persons employed or more (large enterprises).

Analysing the data by the size of companies provides evidence that is required for the formulation and monitoring of SME related policies in the EU, also in regard to their contribution to environmental innovation.

This article refers to all business enterprises covered by the CIS during the reference period 2020 to 2022, for the following 24 EU countries for which data are comparable and complete: Belgium, Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Croatia, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary, Malta, Austria, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, and Finland.

title: Integrated farm statistics - effects of changes in farm coverage
text:
Insert short description for search engines === Introduction ===
This article highlights how changes in farm coverage between 2020 and 2023 have created a methodological break in the time series for some key variables. As such, some developments cannot be interpreted as genuine changes. === Thresholds set in legislation ===
The EU legislation governing farm statistics establishes the minimum requirements for the coverage of [[Glossary:Agricultural holding|agricultural holdings]] (i.e. farms). When defining the national coverage of farms, EU countries apply various sets of thresholds while ensuring compliance with the EU’s minimum legal requirements.
For both 2020 and 2023, the EU’s minimum farm coverage requirements were defined in Articles 3, 5, 6 and 7, as well as Annex II of [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2018/1091/oj Regulation (EU) 2018/1091]. Accordingly, each EU country had to ensure that its core structural data covered those farms and common land agricultural units that met at least one of the following physical thresholds: [[Image:List of legal physical thresholds for 2020 and 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: List of legal physical thresholds for 2020 and 2023
''Source:'' Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2018/1091|alt=A table showing the list of physical thresholds used for the data collections for the reference years 2020 and 2023.]]
In Map 1, the countries that strictly adhered to the legal set of physical thresholds listed in Table 1 are represented by the category "Legal thresholds".
Where the applied thresholds failed to cover at least 98% of the total national [[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|Utilised Agricultural Area]] (UAA, excluding kitchen gardens) and at least 98% of the total national [[Glossary:Livestock unit (LSU)|Livestock Units]] (LSU), the legislation required countries to extend the coverage frame in 2020 by establishing lower and/or additional thresholds. Although this requirement was not in place for 2023, some countries also chose to extend the coverage frame in this way for the 2023 data collection.
Countries that extended the coverage frame in 2023 answered "Yes" to concept 3.6.1.2 of the 2023 [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/quality national quality reports] and are presented in Map 1 by the category “Lower thresholds”. The countries that were required to extend the coverage frame in 2020 had to collect core structural data in the frame extension but not also the module data in the frame extension. Consequently, the module data in 2020 and the core and module data in 2023 do not necessarily ensure the 98 % minimum UAA and LSU requirements in all countries.
By way of exception, the legislation for both the 2020 and 2023 data collections, also allowed countries to set higher physical or equivalent economic thresholds, according to the following conditions: the thresholds presented in Table 1 accounted for over 98% of national agricultural production, as measured by the [[Glossary:Standard_output_(SO)|standard output (SO)]], and that the higher established thresholds also satisfied the minimum 98% coverage requirements for both UAA and LSU. Countries in this situation responded "Yes" to concept 3.6.1.1 of the 2023 national quality reports and are represented in Map 1 by the category “Higher thresholds”. [[Image:Thresholds applied for farms concerning core data in 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Thresholds applied for farms concerning core data in 2023
|alt=A map showing the thresholds used by the countries for the 2023 data collection]] === Relative change of data for core variables between 2020 and 2023 === ''' (analysed over the entire farm populations covered in each year and for subsets of farm populations meeting common size criteria in both years)'''
Table 2 contrasts the relative changes in core data for the entire farm populations surveyed in 2020 and 2023 (referred to as “original populations”), on the one hand, and the populations that meet common size criteria for both years (referred to as “common populations”), on the other.
The common populations for 2020 and 2023 were determined by selecting farms from each year that simultaneously met the size criteria for both 2020 and 2023 within the geographical territory covered in both years.
The analysis compares the relative changes between the two years in key core variables: number of farms (holdings), total UAA, total LSU, economic size of farms (measured in standard output (SO) and labour force directly employed by farms on a regular basis (expressed in [[Glossary:Annual_work_unit_(AWU)|annual work units (AWU)]]).
In both years, many countries covered at least 98% of the total national UAA (excluding kitchen gardens) and at least 98% of the total national LSU. Therefore, where changes in coverage have a significant impact on data, they typically undermine the comparability of other key variables over time, such as the number of farms, legal types of farms, characteristics related to holders and managers, labour force, other gainful activities and, in some cases, specific land use and livestock categories, including kitchen gardens. Where this is the case, trends cannot be directly interpreted from the disseminated data of the original populations. [[Image:Change in core variables 2 (%, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Change in core variables (%, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A table showing the changes in core variables between 2020 and 2023.]] === Changes in the coverage of farms between 2020 and 2023 ===
This section groups EU countries according to whether there were changes in national farm coverage between 2020 and 2023. Where there were changes, their impact on the time series is examined. =====Countries with no change in the national coverage of farms=====
'''Belgium, Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Ireland, France, Croatia, Cyprus, Latvia, Luxembourg, Hungary, the Netherlands, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Finland''' and '''Sweden''' maintained unchanged coverage thresholds and geographical coverage between 2020 and 2023. In their 2023 national quality reports, these countries indicated under concept 15.2.3.1 that: "''There have been no changes''". The relative changes in core variable data are presented in Figures 1-5.
Figures 1, 4 and 5 reveal minor discrepancies for certain countries and core variables between the relative changes in data for original populations and common populations. These differences arise because, despite unchanged farm coverage, the 2020 and/or 2023 farm populations included a small proportion of farms that met the coverage criteria at the data collection design stage but no longer did so during the reference year (due to the fluctuations in crop and animal variables between the design year of the data collection and the reference year). [[Image:Change in the number of farms 5 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Change in the number of farms (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the number of farms between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]]
[[Image:Change in the utilised agricultural area 5 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Change in the utilised agricultural area (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the utilised agricultural area between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]]
[[Image:Change in the total livestock units 5 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Change in the total livestock units (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the total livestock units between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]]
[[Image:Change in the total standard output 5 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Change in the total standard output (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the total standard output between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]]
[[Image:Change in the labour force directly employed by farms on a regular basis 5 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Change in the labour force directly employed by farms on a regular basis (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the labour force directly employed by farms on a regular basis between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]] =====Countries with some changes in the coverage of farms but not enough to warrant the designation of a break in series=====
'''Estonia, Spain''' and '''Austria''' changed their coverage thresholds between 2020 and 2023. However, these changes did not significantly impact the development in the number of farms, the total UAA, the total LSUs, the standard output and the labour force directly employed by farms on a regular basis. In their 2023 national quality reports, these countries indicated under concept 15.2.3.1 that: "''There have been some changes but not enough to warrant the designation of a break in series''".
The following changes were made by the countries: *'''Estonia''' added the threshold of 0.1 hectares for “grapes outdoor” in the 2023 data collection, which was not previously considered in 2020. *'''Spain''' raised some thresholds for the NUTS 2 region ES11 (Galicia) in the 2023 data collection, aligning thresholds across all autonomous communities. In 2020, lower thresholds were used in Galicia to ensure the minimum 98% UAA and LSU coverage. *'''Austria''' introduced an additional threshold for commercial apple and apricot orchards in the 2023 data collection (due to the new data collection module focusing on orchards that year), which applied in addition to the previously used orchard threshold. As Figure 6 illustrates, the change in the number of farms between 2020 and 2023 was identical or nearly identical when comparing the original populations to common populations. This was also the case for the changes in total UAA, total LSU, standard output and the labour force directly employed by farms on a regular basis. [[Image:Change in the number of farms 6 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Change in the number of farms (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the number of farms between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]]
[[Image:Change in the utilised agricultural area 6 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Change in the utilised agricultural area (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the utilised agricultural area between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]]
[[Image:Change in the total livestock units 6 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Change in the total livestock units (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the total livestock units between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]]
[[Image:Change in the total standard output 6 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: Change in the total standard output (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the total standard output between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]]
[[Image:Change in the labour force directly employed by farms on a regular basis 6 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 10: Change in the labour force directly employed by farms on a regular basis (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the labour force directly employed by farms on a regular basis between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]] =====Countries with changes in the coverage of farms that are sufficient to warrant the designation of a break in series=====
'''Bulgaria, Greece, Italy, Lithuania, Malta, Poland''' and '''Slovenia''' revised their coverage thresholds between 2020 and 2023. The adjustments were considered to have significantly impacted the evolution of at least one of the following core variables: number of farms, total UAA, total LSU, standard output and labour force directly employed by farms on a regular basis (see Figures 11-15). In their 2023 [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/quality national quality reports], these countries indicated under concept 15.2.3.1 that: "''There have been sufficient changes to warrant the designation of a break in series''".
Except for '''Malta''', all these countries applied lower thresholds in 2020 but adopted for 2023 the legal set of physical thresholds as listed in Table 1 above. Consequently, they submitted 2020 data for the main and extended frame but only collected data for the main frame in 2023. The thresholds applied are available in the national quality reports - in 2020 for the main and extended frame and in 2023 for the main frame (under point 3.6.1 of these reports). [[Image:Change in the number of farms 7 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 11: Change in the number of farms (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the number of farms between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]]
[[Image:Change in the utilised agricultural area 7 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 12: Change in the utilised agricultural area (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the utilised agricultural area between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]]
[[Image:Change in the total livestock units 7 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 13: Change in the total livestock units (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the total livestock units between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]]
[[Image:Change in the total standard output 7 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 14: Change in the total standard output (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the total standard output between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]]
[[Image:Change in the labour force directly employed by farms on a regular basis 8 (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 15: Change in the labour force directly employed by farms on a regular basis (%, selected EU countries, 2020-2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat calculations |alt=A graph showing the change in the labour force directly employed by farms on a regular basis between 2020 and 2023 for selected EU countries.]]
The main findings are that: *In '''Bulgaria''', the shift in thresholds between 2020 and 2023 significantly affected the number of holdings and the labour force. *In '''Greece''', the change in farm coverage significantly affected the number of holdings. *In '''Italy''', the change in thresholds had a minimal impact on UAA and LSU (as only very small units were excluded), but it significantly affected the number of holdings and the labour force. *In '''Lithuania''', the threshold changes between 2020 and 2023 resulted in the exclusion of the smallest holdings in 2023, affecting the number of holdings, as well as specific crops and livestock species. *'''Malta''' submitted data for both the main and extended frames for 2020 and 2023. However, it excluded from the 2023 population the agricultural holdings having only fallow land and a standard output of 0 euros. This significantly impacted the number of farms, utilised agricultural area and labour force. *In '''Poland''', the threshold changes between 2020 and 2023 affected the number of farms, the utilised agricultural area and the labour force. *In '''Slovenia''', the change in thresholds reduced the coverage of smaller agricultural holdings and, as a result, the 2023 data are not fully comparable to 2020, particularly regarding the number of farms and utilised agricultural area. === Conclusion === This article examines changes in farm coverage between 2020 and 2023, and highlights cases where these changes significantly affect the comparability of data for some main variables during this period. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Data Source for tables and graphs updated v4.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Other articles === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Integrated_farm_statistics_-_impact_of_changes_in_coverage Integrated farm statistics - impact of changes in coverage] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agriculture Agriculture - Statistics Explained] === Database === *'''Detailed datasets''' :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database Agriculture (agr)], see: ::Farm structure (ef) === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/overview Agriculture] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/information-data/agricultural-census Agricultural census 2020] === Publications === *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-049|title=Key figures on the European food chain - 2025 edition}} === Methodology=== *Farm structure: ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/ef_sims.htm ESMS metadata file — ef_esms)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/quality National quality reports] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-25-058 Integrated Farm Statistics Manual, 2023 survey] - 2026 edition *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-reports/w/ks-ft-24-004 Principal quality characteristics of EU countries' Agricultural Censuses for 2020] - 2024 edition === Legislation === *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32018R1091 Regulation (EU) 2018/1091] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 July 2018 on integrated farm statistics and repealing Regulations (EC) No 1166/2008 and (EU) No 1337/2011 *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2021.458.01.0284.01.ENG Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/2286] of 16 December 2021 on the data to be provided for the reference year 2023 pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 of the European Parliament and of the Council on integrated farm statistics as regards the list of variables and their description and repealing Commission Regulation (EC) No 1200/2009 *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32018R1874 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/1874] of 29 November 2018 on the data to be provided for 2020 under Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 of the European Parliament and of the Council on integrated farm statistics and repealing Regulations (EC) No 1166/2008 and (EU) No 1337/2011, as regards the list of variables and their description === External links === '''European Commission''' *[https://commission.europa.eu/topics/agriculture-and-rural-development_en Agriculture and rural development] *DG Agriculture and Rural Development **[https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy_en Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)] ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Article_name'' {{Unit|topic=X_Agriculture}} [[Category:Agriculture, fisheries, and forestry|Integrated farm statistics -
