title: Inland waterways - statistics on container transport
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the inland waterways - statistics on container transport. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 In 2025, container transport accounted for 9.4% of the total inland waterway transport in the EU, based on tonne-kilometres. In 2025, The Netherlands and Germany accounted for the overwhelming majority of EU inland waterway container transport. In 2025, empty containers accounted for 30.4% of inland waterway container transport in the EU, based on TEU-kilometres. This article presents the latest statistical data on inland waterway transport of [[Glossary:Freight_container|containers ]] in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] and other countries connected to the EU inland waterway network. For an overview of the total annual and quarterly inland waterway transport, please refer to the Statistics Explained article [[Inland waterway freight transport - quarterly and annual data]]. === Transport of containers by inland waterways decreased in 2025 === In the EU, the share of container transport in total inland waterway transport performance (in [[Glossary:Tonne-kilometre_(tkm)|tonne-kilometres]]) increased from 9.9% in 2015 to 11.0% in 2017 (see Figure 1). In 2018, the share declined by 0.6 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]], followed by a further drop in 2019 of 0.3 pp, bringing the share down to 10.1%. A temporary rebound occurred in 2020, when the share returned to 10.4%. Thereafter, a downward trend set in: the share declined for four consecutive years, reaching 10.0% in 2021, 9.8% in 2022, 9.5% in 2023, and 9.3% in 2024, before a slight rebound to 9.4% in 2025. Figure 1 Movements of empty containers in the EU in terms of [[Glossary:Twenty-foot_equivalent_unit_(TEU)|twenty-foot equivalent unit]] kilometres (TEU-km) substantially decreased by 7.6% between 2015 and 2016 (see Figure 2). A slight rebound immediately followed in 2017 (+1.7%). In 2018, 2019, and 2020, 3 consecutive declines were registered (-14.8%, -10.3% and, -5.0%, respectively). While an upturn of 3.7% was recorded in 2021, subsequent movements of empty containers expressed in TEU-km continued to show decreases of 6.5% in 2022 and 2.9% in 2023 down to 393 million TEU-km, the lowest level since 2009 (348 million TEU-km). In 2024 and 2025, 2 consecutive modest increase of 0.6%, each, were recorded, suggesting a stabilisation after several years of decline. When looking at movements of loaded containers, the picture is slightly different (see Figure 2). In 2016, movements of loaded containers increased by 4.0% compared with 2015. The positive trend continued in 2017 (+6.4%), culminating in the decade’s peak of 1 123 million TEU-km in 2017. Then, similarly to empty containers, downturns were registered in both 2018 and 2020 (-5.4% and -4.8%, respectively), whereas 2019 was marked by a quite stable evolution (+0.2%). A growth of 4.4% in 2021 was followed by declines of 8.9% in 2022 and 8.1% in 2023. The 2023 value, 886 million TEU-km, is the lowest registered since 2009 (784 million TEU-km). In 2024, loaded movements recovered by 5.1%, but were immediately followed by a drop of 2.2% in 2025 to 911 million TEU-km. Altogether, loaded and empty containers amounted to 1 309 billion TEU-km in 2025, down by 1.3% compared with 2024. Figure 2 International transport of containers accounted for over half of the container transport performance (in TEU-km) in 2015 (51.1%) and 2017 (50.5%), while it came close to this level in 2016 (49.4%) (see Figure 3). International transport evolution was quite erratic, with several year-on-year declines. A notable decrease occurred in 2018, when it dropped by 10.5% compared with 2017. The downward trend continued in 2019 (-2.8%) and 2020 (-4.2%). In 2021, a slight rebound was observed, with a 1.4% increase, followed by 2 sharp declines in 2022 (-9.3%) and 2023 (-15.1%). Thus, 2023 marks the lowest performance in international transport of containers since data are available (i.e. 2007). The year 2024 registered a 1.9% rise over 2023 while a slight decrease was recorded in 2025 (-0.9%). National transport of containers came in second place when measured in TEU-km (34.4% in 2025), followed by transit transport (22.5% in 2025). National transport decreased between 2015 and 2016 (-0.7%), before increasing for 3 consecutive years (+3.2% in 2017, +0.9% in 2018, and +1.9% in 2019). In 2020, national transport decreased by 4.9%. The most noticeable increase was registered in 2021, with a 10.8% growth compared with 2020. In 2022 and 2023, national transport fell by 5.8% and 8.3%, respectively, compared with the previous year. In 2024 and 2025, national transport grew by 6.1% and 0.6%, respectively, compared to the previous year. Transit transport of containers experienced a strong increase in 2016 (+7.7%), followed by a more moderate growth in 2017 (+1.9%). However, in 2018, 2019 and 2020, significant declines were registered (-15.3%, -10.8%, and -6.4%, respectively). In 2021, there was a modest increase of 0.9%, but this was followed by a sharp drop of 9.7% in 2022. A substantial rebound was then recorded in 2023, with growth of 18.7%. In 2024, transit transport continued to expand, rising by 3.7% compared with the previous year. In 2025, the positive trend came to an end, with a 5.0% decrease in transit transport of containers. Figure 3 The performance in the transport of loaded containers in the EU decreased by 2.2% in 2025, when measured in TEU-km (see Table 1), but slightly increased by 0.4%, when measured in TEUs (see Table 2). Looking at the breakdown by type of transport measured in TEU-KM, national transport increased by 1.4% in 2025 compared with 2024. In contrast, international transport fell by 2.7% and transit transport by 5.7%. When expressed in TEUs, national transport rose by 1.1% while international transport decreased by 0.6%. [[Image: Inland waterway transport of loaded containers by type of transport, in selected years, 2015-2025 (thousand TEU-kilometres).png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Inland waterway transport of loaded containers by type of transport, in selected years, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fb4de228-fd35-4ba7-9540-799bee2f6681?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-31T07:48:24Z iww_go_acsize])|alt= Table showing inland waterway transport of loaded containers by type of transport as thousand TEU-kilometres in the EU and some EU Member States for selected years 2015, 2019, 2023, 2024, and 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] At country level, the Netherlands and Germany were by far the main contributors to the inland waterway transport performance of loaded containers (in TEU-km) in 2025, followed by France and Belgium (see Table 1). Altogether, these 4 countries represented 99.8% of the total movements of loaded containers in the EU, when expressed in TEU-km. Amongst these 4 countries, national transport was predominant in France and Belgium, at 94.1% and 57.9% of the total transport of loaded containers, respectively. In the Netherlands, the shares of national and international transport were 41.2% and 35.0%, respectively. In Germany, international transport dominated with 61.3%, while national transport represented only 6.2%. In Germany and the Netherlands, transit transport was quite significant, with shares at 32.5% and 23.8%, respectively, whereas it was less than 1% in Belgium. The Netherlands and Germany were by far the major contributors to the inland waterway transport performance of loaded containers (in TEU) in the EU in 2025, followed by Belgium and France (see Table 2). Amongst these 4 countries, national transport was predominant in France and the Netherlands, at 72.7% and 46.4% of total transport of loaded containers, respectively, whereas international transport in these 2 countries represented 27.3% and 35.0%, respectively. In Germany and Belgium, international transport dominated with 74.0% and 69.6%, respectively. Transit transport was significant in the Netherlands and Germany, with shares at 18.6% and 14.3%, respectively, and it accounted for below 1.5% in Belgium. This reflects the significance of both the Netherlands and Germany as hosts for major transit ports or as a major source or destination for container movements (Rotterdam, Antwerp, and Hamburg). Bulgaria, Luxembourg, Romania, and Hungary recorded significant decreases in inland waterway transport of loaded containers between 2024 and 2025, for both TEU-KM and TEUs. Bulgaria saw a 100.0% decrease in terms of TEU-KM, followed by Luxembourg (-90.3%), Romania (-86.3%) and Hungary (-81.6%). In terms of TEUs, Bulgaria recorded the sharpest decline by 100.0%, followed by Hungary (-90.0%), Romania (-84.2%) and Luxembourg (-49.8%). It should be noted that the contribution of these countries to the total TEU-km performed in the EU is still very low. The shares of the 3 countries combined were 0.05% of the total movements of loaded containers in the EU, based on TEU-km, and 0.1% based on TEUs. France (-12.4% for TEU-KM and -7.5% for TEUs) and Sweden (-7.5% for TEU-KM and -7.7% for TEUs) also experienced large declines. Transport of loaded containers in Germany also declined by 3.9% in terms of TEU-km and 0.5% in terms of TEUs. In contrast, the Netherlands recorded a growth over the same period, by 1.9% for TEU-km and +3.3% for TEUs. Belgium also recorded a growth in terms of TEU-km (+1.1%), but a decline in terms of TEUs (-4.8%). Belgium was the only country to record a growth in transit transport of containers, in 2025 compared with 2024 (+34.8% for TEU-km and +32.2% for TEUs). Bulgaria, France, and Luxembourg did not report any transit transport of containers in 2025. Bulgaria and Romania did not report any international transport of containers in 2025. [[Image: Inland waterway transport of loaded containers by type of transport, in selected years, 2015-2025 (TEUs).png|thumb|center|700px|Table 2: Inland waterway transport of loaded containers by type of transport, in selected years, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/18ef8d25-169a-4db7-8789-7664895ac2b2?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-31T07:48:51Z iww_go_acsize])|alt= Table showing inland waterway transport of loaded containers by type of transport as TEUs in the EU and some EU Member States for selected years 2015, 2019, 2023, 2024, and 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2025, movements of empty containers in the EU showed a slight increase in TEU-km (+0.6%) (see Table 3) and in TEUs (+0.5%) (see Table 4). By type of transport, international transport of empty containers rose in both TEU-km (+3.7%) and TEUs (+4.3%) in the EU, while national transport of empty containers in the EU declined in TEU-km (-0.8%) and in TEUs (-1.4%). Transit transport of empty containers in the EU showed a decrease in TEU-km (-2.9%). At country level, the Netherlands and Germany were again by far the major contributors to the inland waterway transport performance of empty containers (in TEU-km) in 2025, followed by France and Belgium (see Table 3). National transport of empty containers, when based on TEU-km, was predominant in France (91.6% of the total transport of empty containers), Romania (74.8%), Belgium (69.9%), and the Netherlands (50.8%). International transport of empty containers, when based on TEU-km, was predominant in Luxembourg (100%), Hungary (99.9%), Austria (65.6%), and Germany (62.8%). Transit transport of empty containers, when based on TEU-km, was predominant in Bulgaria (100%) and Croatia (100%). [[Image: Inland waterway transport of empty containers by type of transport, in selected years, 2015-2025 (thousand TEU-kilometres).png|thumb|center|700px|Table 3: Inland waterway transport of empty containers by type of transport, in selected years, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/921cb3d8-e723-4a90-8e62-35627169f0d4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-31T07:50:01Z iww_go_acsize])|alt= Table showing inland waterway transport of empty containers by type of transport as thousand TEU-kilometres in the EU and some EU Member States for selected years 2015, 2019, 2023, 2024, and 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at the transport of empty containers in TEUs, the Netherlands and Germany were also by far the major contributors to the inland waterway transport performance of empty containers (in TEUs) in 2025, followed by Belgium and France (see Table 4). National transport of empty containers, when based on TEUs, was predominant in Romania (92.8% of the total transport of empty containers), France (71.1%), and the Netherlands (52.2%). International transport of empty containers, when based on TEUs, was predominant in Hungary (100%), Luxembourg (100%), Austria (81.7%), and Germany (70.6%). Transit transport of empty containers, when based on TEUs, was predominant in Bulgaria (100%) and Croatia (100%). Croatia, Austria, and Hungary recorded significant increases in inland waterway transport of empty containers between 2024 and 2025, for both TEU-KM and TEUs. Austria saw a 587.3% increase in terms of TEU-KM, followed by Croatia (+473.3%) and Hungary (+96.0%). In terms of TEUs, Croatia recorded the sharpest increase by 473.3%, followed by Austria (+133.8%) and Hungary (+94.3%). It should be noted that the contribution of these countries to the total TEU-km performed in the EU is still very low. The Netherlands also experienced growths (+7.4% for TEU-KM and +8.6% for TEUs). Germany also recorded a growth in terms of TEUs (+0.9%), but a decline in terms of TEU-km (-3.7%). By contrast, the other 5 EU countries experienced substantial declines. Notable decreases were recorded in Sweden (-77.6% for both TEU-km and TEUs), Romania (-57.8% for TEU-km and -64.4% for TEUs), Luxembourg (-37.7% for TEU-km and -39.0% for TEUs), Belgium (-19.2% for TEU-km and -16.5% for TEUs), and France (-9.9% for TEU-km and -11.5% for TEUs). Czechia, Poland, Slovakia, and Finland have not reported any empty containers. [[Image: Inland waterway transport of empty containers by type of transport, in selected years, 2015-2025 (TEUs).png|thumb|center|700px|Table 4: Inland waterway transport of empty containers by type of transport, in selected years, 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b529a48d-91d4-467d-b222-0736142ce90b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-31T07:49:19Z iww_go_acsize])|alt= Table showing inland waterway transport of empty containers by type of transport as TEUs in the EU and EU Member States with reporting obligations for selected years 2015, 2019, 2023, 2024, and 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === The shipment of loaded containers accounted for 69.6% of total transport of containers in the EU === At EU level, 69.6% of TEU-km accounted for the shipment of loaded containers in 2025 (see Figure 4). Sweden (99.1%), France (76.5%), Belgium (74.0%), Germany (71.1%) and the Netherlands (67.1%) exceeded the EU level in 2025. The remaining countries had lower shares; Romania: 43.0%, Luxembourg: 11.4%, and Hungary: 0.1%. Bulgaria, Croatia and Austria only reported empty containers. Countries with exclusively or very high levels of empty containers transported on inland waterways have provided methodological clarifications regarding the structure of their transport: empty containers are moved by inland waterways from one port to another, where they are subsequently loaded and then transported further by road or rail. In some cases, for instance in Austria, the empty containers themselves are classified as goods. Figure 4 === 40-foot containers are predominant on EU inland waterways === In terms of the size of loaded containers being transported, 40-foot freight units were dominant at EU level, accounting for 74.3% of all loaded containers in 2025 (see Figure 5). The second most commonly-used type was the 20-foot container with 20.1%, while intermediate containers (>20 feet and <40 feet) made up 4.2%, and containers over 40 feet stood only at 1.4%. Only Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden reported movements of containers over 40-feet; among these, Germany recorded the highest share in 2025, at 1.8% of the total number of containers transported. Figure 5 For empty containers at EU level, the picture looked similar, with intermediate (freight units >20 feet and <40 feet) and very large containers (freight units >40 feet) accounting for only 2.9% and 1.0%, respectively, of the total transport performance of empty containers in TEU-km in 2025 (see Figure 6). 40-foot freight units accounted for 77.6% and 20-foot containers for 18.5%. In most countries, 40-foot containers were the most frequently reported category. In 2025, the exceptions were Croatia and Romania, which reported only 20-foot containers, Luxembourg, where freight units over 20 feet and under 40 feet accounted for the largest share (55.8%), while 40-foot containers represented only 5.3%; and Austria, where freight units over 40 feet accounted for the largest share (79.6%). Figure 6 === Country-to-country flows dominated by the Netherlands, Germany and Belgium === Country-to-country flows in 2025 illustrated the dominance of the 3 countries relevant for inland waterway transport of containers: Belgium, the Netherlands, and Germany. The top 5 flows were between these 3 countries accounting for 70.8% of the total flows in TEU-km (see Table 5). When looking at TEUs, the situation is similar, with the top 6 flows involving these 3 countries and accounting for 92.0% of the total flows in TEUs (see Table 6). However, the ranking of these flows varied, depending on whether transport is measured in TEUs or in TEU-km. For example, the Netherlands to Belgium flow moves in ranking from position 3 in country-to-country flows by TEUs (see Table 6) to position 5 when measured by TEU-km (see Table 5). This is due to the proximity of the 2 countries and the short distances transported between them. [[Image: Top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of containers, 2025 (thousand TEU-kilometres).png|thumb|center|700px|Table 5: Top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of containers, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2d97e986-93ef-4fc5-8d37-20ad84e00321?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-31T07:57:22Z iww_go_actygofl])|alt= Table showing top ten international loading and unloading country flows for inland waterway transport of containers as thousand TEU-kilometres and based on percentage share of total for the year 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] France appeared once among the top 10 flows in 2024, when transport is measured in TEU-km, ranking ninth with the flow from France to Belgium (see Table 5), and 3 times when measured in TEUs (see Table 6). When looking at TEUs, France’s occurrences in top 10 flows recorded the flow from France to Belgium in seventh position, the flow from the Netherlands to France in ninth position and the flow from Belgium to France in tenth position. Switzerland is also present in the top 10 flows, with 3 appearances in positions 6, 7 and 10 when looking at TEU-km; the main flow being the flow from the Netherlands to Switzerland, followed by the flow from Switzerland to Belgium and the flow from Switzerland to the Netherlands (see Table 5). When looking at TEUs, Switzerland appears only once in the top 10 flows with the flow from the Netherlands to Switzerland in eighth position (see Table 6). [[Image: Top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of containers, 2025 (TEUs).png|thumb|center|700px|Table 6: Top 10 international country flows for inland waterway transport of containers, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d2c3e2be-8ca6-4232-9415-dc335f3c1e61?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-31T07:57:42Z iww_go_actygofl])|alt= Table showing top ten international loading and unloading country flows for inland waterway transport of containers as TEUs and based on percentage share of total for the year 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:SE_Article_IWW_containers_2026-09.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== All figures presented in this article have been extracted from the [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] online inland waterways transport database. The related datasets are collected according to {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R0974:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2018/974}} of the European Parliament and of the Council on statistics of goods transport by inland waterways. Regulation (EU) 2018/974 states that data must be supplied by all Member States for which the total volume of goods transported annually by inland waterways exceeds 1 million tonnes. Currently, 17 Member States provide data on a mandatory or voluntary basis: Belgium (BE), Bulgaria (BG), Czechia (CZ), Germany (DE), France (FR), Croatia (HR), Italy (IT), Lithuania (LT), Luxembourg (LU), Hungary (HU), the Netherlands (NL), Austria (AT), Poland (PL), Romania (RO), Slovakia (SK), Finland (FI) and Sweden (SE). Thirteen Member States (previously 12, but since 2022 also Sweden fulfils the requirements for mandatory reporting) have a legal obligation to provide data for inland waterway transport, where transport of goods by containers is one category of cargo classification. The legal act requires only the provision of a reduced annual dataset for countries exceeding the 1 million tonnes threshold but where no international or transit traffic exists. '''Definitions''' '''National inland waterway transport''': Inland waterway transport between two places (a port or place of loading and a port or place of unloading) within a national territory irrespective of the country in which the vessel is registered. It may involve transit through a second country, although for this country this transport must be reported as transit. '''International inland waterway transport''': Inland waterway transport between two places (a port or place of loading and a port or place of unloading) located in different countries. It may involve transit through one or more countries. For the latter countries, this transport must be reported as transit. '''Inland waterway transit transport''': Inland waterway transport through a national territory between two places (a port or place of loading and a port or place of unloading) both located in another national territory or national territories, provided that in the total journey within the national territory, there is no loading and unloading operation. '''TEU (twenty-foot equivalent unit)''' is a statistical unit based on an ISO container measuring 20 feet (6.10 m) to provide a standardised measure for counting containers of various capacities and for describing the capacity of container ships or terminals. One 20-foot ISO container equals 1 TEU. '''EU''' includes data for all Member States that provide data. '''Calculation of EU aggregates''': In Tables 2 and 4, EU international and total goods transport in TEUs is calculated by addressing the issue of double counting. This issue arises because both the country of loading (Country A) and the country of unloading (Country B) report tonnes for the same transport activity. Therefore, simply summing the values reported by individual EU countries is not feasible, as the same transport would be counted twice leading to inflated totals. More precisely, to avoid the issue of double counting, the calculation of EU aggregates for tonnes is currently performed as follows: * EU aggregate for national transport: Total reported for national transport by all reporting EU countries (no risk of double counting); * EU aggregate for international transport: Total reported by the reporting EU country, when it is the unloading country. If the unloading country does not report data, then the data from the loading country is used instead. For example, if goods are transported from Germany (loading country) to Switzerland (unloading country), only the data reported by Germany would be considered in the calculation, as Switzerland does not provide any data. * EU aggregate for total transport: National transport + International transport (Transit transport is not considered). For transit transport measured in TEUs, an EU aggregate equal to the sum of the country figures is not valid because volumes of freight transported are reported by all transit countries through which the transport takes place before reaching the unloading destination. Therefore, the same volume may be reported 2, 3, or more times without the possibility to eliminate multiple counting. At the same time, figures for transit transport are included in the EU national or international transport as they are reported not only by the transit countries but also by the loading and unloading countries. So, for the EU total volume, it is enough to sum the total national and international figures. '''Annual changes in the EU aggregate''' It should be noted that Sweden reported data on containers for the first time in 2022. For this reason, Sweden’s 2022 figures have been excluded when calculating the EU-level change rates between 2021 and 2022. '''Country specific notes''' Belgium: a break in time series can be observed in 2018 due to an improvement in the data collection system. Bulgaria: There was no inland waterway transport of loaded containers in 2017, 2018, 2023 and 2025. There was no inland waterway transport of empty containers in 2023 and 2024. Czechia: There was no inland waterway transport of containers over the period 2015-2025. Italy: No data on inland waterway transport of containers available. Croatia: There was no inland waterway transport of loaded containers over the periods 2016-2019 and 2023-2025. Lithuania: No data on inland waterway transport of containers available. Hungary: There was no inland waterway transport of loaded containers over the periods 2016-2018 and 2020-2021. Austria: There was no inland waterway transport of loaded containers over the period 2015-2025. Poland: There was no inland waterway transport of containers in 2016 and over the period 2018-2025. There was no inland waterway transport of loaded containers in 2017. Romania: There was no inland waterway transport of loaded containers in 2018 and 2020. Slovakia: There was no inland waterway transport of containers over the periods 2017-2020 and 2022-2025. There was no inland waterway transport of loaded containers in 2015, 2016 and 2021. Finland: There was no inland waterway transport of containers over the period 2015-2025. Sweden: Data were delivered on a voluntary basis until 2021. Only a simplified annual dataset was provided until 2021. Data on containers are available only from 2022. '''Symbols''' *":" not available *"-" not applicable *"0" real zero ===Context=== The content of this statistical article is based on data collected within the framework of {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R0974:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2018/974}} of the European Parliament and of the Council on statistics of goods transport by inland waterways. ===Other articles=== *[[Inland waterway freight transport statistics by type of goods]] *[[Inland waterway freight transport - title: Integrated government finance statistics presentation
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of integrated government finance statistics. Data extracted on 22 April 2026 for annual and on 21 July 2026 for quarterly GFS tables Planned article update: 21 October 2026 The 'integrated government finance statistics (GFS) presentation' is a dedicated presentation template for [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] government accounts that shows the economic activities of [[Glossary:Government|government]] in a manner suitable for fiscal analysis. It groups together all government statistics collected by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] specifically for the [[Glossary:General_government_sector|general government sector]] (i.e. excluding public corporations) in the framework of [[Glossary:National_accounts_(NA)|national accounts]], completed by statistical information gathered for administrative purposes. The integrated government finance statistics presentation assures a focus on economic substance over legal form, improves data harmonisation and comparability across countries, and ensures full transparency in the respect of the different statistical concepts and practices.
For recently updated Government Finance Statistics tables, please click on the icon ''Publications'' below. *'''Quarterly GFS tables - ESA 2010 basis''' :*[[Media:QGFS_Tables_2026_07_21.xlsb|Quarterly GFS tables, published 21 July 2026]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] *'''Annual GFS tables - Excel publication - ESA 2010 basis''' :*[[Media:AGFS_Tables_2026-04-22.xlsb|Summary GFS tables for all available years, general government and its subsectors, published 22 April 2026]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] :*[[Media:AGFS_Tables_2026-04-22_S13_only.xlsb|Summary GFS tables for all available years, general government, published 22 April 2026]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]]
===Integrated GFS presentation - introduction=== The GFS presentation shows in an integrated manner: [[Glossary:Total_general_government_revenue|government revenue]], [[Glossary:Total_general_government_expenditure|government expenditure]], government [[Glossary:Deficit|deficit]], transactions in assets, transactions in liabilities, other economic flows (in assets and liabilities), and balance sheets. This presentation is similar to that of business accounting where the profit and loss accounts and the balance sheet are presented together, in a linked manner. This type of GFS presentation is also suitable for fiscal analysis of the various levels of government ([[Glossary:Central_government|central]], regional (or '[[Glossary:State_government|state]]'), [[Glossary:Local_government|local]], [[Glossary:Social_security_fund|social security funds]]). European GFS are defined by reference to the [[Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)|2010 European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010) basis]], the European manual for national accounts. These GFS form the basis for fiscal monitoring in Europe, notably for the statistics related to the [[Glossary:Excessive_deficit_procedure_(EDP)|Excessive deficit procedure (EDP)]]. The approach for compiling and presenting European GFS is to re-arrange the transactions recorded in the various ESA annual and quarterly financial and non-financial accounts for the general government sector. The integrated GFS presentation brings together an analysis of deficit and [[Glossary:Public_debt|debt]], along with their main components. More generally, linkages between stock and flow variables as well as the connection between financial and non-financial accounts are made transparent. This allows for a complete and concise overview of the governments' financial and non-financial positions. Because of the importance of fiscal monitoring, the integrated presentation of GFS is 1 important statistical tool that has been developed in order to improve the assessment of budgetary positions. GFS template tables are presented on both annual and quarterly basis, and they are available in electronic form in the dedicated GFS section of the Eurostat web site. The annual GFS template tables present data for all EU Member States, for the European Union ([[Glossary:EU-27|EU]]) and the [[Glossary:Euro_area|euro area]] ([[Glossary:EA-19|EA19]]) as well as for Iceland, Norway and Switzerland. Annual tables are currently available for the EU and EA-19 from 1995 onwards respectively, while annual data for most individual countries start in 1995. In addition to the presentation in millions of national currency (millions of euro for EU / EA aggregates), data are also presented in percentages of [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|GDP]], and in annual growth rates where applicable. Annual government finance statistics (GFS) template tables are compiled twice per year, coinciding with the official notification of fiscal figures to Eurostat, at the end of April and end of October for data up to year N-1; e.g. in April 2016, 2015 annual data is published for the first time (as well as back series and possible revisions). They comprise tables by subsectors as well as an illustration of consolidation within the general government sector. Quarterly Summary GFS template tables are compiled 4 times per year, coinciding with the transmission to Eurostat of quarterly financial and non-financial accounts for the general government, as well as quarterly government debt. They are released simultaneously to the press releases on quarterly government deficit and debt. '''The most recent publication of quarterly GFS tables presents the EA20, EA19 and EU aggregates. Due to the accession of Croatia to the euro area on 1 January 2023, Croatian data are presented in euro-fixed for periods up to the fourth quarter of 2022, i.e. Croatian kuna (HRK) divided by the [[Glossary:euro|irrevocable exchange rate]].''' ===Revenue and expenditure=== [[Image:Tab1 Presentation of government revenue and expenditure.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Presentation of government revenue and expenditure
''Source:'' Eurostat|alt= Table showing what is included in total revenue and total expenditure. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The summary table of government finance statistics firstly shows total general government revenue as the aggregate of all transactions recorded under resources in the ESA framework, including subsidies receivable in the current accounts and capital transfers receivable recorded in the capital account. [[Glossary:Total general government expenditure|Total general government expenditure]] follows the presentation of revenue. Expenditure is an aggregate of all transactions recorded under positive uses, and subsidies payable, in the current accounts as well as transactions ([[Glossary:Gross capital formation|gross capital formation]], acquisition less disposals of [[Glossary:Non-financial non-produced assets|non-financial non-produced assets]] plus capital transfers payable) in the capital account. A revenue transaction is 1 that increases net worth. Revenue is presented in the tables as the sum of taxes, [[Glossary:Social contributions|net social contributions]], sales (defined as market output, output for own final use and payments for non-market production), other current revenues and capital transfer revenues. Total taxes are composed of taxes on production and imports (so-called indirect taxes), current taxes on income and wealth (direct taxes), and capital taxes (some classifications of taxes include capital taxes as a component of direct taxes). Net social contributions consist of [[Glossary:Actual social contributions|actual social contributions by employers and households]] collected as well as [[Glossary:Imputed social contributions|imputed social contributions]], households' social contribution supplements and social insurance scheme service charges. Total taxes and net social contributions indicate the level of fiscal burden, useful for inter-country comparisons. 'Other current revenues' consist of the categories property income earned, other subsidies on production received and other current transfers. While this latter category is often dominated by other current transfers between different levels of government, these must be consolidated when presenting data for the whole general government. Government expenditure is calculated as the sum of transactions in the following categories: compensation of employees, [[Glossary:Intermediate consumption|intermediate consumption]], [[Glossary:Interest|interest]], subsidies, social benefits, other current expenditure, capital transfers and capital investments. The categories '[[Glossary:Compensation of employees|compensation of employees]]' and '[[Glossary:Intermediate consumption|intermediate consumption]]' form part of the cost of production incurred by the government as a producer. The category 'compensation of employees' includes 'wages and salaries paid' and the 'employers' social insurance contributions' (including imputed social contributions). 'Intermediate consumption' contains the goods and services consumed by the government during its production process. Social benefits consist of social benefits other than social transfers in kind (mainly cash transfers) and of social transfers in kind purchased via market producers (such as the provision, paid by government, of medical services by health care providers classified outside the general government sector). The recording of social benefits expenditure does not include social transfers in kind provided by non-market producers within general government, such as medical services provided by hospitals classified within general government or certain types of social housing. This is to avoid counting such expenditures twice (once as social transfers and once as a cost of production) in the calculation of total expenditure. The category '[[Glossary:Interest|interest]]' includes payments on government liabilities on an accrual basis. Interest expenditure does not include fees and charges made under the service component of interest payments; such expenditures are recorded as 'intermediate consumption'. The category 'other current expenditure' is composed of 'other taxes on production', 'property income other than interest', 'current taxes on income, wealth, etc.', 'other current transfers' and the 'adjustment for the change in pension entitlements'. 'Capital transfers' comprise 'investment grants' and 'other capital transfers'. Last in the sequence, the category 'capital investments' includes 'gross fixed capital formation', among other capital transactions. Disposals of non-financial assets are included as negative investments in this category and not on the revenue side. The GFS presentation of expenditure shows the type of transaction undertaken by the government, and it complements the purpose or function of government expenditure captured in the [[Glossary:Classification of the functions of government (COFOG)|Classification of the functions of government (COFOG)]] typology (for further details, see [[Government expenditure by function – COFOG|article on COFOG statistics]]). ===Government deficit=== The balancing item of the general government in the non-financial accounts is [[Glossary:Net lending net borrowing|net lending]] (positive sign) or [[Glossary:Net lending net borrowing|net borrowing]] (negative sign), i.e. the government surplus or deficit in the integrated GFS presentation, that is total general government revenue minus total general government expenditure. The net lending/ borrowing calculated according to the data transmitted in the context of the ESA 2010 transmission programme is conceptually identical to the so-called Maastricht deficit used for the [[Glossary:Excessive deficit procedure (EDP)|Excessive Debt Procedure]], which is subject to a thorough verification by Eurostat, as well as possible adjustments introduced by Eurostat on the reported figures. [Under ESA 1995, the EDP deficit deviated from the ESA deficit by the recording of some cash flows on selected financial derivatives (e.g. on swaps), which is not the case anymore.] The ESA and EDP deficit may occasionally differ due to differences in vintages. In practice, the data reported by Member States is strictly consistent (during the EDP notifications periods). ===Government financing=== Similar to other institutional units and private companies, the financial account of general government records the transactions in financial assets and liabilities and is included in the integrated presentation of the GFS. The position 'net financial transactions' describes the net financing (i.e. net acquisition of financial assets minus net incurrence of liabilities) of the government and is conceptually equal to the ESA 2010 definition of the government net lending or net borrowing calculated in the non-financial accounts, since a surplus has to be invested or a deficit has to be financed. The discrepancy between the 2 balancing items in the financial and non-financial accounts is a statistical discrepancy due to the use of different data sources for compiling the financial and the non-financial accounts. This statistical discrepancy forms 1 position in the integrated GFS presentation and is 1 way in which the consistency of the data is rendered transparent. It is also an important quality indicator. It is not however a final indication, because some countries mask this discrepancy through adjustments to some financial instruments (traditionally in the 'other accounts' categories). Although this statistical discrepancy shows a relatively high volatility over the years, it has remained below 0.1% of the EU GDP in all years, an indicator of the good quality of the data and consistency of the data sources. Even though this discrepancy is relatively small at the level of the EU and euro area, there are some individual Member States for which this discrepancy is fairly significant, both on an annual and quarterly basis. Under the heading 'government financing' – the financial accounts transactions – details of the 'net acquisition of financial assets' and 'net incurrence of financial liabilities' are also shown. The category 'net acquisition of financial assets' is broken down into the subcategories, or [[Glossary:Financial instruments|financial instruments]], currency and deposits, debt securities, loans, shares and other equity and other financial assets, while the category 'net incurrence of financial liabilities' is shown to consist of currency and deposits, debt securities, loans and other liabilities. ===Other economic flows in government assets and liabilities=== Under the heading 'other economic flows in assets and liabilities' are adjustments to the value of the stock of financial assets and liabilities which are not due to transactions ('net acquisition of financial assets' and 'net incurrence of financial liabilities'). These other changes in stock are relatively important. They primarily reflect 'revaluations' (i.e. holding gains and losses on assets and liabilities, either realised or not) but also, so called 'other changes in volumes' (stemming for example from reclassifications). For the moment, 'other changes in non-financial assets' and 'changes in net worth due to other changes in assets/ liabilities' are not provided by most Member States, even though the GFS presentation includes both categories in order to complete the accounts. ===Government balance sheet=== The government [[Glossary:Financial accounts and balance sheets|balance sheet]] is the stock equivalent of the presentation of government financing described above, containing subcategories consistent with the flow analysis. For the moment, only financial assets and liabilities are collected, though efforts are now under way to collect data on non-financial assets. Showing non-financial assets of general government (mostly amortised fixed assets and non-produced assets mainly constituted by land) allows for the calculation of the general government net worth. Assets and liabilities are valued at market value, notably for debt securities, financial derivatives and shares and other equity. Holding gains/losses on these (realised or not) do not enter government revenue (or expenditure) but are reported in the 'other economic flows'. ===Government debt and link with the deficit=== Table B of the integrated presentation includes the so-called 'stock flow adjustment' (SFA) and [[Glossary:Government debt|gross government debt]] at nominal value (according to the Maastricht definition). The SFA is the difference between the change in the stock of government debt and the flow of annual deficit/surplus. It is widely known that deficits contribute to an increase in debt levels, while surpluses reduce them. However, the change of government debt also reflects other elements than the surplus/deficit. Deficits can also be financed by the sale of financial assets, or alternatively, debt can be used to finance the acquisition of financial assets. Therefore, in addition to the surplus/deficit, a strong co-movement of net acquisition of financial assets exists with the change in debt. The incurrence of liabilities not covered in the Maastricht debt definition as stipulated in the excessive deficit procedure (mainly 'other accounts, payable'), as well as valuation differences and discrepancies, play a smaller role in explaining the change in debt. A positive SFA means that the government debt increases more than the annual deficit (or decreases less than implied by the surplus). The importance of the SFA has been emphasised many times, as an efficient statistical monitoring of fiscal performance requires understanding the [[Glossary:Coherence|coherence]] between the 2 key fiscal indicators: government deficit and debt. Since the 2011 editions of the GFS tables, a new element has been introduced: the 'intergovernmental lending' agreed between government. Up to 2010Q4 the intergovernmental lending figures relate mainly to lending to Greece. From 2011Q1 onwards, intergovernmental lending includes loans made by the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF) - see {{Template:Publication|code=2-27012011-AP|title=Eurostat decision regarding EFSF}}. In order to avoid a "double-counting" at the level of the EU and euro area aggregates, the total value of intergovernmental lending is consolidated. For individual countries, by contrast, intergovernmental lending is reported as a general government asset, and thus is not deducted from debt. '''Memorandum items''' 'Memorandum items' include 'government final consumption expenditure', 'consumption of fixed capital', 'changes in net worth due to savings and capital transfers' and GDP. ===Data sources=== Member States are required to provide the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] with their government deficit and debt statistics before 1 April and 1 October of each year under the terms of the excessive deficit procedure. In addition, Eurostat collects more detailed data on government finances in the framework of the ESA transmission programme, the programme under which Member States submit national accounts data. The main aggregates of general government on an annual basis are provided by the Member States to Eurostat twice a year, whereas statistics on the functions of government (COFOG) and detailed tax and social contribution receipts are transmitted within 1 year after the end of the reference period and within 9 months after the end of the reference period, respectively. The data presented in this article correspond to the main revenue and expenditure items of the general government sector on an annual basis (ESA table 2, received twice a year), the quarterly non-financial accounts for general government (ESA table 25), the quarterly financial accounts for general government (ESA table 27), the quarterly government debt (ESA table 28) and the questionnaire on intergovernmental lending (all received 4 times a year) which are all compiled on a [[Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)|national accounts (ESA 2010) basis]]. Additionally, in annual GFS tables, some data is sourced from EDP tables 1 and 3, which are received twice a year. '''Delineation of general government''' The [[Glossary:General government sector|general government sector]] (S.13) consists of institutional units which are non-market producers whose output is intended for individual and collective consumption, and are financed by compulsory payments made by units belonging to other sectors, and institutional units principally engaged in the redistribution of national income and wealth. (ESA 2010 §2.111) ===Context=== The integrated presentation of GFS carried out by Eurostat allows for a detailed analysis of government fiscal performance through a better understanding of the financial and non-financial operations undertaken by government. It allows inter-country comparisons, to follow the evolution of the main components over time, and to understand better the links between the various variables. It shows how a government finances a possible deficit, and which are the main instruments used. For a more in-depth analysis of specific components, the detailed tables also posted in the Eurostat web site provide further breakdowns: functional classification of government expenditure following the COFOG classification (social protection, education, health, defence, etc.), a breakdown of taxes and social contributions, and a further breakdown for financial instruments. Overall, annual and quarterly GFS tables provide a wealth of integrated information for analysts, researchers, and policy makers. ===Other articles=== *[[Government finance statistics]] *[[Government finance statistics - title: Intergenerational transmission of disadvantages - statistics
text:
Intergenerational transmission of advantages and disadvantages from parents to today's adults and showing how this affects the current standard of living of the population. Data extracted in October 2024 Planned article update: October 2030 In 2023, the at-risk-of-poverty rate for EU adults aged 25 to 59 years was higher for those who faced difficult financial situations around age 14 (20%), compared with those who grew up in better financial conditions (12.4%). In 2023, the at-risk-of-poverty rate for people aged 25 to 59 years was 10.6 percentage points lower for those whose parents had higher education (8.5%) compared with those with less-educated parents (19.1%) across most EU countries. In 2023, most people with tertiary education aged 25 to 59 years in the EU had parents with upper secondary (39.5%) or tertiary education (34.1%), while 26.4% had parents with lower education levels. In 2023, 13.0% of people aged 25 to 59 years in the EU with low education levels reported being unable to afford basic school needs at around age 14, amounting to only 1.5% of those with tertiary education. This article presents data from 2023 on people aged 25 to 59 years living in private households in the European Union (EU), focusing on how early socio-economic conditions shape current ones. More specifically, the financial situation of households when the respondent was around 14 years old and parental educational attainment play a critical role in determining the risk of poverty and educational achievement in adulthood. Additionally, the inability to afford basic school needs when the respondents were around 14 years old is examined in relation to current educational level. === Key findings === In 2023, differences in at-risk-of-poverty rates and educational outcomes for people aged 25 to 59 years in the EU were associated with their household's financial situation around age 14 and their parents' level of education: *The at-risk-of-poverty rate was 20.0% for people who considered their household's financial situation as bad at around age 14, whereas it was 12.4% for people who considered their household's financial situation as good. *The at-risk-of-poverty rate was lower (8.5%) for those who had tertiary-educated parents as compared with those with low-educated parents (19.1%). *The majority of people with tertiary education had parents with either upper secondary (39.5%) or tertiary education (34.1%), while only 26.4% had parents with lower education levels. *People with low education levels were more likely to report being unable to afford basic school needs at around age 14 compared with those with higher education. === Current at-risk-of-poverty rate in relation to the socio-economic characteristics of households when respondents were 14 years old === '''At-risk-of-poverty rate higher for people who experienced a bad household financial situation around age 14''' In 2023, the at-risk-of-poverty rate in the EU for people aged 25 to 59 years was 20.0% among those who considered their household's financial situation to have been bad when they were around 14 years old, compared with 12.4% for those who considered their household's financial situation to have been good. Across the EU countries, Bulgaria (48.1%) and Romania (42.1%) recorded the highest at-risk-of-poverty rates for those who considered their household's financial situation to have been bad when they were around 14 years old, while Czechia (9.5%) and Denmark (8.5%) had the lowest. For those who considered their household's financial situation to have been good, the highest rates were observed in Spain (16.6%), Greece, Latvia (both 14.9%), Romania (14.6%), Bulgaria, and Italy (both 14.4%). The lowest rates for this group were found in Czechia (6.2%), Hungary (7.5%), Belgium, and Ireland (both 7.7%). [[Image:Figure1 igtp01.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: People aged 25 to 59 years at risk of poverty, 2023
by level of financial situation of their households when respondent was around 14 years old (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_igtp04}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing people aged 25 to 59 years at risk of poverty by percentage level of financial situation of their households when respondent was around 14 years old, in the EU, individual EU countries, Norway, Switzerland and Türkiye. Each country has two columns representing good and bad for the year 2023.]] The difference in at-risk-of-poverty rates between those who considered their household's financial situation to have been good and bad when they were around 14 years old averaged 7.6 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] across the EU. The largest differences were observed in Bulgaria (33.7 pp) and Romania (27.5 pp), while Denmark was the only country where the at-risk-of-poverty rate was slightly lower for those who considered their household's financial situation to have been bad (-0.4 pp). Other countries with relatively small differences included Finland (0.9 pp) and Slovenia (0.5 pp). [[Image:Figure2 igtp04.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Difference in the at-risk-of-poverty rate for people 25 to 59 years old based on whether their household's financial situation was bad or good when they were around 14 years old, 2023 (pp)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_igtp04}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing percentage point difference in the at-risk-of-poverty rate for people aged 25 to 59 years based on whether their household's financial situation was bad or good when they were around 14 years old, in the EU, individual EU countries, Norway, Switzerland and Türkiye for the year 2023.]] '''At-risk-of-poverty rate was lower for people with highly educated parents'''
In 2023, the at-risk-of-poverty rate in the EU for people aged 25 to 59 years was 19.1% for those whose parents had less than primary, primary, or lower secondary education (levels 0-2). This rate decreased to 10.2% for those whose parents had upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (levels 3 and 4) and further to 8.5% for those whose parents had tertiary education (levels 5-8). Across the EU, the highest at-risk-of-poverty rates for people whose parents had lower education levels were recorded in Romania (40.8%) and Bulgaria (39.2%), while the lowest were in Denmark (7.4%) and Finland (8.8%). For people whose parents had upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education, the highest rates were found in Latvia (15.7%), Estonia (14.6%), Lithuania (14.5%), Greece (14.1%), and Spain (14.4%), while the lowest were in Czechia (4.7%), Ireland, and Hungary (both 6.4%). For people whose parents had tertiary education, the highest at-risk-of-poverty rates were recorded in Austria (14.5%), Slovakia (12.2%), Sweden (11.9%), Estonia (11.6%), and Spain (11.2%). The lowest rates were in Romania (1.5%) and Czechia (2.9%). In most EU countries, the at-risk-of-poverty rate was lower for people whose parents had higher levels of education. However, Denmark and Finland were exceptions, where the rate was slightly higher for those whose parents had tertiary education compared with those with lower-educated parents. [[Image:Figure3 igtp03.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: People aged 25 to 59 years at risk of poverty, 2023
by educational attainment level of their parents (%)
''Source:'' {{Stable link|title=Eurostat|code=ilc_igtp03}}|alt= Scatter chart showing people aged 25 to 59 years at risk of poverty by percentage educational attainment level of their parents, in the EU, individual EU countries, Norway, Switzerland and Türkiye. Each country has three scatter plots representing ISCED levels zero to two, levels three and four, levels five to eight for the year 2023.]] === Educational attainment level in relation to parental education === '''Largest share of people with tertiary education came from parents with upper secondary or tertiary education''' In 2023, 26.4% of people aged 25 to 59 years in the EU with tertiary education had parents with less than primary, primary, or lower secondary education (levels 0-2). This share was 39.5% for those whose parents had upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (levels 3 and 4), and 34.1% for those whose parents had tertiary education (levels 5-8). Spain (49.8%), Portugal (37.6%) and Greece (34.5%) recorded the highest shares of people with tertiary education whose parents had lower levels of education, with the lowest shares observed in Bulgaria (3.9%) and Romania (4.0%). Spain (49.8%), Portugal (37.6%), and Greece (34.5%) had the highest shares of people with tertiary education whose parents had lower education levels, while the lowest were recorded in Bulgaria (3.9%) and Romania (4.0%). For people whose parents had upper secondary education, Romania (74.3%) and Poland (66.4%) had the highest shares. Among those whose parents had tertiary education, Estonia (59.6%) and Sweden (57.7%) reported the highest shares, while Romania (21.7%) and Italy (26.0%) had the lowest. [[Image:Figure4 igtp01.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: People aged 25 to 59 years with tertiary education, 2023
by educational attainment level of their parents (%)
''Source:'' {{Stable link|title=Eurostat|code=ilc_igtp01}}|alt= Queued horizontal bar chart showing percentage of people aged 25 to 59 years with tertiary education by educational attainment level of their parents, in the EU, individual EU countries, Norway, Switzerland and Türkiye. Totalling 100 percent, each country bar has three queues representing the ISCED levels zero to two, levels three and four, levels five to eight of the parents for the year 2023.]] === Inability to afford basic school needs at around age 14 and current educational attainment === '''Higher percentages of individuals aged 25 to 59 years with lower education levels reported being unable to afford basic school needs at around age 14'''
In 2023, 13.0% of people aged 25 to 59 years in the EU who had less than primary, primary, or lower secondary education (levels 0-2) reported being unable to afford basic school needs when they were around 14 years old. This percentage decreases with higher educational attainment: 3.6% for those with upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (levels 3 and 4), and just 1.5% for those with tertiary education (levels 5-8). Across EU countries, the highest percentages of people with lower education levels (levels 0-2) who reported being unable to afford basic school needs at around age 14 were observed in Romania (33.6%) and Slovakia (33.2%). By contrast, the lowest percentages were recorded in Finland (3.5%) and Czechia (7.1%). For those with upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (levels 3 and 4), the highest percentages were in Cyprus (10.4%) and Greece (8.4%), with the lowest in Finland (0.9%), Czechia (1.2%) and Croatia (1.2%). Among people with tertiary education (levels 5-8), the highest percentages were recorded in Greece (4.3%) and Denmark (3.8%), while Croatia, Czechia, Portugal, Bulgaria, Finland, France and Slovenia reported percentages below 1.0%. [[Image:Figure5 igtp08.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: People aged 25 to 59 years unable to afford basic school needs when they were around 14 years old, 2023
by current educational attainment level (%)
''Source:'' {{Stable link|title=Eurostat|code=ilc_igtp08}}|alt= Scatter chart showing people aged 25 to 59 years unable to afford basic school needs when they were around 14 years old, in the EU, individual EU countries, Norway, Switzerland and Türkiye. Each country has three scatter plots representing ISCED levels zero to two, levels three and four, levels five to eight for the year 2023.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=LCIE 2024 Intergenerational transmission of disadvantages FINAL.xlsx|title=Intergenerational transmission of disadvantages - tables and graphs}} === Data sources === The data used in this article are derived from the EU Statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC). EU-SILC data are compiled annually and are the main source of statistics that measure income and living conditions in Europe; it is also the main source of information used to link different aspects relating to the quality of life of households and individuals. The reference population for the information presented in this article is all private [[Glossary:Household_-_social_statistics#:.7E:text.3DCollective_households_or_institutional_households_.28as_opposed_to.2Creligious_institutions.2C_boarding_houses_and_workers.E2.80.99_hostels.2C_etc.|households]] and their current members residing in the territory of an EU Member State (or non-member country) at the time of data collection; people living in collective households are generally excluded from the target population. The data for the EU are population-weighted averages of national data. The reference period for individuals' characteristics is 2023. The data is available for the 26 Member States (data for Germany is unavailable) as well as Norway, Switzerland, and Türkiye. The EU-SILC 2023 six yearly module Intergenerational transmission of disadvantages & Housing difficulties collects data on family conditions and housing challenges experienced by individuals. The section on 'Intergenerational transmission of disadvantages' examines key aspects of respondents' upbringing when they were around 14 years old. It includes information on the type of household, parental presence, education and activity status, as well as the financial situation of the household. The module also explores access to basic school needs, regular meals, and holidays when respondent was around 14 years old. The data on educational attainment levels is collected and classified according to [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED) ISCED 2011]. It is divided into three categories: high (short-cycle tertiary education, bachelor's or equivalent, master's or equivalent, and doctoral or equivalent levels), medium (upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education), and low (less than primary, primary, or lower secondary education). === Context === Parental educational attainment and socioeconomic status are critical in shaping the risk of poverty and social exclusion in adulthood, providing insight into how inequalities persist across generations. [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2020/2175/oj Commission delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/2175] specifies that the 2023 SILC survey will collect three yearly variables on Labour market and housing, six yearly variables on Intergenerational transmission of disadvantages & Housing difficulties, as well as an ad hoc subject on Households energy efficiency. The findings from this module are highly relevant for policymakers, as they provide crucial data to inform the design and implementation of policies aimed at poverty alleviation, aligned with the [https://commission.europa.eu/energy-climate-change-environment/overall-targets-and-reporting/2030-targets_en EU2030 targets]. The data also supports efforts to promote social mobility, particularly through educational policies, and enables preventive measures by addressing childhood poverty, in line with the [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1428&langId=en EU Child Guarantee]. ===Other articles=== *All articles from [[Living conditions in Europe|Living condtions]] *[[Living conditions in Europe The association of statistics and geography has the potential to generate information far beyond the simple representation of data on a map. Linking numerical and geo-referenced statistics in spatial analysis may help reveal relationships and phenomena which are difficult to discover by more traditional analyses of statistical databases. ''Integration of statistical and geospatial information – experiences and observations from national statistical authorities'' presents details of projects enacted with grants provided during the first nine years of this initiative, showcasing the broad range of applications that may be developed using geospatial information. As well as being available here online, the content is contained in two PDF publications: *the first for the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-statistical-reports/-/ks-ft-19-004 project years 2012–2015] and *the second for the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-statistical-reports/-/ks-ft-23-006 project years 2016–2020]. {{Unit|topic=X_Regions}} [[Category:General and regional statistics - methodological publications|Integration of statistical and geospatial information]] [[Category:Online publications|Integration of statistical and geospatial information]]

title: International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED)
text:
<pdftheme>3</pdftheme>

'''ISCED''' is the reference international classification for organising education programmes and related qualifications by levels and fields. ISCED 2011 (levels of education) has been implemented in all EU data collections since 2014. ISCED-F 2013 (fields of education and training) has been implemented since 2016.

<articlecontent>
<sesection>
===Background===

Education systems vary a lot between countries. International data on education should therefore be based on a classification which proposes, for all countries of the world, sound criteria for the allocation of education programmes to levels which can be considered as comparable.

The ISCED classification - International Standard Classification of Education - was developed by [http://en.unesco.org/ UNESCO] in the mid-1970s and was first revised in 1997. A further review of ISCED was undertaken between 2009 and 2011 involving extensive global consultations with countries, regional experts and international organisations. Finally, ISCED 2011 was adopted by the UNESCO General Conference in November 2011. 

[https://www.uis.unesco.org/en/methods-and-tools/isced '''ISCED 2011'''] '''(levels of education)''' took into account the changes in education systems occurred over the last decade, mainly relating to the  [https://education.ec.europa.eu/education-levels/higher-education/inclusive-and-connected-higher-education/bologna-process Bologna process in tertiary education], but also to the expansion of education programmes for very young children. Additionally, for the first time, ISCED 2011 is clearly not only a classification of levels of education programmes (ISCED-P) but also a classification of educational attainment (ISCED-A) in terms of qualifications resulting from formal education programmes. With ISCED 2011 education programmes/qualifications can be coded up to 3-digit-level. The majority of codes are the same for ISCED-P and ISCED-A but there are also some exceptions, in particular in the case of short programmes for which educational attainment is downgraded to the lower ISCED level.'''

[https://www.uis.unesco.org/en/methods-and-tools/isced '''ISCED-F 2013'''] - '''ISCED Fields of Education and Training 2013''' - is a classification of fields of education, which accompanies ISCED 2011. 
ISCED-F 2013 contains 11 broad fields (2 digits), 29 narrow fields (3 digits) and about 80 detailed fields (4 digits).
</sesection>

<sesection>
===Implementation of ISCED 2011 (levels of education)===

ISCED 2011 has been implemented in all EU data collections as from 2014. In household/individuals surveys, ISCED 2011 has been implemented as from reference year 2014 (see {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32013R0317:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) No 317/2013}}) and in administrative data collections on education systems (UOE) as from school year 2012/13 (see {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32013R0912:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) No 912/2013}}).

'''Methodological support'''

Methodological support was developed for the implementation of ISCED 2011.

* The [https://circabc.europa.eu/w/browse/c2dc65ad-5163-4935-b0c2-e5ea1f44929b ISCED 2011 operational manual], elaborated by UIS, OECD and Eurostat, provides guidelines for classifying national education programmes and related qualifications according to ISCED 2011. It was developed for national statisticians reporting data on education to international organisations and for all users interested in better understanding these data. 

* For statisticians working on the household/individuals surveys including the variable "Educational attainment", [https://circabc.europa.eu/w/browse/c2dc65ad-5163-4935-b0c2-e5ea1f44929b Guidelines on the measurement of educational attainment in household surveys] can serve as a methodological support.

* The UOE (UNESCO-OECD-Eurostat) data collection (from administrative data sources - on pupils/students, graduates, expenditure, teachers, languages and regional data) uses the [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/d14c857a-601d-438a-b878-4b4cebd0e10f/library/b1c46d80-0461-48ef-92a5-30f16e9d2b10 UOE Manual on concepts, definitions and classifications].

National integrated ISCED mappings are available [https://circabc.europa.eu/w/browse/c2dc65ad-5163-4935-b0c2-e5ea1f44929b here].
An ISCED integrated mapping is a table including information on national educational programmes and qualifications, their main characteristics and coding in ISCED 1997 and ISCED 2011.
</sesection>

<sesection>
===Correspondence between ISCED 2011 and ISCED 1997===

'''Levels of education in ISCED 2011'''

Compared to ISCED 1997 which had seven levels of education, ISCED 2011 has nine education levels, from level 0 to level 8 (tertiary education is more detailed):
* ISCED 0: Early childhood education (‘less than primary’ for educational attainment)
* ISCED 1: Primary education
* ISCED 2: Lower secondary education
* ISCED 3: Upper secondary education
* ISCED 4: Post-secondary non-tertiary education
* ISCED 5: Short-cycle tertiary education
* ISCED 6: Bachelor’s or equivalent level
* ISCED 7: Master’s or equivalent level
* ISCED 8: Doctoral or equivalent level

'''Correspondence between ISCED 2011 and ISCED 1997 levels (at 1 digit)'''

[[Image:Correspondence between ISCED 2011 and ISCED 1997 levels new .png|thumb|centre|500px]]

'''Correspondence between ISCED 2011 and ISCED 1997 (aggregated levels)'''

Eurostat’s online tables on or by educational attainment level (mainly from the EU Labour Force Survey but also from EU Statistics on Income and Living Conditions and other EU household/individuals surveys) present data for three main aggregates: low - medium - high level of education. The correspondence between ISCED 2011 and ISCED 1997 at this level of aggregation is as follows:

[[Image:Correspondence between ISCED 2011 and ISCED 1997 levels - aggregated level new.png|thumb|centre|500px]]
 
At this level of aggregation data are considered as comparable over time for all available countries (i.e. no significant level shift breaks) except Austria and Estonia:
* The level shift break in Austria is due to the reclassification of a programme spanning levels: the qualification acquired upon successful completion of higher technical and vocational colleges is allocated in ISCED 2011 to ISCED level 5; under ISCED 1997 the same qualification was reported on ISCED level 4, but earmarked as equivalent to tertiary education.
* The level shift break in Estonia is due to the reclassification of a programme that can last between 6 months and 3.5 years: the qualification acquired upon successful completion of 'vocational courses based on basic education' is allocated in ISCED 2011 to ISCED level 2; under ISCED 1997 this was reported as level 3.

In the online tables, the code list “ISCED11” is used and the change to ISCED 2011 as from 2014 is indicated through the flag ‘b’ (break in time series).
</sesection>

<sesection>
===ISCED 1997 (fields) and ISCED-F 2013===

2016 was the first year of implementation of the revised classification of fields of education and training - ISCED-F 2013 in EU data collections: in administrative data collections on education systems (UOE) it concerned school year 2014/15 and in household/individuals surveys reference year 2016.  

Broad fields of education in ISCED 1997:
:0 – General programmes
:1 – Education
:2 – Humanities and arts
:3 – Social sciences, business and law
:4 – Science
:5 – Engineering, manufacturing and construction
:6 – Agriculture
:7 – Health and welfare
:8 – Services

Broad fields of education in ISCED-F 2013:
:00 – Generic programmes and qualifications
:01 – Education
:02 – Arts and humanities
:03 – Social sciences, journalism and information
:04 – Business, administration and law
:05 – Natural sciences, mathematics and statistics
:06 – Information and Communication Technologies
:07 – Engineering, manufacturing and construction
:08 – Agriculture, forestry, fisheries and veterinary
:09 – Health and welfare
:10 – Services  

For more information on ISCED-F 2013 and in particular the correspondence between ISCED 1997 (fields) and ISCED-F 2013, please see [https://circabc.europa.eu/w/browse/48062305-0a21-4500-a3ab-e8264bf7fcec here]
</sesection>
</articlecontent>
