(difference between the number of enterprises purchasing and supplying services outside of the EU)
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gvc_ps}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=gvc_ss}} |alt=A bar chart showing purchasing vs supplying services outside of the EU - trade balance as percentage of all enterprises engaging in international services trade from 2021 to 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Constraints and transformation drivers affecting global value chains in the EU === GVCs in the EU have faced a range of constraints, including rising input costs, transport disruptions, supply shortages and regulatory measures. Energy-related input costs were the most widespread constraint, affecting 62% of enterprises (Figure 15)For Figures 7, 15 and 16, the percentages shown represent the share of enterprises reporting a moderate or high impact for each individual constraint. In this case, enterprises were required to select only 1 level of impact per constraint – either ‘Not applicable’, ‘No impact’, ‘Moderate impact’ or ‘High impact’. The figures display the sum of the shares for moderate and high impact. These shares do not add up to 100%, as they exclude responses indicating ‘Not applicable’ or ‘No impact’. If all 4 response categories were shown, their combined total would reach 100% for each constraint.. COVID-19-related limitations (56%) and higher non-energy input costs (55%) affected more than half of enterprises. Supply shortages were reported by 49% of enterprises, and transport bottlenecks by 47%. Environmental policy-related drivers affected 38% of enterprises, while comparatively few enterprises reported sanctions on Russia as impactful (28%). [[Image:Figure_15_Constraints_affecting_global_value_chains_in_the_EU_(2021-23).png|thumb|center|725px|Figure 15: Constraints affecting global value chains in the EU, 2021-2023
Source: ''Eurostat'' (gvc_effgvc)|alt= A bar chart illustrating the percentage of enterprises reporting different GVC effects.]] In response to constraints encountered, enterprises adopted several reorganisation strategies between 2021 and 2023, most commonly digitalising GVC processes, strengthening partnerships within the EU, prioritising reliable suppliers and building buffer inventories. Some enterprises also explored farshoring and broader supplier diversification. Digitalisation was the most frequently reported strategy, with 32% of enterprises increasing digitalisation of GVC processes, followed by prioritising reliable suppliers (30%) and nearshoring within the EU (29%) (Figure 16). Increasing inventories was reported by 28% of enterprises, while farshoring and expanding supplier networks were less common (18% and 17%). Most strategies were applied to a moderate extent. For example, digitalisation increased moderately for 24% of enterprises and to a high extent for 8%. Nearshoring was moderate for 24% and high for 5%. Farshoring (15% moderate, 3% high) and expanding supplier networks (15% moderate, 2% high) remained the least used. Overall, the data show that enterprises reorganised their GVCs mainly through incremental rather than large-scale adjustments. [[Image:Figure_16_Reorganisation_of_global_value_chains_in_response_to_business_constraints_(2021-23).png|thumb|center|725px|Figure 16: Reorganisation of global value chains in response to business constraints, 2021-2023
Source: ''Eurostat'' (gvc_effgvc)|alt= A bar chart showing the share of enterprises adopting specific GVC reorganisation strategies in response to business constraints. Increased digitalisation, nearshoring within the EU, and prioritising reliable suppliers were the most commonly reported strategies.]] === The way forward === The survey shows interesting results and changes in modern Europe regarding globalisation, and the main takeaway is that most sourcing still stays within Europe. In general, the sourcing direction shows that enterprises in countries with smaller, open economies with high labour costs source the most to enterprises in other countries. There are indications that the sourcing wave of ICT services from the beginning of the 2000s is declining, with management and administrative services surpassing them in total sourcing in Europe. Sourcing patterns are interesting for policymakers in Europe, and there are often debates about sourcing as an agent of globalisation and its positive or negative effects on an economy. Keeping in mind the scarcity of statistical data on sourcing, this survey should provide new insight into the effects and motivations of sourcing. The survey also captures some elements of the GVC arrangements of European enterprises. These results show that enterprises purchasing high-value goods and services from abroad are more numerous than those supplying high-value goods and services. Additionally, the survey aimed to capture the effects of global constraints on GVCs of enterprises. The first results show that European enterprises were highly affected by different constraints during 2021-2023. The following survey should capture the changes that have happened as well as provide information on new, emerging concepts. It might offer a more detailed and accurate view of the type of jobs lost and facilitate breaking down almost any enterprise characteristic or strategy, such as employment and wages, technology adoption, training and skill requirements and others. The next survey will be the second regular data collection governed by the statistical regulation on European business statistics (EBS), {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R2152:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2019/2152}}, for the reference period 2024-2026. The specific set of questions may differ between data collection rounds; this will allow incorporating questions on new trends and factors affecting GVCs. The GVC survey sheds some new light on the complex issue of GVC, which also includes international sourcing and strives to pave a way forward for new statistical developments. ===Feedback=== To help Eurostat improve these experimental statistics, users and researchers are kindly invited to give us their [mailto:ESTAT-GVC@ec.europa.eu?subject=Feedback_on_experimental_statistics feedback by email] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=SE article-ready table 2021-23 v8.xlsx|title=International sourcing, business functions and GVCs: figures and tables}} === Data sources=== One of the first efforts to measure the GVC phenomenon in Europe came with the [[Glossary:Sourcing|international sourcing]] (IS) survey in 2007. Since 2007, Eurostat has supported and actively contributed to developing and establishing the IS and GVC surveys which were carried out in 2012, 2018, 2021 and the latest one in 2024. These efforts culminated with the international sourcing survey (now renamed GVC survey) being included as official statistics in {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R2152:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2019/2152}} on European Business Statistics ('the EBS Regulation'). Under the EBS Regulation and as described in the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32022R0918:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2022/918}} (GVC Implementing act) that was adopted on 13 June 2022, the survey's scope has increased to encompass the GVC arrangements and impact on the EU Member States. The survey will take place every 3 years; targeted topics may change between consecutive surveys to better capture globalisation trends and policy requirements. The data presented in this article refers to the population of enterprises with 50 or more persons employed in the period 2021-2023 in the reporting 22 EU Member States (except Croatia, Cyprus, Estonia, Luxembourg and Slovenia) and the EFTA country Norway. The GVC statistics cover [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] Rev.2 (Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community) sections B to N, which, broadly speaking, covers the business economy. The data was collected in 2024 and shows cumulative data for the period 2021-23 '''Definitions''' '''Global Value Chains (GVC):''' GVC comprise the full range of cross-border activities required to bring a product or service from conception through the different production and delivery phases to final consumers. '''GVC trade:''' Refers to an international trade that takes place in a GVC. Most commonly, this includes trade in intermediate goods and services. '''COVID-19 events:''' These events resulted directly from the COVID-19 outbreak, hampering or enabling an enterprise's business activity. Examples are government lockdowns, shutting down sales points, and positive events such as increased sales of protection masks. '''Sourcing activities''' ''Sourcing:'' The total or partial movement of business functions (core or support business functions) currently performed in-house of a resident enterprise to either non-affiliated (external suppliers) or affiliated enterprises located either domestically or abroad. ''International sourcing:'' The total or partial movement of business functions (core or support business functions) currently performed in-house or domestically sourced by the resident enterprise to either non-affiliated (external suppliers) or affiliated enterprises located abroad. ''Sourcing does not include:'' Expansion domestically or abroad; for example, a set-up of a new production line domestically or abroad without a movement of business functions domestically or abroad (core or support business functions) nor reduction of activity and jobs in the concerned enterprise. ''Insourcing and outsourcing:'' The survey distinguishes between international sourcing to a foreign affiliate or daughter company within the same multinational enterprise group — so-called insourcing — and sourcing to external providers, called outsourcing. '''Business functions''' ''Core business function:'' Production of final goods or services intended for the market or third parties carried out by the enterprise and yielding income. Core business function equals, in most cases, the primary activity of the enterprise. It may also include other (secondary) activities if the enterprise considers them part of its core functions. ''Support business function:'' Support business functions (ancillary activities) are carried out to permit or facilitate the production of goods or services intended for the market/for third parties by the enterprise. The support business functions' outputs are not intended directly for the market/for third parties. The business functions are divided into:
1. Production of goods and materials for the market (Manufacturing, processing, assembly, refining, printing and binding, casting of metals, building of ships, mining, extraction of gas and oil, stone quarrying, power generation (except trade of electricity), development of building projects, civil engineering, specialised construction tasks, including demolition.
2. Transport, logistics and storage * Transportation and logistics (road, water, rail and air transport activities, passenger and cargo transport, postal services) * Warehousing and storage (warehousing, storage, packaging) 3. Marketing, sales, and after-sales service * Marketing and after-sales services (advertising and media representation, market research and public opinion polling, call centers) * Sales (retail and wholesale, trade of gas and electricity, sales agents and real-estate trading) 4. Information and communication technology services * Information and communication technology services (software publishing and computer consultancy activities, programming and broadcasting tasks, telecommunications tasks, data processing and hosting, web portals and related information service tasks, installation of mainframe computers, maintenance and repair of computers and communications systems) * Software programming (computer programming, consultancy and related tasks) 5. Management and administration * Management (financial services e.g. banking, insurance, financial leasing, fund management; activities of head offices, HRM activities) * Administration (financial markets administration, legal tasks, bookkeeping, accounting and auditing, office administration and business support services, public administration services) 6. Engineering and related technical services (e.g.: support tasks for raw material extraction, sound recording and video production, architectural and engineering tasks and technical analysis)
7. Research and development (e.g.: research and experimental development in the area of natural sciences and engineering, social sciences and humanities)
8. Other business functions * Facility management (accommodation e.g. hotels and camps, food and beverage services e.g. cafes and restaurants, landscape services, libraries, museums, sports centres) * Maintenance and repair services (maintenance and repair of non-ICT electronic equipment, transportation vehicles, personal and household goods) * Other services (water, waste collection and sewerage, remediation services, professional services e.g. photography and translation, travel agency activities, rental and operational leasing activities, security, education, human health activities and residential care, social services, creative and arts activities, gambling and betting, sports activities excluding facility management) '''Enterprise:''' The statistical unit of this survey is the enterprise. The enterprise is the smallest combination of legal units that is an organisational unit producing goods or services, which benefits from a certain degree of autonomy in decision making, especially for the allocation of its current resources. An enterprise carries out one or more activities at one or more locations. An enterprise may be a sole legal unit but can also be part of an enterprise group. The head of an enterprise group can either be located in the same country as the enterprises or in another country. '''Jobs lost:''' The enterprises are asked to estimate the total number (gross) of domestic jobs lost in the responding enterprises as a result of international sourcing. Domestic job losses in the responding enterprises that have taken place due to reasons other than international sourcing (e.g. domestic lay-offs, poor business cycle, etc.) are not included here. Even if jobs (business functions) have been moved abroad, the persons previously performing these functions may still be employed in the company carrying out other tasks (may also be new tasks related to jobs created because of international sourcing). In these cases, the jobs should still be counted as jobs lost. Therefore, generally speaking, the "jobs lost" concept has nothing to do with the observed change in the number of employees and self-employed persons of the enterprise. An enterprise may, e.g. record "jobs lost" due to international sourcing and still record an increase in its "number of employees and self-employed persons". '''Jobs created:''' The enterprises are asked to estimate the total number (gross) of domestic jobs created in the responding enterprises as a result of international sourcing. Domestic jobs created in the responding enterprises due to reasons other than international sourcing (e.g. expansion abroad) are not included here. A common reason for job creation is the increased availability of funds due to international sourcing. These funds, in turn, can lead to job creation in another business function (e.g. outsourcing some IT personnel led to some cost savings, which enabled the enterprise to hire more sales staff). The respondents estimate this variable in a direct link with international sourcing, as job creation is difficult to back up with hard data. === Other articles === *[[Global_value_chain_disruptions_and_enterprise_responses_in_the_EU|Global value chain disruptions and enterprise responses in the EU]] *[[Linking_statistics_on_international_sourcing_with_other_business_statistics|Linking statistics on international sourcing with other business statistics]] *[[Economic_globalisation_indicators|Economic globalisation indicators]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/globalisation-businesses/database Global value chains and international sourcing statistics (gvc)] === Dedicated section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/globalisation-businesses/information-data#Available%20data Economic globalisation: globalisation in business statistics] === Publications === *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-23-017|title=European business statistics compilers’ manual for global value chains – 2023 edition}} === Methodology === [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/gvc_esms.htm GVC ESMS metadata file]. ===External links=== *[https://unstats.un.org/unsd/classifications/Econ/Download/Manual_on_the_Classification_of_Business_Functions_WEB_2024-08-19.pdf Manual on the Classification of Business Functions] *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32022R0918:EN:NOT|title=GVC Implementing Regulation 2022/918}} *[https://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/docserver/9abfa931-en.pdf?expires=1568370377&id=id&accname=id24042&checksum=FCA252EA4DCA42F375D47F625F0E2EA6 Multinational enterprises in domestic value chains]- Cadestin, C., et al. (2019), OECD Science, Technology and Industry Policy Papers, No. 63, OECD Publishing, Paris *[https://www.oecd.org/sti/ind/global-value-chains.htm Global Value Chains (OECD)] *[https://unstats.un.org/unsd/business-stat/GVC/ Global Value Chains (UNSD)] === Footnotes === {{Unit|topic=X_Foreign_direct_investment}} [[Category:Industry, trade, and services|International sourcing, business functions and global value chains]] [[Category:Globalisation of businesses|International sourcing, business functions and global value chains]] [[Category:Experimental statistics|International sourcing, business functions and global value chains]] [[Category:Statistical article|International sourcing, business functions and global value chains]] [[Category:December2028|International sourcing, business functions and global value chains]]

title: International trade in goods - an overview
text:
EU statistics provide an overview of International trade in goods for the EU and the member states. Data extracted in August 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 In 2025, the value of trade in goods between EU Member States was 1.6 times as high as the value of trade in goods between the EU and non-EU countries. Both EU exports and imports increased beween 2024 and 2025. This article provides an overview of developments in [[Glossary:International_trade_in_goods_statistics_(ITGS)|trade in goods]] across the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]]. It details patterns of growth (in both value and volume terms), the split between [[Glossary:Intra-EU|intra-EU]] trade and [[Glossary:Extra-EU|extra-EU]] trade, the performance of individual [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU countries]], and changes in the terms of trade. This article also forms part of the publication on ''[[Globalisation_patterns_in_EU_trade_and_investment|Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment]]'', which presents a summary of recent EU statistics on the economic aspects of globalisation, with a focus on trade and investment patterns. === Overview=== '''''Since 2008, the value of goods imported into the EU has risen at a faster pace than the value of goods exported outside the EU''''' EU international trade in goods reached a relative peak in 2008 (see Figure 1), when [[Glossary:Import|imports]] were valued at €1 555 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] and the value of [[Glossary:Export|exports]] was somewhat lower, €1 421 billion; as such the EU had a [[Glossary:Trade_deficit|trade deficit]] of €134 billion. The impact of the global financial and economic crisis resulted in a rapid decline in the EU’s international trade in goods; the value of extra-EU exports fell by 16.7% in 2009, while there was an even greater reduction (-23.2%) in the value of extra-EU imports. However, there was a swift recovery in trade activity, as EU exports had already risen above their pre-crisis value in 2010, while the same pattern was observed for EU imports by 2011; both EU imports and exports continued to grow in 2012. '''''The downturn in the value of EU imports starting in 2012 may be linked to the fall in the price of oil''''' Thereafter, somewhat different patterns of development were observed for EU exports and imports — reflecting, at least in part, the development of oil prices. Between 2012 and 2016, the value of extra-EU imports fell, while the value of EU exports continued to grow. After 2016, imports also started to grow again, reaching €1 940 billion in 2019. In that same year, exports reached €2 132. In 2020, largely due to the COVID-19 pandemic, both imports (-11.6%) and exports (-9.4%) fell sharply. However, since then, they have more than recovered, with exports reaching €2 646 billion and imports reaching €2 532 billion in 2025. Between 2008 and 2020, the value of EU exports of goods has generally expanded at a faster pace than the value of EU imports, which has led to a significant change in the EU’s [[Glossary:Trade_balance|trade balance]] for goods (the difference between exports and imports). The EU had a trade deficit for goods of €134 billion in 2008, although this had been reversed by 2012 when a surplus of €68 billion was recorded. Due to high energy prices, the surplus turned into a deficit of €432 billion in 2022. In the following years this recovered quickly, reaching a surplus of €114 billion in 2025. Figure 1 ===Variations by EU countries=== '''''During the period 2002-2025, the fastest growth rates for trade in goods were recorded among countries that had joined the EU in 2004 or more recently''''' Looking at developments within the individual EU countries, Figure 2 shows the overall rate of change in the value of imports and exports between 2002 and 2025; it is worth noting that these statistics relate to total trade flows (in other words, both intra-EU and extra-EU trade). It is also interesting to note that countries with the highest overall growth in total trade (the sum of imports and exports) tended to be characterised by higher rates of export growth (when compared with import growth rates), while countries with relatively low overall growth in total trade tended to report higher rates of import growth. Growth rates of more than 300% in total trade between 2002 and 2025 were recorded in 12 of the 13 countries that joined the EU in 2004 or more recently: *Latvia *Lithuania *Bulgaria *Poland *Romania *Slovakia *Slovenia *Czechia *Estonia *Croatia *and Cyprus. These growth rates may, at least in part, be explained by these countries' process of integration into both global markets and (in particular) the [[Glossary:Single_market|European single market]], following reforms which led to switching from centrally-planned to market-based economic models. The highest overall growth in the value of exported goods between 2002 and 2025 was recorded in Cyprus (an increase of 1124%). There were also countries that recorded increases of more than 600%: *Poland *Latvia *Bulgaria *Slovenia *and Slovakia. By contrast, growth rates for exports were below 100% in: *France *Malta *Finland *and Luxembourg. The highest growth rate for imported goods was recorded by Slovenia (609%). There were also countries that recorded growth rates above 500%: *Romania *Slovakia *Poland *and Bulgaria. By contrast, growth rates for imports below 100% was registered only in Luxembourg. [[Image:Overall_change_for_the_value_of_trade_in_goods,_2002-2025_(%).png|centre|700px|Figure 2: Overall change for the value of trade in goods, 2002-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f36b7a30-b707-4344-b462-d8c6513aa655?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-28T10:34:32Z ext_lt_intratrd]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1c8bf0df-7966-4610-b270-055b6584b4bd?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-28T10:35:31Z ext_lt_intercc])|alt= a scatter graph showing the overall change for the value of trade in goods between 2002 to 2024, in the EU, EU Member States and the EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Germany had the highest trade surplus for goods in 2025''''' Figure 3 presents a comparison between 2002 and 2025 for the trade balance for goods. In 2025, Germany had the highest trade surplus in goods (€202 billion). This was followed at some distance by the surpluses recorded in Ireland (€116 billion) and the Netherlands (€103 billion). At the other end of the range, the trade deficit for trade in goods in France amounted to €94 billion, which was much higher than the next largest deficit, recorded in Spain (€66 billion). Figure 3 '''''The value of intra-EU trade in goods was 1.6 times as high as the value of extra-EU trade in goods in 2025''''' Although trade flows within the single market may not appear (at first sight) to be particularly ‘global’ in nature, and could be considered by some as ‘protectionist’ or ‘inward-looking’, it is important to note that some of these intra-EU flows result from the activities of European or multinational enterprises producing goods on foreign territories; for example, German or Japanese cars manufactured in Slovakia or Romania, from where they may be exported tariff-free to other parts of the single market. A comparison between intra-EU trade (between [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU countries]]) and extra-EU trade (between EU Member States and non-member countries) reveals that the former was 1.6 times as high as the latter in 2025; this comparison is made on the basis of total trade (in other words, the sum of imports and exports) - see Table 1. ===The relative significance of different products === '''''A high proportion of the goods imported into the EU are primary goods''''' Table 1 provides more detailed information — based on the [[Glossary:Standard international trade classification (SITC)|Standard International Trade Classification (SITC)]] — concerning the relative significance of different products within intra-EU and extra-EU trade. The intrinsic nature of different goods means that some are largely restricted to national markets or trade within the single market (intra-EU trade), whereas others are more openly traded on global markets. For example, the perishable nature of some food products may, at least in part, explain why food, drinks and tobacco accounted for 11.8% of all intra-EU exports in 2025, while their share of extra-EU exports was somewhat lower, at 8.1%. On the other hand, the scarcity or a complete lack of natural resource endowments may explain, at least to some degree, why some goods are imported from extra-EU partners; this is the case for mineral fuels and related materials, which accounted for 16.4% of all extra-EU imports, compared with a 5.6% share of intra-EU imports. [[Image:Structure of EU international trade in goods, 2002 and 2025 (share in total, %).png|thumb|700px|Table 1: Structure of EU international trade in goods, 2002 and 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_lt_intratrd__custom_22251201/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=1a7b5bdb-5ae3-4ca5-b409-ef20cf6294b0&c=1785319315000 ext_lt_intratrd])|alt= a table showing the structure of EU international trade in goods in 2002 and 2024 with the categories of goods based on the Standard International Trade Classification. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Intra-EU and extra-EU flows=== '''''In 2025 Ireland, Slovenia, and Cyprus were the only EU countries that had a higher share of their trade in goods with non-member countries''''' Figure 4 provides an analysis at an aggregate level for total trade in goods showing which EU countries had a higher propensity to trade within the single market (intra-EU trade) and which had a higher proportion of their total trade with non-member countries (extra-EU trade). The proportion of total trade in goods that was accounted for by intra-EU and extra-EU flows varied considerably across the countries, reflecting to some degree historical ties and geographical location. In 2025, more than three quarters of the trade conducted in the following countries was with intra-EU partners: *Luxembourg (85.2%) *Slovakia (79.5%) *Estonia (78.9%) *Latvia (77.1%) *and Czechia (75.7%). There were 14 additional countries where the share of intra-EU trade in total trade was within the range of 60-75%. In 5 countries, the share was between 50% and 60%. The only countries to report more extra-EU than intra-EU trade were: *Ireland (36.4%) *Slovenia (45.5%) *and Cyprus (48.6%). Figure 4 ===Volume of goods === '''Exports (+23.5%) and imports (+28.0%) of goods grew between 2002 and 2025 despite setbacks in 2009 and 2023''' Figure 5 extends the analysis of international trade developments to cover extra-EU volume [[Glossary:Index_number|indices]] for trade in goods. The patterns of development for EU trade were broadly similar to those in value terms (see Figure 1) during the period 2002-2008. There was a sizeable contraction in the volume of goods traded in 2009, as the global financial and economic crisis impacted on the level of trade with non-member countries. Between 2009 and 2025 extra-EU imports increased by 18.3%, while exports increased by 15.2%. Figure 5 ===EU terms of trade=== '''''Between 2002 and 2025, the EU’s terms of trade declined''''' Figure 6 shows the development of extra-EU unit value indices during the period 2002-2025. Unit value indices are used as a proxy for changes in import and export prices, while the terms of trade index compares export unit values with import unit values, showing how the relative prices of exports and imports are changed. A more detailed explanation of these terms is provided in the Data sources section of this article. The unit values of EU imports and exports rose during the period 2002-2025. The overall change for imports was 64.0 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] while that for exports 70.8 pp. As a result, the EU terms of trade index increased by 0.3 pp. Figure 6 The information presented in Figure 7 extends the analysis of terms of trade to the individual EU countries; note the data concerns trade flows with the rest of the world (in other words, both intra-EU and extra-EU trade). Between 2002 and 2025, due to high prices for energy products in 2025, there were 19 countries whose terms of trade indices had deteriorated. The largest drop in terms of trade was in Ireland, while Bulgaria had the largest increase. Figure 7 '''''EU terms of trade improved for a majority of its main partners''''' EU terms of trade indices can also be analysed on the basis of bilateral indices for selected trade partners. With 19 of the 29 partners, the terms of trade shown in Figure 8 improved between 2002 and 2025, most notably for: *Singapore (+64.6 pp) *and Taiwan (+58.5 pp). The largest falls were seen in: *Australia (-41.8 pp) *Nigeria (-45.0 pp) *Ukraine (-45.6 pp) *and Brazil (-46.5 pp). Figure 8 The final analysis in this article presents information on the overall change in EU terms of trade for a number of selected products (based on the SITC) between 2002 and 2025, as shown in Figure 9. At the start of this period, terms of trade indices were below parity for only two products: chemicals and related materials, and machinery and transport equipment. By 2025, this situation had changed, and all product groupings had terms of trade above parity (with the exception of food, drinks and tobacco). The largest improvement in this period was for chemicals and related products (+13.6 points), while [[Glossary:Raw_material|raw materials]] (-27.4 points) had the largest decrease. Figure 9 === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Globalisation_chapter_2.1_2026.xlsx|title=International trade in goods - overview: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== Statistics on international trade in goods distinguish between intra-EU and extra-EU trade. *Intra-EU statistics concern transactions that occur within the EU, in other words, exports of goods leaving one EU Member State that are destined to arrive in another. The advent of the single market on 1 January 1993 and the removal of customs formalities between EU Member States resulted in a loss of information and required the establishment of a new data collection system — [[Glossary:Intrastat|Intrastat]] — which is closely linked to VAT systems and is based on collecting data directly from taxable persons (traders). *Extra-EU statistics record flows of goods exported and imported between the EU and non-member countries; note that goods ‘in transit’ through an EU Member State are excluded. Extra-EU trade statistics are collected through a different system — Extrastat — which uses records of trade transactions for customs declarations that are gathered by customs authorities. *The trade balance is the difference between exports and imports. When exports are higher than imports, the balance is positive and this is called a trade surplus. In contrast, if exports are lower than imports, the balance is negative and this is called a trade deficit. '''Terms of trade''' Unit value indices provide a proxy for the price of imports and exports: changes in the (relative) price of specific products/goods can have a major impact on the trade performance and the structure of trade in individual EU countries. For example, if the price of oil doubles then it is possible that some countries (with a high degree of energy dependency) may see their trade position move from a surplus to a deficit. The terms of trade index presents, for an individual country or geographical aggregate, the ratio between the unit value indices for exports and imports; if the terms of trade are higher than 100%, then the relative price of exports is greater than the relative price of imports. If a country’s terms of trade improve, then for every unit of exports that it sells abroad, it is able to purchase more units of imported goods. That said, an improvement in the terms of trade may also mean that the price of a country’s exports becomes relatively more expensive on global markets and depending upon the scarcity of these goods (and the availability of possible substitutes), such an increase may have a direct impact on the volume of goods that are exported and could reduce a country’s trade balance. === Context === The EU has a relatively open trade regime, which has helped it build relationships with a wide range of trading partners. The EU is deeply integrated into global markets, and this is likely to continue, as advances in transport and communication continue to encourage producers to trade goods (and services) worldwide. EU policymakers see the promotion of international trade (and investment) with the rest of the world as a key driver of economic growth and job creation. The EU is one of the world’s biggest players in global trade. The EU has achieved this position, at least in part, by acting in a united way with a single voice, rather than having 27 national trade strategies: the EU countries share a single market, a single external border and a single external trade policy within the [[Glossary:World Trade Organization|World Trade Organisation (WTO)]], where the rules of international trade are agreed and enforced. ===Other articles === *[[Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment]] ===Thematic section=== [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/overview International trade in goods - dedicated section] ===Database=== [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/database International trade in goods - database] ===Data visualisations=== * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/visualisations International trade in goods - visualisations] ===Methodology=== [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/methodology International trade in goods - methodology] ===Legislation=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/legislation International trade in goods - legislation] ===External links=== *[https://trade.ec.europa.eu/ European Commission - DG Trade] *[http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2017:240:FIN European Commission — reflection paper on harnessing globalisation (COM(2017) 240)] {{Unit|topic=X_International_trade_goods}} [[Category:International trade|International trade]] [[Category:International trade in goods|International trade in goods - an overview]] [[Category:Statistical article|International trade in goods - an overview]] [[Category:Vistool|International trade in goods - an overview]] [[Category:September2027|International trade in goods - an overview]]

title: International trade in goods - selected topics
text:
Statistics on international trade in goods between the EU and main trading partners, with analysis on modes of transport, tariffs and currencies for imports and exports. Data extracted in August 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 The United States, the United Kingdom and Switzerland were the 3 largest destinations for EU exports of goods in 2025. China, the United States and the United Kingdom and Switzerland were the 3 largest origins for EU imports of goods in 2025. Maritime transport accounted for the largest share of both imports to and exports from the EU in 2025.
This article shows 4 aspects of international trade in goods. It starts with identifying the EU’s main trading partners and the development of their imports from and exports to the EU. Subsequently, it analyses the various modes of transport used to transport goods, the tariffs applied to goods and the main currencies in which trade was invoiced. === Main partners for EU trade === In 2025, almost half (49.8%) of the value of all the EU’s exports of goods went to just 4 countries: the United States, the United Kingdom, Switzerland and China (see Figure 1). Among this grouping of countries, the relative share of exports to China rose most sharply between 2002 and 2025 (up 4.3 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]]), increased slightly for Switzerland, decreased somewhat for the United States and decreased considerably for the United Kingdom (down 9.8 pp). [[Image:EU exports of goods, 2002 and 2025.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 1: EU exports of goods, 2002 and 2025
''Source:'' [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b7204798-8eda-4e92-8a31-0022bdddf13e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-24T07:11:58Z Eurostat Comext DS-059331]|alt= Two pie charts showing EU exports of goods to the top six country partners with the highest value of exports in percentages. One pie chart presents the year 2002 and the other 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] China accounted for 22.6% of the value of all goods imported by the EU in 2025. The United States, the United Kingdom and Switzerland were the next largest partners for goods imported (see Figure 2). The largest increase in the relative share of imports between 2002 and 2025 was for China (up 14.7 pp), with the steepest decline was for the United Kingdom (down 11.6 pp). [[Image:EU imports of goods, 2002 and 2025.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 2: EU imports of goods, 2002 and 2025
''Source:'' [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b7204798-8eda-4e92-8a31-0022bdddf13e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-24T07:11:58Z Eurostat Comext DS-059331]|alt= Two pie charts showing EU imports of goods to the top six country partners with the highest value of imports in percentages. One pie chart presents the year 2002 and the other 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The EU ran a trade deficit for goods with China (€372 billion) in 2025 and Norway (€32 billion) - see Figure 3. By contrast, the EU recorded trade surpluses with the United States (€198 billion), the United Kingdom (€186 billion), Switzerland (€76 billion) and Türkiye (€11 billion). Figure 3 '''''Realignment of the EU's principal partners for trade in goods towards emerging economies''''' Absolute figures show that EU trade in goods is relatively concentrated with respect to its principal partners. However, there has been a considerable realignment of the EU's trading relationships in recent years, with a shift in bilateral trading relationships towards emerging economies. In contrast, trade flows with traditional partners tended to develop at a much slower pace. Emerging economies have captured an increasing share of global trade. Regarding EU exports between 2002 and 2025, the value of goods destined for Ukraine (+513%) and China (+509%) rose most sharply among the main partners (see Figure 4). For EU imports, the value of goods from China rose most sharply among the partners (+676%) between 2002 and 2025), followed by India (+546%), and Mexico (+503%). The pace of growth was much slower for some of the EU's more traditional trading partners and developed world economies. For example, there were low growth rates for both imports from and exports to the United Kingdom, Japan and Hong Kong. Due to trade restrictions, imports from and exports to Russia declined between 2002 and 2025. [[Image:Extra-EU trade developments for goods, selected partners, 2002-2025.png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 4: EU trade developments for goods, selected partners, 2002-2025
''Source:'' [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/66605d38-999e-439f-b3e1-02876d71da2f?lang=en Eurostat Comext DS-059331]|alt= Scatter chart showing change for the value of EU trade of goods in percentages. On the x-axis are exports and imports are on the y-axis. Each scatter plot represents an EU trading partner country in the years 2002 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === EU trade by mode of transport === A wide range of factors can influence an enterprise’s choice of transport mode when trading goods. These include the destination country, the size and weight of the goods, the required speed of delivery (for example, perishable goods), rules and regulations (for example, concerning the transport of animals), and environmental or safety considerations (for example, hazardous goods). In 2025, around half (50.2%) of the value of goods imported into the EU arrived by sea, while 40.4% of goods exported from the EU travelled by maritime transport (see Figure 5). A further 20.7% of the EU’s imports of goods and 29.1% of its exports travelled by air. The other main mode of transport was road vehicles: 19.5% of the value of goods imported into the EU came by road, as well as 24.9% of the EU's exports. Other modes of transport, including railways and pipelines accounted for relatively minor shares. Figure 5 Figure 6 presents a similar overview but based on the weight (tonnes) of goods rather than their value. It highlights that maritime transport held even greater relative importance in these terms, accounting for 73.3% of EU imports and 72.6% of EU exports in 2025. Air transport accounted for just 0.3% of the weight of the EU’s imported goods and 2.9% of exported goods in 2025. The stark contrast between these shares and air transport’s much higher shares in value terms underscores the high unit value of goods typically transported by air. Figure 6 === EU imports by tariff regime === Trade agreements help European enterprises compete more effectively and increase their exports to countries and regions outside the EU. They also improve access for EU importers to raw materials and essential components, while offering consumers a wider range of products. Such agreements can include commitments from partner governments to uphold human rights, labour rights, and environment protections - for example, by addressing workplace safety or promoting gender equality. The EU benefits from being one of the most open economies in the world, with approximately 70% of its imports entering at zero tariff – whether under Most Favoured Nation (MFN) or preferential trade agreements). Figure 7 presents information for 2025 on the share of goods imported into the EU from selected partners according to the different tariff rates applied. Among selected partners, Argentina had the lowest share of zero-tariff imports (at 22%) and Nigeria the highest (at 96%). The share of zero-tariff imports from the United States was 72% and from China was 42%. Figure 7 Between 2002 and 2012, the share of imports subject to zero tariffs fluctuated but, overall, rose from 67% to 72%. Over the subsequent 12 years, this share continued to fluctuate, standing again at 70% in 2025 – despite having dropped as low as 63% in 2020. Since many energy products are imported duty-free, the share of zero tariff imports is strongly influenced by fluctuations in the prices of petroleum oil and natural gas. Figure 8 === Trade by invoicing currency === Goods imported and exported by the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] can be invoiced in a range of currencies. The following analysis focuses on the trade in goods by invoicing currency (TIC) of the EU with countries outside the EU in 2025. It provides information on the share of trade declared in euros, US dollars, EU countries' currencies other than the euro and other currencies of countries outside the EU (further denoted as other currencies) for imports and exports. The TIC data collection is only mandatory in even reference years. === US dollar most used for EU imports, euro most used for EU exports in 2025 === Figure 9 shows that the US dollar was the most used currency for imports into the EU in 2025, with a share of 51%. The euro was the second most used currency with a share of 40%. The share of EU countries' currencies other than the euro was 2%. Other currencies had a share of 7%. Compared with imports, the positions of the euro and the US dollar are reversed for EU exports. The share for the euro in 2025 was 51%, ahead of the US dollar with 33%. EU countries' currencies other than the euro had a share of 2% and other currencies had a share of 14%. Figure 9 Looking at imports based on the [[Glossary:Standard_international_trade_classification_(SITC)|Standard International Trade Classification (SITC)]] sections (see Figure 10), the US dollar stands out as the main currency used for imports of petroleum products (SITC 33) with a share of 87% in 2025. In manufactured goods (SITC 5-8) the US dollar (46%) was also the main currency just ahead of the euro (43%). In primary goods (SITC 0-4) excluding petroleum, the euro (47%) had the highest share ahead of the US dollar (45%). Figure 10 In EU exports of petroleum products, the US dollar (70%) is also the most used currency in 2025, although somewhat less dominant than in imports. With 62% the euro is the most used currency in primary goods ahead of the US dollar with 23%. In manufactured goods the euro has a share of 50%, the US dollar followed with 32% (see Figure 11). Figure 11 === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Globalisation selected topics Aug 2026.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== EU data is taken from [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat's]] [[Glossary:COMEXT|COMEXT]] database. COMEXT is the reference database for international trade in goods. It provides access not only to both recent and historical data from the EU countries but also to statistics of a significant number of non-EU countries. International trade aggregated and detailed statistics disseminated via the Eurostat website are compiled from COMEXT data according to a monthly process. Data are collected by the competent national authorities of the EU countries and compiled according to a harmonised methodology established by EU regulations before transmission to Eurostat. For extra-EU trade, the statistical information is mainly provided by the traders on the basis of customs declarations. EU data are compiled according to EU guidelines and may, therefore, differ from national data published by the EU countries. Statistics on extra-EU trade are calculated as the sum of trade of each of the 27 EU countries with countries outside the EU. In other words, the EU is considered as a single trading entity and trade flows are measured into and out of the area, but not within it. The United Kingdom is considered as an extra-EU partner country for the EU for the whole period covered by this article. However, the United Kingdom was still part of the internal market until the end of the transitory period (31 December 2020), meaning that data on trade with the United Kingdom were still based on statistical concepts applicable to trade between the EU countries. Consequently, while imports from any other extra-EU trade partner are grouped by country of origin, the United Kingdom data reflected the country of consignment. '''Methodology''' According to the EU concepts and definitions, extra-EU trade statistics (trade between EU countries and non-EU countries) do not record exchanges involving goods in transit, placed in a customs warehouse or given temporary admission (for trade fairs, temporary exhibitions, tests, etc.). This is known as 'special trade'. The partner is the country of final destination of the goods for exports and the country of origin for imports. '''Unit of measure''' Trade values are expressed in millions or billions (1 000 millions) of euros. They correspond to the statistical value, i.e. to the amount which would be invoiced in the event of sale or purchase at the national border of the reporting country. It is called a [[Glossary:FOB|FOB]] value (free on board) for exports and a [[Glossary:CIF|CIF]] value (cost, insurance, freight) for imports. === Context === Trade is an important indicator of Europe's prosperity and place in the world. The bloc is deeply integrated into global markets both for the products it sources and the exports it sells. The EU trade policy is one of the main pillars of the EU's relations with the rest of the world. Because the 27 EU countries share a single market and a single external border, they also have a single trade policy. EU countries speak and negotiate collectively, both in the [[Glossary:World_Trade_Organization|World Trade Organisation]], where the rules of international trade are agreed and enforced, and with individual trading partners. This common policy enables them to speak with one voice in trade negotiations, maximising their impact in such negotiations. This is even more important in a globalised world in which economies tend to cluster together in regional groups. The openness of the EU's trade regime has meant that the EU is the biggest player on the global trading scene and remains a good region to do business with. Thanks to the ease of modern transport and communications, it is now easier to produce, buy and sell goods around the world which gives European companies of every size the potential to trade outside Europe. === Other articles === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=International_trade_-_goods International trade in goods - other articles] === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/overview International trade in goods - dedicated section] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/database International trade in goods - database] ===Data visualisations=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/visualisations International trade in goods - visualisations] ===Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/methodology International trade in goods - methodology] ===Legislation=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/legislation International trade in goods - legislation] ===External links=== *[https://trade.ec.europa.eu/ European Commission - DG Trade] ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/International_trade_in_goods_-_selected_topics'' {{Unit|topic=X_International_trade_goods}} [[Category:International trade|International trade in goods - selected topics]] [[Category:International trade in goods|International trade in goods - selected topics]] [[Category:Statistical article|International trade in goods - selected topics]] [[Category:Vistool|International trade in goods - selected topics]] [[Category:September2027|International trade in goods - selected topics]]

title: International trade in goods by enterprise characteristics
text:
Recent EU statistical data is provided on International trade in goods by enterprise characteristics. Data extracted in May 2026 Planned article update: June 2027 In 2024, 71% of the EU enterprises engaged in trade were importers only. Domestic-controlled enterprises accounted for the majority of EU exports while foreign-controlled enterprises accounted for the majority of EU imports in 2024. Over the last few decades, there has been a rapid expansion in the level of international trade in goods. Trade in goods is viewed as one of the most important drivers of globalisation as demonstrated by ''[[Globalisation_patterns_in_EU_trade_and_investment|Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment]]'', an online [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publication presenting a summary of recent [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] statistics on economic aspects of globalisation, focusing on patterns of EU trade and investment. Yet, aside from a range of studies on relatively large, foreign owned enterprises, little is published regarding the characteristics of enterprises trading across international borders - this subject is covered in more detail within this article. Traditionally, international trade statistics have shown movements of goods between countries and by goods category, they have not provided explicit information as to the characteristics of those enterprises behind such trade flows. In a globalised world, this information is of particular interest to policymakers as they attempt to understand how economies are becoming increasingly interconnected.
'''Statistics on international trade in goods by enterprise characteristics''' Statisticians have looked at using international trade in goods statistics in conjunction with business statistics to provide an enriched analysis of the characteristics of enterprises engaged in international trade, for example, providing information as to their economic activity, their size or the concentration of trade. This can help identify differences between enterprises that trade internationally and those that do not. This has been made possible by linking microdata concerning international trade with business register information. Note that only aggregated results are presented thereby protecting the confidential nature of this information. The statistics used in this article were initially divided between enterprises which trade internationally and those enterprises which are active only within their domestic market as research has shown that international traders differ considerably from enterprises that operate solely within their domestic market. The group of international traders was then further subdivided into importers, exporters and two-way traders (enterprises which both imported and exported).
===Trade by type of trader=== Figure 1 presents aggregated information for the EU countries detailing the composition of those enterprises that were engaged in trade. In 2024, 70.6% of EU enterprises engaged in trade were only importers, while 21.3% were two-way traders, the remaining 8.1% were only exporters. Importers are of interest to policymakers insofar as they facilitate access to new goods and services that were otherwise not easily available, whereas exporters are of interest due to their potential for job creation (that may be linked to economic growth that results from expanding into new markets). An analysis by [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] divisions reveals that there were considerable differences with respect to the make-up of those enterprises engaged in trade across different economic activities. In 2024, in the EU, the highest proportions of two-way traders were recorded for manufacturing activities. Whereas, for most services it was more commonplace to find that the largest proportion of enterprises engaged in trade were importers only. [[Image:Trade by type of trader and economic activity, EU, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Trade by type of trader and by economic activity, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4d49dc09-4241-4987-8548-9f1eccab5d7b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-06T10:41:53Z ext-tec06])|alt= Queued horizontal bar chart showing trade by type of trader and by economic activity as percentage pf enterprises engaged in trade. A list of NACE activities is shown as individual bars totalling 100 percent, each with three queues representing importer only, exporter only and two-way trader for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 2 compares the number of enterprises to the value of trade. It reveals that two-way traders accounted for the vast majority of total trade in value terms: across the EU, two-way traders accounted for 95.4% of all goods traded in 2024. This would tend to suggest that a high proportion of importers only and exporters only tend to trade with relatively few countries and/or relatively few (low value) transactions, whereas two-way traders were more inclined to have a larger number of transactions and a wider range of trade partners. [[Image:Trade by type of trader, EU, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Trade by type of trader, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a8b679f7-01e0-4810-8aa3-81c409e0a322?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T09:16:13Z ext-tec06])|alt= Two pie charts showing number of enterprises and value of trade by type of trader as a percentage of the total in the EU, for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Trade by enterprises size class=== Figures 3 to 6 how that a relatively high share of total trade value is generated by a small number of large traders. In 2024, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs, defined as enterprises with fewer than 250 employees) represented 98.4% of enterprises engaged in intra-EU imports but accounted for only 45.6% of the value of imports. By contrast, large enterprises (with 250 or more employees) represented 1.1% of importing enterprises while accounting for 54.1% of the value of imports. [[Image:Intra-EU imports by size class, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Intra-EU imports by size class, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/515faefb-24f8-4256-8324-4bee4be3336b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T09:20:26Z ext-tec01])|alt= Two pie charts showing number of enterprises and value of trade by size class as a percentage of the total for intra-EU imports, for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, SMEs accounted for 97.1% of enterprises engaged in intra-EU exports and generated 39.4% of the total export value, while large enterprises represented 2.3% of exporting enterprises and generated 60.3% of the total export value. [[Image:Intra-EU exports by size class, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Intra-EU exports by size class, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/00f6009a-ddf4-4c29-8276-c46e74eb1ae3?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T09:21:02Z ext-tec01])|alt= Two pie charts showing number of enterprises and value of trade by size class as a percentage of the total for intra-EU exports, for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, SMEs represented 95.1% of enterprises engaged in extra-EU imports but accounted for only 38.6% of the value of imports. By contrast, large enterprises represented 3.2% of importing enterprises while accounting for 61.1% of the value of imports. [[Image:Extra-EU imports by size class, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Extra-EU imports by size class, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d680f048-364b-4239-9a80-1a376b10e912?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T09:21:27Z ext-tec01])|alt= Two pie charts showing number of enterprises and value of trade by size class as a percentage of the total for extra-EU imports, for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, SMEs represented 95.2% of enterprises engaged in extra-EU exports but accounted for only 28.6% of the value of exports. By contrast, large enterprises represented 4.1% of exporting enterprises while accounting for 71.3% of the value of exports. [[Image:Extra-EU exports by size class, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Extra-EU exports by size class, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0db64a67-5537-4dd9-beae-11663486cc11?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T09:21:53Z ext-tec01])|alt= Two pie charts showing number of enterprises and value of trade by size class as a percentage of the total for extra-EU exports, for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Comparing the information from Figures 3 to 6, shows that large enterprises had higher shares in exports than in imports and higher shares in extra-EU trade than in intra-EU trade.
===Trade by enterprise ownership=== The final section of this article analyses the share of international trade by enterprise ownership, an area that is of considerable interest to policymakers when trying to establish the impact of globalisation on economic performance. When interpreting the figures below, readers should be aware that it was not possible to determine the type of ownership for all enterprises. Across the EU countries, foreign owned enterprises accounted for 51.3% of the total value of extra-EU imports in 2024, which was approximately 3 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp) higher than the share accounted for by domestically owned enterprises (48.3%). A large majority of the number extra-EU importers were domestically owned (90.4%) while foreign owned extra-EU importers accounted for 8.3% [[Image:Extra-EU imports by type of ownership, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Extra-EU imports by type of ownership, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/21dd7726-2a01-42ed-9f4d-b2f657fa7e17?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T09:26:26Z ext-tec07])|alt= Two pie charts showing number of enterprises and value of trade by type of ownership as a percentage of the total for extra-EU imports, for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The situation was quite different for exports, as enterprises controlled by domestic owners had a majority (55.5%) of the total value of extra-EU exports, which was approximately 11 pp higher than the share accounted for by foreign owned enterprises (44.3%). A large majority of the number extra-EU exporters were domestically owned (89.0%) while foreign owned extra-EU exporters accounted for 10.3%. [[Image:Extra-EU exports by type of ownership, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Extra-EU exports by type of ownership, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/aa5c2229-2459-41b9-9a11-f580ae14a191?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T09:27:18Z ext-tec07])|alt= Two pie charts showing number of enterprises and value of trade by type of ownership as a percentage of the total for extra-EU exports, for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=TEC-2024.xlsx|title=International trade in goods by enterprise characteristics: tables and figures}} ===Other articles=== *[[Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment]] ===Thematic section=== [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/overview International trade in goods - dedicated section] ===Database=== [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/database International trade in goods - database] ===Data visualisations=== * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/visualisations International trade in goods - visualisations] ===Methodology=== [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/methodology International trade in goods - methodology] ===Legislation=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-goods/legislation International trade in goods - legislation] ===External links=== *[https://trade.ec.europa.eu/ European Commission - DG Trade] *[http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2017:240:FIN European Commission — reflection paper on harnessing globalisation (COM(2017) 240)] {{Unit|topic=X_International_trade_goods}} [[Category:International trade|International trade in goods by enterprise characteristics]] [[Category:International trade in goods|International trade in goods by enterprise characteristics]] [[Category:Globalisation of businesses|International trade in goods by enterprise characteristics]] [[Category:Internationally trading enterprises|International trade in goods by enterprise characteristics]] [[Category:Statistical article|International trade in goods by enterprise characteristics]] [[Category:June2027|International trade in goods by enterprise characteristics]]

title: International trade in goods and services by end use
text:
This article presents data on international trade, broken down by broad economic categories Data extracted in May 2026 Planned article update: June 2027 In 2025, intermediate services made up 71% of total services extra-EU exports and 82% of total services extra-EU imports. In 2025, intermediate goods made up 52% of total goods extra-EU exports and 57% of total goods extra-EU imports. [[Image:Extra-EU imports of goods and services by end-use, 2017-2025_(2017=100).png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01__custom_16942921/default/table?lang=en ext_ser_bec01], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e418e0a6-33a0-472d-8812-1f5cb0b8a140?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-06T06:35:01Z ds-059329] and own calculations)|alt= a line chart with five lines showing the Extra-EU imports of goods and services by end-use, from 2017 to 2025. The lines show, intermediate services, final services, intermediate goods, capital goods and final goods. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The latest revision of the Broad Economic Categories (BEC) classification now offers a new perspective and enables a novel analytical approach to international trade. Unlike traditional classifications, which focus on what is traded, BEC provides insights into the end-use of goods and services, distinguishing between: *Intermediate use (inputs for further production), *Final use (consumption by households, governments, or non-profit institutions), and *Capital formation (goods used for investment, such as machinery or infrastructure). This end-use perspective is particularly valuable for analysing global value chains (GVCs), where intermediate goods and services play a critical role. GVC encompass the entire range of activities required to bring a product from its initial conception and design through to production, marketing, distribution, and after-sales support for the final consumer. Intermediate goods and services– such as components, raw materials, and business services– are the building blocks of GVCs, linking producers and suppliers across borders. A typical illustration of GVCs in action is the automotive sector. Car manufacturers source components– such as engines, electronics, and batteries– from geographically dispersed suppliers, assembling them in central production hubs. This complex, interconnected process is facilitated by: *Lower transport and labour costs, *Advances in communication technologies, and *Efficient logistics networks. However, this interdependence also introduces vulnerabilities. Disruptions, whether caused by geopolitical conflicts, pandemics, natural disasters, or logistical bottlenecks, can have cascading effects across GVCs. For instance, a shortage of semiconductors in one region can halt vehicle production thousands of miles away, highlighting the fragility of modern supply chains. This article represents an initial exploration of EU exports and imports of goods and services by end-use, classified according to the BEC Rev.5 framework. As this is a novel analytical approach, the data presented are experimental and partly based on estimates. The methodologies underpinning these estimates– including data sources, conversion processes, and limitations are detailed in the "Methodology" section. ===Main conclusions=== * Between 2017 and 2025, the EU’s exports saw the highest growth in the following categories (measured in [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp)): intermediate services (+66 pp), final services (+61 pp) and intermediate goods (+48 pp). These categories outpaced all other goods and services, reflecting the EU’s deepening integration into global value chains (GVCs) and the rising demand for services as intermediate inputs. *In 2025 compared to 2024, the trend shifted slightly: intermediate services exports declined by 1 pp, while final services exports continued to grow (+6 pp). * Over the period 2017 to 2025, EU imports of intermediate categories recorded the most significant increases: intermediate services (+75 pp) and intermediate goods (+47 pp). This growth underscores the EU’s increasing reliance on foreign intermediate inputs to support domestic production and service provision. * In 2025, intermediate goods and services dominated EU trade (71% of total services exports and 82% of total services imports), while intermediate goods made up 52% of total goods exports and 57% of total goods imports. These shares highlight the central role of intermediate inputs in the EU’s economic interactions with the rest of the world. * In 2025, intermediate services were most prevalent in the category ‘ICT, media, computers, business and financial services’ accounting for the largest share of both extra-EU exports and imports. This reflects the growing digitalisation of GVCs and the increased demand for cross-border business and financial services. * In 2025, intermediate goods categories differed between exports and imports: extra-EU exports were most prevalent in the category 'Health, pharmaceuticals, education, cultural, sport', while for imports they had the largest share in ‘Mining, quarrying, refinery, fuels, chemicals, electricity, water, waste treatment'. === International trade by end-use === Between 2017 and 2019, EU exports increased across all categories (Figure 1). However, the COVID-19 pandemic led to a sharp decline in exports for all types of goods and services. The most significant drop was observed in final services, followed by capital goods. In 2020, final services experienced the steepest decline - falling 25 pp below 2017 levels for exports and 30 pp for imports. This dramatic downturn was largely due to the health and sanitary restrictions implemented in response to COVID-19, particularly in the first half of 2020. Final services are primarily driven by travel-related activities, such as expenditures by foreign tourists and travelers. With international travel virtually halted or severely restricted for much of 2020, the impact is clearly reflected in the decline of final services during that year. In contrast, the declines in goods were less pronounced but still notable. By 2022, exports across all categories of goods and services had reached their highest levels since 2017. Despite the fluctuations during the following years in 2025 (compared to 2022 levels) all categories recorded growth, except final goods (-2 pp). When compared to 2017 levels, all categories recorded growth by 2025. Intermediate services saw the highest increase, rising by 66 pp, followed by final services (+61 pp), intermediate goods (+48 pp), capital goods (+23 pp), and final goods (+17 pp). [[Image:Extra-EU exports of goods and services by end-use, 2017-2025_(2017=100).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Extra-EU exports of goods and services by end-use, 2017-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01__custom_16942921/default/table?lang=en ext_ser_bec01], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e418e0a6-33a0-472d-8812-1f5cb0b8a140?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-06T06:35:01Z ds-059329] and own calculations)|alt= a line chart with five lines showing the Extra-EU exports of goods and services by end-use from 2017 to 2025. The lines show, intermediate services, final services, intermediate goods, capital goods and final goods. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] As with exports, total EU imports of goods and services declined in 2020 compared to 2019, with the steepest drop again observed in final services (Figure 2). Imports of final services began to recover after 2020, surpassing pre-COVID levels in 2022 and reaching their peak in 2025 - standing 44 pp above 2017 levels. Compared to 2024, final services imports grew by 5 pp in 2025. EU imports of intermediate services experienced only a slight decline in 2020, rebounded in 2021, and continued to grow steadily in the following years. They peaked in 2025 at 75 pp above 2017 levels. All categories of goods saw declines in imports in 2020. The sharpest decrease was in intermediate goods (-16 pp), followed by final goods (-9 pp) and capital goods (-7 pp). By 2022, imports of intermediate and final goods reached their highest levels for the observed period. The increase was particularly strong for intermediate goods, driven largely by a surge in energy prices. However, this upward trend reversed in 2023 and 2024, with imports of intermediate goods, capital goods, and final goods all declining compared to 2022. Then, in 2025 all goods categories showed substantial growth over 2017 levels: intermediate goods increased by 47 pp, capital goods by 40 pp, and final goods by 32 pp. [[Image:Extra-EU imports of goods and services by end-use, 2017-2025_(2017=100).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Extra-EU imports of goods and services by end-use, 2017-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01__custom_16942921/default/table?lang=en ext_ser_bec01], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e418e0a6-33a0-472d-8812-1f5cb0b8a140?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-06T06:35:01Z ds-059329] and own calculations)|alt= a line chart with five lines showing the Extra-EU imports of goods and services by end-use, from 2017 to 2025. The lines show, intermediate services, final services, intermediate goods, capital goods and final goods. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figures 3 and 4 provide further insight by presenting goods and services trade broken down by end-use (intermediate consumption, final consumption and capital goods). In 2025, intermediates services are predominant: 71% of the exported and 82% of the imported services were intermediate services (that means that about 2 to 3 times as many intermediate services are traded as final services). [[Image:Extra-EU trade in services by end use, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Extra-EU trade in services by end-use, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01__custom_16942921/default/table?lang=en ext_ser_bec01] and own calculations)|alt=two pie charts showing extra-EU trade in services by end-use in 2025 the first pie chart shows imports and the second pie chart shows exports the segments show intermediate services and final services. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
In goods, 52% of the exported and 57% of the imported goods are intermediate goods. By comparison, capital goods accounted for 23% of exports and 17% of imports, while final goods accounted for 24% for exports and 26% for imports. [[Image:Extra-EU trade in goods by end use, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Extra-EU trade in goods by end-use, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e418e0a6-33a0-472d-8812-1f5cb0b8a140?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-06T06:35:01Z ds-059329] and own calculations)|alt=Two pies charts showing Extra-EU trade in goods by end-use in 2025 one pie chart shows exports and the second pie chart shows imports. The segments show Intermediate goods Capital goods and Final goods. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === International trade in intermediate goods and services by broad economic category === Figures 5 and 6 show the distribution of extra-EU trade of intermediate goods and services by broad economic categories in 2025. In 2025, the most exported and imported intermediate services to/from the EU were 'ICT, media, computers, business and financial services' (almost 58% for exports and 62% for imports), followed by 'Transport equipment and services, travel, postal services' (about 21% for exports and 19% for imports), and 'Health, pharmaceuticals, education, cultural, sport services' (about 9% for exports and 11% for imports).
