title: International trade in goods by type of good
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the international trade in goods by type of good. Data extracted in August 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 In 2025, machinery and transport equipment accounted for 38.9% of all goods exported from the EU and for 33.8% of all goods imported into the EU. In 2025, the United States was the main destination for EU exports of medicinal and pharmaceutical products, and iron and steel. ''[[Globalisation_patterns_in_EU_trade_and_investment|Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment]]'' is an online [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publication presenting a summary of recent [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] statistics on economic aspects of globalisation, focusing on patterns of EU trade and investment. This article examines in more detail the different types of goods that are traded between nations. Globalisation, falling trade costs and technological progress are thought to have driven the international fragmentation of production and the development of international production/supply chains. These changes to the way in which goods (and services) are produced, has resulted in manufacturing processes being split into different stages so that intermediate inputs may be sourced from the most efficient producers, even if they are spread across disparate locations. As a result, the relative importance of intermediate goods - the inputs which connect different production stages together - as a share of total trade has risen at a rapid pace. ===International trade in goods - developments by broad economic category===
'''Statistics on international trade in goods by broad economic category (BEC)''' As global production chains have developed into complex production networks it has become increasingly difficult, from a statistical perspective, to measure where specific (end) goods are made and by whom. Indeed, an analysis of international trade developments based on gross measures has become less accurate, as intermediate goods (parts and components) may be counted several times as they cross borders to be used at various stages of the manufacturing process. The classification of international trade statistics by [http://unstats.un.org/unsd/trade/classifications/bec.asp broad economic category (BEC)] is managed by the United Nations. These statistics permit the conversion of international trade data based on the standard international trade classification (SITC) into three end-use categories: capital goods, intermediate goods and consumption goods.
'''''The share of intermediate goods in all extra-EU imports peaked in 2011-22''''' Figure 1 shows the development of the share of intermediate goods in total trade for the [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU]] over the period covering 2017-2025. Until 2024, this share was highest for extra-EU imports and lowest for extra-EU exports with intra-EU exports falling in between. This should come as no surprise since raw materials and energy are more abundant in extra-EU imports than in extra-EU exports which are dominated by manufactured goods. The share of intermediate goods for extra-EU imports, measured in value, peaked in 2022 at 60.5% and fell back to 56.7% in 2025. It should be noted that price fluctuations of energy products have a substantial impact on the share of trade in intermediate goods. Figure 1 The predominance of intermediate goods in total trade is shown in Figure 2. Across the EU, intermediate goods accounted for just over half (52.1%) of all goods that were exported in 2025. For comparison, capital goods (23.3%) and consumption goods (24.5%) each accounted for around a quarter of all exported goods. In imports the share of capital goods (16.8%) was lower than in exports while consumption goods (26.6%) had a higher share in exports than in imports. Figure 2 '''''Shares of intermediate products in total trade vary considerably among EU countries''''' In 2025, a majority of the EU countries reported that intermediate goods contributed more than half of their total trade in value terms, both for imports (17 EU countries) and exports (16 EU countries); note these were not the same EU countries for each trade flow (see Figures 3 and 4). The share of intermediate goods in total exports was over 60% in Ireland (79.0%), Slovenia (68.9%), Malta (68.4%), Bulgaria (63.6%) and Finland (60.6%) and below 40% only in Cyprus (18.8%). The share of intermediate goods in total imports was highest in Slovenia (66.6%), and Slovakia (60.6%) while only Cyprus (34.2%) had a share below 40%. Figure 3 Figure 4 ===International trade in goods - developments for key product groups=== Historically, the biggest shifts in international trade by product resulted in a marked decline in the relative contribution of agricultural products to total trade, while the share of manufactured goods increased. When asked to picture globalisation today, many people are likely to imagine a cargo ship transporting large quantities of manufactured goods to distant markets on the other side of the world. A closer examination reveals that the bulk of international trade in goods is relatively concentrated within some key product groups, while there are many goods where the level of international trade remains quite low. Indeed, as noted in the article [[International trade in goods - an overview]], the intrinsic nature of some goods (for example, those with a limited shelf-life or those that are bulky) means that they are principally consumed within domestic or neighbouring markets. '''''In 2025, machinery and transport equipment accounted for €1 028 billion or 39.7% of all goods exported from the EU.''''' Figure 5 shows the development of extra-EU exports for the top level headings from the [[Glossary:Standard_international_trade_classification_(SITC)|standard international trade classification (SITC)]]. One of the most striking aspects is the high value of machinery and transport equipment, which was €1 028 billion in 2025 (39.7% of all exports). The next highest values were recorded for chemicals and related products (€604.1 billion, 23.3%) and other manufactured goods (€555 billion, 21.5%) while food, drinks and tobacco (€215 billion, 8.3%), mineral fuels, lubricants and related materials (€117 billion, 4.5%) and raw materials (€69 billion, 2.7%) accounted for much lower shares. Looking at developments during the period 2002-2025, the impact of the global financial and economic crisis in 2009 and the COVID-19 crisis in 2020 on the different product headings is evident. In 2009 exports decreased sharply for all product groups. By contrast, in 2020 exports of chemicals, food, drinks and tobacco and raw materials were much less impacted than exports of machinery and transport equipment, other manufactured goods and mineral fuels. A comparison of developments for EU exports between 2002 and 2025 reveals that in absolute terms machinery and transport equipment (+€571 billion) increased the most. In relative terms its value was 2.3 times as high as in 2002, which was similar to the growth of other manufactured goods (2.1 times as high) but much lower that mineral fuels which in 2025 were 4.9 times as high as in 2002. By comparison, the exports values in the other three groups in 2025 were between 3 and 4 times as high as in 2002. Figure 5 '''''A-typical development for imports of mineral fuels, lubricants and related materials due to fluctuation of oil prices''''' Complementary information on developments for EU imports is presented in Figure 6 (based on the same product headings). Due to sharply increasing prices, mineral fuels, lubricants and related materials temporarily became the largest product group in imports in 2022 but dropped to third place in 2025 (€415 billion, 16.6%). In 2025 it was preceded by machinery and transport equipment (€855 billion, 34.3%) and other manufactured goods (€605 billion, 23.3%). All products follow the same pattern, a decline in 2009 followed by a recovery in the following years. The COVID-19 pandemic caused a large drop in 2020 but a strong recovery followed in 2021 and 2022. Over the whole period, imports of machinery and transport equipment increased most (+€516 billion), followed by other manufactured goods (+€378 billion) and mineral fuels (+€262 billion). In relative terms chemicals and related products increased the most, being 3.6 times as large in 2025 as in 2002. Figure 6 Figure 7 shows the values by product heading in EU exports, imports and trade balance in 2025. The EU had a trade surplus for machinery and vehicles (€173 billion), chemicals and related products (€256 billion) and food, and drinks and tobacco (€40 billion). By contrast it had a deficit in mineral fuels and lubricants etc. (-€298 billion), other manufactured goods (-€49 billion), and raw materials (-€29 billion). Figure 7 ===International trade in goods - focus on selected product groups === This final section in this article looks in more detail at international trade developments for a selected group of specific products, where globalisation has had a significant impact on industrial structure and conduct *medicinal and pharmaceutical products (SITC 54) *iron and steel (SITC 67) *motor cars (SITC 781) *articles of apparel and clothing accessories (SITC 84). The share of these 4 selected products in extra-EU trade is presented in Figure 8. Between 2002 and 2025 the share for medicinal and pharmaceutical products in total exports rose by 9.1 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]], while the shares for the other three fell. For imports, the share for medicinal and pharmaceutical products in total imports rose by 2.3 pp, somewhat more than the increase for motor cars (0.3 pp) and iron and steel (0.2 pp) while articles of apparel and clothing accessories (-0.1 pp) dropped slightly. These changes should be interpreted with caution as they are the result of a combination of changes in quantities as well as changes in prices. Figure 8 '''Medicinal and pharmaceutical products''' Extra-EU exports of medicinal and pharmaceutical products were valued at €366 billion in 2025, compared with extra-EU imports of €146 billion; as such, the EU had a trade surplus of €220 billion. According to the European Commission's Directorate-General for Trade, the most common trade impediments faced by pharmaceutical exporters are a range of burdensome and costly registration, licensing and certification procedures; the EU aims to redress these through its bilateral trade agreements or by tackling individual barriers as part of its market access partnerships. The United States was the EU's main trading partner for exports of medicinal and pharmaceutical products (see Figure 9). More than two-fifths (43.8%) of EU exports in 2025 were destined for the United States; considerably higher than in 2002, when the United States accounted for a 30.9% share of the EU's exports of medicinal and pharmaceutical products. The next largest EU export markets were Switzerland (16.3% of all exports in 2025), the United Kingdom (5.6%) and China (3.8%). Imports of medicinal and pharmaceutical products into the EU were even more dominated by the EU's main trading partners, as almost four-fifths of the goods imported in 2025 originated from the United States (41.3%), Switzerland (28.3%) and China (9.0%) combined; the next highest share was recorded for imports originating in the United Kingdom (6.4%) (see Figure 10). Figure 9 Figure 10 Among the EU countries in 2025, extra-EU exports of medicinal and pharmaceutical products were relatively concentrated in Ireland (25.5% of the EU's exports), Germany (18.6% ), Belgium (10.6%) and Italy (9.9%); all 4 had the United States as their main export destination (see Table 1). For Ireland, medicinal and pharmaceutical products made up 53.3% of their total exports. Italy (18.9%), Belgium (17.0%), Germany (16.5%), and the Netherlands (11.7%) and recorded the highest shares of extra-EU imports of medicinal and pharmaceutical products in 2025, and were the only EU countries with double-digit shares (see Table 2). [[Image:Exports of medicinal and pharmaceutical products (SITC 54), 2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: Exports of medicinal and pharmaceutical products (SITC 54), 2025

There are columns for Total exports (€ million), Share of total goods exported, Extra-EU exports (€ million), Share of extra-EU exports, Main intra EU partner, Value main intra EU partner (€ million), Main extra EU partner and Value main extra EU partner (€ million). For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:Imports of medicinal and pharmaceutical products (SITC 54), 2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 2: Imports of medicinal and pharmaceutical products (SITC 54), 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a4d89151-6454-455f-8f5e-181f4f6589a5?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-25T06:41:41Z ds-059331])|alt= Table showing imports of medicinal and pharmaceutical products in 2025 by Member States. There are columns for Total imports (€ million), Share of total goods imported, Extra-EU imports (€ million), Share of extra-EU imports, Main intra EU partner, Value main intra EU partner (€ million), Main extra EU partner and Value main extra EU partner (€ million). For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Iron and steel''' The iron and steel industry is often seen as being of strategic importance. In the last couple of decades there has been a pattern of industrialised nations relocating some of their iron and steel production facilities to developing countries; this has been driven, at least in part, by a desire to relocate production facilities closer to coal and iron ore supplies. Between 2002 and 2025 a growing share of EU exports of iron and steel were destined for Türkiye (its share rising from 5.1% in 2002 to 7.7% in 2025 (see Figure 11). The United States (18.9%) and the United Kingdom (14.7%) were the EU's main export destinations. Alongside a rapid shift in global output of iron and steel, there were also major changes to trade patterns. These were particularly evident during the last few years, as Chinese economic growth slowed, resulting in excess Chinese capacity being redirected to foreign markets. In 2002, China accounted for just 2.1% of the EU's imports of iron and steel (see Figure 12). By 2025 the share of EU imports originating from China had jumped to 13.5% becoming the largest origin for imports of iron and steel ahead of Türkiye (10.7%) and India (9.0%). Figure 11 Figure 12 The EU had a trade deficit of 7.7 billion in 2025 for iron and steel. In 2025, the leading exporter among the EU countries was Germany (€29.0 billion) followed by Italy (€19.5 billion) - see Table 3. It is interesting to note that iron and steel products accounted for 10.2% of all goods exported from Luxembourg in 2025, the next highest share being recorded in Finland (6.0%). Extra-EU iron and steel imports into the EU from non-member countries were valued at €42.6 billion in 2026. Table 4 shows that Germany had the highest value (€27.1 billion) of iron and steel imports among the EU countries, followed by Italy (€20.8 billion) (see Table 4). Germany and Italy were the main origin of iron and steel imports for a large number of EU countries while there were also several EU countries reporting that their principal origin of imports was a neighbouring country. [[Image:Exports of iron and steel (SITC 67), 2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 3: Exports of iron and steel (SITC 67), 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d2a2db80-774f-4761-b5c8-a11d5a0e08d7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-25T06:43:18Z ds-059331])| alt= Table showing exports of iron and steel in 2025 by Member States. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] [[Image:Imports of iron and steel (SITC 67), 2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 4: Imports of iron and steel (SITC 67), 2025

There are columns for Total imports (€ million), Share of total goods imported, Extra-EU imports (€ million), Share of extra-EU imports, Main intra EU partner, Value main intra EU partner (€ million), Main extra EU partner and Value main extra EU partner (€ million). For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Motor cars''' The car industry has undergone a considerable change in recent years, with increased production from new producers in emerging markets, while traditional car manufacturers have faced structural issues associated with falling domestic sales and overcapacity. The industry remains dominated by a small number of global players who tend to have a presence on most continents as a result of takeovers, joint ventures, alliances and other forms of collaboration. The car industry is often seen as a pioneer for new methods of industrial organisation and is a leading exponent of global value chains, sourcing intermediate inputs from around the world and delivering these 'just-in-time' for assembly. While car production has diversified geographically, Europe's automotive industry is concentrated in the hands of a small number of groups, including Volkswagen, Daimler, BMW, Fiat Chrysler, PSA and Renault. It should also be noted that overseas carmakers have a considerable presence manufacturing cars within the single European market, for example: General Motors in Germany and Austria; Ford in Spain; or Hyundai in Czechia. It is important to note that the statistics presented below relate to imports and exports of motor cars between national territories, regardless of the ownership of the production facilities where these cars are made. In 2025, the United Kingdom (23.2% of the total) and the United States (19.9%) were the main destinations for EU exports of motor cars, while Türkiye (9.9%) was the third highest destination - see Figure 13. It is interesting to note that, while the share of EU exports destined for the United States and the United Kingdom declined by 9.6 pp and 11.1 pp respectively between 2002 and 2025, the share of exports destined for Türkiye rose by 9.0 pp. Over four-fifths of the EU's imports of motor cars in 2025 originated from 6 countries: China (18.5% of the total), Japan (15.1%), Türkiye (13.5%), the United Kingdom (13.2%), South Korea 11.7%), and the United States (9.3%) - see Figure 14. It is interesting to note the rapid decline in the share of EU motor car imports that originated from Japan (-16.7 pp) and the United Kingdom (-21.5 pp). These developments reflect the establishment of Japanese manufacturing bases within the EU, and also the growing shares of China (+18.4 pp), Türkiye (+9.9 pp) and Morocco (+5.98 pp). Figure 13 Figure 14 Germany was, by far, the leading exporter of motor cars among the EU countries in 2025 (see Table 5). Over half (51.5%) of all cars exported from the EU originated from Germany, far ahead of Slovakia (7.8%), Spain (6.5%) and Czechia (5.8%); none of the remaining EU countries accounted for more than 5.0% of exports. The United States was the main market for cars exported from Germany, while Germany was the largest export partner for a majority of the EU countries. Germany was also the largest importer of motor cars among the EU countries in 2025 (see Table 6); it accounted for 24.4% of imports from outside the EU, followed by Belgium (22.5%). The largest share of German extra-EU imports originated from the United States, while Germany was the main origin of imports for a large majority of other EU countries. [[Image:Exports of motor cars (SITC 781), 2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 5: Exports of motor cars (SITC 781), 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5cfe8443-ddf0-43e0-a0c1-0417c812cf57?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-25T06:45:43Z ds-059331])|alt= Table showing exports of motor cars in 2025 by Member States. There are columns for Total exports (€ million), Share of total goods exported, Extra-EU exports (€ million), Share of extra-EU exports, Main intra EU partner, Value main intra EU partner (€ million), Main extra EU partner and Value main extra EU partner (€ million). For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] [[Image:Imports of motor cars (SITC 781), 2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 6: Imports of motor cars (SITC 781), 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5cfe8443-ddf0-43e0-a0c1-0417c812cf57?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-25T06:44:28Z ds-059331])| alt= Table showing imports of motor cars in 2025 by Member States. There are columns for Total imports (€ million), Share of total goods imported, Extra-EU imports (€ million), Share of extra-EU imports, Main intra EU partner, Value main intra EU partner (€ million), Main extra EU partner and Value main extra EU partner (€ million). For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Apparel and clothing accessories''' The apparel and clothing accessories industry is another interesting case-study in terms of the impact of globalisation. It is characterised by distant supply chains, with subcontractors manufacturing large quantities of mass-produced clothing (often with very low labour costs); even high-end production, such as designer clothes, are predominantly manufactured away from their country of design, although their manufacture may be closer to home (for example, in other European countries with lower labour costs). Consumers are generally considered to have benefited from the impact of globalisation in the clothing industry, as prices have been kept extremely low and a wide-range of ever-changing fashions are rapidly made available on the high street. On the other hand, the relocation of the clothing industry towards emerging and subsequently developing economies, principally in Asia, led to widespread job losses in Europe (and North America). As with the iron and steel industry, the clothing sector is also characterised by overcapacity, which some manufacturers may use to their advantage in order to apply downward pressure on prices agreed with subcontractors. While China and India were at the forefront of the initial relocation of the clothing industry, the situation has subsequently evolved, with India specialising in high-end textiles and Chinese investment often being directed towards establishing new manufacturing facilities in countries such as Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Laos or Cambodia. The largest destinations of EU exports of articles of apparel and clothing accessories were Switzerland (15.8%), the United Kingdom (13.0%) and the United States (12.8%) - see Figure 15. China was the main origin of EU imports for articles of apparel and clothing accessories, its share of the EU import market rose from 23.4% in 2002 to 31.0% in 2025 (see Figure 16). Türkiye (8.8%) and India (5.1%) followed at some distance. A relatively high share of EU imports (48.1%) originated from the rest of the world, suggesting that the manufacture of clothing was being relocated to a wide range of countries. Figure 15 Figure 16 In 2025, the EU ran a trade deficit (€58 billion) for articles of apparel and clothing accessories. The principal export markets for EU countries were other EU countries or nearby countries such as Switzerland, Norway and the United Kingdom. Croatia (4.5%) was the EU country with the highest share for articles of apparel and clothing accessories in total exports (see Table 7). China was the main origin of apparel and clothing accessory imports for 8 of the EU countries. However, when considering only extra-EU partners, China was the main origin for 25 of the EU countries. Germany, France, Spain and the Netherlands were the only EU countries to import more than €10 billion of apparel and clothing accessories from countries outside the EU, in 2025. When considering total (extra-EU + intra-EU) imports, Italy, Poland and Belgium also imported more than €10 billion (see Table 8). title: International trade in services
text:
EU statistics provide information on international trade in services in the EU and its member states. Data extracted in December 2025. Planned article update: December 2026. In 2024, EU exports of services to non-member countries reached €1 568 billion, with Ireland recording the highest value (€334 billion). In 2024, EU imports of services from non-member countries reached €1 374 billion, with Ireland recording the highest value (€356 billion). In 2024, the United States was the EU's largest trading partner for exports and imports of services, followed by United Kingdom. This article describes the major developments of international trade in services in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], and the EU Member States. Furthermore, it provides information about the EU's main trading partners for services. ===General overview=== Services play an important role in all modern economies. A resilient tertiary service sector, as well as increased availability of services, may boost economic growth and enhance industrial performance. In an increasingly globalised world, services such as finance, insurance, transport, logistics and communications deliver key intermediate inputs and thereby provide crucial support to the rest of the economy. Figure 1 presents the year-to-year development of the sum of exports and imports for the [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU]]'s transactions of goods and services with non-member countries (in other words, trade outside of the EU, also known as extra-EU trade), for the years 2001 to 2024; these data are based on quarterly balance of payments statistics. During this period, the EU's volume of services transactions with non-member countries increased each year with the exception of 2003, 2009 and 2020. 2009 is the year in which the global financial and economic crisis was at its peak and the EU's transactions in services fell by 8.3%. The significant dip in 2020 by 10.1% was due to the COVID-19 pandemic and associated measures. The EU volume of services trade increased again in 2021 by 11.1%, as well as in 2022 by 23.7% (largest increase recorded in the entire period), 4.1% in 2023 and 7.5% in 2024. In the period 2002 to 2024, the EU net surplus of services, in other words the value of exports minus the value of imports, was always positive, with a maximum of €209 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] in 2022. In the period from 2012 to 2017, growth for the EU's international trade in services was higher than for international trade in goods, this trend reversed in 2018 but returned in 2019. In 2020 services recorded the same drop as goods. In 2021 and 2022 goods recorded a significantly higher growth rate than services. In 2023 and 2024 services recorded a growth while goods dropped significantly. [[Image: F1-ITSS data 2024.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Annual change in international trade (exports plus imports) with non-member countries (extra-EU), EU, 2001-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/BOP_EU6_Q__custom_19073233/default/table bop_eu6_q])|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing annual change in international trade (exports plus imports) with non-member countries (extra-EU), in the EU from 2001 to 2024, the bars show goods and services. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] From 2010 to 2019 the EU's exports of services to non-member countries increased every year, from €559 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] in 2010 to €1 097 billion in 2019. As a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, in 2020 exports dropped to €953 billion but in 2021 exports recovered with €1 129 billion and reached €1 568 billion in 2024. During the same period, EU imports of services from non-member countries progressed from €487 billion in 2010 to €1 045 billion in 2019, before decreasing to €945 billion in 2020. In 2021 imports rebounded to 991 billion, reaching €1 374 billion in 2024 (see Figure 2). [[Image: F2-ITSS data 2024.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: International trade in services with non-member countries (extra-EU), EU, 2010-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_tot__custom_19362997/default/table bop_its6_tot])|alt= a double vertical bar chart with one line showing international trade in services with non-member countries (extra-EU), in the EU from 2010 to 2024. The bars show exports and imports and the line shows balance. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The 2024 data show that Ireland was the EU country with the highest value of exports of services to non-member countries, its €334 billion of exports equivalent to 21.3% of the EU total – see Figure 3. The next highest levels of exports to non-member countries were recorded by Germany (€240 billion or 15.3%), France (€201 billion or 12.8%) and the Netherlands (€161 billion or 10.3%). Ireland had the highest level of services imports from non-member countries with €356 billion or 25.9% of the EU total; Germany (€243 billion or 17.7%), France (€151 billion or 11.0%) and the Netherlands (€139 billion or 10.1%) followed. [[Image: F3-ITSS data 2024.png |thumb|center|800px|Figure 3: Share of EU countries in international trade in services with non-member countries (extra-EU), 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det__custom_19358111/default/table bop_its6_tot])|alt= two pie charts showing share of EU countries in international trade in services with non-member countries (extra-EU) in 2024, one chart shows imports and the other exports, the segments show the countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 4 presents the analysis of trade in services between EU countries (intra-EU trade) – rather than with non-member countries. In 2024, Germany recorded the largest value of services exports to other EU countries (€195 billion or 12.8%), followed by France (€171 billion or 11.2%) and the Netherlands (€162 billion or 10.7%). Again Germany was the largest importer of services from other EU countries, with imports valued at €258 billion or 19.1%, ahead of France (€164 billion or 12.1%) and the Netherlands (€148 billion or 11.0%). [[Image: F4-ITSS data 2024.png|thumb|center|800px|Figure 4: Share of EU countries in international trade in services within the EU (intra-EU), 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det__custom_19358140/default/table bop_its6_tot])|alt= two pie charts showing share of EU countries in international trade in services within the EU (intra-EU) in 2024, one chart shows imports and the other exports, the segments show the countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, the division of total trade volume in services (sum of imports and exports) between trade with non-member countries on one hand and trade with other EU countries on the other hand varied significantly among the EU countries (see Figure 5). This reflected, to some extent, either the geographical proximity or historical trade associations. Hence, Ireland (76.2%) exhibited a large proportion of international trade in services transactions occurring outside the EU, as did Cyprus (61.6%) and Greece (59.9%). [[Image: F5-ITSS data 2024.png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Distribution of intra-EU and extra-EU trade (exports plus imports) in services, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det__custom_19358183/default/table bop_its6_tot])|alt= a vertical stacked bar chart showing the distribution of intra-EU and extra-EU trade (exports plus imports) in services in 2024, the stacks show, trade with EU countries and and trade with non member countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] At the other end of the spectrum, 78.1% of Slovakia's international trade in services transactions were recorded with other EU countries, followed by Austria with 75.1% and Slovenia with 74.1%. For 2024, the EU average shows that 49.4% of all international services transactions took place within the EU, and 50.6% were with non-member countries. ===Main trading partners=== Figure 6 presents the EU's main trading partners for services. Between 2023 and 2024 the EU's exports of services increased for all of its main partners, except for Singapore for which they decreased. The imports increased as well for all main partners except for Canada. [[Image: F6-ITSS data 2024.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Trade in services with non-member countries (extra-EU), main partners, EU, 2023 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det__custom_19358522/default/table bop_its6_det])|alt=The figure presents the EU's main trading partners for services. Between 2023 and 2024 the EU's exports of services increased for all of its main partners, except for Singapore for which they decreased. The imports increased as well for all main partners except for Canada. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 7 shows the share of the main partners for services exports and imports. In 2024, the United States, the United Kingdom and Switzerland were the largest destination for EU exports of services, with trade valued at €344 billion, €294 billion and €162 billion respectively, representing 21.9%, 18.8% and 10.4% of all exports to non-member countries (see Figure 7). All the countries shown in Figure 7 collectively received about 70.8% of all exports of services from the EU to non-member countries in 2024. [[Image: F7-ITSS data 2024.png|thumb|center|800px|Figure 7: Trading partners' share of EU international trade in services with non-member countries (extra-EU), 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det__custom_19358708/default/table bop_its6_det])|alt= two pie charts showing the trading partners' share of EU international trade in services with non-member countries (extra-EU) in 2024, the first pie chart shows exports and the second pie chart shows imports. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The top 3 countries of origin for EU imports of services were the same as the destinations with the 3 largest shares of EU exports of services (see Figure 7). Again the United States account for the largest value of imported services, some €483 billion which is equivalent to 35.1% of the total imports from non-member countries. The next largest shares are from the United Kingdom with 18.0% and Switzerland with 7.2%. All the countries shown in Figure 7 collectively account for about 77.5% of all EU services imported from non-member countries in 2024. === Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=International trade in services data Dec2025 V3.xlsx |title=International trade in services data Dec2025}} ===Data sources=== Statistics on international trade in services provide the monetary value of such trade, with an analysis by the type of service (for example computer services or legal services) and by partner country. These statistics are produced from the transactions recorded under a country's balance of payments, which captures all transactions that take place between an economy's residents and non-residents. Furthermore, international trade in services statistics distinguishes between transactions between EU Member States (intra-EU transactions) and transactions with non-member countries (extra-EU transactions). The total includes international transactions with all countries of the world and comprises intra-EU and extra-EU transactions. The transmission of data on international trade in services to [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] is covered by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32005R0184:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 184/2005}} of the [[Glossary:European Parliament (EP)|European Parliament]] and of the [[Glossary:Council of the European Union|Council]]. The main methodological references used for the production of statistics on international trade in services are the following: *the [[Glossary:International Monetary Fund|International Monetary Fund's (IMF's)]] Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (BPM6); *the [[Glossary:United Nations|United Nations]]' [http://unstats.un.org/unsd/tradeserv/TFSITS/manual.htm manual on statistics of international trade in services (MSITS 2010)]; *the [https://unstats.un.org/unsd/classifications/Family/Detail/101 extended balance of payments services classification (EBOPS 2010)]. The data presented in this article are based upon the BPM6 methodology which was adopted by the EU Member States from reference year 2013 onwards. On a voluntary basis, some Member States have provided data according to the BPM6 methodology back to the 2010 reference year. In order to calculate the EU aggregate for earlier years — using data provided according to the previous (BPM5) methodology — Eurostat estimated the missing values for those Member States where data prior to 2013 were not available. EU data for the total international trade in services for years before 2010 are available from the quarterly balance of payments. It should be noted that for the years for which data are available from both sources (quarterly balance of payments and annual international trade in services), the values for these 2 sources are somewhat different. The differences may be due to revisions in quarterly data, differences in coverage and possibly also to different compilation practices. ===Context=== The provision of services contributes a substantial share of the EU's economic wealth and accounts for more than 50% of GDP in each of the EU Member States. Nevertheless, the value of exports and imports of goods is generally 2 to 3 times higher than that of services. Part of this imbalance may be due to the nature of some services, for example, professional services that are bound by distinct national legislation. Another difference between goods and services concerns the immediacy of the relationship between supplier and consumer: many services are non-transportable, in other words they require the physical proximity of the service provider and consumer, which implies that many services transactions involve factor mobility. For international trade in non-transportable services to take place, either the consumer must go to the service provider or the service provider must go to the consumer. Thus, an important feature of services is that they are provided via various modes of supply. Often services are tailored according to the client's needs and wishes and so tend not to be homogeneous or mass-produced. As such, services cover a heterogeneous range of products and activities that are difficult to encapsulate within a simple definition, while services may also be difficult to separate from the goods with which they may be associated or bundled. International organisations increasingly recognise that there is a need to explore means of gathering further information as to how services are provided, thus perhaps enabling, in the future, better policy-making internationally and, at the same time, offering complementary information for the purposes of bilateral or multilateral negotiations in trade in services; some first steps have already been undertaken in this direction. In parallel, some initiatives were initiated in order to provide answers to questions such as: who are the services traders, are service traders foreign-owned, and how many people do service traders employ? As such, a first set of experimental data on services trade by enterprise characteristics (STEC) have been collected. These try to measure international trade in services transactions by using data from different data sources. For example, this has been done by linking enterprise based data (from business registers) and data on services traders using a common identifier, namely the business register code. Data compilers involved in this experiment created a cross-classification in order to obtain new data which characterise the set of businesses involved in trade in services. Despite the fact that the level of international trade in services in the EU is equivalent to one-third of the equivalent level for goods, there are a number of reasons to believe that the share of services may grow in future years. Technological developments have increased the tradability of some services, for example by simplifying web-based services in services such as finance, education, health and government, among others. Furthermore, liberalisation efforts are likely to ease and therefore stimulate international trade in services. Globally, the inclusion of services in the Uruguay Round of trade negotiations led to the general agreement on trade in services (GATS) that entered into force in January 1995. The GATS aims to ensure increased transparency and predictability of relevant rules and regulations and to promote progressive liberalisation through successive rounds of negotiation. Within the EU, the objective of {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32006L0123:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2006/123/EC}} of 12 December 2006 on services in the internal market was to eliminate obstacles to trade in services. By doing so, the development of cross-border operations will be encouraged, making it easier for service businesses to set up or sell their services elsewhere in the EU. The Directive requires EU Member States to set up 'points of single contact' to assist business through the provision of information relating to offering services abroad. The Directive is intended to improve [[Glossary:Competitiveness|competitiveness]], not just of service enterprises but also of EU businesses as a whole, while providing greater choice and improved quality for consumers. At the end of May 2012, the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] confirmed that all EU Member States had officially transposed the Services Directive into national law. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Balance_of_payments|All articles on balance of payments]] *[[Balance of payments and international investment position manual (BPM6)]] *[[EU international trade in transport services]] *[[EU international trade in other business services]] *[[Measuring international trade in services - from BPM5 to BPM6]] *[[Services trade by enterprise characteristics - STEC]] *[[Services trade statistics by modes of supply]] *[[Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment]] - online publication ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det__custom_15159709/default/table?lang=en Balance of payments - international transactions (bop_6)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-services/database International trade in services, geographical breakdown (BPM6) (bop_its6)] ===Thematic section=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-trade-in-services/overview International trade in services — Overview] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Economic_globalisation_indicators Economic globalisation indicators] *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=balance_of_payments}} Balance of payments] ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=bop_6_esms|title=Balance of payments - international transactions}} (ESMS metadata file — bop_6_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=bop_its6_esms|title=International trade in services, geographical breakdown}} (ESMS metadata file — bop_its6_esms) ===External links=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/trade/ European Commission — Trade] *[http://www.imf.org/external/np/sta/itserv/methdev.htm International Monetary Fund (IMF) — International Trade in Services: Recent Methodological Developments] *[http://unstats.un.org/unsd/tradeserv/TFSITS/newsletter.htm Newsletter of the Interagency Task Force on Statistics of International Trade in Services] *[https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/services-trade.html OECD — Services trade] *[http://unstats.un.org/unsd/tradeserv/TFSITS/manual.htm United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) — Manual on Statistics of International Trade in Services 2010 (MSITS 2010)] {{Unit|topic=X_International_trade_services}} [[Category:International trade|International trade in services]] [[Category:International trade in services|International trade in services]] [[Category:Statistical article|International trade in services]] [[Category:December2026|International trade in services]]

title: International trade in services statistics by broad economic categories
text:
This article presents data on trade in services, broken down by broad economic categories Data extracted in May 2026 Planned article update: June 2027 In 2025, intermediate services—those used as inputs for other economic activities—accounted for 71% of the EU’s total exports and 82% of its imports. These shares highlight the EU’s deep integration into global value chains, reflecting its role both as a key supplier as well as a major destination for intermediate services. International trade in services is typically measured using the Extended Balance of Payments Services (EBOPS 2010) classification, which categorises services by type (e.g., transport, travel, or financial services). However, EBOPS does not distinguish how these services are used—whether as intermediate inputs for production, or final consumption. The [[Glossary:Broad_economic_categories_(BEC)|broad economic categories (BEC Rev.5) classification]] addresses this gap by organising services based on their economic purpose. This approach provides critical insights into: * The EU’s role in global value chains (GVCs), * Dependencies on intermediate services, and * Vulnerabilities in cross-border supply networks. By analysing trade through the BEC framework, policymakers can better assess: * Strategic dependencies (e.g., reliance on non-EU suppliers for critical services), * Resilience gaps, and * Policy responses (e.g., diversification, nearshoring, or stockpiling). This article presents updated EU data (2016–2025) on services trade by BEC, derived from the conversion of [[Glossary:International_trade_in_services_statistics_(ITSS)|international trade in services statistics]] (ITSS) from the EBOPS 2010 classification into the classification by Broad Economic Categories [https://unstats.un.org/unsd/trade/classifications/SeriesM_53_Rev.5_17-01722-E-Classification-by-Broad-Economic-Categories_PRINT.pdf (BEC Rev.5)]. The 2025 figures are preliminary and should be interpreted with caution. This article is a first step in the analysis of EU exports and imports of services by end-use. The data are still in an experimental phase, partly based on assumptions and estimates, as explained in the "Methodology" section. === General overview - Why broad economic categories matter for GVCs === International Trade in Services Statistics (ITSS) are typically reported using the EBOPS 2010 classification, which groups services by type rather than by their intended economic use (see also [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/BOP_ITS6_DET/default/table?lang=en Eurostat's online database]). This article uses the Broad Economic Categories (BEC) classification to provide a complementary perspective—focusing on the end use of services, specifically distinguishing between intermediate services (used as inputs in production) and final services (for end consumption). This distinction is crucial for analyzing Global Value Chains (GVCs), where intermediate services play a key role as production inputs. Driven by globalization, falling trade costs, and rapid technological advances, service and manufacturing processes have become increasingly fragmented into specialized stages. This allows firms to source intermediate inputs globally, enhancing efficiency, quality, and competitiveness. The analysis covers EU-level data from 2015 to 2024 and includes 2024 data for individual EU countries. Figures for 2024 are preliminary estimates based on annualized quarterly data. While only the 12 main EBOPS categories are available, Eurostat has estimated detailed subcategories using historical patterns. Due to the scope and nature of the data, the analysis remains descriptive, and conclusions should be interpreted cautiously, avoiding broad generalizations. ===Main conclusions=== * Intermediate services dominate EU extra-EU trade, accounting for 71% of exports and 82% of imports in 2025, reflecting their crucial role as inputs in global production networks. * Both intermediate and final services trade have grown steadily over the past decade, with a sharp pandemic-induced dip in 2020 followed by a strong recovery, especially in intermediate services. * The COVID-19 pandemic heavily impacted final services trade (travel, tourism), causing a sharper decline and slower recovery compared to intermediate services, which showed resilience. * The EU is a net exporter of final services but relies heavily on importing intermediate services, highlighting its role as a major consumer of foreign inputs for production. * Northern and Benelux EU countries specialize in intermediate services trade, while Southern and smaller countries tend to have lower shares, reflecting diverse economic structures. * Key sectors like ICT, business, financial services dominate intermediate trade, whereas Health and education services show higher import dependence, illustrating a complex and diversified EU service trade profile. === Trends in the EU trade in services by end-use === '''''Intermediate services dominate EU trade.''''' '''''In 2025, intermediate services made up 71% of total services extra-EU exports and 82% of total services extra-EU imports.''''' '''''ICT, media, computers, business and financial services being the largest intermediate service category in 2025.''''' == Key observations: == * Both intermediate and final services imports and exports have trended upward over the decade, signaling the EU’s increasing dependence on international services for both production inputs and final consumption. * The sustained growth in intermediate services underscores their growing strategic importance in the globalized economy and their critical role as inputs in complex production networks and in global production and supply chains. * Final services were more vulnerable to pandemic disruptions due to their reliance on consumer activities such as travel and tourism but have demonstrated steady recovery. The EU international trade in service flows demonstrate a steady growth in both exports and imports from 2016 to 2019, with exports rising from €877 billion to €1.1 trillion (a rise of above 25%) and imports from €803 billion to €1.0 trillion (an increase of above 30%). In 2020 followed a sharp decline due to the COVID-19 pandemic, with exports dropping by 13% and imports by 10% compared to 2019. A strong recovery is observed for the years after 2020, with exports reaching a provisional high of €1.58 trillion in 2025, 44% above 2019 levels and almost 80% above 2016 levels; imports also increased to €1.43 trillion, 36% higher than pre-pandemic and 78% above 2016 levels. Overall, the data highlight the EU’s increasing engagement in global services trade, with resilience and growth after pandemic disruptions. So, over the decade, exports grew by nearly 80% and imports by around 77%. [[Image:Extra-EU trade in services, 2016-2025_(€ million).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Extra-EU trade in services, 2016-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det])|alt= Combined vertical bar chart showing EU international trade in services with extra-EU partner in euro millions. The columns represent balance and two lines represent export and import over the years 2016 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] While Figure 1 shows the overall EU exports and imports of services, it does not specify their end use. This distinction is provided in Figure 2, which illustrates the evolution of EU exports and imports of both intermediate and final services over the period 2016 to 2025. [[Image:Extra-EU exports and imports of services by end use, 2016-2025_(€ million).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Extra-EU exports and imports of services by end use, 2016-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01__custom_16942921/default/table?lang=en ext_ser_bec01], and own calculations)|alt= Line chart showing EU intermediate and final services exports with extra-EU partner in euro millions. Four lines represent intermediate services exports, intermediate services imports, final services exports and final services imports over the years 2016 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The intermediate services exports grew steadily from €596 billion (2016) to €746 billion (2019), reflecting growing demand for services that support further production or processing abroad. Final services exports also rose from €247 billion (2016) to €310 billion (2019). There was a slight decline for the intermediate services in 2020 to about -1.3% compared to 2019, likely due to disruptions caused by COVID-19. However, this drop is relatively modest compared to final services, being severely impacted of the pandemic. In 2020, final services exports dropped sharply to around €203 billion, a decrease of approximately 35% compared to 2019 level. This sharp decline can be attributed to restrictions on travel, tourism, and other consumer-facing services. From 2021 onwards, intermediate services exports recovered strongly, reaching a provisional high of approximately €1.09 trillion in 2025, or 46% higher compared to pre-COVID 19 level and an overall increase of roughly 83% from 2016. This rebound highlights the resilience and critical role of intermediate services in global value chains. Final services exports started to recover in 2021 but remained below pre-pandemic levels. By 2022, exports exceeded the 2019 value. This positive trend continued, with provisional figures for 2025 indicating further growth to about €438 billion, reflecting a robust rebound in travel, tourism, and other final service categories. Between 2016 and 2019, imports of both intermediate and final services steadily increased, reflecting growing demand for foreign services in the EU. Intermediate services imports rose from €616 billion in 2016 to over €823 billion in 2019, showing robust growth driven by the expanding role of global value chains and cross-border outsourcing. Final services imports also grew steadily but at a lower scale, increasing from about €163 billion in 2016 to nearly €193 billion in 2019. The year 2020 marked a sharp decline in imports for both categories, largely due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Intermediate services imports decreased slightly from €823 billion to €813 billion, indicating some resilience in essential business services despite global disruptions. Final services imports were more severely impacted, dropping by nearly 37%, likely reflecting reduced travel, tourism, and other consumer-related services heavily affected by pandemic restrictions. Following 2020, imports recovered steadily. Intermediate services imports rebounded quickly, surpassing pre-pandemic levels by 2021 and reaching a peak of approximately €1.14 trillion in 2025, an overall increase of roughly 85% from 2016. This growth highlights the increasing integration of intermediate services in EU production processes and global supply chains. Final services imports showed a strong recovery but at a more moderate pace compared to intermediate services. From the pandemic low of €121 billion in 2020, imports rose steadily to around €250 billion in 2026, exceeding the 2019 pre-pandemic level by nearly 30%. This gradual rebound likely corresponds to the resumption of international travel, tourism, and other final services consumption. The analysis of services by end-use provides further insight into the effects of globalisation processes - for a more detailed discussion see the Context section. === EU trade exports and imports of services by end-use === '''''In 2025, intermediate services made up 71% of total services extra-EU exports and 82% of total services extra-EU imports.''''' == Key observations: == * Overall, the share of intermediate services exports remains consistently around 71-78%, indicating a stable and prominent role for intermediate services in the EU’s service export profile. Final services exports maintain a significant but smaller share, closely tied to consumer demand and sensitive to external shocks. * Despite fluctuations, intermediate services imports maintain a dominant share of around 80% in the long term, confirming their critical role in the EU’s service import structure. Final services imports remain a smaller but recovering component. From 2016 to 2025, the EU both imported and exported large volumes of intermediate services to/from non-EU countries (see Figures 3.a and 3.b), reflecting deep integration in global value chains (GVCs). Intermediate services consistently make up a larger share of total services trade, accounting for approximately 71-78% of exports and 78-87% of imports over the period. This reflects their fundamental role as production inputs within global value chains. Final services have a larger share in exports (22-29%) compared to imports (13-22%), driven by sectors like travel and tourism where the EU is a net service provider to non-EU countries. During the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2021), the share of final services dropped sharply in both exports and imports but more drastically in imports (from 19% to 13%) than exports (from 29% to 22%), reflecting severe disruptions in consumer-related imports such as travel services. By 2025, final services shares in both exports and imports are rebounding toward pre-pandemic levels, while intermediate services shares remain dominant but slightly reduced post-pandemic. The comparison between the share of intermediate and final services in EU trade highlights the EU’s dual role as a major exporter of consumer-oriented final services and a large importer of intermediate services essential for production. The pandemic amplified these dynamics, but both trade flows show resilient recovery. Figure 3.a. presents the evolution of exports of intermediate and final services from the EU to non-EU countries over a decade (2016 to 2025). [[Image:Extra-EU services exports by end use, 2016-2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3.a: Extra-EU services exports by end use, 2016-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01__custom_16942921/default/table?lang=en ext_ser_bec01], and own calculations)|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage EU exports with extra-EU partner over the years 2016 to 2025. Totalling 100 percent, each year's column has two stacks representing intermediate services and final services. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Throughout 2016-2025, intermediate services exports consistently accounted for about 71-78% of total Extra-EU services exports, underscoring their dominant role in the EU’s international services trade. In 2020 and 2021, the share of intermediate services exports increased sharply to around 78%, as final services exports were severely impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic (falling from 29% to 22%). This reflects the relative pandemic resilience of intermediate services compared to the consumer-focused final services. From 2022 onwards, final services exports recovered strongly, pushing their share back up to around 29% in 2025, while intermediate services’ share declined slightly but remained the majority, making up to 71% of total services.
Figure 3.b. presents the evolution of imports of intermediate and final services from the EU to non-EU countries over a decade (2016 to 2025). [[Image:Extra-EU services imports by end use, 2016-2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3.b: Extra-EU services imports by end use, 2016-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01__custom_16942921/default/table?lang=en ext_ser_bec01], and own calculations)|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage EU imports with extra-EU partner over the years 2016 to 2025. Totalling 100 percent, each year's column has two stacks representing intermediate services and final services. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Intermediate services imports consistently represent the majority share of extra-EU services imports, ranging from 78% in 2016 to a peak of 87% during the pandemic in 2020, highlighting their importance as inputs in EU production and supply chains. In 2025 intermediate services accounted for 82% of total imports. The final services imports share dropped significantly from around 19-22% pre-pandemic to a low of 13-14% in 2020-2021, reflecting steep declines in consumer-related service imports such as travel and tourism due to COVID-19 restrictions. From 2022 onwards, final services imports began recovering, with their share rising back to around 18% by 2025, indicating renewed demand for consumer services as restrictions eased.
=== EU trade in intermediate and final services by broad economic categories === '' '''In 2025, EU international services trade has a diversified and complex nature.''''' == Key observations: == * The EU’s service trade is heavily concentrated in ICT, media, business, and financial services, which dominate both intermediate and final consumption categories. * There is a close balance in intermediate services trade overall, reflecting the EU’s active participation in global value chains as both a buyer and seller of business inputs. * The EU is a net exporter of final services, particularly in ICT and transport-related services, indicating strong global competitiveness in consumer-facing service sectors. * Health, pharmaceuticals, and education-related services show higher intermediate imports than exports, suggesting dependency on foreign suppliers for these inputs. * The distribution of service trade by sector underlines the diversified and complex nature of EU international services trade in 2025. Figures 4.a-4.d present an analysis of EU intermediate and final services trade broken down by broad economic categories in 2025. In 2025, the largest intermediate trade category is ICT, media, computers, business, and financial services (€630 billion exports or 58% of total exports; €705 billion imports or almost 62% of total imports), representing over half of total intermediate trade. Transport equipment and related services follow, with exports (€228 billion or 21%) slightly exceeding imports (€213 billion or 19%). The third category is Health, pharmaceuticals, education, cultural and sport services and it shows higher imports (€124 billion; 11%) than exports (€99 billion; 9%), indicating EU reliance on these services. Other sectors like Agriculture, Mining, and Construction show moderate trade volumes in intermediate services. [[Image:Extra-EU intermediate services exports by BEC items, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4.a: Extra-EU intermediate services exports by BEC items, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01__custom_16942921/default/table?lang=en ext_ser_bec01], and own calculations)|alt= Pie chart showing percentage EU intermediate services by BEC items exports with extra-EU partner for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image: Extra-EU intermediate services imports by BEC items, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4.b: Extra-EU intermediate services imports by BEC items, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01__custom_16942921/default/table?lang=en ext_ser_bec01], and own calculations)|alt= Pie chart showing percentage EU intermediate services by BEC items imports with extra-EU partner for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
In 2025, the total final services exports (€438 billion) substantially exceed imports (€250 billion), showing the EU is a net exporter of final services. The largest final service export category is ICT, media, business and financial services (€208 billion), more than double corresponding imports (€92 billion). The sector contributes for 48% of the final services exports and 37% of the final services imports. Transport equipment, travel, and postal services also show strong net export positions (€104 billion exports or 24% of total exports vs €71 billion imports or 29% of total imports). Health, pharmaceuticals, education, cultural, and sport services again show more exports (€87 billion or 20% of total exports) than imports (€60 billion 24% of total imports). Other sectors contribute smaller shares to final services trade. [[Image:Extra-EU final services exports by BEC items, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4.c: Extra-EU final services exports by BEC items, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01__custom_16942921/default/table?lang=en ext_ser_bec01], and own calculations)|alt= Pie chart showing percentage EU final services by BEC items exports with extra-EU partner for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:Extra-EU final services imports by BEC items, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4.d: Extra-EU final services imports by BEC items, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01__custom_16942921/default/table?lang=en ext_ser_bec01], and own calculations)|alt= Pie chart showing percentage EU final services by BEC items imports with extra-EU partner for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Focus on country-level of intermediate services=== '''''EU countries having diverse economic structures and trade roles.''''' == Key observations == * Intermediate services form a crucial component of EU international trade (71% of exports and 81% of imports), underscoring the EU’s integration in global value chains and reflecting strong external dependence on intermediate services for production inputs. * Member States exhibit diverse patterns based on the structure of their economy: for example Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, Finland and Lithuania tend to specialize more in intermediate services exports (above 80%), while Malta, Spain, Portugal and Croatia have a comparatively lower focus on intermediate services (below 47% of exports). * The higher share of intermediate services in imports versus exports suggests the EU relies more on foreign intermediate inputs than it supplies abroad, reflecting its role as a major consumer within global production networks. * The countries' patterns in intermediate services highlight the diverse economic structures and trade roles across EU countries, with implications for policy on services trade and value chain integration. The EU average share of intermediate services is 72% for exports and 82% for imports, showing that intermediate services constitute a larger proportion of imports than exports in the EU’s external trade. Figures 5 and Figure 6 show the relative shares of intermediate services in the exports and imports of each EU countries in 2025, with partner Extra-EU. These results should be viewed with some caution, as Eurostat estimated the split of some EBOPS items to their constituents, for some EU countries. [[Image:Extra-EU exports of intermediate services by Member State, 2025 (share in total exports of services).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Extra-EU exports of intermediate services by Member State, 2025 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01__custom_16942921/default/table?lang=en ext_ser_bec01], and own calculations)|alt= Horizontal bar chart showing percentage exports of intermediate services in the EU and individual EU Member States for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:Extra-EU imports of intermediate services by Member State, 2025 (share in total imports of services).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Extra-EU imports of intermediate services by Member State, 2025 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01__custom_16942921/default/table?lang=en ext_ser_bec01], and own calculations)|alt= Horizontal bar chart showing percentage imports of intermediate services in the EU and individual EU Member States for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Northern and Benelux countries dominate intermediate services exports, with Denmark (89%), Netherlands (87%), Belgium (86%), Germany (83%) and Finland (82%) leading, reflecting strong specialization in intermediate service provision. In imports, Ireland (93%), Malta (89%), Denmark (87%), Netherlands and Belgium (each 86%), and Cyprus (85%) show the highest shares, highlighting a greater reliance on intermediate services as inputs for production. Croatia stands out with the lowest shares in both exports (31%) and imports (42%), indicating a different service trade profile focused less on intermediate services. === Data sources === Eurostat publishes detailed statistics on international trade in services, broken down by partner country/region and type of service. These data are compiled as part of the balance of payments (BoP) statistics, which record an economy’s transactions with the rest of the world. The compilation of BoP statistics follows the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) [https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/bop/2007/bopman6.htm sixth edition of the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (BPM6)]. The international Manual on Statistics of International Trade in Services (MSITS 2010) provides further information on the compilation of ITS statistics. The primary data source for this article is the Eurostat dataset (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/bop_its6_det/default/table?lang=en bop_its6_det], which provides detailed international trade in services statistics (ITSS) by service type and partner. Eurostat converts these data from EBOPS 2010 items to BEC Rev.5 codes using a fine-tuned correlation table that assigns modelled allocation shares to each service category. This table is available on the Eurostat website table published on Eurostat website and ensures consistent mapping between the two classifications. Missing items were estimated, and assumptions or modelling is used to derive the use type when information is not available. Eurostat disseminates data trade statistics by broad economic categories Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ext_ser_bec01/default/table?lang=en&category=ext_ser ext_ser_bec01]). === Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=International_trade_in_services_by_broad_economic_categories_2025.xlsx|title=BEC services 2025}} === Context === Measuring intermediate and final services; and the use of BEC Rev.5 classification The classification by Broad Economic Categories [https://unstats.un.org/unsd/trade/classifications/SeriesM_53_Rev.5_17-01722-E-Classification-by-Broad-Economic-Categories_PRINT.pdf (BEC Rev.5)] is an international product classification, mainly designed to provide a set of broad product categories for analysing trade statistics. BEC is a high-level aggregation of existing detailed product classifications, such as the Standard International Trade Classification (SITC), the Harmonised Commodity and Coding System (HS) and the Central Product Classification (CPC). For international trade in goods a classification distinguishing intermediate, final consumption and capital goods already existed. The new BEC Rev. 5 classification improves on this classification and for the first time extends the classification to include also services. This allows the distinction in intermediate services and final consumption services. Table 1 shows the end-use categories of goods and services in BEC Rev. 5. [[Image:T1Goods and services categories.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: Goods and services categories
''Source:'' [https://unstats.un.org/unsd/trade/classifications/Manual%20of%20the%20Fifth%20Revision%20of%20the%20BEC%20(Unedited).pdf Eurostat and UNSD, BEC Rev. 5]|alt= Table showing goods and services belonging to categories. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The main analytical use of the BEC classification is to understand the predominant use of goods and services: either final use (final consumption), or as inputs to other economic activities (intermediate consumption). Figure 7 gives an overview of the structure of BEC Rev.5. [[Image:Structure of the BEC Rev5 classification.PNG |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Structure of the BEC Rev.5 classification
''Source:'' [https://unstats.un.org/unsd/trade/classifications/SeriesM_53_Rev.5_17-01722-E-Classification-by-Broad-Economic-Categories_PRINT.pdf UNSD, BEC Rev.5]|alt= Process flow chart showing structure of the Broad Economic Categories Rev.5 classification. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 8 shows the service flows (e.g. intermediate or final consumption) in the context of the broad economic categories discussion. [[Image:Services Flows.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Services Flows
''Source:''[https://unstats.un.org/unsd/trade/classifications/Manual%20of%20the%20Fifth%20Revision%20of%20the%20BEC%20(Unedited).pdf Eurostat and UNSD, BEC Rev. 5] |alt= Flow chart showing service flows. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] A [https://unstats.un.org/unsd/trade/classifications/bec.asp#background correlation table] between EBOPS 2010, CPC and BEC Rev.5 was also developed to accompany the BEC Rev.5 documentation. Based on this correlation table, Eurostat calculated the distribution of the EBOPS items to the relevant BEC Rev.5 categories, where an EBOPS item corresponds to two or more BEC categories (and in particular for cases when a single EBOPS item corresponds to categories of intermediate as well as final use). Using this fine-tuned correlation table, Eurostat mapped the EU services by EBOPS to BEC categories, and calculated the final and intermediate consumption services trade. Globalisation and services Globalisation has transformed the way products and services are produced, traded, and delivered across borders. To remain competitive, producers increasingly move away from traditional vertically integrated models toward more fragmented production structures. This fragmentation—also known as the international division of labour—breaks down the production process into specific tasks or stages, many of which are outsourced or offshored to other countries. This shift has been enabled by several key developments: the lowering of trade barriers, organisational innovations, and major advances in information and communication technologies (ICT). These changes have significantly reduced coordination and transaction costs, making it easier and cheaper for firms to operate production networks that span multiple countries. In particular, high labour costs and regulatory constraints in advanced economies have accelerated the relocation of many production activities to emerging and developing economies.Source: UNECE Guide to measuring global production - see: https://www.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/stats/documents/ece/ces/bur/2014/Guide_to_Measuring_Global_Production_-_CES.pdf. As a result, goods and services exported from one country are often the product of inputs—especially intermediate services and goods—sourced from several other countries. Therefore, the value and characteristics of a country’s exports increasingly reflect a complex web of international production linkages, not just the capabilities of the final exporter. This interconnected system is known as a global value chain (GVC). GVCs encompass all stages of cross-border production and service delivery—from initial design and input sourcing, through processing and assembly, to marketing and final consumption. In this context, the distinction between trade in intermediate and final services becomes crucial. Intermediate services—such as IT, financial, logistics, and professional services—play a vital role as inputs in other production processes. By definition, all trade in intermediate services occurs within GVCs, as both the supplier and recipient are engaged in cross-border production networks. Understanding the flow of these services is therefore essential to fully grasp the nature of global trade in the modern economy. ===Methodology=== === Methodology=== '''1. Input''' The conversion from EBOPS 2010 items to BEC Rev.5 categories was made using the fine-tuned [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/c1b49c83-24a7-4ff2-951c-621ac0a89fd8/library/5f521524-427e-402d-bbbc-3d08d14e7c80/details correlation table], published on Eurostat web site with the modelled allocation shares. This table is based on a correspondence table between the Classification by Broad Economic Categories revision 5 (BEC Rev. 5), the Central Product Classification, version 2.1 (CPC 2.1) and the Extended Balance of Payments Services Classification, version 2010 (EBOPS 2010), published by the UNSD. The fine-tuned table builds upon the [https://unstats.un.org/unsd/trade/classifications/bec.asp EBOPS-CPC-BEC conversion table] and provides modelled allocation shares of the EBOPS items to the relevant BEC Rev.5 categories (the estimations are evidence based and applicable for the EU). More specifically, in the cases where a single EBOPS item corresponds to more than one BEC codes, Eurostat used additional information and modelling techniques to split the EBOPS code among the respective BEC categories.
