title: Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - statistics on taxation
text:
Experimental results are presented on the joint distribution of income, consumption and wealth. Data extracted in February 2026 Planned article update: March 2028
EXPERIMENTAL
 In around 2020, the median [[Glossary:Value_added_tax_(VAT)|value added tax (VAT)]] paid by households as a share of their [[Glossary:Gross_income|gross income]] varied a lot across EU countries, ranging between 4.9% for Poland and 18.6% for Hungary (Map 1). [[Image:ICW_SEtax_Map1_2020_Median-VAT-out-of-gross-income.png|Map 1: Median amount of VAT paid by households as a share of their gross income (%), around 2020.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/icw_tax_01/default/table?lang=en icw_tax_01])|thumb|center|700px|alt= a map showing the median amount of VAT paid by households as a share of their gross income (%), around 2020 in the EU Member States. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article elaborates further on the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics experimental statistics] on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-consumption-wealth income, consumption and wealth] presenting 3 waves with reference years 'around 2010', 'around 2015' and 'around 2020' Exact reference years of ICW data are reported here: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:Table1_HBS-HFCS_reference_years.png Table HBS-HFCS reference years].. It is based on data resulting from the statistical matching of household surveys on income and consumption expenditure described in [[Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - methodology]]. The joint income and consumption dataset enables us to observe simultaneously how much money households receive and how much they spend in a certain year. By combining these 2 economic dimensions with data on taxes paid by households on their income and expenditures, one can assess the impact of direct and VAT taxation on different groups of households, particularly on different income groups. === VAT as a share of gross income === Differentiating this picture by looking at different income groups (Figure 1), where the quintiles are based on household [[Glossary:Disposable_income|disposable income]], shows large variation not only across countries, but even more so across different income groups within countries. For all countries, the median share of gross income used to pay VAT decreases from the higher- to the lower-income groups. The variation across the income distribution may be wider in some countries than in others. However, in 11 out of 25 countries, half of the households in the 1st income quintile pay more than 12% of their gross income on VAT, while in the vast majority of countries half of the households in the top disposable income quintile pay no more than 9% of household gross income on VAT. The most extreme case is Hungary where the median VAT paid ranges from 36.3% to 12.3%, respectively. [[Image:F1_Median_VAT_paid_by_households_as_a_percentage_of_their_gross_income_by_income_quintile,_around_2020_(%).png |Figure 1: Median VAT paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by income quintile, around 2020.
Countries ordered by the median VAT paid out of gross income for the total population.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/icw_tax_03/default/table?lang=en icw_tax_03])|thumb|center|700px|alt=a vertical bar chart showing the median VAT paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by income quintile, around 2020 in the EU Member States. The bars show the first to fifth quintile. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] VAT as a share of gross income (Figure 2) exhibited, in general, a high variability across household types. In most countries, single-person households turned out to be more heavily taxed in proportion to their income than the other household types. The relatively low incomes in such households normally result in a higher share of income spent on consumption, and therefore on VAT. [[Image:F2_Median_VAT_paid_by_households_as_a_percentage_of_their_gross_income_by_household_type,_around_2020_(%).png |Figure 2: Median VAT paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by household type, around 2020.
Countries ordered by the median VAT paid out of gross income for the total population.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/icw_tax_02/default/table?lang=en icw_tax_02])|thumb|center|700px|alt= a vertical bar chart with six bars showing the median VAT paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by household type around 2020 in the EU Member States. The bars show, one adult, three adults and more two adults with dependent children, two adults, one adult with dependent children three adults and more with dependent children. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 3 shows that the VAT paid as a share of income can be linked to the life cycle. In many EU countries, households whose reference person is under 30 years faced a high median VAT rate as a share of their income, which sometimes was even the highest across age classes, like in Malta, Spain, Cyprus, Greece and Slovakia. This level generally decreases with age, and in most cases increases again for the higher-age groups. The pattern seems to be driven by the change in income over the life cycle as households with the reference person at a lower or higher age tend to have higher marginal propensity to consume. [[Image:F3_Median_VAT_paid_by_households_as_a_percentage_of_their_gross_income_by_age_of_the_reference_person,_around_2020_(%).png |Figure 3: Median VAT paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by age of the reference person, around 2020.
Countries ordered by the median VAT paid out of gross income for the total population.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/icw_tax_01/default/table?lang=en icw_tax_01])|thumb|center|700px|alt= a vertical bar chart with six bars showing the median VAT paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by age of the reference person, around 2020 in the EU Member States. The bars show the ages, less than 30, between 30 and 44 between 45 and 54, between 55 and 64, between 65 and 74 and 75 and more. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Direct taxation === To analyse the overall tax burden on households in the EU and compare it across different household groups, it is necessary to consider the different fiscal policies, not only those on VAT, but also on direct taxation. In this article, direct taxation refers to taxes on income as well as [[Glossary:Social_contributions|social contributions]], as defined in the EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC). In addition, they also include regular taxes on wealth, i.e. taxes that are payable on a periodic basis on the ownership of property assets, taxes on wealth as a whole, net of indebtedness, or any tax on valuables. The median direct tax paid as a share of gross income varies widely across EU countries, ranging from 7.7% in Estonia to over 30% in Greece and Denmark in the period around 2020 (Map 2). More importantly, in a social context, the overall median tax rate, is the way in which national tax systems spread the burden and thereby partly mitigate the large differences in gross income between low- and high-income groups. [[Image:ICW_SEtax_Map2_2020_Median-direct-taxation-out-of-gross-income.png|Map 2: Median amount of direct taxes paid by households as a share of their gross income (%), around 2020.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/icw_tax_04/default/table?lang=en icw_tax_04])|thumb|center|700px|alt= a map showing the median amount of direct taxes paid by households as a share of their gross income (%), around 2020 in the EU Member States. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Most EU countries apply a progressive system of direct taxation, which means that the share of gross income spent for paying direct taxes increases as income grows (Figure 4). [[Image:Figure_4_Median_amount_of_direct_taxes_paid_by_households_as_a_percentage_of_their_gross_income_by_income_quintile,_around_2020_(%).png|Figure 4: Median amount of direct taxes paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by income quintile, around 2020.
Countries ordered by the median direct taxes paid out of gross income for the total population.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/icw_tax_06/default/table?lang=en icw_tax_06])|thumb|center|700px|alt=a vertical bar chart showing the median amount of direct taxes paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by income quintile, around 2020 in the EU Member States. The bars show the first to fifth quintile. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Direct and VAT taxation as a share of gross income === Figure 5 shows the spread of the tax burden (VAT and direct taxes combined) over different income groups for the period around 2020. In most countries, the regressive pattern observed for VAT paid as a share of gross income was largely mitigated by direct taxes that are normally designed to shift the fiscal burden towards the top of the income (and possibly wealth) distribution. [[Image:F5 Median amount of direct taxes plus VAT paid by households as a perc of their gross income by income quintile, 2020 (%).png|Figure 5: Median amount of direct taxes plus VAT paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by income quintile, around 2020.
Countries ordered by the median taxes paid out of gross income for the total population.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/icw_tax_09/default/table?lang=en icw_tax_09])|thumb|center|700px|alt=a vertical bar chart showing the median amount of direct taxes plus VAT paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by income quintile, around 2020 in the EU Member States. The bars show the first to fifth quintile. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 6 shows that there was no clear pattern for the incidence of VAT and direct taxation across household types in the period around 2020. In some countries the tax burden seemed to increase in relation to household size, while in others it was similar across the different household types. [[Image:F6 Median amount of direct taxes plus VAT paid by hh as a percentage of their gross income by household type, around 2020 (%).png|Figure 6: Median amount of direct taxes plus VAT paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by household type, around 2020.
Countries ordered by the median taxes paid out of gross income for the total population.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/icw_tax_08/default/table?lang=en icw_tax_08])|thumb|center|700px|alt= a vertical bar chart with six bars showing the median amount of direct taxes plus VAT paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by household type, around 2020 in the EU Member States. The bars show, one adult, three adults and more two adults with dependent children, two adults, one adult with dependent children three adults and more with dependent children. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Opposite to the VAT paid by households across the life cycle (Figure 3), a higher share of income spent on both direct taxes and VAT is observed for those groups whose reference person is aged between 30 and 65 years, in the period around 2020 (Figure 7). Noticeably, households whose reference person is 65 years and over, paid the lowest taxes in relation to their gross income, which is mainly driven by the drop in direct taxation for this age group. [[Image:F7 Median amount of direct taxes plus VAT paid by hh as a percentage of their gross income by age, around 2020 (%).png|Figure 7: Median amount of direct taxes plus VAT paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by age of the reference person, around 2020.
Countries ordered by the median taxes paid out of gross income for the total population.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/icw_tax_07/default/table?lang=en icw_tax_07])|thumb|center|700px|alt= a vertical bar chart with six bars showing the median amount of direct taxes plus VAT paid by households as a percentage of their gross income by age of the reference person, around 2020 in the EU Member States. The bars show the ages, less than 30, between 30 and 44 between 45 and 54, between 55 and 64, between 65 and 74 and 75 and more. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === VAT taxation as a share of expenditure === Figure 8 presents the share of VAT in the overall expenditure on consumption and how it related to disposable income levels in the period around 2020. Due to reduced VAT rates on food and some other essential products, and because low-income households spend more on such essential items than on other items compared with high-income households, the average rate of VAT on expenditure is generally lower for low-income households than for high-income households. In some countries (Denmark, Germany, Croatia, Latvia, Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Slovenia and Finland), the more income households earned, the more VAT they paid on their expenditure. This pattern may have been a result of using reduced or zero rates targeted at lower income groups in the national VAT policies. In the other countries this effect is rather limited, with households of all income levels paying a similar share of VAT on their expenditure. [[Image:Figure_8_Share_of_VAT_in_the_overall_consumption_expenditure_of_households_by_income_quintile,_around_2020_(%).png |Figure 8: Share of VAT in the overall consumption expenditure of households by income quintile, around 2020.
''Source:'' Eurostat (experimental statistics: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/icw_res_02/default/table?lang=en icw_res_02], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/icw_tax_10/default/table?lang=en icw_tax_10]), (Household Budget Survey: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hbs_str_t211/default/table?lang=en hbs_str_t211]) |thumb|center|700px|alt= a vertical bar chart showing the share of VAT in the overall consumption expenditure of households by income quintile, around 2020 in the EU Member States. The bars show the first to fifth quintile. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Limitations === The observations in this article are subject to some uncertainty. While the direct taxes are covered quite comprehensively with income and wealth taxes and social contributions, there are still some taxes such as local taxes that are not included in the analysis. Likewise, indirect taxes in this article are only represented by VAT and no other excise taxes. In addition, the automatised application of VAT rates on the [[Glossary:Classification_of_individual_consumption_by_purpose_(COICOP)|Classification of individual consumption by purpose (COICOP)]] items has limitations where national rules are very specific for certain items. This is even more relevant for the 2020 wave, where an extremely specific exemption was applied during the COVID-19 pandemic years on a country-by-country basis. Furthermore, the estimates presented here are based on the statistical matching of data from 2 different surveys and their quality may vary across countries, as do the exact reference years. ===Feedback=== To help Eurostat improve these experimental statistics, please send us your [mailto:ESTAT-ICW@ec.europa.eu?subject=Feedback_on_experimental_statistics feedback by email]. === Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=DataFiguresSE3_icw_taxation_2020wave_v3_2026.xlsx|title=Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth – statistics on taxation - Graphs and tables}} [https://github.com/eurostat/statistics-coded/blob/master/popul/living-conditions/income-consumption-wealth_r/icw3.R Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth – statistics on taxation - Link to the scripts generating the figures] === Data sources=== The income data for the joint dataset used in this article comes from the [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]], governed by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R1700:EN:NOT|title=Regulation 1700/2019}} (more information on the legal framework can be found in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/legislation legislation] part of the thematic section on income and living conditions statistics on Eurostat's web page). The consumption expenditure data are from the [[Glossary:Household_budget_survey_(HBS)|Household Budget Survey (HBS)]]. Information on assets and liabilities is from the [https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/economic-research/research-networks/html/researcher_hfcn.en.html Household Finance and Consumption Survey (HFCS)]. The HFCS is run by national central banks and coordinated by the European Central Bank. The EU-SILC, HBS and HFCS data are matched according to the year of reference for HBS in order to obtain a fused dataset containing household-level information on both income and consumption. For more details on the statistical matching and the methodology used in the data, see the Statistics Explained article [[Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - methodology]]. '''Gross income''' is collected as variable HY010 in the EU-SILC and comprises the sum of gross personal income components for all household members (wages, self-employment income, pensions and benefits) plus gross income components at household level. '''Disposable income''' is collected as variable HY020 in the EU-SILC and comprises the total amount of money households have available for spending and saving after subtracting income taxes and pension contributions. '''Consumption''' is described according to the [[Glossary:Classification_of_individual_consumption_by_purpose_(COICOP)|Classification of individual consumption by purpose (COICOP)]] for each household. Total consumption is obtained by adding up all COICOP items. '''Direct taxation''' is estimated through variables collected in EU-SILC: HY120 'regular tax on wealth' and HY140 'Tax on income and social contributions'. Regular taxes on wealth refers to taxes that are payable on a regular basis on the ownership or use of land/buildings by their owners. It also includes taxes on net wealth or on valuables. HY140 includes taxes on income, profits and capital gains, as well as social insurance contributions paid by employees, self-employed individuals and if applicable unemployed and retired individuals. The figures on direct taxation as a share of gross income are obtained by dividing the sum of HY120 and HY140 by HY010. '''VAT''' is a tax paid by consumers on top of what they spend for consumption. Even if VAT collection may involve many parts of the economy (generally firms, or any seller of goods or services, are taxed), the households that consume in the country are those that end up paying the tax. Also, within the EU, it does not matter whether or not a household lives in the country where it consumes. VAT applies to goods and services sold in the EU, including between EU countries; goods and services sold outside the EU are not subject to VAT. In the EU, all countries have a 'multi-rate' system, with a 'standard' rate as a general rule and reduced/super-reduced/zero rates as exceptions for specific goods and services. Under European tax rules, the standard rate should not be below 15%, while the reduced rates (1 or 2 reduced rates may apply to a specific list of goods and services defined by the rules) should not be below 5%. For more information, see the [https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/taxation/vat_en Commission's documentation on VAT]. In this article, the '''VAT''' paid by households is calculated by applying the [https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/taxation/vat/vat-directive/vat-rates_en rates obtained from the European Commission's Directorate-General for Taxation and Customs Union] to data obtained through multiplying the average household consumption ({{Template:Publication|code=icw_res_02|title=icw_res_02}}) and the consumption structure of households ({{Template:Publication|code=hbs_str_t211|title=hbs_str_t211}}). This means a VAT rate is applied to every COICOP item. This makes it possible to compute the VAT that is paid by each household, assuming that every expense reported by the household occurred on the national territory and that none of the reported expenses occurred in the black economy. For each country the VAT rates of the most recent year <= 2020 are used. Then, depending on whether the VAT is paid as a share of total expenditure or as a share of gross income, this rate is divided by the total consumption expenditure or gross income, respectively, in the income-consumption matched dataset with HBS and EU-SILC income for the reference year 'around 2020'. Then, the median of those shares is presented according to the different household breakdowns. === Other articles === *[[Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - main indicators]] *[[Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - methodology]] *[[Living conditions in Europe - income distribution and income inequality ]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-consumption-wealth Income, consumption and wealth - experimental statistics], see: :Household economic resources (icw_res) :Saving rates (icw_sr) :Poverty (icw_pov) :Taxation (icw_tax) ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics Experimental statistics] === Publications === '''Others''' *De Agostini P., Capéau B., Decoster A., Figari F., Kneeshaw J., Leventi C., Manios K., Paulus A., Sutherland H., Vanheukelom T., [https://www.microsimulation.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/publications/emtn-3.0.pdf Euromod Extension to Indirect Taxation: Final Report], Euromod Technical Note Series, 2017. *OECD/KIPF, [http://dx.doi.org/10.1787/9789264224520-en The Distributional Effects of Consumption Taxes in OECD Countries], OECD Publishing, 2014. === Legislation === *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32006L0112:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 112/2006}} of 28 November 2006 on the common system of value added tax *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/LSU/?uri=CELEX:32006L0112 Summaries of EU Legislation: The EU's common system of value added tax (VAT)] === Footnotes === ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Article_name'' {{Unit|topic=X_Social_statistics}} [[Category:Household_income,_expenditure_and_debt|Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - statistics on taxation]] [[Category:Living_conditions|Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - statistics on taxation]] [[Category:Statistical_article|Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - statistics on taxation]] [[Category:Experimental statistics|Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - statistics on taxation]] [[Category:March2028|Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - statistics on taxation]]

title: Job vacancy statistics
text:
EU statistics are provided on job vacancy. Data extracted in June 2026 Planned article update: 15 September 2026 2.3% of jobs in the euro area and 2.1% of jobs in the EU were vacant in Q1 2026. With 4.0%, the Netherlands had the highest job vacancy rate in the EU in Q1 2026. |alt= Interactive line chart showing quarterly job vacancy rates, not seasonally adjusted in percentages. Two lines represent the EU and the Euro Area for quarter one of 2014 through to quarter one of 2026. This article gives an overview of recent quarterly and annual job vacancy statistics, notably the [[Glossary:Job_vacancy_rate_(JVR)|job vacancy rate (JVR)]] in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU) ]], Iceland, Norway and Switzerland. EU policies in the area of job vacancies aim to improve the functioning of the [[Glossary:Labour_market|labour market]] by trying to help match supply and demand more closely. The [https://eures.europa.eu/index_en European Jobs and Mobility Portal (EURES)] was set up in order to enable job seekers to consult all vacancies publicised by the employment services of each EU country. ===Job vacancies: latest developments=== The job vacancy rate (not seasonally adjusted) in the [[Glossary:Euro_area|euro area]]Euro area (EA) - Up to 31 December 2025, the euro area included Belgium, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Croatia, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, Portugal, Slovenia, Slovakia and Finland (EA20). From 1 January 2026, the euro area also includes Bulgaria (EA21). The aggregate data series commented on in this article refer to the official composition of the euro area in the most recent quarter for which data are available, hence EA21. was 2.3% in Q1 2026, up from 2.2% in Q4 2025 and down from 2.4% in Q1 2025. In the [[Glossary:EU_enlargements|EU]], the job vacancy rate was 2.1% in Q1 2026, unchanged from Q4 2025 and down from 2.2% in Q1 2025, as shown in Table 1. [[Image:Quarterly job vacancy rates not seasonally adjusted,Q1 2025 - Q1 2026 V1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Quarterly job vacancy rates not seasonally adjusted, Q1 2025 - Q1 2026
''Source:''Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fffeddf2-4505-4b04-8886-01657b84f4bb?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-16T05:12:13Z (jvs_q_r21)]|alt= Table showing quarterly job vacancy rates not seasonally adjusted for the EU, Euro area, individual EU countries and some EFTA countries in percentages for the first quarter of 2025 through to the first quarter of 2026. The last column shows the changes between quarter one of 2026 and quarter four of 2025 in percentage points. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among EU countries for which comparable data are available (see [[#Data_sources|''Data sources'']] for information concerning coverage), the highest job vacancy rates in Q1 2026 were recorded in the Netherlands (4.0%) and in Belgium (3.4%), followed by Malta (3.3%) and Austria (3.1%). The lowest rates were observed in Romania (0.6%) and Poland (0.8%) followed by Bulgaria, Spain and Slovakia (all 0.9%). [[Image:Figure 1 Job vacancy rates not seasonally adjusted Q1 2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Job vacancy rates not seasonally adjusted, Q1 2026
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2253b612-aec6-4728-98df-96a14f47853c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-16T05:19:55Z (jvs_q_r21)]|alt= Vertical bar chart showing job vacancy rates not seasonally adjusted for the EU, Euro area, individual EU countries and some EFTA countries in percentages for the third quarter of 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Compared with the same quarter of the previous year, the job vacancy rate increased in 3 EU countries, remained stable in 8 EU countries and decreased in 16 EU countries. The largest increases were observed in Malta (+0.4 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]]), Portugal and Slovenia (both +0.2 pp). Except for Czechia, impacted by a methodological break in the first quarter of 2025, the largest decreases were recorded in Belgium (-0.7 pp), Austria (-0.5 pp), Denmark and Italy (both -0.4 pp) and France (-0.3 pp). Figure 2 presents information for annual job vacancy rates in 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025. In the euro area and the EU, job vacancy rates slightly declined in 2023, sizeably more in 2024 and 2025. [[Image:Job_vacancy_rates,_2022,_2023,_2024,_and_2025_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Job vacancy rates, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/jvs_a_rate_r2__custom_20580135/default/table (jvs_a_rate_r2)]|alt= Scatter chart showing job vacancy rates in percentages. Four different scatter marks represent the percentages in a linear form for each of the EU, Euro area, individual EU countries and some EFTA countries for the years 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Job vacancies: a backwards glance=== In the euro area, the job vacancy rate declined at the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic (-0.5 pp in 2020), before rebounding in 2021 and 2022 (+0.7 pp in both years; see Figure 3). It diminished in 2023 (-0.2 pp) and then further decreased in 2024 (-0.4 pp) and 2025 (-0.3 pp). A similar pattern was observed in the EU. The pandemic led to a decline in the job vacancy rate in 2020 (-0.5 pp), followed by a strong recovery in 2021 and 2022 (+0.6 pp in both years). From 2023 onwards, the rate decreased again, by -0.2 pp in 2023, -0.4 pp in 2024, and -0.3 pp in 2025. [[Image:Annual change in job vacancy rates, 2011 2025 (percentage points).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Annual change in job vacancy rates, 2011-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/jvs_a_rate_r2__custom_20580179/default/table (jvs_a_rate_r2])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the annual change in job vacancy rates in percentage points. Two adjoining vertical columns represent the EU and Euro area for each of the years 2011 through to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 4 presents the development of the seasonally adjusted quarterly job vacancy rates in the euro area and in the EU between 2011 and 2026 (Q1 2026). [[Image:Figure_4_Quarterly_job_vacancy_rates_seasonally_adjusted_Q1_2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4 Quarterly job vacancy rates seasonally adjusted 2011-2026 (Q1 2026)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/jvs_q_nace2__custom_20580214/default/table (jvs_q_nace2)]|alt= Line chart showing quarterly job vacancy rates, seasonally adjusted in percentages. Two lines represent the EU and the Euro area for quarter one of 2011 to quarter one of 2026. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Job vacancies: a breakdown by economic activity=== Figure 5 presents the job vacancy rates of the euro area and the EU by economic activity, in Q1 2026. Data are displayed from section B to section N of the NACE Rev. 2.1 classification, for which data are available from all EU countries. The highest job vacancy rates, for the EU and the euro area, respectively, were recorded in * Section O: ‘Administrative and support service activities’ that includes temporary employment agencies (3.2% in the euro area, 3.1% in the EU), * Section I: 'Accomodation and food service activities' (3.2% in the euro area, 3.0% in the EU), * Section F: ‘Construction’ (3.1% in the euro area, 2.8% in the EU), * Section K: ‘Telecommunication, computer programming, consulting, computing infrastructure and other information service activities’ (2.8% in the euro area, 2.6% in the EU), and * Section N: ‘Professional, scientific and technical activities’ (2.5% in the euro area, 2.4% in the EU). [[Image:Job vacancy rate by NACE section Q1 2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Job vacancy rate by NACE section, euro area and EU, Q1 2026
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/jvs_q_r21__custom_21845141/default/table (jvs_q_nace2.1)]|alt= Bar chart showing the job vacancy rate by NACE section, for the euro area and the EU, first quarter of 2026. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Job vacancy rate by occupation and NUTS 1 region – experimental statistics=== Labour shortages are among the main challenges faced by the EU industry: ''‘Europe is close to full employment. Instead of millions of people looking for jobs, millions of jobs are looking for people. Labour and skills shortages are reaching record levels – both here and across all major economies. It is also one of the most significant bottlenecks for our competitiveness ([https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/SPEECH_23_4426 State of the Union 2023])’.'' It is therefore important to provide policy makers and social partners, at national and European levels, with adequate data on the demand side of the labour market. This data need is only partly met with the existing job vacancy statistics that are not available by occupation and region although this would be necessary for a detailed assessment of recruitment bottlenecks. Indeed, collecting these additional breakdowns from statistical surveys would sizably increase the cost and burden for respondents. Eurostat used instead data on online job advertisements (‘OJA’), from Eurostat’s Web Intelligence Hub, and EU-LFS data on the number of employees (‘SAL’), to break down the total number of job vacancies and occupied posts, respectively, by occupation and region. The job vacancy rate is then derived, at the three digits level of the classification of occupations (ISCO) and by NUTS 1 region and disseminated as “experimental statistics”. For detailed information on its calculation, please refer to our [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/7894008/22626615/methodological-note.pdf/0a21a711-f046-ed22-6417-c3d886a9ca82?t=1764345096884 methodological note]. [[Image:Top 10 occupations with the highest job vacancy rate in the EU in 2024 Experimental statistics, (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Top 10 occupations with the highest job vacancy rate in the EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0d898fb1-485d-4398-a8d9-a0ecbd9a88b2?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-12T12:20:40Z (jvs_a_isco3_r1)]|alt= a horizontal bar chart showing the top 10 occupations with the highest job vacancy rate in the EU in 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In the EU, in 2024, 'Sales, marketing, and development managers' recorded the highest job vacancy rate (8.4%), ahead of 'Manufacturing labourers' and 'Other clerical support workers' (both 7.3%). 'Other sales workers' (6.1%) and 'Artistic, cultural and culinary associate professionals' (6.0%) complete the top 5 occupations with the highest job vacancy rates (see Figure 6). Some occupations such as healthcare workers and teachers are not shown on the chart although they may also face recruitment difficulties. This could be because these positions are often not advertised on the web. In particular, the following ISCO positions have been excluded from the dataset due to their under-representation in OJA data: 'OC234 Primary School and Early Childhood Teachers', 'OC233 Secondary Education Teachers', 'OC541 Protective Services Workers', 'OC335 Government Regulatory Associate Professionals', 'OC411 General Office Clerks', 'OC521 Street and Market Salespersons', 'OC711 Building Frame and Related Trades Workers', 'OC412 Secretaries (general)', 'OC322 Nursing and Midwifery Associate Professionals', 'OC921 Agricultural, Forestry and Fishery Labourers'. On the contrary, IT related occupations may be over-represented in OJA data. In addition, ISCOs representing less than 0,1% of the total number of employees were excluded, namely 'OC131 Production Managers in Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries', 'OC223 Traditional and Complementary Medicine Professionals', 'OC224 Paramedical Practitioners', 'OC225 Veterinarians', 'OC323 Traditional and Complementary Medicine Associate Professionals', 'OC324 Veterinary Technicians and Assistants', 'OC613 Mixed Crop and Animal Producers', 'OC621 Forestry and Related Workers', 'OC622 Fishery Workers, Hunters and Trappers', 'OC631 Subsistence Crop Farmers', 'OC632 Subsistence Livestock Farmers', 'OC633 Subsistence Mixed Crop and Livestock Farmers', 'OC634 Subsistence Fishers, Hunters, Trappers and Gatherers', 'OC835 Ships' Deck Crews and Related Workers', 'OC951 Street and Related Service Workers' and 'OC952 Street Vendors (excluding Food)'. Figure 7 displays the most demanded skills in the EU (in native language) in 2024. [[Image:Wordcloud 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Most frequently sought skills in online job advertisements in the EU in 2024
''Source: Eurostat Web Intelligence Hub''|alt= a word cloud showing the most frequent occupations sought in online job advertisements.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Job_vacancy_statistics_2026Q1_update_16_June_2026.xlsx|title=Job vacancy statistics: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publishes quarterly and annual data on the number of [[Glossary:Job_vacancy_rate_(JVR)|job vacancies]] and the number of [[Glossary:Occupied_post|occupied posts]]. This information is collected on a quarterly basis from the national statistical authorities under the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32008R0453 Regulation on quarterly statistics on Community job vacancies]. The data may be analysed by [[Glossary:NACE|economic activity]] at the [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE]] section level and by [[Glossary:Enterprise_size|size of enterprise]], while data are collected on a voluntary basis by [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_occupations_(ISCO)|occupation]] or by [[Glossary:Nomenclature_of_territorial_units_for_statistics_(NUTS)|region]]. Annual data for the job vacancy rate are unadjusted information calculated directly from the quarterly data. Some of the data provided by the EU countries fail to match common criteria and there may be differences in the [[Glossary:Coverage|coverage]] between countries. As a result, there are currently no EU totals for the actual numbers of job vacancies or occupied posts, work is currently underway to remove these differences in coverage. Note that the data presented for Denmark relates to NACE Sections B to N, rather than the broader aggregate of NACE Sections B to S used for the other EU countries. In France and Italy, 'Public administration and defence; compulsory social security' (NACE Rev. 2 section O) is not surveyed while public institutions are not fully covered in 'Education' as well as 'Human health and social work activities' (NACE Rev. 2 sections P and Q). Due to a methodological change there is a break in series for Czechia in 2025Q1. Primary data are collected by the Labour Office from administrative sources. With the introduction of an amendment to the Employment Act (No 470/2024), in force from 1 January 2025, vacancies older than 6 months are automatically closed unless the employer registers them again. As a consequence, since the first quarter of 2025 the number of vacancies have been sizably lower compared with previous periods. The EU and euro area job vacancy rates are calculated on the basis of the information that is available, no estimates are made for missing or incomplete data. The source dataset for online job advertisements covers over 100 million ads posted in EU countries, collected from several hundred web sources including job search engines and public employment services' websites. To the extent possible, automatic systems filter out multiple postings for the same vacancy. Online job advertisements usually include data on the characteristics of the job (e.g. occupation and location), of the employer (e.g. economic activity) and requirements (e.g. education/skills). This information, only available as unstructured data (natural language text), is processed and classified according to main international classifications. ===Context=== Job vacancy statistics provide information on the level and structure of labour demand. The job vacancy rate may, in part, reflect the unmet demand for labour, as well as potential mismatches between the skills and availability of those who are [[Glossary:Unemployed|unemployed]] and those sought by employers. Job vacancy statistics are used by the [[Glossary:European_Commission|European Commission]] and the [[Glossary:European_Central_Bank_(ECB)|European Central Bank (ECB)]] to analyse and monitor the development of the labour market at national and European level. These statistics are also a key indicator used for an assessment of the [[Glossary:Business_cycle|business cycle]] and for a structural analysis of the economy. Policy developments in this area have focused mainly on trying to improve the labour market by matching supply and demand more closely, through: *modernising and strengthening labour market institutions, notably employment services; *removing obstacles to worker mobility across Europe; *better anticipating skill needs, labour market shortages and bottlenecks; *managing economic [[Glossary:Migration|migration]]; *improving the adaptability of workers and enterprises so that there is a greater capacity to anticipate, trigger and absorb economic and social change. The European jobs and mobility portal ([https://eures.europa.eu/index_en EURES]) was set-up with the aim of providing job seekers in the EU with the opportunity to consult all job vacancies publicised in each of the EU countries' employment services. The website provides access to a range of job vacancies from 31 European countries (27 EU countries, as well as Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland). In March 2022, there were almost [https://eures.europa.eu/eu-talent-pool-pilot_en nearly 4.0 million vacant posts advertised] in EURES. [http://www.europeanjobdays.eu/en/about European job days] are another EU initiative in this domain, with hundreds of events being organised across Europe. These aim to raise awareness about the opportunities and practicalities of living and working in another European country, encouraging mobility throughout the EU and putting job candidates in touch with employers who have job vacancies. Such events typically include job fairs, seminars, lectures, workshops and cultural events, all aimed at improving labour mobility. ===Other articles=== *[[Job vacancy and unemployment rates - Beveridge curve|Job vacancy and unemployment rates — Beveridge curve]] *[[Employment - annual statistics]] *[[Labour market statistics at regional level]] *[[Unemployment statistics]] *[[Unemployment statistics at regional level]] ===Publications=== See also the latest: *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-euro-indicators/w/3-18032026-bp News release dated 16 June 2026: Euro area job vacancy rate at 2.3%.] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/labour-market/database Job vacancy statistics (jvs)], see: :Job vacancy statistics by NACE Rev. 2.1 activity - title: Investments in climate change mitigation
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the investments in climate change mitigation. Data extracted in January 2026 Planned article update: December 2026 Private investment in climate change mitigation in the EU has increased in line with gross domestic product (GDP) since 2005, reaching €138.1 billion or 0.8% of GDP in 2023. [[Image: Private investment in climate change mitigation EU 2005-2023_1.jpg|Private investment in climate change mitigation, EU, 2005-2023 (% of GDP)|800px| alt= An image showing the private investment in climate change mitigation in the EU between 2005 and 2023. The vertical axis displays the percentage of GDP, while the horizontal axis displays the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_ac_ccminv}}

This article is a part of the Eurostat online publication [[Statistics_on_climate_change_mitigation|Statistics on climate change mitigation]]. It analyses private [[Glossary:Gross_investment_in_tangible_goods_-_SBS|investment]] in [[Glossary:Climate_change_mitigation|climate change mitigation]] in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]]. This investment aims to reduce the emissions of [[Glossary:Greenhouse_gas_(GHG)|greenhouse gases]], for example by promoting low-carbon technologies or a switch to [[Glossary:Renewable_energy_sources|renewable energy sources]]. As far as possible, this article indicates which part of the economy (according to the [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE]] classification) is the investor (see '''Data sources''' at the end of this article for further details).
'''Note on data coverage''' The data presented in this article have been modelled and estimated based on investment data from Eurostat’s [[Glossary:Structural_business_statistics_(SBS)|structural business statistics (SBS)]]. Data from SBS cover the [[Glossary:Business_economy|business economy]], which includes industry, construction and services, while other economic sectors and public administration are outside the scope. The data presented in this article therefore only refer to private investment by the business economy related to climate change mitigation, whereas investment from the general government and from households is not included. Keeping this scope in mind is important when interpreting the data presented below (also in relation to investment needs stated in policy documents and other studies). A more comprehensive collection of data is planned to be made available in 2026 through Eurostat’s [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Environmental_accounts_-_establishing_the_links_between_the_environment_and_the_economy environmental accounts], which will cover additional sectors and economic activities.
=== Evolution of private investment in climate change mitigation === According to Eurostat estimates, private [[Glossary:Gross_investment_in_tangible_goods_-_SBS|investment]] in climate change mitigation in the EU has seen an overall increasing trend since 2005. In 2023, it reached €138.1 billion (in current prices), which corresponds to 0.8% of the EU’s [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]]. Chain-linked data, which allow for comparisons over time by removing the effect of price changes, show a 164% increase in private investment related to climate change mitigation in the EU between 2005 and 2023 (see '''Figure 1'''). In relation to GDP, investment remained at around 0.5% between 2008 and 2017. It had been increasing since then, with especially strong growth in 2022 and 2023, reaching 0.8% of GDP in 2023 – the highest value recorded (switch to unit ‘% of GDP’ in '''Figure 1''').

Figure 1 === Investment in climate change mitigation by economic activity === Around 85% of private investment in the EU was carried out by 2 [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|economic activities]]. In 2023, transportation and storage accounted for 43% of total private [[Glossary:Gross_investment_in_tangible_goods_-_SBS|investment]], followed by electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply (hereinafter referred to as ‘electricity and gas supply’), which accounted for 42% (see '''Figure 2'''). Virtually all investment from these 2 sectors went into ‘low-carbon transport technologies and services’ and ‘renewable energy production, transmission and storage’ (hereinafter referred to as ‘renewable energy’). Between 2005 and 2023, the share of investment from the transportation and storage sector fell from 65% to 43%. At the same time, investment from electricity and gas supply increased from 20% to 42%. Throughout the available period, these 2 sectors accounted for around 80% to 90% of total investment in climate change mitigation in the EU. The manufacturing sector showed a small but steady gain over time and accounted for 10% of private investment in climate change mitigation in 2023. Investment in this sector mainly related to ‘renewable energy’, ‘[[Glossary:Energy_efficiency|energy efficiency]] technologies’ and ‘planning, construction, and installation services’. Investment from the construction sector lost in relative importance and only accounted for 5% in that year. Virtually all of the investment in this sector was related to ‘planning, construction, and installation services’.

Figure 2 '''Climate change mitigation investment by economic activity in relation to gross value added''' [[Glossary:Gross_value_added|Gross value added]] measures the contribution of each economic activity to the whole economy and is thus a suitable measure for putting the investment figures presented above into perspective. The 2 largest investors in climate change mitigation at EU level – transportation and storage as well as electricity and gas supply – also recorded the highest investment shares of gross value added (see '''Figure 3'''). In 2023, climate change mitigation investment in electricity and gas supply amounted to around 15% of the sector’s gross value added. For transportation and storage, the investment share was around 8%. In contrast, climate change mitigation investment in construction and manufacturing accounted for less than 1% of these sectors’ gross value added. The investment share of electricity and gas supply has increased since 2005 when it was about 5%, peaking at just above 15% in 2020 and 2021. In 2022, it dropped to about 13% but recovered already the next year, reaching almost 15% in 2023. Transportation and storage has also recorded an increase in its investment share since 2013, albeit at a slower pace, peaking at almost 8% in 2020 and 2023. This means that in these 2 economic activities, investment in climate change mitigation grew more strongly than gross value added over the past decade. In contrast, the investment shares for construction and manufacturing have remained below 1% of gross value added since 2009, although both shares have been slowly growing since 2021.

Figure 3 === Investment in climate change mitigation across EU countries === In 2023, Lithuania reported the highest shares of [[Glossary:Gross_investment_in_tangible_goods_-_SBS|investment]] in climate change mitigation, with 2.6% of GDP, followed by Denmark, Finland and Estonia with 1.9%, 1.7%, and 1.6%, respectively (see '''Map 1'''). Ireland, Malta, and Luxembourg had the lowest investment shares with less than 0.1% of GDP. Map 1: Private investment in climate change mitigation
(% of GDP) Investment in climate change mitigation has evolved quite dynamically across EU countries. Between 2005 and 2023, 18 countries increased their investment shares, with Finland showing the strongest growth from 0.3% of GDP in 2005 to 1.7% of GDP in 2023 (switch to 2005 in '''Map 1'''). In contrast, 9 countries reported a decrease in their investment shares over this period, with the most dramatic drop recorded in Latvia (from 3.3% of GDP in 2005 to 1.5% of GDP in 2023) and Romania (from 2.3% to 1.0%). As a result, the investment in climate change mitigation has grown relative to GDP at EU level. '''Figure 4''' shows the trends in investment in climate change mitigation across EU countries, both in absolute terms and in relation to GDP. In absolute terms, the main drivers of the growth in climate change mitigation investments were Germany and France, who increased their investments by 356% and 312%, respectively, between 2005 and 2023.

Figure 4

'''Figure 5''' shows the distribution of investment in climate change mitigation by economic activity for each country. In 17 countries, most investment took place in electricity and gas supply in 2023. In a further 8 countries, and at EU level, transportation and storage was the major investor. In Hungary, most of the investment took place in manufacturing, while construction was the major investor in Luxembourg.

Figure 5

'''Figure 6''' shows the investment share for each of the 3 main economic activities – transportation and storage, electricity and gas supply, and manufacturing – across EU countries in 2023. In Malta, Cyprus, France, and Belgium, transportation and storage accounted for more than 60% of total investment in climate change mitigation. Electricity and gas supply was the major investor in climate change mitigation in Finland, Estonia, Greece, and Austria, with a share of more than 70%. The country pattern for manufacturing is more skewed; while this activity accounted for more than 50% of total investment in Hungary, 27% in Slovenia, 26% in Sweden and 22% in Poland, it remained below 20% in all other countries.

Figure 6 === Data sources === While the [[Glossary:European_Environmental_Economic_Accounts|environmental accounts]] are a multipurpose data system defined in the [https://seea.un.org/ System of Environmental-Economic Accounting] (SEEA), they do not yet measure some emerging environmental policy themes such as climate change mitigation. Eurostat, in cooperation with the Member States, is working to put in place data requirements on climate change mitigation investments. The first collection of national data using the environmental accounts framework and additional data sources is expected to be disseminated in 2026. '''Methodological Notes:''' *The data presented refers to private investments, i.e. investments by businesses. The estimates are based on a methodology developed by Eurostat for defining private investments in climate change mitigation, consisting of the following steps: 1) Define what climate change mitigation is. 2) Delineate economic activities relating to climate change mitigation. *As regards the first point, the climate change mitigation sector is a sub-sector of the whole economy that substantially reduces greenhouse gas emissions by source or from the atmosphere. It reflects the internationally accepted definition by the [https://unfccc.int/ United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change] (UNFCCC) which is based on the [https://www.ipcc.ch/ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] (IPCC). The estimation method makes assumptions about the share of investment in climate change mitigation that should be applied to each economic activity. *As regards the second point, the investments are defined using the structural business statistics concept of ‘investment in tangible goods’. This is more restrictive than the concept of ‘gross fixed capital formation’, which reflects investments in both tangible and intangible goods. Please note that in most countries, the estimates do not cover agriculture, forestry and fishing ([[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community - NACE]] A) and data for this economic activity are therefore not available for the EU aggregate. In environmental accounts, the data are organised by economic activity, using the [[Glossary:NACE|NACE classification]]. This arrangement makes it possible to supplement national accounts with an integrated environmental-economic analysis. The scope encompasses production by all businesses resident in a country, including those operating ships, aircraft and other transportation equipment in other countries. The NACE Rev. 2 groups used in this article are: *Agriculture, forestry and fishing — NACE Rev. 2 Section A *Mining and quarrying — NACE Rev. 2 Section B *Manufacturing — NACE Rev. 2 Section C *Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply — NACE Rev. 2 Section D *Water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities — NACE Rev. 2 Section E *Construction — NACE Rev. 2 Section F *Transportation and storage — NACE Rev. 2 Section H *Services (except transportation and storage) — NACE Rev. 2 Sections G to U, excluding H, in other words all remaining economic activities as defined in NACE without transportation and storage *Total — all NACE activities === Context === In the European Union, [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02011R0691-20250101&qid=1738585552360 Regulation (EU) 691/2011 on European environmental economic accounts] (including its amendments in 2014 and 2022) has established a common framework for the collection, compilation, transmission and evaluation of [[Glossary:European_Environmental_Economic_Accounts|European environmental economic accounts]], for the purpose of setting up environmental economic accounts as satellite accounts to the European System of Accounts (ESA). The environmental economic accounts in the Regulation are grouped in the following 6 modules: * [[Glossary:Air_emissions_accounts_(AEA)|Air emissions accounts]] * [[Glossary:Economy-wide_material_flow_accounts_(EW-MFA)|Economy-wide material flow accounts]] * [[Glossary:Environmental_tax|Environmental taxes]] * [[Glossary:Classification_of_environmental_protection_activities_(CEPA)|Environmental protection expenditure]] accounts * [[Glossary:Environmental_goods_and_services_sector_(EGSS)|Environmental goods and services sector (EGSS)]] accounts * [[Glossary:Physical_energy_flow_accounts_(PEFA)|Physical energy flow accounts]] More information on these modules can be found through [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/environment/overview Eurostat’s dedicated section on environment]. The most recent amendment of the Regulation - through [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202403024 Regulation (EU) 2024/3024] - introduced 3 further modules: * Forest accounts * Environmental subsidies and similar transfers accounts * Ecosystem accounts Preparing the implementation of these new modules is one of the key objectives of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/1798247/6191525/European+Strategy+for+Environmental+Accounts/ European Strategy for environmental accounts (ESEA)] for the period 2024-2028. In line with the EU’s commitment to tackling environmental challenges and becoming climate-neutral, the environmental accounts are vital for providing better information for supporting Europe's [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/competitiveness_en sustainable prosperity and competitiveness] and its [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/quality-life_en quality of life as] well as for implementing the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/environment-action-programme-2030_en 8th Environmental Action Programme] and the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/sustainable-development-goals_en Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)]. *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Greenhouse_gas_emission_accounts Greenhouse gas emission accounts] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Energy_accounts Energy accounts] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Greenhouse_gas_emission_footprints Greenhouse gas emission footprints] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Investments_in_environmental_protection Investments in environmental protection] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Environmental_accounts_-_establishing_the_links_between_the_environment_and_the_economy Environmental accounts - establishing the links between the environment and the economy] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/explore/all/envir?lang=en&subtheme=env.env_egs&display=list&sort=category Environmental goods and services sector] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_ccminv/default/table?lang=en Investments in climate change mitigation by NACE Rev. 2 activity (env_ac_ccminv)] === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/environment/overview Environment] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/climate-change/overview Climate change] === Publications === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-ra-07-015 NACE Rev. 2 -
