title: Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - main indicators
text:
Experimental results are presented on the joint distribution of income, consumption and wealth. Data extracted in February 2026 Planned article update: January 2028
EXPERIMENTAL
 In 2020, 9.8% of households in the EU were in the lowest quintiles of both income and consumption expenditure distributions. These households received 3.5% of the total disposable income, spent 3.8% of consumption expenditure and accumulated 4% of total net wealth in 2020. [[Image:Highlight_Figure_Households_bottom_quintiles_income_and_consumption(%_share_around_2020).png|Share of households (%) in the bottom quintiles of both income and consumption expenditure distributions, and share of disposable income, consumption expenditure, and net wealth held by these households, 'around 2020'.
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=icw_res_01|title=icw_res_01}})|thumb|center|700px|alt= a combined vertical bar/ line chart showing the share of households falling in the bottom 20% of income and consumption expenditure distributions (diamonds) and and the share of disposable income, consumption expenditure and net wealth held by these households. The chart refers to ICW 2020 wave. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article presents indicators compiled from a joint dataset that is constructed using statistical matching of microdata from household income, consumption expenditure and wealth surveys (see [[Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - methodology|Statistics Explained article on methodological issues]]). The indicators are presented with reference years 'around 2010', 'around 2015' and 'around 2020'Exact reference years of ICW data are reported here: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=File:Table1_HBS-HFCS_reference_years.png because the source data from the countries spread over 3 years around these years. The joint datasets for Italy for all 3 reference years and for the Netherlands for 'around 2010' were not available due to partly missing consumption expenditure data. Moreover, no consumption expenditure data for Sweden were available for the 'around 2020' reference year. The indicators for those reference yeas were therefore not available for the analysis in this article. Due to the lack of national data, consumption expenditure for Cyprus, France and Malta for 'around 2020' were extrapolated from the 'around 2015' data with [[Glossary:Harmonised_index_of_consumer_prices_(HICP)|HICP]] based deflators. === Income, consumption and wealth inequalities === '''Saving disparities''' In order to understand the dynamics of wealth inequality, it is essential to describe the process of asset accumulation and therefore saving behaviours. Saving flows may be defined as the residual between income and consumption, i.e. what is left from income at the end of the period after expenditures for consumption. If income is higher than consumption, this residual is invested in (financial or real) assets and will constitute a part of the wealth held by a household. If consumption expenditure is higher than income, the household will have to finance its consumption not only from income, but also by contracting debt or selling assets. The fact that a household cannot finance its consumption entirely from its income may be a good indication of financial difficulties. As shown in Figure 1, the proportion of households whose yearly expenditures are higher than their income ('dissaving households') varies greatly across countries, although this indicator must be interpreted with caution, as it may be affected by significant measurement errors. Similarly, a saving rate close to zero suggests that the household is unable to save and is more likely to restrict its expenditures, thereby risking not being able to meet all its needs. Saving rates are computed by dividing savings (the difference between total disposable income and total consumption at the end of year X) by the total disposable income of the household during the same year. [[Image:F1_Households_with_consumption_expenditure_higher_than_income_.png |Figure 1: Share of households (%) with consumption expenditure higher than income 'around 2015' and 'around 2020'
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=icw_pov_03|title=icw_pov_03}}).|thumb|centre|700px|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing the Proportion of households with expenditure higher than income in the EU and Member States. The bars show the years 2015 and 2020. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The median household saving rate (when households are ranked according to their saving rates, half are above this rate and half are below) can be looked at as another distributional indicator. In 'around 2020', for example, half of all households in the EU were able to save over 26% of their annual income (up from 21% in 'around 2015'). This trend is reflected in most countries, apart from a few exceptions, such as Finland and France where 'around 2020' saving rates dropped compared with 'around 2015' results, and Romania, where the situation of households was even more difficult, as over half of the households could not fully fund their expenditure with own income (Figure 2). [[Image:F2_Median_saving_rates_of_households_(%_share_around_2015_and_around_2020).png |Figure 2: Median saving rates (%) of households 'around 2015' and 'around 2020'
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=icw_sr_03|title=icw_sr_03}}).|thumb|center|700px|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing the Median saving rates in percentage of households 'around 2015' and 'around 2020' in the EU and the member States. The bars show the years 2015 and 2020. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ''' Inequality in households' income, consumption, savings and wealth''' The [[Glossary:Gini_coefficient|gini coefficient]] is the most common indicator used to measure income inequality, wealth inequality or consumption inequality within a group, where 0 expresses perfect equality, meaning that everyone has the same economic resources, and 100 represents complete inequality, with all the resources belonging to only 1 person or household. Wealth is in general far more unevenly distributed than income or consumption. Figure 3 shows the Gini coefficients for households' income, consumption expenditures, savings and wealth for EU countries in 'around 2020'. The coefficients range between 27 and 41 for consumption expenditures and between 29 and 47 for income across available countries. For the other 2 variables, the distribution is less equal with the Gini coefficients varying across countries between 46 and 72 for wealth and between 49 and 78 for savings. [[Image:F3_Expenditures,_income,_savings_and_wealth_(Gini_coefficients_around_2020).png|Figure 3: Gini coefficients for income, expenditures, savings and wealth, 'around 2020'
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=icw_sr_05|title=icw_sr_05}})|thumb|centre|700px|alt=a vertical bar chart with four bars showing the Gini coefficients for income, expenditures, savings and wealth in the EU and the EU Member States. The bars show expenditure, income, savings and wealth. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Interplay between indicators === Apart from the accounting exercise of computing savings from income and consumption at household level, it is also interesting to focus on the interplay between the various indicators of vulnerability described above. In particular, individuals who are poor according to the usual income-based definition and at the same time vulnerable with respect to their consumption expenditure levels may be of interest, as they combine several dimensions of poverty. Figure 4 shows the intersection between the [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|at-risk-of-poverty (AROP)]] indicator and the indicator based on consumption expenditures; the dark gold coloured segment shows the estimated proportion of the population affected by both types of vulnerability. In 'around 2020', share of income-poor population as measured by AROP alone for the EU was around 9%, exceeding 11% for 3 EU countries (Spain, Estonia and Bulgaria). Observing how the proportion of vulnerable people changes when taking account of consumption, about 24% of the EU population was either at risk of poverty due to low income or had low levels of consumption expenditure in 'around 2020'. At national level, in 12 countries, 1 person in 4 was either income or expenditure poor, while in Luxembourg, Latvia, Spain, Lithuania and Estonia this was almost 1 in 3. [[Image:Fig4 Population at-risk-of-poverty (AROP).png|Figure 4: Proportion of the population (%) at-risk-of-poverty (AROP) or having low level of consumption expenditure or both, 'around 2020'
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=icw_pov_01|title=icw_pov_01}}). |thumb|centre|700px|alt=a vertical stacked bar chart showing the Intersection between at-risk-of-poverty and low levels of expenditure 'around 2020' in the EU and the EU Member States. The bars show only at-risk-of-poverty, at-risk-of-poverty and low levels of expenditure and not at-risk-of-poverty and low levels of expenditure. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The data showed that only a small proportion of households were 'dissaving' and had low levels of consumption expenditure at the same time (see Figure 5), i.e. their consumption expenditure was not below 60% of the median consumption expenditure the total households in their country although their income was lower than their consumption expenditure. In 'around 2020', the share of households in the EU facing a combination of the 2 types of vulnerability was 2.1%. The highest shares were observed for Romania (7.5%), Croatia (4.3%), Latvia (3.2%) and Spain (3.1%), while for all other EU countries they were 3% or below. [[Image:Fig5 Intersection between dissaving households and low levels of expenditure.png|Figure 5: Intersection between dissaving households and low levels of expenditure 'around 2020'
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=icw_pov_04|title=icw_pov_04}}).|thumb|centre|700px|alt=a vertical stacked bar chart showing the Intersection between dissaving households and low levels of expenditure 'around 2020' in the EU and the EU Member States. The bars show dissaving households, no low expenditure, dissaving households, with low expenditure saving households, with low expenditure. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Consumption expenditures by income === The joint dataset of households' income and consumption may be used to show distributions of median consumption expenditure over different income groups (Figure 6). A steep increase in consumption expenditure with available income is observed, which is particularly pronounced at the top of the distribution in most countries. [[Image:F6_Median_consumption_by_income_decile_(in_1_000_PPS_around_2020).png |Figure 6: Median consumption (1 000 [[Glossary:Purchasing_power_standard_(PPS)|purchasing power standard (PPS)]]) by income decile, 'around 2020'
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=icw_sr_06|title=icw_sr_06}}). |thumb|center|700px|alt=a vertical bar chart also showing percentiles on the Median consumption by income decile 'around 2015', in 1000 in terms of Purchasing Power Standard. In the EU, the EU Member States and the United Kingdom. The bar shows the first to tenth percentile. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The aggregate propensity to consume is defined as the percentage of income spent on average on goods and services. It is derived by using the national accounts approach for the household sector, in which all household income and consumption flows are aggregated at national level. The aggregate consumption expenditure is divided by the aggregate income. The complement of the aggregate propensity to consume is the aggregate saving rate, which reflects the saving behaviour of the population as a whole. Figure 7 demonstrates how lower income groups have to spend a considerably higher part of their income on goods and services than higher income groups, thereby preventing them from saving part of their income, or even dissaving as is the case for the first income quintile in almost all EU countries. [[Image:Fig7 Aggregate propensity to consume by income quintile.png|Figure 7: Aggregate propensity to consume (%) by income quintile, 'around 2020'
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=icw_sr_10|title=icw_sr_10}}).|thumb|centre|700px|alt=a vertical bar chart showing the Aggregate propensity to consume by income quintile by percentage around 2020 In the EU and the EU Member States. The bars show the first to fifth quintile. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Saving behaviours === '''The role of life cycle''' People's saving behaviour may vary over their lifetime, as they tend to adjust their consumption in order to smooth out income variations. In particular, younger and older people will tend to have lower saving rates, since they are generally earning less than they will earn on average over their lifetime. At EU level, the joint dataset reflects this behaviour well (Figure 8). Furthermore, households with a reference person below 35 years of age, more often save less than households whose main earner is older. Yet, there is considerable variation across countries, and for example, the decrease of saving rates after retirement (age groups 65+), does not occur in about one-third of the countries. [[Image:F8_Median_saving_rate_by_age_of_the_household_reference_person_(%_around_2020).png |Figure 8: Median saving rate (%) by age of the household reference person, 'around 2020'
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=icw_sr_01|title=icw_sr_01}}).|thumb|centre|700px|alt=a bar chart with seven bars showing the Median saving rate by age of the household reference person 'around 2020 in the EU and the EU Member States. The bars show the ages, less than 35, between 35 and 44 between 45 and 54, between 55 and 64, between 65 and 74 and other. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Household structure and vulnerability''' Saving behaviour is also linked to household structure. The data show that, in most countries, a single parent with children is more likely to have a low saving rate. However, the situation varies considerably across the EU (see Figure 9). [[Image:F9_Median_saving_rate_by_type_of_household_(%_around_2020).png |Figure 9: Median saving rate (%) by type of household, 'around 2020'
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=icw_sr_02|title=icw_sr_02}}).|thumb|centre|700px|alt=a vertical bar chart with six bars showing the Median saving rate by type of household 'around 2020' in the EU and the EU Member States. The bars show, one adult, three adults and more two adults with dependent children, two adults, one adult with dependent children three adults and more with dependent children. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Income and savings''' Saving rates increase with income, i.e. the share of income not used for consumption increases with income (see Figure 10). The median saving rate for the first income quintile (the 20% of households with the lowest income) for the EU in 2020 was -3% reflecting well the overall situation in the EU countries, where only 9 countries showed positive saving rates: Poland, Cyprus, Estonia, France, Lithuania, Portugal, Czechia, Slovenia and Latvia. By contrast, Romania (-62.3%), the Netherlands (-28.8%), Greece (-15.7%) and Austria (-15.2%), showed the most pronounced negative saving rates for households belonging to the bottom income quintile. For Romania, even the median household in the second and the third income quintiles recorded a negative saving rate. Highest median saving rates are attained for all countries in the last income quintile (the 20% of households with the highest income). The difference in saving rates of households in the lowest and the highest income quintile for the EU was about 49 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp), exceeding 60 pp for Romania, the Netherlands, Denmark, Belgium and Spain. [[Image:F10_Median_saving_rate_of_households_by_income_quintile_(%_around_2020).png |Figure 10: Median saving rate (%) of households by income quintile, 'around 2020'
''Source:'' Eurostat ({{Template:Publication|code=icw_sr_03|title=icw_sr_03}}).|thumb|centre|700px|alt=a vertical bar chart showing the Median saving rate of households by income quintile in the EU, the EU Member States and the United Kingdom The bars show the first to fifth quintile. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Feedback=== To help Eurostat improve these experimental statistics, users and researchers are kindly invited to give us their [mailto:ESTAT-ICW@ec.europa.eu?subject=Feedback_on_experimental_statistics feedback by email] === Source data for tables and graphs=== *[[Media:DataFiguresSE1 graphs 2026v2.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] *[https://github.com/eurostat/statistics-coded/blob/master/popul/living-conditions/income-consumption-wealth_r/icw1.R Link to the scripts generating the figures] === Data sources=== The income data for the joint dataset used in this article comes from the [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]], governed by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R1700:EN:NOT|title=Regulation 1700/2019}} (more information on the legal framework can be found in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/legislation legislation] part of the thematic section on income and living conditions statistics at Eurostat's web page). The consumption expenditure data is from the [[Glossary:Household_budget_survey_(HBS)|Household Budget Survey (HBS)]]. Information on assets and liabilities is from the [https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/economic-research/research-networks/html/researcher_hfcn.en.html Household Finance and Consumption Survey (HFCS)]. The HFCS is run by National Central Banks and coordinated by the European Central Bank. The EU-SILC, HBS and HFCS data are matched according to the year of reference for HBS to obtain a fused dataset containing household-level information on both income and consumption. For more details on the statistical matching and the methodology used in the data, please see Statistics Explained article [[Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - methodology]]. ===Other articles === *[[Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - methodology]] ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics Experimental statistics] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-consumption-wealth Income, consumption and wealth - experimental statistics], see: :*Household economic resources (icw_res) :*Saving rates (icw_sr) :*Poverty (icw_pov) === Publications === '''Statistical books''' *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-05-14-075|title=Monitoring social inclusion in Europe - 2017 edition}} '''Others''' *Törmälehto V.-M., Kannas O., Säylä M., [http://old.iariw.org/papers/2012/TormalehtoPaper.pdf Integrated measurement of household-level income, wealth and non-monetary well-being in Finland], 32nd General Conference of the International Association for Research in Income and Wealth, 2012. *Eurosystem Household Finance and Consumption Network, [https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/pdf/other/ecbsp2en.pdf?2180f869d12ccc366869c9419b3da32e|The Eurosystem Household Finance and Consumption Survey-Results from the First Wave], 2012. *Lequiller F., Blades D., [http://dx.doi.org/10.1787/9789264214637-en Understanding National Accounts], OECD Publishing, 2014. *Balestra C., Oehler F. [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3888793/15984035/KS-TC-22-003-EN-N.pdf/4e7e6c11-6c59-dea9-12d3-2ca21c7cc0ea?version=3.0&t=1674810934598 Measuring the joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth at the micro level - Methodological issues and experimental results], 2023. ===Legislation === *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32003R1177:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1177/2003}} of 16 June 2003 concerning Community statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/LSU/?uri=CELEX:32003R1177 Summaries of EU Legislation: EU statistics on income and living conditions] *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32005R1553:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1553/2005}} of 7 September 2005 amending Regulation 1177/2003 concerning Community statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32006R1791:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1791/2006}} of 20 November 2006 adapting certain Regulations and Decisions in the fields of ... statistics, ..., by reason of the accession of Bulgaria and Romania === External links === *[https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/economic-research/research-networks/html/researcher_hfcn.en.html Website of ECB's Household Finance and Consumption Survey] === Footnotes === ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Article_name'' {{Unit|topic=X_Social_statistics}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - title: Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - methodology
text:
EXPERIMENTAL
 This article outlines Eurostat’s methodology for producing experimental joint statistics on income, consumption and wealth (ICW) at the micro level for EU countries. The article first introduces the conceptual foundation for integrating these three dimensions. It then explores the approaches based on integrated surveys and data linkage with non-survey sources. The core of the article explains how statistical matching is applied by Eurostat to integrate ICW data. Finally, the article analyses the quality of the matched dataset. === Conceptual foundation for Eurostat’s integrated approach to ICW === The Stiglitz Report, which was published in 2009, emphasised the importance of going beyond [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]] to better capture the well-being of individuals and households (Stiglitz et al., 2009)See the full references and links to the cited publications under Publications.. One of its key recommendations highlighted that the most meaningful measures of material living standards are likely to come from considering jointly the ICW levels of households or individuals. This recommendation laid the conceptual foundation for the combined ICW approach, which aims to provide a more integrated and refined understanding of economic well-being by recognising that income flows, spending behaviour and asset ownership jointly shape households’ living conditions. Building on this multidimensional perspective, the Report called for surveys to collect information on the joint distribution of the key dimensions of quality of life assessing their interlinkages at the individual level. This recommendation has posed a practical challenge for the European Statistical System to consider such multidimensional and person-centred measures in a harmonised way across the EU. === Integrated surveys and data linkage === The most comprehensive dataset combining income, consumption and wealth is likely to result from an integrated survey approach, where these variables are jointly observed. This may involve collecting all relevant data through a single unified survey or by linking multiple coordinated surveys conducted on the same population sample. However, this approach is rarely implemented in practice, as it significantly increases the response burden, which can lead to lower participation rates and potentially compromise the quality of the collected data. Another option for obtaining joint ICW data is data linkage with non-survey sources. Instead of collecting all relevant information through surveys, this method integrates as many variables as possible – particularly economic ones – from non-survey sources such as administrative records (e.g. tax or social security registers). Integration between survey data and administrative sources can be carried out through unique identifiers. These are specific pieces of information, such as social security numbers or tax identification codes, that enable deterministic (exact) linking of records across different datasets, ensuring consistent integration of information about the same individual or household. When such unique identifiers are unavailable or incomplete, probabilistic linkage can be used instead. Data linkage can significantly reduce the response burden when conducting surveys. However, non-survey sources often diverge from statistical definitions and classifications, creating a trade-off between reducing response burden and maintaining conceptual consistency. Furthermore, access to administrative data is often limited. === Statistical matching === Given the constraints associated with integrated surveys and data linkage, statistical matching has emerged as a feasible alternative. It is a model-based approach that combines variables – referred to as target variables – from multiple datasets, each based on a survey conducted on a distinct sample from the same population. This integration is achieved using a set of variables common to the datasets, with the expectation that individuals or households who are similar in terms of these common variables are also similar with respect to the target variables. Additionally, the modular approach In the modular approach, a survey collects detailed information on one dimension (e.g. income), while information on other dimensions (e.g. consumption or wealth) is limited and collected through a survey module. The resulting data from this module frequently need to be complemented with information from external sources. This is typically achieved through statistical imputation techniques such as matching, using module variables that overlap with external sources. can be regarded as a complementary solution that supports data integration, particularly when combined with statistical matching techniques. === Harmonised ICW matching approach for the EU === In line with the Stiglitz Report, the Vienna Memorandum, which was adopted at the 2016 Conference of the Directors-General of the National Statistical Institutes, called for developing integrated ICW statistics for EU countries in the short to medium term, using a model-based approach to combine data from multiple sources. In response, Eurostat started to compile and release experimental statistics based on the joint ICW distribution at the micro level. The latest Eurostat estimates for the main indicators are available in the Statistics Explained article [[Joint_distribution_of_household_income,_consumption_and_wealth_-_main_indicators|Joint_distribution_of_household_income,_consumption_and_wealth_-_main_indicators]]. In parallel, some EU countries took action at national level to produce their own joint distribution estimates. === Data sources === In the ICW matching process, Eurostat integrates data from three different surveys to produce joint information on ICW at the micro level. In particular, national micro data on income and consumption are available from the [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC)]] and the [[Glossary:Household_budget_survey_(HBS)|Household Budget Survey (HBS)]], respectively. Data on household wealth are available from the [https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/ecb_surveys/hfcs/html/index.en.html Household Finance and Consumption Survey (HFCS)], a harmonised survey coordinated by the European Central Bank and conducted in multi-year waves by national central banks in most EU countries (see Table 1). It collects information on households’ assets and liabilities, as well as partial data on their income and consumption. === Alignment of reference periods === To ensure data comparability in the resulting joint dataset, Eurostat aligns the reference periods across the EU-SILC, the HBS and the HFCS datasets. Since the HBS is conducted every five years and its reference period may vary across countries, the annual EU-SILC is selected to correspond to the HBS reference period. For wealth, the HFCS survey year closest to the HBS reference period is used for each country where HFCS data are available. Table 1 presents the reference periods across surveys, grouped into three waves: ‘around 2010’, ‘around 2015’ and ‘around 2020’. [[Image:Table1 HBS-HFCS reference years.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Exact reference years of the ICW data |alt= Table illustrating the exact reference year of the HBS and HFCS surveys used in the matching for each country]] === Conceptual definitions of target variables === By integrating survey data, Eurostat aims to achieve conceptually harmonised variables. Below are the definitions of ICW variables used in constructing the joint distribution. '''Income''' is represented by the annual household disposable income from the EU-SILC. This includes all monetary income received by any member of the household (e.g. income from employment, self-employment, social benefits and property income), as well as income received at household level, after the deduction of taxes and social contributions. It excludes * imputed rent, i.e. money that one saves by not paying full (market) rent when living in own accommodation or in accommodation rented at a price lower than the market rent * non-monetary income components, such as the value of goods produced for own consumption, social transfers in kind and non-cash employee income (except for the use of company cars, which is included) For '''consumption''', annual monetary household consumption is derived from the HBS by subtracting imputed rents and other non-monetary expenditures from total consumption expenditureIt should be noted that consumption expenditure includes the full purchase costs of consumer durables (i.e. long-lasting goods that households use over time such as cars, washing machines, furniture and computers), although, strictly speaking, only the annual service provided by such durables should be regarded as consumption (e.g. a € 1 000 durable that lasts 10 years provides € 100 of service per year).. Two '''wealth''' variables are used from the HFCS * household net wealth, defined as total assets minus total liabilities * total assets Total assets consist of real assets (e.g. the value of the household’s main residence, other real estate property and vehicles) and financial assets (e.g. deposits, investments in mutual funds, private pension plans and whole life insurance policies but not the current value of public and occupational pension plans). Total liabilities (debt) include, for example, outstanding amounts on mortgages for the main residence and other real estate properties. === Statistical matching via hot-deck methods === To create a joint distribution of ICW, Eurostat applies a statistical matching approach based on hot-deck imputation. This is a widely used non-parametric method in which missing values in one dataset are imputed by assigning observed values from similar records in another dataset. As part of this process, it is necessary to determine which dataset will act as the recipient (where information is missing) and which will serve as the donor (providing the missing information). In Eurostat’s ICW matching process, the EU-SILC dataset serves as the recipient, while the HBS and HFCS datasets serve as donor datasets. When the matching is performed at the household level, as is the case in Eurostat’s ICW matching, the process is as outlined below (Figure 1). * the recipient dataset contains one or more target variables, denoted Y (e.g. income), that are not available in the donor dataset * the donor dataset contains one or more different target variables, denoted Z (e.g. consumption), that are not available in the recipient dataset * a household record from the donor dataset with value(s) for Z is matched to a similar household record in the recipient dataset with value(s) for Y, using the matching variables X, which are common to both datasets * this approach relies on the expectation that households similar with respect to X are also similar with respect to Y and Z * as a result, a matched dataset is produced containing household records with values for variables X, Y and Z [[Image:Combining recipient and donor datasets.JPG|Figure 1: Combining two datasets through statistical matching|thumb|centre|700px|alt=Picture illustrating how variables from different sources are combined in the matched dataset]] === Conditional independence assumption === The conditional independence assumption (CIA) is a fundamental principle in statistical matching and is essential for ensuring the validity of the procedure (D’Orazio et al., 2006). It states that the target variables Y and Z are conditionally independent given the matching variables X. In other words, once X is known, knowing the value of Y provides no additional information about Z, and vice versa. This implies that the statistical relationship between Y and Z is fully accounted for by X. While the CIA cannot be formally tested in the matched dataset – since the target variables Y and Z are not jointly observed – its plausibility can be supported by incorporating proxy variables into the set of matching variables X (Zhang, 2015). Each of these proxy variables is conceptually related to and strongly associated with at least one target variable from either Y or Z. Including such proxies enhances the explanatory power of the matching variables X, making it more reasonable to assume that X sufficiently captures the relationship between the target variables Y and Z. This, in turn, helps support the plausibility of the CIA (see also the [[#Quality assessment of the matching results|Quality assessment of the matching results]]). === Random hot-deck matching between EU-SILC and HBS === When more than two donor datasets are to be combined with a single recipient dataset, the matching process is typically carried out in sequence. In Eurostat’s ICW matching process, the HBS dataset is first matched to the EU-SILC dataset to impute consumption data and then the HFCS dataset is matched separately to the SILC-HBS dataset to impute wealth data. Random hot-deck imputation is used when matching the HBS donor dataset with the EU-SILC recipient dataset. In this method, both the donor and the recipient dataset are grouped into strata, or donation classes, based on shared categorical matching variables. Within each stratum, a donor record is randomly selected to provide the missing information for a recipient record. All variables common to both the HBS (donor) and the EU-SILC (recipient) dataset that are considered as potential matching variables are * population density level * household size * household type * age of the reference person * level of education of the reference person * activity status of the reference person * occupation status of the reference person * country of origin of the reference person * tenure status of the household * rent paid by tenants (quartiles) * 20-quantiles of income * main source of income of the reference person These potential matching variables are harmonised across both datasets, resulting in categorical variables with aligned categories across the two datasets. For variables related to the reference person, the definition provided by the Canberra Group (UNECE, 2011) is followed, identifying the reference person in a household as the adult with the highest income. Among the potential matching variables is income, which – although available in the HBS – is not of sufficient quality for direct analysis of income-consumption relationships. However, when transformed into income quantiles on an ordinal scale (i.e. ranked categories), it serves as a valuable proxy for total disposable income in the EU-SILC dataset, thereby supporting the plausibility of the CIA (see also the [[#Quality assessment of the matching results|Quality assessment of the matching results]]). The selection of matching variables begins by applying the Hellinger distance measure to each common variable to identify those with similar distributions across the two datasets. In line with D’Orazio et al. (2006), a parsimonious set of matching variables is then selected from this pool. The below steps are applied for each country. * Step 1: A linear backward selection regression model is applied to identify up to n of the most relevant matching variables based on their ability to explain variations in HBS consumption. This backward selection starts with all potential variables, systematically removes them one by one and stops according to a predefined criterion (e.g. adjusted R2). * Step 2: Both datasets are stratified according to the selected matching variables. This stratification is retained only if, for most strata (at least 90%), the condition is met that the number of household records in the EU-SILC is no more than three times the number of household records in the HBS, accounting for the relative sample sizes of both datasets. * Step 3: If the threshold condition is not satisfied, the process is repeated with the selection of up to n−1 matching variables. As a result of the selection process, each country may have a different final set of matching variables. However, the underlying methodology remains harmonised across the EU. Moreover, income categorised into 20 quantiles has been selected as a matching variable for all countries through backward selection. The selected matching variables are then used to define strata, grouping together households with similar characteristics in both datasets. After stratification, each EU-SILC household record receives a consumption value from a randomly selected HBS household record within the same stratum – that is, from a household with similar characteristics. This process results in a matched SILC-HBS (income-consumption) dataset. Building on the methodology proposed by Renssen (1998), the EU-SILC weights in the matched dataset are subsequently recalibrated to account for both EU-SILC and HBS margins. The targeted margins are * average consumption (HBS) * average consumption by COICOP 2-digit level (HBS) * mean consumption by income quintile (in purchasing power standards) (HBS) * equivalised disposable household income by income decile (EU-SILC) * number of individuals at risk of poverty (EU-SILC) === Rank hot-deck matching between SILC-HBS and HFCS === Rank hot-deck imputation is employed to match the donor HFCS dataset with the recipient SILC-HBS (income-consumption) dataset. While similar to the random hot-deck approach in that both datasets are grouped into strata, or donation classes, based on shared categorical matching variables, the rank hot-deck method differs in the following steps. Within each stratum, records are ranked according to a shared continuous matching variable. Subsequently, for each recipient record, the donor record with the closest rank is selected to provide the missing information. Three variables common to both the HFCS (donor) and the SILC-HBS (recipient) dataset are used as matching variables for stratification. These are * household type * tenure status of household * food consumption (quintiles) The matching variables are harmonised across both datasets, resulting in categorical variables with aligned categories across the two datasets. These harmonised variables are then used to define strata, grouping together households with similar characteristics in both datasets. In each stratum, records from the HFCS and the SILC-HBS datasets are ranked based on the continuous matching variable of gross income, which is common to both. Although the levels of gross income may differ between the surveys, it is assumed that the relative ranking among households is consistent, allowing for comparable household rankings across datasets. For each recipient record, the donor record with the closest rank is selected to provide the missing information on net wealth and total assets, resulting in the matched ICW dataset. Both gross income and food consumption serve as proxy variables in this process. Gross income is closely related to total disposable income, while food consumption is strongly associated with total consumption expenditure. Including these proxies in the set of matching variables increases the plausibility of the CIA (see also the [[#Quality assessment of the matching results|Quality assessment of the matching results]]). === Final estimates === Statistical matching procedures can be repeated multiple times, following the multiple imputation principles introduced by Rubin (1987) to account for the uncertainty inherent in the process. In Eurostat’s ICW matching process, the matching is performed over 30 iterationsInitially, 1 000 iterations were applied, followed by 100 iterations. It was observed that 30 iterations provided sufficiently similar and robust final estimates, indicating that further iterations did not significantly alter outcomes., each producing a plausible joint distribution of ICW. For each iteration, estimates such as medians or ratios are calculated. Final estimates are obtained by averaging the results across all iterations, while the variability among them provides a measure of the uncertainty introduced by the matching process. === Quality assessment of the matching results === The quality of statistical matching can be assessed using a multilevel framework of validity, as proposed by Rässler (2002). The first level, marginal validity, assesses whether the marginal distributions of target variables in the donor datasets are preserved in the matched dataset. In the ICW matching process, the distribution of total consumption in the HBS dataset is compared with that in the matched ICW dataset. As illustrated in Figure 2 for Belgium, the percentile distributions align closely, indicating a good approximation of the original distribution of consumption. A similar pattern is observed for most other countries. [[Image:Comparison of percentile distributions of consumption2.png|Figure 2: Comparison of percentile distributions of consumption in the donor HBS dataset and the matched ICW dataset, Belgium, 'around 2020' ''Source:'' Eurostat (own calculations)|thumb|centre|700px| alt= a line plot showing the comparison of percentile distribution of consumption in the donor dataset (HBS) and in the matched ICW dataset for Belgium, 'around 2020']] A comparison for total assets is presented in Figure 3, using the donor HFCS dataset and the matched ICW dataset. For Belgium, the alignment appears less strong than for total assets, a pattern also observed for most other countries. [[Image:Comparison of percentile distributions of total assets2.png| Figure 3: Comparison of percentile distributions of total assets in the donor HFCS dataset and the matched ICW dataset, Belgium, 'around 2020' ''Source:'' Eurostat (own calculations)|thumb|centre|700px| alt= a line plot showing the comparison of percentile distribution of total assets in the donor dataset (HFCS) and in the matched ICW dataset for Belgium, 'around 2020']] The second level of validation, known as conditional validity, examines whether the relationships between the matching variables and the target variables are preserved after matching. In the ICW matching process, this is assessed by comparing Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients between the matching and target variables in the matched dataset with those in the donor datasets. The correlation structures, in terms of both strength and direction, are largely maintained, indicating that the statistical associations observed prior to matching are reasonably preserved. The third level of statistical matching quality, known as joint validity, refers to the extent to which the reconstructed joint distribution of the target variables plausibly reflects their true relationship. Achieving joint validity is particularly challenging because the true joint distribution is unknown. This is where the CIA plays a central role. As the CIA cannot be directly tested using the matched dataset – since the target variables are not jointly observed – Eurostat indirectly assessed its plausibility using auxiliary data from the EU SILC module on over-indebtedness, consumption and wealth for the reference years 2017 and 2020. The availability of both income and consumption data in the over-indebtedness, consumption and wealth module makes it possible to compute their correlation given the 20-quantiles of income. When the effect of this matching variable is controlled for, the correlation between income and consumption is substantially reduced and, in most cases, is not statistically significant. This suggests that using this variable as a proxy in matching income and consumption between the EU-SILC and the HBS captures well the relationship between the target variables. A similar approach is applied to assess the matching of income and wealth between the SILC-HBS and the HFCS, where gross income is used as a proxy in the matching variables. Controlling for gross income substantially reduces the correlation between income and wealth, strengthening the assumption that this variable explains much of the relationship between income and wealth. All these findings relating to the proxy variables offer some support for the plausibility of the CIA in the matched ICW dataset. === See also === *[[Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - main indicators]] *[[Joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth - statistics on taxation]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-consumption-wealth Income, consumption and wealth - experimental statistics] === Publications === * Balestra, C. and F Oehler (2023), [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-working-papers/w/ks-tc-22-003 Measuring the joint distribution of household income, consumption and wealth at the micro-level – Methodological issues and experimental results – 2023 edition], Eurostat and OECD, Luxembourg. * Browning, M., T. Crossley and G. Weber (2003), “Asking Consumption Questions in General Purpose Surveys”, The Economic Journal, Vol. 113/491, pp. F540-F567. * Coli, A., R. Istatkov, H. Jayyousi, F. Oehler, O. Tsigkas (2022), [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-working-papers/-/ks-tc-21-010 Distributional national account estimates for household income and consumption: methodological issues and experimental results - 2022 edition], Eurostat and OECD, Luxembourg. * DGINS Conference (2016), [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/13019146/13237859/DGINS+Memorandum+2016.pdf/4ebdf162-1b20-4d9e-a8c7-ae880eca9afd?t=1501752851000 Vienna Memorandum], Directors General of the National Statistical Institutes (DGINS), Vienna. * D'Orazio, M., M. title: Key figures for European Neighbourhood East countries
text:
This article is part of an online Eurostat publication that provides a statistical overview over the European Neighbourhood Policy-East (ENP-East) countries. The article presents statistics on various main topics for Moldova, Georgia, Ukraine, Armenia and Azerbaijan and compares these with the EU. The statistics presented include data from their respective thematic articles. Data extracted in January 2026. Planned article update: March 2027. In 2024, population density in the ENP-East countries ranged from 64.6 inhabitants per km² in Georgia to 118.0 in Azerbaijan, the only country in the region with a higher density than the EU average (109.3; 2023 data). In 2024, GDP per capita in the ENP-East countries remained far below the EU level (€39 940), with the highest value recorded in Georgia (€8 541), at around one fifth of the EU average, while Ukraine reported the lowest level (€4 077; 2021 data). Income inequality remained higher in most ENP-East countries than in the EU in 2024: the Gini coefficient stood at 35.9 in Moldova, 34.8 in Armenia (2023 data) and 34.4 in Georgia, compared with 29.4 in the EU. Moldova stood out in the ENP-East countries with very high energy productivity (€20.1 per kg of oil equivalent; 2023 data), more than double the EU average (€10.0), while Georgia and Azerbaijan recorded much lower levels (€2.7). In 2024, household internet access in the ENP-East countries ranged from 74.1% in Moldova to 91.5% in Georgia, remaining below the EU average of 94.2%. This article is part of an [[European_Neighbourhood_Policy_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]]. It presents information on 5 [[Glossary:European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP)|European Neighbourhood Policy-East (ENP-East)]] countries, namely, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, the Republic of Moldova and Ukraine, compared with the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are also [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries]]. The European Council granted Moldova and Ukraine candidate status on 23 June 2022 and Georgia on 14 December 2023. This article does not contain any data on Belarus, as statistical cooperation with Belarus has been suspended as of March 2022. Data shown for Georgia exclude the regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia over which the government of Georgia does not exercise control. The data managed by the National Bureau of Statistics of the Republic of Moldova does not include data from the Transnistrian region over which the government of the Republic of Moldova does not exercise control. Since 2014, data for Ukraine generally exclude the illegally annexed Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the City of Sevastopol and the territories which are not under control of the Ukrainian government. For Ukraine official statistics for 2022-2025 were not fully produced due to the martial law. It will gradually be produced and disseminated as defined by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine, taking into account the specific conditions of producing statistics during Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. This article presents, among others: statistics on [[Glossary:Population_density|population density]], [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]], measured in € per capita; inequality of disposable income measured by [[Glossary:Gini_coefficient|Gini coefficient]], energy productivity expressed in [[Glossary:Gross_value_added|gross value added (GVA)]] per kilogram of oil equivalent (kgoe) and households with [[Glossary:Internet_access|internet access]]. The indicators presented have been selected based on the importance of the policy areas and social issues they inform, as well as the availability of data. ===Population density=== Data on population density, measured in inhabitants per square kilometre (km2), is illustrated in Figure 1 for the ENP-East countries and compared with the EU. Among the ENP-East countries, Azerbaijan recorded the highest estimated population density in 2024, at 118.0 inhabitants per km2, and remained the only country in the region with a density higher than the EU average (109.3 inhabitants per km2; 2023 data, estimated and provisional). Armenia followed with a density of 103.4 inhabitants per km2. Moldova had a notably lower density, at 79.8 inhabitants per km2 (estimated and provisional data), while Georgia recorded the lowest estimated population density among the ENP-East countries shown, at 64.6 inhabitants per km2. Data for Ukraine are not available. [[Image: ENPE26_Pop density.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Population density, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1dd3cf6c-56b0-4fc9-97f8-c5f618123cd7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:47:12Z demo_r_d3dens]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b86a6f90-4911-41b8-bc91-367a78d244ef?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:46:31Z enpe_demo_r_d3dens])|alt=Visual showing population density in inhabitants per square kilometres for 2024 in the EU, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Moldova and Georgia. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Gross domestic product (GDP) per capita=== GDP per capita is a broad economic indicator that can be used for a basic comparison of living standards, as it adjusts for differences in population size and facilitates comparisons between countries. Georgia recorded the highest GDP per capita among the ENP-East countries in 2024, at €8 541 per capita. This level corresponded to slightly over one fifth of the EU average, which stood at €39 940 per capita. Armenia followed with €7 908 per capita, while Moldova recorded €7 001 (provisional data). At a somewhat lower level, GDP per capita in Azerbaijan amounted to €6 730. Ukraine had the lowest GDP per capita among the ENP-East countries, estimated at €4 077 (2021 data), almost 10 times lower than the EU average (see Figure 2). Overall, GDP per capita levels across the ENP-East countries are relatively close to one another, with the highest value a little more than double the lowest. This contrasts with the much wider dispersion observed [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6fb14291-6607-42a0-a1e6-0349c4b6634b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-09T08:30:09Z within the EU], where GDP per capita levels vary far more strongly between EU countries. [[Image: ENPE26_GDP_per capita.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Gross domestic product (GDP) per capita, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cbfe46d2-1193-4cb5-8267-35ac5e79f349?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:23:05Z nama_10_pc]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/efaff938-5ff0-46b2-bee5-e7333b6a9b4c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:19:25Z enpe_nama_10_gdp])|alt=Visual showing GDP in euro per capita for 2024 in the EU, Georgia, Armenia, Moldova, Azerbaijan and Ukraine. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Income inequality=== Income inequality, measured by the [[Glossary:Gini_coefficient|Gini coefficient]] of equivalised disposable income, is presented in Figure 3 for the ENP-East countries and the EU. The Gini coefficient captures how unevenly income is distributed within a population. A coefficient of 0 expresses perfect equality where everyone has the same income, while a coefficient of 100 expresses full inequality where only one person has all the income. The disposable income of a household is its net income after taxes and social contributions but including social benefits received; equivalised means that the composition of each household is weighted according to the number of adults and children living in it. Across the ENP-East countries, income inequality remains higher than in the EU. In 2024, the EU recorded a Gini coefficient of 29.4, while all ENP-East countries with recent data reported clearly higher values. Moldova had a Gini coefficient of 35.9 in 2024. Armenia recorded 34.8 (2023 data), reflecting a notable reduction compared with 2014. The largest improvement was observed in Georgia, where income inequality declined sharply from 41.2 in 2014 (the highest level among the ENP-East countries for which data is available) to 34.4 in 2024, bringing it closer to the levels seen in Moldova and Armenia. An exception within the ENP-East region is Ukraine, which recorded a comparatively low Gini coefficient of 23.0 (2014 data; no recent data available), well below the EU average and lower than in the other ENP-East countries. Data for Azerbaijan are not available. [[Image: ENPE26_Income_inequality.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Income inequality, 2014 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8b6ae9bc-4622-4024-8081-6b42db13119c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T10:46:44Z ilc_di12]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b8d5280d-2ad9-4892-8c59-5f345458a1ec?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T10:40:43Z enpe_ilc_di12])|alt=Visual showing the income inequality for 2014 and 2024 in the EU, Moldova, Armenia, Georgia and Ukraine. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Energy productivity=== Figure 4 presents the energy productivity of the ENP-East countries for 2024, compared with the EU. Energy productivity is an economic indicator that measures the amount of economic output achieved per unit of energy consumed by the economy, with higher values indicating more efficient use of energy in creating economic value. It is expressed in euro of [[Glossary:Gross_value_added|gross value added (GVA)]] per [[Glossary:Kilograms_of_oil_equivalent_(kgoe)|kilogram of oil equivalent]] (€/kgoe). Among the ENP-East countries, Moldova recorded by far the highest energy productivity, at €20.1 per kgoe (2023 data), more than double the EU average of €10.0 per kgoe. Armenia followed at a much lower level, with €5.8 per kgoe (2023 data), remaining below the EU average. Energy productivity in Georgia and Azerbaijan was substantially lower, at €2.7 per kgoe in both countries, indicating a relatively energy-intensive economic structure. Data for Ukraine are not available. Overall, apart from Moldova, energy productivity in the ENP-East countries remained well below the EU level, pointing to differences in economic structure, technological development and energy efficiency. As with other countries, these indicators are influenced not only by energy use but also by the composition of economic activity and relative price levels. [[Image: ENPE26_Energy productivity.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Energy productivity, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9cdba3e5-817b-4982-84fa-f7715b5b8dcb?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:58:22Z nrg_ind_ep]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/711b2aaa-7eec-4c57-8fb8-bde42579b957?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-13T08:19:18Z enpe_nrg_prod])|alt=Visual showing the energy productivity for 2024 in the EU, Moldova, Armenia, Georgia and Azerbaijan. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Households with internet access=== Figure 5 presents the share of households with internet access in the ENP-East countries for 2024, compared with the EU. This indicator reflects the level of digital connectivity among households and provides an insight into access to online services and information. In 2024, household internet access in the ENP-East countries remained below the EU average of 94.2%. Georgia recorded the highest level among the ENP-East countries, with 91.5% of households having internet access, followed closely by Azerbaijan at 90.2%. These levels indicate a relatively high degree of household connectivity, although still slightly lower than in the EU. More moderate levels of access were observed in Ukraine, where 82.7% of households had internet access (2021 data), and in Armenia, with 80.0% (2023 data). Moldova recorded the lowest share among the ENP-East countries, at 74.1% in 2024. [[Image: ENPE26_H_internet access.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Households with internet access, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c16c439e-cddc-41e6-913f-f3d44e2ec36e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-24T13:43:07Z isoc_ci_in_h]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1f147e0d-c670-4e02-90c5-201d807bb414?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-24T13:41:12Z enpe_isoc_ci_in_h])|alt=Visual showing the shares of households that had internet access in the EU, Georgia, Azerbaijan, Ukraine, Armenia and Moldova in 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== {{Template:Excel|filename=ENPE26_Key Figures_v1.xlsx|title=European Neighbourhood Policy — East countries — Key figures: tables and visuals}} ===Data sources=== The data for ENP-East countries are supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country on a voluntary basis. The data result from an annual data collection cycle that has been established by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]. These statistics are available free-of-charge on Eurostat's website, together with a range of additional indicators for ENP-East countries covering most socio-economic topics. Eurostat collects population data from EU countries and other countries participating in its demography data collection exercise, including the ENP-East countries. The recommended definition is the 'usual resident population' and represents the number of inhabitants on 1 January of the year in question (or, in some cases, on 31 December of the previous year). The [[Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)|European system of national and regional accounts (ESA)]] provides the methodology for national accounts in the EU. In the ENP-East countries the national accounts data presented in this article were generally collected according to the internationally agreed [[Glossary:System_of_national_accounts_(SNA)|2008 System of national accounts (2008 SNA)]]. The European Standard for National Account, [[Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)|ESA 2010]], is consistent with the 2008 SNA. [[Glossary:EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]] provides for harmonised data on income, poverty, social inclusion and living conditions in the EU and a number of other European countries. In the ENP-East countries, statistics on income and living conditions are collected through household surveys such as income and living conditions surveys, household budget surveys, labour force surveys or similar, based on internationally agreed methodologies and recommendations. Energy productivity is calculated as units of GDP per unit of energy. The energy data are generally taken from energy balances and GDP from the national accounts. For energy statistics, definitions, concepts and methodology are harmonised at international level. The methodology is described in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/NRG-2004 Energy Statistics Manual]. For EU statistics, the main legislation is [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:32008R1099:EN:NOT Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008] on energy statistics. For energy balances, the methodology is not harmonised at international level - international organisations as well as national administrations apply various approaches when constructing energy balances. Eurostat's [[Glossary:EU_survey_on_the_use_of_ICT_in_households_and_by_individuals|survey on ICT usage in households and by individuals]] is an annual survey used to benchmark ICT-driven developments. Data from ENP-East countries are typically based on income and living conditions surveys, household budget surveys, or other household surveys. ===Context=== On 2 July 2021, the European Commission and the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy presented the [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/IP_21_3367 Eastern Partnership: a Renewed Agenda] for cooperation with the EU's Eastern partners. This agenda is based on the five long-term objectives, with resilience at its core, as defined for the future of the [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/european-neighbourhood-policy/eastern-partnership_en Eastern Partnership (EaP)] in the Joint Communication [https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eeas/joint-communication-eastern-partnership-policy-beyond-2020-reinforcing-resilience-%E2%80%93-eastern_en Eastern Partnership policy beyond 2020: Reinforcing Resilience – an Eastern Partnership that delivers for all] in March 2020. It is further elaborated in the Joint Staff Working Document [https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eastern-partnership/joint-staff-working-document-recovery-resilience-and-reform-post-2020-eastern-partnership-priorities_en Recovery, resilience and reform: post 2020 Eastern Partnership priorities], amongst others defining the 'Top Ten Targets for 2025'. The Eastern Partnership’s agenda for recovery, resilience and reform is underpinned by an 'Economic and Investment Plan for the Eastern Partnership (EaP): Investing in resilient and competitive economies and societies' (Annex I of the Joint Staff Working Document). More detailed overviews are given in a [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/document/download/94735c00-2cfa-4ef7-92a6-41515b8b466d_en Factsheet on the Eastern Partnership Joint Communication], presenting the policy objectives and the specific priorities, as well as in a [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/document/download/d675e1d6-fd68-45fa-a671-80a69a117f1f_en Factsheet on EU-Eastern Neighbourhood Flagship projects 2023-2024]. The [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/news/eastern-partnership-summit-joint-declaration-2021-12-15_en Joint Declaration of the Eastern Partnership Summit 'Recovery, Resilience and Reform'] of 15 December 2021 reaffirmed the strong commitment to a strategic, ambitious and forward-looking Eastern Partnership. At the [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/meetings/international-ministerial-meetings/2023/12/11/ Eastern Partnership Foreign Affairs Ministerial meeting of 11 December 2023], the EU, EU countries and partners declared that they will step up their efforts to implement the Eastern Partnership’s agenda for recovery, resilience and reform, as well as tackling challenges related to the ongoing consequences of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine for the entire region. On 14-15 December 2023, the European Council decided to [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2023/12/14/european-council-conclusions-on-ukraine-enlargement-and-reforms/ open accession negotiations] with Moldova and Ukraine, and granted the status of candidate country to Georgia. In cooperation with its ENP partners, Eurostat has the responsibility to promote and implement the use of European and internationally recognised standards and methodology for the production of statistics, necessary for designing and monitoring policies in various areas. Eurostat manages and coordinates EU efforts to increase the capacity of the ENP countries to develop, produce and disseminate good quality data according to European and international standards. Additional information on the policy context of the ENP is provided on the website of [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/index_en Directorate-General Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood (ENEST)]. A regional statistical cooperation programme, STAT-East, is in place since January 2026 to strengthen partner countries’ statistical capacity to develop, produce and disseminate high-quality statistics and to reinforce the independence and institutional capacity of national statistical systems. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Non-EU_countries|All articles on non-EU countries]]
