title: Latest developments in income dynamics and poverty
text:
test test test Data extracted in May 2025 Planned article update: May 2027
EXPERIMENTAL
 At the EU level, 16.3% of the population were at risk of poverty according to the EU-SILC 2025 (covering 2024 income). Flash estimates for 2025 income point to overall stability, with a slight increase in the at-risk-of-poverty rate to 16.4%, compared with 16.3% in 2024. [[Image:At-risk-of-poverty rate, EU, 2019-2025 income years (% of population)V1.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bae09bca-6bc5-4964-854e-63a3c56d0c42?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T14:15:40Z ilc_li02], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/d/experimental-statistics/main-tables-flash-estimates-2025 (flash estimates)]|alt= A line chart showing the change in at-risk-of-poverty rate between 2019 and 2025 in the EU, by percentage of population. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article provides the latest developments in terms of income dynamics and poverty. All figures provided are based on structural and detailed indicators from European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions ([[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU-SILC]]), complemented with [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators flash estimates (FE)]. Since the EU-SILC income data refer to the previous year, Eurostat compiled flash estimates of the 2025 income to predict the evolution of the at-risk-of-poverty rate for the upcoming EU-SILC 2026. * EU-SILC 2025 results show that the [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|at-risk-of-poverty rate]] (AROP) at the EU level increased slightly, by 0.1 percentage points (pp), to 16.3% between 2023 and 2024 income years. EU-level flash estimates for 2025 income indicate a slight statistically non-significant increase, with the AROP rate expected to reach 16.4%. * Median [[Glossary:Equivalised_disposable_income|equivalised disposable income]] in Euro at the EU level, according to the EU-SILC 2025 results, increased by 6.2% from 2023 to 2024 income years. For 2025 income, flash estimates nowcast an overall increase of 3.5%, with statistically significant positive changes expected in all countries. This points to a slowdown, as the estimated increase is nearly half the rate observed over the previous 3 years, when increases consistently exceeded 6%. * EU-SILC 2025 data show that, at the EU level, real income in 2024 was 3.6% higher than the previous income year. Flash estimates for 2025 income point to a statistically significant increase of 1.2%. Real income in 2025 is nowcast to increase in 17 of the 25 countries for which estimates are available, and remain stable in Belgium, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, Austria, Romania and Sweden. By contrast, Estonia is expected to record a decrease. === At-risk-of-poverty rate === EU-SILC 2025 shows that 72.4 million people in the EU (16.3% of the population) were at risk of poverty. This share increased by 0.1 pp compared with EU-SILC 2024. Because EU-SILC income data refer to the previous year, Eurostat produced flash estimates for 2025 income to predict the evolution of AROP for the upcoming EU-SILC 2026. Flash estimates show a slight, statistically non-significant increase (0.1 pp) in AROP based on 2025 income at EU level. [[Image:At-risk-of-poverty rate, EU, 2019-2025 income years (% of population)V1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Change in at-risk-of-poverty rate, EU, 2019-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bae09bca-6bc5-4964-854e-63a3c56d0c42?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T14:15:40Z ilc_li02], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/d/experimental-statistics/main-tables-flash-estimates-2025 (flash estimates)]|alt= A line chart showing the change in at-risk-of-poverty rate between 2019 and 2025 in the EU, by percentage of population. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 1 shows the AROP rate in EU-SILC 2025 (2024 income), together with AROP flash estimates for 2025 income. According to EU-SILC 2025, Lithuania (22.6%), Latvia (22.0%), and Bulgaria (21.2%) recorded the highest at-risk-of-poverty rates. Denmark, Belgium, and Czechia reported the lowest shares (11.8%, 10.9% and 9.6%, respectively). Flash estimates are presented by arrows indicating the expected direction and size of the change. For 2025, AROP is expected to remain stable in most countries (18), decrease in Spain and Romania, and increase in 5 (Germany, Ireland, Croatia, Hungary and Slovenia). [[Image:At-risk-of-poverty rate by country, 2024-2025 income years Country V1.png|thumb|centre|500px|Table 1: At risk of poverty rate by country, 2024-2025 income
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/17027dca-c809-40a9-a8fb-6acbd628e240?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T14:17:26Z ilc_li02], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/d/experimental-statistics/main-tables-flash-estimates-2025 (flash estimates)]|alt= A table showing the change in at-risk-of-poverty rate by country between 2024 and 2025 in the EU. The columns present the percentage of population and the year-on-year change in percentage points. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Median equivalised disposable income === Figure 2 shows that, according to EU-SILC 2025 data, income at EU level increased in 2024 by 6.2% in nominal terms, and by 3.6% in real terms. Flash estimates indicate that, in 2025, EU income will continue to increase in both nominal and real terms by around 3.5% and 1.2%, respectively. [[Image:Median income, nominal versus real terms, EU, 2019-2025 income yearsV1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Change in median equivalised disposable income, nominal vs real terms, EU, 2019-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/adb77ddc-5172-410e-85fe-f9329f6362ca?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T14:22:19Z ilc_di01] , [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cbd424e1-401d-4d8d-bc15-ad36315d9df1?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T14:20:35Z prc_hicp_aind] , [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/d/experimental-statistics/main-tables-flash-estimates-2025 (flash estimates)]|alt= A line chart showing the change in median equivalised disposable income, nominal vs real terms between 2019 and 2024 in the EU. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 2 displays changes in median income at national level, in both nominal and real terms, from the EU-SILC 2025 (2024 income year), together with flash estimates for the 2025 income year. Between the 2023 and 2024 income years (covered by EU-SILC 2024 and 2025, respectively), median income increased in all EU countries except Luxembourg, where it declined by 1.5%This figure is flagged with a break in series . Among countries with increases, Slovakia (27.7%) and Croatia (22%) reported the strongest growth, while Belgium (2.8%) recorded the smallest increase. In real terms over the same period, 3 countries showed negative changes (Romania -0.8%, Belgium -1.5% and Luxembourg -3.7%). Of the remaining 22 countries, where real income in 2024 (EU-SILC 2025) was higher than in 2023 (EU-SILC 2024), Slovakia (23.8%) and Croatia (17.3%) experienced the steepest increases. Flash estimates in nominal terms for 2025 income show positive changes for all 25 countries for which estimates are available. In real terms, the nowcast median disposable income is estimated to increase in 17 of the 25 countries, and to remain stable in Belgium, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, Austria, Romania and Sweden. By contrast, Estonia is expected to see a statistically significant decrease. [[Image:Median_income_by_country,_nominal_versus_real_terms_(2024-2025_income_years)_Country20260522a.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Median equivalised disposable income by country, nominal vs real terms
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1e873428-ff5f-4eeb-b027-eabe4f2b6a01?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T14:32:56Z (ilc_di01)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/93948841-0826-46c2-a369-5afa42c68d34?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T14:34:12Z (prc_hicp_aind)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/d/experimental-statistics/main-tables-flash-estimates-2025 (flash estimates)]|alt= A table showing the median equivalised disposable income by country, nominal vs real terms between 2023 and 2024 in the EU. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Feedback === To help Eurostat improve these experimental statistics, users and researchers are kindly invited to give us their [mailto:ESTAT-FLASH-EST-INCOME@ec.europa.eu?subject=Feedback_on_experimental_statistics feedback by email] === Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=Data_for_SE_Latest_developments_in_income_dynamics_and_poverty_20260522a.xlsx |title=Download data}} === Data sources === The [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU-SILC]] indicators provide insights on the economic wellbeing and other living conditions on EU residents, based on data collected during a specific year, denoted as N. These data cover both household characteristics in year N and income for year N-1. Income for year N-1 is used to estimate income in year N within EU-SILC. To reflect differences in household size and composition and thus enable comparisons of income levels, the concept of equivalised disposable income is applied. It is calculated as total net (disposable) household income divided by the number of 'equivalent adults', using a standard (equivalence) scale. [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Eurostat flash estimates] complement structural and detailed EU-SILC indicators to capture the latest income changes, particularly relevant in times of crisis. Flash estimates are based on modelling and microsimulation techniques The flash estimates for Sweden are based on the national microsimulation model that consider the complex interaction between labour market developments, economic and monetary policies, and the implementation of social reforms. For this purpose, Eurostat uses the latest information on labour from the [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(EU-LFS)|EU Labour Force Survey]] together with the [https://euromod-web.jrc.ec.europa.eu/overview/what-is-euromod EUROMOD ] EUROMOD is a tax-benefit microsimulation model for the EU and UK that enables researchers and policy analysts to calculate the effects of taxes and benefits on household incomes and work incentives. Initially developed by the Institute for Social and Economic Research (ISER) at the University of Essex, it is now maintained, developed, and managed by the Joint Research Centre (JRC) of the European Commission, in collaboration with Eurostat and national authorities from the EU countries microsimulation model, which provides the effects of direct taxes, social security contributions and benefits on household income. The [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|at-risk-of-poverty rate]] (AROP) is the share of people whose equivalised disposable income (after [[Glossary:Social_transfers|social transfer]]) is below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold, set at 60% of the national [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Median median ] equivalised disposable income after social transfers. Income in real terms reflects the level of the equivalised disposable income after adjusting for price changes. The price deflator used is the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) with 2019 as the base year. This index measures changes in prices of consumer goods and services purchased by households relative to 2019. More information on inflation is available here: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Consumer_prices_-_inflation#Inflation:_price_changes_over_time_in_the_European_Union Consumer prices - inflation]. EU-SILC data on median in real terms derived using a combination of 2 data sources: * Distribution of income by quantiles ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/44a89755-870d-4f37-b6c4-5f2ce75155fa?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-21T15:13:07Z ilc_di01]) * HICP - annual data (average index and rate of change)([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/tec00027/default/table?lang=en prc_hicp_aind]) === Context === Indicators on poverty and income inequality are based on EU statistics on income and living conditions ([[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU-SILC]]). The [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|AROP ]] rate is part of the at risk of poverty or social exclusion rate defined in the framework of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:The_European_Pillar_of_Social_Rights_Action_Plan_(EU_2030_targets) EU 2030 target on poverty and social exclusion (AROPE)]. Providing timelier social statistics – especially indicators on income poverty and inequality – is a priority for the Commission and the [[Glossary:European_statistical_system_(ESS)|European Statistical System]]. To better monitor the effectiveness of social policies at EU level, [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Flash Estimates (FE)] offer early indicative results for income year N, until EU-SILC N+1 data become available. These estimates, which are part of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics experimental statistics] produced by Eurostat, are releases significantly earlier than the survey data. For example, flash estimates for income year 2025 are published in May 2026 and anticipate EU-SILC 2026, which also refers to income year 2025 but is scheduled for release in April 2027. === See also === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Living_conditions_in_Europe_-_poverty_and_social_exclusion Living conditions in Europe - poverty and social exclusion - Statistics Explained (europa.eu)] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/database EU-SILC - database] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/d/experimental-statistics/main-tables-flash-estimates-2025 Flash estimates on income and poverty indicators - main tables ] === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/income-inequality-poverty-indicators Income inequality and poverty indicators] *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=income_social_inclusion_living_conditions}} Income, social inclusion and living conditions] === Publications === *{{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-034|title=Flash estimates of income distribution: capturing labour market dynamics – 2025 edition}} *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/d/experimental-statistics/flash-estimate-income-inequalities-poverty-indicators-experimental-results-2025 Flash estimates on income inequalities and poverty indicators -experimental results - 2025] *{{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-032|title=Key figures on European living conditions – 2025 edition}} === Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/d/experimental-statistics/methodological-note-flash-estimates-2025 Flash estimates on income and poverty indicators - methodological notes] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/methodology EU SILC methodology] === Legislation === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/legislation Income and living conditions - legislation] === Visualisations === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RSI Regional Statistics Illustrated] === External links === *[https://euromod-web.jrc.ec.europa.eu/ EUROMOD Tax-benefit microsimulation model for the European Union] *[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/european-pillar-social-rights-building-fairer-and-more-inclusive-european-union_en European Pillar of Social Rights] *[https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=830&langId=en European Commission — Directorate General for Employment, Social Affairs & Inclusion — Indicators' Sub-Group of the Social Protection Committee] === Footnotes === {{Unit|topic=X_Social_statistics}} [[category:Population and social conditions|Latest developments in income dynamics and poverty]] [[Category:Income and living conditions|Latest developments in income dynamics and poverty]] [[Category:Living conditions|Latest developments in income dynamics and poverty]] [[Category:Household income, expenditure and debt|Latest developments in income dynamics and poverty]] [[Category:Statistical article|Latest developments in income dynamics and poverty]] [[Category:Experimental statistics|Latest developments in income dynamics and poverty]] [[Category:May2027|Latest developments in income dynamics and poverty]]

title: Labour market statistics at regional level
text:
Eurostat regional yearbook; 2026 edition; flagship publication; EU; regional statistics; NUTS; labour market; employment; focus on young people in the labour market; unemployment; employment rates; gender employment gap; young people neither in employment nor in education and training; NEETs; unemployment rate; long-term unemployment rate [[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH04 RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|380px|''Source:'' Eurostat]] Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 This article forms part of the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026]'', an annual [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications flagship publication]. It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the [[Glossary:EU|EU]], [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate]] countries. A [[Regional_yearbook_introduction#A_short_reading_guide|short reading guide]] is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps. All but 1 of the EU regions had an employment rate of at least 50.0% in 2025, with the lowest level recorded in the French outermost region of Mayotte (36.9%). Relatively low rates were recorded in some other outermost regions of France, as well as southern Italy and the Spanish autonomous regions of Ciudades de Ceuta y Melilla. In 2025, NEET rates were below 9.0% in every region of the Netherlands, Slovenia and Sweden, as well as in Luxembourg and Malta.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:SDG wheel icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:Compet and SDG wheel icons RYB2026_small.png|left]]
[[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH04_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/194b8ae4-edc2-4b87-a518-a704bd1950c3?lang=en lfst_r_lfe2emprt)]|alt="An infographic showing the ten EU regions with the highest employment rates for people aged 20 to 64. Data are shown in percent for 2025. Data are presented for the EU and selected NUTS level 2 regions with the highest rates. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image."]]
On 4 March 2021, the European Commission set out its ambition to build a stronger, more social EU by focusing on jobs and skills, paving the way for a fair, inclusive and resilient socio-economic recovery from the COVID-19 crisis. ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2021:102:FIN The European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan]'' (COM(2021) 102 final) outlines specific actions and headline targets to improve [[Glossary:Employment|employment]], skills and social protection across the EU. One of its principal targets is to have, by 2030, an EU [[Glossary:Employment rate|employment rate]] of at least 78% among people aged 20 to 64. Employment and social policies offer a broad range of practical benefits for people living in the EU, including employment support, mobility within the labour market, skills development, social protection and inclusion, as well as range of different rights at work. In 2025, there were 259.7 million people aged 20 to 64 in the EU (those considered to be of core working age). Of these, the [[Glossary:Labour force|labour force]] was composed of 209.9 million people, of which 197.7 million were [[Glossary:Employed person - LFS|employed]] and 12.1 million were [[Glossary:Unemployed|unemployed]] (not employed, actively seeking and available for work). There were 49.8 million people [[Glossary:People_outside_the_labour_force|outside the labour force]], for example students, retired people (if under the age of 65), people caring for other family members, volunteers and those unable to work due to a long-term illness or disability. Across NUTS level 2 regions, the Polish capital region of Warszawski stołeczny (86.9%) and the Czech capital region of Praha (86.0%) recorded the highest employment rates in 2025 among people aged 20 to 64. There were 2 other capitals that also ranked among the 10 EU regions with the highest employment rates: Sostinės regionas in Lithuania and Noord-Holland in the Netherlands. This chapter examines employment and unemployment patterns across EU regions, offering a detailed analysis of regional labour markets, with a focus on young people. It highlights key indicators such as employment rates, [[Glossary:Young_people_neither_in_employment_nor_in_education_and_training_(NEET)|young people who are neither in employment nor in education and training (NEET)]] and unemployment rates, providing an insight into regional disparities. ===Employment===
'''More about the data: employment rate targets''' One of the EU’s key policy objectives is to increase the number and share of people in work. This goal has been central to [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/eu-employment-policies_en EU employment policies] since the launch of the European employment strategy in 1997 and was subsequently integrated into the Lisbon and Europe 2020 strategies. The employment rate is a key indicator in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/dashboard/social-scoreboard/ social scoreboard], which monitors the implementation of the [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/european-pillar-social-rights-building-fairer-and-more-inclusive-european-union_en European Pillar of Social Rights]. By 2030, the EU has set a target of having an employment rate of at least 78% among its core working-age population (those aged 20 to 64). This age range reflects the growing share of young people who remain within education into their late teens and beyond, potentially limiting early labour market participation, while most EU residents retire by the age of 65. Individual EU countries have different employment rate targets. To achieve the overall EU target of 78% by 2030, individual countries presented and agreed national targets in June 2022. These are generally higher for countries that already had relatively high rates. For example, the target for Hungary has been set at 85.0%, for Malta at 84.6% and for Germany at 83.0%. The employment rate is also included in the EU’s [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/overview sustainable development goals (SDGs)] indicator set. Goal 8 seeks to promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, through full and productive employment and decent work for all.
'''''In 2025, the EU’s employment rate was 1.9 percentage points below its 2030 target''''' Prior to the COVID-19 crisis, the EU’s employment rate for the core working-age population (people aged 20 to 64) increased steadily for 6 consecutive years, reaching 72.7% by 2019. This upward development was interrupted in 2020 when the pandemic contributed to a fall of 1.0 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]]. However, the employment rate rebounded in 2021, returning to above its pre-pandemic level, and continued to rise in subsequent years, with particularly sharp increases in 2021 (up 1.4 points) and 2022 (up 1.5 points). By 2025, the EU’s employment rate had climbed to an all-time high (time series starts in 2009) of 76.1%, which was 1.9 points below the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan target for 2030. '''Map 1''' shows the employment rate in 2025 for NUTS level 2 regions. Almost half (47.1%) of all EU regions – 115 out of 244 regions – had already reached or surpassed the EU’s target of 78.0% by 2025. These 115 regions were found in clusters, with high concentrations in Czechia (all 8 regions), Denmark (4 out of 5 regions), Germany (34 out of 38 regions; the exceptions being Bremen, Berlin, Düsseldorf and Arnsberg), Ireland (all 3 regions), Hungary (6 out of 8 regions), the Netherlands (all 12 regions), Portugal (7 out of 9 regions), Slovakia (3 out of 4 regions) and Sweden (all 8 regions); this group also included Estonia, Cyprus and Malta. In 2025, a small group of 6 regions recorded the highest employment rates among NUTS level 2 regions, with rates of at least 85.0%: *Warszawski stołeczny, the Polish capital region (86.9%) *Praha, the Czech capital region (86.0%) *the archipelago of Åland in Finland (85.5%) *Utrecht in the Netherlands (85.4%) *the southern German region of Oberbayern (85.1%) *the northern Swedish region of Mellersta Norrland (85.0%). Beyond these 6 regions, a further 23 regions posted employment rates of at least 83.5% in 2025. These regions were concentrated in Germany (9 regions) and the Netherlands (6 regions), while Hungary and Sweden each accounted for 2 regions. The remaining regions in this group of 23 were distributed across Czechia, Lithuania, Malta and Slovakia (with a single region from each). In 2025, all multi-regional northern, eastern and southern EU countries reported that their capital region had a higher employment rate than their national average. For example, Romania’s capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov had an employment rate of 81.1%, which was 12.1 percentage points above the national average of 69.0%. By contrast, this pattern was reversed in 3 western EU countries – Belgium, Germany and Austria – where the capital regions recorded employment rates that were below their respective national averages. Indeed, a closer inspection reveals that Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest (63.9%) and Wien (71.3%) registered the lowest employment rates across all regions of Belgium and Austria, respectively. '''''In 2025, the French outermost regions of Mayotte and Guyane and the southern Italian regions of Calabria, Campania and Sicilia recorded the lowest employment rates''''' Many of the regions with relatively low employment rates were rural, sparsely populated, or regions on the periphery of the EU. This pattern was particularly apparent in southern regions of Spain and Italy, much of Greece, some regions in Romania, and the outermost regions of France. These regions were typically characterised by limited employment opportunities, especially for individuals with intermediate and high skill levels. Former industrial heartlands form another group of regions characterised by relatively low employment rates. Some of these have witnessed the negative impact of globalisation on traditional sectors of their economies (such as coal mining, steel or textiles manufacturing). Examples include a band of regions running from north-east France into the Région wallonne (Belgium). In 2025, approximately a quarter of all EU regions – 64 out of 244 regions – recorded employment rates below 74.0%. Among others, this group comprised: *11 French regions, including all 5 outermost regions; Mayotte and Guyane recorded the lowest employment rates in the EU, at 36.9% and 50.0%, respectively *11 Italian regions, concentrated almost exclusively in central and southern Italy, with the lowest rates observed in Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicilia (51.4%) *11 out of 13 Greek regions, the exceptions being Kriti and Peloponnisos *11 Spanish regions, many of them peripheral, island or predominantly rural regions *7 of the 8 Romanian regions, the exception being the capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov *the capital regions of Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest in Belgium (63.9%), Lazio in Italy (69.3%), Wien in Austria (71.3%) and Attiki in Greece (73.1%); Luxembourg (73.9%) also recorded a relatively low employment rate.

At the other end of the range, the lowest regional disparities in employment rates – with a coefficient of variation of 2.0% or less – were recorded in the [[Glossary:Nordic Member States|Nordic EU countries]] of Finland and Sweden, as well as the Netherlands and Portugal. '''Figure 1''' shows that regional employment rates converged to some degree between 2015 and 2025. The coefficient of variation for the EU as a whole fell from 12.5% to 9.2%. In 15 (out of 17) EU countries for which data are available, the disparities between inter-regional employment rates narrowed. The largest falls – in relative terms – occurred in Finland, Portugal and Spain, where the coefficient decreased by at least 40%. By contrast, Denmark and Romania were the only EU countries to report an increase in regional disparities, rising 22.2% and 2.6%, respectively.

'''''The EU’s gender employment gap was 9.7 percentage points in 2025''''' The gender employment gap is included in the EU’s SDGs indicator set. Goal 5 seeks to achieve gender equality by, among other actions, ending all forms of discrimination, violence, and any harmful practices against women and girls, while promoting women’s social and economic empowerment. Long-standing challenges related to female participation in the labour force are reflected in persistent gender gaps in employment and pay. These gaps exist for a variety of reasons, including: *women often bear a disproportionate share of unpaid care and household chores that may limit their availability for paid employment *gender bias and discrimination when hiring, promoting and paying women *fewer women in leadership positions to draw attention to gender-related policies or to mentor more junior female staff *a lack of affordable childcare and support for working parents *disincentives in tax and benefit system that can lead to second earners bearing a higher tax burden when they choose to participate in the labour market *occupational segregation, with women often concentrated in specific activities that are characterised by lower wages and/or fewer opportunities for career development. In 2025, the EU employment rate for men aged 20 to 64 was 80.9%, while the corresponding rate for women of the same age was considerably lower, at 71.2%. This resulted in a gender employment gap – defined here as the difference between male and female employment rates – of 9.7 percentage points. As part of its broader target to increase the overall employment rate to 78% by 2030, the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan also includes a subgoal of halving the gender employment gap. This implies reducing the gap to 5.7 percentage points by 2030, equivalent to an average annual decrease of 0.5 points from 2019 onwards. According to the latest available data, the gender employment gap in the EU fell from 10.0 percentage points in 2024 to 9.7 points in 2025. '''''In 2025, more than a quarter of EU regions already had a gender employment gap below the 2030 target''''' As noted above, regions with relatively narrow gender employment gaps are often characterised by high overall employment rates, which may reflect more inclusive labour markets, higher female participation and greater availability of part-time or flexible working arrangements. In 2025, 65 out of 244 NUTS level 2 regions – corresponding to more than a quarter of all EU regions – recorded a gender employment gap of less than 5.7 percentage points, thereby already surpassing the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan target for 2030 (see '''Map 2'''). These 65 regions were mainly concentrated in France (14 regions), Germany (12 regions), Sweden (7 out of 8 regions), Belgium (5 regions), Portugal (5 regions) and Finland (all 5 regions); among others, they also included all of the Baltic regions, as well as both regions in Slovenia. Some of the lowest gender employment gaps were recorded in Baltic and Nordic regions. In 2025, there were 8 regions where the gap between male and female employment rates was less than 1.0 percentage points. In 5 of these regions, male employment rates remained slightly higher. This group included: *the Finnish regions of Etelä-Suomi, Länsi-Suomi (both 0.1 percentage points) and Åland (0.7 percentage points) *Estonia (0.5 percentage points) *the Lithuanian region of Vidurio ir vakarų Lietuvos regionas (0.7 percentage points). Furthermore, there were 3 regions that reported higher female (than male) employment rates: *the Lithuanian capital region of Sostinės regionas, where the female employment rate was 3.3 points higher than the male rate *the French outermost regions of Martinique and Guadeloupe, where female employment rates exceeded male rates by 5.0 and 1.0 percentage points, respectively. This atypical pattern may reflect a combination of factors, including higher male participation in informal or seasonal activities (such as fishing), alongside higher levels of female employment in the relatively stable public-sector and service-sector occupations. '''''The widest gender employment gaps were recorded in the central Greek region of Sterea Elláda and the southern Italian regions of Puglia, Campania and Sicilia''''' Despite some progress in reducing the gender employment gap, female employment rates continue to lag behind male rates in the vast majority of EU regions. Regions with wider gaps are often characterised by high unemployment, weaker and more informal labour markets, and a higher share of women outside the labour force. Low female employment rates may reflect a combination of constraints: women are more likely to take on unpaid family and caregiving responsibilities, while limited access to affordable childcare and support for older people, alongside persistent expectations around traditional family roles, can further reduce their participation in paid employment. In 2025, 26 NUTS level 2 regions reported gender employment gaps of at least 18.0 percentage points. These regions were concentrated in southern and eastern EU countries: *10 of the 13 regions in Greece (the exceptions being Attiki, Ipeiros and Kriti) *8 regions in Italy, 7 of which were in the south (the exception being Veneto) *5 of the 8 regions in Romania (the exceptions being Bucureşti-Ilfov, Nord-Vest and Vest) *the Spanish autonomous regions of Ciudad de Melilla and Ciudad de Ceuta *the French outermost region of Mayotte. At the very upper end of the distribution, the widest gender employment gaps in the EU were observed in: *the central Greek region of Sterea Elláda, which recorded a gender employment gap of 29.0 percentage points in 2025; this may reflect, at least in part, a high male employment rate (the highest in Greece), with a concentration of jobs in traditionally male-dominated industrial sectors *the southern Italian regions of Puglia (28.7 percentage points), Campania (28.2 points), Sicilia (28.1 points), Calabria (25.4 points) and Basilicata (25.3 points) *Sud-Muntenia in southern Romania (25.1 points), the only other region in the EU with a gap of at least 25.0 percentage points.

'''More about the data: employment rates by educational attainment''' An individual’s level of educational attainment can play a key role when seeking employment. People with a tertiary level of educational attainment (as defined by the [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|international standard classification of education (ISCED 2011 levels 5 to 8)]]) generally enjoy the most success when trying to find work. They also tend to be better shielded from the risks of unemployment than their peers with lower levels of educational attainment. The data presented in this section concern people aged 25 to 64, as this represents a cohort of individuals who have generally completed their education or training and are most likely to be actively participating in the labour market. As such, it excludes younger individuals who may still be studying, as well as older individuals who may be in retirement.
In 2025, 185.1 million people aged 25 to 64 were employed across the EU. The largest share of this cohort consisted of people with an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (ISCED levels 3 to 4; 44.3%), closely followed by those with a tertiary level of educational attainment (ISCED levels 5 to 8; 41.5%). A relatively small share of the EU workforce had no more than a lower secondary education (ISCED levels 0 to 2; 14.1%). The strong links between educational attainment and employment opportunities are reflected in the latest EU employment rates for 2025: *58.9% for people with no more than a lower secondary education (hereafter referred to as a low level of education) *78.5% for people with an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (a medium level of education) *88.1% for people with a tertiary level of education (a high level of education). '''Map 3''' presents employment rates in 2025 for people aged 25 to 64 according to these 3 different levels of educational attainment. *There were 53 NUTS level 2 regions where fewer than half of all people with a low level of education were in employment. By contrast, employment rates for people with medium or high levels of education exceeded 50.0% in every region of the EU. *There were 83 NUTS level 2 regions where at least 90.0% of all people with a high level of education were in employment. By contrast, employment rates for people with low or medium levels of education remained consistently below 90.0% across every region of the EU. '''''In 2025, the Slovak region of Východné Slovensko recorded an employment rate of 25.6% among people with a low level of education, the smallest share among EU regions''''' The first part of '''Map 3''' shows employment rates for people aged 25 to 64 with a low level of education. In 2025, there were 53 NUTS level 2 regions with employment rates below 50.0% for this cohort. This group included two capital regions: Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest (Belgium) and Grad Zagreb (Croatia). These 53 regions were mainly concentrated in: *eastern EU countries (excluding Czechia, Hungary and Slovenia) *Belgium, particularly in the south *north-eastern France and the outermost regions of France *southern Italy. In 2025, the lowest employment rates for people aged 25 to 64 with a low level of education were recorded in the eastern Slovak region of Východné Slovensko (25.6%) and the French outermost regions of Mayotte (27.0%) and Guyane (28.3%); in other words, around a quarter of people in this cohort were in employment. A further 8 regions reported employment rates below 40.0%: *the Romanian regions of Sud-Est (36.9%), Sud-Vest Oltenia (37.1%) and Centru (38.4%) *Panonska Hrvatska in Croatia (37.6%) *Severozapaden in Bulgaria (38.3%) *the southern Italian regions of Campania (38.6%) and Sicilia (38.8%) *the French outermost region of Guadeloupe (39.2%). '''''Employment rates for people with a medium level of education were generally low across southern Italy, with Calabria recording the lowest rate (56.0% in 2025)''''' The second map shows employment rates for people aged 25 to 64 with a medium level of education. In 2025, there were 10 NUTS level 2 regions that recorded an employment rate of at least 87.0% for this cohort, they included: *4 regions from Czechia (including the capital region of Praha) *3 regions from Portugal *Malta *Åland in Finland *Pest in Hungary. At the lower end of the distribution, there were 3 regions where, in 2025, fewer than 60.0% of people with a medium level of education were in employment: *the southern Italian regions of Calabria (56.0%) and Campania (59.2%) *the Belgian capital region – Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest (58.3%). '''''The highest employment rate among tertiary-educated people was recorded in the Portuguese Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6% in 2025)''''' The third map shows employment rates for people aged 25 to 64 with a high level of education. In 2025, there were 83 NUTS level 2 regions across the EU that recorded employment rates of at least 90.0% for this cohort. These regions were mainly clustered across: *Bulgaria (all 6 regions) *Croatia (3 out of 4 regions) *Lithuania (both regions) *Hungary (all 8 regions) *the Netherlands (8 out of 12 regions) *Poland (16 out of 17 regions) *Portugal (8 out of 9 regions) *Romania (all 8 regions) *Slovenia (both regions) *Slovakia (all 4 regions) *Malta had a similarly high level. The highest proportion of tertiary-educated people in employment was recorded in the Portuguese island region of Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%). Employment rates above 93.0% were also observed in 5 regions located in eastern EU countries: *the capital regions of Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (93.6%), Warszawski stołeczny in Poland (93.5%) and Bratislavský kraj in Slovakia (93.3%) *the Romanian regions of Nord-Est (93.4%) and Centru (93.3%). In 2025, employment rates for people aged 25 to 64 with a tertiary level of education were generally higher in capital regions than their respective national averages. This may reflect the ability of capital regions to attract highly qualified individuals, exerting considerable ‘pull effects’ through the diverse educational, employment and social/lifestyle opportunities that they offer. This pattern was particularly evident in several eastern and southern EU countries, for example: *in Czechia, the employment rate for tertiary-educated people in the capital region of Praha was 2.6 percentage points above the national average *in Spain, the rate in the capital region of Comunidad de Madrid was 2.2 percentage points above the national average. A similar, although less pronounced, situation was observed in Slovakia, Greece, Croatia, Poland, Denmark, Bulgaria and Lithuania, where the gap between these 2 rates also exceeded 1.0 percentage points. By contrast, there were 4 western EU countries where employment rates for tertiary-educated people in the capital region were at least 1.0 percentage points below the national average: *in Belgium, the employment rate for tertiary-educated people in the capital Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest was 6.1 percentage points below the national average *in Austria, the rate in the capital region of Wien was 4.5 percentage points below the national average. A similar, although less pronounced, pattern was observed in Germany and France, where the gap between the capital region and the national rate was 2.9 and 1.0 percentage points, respectively. There were 4 regions across the EU where, in 2025, the employment rate for people aged 25 to 64 with a high level of education was below 78.5%. These regions were predominantly rural, typically characterised by relatively large agricultural sectors and more limited opportunities for highly skilled employment. They were exclusively located in southern EU countries: *3 regions in Italy – Calabria (73.1%, the lowest rate in the EU), Sicilia and Campania *Ionia Nisia (75.8%) in Greece.

'''More about the data: young people neither in employment nor in education and training (NEET)''' The share of young people (aged 15 to 29) who are neither in employment nor in education and training (NEET) provides a useful measure for studying the vulnerability of young people in terms of their labour market participation and social exclusion. The NEET rate is expressed relative to the total population of the same age (15 to 29); the numerator includes not only young people who are unemployed but also young people who are outside the labour force for reasons other than education or training (for example, because they are unable to work for health reasons, caring for family members, volunteering or travelling). Within the framework of the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan, the EU has set a policy target to reduce the NEET rate from 12.6% (in 2019) to 9.0% by 2030. This target forms part of broader efforts to strengthen labour market participation and improve social inclusion among young people. Lowering the share of young people who are neither in employment nor in education and training is also considered important for helping to address skills shortages and supporting the EU’s long-term economic competitiveness. The NEET rate is also included in the EU’s SDG indicator set. Goal 8 seeks to promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all.
'''''In 2025, 11.0% of young people aged 15 to 29 in the EU were neither in employment nor in education and training''''' Economic crises tend to impact young people disproportionately, as they are more likely to work under temporary and other atypical contracts that are easier to terminate. The NEET rate helps assess the share of young people who have not transitioned from education or training to employment. It is generally seen as a more comprehensive measure than the unemployment rate, as it more closely reflects young people’s risk of social and labour market exclusion. Having peaked at 16.1% in 2013, the EU’s NEET rate subsequently fell during 6 consecutive years. The COVID-19 pandemic reversed this trend, pushing the NEET rate up to 13.8% in 2020, after which it resumed its downward trajectory. By 2025, it stood at 11.0%, marking a modest decrease of 0.1 percentage points compared with the previous year. Of the 241 NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available in 2025, 146 regions recorded NEET rates below the EU average of 11.0%. A further 93 regions reported rates above the EU average, while 2 regions – Latvia and Etelä-Suomi in Finland – had the same rate as the EU (see '''Map 4'''). This uneven split suggests a skewed distribution, with relatively few high values pulling the EU average upward. At the upper end of the distribution, 27 regions recorded NEET rates of at least 16.0% among young people aged 15 to 29. The highest rates were generally observed in predominantly rural regions of southern and eastern EU countries, as well as in the French outermost regions. Within this group, 5 regions had NEET rates of at least 25.0%, including: *the French outermost regions of Mayotte (47.2%), Guyane (31.9%) and La Réunion (25.2%), with Mayotte recording the highest NEET rate in the EU *the Romanian regions of Sud-Vest Oltenia (27.9%) and Sud-Est (26.3%) *the Bulgarian region of Severozapaden (25.3%). '''''The lowest NEET rate was in the Hungarian capital region of Budapest, 3.8% in 2025''''' In 2025, 87 NUTS level 2 regions reported a NEET rate of 9.0% or less (the EU’s policy target to be reached by 2030). This group was mainly concentrated in northern Belgium (5 regions, mainly from Vlaams Gewest), Czechia (6 out of 8 regions), Ireland (2 out of 3 regions), northern and central Italy (7 regions), the Netherlands (all 12 regions), Slovenia (both regions), Slovakia (3 out of 4 regions) and Sweden (all 8 regions); it also included Luxembourg and Malta. Looking in more detail at the lower end of the distribution, 24 regions recorded NEET rates below 6.5% in 2025, including: *the capital regions of Hungary, Czechia, Poland, the Netherlands, Bulgaria and Sweden; the Hungarian capital region of Budapest recorded the lowest rate in the EU, at 3.8% *a further 9 regions from the Netherlands (in addition to the capital region of Noord-Holland), with the lowest rate in Utrecht (4.0%); the only Dutch regions to record rates above 6.5% were Drenthe and Friesland *4 regions from Sweden (in addition to the capital region of Stockholm), with the lowest rate observed in Sydsverige (4.6%) *5 other regions with particularly low rates, dispersed across the EU, including Schwaben in southern Germany, Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen in northern Italy, Nyugat-Dunántúl in western Hungary, Prov. West-Vlaanderen in northern Belgium and Centro in Portugal. In 2025, capital regions in the EU generally recorded lower NEET rates than their national averages. There were only 5 exceptions observed among multi-regional EU countries, where the rate in the capital region was higher than the national average: *Berlin in Germany (13.9%), where the share of young people neither in employment nor in education or training was 4.4 percentage points above the national average (9.5%) *Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest in Belgium (12.8%), 3.0 points above the national average (9.8%) *Wien in Austria (12.9%), 2.6 percentage points above the national average (10.3%) *Lazio in Italy (13.7%), slightly above the national average (13.3%) *Eastern and Midland in Ireland (8.3%), marginally above the national average (8.1%).

High levels of youth unemployment can lead to considerable economic and social challenges. Indeed, persistent unemployment among young people is likely to increase the risk of poverty, social exclusion and mental health issues, while reducing lifetime earnings and productivity. It may also contribute to concerns about social cohesion and public confidence in institutions. Youth employment is a key priority, with the EU aiming to reduce youth unemployment and increase the youth employment rate, ensuring young citizens have access to opportunities. The [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/eu-employment-policies/youth-employment-support/reinforced-youth-guarantee_en Youth Guarantee], reinforced in 2020, provides young people with an offer of employment, education, apprenticeship or traineeship within 4 months of becoming unemployed or leaving education. Unemployment rates in the EU vary considerably as a function of age: in 2025, they were highest among young people aged 15 to 29 (11.7%) and lowest among people aged 45 to 54 and aged 55 to 64 (both 4.4%). Subject to data availability, young people systematically faced the highest unemployment rates in every NUTS level 2 region. For example, in the Croatian capital region of Grad Zagreb, the unemployment rate of young people (12.2%) was 4.1 times as high as the overall rate (3.0%), while in the southern Italian region of Sicilia, the unemployment rate of young people (27.2%) was 15.0 percentage points higher than the overall rate (12.2%). '''Map 5''' illustrates the distribution of youth unemployment rates among people aged 15 to 29 across NUTS level 2 regions. In 2025, the highest youth unemployment rates were mainly concentrated in southern EU countries, although several regions in Belgium, France, Romania and Sweden also recorded relatively high rates. By contrast, some of the lowest rates were observed in a band of regions extending from the Netherlands, Germany, northern Italy and Austria through parts of Poland, Czechia and Hungary. In 2025, particularly high youth unemployment rates – of at least 25.0% – were recorded in 11 regions across the EU, including: *the Spanish autonomous regions of Ciudades de Ceuta y Melilla and the western Spanish region of Extremadura *all 5 of the French outermost regions – Mayotte, Martinique, Guadeloupe, Guyane and La Réunion – as well as the French island region of Corse (2024 data) *the southern Italian regions of Campania and Sicilia. At the lower end of the distribution, the lowest youth unemployment rates were generally observed in predominantly urban regions, including several capital regions. In total, there were 9 regions in the EU that recorded rates below 5.0%: *3 capital regions in eastern EU countries – Yugozapaden (Bulgaria), Warszawski stołeczny (Poland) and Praha (Czechia) *2 additional regions in Czechia – Střední Čechy and Jihovýchod *Weser-Ems in north-western Germany *Nyugat-Dunántúl in western Hungary *Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen in northern Italy (2024 data) *Zeeland in the south-west of the Netherlands, which recorded the lowest youth unemployment rate in the EU, at 3.6%. From an economic perspective, unemployment reflects unused labour capacity and can reduce a country’s or region’s productive potential. It also leads to lower tax revenues and higher public spending on social benefits. At the same time, unemployment has significant social impacts. It results in a loss of income for individuals. Beyond these financial effects, it is also associated with a higher risk of poverty, social exclusion, debt and homelessness, and may have adverse effects on (mental) health and overall well-being.
'''More about the data: the unemployment rate''' Within this section, data are presented for people aged 15 to 74; this is the standard age range used by Eurostat and the [[Glossary:International Labour Organization (ILO)|International Labour Organization (ILO)]] for analysing unemployment. The unemployment rate is defined as the share of unemployed people (aged 15 to 74) in the total labour force (in other words, employed and unemployed people) of the same age group. Note that the unemployment rate is not the opposite of the employment rate, as the two indicators use different denominators: the unemployment rate is based on the labour force, while the employment rate is based on the population.
The EU unemployment rate fell from a peak of 11.6% in 2013, declining over 6 consecutive years to 6.8% by 2019. With the onset of the COVID-19 crisis, the rate increased 0.4 percentage points in 2020 and remained almost unchanged in 2021 (down 0.1 points), as the pandemic continued to affect much of the EU economy. Following a marked decline in 2022, unemployment continued to fall in 2023 and 2024 at a more moderate pace, reaching its lowest rate since the start of the time series in 2009. The rate was unchanged in 2025, at 6.0%. In 2025, there were 13.3 million unemployed people aged 15 to 74 across the EU. Compared with 2024, the number of unemployed people in 2025 was 223 000 higher. '''Map 6''' presents unemployment rates (for people aged 15 to 74) across NUTS level 2 regions. In 2025, the distribution of regional unemployment rates was slightly skewed towards lower values: of the 241 NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available, 103 had rates above the EU average of 6.0%, while 137 were below this level; Piemonte (northern Italy) reported an unemployment rate equal to the EU average. The highest regional unemployment rates were generally concentrated in southern EU countries and France’s outermost regions, while the lowest rates were mainly observed across eastern EU countries and parts of southern Germany and northern Italy. In 2025, 23 regions across the EU reported unemployment rates of at least 10.0%, as shown by the darkest shade in '''Map 6'''. At the upper end of the distribution, the Spanish autonomous region of Ciudad de Melilla and the French outermost region of Mayotte recorded the highest rates, both 24.9%, closely followed by Ciudad de Ceuta (24.3%). Leaving these atypical Spanish and French regions aside, the highest unemployment rates – above 12.0% – were observed in: *the north-western Greek region of Dytiki Makedonia *several other Spanish regions – Andalucía, Extremadura, Canarias, Castilla-La Mancha and Región de Murcia *the southern Italian regions of Campania and Sicilia *the Belgian capital region of Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest. '''''The Czech region of Střední Čechy (which surrounds the capital region of Praha) reported the lowest regional unemployment rate in the EU, at 1.5% in 2025''''' At the lower end of the distribution, there were 25 regions with unemployment rates below 3.0% in 2025, as shown by the lightest shade in '''Map 6'''. These regions were mainly concentrated in Czechia (5 regions), Germany and Poland (both 7 regions). There were a number of other regions that recorded rates below this level including Yugozapaden (the Bulgarian capital region), Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen and Provincia Autonoma di Trento (northern Italy), Zeeland (the Netherlands), Bucureşti-Ilfov (the capital region of Romania) and Bratislavský kraj (the capital region of Slovakia). The Czech region of Střední Čechy (which surrounds the capital region of Praha) recorded the lowest unemployment rate in the EU, at 1.5%. Unemployment rates in the capital regions of multi-regional eastern and Baltic EU countries were consistently below their national averages. In 2025, this pattern was particularly pronounced in Romania and Slovakia, where national rates were 3.4 and 2.2 times as high as than those in Bucureşti-Ilfov and Bratislavský kraj, respectively. By contrast, capital regions in most western and Nordic EU countries recorded higher unemployment rates than their national averages. This pattern was observed for Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Ireland, France, Austria, Finland and Sweden. In this group of countries, capital regions often recorded the highest regional unemployment rate; the only exceptions were France and Sweden. The contrast was most evident in Belgium, where Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest recorded an unemployment rate of 12.6%, which was more than twice the national average (6.4%). A comparable, although less pronounced, pattern was observed in the German and Austrian capital regions of Berlin and Wien, as their unemployment rates were 1.7 times as high as their respective national averages. High rates often signal structural issues in the labour market, skill mismatches or economic stagnation, leading to income loss, social exclusion and increased pressure on public welfare systems and community well-being. A ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32016H0220(01) Council recommendation on the integration of the long-term unemployed into the labour market]'' (2016/C 67/01) includes 3 key steps (aimed at supporting vulnerable groups): *encouraging registration with an employment service *providing individual in-depth assessments *offering job integration agreements. In March 2024, the European Commission presented an [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-sets-out-actions-tackle-labour-and-skills-shortages-2024-03-20_en action plan to tackle labour and skills shortages] driven by demographic changes, emerging skill demands and poor working conditions. Building on existing initiatives – including the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan – it supports training, mobility and attracting talent – one of its key measures is the financing of new projects aimed at achieving zero long-term unemployment. Furthermore, a range of active labour market policies, including job training and upskilling, wage subsidies for hiring long-term unemployed people, public employment programmes, job matching services and school-to-work transition programmes are funded through EU cohesion instruments. In 2025, 4.2 million people across the EU had been unemployed for more than a year. The long-term unemployment ratio – which is defined as the share of unemployed people (aged 15 to 74) that has been unemployed for 12 months or more – stood at 31.6%. '''Map 7''' shows the long-term unemployment ratio (for people aged 15 to 74) across NUTS level 2 regions. Of the 207 regions for which data are available in 2025, 86 recorded ratios above the EU average of 31.6%, while 120 were below and 1 recorded the same rate. The highest ratios were predominantly concentrated in a cluster of regions in Baltic, southern and eastern EU countries, as well as in southern Belgium, eastern Germany and the French outermost regions. There were 27 regions across the EU where the long-term unemployment ratio was at least 50.0% (indicating that at least half of all unemployed people had been without work for at least a year). Such patterns may reflect structural characteristics of regional labour markets, including skills mismatches, limited job creation, and broader economic conditions such as deindustrialisation or economies with a high reliance on agriculture and a limited industrial or service base, often accompanied by outward migration of younger populations. This group of 27 regions included: *all 4 regions in Slovakia (2024 data for Bratislavský kraj), with the easternmost region of Východné Slovensko recording the highest ratio in the EU, with almost three quarters (72.5%) of unemployed people without work for at least a year *8 of the 13 regions in Greece, with the highest ratio observed in Sterea Elláda (66.9%) *9 of the 21 regions in Italy, predominantly in the southern half of the country, with the highest ratio recorded in Molise (70.1%) *the Spanish autonomous regions of Ciudades de Ceuta y Melilla *the northern Bulgarian region of Severen tsentralen *the French outermost regions of Mayotte and Guadeloupe *the Romanian capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov. In 2025, there were 13 regions across the EU where the long-term unemployment ratio was below 15.0% (as shown by the lightest shade in '''Map 7'''). These regions were concentrated in the Netherlands, with Utrecht recording the lowest ratio in the EU, at 11.0%. The remainder of this group of 13 regions was composed of: *6 additional regions from the Netherlands *3 of the 5 regions in Denmark, including the capital region of Hovedstaden *2 regions in north-west France, Bretagne and Pays de la Loire *Prov. West-Vlaanderen in northern Belgium.

Eurostat compiles and publishes labour market statistics for the EU and individual EU countries, as well as for EU regions. In addition, data are also available for 3 EFTA countries – Iceland, Norway and Switzerland – and several candidate countries – Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Serbia and Türkiye – and their statistical regions. The EU-LFS population generally consists of people aged 15 or over living in private households; definitions are aligned with those provided by the International Labour Organization (ILO). EU-LFS microdata are collected through a survey to obtain information on an individual’s demographic background, labour status, employment characteristics of their main job, hours worked, employment characteristics of their second job (if relevant), time-related underemployment, the search for employment, education and training, previous work experience of people not in employment and their income. These statistics are aggregated by region and are generally published down to NUTS level 2. When evaluating regional information from the EU-LFS, it is important to bear in mind that the information presented relates to the region where the respondent has their usual residence and that this may be different to the region where their place of work is situated as a result of commuter flows. The collection of EU-LFS data up to and including reference year 2020 was conducted by national statistical authorities in accordance with ''Council Regulation (EEC) No 577/98''. A new legal basis was introduced for EU-LFS data from 2021 onwards: ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32019R1700 Regulation (EU) 2019/1700] establishing a common framework for European statistics relating to persons and households, based on data at individual level collected from samples''. Furthermore, ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2019/2240 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2240]'' specifies the technical items of the dataset, establishing formats for the transmission of information and specifying the detailed arrangements and content of the quality reports on the organisation of the sample survey. This change in legal basis implies a break in series between 2020 and 2021; results obtained before and after 1 January 2021 are consequently not fully comparable. Some countries/regions have other quality concerns that may impact geographical comparability. *Changes in survey methodology led to a break in series for German data in 2020. Therefore, data for Germany from 2020 onwards should not be compared directly with those for previous years. In addition, data collection during 2020 was impacted by technical issues and COVID-19 measures and hence there is a low degree of reliability for some regions. For more information, please refer the online methodological publication for the [[EU_labour_force_survey|EU’s labour force survey]]. ==== Indicator definitions ==== The '''labour force''' includes all people who were either employed or unemployed during the reference week. This aggregate includes people offering their work capacity on the labour market: as such it reflects the supply side. In the context of the EU-LFS, employed people include those aged 15 to 89 who, during the reference week, performed work – even if just for 1 hour – for pay, profit or family gain. Alternatively, the person was not at work, but had a job or business from which they were temporarily absent, for example due to illness, holiday, maternity or paternity leave, job-related training, paid parental leave or working time arrangements. This definition follows guidelines of the [https://www.ilo.org/ International Labour Organization (ILO)]. Within this publication, most labour force indicators are for a narrower definition of core working-age people, namely people aged 20 to 64. '''Employment rate''' The employment rate is the percentage of employed people in relation to the comparable population. The comparison is generally made within the population of core working-age (defined within this publication as people aged 20 to 64). Regional labour market disparities are measured using the population-weighted coefficient of variation. This indicator compares the standard deviation of regional employment rates with the national employment rate, while weighting each region by its population size. The aggregated EU value is calculated using all available regions in EU countries. However, dispersion across countries are only published for countries that have more than 4 NUTS level 2 regions. As a result, data are not presented for Estonia, Ireland, Croatia, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Slovenia or Slovakia; equally, they are not published for Iceland, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia or Serbia. The gender employment gap is defined as the employment rate for men minus the employment rate for women (among people aged 20 to 64). Employment rates may be calculated for other cohorts according to a range of socio-economic criteria, for example, by educational attainment. Within this publication, the employment rate of people with different levels of educational attainment concerns people aged 25 to 64 who had completed: *no more than a lower secondary education (as defined by the [[International_Standard_Classification_of_Education_(ISCED)|international standard classification of education (ISCED)]] levels 0 to 2) *an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (as defined by ISCED levels 3 to 4) *a tertiary level of education (as defined by ISCED levels 5 to 8) – in other words, people who had completed a short-cycle tertiary education, bachelor’s, master’s or doctoral (PhD) degree. '''Young people neither in employment nor in education or training (NEET)''' The share of young people who are neither in employment nor in education and training, abbreviated as NEET, corresponds to the share of the population (of a given age group and sex) that is not employed and not involved in further (formal or non-formal) education or training during the 4 weeks ending with the reference week. The numerator refers to people meeting these 2 conditions, while the denominator is the population (of the same age group and sex), excluding respondents who did not answer the question in the survey about participation in regular (formal) education and training. For the purpose of this publication, the share of young people neither in employment nor in education or training relates to people aged 15 to 29. '''Unemployment''' Eurostat‘s unemployment statistics are based on guidelines provided by the ILO. Unemployed people are those aged 15 to 74 who are without work, but who have actively sought employment in the 4 weeks preceding the survey’s reference week (or have already found a job to start within the subsequent 3 months) and are available to begin work within the following 2 weeks. The unemployment rate is defined as the number of unemployed people expressed as a percentage of the labour force of the same age (defined within this publication as people aged 15 to 74). The youth unemployment rate is defined as the number of unemployed people aged 15 to 29 expressed as a percentage of the labour force of the same age. Long-term unemployment refers to unemployed people aged 15 to 74 whose duration of unemployment is 12 months or more. The long-term unemployment ratio is the number of long-term unemployed people expressed as a percentage of the number of unemployed people of the same age. ===Context=== '''Safeguarding jobs and ensuring fair working conditions''' Since 2020, the European Commission has introduced several initiatives to support labour market resilience in line with the European Pillar of Social Rights. *''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:32020R0672 Council Regulation (EU) 2020/672]'' established the [https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/eu-financial-assistance/sure_en European instrument for temporary support to mitigate unemployment risks in an emergency (SURE)] to protect jobs and protect income during the COVID-19 crisis. *The [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/eu-employment-policies/youth-employment-support_en Youth employment support] initiative reinforced the [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/eu-employment-policies/youth-employment-support/reinforced-youth-guarantee_en Youth Guarantee], providing additional support to vocational training, apprenticeships and entrepreneurship opportunities for young people. *The [https://commission.europa.eu/funding-tenders/find-funding/eu-funding-programmes/just-transition-fund_en Just Transition Fund] helps communities manage the socio-economic costs/effects of the shift to a climate-neutral economy. *''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2022/2041/oj Directive (EU) 2022/2041 on adequate minimum wages in the European Union]'' promotes fair minimum wages, strengthens collective bargaining and supports upward social convergence across EU countries. *A ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=oj:JOC_2023_041_R_0001 Council Recommendation on adequate minimum income ensuring active inclusion 2023/C 41/01]'' complements earlier initiatives by addressing income protection for individuals outside employment. *The EU has also addressed emerging forms of employment through ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/2831 Directive (2024/2831) on improving working conditions in platform work]'' – an initiative aimed at strengthening conditions for those working with digital labour platforms (for example, food delivery riders or taxi drivers). *The ''[https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/union-skills_en Union of skills]'' (COM(2025) 90 final) aims to strengthen lifelong learning, upskilling and reskilling opportunities, support enterprise competitiveness – particularly for SMEs – and improve the transparency and recognition of skills and qualifications across the EU. '''Promoting gender equality in the labour market''' The European Commission adopted ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0097 A Roadmap for Women’s Rights]'' (COM(2025) 97 final) in March 2025. It addresses emerging gender equality challenges, including technology-facilitated discrimination through a ‘Declaration of principles for a gender-equal society’. Although inequalities still exist, the EU has made significant progress in terms of gender equality over recent decades. The European Commission’s [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/gender-equality/gender-equality-strategy_en Gender equality strategy 2026–30] aims to build on this by countering gender stereotypes, promoting gender mainstreaming (including gender perspectives, for example in policies, to promote equality), closing gender gaps and increasing women’s participation in decision-making. The strategy aims to strengthen action across several policy areas, including: *tackling gender-based cyberviolence *enhancing women’s health (for example, through work addressing the social and economic impacts of the women’s health gap, including conditions such as menopause) *reducing gender gaps in employment and promoting equality in the labour market *ensuring that EU funding is gender-sensitive. '''Investing in people: funding and skills development''' The [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/funding/european-social-fund-plus-esf_en European Social Fund Plus (ESF+)] is the EU’s main financial instrument for investing in people. With a budget of €142.7 billion allocated for 2021 to 2027, it supports employment, social inclusion, poverty reduction and youth investment. The ESF+ is central to advancing the European Pillar of Social Rights and the post-pandemic recovery. To respond to changes in labour markets – especially those driven by the green and digital transitions – the EU has prioritised skills development through initiatives such as the ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0274 European Skills Agenda for sustainable competitiveness, social fairness and resilience]'' (COM(2020) 274 final), the [https://year-of-skills.europa.eu/index_en European Year of Skills] launched in 2023 and extended into 2024, and ''The Union of Skills''. '''Towards a fair and inclusive future labour market''' Labour markets across the EU are adapting to technological progress, demographic change and sustainability goals. Policymakers have introduced measures to improve employment access for underrepresented groups at risk of exclusion – such as young people, older workers and people with disabilities – while, at the same time, supporting regional adaptation to structural change. The growth of platform work and other non-standard forms of employment has also reinforced the need for fair working conditions. A key initiative in this area is the ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52024DC0131 Labour and skills shortages in the EU: an action plan]'' (COM(2024) 131 final) which provides a coordinated policy response to persistent labour market imbalances, focusing on: *increasing labour market participation among underrepresented groups *advancing skills development and
