title: Living conditions in Europe - energy efficiency in households
text:
test test test Data extracted in June 2026 No planned article update In 2025, 23.9% of EU residents lived in dwellings with improved energy efficiency in the previous 5 years, a decrease of 1.9 percentage points compared with 2023 (25.8%). In 2025, people in the EU at risk of poverty or social exclusion were less likely to report living in dwellings with improved energy efficiency (17.4%) than those not at risk (25.6%). In 2025, reported energy-efficiency improvements in the EU were more common among homeowners (26.9%) and people living in houses (30.5%) than among tenants (16.7%) and people living in flats (16.6%). In 2025, people in the EU living in more recently constructed dwellings were less likely to experience difficulty keeping their homes adequately warm or to have arrears on utility bills. [[image:Dwelling-energy-efficiency-improvments-2025.jpg|thumb|centre|700px]] This article presents data on energy efficiency and energy poverty among people living in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union]] (EU), focusing on those * whose [[Glossary:Dwelling|dwellings]] have had their energy efficiency improved in the last 5 years * who cannot afford to keep their home adequately warm * who live in [[Glossary:Household|households]] with arrears on utility bills. The analysis is broken down by [[Glossary:At risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)|risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)]], tenure status, type of building, and year of construction of the dwelling, illustrating how these factors may affect some aspects of living conditions. === Energy efficiency improvements === '''Energy efficiency improvements slightly lower in 2025 than in 2023''' In 2025, 23.9% of the EU population reported living in a dwelling in which the energy efficiency had been improved within the last 5 years (Figure 1). This represents a decrease of 1.9 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] compared with 2023 (25.8%). Between 2023 and 2025, 11 [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU countries]] reported an increase, while 15 reported a decrease. The largest increases were observed in Cyprus, Austria, Spain, Portugal and Luxembourg, while the largest decreases were in Estonia, Slovakia, Croatia, Italy and Lithuania. In 2025, the Netherlands (60.5%) had the highest proportion of the population reporting energy efficiency improvements to their dwelling in the previous 5 years, followed by Denmark (34.0%), France and Slovenia (both 33.3%). At the other end of the scale, Italy (2.6%) had the lowest rate, followed by Malta (7.8%) and Greece (9.5%). [[Image:FIGURE 1 People living in dwellings with improved energy efficiency .png |thumb|centre|700px| Figure 1: People living in dwellings with improved energy efficiency over the last 5 years, 2025 and 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b7f2af29-9cb4-4719-96eb-ac1907e2a6a8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-03T07:03:07Z ilc_enevh_01] )|alt=Chart showing showing the share of people in the EU living in dwellings in which energy efficiency imporved in the last 5 years, for the year 2025 and 2023 for EU countries as well as EFTA (NO) and some candidate countries. The largest increases were observed in Cyprus, Austria, Spain, Portugal and Luxembourg, while the largest decreases were in Estonia, Slovakia, Croatia, Italy and Lithuania.]] '''People at risk of poverty or social exclusion report fewer energy-efficiency improvements in their dwellings''' In 2025, 17.4% of the people in the EU at risk of poverty or social exclusion reported that the energy efficiency of their dwelling had been improved in the last 5 years, compared with 25.6% among those not at risk (Figure 2). The Netherlands had the highest proportion of people reporting energy-efficiency improvements to their dwelling in the last 5 years, both among those at risk of poverty or social exclusion (45.3%) and those not at risk (63.3%). Among people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, Austria (30.4%), Poland (28.8%) and Estonia (28.1%) had the next highest rates, while Italy (1.5%), Malta (2.9%) and Greece (7.9%) had the lowest. For people not at risk, the Netherlands was followed by Denmark (36.4%), France (35%) and Portugal (34.7%), while Italy (2.9%), Malta (9.0%) and Greece (10.1%) had the lowest rates for this group. The largest gap between these 2 groups was observed in the Netherlands (18 pp), followed by Cyprus (13.6 pp), Denmark (13.5 pp) and Luxembourg (12.6 pp). [[Image:Figure 2 People living in dwellings with improved energy efficiency .png |thumb|centre|700px| Figure 2: People living in dwellings with improved energy efficiency over the last 5 years, by risk of poverty or social exclusion, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/71073764-fe2c-4e4a-8a3c-c37b622156f8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-03T07:09:50Z ilc_enevh_01]) |alt=Chart showing showing the share of people in the EU living in dwellings in which energy efficiency improved in the last 5 years by risk of poverty or social exclusion situation, for the year 2025 for EU countries as well as EFTA (NO) and some candidate countries. Blue bars represent people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, while yellow bars represent people who are not at risk. The red dots represent the total population.]] '''Fewer energy efficiency improvements for tenants and people living in flats''' In 2025, 16.7% of tenants in the EU reported energy efficiency improvements of their dwelling over the last 5 years, compared with 26.9% of owners (Figure 3). Among tenants, the highest share was recorded in the Netherlands (39.9%), followed by Slovenia (28.5%), Austria (27.9%), Estonia (25.3%) and Portugal (25.2%), while Italy (1.7%), Malta (5.3%) and Greece (6.3%) had the lowest rates. Among owners, the Netherlands again had the highest share (69.7%), followed by Denmark (42.9%), Sweden (39.6%), France (39.1%) and Belgium (36.3%), while Italy (2.8%), Malta (8.7%) and Greece (10.9%) had the lowest rates. The largest gaps between owners and tenants were observed in the Netherlands (29.8 pp), Ireland (23.3 pp), Sweden (23.0 pp) and Denmark (21.6 pp). [[Image:Figure 3 People living in dwellings with improved energy .png |thumb|centre|700px| Figure 3: People living in dwellings with improved energy efficiency over the last 5 years, by tenure status, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7e94a78f-8a83-4b4b-9c42-5c0b0dec4699?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-03T07:21:43Z ilc_enevh_01]) |alt=Chart showing showing the share of people in the EU living in dwellings in which energy efficiency improved in the last 5 years by tenure status, for the year 2025 for EU countries as well as EFTA (NO) and some candidate countries. Blue bars represent the share of people who are tenants, while yellow bars represent owners. The red dots represent the total population.]] In 2025, 16.6% of people living in flats in the EU reported that the energy efficiency of their dwellings had been improved in the last 5 years, compared with 30.5% of people living in houses (Figure 4). Portugal (34.1%), the Netherlands (33.4%), Austria and Slovenia (both 28.3%) had the highest proportions of people living in flats with energy efficiency improvements, while Italy (2.6%), Malta (6.8%) and Greece (8.3%) had the lowest. Among people living in houses, the Netherlands (68.3%) had the highest proportion, followed by Sweden (43.7%), Denmark (40.2%) and Luxembourg (39.2%), while Italy (2.6%), Malta (9.6%) and Greece (11.4%) had the lowest. The largest gaps between people living in houses and people living in flats were observed in the Netherlands (34.9 pp), Sweden (24.8 pp) and Luxembourg (23.4 pp). [[Image:Figure 4 People living in dwellings with improved energy efficiency .png |thumb|centre|700px| Figure 4: People living in dwellings with improved energy efficiency over the last 5 years, by type of building, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_enevh_01__custom_21891842/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=4e36f831-4979-4f87-b94f-e8eb827ef395&c=1781876951000 ilc_enevh_01]) |alt=alt=Chart showing showing the share of people in the EU living in dwellings in which energy efficiency improved in the last 5 years by risk of poverty or social exclusion situation, for the year 2025 for EU countries as well as EFTA (NO) and some candidate countries. Blue bars represent people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, while yellow bars represent people who are not at risk. The red dots represent the total population.]] === Energy poverty and year of construction === '''Inability to keep home warm is less common for people living in more recently built buildings''' In 2025, the proportion of people in the EU who were unable to keep their home adequately warm was lowest (4.8%) among those living in dwellings built in 2011 or later (Figure 5). People living in dwellings built between 2001 and 2010 reported the second lowest proportion (7.2%), followed by those living in dwellings built between 1981 and 2000 (8.9%), between 1961 and 1980 (9.8%), and in 1960 or before (10.1%). A similar pattern is observed for people not at risk of poverty or social exclusion: the lowest proportions of those unable to keep their home adequately warm were reported for people living in dwellings built in 2011 or later (2.9%) and between 2001 and 2010 (4.1%). For people at risk, the proportion was lower for those living in dwellings built in 2011 and later (15.8%), while people living in older dwellings reported shares between 23.9% and 24.3%. [[Image:Fig_5_People_unable_to_keep_home_adequately_warm,_by_construction_year_and_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion,_EU,_2025_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px| Figure 5: People unable to keep home adequately warm, by construction year and risk of poverty or social exclusion, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2337193d-f7a7-414e-ba76-af2fd1b98cb3?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-03T07:30:33Z ilc_enevh_02]) |alt=Chart showing showing the share of people in the EU unable to keep home adequately warm by year of construction and risk of poverty or social exclusion. Blue bars represent people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, while yellow bars represent people who are not at risk. The red dots represent the total population.]] '''Arrears on utility bills are less common for people living in more recently built buildings''' In the EU in 2025, the proportion of people living in households with arrears on utility bills was lowest (5.2%) among people living in dwellings built in 2011 or after (Figure 6). People living in dwellings built between 2001 and 2010 reported the second lowest proportion (6.2%), followed by those living in dwellings built between 1981 and 2000 (6.7%), in 1960 or before (6.9%), and between 1961 and 1980 (7.9%). A similar pattern is observed for people not at risk of poverty or social exclusion: the lowest proportion of those having arrears on utility bills was reported for people living in dwellings built in 2011 and after (3.2%), followed by those built between 2001 and 2010, and in those built in 1960 or before (both 3.5%). For people at risk, the proportion of those having arrears on utility bills was lower for those living in dwellings built in 2011 or after (16.6%) and those built in 1960 or before (17.6%), with those living in other dwellings reporting higher shares (between 19.1% and 20.7%). [[Image:Fig_6_People_in_households_with_arrears_on_utility_bills,_by_construction_year_and_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion,_EU,_2025_(%_).png |thumb|centre|700px| Figure 6: People in households with arrears on utility bills, by construction year and risk of poverty or social exclusion, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/45a55ea3-eb79-4a3e-a820-a967db63c505?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-13T09:31:13Z ilc_enevh_03]) |alt=Chart showing showing the share of people in the EU unable to keep home adequately warm by year of construction and risk of poverty or social exclusion. Blue bars represent people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, while yellow bars represent people who are not at risk. The red dots represent the total population.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Living_conditions_in_Europe_-_energy_efficiency_in_household_rev2.xlsx|title=Living conditions in Europe – energy efficiency in households: tables and figures}} === Data sources === The data used in this article come from [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]]. EU-SILC data are compiled annually and serve as the main source of statistics measuring income and living conditions in Europe. They are also the primary source of information linking various aspects of [[Glossary:Household|households]] and individual quality of life. The reference population for the information presented in this article covers all private households and their current members living in the territory of an EU Member State (or non-EU member country) at the time of data collection. Those living in collective households are generally excluded from the target population. EU figures are population-weighted averages of national data. The EU-SILC 2025 ad hoc subject module ‘Energy and the environment’ focuses on key social aspects of the green transition, addressing information gaps and supporting stronger future monitoring and evaluation. === Context === [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R2527 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/2527] states that the ad hoc subject on ‘Energy and the environment’ collected in 2025 in accordance with [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ%3AL%3A2020%3A054%3ATOC Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/256] is of key importance, especially in view of the Commission Communication [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52021DC0550 ‘Fit for 55’]. The module covers several key topics, including household energy efficiency. The indicator ‘Energy efficiency improvements of the dwelling in the last 5 years’ measures the extent to which residential properties have been renovated to improve energy performance. It includes all measures that affect the thermal conditions of the dwelling. Key renovation activities covered by this indicator include upgrading of thermal insulation in external walls, roofs, or floors; replacing single-glazed windows with double or triple-glazed ones; and installing more efficient heating systems. It covers both comprehensive building-wide renovations and those specific to individual dwellings. Renovations may be carried out by the household itself or by external parties, such as property owners. Changes in renovation activity over time and across countries may partly reflect differences in national subsidy programmes. The ‘year of construction of the main dwelling’ indicates when the household’s dwelling was completed or, if it underwent a major renovation, the year that renovation was finished. A major renovation is an extensive modernisation of the building, including installing insulation and replacing the roof, electrical system and heating system. The percentage of people who are unable to keep their home adequately warm measures the extent to which the population can afford to heat their home, while the percentage of people in households with arrears on utility bills measures the extent to which the population faces financial difficulties in paying utility bills (for example heating, electricity, gas, water). Both indicators are collected annually and used to assess energy poverty in the EU. ===Other articles=== * [[Living conditions in Europe|All articles from Living conditions]] *[[Living conditions in Europe - title: Living conditions in Europe - childcare arrangements
text:
Living conditions in Europe is an online Eurostat publication that analyses income and living conditions across the EU. This article covers childcare arrangements for the EU population. Data extracted in September 2025 Planned update: October 2026 In 2024, 99.7% of children in the EU aged between 1 year older than the compulsory school age and 12 years of age were in formal education. In the EU, the percentage of children aged between 3 years and the minimum compulsory school age, who were not in formal childcare or education, was higher for those at risk of poverty or social exclusion (17.6%) compared with those not at risk (8.7%) in 2024. In 2024, 13.9% of children in the EU aged between 3 years and the minimum compulsory school age who were at risk of poverty or social exclusion, were 25 hours or more per week in formal childcare or education. ===Childcare arrangements=== '''The number of children in the EU receiving formal childcare increases with age''' In 2024, 50.7% of children in the [[Glossary:EU|EU]] aged 1 to 2 years received [[Glossary:Children_in_formal_childcare_or_education|formal childcare or education]], while for children aged between 3 years and the minimum compulsory school age, the share was 89.3%. Among children aged 1 year older than the compulsory school age to 12 years of age, 99.7% received formal childcare or education (Figure 1). For children aged 1 to 2 years, 49.4% did not receive any formal childcare. Within this age group, 13.8% were in formal childcare for less than 25 hours per week, while 36.9% received 25 hours or more of formal childcare or education. Among children aged between 3 years and the minimum compulsory school age, 68.5% were in formal childcare or education for at least 25 hours per week, 20.8% received less than 25 hours per week, and 10.8% did not receive any formal childcare or education. For children aged between 1 year older than the compulsory school age and 12 years old, only 0.3% did not receive any formal childcare or education, 15.5% received less than 25 hours of formal childcare or education, and the majority (84.2%) received at least 25 hours per week.
[[Image:Fig1_Children in formal childcare or education, by age and duration of care, EU, 2024_(% of children in each age group).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Children in formal childcare or education, by age and duration of care, EU, 2024.
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_caindform25}}|alt=A set of three pie charts showing the share of children in formal childcare or education by age of child and duration of care at EU level in 2024 as a percentage in the EU. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''In the EU, children aged between 3 years and the minimum compulsory school age who were at risk of poverty or social exclusion received less formal childcare or education compared with those not at risk''' In 2024, 17.6% of children in the EU aged between 3 years and the minimum compulsory school age who were [[Glossary:At_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_(AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)]] were not in any formal childcare or education, compared with 8.7% of children not at risk (Figure 2).
[[Image:Fig2_Children in formal childcare or education aged between 3 years and the minimum compulsory school age by duration of care and AROPE situation, EU, 2024 _(% of children in the respective AROPE situation).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Children in formal childcare or education aged between 3 years and the minimum compulsory school age by duration of care and AROPE situation, EU, 2024.
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_caindform25b}}|alt=Two pie charts showing the share of children in formal childcare or education aged between 3 years and the minimum compulsory school age by duration and at risk of poverty status at EU level in 2024 as a percentage in the EU. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''The highest rates of formal childcare among at-risk-of-poverty-or-social-exclusion (AROPE) children were recorded in Spain, Bulgaria and Italy''' In 2024, 13.9% of children in the EU aged between 3 years and the minimum compulsory school age were at risk of poverty or social exclusion and received 25 hours or more formal childcare or education per week (Figure 3). Across EU countries, the highest percentages were recorded in Spain (31.7%), Bulgaria (27.7%) and Italy (22.0%), while the lowest were in Romania (3.9%), Ireland (4.6%) and Austria (5.7%). [[Image:Fig3_Children at-risk-of-poverty-or-social-exclusion aged between 3 years old and the minimum compulsory school age received 25 hours or more formal childcare or education per week, 2024_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Children at-risk-of-poverty-or-social-exclusion, aged between 3 years and the minimum compulsory school age receiving 25 hours or more formal childcare or education per week, 2024.
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_caindform25}}|alt=A bar chart showing the share of children in formal childcare or education aged between 3 years and the minimum compulsory school age at risk of poverty and receiving 25 hours or more of formal childcare or education per week as a percentage in the EU, the EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=LCIE_Childcare_arrangements_2024_data.xlsx|title=Childcare arrangements: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data used in this article are derived from the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions European Statistics on income, social inclusion and living conditions] (EU-SILC). EU-SILC data are compiled annually and are the main source of statistics that measure income and living conditions in Europe; they are also the main source of information used to link different aspects relating to the quality of life of [[Glossary:Household_-_social_statistics|household]] and individuals. The reference population for the information presented in this article is all private households and their current members residing in the territory of an EU Member State (or a non-member country) at the time of data collection; persons living in collective households were excluded from the target population. The data for the EU are population-weighted averages of national data. The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/ilc_sieusilc.htm#ref_periodDisseminated reference period] for information on income is 2023, while the other households’ characteristics are referenced to 2024. ===Context=== Formal childcare is a formal education programme that is institutionalized, intentional and planned through public organizations and recognized private bodies, in line with the formal education definition of [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|ISCED 2011 classification]]. Other types of childcare may include care that is provided by a professional child-minder at the child’s home or at the child-minders’ home, as well as care provided by grandparents, other household members (not parents), other relatives, friends or neighbours. Following the Council Recommendation of 8 December 2022 on early childhood education and care: [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32022H1220(01) the Barcelona Targets] for 2030 (2022/C 484/01), Eurostat defined in 2023 a new indicator for measuring ‘Children in formal childcare or education by age group and duration’, setting the threshold for the number of hours in formal childcare or education at 25 hours per week, and breaking down the indicator by the [[Glossary:At_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_(AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)]] status {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_caindform25}} and by income quintile {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_caindform25q}}. Furthermore, an additional indicator is available showing the share of children in formal childcare or education from the population of children in their respective AROPE situation {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_caindform25b}}. In addition, together with the three age groups already available in the previous indicator {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_caindformal}}, an additional age group has been added for children aged 1 or 2 years old. === Other Articles === *[[Living conditions in Europe|Living conditions in Europe - Statistics Explained (europa.eu)]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/database/ Income and living conditions database] === Thematic section === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=income_social_inclusion_living_conditions}} Income and living conditions] === Publications === *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-032|title=Key figures on European living conditions – 2025 edition - Eurostat}} === Selected Datasets === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=ilc_ca Childcare arrangements] === Methodology === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/ilc_sieusilc.htm ESMS metadata file — ilc_esms] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/information-data Income and living conditions — information on data] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/methodology Income and living conditions — methodology] ===External links=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=830&langId=en European Commission — Directorate General for Employment, Social Affairs & Inclusion: Indicators' Sub-Group of the Social Protection Committee] *[https://op.europa.eu/webpub/empl/european-pillar-of-social-rights/en/ European pillar of social rights] *[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/social-protection-social-inclusion/addressing-poverty-and-supporting-social-inclusion/investing-children/european-child-guarantee_en European child guarantee] ===Legislation=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/legislation Income and living conditions - legislation] {{Unit|topic=X_Living_conditions}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Living conditions in Europe — childcare arrangements]] [[Category:Income and living conditions|Living conditions in Europe — childcare arrangements]] [[Category:Household composition and family situation|Living conditions in Europe — childcare arrangements]] [[Category:Statistical article|Living conditions in Europe — childcare arrangements]] [[Category:October2026|Living conditions in Europe — childcare arrangements]]

title: Living conditions in Europe - housing and renting difficulties
text:
Living conditions in Europe - housing and renting difficulties Data extracted in September 2024. Planned article update: September 2030. In 2023, 4.9% of people aged 16 or older in the EU reported experiencing housing difficulties in their lifetime. In 2023, 8.5% of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in the EU reported experiencing housing difficulties in the past, with men (9.0%) more affected than women (8.1%). In 2023, 26.5% of people in the EU reported that they had overcome housing difficulties by finding a job. Households in the EU with dependent children (18.1%) were more likely to experience renting difficulties in the last 12 months than those without (10.2%), as reported in 2023. People at risk of poverty in the EU were more likely to experience renting difficulties in their lifetime, with rates decreasing from 22.1% for those aged 16-29 to 12.9% for people aged 65 or older, as reported in 2023. [[image:People-experiencing-housing-difficulties-lifetime-current-risk-poverty-social-exclusion-2023.png|700px|centre|alt=An infographic showing the share of people in the having experienced housing difficulties in their lifetime as reported in 2023. Data are shown as percentage by current risk of poverty and social exclusion for the EU, the EU Member States and the EFTA country Norway.]] Data on housing difficulties is crucial to show the living conditions and quality of life of people in Europe. It enables policymakers to take informed decisions, identify vulnerable groups of the population, and understand the impact of housing challenges in households and in society. This article presents data on people aged 16 years or over living in private households in the European Union (EU) in 2023, focusing on those who have experienced housing difficulties in their lifetime and those who have faced renting difficulties in the last 12 months. Reasons for experiencing and overcoming housing difficulties are also examined. Past housing difficulties refer to situations where an individual lacked a permanent and stable home in their lifetime, forcing them to rely on temporary accommodation, excluding temporary displacements due to unforeseen events but with a permanent home to return to. The analysis is broken down by sex, age, risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE), and household composition, highlighting how these factors impacted such situations === Key findings === In 2023, 4.9% of people in the EU aged 16 or older reported experiencing housing difficulties in their lifetime. * People at risk of poverty or social exclusion were more affected, with 8.5% experiencing housing difficulties in the past, compared with 3.9% among those not at risk. * Among those at risk of poverty, 9.0% of men reported experiencing housing difficulties in their lifetime, compared with 8.1% of women. * The most common cause of housing difficulties was reasons linked to family or relationships (30.0%). * 26.5% of people in the EU reported that they had overcome housing difficulties by finding a job. In 2023, 13.0% of the EU population aged 16 or older reported renting difficulties in the last 12 months. * Households with dependent children were more affected by renting difficulties (18.1%) compared with those without children (10.2%). * Renting difficulties decreased with age, from 14.8% for people aged 16 to 29 years to 6.7% for those aged 65 or older. === Housing difficulties === '''Experiencing housing difficulties was more frequent among men at risk of poverty or social exclusion''' In 2023, 4.9% of people aged 16 or older in the EU reported experiencing housing difficulties in their lifetime, with a marginal difference between men (4.9%) and women (4.8%). The highest rates of housing difficulties were observed in Cyprus (11.2%), Finland (10.8%), Denmark (9.4%), France and Sweden (both 9.1%). Conversely, the lowest rates were recorded in Hungary and Poland (both 0.8%), Italy (1.2%), Slovakia (1.3%) and Bulgaria (1.5%). Most EU countries recorded gender differences in housing difficulties of less than 1.0 percentage point (pp). Exceptions included Ireland, where women had a 2.0 pp higher rate than men (8.2% vs. 6.2%), Latvia with a 1.1 pp difference, and Slovenia with a 1.0 pp difference. In contrast, in Austria, men reported a 1.1 pp higher rate than women. In 2023, 8.5% of people in the EU at risk of poverty or social exclusion reported experiencing housing difficulties in their lifetime, compared with 3.9% among those not at risk. Among those at risk of poverty in the EU, men (9.0%) were more affected by housing difficulties than women (8.1%). Most Member States reported higher rates of housing difficulties among men at risk of poverty compared with women. The largest gaps were observed in Sweden (7.8 pp), the Netherlands (5.4 pp), and Austria (3.4 pp). In contrast, women were more affected in Ireland (5.0 pp) and Estonia (1.2 pp). For those not at risk of poverty, no gender gap was observed at EU level, though variations were observed across the EU countries. The largest gap was in the Netherlands (2.2 pp), with women reporting higher rates of housing difficulties. Latvia (1.1 pp) and Slovenia (1.0 pp) also showed gaps where women reported higher rates. In contrast, men were more affected in Estonia and Finland (both 1.3 pp), as well as in Austria (0.9 pp) and France (0.6 pp). [[Image:People_having_experienced_housing_difficulties_in_their_life,_2023_Analysed_by_sex_and_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_situation_(%_population_aged_16_or_older)_04-10-2024.png |thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: People having experienced housing difficulties in their life, 2023
(Analysed by sex and risk of poverty or social exclusion situation (% population aged 16 or older))
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_lvhd01}}|alt=A table showing the share of people in the EU having experienced housing difficulties in their life, as reported in 2023. Data are analysed by sex and risk of poverty or social exclusion situation, and shown as percentage of the population aged 16 or older for the EU, the EU Member States and the EFTA country Norway. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Relationship or family matters mostly behind housing difficulties in the EU''' In 2023, 30.0% of people in the EU aged 16 or older reported experiencing housing difficulties in their lifetime due to relationship or family reasons, (Figure 1). Financial reasons accounted for 25.9%, followed by job loss or inability to find a job (7.3 %), and the end of a rental contract (5.2 %). Less frequent reasons included uninhabitable accommodation (4.0%), health reasons (2.0%), and leaving an institution after a long stay with no home to return to (1.1%). Other reasons were reported by 24.5 % of people. [[Image:People_having_experienced_housing_difficulties_in_their_life,_EU,_2023_Analysed_by_reason_(%_population_aged_16_or_older)_04-10-2024.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: People having experienced housing difficulties in their life, EU, 2023
(Analysed by reason (% population aged 16 or older))
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_lvhd05}}|alt=A pie chart showing the share of people in the EU havn experienced housing difficulties in their life, as reported in 2023. Data are analysed by reason and shown as percentage of the population aged 16 or older. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Finding a job was the most common solution to overcome housing difficulties''' In 2023, 26.5% of people in the EU aged 16 or older reported that they had overcome housing difficulties by finding a job (Figure 2). Moving into social or subsidised private housing accounted for 20.4%, while relationship or family reasons were cited by 14.1%. Health reasons contributed to 1.1%, while 37.9% of people reported other reasons. [[Image:People_having_overcome_housing_difficulties_experienced_in_their_life,_EU,_2023_Analysed_by_reason_(%_population_aged_16_or_older)_04-10-2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: People having overcome housing difficulties experienced in their life, EU, 2023
(Analysed by reason (% population aged 16 or older))
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_lvhd06}}|alt=A pie chart showing the share of people in the EU having overcome housing difficulties that they experienced in their life, as reported in 2023. Data are analysed by reason and shown as percentage of the population aged 16 or older. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Renting difficulties === '''Renting difficulties were higher among households with dependent children in most EU countries''' In 2023, 13.0% of the EU population aged 16 or over reported renting difficulties in the last 12 months (Figure 3). Households with dependent children were more affected, with 18.1% experiencing difficulties, compared with 10.2% of households without children. Greece (26.1%), France (24.1%), and Spain (17.2%) had the highest overall rates of renting difficulties, while the lowest rates were observed in Romania (0.3%), Slovakia (1.1%), Belgium (4.3%), Germany and Hungary (both 4.7%). For households with dependent children, France (33.2%), Greece (26.3%), and Spain (20.8%) reported the highest rates, while Romania (less than 0.0%), Slovakia (1.2%), and Bulgaria (3.7%) had the lowest. Among households without dependent children, Greece (25.9%), France (18.0%), and Slovenia (15.3%) faced the most difficulties, while the lowest rates were found in Romania (0.4%), Slovakia (1.1%), and Cyprus (2.5%). Most EU countries reported higher rates of renting difficulties among households with dependent children compared with those without. The widest gaps were observed in France (15.2 pp) and Cyprus (12.1 pp). In contrast, minimal differences were observed in Slovakia (0.1 pp) and Greece (0.4 pp). Notably, households without dependent children reported higher renting difficulties than those with children in Lithuania (7.3 pp), Bulgaria (5.4 pp), Slovenia (3.7 pp), Croatia (0.6 pp), and Romania (0.4 pp). [[Image:People_having_experienced_renting_difficulties_in_the_last_12_months,_2023_Analysed_by_household_composition_(%_population_aged_16_or_older)_04-10-2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: People having experienced renting difficulties in the last 12 months, 2023
(Analysed by household composition (% population aged 16 or older))
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_lvhd13}}|alt=A multi bar chart showing the share of people in the EU having experienced renting difficulties in the last 12 months, as reported in 2023. Data are analysed by household composition and shown as percentage of the population aged 16 or older for the EU, the EU Member States and the EFTA country Norway. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''People aged 30 to 54 and at risk of poverty or social exclusion reported the highest percentage of renting difficulties compared with other age groups''' In 2023, the rate of people in the EU that reported experiencing renting difficulties in the last 12 months decreased with age (Figure 4). Younger people aged 16 to 29 years (14.8%) and those aged 30 to 54 years (14.7%) reported the highest rates, while the rates decreased to 12.8% for those aged 55 to 64 years and further to 6.7% for people aged 65 years or over. The same pattern was observed among those not at risk of poverty or social exclusion, with renting difficulties decreasing from 10.6% for those aged 16 to 29 years to 4.1% for those aged 65 or older. Among people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, renting difficulties were notably higher, peaking at 27.7% for people aged 30 to 54 years. High rates were also observed among people aged 55 to 64 years (24.0%) and 16 to 29 years (22.1%), with a decrease to 12.9% for those aged 65 years or older. [[Image:People_having_experienced_renting_difficulties_in_the_last_12_months,_EU,_2023_Analysed_by_age_and_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_situation_(%)_04-10-2024.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: People having experienced renting difficulties in the last 12 months, EU, 2023
(Analysed by age and risk of poverty or social exclusion situation (%))
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_lvhd08}}|alt=A multi bar chart showing the share of people in the EU having experienced renting difficulties in the last 12 months, as reported in 2023. Data are analysed by age and risk of poverty or social exclusion situation and shown as percentage. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=LCIE_2024_-_Housing_and_renting_difficulties_.xlsx|title=Housing and renting difficulties: tables and figures}} === Data sources === The data used in this article are derived from the EU Statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC). EU-SILC data are compiled annually and are the main source of statistics that measure income and living conditions in Europe; it is also the main source of information used to link different aspects relating to the quality of life of households and individuals. The reference population for the information presented in this article is all private households and their current members residing in the territory of an EU Member State (or non-member country) at the time of data collection; people living in collective households are generally excluded from the target population. The data for the EU are population-weighted averages of national data. The reference period for individuals' characteristics is 2023. The data is available for the 27 Member States as well as the EFTA countries Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and the candidate countries Serbia, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Albania and Türkiye. The six-yearly module Intergenerational transmission of disadvantages and housing difficulties collects data on family conditions and housing challenges experienced by individuals. The section on “housing difficulties” covers different aspects of having experienced past housing difficulties in a person’s lifetime, including reasons for such difficulties, duration of the most recent experience, and how individuals overcame these challenges, as well as specific questions on renting difficulties. Housing difficulties are defined as situations where a person had no place of their own (either owned or rented) and was forced to stay with friends or family, use emergency or temporary accommodation, live in a place not intended as a permanent home, or sleep in a public space. Temporary displacement due to unforeseen events, such as natural disasters or emergencies, is not considered housing difficulties if the person still had a permanent residence (either owned or rented) to return to. The respondent should not be considered to have had housing difficulties if they were forced to leave their home for a few days due to an unforeseen event such as the risk of an earthquake, fire in the neighbourhood or evacuation of the neighbourhood because a bomb was being defused, etc., but they still had a place of their own that they could return or move into. If a person experienced housing difficulties more than once during their lifetime, only the most recent occurrence is reported. Renting difficulties occur when an individual is unable to cover the cost of their accommodation, during the last 12 months, using their own resources, without having to borrow money, take out a loan, or resort to other financial means to pay their rent. === Context === [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2020/2175/oj Commission delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/2175] specifies that the 2023 SILC survey will collect three-yearly variables on labour market and housing, six-yearly variables on intergenerational transmission of disadvantages and housing difficulties, as well as an ad hoc subject on households energy efficiency. ===Other articles=== *All articles from [[Living conditions in Europe|Living condtions]] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-HC-23-001&language=en Key figures on European living conditions – 2023 edition] *[[Living conditions in Europe - title: Living conditions in Europe - housing
text:
Living conditions in Europe is an online Eurostat publication that analyses income and living conditions across the EU. This article covers housing quality. Data extracted: November 2025 Planned article update: December 2026 In 2024, 68.4% of people in the EU lived in owner-occupied homes, while 31.6% lived in rented accommodation. In 2024, 16.9% of people in the EU lived in overcrowded households. The highest rates were observed in Romania (40.7%) and Latvia (39.3%), while the lowest were in Cyprus (2.4%) and Malta (4.4%). In 2024, 9.2% of people in the EU could not afford to keep their homes adequately warm, a decrease from 10.6% in 2023. In 2024, 8.2% of the EU population spent 40% or more of their household disposable income on housing, with the highest rates recorded in Greece (28.9%) and Denmark (14.6%), and the lowest in Cyprus (2.4%) and Croatia (3.7%). 10.1% of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE) in the EU felt discriminated against when looking for housing in 2024, compared with 4.7% of those not at risk. This article explores the housing landscape within the [[Glossary:EU_enlargements|European Union (EU)]] in 2024, focusing on various aspects of households’ living conditions. The analysis covers the distribution of the population based on tenure status, [[Glossary:overcrowding_rate|overcrowding rate]], the ability to keep the home adequately warm, the prevalence of [[Glossary:Housing_cost_overburden_rate|housing cost overburden]] and satisfaction with dwellings. All figures are based on [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]] available from [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database Eurostat's online database]. EU-SILC data are available for all EU countries, as well as for most of the [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]]. ===Housing conditions=== '''In 2024, nearly 7 out of 10 people in the EU owned the dwelling they lived in''' In 2024, 68.4% of people in the EU lived in owner-occupied dwellings, while 31.6% resided in rented accommodation (see '''Figure 1'''). In the EU, 44.2% owned their dwellings outright, free from a mortgage or housing loan, whereas 24.3% were owners with a mortgage or loan. Concerning tenants, 21.1% of people in the EU paid market rent, and 10.5% lived in dwellings with rent at a reduced price or for free. [[Image:Fig1_Population distribution by tenure status at EU level, 2024_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Population distribution by tenure status at EU level, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_lvho02__custom_19118084/default/table ilc_lvho02])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing percentage population distribution by tenure status at EU level. Six columns represent owner occupied without mortgage, owner-occupied with mortgage, owner-occupied total, tenant rent at market price, tenant reduced rent and tenant total for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''The highest percentages of people living in overcrowded households in 2024 were observed in Romania and Latvia while the lowest were in Cyprus, Malta and the Netherlands''' In 2024, 16.9% of people in the EU lived in overcrowded households. '''Map 1''' shows that overcrowding rates above 30% were recorded in Romania (40.7%), Latvia (39.3%), Bulgaria (33.8%), Poland (33.7%) and Croatia (31.7%). By contrast, the lowest rates, below 5.0%, were observed in Cyprus (2.4%), Malta (4.4%), and the Netherlands (4.6%). [[Image:MAP_overcrowded_V2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: People living in an overcrowded household, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_lvho05a__custom_19118119/default/table ilc_lvho05a])]] Map 1: People living in an overcrowded household, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_lvho05a__custom_19118119/default/table ilc_lvho05a]) '''The share of people living in households unable to keep their home warm decreased in the majority of EU countries in 2024 compared with 2023''' In 2024, 9.2% of people in the EU lived in households unable to afford to keep their home adequately warm (see '''Figure 2'''). Among EU countries, the lowest rates were observed in Finland (2.7%), Slovenia and Poland (both at 3.3%). By contrast, the highest rates were recorded in Bulgaria and Greece (both at 19.0%). [[Image:Fig2_People living in households unable to keep their home adequately warm, 2023-2024_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: People living in households unable to keep home adequately warm, 2023-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_mdes01__custom_19118906/default/table ilc_mdes01])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing percentage share of the population unable to keep home warm in the EU, individual EU countries, Norway, Switzerland, Serbia and Türkiye. Each country has two columns representing the year 2023 and 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Compared with 2023, the percentage of people in the EU living in households unable to keep their homes adequately warm decreased by 1.4 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp), going from 10.6% to 9.2% in 2024, as shown in '''Figure 3'''. Among EU countries, 5 recorded an increase in the percentage of people unable to keep their homes adequately warm between 2023 and 2024. The highest increases were observed in Luxembourg (+1.5 pp), Malta (+1 pp), and Slovakia (+0.2 pp). Conversely, 21 EU countries reported a decrease during the same period. The largest decreases were recorded in Portugal (-5.1 pp), Spain (-3.3 pp), and Cyprus and Denmark (both -2.5 pp) (see '''Figure 3'''). The Netherlands was the only country where the situation remained stable, with the same percentage (7.1%) recorded both in 2023 and 2024. [[Image:Fig3_Difference in the percentage of people unable to keep their home adequately warm, 2023-2024_(percentage points)_rev.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Difference in the percentage of people unable to keep their home adequately warm, 2023-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_mdes01__custom_19118906/default/table ilc_mdes01])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing percentage share of the population unable to keep home warm in the EU, individual EU countries, Norway, Switzerland, Serbia and Türkiye. Each country has one column showing the difference in percentage points between 2023 and 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Housing discrimination and affordability=== '''10.1% of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE) in the EU felt discriminated against when looking for housing in 2024''' In 2024, 5.8% of people aged 16 and over in the EU reported feeling discriminated against when looking for housing ('''Figure 4'''). Among those at risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE), this share was notably higher at 10.1% compared with 4.7% for people not at risk. At country level, all EU countries recorded values below 10.0% for the total population. Spain (9.0%), Slovenia (8.9%) and France (8.3%) had the highest shares of people feeling discriminated against when looking for housing, while Croatia (0.4%), Hungary (0.7%), and Italy and Romania (both 0.9%) reported the lowest. When looking at people at risk of poverty and social exclusion, the percentages varied significantly, with much higher values. The highest shares were recorded in Belgium (17.0%), Cyprus (16.6%), Spain (15.9%) and France (15.5%), whereas Croatia (0.3%), Italy (1.7%), and Hungary and Malta (both 2.2%) had the smallest proportions. In 24 EU countries, feeling discriminated against when looking for housing was more common among people at risk of poverty and social exclusion than for people not at risk. The opposite trend was evidenced only in Greece (2.7% for people at risk compared with 3.5% for not at risk), Malta (2.2% vs. 3.6%) and Croatia (0.3% vs. 0.4%) where higher values were recorded among people not at risk. The highest gaps in self-perceived discrimination when looking for housing between people at risk of poverty or social exclusion and those not at risk were observed in Cyprus (14.7 pp), Belgium (11.3 pp), and Spain and Czechia (both 9.2 pp). The smallest gaps were reported in Estonia (0.6 pp) and Latvia (0.8 pp), while Lithuania had the same share for both groups (2.5%). [[Image:People feeling discriminated against when looking for housing, by at risk of poverty or social exclusion, 2024 v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: People feeling discriminated against when looking for housing, by at risk of poverty or social exclusion, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_atsd01__custom_19296619/default/table ilc_atsd01])|alt= Chart showing the percentage of people aged 16 or older who feel discriminated against when looking for housing in 2024, broken down by risk of poverty or social exclusion across the EU, individual EU countries, Switzerland, Norway, Albania, Türkiye and Serbia. Each country has three data points: a green rhombus for the total population, an orange square for people at risk of poverty or social exclusion and a blue dot for people not at risk of poverty or social exclusion. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''In 2024, housing cost overburden rate above 9.0% in 5 EU countries''' In 2024, 8.2% of people in the EU lived in households spending 40% or more of their disposable income on housing. The housing cost overburden rate varied considerably across the EU countries (see '''Map 2'''). Greece recorded the highest housing cost overburden rate at 28.9%. Other countries with rates above 9.0% included Czechia (9.2%), Sweden (10.6%), Germany (12.0%) and Denmark (14.6%). By contrast, the lowest housing cost overburden rates, below 4%, were observed in Slovenia (3.8%), Croatia (3.7%) and Cyprus (2.4%). [[Image:MAP_Cost_Overburden_V2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 2: People living in households with housing cost overburden, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_lvho07a__custom_19119035/default/table ilc_lvho07a])]] Map 2: People living in households with housing cost overburden, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_lvho07a__custom_19119035/default/table ilc_lvho07a]) === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=LCIE Housing 2025 rev v3.xlsx|title=Housing: maps, tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data used in this article are derived from EU statistics on income and living conditions [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]]. EU-SILC is carried out annually and is the main survey that measures income and living conditions in Europe. It is also the main source of information used to link different aspects relating to the quality of life of households and individuals. The reference population for the information presented in this article is all private [[Glossary:Household_-_social_statistics|households]] and their current members residing in the territory of an EU Member State at the time of data collection; persons living in in institutions are generally excluded from the target population. The data for the EU are population-weighted averages of national data. The [[Glossary:Overcrowding_rate|overcrowding rate]] is determined by the percentage of the population residing in a dwelling with an insufficient number of rooms, based on household size, family composition, and the ages of its occupants. The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Inability_to_keep_the_house_adequately_warm ability to keep the house adequately warm] explicitly focuses on affordability - whether a household can financially afford to keep the home adequately warm - regardless of whether there is an actual need for heating due to climatic conditions. The [[Glossary:Housing_cost_overburden_rate|housing cost overburden rate]] measures housing affordability as the percentage of the population living in households where the total housing costs (’net’ of housing allowances) represent more than 40% of disposable income (’net’ of housing allowances). Housing costs refer to the monthly expenditures connected with a household’s occupancy of their accommodation. These costs include utilities (water, electricity, gas, heating) based on actual usage. Only costs that are actually paid are considered, regardless of the payer. For owners, housing costs encompass mortgage interest payments (net of tax relief), structural insurance, mandatory services and charges (like sewage and refuse removal), regular maintenance and repairs, taxes, and utilities. Tenants (both at market and reduced prices) have similar housing costs, including rental payments, structural insurance (if paid by tenants), services and charges (if paid by tenants), taxes on dwelling (if applicable), regular maintenance and repairs, and utilities. Rent-free tenants incur housing costs potentially covering structural insurance, services and charges, dwelling taxes (if applicable), regular maintenance and repairs, and utilities. In all cases, housing benefits are not deducted from the total housing cost. Finally, the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Satisfaction_with_the_dwelling satisfaction with their dwelling] measures individuals’ satisfaction with their dwelling classified into levels (e.g. very high, good, low, very low). It further analyses these levels in relation to [[Glossary:At_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_(AROPE)|the risk of poverty]] threshold, highlighting disparities between those who are at risk of poverty and those not. The indicator presented in this article focuses on people reporting "very high" or "good" level of satisfaction with their dwellings. ===Context=== According to the European Commission's [https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/e6cd4328-673c-4e7a-8683-f63ffb2cf648_en?filename=Political%20Guidelines%202024-2029_EN.pdf Political Guidelines 2024-2029], affordable and sustainable housing is a key priority for the [https://commission.europa.eu/about/commission-2024-2029_en Commission 2024-2029]. Such guidelines emphasise the need to address the housing crisis in Europe, where many citizens struggle to access decent and affordable housing. The Commission aims to promote policies that increase the supply of affordable housing, improve energy efficiency in buildings and support vulnerable populations such as low-income households and the homeless. Notably, a newly appointed Commissioner has been tasked with overseeing a dedicated ’Energy and Housing’ portfolio, underscoring the Commission’s commitment to tackle the interlinked challenges of energy and housing. By prioritising housing, the Commission seeks to improve the quality of life for European citizens, promote social cohesion and contribute to a more sustainable and inclusive future for all. === Other articles === '''Online publication''' *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Living_conditions_in_Europe All articles from Living conditions in Europe] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)_methodology_-_people_at_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) methodology - people at risk of poverty or social exclusion] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Living_conditions_in_Europe_-_poverty_and_social_exclusion Living conditions in Europe - title: Living conditions in Europe - income distribution and income inequality
text:
Living conditions in Europe is an online Eurostat publication that analyses income and living conditions across the EU. This article covers income distribution and income inequality. Data extracted in November 2025. Planned article update: November 2026. In 2024, the median annual equivalised disposable income was 21 245 PPS per inhabitant in the EU; over one quarter of it (5 847 PPS) was received as social transfers from governments (e.g. pensions, social benefits, etc.). The at-risk-of-poverty rate anchored to 2019 decreased to 14.1% in 2024, down from 16.5% in 2019. In 2024, the Gini coefficient for the EU was 29.4, with the highest levels of inequality in terms of disposable income in the EU reported in Bulgaria (38.4), Lithuania (35.3) and Latvia (34.2), and lowest in Slovakia (21.7), Czechia (23.7) and Slovenia (23.8). In the EU in 2024, the share of people at risk of poverty exceeded 45% only in one region in France’s overseas departments, while 28 regions in the EU had rates below 10%. This article focuses on income distribution and poverty risk in the [[Glossary:EU_enlargements|European Union (EU)]] in 2024. It examines median disposable income, the role of social transfers, regional disparities in poverty risk, and income inequality as measured by the [[Glossary%3AGini_coefficient|Gini coefficient]]. All figures are based on [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]] available from [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database Eurostat's online database]. EU-SILC data are available for all EU Member States, as well as for most of the EFTA and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]]. ===Income distribution=== '''Median annual disposable income in 2024 highest in Luxembourg and lowest in Hungary''' In 2024, the [[Glossary:Equivalised_disposable_income|median annual disposable income]] was 21,245 PPS ([[Glossary:Purchasing_power_standard_(PPS)|purchasing power standard]]) per inhabitant in the EU. Across the EU countries, it ranged from 37,781 PPS in Luxembourg and 29,758 PPS in Austria to 11,199 PPS in Hungary and 11,433 PPS in Slovakia. Figure 1 shows the contribution of [[Glossary:Social transfers|social transfers]] to disposable income. This information is split between transfers for pensions and other social transfers, for example, social security benefits and social assistance that aim to alleviate or reduce the risk of poverty. In 2024, in the EU, social transfers (including pensions) accounted for 5,847 PPS of the median disposable income, 1,613 PPS from transfers other than pensions. Among the EU countries, there were considerable variations in the contribution made by social transfers to median disposable income in 2024. The largest transfers were observed in Luxembourg, where social transfers (including pensions) increased the median disposable income by 10,015 PPS per inhabitant. Social transfers (including pensions) were also relatively high in Austria (8,141 PPS) and France (7,606 PPS). In 2024, social transfers excluding pensions contributed more than 2,000 PPS per inhabitant to median disposable income in Belgium (2,686 PPS), Austria (2,442 PPS), Sweden (2,273 PPS), Estonia (2,254 PPS) and Ireland (2,233 PPS). [[Image:Fig1_Median equivalised disposable income and magnitude of social transfers, 2024_(PPS per inhabitant).png|thumb|centre|850px|Figure 1: Median equivalised disposable income and magnitude of social transfers, 2024
(PPS per inhabitant)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_di03__custom_18724193/default/table (ilc_di03)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ILC_DI13__custom_18724207/default/table (ilc_di13)] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ILC_DI14__custom_12455581/default/table?lang=en (ilc_di14)]|alt= Combined stacked bar chart and scatter chart showing median equivalised disposable income and magnitude of social transfers as PPS per inhabitant in the EU, individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Türkiye, Albania, Serbia, Montenegro and North Macedonia for the year 2024. Each country column contains two stacks representing pensions and social transfers other than pensions. The scatter plot for each country represents total disposable income. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''The at-risk-of-poverty rate in the EU decreased between 2019 and 2024''' Figure 2 shows that the at-risk-of-poverty rate anchored to 2019 decreased across the EU, reaching 14.1% in 2024, compared to 16.5% in 2019. This decline reflects an overall improvement in living standards for low-income groups. It suggests that the real equivalised disposable incomes of these groups, adjusted for inflation, have increased compared to the 2019 baseline, lifting many out of poverty. The largest reductions were observed in Romania (down 17.3 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] to 6.5%) and Bulgaria (down 14.2 pp to 8.4%). The lowest decreases were recorded in Austria (down 0.8 pp to 12.5%) and Czechia (down 0.9 to 9.2%). However, some countries recorded increases in their anchored at-risk-of-poverty rates. Denmark saw its rate rise by 0.1 pp to 12.6%, while Finland experienced an increase of 1.1 pp, reaching 12.7% in 2024. Germany reported a more significant rise of 2.3 pp to 17.1%, and Slovakia recorded the largest increase together with France, up 3.5 pp to 15.4% and 17.1%, respectively. [[Image:Fig2_At-risk-of-poverty rate anchored to 2019, 2019 and 2024_(%).png|thumb|centre|850px|Figure 2: At-risk-of-poverty rate anchored to 2019, 2019 and 2024 (%), ranked by year 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_li22__custom_18724713/default/table (ilc_li22)]|alt= Combined stacked bar chart and scatter chart showing at-risk-of-poverty rates anchored to 2019 for the EU as a whole, EU Member States, Norway, Switzerland and Türkiye in 2019 and 2024.]]
===Income inequality=== Median disposable income provides a measure of average living standards, but it does not capture the distribution of income within the population. The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Gini_coefficient Gini coefficient] gives the extent to which the distribution of income within a country deviates from a perfectly equal distribution. A Gini value of 100 means that only one person receives all the income in the country, while a Gini value of 0 means that income is distributed equally across the population. '''Income inequality as measured by Gini coefficient above the EU average in 14 EU countries''' In 2024, the Gini coefficient for the EU was 29.4, as shown in Map 1. The highest income disparities among the EU countries were recorded in Bulgaria (38.4), Lithuania (35.3) and Latvia (34.2). In Germany, Denmark and Croatia, the Gini coefficients were close to the EU average. Income was more evenly distributed in Slovakia, Czechia, Slovenia and Belgium, where the Gini coefficient was less than 25.0.
Map 1: Gini coefficient for equivalised disposable income per inhabitant, 2024 (Scale from o to 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_di12__custom_18725191/default/table ilc_di12]) [[Image:MAP GINI2024 GISCO V5.png|thumb|centre|850px|Map 1: Gini coefficient for equivalised disposable income per inhabitant, 2024 (Scale from 0 to 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([ttps://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_li41__custom_18893793/default/tablen ilc_di12])|alt=Map showing the Gini coefficient for equivalised disposable income per inhabitant in the EU for the year 2024.]] '''Regional disparities observed in shares of people at risk of poverty across the EU''' Map 2 shows the share of people [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|at risk of poverty]] at regional [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/nuts NUTS] level 2 in 2024. Among all EU regions, one region in France’s overseas departments (Guyane) recorded the highest percentage of people at risk of poverty, with a percentage of 53.3%. Across the EU, 10 regions had a share of people at risk of poverty ranging from 30.0% to 41.4%. These regions specifically include two of France’s overseas departments (La Réunion and Guadalupe), two of Spain’s autonomous cities (Ciudad de Ceuta and Ciudad de Melilla), four regions in Italy (Campania, Calabria, Puglia and Sicilia), and two regions in Greece (Dytiki Elláda and Voreio Aigaio). On the other hand, 28 NUTS level 2 regions in the EU recorded shares of people at risk of poverty below 10% in 2024. These included five NUTS Level 2 regions each in Italy (Marche, Valle d’Aosta, Emilia Romagna, Provincia autonoma di Trento and Provincia autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen), Belgium (Prov. Limburg, Prov. Oost-Vlaanderen, Prov. Vlaams-Brabant, Prov. West-Vlaanderen and Prov. Brabant wallon) and in Czechia (Praha, Jihovýchod, Střední Čechy, Jihozápad and Severovýchod), three regions in Hungary (Budapest, Közép-Dunántúl and Nyugat-Dunántúl), two regions in Poland (Śląskie and Warszawski stołeczny) and Austria (Burgenland and Salzburg), and one region each in Finland (Helsinki-Uusimaa), Slovakia (Bratislavský kraj), Spain (Pais Vasco), Denmark (Sjælland) and Romania (Bucureşti-Ilfov).
Map 2: People at risk of poverty by NUTS 2 regions, 2024
(% of people)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_li02/default/table?lang=en ilc_li02]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_li41/default/table?lang=en ilc_li41]) [[Image:MAP AROP2024V2.png|thumb|centre|850px|Map 2: People at risk of poverty by NUTS 2 regions, 2024
(% of people)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_li02/default/table?lang=en ilc_li02]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_li41/default/table?lang=en ilc_li41])|alt=Map showing the share of people at risk of poverty in the EU by NUTS 2 regions for the year 2024.]] === Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=SE_article_Income_distribution_and_income_inequality_2024_v3.xlsx|title=Income distribution and inequality: maps and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data used in this article are derived from [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]]. EU-SILC data are compiled annually and are the main source of statistics that measure income and living conditions in Europe. It is also the main source of information used to link different aspects relating to the living conditions of households and individuals. The reference population for the information presented in this article is all private [[Glossary:Private_household|households]] and their current members residing in the territory of an EU Member State (or non-EU member country) at the time of data collection. Persons living in collective households and in institutions are generally excluded from the target population. The data for the EU are population-weighted averages of national data. The reference time for information on income is 2023, while the other households’ characteristics are referenced to 2024. ===Context=== To consider differences in household size and composition, and thus enable comparisons of income levels across countries and population groups, the concept of [[Glossary:Equivalised disposable income|equivalised disposable income]] is used. This measure is based on the total net (also referred to as disposable) household income divided by the number of “equivalent adults” in the household, using a standard (equivalence) scale. Eurostat employs the “modified OECD scale”, which assigns a weight of 1.0 to the household head, 0.5 to each additional adult (aged 14 and over), and 0.3 to each child (aged under 14). The weights are summed to calculate an equivalised household size, which is then used to divide the total household income and determine the equivalised disposable income attributed to each household member. For the anchored [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|at-risk-of-poverty]] rate, the equivalised disposable income is compared to a fixed poverty threshold, which is calculated using the income distribution of the base year (2019). This anchored poverty line remains constant over time but is adjusted for inflation to maintain its real value. The anchored poverty threshold enables comparisons across years, providing a consistent baseline to assess changes in living standards for low-income groups. The median of the equivalised disposable income distribution is typically used in the EU as a key measure for analysing standards of living within each economy. It is simply the income level that divides the population into two groups of equal size: one group encompasses half the population with a level of disposable income above the median and the other group encompasses the half of the population with a level of disposable income below the median. The use of the median (rather than the arithmetic mean) avoids any potential distortion that may be caused by the existence of extreme values, such as a few extremely rich households that may raise the arithmetic mean. The at-risk-of-poverty rate is part of the [[Glossary:At_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_(AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion rate (AROPE)]]. The AROPE ratio is the share of the total population which is at risk of poverty or social exclusion. The headline target [[Glossary:The_European_Pillar_of_Social_Rights_Action_Plan_(EU_2030_targets)|(EU2030 target)]] on poverty and social inclusion of [[Glossary:The_European_Pillar_of_Social_Rights_Action_Plan_(EU_2030_targets)|the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan]] is to reduce the number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion by at least 15 million by 2030. Progress towards this target is monitored through the AROPE rate, published by Eurostat. ===Other articles=== '''Online publication''' *All articles from [[Living_conditions_in_Europe|''Living conditions in Europe'']] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)_methodology_-_people_at_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) methodology -
