title: Living conditions in Europe - self-perceived discrimination
text:
Living conditions in Europe is an online Eurostat publication that analyses income and living conditions across the EU. This article covers self-perceived discrimination. Data extracted in July 2025 Planned article update: July 2031 In 2024 in the EU: * 5.9% of people aged 16 and over reported feeling discriminated against when looking for housing; the rate was higher among people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, reaching 10.1%, compared with 4.7% for those not at risk. * *4.1% of people without disabilities (activity limitations) have felt discriminated against when interacting with public services. For people with a disability, the share was more than twice as much, 9.3%. * * people born abroad were nearly 3 times more likely to feel discriminated against in public spaces (7.7%) than native-born (2.7%).
This article focuses on self-perceived discrimination across different life situations and contexts (for example, looking for housing in the past 5 years, and education, public services, and public spaces in the past 12 months) in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Drawing on data from the [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions]] (EU-SILC) 6-yearly module on ‘access to services’, the findings highlight that people [[Glossary:At_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_(AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)]], individuals with a disability ([[Glossary:Activity limitation|activity limitations]]), and those living in a country other than their country of birth are more likely to feel discriminated against. ===Self-perceived discrimination higher among people at risk of poverty or social exclusion=== In 2024, 5.9% of people aged 16 and over reported having felt discriminated against when looking for housing. Moreover, 5.2% of them felt discriminated against when in contact with public services or administrative offices, 3.4% in public spaces and 2.6% in education. People at risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE) in the EU reported feeling discriminated against twice as often as those not at risk across all surveyed life situations (see Figure 1). The gap in self-perceived discrimination between people at risk of poverty or social exclusion and those who are not at risk of poverty or social exclusion was largest when looking for housing (10.1% compared with 4.7%) and when contacting public services or administrative offices (9.2% compared with 4.2%). While self-perceived discrimination in public spaces and education was less frequent overall, they remained more prevalent among people at risk of poverty or social exclusion: 5.7% reported such experiences in public spaces and 4.4% declared having felt discriminated against when in education. For people who were not at risk of poverty or social exclusion, these percentages were 2.8% and 2.1%, respectively. [[Image:F1_Self-perceived discrimination by life situation and at risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE) situation, EU, 2024_(%)_rev.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Self-perceived discrimination by life situation and at risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE) situation, EU, 2024 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_atsd01}}|alt=Vertical bar chart showing the share of self-perceived discrimination across four life situations in the EU for the year 2024 for people not at risk of poverty or social exclusion, people at risk of poverty or social exclusion. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===People with a disability (activity limitation) report experiencing more discrimination than those without=== In 2024, in the EU, 8.3% of people with a disability (activity limitation) felt discriminated against when looking for housing. This is approximately 1.6 times higher than the percentage for people with no disability (at 5.3%, see Figure 2). The gap in self-reported discrimination is even wider when contacting public services and administrative offices, with 9.3% of people with activity limitations reporting self-perceived discrimination, which is 2.3 times higher than the figure for those without such limitations (4.1%). When interacting with educational institutions, more people with a disability reported discrimination than people without a disability (4.1% compared with 2.3%). The ratio was similar for self-perceived discrimination in public spaces, with more reports for people with a disability (4.9%) compared with people without (2.9%). [[Image:F2_Self-perceived discrimination by life situation and disability status (activity limitation), EU, 2024_(%)_rev.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Self-perceived discrimination by life situation and disability status (activity limitation), EU, 2024 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_atsd01}}|alt=Vertical bar chart showing self-perceived discrimination across four life situations in the EU for the year 2024 for people with no activity limitations and people with activity limitations. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Foreign-born people more likely to feel discriminated against than native-born people=== In 2024, 13.7% of men born abroad reported feeling discriminated against when looking for housing, as shown in Figure 3. This rate is 3.4 times higher than that of native-born men (4.0%). Similarly, 11.6% of women born abroad reported feeling discriminated against, which is 2.5 times higher than the rate for native-born women (4.7%). Self-perceived discrimination in public spaces was much higher for men born abroad (at 7.5%) than among native-born men (2.4%). Overall, women reported having experienced discrimination in public spaces more than men, with rates of 7.9% for foreign-born women and 3.1% for native-born women. When in contact with public services, men and women born abroad reported similar levels of discrimination, with around 9.7% for each group. Among those native-born, women reported slightly higher rates of self-perceived discrimination (4.6%) than native-born men (4.4%). Men born abroad reported discrimination when interacting with educational institutions nearly twice as high as native born (3.7% compared with 1.9%). In the same context, women were more likely than men to have felt discriminated against, with rates of 4.8% for foreign-born and 2.6% for native-born women. [[Image:F3_Self-perceived discrimination by life situation, country of birth and sex, EU, 2024_(%)_rev.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Self-perceived discrimination by life situation, country of birth and sex, EU, 2024 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_atsd02}}|alt=Vertical bar chart showing self-perceived discrimination in the EU for the year 2024 across four life situations. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''The share of self-perceived discrimination while in contact with public services was highest in Estonia, the Netherlands and Germany''' In 2024, 5.2% of people in the EU reported having felt discriminated against while in contact with public services or administrative offices (see Figure 4), but shares varied widely across the EU countries. Self-perceived discrimination in this life situation was highest in Estonia (10.1%), followed by the Netherlands (8.2%), Germany (7.9%), Austria (7.8%) and Spain (7.7%). By contrast, Italy (1.5%), Croatia (1.9%) and Hungary (2.2%) recorded relatively low levels of self-perceived discrimination. [[Image:F4_Self-perceived discrimination when in contact with public services or administrative offices by country, 2024_(%)_rev.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Self-perceived discrimination when in contact with public services or administrative offices by country, 2024 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_atsd01}}|alt=Vertical bar chart showing self-perceived discrimination in the EU for the year 2024 when in contact with public services or administrative office in the EU, individual EU countries, Norway, and Türkiye. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Self-perceived discrimination in public spaces was 2.9 times higher for foreign-born people compared with native-born in the EU=== Figure 5 illustrates that, on average across the EU, 2.7% of native-born people reported having experienced discrimination in public places. For people born abroad, this share was nearly 3 times higher, at 7.7%. In general, countries with high levels of self-perceived discrimination tend to show elevated rates for both groups, though the gap between them may vary. For instance, in Croatia, the proportions of self-perceived discrimination were similar between the 2 groups, with 0.7% for natives and 0.8% for those born abroad. By contrast, the Netherlands showed a stark disparity, with 5.5% of native-born reporting self-discrimination when in contact with public services compared with 18.0% for foreign-born people. The largest gaps in self-perceived discrimination between native-born and people born abroad were observed in Poland, Portugal, Czechia and Italy, where people born abroad reported feeling discriminated in public spaces at more than 5 times the rate of native-born. [[Image:F5_Self-perceived discrimination in public spaces by country of birth, 2024_(%)_rev.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Self-perceived discrimination in public spaces by country of birth, 2024 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_atsd02}}|alt=Vertical bar chart showing self-perceived discrimination in public spaces in the EU for the year 2024 for individual EU countries, Norway, and Türkiye. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Self-perceived_discrimination_rev2.xlsx|title=Self-perceived discrimination: tables and figures}} === Data sources === The data used in this article are derived from the EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC). EU-SILC are collected annually and are the main source of statistics that measure income and living conditions in Europe; it is also the main source of information used to link different aspects relating to the quality of life of households and individuals. The reference population for the information presented in this article is all private households and their current members residing in the territory of an EU Member State (or a non-member country) at the time of data collection; people living in collective households are generally excluded from the target population. The data for the EU are population-weighted averages of national data. The reference period for individuals' characteristics is 2024. The statistics presented cover the EU as a whole, its individual Member States, one [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA]] country (Norway), as well as the [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]] Serbia and Türkiye. The 6-yearly module on ‘access to services’ collects information on different topics, such as use of services, including care services and services for independent living; self-perceived discrimination; affordability of services; unmet needs for services. The section on '''self-perceived discrimination''' covers information on whether the respondent felt discriminated against at any time in the past 12 months (even only once) when in contact with administrative offices or public services (including job centre, health and social services), feeling discriminated in education, and feeling discriminated in public spaces (shops, cafés, restaurants, leisure facilities, etc). It also includes information on whether the respondent felt discriminated against at any time in the past 5 years (even if only once) when looking for housing. It is important to note that '''subjective perceptions of discrimination''', as measured through surveys, can be influenced by various factors, including individuals’ awareness, expectations, the legal context (e.g. availability of anti-discrimination laws or complaint mechanisms) and the degree of societal acceptance. As a result, these factors can significantly impact the reporting of discrimination and affect the comparability of data across different population groups, countries, or cultural settings. For information related to country of birth, '''native-born''' designates individuals who were born in the reporting country, while '''foreign-born''' applies to those born abroad, regardless of their current citizenship or legal status. '''Concepts:''' '''Discrimination''' is the unfair or prejudicial treatment of people and groups based on the protected characteristics in EU law: sex, age, disability, religion or belief, ethnic or racial origin, and sexual orientation. '''Self-perceived discrimination''' refers to the self-reported experience of discrimination. It is measured by asking individuals if they have felt, in the last 12 months (last 5 years for housing), personally discriminated against in a certain number of situations. '''Discrimination when looking for housing''' includes situations where the interviewee suffered hardship when looking to rent or buy real estate. This can mean refusing to rent and sell, expressing preferences for tenants or buyers or treating them less favourably on the basis of the protected grounds. '''Discrimination in education''' includes discrimination happening before admission, for instance through refusing to register a child, or during the education process with inconsistent enforcement of policy and discipline according to the protected grounds. Discrimination can target children and parents alike. '''Discrimination in public services or administrative offices''' refers to public-owned and managed institutions, including job centres and health related services, where a person occupying public functions might have charged the interviewee more, might have denied help or have the interviewee’s benefits interrupted on the basis of discriminatory behaviour. '''Discrimination in public spaces''' refer to a wide array of places such as cafes, shops, sports facilities in which people may have been denied service, have been served lower quality goods or services, or have been charged more than other individuals for instance. '''At risk of poverty or social exclusion''', abbreviated as AROPE, corresponds to the sum of people who are either at risk of poverty, or severely materially and socially deprived, or living in a household with a very low work intensity. People are included only once even if they are in more than one of these situations. '''Disability''' is approximated according to the concept of [[Glossary:Activity limitation|global activity limitation]], which is defined as a limitation – because of health problems – in carrying out usual activities (for at least the previous 6 months). This is considered to be an adequate proxy for disability, both by the scientific community and organisations representing people with disabilities. This definition is also in line with the concept of disability as set out in the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=LEGISSUM%3Aem0047 European disability strategy 2010-2020] and its successor, the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030-easy-read-version_en Strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities 2021-2030]. '''People born abroad or foreign-born''' refers to people, citizens of the country they were interviewed in or not, who were born in a country different from the one reporting. === Context === Equality and non-discrimination are core values of the EU and have strong foundations in the EU treaties, in the Charter of Fundamental Rights and in equal treatment directives. The [[Glossary:Treaty_on_European_Union|Treaty on European Union]] (TEU) called for a Union that would respect “human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and respect for human rights, including the rights of persons belonging to minorities” (Article 2) and would combat social exclusion and discrimination (Article 3). Sex, age, racial or ethnic origin, disability, religion and sexual orientation are the main protected grounds under EU treaties and legislation. Equality and non-discrimination are at the heart of the Commission’s agenda, through the first EU strategy on combating antisemitism and fostering Jewish life (2021-2030) and the Union of Equality initiatives adopted in 2020 and 2021, namely the EU Roma Strategic Framework, the Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, the Gender Equality Strategy, the LGBTIQ Equality Strategy and the EU Anti-racism Action Plan. The last 3 will be updated and extended in accordance with [https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/e6cd4328-673c-4e7a-8683-f63ffb2cf648_en?filename=Political%20Guidelines%202024-2029_EN.pdf President Von der Leyen’s political guidelines (2024-2029)]. The [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/gender-equality/gender-equality-strategy_en Gender Equality Strategy 2020–2025] and the Roadmap for Women’s Right aim to achieve gender equality, uphold and develop women’s rights and address gender equality challenges, such as gender stereotypes, technology-facilitated bias, discrimination, and violence. The [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/combatting-discrimination/racism-and-xenophobia/eu-anti-racism-action-plan-2020-2025_en EU Anti-racism Action Plan 2020-2025], launched in 2020, seeks to tackle racism at all levels, from encouraging diversity to identifying structural racism and collecting data on hate crimes. The [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030_en Strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities 2021-2030] aims to improve the lives of disabled people. Among its objectives are the enjoyment of basic human rights, the provision of equal opportunities and access to society and economic life, and the elimination of discrimination based on disability. These goals also align with the [https://sdgs.un.org/goals United Nation’s Sustainable Development Goals for 2030] amongst which are achieving gender equality, reducing inequalities in general and promoting inclusive societies. To achieve these goals, the report “[https://hlpf.un.org/tools/a-human-rights-based-approach-to-data-leaving-no-one-behind-in-the-2030-agenda-for A Human Rights-Based Approach to Data. Leaving no one Behind in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development]” offers insights into data collection and disaggregation to quantify the completion of the goals. Providing statistics, which are disaggregated by protected grounds for discrimination, allows for detailed monitoring of the EU’s goals to build a [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/justice-and-fundamental-rights/equality-and-inclusion_en Union of Equality]. Many of Eurostat’s indicators are disaggregated by sex, age, activity limitations (as a proxy of disability), and country of birth. [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2022.325.01.0016.01.ENG Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2498] specifies that the 2024 EU-SILC survey will collect 6-yearly variables on access to services. === Other articles === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Living_conditions_in_Europe_-_poverty_and_social_exclusion Living conditions in Europe – poverty and social exclusion] (online publication) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Gender_statistics Gender statistics] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Self-perceived_discrimination_at_work_-_statistics Self-perceived discrimination at work – statistics] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Disability_statistics_-_housing_conditions Disability statistics – housing conditions] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Migrant_integration_statistics_-_housing Migrant integration statistics – housing] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Young_people_-_housing_conditions Young people – housing conditions] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database Database – Eurostat] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/equality-non-discrimination/database Database – Equality and non-discrimination] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/database Database – Income and living conditions] === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/equality-non-discrimination/overview Overview – Equality and non-discrimination - title: Living conditions in Europe - poverty and social exclusion
text:
Living conditions in Europe is an online Eurostat publication that analyses income and living conditions across the EU. This article covers poverty and social exclusion. Data extracted in: April 2025 Planned article update: April 2027 In 2025, 92.7 million people in the EU were at risk of poverty or social exclusion; this was equivalent to 20.9% of the EU population. The risk of poverty or social exclusion in the EU was, in 2025, higher for women than for men (21.9% compared with 19.8%). In 2025, at the EU level, working status significantly influenced the at-risk-of-poverty-or-social-exclusion rate, ranging from 10.9% for employed people to 66.3% for the unemployed individuals. Over one-fifth (22.1%) of the EU population living in households with dependent children was at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025. [[Image:Poverty and social exclusion Apr2026_bars_1920px.jpg|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/36c503c8-0106-47d1-b830-4c3b0da37837?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-24T12:10:58Z/default/table ilc_peps01n])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in the EU and individual EU Member States as a percentage of total population for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article is part of a set of statistical articles that form Eurostat's online publication, ''[[Living_conditions_in_Europe|Living conditions in Europe]]'' and focuses on people [[Glossary:At_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_(AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion]], presenting some key results from the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union's (EU)]] [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]]. This data collection covers EU countries, as well as most of the [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]].
===Poverty or social exclusion=== '''Over one in five people in the EU were at risk of poverty or social exclusion''' In 2025, there were around 92.7 million people in the EU at risk of poverty or social exclusion, which was equivalent to 20.9% of the total population. The AROPE rate varied considerably across the EU countries. Bulgaria (29.0%), Greece (27.5%) and Romania (27.4%) reported the highest shares of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025. By contrast, the Netherlands, Slovenia, Poland and Czechia presented shares below 16.0%. '''Component indicators which contribute to an analysis of the risk of poverty or social exclusion''' '''Figure 1''' provides an analysis for the EU population of the various components of risks of poverty or social exclusion. Among the 92.7 million people within the EU who faced the risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025, some 5.7 million lived in households experiencing simultaneously all 3 poverty and social exclusion risks. There were 11.6 million people in the EU living both at risk of poverty and in a household with very low work intensity (but not severely materially and socially deprived); 8.1 million were at risk of poverty and at the same time severely materially and socially deprived (but not in a household with very low work intensity); almost 1.5 million lived in households with very low work intensity while experiencing severe material deprivation (but were not at risk of poverty). [[Image:Poverty and social exclusion Apr2026 Venn2 1920px.jpg|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, by type of risk, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0a40baba-2f93-4366-8761-6302a1f83ab8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-24T11:50:07Z/default/table ilc_pees01n])|alt= Venn diagram showing number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in millions within the EU analysed by type of risk. For the year 2025, three types of risk are analysed, namely, at risk of poverty, severely materially and socially deprived and lastly, living in household with very low work intensity. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''The profile of people in the EU at risk of poverty or social exclusion''' Women, young adults aged 18-24 years, people with a low level of educational attainment and unemployed people were, on average, more likely to be at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025 than other groups within the EU population (see '''Figure 2'''). [[Image:Fig_2 People at risk of poverty or social exclusion, analysed by socio-economic characteristics, EU, 2025_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: People at risk of poverty or social exclusion, by socio-economic characteristics, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/df53a2b8-b806-4ab2-8a47-32aa3c9cff37?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-24T12:00:30Z/default/table ilc_peps01n]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/236151dd-716f-4ea5-b439-78b2fbce4ca4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-24T12:01:07Z/default/table ilc_peps02n]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1d24ae7f-43e3-499c-940e-eec38e28d895?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-24T12:01:28Z/default/table ilc_peps04n])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in percentages analysed by socio-economic characteristic in the EU for the year 2025. 14 columns divided into four sections represent 1, sex – female and male; 2, age in years – less than 18, 18 to 24, 25 to 49, 50 to 64, 65 and over; 3, education – low, medium, high and 4, activity status – employed, unemployed, retired and other inactive. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Women and young adults were more at risk of poverty or social exclusion''' When analyzed by sex, the risk of poverty or social exclusion in the EU was higher for women than it was for men (21.9% compared with 19.8%). Concerning age, the highest risk of poverty or social exclusion in the EU was recorded for young adults aged 18-24 years (26.3%), while the lowest risk was recorded for adults aged 65 years or over (18.8%). Moreover, the risk of poverty or social exclusion was 19.1% for adults aged 25-49 years and 20.8% among the population aged 50-64 years. The youngest age group, people aged less than 18 years, recorded a relatively high risk of poverty or social exclusion (24.3%). '''In addition to age, educational attainment had a considerable impact on the risk of poverty or social exclusion''' At EU level, more than one-third (34.2%) of all people aged 18 years or over with a low educational attainment level ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=International_Standard_Classification_of_Education_(ISCED) International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED)] levels 0-2) were at risk of poverty or social exclusion, compared with 10.3% of people in the same age group with a tertiary (high) level of educational attainment (ISCED levels 5-8). The corresponding percentage for people with a medium level of educational attainment (ISCED levels 3-4) was 19.2%. '''Unemployed people faced a particularly high risk of poverty or social exclusion''' In the EU, 66.3% of the [[Glossary:Unemployment|unemployed]] aged 18 years or over were at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025. [[Glossary:Inactive|Inactive people]] (other than in retirement) faced the second-highest risk on the basis of an analysis by activity status, with 44.3% at risk. For comparison, the share of people in retirement who were at risk of poverty or social exclusion was 17.6% and the share of [[Glossary:Employed_person|employed people]] in such situation was 10.9%. '''At the EU level, households with dependent children faced a slightly higher risk of poverty or social exclusion than those without''' More than one-fifth (22.1%) of people living in households with [[Glossary:Dependent_children|dependent children]] in the EU were at risk of poverty or social exclusion which was slightly higher than the respective share among households without dependent children (19.8%). Nevertheless, these rates varied considerably across the EU countries. For people living in households with dependent children, the rate ranged from peaks of 29.9% in Spain, 29.4% in Romania and 29.1% in Bulgaria down to 12.2% in Cyprus, 11.7% in the Netherlands and 10.4% in Slovenia (see '''Figure 3''' ). For those living in households without dependent children, the rates varied from 33.4% in Latvia, 32.3% in Lithuania and 28.9% in Bulgaria to 12.8% in Luxembourg, 12.3% in Slovakia and 9.6% in Czechia. [[Image:Fig 3 People at risk of poverty or social exclusion for households with or without dependent children, 2025_fnl.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: People at risk of poverty or social exclusion for households with or without dependent children, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c44a6618-bbc3-475e-b8f7-3a1658a353b5?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-24T12:05:16Z/default/table ilc_peps03n])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion for households with or without dependent children as percentages in the EU, euro area, individual EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries for the year 2025. Each country has two columns representing those living in households without dependent children and those living in households with dependent children. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=Living_conditions_in_Europe_-_poverty_and_social_exclusion_fnl.xlsx|title=Poverty and social exclusion: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data used in this article are derived from the [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]] data collection. EU-SILC data are compiled annually and are the main source of statistics that measure income and living conditions in Europe; it is also the main source of information used to link different aspects relating to the quality of life of [[Glossary:Household|households]] and individuals. The reference population for the information presented in this article is all private households and their current members residing in the territory of an EU Member State (or non-EU member country) at the time of data collection; people living in collective households and in institutions are generally excluded from the target population. The data for the EU are population-weighted averages of national data. The data on educational attainment levels is collected and classified according to [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=International_Standard_Classification_of_Education_(ISCED) ISCED 2011]. It is divided into three categories: high (short-cycle tertiary education, bachelor's or equivalent, master's or equivalent, and doctoral or equivalent levels), medium (upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education), and low (less than primary, primary, or lower secondary education). ===Context=== The [[Glossary:At_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_(AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion]] rate, abbreviated as AROPE, corresponds to the sum of people who are either [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|at risk of poverty]], or [[Glossary:Severe material and social deprivation rate (SMSD)|severely materially and socially deprived]] or [[Glossary:Persons living in households with very low work intensity|living in a household with a very low work intensity]] (also know as (quasi-)jobless households). The AROPE ratio is the share of the total population which is at risk of poverty or social exclusion. The headline target (EU2030 target) on poverty and social inclusion of the [[Glossary:The European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan (EU 2030 targets)|European Pillar of Social Rights]] Action Plan is to reduce the number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion by at least 15 million by 2030. Progress towards this target is monitored through the AROPE rate, published by Eurostat. To calculate the number or share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, three separate measures are combined. This indicator covers individuals who are in at least one of the following situations: • '''People at risk of poverty''', that is, those with an equivalised disposable income below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold, defined as 60% of the national median equivalised disposable income after social transfers; • '''People experiencing severe material and social deprivation''', that is, those who face and enforced lack at least seven out of thirteen deprivation items (six related to the individual and seven related to the household) considered necessary and desirable for an adequate life; • '''People aged less than 65 years living in households with very low work intensity''', that is, those living in households where the adults (those aged 18-64, but excluding students aged 18-24 and people who are retired according to their self-defined current economic status or who receive any pension (except survivors pension), as well as people in the age bracket 60-64 who are inactive and living in a household where the main income is pensions) worked a working time equal or less than 20% of their total combined work-time potential during the previous year. In 2021, the AROPE indicator was modified. The severe material deprivation rate component was revised, defining a new severe material and social deprivation rate (SMSD) based on a revised list of items, and the people living in very low work intensity households indicator relating to people living in a household with a very low work intensity was redefined. The revised AROPE indicator is used to monitor the headline target on poverty and social inclusion of the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan. === Other articles === *[[Living conditions in Europe|All articles from ''Living conditions in Europe'']] *[[EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) methodology - people at risk of poverty or social exclusion]] *[[Living conditions in Europe - income distribution and income inequality ]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/database Income and living conditions - detailed datasets (ilc)] === Thematic section === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=income_social_inclusion_living_conditions}} Income, social inclusion and living conditions] === Publications === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-key-figures/w/KS-01-25-032 Key figures on European living conditions – 2025 edition - Eurostat] === Methodology === *{{Template:Esms|code=ilc_sieusilc|title=Income and living conditions}} (ESMS metadata file — ilc_esms) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/information-data Income and living conditions — information on data ] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/methodology Income and living conditions — methodology] === Legislation === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/legislation Income and living conditions - legislation] ===External links=== *[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/social-protection-social-inclusion/social-protection-committee/indicators-sub-group_en European Commission — Directorate General for Employment, Social Affairs & Inclusion: Indicators’ Sub-Group of the Social Protection Committee] *[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/index_en European Commission — Directorate General for Employment, Social Affairs & Inclusion: Employment and social analysis] {{Unit|topic=X_Living_conditions}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Living conditions in Europe — poverty and social exclusion]] [[Category:Income and living conditions|Living conditions in Europe — poverty and social exclusion]] [[Category:Poverty and social exclusion|Living conditions in Europe — poverty and social exclusion]] [[Category:Statistical article|Living conditions in Europe — poverty and social exclusion]] [[Category:April2027|Living conditions in Europe — poverty and social exclusion]]

title: Living conditions in Europe - monetary poverty among the elderly
text:
Overview of gender disparities in pensions and poverty among older people in the EU, including gaps in pension income, coverage rates, at‑risk‑of‑poverty indicators and differences in the aggregate replacement ratio for pensions . Data extracted in December 2025 Planned article update: January 2027 In 2024, the average pension for women aged 65 years or over in the EU was 24.5% lower than those for men. In 2024, the at-risk-of-poverty rate for women aged 65 years or over was higher than that for men in the same age group in 22 EU countries. Minor disparities in pension adequacy were recorded at EU level in 2024, with a gender difference in the aggregate replacement ratio standing at 0.03 percentage points. This article examines monetary poverty among those aged 65 years or over, using various statistical indicators such as the average and median gender pension gaps, pension coverage rate, at-risk-of-poverty rate of pensioners, and gender differences in the aggregate replacement ratio for pensions. All figures are from [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]] accessible via [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database Eurostat’s online database]. EU-SILC data cover all EU countries, and most [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]]. === EU average gender pension gap was 24.5% in 2024 === In 2024, the average gender pension gap for those aged 65 years or over in the EU was 24.5%, showing that, on average, women’s pensions were around one quarter lower than those of men, as shown in '''Figure 1'''. The largest gaps were recorded in Malta (40.3%), the Netherlands (36.3%) and Austria (35.6%), while the smallest were noted in Estonia (5.6%), Slovakia (8.4%), Czechia and Hungary (both 9.6%). [[Image:Average gender pension average gap, 2024_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 1: Average gender pension gap, 2024.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_pnp13__custom_19892665/default/table ilc_pnp13]) |alt=Bar chart showing the gender pension average gap in 2024 across EU, EFTA and some candidate countries. Data are shown as percentages. The EU average is around 25%, with the highest gaps in Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, and Luxembourg.]] ===EU median gender pension gap was 24.9% in 2024=== In 2024, the median gender pension gap among people aged 65 years or over in the EU was 24.9%, as shown in '''Figure 2'''. The largest gaps were recorded in Luxembourg (43.3%), Spain (41.1%) and the Netherlands (39.6%), while the smallest were noted in Estonia (-0.3%), Hungary (0.4%) and Denmark (2.7%). Estonia was the only country with a slightly negative gap in 2024, indicating women’s median pension was marginally higher than men’s. Hungary and Estonia reported values close to zero, showing near-equal pensions for men and women. The difference between median and average values varied across EU countries. The countries with the largest differences were Denmark (12.9 percentage points (pp)), Belgium (11.0 pp) and Hungary (9.2 pp). In these cases, the average was higher than the median, indicating high pensions among men, which elevate the average and widen the gap. Conversely, in Spain (-11.9 pp), Luxembourg (-10.6 pp) and Portugal (-6.5 pp), the median gender pension gap was larger than the average value. [[Image:Average and median gender pension gaps, 2024_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 2: Average and median gender pension gaps, 2024.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_pnp13__custom_19892665/default/table ilc_pnp13] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_pnp13m__custom_19898030/default/table ilc_pnp13m]) |alt=Chart showing the gender pension gap in 2024 for EU countries as well as EFTA and some candidate countries, comparing average and median values. Each country has two markers: a blue dot for the average gap and a yellow dot for the median gap. Among EU Member States, the largest gaps appear in Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, and Luxembourg. Countries such as Hungary, Slovakia, and Estonia show much smaller gaps. In most EU countries, the average value is higher than the median.]] ===Men aged 65 years or over were more likely to receive a pension than women=== The gender coverage rate in pensions at EU level was 4.1 pp in 2024, suggesting women were less likely than men to receive a pension. Spain (19.5 pp), Greece (12.1 pp), and Italy (10.4 pp) saw the largest gender gaps in pension coverage, favouring men. Conversely, Denmark and Bulgaria (both −2.6 pp), the Netherlands and Poland (both −1.3 pp) had gaps favouring women. Estonia was the only country with a zero value, indicating equal pension coverage for men and women. Additionally, 12 countries reported values between -1.0 and +1.0 pp, suggesting near-parity in coverage. [[Image:Fig4_Gender coverage rate in pension, 2024_(percentage points, population aged 65 years or over).png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 3: Gender coverage rate in pension, 2024.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_pnp14__custom_19503729/default/table ilc_pnp14]) |alt=Bar chart showing the gender coverage rate in pensions in 2024 for EU countries, Norway, Switzerland, Türkiye and Serbia, measured in percentage points for the population aged 65 or over. Spain and Greece display the highest positive gender coverage differences, followed by Italy and Malta. Several EU countries, including Finland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Poland, Bulgaria, Denmark, and Lithuania, show slightly negative values, indicating higher coverage for women than men. The EU average is 4.1.]] ===Women aged 65 years or over faced higher at-risk-of-poverty rate than men in 22 EU countries === At EU level in 2024, the difference in the [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|at-risk-of-poverty (AROP)]] rate between men and women aged 65 years or over was -5.6 pp, indicating a higher AROP rate for women. Only 5 countries reported positive AROP differences, where men faced a greater risk than women, as shown in '''Figure 4'''. Women over 65 years were less at risk of poverty than men in Luxembourg (1.9 pp), Sweden (1.3 pp), and Denmark (0.7 pp), whereas the opposite was particularly evident in Malta (-18.6 pp), Lithuania (-13.3 pp), Austria (-13.0 pp), and Portugal (-12.5 pp). Gender differences in the AROP rate were wider among people aged 65 years or over than among those under 65 years; however, this pattern was not observed in all countries. At EU level, the gender difference in the AROP rate was -1.9 pp for women under 65 years and -5.6 pp for those aged 65 years or over. Countries where this difference was more pronounced were Portugal (8.4 pp for women younger than 65 years and -12.5 pp for women aged 65 years or over, resulting in -20.9 pp difference), Lithuania (-20.0 pp difference), Ireland (-18.7 pp) and Bulgaria (-17.2 pp). Although women aged 65 years or over generally faced a higher risk of poverty than those under 65 years, relative to men in the same age groups, there were 5 EU countries where this pattern was reversed: Luxembourg (+9.2 pp difference), Slovenia (+4.1 pp), Denmark (+2.5 pp), Germany (+1.3 pp) and France (+0.7 pp). A positive difference indicates that younger women faced a greater relative disadvantage compared to men than older women did. [[Image:Gender differences in the at-risk-of-poverty rate by age, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 4: Gender differences in the at-risk-of-poverty rate by age, 2024.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_pnp12__custom_19599319/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=3f2df02a-e947-4953-95d2-5cee632e09a6&c=1771332208000 ilc_pnp12]) |alt=Bar chart showing gender differences in the at‑risk‑of‑poverty rate in 2024, measured in percentage points for EU countries, Norway, Switzerland, Türkiye and Serbia with separate values for people under 65 and those aged 65 or over. Green bars represent the population below 65, yellow bars the population aged 65 and over. ]] ===Gender difference in the aggregate replacement ratio at EU level indicates minor disparities in pension adequacy=== Looking at the [[Glossary:Aggregate_replacement_ratio|aggregate replacement ratio (ARR)]], which measures how similar the pension is compared to working life income, the difference between the genders at the EU level in 2024 was 0.03 pp. This shows that men had pensions that were slightly more similar to their working-age earnings than women. Spain (0.18 pp), Italy (0.11 pp), and Poland (0.10 pp) had the highest values, reflecting a larger male advantage. In contrast, Luxembourg (−0.11 pp), Germany (−0.07 pp), and Czechia (−0.06 pp) had the lowest values, indicating a female advantage. Malta and Croatia reported no difference, suggesting identical income replacement levels for men and women post-retirement. [[Image:Fig6_Gender differences in the aggregate replacement ratio for pensions (excluding other social benefits), 2024_(percentage points).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Gender differences in the aggregate replacement ratio for pensions (excluding other social benefits), 2024.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_pnp11__custom_19421340/default/table ilc_pnp11]) |alt=Bar chart showing gender differences in the aggregate replacement ratio for pensions in 2024, measured in percentage points for EU countries, Norway, Switzerland, Türkiye and Serbia.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Monetary poverty of the elderly_2024_v6.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === The data used in this article are derived from [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]]. EU-SILC data are compiled annually and are the main source of statistics that measure income and living conditions in Europe. It is also the main source of information for linking various aspects of [[Glossary:household|households]]’ and individuals’ quality of life. The reference population for the information presented in this article is all private households and their current members residing in the territory of an EU Member State (or non-EU member country) at the time of data collection. Individuals in collective households are generally excluded from the target population. EU data represent population-weighted averages of national data. === Context === The average gender pension gap is defined as the percentage difference between women’s and men’s average (gross) pension income. Pension income includes old-age benefits, survivors’ benefits and regular pensions from individual private plans. The median gender pension gap is defined as the percentage difference between women’s and men’s median (gross) pension income. Pension income includes old-age benefits, survivors’ benefits and regular pensions from individual private plans. The gender coverage rate is the difference between the proportion of women who do not receive a pension compared to men, expressed in percentage points. A positive value indicates that men are more likely to receive a pension than women, while a negative value indicates the opposite. The gender difference in the at-risk-of-poverty rate presented is defined as the absolute difference between men and women in the [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|at-risk-of-poverty (AROP)]] (i.e. not only those receiving a pension), measured in percentage points. The [[Glossary:Aggregate_replacement_ratio|aggregate replacement ratio (ARR)]] is the gross median individual pension income of those aged 65–74 years relative to the gross median individual earnings from work of those aged 55-64, excluding other social benefits. Gender differences in the ARR are defined as the absolute difference between men and women in the aggregate replacement ratio (ARR). By measuring the level of older people’s pensions relative to the income from work of people in the decade before retirement, the aggregate replacement ratio reflects the overall adequacy of pensions in the transition from work to retirement. This indicator is used in the Pension Adequacy Report, published triennially by the European Commission and the Social Protection Committee, which is an EU policy monitoring instrument that assesses whether Member States’ pension systems provide adequate income in old age while tracking poverty risks, replacement rates, and reform impacts. === Database === * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/database/ Income and living conditions database] === Thematic section === * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/overview Income and living conditions] === Publications === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-key-figures/w/KS-01-25-032 Key figures on European living conditions – 2025 edition - Eurostat] === Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/ilc_sieusilc.htm ESMS metadata file — ilc_esms] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/information-data Income and living conditions - information on data] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/methodology Income and living conditions - methodology] === External links === *[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/social-protection-social-inclusion/social-protection-committee/indicators-sub-group_en European Commission — Directorate General for Employment, Social Affairs & Inclusion: Indicators’ Sub-Group of the Social Protection Committee] *[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/index_en European Commission — Directorate General for Employment, Social Affairs & Inclusion: Employment and social analysis] *[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/pension-adequacy-report-current-and-future-income-adequacy-old-age-eu_en Pension adequacy report - Current and future income adequacy in old age in the EU, 2024] === Legislation === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/legislation Income and living conditions - legislation] {{Unit|topic=X_Living_conditions }} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Living conditions in Europe -
