title: Living conditions in Europe - subjective poverty statistics
text:
EU subjective poverty statistics provide an analysis of the living conditions in Europe. Data extracted in October 2025. Planned article update: November 2026. In 2024, the subjective poverty rate in the EU (17.4%) was 1.7 percentage points lower than in 2023 (19.1%). In 2024, in the EU, people under 18 had the highest rate of subjective poverty (20.6%), followed by those aged 18-64 (17.3%) and those aged 65 and over (14.9%). In 2024, in the EU, people with low education levels were most likely to be considered subjectively poor (27.0%), followed by those with medium education (16.5%). In contrast, this rate was only 8.5% for individuals with high education levels. In 2024, unemployed individuals in the EU were most likely to be considered subjectively poor (42.0%), followed by other inactive persons (24.7%). In contrast, the subjective poverty rate was lower among retired persons (14.2%) and employed persons (13.5%). [[Image:People considered to be subjectively poor by socio-economic characteristics, EU, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|People considered to be subjectively poor, by socio-economic characteristics, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_sbjp01}} {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_sbjp02}} {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_sbjp03}} |alt= Vertical bar chart showing the percentage of population considered to be subjectively poor in 2024. 13 bars are shown as total, age, sex, education and activity status.]] === Subjective poverty is more prominent for women than for men === In 2024, 17.4% of people in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union]] (EU) were considered to be subjectively poor (Figure 1), a decrease of 1.7 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp) from 2023. The rate was 17.0% for men and 17.8% for women. [[Image:Fig1_People considered to be subjectively poor, by sex, 2024_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: People considered to be subjectively poor, by sex, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_sbjp01}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the percentage of population considered to be subjectively poor by sex in 2024. EU countries, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries are shown.]] At national level, the lowest percentages of the subjective poverty rate were observed in the Netherlands and Germany (both at 7.3%), Luxembourg (8.5%) and Finland (9.0%), while the highest rates were seen in Greece (66.8%), Bulgaria (37.4%) and Slovakia (28.7%). In 9 EU countries, more than 1 in 5 people were considered subjectively poor. The subjective poverty rate was higher among women than men in all EU countries, except in Germany and the Netherlands, where it was the same for both sexes. === Subjective poverty was more prevalent among people under 18 than among those aged 65 and over === Concerning age (Figure 2), the subjective poverty rate in the EU in 2024 was generally highest for people under 18 (20.6%) and lowest among people aged 65 and over (14.9%). However, in Bulgaria, Greece, Slovakia, Latvia, Romania, Croatia, Slovenia, Poland, Lithuania and Estonia, the subjective poverty rate was highest among the older population (people aged 65 and over). [[Image:Fig2_People considered to be subjectively poor, by age, 2024_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: People considered to be subjectively poor, by age, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_sbjp01}}|alt= Linear chart with markers, the lines are removed showing the percentage of population considering themselves to be subjectively poor by age in 2024. EU countries and Norway, Switzerland, Iceland, Türkiye, Serbia, North Macedonia, Montenegro and Albania are shown.]] === People with low education levels were 3 times more likely to be considered subjectively poor than those with high education levels === In 2024, over one quarter (27.0%) of the EU population with a low educational attainment level ([[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|ISCED]] levels 0-2) were considered to be subjectively poor (Figure 3). This rate was 3 times lower (8.5%) among those with a high education (ISCED level 5-8). On the other hand, the percentage for people with a medium educational attainment level (ISCED level 3 and 4) was 16.5%, nearly twice as high compared with those with high education levels. [[Image:Fig3_People considered to be subjectively poor, by education attainment level, 2024_(% of population aged 18 and over).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: People considered to be subjectively poor, by education attainment level, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_sbjp02}}|alt= Combo chart showing the percentage of population considered to be subjectively poor by education in 2024. EU countries and Norway, Switzerland, Iceland, Türkiye, Serbia, North Macedonia, Montenegro and Albania are shown.]] Significant differences in subjective poverty rates were observed between high- and low-educated population groups across EU countries. The largest gaps were recorded in Bulgaria (43.3 pp), Slovakia (42.8 pp) and Hungary (38.8 pp), while the smallest gaps were in Finland (3.0 pp), Luxembourg (5.7 pp), Sweden and Estonia (both 7.6 pp). In 11 countries, the difference reached 20 pp or more. In Hungary, Lithuania, Romania and Poland, the subjective poverty rate among people with low education levels was more than 5 times higher than among those with high education. === People considered to be subjectively poor outnumber those at risk of poverty in most EU countries === In the EU in 2024, the share of people who were considered to be subjectively poor (17.4%) (Map 1) was higher than the [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|at-risk-of-poverty rate]] (16.2%) (Map 2), a difference of 1.2 percentage points (pp) (Figure 4). Higher levels of people considered to be subjectively poor were observed in Eastern and Southern Europe, with substantial differences between subjective poverty and at-risk-of-poverty rates. In total, 16 EU countries recorded a higher share of people who were considered to be subjectively poor than those at risk of poverty. Greece showed the largest gap, with 66.8% of people who were considered to be subjectively poor, compared with 19.6% at risk of poverty, a difference of 47.2 pp. Other countries with notable gaps included Bulgaria (15.7 pp), Slovakia (14.2 pp) and Cyprus (6.2 pp). In Malta and Italy, the gap was minimal at 0.2 pp and -0.2 pp, respectively. In these 2 countries, the two rates nearly aligned, with values close to 17.0% in Malta and 19.0% in Italy. Moreover, Estonia recorded the largest negative gap, with 9.8% of people who were considered to be subjectively poor compared with 20.2% at risk of poverty, a difference of 10.4 pp. Other countries with notable negative gaps included Lithuania (-10.1 pp), Luxembourg (-9.6 pp) and Germany (-8.2 pp). [[Image:People-considered-subjectively-poor-2024.png|100px|centre|Map 1: People considered to be subjectively poor, 2024 (%) ]]
Map 1: People considered to be subjectively poor, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_sbjp01/default/table?lang=en ilc_sbjp01])

[[Image:People-risk-poverty-2024.png|100px|centre|Map 2: People at-risk-of-poverty, 2024 (%)]]
Map 2: People at-risk-of-poverty, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_sbjp02/default/table?lang=en ilc_li02])

[[Image:Fig4_Difference between subjective poverty and at-risk-of-poverty rates, 2024_(pp).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Difference between subjective poverty and at-risk-of-poverty rate, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_sbjp01}} {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_li02}} |alt= Combo chart showing the difference between subjective poverty and at-risk-of-poverty rate in 2024. EU countries and Norway, Switzerland, Iceland, Türkiye, Serbia, North Macedonia, Montenegro and Albania are shown.]]
=== Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Subjective poverty updated to 2024 data v3.xlsx|title=Subjective poverty statistics: tables and figures}} === Data sources === The data used in this article are derived from the [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|European Statistics on income, social inclusion and living conditions]] (EU-SILC). EU-SILC data are compiled annually and are the main source of statistics that measure income and living conditions in Europe; it is also the main source of information used to link different aspects relating to the quality of life of [[Glossary:Household|households]] and individuals. The reference population for the information presented in this article is private households and their current members residing in the territory of an EU Member State (or non-member country) at the time of data collection; persons living in collective households were excluded from the target population. The data for the EU are population-weighted averages of national data. The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/ilc_sieusilc.htm#ref_periodDisseminated reference period] for information on income is 2023, while the other households’ characteristics are referenced to 2024. === Context === [[Glossary:Subjective poverty|Subjective poverty]] is a newly developed area with the idea of supplementing the well-known and traditional poverty indicators such as at-risk-of-poverty, material and social deprivation, people living in quasi-jobless households etc. Subjective poverty is a concept developed based on the EU-SILC variable ‘ability to make ends meet’. Contrary to the relative poverty measure, the at-risk-of poverty rate indicator (calculated based on the ranking of the households’ income at country level), the aim of subjective poverty is to assess the respondents’ perception of the difficulties experienced by the household in making ends meet. The assessment takes into account the households’ material wellbeing situation including income, expenditure, debt and wealth. The EU-SILC variable has six response categories: * With great difficulty; * With difficulty; * With some difficulty; * Fairly easy; * Easily; * Very easily. Subjective poverty is based on a combination of the top two categories of the variable. A household that answered “With great difficulty” or “With difficulty” is considered to fall under subjective poverty. This approach is more conservative than the approach based on the minimum income question (or lowest income to make ends meet). The minimum income question approach of subjective poverty was developed mid- 20th century, and it is a model-based approach.
The [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|at-risk-of-poverty rate]] is defined as the share of people with an equivalised disposable income (after social transfer) below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold, which is set at 60% of the national median equivalised disposable income after social transfers.
Used classification: Educational attainment level is classified according to [[Glossary:ISCED|ISCED]] — the international standard classification of education. The (latest) 2011 version has the following levels: * ISCED level 0 — early childhood education; * ISCED level 1 — primary education; * ISCED level 2 — lower secondary education; * ISCED level 3 — (upper) secondary education; * ISCED level 4 — post-secondary non-tertiary education; * ISCED level 5 — short-cycle tertiary education; * ISCED level 6 — bachelor’s or equivalent level; * ISCED level 7 — master’s or equivalent level; * ISCED level 8 — doctoral or equivalent level. === See also === *[[Living conditions in Europe|All articles from ''Living conditions in Europe'']] *[[EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) methodology - people at risk of poverty or social exclusion]] *[[Living conditions in Europe - income distribution and income inequality ]] *[[Living conditions in Europe - poverty and social exclusion]] *[https://unece.org/info/publications/pub/400551 UNECE guidelines on Subjective poverty] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/database/ Income and living conditions database] === Thematic section === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=income_social_inclusion_living_conditions}} Income and living conditions] === Publications === *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-032|title=Key figures on European living conditions – 2025 edition - Eurostat}} === Methodology === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/ilc_sieusilc.htm ESMS metadata file — ilc_esms] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/information-data Income and living conditions — information on data] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/methodology Income and living conditions — methodology] === Legislation === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/legislation Income and living conditions - legislation] {{Unit|topic=X_Living_conditions}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Living conditions in Europe - subjective poverty statistics]] [[Category: Income and living conditions|Living conditions in Europe - subjective poverty statistics]] [[Category:Statistical article|Living conditions in Europe - subjective poverty statistics]] [[Category:November2026|Living conditions in Europe - subjective poverty statistics]]

title: Living conditions in Europe - work intensity
text:
Living conditions in Europe is an online Eurostat publication that analyses income and living conditions across the EU. This article covers labour market conditions for the EU population. Data extracted in November 2025 Planned article update: December 2026 In 2024, 7.9% of the EU population aged 0-64 years lived in households with very low work intensity. Belgium reported the highest rate (11.4%) and Slovenia the lowest (3.5%). Significant regional disparities in very low work intensity rates were recorded in France, Italy and Germany, in 2024. In 2024, 6.5% of EU households with children and 10.3% of those without faced very low work intensity, with Denmark showing the highest differences between the 2 groups. This article focuses on the population aged 0-64 years living in households with very low work intensity (also known as the [[Glossary:Persons living in households with very low work intensity|share of persons living in (quasi-)jobless households]]) within the [[Glossary:EU_enlargements|European Union (EU)]] in 2024. The analysis is carried out over time, at national and regional levels and considering households’ composition as well as their socio-economic characteristics. All figures are based on [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]] available from [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database Eurostat's online database]. EU-SILC data are available for all EU Member States, as well as for most of the [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]]. ===Persons living in households with very low work intensity (share of persons living in (quasi-)jobless households)=== '''Very low work intensity in 2024 highest in Belgium and lowest in Slovenia''' In 2024, 7.9% of the EU population aged 0-64 years lived in households with very low work intensity (see Figure 1). Across EU countries, the percentage ranged widely, from just 3.5% in Slovenia and 3.9% in Luxembourg to as high as 11.4% in Belgium, with Denmark and Germany also reporting elevated levels at 10.6% and 10.0%, respectively. [[Image:Fig1_People living in households with very low work intensity, _2023 and 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: People living in households with very low work intensity, 2023 and 2024.
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_lvhl13n__custom_18844413/default/table (ilc_lvhl13n)]|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the persons living in households with very low work intensity as percentage of population aged 0 to 64 years in the EU, individual EU countries, Norway, Switzerland, Serbia and Türkiye. Each country has two columns comparing the year 2023 with 2024.]] '''Profile of people in the EU living in households with very low work intensity''' In the EU in 2024, women and people with a low level of educational attainment were, on average, more likely to live in households with very low work intensity (see Figure 2). When analysed by sex, very low work intensity in the EU was higher for women than for men (8.3% and 7.5%, respectively) in 2024. In terms of educational attainment, at EU level, 17.1% of all people aged from 18 to 64 years with a low level of educational attainment ([[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|ISCED]] levels 0-2) lived in households with very low work intensity, compared with 4.1% of people in the same age group with a high level of educational attainment (ISCED levels 5-8). The corresponding percentage for people with a medium level of educational attainment (ISCED levels 3-4) was 7.3%. [[Image:Fig2_People living in households with very low work intensity analysed by sex and educational attainment, EU, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: People living in households with very low work intensity analysed by sex and educational attainment, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_lvhl11n__custom_18843524/default/table (ilc_lvhl11n)] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_lvhl14n__custom_18864164/default/table (ilc_lvhl14n)]|alt= Vertical bar charts showing the percentage of people aged 0–64 living in households with very low work intensity in the EU in 2024. The data is categorised by sex (with separate columns for females and males) and by education level (with columns for low, medium, and high education).]] '''Twelve EU countries showed an increase in the share of people living in households with very low work intensity between 2023 and 2024''' In 2024, the percentage of the EU population aged 0-64 years living in households with very low work intensity was slightly lower than in 2023 (see Figure 3), decreasing from 8.1% to 7.9%. The largest decreases in the share were observed in Portugal (1.5 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp)), Ireland (1.4 pp) and Romania (0.9 pp). Increases were observed in 12 EU countries, with the largest in Lithuania (1.4 pp), Bulgaria and Malta (both 0.9 pp), Belgium and Denmark (both 0.8 pp). [[Image:Fig3_Share of people living in households with very low work intensity between 2023 and 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Share of people living in households with very low work intensity between 2023 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_lvhl13n__custom_18844413/default/table= (ilc_lvhl13n)]|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the change in percentage points in the share of people aged 0 to 64 living in households with very low work intensity between 2023 and 2024 in the EU, individual EU countries, Switzerland, Norway, Serbia and Türkiye.]] '''Very low work intensity rates higher among people living in households without dependent children''' In 2024, the proportion of the EU population aged 0-64 years living in very low work-intensity households was 6.5% for people living in households with [[Glossary:Dependent children|dependent children]], compared with 10.3% for households without dependent children (see Figure 4), reflecting a difference of 3.8 pp. Countries that experienced values greater than 15.0% of people living in households without dependent children with very low work intensity were Denmark (17.6%) and Belgium (16.8%). [[Image:Fig4_People living in households with very low work intensity, analysed by household type, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: People living in households with very low work intensity, analysed by household type, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_lvhl13n__custom_18844413/default/table= (ilc_lvhl13n)]|alt= Vertical bar chart showing share of population living in households with very low work intensity as percentage of population aged 0 to 64 years analysed by household type in the EU, individual EU countries, Norway, Switzerland, Serbia and Türkiye. Each country has two columns representing households without dependent children and households with dependent children for the year 2024.]] '''Very low work intensity rates higher among people living in households without dependent children''' The presence of [[Glossary:Dependent children|dependent children]] influenced the share of the population living in households with very low work intensity. In 2024, in the EU, the gap was 3.8 pp lower for people in households with dependent children compared to those without. Among EU countries, Denmark and Greece showed the largest difference, with rates 12.2 pp and 8.6 pp lower, respectively, for households with dependent children. Romania and Bulgaria were the only EU countries where the rate was higher for households with dependent children, with a difference of 0.6 pp and 0.8 pp, respectively, as shown in Figure 5. [[Image:Fig5_Gap between households, with and without dependent children, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Gap between people living in households with very low work intensity, with and without dependent children, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_lvhl13n__custom_18844413/default/table= (ilc_lvhl13n)]|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the change in percentage points in the share of people aged 0 to 64 living in households with very low work intensity with and without dependent children in 2024 in the EU, individual EU countries, Switzerland, Norway, Serbia and Türkiye.]] '''Lowest inter-regional disparities in very low work intensity rates in Slovenia, Finland and Ireland''' Map 1 illustrates the share of the EU population aged from 0-64 years living in households with very low work intensity at the [[Glossary:Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)|NUTS]] level 2 in 2024. Among all EU regions, Guyane (France) reported the highest regional share, with more than one third (35.4%) facing such conditions. In addition, several other regions within the EU reported elevated rates of very low work intensity, exceeding 20.0%. These regions included Campania (24.4%) in Italy, La Réunion (21.9%) and Guadeloupe (23.5%) in France, Bremen (22.9%) in Germany, Ciudad de Ceuta (21.9%) in Spain, Province Hainaut (20.6%) and Region de Bruxelles-Capitale (20.2%) in Belgium. Conversely, 70 regions (including Cyprus, Malta and Luxembourg) had a share below 5.0%. Significant inter-regional disparities in very low work intensity rates were observed in France, Italy and Germany, with variations exceeding 18 pp. By contrast, Slovenia, Finland and Ireland had inter-regional differences of less than 3.5 pp.
Map 1: People living in households with very low work intensity, 2024. NUTS 2 regions.
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_lvhl13n/default/table?lang=en ilc_lvhl13n]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_lvhl21n/default/table?lang=en ilc_lvhl21n]) === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=LCIE_2024_Work_intensity_v3.xlsx|title=Work Intensity: maps, tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data used in this article are derived from [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC) EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]. EU-SILC data are compiled annually and are the main source of statistics that measure income and living conditions in Europe. It is also the main source of information used to link different aspects relating to the quality of life of [[Glossary:Household|households]] and individuals. The reference population for the information presented in this article is all private households and their current members residing in the territory of an EU Member State (or non-EU member country) at the time of data collection. Persons living in collective households are generally excluded from the target population. The data for the EU are population-weighted averages of national data. ===Context=== The [[Glossary:Persons_living_in_households_with_very_low_work_intensity|work intensity]] of a household is the ratio of the total number of months that all adults household members have worked during the income [[Glossary:Reference_period|reference year]] and the total number of months the same household members theoretically could have worked in the same period. 'Adults' refers to people aged 18 to 64 years. Students aged 18 to 24 years; people who are retired according to their self-defined current economic status or who receive any pension (except survivor’s pension); and people in the age bracket 60 to 64 years who are inactive and living in a household where the main income is pensions, are not taken into account. Work intensity is considered very low when the adults of the household had a working time equal to or less than 20% of their total combined work-time potential during the previous year. By contrast, work intensity is considered very high when the adults of the household had a working time more than 85% of their total combined work-time potential. The very low work intensity indicator (VLWI) is part of the at risk of poverty or social exclusion rate defined in the framework of the [[Glossary:The_European_Pillar_of_Social_Rights_Action_Plan_(EU_2030_targets)|EU 2030 target on poverty and social exclusion]]. The [[Glossary:At risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)]] indicator corresponds to the sum of persons who are either at [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|risk of poverty]], or [[Glossary:Severe material and social deprivation rate (SMSD)|severely materially and socially deprived]] or [[Glossary:Persons living in households with very low work intensity|living in a household with a very low work intensity]] - (quasi-)jobless households. The headline target ([[Glossary:The_European_Pillar_of_Social_Rights_Action_Plan_(EU_2030_targets)|EU2030 target]]) on poverty and social inclusion of the [[Glossary:The_European_Pillar_of_Social_Rights_Action_Plan_(EU_2030_targets)|European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan]] is to reduce the number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion by at least 15 million by 2030. Progress towards this target is monitored through the AROPE rate, published by Eurostat. Educational attainment level is classified according to the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=International_Standard_Classification_of_Education_(ISCED) international standard classification of education (ISCED)]: * ISCED level 0 — early childhood education; * ISCED level 1 — primary education; * ISCED level 2 — lower secondary education; * ISCED level 3 — (upper) secondary education; * ISCED level 4 — post-secondary non-tertiary education; * ISCED level 5 — short-cycle tertiary education; * ISCED level 6 — bachelor's or equivalent level; * ISCED level 7 — master's or equivalent level; * ISCED level 8 — doctoral or equivalent level. For this article, the levels are grouped as follows: low education (levels 0–2), medium education (levels 3–4), and high education (levels 5–8). === See also === '''Online publication''' *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Living_conditions_in_Europe All articles from Living conditions in Europe] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)_methodology_-_people_at_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) methodology - people at risk of poverty or social exclusion] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Living_conditions_in_Europe_-_poverty_and_social_exclusion Living conditions in Europe - Eurostat] === Methodology === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/ilc_sieusilc.htm ESMS metadata file — ilc_esms] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/information-data Income and living conditions - title: Living conditions in Southern Mediterranean countries
text:
This article is part of an online Eurostat publication that provides a statistical overview over the Southern Mediterranean countries. The article presents statistics on recent economic developments for Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Palestine and Tunisia and compares these with the EU. Data extracted in February 2026. Planned article update: June 2027. Israel and Palestine exhibited the largest income inequalities among the available Southern Mediterranean countries, with Gini coefficients of 34.5 and 34.4 (both 2023 data). The EU average was significantly lower, at 29.4 in 2024. Consumer price inflation in Palestine (West Bank only, data unavailable on Gaza) was sharply up to 53.6% in 2024, the highest among the Southern Mediterranean countries. Inflation in Lebanon was 45.2%, its lowest rate since 2019. In comparison, in 2024 inflation was 2.6% in the EU. In 2024, long-term unemployment stood at 10.0% of the labour force in Tunisia and 8.2% in Morocco, the highest rates among the available Southern Mediterranean countries. In contrast, long-term unemployment was 0.2% in Israel. In the EU, the rate stood at 1.9%. This article is part of an [[European_Neighbourhood_Policy_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]]. It presents information on 9 [[Glossary:European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP)| Southern Mediterranean]] countries, namely, Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Palestine ''This designation shall not be construed as recognition of a State of Palestine and is without prejudice to the individual positions of the Member States on this issue.'' and Tunisia. Information on these countries is compared with developments in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]]. This article does not contain any data on Syria, as cooperation with Syria was suspended from 2011 until recently, and no data are collected yet. Lebanon data does not account for Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon. Given that data collection for the Southern Mediterranean countries is non-obligatory and subject to various changes related to the political and geographical context, data availability may often show inconsistency over the entire period presented or for recent years. This article includes information on [[Glossary:Inequality_of_income_distribution|income inequality]] measured by the [[Glossary:Gini_coefficient|Gini coefficient]], the development in [[Glossary:Consumer price index (CPI)|consumer prices]], [[Glossary:Long-term unemployment|long-term unemployment]], as well as the shares of the populations living below the respective national poverty lines. === Income inequality=== The [[Glossary:Gini_coefficient|Gini coefficient]] captures how unevenly income is distributed within a population. A coefficient of 0 expresses perfect equality where everyone has the same income, while a coefficient of 100 expresses full inequality where only one person has all the income. The disposable income of a household is its net income after taxes and social contributions but including social benefits received; equivalised means that the composition of each household is weighted according to the number of adults and children living in it. In Figure 1, the Gini coefficients for [[Glossary:Equivalised_disposable_income|equalised disposable income]] in the Southern Mediterranean countries are presented and compared with the coefficient for the EU. Among the Southern Mediterranean countries, income inequality was highest in Israel and Palestine, with Gini coefficients of 34.5 and 34.4 (both 2023 data), respectively. For Israel, this represented a decrease in income inequality since 2014, when the coefficient stood at 37.6. For Palestine, 2014 data are not available. In Tunisia, the Gini coefficient was 36.5 (2015 data, 2024 data not available), somewhat lower than that reported by Israel in 2014. The lowest income inequality among the Southern Mediterranean countries with available data was measured in Egypt, with a Gini coefficient of 27 in 2022, down from 30 in 2013 (decimals not provided). Data are not available for Algeria, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya and Morocco. In comparison, the Gini coefficient of income inequality stood at 29.4 in the EU in 2024. This was lower than a decade earlier, with the coefficient at 30.9 in 2014 (break in time series in 2020). [[Image: ENPS26_Income inequality, 2014 and 2024_(Gini coefficient).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Income inequality, 2014 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e9febc01-560e-4a16-b3b9-9fefb4ddd3e3?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:39:51Z ilc_di12]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f77f1aae-794b-46a0-ba21-9495c8d158b5?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:52:16Z enps_ilc_di12])|alt=Bar chart showing the income inequality measured by the Gini coefficient in the EU, Egypt, Israel, Palestine and Tunisia for the years 2014 and 2024. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] ===Consumer prices=== A [[Glossary:Consumer_price_index_(CPI)|consumer price index (CPI)]], in the EU countries the [[Glossary:Harmonised_index_of_consumer_prices_(HICP)|harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)]], is an indicator that measures changes in the prices of a ‘basket’ of goods and services bought by households. The index is used to assess inflation in consumer prices in an economy. Consumer prices in the EU remained relatively stable between 2014 and 2020, with the index increasing only moderately from 99.9 to 105.8 (2015 = 100). A more pronounced rise was observed from 2021 onwards, with the index reaching 129.7 in 2024. Reflecting global economic disruptions, notably post-pandemic economic shifts and Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, inflation accelerated to 9.2% in 2022 before slowing to 2.6% in 2024. Over the whole period 2014-2024, consumer prices in the EU increased by 29.8%. Among the Southern Mediterranean countries, developments were considerably more heterogeneous. Considering its steep increase in consumer prices over the period 2014-2024, Lebanon’s data are presented in a separate chart with a different scale from than the chart for the other Southern Mediterranean countries and the EU. Between 2014 and 2019, consumer prices in Lebanon remained relatively stable, with only moderate year-on-year changes, the index reaching 113.1 in 2019 after a slight decline in 2016 (deflation of 0.8% compared with 2015). From 2020 onward, consumer prices rose sharply. The index stood at 6 742.1 in 2024, almost 70 times its 2014 level. This inflationary spiral reflected the effects of multiple crises, including collapse in the banking sector, sovereign debt default, the COVID-19 pandemic, the explosion at the port of Beirut, and the (recent) increase in hostilities in Lebanon. Egypt also experienced a strong and sustained increase over the period, with consumer prices rising from 100.0 in 2015 to 397.9 in 2024, almost a fourfold increase. The upward trend was continuous throughout the period, with particularly pronounced accelerations after 2016 and again from 2021 onwards, when the index moved from 203.4 to 397.9. This overall trend is associated with notable fluctuations in inflation rates. In 2017, inflation peaked at 29.5%, following subsidy reforms and a sharp currency devaluation. A further surge was recorded in 2023, with inflation climbing to 33.9%, driven by rising commodity prices, supply chain disruptions and currency pressures. This continued into 2024, albeit at a somewhat slower pace at 28.3%. Tunisia and Algeria recorded continuous increases in consumer prices over the period, with a steady upward trend extending throughout the decade and into 2024. Over the period 2014-2024, consumer prices rose by 85% in Tunisia and by 71% in Algeria (estimated data). In Tunisia, the index increased from 95.4 in 2014 to 176.8 in 2024, while in Algeria it rose from 95.4 to 163.0, confirming a broadly comparable inflationary trajectory in both countries. In both cases, inflation peaked in 2023, at 9.3% before moderating in 2024 to 7.0% and 4.0%, respectively. Although Palestine experienced a similar overall increase to Tunisia and Algeria, with consumer prices rising by 74% over the period 2014-2024 (2014-2016 and 2018-2024 estimated), this development was largely driven by a sharp increase of 53.6% in 2024. Between 2014 and 2021, annual inflation remained moderate, ranging between -0.2% (2016) and 1.6% (2019). Moderate surges were observed in Jordan and Israel, where consumer price indices followed a relatively steady upward path until 2021 before easing in pace and remaining lower than in most other Southern Mediterranean countries. In Jordan, the index rose from 100.9 in 2014 to 118.4 in 2024 (2014-2018 estimated), while in Israel it increased from 100.6 to 114.6 over the same period, indicating a contained overall increase compared with other countries in the region. A similar moderate pattern was observed in Morocco over 2014–2022. A notable shift occurred in 2022, as inflation accelerated across the region, peaking at 6.6% in Morocco and reaching 4.3% in both Israel and Jordan. In Libya, for the period with available data, consumer prices remained at a high level, with the index standing at 238.8 in 2017, rising to 270.2 in 2018 and easing slightly to 266.7 in 2019. No data are available for the other years under review. [[Image: ENPS26_Consumer prices, 2014-2024 (index 2015 = 100).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Consumer prices, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8fd92790-3521-4cf6-8321-3b5495f6dc1f?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T14:59:11Z prc_hicp_aind]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c5118a09-d580-4f2f-85ab-c40a1bec7f5f?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T14:59:47Z enps_cpi])|alt=Line chart showing the development in the consumer price index in the EU, Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Morocco, Palestine and Tunisia for the years 2014 to 2024. Lebanon is presented in a separate line chart, due to difference in scale. The lines are coloured according to country. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] ===Long-term unemployment=== The [[Glossary:Long-term_unemployment|long-term unemployment]] rate presented in Figure 3 represents the percentage of the [[Glossary:Labour_force|labour force]] that is unemployed and has been actively seeking employment for at least a year. Unemployment results in a loss of income, and if it persists long-term it increases the risk of [[Living conditions in Europe - poverty and social exclusion|falling into poverty.]] Between 2014 and 2024, long-term unemployment varied significantly across Southern Mediterranean countries. Throughout this period, Palestine had one of the highest long-term unemployment rates in the region. From 2014 to 2022, the level remained relatively stable at between 8.8% and 12.0%. A sharp rise to 16.5% in 2023 coincided with the outbreak of open conflict with Israel. This led to a break in the geographical coverage: from 2023 on, data cover the West Bank only, as data are unavailable for Gaza. However, the rate fell sharply, by 10.0 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]], to 6.5% in 2024. In contrast, Israel maintained the lowest long-term unemployment rate among the Southern Mediterranean countries 2014-2024, not exceeding 0.5% in any year. This was substantially lower than in the EU during this period. Algeria, Morocco (2017-2024 estimated data) and Tunisia generally recorded long-term unemployment rates in the range between 5.1% and 8.9%, with relatively limited fluctuations within the period 2014-2024. The only exception was the rate for Tunisia in 2024, at 10.0%. However, data are only available for 2014-2019 for Algeria, and 2019-2022 and 2024 for Tunisia. Egypt stood out with relatively low long-term unemployment rates in 2014 (3.5%) and 2015 (2.7%). In 2016, the rate rose sharply to a peak at 10.4%, but decreased gradually in the subsequent years to 3.0% in 2021, the most recent year available. For Lebanon, data (estimated) for the long-term unemployment rate are only available for 2018 (6.3%) and 2022 (14.3%). Data are not available for Jordan and Libya. In the EU, the long-term unemployment rate declined steadily from 5.4% in 2014 to 1.9% in 2024, with an exception in 2021 when it increased by 0.4 percentage points following the COVID-19 pandemic. [[Image: ENPS26_Long-term unemployment rate, 2014-2024_(% of labour force).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Long-term unemployment rate, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fa11ec5d-cfe4-4e90-80c3-d30eb89ad697?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:37:05Z une_ltu_a]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c980d279-7162-4eaa-b7a9-571af716629e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T14:40:13Z enps_lfsa_urgan2])|alt=Line chart showing the development in long-term unemployment in the EU, Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Lebanon, Morocco, Palestine and Tunisia for the years 2014 to 2024. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] ===Persons living below the national poverty line=== The poverty rate as defined by the national poverty line corresponds to the share of the population that fails to meet the standard considered necessary to cover basic needs. National poverty lines are generally applying a 'cost of basic needs' approach to estimate poverty, defined through required calories per capita and a common food and non-food basket for all households. The 'poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines' is normally estimated based on national household surveys on income, expenditure, consumption and living conditions. This ratio is presented in Figure 4. It should be noted that the rates at national poverty lines are not suited to compare countries, as the national poverty lines are specific to each country. There are also limitations to comparability caused by differences in available reference years, geographic coverage, and in some cases estimations. The Southern Mediterranean countries showed wide variation in the shares of people living below their respective national poverty lines. Egypt had the highest rate at 29.7% (2020 data), followed by Israel (18.2%; 2023 data), Tunisia (16.6%; 2021 data), and Palestine (11.5%; 2023 data; West Bank only, data unavailable on Gaza). Morocco stood out with an estimated rate of 3.9% (2022 data), by far the lowest among the Southern Mediterranean countries with available data. Data for Algeria, Jordan, Lebanon and Libya are not available. A national poverty line is not defined for the EU as a whole, since such thresholds are, by definition, established separately by each individual country. [[Image: Persons living below the national poverty line, 2024 v2.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Persons living below the national poverty line, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a4362d89-47f3-4d46-8854-adc77c061fd9?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:49:08Z enps_ilc_natln])|alt=Bar chart showing the share of the total population living below the national poverty line in Egypt, Israel, Morocco, Palestine and Tunisia in 2024. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] === Notes === === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=ENPS26 Living conditions V4.xlsx|title=European Neighbourhood Policy — South countries — living conditions: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data for Southern Mediterranean countries are supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country on a voluntary basis. The data result from an annual data collection cycle that has been established by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]. These statistics are available on Eurostat's website, together with a range of different indicators covering most socio-economic areas. For the EU, the [[Glossary:EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]] is a key source for data on living conditions of the European population. It aims to collect timely and comparable data on income, poverty, social inclusion and living conditions. Eurostat's website provides an overview of [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/legislation legislation related to EU-SILC], as well as an online publication on [[EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) methodology]] and an overview article over main results on [[Living conditions in Europe - poverty and social exclusion]]. In this article, SILC data are complemented by household consumer prices sourced from the [[Glossary:Harmonised_index_of_consumer_prices_(HICP)|Harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)]] and unemployment data from the [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(EU-LFS)|Labour Force Survey (LFS)]]. In the Southern Mediterranean countries, data are generally collected through national household surveys on income, expenditure, consumption and living conditions, such as the Household Income and Expenditure Surveys (HIES)See e.g. the [https://webapps.ilo.org/surveyLib/index.php/collections/HIES International Labour Organization's Survey Catalogue].. In the Southern Mediterranean countries, poverty estimates are generally based on surveys such as the National survey on consumer spending and household standard of living in Algeria, the Household income, expenditure and consumption survey (HIECS) in Egypt, the Household expenditure and income survey (HEIS) in Jordan, the National household consumption and expenditure survey (ENCDM) in Morocco and the National survey on the budget, consumption and standard of living of households (EBCNV) in Tunisia. These representative surveys are generally carried out at regular intervals, e.g. on average every two years in Egypt and every seven years in Morocco. ===Context=== EU cooperation with the Southern Mediterranean countries is guided by the [https://north-africa-middle-east-gulf.ec.europa.eu/what-we-do/pact-mediterranean_en Pact for the Mediterranean ‘One Sea, One Pact, One Future’]. The Pact reflects the EU’s commitment to strengthening its partnership with the southern Mediterranean countries and to building a common Mediterranean space that is connected, prosperous, resilient and secure, based on shared interests and joint responsibility. The Pact for the Mediterranean ‘One Sea, One Pact, One Future’ sets out a long-term vision to foster shared prosperity, stability, and sustainable development across the Euro-Mediterranean region. It establishes a strategic framework for cooperation, built around three interlinked thematic “pillars”: I. People: driving force for change, connections and innovation; II. Stronger, more sustainable and integrated economies, and III. Security, preparedness and migration management. Its core objectives include strengthening economic integration through enhanced trade, investment, and digital connectivity; accelerating the green and just transition by aligning climate action, renewable energy cooperation, and water security; and promoting human development via education, youth employment, and social cohesion initiatives. The Pact also aims to deepen political dialogue to address common security challenges, like migration, while reinforcing democratic governance. The Pact for the Mediterranean was endorsed by the EU and southern Mediterranean partners in November 2025 on the occasion of the 30th anniversary of the Barcelona process, with the European Council welcoming the Pact in its conclusions 20 November 2025. The [https://www.eeas.europa.eu/sites/default/files/joint_staff_working_document_renewed_partnership_southern_neighbourhood.pdf Economic and Investment Plan for the Southern Neighbours] complements this agenda. In cooperation with its Southern Mediterranean partners, Eurostat has the responsibility to promote and implement the use of European and internationally recognised standards and methodology for the production of statistics, necessary for designing and monitoring policies in various areas. Eurostat manages and coordinates EU efforts to increase the capacity of the Southern Mediterranean countries to [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-catalogues/-/KS-32-11-955?inheritRedirect=true&redirect=%2Feurostat%2Fen%2Fpublications%2Fleaflets develop, produce and disseminate good quality data] according to European and international standards. Additional information on the policy context of the Southern Mediterranean region is provided on the website of [https://north-africa-middle-east-gulf.ec.europa.eu/index_en Directorate-General for Middle East, North Africa and the Gulf (DG MENA)]. The EU has been supporting statistical capacity building in the region for a number of years, among others by providing technical assistance to national statistical authorities and by sharing best practice and transferring know-how. A key tool for this statistical cooperation is the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Statistical_cooperation_-_European_Neighbourhood_Policy-South_(ENP-S) MEDSTAT programme], a multiannual regional cooperation programme for statistics addressing common issues and requirements. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Non-EU_countries|All articles on non-EU countries]] *[[European_Neighbourhood_Policy_countries_-_statistical_overview|European Neighbourhood Policy countries — statistical overview]] — online publication *[[International_statistical_cooperation|Statistical cooperation]] — online publication *[[Income and living conditions|Income and living conditions]] – overview over all articles on income and living conditions *[[EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)_methodology|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) methodology]] - online publication ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=enps Southern European Neighbourhood Policy Country (ENP-South) (enps)], see: :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=enps_pop Population and social conditions (enps_pop)] ::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=enps_livcon Living conditions (enps_livcon)] :::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=enps_incom Income distribution (enps_incom)] :::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=enps_pov Relative poverty (enps_pov)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=ilc Income and living conditions (ilc)], see: :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=ilc_pe People at risk of poverty or social title: Living conditions in European Neighbourhood East countries
text:
This article is part of an online Eurostat publication that provides a statistical overview over the European Neighbourhood Policy-East (ENP-East) countries. The article presents statistics on living conditions for Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine and compares these with the EU. Data extracted in January 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 Moldova, Armenia and Georgia all recorded larger income inequalities than the EU in 2024, with Gini coefficients at 35.9, 34.8 (2023) and 34.4, respectively. The EU had a Gini coefficient of 29.4. In 2024, long-term unemployment climbed to 7.1% in Armenia, fell to 5.0% in Georgia and stayed stable at 2.1% in Azerbaijan. All were above the 1.9% in the EU. In contrast, Moldova recorded long-term unemployment of just 0.6%. All European Neighbourhood East countries observed higher at-risk-of-poverty rates than the EU in 2024. The highest rate was recorded in Armenia, at 23.7% of the population (2023 data), the lowest in Georgia, at 18.9%. In the EU, the rate was 16.2%. This article is part of an [[European_Neighbourhood_Policy_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]]. It presents information on 5 [[Glossary:European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP)|European Neighbourhood Policy-East (ENP-East)]] countries, namely, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine. Information on these 5 countries is compared with the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are also [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]]. The European Council granted Moldova and Ukraine candidate status on 23 June 2022 and Georgia on 14 December 2023. This article does not contain any data on Belarus, as statistical cooperation with Belarus has been suspended as of March 2022. Data shown for Georgia exclude the regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia over which the government of Georgia does not exercise control. The data managed by the National Bureau of Statistics of Moldova does not include data from the Transnistrian region over which the government of Moldova does not exercise control. Since 2014, data for Ukraine generally exclude the illegally annexed Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the City of Sevastopol and the territories which are not under control of the Ukrainian government. For Ukraine official statistics for 2022-2025 were not fully produced due to the martial law. It will gradually be produced and disseminated as defined by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine, taking into account the specific conditions of producing statistics during Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. The article includes information on [[Glossary:Inequality_of_income_distribution|income inequality]] measured by the [[Glossary:Gini_coefficient|Gini coefficient]], the [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|risk of poverty]] after [[Glossary:Social transfers|social transfers]], [[Glossary:Long-term_unemployment|long-term unemployment]], as well as the development in [[Glossary:Consumer_price_index_(CPI)|consumer prices]]. ===Income inequality=== The [[Glossary:Gini_coefficient|Gini coefficient]] measures inequality in how income is distributed within a country. A coefficient of 0 expresses perfect equality where everyone has the same income, while a coefficient of 100 expresses full inequality where only one person has all the income. Figure 1 presents the Gini coefficients for [[Glossary:Equivalised_disposable_income|equivalised disposable income]]. This income is the total income of a household (including social benefits) after taxes and social contributions, divided by the number of household members. To compare households of different sizes and compositions, households are 'equivalised' by counting the first adult in the household as 1.0, all other adults (aged 14 and over) as 0.5, and children (aged under 14) as 0.3. From 2014 to 2024, income inequality fell substantially in Georgia. Its Gini coefficient decreased from 41.2 in 2014, the highest among the available ENP-East countries that year, to 34.4 in 2024. This corresponded to a decrease by -6.8 over this period and brought the Gini coefficient down to roughly the same level as in Moldova and Armenia. Except for Ukraine, income inequality decreased or remained stable in the other ENP-East countries for which data are available. In Armenia, the Gini coefficient fell by -2.5 to 34.8 (2023 data instead of 2024). In Moldova, it stayed relatively stable. At 35.9, it was the highest among the ENP-East countries in 2024. Ukraine stood out with significantly less income inequality than in the other ENP-East countries and also less than in the EU. In 2014, the Gini coefficient of income inequality stood at 23 in Ukraine (only rounded figures available before 2017). However, in contrast to the other ENP-East countries, income inequality in Ukraine increased to a coefficient of 24.4 by 2021, the most recent year available. It should be noted that Ukraine uses a different calculation of equivalised households, thus its Gini coefficient is not directly comparable with those of the other ENP-East countries and the EU. [[Image: ENPE26_Income inequality, 2014 and 2024_(Gini coefficient)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Income inequality, 2014 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8b6ae9bc-4622-4024-8081-6b42db13119c?lang=en ilc_di12]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a542665b-cd87-421a-a4e9-d00a0ad1426a?lang=en enpe_ilc_di12])|alt=Bar chart showing the Gini coefficient of equivalised disposable income in the EU, Moldova, Armenia, Georgia and Ukraine, for the years 2014 and 2024, respectively. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Consumer prices=== The [[Glossary:Consumer_price_index_(CPI)|consumer price index (CPI)]] is an indicator that measures changes in the price level of goods and services purchased by households. The index is used to assess inflation in an economy. In the EU, the [[Glossary:Harmonised_index_of_consumer_prices_(HICP)|Harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)]] is used to provide a consistent CPI for the EU as a whole and one that is directly comparable between EU countries. Between 2014 and 2024, all ENP-East countries experienced periods of high inflation. By 2024, the consumer price index (2015=100) had exceeded 200 for Ukraine (2023 data) and Moldova, stood between 200 and 150 for Azerbaijan and Georgia, but remained lower than 150 (and lower than in the EU) in Armenia. Across the region, inflation accelerated considerably in 2021, peaking in 2022. Despite inflation slowing down in 2023, it remained high in several countries. However, it slowed further in 2024. Generally, this trend followed international developments, with inflation pressures from disruptions in international supply chains following the COVID-19 pandemic and from Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine starting in 2022. Over the period 2014-2024, Ukraine experienced some of the highest inflation rates among the ENP-East countries. In addition, Ukraine recorded the highest year-on-year increases in consumer prices each year from 2016 to 2019 and the second highest from 2021 to 2023 (2014 and 2024 data not available), peaking at 20.2% in 2022. Moldova also recorded high annual inflation rates throughout the period, although lower than in Ukraine. The exception was in 2022, when Moldova recorded the highest inflation among these countries, at 28.8%. Azerbaijan recorded sharp increases in consumer prices in 2016 and 2017, with inflation surging to 12.4% and 13.0%, respectively. Apart from 2024 (1.1%), Georgia experienced inflation above 2.0% throughout the period, peaking at 11.9% in 2022. Inflation in Armenia was more volatile, with deflation in 2016 (-1.4%) and inflation of 2.5% or less during most of the period. Armenia experienced the most moderate increase in 2022, with a rate of 8.6%. From 2014 to 2024, consumer prices in Armenia increased less than in the EU. In the EU, consumer prices grew by less than 2.0% per year in the period 2014-2020. Inflation accelerated in 2021 to a peak at 9.2% in 2022, before easing back down to 2.6% in 2024. [[Image:ENPE26 Consumer prices, 2014-2024_(index 2015 = 100).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Consumer prices, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8fd92790-3521-4cf6-8321-3b5495f6dc1f?lang=en prc_hicp_aind]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/76a70469-794d-4e5b-a86f-cdadd994731a?lang=en enpe_cpi])|alt=Line chart showing the development in the consumer price index in the EU, Ukraine, Moldova, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Armenia for the years 2014 to 2024. The lines are colour coded according to country. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Long-term unemployment=== The [[Glossary:Long-term_unemployment|long-term unemployment]] rate represents the share of the [[Glossary:Labour_force|labour force]] that is unemployed and has been actively seeking employment for at least a year. Unemployment results in a loss of income, and if it persists long-term it increases the risk of [[Living conditions in Europe - poverty and social exclusion|falling into poverty]]. From 2014 to 2024, long-term unemployment generally declined or remained stable across the ENP-East region. Armenia, despite having the highest rates among the ENP-East countries throughout this period, overall recorded reduced long-term unemployment. The exception was a peak at 11.2% in 2015, and a 0.6 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp) increase to 7.1% in 2024. Georgia also recorded high rates of long-term unemployment over the period, with rates at 5.0% or more every year except 2019, peaking at 7.2% in 2021. Long-term unemployment in Ukraine was relatively low between 2014 and 2021, the most recent year available. However, the rate fluctuated year-on-year in the range between 1.0% (2019) and 2.5% (2017). In 2021, the last year for which data are available, long-term unemployment in Ukraine was 2.4%. Moldova's long-term unemployment rates were the lowest among the ENP-East countries. In 2014, the rate stood at 0.9%. With the exception of 2015 (1.4%), long-term unemployment remained below 1.0% of the labour force 2014-2024. Between 2014 and 2024, the EU’s long-term unemployment rate declined steadily from 5.4% to 1.9%, despite a temporary post-pandemic increase in 2021. [[Image:ENPE26 Long-term unemployment rate, 2014-2024_(% of labour force).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Long-term unemployment rate, 2014-2024
''Source:'' ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c026fe64-bfed-4a64-bff2-f47ba5386438?lang=en une_ltu_a]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f74df3b2-6fc8-489a-b164-f3443dd3e6c0?lang=en enpe_lfsa_urgan2])|alt=Line chart showing the development in long-term unemployment in the EU, Armenia, Georgia, Ukraine, Azerbaijan and Moldova for the years 2014 to 2024. The lines are colour coded according to country. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===People at risk of poverty === The [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|at-risk-of-poverty rate]] measures the share of people with an [[Glossary:Equivalised_disposable_income|equivalised disposable income]] below the national at-risk-of-poverty threshold. The at-risk-of-poverty threshold is set at 60% of the national [[Glossary:Median|median]] equivalised disposable income. The poverty threshold is set independently for each country, thus the indicator reflects low income compared with other residents within the same economy. The indicator is calculated after [[Glossary:Social_transfers|social transfers]]. Except for 2018, Armenia’s at-risk-of-poverty rate was the highest among the ENP-East countries throughout the period 2014-2024. Despite this, the rate fell from 30.0% in 2014 to 23.7% in 2023 (2024 not available), an improvement by -6.3 pp. However, a change in methodology in 2019 likely contributed to an upward shift by +2.9 pp, before the rate resumed its downward trend from 2021 on. In Ukraine, the at-risk-of-poverty rate remained relatively stable over the period 2014-2021 (data not available from 2022 onwards), standing at 23.4% in both 2014 and 2021. The rate fluctuated during this period, with a notable decrease in 2020 (-2.1 pp) followed by an increase in 2021 (+1.1 pp). The at-risk-of-poverty rate in Moldova was at a similar level to that of Ukraine, falling from 25.3% in 2014 to 21.5% in 2024, albeit with considerable fluctuations in-between. A change in methodology in 2019, coinciding with a -3.1 pp lower rate, limits comparability with previous years. Despite fluctuations, Georgia experienced a downward trend in the share of the population at risk of poverty, overall falling by -2.5 pp from 21.4% in 2014 to 18.9% in 2024. Georgia’s at-risk-of-poverty rate was the lowest in the ENP-East region during the period, remaining below 20.0% since 2020. The EU witnessed a relatively stable rate of people at risk of poverty, decreasing from 17.3% in 2014 to 16.2% in 2024 (-1.1 pp). Year-on-year changes were limited to between -0.6 pp (2017) and +0.2 pp (2020). The at-risk-of-poverty rate in the EU was lower than in any of the ENP-East countries throughout the period 2014-2024. [[Image:ENPE26 People at risk of poverty, after social transfers, 2014-2024_(% of total population).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: People at risk of poverty, after social transfers, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/72468d6a-c408-4a2c-ba38-ea0455064574?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T10:58:27Z ilc_li02]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2b081ea8-abfd-4fdc-a022-40124f1884dc?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T10:59:16Z enpe_ilc_li09a])|alt=Line chart showing the development in share of the population that were at risk of poverty after social transfers, measured in per cent of the total population, in the EU, Armenia, Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia for the years 2014 to 2024. The lines are colour coded according to country. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= ENPE26_Living_conditions_v3.xlsx|title=Living conditions in European Neighbourhood East countries: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data for ENP-East countries are supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country on a voluntary basis. The data result from an annual data collection cycle that has been established by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]. These statistics are available free of charge on Eurostat’s website, together with a range of additional indicators for ENP-East countries covering most socio-economic topics. For the EU, the [[Glossary:EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]] is a key source for data on living conditions of the European population. It aims to collect timely and comparable data on income, poverty, social inclusion and living conditions, in both monetary and non-monetary terms. The data are generally collected for private households and household members. The legal basis for this data collection exercise is [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.LI.2019.261.01.0001.01.ENG Regulation (EU) 2019/1700] establishing a common framework for European statistics relating to persons and households, based on data at individual level collected from samples. In this article, SILC data are complemented by household consumer prices data sourced from the [[Glossary:Harmonised_index_of_consumer_prices_(HICP)|Harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)]] and unemployment data from the [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(EU-LFS)|Labour Force Survey (LFS)]]. ===Context=== The European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP) provides the overarching framework for relations between the European Union and its eastern partner countries, aiming to promote stability, prosperity and cooperation in the region. Within this framework, the [https://neighbourhood-enlargement.ec.europa.eu/european-neighbourhood-policy/eastern-partnership_en Eastern Partnership (EaP)] serves as a key policy initiative to strengthen political association, economic integration and institutional cooperation between the EU and its eastern neighbours. On 2 July 2021, the European Commission and the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy presented the [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/IP_21_3367 Eastern Partnership: a Renewed Agenda] for cooperation with the EU's Eastern partners. This agenda is based on the five long-term objectives, with resilience at its core, as defined for the future of the Eastern Partnership (EaP) in the Joint Communication [https://eeas.europa.eu/headquarters/headquarters-homepage/76166/joint-communication-eastern-partnership-policy-beyond-2020-reinforcing-resilience-%25E2%2580%2593-eastern_en Eastern Partnership policy beyond 2020: Reinforcing Resilience – an Eastern Partnership that delivers for all] in March 2020. The Eastern Partnership’s agenda for recovery, resilience and reform is underpinned by an 'Economic and Investment Plan for the Eastern Partnership (EaP): Investing in resilient and competitive economies and societies' (Annex I of the Joint Staff Working Document). More detailed overviews are given in a [https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/document/download/94735c00-2cfa-4ef7-92a6-41515b8b466d_en Factsheet on the Eastern Partnership Joint Communication], presenting the policy objectives and the specific priorities, as well as in a [https://neighbourhood-enlargement.ec.europa.eu/document/download/d675e1d6-fd68-45fa-a671-80a69a117f1f Factsheet on EU-Eastern Neighbourhood flagship projects 2023-2024]. The [https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/news/eastern-partnership-summit-joint-declaration-2021-12-15_en Joint Declaration of the Eastern Partnership Summit 'Recovery, Resilience and Reform'] of 15 December 2021 reaffirmed the strong commitment to a strategic, ambitious and forward-looking Eastern Partnership. At the [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/meetings/international-ministerial-meetings/2023/12/11/ Eastern Partnership Foreign Affairs Ministerial meeting of 11 December 2023], the EU, member states and partners declared that they will step up their efforts to implement the Eastern Partnership’s agenda for recovery, resilience and reform, as well as tackling challenges related to the ongoing consequences of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine for the entire region. On 14-15 December 2023, the European Council decided to [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2023/12/14/european-council-conclusions-on-ukraine-enlargement-and-reforms/ open accession negotiations] with Moldova and Ukraine, and granted the status of candidate country to Georgia. In cooperation with its ENP partners, Eurostat has the responsibility to promote and implement the use of European and internationally recognised standards and methodology for the production of statistics, necessary for designing and monitoring policies in various areas. Eurostat manages and coordinates EU efforts to increase the capacity of the ENP countries to develop, produce and disseminate good quality data according to European and international standards. Additional information on the policy context of the ENP is provided on the website of [https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/index_en Directorate-General Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood (ENEST)]. A regional statistical cooperation programme, STAT-East, is in place since January 2026 to strengthen partner countries’ statistical capacity to develop, produce and disseminate high-quality statistics and to reinforce the independence and institutional capacity of national statistical systems. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Non-EU_countries|All articles on non-EU countries]] title: Living conditions in enlargement countries
text:
This article presents information on living conditions and income distribution, as well as unemployment and consumer prices, for the enlargement countries. It presents data for Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Kosovo*, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, Türkiye and Ukraine, and compares these with the corresponding data for the EU. Data from April 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 Between 2015 and 2024, the EU’s median annual income increased by 35.8%, from 15 641 to 21 245 PPS per capita. Income levels remained lower in the enlargement countries, albeit several recorded stronger growths. Median income more than doubled in Türkiye between 2015 and 2025, rose by nearly 90% in Serbia between 2015 and 2024, and increased by 67% in North Macedonia between 2015 and 2023. In 2015, income inequality was significantly higher in enlargement countries than in the EU, as reflected in their elevated Gini coefficients. By 2025, these had moved closer to the EU level, ranging from 30.2 in Albania (2023 data) to 31.9 in Serbia (2024 data), compared with 29.4 in the EU (2024 data). Türkiye was the only exception, where the coefficient increased to 43.9 in 2025. Between 2015 and 2025, most enlargement countries followed HICP trends similar to those in the EU where prices rose by 32.9%. In contrast, Türkiye diverged distinctly, with the index rising from 100 in 2015 to 1 221.2 in 2025. From 2015 to 2025, Türkiye consistently recorded the lowest long-term unemployment rate among the enlargement countries, while North Macedonia showed the highest levels despite a marked decline from 21.3% in 2015 to 7.8% in 2025. This article is part of an [[Enlargement_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]]. It presents information on the [[Glossary:Candidate countries|enlargement countries]] and compares this information with the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. The data used in this article have all been submitted to and validated by Eurostat's subject matter units, following the same process as for the EU countries. For Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine, data on living conditions are not yet transmitted according to this process and are therefore not yet available. However, data on Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are also presented in the [[European Neighbourhood Policy countries - statistical_overview| Statistics Explained articles for European Neighbourhood Policy - East]] countries; these articles are based on annual indicators supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country. The article includes information on [[Glossary:Median|median]] [[Glossary:Equivalised disposable income|equivalised disposable income]] and the [[Glossary:Gini coefficient|Gini coefficient]], the [[Glossary:Harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)|harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)]], [[Glossary:Long-term_unemployment|long-term unemployment rate]] and people [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty_rate|at-risk-of-poverty]]. ===Median equivalised annual net income (PPS per capita)=== [[Glossary:Equivalised income|Equivalised income]] adjusts a [[Glossary:Household|household’s]] total income according to its size and composition, making it possible to fairly compare households of different types. This method applies a standard scale that assigns varying weights to adults and children, reflecting their shared living expenses. Equivalised means that the composition of each household is weighted according to the number of adults and children living in it. Income is presented in [[Glossary:Purchasing_power_standard_(PPS)|purchasing power standards (PPS)]], a unit that accounts for price-level differences between countries, thereby improving comparability. Table 1 compares the [[Glossary:Median|median]] annual net income expressed in PPS per capita in the enlargement countries and in the EU for the years 2015-2025. The highest median annual income among the enlargement countries over the period was observed in Türkiye in 2025 (11 403 PPS per capita), at about half of the level recorded in the EU in 2024 (21 245 PPS per capita, the most recent year for which EU data are available). The fluctuations in the purchasing power of income in Türkiye were significantly affected by the exceptionally high inflation in the country since 2021. Until 2023, Serbia and North Macedonia led enlargement countries in median annual income at 7 752 and 7 609 PPS, respectively, before Türkiye surpassed them. North Macedonia’s data show a break in timeseries in 2021. The median annual income in 2022 in Montenegro (more recent data not available) was 7 309 PPS per capita. This figure positioned Montenegro between Serbia and North Macedonia for that year. In Albania the median equivalised annual income almost doubled from 3 589 PPS per capita in 2017 to 6 174 PPS per capita in 2023 (latest available data). Although notable growth, it remains at about one-third of the EU median (19 903 PPS per capita in 2023). For Kosovo''This designation is without prejudice to positions on status and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo Declaration of Independence.'', only data for 2018 are available, when it recorded the lowest median annual income among the enlargement countries (3 953 PPS per capita), only slightly below Albania (4 003 PPS per capita). Data are not available for Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the EU, median annual income increased by 35.8% between 2015 and 2024, from 15 641 to 21 245 PPS per capita. The series shows a steady upward trend, with 2018 recorded as an estimated value (16 938 PPS). No data are available for 2025. Overall, median income levels in enlargement countries increased over time, indicating gradual convergence dynamics, but substantial gaps remain both within the region and relative to the EU. Stronger gains were observed in countries such as Türkiye, Serbia, and North Macedonia, while Albania and Kosovo remained at lower income levels despite steady growth, and Montenegro occupied a mid-range position in the latest available data.
