For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Gini coefficient of equivalised disposable income=== The [[Glossary:Gini coefficient|Gini coefficient]] captures how unevenly income is distributed within a population. A coefficient of 0 expresses perfect equality where everyone has the same income, while a coefficient of 100 expresses full inequality where only one person has all the income. The disposable income of a household is its net income after taxes and social contributions but including social benefits received. Figure 1 displays the Gini coefficients for [[Glossary:Equivalised disposable income|equivalised disposable income]], defined as the total income of a household, after taxes and other deductions, that is available for expenditure or saving. This figure is divided by the number of household members, with each member adjusted into equalised adults according to the modified [[Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)|OECD]] equivalence scale, which assigns weights based on age to achieve comparability among household members. Gini coefficients are listed for 2015 and 2025, or for the nearest available years. In 2015, enlargement countries exhibited greater income inequality than the EU, as reflected by their higher Gini coefficients. The highest coefficient was recorded in Kosovo: 46.6 (2018 data, the only available observation). Based on the most recent data, Gini coefficients have converged towards the EU level, with values ranging from 30.2 in Albania (2023 data) to 31.9 in Serbia (2024 data), as opposed to the EU’s coefficient of 29.4 (2024 data). Türkiye was an outlier, recording a coefficient of 43.9 in 2025. Data for Bosnia and Herzegovina are unavailable. The convergence pattern in income inequality (Gini coefficients) is most clearly illustrated by Serbia, where inequality declined significantly, with the coefficient dropping from 40.0 in 2015 to 31.9 in 2024 (-20.3%). Similar reductions over 2015-2025 were observed in Albania, Montenegro, and North Macedonia, with declines of 17.9%, 13.7%, and 10.1%, respectively. In contrast, Türkiye diverged from this pattern, with the coefficient increasing by 4.8%, from 41.9 to 43.9 over the same period. Data availability and comparability vary across countries. For Albania, 2017 data were used instead of 2015 and 2023 data instead of 2025. For Montenegro and North Macedonia, 2022 and 2023 data, respectively, were used instead of 2025. For Serbia and the EU, 2024 data were used instead of 2025. In addition, there were breaks in the time series between 2015 and 2025 for the EU and North Macedonia. In the EU, the Gini coefficient declined by 4.5%, from 30.8 in 2015 to 29.4 in 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Harmonised index of consumer prices=== A [[Glossary:Consumer price index (CPI)|consumer price index (CPI)]] is an economic indicator that tracks changes in the price levels of a specified basket of goods and services typically purchased by households. The index is used to assess inflation in an economy. The [[Glossary:Harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)|harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)]] serves as a unified measure of the consumer price index across the EU, ensuring both consistency and direct comparability among countries. Figure 2 presents the HICP (2015=100) for the enlargement countries and the EU. It should be noted that for enlargement countries, compliance with HICP methodological requirements has not been fully assessed by Eurostat, and comparability may therefore vary. With the exception of Türkiye, enlargement countries’ harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP) followed a pattern similar to the EU: moderate growth from 2015-2019, slowed inflation in 2020 during the COVID-19 crisis, and accelerated price increases in 2021-2022 due to economic recovery and supply chain issues. The Russian war of aggression against Ukraine in 2022 further exacerbated consumer price pressures, resulting in even sharper increases in inflation. Finally, during 2023-2025 a gradual decline in HICP was observed, although it continued to stand above pre-COVID levels. Between 2015 and 2019, HICP year-on-year changes in the enlargement countries (excluding Türkiye) ranged from a decrease of 0.1% in Montenegro (2016) to an increase of 3.3% in Serbia (2017). In 2020, most of these countries, including Türkiye, but excluding Albania and North Macedonia, recorded smaller annual increases in the HICP compared to previous years. In 2021, the HICP increased significantly, ranging from 2.3% in Albania to 4.0% in Serbia, while Türkiye experienced a 19.6% rise. In 2022 every enlargement country except Albania registered HICP growth exceeding 11%; Albania's increase was 6.6%. The HICP trend in Türkiye showed an almost exponential rise, with the index climbing from 100 in 2015 to 1 221.2 by 2025 – more than 12 times higher. This pattern resulted from extraordinary year-on-year increases in Türkiye's HICP, notably a 72.3% surge in 2022, which then gradually decreased to 34.9% by 2025. Between 2015 and 2024, the HICP index increased gradually across enlargement countries, prior to the levels observed in 2025. By 2025, values ranged from 133.4 in Albania to 157.3 in Serbia, indicating cumulative price level increases of roughly one-third to one-half compared with the 2015 base year. North Macedonia (149.1), Montenegro (141.8), Kosovo (135.1), and Albania (133.4) clustered at comparatively lower levels. Serbia (157.3) stood out with the second highest index among the enlargement countries, albeit far below the index in Türkiye (1 221.2). In contrast, the EU recorded an HICP index of 132.9 in 2025, broadly in line with the lowest values observed among enlargement countries such as Albania and Kosovo. Excluding Türkiye as an outlier, the EU’s price level increase over the period 2015-2025 was comparable to that of most enlargement countries, remaining within the lower range and well below the higher values observed in Serbia and North Macedonia. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Long-term unemployment rate=== The [[Glossary:Long-term unemployment|long-term unemployment]] rate represents the proportion of the [[Glossary:Labour force|labour force]] (which includes both employed and unemployed persons) that is unemployed and has been actively seeking work for at least one year. Unemployment results in a loss of income, and if it persists long-term it increases the risk of [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Living_conditions_in_Europe_-_poverty_and_social_exclusion falling into poverty]. The data cover persons aged 15 to 74 years. Figure 3 shows the long-term unemployment rate in the years 2015 to 2025 for the enlargement countries and the EU. Data for Albania and Kosovo are not available. Overall, the long-term unemployment rates decreased steadily over the period, in both the enlargement countries and the EU, except for Türkiye and Montenegro. In Montenegro, the rate declined from 13.5% in 2015, to 11.4% in 2018, before increasing again from 2019, reaching 13.4% in 2020; no more recent data available. The most significant reductions in long-term unemployment occurred in North Macedonia and Serbia. In 2015, North Macedonia recorded the highest rate at 21.3%. By 2025, this figure had fallen to 7.8%, representing a drop of 13.5 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points (pp)]] (break in time series in 2021). Serbia recorded a steady decline in its long-term unemployment rate, dropping from 10.7% in 2015 to 3.5% in 2025, a decrease of 7.2 percentage points over the period. Data for Bosnia and Herzegovina, available from 2021 onwards, indicate a marked decline in the long-term unemployment rate, from 13.4% in 2021 to 9.1% in 2025. In Montenegro, by contrast, the rate remained broadly stable between 2015 and 2020, with temporary declines during 2017-2019 offset by a subsequent increase, leaving the rate almost unchanged overall (13.5% in 2015 and 13.4% in 2020). Between 2015 and 2025, Türkiye consistently recorded the lowest long-term unemployment rate among the enlargement countries for which data were available. From 2015 to 2018 and again in 2023-2025, the rate remained below the EU average. Unlike the overall downward trend observed elsewhere, Türkiye experienced a gradual increase from 2.2% in 2015 to 3.2% in 2019, when it exceeded the EU rate of 2.8%, before declining markedly to 1.5% in 2025 (break in time series in 2021). Within the EU, the long-term unemployment rate declined steadily from 4.9% in 2015 to 1.9% in 2025. The only interruption to the downward trend was a temporary increase to 2.8% in 2021, representing a rise of 0.4 percentage points compared with 2020. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Risk of poverty=== The [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|at-risk-of-poverty rate]] measures the share of people that have [[Glossary:Equivalised disposable income|equivalised disposable income]] below the national at-risk-of-poverty threshold. The at-risk-of-poverty threshold is set at 60% of the national median equivalised disposable income; it is thus defined separately for each country. This indicator can be calculated either before social transfers or after social transfers. The difference between the two reflects the proportion of the population moved above the threshold as a result of receiving social transfers. Social transfers include items such as pensions, [[Glossary:Unemployment|unemployment]] benefits, family benefits, sickness benefits, housing allowances, as well as other social assistance and benefits. As the poverty threshold is set independently for each enlargement country, the indicator reflects low income in comparison with other residents in the same economy. This does not necessarily imply an extremely low standard of living. Figure 4 shows the risk-of-poverty rate after social transfers, representing the proportion of people still at risk of poverty despite receiving support (social transfers). The graph clearly shows that the at-risk-of-poverty rate is higher in the enlargement countries than in the EU, with the EU line remaining below those of the enlargement countries throughout the period. In the EU, the observed proportion of people at risk of poverty after social transfers is generally quite stable or slightly declining, with occasional fluctuations. Based on recent available data, the share of people at risk of poverty after receiving social transfers varies across the enlargement countries. It stood at 19.7% in both Albania (2023 data) and Serbia (2024 data), while Kosovo recorded a higher rate of 27.9% in 2018, the only available observation. In the other enlargement countries, the rate situates within this range. The most significant decrease in the proportion of the population at risk of poverty after social transfers was observed in Serbia, where it declined by 7 pp from 26.7% in 2015 to 19.7% in 2024. In Türkiye, the significant increase observed in 2024 and 2025 resulted in an end-period level 0.9 percentage points higher than in 2015 Data are not available for Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the EU the proportion of the population at risk of poverty after social transfers decreased by 1.2 pp from 17.4% in 2015 to 16.2 in 2024 (data for 2025 are not available). For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=CPC26_Living_conditions_V3_.xlsx|title=Enlargement countries – living conditions: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data used in this article are mainly derived from [[Glossary:EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]], a key source for data on living conditions of the European population. It aims to collect timely and comparable data on income, poverty, social inclusion and living conditions. Eurostat's website provides an overview of legislation related to EU-SILC, as well as an online publication on its methodology and an overview article presenting main results on living conditions in Europe - poverty and social exclusion. Among the enlargement countries, Türkiye started the full implementation of EU-SILC in 2006, while North Macedonia launched it in 2010, Montenegro and Serbia in 2013, Albania in 2017, Kosovo in 2018 and Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2022. The legal basis for this data collection exercise is [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:32019R1700:EN:NOT Regulation (EU) 2019/1700] establishing a common framework for European statistics relating to persons and households, based on data at individual level collected from samples (Integrated European Social Statistics – IESS). The main source for European labour force statistics is the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|European Union labour force survey (EU LFS)]]. This [[Glossary:Household|household]] survey is carried out in all EU Member States in accordance with European legislation and provides figures at least every quarter. Among the enlargement countries, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia and Türkiye have implemented the EU-LFS instrument and conduct the labour force survey according to the same guidelines, methodology and standards as the EU countries. Information concerning the current statistical legislation on statistics on employment and unemployment can be found in the 'Legislation' section of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/lfs dedicated section on 'Employment and unemployment (Labour Force Survey – LFS)'] on Eurostat's website. The [[Glossary:Harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)|harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP)]] measures the changing cost of a fixed basket of goods and services over time. The HICP is computed as a [[Glossary:Laspeyres price index|'Laspeyres-type price index']] according to harmonised definitions. It is an important basis for comparisons of consumer price inflation in the EU. National HICP data are calculated by the national statistical institutes, while the country-special aggregates and the European aggregates are produced by Eurostat. Eurostat publishes HICP data for several of the enlargement countries. Consumer price indices that classify products according to the [https://showvoc.op.europa.eu/#/datasets/ESTAT_European_Classification_of_Individual_Consumption_according_to_Purpose_%28ECOICOP%29/data European Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose (ECOICOP)] are available for Albania since 2015, Montenegro since 2014, North Macedonia since 2004, Serbia since 2005 and Kosovo since 2015. HICP data for Türkiye according to ECOICOP are not available. Information concerning the current statistical legislation on the harmonised indices of consumer prices can be found in the 'Legislation' section of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/hicp/overview dedicated section on 'Harmonised indices of consumer prices (HICP)'] on Eurostat's website. While basic principles and institutional frameworks for producing statistics are already in place, the enlargement countries are expected to increase the volume and quality of their data progressively, and to transmit these data to Eurostat in the context of the EU enlargement process. [[Glossary:European statistical system (ESS)|European statistical system (ESS)]] standards in the field of statistics require the existence of a statistical infrastructure based on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/quality/european-quality-standards/european-statistics-code-of-practice principles] such as professional independence, impartiality, relevance, confidentiality of individual data and easy access to official statistics; they cover methodology, classifications and standards for production. Eurostat assesses and supports the alignment of statistical production in the enlargement countries with the EU acquis in the field of statistics. Eurostat supports the national statistical offices and other producers of official statistics through a range of initiatives, such as statistical projects, training courses, traineeships, study visits, workshops and seminars, and participation in meetings within the ESS. The ultimate goal is the provision of harmonised, high-quality data that conforms to European and international standards. ===Context=== Rising costs of living have a direct and indirect impact on the general population, but in particular on vulnerable groups such as the elderly, people with disabilities, young people, low-wage earners, part-time workers and people with precarious work contracts. In recent years, pressure on living conditions of households has increased through rising consumer prices, together with a generally uncertain economic environment. The EU and the EU countries operate an open method of coordination for social protection and social inclusion. This aims to promote social cohesion and equality through adequate, accessible and financially sustainable social protection systems and social inclusion policies. As such, the EU provides a framework for national strategy development, as well as the opportunity to discuss and learn from best practices and to coordinate policies between EU Member States in areas such as [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1226&langId=en building a fairer and more inclusive EU], [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?langId=en&catId=750 social protection and social inclusion], and [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=752&langId=en pensions]. At the start of March 2021, the European Commission outlined its ambition for an EU that focuses on education, skills and jobs for the future and targets a fair, inclusive and resilient socioeconomic recovery. The [https://op.europa.eu/webpub/empl/european-pillar-of-social-rights/en/ European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan] outlines a range of actions designed to promote social rights through the active involvement of social partners and civil society. It also proposes employment, skills and social protection headline targets for the EU. One of the headline targets relates specifically to living conditions, namely that the number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion should decrease by at least 15 million persons (of which, at least five million should be children) between 2019 and 2030. The Action Plan highlights how the principles of the social pillar might be implemented, with the aim of building a stronger social Europe by 2030. Additional information on statistical cooperation with the enlargement countries is provided in the Statistics explained background article [[Enlargement policy and statistical cooperation]]. === title: Long term developments in industrial production - results from short-term statistics
text:
This article describes the development of industrial production and in particular the evolution of manufacturing in the EU, the euro area and the EU Member States since the year 2000 on the basis of short-term business statistics. Data extracted in July 2025 Next update: 2028 Between 2000 and 2024 industrial production increased by an average rate of 0.6% per year in the EU. The highest average growth rates were observed in Ireland (5.6%), and Poland (4.9%). The largest decreases were observed in Italy (-1.1%), and Portugal (-0.9%). European manufacturing industries developed in very different ways between 2000 and 2024. While the production of pharmaceutical products grew by an average rate of 5.7% and the production of computers by 2.0% per year the production of wearing apparel fell by an average of 5.3% per annum. [[Image: Long-term developments in industrial production 1920pxREV.jpg|thumb|center|500px| Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpr_a}}]] ==Overview== This article describes the development of industrial production and in particular the evolution of manufacturing in the EU, the euro area and the EU countries since the year 2000 on the basis of [[Short-term business statistics introduced|short-term business statistics]]. The analysis is based on the current composition of the EU, covering [[Glossary:EU enlargements|27 countries]]. The main purpose of short-term business statistics (or simply short-term statistics, STS) is to describe the most recent changes in the activities of European businesses in industry, construction, trade, and services to help policy makers to plan, monitor, and assess their fiscal and monetary policies. However, STS provide time series of major economic aggregates (e.g. production, turnover, prices, employment) which often go back to the year 2000 (and sometimes even beyond that). Therefore, the data can also be used to analyse long-term trends in European economies. Industry, in this article, refers to economic activities in [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] sections B (mining and quarrying), C (manufacturing), and D (electricity, gas, steam, air conditioning supply). Note that water supply and waste management, which are grouped together in NACE section E, are not included in the industry and energy definitions used in this article. These latter activities account for around 4% of the sum of activities in a more comprehensive definition of industries, i.e. NACE sections B, C, D, and E (Table 1). Unfortunately, the coverage of industry section E in STS is not sufficient for a detailed analysis. Manufacturing accounts for around 84% of total industry (B, C, D, E), and the emphasis of this article will therefore be on manufacturing activities. [[Image: Table 1 Share of different industries in total industrial value added, EU, 2022.png|thumb|center|500px|Table 1: Share of different industries in total industrial value added, EU, 2022
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sbs_sc_ovv}}|alt= A table showing the share of different industries in total industrial value added in the EU in 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Since the emphasis of STS is on the changes in the economy, STS provides indices and growth rates but not data in absolute values. In order to show the long-term trends most clearly, all indices in this article have been re-referenced to the year 2000 (2000 = 100). Note however that the indices are calculated with weights from the base year 2021, i.e. the relative significance of the various industries is based on the situation in 2021. (For more on basing and referencing indices see [[Short-term business statistics - base year 2021|here]].) This article does not discuss in detail the effects of the COVID-19 epidemic on industrial production since there is a [[Impact of Covid-19 crisis on industrial production|special article]] on that particular subject. ==General trends in industrial production 2000 – 2025== Figure 1 shows the evolution of the three NACE sections mining and quarrying, manufacturing, and energy (i.e. electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply) that compose total industry. [[Image:Figure 1 Production in total industry and main industry sections, EU, 2000-2025 Monthly data, calendar and seasonally adjusted, 2000=100.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 1: Production in total industry and main industry sections, EU, 2000-2025
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpr_m}}|alt= a line chart with 4 lines showing monthly data for production in total industry and main industry sections in the EU from 2000-2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] As Figure 1 shows, the production of energy (electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply) stagnated over the long term. Moreover, this energy related production was less affected by the financial and economic crisis than many other industries. Mining and quarrying activities also more or less stagnated in the early years of the 2000s. During the financial and economic crisis these activities declined relatively strongly. After the crisis mining and quarrying activities did not fully recover and their development since then shows a stable downward path. In total, the index of mining and quarrying decreased by more than 50 points between January 2000 and spring 2005, i.e. the size of these activities was effectively halved over the last two and a half decades. European manufacturing increased rather dynamically in the years immediately preceding the financial and economic crisis of 2008 and 2009. During the crisis, manufacturing dropped by almost 9.0% per year, but it recovered relatively quickly in the years 2010, 2011 and 2012 – however without quite regaining the pre-crisis level which was only reached in 2018. During the COVID-19 crisis in 2020, production levels fell much more than in 2008/2009; recovery was however also more dynamic. Figure 2 shows the evolution of the industrial production index since the year 2000 together with the evolution of the [[Glossary:Main industrial grouping (MIG)|main industrial groupings (MIGs)]]. MIGs combine different industries with common characteristics into specific aggregates. The MIGs are intermediate goods (e.g. raw materials), energy (e.g. mining activities, electricity, gas, and steam), capital goods (e.g. machinery, motor vehicles), durable consumer goods (e.g. consumer appliances, furniture), and non-durable consumer goods (e.g. food, clothing). All indices show roughly the same general development pattern since they all clearly reflect the economic and financial crisis in 2008/2009 and the COVID-19 crisis. There are, however, marked differences in the long-term trends. Between early 2020 and the first quarter of 2025 the total industry index increased by almost 20 percentage points. Over the same period the index for intermediate goods remained almost stable. The production index for energy dropped by around 16 points and the index for durable consumer goods by 13 points. The index for capital goods increased by 36 points and the index for non-durable consumer goods by 50 points. [[Image:Production in Main Industrial Groupings (MIGs), EU, 2000-2025 monthly data, calendar and seasonally adjusted, 2000=100.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 2: Production in Main Industrial Groupings (MIGs), EU, 2000-2025
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpr_m}}|alt= a line chart with 6 lines showing monthly data production in main industrial groupings (MIGs) in the EU from 2000-2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Although they combine industries that share important characteristics, the main industrial groupings also hide some differences between the developments of the specific industries of which they are composed. Figure 3, therefore, presents the industries (at NACE rev. 2 division level) with the strongest positive and the strongest negative trends. The most dynamic development by far can be noted in the pharmaceutical industry; the monthly index level increased by more than 300 points, meaning that the production in this industry quadrupled over the period 2000-2025. A very strong increase was also recorded for the manufacturing of computers, electronic and optical goods, which increased by more than 60 points. The monthly production levels for tobacco, on the other hand, declined by more than 50 points, i.e. the production was more than halved between 2000 and 2025. The index for the production of wearing apparel lost even more than 70 points. [[Image:Figure 3 Manufacturing, fastest declining and growing industries, EU, 2000-2025 monthly data, calendar and seasonally adjusted, 2000 = 100.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 3: Manufacturing, fastest declining and growing industries, EU, 2000-2025 monthly data, calendar and seasonally adjusted, 2000 = 100
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpr_m}}|alt= a line chart with 5 lines showing monthly production in manufacturing and the two fastest growing and the two slowest growing manufacturing industries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at specific industries, the development of the pharmaceutical industry and the wearing apparel industry differs most significantly from the evolution of total industry. However, there are also some other industries that develop either more dynamically than total industry or which are in general decline. Table 2 is based on the average annual rates of change for the industries in all countries for the years 2000 – 2024. It shows, for the European Union, the euro area and the individual countries, those industries that in this period had the highest growth rates (first, second and third) as well as those industries that had the lowest average rates of growth or even rates of decline. [[Image: Strongest and weakest growth industries, 2000 - 2024.png |thumb|center|800px|Table 2: Strongest and weakest growth industries, 2000 - 2024
Source: Eurostat, special calculations {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpr_a}}|alt= a table naming, for all EU countries and for Norway and North Macedonia the three fastest and the three slowest growing industries.]] Table 2 confirms the dynamic growth of the pharmaceutical industry in the EU, which is also visible in the country results. This activity appears for 9 countries (for which data are available) as one of the three fastest growing industries. Other industries that are regularly among the most dynamic industries at county level are electrical equipment, motor vehicles, machinery, and computers and electric and optical equipment. At the other end of the spectrum are the industries that declined during the last 25 years. Apart from the industry for wearing apparels, industries that have considerably lost importance are the production of tobacco, leather products and textiles. Also on the decline are the various sub-sectors of mining and quarrying (mining of coal and lignite, extraction of petroleum and gas, mining of metal ores). It should be noted that the analysis of the fastest growing and declining industries cannot be based on all EU countries. For Ireland, manufacturing data are mostly confidential since 2010. Moreover, because of their relatively low weight in the EU-aggregates several countries are not required to transmit data that are sufficiently detailed for this type of analysis. While the industries mentioned above show a trend that is rather different from manufacturing as a whole, it is interesting to observe that the production of rubber and plastic is very similar to the development of total manufacturing although this industry only makes up around 4 to 5 % of the total EU production value. The graphs for total manufacturing and for the manufacturing of rubber and plastic products are difficult to distinguish in Figure 2 and are therefore presented again in Figure 4 with a different axis formatting. [[Image:Total manufacturing, rubber and plastic production, EU, 2000-2025 monthly data, calendar and seasonally adjusted, 2000 = 100.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 4: Total manufacturing, rubber and plastic production, EU, 2000-2025 monthly data, calendar and seasonally adjusted, 2000 = 100
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpr_m}}|alt= a line chart with 2 lines showing monthly production in manufacturing and monthly production of rubber and plastic products.]] ==Before and after the financial and economic crisis== Between 2000 and 2007, industrial production in the EU increased by an average annual rate of 2.0%, manufacturing increased on average by 2.1% per year. In 2008, and in particular in 2009, industrial production dropped significantly (-8.3%). In the following years, industrial production recovered, but it decreased again in 2012 and 2013. Since 2014, industrial production was again on an upward trend but not to the extent of its dynamic development of the pre-crisis years. In 2020, the COVID-19 crisis had a strong negative effect on industrial production. Table 3 summarises the average annual growth rates for all industries in the EU for the period 2000-2024, for the years before, during and after the financial and economic crisis in 2008 and 2009, and also reports the 2020 rates of change which were strongly influenced by the COVID-19 crisis. [[Image: Table 3 EU, Industries average annual growth rates during different periods.png|thumb|center|500px|Table 3: EU, Industries annual growth rates during different periods
Source: Eurostat, special calculations {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpr_a}}|alt= a table showing the average annual growth rates for the various manufacturing industries for different time periods. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The rates in Table 3 suggest that the economic and financial crisis did not only lead to a massive reduction in industrial production at the time (2008/2009), but that afterwards the economic development was also much less dynamic than it had been before. To give an idea of the magnitude of these effects, Figure 5 shows the actual development of industrial production as well as the trend of production based on the average rate of change in the years 2000 – 2007, i.e. assuming that the growth rates of the years 2000-2007 had continued until spring 2025. The graph shows that under this assumption, the level of production in the EU would have reached around 170 points in early 2025, which is around 50 % higher than the index level that was actually reached by that time. Note that this simulation is of course entirely hypothetical; even without the financial and economic crisis there might not have been a continuation of the 2000-2007 trend for other reasons. Figure 5 also shows the hypothetical prolongation of the trend of the years 2011-2019, i.e. the average growth rate of the years between the economic and financial crisis and the COVID-19 crisis. It becomes apparent that the pandemic resulted in a massive reduction of industrial production, but this shock was relatively short. The growth performance in its wake was very similar to the development before and in early 2025 the actual level of industrial production and the hypothetical level resulting from the 2011-2019 performance are very similar. [[Image: Total industry, actual development and prolongation of the trend, EU, 2000-2007 and 2011-2019 Fig 5.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 5:Total industry, actual development and prolongation of the trend, EU, 2000-2007 and 2011-2019, monthly data, calendar and seasonally adjusted, 2000=100
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpr_m}}}|alt= a figure showing the actual development of the total industrial production index and two trend lines, one that prolongates the average annual growth of the years 2000-2007 and one that prolongates average annual growth of the years 2011-2019.]] The simulation shows quite different results for different industries. The largest difference between the actual development and the projection of the 2000-2007 trend for the index can be found for printing and the reproduction of recorded media, for basic metal products and the manufacturing of motor vehicles and trailers (Figure 6). The production of leather and tobacco products, and of wearing apparel present almost exactly the opposite development. These three industries were already declining in the years before the financial and economic crisis and while their output also dropped during the crisis itself, their decline was not very pronounced afterwards. For the production of pharmaceuticals and computers the difference between the 2000-2007 trend prolongation and the actual development is also not so big since these industries actually developed rather strongly since the year 2000. [[Image:Manufacturing industries, EU percentage difference between prolongation of trend 2000-2007 and actual February 2020 index.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 6: Manufacturing industries, EU percentage difference between prolongation of trend 2000-2007 and latest 2025 index
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpr_m}}|alt= a bar chart that shows, for each manufacturing industry the difference between the actual index level in 2024 and the index level that would have resulted if the growth of the years 2000-2007 had continued.]] As mentioned above, the impact of the COVID-19 crisis on industrial production is analysed in a [[Impact of Covid-19 crisis on industrial production|dedicated article]]. ==Country analysis== Just as the various industries have developed in a very different fashion since the year 2000 so did the industrial production of the EU countries (Table 4). Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Estonia were the EU countries with the fastest industrial growth between 2000 and 2024; these countries had average annual growth rates of more than 4%. [[Image: Countries average annual industry growth rates during different periods.png|thumb|center|500px|Table 4: Countries average annual industry growth rates during different periods
Source: Eurostat, special calculations {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpr_a}}|alt= a table showing the average annual growth rates for EU countries and other countries for different time periods. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The highest annual average growth was recorded in Ireland (5.6%). Ireland presents a rather special case; while the country already showed an above average development in industrial growth between 2000 and 2014, its statistics were heavily revised in 2015 and, as a consequence, the index of industrial production increased massively between 2014 and 2015. Since then, the country’s industrial production statistics stayed on a rather high level overall, but depicted strong cyclical movements. [[Image: Industrial production, EU and fastest developing countries, Monthly data, calendar and seasonally adjusted, 2000 = 100.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 7: Industrial production, EU and fastest developing countries, Monthly data, calendar and seasonally adjusted, 2000 = 100
2000 = 100, Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpr_m}}|alt= a figure showing the average annual growth rates for the various manufacturing industries for different time periods. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In Italy, Portugal, Spain, Greece, France and Luxembourg, industrial production contracted during the years 2000 – 2024. In general the reductions in industrial production occurred during the financial crisis and afterwards production only partly recovered and more or less stagnated. The exception to this is Greece which shows a positive development since 2021. [[Image: Industrial production, EU and slowest developing countries, Monthly data, calendar and seasonally adjusted, 2000 = 100.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 8: Industrial production, EU and slowest developing countries, Monthly data, calendar and seasonally adjusted, 2000 = 100
2000 = 100, Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpr_m}}|alt= a line chart with 5 lines showing monthly monthly industrial production in the EU and in the the two fastest growing and the two slowest growing EU countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In the same way as for the manufacturing industries (see Figure 6), a difference can be calculated between the total industry level which countries had actually reached in early 2025 and the level they would have – hypothetically – reached if the growth trend of the years 2000 – 2007 had continued (Figure 9). The differences between countries are quite remarkable. Between the year 2000 and the year 2007, Bulgaria had an annual growth rate of 7.8%. Had this trend continued, the Bulgarian industrial production would have been around 270% higher in Spring 2025 than it actually was – a result of the strong pre-crisis growth on the one hand and the comparatively moderate annual growth of 1.9% after the financial and economic crisis (which was however still higher than the EU average) on the other hand. [[Image:Figure 9 EU and Member States, total industry, percentage difference between prolongation of trend 2000-2007 and latest 2025 index.png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 9: EU and Member States, total industry, percentage difference between prolongation of trend 2000-2007 and latest 2025 index
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpr_m}}|alt= a bar chart showing, for each EU Member State, the difference between the actual index level of industrial production index in 2024 and the index level that would have resulted if the trend of the years 2000-2007 had continued.]] For the EU as a whole the difference between the actual Spring 2025 value and the level that would have been reached with a continuation of the 2000 – 2007 trend is much lower (about 50%). In Denmark and Romania, for example, the industrial development was more dynamic after the financial and economic crisis than before. In Denmark the most recent development was so positive that the actual development of industrial production is even higher than the level that would have been resulted if the production trend of the years 2000 – 2007 had continued. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Industry long term developments in STS Figures and Tables 2025 23-07-25.xlsx |title=tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== Despite its name the industrial production index is not intended to measure production but should – in theory – reflect the development of value added in the different branches of industry. This means that the inputs obtained by one branch from another must be deducted from its gross output. In this way, double counting of production is prevented and the degree of vertical integration of branches should not influence the results for the indicator. In practice, however, it is difficult to collect value-added data on a monthly basis. Most statistical institutes therefore derive monthly production data from other sources including [[Glossary:Deflated|deflated]] [[Glossary:Turnover - SBS|turnover]], physical production data, labour input, intermediate consumption of raw materials and energy etc. [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publishes, on a monthly basis, the industrial production index for the EU, for the [[Glossary:Euro area|euro area]] and the EU Member States; data are also collected for several non-EU countries. Data are presented in [[Glossary:Working-day adjustment|calendar adjusted/working-day adjusted]] and in [[Glossary:Seasonal adjustment|seasonally adjusted]] form. The data in this article were calculated with 2021 as the [[Short-term business statistics - base year 2021|base year]] (=100). ===Context=== The industrial production index is one of the most important short-term statistics indicators. It is used to identify turning points in the economic development at an early stage and to assess the future development of [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|GDP]]. In order to serve this purpose it is available on a monthly basis in a detailed activity breakdown and with a rather short delay (1 month and 10 days). The industrial production index is one of the so-called '[[Glossary:Principal European economic indicators (PEEI)|Principal European economic indicators (PEEI)]]' which are used to monitor and steer economic and monetary policies in the EU and in the euro area. === Other Articles === *[[Short-term business statistics (STS)]] === Publications === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/short-term-business-statistics/publications All STS News Releases] *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-SF-13-001|title=High-technology and medium-high technology industries main drivers of EU-27's industrial growth, Statistics in focus 1/2013}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-SF-11-036|title=Industrial output in the EU and euro area, Statistics in focus 36/2011}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-SF-10-021|title=The economic crisis in the non-financial business economy – where was it more heavily felt?, Statistics in focus 21/2010}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-SF-09-097|title=Recession in the EU-27: length and depth of the downturn varies across activities and countries, Statistics in focus 97/2009}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-SF-09-017|title=Recession in the EU-27: output measures, Statistics in focus 17/2009}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-SF-08-061|title=Industrial production indices – global developments, Statistics in focus 61/2008}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-SF-07-068|title=Evolution of high-technology manufacturing and knowledge intensive services, Statistics in focus 68/2007}} === Selected Datasets === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/short-term-business-statistics/database Short-term business statistics (t_sts)], see: :Industry (NACE Rev.2) (t_sts_ind) For more on the legal base see [[Short-term business statistics - legal base|the background article]]. === External links === *[http://unstats.un.org/unsd/statcom/doc10/BG-IndustrialStats.pdf United Nations Statistics Division: International Recommendations for the Index of Industrial production (2010)] {{Unit|topic=X_Short-term_statistics}} [[Category:Industry, trade, and services|Long term developments in industrial production - results from short-term statistics]] [[Category:Short-term business statistics (STS)|Long term developments in industrial production - results from short-term statistics]] [[Category:Industry short-term statistics|Long term developments in industrial production - results from short-term statistics]] [[Category:Statistical article|Long term developments in industrial production - results from short-term statistics]] [[Category:Industrial production|Long term developments in industrial production - results from short-term statistics]] [[Category:July2028|Long term developments in industrial production - results from short-term statistics]]

title: MEETS programme - framework for business-related statistics
text:
This article is part of an [[MEETS programme - results|online publication]] presenting the results of the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] programme 'Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics', or MEETS for short, which ran from 2009 to 2013 with the objectives of adjusting European business statistics to new needs and reducing the burden on [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]]. The article presents the results for the programme's '''second objective''', to achieve a streamlined framework for business-related statistics, which was put into practice through three actions: *the integration of concepts and methods within the legal framework (action 2.1), to be implemented via projects on consistency; *the establishment of a Community register of multinational enterprise groups (action 2.2), which should cover the links between units across border; *the development of [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] sampling schemes (action 2.3). === Harmonising methodologies used across relevant statistical areas === '''''Action 2.1: Integrating concepts and methods within the legal framework''''' Until recently, many statistical projects as well as the legal regulations and compulsory methodologies governing such projects were, to some degree, characterised by a certain ‘stove-pipe principle’, which did not pay much attention to the requirements, concepts and definitions in related statistical areas. Different data definitions and methodologies are in use for trade and business statistics. In addition, as they often deal with cross-cutting issues, there is potential for overlapping and redundancy. This first action aimed at an increased harmonisation of the methodologies used across the relevant statistical areas. More consistency between all trade and enterprise related statistics will help to increase the analytical potential of the entire system of enterprise statistics, because different statistical information might then be combined in a coherent framework. In addition, more consistency could help to save resources for the NSIs and reduce the response burden on those enterprises providing the source of data. '''Consistency between legal acts on statistics''' To tackle these issues, the European Statistical System Networks (ESSnet) on Consistency of concepts and methods of business-related statistics was set up and organised around three projects. The 2010 project on 'Statistical units' provided revised definitions of the statistical units enterprise, enterprise group, kind of activity unit and local kind of activity unit. The target was the improvement of the old enterprise definition and operational rules and a data model to enforce uniform implementation. The kind of activity unit and local kind of activity unit were reformulated in order to make application easier. In the future, they will be applied to very big units. The second project on 'Target population, frames, reference periods, classifications and their applications' (2011) developed recommendations for harmonisation of business registers. By making them the backbone of business statistics more consistency between the domains may be achieved. In terms of size classes and classification, a breakdown is proposed as well as concepts for consistent reference periods. The proposals are targeted at achieving output consistency and developing integrated systems for statistical production. The 2012 project on 'Characteristics and their definitions' issued recommendations for a system of variables with consistent and standardised terminology and uniform definitions for all statistical domains, including inclusions and exclusions and explicit references to related variables, as well as methodological guidelines. '''Deliverables on CROS portal:''' [http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/deliverables-2 Project on Statistical Units (01/01/2011 - 31/12/2012)]
[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/consistency-mbga2 Project on target population, frames, reference periods, classifications and their applications (01/01/2012 - 31/12/2013)]
[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/deliverables Project on characteristics and their definitions (31/08/2012 - 31/12/2013)]
'''Further Links:''' [http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/deliverable-53-part-1-definition-statistical-unit-enterprise Final report of the project on statistical units part 1]
[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/deliverable-53-part-2-definition-statistical-units-kind-activity-unit-and-local-kind Final report of the project on statistical units part 2]
[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/deliverable-210310-essnet-consistency-wp2-report-proposals Final report of the project on target population, frames, reference periods, classifications and their applications]
[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/deliverable-31-report-proposed-adjustments Final report of the project on project on characteristics and their definitions]
'''Consistency between BoP and international transactions statistics''' The project was split into two subprojects. The project "Improvement of consistency between BoP and trade statistics" provided funds for improving CIF/FOB methodology and also the data related to goods for processing in the Member States. The project provided funds for exploring the possible ways to close the gap between the two statistical domains. === Developing statistics on enterprise groups === '''''Action 2.2: To establish a community register of multinational enterprise groups''''' '''EuroGroups Register (EGR)''' The aim of the [http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/egr-objectives EuroGroups Register (EGR)] is to provide consistent and coordinated survey frames for producing quality statistics measuring globalisation; mainly for [[Glossary:Foreign_affiliates_statistics_(FATS)|Foreign affiliates statistics (FATS)]] and [[Glossary:Foreign_direct_investment_(FDI)|Foreign direct investment (FDI)]]. The methodological development was done with the support of an ESSnet. In 2009 the methodology and the EGR system version 1.0 were set up, as well as the organisational network for the data exchange between Eurostat and ESS members. The yearly frame population produced by the EGR was extended from the largest 5000 multinational enterprise groups (MNEs) with an interest in the EU in 2009 and 2010 to 10 000 MNEs in 2011. In 2012, the EGR started to be upgraded toward version 2.0, with the aim to improve efficiency, [[Glossary:Timeliness|timeliness]] and consistency with respect to the EGR 1.0. The methodology of EGR 2.0 aims at full coverage for FATS and FDI and at associating national central banks. EGR 2.0 requires remote access for users and producers in the ESS; therefore it has to operate in a secure environment. Due to delays in the Secured Infrastructure for Confidential Data Access (SICON) project, EGR 2.0 was not yet fully operational in 2013 even though the methodological development was completed.
At national level, the implementation of the EGR and its integration with national statistical business registers was co-financed by individual grant agreements. '''Deliverables on CROS portal:''' [http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/egr-sga1 Project period 1 (2008 - 2009)]
[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/egr-sga2 Project period 2 (2009 - 2010)]
[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/egr-sga3 Project period 3 (2010 - 2012)]
[http://www.cros-portal.eu/node/6196 Project period 4 (2012 - 2014)]
'''Profiling''' The ESSnet on [http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/profiling profiling] of large and complex multinational enterprise groups developed methodology and guidelines for profiling multinational and complex enterprise groups. They tested the methodology proposed and supported the implementation of operating methods for the profiling model in the ESS (in particular in ESS members which did not participate in the ESSnet) via e.g. training and coaching sessions. Eurostat is developing an Interactive Profiling Tool (IPT) to facilitate the easy exchange of information between ESS members while simultaneously respecting confidentiality rules. The ESSnet Profiling assisted Eurostat in defining and testing the tool. The ESSnet Profiling worked closely together with the ESSnet Consistency in the development of the revised definition of the enterprise and operational rules. '''Deliverables on CROS portal:''' [http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/final-report-profilingsga1 Final report/Executive summary project period 1]
[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/deliverables-wpa-feasibility-study-profilingsga1 Report on work package A: feasibility study]
[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/deliverableswp-b-statistical-units-profilingsga1 Work package B (partial): statistical units]
'''Further Links:''' [http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/b3-essnet-profilingwp-bpreliminary-reportv1-07-02-2012 Methodology of profiling (WPB) preliminary report] === Setting EU sampling schemes === '''''Action 2.3: Conducting community surveys to minimise burden on enterprises''''' EU sampling schemes aim at providing reliable EU aggregates in order to reduce the burden for Member States for those statistical data for which an EU aggregate satisfies the users’ needs. Some methodologies for EU sampling schemes were developed for selected business statistics domains such as space-related activities including e.g. space transport, [[Glossary:Structural_business_statistics_(SBS)|Structural business statistics]] for enterprises with 250-499 employees, outward [[Glossary:FATS|FATS]], [[Glossary:ICT|ICT]] investment and expenditure and culture statistics. A pilot data collection aiming at testing and evaluating the methodology had to be cancelled due to a low response rate to the call for proposals. === See also === *[[MEETS programme - results ]] === Dedicated section === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=european_business}} Structural business statistics] === Publications === *[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/external-study-detail-evaluation-legal-acts External study on detail evaluation of the legal acts in the areas of statistics which were identified by member states as areas to revision] === Legislation=== *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52009DC0404:EN:NOT|title=Communication COM(2009) 404}} on the production method of EU statistics: a vision for the next decade *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008D1297:EN:NOT|title=Decision 1297/2008/EC}} of 16 December 2008 on a Programme for the Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics (MEETS) *[[Media:MEETS_project_overview,_key_results_and_follow-up.docx|MEETS project overview, key results and follow-up]] (downloadable Word document) *[http://epp.eurostat.ec.europa.eu/portal/page/portal/ess_eurostat/statistical_programmes Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics (MEETS)] *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52010DC0813:EN:NOT|title=Report COM(2010) 813}} on the implementation of Decision 1297/2008/EC of 16 December 2008 on a Programme for the Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics (MEETS) === External links === *[http://www.cros-portal.eu Cros portal] *[MEETS programme - framework for business-related statistics EuroGroups Register website] {{Unit|topic=X_Dissemination}}  [[Category:Industry, trade, and services|MEETS programme - framework for business-related statistics]] [[Category:Structural business statistics (SBS)|MEETS programme - framework for business-related statistics]] [[Category:Background_article|MEETS programme - framework for business-related statistics]]

title: MEETS programme
text:
<highlight title=false>
This article is part of an [[MEETS programme - results|online publication]] presenting the results of the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] programme 'Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics', or MEETS for short, which ran from 2009 to 2013 with the objectives of adjusting European business statistics to new needs and reducing the burden on [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]].
 
Business and trade statistics are facing major challenges: the world economy has become more integrated, and statistics have to respond by adequately reflecting the new phenomena. At the same time there is strong pressure to cut red tape and reduce the burden on business. New ways of producing business statistics, taking advantage of technological progress, need to be explored. 

To address this, the [[Glossary:European Parliament (EP)|European Parliament]] and the [[Glossary:Council of the European Union|Council]] adopted the MEETS programme in December 2008. The programme, which ran over a period of five years from 2009 to 2013, helped to adapt business statistics to new needs and also adjusted the statistical production systems to reduce the burden on [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]]. It provided substantial financial resources - an overall amount of 42.5 million euros - to support development in several areas in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] Member States and [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA]] Member States. 

The strategy was fully in line with the vision of European statistics for the next decade as defined in {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52009DC0404:EN:NOT|title=Communication COM(2009) 404}} on the production method of EU statistics: a vision for the next decade; its legal basis is {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008D1297:EN:NOT|title=Decision 1297/2008/EC}} of 16 December 2008 on a Programme for the Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics (MEETS). 
</highlight>

<articlecontent>
<sesection>
=== Objectives and work programmes  ===

The programme contributed to achieving the following general objectives: 

(1) '''Review priorities and develop target sets of indicators for new areas''' 

was about identifying and deciding on which new areas to describe and reviewing old requirements affected by changing economic structures.

(2) '''Achieve a streamlined framework for business-related statistics''' 

was about integration of different areas of business statistics, including coordination of legal acts, harmonisation of methodologies and linking and harmonising statistical classifications and business registers with related sources. The objective also required the inclusion of multinational groups and data collection on such groups. 

(3) '''Support the implementation of a more efficient way of producing enterprise and trade statistics''' 

was about integration of data collection and data processing. The objective was to more effectively use existing data through integrating data already collected into a single system or by using microdata linking techniques. Additionally, efforts were directed at increasing the use of administrative data and taking advantage of the harmonisation of accounting standards. 

(4) '''Modernise Intrastat''' 

was about improving the simplified Intrastat system through work on harmonising methods, enhancing the use of administrative data and Information and Communication Technology (ICT) improvements. 

For all the objectives, broad actions have been defined in the legal basis. They were implemented through annual work programmes adopted by the Commission after consultation of the relevant technical bodies. 

For more information on the annual work programmes see: 

*[http://epp.eurostat.ec.europa.eu/portal/page/portal/about_eurostat/documents/1_EN_ACT_part1_v3.pdf Commission Decision] of 25 October 2012 on the annual work programme for 2013 for the implementation of Decision 1297/2008/EC on a Programme for the Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics (MEETS); 
*[http://epp.eurostat.ec.europa.eu/portal/page/portal/about_eurostat/documents/Commission_Decision_MEETS_2012.pdf Commission Decision] of 28 October 2011 on the annual work programme for 2012 for the implementation of Decision 1297/2008/EC on a Programme for the Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics (MEETS); 
*[http://epp.eurostat.ec.europa.eu/portal/page/portal/grants/documents/Tab/Commission%20Decision%20_MEETS%202011.pdf Commission Decision] of 26 November 2010 on the annual work programme for 2011 for the implementation of Decision 1297/2008/EC on a Programme for the Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics (MEETS); 
*[http://epp.eurostat.ec.europa.eu/portal/page/portal/grants/documents/Tab/MEETS2010_EN_.pdf Commission Decision] of 30 November 2009 on the annual work programme for 2010 for the implementation of Decision 1297/2008/EC on a Programme for the Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics (MEETS); 
*[http://epp.eurostat.ec.europa.eu/portal/page/portal/grants/documents/Tab/DF_MEETS_2009_EN.pdf Commission Decision] of 24 April 2009 on the annual work programme for 2009 for the implementation of Decision 1297/2008/EC on a Programme for the Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics (MEETS).
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== MEETS – part of an overall strategy  ===

The ‘Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council on the production methods of EU statistics: a vision for the next decade’ provides a comprehensive and holistic approach to changing the way European statistics are produced. The objective is to increase the overall efficiency and effectiveness of the system and to ensure that new user demands can be met in the future. It describes the fundamental dilemma posed by increasing demands, resource constraints and the need to reduce burden on respondents. It also calls for close cooperation within the [[Glossary:European statistical system (ESS)|European statistical system (ESS)]] to achieve the necessary efficiency gains. 

The MEETS programme is the application of this vision to the area of business and trade statistics. ESSnets are a way to develop new projects where a few Member States interested in a specific domain actively collaborate on a common task and then disseminate the results to those not participating. This helps to harness synergies, to save costs and to share best practice while developing specific actions beneficial for the whole of the ESS. ESSnets have been set up for the main projects: 

*Consistency of concepts and methods for business and trade-related statistics; 
*Use of [[Glossary:Administrative_data|administrative data]], data warehouse and linking;  
*Methodology for modern business statistics

These projects are described in more detail below.    
The following figure shows the main links between the MEETS programme and the 'Vision':  

[[Image:Vision_and_MEETS.png|thumb|center|700px|700px]]  
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Main projects ===

'''Consistency of concepts and methods for business and trade-related statistics'''  

Business statistics are compiled in accordance with EU legislation, which has developed over the years and is not necessarily consistent in terms of concepts, scope, definitions, methodology, etc. The European Statistical System Networks (ESSnet) on Consistency analysed the possible lack of consistency of concepts and methods of business and trade related statistics. 

The ESSnet provided revised definitions of the statistical units enterprise, enterprise group, kind-of-activity and local kind-of-activity unit together with operational rules and a data model to enforce uniform implementation. The drafts are being fine-tuned by a Task Force on Statistical Units launched by Eurostat in 2013 and a study was done on the impact on the implementation of the revised definition of enterprises in business statistics. Further testing of the methodology was done in 2014. Further deliverables of the ESSnet were recommendations for a method to classify statistical units, applied in a comparable manner over all statistical domains, comparable breakdowns as well as a methodology for a frame population in business statistics. In addition, the ESSnet provided recommendations for a system of variables with consistency and standardised terminology and definitions for all statistical domains including methodological guidelines. 

The results will feed into the Framework Regulation Integrating Business and Trade Statistics (FRIBS), which will simplify and harmonise existing legislation. 

For more information see: 

*[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/consistency-0 Consistency on ESSnet portal] 
*[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/external-study-detail-evaluation-legal-acts External study on detail evaluation of the legal acts in the areas of statistics which were identified by member states as areas to revision]


'''EuroGroups register (EGR)'''  

The aim of the EuroGroups Register is to provide consistent and coordinated survey frames for producing quality statistics measuring globalisation; mainly for Foreign Affiliates Statistics (FATS) and Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). 

In 2009 the ESSnet on EGR methodology set up EGR version 1.0 and the organisational network for data exchange between Eurostat and ESS.

For more information see the [http://epp.eurostat.ec.europa.eu/statistics_explained/index.php/EuroGroups_register EGR article], as well as: 

*[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/egr-0 ESSnet - EGR]; 
*[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/profiling ESSnet - Profiling]; 
*[http://egr.istat.it/ EuroGroups Register] (dedicated website); 




'''Use of existing data in the statistical system'''  

The following MEETS projects under objective 3 dealt with data linking: 

*Data warehousing and data linking in statistical data production (ESSnet). The aim of the ESSnet was to define a functional model for a data warehouse to serve as the basis for assessing all issues raised in the ESSnet in a generic and standardised way. 
*Linking of microdata on international sourcing (ESSnet and individual grants). The measurement and analysis of international sourcing and its consequences for European economies was one of the key objectives of this project. Another important objective was to develop a methodology for measuring the global value chain (GVC). 
*Linking of microdata on international trade and business statistics. The main objective of the project was to develop indicators that combine variables from external trade and business statistics. 
*Linking of microdata on ICT usage (ESSnet). This ESSnet addressed the development of a microdata linking approach to analyse the impact of ICT on the economic performance of enterprises. It also investigated in more detail how to adjust national survey strategies to optimise the results of microdata linking in the future. 
*Methodology for modern business statistics - Memobust (ESSnet). The overall objective was to identify best practices and develop a common methodology and ESS guidelines for the efficient and integrated production of business statistics.

For more information see: 

*[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/data-warehouse ESSnet - Data Warehouse] (data warehousing and data linking on ESSnet portal); 
*[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/memobust ESSnet - Memobust] (methodology for modern business statistics).


'''Use of data already existing in the economy'''  

The following activities under objective 3 aimed to improve the use of existing data in the economy: 

*ESSnet on the use of administrative and accounts data for business statistics (ESSnet AdminData): its main objective was to investigate the possibilities of making wider use of administrative data for business statistics, to make good practices available to NSIs and to prepare some recommendations in this area. The ESSnet focused on the common problems arising from the use of different data sources for producing business statistics. 
*Individual grants to national statistical institutes for the use of administrative data: the aim was to support national statistical institutes in implementing more efficient ways of producing enterprise statistics and in improving the quality of statistical data. 
*Facilitation of data transfer from enterprises to national statistical institutes: grants were provided to national statistical institutes to introduce data collection systems that could simplify the reporting burden on businesses and to continue investigating the possibilities of using XBRL for statistical purposes.

For more information see: 

*[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/use-administrative-and-accounts-data-business-statistics ESSnet - AdminData] (use of administrative and accounts data for business statistics); 
*[http://essnet.admindata.eu/ Admin Data Wiktionary - The Use Of Administrative And Accounts Data For Business Statistics].


'''Modernisation of international trade statistics'''  

The following projects aimed to meet objective 4 of the MEETS programme: 

*Harmonising methods to improve quality in [[Glossary:Intra-EU|intra-EU]] trade statistics (procurement and individual grants). The aim was to improve the quality of Intrastat data by defining a list of quality items and precise quality requirements and by providing recommendations. 
*Better use of administrative data in Intrastat (individual grants). Support was provided for Member State actions to increase and improve the use of administrative data for the compilation of Intrastat data resulting in better data quality while reducing the response burden for enterprises. 
*Development of tools and methods for data exchange (former XT-NET) (procurement and individual grants). The objective of the project was to consolidate and further develop tools and standards in order to facilitate the supply of data on multinational enterprises and improve data quality to enable automated data exchange among Member States and Eurostat. 
*Improvement of data exchange systems in external trade statistics (procurement).
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Results  ===

The results of the MEETS programme were achieved by numerous deliverables of the participating National Statistical Institutes (NSIs). For a detailed overview please click [http://epp.eurostat.ec.europa.eu/statistics_explained/index.php?title=MEETS_programme_-_results&stable=0&redirect=no here]. 
</sesection>
</articlecontent>
