title: MEETS programme - introducing results
text:
<highlight title=false>
This article is a general introduction to an [[MEETS programme - results|online publication]] presenting the results of the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] programme 'Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics', or MEETS for short, which ran from 2009 to 2013 with the objectives of adjusting European business statistics to new needs and reducing the burden on [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]].
 
The two most important reasons for launching the MEETS programme were demands for cost reductions and the need to increase the relevance of European business statistics. In addition, the deepening of European integration in a number of areas created new statistical needs. 

Business statistics should be able to provide new indicators based on timely and high quality statistical information about structural changes in the European economy and its business sector. The MEETS programme dedicated resources to modernise the statistical production system and to satisfy emerging data needs. 
</highlight>

<articlecontent>
<sesection>
=== Four objectives - many results  ===

The MEETS programme achieved many important results within its four main objectives. 

(1) '''Review priorities and develop target sets of indicators for new areas''' was about identifying and deciding on which new areas to describe and on reviewing old requirements because of changing economic structures: 

*An external study identified inconsistencies, further analysed by projects under objective 2. 
*New indicators related to entrepreneurship like "culture for entrepreneurship", "access to finance" and "innovation and technology".

(2) '''Achieve a streamlined framework of business-related statistics''' was about integration of different areas of business statistics including coordination of legal acts and harmonisation of methodologies, classifications and business registers: 

*Identification of inconsistencies and their reasons accompanied by recommendations which included revised definitions and operational rules for statistical units, a method to classify statistical units in a comparable manner across statistical areas, comparable breakdowns, measures to harmonise business registers and recommendations for a system of variables with consistent and standardised terminology and definitions for all statistical areas. 
*The EuroGroups Register (EGR) with a yearly frame population 10 000 multinational enterprise groups (MNEs) providing consistent and coordinated survey frames for [[Glossary:Foreign_affiliates_statistics_(FATS)|Foreign Affiliates Statistics (FATS)]] and [[Glossary:Foreign_direct_investment_(FDI)|Foreign Direct Investments (FDI)]]. 
*Guidelines, documentation and training support for profiling of MNEs.

(3) '''Support the implementation of a more efficient way of producing enterprise and trade statistics''' was about more efficiently using existing data, increasing use of administrative data and exploiting harmonised accounting standards: 

*Guidelines, models and recommendations for building a statistical data warehouse. 
*Several data linking projects including production of statistics on international trade by enterprise characteristics based on linking trade data and business register information, measurement of global value chains through linking SBS ([[Glossary:Structural business statistics (SBS)|Structural Business Statistics]]) microdata and other business statistics and analysis of [[Glossary:Information and communication technology (ICT)|ICT]] (Information and Communication Technology) impact via linking data from [[Glossary:Information and communication technology (ICT)|ICT]] usage, innovation, SBS and business registers. 
*Methodological development concerning design, data collection and [[Glossary:Estimation|estimation]] and summarisation of business statistics methods in the coherent framework of an electronic handbook. 
*Recommendations for use of administrative data for business statistics including overview of national practices, estimation methods when using incomplete data sets, list of indicators for assessing quality of business statistics based on administrative data. 
*Handbook with assessment of feasibility of collecting high quality statistics from Internet and other big data sources.

(4) '''Modernise [[Glossary:Intrastat|Intrastat]]''' was about improving and simplifing the Intrastat system through work on harmonising methods, enhancing the use of administrative data and ICT improvements: 

*Guidelines and support for implementation of Intrastat and Extrastat legislation to promote harmonised practices and reduced asymmetries at detailed and aggregated level. 
*Enhanced use of administrative data, VAT (Value Added Tax) and VIES (Value Added Tax Information Exchange) data. 
*Development of tools and methods for data exchange within Intrastat.

More information about these and other results achieved can be found under each of the [http://epp.eurostat.ec.europa.eu/statistics_explained/index.php?title=MEETS_programme_-_results&stable=0&redirect=no four objectives]. 

There is also a detailed [[Media:MEETS_project_overview,_key_results_and_follow-up.docx|table of all MEETS actions and projects]] with their respective results (downloadable Word document).
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== How were the results achieved? ===

The MEETS programme was adopted by the [[Glossary:European_Parliament_(EP)|European Parliament]] and the [[Glossary:Council|Council]] in December 2008. The programme was closed down by the end of 2013. It provided financial resources of 42.5 million euros to support development within several areas in the ESS (European Statistical System). 


'''European statistical system networks (ESSnets)''' 

Grants to European statistical system networks (ESSnets) were the most common instrument for financing the work. The idea behind projects organised in ESSnets is to use results achieved by the cooperation of a few national statistical institutes to the benefit of the whole [[Glossary:European_statistical_system_(ESS)|European statistical system (ESS)]]. 

The aim is that sharing the results achieved will reduce the total costs needed for solving common problems. Therefore the transfer of results to non-participating countries is very important. Several ESSnets provided results within areas such as consistency of concepts and applied methods, EGR, microdata linking and data warehousing, use of [[Glossary:Administrative_data|administrative data]], design and implementation of business surveys and profiling of large and complex enterprises. 72 % of the ESS members participated in at least one MEETS financed ESSnet.

{| border="1" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="2" width="35%"
|-
|   
| '''ESS members participating''' 
| '''ESS members not participating''' 
| '''Total'''
|-
| '''At least one ESSnet''' 
| 23 
| 9 
| 32
|-
| '''At least one individual grant''' 
| 28 
| 4 
| 32
|}

'''Table 1''': Number of ESS Member States<ref>In total 32: the 28 EU Member States + Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland</ref> participating in at least one ESSnet or at least one individual grant 


'''Individual grants'''  

In parallel, a substantial number of individual grants were also used to support the work of ESS members within areas such as EGR, linking of microdata, use of administrative data, facilitation of data transfer from enterprises to NSIs, better use of administrative data, modernisation of [[Glossary:Intrastat|Intrastat]]. Almost 90 % of the ESS members participated in at least one of the individual grants of the MEETS programme. 


'''Procurements'''  

A number of procurement contracts were used to acquire services within areas such as evaluation of legal acts, development of combined external trade and business statistics, usage of Internet as a data source, a combined nomenclature aid for Intrastat declarants, tools and methods for data exchange in [[Glossary:Intrastat|Intrastat]], implementation and testing of profiling, and development of EU sampling schemes to produce EU [[Glossary:Aggregate|aggregates]]. 
</sesection>

title: MEETS programme - priorities and new sets of indicators
text:
This article is part of an [[MEETS programme - results|online publication]] presenting the results of the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] programme 'Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics', or MEETS for short, which ran from 2009 to 2013 with the objectives of adjusting European business statistics to new needs and reducing the burden on [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]]. The article focuses on the programme's actions 1.1 (Identifying areas of lesser importance) and 1.2. In a changing world, statistical needs have to be reviewed, because new needs emerge (action 1.2) and others become less important or even obsolete (action 1.1).  === Action 1.1: Identifying areas of lesser importance === To identify areas of lesser importance, two actions were undertaken, a study on legal acts and a so-called 'filter exercise'. '''Study on legal acts on business statistics identified for revision by Member States''' In 2009 an [http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/external-study-detail-evaluation-legal-acts external study] evaluating legal acts in areas of statistics identified for revision was subcontracted. The study revealed a considerable degree of consistency in concepts and definitions between closely related fields but also identified some stand-alone projects and a number of inconsistencies. The study was the basis for the work of the European Statistical System Networks (ESSnet) on Consistency of concepts and methods of business and trade related statistics [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/MEETS_programme_-_framework_for_business-related_statistics (objective 2)]. '''Filter exercise''' The filter exercise was carried out by Eurostat in close co-operation with National Statistical Institutes (NSIs). It identified which legal acts or parts of legal acts in the area of business statistics should be looked at more closely. For [[Glossary:Structural_business_statistics_(SBS)|Structural business statistics (SBS)]] a number of variables to be deleted were validated by the European Statistical Advisory Committee (ESAC). For [[Glossary:Short-term_statistics_(STS)|Short-term statistics]] (STS) the user consultation was carried out in the context of the rolling reviews in this area, consisting of a user survey, a survey among NSIs and a process review in [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]. The proposals for both data collections were referred back to the relevant working groups. In 2010 the European Statistical System Committee (ESSC) adopted a new strategy-driven approach where the areas of lesser importance in business and trade statistics were identified within the framework of the annual strategic review of Eurostat’s priorities. Consequently, this action was removed from the responsibilities of the MEETS programme. === Action 1.2: Developing new areas=== Globalisation and entrepreneurship are policy areas for which statistics are not yet full developed. In the area of globalisation two main projects were launched, while a third one focused on entrepreneurship. '''Statistics on enterprise groups''' The aim of the project “development of statistics on enterprise groups” was to identify useful and meaningful indicators based on enterprise groups as the observation unit and to test the feasibility of collecting these indicators. A study was carried out to identify useful and meaningful statistical indicators based on the [[Glossary:Small_and_medium-sized_enterprises_(SMEs)|small and medium sized enterprise]] group as [[Glossary:Observation_unit|observation unit]]. In addition, methodological work was launched in the priority area “intra-group trade” and “research, development and innovation”. The outcome of the project was a set of recommendations on how best to collect the data in the two areas concerned as well as a methodological basis for ESS data collection on enterprise groups via parent companies. An initial assessment of this methodological work will be integrated in the activities of the ESSnet on 'Profiling of Large and Complex Multinational Enterprise Groups' [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/MEETS_programme_-_framework_for_business-related_statistics (objective 2)]. '''Economic indicators on globalisation''' A study on globalisation indicators availability, data collection and [[Glossary:Data_dissemination|dissemination]] of the information was launched to analyse the availability and calculation methods of indicators proposed in the [[Glossary:Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development_(OECD)|OECD]] [http://www.oecd.org/science/sci-tech/oecdhandbookoneconomicglobalisationindicators.htm Handbook on Economic Globalisation Indicators].  Further methodological work and the organisation of the pilot data collection to test the feasibility of economic globalisation indicators took place within the framework of the ESSnet on Measuring Global Value Chains [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/MEETS_programme_-_towards_more_efficient_enterprise_and_trade_statistics&stable=0&redirect=no (objective 3)].
'''Entrepreneurship''' To underpin policies related to entrepreneurship, indicators such as [[Business_demography_statistics|business demography]] and employer business demography have been developed in cooperation with the OECD in the frame of the joint [http://www.oecd.org/industry/business-stats/theentrepreneurshipindicatorsprogrammeeipbackgroundinformation.htm Entrepreneurship Indicators Programme] (EIP). Two groups of determinants of entrepreneurial activity recognised within the EIP, knowledge creation and diffusion, and [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-statistical-books/-/KS-31-12-758 culture and capabilities] have been investigated during workshops. External finance is essential for all [[Glossary:Enterprises_-_SBS|enterprises]] to increase [[Glossary:Productivity|productivity]], [[Glossary:Innovation|innovation]], conquer new markets or, more generally, to create employment and wealth; easy access to finance is especially crucial, however, for [[Glossary:Small_and_medium-sized_enterprises_(SMEs)|small and medium-sized enterprises]] (SMEs). A survey on [[Archive:Access to finance statistics|access to finance]] in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union]] (EU) coordinated by Eurostat allowed for the first time an analysis of the situation based on statistical data of a sound quality. Provisions for mandatory data collection on employer and high-growth enterprises within the ESS have been laid down and will come into force in the first half of 2014. === See also === *[[MEETS programme - results ]] (online publication) === Dedicated section === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=european_business}} Structural business statistics] === Publications === *[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/external-study-detail-evaluation-legal-acts External study on detail evaluation of the legal acts] === Legislation=== *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52009DC0404:EN:NOT|title=Communication COM(2009) 404}} on the production method of EU statistics: a vision for the next decade *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008D1297:EN:NOT|title=Decision 1297/2008/EC}} of 16 December 2008 on a Programme for the Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics (MEETS) *[[Media:MEETS_project_overview,_key_results_and_follow-up.docx|MEETS project overview, key results and follow-up]] (downloadable Word document) *[http://epp.eurostat.ec.europa.eu/portal/page/portal/ess_eurostat/statistical_programmes Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics (MEETS)] *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52010DC0813:EN:NOT|title=Report COM(2010) 813}} on the implementation of Decision 1297/2008/EC of 16 December 2008 on a Programme for the Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics (MEETS) === External links === *[http://www.cros-portal.eu Cros portal] *[http://egr.istat.it/ EuroGroups Register website] {{Unit|topic=X_Dissemination}}  [[Category:Industry, trade, and services|MEETS programme - priorities and new sets of indicators]] [[Category:Structural business statistics (SBS)|MEETS programme - priorities and new sets of indicators]] [[Category:Background_article|MEETS programme - priorities and new sets of indicators]]

title: MEETS programme - towards more efficient enterprise and trade statistics
text:
<highlight title=false>
This article is part of an [[MEETS programme - results|online publication]] presenting the results of the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] programme 'Modernisation of European Enterprise and Trade Statistics', or MEETS for short, which ran from 2009 to 2013 with the objectives of adjusting European business statistics to new needs and reducing the burden on [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]].
 
It presents the results for its '''third objective''', increased integration of data collection and [[Glossary:Data_processing|data processing]]. This objective was to allow for a more effective use of already existing statistical information and, additionally, to encourage the increased use of administrative data sources, either through integrating all collected data into a single system or through using microdata linking techniques. More specific issues treated under this objective include ensuring the quality of data collected from different sources, standard [[Glossary:Estimation|estimation]] techniques and assessing the differences between accounting concepts and statistical variables. 
</highlight>

<articlecontent>
<sesection>
=== Use of existing data===

'''''Action 3.1: Making better use of data that already exist in the statistical system including the possibility of estimates'''''

New or current statistical information required could be obtained by linking together existing types of business statistics without the need to increase the burden on enterprises. The aim of action 3.1 is to exploit the potential of business statistics in a more efficient way.

'''Data warehousing and data linking in statistical data production'''  

The work on “data warehousing and data linking in the production of business statistics” was carried out by an European Statistical System Networks (ESSnet) set up in 2010. The ESSnet first established an overview of the state of the art and future needs in integrated business data systems of the ESS members. On this basis it established a work programme focussing on the creation of a set of guidelines, models and recommendations for building a statistical data warehouse. The results include a generic architecture detailing its processes and metadata and providing some insight into methodological aspects. The impressive set of deliverables was presented in a handbook guiding the users during the entire process of setting up a statistical data warehouse. As the development of integrated systems requires a long period of time and to enable the ESS members to continue using each other’s experience after the end of the MEETS programme, Eurostat and part of the ESSnet have created the centre of competence for data warehousing.

[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/data-warehouse Data warehousing and data linking on CROS portal]

'''Deliverables on CROS portal:'''

[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/data-warehouse-sga1 Project period 1 (4/10/2010 – 3/10/2011)]

[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/data-warehouse-sga2 Project period 2 (4/10/2011 – 3/10/2013]

'''Further links:'''
 
[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/dwh-sga2-wp4-45-overall-handbook-how-set-s-dwhv04 Overall handbook on how to set up a statistical data warehouse]

[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/final-report-sga2 Final report]

'''Methodology for modern business statistics'''  

The ESSnet on “Methodology for modern business statistics”(MEMOBUST) set up in 2010 provided methodological guidance to support the modernisation and integration of business statistics in the ESS. In addition to methodological developments concerning specific production steps (design, data collection and estimation), the project summarised the body of business statistics methods in the coherent framework of an electronic handbook. The project has also reused work done by previous projects.
The handbook will serve in the future as a reference work both for subject matter statisticians and methodologists. It can also be used as basis for training. A possible follow-up by a centre of competence is under consideration.

[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/memobust Methodology for modern business statistics on CROS portal]

'''Deliverables on CROS portal:'''

[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/handbook-methodology-modern-business-statistics Handbook on Methodology for Modern Business Statistics]

'''Further links:'''

Background material:   
[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/handbook-design-and-implementation-business-surveys-1998 Handbook on design and implementation of business surveys (1998)]

'''Linking of microdata on international sourcing (global value chains)''' 

The ESSnet on Measuring Global Value Chains (ESSnet GVC) consisted of 6 work packages:

1. [http://cros-portal.eu/content/d11-final-draft-august-2013-main-indicators-framework Development of indicators on economic globalisation]

In this work package three sets of indicators are being developed: [http://cros-portal.eu/content/d12-final-draft-august-2013-main-indicators-fact-sheets main indicators] (country level), [http://cros-portal.eu/content/d13-final-draft-august-2013-supplemental-indicators-fact-sheets supplemental indicators] (breakdowns of the main indicators available in the ESS) and experimental indicators (breakdowns not available in the ESS but resulting from MicroData Linking – not yet published).

2. Survey on global value chains/international sourcing

This work updated the previous survey on international sourcing and its guidelines and gave methodological support to the countries carrying out the survey. This resulted in a [http://cros-portal.eu/content/d21a-isgvc-questionnaire-final-version new survey] and [http://cros-portal.eu/content/d21c-isgvc-definitions-05mar2012 accompanying definitions and guidelines].

3. Microdata linking (MDL)

This project developed a methodology and computer code for linking data from structural business statistics, foreign affiliate statistics, international trade, research and development (R & D) and global value chains/international sourcing and produced input for the experimental indicators mentioned above.

4. Linking of inward and outward foreign affiliate statistics (FATS) with business registers
 
The goal of this project was to match inward [[Glossary:Foreign_affiliates_statistics_(FATS)|FATS]] of countries with the corresponding outward FATS data. Possible reasons for non-matching were analysed and suggestions for improvements were made. [http://www.google.com/url?sa=t&rct=j&q=&esrc=s&frm=1&source=web&cd=1&cad=rja&ved=0CCYQFjAA&url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.dst.dk%2F~%2Fmedia%2FKontorer%2F11-Erhvervslivets-udvikling%2Fgvc-workshop%2FMc%2520Mahon-Mirroring%2520foreign%2520affiliate%2520statistics_27%252011%25202013-pdf.pdf&ei=88IEU6XKAYS6ygOe9IKgAw&usg=AFQjCNGajnTqztNdAnBccjFP4szeRDD8Dg&sig2=76k63w1Q3z8PB0rYpEB4xQ The results (pdf)] were presented in the Copenhagen workshop mentioned below.

5. Dissemination of the results of the work packages

Apart from the reports mentioned above, an [[Archive:International sourcing of business functions|article on International sourcing of business functions]] has been published. In 2014 three or four more articles will be published that can be accessed from the  [http://cros-portal.eu/content/global-value-chains-0 CROS-portal on Global Value Chains] where also a [http://cros-portal.eu/content/global-value-chains-0 complete list of deliverables] can be found.

6. Co-ordination, administration and organisation of meetings/seminars/workshops

This included not only the organisation of the taskforces and meetings of the steering groups but also the organisation of and participation in several workshops. This included the presentation of two articles for the ISI World Statistics congress 2013 in Hong Kong on [http://2013.isiproceedings.org/Files/STS024-P5-S.pdf Measuring International Organisation of Enterprises and Sourcing of Business Functions (pdf)] and [http://2013.isiproceedings.org/Files/STS024-P1-S.pdf A measurement framework and a narrative on global value chains and economic globalization (pdf).] Among the workshops organised were [http://www.google.be/url?sa=t&rct=j&q=&esrc=s&source=web&cd=5&cad=rja&ved=0CFYQFjAE&url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.dst.dk%2F~%2Fmedia%2FKontorer%2F11-Erhvervslivets-udvikling%2Fgvc-workshop%2FSummary-of-Europe-in-a-Globalised-World-workshop.pdf&ei=Pr0EU8vRLeTMygP6qIJo&usg=AFQjCNGZj5gGCClRd6Qo8b3cNm8TOGFddg&sig2=6JjmZf8LBLBV15VFspTquA&bvm=bv.61535280,d.bGQ Europe in a globalised world (pdf)] (Copenhagen - December 2013), [http://www.cso.ie/en/media/csoie/newsevents/documents/eurostatseminar/PanelQs.pptx Global Value Chains and economic globalisation] (Dublin – April 2013) and a [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/portal/page/portal/pgp_ess/news/ess_news_detail?id=129439305&pg_id=2737&cc=ESTAT_EUROSTAT Eurostat workshop on Global Value Chains] (Luxembourg October 2012).

Another achievement of the ESSnet GVC has been the publication of a report by Dr. Timothy Sturgeon of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology titled [http://unstats.un.org/unsd/trade/events/2014/mexico/documents/session1/Eurostat-GVCs-and-Economic-Globalization-Sturgeon-report-04-2013.pdf Global Value Chains and Economic Globalization - Towards a New Measurement Framework (pdf)] which makes an assessment of the data-gaps related to Global Value Chains and International Sourcing and provides a vision for improving the statistics on this subject.

'''Linking microdata on external trade and business statistics''' 

In 2009 the project on data linking of trade and business statistics used an external study to develop the methodological framework producing statistical indicators on external trade by business characteristics, and pilot data collection tested its feasibility. In 2013 ESS members developed and compiled an extended set of indicators based on trade and business microdata. The new indicators will be included in the TEC (trade by enterprise characteristics) database. A compilers’ guide for the production of statistics on international trade by enterprise characteristics based on the linkage between trade data and business register information is available. In addition, a first set of trade by enterprise characteristics indicators for services was developed.

'''Linking of microdata on ICT usage'''  

:'''ESSnet on linking of microdata on ICT usage (ESSLimit, 2010-2012)''' 

The methodology for linking of microdata on [[Glossary:ICT|ICT]] usage builds on the [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] ICT Impacts Project (also known as the Feasibility Study), carried out in 2006-2008. The Feasibility Study developed a Distributed Microdata (DMD) approach and tested it on linked data (with a main focus on the ICT usage) provided by 13 National Statistical Offices for the year 2001-2005. 
The [http://cros-portal.eu/content/esslimit-1 ESSnet on Linking of Microdata on ICT usage, ESSLimit] (2010-2012) was launched with the objective to address the main methodological issues revealed by the Feasibility Study and to explore the use and impact of ICT in the business sector. The Project involved 15 National statistical offices and extended the previous project by both including more recent years and adding new data dimensions (mainly from the Community Innovation Survey) to the linked data. The main achievements of the Project are:

*setting up an infrastructure for DMD analysis;
*harmonisation of the national microdata;
*generation of linked microdata at national level;
*production of metadata at industry level across multiple countries and time periods for data warehousing purposes;
*analysis of topics pertaining to seven priority areas of [http://ec.europa.eu/digital-agenda Digital Agenda for Europe];
*a study on survey methodologies to improve quality of linked [[Glossary:Dataset|datasets]] and a protocol on access to partially confidential data.

The approach developed permits the production of indicators comparable across countries, and auditable back to source data. Moreover, it allows the generation of data which can be used for analysis of performance differences in ICT use across countries and industries. It prepared the grounds for making the micro-aggregated dataset (which is an output of the data linking process and the analysis of the linked datasets) available for research purposes via the safe centre facilities of Eurostat. Within the project, a cross-country dataset was built from aggregation of comparable enterprise-level data at a relatively disaggregated industry level across multiple countries and time periods. A public version of this dataset can be downloaded from the link below.

The work on survey strategies was used as an input for the coordination and harmonisation of business statistics within the Framework Integrating Business Statistics (FRIBS).

[http://cros-portal.eu/content/esslimit-1 ESSLimit on CROS portal]

'''Deliverables on CROS portal:''' 	

[http://cros-portal.eu/content/1-final-report Final Report]

[http://cros-portal.eu/content/2-annexes-data-description Annexes (data description)]

[http://cros-portal.eu/content/micro-aggregated-data Micro-aggregated data]

:'''ESSnet on linking of microdata to analyse ICT impact (ESSLait, 2013)''' 

The [http://www.cros-portal.eu/projectdetail/1409 ESSnet on linking of microdata to analyse ICT impact (ESSLai)] built on its predecessor, the ESSLimit Project (2010-2012), and had a general scope i) to apply and improve the methodology for data linking and ICT impact analysis that was developed in the ESSLimit Project and the ICT Feasibility Study (see below), and ii) to generate micro-aggregate datasets for future use. The earlier projects demonstrated that a wealth of information can be extracted by microdata linking, through which information already available can be analysed in completely new ways. This final phase of ICT impacts work fits well with the goals of the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/european-statistical-system/statistical_programmes MEETS programme] (i.e. efficient production of statistics and secondary use of data) while the analytical work relates to the themes of the [http://ec.europa.eu/digital-agenda/ Digital Agenda for Europe].

The project involved partners from 14 European statistical offices, supported by academic advisors. It used the general infrastructure developed by its predecessor projects to link and coordinate the data management in the European statistical offices. This infrastructure enables a harmonised approach to analysing the impact of ICT usage by firms through the Distributed Microdata (DMD) approach. A common protocol is used to extract micro-aggregated information from each country’s firm-level datasets. This involves the linking of firm-level datasets by participating statistical offices, and the subsequent application of a common software tailored to extract the indicators and statistical data (means, distributions, etc) from the data. This approach guarantees the cross-country comparability of results to the highest possible degree while still allowing information on underlying distributions and correlations to be obtained without impairing national rules of confidentiality. Moreover, the infrastructure allows external researchers to run their own tests on data: harmonised microdata onsite at national statistical offices enable the easy implementation of additional analyses through the writing of analytical add-on modules for the code.

[http://cros-portal.eu/projectdetail/1409 ESSLait on CROS portal]

'''Deliverables on CROS portal:'''

[http://cros-portal.eu/content/final-report-5 Final report]

[http://cros-portal.eu/content/mmd-and-research-infrastructure Description of the micro moments database and research infrastructure]

[http://cros-portal.eu/content/metadata-repository Description of the metadata repository]

[http://cros-portal.eu/content/micro-aggregated-data-0 Micro-aggregated data]
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Making better use of data that already exist in the economy (Action 3.2)  ===

Statistical information is sometimes collected twice: first for administrative purposes, such as taxes, and then for statistical purposes, in surveys. Two projects were launched to avoid such a double burden.

'''Use of administrative data'''  

The ESSnet on the use of administrative and accounts data, which was launched in 2009, investigated the practical issues related to the use of these data for business statistics purposes. The main results achieved concern the preparation of the overview of national practices on the use of administrative data, the description of the methods used for estimation of incomplete data sets when using administrative data for short-term statistics, and the production of a list of indicators for assessing the quality of business statistics based on administrative data. In addition, the ESSnet provided information on links from statistical characteristics to the International Accounting Standards (IAS)/International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) and EU accounting directives.

[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/use-administrative-and-accounts-data-business-statistics Use of administrative data on CROS portal]

'''Deliverables on CROS portal:'''

*[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/admindata-sga-1 Project period 1 (16/09/2009 to 31/03/2010)]
*[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/admindata-sga-2 Project period 2 (28/04/2010 to 30/06/2011)]
*[http://www.cros-portal.eu/content/admindata-sga-3 Project period 3 (01/07/2011 to 31/12/2013)]

'''Using the internet as a data source for official statistics''' 

ICT and the internet are generating huge amounts of data with the potential to be exploited as statistical data. In 2013, Eurostat launched a project to assess the feasibility of employing modern methodologies and indicators for collecting high quality statistics from non-traditional sources such as the Internet or other big data sources. The experiences were summarised in a preliminary handbook which can be applied by NSIs. Big data repositories were also identified and their potential for official statistics analysed. This included negotiations with big data owners on conditions for data usage by NSIs and development of criteria for assessing required quality aspects. The results of the project will contribute to a broader initiative from the ESS on “Big Data and Official Statistics” .
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Better data extraction, transmission and treatment tools  ===

'''''Action 3.3: Developing tools for the more efficient extraction, transmission and treatment of data''''' 

New ICT offer opportunities for simplified reporting. This may be achieved by using company accounts and other financial reports drawn up according to international accounting standards, and appropriate technical standards for such reports. 

'''Facilitation of data transfer from enterprises to NSIs, Accountancy data'''  

Grants aided national statistical institutes to implement online data collection and electronic questionnaires, and conversion tables between GAAP ('generally accepted accounting principles') and statistical characteristics and XBRL (Extensible business reporting language). 

'''Use of customs data (Extrastat)'''  

'''Making better use of customs data for compiling statistics on the trading of goods with non-member countries (Extrastat)'''  

The project “Making better use of customs data in external trade statistics (Extrastat)” helped ESS members to adapt their data collections systems to the new customs systems of the Modernised Customs Code.
</sesection>
</articlecontent>

title: Living conditions statistics at regional level
text:
Eurostat regional yearbook; 2026 edition; flagship publication; EU; regional statistics; NUTS; living conditions; people at risk of poverty or social exclusion; focus on housing; criminal justice; at-risk-of-poverty rate; severe material and social deprivation; households with very low work intensity; housing cost; arrears on mortgage, rent, utility bills or hire purchase; burglaries; intentional homicide [[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH05_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|380px|''Source:'' Eurostat]] Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 This article forms part of the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026]'', an annual [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications flagship publication]. It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the [[Glossary:EU|EU]], [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate]] countries. A [[Regional_yearbook_introduction#A_short_reading_guide|short reading guide]] is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps. In 2025, the French outermost region of Guyane was the only region across the EU to report more than half (54.8%) of its population at risk of poverty or social exclusion; the next highest shares were recorded in the southern Italian regions of Calabria (45.3%) and Sicilia (43.7%). In 2024, there was a high incidence of police-recorded burglaries of private residential properties in the eastern Belgian region of Prov. Liège and the central Danish region of Midtjylland.

By global standards, most people living in the European Union (EU) enjoy relatively high standards of living. This reflects the EU’s relatively high levels of income and wealth, as well as its well-established network of [[Glossary:Social protection|social protection]] systems that provide a safety net for those in need. Nevertheless, 92.7 million people in the EU – or 20.9% of the population – were [[Glossary:At risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion]] in 2025. Across the NUTS level 2 regions of the EU, the French outermost region of Guyane recorded the highest rate, at 54.8%. It was the only region in the EU where more than half of the population faced such a risk (see the infographic above for more information). Sociodemographic characteristics such as age, educational attainment, sex and country of birth / citizenship can influence an individual’s living conditions. Wider societal developments – including globalisation – together with major shocks such as the global financial and economic crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, the impact of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, the cost-of-living crisis or recent developments in Iran and the wider region – can also have a significant impact. In some cases, these events can rapidly reverse more gradual, long-term reductions in inequality. Since late 2021, living conditions across the EU have been shaped by sustained pressures on household budgets, with the cost of living remaining a key concern for many families. Housing affordability has deteriorated as a result of rising rents, house prices and mortgage costs. At the same time, volatile energy prices have continued to put a strain on household finances, reinforcing broader affordability challenges. This chapter of the ''Eurostat regional yearbook'' includes a special focus on housing (see below). ===People at risk of poverty or social exclusion=== Absolute poverty is a lack of basic human needs, for example, food, shelter, water, sanitation facilities, health or education; in other words, a situation where a [[Glossary:Household - social statistics|household’s]] income is insufficient to afford the basic necessities of life. By contrast, relative poverty concerns a situation where a household’s income is below a certain percentage of the [[Glossary:Median|median]] household income of the country where they live.
'''More about the data: at risk of poverty or social exclusion''' The indicator for people at risk of poverty or social exclusion is based on measures of relative poverty, severe material and social deprivation, and quasi-joblessness. The number/rate of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion combines these criteria to cover people who are in at least 1 of the following situations: *[[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|at risk of poverty]] – people with an [[Glossary:Equivalised disposable income|equivalised disposable income]] (after [[Glossary:Social transfers|social transfers]]) below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold, which is set at 60% of the national median equivalised disposable income *facing [[Glossary:Severe_material_and_social_deprivation_rate_(SMSD)|severe material and social deprivation]] – people unable to afford at least 7 out of 13 deprivation items (6 related to the individual and 7 related to the household) that are considered desirable, or even necessary, to lead an adequate quality of life *[[Glossary:Persons living in households with very low work intensity|living in a household with very low work intensity]] – where adults aged 18 to 64 years (excluding students aged 18 to 24 years and retired people under the age of 65 years) worked for 20% or less of their combined potential working time during the previous 12 months. For [[Glossary:EU-SILC|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]]: *data for the Finnish regions of Länsi-Suomi and Åland are aggregated (the same value is shown for both regions) *due to changes in regional boundaries, data are only available for the reference years of 2024 and 2025 (no earlier years) for Utrecht, Zuid-Holland (both the Netherlands), Centro, Grande Lisboa, Península de Setúbal, Alentejo and Oeste e Vale do Tejo (all Portugal) *there is no information for Mayotte in France *an earlier reference year is sometimes used for individual regions/countries (see specific footnotes under each map/figure for more information).
On 4 March 2021, the European Commission presented its vision for a stronger social Europe, aiming to reinforce education, skills and employment policies as part of a fair and inclusive recovery from the COVID-19 crisis. The initiative also sought to reduce inequalities, combat discrimination and support vulnerable groups at risk of poverty and social exclusion. The [https://op.europa.eu/webpub/empl/european-pillar-of-social-rights/en/ European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan] sets out a range of policy commitments and establishes [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/european-pillar-social-rights-building-fairer-and-more-inclusive-european-union/european-pillar-social-rights-action-plan_en 3 headline EU targets to track progress]; 1 of these targets seeks to reduce the number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion by at least 15 million people by 2030 (compared with 2019 levels), including at least 5 million children. As noted above, there were 92.7 million people in the EU facing the risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025. This social vulnerability is spread across the overlapping risks of poverty, severe material and social deprivation, and very low work intensity; '''Figure 1''' provides more information on the layered patterns of social disadvantage. Among these, 72.4 million were at risk of poverty: *46.9 million people, were at risk of poverty but not severely materially and socially deprived and not living in a household with very low work intensity *11.6 million people were at risk of poverty and were living in a household with very low work intensity, but were not severely materially and socially deprived *8.1 million were at risk of poverty and were severely materially and socially deprived, but were not living in a household with very low work intensity *5.7 million people faced all 3 of these risks simultaneously. Among those not at risk of poverty, 11.5 million people across the EU in 2025 were severely materially and socially deprived, 7.3 million were living in a household with very low work intensity, and 1.5 million experienced both these forms of deprivation and very low work intensity concurrently.

===People at risk of poverty=== In 2025, 72.4 million people in the EU were at risk of poverty (after social transfers), representing 16.3% of the population, some 0.1 percentage points higher than in 2024. Some of the highest regional rates for people at risk of poverty were concentrated in southern, eastern and Baltic EU countries. By contrast, some of the lowest rates were recorded in a cluster of regions stretching from central/northern Italy through Austria and southern Germany, into Hungary, Czechia and Poland. Another cluster of regions with low rates was found in northern Belgium and the Netherlands, while several capital regions also recorded relatively low rates.
'''More about the data: at-risk-of-poverty rate''' The at-risk-of-poverty rate (after social transfers) is 1 of 3 criteria used to identify people who are at risk of poverty or social exclusion. It identifies the proportion of the population who live in a household with an annual equivalised disposable income that is below 60% of the national median. While the threshold is the same for all EU countries in percentage terms (60%), it varies in monetary terms as median incomes differ – sometimes considerably – between countries.
'''Map 2''' shows the at-risk-of-poverty rate for NUTS level 2 regions. In 2025, the regional distribution of this rate was somewhat skewed: there were 108 regions that recorded a rate above the EU average of 16.3%, while the remaining 135 regions had lower than average rates. '''''In 2025, the French outermost region of Guyane reported the highest at-risk-of-poverty rate''''' The French outermost regions of Guyane (50.7%) and La Réunion (36.4%), the autonomous Spanish regions of Ciudad de Melilla (39.3%) and Ciudad de Ceuta (37.0%), and the southern Italian regions of Sicilia (38.4%) and Campania (35.6%) recorded the highest at-risk-of-poverty rates among NUTS level 2 regions. These were the only regions across the EU where more than a third of the population was at risk of poverty in 2025. An additional 22 regions had at-risk-of-poverty rates covering between a quarter and a third of their populations. Together, these 28 regions with the highest at risk of poverty rates are shown in the darkest shades in '''Map 2'''. '''''… while the lowest rates were recorded in the Slovak and Romanian capital regions of Bratislavský kraj and Bucureşti-Ilfov''''' By contrast, at the lower end of the distribution, there were 20 NUTS level 2 regions where the at-risk-of-poverty rate was below 9.0% in 2025 (as shown by the lightest shade). Many of these regions were predominantly urban regions (including capitals) and/or regions characterised by relatively low unemployment rates and relatively high standards of living. This group of 20 regions included: *4 regions each from northern Belgium, Hungary (including Budapest) and northern Italy *3 regions from Poland (including Warszawski stołeczny) *2 regions from Czechia (including Praha) *the capital regions of Bratislavský kraj and Bucureşti-Ilfov *Burgenland from eastern Austria. These 20 regions with a relatively low risk of poverty in 2025 included 5 capital regions, all from eastern EU countries: Bratislavský kraj in Slovakia (1.4%), Bucureşti-Ilfov in Romania (2.7%), Warszawski stołeczny in Poland (6.1%), Praha in Czechia (6.8%) and Budapest in Hungary (7.2%). The next lowest shares among capital regions were observed in the Irish and Finnish capital regions of Eastern and Midland (10.4%) and Helsinki-Uusimaa (10.8%). While Bratislavský kraj and Bucureşti-Ilfov had, by far, the lowest at-risk-of-poverty rates in 2025, rates below 6.0% were also recorded in: *the northern Italian regions of Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen and Valle d’Aosta/Vallée d’Aoste *the northern Belgian regions of Prov. West-Vlaanderen and Prov. Vlaams-Brabant.

===Severe material and social deprivation, and economic strain=== The severe material and social deprivation rate measures the share of people whose living conditions are severely constrained by an enforced lack of items that are necessary and desirable to lead an adequate life. It reflects enforced inability to afford basic goods, services or social activities – such as a meal with protein, adequate heating, or spending social time with family and/or friends. The EU’s severe material and social deprivation rate rose during the cost-of-living crisis, peaking at 6.8% in 2023. A year later, it fell 0.4 percentage points, returning to its pre-crisis level, with an additional modest reduction the following year (down 0.1 points). In 2025, there were 26.9 million people across the EU that were facing severe material and social deprivation; this was equivalent to 6.3% of the total population.
'''More about the data: severe material and social deprivation''' The severe material and social deprivation rate is 1 of 3 criteria used to identify people at risk of poverty or social exclusion. It is defined as the share of people who are unable to afford at least 7 out of 13 items (6 related to the individual and 7 related to the household) that are considered desirable – or even necessary – to lead an adequate quality of life. '''List of items related to the individual''' *having an internet connection *replacing worn-out clothes by some new ones *having 2 pairs of properly fitting shoes (including a pair of all-weather shoes) *spending a small amount of money each week on themselves *having regular leisure activities *getting together with friends/family for a drink/meal at least once a month '''List of items related to the household''' *capacity to face unexpected expenses *capacity to afford paying for 1-week annual holiday away from home *capacity to being confronted with payment arrears (on mortgage or rental payments, utility bills, hire purchase instalments or other loan payments) *capacity to afford a meal with meat, chicken, fish (or vegetarian equivalent) every 2nd day *ability to keep home adequately warm *have access to a car/van for personal use *replacing worn-out furniture
'''''In 2025, the highest severe material and social deprivation rates were recorded in the south-eastern corner of the EU: in Sud-Est (Romania), more than a quarter of the population faced such deprivation''''' '''Map 3''' shows the regional distribution of severe material and social deprivation rates. In 2025, the highest rates among NUTS level 2 regions were concentrated in Greece, Romania, Bulgaria, the outermost regions of France and Hungary. The lowest rates were observed in northern and central Italy, Slovenia, Austria, Croatia, the Netherlands, Poland and northern Sweden. Of the 243 regions for which data are available, 155 had rates below the EU average of 6.3%, 3 had the same rate, and 85 recorded higher than average rates. In 2025, Sud-Est in Romania (27.2%) recorded the highest severe material and social deprivation rate. It was the only EU region where more than a quarter of the population was affected by the enforced inability to afford basic goods, services or social activities. There were 3 other regions in the EU where more than a fifth of the population faced severe material and social deprivation: *Ionia Nisia in Greece (23.3%) *Yugoiztochen in Bulgaria (21.1%) *Guyane in France (also 21.1%). At the other end of the distribution, every region of Czechia, Denmark, Croatia, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Slovenia, Finland and Sweden had a severe material and social deprivation rate that was below the EU average of 6.3% in 2025; this was also the case in Estonia, Cyprus, Latvia, Luxembourg and Malta. In 2025, there were 10 regions in the EU with severe material and social deprivation rates of less than 1.0%: *the Italian regions of Provincia Autonoma di Trento (which had the lowest rate in the EU), Molise and Valle d’Aosta/Vallée d’Aoste *the Dutch regions of Zeeland, Drenthe and Groningen *the Austrian regions of Salzburg and Tirol *the Polish regions of Opolskie and Małopolskie.

By contrast, Finland recorded the smallest degree of inter-regional variation in severe material and social deprivation rates in 2025. There were also relatively small differences between the regions in Denmark (where the highest rate was 1.6 times as high as the lowest) and in Ireland (1.7 times as high).

===People living in a household with very low work intensity=== In 2025, there were 26.1 million people (aged 0 to 64) across the EU living in a household with very low work intensity, representing 7.9% of this subpopulation.
'''More about the data: very low work intensity''' The share of people (aged 0 to 64) living in a household with very low work intensity is 1 of the 3 criteria used to identify people at risk of poverty or social exclusion. Working-age adults with low work intensity are defined as people aged 18 to 64 (excluding students aged 18 to 24 and retired people under the age of 65) who worked for 20% or less of their combined potential working time during the previous 12 months. Households composed only of children, of students younger than 25 and/or of people aged 65 or more are excluded from the calculation of this indicator.
'''''In 2025, 7.9% of the EU population was living in a household with very low work intensity''''' Out of the 243 NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available, 98 recorded shares of people living in households with very low work intensity above the EU average (7.9%). By contrast, 139 regions reported lower than average shares, while a further 6 regions had the same share as the EU average. '''Map 4''' highlights the EU regions with a relatively high share of people living in households with very low work intensity (as shown by the darkest shade). In 2025, there were 23 regions with shares of at least 13.0%, distributed across several EU countries: *6 regions from Italy, located in the south or on islands *5 regions from France, the northern region of Nord-Pas de Calais and 4 outermost regions (no data for Mayotte) *4 predominantly urban regions from Germany, including the capital region of Berlin *3 regions from Belgium, including the capital Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest *2 autonomous regions from Spain, Ciudad de Ceuta and Ciudad de Melilla *the Lithuanian region of Vidurio ir vakarų Lietuvos regionas *the north-western Bulgarian region of Severozapaden *the capital region of Austria, Wien. In 2025, the highest proportion of people living in a household with very low work intensity was recorded in the French outermost region of Guyane (29.5%). Along with the Spanish autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla, as well as 2 other French outermost regions, there were 3 additional regions in the EU where more than a fifth of the population lived in such households: *Bremen in northern Germany (22.7%) *the Belgian capital Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest (22.1%) *Campania in southern Italy (20.3%). By contrast, there were 27 regions in the EU where fewer than 3.5% of people were living in a household with very low work intensity in 2025 (as shown by the lightest shade in '''Map 4'''). These regions were distributed across 12 different EU countries. *The EU countries with the highest numbers of regions included Italy (4 northern regions), Hungary (4 western regions), Poland (4 regions) and Slovakia (3 western regions). *Overall, this group was geographically concentrated in eastern EU countries, although it also included several regions in the south and west: **in addition to the 4 northern Italian regions, it also included Ionia Nisia (Greece) and Algarve (Portugal) **as well as Tirol and Salzburg (both Austria) and Zeeland (the Netherlands). *This group of 27 regions also included 6 capital regions, all located in eastern EU countries: Bratislavský kraj (0.6%), Bucureşti-Ilfov (0.9%), Grad Zagreb (1.6%), Warszawski stołeczny (1.9%), Praha (2.7%) and Budapest (2.8%). *The lowest regional share was recorded in Valle d’Aosta/Vallée d’Aoste (0.0%) in northern Italy.

===Focus on housing=== Housing affordability has become an increasingly important dimension of economic strain, as housing costs have risen rapidly in many parts of the EU. Higher rents, rising mortgage interest rates and increasing house prices have reduced the disposable income available for other essential expenditures, particularly among low-income households, young people and tenants living in predominantly urban regions. In some regions, a shortage of housing supply has further intensified affordability pressures, contributing to wider inequalities in living conditions and financial security.
'''More about the data: housing cost overburden rate''' The [[Glossary:Housing_cost_overburden_rate|housing cost overburden rate]] is defined as the share of the population living in a household where housing costs represent more than 40% of total disposable household income (both the numerator and denominator are expressed net of housing allowances). Housing costs include the total amount of money regularly spent to maintain a household, not limited to rent or mortgage payments. They comprise essential expenses such as utilities (electricity, gas, water), service charges, regular maintenance and repairs, property-related taxes and home insurance. These costs exclude non-essential or discretionary expenditures such as furniture, household appliances or home improvements. The housing cost overburden rate is used in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/dashboard/social-scoreboard/ Social Scoreboard] of the European Pillar of Social Rights, which monitors progress in the context of the [https://reforms-investments.ec.europa.eu/european-semester_en European Semester].
'''''The highest housing cost overburden rate in 2025 was recorded in the Greek region of Anatoliki Makedonia, Thraki (33.9%)''''' According to the most recent data available, 7.7% of the EU’s population were overburdened by housing costs in 2025. This marked a decrease of 0.5 percentage points compared with 2024 (when the rate was 8.2%). The housing cost overburden rate was generally higher in predominantly urban regions than in predominantly rural regions. '''Map 5''' shows the cost of housing accounted for more than 40% of household budgets in a high proportion of households across Greece and Denmark, as well as in most western regions of Germany and in several capital regions. In 2025, there were 20 NUTS level 2 regions in the EU where at least 16.0% of the population faced a housing cost overburden (as shown by the darkest shade in '''Map 5'''). These 20 regions included: *all 13 regions from Greece *all 5 regions from Denmark *Trier from western Germany *the Belgian capital Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest. In 2025, the housing cost overburden rate in Greece ranged from a low of 18.5% in Kriti to a high of 33.9% in the northern region of Anatoliki Makedonia, Thraki; the highest rate in the EU. The western Greek region of Peloponnisos (33.3%) was the only other region in the EU where at least one third of the population lived in a dwelling where housing costs exceeded 40% of disposable household income. In Denmark, the highest rate was observed in the capital region of Hovedstaden (26.6%), while the remaining 4 Danish regions had broadly similar shares, ranging from 21.0% to 22.6%. Outside Greece and Denmark, Trier in Germany recorded the highest housing cost overburden rate, at 18.1%. This may be linked, at least in part, to cross-border commuting, with many residents living in Germany but working in Luxembourg. This demand pressure can contribute to higher rents and house prices, particularly in nearby commuter towns and villages. '''''The lowest housing cost overburden rate in 2025 was recorded in the Slovak capital region of Bratislavský kraj (1.6%)''''' At the lower end of the distribution, there were 15 NUTS level 2 regions where the housing cost overburden rate was less than 3.0% in 2025. These 15 regions were distributed over 6 different EU countries, with 5 regions located in Poland (4 of which were in the east), 3 regions in Italy, as well as 2 regions in each of Croatia, Romania and Slovakia; Cyprus also had a low rate. In 2025, the lowest housing cost overburden rate in the EU was observed in the Slovak capital region of Bratislavský kraj (1.6%). The rate in Anatoliki Makedonia, Thraki was therefore 21.2 times as high as the rate recorded in Bratislavský kraj, while the EU average was 4.8 times as high as this lowest rate. The Slovak capital region was somewhat atypical among regions with low housing cost overburden rates, as the only other capital region in this group was Grad Zagreb in Croatia, while most of the remaining regions with low values were predominantly rural.

'''More about the data: economic strain''' Economic strain refers to a set of indicators that measure self-perceived financial difficulties of households. This concept is covered by a group of indicators collected as part of the EU-SILC survey, designed to capture material hardship and/or financial stress. While economic strain is not generally used as a headline indicator within EU policy development, it does play a key role in understanding living conditions and poverty (beyond income-based measures). Various measures of economic strain are included in composite indicators such as the severe material and social deprivation rate. Some of the most common measures include, whether households: *have arrears on mortgage/rent, utility bills, hire purchase instalments or other loan payments *can keep their home adequately warm.
'''''In 2025, almost 1 in 10 people across the EU faced arrears on mortgage, rent, utility bills or hire purchase''''' Economic strain has gained renewed attention in light of the ongoing cost-of-living crisis. Rising inflation, surging energy prices and challenges around housing affordability have placed considerable pressure on household budgets, particularly among vulnerable groups. Indicators of economic strain can reveal growing disparities in financial resilience, which may be used to understand where support is most needed. '''Map 6''' focuses on the share of individuals falling behind on payments for mortgages, rent, utilities or hire purchase agreements. In 2025, these issues affected 9.2% of the EU population. The highest regional shares across NUTS level 2 regions were recorded in the south-eastern part of the EU, as well as in some of the French outermost regions. In 2 western regions of Greece, more than half of the population was falling behind on payments for mortgages, rent, utilities or hire purchase agreements in 2025: *the highest share in the EU was recorded in the island region of Ionia Nisia, where approximately two thirds (66.3%) of the population faced such an economic strain *the second highest share was in the mainland region of Dytiki Elláda (50.7%). The share of people in arrears on mortgage, rent, utility bills or hire purchase payments was more than twice the EU average in 24 regions, as shown by the darkest shade in '''Map 6'''. This group included all 13 regions of Greece (which recorded the 13 highest regional shares in the EU), 4 regions of Bulgaria, 3 regions of Romania, as well as 2 French outermost regions and the autonomous Spanish regions of Ciudad de Ceuta and Ciudad de Melilla. By contrast, the northern Italian region of Provincia Autonoma di Trento (0.6%) had the lowest share of people falling behind on payments for mortgages, rent, utilities or hire purchase agreements in 2025. There were 21 other regions across the EU where the share of people in arrears was less than 3.0%: *6 regions from central and eastern Poland *4 regions from northern Belgium *3 regions from Czechia, including the capital region of Praha *3 further regions from northern Italy (in addition to Provincia Autonoma di Trento) *2 regions from the east of the Netherlands (NUTS level 1) *single regions from Germany and Hungary *the capital region of Bratislavský kraj in Slovakia. '''''In the Greek region of Dytiki Elláda, more than 3 in 10 people were unable to keep their home adequately warm in 2025''''' In 2025, some 8.8% of the EU population lived in a household that struggled to keep their home adequately warm. By contrast, across many regions of Belgium and Finland, a relatively small proportion of people lived in households unable to keep their home adequately warm. Antwerpen (which had the lowest share in the EU, at 0.4%) *4 regions from Finland *2 regions from each of Germany, Italy and Poland (including the capital region of Warszawski stołeczny) *single regions from Czechia, Hungary and Sweden *Bratislavský kraj, the capital region of Slovakia.

'''More about the data: crime and criminal justice statistics''' The statistics presented in this section are based on official figures for police-recorded offences (criminal acts), classified according to the [https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/data-and-analysis/statistics/iccs.html International classification of crime for statistical purposes (ICCS)]. The number of police-recorded crimes varies considerably across the EU. This may reflect, among other factors, differences in the likelihood of reporting crimes to the police (especially minor offences), variations in national legislation and different police practices for recording crimes. As such, Eurostat advises against cross-country comparisons; instead, the data presented in this section should be analysed within individual countries (inter-regional comparisons). The data shown in this section are based on crime rates, defined as the number of police-recorded crimes per 100 000 inhabitants for NUTS level 2 regions. Only national data are available for the Netherlands and Sweden, while data for Italy (as well as Albania) refer to 2023. [[Glossary:Domestic_burglary|Domestic burglary]] is defined as breaking in and stealing, in other words, getting unauthorised access to a dwelling for theft or intent of theft (with or without forcing locks, doors, windows and so on). Theft is defined as taking property unlawfully – without violence, force, threat, coercion or deception – with the intent to keep it permanently without consent. [[Glossary:Intentional_homicide|Intentional homicide]] is defined as killing a human being wilfully and illegally; in other words, the intent was to cause death or serious injury, but not necessarily that it was planned beforehand. This is a wider concept than murder, for which also planning and other criteria are considered. Intentional homicide statistics: *include murder, deadly assault, assassination, terrorism, femicide, infanticide, voluntary manslaughter, extrajudicial killings and illegal killing by police or military *exclude attempted homicide, justifiable self-defence, assisted suicide, euthanasia and abortion. Special care should be taken when analysing the statistics presented below, as there may be very low counts of intentional homicides in some regions. Counts can vary considerably over time, especially in jurisdictions with small populations, whereby a small increase/decrease in the number of homicides may lead to a relatively large change in crime rates from 1 year to the next. You can find more information about how crimes are classified across EU regions in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/crim_gen_reg_esms.htm metadata].
Based on the latest information available, there were an estimated 700 700 police-recorded domestic burglaries across the EU in 2024 (including 2021 data for Luxembourg and excluding Ireland, Cyprus and Hungary). '''Figure 6''' highlights the regional distribution of police-recorded offences for domestic burglaries in 2024. Note these figures are normalised, using incidence rates per 100 000 inhabitants to enable more relevant comparisons between regions of different population sizes. *In Germany, Croatia, Lithuania, Austria, Slovenia and Slovakia, the capital regions of Berlin, Grad Zagreb, Sostinės regionas, Wien, Zahodna Slovenija and Bratislavský kraj – recorded the highest incidence rates for domestic burglaries. *By contrast, none of the remaining capital regions in multi-regional EU countries recorded the lowest incidence rate for domestic burglaries. In relative terms (compared with national averages), the highest incidences of domestic burglaries were recorded in the German capital region of Berlin, where burglaries were 2.5 times as likely as the national average. Relatively high indices (more than 1.5 times the national average) were also observed in: *the Portuguese island region of Região Autónoma dos Açores *the Austrian capital region of Wien *the south-western Polish region of Dolnośląskie *the eastern Spanish region of Comunitat Valenciana *the north-western Bulgarian region of Severozapaden *the central Greek region of Sterea Elláda.
