title: Maritime transport of goods - quarterly data
text:
Main results from quarterly statistics on maritime transport of goods in the European Union, plus Norway, Montenegro and Türkiye. Data extracted in March 2026 Planned article update: 25 September 2026 846.0 million tonnes of goods were handled in the main EU ports in Q3 2025. The gross weight of goods handled in the main EU ports increased by 2.4% in Q3 2025 compared with the same quarter of 2024. |alt= Interactive line chart showing gross weight of seaborne goods as millions of tonnes handled in EU main ports over the period Q3 2019 to Q3 2025. This article presents the main results from quarterly statistics on maritime transport of goods in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]], plus figures for Norway, Montenegro and Türkiye. It covers the [[Glossary:Gross_weight|gross weight]] of goods handled in the [[Glossary:Main_ports|main European ports]], by type of cargo, direction, reporting country and various partner regions. These data are complemented by maritime transport flows with the main [[Glossary:Extra-EU|extra-EU]] partners. The article contains data for Q3 2025. Please note that the quarterly port activity figures are provisional and subject to revisions. === Gross weight of goods handled in the main EU ports increased by 2.4% in Q3 2025=== At 846.0 million tonnes, the gross weight of goods handled in the main [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU]] ports increased by 0.7% in Q3 2025 compared with the previous quarter and increased by 2.4% versus the same quarter of 2024 (Figures 1 and 2). After a steady recovery, following the economic crisis and a peak in activity reached in Q2 2019, maritime transport then observed a downward trend until Q2 2020, as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. A partial recovery continued until Q2 2022. After that, a new declining trend was observed, mainly attributed to the restrictions on freight transport with Russia, following its military aggression against Ukraine. Looking at the overall annual change, EU port activity in terms of gross weight of goods handled increased by 0.1% compared with the previous period (Figure 2). [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports by direction, EU, Q3 2013 - Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports by direction, EU,
Q3 2013 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/df0ca7d3-e4f9-4f8b-8e6e-4c8b5f145169?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-09T12:06:21Z mar_qg_qm_ewhd])|alt= Line chart showing gross weight of seaborne goods as millions of tonnes handled in EU main ports by direction. Three lines represent total, inwards and outwards over the period Q3 2013 to Q3 2025. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] === Inward movement of goods represented 63.2% of the total volume of goods handled in the main EU ports in Q3 2025 === In Q3 2025, 63.2% of the total volume of goods handled in the main EU ports were inward movements, a slight increase of 0.3 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp) compared with the previous quarter. This share increased by 1.0 pp compared with Q3 of the previous year. Compared with Q3 2024, inward movements of goods to the main EU ports increased by 4.0%, to 534.6 million tonnes in Q3 2025. Outward movements decreased by 0.3% to 311.4 million tonnes. When looking at the overall annual aggregate, inward movements of goods increased by 2.1% and outward movements decreased by 3.2%. [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports, EU, Q3 2013 - Q3 2025 (% change rate on same quarter of previous year and annual change rate).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports, EU,
Q3 2013 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/21921e82-9072-416c-ab82-24e6fa3ab201?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-25T13:01:38Z mar_qg_qm_ewhd])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing gross weight of seaborne goods handled in the EU's main ports, as a percentage change rate for the previous year's same quarter and annual change rate over the period Q3 2013 to Q3 2025. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] === Liquid bulk goods increased by 4.2% in Q3 2025 compared with the same quarter of 2024 === Compared with the same quarter of 2024, liquid bulk goods (+4.2%) increased substantially in Q3 2025. [[Glossary:Roll_on_-_roll_off|Roll on - roll off (Ro-Ro)]] units also increased by 2.3%, followed by dry bulk goods (+2.0%) and large containers (+1.1%). By contrast, other cargo decreased by 2.1%. When looking at the overall annual change, liquid bulk goods and dry bulk goods decreased by 1.5%. By contrast, large containers increased by 2.7%, followed by other cargo (+2.0%) and Ro-Ro mobile units (+1.5%) (Figure 3). [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports by type of cargo, EU, Q3 2023 - Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports by type of cargo, EU,
Q3 2023 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5f9016cd-44b4-413e-89ef-ecc85a1a3f52?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-25T13:07:12Z mar_qg_qm_ewhk])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing gross weight of seaborne goods as millions of tonnes handled in EU main ports by type of cargo. The columns represent the nine quarters from Q3 2023 to Q3 2025. Each column has five stacks representing liquid bulk goods, dry bulk goods, large containers, ro-ro mobile units and other cargo. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] === The Netherlands, Italy and Spain each handled more than 120 million tonnes of goods in Q3 2025 === In Q3 2025, the Netherlands, Italy and Spain were the EU countries with the largest amount of maritime freight handled in their main ports, each handling more than 120 million tonnes of goods (Figure 4). [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports, Q3 2024, Q2 2025 and Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports,
Q3 2024, Q2 2025 and Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9e46c2a9-887b-4341-b19c-71efa4cd6532?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-25T13:53:00Z mar_qg_qm_cwh])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing gross weight of seaborne goods as millions of tonnes handled in the main ports of individual EU countries, EFTA countries and Candidate countries. Each country has three bars representing Q3 2024, Q2 2025 and Q3 2025. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] In Q3 2025, 9 of the [[Glossary:Coastal_Member_States|maritime EU countries]] recorded a decrease in the tonnes of goods handled in their main ports, compared with the same quarter of 2024 (Table 1). In relative terms, the largest decrease was observed for Malta (-19.2%), followed by Estonia (-14.3%), Croatia (-5.4%) and Bulgaria (-5.0%). By contrast, Cyprus reported the highest increase in main port activity in this period (+36.8%), followed by Romania (+9.5%) and France (+7.6%). When looking at the overall annual change, 10 EU countries recorded a decrease. The largest drop was recorded by Malta (-40.7%; this large change in percentage should be considered in relation to a low initial value), followed by Romania (-16.8%), Bulgaria (-9.5%) and Estonia (-9.3%). By contrast, the most noticeable growth was observed in Cyprus (+35.6%), followed by Lithuania (+8.0%) and Ireland (+6.4%). [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports, in selected quarters, Q3 2023 - Q3 2025.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports, in selected quarters,
Q3 2023 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2e194edd-4a29-43c0-a5ab-b1c0d7ed566f?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-25T13:12:37Z mar_qg_qm_cwh])|alt= Table showing the gross weight of seaborne goods as millions of tonnes and percentage change over past quarters handled in main EU ports of the individual EU countries, EFTA countries and Candidate countries for Q3 2023 to Q3 2025. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] === In Q3 2025, the main maritime trade flow was inward movements of large containers from China === It is worth noting that the figures presented in this section may be influenced by variations in the level of transport reported with unknown partner regions. At 541 million tonnes, [[Glossary:Short_sea_shipping_(SSS)|short sea shipping]] tonnages to and from the main EU ports increased by 1.7% in Q3 2025, compared with the same quarter in 2024. [[Glossary:Deep_sea_shipping|Deep sea shipping]] tonnages also increased by 4.8%, to 295 million tonnes (Figure 5). When looking at the overall annual change, short sea shipping increased by 0.6% while deep sea shipping fell by 0.7%, compared with the previous period. [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports by type of shipping, EU, Q3 2023 - Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports by type of shipping, EU,
Q3 2023 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5c1a0fda-c92d-4289-adef-bd8e01d7a400?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-25T13:18:36Z mar_qg_qm_ewhg])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing the gross weight of seaborne goods as millions of tonnes handled in EU main ports by type of shipping from Q3 2023 to Q3 2025. Each column has three stacks representing short sea shipping, deep sea shipping and unknown. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] Between Q3 2024 and the same quarter of 2025, international extra-EU transport increased by 4.2%, national transport by 1.4% and international intra-EU transport by 0.3% (Figure 6). When looking at the overall annual change, national transport by 1.7% and international extra-EU transport increased by 0.4% while intra-EU transport decreased by 1.1% [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports by type of transport, EU, Q3 2023 - Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports by type of transport, EU,
Q3 2023 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/86b7d7b3-0362-4952-981b-d2e0cd10d252?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-25T13:21:42Z mar_qg_qm_ewht])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing gross weight of seaborne goods as millions of tonnes handled in the main EU ports by type of transport from Q3 2023 to Q3 2025. Each column has four stacks representing international extra-EU, international intra-EU, national and unknown. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] The increase in international extra-EU transport in Q3 compared with the same quarter in 2024 was mainly due to increases in seaborne transport with all extra-EU regions: Africa (+8.5 million tonnes or +8.8%), America (+7.6 million tonnes or +5.9%) and 'Asia & Oceania' (+1.8 million tonnes or +1.6%) (Figure 7). When looking at the overall annual change, seaborne transport with 'Asia & Oceania' decreased by 6.2%. By contrast, seaborne transport with America increased by 5.4%, 'Europe except EU' by 1.1% and Africa by 0.5%. [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports by partner regions, EU, Q3 2023 - Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 7: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports by partner regions, EU,
Q3 2023 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4cfb6fd9-4ef5-4f02-9b51-6aece49d672c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-25T13:22:39Z mar_qg_qm_ewhg])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing gross weight of seaborne goods as millions of tonnes handled in EU main ports by partner regions from Q3 2023 to Q3 2025. Each column has five stacks representing the EU, Europe except EU, America, Asia & Oceania, Africa and unknown. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] In terms of the total gross weight of goods, the United States of America (USA) remained the EU's largest maritime freight transport partner in Q3 2025, for 14 consecutive quarters. The United Kingdom (UK) was the EU's second-largest maritime freight transport partner in Q3 2025, followed by Norway, China and Türkiye. Brazil, Russia, Egypt, Canada and Morocco completed the top 10 of extra-EU partner countries (Figure 8). EU transport with the USA and the UK together, accounted for almost one-quarter (23.6%) of total extra-EU maritime transport. Maritime transport in Q3 2025 between the EU and the extra EU partner countries increased for all countries from the top 10, except for the United Kingdom, when compared with the same quarter of 2024. The largest increases were recorded for Morocco (+14.4%), Russia (+13.9%) and Canada (+11.5%). On the other hand, maritime transport between the EU and the United Kingdom decreased by 0.2% in Q3 2025 compared with the same quarter of 2024. When looking at the overall annual change, transport between the EU and Canada (+11.8%), Morocco (+7.8%), Türkiye (+5.6%), the US (+4.4%), Russia (+3.6%), Norway (+0.7%) and the United Kingdom (+0.2%) increased. By contrast, the highest decrease was observed for transport between the EU and Egypt (-6.8%), followed by China (-5.0%). [[Image: Top 10 extra EU partner countries in maritime transport, EU, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 8: Top 10 extra-EU partner countries in maritime transport, EU,
Q3 2024 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e7e64e48-c9ce-45ea-aa41-2145d8960a93?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-25T13:31:34Z mar_qg_qm_ewhp])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the top ten extra-EU partner countries in maritime transport as millions of tonnes in the USA, UK, Norway, China, Türkiye, Brazil, Russia, Egypt, Canada and Morocco. Each country has five columns representing the quarters Q3 2024 to Q3 2025. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] A substantial share of seaborne transport with China is made up of inward movements of large containers to the main EU ports, followed by Norway for crude oil and the USA for liquefied gas (Figure 9). In Q3 2025, the main maritime trade flow was the inward movements of large containers from China, with 18.5 million tonnes. Inward movements of crude oil from Norway were second, with 14.4 million tonnes. When looking at outward movements, Ro-Ro mobile units to the UK was the main maritime trade flow (11.6 million tonnes), followed by large containers to China and oil products to the UK (5.5 million tonnes both). In Q3 2025, the top 20 trade flows were largely dominated by inward movements of liquid bulk goods (crude oil, liquefied gas and oil products), with the following exceptions: large containers to and from China, Ro-Ro mobile units to and from the United Kingdom, ores from the East coast of Canada, other dry bulk goods from Norway, agricultural products from Brazil and large containers from Türkiye. [[Image: Top 20 extra EU maritime trade flows, EU, Q3 2024, Q2 2025 and Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 9: Top 20 extra-EU maritime trade flows, EU,
Q3 2024, Q2 2025 and Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c115e08f-22fb-4322-9cf4-cf2e849cd24c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-25T13:41:49Z mar_qg_qm_ewh])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the top 20 extra-EU maritime trade flows by partner as millions of tonnes. Seventeen partner regions have 3 columns representing Q3 2024 inwards, Q2 2025 inwards and Q3 2025 inwards. Three partner regions have three columns representing Q3 2024 outwards, Q2 2025 outwards and Q3 2025 outwards. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] In Q3 2025, compared with the same quarter of 2024, the most noticeable increases were recorded for liquefied gas from the East coast of USA (+87.7%), crude oil from Libya (+40.7%), agricultural products from Brazil (+39.5%), crude oil from the Black Sea of Russia (+33.3%) and from Nigeria (+10.9%) and ores from the East coast of Canada (+10.0%). By contrast, large decreases were observed for crude oil from the East coast of the USA (-15.0%) and from Iraq (-12.5%) (Table 2). When looking at the overall annual change, 10 out of the top 20 maritime trade flows increased compared with the previous period. The highest increase was registered in the inward movements of liquefied gas from the East coast of the USA (+30.0%), followed by inward movements of crude oil from Libya (+20.1%), inward movements of crude oil from the Black Sea of Russia (+13.5%), inward movements of agricultural products from Brazil (+9.9%) and inwards movements of crude oil from Brazil (+8.3%). By contrast, the highest drops were recorded for the inward movements of crude oil from the East coast of the USA (-18.9%) and inward movements of crude oil from Iraq (-18.6%). [[Image: Top 20 extra EU maritime trade flows, EU, in selected quarters, Q3 2023 - Q3 2025.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 2: Top 20 extra-EU maritime trade flows, EU, in selected quarters,
Q3 2023 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8287aefa-5563-4523-b4be-49c0594249f6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-25T13:40:46Z mar_qg_qm_ewh])|alt= Table showing the top 20 extra-EU maritime trade flows to EU main ports as millions of tonnes and percentage change over past quarters for Q3 2023 to Q3 2025. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Maritime_transport_of_goods_EU_2025Q3.xlsx|title=Maritime transport of goods - quarterly data: tables and figures}} === Data sources and availability === The content of this statistical article is based on data collected within the framework of the EU maritime transport statistics {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0042:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/42/EC}} on statistical returns in respect of carriage of goods and passengers by sea. EU aggregates refer to the total of 22 [[Glossary:Coastal_Member_States|maritime Member States]]. Czechia, Luxembourg, Hungary, Austria and Slovakia have no maritime ports. Norway and Iceland provide [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] with data as members of the [[Glossary:European_Economic_Area_(EEA)|European Economic Area (EEA)]]. However, quarterly data are currently not available for Iceland. The EEA country Liechtenstein has no maritime ports. The EU candidate countries Montenegro and Türkiye provide data on a voluntary basis. 'Main ports' are ports handling more than 1 million tonnes of goods annually (however, data for some smaller ports may be included in the published results). Data are presented at the level of '[[Glossary:Statistical_port|statistical ports]]'. A statistical port consists of one or more ports, normally controlled by a single port authority, able to record ship and cargo movements. All figures are based on a port's total (inward + outward) declarations. The results represent the 'handling' of goods in ports. The '[[Glossary:Short_sea_shipping_(SSS)|short sea shipping]]' aggregate (in Figure 5) includes partner ports geographically situated in Europe, on the Mediterranean or on the Black Sea. '[[Glossary:Deep_sea_shipping|Deep sea shipping]]' is the complementary geographical aggregate, covering maritime transport of goods on intercontinental routes, crossing oceans. A more extensive definition of 'short sea shipping' is available in the article [[Maritime_transport_statistics_-_short_sea_shipping_of_goods|Maritime transport statistics - short sea shipping of goods]]. The concept of maritime transport trade (in Figure 9 and Table 2) is defined using the following 3 variables: # '''Direction''': 'inwards' transport is distinguished from 'outwards' transport. # '''Partner geographical area''' (partner region): usually this corresponds to one country, with the exception of countries of such a size and/or geographical position that the location of individual ports may be quite different and may have a strong impact on the maritime route followed. For example, the ports of the United States of America are grouped in 2 geographical areas: East Coast (including Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, Great Lakes and Puerto Rico) and West Coast (Pacific). # '''Type of cargo''': the following thirteen cargo types are used in Figure 9 and Table 2: liquefied gas, crude oil, oil products, other liquid bulk goods, ores, coal, agricultural products, other dry bulk goods, large containers, Ro-Ro mobile units, forestry products, iron/steel products and other general cargo. The first 4 types constitute 'liquid bulk', the subsequent 4 types 'dry bulk' and the last 3 types 'other general cargo not elsewhere specified', as presented in Figures 3 and 11 to 16. '''Abbreviations''' {| style="background-color: #f5faff; vertical-align: top" class="wikitable" |- |:|| not available |- | -|| not applicable |- | Nes|| Not elsewhere specified |- | Ro-Ro|| Roll-on/roll-off |- | TEU || Twenty-foot Equivalent Unit |} '''Quarterly data''' are in general provisional. Revisions may be made by countries as more complete information becomes available or as a result of quality checks. More specifically, when the complete set of annual data emerges, this usually involves some revision of quarterly data for some countries. The basic results (in million tonnes) and the derived indicators (growth rates) shown in the figures and tables are rounded. However, they are all based on non-rounded original data, as available in Eurostat's database. '''Specific remarks''' for data up to and including Q3 2025: * There is a break in time series from Q1 2015 due to methodological improvement in the data reported by the Netherlands. * Starting from Q1 2013 , the quarterly figures for Germany include data for all national ports (both main ports and minor ports). * The quarterly data for port activity in France have been partially estimated by Eurostat for the period Q1 2010 - Q1 2016. These data are to be considered as provisional and are likely to be revised. In general, such estimates reduce the accuracy of the statistics at detailed levels. * Starting from Q1 2019 , the statistical coverage of data has improved for Greece, having more ports reporting quarterly data. Starting from Q1 2023, the statistical coverage of data has again improved for Greece, having more ports reporting quarterly data. * Starting from Q1 2011 , the quarterly figures for Spain include data for a number of regional ports outside the state-controlled port system. * Starting from Q1 2018 , quarterly figures for Portugal include data for all national ports (both main ports and minor ports). * Starting from Q1 2013 , the quarterly figures for Sweden include data for all national ports (both main ports and minor ports). Until 2023, data for Sweden include inland waterway transport. The share of inland waterway transport is less than 3% of all goods handled in Swedish ports. Due to revisions of the underlying data, figures in this article may differ from figures currently or previously available on Eurostat's website. ===Context=== The content of this statistical article is based on data collected within the framework of the EU maritime transport statistics {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0042:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/42/EC}} of 6 May 2009 on statistical returns in respect of carriage of goods and passengers by sea, which is a recast of the original Council {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31995L0064:EN:NOT|title=Directive 95/64/EC}} of 8 December 1995. ===Other articles=== *[[Maritime transport of goods at port level - quarterly data]] *[[Freight transport statistics - modal split]] *[[Maritime vessels statistics]] *[[Maritime transport statistics - short sea shipping of goods]] ===Publications=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/publications All transport publications online] *{{Template:Publication|code= KS-01-25-057 |title=Key figures on European transport - 2025 edition}} ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/database Transport], see: :Maritime transport (mar) ::Maritime transport - main annual results (mar_m) ::Maritime transport - title: Maritime transport of goods - annual data
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the annual maritime transport of goods. Data extracted in November 2025. Planned update: December 2026. EU ports handled 3.4 billion tonnes of goods in 2024. The Netherlands remained the largest maritime freight transport country in Europe in 2024. Rotterdam, Antwerp-Bruges and Hamburg maintained their positions as Europe's top 3 ports in 2024. |alt= A dynamic bar chart showing the gross weight of seaborne freight handled in 2023. This article presents the latest statistical data on goods handling and vessels traffic in [[Glossary:Port|ports]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], the [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA countries]] Iceland and Norway and the [[Glossary:candidate countries|candidate countries]] Montenegro and Türkiye. It also covers maritime transport flows with the main partner geographical areas, as well as individual results for major EU ports. This article contains data for 2024. === Seaborne goods handled in EU ports slightly decreased by 0.2% in 2024 === The total [[Glossary:Gross-gross weight|gross weight of goods]] handled by EU ports was estimated at 3.4 billion tonnes in 2024 (Figure 1), remained relatively stable compared with 2023 (-0.2%). The decline in goods handled in 2023 and 2024 compared with 2022, can be mainly attributed to the restrictions on goods transport with Russia, after its military aggression against Ukraine. Despite the rebound after the substantial fall observed in 2020, most probably due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent restrictions put in place in the EU and worldwide, the 2022 levels were still slightly lower than those observed in 2018 and 2019. Before the downturn in 2020, EU port freight activity followed a positive trend from 2014 onwards, showing a slight upturn in recovery after the economic crisis in 2009. [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in all ports by direction, EU, 2009-2024 (million tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in all ports by direction, EU, 2009-2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_aa_cwh__custom_18763215/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=1e4230d4-cd17-4eb9-9a53-5527f73314f9&c=1762351127000 mar_mg_aa_cwh]) |alt= a stacked bar chart showing the gross weight of seaborne goods handled in all ports by direction in the EU from 2009 to 2024 in million tonnes. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The Netherlands remained the largest maritime goods transport country in Europe in 2024, while Rotterdam, Antwerp-BrugesStarting from 2022, the ports Antwerpen and Zeebrugge have been merged and the data are reported under the new port name Antwerp-Bruges. and Hamburg maintained their positions as the 3 largest goods ports in the EU. Among the EU countries, the seaborne freight-per-capita ratio varied from 29.9 tonnes per inhabitant in the Netherlands to 3.1 tonnes per inhabitant in Romania in 2024. The EU average was 7.5 tonnes per inhabitant (Figure 2). The EFTA country Norway recorded the highest ratio of countries reporting maritime data to Eurostat, with 38.1 tonnes per inhabitant in 2024. [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in all ports, 2024_(tonnes per capita).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in all ports, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_aa_cwh__custom_18763110/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=8e8c0623-8d5d-4b91-90c0-4677f6b2abb3&c=1762350864000 mar_mg_aa_cwh])|alt= a vertical bar chart showing the gross weight of seaborne goods handled in all ports in 2024 in the EU, Norway, Iceland, Türkiye and Montenegro. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === The Netherlands is the EU's largest maritime goods transport country=== The Netherlands reported the largest volume of seaborne goods handled in Europe in 2024. At 538 million tonnes, the volume of seaborne goods handled in Dutch ports represented 16.0% of the EU total in 2024. The Netherlands was followed by Italy and Spain, with respective shares of 14.6% and 14.5% (Figure 3). [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in all ports, 2014, 2023 and 2024 (million tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in all ports, 2014, 2023 and 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_aa_cwh__custom_18763215/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=1e4230d4-cd17-4eb9-9a53-5527f73314f9&c=1762352952000 mar_mg_aa_cwh])|alt= a vertical bar chart with three bars showing the gross weight of seaborne goods handled in all ports in 2014, 2023 and 2024, the bars show the years, in the EU, Norway, Iceland, Türkiye and Montenegro. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among other countries reporting maritime freight data to Eurostat, the [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate country]] Türkiye handled 525 million tonnes of goods in 2024, placing this country between the Netherlands and Italy in terms of total tonnage of seaborne goods handled. Compared with 2023, half of the 22 EU [[Glossary:Coastal Member States|coastal countries]] registered a growth in port freight activity in 2024. Lithuania registered the largest relative increase (+6.1%), followed by Portugal (+4.3%). Conversely, the biggest relative decline was recorded in Malta (-37.9%), followed by Romania (-14.1%), Croatia (-10.1%), Poland (-8.9%), Latvia (-7.1%) and Estonia (-5.6%). All in all, 8 EU countries recorded decreases in port freight activity in the 10-year period between 2014 and 2024. The steepest relative falls were observed for Latvia (-53.3%), Estonia (-50.2%), Finland (-11.9%), Germany (-9.8%) and France (-9.5%). By contrast, Poland registered the largest relative increase (+80.7%), followed by Romania (+36.1%), Malta (+29.4%), Cyprus (+24.5%) and Slovenia (+20.9%). Four other EU countries registered growths of more than 10% over the same period, while 5 additional EU countries recorded growths between 1% and 9%. The candidate countries Montenegro and Türkiye also reported noticeable increases: +98.5% and +38.6%, respectively. Inward movements of goods to EU countries remained relatively stable (+0.1%) at 2.1 billion tonnes in 2024 compared with 2023, whereas outwards movements slightly decreased by 0.7%, to just under 1.3 billion tonnes. Inward movements accounted for 61.9% of the total tonnes of goods handled in the EU ports (Figure 4). The share of inward movements on total remained relatively stable between 2009 and 2024, fluctuating between 62.1% in 2009 and 59.0 in 2015 and 2016. Liquid bulk goods, such as crude oil and oil products, made up a substantial proportion of the inward tonnage. [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in all ports by direction, 2024_(%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in all ports by direction, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_aa_cwhd__custom_18764131/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=1f9c344b-c750-4231-9c9e-991197dcd5ce&c=1762353554000 mar_mg_aa_cwhd])|alt= a stacked bar chart showing the gross weight of seaborne goods handled in all ports by direction in 2024, in the EU, Iceland, Norway, Türkiye and Montenegro, the stacks show inwards and outwards. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] More seaborne goods are unloaded from vessels than loaded onto vessels in most EU countries. Malta had the most shares of unloaded goods in 2024, with 89.8% of the total tonnes of seaborne goods recorded as inward movements to their ports. By contrast, Latvia, Estonia, Bulgaria, Romania, the EFTA countries Norway and Iceland and the candidate country Montenegro all had more outward movements of goods than inwards movements. === In 2024, liquid bulk made up 37.3% of the total cargo handled in the main EU ports=== Liquid bulk goods accounted for 37.3% of the total cargo handled in the main EU ports in 2024 (Figure 5), followed by containerised goods (24.7%), dry bulk goods (20.6%), and goods transported on [[Glossary:Ro-Ro|Ro-Ro]] mobile units (12.4%). The largest volumes of liquid bulk goods were handled in the Netherlands (255 million tonnes), followed by Italy (196 million tonnes) and Spain (179 million tonnes). France recorded the largest share of liquid bulk goods as a percentage of the total tonnages passing through its main ports in 2024 (49.5%). Liquid bulk goods were predominant in 12 EU countries. This was also the case for the EFTA country Norway (47.6%). [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne freight handled in main ports by type of cargo, 2024_(%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports by type of cargo, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_am_cwhc__custom_18771059/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=283c2eb0-f910-40ce-97cf-36475a15c6bd&c=1762410740000 mar_mg_am_cwhc])|alt= a stacked vertical bar chart showing the gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main ports by type of cargo in 2024 in the EU, Norway, Türkiye and Montenegro, the stacked bars show liquid bulk goods, dry bulk goods, large containers Ro-Ro mobile units and other cargo. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] With 132 million tonnes in 2024, Dutch ports also handled the largest volumes of dry bulk goods in the EU, followed by Spain with 95 million tonnes. The tonnages of dry bulk goods handled in these 2 EU countries in 2024 were lower than the 188 million tonnes reported by the candidate country Türkiye. Romania had the highest shares of dry bulk goods as a percentage of the total tonnages in 2024 (50.7%), largely due to substantial outward movements of agricultural products from its ports. Latvia (49.4%) and Denmark (29.5%) were the other EU countries where dry bulk goods were predominant. This was also the case for the candidate countries Montenegro and Türkiye (63.1% and 35.8%). Containers were the dominant type of cargo handled in Slovenian, Belgian, German and Portuguese ports in 2024, with shares of 43.4%, 41.4%, 39.8% and 38.5%, respectively, of the total cargo passing through the ports of the 4 countries. The largest volumes of containerised goods, however, were handled in Spanish and Belgian ports, with 155 million tonnes and 114 million tonnes, respectively. The 2 top container countries were followed by Germany and the Netherlands with 109 and 108 million tonnes of containerised, respectively. The share of Ro-Ro mobile units in the total tonnage of goods was the largest for Estonia (33.9%), Ireland (32.1%) and Malta (25.6%), reflecting the importance of Ro-Ro ferry traffic in the seaborne transport of these countries. In tonnage terms, Italy (97 million tonnes) recorded the largest EU volumes of goods transported on Ro-Ro mobile units in 2024. === In 2024, the largest individual goods category handled in the main EU ports was 'Coal and lignite; crude petroleum and natural gas'=== Figure 6 presents the share of the type of goods (according to the [[Glossary: NST_2007|NST 2007 classification)]] handled in the main EU ports. It is significant to note that the high share of unidentifiable goods reported impacts the results presented. At EU level, the main types of goods (according to the NST 2007 classification) handled in the main EU ports were 'Coal and lignite; crude petroleum and natural gas' (19.0%) and 'coke and refined petroleum products' (16.5%), in 2024. These two categories represented over one third of all goods handled in the main EU ports. [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main EU ports by type of goods, 2024_(%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Gross weight of seaborne goods handled in main EU ports by type of goods, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_am_cwhg__custom_18771091/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=4c16b56d-abeb-4f61-9fe4-c3011d9e9a74&c=1762411311000 mar_mg_am_cwhg])|alt= a pie chart showing the gross weight of seaborne freight handled in main EU ports by type of goods in 2024, the segments show eight different categories of goods. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Rotterdam, Antwerp-Bruges and Hamburg maintained their positions as Europe's top 3 ports in 2024=== Rotterdam, Antwerp-Bruges and Hamburg, all located on the North Sea coast, maintained their positions as the EU's top 3 ports in 2024, both in terms of gross weight of goods handled and volume of containers handled in the ports. The 20 largest cargo ports accounted for half (49.8%) of the total tonnage of goods handled in the EU ports in 2024. The largest port in Europe, Rotterdam in the Netherlands, on its own accounted for 11.8% of the total tonnage handled in the EU ports (Figure 7). Among the top 20 EU ports, the tonnes of goods handled in 2024 decreased in 7 ports compared with 2023. The steepest falls were recorded by Constanţa (-14.3%) and Gdańsk (-11.0%). By contrast, Sines reported the highest growth, with +10.7%, followed by Göteborg (+10.1%), Gioia Tauro (+8.7%), Bremerhaven (+8.4%) and Barcelona (+7.9%). [[Image: Top 20 EU ports handling goods, 2014, 2023 and 2024 (million tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Top 20 EU ports handling goods, 2014, 2023 and 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_aa_pwhd__custom_18771251/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=abf1e638-b544-41e6-aa1e-187e96463a6c&c=1762412868000 mar_mg_aa_pwhd])|alt= a horizontal bar chart with three bars showing the Top 20 EU ports handling goods for 2014, 2023 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] While inward activity was prevalent in 16 of the top 20 ports, the ports of Bremerhaven (53.5%), Constanţa (51.2%), Gioia Tauro (51.1%) and Valencia (50.9%) marginally recorded more outward than inward movements of goods (Figure 8). [[Image: Top 20 EU ports handling goods by direction, 2024_(%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Top 20 EU ports handling goods by direction, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_aa_pwhd__custom_18771395/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=c8cc6043-8225-4112-b4e1-7474432a39f4&c=1762413608000 mar_mg_aa_pwhd])|alt= a horizontal stacked bar chart showing the top 20 EU ports handling goods by direction in 2024, the stacks show inwards and outwards. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among the top 20 cargo ports, Gioia Tauro (92.2% of total tonnage in 2024), Bremerhaven (90.7%), Piraeus (84.8%), Valencia (73.5%) and Hamburg (64.7%) stood out as the most specialised in container handling. The most specialised in handling liquid bulk goods were Trieste (76.7%) and Marseille (67.1%); the most specialised in handling dry bulk goods were 'Zeeland Seaports' (56.2%) and Constanţa (50.4%); the most specialised in handling goods transported on Ro-Ro mobile units was Göteborg (22.6%) (Figure 9). [[Image: Top 20 EU ports handling goods by type of cargo, 2024 (%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: Top 20 EU ports handling goods by type of cargo, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_am_pwhc__custom_18771602/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=3dfa2381-709e-4191-8f0d-0e2f88091079&c=1762414384000 mar_mg_am_pwhc])|alt=a horizontal stacked bar chart showing the top 20 EU ports handling goods by type of cargo in 2024, the stacked bars show liquid bulk goods, dry bulk goods, large containers Ro-Ro mobile units and other cargo. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] All in all, 8 of the top 20 EU cargo ports in 2024 were located on the Mediterranean, 7 on the North Sea coast of Europe, 3 ports on the Atlantic coast, 1 port in the Baltic Sea and 1 port in the Black Sea (Map 1). Whether a country makes the top 20 list of cargo ports can sometimes depend on the structure of its national port system. Denmark and Finland, for instance, are countries with numerous medium-sized ports, all handling volumes of goods lower than the 36 million annual tonnes required to make the top 20 list. [[File:Maritime-ports.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 1: Maritime cargo ports by gross weight of goods handled, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=mar_mg_aa_pwhd}}|alt= The map shows the main cargo ports in individual European countries, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries by gross weight of goods handled in 2024, measured in million tonnes. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Most EU maritime goods transport is with extra-EU partners === Unlike the statistics presented earlier in this article, the data in Table 1 and Figure 10 do not present the total handling of goods in ports (inward movements plus outward movements in the ports), but show the movement of seaborne transport of goods between the main European ports and their partner ports. As far as possible, double counting of the same goods being reported as outward transport in one port and inward transport in another, is excluded in these figures (see data sources). [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne goods transported to_from main ports, in selected years, 2014-2024 (million tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Gross weight of seaborne goods transported to/from main ports, in selected years, 2014-2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_am_cwt/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=8cb3c62e-7784-4f1d-b17a-9f4db1f7492c&c=1762419676000 mar_mg_am_cwt])|alt= a table showing the gross weight of seaborne goods transported to/from main ports, in selected years, 2014-2024 in the EU, Norway, Montenegro and Türkiye. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] At 2.8 billion tonnes, the EU seaborne transport of goods remained relatively stable between 2023 and 2024 (-0.1%) (Table 1). Most of these goods (68.4%) were transported to or from ports outside the EU (international extra-EU transport), making maritime transport the most common mode for long-distance transport of goods to or from the EU, in tonnage terms. Cross-border transport between ports in the EU (international intra-EU transport) made up 21.2% of the maritime transport of goods in 2024, while transport of goods between national ports made up 8.5% of the total EU maritime transport (Figure 10). [[Image: Seaborne transport of goods between main ports in the reporting country and their partner ports grouped by main geographical areas, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 10: Seaborne transport of goods between main ports in the reporting country and their partner ports grouped by main geographical areas, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_am_cwtt__custom_18773578/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=5788119a-7c3d-4ef9-881b-f0cc27ab9be8&c=1762420374000 mar_mg_am_cwtt])|alt=a vertical stacked bar chart showing the seaborne transport of goods between the main ports in the reporting country and their partner ports, grouped by main geographical areas in 2023, in the EU, Norway, Türkiye and Montenegro, the stacks show national, international intra-EU, international extra-EU and unknown. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In countries with long shorelines or many islands, such as Italy, Greece and the EFTA country Norway, the share of national seaborne transport tends to be relatively high (19-24% in 2024). Countries like Estonia, Malta, Finland, Sweden, Cyprus, Latvia, Denmark and Ireland, however, had high shares of international intra-EU transport (above 50% in 2024), because their main maritime freight transport partners are found within the EU. Other countries, such as Bulgaria, Romania, the Netherlands, Slovenia, Belgium, Spain, France, Croatia, Germany, Portugal (above 59% in 2024), have high shares of extra-EU transport, based on their geographical position or the 'deep-sea' nature of the transport activities prevailing in their main ports. Map 2 illustrates the largest maritime transport flows between the EU and the main international partners. As shown in the map, most of the EU's top 10 maritime flows of goods in 2024 were inward flows, except for the outward flow to the United Kingdom and the East Coast of the USA. In declining order, these were the inward flows of goods from the East Coast of the USA (8.7% of the total extra-EU seaborne transport in 2024), the outward flow to the United Kingdom, the inward flows from Norway (each 5.5%), the United Kingdom (4.8%), China, Brazil (each 4.0%), Türkiye (3.9%), Egypt (3.2%), the outward flow to the East Coast of the USA (2.4%), and the inward flow from the Black Sea area of Russia (2.2%). [[File:Top-20-extra-eu-maritime-flows.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 2: Top 20 extra-EU maritime flows
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/information-data/maritime-transport mar_go])|alt= The map illustrates the top 20 maritime trade routes between the European Union (EU) and non-EU countries for 2024, based on the gross weight of goods handled in main ports. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === In 2024, 100.9 million TEUs of containers were handled in the main EU ports === In 2024, the volume of containers handled in the main EU ports reached a peak at 100.9 million [[Glossary:Twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU)|twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs)]] (Figure 11), after an increase by 4.4% compared with 2023. When looking at empty containers, the increase in 2024 was more substantial (+5.5%) compared with the increase in the handling of loaded containers (+4.1%). [[Image: Volume of containers handled in main ports, EU, 2009-2024_(million TEUs).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 11: Volume of containers handled in main ports, EU, 2009-2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_am_cvh__custom_18773715/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=40aad2c1-d5dc-4452-be1f-ac83baea91c5&c=1762420675000 mar_mg_am_cvh])|alt= a line chart with three lines showing the volume of containers handled in main ports in the EU from 2009-2024, the lines show, total, empty and loaded. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Spain reported the largest volumes of containers handled in Europe in 2024. At 18.8 million TEUs, the volume of containers handled in Spanish ports represented 18.6% of the EU total in 2024 (Figure 12). Spain was followed by the Netherlands (13.9% of the EU total), Italy (13.7%), Germany (13.2%) and Belgium (12.3%). All together, these 5 countries had 71.7% of the containers handled in main EU ports in 2024. [[Image: Volume of containers handled in main ports, 2014, 2023 and 2024 (million TEUs).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 12: Volume of containers handled in main ports, 2014, 2023 and 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_am_cvh__custom_18774016/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=b4b91432-447a-4974-b70d-390b090c7c52&c=1762421412000 mar_mg_am_cvh])|alt= a vertical bar chart with three bars showing the Volume of containers handled in main ports in 2014, 2023 and 2024, in the EU countries, Norway, Türkiye and Montenegro. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] All countries reported more loaded containers than empty containers. The shares of empty containers handled was the least in Malta and Italy (1.6% and 8.2% of the containers handled in the main ports of the country, respectively) and the most in Finland (37.2%) (Figure 13). [[Image: Volume of containers handled in main ports by loading status, 2024_(%, based on TEUs).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 13: Volume of containers handled in main ports, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_am_cvh__custom_18778768/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=99e77cc8-4a06-405c-ad7f-ec84d9b3805c&c=1762432062000 mar_mg_am_cvh])|alt=a vertical stacked bar chart showing the volume of containers handled in main ports by loading status in 2024 in the EU, Norway and Türkiye. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] With 13.4 million TEUs handled, Rotterdam was EU’s largest container port in 2024 (Figure 14). Rotterdam was followed by Antwerp-Bruges with 12.4 million TEUs and Hamburg with 7.8 million TEUs handled in total. All in all, 14 of the top 20 container ports recorded increases in the number of TEUs handled compared with 2023. In relative terms, the largest growth was observed for HAROPA Since 2022, Le Havre and Rouen have been merged and the data are now reported under the new port name, HAROPA (+18.6%), followed by Barcelona (+18.5%), Constanţa (+16.0%), entering the top 20, Sines (+14.7%), Valencia (+14.2%) and Algeciras (+13.4%). By contrast, the steepest relative falls amongst the top 20 EU container ports were recorded by La Spezia (-27.6%), losing 2 positions compared to 2023, and Gioia Tauro (-14.2%). [[Image: Top 20 EU ports handling containers, 2014, 2023 and 2024 (million TEUs).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 14: Top 20 EU ports handling containers, 2014, 2023 and 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_am_pvh__custom_18779286/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=b7c51a66-ff7d-47c6-9a44-cf15ec7d7233&c=1762433345000 mar_mg_am_pvh])|alt= a horizontal bar chart with three bars showing the top 20 EU ports handling containers, 2014, 2023 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] All top 20 EU container ports reported more loaded containers than empty containers. The shares of empty containers handled was the lowest in Genova (2.9% of the containers handled in the main ports of the country) and the highest in Klaipėda (34.7%) (Figure 15). [[Image: Top 20 EU ports handling containers by loading status, 2024_(%, based on TEUs).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 15: Top 20 EU ports handling containers by loading status, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mg_am_pvh__custom_18779342/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=71c963ea-8850-4bb6-a889-3ccd8f7dea01&c=1762433767000 mar_mg_am_pvh])|alt= a horizontal stacked bar chart showing the top 20 EU ports handling containers by loading status in 2024, the bars show loaded and empty. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= SE_Article_Maritime_Freight_2025-11.xlsx |title= Maritime ports freight statistics: tables and figures}} === Data sources === This article presents the trends in goods transport in European Union (EU) ports and also includes figures for Iceland, Norway, Montenegro and Türkiye. The content is based on data collected within the legal framework for EU maritime transport statistics, i.e. {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0042:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/42/EC}} of the European Parliament and of the Council of 6 May 2009 on statistical returns in respect of carriage of goods and passengers by sea and later amendments. Directive 2009/42/EC is a recast of the original Council {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31995L0064:EN:NOT|title=Directive 95/64/EC}} of 8 December 1995. The EU aggregates in the statistics refer to the total of 22 [[Glossary:Coastal Member States|maritime EU countries]]. Czechia, Luxembourg, Hungary, Austria and Slovakia have no maritime ports. Norway and Iceland provide [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] with data as members of the [[Glossary:European Economic Area (EEA)|European Economic Area (EEA)]]. The EEA country Liechtenstein has no maritime ports. Montenegro and Türkiye provide data as [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries]]. 'Main ports' are ports handling more than one million tonnes of goods annually (however, data for some smaller ports may be included in the published results). Data are presented at level of '[[Glossary:Statistical port|statistical ports]]'. A statistical port consists of one or more ports, normally controlled by a single port authority, able to record ship and cargo movements. '''Explanatory notes:''' Please note that data can be subject to revision and the latest data are available in Eurostat's online database. Basic results and derived indicators (such as growth rates and shares in % of the total) in the tables are rounded. However, the figures are based on the non-rounded original data. As a result, the sum of shares in % of the total, as shown in the tables, is not necessarily equal to 100%. Explanatory notes for countries are available in the {{Template:Esms|code=mar_esms|title=metadata on the Eurostat website}}. Starting from 2011, the figures for Spain include data for a number of minor regional ports outside the state-controlled port system. There is a break in time series from 2015 due to methodological improvements in data reported by the Netherlands. Montenegro started to report data on seaborne transport in 2012. Data have been partially estimated by Eurostat for a number of French ports for the period 2009-2016. Detailed data on main ports are not available for Iceland. '''Type of cargo (Figures 5 and 9):''' * Liquid bulk: liquefied gas, crude oil, oil products, other liquid bulk goods. * Dry bulk: ores, coal, agricultural products (e.g. grain, soya, tapioca), other dry bulk goods. * Large containers: 20 ft freight units, 40 ft freight units, freight units > 20 ft and < 40 ft, freight units > 40 ft. * Ro-Ro mobile units: a) Mobile self-propelled units: road goods vehicles and accompanying trailers, passenger cars, motorcycles and accompanying trailers/caravans, passenger buses, trade vehicles (including import/export motor vehicles), live animals on the hoof, other mobile self-propelled units. b) Mobile non-self-propelled units: unaccompanied road goods trailers and semi-trailers, unaccompanied caravans and other road, agricultural and industrial vehicles, rail wagons, shipborne port-to-port trailers and shipborne barges engaged in goods transport, other mobile non-self-propelled units * Other cargo: forestry products, iron and steel products, other general cargo. The category 'large container' includes containers having a length of 20 feet or more. Smaller containers are included in the category 'other cargo'. As a general rule, the container figures are limited to lift-on lift-off containers (Lo-Lo). '''Transport calculation (Table 1 and Figure 10):''' In order to estimate maritime transport of goods between ports, the issue of 'double counting', the transport of the same goods being declared by both the port of loading (as outward movements) and the port of unloading (as inward movements) has to be addressed. Generally, when both the port of loading and the port of unloading are situated within the same statistical aggregate, only the incoming flows of goods declared by ports are summed up to determine the total maritime transport within the aggregate ('elimination of double counting'). The algorithm for the elimination of double counting is applied at statistical port level. Thus, the total maritime transport per country excludes the double counting of maritime transport within the country. Similarly, the total maritime transport for the EU excludes the double counting of national and international intra-EU maritime transport (see {{Template:Esms|code=mar_esms|title=metadata on the Eurostat website}} for more information). Please note that the recording of unknown ports of loading or unloading may have influenced the transport figure calculations, as well as the shares of maritime transport allocated to intra-EU, extra-EU and national maritime transport. '''Type of vessel (Figure 17):''' * Liquid bulk: oil tanker, chemical tanker, LG tanker, tanker barge, other tanker. * Dry bulk: bulk/oil carrier, bulk carrier. * Container: full container. * Cargo, specialised: barge carrier, chemical carrier, irradiated fuel, livestock carrier, vehicle carrier, other specialised. * Cargo, non-specialised: reefer, Ro-Ro passenger, Ro-Ro container, other Ro-Ro cargo, combination carrier general cargo/passenger, combination carrier general cargo/container, single-decker, multi-decker. * Passenger: passenger (excluding cruise passenger vessels). * Other: cruise ships, offshore supply, dry cargo barges, tugs, miscellaneous, unknown type of vessel. '''Special symbols used in the tables''' ':' not available '-' not applicable === Context === The content of this statistical article is based on data collected within the framework of the EU maritime transport statistics Directive, i.e. {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0042:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/42/EC}} of the European Parliament and of the Council of 6 May 2009 on statistical returns in respect of carriage of goods and passengers by sea (OJ L141 of 6.6.2009, page 29), which is a recast of the original {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31995L0064:EN:NOT|title=Council Directive 95/64 (EC)}} of 8 December 1995. The basic legal act ({{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0042:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/42/EC}}) was amended by: *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32010D0216:EN:NOT|title=Commission Decision 2010/216/EC}} of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 April 2010, OJ L 94, 15.4.2010, p. 33-40 *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32010R1090:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 1090/2010}} of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 November 2010, OJ L 325, 9.12.2010, p. 1-3 *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012D0186:EN:NOT|title=Commission Delegated Decision 2012/186/EU}} of 3 February 2012 OJ L 101 of 11.4.2012 pp. 5-14. The following legal acts include respectively the last official version of the list of ports and some dissemination aspects: *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32001D0423:EN:NOT|title=Commission Decision 2001/423/EC}} of 22 May 2001 (on dissemination) OJ L 151 of 07.06.2001 p. 41 *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018D1007:EN:NOT|title= Commission Delegated Decision (EU) 2018/1007}} of 25 April 2018 supplementing Directive 2009/42/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards the list of ports and repealing Commission Decision 2008/861/EC (Text with EEA relevance.) OJ L 180, 17.7.2018, p. 29–71 ===Other articles=== *[[Freight transport statistics - modal split]] *[[Maritime transport of goods - quarterly data]] *[[Maritime transport statistics - short sea shipping of goods]] ===Publications=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/publications All transport publications online] *{{Template:Publication|code= KS-01-24-021 |title=Key figures on European transport - 2024 edition}} ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/database Transport], see detailed datasets: :Maritime transport (mar) ::Maritime transport - main annual results (mar_m) ::Maritime transport - short sea shipping - main annual results (mar_s) ::Maritime transport - passengers (mar_pa) ::Maritime transport - goods (mar_go) ::Maritime transport - vessel traffic (mar_tf) ::Maritime transport - regional statistics (mar_rg) ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=transport}} Transport] ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=mar_esms|title=Maritime transport}} (ESMS metadata file — mar_esms) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/29567/3217334/Reference_Manual_Maritime_May_2023.pdf Reference Manual on Maritime Transport Statistics] *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-19-004|title=Glossary for transport statistics - 5th edition - 2019}} === Notes === {{Unit|topic=X_Transport}} [[Category:Transport|Maritime transport of goods - annual data]] [[Category:Maritime|Maritime transport of goods - annual data]] [[Category:Statistical article|Maritime transport of goods - annual data]] [[Category:December2026|Maritime transport of goods - annual data]]

title: Maritime transport of goods at port level - quarterly data
text:
Main results from quarterly statistics on maritime transport of goods in the European Union ports. Data extracted in March 2026 Planned article update: 25 September 2026 Rotterdam continues to lead the EU in port activity, with 99.0 million tonnes of goods handled in Q3 2025. [[Image: Top 5 EU maritime ports, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png |thumb|center|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/527298e8-8eb0-4781-a6ff-fb19141e7aeb?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-26T08:22:21Z mar_qg_qm_pwh])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the top five EU maritime ports as millions of tonnes. Each port, namely, Rotterdam, Antwerp-Bruges, Hamburg, Gdansk and HAROPA, has five columns representing the quarters Q3 2024 to Q3 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article presents quarterly statistics on maritime transport of goods in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] ports. It covers the [[Glossary:Gross_weight|gross weight]] of goods handled in the [[Glossary:Main_ports|main EU ports]], by type of cargo. The article contains data for Q3 2025. Please note that the quarterly port activity figures are provisional and subject to revision. === Rotterdam remained the EU port with the highest activity in Q3 2025 === Rotterdam was by far the EU port with the highest activity in Q3 2025, with 99.0 million tonnes of gross weight of goods handled (Figure 1). The second main port was Antwerp-Bruges, which handled 56.5 million tonnes. The third port was Hamburg with 25.3 million tonnes. The fourth and fifth ports were Gdansk and HAROPA, with 20.8 million tonnes and 20.5 million tonnes, respectively. Gdansk increased by 15.4% compared with Q3 2024. In the same period, 3 other ports in the top 5 increased: HAROPA by 9.2%, Hamburg by 4.3% and Rotterdam by 0.5%. On the opposite, Antwerp-Bruges is the only port of the top 5 which recorded a decrease compared with Q3 2024 (-2.7%). When looking at the overall annual change, 3 ports of the top 5 decreased: Antwerp-Bruges by 3.7%, Rotterdam by 2.2% and HAROPA by 1.7%. By contrast, Hamburg increased by 2.5% and Gdansk by 0.9%. [[Image: Top 5 EU maritime ports, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Top 5 EU maritime ports, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/527298e8-8eb0-4781-a6ff-fb19141e7aeb?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-26T08:22:21Z mar_qg_qm_pwh])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the top five EU maritime ports in millions of tonnes. Each port, namely, Rotterdam, Antwerp-Bruges, Hamburg, Gdansk and HAROPA, has five columns representing the quarters Q3 2024 to Q3 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at liquid bulk, Rotterdam was by far the main EU port in Q3 2025, followed by Antwerp-Bruges, Trieste, Marseille and HAROPA (Figure 2). Only Antwerp-Bruges decreased by 1.0% compared with the same quarter of the previous year. By contrast, Trieste registered the largest increase by 11.3%, followed by Marseille (+9.8%), HAROPA (+9.4%) and Rotterdam (+1.0%). When looking at the overall annual change rate compared with the previous period, Marseille increased by 8.1% and Trieste by 4.5%. By contrast, Antwerp-Bruges decreased by 14.2%, Rotterdam by 2.5% and HAROPA by 1.8%. [[Image: Top 5 EU maritime ports for liquid bulk, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Top 5 EU maritime ports for liquid bulk, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cf7ac881-0c96-4c30-b1ca-dac61df75215?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-26T08:26:08Z mar_qg_qm_pwhl])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the top five EU maritime ports for liquid bulk in millions of tonnes. Each port, namely, Rotterdam, Antwerp-Bruges, Trieste, Marseille and HAROPA, has five columns representing the quarters Q3 2024 to Q3 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at dry bulk, Rotterdam was again the main EU port in Q3 2025, followed by Amsterdam, Constanta, Zeeland Seaports and Hamburg (Figure 3). Compared with the same quarter of 2024, all of the top 5 increased: Zeeland Seaports by 21.7%, Constanta by 18.3%, Amsterdam by 4.8%, Hamburg by 4.4% and Rotterdam by 2.3%. When looking at the overall annual change rate compared with the previous period, 2 of the top 5 increased: Zeeland Seaports (+3.1%) and Amsterdam (+2.8%). By contrast, Constanta registered the largest decrease (-25.9%), Hamburg (-5.3%) and Rotterdam (-3.0%). [[Image: Top 5 EU maritime ports for dry bulk, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Top 5 EU maritime ports for dry bulk, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/eaac90a1-ca91-4e49-8aab-70abce9f1e8c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-26T08:28:34Z mar_qg_qm_pwhb])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the top five EU maritime ports for dry bulk in millions of tonnes. Each port, namely, Rotterdam, Amsterdam, Constanta, Zeeland Seaports and Hamburg, has five columns representing the quarters Q3 2024 to Q3 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In the large container cargo segment, Antwerp-Bruges remained the main EU port in Q3 2025, followed by Rotterdam. Hamburg, Valencia and Algeciras completing the top 5 EU ports (Figure 4). Four out of the 5 ports decreased compared with the same quarter of the previous year. The largest decrease was registered by Algeciras (-9.6%), leading to an overall annual change of -7.9%. Antwerp-Bruges decreased by 5.8% compared with the same quarter of the previous year, with an overall annual change of +2.7%. Valencia decreased by 4.4% compared with the same quarter of the previous year, with an overall annual change of -1.1%. Rotterdam decreased by 1.4% compared with the same quarter of the previous year, with an overall annual change of -1.4%. Compared with the same quarter of the previous year, there was a 4.5% increase in Hamburg, with an overall annual change of +5.5%. [[Image: Top 5 EU maritime ports for large containers, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Top 5 EU maritime ports for large containers, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/888c61d6-4dc4-431d-b246-a876030a011f?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-26T08:30:27Z mar_qg_qm_pwhc])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the top five EU maritime ports for large containers in millions of tonnes. Each port, namely Antwerp-Bruges, Rotterdam, Hamburg, Valencia and Algeciras, has five columns representing the quarters Q3 2024 to Q3 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at the number of [[Glossary:Twenty-foot_equivalent_unit_(TEU)|twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs)]] handled in the same period (Figure 5), the ranking was different to the one based on tonnes of containerised goods. Indeed, Rotterdam took the first place in front of Antwerp-Bruges. Four out of the 5 ports increased in Q3 2025 compared with the same quarter of 2024: Algeciras (+11.9%), Hamburg (+11.1%), Rotterdam (+3.4%) and Valencia (+3.4%). By contrast, Antwerp-Bruges decreased by 3.9% in Q3 2025 compared with the same quarter of 2024. Regarding the overall annual change compared with the previous period, Hamburg recorded the highest increase (+9.0%), followed by Valencia (+4.9%), Rotterdam and Antwerp-Bruges (+3.9% both) and Algeciras (+2.7%). [[Image: Top 5 EU maritime ports for large containers, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025 (thousand TEUs).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Top 5 EU maritime ports for large containers, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/686c0b3d-fb50-4fcb-a4cb-2927a9235b51?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-26T08:32:15Z mar_qg_qm_pvh])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the top five EU maritime ports for large containers in thousands of TEUs. Each port, namely Rotterdam, Antwerp-Bruges, Hamburg, Algeciras and Valencia, has five columns representing the quarters Q3 2024 to Q3 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at the tonnage of Ro-Ro mobile units, the picture is different compared with the other types of cargo. Antwerp-Bruges was the largest EU Ro-Ro port in Q3 2025. It was followed by Rotterdam, Calais, Dublin and Lubeck (Figure 6). Compared with the same quarter of 2024, all ports from the top 5 increased. Antwerp-Bruges recorded the highest increase by 4.2%, followed by Lubeck (+2.5%), Calais (+1.6%), Dublin (+0.7%) and Rotterdam (+0.4%). When looking at the overall annual change compared with the previous period, the same 3 ports decreased: Dublin (-2.9%), Calais (-2.0%) and Rotterdam (-0.1%). On the other hand, Lubeck increased by 2.7% and Antwerp-Bruges by 1.0%. [[Image: Top 5 EU maritime ports for Ro-Ro mobile units, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Top 5 EU maritime ports for Ro-Ro mobile units, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/69cd2e0b-533e-4a23-8f6b-339165265c65?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-26T08:36:17Z mar_qg_qm_pwhr]) |alt= Vertical bar chart showing the top five EU maritime ports for Ro-Ro mobile units in millions of tonnes. Each port, namely Antwerp-Bruges, Rotterdam, Calais, Dublin and Lubeck, has five columns representing the quarters Q3 2024 to Q3 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at the tonnes for other general cargo, Antwerp-Bruges ranked first in Q3 2025, followed by Valencia, Rotterdam, Ravenna and Amsterdam (Figure 7). Ravenna decreased substantially compared with the same quarter of 2024, by 16.3%. Rotterdam recorded a lower decrease compared with the same quarter of 2024 (-1.8%). By contrast, Antwerp-Bruges increased by 8.3% over the same period, followed by Amsterdam (+5.9%) and Valencia (+1.8%). When looking at the overall annual change rates compared with the previous period, Rotterdam decreased by 2.7%, Valencia by 0.9%, Amsterdam by 0.6% and Ravenna by 0.2%. By contrast, only Antwerp-Bruges registered a increase by 4.3%. [[Image: Top 5 EU maritime ports for other general cargo, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025 (million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 7: Top 5 EU maritime ports for other general cargo, Q3 2024 - Q3 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fcfca013-b7c4-4f2d-890d-402446496292?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-26T08:38:00Z mar_qg_qm_pwho])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the top five EU maritime ports for other general cargo in millions of tonnes. Each port, namely Antwerp-Bruges, Valencia, Rotterdam, Ravenna and Amsterdam, has five columns representing the quarters Q3 2024 to Q3 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Maritime transport of goods EU 2025Q3-Ports.xlsx|title=Maritime transport of goods at port level - quarterly data: tables and figures}} === Data sources and availability === The content of this statistical article is based on data collected within the framework of the EU maritime transport statistics {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0042:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/42/EC}} on statistical returns in respect of carriage of goods and passengers by sea. Data are presented at the level of '[[Glossary:Statistical_port|statistical ports]]'. A statistical port consists of 1 or more ports, normally controlled by a single port authority, able to record ship and cargo movements. All figures are based on a port's total (inward + outward) declarations. The results represent the 'handling' of goods in ports. # '''Type of cargo''': the following 13 cargo types are used: liquefied gas, crude oil, oil products, other liquid bulk goods, ores, coal, agricultural products, other dry bulk goods, large containers, Ro-Ro mobile units, forestry products, iron/steel products and other general cargo. The first 4 types constitute 'liquid bulk', the subsequent 4 types 'dry bulk' and the last 3 types 'other general cargo not elsewhere specified'. '''Abbreviations''' {| style="background-color: #f5faff; vertical-align: top" class="wikitable" |- |:|| not available |- | -|| not applicable |- | Nes|| Not elsewhere specified |- | Ro-Ro|| Roll-on/roll-off |- | TEU || Twenty-foot Equivalent Unit |} '''Quarterly data''' are in general provisional. Revisions may be made by countries as more complete information becomes available or as a result of quality checks. More specifically, when the complete set of annual data emerges, this usually involves some revision of quarterly data for some countries. The basic results (in million tonnes) and the derived indicators (growth rates) shown in the figures are rounded. However, they are all based on non-rounded original data, as available in Eurostat's database. '''Specific remarks''' for data up to and including Q3 2025: * Starting from Q1 2022, the ports Antwerpen and Zeebrugge have been merged and the data are reported under the new port name Antwerp-Bruges. * Starting from Q1 2022, the ports Le Havre and Rouen have been merged and the data are reported under the new port name HAROPA. Due to revisions of the underlying data, figures in this article may differ from figures currently or previously available on Eurostat's website. ===Context=== The content of this statistical article is based on data collected within the framework of the EU maritime transport statistics {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0042:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/42/EC}} of 6 May 2009 on statistical returns in respect of carriage of goods and passengers by sea, which is a recast of the original Council {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31995L0064:EN:NOT|title=Directive 95/64/EC}} of 8 December 1995. ===Other articles=== *[[Maritime transport of goods -
