The following legal acts include the last official version of the list of ports and some dissemination aspects, respectively: *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32001D0423:EN:NOT|title=Commission Decision 2001/423/EC}} of 22 May 2001 (on dissemination) OJ L 151 of 07.06.2001 p. 41 *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018D1007:EN:NOT|title=Commission Delegated Decision (EU) 2018/1007}} of 25 April 2018 supplementing Directive 2009/42/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council as regards the list of ports and repealing Commission Decision 2008/861/EC (Text with EEA relevance.), OJ L 180, 17.7.2018, p. 29–71 {{Unit|topic=X_Transport}} [[Category:Transport|Maritime transport of goods at port level - quarterly data]] [[Category:Freight|Maritime transport of goods at port level - quarterly data]] [[Category:Maritime|Maritime transport of goods at port level - quarterly data]] [[Category:Statistical article|Maritime transport of goods at port level - quarterly data]] [[Category:September2026|Maritime transport of goods at port level - quarterly data]]

title: Maritime transport statistics - short sea shipping of goods
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the short sea shipping of goods. Data from March 2026 Planned update of the article: March 2027 The total gross weight of goods transported as part of EU short sea shipping was estimated at more than 1.6 billion tonnes in 2024. Italy was the main short sea shipping country in the EU in 2024, with a share of 15.6% of the total EU short sea shipping tonnage. |alt=a dynamic vertical bar chart with three bars showing the short sea shipping of freight in the years, 2014, 2023 and 2024. This article presents recent [[Glossary:Short sea shipping|short sea shipping]] (SSS) statistics of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], covering the transport of goods between [[Glossary:Main ports|main ports]] in the [[Glossary:EU|EU Member States]] and ports situated in geographical Europe or in non-European countries on the Mediterranean Sea and the Black Sea. In addition to the EU Member States, short sea shipping statistics are also available for main ports in the [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA country]] Norway and the [[Glossary:candidate_countries|candidate countries]] Montenegro and Türkiye. The results are broken down by country, sea region and type of cargo. It should be noted that the figures presented in this article are influenced by variations in the level of transport reported with unknown partner ports (see methodological notes). ===EU short sea shipping increased by 3.1% in 2024 compared with 2023=== The overall increase in short sea shipping recorded by the main EU ports consolidated the gradual recovery seen in EU short sea shipping following the economic downturn in Europe in 2009 and reached a new high in 2019 (Figure 1). However, this positive trend was put to an end in 2020 most probably because of the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent restrictions put in place in the EU and worldwide. In 2021, a partial recovery was observed. In 2022 and 2023, there were 2 consecutive drops, reaching a low point but still 3.6% higher than in 2009. The total [[Glossary:Gross weight|gross weight of goods]] transported as part of EU short sea shipping was estimated at more than 1.6 billion tonnes in 2024, an increase of 3.1% from the previous year. [[Image: Gross weight of seaborne freight transported to_from main ports by type of shipping, EU, 2008-2024_(million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px| Figure 1: Gross weight of seaborne freight transported to/from main ports by type of shipping, EU, 2008-2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ff121e8a-21e7-440a-8723-6d8d6d7f4aeb?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:10:42Z mar_sg_am_cw])|alt= a line chart with two lines showing the gross weight of seaborne freight transported to and from main ports by type of shipping in the EU from the year 2008 to 2024. The lines show short sea shipping and other seaborne transport. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Short sea shipping made up 58.3% of the total sea transport of goods to and from the main EU ports in 2024, 1.9 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] more compared with 2023. When looking at the reporting countries, the share of short sea shipping in total sea transport varies considerably. The predominance of short sea shipping of goods over [[Glossary:Deep sea shipping|deep sea shipping]] was particularly pronounced in Estonia, Cyprus, Finland, Sweden, Ireland, Malta, Denmark, Lithuania, Greece, Italy, Poland, Bulgaria, Latvia and Croatia, and as well as in the EFTA country Norway and in the candidate countries Montenegro and Türkiye, all with short sea shipping shares of 70% or more in their main ports (Figure 2). [[Image: Short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport, 2024_(%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport, 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f2939a0c-c926-4cd7-a6a8-68457843cc7c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:12:49Z mar_sg_am_cw])|alt=a vertical stacked bar chart showing the share of short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport in 2024, in the EU, EU Member States some EFTA countries and some candidate countries. The stacks show short sea shipping and other seaborne transport. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Geographical considerations, such as long coastlines or many inhabited islands, play a part in explaining the high share of short sea shipping in most of these countries. A large volume of [[Glossary:Feeder_services|feeder services]] to or from [[Glossary:Hub_port|hub ports]] also explains the high degree of short sea shipping transport in countries which function as regional trans-shipment points. By contrast, the share of short sea shipping is lower in countries with major ports focused on intercontinental trade. In 2024, it was lower than 64% in Romania, Portugal, Germany, Slovenia, France, Belgium, Spain and the Netherlands. ===Italy, the Netherlands and Spain accounted for 39.2% of EU short sea shipping in 2024=== Italy was the major short sea shipping country in the EU in 2024, with 304 million tonnes, representing a share of 15.6% of the total tonnages of EU short sea shipping in 2024. The Netherlands followed with 239 million tonnes and then Spain with 221 million tonnes of short shipped goods recorded in their main ports (Figure 3). [[Image: Short sea shipping of freight, 2014, 2023 and 2024_(million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Short sea shipping of freight, 2014, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/30e0d921-7dd4-4edf-8690-fcc2957f4e0b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:13:29Z mar_sg_am_cw])|alt= a vertical bar chart with three bars showing short sea shipping of freight in the years 2014, 2023 and 2024, in the EU Member States some EFTA countries and some candidate countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among the EU countries, 13 out of 22 registered a growth in short sea shipping between 2023 and 2024. The largest relative increase was recorded by Lithuania (+12.9%), followed by Portugal (+8.8%) and Slovenia (+7.3%). By contrast, the largest relative decreases in short sea shipping among the EU countries were recorded by Malta (-39.1%), Croatia (-9.1%) and Romania (-6.3%). The candidate country Montenegro also recorded a noticeable drop by 9.6%. In 2024, inward movements accounted for 57.8% of the total tonnes of goods handled in the EU ports that were involved in short sea shipping transport (Figure 4). More seaborne goods were unloaded from than loaded onto vessels in most EU countries. Malta, Cyprus and Poland had the highest shares of unloaded goods in 2024, with respective shares of 90.3%, 82.6% and 70.1% of the total tonnes of short sea shipped goods recorded as inward movements to their ports. By contrast, Latvia, Estonia, Bulgaria and the EFTA country Norway had more outward movements of short sea shipped goods than inwards movements. [[Image: Short sea shipping of freight by direction, 2024_(%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Short sea shipping of freight by direction, 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2de91fda-1356-42fc-9b5c-cf7a0452b538?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:14:12Z mar_sg_am_cwd])|alt= a vertical stacked bar chat showing short sea shipping of freight by direction in 2024 in the EU, EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries, the stacks show inwards and outwards. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The short sea shipping of goods between main EU ports and ports located in the Mediterranean Sea reached 647 million tonnes in 2024. This accounted to 35.7% of the total EU short sea shipping tonnages for all sea regions in 2024. The Mediterranean Sea was followed by the North Sea and the Baltic Sea, with shares of 26.1% and 16.2% of the total EU short shipping tonnages, respectively (Figure 5). [[Image: Short sea shipping of freight by sea region of partner ports, 2024_(%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px| Figure 5: Short sea shipping of freight by sea region of partner ports, 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1f75dd82-7ed5-4425-bacd-667ec939c603?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:14:58Z mar_sg_am_cws])|alt=a stacked vertical bar chart showing the short sea shipping of freight by sea region of partner ports in 2024 in the EU, EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries. The stacks show the Atlantic Ocean, Black Sea, Mediterranean Sea, North Sea and others. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] For most countries, the highest share of their short sea shipping of goods was with partner ports located in the same sea region or sea regions. There are some exceptions, like Poland and Romania. Poland is located on the Baltic Sea, but a majority (51.7%) of the short sea shipping of goods came from or was destined for ports located on the North Sea. Romania is located on the Black Sea, but a majority (60.2%) of the short sea shipping of goods came from or was destined for ports located on the Mediterranean Sea. By comparison, countries with large ports that act as hub ports or trans-shipment points will tend to have substantial short sea shipping with ports in several sea regions. === Liquid bulk remained the dominant type of cargo in EU short sea shipping === As in previous years, liquid bulk remained the dominant type of cargo in EU short sea shipping. At 640 million tonnes, liquid bulk accounted for 38.9% of the total short sea shipping of goods to and from main EU ports in 2024 (Figure 6). Liquid bulk was followed by dry bulk at 335 million tonnes (20.3%), containers at 294 million tonnes (17.9%) and [[Glossary:Roll on - roll off|roll on - roll off (Ro-Ro)]] units at 275 million tonnes (16.7%). For liquid bulk, Italy had the largest volume of short sea shipping in 2024 (132 million tonnes), followed by the Netherlands (120 million tonnes). The Netherlands led the EU rankings for short sea shipping of dry bulk goods (49 million tonnes). Italy was the main country in terms of short sea shipping of goods in containers (68 million tonnes) and also in terms of Ro-Ro units (59 million tonnes). [[Image: Short sea shipping of freight by type of cargo, 2024_(%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Short sea shipping of freight by type of cargo, 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/18212fd5-3c08-4964-8d60-239e7e44d522?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:15:53Z mar_sg_am_cwk])|alt=a stacked vertical bar chart showing Short sea shipping of freight by type of cargo, in 2024, in the EU, EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries. The stacks show liquid bulk, dry bulk, containers, Ro-Ro units, other cargo. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Short sea shipping of liquid bulk goods was dominant in almost all sea regions in 2024, even though the composition of the short sea shipping cargo varies among the sea regions. The exception concerns the Baltic Sea for Ro-Ro units. While liquid bulk goods accounted for 48.3% of total short sea shipping of goods in the Black Sea, the comparable figure for the Atlantic Ocean was only 32.2% of the total. By contrast, the share of dry bulk goods in the short sea shipping of each sea region is more evenly distributed, with a range from 14.0% in the Mediterranean Sea to 40.7% in the Black Sea (Figure 7). [[Image: Short sea shipping of freight by type of cargo for each sea region of partner ports, EU, 2024_(%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 7: Short sea shipping of freight by type of cargo for each sea region of partner ports, EU, 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/04ba3c59-34f3-48ab-89b0-a7b9c4c45b9b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:16:22Z mar_sg_am_ewx])|alt= a stacked bar chart showing short sea shipping of freight by type of cargo for each sea region of partner ports in the EU in the year 2024. The stacks show liquid bulk, dry bulk, containers, Ro-Ro units, other cargo. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Goods transported in containers accounted for 24.4% of the short sea cargo in the Mediterranean Sea in 2024, while it only made up 7.3% of short sea shipping in the Black Sea. Similarly, goods transported on Ro-Ro units accounted for 28.9% of short sea shipping in the Baltic Sea. By contrast, short sea shipping of goods on Ro-Ro units was barely registered in the Black Sea (0.5%). === Short sea shipping of containers in the main EU ports reached a peak in 2024=== In terms of number of twenty-foot equivalent units [[Glossary:Twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU)|(TEUs)]], short sea shipping of containers in the main EU ports reached a peak in 2024, at 36.4 million TEUs, after an increase by 8.9% compared with 2023. Loaded containers increased by 8.2%, to 29.0 million TEUs, in 2024, compared with the previous year, transport of empty containers increased by 11.8% to 7.4 million TEUs (Figure 8). Please note that the figures and growth rates may be influenced by changes in data quality for certain countries (see methodological notes). [[Image: Short sea shipping of containers by loading status, EU, 2008-2024_(million TEUs).png|thumb|center|700px| Figure 8: Short sea shipping of containers by loading status, EU, 2008-2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/20be7cde-8f52-4d04-869f-42667373ffb9?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:18:00Z mar_sg_am_cv])|alt= a line chart with two lines showing the short sea shipping of containers by loading status in the EU from the year 2008 to the year 2024, the lines show loaded and empty. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, Italy was the major country for short sea shipped goods in containers in the EU, with 9.1 million TEUs. Spain followed with 6.6 million TEUs and then Germany with 5.1 million TEUs recorded in their main ports (Figure 9). Decreases in 2024 compared with 2024 were observed in 4 out of the 22 maritime EU countries. The highest decrease was observed for Malta (-14.3%), followed by Sweden (-4.3%), Italy (-1.4%) and Romania (-1.0%). By contrast, Denmark (+45.5%), Spain (+21.7%), Slovenia (+19.2%), Estonia (+18.2%), Latvia (+17.4%), Germany (+14.8%), Belgium (+12.6%), Portugal (+11.9%), Ireland (+10.5%) and Greece (+10.0%) recorded substantial growth in short sea shipping of containers (in TEUs) compared with 2023. [[Image: Short sea shipping of containers, 2014, 2023 and 2024_(million TEUs).png |thumb|center|700px| Figure 9: Short sea shipping of containers, 2014, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/708802be-01d9-4931-af9d-79ba746a5d20?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:18:52Z mar_sg_am_cv])|alt=a vertical bar chart with three bars showing the short sea shipping of containers for the years 2014, 2023 and 2024 in the EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] At EU level, the loaded containers represented 79.8% of all containers short sea shipped (in TEUs) in 2024 (Figure 10). All reporting countries transported more loaded containers than empty ones. Malta had the highest share of loaded containers (97.9%), followed by Italy (91.7%) while Cyprus had the lowest (60.8%). [[Image: Short sea shipping of containers by loading status, 2024_(%, based on TEUs).png|thumb|center|700px| Figure 10: Short sea shipping of containers by loading status, 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4d6d8441-6030-41d3-86b5-449206714984?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:19:18Z mar_sg_am_cv)]|alt= a vertical bar chart showing the short sea shipping of containers by loading status in the year 2023 in the EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Maritime transport short sea shipping 2026-03.xlsx |Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== The statistics in this article are based on data collected under {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0042:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/42/EC}} of 6 May 2009 on statistical returns in respect of carriage of goods and passengers by sea. The relevant data on port of loading and unloading of the goods is mainly collected for [[Glossary:Main_ports| main ports]], passengers by sea. The relevant data on port of loading and unloading of the goods is mainly collected for main ports, which are defined as ports handling more than one million tonnes of goods annually. Data are collected at level of [[Glossary:Statistical port|statistical ports]]. The [[Glossary:Short_sea_shipping|short sea shipping (SSS)]] statistics present seaborne transport of goods between *main ports in the [[Glossary:Coastal_Member_States|maritime EU Member States]] *main ports in the maritime EU Member States and non-EU partner ports situated in geographical Europe or in non-European countries on the Mediterranean and on the Black Sea. In consequence, the article covers short sea shipping of goods to and from main ports in the 22 maritime EU Member States (Czechia, Luxembourg, Hungary, Austria and Slovakia have no maritime ports). The partner ports are situated *in the maritime EU Member States *in the maritime [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA countries]] Iceland and Norway *in the maritime [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]] Albania, Georgia, Moldova, Montenegro, Türkiye and Ukraine *in the United Kingdom (European ports) *on the Baltic Sea (Russia) *on the Mediterranean (Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Occupied Palestinian territories, Syria, and Tunisia) *on the Black Sea (Georgia, Moldova, Russia and Ukraine). In addition to the maritime EU Member States, similar short sea shipping statistics are also available for seaborne transport to and from main ports in Norway, Montenegro and Türkiye. The definition of short sea shipping is derived from the Communication of the Commission COM (1999) 317 on the development of Short Sea Shipping in Europe. In consequence, the concept of short sea shipping includes both regular short sea shipping and feeder services (short sea shipping between ports for freight to be consolidated or redistributed to or from a deep sea service in one of the ports in a network [hub ports]). The category other seaborne transport in the tables and figures includes both deep sea shipping and transport with unidentified partner ports (unknown ports). '''Sea regions''' The following sea regions have been taken into account to group the short sea shipping partner ports: the Baltic, the North Sea, the Atlantic Ocean (including the English Channel and the Irish Sea), the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. '''1. The Baltic''': *Danish ports below the Helsingborg–Korsør–Nyborg–Kolding line (including Helsingør). *All ports of Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland as well as German and Russian ports on the Baltic. *The Swedish ports on the Baltic from Helsingborg (included). '''2. The North Sea''': *All ports of Norway, the Netherlands and Belgium as well as the ports of Germany on the North Sea. *Swedish ports on the North Sea from Helsingborg (excluded). *Danish ports on north of the Helsingborg–Korsor–Nyborg–Kolding line and North Denmark (excluding Helsingør). Faroe Islands. *United Kingdom: ports on the east coast of Great Britain from Ramsgate (included) to Cape Wrath in Scotland, the Shetland Islands and Orkney Islands. '''3. The Atlantic Ocean''': *All ports of Ireland, Portugal (including Açores and Madeira) and Iceland. *French ports on the Atlantic Ocean and on the Channel, up to the Belgian border. *Spanish ports on the Atlantic Ocean to Tarifa (included); Canary Islands are included. *United Kingdom: ports of Great Britain on the Channel (from Ramsgate excluded) and the west coast to Cape Wrath in Scotland; ports in Northern Ireland. '''4. The Mediterranean''': *Spanish ports on the Mediterranean from Tarifa (excluded). *French ports on the Mediterranean. *All ports of Malta, Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Montenegro, Albania, Greece, Cyprus, Syria, Lebanon, Occupied Palestinian territory, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria and Gibraltar. *Ports of Morocco, Egypt and Israel on the Mediterranean. *Ports of Türkiye on the Mediterranean (including the ports on the Bosporus). '''5. The Black Sea''': *All Black Sea ports excluding the ports on the Bosporus. '''6. Others''': *Non-identified ports of Denmark, Germany, Spain, France, Sweden, the United Kingdom, Israel, Morocco, Russia, Türkiye and Egypt; river ports of EU countries. Please note that ports located in Morocco–West Africa, Egypt–Red Sea, Israel–Red Sea and Russia–Barents and White Seas are not part of the European short sea shipping area. '''Comparability over time and between countries''' '''Exclusion of double counting''' All the results shown in this publication are calculated based on the statistics declared by main ports vis-à-vis their partner ports. To estimate the seaborne transport of goods between the ports, any double counting of the same cargo being declared by both the port of loading as outward movements of goods and the port of unloading as inwards movements of goods has to be excluded. In cases where data is collected for both the port of loading and the port of unloading, the double counting is excluded by only taking the inwards movements in ports into account when calculating the total transport on the maritime routes in question. The algorithm for this exclusion of double counting is applied at statistical port level. The total SSS per country excludes the double counting in the national transport declarations. The total SSS for the EU excludes the double counting of national and international intra-EU transport declarations. The total aggregates per country may therefore differ from the sum of inwards and outwards declarations for the country. Similarly, the total aggregates for the EU may differ from the sum of inwards and outwards declarations and from the sum of the country totals. '''Specific remarks on figures''' '''Figures 1 and 2:''' The category 'other seaborne transport' includes both deep sea shipping and transport with unidentified partner ports (unknown ports). It should be noted that the share of unknown partner ports in the total seaborne transport, at EU level, was 2% between 2008 and 2014, 2019, 2023 and 2024, 3% in 2015 and 2018, 1% in 2020 and 2021 and 4% in 2016, 2017 and 2022. '''Figures 6 and 7:''' * Liquid bulk: liquefied gas, crude oil, oil products and other liquid bulk goods. * Dry bulk: ores, coal, agricultural products (e.g. grain, soya, tapioca), other dry bulk goods. * Large containers: 20 ft freight units, 40 ft freight units, freight units > 20 ft and < 40 ft, freight units > 40 ft. * Ro-Ro mobile units: a) Mobile self-propelled units: road goods vehicles and accompanying trailers, passenger cars, motorcycles and accompanying trailers/caravans, passenger buses, trade vehicles (including import/export motor vehicles), live animals on the hoof, other mobile self-propelled units. b) Mobile non-self-propelled units: unaccompanied road goods trailers and semi-trailers, unaccompanied caravans and other road, agricultural and industrial vehicles, rail wagons, shipborne port-to-port trailers and shipborne barges engaged in goods transport, other mobile non-self-propelled units. * Other cargo: forestry products, iron and steel products, other general cargo. The category 'other cargo' includes data for unknown type of cargo. '''Figure 8:''' At EU level, the share of unknown partner ports in the total seaborne transport of containers, based on TEUs, was 3% in 2009 and 2010, 4% in 2008, between 2015 and 2018, 2020 and 2021, 5% in 2011, 2019 and 2023, 6% in 2022 and 2024, 7% in 2012, 8% in 2013 and 2014. '''Country specific remarks''' Explanatory notes for countries are available in the metadata on the Eurostat website. Additional information related to this article are mentioned hereafter. Significant shares of declarations to and from unknown partner ports have several consequences: the volume of SSS and its share in total seaborne transport are probably underestimated and the change rates of SSS may not be reliable. '''Spain (ES)''' The share of declarations to and from unknown partner ports was 4% in 2014 while it was less than 0.5% in 2023 and 2024. For container statistics, the share of unknown partner ports was 7% in 2014 and 2023 and 9% in 2024. '''France (FR)''' Taking into account the definition of European short sea shipping, the figures do not include transport with the French overseas territories (Départements d'Outre Mer/Collectivités d'Outre Mer). The quarterly data for port activity in France have been partially estimated by Eurostat for the period 2009-2016. The data reported by France contain a significant share of declarations to and from unknown partner ports in 2023 (11%) and 2024 (9%). This share was 3% in 2014. For container statistics, the share of unknown partner ports was 5% in 2014, 15% in 2023 and 19% in 2024. '''Netherlands (NL)''' For container statistics, the share of unknown partner ports was significant in 2014 (41%). This share was 18% in 2023 and 2024. '''Sweden (SE)''' For container statistics, the share of unknown partner ports was 8% in 2023 and 7% in 2024, while it was less than 1% in 2014. ===Context=== The content of this statistical article is based on data collected under the EU maritime transport statistics Directive ({{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0042:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/42/EC}} of 6 May 2009 on statistical returns in respect of carriage of goods and passengers by sea), which is a recast of the original Council {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31995L0064:EN:NOT|title=Directive 95/64/EC}} of 8 December 1995. The basic legal act (Directive 2009/42/EC) was amended by: *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32010D0216:EN:NOT|title=Commission Decision 2010/216/EC}} of 14 April 2010 OJ L 94 of 15.4.2010 pp. 33-40 *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32010R1090:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 1090/2010}} of 24 November 2010 OJ L 325 of 09.12.2010 pp. 1-3 *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012D0186:EN:NOT|title=Commission Delegated Decision 2012/186/EU}} of 3 February 2012 OJ L 101 of 11.4.2012 pp. 5-14. The following legal acts include respectively the last official version of the list of ports and several dissemination aspects: *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018D1007:EN:NOT|title=Commission Delegated Decision (EU) 2018/1007}} of 25 April 2018 (Port list) OJ L 180 of 17.7.2018 pp. 29-71 *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32001D0423:EN:NOT|title=Commission Decision 2001/423/EC}} of 22 May 2001 (on dissemination) OJ L 151 of 07.06.2001 p. 41 ===Other Articles=== *[[Freight transport statistics - modal split]] *[[Maritime vessels statistics]] *[[Maritime transport of goods - quarterly data]] *[[Maritime transport of goods at port level - quarterly data]] *[[Maritime transport statistics - short sea shipping of goods at port level]] ===Publications=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/publications All transport publications online] *{{Template:Publication|code= KS-01-25-057 |title=Key figures on European transport - title: Maritime transport statistics - short sea shipping of goods at port level
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the short sea shipping of goods at port level. Data from March 2026 Planned update of the article: March 2027 The top 20 EU ports accounted for 42.1% of EU short sea shipping in 2024. In 2024, the top 5 ports for containers handled 41.9% of the total short sea shipped container goods in main EU ports, in terms of gross weight of goods. [[Image: Top 20 short sea shipping EU ports, 2014, 2023 and 2024_(million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a9a0cd02-7935-44f6-a83b-bd3062f4acc8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:20:39Z mar_sg_am_pw]) |alt=a bar chart with three bars showing the top 20 short sea shipping EU ports in the years 2014, 2023 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article presents recent [[Glossary:Short sea shipping|short sea shipping]] (SSS) statistics in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] ports, covering the transport of goods between [[Glossary:Main ports|main ports]] in the [[Glossary:EU|EU countries]] and ports situated in geographical Europe or in non-European countries on the Mediterranean Sea and the Black Sea. The results are broken down by type of cargo. Unlike statistics presented in the article [[Maritime transport statistics - short sea shipping of goods]], the figures at port level presented hereafter do not estimate the seaborne transport of goods between the main EU ports and their partner ports in the short sea shipping area (where double-counting is excluded), but present the handling of short sea shipped goods in the main EU ports. === The top 20 EU ports accounted for 42.1% of EU short sea shipping in 2024 === The top 20 ports accounted for 42.1% of the total short sea shipped goods handled in the main EU ports in 2024. Rotterdam remained the largest EU port for short sea shipping, handling a total of 161 million tonnes of short sea shipped goods in 2024. Among the other top 3 ports, Antwerp-BrugesStarting from the first quarter of 2022, the ports of Antwerpen and Zeebrugge have been merged and the data are reported under the new port name Antwerp-Bruges. handled 122 million tonnes of short shipped goods in 2024 and Gdansk handled 59 million tonnes (Figure 1). Amongst the top 20 EU ports, 4 registered a decrease in 2024 compared with 2023. Constanta reported the highest fall, with -6.1%, followed by Marseille (-6.0%), Gdansk (-3.2%) and HAROPAStarting from the first quarter of 2022, Le Havre and Rouen have been merged and the data are reported under the new port name HAROPA. (-1.4%). By contrast, Barcelona (+16.1%) reported the highest increase over the same period and was followed by Valencia (+12.9%), Gioia Tauro and Bremerhaven (both +11.3%), Klaipeda (+10.6%) and Göteborg (+10.0%). [[Image: Top 20 short sea shipping EU ports, 2014, 2023 and 2024_(million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Top 20 short sea shipping EU ports, 2014, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a9a0cd02-7935-44f6-a83b-bd3062f4acc8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:20:39Z mar_sg_am_pw]) |alt=a bar chart with three bars showing the top 20 short sea shipping EU ports in the years 2014, 2023 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Amongst the top 20 EU ports, 5 ports, Rotterdam, Antwerp-Bruges, Hamburg, HAROPA and Barcelona, handled more deep sea shipping than short sea shipping of goods. By contrast, all the other top 20 ports for short sea shipping handled more short sea than deep sea shipped goods (Figure 2). In particular, 98.5% of the goods handled in the port of Dublin were short sea shipped. [[Image: Short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 20 short sea shipping EU ports, 2024_(%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 20 short sea shipping EU ports, 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/979964c9-6b0e-4432-8669-4d7b393c4af5?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:21:08Z mar_sg_am_pw])|alt=a horizontal stacked bar chart showing short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 20 short sea shipping EU ports in the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Rotterdam handled 11.6% of the total short sea shipped liquid bulk goods reported by the main EU ports in 2024 === At 91 million tonnes, Rotterdam handled 11.6% of the total short sea shipped liquid bulk goods reported by the main EU ports in 2024, by far the largest volume of short sea shipped liquid bulk for any EU port (Figure 3). With 34 million tonnes each, Gdansk and Trieste were the only ports the top 5 recording an increase (+7.8% and +7.6%, respectively) in 2024, compared with 2023. [[Image: Top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for liquid bulk, 2014, 2023 and 2024_(million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for liquid bulk, 2014, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f25e5628-77e0-43d6-8818-1ef6b996560e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:21:36Z mar_sg_am_pwl])|alt=a horizontal bar chart with three bars showing the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for liquid bulk for the years 2014, 2023 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, the share of short sea shipped liquid bulk on the total sea transport of liquid bulk was particularly pronounced in the ports of Gdansk (86.7%) and Trieste (82.2%), see Figure 4. [[Image: Short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for liquid bulk, 2024_(%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for liquid bulk, 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/280c7793-8d84-441f-a276-2f1500bade43?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:21:58Z mar_sg_am_pwl])|alt= a horizontal stacked bar chart showing the short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for liquid bulk in the year 2023. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Amsterdam was the EU’s largest port for short sea shipping of dry bulk goods === Constanţa lost its position as the largest port for short sea shipping of dry bulk goods attained in 2023 after a large drop of 28.4% in 2024 compared to the previous year (Figure 5). Constanţa was overpassed by Amsterdam (18 million tonnes) and Rotterdam (16 million tonnes) . All the other ports of the top 5 recorded large increases compared with the previous year (more than 10%). [[Image: Top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for dry bulk, 2014, 2023 and 2024 (million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for dry bulk, 2014, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6c51203c-ad2a-49de-bac1-133ec62c319f?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:22:20Z mar_sg_am_pwb])|alt= a horizontal bar chart with three bars showing the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for dry bulk for the years 2014, 2023 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, the share of short sea shipped dry bulk on the total sea transport of dry bulk was higher than 50% in Gent (Ghent) (53.7%), Constanţa (53.2%) and Zeeland Seaports (52.4%). In Rotterdam, the share was 23.7% while in Amsterdam it was 48.9% (Figure 6). [[Image: Short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for dry bulk, 2024_(%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for dry bulk, 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9be004fb-4e46-4886-bd68-2208a4c455fa?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:22:41Z mar_sg_am_pwb])|alt= a horizontal stacked bar chart showing the short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for dry bulk in the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === The top 5 ports for containers handled 41.9% of the total short sea shipped container goods in main EU ports=== Antwerp-Bruges and Rotterdam were the EU’s 2 largest ports for short sea shipped goods in containers with 43 and 33 million tonnes in 2024, respectively (Figure 7). Altogether, the 2 ports represented 20.9% of total short sea shipped goods in containers reported by the main EU ports in 2024. All top 5 ports registered increases between 2023 and 2024. The largest growth was recorded by Antwerp-Bruges (+14.3%), followed by Hamburg (+10.8%) and Gioia Tauro (+10.2%). Unlike dry bulk segment, for instance, short sea shipping of goods in containers is concentrated around a limited number of main hub ports. In 2024, the top 5 ports for containers handled 41.9% of the total short sea shipped container goods in main EU ports, in terms of gross weight of goods. [[Image: Top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for containers, 2014, 2023 and 2024 (million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 7: Top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for containers, 2014, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3df16ac2-595f-42b4-b09d-30dd51513199?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:23:02Z mar_sg_am_pwc])|alt= a horizontal bar chart with three bars showing the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for containers in the years 2014, 2023 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, the share of short sea shipped goods in containers on the total sea transport of goods in containers was below 50% for Antwerp-Bruges, Rotterdam and Hamburg, while Gioia Tauro and Piraeus had shares of 90.9% and 64.1%, respectively (Figure 8). [[Image: Short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for containers, 2024_(%, based on tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 8: Short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for containers, 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4215bf69-e92e-45dc-8f6e-91744a26c3e6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:23:33Z mar_sg_am_pwc])|alt=a horizontal stacked bar chart showing the short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for containers in the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Antwerp-Bruges was the largest port for short sea shipped goods on roll-on and roll-off units === Antwerp-Bruges was the largest port for short sea shipped goods on roll-on and roll-off (Ro-Ro) units with 20 million tonnes in 2024 (Figure 9). Compared with 2023, all top 5 ports recorded decreases, except for Lubeck where the increase was +2.5%. Calais recorded the highest fall, with -3.5%. [[Image: Top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for roll-on and roll-off units, 2014, 2023 and 2024 (million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 9: Top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for roll-on and roll-off units, 2014, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bcdd70cd-604d-4950-929c-bddfbe3a11c8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:24:10Z mar_sg_am_pwr])|alt= a horizontal bar chart with three bars showing the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for roll-on and roll-off units for the years 2014, 2023 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, the goods on Ro-Ro units were exclusively short sea shipped in Calais, Lubeck and Dublin, while short sea shipping of goods on Ro-Ro units represented 90.9% of the total sea transport of goods on Ro-Ro units in Antwerp-Bruges and 99.7% in Rotterdam (Figure 10). [[Image: Short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for roll-on and roll-off units, 2024.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 10: Short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for roll-on and roll-off units, 2024
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/354100e2-e814-45ed-8f31-bc714c063864?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-24T15:24:31Z mar_sg_am_pwr])|alt=a horizontal stacked bar chart showing the short sea shipping of freight in total sea transport for the top 5 short sea shipping EU ports for roll-on and roll-off units in the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media: Maritime transport short sea shipping_2026-03-Port.xlsx |Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== The statistics in this article are based on data collected under {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0042:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/42/EC}} of 6 May 2009 on statistical returns in respect of carriage of goods and passengers by sea. The relevant data on port of loading and unloading of the goods is mainly collected for [[Glossary:Main_ports| main ports]], passengers by sea. The relevant data on port of loading and unloading of the goods are mainly collected for main ports, which are defined as ports handling more than one million tonnes of goods annually. Data are collected at level of [[Glossary:Statistical port|statistical ports]]. The [[Glossary:Short_sea_shipping|short sea shipping (SSS)]] statistics present seaborne transport of goods between *main ports in the [[Glossary:Coastal_Member_States|maritime EU Member States]] *main ports in the maritime EU Member States and non-EU partner ports situated in geographical Europe or in non-European countries on the Mediterranean Sea and the Black Sea. As a result, this article covers short sea shipping of goods to and from main ports in the 22 maritime EU Member States (Czechia, Luxembourg, Hungary, Austria and Slovakia have no maritime ports). The partner ports are situated *in the maritime EU Member States *in the maritime [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA countries]] Iceland and Norway *in the maritime [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]] Montenegro, Moldova, Georgia, Albania, Türkiye and Ukraine *in the United Kingdom (European ports) *on the Baltic Sea (Russia) *on the Mediterranean (Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Occupied Palestinian territories, Syria, and Tunisia) *on the Black Sea (Georgia, Moldova, Russia and Ukraine). In addition to the maritime EU Member States, similar short sea shipping statistics are also available for seaborne transport to and from main ports in Norway, Montenegro and Türkiye. The definition of short sea shipping is derived from the Communication of the Commission COM (1999) 317 on the development of Short Sea Shipping in Europe. As a result, the concept of short sea shipping includes both regular short sea shipping and feeder services (short sea shipping between ports for freight to be consolidated or redistributed to or from a deep sea service in one of the ports in a network (hub ports). Please note that ports located in Morocco–West Africa, Egypt–Red Sea, Israel–Red Sea and Russia–Barents and the White Sea are not part of the European short sea shipping area. '''Figures 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10:''' The category ‘other seaborne transport’ includes both deep sea shipping and transport with unidentified partner ports (unknown ports). It should be noted that the share of unknown partner ports in the total seaborne transport is less than 7% in 2014, 2023 and 2024 for all the mentioned ports, except for Marseille in 2023 (11%) and 2024 (12%). When looking at each type of cargo, this share is lower than 8% for all ports, except for Marseille for liquid bulk goods in 2023 (11%) and 2024 (9%) and Rotterdam for containers in 2014 (9%). ===Context=== The content of this statistical article is based on data collected under the EU maritime transport statistics Directive ({{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0042:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/42/EC}} of 6 May 2009 on statistical returns in respect of carriage of goods and passengers by sea), which is a recast of the original Council {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31995L0064:EN:NOT|title=Directive 95/64/EC}} of 8 December 1995. The basic legal act (Directive 2009/42/EC) was amended by: *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32010D0216:EN:NOT|title=Commission Decision 2010/216/EC}} of 14 April 2010 OJ L 94 of 15.4.2010 pp. 33-40 *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32010R1090:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 1090/2010}} of 24 November 2010 OJ L 325 of 09.12.2010 pp. 1-3 *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012D0186:EN:NOT|title=Commission Delegated Decision 2012/186/EU}} of 3 February 2012 OJ L 101 of 11.4.2012 pp. 5-14. The following legal acts include respectively the last official version of the list of ports and some dissemination aspects: *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018D1007:EN:NOT|title=Commission Delegated Decision (EU) 2018/1007}} of 25 April 2018 (Port list) OJ L 180 of 17.7.2018 pp. 29-71 *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32001D0423:EN:NOT|title=Commission Decision 2001/423/EC}} of 22 May 2001 (on dissemination) OJ L 151 of 07.06.2001 p. 41 ===Other Articles=== *[[Freight transport statistics - title: Maritime vessels statistics
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the maritime vessels. Data extracted in November 2025. Planned update: January 2027. In 2024, 2.2 million vessels entered the main EU ports. Greece recorded the largest number of vessel port calls in 2024. The average size of vessels calling at main EU ports is estimated at 7 716 gross tonnage per vessel. |alt= A dynamic bar chart showing the average size of vessels calling at main EU ports from 2009 to 2024. This article presents the latest statistical data on vessels traffic in main [[Glossary:Port|ports]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], the [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA country]] Norway and the [[Glossary:candidate countries|candidate countries]] Montenegro and Türkiye. This article contains data for 2024. === In 2024, 2.2 million vessels entered the main EU ports === In 2024, the number of vessels calling (handling freight or embarking and disembarking passengers) in main EU ports was estimated at 2.2 million, an increase of 2.4% from the previous year. Greece had the largest number of port calls in 2024 (488 053 vessels), followed by Italy (430 627 vessels), Denmark (301 205 vessels), Croatia (284 012 vessels), Spain (205 622 vessels) and Germany (115 012 vessels) (Table 1). [[Image: Vessels in main ports, in selected years, 2014-2024 (number).png|thumb|centre|750px|Table 1: Vessels in main ports, in selected years, 2014-2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mt_am_csvi__custom_18985371/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=658e7b3d-0599-4d55-9f80-b90ff6789c61&c=1763634252000 mar_mt_am_csvi])|alt= A table showing the vessels in main ports, in selected years, 2014-2024, in the EU, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Fifteen countries recorded an increase in 2024 compared with 2023: Spain registered the largest increase (+15.7%), followed by Italy (+7.5%), Malta (+6.9%) and Poland (+5.1%), while 11 other EU countries recorded increases less than 5%. Among the remaining EU countries, Denmark registered the largest decrease (-7.8%), followed by Cyprus (-4.9%). Germany recorded the least decline by 0.4% compared with 2023. Compared with 2014, 12 EU countries registered increases. The largest increases were recorded in Malta (+110.9%), followed by Croatia (+45.8%) and Spain (+45.4%). By contrast, the largest decreases were recorded by Finland (-25.2%), Latvia (-21.5%) and Denmark (-16.7%). The candidate country Türkiye also decreased by 6.3%. === The average size of vessels calling at main EU ports is estimated at 7 716 gross tonnage per vessel=== In 2024, the estimated gross tonnage (GT) of the vessels calling in EU ports increased to 16.8 billion GT (+1.0% from the previous year). Spain recorded the largest gross tonnage of vessels calling at its main ports in 2024 with 2.84 billion GT, followed by Italy (2.78 billion GT) (Table 2). Ten countries recorded an increase in 2024 compared with 2023. Spain registered the largest increase (+5.5%), followed by Slovenia (+5.1%), Finland and Poland (both +4.2%) and France (+3.7%). Among the remaining EU countries, Cyprus recorded the largest decrease (-20.5%), followed by Romania (-12.0%), Latvia (-9.9%), Bulgaria (-6.8%), Malta (-6.7%), the Netherlands (-4.2%) and Belgium (-4.1%), whereas the other 5 EU countries recorded a decrease of less than 3%. Compared with 2014, all countries registered increases except Latvia, Finland and Germany (-29.8%, -4.6% and -0.7%, respectively). The largest increase was recorded by Croatia (+62.8%), followed by Poland (+60.9%) and Spain (+53.6%). Ten EU countries registered increases between 20% and 50% and the remaining EU countries registered increases less than 20%. The EFTA country Norway and also the candidate country Türkiye registered substantial increases (+129.5% and +29.4%, respectively). [[Image: Gross Tonnage of vessels in main ports, in selected years, 2014-2024 (thousand).png|thumb|centre|750px|Table 2: Gross tonnage of vessels in main ports, in selected years, 2014-2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mt_am_csvi__custom_18985393/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=c7e754b3-82fa-47da-8081-5c0b9003fc76&c=1763634289000 mar_mt_am_csvi]) |alt= A table showing the gross tonnage of vessels in main ports, in selected years, 2014-2024, in the EU, some EFTA countries, and some candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, the average size of vessels calling at the main EU ports decreased by 1.4%, to 7 716 GT, compared with the previous year (Figure 1). [[Image: Average size of vessels calling at main ports, EU, 2009-2024_(gross tonnage per vessel).png|thumb|centre|750px|Figure 1: Average size of vessels calling at main ports, EU, 2009-2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mt_am_csvi__custom_18985509/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=2cbb713c-9b60-4baa-9175-5a2b17d91e2a&c=1763634565000 mar_mt_am_csvi])|alt= A vertical bar chart showing the average size of vessels calling at the main ports in the EU from 2009-2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, Belgium remained the EU country which registered the largest average size of vessels at the main ports, followed by France and Slovenia. The candidate country Montenegro also recorded a high than average size of vessel, compared with that of the top 3 EU countries (Figure 2). Compared with 2023, the largest increase was registered by Denmark (+6.3%), whereas the largest decrease was recorded by Cyprus (-16.4%). Among the EU countries, 19 saw increases compared with 2023, while only 3 EU countries decreased compared with 2014. [[Image: Average size of vessels calling at main ports, 2014, 2023 and 2024_(gross tonnage per vessel).png|thumb|centre|750px|Figure 2: Average size of vessels calling at main ports, 2014, 2023 and 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mt_am_csvi__custom_18985594/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=e6c84f8a-8c28-4670-97b4-d0345207bc09&c=1763634781000 mar_mt_am_csvi])|alt= A vertical bar chart showing the average size of vessels calling at the main ports in the EU, some EFTA countries and candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Vessels in the category 'Cargo, non-specialised' (which includes [[Glossary:Ro-Ro|Ro-Ro vessels]]) made the highest share of calls to the main EU ports in 2024 (69.9% of the vessels and 58.9% of the gross tonnage). When based on the number of vessels, the next category was passenger vessels (19.6%), which excluded cruise passengers, followed by liquid bulk vessels (3.8%) and container vessels (3.1%) (Figure 3). When looking at the shares based on gross tonnage, container vessels came second, with 15.6%, followed by cruise passenger vessels (9.5%), liquid bulk vessels (8.1%) and dry bulk vessels (3.4%). Passenger vessels represented only 1.8% based on gross tonnage, indicating their lower size compared with the other types of vessels. [[Image: Vessels in main ports by type of vessel, EU, 2024.png|thumb|centre|750px|Figure 3: Vessels in main ports by type of vessel, EU, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_mt_am_csvi__custom_18985738/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=bc1b3e8a-b0e3-46e3-ba4f-09d0e7bcdb16&c=1763635053000 mar_mt_am_csvi])|alt= Two pie charts showing the vessels in main ports by type of vessel in the EU in 2024, the first pie chart is %-based on number of vessels, and the second pie chart is %-based on gross tonnage. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Reggio Di Calabria was the largest EU port in terms of number of vessels === The top 20 ports accounted for 29.9% of the total number of vessels in the reporting countries in 2024. The port of Reggio Di Calabria was the largest EU port in 2024, with more than 57 000 vessels (Figure 4). Fifteen ports out of the top 20 increased, compared with 2023. Among the top 20 ports in 2024, Napoli recorded the largest increase in 2024 compared with the previous year (+26.3%), followed by Porto d'Ischia (+12.1%), Mgarr- Gozo (+5.7%) and Capri (+5.4%). By contrast, Algeciras (-7.0%), Rotterdam (-2.3%), Palma de Mallorca (-1.3%), Paloukia Salaminas and Perama recorded falls in 2024 compared with 2023. Compared with 2023, only one port entered the top 20: Capri replaced Procida. [[Image:Top 20 EU maritime ports in terms of number vessels, 2014, 2023 and 2024 (thousand).png|thumb|centre|750px|Figure 4: Top 20 EU maritime ports in terms of number vessels, 2014, 2023 and 2024
''Source'': Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/mar_tf_qm__custom_18985989/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=9f1d0853-892a-4d6f-bfc6-5cb14c613ab7&c=1763635470000 mar_tf_qm])|alt= a horizontal bar chart with three bars showing the Top 20 EU maritime ports in terms of number vessels for 2014, 2023 and 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= SE_Article_Maritime_Vessels_2025-11.xlsx|title= Maritime ports vessel statistics: tables and figures}} === Data sources === This article presents the trends in vessel traffic in the main European Union (EU) ports and also includes figures for Norway, Montenegro and Türkiye. The content is based on data collected within the legal framework for EU maritime transport statistics, i.e. {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0042:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/42/EC}} of the European Parliament and of the Council of 6 May 2009 on statistical returns in respect of carriage of goods and passengers by sea and later amendments. Directive 2009/42/EC is a recast of the original Council {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31995L0064:EN:NOT|title=Directive 95/64/EC}} of 8 December 1995. The EU aggregates in the statistics refer to the total of 22 [[Glossary:Coastal Member States|maritime Member States]]. Czechia, Luxembourg, Hungary, Austria and Slovakia have no maritime ports. Norway provides [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] with data as members of the [[Glossary:European Economic Area (EEA)|European Economic Area (EEA)]]. The EEA country Liechtenstein has no maritime ports. Data for Iceland are not available as the country does not have detailed reporting of data sets and does not report data on vessels. Montenegro and Türkiye provide data as [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries]]. 'Main ports' are ports handling more than one million tonnes of goods or more than 200 000 passengers annually (however, data for some smaller ports may be included in the published results). Data are presented at level of '[[Glossary:Statistical port|statistical ports]]'. A statistical port consists of one or more ports, normally controlled by a single port authority, able to record ship and cargo movements. '''Explanatory notes:''' Please note that data can be subject to revision and latest data are available in Eurostat's online database. Basic results and derived indicators (such as growth rates and shares in % of total) in the tables are rounded. However, the figures are based on the non-rounded original data. As a result, the sum of shares in % of total, as shown in the tables, is not necessarily equal to 100%. Explanatory notes for countries are available in the {{Template:Esms|code=mar_esms|title=metadata on the Eurostat website}}. Starting from 2011, the figures for Spain include data for a number of minor regional ports outside the state-controlled port system. There is a break in time series from 2015 due to methodological improvement in the data reported by the Netherlands. Montenegro started to report data on vessel traffic in 2018. Detailed data on main ports are not available for Iceland, as the country has not provided detailed reporting. '''Type of vessel (Figure 3):''' * Liquid bulk: oil tanker, chemical tanker, LG tanker, tanker barge, other tanker. * Dry bulk: bulk/oil carrier, bulk carrier. * Dry cargo barge. * Container: full container. * Cargo, specialised: barge carrier, chemical carrier, irradiated fuel, livestock carrier, vehicle carrier, other specialised. * Cargo, non-specialised: reefer, Ro-Ro passenger, Ro-Ro container, other Ro-Ro cargo, combination carrier general cargo/passenger, combination carrier general cargo/container, single-decker, multi-decker. * Passenger: passenger (excluding cruise passenger vessels). * Cruise passenger. * Unknown type of vessel.
