title: Migrant integration statistics - employment conditions
text:
European statistics on main employment conditions indicators among foreign-born persons and foreign citizens compared with nationals and native-born persons: share of self-employment, temporary employees and part-time employment. Data extracted: 17 June 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 Between 2015 and 2025, non-EU citizens consistently had the highest share of employees aged 20-64 with a temporary contract. In 2025, this share fell to its lowest level over the period, at 22.1%, compared with 12.4% for citizens of other EU countries and 10.7% for nationals. This article presents European statistics for 3 employment condition indicators: [[Glossary:Self-employed|self-employment]], [[Glossary:Temporary employment|temporary employment]], and part-time employment. These indicators are analysed according to individuals’ citizenship and their migration status. Individuals are classified by citizenship as either nationals or non-nationals of the country in which they reside. Non-nationals are further divided into 2 groups: those who hold a citizenship of another EU country and those who hold a citizenship of a non-EU country. Migration status is defined according to individuals’ country of birth and, where relevant, their parents’ country of birth. Individuals are grouped as either native-born or foreign-born. Native-born individuals are further classified into 3 groups based on the birthplace of their parents, in order to reflect on a possible migrant background. As a result, the 4 migration status categories used are: native-born with 2 native-born parents, native-born with 1 foreign-born parent, native-born with 2 foreign-born parents, and foreign-born persons. This article forms part of the online publication on [[Migrant_integration_statistics - facts and figures|migrant integration statistics]]. ===Overview === The [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|EU labour force survey (EU-LFS)]] is the data source for this article which is concentrating on the age group 20-64 years. This age group is the focus for employment analyses in the [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/migrant-integration/eu-integration-policy_en#action-plan-on-integration-and-inclusion-2021-2027 Action Plan on integration and inclusion 2021–2027]. This article examines 3 key indicators by citizenship over the period from 2005 to 2025: self-employment, temporary contracts, and part-time employment. Between 2005 and 2025, citizens of other EU countries and non-EU citizens consistently recorded:
  • lower shares of self-employed people
  • higher shares of temporary contracts
  • higher shares of part-time employment
compared to nationals.
The share of self-employed people remained highest among nationals throughout the period, although it followed a slight downward trend, reaching its lowest point in 2023 (13.5%) and remaining stable through 2025 (Figure 1). For citizens of other EU countries and non-EU citizens, the shares varied over the period and stood at 10.9% and 10.1%, respectively, in 2025. Figure 1 Between 2005 and 2025, non-EU citizens consistently recorded the highest shares of employees with temporary contracts, while nationals recorded the lowest (Figure 2). In recent years, the share decreased across all 3 groups, reaching its lowest level in 2025: 22.1% for non-EU citizens, 12.4% for citizens of other EU countries and 10.7% for nationals. Figure 2 Between 2005 and 2025, nationals consistently recorded the lowest shares of part-time employment (Figure 3). In recent years, the share declined across all 3 groups, most notably among non-EU citizens. In 2025, it stood at 21.8% for non-EU citizens, 20.0% for citizens of other EU countries and 16.6% for nationals. Figure 3 ===Self-employment=== In 2025, nationals showed the highest share of self-employment in total employment at EU level (13.5%), followed by citizens of other EU countries (10.9%) and non-EU citizens (10.1%). Greater variability was observed at country level. Nationals recorded particularly high shares in Greece and Italy, while citizens of other EU countries showed the highest shares in Croatia and Portugal. At EU level, the share of self-employed was consistently higher for males across all citizenship groups. Figure 4 In 2025, the share of self-employment at EU level was highest among native-born with 2 native-born parents (13.8%) and lowest among native-born with both parents born abroad (9.3%) (Figure 5). Differences across groups varied considerably across countries. Greece recorded the highest share overall among native-born persons with 2 native-born parents (25.5%), and the lowest share among native-born persons with 2 foreign-born parents (4.1%). At EU level, men had a higher share of self-employment than women, regardless of migration background. Figure 5 ===Temporary employment=== In 2025, nationals recorded the lowest share of employees with temporary contracts at EU level (10.7%), while non-EU citizens recorded the highest share (22.1%). Citizens of other EU countries recorded an intermediate share (12.4%) (Figure 6). Differences across citizenship groups varied considerably across countries, with the highest shares overall observed among non-EU citizens in Cyprus, the Netherlands and Poland, all exceeding 40%. At the EU level, female employees had a higher share of temporary contracts than males across all citizenship groups. Figure 6 In the EU in 2025, foreign-born employees (16.1%) and native-born employees with both parents born abroad (15.9%) had a higher share of temporary contracts than native-born employees with 1 parent born abroad (13.6%) and native-born employees with 2 native-born parents (10.2%) (Figure 7). This pattern was observed for both women and men. Women had a higher share of temporary contracts than men, regardless of migration background. Among countries with available data for all 4 groups, the greatest variability between groups was observed in Italy, followed by Spain and Portugal. Figure 7 ===Part-time employment=== In the EU in 2025, part-time employment was lowest among nationals (16.6%), while non-EU citizens recorded the highest share (21.8%). Citizens of other EU countries stood between the 2 groups, at 20.0% (Figure 8). The share of part-time employment varied across countries and citizenship groups. Among countries with available data for all 3 citizenship groups, the largest disparities between groups were observed in the Netherlands, followed by Finland and France. Women had considerably higher shares of part-time employment than men across all citizenship categories. Figure 8 In the EU in 2025, part-time employment was most prevalent among native-born people with 2 parents born abroad (23.6%), followed by native-born people with 1 parent born abroad (23.4%) and foreign-born people (21.1%). In contrast, the lowest rate was recorded among native-born people with 2 native-born parents (15.6%) (Figure 9). This pattern was also observed among women. Among men, however, the highest rate was recorded among native-born people with 1 parent born abroad. Women reported higher rates of part-time employment than men, regardless of migration background. Among EU countries with available data for all 4 groups, the largest disparities between groups were observed in Spain, Ireland and Denmark. Figure 9 ===Data sources=== The data presented in this article are from the [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)|EU labour force survey (EU-LFS)]], the largest household sample survey in the EU. The survey covers the resident population, defined as all people usually residing in private households. As such, persons living in collective households are excluded from the target population. Usual residence means the place where a person normally spends the daily period of rest, regardless of temporary absences for purposes of recreation, holidays, visits to friends and relatives, business, medical treatment or religious pilgrimage. The data for the EU are aggregated results for the 27 EU countries. For more information on the data sources used, please consult the online publication [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey EU Labour Force Survey]. Due to the sampling nature of the survey, some data have low reliability or are not published due to very low reliability or confidentiality. For figures by citizenship, shares are taken directly from Eurostat's dissemination database; for those by migration status, shares are calculated using data from the same source. '''Main concepts''' An [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Employed_person_-_LFS employed person] is someone aged 15-89 years who, during the reference week of the labour force survey, performed work – even if just for one hour a week – for pay, profit or family gain. Also included are people who were not at work but had a job or business from which they were temporarily absent due to illness, holiday, industrial dispute or education and training. An [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Employee_-_LFS employee] is a particular type of employed person. Employees work for a public or private employer and receive compensation in the form of wages, salaries, payment by results, or payment in kind; non-conscript members of the armed forces are also included. Employees are not self-employed or contributing family workers. [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Self-employed_-_LFS Self-employed] persons are defined as persons who work in their own business (including professional practices, farms, shops and other businesses) for the purpose of earning a profit. An employee is considered as having a [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Temporary_employment temporary job] if employer and employee agree that its end is determined by objective conditions, such as a specific date, the completion of an assignment, or the return of an employee who is temporarily replaced: in such cases the employee has a contract of limited duration (as opposed to one of unlimited duration). The distinction between full-time and part-time work is generally based on a spontaneous response by a respondent to the labour force survey. ===Context=== In November 2020, an [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/migrant-integration/eu-integration-policy_en#action-plan-on-integration-and-inclusion-2021-2027 Action Plan on integration and inclusion 2021–2027] (COM(2016) 377 final) was adopted with the purpose of fostering social cohesion and building inclusive societies for all. Inclusion for all is about ensuring that all policies are accessible to and work for everyone, including migrants and EU citizens with migrant background. This plan includes actions in 4 sectoral areas (education and training, employment and skills, health and housing) as well as actions supporting effective integration and inclusion in all sectoral areas at the EU, Member State and regional level, with a specific attention paid to young people. Recent developments for the EU's overall immigration policy can be found in the [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en Pact on Migration and Asylum] that entered into application on 12 June 2026. The revised Reception Conditions Directive and the Qualifications Regulation, which are part of the Pact on Migration and Asylum, include important provisions on integration. The Pact provides a comprehensive approach that delivers a common European response to migration. It allows the EU to manage migration in a fair and sustainable way, ensuring solidarity between countries while also providing certainty and clarity for people arriving in the EU and protecting their fundamental rights. The Pact will ensure that countries share the effort responsibly, showing solidarity with the ones that protect our external borders and with those facing particular migratory pressure, while preventing irregular migration to the EU. The Pact also gives the EU and its countries the tools to react rapidly in situations of crisis, when countries are faced with large numbers of arrivals or when a third-country or non-State entity tries to instrumentalise migrants in order to destabilise our Union. More information on the policies and legislation in force in this area can be found in an [[Migrant_integration_statistics_introduced|introductory article on migrant integration statistics]]. ===Other title: Migrant integration statistics - health
text:
EU statistics on overview of the self-reported health status of non-nationals. Data extracted on 21 October 2025 Planned article update: November 2026 In 2024, the self-perceived health of non-nationals was less favourable than that of nationals for each age group (16-44 years old, 45-64 years old and 65 years old or older), particularly for non-EU citizens 65 years old or older. In 2024, citizens of other EU countries had the highest percentage of unmet needs for medical examination at 4.2%, while nationals reported the lowest at 3.9%. Non-EU citizens fell in between, with 4.0%. In 2024, 6.2% of non-EU citizens reported unmet needs for dental examination, compared with 5.5% of citizens of other EU countries and 4.6% of nationals. This article presents an overview of the self-reported health status of non-nationals and compares it with nationals. The first part of the article focuses on self-perceived health – the indicator giving an overall assessment by respondents of their health in general. The second part of the article examines self-reported unmet needs for both medical and dental examinations or treatments. The information presented in the article refers to people aged 16 years and over. Non-nationals refer to persons living in a reporting country who do not hold its citizenship. They can be divided into two groups: EU citizens living in an EU country other than their country of citizenship (citizens of other EU countries), and non-EU citizens living in the EU (non-EU citizens). Nationals are EU citizens living in their country of citizenship. This article forms part of the online publication on [[Migrant_integration_statistics - facts and figures|migrant integration statistics]]. === Self-perceived health === [[Glossary:Self-perceived health|Self-perceived health]] is surveyed through a question about how a person perceives their health in general, using the following answer categories: very good, good, fair, bad or very bad. It refers to a person's health in general rather than their current (possibly temporary) state of health and concerns physical, social and emotional functions and biomedical signs and symptoms. Figures 1 to 4 below present the share of individuals reporting bad or very bad health.
Figure 1 shows the percentage of individuals reporting a bad or very bad state of self-perceived health by citizenship from 2015 to 2024. Among citizens of other EU countries, perceptions of poor health varied over time: 7.7% in 2015, a decline to 5.9% in 2017, followed by an increase to 8.4% by 2024. Non-EU citizens initially reported a decrease in poor health perception from 7.5% in 2015 to 5.9% in 2017; however, this percentage rose significantly, peaking at 9.4% in 2020, before stabilizing around 7.5% in 2024. Nationals of the reporting country maintained more stable levels of poor self-perceived health, starting at 9.8% in 2015, decreasing to 8.6% in 2017, and remaining around 8.8% to 8.9% in the following years, with a slight decrease to 8.6% in 2024. Figure 1 The differences in levels of bad or very bad self-perceived health among the 3 population subgroups are affected by their varying age structures: nationals are likely to have an age distribution with higher proportion of older people, which can contribute to higher rates of bad or very bad state of self-perceived health. By contrast, non-nationals tend to be younger on average, which may explain their comparatively lower percentages in the same category. For this reason, a proper comparison between nationals and non-nationals must account for age as a factor.
Figure 2 illustrates how the levels of self-perceived bad or very bad health varied by age and citizenship within the EU in 2024. Among those aged 16 to 44, the percentages were similar across all groups: non-EU citizens and citizens of other EU countries both recorded 2.9%, while nationals were slightly lower at 2.8%. However, as age increased, differences became more pronounced. For ages 45 to 64, both groups of non-nationals reported higher rates of poor self-perceived health, at 12.1%, compared to 7.9% among nationals. In the 65+ group, non-EU citizens had the highest rate at 24.6%, followed by citizens of other EU countries at 20.8%, and nationals at 17.8%. Figure 2 Figure 3 shows that differences between women and men in health perceptions vary across groups of population, with women exhibiting worse health perceptions regardless of citizenship. Among nationals, 9.5% of women reported poor health compared to 7.7% of men. Similarly, among citizens of other EU countries, 8.9% of women perceived their health as bad or very bad compared to 7.9% of men. For non-EU citizens, the pattern persisted, with 7.9% of women reporting poor perceived health versus 7.0% of men. Figure 3 The analysis of self-perceived health reveals significant variations among nationals, citizens of other EU countries, and non-EU citizens across different countries (Figure 4). For nationals, Latvia had the highest percentage of bad or very bad self-perceived health at 13.2%, followed by Lithuania and Portugal at 12.3% each, and Croatia at 12.2%, while Ireland (4.8%) and Malta (4.6%) reported much lower figures. Citizens of other EU countries living in France and Portugal stood out with 16.1% perceiving their health as bad or very bad, notably higher than in other EU countries. By contrast, Slovakia (0.5%), Malta (1.5%), Cyprus and Italy (1.7% each) showed much lower percentages. Lastly, for non-EU citizens, Latvia had the highest rate at 28.6%, likely due to the significant number of [[Glossary:Recognised non-citizen|recognised non-citizens]] (mainly former Soviet Union citizens, permanently resident in the country but not holding any other citizenship) with an older age structure compared with non-EU citizens in other countries. Austria (12.9%), France (12.3%) and Estonia (12.2%) also reported higher percentages, while Bulgaria (0.0%), Italy (1.4%), Cyprus (1.6%) and Malta (1.9%) had much lower rates. Figure 4 === Unmet medical and dental examination or treatment needs === Figure 5 provides data on the percentage of people with [[Glossary:Self-reported unmet need for medical care | self-reported unmet needs for medical examinations]] by citizenship within the EU from 2015 to 2024. Citizens of other EU countries showed a significant decline from 4.0% in 2015 to 1.4% in 2017, but their unmet needs rose again to 4.2% by 2024. Non-EU citizens reported a higher level of unmet needs initially, at 7.8% in 2015, which then fell to 3.0% by 2017 and fluctuated around 4.0% in 2024. Citizens of the reporting country saw a decline from 5.3% in 2015 to 3.2% in 2017, stabilising at 3.9% in 2024. Figure 5 Figure 6 shows the percentage of people with self-reported unmet needs for dental examinations by citizenship within the EU from 2015 to 2024. Citizens of other EU countries initially reported unmet dental needs at 6.8% in 2015, experiencing fluctuations with a low of 3.6% in 2019 and rising to 5.5% in 2024. Non-EU citizens consistently reported higher unmet dental needs, starting at 10.8% in 2015, decreasing to 5.5% in 2017, and stabilizing around 6.2% by 2024. For nationals, the share declined from 6.5% in 2015 to 3.9% in 2017, with a gradual increase to 4.6% in 2024. Figure 6 Figure 7 shows that unmet medical needs increased with age for all 3 citizenship groups, peaking at 6.4% among non-EU citizens aged 65 years and over. Citizens of other EU countries reported the highest percentage of unmet medical needs in the age groups 16-44 years (3.8%) and 45-64 years (4.4%). Figure 7 As for the self-reported unmet needs for dental examinations, Figure 8 reveals that non-EU citizens consistently showed the highest unmet needs across all age groups, especially among those aged 45-64 years (7.3%). In comparison, nationals had the lowest levels of unmet needs across all age groups. Figure 8 In Figure 9, which covers unmet needs for medical examinations by sex, women consistently reported higher unmet needs than men across all citizenship groups. Among nationals, 4.3% of women reported unmet needs compared with 3.5% of men. Among citizens of other EU countries, 4.4% of women reported unmet needs, while men reported 3.9%. Non-EU citizens followed the same pattern, with 4.6% of women reporting unmet needs compared with 3.4% of men. Figure 9 In Figure 10, which focuses on unmet needs for dental examinations, the gender gap remains for nationals (4.7% of women to 4.5% of men) and non-EU citizens (6.4% compared with 6.0%). For citizens of other EU countries, the situation was reversed, with men reporting higher unmet needs at 5.7%, slightly more than the 5.3% reported by women. Figure 10 Figures 11 and 12 provide data on the share of people self-reporting unmet needs for medical and dental examinations or treatment in 2024 across EU countries, broken down by citizenship. For medical examinations or treatment, across the EU, 3.9% of nationals reported unmet needs, compared with 4.2% of citizens of other EU countries and 4.0% of non-EU citizens (Figure 11). The countries with the highest shares of unmet medical needs among nationals were Greece (13.6%) and Denmark (11.3%). Among non-nationals, Portugal and Denmark showed the highest percentages for citizens from other EU countries (15.2% and 13.9%, respectively), whereas Latvia and Denmark stood out with the highest percentages for non-EU citizens (20.2% and 17.7%, respectively). Figure 11 For dental examinations or treatment, the share of unmet needs was higher across the EU: 4.6% of nationals reported unmet needs, compared with 5.5% for citizens of other EU countries and 6.2% for non-EU citizens (Figure 12). Greece and Denmark had the highest unmet dental needs for both nationals (15.3% and 11.5%, respectively), and citizens of other EU countries (19.3% and 15.1%, respectively), while Denmark (17.4%) and Latvia (16.8%) reported the highest rates for non-EU citizens. Figure 12 === Source data for graphs === The data displayed in these visualisations are taken directly from the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database Eurostat online database] for the reference year(s) mentioned in the visualisations. The accompanying text is from 21 October 2025 and reflects the data situation at that time. For information on data reliability, series breaks, and differing definitions, the relevant flags can be consulted in the online datasets. === Data sources === The data used in the article concerning self-perceived health and unmet needs for health care are derived from [[Glossary:EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]]. This source is documented in more detail in this [[Health_variables_in_SILC_-_methodology|background article]] which provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. Data refer to the population aged 16 years and over. The indicators presented in this article are derived from self-reported data so they are, to a certain extent, affected by respondents' subjective perception as well as by their social and cultural background. Despite their subjective nature, the statistics that are presented are relevant and reliable estimators of the health status of populations as well as good predictors of health care needs; they are useful for trend analysis and for measuring socioeconomic disparities. EU-SILC does not cover the institutionalised population, for example, people living in health and social care institutions whose health status is likely to be worse than that of the population living in private households. It is therefore likely that, to some degree, data sources under-estimate health problems. Another factor that may influence the results shown is the different organisation of health care services, be that nationally or locally. Furthermore, the indicators presented are not age-standardised and thus reflect the current national age structures. Finally, the implementation of EU-SILC was organised nationally, which may impact on the results presented, for example, due to differences in the formulation of questions or their precise coverage. === Context === Good health is an asset. It is not only of value to the individual as a major determinant of quality of life, well-being and social participation, but it also contributes to general social and economic growth. Many factors influence the health status of a population and these can be addressed by health and other policies regionally, nationally or across the EU. Indicators on health status are given high importance in EU health policies. The monitoring of health status of populations was included in the overarching EU strategy ''{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52007DC0630:EN:NOT|title=Together for Health: A Strategic Approach for the EU 2008–2013}}'' (COM(2007) 630 final) and in the more recent ''{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52013SC0043:EN:NOT|title=Investing in health}}'' working document and the [https://health.ec.europa.eu/funding/eu4health-programme-2021-2027-vision-healthier-european-union_en EU4Health programme 2021–2027 – a vision for a healthier European Union]. Health status monitoring is also important for more topical policies such as [https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/active-and-healthy-living-digital-world active and healthy living in the digital world], [https://health.ec.europa.eu/social-determinants/overview_en health inequalities], and social protection and social inclusion. In November 2020, the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0758 action plan on integration and inclusion 2021-2027 (COM(2016) 377 final)] was adopted. The action plan builds on the achievements of the 2016 action plan and goes further by bringing forward new actions and a stronger framework to promote integration and inclusion, focusing on the essentials of successful integration and inclusion into a host society: education and training, employment and skills, health and housing. In September 2020, the European Commission presented the [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en Pact on Migration and Asylum]. Following the adoption by the European Parliament in April 2024 and by the Council in May 2024, the new rules on migration introduced by the Pact entered into force in June 2024 and will enter into application in June 2026. The Pact includes important provisions on integration and provides a comprehensive approach that delivers a common European response to migration. It allows the EU to manage migration in a fair and sustainable way, ensuring solidarity between countries while also providing certainty and clarity for people arriving in the EU and protecting their fundamental rights. ===Other articles=== *[[Migrant integration statistics - facts and figures]] *[[Migrant integration statistics introduced]] *[[EU population diversity by citizenship and country of birth]] *[[Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/migrant-integration/publications All publications on migrant integration] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/managed-migration/publications All publications on asylum and managed migration] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Health All publications on health] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/migrant-integration/database Migrant integration (mii)], see: :Health (mii_health) ::Health status (mii_hlth_state) ::Health determinants (mii_hlth_det) ::Health care (mii_hlth_care) ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/migrant-integration Migrant integration] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/overview Health] ===Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/migrant-integration/methodology Migrant integration statistics — methodology] *[[EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) methodology|Statistics on income and living conditions]] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Health_variables_in_SILC_-_methodology Health variables in SILC - title: Migrant integration - demographic vital events
text:
[[Image:Underconstructioniconblue.jpg|thumb|center|200px|PAGE UNDER CONSTRUCTION !!!]] THEME NUMBER test test test Data extracted in September 2022 Planned article update: September 2023 In 2020, the fertility rate of non-national women in the EU was 37.0 % higher than that of national women (1.97 live births per woman versus 1.44). In 2020, slightly more than half of this difference (50.7%) is explained by the fertility rates of 15-24-year-old women. In 2020, the total mortality rate of non-nationals (3.6 °/°°) is less than one third of that of nationals (11.1 °/°°). In 2020, the mortality rate of non-nationals (0.4 °/°°) is only higher than that of nationals (0.3 °/°°) for children aged less than 16-years-old. [[Image:F1_Fertility_rates_in_the_EU,_2020.png|thumb|centre|600px|]] This article compares the recorded fertility rate and the mortality rate for the year 2020 of nationals and non-nationals (foreign citizens and stateless) in EU and EFTA countries. This comparison aims to highlight the main differences between nationals and non-nationals for those two demographic indicators. In addition to analysing those two indicators at aggregate level, an analysis by age group or individual age is carried out to show some specific characteristics of nationals and non-nationals in terms of their fertility and mortality rates. === Fertility rate by main groups of citizenship in EU and EFTA countries ===
[[Image:T1_Fertility_rates,_2020.png|thumb|centre|500px|Table 1: Fertility rates, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_faczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] Fertility rates for the year 2020 have been calculated for nationals and non-nationals based on population and live births tables by age (number of live births in an age group in 2020 divided by the average number of women in the same age group between 1 January 2020 and 2021). At EU level (Figure 1) in 2020, the fertility rate of non-nationals (1.97) was almost 37% higher than that of nationals (1.44). The fertility rate of the total EU population (nationals and non-nationals) was 1.50, which is 4% higher than that of nationals alone. [[Image:F1_Fertility_rates_in_the_EU,_2020.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 1: Fertility rates in the EU, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_faczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] Looking at the fertility rates of non-nationals in the 27 EU Member States, (Figure 2), we can see that they were higher than the EU average in 9 Member States. The highest rate (3.25) was recorded in France. On the other end of the scale, values lower than 1.3 were recorded in 5 countries, and the lowest rate (0.72) was observed in Hungary. [[Image:F2_Fertility_rates_of_non-nationals,_2020.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 2: Fertility rates of non-nationals, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_faczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] In the table showing the difference between the fertility rates of non-nationals and nationals (Figure 3) we see that 8 of the 9 Member States with a higher fertility rate for non-nationals than the EU average are also above the EU average for this indicator, with Italy replacing Sweden in the top 9. The highest difference (1.58) is recorded in France followed by Romania (0.97) and Lithuania (0.91). On the opposite end of the scale, the fertility rate of non-nationals is lower than fertility rate of nationals in 8 Member States, with lowest values observed in Hungary (-0.90), Bulgaria (-0.72) and Croatia (-0.63). [[Image:F3_Difference_between_fertility_rates_of_non-nationals_and_nationals,_2020.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 3: Difference between fertility rates of non-nationals and nationals, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_faczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] In terms of the impact that the fertility of non-nationals had on the total fertility rate in 2020 (Figure 4), this resulted in total fertility rate higher than the EU average in 9 Member States. The highest (10%) was observed in Luxembourg and values equal or higher than 7% were recorded in France, Belgium, Germany, Italy and Austria. In 9 Member States, the influence of the fertility rate of non-nationals on the total fertility rate was negative, in particular in Estonia, Denmark and Malta. The scale of the impact depends on two things: the difference between the fertility rates of nationals and non nationals; and the weight of the non-national population as a percentage of the total population in each country. [[Image:F4_Impact_of_the_fertility_rate_of_non-nationals_on_the_fertility_rate_of_the_total_population,_2020_(%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 4: Impact of the fertility rate of non-nationals on the fertility rate of the total population, 2020
(%)
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_faczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] === EU-level comparison of age-specific fertility rates between nationals and non-nationals === The age-specific fertility rate (fertility rate by mother’s age) is calculated as the ratio of the number of live births of mothers of age x to the average female population of age x. The total fertility rate presented above is subdivided by the age of women in a given year, in this case 2020. This provides us with an estimate on the mean number of children that would be born alive to a woman during her lifetime if she were to pass through her childbearing years conforming to the fertility rates by age of a given year and surviving. Figure 5 looks at the age-specific fertility rates of national (blue curve) and non-national (orange curve) women living in the EU for each year of age between 15 and 49. It shows that the age-specific fertility rate of non-national women is higher than that of national women for each of these years of age. The peak of the curve for nationals, which indicates the age at which women are the most fertile, is 31 years old whereas the peak for non-national women is slightly earlier at 30 years old. The other main pattern is the faster increase in the fertility rate of non-nationals compared with nationals at the beginning of the curve (ages 15-24), with the distance between the two curves narrowing for ages 25-32. From the age of 33, the distance between the two curves increases again but the difference is less pronounced. [[Image:F5_Age_specific_fertility_rates_(between_15_and_49_years_old)_of_nationals_and_non-nationals_in_the_EU,_2020_.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 5: Age specific fertility rates (between 15 and 49 years old) of nationals and non-nationals in the EU, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_faczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] To better analyse the difference in the distribution of the age-specific fertility rates of national and non-national women in the EU, Figure 6 shows the cumulative difference between fertility rates of both groups in 2020. More than half of the total difference (50.7%) is observed for women aged between 15 and 24, whereas almost 30% of the difference is recorded for women aged between 25 and 34. Furthermore, although the age-specific fertility rates of non-national women are higher than that of national women at all ages, most of this difference results from the difference in the number of young mothers, in particular those aged between 18 and 26. [[Image:F6_Cumulative_difference_by_age_between_age_specific_fertility_rates_of_non-nationals_and_nationals_in_the_EU,_2020_(%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 6: Cumulative difference by age between age specific fertility rates of non-nationals and nationals in the EU, 2020
(%)
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_faczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] === Mortality rate by age groups === Mortality rates for 2020 have been calculated for nationals and non-nationals (including people who are stateless) based on population and death data subdivided by age (number of deaths in a given age group in 2020 divided by the average population between 1 January 2020 and 2021). This indicator could provide some insights into the ‘robustness’ of non-nationals compared with nationals. The ratio (EU, 2020) between the mortality rates by age group of non-national and nationals is presented in Figure 7. For the total population, the mortality rate of non-nationals is slightly less than one third of that of nationals. Looking at the data by age group, the mortality rates of non-nationals aged 16 and over are between two thirds and three quarters of that observed for nationals. Furthermore, the mortality rate of non-nationals is higher than that of nationals only for youngsters under the age of 16. This pattern, which may be surprising, results from several factors, including: * the different age structure of non-nationals and nationals when considering the total population; * the fact that non-nationals may return to their country of citizenship when becoming more fragile or older; * non-nationals may acquire the citizenship of their country of residence; * the existence of a ‘healthy migrant paradox’ or selection effect reflecting the fact that, in order to migrate, the migrant population needs to be in good health; * the declaration of death of a non-national citizen may be recorded only in the country of citizenship, particularly if the funeral takes place in that country. [[Image:F7_Ratio_between_mortality_rates_of_non-nationals_and_mortality_rate_of_nationals_by_age_group_in_the_EU,_2020.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 7: Ratio between mortality rates of non-nationals and mortality rate of nationals by age group in the EU, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_maczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] On the higher mortality rate of non-nationals aged less than 16, in Figure 8 which compares the mortality rates of non-nationals and nationals for each age, we see that infant mortality (deaths of new-borns aged 0-12 months) is not the cause of higher mortality in non-nationals, but that this higher rate of mortality occurs between the ages of 1 and 22. For people aged above 22, non-nationals have a lower mortality rate than nationals, in particular for the two following age groups: 25-36-years-old and more than 90-years-old. [[Image:F8_Comparison_between_mortality_rates_by_age_of_nationals_and_foreign_citizens_in_the_EU_in_2020_(logarithm_scale)_.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 8: Comparison between mortality rates by age of nationals and foreign citizens in the EU in 2020 (logarithm scale)
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_maczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] Table 2 presents the mortality rates by age group of non-nationals living in EU Member States and EFTA countries whereas Figures 9.a to 9.d compare them in a scatter plot. We see that the mortality rates of non-nationals aged over 16 are higher than those of nationals in some Member States: particularly in Latvia and Estonia, but also in Lithuania, France and Cyprus. In Baltic countries, the non-nationals are very often those that did not migrate during their lifetime, but rather found themselves in a different country after the collapse of the Soviet Union. This population group is exposed to additional risks such as an unhealthy lifestyle, in particular alcohol addiction. [[Image:T2_Mortality_rates_by_age_groups_and_citizenship_in_the_EU_in_2020_(°_°°).png|thumb|centre|500px|Table 2: Mortality rates by age groups and citizenship in the EU in 2020
(°/°°)
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_maczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] [[Image:F9a_Mortality_rates_of_nationals_and_non-nationals_aged_0-15_years,_2020.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 9a: Mortality rates of nationals and non-nationals aged 0-15 years, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_maczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] [[Image:F9b_Mortality_rates_of_nationals_and_non-nationals_aged_16-44_years,_2020.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 9b: Mortality rates of nationals and non-nationals aged 16-44 years, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_maczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] [[Image:F9c_Mortality_rates_of_nationals_and_non-nationals_aged_45-64_years,_2020.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 9c: Mortality rates of nationals and non-nationals aged 45-64 years, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_maczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] [[Image:F9d_Mortality_rates_of_nationals_and_non-nationals_aged_65_years_or_over,_2020.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 9d: Mortality rates of nationals and non-nationals aged 65 years or over, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_maczc}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_pop2ctz}}]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Migrant_integration_statistics_-_demographic_vital_events.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === '''Number of live births in the population''': Eurostat data set on Live births by mother's age and citizenship ''(demo_faczc)'' Statistics on live births are collected from the EU and EFTA National Statistical Institutes. Live births are defined as births of children that showed any sign of life. It is the total number of births excluding stillbirths. '''Number of deaths in the population''': Eurostat dataset on deaths by age, sex and citizenship ''(demo_maczc)'' Statistics on deaths are collected from the EU and EFTA National Statistical Institutes. The recommended definition of the population is the 'usually resident population' and means all the persons having their usual residence in a Member State at the reference time. In accordance with this concept, the following persons are considered to be usually residents of the geographical area in question: those who have lived in their place of usual residence for a continuous period of at least 12 months before the reference date or those who arrived in their place of usual residence during the 12 months before the reference date with the intention of staying there for at least one year. Where the circumstances described above cannot be established, 'usual residence' can be taken to mean the place of legal or registered residence. Deaths statistics should refer to the same concept used for population statistics. [[Image:Table data sources.PNG|thumb|centre|600px|]] === Context === Vital events have a major influence on population change and on the structure of population which are increasingly used to support policymaking and to enable the monitoring of demographic behaviour within political, economic, social and cultural contexts. These statistics broken down by main group of citizenship may be used to support a range of different analyses, including studies relating to the future composition of EU population and its effects on the inclusion and integration policies of the EU. It concerns for example demographic developments that focus on the structure and weight of working-age population. In November 2020, an [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/system/files_en?file=2020-11/action_plan_on_integration_and_inclusion_2021-2027.pdf Action plan on Integration and Inclusion 2021-2027] (COM(2016) 377 final) was adopted with the purpose of fostering social cohesion and building inclusive societies for all. Inclusion for all is about ensuring that all policies are accessible to and work for everyone, including migrants and EU citizens with migrant background. This plan includes actions in four sectoral areas (education and training, employment and skills, health and housing) as well as actions supporting effective integration and inclusion in all sectoral areas at the EU, Member State and regional level, with a specific attention paid to young people. *[[Migrant_integration_statistics - facts and figures|Migrant integration statistics]] title: Migrant integration statistics - migration status and household composition
text:
Statistics on the demographic characteristics of foreign-born people and their descendants in the EU. Native-born and foreign-born populations. Data extracted on 21 July 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 Between 2021 and 2025, the share of foreign-born people in the EU population aged 15 - 74 increased from 13.0% to 15.2%. The share of native-born people with one foreign-born parent rose from 4.1% to 4.4%, and those with 2 foreign-born parents from 2.9% to 3.3%. The article presents statistics on the migration status of people aged 15 - 74 years usually residing in private households in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. It examines both the main characteristics of people residing in private households in the EU and the household composition according to migration status, focusing on different household types such as single-adult and multi-adult households. Migration status is defined according to individuals’ country of birth and, where relevant, their parents’ country of birth. Individuals are grouped as either native-born or foreign-born. Native-born individuals are further classified based on the birthplace of their parents, in order to reflect on the possible migrant background. As a result, the migration status categories used are: native-born with 2 native-born parents, native-born with one foreign-born parent, native-born with 2 foreign-born parents, and foreign-born persons. Additional analysis by citizenship classifies individuals as either nationals or non-nationals of the country in which they reside. Non-nationals are further divided into 2 groups: those who hold a citizenship of another EU country and those who hold a citizenship of a non-EU country. The types of households have been categorised based on the migration background. For single-adult households, the household migration background reflects the migration background of that person *'''household of native-born with native background''': household where the adult is a native-born person with both parents native-born *'''household of native-born with foreign background''': household where the adult is a native-born with one or both parents born abroad *'''household of foreign-born''': household where the adult is a foreign-born. For multi-adult households, the same three categories apply when all members share the same migration background. However, adults of a household may have different migration backgrounds. Therefore, one additional category is included *'''mixed household''': households where at least 2 adults have different migration backgrounds, including native-born with a native background, native-born with a foreign background, and foreign-born. In addition, there are households where the migration background is not available. These are mostly households where the majority of adults are aged 75 years and over and for whom no information on the migration background of their parents was surveyed. In the following sections, to facilitate the reading of the figures and the comparison between the household migration background, these households where the migration background is not available, were excluded from the analysis. This article forms part of the online publication on [[Migrant_integration_statistics - facts and figures|migrant integration statistics]]. ===Overview=== In 2025, 90.2% of the EU population aged 15–74 were citizens of the country in which they resided (Figure 1), while 6.6% were citizens of non-EU countries and 3.2% were citizens of another EU country. Looking instead at migration background, most of the population (77.0%) were native-born with 2 native-born parents, while 15.2% were foreign-born, 4.4% were native-born with one foreign-born parent and 3.3% were native-born with 2 foreign-born parents. Figure 1 ===Main characteristics of foreign-born people and their descendants=== The distribution of the population by migration background varied considerably across the EU countries (Figure 2). Luxembourg stood out in the EU as the only country where more than half of the population aged 15 - 74 was foreign-born (56.1%). This was far above the EU pattern, where native-born people with native-born parents remained the clear majority. Malta (36.7%) and Cyprus (32.0%) also recorded exceptionally high shares of foreign-born people, placing them well above most other EU countries. On the other hand, in Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia and Poland, foreign-born people accounted for only a small share of the population. Figure 2 Focusing only on people residing in their country of citizenship, the age distribution in 2025 differed markedly by migration status (Figure 3). At EU level, native-born citizens with both parents born abroad were the youngest group, with 44.2% aged 15 - 29 and only 19.8% aged 55 - 74. By contrast, foreign-born citizens were concentrated in the older age groups: only 12.4% were aged 15 - 29, while 50.7% were aged 30 - 54 and 36.8% were aged 55 - 74. The age distribution of native-born citizens with both parents native-born and of native-born citizens with one parent born abroad was more balanced, although in both groups the largest share was aged 30 - 54. Figure 3 In 2025, people aged 15 - 74 with a migrant background in the EU were more concentrated in cities than native-born people with both parents native-born (Figure 4). The share living in cities was 54.5% among native-born people with both parents foreign-born and 53.5% among foreign-born people, compared with 44.9% for those with one parent born abroad and 36.8% for native-born people with both parents native-born. By contrast, rural residence was most common among native-born people with both parents native-born (28.1%), while it was less than half that level among foreign-born people (12.9%) and native-born people with both parents foreign-born (12.3%). The differences were smaller in towns and suburbs, where all groups recorded shares of around one third, ranging from 33.2% to 35.1%. Figure 4 ===Household composition=== Figure 5 shows that, in 2025, households composed of native-born people with a native background remained the largest group in the EU, accounting for 27.3% of single-adult households and 45.8% of multi-adult households. Between 2021 and 2025, their share increased among single-adult households, by 0.6 percentage points, while it declined by 3.1 percentage points among multi-adult households. At the same time, the share of foreign-born households increased steadily in both household types, rising from 5.0% in 2021 to 6.0% in 2025 among single-adult households, and from 5.5% to 6.4% among multi-adult households. The share of households composed of native-born people with a foreign background increased at lower pace among single-adult households, from 2.7% to 3.0%, while it remained stable among multi-adult households, between 1.0% to 1.1%. Mixed households represented around one tenth of multi-adult households over the whole 2021-2025 period. Figure 5 In 2025, at EU level, single-adult households were most commonly composed of native-born people with native-born parents (Figure 6). The share of such households was particularly high in Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Poland, Hungary, Greece and Lithuania, where it exceeded 90.0% in each case. By contrast, Malta (60.9%) and Luxembourg (57.5%) recorded high proportions of single-adult households of foreign-born people, while Latvia and Estonia reported a notable presence of households with native-born people who had one or 2 foreign-born parents. In the case of multi-adult households, the most common group across the EU remained those composed of native-born people with native-born parents. Smaller shares were observed for households composed of foreign-born people, for mixed households, and for native-born people with one or 2 foreign-born parents. Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Poland, and Hungary had a particularly high share of households composed of native-born people with native-born parents, all above 90.0%. Luxembourg, Malta and Cyprus recorded high proportions of households composed of foreign-born people (45.0%, 28.1% and 25.1%, respectively). Mixed households were more frequent in Luxembourg, Latvia, Estonia, Belgium, and France. Figure 6 In 2025, across the EU, among all households, mixed households were the most likely to have children (39.6%), followed by households of foreign-born persons (31.8%), while households of native-born persons with a foreign background were the least likely (15.8%) (Figure 7). Among single-adult households, those with children were least common among native-born persons with a native background (8.9%) and most common among foreign-born people (11.6%). Among multi-adult households, those of foreign-born people were the most likely to have children (50.9%), while the shares were lower among households of native-born people, regardless of whether they had native-born or foreign-born parents. Figure 7
===Source data for graphs=== The data displayed in these visualisations were calculated using data from 3 Eurostat datasets: * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfsa_pganedm/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=7bec084f-4c22-46b0-bb14-dcdc01b27d56&c=1749481086660 Population by sex, age, migration status, citizenship and educational attainment level [lfsa_pganedm]]; * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfst_r_pgaum__custom_17589412/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=75327873-2422-464f-a3df-e512b4474d01&c=1753457699895 Population by sex, age, migration status and degree of urbanisation [lfst_r_pgaum]] * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfst_hhmgscomp/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=824ac8ce-6a05-435a-a22d-128df749da12&c=1753278625311 Number of households by migration status, working status and household composition [lfst_hhmgscomp]] Information on data reliability, series breaks, and differing definitions, flags can be consulted in the online datasets. ===Data sources=== The data presented in this article are from the EU [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)| labour force survey (EU-LFS)]], the largest household sample survey in the EU. The survey covers the resident population in private households. As such, people living in collective households are excluded from the target population. The concept of usual residence is used, which means the place where a person normally spends the daily period of rest, regardless of temporary absences for purposes of recreation, holidays, visits to friends and relatives, business, medical treatment or religious pilgrimage. The data for the EU are aggregated results for the 27 EU countries. For more information on the data sources used, please consult the online publication [[EU_labour_force_survey|EU labour force survey]]. Due to the sampling nature of the survey, some data have low reliability or are not published due to very low reliability or confidentiality. '''Calculation of shares in totals''' All the figures in this article present shares of a total. For some of the analysed breakdowns, e.g. by migration status, citizenship, household composition there is a certain amount of non-response (also called ’not stated’ or ’unknown’). Wherever possible, the calculation of shares in this article is based on a total excluding the number of people classified in the not stated or unknown categories. As such, all exhaustive breakdowns presented in graphs should sum to 100.0% (allowing for rounding errors). ===Context=== The data in this article provide information not only on foreign-born persons living in the EU but also about native-born persons with at least one foreign-born parent. Successful integration may lead to economic and social benefits for migrants and their children, and for the society where they live. More information on the policies and legislation in force in this area can be found in an introductory article: [[Migrant_integration_statistics_introduced|Migrant integration statistics introduced]]. ===See also=== *[[:Category: Migration and asylum |All articles on migration and asylum]] '''Online publications''' *[[Migrant integration statistics - title: Migrant integration statistics - housing
text:
European statistics on main housing indicators among foreign citizens contrasted with nationals: home ownership rate, overcrowding rate and housing cost overburden rate. Data extracted on 10 September 2025. Planned article update: October 2026. In 2024, the home ownership rate among nationals (73.6%) was more than 3 times higher than that of non-EU citizens (22.9%) and nearly twice as high as that of citizens of other EU countries (37.0%). In 2024, 33.0% of non-EU citizens lived in overcrowded housing; for citizens of other EU countries, the share was 19.8%, while for nationals it was 13.7%. In 2024, the housing cost overburden rate stood at 18.8% for non-EU citizens, compared with 16.1% for citizens of other EU countries and 7.6% for nationals. This article presents European statistics for 3 main housing indicators: [[Glossary:Home ownership|home ownership]], [[Glossary:Overcrowding rate|overcrowding]] and [[Glossary:Housing cost overburden rate|housing cost overburden]] rates. These rates are analysed according to an individual’s citizenship. The data presented in this article come from the [[Glossary:EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]] and the analysis is done for the population aged 18 years and over. This article forms part of the online publication on [[Migrant_integration_statistics - facts and figures|migrant integration statistics]]. The three indicators are also visualized in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/dashboard/migrant-integration-inclusion/ Migrant Integration and Inclusion Dashboard].
===Home ownership rate=== Between 2015 and 2024, [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Home_ownership home ownership] was more common among nationals than among foreign citizens, both from other EU countries and non-EU countries (Figure 1). Over this period, the ownership rate among nationals increased slightly, from 72.7% in 2015 to 73.6% in 2024. By contrast, it fluctuated around 40% for other EU citizens, settling at 37.0% in 2024, and declined steadily for non-EU citizens, from 31.7% in 2015 to 22.9% in 2024, thereby further widening the gap with nationals. Figure 1 In 2024, in the EU, the home ownership rate remained high among nationals (Figure 2), with the highest rates recorded in Romania (94.4%) and Slovakia (94.1%), and the lowest in Germany (52.3%), Denmark (60.2%) and Austria (61.2%). For non-EU citizens, home ownership varied widely across countries, with highest rates in Bulgaria (82.3%) and Latvia (78.1%) and particularly low rates in Austria (14.8%), Slovenia (15.8%), and Germany (16.3%). Citizens of other EU countries generally had higher ownership rates than non-EU citizens, with exceptions in Ireland (35.9% for non-EU citizens, compared with 35.4% for other EU countries) and Latvia (78.1% compared with 75.8%). In Poland, the highest home ownership rate was recorded among citizens of other EU countries (90.1%) rather than among nationals (87.9%), while in Slovakia, the rate for other EU citizens was equal to that of nationals (94.1%). Figure 2
===Overcrowding rate=== Between 2015 and 2024, in the EU, the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Overcrowding_rate overcrowding rate] remained considerably higher among non-EU citizens than among nationals and citizens of other EU countries (Figure 3). Over the decade, the overcrowding rate for nationals declined slightly (from 15.7% in 2015 to 13.7% in 2024), while for non-EU citizens it increased (from 31.7% in 2015 to 33.0% in 2024), peaking in 2021 (35.9%), before returning to lower levels. At the start of the period, overcrowding rate for citizens of other EU countries (16.1%) was similar to that of nationals (15.7%). Over the decade, however, the rate of citizens of other EU countries increased to 19.8% in 2024, moderately increasing the gap between the 2 groups. Figure 3 Figure 4 shows that in 2024, in the EU, the overcrowding rate was highest among non-EU citizens in Romania (61.6%) and Poland (58.0%), and lowest in Ireland (4.4%) and Cyprus (7.0%). Among nationals, highest rates were recorded in Romania (35.6%) and Latvia (35.4%), with lowest in Cyprus (1.3%) and Malta (2.4%). For citizens of other EU countries, overcrowding rates were highest in Slovakia (49.9%) and Latvia (44.4%), and lowest in Malta (0.6%) and Hungary (4.2%). When availability of data allows comparison between the 3 groups, the overcrowding rate was generally highest among non-EU citizens, except in Ireland, Croatia and Latvia, where the highest rates were observed among citizens of other EU countries. Conversely, lowest rates were usually among nationals, except in Malta and Portugal, where the lowest rates were among other EU citizens, and in Croatia, where the lowest rates were observed among non-nationals. The greatest variation between the groups was observed in Poland, Austria and Sweden. Figure 4
===Housing cost overburden rate=== Between 2015 and 2024, the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Housing_cost_overburden_rate housing cost overburden rate] remained consistently higher among foreign citizens than among nationals (Figure 5). In the EU, the housing cost overburden rate for nationals gradually declined in the first part of the period, from 10.7% in 2015 to 7.2% in 2020, before stabilizing at 7.6% in 2024. Non-EU citizens faced higher and more fluctuating rates, showing a clear downward trend from 27.1% in 2015 to 18.8% in 2024. Citizens of other EU countries experienced a decline from 21.1% in 2015 to 16.1% in 2024, consistently remaining between the levels of nationals and non-EU citizens. Figure 5 Figure 6 shows that in the EU in 2024, the housing cost overburden rate was lowest among nationals (7.6%) and highest among foreign citizens, with non-EU citizens (18.8%) above citizens of other EU countries (16.1%). The same pattern was also observed in most countries with data available for all 3 groups, with some exceptions. In Denmark, non-EU citizens had lower rate (15.2%) than the other 2 groups (16.5% for nationals and 27.8 for other EU citizens), while citizens of other EU countries recorded higher rates than nationals and non-EU citizens in Denmark (27.8%), Estonia (17.5%), Italy (17.1%), Germany (15.2%), Slovenia (13.3%) and Latvia (12.7%). The greatest differences between the 3 groups were observed in Portugal, the Netherlands, Czechia and Spain. Figure 6 ===Source data for graphs=== The data displayed in the visualisations come directly from [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/migrant-integration/database Eurostat’s online database] for the reference year(s) mentioned in the visualisation. The accompanying text is from 10 September 2025 and reflects the data situation at that moment in time. For information on data reliability, series breaks, and differing definitions, flags can be consulted in the online dataset. ===Data sources=== The data used in this article are derived from EU-SILC. EU-SILC data are compiled annually and are the main source of statistics that measure income and living conditions in Europe; it is also the main source of information used to link different aspects relating to the quality of life of [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Household_-_social_statistics households] and individuals. The reference population for the information presented in this article is all private households and their current members residing in the territory of an EU country (or non-EU country) at the time of data collection; people living in collective households and in institutions are excluded from the target population. The data for the EU are population-weighted averages of national data. The reference period for individuals' characteristics is 2024. The statistics presented cover the EU as a whole, its individual Member States, one EFTA country (Norway), as well as the candidate countries Serbia and Türkiye. In several EU countries, the classification of foreign citizens identifies a small sample of observations, therefore some data cannot be published due to very low reliability. ===Context=== Housing is considered an important element for the well-being of individuals. The quality and affordability of housing is often seen as crucial for measuring living standards and social inclusion/exclusion. Being able to afford housing of adequate/decent quality in a safe environment is a basic need, as a [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Dwelling dwelling] should provide shelter, adequate space for its occupants to live, eat and sleep, as well as a degree of privacy for the household as a whole and for its individual members. In November 2020, the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0758 action plan on integration and inclusion 2021–2027] (COM(2016) 377 final) was adopted with the purpose of fostering social cohesion and building inclusive societies for all. Inclusion for all is about ensuring that all policies are accessible to and work for everyone, including migrants and EU citizens with migrant background. This plan includes actions in four sectoral areas (education and training, employment and skills, health and housing) as well as actions supporting effective integration and inclusion in all sectoral areas at the EU, EU country and regional level, with a specific attention paid to young people. More information on the policies and legislation in force in this area can be found in an [[Migrant_integration_statistics_introduced|introductory article on migrant integration statistics]]. ===Other
