title: National accounts 2024 benchmark revision - impact on sector accounts
text:
national accounts; 2024 coordinated benchmark revision of sector accounts; harmonised European revision policy; gross disposable income of households; value added of non-financial corporations. Data extracted in February 2025. No planned article update. The gross disposable income in 2019 of households in the EU was 1.2% higher after the benchmark revision. The gross value added in 2019 of non-financial corporations in the EU was 0.4% lower after the benchmark revision. |alt=Dynamic interactive line chart with 2 lines showing, in percent, the impact of the 2024 benchmark revision on the gross disposable income of households and the gross value added of non-financial corporations. Data are shown for 1999 to 2022 for the European Union. This article presents [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] statistics derived from European sector accounts, which form part of the [[Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)|European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)]]. Data are provided for the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], the [[Glossary:Euro_area|euro area]], EU countries and some [[Glossary:Candidate countries|enlargement]] countries. In 2024, 26 [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU countries]] participated in a coordinated benchmark revision of [[Glossary:National_accounts_(NA)|national accounts]] in line with recommendations of the harmonised European revision policy (HERP). National statistical authorities took the opportunity to improve the quality of their national accounts estimates further by introducing methodological or compilation changes as well as using new data sources. This had some effect on countries’ data; this in turn impacted estimates for the EU and the euro area. In line with the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-catalogues/-/KS-02-18-142 European statistics code of practice], this article communicates the main results of the 2024 coordinated benchmark revisions in a transparent way. While this benchmark revision exercise has impacted all national accounts data, it has impacted various sectors and indicators differently. This article focuses on [[Glossary:Household disposable income|gross disposable income]] of households and [[Glossary:Gross value added|gross value added]] of [[Glossary:Non-financial corporations sector|non-financial corporations (also referred to as businesses]]. *Gross household adjusted disposable income provides a measure of the financial resources that are available to households, after taxes and other deductions have been made. *Gross value added is defined as output (at basic prices) minus [[Glossary:intermediate consumption|intermediate consumption]] (at purchaser prices). The article analyses time series starting in 1995 and ending in 2022. For the EU, the euro area and a few countries, slightly shorter time series are presented; for example, the time series for the EU and the euro area start in 1999. For each [[Glossary:Economic indicator|indicator]] and year, 2 values are compared, having been extracted in February 2024 (before the 2024 benchmark revision) and in February 2025 (after the benchmark revision). *Note that Luxembourg and Türkiye didn’t undertake the benchmark revision in 2024 and so any revisions between these 2 extractions reflect routine updates only. *For all other countries, the changes reflect the impact of the benchmark revision, as well as routine updates. Revisions were generally smaller for earlier years and larger for more recent years, due to a combination of routine updates and the benchmark revision. Because routine updates tend to have their greatest impact on recent years (2020-2022), the main focus of this article is on the years 2015 to 2019, in particular on 2019. This period has been chosen in the expectation that routine updates after 1 January 2024 would have been minimal and so the calculated revisions reflect principally the impact of the 2024 benchmark revision exercise. The overall results of the implementation of the 2024 benchmark revision exercise for 2019 data can be summarised as follows. *Gross disposable income of households for the EU was revised upwards by 1.2%, while for the euro area it was revised upwards by 1.1%. *Gross value added of non-financial corporations (businesses) for the EU was revised downwards by 0.4%, while for the euro area it was revised downwards by 0.5%. ===Gross disposable income of households=== The earliest years in the EU’s time series for gross disposable income of households recorded the smallest revisions, around 0.2% to 0.4% for the 3 years from 1999 to 2001 – see Figure 1. Revisions increased from 0.6% for 2002 to 1.0% for 2006 and then remained between 0.9% and 1.1% for all years through to 2018. A slightly larger revision (up 1.2%) was observed in 2019 and then a more typical revision of 0.9% in 2020. The revisions in 2021 (up 1.4%) and 2022 (up 2.2%) were notably larger and this may reflect the impact of routine updates alongside the benchmark revisions. For the euro area, the revisions were slightly larger from the start of the series (1999) through until 2018. For the 3 most recent years (2019 to 2022), the revisions for the euro area were marginally smaller than for the EU. [[Image:Revisions of gross disposable income of households, 1999–2022 (% revision)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 1: Revisions of gross disposable income of households, 1999–2022
(% revision)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_ki}}|alt=A line chart showing the impact of revisions on gross disposable income of households. Data are shown in percent, for 1999 to 2022, for the EU and the euro area. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] Table 1 summarises the revisions of gross disposable income of households for the period from 1995 to 2022, presenting average revisions for 5-year periods as far as these are available. *The smallest revisions, regardless of whether they were negative or positive, were recorded in the 2 earliest 5-year periods (1995 to 1999 and 2000 to 2004). *As expected, because of the impact of routine updates, the largest revisions tended to be in the most recent period (2020 to 2022). *The EU countries with the largest average revisions were **Romania, with relatively large negative revisions in the 5-year periods from 2005 to 2019 **Latvia and Lithuania, with negative revisions in all 5-year periods, with the largest revisions in the 5-year periods from 2000 to 2004 onwards **Malta, with positive revisions from 2000 to 2004 onwards, with relatively large positive revisions in the 5-year periods from 2005 to 2009 onwards **Cyprus and Czechia, with positive revisions in all 5-year periods, with the largest revisions in the period from 2020 to 2022. [[Image:Revisions of gross disposable income of households, 1995–2022 (% revision, averages)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: Revisions of gross disposable income of households, 1995–2022
(% revision, averages)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_ki}}|alt=A table showing the impact of revisions on gross disposable income of households. Data are shown in percent, for 5-year periods from 1995 to 2019 and for 2020 to 2022, for the EU and the euro area as well as for EU and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] Figure 2 focuses on revisions to gross disposable income of households in the years from 2015 to 2019; these years were selected as they are a) relatively recent and b) expected to be less impacted by routine updates. This figure shows the average revision during this period, which was 1.1% in both the EU and the euro area. *16 EU countries recorded positive average revisions, peaking at 6.8% in Malta. *The remaining 11 EU countries recorded negative average revisions, with the largest negative revision in Romania (-9.0%). The latter was mainly explained by an improvement of the estimate of [[Glossary:Remittances|remittances]] tranferred by Romanians working abroad, which led to a large decrease of their values. [[Image:Revisions of gross disposable income of households, 2015–19 (% revision, averages)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 2: Revisions of gross disposable income of households, 2015–19
(% revision, averages)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_ki}}|alt=A column chart showing the impact of revisions on gross disposable income of households. Data are shown in percent, for 2015 to 2019, for the EU and the euro area as well as for EU and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] '''Impact of national revisions on the EU totals''' Figure 3 shows the average revision of the EU’s gross disposable income of households for each year from 1999 to 2022. The horizontal bar shown for each year represents the EU’s percentage revision (which is the same as the line shown for the EU in Figure 1). The columns show the contributions of EU countries (in percentage points) to the EU revision. The contributions of the 5 EU countries with the biggest contributions to the EU’s revisions of gross disposable income of households over this whole period – Germany, Italy, Spain, Poland and France – are shown individually; the combined net contribution of all other countries is also shown. *For every year, the contributions of the 5 individual countries shown in the figure were positive. *From 1999 to 2016, the net contribution of all other EU countries combined was negative. *In 2017 and 2018, the net contribution of all other EU countries combined was almost nothing (+/- 0.01 percentage points). *From 2019, the net contribution of all other EU countries combined was positive. [[Image:Revisions of gross disposable income of households, 1999–2022 (EU countries, percentage point contributions to the EU revision; EU, % revision)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 3: Revisions of gross disposable income of households, 1999–2022
(EU countries, percentage point contributions to the EU revision; EU, % revision)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_ki}}|alt=A stacked column chart showing the impact of revisions on gross disposable income of households for the EU in percent and the contribution of EU countries to the revisions of gross disposable income of households for the EU in percentage points. Data are shown for 1999 to 2022, for the EU, the 5 EU countries with the largest contributions to the EU revisions and an aggregate for the remaining EU countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] '''Revision of components''' Gross disposable income can be analysed according to its components. The revision of gross disposable income equals the sum of the revisions to the following components *[[Glossary:Compensation of employees|compensation of employees]] *[[Glossary:Gross operating surplus (GOS) - NA|gross operating surplus and gross mixed income]] *net [[Glossary:Allocation of primary income account|property income]] and other net [[Glossary:Current transfers|current transfers]] *social benefits *current taxes and net [[Glossary:Social contributions|social contributions]]. Table 2 shows the average impact of the revisions between 2015 and 2019 for gross disposable income and each of its components. *For the EU and the euro area, the component most strongly impacted by the revisions was compensation of employees, in both cases with an upward revision. The next largest revisions were for the gross operating surplus and gross mixed income, which also had positive revisions. *For 10 EU countries, the component most strongly impacted by the revisions was net property income and other net current transfers. Malta and Poland recorded the largest positive revisions for this component, while Romania and Lithuania recorded the largest negative revisions. In the case of Malta, [[Glossary:Balance of payments|balance of payments]] and administrative data were used to improve the estimates of [[Glossary:Interest|interest]] received and distributed income of corporations. This implied a considerable increase in Maltese property income in 2015 and 2016. *For 9 EU countries, the component most strongly impacted by the revisions was gross operating surplus and gross mixed income. Malta recorded the largest positive revision for this component and Latvia the largest negative revision. The large revision upwards of gross mixed income of households in Malta was mainly due to the integration of the ''Census of population and housing 2021''. It led to a change in methodology to calculate imputed rents in Malta (from the user-cost method to the stratification method), large revisions in actual rentals and exhaustiveness adjustments. The gross operating surplus of households was revised downwards considerably in Latvia, due to a revision (around -30%) in output for own final use. The revision in Latvia of the data for the [[Glossary:Consumption of fixed capital (CFC)|consumption of fixed capital]] and net accrued [[Glossary:Fixed capital|fixed capital]] impacted the values for own-account production of housing services by owner-occupiers (the main component of output for own final use). The integration of the results of the Population and Housing Census 2021 also affected own-account production of housing services by owner-occupiers, as Latvia applies the user-cost method because the rental market is very small. *For Germany, Ireland, Hungary, the Netherlands and Sweden, the component most strongly impacted by the revisions was compensation of employees, with all reporting positive revisions. *For Bulgaria (2015 to 2017) and Cyprus, the component most strongly impacted by the revisions was social benefits, with Cyprus reporting a positive revision and Bulgaria a negative one. *For France, the component most strongly impacted by the revisions was current taxes and net social contributions, with a negative revision. [[Image:Revisions of gross disposable income of households and its components, 2015–19 (% revision, averages)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 2: Revisions of gross disposable income of households and its components, 2015–19
(% revision, averages)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_ki}}|alt=A table showing the impact of revisions on gross disposable income of households and its components. Data are shown in percentages as an average for 2015 to 2019 for the EU and the euro area as well as for EU and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] ===Gross value added of non-financial corporations (businesses)=== The earliest years in the EU’s time series for gross value added of non-financial corporations recorded the largest negative revisions, around -0.8% or -0.9% from 1999 to 2004 – see Figure 4. Revisions then remained between -0.5% and -0.7% from 2005 to 2017. Smaller negative revisions (-0.2% to -0.4%) were recorded from 2018 to 2020 after which the revisions turned positive, up 0.2% in 2021 and 1.1% in 2022. The revision in 2022 was notably larger than in other years and may reflect the impact of routine updates alongside the benchmark revisions. For the euro area, the revisions were somewhat more negative from the start of the series (1999) through until 2013. In 2014, EU and euro area revisions were almost identical. Thereafter, there was no clear pattern, with EU and euro area revisions broadly similar. [[Image:Revisions of value added of non-financial corporations, 1999–2022 (% revision)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 4: Revisions of value added of non-financial corporations, 1999–2022
(% revision)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_ki}}|alt=A line chart showing the impact of revisions on gross value added of non-financial corporations. Data are shown in percent, for 1999 to 2022, for the EU and the euro area. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] Table 3 summarises the revisions of gross value added of non-financial corporations for the period from 1995 to 2022, presenting average revisions for 5-year periods as far as these are available. *The largest and smallest revisions aren’t found in a particular part of the time series. For example, the single largest positive revision for any country was for Malta for 2020 to 2022 (which may be explained by routine revisions), while the single largest negative revision was for Greece for 1995 to 1999. *The EU countries with the largest average revisions were **Greece, with negative revisions in all 5-year periods, with relatively large negative revisions in the 5-year periods from 1995 to 2004. **Croatia, with negative revisions in most but not all 5-year periods, with relatively large negative revisions in 2010 to 2014 and 1995 to 1999. **Ireland, with positive revisions in 5-year periods from 2010 to 2014 onwards, with relatively large positive revisions in the 5-year period from 2015 to 2019. [[Image:Revisions of value added of non-financial corporations, 1995–2022 (% revision, averages)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 3: Revisions of value added of non-financial corporations, 1995–2022
(% revision, averages)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_ki}}|alt=A table showing the impact of revisions on gross value added of non-financial corporations. Data are shown in percent, for 5-year periods from 1995 to 2019 and for 2020 to 2022, for the EU and the euro area as well as for EU and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] Figure 5 focuses on revisions to gross value added of non-financial corporations in the years from 2015 to 2019. This figure shows the average revision during this period, which was -0.4% in both the EU and the euro area. *9 EU countries recorded positive average revisions, peaking at 4.4% in Ireland. *The remaining 17 EU countries (other than Luxembourg, for which no revisions were recorded) recorded negative average revisions, with the largest negative revision in Greece (-2.6%). [[Image:Revisions of value added of non-financial corporations, 2015–19 (% revision, averages)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 5: Revisions of value added of non-financial corporations, 2015–19
(% revision, averages)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_ki}}|alt=A column chart showing the impact of revisions on gross value added of non-financial corporations. Data are shown in percent, for 2015 to 2019, for the EU and the euro area as well as for EU and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] '''Impact of national revisions on the EU totals''' Figure 6 shows the average revision of the EU’s gross value added of non-financial corporations for each year from 1999 to 2022. The horizontal bar shown for each year represents the EU’s percentage revision (which is the same as the line shown for the EU in Figure 4). The columns show the contributions of EU countries (in percentage points) to the EU revision. The contributions of the 5 EU countries with the biggest contributions to the EU’s revisions of gross value added of non-financial corporations over this whole period – France, Germany, the Netherlands, Italy and Ireland – are shown individually; the combined net contribution of all other countries is also shown. *For every year, the contribution of France was negative, as it was for Italy in every year except for 2022. *Germany’s contribution was negative most years; among the exceptions, the most notable were the positive contributions in 2010, 2018 and 2022. *The Netherlands’ contribution was negative from 1999 to 2014 and positive thereafter. *From 1999 to 2009, there was no revision for Ireland; thereafter, the contribution of Ireland was positive. *The net contribution of all other EU countries combined was negative from 1999 to 2017 and positive for the 5 most recent years. [[Image:Revisions of value added of non-financial corporations, 1999–2022 (EU countries, percentage point contributions to the EU revision; EU, % revision)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 6: Revisions of value added of non-financial corporations, 1999–2022
(EU countries, percentage point contributions to the EU revision; EU, % revision)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_ki}}|alt=A stacked column chart showing the impact of revisions on gross value added of non-financial corporations for the EU in percent and the contribution of EU countries to the revisions of gross value added of non-financial corporations for the EU in percentage points. Data are shown for 1999 to 2022, for the EU, the 5 EU countries with the largest contributions to the EU revisions and an aggregate for the remaining EU countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] '''Revision of components''' Gross value added can be analysed according to its components. The revision of gross value added equals the sum of the revisions to the following components *gross operating surplus *compensation of employees *other taxes less [[Glossary:Subsidies|subsidies]] on production. Table 4 shows the average impact of the revisions between 2015 and 2019 for gross value added and each of its components. *For the EU and the euro area, the component most strongly impacted by the revisions was other taxes less subsidies on production, with large negative revisions. The next largest revision was for the compensation of employees, which had positive revisions for both the EU and the euro area. *For 16 EU countries, the component most strongly impacted by the revisions was gross operating surplus. Ireland recorded the largest positive revision for this component and Greece and Finland the largest negative revisions. *For Spain, Hungary, Malta, Portugal and Slovenia, the component most strongly impacted by the revisions was compensation of employees. Among these countries, Malta and Hungary recorded the largest positive revisions for this component and Slovenia the largest negative revision. *For Germany, Estonia, Croatia, Italy and Poland, the component most strongly impacted by the revisions was other taxes less subsidies on production. These 5 countries all recorded negative revisions, with the largest in Italy and Germany. In the case of Germany, following Eurostat recommendations, the surcharge levied on electricity consumers is no longer classified as part of the electricity price, but rather as other product taxes. Consequently, other taxes less subsidies on production were revised upwards, which implied a decrease in gross value added. [[Image:Revisions of value added of non-financial corporations and its components, 2015–19 (% revision, averages)_NA2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 4: Revisions of value added of non-financial corporations and its components, 2015–19
(% revision, averages)
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=nasa_10_ki}}|alt=A table showing the impact of revisions on gross value added of non-financial corporations and its components. Data are shown in percentages as an average for 2015 to 2019 for the EU and the euro area as well as for EU and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=Sector accounts 2024 benchmark revisions_NA2025.xlsx|title=Sector accounts 2024 benchmark revisions: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''Benchmark revision''' Benchmark revisions are coordinated major revisions carried out at least once every 5 years to incorporate new data sources and major changes in international statistical methodology. In national accounts, they aim to ensure a maximum degree of consistency within national accounts. In other words, they should be implemented to obtain a long time series and ensure consistency across countries. In line with the implementation of a harmonised European revision policy (HERP), 26 EU countries carried out coordinated benchmark revisions of national accounts in 2024; Luxembourg postponed the benchmark revision to 2027. This means that the 2024 benchmark revision covered countries that account for 99% of EU / euro area economic activity. Three of the [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] countries – Iceland, Norway and Switzerland – plan to carry out the benchmark revision in 2025. Before and during the benchmark revision exercise, a coordinated communication strategy was implemented through Eurostat’s dedicated section on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-2010/data-revision benchmark revisions]. This was progressively updated and covers various aspects *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/737960/9861115/2024-benchmark-revision-overview.pdf/c6286ffa-8949-c032-2e95-8b4d297cf8eb?t=1709215434771 Overview on requirements and main expected changes] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/737960/0/Overviews-national-communication-data-release-dates.pdf/a8250741-13b2-4e10-aaf5-6c5d3c3c3dba?t=1723109111463 Overviews on national communication and data release dates] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/737960/0/Information-on-cooridation-and-consistency-of-benchmark-implementation.pdf/f3eb3e76-0af1-928a-13ad-383b0c7229db?t=1722427021181 Information on coordination and consistency of benchmark implementation] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/737960/0/Progress-of-benchmark-implementation-with-metadata.pdf/912b4844-9a7a-f174-71f8-3d326622eb6d?t=1729694788775 Progress of benchmark data publication and associated metadata] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/737960/0/Information-on-GDP-impacts-and-main-changes.pdf/cd4fbf82-8bf9-32e5-4185-85bd150496d0?t=1726225014830 Information on GDP impacts and main changes]. Country-specific [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/24987/6624264/Country_specific_metadata_on_particularities.pdf/c2002d80-aded-1cf5-0d59-60eba493e37d?t=1697102466339 metadata on data particularities] were also published for a number of countries. The analysis in this article is based on the annual sector accounts data, including 2024 benchmark revisions transmitted in May-October of 2024. It compares the latest annual transmissions before the announced benchmark revision date and the first annual transmission after the announced benchmark revision date. Data for the EU and the euro area were compiled by aggregating the values from each EU country. Since September 2014, data transmission has been in line with {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32013R0549:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 549/2013}} of the European Parliament and of the Council on the European system of national and regional accounts in the European Union. This required EU countries to transmit their main GDP aggregates based on the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-2010/overview European system of national and regional accounts 2010 (ESA 2010)]. In March 2023, {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32023R0734:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 734/2023}} amended Regulation (EU) No 549/2013, introducing updates and repealing 11 legal acts in the field of national accounts to ensure the continued relevance and coherence of the national accounts framework. This has been applicable for transmissions since 1 September 2024, unless temporary derogations were granted by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32024D1251:EN:NOT|title=Decision (EU) 1251/2024}}. '''Institutional sectors''' [[Glossary:Institutional sector|Institutional sectors]] within national accounts bring together economic units with broadly similar characteristics and behaviour. The 5 sectors which make up the domestic economy are non-financial corporations, financial corporations, general government, households and non-profit institutions serving households (NPISH). '''''The household sector''''' The household sector consists of individuals or groups of individuals as consumers, as entrepreneurs (producing market goods, non-financial and financial services) and as producers of goods and non-financial services exclusively for their own final use. In general, sole proprietorships and most partnerships that don’t have an independent legal status are considered to be part of the household sector, rather than as corporations (financial or non-financial). However, there are sometimes practical difficulties in delineating ‘quasi-corporations’ (unincorporated businesses with the characteristics of companies) between corporations and the household sector; this may influence the scope and comparability of the data presented as well as the internal consistency of the full set of accounts. As stated above, data for the household sector in this article are shown including information on the sector of non-profit institutions serving households. The latter is relatively small and includes, for example, charities, relief and aid organisations, religious groups, consumer associations, sports and recreational clubs, professional societies, trade unions and political parties. These institutions provide goods or services to households for free or at considerably reduced prices. Their main resources are derived from voluntary contributions in cash or in kind from households (in their capacity as consumers), payments made by general government, or property income. '''''The non-financial corporations sector''''' The non-financial corporations sector consists of institutional units which are independent legal entities and market producers, and whose principal activity is the production of goods and non-financial services. It may be divided into 3 subsectors covering: public non-financial corporations, national private non-financial corporations and foreign controlled non-financial corporations. In general, sole proprietorships and most partnerships that don’t have an independent legal status are considered to be part of the household sector, rather than corporations (financial or non-financial). However, there are sometimes practical difficulties in delineating ‘quasi-corporations’ (unincorporated businesses with the characteristics of companies) between corporations and the household sector. This may influence the scope and comparability of the data presented as well as the internal consistency of the full set of accounts. '''Indicator definitions''' '''''Gross disposable income''''' Gross disposable income is the result of all current transactions before consumption. It excludes exceptional resources/uses such as capital transfers, holding gains/losses and the consequences of natural disasters. It reflects the net resources, earned during the period, which are available for consumption and/or saving. The aggregate therefore consists of net wages, the gross operating surplus and mixed income, net [[Glossary:Allocation of primary income account|property income]] (note that financial intermediation services indirectly measured (FISIM) is a component reallocated from property income to consumption within national accounts), social benefits, and other transfers, reduced by any taxes paid and pension contributions. In other words, it is the total amount of resources that a household has left available to spend or save once income taxes and pension contributions have been subtracted. '''''Value added''''' Gross value added is defined as output (at basic prices) minus intermediate consumption (at purchaser prices); it is the balancing item of the national accounts’ production account. Value added can be analysed by industry and by institutional sector. The sum of value added over all industries or sectors plus taxes on products minus subsidies on products gives [[Glossary:gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product]]. '''Symbols''' In tables, a colon ‘:’ is used to show where data aren’t available. ===Context=== Non-financial sector accounts form part of the national accounting framework and are compiled in the EU in accordance with the ESA 2010. They are an indispensable tool for analysing developments concerning production, the distribution of income, savings and investment by various institutional sectors, including households and non-financial corporations. Sector accounts provide important indicators for national and EU decision making. It is, therefore, important that regular quality improvements are introduced in the data sources and methods. This is achieved through data revisions in line with the [https://www.cmfb.org/main-topics/revision-policy harmonised European revision policy]. The most important changes are introduced with the benchmark revisions typically carried out every 5 years. ===Other articles=== *[[European system of national and regional accounts - ESA 2010|European system of national and regional accounts – ESA 2010]] – background article *[[Households - title: National accounts - main GDP aggregates and related indicators
text:
2 Data from October 2012 This article presents key messages from selected [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] annual [[Glossary:National accounts (NA)|national accounts]] figures, together with some practical and methodological background information. National accounts are a powerful source of information for studying many aspects of the economy. The main [[Glossary:Aggregate|aggregates]], covering the annual and quarterly [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]] and its components, are among the most significant indicators of the state of any economy, be it at a national or European level. Data on the evolution of GDP, production, expenditure and income as well as related indicators (e.g. on [[Glossary:Employment|employment]] and [[Glossary:Productivity|productivity]]) are often headline figures and are of key interest to users. While typical users of quarterly national accounts (QNA) figures, such as market analysts, forecasters or economic and monetary policy advisors are primarily interested in assessing the state of the current [[Glossary:Business cycle|business cycle]], users of annual national accounts data (ANA) are typically interested in analysing structural changes in the economy from a medium-term perspective. === Economic size === '''Nominal GDP''' The EU economic data are the result of aggregating the data for the individual economies of [[Glossary:EU enlargements|27 Member States]]. They are fairly heterogeneous in terms of size, income levels, economic structure and recent economic performance. Table 1 provides an overview of the relative size of their economies between 2001 and 2011 based on GDP measured at current prices and current [[Glossary:Exchange rate|exchange rates]]. Member States are sorted in descending order according to their share in [[Glossary:EU-27|EU-27]] GDP in 2011. They have been classified into three groups. A first group of five large Member States accounted for more than 70 % of the EU-27 economy in 2011 (71 %). A second group of 12 medium-sized Member States accumulated about one quarter (26 %) of EU GDP. Lastly, a group of 10 small Member States represented just 3% of the EU economy. [[Image:Gross domestic product at market prices 2011.png|thumb|centre|500px|Table 1: Comparison of countries' economic size in relation to the EU-27;
Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=nama_gdp_c}}]] The table provides some interesting facts. For example, the Member State with the largest economy (Germany) is more or less the same size as the combined economies of the twenty smaller Member States. It therefore follows that the main features of the EU economy chiefly result from developments in the largest Member States. This is the case even if their respective share of EU GDP has decreased since 2001 excepted in France and Spain. All medium-sized and small Member States have maintained, and in most cases increased their relative weights since 2001, however four countries (Greece, Ireland, Hungary and Lithuania) faced a slight decrease since 2008. Member States that [[Glossary:EU enlargements|joined the EU after 2004]] benefited from economic growth above the EU average until the economic and financial crisis in 2008. These figures not only reflect changes in Member States' respective growth but also differences in price levels among countries du to exchange rate fluctuations as the currencies of many EU Member States lost ground against the [[Glossary:Euro|euro]] between 2007 and 2009. '''GDP in PPS''' The influence of exchange rate effects and differing population sizes on the comparability of nominal GDP levels across countries over time underlines the importance of [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP) in purchasing power standards|GDP per capita expressed in purchasing power standards (PPS)]] for comparing relative income levels. Figure 1 shows adjusted GDP figures per inhabitant, indexed to EU-27=100 for the years 2006, 2010 and 2011. Based on the figures of 2011, Luxembourg stands with an index of 271.7 while the Netherlands, Ireland, Austria and Sweden had an index of 25 % above the EU average. On the other side eight countries – Slovakia, Estonia, Lithuania, Hungary, Poland, Latvia, Romania and Bulgaria were more than 25 % below the EU-27 average. Although comparisons through time should be taken with caution as many factors affect the way PPS figures change, the comparison with 2005 figures suggests some convergence in GDP per capita as countries that were relatively poorer grew faster than in the relatively richer countries. [[Image:GDP per capita in purchasing power standards (PPS).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 1: GDP per capita in purchasing power standards (PPS), EU-27=100;
Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=nama_gdp_c}}]] Though GDP in PPS is a standard measure for comparing income levels across countries, it is not always the most appropriate indicator. Indeed, GDP is based on the concept of domestic production and as such does not account for net [[Glossary:Allocation of primary income account|primary income]] transfers with the rest of the world. This is the case of Luxembourg where a significant part of the wages and salaries paid in relation to domestic production go to cross-border commuters. In Ireland the difference was due to the major presence of foreign multinational corporations. Their profits were included in Irelands GDP, but the dividends repatriated by the multinationals were not reflected in [[Glossary:Gross national income (GNI)|gross national income (GNI)]]. The next sections analyse further the main components of EU GDP in order to highlight the sources of EU growth and its main features but also the origin of disparities that exist among member States. === Economic growth === '''Comparing annual growth rates''' Figure 2 gives an overview of [[Glossary:Chain index|GDP in volume]] growth for the EU, the [[Glossary:Euro area|euro area]], US and Japan for the period 2001-2011. EU-27 and the euro area GDP presented a similar trend. Following a period of relative strong growth between 2001 and 2007, the financial and economic crisis let to a sharp worsening of the global economic situation. In 2008 GDP growth rates declined and even turned negative in 2009 reaching -4.3 % and 4.4% in both the EU and the euro area. However the economy showed a significant recovery the following years with a rate of 1.5 % in the EU and of 1.4 % in the euro area in 2011. [[Image:GDP volume growth between 2001 and 2011.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 2: GDP volume growth between 2000 and 2010, change on previous period (%);
Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=nama_gdp_k}}]] While the european economy grew at a rate of 1.5% on average in 2011, disparities in growth patterns remained within the EU. As Figure 3 shows it, the growth in Greece (-7.1%), Portugal (-1.7%) turned to be negative for this period meanwhile it appeared to be above 5 % in Estonia (+8.3 %), Lithuania (+5.9 %) and Latvia (+5.5 %). [[Image:GDP volume growth in 2011.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 3: GDP volume growth in 2010, change on previous period (%);
Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=nama_gdp_k}}]] GDP volume growth in selected non-EU countries has generally recovered in 2011 compared to the negative growth rates experienced in 2009. However, the growth rates (excepted in the case of Turkey) did not reach the level before 2008 and remained even negative for Japan (-0,8 %). The GDP volume change gives a rough indication of the short-term evolution of living standards. However over longer periods the increase in volume GDP does not necessarily translate into an improvement in living standards: changes in population should be taken into consideration. For short-term economic analysis (quarter-on-quarter or year-on-year developments), population changes are relatively small and therefore the GDP volume change in GDP is a very good approximation of the increase in living standards. '''Breaking down medium-term growth''' Figure 4 shows the average annual GDP volume growth broken down into [[Glossary:Per capita|per-capita]] and average population changes for 2001-2011.The EU-27 experienced an average annual GDP volume growth rate of 1.3 % between 2001 and 2011. However, the average annual GDP volume growth rate per capita was only of 0.9 %. This difference comes from a 0.4 % average annual increase in population. Most of the [[Glossary:EU enlargements|"new" Member States]] have volume growths that are above the EU average. However, six of them experienced a negative growth in population. This is the case for Estonia and Hungary (-0.2 %), Romania (-0.5 %), Bulgaria (-0.6 %), Latvia (-1.3%) and Lithuania (1.4 %) . This downward trend in population shows in these countries that GDP per capita growth outstripped GDP in volume growth. On the other hand, most of the [[Glossary:EU-15|“old” 15 Member States]] faced a GDP growth per capita lower than the volume growth, as the population increased. Among the non-EU countries analysed here, GDP volume growth also mostly exceeded GDP per capita growth due to a growing population effect. In fact, the United States and Japan provide good examples of the shortcomings of focusing on the GDP volume growth rate only. While the US experienced a volume growth 2.5 times higher than in Japan between 2001 and 2011, increases in GDP per capita were actually the same for both countries because the population in the United States grew faster than in Japan. [[Image:Average annual growth of volume GDP for the period 2001-2011 (%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 4: Average annual growth of volume GDP for the period 2001-2011 (%);
Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=nama_gdp_k}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_aux_pem}}]] '''The sources of growth''' In Figure 5, GDP in volume per person growth is further broken down into the contributions to the growth of [[Glossary:Labour productivity|labour productivity per person employed]] and the growth of persons employed divided by the population for the period 2001–2011. Overall, it can be seen that more than two thirds of EU-27 and euro area ([[Glossary:EA-17|EA-17]]) growth stemmed from higher labour productivity. The most impressive gains in productivity were displayed by Romania (+5.4 %), Latvia (+4.5 %) and Lithuania (+4.1 %). It is interesting to note that the countries experiencing the highest gains in labour productivity were the eastern European new Member States. The only EU countries that faced negative labour productivity growth were Luxembourg (-0.2 %) and Italy (-0.3%). The EU [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries]] have also experienced significant productivity gains. On the other hand, the highest increase in [[Glossary:Employment rate|employment ratios]] was observed for Luxembourg (+2.9 %), Cyprus (+2 %) and Malta (+1.4 %). The respective EU-27 and EA-17 average growth rates were both 0.5 % per year. Four countries showed a negative employment ratio namely Latvia, Portugal, Hungry and Romania while outside the EU it was the case of Japan. [[Image:Labour productivity and input to average GDP per capita growth (%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 5: Contributions of labour productivity and input to average GDP per capita growth (%);
Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=nama_gdp_c}},{{Stable link|title=|code=nama_aux_lp}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_aux_pem}}]] Following analysis of the overall GDP aggregate, the remainder of this investigation focuses specifically on the structure of, and changes, in, main output, expenditure and income aggregates. === Further analysis of main GDP aggregates === A core selection of national accounts data focuses on developments at the aggregate level of the total economy. For instance, GDP is a central measure of the economic performance of a country (or region). It can be calculated using three approaches: the [[Glossary:Output approach|output approach]], which sums the gross value added of various industries, plus taxes and minus subsidies on products; the [[Glossary:Expenditure approach|expenditure approach]], which sums the final use of goods and services (final consumption and gross capital formation), plus exports and minus imports of goods and services (external balance); and the [[Glossary:Income approach|income approach]], which sums compensation of employees, net taxes on production and imports, gross operating surplus and mixed income. Figure 6 presents the respective size of these aggregates for the EU. [[Image:Size of main GDP aggregates 2011.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 6: Size of main GDP aggregates (in 2010,% of total EU-27 GDP);
Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=nama_gdp_c}}]] '''The production side''' Starting from the [[Glossary:Output approach|production side]], Figure 7 presents the breakdowns of EU-27 [[Glossary:Gross value added|gross value added]] by 10 industries according to the revised classification [[Glossary:Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)|NACE Rev.2]]. [[Image: EU gross value added by industry, 2001-2011.png|thumb|centre|500px| Figure 7: EU gross value added by industry, % of total, 2001-2011;
Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=| code=nama_nace10_c }}]] In 2011, the seven services industries combined made up more than 70% of the EU-27's total gross value: public administration, defence, education, human health and social work activities (19.1%), wholesale and retail trade, transport, accommodation and food service activities (19.5%), real estate activities (10.3 %), professional, scientific and technical activities; administrative and support service activities (10 %), financial and insurance activities (5.7 %), information and communication (4.6 %), arts, entertainment and recreation; other service activities; activities of household and extra-territorial organizations and bodies (3.5 %). Manufacturing generated 15.5% of the total gross value added, construction 6,2 %, other industries and agriculture, hunting, forestry and fishing accounted for respectively 4 % and 1.7 % of the total GVA. Looking at the evolution of GVA on a longer term perspective, one can see that the weights of [[Glossary:Industry|industries]] slightly decreased while the service sector expanded between 2001 and 2011. [[Glossary:Manufacturing|Manufacturing]] showed the highest loss of weight among industries as it accounted for 18 % of GDP in 2001 and only to 15.5 % in 2011. Agriculture, forestry and fishing remained on a steady downward trend around 2 %. On the other side, three main items drove the service sector expansion. Financial and insurance activities gained 0.9% and real estate activities 0.5% share of GDP throughout the period while public administration, defence, education, human health and social work activities accounted for almost 20 % of EU GDP in 2011 compared to 17.8% in 2001. Figure 8 shows on the basis of 2011 figures that the structure of GVA vary significantly across member states . The countries presenting the highest share in industries were Romania (48.4 %), Slovakia (39.5 %) and the Czech Republic (39.1 %). The share of manufacturing was highest in Slovakia, Ireland, the Czech Republic and Hungary (above 22 %). Construction activities exceeded 10% in Spain and Romania while agricultural GVA was highest in Romania, Bulgaria and Latvia where it was above 5 %. On the other hand the services based economies appeared to be Luxembourg, Greece, Cyprus and Malta with shares of GVA around 80 %. Public administration activities were the highest in Denmark and Sweden. Lithuania, Latvia, Poland and Greece had the largest share in wholesale and retail trade above 25%. Italy, France and Greece presented a substantive high share in real estate where they accounted for more than 13 %. Malta showed a significantly higher share (above 11 % of GVA) in other services compared to the other Member States. [[Image:Country comparison of value added by industry, 2011.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 8: Country-to-country comparison of value added by industry, % of total, 2011;
Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=nama_nace10_c}}]] '''The expenditure side''' Figure 9 shows the respective EU-27 shares of GDP of each [[Glossary:Expenditure approach|expenditure component]] for the period 2001-2011. Private final consumption was by far the most important component representing around 58 % of EU GDP throughout the period. Government final consumption and [[Glossary:Gross capital formation|gross capital formation]] accounted respectively for 21.7 % and 19.2 % of GDP in 2011. While the weight of government final consumption showed on overall an upward trend since 2001, the weight of gross capital formation was more versatile during this period. It increased between 2003 and 2007, reaching its highest level in 2007 with 22.1 % and decreased to 18.3 % of GDP in 2009, its lowest level of the decade. Even if the share of the external balance of goods and services does not represent a large part of GDP (1.2 %), it is worthwhile to note that [[Glossary:Exports - NA|exports]] and [[Glossary:Imports - NA|imports]] accounted respectively for 43.7 % and 42.5 % of GDP in 2011. [[Image:Main EU expenditure components, 2001-2011.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 9: Main EU expenditure components, % of GDP, 2001-2011;
Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=nama_gdp_c}}]] Figure 10 shows sizeable differences in the weight of expenditure components among countries in 2011 and the inverse relation that exists between final private and government consumption. For instance the Netherlands (45%), Sweden (47.8 %) and Denmark (48.6 %) had relatively low share of private final consumption but the highest shares in government final consumption (above 26% of GDP). On the other hand, Greece, Cyprus and Portugal had the highest share (beyond 65 %) in private final consumption but presented a relatively low share of government final consumption expenditures. Luxembourg break with this relation as it showed a low weight in both private and government final consumption. The reason behind these figures is that wages and salaries of cross-border workers are spent abroad. [[Image:Main expenditure components by country, 2011.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 10: Main expenditure components by country,% of GDP, 2011;
Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=nama_gdp_c}}]] Gross capital formation was highest in Romania and Latvia with investments expenditures above 25 % of GDP. Those economies have higher share of GDP in industry while the Greece, the UK, Malta and Ireland that are more services oriented presented the lowest weights in terms of gross capital formation expenditures. Luxembourg and Ireland showed a particularly strong external balance of goods and services that can be explained by their specific particularities in terms of large cross-border-income, goods and services flows. For instance, in Luxembourg, the significant purchases of fuel, cigarettes and alcohol by non-residents is counted as exports of services. On the other hand Romania and Greece presented a significant negative external balance of respectively -5.2 % and -8.1 % of GDP. '''The income side''' Figure 11 shows the relative share of EU-27 GDP for each component of the [[Glossary:Income approach|income side]]. Compensation of employees presents a relatively constant share around 50 % of GDP for the period 2001-2011, with a downward trend of 2 percentage points between 2001 and 2007. This is mostly explained by the wages and salaries, as the weight of employer’s social contributions did not change that much throughout that period. [[Image:EU income components in GDP between 2001 and 2011 (%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 11: Changes in the share of EU income components in GDP between 2001 and 2011 (%);
Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=nama_gdp_c}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_inc_c}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_nace10_c}}]] The share of [[Glossary:Gross operating surplus (GOS) - NA|gross operating surplus and mixed income]] grew until 2007 but this effect reversed in 2008 and 2009 due to the financial and economic crisis. It finally stabilised around 39% of GDP in 2011. The [[Glossary:Taxes on production and imports|taxes on production and imports]] less [[Glossary:Subsidies|subsidies]] component showed a similar trend with a share of GDP of 11,8 % in 2011. Figure 12 offers a cross country comparison of compensation of employees in 2010 and 2011. Average compensation per employee in 2011 was EUR 32 959 in the EU and EUR 36 677 in the euro area. The figure highlights the deep disparities that exist between Member States. Indeed, while Luxembourg, Denmark and Belgium showed the highest average compensation of employees (above EUR 50 000) the lowest appeared to be in Bulgaria (EUR 5 781). [[Image:Average compensation per employee, 2010-2011 (EUR).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 12: Average compensation per employee, 2009-2010 (EUR);
Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=nama_nace10_c}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=nama_nace10_e}}]] === Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=Main_aggregates_tables_and_figures.xls|title=National accounts: tables and figures}} ===Other articles=== *[[European sector accounts - background]] (background article) *[[National accounts - an overview]] *[[National accounts and GDP]] *[[Update of the SNA 1993 and revision of ESA95]] (background article) ===Tables=== *[{{Template:Main tables|dedicated_section=national_accounts}} National accounts (including GDP) (t_na)], see: :Annual national accounts (t_nama) :Quarterly national accounts (t_namq) ===Database=== *[{{Template:Database|dedicated_section=national_accounts}} National accounts (including GDP) (na)], see: :Annual national accounts (nama) :Quarterly national accounts (namq) ===Dedicated section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=balance_of_payments}} Balance of payments] *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=sector_accounts}} European sector accounts] *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=national_accounts}} National accounts (including GDP)] *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=purchasing_power_parities}} Purchasing power parities (PPPs)] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-CD-11-001|title=Eurostat Yearbook 2011; Economy and finance – national accounts}} *{{Template:Publication|code=CA-80-93-436|title=NACE Rev. 1 – statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community}} (publication) ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=nama_esms|title=Annual national accounts}} (ESMS metadata file — nama_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=nasa_esms|title=Annual sector accounts}} (ESMS metadata file — nasa_esms) *{{Template:Publication|code=CA-15-96-001|title=European system of accounts ESA 1995}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-BE-06-002|title=Eurostat-OECD methodological manual on purchasing power parities}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-41-01-543|title=Handbook on price and volume measures in national accounts}} *{{Template:Esms|code=namq_esms|title=Quarterly national accounts}} (ESMS metadata file - namq_esms) ===Legislation=== *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32007R1392:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1392/2007}} of 13 November 2007 amending Regulation (EC) No 2223/96 with respect to the transmission of national accounts data. ===External links=== *[http://unstats.un.org/unsd/nationalaccount/sna2008.asp United Nations Statistics Division 2008 SNA] *[http://unstats.un.org/unsd/nationalaccount/sna1993.asp United Nations Statistics Division 1993 SNA] {{Unit|topic=X_National_accounts_methods}} [[Category:Economy and finance|National accounts – main GDP aggregates and related indicators]] [[Category:National accounts (incl. title: National accounts and GDP
text:
National accounts statistics are the source of important economic indicators for the European Union (EU) and its EU countries, such as gross domestic product (GDP), which measures the overall size of an economy. Data extracted on 21 July 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 In 2025, EU GDP was 1.4% higher in real terms than in 2024. All expenditure components contributed to the growth of GDP in 2025. |alt=Dynamic interactive line chart with 5 lines showing, in percent, the real rate of change of GDP compared with the previous year from 2006 to 2025. The lines show the European Union, the euro area, China including Hong Kong, Japan and the United States and. [[Glossary:National accounts (NA)|National accounts]] are the source for a multitude of well-known [[Glossary:Economic indicator|economic indicators]] that are presented in this article. [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|Gross domestic product (GDP)]] is the most frequently used measure for the overall size of an economy. Derived indicators such as GDP [[Glossary:Per capita|per inhabitant (per capita)]] – for example, in euro or adjusted for differences in price levels (as expressed in [[Glossary:Purchasing power standard (PPS)|purchasing power standards, PPS]]) – are widely used for a comparison of living standards; they are also used to monitor economic convergence or divergence within the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Moreover, the development of specific GDP components and related indicators, such as those for economic [[Glossary:Output|output]], [[Glossary:Import|imports]] and [[Glossary:Export|exports]], domestic (private and public) [[Glossary:Intermediate and final consumption|consumption]] or [[Glossary:Investment - NA|investments]], as well as data on the distribution of [[Glossary:Income approach|income]] and [[Glossary:Saving|savings]], can give valuable insights into the main drivers of economic activity. These can serve as the basis for the design, monitoring and evaluation of specific EU policies. This article is published every year with annual data. The 2026 edition describes the situation from 2006 up to (and including) the year 2025. As a consequence, the time series covers the global financial and economic crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic and the cost-of-living crisis. While these crises have impacted the economy as a whole, they have impacted various sectors differently as well as differing in terms of the type of expenditure, such as consumption and investment. This should be borne in mind when analysing time series, for example when comparing data for the most recent years – 2020 to 2025 – with each other and with data for 2019 and earlier years. ===Developments for GDP in the EU: the rebound observed in 2021 continued through to 2025 but in a more subdued manner=== The global financial and economic crisis resulted in a severe recession in the EU in 2009 (see Figure 1), followed by a recovery in 2010. The crisis started earlier in Japan, with a negative annual rate of change for GDP (in real terms) already recorded in 2008, a deepening in 2009 and a rebound in 2010. By contrast, economic output in China (including Hong Kong) continued to grow at a rapid pace during the global financial and economic crisis (close to 10% each year), slowing somewhat in subsequent years, but remaining considerably higher than in any of the other economies shown in Figure 1 for almost every year. The global financial and economic crisis was already apparent in the EU in 2008 when there had been a considerably lower rate of increase for GDP than in 2007 (down from 3.1% in 2007 to 0.6% in 2008) and this was followed by a 4.3% decrease in GDP in 2009. The recovery in the EU saw the index of GDP (based on chain linked volumes) increase 2.1% in 2010 and there was a further gain of 1.9% in 2011. The recovery wasn’t sustained: GDP contracted 0.8% in 2012 and the change in 2013 was negligible (0.0%). A series of positive rates of change was recorded thereafter, with growth relatively stable between 1.6% and 2.8% each year from 2014 to 2019. In 2020, the EU recorded a real decrease in GDP of 5.6% as the initial impact of the COVID-19 crisis was felt; this was considerably larger than the decrease in activity in 2009 during the global financial and economic crisis. Equally, the rebound in activity in 2021, up 6.4%, was stronger than that observed in 2010, while there were further expansions in all the following years, albeit at a lower rate. In the [[Glossary:Euro area|euro area]], the corresponding rates of change were similar to those recorded in the EU: the contractions recorded in 2009, 2012 and 2020 were stronger (down by 4.5%, 0.9% and 6.0% respectively) than in the EU, while in 2013 a fall of 0.2% was recorded (when there was no change in the EU). The rate of change in the euro area was frequently slightly lower than in the EU, 0.1 or 0.2 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points (pp)]] lower most years from 2006 to 2018. This gap was somewhat larger in 2019 (0.3 pp) and 2020 (0.4 pp) compared with earlier years. Over the whole period from 2006 to 2025, real GDP growth in the euro area (up 21.0%) was weaker than that in the EU as a whole (up 24.6%). [[Image:Figure 1 Real GDP rate of change, 2006–25 (% change compared with the previous year) V1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Real GDP rate of change, 2006–25

However, in 2012 this development changed, as just under half (13) of the EU countries reported economic expansion. Thereafter, a majority of EU countries once again recorded growth, with the number of countries recording a positive rate of change reaching 15 in 2013 and rising to 23 in 2014 and 26 in 2015 and 2016. All 27 EU countries recorded a positive rate of change in 2017 (the 1st time this had occurred since 2007) and did so again in 2018 and 2019. Lithuania also experienced growth in 2021, up 6.4%, while Ireland’s growth reached 16.6%. *In 2022, Luxembourg and Estonia recorded a decreases of 1.1% and 1.2% respectively, while all other EU countries continued to record growth. Ireland recorded the fastest growth for the 3rd consecutive year, up 8.2%. Austria and Portugal were the only EU countries to record faster growth in 2022 than in 2021. *In 2023, the rates of change were much more mixed; 17 EU countries recorded increases and 9 recorded decreases. This reflected the tailing off of the rebound from the COVID-19 crisis and the impact of the cost-of-living crisis. Ireland recorded its 1st annual decrease in GDP in 2023, after 10 consecutive annual increases. *In 2024 and 2025, economic growth improved further across the EU. The number of EU countries recording an increase in GDP grew to 23 in 2024 and to all 27 Member States in 2025. In 2025, the lowest growth was recorded in Germany (0.2%), Italy and Hungary (both 0.5%). The fastest growth was 8.0% in Ireland. Less than half of the EU countries (9) recorded a higher rate of change in 2025 than in 2024. '''Average annual GDP growth of 1.2% over the last 19 years in the EU and 1.0% in the euro area''' When analysing developments over the last 19 years, the global financial and economic crisis reduced the overall performance of EU economies, and the COVID-19 crisis caused an additional decline. The annual average growth rates of GDP in the EU and the euro area between 2006 and 2025 were 1.2% and 1.0%, respectively (see Table 1). By comparison, between 2010 (the 1st year after the low point of the global and financial crisis) and 2019 (the last full year before the COVID-19 crisis) the average for the EU was 1.5% and for the euro area it was 1.3%. The highest growth rates between 2006 and 2025 among EU countries were recorded for Malta (average annual growth for GDP of 5.4%) and Ireland (5.0%; this includes an exceptional increase in 2015 reflecting the activities of multinational enterprises). Poland (3.6%), Cyprus, Lithuania (both 2.7%) and Romania, Slovakia (both 2.6%) had the next highest average growth rates. By contrast, the real development of GDP between 2006 and 2025 was negative overall in Greece, down on average 0.6% per year. Cross-country comparisons are often made using purchasing power standards (PPS) which are values adjusted to account for differences in price levels between countries. Note that the data shown in Figures 2 and 3 and in Table 2 are in current prices and shouldn’t be used for calculating rates of change because of inflation and exchange rate fluctuations. In 2025, GDP in the EU was 18.8 trillion PPS (18 800 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] PPS) – note that 1 PPS equals 1 euro (€) for the EU. PPS figures are intended for cross-country comparisons rather than for temporal comparisons since they can’t be considered as time series for methodological reasons. Nevertheless, it is interesting to note that China historically had a lower level of economic output than either the EU or the United States, but that this situation changed with the rapid transformation and continued expansion of the Chinese economy. China’s GDP in PPS reached a level in 2013 that was – for the 1st time – higher than that recorded for the EU. In 2014, China’s GDP in PPS surpassed that of the United States. By contrast, GDP per inhabitant in PPS in Bulgaria and Greece was just over two thirds (68%) the EU average. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] ===Gross value added in the EU analysed by economic activity=== '''Close to three quarters of the EU’s total value added in 2025 was generated within services''' Looking at GDP from the output side, Table 3 gives an overview of the relative importance of 10 economic activities (as defined by [[Glossary:Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)|NACE Rev. 2]]) in terms of their contribution to total gross value added at current basic prices. Between 2006 and 2025, 2 of the 3 largest activities in the EU experienced a fall in their share of total value added: industry’s share declined from 20.8% in 2006 to 19.1% in 2025; and the contribution of distributive trades, transport, accommodation and food services fell from 19.1% to 18.8%. By contrast, the share of public administration, defence, education, human health and social work activities increased, from 18.2% to 19.0%. Professional, scientific, technical, administrative and support services increased its share of value added by 1.8 pp between 2006 and 2025, the largest percentage point increase recorded among the 10 activities shown; it moved to become the 4th largest activity with an 11.9% share. Real estate activities dropped from 4th to 5th largest despite its stable share of 10.7%. The 2nd largest increase was observed for the share of information and communication activities, up from 4.7% to 5.6%, moving ahead of financial and insurance activities. The share for agriculture, forestry and fishing remained stable at 1.8% between 2006 and 2025. The remaining activities recorded falls in their share of output in the EU between 2006 and 2025: the share of construction was down from 6.2% to 5.5%; the share for financial and insurance activities was down from 5.0% to 4.6%; a fall was also observed for arts, entertainment and recreation, other services and activities of household and extra-territorial organisations and bodies, down from 3.3% to 3.1%. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] Services contributed 73.7% of the EU’s total gross value added in 2025 compared with 71.1% in 2006. The relative importance of services was particularly high in Luxembourg, Malta, Cyprus, France, Belgium, Greece, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain, where they accounted for more than three quarters of total value added. By contrast, the share of services was below two thirds in Slovakia, Slovenia and Czechia, and was lowest in Ireland at 63.9%; all of these EU countries recorded above-average shares for industry, particularly Czechia. '''Diverging developments of economic activities interrupted by the global financial and economic crisis and the COVID-19 crisis''' Structural change in the EU is, at least in part, a result of phenomena such as technological change, developments in relative prices, outsourcing and globalisation, often resulting in manufacturing activities and some services (those that can be provided remotely, such as online or through call centres) being moved to regions with lower labour-cost, both within and outside the EU. Furthermore, several activities were particularly affected by the global financial and economic crisis and its aftermath, the COVID-19 crisis and/or by the cost-of-living crisis; recovery from the more recent crises has been uneven when analysed in terms of developments for real gross value added by activity. *Information and communication activities recorded growth every year between 2010 and 2025. Furthermore, this was 1 of only 2 activities among those shown in Figures 4 and 5 that recorded growth at the start of the COVID-19 crisis (in 2020), expanding by 2.3%. The latest rate of change was growth of 4.0%, the largest increase of the 10 activities shown in these 2 figures. Output from information and communication activities more than doubled (up 108.4%) between 2010 and 2025, by far the largest growth among all 10 activities. *The development for distributive trades, transport, accommodation and food services shows a clear interruption in 2020. A much weaker fall in 2013 (down 0.3%) was the only negative rate of change before 2020. The 13.0% fall in 2020, largely reflecting the COVID-19 containment measures, was the 2nd largest fall in 2020 among the 10 activities. Looking at the whole period from 2010 to 2025, overall growth was 25.1%. *Industrial output increased consistently for 6 consecutive years prior to the COVID-19 pandemic but fell 6.1% in 2020 the COVID-19 related restrictions had an impact. Output rebounded 7.8% in 2021 and 1.4% in 2022, before another contraction in 2023 (down 1.6%). Overall, industrial output was 19.3% higher in 2025 than in 2010. *Between 2010 and 2013, output from agriculture, forestry and fishing fluctuated a little before a relatively strong increase of 6.2% in 2014. Since then, these activities again have shown little volatility, with rates of change between -2.0% and 2.0%. Overall, output of agriculture, forestry and fishing was 8.1% higher in 2025 than it had been in 2010. *Construction recorded the deepest and longest contraction following the global financial and economic crisis. The 1.6% increase recorded in 2015 was the 1st annual growth in 8 years and was followed by growth between 0.9% and 2.6% through to 2019. In 2020, construction output fell for the 1st time since 2014, down 4.6%. This was followed by a rebound of 3.8% in 2021, and alternating negative and positive growth in the years thereafter. Despite the period of sustained growth between 2015 and 2019 and growth in 2021, 2023 and 2025, construction output in 2025 remained 3.2% lower than it had been in 2010. This was the only overall fall among the 10 activities. As such, GDP in 2024 was 7.2% above its 2019 pre-COVID level. Figure 7 focuses the analysis on the development of the EU’s GDP components from the expenditure side. *[[Glossary:Final consumption expenditure|Final consumption expenditure]] rose overall by 23.4% in volume terms between 2006 and 2025 (see Figure 7), despite slight falls in 2009, 2012 and 2013, and a larger fall in 2020 (down 4.8%). *Final consumption expenditure of general government rose notably faster than final consumption expenditure as a whole, up 33.0% between 2006 and 2025 despite a slight fall in 2012. Final consumption expenditure of general government increased 1.2% in 2020, the only expenditure item shown in Figure 7 to record an increase during the year that the COVID-19 crisis started. *During the same period (2006–25), [[Glossary:Gross capital formation|gross capital formation]] was relatively volatile: it increased from 2006 to 2007 by 7.0% and fell by a greater amount (18.1%) between 2007 and 2009 (during the global financial and economic crisis). It then increased by 8.4% between 2009 and 2011 and fell by 8.1% between 2011 and 2013. A subsequent period of regular growth resulted in an overall increase of 29.4% between 2013 and 2019. A fall of 6.4% was observed in 2020, a larger fall than for the final consumption expenditure items shown in Figure 7. Equally, the rebound in gross capital formation in 2021 and 2022 (up 8.3% and 4.0%, respectively) was larger than for final consumption expenditure. In 2023 and 2024, gross capital formation fell 3.2% and 1.4%, respectively, before increasing again in 2025, with 3.6%. *The growth in exports of goods and services exceeded the growth in imports in 2008, between 2010 and 2013, in 2017, 2021, 2023 and 2024, whereas imports grew faster (or decreased less) in the other years since 2006. In 2020, the volume of exports fell 8.2% compared with 2019, while imports fell 7.6%. In 2021 and 2022, the volume of exports and of imports rebounded strongly while in 2023 exports and imports contracted again, albeit slightly. Growth of import and export resumed in 2024 and increased in 2025. Exports were 64.6% higher in 2025 than in 2006, whereas the equivalent increase for imports was 61.6%. However, increases in investment were observed in each of the next 6 years, rising in the range of 2.9% to 5.2% each year. As for most other expenditure indicators, this period of growth ended abruptly in 2020 when investment fell by 6.4%. A strong rebound of 8.3% in 2021 was reinforced by growth of 4.0% in 2022.
