title: Population and housing census 2021 - EU population size and structure
text:
Statistics from the 2021 population and housing census. Characteristics of the population size and population structure in the European Union (EU), degree of urbanisation (DEGURBA), local administrative units (LAU), regions (NUTS), national data; population pyramid, population analysed by sex, population analysed by age; young-age dependency, old-age dependency, total age dependency, median age; legal marital status. Data extracted September 2025 Planned article update: no planned update According to the 2021 population and housing census, there were 443.9 million people living in the EU. The median age of the EU population was 44.3 years. There were 227 million females and 217 million males in the EU, equivalent to 104.6 females for every 100 males. In 4 EU countries – Malta, Luxembourg, Sweden and Slovenia – there were more males than females. According to the 2021 population and housing census, 15.0% of the EU population were children younger than 15 years, 64.0% were people aged 15 to 64 years, 18.0% were people aged 65 to 84 years and 3.0% were aged 85 years or over. Among the 377.2 million people aged 15 years or over in the EU in 2021, nearly half (49.1%) were married or in a registered partnership, just over a third (34.3%) were single, 7.9% were widowed and another 7.9% were divorced; the marital status of 0.8% of people was unknown. [[Image:Population pyramid, EU, 2021_(% of the total population, single years of age)_PHCensus2021.png|thumb|centre|700px|Highlight: Population pyramid, EU, 2021
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21agr2}}|alt=A population pyramid showing single year age for males and females. Data are shown in percent, for 2021, for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] A [[Glossary:Census|population and housing census]] counts the entire [[Glossary:Population_figure|population]] and housing stock of a given country; this is conducted typically every 10 years. This article is part of an online publication concerning the results of the 2021 population and housing census. A person’s age reflects the number of completed years at the census reference date. === Age and sex structure of the population === '''Age structure''' '''''In 2021, 443.9 million people lived in the EU''''' According to the 2021 population and housing census, the population of the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] was 443.9 million. Children younger than 15 years accounted for 15.0% of the population, people aged 15 to 64 years accounted for nearly 2 in 3 people (64.0%), while people aged 65 to 84 years accounted for 18.0%, leaving 3.0% of the population aged 85 years or over. As such, there were 93.0 million people aged 65 years or over, of which 13.0 million were aged 85 years or over. [[Image:Distribution of the population by age, 2021_(%)_PHCensus2021.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Distribution of the population by age, 2021
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21ctz_r3}}|alt=A stacked column chart showing the distribution of the population by age, distinguishing people younger than 15 years, people aged 15 to 64 years, people aged 65 to 84 years and people aged 85 years or over. Data are shown in percent, for 2021, for the EU as well as for EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''In 2021, the young-age dependency ratio was highest across the EU in rural areas and lowest in cities''''' The [[Glossary:Young-age_dependency_ratio|young-age dependency ratio]] is calculated as the number of people younger than 15 years relative to the number aged 15 to 64 years, expressed as a percentage. In the EU in 2021, this ratio was 23.5%. Across the 3 different [[Glossary:Degree_of_urbanisation|degrees of urbanisation]], the young-age dependency ratio was highest in [[Glossary:Rural_area|rural areas]] (24.4%) and lowest in [[Glossary:City|cities]] (22.5%), with the ratio for [[Glossary:Town_or_suburb|towns and suburbs]] between these 2 values (23.8%). Although 10 EU countries showed a similar pattern to that of the EU, with the lowest young-age dependency ratio in cities and the highest in rural areas, most did not. For example, in Croatia, Lithuania and Portugal the pattern was reversed. While the highest ratio was observed in towns and suburbs in Denmark, Germany, Greece, Spain, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, the Netherlands, Romania, Slovenia and Sweden, the lowest ratio was observed in towns and suburbs in Belgium, Bulgaria and Slovakia. [[Image:Young-age dependency ratio, by degree of urbanisation, 2021_(%)_PHCensus2021.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Young-age dependency ratio, by degree of urbanisation, 2021
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21ctz_r3}} and [https://ec.europa.eu/CensusHub the CensusHub]|alt=A combined column chart and high-low chart showing the young-age dependency ratio. The columns show the national ratio and the high-low markers show the ratio by degree of urbanisation. Data are shown in percent, for 2021, for the EU as well as for EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''In 2021, the old-age dependency ratio was highest across the EU in rural areas and lowest in cities''''' The [[Glossary:Old-age_dependency_ratio|old-age dependency ratio]] is calculated as the number of people aged 65 years or over relative to the number aged 15 to 64 years, expressed as a percentage. In the EU in 2021, this ratio was 32.7%. Across the 3 different degrees of urbanisation, the old-age dependency ratio was highest in rural areas (35.7%) and lowest in cities (30.0%), with the ratio for towns and suburbs between these 2 values (33.9%). Nine EU countries showed a similar pattern to that of the EU, with the lowest old-age dependency ratio in cities and the highest in rural areas. On the contrary, in Malta, Poland and Slovakia the pattern was reversed. While the highest ratio was observed in towns and suburbs in Belgium, Czechia, Germany, Estonia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary and Slovenia, the lowest ratio was observed in towns and suburbs in Greece, Spain, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Portugal and Romania. [[Image:Old-age dependency ratio, by degree of urbanisation, 2021_(%)_PHCensus2021.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Old-age dependency ratio, by degree of urbanisation, 2021
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21ctz_r3}} and [https://ec.europa.eu/CensusHub the CensusHub]|alt=A combined column chart and high-low chart showing the old-age dependency ratio. The columns show the national ratio and the high-low markers show the ratio by degree of urbanisation. Data are shown in percent, for 2021, for the EU as well as for EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] As noted earlier, the young-age dependency ratio in the EU in 2021 was 23.5%. Across the [[Glossary:Nomenclature_of_territorial_units_for_statistics_(NUTS)|NUTS]] level 3 [[Glossary:Region|regions]] of the EU, this ratio was highest in the French outermost region of Guyane, at 53.0%. The next highest ratios were also in France, 34.2% in another outermost region, La Réunion, and 34.1% in Seine-Saint-Denis, in the north-east of the French capital city. Among the 75 EU regions where the ratio was 28.5% or higher (as shown by the dark blue shade in Map 1), 40 were in France, 10 were in Sweden and 7 were in Ireland; the capital region of Dublin (26.7%) was the only region in Ireland to have a rate below 28.5%. At the other end of the range, the regions with the lowest ratios were La Gomera (part of the Canary Islands, 14.6%), Zamora in north-west Spain (15.5%) and Oristano in western Sardinia (15.6%). [[Image:Young-age dependency ratio, NUTS level 3 regions, 2021_(%)_PHCensus2021.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Young-age dependency ratio, NUTS level 3 regions, 2021
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21ctz_r3}}|alt=A choropleth map showing the young-age dependency ratio. Data are shown in percent, for 2021, for the EU as well as for level 3 regions of EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The old-age dependency ratio in the EU in 2021 was 32.7%. Across the NUTS level 3 regions of the EU, this ratio was highest in the inland northern Portuguese region of Alto Tâmega e Barroso, at 62.6%. The next highest ratios were in Arr. Veurne (Belgium, 61.2%), Suhl, Kreisfreie Stadt (Germany, 61.1%) and Evrytania (Greece, 60.3%). Among the 158 level 3 regions in the EU where the old-age dependency ratio was 43.5% or higher (as shown by the dark blue shade in Map 2), 61 were in Germany, 24 were in France, 21 in Italy, 12 in Portugal and 10 each in Bulgaria, Greece and Finland. There are a number of reasons for regions to have high old-age dependency ratios including a long-term decline in birth rates, immigration of older people (for example in regions popular with retired people) and emigration of younger or working-age people (for example in regions with more limited educational or employment opportunities). The region with the lowest ratio was the French outermost region of Guyane (9.4%), with Fuerteventura (part of the Canary Islands, 15.0%) recording the next lowest ratio. [[Image:Old-age dependency ratio, NUTS level 3 regions, 2021_(%)_PHCensus2021.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 2: Old-age dependency ratio, NUTS level 3 regions, 2021
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21ctz_r3}}|alt=A choropleth map showing the old-age dependency ratio. Data are shown in percent, for 2021, for the EU as well as for level 3 regions of EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 1 presents a summary of young- and old-age dependency ratios. For each of these ratios, data are presented for the national ratio as well as the lowest and highest ratios for the [[Glossary:Local_administrative_unit_(LAU)|municipalities]] of each country. There were several EU countries where the minimum in municipalities was 0.0% for both ratios. This was the case in Germany, Greece, Spain, France and Cyprus: in other words, in each of these countries there was at least 1 municipality where there were some people aged 15 to 64 years and no people younger than 15 years and at least 1 municipality where there were some people aged 15 to 64 years and no people aged 65 years or over. Many of these municipalities are likely to be very small, with low numbers of inhabitants. Note that the data shown are ratios, not shares. As such, values greater than 100.0% occur where there are more children younger than 15 years than people aged 15 to 64 years or more people aged 65 years or more than people aged 15 to 64 years. For example, in France the young-age dependency ratio was 225% in Volvent (in the Drôme department of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes administrative region), while the old-age dependency ratio was 720% in Annoux (in the Yonne department of the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté administrative region). [[Image:Population age indicators, 2021_(%)_PHCensus2021.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Population age indicators, 2021
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21ctz_r3}} and [https://ec.europa.eu/CensusHub the CensusHub]|alt=A table showing the young- and old-age dependency ratios. For each of these ratios, data are presented for the national ratio as well as the lowest and highest ratios across the municipalities of each country. Data are shown in percent, for 2021, for the EU as well as for EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''In 2021, the median age of the EU population was 44.3 years''''' The [[Glossary:Median_age|median age]] of a population is the age that divides that population into 2 groups of equal size, with half of the people younger than the median age and half older. In 2021, the median age of the EU’s population was 44.3 years; in other words, there were equal numbers of people younger and older than 44.3 years. Among EU countries, the median age was lowest in Ireland (39.0 years), Luxembourg (39.7 years), Cyprus (40.0 years), Malta (40.5 years) and Sweden (40.7 years), while it was highest in Italy (48.0 years). [[Image:Median age of the population, 2021_(years)_PHCensus2021.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Median age of the population, 2021
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21agr2}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21ctz_r3}}|alt=A column chart showing the median age of the population in years. Data are shown for 2021, for the EU as well as for EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Analysis by sex''' In 2021, there were 227.0 million females and 216.9 million males in the EU, equivalent to a ratio of 104.6 females for every 100 males. In 23 of the EU countries, there were more females than males, with the reverse situation observed in Malta (92.4 females for 100 males), Luxembourg (98.5), Sweden (98.7) and Slovenia (99.0). At the other end of the scale, the 3 highest ratios of females to males were in the [[Glossary:Baltic_Member_States|Baltic EU countries]], with ratios of 116.3 females to 100 males in Latvia, 115.4 to 100 in Lithuania and 110.3 to 100 in Estonia; a similar ratio (110.2 females to 100 males) was also observed in Portugal. In the EU, the ratio of females to males in 2021 was highest in cities (107.4 females per 100 males) and lowest in rural areas (100.6), with the ratio for towns and suburbs between these 2 values (104.4). Almost all of the EU countries showed a similar pattern to that of the EU, with the lowest females to males ratio in rural areas and the highest in cities. There were 2 exceptions: in Malta, the highest ratio was in rural areas and the lowest in towns and suburbs; in Luxembourg, the highest ratio was in towns and suburbs and the lowest in cities. [[Image:Number of females for 100 males, 2021_(number)_PHCensus2021.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Number of females for 100 males, 2021
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21ctz_r3}} and [https://ec.europa.eu/CensusHub the CensusHub]|alt=A combined column chart and high-low chart showing the number of females for 100 males. The columns show the national ratio and the high-low markers show the ratio by degree of urbanisation. Data are shown as a number, for 2021, for the EU as well as for EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Marital status of the population=== '''Analysis by marital status''' EU population by sex, single year of age (aged 15 and over) and legal marital status is presented in the Population pyramid by marital status (Fig 6), without unknown status. [[Image:Population pyramid by legal marital status, 2021_PHCensus2021.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Population pyramid by legal marital status, 2021
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21_m}} and [https://ec.europa.eu/CensusHub the CensusHub]|alt=Aalt=A population pyramid showing the distribution of the population aged 15 years or over by marital status. Data are shown in absolute numbers, for 2021, for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among the 377.2 million people aged 15 years or over in the EU in 2021, nearly half (49.1%) were [[Glossary:Marriage|married]] or in a registered partnership, just over a third (34.3%) were single, 7.9% were widowed and another 7.9% were [[Glossary:Divorce|divorced]]; the marital status of 0.8% of people aged 15 years or over was unknown. Across EU countries, the share of people aged 15 years or over who – in 2021 – were: *married or in a registered partnership ranged from 36.2% in Estonia to 56.5% in Cyprus; along with Cyprus, more than half of people in this age group were married or in a registered partnership in Poland, Greece, Malta, Romania, Croatia, Italy and Luxembourg *single ranged from 26.3% in Romania to 44.0% in Sweden *widowed ranged from 4.9% in both Malta and Sweden (which had the second lowest share of people who were married or in a registered partnership) to 13.0% in Bulgaria *divorced ranged from 1.6% in Malta (where divorce has only been legal since October 2011) to 15.0% in Estonia; the share of divorced people in the population aged 15 years or over was above 10.0% in all of the [[Glossary:Nordic_Member_States|Nordic]] and Baltic EU countries, as well as in Czechia, Hungary and Belgium. [[Image:Distribution of the population aged ≥ 15 years by marital status, 2021_(%)_PHCensus2021.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Distribution of the population aged ≥ 15 years by marital status, 2021
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21m}}|alt=A stacked column chart showing the distribution of the population aged 15 years or over by marital status. Data are shown in percent, for 2021, for the EU as well as for EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''In 2021, the share of single people in the EU population was highest in cities and lowest in rural areas''''' In 2021, the share of single people in the EU population was highest in cities (47.1%) and lowest in rural areas (41.9%), with the share for towns and suburbs (42.6%) between these 2 values but notably closer to the share for rural areas. More than half of the EU countries showed a similar pattern to that of the EU, with the lowest share in rural areas and the highest in cities. *The reverse situation was observed in Estonia, Latvia, Romania and Slovakia, with the highest share in rural areas and the lowest in cities. *In Poland, the share was lowest in towns and suburbs and highest in rural areas. *In Cyprus, the share was marginally higher in towns and suburbs than in cities. *In Belgium, Lithuania, Hungary and Slovenia, the share was lowest in towns and suburbs, rather than in rural areas. In Lithuania, the gap in the share of single people analysed by degree of urbanisation was narrowest, at 1.3 points between cities (39.7%) and towns and suburbs (38.4%). By contrast, the difference was widest in Denmark, 14.1 points between cities (57.4%) and rural areas (43.3%). [[Image:Share of single people in the population, by degree of urbanisation, 2021_(%)_PHCensus2021_2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Share of single people in the population, by degree of urbanisation, 2021
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21m}} and [https://ec.europa.eu/CensusHub the CensusHub]|alt=A combined column chart and high-low chart showing the share of single people in the population. The columns show the national share and the high-low markers show the share by degree of urbanisation. Data are shown in percent, for 2021, for the EU as well as for EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] As noted earlier, the share of people aged 15 years or over who were single in 2021 was 34.3% in the EU. Across the NUTS level 3 regions of the EU, this share was highest in the French outermost region of Guyane (74.1%). This was followed – at some distance – by another French outermost region, Martinique (57.6%), the Danish capital region Byen København (56.5%) and the 2 other French outermost regions for which data are available, Guadeloupe (55.4%) and La Réunion (52.5%). There were 4 other regions that had shares above 50.0%: Paris and Groot-Amsterdam, in other words, the French and Dutch capital regions; Jämtlands län in the Norrland pert of Sweden; Heidelberg, Stadtkreis in south-west Germany. The 9 regions with the lowest shares were all in Poland, with the lowest share in the north-west of the country, in Miasto Szczecin (17.0%). [[Image:Share of single people in the population aged ≥ 15 years, NUTS level 3 regions, 2021_2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 3: Share of single people in the population aged ≥ 15 years, NUTS level 3 regions, 2021
'' Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=cens_21m_r3}}|alt=A choropleth map showing the share of single people in the population aged 15 years or over. Data are shown in percent, for 2021, for the EU as well as for level 3 regions of EU and EFTA countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and figures === {{Template:Excel|filename=Population_and_housing_census_2021_-_EU_population_size_and_structure.xlsx|title=Population and housing census 2021 – EU population size and structure: tables and figures}} === Data sources === '''2021 population and housing census''' The source of the data in this article is the 2021 population and housing census. Typically, every 10 years a population and housing census counts the entire population and housing stock of a given country. The population part of the census provides information on the population’s main geographic, demographic, social and economic characteristics, as well as household and family characteristics. This census provides a precise and geographically detailed count of the population and is a rich source of statistical information. '''Population coverage''' The census population aims to include all people who have their ‘usual residence’ in the place of enumeration; in other words, people who have lived there for a year or moved there within the previous year and have the intention to stay for at least 1 year. Ideally, where a person ‘lives’ is based on their place of ‘daily rest’. People who are temporarily absent from the place of enumeration are included, while people who are temporarily present are excluded. This concerns, for example, people in short-term military service, children with 2 homes, merchant seamen and fishermen at sea, foreign diplomats, naval personnel and military forces (and their families). '''Definitions of key concepts''' Concerning ''marital status'', a person is single if they have never married and never been in a registered partnership. The concepts of marriage and registered partnership are treated in the census as equivalent statuses; these include same-sex partnerships insofar as they are legally recognized. This category also includes the concept of being legally separated, for example if a registered partnership is legally dissolved. The category of widowed also includes the concept of a registered partnership having ended with the death of partner (and the survivor not having remarried or entered into a registered partnership). ===Context=== Population and housing censuses provide essential statistical input for formulating and evaluating policies, for administration and for research. A common programme of comparable census data throughout the EU not only supports EU-wide activities but also make it easier for local, regional and national policymakers to study their situation within an EU context. The EU programme for the 2021 population and housing censuses has been considerably revised when compared with the 2011 census. The aim of this revision was to simplify and reduce the size of the datasets to be transmitted, while at the same time keeping up with major policy needs of the EU. === Footnotes === === See also === title: Population in Southern Mediterranean countries
text:
This article is part of an online Eurostat publication that provides a statistical overview over the Southern Mediterranean countries. The article presents statistics on recent population changes for Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Palestine and Tunisia and compares these with the EU. Data extracted in March 2026 Planned article update: June 2027 Among the Southern Mediterranean countries, the share of people aged 65 and older ranged from 2.8% in Libya (2020 data) to 12.7% in Israel (estimated), compared with a provisional 21.6% in the EU (2024 data). Population density across the Southern Mediterranean countries ranges from 4 inhabitants per square kilometre in Libya (2020 data) to 921 in Palestine (2024 data), compared with an estimated 110 in the EU (2024 data). In 2024, Israel was the only Southern Mediterranean country where life expectancy exceeded that of the EU for both men (81.3 versus 79.2 years) and women (85.4 versus 84.4 years). Palestine recorded the lowest life expectancy in the region: 73.4 years for males and 75.6 for females. [[File: ENPS26_Natural population change, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a074a219-0b4d-4a2a-9806-33f7daf9532c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:55:57Z demo_gind]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/728dd3af-4b09-424b-a322-b71cfbed2c06?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-30T09:55:29Z enps_demo_gind])|alt=Infographic showing the natural population change in the EU and the European Neighbourhood South countries in 2024. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] This article is part of an [[European_Neighbourhood_Policy_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]]. It presents information on 9 [[Glossary:European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP)| Southern Mediterranean]] countries, namely, Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Palestine ''This designation shall not be construed as recognition of a State of Palestine and is without prejudice to the individual positions of the Member States on this issue.'' and Tunisia. Information on these countries are compared with developments in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. This article does not contain any data on Syria, as cooperation with Syria was suspended from 2011 until recently and no data are collected yet. Lebanon data does not account for Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon. Given that data collection for Southern Mediterranean countries is non-obligatory and subject to various changes related to the political and geographical context, data availability may often show inconsistency over the entire period presented or for recent years. This article includes information on [[Glossary:Population|population]] levels and structure as well as [[Glossary:Population_density|population density]], [[Glossary:Natural_population_change|natural change in the population]] and [[Glossary:Life expectancy|life expectancy]] at birth. ===Population during 2014-2024=== The [[Glossary:Population_figure|population]] (or usual resident population) represents the number of inhabitants of a country. Eurostat uses the reference date 1 January of the year in question. In some cases, the 31 December of the previous year is used instead. Growth in the EU population remained modest over 2014-2024, increasing by around 7.0 million persons overall (1.6%), reflecting a generally slow upward trend. The only notable interruption occurred in 2021, when the population declined slightly before recovering in subsequent years and reaching a new peak in 2024 at 449.3 million persons. Annual growth remained low throughout, typically below 0.3%, indicating subdued demographic expansion. The Southern Mediterranean region displays a pattern of sustained population growth, with a distinction between high-growth countries (notably Jordan and Palestine), more moderate and stable growth patterns (Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia and Israel), and countries with significant data constraints affecting temporal coverage. Egypt recorded the largest absolute increase, rising from 88.5 million in 2014 to 105.9 million in 2024. Population growth was particularly strong in the early part of the period, with annual increases above 2% in 2014-2015, followed by a temporary contraction in 2017 (-0.67%) and a subsequent rebound in 2018 (4.52%). Thereafter, growth steadily slowed, declining to around 1.4% by 2022. Morocco and Tunisia followed more gradual growth trends, with populations increasing steadily from 33.8 million (2014) to 37.0 million (2023) for Morocco and from 10.9 million (2014) to 11.9 million (2023) for Tunisia, and with relatively stable but moderating growth rates, particularly in Tunisia where growth fell below 1 % during 2018-2023. Israel exhibited sustained growth, rising from 8.1 million in 2014 to 9.9 million in 2024, with relatively stable annual increases generally between 1.6% and 2.6%, and a slight strengthening in the most recent years. Higher growths were observed in Jordan and Palestine. Jordan’s population expanded from 8.8 million in 2014 to 11.5 million in 2023 (the latest year with data available). A strong increase was recorded at the beginning of the period (8.6% in 2015), followed by significantly lower growth, thereafter, declining to 2.5% in 2016 and 1.9% in 2023. Palestine recorded sustained population growth, increasing from 4.4 million in 2014 to 5.5 million in 2024, with relatively stable annual increases, including 2.3% in 2015 and 2.7% in 2019. Data for Algeria, Libya, and Lebanon are incomplete, with breaks in the time series and missing observations limiting comparability over the full period. Algeria recorded a steady increase of its population from 38.7 million in 2014 to 44.6 million in 2021, with annual growth gradually moderating over the period. Libya’s population increased from 6.2 million in 2014 to 6.9 million in 2020, before the series is interrupted thereafter. Lebanon shows no continuous time series for population levels, with only a single observation available in 2018 (4.8 million). [[Image: Population, 2014-2024 (million persons) V1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Population, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cbabd486-04a2-49db-a622-a68a09469a6e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:54:27Z demo_pjan]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d573c01a-dff5-4c83-ada5-43cc940a97b7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:53:52Z enps_demo_pjangr])|alt=Table showing the population as of 1st of January between 2014 and 2024 in the EU and the ENP-South region countries. The table shows the population in million persons for each of the countries and the EU. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] ===Population by sex=== Figure 1 presents the share of women and men in total population in the Southern Mediterranean countries and the EU in 2024. In 2024, the EU’s population had a slight gender imbalance, with women making up 51.1% of the total, compared to 48.9% for men (provisional data). In the Southern Mediterranean region, the distribution was generally more balanced, with women and men close to parity in Morocco (50.2% and 49.8%, 2023 data), Tunisia (50.4% and 49.6%, 2023 estimated) and Israel (50.2% and 49.8%). Palestine showed a slight male majority (49.2% women and 50.8% men, 2024 data). Egypt and Algeria (2021 data) showed a moderate male majority, with women representing 48.6% and 49.3% respectively, while men accounted for 51.4% and 50.7%. A stronger male predominance was observed in Jordan (2023 data), where men represented 52.9% of the population and women 47.1%. Libya also displayed a slight male majority (50.7% men, 49.3% women, 2020 data). Data for Lebanon are not available. Overall, a balanced gender distribution was observed in Morocco, Tunisia and Israel, with only limited differences across the other Southern Mediterranean countries. However, comparability is affected by differences in reference years and data availability across countries. [[Image: ENPS26_Share of women and men in total population, 2024_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Share of women and men in total population, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fa781070-7fa7-4a53-86f7-022d65be05a1?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T14:02:43Z demo_pjan]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b22b1882-736d-45ae-a9d9-02ff66d535c5?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T14:02:08Z enps_demo_pjan])|alt=Horizontal stacked bar chart showing the share of women and men in total population for the year 2024. The figure presents the EU and the ENP-South region countries. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] ===Population by age class=== As shown in Figure 2, in 2024 the EU population comprised 14.6% of children (less than 15 years), 63.8% of persons of working age (15-64 years) and 21.6% of persons aged 65 years and over. The share of people aged 65 years and over exceeded that of children by 7.0 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points (pp)]]. By contrast, in the Southern Mediterranean countries the age structure was generally younger, with a higher share of children than in the EU across all countries. Regarding the share of children in the total population in the Southern Mediterranean countries, the highest proportions were recorded in Palestine (37.2%), Jordan (34.3%, 2023 data) and Egypt (34.3%, 2023 data), followed by Libya (31.3%, 2020 data), Algeria (30.6%, 2021 data, provisional) and Israel (27.2%, estimated). Lower shares were observed in Morocco (24.9%, 2023 data) and Tunisia (24.6%, 2023 data). No recent data are available for Lebanon. The share of persons aged 65 years and over remained relatively low in most Southern Mediterranean countries, particularly in Libya (2.8%, 2020 data), Palestine (3.5%), Jordan (3.7%, 2023 data), and Egypt (3.9%, 2023 data). Higher values were recorded in Tunisia (9.9%, 2023 data, estimated), Morocco (8.2%, 2023 data) and Algeria (6.9%, 2021 provisional). Israel showed a higher proportion of persons aged 65 years and over (12.7%, estimated), while no recent data are available for Lebanon. Overall, the Southern Mediterranean region displays a younger age structure compared with the EU, with a higher share of children and a lower share of people aged 65 years and over, although notable differences exist across countries. [[Image: ENPS26_Population by age class, 2024_(% of total).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Population by age class, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4799cc8d-439d-4b83-9d8c-7adfadb8f1ce?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-03T06:17:00Z demo_pjanbroad]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f5b48743-549d-45b6-bf53-e2a200b89a0d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T14:00:42Z enps_demo_pjangr])|alt=Horizontal stacked bar chart showing population by age class for the year 2024 as a percentage of total population. The figure presents the EU and the ENP-South region countries. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] ===Population density=== Data on [[Glossary:Population_density|population density]], measured in inhabitants per square kilometre (km2), is illustrated in Figure 3 for the Southern Mediterranean countries and compared with the EU. In 2024, the population density in the EU stood at 109.7 inhabitants per km2 (estimated, provisional). In the Southern Mediterranean region, population density varied considerably across countries, reflecting differences in population size and land area. Palestine recorded by far the highest density, at 920.9 inhabitants per km2, followed by Israel with 434.8 (estimated). Jordan’s population density (129.7, 2023 data) was closer to the EU average, while significantly lower levels were observed in Morocco (46.0, 2021 data) and Algeria (18.7, 2021 data). Libya recorded a very low population density of 4.1 inhabitants per km2 (2020 data), reflecting its large territory and relatively small population. Data for Lebanon, Tunisia and Egypt are not available. Overall, the Southern Mediterranean region shows a wide dispersion in population density, ranging from very high concentrations in smaller or more urbanised territories to very low densities in geographically large countries. [[Image: ENPS26_Population density, 2024_(inhabitants per km2).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Population density, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d4cb10a2-b0ca-4573-8c0d-017c04279284?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:59:30Z demo_r_d3dens]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/de07d30b-a53b-4f5f-a749-65217553e751?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:58:55Z enps_demo_dens])|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing population density in the EU and the countries in the ENP-South region for 2024. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] === Natural population change=== Population change can happen in two ways: either by [[Glossary:Natural_population_change|natural change]] or by [[Glossary:Migration|net migration]]. The natural population change is the difference between the number of live births and the number of deaths during a given period, usually 1 year. Data for the Southern Mediterranean countries is illustrated in Figure 4 for 2024 as the crude rate of population growth. The latter is defined as the ratio of total population growth during the year to the average population of the area in question that year. The value is expressed per 1 000 inhabitants. Across the EU, the natural population change rate was negative, at -2.8 per 1 000 inhabitants (provisional), indicating that the number of deaths exceeded the number of births. In contrast, the Southern Mediterranean countries with available data recorded positive natural population change. Palestine stood out with by far the highest rate, at 24.7 per 1 000 inhabitants, followed by Israel (13.3) and Egypt (12.8). Morocco and Jordan also recorded relatively high natural increases, at 10.6 and 10.0 per 1 000 inhabitants, respectively (both 2023 data). Tunisia showed a more moderate rate of 4.5 per 1 000 inhabitants (2021 data). Overall, the Southern Mediterranean region is characterised by consistently positive natural population change, albeit with considerable variation in magnitude across countries. [[Image: ENPS26_Natural population change, 2024_(per thousand persons)-2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Natural population change, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7c45b1f3-1499-47a1-a1e5-8d07a9905174?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:58:22Z demo_gind]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/07a8ea9b-9cc0-44b1-a6c3-0378cf2f4aff?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:57:52Z enps_demo_gind])|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing natural population change in the EU and the countries in the ENP-South region for 2024. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] ===Life expectancy at birth=== [[Glossary:Life_expectancy|Life expectancy]] at birth represents the average number of years a newborn can expect to live if subjected throughout life to the prevailing [[Glossary:Mortality|mortality]] conditions, that is, the probabilities of dying at each age. It provides a concise measure of overall population health and longevity, allowing for comparisons across countries and overtime. Differences in life expectancy often reflect variations in healthcare, living conditions, and broader demographic trends, making it a key indicator for understanding population dynamics in both the EU and the Southern Mediterranean countries. Across the EU, life expectancy at birth increased between 2014 and 2024 for both sexes, reaching 79.2 years for males and 84.4 years for females in 2024 (estimated, provisional), as shown in Figure 5. In the Southern Mediterranean region, life expectancy at birth also showed an overall increase over the period in the countries with available data. Israel recorded the highest levels in the region, with life expectancy rising from 80.3 to 81.3 years for males and from 84.1 to 85.4 years for females between 2014 and 2024 (noting a break in the time series). Morocco and Tunisia also registered notable gains, with male life expectancy reaching 75.3 and 74.7 years, and female life expectancy 78.8 and 79.3 years, respectively (2022 and 2023 data, respectively). In Jordan and Palestine, more moderate increases were observed. In Jordan, life expectancy rose to 73.8 years for males and 77.0 years for females (2023 data), while in Palestine it reached 73.4 and 75.6 years, respectively. Data for Egypt and Algeria are unavailable for 2024, while Libya and Lebanon have no data for 2014 and 2024. Overall, the Southern Mediterranean region shows a general upward trend in life expectancy at birth, alongside persistent differences in levels between countries and between sexes. [[Image: ENPS26_Life expectancy at birth by sex, 2014 and 2024_(years).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Life expectancy at birth by sex, 2014 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7c378c31-6047-4fff-827b-db1491e8b183?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:57:03Z demo_mlexpec]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/711db8b7-1131-43c3-8a06-8ea52feb8831?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:56:30Z enps_demo_mlexpec])|alt=Double vertical bar chart showing life expectancy at birth by sex in the EU and the countries in the ENP-South region. The bars show the years 2014 and 2024. For more details, see the link to the dataset below]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= ENPS26_Population_V2.xlsx|title=European Neighbourhood Policy — South countries — population: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data for Southern Mediterranean countries are supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country on a voluntary basis. The data result from an annual data collection cycle that has been established by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]. These statistics are available free-of-charge on Eurostat's website, together with a range of different indicators covering most socio-economic areas. Eurostat provides a wide range of demographic data, including statistics on [[Glossary:Population_figure|population]] at national and regional level, as well as for various demographic events influencing the size, the structure and the specific characteristics of these population data. Eurostat collects data from EU countries and other countries participating in its demography data collection exercise, including the Southern Mediterranean countries. The recommended population definition is the 'usual resident population' and represents the number of inhabitants on 1 January of the year in question (or, in some cases, on 31 December of the previous year). ===Context=== Population statistics are widely used to compare statistics relating to regions or countries that are inevitably of different sizes. Population is used as the denominator to normalise these data on a per capita (per person) basis. Examples include government expenditure per capita between regions; hospital beds per thousand population; school places per thousand children within a specific age range. Population statistics are used both in policy development and in discussion of its outcomes. EU cooperation with the Southern Mediterranean countries is guided by the [https://north-africa-middle-east-gulf.ec.europa.eu/what-we-do/pact-mediterranean_en Pact for the Mediterranean ‘One Sea, One Pact, One Future’]. The Pact reflects the EU’s commitment to strengthening its partnership with the southern Mediterranean countries and to building a common Mediterranean space that is connected, prosperous, resilient and secure, based on shared interests and joint responsibility. The Pact for the Mediterranean ‘One Sea, One Pact, One Future’ sets out a long-term vision to foster shared prosperity, stability, and sustainable development across the Euro-Mediterranean region. It establishes a strategic framework for cooperation, built around three interlinked thematic “pillars”: I. People: driving force for change, connections and innovation; II. Stronger, more sustainable and integrated economies, and III. Security, preparedness and migration management. Its core objectives include strengthening economic integration through enhanced trade, investment, and digital connectivity; accelerating the green and just transition by aligning climate action, renewable energy cooperation, and water security; and promoting human development via education, youth employment, and social cohesion initiatives. The Pact also aims to deepen political dialogue to address common security challenges, like migration, while reinforcing democratic governance. The Pact for the Mediterranean was endorsed by the EU and southern Mediterranean partners in November 2025 on the occasion of the 30th anniversary of the Barcelona process, with the European Council welcoming the Pact in its conclusions 20 November 2025. The [https://www.eeas.europa.eu/sites/default/files/joint_staff_working_document_renewed_partnership_southern_neighbourhood.pdf Economic and Investment Plan for the Southern Neighbours] complements this agenda. In cooperation with its Southern Mediterranean partners, Eurostat has the responsibility to promote and implement the use of European and internationally recognised standards and methodology for the production of statistics, necessary for designing and monitoring policies in various areas. Eurostat manages and coordinates EU efforts to increase the capacity of the Southern Mediterranean countries to [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-catalogues/-/KS-32-11-955?inheritRedirect=true&redirect=%2Feurostat%2Fen%2Fpublications%2Fleaflets develop, produce and disseminate good quality data] according to European and international standards. Additional information on the policy context of the Southern Mediterranean countries is provided on the website of [https://north-africa-middle-east-gulf.ec.europa.eu/index_en Directorate-General for Middle East, North Africa and the Gulf (DG MENA)]. The EU has been supporting statistical capacity building in the region for a number of years, among others by providing technical assistance to national statistical authorities and by sharing best practice and transferring know-how. A key tool for this statistical cooperation is the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Statistical_cooperation_-_European_Neighbourhood_Policy-South_(ENP-S) MEDSTAT programme], a multiannual regional cooperation programme for statistics addressing common issues and requirements. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Non-EU_countries|All articles on non-EU countries]]
