title: Population projections in the EU
text:
EU statistics presents the latest EUROPOP2025 population projections for the European Union covering the period 2025 to 2100. Data extracted in April 2026 Planned update date: April 2027 The EU population is projected to increase from 451.8 million in 2025 and peak at 453.3 million in 2029 (+0.3%), then gradually decrease to 445.0 million in 2050 and to 398.8 million in 2100. Median age of the EU population expected to increase by 6.6 years between 2025 and 2100. Proportion of people aged 65 years and older in the EU to more than double by 2100. This article focuses on projected developments of the population size and structure for all [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] Member States and 3 of the 4 [[Glossary: European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|European Free Trade Association (EFTA)]] countries, covering the period 2025 to 2100, based on the latest EUROPOP2025 population projections released by Eurostat on 16 April 2026. The size and composition of a population changes over time as a function of 3 demographic events: [[Glossary:Birth|births]], [[Glossary:Death|deaths]] and [[Glossary:Migration|migratory]] flows. The main outcome of the current levels of [[Glossary:Fertility|fertility]] and [[Glossary:Mortality|mortality]] in the EU is a progressive ageing of the population. This is an ongoing demographic process and its consequences are analysed by policymakers from social, economic and labour-related perspectives. EUROPOP2025 are deterministic projections, or 'what-if' population projections, based on assumptions formulated on a future course of fertility, mortality and migration. The scenario is that of partial convergence among the countries included in EUROPOP2025 in fertility, mortality and migration developments. The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Population_projections_in_the_EU_-_methodology methodology used in this projection round] builds heavily upon the previous projections exercises and their methodological reports are useful complements. ===Projected changes in population totals=== EUROPOP2025, the latest [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/population-projections population projections] released by Eurostat on 16 April 2025, provide the baseline projections for population developments from 2025 to 2100 for 30 European countries: all of the EU countries and 3 EFTA countries (Iceland, Norway and Switzerland), using data for population on 1 January 2025 as a starting point. Eurostat's population projections result from the application of a set of assumptions on future developments for fertility, mortality and net migration. The projections should not be considered as forecasts, as they show what would happen to the resulting population structure if the set of assumptions are held constant over the entire time horizon under consideration; in other words, the projections are 'what-if' scenarios that track population developments under a set of assumptions. As these projections are made over a relatively long time horizon, statements about the likely future developments of the EU's population should be treated with caution and interpreted as only 1 of a range of possible demographic developments. The additional available projection scenarios published show the wide range of possible outcomes under different assumptions. This article presents the main results of the baseline projections and includes the most recent official statistics available at the time of writing this article; for a more detailed presentation of the latest published data for the reference year 2024, please refer to the article on [[Population_and_population_change_statistics|population and population change statistics]]. '''''EU population projected to grow very slightly until 2029, followed by an increasingly steep decline until the end of the century''''' The EU population is projected to slightly increase from 451.8 million in 2025 to 453.3 million in 2029 (+0.3%), then gradually decrease to 445.0 million in 2050 and then accelerate its decline to 398.8 million in 2100, with an overall decrease of 53.0 million (-11.7%) from 2025 to 2100 (see Figure 1). Figure 1 '''''In 2100, Germany will remain the most populous EU country followed by France and Spain ''''' Between individual countries, the changes in the projected population structure vary considerably, both in terms of when the highest level of population will be reached and the direction and magnitude of change. In terms of total population, Germany will remain the largest country, despite a projected decline from 83.6 million in 2025 to 74.7 in 2100. It is followed by France with a projected total of 67.2 million in 2100 (down from 68.8 million in 2025) and Spain, which is projected to grow from 49.1 million to 49.8 million. Despite being projected to grow substantially, Malta and Luxembourg are projected to remain the least populous countries, with both projected populations remaining under 1 million. Figure 1 shows the trajectory of projected populations for all countries and aggregates between 2025 and 2100. Figure 2 shows the increase in % from 2025 to selected time periods, and for different age groups. In both figures, individual countries can be selected in the drop-down menu. An increase in the number of inhabitants is projected for 9 EU countries and for all 3 EFTA countries considered here. Population numbers are projected to rise by more than 25.0% until 2100 in 2 countries: Luxembourg (+36.4%), and Malta (+26.0%). Of the remaining countries, growth between 10.0% - 20% is projected for Sweden and Ireland. By contrast, the total population is projected to fall between 2025 and 2100 in 18 EU countries. Among these, there will be a relatively modest decline in the total number of people living in France and Austria, where the population is projected to contract by less than 5%. Declines of about 10% of the total population are projected for Germany, Slovenia, Finland and Czechial. The largest declines – with the total number of inhabitants between 2025 and 2100 falling by more than 30.0% – are projected for Poland (-31.6%), Lithuania (-33.4%) and Latvia (-33.9%). Figure 2 ===Impact of births, deaths and migration on population change=== At EU level, over the entire period between 2025 and 2100, a higher number of deaths than live births is projected, resulting in a continuous negative natural change (the difference between births and deaths). Figure 3 shows the projected developments for each vital event, as well as net migration, with the widest gap between the numbers of deaths and births projected for the decade from 2055 to 2064, exceeding 2.5 million persons. At country level, Eurostat's projections indicate that there will be considerable differences in [[Glossary:Natural population change|natural population changes]] developments during the period from 2025 to 2100, with: *An initial positive natural population change, but an overall negative balance over the projections' horizon – for 6 EU countries (Sweden, Luxembourg, Ireland, Cyprus, Malta, Denmark) and the 3 EFTA countries; *Negative natural change in each year of the projections' horizon – for the remaining EU countries. Figure 3 Migratory patterns – immigration and emigration – also have an impact on the total population as well as the population age structures, resulting from either positive net [[Glossary:Migration|migration]] (more people arriving in a country than leaving it) or negative net migration (more people leaving a country than arriving), and how both migration flows are distributed over the age groups. In the EUROPOP2025 projections, high and persistent positive net migration is the only factor contributing to population growth for those countries that are projected to grow over the time period between 2025 to 2100. In those EU countries which are characterised by positive net migration, it is possible that the process of population ageing may be slowed down, as migrant populations often have a high share of working-age persons. However, some countries have sizeable net immigration of pension-aged persons, such that positive net migration can also contribute to ageing. Also with negative net migration, the ageing process may be accelerated, as those leaving the country may also be relatively young, thereby reducing the number of working-age persons in the population, while also reducing the fertility rate. Table 1 shows the cumulative contributions of natural population change and net migration to the total [[Glossary:Population change|population change]] in the EU and for all EU countries until 2100. Over the period 2025 to 2100, Eurostat's projections suggest that there will be 253.0 million births and 409.8 million deaths in the EU, equivalent to a rounded net reduction of 156.7 million people due to natural changes in the population. The cumulated net migration is projected to contribute an increase of 103.7 million persons, resulting in an overall decrease of 53.0 million people in the total EU population. [[Image:Demographic balances, 1 January 2025-2100 (thousands) v3.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Demographic balances, 1 January 2025-2100
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=proj_25ndbi}}|alt= Table showing demographic balances in thousands for the EU, individual EU Member States and the three EFTA countries.]] ===Projected changes in population composition=== The Eurostat baseline scenario projects that the current pattern of population ageing in the EU is likely to continue until 2100, with both the size and the proportion of older persons in the total population increasing. Various demographic indicators are used to analyse the shift in age distribution towards older ages, including: *the [[Glossary:Median age|median age]]; *the proportion of population in each of the main demographic age groups - children (defined here as those aged 0-14 years), the working-age population (15-64 years) and the elderly population (65 years and over); and, *age-dependency ratios - such as the [[Glossary:Young-age dependency ratio|young-age dependency ratio]], the [[Glossary:Old-age dependency ratio|old-age dependency ratio]] or [[Glossary:Total-age dependency ratio|total-age dependency ratio]]. Figure 4 shows that during the period 2025 to 2100, the median age of the EU population is projected to increase by 6.6 years to reach 51.5 years in 2100. All countries are expected to experience an increase in the median ages of their population. Malta, Cyprus, Ireland, Luxembourg, Lithuania and Poland are projected to see their median ages rising by more than 10 years. The smallest increases below 6 years are projected for Bulgaria, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Greece, Slovenia and Czechia. Overall, the youngest populations are projected to be Bulgaria, the Netherlands, and Germany, with median ages just below 50 years. On the other side of the spectrum, projections indicate that by the end of the century, the median age is likely to rise above 53.0 years in 7 countries: Lithuania, Malta, Cyprus, Italy, Spain, Portugal, and Poland. The exact projected median ages for all countries and specific time periods can be selected and read off the interactive Figure 4. Figure 4 '''''Share of people aged 65 and over in the EU projected to more than double until 2100''''' The projected relative and absolute sizes of different age groups follow contrasting developments (see Figure 5). The proportion of young people (0-19 years old) in the EU total population is projected to decline in both relative and absolute terms, from a share of 23.3% (99.4 million) at the beginning of 2025 to 16.7% (66.6 million) in 2100. The share of working-age population (20-64 years old) in the EU total population is projected to decrease from 58.3% (263.2 million) at the beginning of 2025 to 49.7% (198.4 million) in 2100, representing an overall reduction of 64.9 million persons. The proportion of elderly (65 years and over) in the EU total population is projected to increase from 12.4% (99.0 million) at the beginning of 2025 to 33.6% (133.8 million) in 2100. As such, the share of elderly persons is projected to rise by +17.8 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points (pp)]], corresponding to additional 34.8 million persons by 2100. With the overall EU population declining by 2100, this is the only main demographic age group that is projected to grow considerably, both in relative and absolute terms, indicating an acceleration of population ageing. Figure 5 The shift in population structure towards older ages is projected to continue in all EU countries and all 3 EFTA countries covered here. Figure 6 provides a different graphical presentation of changes in the EU population between 2025 and 2100 by superimposing 2 [[Glossary:Population_pyramid|population pyramids]]. Each pyramid shows the distribution of the population by single year of age and sex, where the length of the bars corresponds to the number of people in a given age group for that sex in the total population. Comparing population pyramids over time shows how individual generations move through age groups and change in size as they age, and in this specific example, how the total and relative size of population by age changes between 2025 and 2100. The differences between these pyramids highlight the changes that will occur in the projected population structure of the EU between 2025 and 2100: *the population of children and young people is projected to decrease due to a lower number of births; this narrowing process is known as 'ageing at the bottom' (of the population pyramid); *the working-age population is projected to shrink considerably, increasing its burden of supporting the elderly; *the elderly population is projected to grow much larger – as shown by the broadening at the top of the pyramid – reflecting the ageing of the EU's population as a result of lower mortality rates; Figure 6 ''''' Projected age dependency ratios''''' Demographic dependency ratios are based on the age structure of the population rather than their employment status, and they can be defined using different age groups. They generally express the burden on the working-age population by calculating the proportion of dependents – persons below or above the age defined as working age, or both. Figure 7 shows the developments of different projected age-dependency ratios for the EU, covering the period 2025 to 2100. According to the projections, the young-age dependency ratios will be relatively constant throughout the projection period, oscillating between 20.2-23.0% for the age group 0-15 years, and around 33.6-34.0%, if the young age group is extended to cover persons 0-19 years old. However, the old-age dependency ratios are projected to increase rapidly until 2050, reflecting the ongoing retirement of baby-boomers and subsequent age cohorts and then keep growing at a lower rate until the end of the century. Both old-age dependency ratios (for the 2 working age groups of 15 to 64 years, and 20 to 64 years) are projected to increase substantially, from 34.4% in 2025 to 61.9% in 2100 and from 37.6% in 2025 to 67.5% in 2100. Therefore, while in 2025 there was roughly 1 elderly person for every 3 people of working age, it is projected that in 2100 there may be up to 2 elderly persons for the same number of people of working age. Among all EU countries and EFTA countries, old-age dependency ratios are projected to increase strongly. However, the dynamics over time between countries differ, with some countries projected to have almost linearly increasing old-age dependency ratios, while others exhibit periods of deceleration and acceleration of this indicator. In Figure 7, all available dependency ratios can be selected individually or together for each country. Figure 7 ===Alternative scenarios=== The population projections produced by Eurostat are deterministic projections, and a specific set of assumptions for fertility, mortality and migration fully determines the projected population. In such a deterministic approach baseline projections are constructed to reflect the most plausible continuation of observed trends, drawing on recent data and a common model, while the alternative scenarios are designed to explore the demographic consequences of systematically more pessimistic or optimistic assumptions across all components simultaneously. This scenario-based framework does not assign probabilities to any particular outcome; instead, it offers a structured range of plausible futures that can inform policy planning. The distance between the high and low scenario variants provides a practical, if implicit, indication of projection uncertainty, acknowledging that demographic behaviour – particularly fertility and international migration – is subject to considerable volatility over longer time horizons. In addition to the baseline assumptions, Eurostat therfore also formulates alternative scenarios, or sensitivity tests, to give insights into the impact changes in the assumptions have on the projected population. For the EUROPOP2025 round, these scenarios are lower fertility, lower mortality, as well as zero net migration, lower non-EU immigration and higher non-EU immigration. An additional migration scenario describes later convergence of migration flows, and a higher migration replacement rate. Figure 8 shows the projected population for the baseline along with all available scenarios. Figure 8 === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=EUROPOP2025 SE table v2.xlsx|title=Excel file}} ===Context=== Europeans are living longer and healthier lives than ever before. Along with an increase in longevity, Europe is witnessing an overall ageing population, which brings with it both opportunities and challenges. Eurostat's population projections indicate that population ageing will continue across all of the EU Member States and the 3 EFTA countries covered here. The EU population is projected to be lower in 2100 than it was in 2025 and its structure will be increasingly old, with a considerable reduction in the number and share of working-age persons. The ageing process may be highlighted through the increasing number of very old persons, whereby the elderly population is itself in the process of ageing. While migration has the potential to help delay the ageing process in some of the EU Member States, it may also speed up the process of ageing in those Member States which are characterised by a relatively high proportion of their working-age population leaving, for example in search of more attractive jobs. Indeed, the latest projections indicate that age dependency ratios are likely to continue to increase, highlighting challenges for public expenditure in relation to pensions, healthcare and long-term care costs. Information on the work of the European Commission 2019-2024 to tackle the impact of demographic change in Europe can be found in the [https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/priorities-2019-2024/new-push-european-democracy/impact-demographic-change-europe_en European Commission dedicated pages]. ===Other articles=== *[[Population projections in the EU - methodology]] *[[Population and population change statistics]] *[[Population structure and ageing]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/population-projections/database Population projections (proj)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/demography-population-stock-balance/database Population (demo_pop)] ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/overview Population and Demography overview] ===Legislation=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-15-002|title=Demographic statistics: a review of definitions and methods of collection in 44 European countries}} ===External links=== *[https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/publications/2024-ageing-report-economic-and-budgetary-projections-eu-member-states-2022-2070_en 2024 Ageing Report: Economic and Budgetary Projections for the EU Member States (2022-2070)] *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0241&from=EN Report from the European Commission on the impact of demographic change - 2020] *[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/new-push-european-democracy/impact-demographic-change-europe_en The impact of demographic change in Europe] {{Unit|topic=X_Population}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Population projections in the EU]] [[Category:Population and demography|Population projections in the EU]] [[Category:Population size and projections|Population projections in the EU]] [[Category:Statistical article|Population projections in the EU]] [[Category:Vistool|Population projections in the EU]] [[Category:April2027|Population projections in the EU]]

title: Population in enlargement countries
text:
An overview of demographic developments in the enlargement countries is given, including information for the number of inhabitants, sex and age distribution, population density, natural population change, migration and life expectancy. Data extracted in May 2026. Planned article update June 2027 Among the enlargement countries, between 2015 and 2025, the population increased only in Türkiye, from 77.7 million to 85.7 million inhabitants. In contrast, Albania and Moldova both saw continuous declines, from 2.9 million to 2.4 million). In 2025, Serbia was the only enlargement country where the share of the elderly population (22.7%) exceeded the EU average (22.0%). Conversely, the share of young people (less than 15 years old) was above the EU average (14.4%) in most enlargement countries, peaking at 23.8% in Kosovo'' This designation is without prejudice to positions on status and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo Declaration of Independence.'' (2022 data), while Serbia matched the EU average. [[File: CPC26_natural population change_2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|'' Source:''Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/80491fc0-616a-49ba-a78a-d574e33c05ad?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:30:06Z demo_gind])|alt= Infographic showing the natural population change in the EU, Kosovo, Türkiye, Montenegro, Albania, Georgia, North Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine in 2024.]] This article is part of an [[Enlargement_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]] and provides information on a range of population statistics for the enlargement countries compared with developments in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. The data used in this article have all been submitted to and validated by Eurostat's subject matter units, following the same process as for the EU countries. Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are usually included in the set of articles covering the enlargement countries. However, data on Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are also presented in the [[European Neighbourhood Policy countries - statistical_overview|Statistics Explained articles for European Neighbourhood Policy - East]] countries; these articles are based on annual indicators supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country. Data shown for Georgia exclude the regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia over which the government of Georgia does not exercise control. The data managed by the National Bureau of Statistics of Moldova does not include data from the Transnistrian region over which the government of Moldova does not exercise control. Since 2014, data for Ukraine generally exclude the illegally annexed Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the City of Sevastopol and the territories which are not under control of the Ukrainian government. For Ukraine official statistics on population for 2022-2025 were not fully produced due to the martial law. It will gradually be produced and disseminated as defined by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine, taking into account the specific conditions of producing statistics during Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. Statistics on changes in the population and its structure are increasingly used to support policy making and provide an opportunity to monitor demographic behaviour within an economic, social and cultural context. Aside from basic data on [[Glossary: Population_figure|population]] levels and structure, this article also provides information on [[Glossary:Population_density|population density]], [[Glossary:Natural_population_change|natural population change]], [[Glossary:Life expectancy|life expectancy]] at birth by sex and [[Glossary: Migration|annual net migration plus statistical adjustment]]. ===Population=== The recommended definition of total population is the ‘usual resident population’, which represents the number of inhabitants of a given area. Eurostat uses the reference date of 1 January of the year in question to ensure harmonised comparability. In some cases, however, the date of 31 December of the previous year is used, due to national production and data transmission practices. Data on the total population for the enlargement countries and the EU is shown in Table 1 for the years 2015-2025. Data for Bosnia and Herzegovina are not available for the period, data for Ukraine are missing for 2023-2025 and for Kosovo for 2015 and 2023-2025. Several countries report breaks in time series, notably Serbia (2023) and North Macedonia (2022), which should be considered when interpreting developments over time. Breaks in time series are also reported for the EU in 2017, 2021 and 2023. Over the period 2015–2025, the EU population increased moderately overall, rising from 442.9 million to 450.7 million persons (2021-2025 provisional). Annual growth rates remained relatively low and stable, generally between 0.1% and 0.2% up to 2020. The EU population then declined slightly in 2021 (-0.3%) before returning to moderate growth from 2023 onwards (0.4% in both 2023 and 2024, and 0.3% in 2025). Among the enlargement countries, Türkiye recorded the strongest and most sustained population growth, increasing from 77.7 million persons in 2015 to 85.7 million in 2025. Annual growth ranged from 1.3% in 2016 to 1.5% in 2019 and 1.4% in 2020, before slowing in subsequent years, although population growth remained positive throughout the period. By contrast, Moldova, Serbia and Albania experienced persistent population declines. Moldova’s population fell from 2.9 million persons in 2015 to 2.4 million in 2025, with annual decreases accelerating to -3.6 % in 2024. Serbia’s population declined from 7.1 million to 6.6 million persons over the same period, including a marked decrease of -2.4 % in 2023, coinciding with a break in time series. Albania remained broadly stable until 2020 before entering a more pronounced downward trend. Population developments in Georgia and Montenegro were comparatively stable. Georgia and Montenegro both showed stability over the period, with populations remaining unchanged at around 3.7 million and 0.6 million persons respectively. North Macedonia also remained broadly stable until 2021, before recording a decline in 2022 (-11.1 %) linked to a break in time series. Kosovo recorded a broadly stable population of around 1.8 million persons between 2016 and 2022. Data for subsequent years are not available. Ukraine’s population decreased continuously from 42.8 million persons in 2015 to 41.0 million in 2022, with annual declines gradually intensifying over the period; data for subsequent years are not available. [[Image: CPC26_Population, 2015-2025 (million persons).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Population, 2015-2025''
Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_pjan}}|alt= table showing the population by sex for the years 2015 to 2025 for the EU, Albania, Georgia, Kosovo, Montenegro, Moldova, North Macedonia, Serbia, Türkiye, Ukraine. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Share of women and men in total population=== Figure 1 presents the share of women and men in total population in enlargement countries and the EU in 2025. Data are not available for Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the EU, women slightly outnumbered men (51.0% compared with 49.0%), reflecting a typical demographic pattern driven mainly by higher female life expectancy and higher male mortality at older ages. Across the enlargement countries, the gender distribution of the population is generally balanced, with several countries clustering around an almost equal distribution between women and men, such as Montenegro (50.8% women), North Macedonia and Albania (50.5% women for both) and Kosovo (50.9% women, 2022 data). A small number of countries exhibit a wider gap from parity. A female majority is observed in Ukraine (53.6% women and 46.4% men; 2022 data) and Moldova (52.9% women and 47.1% men). In Türkiye, the population is evenly distributed between women and men (50.0% each). Differences in the gender composition of the population across enlargement countries remain limited and are largely driven by structural demographic factors, in particular differences in age composition and gender specific mortality patterns. Compared with the EU, where a slight female majority is consistently observed, the enlargement region shows broadly similar demographic patterns, with differences between male and female population shares remaining contained in a small number of countries. [[Image: CPC26_Share of women and men in total population, 2025_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Share of women and men in total population, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/00e322c1-1f23-4de1-9c8f-e7b0920658ca?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:24:05Z demo_pjan])|alt= horizontal stacked bar chart showing the share of women and men as a percentage of the total population for the EU, Albania, Georgia, Kosovo, Montenegro, Moldova, North Macedonia, Serbia, Türkiye, Ukraine for the year 2025. Each line has two stacked sections, totalling one hundred percent, representing the percentage of the women and men, respectively. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Population by age class === Figure 2 presents the distribution of the population by age class in enlargement countries and the EU in 2025, distinguishing between persons aged less than 15 years, 15–64 years, and 65 years and over. Overall, the data point to a relatively diverse age structure across the enlargement countries and the EU, with noticeable differences in the balance between working-age and dependent populations. In the European Union, the population is characterised by a relatively advanced ageing profile, with 22.0% aged 65 and over and 14.4% aged below 15 years. The working-age population (15–64 years old) accounts for 63.7% of the total (EU 2025 data provisional). This reflects a long-term demographic transition driven by sustained low fertility and increasing life expectancy. Across the enlargement countries, the age structure is more heterogeneous. A relatively young population is observed in several cases, most notably in Kosovo (23.8% aged below 15 years, 2022 data) and Türkiye (20.9% aged below 15 years), both characterised by a comparatively high share of children and a low proportion of older persons aged 65 years and over (9.1% and 10.6% respectively). A similar but less pronounced pattern is observed in Georgia (19.2% aged below 15 years) and Moldova (2025 provisional) (19.3% aged below 15 years), indicating a relatively younger demographic profile. At the same time, several countries are closer to the EU ageing profile, with higher shares of older persons aged 65 years and over, notably Serbia (22.7% aged 65 years and over) and Albania (21.2% aged 65 years and over), alongside lower shares of children aged below 15 years and a more advanced stage of demographic ageing. Intermediate patterns are observed in countries such as Montenegro and North Macedonia, where the age distribution remains relatively balanced between younger and older cohorts. The share of the working-age population (15–64 years) remains comparatively high in several enlargement countries relative to the European Union average (63.7%). The highest proportions are observed in Türkiye (68.4%), Ukraine (67.4%, 2022 data), and Kosovo (67.1%, 2022 data), indicating a demographic structure characterised by a comparatively large working-age population and lower old-age dependency. Relatively elevated shares are also recorded in North Macedonia (65.0%), Montenegro (64.8%), and Georgia (64.2%). Conversely, Moldova (62.4%) and Serbia (62.8%) remain below the EU average, reflecting comparatively older population structures. Overall, the enlargement region displays a dual demographic pattern, with some countries still characterised by relatively young populations, while others — notably Serbia and Albania — are already approaching or converging towards an ageing structure similar to that of the European Union. Differences across countries reflect varying stages of the demographic transition, particularly differences in fertility decline, longevity, and past migration dynamics. [[Image: CPC26_Population by age class, 2025_ (% of total).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Population by age class, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d5ee1705-3059-4350-a5e8-62ba5ad93508?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:26:37Z demo_pjangroup])|alt= horizontal stacked bar chart showing the categories of population aged: less than 15 years old, 15-64 years old and 65 years and over as a percentage of the total population for the EU, Albania, Georgia, Kosovo, Montenegro, Moldova, North Macedonia, Serbia, Türkiye, Ukraine for the year 2025. Each line has three stacked sections, totalling one hundred percent, representing the percentage each category of age in one hundred. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Population density === Data on population density, measured in inhabitants per square kilometre (km2), is illustrated in Figure 3 for the enlargement countries compared with the EU. The EU recorded a population density of 109.7 inhabitants per km2 in 2024, based on estimated and provisional data. Among the enlargement countries with available data, Türkiye recorded the highest population density in 2024, at 111.6 inhabitants per km2. Serbia followed at 90.5, Albania at 84.6, ahead of North Macedonia at 73.3 (both estimated) and Montenegro at 45.8 inhabitants per km2. The observed variation in population density across the enlargement countries is associated with differences in territorial extent and in the distribution of the population across cities, towns and rural areas. [[Image: CPC26_Population density, 2024_(inhabitants per km²).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Population density, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/55625f9d-b2a9-43f5-89b2-5811a1e1157b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:28:42Z demo_r_d3dens])|alt= horizontal bar chart showing population density measured in number of inhabitants per km² for the EU, Montenegro, Moldova, North Macedonia, Georgia, Albania, Serbia, Türkiye and Ukraine in 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Natural population change=== Population change can happen in two ways: either by natural change or by net migration. The natural population change is the difference between the number of live births and the number of deaths during a given period, usually 1 year. Data for the enlargement countries is illustrated in Figure 4 for 2024 as the crude rate of population growth. The latter is defined as the ratio of total population growth during the year to the average population of the area in question that year. The value is expressed per 1 000 persons. The EU recorded a natural population change of -2.8 per thousand persons in 2024 (estimated, provisional), indicating that deaths continued to exceed births overall. Of the enlargement countries with available data, Kosovo recorded the highest natural population change, at 5.5 per thousand persons (2021 data), followed closely by Türkiye at 5.2. Montenegro and Albania also recorded positive rates, at 1.0 and 0.5 respectively. By contrast, Ukraine recorded a natural population change of -7.8 per thousand persons (2020 data), representing the most pronounced decline, followed by Serbia at -5.7, Moldova at -4.1 (estimated, provisional), Bosnia and Herzegovina (provisional) at -3.2, North Macedonia at -2.3 and Georgia at -1.2. [[Image: CPC26_Natural population change, 2024_(per thousand persons).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Natural population change, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/80491fc0-616a-49ba-a78a-d574e33c05ad?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:30:06Z demo_gind])|alt= horizontal bar chart showing the annual crude rate of the natural change for the EU, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Moldova, North Macedonia, Georgia, Albania, Serbia, Türkiye, Ukraine and Kosovo for 2024. The crude rate is determined as the number of live births minus deaths in a year, divided by total population, expressed in thousands of persons. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Life expectancy at birth by sex === [[Glossary:Life_expectancy|Life expectancy at birth]] represents the life average number of years a newborn can expect to live if subjected throughout life to the prevailing mortality conditions, that is, the probabilities of dying at each age. It provides a concise measure of overall population health and longevity, allowing for comparisons across countries and overtime. Differences in life expectancy often reflect variations in healthcare, living conditions, and broader demographic trends, making it a key indicator for understanding population dynamics in both the EU and the enlargement countries. Figure 5 presents life expectancy at birth in 2014 and 2024 in the enlargement countries and the EU. Data are not available for Bosnia and Herzegovina (2014 and 2024) and Kosovo (2024). Life expectancy at birth increased between 2014 and 2024 in the EU, rising from 77.9 to 78.9 years for males and from 83.7 to 84.1 years for females (estimated, provisional). In 2024, women continued to live longer than men, with a gender gap of 5.2 years. In most enlargement countries for which data are available, life expectancy at birth also increased over the period considered, although developments differed by country and sex. Albania recorded one of the largest increases, with male life expectancy rising from 76.4 to 78.4 years and female life expectancy from 80.1 to 82.4 years. More moderate changes in life expectancy were observed in Serbia, Georgia and Moldova. Serbia recorded increases of 1.1 years for males and 0.5 years for females between 2014 and 2024, while in Georgia gains amounted to 0.6 years and 1.1 years respectively. Moldova also recorded increases, particularly for females, with male life expectancy rising by 0.5 years and female life expectancy by 1.5 years (based on 2012 and 2023 data respectively instead of 2014 and 2024, estimated and provisional). By contrast, North Macedonia recorded declines between 2014 and 2021, the latest year available, with male life expectancy falling from 73.5 to 71.1 years and female life expectancy from 77.5 to 75.5 years. Ukraine remained one of the countries with the lowest life expectancy levels, despite increases between 2014 and 2019 (latest data available), especially for females, whose life expectancy rose from 76.7 to 78.3 years. In all countries presented, females consistently had higher life expectancy at birth than males. The gender gap was particularly pronounced in Ukraine and Moldova, where female life expectancy exceeded male life expectancy by around 10 years. Breaks in time series are reported for the EU, Montenegro, Georgia, Albania, Serbia, Türkiye and North Macedonia. Data for Moldova (2012 data instead of 2014 and 2023 instead of 2024), North Macedonia (2021 data instead of 2024), Ukraine (2019 data instead of 2024) and Kosovo (2016 data instead of 2014) refer to different reference years. [[Image: CPC26_Life expectancy at birth by sex, 2014 and 2024_(years).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Life expectancy at birth by sex, 2014 and 2024
''Source:''Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/faaffd03-e277-40a7-a8b3-72cc4dfb216d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:31:28Z demo_mlexpec])|alt= vertical bar chart showing the life expectancy at birth by sex for the EU, Montenegro, Moldova, North Macedonia, Georgia, Albania, Serbia, Türkiye and Ukraine, measured in years. Four columns for each country represent life expectancy for men and women separately, for the years 2014 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Annual net migration=== Besides natural population change, net migration is the second component determining whether a population increases or decreases. Annual net migration is the difference between the number of immigrants (people entering an area) and emigrants (people leaving an area). In population change statistics, net migration also includes statistical adjustments used to reconcile differences between demographic events recorded during the year and the observed total population change. Net migration plus statistical adjustment is calculated as the difference between total population change and natural population change (births minus deaths). It therefore reflects not only the balance between immigration and emigration, but also any residual or unexplained changes in population numbers between two consecutive 1 January reference dates. This measure is important because it captures both migration flows and corrections for statistical discrepancies in population accounting. Data for the enlargement countries, as well as the EU, is shown in Figure 6 for the period 2020-2024. Breaks in the time series and missing annual data are present for several enlargement countries. Annual net migration plus statistical adjustment showed strong volatility over the period 2020–2024 in most enlargement countries, reflecting marked year-on-year fluctuations and, in several cases, shifts between positive and negative balances. Overall, developments were characterised by a sharp deterioration in 2021 in several countries, followed by partial rebounds in 2022, while results in 2023–2024 were more heterogeneous. Albania, North Macedonia and Türkiye are shown separately in the figure due to the scale of their values. A pattern of high volatility was observed in Türkiye, with a large positive balance recorded in 2021 (552 554), offset by negative values in 2020 and in subsequent years. In 2023 and 2024, the balances stood at -339 770 and -155 631 respectively. This indicates a significant reversal following the 2021 peak, with sustained negative contributions in the most recent years. Albania and Moldova consistently recorded negative balances over the period, with particularly pronounced declines in Albania in 2023 (-373 174). Serbia recorded a strong negative net migration plus statistical adjustment in 2022 (-109 405), while values for the other years shown (2020 – 2021, 2023-2024) remained at or close to balance. Georgia also recorded pronounced fluctuations in annual net migration plus statistical adjustment over the period. The balance shifted from a positive value in 2020 (15 732) to a negative value in 2021 (-25 966), before rebounding strongly in 2022 (54 509). It then returned to negative territory in 2023 (-39 207), followed by a renewed positive balance in 2024 (14 386). By contrast, Montenegro exhibited comparatively moderate movements, shifting from small negative values in 2020–2022 to a positive balance in 2023 (6 304), before returning to a slightly negative value in 2024 (-1 001). North Macedonia recorded a very large negative value in 2021 (-221 826), followed by much smaller values in subsequent years and a return to a slight positive balance in 2024 (505). Bosnia and Herzegovina showed negative values in 2022 and 2023, before turning slightly positive in 2024 (476). Kosovo recorded a positive balance in 2020 (2 819) and a negative balance in 2021 (-34 026), while data for subsequent years are not available. Data for Ukraine are only available for 2020 (9 316 persons). Overall, the series are characterised by substantial volatility and, in several cases, pronounced one-off movements in specific years, particularly in 2021 and 2023. For Bosnia and Herzegovina, data for 2020–2021 are not available and data for 2022–2024 are provisional; for Moldova, data are estimated and data for 2021–2024 are provisional; for Kosovo, data for 2020 are provisional and data for 2022–2024 are not available; and for Ukraine, data for 2021–2024 are not available. [[Image: CPC26_Annual net migration plus statistical adjustment, 2020-2024 (persons).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Annual net migration plus statistical adjustment, 2014 and 2024
''Source:''Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b0fd319e-81ec-4697-8957-022a92b2bba4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:32:48Z demo_gind])|alt= two line charts showing the annual net migration plus statistical adjustment for Albania, North Macedonia and Türkiye on the left hand side of the figure, and the annual net migration plus statistical adjustment for Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia Kosovo, Montenegro, Moldova, Serbia, and Ukraine on the right hand side, measured in persons, for the years 2020 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=CPC26_Population_v2.xlsx|title=Enlargement countries-Population: tables and figures }} ===Data sources=== Eurostat assesses and supports the alignment of statistical production in the enlargement countries with the EU acquis in the field of statistics. Eurostat supports the national statistical offices and other producers of official statistics through a range of initiatives, such as pilot surveys, training courses, traineeships, study visits, workshops and seminars, and participation in meetings within the European Statistical System. The ultimate goal is the provision of harmonised, high-quality data that conforms to European and international standards. [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] provides a wide range of demographic data, including statistics on population at national and regional level, as well as for various demographic events influencing the size, the structure and the specific characteristics of these populations. These statistics are available on Eurostat’s website. The population figures transmitted by the countries can either be based on data from the most recent population and housing census, typically carried out every 10 years, adjusted by the population change (live births, deaths, immigration and emigration) since the last census, or be based on population registers. The estimates of population produced using the population change components since the last census should be revised once the census results become available, revising and rebasing the population statistics series for the previous decade. Since 2016, the enlargement countries have provided annual demographic estimates directly to Eurostat’s unit responsible for population and migration statistics; these data have been used in this article. The same process applies to Eurostat’s regular collection of population data from EU Member States and EFTA countries. Among other steps, this process includes validation of the data received from the reporting countries. In some cases, enlargement countries have implemented major statistical adjustments in a single year when the precise results of a census become available, if retrospective adjustments of the population estimates for the previous decade are not feasible. This leads to a break in the time series. Population data for North Macedonia has been revised based on the 2021 census results which was released on 30 March 2022. A break appears in the time series as the revision has not been done backwards. ===Context=== Population statistics are widely used to compare statistics relating to regions or countries that are inevitably of different sizes. Population is used as the denominator to normalise these data on a per person (per person) basis. Examples include government expenditure per capita between regions; hospital beds per thousand population; school places per thousand children within a specific age range. Population statistics are used both in policy development and in discussion of its outcomes. Population statistics are the basis for distributing seats in democratic assemblies, where these are allocated geographically. Population statistics are also used in business decisions, both at local level and in focusing on specific age ranges. These statistics are used to analyse ageing population and its effects on the labour force and the age dependency ratio, thus supporting social and employment policies. Information concerning the current statistical legislation on population and demography statistics can be found at the following links: *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/population-housing-censuses/legislation Population and housing censuses] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/demography-population-stock-balance/legislation Demography, population and stock & balance] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/population-projections/legislation Population projections] While basic principles and institutional frameworks for producing statistics are already in place, the enlargement countries are expected to increase progressively the volume and quality of their data and to transmit these data to Eurostat in the context of the EU enlargement process. In cooperation with its ENP partners, Eurostat has the responsibility to promote and implement the use of European and internationally recognised standards and methodology for the production of statistics, necessary for designing and monitoring policies in various areas. Eurostat manages and coordinates EU efforts to increase the capacity of the ENP countries to [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-catalogues/-/KS-32-11-955?inheritRedirect=true&redirect=%2Feurostat%2Fen%2Fpublications%2Fleaflets develop, produce and disseminate good quality data] according to European and international standards. To do so, Eurostat supports the national statistical offices and other producers of official statistics through a range of initiatives, such as statistical projects, training courses, traineeships, study visits, workshops and seminars, and participation in meetings within the [[Glossary:European statistical system (ESS)|European Statistical System (ESS)]]. Additional information on statistical cooperation with the enlargement countries is provided in the Statistics explained background article [[Enlargement policy and statistical cooperation]]. === Footnotes === <'''footnote text will be automatically inserted if reference tags are used in article content text (use reference icon on ribbon)'''> ===Other articles=== *[[Enlargement_countries_-_statistical_overview|Enlargement countries — statistical overview]] *[[International_statistical_cooperation|International statistical cooperation]] — online publication *[[Population and demography]] *[[Population and population change statistics]] — online publication *[[Population structure and ageing]] — online publication ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=demo Demography and migration (demo)], see: :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=demo_gind Population change - Demographic balance and crude rates at national level (demo_gind)] :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=demo_pop Population (demo_pop)] :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=demo_fer Fertility (demo_fer)] :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=demo_mor Mortality (demo_mor)] ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-cooperation/regional-cooperation/enlargement Enlargement countries] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography Population] ===Publications=== *'''Factsheets''' :{{Template:Publication|code=KS-04-23-313|title=Basic figures on the candidate countries and potential candidates — Factsheets}} — 2023 edition :{{Template:Publication|code=KS-05-22-089|title=Basic figures on Western Balkans and Türkiye — Factsheets}} — 2022 edition :{{Template:Publication|code=KS-08-21-097|title=Basic figures on enlargement countries — Factsheets}} — 2021 edition ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=demo_gind_esms|title=Population change - Demographic balance and crude rates at national level}} (ESMS metadata file — demo_gind_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=demo_pop_esms|title=Population}} (ESMS metadata file — demo_pop_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=demo_fer_esms|title=Fertility}} (ESMS metadata file — demo_fer_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=demo_mor_esms|title=Mortality}} (ESMS metadata file — demo_mor_esms) ==External links== *[https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/enlargement-and-eastern-neighbourhood_en European Commission — Directorate-General for Enlargement and the Eastern Neighbourhood (DG ENEST)] {{Unit|topic=X_International_statistical_cooperation}} [[Category:General and regional statistics|Population in enlargement countries]] [[Category:International cooperation|Population in enlargement countries]] [[Category:EU enlargement countries|Population in enlargement countries]] [[Category:Non-EU_countries|Population in enlargement countries]] [[Category:Statistical_article|Population in enlargement countries]] [[Category:July2027|Population in enlargement countries]]

title: Population projections at regional level - EUROPOP2019
text:
Data extracted in March 2021 No planned article update 2 out of 3 EU regions at NUTS level 3 are projected to have a smaller population in 2050. The median age of population is projected to increase by 4 years on average across regions up to 49.1 years in 2050. Population is projected to increase in almost 3 out of 5 urban regions and to decrease in 4 out of 5 rural regions by 2050. [[Image:Map1 Projected relative change of the population, by NUTS 3 regions, 2019–50.png|thumb|centre|700px|Projected relative change of the population, by NUTS 3 regions, 2019–50
(%)
''Source'': Eurostat, EUROPOP2019, online data codes {{Stable link|title=|code=proj_19rp3}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=proj_19np}}| alt= A map showing the projected relative change of the population, by NUTS 3 regions between 2019 and 2050. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article describes the results of the [[Glossary:Projection|population projections]] of regional demographic patterns across 31 countries (the 27 [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] Member States and the 4 [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|European Free Trade Association (EFTA)]] countries). It presents a concise summary of the results at regional [[Glossary:NUTS|NUTS]] level 3 from the Eurostat Population Projections 2019-based — EUROPO2019. For the sake of simplicity and unless otherwise specified,'EU+' is the EU-27 plus the 4 EFTA Member States (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, and Switzerland). These regional population projections are based on population and vital events data up to 2018 corresponding to NUTS 2016 classification, which divides the economic territories of the 31 countries in 1216 geographical statistical units at NUTS level 3. Although these projections cover a time horizon that reaches the end of the century, the results presented in this article refer to the year 2050 and to the regional level only. The regional projections should be interpreted as a breakdown of the broader national projections consistent with the overall assumption of partial demographic convergence, rather than as an independent set of projections. In fact, the methodology of the Eurostat population projections is based on the main assumption that socio-economic differences between EU+ countries will fade out in the very long term. Values of major demographic indicators are thus so as to converge across countries in the very long term, but it has not been assumed that full convergence would be achieved, leading to countries equal in their demographic elements. It is rather an assumption of countries moving together and getting – demographically speaking – closer, due to the influence exerted by the (converging) socio-economic drivers. All the results here presented should be understood as one of the possible outcomes of a hypothetical scenario of partial convergence across regions to the national values, which follow the partial convergence as summarised above. Therefore, each result should be read as preceded by the sentence “''according to a scenario of partial convergence,''…” ===Projected changes in regional populations=== '''''Two-thirds of the regions are projected to have lower populations in 2050 than in 2019''''' Among the 1216 NUTS level 3 regions for which data are shown in Map 1, 802 are projected to have a lower population in 2050 than in 2019, while about half that number, 414 regions, are projected to have a higher population. The regions with the largest population relative decreases are mostly along the eastern EU border, from Finland through the [[Glossary:Baltic_countries|Baltic countries]] down to Romania and Bulgaria; along the southern continental border, namely in Greece and southern Italy; and along the south-western continental border, particularly in Portugal and in north-western Spain. The regions with the largest population relative increases are mostly on the north-western part of the European continent, namely in Ireland, Iceland, Sweden and Norway. Cross-border areas with larger projected population decreases (above 20 %) are noticeable in southern Latvia to northern Lithuania, southern Romania to northern Bulgaria and north-eastern Portugal to north-western Spain. Within countries, geographic clusters of projected population decline can be seen in Germany (eastern part), Greece (central continental part), Spain (central and north-western part), France (central part), Croatia (eastern part), Italy (southern part and islands), Portugal (eastern part) and Finland (central-eastern part). For Belgium, Denmark, Ireland, Austria, Netherlands, Sweden, Iceland, Norway and Switzerland the number of regions with projected population increase by 2050 is larger than the number of regions with population decrease. '''''All capital city regions always have a projected population change that is higher than the national average, either more positive or less negative ''''' The analysis of the variability of projected population change within a country can be narrowed to the capital cities. Between 2019 and 2050, in 22 of the 28 multi-regional countries, the population of the region hosting the capital city is projected to increase. For Höfudborgarsvædi (Iceland), Malta, Dublin (Ireland), Stockholms län (Sweden) and Oslo (Norway) this increased is by more than 25 %. Cyprus, Luxembourg and Liechtenstein, which have only one NUTS level 3 region, are all projected to have a higher population in 2050. '''''Population is projected to increase in almost 3 out of 5 urban regions and to decrease in 4 out of 5 rural regions''''' Another way to analyse the results of these population projections is from the [[Glossary:Urban-rural typology|urban-rural perspective]], which is applied to NUTS level 3 regions based on specific criteria. In the presentation of the results that follows, it is assumed that the classification of a NUTS 3 region by urban-rural typology does not change over time. Therefore, the projected outcomes should be read as referring to regions classified predominantly urban, intermediate or predominantly rural as of 1 January 2019. On 1 January 2019, 40.2 % of EU+ population was concentrated in the predominately urban regions (251), 39.2 % was living in the intermediate regions (542) and 20.6 % in the predominately rural regions (463), showing the differences that exist in the territorial distribution of populations across EU+. For a small number of regions, 21, spread over 8 countries (Lithuania, Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Germany, France, Croatia and Spain), the projected decreased population by 2050 is the result of higher negative net migration, which exceeds the natural change (group D). For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=EUROPOP2019-population projections regions NUTS3 (NUTS 2016).xlsx|title=EUROPOP2019 population projections regions NUTS 3 level: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== EUROPOP2019 projections at subnational level were produced for regions NUTS level 3, for all EU and EFTA countries, and are consistent with the population projections at national level, using population data on 1 January 2019 as starting point. They are the result from the application of a set of assumptions on future developments for fertility, mortality and migration. The projections should not be considered as forecasts, as they show what would happen to the population structure if the set of assumptions are held constant over the entire time horizon under consideration; in other words, the projections are ‘what-if’ scenarios that track population developments under a set of assumptions. As these population projections are made over a relatively long time horizon, statements about the likely future developments for the EU and EFTA population should be taken with caution, and interpreted as only one of a range of possible demographic developments. The EUROPOP2019 population projections at regional level where produced for regions NUTS 3 level using the NUTS 2016 classification. '''[[Glossary:NUTS|NUTS]]''' The data presented in this article are based exclusively on the 2016 version of NUTS (the Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics). It covers all 1169 regions classified as NUTS level 3 and the 47 Statistical Regions (SR) agreed between the European Commission and EFTA countries. Statistical regions are defined according to principles similar to those used in the establishment of the NUTS classification. '''Methodological note''' Whether the combined effect of net migration and natural change results in population growth or decline depends upon the relative size of the former components. Each of the 4 sectors identified above in the Figure 5 can be further split into 2 equal areas by drawing the diagonals. By doing so, there are 8 groups, described moving clockwise from the top right sector in the plot of Figure 5: 1. Positive natural change (N+) and positive net migration (M+): :: a. M+ < N+ : population growth, with positive natural change stronger than positive net migration :: b. M+ > N+ : population growth, with positive net migration stronger than positive natural change 2. Negative natural change (N-) and positive net migration (M+) :: a. M+ > N-: population growth due to positive net migration compensating negative natural change :: b. M+ < N-: population decline due to negative natural change stronger than positive net migration 3. Negative natural change (N-) and negative net migration (M-): :: a. M- < N-: population decline, with negative natural change stronger than negative net migration :: b. M- > N-: population decline, with negative net migration stronger than negative natural change 4. Positive natural change (N+) and negative net migration (M-): :: a. M- > N+: population decline due to negative net migration stronger than positive natural change :: b. M- < N+: population growth due to positive natural change compensating negative net migration From the perspective of population growth or decline, the regions can then be grouped as follow: : A. Regions with population growth mainly due to positive natural change: former groups 1a and 4b (respectively N+ > M- and N+ > M+) : B. Regions with population growth mainly due to positive net migration: former groups 1b and 2a (respectively N+ < M+ and N- < M+) : C. Regions with population decline mainly due to negative natural change: former groups 2b and 3a (respectively N- > M+ and N- > M-) : D. Regions with population decline mainly due to negative net migration: former groups 3b and 4a (respectively N- < M- and N+ < M-) === Other Articles> === *[[Population_statistics_at_regional_level|Population statistics at regional level]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/population-projections/database Population projections - detailed datasets (proj)], see: ::Population projections at regional level (2019-2100) - EUROPOP2019 (proj_19r) :::Population on 1st January by age, sex, type of projection and NUTS 3 region (proj_19rp3) :::Assumptions for fertility rates by age, type of projection and NUTS 3 region (proj_19raasfr3) :::Assumptions for probability of dying by age, sex, type of projection and NUTS 3 region (proj_19raasmr3) :::Assumptions for net migration by age, sex, type of projection and NUTS 3 region (proj_19ranmig3) :::Projected life expectancy by age (reached during the year), sex, type of projection and NUTS 3 region (proj_19ralexp3) :::Demographic balances and indicators by type of projection and NUTS 3 region (proj_19rdbi3) === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/population-projections Population projections] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/overview Population and Demography overview] *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=regions}} Regions] === Publications === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3217494/11348978/KS-HA-20-001-EN-N.pdf/f1ac43ea-cb38-3ffb-ce1f-f0255876b670?t=1601901088000 Eurostat regional yearbook — 2020 edition] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/15234730/15241943/KS-HA-21-001-EN-N.pdf/202462e1-b947-a2c5-6da2-c3d999018134?t=1667396809671 Eurostat regional yearbook — 2021 edition] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/15234730/15242104/KS-HA-22%E2%80%91001-EN-N.pdf/ffb89e8c-a7c9-517e-101f-13462ba1cf65?t=1667398021883 Eurostat regional yearbook — 2022 edition] === Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/proj_19n_esms.htm Population projections EUROPOP2019 -
