title: Population in European Neighbourhood East countries
text:
This article is part of an online Eurostat publication that provides a statistical overview over the European Neighbourhood Policy-East (ENP-East) countries. The article presents statistics on the population and its characteristics for Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine and compares these with the EU. Data extracted in January 2026. Planned article update: March 2027. Among the European Neighbourhood East countries, in 2024, the share of people aged 65 years and over in the population ranged from 9.1% in Azerbaijan to 17.6% in Ukraine (2022 data). In the EU, this age group accounted for 21.6% of the population. The population density in the European Neighbourhood East countries varied between 64.6 inhabitants per km2 in Georgia and 118.0 in Azerbaijan in 2024. In comparison, the population density in the EU was 109.3 (2023 data). The EU’s natural population change rate was -2.8 per 1 000 people in 2024 (provisional), meaning number of deaths exceeded the number of births. In the European Neighbourhood East region, Azerbaijan (4.3) and Armenia (2.7) saw population growth, while Georgia, Moldova, and Ukraine (2020 data) – like the EU – experienced declines. [[File: ENPE26_Rate of natural pop increase.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6aaa9225-22f9-4aaa-bb0f-58f0ee29bf4c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:50:35Z demo_gind])|alt= Infographic showing the natural population change in the EU, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine in 2024. The data are represented as horizontal line, sorted by value.]] This article is part of an [[European_Neighbourhood_Policy_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]]. It presents information on 5 [[Glossary:European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP)|European Neighbourhood Policy-East (ENP-East)]] countries, namely, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine. Information on these 5 countries is compared with developments in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are also [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries]]. The European Council granted Moldova and Ukraine candidate status on 23 June 2022 and Georgia on 14 December 2023. This article does not contain any data on Belarus, as statistical cooperation with Belarus has been suspended as of March 2022. Data shown for Georgia exclude the regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia over which the government of Georgia does not exercise control. The data managed by the National Bureau of Statistics of Moldova does not include data from the Transnistrian region over which the government of Moldova does not exercise control. Since 2014, data for Ukraine generally exclude the illegally annexed Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the City of Sevastopol and the territories which are not under control of the Ukrainian government. For Ukraine official statistics for 2022-2025 were not fully produced due to the martial law. It will gradually be produced and disseminated as defined by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine, taking into account the specific conditions of producing statistics during Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. Statistics on changes in the population and its structure are increasingly used to support policy making and provide an opportunity to monitor demographic behaviour within an economic, social and cultural context. Aside from basic data on [[Glossary:Population|population]] levels and structure, this article also provides information on [[Glossary:Population_density|population density]], [[Glossary:Natural_population_change|natural change in the population]], [[Glossary:Migration|annual net migration plus statistical adjustment]] and [[Glossary:Life_expectancy|life expectancy]] at birth by sex. ===Population during 2014-2024=== Data on the total population for the ENP-East countries and the EU is shown in Table 1 for the years 2014-2024. Ukraine’s data for 2023-2024 are not available. Due to a break in times series in 2015 for Moldova, Georgia, Azerbaijan and Ukraine along with missing 2014 (and 2022) data for Armenia, trend analysis for ENP-East countries begins only from 2015 onwards. Among the ENP-East countries, Moldova recorded a continuous population decline from 2.87 million in 2015 to 2.42 million in 2024. Between 2015 and 2024, Georgia’s population remained broadly stable, fluctuating near 3.7 million. Azerbaijan stands out as the only country in this group with sustained population growth throughout the period, rising from 9.59 million in 2015 to 10.18 million in 2024. Armenia’s population decreases slightly from 3.01 million in 2015 to 2.99 million in 2024. Ukraine saw a population decline of around 4.1 %, from 42.76 million in 2015 to 41.0 million in 2022, with data for 2023 and 2024 not available. Over the period 2014-2024, the EU population grew moderately (from 442.3 million persons to 449.3 million persons) reflecting overall stability despite a temporary decline in 2021 linked to the Covid-19 pandemic and to the effects of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine on migration flows. By contrast, population trends in the ENP-East countries were more heterogeneous: Azerbaijan continued to grow steadily, Armenia remained broadly stable, while Moldova and Ukraine experienced notable declines over the period. [[Image: ENPE26_Population, 2014-2024 (million persons)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Population, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/55688ca6-6b98-453e-9764-d8429990276b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:49:51Z demo_pjan])|alt=Table showing the population for the years 2014 to 2024 for the EU, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine.]] ===Share of women and men in total population=== Figure 1 shows that in 2024, women made up 51.1% of the EU population, compared with 48.9% men. This reflects a small and stable difference in the sex distribution across most EU countries. Across the ENP-East economies, the share of women is generally higher than in the EU. Azerbaijan is an exception, with 50.2%. The share of women in total population reaches up to 53.6% in Ukraine (2022 data). Georgia, Armenia, and Moldova also exhibit a pronounced female majority. This pattern is particularly notable in Ukraine and Moldova, where women constitute over 53% of the population, highlighting regional demographic trends influenced by life expectancy differences, migration, and historical population shifts. The share of men across most ENP-East countries ranges between 46% and 48%, remaining below 47% in Ukraine and Moldova and generally lower than the EU average of 48.9%, except in Azerbaijan, where it is higher at 49.8%. [[Image: ENPE26_Share of women and men in total population, 2024_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Share of women and men in total population, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/42699abe-dedf-4e4e-a070-5be6a79b7e50?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:49:07Z demo_pjan])|alt=Horizontal stacked bar chart showing the share of women and men in total population for the EU, Moldova, Georgia, Ukraine, Armenia and Azerbaijan for the year 2024.]] ===Population by age class=== As shown in Figure 2, in 2024 the EU population comprised 14.6% children (less than 15 years), 63.8% working-age people (15-64 years), and 21.6% older people (65 years and over). The share of older people exceeded that of children by 7.0 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]], up from 6.4 pp in 2023, indicating a slight widening of the gap. The EU’s population is ageing, as consistently low birth rates and higher life expectancy transform the shape of its [[Glossary:Population_pyramid|age pyramid]]. As a result, the share of working-age people is shrinking while the proportion of older people is rising. This seems to place growing pressure on the working-age population to support social expenditure for pensions, healthcare, and other services. By contrast, in Azerbaijan, Georgia and Armenia the share of young people exceeded that of the elderly, with the largest difference in Azerbaijan at 12.1 pp. In Moldova, the shares of younger and older people were almost identical (0.1 pp). In Ukraine (2022 data) the share of older people was slightly higher than that of children (2.7 pp), although the difference was smaller than in the EU (7.0 pp). Consequently, the working-age population ranges from 64.2% in Armenia to 69.6% in Azerbaijan, with Moldova at 65.1%, Georgia at 64.3%, and Ukraine at 67.4% at the higher end. Overall, these patterns reflect generally younger population structures compared with the EU, driven by higher fertility and lower life expectancy including a gender gap in life expectancy, with clear variation between countries. [[Image: ENPE26_Population by age class, 2024_(% of total).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Population by age class, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1ced4753-4965-4615-9f91-d39dc38d37d8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-06T14:29:48Z demo_pjanbroad])|alt=Horizontal stacked bar chart showing the population by age class for the EU, Moldova, Georgia, Ukraine, Armenia and Azerbaijan for the year 2024.]] ===Population density=== Data on population density, measured in inhabitants per square kilometre (km2), is illustrated in Figure 3 for the ENP-East countries and compared with the EU. Population density in the ENP-East region varies widely, reflecting differences in geography, urbanisation, and settlement patterns compared with the EU. In 2024, among the ENP-East countries, Azerbaijan had the highest density at 118.0 inhabitants per km2 (provisional), making it the sole country above the EU average of 109.3 inhabitants per km2 (2023 data, provisional). Armenia, with 103.4 inhabitants per km2, was slightly less densely populated than the EU. Moldova and Georgia recorded lower densities, at 79.8 and 64.6 inhabitants per km2, respectively. The most recent data available for Ukraine refers to 2014, when the population density was 75.3 inhabitants/km2. [[Image: ENPE26_Population density, 2024_(inhabitants per km2).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Population density, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1dd3cf6c-56b0-4fc9-97f8-c5f618123cd7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:47:12Z demo_r_d3dens]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b86a6f90-4911-41b8-bc91-367a78d244ef?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:46:31Z enpe_demo_r_d3dens])|alt=Line chart showing population density in inhabitants per square kilometre for 2024 in the EU, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Georgia and Moldova.]] === Natural population change === Population change can happen in two ways: either by natural change or by net migration. The natural population change is the difference between the number of live births and the number of deaths during a given period, usually 1 year. Data for the ENP-East countries is illustrated in Figure 4 for 2024 as the [[Glossary:Population_change|crude rate of population growth]]. The latter is defined as the ratio of total population growth during the year to the average population of the area in question that year. The value is expressed per 1 000 inhabitants. Across the EU, the natural population change rate was negative, at -2.8 per 1 000 inhabitants (provisional), indicating that the number of deaths exceeded the number of births. Among the ENP-East countries, Azerbaijan and Armenia recorded positive rates, at 4.3 and 2.7 per 1 000 inhabitants, respectively, reflecting a natural increase in their population. By contrast, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine experienced natural decreases, with the most pronounced decline observed in Ukraine at -7.8 per 1 000 inhabitants (2020 data), followed by Moldova at -4.1 per 1 000 (provisional) and Georgia at -1.2 per 1 000. Overall, the data highlight a clear contrast between countries with continuing natural population growth in the South Caucasus (especially Azerbaijan and Armenia) and persistent decline in Eastern Europe, underlining regional differences in fertility and mortality patterns, even over a short-term observation period. [[Image: ENPE26_Natural population change, 2024_(per thousand persons).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Natural population change, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b7e939e1-dd91-4a49-afe0-018283f8b176?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:46:01Z demo_gind])|alt=Clustered bar chart showing natural population change for 2024 in the EU, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine.]] === Life expectancy at birth by sex === Life expectancy at birth represents the average number of years a newborn can expect to live if subjected throughout life to the prevailing mortality conditions, that is, the probabilities of dying at each age. It provides a concise measure of overall population health and longevity, allowing for comparisons across countries and overtime. Differences in life expectancy often reflect variations in healthcare, living conditions, and broader demographic trends, making it a key indicator for understanding population dynamics in both the EU and the enlargement and neighbouring countries. Figure 5 presents life expectancy at birth by sex for 2014 and 2024. In the EU, life expectancy increased over the period, reaching 79.2 years for men and 84.4 years for women in 2024, consistent with gradual improvements in longevity and overall health conditions. Across the ENP-East countries, life expectancy remains generally lower than in the EU, with distinct differences between countries and between sexes. In Moldova, the most pronounced recent gains occurred among women. Their life expectancy climbed from 74.9 years in 2014 to 76.4 years in 2024. Men experienced a smaller increase, from 67.0 to 67.5 years. Georgia records more stable values, with male life expectancy unchanged at 69.9 years and a slight decline for women from 78.2 to 77.5 years. For Ukraine, Armenia, and Azerbaijan, 2024 data are not available. The graph indicates that in 2014 life expectancy at birth remained below the EU average for both sexes, with women consistently living longer than men by around 7-8 years. Overall, the EU demonstrates higher longevity and sustained improvements over the decade, whereas the ENP-East countries, though exhibiting some progress in specific cases, continue to display lower life expectancy and wider gender gaps, underscoring persistent regional differences in health and mortality. [[Image: ENPE26_Life expectancy at birth by sex, 2014 and 2024_(years).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Life expectancy at birth by sex, 2014 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/370f2a1d-4ac2-45b5-9cd2-6e2a90897d54?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:45:13Z demo_mlexpec])|alt=Clustered column chart showing life expectancy at birth by sex for 2014 and 2024 in the EU, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine.]] ===Annual net migration plus statistical adjustment=== Net migration plus statistical adjustment is a demographic metric calculated as the difference between total population change and natural change (births minus deaths). It covers net migration (immigrants minus emigrants) plus any other, unexplained changes in population numbers between two consecutive 1 January dates. The measure is crucial for understanding that population changes are not just due to births, deaths, and registered migration, but also include corrections for statistical discrepancies. Figure 6 shows the related trends for the ENP-East countries and the EU during 2020-2024In the context of the annual demographic balance, Eurostat produces net migration figures by taking the difference between total population change and natural change; this is referred to as ''net migration plus statistical adjustment.''. Annual net migration plus statistical adjustment between 2020 and 2024 shows changes in migration patterns across the ENP-East countries. Armenia recorded positive net migration in 2020 and again in 2023, followed by a strong increase in 2024 to 76 893 persons. In Georgia, net migration fluctuated between positive and negative values over 2020-2024, ranging from -39,207 to +54,509 persons. Azerbaijan also noted fluctuations, including a large negative balance in 2022 of 91 257 persons, before shifting back to positive figures in 2023 and 2024. In Moldova, though, net migration remained negative throughout 2020-2024, highlighting particularly large losses in 2021 (-62 411) and 2023 (-79 813). The 2020-2024 data are provisional. For Ukraine, only 2020 data are available (+9 316 persons), preventing comparability over time. Overall, the figures emphasize the pronounced instability of migration dynamics in the region during 2020-2024, influenced by economic conditions, geopolitical developments and data revisions, and highlight substantial differences in migration patterns across ENP-East countries. [[Image: ENPE26_Annual net migration plus statistical adjustment, 2020-2024_(persons)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Annual net migration plus statistical adjustment, 2020-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cc45f53b-78b2-4b27-a740-4bd377e81c66?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:51:50Z demo_gind])|alt=Line chart showing annual net migration plus statistical adjustment for 2020-2024 in Azerbaijan, Armenia, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine.]] === Notes === === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= 01_ENPE26_Population_Infographic_V1.xlsx|title=European Neighbourhood Policy — East countries — Population: infographic}} *{{Template:Excel|filename=01_ENPE26_Population_V4.xlsx|title=European Neighbourhood Policy — East countries — Population: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data for ENP-East countries are supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country on a voluntary basis. The data result from an annual data collection cycle that has been established by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]. These statistics are available free-of-charge on Eurostat's website, together with a range of different indicators covering most socio-economic areas. Eurostat provides a wide range of demographic data, including statistics on population at national and regional level, as well as for various demographic events influencing the size, the structure and the specific characteristics of these populations. Eurostat collects data from EU countries and other countries participating in its demography data collection exercise, including the ENP-East countries. The recommended population definition is the 'usual resident population' and represents the number of inhabitants on 1 January of the year in question (or, in some cases, on 31 December of the previous year). ===Context=== Population statistics are widely used to compare statistics relating to regions or countries that are inevitably of different sizes. Population is used as the denominator to normalise these data on a per person (per capita) basis. Examples include comparisons of government spending per person across regions; hospital beds per thousand population; school places per thousand children within a specific age range. Population statistics are used both in policy development and in discussion of its outcomes. These statistics are used to analyse ageing population and its effects on the labour force and the age dependency ratio, so informing social and employment policies. On 2 July 2021, the European Commission and the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy presented the [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/IP_21_3367 Eastern Partnership: a Renewed Agenda] for cooperation with the EU's Eastern partners. This agenda is based on the 5 long-term objectives, with resilience at its core, as defined for the future of the [https://neighbourhood-enlargement.ec.europa.eu/european-neighbourhood-policy/eastern-partnership_en Eastern Partnership (EaP)] in the Joint Communication [https://eeas.europa.eu/headquarters/headquarters-homepage/76166/joint-communication-eastern-partnership-policy-beyond-2020-reinforcing-resilience-%25E2%2580%2593-eastern_en Eastern Partnership policy beyond 2020: Reinforcing Resilience – an Eastern Partnership that delivers for all] in March 2020. The Eastern Partnership’s agenda for recovery, resilience and reform is underpinned by an 'Economic and Investment Plan for the Eastern Partnership (EaP): Investing in resilient and competitive economies and societies' (Annex I of the Joint Staff Working Document). More detailed overviews are given in a [https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/document/download/94735c00-2cfa-4ef7-92a6-41515b8b466d_en Factsheet on the Eastern Partnership Joint Communication], presenting the policy objectives and the specific priorities, as well as in a [https://neighbourhood-enlargement.ec.europa.eu/document/download/d675e1d6-fd68-45fa-a671-80a69a117f1f Factsheet on EU-Eastern Neighbourhood flagship projects 2023-2024]. The [https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/news/eastern-partnership-summit-joint-declaration-2021-12-15_en Joint Declaration of the Eastern Partnership Summit 'Recovery, Resilience and Reform'] of 15 December 2021 reaffirmed the strong commitment to a strategic, ambitious and forward-looking Eastern Partnership. At the [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/meetings/international-ministerial-meetings/2023/12/11/ Eastern Partnership Foreign Affairs Ministerial meeting of 11 December 2023], the EU, EU countries and partners declared that they will step up their efforts to implement the Eastern Partnership’s agenda for recovery, resilience and reform, as well as tackling challenges related to the ongoing consequences of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine for the entire region. On 14-15 December 2023, the European Council decided to [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2023/12/14/european-council-conclusions-on-ukraine-enlargement-and-reforms/ open accession negotiations] with Moldova and Ukraine, and granted the status of candidate country to Georgia. In cooperation with its ENP partners, Eurostat has the responsibility to promote and implement the use of European and internationally recognised standards and methodology for the production of statistics, necessary for designing and monitoring policies in various areas. Eurostat manages and coordinates EU efforts to increase the capacity of the ENP countries to develop, produce and disseminate good quality data according to European and international standards. Additional information on the policy context of the ENP is provided on the website of [https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/index_en Directorate-General Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood (ENEST)]. A regional statistical cooperation programme, STAT-East, is in place since January 2026 to strengthen partner countries’ statistical capacity to develop, produce and disseminate high-quality statistics and to reinforce the independence and institutional capacity of national statistical systems. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Non-EU_countries|All articles on non-EU countries]] *[[European_Neighbourhood_Policy_countries_-_statistical_overview|European Neighbourhood Policy countries — statistical overview]] — online publication *[[International_statistical_cooperation|Statistical cooperation]] — online publication *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Population_and_demography All articles on population and demography] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=enpe Eastern European Neighbourhood Policy Country (ENP-East) (enpe)], see: :Population and social conditions (enpe_pop) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/demography-population-stock-balance/database Population and demography - detailed datasets (demo_pop)] ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/international-cooperation/regional-cooperation/european-neighbourhood-policy Eastern European Neighbourhood Policy countries (ENP-East)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography Population and demography] ===Publications=== '''''Factsheets''''' *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-FU-23-001|title=Basic figures on the European Neighbourhood Policy-East countries — 2023 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-FU-22-001|title=Basic figures on the European Neighbourhood Policy-East countries — 2022 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-FU-21-001|title=Basic figures on the European Neighbourhood Policy-East countries — 2021 edition}} '''''Leaflets''''' *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-04-19-762|title=Basic figures on the European Neighbourhood Policy — East countries — 2020 edition}} ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=enpe_esms|title=Eastern European Neighbourhood Policy countries (ENP-East)}} (ESMS metadata file — enpe_esms) ===External links=== *European External Action Service (EEAS): [https://eeas.europa.eu/diplomatic-network/european-neighbourhood-policy-enp_en European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP)] and [https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eeas/eastern-partnership_en Eastern Partnership (EaP)] *Directorate-General for Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood (DG ENEST)): [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/european-neighbourhood-policy_en European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP)] and [https://neighbourhood-enlargement.ec.europa.eu/european-neighbourhood-policy/eastern-partnership_en Eastern Partnership (EaP)]. *Joint Communication JOIN(2020) 7 final: [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=JOIN:2020:7:FIN Eastern Partnership policy beyond 2020: Reinforcing Resilience - title: Population projections at regional level
text:
Insert short description for search engines Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: July 2030 Population is projected to fall in 70% of EU NUTS 3 regions by 2050. By 2050, the average median age is projected to rise to 50.1 years, an average increase of 3.8 years across all regions. Projected relative population change, 2025–2050, by NUTS 3 regions
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/97ad7bb0-4acb-4753-8a63-95e64084b857?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-07T12:38:53Z proj_25rp5] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/36fa2632-8517-45e2-a567-0dfa854af8e8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-07T12:39:51Z proj_25np])

This article describes the results of the latest [[Glossary:Projection|population projections]] of regional demographic patterns across the 27 [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]countries. It presents a concise summary of the results at regional [[Glossary:NUTS|NUTS]] level 3 based on the Eurostat Population Projections 2025-based — EUROPOP2025. The Joint Research Centre, with support from [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], produced these projections applying an updated methodology that builds on the approach developed for the EUROPOP2019 projection round. These regional population projections use population and vital events data up to 2024 and follow the NUTS 2024 classification, which divides the economic territory of the 27 countries in 1 165 geographical statistical units at NUTS level 3. Although the projections extend to the end of the century, the results in this article focus on 2050 and on the regional level only. For a presentation of the EUROPOP2025 data at national level, please refer to the article on "[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Population_projections_in_the_EU#Population_projections Population projections in the EU]”. All results in this article reflect one possible outcome under a hypothetical scenario of partial convergence — first at the level of countries, and then at the level of regions converging towards their national values. Every result should therefore be read with the implicit qualifier “''according to a scenario of partial convergence,''…” ===Population changes across regions=== '''''Population is projected to decline in 7 out of 10 regions between 2025 and 2050''''' Of the 1 165 NUTS level 3 regions shown in Map 1, population in 836 regions (71.8%) is projected to be lower in 2050 than in 2025, while 329 regions (28.2%) are projected to have higher populations. The sharpest relative declines by 2050 are projected along the EU’s eastern border, from Finland through the [[Glossary:Baltic_states|Baltic States]] to Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria. Marked declines are also expected along the southern continental border, particularly in Greece, Croatia, southern Italy, Portugal and Spain. In Germany, several regions are also projected to lose population by 2050, particularly in parts of eastern Germany. By contrast, the largest relative population increases are projected mainly in northern and western Europe, particularly in regions of Sweden, Ireland, France and Spain. Overall, these projections point to an increasingly uneven demographic landscape across the EU, with some regions facing sustained population loss while others continue to expand. '''Map 1:''' Projected relative population change, 2025–2050, by NUTS 3 regions
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/97ad7bb0-4acb-4753-8a63-95e64084b857?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-07T12:38:53Z proj_25rp5] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/36fa2632-8517-45e2-a567-0dfa854af8e8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-07T12:39:51Z proj_25np])

'''''Population projected to decline by at least 15% by 2050 in half of the regions along the EU’s eastern border''''' Figure 1 shows that the direction and scale of projected population change vary considerably across countries. Among countries with 2 or more NUTS 3 regions (all except Luxembourg and Cyprus), only 2 are projected to have no regions experiencing population loss by 2050, and 2 countries are projected to have no growth in any of their NUTS 3 regions. Overall, the current projections indicate that most countries are projected to lose half or more of their regions by 2050. In Latvia and Lithuania, all 15 NUTS 3 regions are projected to experience population decline by 2050 compared with 2025, with most regions losing at least 15% of their population. In Estonia, all but one region are projected to shrink by at least 10%. In Poland, Romania and Bulgaria, most regions are projected to see populations declines of at least 15%, while in Finland, Slovakia and Hungary, a majority of regions are also projected to record decreases, generally of more than 10%. [[Image:Fig1 NUTS Regions pop increase decrease 2025 2050 v1.png|thumb|left|700px|
'''Figure 1:''' Share of NUTS 3 regions with increased/decreased population, 2025-2050
''Source'': Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9c403d3c-2e71-4ca9-ad70-ede08dc12970?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-07T12:47:33Z proj_25rp5])| alt= A horizontal bar chart showing the share of NUTS 3 regions with increased/decreased population between 2025 and 2050 in EU countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''In 18 of the 25 multi-regional countries, the population is projected to decrease in the majority of regions by 2050''''' Among the EU countries with the largest national populations, the number of regions whose population is projected to decline exceeded the number of regions whose population is projected to grow in Germany (324 out of 400 regions), France (52 out of 101 regions) and Italy (92 out of 107 regions). By 2050, most regions in the 9 EU countries on the eastern border are projected to see population decline, as are more than 80% of regions in Greece, Czechia, Croatia and Portugal. In Ireland, Malta, Belgium, Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands and Spain, more regions are projected to see population increases than decreases by 2050. In Ireland and Malta, every region is projected to have higher population in 2050 than in 2025; the same holds for 42 of the 44 regions in Belgium. '''''In most capital city regions, projected population change is above the national average, either more positive or less negative''''' Focusing on capital cities highlights the variation in projected population change within countries. Between 2025 and 2050, the population of the capital city region is projected to increase in 19 of the 25 multi-regional countries. For Madrid (Spain), Malta, Dublin (Ireland) and Bratislavský kraj (Slovakia), this increase exceeds 20%. In 9 countries, the capital city region records the highest projected population change between 2025 and 2050 among all regions in the country — Denmark, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia and Malta. By 2050 almost 90% of the capital city regions (22) are projected to have a population change above the national average, with differences ranging from +29.5 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] to -6.8 pp. In 10 capital city regions (in Bulgaria, Czechia, Germany, Estonia, Finland, Croatia, Italy, Portugal, Slovenia and Slovakia), positive projected population change contrasts with a negative national average. Cyprus and Luxembourg, which each have a single NUTS level 3 region, are both projected to have higher populations in 2050. ===Population ageing across regions=== '''''Median age is projected to increase between 2025 and 2050 in almost all EU regions''''' Map 2 shows the [[Glossary:Median age|median age]] of the population in NUTS 3 regions on 1 January 2025 and 2050. Population ageing over this period is reflected in an unweighted average increase in the median age to 50.1 years by 2050, corresponding to a rise of 3.8 years across all regions. [[Image:Map2_Median_ages_2025_2050_v2.png|thumb|center|700px|
'''Map 2:''' Median age of population, 2025 and 2050, by NUTS 3 regions
(years)
''Source'': Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0d7e732b-4078-4cf4-9400-0b7f8d526324?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-07T12:36:37Z proj_25rpind])| alt= A map showing the median age of population, by NUTS 3 regions in 2025 and 2050. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Ageing is likely to rise at varying rates across regions. It is projected to be fastest in regions of Lithuania, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Malta and Italy, where the median age could rise by at least 8.0 years between 2025 and 2050. In most regions along the EU’s eastern and southern borders, the median age is projected to reach at least 41.4 years, with the vast majority exceeding 50.0 years. Ageing is also anticipated in north-western Europe, although median ages in most regions there are likely to remain below 48.0 years. By contrast, regions with relatively older populations in 2025 — including many parts of Germany — are projected to age more slowly, resulting in a gradual convergence in median age across regions. 30 regions, mostly in Bulgaria and Germany, are projected to have younger populations, with median age likely to decrease by up to 5.0 years. '''''By 2050, 9 in 10 regions are projected to have at least one quarter of their population aged 65 years and over''''' Population ageing can also be measured by looking at the share of specific age groups in the total population or by using age dependency ratios, i.e. ratios between age groups. The share of people aged 65 and over is projected to increase from an average of 23.4% in 2025 to 30.5% in 2050, a rise of 7.2 pp. In 2025, nearly 30% of EU regions (357) already had at least one quarter of their population aged 65 or over. These regions were mainly located in Sweden and Finland, extending through to eastern Germany, southern France, Portugal, Spain, central and northern Italy, and across Bulgaria and Greece. By 2050, this share is projected to rise sharply to 90% of regions (1 040). A similar pattern is projected for population aged 80 years and over as share of the total population. Across all 1 165 NUTS level 3 regions, the proportion of people aged 80 years and over averaged 6.7% in 2025 and is projected to reach 11.8% by 2050, an increase of 5.1 pp. By 2050, the share of population aged 80 years and over is projected to reach or exceed 13.9% — the highest regional value observed in 2025 (Evrytania, Greece) — in 246 regions. Most of these regions are located in southern European countries (Greece, Italy, Spain, and Portugal) and in France and Germany. Overall, three quarters of all regions are projected to have at least 10.0% of their population aged 80 years and over by 2050. The increasing share of older people in the population also has implications for the balance between age groups. These can be assessed using the [[Glossary:Old-age dependency ratio|old-age dependency ratio]], which measures the number of people aged 65 years and over relative to the working-age population (aged 15–64 years considered in this article). [[Image:Map3_Old_Age_Dependency_Ratios_2025_2050_v3.png|thumb|center|700px|
'''Map 3:''' Old age dependency ratios, 2025 and 2050, by NUTS 3 regions
(%)
''Source'': Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/571596a2-b53b-481b-98b3-61066322fb21?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-07T12:34:57Z proj_25rpind])|alt=A map showing the projected old-age dependency ratio - OLDDEP1, by NUTS 3 regions, 2025 and 2050. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Map 3 shows the old-age dependency ratio in 2025 and 2050 for all 1 165 NUTS level 3 regions. By 2050, the ratio is projected to exceed 50% in 6 out of 10 regions (710), meaning that there will be one person aged 65 years and over for at most 2 people of working age in these regions. Across all regions, the combined effect of the projected increase in the population aged 65 years and over and the decline in the working-age population is expected to raise the old-age dependency ratio from a simple unweighted average of 37.6% in 2025 to 54.5% by 2050, an increase of 16.8 pp. ===Demographic drivers of projected population change across regions=== The EUROPOP2025 regional projections have been estimated on the basis of 5-year age groups, and 5-year intervals. Population change is therefore defined as the difference in the size of a population between the beginning and the end of 5 calendar years. It has 2 components: *(N) [[Glossary:Natural_population_change|natural change]], defined as the aggregated number of live births over 5 years minus the aggregated number of deaths over 5 years, i.e. the change in population due to vital events; and *(M) [[Glossary:Net_migration|net migration]], defined as the aggregate number of immigrants minus the aggregate number of emigrants over 5 years. The direction of population change (positive or negative) depends on the combined effect of the 2 components. Accordingly, all 1 165 NUTS level 3 regions can be classified into 4 main groups based on the combination of natural change and net migration. * Positive natural change (N+) and positive net migration (M+) * Negative natural change (N-) and positive net migration (M+) * Negative natural change (N-) and negative net migration (M-) * Positive natural change (N+) and negative net migration (M-) '''''Net migration is the main driver for population growth by 2050 for almost 3 out of 10 regions''''' Almost one-third of the regions (329 out of 1 165 NUTS 3 regions) is projected to have a higher population in the year 2050 compared with 2025, mainly due to overall positive natural change (group A) or positive net migration (group B). Positive natural change is projected to be the main driver of population growth by 2050 in just 21 regions (group A). These regions are spread across 6 countries — Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands and Spain — with more than half of them located in France. Net migration, the other component of population change, is projected to be the main driver of population growth by 2050 in 308 regions (26.4%), classified in group B. Among multi-regional countries, at least half of the regions are projected to belong to this group in Denmark and Sweden (northern Europe), Ireland, Belgium and the Netherlands (western Europe), and Spain (southern Europe). In Ireland and Malta, net migration is projected to be the main driver of population growth in all regions by 2050. The same is projected for the single-region countries of Cyprus and Luxembourg. '''''Negative natural change is the main driver for the population decline by 2050 for 7 out of 10 regions''''' Compared with 2025, the population is projected to decline in 820 regions (70%) by 2050 as a result of natural decrease (group C). In these regions, positive net migration, where present, is not expected to offset the excess of deaths over live births. By 2050, at least 80% of the regions in 13 EU countries are projected to experience population decline driven by negative natural change. These countries include Finland; the Baltic States; countries in Central and Eastern Europe (Poland, Czechia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria); and southern European countries (Greece, Croatia, Italy, Portugal). For a small number of regions, 16, spread over 7 countries (Slovakia, Romania, Bulgaria, Germany, France, Spain, Greece), the projected decreased population by 2050 is the result of higher negative net migration, which exceeds the natural change (group D). [[Image:Table 1 Population change 2025 2049.png|thumb|centre|700px|
'''Table 1:''' Population change by group of demographic balance components, 2025-2049
''Source'': Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1ff46b53-4551-47a7-8bc9-31eac62ceb90?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-07T12:55:26Z proj_25rbal])| alt= A table showing the population change by group of demographic balance components between 2025 and 2050. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=EUROPOP2025 population projections by NUTS 3 regions (NUTS 2024) FINAL.xlsx|title=EUROPOP2025 population projections by NUTS 3 regions (NUTS 2024): maps graph and table}} ===Data sources=== The EUROPOP2025 subnational population projections were produced for all NUTS level 3 regions in the 25 EU Member States that have more than one NUTS3 region. They are consistent with the national population projections and use the population on 1 January 2025 as the baseline. The projections are based on a set of assumptions about future developments in fertility, mortality and migration. These projections should not be interpreted as forecasts. Rather, they illustrate how the population would evolve if the underlying assumptions remained unchanged throughout the projection period. In other words, they represent what-if scenarios that describe possible population developments under a specific set of demographic assumptions. As the projections cover a relatively long time horizon, they should be interpreted with caution. They represent only one of a range of possible demographic futures for the populations of the EU Member States. The regional EUROPOP2025 projections were produced for all 1 165 NUTS level 3 regions, based on the [[Glossary:NUTS|NUTS]] 2024 classification (the Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics). '''Methodological note''' Whether the combined effect of natural change and net migration results in population growth or decline depends on the direction and relative magnitude of these 2 demographic components. The 4 groups (A–D) presented in Table 1 are derived from 8 demographic scenarios, reflecting all possible combinations of positive or negative natural change and net migration, as well as the component that has the greater influence on the overall population change. These scenarios are described below. 1. Positive natural change (N+) and positive net migration (M+): : a. M+ < N+ : population growth, with positive natural change stronger than positive net migration : b. M+ > N+ : population growth, with positive net migration stronger than positive natural change 2. Negative natural change (N-) and positive net migration (M+): : a. M+ > N- : population growth due to positive net migration compensating negative natural change : b. M+ < N- : population decline due to negative natural change stronger than positive net migration 3. Negative natural change (N-) and negative net migration (M-): : a. M- < N- : population decline, with negative natural change stronger than negative net migration : b. M- > N- : population decline, with negative net migration stronger than negative natural change 4. Positive natural change (N+) and negative net migration (M-): : a. M- > N+ : population decline due to negative net migration stronger than positive natural change : b. M- < N+ : population growth due to positive natural change compensating negative net migration From the perspective of population growth or decline, the regions can then be grouped as follow: : A. Regions with population growth mainly due to positive natural change: subgroups 1a and 4b : B. Regions with population growth mainly due to positive net migration: subgroups 1b and 2a : C. Regions with population decline mainly due to negative natural change: subgroups 2b and 3a : D. Regions with population decline mainly due to negative net migration: subgroups 3b and 4a ===Context=== These regional projections are a disaggregation of the national projections and follow the overall assumption of partial demographic convergence, rather than forming a separate set of projections. Eurostat's national-level population projections assume that socio-economic differences between EU countries will gradually diminish over the very long term. Major demographic indicators are therefore projected to move closer across countries, though not to full convergence — countries are not expected to become identical in their demographic profiles. Instead, countries are assumed to become more similar demographically as socio-economic conditions converge. === Other Articles> === *[[Population_projections_in_the_EU#Population_projections|Population projections in the EU]] *[[Population_statistics_at_regional_level|Population statistics at regional level]] *[[Population_and_population_change_statistics|Population and population change statistics]] *[[Population_structure_and_ageing|Population structure and ageing]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/population-projections/database Population projections - detailed datasets (proj)], see: :Population projections at regional level (2025-2100) - EUROPOP2025 (proj_25r) ::Population on 1st January by age group, sex, type of projection and NUTS 3 region (proj_25rp5) ::Assumptions for total fertility rates, type of projection and NUTS 3 region (5-year averages) (proj_25raasfr) ::Projected life expectancy at birth, by sex, type of projection and NUTS 3 region (5-year averages) (proj_25ralexp) ::Demographic balances by type of projection and NUTS3 region (5-year aggregates) (proj_25rdbal) ::Population structure indicators by type of projection and NUTS3 region (proj_25rpind) === Thematic section === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/population-projections Population projections] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/overview Population and Demography overview] *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=regions}} Regions] === Publications === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/15234730/22226461/KS-01-25-037-EN-N.pdf/d1e913e6-7903-cabc-4171-73cb06225f1a?version=6.0&t=1761314134077 Eurostat regional yearbook — 2025 edition] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/interactive-publications/demography-2026 Demography of Europe – 2026 edition] === Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/proj_25r_esms.htm Reference metadata - 'Population projections at regional level (2025-2100) - EUROPOP2025] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Population_projections_in_the_EU_-_methodology Population projections in the EU - methodology at] === Visualisations === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RSI/ Regional Statistics Illustrated] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/interactive-publications/demography-2026 Demography of Europe – 2026 edition] === External links === *[https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/publications/2024-ageing-report-economic-and-budgetary-projections-eu-member-states-2022-2070_en 2024 Ageing Report. Economic and Budgetary Projections for the EU Member States (2022-2070)] * [https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/information-sources/cohesion-report_en Ninth Report on Economic, Social and Territorial Cohesion] *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0241&from=EN Report from the European Commission on the impact of demographic change - 2020] * [https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/priorities-2019-2024/new-push-european-democracy/impact-demographic-change-europe_en The impact of demographic change in Europe] {{Unit|topic=X_Social_statistics}} ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Statistics_on_regional_population_projections'' [[Category:Population and social conditions|Population projections at regional level]] [[Category:Population and demography|Population projections at regional level]] [[Category:Population size and projections|Population projections at regional level]] [[Category:Statistical article|Population projections at regional level]] [[Category:July2030|Population projections at regional level]]

title: Population projections in the EU - methodology
text:
<newarticle pic="Rawpixel.com shutterstock 248784517 RV.jpg"> </newarticle>

<metadescription>EU methodological statistics on the population projections in the EU</metadescription>

<highlight title=false>

<vistool>
      <script>{ 
"utility": "wcloud",
    "url": "https://europa.eu/assets/wcloud/widgets/202507/839efcc0-574b-11f0-8a71-5b8e7bbdd96c/uec.json"
}</script>
<caption> </caption>
</vistool>

Population projections are 'what-if scenarios' that aim to show, for a long-time period, the hypothetical developments of the population size and its structure based on sets of assumptions for fertility, mortality and migration. These assumptions for future fertility, mortality and migration are based on observed demographic trends and the assumption of partial convergence of these trends for all EU Member States. Population projections are not forecasts, and do not take into account current or future policies in the Member States. Population projections published by Eurostat may differ substantially from projections published by other organisations such as the [https://population.un.org/wpp/ UN], or by projections published nationally due to differences in these assumptions, adoption of different models or specifications in the same model, as well as different input data. This is notably true of the migration component, which is the most volatile and the most difficult element of population change to estimate.
The purpose of this article is to provide information about Eurostat’s methodology and the assumptions used in the estimation of the latest long-term and short-term population projection rounds.

</highlight>

<articlecontent>

<sesection>

=== Eurostat's mandate ===

As the statistical office of the EU, Eurostat was initially called upon to prepare population projections so that the EU could assess and address the impact of the EU population’s ageing on public finances in the EU. Later, the interest in and use of population projections grew to cover other topics on the EU agenda. Today’s population projections are typically produced in a 3-year cycle, publishinge EU/EFTA, national and in irregular time-spans, regional results. While published projection results are now used in a number of policy products, this timeline remains strongly driven by public finance policy needs within the EU. 
The latest long-term projections were published on 15 April 2026, covering the period from 2025 to 2100. These long-term projections are covered by a mandate from the ECOFIN council, and will serve as important input to the Ageing Report  prepared by the [https://economic-financial-policy-committees.europa.eu/economic-policy-committee/working-groups/working-group-ageing-populations-and-sustainability-awg_en EPC Working Group on Ageing Populations and Sustainability], to be published in 2027. These long-term projections will be updated in  April 2027 and April 2028 with the newest available demographic data, to support the work of the [https://economic-financial-policy-committees.europa.eu/economic-policy-committee/working-groups/potential-output-working-group-powg_en EPC Potential Output Working Group], and as input for the spring and fall semester. 


</sesection>

<sesection>

=== General methodological approach ===
The cohort-component method is the framework used by Eurostat to produce demographic projections. It builds directly on the familiar principle of demographic balance, according to which population change is determined by births, deaths, and migration. Rather than applying this principle only at the level of the total population, the cohort-component method operationalizes it at a more detailed level by tracking changes separately for groups defined by age and sex.
The central idea is to follow cohorts–groups of individuals born in the same year–as they move through time. At each step – each year -  of the projection, individuals age into the next age group, while their numbers are adjusted to account for mortality and migration. In this way, each cohort evolves according to the same basic demographic accounting logic: its size decreases through deaths, may increase or decrease through migration, and shifts forward as its members grow older.
A special role is played by the youngest age group, which enters the population through births. The number of births in each period is determined by the number of women of child-bearing age in the population and their assumed fertility rates. These births form a new cohort that is then subject to the same processes of mortality, aging, and migration as all other cohorts.
The method is therefore structured around 3 core components: fertility, mortality, and migration. Fertility generates new births into the population; mortality rates determine the number of deaths of individuals as they age; and migration redistributes population across age groups through inflows and outflows, with a net positive or net negative effect on total population. Each component is applied in a consistent and systematic way across the projection horizon.
In practice, the projection proceeds iteratively. Starting from a baseline population disaggregated by age and sex, cohorts are advanced forward year by year by applying mortality rates and migration assumptions. Births are then calculated and added as a new youngest cohort. Repeating this process for each year yields a projected population that evolves both in size and in age structure.
Conceptually, the cohort-component method can be understood as a disaggregated implementation of the demographic balance equation. While the balance equation describes changes in the total population, the cohort-component approach applies the same logic at the level of individual cohorts. The aggregate population at any point in time is simply the sum of these cohort-specific dynamics.
This disaggregation is crucial because it allows the model to capture changes in population structure. In particular, it reflects how the age distribution of a population influences future demographic outcomes–for example, how large cohorts entering reproductive ages can lead to increases in the number of births even if fertility rates remain constant. By incorporating these structural dynamics, the cohort-component method provides a coherent and flexible framework for projecting population change under specified assumptions about future fertility, mortality, and migration.
Three independent models are used to derive the assumptions for each component in the same way for each country. The migration model contains in turn 3 different components for immigration, and 3 for emigration. In all models, the partial convergence assumption is the most important driver of the model. Unless otherwise stated, each model is applied to all countries in the same way. The output of the models is expressed respectively in age-specific fertility rates; age- and sex-specific mortality rates; age- and sex- and geo-specific emigration rates ; and age-, sex- and geo-specific immigration levels for each of the years covered by this projection exercise. Population by age and sex is calculated by recursively applying the changes brought by the stated assumptions on fertility, mortality and migration, as described above.
The projections methodology is developed mainly for the EU Member States, which remain the main focus of the exercise. EU aggregate results are derived by aggregating projected population or indicators for all Member States. EU aggregates for assumptions are not published, as no assumptions are formulated for the EU as a whole. Results are also produced for EFTA countries, with an adapted migration model. Population projections are produced and published by sex and single age.
To give an impression of the impact of different assumptions on the projected population, Eurostat publishes in addition to the baseline model a number of alternative scenarios: lower fertility,  lower mortality, zero net migration, higher and lower non-EU immigration, and a slower convergence migration scenario with additional replacement migration.

===Partial convergence assumption===

One of the main drivers of the models used to derive fertility, mortality and migration assumptions for Eurostat’s population projections is the assumption of partial convergence of all EU Member States’ demographic development over time.  This assumption is built on the premise that continuing European integration and income convergence drives a number of socio-economic factors that directly and indirectly influence demographic developments, leading to partial convergence of these demographic factors over time. One example of partial convergence is the development of the infant mortality rate in the EU over the last 65 years. Figure 1 shows how the spread of these rates observed in 1960 has diminished over time, approaching very similar values for all EU countries in 2024.

In the Eurostat population projections, partial convergence is modelled by setting a convergence value for fertility, mortality and migration outside the horizon covered by population projections. For each country, fertility, mortality and migration assumptions are derived by interpolating the country-specific trajectory at the beginning of the projection with this convergence value outside the projection horizon. By design, this implies that values for all countries will converge partially, but never fully, during the projection horizon. The speed of convergence is controlled by the interpolation function chosen, the choice of introducing a mid-term year or not, and the distance between the final year of projections and the convergence year outside the projection horizon.  How partial convergence for each of the driver of population change is modelled, is explained in each section discussing the relevant model.

=== EUROPOP2025 ===

EUROPOP2025 refers to the national population projections Eurostat published in April 2025 for all the EU and EFTA countries (with the exception of Liechtenstein). The time horizon spans from the year 2025 (also called the base year of the projections) to 2100. 
The data used in EUROPOP2025 are mostly official statistics that the NSIs provided to Eurostat. Some are from the latest regular Eurostat demographic data collection, which were sent by the countries in December 2025 and disseminated by Eurostat in early 2026 in the Eurostat public database. These data refer to events that occurred in 2024 and to the population at the end of the period (i.e. on 1 January 2025). These were the latest detailed data available to Eurostat when the projections were made. On a voluntary basis, total numbers of live births and deaths as well as migration flows referring to 2025 have also been collected as special input for the projections. However, considering that they are not always entirely based on recorded data and that they are further elaborated before being used, they are described below in the section on assumptions.

====Assumptions for fertility====

The total fertility rate (TFR) is a major determinant of population growth. It refers to the average number of children women would bear during their reproductive years if they had the same probability of having a child at each age as observed in the current time period. This is not the same as a measure of the number of births a cohort of women actually has once they have reached the end of their child-bearing years. This is referred to as Completed Cohort Fertility. The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) and Completed Cohort Fertility (CCF) each have distinct strengths and limitations. TFR is a timely, year-to-year indicator of fertility trends, making it useful for monitoring short-term changes and informing immediate policy decisions. However, it is highly sensitive to the timing of births–especially postponement–which can distort the true level of fertility by underestimating eventual childbearing. In contrast, CCF offers a more accurate and stable measure of actual reproductive outcomes by tracking real cohorts through their full childbearing years. While it avoids the tempo distortions that affect TFR, its main limitation is that it is only available with a significant time lag, limiting its relevance for understanding current behaviors or conditions significantly. As such, TFR is better for current diagnostics, whereas CCF is more suited for evaluating long-term fertility outcomes. TFR is generally used in population projections because it reflects the fertility patterns of all reproductive-age women in a given year, allowing to estimate future births without waiting for cohorts to complete their fertility. Eurostat’s assumptions on fertility are formulated based on past observed TFR for each country.

Since 2001, Eurostat publishes EU averages of TFR. The observed value has been relatively stable around 1.5, reaching highs of 1.57 in 2010 and 2016. Since 2016, the TFR has steadily declined, though at a slow pace until about 2021, after which the rate has plummeted to 1.34 in 2024, an al-time low. During these years, total fertility rates have fallen in almost all EU Member States. More details on current fertility data in the EU and the Member States is available in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Fertility_statistics Statistics Explained article]. Based on these long-term and recent developments, the model to derive fertility assumptions for the EUROPOP2025 round is driven by 2 hypotheses: first, the current, very low fertility rates observed in most EU Member States are at least partially due to the deferment of births. This means that due to individual preferences, as well as economic and political uncertainty, persons delay pregnancy,<ref>Beaujouan, E. (2023). Delayed Fertility as a Driver of Fertility Decline?. In: Schoen, R. (eds) The Demography of Transforming Families. The Springer Series on Demographic Methods and Population Analysis, vol 56. Springer, Cham.</ref> Given the ongoing political and socio-economic situation, further decreases may be possible.  In addition, societal attitudes have shifted, and births at older ages have become more accepted<ref>Lazzari E, Compans MC, Beaujouan E. Change in the perceived reproductive age window and delayed fertility in Europe. Popul Stud (Camb). 2025 Mar;79(1):81-101. doi: 10.1080/00324728.2023.2298678. Epub 2024 Mar 1. </ref>. Thus, some of the births that have not taken place in recent years may  take place later. However, there is evidence that delaying births generally leads to a lower overall fertility rate, particularly in countries where mothers' age at first birth is high. The implications for the EUROPOP2025 round are that there is an expectation of some recovery of TFR on average, but that in the long-run, fertility will remain relatively low. Along the same line, for the distribution of births over the age of the mother made, the assumption of the continuation of the trend of [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Fertility_statistics#Women_in_the_EU_are_becoming_mothers_later_in_life increasing mean age of mother] is implemented 
Assumptions are formulated for the future values of the total fertility rate (TFR), which are then broken down by age-specific fertility rates (ASFR) for each year in the projection horizon. The model combines a country-specific trend extrapolation covering the time period 2025 and 2026, a return to a mid-term value between 2026 and 2035, and the partial convergence assumption from 2036 to 2100.

''Country specific estimates for 2025 and 2026''

At the beginning of the projections period, available monthly live birth time series which cover the first 6 months of 2025 are used to nowcast the number of live births for 2025 and 2026 using seasonal exponential smoothing. These figures are combined with the latest observed population to derive TFR for both years. For countries that deliver the total number of live births for reference year 2025 to Eurostat in a voluntary data collection, the forecasted number for 2025 is calibrated to the observed data, and forecasts for 2026 are re-run. 

''Derivation of and interpolation with mid-term value: 2027-2034''

To model a slight recovery of fertility in the near future, a mid-term value in 2034 is derived by calculating the simple average of the last 5 years of observed TFR data published in the Eurostat database (i.e. the average of TFR from 2020 to 2024 included). TFR values between 2027 and 2034 are derived by simple linear interpolation.

''Partial convergence assumption: 2035-2100 ''

The partial convergence is modelled by assuming a tendency of fertility in all countries to converge towards an ultimate value never reached during the horizon of the projections; this value is set to 1.64 for the EUROPOP2025 round, and its 2 rounds of updates to be published in 2027 and 2028. This value has been derived using the freeze rate method of projecting TFR of the EU member frontrunners in fertility development, defined as the cluster A countries<ref>Lesthaeghe, Ron. “The Second Demographic Transition, 1986–2020: Sub-Replacement Fertility and Rising Cohabitation—a Global Update.” Genus 76, no. 1 (June 9, 2020): 10. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41118-020-00077-4.</ref> <ref>Lesthaeghe, Ron, and Iñaki Permanyer. “European Sub-Replacement Fertility: Trapped or Recovering.” Population Studies Center Research Report, no. 14–822 (2014).</ref>, or the upper branch of the fertility fork<ref>Rindfuss, Ronald R., Minja Kim Choe, and Sarah R. Brauner-Otto. “The Emergence of Two Distinct Fertility Regimes in Economically Advanced Countries.” Population Research and Policy Review 35, no. 3 (June 1, 2016): 287–304. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11113-016-9387-z.</ref>. These are: Ireland, Sweden, France, Denmark, Finland, Belgium and the Netherlands. 
For justification in using the freeze rate method, please see (Bohk-Ewald et al., 2018)<ref>Bohk-Ewald, Christina, Peng Li, and Mikko Myrskylä. “Forecast Accuracy Hardly Improves with Method Complexity When Completing Cohort Fertility.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America 115, no. 37 (September 11, 2018): 9187–92. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1722364115</ref> and (Hilton et al., 2019)<ref>Hilton, Jason, Erengul Dodd, Jonathan J. Forster, Peter W. F. Smith, and Jakub Bijak. “Comparing Fertility Forecasting Methods: How Do Parametric Mixture Models Perform?,” 2019.</ref>. 
TFR values between the mid-term value in 2034 and the end of the projection horizon in 2100 are derived by simple linear interpolation of the mid-term year value, with the convergence value of 1.64 in 2150. Assumptions for the total fertility rate for each country can be seen in Figure 2.

====Assumptions for mortality====

Mortality patterns in 2020 and the following years have been massively impacted by an increase in mortality rates due to the COVID-19 epidemic. The impact has led to drops or stagnation of life expectancy in all European countries, though the timing and extent of this impact was not uniform across all countries<ref>Schöley, J., Aburto, J.M., Kashnitsky, I. et al. Life expectancy changes since COVID-19. Nat Hum Behav 6, 1649–1659 (2022). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-022-01450-3</ref>. Overall, persons in the EU had a life expectancy at birth of 80.1 in 2021, down from 80.4 in 2020 and 81.3 in 2019. In past projections, the assumptions formulated for mortality were based on the idea that in 2022 and 2023 the mortality rates had not completely aligned with levels observed before the epidemic, but that they would fully return to pre-epidemic level by 2024 across the EU.

Given that the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Mortality_and_life_expectancy_statistics life expectancy at birth in 2024] for men and women in the EU has exceeded the 2019 life expectancy , and has reached or exceeded 2019 levels for all but 2 Member States, no specific adjustment to assumptions are made due to the effect of COVID-19.  This means that from 2025 on, age- and sex-specific mortality rates are assumed to partially converge towards a common (sex-specific) mortality profiles, which incorporate some information from previous mortality trends of selected countries. The derivation of these convergence profiles is described in detail in the methodological document that will be made available in the metadata. They differ significantly from common mortality profiles used in previous projection rounds due to the recent slowdown in improvements in mortality of neonates and persons below the age of 20.<ref>Hucko A, Weigel R, Nizamov F, Black M. Child and adolescent mortality in the WHO European Region: Concerning trends requiring urgent action. Public Health Pract (Oxf). 2025 Oct 9</ref>  The interpolation function applied is a simple decay function with an exponent of 1.8.  Age-specific mortality rates for the base year are computed using the average person-years at risk and the average number of deaths over the most recent 5 observed years. The COVID-19 years (2020 and 2021) for ages 26 and above are treated as outliers and excluded. For ages 85 and above, the mortality rates are replaced with estimates from the coherent Kannisto model to ensure plausible old-age trajectory and to prevent divergence between male and female mortality. The log-transformed mortality rates are then smoothed using weighted smoothing splines with a regularisation parameter. Weights are chosen empirically to preserve the characteristic patterns of infant mortality and the young-adult mortality hump. The regularisation parameter is reduced for countries with larger populations, which require less smoothing. The mortality rate at age 0 is not smoothed. Mortality rates at ages with missing or insufficient-quality data are interpolated.
Figures 4a and 4b show, on a logistic scale, the resulting ASMR for each year of the projection horizon. The data for each country can be selected in the drop-down menu. 
The projected life expectancy for men and women shown in Figure 5 for each country is a direct result of the assumptions made for the age-specific mortality rates.
