title: Population and housing census 2021 - population grids
text:
<newarticle pic="Rawpixel.com shutterstock 551117140 RV.jpg"></newarticle> 

<metadescription>EU statistics on population and housing census  in 2021 and population grids</metadescription>

<updatedata>
Data extracted in June 2025

Planned article update: 2030
</updatedata>


<highlight>

<highlight-message>The 1 km² population grid data from the 2021 EU population and housing censuses – initially published in March 2023 - have been updated with final data.</highlight-message>

<highlight-message>As opposed to the provisional data previously released, these updated data include information on several important variables in addition to the population total.</highlight-message>


This article presents harmonised [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Population_grid_cell population grid] 1 km² grid data that are available for the European Union and three EFTA countries. The datasets are based on data collected under the 2021 EU Census Programme. 

The interactive visualization below shows grid data for the total population in 2021.

<embedgraph src="https://ec.europa.eu/assets/estat/E/E4/gisco/website/stat_expl/population_grid/grid_maps/main_map.html?sty=colorCh%22%20allow=%22fullscreen"fullscreen allowfullscreen="true" frameborder="0" height="630px" width="700px"|alt= Interactive map showing the total population in the year 2011 and/or 2021 and the population changes over the ten years in Europe. The population grids are classified within ranges of the population change in number of inhabitants.></embedgraph>

</highlight>


<articlecontent>

<sesection>

=== Background information  ===

The information presented in this article is based on population grids data produced as part of the 2021 population and housing censuses in the EU. 
The grid data consist of statistics that are geographically referenced to a system of square grid cells in a common European reference grid net with Cartesian coordinates. The use of a common European-level grid allows analyses to be undertaken for areas that cross national boundaries.

Traditionally, official statistics are reported in accordance with a hierarchical system of administrative and statistical units ranging from the local to the EU level and usually under the control of an official authority. In the EU, the Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS) is the most important example of such an output system. While this is excellent for accounting purposes, and for reporting to the respective authorities administering services within the territory, it is not suitable for studying causes and effects of many socioeconomic and environmental phenomena, such as flooding, commuting, mobility, leisure time, and urban sprawl to name but a few. 
When studying such phenomena, a system of grids<ref>A system for the coordinate grid was constructed using the Lambert Azimuthal Equal-Area projection based on the European Terrestrial Reference System 1989 (ETRS89-LAEA), which was designated as the European standard under the INSPIRE (Infrastructure for Spatial Information in the European Community) Directive 2007/2/EC. This alignment marked a major step forward, particularly in ensuring the usability of grid data across national borders and enabling seamless pan-European analysis.</ref>  with equal-size cells has many advantages:	
* grid cells all have the same size allowing for easy comparison
* grids are stable over time
* grids can be easily integrated with other scientific data (e.g. meteorological information)
* grid systems can be constructed hierarchically in terms of cell size thus matching the study area and grid cells can be assembled to form areas reflecting a specific purpose and study area (mountain regions, water catchments).


</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Distribution of European population ===

The total population of the EU Member States and 3 EFTA countries considered here was 455,671,735 residents.
Out of the 4 595 749 1 km² grid cells, 1 901 599 were populated, while 2 694 150 grid cells had no resident population. This means that approximately 59 out of every 100 grid cells were uninhabited. Among the inhabited cells, 53 864 had a resident population of just 1 person. 

France holds the largest share of the overall grid area, accounting for approximately 12% of the total grid cells. It is followed by Spain with 11% and Sweden with 10% from all grid cells.
Spain and Sweden have the highest number of uninhabited grid cells, contributing 8.6% and 7.5%  of all uninhabited cells, respectively. In terms of populated cells, Finland alone accounts for more than 5% of inhabited grid cells.

The census population grid data provide insights into the most densely populated areas across Europe. The three 1 km² grid cells with the highest population counts, based on the 2021 population and housing censuses, are in Spain: with 56 034 and 54 044 people in the grid cells respectively and in France with 51 525 people. 		 		 

</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Population density classes ===

A population refers to a group of individuals living within a specific area. The number of these individuals, divided by the surface area that they occupy, determines the population density. Population density is used to describe the location, growth and many other indicators in relation to urbanisation, immigration and population demographics, and is very useful for many policy domains such as ecology, epidemiology and infrastructure. It is therefore important to keep track of population density and its changes for small areas, using geographically detailed population data.

[[Image: Population distribution by density classes, 2021.png| Table 1: Population distribution by density classes, 2021|thumb|centre|600px|alt= Table 1:Population distribution by density classes. Table is showing population distribution by density classes in 2021.]]



According to the 2021 population grid data, the population is distributed unevenly by density class across the 1,901,599 populated 1 km² grid cells. Based on population density, around 64.5% of the population in the EU and EFTA countries lives in grid cells with at least 1,000 people.
Although the densest grid class (≥5,000 people) represents about 0.7% of populated grid cells, it houses over 124 million people, accounting for more than 27% of the total population.
In contrast, the largest number of populated grid cells — 762,201, or 40% — belong to the 2–19 people per cell category accommodating 1.4% of the population. This highlights the vast spatial spread of low-density areas.
Low-density cells (fewer than 100 people) make up over 71% of all populated grid cells but house about 13% of the population.
Grid cells with only 1 resident making 2.8% of all populated cells (Table 1). 

The following animation visualises population in the EU by 25 km². 
A glimpse at the distribution of the population over such squares reveals that 38% of them have only 1 to 500 people as residents, while the most densely populated areas (more than 10,000 people per a 25 km² make up only about 5% of the total.

<embedgraph src="https://ec.europa.eu/assets/estat/E/E4/gisco/website/stat_expl/population_grid/regl_animation/" frameborder="0" height="430px" width="730px"|alt= Animated vertical bar chart and map showing population number of inhabitants per 25 km² area. The animation emphasises how similar data can be interpreted.></embedgraph>


</sesection>
<sesection>
=== Population of European capitals ===

[[Image: Population of capital cities in the EU, 2021 Based on data presented for the population grids.png|Table 2: Population of capital cities in the EU, 2021 |thumb|centre|500px|alt= Table is showing population of capital cities in the EU, for the year 2021.]]


The population grid is used to produce the grid cell classification to define cells that belong to an urban centre. By definition, a city is a [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Local_administrative_unit_(LAU) local administrative unit] or a group of local administrative units where a majority of the population lives in an urban centre of at least 50,000 inhabitants. Examples of local administrative units include a municipality or a commune. A coherent and harmonised methodology that delineates cities is the basis of the production of comparable datasets. This basis is laid down in Commission Regulation (EU) No 2019/1130 on the uniform conditions for the harmonised application of territorial typologies.

It is common that capital cities include a single urban centre located in a single local administrative unit with very high population. Some capital cities can contain more than 1 urban centre; or 1 urban centre that covers two different parts of the city, as in the case of Budapest. Moreover, some capitals have outgrown their central local administrative unit, such as Athens, Copenhagen, Paris or Valletta.

According to the population grid data from the 2021 population and housing census, the total capital city population in the EU was 48,896,347, which is close to 11% of the total EU population enumerated in 2021. More than 20% of the total capital city population lived in the biggest capital city, Paris. The second largest capital is Madrid with half the population of Paris. The smallest capital city, Luxembourg, has a population of only about 1.3% of the population of the biggest capital city (Table 2).

The map below allows the user to zoom in on different capital cities by selecting them from the drop-down menu at the top left.

<embedgraph src="https://ec.europa.eu/assets/estat/E/E4/gisco/website/stat_expl/population_grid/grid_maps/capitals.html" allow="fullscreen" allowfullscreen="true" frameborder="0" height="630px" width="700px"|alt= Interactive map showing the population for the year 2021 by capital cities in Europe. The population grids are classified within ranges of the number of inhabitants.></embedgraph>


The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Degree_of_urbanisation degree of urbanisation] is a classification of the character of an area using 1 km² grid cells, according to their population density, population size and contiguity (neighbouring cells). The latest update of the classification is based on the 2021 population census grids. Based on the share of local population living in urban clusters and in [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Urban_centre urban centres], local administrative units are classified into three types of area

*[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:City Cities] (densely populated areas)
*[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Town_or_suburb Towns and suburbs] (intermediate density areas)
*[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Rural_area Rural areas] (thinly populated areas)

The map below visualises the degree of urbanisation by providing a view on urban and rural areas.



<embedgraph src="https://ec.europa.eu/assets/estat/E/E4/gisco/website/stat_expl/population_grid/grid_maps/degurba.html" allow="fullscreen" allowfullscreen="true" frameborder="0" height="630px" width="700px"|alt= Interactive map showing degree of urbanisation in Europe for the year 2021. The map grids are classified based on ranges for city, town, suburb, village, dispersed rural and mostly uninhabited.></embedgraph>



</sesection>


<datadetails>
=== Source data for tables and figures ===

{{Template:Excel|filename=Population distribution on grids in 2021.xlsx|title=Population distribution on grids}}

=== Data sources ===

The data source used to produce population grids was the 2021 population and housing census. The sources for census data differ between countries and census rounds. Four main census approaches according to the Art. 4 of Regulation (EC) No 763/2008, were applied by countries in 2021: traditional, register based, rolling and combined census.
Grid data for Iceland is not available and grid data from France does not include ''Régions Ultrapériphériques Françaises''.
Eurostat classifies the values on the grid cells as final. The data to be provided on 1 km² grid from the 2021 population and housing census is laid down in Regulation (EU) 1799/2018 and is as follows: with a deadline of 31 December 2022 for the total population on grids, and with a deadline of 31 March 2024
* sex (males, females)
* age (under 15, 15 to 64, 65 and over)
* employed persons(voluntary bases, not provided by Germany and France)
* place of birth (in the reporting country, in another EU country, outside the EU)
* usual residence 12 months before the census date (unchanged, within the reporting country, outside of the reporting country)

The census  grid dataset is referenced to a common 1 km² reference grid, that is defined by the INSPIRE framework, more specifically by Regulation (EU) No 1089/2010  that specifies the grid to be used (the ETRS89-LAEA coordinate reference system). The geo-referenced population dataset from the 2021 population and housing censuses in the EU can be accessed at the Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/gisco/geodata/population-distribution/population-grids GISCO website].

=== Methodology ===

To create population grids for the 2021 population and housing census round, 30 countries in the European Statistical System applied mostly the aggregation method. As described in the Statistics Explained article on [[Population_grids|Population grids]], there are usually three methodology types that are used to attribute a number of inhabitants to each square kilometre cell:

'''Aggregation method''':
Grids are produced by aggregating geo-referenced micro data (also called bottom-up approach). This method requires the availability of data that has been geocoded to a geographical location, followed by the aggregation into the square kilometre. This was the method used by 25 Member States and three EFTA countries (Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia, Germany, Denmark, Estonia, Ireland, Spain, Italy, Croatia, Hungary, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland, Sweden, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland).

'''Disaggregation method''':
In the absence of geocoded micro data this method produces grids, using statistical data for the lowest available administrative/territorial units in combination with auxiliary spatial data (also called top-down approach). Data on land use and land cover is used to estimate the population within a particular administrative region into the square kilometre cells of that region. None of the Member States used this method for the 2021 population and housing census.

'''Hybrid method''':
The hybrid method combines aggregation and disaggregation techniques and represents a compromise between accuracy and availability of data. The aim is to maximise the quality of the data over disaggregation alone, e.g. for different parts of a country. The term hybrid could also refer to the source data, meaning a combination of different data sources with the aim of establishing a geocoded framework. The hybrid method was used by two Member States (Greece and France).

Population census data at a 1 km² grid level have the same scale, the same resolution and the same delineation across countries, in order to allow easy combinations to be used in cross-cutting comparable analysis. 
Population grid data on totals show the estimated number of people residing in each grid cell and allows for a visualisation of the residential distribution of the European population.
All grid cells have an identification according to the INSPIRE specification, according to the ETRS89-LAEA coordinate reference system mentioned above.

The population grid data from the 2021 population and housing census contains the total population at the place of usual residence.
Some countries chose to apply various statistical disclose control (SDC) methods to protect the grid data. Information on the application of SDC methods has been supplied by all countries in the national metadata files.

Land surface area information was calculated for seven countries (Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, France, the Netherlands, Romania and Slovakia), where more precise geographical information than 1ha was not available at national level. The land surface parameters for these countries are based on the CORINE dataset (minimum mapping unit 25ha) and the EBM administrative boundaries (Map scale 1:100 000).

For the current release of total population grids, the following set of controls, checks and improvements were applied:

* Revision of changes compared to provisional 2021 data in the population, land surface, flags values; 
* Harmonisation of coastlines and border areas; 
* Revision of unpopulated units.

</datadetails>

<context>
=== Context  ===

The dissemination of Union-wide harmonised census topics on a constant area grid, in particular on a 1 km² grid, is a key European statistical output for evidence-based policymaking. The collection of geocoded population data addresses a common need across the Union for reliable, and comparable information on population distribution with sufficient spatial resolution, founded on harmonised output requirements and intended for pan-European regional policymaking. 
As a result, harmonised, spatially resolved demographic information across the Union collected and disseminated; 1 dataset per Member State was collected, containing selected topics of the 2021 population and housing census geocoded to a 1 km²  grid. 
To achieve comparable harmonised outputs across the Union, a Union-wide constant area grid consisting of 1 km² cells was determined. 
The specific topics and their breakdowns as well as the detailed programme to be disseminated on this 1 km² grid was established by a temporary direct statistical action. 
The total population in the grid cells was disseminated in 2023, 2024 and updated in 2025.



</context>
</articlecontent>

title: Preliminary GDP flash estimate in 30 days for Europe/bg
text:
<pdftheme>2</pdftheme>
=Предварителни експресни оценки на БВП на Европа за 30 дни=

<highlight title=false>
От 29 април 2016 г. нататък [[Glossary:Eurostat|Евростат]] ще публикува предварителни експресни оценки на тримесечните данни за [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|БВП]] на [[Glossary:Euro_area|еврозоната (ЕЗ)]] и [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|Европейския съюз (ЕС)]] около 30 дни след края на съответното тримесечие (t+30). Това по-ранно публикуване е постижение на [[Glossary:European_statistical_system_(ESS)|Европейската статистическа система]], тъй като държавите членки ще предоставят на Евростат националните си оценки две седмици по-рано в сравнение с предишната практика.

Методологията в основни линии остава същата като досега прилаганата методология за експресните оценки на БВП, които се публикуват 45 дни след края на съответното тримесечие (t+45)<ref>Повече информация има на тази  [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/24987/725066/Estimating_GDP_flashes.pdf/7482fff6-a662-4b77-9877-f61ed519c5f5 връзка.] </ref>. Основната разлика е използването на по-ранни предварителни оценки на държавите. Поради по-ранния срок често данните за третия месец от тримесечието трябва (поне отчасти) да са изчислени приблизително от държавите членки.
</highlight>

<articlecontent>
<sesection>
===Как се изготвят предварителните експресни оценки?===

Накратко, по-голямата част от държавите — членки на ЕС, предават на Евростат оценките си за прираст на БВП един ден преди договорения срок за публикуване. Тази група включва държавите членки, които вече публикуват оценките си след t+30 дни, както и няколко държави членки, които предоставят на Евростат поверителни оценки. След това Евростат сумира темповете на тримесечния прираст на БВП на държавите, като използва теглото на държавите в годишния БВП, за да получи оценките за темповете на прираст на БВП на ЕС и еврозоната. 

Решението за публикуване след t+30 на експресните оценки на БВП на ЕЗ/ЕС се основава на резултатите от пилотна фаза за тримесечията от периода 2012 г. — 2015 г. При последните пробни оценки за четвъртото тримесечие на 2015 г. покритието на държавите достигна 91 % от БВП на [[Glossary:EU-28|ЕС-28]] и 94 % от БВП на [[Glossary:EA-19|ЕЗ-19]].
</sesection>

<sesection>
===Надеждни ли са тези предварителни оценки?===

Тъй като експресните оценки са готови по-рано от традиционните, е налице компромисно решение по отношение на актуалността и точността. Въз основа на 16-те пробни оценки очакваната обичайна ревизия при t+45 за темповете на прираст на БВП, публикувани при t+30 (закръглени до един знак след десетичната запетая), би била -0,1, 0,0 или +0,1 процентни пункта за еврозоната и ЕС. При внезапна драматична промяна в икономическото развитие, като тази през второто тримесечие на 2008 г. поради финансовата криза, могат да се очакват по-големи ревизии.

Изпробвани спрямо предварително зададени критерии за качество, очакваните ревизии отговориха на изискванията<ref>Вж. статистическия работен документ на Евростат „Експресни оценки на БВП на еврозоната и Европейския съюз за 30 дни“, който (ще) се публикува на 29 април 2016 г.  [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/national-accounts/methodology/european-accounts/estimation-european-main-aggregates на уебсайта] на  Евростат.</ref> . На фигура 1 по-долу са дадени разликите в темповете на прираст (незакръглени) при t+30 (пробни оценки), t+45 и t+65 дни за периода от първото тримесечие на 2012 г. до четвъртото тримесечие на 2015 г. На горната графика са дадени темповете на прираст за ЕЗ, а на долната — за ЕС.

title: Population statistics at regional level
text:
Eurostat regional yearbook; 2026 edition; flagship publication; EU; regional statistics; NUTS; population; demography; population structure; median age; population change; net migration; fertility; childbirth Data extracted in March and April 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 This article forms part of the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026]'', an annual [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications flagship publication]. It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the [[Glossary:EU|EU]], [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate]] countries. A [[Regional_yearbook_introduction#A_short_reading_guide|short reading guide]] is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps. On 1 January 2025, Mayotte – an outermost region of France – had the highest young-age dependency ratio in the EU (123.3%); the Belgian coastal region of Arr. Veurne had the highest old-age dependency ratio (75.1%). At the start of 2025, the highest regional shares of working-age people were observed in the Danish capital region of Byen København and the Spanish island region of Eivissa y Formentera, each with a share of 68.9%.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:Compet_icon_RYB2026_small.png|left]]
[[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH01_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/34dce455-95d3-43bf-9e6c-bb12eda40a65?lang=en demo_r_pjangrp3])|alt=An infographic showing the NUTS level 3 regions in the EU with the highest shares of younger and older people. Data are shown for three population pyramids with information for: Mayotte in France that had the highest young-age dependency ratio; the EU as a whole; Arrondissement Veurne in Belgium that had the highest old-age dependency ratio. Data are shown for 5-year age classes by sex as a percentage of the total population on 1 January 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Population events such as births, deaths and migratory flows shape demographic changes over time to impact the structure of the EU’s population. Demographic developments are also impacted by irregular shocks, such as the COVID-19 crisis, Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine or more recent developments in Iran and the wider region. On 1 January 2025, there were 450.6 million people living in the EU. During the course of 2024, the EU’s [[Glossary:Population|population]] increased by 1.3 million (up 0.3%). This rise resulted exclusively from [[Glossary:Migration|migratory]] flows, as [[Glossary:Natural_population_change|natural population change]] was negative, with 1.3 million more [[Glossary:Death|deaths]] than [[Glossary:Birth|births]]. [[Glossary:Migration|Net migration]] – the difference between the number of immigrants and emigrants, after statistical adjustments – amounted to 2.4 million people across the EU. This total reflects, among other factors, migrants moving for work, family reunification or international protection (including the movement of displaced people, for example, from Ukraine). The [[Glossary:Population_pyramid|population pyramids]] shown in the infographic above highlight the considerable difference in age structures across [[Glossary:Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)|NUTS]] level 3 regions. On 1 January 2025, the French outermost region of Mayotte had the highest young-age dependency ratio in the EU, while the Belgian coastal region of Arr. Veurne recorded the highest old-age dependency ratio. To illustrate the contrast in age structures: *15.7% of Mayotte’s population was aged under 5, compared with 3.1% in Arr. Veurne *36.7% of Arr. Veurne’s population was aged 65 or more, compared with 2.7% in Mayotte. ===Population structure === Demographic developments across the EU are far from uniform, with considerable variations both between and within individual countries. The EU’s population structure is evolving as a result of several different factors, including population ageing, changing fertility and mortality patterns, and migration flows. Increased mobility – particularly among younger people – is also reshaping where people live, as individuals move in search of education, employment and improved living conditions. As a result, population change is unevenly distributed, contributing to shifting regional dynamics and altering the balance between different types of territories. The EU’s population distribution spans various settlement types, each characterised by distinct demographic and economic features, including: *major urban areas that tend to attract younger populations, with a high share of people living alone, relatively high living costs, diverse educational opportunities and dynamic labour markets *commuter belts/suburban areas, which are often populated by families *former industrial heartlands, characterised by economic decline, lower living costs, relatively high levels of unemployment, poverty and social exclusion *coastal and countryside locations, some of which are viewed as retirement locations for relatively affluent pensioners *other rural and remote regions which frequently exhibit declining population numbers, ageing populations, limited job opportunities and lower access to services. The [[Glossary:Median age|median age]] is an indicator that helps summarise the pace at which population structures have changed. During the last 2 decades, the median age of the EU population increased 5.3 years, up from 39.6 years on 1 January 2005 to 44.9 years by 1 January 2025. The regional distribution of median ages is moderately skewed. As of 1 January 2025, 745 NUTS level 3 regions had a median age above the EU average, 14 had a value that was the same as the EU (44.9 years), while 406 regions were below this level. *At the upper end of the distribution, 191 regions had a median age of at least 50.0 years. A relatively large number were located in Germany (75 regions), predominantly in the eastern part of the country, and in Italy (47 regions). The remaining regions with similarly high median ages were mainly found in Bulgaria, Greece, France (13 regions each), Portugal (10 regions) and Spain (9 regions). *At the lower end of the distribution, 2 outermost regions of France had, by far, the lowest median ages in the EU. There were also relatively low median ages recorded in a number of predominantly urban regions (including capital regions and regions that border/surround their capital). '''''At the start of 2025, rural regions recorded some of the highest median ages …''''' '''Map 1''' highlights those regions with the highest and lowest median ages, as of 1 January 2025. There were 7 regions in the EU that reported a median age above 55.0 years: *Evrytania (57.8 years), a mountainous region in central Greece *Arr. Veurne (57.2 years), a rural/coastal region in north-western Belgium *Alto Tâmega e Barroso (56.6 years), a mountainous region in northern Portugal *the eastern German regions of Suhl Kreisfreie Stadt, Spree-Neiße, Mansfeld-Südharz and Greiz (55.1 to 56.1 years). '''''… while some of the lowest median ages were in and around capital cities''''' Capital regions often exert a considerable pull on inter-regional and international migrants, as they tend to provide a diverse range of educational and employment opportunities. This process can lead to a shift in population structures, with younger people accounting for a growing share of the population in predominantly urban regions; over time, this pattern may self-reinforce, insofar as populations with younger age structures are more likely to have relatively high birth rates. As of 1 January 2025, the French outermost regions of Mayotte and Guyane had the lowest median ages in the EU (18.1 years and 27.5 years, respectively). This reflects their relatively young population structures and high fertility rates. Beyond these outermost regions and the Spanish autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla, some of the lowest median ages were recorded in: *capital regions, including the Danish capital of Byen København (34.2 years), the Belgian capital of Arr. de Bruxelles-Capitale/Arr. Brussel-Hoofdstad (36.1 years), the Dutch capital of Groot-Amsterdam and the Irish capital of Dublin (both 38.2 years) *regions bordering or surrounding capitals, such as Seine-Saint-Denis (36.1 years), Val-d’Oise (37.6 years) and Essonne (38.2 years) in France *other predominantly urban regions that are home to renowned academic institutions, diverse populations and dynamic labour markets, like Heidelburg (35.8 years), Freiburg im Breisgau (37.9 years) and Darmstadt (38.0 years) in Germany. Map 1: Median age
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a866ffd3-1669-40bf-90f4-c91699bcbc4c?lang=en demo_r_pjanind3] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9e29327c-1a2a-4d07-aa5c-d818749f70fd?lang=en demo_r_pjanind]) [[Image:Median age (years, by NUTS 3 regions, 1 January 2025)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Median age
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a866ffd3-1669-40bf-90f4-c91699bcbc4c?lang=en demo_r_pjanind3] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9e29327c-1a2a-4d07-aa5c-d818749f70fd?lang=en demo_r_pjanind])]] '''''As of 1 January 2025, the Danish capital region of Byen København and the Spanish island region of Eivissa y Formentera had the highest shares of working-age people in the EU''''' Europe is experiencing population ageing, reflected in economic and social pressures arising from low birth rates, a shrinking workforce and a growing share of retirees (driven in part by increased longevity). As this demographic shift progresses, the size, productivity and participation of the working-age population become increasingly critical. This is evident in key policy areas such as the sustainability of pension systems, the financing of healthcare provision and the maintenance of labour market stability. Taken together, these dynamics underline the central role of working-age people in supporting long-term economic and social resilience. For the purpose of this publication, the working-age population is defined as individuals aged 20 to 64. During the past 2 decades, the EU’s age dependency ratio – which shows the number of ‘dependents’ (people aged under 20 and people aged 65 or over) relative to the working-age population – has increased rapidly. On 1 January 2005, it stood at 63.4%, meaning there were about 1.6 working-age adults for every dependent. By 1 January 2025, this ratio had risen to 71.6%, meaning there were about 1.4 working-age adults for every dependent, as the share of the working-age population fell to 58.3% of the total. As of 1 January 2025, there were 39 NUTS level 3 regions where the share of the working-age population was at least 63.0%. As shown by the darkest shade in '''Map 2''', this group was largely concentrated in Germany (22 regions), while also including a number of island regions in Spain, as well as several capital regions and regions in close proximity to them. Apart from the Spanish islands, these 39 regions were often predominantly urban, reflecting the concentration of education and employment opportunities in major population centres. At the top end of the distribution, more than two thirds of the population were of working age in: *the Danish capital region of Byen København (68.9%) *3 island regions of Spain – Eivissa y Formentera (68.9%), Fuerteventura (68.3%) and Lanzarote (67.3%). As of 1 January 2025, there were 189 NUTS level 3 regions in the EU where the working-age population accounted for less than 55.0% of the total population. Some of the lowest shares of working-age people were found in predominantly rural regions, including inland Portugal, much of rural France, as well as most of eastern Germany and rural areas in Bulgaria, Greece and the Nordic EU countries. This pattern may be linked to rural depopulation (particularly in sparsely populated regions), as young adults move to large cities/metropolises, coastal hubs or abroad for work and/or study, leaving behind older populations and thereby reducing the share of the working-age residents. In addition, some predominantly rural regions may experience inward migration of retirees, attracted by lower living costs and perceived advantages such as less congestion, noise and crime, which further increases the proportion of older residents. At the bottom end of the distribution, there were 6 regions across the EU where the working-age population accounted for less than half of the total population on 1 January 2025: *the relatively peripheral regions of Bornholm in Denmark and Arr. Veurne in Belgium, characterised by limited job opportunities, outward migration of working-age residents and some inflow of domestic retirees *the sparsely populated regions of Creuse and Lot in south-west France and Etelä-Savo in south-east Finland *the French outermost region of Mayotte, which is an outlier, characterised by a very high fertility rate and a high share of children below working age.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]]
Map 2: Working-age people
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/99cdd154-798a-46be-8510-809d25ac1b66?lang=en demo_r_pjanind3] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/760804d6-a1fa-46b2-a950-b2b7b83f0a54?lang=en demo_r_pjanind]) [[Image:Compet_icon_RYB2026_small.png|left]] [[Image:Working-age people (% of total population, by NUTS 3 regions, 1 January 2025)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 2: Working-age people
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/99cdd154-798a-46be-8510-809d25ac1b66?lang=en demo_r_pjanind3] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/760804d6-a1fa-46b2-a950-b2b7b83f0a54?lang=en demo_r_pjanind])]] Across the EU, the population grew, on average, by 0.2% each year during the period from 2014 to 2024. The highest growth rates were observed in Malta, Luxembourg, Ireland and Cyprus, at between 1.2% and 2.7% per year on average. By contrast, population decline was recorded in 9 Baltic, eastern and southern EU countries, with the largest decrease in Bulgaria (down 0.9% per year on average). '''Figure 1''' presents an analysis of population change across NUTS level 3 regions, highlighting those regions with the highest and lowest average growth rates over the period 2014 to 2024. The French outermost region of Mayotte had the fastest growing population, up on average by 3.6% each year during the period under consideration. The only other region to report growth of more than 3.0% each year was Ilfov in Romania (which completely surrounds the capital region of Bucureşti). In several EU countries, the fastest population growth was often recorded in the capital region or a region within close proximity or surrounding the capital. This was the case in: Dublin (Ireland), Uppsala län (Sweden), Wien (Austria), Flevoland (the Netherlands), Byen København (Denmark), Põhja-Eesti (Estonia), Středočeský kraj (Czechia), Helsinki-Uusimaa (Finland), Osrednjeslovenska (Slovenia), Oeste (Portugal), Bratislavský kraj (Slovakia), Vilniaus apskritis (Lithuania), Pest (Hungary), Warszawski zachodni (Poland), Ilfov (Romania), Rīga (Latvia) and Sofia stolitsa (Bulgaria). Of the 1 165 regions for which data are available, a minority (512 regions) experienced a decline in population during the period from 2014 to 2024. The largest decrease was recorded in the Bulgarian capital region of Sofia, where the population fell by an average of 4.1% each year – by far the biggest decline in the EU. The second largest decline was also observed in Bulgaria, in Vidin (down 2.5% each year), followed Vukovarsko-srijemska županija in Croatia (down 2.2% each year). Some EU countries are characterised by pronounced differences in population change across their regions. This typically reflects the influence of capital regions, uneven economic development and/or patterns of internal migration that are not visible when analysing national averages. A closer examination of regional demographic developments shows that Bulgaria, Romania, France and Poland recorded the widest ranges in population change: *in Bulgaria, the strongest growth was recorded in the capital region of Sofia (stolitsa), where the population increased at an annual rate that was 5.0 percentage points higher than in the surrounding region of Sofia *the highest rate of change in Romania was recorded in Ilfov, which surrounds the capital region of Bucureşti; average population growth in this suburban region was 5.0 percentage points higher than in the south-western region of Caraș-Severin *the highest regional growth rate in France – and indeed in the entire EU – was observed in the outermost island region of Mayotte, where annual population growth exceeded that recorded in the eastern region of Haute-Marne by 4.3 percentage points *in Poland, the highest average annual growth rate was recorded in Warszawski zachodni, a suburban region to the west of the capital, while the lowest rate was observed in the eastern region of Chełmsko-zamojski, some 3.1 percentage points lower. [[Image:Average annual rate of population change (%, by NUTS 3 regions, 2014–24)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Average annual rate of population change
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6682d901-4bc8-4c9d-90f4-6fb8f3e8eea1?lang=en demo_r_gind3] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/df05f386-9bab-4d27-9667-7b047e108aba?lang=en demo_gind])|alt=A high-low chart showing information for the average annual rate of population change. Data are shown in percent for the period 2014 to 2024. Data are shown for the regions in each country with the highest and lowest rates, as well as for the national average. Data are shown for level 3 regions in EU, EFTA and candidate countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Maps 3 and 4''' provide a more detailed analysis of regional population developments. Before examining the individual components of population change – namely, natural change and net migration – this section highlights some of the largest increases and decreases in regional populations. The regions of the EU were relatively evenly divided between those recording population growth and those experiencing a decline between 1 January 2014 and 1 January 2025, as the population increased in 653 NUTS level 3 regions, while 512 regions recorded a decrease. '''''Population growth above 20% was largely concentrated in island, peripheral and capital regions''''' There were 7 regions that recorded overall population growth of more than 20.0% between 1 January 2014 to 1 January 2025, with several of these located in peripheral areas. *The highest increase was recorded in the French outermost region of Mayotte, where the population grew 47.2% (an annual average of 3.6%). *A similarly high growth rate was observed in the Romanian region of Ilfov that surrounds the capital region of Bucureşti, its population increased 44.6%. *Both regions that together make up Malta also recorded substantial growth: the main island region of Malta saw its population rise 34.5%, while Gozo and Comino/Għawdex u Kemmuna recorded an increase of 29.6%. *Luxembourg – which forms a single region at this level – saw its population grow 24.1%. *The Irish capital region of Dublin recorded population growth of 21.5%. *The final region to record growth above 20.0% was the Spanish island region of Fuerteventura, with an overall increase of 21.3% during the period under consideration. '''''3 of the 4 EU regions where population declined by more than 20% were located in Bulgaria''''' The largest decreases in population between 1 January 2014 and 1 January 2025 were concentrated in regions across Bulgaria and, to a lesser degree, Croatia. There were 4 regions where the population declined by at least 20.0%. *The most pronounced decrease was recorded in the Bulgarian region of Sofia, which surrounds the capital region, where the population fell by 37.2%. *The north-western Bulgarian region of Vidin also recorded a considerable fall, its population decreasing 24.4%. *In eastern Croatia, the region of Vukovarsko-srijemska županija recorded a population decrease of 21.5%. *The relatively sparsely populated region of Smolyan in southern Bulgarian was the only other region to report a decline of more than 20.0% during the period under consideration; its population fell 21.1%. '''''Madrid recorded the largest absolute population increase, followed by Barcelona and Stockholm''''' Between 1 January 2014 and 1 January 2025, the largest population increases – in absolute terms – were concentrated in a number of predominantly urban regions, many of which were capital regions. *The Spanish capital region of Madrid recorded, by far, the largest increase, with its population rising by 741 300 people. The second largest increase was also recorded in Spain, as the population of Barcelona grew by 500 200 during the period under consideration. *There was relatively large gap to the Swedish capital region of Stockholm, which recorded the third highest increase (up 310 300). *There were 3 other regions that recorded population growth of more than 250 000 people: the Irish capital region of Dublin (up 274 900), the German capital region of Berlin (up 263 400) and the Austrian capital region of Wien (up 261 500). '''''Population declines of more than 50 000 people were mainly concentrated in eastern EU regions, while the largest falls were recorded in predominantly urban regions such as Bucureşti, Paris, Sofia and Napoli''''' There were 28 regions across the EU where the population fell – in absolute terms – by more than 50 000 people between 1 January 2014 and 1 January 2025. *Most of these regions were located in eastern EU countries: **Poland (16 regions) **Romania (5 regions) **as well as single regions from each of Bulgaria and Hungary. *There were also relatively large falls in: **Italy (3 regions) **France (a single region) **Latvia (also a single region). *Within this group of 28 regions, there were 4 predominantly urban regions that recorded the largest declines, with their populations falling by more than 100 000 people: **the Romanian capital region of Bucureşti (down 156 000) **the French capital region of Paris (down 154 900) **the Bulgarian region of Sofia, which surrounds the capital (down 132 900) **the southern Italian region of Napoli (down 114 600). '''''There were relatively few regions in the EU where the population grew as a result of natural change between 2014 and 2024''''' The EU recorded a crude rate of natural population change of -1.6‰ over the period from 1 January 2014 to 1 January 2025. Overall, negative rates of natural change were widespread across the EU, with more than 4 out of every 5 NUTS level 3 regions (963 out of the 1 165 for which data are available, or 82.7%) recording a negative rate during the period under consideration. Positive crude rates of natural population change were limited to a small number of EU countries: every region in Ireland recorded a positive rate, as did both regions in Malta, alongside Cyprus and Luxembourg. By contrast, negative rates of natural population change were widespread, with several EU countries recording declines across every region. This was the case in Bulgaria, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania and Hungary. A similar pattern was observed in Italy, where Bolzano-Bozen was the only region to record a positive rate. Negative crude rates of natural population change indicate that deaths exceeded births over the period from 1 January 2014 to 1 January 2025. In several regions, this imbalance was particularly pronounced, with persistently low rates of natural change, reflecting ageing populations and relatively low fertility levels. There were several clusters of regions where the crude rate of natural population change reflected a decrease below 10‰, see '''Map 3''', including: *15 regions in Bulgaria, concentrated in the north *6 regions in eastern Germany *4 interior regions of Portugal *2 regions in the north-western Spain *2 regions in northern Greece *2 easternmost regions in the Baltic countries of Latvia and Lithuania *single regions in central France, western Croatia and southern Romania. Map 3: Crude rate of natural population change
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6682d901-4bc8-4c9d-90f4-6fb8f3e8eea1?lang=en demo_r_gind3] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/df05f386-9bab-4d27-9667-7b047e108aba?lang=en demo_gind]) [[Image:Crude rate of natural population change (‰, by NUTS 3 regions, 2014–24)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 3: Crude rate of natural population change
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6682d901-4bc8-4c9d-90f4-6fb8f3e8eea1?lang=en demo_r_gind3] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/df05f386-9bab-4d27-9667-7b047e108aba?lang=en demo_gind])]] '''''Most Iberian, western and northern EU regions recorded positive population growth from net migration between 2014 and 2024''''' Net migration plays a key role in shaping population change across the EU, often offsetting negative natural population change. That said, the crude rate of net migration varied considerably across EU countries, reflecting differences in economic opportunities, labour market conditions and patterns of internal and international migration. '''Map 4''' illustrates these spatial differences, highlighting regions where net migration made a positive or negative contribution to overall population change.
'''More about the data: measuring net migration''' Note that statistics on net migration and statistical adjustment might be affected by statistical inaccuracies or by methodological differences in the 2 components of this indicator. Besides the difference between inward and outward migration, net migration and statistical adjustment may also cover other changes observed in the population figures between consecutive years that cannot be attributed to births, deaths, immigration or emigration. Crude rates of net migration at regional level capture population movements into and out of a region, and therefore include flows from within the same country, from other EU countries and from non-EU countries. In many regions, a considerable share of inward migration consists of people moving from other parts of the same country, for example for education, employment or retirement reasons. These flows are particularly evident: *in capital and other metropolitan regions, as well as in their neighbouring regions (which may benefit from their proximity to major urban labour markets and comparatively lower housing costs) *in coastal regions, which may be attractive retirement destinations. Elsewhere, net migration may be strongly influenced by international flows. This is particularly relevant for some peripheral regions of the EU, which may act as entry points for non-EU migrants.
The EU recorded a crude rate of net migration and statistical adjustment of 3.4‰ over the period from 1 January 2014 to 1 January 2025. Positive rates of change were widespread across most Iberian, western and northern EU regions. Indeed, more than three quarters of NUTS level 3 regions (892 out of the 1 165 for which data are available, or 76.6%) recorded a positive rate during the period under consideration. There were 73 regions across the EU where the crude rate of net migration and statistical adjustment was at least 10.0‰ between 1 January 2014 and 1 January 2025. The highest numbers of regions were recorded in some of the largest EU countries, including Germany (28 regions), Spain (9 regions) and France (8 regions). *In Germany, the highest rate was recorded in the Barnim, a commuter region located to the north-east of Berlin, where the crude rate of net migration and statistical adjustment stood at 15.2‰. *In Spain, the highest rate was observed in El Hierro, at 15.7‰. This may, at least in part, reflect its role as an initial reception point for some migrant arrivals, rather than long-term settlement. *In France, the highest rate was recorded in Corse-du-Sud, at 13.6‰. Within the group of 73 regions where the crude rate of net migration and statistical adjustment was at least 10.0‰ there were several capital regions with relatively high growth rates: *Malta (25.7‰) *the Czech capital region of Hlavní město Praha (14.7‰) *the Slovak capital of Bratislavský kraj (13.9‰) *the Bulgarian capital of Sofia (stolitsa) (11.4‰) *the Irish capital of Dublin (11.3‰) *the Austrian capital of Wien (11.1‰). There were several clusters of regions that recorded negative crude rates of net migration and statistical adjustment over the period from 1 January 2014 and 1 January 2025. This was the case, for example, in much of northern France, southern Spain, southern Italy and parts of Greece. Negative rates were also widespread across most eastern EU countries, as well as in Latvia and Lithuania. At the lower end of the distribution, there were 3 regions in the EU where the crude rate of net migration and statistical adjustment was lower than -10.0‰, indicating sustained net outflows of population relative to the size of the resident population. This may reflect a combination of internal migration towards other regions within the same country, including nearby regions within commuting distance, as well as outward movement to other EU countries or non-EU countries, often linked to differences in labour market opportunities. In some cases, additional factors such as geographic remoteness or limited local labour market opportunities may also contribute to outward migration. The regions were: *Sofia in Bulgaria (-35.6‰) *Paris in France (-12.0‰) *Smolyan in Bulgaria (-10.5‰). Map 4: Crude rate of net migration
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b2913573-8787-4ef6-a6e1-2527f89a9b31?lang=en demo_r_gind3] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c5d1afdd-e7ee-4926-819b-b58cc97fcc0c?lang=en demo_gind]) [[Image:Crude rate of net migration (‰, by NUTS 3 regions, 2014–24)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 4: Crude rate of net migration
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b2913573-8787-4ef6-a6e1-2527f89a9b31?lang=en demo_r_gind3] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c5d1afdd-e7ee-4926-819b-b58cc97fcc0c?lang=en demo_gind])]] ===Fertility ===
'''More about the data: measuring fertility''' The [[Glossary:Fertility|total fertility rate]] is the average (mean) number of children who would be born to a woman during her lifetime, if she were to spend her childbearing years conforming to the age-specific fertility rates of a given year. The natural replacement rate – the average number of live births per woman required to keep the population size constant in the absence of migration – is estimated to be around 2.10 children per woman for developed countries.
The number of live births across the EU was 5.1 million in 1990. Some 30 years later it had declined to 4.1 million. After a modest rebound in 2021, the downward trend resumed. The decline in births then accelerated in 2022 and 2023, falling 5.1% and 5.4%, respectively, before slowing somewhat to a 3.1% decrease in 2024. The most recent data available indicate that there were 3.6 million live births, representing an overall decrease of 30.2% compared with 1990. In 2024, the EU’s total fertility rate was 1.34 live births per woman; this was the lowest rate recorded since the start of the time series in 2001. Over the last 2 decades, the fertility rate remained consistently below the natural replacement rate of 2.10, fluctuating within the range of 1.34 to 1.57 live births per woman. '''''Several of France’s outermost regions recorded some of the highest fertility rates in the EU''''' '''Map 5''' shows the distribution of total fertility rates across NUTS level 3 regions. In 2024, the regional distribution was somewhat skewed: among the 1 165 regions for which data are available, 439 regions (37.7%) recorded total fertility rates below the EU level, while 714 regions (61.3%) had rates above the EU level; 12 regions had the same fertility rate as the EU average. The highest total fertility rates in the EU were recorded across Bulgaria and France. Relatively high rates (of at least 1.75 live births per woman) were observed in 14 regions from each of Bulgaria and France, 6 regions from Germany (2023 data), 3 regions from Slovenia, 2 regions from each of Hungary, the Netherlands and Romania, as well as single regions from Ireland, Greece, Croatia and Slovakia. By contrast, total fertility rates were particularly low in Spain (most notably in the north-west and certain island regions) and across much of Italy (notably in Sardegna). The lowest rates (less than 1.00 live births per woman) were observed in 16 Spanish regions, 7 Polish regions, 5 Italian regions, 3 Greek regions, as well as 2 regions from each of Germany (2023 data) and Lithuania. A more detailed analysis of the latest regional data for 2024 reveals that: *by far the highest total fertility rates in the EU were observed in the French outermost regions of Mayotte (3.51 live births per woman) and Guyane (3.10 live births per woman), while La Réunion (2.11 live births per woman) also recorded a rate that was slightly above the natural replacement level *the Bulgarian regions of Sliven (2.58 live births per woman) and Yambol (2.42 live births per woman) were the only other regions across the EU to record total fertility rates above the natural replacement level *at the lower end of the distribution, 4 island regions in Spain’s Canarias recorded the lowest total fertility rates in the EU; La Palma had the lowest rate at 0.76 live births per woman, with only slightly higher values in Tenerife, La Gomera and Gran Canaria *leaving aside these Spanish island regions, the next lowest total fertility rates were observed in the sparsely populated Greek regions of Evrytania and Fokida, the Italian island regions of Cagliari and Sud Sardegna, and the north-western Spanish regions of Ourense and Pontevedra *it was relatively common for the lowest total fertility rate within a country to be recorded in the capital region; this was the case for Byen København (Denmark), Põhja-Eesti (Estonia), Dublin (Ireland), Rīga (Latvia), Budapest (Hungary), Malta (Malta) and Groot-Amsterdam (the Netherlands) *otherwise, some of the lowest fertility rates in the EU were typically observed in other large metropolitan regions and in selected regions characterised by a high concentration of students (for example, certain regions in Germany). Map 5: Total fertility rate
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/26b02271-c787-4394-8182-ff844e6d6949?lang=en demo_r_find3] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b9f9daaf-f338-4aaa-ba7d-7ba5f43f7205?lang=en demo_find]) [[Image:Total fertility rate (average number of live births per woman, by NUTS 3 regions, 2024)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 5: Total fertility rate
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/26b02271-c787-4394-8182-ff844e6d6949?lang=en demo_r_find3] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b9f9daaf-f338-4aaa-ba7d-7ba5f43f7205?lang=en demo_find])]] '''''Women in the EU are giving birth later in life''''' A growing proportion of women in the EU are giving birth later in life, which helps explain, at least in part, relatively low fertility levels. This may be linked, among other factors, to: *higher female participation in further education and/or a growing share of women choosing to establish a career before starting a family *lower levels of job security (for example, due to precarious employment) *rising costs for raising children and housing.
'''More about the data: the median age of women at childbirth''' The median age at childbirth is the value that divides all recorded ages of mothers at childbirth into 2 equal halves when they are arranged in ascending order. In other words, half of all births occur to mothers younger than this age and half to mothers older. It is generally considered a more robust indicator of the ‘typical age’ at childbirth, as it is less sensitive to extreme values at either end of the distribution. Eurostat also publishes the mean age of women at childbirth: this is calculated as a weighted average of the mother’s ages at childbirth, using age specific fertility rates as weights. The mean value can be influenced by extreme observations, such as cases where a small number of women give birth at unusually young or older ages, which may shift the average away from the central tendency of the distribution.
Across the EU, the median age of women at childbirth rose from 31.0 to 31.9 years between 2014 and 2024. During this decade, the rise in the median age had a fairly regular pattern of development, with modest annual increases interspersed with occasional years of stability. '''''In 2024, the predominantly urban region of Voreios Tomeas Athinon, located to the north of the Greek capital, recorded the highest median age for mothers at childbirth …''''' '''Figure 2''' shows that in 2024, among NUTS level 3 regions: *some of the highest median ages of mothers at childbirth were observed in southern EU countries, although relatively high values were also recorded in Ireland and Luxembourg *the highest median ages were recorded in and around the Greek capital: Voreios Tomeas Athinon (to the north; 35.7 years), Notios Tomeas Athinon (to the south; 34.7 years) and Kentrikos Tomeas Athinon (the capital region; 34.3 years); a similarly high value was also observed in the Greek island region of Lefkada (34.7 years) *several regions in the northern and north-western Spain also recorded high median ages, including: A Coruña, León (both 34.7 years), Pontevedra (34.5 years), Bizkaia, Valladolid (both 34.3 years), Cantabria, Gipuzkoa (both 34.2 years) and Ourense (34.1 years) *3 regions on the Italian island of Sardegna recorded relatively high median ages – Cagliari (34.7 years), Oristano (34.3 years) and Sud Sardegna (34.2 years) – while the Italian capital region of Roma also recorded a high median age (34.1 years) *the predominantly rural Irish region of West also had a relatively high median age (34.3 years). Across the 25 EU countries for which regional data are available, capital regions consistently recorded median ages of mothers at childbirth that were higher than the national average. There were 14 countries where the capital region had the highest median age within the national territory. This pattern likely reflects a combination of factors, among which, higher housing costs, longer periods spent in education, higher female labour market participation, greater career orientation and consequently delayed family formation. Across all capital regions of EU countries, the median age of mothers at childbirth in 2024 ranged from 31.7 years in Osrednjeslovenska (Slovenia) to 34.3 years in Kentrikos Tomeas Athinon (Greece). Relatively low median ages are broadly associated with earlier entry into family formation, which tends to be more common in regions characterised by, among other factors, lower levels of educational attainment, weaker labour market participation and different socio-economic structures and cultures compared with higher-income or more urbanised parts of the EU. In 2024, there were 11 EU regions where the median age of mothers at childbirth was below 27.0 years. All 11 of these regions were located in Bulgaria (6 regions) or Romania (5 regions). The lowest values were observed in: *the south-eastern Bulgarian regions of Sliven (23.2 years) and Yambol (24.6 years), both of which recorded total fertility rates above the natural replacement level, while a relatively low median age was also observed in the northern Bulgarian region of Lovech (25.7 years) *the southern Romanian regions of Călăraşi (25.7 years) and Ialomiţa (26.0 years). [[Image:Median age of mothers at childbirth (years, by NUTS 3 regions, 2024)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Median age of mothers at childbirth, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/77e86d24-9d90-4800-886a-e51f1a066401?lang=en demo_r_find3] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b423558d-22ae-4a9c-8c09-3c4510de485f?lang=en demo_find])|alt=A high-low chart showing information for the median age of mothers at childbirth. Data are shown in years for 2024. Data are shown for the regions in each country with the highest and lowest median ages, as well as for the national average. Data are shown for level 3 regions in EU, EFTA and candidate countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Source data for figures and maps=== {{Template:Excel|filename=RYB2026 CH01 Population.xlsx|title=Regional population statistics}} ===Data sources=== ==== Regional demographic statistics ==== Eurostat collects a wide range of regional demographic statistics, including data on population numbers and various demographic events which influence the population’s size, structure and specific characteristics. Regional demographic statistics may be used for a wide range of planning, monitoring and evaluating actions, for example, to: *study population ageing and its effects on sustainability and welfare *evaluate the economic impact of demographic change *calculate ratios relative to the size of the population – for example, regional GDP per inhabitant – which is a key measure when allocating [[Glossary:Structural fund|structural funds]] to economically less advantaged regions. Demographic statistics include information on: *the usual resident population, which counts the number of people living in a given area on 1 January (or, in some cases, 31 December of the previous year) *the number of live births *the number of deaths. These statistics are presented for different NUTS levels within the EU, EFTA and candidate countries. '''NUTS level 2''' *Population by sex, age and region of residence *Live births by mother’s age, mother’s year of birth and mother’s region of residence *Deaths by sex, age, year of birth and region of residence *Life table by age and sex *Infant mortality and infant mortality rates '''NUTS level 3''' *Population by sex, 5-year age group and region of residence *Live births by 5-year age group of the mothers and region of residence *Deaths by week, sex, 5-year age group and region of residence *Demographic balance and crude rates (population change, natural change, net migration including statistical adjustment, crude birth and death rates, and crude rates of population change) *Population structure indicators (shares of various population age groups, dependency ratios and median ages) *Fertility indicators (total fertility rate, mean age of woman at childbirth, median age of women at childbirth) *Population density Regional demography statistics are collected in accordance with Article 3 of ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32013R1260 Regulation (EU) No 1260/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 November 2013 on European demographic statistics]'' and the implementing measures laid out in ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32014R0205 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 205/2014 of 4 March 2014]''. Eurostat has collected regional demographic data according to this legal basis since the reference year 2013. Before that date, national statistical offices provided regional demographic data on a voluntary basis. ==== Indicator definitions ==== '''Age dependency ratios''' Age dependency ratios typically compare economically dependent people with those who are not. For the purpose of this chapter, the economically dependent population is defined as the sum of people aged less than 20 and people aged 65 or over; these 2 groups are generally considered to be economically inactive, either because they are probably still in education or because they are probably retired from the labour force. By contrast, the economically productive population consists of people of working age, defined here as those aged 20 to 64. '''Crude rate of natural population change''' Natural population change is the difference between the number of live births and deaths during a given time period (usually 1 year); it can be positive or negative. The crude rate of natural population change is the ratio of natural population change to the average population; the value is expressed per 1 000 inhabitants. '''Crude rate of net migration plus statistical adjustment''' Net migration is the difference between the number of immigrants and the number of emigrants. In the context of the annual demographic balance, Eurostat produces net migration figures by taking the difference between total population change and natural change; this concept is referred to as net migration plus statistical adjustment. The crude rate of net migration plus statistical adjustment is the ratio of net migration plus statistical adjustment to the average population; the value is expressed per 1 000 inhabitants. '''Fertility''' Fertility is the ability to conceive (become pregnant) and give birth to children. The total fertility rate is defined as the mean number of children who would be born to a woman during her lifetime, if she were to spend her childbearing years conforming to the age-specific fertility rates that have been measured in a given year. A birth is defined as the start of life when a child emerges from the body of its mother. The total number of births includes both live births and stillbirths (foetal deaths). A live birth is the birth of a child who shows any sign of life. The number of live births refers to the number of births excluding stillbirths. The median age of women at childbirth is the age that divides the population of mothers at childbirth into 2 numerically equal groups, meaning half of the mothers are younger than the median age and half are older. The median age of women at childbirth tends to be relatively high in developed economies. '''Median age''' The median age is the age that divides a population, ranked by age, into 2 equal-sized groups. '''Population''' For population statistics, Eurostat recommends the use of the ‘usually resident population’ of a given area. The number of inhabitants is compiled for 1 January of the year in question (or, in some cases, on 31 December of the previous year). Countries can also base their population statistics on the most recent census, adjusted by the components of population change since then, or on population registers. The average population during a calendar year is calculated as the arithmetic mean of the population on 1 January of the reference year and of the following year. This measure is used, among other purposes, in the calculation of demographic indicators, such as crude rates per 1 000 people. '''Population change''' Population change is the difference in the size of a population between the end and the beginning of a given time period (usually 1 year). Population change has 2 components: *natural population change (the number of live births minus the number of deaths) *net migration (the number of immigrants minus the number of emigrants) plus statistical adjustments. '''Working-age people''' The share of working-age people in the total population is defined as the number of people aged 20 to 64 as a share of the total population, in percent. ===Context=== Demographic developments across the EU have been influenced by a combination of factors, including advances in medicine and public health, socio-economic transformations, shifting cultural norms, patterns of migration and increasing urbanisation, which have shaped the population’s size, structure and distribution. Policymakers can regulate some of the perceived issues linked to demographic transition through actions that prevent, delay or address demographic imbalances, for example, by introducing measures that impact fertility rates, population ageing and/or the flow of migrants (nationally and internationally). These actions can be direct (for example, vaccination programmes for young children or asylum reception policies for displaced persons) or indirect (for example, tax breaks or social transfers that provide an incentive for people to have (more) children). Prolonged life expectancy represents a considerable social achievement. However, when coupled with historically low fertility rates, it has led to a major change in the structure of the EU’s population, with a growing share of elderly people. These developments may pose a range of societal challenges, with a higher proportion of the population considered as unproductive or inactive (those aged 65 or over), while relatively few younger people enter the labour force. The growing number of very old people in the EU also impacts the sustainability of welfare, health and care systems and may require the development of a broad range of new services to meet the specific demands of an increasingly frail population. Population ageing is already apparent in several EU countries. It manifests itself through labour market shortages for certain occupations and puts the EU’s long-term economic prosperity and competitiveness at risk. Policymakers can alleviate these challenges to some degree through initiatives that encourage, among other actions, more flexible working opportunities, better provision of childcare and prolonged labour market participation by older people. The European Commission has addressed the on-going demographic transition by adopting: *a ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=COM:2021:0050:FIN Green Paper on Ageing – Fostering solidarity and responsibility between generations]'' (COM(2021) 50 final) *''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52021DC0345 A long-term vision for the EU’s rural areas – Towards stronger, connected, resilient and prosperous rural areas by 2040]'' *a Communication on ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52023DC0032 Harnessing talent in Europe’s regions]'' (COM(2023) 32 final) *a Communication on ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52023DC0577 Demographic change in Europe: a toolbox for action]'' (COM(2023) 577 final) *a Communication on the ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52026DC0045 European Asylum and Migration Strategy]'' (COM(2026) 45 final) *a Communication on a ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52026DC0110 Strategy for Intergenerational Fairness]'' (COM(2026) 110 final). In July 2026, the European Commission published a Staff Working Document on ''[https://commission.europa.eu/system/files/2026-07/Demography_Report_2026.pdf Demographic transformation in the EU: understanding change and adapting to its consequences]'' which provided analyses of long-term demographic trends as well as population projections through to 2100. The European Commission addresses the impact of demographic change through a range of policy initiatives: *a [https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/whats-new/newsroom/27-10-2023-harnessing-talent-in-europe-commission-launches-the-demography-toolbox_en demography toolbox] to support EU countries in addressing demographic change *an [https://knowledge4policy.ec.europa.eu/atlas-demography_en atlas of demography] providing territorial and regional indicators *a long-term vision for EU rural areas *a [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/news/european-care-strategy-caregivers-and-care-receivers-2022-09-07_en European care strategy] *a [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/rights-child/eu-strategy-rights-child-and-european-child-guarantee_en strategy on the rights of the child] (including the EU’s child guarantee, measures to combat child sexual abuse and initiatives for a better and safer internet for children) *actions to address loneliness and social isolation in the EU. =Předběžný bleskový odhad HDP za Evropu již 30 dní po skončení čtvrtletí=
<highlight title=false>
Od 29. dubna 2016 bude [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] pravidelně zveřejňovat předběžné bleskové odhady čtvrtletního [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|HDP]] za [[Glossary:Euro_area|eurozónu (EZ)]] a za [[Glossary:EU-28|Evropskou unii (EU)]] přibližně 30 dní po skončení čtvrtletí (t+30). Rychlejší zveřejňování je umožněno díky [[Glossary:European_statistical_system_(ESS)|Evropskému statistickému systému]], v rámci kterého členské státy nyní poskytují Eurostatu své národní odhady o dva týdny dříve.

Metodika do velké míry odpovídá stávající metodice pro bleskové odhady HDP zveřejňované 45 dní po skončení čtvrtletí (t+45)<ref>Další informace získáte kliknutím na tento [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/24987/725066/Estimating_GDP_flashes.pdf/7482fff6-a662-4b77-9877-f61ed519c5f5 odkaz.] </ref> . Hlavní rozdíl spočívá v použití předběžnějších odhadů z jednotlivých zemí. Vzhledem k dřívějšímu termínu musí členské státy údaje za třetí měsíc čtvrtletí mnohdy (alespoň částečně) odhadovat.
</highlight>

<articlecontent>
<sesection>
===Jak se předběžný bleskový odhad sestavuje?===

Většina členských států EU předává Eurostatu své odhady růstu HDP jeden den před dohodnutým datem zveřejnění. Do této skupiny patří ty členské státy, které již nyní zveřejňují své odhady 30 dní po skončení období, a také řada členských států, které předávají Eurostatu důvěrné předběžné údaje. Eurostat poté agreguje mezičtvrtletní tempa růstu použitím váženého ročního HDP jednotlivých zemí, čímž se získají odhady tempa růstu HDP za EU a eurozónu. 

Rozhodnutí začít zveřejňovat bleskové odhady HDP EZ/EU 30 dní po skončení čtvrtletí vychází z výsledků testovací fáze za jednotlivá čtvrtletí v období let 2012–2015. V posledních testovacích odhadech za 4. čtvrtletí 2015 (2015Q4) bylo pro HDP dosaženo 91% pokrytí zemí [[Glossary:EU-28|EU-28]] a 94% pokrytí zemí [[Glossary:EA-19|EZ-19]]. 
</sesection>

<sesection>
===Je předběžný odhad spolehlivý?===

Jelikož jsou bleskové odhady k dispozici dříve než tradiční odhady, jde o kompromis mezi včasností a přesností. Z 16 testovacích odhadů vyplývá, že by očekávaná typická revize tempa růstu HDP zveřejňovaného v termínu t+30 na úrovni přesnosti zveřejňovaných hodnot (tj. se zaokrouhlením na jedno desetinné místo) v čase t+45 představovala –0,1, 0,0 nebo +0,1 procentního bodu za eurozónu i EU. V případě náhlé dramatické změny vývoje ekonomiky, jako tomu bylo v 2. čtvrtletí 2008 v souvislosti s finanční krizí, mohou být revize větší.

Očekávané revize byly úspěšně testovány na základě předem stanovených kritérií kvality<ref>Viz statistický pracovní dokument Eurostatu „Euro area and European Union GDP flash estimates at 30 days“ s datem zveřejnění na [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/national-accounts/methodology/european-accounts/estimation-european-main-aggregates internetových stránkách] Eurostatu dne 29. dubna 2016.</ref> . Na obrázku 1 jsou znázorněny rozdíly v (nezaokrouhlených) tempech růstu zveřejněných 30 dní (t+30) (testovací odhady), 45 dní (t+45) a 65 dní (t+65) po skončení daného čtvrtletí za období 2012Q1–2015Q4. V horním grafu jsou zobrazena tempa růstu EZ a ve spodním grafu tempa růstu EU.

[[Image:The growth rates (in %) of EA (upper graph) and the EU (lower graph) final CZ.png|thumb|center|600px|'''Obrázek 1: Tempo růstu (v %) EZ (horní graf) a EU (spodní graf) v termínech t+30 (test), t+45 a t+65 dní''']]
</sesection>
</articlecontent>

===Tematické sekce===
