title: Preventive health care expenditure statistics
text:
Statistics on healthcare expenditure for prevention. Data for the European Union and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. Data extracted in March 2026. Planned article update: May 2027. EU countries spent €62.8 billion on preventive health care in 2023. Preventive health care expenditure in the EU was equivalent to 0.36% of GDP in 2023. This article forms part of the online publication [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] and, more specifically, is part of the domain of [[Healthcare expenditure statistics - overview|healthcare expenditure statistics]]. It presents key statistics on preventive healthcare expenditure in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] for the reference year 2023. With the release of 2023 data, the data in this article relate to information on preventive healthcare expenditure during the calendar year in which the [[Glossary:World Health Organization (WHO)|World Health Organization (WHO)]] declared the end of the pandemic phase of COVID-19. Preventive healthcare expenditure in the EU was 33.6% lower in current price terms in 2023 than in 2022. Relative to GDP, preventive healthcare expenditure decreased from 0.59% of GDP in 2022 to 0.36% in 2023. This reflects the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the 2022 data, in particular for the category of immunisation programmes (which includes vaccination campaigns). Within the health sector, preventive care involves ‘any measure that aims to avoid or reduce the number or severity of injuries and diseases, their sequelae and complications’ Pomey et al. (2000) in [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf A system of Health Accounts 2011, revised edition] page 100.. This type of care is based on a health promotion strategy that enables people to improve their health by controlling some immediate determinants [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf A System of Health Accounts 2011, revised edition] page 100.. Preventive healthcare includes interventions for both individual and collective consumption. According to the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf/60aa44b0-2738-4c4d-be4b-48b6590be1b0 2011 edition of the system of health accounts (SHA 2011)], preventive healthcare aims to reduce the ‘risks before they generate some effects’ [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf A System of Health Accounts 2011, revised edition] page 100. and to detect diseases as early as possible. Activities aimed at ‘reducing the negative impact of an already established disease or injury by an attempt to avoid worsening and complications and then therapy’ are therefore outside the scope of preventive healthcare [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf A System of Health Accounts 2011, revised edition] page 100.. For some countries, it can be difficult to identify expenditure on preventive healthcare separately from expenditure on curative and rehabilitative care Preventive actions such as check-ups provided during a contact with a general practitioner might be included in expenditure for curative care., leading to an underestimation in this area. ===Preventive healthcare in the EU accounted for 0.36% of GDP in 2023=== '''Relative to GDP, Germany and the Netherlands spent the highest amount on preventive healthcare in 2023''' Current expenditure on preventive healthcare can be analysed in absolute terms (euros), relative to GDP or per inhabitant (see the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d25f69be-2892-4229-a6d7-b518549bd527?lang=en average population]), as presented later in this article. Relative to the size of their economies, Germany and the Netherlands had the highest expenditure on preventive healthcare in 2023 among EU countries, at 0.56% and 0.52%, respectively, of their [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]]. Finland (0.48%) and Austria (0.47%) had the next highest ratios, while the remaining countries had ratios below 0.40% of GDP (see Figure 1 and Table 1). Romania (0.07%) and Malta (0.08%) recorded the lowest ratios and were the only EU countries to allocate less than 0.10% of their GDP to expenditure on preventive healthcare in 2023. [[Image:Current_expenditure_on_preventive_healthcare_relative_to_GDP,_2023_(%)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Current expenditure on preventive healthcare relative to GDP, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (dataset code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/58324fab-0453-4746-af89-c53c88e98e5d?lang=en hlth_sha11_hchp])|alt=A column chart showing current expenditure on preventive healthcare relative to GDP in percent. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In absolute terms, total expenditure on preventive healthcare for all EU countries amounted to €62.8 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] in 2023: *Germany spent €23.6 billion on preventive healthcare, recording, by far, the highest value among EU countries *Italy (€8.3 billion), France (€7.5 billion), the Netherlands (€5.4 billion), Spain (€4.6 billion) and Austria (€2.2 billion) were the only other EU countries to spend more than €2.0 billion on preventive healthcare in 2023 *at the other end of the ranking, Malta (€17.2 million), Cyprus (€38.4 million) and Latvia (€73.3 million) recorded the lowest values across the EU; they were the only EU countries to spend less than €100 million on preventive healthcare in 2023. These levels of expenditure are partly proportional to the size of the population; an analysis of the expenditure per inhabitant can account for differences in the size of the population. [[Image:Current_expenditure_on_preventive_healthcare,_2023_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Current expenditure on preventive healthcare, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (dataset code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6156b743-1ab8-4f27-8b03-0df46c798d16?lang=en hlth_sha11_hchp] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hlth_sha11_hc__custom_15919869/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=3398529f-ea67-4bf7-9fab-1d4c15d0a221&c=1742830743092 hlth_sha11_hc])|alt=A table showing current expenditure on prevent healthcare. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The data are shown in millions of euro, euro per inhabitant, millions of PPS, PPS per inhabitant, as a share of current healthcare expenditure in percent, and relative to GDP in percent. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===There were 10 EU countries that spent more than €100 per inhabitant on preventive healthcare in 2023=== '''With expenditure of €303.9 and €283.5 per inhabitant, respectively, the Netherlands and Germany spent the most relative to their population size''' Taking account of population size, the Netherlands (€303.9 per inhabitant) and Germany (€283.5 per inhabitant) had the highest levels of preventive healthcare expenditure in 2023 among EU countries (see Table 1). At the opposite end of the scale, Romania (€12.2 per inhabitant) and Poland (€24.5 per inhabitant) reported the lowest values per inhabitant. Comparing the highest and lowest values, those of the Netherlands and Romania, shows that preventive healthcare expenditure per inhabitant was approximately 25 times as high in the Netherlands as in Romania. Table 1 also shows the level of expenditure on preventive healthcare measured in [[Glossary:Purchasing_power_standard_(PPS)|purchasing power standards (PPS)]], which take account of the price level differences between countries; these data expressed in relation to the number of inhabitants are also shown in Figure 2. *Among EU countries, Germany had the highest value in absolute terms in 2023, with expenditure on preventive healthcare of 21.7 billion PPS. *Based on the ratio of preventive healthcare expenditure per inhabitant (measured in PPS terms), Germany (260.0 PPS per inhabitant) and the Netherlands (250.9 PPS per inhabitant) spent the most on preventive healthcare in 2023, followed by Austria (208.1 PPS per inhabitant) and Finland (182.3 PPS per inhabitant). *Romania, Malta, Poland and Cyprus were at the other end of the ranking, with expenditure per inhabitant below 50.0 PPS in 2023. Figure 2 shows that EU countries with relatively high levels of expenditure on preventive healthcare per inhabitant in euro terms tended to have lower ratios in PPS terms; the reverse was observed for EU countries with relatively low levels of expenditure. Unsurprisingly therefore, the ratio between the highest and lowest levels of preventive healthcare expenditure per inhabitant when measured in PPS (taking account of price level differences) – based on a comparison between Germany and Romania – was considerably smaller (12 : 1) in 2023 than the ratio in euro terms (25 : 1; as noted earlier). [[Image:Current_expenditure_on_preventive_healthcare_per_inhabitant,_2023_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Current expenditure on preventive healthcare per inhabitant, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (dataset code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/28589e6a-d176-4777-8539-9cabad4d146f?lang=en hlth_sha11_hchp])|alt=A bullet chart showing current expenditure on preventive healthcare per inhabitant. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. Columns are shown for data in euro per inhabitant and markers are shown for data in PPS per inhabitant. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Among EU countries, spending on preventive healthcare ranged between 0.9% and 5.2% of current healthcare expenditure in 2023=== '''The Netherlands, Germany, Croatia, Italy and Finland recorded the highest shares of health expenditure on preventive healthcare''' At 3.7% of current healthcare expenditure across the EU, preventive healthcare was a smaller function within the system of health accounts in 2023 than in 2022 (5.7%) or 2021 (6.2%), but marginally larger than in 2020 (3.6%). In 2023, the share of preventive healthcare expenditure in total health expenditure was highest among EU countries in the Netherlands, Germany, Croatia, Italy and Finland, all with shares between 4.6% and 5.2% – see Figure 3. Austria and Estonia reported the next highest shares, 4.3% and 4.2%, respectively; all other countries reported shares below 3.5%. At the other end of the ranking, 5 EU countries reported shares below 2.0%: Malta (0.9%), Romania (1.3%), Cyprus (1.5%), Poland (1.7%) and Belgium (1.8%). [[Image:Preventive_healthcare_expenditure_as_a_share_of_current_expenditure_on_healthcare,_2023_(%)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Preventive healthcare expenditure as a share of current expenditure on healthcare, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (dataset code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a1e263df-fb56-4b6b-a586-cd1a476e68b1?lang=en hlth_sha11_hchp])|alt=A column chart showing preventive healthcare expenditure as a share of current expenditure on healthcare in percent. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Preventive healthcare mainly financed by government schemes=== '''In Malta, Spain and Denmark, preventive healthcare was almost entirely financed by government schemes in 2023''' '''Healthcare financing schemes''' are a structural component of healthcare financing systems: they are the types of financing arrangements through which people obtain health services [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf A System of Health Accounts 2011, revised edition] page 164.. Figure 4 shows that '''government schemes''' were the main mechanism for financing preventive healthcare in 2023, accounting for 55.6% of expenditure in the EU and more than half of expenditure in 14 EU countries: shares varied among these countries from 59.0% in Hungary to 95.7% in Latvia, 97.5% in Denmark and 100.0% in Malta. In 6 more EU countries, government schemes accounted for a larger share than for any other financing schemes but less than half (between 41.4% and 49.7%) of all preventive healthcare expenditure. '''Compulsory contributory health insurance schemes''' and compulsory medical saving accounts (CMSA), which are generally part of the social security system, were the second largest financing mechanism across the EU in 2023, accounting for a 28.0% share of the EU’s total preventive healthcare expenditure. These mechanisms contributed a majority of the financing of preventive healthcare in Croatia (65.8%), Czechia (64.9%), Slovakia (62.2%) and Lithuania (51.1%), as well as the largest share (but below 50.0%) in Germany, Slovenia and France. In 2023, '''enterprise financing schemes''' accounted for 10.5% of preventive healthcare expenditure in the EU. In 10 EU countries, this share exceeded 10.0%, with the highest shares in Portugal (39.2%) and Poland (27.9%). With an average share of 1.9%, '''household out-of-pocket payments''' did not play a significant role in the financing of preventive healthcare within the EU in 2023. The relative contribution of this means of financing was highest in Cyprus (24.1%), Ireland (12.5%) and the Netherlands (10.6%). [[Image:Expenditure on preventive healthcare analysed by financing scheme, 2023 (%)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Expenditure on preventive healthcare analysed by financing scheme, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (dataset code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7dac16b4-0c8a-4a57-a4ce-5f4741950d20?lang=en hlth_sha11_hchf])|alt=A stacked column chart showing the share of expenditure on preventive healthcare by financing scheme as a percentage of all preventative healthcare expenditure. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The stacks for each country sum to 100% and present the shares for government schemes, compulsory contributory health insurance schemes, enterprise financing schemes, household out-of-pocket payments, and other financing schemes. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Preventive healthcare mainly delivered by providers of preventive health care in 2023=== Healthcare providers are ‘organisations and actors that deliver healthcare goods and services as their primary activity, as well as those for which healthcare provision is only one among a number of activities. They vary in their legal, accounting, organisational and operating structures’ [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf A System of Health Accounts 2011, revised edition] page 122.. '''Providers of preventive care accounted for more than half of preventive healthcare expenditure in 10 EU countries in 2023''' Figure 5 shows that there were 2 main providers of preventive healthcare in the EU. *'''Providers of preventive care''', which include ‘organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population as a whole, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity’ [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf A System of Health Accounts 2011, revised edition] page 145.. Across the EU, providers of preventive care accounted for close to an absolute majority of current expenditure on preventive care in 2023 (46.5%). *'''Providers of ambulatory healthcare''', defined in the system of health accounts as ‘establishments that are primarily engaged in providing healthcare services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services’ [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf A System of Health Accounts 2011, revised edition] page 135.. Providers of ambulatory healthcare accounted for more than a third of the EU’s current expenditure on preventive healthcare in 2023 (36.3%). In 2023, there were 10 EU countries where '''providers of preventive care''' accounted for an absolute majority of current expenditure on preventive healthcare and in 4 more these providers accounted for less than half of all expenditure but for more than any other type of provider. The largest shares of expenditure for providers of preventive care were observed in Slovakia (94.6%), Malta (73.0%) and Italy (71.5%). '''Providers of ambulatory healthcare''' accounted for an absolute majority of current expenditure on preventive healthcare in 4 EU countries and in 7 more these providers accounted for less than half of the total but for more than any other type of provider. The largest share of expenditure recorded for providers of ambulatory healthcare was observed in Finland (89.1%). In 2 EU countries, the largest provider of preventive healthcare in 2023 was neither of the 2 principal types of providers – preventative care or ambulatory healthcare – which dominated across the EU as a whole. *The '''rest of the economy''' category accounted for 37.5% of preventive healthcare expenditure in Bulgaria. This heading encompasses households as providers of home health care and other industries as secondary providers of health care. For comparison, the average share in the EU was 6.6%. *In Romania, '''hospitals''' had the largest share of preventive healthcare expenditure, at 45.5%. The EU average was 2.5%. Note that in Greece and France there are particularly large shares of expenditure for which the provider is unknown. [[Image:Expenditure_on_preventive_healthcare_analysed_by_provider,_2023_(%)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Expenditure on preventive healthcare analysed by provider, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (dataset code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4d49057f-5288-42cf-ac07-2fb152fbf77c?lang=en hlth_sha11_hchp])|alt=A stacked column chart showing the share of expenditure on preventive healthcare by provider as a percentage of all preventive healthcare expenditure. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU and for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The stacks for each country sum to 100% and present the shares for providers of preventive care, providers of ambulatory healthcare, hospitals, residential long-term care facilities, providers of ancillary services, providers of healthcare system administration and financing, the rest of economy, and all other providers. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== {{Template:Excel|filename=Preventive healthcare expenditure_Health2026.xlsx|title=Preventive healthcare expenditure data: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''Tables in this article use the following notation''': *values in italic show where a value is provisional *a colon ‘:’ is used to show where data are not available. '''Key concepts''' Current expenditure on health care equals ‘final consumption expenditure of resident units on health care goods and services, including the health care goods and services provided directly to individual persons as well as collective health care services’ [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf A System of Health Accounts 2011, revised edition] page 38.. Healthcare expenditure is primarily concerned with healthcare goods and services that are consumed by resident units, irrespective of where that consumption takes place (it may be in the rest of the world) or who is paying for it. As such, exports of healthcare goods and services (to non-resident units) are excluded, whereas imports of healthcare goods and services for final use are included. '''System of health accounts''' [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], the [[Glossary:Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development_(OECD)|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)]] and the WHO established a common framework for a joint healthcare data collection exercise. The data collected relate to healthcare expenditure following the [[Glossary:System_of_health_accounts_(SHA)|system of health accounts (SHA)]] methodology. The system of health accounts shares the goals of the [[Glossary:System of national accounts (SNA)|system of national accounts (SNA)]] ‘to constitute an integrated system of comprehensive, internally consistent and internationally comparable accounts, which should as far as possible be compatible with other aggregated economic and social statistical systems’. Health accounts provide a description of the financial flows related to the consumption of healthcare goods and services from an expenditure perspective. Health accounts are used in 2 ways: *internationally, where the emphasis is on a selection of comparable expenditure data *nationally, with more detailed analyses of healthcare spending and a greater emphasis on comparisons over time. In 2011, and as a result of 4 years of extensive and wide-reaching consultation, Eurostat, the OECD and the WHO released an updated manual for the collection of health accounts, [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/3859598/7985806/KS-05-19-103-EN-N.pdf A System of Health Accounts 2011, revised edition]. The core set of SHA tables addresses 3 basic questions. *What kinds of healthcare goods and services are consumed? *Which healthcare providers deliver them? *Which financing schemes are used to deliver them? Healthcare expenditure is recorded based on the [[Glossary:International_classification_for_health_accounts_(ICHA)|international classification for health accounts (ICHA)]]. *Healthcare expenditure by financing schemes (ICHA-HF) – which classifies the types of financing arrangements through which people obtain health services; healthcare financing schemes include direct payments by households for services and goods and third-party financing arrangements. *Healthcare expenditure by function (ICHA-HC) – which details the split in healthcare expenditure following the purpose of healthcare activities, such as, curative care, rehabilitative care, long-term care or preventive care. *Healthcare expenditure by provider (ICHA-HP) – which classifies units contributing to the provision of healthcare goods and services, such as hospitals, residential facilities, ambulatory healthcare services, ancillary services or retailers of medical goods. OECD guidelines for reporting preventive care have been published as [https://www.oecd.org/els/health-systems/Expenditure-on-prevention-activities-under-SHA-2011_Supplementary-guidance.pdf Expenditure on Prevention Activities under SHA 2011: Supplementary Guidance – March 2017 version]. '''Healthcare expenditure – methodology''' {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32015R0359:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/359 of 4 March 2015 as regards statistics on healthcare expenditure and financing}} established the collection of data on healthcare expenditure according to SHA 2011 methodology. This regulation applied to data from reference years 2014 until 2020. [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2021.387.01.0110.01.ENG Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/1901 of 29 October 2021 as regards statistics on healthcare expenditure and financing] covers data from the 2021 reference year onwards. These regulations lay down rules for the development and production of European statistics in the area of healthcare expenditure and financing. The background article [[Healthcare expenditure statistics - methodology|Healthcare expenditure statistics – methodology]] documents healthcare expenditure statistics. It provides more information on the scope of the data, the legal framework, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. ===Context=== Health systems across the globe are developing in response to a multitude of factors, including: *new medical technology and improvements in knowledge *new health services and greater access to them *changes in health policies to address specific diseases and demographic developments *new organisational structures and more complex financing mechanisms. However, access to healthcare and greater patient choice is increasingly being considered against a background of financial sustainability. Europe is home to some of the lowest levels of income/wealth inequality, as well as some of the highest standards for working conditions and broad social protection. At the Gothenburg Summit in 2017, the European Parliament, the Council and the European Commission proclaimed the [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/european-pillar-social-rights-building-fairer-and-more-inclusive-european-union/european-pillar-social-rights-action-plan/social-protection-and-inclusion_en#promoting-health-and-care European Pillar of Social Rights]. This set out 20 key principles for guiding the EU towards a strong, social Europe that is fair, inclusive and full of opportunity in the 21st century. Under the action plan for social protection and inclusion, the European Commission acts to promote health and care systems; these were under considerable strain during the COVID-19 pandemic. Reforms and investments in health systems are required to: *increase their resilience and capacity to manage current and future crises *reinforce primary health care and mental health *improve access to quality health care for all and reduce social, territorial and economic inequalities in health. The European Commission aims to build a strong [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0724&from=EN European Health Union] in which all EU countries prepare and respond together to health crises, where medical supplies are available, affordable and innovative, and where countries work together to improve prevention, treatment and aftercare for diseases. title: Primary education statistics
text:
EU statistics are provided on primary education: pupils, numbers of teachers and pupil-teacher ratios. Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: May 2027 In 2024, there were 23.2 million primary school pupils and 1.92 million primary school teachers across the EU (including 2023 data for some countries). In 2024, 85.6% of primary school teachers in the EU in 2024 were women. Of all primary school teachers, 19.7% were under 35 years old, 42.1% were aged 35-49 years and 38.1% were aged 50 years or over. In 2024, the average number of pupils per teacher in primary education across the EU was 13.2, ranging from an average of 7.4 in Greece to 18.2 in Romania. This article presents statistics on [[International_Standard_Classification_of_Education_(ISCED)|primary education]] ([[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|ISCED]] level 1) in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] and forms part of the online publication ''[[Education_and_training_in_the_EU_-_facts_and_figures|Education and training in the EU – facts and figures]]''. School helps young people acquire basic life skills and competences that are necessary for their personal development. The quality of a pupil’s early school experience affects not only their development, but also their future place in society, level of educational attainment and employment opportunities. Primary education follows early childhood education and provides the foundations of formal education, preparing pupils with the skills and knowledge needed for the secondary level of their education. The quality of (primary) education may be linked to teaching standards, which in turn are related to the demands placed upon teachers, the training they receive, the roles they are asked to fill and the resources that are made available for them to carry out their tasks. Equally, the quality of education may show local or regional variations, related to a variety of socio-demographic factors. ===Participation=== In the EU, there were 23.2 million pupils in primary education in 2024 (including 2023 data for Czechia and Ireland). The number of pupils found in primary education in each of the EU countries reflects their population size, demographic structure, as well as differences in the typical age for starting primary education and the age at which children should start their compulsory formal education. [[Image:Number of primary education pupils, 2024_(1 000)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Number of primary education pupils, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a9b2e6e9-534c-4e8c-a2e3-5d319759346d?lang=en educ_uoe_enrp04])|alt=A column chart showing the number of primary education pupils. Data are shown for 2024 for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The largest number of primary education pupils in 2024 among the EU countries was 4.1 million in France. This was notably larger than in Germany, Spain and Italy, which had 3.3 million, 2.8 million and 2.6 million pupils, respectively. [[Image:Distribution of pupils in primary education by type of institution, 2024_(%)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Distribution of pupils in primary education by type of institution, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f6bc7316-d574-472f-9233-0439335e6296?lang=en educ_uoe_enrp04])|alt=A stacked column chart showing the percentage distribution by type of institution of pupils in primary education. Each column has three stacks representing public, private dependent and private independent institutions. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Across the EU as a whole, 83.6% of primary education pupils in 2024 were in public institutions, with the remainder in private institutions According to the UOE classification, the distinction between public and private is made according to whether a public agency or a private entity has the overall control of the institution and not according to which sector provides the majority of the funding. If a private institution receives the majority of funding from a public agency it is considered to be dependent; if not, it is independent.. The split between public and private institutions was heavily skewed among the EU countries, as 21 of the 27 had a share of primary pupils in public institutions that was above the average for the EU. The 6 with shares of primary pupils in private institutions below the EU average were Denmark, Hungary, Spain, Malta, Belgium and the Netherlands. The Netherlands and Belgium were the only EU countries where a majority (74.4% and 54.0%, respectively) of primary pupils were in private education. In the 6 EU countries with higher-than-average shares of primary pupils in private institutions, private dependent institutions had a larger – often much larger – share of primary pupils than did private independent institutions. A majority of primary pupils in the Netherlands (74.0%) and Belgium (53.2%) were educated in private dependent institutions, with the next highest shares in this type of institution recorded in Spain (27.8%) and Malta (27.6%); 4 other EU countries – Denmark, Hungary, France and Sweden – recorded shares above 10.0%. The highest shares of primary pupils in private independent institutions were 14.1% in Cyprus and 14.0% in Malta; Portugal and Luxembourg also had shares above 10.0%. ===Number of teachers and pupil-teacher ratios=== [[Image:Pupil-teacher ratios and the number of teachers in primary education, 2024_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Pupil-teacher ratios and the number of teachers in primary education, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/14aa2c81-0654-4862-987f-f53e52396eef?lang=en educ_uoe_perp01] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/badea71c-94fa-4d69-9acb-5f0a3465a21f?lang=en educ_uoe_perp04])|alt=A table showing pupil-teacher ratios and the number of teachers in primary education. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The [[Glossary:Pupil-teacher ratios|pupil-teacher ratio]] is a measure which may be used indirectly to analyse the quality of schooling. This provides an indication of the average number of pupils there are for each teacher (see Table 1). In 2024, the average for the EU was 13.2 primary education pupils per teacher. In 2024, the lowest pupil-teacher ratios for primary education were recorded in Greece and Luxembourg, with ratios of 7.4 and 8.2 pupils per teacher, respectively; these were the only EU countries to report ratios below 10.0. At the other end of the range, pupil-teacher ratios above 15.0 primary education pupils per teacher were reported in Germany, the Netherlands, Czechia (2023 data) and France (excluding independent private institutions), with the highest ratio recorded in Romania (18.2 pupils per teacher). There were 1.83 million primary education teachers in the EU in 2024; note that the figure excludes teachers in independent private institutions for France, includes lower secondary education teachers for Slovenia and excludes data for Czechia, Ireland and Croatia. Including 2023 data for Czechia, Ireland and Croatia gives a total of around 1.92 million. The largest number of primary education teachers in 2024 among the EU countries was (to the nearest thousand) 284 000 in Germany. After Germany, the highest figures were in Italy (251 000), Spain (248 000) and France (242 000; incomplete). ===Sex and age of teachers=== In primary education, there is a clear dominance of female over male teachers. Across the EU (including 2023 data for Czechia, Ireland and Croatia), there were 273 000 male teachers in primary education in 2024 compared with 1.6 million female teachers. [[Image:Sex distribution of teachers in primary education, 2024_(%)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Sex distribution of teachers in primary education, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/249f7755-1814-414c-8c9b-d0f296f56185?lang=en educ_uoe_perp01])|alt=A stacked column chart showing the distribution by sex of teachers in primary education. Each column has two stacks representing male and female teachers. Data are shown for 2024 for EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The share of female primary education teachers averaged 85.6% across the EU in 2024, with male teachers accounting for the remaining 14.4%. The share of male teachers was below 10.0% in 9 EU countries, below 20.0% in 22 EU countries, and below a third in all EU countries. The lowest share of male primary education teachers in 2024 was 3.9% in Lithuania; the highest share was 32.8% in Denmark. [[Image:Age distribution of teachers in primary education, 2024_(%)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Age distribution of teachers in primary education, 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cd05298c-2e5b-4977-8bd6-92983d276236?lang=en educ_uoe_perp01] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0302b66e-9cc4-4e87-8d65-f4ef36f876b0?lang=en educ_uoe_perd01])|alt=A stacked column chart showing the age distribution of teachers in primary education. Each column has three stacks representing the following age groups: younger than 35 years, 35 to 49 years and 50 years or over. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, around a fifth (19.7%) of primary education teachers in the EU were younger than 35 years of age. The largest age cohort was for teachers aged 35 to 49 years with a 42.1% share, followed by older teachers (those aged 50 years or over) with a share of 38.1%. Note that the shares for these 3 age classes do not sum to 100.0% for the EU due to the age of some teachers, mainly in Germany and Ireland, being unknown. For comparison, 28.1% of all people employed in the EU were under the age of 35 years, 36.7% were aged 35 to 49 years and 35.2% were aged 50 years or over. The share of older primary education teachers was above 20.0% in 24 EU countries and above 30.0% in 20 of these. The highest shares of older primary education teachers were observed in Italy (58.2%) and Lithuania (57.3%). The 3 EU countries with shares for older teachers that were below 20.0% were Ireland (2023 data), Malta and Luxembourg. Malta and Luxembourg recorded particularly high shares of younger primary education teachers, approximately double the EU average. === Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=Primary education statistics_ET2026.xlsx|title=Primary education statistics: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''Source''' The standards for international statistics on education are set by 3 organisations *the [[Glossary:United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)|United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)]] institute for statistics (UIS) *the [[Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)]] *[[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], the statistical office of the EU. The source of data used in this article is a [[Glossary:UOE data collection|joint UNESCO/OECD/Eurostat (UOE) data collection]] on education statistics and this is the basis for the core components of Eurostat’s database on education statistics; in combination with the joint data collection Eurostat also collects data on regional enrolments and foreign language learning. More information about the joint data collection is available in an article on the [[UNESCO_OECD_Eurostat_(UOE)_joint_data_collection_%E2%80%93_methodology|UOE methodology]]. '''Classification''' The [https://www.uis.unesco.org/en/methods-and-tools/isced?hub=175 international standard classification of education (ISCED)] is the basis for international education statistics, describing 9 different [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|levels of education]]. '''Key concepts''' Pupil-teacher ratios are calculated by dividing the number of [[Glossary:Full-time equivalent (FTE)|full-time equivalent]] pupils and students in each level of education by the number of full-time equivalent teachers at the same level. This ratio should not be confused with average class size, which refers to the number of students in a given course or classroom. '''Symbols''' In tables, a colon ‘:’ is used to show where data are not available. Data in italics are estimates or provisional. ===Context=== Age is generally the sole criterion for admission to [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/Annexes/educ_uoe_enr_esms_an_6.xlsx compulsory primary education]. This starts in most of the EU countries when children reach 6 years of age. Bulgaria, Estonia, Croatia and Finland have a compulsory starting age for primary education of 7 years, while Malta (5 years) has a younger starting age. Although education is compulsory at 5 or 6 years of age in Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Sweden, this is at early childhood education level, not primary education which starts at 7 years. More information about the starting age of compulsory primary education is provided in national quality reports (national metadata) attached to the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/educ_uoe_enr_esms.htm metadata for administrative data on enrolments]. Note that in close to half of the EU countries it is also compulsory for young children to attend pre-primary education (usually at 5 years of age). Among EU countries, primary education typically lasts 6 years, although its duration can range between 4 and 7 years; as a result, it lasts until a child is aged 10 to 12 years. Primary education programmes are typically designed to provide students with fundamental skills in reading, writing and mathematics (in other words, literacy and numeracy) and to establish a solid foundation for learning and understanding core areas of knowledge, personal and social development, in preparation for lower secondary education. It focuses on learning at a basic level of complexity with little, if any, specialisation. === Footnotes === ===Other articles=== *[[Education_and_training_in_the_EU_-_facts_and_figures|Education and title: Preventable and treatable mortality statistics
text:
EU statistics are presented on avoidable (also called amenable) deaths focusing on people aged less than 75 years. Avoidable deaths relate to deaths from treatable or preventable diseases or conditions. Data from March 2026 Planned article update: April 2027 In the EU, 1.56 million people aged less than 75 years died in 2023; the total number of avoidable deaths within this cohort was 1.03 million. Among people aged less than 75 years, the 3 leading causes of avoidable deaths in 2023 in the EU were ischaemic heart diseases, lung cancer and cerebrovascular diseases. In the EU, standardised mortality rates for both treatable and preventable diseases or conditions were higher for males than for females in 2023. This pattern was repeated in all of the EU countries. In 2023, Luxembourg had the lowest standardised death rate in the EU for treatable diseases or conditions (51.7 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants), followed by Sweden, France and Belgium, all with rates between 58.4 and 58.8 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants. |alt=A dynamic triple column chart showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for treatable diseases or conditions among people aged less than 75 years. Data are analysed by sex. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. This article presents statistics for the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] on 2 indicators of avoidable mortality, namely deaths from treatable and deaths from preventable diseases or conditions. The concept of treatable and preventable mortality is based on the idea that certain deaths (for specific diseases or conditions defined by the [https://icd.who.int/browse10/2019/en ICD classification] – see the [[Preventable and treatable mortality statistics#Data sources|Data sources]] section) could be ‘avoided’ among people aged less than 75 years. In other words, these avoidable deaths would not have occurred at this stage if there had been more effective public health and/or medical interventions in place See the discussions in Nolte E. and M. McKee (2004): ''Does Health Care Save Lives? Avoidable Mortality Revisited'', Nuffield Trust, London; and Gay J. et al. (2011): ''Mortality Amenable to Health Care in 31 OECD Countries'', OECD Health Working Papers No. 55, OECD.. *The concept of preventable causes of death covers deaths which could have been avoided by public health interventions focusing on wider determinants of public health, such as behaviour and lifestyle factors, socioeconomic status, and environmental factors. *The diseases or conditions that can be largely prevented and that can also be treated once they have occurred are attributed to the preventable category. *A disease/condition is considered as treatable if a death from this disease/condition could have been avoided through optimal quality [[Glossary:Healthcare|health care]]. *In cases where there is no strong evidence of predominance of preventability or treatability diseases or conditions, they are allocated on a 50%-50% basis to the 2 categories. This article is included in a set of statistical articles concerning health status in the EU which forms part of the online publication ''[[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]]''. ===Number and rate of avoidable deaths=== '''''In 2023, deaths from avoidable diseases or conditions among people aged less than 75 years amounted to 1.03 million in the EU''''' A total of 1.03 million deaths in 2023 among people aged less than 75 years – equivalent to a [[Glossary:Standardised_death_rate_(SDR)|standardised death rate]] of 237.7 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants – could have been avoided in the EU. Some 376 000 of these deaths – equivalent to a standardised death rate of 86.8 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants – were deaths from diseases or conditions that are treatable; 655 000 deaths – equivalent to 150.9 deaths per 100  000 inhabitants – could have been prevented. Figure 1 shows data for standardised death rates of avoidable mortality, comparing the rates for preventable diseases or conditions with those for treatable ones. These standardised death rates are compiled using the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-ra-13-028 European standard population]. [[Image:Standardised death rates for avoidable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, 2023_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Standardised death rates for avoidable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d47758bc-df7b-485b-8e68-bcbc8a2dab46?lang=en hlth_cd_apr])|alt=A high-low chart showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for avoidable diseases or conditions for people aged less than 75 years. The markers for each country show the rates for preventable and for treatable mortality. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In all EU countries, standardised death rates for treatable diseases or conditions were lower than for preventable diseases or conditions in 2023. The largest absolute gap in 2023 was recorded in Hungary, where there were 128.0 more deaths per 100 000 inhabitants from preventable than treatable diseases or conditions. The narrowest gap was in Cyprus, where the difference was 26.8 deaths per 100 00 inhabitants. The lowest death rate for treatable diseases or conditions was recorded in Luxembourg, at 51.7 per 100 000 inhabitants. The highest death rate for treatable diseases or conditions was 199.7 per 100 000 inhabitants in Romania. Latvia, Bulgaria, Hungary, Lithuania and Slovakia also recorded rates above 160.0 per 100 000 inhabitants. In 2023, the lowest death rate for preventable diseases or conditions was recorded in Cyprus, at 89.7 per 100 000 inhabitants. Italy, Malta, Sweden, Luxembourg and Spain also recorded rates under 120.0 per 100 000 inhabitants. The highest death rates for preventable diseases or conditions were 309.0 per 100 000 inhabitants in Latvia and 300.4 per 100 000 inhabitants in Hungary. Lithuania and Romania also recorded rates above 250.0 per 100 000 inhabitants. ===Avoidable death rates by sex=== '''''Mortality rates in the EU were higher for males than for females for avoidable diseases or conditions''''' In 2023, mortality rates for treatable diseases or conditions among people aged less than 75 years were consistently higher for males than for females – see Figure 2. Among the EU countries, the narrowest gap between the 2 sexes (the difference between the rates for males and for females), in relative terms, was observed for the Netherlands, followed by Malta, Luxembourg, France, Belgium, Italy, Ireland and Sweden. The widest gaps for treatable diseases or conditions were reported for the [[Glossary:Baltic_Member_States|Baltic countries]] – Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia – which were the only EU countries to report rates for males that were at least 2.0 times as high as those for females. For males, Luxembourg (53.5 per 100 000 inhabitants) reported the lowest death rate for treatable diseases or conditions in 2023, while Latvia and Romania (272.2 and 267.2 per 100 000 inhabitants, respectively) reported the highest rates. For females, the lowest mortality rate for treatable diseases or conditions was reported by Spain (49.5 per 100 000 inhabitants) and the highest rates by Romania and Bulgaria (143.6 and 131.9 per 100 000 inhabitants, respectively). [[Image:Standardised death rates for treatable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, by sex, 2023 (per 100 000 male female inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Standardised death rates for treatable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, by sex, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/08455f15-1ded-4bfb-8d24-5deeef7b23ad?lang=en hlth_cd_apr])|alt=A high-low chart showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for treatable diseases or conditions among people aged less than 75 years. The markers for each country show the rates for males and for females. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Preventable mortality rates were also consistently higher for males than for females in 2023 – see Figure 3. Gaps between the 2 sexes were wider for preventable diseases or conditions than for treatable ones. Among the EU countries, the narrowest gap (in relative terms) for preventable diseases or conditions was observed for the Netherlands, with the rate for males 1.6 times as high as the rate for females. In 22 of the EU countries, the death rate for preventable diseases or conditions for males was more than double the rate for females. In 9 of the EU countries, the rate for males was at least 3.0 times as high as the rate for females. The widest gap was recorded in Latvia, with the rate for males 3.6 times as high as the rate for females. For males, Sweden (135.1 per 100 000 inhabitants) reported the lowest death rate among the EU countries for preventable diseases or conditions in 2023. Latvia (519.7 per 100 000 inhabitants) reported the highest rate. For females, the lowest mortality rate for preventable diseases or conditions was reported by Cyprus (44.8 per 100 000 inhabitants), whereas Hungary (181.1 per 100 000 inhabitants) reported the highest rate. [[Image:Standardised death rates for preventable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, by sex, 2023_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Standardised death rates for preventable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, by sex, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a86076bc-d618-4983-9c76-7f98a323c2af?lang=en hlth_cd_apr])|alt=A high-low chart showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for preventable diseases or conditions among people aged less than 75 years. The markers for each country show the rates for males and for females. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Leading causes of avoidable deaths=== Table 1 lists the main avoidable diseases or conditions in the EU in terms of their number of deaths in 2023. The 12 individual diseases or conditions that are listed collectively accounted for 69.4% of the total number of deaths from avoidable diseases or conditions. They accounted for 71.5% of all deaths from treatable diseases or conditions and 68.3% of all preventable deaths. By far the most common causes of avoidable deaths in the EU were ischaemic heart diseases (146 000 deaths) and lung cancer (136 000 deaths). Ischaemic heart diseases are split between treatable and preventable diseases, while lung cancer is considered as a preventable cause of death. The largest numbers of deaths from purely treatable diseases or conditions were 57 000 from colorectal cancer and 40 000 from breast cancer (females only). [[Image:Leading causes of avoidable deaths, people aged less than 75 years, EU, 2023 (number) v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Leading causes of avoidable deaths, people aged less than 75 years, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/29055162-4918-4720-92ea-81a8ed4bb800?lang=en hlth_cd_apr] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hlth_cd_aro__custom_20466470/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=6c0044c7-3aa3-49de-822f-924ee7540e55&c=1773160580387 hlth_cd_aro])|alt=A table showing the number of deaths from the leading causes of avoidable deaths among people aged less than 75 years. The table lists a total for all diseases or conditions, data for 12 individual diseases and conditions and data for a residual category. For each of these, it shows the numbers for all avoidable deaths, for treatable deaths and for preventable deaths. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''The leading cause of death for treatable diseases or conditions was ischaemic heart diseases''''' Figure 4 shows the leading causes of death in the EU for avoidable diseases or conditions in 2023. The EU standardised rate of deaths from treatable diseases or conditions from ischaemic heart diseases was 16.6 per 100 000 inhabitants in 2023, equivalent to 19.1% of the total death rate from treatable diseases or conditions. Colorectal cancer (13.0 per 100 000 inhabitants), breast cancer among females only (9.2 per 100 000 inhabitants) and cerebrovascular diseases (8.6 per 100 000 inhabitants) were the next most common causes of death among treatable diseases or conditions. Collectively, the 7 treatable diseases or conditions shown in Figure 4 accounted for 70.9% of the overall standardised death rate from treatable diseases or conditions. [[Image:Standardised death rates for avoidable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, EU, 2023_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Standardised death rates for avoidable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3c8c214b-2882-4d2e-9aed-d7a6280febb5?lang=en hlth_cd_apr])|alt=A bar chart showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for avoidable diseases and conditions among people aged less than 75 years. The chart is divided in 2 sections, listing 7 treatable diseases and 7 preventable diseases, each section also showing a residual category for other causes. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''The leading causes of preventable deaths were lung cancer and ischaemic heart diseases''''' The EU standardised rate of preventable deaths for lung cancer was 30.8 per 100 000 inhabitants in 2023, equivalent to 20.4% of the total death rate from preventable deaths. Ischaemic heart diseases (16.6 per 100 000 inhabitants), alcohol-specific disorders and poisonings (11.7 per 100 000 inhabitants) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (10.0 per 100 000 inhabitants) were the next most common causes of preventable deaths. The 7 preventable diseases or conditions shown in Figure 4 collectively accounted for 63.1% of the overall death rate from preventable diseases or conditions. ===Leading causes of avoidable death – analysis by sex=== In 2023, the distribution of treatable diseases or conditions in the EU varied somewhat for males and females, reflecting the fact that some of the major causes of death are sex specific to a large or even exclusive extent. Among females, the leading cause of death from treatable diseases or conditions was breast cancer: this disease alone was responsible for close to a quarter (24.6%) of the death rate from all treatable diseases or conditions among females, reflecting a standardised death rate of 17.7 per 100 000 female inhabitants. Cancer of the uterus (3.7 per 100 000 female inhabitants) was also among the top causes of death shown in Figure 5 and is sex specific. For diseases common to males and females, the most frequent causes of death for treatable diseases or conditions in the EU were ischaemic heart diseases (26.3 per 100 000 male inhabitants and 7.8 per 100 000 female inhabitants) and colorectal cancer (16.8 per 100 000 male inhabitants and 9.7 per 100 000 female inhabitants). The largest difference between sexes was observed for ischaemic heart disease which had a standardised death rate that was 3.4 times as high among males as among females. [[Image:Standardised death rates for treatable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, EU, 2023 (per 100 000 male female inhabitants) v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Standardised death rates for treatable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/241c4b07-61e1-407e-b038-4b9f15ff40fb?lang=en hlth_cd_apr])|alt=A double bar chart showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for treatable diseases and conditions among people aged less than 75 years. The bars show 14 diseases and a residual category. Data are analysed by sex. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] For preventable deaths, the 2 leading causes of death in the EU in 2023 were the same for males and for females: lung cancer and ischaemic heart diseases. Standardised death rates were higher among males than among females for all of the diseases or conditions presented in Figure 6. The greatest difference between the sexes was observed for oesophagus cancer, which was 4.8 times as high among males as among females (5.5 deaths per 100 000 male inhabitants and 1.2 deaths per 100 000 female inhabitants). Rates for males were 4.2 times as high for intentional self-harm (13.6 deaths per 100 000 male inhabitants and 3.2 deaths per 100 000 female inhabitants), 4.1 times as high for lip, oral cavity and pharynx cancer (7.0 per 100 000 male inhabitants and 1.7 per 100 000 female inhabitants), and 4.0 times as high for transport accidents (7.1 per 100 000 male inhabitants and 1.8 per 100 000 female inhabitants). [[Image:Standardised death rates for preventable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, EU, 2023 (per 100 000 male female inhabitants) v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Standardised death rates for preventable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, EU, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/99ca5eaa-f7a3-41c2-a3ac-e2e3be51891b?lang=en hlth_cd_apr])|alt=A double bar chart showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for preventable diseases and conditions among people aged less than 75 years. The bars show fourteen diseases and a residual category. Data are analysed by sex. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Leading causes of avoidable death – analysis by EU country=== In 2023, the 5 most common causes of death in the EU from treatable diseases or conditions (ischaemic heart diseases, colorectal cancer, breast cancer, cerebrovascular diseases and pneumonia) accounted for 62.2% of the death rate for all treatable diseases or conditions. These 5 causes (as well as a residual category for all other causes) are presented in Figure 7. The share of these 5 common causes in all deaths ranged among the EU countries from 49.7% in Estonia to 70.3% in Slovenia. In 2023, among these 5 leading causes of death across the EU from treatable diseases or conditions, ischaemic heart disease had the highest standardised death rate in 20 EU countries. In the remaining 7 – Croatia, Denmark, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain – the highest rate was observed for colorectal cancer. [[Image:Standardised death rates for the top 5 treatable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, 2023 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Standardised death rates for the top 5 treatable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3fae24b7-6bd9-4bd1-9881-373381de9ad5?lang=en hlth_cd_apr])|alt=A stacked bar chart showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants among people aged less than 75 years. The stacks show the top five treatable diseases and conditions as well as a residual category. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The 5 most common causes of preventable deaths (lung cancer, ischaemic heart diseases, alcohol-specific disorders and poisonings, chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder, and cerebrovascular diseases) in the EU in 2023 accounted for 51.5% of the death rate for all preventable deaths. These 5 cases (as well as a residual category for all other causes) are presented in Figure 8. The share of these 5 common causes in all deaths ranged among the EU countries from 43.0% in Portugal to 63.3% in Hungary. Among these 5 leading causes of preventable deaths in the EU in 2023, lung cancer had the highest standardised death rate in 20 EU countries. In Bulgaria, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania and Slovakia, the highest rate was observed for ischaemic heart diseases. In Estonia and Finland, the highest rate was for alcohol-specific disorders and poisonings. [[Image:Standardised death rates for the top 5 preventable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, 2023 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Standardised death rates for the top 5 preventable diseases or conditions, people aged less than 75 years, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a8fe8261-9ca3-4f39-b75d-f98e7bd64c22?lang=en hlth_cd_apr])|alt=A stacked bar chart showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants among people aged less than 75 years. The stacks show the top five preventable diseases and conditions as well as a residual category. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Potential years of life lost in the EU in 2023=== As noted earlier, 1.03 million EU residents died in 2023 from avoidable (preventable or treatable) causes, equivalent to 66.3% of all deaths before the age of 75 years. Over the course of 2023, a total of 3 166 [[Glossary:Potential years of life lost|potential years of life were lost]] per 100 000 inhabitants through avoidabel causes of deaths of EU residents aged less than 75 years. This rate is calculated by summing the number of years between the age at death and 75 years for each premature death from preventable or treatable causes and then expressing this total relative to the size of the age-standardised population aged less than 75 years. A total of 2 015 potential years of life were lost per 100 000 inhabitants through preventable deaths, while 1 151 potential years of life were lost per 100 000 inhabitants through treatable deaths. In 2023, the highest rates of potential years of life lost were generally observed among Baltic and eastern EU countries, while lower rates were generally observed in [[Glossary:Nordic_Member_States|Nordic]], western and southern EU countries; an exception was Slovenia, which had a lower rate than those of Finland and Germany. Among EU countries, the highest number of potential years of life lost through preventable or treatable deaths was 7 158 per 100 000 inhabitants in Latvia; the lowest was 1 974 per 100 000 inhabitants in Luxembourg. In 2023, preventable deaths consistently accounted for more than half of all potential years of life lost among deaths before the age of 75 years. The lowest share for preventable deaths was 54.9% in Bulgaria, while the highest share was 73.8% in Estonia; the share across the whole of the EU was 63.6%. [[Image:Potential years of life lost through deaths from treatable and preventable diseases, deaths before age 75 years, 2023_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: Potential years of life lost through deaths from treatable and preventable diseases, deaths before age 75 years, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ed35cc9e-9d62-49f2-957a-c176cad3661a?lang=en hlth_cd_ptpyll])|alt=A stacked bar chart showing the number of potential years of life lost per 100 000 inhabitants through deaths among people aged less than 75 years. The stacks show data for treatable diseases and for preventable diseases. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=Preventable_and_treatable_mortality_statistics_Health2026.xlsx|title=Preventable and treatable mortality statistics: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The definitions of avoidable deaths are based on the following. *A disease/condition leading to a death is treatable if, in the light of medical knowledge and technology at the time of death, all or most deaths from that cause could be avoided through optimal quality health care. *A disease/condition leading to a preventable death is a disease/condition which, in the light of understanding of the determinants of health at the time of death, all or most deaths from that cause could be avoided by public health interventions in the broadest sense. To calculate treatable and preventable mortality, the initial step is to define which diseases or conditions cause deaths that could – potentially – have been avoided through optimal quality health care (deaths from treatable diseases or conditions) and through public health interventions (preventable deaths). In 2018, the [[Glossary:Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development_(OECD)|OECD]] and [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] worked together with an expert group to develop new lists of treatable and preventable causes of mortality. These lists built on earlier work carried out by researchers (such as Nolte E. and M. McKee (2004 and 2011)), by some OECD countries, and by an ad-hoc Eurostat task force. The list was slightly revised in November 2019. The complete list of diseases or conditions considered to cause avoidable deaths is available as an [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/Annexes/hlth_cdeath_sims_an_5.pdf annex to the metadata] for Eurostat’s causes of death statistics. The age up to which a death can be considered avoidable is set at 74 years (inclusive) to reflect life expectancy. The list of diseases or conditions and the age limit reflect current health expectations, medical technology and knowledge, and developments in healthcare public policy. As such, they are subject to change. For example, the data for 2020, 2021 and 2023 include COVID-19 as a preventable disease. The next step in the calculation of treatable and preventable mortality is the summation of all deaths within the age limit where the underlying cause of death was included in the list of diseases or conditions for avoidable deaths. The statistics used to calculate avoidable mortality indicators are causes of death data; these include detailed information on the underlying cause of death of the deceased. More information on the methodology used for statistics on the causes of death is available in a background article on the [[Causes_of_death_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of causes of death statistics]]. The data for causes of death are included in an annual data collection with a legal basis requiring all EU countries to send complete data to Eurostat. Note that some diseases or conditions are considered to be treatable and preventable. An example is ischaemic heart diseases, from which a death might be avoided through timely and effective health care (for example through thrombolytic therapy) and/or through effective public health intervention to reduce the underlying risk factors (for example reduced salt intake). The causes of death that can be both largely prevented and that can be treated once they have occurred are attributed to the preventable category on the rationale that if these diseases or conditions are prevented, there would be no need for treatment. The number of deaths for a specific disease/condition are generally not fractioned as being partly preventable and partly treatable given the lack of evidence to do this accurately and systematically. An exception is when there is no strong evidence of predominance, in which case a 50%-50% allocation is used. As such, any double counting of the same death between the 2 lists is avoided; therefore, the number of deaths according to the 2 lists can be aggregated to provide a broad assessment of the relative importance of prevention and healthcare interventions in reducing the number of avoidable deaths. Annual data on the 2 types of avoidable deaths are provided in absolute numbers and as standardised death rates. Since most causes of death vary significantly by age and according to sex, the use of standardised death rates improves comparability over time and between countries as death rates can be measured independently of a population’s age structure: standardised death rates are calculated based on the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-ra-13-028 European standard population]. Note that the standardised death rates used in this article are calculated per 100 000 inhabitants aged less than 75 years. ===Context=== Assessing the performance of healthcare systems is of increasing importance in the EU. While avoidable mortality indicators are not meant to be a definitive measure of the quality of the health care in EU countries, they provide some indication of the quality and performance of health care and of (wider) public health policies. In addition to health care and public health policies, other factors related to the likelihood that individuals may contract a disease or seek medical advice – such as education, social background, health beliefs, levels of concern, costs of diagnosis and treatment – are likely to influence the number of avoidable deaths See page 18 of Nolte E. and M. McKee (2004), ''Does Health Care Save Lives? Avoidable Mortality Revisited'', Nuffield Trust, London.. Improvements in health policies should translate into lower numbers of avoidable deaths. However, there is often a long time-lag between implementation of health (care) policies and changes in mortality rates and therefore any conclusions need to be drawn with caution. === Footnotes === ===Other articles=== *[[Health in the European Union - facts and figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]] *[[Cancer statistics|Cancer statistics]] *[[Cardiovascular diseases statistics|Cardiovascular diseases statistics]] *[[Causes of death - monthly statistics|Causes of death – monthly statistics]] *[[Causes of death statistics|Causes of death statistics]] *[[Respiratory diseases statistics|Respiratory diseases statistics]] *[[Cancer statistics - specific cancers|Specific cancers]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/database Health (hlth)] :Causes of death (hlth_cdeath) ::Public health themes (hlth_cd_pbt) :::Treatable and preventable mortality of residents by cause and sex (hlth_cd_apr) :::Causes of death - potential years of life lost by treatable and preventable diseases (hlth_cd_ptpyll) ===Thematic section=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/health/overview Health] ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=hlth_cdeath_sims|title=Causes of death statistics}} (ESMS metadata file – hlth_cdeath_sims) *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-020|title=Causes of death statistics manual}} – 2025 edition ===External links=== *[https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/health-and-food-safety_en European Commission, Directorate General Health and Food Safety], see: **[https://health.ec.europa.eu/index_en Public health] **[https://health.ec.europa.eu/health-systems-performance-assessment/overview_en Health systems performance assessment] ''View this article online at {{fullurl:{{PAGENAME}}}}'' {{Unit|topic=X_Health}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Preventable and treatable mortality statistics]] [[Category:Health|Preventable and treatable mortality statistics]] [[Category:Mortality and life expectancy|Preventable and treatable mortality statistics]] [[Category:Statistical article|Preventable and treatable mortality statistics]] [[Category:April2027|Preventable and treatable mortality statistics]]

title: Preliminary GDP flash estimate in 30 days for Europe/sk
text:
<pdftheme>2</pdftheme>
=Predbežný rýchly odhad HDP za Európu už 30 dní po skončení referenčného štvrťroka=

<highlight title=false>
Od 29. apríla 2016 bude [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] zverejňovať predbežné rýchle odhady štvrťročného [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|HDP]] za [[Glossary:Euro_area|eurozónu (EZ)]] a za [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|Európsku úniu (EÚ)]] približne 30 dní po skončení štvrťroka (t + 30). Toto skoršie zverejňovanie je výsledkom [[Glossary:European_statistical_system_(ESS)|Európskeho štatistického systému]], keďže členské štáty prispievajú tým, že svoje vnútroštátne odhady zasielajú Eurostatu oproti minulosti o dva týždne skôr.

Metodika zodpovedá najmä súčasnej metodike pre rýchle odhady HDP zverejňované 45 dní po skončení štvrťroka (t + 45)<ref>Ďalšie podrobnosti sú k dispozícii na tejto [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/24987/725066/Estimating_GDP_flashes.pdf/7482fff6-a662-4b77-9877-f61ed519c5f5 webovej stránke].</ref>. Hlavný rozdiel spočíva v tom, že sa za krajiny používajú predbežnejšie odhady. Vzhľadom na skoršiu lehotu musia členské štáty údaje za tretí mesiac štvrťroka často (aspoň čiastočne) odhadovať. 
</highlight>

<articlecontent>
<sesection>
===Ako sa zostavuje predbežný rýchly odhad?===

Stručne povedané, väčšina členských štátov EÚ zasiela Eurostatu odhady údajov o raste HDP jeden deň pred dohodnutým dátumom zverejnenia. Do tejto skupiny patria tie členské štáty, ktoré svoje odhady už zverejňujú v lehote t + 30, ako aj viaceré členské štáty, ktoré Eurostatu zasielajú dôverné odhady. Eurostat potom agreguje medzikvartálne tempá rastu jednotlivých krajín použitím váženého ročného HDP jednotlivých krajín, na základe čoho získa odhady údajov o tempe rastu HDP za EÚ a eurozónu.

Rozhodnutie začať zverejňovať rýchle odhady HDP EZ/EÚ v lehote t + 30 je založené na výsledkoch testovacej fázy za štvrťroky 2012 – 2015. V posledných skúšobných odhadoch za štvrťrok 2015Q4 pokrytie krajín dosiahlo 91 % HDP za [[Glossary:EU-28|EÚ-28]] a 94 % HDP za [[Glossary:EA-19|EZ-19]].
</sesection>

<sesection>
===Je predbežný odhad spoľahlivý?===

Keďže rýchle odhady sú k dispozícii skôr ako klasické odhady, ide o kompromis medzi včasnosťou a presnosťou. Na základe 16 skúšobných odhadov by očakávaná typická revízia v lehote t + 45 v prípade tempa rastu HDP zverejňovaného v lehote t + 30 (zaokrúhlená na jedno desatinné miesto) predstavovala –0,1, 0,0 alebo +0,1 percentuálneho bodu za eurozónu aj za EÚ. V prípade náhlej výraznej zmeny hospodárskeho vývoja, ako to bolo v 2008Q2 v súvislosti s finančnou krízou, je možné očakávať väčšie revízie.

Očakávané revízie boli úspešne testované podľa vopred určených kvalitatívnych kritérií<ref>Pozri štatistický pracovný dokument Eurostatu „Euro area and European Union GDP flash estimates at 30 days“ zverejnený 29. apríla 2016 na [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/national-accounts/methodology/european-accounts/estimation-european-main-aggregates webovej stránke] Eurostatu.</ref>. Na obrázku 1 vidieť rozdiely v (nezaokrúhlenej) miere rastu v lehote t + 30 (skúšobné odhady) a v lehotách t + 45 a t + 65 dní za 2012Q1 – 2015Q4. V hornom grafe je zobrazené tempo rastu za EZ a na spodnom grafe za EÚ.

[[Image:The growth rates (in %) of EA (upper graph) and the EU (lower graph) final SK2.png|thumb|center|600px|'''Obrázok 1: Miery rastu (v %) v EZ (horný graf) a EÚ (spodný graf) v lehote t + 30 (test), t + 45 a t + 65 dní''']]
</sesection>
</articlecontent>

<dedicatedsection>
===Tematická sekcia ===
*[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/national-accounts/methodology/european-accounts/estimation-european-main-aggregates National accounts (including GDP)] (v angličtine)
</dedicatedsection>

<notes>
=== Referencie ===

<references />
</notes>
