title: R&D personnel
text:
EU statistics on science and technology personnel are key indicators for measuring the knowledge-based economy and its developments. Data extracted in January 2026 Planned article update: January 2027 The number of full-time equivalent researchers in the EU increased by more than 47.3% between 2014 and 2024, from 1.50 to 2.21 million. More than half (57.0%) of full-time equivalent researchers in the EU worked in business enterprises, 31.6% in higher education and 10.1% in the government sector in 2024. [[Image:Figure 4 R&D personnel by sector, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|R&D personnel by sector, 2024
(% of total employment, based on full-time equivalents)|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing R and D personnel by sector as percentage of total employment, based on full-time equivalents in the EU, euro area, individual EU countries, EFTA countries and some candidate countries. Each country bar has four queues representing business enterprise sector, government sector, higher education sector and private non-profit sector for the year 2024.]] This article analyses preliminary data for 2024 on research and development (R&D) personnel, [[Glossary:Research_and_development_(R_&_D)_personnel_and_researchers|researchers]], [[Glossary:Human resources in science and technology (HRST)|human resources in science and technology (HRST)]] and doctorate/PhD students in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Statistics on science and technology personnel are key indicators for measuring the knowledge-based economy and its developments, for example, providing information on the supply of and demand for, highly qualified science and technology specialists. ===Researchers=== The number of [[Glossary:Researcher|researchers]] in the [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU]] has increased in recent years: there were 2.15 million researchers (in [[Glossary:Full-time equivalent (FTE)|full-time equivalents (FTE)]]) employed in the EU in 2024 (see Figure 1), which marked an increase of 679 000 when compared with 2014. The number of researchers (FTE) increased strongly in Poland (+82.7%) and Cyprus (+81.2%). Moreover, it increased by more than 60% in Greece (70.1%), Hungary (68.7%), Portugal (68.2%), Sweden (63.9%) and in Belgium (60.7%) between 2014 and 2024. At the opposite end of the range, with small growth rates were Latvia (15.8%) and Lithuania (17.7%). Among the non-EU member countries shown in Figure 1, the number of researchers in China (excluding Hong Kong) reached 3.01 million in 2023. There was a rapid growth noted in China, where the number of researchers more than doubled compared with 2013. South Korea also recorded a rapid increase in the number of researchers (up overall by 52.3%) between 2013 and 2023. In the United States the growth rate was 38.3% (between 2013 and 2022). The number of researchers rose by 5.9% in Japan between 2013 and 2023. Among the candidate countries, the number of researchers in Türkiye more than doubled during the period 2013-2023. [[Image:Figure 1 Name of researchers.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Number of FTE researchers, 2014 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=rd_p_persocc}} and [https://stats.oecd.org/ OECD database]|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing number of researchers as thousand full time equivalents in the EU, euro area, individual EU countries, EFTA countries, some candidate countries, China except for Hong Kong, United States, Japan and South Korea. Each country has two bars representing the years 2014 and 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] An analysis of R&D personnel by sector in 2024 (see Figure 2) shows that in the EU there was a high concentration of researchers in the business enterprise sector (57.0%) and the higher education sector (31.6%), while 10.1% of the total number of researchers were working in the [[Glossary:General government sector|government sector]]. The relative importance of the different sectors varied considerably across the EU countries, with the business sector accounting for three-fifths or more of all researchers in Sweden, the Netherlands, Hungary, Austria, Germany, France, Belgium and Finland. By contrast, the countries with the highest share of researchers working in the government sector were Romania (30.4%), Bulgaria (27.5%), Croatia (23%) and Luxembourg (22.1%). A majority of researchers working in Latvia (53.6%), Lithuania (52.5%) and Croatia (50.8%) were employed within the higher education sector. This sector also accounted for a high share (although less than 50%) of all researchers in Portugal, Slovakia, Ireland, Greece, Malta, Cyprus, Luxembourg, Spain and Estonia. In terms of its number of researchers, the private non-profit sector was the smallest in all EU countries, its highest share (10.4% of all researchers) was recorded in Cyprus, while the next highest shares were in Italy (2.9%) and Germany (2.4%). In the remaining 21 countries for which the data for this sector are available, it ranged between 0.0% and 1.9%. [[Image:Figure 2 Researchers by sector, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Researchers by sector, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=rd_p_persocc}} and [https://stats.oecd.org/ OECD database]|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing researchers by sector as percentage of total number of researchers based on full time equivalents in the EU, euro area, individual EU countries, EFTA countries, some candidate countries, China except for Hong Kong, United States, Japan and South Korea. Totalling 100 percent, each country bar has four queues representing business enterprise sector, government sector, higher education sector and private non-profit sector for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] An analysis by sex shows that men accounted for approximately two-thirds (65.7%) of the EU's researchers in 2023 (expressed in head count). The share of women in the total number of researchers was close to parity in Croatia, Lithuania, Latvia, Bulgaria and Romania, all above 45% (see Figure 3). The gender gap was the largest in Czechia, Hungary and Germany where women made up less than 30% of all researchers. [[Image:Figure 3 Researchers by sex, 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Researchers by sex, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=rd_p_persocc}} and [https://stats.oecd.org/ OECD database]|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing researchers by sex as percentage of total number of researchers based on head count in the EU, euro area, individual EU countries, EFTA countries, some candidate countries, Japan and South Korea. Totalling 100 percent, each country bar has two queues representing women and men for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===R&D personnel=== R&D personnel in all sectors together accounted for more than 2.0% of the total [[Glossary:Employment|employment]] in Sweden, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Austria, Netherlands, and Germany compared with an EU average of 1.7%. (Note: these figures are based on information in full-time equivalents.) Aside from the above countries mentioned, the share of R&D personnel in the total employment ranged from 0.5% in Romania and Cyprus to 1.9% in Slovenia (see Figure 4). [[Image:Figure 4 R&D personnel by sector, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: R&D personnel by sector, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=rd_p_perslf}}|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing R and D personnel by sector as percentage of total employment, based on full-time equivalents in the EU, euro area, individual EU countries, EFTA countries and some candidate countries. Each country bar has four queues representing business enterprise sector, government sector, higher education sector and private non-profit sector for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Human resources in science and technology=== [[Glossary:Human resources in science and technology (HRST)|Human resources in science and technology (HRST)]] provide information concerning the demand for and the supply of people with high qualifications in science and technology. Around 80.1 million people in the EU were employed in science and technology (S&T) occupations in 2024, this made up one-third (36.5%) of the total labour force aged 15-74 years (see Figure 5). Persons in S&T occupations accounted for well over half of the total labour force in Luxembourg (60.2%) in 2024 and for more than two fifths in Sweden (47.3%), the Netherlands (47.2%), Denmark (42.9%), Germany (41.7%), Finland (41.0%) and Belgium (40.0%). By contrast, the lowest shares of people working in science and technology occupations were recorded in Romania (23.7%), Greece (25.8%), Spain (28.7%) and Bulgaria (29.6%). The concept of human resources in science and technology in the [http://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/science-and-technology/measurement-of-scientific-and-technological-activities_9789264065581-en Canberra manual] is based on a broad understanding of science. HRST by education covers all fields of study, in other words anybody who successfully completed a [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|tertiary level education]]. The HRST 'core' (HRSTC) — which is made up of people who possess a tertiary level education and who are employed in science and technology occupations — amounted to 55.2 million persons in 2024 across the whole EU and accounted for one-quarter (25.1%) of the total labour force. Concerning the HRST 'core', Romania (16.8%), Italy (18.0%), Czechia (20.4%) and Slovakia (20.5%) were the EU countries reporting the lowest figures of their labour force in that category in 2024. At the other end of the scale, HRSTC accounted for more than one-quarter of the labour force in Luxembourg (48.4%), Sweden (34.5%), Belgium (32.2%), Ireland (31.9%), Cyprus (31.0%), the Netherlands (30.8), Finland (30.1%), Denmark (30.0%), Lithuania (29.9%), France (29.7%), Poland (27.7%), Slovenia (25.9%) and Estonia (25.7%) (see Figure 5). [[Image:Figure 5 Human resources in science and technology, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Human resources in science and technology, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hrst_st_ncat}}|alt= Horizontal bar chart showing human resources in science and technology as percentage of active population aged 15-74 years in the EU, euro area, individual EU countries, EFTA countries and some candidate countries. Each country has two bars representing HRSTO people working in an S and T occupation and HRSTC people who have a tertiary education and work in an S and T occupation for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Between 2014 and 2024 there was a considerable increase in the relative importance of people classified as HRST 'core' within the EU's labour force, as their share rose by 6.2 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points]] (pp) (see Figure 6) from 18.9% to 25.1% in 2024. In fact, this share increased in all EU countries. The largest increases in the relative importance of the HRST core workforce were recorded in Cyprus (8.8 pp), Sweden (8.1 pp), the Netherlands and France (both with 8.0 pp), Poland and Ireland (both with 7.8 pp)Portugal (7.7 pp), Croatia (7.2 pp), Slovakia (7.1 pp) and Luxembourg (6.9 pp). [[Image:Figure 6 People with tertiary education and employed in science and technology, 2014 and 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: People who have a tertiary education and work in a science and technology occupation, 2014 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=hrst_st_ncat}}|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing people with tertiary education and employed in science and technology as percentage of active population aged 15 to 74 years in the EU, euro area, individual EU countries, EFTA countries and some candidate countries. Each country has two bars representing the years 2014 and 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Science and technology graduates=== Moving away from the broad definitions of HRST, Figures 7 and 8 look at the [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|international standard classification of education]] (ISCED) levels 5-8 (tertiary education) in the field of science and technology covering natural sciences, mathematics and statistics; information and communication technologies; engineering, manufacturing and construction. Within the EU (2023 data), there were 22.4 graduates of these science and technology fields of education per 1 000 persons aged 20 to 29 years. Among the EU countries (2023 data), relatively high ratios — above 20.0 graduates per 1 000 persons aged 20 to 29 years — were recorded in Ireland, Finland, France, Denmark, Austria, Germany, Spain, Portugal, Slovenia, Greece, Croatia, Sweden and Italy. In Ireland this ratio peaked at 39.5 graduates per 1 000 persons aged 20 to 29 years. This indicator should be interpreted cautiously because graduates are typically counted where they complete their studies, including non-resident or internationally mobile graduates who may return to their home country, after their graduation. Countries that host many international students may therefore record higher values, whereas countries whose residents earn degrees abroad may record lower values. This may explain the particularly low values inin some of the smallest EU countries, namely Luxembourg (6.1 graduates from science and technology fields of education per 1 000 persons aged 20 to 29), Malta (10.7) and Cyprus (12.0). [[Image:Figure 7 Science and technology graduates, 2013 and 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Science and technology graduates, 2013 and 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=educ_uoe_grad04}}|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing science and technology graduates with tertiary graduate levels 5 to 8 per 1000 persons aged 20 to 29 years in the EU, individual EU countries, EFTA countries and some candidate countries. Each country has two bars representing the years 2013 and 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] An analysis by sex of graduates in natural sciences, mathematics and statistics; information and communication technologies; engineering, manufacturing and construction shows that men (aged 20-29 years) are more likely to graduate in these fields than women. In 2023, the EU registered 29.0 male tertiary graduates in science and technology per 1 000 men aged 20-29 years and 15.5 female tertiary graduates per 1 000 women of the same age, a difference of 13.5 per 1 000. A gender gap was observed in all EU countries in 2023, ranging from 4.0 per 1 000 in Luxembourg, 4.6 per 1 000 in Malta and 4.9 per 1 000 in Romania to 21.4 per 1 000 in Ireland. [[Image:Figure 8 Science and technology graduates by sex, 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Science and technology graduates by sex, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=educ_uoe_grad04}}|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing science and technology graduates by sex with tertiary graduate levels 5 to 8 per 1000 persons aged 20 to 29 years in the EU, individual EU countries, EFTA countries and some candidate countries. Each country has two bars representing women and men for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Doctoral students=== A similar but more specific measure of a country's potential research capability is provided by the number of doctoral (PhD) students (see Figure 9). In 2023, there were an estimated 721 000 doctoral students in the EU. Women accounted for slightly less than half (an estimated 49.4%) of doctoral students in the EU in 2023. The gender split of doctoral students across the EU countries was typically quite balanced: women accounted for more than half of all the doctoral students in 16 out of the 27 EU countries in 2023, their share peaking at 61.0% in Latvia, 56.9% in Cyprus and at 56.5% in Lithuania. Among the 11 EU countries where a higher number of male than female PhD students was observed, the share of men peaked at 57.0% in Luxembourg, 55.3% in Czechia and at 54.0% in Austria. [[Image:Figure 9 Number of PhD students by sex, 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: Number of PhD students by sex, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=educ_uoe_enrt01}}|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing number of PhD students by sex as thousands in the EU, individual EU countries, EFTA countries and some candidate countries. Each country has two bars representing women and men for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In relative terms, the broad group covering science and technology accounted for 39.9% of the doctoral students in the EU in 2023 (Figure 10). Among the EU countries, natural sciences, mathematics and statistics; information and communication technologies; engineering, manufacturing and construction fields of education accounted for more than half of all doctoral students only in Luxembourg (63.1%) and Italy (54.5%). These fields were also very popular among students in France, Czechia, Estonia, Lithuania, Poland, Belgium, Ireland, Denmark, Croatia, Sweden and Germany where the shares ranged between 48.0% and 40.5%. The lowest proportion of PhD students in S&T fields of education was recorded in Malta (9.3%), Latvia (24.8%) and Bulgaria (25.3%). Among the remaining doctoral fields in the EU, the largest shares were health, welfare and services (22.2%), social science, business and law (18.5%) education, arts and humanities (16.0%), and agriculture and veterinary (2.9%). [[Image:Figure 10 PhD students by field of education, 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 10: PhD students by field of education, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=educ_uoe_enrt03}}|alt=Horizontal bar chart showing PhD students by field of education as percentage of total PhD students in the EU, individual EU countries, EFTA countries and some candidate countries. Totalling 100 percent, each country bar has five queues representing science and technology, social science, business and law, education arts and humanities, health and welfare, services, agriculture and veterinary and lastly, unknown for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Copy of Excel Personnel preliminary 2024 20260105.xlsx|title=R & D personnel: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''R&D personnel''' Statistics on R&D personnel are compiled using guidelines laid out in the 7th edition of the [https://www.oecd.org/sti/frascati-manual-2015-9789264239012-en.htm Frascati manual], published in 2015 by the [[Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)|OECD]]; the manual was updated with improved guidelines reflecting changes in the way that R & D is funded and carried out — see the [http://www.oecd.org/sti/frascati-manual-2015-9789264239012-en.htm Frascati manual 2015]. R&D personnel include all persons employed directly within R&D, as well as persons supplying direct services (such as managers, administrative staff and clerical staff). For statistical purposes, indicators on R&D personnel are compiled as both head counts (HC) and as full-time equivalents (FTEs). Researchers are a subcategory of R&D personnel and are professionals engaged in the conception or creation of new knowledge. They conduct research and improve or develop concepts theories, models, techniques instrumentation, software, or operational methods (Frascati manual 2015, pp 162, paragraph 5.35). '''Human resources in science and technology (HRST)''' Statistics on human resources in science and technology (HRST) are compiled using guidelines laid out in the Canberra manual, prepared in cooperation between the OECD, [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]], [[Glossary:United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)|UNESCO]] and the [[Glossary:International Labour Organization (ILO)|International Labour Organisation (ILO)]] and published in 1995. HRST data can be analysed by sex, age, region, sector of activity, occupation, educational attainment and fields of education (although not all combinations are possible). Data relating to stocks of HRST provide information on the number of HRST at a particular point in time, these stock data relate to the employment status as well as the occupational and educational profiles of individuals. HRST based on education (HRSTE) are persons having successfully completed tertiary education, defined as levels 5, 6, 7 or 8 of the 2011 version of the [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|international standard classification of education (ISCED)]]. Previously it was defined as levels 5 (a or b) or 6 of the 1997 version of ISCED. HRST based on occupation (HRSTO) are persons who are employed in science and technology occupations as 'professionals' or 'technicians and associate professionals' within the [https://ilostat.ilo.org/methods/concepts-and-definitions/classification-occupation/ International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO)]. Persons who fulfil both the education and the occupation criteria are classified as the HRST 'core' (HRSTC). Information on HRST flows from education are obtained from a UNESCO/OECD/Eurostat questionnaire on education and can be used to provide a measure of the current and future supply of HRST from the education system, in terms of actual inflows (graduates from the reference period) and potential inflows (students participating in higher education during the reference period). '''Science, technology and innovation''' Since the beginning of 2021, the collection of R&D statistics is based on Commission Implementing {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32020R1197:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 1197/2020}} of 30 July 2020. Statistics on science, technology and innovation were collected based on Commission Implementing {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012R0995:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 995/2012}} concerning the production and development of Community statistics on science and technology until the end of 2020. Science and technology graduates are defined as the number of new graduates from all public and private institutions completing science and technology related graduate and postgraduate studies in the reference year. To facilitate comparisons, the number of graduates may be expressed relative to the total number of persons aged 20-29 years and 25-29 years. '''Doctoral students''' Indicators based on the number of doctoral (PhD) students give an idea of the extent to which countries will have researchers at the highest level of education in the future. The data relate to the number of students in the reference year, they do not refer to the number of new graduates or to the total number (stock) of graduates in the labour market that year. The number of doctoral students is measured as students enrolled in ISCED 2011 level 8: this level concerns tertiary programmes which lead to the award of an advanced research qualification. Programmes at this ISCED level are devoted to advanced study and original research and are typically offered only by research-oriented tertiary educational institutions such as universities. Doctoral programmes exist in both academic and professional fields. ===Context=== The [http://ec.europa.eu/research/era/index_en.html European Research Area (ERA)] is composed of all research and development activities, programmes and policies in Europe which involve a transnational perspective and researchers' mobility. The recent document [https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/e6cd4328-673c-4e7a-8683-f63ffb2cf648_en?filename=Political%20Guidelines%202024-2029_EN.pdf Political Guidelines for the next European Commission 2024-2029], put investment in R&D 'at the centre of our economy. We will increase our '''''research spending''''' to focus more on strategic priorities [...]. Europe must also be at the cutting edge between emerging science, tech and industry, the nexus that will make this tech revolution faster and more transformative.' These Political Guidelines reconfirm the May 2021 Communication Global Approach to Research and Innovation adopted by the European Commission (Communication on a Global Approach to Research and Innovation — Europe's strategy for international cooperation in a changing world [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52021DC0252&qid=1634106511540 (COM(2021) 252 final)]) and the Communication on [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/f8f19fc4-2888-11eb-9d7e-01aa75ed71a1/ 'A new ERA for Research and Innovation'] (COM/2020/628 final). These programmatic documents underline the EU's desire to play a leading role in supporting international research and researchers' mobility, while delivering innovative solutions that support green and digital solutions in line with the sustainable development goals. It engages the EU to promote resilience, prosperity, competitiveness, economic and social well-being. These documents reiterate the European Commission adopted Communication of May 2008 to launch an initiative titled, ''{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52008DC0317:EN:NOT|title=Better careers and more mobility: a European partnership for researchers}}'' (COM(2008) 317 final). The goal of this initiative was to improve the mobility of researchers and to enhance the diffusion of knowledge throughout Europe, by balancing demand and supply for researchers at a European level, helping create centres of excellence and improving the skills of researchers in Europe. With this in mind, the EU and its Member States set-up a pan-European initiative — [http://euraxess.ec.europa.eu/ EURAXESS: researchers in motion] — which is designed to deliver information and support researcher mobility and career development, while enhancing scientific collaboration between Europe and the world. The same gateway is also used to promote the European Commission's initiative titled ''[http://euraxess.ec.europa.eu/jobs/science4refugees Science4Refugees]'', which is designed to help refugee researchers find jobs and to support refugee scientists in finding European researchers with whom they may discuss problems, find solutions and study together. In December 2008, the Competitiveness Council adopted a definition for a {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52009XG0131(01):EN:NOT|title=2020 vision for the ERA}}. According to the opening statement of this vision, all players should benefit from: the 'fifth freedom', introducing the free circulation of researchers, knowledge and technology across the ERA; attractive conditions for carrying out research and investing in R & D intensive sectors; Europe-wide scientific competition, together with the appropriate level of cooperation and coordination. This vision is part of the wider goals contained within the [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/6a915e39-0aab-491c-8881-147ec91fe88a/language-hr Europe 2020 strategy] for smart, sustainable and inclusive growth. In 2018 the Commission proposed an ambitious €100 billion research and innovation programme - Horizon Europe - to succeed Horizon 2020. Horizon Europe was subsequently adopted and launched for 2021–2027 with a budget of around €95.5 billion in current prices (including NextGenerationEU funding). The [https://marie-sklodowska-curie-actions.ec.europa.eu/ Marie Sklodowska-Curie actions], aim to support the career development and training of researchers — with a focus on innovation skills — in all scientific disciplines through worldwide and cross-sector mobility. ===Other articles=== *[[Human resources in science and technology]] *[[R&D expenditure]] ===Publications=== title: Recent developments in industry, construction, trade and services – short-term statistics data
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the recent developments in industry, construction, trade and services. Data extracted in December 2025 Planned article update: March 2027 Services production developing dynamically during recent years. Trade and construction production stagnating. Slight increase in industrial production. [[Image:EU, Index of production, industry, construction, services, and trade volume (2021 = 100).png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e6bb3f4c-2fc0-46c0-ba7f-dc3364c5baca?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-15T10:08:38Z sts_inpr_m]) ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sts_copr_m__custom_19386940/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=ddeb739e-2efe-4eb7-83a9-fe5ceb072757&c=1766052215000 sts_copr_m]) ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e3d301a4-78da-488f-8060-d4eb24bc41ac?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-08T09:46:41Z sts_sepr_m]) ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6415df33-3b44-487d-b35a-2946c1d93e19?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-08T11:08:23Z sts_trtu_m])|alt= Line chart showing index of production in the EU. Four lines representing services, construction and industry production as well as the total trade volume, monthly values from 2020 to 2025. 2021 is indexed at 100. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Production indices are business indicators, which measure the monthly changes of the price adjusted output of industry, construction and services. The trade volume measures the price-adjusted turnover in trade. ===Main economic influences since 2020=== In early 2020, the first cases of COVID-19 were diagnosed in Europe and around mid-March 2020 [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU countries]] began to introduce containment measures to fight the pandemic. The measures varied considerably from one country to the other and included the closing of bars, restaurants, hotels shops and many other businesses. The majority of measures were maintained in April and abandoned or reduced in scope and severity in May 2020. With increasing COVID-19 cases, containment measures were tightened again after the summer of 2020 and further increased in autumn and winter. Since March 2021, many measures have gradually been lifted. In early 2022, measures were further reduced or completely phased out. In general, the strictness, length and nature of the COVID-19 measures in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|EU]] were quite heterogeneous. The COVID-19 pandemic and the containment measures taken by EU countries were not the only factors that influenced economic development in recent years. The Russian military aggression against Ukraine and embargo measures since March 2022 have also affected production levels in the EU as well as trade volumes and are reflected in [[Glossary:Short-term_statistics|short-term statistics]] (STS) data. Moreover, as a result of worldwide containment measures, supply chains were disrupted and prices for many goods, especially energy, strongly increased. [[Image:EU, Index of production, industry, construction, services, and trade volume (2021 = 100).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: EU, Index of production, industry, construction, services and trade volume
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e6bb3f4c-2fc0-46c0-ba7f-dc3364c5baca?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-15T10:08:38Z sts_inpr_m]) ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sts_copr_m__custom_19386940/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=ddeb739e-2efe-4eb7-83a9-fe5ceb072757&c=1766052215000 sts_copr_m]) ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e3d301a4-78da-488f-8060-d4eb24bc41ac?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-08T09:46:41Z sts_sepr_m]) ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6415df33-3b44-487d-b35a-2946c1d93e19?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-08T11:08:23Z sts_trtu_m])|alt= Line chart showing index of production in the EU. Four lines representing services, construction and industry production as well as the total trade volume, monthly values from 2020 to 2025. 2021 is indexed at 100. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 1 provides an overview of the development of EU production indices for industry, construction and services (excluding financial and public services) as well as for the total trade volume (comprising the sale of motor vehicles, wholesale trade and retail trade). All 4 branches of the economy experienced unprecedented decreases in activity around March and April 2020. The COVID-19 crisis was followed by a recovery period and about a year later the former production levels had been re-reached to a more or less greater extent. In early 2022, the development in the 4 economic areas began to differ. Industrial and construction production as well as trade stagnated or slowly declined while the production of services remained on a rather steady upward path. According to the latest data (October 2025 for industry and construction, September 2025 for services and total trade). Services production is now 16% higher than in early 2020. The trade volume and the level of construction production is almost the same and industrial production only around 2 % higher than in February 2020 (i.e. just before the outbreak of the pandemic). ===Industry=== In most industrial sectors, the COVID 19 induced fall in production started in March 2020. There were only a few exceptions to this general trend, i.e. the mining of ores, the manufacture of paper, pharmaceutical products and computers. In these industries, the drop in production took place one month later, in April 2020. The only industry that appears not to have been affected by the crisis was the manufacturing of tobacco products. This industry, however, had already been on a steadily declining trend for several years (for more details see the article on [[Long term developments in industrial production - results from short-term statistics |Long term developments in industrial production - results from short-term statistics]]). Already in May 2020, industrial production began to recover on a broad level. Some industries reached their pre-crisis level again in August or September 2020 but total industry and several sub-sectors only surpassed the pre-crisis level in November 2020. For a number of industries, the recovery took even longer (e.g. food products). With the Russian attack on Ukraine the development of the various branches in industry started to differ relatively strongly (Figure 2). Some industries are now on a considerable higher level than in early 2020 (e.g. pharmaceutical products, transport equipment other than automobiles) while some other industries are nowadays at a considerably lower level (e.g. chemical products). [[Image:EU, Index of industrial production, total and selected industries (2021 = 100) v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: EU, Index of industrial production, total and selected industries
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sts_inpr_m__custom_19339893/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=e6bb3f4c-2fc0-46c0-ba7f-dc3364c5baca&c=1765793318000 sts_inpr_m])|alt= Line chart showing index of industrial production in the EU. Five lines represent total and selected industries' monthly values from 2020 to 2025. 2021 is indexed at 100. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Construction=== Total production in construction went down by more than 26% between February and April 2020. The construction of buildings fell by around 14%, whereas civil engineering work dropped by 20% and the production of specialised construction activities by 25% (Figure 3). [[Image:EU, Index of construction production (2021 = 100).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: EU, Index of construction production
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sts_copr_m__custom_19386940/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=ddeb739e-2efe-4eb7-83a9-fe5ceb072757&c=1766052215000 sts_copr_m])|alt= Line chart showing index of production in the EU. Four lines represent the monthly production of total construction, buildings, civil engineering, and specialised activities from 2020 to 2025. 2021 is indexed at 100. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In May 2020 a recovery set in, however, production levels dropped again in the first months of 2021. Only in early 2022 the pre-COVID-19 crisis level was surpassed. Since early 2022, production levels in construction dropped again – except for civil engineering. All in all, production levels in construction are more or less the same today as before the pandemic. ===Services=== In the first months of 2020, the COVID-19 crisis and the resulting containment measures by governments had a strong effect on the production of services. Within just 2 months, from February 2020 to April 2020, their production (excluding financial and public services) in Europe fell by around 17%. The development was quite heterogeneous. Most affected were accommodation and food services, i.e. mainly hotels and restaurants (Figure 4a). As a result of the lockdowns, social distancing measures, restricted access and reduced demand, their production fell by more than three-quarters. Until the summer of 2020 a recovery set in, but in the autumn and winter the production of accommodation and food services dropped again due to renewed containment measures. In late spring 2021 a second recovery phase started which was briefly interrupted during the winter 2021/2022. In spring 2022 the production of accommodation and food services reached about 92% of the pre-COVID-19 pandemic level, since then the production stagnated. During the COVID-19 pandemic, transport services declined by around 19%, in particular air transport was severely hit by the travel restrictions. The production of information services dropped by almost 4%; most strongly hit were the production of motion pictures, TV shows and similar activities. Professional and technical services decreased by almost 9%, administrative and support services and even real estate activities declined by 15% (Figure 4b). A clear effect of Russia's invasion of Ukraine on service production levels is not directly visible. In 2022 and 2023 service production increased more dynamically than the production in industry and construction and the trade volume. In particular, information and communication services developed quite dynamically while real estate activities stagnated. [[Image:EU, Index of food and accomodation services production (2021 = 100).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4a: EU, Index of food and accommodation services production
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sts_sepr_m__custom_19244700/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=e3d301a4-78da-488f-8060-d4eb24bc41ac&c=1765187201000 sts_sepr_m])|alt= Line chart showing index of production for food and accommodation services from 2020 to 2025. 2021 is indexed at 100. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:EU, Index of services production (2021 = 100).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4b: EU, Index of services production
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sts_sepr_m__custom_19244700/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=e3d301a4-78da-488f-8060-d4eb24bc41ac&c=1765187201000 sts_sepr_m])|alt= Line chart showing index of services production in the EU. Six lines represent total and selected services' monthly production from 2020 to 2025. 2021 is indexed at 100. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Trade=== The total trade volume in the EU, comprising retail trade, wholesale trade and the trade (and repair) of motor vehicles, decreased by more than 22% between February and April 2020. There were, however, significant differences between the various trade categories. Retail trade was reduced by around 20% but this reduction mainly concerned the sales of non-food articles, the retail sale of food products (including beverages and tobacco) fell by less than 1% and was soon back to a level that was close to what it had been before the COVID-19 crisis (Figure 5). [[Image:EU, Index of trade volume (2021 = 100).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: EU, Index of trade volume
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sts_trtu_m__custom_19246467/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=6415df33-3b44-487d-b35a-2946c1d93e19&c=1765192103000 sts_trtu_m])|alt= Line chart showing index of trade volume in the EU. Eight lines represent total and selected trade monthly volumes from 2020 to 2025. 2021 is indexed at 100. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The situation was especially dramatic for the trade volume of motor vehicles, which fell by more than half and the trade volume of fuel, which dropped by around 45%. In the meantime however the sales of automobiles have recovered. Wholesale trade decreased by around 3% since early 2020. Internet sales developed very dynamically in the early period of the pandemic, increasing by 20% between February and April 2020. After May 2020, a certain consolidation set in and internet sales dropped again for 2 months. However, with the exception of some temporary reductions in the second half of 2020, internet sales generally increased quite fast for around 1 year between the summer of 2020 and the spring of 2021. In summer 2021 internet sales declined again and have since then developed rather dynamically. Since early 2022 the retail trade volume increased by around 6%. This was largely due to increases in the sales of non-food products. The sales volume of food products declined by around 1%, probably as a result of price increases since 2022. ===Average growth rates for production and trade volume=== Table 1 presents the aforementioned developments in the form of average monthly rates of change for the period before the COVID-19 crisis, i.e. for the years 2015-2019, for the peak of the crisis, i.e. the months February to April 2020 and for the time between May 2020 and January 2022 (recovery period before the war in Ukraine) and the latest available data (October 2025 for industry and construction, September 2025 for services and trade). [[Image:Average monthly rates of change in production and trade volume, before, during and after the main COVID-19 crisis v3.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Average monthly rates of change in production and trade volume, before, during and after the main COVID-19 crisis
''Source:'' Eurostat (special calculations) {{Stable link|title=|code=sts_inpp_a}}, ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sts_inpr_m__custom_19341118/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=0a0348ba-1c44-4851-9f68-7b24b68a261c&c=1765796145000 sts_inpr_m]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sts_copr_m__custom_19386940/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=ddeb739e-2efe-4eb7-83a9-fe5ceb072757&c=1766052215000 sts_copr_m]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/89e607a7-3741-4288-b3d8-c403043c334f?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-15T11:15:01Z sts_sepr_m]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/366d5c81-f9d3-4f25-8ce4-803e1687ee33?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-15T11:05:31Z sts_trtu_m])|alt= Table showing average percentage monthly rates of change in production and trade volume before, during and after the main Covid-19 crisis in industry, construction, services and trade from the year 2015 to 2025. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In general, the average monthly growth in production and trade volume was relatively low between 2015 and 2019. The highest average increases were recorded for the production of pharmaceuticals (0.5% per month) and for information and communication services as well as for the trade in motor vehicles (both 0.4% per month). In March and April 2020, the general growth patterns were severely disrupted, in some areas with decreases of more than 50% within just 2 months. The recovery after the peak of the pandemic until early 2022 is recorded in the third column of Table 1, which shows comparatively high average growth rates, that are largely influenced by the recovery process in the summer of 2020. The development since February 2022, i.e. the start of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine, is shown in the last column. The highest average monthly increases in production levels were recorded for pharmaceuticals (0.7%), accommodation and food services (0.5 %), and information and communication activities (0.4%). Decreases were found for the production of chemical products (-0.5%), as well as for the production of computers and electrical equipment and the construction of buildings (both -0.2%). ===Industrial producer prices=== The development of total (domestic and non-domestic) industrial producer prices does not display major effects of the COVID-19 pandemic (Figure 6), most prices remained quite stable during the peak of the pandemic and also in subsequent months. Different from the general trend, prices for several energy products recorded 2-digit declines during the first half of 2020. [[Image:EU, Total output prices for selected industries 2020-2025 (2021 = 100), unadjusted data.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: EU, Total output prices for selected industries 2020 - 2025, unadjusted data (2021 = 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/sts_inpp_m__custom_19247634/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=e1a284f5-0b1f-44f3-a7be-536bff039c7a&c=1765195107000 sts_inpp_m])|alt= Line chart showing index of output prices in the EU as unadjusted data. Six lines represent total and selected industries' monthly prices from 2020 to 2025. 2021 is indexed at 100. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In the second half of 2021, a steep and rather steady rise in many producer prices set in. Between June 2021 and September 2022, the producer prices for total industry increased by 36%. Prices for the extraction of crude petroleum and natural gas increased by more than 300%. The prices of other energy industries also rose dramatically. Producer prices for electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning more than doubled, prices for coke and refined petroleum products saw a total increase of more than 60%. Since autumn 2022 industrial producer prices and in particular prices for energy products or energy related products and mining activities started to fall. However, price levels in October 2025 were still significantly higher than in the summer of 2021. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Recent developments STS December 2025 v2.xlsx|title=tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== Despite their name, the production indices are not intended to measure production but should – in theory – reflect the development of value added in the different branches of industry, construction and services. This means that the inputs obtained by one branch from another must be deducted from its gross output. In this way, double counting of production is prevented and the degree of vertical integration of branches should not influence the results for the indicator. In practice, however, it is difficult to collect value-added data on a monthly basis. Most statistical institutes, therefore, derive monthly production data from other sources including [[Glossary:Deflated|deflated]] [[Glossary:Turnover - SBS|turnover]], physical production data, labour input, intermediate consumption of raw materials and energy etc. [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publishes, on a monthly basis, production indices for [[Industrial production (volume) index overview|industry]], [[Construction production (volume) index overview|construction]] and [[Services production (volume) index overview|services]] for the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|EU]], for the [[Glossary:Euro area|euro area]] and the EU countries; data are also collected for several non-EU countries. For trade, a genuine production index is not available; instead, an index of [[Glossary:Volume of sales index|trade volume]] (price-adjusted turnover) is published. Data are presented in [[Glossary:Working-day adjustment|calendar adjusted]] and in [[Glossary:Seasonal adjustment|calendar and seasonally adjusted]] form. The data in this article were calculated with the [[Short-term business statistics - base year 2021|base year 2021]]. ===Context=== Production and trade volume indices are among the most important short-term statistics indicators. They are used to identify turning points in the economic development at an early stage and to assess the future development of [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|GDP]]. In order to serve this purpose they are now available on a monthly basis in a detailed activity breakdown. STS production indices also figure prominently among the so-called '[[Glossary:Principal European economic indicators (PEEI)|Principal European economic indicators (PEEI)]]' which are used to monitor and steer economic and monetary policies in the EU and in the euro area. ===Other articles=== *[[Industrial production (volume) index overview]] *[[Industrial producer price index overview]] *[[Construction production (volume) index overview]] *[[Services production (volume) index overview]] *[[Retail trade volume index overview]] ===Selected datasets=== :Construction, building and civil engineering (NACE F) (t_sts_cons) ::Production in construction (teiis500) :Trade and services (t_sts_ts) ::Wholesale and retail trade (NACE G) (t_sts_wrt) ::Services (t_sts_ser) ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/short-term-business-statistics/database Short-term business statistics (sts)], see: :Industry (sts_ind) ::Production in industry (sts_ind_prod) :Construction, building and civil engineering (sts_cons) ::Production in construction (sts_cons_pro) :Trade and services (sts_ts) ::Wholesale and retail trade (NACE G) (sts_wrt) ::Services (sts_os) ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=short_term_business_statistics}} Short-term business statistics] ===Methodology===
