title: Regional accounts - an analysis of the economy for NUTS level 3 regions
text:
Regional EU statistics on GDP (NUTS level 3) may be used to provide a broad measure of the concentration of economic activity, labour productivity and specialisation. Data extracted in February 2026. Planned article update: February 2027. 20% of the EU’s GDP was generated in 74 NUTS level 3 regions, which collectively covered 1.4% of the EU’s surface area. Compared with the average for the EU, regional labour productivity increased markedly between 2013 and 2023 in South-West, Dublin, Mid-West, West (all Ireland). [[File:Classification of regions based on their GDP per inhabitant in PPS, 2023 (NUTS level 3 regions)_NA2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3edea12e-d6ab-46cd-ab3e-d547d9bae3c1?lang=en nama_10r_3gdp] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/96004425-3401-4794-adf4-7f73dbd59700?lang=en nama_10r_3popgdp])|alt=A map showing the classification of NUTS level 3 regions into 5 groups based on their GDP per inhabitant in PPS. Data are shown for 2023 for level 3 regions of EU countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] This article provides an analysis of regional accounts data for the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union’s (EU)]] [[Glossary:NUTS|NUTS]] level 3 regions. Regional data at level 3 provide more granular (detailed) information than the data at level 2; Eurostat publications commonly present the latter. Based on the 2024 version of NUTS, there are 1 165 level 3 regions in the EU compared with 244 level 2 regions. The use of level 3 data makes it possible to have a regional analysis for several of the EU countries that only have a single level 2 region: there are only 2 EU countries – Cyprus and Luxembourg – that remain a single region at level 3. Furthermore, level 3 offers a more enlightening regional analysis for EU countries with only 2 or 3 regions at level 2, namely Ireland, Lithuania and Slovenia. For these EU countries, a level 2 analysis may be particularly unbalanced due to the dominance of the region that contains the capital city; note that this can also happen at level 3 for EU countries with only 2 or 3 regions. Equally, the information available at level 3 is much more detailed than that at level 2 for some of the larger EU countries. Most notably, Germany has 400 level 3 regions compared with 38 level 2 regions. While a regional analysis is more detailed at level 3 than at level 2, data are available for far fewer national accounts variables. For example, there are no regional accounts data on the compensation of employees, hours worked, investment or household accounts. The information available from regional accounts for level 3 concerns [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]] and [[Glossary:Population figure|population]], as well as a relatively aggregated activity analysis (depending on the EU country, either for 6 or for 10 economic activities according to [[Glossary:Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Community (NACE)|NACE]]) for [[Glossary:Gross value added|gross value added]] and [[Glossary:Employment|employment]].
'''Statistics on regions – the NUTS classification''' At the heart of regional statistics is the NUTS classification – a classification of territorial units for statistics. This regional classification for EU countries is based on a hierarchy of regions and subdivides each EU country into regions that are classified according to three different levels, covering levels 1, 2 and 3 from larger to smaller areas. Some EU countries have a relatively small population and may therefore not be subdivided at some (or even all) of the different levels of the NUTS classification. For example, Estonia, Cyprus, Latvia, Luxembourg and Malta are each composed of a single level 2 region according to the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/nuts/history 2024 version of the classification], while Cyprus and Luxembourg are also composed of a single level 3 region. Table 1 provides an overview of the number of NUTS regions in the EU as a whole and in individual EU countries.

[[Image:Number of NUTS 2024 regions_NA2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Number of NUTS 2024 regions
'' Source:'' Eurostat|alt=A table showing the number of level 1, level 2 and level 3 regions in each country. Data are shown as a count for the EU as well as for individual EU countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] ===Regional concentration of economic activity within the EU=== Map 1 shows the regional concentration of economic activity within the EU. For each region, GDP per inhabitant (also referred to as GDP per capita) has been calculated based on GDP data presented in [[Glossary:Purchasing power standard (PPS)|purchasing power standards (PPS)]].
'''GDP in PPS''' GDP expressed in PPS is calculated by applying [[Glossary:Purchasing power parities (PPPs)|purchasing power parities]], the latter being indicators of price level differences between countries. The use of purchasing power parities rather than market exchange rates to convert currencies makes it possible to compare the output of economies and the material welfare of their inhabitants in real terms, in other words, to control for differences in price levels. By convention, the GDP of the EU as a whole in PPS has the same value as in euro. By contrast, these values (in PPS and euro) are different for individual EU countries and regions, depending on the underlying price level differences. '''GDP per inhabitant''' By presenting indicators as ratios to the number of inhabitants in each region, the data are standardised to take account of the different size (in population terms) of each region.
The 1 165 regions in the EU for which data are available have been sorted based on the value of their GDP per inhabitant. They have then been grouped into 5 roughly equal parts, each accounting for 3.5 trillion (thousand [[Glossary:Billion|billion]]) PPS of GDP in 2023, in other words one fifth (20%) of the [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU’s]] total GDP. Just 74 level 3 regions made up the top fifth of the EU economy in 2023. These included 50 German regions (which together contributed 32% of the GDP within this group), 3 regions each from the Netherlands and Austria, 2 regions each from Belgium, Denmark, Ireland, France, Italy and Poland and 1 region each from Czechia, Hungary, Luxembourg, Romania, Slovakia and Sweden. These 74 regions covered an area of 58 170 square kilometres, representing 1.4% of the total area of the EU. The other groups (second to fifth) are composed of 130, 203, 330 and 428 level 3 regions, respectively. [[File:Classification of regions based on their GDP per inhabitant in PPS, 2023 (NUTS level 3 regions)_NA2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Classification of regions based on their GDP per inhabitant in PPS, 2023
(NUTS level 3 regions)
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3edea12e-d6ab-46cd-ab3e-d547d9bae3c1?lang=en nama_10r_3gdp] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/96004425-3401-4794-adf4-7f73dbd59700?lang=en nama_10r_3popgdp])|alt=A map showing the classification of NUTS level 3 regions into five groups based on their GDP per inhabitant in PPS. Data are shown for 2023 for level 3 regions of EU countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] There are 2 issues to keep in mind when using GDP per inhabitant measured in PPS as an indicator of the economic situation in a region. First, commuting flows are very important for certain EU countries and/or regions. The economic activity taking place in region A may result from the work of many people living in a neighbouring or nearby region B, which may even be in another EU country. Dividing the GDP of region A by the population of region A, results in a GDP per inhabitant of region A which appears to be relatively high. Two neighbouring level 3 regions in Germany – Wolfsburg and Helmstedt – illustrate this situation. Wolfsburg was the level 3 region with the highest GDP per inhabitant in 2023 in the EU, at 164 900 PPS, while the neighbouring region of Helmstedt had a GDP per inhabitant of 24 700 PPS. This difference in GDP per inhabitant – 6.7 times as high in Wolfsburg as in Helmstedt – is mainly explained by commuting flows. Secondly, the use of national PPS (as regional ones are not available) overstates the GDP per inhabitant in PPS in relatively expensive regions within any given EU country, while the values for relatively cheaper regions within an EU country are understated. The French regions of Paris and Mayotte are good examples. Applying the national PPS underestimates the price level in Paris and overestimates the price level in Mayotte. There are no official estimates of regional variations in price levels across the EU. However, estimates based on detailed data for consumer prices in Germany indicate that the regional variation may be as high as 26%, between level 3 regions, in particular, due to housing costs Weinand, S. & L. von Auer (2019): ''Anatomy of regional price differentials: Evidence from micro price data'', [http://www.bundesbank.de/resource/blob/776256/9c7f0381e6efdf649eccd33aab0ff297/mL/2019-02-08-dkp-04-data.pdf Discussion Paper 4/2019], Deutsche Bundesbank, Frankfurt am Main.. Bearing these issues in mind, Table 2 shows what percentage of the GDP for each EU country belonged to each of the 5 groups (classified according to the value of GDP per inhabitant in each region) for the year 2023. Looking at the bottom (fifth) 20% group, it includes regions that represent 61.0% of the national economy in Slovakia and also more than 50% in Hungary, Greece, Poland, Romania, Croatia and Bulgaria. By contrast, this group includes regions with less than 10% of the national economy in Belgium, Germany, Malta, Ireland and Austria, while no regions were in this group in Denmark, the Netherlands, Finland and Sweden, nor in Cyprus and Luxembourg (which are both mono-regional). The impact of commuting, among other factors (such as sectoral concentration and agglomeration economies), is visible, as the capital regions of Hungary, Poland, Romania and Slovakia are part of the top 20% group while most of the remaining regions of these countries are included in the bottom group. [[Image:Share of national GDP contributed by NUTS level 3 regions classified to each of the EU's five GDP groups, 2023 (%)_NA2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Share of national GDP contributed by NUTS level 3 regions classified to each of the EU’s five GDP groups, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3edea12e-d6ab-46cd-ab3e-d547d9bae3c1?lang=en nama_10r_3gdp] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/96004425-3401-4794-adf4-7f73dbd59700?lang=en nama_10r_3popgdp])|alt=A table showing the share of national GDP contributed by NUTS level 3 regions classified to each of the EU’s five GDP groups. Data are shown in percent for 2023 for EU countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Another interesting aspect of the concentration of regional economic activity concerns developments observed over time. Map 2 classifies the level 3 regions for which data are available according to 2 different criteria: whether their share of EU GDP decreased or increased between 2013 and 2023 and whether their share of national GDP decreased or increased during the same period. [[Image:Change in the regional share of national and EU GDP in PPS, 2013–23 (NUTS level 3 regions)_NA2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 2: Change in the regional share of national and EU GDP in PPS, 2013–23
(NUTS level 3 regions)
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f7f6835e-5d44-41bb-a422-58a4cebc8f25?lang=en nama_10r_3gdp])|alt=A map showing the change in the share of the GDP of NUTS level 3 regions in national and in EU GDP. Data are shown for 2013 to 2023 for level 3 regions of EU countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] All 19 level 3 regions in Finland saw their share of the EU’s GDP decrease between 2013 and 2023. This share decreased in 51 of 52 regions in Greece, 103 of 107 regions in Italy, 93 of 101 regions in France, 19 of 21 regions in Sweden, 325 of 400 regions in Germany, 8 of 10 regions in Lithuania, 6 of 8 regions in Slovakia, 20 of 35 regions in Austria and 21 of 40 regions in the Netherlands. A majority of regions in the remaining EU countries increased (or maintained) their share of the EU’s GDP. For example, all 12 Slovenian level 3 regions increased their share of the EU’s GDP between 2013 and 2023, as did all 8 Irish regions, both Maltese regions and the single regions of Cyprus and Luxembourg. Looking at the share of each region in national GDP (rather than in the EU total), 7 of the 8 Irish regions saw their share decrease, as was the case for 23 of the 28 Bulgarian regions, 4 of the 5 Estonian regions, 8 of the 10 Lithuanian regions, 15 of the 20 Hungarian regions, 9 of the 12 Slovenian regions. In some cases, the decreases in the shares were mainly explained by relatively large increases in the capital regions. For example, in the Lithuanian capital, Vilniaus apskritis, the share of national GDP increased from 39.4% to 45.5%. Notable exceptions included: *Ireland, where the only region to record an increase was South-West, up from a 14.3% share of national GDP to 24.5% *Estonia, where the only region to record an increase was Lõuna-Eesti, up from 16.6% to 18.5%. Decreases were also observed in at least half of the regions of most of the other EU countries. By definition, in the mono-regional countries (Cyprus and Luxembourg) there was no change in the share of national GDP. A majority of regions increased (or maintained) their share of national GDP in Slovakia (6 of 8 regions), Denmark (6 of 11 regions) and Austria (18 of 35 regions). Increases in the share of national GDP were observed for half (37) of the 74 regions in the top 20% of the EU economy (as identified in Map 1). These included the capital regions of Denmark, Hungary, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania and Sweden; the others were mainly concentrated in Germany (19 regions), Italy (2 regions), the Netherlands (2 more regions) and Austria (2 regions). By contrast, the capital regions of Belgium, Ireland, France and Slovakia were in the top 20% of the EU economy but recorded falls in their national shares, as was the case for 31 German regions – including, among others, Hamburg, Frankfurt am Main (Kreisfreie Stadt), Düsseldorf (Kreisfreie Stadt), Nürnberg (Kreisfreie Stadt) and Bonn (Kreisfreie Stadt) – as well as Hauts-de-Seine in France and Linz-Wels in Austria. ===Regional labour productivity=== In the first part of this article, regions were initially categorised by their GDP per inhabitant, which is the result of dividing GDP by the population. This section focuses on [[Glossary:Labour productivity|labour productivity]]. For this analysis, gross value added is used instead of GDP, with labour productivity calculated as gross value added per person employed. This is presented in euro rather than in PPS, as gross value-added data are not available in PPS; note that the PPS data for GDP are calculated from the expenditure approach for compiling GDP rather than the output approach which is used as the basis for data on gross value added. Another factor to consider before interpreting the results is that the average hours worked per person varies considerably across EU countries, regions and economic activities. People working in EU countries with higher productivity usually work fewer hours than people employed in EU countries that display lower levels of labour productivity. Furthermore, the productivity of an economy as a whole reflects the productivity of its different economic activities (implicitly weighted by the number of people employed in each activity). A region specialised in activities with a higher labour productivity will have a higher overall productivity than a region specialised in activities with a lower labour productivity, even if the productivity for each activity is the same in both regions. [[Image:Labour productivity of NUTS level 3 regions, 2023 (EUR per person employed)_NA2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 3: Labour productivity of NUTS level 3 regions, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bc8deaac-7f25-4f74-96b1-86fd475e024f?lang=en nama_10r_3gva] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/13e0b56d-4288-4dbb-a74c-fe9c2789e167?lang=en nama_10r_3empers])|alt=A map showing the labour productivity of NUTS level 3 regions. Data are shown in euro per person employed for 2023 for level 3 regions of EU countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Map 3 shows a distribution of regional gross value added based on a region’s labour productivity. The first step was to calculate the labour productivity for each level 3 region. Five classes of labour productivity were defined, each containing approximately the same number of level 3 regions, starting from the highest of €83 000 or more of gross value added per person employed down to the lowest where labour productivity was less than €40 000 per person employed. Once each region had been assigned to 1 of these 5 classes based on its labour productivity, the value added of the regions within each class were combined; from this value a distribution of national gross value added was calculated (see Table 3). Map 3 clearly shows the differences in labour productivity measured in euros between western and [[Glossary:Nordic_Member_States|Nordic]] regions on one hand and southern, eastern and [[Glossary:Baltic_Member_States|Baltic]] regions on the other. Table 3 shows what share of value added was contributed by regions classified to each of the labour productivity classes. The Nordic EU countries (Denmark, Finland and Sweden), Luxembourg, Ireland, Belgium, Austria and the Netherlands recorded the majority of their value added in their most productive regions. The only other EU countries with any regions that had an average labour productivity of at least €83 000 per person employed were Germany (47.5% of national value added), France (45.1%) and Italy (19.7%). [[Image:Share of national gross value added contributed by NUTS level 3 regions classified to specified labour productivity classes, 2023 (%)_NA2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Share of national gross value added contributed by NUTS level 3 regions classified to specified labour productivity classes, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bc8deaac-7f25-4f74-96b1-86fd475e024f?lang=en nama_10r_3gva] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/13e0b56d-4288-4dbb-a74c-fe9c2789e167?lang=en nama_10r_3empers])|alt=A table showing the share of national gross value added contributed by NUTS level 3 regions classified to specified labour productivity classes. Data are shown in percent for 2023 for EU countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] For each level 3 region, Figure 1 shows the change between 2013 and 2023 in a productivity index that has been calculated relative to the EU average. After deriving the level of labour productivity as described above, a ratio was calculated to show the labour productivity of each region relative to the average for the EU, with this ratio expressed as a percentage; by definition, the productivity index = 100 for the EU. The [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage point]] difference in this ratio between 2013 and 2023 was calculated and this is shown in the figure. Between 2013 and 2023, all of the level 3 regions in Bulgaria, Czechia, Estonia, Ireland, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Malta, Romania, Slovenia and Slovakia reported an increase in labour productivity compared with the EU average. This was also the case in all but 1 region in Poland. By contrast, none of the level 3 regions in Greece, Spain, Italy or Sweden reported an increase in labour productivity compared with the EU average, while only 2 regions in France reported an increase. Concerning mono-regional countries, Cyprus and Luxembourg both recorded decreases. [[Image:Change in the relative labour productivity of NUTS level 3 regions, 2013 to 2023 (percentage points, based on an index with EU = 100)_NA2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Change in the relative labour productivity of NUTS level 3 regions, 2013 to 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d382199f-9132-4124-b153-5d78e32cf4f4?lang=en nama_10r_3gva] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/71ce1fbb-136a-4aed-b027-0a44366ed033?lang=en nama_10r_3empers])|alt=A high-low chart showing the change in the relative labour productivity of NUTS level 3 regions. Data are shown in percentage points for the change from 2013 to 2023 for level 3 regions of EU countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The regions with the largest increases in relative labour productivity were the Irish regions of South-West, Dublin, Mid-West and West, with increases of 286, 105, 66 and 43 percentage points, respectively. These were followed by Spree-Neiße and Weimarer Land in Germany (up 42 and 41 percentage points, respectively) and the Romanian capital region, Bucureşti, also with an increase of 41 percentage points. Apart from Bucureşti, these regions all had a labour productivity in 2013 that was already above the EU average. At the other end of the range, the largest decrease in relative labour productivity was recorded in the Dutch region of Delfzijl en omgeving (down 299 percentage points). This was followed by another Dutch region, Overig Groningen (down 59 percentage points), the Greek region of Grevena, Kozani (down 55 percentage points) and the French overseas region of Guyane (down 52 percentage points). These regions all had above average relative labour productivity in 2013 but by 2023 Grevena, Kozani and Guyane both recorded below average values. ===Regional specialisation=== The final section of this article looks at regional specialisation of level 3 regions. For this purpose, the Krugman specialisation index is used. In this implementation, the index measures the extent to which the structure of a region’s output (value added) differs from the average for the EU. If the index is close to 0, it implies that the economic structure of the region is very similar to that of the EU (as a whole). The structure has been analysed based on 6 economic activities which collectively cover the whole economy and for which data are available for all level 3 regions. There were 27 level 3 regions in the EU for which the Krugman index was above 0.60 in 2023. These relatively high levels can mainly be attributed to a high degree of specialisation in industry. The exceptions were the Greek island region of Zakynthos and the French overseas region of Mayotte: *Zakynthos had a high specialisation in the category covering wholesale and retail trade, transport, accommodation and food service activities, and information and communication, reflecting the fact that it is a popular tourist destination *Mayotte had a high specialisation in the category covering public administration and defence; compulsory social security; education; human health and social work activities; arts, entertainment and recreation, repair of household goods and other services. An index above 0.60 was observed in 16 German regions, 3 regions in each of Bulgaria and Poland, 2 Greek regions and 1 region each in Ireland, France and Croatia. [[Image:Krugman regional specialisation index for value added, 2023 (NUTS level 3 regions)_NA2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 4: Krugman regional specialisation index for value added, 2023
(NUTS level 3 regions)
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9cb80d78-050a-46b6-b17e-9c576e7bea0a?lang=en nama_10r_3gva] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/21524f65-fc1b-4690-9fbe-ccca25e13b30?lang=en nama_10_a10])|alt=A map showing the Krugman regional specialisation index for value added. Data are shown for 2023 for level 3 regions of EU countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Regional accounts - an analysis of the economy for NUTS level 3 regions_NA2026.xlsx|title=Regional accounts – an analysis of the economy for NUTS level 3 regions: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The [[Glossary:European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)|European system of national and regional accounts (ESA 2010)]] is the latest internationally compatible accounting framework for a systematic and detailed description of the EU economy. [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-2010/overview ESA 2010] has been implemented since September 2014 and is consistent with worldwide guidelines on national accounting, as set out in the [[Glossary:System of national accounts (SNA)|system of national accounts (2008 SNA)]]. ESA 2010 provides the basis for the consistent, comparable, reliable and up-to-date compilation of economic statistics for EU countries. Regulation (EU) No 549/2013 of the European Parliament and the Council on the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32013R0549:EN:NOT|title=European system of national and regional accounts in the European Union}} provides the legal framework for these statistics. ESA 2010 is not restricted to annual national accounting, as it also applies to quarterly and shorter or longer period accounts, as well as to regional accounts. It is harmonised with the concepts and classifications used in many other social and economic statistics (for example, statistics on employment, business or international trade) and as such serves as a central reference for socioeconomic statistics. '''2024 benchmark revision''' Benchmark revisions are coordinated major revisions carried out at least once every 5 years to incorporate new data sources and major changes in international statistical methodology. In national accounts, they aim to ensure a maximum degree of consistency within national accounts. In other words, they should be implemented to obtain a long time series and ensure consistency across countries. For further information, please refer to the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/Annexes/reg_eco10_esms_an_Metadata_file_on_data_release.docx associated metadata]. ===Context=== In her
