title: Regional yearbook foreword
text:
Eurostat regional yearbook; 2026 edition; flagship publication; EU; regional statistics; NUTS; foreword; Mariana Kotzeva [[Image:Regional_yearbook_foreword_2026_MK.jpg|thumb|right|300px|300px|alt=A photograph of Eurostat’s Director-General, Mariana Kotzeva.]] Welcome to the 2026 edition of the ''Eurostat regional yearbook'', the longest-running flagship publication of the statistical office of the European Union. With a history spanning 55 years, the yearbook has for decades guided readers through the development, diversity, and dynamism of Europe’s regions. The 2026 edition brings together data from the 27 EU countries, 4 EFTA countries, and 9 candidate countries, offering a wide range of economic, social, and environmental findings. Since its debut in 1971, the yearbook has continued its tradition of providing detailed figures and maps, now enhanced with the vivid infographics for which Eurostat has become well known. With compelling visualisations and accessible explanations, the ''Eurostat regional yearbook'' transforms data into meaningful statistical insights. It offers trusted evidence to guide policymakers and strengthen cohesion, and it fosters a richer understanding of Europe’s regions for journalists, researchers, students, and inquisitive citizens alike. While remaining a valuable source of information for a broad spectrum of users, the yearbook has continued to evolve with economic, social and environmental changes, in step with new technologies and the transformations that they have brought. Among the novelties in this edition are sections on landscape features and precision farming, as well as extended analyses of diseases of the circulatory system, young people in the labour market, and housing. The ''Eurostat regional yearbook'' is available on Eurostat’s [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat website] as a [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/product?code=KS-01-26-039 PDF file] and through [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Statistics Explained], a section which provides explanatory articles and interactive maps. The most recent and detailed datasets can be accessed via Eurostat’s comprehensive [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database database]. Complementing the yearbook, readers can further explore Europe’s regions through the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/visualisations/my-region/ My region] data visualisation tool and the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/interactive-publications/regions-2026 Regions in Europe] interactive publication. I hope this edition of the yearbook serves as a valuable and informative reference, deepening your knowledge of Europe’s regions. '''Mariana Kotzeva'''
Director-General, Eurostat



This article forms part of the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026]'', an annual [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications flagship publication]. It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the EU, EFTA and candidate countries. {{Unit|topic=X_Regions}} [[Category:General and regional statistics|Regional yearbook foreword]] [[Category:Regions and cities|Regional yearbook foreword]] [[Category:Regional_yearbook|Regional yearbook foreword]]

title: Remittances according to the BPM6 manual
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of remittances according to the BPM6 manual for the EU and the member states. [[Glossary:Remittances|Remittances]] are an important measure derived from [[Glossary:Balance_of_payments|balance of payments]], which regularly receive attention in research and media. Remittances represent an important source of funding for households from other economies, arising mainly from the temporary or permanent movement of resident household members to abroad. By contributing to the [[Glossary:Gross_national_income_(GNI)|GNI]] and the disposable income of recipient countries, lower income countries around the world and within the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|EU]], benefit from this type of extra funding with regard to economic growth and poverty reduction. === Relevant components for the various remittances measures according to the BPM6 === In the 6th edition of the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (BPM6), remittances were introduced as a cumulative measure resulting in three aggregation levels: personal remittances, total remittances and total remittances including transfers to [[Glossary:Non-profit_institutions_serving_households_(NPISH)|non-profit institutions serving households (NPISHs)]]. These measures overall consist of two standard (personal transfers and compensation of employees) and additional supplementary components presented in BPM6, Table A5.1 and Table A5.2. The components are a mix of goods, services, primary, secondary income and capital account items and provide for measuring in a cumulative sequence, personal remittances (R1), total remittances (R2) and total remittances and transfers to NPISH (R3). The 2009 International Transactions in Remittances: Guide for Compilers and Users (RCG) is the compilation guide based on the concepts set out in BPM6. '''Personal Remittances:'''
Personal transfers
+ Compensation of employees less taxes, social contributions, expenditures for transport and travel
+ Capital transfers between households '''Total Remittances:'''
Personal Remittances
+ Social benefits '''Total Remittances and Transfers to NPISHs:'''
Total Remittances
+ Current and Capital transfers to NPISHs === The components in detail=== The components are referenced with their database identifier codes. '''For compiling personal remittances:''' '''Personal transfers (D752)'''
Personal transfers consist of all current transfers in cash or in kind between resident and non-resident households (BPM6, A5.7), disregarding the underlying source of income, the relationship between the households or the purpose of the transfer. Personal transfers replaced the BPM5 concept of “workers’ remittances” (a BPM6 memo-item), which was limited to what migrants send home to their immediate household members from their new place of employment abroad. '''Compensation of employees (D1)'''
[[Glossary:Compensation_of_employees|Compensation of employees]] refers to the income of border, seasonal and other short-term workers, who work in an economy where they are not residents (BPM6, A5.12). The income is remuneration in return for labour input, where an employer-employee relationship is present and both are residents of different economies (BPM6, 11.10). The earnings of individuals from the provision of services to another economy are, however, not included. To obtain the net value of compensation relevant for calculating personal remittances, supplementary items such as paid taxes, social contributions, transport and travel expenses, as well as personal expenses of seasonal, short-term employees and cross-border commuters need to be deducted. '''Current taxes on income and wealth payable by border, seasonal and other short-term workers (D5Z)'''
Taxes on income and wealth are mainly taxes levied on the income earned by non-resident short-term workers and cross-border commuters from the provision of their labour and payable to the host economy. They are a supplementary item (BPM6, 12.28) of other sectors other current transfers. For the purpose of personal remittances, these transfers need to be deducted from compensation of employees (D1). '''Social contributions related to employment of border, seasonal and other short-term workers (D61Z)'''
Non-resident short-term workers and cross-border commuters make social contributions to social insurance schemes (public or employment-related schemes, funded or unfunded pension schemes) of the host economy where they are employed. Because the amount payable by employers is also included in the compensation of employees, the total of actual and rerouted contributions (on behalf of the employer) are payable by the employee and recorded as other current transfers supplementary item (BPM6, 12.32). For the purpose of personal remittances, these transfers need to be deducted from compensation of employees (D1). '''Passenger services in form of transport and travel payable by border, seasonal and other short-term workers (SCAZ)'''
Passenger services relate to services expenses on international transport that border, seasonal and other short-term workers pay for their commute to the place of employment in the host economy. Expenditures on local transportation of non-resident employees within their host economies are covered under travel services. These subcomponents of transport and travel, respectively (BPM6, 10.76), are deducted from compensation of employees (D1) for calculating personal remittances. '''Personal expenses: Acquisition of goods and services by border, seasonal and other short-term workers (SDA1)'''
The acquisition of goods and services for personal use by cross border, seasonal and other short-term workers in the host economy are a subcomponent of business travel services (BPM6, 10.93). It should be noted that expenditures by seasonal or cross-border workers for durable and valuable goods are included in the goods account and would need to be subtracted as well from the gross compensation (D1). '''Capital transfers between households (D99R1)'''
Infrequent and extraordinary large capital transfers, such as donations or inheritances, in which the ownership of assets changes between resident and non-resident households, may be identified separately when considered significant (BPM6, 13.35). Capital transfers between households are a supplementary item in the capital account. '''For compiling Total remittances and Total remittances and transfers to NPISHs:''' '''Social benefits (D62)'''
Social benefits relate to international current transfers receivable from social security or pension funds, but also any other sickness, unemployment, housing or education schemes in the context of employment in another economy (BPM6, 12.40). Social benefits is a supplementary item within the secondary income and has to be included to arrive at the concept of total remittances (BPM6 A5.14). '''Current transfers to NPISH (D751) and Capital transfers to NPISH (D99R2)'''
Current and capital transfers to NPISHs from any sector of the sending economy (households, corporations, governments, and non-profit institutions) include funds and non-cash items that flow indirectly to households through non-profit institutions (BPM6, A5.15). Current transfers received by and sent to NPISHs are supplementary items within the miscellaneous current transfers of secondary income; capital transfers are supplementary in the other capital transfers of the capital account. === The measures in detail from the perspective of the recipient economy === '''Personal remittances (R1)'''
Personal remittances are defined as current and capital transfers in cash or in kind receivable by resident households from non-resident households plus net compensation of employees receivable by resident workers that temporarily work abroad or are cross-border commuters. In order to obtain a net value for compensation of employees, four supplementary components concerning taxes, social contributions, transport and personal expenses have to be deducted from the corresponding standard component (BPM6, A5.10). ::'''R1 = D752 + [D1 – (D5Z + D61Z + SCAZ + SDA1)] + D99R1''' '''Total remittances (R2)'''
Total remittances are the sum of personal remittances receivable and social benefits receivable; thus, the measure additionally includes cross-border transfers of acquired benefits from social security and pension funds abroad. (BPM6, A5.14). ::'''R2 = R1 + D62''' '''Total remittances and transfers to NPISHs (R3)'''
This measure includes total remittances receivable plus current and capital transfers receivable by resident NPISHs. This adds donations in cash or in kind, cross-border sponsorships, aid programs in relation to health, educational and cultural development from non-resident governments and the private sector to resident charitable organisations (NPISHs). This measure is defined in a broader context beyond the limits of migration-related transfers and donations, and is a more general indicator of the impact of international development programs and activities. ::'''R3 = R2 + D751 + D99R2''' === The current data situation for compiling remittances measures according to the BPM6 === In June 2014, BPM6 was introduced in European balance of payments statistics in line with EC Regulations 184/2005 and 555/2012 on community statistics concerning balance of payments, international trade in services and foreign direct investment. Currently, only the two standard components for remittances (personal transfers and compensation of employees) are readily available for the calculation of remittances measures. Consequently, Eurostat cannot compile the broader measures of R2 and R3. Due to the lack of supplementary components, also the compilation of personal remittances (R1) is incomplete, resulting from compensation of employees being available predominantly on a gross basis without the availability of the four supplementary items that need to be deducted, as well as missing cross-border capital transfers between households. In summary, currently no remittances measures in European statistics are available that strictly adhere to the BPM6 concepts. For the needs of macroeconomic management and surveillance, it is however already of interest to assess personal transfers and gross values for compensation of employees; see: Eurostat Statistics Explained article: [[Personal transfers and compensation of employees]]. The World Bank publishes annual data of estimates for personal remittances as part of its World Development Indicators Data starting from 2005 are available according to the BPM6., using the sum of the two standard components. '''Possible reasons for the missing components:''' '''(1) Voluntary character of supplementary components in the BPM6'''
The reporting of supplementary items related to the calculation of remittance measures is considered voluntary, thus remaining at the discretion and needs of the compiler (BPM6, A5.9). Through this, the BPM6 allows compilers to keep a cost-benefit balance in their statistical production processes. '''(2) Relative insignificance of remittances flows in some economies '''
In some advanced economies, remittances inflows to households may appear of minor importance compared to other international transaction volumes in their balance of payments statistics. As a consequence, data production of these items may rank lower in priority and the production of voluntary data is deemed too costly. The lack of resources and source data may also be a constraint in lower income economies, even though these transfers may constitute a significant source of income in these recipient economies. '''(3) Heterogeneous character of remittances transactions'''
Due to its heterogeneous character, compilation of data on remittances requires a combination of data sources, which makes the underlying data production process more complex For full description and discussion of data sources, see RCG Chapter 4.. While data from the international transactions reporting systems (ITRS) cannot be considered complete as they only cover transactions conducted through formal channels in the financial sector, the collection of survey data may be less timely and frequent (RCG, 5.10), and is more costly. Surveys relating to households and specifically to border, seasonal and other short-term workers are demanding to the compiler with respect to the target population of the recipient counterparts; the survey would have to rely on sampling due to cost-benefit reasons and would require further quality interventions (estimations, secondary data sources, and adjustments). Consequently, compiling data on remittances is less straightforward compared to other balance of payments items, and thus, the immediate availability of consistent data cannot be expected. '''(4) Bilateral asymmetries'''
For the European balance of payments statistics, compilers report geographical breakdowns for transactions related to personal transfers and compensation of employees. These bilateral breakdowns by countries are vital for further quality analysis as they provide valuable information on the most relevant remittance corridors (RCG, 6.12). === Other articles === *[[Personal_transfers_and_compensation_of_employees|Personal transfers and compensation of employees]] *[[Balance of payments and international investment position manual (BPM6)]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/balance-of-payments/database Balance of payments (bop)], see: : Personal transfers and compensation of employees (bop_rem6) ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20230126-1 News article - Extra-EU personal transfers in 2021] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-eurostat-news/-/ddn-20220107-1 News article - Amounts sent to non-EU countries by EU residents in 2020] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-eurostat-news/-/ddn-20211214-1 News article - EU residents sent €34.1 billion in 2020 to non-EU countries] ===Methodology=== *[http://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/bop/2007/bopman6.htm Balance of payments and international investment position manual, Washington D.C., IMF 2009, 6th edition (BPM6)] *[https://www.imf.org/external/np/sta/bop/2008/rcg/pdf/guide.pdf International Transactions in Remittances: Guide for compilers and users, Washington D.C., IMF 2009 (RCG)] ===Legislation=== *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32005R0184:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 184/2005}} of 12 January 2005 on Community statistics concerning balance of payments, international trade in services and foreign direct investment. * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=legissum:070204_1 Summaries of EU Legislation: EU statistics — balance of payments, trade in services and foreign direct investment] *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012R0555:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 555/2012}} of 22 June 2012 amending Regulation (EC) No 184/2005 on Community statistics concerning balance of payments, international trade in services and foreign direct investment, as regards the update of data requirements and definitions. ===External links=== *[http://data.worldbank.org/indicator/BX.TRF.PWKR.CD.DT World Bank DataBank] === Footnotes === <'''footnote text will be automatically inserted if reference tags are used in article content text (use reference icon on ribbon)'''> {{Unit|topic=X_Balance_of_payments}} [[Category:Economy and finance|Remittances according to the BPM6]] [[Category:Balance of payments|Remittances according to the BPM6]] [[Category:Background article|Remittances according to the BPM6]]

title: Renewable energy statistics
text:
Statistics on renewable energy sources in the EU cover their production and share in energy consumption. Data extracted on 13 July 2026 Planned article update: December 2026 In 2025, renewables made up 26.2% of energy consumed in the EU, up from 25.2% in 2024. Renewable electricity accounted for 49.9% of all electricity consumed in the EU in 2025, up from 47.5% in 2024. Renewable energy made up 27.3% of energy used for heating and cooling in 2025, up from 26.7% in 2024. [[Image:Share_of_energy_from_renewable_sources_2025_Graphic_Designer.jpg|thumb|center|700px|alt= Vertical bar chart showing overall share of energy from renewable sources as percentages in the EU, EU countries, and Norway for the year 2025.]] This article provides the most recent statistics on the share of [[Glossary:Renewable energy sources|energy from renewable sources]] overall and in 3 consumption areas ([[Glossary:Electricity|electricity]], heating and cooling, and transport) in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Renewable energy sources include wind power, solar power (thermal, photovoltaic, and concentrated), hydropower, tidal power, geothermal energy, ambient heat captured by heat pumps, [[Glossary:Biofuels|biofuels]], and the renewable part of [[Glossary:Waste|waste]]. The use of renewable energy has many potential benefits, including a reduction in [[Glossary:Greenhouse gas (GHG)|greenhouse gas]] emissions, the diversification of energy supplies, and a reduced dependency on [[Glossary:Fossil fuel|fossil fuel]] markets (in particular, oil and gas). The growth of renewable energy sources may also stimulate employment in the EU, through the creation of jobs in new 'green' technologies, which will be one of the cornerstones of the [https://energy.ec.europa.eu/strategy/energy-union_en Energy Union] and the [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/clean-industrial-deal_en Clean Industrial Deal]. All 2025 data in this article are provisional and based on early estimates. Where 2025 data are not available, 2024 data are shown instead. ===Share of renewable energy reached 26.2% in 2025 === According to provisional data, the EU reached a 26.2% share of its gross [[Glossary:Final_energy_consumption|final energy consumption]] from renewable sources in 2025, around 1 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage point (pp)]] higher than in 2024 and almost 3 times higher than in 2004 (9.6%). [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202302413 EU Directive 2023/2413] on the promotion of the use of energy from renewable sources has revised the EU's 2030 renewable energy target from 32% to 42.5% (with an aim to increase it to 45%). Therefore, EU countries need to intensify their efforts to collectively comply with the EU target for 2030, which requires increasing the share of renewable energy sources in the EU's gross final energy consumption by more than 16 pp in just 5 years. Figure 1 shows the latest data available for the share of renewable energies in gross final energy consumption. [[Image:Share of energy from renewable sources, 2025 (%).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Share of energy from renewable sources, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nrg_ind_ren__custom_22125475/default/table (nrg_ind_ren)]|alt=a vertical bar chart share of energy from renewable sources 2025 as a percentage of gross final energy consumption in the EU countries and some of the EFTA and candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Sweden had the highest share among the EU countries, with 65.4% of its gross final energy consumption coming from renewable sources in 2025. Sweden’s main renewable energy sources, in descending order, were solid biomass, hydro, and wind. Finland followed with 53.0%, relying mainly on solid biomass, followed by wind and hydropower. Denmark had the next-highest share at 48.2%, with solid biomass contributing the most, followed by wind and biogas. The lowest shares of renewables were recorded in Belgium (14.9%), Slovakia (16.3%), and Ireland (17.2%). Table 1 presents data for all reporting countries. [[Image:Overall share of energy from renewable sources, 2004-2025 (% of gross final energy consumption).png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Share of energy from renewable sources, 2004-2025
''Source'': Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nrg_ind_ren__custom_22125457/default/table (nrg_ind_ren)]|alt=a table showing the share of energy from renewable sources from 2004 to 2025 as a percentage of gross final energy consumption in the EU countries and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries, and potential candidates. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Some countries used statistical transfers to maintain higher levels than their 2020 targets (which is an obligation for the 2021-2030 period) or simply to increase their share. Statistical transfers are agreements between EU countries to transfer a specified amount of energy from renewable sources from one EU country to another. See Table 1a for more details on the statistical transfers reported for reference year 2024 (data for 2025 are not yet available). [[Image:Statistical_transfers_reported_by_countries_for_reference_year_2024_(thousand_tonnes_of_oil_equivalent,_ktoe).png |thumb|center|700px|Table 1a: Statistical transfers reported by countries for reference year 2024
''Source'': Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nrg_ind_stjpjss__custom_19370105/default/table (nrg_ind_stjpjss)]|alt=a table showing the statistical transfers reported by countries for the reference year 2024 in thousand [[Glossary:Tonnes_of_oil_equivalent|tonnes of oil equivalent]] for the amount deducted from the share of renewables and the amount added for the share of renewables from one Member State to another Member State. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The rest of this article's statistical findings deal with the developments from 2004 to 2025 in the share of energy from renewable sources in 2 areas: electricity and heating and cooling, and from 2004 to 2024 in the share of energy from renewable sources in transport (data for 2025 are not yet available). === Renewables account for almost 50% of total electricity in 2025 === In 2025, renewable energy sources made up 49.9% of [[Glossary:Gross_electricity_consumption|gross electricity consumption]] in the EU, more than 2 pp higher than the previous year (47.5% in 2024). The growth in [[Glossary:Gross_electricity_generation|electricity generated]] from renewable energy sources during the period 2015 to 2025 largely reflects an expansion in 2 renewable energy sources across the EU, namely wind power and solar power. Looking at detailed data (available only up to 2024), wind power and hydropower accounted for almost two-thirds of the total electricity generated from renewable sources (38.0% and 26.4%, respectively). The remaining one-third of electricity generated was from solar power (23.4%), solid biofuels (5.8%) and other renewable sources (6.1%). Solar photovoltaic power is the fastest-growing source: in 2008, it accounted for 1%. This means that the growth in electricity from solar power has been dramatic, rising from just 7.4 [[Glossary:Terawatt_hours_(TWh)|terawatt hours (TWh)]] in 2008 to 304 TWh in 2024 (for more information, visit the Eurostat dataset [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nrg_ind_ured__custom_22126737/default/table (nrg_ind_ured)] The share of energy from renewable sources in electricity is presented in Figure 2. [[Image:Share of energy from renewable sources in gross electricity consumption, 2025 (%).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Share of energy from renewable sources in gross electricity consumption, 2025
''Source'': Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nrg_ind_ren__custom_22125498/default/table (nrg_ind_ren)]|alt=A vertical bar chart showing share of energy from renewable sources in gross electricity consumption for 2025 in the EU countries and some of the EFTA and candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] According to provisional data, among the EU countries, more than 75% of electricity consumed in 2025 was generated from renewable sources in Austria (90.8%), Sweden (89.2%), and Denmark (77.7%). The consumption of electricity from renewable sources was also higher than 60% in Portugal (65.6%), Greece (60.9%), and Spain (60.7%). At the other end of the scale, the share of electricity from renewable sources was less than 25% in Malta (11.2%), Czechia (19.2%), Luxembourg (23.3%), and Slovakia (24.1%). The [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA ]]countries Norway and Iceland, as well as the [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate country]] Albania, produced more electricity from renewable sources than the total amount of electricity they consumed in 2025 (Norway) and 2024 (Iceland and Albania), therefore leading to shares higher than 100%. In some of these cases, the effect comes from higher production than consumption with net exports (Norway, which stands at 122%) or real share at 100%, but hydro normalisation brings the share result to a higher level (Iceland with 102.4% and Albania with 105.2%). For more details, see Table 2. [[Image:Share of energy from renewable sources in gross electricity consumption, 2004-2025 (%).png |thumb|center|700px|Table 2: Share of energy from renewable sources in gross electricity consumption, 2004-2025
''Source'': Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nrg_ind_ren__custom_22125518/default/table (nrg_ind_ren)]|alt=A table showing the share of energy from renewable sources in gross electricity consumption, from 2004 to 2025 as a percentage of gross final electricity consumption in the EU countries and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries, and potential candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===27.4% of energy used for heating and cooling from renewable sources=== In 2025, renewable energy accounted for 27.4% of total energy use for heating and cooling in the EU, increasing from 11.7% in 2004. Developments in the industrial sector, services, and households contributed to this growth. Ambient energy captured by heat pumps for heating and renewable cooling are also taken into account. Country-level data, which are available only up to 2024, are presented in Figure 3. [[Image:Share_of_energy_from_renewable_sources_for_heating_and_cooling,_2024_(%).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Share of energy from renewable sources for heating and cooling, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nrg_ind_ren__custom_19370127/default/table (nrg_ind_ren)]|alt=A vertical bar chart showing the share of energy from renewable sources for heating and cooling in 2024 in the EU countries and some of the EFTA and candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among the EU countries, the share of energy from renewable sources in heating and cooling in 2024 was more than 50% in Sweden and Estonia (both at 67.8%), Finland (62.6%), Latvia (61.8%), Malta (59.2%), Denmark (56.4%), and Lithuania (52.1%). The EFTA country Iceland also stood out with a 79.5% share. At the other end of the scale, the EU countries with a share of energy from renewable sources in heating and cooling of less than 20% were Ireland (7.9%), the Netherlands and Belgium (both 11.3%), Germany (17.7%), and Luxembourg (19%), see Table 3. [[Image:Share_of_energy_from_renewable_sources_for_heating_and_cooling,_2004-2024_(%).png|thumb|center|700px|Table 3: Share of energy from renewable sources in heating and cooling, 2004-2024
''Source'': Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nrg_ind_ren__custom_19370073/default/table (nrg_ind_ren)]|alt=A table showing the share of energy from renewable sources in heating and cooling from 2004 to 2024 in the EU countries and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries, and potential candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===11.2% of renewable energy used in transport activities in 2024=== The average share of energy from renewable sources in transport increased from 1.4% in 2004 to 11.2% in 2024. By 2030, EU countries must either increase the share of renewable energy used in transport to at least 29% or reduce the greenhouse gas intensity of transport fuels by at least 14.5%. Renewable energy used in transport includes liquid biofuels, renewable hydrogen, biomethane, ‘green’ electricity, etc. The share of energy from renewable sources in transport is presented in Figure 4. [[Image:Share of energy from renewable sources in transport, 2024 (%).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Share of energy from renewable sources in transport, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nrg_ind_ren__custom_19370122/default/table (nrg_ind_ren)]|alt=A vertical bar chart showing the share of energy from renewable sources in transport, 2024, as a percentage of gross final energy consumption in the EU countries and some of the EFTA and candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among EU countries, the share of renewable energy in transport fuel consumption ranged from highs of 26.4% in Sweden and 20.3% in Finland down to less than 5% in Croatia (0.9%) and Greece (3.9%). The EFTA country Norway also reported a high share of renewable energy in transport fuel consumption (33.6%), while the candidate and potential candidate countries all show a very low share of renewable energy in transport (from zero to around 1%). The share of energy from renewable sources in transport is presented in Figure 4. More details on the share of energy from renewable sources in transport can be found in Table 4. [[Image:Share_of_energy_from_renewable_sources_in_transport,_2004-2024_(%).png |thumb|center|700px|Table 4: Share of energy from renewable sources in transport, 2004-2024
''Source'': Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nrg_ind_ren__custom_19370076/default/table (nrg_ind_ren)]|alt=A table showing the share of energy from renewable sources in transport from 2004 to 2024 as a percentage of final energy consumption in transport in the EU countries and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries, and potential candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=Renewable_energy-tables_and_figures_2025_prov.xlsx|title=Renewable energy: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data presented in this article are based on energy statistics covered by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R1099:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008}} on energy statistics. In addition, the methodology laid down in {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009L0028:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2009/28/EC}} (also known as RED I) is used until reference year 2020. From 2021 until 2024, the calculation of the share of energy from renewable sources follows the accounting rules set down in {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018L2001:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2018/2001/EU}} (also known as RED II) on the promotion of the use of energy from renewable sources. Due to the change of legal basis, a break in series occurs between 2020 and 2021. Another important aspect to take into account when comparing 2020 with 2021 data is the lifting of restrictions linked to the COVID-19 pandemic, which produced an increase of energy consumption and a possible decrease of the share of renewables. Readers are encouraged to analyse the differences between both Directives (RED I and RED II), the energy market and all national specificities before drawing any conclusions from the comparison of year 2021 with previous time series. Analysing the break in series between 2020 and 2021, there are some cases in which the share of renewables substantially changed: *Bulgaria: more than 6 pp decrease, due to the inability to report a certain part of their solid and gaseous biofuels as compliant. This might change in the future once it can benefit from a certification procedure. *Denmark: around 10 pp increase, due to the reduction in its statistical transfers (as seller). *Estonia: around 7.5 pp increase, mainly because it started to report the use of heat pumps for heating purposes (which, although already existent, Estonia had not reported them previously). *Ireland: more than 3.5 pp decrease, due to its decision not to use statistical transfers in 2021, as well as its inability to report a certain part of its solid and gaseous biofuels as compliant. Data are available for all EU countries, as well as Norway, Iceland, Montenegro, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Albania, North Macedonia, Kosovo*, Georgia, and Moldova. In general, data are complete and comparable across countries. ''Kosovo*: This designation is without prejudice to positions on status, and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo declaration of independence.'' From reference year 2025 onwards, calculations follow the methodology introduced by [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202302413 Directive 2023/2413] (also known as RED III). The most significant change introduced by RED III affects the share in transport, which goes down by several percentage points due to the increase of the transport scope. Statistical revisions in datasets submitted by reporting countries in their annual energy questionnaires have played a role in the change in data over a long period. As a consequence of the Renewable Energy Directive and the requirement of the Energy Statistics Regulation to report detailed energy consumption data in households, countries are monitoring the flows of renewable energy commodities in their economies more closely. A very significant case is the consumption of biomass, where countries are launching new, more detailed surveys that usually result in higher quantities of biomass and therefore an increase of the final energy consumption of biomass. As a consequence of several countries revising their data, significant increases have been observed in their share of energy from renewable sources (e.g. Croatia, France, Lithuania, Hungary, and recently, Poland). '''Gross final consumption of energy''' is defined in RED I as the energy commodities delivered for energy purposes to industry, transport, households, services (including public services), agriculture, forestry and fisheries, including the consumption of electricity and heat by the energy branch for electricity and heat production and including losses of electricity and heat in distribution and transmission. The concept of transport fuel production is included in the definition in RED II, but will disappear with the implementation of RED III. Energy production from non-renewable municipal wastes was deduced from the contribution of biomass to heating and electricity generation. Consumption for pipeline transport was included in gross final consumption of energy, in line with the sectoral classification of the Energy Statistics Regulation. To improve accuracy and consistency with national statistics in calculating renewable energy shares, '''national calorific values''' were used, where available, for converting quantities of all energy products into energy units, instead of the default calorific values. The exception is the use of fuels in transport, where calorific values from Annex III of RED I or RED II are used. '''Data for the period 2004-2010''': RED I did not yet exist or had not been transposed into national legislation. The values in these years are not used for any measurement of legislative compliance with the indicative trajectory defined in part B of Annex I of the Directive (RED I). RED I stipulates that only biofuels and bioliquids that fulfil sustainability criteria should be counted for the targets. It was decided that for the years 2004-2010 all biofuels and bioliquids would be counted towards the numerator of the share of energy from renewable sources. '''Data for 2011 - 2020''': Compliance with Article 17 (Sustainability criteria for biofuels and bioliquids) has to be assessed with respect to Article 18 (Verification of compliance with the sustainability criteria for biofuels and bioliquids). As of reference year 2011, countries are to report as compliant only those biofuels and bioliquids for which compliance with both Article 17 and Article 18 can be fully demonstrated. Only reported compliant biofuels and bioliquids are counted towards the respective shares of renewables. In some countries, consumption of biofuels and bioliquids in the period 2011-2015 were not certified as compliant (sustainable) due to late implementation of RED I. While the share of renewable energy as a whole has been increasing since 2004, between 2010 and 2011, its share in transport decreased. This can be attributed in part to the total absence of compliant biofuels reported by several EU countries (countries did report some biofuel use, but none or very little of it was compliant in 2011). As some countries had not yet fully implemented all provisions of the Renewable Energy Directive, some biofuels and bioliquids were not counted as compliant (sustainable) in the period 2011-2015. '''Data for 2021 and onwards''': Compliance with Article 29 ('Sustainability and greenhouse gas emissions saving criteria for biofuels, bioliquids and biomass fuels') has to be judged also with respect to Article 30 ('Verification of compliance with the sustainability and greenhouse gas emissions saving criteria'). As of data from the second half of 2021, countries should report as compliant only those biofuels, bioliquids, and biomass fuels for which compliance with Articles 29 and 30 can be fully demonstrated. Otherwise (even when compliance cannot be demonstrated because there is not a national legal basis in place), biofuels, bioliquids, and biomass fuels should not be reported as compliant and do not count towards the numerator of the share of energy from renewable sources. The share of electricity from renewable energy sources is defined as the ratio between electricity produced from renewable energy sources and gross national electricity consumption. As stipulated in the Renewable Energy Directive, gross final consumption of '''electricity from renewable sources''' is the electricity produced from renewable energy sources. This includes hydropower plants (excluding hydropower electricity produced from pumped storage plants using water previously pumped uphill), as well as electricity generated from solid biofuels/wastes, wind, solar, and geothermal installations. The Directive also requires electricity production from hydropower and wind power to be normalised. Given the 15-year normalisation requirement for hydropower production and the availability of energy statistics (for the EU, starting from 1990), time series of this indicator before 2004 are not available. With the implementation of RED III, electricity used to produce renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBO) shall not be counted towards the quantity of renewable electricity in the electricity sector, as RFNBO are to be accounted for in the final sector of consumption. For the purpose of calculating the share of '''renewable energy in heating and cooling''', final consumption of energy from renewable sources is defined as the final consumption of renewable energy in industry, households, services, agriculture, forestry, and fisheries for heating and cooling purposes, plus district heating produced from renewables. The total final consumption for heating and cooling is the final consumption of all energy commodities, except electricity, for purposes other than transport, plus the consumption of heat for own use at electricity and heat plants, and heat losses in networks. For more detailed definition, please see the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/energy/database/additional-data#Short%20assessment%20of%20renewable%20energy%20sources%20(SHARES) SHARES tool manual]. ===Context=== Becoming the world's first climate-neutral continent by 2050 is the greatest challenge and opportunity of our times. To achieve this, on 11 December 2019 the European Commission presented the [https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en European Green Deal] ({{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52019DC0640:EN:NOT|title=COM(2019) 640 final}}), the most ambitious package of measures that should enable European citizens and businesses to benefit from a sustainable green transition. Measures accompanied by an initial roadmap of key policies range from ambitiously cutting emissions, to investing in cutting-edge research and innovation, to preserving Europe's natural environment. Above all, the European Green Deal sets a path for a transition that is just and socially fair. It is designed in such a way as to leave no individual or region behind in the great transformation ahead. Some of the objectives of the Green Deal will become part of the Clean Industrial Deal. It is an integral part of the Commission's strategy to implement the United Nation's 2030 Agenda and the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi Sustainable Development Goals] to boost Europe's innovation and competitiveness, and many other priorities announced in President von der Leyen's political guidelines. The [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] has set out several energy strategies for a more secure, sustainable, and low-carbon economy. Aside from combating climate change through a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, the use of renewable energy sources is likely to result in more secure and diverse energy supply, less air pollution, as well as job creation in environmental and renewable energy sectors. Building on the 20% target for 2020, on 11 December 2018, the EU adopted RED II on the promotion of the use of energy from renewable sources, whose last amendment by RED III includes a binding renewable energy target for the EU for 2030 of 42.5% with the aim to achieve 45%. On 18 May 2022, the Commission published the [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/energy/repowereu_en REPowerEU plan], which sets out a series of measures to rapidly reduce EU's dependence on Russian fossil fuels well before 2030 by accelerating the clean energy transition. The REPowerEU plan is based on 3 pillars: saving energy, producing clean energy and diversifying the EU's energy supplies. ===Other articles=== *[[Calculation methodologies for the share of renewables in energy consumption]] *[[Energy statistics introduced]] *[[Energy statistics - an overview]] *[[Electricity production, consumption and market overview]] *[[Energy production and imports]] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-26-007|title=Energy in Europe (2026 edition)}} *{{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-063|title=Sustainable development in the European Union — Monitoring report on progress towards the SDGs in an EU context (2026 edition)}} ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=nrg_ind_share Database folder - Share of energy from renewable sources] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/energy/database/additional-data#Short%20assessment%20of%20renewable%20energy%20sources%20(SHARES) Website - Share of energy from renewable sources] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/energy/database Energy - selected datasets (t_nrg)], see: :Energy statistics - main indicators (t_nrg_ind) :Energy statistics - quantities (t_nrg_quant) ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=energy}} Energy] ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Publication|code=NRG-2004|title=Energy Statistics Manual}} *{{Template:Esms|code=nrg_quant_esms|title=Energy statistics — quantities}} (ESMS metadata file — nrg_quant_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=nrg_ind_share_esmsip2|title=Share of energy from renewable sources (nrg_ind_share)}} (ESMS metadata file — nrg_ind_share_esmsip2) ===External links=== *[http://www.eurobserv-er.org EURObserv'ER] *[https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/renewable-energy_en European Commission — Directorate-General for Energy — Renewable energy] *[https://energy.ec.europa.eu/index_en/ Europe's Energy Portal] *[https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/international-cooperation/international-organisations-and-initiatives/international-renewable-energy-agency_en International Renewable Energy Agency] *[https://www.iea.org/energy-system/renewables?language=en International Energy Agency (IEA) — Renewables] *[https://www.ca-res.eu/ Concerted Action on Renewable Energy Sources Directive] {{Unit|topic=X_Energy}} [[Category:Environment and energy|Renewable energy statistics]] [[Category:Energy|Renewable energy statistics]] [[Category:Energy and environment|Renewable energy statistics]] [[Category:Environment - title: Residence permits - statistics on first permits issued during the year
text:
Statistics on residence permits issued to non-EU citizens provide valuable information for assessing migration and international protection policies. Data extracted in 11 September 2026 Planned article update: September 2026 In 2025, around 3.9 million first residence permits were issued in the EU to non-EU citizens, a 10.1% increase (+355 350) compared with 2024. In 2025, among the 10 top citizenships of non-EU nationals who received first residence permits, the highest relative increase compared with 2024 were observed for Brazil (up 113.3%), followed by Colombia (+43.4%) and India (+18.4%). In 2025, employment was the main reason for non-EU citizens obtaining first residence permits in the EU (representing 33.6% of all first residence permits). |alt=A dynamic line chart with four lines showing the annual changes in first residence permits issued, by reason in the EU from 2016 to 2025. The four lines show family education, employment and other reasons. This article presents [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] statistics on first [[Glossary:Residence permit|residence permits]] issued to non-EU citizens during the reference year 2024. Persons benefitting from temporary protection, i.e. persons who left Ukraine due to Russia’s invasion, are not covered by the data on residence permits; see the methodological section below. === First residence permits — an overview === In 2025, around 3.9 million first residence permits were issued in the EU to citizens of non-EU countries. This latest figure reached the highest level of first residence permits issued— since records began in 2008 — representing an increase of 10.1% (355 350 more permits) compared with 2024 (Figure 1). The increase was mainly due to an increased number of first permits issued for employment (179 701 permits more, or +16.1%), family reasons (133 941 permits more, or +14.1%) and education reasons (49 623 permits more, or +9.0%). Permits issued for other reasons (including international protection) saw a small decrease in comparison with 2024 (7 915 permits less, or -0.9%). In 2025, 1.3 million first residence permits were issued for employment-related reasons, representing 33.6% of all first residence permits issued. Family reasons accounted for 28.1%, education reasons for 15.5%, while other reasons, including international protection, accounted for 22.8%. Figure 1 Among the EU countries, Spain issued the highest number of first residence permits (635 438 permits representing 16.5% of all first permits issued in the EU). Germany followed with 605 292 permits (or 15.7%), Poland with 467 314 (or 12.1%), Italy with 433 099 (or 11.2%) and France with 377 462 (or 9.8%). These 5 countries accounted for almost two-thirds (65.2%) of all first residence permits issued in the EU in 2025 (Figure 2). The largest relative increase in the total number of first permits issued in 2025 when compared with 2024 was recorded in Portugal (+154.9%; from 121 872 in 2024 to 310 639 in 2025), followed by Romania (+30.7%; from 57 111 to 74 664), Italy (+25.0%; from 346 411 to 433 099) and Slovakia (+24.9%; from 18 959 to 23 686). Other notable increases were observed in Bulgaria (+19.9%) and Cyprus (+14.0%). The most significant relative decrease in the total number of permits issued in 2025 compared with 2024 were recorded in Croatia (-43.3%; from 89 809 in 2024 to 50 963 in 2025), Greece (-20.6%; from 87 932 to 69 786) and Austria (-15.5%; from 65 668 to 55 486). Figure 2 Compared with the population of each EU country, the highest ratio of first residence permits per 1 000 persons in 2025 was recorded in Malta (57 permits issued per 1 000 persons), Cyprus (47) and Portugal (27). The lowest ratio was observed in Slovakia, Czechia, Romania, Estonia and Bulgaria each with 4 permits per 1 000 persons. In total in EU, there were 9 first residence permits issued per 1 000 persons in 2025 (Figure 3). Figure 3 ===First residence permits by reason=== '''Employment''' In 2025, employment was the most common reason for issuing residence permits in 13 EU countries. The highest shares were observed in Croatia (93.0%), Romania (81.5%), Lithuania (78.5%) and Portugal (77.4%) (Figure 4). Poland with 318 186 first permits was the main destination for non-EU citizens (mainly Ukrainians and Belarusians) entering the EU for work reasons (Figure 1). The next most common destinations for work were Portugal (240 523 permits), Spain (115 040 permits) and Germany (108 091 permits). These 4 EU countries issued more than half of all first permits for employment reasons in the EU (60.3%). Figure 4 '''Family formation and reunification''' Family-related reasons were the most common reason for issuing residence permits in 8 EU countries. In Luxembourg (56.7%), Sweden (50.5%), Finland (48.3%), Belgium (47.4%), Spain (43.4%) and Italy (40.8%), family-related reasons accounted for more than 40.0% of all the permits issued at national level, followed by Germany (37.3%) and Netherlands (35.8%). Spain (275 869), Germany (225 591), Italy (176 876) and France (90 959) were the EU countries with the highest number of first residence permits issued in 2025 for family-related reasons. '''Education and study''' Ireland, Denmark and France were the only 3 EU countries where the most common reason for granting a residence permit was related to education (respectively 47.6%, 36.7% and 31.4%) in 2025. In absolute terms, France (118 404 permits), Germany (112 500 permits) and Spain (105 419 permits), emerged as the top choice for non-EU students seeking educational opportunities within the EU. '''Other reasons''' Figure 4 also shows the number of first residence permits issued for other reasons, such as international protection or other types of residence (e.g. pensioners). In 2025, 3 EU countries reported other reasons as the most common basis for granting residence permits: Greece (54.8%), Estonia (45.8%) and Austria (38.4%) of all first permits issued at the national level. '''First residence permits by sex''' In 2025, males accounted for 55.7% of the total number of first residence permits issued in the EU, compared with 44.3% for females. The primary reason for issuing a first residence permit to males was for employment-related reasons (22.8% of the total), while the corresponding share for females only accounted for 10.8% (Figure 5). In contrast, 16.4% of all permits issued for females were for family-related reasons; this share was higher than the corresponding proportion recorded for males (11.7%). Almost the same percentages of permits were issued to males and females for education-related reasons, respectively 7.9% and 7.6%. For other reasons, the percentage was higher for males (13.3%) than for females (9.5%). Figure 5 ===First residence permits by citizenship and by destination in the EU=== In 2025, citizens of Ukraine (335 096, or 8.7% of the total number of first residence permits issued) received the highest number of first residence permits in the EU, ahead of citizens of India (227 577, or 5.9%) and Morocco (202 054, or 5.2%) (Figure 6). Figure 6 Figure 6 also shows the development of the number of first residence permits that were issued between 2023 and 2025 for the 10 top citizenships. The top 10 ranking changed for some of the citizenships between 2023 and 2025. Belarus and Syria remained among the largest groups despite declining numbers. Colombia rose in the ranking, and by 2025 Brazil and Pakistan entered the top 10, replacing Bangladesh and Afghanistan. In 2025 compared with 2024, among countries that were already in the top 10 in previous years, the highest relative increases were observed for Colombia (+43.4%), India (+18.4%), Türkiye (+14.0%) and Ukraine (+13.6%). The only decreases were observed for Syria (-42.1%) and Belarus (-15.5%). There are several factors that influence the destination chosen by citizens of non-EU countries granted residence permits, including: geographical proximity (for example, a high number of Ukrainians and Belarusians sought residence in Poland, a high number of Albanians in Greece, and a high number of Moroccans in Spain and France); historical and linguistic links (for example, a high number of Venezuelans, Colombians and Peruvians sought residence in Spain, a high number of Moroccans, Algerians and Tunisians in France, and a high number of Brazilians sought residence in Portugal); or established migrant networks (for example, a high number of Turkish citizens sought residence in Germany) (Table 1). [[Image: T1_Top_5_non-EU_countries_whose_citizens_received_a_first_resident_permit_in_2025_v2.png |thumb|centre|750px|Table 1: Top 5 non-EU countries whose citizens received a first resident permit in 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_resfirst}}|alt=A table showing the top 5 non-EU countries whose citizens received a first resident permit in 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Poland was the principal destination for Ukrainian citizens, representing 72.0% of all first resident permits issued to Ukrainians in the EU in 2025 (Table 2). Similarly, the principal destination for citizens of Belarus was also Poland (87.1% of all first resident permits issued to citizens of Belarus in the EU). Spain was the most popular destination for citizens Morocco (43.8%), while Germany was for citizens of India (21.5%) and Portugal for Brazilian citizens (67.9%). [[Image: T2_Top_5_non-EU_countries_whose_citizens_received_first_residence_permits_in_the_EU,_by_reason.png|thumb|centre|750px|Table 2: Top 5 non-EU countries whose citizens received first residence permits in the EU, by reason and by EU country issuing the permit, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_resfirst}}|alt=A table showing the top 5 non-EU countries whose citizens received first residence permits in the EU, by reason and by EU country issuing the permit for the year 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 2 focuses also on the top 5 countries whose citizens received first residence permits in the EU by reason and by 3 leading EU countries issuing a permit. In 2025, Moroccans were the largest group to receive residence permits for family-related reasons, with more than half issued in Spain (51.7%). Indians were the largest group to receive residence permits for education-related reasons, with 39.5% issued in Germany. Ukrainians and Brazilians were granted the highest numbers of first residence permits issued for employment-related reasons, with 86.3% of permits for Ukrainian citizens issued by Poland and 90.3% of permits for Brazilian citizens issued by Portugal. Afghans topped the list of permits issued for other reasons, of which 41.9% were granted in Germany. Figure 7 looks in more detail at the reasons for granting permits to citizens of particular countries. Around two-thirds of Ukrainians who were granted a residence permit in the EU in 2025 received their permit for employment-related reasons. Employment was also the principal reason for granting residence permits in the EU to Brazilians (64.5%), Belarusians (56.6%) and Indians (44.6%). Family was the prevailing reason for permits granted to Moroccans (47.9%), Colombians (37.7%), Turkish citizens (35.7%) and Pakistanis (34.5%). Permits for education were primarily issued to Chinese (31.7%), while other reasons were predominant for Syrians (57.3%). Figure 7 === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Residence_permits_statistics_2025_.xlsx|title=Residence permits statistics: tables}} ===Data sources=== The statistics used for this article are provided to [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] by the responsible authorities in each of the EU and EFTA countries, principally Ministries of the Interior or Home Affairs or various immigration agencies. The data are based entirely on administrative sources supplied to Eurostat as part of an annual residence permits data collection exercise in accordance with the provisions of Article 6 of [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:32007R0862:EN:NOT Regulation (EC) No 862/2007] on Community statistics on migration and international protection. Commission [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32010R0216 Regulation (EU) No 216/2010] implementing Regulation (EC) No 862/2007 gives the definitions of the reasons for the residence permits statistics. Limitations in data availability affect the information presented in this article: * Break in series for Poland in 2018 (employment and other reasons), Greece in 2021 (other reasons), Italy in 2022 (other reasons), Spain in 2023 (education reasons), Hungary in 2024 (education and other reasons) and Portugal (employment reasons). * The note on low reliability in Irish data highlights limited data quality reported by the Irish authorities. The process of generating residence permits data involves both the Irish Police and the Department of Justice for which an old information system is currently used. The current system’s limitations, which omits unique identifiers of persons, and requires manual data checks, may lead to potential quality issues. According to Irish authorities a comprehensive modernisation programme of the information systems to ensure more accurate data management is in progress. The data on residence permits may be analysed by: reporting country, citizenship of the permit holder, reason for the permit being issued, and length of validity of the permit. From reference period 2010 onwards, data on residence permits were collected on a voluntary basis by age and by sex, becoming mandatory data collection for the 2021 reference period onwards. Residence permits statistics are available as both flows and stocks. * Data related to residence permits granted during the reference year (flows): the data published under this category contain information about first residence permits issued during the reference year and information about any change of residence status of immigrants during the reference year; * Data related to residence permits valid at the end of the reference year (stock of permits): the data published under this category contain information about the number of valid permissions to stay at the end of the reference year and long-term legal residence status at the end of the reference year. It should be noted that certain methodological aspects are not fully harmonised between the reporting countries due to different legal or information technology systems. Therefore, the results that are presented in this article should be interpreted with care and readers are advised to make reference to the metadata file on [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/migr_resval_esms.htm residence permits statistics.] Starting with the 2021 reference period, there were several improvements in the data collection, including methodological aspects. These changes were introduced through the implementation of [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32020R0851 Regulation (EU) 851/2020] amending Regulation (EC) No 862/2007. More details are available in the following document: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/Annexes/migr_resval_esms_an_9.pdf 2023 Residence Permits Technical Guidelines.] ===Methodological note=== Residence permits data collection refers to residence permits as any authorisation issued by the national authorities of a EU country allowing a third-country national (non-EU citizen) to stay legally on its territory. Persons benefitting from temporary protection are not included in any of the Residence permits statistics. Temporary protection status is considered to be of a different administrative nature to that of the authorisations to reside reported in the residence permits data collection. These persons are subject of a separate data collection on Temporary Protection (TP); see data on temporary protection [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/asylum/database?node_code=migr_asytp here] and the statistics explained article [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Temporary_protection_for_persons_fleeing_Ukraine_-_monthly_statistics here]. ===Context=== The residence permits are a significant component of the migration area, being linked to the national and European migration context and policies. Migration policies within the EU are built upon solidarity and responsibility, taking into account the contribution that immigrants make to the EU. Within the European Commission, the Directorate-General for Migration and Home Affairs is responsible for immigration policy. As recent development in the area of migration, the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/promoting-our-european-way-life/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en Pact on Migration and Asylum], was adopted by the European Parliament in April 2024 and by the Council in May 2024. This Pact provides a common European response to migration. It allows the EU to manage migration in a fair and sustainable way, ensuring solidarity between countries while also providing certainty and clarity for people arriving in the EU and protecting their fundamental rights. More information regarding the EU’s migration policy can be accessed on the European Commission’s [https://commission.europa.eu/about-european-commission/departments-and-executive-agencies/migration-and-home-affairs_en website]. === Footnotes === ===Other articles===
