title: Regional yearbook introduction
text:
Eurostat regional yearbook; 2026 edition; flagship publication; regional statistics; NUTS; introductory chapter; reading guide; policy background. Planned article update: September 2027 This article forms part of the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026]'', an annual [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications flagship publication]. It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], as well as statistics for the regions of [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|European Free Trade Association (EFTA)]] and [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate]] countries. A [[Regional_yearbook_introduction#A_short_reading_guide|short reading guide]] is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps. Shifting geopolitics, artificial intelligence and climate change are redefining the global landscape. In response, the EU is focusing on strengthening business competitiveness as a central pillar of its economic strategy. While global in ambition, the United Nations’ sustainable development goals are ultimately delivered locally. Across EU regions, the shared objectives of Agenda 2030 promote sustainable prosperity, address inequality, accelerate the shift to clean energy and strengthen inclusive, resilient communities. [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], the statistical office of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], collects, compiles and publishes statistics for the EU, including statistics for the regions of the EU, EFTA and candidate countries. Data can play a crucial role in shaping and evaluating effective policies and responses to the challenges that arise in a world characterised by rapid change and uncertainty. This edition of the ''Eurostat regional yearbook'' provides statistical insights into a range of pressing challenges, from climate change to competitiveness. By leveraging accurate and timely data, policymakers can make informed decisions that drive resilience and sustainable growth. This edition of the ''Eurostat regional yearbook'' focuses on 2 key policy areas.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]]
 [[Image:Compet icon RYB2026 small.png|left]] The European Commission’s [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/competitiveness_en new plan for Europe’s sustainable prosperity and competitiveness] aims to strengthen economic growth while ensuring environmental and social sustainability. Through balancing economic resilience with climate goals, the plan aspires to create high-quality jobs, reinforce global competitiveness and uphold the EU’s commitment to a fair, green and prosperous future for all its citizens. The ''Eurostat regional yearbook'' identifies regional indicators that can be used to measure sustainable prosperity and competitiveness by placing a logo next to them. The indicators are aligned with those highlighted in ''[https://commission.europa.eu/topics/eu-competitiveness/draghi-report_en The future of European competitiveness]'', a report produced by Mario Draghi for the European Commission.
[[Image:SDG wheel icon RYB2026.png|50px]]
 [[Image:SDG wheel icon RYB2026 small.png|left]] The [[Glossary:United_Nations_(UN)|United Nations’ (UN)]] [https://sdgs.un.org/2030agenda 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development] is a long-term strategy that aims to meet a range of economic, social and environmental goals. Developments are traced through 17 [https://sdgs.un.org/goals sustainable development goals (SDGs)] and 169 targets. Eurostat monitors progress in an EU context, coordinating a review of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/database EU SDG indicator set] and publishing annual monitoring reports. This edition of the ''Eurostat regional yearbook'' identifies regional indicators that can be used to measure progress towards the SDGs by placing a logo next to them. ===European statistics=== '''Subnational statistics''' EU countries are often compared statistically, but differences in size can make such comparisons challenging. For instance, on 1 January 2025, Malta and Luxembourg – the EU’s least populous countries – had 574 000 and 682 000 inhabitants, respectively. By contrast, Germany – the most populous – had 83.6 million inhabitants. There are considerable differences between and within countries as regards their territorial composition. For example, Ireland, Finland and Sweden are generally rural and sparsely populated, while Malta and the [[Glossary:Benelux|Benelux]] countries have much higher levels of population density. Similarly, there can be considerable diversity within individual EU countries. For example, contrast the densely populated, urbanised areas of Nordrhein-Westfalen in the west of Germany (which had an average of 533 inhabitants per square kilometre in 2024) with the sparsely populated, largely rural, north-eastern region of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (with an average of 70 inhabitants per square kilometre). In a similar manner, there are considerable differences between regions of France: for example, contrast the bustling pace of life in the capital region of Paris (which had an average of 20 148 inhabitants per square kilometre in 2024) with the more sedate pace of rural life in the central/southern region of Lozère (with an average of 15 inhabitants per square kilometre). Looking at regional data within EU countries often provides clearer insights by highlighting internal disparities, such as Italy’s north-south divide or Germany’s east-west divide. For example, Germany and Poland have several large cities spread across the country (a polycentric economic structure), while France and Romania tend to have economic development concentrated in their respective capitals (a monocentric pattern). Over the past few years, Eurostat has expanded its range of statistics beyond national and regional information to cover other territorial typologies. These alternatives address the needs of policymakers, particularly within the context of cohesion and territorial developments, using 2 broad headings: *regional typologies *local typologies that are based on data for [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/nuts/local-administrative-units local administrative units (LAUs or municipalities)]. With this in mind, ''{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32017R2391:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2017/2391 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 December 2017 as regards the territorial typologies (Tercet)}}'' established a common statistical classification of territorial units. It consolidates and facilitates the collection, compilation and dissemination of European statistics at different territorial levels. '''Statistics on regions – the NUTS classification''' The [[Glossary:Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)|classification of territorial units for statistics]] – known as NUTS – underpins EU regional statistics. It is hierarchical, dividing each EU country into regions of decreasing size: NUTS levels 1, 2 and 3 regions. The {{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-23-010|title=2024 edition of the NUTS classification}} provides the basis for classifying regional information in this year’s ''Eurostat regional yearbook''. For example, Italy has 107 NUTS level 3 regions, which form 21 NUTS level 2 regions and 5 NUTS level 1 regions. Some smaller EU countries are not divided at all, or at only certain levels of the classification. Estonia, Cyprus, Latvia, Luxembourg and Malta each consist of a single NUTS level 2 region covering their entire territory, while Cyprus and Luxembourg are also composed of just a single NUTS level 3 region. For EFTA and candidate countries, the concept of ‘statistical regions’ replaces NUTS. For most countries, bilateral agreements with Eurostat apply the same principles as the NUTS classification. Liechtenstein and Montenegro each consist of a single region (at every level of the classification). As of April 2026, no regional breakdowns had been agreed for Bosnia and Herzegovina (other than levels 1 and 2), the Republic of Moldova or Georgia; in this publication, each comprises a single region covering its entire territory. '''Table 1''' provides an overview of the number of NUTS/statistical regions that exist in each of the EU and non-EU countries. [[Image:Number of NUTS 2024 regions and statistical regions_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Number of NUTS 2024 regions and statistical regions
''Source:'' Eurostat|alt=A table showing the count of NUTS 2024 regions and statistical regions for levels 1, 2 and 3. Data are shown for the EU and EU, EFTA and candidate countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] Most of the regional statistics shown in the ''Eurostat regional yearbook'' are for NUTS level 2 regions. However, subject to data availability, some maps and figures are shown for either NUTS level 1 regions (more aggregated geographical information) or NUTS level 3 regions (the most detailed level of regional information). The latter are only available for a limited selection of indicators that cover topics such as demography, economic accounts, business statistics, tourism statistics and environmental statistics. '''''The NUTS regulation''''' The NUTS classification is defined in ''{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32003R1059:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1059/2003 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 May 2003 on the establishment of a common classification of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)}}''. The classification is periodically reviewed by the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] amending the regulation to reflect administrative changes within EU countries. The NUTS regulation specifies that there should be a minimum period of 3 years stability during which time the classification should not be changed. Exceptions are made when the accession (or departure) of an EU country occurs. Since 2003, the NUTS classification has been amended several times (see Figure 1), due to: *regular amendments *changes in the membership of the EU *changes to the territorial boundaries of existing EU countries (for example, the inclusion of the French region of Mayotte). [[Image:History of NUTS_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: History of NUTS
''Source:'' Eurostat|alt=A figure/diagram showing the history of the NUTS classification. Information is shown for changes to the legal status of the collection of regional data from 1999. The figure shows the periods covered by each version of the NUTS classification, including NUTS 2024 (which is the basis for the regional data presented in this edition of the Eurostat regional yearbook). The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] The European Commission adopted the seventh amendment of the NUTS classification (''{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32023R0674:EN:NOT|title=Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 2023/674}}'') in December 2022. It applies to any data that are transmitted to Eurostat for reference periods starting from 1 January 2024. This version of NUTS – commonly referred to as NUTS 2024 – is the basis for classifying regional statistics in the 2026 edition of the ''Eurostat regional yearbook''. It provides a framework for regional statistics in the EU, delineating: *92 regions at NUTS level 1 *244 regions at NUTS level 2 *1 165 regions at NUTS level 3. With the switch to NUTS 2024, Eurostat tried to recode historical statistics (data for earlier reference periods) to the new classification, although this was only partially possible. As a result, data are not always available for a complete set of regions, especially when simple recoding or aggregation was not feasible. Sometimes, the lack of historical data under NUTS 2024 makes time-series analyses challenging, although EU countries attempt to back-calculate key regional statistics to improve data availability.
'''''More about the data: the main principles of the NUTS classification''''' '''Principle 1''': NUTS favours administrative divisions. If available, administrative structures are used for the different NUTS levels. In EU countries where there is no administrative layer corresponding to a particular level of NUTS, so-called non-administrative regions are created by aggregating smaller administrative regions. '''Principle 2''': the NUTS regulation defines minimum and maximum population thresholds for the size of NUTS regions (see '''Table 2''') to ensure a basic degree of comparability. Different rules apply to administrative and non-administrative layers. Deviations from these thresholds are only possible when particular geographical, socioeconomic, historical, cultural or environmental circumstances exist.
[[Image:Population size constraints for NUTS 2024 regions (number of inhabitants)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Population size constraints for NUTS 2024 regions
''Source:'' Eurostat|alt=A table showing the minimum and maximum population size constraints used to determine NUTS 2024 regions. Information is shown for the number of inhabitants, presenting the upper and lower thresholds for NUTS levels 1, 2 and 3. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article.]] '''Other territorial typologies''' Grid-based statistics provide an alternative to regional statistics based on administrative boundaries. They divide territories into uniform grid cells, offering detailed spatial data with a high degree of geographical resolution. For example, the population and housing census is conducted every decade to provide grid statistics composed of cells measuring 1 km2. Eurostat uses grid-based statistics to analyse, among other subjects, population, transport, the environment, agriculture and accessibility. Other territorial typologies allow analyses to be extended to cover topics such as [[Glossary:City|cities]] and [[Glossary:Commuting_zone|commuting zones]], or the [[Glossary:Degree of urbanisation|degree of urbanisation]]. While these statistics remain highly relevant for policy debate in the EU, an editorial decision was taken when compiling the 2025 edition of the publication to concentrate on regional statistics and this approach has been maintained for the 2026 edition. Readers interested in subnational statistics based on other territorial typologies can refer to the following publications: *[[Rural_Europe|Rural Europe]] (online publication) *[[Urban_Europe|Urban Europe]] (online publication) *[[Territorial_typologies_manual|Territorial typologies manual]] (online publication). ===Policy context=== European policymaking faces a dual challenge: setting broad objectives for the EU while addressing the specific needs of national and regional territories. The territorial dimension of EU policy is increasingly recognised as essential for issues such as job creation and the transition to a green and digital economy. Recent challenges within the EU – including economic uncertainty, defence and security concerns, migration pressures, geopolitical developments, public health challenges, and broader social and environmental changes – highlight the complexity of implementing coherent policies at the local, regional, national and international levels. '''Cohesion policy''' '''''What is cohesion policy?''''' The EU’s [[Glossary:Cohesion_policy|cohesion policy]] is designed to strengthen economic, social and territorial cohesion within the EU. It aims to promote job creation, business competitiveness, economic growth, social inclusion and sustainable development, thereby impacting the overall quality of life. The bulk of cohesion policy funding is concentrated on less developed EU regions with the goal of helping these regions to catch up and to reduce the economic, social and territorial disparities that exist across the EU. Although cohesion policy covers every region of the EU, most of the funds are targeted at regions where [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]] per inhabitant is less than 75% of the EU average. During the period [https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/2021-2027_en 2021 to 2027], the framework for regional development and cohesion policy focuses on 5 key policy objectives: *'''a more competitive and smarter Europe''', promoting innovation, digitalisation, economic transformation and support to SMEs *'''a greener Europe''', transitioning towards a ‘net zero’ economy, while implementing the [https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-paris-agreement Paris Agreement] *'''a more connected Europe''', enhancing mobility *'''a more social and inclusive Europe''', supporting social inclusion, equal access to healthcare, quality employment, education and skills *'''a Europe closer to citizens''', fostering the sustainable and integrated development of locally led strategies. '''''Cohesion policy: how is it delivered?''''' Cohesion policy is delivered through several specific funds. They are the main financial instruments used to promote economic, social and territorial cohesion across the EU. *The '''[https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/funding/erdf_en European Regional Development Fund (ERDF)]''' aims to strengthen economic, territorial and social cohesion in the EU by correcting development imbalances between the regions. *The '''[https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/funding/cohesion-fund_en Cohesion Fund (CF)]''' aims to reduce economic and social disparities and to promote sustainable development in EU countries with a gross national income per inhabitant below 90% of the EU average. *The '''[https://ec.europa.eu/european-social-fund-plus/en European Social Fund Plus (ESF+)]''' provides support for people, with a focus on improving employment and education opportunities across the EU, as well as the situation of the most vulnerable people. *The '''[https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/funding/just-transition-fund_en Just Transition Fund (JTF)]''' aims to support territories facing serious socioeconomic challenges arising from the transition towards climate neutrality. It addresses the social, employment, economic and environmental impacts of the transition. '''''Cohesion policy: how is the budget decided?''''' Political agreement on the [https://interreg-rohu.eu/en/the-new-cohesion-policy-legislative-package-for-the-2021-2027-period-has-been-published/ legislative package for cohesion policy for 2021 to 2027] was adopted in the middle of 2021, with the multiannual financial framework including a total of €392 billion for regional development and cohesion. For more information, see the [https://cohesiondata.ec.europa.eu/stories/s/2021-2027-EU-allocations-available-for-programming/2w8s-ci3y/ budget allocations for EU cohesion policy 2021 to 2027].
'''''More about the data: the NUTS classification – an objective basis for the allocation of cohesion policy funding''''' Statistics from regional accounts are used in the allocation of cohesion policy funds, with the NUTS classification providing the basis for regional boundaries and geographic eligibility. During the period 2021 to 2027, eligibility for cohesion policy funds is based on NUTS level 2 regions being ranked and classified into the following groups: *less developed regions, where GDP per inhabitant (in [[Glossary:Purchasing_power_standard_(PPS)|purchasing power standards (PPS)]]) was less than 75% of the EU average *transition regions, where GDP per inhabitant was 75% to 100% of the EU average *more developed regions, where GDP per inhabitant was greater than 100% of the EU average. Additional criteria, such as youth unemployment, education levels, climate change, demographic developments and migrant integration, have been introduced to address regional challenges better.
The EU assigns the bulk of the cohesion policy budget to regions whose development lags behind the EU average, aiming to reduce economic, social and territorial disparities. Less developed and transition regions – predominantly located in the south or the east of the EU, the Baltic countries and several [https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/policy/themes/outermost-regions_en outermost regions] – benefit from 90% of the ERDF and ESF+ resources. '''Other policy areas that impact on subnational areas''' '''''Urban development policy in the EU''''' The EU’s urban development policy integrates economic, social, cultural and environmental aspects through coordinated measures such as urban renewal, education opportunities, social inclusion, crime prevention and environmental protection. For more information: *[https://www.urban-initiative.eu/ European Urban Initiative (EUI)] *[https://www.urbanagenda.urban-initiative.eu/sites/default/files/2022-10/ljubljana_agreement_2021_en.pdf Ljubljana agreement] *[https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/information-sources/publications/brochures/2020/new-leipzig-charter-the-transformative-power-of-cities-for-the-common-good_en New Leipzig Charter – the transformative power of cities for the common good] *[https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/policy/themes/urban-development/agenda/pact-of-amsterdam.pdf Pact of Amsterdam] *[https://www.urbanagenda.urban-initiative.eu/ Urban Agenda for the EU]. '''''Rural development policy in the EU''''' Rural areas are fundamental to the European way of life and play an important role in supporting the EU’s economic resilience and prosperity, while offering potential to strengthen Europe’s competitiveness. While several rural areas face challenges such as demographic decline, fewer job opportunities and limited-service provision, they remain central not only to food production, but also to important productive activities in, among others, manufacturing, energy or the bioeconomy, while benefiting from place-specific advantages that can attract firms and support innovation and experimentation. For more information: *[https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy_en Common agricultural policy] *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52021DC0345 Long-term vision for the EU’s rural areas – Towards stronger, connected, resilient and prosperous rural areas by 2040] *[https://rural-vision.europa.eu/action-plan_en Rural action plan] *[https://ruralpact.rural-vision.europa.eu/rural-pact_en Rural pact] *[https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/overview-vision-agriculture-food/vision-agriculture-and-food_en Vision for Agriculture and Food]. '''''Multi-annual financial framework 2028–34''''' On 16 July 2025, the European Commission adopted proposals for the multi-annual financial framework (MFF) 2028–34 with the overall aim of a more policy-oriented, simpler, impactful and responsive budget to help EU countries and their regions address priorities and challenges in the most effective, inclusive and efficient way, drawing on all the lessons learned from the current programmes. This includes a proposal establishing the European Fund for: *economic, social and territorial cohesion *agriculture and rural development *fisheries and maritime policy *prosperity and security. The goal is to allow a more differentiated and qualitative approach to deliver on EU priorities, tailored to each country’s national and regional challenges through 27 partnership plans. The proposal brings together – under a single rulebook – instruments and policies that are currently covered by 14 different funds. The national and regional partnership plans will benefit from €783 billion in total, including €453 billion for cohesion policy, rural development and fishing communities, out of which at least €218 billion shall be allocated to less developed regions. Negotiations on the next MFF proposals are underway with a view to reach a timely agreement. For more information, see the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/eu-budget/long-term-eu-budget/eu-budget-2028-2034_en 2028–34 EU budget for a stronger Europe]. '''''European Committee of the Regions''''' The [https://cor.europa.eu/en European Committee of the Regions (CoR)] – the EU’s assembly of locally and regionally elected representatives – gives a voice to regions, cities and municipalities in the EU decision-making process. For its 2025 to 2030 mandate, the CoR has identified 3 overarching priorities: *''cohesion'', to increase competitiveness and promote balanced territorial development, ensuring that no region is left behind; *''resilience'', to strengthen the capacity of local and regional communities to address economic, social, environmental and security challenges; and *''proximity'', to bring the EU closer to citizens by empowering local and regional authorities and reinforcing democratic participation. Every year in October, the CoR publishes its ''[https://www.cor.europa.eu/en/plenaries-events/state-regions-and-cities-european-union-2026 Annual Report on the State of the Regions and Cities]''. [[Image:European_week_of_regions_and_cities_RYB2026.png|centre|600px|alt=An image of a banner used to advertise the 2026 edition of the European week of regions and cities.]] The [https://regions-and-cities.europa.eu/ European Week of Regions and Cities] is an annual multi-day event which allows regions and cities to showcase their capacity to encourage growth and job creation, implement EU cohesion policy and support good governance. The 24th European Week of Regions and Cities will be held from 12 to 14 October 2026 under the headline of ‘Strong Europe, strong regions’. '''''Strategic agenda 2024 to 2029''''' In June 2024, following the [[Glossary:European_Parliament_(EP)|European Parliament]] elections, the [[Glossary:European_Council|European Council]] adopted a [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/european-council/strategic-agenda-2024-2029/ strategic agenda] for the period from 2024 to 2029. It addresses global instability, economic challenges and threats to the rules-based order, focusing on 3 main pillars: *a free and democratic Europe – upholding fundamental rights and democratic values *a strong and secure Europe – enhancing defence and security measures *a prosperous and competitive Europe – promoting economic growth and sustainability. '''''Sustainable prosperity and competitiveness''''' Subsequently, the European Commission re-aligned its work programme, detailing 7 key priority areas. This publication focuses on 1 of these, namely, ''[https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/competitiveness_en A new plan for Europe’s sustainable prosperity and competitiveness]'', which is considered central to improving citizens’ economic and social well-being, increasing their purchasing power, creating good jobs, assuring high-quality goods and services, and reinforcing Europe’s sovereignty in strategic sectors. For more information: *[https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/competitiveness-compass_en Competitiveness compass] *[https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/clean-industrial-deal_en Clean industrial deal] *[https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/ai-continent_en AI continent action plan] *[https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/data-union European Data Union strategy] *[https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/union-skills_en Union of skills]. '''''Sustainable development goals''''' The 17 sustainable development goals (SDGs) provide a global policy framework until 2030 for stimulating action in areas of critical importance related to people, the planet, prosperity, peace and partnership. On 22 November 2016, the European Commission adopted the Communication, ''{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52016DC0739:EN:NOT|title=Next steps for a sustainable European future – European action for sustainability}}'' (COM(2016) 739 final). It detailed the importance of the SDGs, identified EU policies that contribute to the implementation of SDGs and announced plans for regular monitoring within an EU context. For more information: *[https://sdgs.un.org/2030agenda 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development] *[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/sustainable-development-goals/eu-approach-sdgs-implementation_en EU approach to SDGs implementation] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/overview Eurostat monitoring – SDGs overview]. ===Reading guide=== '''''Coverage''''' Each chapter in the ''Eurostat regional yearbook'' presents statistical information in the form of maps, figures and infographics, accompanied by descriptive analyses highlighting the main findings. Information is shown for 13 different subjects: population, health, education and training, the labour market, living conditions, the digital society, the economy, business, research and innovation, tourism, transport, the environment and agriculture. The ''Eurostat regional yearbook'' contains regional statistics for the EU countries, alongside data for several non-EU countries: EFTA countries (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland) and candidate countries (Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Moldova, Georgia, North Macedonia, Albania, Serbia, Türkiye and Ukraine). The geographical descriptions used within this publication to group EU countries – for example, as ‘northern’, ‘eastern’, ‘southern’ or ‘western’ – are not intended as political categorisations. Rather, these references relate to the geographical location of 1 or more EU countries, based on the [https://op.europa.eu/en/web/eu-vocabularies/concept-scheme/-/resource?uri=http://eurovoc.europa.eu/100277 geography domain] of the European Commission’s [https://op.europa.eu/s/yZvL multilingual thesaurus (Eurovoc)]. The designations employed and the presentation of material in maps and figures does not imply the expression of any opinion whatsoever on the part of the EU concerning the legal status of any country, territory or area or of its authorities, or concerning the delimitation of its frontiers or boundaries. '''''Timeliness''''' Eurostat compiles the information used in this publication from a wide range of surveys and data collection exercises. As a result, there may be differences in the latest available reference year between chapters and indicators, as each aims to show the latest information available. In general, 2025 data are available for demography (as used in the chapter on population), the labour force survey (as used in the chapters on education and training and on the labour market), statistics on income and living conditions (as used in the chapter on living conditions) and the information society survey (as used in the chapter on the digital society). Otherwise, the most recent reference period is generally 2024. [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat Eurostat’s website] may have more up-to-date data due to the continuous nature of data collection and processing (resulting in updates and new reference periods being added throughout the year). Online data codes are provided below each of the maps and figures as part of the source; these codes can be used to access the most recent data. '''''How to interpret the maps''''' Most maps in the ''Eurostat regional yearbook'' are choropleth maps, using coloured shades to highlight regional differences. Typically, 6 sequential colours are used, from light (low values) to dark (high values), based on normalised data such as proportions, rates or ratios, rather than absolute values (which could introduce bias linked to the size of each region). Some maps use more or fewer classes, while different colours may be applied (for example, if there are specific colour conventions inherent to a particular indicator). Class boundaries presented in the maps are generally based on the distribution of regional values for EU regions (therefore excluding EFTA and candidate country regions). The lower boundaries are usually based on the 10th and the 25th percentiles, the middle on the 50th percentile, and the upper boundaries on the 75th and the 90th percentiles. As such, the lightest and darkest shades in maps generally portray those EU regions with the lowest/highest 10% of values. The values within each class range from the lower boundary (inclusive) to the upper boundary (exclusive). When multiple maps are shown together – for example, employment rates by educational attainment in [[Education_and_training_statistics_at_regional_level|Chapter 3]] – a common classification scheme is used to facilitate comparisons across the maps. The highest and lowest values in each legend indicate the maximum and minimum values in the corresponding dataset. These are calculated using all regions shown on the map and may therefore refer to regions in the EU, EFTA or candidate countries. For small multiple maps (that is, maps composed of more than 1 map), the maximum and minimum values are calculated using all data displayed across the entire set of maps. Some choropleth maps use diverging colour schemes to show variations around a specific EU policy target or to highlight regions above/below an index value, such as the EU average (= 100). Bivariate choropleth maps display information for two indicators simultaneously. For example, [[Health_statistics_at_regional_level|Chapter 2]] presents a map showing the average number of inhabitants per hospital bed and per doctor, using 9 shades organised in a 3*3 grid, from light (low for both indicators) to dark (high for both). Proportional circle maps display absolute values, such as the number of people employed in science and technology. Circle size reflects the underlying number, while colour or shade can be used to indicate complementary information, such as this subpopulation’s share of the overall labour force. Finally, coxcomb maps are used to visualise regional data using segmented circles, with the size of each segment representing the absolute values for each month. In [[Tourism_statistics_at_regional_level|Chapter 10]], this type of map is used to depict the number of guest nights spent in tourist accommodation. Coloured shading is used to distinguish between the nights spent by domestic and international tourists, making it easy to see both seasonal variations and the origin of tourists at a glance. Within this edition of the ''Eurostat regional yearbook'', the map legends have been adapted to include information for the minimum and maximum values displayed in each map. Unlike the class boundaries, which are based solely on data for EU regions, these minimum and maximum values refer to the full range of data shown and may therefore correspond to regions outside the EU (in EFTA or candidate countries). '''''Metadata''''' Eurostat data are consistently published with accompanying metadata, providing background information on the main sources as well as specific information on individual indicators and data cells. Metadata for individual data cells, often referred to as flags, indicate the status of data, such as whether it is estimated, provisional or forecasted. To limit the amount of information displayed under each figure or map, this publication generally omits detailed flags. No distinction is made between data cells that are unavailable, of poor quality or confidential; rather, these data points are all shown/labelled as ‘not available’. Data with break in series, different definitions, or low reliability are documented in the metadata notes below each figure or map. Readers seeking more detailed metadata are encouraged to use the online data codes provided as part of each source. '''''Missing data''''' In figures, missing data for EU regions are indicated in footnotes (no information is presented for non-EU countries). Many figures focus exclusively on data for EU regions – for example, charts showing the 10 EU regions with the highest or lowest values for a particular indicator. In maps, missing data are shown in dark grey, while countries outside the spatial coverage adopted for this edition (EU, EFTA and candidate countries) are shown in a lighter grey. During data processing, missing values were filled, whenever possible, using data from the previous year at the same NUTS level. If such data were unavailable, values from more aggregated NUTS levels or national data were used. Any exceptions, including differences in reference period or NUTS level, are documented in the notes or footnotes. In some exceptional cases, estimates were made to fill the gaps in the datasets; these are also mentioned in the accompanying notes. For countries with few or no regional values, national data were used to fill gaps; these exceptions are noted. Furthermore, the source data codes (online data codes) have been adapted to reflect any additional national data tables that may have been used. When a figure or map covers more than 1 territorial level (for example, some countries only have national data), commentary on the number of regions meeting a criterion refers to the available data, reflecting the actual NUTS levels or national data employed. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:RYB2026 CH00 Introduction.xlsx|Download Excel file]] title: Residence permits - statistics on stock of permits at the end of the year
text:
Statistics on EU residence permits granted to non-EU citizens provide valuable information for assessing migration and international protection policies; the information in this article concerns the total stock of permits (which may be contrasted to the number of permits that are granted each year). Data extracted: 11 September 2026. Planned article update: September 2027. At the end of 2025, there were 27.8 million residence permits held by non-EU citizens in the EU. Family was the main reason for residence permits held by non-EU citizens in the EU at the end of 2025, accounting for 32.4% of the total. Moroccan (2.2 million), Turkish (2.0 million) and Ukrainian (1.7 million) citizens were the 3 main citizenships holding residence permits in the EU at the end of 2025. This article provides an overview of the stock of valid residence permits granted to non-EU citizens at the end of 2025. In addition, it presents the developments of the stock between the end of 2016 and the end of 2025. Different aspects are analysed, such as the reasons for issuing the permits, the duration of permits and the citizenship of persons to whom the permits were granted. This article does not include information on temporary protection of refugees from Ukraine in EU countries resulting from Russia's military aggression against that country. Note that a complementary article provides information on the [[Residence permits - statistics on first permits issued during the year|number of first residence permits issued during the year]]. ===Non-EU citizens with a residence permit === At the end of 2025, there were 27.8 million residence permits granted to non-EU citizens. Germany (5.9 million permits), France (4.4 million), Spain and Italy (4.3 million each) together accounted for 68.1% of the total residence permits granted to non-EU citizens (Figure1). Figure 1 The number of persons holding residence permits relative to the EU population was 62 permits per thousand people at the end of 2025. Among the EU countries, the highest ratios were observed in Malta (230 permits per thousand people), Cyprus (204), Estonia (137) and Latvia (131), while the lowest were recorded in Poland (29) Hungary (22), Bulgaria (21) and Romania (12) (Map 1). Map 1: Stock of residence permits granted to non-EU citizens relative to the size of the population, 2024 (number per 1 000 persons) Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_resvalid}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_gind}} ===Stock of residence permits granted to non-EU citizens at the end of 2025=== The stock of residence permits granted to non-EU citizens to reside in the EU increased by 4.6% between the end of 2024 and the end of 2025 (Figure 2). Among all EU countries, 19 reported an increase of the stock. The highest rate was recorded in Romania where the stock of permits granted to non-EU citizens increased by 42.6%, followed by Cyprus (up 23.7%), Bulgaria (up 12.7%) and Malta (up 12.3%). By contrast, 8 countries reported a decline in the stock of permits, with the largest decreases observed in Poland (down 9.7%), Hungary (down 4.2%), Croatia (down 4.0%) and Lithuania (down 3.9%). Among the 4 EU countries with the largest stocks of resident permits, Italy recorded the highest increase, as the number of permits rose by 9.1%. Increases were also recorded in Germany (up 5.6%), Spain (up 5.4%) and France (up 3.4%). Figure 2 Figure 3 provides an analysis of the reasons for which the valid residence permits were granted. At the end of 2025, around one-third (32.4%) of all valid residence permits granted to non-EU The categories for refugee and subsidiary protection status exclude data from Austria, Malta, and Hungary, as well as partial data from Spain for subsidiary protection, due to missing data for the reference year 2025. citizens were for family-related reasons, with lower shares for employment reasons (22.3%), refugee and subsidiary protection status (14.7%) or education reasons (4.7%). Residence permits classified for ’other reasons’ accounted for 25.9% of all permits. At the end of 2025, among the EU countries, more than half of all the residence permits valid in Belgium (56.2%) were family-related while this share was slightly lower in Luxembourg (51.9%) and Sweden (51.1%). Germany (2.2 million), Italy (1.7 million), Spain (1.6 million) and France (1.5 million) recorded the highest absolute numbers of valid permits issued for this reason. More than half of the stock of residence permits for non-EU citizens at the end of 2025 was granted for employment reasons in Croatia (79.0%), Lithuania (68.1%), Romania (65.5%). Malta (65.2%), Slovakia (59.3%) and Poland (57.0%). In absolute terms, Italy registered the highest number of residence permits for employment reasons (1.8 million), considerably greater than in Germany (615 957) and Poland (601 428), where the second and third highest numbers were observed. In Germany, refugee and subsidiary protection status accounted 44.8% of all residence permits for non-EU citizens at the end of 2025, followed by Sweden (20.4%), Belgium (16.3%), the Netherlands (16.0%) and France (14.4%). In absolute terms, Germany reported the highest number of valid residence permits for non-EU citizens concerning refugee status and subsidiary protection (2.7 million), followed by France (637 634), Italy (158 671) and Netherlands (132 927). Figure 3 At the end of 2025, 92.4% of residence permits at EU level were valid for 12 months or more, compared with 5.5% valid for 6 to 11 months and 2.1% valid for 3 to 5 months (Figure 4). This predominance of permits valid for at least 12 months was observed across all the EU countries except Croatia, where most permits were valid for 6 to 11 months. The share of residence permits valid for 12 months or longer ranged from 62.9% in Portugal and 74.4% in Ireland up to 100% in Greece. The highest share of residence permits with a validity period of 6 to 11 months was observed in Croatia (55.4%). Meanwhile, Portugal had the highest percentage of residence permits valid for 3 to 5 months, at 21.5%. Figure 4 ===Developments for the stock of residence permits=== Across the EU, there was an increase of 53.4% between the end of 2016 and the end of 2025 in the stock of residence permits granted to non-EU citizens. The most rapid increase was recorded for residence permits valid for refugee or subsidiary protection status, from 1.2 million to 4.1 million (up 251.7%) (Figure 5). In relative terms, between the end of 2016 and the end of 2025, the increase in the stock of permits was considerable for employment (up 120.7%) and education reasons (up 96.8%), while it was smaller for family (up 28.6%) and other reasons (up 10.9%). Figure 5 Figure 6 presents developments among the 4 EU countries having the largest number of permits between the end of 2016 and the end of 2025. In Germany, the stock of residence permits increased from 4.1 million in 2016 to 5.9 million in 2025, despite a drop in 2020 and a slight decrease in 2024.In France, the number of permits rose every year, from 2.7 million in 2016 to 4.4 million in 2025; a similar trend was observed in Spain, up from 2.6 million in 2016 to 4.3 million in 2025. In Italy, the stock of residence permits slightly declined from 3.7 million to 3.4 million between 2016 and 2020, before gradually increasing again to 4.3 million by 2025. Figure 6 Between the end of 2016 and the end of 2025, the increase in the stock of residence permits in the EU was influenced by a rapid rise in the number of permits granted to persons benefiting from refugee or subsidiary protection status. Figure 7 shows that these permits rose from 0.3 million at the end of 2016 to 1.7 million by the end of 2025 while refugee status increased from 0.9 million to 2.4 million over the same period. Figure 7 ===Citizenship of the permit holders=== Map 2 provides an overview of the countries of citizenship of the holders of residence permits in the EU at the end of 2025. The stock of residence permits was highest for citizens of Morocco (2.2 million) and Türkiye (2.0 million), followed by citizens of Ukraine (1.7 million), China (including Hong Kong) (1.2 million), Syria (1.1 million) and India (1.0 million). These were the only countries whose citizens held more than one million residence permits. The next highest numbers were recorded for United Kingdom (919 297), Russia (876 625), Albania (875 105) and Algeria (804 725). By the end of 2025, citizens of these 10 countries accounted for almost a half (45.7%) of the total stock of residence permits held by non-EU citizens in the EU. Map 2: Distribution of residence permits in the EU by country of citizenship of the permit holders, 2025 (number of permits) Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_resvalid}}

Table 1 provides a more detailed analysis for the top 10 countries with the highest stock of permits (as identified above). It shows for example that 81.8% of all residence permits held by Algerian citizens were reported by France, while Germany reported 68.7% of permits held by Syrian citizens and close to two-thirds (64.3%) of those held by Turkish citizens. The next highest shares of residence permits were observed for Albanian citizens in Italy (46.6%), British citizens in Spain (44.5%), Moroccan citizens in Spain (42.4%) and Ukrainian citizens in Poland (35.9%). [[Image:T1_Distribution_of_residence_permits_by_main_issuing_EU_countries,_2025.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: Distribution of residence permits by main issuing EU countries, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=migr_resvalid}}|alt=A table showing the stock of residence permits for residing in the EU among the 10 non-EU countries whose citizens held the largest number of permits. It also shows the three EU countries that granted the highest number of permits to citizens of each of these 10 non-EU countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Developments for residence permits by citizenship and by reason=== For several of the top 10 countries of citizenship of the permit holders, between the end of 2021 and the end of 2025 there was a clear change in the stock of residence permits (Figure 8), with some variations in 2021. *The stock of residence permits for Indian citizens increased noticeably over this period. The sharpest rise was recorded in 2022, followed by continued growth, with the stock reaching its highest level in 2025. *China (including Hong Kong), Algeria and Morocco recorded more moderate increases, with Morocco remaining the citizenship with the highest number of valid residence permits overall. *The number of residence permits held by citizens of Albania and Syria remained relatively stable between 2021 and 2025, at around 0.8–0.9 million for Albanians and 0.9–1.1 million for Syrians. *The situation for the United Kingdom was exceptional, reflecting its withdrawal from the EU on 31 January 2020. The number of residence permits held by British citizens remained broadly stable at around 0.9 million between 2021 and 2025. Figure 8 Among the top 10 non-EU countries whose citizens had the highest numbers of permits to reside in the EU at the end of 2025, Figure 9 provides a more detailed analysis according to the reasons for which the permits were granted. Among Albanian citizens, 46.3% had a permit granted for family-related reasons. As with citizens of Albania, family was also the principal reason for granting residence permits to citizens of Morocco (43.8%), Russia (37.2%) and China (including Hong Kong) (32.1%). For citizens of Türkiye, family-related reasons and refugee or subsidiary protection status accounted for similar shares (36.5% each), with family-related permits slightly higher in absolute terms. Employment-related reasons were predominant among Indians (46.0%) and Ukrainians (44.0%). Most Syrian citizens had a permit granted for reasons related to their refugee or subsidiary protection status 77.0%. Citizens of the United Kingdom (80.4%) and Algeria (44.4%) mainly benefited from residence permits granted for other reasons. Figure 9 === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Residence_permits-statistics_on_stocks_of_valid_permits_2025.xlsx|title=Statistics on the stock of residence permits: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data used in this article – based entirely on administrative sources – are supplied to Eurostat as part of an annual residence permits data collection exercise according to the requirements of Article 6 of [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:32007R0862:EN:NOT Regulation (EC) No 862/2007] on Community statistics on migration and international protection. Commission Regulation [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:32010R0216:EN:NOT (EU) No 216/2010] on Community statistics on migration and international protection, as regards the definitions of categories of the reasons for issuing residence permits, provides the list and definition of reasons for residence permits being issued. Since the 2008 reference year, Eurostat has collected data on permits that have been granted to nationals of non-member countries to reside in the EU. Data on residence permits may be analysed by: *reporting country – the EU country (or EFTA country) granting the residence permit; *citizenship of the permit holder; *reason for the permit being issued – family formation and reunification; education and study; remunerated activities (employment); refugee status; subsidiary protection status; other reasons; *the length of validity of the permit – for at least 3 months but less than 6 months; for at least 6 months but less than 12 months; for 12 months or longer. Statistics on residence permits are available as both stocks and flows. Data on stocks relate to all residence permits at the end of the reference year, in other words, the total stock of residence permits including renewed permits. Certain methodological aspects are not fully harmonised between the reporting countries due to different legal and/or information technology systems. Therefore, the results that are presented in this article should be interpreted with care and readers are advised to make reference to the metadata file on [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/migr_resval_esms.htm residence permits statistics]. The "u" flag in Irish stock residence permits data highlights limited data quality reported by the Irish authorities. For the process of generating resident permits data that involves both the Irish Police and the Department of Justice an old information system is currently being used. The current system's limitations, which misses unique identifier of persons, require manual data checks, which may lead to potential quality issues. According to the Irish authorities, a comprehensive modernisation programme of the information systems to ensure more accurate data management is in progress. ===Context=== Migration policies within the EU are built upon solidarity and responsibility, taking account of the contribution that immigrants make to the EU's economic development and performance. Within the [[Glossary:European Commission|European Commission]], the [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/index_en Directorate-General for Migration and Home Affairs] is responsible for immigration policy. EU policy measures on legal immigration cover the conditions of entry and residence for certain categories of immigrants. The [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32011L0098 Single Permit Directive (2011/98/EU)] establishes rules for a single application/permit and equal treatment provisions for non-EU citizens. The legislation does not apply to certain categories of non-EU citizens, such as highly qualified workers subject to the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32021L1883 EU Blue Card Directive], some students, or various persons working temporarily (for example, as seasonal workers or au pairs), or to migrants who have lived in the EU for at least 5 years and have applied and been granted long-term residence status, as defined in [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32003L0109 Council Directive 2003/109/EC concerning the status of third-country nationals who are long-term residents]. Equally, the legislation concerning the Single Permit Directive does not apply in Denmark or Ireland (each of which has special arrangements for immigration and asylum policy). All relevant legal acts and information regarding the EU's immigration policy can be accessed on the [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/index_en European Commission's website]. In September 2020, the European Commission presented the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/promoting-our-european-way-life/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en/ Pact on Migration and Asylum] which was adopted by the European Parliament in April 2024 and by the Council in May 2024 and will start to apply as of July 2026. The Pact on Migration and Asylum is a comprehensive approach that delivers a common European response to migration. It allows the EU to manage migration in a fair and sustainable way. ===Footnotes=== ===Other articles=== '''Residence permits'''
