The final part of this chapter provides a regional analysis of human resources in science and technology by sex. The EU actively promotes gender equality in the fields of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, through a broad range of policies/initiatives, including gender equality plans within the EU’s research framework programme called [https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe_en Horizon Europe]. The [https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/strategy/strategy-research-and-innovation/our-digital-future/european-research-area_en European research area] and the [https://eige.europa.eu/ European Institute for Gender Equality] both promote initiatives such as gender mainstreaming, training programmes, and networking opportunities for female scientists and engineers. In 2025, there were 20.2 million [[Glossary:Scientists_and_engineers|scientists and engineers]] in the EU. A minority (40.8 %) of the scientists and engineers in the EU were female. '''Map 5''' shows the total number of female scientists and engineers (indicated by the size of each circle) and their share of all scientists and engineers (indicated by the shade of each circle). In 2025, there were 8.2 million female scientists and engineers in the EU. In 2025, the highest numbers of female scientists and engineers were observed in some of the EU’s most populous regions. Among NUTS level 1 regions, the French capital region of Ile-de-France recorded the highest count, with 336 300. It was followed by a group of regions with very similar levels, ranging between 265 100 and 281 400 female scientists and engineers: Nordrhein-Westfalen and Bayern in Germany, Este in Spain, West-Nederland in the Netherlands and Continente in Portugal. There were 10 NUTS level 1 regions where females accounted for more than half of all scientists and engineers in 2025. A majority of these were located in southern EU countries: 4 regions from Spain, 2 from Portugal and a single region from Greece; the remaining 3 regions included Makroregion centralny in Poland, the northernmost region of Sweden and the French outermost regions. Most of this group had relatively small numbers of scientists and engineers. The highest count was observed in Noreste (Spain), with 102 700 female scientists and engineers, the 27th highest value among the 91 regions for which data are available. Although females accounted for a majority (60.0%) of the scientists and engineers in Região Autónoma dos Açores (Portugal; the second highest share), they numbered 4 800, which was the second lowest count, larger only than in the French island region of Corse. At the lower end of the distribution, there were 14 regions in the EU where females accounted for less than 35.0% of all scientists and engineers in 2025. A majority of these regions (8 out of 14) were concentrated in Germany, including several with a strong industrial base, such as Baden-Württemberg (32.2%), Bayern (34.8%) and Nordrhein-Westfalen (34.9%). The lowest share of female scientists and engineers was observed in the central Hungarian region of Közép-Magyarország, where 68 100 females accounted for 31.6% of all scientists and engineers. There were 5 other regions across the EU where females accounted for less than a third of all scientists and engineers: Manner-Suomi (mainland Finland; 31.8%), Slovakia (also 31.8%), the south-western German regions of Baden-Württemberg (32.2%) and Saarland (32.8%) and Nord-Est (Italy; 33.2%).

They provide the detailed rules about the production of European statistics on science and technology (for example, datasets, analyses, frequency or transmission timetable to be respected by the EU countries). The methodology for R&D statistics is laid down in the ''[https://www.oecd.org/publications/frascati-manual-2015-9789264239012-en.htm Frascati manual]'' (OECD, 2015). It provides guidelines for collecting and reporting data on research and experimental development, with definitions of basic concepts and classifications for compiling R&D statistics. R&D intensity is defined as R&D expenditure relative to gross domestic product (GDP), expressed as a percentage. R&D personnel include all persons employed directly within R&D, as well as persons supplying direct services (such as managers, administrative staff and clerical staff). For statistical purposes, indicators on R&D personnel are compiled as both head counts and as full-time equivalents (FTEs). A researcher is a professional engaged in the conception or creation of new knowledge. A researcher conducts research and improves or develops concepts, theories, models, techniques instrumentation, software or operational methods. '''Human resources in science and technology (HRST)''' Regional data on human resources in science and technology (HRST) are derived from the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|European Union’s labour force survey (EU-LFS)]], whose legal basis, starting with survey year 2021, is an integrated European social statistics (IESS) regulation – ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.LI.2019.261.01.0001.01.ENG Regulation (EU) No 2019/1700 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 October 2019 establishing a common framework for European statistics relating to persons and households, based on data at individual level collected from samples]''. The methodology for statistics on HRST is laid down in the ''[http://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/science-and-technology/measurement-of-scientific-and-technological-activities_9789264065581-en Canberra manual]'' (OECD, 1995), which lists all HRST concepts and provides definitions of human resources devoted to science and technology in terms of qualification (levels and fields of study) and occupation. Data on HRST concern stocks of human resources. An HRST stock is defined as the ‘number of people at a particular point in time who fulfils the conditions of the definition of HRST’. The Canberra manual states that HRST comprise those individuals who: *have successfully completed a tertiary level of education (ISCED levels 5 to 8) in a science and technology field and/or *are employed in a science and technology occupation (regardless of their educational background). This results in 3 different HRST categories: *HRST by education – people with a tertiary level of education in science and technology *HRST by occupation – people employed in science and technology occupations *core HRST – people who meet both of the above criteria, in other words, they have a tertiary level of education in a science and technology field and they are employed in a science and technology occupation. Scientists and engineers are people who conduct research, improve or develop concepts, theories and operational methods and/or apply scientific knowledge relating to fields which are covered by one of the following occupations defined in the [https://ilostat.ilo.org/methods/concepts-and-definitions/classification-occupation/ International standard classification of occupations (ISCO-08)]: *21 Science and engineering professionals; *22 Health professionals; *25 Information and communications technology professionals. Scientists and engineers refer to people who, working in those capacities, use or create scientific knowledge and engineering and technological principles. In other words, persons with scientific or technological training who are engaged in professional work on science and technology activities, high-level administrators and personnel who direct the execution of science and technology activities. ===Context=== Europe is often said to have an innovation deficit. A European Commission communication, ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52021PC0574 Path to the Digital Decade]'' (COM(2021) 574 final) reiterates that, despite strong research and invention capacities, Europe continues to lag behind in the diffusion and commercialisation of innovation. This persistent gap may be linked, at least in part, to risk aversion among EU businesses and financial systems, which can hinder the ability to identify and scale disruptive research and breakthrough technologies. A recent report by the Directorate-General for Research and Innovation titled ''[https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/news/all-research-and-innovation-news/combining-regional-strengths-narrow-eu-innovation-divide-2024-06-20_en Combining regional strengths to narrow the EU innovation divide]'' suggests that the innovation divide across EU regions is due to a concentration of innovation-critical factors – such as talent and funding – in hubs (a defining feature of strong innovation ecosystems). The report argues that synergies with other policies, such as skills and economic redistribution, should be encouraged in order to maximise research and innovation policy impacts. A highly skilled workforce is a cornerstone of research and innovation, driving scientific progress, technological development and long-term competitiveness. Strengthening skills across the EU is considered essential to support science and technology sectors and to enable the economy to adapt to the green and digital transitions. The EU has intensified its efforts to promote gender equality in science, technology and innovation through targeted policy initiatives. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0152 Gender Equality Strategy 2020–25] (COM(2020) 152 final) had the goal of eliminating disparities and fostering inclusive workplaces by enhancing women’s participation – particularly in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields. Complementing this, the [https://projects.research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/en/knowledge-publications-tools-and-data/interactive-reports/she-figures-2024 She Figures] report provides essential data to inform policy and monitor progress on gender equality in research and innovation. In addition, the [https://marie-sklodowska-curie-actions.ec.europa.eu/ Marie Skłodowska-Curie actions] promote gender balance in research teams and seek to reduce bias in recruitment and evaluation, thereby supporting the advancement of women’s careers in research. '''Horizon Europe''' Since their launch in 1984, the EU’s framework programmes for research have played a leading role in multidisciplinary research and innovation. In December 2020, a [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/IP_20_2345 political agreement] was reached on [https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe_en Horizon Europe], the EU’s 9th framework programme for research and innovation, which runs until 2027. With a total budget of €93.5 billion, mostly drawn from the EU’s multiannual financial framework for 2021–27, Horizon Europe represents the largest EU research and innovation programme to date. The programme’s [https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe/strategic-plan_en# 2nd strategic plan] (2025–27) outlines 3 key orientations: *the green transition *the digital transition *a more resilient, competitive, inclusive and democratic Europe. Within Horizon Europe, 5 missions have been identified to enhance the effectiveness of funding by pursuing clearly defined targets: *adaptation to climate change *cancer *restoring our oceans and waters *climate-neutral and smart cities *a soil deal for Europe. '''European research area (ERA)''' The [https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/strategy/strategy-research-and-innovation/our-digital-future/european-research-area_en European research area (ERA)], launched in 2000, aims to create a single, borderless market for research, innovation and technology across the EU. It supports better alignment of national policies, the free circulation of researchers, and stronger cross-border cooperation and competition. In September 2020, the European Commission published a communication on ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2020:628:FIN A new ERA for Research and Innovation]'' (COM(2020) 628 final). It acknowledged stagnating EU performance in research and innovation, especially in the light of emerging competition, notably from Asia. Drawing on lessons from the COVID-19 crisis, the communication proposed revitalising the ERA to support the EU’s prosperity, autonomy and global competitiveness through a stronger focus on green and digital transitions, resilience and preparedness to face future crises and innovation leadership. The ''[https://european-research-area.ec.europa.eu/era-policy-agenda-2025-2027 European research area policy agenda 2025–27]'' builds on earlier initiatives and reinforces efforts to create a more cohesive and effective ERA. It has 3 main building blocks: *a policy narrative – to set the scene for broader goals and ambitions *11 structural policies – to outline long-term undertakings such as enabling open science and data reuse, advancing inclusive and intersectional gender equality, improving research careers and strengthening links with higher education, and fostering greater trust in science through public engagement and communication *8 ERA actions – time-bound objectives or pilot initiatives to fill specific gaps concerning new or emerging issues, such as: **facilitating and accelerating the responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI) in science **equity in open science **advancing the European [https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/strategy/support-policy-making/scientific-support-eu-policies/science-policy_en Science for Policy (S4P)] to improve policymaking **enhancing research security across the EU. ===Other articles=== *[[Government_budget_allocations_for_R%26D_(GBARD)|Government budget allocations for R&D (GBARD)]] *[[Human resources in science and technology]] *[[R&D expenditure]] *[[R&D personnel]] *[[SDG_9_-_Industry,_innovation_and_infrastructure|Sustainable development goal 9 (SDG 9) – Industry, innovation and infrastructure]] ===Publications=== '''News title: Resource productivity statistics
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the resource productivity. Data extracted in June 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 Resource productivity in the EU economy has increased by 50% in the period 2000-2025. At EU country level, resource productivity increased in nearly all countries between the year 2000 and 2025. It more than doubled in Ireland, Spain, Slovakia and the Netherlands. Almost half of EU countries, and the EU economy as a whole, achieved absolute decoupling of resource use from economic activities in the period 2000-2025. |alt= Dynamic line chart with three lines showing resource productivity in comparison to GDP and DMC in the EU from 2000 to 2024. This article presents recent statistics on [[Glossary:Resource productivity|resource productivity]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] and its EU countries. Since the year 2000, the EU's resource productivity has increased by 50.0%. Resource productivity quantifies the relation between economic activity - expressed by [[Glossary:GDP|gross domestic product (GDP)]] - and the consumption of material resources - measured as [[Glossary:Domestic material consumption|domestic material consumption (DMC)]] which is an indicator derived from [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/environment/information-data/material-flows-resource-productivity economy-wide material flow accounts (EW-MFA)]. Resource productivity is an important indicator of the sustainable development goal 12 '[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/database/responsible-consumption-and-production responsible consumption and production]'. === Resource productivity of the EU and EU countries over time === Resource productivity is measured as [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]] over [[Glossary:Domestic material consumption|domestic material consumption]] (DMC). The latter measures the total amount of materials directly consumed in an economy by businesses for economic production and by households. The former is a basic measure of the overall size of a country's economy. Two different unit of measure of GDP are used in this article: *GDP expressed in chain-linked [[Building_the_System_of_National_Accounts_-_volume_measures|volumes]] is used for comparisons over time as it shows the development of the economic aggregate excluding inflation; *GDP expressed in current prices converted into [[Glossary:Purchasing power standard (PPS)|purchasing power standards (PPS)]] is used for cross-country comparisons in a specific year as PPS remove differences in price levels between countries. [[Image:Resource productivity in comparison with GDP and DMC, EU, 2000-2025_(Index 2000 = 100)_v2.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Resource productivity in comparison with GDP and DMC, EU, 2000-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nama_10_gdp__custom_21937040/default/table (nama_10_gdp)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_mfa__custom_21936970/default/table (env_ac_mfa)] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_rp__custom_21936999/default/table (env_ac_rp)]|alt= a line chart with three lines showing resource productivity in comparison to GDP and DMC in the EU from 2000 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Since 2000, the resource productivity of the [[Glossary:EU|European Union (EU)]] economy increased by 50.0%. This growth happened mainly with and after the global financial crisis of 2007-2008. Before the crisis, resource productivity had remained rather stable. The COVID-19 recession caused a moderate decline between 2019 and 2020, then the trend of resource productivity continued to expand up to 2024. Reource productivity declined by 1.8% in 2025.(see Figure 1). An analysis of the resource productivity components, namely GDP and DMC, helps to explain these developments. Before 2007-08, GDP and DMC had been increasing almost in parallel resulting in a more or less stable resource productivity. Between 2008 and 2016, the two components decoupled, i.e. developed in reverse directions. Between 2016 and 2021, both components seemed to re-couple again, i.e. show rather parallel annual change patterns. With the on-set of the recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic since 2021 we see a strong decoupling, with GDP increasing by 5.0% from 2021 to 2024 while DMC has decreased by more than 7.0% over the same period. The global financial crisis in 2007-08 had a very different impact on the resource productivity of the EU than the COVID-19 recession. While the former triggered a significant growth in resource productivity, the latter caused a moderate decrease, which, however, remained less pronounced than the GDP fall between 2019 and 2020. During the global financial crisis and the following years, the consumption of materials – in particular for construction, i.e. gross capital formation – dropped much more than the GDP and stayed at low levels until 2016. On the other hand, the COVID-19 pandemic caused a much more significant shrinking of the EU economy compared with the global financial crisis, while material consumption decreased moderately, in particular because the consumption of construction material and biomass almost remained unchanged. At EU country level, resource productivity developed quite differently (see Table 1). It increased in nearly all countries between the year 2000 and 2025. In Ireland, Spain, Slovakia and the Netherlands, resource productivity has more than doubled. Despite the COVID-19 recession, resource productivity increased between 2019-22 in many countries, most notably in Ireland, Hungary and Malta. [[Image:Resource productivity - GDP_ DMC by country, 2000-2025_v2.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Resource productivity - GDP_ DMC by country, 2000-2025
''Source'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_rp__custom_21940773/default/table (env_ac_rp)]|alt= a table showing resource productivity by country by 2000 to 2025 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Variation of resource productivity across EU countries === Expressed in GDP in PPS over DMC, the resource productivity amounts to 3 €/kg for the aggregated EU economy in 2025. The ratio varies considerably across EU countries from around 1 €/kg (Romania, Finland, Estonia and Bulgaria) to countries - the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Italy, Belgium, Spain, Germany, Malta, France and Ireland - above the EU average (see Table 2). There is no clear linear relationship between GDP and DMC across EU countries. There are countries such as Romania with low GDP and high DMC, as well as countries with high GDP and low DMC (e.g. the Netherlands). Further, there are countries with low DMC and low GDP (e.g. Greece) as well as with high DMC and high GDP (e.g. Ireland and Luxembourg). [[Image:Resource productivity, GDP and DMC by country, 2025_v2.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 2: Resource productivity, GDP and DMC, by country, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nama_10_gdp__custom_21940807/default/table?page=time:2025 (nama_10_gdp)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_gind__custom_21940816/default/table?page=time:2025 (demo_gind)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_mfa__custom_21940795/default/table?page=time:2024 (env_ac_mfa)] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_rp__custom_21940785/default/table?page=time:2024 (env_ac_rp)]|alt= a table showing resource productivity, GDP and DMC, by country in 2025 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === DMC and GDP growth rates in the EU and EU countries - decoupling economic growth from material consumption === Looking at the long term 2000-2025 [[Glossary:Annual_average_growth_rate_(AAGR)|annual average change rates (AAGR)]] of DMC and GDP provides an insight on the degree of decoupling between DMC (pressure on the environment) and GDP (economic growth). Table 3 illustrates how far decoupling has been achieved in the EU economy. Absolute decoupling, i.e. absolute decrease of DMC while GDP increases, was achieved by twelve EU countries over the reporting period, and the EU economy as a whole. It is important to note that this outcome should be further investigated as it could also be the result of outsourcing material-intensive production to other parts of the world. However, those aspects of dislocated environmental pressures through trade are not covered by the DMC indicator. More comprehensive data which reflect materials embodied in trade can be found in [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Material_flow_accounts_-_flows_in_raw_material_equivalents Material flow accounts - flows in raw material equivalents] [[Image:Annual average growth rates (AAGR) of DMC and GDP by country, 2000-2025_v3.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 3: Annual average growth rates of DMC and GDP by country, 2000-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nama_10_gdp__custom_21940822/default/table?page=time:2025 (nama_10_gdp)] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_ac_mfa__custom_21940821/default/table?page=time:2024 (env_ac_mfa)]|alt= a table showing changes of DMC and GDP by country from 2000 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Resource_productivity_statistics_June2026-v5.xlsx|Resource productivity: tables and figures]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png| 20px|link=http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/images/9/9c/Resource_productivity.xls]] ===Data sources=== This article uses data from economy-wide material flow accounts (EW-MFA), which are one of the European environmental economic accounts (see {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02011R0691-20140616:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 691/2011}} on European environmental economic accounts). Economy-wide material flow accounts (EW-MFA) provide an aggregate overview, in thousand tonnes per year, of the material flows into and out of an economy. EW-MFA cover solid, gaseous, and liquid materials, except for bulk flows of water and air. Material inputs into national economies include domestic extraction of material originating from the domestic environment and physical imports originating from other economies. Material outputs from national economies include materials released to the domestic environment (e.g. emissions to air, water and soil) and physical exports to other economies. Material flows within the economy are not represented in EW-MFA. A variety of material flow-based indicators are derived from EW-MFA amongst which the following: '''[[Glossary:Domestic_material_consumption_(DMC)|Domestic material consumption (DMC)]]''' measures the total amount, in tonnes, of material directly used in an economy, i.e. by resident businesses, governments and other institutions for economic production or by households. DMC equals the domestic extractions of materials plus imports minus exports. At the same time, DMC is the amount of materials that become part of the material stock within the economy or are released back to the environment in form of e.g. emissions to air. '''[[Glossary: Resource_productivity|Resource productivity]]''' is defined here as GDP divided by DMC. It is important to note that GDP is expressed in different measurement units, of which the following are used to calculate three different resource productivity ratios. The appropriate choice depends on the context of the analysis: * € per kg using chain-linked volume data for GDP, to be used for analysing developments in real terms over time; * PPS per kg using current price data for GDP expressed in purchasing power standards (PPS); PPS are artificial currency units that remove differences in purchasing power between economies by taking account of price level differences; these can be used when comparing across different economies at one point in time (for one particular year); * € per kg using current price data for GDP, which could be used when analysing a single economy at one point in time (for one particular year). See also [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/env_ac_mfa_sims.htm MFA metadata]. '''Decoupling''' The term decoupling refers to breaking the link between an environmental and an economic variable. As defined by the [[Glossary: Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development_%28OECD%29|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)]], decoupling occurs when the growth rate of an environmental pressure (for example, DMC) is less than that of its economic driving force (for example, GDP) over a given period. Decoupling can be either absolute or relative. Absolute decoupling is said to occur when the environmental variable is stable or decreases while the economic driving force increases. Decoupling is said to be relative when the rate of change of the environmental variable is less than the rate of change of the economic variable. ===Context=== Eurostat's environmental accounts and statistics inform policy making under the [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029_en European Commission's 2024-2029 priorities]. In this context, the [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/competitiveness_en plan for Europe's sustainable prosperity and competitiveness] works towards a more circular and resilient economy to shift to a more sustainable pattern of production and consumption, retaining the value of resources in our economy for longer. Further reading: [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/circular-economy-action-plan_en The 2020 Circular Economy Action Plan for a Cleaner and More Competitive Europe and the Circular Economy Act] ===Other articles=== *[[Material flow accounts and resource productivity]] *[[Physical imports and exports]] *[[Material flow accounts - title: Residence permits – statistics on authorisations to reside and work
text:
The article shows an overview of the 2023 statistics based on the results of data collection for specific EU directives. Data extracted: 18 December 2025. Planned article update: December 2026. In 2024, more than 4.6 million non-EU citizens obtained the right to both reside and work in the EU through the single permit administrative procedure. In 2024, Indian citizens received the highest number of authorisations to reside for study, research and other activities (52 890 authorisations), continuing the growth observed over the previous year. A total of 273 897 authorisations for seasonal work in the EU were issued to non-EU citizens in 2024, 43% increase compared with 2023. This article presents statistics on authorisations to reside and work issued by EU countries on the basis of specific EU directives, which require harmonised rules for non-EU citizens allowing them to receive legal residence and employment rights. ===Overview of EU directives at EU and national level=== Table 1 shows that single permits represent by far the largest legal path to obtaining residence and working rights in the EU. More than 4.6 million single permits were issued in the EU in 2024, representing a significant number of non-EU citizens benefiting from the simplified procedure of issuing residence rights together with a work permit. The 4 other types of authorisations refer to specific groups of non-EU citizens being granted the right to work in EU countries. 475 138 residence permits were issued under the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2016/801/oj Student and researchers (SR) Directive], 273 897 under the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32014L0036 Seasonal Workers (SW) Directive], 78 096 under the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32021L1883 EU Blue Card (BC) Directive] and 10 230 under the Intra-corporate transfers under the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32014L0066 Intra-corporate transfers (ICT) Directive]. [[Image:Residence_permits_issued_under_the_EU_directives,_2024_V2.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: Residence permits issued under EU Directives, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_resbc11__custom_19379758/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=d15decc7-7a5d-4925-b9ea-1cae5ac99609&c=1765984526000 migr_resbc11]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_ressing__custom_19223531/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=b4518dbf-1a46-452e-a8d9-c261768e0cbe&c=1764945349000 migr_ressing]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/447f40b5-fab0-4851-9e19-17a963b0a50f?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-05T15:49:34Z migr_ressw1_1]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/880c3746-bd0d-4931-bfdf-99af724d231a?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-08T08:14:01Z migr_resict1_1]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7002a410-0106-4675-afb5-debceba01770?lang=en&createdAt=2025-12-08T08:14:49Z migr_ressrath])|alt=Table with columns on the number of residence permits issued under the 5 EU directives in 2024 (Single permits, EU Blue Card holders, Seasonal work, Intra-corporate transfers, Students, researchers and other categories) and rows with the reporting countries. The share of number of residence permits in the EU total is also shown for each country and directive. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Single procedure for non-EU citizens to reside and work in the EU=== '''''More than 4.6 million single permits were issued in the EU in 2024''''' The number of single permits issued has risen for two consecutive years, reaching 4 607 257 in 2024. This was the highest number recorded, representing an increase of 13.6 % compared with 2023 (4 056 150 single permits issued) and 28.0 % compared with 2022 (3 598 032). '''''More than 60% of single permits issued in 2024 were extensions of an existing residence permit''''' In 2024, more than two-thirds of single permits issued in the EU were extensions of residence permits (67.6% or 3 113 809), which can be broken down to either renewals (61.9%) or change of status (5.7%) of existing residence permits (Figure 1). The remaining 32.4% (1 493 448) of single permits were issued for the first time i.e. an inflow in the reporting EU country. Nearly two-thirds of the total number of single permits (61.9%) issued in the EU were issued by 3 countries in 2024: Portugal (1 214 086, 26.4% of the total), France (993 247 permits, 21.6%), and Spain (644 194, 14.0%) (Table 1). Figure 1 ===EU Blue Cards issued to highly qualified non-EU citizens=== '''''More than 78 000 EU Blue Cards issued in 2024''''' The overall trend of EU Blue Cards issued in the EU shows a positive trend since 2016, except for 2020 when a decrease of 3.6% was recorded due to the COVID-19 pandemic and a decrease of 12.3% in 2024 probably due to the revision of the EU Blue Cards Directive (Figure 2). 78 096 EU Blue Cards were granted to non-EU citizens in 2024 after a record number of 89 055 in 2023, when an increase of 8.8% was recorded compared with the 81 846 EU Blue Cards granted in 2022. Figure 2 '''''Germany issued 56 252 EU Blue Cards in 2024 (72.0% of all EU Blue Cards issued)''''' Table 1 shows that, in 2024, the majority of EU Blue Cards in the EU (89.5%) were issued in 5 countries: Germany (56 252, 72.0% of the total), Poland (5 853, 7.5%), Hungary (2942, 3.8%), France (2 775, 3.6%) and Spain (1 924 or 2.5%). Conversely, 6 EU countries issued less than 100 EU Blue Cards in 2024: Greece (95 EU Blue Cards), Sweden (62), Estonia (41), Slovakia (32), Portugal (16) and Cyprus issued no EU Blue Cards. '''''Citizens of India were granted the highest number of EU Blue Cards in 2024''''' The top 10 countries whose citizens were granted EU Blue Cards in 2024 accounted for nearly two-thirds (63.3%) of the total 78 096 cards issued in the EU in 2024 (Figure 3). Of these, 16 268 EU Blue Cards were granted to citizens of India, representing 20.8% of all EU Blue Cards issued in the EU. The next largest numbers were for citizens of Russia (6 657 EU Blue Cards, 8.5% of the total), Türkiye (5 645, 7.2%), China (4 550, 5.8%), Belarus (3 533, 4.5%), Ukraine (3 524, 4.5%) and Iran (3503, 4.5%). In this top 10 countries list, 3 countries recorded less than 2 000 EU Blue Cards issued to the citizens of Syria (1 955), Tunisia (1 889), and United States (1 884). Figure 3 ===Authorisations for seasonal work=== '''''273 897 authorisations for seasonal work were issued in 2024''''' The total number of authorisations for seasonal work granted to non-EU citizens in the EU rose by 42.8 %, from 191 840 residence permits issued in 2023 to 273 897 in 2024. This follows the trend from the previous year, when 20.5 % more authorisations for seasonal work were granted compared with 2022. Figure 4 '''''Italy issued 146 099 authorisations for seasonal work in 2024''''' Table 1 shows that, in 2024, most authorisations for seasonal work in the EU were issued in the following 5 countries: Italy (146 099, 53.3% of the total), France (41 700, 15.2%), Spain (20 810, 7.6 %), Croatia (16 555, 6.0%) and Greece (15 206, 5.6%). On the opposite side of the ranking, 8 EU countries issued less than 100 authorisations for seasonal work in 2024: Cyprus (83), Slovakia (29) and Romania (19), and no authorisations to reside for seasonal work were issued in Hungary, Luxembourg, Malta, Portugal and the Netherlands. '''''Citizens of Morocco were granted the highest number of authorisations to reside for seasonal work in the EU in 2024''''' The top 5 countries whose citizens were granted authorisations for seasonal work in 2024 accounted for more than two-thirds (69.4%) of the total 273 897 authorisations for seasonal work issued in the EU in 2024 (Figure 5). Of these, 76 579 authorisations were granted to citizens of Morocco, which represented 28.0% of all authorisations for seasonal work issued in the EU. The next largest numbers and shares were for citizens of Bangladesh (53 567 authorisations for seasonal work, 19.6%), India (39 137, 14.3%), Tunisia (12 675, 4.6%) and Pakistan (8 240, 3.0%). Figure 5 === Authorisations for intra-corporate transfers === '''''10 230 authorisations for intra-corporate transfers were issued in 2024''''' The number of intra-corporate transfer authorisations (referring to persons posted from a company operating outside the EU to a branch in one of the EU countries) granted to non-EU citizens changed the trend between 2021 and 2024, rising sharply from 6 260 in 2021 to over 10 000 in 2022–2023, and recording a slight decrease between 2023 and 2024 (from 10 846 to 10 230, a 5.7% drop). Figure 6 '''''The Netherlands issued nearly one-quarter of all authorisations to reside for intra-corporate transfers in 2024''''' Table 1 shows that, in 2024, most authorisations for intra-corporate transfers granted in the EU (82.9%) were issued by 5 countries: the Netherlands (2 400, 23.5% of the total), Hungary (1 985, 19.4%), France (1 784, 17.4%), Germany (1 556, 15.2%), and Spain (751, 7.3%). On opposite side of the ranking, 7 EU countries issued less than 20 authorisations in 2024: Slovakia (18 authorisations), Malta (12), Latvia (11), Portugal (4), Poland (1), and no authorisation to reside for intra-corporate transfers was issued in Estonia and Cyprus. '''''Citizens of India were granted the highest number of authorisations to reside for intra-corporate transfers in the EU in 2024''''' The top 5 countries whose citizens were granted authorisations for intra-corporate transfers in 2024 accounted for nearly three-quarters (74.1%) of the total 10 230 authorisations issued (Figure 7). Of these, 3 346 authorisations were granted to citizens of India, which represented 32.7% of all authorisations for intra-corporate transfers issued in the EU. The next largest numbers and shares were for citizens of China (2 181 authorisations for intra-corporate transfers, 21.3% of the total), South Korea (816, 8.0%), United Kingdom (653, 6.4%) and the United States (589, 5.8%). Figure 7 === Authorisations for students and researchers (and other related categories) === '''''In 2024, 475 138 of authorisations for study, research and other activities were issued in the EU''''' The total number of authorisations for study, research and other related activities (authorisations issued to trainees, volunteers, school pupils and au pairs) granted to non-EU citizens in the EU increased between 2022 and 2024 (Figure 8). In 2022, 421 974 authorisations for students and researchers and other related categories were issued in the EU, followed by an increase in the following two years: 6.8% increase in 2023 (450 848 authorisations issued) and 5.4% increase in 2024 (475 138). Figure 8 '''''Germany issued nearly one-third of all authorisations for study, research and other activities in 2024''''' Table 1 shows that, in 2024, about three quarters of total authorisations for study, research and other activities in the EU were issued in the following 5 countries (75.1%): Germany (131 098, 27.6% of the total), France (118 430, 24.9%), Spain (59 384, 12.5%), the Netherlands (25 961, 5.5%) and Hungary (22 132, 4.7%). On the other side of the ranking, 4 countries issued less than 1000 authorisations: Estonia (782 authorisations), Croatia (522), and Ireland (400) while no authorisations to reside for study, research and other activities were issued in Greece. '''''Citizens of India were granted the highest number of authorisations to reside for study, research and other activities, in the EU in 2024''''' The top ten countries whose citizens were granted authorisations for study, research and other activities in 2024 accounted for nearly half of the total authorisations (47.4%) (Figure 9). Of these, 52 890 authorisations were granted to citizens of India, which represented 11.1% of all such authorisations in the EU. The next largest numbers were for citizens of China (43 985 authorisations, 9.3%), Morocco (22 918, 4.8%), United States (21 694, 4.6%), Türkiye (18 711, 3.9%), Iran (16 146, 3.4%), Pakistan (13 421, 2.8%), Brazil (12 049, 2.5%), Algeria (11 916, 2.5%), and Colombia (11 680 2.5%). All these 10 countries excepting China and Algeria recorded an increase in the last 2 years (2023 and 2024) (Figure 9). The greatest increase in 2024 in absolute numbers in comparison with 2023 was recorded by citizens of Iran (+9 181), Pakistan (+4 304) and Brazil (+4 075. A decrease was recorded by China (-3 009) and Algeria (-1 405). Figure 9 === Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=Residence_permits_-_statistics_on_authorisations_to_reside_and_work_MIGR2025_V2.xlsx|title=Residence permits – statistics on authorisations to reside and work: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The statistics presented in this article are collected by Eurostat on the basis of EU legal acts, covering specific areas of the legal migration of non-EU citizens to the EU countries: statistics on Single Permits, statistics on EU Blue Cards, statistics on Intra-Corporate Transfers, statistics on Seasonal Workers and statistics on Students and Researchers and other related categories. EU directives are European Union (EU) legal acts that are transposed by EU Member States so they become law in the Member States. See more details here: [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/european-union-directives.html EUR-Lex - European Union directives]. For more technical aspects and guidelines in relation to the collection of these statistics, please refer to definitions and methodological concepts. ===Context=== The topic of residence permits issued under the EU directives refers to the EU legal migration policy on working area that facilitates a balanced common EU migration policy from which migrants, countries of origin, and countries of destination benefit. These EU legal acts are part of the legal migration policy that support the EU's green and digital transition, while making European societies more cohesive and resilient. In practice, the EU has developed rules to harmonise Member States' conditions of entry and residence for certain categories of nationals from non-EU countries. This includes entry and residence for labour purposes, such as highly qualified workers, seasonal workers, intra-corporate transfers, students and researchers and other categories. Single permit procedure is also important in this context, expressing the policy that promotes simplified procedure of issuing the residence permits for different reason together with the right to work, helping the integration of migrants and reducing the bureaucracy at the same time. For further information on these and other measures (seasonal workers and intra-corporate transferees) please refer to the European Commission webpage on [https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/networks/labour-migration-platform_en labour migration]. ===Other articles=== '''Residence permits''' title: Resources and green transformation in Southern Mediterranean countries
text:
This article is part of an online Eurostat publication that provides a statistical overview over the Southern Mediterranean countries. The article presents statistics on recent economic developments for Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Palestine and Tunisia and compares these with the EU. Data extracted in February 2026 Planned article update: June 2027 In 2024, Algeria's water abstraction was 10 389 million cubic metres of freshwater, the highest among the Southern Mediterranean countries for which data are available. In 2024, Morocco’s primary energy production was dominated by renewables, which accounted for 84.7% of total primary energy production, confirming its leading position in the green energy transition among the Southern Mediterranean countries. In 2024, Algeria was the only net exporter of energy among the Southern Mediterranean countries for which data are available, with net energy exports of 91.0 million tonnes of oil equivalent. This article is part of an [[European_Neighbourhood_Policy_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]]. It presents information on nine [[Glossary:European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP)|Southern Mediterranean]] countries, namely Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Palestine This designation shall not be construed as recognition of a State of Palestine and is without prejudice to the individual positions of the EU Member States on this issue. and Tunisia. Information on these countries is compared with developments in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union]]. This article contains no data on Syria, as cooperation with Syria was suspended from 2011 until recently and no data are collected yet. Lebanon data does not account for Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon. Given that data collection for Southern Mediterranean countries is non-obligatory and subject to various changes related to the political and geographical context, data availability may often show inconsistency over the entire period presented or for recent years. The article presents a range of resources and green transformation indicators such as annual freshwater abstraction, [[Glossary:Primary energy production|primary energy production]], net import of energy and [[Glossary:Gross inland energy consumption|gross inland energy consumption]]. Energy is an important issue due to various reasons. These include the fluctuation in energy prices, disruptions in energy supplies, and growing concerns about how human activities affect climate change, especially the rise in greenhouse gas emissions. The Southern Mediterranean countries experience many of the environmental issues faced globally. Issues like water quality, water scarcity, soil erosion, and desertification are particularly significant. Water is vital for life and plays a crucial role in the economy, especially in agriculture. However, it is becoming increasingly scarce in many Southern Mediterranean countries. ===Annual freshwater abstraction=== Figure 1 compares [[Glossary:Water_abstraction|annual freshwater abstraction]] in the Southern Mediterranean countries from 2014 to 2024, in million cubic metres (m3). 'Annual freshwater abstraction' measures the total volume of freshwater withdrawn from surface and groundwater sources over a year, regardless of its subsequent use or whether it is returned to the environment. In Algeria, freshwater abstraction increased sharply between 2014 and 2020, rising from 4.8 billion m3 in 2014 to a peak of 10.5 billion m3 in 2020. This corresponds to more than a doubling of abstraction levels over the period. After a slight decrease in 2021, abstraction resumed an upward trend, reaching 10.4 billion m3 in 2024, close to its peak level. Algeria consistently recorded the highest freshwater abstraction among the Southern Mediterranean countries throughout the period. In Morocco, freshwater abstraction fluctuated but showed an overall downward trend between 2014 and 2021 (more recent data not available). After reaching a peak of 10.2 billion m3 in 2015, abstraction declined to 6.7 billion m3 in 2021, representing a reduction of 34.4%. The most pronounced decrease occurred in 2020 (-20.4% compared with 2019). Freshwater abstraction in Israel remained relatively stable over the period 2014-2024, ranging between 1.1 to 1.5 billion m3. After increasing to a peak of 1.5 billion m3 in 2021, abstraction declined slightly in 2023 before rising again to 1.5 billion m3 in 2024, indicating overall stability with moderate year-on-year variation. In Jordan, freshwater abstraction showed a generally upward trend between 2015 and 2023 (data for 2014 and 2024 not available). Abstraction increased from 1.0 billion m3 in 2015 to 1.2 billion m3 in 2023, reflecting a gradual rise of 19.2%. A temporary decline was observed in 2021, but the upward trend resumed thereafter. Palestine recorded a moderate but overall increasing trend in freshwater abstraction between 2014 and 2022 (more recent data not available). Abstraction rose from 0.28 billion m3 in 2014 to a peak of 0.35 billion m3 in 2020, before declining slightly and stabilising at around 0.34 billion m3 in 2021 and 2022. Egypt reported 62 million m3 in 2016 (more recent data not available). Overall, the data highlight contrasting developments across the Southern Mediterranean countries, with strong increases in Algeria, a marked decline in Morocco, and more stable or moderately increasing trends in Israel, Jordan and Palestine, reflecting differing levels of water availability, demand pressures and resource management strategies. [[Image: ENPS26_Annual freshwater abstraction, 2014-2024_(million m3).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Annual freshwater abstraction, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/db6db897-84f3-43c0-9318-7eeaf196a314?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T14:10:18Z enps_env_wat_abs])|alt=Line chart on annual freshwater abstraction from 2014 to 2024 in Southern Mediterranean countries. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] ===Primary energy production by sources=== [[Glossary:Primary_production_of_energy|Primary energy production]] refers to energy commodities extracted or captured directly from natural resources, such as [[Glossary:Solid_fuels|solid fuels]], [[Glossary:Crude_oil|crude oil]], natural gas, [[Glossary:Nuclear_heat|nuclear heat]] and hydroelectric power; and [[Glossary:Renewable_energy_sources|renewables]] sources. Crude oil production covers fuel extracted within national boundaries, including offshore areas. Natural gas production refers to dry gas measured after purification and the removal of natural gas liquids and sulphur. Energy generated through transformation processes, such as electricity or heat produced in thermal power plants, is not considered primary energy production. Levels of primary energy production can vary significantly from year to year due to changes in demand linked to economic conditions and heating needs, fluctuations in energy prices driven by international markets, and weather conditions affecting hydroelectric and renewable energy sources. Longer-term developments may also reflect the emergence of new energy sources or the depletion or replacement of existing ones. Figure 2 shows that in Algeria, primary energy production in 2024 was almost entirely based on natural gas (58.3%) and crude oil and petroleum products (41.7%). A similarly strong reliance was observed in Egypt (2023 data), where natural gas represented 59.5% and crude oil 32.6%, with only a limited contribution from renewables (4.2%). In Israel, primary energy production was dominated by natural gas, which accounted for 90.3% of the total in 2024, while renewables contributed a relatively small share (6.3%). In contrast, Morocco showed a different production structure, largely based on renewable energy, which accounted for 84.7% of primary energy production in 2024, complemented by smaller contributions from other sources (11.7%). Tunisia presented a more diversified energy mix, with crude oil and petroleum products (41.3%) and natural gas (40.4%) accounting for the majority of production, while renewables contributed 16.4%. The structure of primary energy production in the EU was more diversified in 2024, compared with the Southern Mediterranean countries, with renewables (48.1%) and nuclear heat (28.2%) representing the largest shares, followed by solid fuels (12.3%), natural gas (5.1%) and crude oil and petroleum products (3.3%). Overall, the data highlight a clear contrast within the Southern Mediterranean countries, with some countries remaining heavily reliant on fossil fuels, while others, particularly Morocco, show a strong orientation towards renewable energy sources, whereas the EU maintains a broadly diversified energy mix. [[Image: ENPS26_Primary energy production by sources, 2024_(% of total primary production).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Primary energy production by sources, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/34eae00a-dabb-4299-9f6a-a3eb864537ff?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:11:39Z (nrg_bal_s)] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3b327242-d663-4829-ab13-9869ac3a37b3?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T14:57:34Z (enps_nrg_pprd)]|alt=Stacked column chart showing primary energy production by sources for 2024, as a percentage of total primary energy production, in the EU and Southern Mediterranean countries. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] ===Net import of energy=== Net energy imports are calculated as energy imports minus energy exports. Imports include all energy products entering a country, excluding quantities in transit (for example via gas or oil pipelines). Exports cover all energy products leaving the country. Negative values indicate net exports, meaning that exports exceeded imports. Figure 3 presents net energy imports for the Southern Mediterranean countries for the period 2014-2024, measured in thousand [[Glossary:Tonnes_of_oil_equivalent_(toe)|tonnes of oil equivalent (toe)]]. In Morocco, net energy imports showed an upward trend over the period, increasing from 19 457 thousand toe in 2014 to 21 900 thousand toe in 2024 (+12.6%), despite some fluctuations. This reflects a continued reliance on imported energy to meet growing domestic demand. In Egypt, net energy imports fluctuated over the period. After rising sharply to 16 064 thousand toe in 2017, Egypt was a net exporter in 2019 (-2 860 thousand toe). Thereafter, the trend reversed, with imports increasing again to 7 167 thousand toe in 2023 (2024 data not available), indicating a renewed dependence on external energy supply. Tunisia recorded a gradual increase in net energy imports from 4 146 thousand toe in 2014 to 6 815 thousand toe in 2024 (+64.4%). Despite some year-on-year variation, the overall trend points to rising import needs. Net energy imports in Jordan increased steadily from 8 433 thousand toe in 2014 to 9 277 thousand toe in 2017 (more recent data not available). Lebanon showed a downward trend in net energy imports in recent years. After peaking at 8 472 thousand toe in 2017, imports declined to 5 028 thousand toe in 2024, despite a temporary increase in 2023. In Palestine, net imports followed a gradual upward trend, reaching 1 690 thousand toe in 2019 (more recent data not available). In Israel, net energy imports declined strongly over the period, falling from 15 682 thousand toe in 2014 to 1 083 thousand toe in 2024. This substantial decrease reflects a reduced reliance on imports, likely linked to increased domestic energy production, particularly natural gas. Libya recorded net exports over the available period (data up to 2020), with values ranging between 5 134 thousand toe in 2019 and 3 773 thousand toe in 2020. Algeria remained a large net exporter of energy throughout the period. Net exports were already very high in 2014 (95 325 thousand toe), peaked at 105 520 thousand toe in 2016, and, despite some fluctuations, remained at similarly high levels in recent years, reaching 90 968 thousand toe in 2024. For the EU, net energy imports increased from 798 910 thousand toe in 2014 to a peak of 908 439 thousand toe in 2019. After a sharp decline in 2020 (-12.8%), imports partially recovered in 2021 and 2022, before decreasing again to 759 968 thousand toe in 2024. Overall, the Southern Mediterranean region displays contrasting patterns, with countries such as Morocco and Tunisia showing increasing dependence on energy imports, while Algeria and Libya continued to be net exporters of energy and Israel has significantly reduced its reliance on imported energy. [[Image: ENPS26_Net energy imports, 2014-2024 (thousand tonnes of oil equivalent).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Net energy imports, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/39759460-207c-4324-b592-e032b41d05df?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T14:55:58Z nrg_bal_s]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9f391daa-d82f-4564-870c-46a704cc3121?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T14:56:48Z enps_nrg_imp])|alt=Line chart showing net energy imports from 2014 to 2024 in the EU and Southern Mediterranean countries. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] ===Gross inland energy consumption=== [[Glossary:Gross_inland_energy_consumption|Gross inland energy consumption]] is the energy that a country requires to meet its internal (national) demand. It covers consumption by the energy sector itself; distribution and transformation losses; final energy consumption by end users; non-energy use by end users (such as feedstock for the petrochemical industry, lubricants); and statistical differences. It represents the total energy demand of a country or region from all sources necessary to satisfy inland consumption. In Israel, gross inland energy consumption per capita followed a gradual downward trend over the period 2014-2023, decreasing from 2 622 [[Glossary:Kilograms_of_oil_equivalent_(kgoe)|kilogrammes of oil equivalent (kgoe)]] per capita to 2 506 kgoe/capita (see Figure 4). Despite some fluctuations, including temporary increases in 2015, 2018 and 2022, the overall pattern indicates a moderate decline in energy use per person. In 2024, gross inland energy consumption decreased further to 2 458 kgoe/capita, but this data is affected by a break in time series. In Algeria, energy consumption per capita fluctuated over the period 2014-2021 (more recent data not available), remaining broadly stable overall. It ranged between 1 448 kgoe/capita in 2015 and 1 594 kgoe/capita in 2019. Tunisia recorded a fluctuating trend over the period 2014-2023 (2024 data not available). After falling to a low of 807 kgoe/capita in 2016, consumption increased to 998 kgoe/capita in 2018, before declining again to 931 kgoe/capita in 2023. Overall, levels remained broadly stable compared with the beginning of the period. In Egypt, energy consumption per capita rose from 901 kgoe/capita in 2014 to a peak of 1 004 kgoe/capita in 2017, before following a gradual downward trend to 881 kgoe/capita in 2023 (2024 data not available). Morocco showed a generally upward trend between 2014 and 2023 (2024 data not available), increasing from 589 kgoe/capita in 2014 to 643 kgoe/capita in 2023. In Palestine, energy consumption per capita increased overall from 388 kgoe/capita in 2014 to a peak of 479 kgoe/capita in 2022, before decreasing to 435 kgoe/capita in 2023 (more recent data not available). Data for Lebanon and Libya are too limited to allow a meaningful assessment of trends. In Jordan, energy consumption fluctuated between 2014 and 2018 (more recent data not available), ranging between 900 kgoe/capita in 2015 and 1 009 kgoe/capita in 2014. For the EU, gross inland energy consumption per capita peaked in 2017 at 3 354 kgoe/capita before declining sharply in 2020, largely due to reduced activity during the Covid-19 pandemic. After a partial rebound in 2021, consumption resumed its downward trend, falling to 2 888 kgoe/capita in 2024. Overall, gross inland energy consumption per capita in Southern Mediterranean countries remained well below EU levels, with diverse national trends reflecting differences in economic development, energy efficiency and energy systems. [[Image: ENPS26_Gross inland energy consumption, 2014-2024_(kilogrammes of oil equivalent per capita).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Gross inland energy consumption, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0418bbed-dfab-4d44-b8ef-98d129718aa6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:01:33Z nrg_bal_s]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/062af588-3ad0-4db4-b954-2bbfb413ae43?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:04:48Z demo_gind]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0657306c-6af3-40b3-b106-489ef10dd9f8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T14:06:04Z enps_nrg_gic])|alt=Line chart showing gross inland energy consumption, from 2014 to 2024 in the EU and Southern Mediterranean countries. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] ===Renewable energy in gross final energy consumption=== Renewable energy in gross final energy consumption measures how much of the energy actually used in an economy comes from renewable sources, expressed as a percentage of total energy use. In Morocco, the share of renewables remained relatively stable over the period 2014-2024, fluctuating around 10-11% (see Figure 5). After a slight decline between 2015 and 2017, the share gradually increased again, reaching 11.8% in 2024, the highest level observed over the period. Palestine recorded comparatively high shares of renewable energy, although with some volatility. The share declined from 13.8% in 2014 to 9.9% in 2017, before partially recovering in subsequent years and stabilising at around 10-11% up to 2023 (more recent data not available). In Israel, the share of renewables increased steadily throughout the period, rising from 3.0% in 2014 to 8.3% in 2023 (more recent data not available). This continuous growth indicates gradual progress in the uptake of renewable energy, although levels remained below those observed in Morocco and Palestine. Tunisia showed a moderate increase in the share of renewables between 2017 and 2020, rising from 10.6% to 12.2%. This was followed by some fluctuation, before a sharp decrease to 5.3% in 2024, the lowest level recorded over the available period. This sharp decrease was due to a reduction of the renewable energy consumption in households. In Algeria, the share of renewables remained low and broadly unchanged, at around 0.1-0.2% between 2015 and 2024, highlighting the continued dominance of fossil fuels in the energy mix. At EU level, the share of renewables increased steadily from 17.4% in 2014 to 25.2% in 2024, reflecting sustained progress towards renewable energy targets, which aim to increase the share of renewables in gross final energy consumption as part of the transition to climate neutrality. Overall, the data show varying degrees of progress across the Southern Mediterranean countries, with gradual increases in some cases, such as Israel and Morocco, contrasting with stagnation in Algeria and more recent declines in Tunisia, while the EU maintained a consistent upward trend in the share of renewable energy. [[Image: ENPS26_Renewable energy in gross final energy consumption, 2014-2024_(% of total consumption).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Renewable energy in gross final energy consumption, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/54b4212e-40ae-4ccc-9220-70af9fb1d712?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:56:59Z nrg_ind_ren]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c3ce5855-4183-4e55-ae95-5642fecb2528?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-06T14:55:00Z enps_nrg_rnew])|alt=Line chart showing renewable energy in gross final energy consumption from 2014 to 2024 as a percentage of total consumption in the EU and Southern Mediterranean countries. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=ENPS26_Resources and green transformation_V2.xlsx|title= Southern Mediterranean countries — Resources and green transformation: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data for Southern Mediterranean countries are supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country on a voluntary basis. The data that are presented in this article result from an annual data collection cycle that has been established by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]. These statistics are available on Eurostat's website, together with a range of different indicators covering most socio-economic areas. '''Energy''' For EU statistics, the main legislation covering the collection of statistics in relation to energy quantities is [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:32008R1099:EN:NOT Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 October 2008 on energy statistics. Since its adoption, it has been amended several times and a [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:02008R1099-20171130:EN:NOT consolidated] version is available. A summary of the relevant legislation is also available on Eurostat's website, under '[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/energy/legislation Legislation]' on the dedicated section for [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/energy/overview Energy statistics]. '''Environment''' Eurostat, in close partnership with the [[Glossary:European Environment Agency (EEA)|European Environment Agency (EEA)]], provides environmental statistics, accounts and indicators supporting the development, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of the EU's environmental policies, strategies and initiatives. The collection of water statistics within the EU is based on information demands linked to the [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/water/water-framework/index_en.html Directive 2000/60/EC Water Framework Directive (WFD)]. Eurostat and the [[Glossary:OECD|OECD]] jointly administer a questionnaire on inland waters among EU Member States, candidate countries and potential candidates. Data collection is voluntary although there is an initiative to establish a legal framework for the collection of water statistics. A large amount of data and other information on water is accessible via [http://water.europa.eu/ WISE], the water information system for Europe, which is hosted by the [http://www.eea.europa.eu/ European Environment Agency (EEA)] in Copenhagen. ===Context=== The EU's long-term strategy for reducing greenhouse gas emissions was laid out in November 2018, with the aim of making Europe the world's first climate-neutral continent by 2050. In December 2019, the European Commission presented the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en European Green Deal], set out in [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52019DC0640&qid=1713270488420 Communication COM(2019) 640 final]. The European Green Deal is a growth strategy that aims to transform the EU into a fair and prosperous society, with a modern, resource-efficient and competitive economy where there are no net emissions of greenhouse gases by 2050 and where economic growth is decoupled from resource use. The Green Deal is an integral part of this Commission's strategy to implement the [https://sdgs.un.org/2030agenda United Nation’s 2030 Agenda] and the [https://sdgs.un.org/goals Sustainable Development Goals]. In June 2021, the [https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/european-green-deal/european-climate-law_en European Climate Law], [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32021R1119 Regulation (EU) 2021/1119], was adopted. The European Climate Law makes the goal set out in the European Green Deal to become climate-neutral by 2050 a legal obligation for the EU and its Member States. It sets the framework for actions for reducing greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% levels by 2030, compared with 1990 levels, and reach climate neutrality in the EU by 2050. The Climate Law is complemented by the [https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/european-green-deal/european-climate-pact_en European Climate Pact] and the [https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/european-green-deal/2030-climate-target-plan_en 2030 Climate Target Plan]. In order to [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal/delivering-european-green-deal_en deliver the European Green Deal] and reduce the EU's greenhouse gas emissions by 55% by 2030, the European Commission proposed the '[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal/delivering-european-green-deal/fit-55-delivering-proposals_en Fit for 55]' package in June 2021. The 'Fit for 55' package is the EU's key plan to turn the climate goals into EU law and comprises [https://commission.europa.eu/publications/legal-documents-delivering-european-green-deal_en a set of proposals for revision of existing legislation and new initiatives in a wide range of areas]. By October 2023, the [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_23_4754 final legislation of the ‘Fit for 55' package] had been adopted. Since the adoption of the European Climate Law and the ‘Fit for 55’ package, further legislative measures have been adopted to operationalise and strengthen the EU’s climate objectives. These include revised targets for renewable energy and energy efficiency, reforms of the EU emissions trading system, and new instruments such as the [https://trade.ec.europa.eu/access-to-markets/en/news/carbon-border-adjustment-mechanism-cbam Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism]. More recently, industrial policy initiatives such as the [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/green-deal-industrial-plan/net-zero-industry-act_en Net-Zero Industry Act] and the [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/green-deal-industrial-plan/european-critical-raw-materials-act_en Critical Raw Materials Act] aim to support the EU’s transition to a climate-neutral economy while strengthening its strategic autonomy. EU cooperation with the Southern Mediterranean countries is guided by the [https://north-africa-middle-east-gulf.ec.europa.eu/what-we-do/pact-mediterranean_en Pact for the Mediterranean ‘One Sea, One Pact, One Future’]. The Pact reflects the EU’s commitment to strengthening its partnership with the southern Mediterranean countries and to building a common Mediterranean space that is connected, prosperous, resilient and secure, based on shared interests and joint responsibility. The Pact for the Mediterranean ‘One Sea, One Pact, One Future’ sets out a long-term vision to foster shared prosperity, stability, and sustainable development across the Euro-Mediterranean region. It establishes a strategic framework for cooperation, built around three interlinked thematic “pillars”: I. People: driving force for change, connections and innovation; II. Stronger, more sustainable and integrated economies, and III. Security, preparedness and migration management. Its core objectives include strengthening economic integration through enhanced trade, investment, and digital connectivity; accelerating the green and just transition by aligning climate action, renewable energy cooperation, and water security; and promoting human development via education, youth employment, and social cohesion initiatives. The Pact also aims to deepen political dialogue to address common security challenges, like migration, while reinforcing democratic governance. The [https://north-africa-middle-east-gulf.ec.europa.eu/document/download/72003d02-fa03-418f-b541-d9588aafcd3e_en?filename=JOIN_2025_26_F1_COMMUNICATION_FROM_COMMISSION_TO_INST_EN_V7_P1_4391705.PDF Pact for the Mediterranean] was endorsed by the EU and southern Mediterranean partners in November 2025 on the occasion of the 30th anniversary of the Barcelona process, with the European Council welcoming the Pact in its conclusions 20 November 2025. The [https://www.eeas.europa.eu/sites/default/files/joint_staff_working_document_renewed_partnership_southern_neighbourhood.pdf Economic and Investment Plan for the Southern Neighbours] complements this agenda. In cooperation with its Southern Mediterranean, Eurostat has the responsibility to promote and implement the use of European and internationally recognised standards and methodology for the production of statistics, necessary for designing and monitoring policies in various areas. Eurostat manages and coordinates EU efforts to increase the capacity of the Southern Mediterranean countries to [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-catalogues/-/KS-32-11-955?inheritRedirect=true&redirect=%2Feurostat%2Fen%2Fpublications%2Fleaflets develop, produce and disseminate good quality data] according to European and international standards. Additional information on the policy context of the Southern Mediterranean region is provided on the website of [https://north-africa-middle-east-gulf.ec.europa.eu/index_en Directorate-General for Middle East, North Africa and the Gulf (DG MENA)]. The EU has been supporting statistical capacity building in the region for a number of years, among others by providing technical assistance to national statistical authorities and by sharing best practice and transferring know-how. A key tool for this statistical cooperation is the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Statistical_cooperation_-_European_Neighbourhood_Policy-South_(ENP-S) MEDSTAT programme], a multiannual regional cooperation programme for statistics addressing common issues and requirements. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Non-EU_countries|All articles on non-EU countries]]
