title: Resources and green transformation in European Neighbourhood East countries
text:
This article is part of an online Eurostat publication that provides a statistical overview over the European Neighbourhood Policy-East (ENP-East) countries. The article presents statistics on resources and the transition towards a green economy and society for Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine and compares these with the EU. Data extracted in January 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 In 2024, Azerbaijan is the only net exporter of energy among the European Neighbourhood East countries, with estimated net energy exports of almost 48 million tonnes of oil equivalent. In 2024, gross inland energy consumption per capita in ENP-East countries remained well below the EU level (2 888 kilogramme of oil equivalent per capita), ranging from around 1 300 kgoe in Armenia to about 1 800 kgoe in Azerbaijan. Azerbaijan recorded by far the highest freshwater use among the ENP-East countries, reaching around 8.9 billion cubic metres in 2024. This article is part of an [[European_Neighbourhood_Policy_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]]. It presents information on 5 [[Glossary:European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP)|European Neighbourhood Policy-East (ENP-East)]] countries, namely, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine. Information on these countries is compared with the developments in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are also [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries]]. The European Council granted Moldova and Ukraine candidate status on 23 June 2022 and Georgia on 14 December 2023. This article does not contain any data on Belarus, as statistical cooperation with Belarus has been suspended as of March 2022. Data shown for Georgia exclude the regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia over which the government of Georgia does not exercise control. Except for the amount of freshwater used until 2022, the data managed by the National Bureau of Statistics of Moldova does not include data from the Transnistrian region over which the government of Moldova does not exercise control. Since 2014, data for Ukraine generally exclude the illegally annexed Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the City of Sevastopol and the territories which are not under control of the Ukrainian government. For Ukraine official statistics for 2022-2025 were not fully produced due to the martial law. It will gradually be produced and disseminated as defined by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine, taking into account the specific conditions of producing statistics during Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. Where a table or graph refers to a single reference year (for example, 2024), or where annual data are unavailable for certain countries, the most recent available data within the preceding five years are used. Where both the start and end years are intended to be shown but the corresponding data series are not available, data from the closest possible years are presented instead (for example, 2023 data instead of 2024). The article presents a range of resources and green transformation indicators such as [[Glossary:Freshwater withdrawals|freshwater use]], [[Glossary:Municipal waste|generation of municipal waste]], [[Glossary:Primary energy production|primary energy production]], [[Glossary:Import|import]] of energy, [[Glossary:Gross inland energy consumption|gross inland energy consumption]], consumption of [[Glossary:Renewable energy sources|renewable energy]] and energy productivity. ===Annual freshwater use=== Figure 1 compares annual [[Glossary:Freshwater_resources|freshwater]] [[Glossary:Water_use|use]] in the ENP-East countries from 2013 to 2023, in million cubic metres (m3). Annual freshwater use measures how much freshwater is used by main categories of end users like households and economic sectors such as services, agriculture and industry. The use of freshwater in Azerbaijan increased steadily between 2014 and 2021, rising from 7.6 billion m3 in 2014 to a peak of 9.8 billion m3 in 2021. This corresponds to an overall growth of 28.6% over that period. After 2021, freshwater use declined, falling slightly to 9.7 billion m3 in 2022 and more sharply in 2023 (-8.2%) to 8.9 billion m3. Consumption stabilised in 2024 at 8.9 billion m3. Despite the recent decrease, Azerbaijan continued to record by far the highest freshwater use among the ENP-East countries throughout the entire period. In Ukraine, freshwater use followed a strong downward trend over the period 2014-2024. Consumption fell from 8.1 billion m3 in 2014 to 3.5 billion m3 in 2024, representing an overall reduction of 56.2%. Particularly sharp decreases were recorded in 2015 (-19.1%) and again between 2021 and 2022 (-39.9%), when freshwater use dropped from 5.6 billion m3 to 3.4 billion m3. A small increase was observed in 2023 (+5.2%), before consumption decreased slightly again in 2024 (-0.7%). This steep decline is likely linked to disruptions in water supply and usage caused by Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. Freshwater consumption in Armenia showed fluctuating but overall moderate growth during the period. After increasing from 2.1 billion m3 in 2014 to a peak of 2.5 billion m3 in 2015 (+19.9%), freshwater use declined in subsequent years, reaching a low of 1.9 billion m3 in 2018. From 2019 onwards, consumption generally increased again, rising to 2.4 billion m3 in 2022. Following a decrease in 2023 (-6.6%), freshwater use rose strongly in 2024 to 2.6 billion m3, the highest level observed for Armenia over the period. Between 2014 and 2023 (2024 data not available), freshwater use in Georgia was characterised by two distinct phases. From 2014 to 2018, consumption declined sharply from 1.6 billion m3 to just under 1.0 billion m3, with the steepest reduction occurring in 2016 (-19.7%, compared with 2015). From 2019 onwards, the trend reversed, with a strong increase of 27.9% in 2019 followed by further growth to reach 1.5 billion m3 in 2021. After a significant decrease in 2022 (-18.9%), freshwater use increased again in 2023 to 1.3 billion m3. Among the ENP-East countries, Moldova continued to show the lowest and most stable levels of freshwater use up to 2022, with annual consumption fluctuating only marginally between 0.78 and 0.79 billion m3. From 2023 onwards, a break in the time series occurred due to the exclusion of data from the Transnistrian region. As a result, reported freshwater use dropped sharply to 0.12 billion m3 in 2023 and remained at a similarly low level in 2024 (0.13 billion m3). Data on freshwater use is not available for the EU. [[Image: ENPE26_Annual freshwater use, 2014-2024_(million m3)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Annual freshwater use, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/36dab9ad-d92f-4d68-b48a-0b9e02b088b3?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:13:51Z enpe_env_wat_use])|alt=Line chart on annual freshwater use from 2014 to 2024 in Azerbaijan, Ukraine, Armenia, Georgia and Moldova.]] ===Municipal waste generated=== Figure 2 presents the development in quantities of municipal waste generated across the EU, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine over the period 2014-2024, measured in kilogramme per inhabitant (kg/capita). In Georgia, the generation of municipal waste increased almost continuously from 208 kg/capita in 2015 (earlier data not available) to 299 kg/capita in 2023 (2024 data not available). Apart from a slight decrease in 2020, year-on-year growth was observed throughout the period. Overall, this corresponded to an increase of 91 kg/capita (+43.8%) between 2015 and 2023. In Azerbaijan, municipal waste generation rose strongly over the period 2014-2024. Following a low level of 143 kg/capita in 2014, waste generation increased almost continuously, to 297 kg/capita in 2024. This represents an overall increase of 154 kg/capita (+107.7%) over the period, by far the largest increase among the ENP-East countries. In Moldova, data on municipal waste generation are available only for the period 2020-2023. Over this limited period, municipal waste generation increased from 260 kg per capita in 2020 to 291 kg per capita in 2021, before declining to 281 kg per capita in 2022 and further to 220 kg per capita in 2023 (provisional). Given the short time series, trends should be interpreted with caution. In Armenia, municipal waste generation remained relatively stable between 2015 (2014 data not available) and 2019, fluctuating between 158 and 167 kg/capita. A notable increase was observed in 2020, when waste generation reached 194 kg/capita. After returning to 164 kg/capita in 2021, municipal waste fell to 146 kg/capita in 2023 (2022 data not available), before increasing sharply to 213 kg/capita in 2024, the highest level recorded for Armenia over the period. The generation of municipal waste in Ukraine fluctuated considerably between 2014 and 2022 (more recent data not available). Despite some year-to-year fluctuations, municipal waste generation rose from 214 kg/capita in 2014 to a peak of 257 kg/capita in 2020, before declined slightly to 253 kg/capita in 2021. In 2022, following Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, reported municipal waste dropped sharply to 181 kg/capita (-28.5% compared with 2021). For the EU, municipal waste generation per capita showed an upward trend from 479 kg/capita in 2014 to a peak of 534 kg/capita in 2021. This corresponds to an increase of 55 kg/capita (+11.5%) over the period. Since then, waste generation declined to 514 kg/capita in 2022 and further to 511 kg/capita in 2023 (2024 data not available). It should be noted that significant growth in generated municipal waste, as in the case of Azerbaijan, may reflect not only increased consumption but also improvements in waste collection coverage and reporting by municipalities. [[Image: ENPE26_Municipal waste generated, 2014-2024_(kg per capita)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Municipal waste generated, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cd11169d-72ee-47fb-aa9e-323f690e1a44?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:12:45Z env_wasmun]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/28779625-c361-43ae-b890-e5a74be3809b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:12:13Z enpe_env_wasgenm])|alt=Line chart on municipal waste generated from 2014 to 2024 in the EU, Georgia, Azerbaijan, Moldova, Armenia and Ukraine.]] ===Primary energy production by sources=== [[Glossary:Primary_production_of_energy|Primary energy production]] refers to energy commodities extracted or captured directly from natural resources, such as [[Glossary:Solid_fuels| solid fuels]], [[Glossary:Crude_oil|crude oil]], natural gas, [[Glossary:Nuclear_heat|nuclear heat]] and hydroelectric power; and [[Glossary:Renewable energy sources|renewables]] sources. Crude oil production covers fuel extracted within national boundaries, including offshore areas. Natural gas production refers to dry gas measured after purification and the removal of natural gas liquids and sulphur. Energy generated through transformation processes, such as electricity or heat produced in thermal power plants, is not considered primary energy production. Energy quantities are commonly expressed in [[Glossary:Tonnes_of_oil_equivalent_(toe)|tonnes of oil equivalent (toe)]]. Levels of primary energy production can vary significantly from year to year due to changes in demand linked to economic conditions and heating needs, fluctuations in energy prices driven by international markets, and weather conditions affecting hydroelectric and renewable energy sources. Longer-term developments may also reflect the emergence of new energy sources or the depletion or replacement of existing ones. Figure 3 shows that in Azerbaijan, crude oil and petroleum products (45.0%) together with natural gas (54.4%) accounted for almost all primary energy production in 2024, representing 99.4% of the total production. This structure contrasts sharply with that of Ukraine, where primary energy production in 2020 (more recent data not available) was more diversified: nuclear heat accounted for 35.1%, natural gas for 27.8% and solid fuels for 22.2%, while renewables contributed a more limited share (8.9%). The remaining ENP-East countries recorded relatively low levels of primary energy production, and their production shares should be interpreted in this context. In Georgia, primary energy production was dominated by renewable sources, mainly hydropower, which accounted for 91.4% (2022 data; more recent data not available). Moldova sourced almost all its primary energy production from renewables in 2023 (99.2%; more recent data not available), although the country remained highly dependent on energy imports. In Armenia, primary energy production in 2023 (more recent data not available) was largely based on nuclear heat (68.8%), complemented by renewables (31.1%). The structure of primary energy production in the EU was relatively diversified in 2024, reflecting differences in resource endowments and energy policies across EU countries. Renewables formed the largest share of EU primary energy production (48.1%), followed by nuclear heat (28.2%). Solid fuels accounted for 12.3%, while natural gas (5.1%) and crude oil and petroleum products (3.3%) played more limited roles. [[Image: ENPE26_Primary production of energy by sources, 2024_(% of total primary production)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Primary production of energy by sources, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/30381ee1-1f5e-4385-b06e-7a354c22abb5?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-03T15:07:40Z nrg_bal_s]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/38228e5d-89a4-48ef-9597-41669bbc29b3?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-12T12:05:38Z enpe_nrg_pprd])|alt=Stacked column chart showing primary production by sources for 2024, as a percentage of total primary production, in the EU, Moldova, Georgia, Ukraine, Armenia and Azerbaijan. The bars show crude oil and petroleum products, solid fuel, natural gas, nuclear heat, renewable, non-renewable and other sources.]] ===Net import of energy=== Net energy imports are calculated as energy imports minus energy exports. Imports include all energy products entering a country, excluding quantities in transit (for example via gas or oil pipelines). Exports cover all energy products leaving the country. Negative values indicate net exports, meaning that exports exceeded imports. Figure 4 presents net energy imports for the ENP-East countries for the period 2014-2024, measured in thousand [[Glossary:Tonnes_of_oil_equivalent_(toe)|tonnes of oil equivalent (toe)]]. Net energy imports in Ukraine fluctuated over the period 2014-2020 (more recent data not available). Net imports increased overall from 27 438 thousand toe in 2014 to 29 487 thousand toe in 2020 (+7.5%), despite substantial year-on-year variation. A peak was recorded in 2017 at 33 167 thousand toe, while notable declines occurred in 2016 and 2020. In Georgia, net energy imports showed a clear upward trend from 3 153 thousand toe in 2014 to 4 561 thousand toe in 2022 (+44.7%; more recent data not available), reflecting rising energy demand. The only interruption to this growth was a temporary decline in 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic. Estimated data for Armenia are available from 2015 onwards. Net energy imports increased steadily from 2 212 thousand toe in 2015 to 3 078 thousand toe in 2022, before declining slightly to 2 991 thousand toe in 2023 (more recent data not available). Apart from a small decline in 2016, the overall trend was upward, indicating growing reliance on imported energy. In Moldova, net energy imports rose from 1 920 thousand toe in 2014 to a peak of 2 306 thousand toe in 2021. This was followed by a decline to 2 181 thousand toe in 2022 and further to 1 944 thousand toe in 2023 (more recent data not available), suggesting a moderation in energy demand or changes in supply conditions. Azerbaijan continued to stand out as a large net exporter of energy throughout the period. Based on estimated data, net exports (negative values) were already very high in 2014 (-45 870 thousand toe) but declined to -40 755 thousand toe in 2017. Thereafter, exports increased again, reaching a peak of -48 246 thousand toe in 2021. In recent years, exports remained at similarly high levels, amounting to -47 869 thousand toe in 2024, the second highest level recorded over the period, underlining Azerbaijan’s role as a major exporter of oil and natural gas. For the EU, net energy imports increased from 798 910 thousand toe in 2014 to a peak of 908 439 thousand toe in 2019. A sharp drop was observed in 2020 (-12.8%) due to reduced energy demand during the Covid-19 pandemic. After a partial recovery in 2021 and 2022, net imports declined again in the next years, falling to 759 968 thousand toe in 2024. [[Image: ENPE26_Net import of energy, 2014-2024_(thousands tonnes of oil equivalent)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Net import of energy, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/38707af6-0686-46a6-821b-b7ff5cbbd662?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-03T15:08:16Z nrg_bal_s]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/774e7ad9-d41f-4503-8df2-d0fb802b9c31?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:07:33Z enpe_nrg_imp])|alt=Line chart showing net import of energy from 2014 to 2024 in the EU, Ukraine, Georgia, Armenia, Moldova and Azerbaijan.]] ===Gross inland energy consumption=== In Ukraine, energy consumption declined overall from 2 340 [[Glossary:Kilograms_of_oil_equivalent_(kgoe)|kilogrammes of oil equivalent (kgoe)]] per capita in 2014 to 2 075 kgoe/capita in 2020 (more recent data not available), despite a temporary increase in 2018 (+5.1%). Larger decreases were recorded in 2015 and 2019, and a break in the time series in 2015 should be taken into account. Overall, consumption fell by 11.3% between 2014 and 2020. Energy consumption in Azerbaijan remained relatively stable between 2014 and 2018, fluctuating around 1 580 kgoe/capita. A strong increase was observed in 2019 (+8.7%), followed by a decline in 2020 (-3.4%). Consumption then rose again to reach a peak of 1 861 kgoe/capita in 2023, before decreasing slightly to 1 815 kgoe/capita in 2024. Overall, Azerbaijan’s energy consumption increased by 14.0% over the period 2014-2024. For Georgia, from 2015 to 2022 (more recent data not available), energy consumption followed a generally upward trend, despite small declines in 2018 and 2020, reaching a high of 1 590 kgoe/capita in 2022. In Armenia, energy consumption fluctuated over the period 2015-2023 (data not available for 2014, 2022 and 2024). After falling to a low of 1 041 kgoe/capita in 2016, consumption increased in most subsequent years, reaching 1 272 kgoe/capita in 2021. Armenia was the only ENP-East country to record an increase in energy consumption during the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020 (+5.8%). Following a data gap in 2022, consumption rose further to 1 296 kgoe/capita in 2023. In Moldova, gross inland energy consumption rose steadily from 907 kgoe/capita to 1 075 kgoe/capita between 2015 and 2018. This was followed by a period of decline in 2019 and 2020, with consumption falling to 1 011 kgoe/capita in 2020. An increase in 2021 brought consumption to a period high of 1 138 kgoe/capita, but this was followed by further declines to 1 050 kgoe/capita in 2022 and 1 024 kgoe/capita in 2023. For the EU, gross inland energy consumption per capita peaked in 2017 at 3 354 kgoe/capita before declining sharply in 2020 to 2 998 kgoe/capita, reflecting reduced activity during the Covid-19 pandemic. After a partial rebound in 2021, consumption resumed its downward trend, falling to 2 888 kgoe/capita in 2024. Despite breaks in the time series and the use of estimates, the overall pattern points to a gradual reduction in per capita energy consumption in the EU in recent years. [[Image: ENPE26_Gross inland energy consumption, 2014-2024_(kilogrammes of oil equivalent per capita)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Gross inland energy consumption, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0418bbed-dfab-4d44-b8ef-98d129718aa6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:01:33Z nrg_bal_s]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/062af588-3ad0-4db4-b954-2bbfb413ae43?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:04:48Z demo_gind]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8484e26d-54b0-490c-9d9e-b3339167d0f4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:00:34Z enpe_nrg_gic])|alt=Line chart showing gross inland energy consumption, from 2014 to 2024 in the EU, Ukraine, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Armenia and Moldova.]] ===Renewable energy in gross final energy consumption=== Among the ENP-East countries, Moldova continued to record the highest share of renewables throughout 2014-2024, exceeding the EU average between 2014-2021. The share increased from 26.2% in 2014 to a peak of 27.8% in 2017, before declining overall to 21.5% in 2022. A partial recovery followed in 2023 (+1.5 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]]), but the share fell again to 20.8% in 2024, confirming a downward trend in recent years. In Georgia, between 2021-2024 (data before 2021 not available), the share of renewables rose overall from 18.3% to 19.5%. Georgia continued to report the second-highest renewable share among the ENP-East countries, with levels closer to those of Moldova and the EU than to the remaining ENP-East countries. In Armenia, the share of renewables fluctuated over the period 2015-2023 (no other data available), peaking at 13.2% in 2016 before declining to a low of 8.4% in 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic. A rebound followed in 2021 to 11.3% (+2.9 pp), after which the share decreased to 10.2% in 2023, remaining slightly below its 2015 level. Ukraine showed a steady increase in the share of renewables from 4.0% in 2014 to 9.2% in 2020 (more recent data not available). Growth was continuous, with annual increases ranging from +0.3 pp to +1.1 pp, indicating gradual progress in the use of renewable energy. Azerbaijan continued to report a very low share of renewables, reflecting its strong reliance on fossil fuels. The share declined from 2.1% in 2014 to around 1.3% during 2020-2022, before increasing to 2.2% in 2024. Despite this recent rise, renewable energy remains marginal in Azerbaijan’s energy mix. At EU level, the share of renewables increased steadily from 17.4% in 2014 to 25.2% in 2024, highlighting sustained progress towards renewable energy targets, which aim to increase the share of renewables in gross final energy consumption as part of the transition to climate neutrality. Overall, the data illustrate differing levels of progress in the green transition across the ENP-East countries, shaped by national energy policies, resource endowments and structural reliance on fossil fuels, while the EU continued its long-term upward trajectory in the share of renewable energy. [[Image: ENPE26_Renewable energy in gross final energy consumption, 2014-2024_(% of total consumption)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Renewable energy in gross final energy consumption, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9909ed4c-0ded-4346-b9ee-7cc8823b5ef8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-03T15:08:49Z nrg_ind_ren]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ccb0f1a3-ef9c-45f5-b116-182c6738b103?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:56:27Z enpe_nrg_rnew])|alt=Line chart showing renewable energy in gross final energy consumption from 2014 to 2024 as a percentage of total consumption in the EU, Moldova, Georgia, Armenia, Ukraine and Azerbaijan.]] ===Energy productivity=== Energy productivity measures how efficiently energy is used to generate economic output. It is calculated as [[Glossary:Gross_value_added|gross value added (GVA)]] divided by gross inland energy consumption and expressed as euros of GVA per kilogramme of oil equivalent (€/kgoe). Higher values indicate that more economic value is produced for each unit of energy consumed, reflecting greater energy efficiency and/or structural shifts in the economy towards less energy-intensive activities. Moldova stands out with a strong upward trend. Energy productivity increased from 9.6 €/kgoe in 2014 to around 12.1 €/kgoe in 2019-2020, before rising sharply to 20.1 €/kgoe in 2023 (more recent data not available). This was the highest level among the ENP-East countries shown, pointing to substantial gains in energy efficiency and/or significant structural economic change. In Armenia, energy productivity was broadly stable at around 2.9-3.3 €/kgoe between 2015 (earlier data not available) and 2018, increased to 3.6 €/kgoe in 2019, and then declined again to 3.1 €/kgoe in 2020-2021. A sharp improvement followed in 2022 and 2023 (more recent data not available), when productivity rose to 4.6 €/kgoe and 5.8 €/kgoe respectively. This marked increase suggests that economic output grew faster than energy consumption in recent years, indicating improvements in energy efficiency and/or a shift towards less energy-intensive economic activities. In Georgia, energy productivity declined from 2.7 €/kgoe in 2014 to 1.8 €/kgoe in 2021, before recovering to 2.7 €/kgoe in 2023 and 2024. This pattern suggests that energy consumption increased faster than economic output during much of the period up to 2021. The subsequent recovery indicates an improvement in the efficiency with which energy was converted into economic output in recent years, bringing productivity back to a level comparable with that observed at the beginning of the period. Azerbaijan recorded very stable energy productivity throughout the period, remaining within a narrow range between 2.6 and 2.9 €/kgoe from 2014 to 2024. This stability points to limited changes in energy efficiency or in the structure of the economy over time. At EU level, energy productivity increased almost continuously from 7.7 €/kgoe in 2014 to 10.0 €/kgoe in 2024. The indicator rose each year over the period, apart from 2021 when it remained at the same level as in 2020 (8.7 €/kgoe). This overall upward trend reflects sustained improvements in energy efficiency and a continued shift towards higher value-added economic activities. Overall, the data highlight contrasting developments across the region, with strong gains in Moldova and Armenia in recent years, stability in Azerbaijan, and more modest improvements in Georgia, while the EU continued its long-term upward trend in energy productivity. [[Image: ENPE26_Energy productivity, 2014-2024_(euro per kilogrammes of oil equivalent)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Energy productivity, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9cdba3e5-817b-4982-84fa-f7715b5b8dcb?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T12:58:22Z nrg_ind_ep]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/711b2aaa-7eec-4c57-8fb8-bde42579b957?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-13T08:19:18Z enpe_nrg_prod])|alt=Line chart showing the energy productivity from 2014 to 2024 in the EU, Moldova, Armenia, Georgia, Azerbaijan and Ukraine.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= ENPE26_Resources_and_green_transformation_V4_.xlsx |title=European Neighbourhood Policy — East countries — Resources and green transformation: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data for ENP-East countries are supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country on a voluntary basis. The data result from an annual data collection cycle that has been established by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]. These statistics are available free of charge on Eurostat’s website, together with a range of additional indicators for ENP-East countries covering most socio-economic topics. '''Energy''' For EU statistics, the main legislation covering the collection of statistics in relation to energy quantities is [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:32008R1099:EN:NOT Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008] of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 October 2008 on energy statistics. Since its adoption, it has been amended several times and a [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:02008R1099-20171130:EN:NOT consolidated] version is available. A summary of the relevant legislation is also available on Eurostat's website, under '[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/energy/legislation Legislation]' on the dedicated section for [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/energy/overview Energy statistics]. '''Environment''' Eurostat, in close partnership with the [[Glossary:European Environment Agency (EEA)|European Environment Agency (EEA)]], provides environmental statistics, accounts and indicators supporting the development, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of the EU's environmental policies, strategies and initiatives. Data on greenhouse gas emissions as reported under the [http://unfccc.int/2860.php United Nations framework convention on climate change (UNFCCC)] are collected by the EEA. Eurostat collects official statistics in relation to a broad selection of subject areas, for example, waste, water, material flows and environmental protection expenditure. Eurostat's data on waste is collected from EU countries on the basis of [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:32002R2150:EN:NOT Regulation (2150/2002/EC) on waste statistics] and is published every two years in line with common methodological recommendations. Landfill is the deposit of waste into or onto land; it includes specially engineered landfill sites and temporary storage of over one year on permanent sites. The definition covers both landfill in internal sites, in other words, where a generator of waste is carrying out its own waste disposal at the place of generation and in external sites. The collection of water statistics within the EU is based on information demands linked to the [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/water/water-framework/index_en.html Directive 2000/60/EC Water Framework Directive (WFD)]. Eurostat and the [[Glossary:OECD|OECD]] jointly administer a questionnaire on inland waters among EU countries, candidate countries and potential candidates. Data collection is voluntary although there is an initiative to establish a legal framework for the collection of water statistics. A large amount of data and other information on water is accessible via [http://water.europa.eu/ WISE], the water information system for Europe, which is hosted by the [http://www.eea.europa.eu/ European Environment Agency (EEA)] in Copenhagen. ===Context=== The EU's long-term strategy for reducing greenhouse gas emissions was laid out in November 2018, with the aim of making Europe the world's first climate-neutral continent by 2050. In December 2019, the European Commission presented the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en European Green Deal], set out in [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52019DC0640&qid=1713270488420 Communication COM(2019) 640 final]. The European Green Deal is a growth strategy that aims to transform the EU into a fair and prosperous society, with a modern, resource-efficient, and competitive economy where there are no net emissions of greenhouse gases in 2050 and where economic growth is decoupled from resource use. The Green Deal is an integral part of the Commission's strategy to implement the [https://sdgs.un.org/2030agenda United Nation’s 2030 Agenda] and the [https://sdgs.un.org/goals Sustainable Development Goals]. In June 2021, the [https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/european-green-deal/european-climate-law_en European Climate Law], [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32021R1119 Regulation (EU) 2021/1119], was adopted. It makes the goal to become climate-neutral by 2050 a legal obligation for the EU and its Member States. It sets the framework for actions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% levels by 2030 and reach climate neutrality in the EU by 2050. The Climate Law is complemented by the [https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/european-green-deal/european-climate-pact_en European Climate Pact] and the [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/api/files/attachment/866232/EU%20Climate%20Target%20Plan%202030%20Key%20contributors%20and%20policy%20Tools.pdf.pdf Climate Target Plan]. To [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal/delivering-european-green-deal_en deliver the European Green Deal], the European Commission proposed the '[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal/delivering-european-green-deal/fit-55-delivering-proposals_en Fit for 55]' package in June 2021. The 'Fit for 55' package is the EU's key plan to turn the climate goals into EU law and comprises [https://commission.europa.eu/publications/legal-documents-delivering-european-green-deal_en a set of proposals for revision of existing legislation and new initiatives in a wide range of areas]. By October 2023, the [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_23_4754 final legislation of the ‘Fit for 55' package had been adopted]. Since the adoption of the European Climate Law and the ‘Fit for 55’ package, further legislative measures have been adopted to operationalise and strengthen the EU’s climate objectives. These include revised targets for renewable energy and energy efficiency, reforms of the EU emissions trading system, and new instruments such as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. More recently, industrial policy initiatives such as the Net-Zero Industry Act and the Critical Raw Materials Act aim to support the EU’s transition to a climate-neutral economy while strengthening its strategic autonomy. On 2 July 2021, the European Commission and the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy presented the [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/IP_21_3367 Eastern Partnership: a Renewed Agenda] for cooperation with the EU's Eastern partners. This agenda is based on the five long-term objectives, with resilience at its core, as defined for the future of the [https://neighbourhood-enlargement.ec.europa.eu/european-neighbourhood-policy/eastern-partnership_en Eastern Partnership (EaP)] in the Joint Communication [https://eeas.europa.eu/headquarters/headquarters-homepage/76166/joint-communication-eastern-partnership-policy-beyond-2020-reinforcing-resilience-%25E2%2580%2593-eastern_en Eastern Partnership policy beyond 2020: Reinforcing Resilience – an Eastern Partnership that delivers for all] in March 2020. It is further elaborated in the Joint Staff Working Document [https://eeas.europa.eu/headquarters/headquarters-homepage/101173/joint-staff-working-document_en Recovery, resilience and reform: post 2020 Eastern Partnership priorities], amongst others defining the 'Top Ten Targets for 2025'. The Eastern Partnership’s agenda for recovery, resilience and reform is underpinned by an 'Economic and Investment Plan for the Eastern Partnership (EaP): Investing in resilient and competitive economies and societies' (Annex I of the Joint Staff Working Document). More detailed overviews are given in a [https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/document/download/94735c00-2cfa-4ef7-92a6-41515b8b466d_en Factsheet on the Eastern Partnership Joint Communication], presenting the policy objectives and the specific priorities, as well as in a [https://neighbourhood-enlargement.ec.europa.eu/document/download/d675e1d6-fd68-45fa-a671-80a69a117f1f Factsheet on EU-Eastern Neighbourhood flagship projects 2023-2024]. The [https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/news/eastern-partnership-summit-joint-declaration-2021-12-15_en Joint Declaration of the Eastern Partnership Summit 'Recovery, Resilience and Reform'] of 15 December 2021 reaffirmed the strong commitment to a strategic, ambitious and forward-looking Eastern Partnership. At the [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/meetings/international-ministerial-meetings/2023/12/11/ Eastern Partnership Foreign Affairs Ministerial meeting of 11 December 2023], the EU, EU countries and partners declared that they will step up their efforts to implement the Eastern Partnership’s agenda for recovery, resilience and reform, as well as tackling challenges related to the ongoing consequences of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine for the entire region. On 14-15 December 2023, the European Council decided to [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2023/12/14/european-council-conclusions-on-ukraine-enlargement-and-reforms/ open accession negotiations] with Moldova and Ukraine, and granted the status of candidate country to Georgia. In cooperation with its ENP partners, Eurostat has the responsibility to promote and implement the use of European and internationally recognised standards and methodology for the production of statistics, necessary for designing and monitoring policies in various areas. Eurostat manages and coordinates EU efforts to increase the capacity of the ENP countries to develop, produce and disseminate good quality data according to European and international standards. Additional information on the policy context of the ENP is provided on the website of [https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/index_en Directorate-General Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood (ENEST)]. A regional statistical cooperation programme, STAT-East, is in place since January 2026 to strengthen partner countries’ statistical capacity to develop, produce and disseminate high-quality statistics and to reinforce the independence and institutional capacity of national statistical systems. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Non-EU_countries|All articles on non-EU countries]] title: Resources and green transformation in enlargement countries
text:
This article presents statistics on the transition towards a green economy and society for the EU [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries and potential candidate]]. It covers Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Moldova, North Macedonia, Georgia, Albania, Serbia, Türkiye, Ukraine and Kosovo. Data from April 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 Freshwater abstraction trends varied widely across the enlargement countries. While Türkiye increased from 52.0 billion cubic metres (m3) in 2014 to 66.0 billion m3 in 2022, Ukraine’s abstraction almost halved, falling from 10.9 billion m3 to 5.7 billion m3 in 2023. In 2024, solid fuels remained the dominant source of primary energy production in Bosnia and Herzegovina (60.3%), Serbia (58.2%) and North Macedonia (53.8%), while renewable energy sources accounted for the largest share in Moldova (99.6%) and Georgia (90.7%). In 2024, Albania and Montenegro had the highest shares of renewables in gross final energy consumption, with shares of 43.1% and 40.8% of total energy consumption, respectively, well above the EU average of 25.2%. This article is part of an [[Enlargement_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]] and provides information on resources and green transformation for the [[Glossary:Candidate countries|enlargement countries]] and compares this with the corresponding data for the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. The data used in this article have all been submitted to and validated by Eurostat's subject matter units, following the same process as for the EU countries. For Moldova, data on annual freshwater abstraction, municipal waste generated and energy productivity are not yet transmitted according to this process and are therefore not yet available. The same applies for Georgia when it comes to data on municipal waste generated and energy productivity, as well as for Ukraine for data on municipal waste generated, renewable energy in gross final energy consumption and energy productivity. However, data on Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are also presented in the [[European Neighbourhood Policy countries - statistical_overview|Statistics Explained articles for European Neighbourhood Policy - East]] countries; these articles are based on annual indicators supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country. Data shown for Georgia exclude the regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia over which the government of Georgia does not exercise control. The data managed by the National Bureau of Statistics of Moldova does not include data from the Transnistrian region over which the government of Moldova does not exercise control. Since 2014, data for Ukraine generally exclude the illegally annexed Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the City of Sevastopol and the territories which are not under control of the Ukrainian government. For Ukraine official statistics for 2022-2025 were not fully produced due to the martial law. It will gradually be produced and disseminated as defined by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine, taking into account the specific conditions of producing statistics during Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. The article presents a range of indicators on resources and green transformation, such as annual [[Glossary:Water_abstraction|freshwater abstraction]], [[Glossary:Municipal waste|municipal waste]] generated, [[Glossary:Primary energy production|primary energy production]], net import of energy, [[Glossary:Gross inland energy consumption|gross inland energy consumption]], the [[Glossary:Share_of_renewable_energy_in_energy_consumption|share of renewable energy in energy consumption]] and energy productivity. === Annual freshwater abstraction=== Figure 1 compares annual [[Glossary:Water_abstraction|freshwater abstraction]] in the enlargement countries from 2014 to 2024, in million cubic metres (m3). Annual freshwater abstraction measures the volume of water removed from natural sources for use by households and economic sectors such as agriculture, industry and services. Among the enlargement countries, Türkiye recorded by far the highest freshwater abstraction levels, increasing steadily from 52.0 billion m3 in 2014 to 66.0 billion m3 in 2022 (latest available data). Ukraine was among the countries with the highest freshwater abstraction volumes over the period, but with an overall decline, from 10.9 billion m3 in 2014 to 5.7 billion m3 in 2023, including a drop of more than 40% between 2021 and 2022. Freshwater abstraction increased overall in Serbia, rising from 3.6 billion m3 in 2014 to 5.2 billion m3 in 2023, despite some fluctuations after the 2019 peak. North Macedonia showed strong variations over the period, reaching 2.7 billion m3 in 2023, the highest level recorded (nevertheless, there was a break in time series in 2015). In Georgia, freshwater abstraction fluctuated between 1.8 and 2.3 billion m3 between 2014 and 2023, ending the period at its highest level. Montenegro also recorded considerable fluctuations between 2020 and 2022 (no other data available), while Albania showed an overall decline, from 1.1 billion m3 in 2017 to 0.8 billion m3 in 2023 (latest available data). KosovoThis designation is without prejudice to positions on status and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo Declaration of Independence. reported the lowest abstraction volumes, increasing from 0.2 billion m3 in 2014 to 0.3 billion m3 in 2019 (latest available data). Overall, the data show differing developments across the enlargement countries, with strong increases in Serbia, Türkiye and North Macedonia, substantial declines in Ukraine and Albania, and more stable or fluctuating patterns in the other countries, reflecting differences in water availability, economic activity and resource management. [[Image: CPC26_Annual freshwater abstraction, 2014-2024 (million m3).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Annual freshwater abstraction, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d33fb5b8-fbbe-4ccf-9c01-75a0c39ee816?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:36:46Z env_wat_abs])|alt=A line chart showing annual freshwater abstraction in million cubic metres for the EU Candidate countries and Kosovo for the years from 2014 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Municipal waste=== Municipal waste consists mainly of waste generated by [[Glossary:Household|households]], although it also includes similar wastes from sources such as shops, offices and public institutions. Waste from agriculture and from industry is excluded. Municipal waste is waste collected by or on behalf of municipalities and disposed through waste management systems. For areas not covered by a municipal waste collection scheme, the reporting countries estimate the amount of waste generated. Among the enlargement countries, Montenegro recorded the highest level of municipal waste generation in the most recent years available, increasing from 479 kilogramme (kg) [[Glossary:Per capita|per capita]] in 2014 to 585 kg/capita in 2024 (see Figure 2). In 2024, this was well above the EU level of 517 kg/capita. North Macedonia and Serbia also showed upward trends. In North Macedonia, waste generation increased from 370 kg/capita in 2014 to 480 kg/capita in 2023 (2024 data not available). In Serbia, it rose from 299 kg/capita in 2014 to 467 kg/capita in 2023 (2024 data not available), despite a slight decline after the 2022 peak. By contrast, Türkiye and Bosnia and Herzegovina showed broadly stable developments. In Türkiye, municipal waste generation ranged between 380 and 426 kg/capita over the period and stood at 402 kg/capita in 2024 (nevertheless, there was a break in time series in 2016). In Bosnia and Herzegovina, it ranged between 329 and 356 kg/capita and stood at 329 kg/capita in 2024. Albania showed a downward trend, with municipal waste generation declining from 425 kg/capita in 2014 to 306 kg/capita in 2023 (2024 data not available). Kosovo also recorded relatively low levels, increasing from 178 kg/capita in 2015 to 267 kg/capita in 2024. In the EU, municipal waste generation per capita increased from 479 kg/capita in 2014 to 517 kg/capita in 2024, despite declines in 2022 and 2023 following a peak in 2021. Differences in municipal waste generation between countries may reflect not only variations in consumption patterns, but also differences in waste collection systems, coverage and reporting practices. [[Image: CPC26_Municipal waste generated, 2014-2024_(kg per capita).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Municipal waste generated, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e2476772-43e3-4835-b194-514e5eabaf42?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:39:03Z env_wasmun])|alt=A line chart showing municipal waste generated in kilogramme per capita for the EU, some of the EU Candidate countries and Kosovo for the years from 2014 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Primary energy production by sources=== [[Glossary:Primary energy production|Primary energy production]] refers to energy commodities extracted or captured directly from natural resources, such as [[Glossary:Solid fuels|solid fuels]], [[Glossary:Crude_oil|crude oil]], natural gas, [[Glossary:Nuclear_heat|nuclear heat]] and hydroelectric power; and [[Glossary:Renewable_energy_sources|renewable energy sources]]. Crude oil production covers fuel extracted within national boundaries, including offshore areas. Natural gas production refers to dry gas measured after purification and the removal of natural gas liquids and sulphur. Energy generated through transformation processes, such as electricity or heat produced in thermal power plants, is not considered primary energy production. Levels of primary energy production can vary significantly from year to year due to changes in demand linked to economic conditions and heating needs, fluctuations in energy prices driven by international markets, and weather conditions affecting hydroelectric and renewable energy sources. Longer-term developments may also reflect the emergence of new energy sources or the depletion or replacement of existing ones. Figure 3 shows considerable differences in the structure of primary energy production across the enlargement countries in 2024. In Kosovo (2023 data), Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia, production was dominated by solid fuels, accounting for 82.7%, 60.3% and 58.2% of total primary energy production, respectively. Solid fuels also represented more than half of production in North Macedonia (53.8%) and Montenegro (50.8%). By contrast, renewable energy sources accounted for the vast majority of primary energy production in Moldova (99.6%) and Georgia (90.7%). Renewable energy sources also represented more than half of total production in Türkiye (55.2%) and Albania (53.5%), while Montenegro and North Macedonia showed a more balanced structure between renewable energy sources and solid fuels. In Albania, crude oil and petroleum products accounted for a substantial share of primary energy production (36.9%), while Türkiye recorded a more diversified energy mix, combining renewables, solid fuels and crude oil. Serbia also displayed a relatively diversified structure, although solid fuels remained dominant. Ukraine (2020 data) showed the most diversified energy mix among the enlargement countries, with nuclear heat accounting for 35.1% of primary production, followed by natural gas (27.8%), solid fuels (22.2%) and renewable energy sources (8.9%). Compared with the enlargement countries, the EU displayed a broadly diversified primary energy production structure in 2024, with renewable energy sources (48.1%) and nuclear heat (28.2%) representing the largest shares, followed by solid fuels (12.3%), natural gas (5.1%) and crude oil and petroleum products (3.3%). Overall, the data highlight substantial differences in energy production structures across the enlargement countries, ranging from strong dependence on solid fuels in several economies to a dominant role for renewable energy in Moldova and Georgia. [[Image: CPC26_Primary energy production by sources, 2024_(% of total primary production).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Primary energy production by sources, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bf716a2c-632c-4a32-bcf8-5eabd20cda11?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:41:15Z nrg_bal_s])|alt=A bar chart showing primary energy production by sources as a share of the total primary production for the EU, EU Candidate countries and Kosovo for 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Net import of energy=== Net energy imports are calculated as energy imports minus energy exports. Imports include all energy products entering a country, excluding quantities in transit (for example via gas or oil pipelines). Exports cover all energy products leaving the country. Negative values indicate net exports, meaning that exports exceeded imports. Figure 4 presents developments in net energy imports for the enlargement countries and the EU over the period 2014-2024, expressed as an index (2014=100). It is to be noted that all enlargement countries and EU were net importers during the entire period analysed. Net energy imports increased strongly in several enlargement countries between 2014 and 2024. Serbia recorded the largest increase, with net imports rising by 74.2 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] compared with 2014, despite some decline after the 2022 peak. Georgia also showed a significant increase (+52.1 pp), while Türkiye (+23.7 pp) and North Macedonia (+19.3 pp) recorded more moderate growth in net imports. Kosovo also experienced a substantial increase in net energy imports (+63.1 pp in 2023 compared with 2014; 2024 data not available). Bosnia and Herzegovina and Moldova recorded more limited increases, at +13.6 pp and +10.9 pp respectively in 2024 compared with 2014. Montenegro showed a more volatile development. After fluctuating considerably over the period, net energy imports in 2024 were 28.4 pp higher than in 2014. Albania also experienced strong fluctuations, but was one of the few enlargement countries to record lower net energy imports in 2024 than in 2014 (-9.6 pp). In Ukraine, net energy imports fluctuated between 2014 and 2020. Compared with 2014, they increased by 20.9 pp in 2017, before remaining at a similarly high level in 2019 (-0.7 pp, compared with 2017) and then declining by 12.7 pp in 2020 compared with the previous year. More recent data are not available. By contrast, net energy imports in the EU decreased overall, standing at -4.5 pp in 2024 compared with 2014, despite fluctuations during the period. Overall, most enlargement countries showed an increase in net energy imports compared with 2014, indicating a growing reliance on imported energy. However, developments differed considerably across countries, with some showing relatively stable trends and others experiencing strong fluctuations over time. [[Image: CPC26_Net import of energy, 2014-2024_(index 2014=100, based on toe).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Net import of energy, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b81c1c57-73c7-4a7c-800e-94d546225330?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:42:16Z nrg_bal_s])|alt=A line chart showing net energy imports as an index (2014=100) for the EU, EU Candidate countries, and Kosovo for the years from 2014 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Gross inland energy consumption=== [[Glossary:Gross_inland_energy_consumption|Gross inland energy consumption]] is the energy that a country requires to meet its internal (national) demand. It covers consumption by the energy sector itself; distribution and transformation losses; final energy consumption by end users; and non-energy use by end users (such as feedstock for the petrochemical industry, lubricants). It represents the total energy demand of a country or region from all sources necessary to satisfy inland consumption. Among the enlargement countries, Serbia recorded the highest level of gross inland energy consumption per capita throughout the period, rising from 1 869 [[Glossary:Kilograms_of_oil_equivalent_(kgoe)|kilogrammes of oil equivalent (kgoe)]] per capita in 2014 to 2 416 kgoe in 2024, despite some fluctuations in earlier years (see Figure 5). Ukraine followed at a somewhat lower level, declining overall from 2 340 kgoe in 2014 to 2 075 kgoe in 2020 (latest available data; break in time series 2015), although remaining above most other enlargement countries over the period considered. Türkiye, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro all recorded a broadly upward trend over time. Türkiye increased from 1 595 kgoe per capita in 2014 to 1 993 in 2024 (break in time series in 2019), while Montenegro rose from 1 567 to 1 817 over the same period. Bosnia and Herzegovina also increased overall, from 1 567 in 2014 to 2 025 in 2024 (provisional data), despite some interruptions in the series. North Macedonia and Georgia also showed sustained growth in energy consumption per capita. North Macedonia increased from 1 310 kgoe in 2014 to 1 396 in 2024, after peaking in 2022. Georgia recorded one of the strongest increases among the enlargement countries, rising from 1 007 in 2014 to 1 655 in 2024 (break in time series in 2015). At the lower end of the scale, Moldova and Albania recorded lower but generally increasing levels over time. Moldova rose from 727 kgoe in 2014 to 1 108 in 2024, while Albania increased from 814 to 936 over the same period, although both series show some fluctuations. Kosovo also showed an upward trend, increasing from 1 218 kgoe in 2014 to 1 501 in 2022 (latest available data). Overall, gross inland energy consumption per capita in the enlargement countries remained well below EU levels, which declined overall from 3 227 kgoe in 2014 to 2 875 in 2024 (break in time series in 2015, 2017 and 2021 to 2023). The results reflect differences in economic structure, levels of development and energy efficiency across the region. [[Image: CPC26_Gross inland energy consumption, 2014-2024_(kilogrammes of oil equivalent per capita).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Gross inland energy consumption, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f63bb178-e6ff-4371-9b8b-803a34291c03?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:43:06Z nrg_bal_s]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c019c42d-e413-4721-aaf1-0e6f0c7a58c8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T13:03:51Z demo_gind])|alt=A Line chart showing gross inland energy consumption in kilogramme of oil equivalent per capita for the EU,EU Candidate Countries and Kosovo, over the years 2014 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Renewable energy in gross final energy consumption=== The [[Glossary:Share_of_renewable_energy_in_energy_consumption|share of renewable energy in gross final energy consumption]] is the ratio between the renewable energy delivered to final consumers and the gross [[Glossary: Final_energy_consumption|final energy consumption]], which is the total energy consumed by end users. Renewable energy sources, also called renewables, are energy sources that replenish (or renew) themselves naturally. Typical examples are hydropower, solar energy, wind and biomass; energy production from these generally vary depending on weather conditions. Among the enlargement countries, Albania and Bosnia and Herzegovina recorded the highest shares of renewable energy in gross final energy consumption in 2024 (or the latest available year). Albania reached 43.1% in 2024 (see Figure 6), despite a decline compared with the peak of 46.6% in 2023, while Bosnia and Herzegovina recorded 40.0% in 2023 (2024 data not available), up substantially from 24.9% in 2014. Montenegro also maintained a high share, at 40.8% in 2024, although this was slightly below its 2014 level of 44.1% At intermediate levels, Serbia reported a share of 25.9% in 2024, slightly above the EU average of 25.2%, following a gradual increase over the period. North Macedonia also recorded an upward trend, reaching 21.8% in 2024, compared with 19.6% in 2014. By contrast, Moldova and Kosovo recorded declining shares over the period. In Moldova, the share fell from 26.2% in 2014 to 20.8% in 2024, while Kosovo declined from 19.5% to 18.0% over the same period, despite some fluctuations in intermediate years. Georgia, for which data are available only from 2021 onwards, recorded a relatively stable share close to 19-20%. Overall, renewable energy accounted for a relatively large share of final energy consumption in several enlargement countries, often exceeding the EU average. However, developments over time were uneven, reflecting differences in energy mix, renewable energy capacity and changes in overall energy consumption patterns. [[Image: Renewable energy in gross final energy consumption, 2014-2024_(% of final energy consumption)_up.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Renewable energy in gross final energy consumption, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a816af74-a504-4934-aafd-691486086aba?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:44:31Z nrg_ind_ren])|alt=A Line chart showing the share of renewable energy as percentage of total consumption for the EU, EU Candidate countries and Kosovo over the years 2014 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Energy productivity=== Energy productivity measures the amount of economic output produced, measured as [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]], per unit of energy input to the production, measured as [[Glossary:Gross available energy|gross available energy (GAE)]]. GAE includes energy needs for energy transformation (including generating electricity), support operations of the energy sector, transmission and distribution losses, final energy consumption (industry, transport, households, services, agriculture and other sectors) and the use of fossil fuel products for non-energy purposes (e.g. as raw material in the chemical industry). Among the enlargement countries, Türkiye recorded the highest energy productivity throughout the period 2014-2024, reaching €7.3 per kilogramme of oil equivalent (kgoe) in 2024, compared with €10.0 per kgoe in the EU (see Figure 7). Türkiye’s energy productivity increased steadily over the decade, rising by €1.0 per kgoe compared with 2014. Albania recorded the second highest energy productivity among the enlargement countries, increasing continuously from €4.1 per kgoe in 2014 to €6.0 per kgoe in 2024. Montenegro also showed a mild upward trend with some fluctuations, increasing from €3.4 per kgoe in 2014 to €4.0 per kgoe in 2024, while North Macedonia increased from €2.9 to €3.8 per kgoe over the same period. Lower levels of energy productivity were observed in Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 2024, energy productivity stood at €2.8 per kgoe in Serbia and €2.6 per kgoe in Bosnia and Herzegovina, although both countries recorded moderate increases compared with 2014. Kosovo also showed some improvement, rising from €2.1 per kgoe in 2014 to €2.5 per kgoe in 2022 (more recent data not available). Energy productivity in the enlargement countries remained below the EU level throughout the period, although most countries recorded gradual improvements over time. [[Image: CPC26_Energy productivity, 2014-2024_(GDP in euro per kg of oil equivalent).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Energy productivity, 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9c20f9c2-2ec2-47d8-addd-502b4f94bf8d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-21T11:45:09Z nrg_ind_ep])|alt=A Line chart showing energy productivity in euro per kilogramme of oil equivalent for the EU, EU Candidate countries and Kosovo over the years 2014 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=CPC26_Resources and green transformation_V4.xlsx|title=Enlargement countries — resources and green transition: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The enlargement countries provide data on energy and waste directly to Eurostat's units responsible for energy and environment statistics, respectively, following the same process as the EU and EFTA countries. These statistics are available on Eurostat's website. Eurostat’s data on municipal waste are collected on the basis of the [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:32002R2150:EN:NOT Regulation on waste statistics (2150/2002/EC)] and are published every 2 years in line with common methodological recommendations. Information concerning the current statistical legislation on waste statistics can be found under [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/waste/legislation 'Legislation'] in Eurostat's dedicated section on Waste statistics. The collection of data on energy quantities is based on [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?qid=1552477653076&uri=CELEX:32008R1099 Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008]. Data are collected from EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. Data cover a variety of energy sources. Basic data on energy quantities are in fuel specific units, such as liquid fuels in thousand tonnes and electricity in [[Glossary:Kilowatt-hour (kWh)|kilowatt-hours]]. Further information regarding the statistical legislation on energy statistics can be found under [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/energy/legislation 'Legislation'] in Eurostat's dedicated section on Energy statistics. While basic principles and institutional frameworks for producing statistics are already in place, the enlargement countries are expected to increase the volume and quality of their data progressively, and to transmit these data to Eurostat in the context of the EU enlargement process. [[Glossary:European statistical system (ESS)| European Statistical System (ESS)]] standards in the field of statistics require the existence of a statistical infrastructure based on principles such as professional independence, impartiality, relevance, confidentiality of individual data and easy access to official statistics; they cover methodology, classifications and standards for production. Eurostat assesses and supports the alignment of statistical production in the enlargement countries with the EU acquis in the field of statistics. Eurostat supports the national statistical offices and other producers of official statistics through a range of initiatives, such as statistical projects, training courses, traineeships, study visits, workshops and seminars, and participation in meetings within the ESS. The ultimate goal is the provision of harmonised, high-quality data that conforms to European and international standards. ===Context=== The EU's long-term strategy for reducing greenhouse gas emissions was laid out in November 2018, with the aim of making Europe the world's first climate-neutral continent by 2050. In December 2019, the European Commission presented the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en European Green Deal], set out in [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52019DC0640&qid=1713270488420 Communication COM(2019) 640 final]. The European Green Deal is a growth strategy that aims to transform the EU into a fair and prosperous society, with a modern, resource-efficient and competitive economy where there are no net emissions of greenhouse gases in 2050 and where economic growth is decoupled from resource use. The Green Deal is an integral part of the Commission’s strategy to implement the [https://sdgs.un.org/2030agenda United Nation’s 2030 Agenda] and the [https://sdgs.un.org/goals Sustainable Development Goals]. In June 2021, the [https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/european-green-deal/european-climate-law_en European Climate Law], [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32021R1119 Regulation (EU) 2021/1119], was adopted. It makes the goal to become climate-neutral by 2050 a legal obligation for the EU and its Member States. It sets the framework for actions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030, compared with 1990 levels, and reach climate neutrality in the EU by 2050. The Climate Law is complemented by the [https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/european-green-deal/european-climate-pact_en European Climate Pact] and the [https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/european-green-deal/2030-climate-target-plan_en 2030 Climate Target Plan]. In order to [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal/delivering-european-green-deal_en deliver the European Green Deal], the European Commission proposed the '[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal/delivering-european-green-deal/fit-55-delivering-proposals_en Fit for 55]' package in June 2021. The 'Fit for 55' package is the EU's key plan to turn the climate goals into EU law and comprises [https://commission.europa.eu/publications/legal-documents-delivering-european-green-deal_en a set of proposals for revision of existing legislation and new initiatives in a wide range of areas]. By October 2023, the [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_23_4754 final legislation of the ‘Fit for 55'] package had been adopted. Since the adoption of the European Climate Law and the ‘Fit for 55’ package, further legislative measures have been adopted to operationalise and strengthen the EU’s climate objectives. These include revised targets for renewable energy and energy efficiency, reforms of the EU emissions trading system, and new instruments such as the [https://trade.ec.europa.eu/access-to-markets/en/news/carbon-border-adjustment-mechanism-cbam Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism]. More recently, industrial policy initiatives such as the [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/green-deal-industrial-plan/net-zero-industry-act_en Net-Zero Industry Act] and the [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/green-deal-industrial-plan/european-critical-raw-materials-act_en Critical Raw Materials Act] aim to support the EU’s transition to a climate-neutral economy while strengthening its strategic autonomy. Energy has been a key feature on the EU's policy agenda for a number of years, largely as a result of fluctuating energy prices; security of supply; and human induced effects of energy use on climate change, in particular, increased levels of greenhouse gas emissions. The use of renewable energy sources is seen as a key element of the EU's energy policy and should help to improve energy security; support the achievement of a carbon neutral society; and decouple energy costs from oil prices. Energy crises have underlined the EU's need to work with its neighbours on energy security, including diversification of energy sources, routes and suppliers. Additional information on statistical cooperation with the enlargement countries is provided in the Statistics explained background article [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Enlargement_policy_and_statistical_cooperation Enlargement policy and statistical cooperation]. === Footnotes === <'''footnote text
