title: Road freight transport by type of goods
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the road freight transport by type of goods. Data extracted in September 2025 Planned article update: 24 September 2026 In 2024, ‘Metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium’ accounted for the largest share (23.0%) of freight transported by road in the EU, measured in tonnes. In the EU, ‘Food products, beverages and tobacco’ constituted 16.7% of tonne-kilometres transported by road in 2024, representing the highest share among all product groups. [[Image: Road freight transport by product group (NST 2007), EU, 2024_(% share in tonnes and tonne-kilometres)_up.png|thumb|centre|800px|Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tg}}
Full names and description of [[Glossary:Standard_goods_classification_for_transport_statistics_(NST)|NST 2007]] codes |alt=Road freight transport by product group. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article presents [[Glossary:Road freight transport|road freight transport]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], focusing on the various types of goods transported. It examines the total national and international road freight transport performed, classified by the type of goods. It also provides information on the transport of dangerous goods. Finally, it offers an overview of road freight transport categorised by cargo type. This article and the articles [[Road freight transport statistics|'Road freight transport statistics']], [[Road freight transport by vehicle characteristics|'Road freight transport by vehicle characteristics']], [[Road freight transport by journey characteristics|'Road freight transport by journey characteristics']] and [[Road freight transport statistics - cabotage|'Road freight transport statistics – cabotage']] present a complete overview of road freight transport in Europe. === Road freight transport by product group ([[Glossary:Standard_goods_classification_for_transport_statistics_(NST)|NST 2007 classification]]) === Tables 1a and 1b present road freight transport by product group, measured in tonnes and [[Glossary:Tonne-kilometre (tkm)|tonne-kilometres (tkm)]], respectively. The data presented cover the period 2020-2024. In terms of tonnes of freight carried, EU road transport declined by 0.7% in 2024 compared with 2023. Over the period 2020-2024, the number of tonnes carried grew at an average annual rate of 0.1% In 2024, 'Metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium' was the largest product group transported in terms of tonnage, accounting for 3 007.2 million tonnes, or 23.0% of the EU total (see Table 1a and Figure 1). This was followed by 'Food products, beverages and tobacco' (1 590.0 million tonnes, 12.2%), and 'Other non-metallic mineral products' (1 562.5 million tonnes and a share of 11.9%). Another major product group was 'Products of agriculture, hunting, and forestry; fish and other fishing products', accounting for 1 287.1 million tonnes, or 9.8%. From 2023 to 2024, the tonnage carried by road decreased in 10 product groups. The largest declines were observed for ‘Coal and lignite; crude petroleum and natural gas’ (-44.8%) and ‘Basic metals; fabricated metal products, except machinery and equipment’ (-8.1%). By contrast, the largest increases were observed for ‘Other goods not elsewhere classified (n.e.c.)’ (+35.6%), ‘Unidentifiable goods: goods which for any reason cannot be identified’ (+17.1%) and ‘Textiles and textile products; leather and leather products’ (+6.7%). In terms of average annual growth over the period 2020-2024, ‘Other goods n.e.c.’ recorded the strongest growth, at 13.0%, followed by ‘Unidentifiable goods: goods which for any reason cannot be identified’ (+7.5%), ‘Textiles and textile products; leather and leather products’ and ‘Mail, parcels’ (both +4.0%). The largest negative rates were recorded by ‘Coal and lignite; crude petroleum and natural gas’ and ‘Metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium’ (-8.7% and -2.0%, respectively). [[Image: Road freight transport by product group, EU, 2020-2024 (million tonnes).png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1a: Road freight transport by product group, EU, 2020-2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tg}}|alt= a table showing the road freight transport by product group in the EU from 2020 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In terms of road freight transport performance measured in tonne-kilometres, total EU performance in 2024 was 0.7% higher than in 2023. The leading category of goods was ‘Food products, beverages and tobacco', accounting for 312.2 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] tkm; its share in the total EU tkm was 16.7% (see Table 1b and Figure 1). This was followed by 'Grouped goods' (236.5 billion tkm and a share of 12.7%) and 'Products of agriculture, hunting, and forestry; fish and other fishing products' (207.6 billion tkm and a share of 11.1%). Another product group that recorded significant transport performance was ‘Other non-metallic mineral products’, with 137.3 billion tkm and a share of 7.4%. The largest increases in tonne-kilometres from 2023 to 2024 were recorded for ‘Unidentifiable goods: goods which for any reason cannot be identified’ (+24.2%, through the absolute values are rather small), followed by ‘Other goods n.e.c.’ (+22.4%) and ‘Goods moved in the course of household and office removals’ (+14.5%). At the other end of the scale, the steepest declines were recorded for ‘Coal and lignite; crude petroleum and natural gas’ (-67.5%, with relatively small values), ‘Basic metals; fabricated metal products, except machinery and equipment’ (-6.3%), and ‘Coke and refined petroleum products’ (-3.9%). Over the period 2020-2024, the strongest average annual growth rate was recorded for ‘Unidentifiable goods: goods which for any reason cannot be identified’ (+11.2%), followed by ‘Other goods n.e.c.’ (+8.6%) and ‘Goods moved in the course of household and office removals’ (+5.7%). The largest declines were recorded for ‘Coal and lignite; crude petroleum and natural gas’, with an average annual growth rate of -7.5%, and ‘Wood and products of wood and cork (except furniture)’ with -1.4%. [[Image: Road freight transport by product group, EU, 2020-2024 (billion tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1b: Road freight transport by product group, EU, 2020-2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tg}}|alt= a table showing the road freight transport by product group in the EU from 2020 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image: Road freight transport by product group (NST 2007), EU, 2024_(% share in tonnes and tonne-kilometres)_up.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 1: Road freight transport by product group (NST 2007), EU, 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tg}}
Full names and description of [[Glossary:Standard_goods_classification_for_transport_statistics_(NST)|NST 2007]] codes |alt= a horizontal bar chart showing the road freight transport by product group (NST 2007 in the EU in 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 2 presents the share of each NST 2007 product group in total EU tonne-kilometres for [[Glossary:Road freight transport|national]] and [[Glossary:Road freight transport|international]] road freight transport. In 2024, the following product groups accounted for larger shares in national than in international transport: 'Agriculture, hunting, forestry, fishing products'; ‘Coal and lignite; crude petroleum and natural gas’; ‘Metal ores, mining and quarrying products’, 'Food, beverages and tobacco', ’Coke and refined petroleum products’; ‘Other non-metallic mineral products’, 'Secondary raw materials; wastes', ‘Mail and parcels’, and ‘Goods moved in removals; baggage; vehicles moved for repair’. All other product groups made up larger share of international than of national road freight transport. [[Image: Road freight transport of each product group (NST 2007) by type of operation, EU, 2024_(% share in tonne-kilometres)_up.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 2: Road freight transport of each product group (NST 2007) by type of operation, EU, 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tg}},{{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_na_tgtt}}
Full names and description of [[Glossary:Standard_goods_classification_for_transport_statistics_(NST)|NST 2007]] codes|alt= a horizontal bar chart showing the road freight transport of each product group (NST 2007) by type of operation in the EU in 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Road freight transport of dangerous goods === Figure 3 presents the share of dangerous goods in total transport performance in tkm of each EU country in 2023 and 2024. It should be noted that data for Italy are not available for 2023, while for Ireland data are not available for both years. The EU countries with the highest shares of dangerous goods in total road transport were Finland (7.3% in 2023; 8.4% in 2024) and Belgium (7.0% in 2023; 6.4% in 2024), followed by Denmark (6.4% in 2023; 5.6% in 2024). Several EU countries recorded shares of dangerous goods between 4.0% and 6.0% in both 2023 and 2024, including France, Spain and Germany. Poland, a major country in terms or road freight transport, recorded shares of 2.6% in 2023 and 2.5% in 2024. Slovakia, Portugal and Lithuania each recorded shares below 2.0% in both years. High differences between the 2 years can be seen for Bulgaria, where the share of dangerous goods in total tkm transported increased from 2.9% in 2023 to 5.5% in 2024, and in Cyprus where the share decreased from 7.0% in 2023 to 4.9% in 2024. [[Image: Road freight transport of dangerous goods, 2023 and 2024_(% share in total tonne-kilometres transported)_v1.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 3: Road freight transport of dangerous goods, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_dg}},{{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= a horizontal bar chart showing the road freight transport of dangerous goods in 2023 and 2024. In the EU, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 2 presents the transport of dangerous goods between 2020 and 2024. Over this period, 15 EU countries registered positive average annual growth rate in the transport of dangerous goods. The highest positive rates were recorded in Bulgaria (+13.0% per year on average), Romania (+9.6%) and Lithuania (+8.1%). At the other end of the scale, the largest negative growth rates over this period were registered in Portugal (-11.6% per year on average), Croatia (-11.3%), Cyprus (-11.2%) and Luxembourg (-10.8%). Twelve EU countries reported increases in transport of dangerous goods, with the largest in Slovakia (+372.7%), Bulgaria (+52.6%), Sweden (+41.9%) and Greece (+29.0%). Substantial decreases were observed in Croatia (-38.6%), Luxembourg (-28.4%) and Cyprus (-25.0%). [[Image: Road freight transport of dangerous goods, 2020-2024 (million tonne-kilometres)_v1.png|thumb|centre|500px|Table 2: Road freight transport of dangerous goods, 2020-2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_dg}}|alt= a table showing the road freight transport of dangerous goods from 2020 to 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 4 illustrates the share of national and international transport performance (in tonnes-kilometres) involving dangerous goods in 2024. In 2024, most of the EU countries recorded higher shares of tkm involving dangerous goods in national transport than in international transport. The main exceptions were Belgium, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Portugal, Slovenia, and Slovakia, where most of the dangerous goods transport was international. [[Image: Road freight transport of dangerous goods by type of operation, 2024_(% share in tonne-kilometres)_v1.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 4: Road freight transport of dangerous goods by type of operation, 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_dg}}|alt= a table showing the road freight transport of dangerous goods by type of operation in 2024 in the EU, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] It should be noted that, since dangerous goods make up only a small share of total road freight, the statistical processing of the survey results for this category entails a higher degree of uncertainty than for non-dangerous goods. === Road freight transport by type of cargo === In 2024, ’Palletised goods’ (i.e., goods transported on pallets) were the main type of cargo transported by road in most of the EU countries (see Table 3). The only exceptions were Cyprus and Luxembourg, where ’Solid bulk goods’ represented the main type of cargo, and Finland where ‘Other cargo not elsewhere specified’ was the most prevalent category. The EU countries with the highest shares of ’Palletised goods’ were Romania (72.3%), Lithuania (71.9%) and Portugal (61.5%). In contrast, the lowest shares were observed in Cyprus (8.5%), Finland (25.8%) and Luxembourg (30.2%). When looking at the sum of ’Palletised goods’ and ’Solid bulk goods’, the only country with an accumulated share below 50% was Finland (43.1%). Road freight transport by type of cargo is an optional variable of the road freight transport survey. Ireland and Italy do not report data by type of cargo, while Denmark reports all cargo as ‘unknown’. [[Image: Road freight transport by type of cargo, 2024 (million tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 3: Road freight transport by type of cargo, 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tcrg}}|alt= a table showing the road freight transport by type of cargo in 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= SE_Types_of_goods_2025_v5.xlsx|title=Road freight transport by type of goods}} === Context === Data presented in this publication were collected in the framework of {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012R0070:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 70/2012}} on statistical returns in respect of the carriage of goods by road (recast). These data are based on sample surveys carried out in the reporting countries, i.e., the EU countries, Norway and Switzerland, and record the road goods transport undertaken by vehicles registered in these countries. Reporting countries use their own national surveys for the collection of data based on returns from road hauliers. The results are microdata referring to vehicles and their linked journeys, providing detailed information on goods transported. At European level, common [[Glossary:Aggregation|aggregation]] procedures have been used which may diverge from national practices. Therefore, differences might occur between the figures in this publication and national values. === Data sources === ==== Country specific notes ==== '''Croatia''': While Croatia had no obligation prior to their accession in 2013, it started to report data from the reference year 2008. '''Malta''': Regulation (EU) No 70/2012 does not apply to Malta, as long as the number of Maltese-registered goods road transport vehicles licensed to engage in international transport does not exceed 400 vehicles. '''Finland''': National and international surveys have been harmonised and follow a common methodology from Q1 2011 onwards, leading to a break in time series in 2011. '''Sweden''': A break in series occurred in 2014 following a change in methodology. On the basis of a specific survey, Sweden corrected the European road freight survey results for trucks participating in the sample which were not in use over the surveyed period. ==== Methodological notes ==== '''EU totals''' calculated in this publication refer to road freight transport reported by the EU countries, excluding Malta which is exempt from reporting road freight statistics. '''Total international transport''' Total international transport includes international transport [[Glossary:Road freight transport|loaded]], [[Glossary:Road freight transport|unloaded]], [[Glossary:Cross-trade|cross-trade]] and [[Glossary:Cabotage|cabotage]]. '''Breakdown by goods groups''' Starting with the reference year 2008, {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32007R1304:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1304/2007}} establishes [[Glossary:Standard goods classification for transport statistics (NST)|NST 2007]] as the sole classification for goods carried in road freight transport. For detailed information on the NST 2007 classification, please refer to ‘[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/metadata/classifications Classifications]’, in Eurostat’s web pages about metadata. '''Dangerous goods''' {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012R0070:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 70/2012}} stipulates the collection of information on different categories of dangerous goods on an obligatory basis. Annex V of the Regulation (EU) No 70/2012 provides the categories to be used. As the carriage of dangerous goods by road represents only a small percentage of total road transport and the data are collected on the basis of sample surveys, the margins of error in any statistics will be substantial. Any figures for the transport of dangerous goods should be treated with caution. '''Type of cargo''' is the appearance of the cargo unit on presentation for transportation. The provision of data according to the type of cargo is optional in the legal basis. As not all EU countries provide this optional variable, the EU aggregate is not calculated. '''Tonne-kilometre (tkm)''': Unit of measure of goods transport that represents the transport of one tonne by road over one kilometre. The distance taken into account is the distance actually run. It excludes the distance covered when the goods road vehicle is being transported by another means of transport. ===Other articles=== *[[Transport#Freight transport|All articles on freight transport]] *[[Road_freight_transport_statistics|Road freight transport statistics]] *[[Road_freight_transport_by_journey_characteristics|Road freight transport by journey characteristics]] *[[Road_freight_transport_by_vehicle_characteristics|Road freight transport by vehicle characteristics]] *[[Road_freight_transport_statistics_-_cabotage|Road freight transport statistics - title: Road freight transport by journey characteristics
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the road freight transport by journey characteristics. Data extracted in August 2024 Planned article update: 10 September 2026 The total road freight transport performance in the EU, measured in tonne-kilometres, increased by an average of 0.9% per year between 2020 and 2024. Hauliers from Poland accounted for the largest share of international transport performance among EU countries in 2024, representing almost one third (32.7%) of the total. In 2024, more than one fifth (21.6%) of the distances travelled by road freight vehicles in the EU was performed by empty vehicles. [[Image: Average loads of road freight transport by type of operation, 2024_(tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px| Average loads of road freight transport by type of operation, 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= an image of a vertical bar chart showing the average loads of road freight transport by type of operation in 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article presents [[Glossary:Road freight transport|road freight transport]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] focusing on journeys performed by road freight vehicles. The article presents the different types of transport operations. It also discusses the average loads carried and average distances over which goods were moved, road freight transport by distance class and the distances travelled by empty road freight vehicles. This article and the articles [[Road freight transport by vehicle characteristics|'Road freight transport by vehicle characteristics']], [[Road freight transport by type of goods|'Road freight transport by type of goods']], [[Road freight transport statistics|'Road freight transport statistics']] and [[Road freight transport statistics - cabotage|'Road freight transport statistics - cabotage']] present a complete overview of road freight transport in Europe. === Road freight transport performance by type of operation (in tonne-kilometres) === In 2024, total European road freight transport performance increased by 0.6% compared with 2023 (from 1 857.0 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] [[Glossary:Tonne-kilometre (tkm)|tonne-kilometres (tkm)]]) to 1 868.7 billion tkm). The average annual growth rate from 2020 to 2024 was 0.9% (see Table 1). Total road freight transport decreased by 0.1% in 2022 and 3.2% in 2023 compared with the previous year, respectively. In 2021, it increased by 6.7% compared with 2020. Over the period 2020-2024, 15 of the 26 EU countries for which data are provided (Malta is exempt, see the chapter ‘Data sources’ below) reported a positive average annual growth rate in road freight transport performance, measured in tonne-kilometres (see Table 1). The largest were observed in Cyprus (+12.0%), Czechia (+5.8%) and Romania (+5.2%). In contrast, the highest negative rates were reported by Bulgaria (-4.6%), Germany (-2.0%), the Netherlands and Finland (both -1.8%). [[Image: Total road freight transport, 2020-2024 (billion tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Total road freight transport, 2020-2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= a table showing the total road freight transport from 2020 to 2024, in the EU, EU Member States and some EFTA countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at the evolution of EU road freight transport from 2020 onwards, the trends observed for [[Glossary:Road freight transport|national road freight transport]] and international road freight transport by loaded vehicles, presented as an index (2020 = 100) based on tonne-kilometres, are very similar to each other (see Figure 1). After declining in 2022–2023, both national and international transport returned to growth in 2023–2024. Although the overall patterns were comparable, international transport recorded somewhat stronger growth than national transport over the period 2020-2024. However, between 2023 and 2024, national road freight transport increased by 0.8 index points, slightly more than international road freight transport by loaded vehicles which grew by 0.4 index points. [[Image: Road freight transport by type of operation, EU, 2020-2024_(based on tonne-kilometres, 2020=100).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Road freight transport by type of operation, EU, 2020-2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt=a line chart with three lines showing the road freight transport by type of operation in the EU from 2020 to 2024; the three lines show national transport loaded, total transport and total international transport-loaded. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 2 shows that the national road freight transport in the EU accounted for 1 146.7 billion tkm in 2024, 0.8% more than in 2023. The average annual growth rate from 2020 to 2024 was 0.8%. Most of the EU countries recorded positive average growth rates over this period (17 out of 26). The highest positive rates were recorded in Estonia (+10.0%), followed by Cyprus (+9.3%), Bulgaria (+9.1%) and Romania (+8.5%). In contrast, the largest negative rates were reported by Portugal (-3.0%), Germany (-2.1%), Finland (-1.9%) and Belgium (-1.2%). [[Image: National road freight transport (loaded), 2020-2024 (billion tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: National road freight transport (loaded), 2020-2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= a table showing the national road freight transport, (loaded) from 2020 to 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some EFTA countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] At EU level, international road freight transport increased by 0.4% in 2024 compared with 2023, rising from 719.1 billion tkm to 721.8 billion tkm. The average annual growth rate was 1.1% between 2020 and 2024 (see Table 3). Close to half of the EU countries (11 out of 26) recorded increases over this period, some of them considerable: Czechia recorded an average annual growth rate of 10.4%, followed by Lithuania with a rate of 4.7%, Croatia with 4.2% and France with 3.7%. At the other end of the scale, among the 11 EU countries for which international transport fell, Bulgaria had the highest negative average annual growth (-10.0%), followed by Sweden (-6.6%), Estonia (-5.4%) and Greece (-5.2%). Denmark, Ireland and Finland recorded the same level of international road freight transport performance in 2024 as in 2020, although with some fluctuations in the years in between. Cyprus reported international transport performance of just 0.1 billion tkm in 2024. [[Image: International road freight transport (loaded), 2020-2024 (billion tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: International road freight transport (loaded), 2020-2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= a table showing the International road freight transport (loaded), from 2020 to 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some EFTA countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The share of international transport in the total road freight transport of a country varies considerably (see Figure 2). Among the EU countries, the highest shares of international transport were registered in Lithuania in both 2023 and 2024 (93.4% and 93.0%, respectively), followed by Luxembourg (92.9% in 2023; 92.7% in 2024) and Slovenia (86.2% in 2023; 87.7% in 2024). The lowest shares were registered in Sweden (5.0% in 2023; 4.6% in 2024), Finland (6.2% in 2023; 6.4% in 2024) and Cyprus (3.6% in 2023; 7.1% in 2024). [[Image: International road freight transport, 2023 and 2024_(% share of total, based on tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: International road freight transport, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= a vertical double bar chart showing international road freight transport from 2023 and 2024, in the EU, EU Member States and some EFTA countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at the shares of the individual EU countries in total EU international road freight transport in 2024 (see Figure 3), Poland continued having the highest share in total tonne-kilometres with 32.7%. International transport made up 64.2% of total road freight transport in tonne-kilometres in Poland in 2024, slightly down from 64.3% in 2023 (see Figure 2). After Poland, Spain followed as the second largest operator of international transport in the EU, with a share of 12.3% in 2024. The share of international transport in total road freight transport in Spain was up from 32.3% in 2023 to 32.6% in 2024 (see Figure 2). [[Image: Share of Member States in total EU international road freight transport, 2024_(%, based on tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Shares of Member States in total EU international road freight transport, 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= a pie chart showing the share of Member States in total EU international road freight transport in 2024, the segments show some of the Member States. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 4 presents the shares of [[Glossary:Cross-trade|cross-trade]] and [[Glossary:Cabotage|cabotage]] in international road freight transport in tkm for 2024. At the EU level, the share of cross-trade transport was 29.2%, while cabotage transport represented 7.2% In 6 EU countries (Bulgaria, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Romania and Slovenia), cross-trade transport represented more than 40% of international transport in tkm. Among these countries, Lithuania stood out with cross-trade of 70.9% of its total international transport. For cabotage, Luxembourg stood out with a share in international transport of 23.5%, which may be explained by the small size and the central geographical location of the country. The next highest shares of cabotage were recorded by Ireland (19.3%) and Finland (16.6%). [[Image: Cross-trade and cabotage in international road freight transport, 2024_(% share in tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Cross-trade and cabotage in international road freight transport, 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= a vertical double bar chart showing cross-trade and cabotage in international road freight transport in 2024, in the EU, EU Member States and some EFTA countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at the distribution of total EU cross-trade transport performance in tkm between the different EU countries in 2024, Poland, Lithuania, Romania and Slovenia recorded the highest shares in the EU total (see Table 4). Poland remained by far the main cross-trade transporter, accounting alone for 38.1% of total EU cross-trade transport. It was followed by Lithuania (20.7%), Romania (8.3%) and Slovenia (4.1%). All other EU countries registered shares below 4.0% in total EU cross-trade. In terms of the average share over the period 2020-2024, the highest shares were registered in Poland (37.7%), Lithuania (18.6%), Romania (8.3%) and Bulgaria (5.5%). During this period, all other EU countries registered average shares in total EU cabotage of less than 5.0%. In 2024, Hungary increased its share of cross-trade transport performance in the EU total by 1.0 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] compared with 2023. Other EU countries with notable increases were Latvia (+0.6 pp), Lithuania and Slovakia (both +0.5 pp). In contrast, the shares in the EU total fell by 1.7 pp in Bulgaria, 0.8 pp in Portugal and 0.3 pp in Poland. [[Image: Cross-trade transport, 2020-2024 (% share of EU total, based on tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 4: Cross-trade transport, 2020-2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}} |alt= a table showing the cross-trade transport from 2020 to 2024 in the EU Member States. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Road freight transport in tonnage and average loads === EU road freight transport measured in tonnes showed only marginal overall growth over the period 2020-2024, increasing from 13 018.4 billion tonnes in 2020 to 13 020.3 billion tonnes in 2024 (0.0%) (see Table 5). The highest positive average annual growth rates over this period were observed in Cyprus (+12.7%), Lithuania (+6.5%) and Estonia (+6.3%). By contrast, significant negative growth rates over the same period were noted in Greece (-4.0%), Portugal, Slovakia and Finland (all -3.0%). Between 2023 and 2024, total EU road freight transport decreased by 0.7% in terms of tonnes carried. Transported tonnage increased in 10 of the EU countries, with the largest increases observed in Estonia (+18.7%), Lithuania (+14.5%) and Italy (+6.6%). In 16 EU countries, the transported tonnage decreased. The sharpest falls were registered in Bulgaria (-10.4%), Portugal (-9.9%) and Hungary (-8.1%). [[Image: Road freight transport, 2020-2024 (million tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 5: Road freight transport, 2020-2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= a table showing the road freight transport, 2020-2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some EFTA countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The 'average load' (in tonnes) presented in this article was calculated by dividing annual freight transport performance (in tonne-kilometres) by the corresponding laden distance travelled (vehicle-kilometres, equivalent to kilometres). At country and EU level, this indicator provides information on the average weight in tonnes carried per kilometre of the laden distance travelled. The indicator is calculated separately for national, international and total transport. For total transport, national and international tonne-kilometres are added and then divided by the total laden distance travelled. The EU average load for total transport was 14.3 tonnes in 2024, with average loads of 13.5 tonnes for national transport and 15.9 tonnes for international transport (see Figure 5). In 2024, Finland had the highest average load in international transport at 22.0 tonnes, followed by Cyprus (19.5 tonnes), France (18.8 tonnes) and Greece (18.1 tonnes). Finland also had the highest average load in national transport, at 18.2 tonnes, ahead of Bulgaria (16.3 tonnes) and Latvia (16.2 tonnes). The average load in national transport in Slovenia was just 5.8 tonnes, 57.0% below the EU average. [[Image: Average loads of road freight transport by type of operation, 2024_(tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Average loads of road freight transport by type of operation, 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= a horizontal bar chart showing the average loads of road freight transport by type of operation in 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some EFTA countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Average distance travelled per tonne of load === The average distance over which 1 tonne of goods is carried has been calculated by dividing tonne-kilometres by tonnes for laden journeys only. This indicator provides information on the average distance travelled per tonne in each country and at EU level. The indicator is calculated separately for national, international and total transport. For total transport, national and international tonne-kilometres for laden journeys are added and then divided by the total tonnes transported. In 2024, the average distance travelled per tonne in total road freight transport in the EU was 143.5 kilometres (km). Within the different types of transport operations, this corresponded to 97.3 km in national road freight transport; 604.3 km in international transport; 722.0 km in cross-trade transport and 280.0 km in cabotage transport (see Figure 6). The average distance travelled per tonne for different types of transport in each EU country is generally affected by the size of the country and its level of involvement in international transport, where longer distances are travelled. Among the EU countries, the average distance travelled per tonne in total transport was substantially higher for hauliers from Lithuania than in most other countries, reaching 480.4 km in 2024. This reflects the importance of international transport for the Lithuanian road freight transport sector. The average distance travelled per tonne for Lithuanian national transport was 91.2 km in 2024, whereas this distance was 922.4 km for international transport, 779.9 km for cross-trade transport and 386.9 km for cabotage transport. At the other end of the scale, the average distance travelled per tonne were much lower for hauliers from Cyprus, with only 26.1 km in total transport in 2024. [[Image: Average distance travelled per tonne by type of operation, 2024_(kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Average distance travelled per tonne by type of operation, 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= a horizontal bar chart showing the average distance travelled per tonne by type of operation in 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some EFTA countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Transport performance by distance class === At EU level, most of the total road freight transport performance in 2024 was carried out over distances between 300 and 999 km (41.3%). This was also the case for most of the EU countries (see Table 6). However, a few countries showed a different pattern with respect to transport performance by distance class. In some islands and countries with an important domestic market, the share of road freight transport over short distances (less than 150 km) was higher: Cyprus, Ireland, the Netherlands and Austria. For Cyprus, 90.1% of transport performance is carried out over distances of less than 150 km. On the other hand, countries where international road transport plays a key role had a higher share of transport performance over long distances; transport over 1 000 km accounted for 40% or more of total tkm in Portugal and Lithuania (45.5% and 44.7%, respectively). The overall trend and distance profile of a country can be assessed by analysing its figures across different distance classes. Regarding the distance class of less than 150 km, a notable increase between 2023 and 2024 was recorded in Estonia (+25.4%). At the other end of the scale, we find Slovenia (-13.4%) and Hungary (-11.6%). For the distance class 150-299 km, Lithuania (+28.8%) and Cyprus (+26.9%) recorded the highest increases, while Hungary and Slovenia recorded decreases of 8.6% and 8.5%, respectively. The distance class 300-999 km showed notable increases in Latvia (+21.8%) and Ireland (+21.4%). Cyprus, Bulgaria and Luxembourg recorded decreases of more than 15% for this distance class (-100.0%, -17.6% and -15.3%, respectively). Lastly, for the distance class of 1 000 km or more, Belgium, Cyprus and France registered the highest increases: 130.6%, 130.3% and 48.9%, respectively. In contrast, Ireland, Bulgaria and Portugal recorded the highest decreases for this distance class, 29.1%, 26.1% and 22.8%, respectively. [[Image: Road freight transport by distance class, 2024 (million tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 6: Road freight transport by distance class, 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_dc}}|alt= a table showing road freight transport by distance class, 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some EFTA countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Empty runnings of road freight vehicles === Figure 7 presents the percentage of vehicle-kilometres recorded for empty runnings in 2024. At EU level, one fifth of total road freight vehicle-kilometres was carried out by empty vehicles (21.6%). This share was higher for national transport than for the total, at around one quarter (25.8%), whereas in international road transport the share of empty vehicle-kilometres was 12.6%. For total road freight transport, 17 of the EU countries recorded a share of vehicle-kilometres travelled by empty vehicles between 15% and 30% in 2024. The share for Cyprus was considerably higher, at 43.7%, which likely indicates that a big share of the road freight performance is linked either to goods imported through ports or construction traffic, both of which are linked to empty journeys in one of the two directions. Road freight performance by empty vehicles was also well above the EU average for Ireland (34.7%), Greece (34.4%) and Austria (34.0%). At the other extreme were Denmark, with only 7.5% vehicle-kilometres by empty vehicles, Lithuania with 11.0% and Belgium with 11.6%. Empty vehicles accounted for a large share of vehicle-kilometres in national transport for almost all countries. In contrast, for international transport, almost all the EU countries reported lower levels of empty running compared with national transport, with the only exceptions Denmark and France. Only a few countries recorded shares of more than 20% of vehicle-kilometres by empty vehicles in international transport in 2024: Austria (22.3%), France (21.0%), Luxembourg (20.9%), Ireland (20.5%) and Germany (20.2%). These figures underline the economic importance of securing loads for return journeys in international transport to minimise empty runs. [[Image: Road transport performed by empty vehicles by type of operation, 2024_(% share in vehicle-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Road transport performed by empty vehicles by type of operation, 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= a horizontal bar chart showing road transport performed by empty vehicles by type of operation in 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some EFTA countries. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= SE_Journey_charact_2025.xlsx|title=Road freight transport by journey characteristics}} === Context=== Data presented in this publication were collected in the framework of {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012R0070:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 70/2012}} on statistical returns in respect of the carriage of goods by road (recast). These data are based on sample surveys carried out in the reporting countries, i.e., the EU countries, Norway and Switzerland, and record the road goods transport undertaken by vehicles registered in these countries. Reporting countries use their own national surveys for the collection of data based on returns from road hauliers. The results are microdata referring to vehicles and their linked journeys, providing detailed information on goods transported. At European level, common [[Glossary:Aggregation|aggregation]] procedures have been used which may diverge from national practices. Therefore, differences might occur between the figures in this publication and national values. ===Data sources=== '''Country specific notes''' '''Bulgaria and Romania''': While Bulgaria and Romania had no obligation prior to accession in 2007, they started reporting data for the reference year 2006. '''Croatia''': While Croatia had no obligation prior to accession in 2013, it started reporting data from reference year 2008. '''Malta''': Regulation (EU) No 70/2012 does not apply to Malta, as long as the number of Maltese-registered goods road transport vehicles licensed to engage in international transport does not exceed 400 vehicles. '''Finland''': National and international surveys have been harmonised and follow a common methodology from Q1 2011 onwards, leading to a break in series in 2011. '''Sweden''': A break in series occurred in 2014 following a change in methodology. On the basis of a specific survey, Sweden corrected the European road freight survey results for trucks participating in the sample which were not in use over the surveyed period. '''Methodological notes''' '''EU totals''' calculated in this publication refer to road freight transport reported by the 27 EU countries excluding Malta which does not report road freight transport statistics. '''International transport loaded and unloaded''': International transport as presented in this publication is based on goods loaded and unloaded in the reporting EU countries. Double counting is avoided since reporting relates only to resident carriers of the reporting countries: the figures sum up the goods transported by resident carriers to all other countries of the world and the goods brought into the reporting country by resident carriers from all other countries of the world. '''Road freight transport performance in tonne-kilometres''' derives only from loaded journeys. Distances travelled by empty vehicles are not considered. ===Other articles=== *[[Transport#Freight transport|All articles on freight transport]] *[[Road_freight_transport_statistics|Road freight transport statistics]] *[[Road_freight_transport_by_type_of_goods|Road freight transport by type of goods]] *[[Road_freight_transport_by_vehicle_characteristics|Road freight transport by vehicle characteristics]] *[[Road_freight_transport_statistics_-_cabotage|Road freight transport statistics - title: Respiratory diseases statistics
text:
EU statistics on the diseases of the respiratory system cover the related deaths, healthcare, and the availability of specialised personnel. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 Diseases of the respiratory system accounted for 7.8% of all deaths in the EU in 2023. In 2024, at least three quarters of all people aged 65 or over in Ireland and Denmark had been vaccinated against influenza, the highest shares among the EU countries. On average in 2023, resident in-patients with diseases of the respiratory system spent between 4.7 days (Denmark) and 10.3 days (Czechia) in hospital. This article presents an overview of [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] statistics related to deaths from diseases of the respiratory system; it also presents information on the influenza vaccination rate, as well as healthcare activities assessed in terms of the number of hospital discharges and average lengths of stay. The respiratory system is a network of organs that are responsible for breathing; the lungs are the primary organ of this system, which also includes the nasal passage, oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles. Diseases of the respiratory system are among the main [[Glossary:Cause of death|causes of death]] in the EU and include conditions such as [[Influenza_statistics|influenza]], chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pneumonia or asthma. Note that the statistics presented in this article do not cover cancer of the respiratory system (such as lung cancer), which is covered in an article on [[Cancer_statistics_-_specific_cancers|statistics on specific cancers]]; diseases of the respiratory system do not include COVID-19. This article is included in a set of statistical articles concerning specific health conditions in the EU which forms part of the online publication [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union – facts and figures]]. ===Deaths from diseases of the respiratory system=== '''''Diseases of the respiratory system accounted for 7.8% of all deaths in the EU in 2023''''' In 2023, there were 380 100 deaths in the EU resulting from diseases of the respiratory system, equivalent to 7.8% of all deaths among residents. Table 1 shows that, in 2023, the proportion of deaths from respiratory diseases peaked in Malta, Denmark and Ireland, at 13.5%, 11.8% and 11.6%, respectively; Portugal, Belgium, Spain, Cyprus and Greece also reported double-digit shares. At the other end of the range, respiratory diseases were the main cause of death for fewer than 4.0% of the population in Lithuania, Latvia, Finland and Slovenia. [[Image:Causes of death – diseases of the respiratory system, residents, 2023_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Causes of death – diseases of the respiratory system, residents, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f6490cd0-2cdb-4af7-96cd-ec00dd0fdf32?lang=en hlth_cd_aro] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/88d0c76f-6ce4-4d2e-ac5b-8fa99fb0b0c1?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A table showing deaths from diseases of the respiratory system among residents, in number, as a share of all deaths and as standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Across the EU, a higher proportion of deaths of males than of females were from diseases of the respiratory system (8.3% compared with 7.4%) in 2023. This situation was repeated in most of the EU countries. The difference – with a higher share among males than females – was most pronounced in Romania (where the gender gap was 2.1 [[Glossary:Percentage point|percentage points]]), Latvia, Spain (both 1.8 percentage points) and Lithuania (1.7 percentage points). While the shares for males and females were approximately the same in France, Malta, Luxembourg and Slovenia, a higher proportion of deaths among females (rather than males) were attributed to diseases of the respiratory system in Greece, the Netherlands (both 0.3 percentage points), Sweden (0.4 percentage points), Denmark (0.9 percentage points) and Ireland (where the share of deaths from respiratory diseases was 1.2 percentage points higher for females than for males). '''''Standardised death rates for respiratory diseases were higher for males than for females''''' The EU’s [[Glossary:Standardised death rate (SDR)|standardised death rate]] for diseases of the respiratory system was 75.2 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2023; the death rate for males (103.0 deaths per 100 000 male inhabitants) was almost twice as high as that for females (57.3 deaths per 100 000 female inhabitants). Standardised death rates for males were higher than those for females in 2023 across all EU countries. The gender difference may, at least in part, be attributed to different smoking habits between the sexes and/or to occupational risks. Standardised death rates from respiratory diseases for males were 2.9 to 3.3 times as high as those for females in all 3 [[Glossary:Baltic Member States|Baltic countries]], while elsewhere they were between 1.3 and 2.2 times as high; the narrowest gender gaps in relative terms were recorded in Sweden, Ireland and the Netherlands, where the rates for males were 1.3 times as high as for females. Table 1 shows that standardised death rates for diseases of the respiratory system were particularly concentrated among older people (347.6 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants aged 65 or over). The EU’s standardised death rate for respiratory diseases among older people was 38 times as high as the standardised death rate for people aged less than 65 years (9.2 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants under 65). This was considerably higher than the same ratio for all causes of death, where the standardised death rate for the older age group was 22 times as high as that for the younger age group. A more detailed analysis of causes of death for diseases of the respiratory system is presented in Table 2. It shows that the main causes of death among respiratory diseases were lower respiratory diseases (chronic or other) and pneumonia, while standardised death rates for asthma and for influenza were considerably lower. [[Image:Standardised death rates – diseases of the respiratory system, residents, 2023 (per 100 000 male_female inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Standardised death rates – diseases of the respiratory system, residents, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/61b7bdc9-fd92-4919-b06c-4fe9eac3d275?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt= A table showing standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for diseases of the respiratory system. Data are analysed by sex and for six types of diseases of the respiratory system. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, the highest standardised death rates for chronic lower respiratory diseases among the EU countries were recorded in Hungary for males (80.6 deaths per 100 000 male inhabitants) and in Denmark for females (60.6 per 100 000 female inhabitants). The lowest rates were recorded in Slovenia for males (18.0 per 100 000 male inhabitants) and Latvia for females (3.7 per 100 000 female inhabitants). In 2023, the highest rates for pneumonia were registered in Slovakia for both sexes (109.7 deaths per 100 000 male inhabitants and 54.8 per 100 000 female inhabitants) and Romania (92.9 per 100 000 male inhabitants and 46.2 per 100 000 female inhabitants). The lowest rates were recorded in Finland (1.4 per 100 000 male inhabitants and 0.8 per 100 000 female inhabitants). In 2023, Austria had the highest standardised death rate for influenza for males (6.3 deaths per 100 000 male inhabitants), while Cyprus had the highest rate for females (4.8 deaths per 100 000 female inhabitants). Slovakia reported the lowest rates, at 0.4 deaths per 100 000 male inhabitants and 0.1 deaths per 100 000 female inhabitants. Among the diseases with much lower mortality rates, Malta recorded the highest standardised death rate in 2023 for asthma and status asthmaticus (also known as acute severe asthma) for males (2.4 deaths per 100 000 male inhabitants) and Estonia the highest death rate for females (2.8 per 100 000 female inhabitants). Greece recorded the lowest rates (0.2 deaths per 100 000 male inhabitants and 0.4 deaths per 100 000 female inhabitants) When there are very few deaths in a group, Eurostat uses confidentiality rules to ensure that disseminated data are confidential. These data are noted with ':' and a 'c' flag. Consequently, certain causes of death are reported as 0.0 per 100 000 people when expressed as standardised death rates, even if there are a few cases. This ensures that individuals cannot be identified.. '''''The standardised death rate for asthma was higher among females''''' With the exception of asthma and status asthmaticus, EU standardised death rates in 2023 for males were higher than those for females for each of the causes of death presented in Table 2. The EU standardised death rate for asthma and status asthmaticus was 1.4 times as high for females (1.3 deaths per 100 000 female inhabitants) as for males (0.9 deaths per 100 000 male inhabitants). For asthma and status asthmaticus, the rates in 2023 for females were higher than the rates for males for 23 of the EU countries. This difference between the sexes was largest in Slovakia, where the female standardised death rate for asthma and status asthmaticus was 2.7 times as high as that recorded for males. Large relative differences were also observed in Spain and Portugal, where the female death rate was at least 2.4 times as high as the male rate; all of the remaining EU countries had rates that were less than 2.0 times as high for females as for males. Among the 4 EU countries where the death rate for asthma and status asthmaticus was higher for males than for females, the largest relative differences were in Poland and Ireland (1.1 times as high among males as among females). For the other causes of death presented in Table 2, the rates for females were rarely higher than those for males. The exceptions were in Cyprus and Luxembourg for influenza and in Sweden for both chronic lower respiratory diseases and other lower respiratory diseases. ===Preventive care – vaccination === '''''At least three quarters of people aged 65 or over in Ireland and Denmark were vaccinated against influenza in 2024''''' Vaccination is an effective measure of preventative care which can reduce the number of deaths and some of the costs associated with influenza epidemics (see the article on [[Influenza_statistics|influenza statistics]] for more information). EU countries have a range of different policies with respect to making influenza vaccines available to the general public. Often these vaccines are targeted at older age groups or other at-risk groups. Figure 1 shows the rate of vaccinations against influenza among people aged 65 or over; there are considerable differences between EU countries. In 2024, at least three quarters of people aged 65 or over in Ireland and Denmark had been vaccinated against influenza. By contrast, fewer than 15% of people aged 65 or over were vaccinated against influenza in Poland and Slovakia (where the rate is for people aged 59 or over). In 20 of the EU countries for which data are presented (see Figure 1 for more information on the coverage), the share of the elderly vaccinated against influenza was higher in 2024 than in 2014. The proportion of the population aged 65 or over that was vaccinated against influenza was at least 20.0 percentage points higher in 2024 than in 2014 in Denmark, Estonia and Sweden. By contrast, the share of people aged 65 or over that was vaccinated fell 13.6 percentage points in Malta and 9.5 percentage points in Hungary. In the remaining 5 countries that reported a fall in the vaccination rate during the period under consideration, this decline was smaller than 4.0 percentage points. [[Image:Influenza vaccination rate, people aged 65 or over, 2014 and 2024 (%)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Influenza vaccination rate, people aged 65 or over, 2014 and 2024
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3ca86a2c-fc45-4017-833e-277b2f22cb4f?lang=en hlth_ps_immu])|alt=A double column chart showing the influenza vaccination rate of people aged 65 or over. Data are shown for 2014 and 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===In-patient respiratory healthcare=== '''''In 2023, approximately 5.4 million resident in-patients with diseases of the respiratory system were discharged from EU hospitals''''' Across the EU in 2023, resident [[Glossary:In-patient|in-patients]] with diseases of the respiratory system (codes J00 to J99) spent a total of 40.3 million days in hospital. By far the highest number of in-patient days was spent in German hospitals (24.0% of the EU total), while Italy (13.3%), France (13.1%) and Spain (10.2%) were the only other EU countries to record double-digit shares; the next highest share was in Poland (6.4%). Around 5.4 million resident in-patients with diseases of the respiratory system were [[Glossary:Hospital discharge|discharged]] from EU hospitals in 2023. Hospital discharges of resident in-patients treated for respiratory diseases accounted for 7.9% of all resident in-patient discharges. Among the EU countries, this share peaked at 11.9% in Spain, with relatively high shares also recorded in Portugal (11.7%), Ireland (11.3%), Cyprus and Romania (both 10.4%); none of the remaining EU countries had shares of more than 9.4%. By contrast, respiratory diseases accounted for a relatively small share of the total number of resident in-patient discharges in Croatia (6.3%), France and Latvia (both 6.5%). Additional information on this topic is available in the article [[Hospital_discharges_and_length_of_stay_statistics|Hospital discharges and length of stay statistics]]. '''''Bulgaria and Romania had highest number of resident in-patient discharges per 100 000 inhabitants''''' Relative to population size, Bulgaria (2 800 per 100 000 inhabitants) and Romania (1 900 per 100 000 inhabitants) recorded the highest resident in-patient discharge rates among those treated for diseases of the respiratory system in 2023 (see Figure 2). The Netherlands had the lowest resident in-patient discharge rates for diseases of the respiratory system, 623 per 100 000 inhabitants. [[Image:Hospital discharge rates for resident in-patients with diseases of the respiratory system, 2023 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Hospital discharge rates for resident in-patients with diseases of the respiratory system, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/79237154-5c71-4f30-bdfd-428fb24eae0e?lang=en hlth_rinpat2])|alt=A column chart showing hospital discharge rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for resident in-patients with diseases of the respiratory system. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''The length of hospital stays for resident in-patients with diseases of the respiratory system was generally close to the average for all types of disease''''' Table 3 presents an analysis of the average length of hospital stays for resident in-patients treated for a respiratory disease in 2022 and 2023. The average hospital stay in 2023 ranged in length from 4.7 days in Denmark, 5.1 days in Sweden and 5.3 days in the Netherlands up to 9.0 days in Portugal, 9.9 days in Italy and a peak of 10.3 days in Czechia. In Lithuania, the average length of a hospital stay for residents treated for a disease of the respiratory system in 2023 was 3.0 days shorter than the average for all diseases. Aside from Lithuania, the average length of a hospital stay due to a disease of the respiratory system was also at least 1.0 days shorter than the average for all diseases in Hungary, Germany, France, Latvia and Finland. By contrast, there were 4 EU countries that reported that the average length of a hospital stay due to a disease of the respiratory system was at least 1.0 days longer than the average for all diseases. The largest difference was observed in Italy (1.7 days); the other countries in this group were Ireland, Belgium and the Netherlands. [[Image:Average length of hospital stay for resident in-patients with diseases of the respiratory system, 2022 and 2023 (days)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Average length of hospital stay for resident in-patients with diseases of the respiratory system, 2022 and 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ac8a8bce-6c9b-4544-820d-c07bed9c2f24?lang=en hlth_ralos1])|alt=A table showing the average length of stay in days for resident in-patients with diseases of the respiratory system. Data are presented for 6 types of respiratory diseases. Data are shown for 2022 and 2023 for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Across the 22 EU countries for which data are available (incomplete data for Bulgaria, Denmark, Greece, Poland and Finland), the average length of a hospital stay for resident in-patients treated for a disease of the respiratory system fell between 2022 and 2023 in 13, was almost unchanged in the Netherlands, and increased in the remaining 8. The largest decreases between 2022 and 2023 in the average time spent in hospital for resident in-patients treated for a disease of the respiratory system were 1.2 days in Estonia and 1.1 days in Cyprus. By contrast, France recorded the largest increase, up 1.3 days. The remainder of Table 3 provides a more detailed analysis of the average length of hospital stays for resident in-patients diagnosed with 5 different types of respiratory diseases. On average, in-patients with pneumonia (codes J12 to J18) and with asthma and status asthmaticus (codes J45 to J46) spent the largest number of days in hospital. These data are of interest, insofar as pneumonia was 1 of the leading causes of death among respiratory diseases, in contrast to asthma, which had a relatively low death rate. The average length of stay for pneumonia ranged from 13.2 days in Estonia to 5.4 days in Sweden. Comparatively, the average stay in hospital for resident in-patients being treated for asthma varied considerably across the EU countries, from highs of 14.2, 13.9 and 13.8 days in Czechia, Germany and Croatia, respectively, to no more than 2.6 days in Denmark and Sweden. For resident in-patients diagnosed with acute upper respiratory infections and influenza (J00-J11), the average length of stay was highest in Portugal (at 6.5 days) and lowest in Denmark (at 2.4 days). Resident in-patients of other acute lower respiratory diseases (J20-J22) in Czechia spent an average of 8.0 days in hospital compared with 2.8 days in Denmark. Leaving aside Czechia (5.6 days), resident in-patients with other diseases of the upper respiratory tract (J60–J99) spent an average of no more than 3.9 days in hospital. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Respiratory diseases_Health2026.xlsx|title=Respiratory diseases: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''Key concepts''' An [[Glossary:In-patient|in-patient]] is a patient who is formally admitted (or ‘hospitalised’) to an institution for treatment and/or care and stays for a minimum of 1 night or more than 24 hours in the hospital or other institution providing in-patient care. An in-patient or day care patient is discharged from hospital when formally released after a procedure or course of treatment (episode of care). A discharge may occur because of the finalisation of treatment, signing out against medical advice, transfer to another healthcare institution or because of death. The number of deaths from a particular cause of death can be expressed relative to the size of the population. A standardised (rather than crude) death rate can be compiled which is independent of the age and sex structure of a population. This is done as most causes of death vary significantly by age and by sex; the standardisation facilitates comparisons of rates over time and between countries Standard population report: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-ra-13-028.. For country-specific notes on causes of death, please refer to the national metadata reports, which can be accessed through the links at the beginning of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/hlth_cdeath_sims.htm European metadata report]. '''Causes of death''' Statistics on causes of death provide information on [[Glossary:Mortality|mortality]] patterns, supplying information on developments over time in the underlying causes of death. This source is documented in more detail in a background article on the [[Causes_of_death_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of causes of death statistics]]. This provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis and the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. Under Commission {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0328:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 0328/2011}}, countries provide causes of death data to Eurostat within 24 months (T+24) after the end of the reference year. Causes of death are currently classified according to the 86 causes in the [[Glossary:European_shortlist_of_causes_of_death|European shortlist]], which is based on the [[Glossary:International classification of diseases (ICD)|International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD)]] 10th revision. Chapter X of the ICD covers diseases of the respiratory system: *J00 to J06 acute upper respiratory infections *J09 to J18 influenza and pneumonia *J20 to J22 other acute lower respiratory infections *J30 to J39 other diseases of upper respiratory tract *J40 to J47 chronic lower respiratory diseases *J60 to J70 lung diseases due to external agents *J80 to J84 other respiratory diseases principally affecting the interstitium *J85 to J86 suppurative and necrotic conditions of lower respiratory tract *J90 to J94 other diseases of pleura *J95 to J99 other diseases of the respiratory system. '''Healthcare resources and activities''' Statistics on healthcare resources (such as beds and personnel) and healthcare activities (such as information on hospital discharges) are documented in a background article on the [[Healthcare_non-expenditure_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of healthcare non-expenditure statistics]]. This provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. For hospital discharges and the length of stay in hospitals, the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/Annexes/hlth_res_esms_an_2.pdf International Shortlist for Hospital Morbidity Tabulation] (ISHMT) is used to classify data from 2000 onwards; Chapter X covers diseases of the respiratory system: * acute upper respiratory infections and influenza (1001) * pneumonia (1002) * other acute lower respiratory infections (1003) * chronic diseases of the tonsils and adenoids (1004) * other diseases of upper respiratory tract (1005) * asthma (1007) * other diseases of the respiratory system (1008). This article presents data on influenza vaccinations, largely derived from administrative sources that are linked to vaccination programmes (see further information in the background article on the [[Healthcare_non-expenditure_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of healthcare non-expenditure statistics]]). For country-specific notes, please refer to the annexes at the end of the national metadata reports, which can be accessed through the links at the beginning of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/hlth_res_esms.htm European metadata report]. The Eurostat {{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-028|title=Healthcare non-expenditure statistics manual}} provides an overview of the classifications, both for mandatory variables and variables provided on a voluntary basis. '''Symbols''' In tables, a colon ‘:’ is used to show where data are not available. Data in italics are estimates or provisional. ===Context=== There are many factors that can affect the health of a person’s respiratory system. Most of these are linked to lifestyle or environmental factors, such as smoking or pollution. Indeed, smoking tobacco is the main cause of lung disease in Europe (note that the data presented in this article do not cover cancer; for further information, see an article on [[Cancer_statistics_-_specific_cancers|specific cancers]]), while it is also considered to be a major contributory factor to the incidence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and the development of asthma in children and adults; furthermore, respiratory diseases also occur among people who are subject to passive smoking. EU countries have taken various tobacco control measures in the form of legislation, recommendations and information campaigns in an attempt to reduce the number of smokers. From a public health perspective, these measures aim to protect citizens from the hazardous effects of smoking and other forms of tobacco consumption. Air pollution is a major respiratory health issue: activities involving the burning of fossil fuels, such as some industrial activities, power generation, vehicle emissions and household heating/cooking, as well as natural phenomena (such as volcanic eruptions or dust storms) have the potential to cause respiratory diseases. Most sources of outdoor air pollution are beyond the control of individuals and require action by urban, national or international policymakers. Societies that reduce air pollution are likely to benefit from a reduced burden from heart disease and lung cancer, as well as chronic and acute respiratory diseases (including asthma). In urban areas, policies that can potentially alleviate air pollution include support for cleaner transport (including the introduction of low emission zones), energy-efficient housing, or better municipal waste management, while in rural areas air pollution may be alleviated by reducing agricultural waste incineration, forest fires and certain agro-forestry activities. Indoor air pollution is also generated by a variety of sources, including human activity (smoking, fuel used for heating or cooking, and the use of cleaning materials), pets, plants, dust or damp, and may be exacerbated by poor ventilation. Influenza is an annual, seasonal infectious disease caused by the influenza virus; it affects Europe in the winter. The majority of people who die from influenza are aged 65 or over and face complications based on chronic diseases such as cardiovascular diseases or chronic lung diseases. During an influenza epidemic, there may be significant costs for health services (associated with caring for those who fall sick) and for businesses in general (lost production because of time taken off work). In February 2026, the European Commission announced plans [https://health.ec.europa.eu/latest-updates/commission-invests-eu225-million-build-next-generation-protection-against-influenza-2026-02-20_en to invest €225 million to build next-generation protection against influenza] with the goal of speeding-up the development of flu vaccines offering protection across a wider range of influenza variants, while expanding production capacity and introducing novel treatments. Chronic respiratory diseases are included as 1 of the 5 main strands covered by the European Commission’s ''[https://health.ec.europa.eu/non-communicable-diseases/healthier-together-eu-non-communicable-diseases-initiative_en Healthier together – EU non-communicable diseases (NCD) initiative]''. The initiative was launched in December 2021 and aims to support EU countries in identifying and implementing effective policies and actions to reduce the burden of major NCDs and improve citizens’ health and well-being. === Footnotes === ===Other articles=== '''Online publications''' *[[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union – facts and figures]]
