title: Road freight transport statistics - cabotage
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the cabotage in the road freight transport. Data extracted in September 2025 Planned article update: 22 October 2026 Cabotage accounted for 4.8% of national road freight transport for hire and reward in the EU in 2024, a slight increase of 0.1 percentage points compared with 2023. More than half of the cabotage in the EU in 2024 was performed in Germany (51.3%). Polish hauliers performed 43.7% of all EU cabotage in 2024. |alt=dynamic a line chart with three lines showing road freight cabotage transport from the year 2020 to the year 2024; the lines show tonnes, tonnes-kilometers and vehicle kilometers. This article presents road freight [[Glossary:Cabotage|cabotage]] transport in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] up to and including 2024. Trends in cabotage are presented both from the perspective of the hauliers performing cabotage in other countries, and from the perspective of the countries where this cabotage takes place. Cabotage is defined as freight transport carried out within one country by hauliers registered in another country. As national transport markets within the EU are not yet fully liberalised, the level of cabotage (together with [[Glossary:Cross-trade|cross-trade]], i.e. transport between two countries carried out by hauliers from a third country), may be seen as a sign of market integration. This article, together with the articles [[Road freight transport statistics|'Road freight transport statistics']], [[Road freight transport by vehicle characteristics|'Road freight transport by vehicle characteristics']], [[Road freight transport by type of goods|'Road freight transport by type of goods']] and [[Road freight transport by journey characteristics|'Road freight transport by journey characteristics']], presents a complete overview of road freight transport in Europe. === Road freight cabotage transport registered an increase in 2024 === From the perspective of a reporting country and its hauliers, cabotage is considered [[Glossary:Road freight transport|international transport]] as it takes place on the territory of another country. From the perspective of the country in which the transport takes place, it could be considered [[Glossary:Road freight transport|national transport]] for hire and reward since goods are transported by foreign trucks from one location to another within the country. As road cabotage transport represents only a small share of [[Glossary:Road freight transport|road freight transport]] for [[Glossary:Road transport type|hire and reward]] in the national territory and as data are collected on the basis of sample surveys, the accuracy of cabotage data is generally lower than the accuracy of other road freight transport variables. The standard error of the data on cabotage transport varies significantly from country to country, whether measured in [[Glossary:Tonne-kilometre (tkm)|tonne-kilometres (tkm)]] or in tonnes. Figure 1 shows the development in road freight cabotage transport in the EU in terms of tonne-kilometres, tonnes and vehicle-kilometres (vkm), presented as indices based on 2020 data (2020=100). From 2020 to 2021, cabotage transport increased before declining sharply in 2022. This trend was similar across all three measurements (tonne-kilometres, tonnes and vehicle-kilometres). However, in 2023, cabotage measured in tonnes and vehicle-kilometres recovered slightly, while cabotage measured in tonne-kilometres recorded a minor decrease. In 2024, increases were recorded again for all 3 measures. In 2024, cabotage transport measured in tonnes was 3.3 index points higher than it had been in 2020. In terms of tonne-kilometres, the cabotage transport index in 2024 was 0.9 points higher than in 2020, while it decreased by 0.8 index points over the same period in terms of vehicle-kilometres. [[Image: Road freight cabotage transport, EU, 2020-2024_(index 2020=100).png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 1: Road freight cabotage transport, EU, 2020-2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= a line chart with three lines showing road freight cabotage transport from the year 2020 to the year 2024; the lines show tonnes, tonnes-kilometers and vehicle kilometers. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Cabotage in hire and reward transport accounted for 4.8% of national tonne-kilometres in the EU in 2024 === The 'cabotage penetration rate in hire and reward transport' is the main indicator used to assess the extent of cabotage within the national transport markets in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|EU]]. It is defined as the share of cabotage transport in the total national transport of a country (sum of national transport for hire and reward and cabotage transport). Thus, it does not include any transport carried out by companies on their own account, using their own trucks and lorries. The cabotage penetration rate in the EU increased slightly from 4.7% in 2023 to 4.8% in 2024 (see Figure 2). In 2024, the highest cabotage penetration rate among the EU countries was recorded in Luxembourg (20.8%), followed by Germany (10.6%), Belgium (10.1%) and Austria (9.5%). Together with France (7.9%), these were the only EU countries with a cabotage penetration rate above 7% in 2024. Luxembourg registered by far the highest increase in its cabotage penetration rate of 20.8% in 2024, rising by 11.0 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] from a rate of 9.8% in 2023. Other significant increases from 2023 to 2024 were recorded in the Netherlands (+1.9 pp), Belgium (+1.1 pp) and Slovakia (+0.7 pp). By contrast, the cabotage penetration rate in Estonia fell by 1.2 pp to 0.7%, down from 1.9% in 2023. In Slovenia, it fell by 0.6 pp to 1.2% in 2024, while Latvia registered a decrease of 0.5 pp to 0.7% in 2024. For the other EU countries, there were only minor or no changes in the cabotage penetration rate from 2023 to 2024. Poland, which is one of the major road transport providers in the EU, recorded a cabotage penetration rate of just 0.2% in 2023 and 0.3% in 2024. [[Image: Cabotage, by country where it takes place 2023 and 2024 V2.png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 2: Cabotage, by country where it takes place, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}},{{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ca_c}}|alt= a horizontal bar chart with two bars showing cabotage, by country where it takes place in the year 2023 and the year 2024 as a percentage share of transport for hire and reward in the national territory, in tonne-kilometres, in the EU, EU countries, Norway and Switzerland. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In terms of transport performance measured in tonne-kilometres, cabotage in the EU increased from 49.4 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] tkm in 2020 to a peak of 52.3 billion tkm in 2021. A decrease to 48.1 billion tkm followed in 2022, but EU cabotage remained largely stable in 2023, with only a minor decrease to 48.0 billion tkm. In 2024, cabotage transport performance in the EU picked up again, rising to 49.9 billion tkm (see Table 1). Germany remained by far the EU country with the highest cabotage performance, with more than double the level of the next country. Although cabotage stood at roughly the same level in 2024 as it had in 2020, at 25.6 billion tkm, it fluctuated between 27.2 (2021) and 26.0 billion tkm (2023) in the years in between. France recorded the second highest cabotage performance among the EU countries, with a slightly lower level in 2024, at 12.2 billion tkm, than in 2020 when it stood at 12.3 billion tkm. France also experienced substantial fluctuations in cabotage in its national transport market, with the cabotage transport performance ranging between 12.9 billion tkm in 2021 and 11.1 billion tkm in 2023. The cabotage performance in other EU countries remained significantly lower, with Italy recording cabotage of 2.9 billion tkm in 2024. All other EU countries registered cabotage performance of less than 2 billion tkm. [[Image: Cabotage, by country where it takes place, 2020-2024 (million tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|600px|Table 1: Cabotage, by country where it takes place, 2020-2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ca_c}}|alt=a table showing the cabotage, by country where it takes place from the year 2020 to the year 2024 in the EU, EU countries, Norway and Switzerland. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Cabotage is not always performed by hauliers from neighbouring countries === Table 2 shows the top 5 cabotage performers among the EU countries, Poland, Lithuania, Romania, Spain and the Netherlands, and in which countries the hauliers from these countries mainly carry out this cabotage (in tonne-kilometres). Until a few years ago, most cabotage transport was carried out in neighbouring countries. However, this has changed in recent years, in particular for hauliers from Poland, Lithuania and Romania. Hauliers from Poland continued to carry out by far the largest share of cabotage transport in the EU. In both 2023 and 2024, Poland accounted for 43.7% of all freight cabotage for hire and reward in the EU (see Figure 3). About three-quarters of the cabotage performed by Polish hauliers took place in Germany. In 2023, cabotage performed in Germany accounted for 77.0% of Polish cabotage performance, decreasing to 71.6% in 2024. Polish hauliers also conducted cabotage operations in France, the Netherlands and Sweden, although at a significantly lower scale. France was the second largest market for Polish cabotage, representing 11.5% in 2023 and 13.3% in 2024, followed by Sweden the third largest market in 2023 with 2.3% and the Netherlands in 2024 with 3.1%. Lithuania was the second largest provider of cabotage transport services, accounting for 13.7% of the total EU cabotage in 2023, rising to 14.7% in 2024. Lithuania performed most of its cabotage in countries with which it had no land borders. The largest share of Lithuania's cabotage performance took place in Germany (39.5% in 2023 and 36.7% in 2024). France came second, with 34.5% in both 2023 and 2024. Italy was the third largest cabotage market for Lithuanian hauliers both in 2023 and 2024 (8.5% and 9.8%, respectively). The third largest provider of cabotage transport in the EU was Romania, with 5.8% of the total EU cabotage performance in 2023 and 5.2% in 2024. The same 2 transport markets, Germany and France, were also the main countries for cabotage by Romanian hauliers. In both 2023 and 2024, Germany had the highest share, at 35.9% and 30.5%, respectively, followed by France with 22.5% in 2023 and 23.2% in 2024. Spain was the fourth largest provider of cabotage transport, with 5.2% in both 2023 and 2024, matching the share of Romania in 2024. Hauliers from the Netherlands had lower shares, with 3.6% in 2023 and 3.5% in 2024. For hauliers from Spain and the Netherlands, neighbouring countries were their main cabotage markets. For Spanish hauliers, the transport market in France accounted for 84.7% of their cabotage in 2023 and 86.6% in 2024. For Dutch hauliers, more than half (56.6% in 2023; 58.5% in 2024) of their cabotage was performed in Germany, and over a quarter in Belgium (28.2% in 2023; 25.2% in 2024). [[Image: Top 5 cabotage performing countries and the countries in which they carry out cabotage, 2023 and 2024.png|thumb|centre|600px|Table 2: Top 5 cabotage performing countries and the countries in which they carry out cabotage, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ca_hac}}|alt= a table showing the top five cabotage performing countries and the countries in which they carry out cabotage in the years 2023 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image: Cabotage in the EU, performed by hauliers from reporting countries, 2023 and 2024 (% share in total EU cabotage tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 3: Cabotage in the EU, performed by hauliers from reporting countries, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= two pie charts showing the cabotage in the EU, performed by hauliers from reporting countries in the years 2023 and 2024, one pie chart shows the year 2023 and one pie chart shows the year 2024 as a percentage share in total EU cabotage, in tonne-kilometres. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === More than half of EU cabotage transport was carried out in Germany in 2024 === In 2023, 54.0% of all cabotage transport in the EU (in tonne-kilometres) was performed on German territory, falling slightly to 51.3% in 2024. Nearly one quarter of the cabotage transport in the EU took place in France, accounting for 23.2% of the total EU cabotage market in 2023 and 24.5% in 2024 (see Figure 4). [[Image: Cabotage in the EU by country in which it takes place 2023 and 2024 V2.png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 4: Cabotage in the EU, by country in which it takes place, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ca_c}}|alt= two pie charts showing the Cabotage in the EU, by country in which it takes place in the years 2023 and 2024, one pie chart shows the year 2023 and one pie chart shows the year 2024 as a percentage share in total EU cabotage, in tonne-kilometres. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 3 shows the 5 EU countries where most cabotage was performed (in tonne-kilometres) and the nationality of the hauliers that performed the largest parts of the cabotage in each of these countries. Polish hauliers performed around two-thirds of all cabotage in Germany, the largest market for cabotage in the EU, in both years, with shares of 64.5% in 2023 and 63.8% in 2024. Lithuania was the second largest cabotage provider, but with far lower shares: 10.4% in 2023, rising to 11.0% in 2024. Polish hauliers also accounted for the largest shares in France, the second largest cabotage market in tonne-kilometres, with 22.4% in 2023 and 24.7% in 2024. Other key cabotage providers in France were Lithuania (21.1% and 21.6%) and Spain (19.6% and 19.1%). Italy was the third largest cabotage market in the EU in terms of volume. Among the top 3 foreign hauliers operating in Italy, Lithuanian hauliers provided the largest share of cabotage (22.0% in 2023; 25.6% in 2024), followed by Polish hauliers (14.9% in 2023; 20.0% in 2024). Romanian hauliers were the third most significant in 2023, but were overtaken by Slovenian hauliers in 2024 (10.8%). Belgium retained its fourth place among the top 5 EU countries where most cabotage was performed in 2023 and 2024. In Belgium, hauliers from Luxembourg performed around one-third of the cabotage (34.1% in 2023 and 32.4% in 2024), closely followed by hauliers from the Netherlands (30.1% in 2023 and 26.9% in 2024). Spain rounded off the top 5 in both 2023 and 2024. In 2024, Portuguese hauliers accounted for 30.9% of the cabotage performed in Spain, a decrease from 43.9% in 2023. [[Image: Top 5 countries with most cabotage performed and the main countries performing it, 2023 and 2024.png|thumb|centre|600px|Table 3: Top 5 countries with most cabotage performed and the main countries performing it, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ca_hac}} |alt= a table showing the top five countries with most cabotage performed and the main countries performing it in the years 2023 and 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Cabotage activity rebounded in 2024 after 2 years of decline === From 2020 to 2024, cabotage performance increased in 13 of the 25 EU countries for which data are available (see Table 4). The highest average annual growth rates in cabotage performed were observed for Sweden (+22.3%), Ireland (+8.4%%), and both Czechia and Finland (+7.2% each). By contrast, the largest decreases over the period 2020-2024 were recorded for hauliers from Greece (-31.2%), ahead of Bulgaria (-15.2%) and Estonia (-9.6%). Cabotage activity in 6 EU countries – Bulgaria, Croatia, Austria, Portugal, Romania, and Slovenia – fell continually since 2020, reaching their lowest levels in 2024. The largest absolute increases in cabotage transport between 2020 and 2024 were recorded by Lithuania (+1.9 billion tkm) and Czechia (+0.4 billion tkm). At the other end of the scale, the largest decreases were recorded by Bulgaria (-0.8 billion tkm), followed by Romania (-0.7 billion tkm) and Poland (-0.5 billion tkm). [[Image: Cabotage performance by haulier's country of registration, 2020-2024 (million tonne-kilometres)_up.png|thumb|centre|600px|Table 4: Cabotage performance by haulier's country of registration, 2020-2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= a table showing the cabotage performance by haulier's country of registration from the year 2020 to the year 2024 in the EU, EU countries, Norway and Switzerland. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Polish hauliers carried by far the largest loads in cabotage transport in 2024=== The trend in volume (in tonnes) of goods transported in cabotage was similar to the trend in tonne-kilometres. Polish hauliers carried by far the largest volume of goods in cabotage in 2024, followed at a considerable distance by Lithuanian and Dutch hauliers (see Figure 5). The highest relative increases between 2023 and 2024 were recorded by Danish hauliers (+53.4%), Irish hauliers (+35.5%) and Lithuanian hauliers (+30.8%). At the other end of the scale, Greece (-91.5%), Italy (-27.8%) and Portugal (-19.6%) recorded the largest decreases from 2023 to 2024. [[Image: Volume of freight transported in cabotage operations, by haulier's registration country, 2023 and 2024 (thousand tonnes).png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 5: Volume of freight transported in cabotage operations, by haulier's registration country, 2023 and 2024
Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=road_go_ta_tott}}|alt= ahorizontal bar chart showing the volume of freight transported in cabotage operations, by haulier's registration country in the years 2023 and 2024, in the EU countries, Norway and Switzerland. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename= SE_Cabotage_2025_up.xlsx|title=Road freight transport - cabotage}} == Context == Data presented in this publication were collected within the framework of {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012R0070:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 70/2012}} on statistical returns in respect of the carriage of goods by road (recast). These data are based on sample surveys carried out in the reporting countries, i.e. the EU countries, Norway and Switzerland, and record the freight transport operations undertaken by road vehicles registered in these countries. Reporting countries use their own national surveys for the collection of data based on returns from road hauliers. The results are microdata referring to vehicles and their linked journeys, providing detailed information on goods transported. At the European level, common [[Glossary:Aggregation|aggregation]] procedures are applied which may diverge from national practices. Differences might therefore occur between the figures in this publication and national values. For the distinction between national and international transport, journey related information is used at European level, which might cause differences compared with values reported by countries that use goods-related information for these statistics. === Data sources === ==== Country specific notes ==== '''Croatia''': While Croatia had no obligation prior to accession in 2013, it started reporting data for the reference year 2008. '''Malta''': Regulation (EU) No 70/2012 does not apply to Malta, as long as the number of Maltese-registered goods road transport vehicles licensed to engage in international transport does not exceed 400 vehicles. '''Finland''': National and international surveys have been harmonised and follow a common methodology from Q1 2011 onwards, leading to a break in time series in 2011. '''Sweden''': A break in series was produced in 2014 following a change in methodology. On the basis of a specific survey, Sweden corrected the European road freight survey results for trucks participating in the sample which were not in use over the surveyed period. ==== Methodological notes ==== '''EU totals''' calculated in this publication refer to road freight transport reported by the EU countries, excluding Malta which is currently exempt from reporting road freight statistics. '''Total transport''' Total transport includes national transport, international transport of goods [[Glossary:Road freight transport|loaded]] in the reporting countries, international transport of goods [[Glossary:Road freight transport|unloaded]] in the reporting countries, [[Glossary:Cross-trade|cross-trade]] and [[Glossary:Cabotage|cabotage]] '''Cabotage''' ''Definition and history'': Cabotage is declared by EU countries for hauliers registered in their country that performed transport on the national territory of another country. From the point of view of the reporting country, it is considered as international transport, from the point of view of the movements of goods, it could be considered as national transport. With the aim of increasing transport efficiency and reducing the number of empty journeys, cabotage transport was gradually introduced in 1990 through authorisation quotas (quantitative restrictions) and further liberalised in 1998 in the 15 EU countries at that time (hauliers are allowed up to three cabotage operations within 7 days following an incoming international carriage). The cabotage regime was extended to the EFTA states (except Switzerland) following the creation of the EEA (European Economic Area). In May 2009, cabotage transport was liberalised between the EU-15 countries (the EU countries prior to the 2004 enlargement) and the countries that joined the EU in 2004. In January 2012, cabotage transport was further liberalised, allowing hauliers from Romania and Bulgaria the same cabotage rights across the EU as those from other EU countries. Since July 2015, cabotage for Croatian hauliers has been permitted in certain EU countries and was later extended to cover all EU countries. In 2020, as part of the EU Mobility Package I, new rules on cabotage were adopted to improve enforcement and ensure fair competition within the EU road transport market. While the basic rule of up to three cabotage operations within seven days remained unchanged, a “cooling-off period” of four days was introduced. This means that after completing cabotage operations in a host country, the same vehicle may not perform cabotage in that country again for four days. The package also introduced enhanced enforcement measures, such as the mandatory return of vehicles to their country of establishment every eight weeks, stricter rules on posting of drivers, and the digitalisation of control procedures through smart tachographs and the Internal Market Information System. The adoption of Mobility Package II in 2020 enhanced the digital enforcement tools, such as smart tachographs and electronic freight information systems, that facilitate compliance with cabotage regulations. ''Cabotage penetration rate'': Share of cabotage transport in total national transport, where total national transport is the sum of national transport (for hire and reward) and cabotage transport (in that country). ''Data reliability'': As road cabotage transport represents only a small percentage of total road transport and as data are collected on the basis of sample surveys, the importance of cabotage could sometimes either be over- or underestimated. Percentage standard error (PSE, 95% confidence interval) of cabotage transport is typically 5-40% for tonnes and 5-30% for tonne-kilometres. Furthermore, variability in cabotage transport performance often occurs due to 'haulage contracts' that have a limited validity. A haulier might thus perform cabotage transport operations in 1 year and lose this market to a transport operator registered in a different country the next year. ===Other articles=== *[[Transport#Freight transport|All articles on freight transport]] *[[Road_freight_transport_statistics|Road freight transport statistics]] *[[Road_freight_transport_by_journey_characteristics|Road freight transport by journey characteristics]] *[[Road_freight_transport_by_vehicle_characteristics|Road freight transport by vehicle characteristics]] *[[Road_freight_transport_by_type_of_goods|Road freight transport by type of goods]] ===Selected Datasets=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/database Transport], see selected datasets: :Road transport (t_road) ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/database Transport], see detailed datasets: :Road transport (road) ::Road freight transport measurement (road_go) ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=transport}} Transport] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-037|title=Eurostat regional yearbook — 2025 edition}} - Flagship publications *{{Template:Publication|code= KS-01-25-003|title=Key figures on Europe – 2025 edition}} - Key figures *{{Template:Publication|code= ks-01-24-021|title=Key figures on European transport — 2024 edition}} - Key figures ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=road_go_esms|title=Road freight transport measurement}} (ESMS metadata file) *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-19-004|title=Glossary for transport statistics — 5th edition — 2019}} - Manuals and guidelines *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/KS-01-25-%20004 Methodologies used in road freight transport surveys in Member States, EFTA and 3 candidate countries — 2025 edition] - Manuals and guidelines *{{Template:Publication|code=ks-gq-24-019|title=Road freight transport methodology — 2025 edition}} - Manuals and guidelines ===Legislation=== *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012R0070:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 70/2012}} on statistical returns in respect of the carriage of goods by road (recast) *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32007R1304:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1304/2007}} of 7 November 2007 amending Directive 95/64, Regulation (EC) No 1172/98, Regulations (EC) No 91/2003 and (EC) No 1365/2006 with respect to the establishment of [[Glossary:Standard goods classification for transport statistics (NST)|NST 2007]] as the unique classification for transported goods in certain transport modes *A wider European legislative framework for international road freight transport is presented by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009R1072:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1072/2009}} of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 October 2009 on common rules for access to the international road haulage market *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32010R0202:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EC) No 202/2010}} amending Regulation (EC) No 6/2003 concerning the dissemination of statistics on the carriage of goods by road {{Unit|topic=X_Transport}} [[Category:Transport|Road freight transport statistics - title: Road freight transport statistics
text:
This article presents the main trends in road freight transport in the European Union up to and including 2025, analysing national and international transport as well as cross-trade transport and cabotage. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 In 2025, total road freight transport in the EU amounted to 1 886 billion tonne-kilometres and nearly 13.3 billion tonnes. In terms of tonne-kilometres, ‘Food products, beverages and tobacco' was the largest group of goods transported by road in the EU in 2025, accounting for 311.1 billion tonne-kilometres. In terms of tonnes, Germany was the territory with the highest freight transport by road in 2025. In 2025, Germany was the origin or destination of almost half of the top 20 country-to-country road freight transport flows within the EU.

This article presents the main trends in [[Glossary: Road freight transport|road freight transport]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] up to and including 2025. National, international, [[Glossary:Cross-trade|cross-trade]] and [[Glossary:Cabotage|cabotage]] transport are all analysed. Road freight transport by type of goods and distance class are also presented, as are goods moved on the national territory of countries and country-to-country flows. This article, together with the articles [[Road freight transport by vehicle characteristics|'Road freight transport by vehicle characteristics']], [[Road freight transport by type of goods|'Road freight transport by type of goods']], [[Road freight transport by journey characteristics|'Road freight transport by journey characteristics']] and [[Road freight transport statistics - cabotage|'Road freight transport statistics - cabotage']] present a complete overview of road freight transport in Europe. ===Total EU road freight transport performance continued to increase in 2025=== In terms of [[Glossary:Tonne-kilometre_(tkm)|tonne-kilometres (tkm)]], European road freight transport increased by 0.6% from 2023 to 2024 (from 1 857 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] tkm to 1 869 billion tkm). In 2025, it increased further, by 0.9% to 1 886 billion tkm (see Table 1 and Figure 1). International transport accounted for almost one quarter (24.4%) of total road freight transport in the EU in 2025. It decreased by 1.5% from 2023 to 2024, followed by a slight increase of 0.3% from 2024 to 2025 (see Table 1). National transport, which represented almost two thirds (62.2%) of the total in 2025, increased by 0.8% in 2024 and 2.2% in 2025. Cross-trade and cabotage transport (together representing 13.4% of the EU total in 2025), fell by 3.7% and 3.0%, respectively, compared with 2024. In 2024, both recorded increases, by 3.4% and 4.7%, respectively. In 2025, Poland (20.2% of EU total tkm) reconfirmed its position as one of the most important countries for road transport in Europe, ahead of Germany (14.7%) and Spain (14.5%). Together, international transport, cross-trade and cabotage made up 60.0% of Poland's transport performance, while national transport represented 40.0%. In 2025, total road freight transport decreased in 13 EU countries compared with 2024, with the most significant declines recorded in Luxembourg (-14.1%), Slovenia (-10.7%) and Estonia (-10.3%). In contrast, 11 EU countries recorded increases, the highest ones in Ireland (+10.5%), Portugal (+10.3%) and Croatia (+7.7%). In Bulgaria and Lithuania, total road freight transport remained stable during these 2 years (see Figure 1). Looking back to 2024, compared with 2023, total road freight transport fell in 10 EU countries, from -18.6% in Bulgaria to -0.4% in Austria and Belgium. In 15 EU countries, total road freight transport increased, from +0.4% in Netherlands to +15.9% in Slovakia, while in Croatia the level remained stable. [[Image:Road freight transport by type of operation, 2023-2025 (million tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Road freight transport by type of operation, 2023-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/265fc63a-9969-4d64-b2a7-2823fe98556a?lang=en road_go_ta_tott])|alt=a table showing the road freight transport by type of operation from 2024 to 2025 in the EU, the EU countries and some of the EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

Figure 1 Road freight transport performance in the EU increased in 2021, following the recovery after the COVID-19 pandemic. The second quarter of 2021 represented a peak, at 496.4 billion tkm (see Figure 2). In 2022, total EU road freight transport remained relatively stable, with a higher performance in the first quarter compared with the same quarter of the previous year (+2.5%) and small decreases in the following 3 quarters (-0.7%, -0.6% and -1.6%, respectively), bringing total transport in 2022 close to the same level as in 2021. The road freight transport performance continued to decrease throughout 2023: -2.3% in the first quarter compared with the same quarter of the previous year, -3.6% in the second quarter, -3.8% in the third quarter, and -3.1% in the last quarter. In the last 2 quarters of 2023, total EU road freight transport fell to levels not recorded since before the COVID-19 pandemic. Road freight transport performance continued to decrease in the first quarter of 2024 compared with the same quarter of the previous year (-1.8%) but started to increase in the next quarters: +0.7% in the second and third quarter and +3.0% in the last quarter. This upward trend continued in 2025 except for the second quarter (-0.7%) while increases were observed in the first (+1.6%), third (+0.9%) and fourth (+1.9%) quarters.

Figure 2 ===The main goods categories transported in 2025 were the same as in 2024, both in terms of tonnes and tonne-kilometres=== In terms of tonnage, European road freight transport increased by 1.8% in 2025, compared with 2024 (from 13 057 million tonnes to 13 291 million tonnes – see Table 2). In 2025, as in previous years, 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products' was the largest product group transported, accounting for 3 041 million tonnes. Other important product groups were 'food, beverages and tobacco' (1 611 million tonnes), 'other non-metallic mineral products' (1 602 million tonnes), and 'agricultural, forestry and fishery products' (1 289 million tonnes). The most notable increases between 2024 and 2025 were recorded for ‘coal and lignite; crude petroleum and natural gas’ (up by 17.8%), ‘unidentifiable goods’ (up by 15.7%) and ‘equipment and material utilized in the transport of goods’ (up by 8.6%). At the other end of the scale, significant decreases were recorded for the product groups ‘textiles and textile products; leather and leather products’ (-6.6%), ‘furniture’ (-2.8%) and ‘removals; motor vehicles moved for repair’ (-2.3%). In terms of tonne-kilometres, ‘food products, beverages and tobacco' continued to dominate road freight transport in 2025, accounting for 311.1 billion tkm, followed by 'grouped goods' (237.1 billion tkm) and 'agricultural products' (206.3 billion tkm). Notable increases between 2024 and 2025 were recorded for ‘unidentifiable goods’ (up by 18.8%), ‘coal and lignite; crude petroleum and natural gas’ (up by 11.7%) and ’coke and refined petroleum products’ (up by 8.2%). The highest decreases were recorded for ‘furniture’ (-11.8%), ‘chemicals; rubber and plastic products ; nuclear fuel’ (-4.1%) and ‘removals; motor vehicles moved for repair’ (-3.3%). [[Image:Road freight transport by group of goods (NST 2007), EU, 2024 and 2025 (thousand tonnes and million tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Road freight transport by group of goods (NST 2007), EU, 2024 and 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/60a03d01-9f04-40b3-a64a-a0e877f4489a?lang=en road_go_ta_tg])|alt=a table showing the road freight transport in the EU in 2024 and 2025, by group of goods according to the classification NST 2007. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Mixed trends in transport across distance classes in 2025=== Most of the EU road freight traffic is carried out within 3 distance classes: from 150 to 299 km, from 300 to 499 km and from 500 to 999 km (see Table 3). In 2025, these 3 distance classes together accounted for 1 142 billion tkm of the total EU road freight transport, an increase of 1.4% compared with 2024. The highest road freight transport performances over these 3 distance classes were recorded in Poland (231 billion tkm), Germany (171 billion tkm) and Spain (158 billion tkm), while the lowest were recorded in Estonia (2 billion tkm), Luxembourg (4 billion tkm) and Latvia (7 billion tkm). [[Image:Road freight transport by distance class, 2024 and 2025 (million tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Road freight transport by distance class, 2024 and 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e110d312-a0b9-414a-8774-48090c4df6d9?lang=en road_go_ta_dctg])|alt=a table showing road freight transport by distance class in the EU, the EU countries and some of the EFTA countries in 2024 and 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 3 shows trends in road freight transport for different distance classes since 2021. Compared with 2021, EU road freight transport decreased in 2022 for the distance classes of less than 150 km (-1.1%), from 150 to 299 km (-1.3%), as well as for the class of over 2 000 km (-2.2%). The remaining distance classes (from 300 to 999 km and from 1 000 to 1 999 km) each recorded increases of 0.8%. Road freight transport fell considerably in all distance classes in 2023: -3.5% for both over 2 000 km and from 300 to 999 km, -3.4% for from 1 000 to 1 999 km, -3.3% for less than 150 km and -2.3% for from 150 to 299 km. In 2024, small increases were recorded compared with the previous year for the distance classes from 150 to 299 km (+1.6%), from 300 to 999 km (+1.4%) and less than 150 km (+0.4%), while the distance classes of over 2 000 km and from 1 000 to 1 999 km recorded decreases (-5.8% and -0.2%, respectively). In 2025 compared with 2024, the trend with increases over the shorter distance classes and decreases or limited changes over the longer distance classes continued: whereas the transport performance increased over distances of less than 150 km (+2.5%), from 150 to 299 km (+2.3%) and from 300 to 999 km (+0.9%), it fell for the class from 1 000 to 1 999 km (-3.6%) and changed only marginally for the class of 2 000 km and over (+0.1%).

Figure 3 Table 4 shows road freight transport by group of goods for 2024 and 2025, measured in tonnes, split between movements of less than 300 km and movements of 300 km or more. The tonnage transported over distances of less than 300 km increased by 1.9% between 2024 and 2025. For transport within this distance range, 'coal and lignite; crude petroleum and natural gas' and ‘unidentifiable goods’ were the product groups that recorded the most significant increases (+20.0% and +14.3%, respectively). The highest decreases were recorded for ‘textiles and textile products; leather and leather products’ (-7.4%) and ‘removals; motor vehicles moved for repair’ (-1.9%). The tonnage transported over 300 km and more increased by 1.1% between 2024 and 2025. The most notable changes were the high increases for ‘unidentifiable goods’ and ‘secondary raw materials; wastes’ (up by 22.5% and 8.0%, respectively). The largest decreases were recorded for ‘furniture’ and ‘removals; motor vehicles moved for repair’ (-8.2% and -6.4%, respectively). [[Image:Road freight transport by distance class and group of goods (NST 2007), EU, 2024 and 2025 (thousand tonnes).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 4: Road freight transport by distance class and group of goods (NST 2007), EU, 2024 and 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1e07a769-3ce5-4a64-bbf9-39d418705d10?lang=en road_go_ta_dctg])|alt=a table showing road freight transport in the EU in 2024 and 2025 by distance class and group of goods according to the classification NST 2007. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===In 2025, Germany, France, Spain, Poland and Italy together accounted for two thirds of the total tonnage transported in the EU=== When looking at total transport in 2025, the tonnes of goods transported within Germany (national transport) or loaded/unloaded in Germany (international transport) represented almost one quarter of the total tonnage (22.3%) in the EU, with France and Spain together almost making up another quarter (12.4% and 12.1%, respectively). These 3 countries, along with Poland (10.6%) and Italy (9.4%), accounted for just over two thirds (66.8%) of the total transport of goods by road in the European Union (see Figure 4). In terms of national transport on their own territory, Germany, France, Spain, Poland and Italy recorded the highest tonnages among the EU countries in 2025 (22.5%, 12.6%, 13.1%, 11.0% and 10.0% of the total national transport in the EU, respectively). Considering international transport (i.e., the sum of goods entering and leaving the country, including cross-trade), the pattern has not changed significantly over the last years. International transport of goods loaded/unloaded in Germany remained the highest tonnage (431 million tonnes), ahead of France (231 million tonnes), the Netherlands (200 million tonnes), and Belgium and Poland (181 million tonnes each).

Figure 4 At the level of EU/extra-EU country-to-country freight transport flows (see Table 5), Switzerland, Norway and the United Kingdom were important trading partners of the EU. The main extra-EU flows have generally been between these countries and the EU countries neighbouring them. In 2024, the main such traffic flows were between Switzerland and Germany (17.3% of the total extra-EU road transport tonnage), followed by the flows between Norway and Sweden (10.1%), Switzerland and France (8.4%), and Ireland and the United Kingdom (5.9%). [[Image:Top 15 country-to-country flows in EU_extra-EU road freight transport, 2025 (million tonnes)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 5: Top 15 country-to-country flows in EU/extra-EU road freight transport, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/105e40e1-b37a-4ae5-82e7-27c1232ebe3c?lang=en road_go_ia_ugtt], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5380eecb-53da-4482-8343-103f01945965?lang=en road_go_ia_lgtt] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/074d733f-3ee7-49f5-838f-26fe43c4d5a4?lang=en road_go_cta_gtt])|alt=a table showing the top 15 country-to-country flows in EU/extra-EU road freight transport in 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 6 shows the tonnage transported in the top 20 country-to-country flows within the EU, as well as the nationality of the most important hauliers and their shares in the respective transport flows. Germany was either the origin or the destination for almost half of the top 20 country-to-country flows in 2025, illustrating the central role of Germany in intra-EU trade flows. However, German hauliers’ share of the transported volumes was less than 50% in all country-to-country flows shown in Table 6, with as little as 3.0% in the flow between Germany and Poland and 4.0% in that between Germany and Spain. German hauliers recorded their highest shares in the transport between Germany and Denmark (39.2%) and between Austria and Germany (29.7%). The share of hauliers from other EU countries in the country-to-country transport flows varied substantially. In 2025, hauliers from other EU countries than the origin and destination countries carried 64.1% of the total volume transported between Germany and Italy, 60.1% between Belgium and Germany, 57.9% between Germany and France, 54.7% between Germany and Denmark, 54.4% between Austria and Italy, and 53.5% between France and the Netherlands. At the other end of the scale, hauliers from other countries accounted for only 1.3% of total tonnes transported between Spain and Portugal; 1.4% between Czechia and Poland; 1.6% between Germany and Poland; and 2.1% between Poland and Slovakia. Among hauliers from other EU countries than the origin and destination, Polish hauliers were by far the most important. Of the top 20 intra-EU country-to-country transport flows in 2025, Polish hauliers were the main transporters from and to other EU countries for 10 connections. Of the remaining 10 connections with ‘other hauliers’, Poland was the origin or destination country in 3 these connections. [[Image:Top 20 country-to-country flows in intra-EU road freight transport, 2025 (million tonnes)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 6: Top 20 country-to-country flows in intra-EU road freight transport, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0510ffe9-b72c-4494-8199-39cb382cb234?lang=en road_go_ia_ugtt], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4f2fe4f5-67e8-4c49-9153-dbc21607c3d7?lang=en road_go_ia_lgtt] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/074d733f-3ee7-49f5-838f-26fe43c4d5a4?lang=en road_go_cta_gtt])|alt=a table showing the top 20 country-to-country flows in intra-EU road freight transport in 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables === *{{Template:Excel|filename= SE_Road_Trends_2026.xlsx|title=Road freight transport statistics}} === Context=== Data presented in this publication were collected in the framework of [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32012R0070 Regulation (EU) No 70/2012] on statistical returns in respect of the carriage of goods by road (recast). These data are based on sample surveys carried out in the reporting countries, i.e., the EU Member States, Norway and Switzerland, and record the road goods transport undertaken by vehicles registered in these countries. Reporting countries use their own national surveys for the collection of data based on returns from road hauliers. The results are microdata referring to vehicles and their linked journeys, providing detailed information on goods transported. At the European level, common [[Glossary:Aggregation|aggregation]] procedures have been used which may diverge from national practices. Differences might therefore occur between the figures in this publication and national values. For the distinction between national and international transport, journey information is used at the European level, which might cause differences compared with corresponding values from countries that use goods information for these statistics. ===Data sources=== '''Country specific notes''' '''Croatia''': While Croatia had no obligation prior to their accession in 2013, it started to report data for the reference year 2008. '''Malta''': Regulation (EU) No 70/2012 does not apply to Malta, as long as the number of Maltese-registered goods road transport vehicles licensed to engage in international transport does not exceed 400 vehicles. '''Finland''': National and international surveys have been harmonised and follow a common methodology from Q1 2011 onwards, leading to a break in time series in 2011. '''Sweden''': A break in series occurred in 2014 following a change in methodology. On the basis of a specific survey, Sweden corrected the European road freight survey results for trucks participating to the sample which were not in use over the surveyed period. '''Liechtenstein''': Starting with the reference year 2014, Liechtenstein is exempted from the reporting of road freight data. '''Methodological notes''' '''EU totals''' calculated in this publication refer to road freight transport reported by the EU Member States, excluding Malta which is exempted from reporting road freight statistics. '''Total transport''' Total transport includes national transport, international transport of goods loaded in the reporting countries, international transport of goods unloaded in the reporting countries, cross-trade and cabotage transport. '''National transport''' Road transport between two places, a place of loading and a place of unloading, located in the same country by a vehicle registered in that country. It may involve transit through one or more countries. '''International transport, loaded and unloaded''' International transport as presented in this publication is based on goods loaded and unloaded in the reporting Member States. Each reporting country reports all activities of a road motor vehicle inside and outside its national territory. There is thus no risk of double counting at European level. '''Breakdown by goods groups''' Starting with the reference year 2008, {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32007R1304:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1304/2007}} establishes [[Glossary:Standard goods classification for transport statistics (NST)|NST 2007]] as the sole classification for goods carried in road freight transport. For detailed information on the NST 2007 classification, please refer to ‘[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/metadata/classifications Metadata classification]’, Eurostat’s Metadata Server. '''Transport by distance class''' Eurostat disseminates road freight transport according to the following distance classes: less than 50 km; 50-149 km; 150-299 km; 300-499 km; 500-999 km; 1 000-1 999 km; 2 000-5 999 km; over 6 000 km. More detailed data and metadata are available in the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database Eurostat dissemination database]. '''Goods entering a country''' The volume of goods entering a country is the sum of international transport and cross-trade unloaded in the country by hauliers from all reporting countries. '''Goods leaving a country''' The volume of goods leaving a country is the sum of international transport and cross-trade loaded in the country by hauliers from all reporting countries. '''Table 1 vs Table 2''' The dissemination tables providing transport performance (in tkm) with a breakdown by group of goods are derived from basic goods transport operations (goods-related information) whereas dissemination tables without a breakdown by group of goods are derived from journey-related information. This may lead to small differences in the total tkm presented in different dissemination tables. '''Figure 4''' This figure presents volumes moved on the territory of each country if there is loading or unloading of the goods. Transit, where neither loading nor unloading takes place in the country traversed, is not included in this figure. The weight of goods in international transport is accounted for both in the country of loading and in the country of unloading. The weight of goods in national transport is accounted for only once. '''Table 5 and Table 6''' Table 5 and Table 6 are based on Eurostat calculations, drawing on several datasets. Table 5 presents the largest road freight transport flows between EU countries and extra-EU countries, while Table 6 presents the largest flows between different EU countries. In addition, Table 6 provides information on the share of carriers from the two loading/unloading countries and the most important other country. The calculation of each trade flow is based on tonnes of goods loaded/unloaded in a reporting EU country of goods unloaded/loaded in an extra-EU country (Table 5) or another EU country (Table 6) and the corresponding flow in the other direction. In addition, data on cross-trade for each flow is added (i.e. transport carried out for the flow by carriers from other reporting countries). Data on tonnes of goods loaded for each country-to-country flow are taken from the dataset [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e7b480b3-29d4-47ab-b514-25db4f714cb8?lang=en road_go_ia_lgtt], goods unloaded from [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e296982e-51f5-45d9-a318-f5045c8da5c0?lang=en road_go_ia_ugtt], and cross-trade from [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d1779e08-6cbe-4148-9854-74beb867ff72?lang=en road_go_cta_gtt]. ===Other articles=== *[[Transport#Freight transport|All articles on freight transport]] *[[Road_freight_transport_by_journey_characteristics|Road freight transport by journey characteristics]] *[[Road_freight_transport_by_type_of_goods|Road freight transport by type of goods]] *[[Road_freight_transport_by_vehicle_characteristics|Road freight transport by vehicle characteristics]] *[[Road_freight_transport_statistics_-_cabotage|Road freight transport statistics - cabotage]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/database Transport], see: :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=road Road transport (road)] ::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=road_go Road freight transport measurement (road_go)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/database Transport], see: :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=t_road Road transport (t_road)] ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=transport}} Transport] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-057|title=Key figures on European transport — 2025 edition}} - Key figures *{{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-037|title=Eurostat regional yearbook — 2025 edition}} - Flagship publications *{{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-003|title=Key figures on Europe – 2025 edition}} - Key figures ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=road_go_esms|title=Road freight transport measurement}} (ESMS metadata file) *{{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-048|title=Glossary for transport statistics — 6th edition — 2026}} - Manuals and guidelines *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-062|title=Methodologies used in road freight transport surveys in Member States, EFTA and 3 candidate countries — 2025 revised edition}} - Manuals and guidelines *{{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-070|title=Road freight transport methodology — 2025 revised edition}} - Manuals and guidelines ===Legislation=== *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32012R0070:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 70/2012}} of 18 January 2012 on statistical returns in respect of the carriage of goods by road (recast) *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32007R1304:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1304/2007}} of 7 November 2007 amending Directive 95/64, Regulation (EC) No 1172/98, Regulations (EC) No 91/2003 and (EC) No 1365/2006 with respect to the establishment of NST 2007 as the unique classification for transported goods in certain transport modes {{Unit|topic=X_Transport}} [[Category:Transport|Road freight transport statistics]] [[Category:Freight|Road freight transport statistics]] [[Category:Road|Road freight transport statistics]] [[Category:Statistical_article|Road freight transport statistics]] [[Category:July2027|Road freight transport statistics]]

title: Road safety statistics in the EU
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the road safety statistics in the EU. Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: April 2027 In 2024, 19 934 persons were killed in road accidents in the EU, a decrease of 2.2% compared with 2023. In 2024, 78 persons per million inhabitants were killed in road accidents in Romania, the highest rate in the EU. People aged 25 to 49 years old accounted for almost one third of road fatalities in the EU in 2024. |alt= A dynamic line chart showing the road accident fatalities from the year 2014 to the year 2024. This article focuses on the number of [[Glossary:People_killed_in_road_accidents|persons killed in road accidents]] in 2024. The data are extracted from the CARE database (the Community database on road accidents resulting in death or injury). CARE contains detailed data on individual accidents collected by the [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU countries]] from police and hospital sources. This allows for a high level of disaggregation. However, data consolidation takes a considerable amount of time. For Greece, Cyprus, Malta, Portugal and Slovenia, where breakdown data (by age, type of road, sex and mode of transport) are missing for 2024, the distributions were estimated by applying the 2023 percentage shares to the reported 2024 totals. As a result, EU aggregates for these breakdowns combine reported and estimated data. === The number of persons killed in road traffic accidents fell by 17.4% between 2014 and 2024 === In 2003, the [[Glossary:European_Commission|European Commission]] adopted its third [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52010DC0389#:~:text=On%202%20June%202003%2C%20the,of%20infrastructure%20and%20users%27%20safety. European action programme for road safety], which aimed to halve the number of road deaths by 2010. While the initial target was not quite met by the end of 2010, it was decided to continue with the objective of halving the overall number of road deaths in the EU by 2020, using 2010 as the baseline. In 2021, the European Commission introduced the [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/d7ee4b58-4bc5-11ea-8aa5-01aa75ed71a1 EU road safety policy framework 2021-2030] which sets up new interim targets to reduce the number of road deaths by 50% between 2020 and 2030 and forms part of the ‘Vision Zero’ objective - zero fatalities and serious injuries on European roads by 2050. Since 2021, the European Commission has complemented this framework with several initiatives to strengthen road safety, notably through the [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/policies/road-transport/ Road Safety Package] adopted in March 2023. This package includes proposals to revise driving licence rules, improve the cross-border enforcement of traffic offences, and enhance cooperation between EU countries.
Figure 1 The number of persons killed in road traffic accidents has fallen considerably over the last 10 years: the number of fatalities in the EU countries fell by 17.4% between 2014 and 2024. Overall, the trend over this period has been downward, however increases were recorded in certain years, notably in 2015, 2021 and 2022, when fatalities rose by 0.9%, 5.8% and 3.7%, respectively compared with the previous years. However, lockdowns and other mobility restrictions related to the COVID-19 pandemic across Europe may have had an impact on the number of fatalities in 2020 (-17.3% compared to 2019), as traffic levels were significantly reduced during this period. The target of halving the number of fatalities in 2020 compared with 2010 was not met, despite traffic being significantly reduced in 2020 (-36.4%, from 29 611 to 18 838). === In 2024, 78 persons per million inhabitants were killed in road accidents in Romania, the highest in the EU === Figure 2 presents the number of persons killed in road accidents in 2024 per million inhabitants. Overall, the rate of road fatalities in the EU was 44 per million inhabitants in 2024. There are considerable differences between EU countries, as well as between EFTA countries. Sweden, Malta, Denmark and Luxembourg reported the lowest numbers, with 20, 21, 24 and 27 fatalities per million inhabitants, respectively. In contrast, Romania reported the highest rate with 78 fatalities per million inhabitants.
Figure 2 Among the EU countries, 10 recorded 50 fatalities or more per million inhabitants, namely Romania, Bulgaria, Greece, Croatia, Latvia, Portugal, Hungary, Poland, Italy and Estonia, listed in descending order from the highest to the lowest. These countries may need to prioritize road safety measures to reduce the number and severity of accidents. Three EFTA countries, Norway, Switzerland and Iceland reported relatively low rates of 16, 28 and 34 persons killed in road accidents per million inhabitants in 2024, respectively. Liechtenstein recorded 75 road fatalities per million inhabitants in 2024. However, this high rate is due to its small population size and corresponds to only 3 fatalities. Figure 3 shows that within the EU, Malta had the lowest number of persons killed in road accidents in 2014, 2023 and 2024, with only 10, 16 and 12 fatalities, respectively. Meanwhile, Italy recorded the highest number of fatalities in 2014 (3 381 persons killed), while France recorded the highest numbers in 2023 (3 154) and 2024 (3 181). In 2024, 3 EU countries registered more than 2 000 fatalities: Germany, France and Italy, compared with 4 countries in 2014: Germany, France, Italy and Poland. Five countries registered less than 100 fatalities in 2024: Estonia, Cyprus, Luxembourg, Malta and Slovenia. Among the EFTA countries, Switzerland registered the highest number of fatalities in all 3 of these reference years.
Figure 3 All EU countries registered a decrease in the number of persons killed in road accidents between 2014 and 2024, except for 3: Spain, Malta and the Netherlands. Compared with 2023, 6 EU countries saw an increase in the number of fatalities. France, with 27 more fatalities in 2024, registered the largest increase in absolute terms. Twenty-one EU countries registered a decrease, especially Germany, which registered 69 fewer fatalities in 2024 compared with 2023. === Men accounted for around three quarters of road accident fatalities between 2014 and 2024 === Figure 4 highlights the evolution of road accident fatalities over the years, broken down by sex. Comparing 2014 with 2024, there has been a 12.6% decrease in male fatalities and a 18.4% decrease in female fatalities.
Figure 4 Over the period 2014-2016, the number of road accident fatalities for males and females remained approximately at the same level (considering a distribution of fatalities by sex of the Unknown category). From 2017 to 2019, fatalities for both males and females showed a gradual decline. Male fatalities decreased from 17 802 in 2017 to 17 509 in 2019 (-1.6%), while female fatalities fell from 5 562 to 5 199 (-6.5%). This downward trend was interrupted in 2020, when fatalities dropped markedly due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the associated reduction in traffic levels. In that year, male fatalities fell to 14 674 (-16.2% compared with 2019), while female fatalities decreased to 4 124 (-20.7% compared with 2019). In the following years, fatalities increased again in 2021 and 2022, reaching 15 932 for males and 4 680 for females in 2022. A slight decline was then observed in 2023, followed by a further decrease in 2024, when fatalities fell to 15 332 for males and 4 552 for females. Over the whole 2016-2024 period, the distribution of fatalities by sex remained relatively stable. Males consistently accounted for around three quarters of all fatalities (ranging from 75.8% in 2016 to 77.9% in 2020 and 2021), while females represented around 23%. [[Image: Road accident fatalities by sex, 2019, 2024 (number).png|thumb|center|700px|Table 1: Road accident fatalities by sex, EU, 2019, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9f4722de-074d-446b-843d-6ebc21ecea1b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-14T10:01:04Z tran_sf_roadus])|alt= a table showing Road accident fatalities by sex in the years 2019 and 2024 in the EU, EU countries, EFTA countries and Serbia. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Among the EU countries and the EFTA countries, Poland, Lithuania and Slovenia registered the largest decreases in persons killed in road accidents between 2019 and 2024, with decreases of 34.8% for Poland and 33.3% for both Lithuania and Slovenia. Only 5 countries registered an increase over this period: Estonia, Iceland, Ireland, Spain, and Switzerland with increases ranging from 1.7% to 116.7%. In terms of male fatalities, 3 EU countries recorded increases over this period: Estonia (+48.6%), Ireland (+21.0%) and Spain (+3.0%). Among the 9 EU countries that recorded a decrease of 20% or more in male fatalities, the largest reductions were observed in Slovenia (-36.1%) and Poland (-35.9%). As regards female fatalities, 5 EU countries registered an increase: Ireland, Greece, Latvia, the Netherlands and Sweden, ranging from 0.6% to 25.7%. By contrast, 6 countries recorded decreases of 30% or more, with the largest reductions observed in Malta (-60.0%), Lithuania (-52.1%), and Luxembourg (-50.0%). When looking at EFTA countries, between 2019 and 2024, Switzerland recorded increases in fatalities for both males (+35.3%) and females (+29.2%). Iceland also showed large increases. However, these should be interpreted with caution due to the low absolute number of fatalities. By contrast, Norway recorded decreases over the same period for both males (-15.4%) and females (-30.0%). In Finland, Greece, Italy, Lithuania, Luxembourg and Malta, males accounted for more than 80% of the fatalities in 2024. Concerning females, Iceland and the Netherlands, were the only countries where women made up more than 30% of the fatalities (30.2% and 30.8% respectively). With respect to the total number of fatalities, only 3 EU countries registered more than 2 000 fatalities in 2024: France, Germany and Italy. These countries accounted for almost half (45.1%) of all fatalities in the EU. === In 2024, people aged 25-49 accounted for almost one third of road fatalities in the EU === Figure 5 shows that people aged from 25 to 49 years accounted for the highest share of fatalities, representing 31.1% of reported deaths in 2024. This age group is followed by those aged 65 years or over, with 30.7% of fatalities. Together, these 2 groups represented just over 60% of all road accident fatalities in the EU.
Figure 5 The age group between 50 and 64 years accounted for 21.4% of the total fatalities, while individuals aged 18 to 24 years made up 12.1%. Among younger age groups, the age group 15 to 17 years old represented 2.3% of the total fatalities, and those less than 15 years old accounted for 1.9%. [[Image: Road accident fatalities by age, 2024 (percentage shares)_v1.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 2: Road accident fatalities by age, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ac940c47-5ca5-4389-a4c0-285f1d2416c7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-14T13:32:39Z tran_sf_roadus])|alt=a table showing Road accident fatalities by age in the year 2024 in the EU, EU Member States, EFTA countries and Serbia. The columns show the different age categories. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 2 shows that in majority of EU countries, people aged less than 18 years old accounted for less than 10% of the fatalities in 2024, with the exception of Malta (12.5%), Finland (11.6%) and Estonia (10.1%). The age group 65 years old and older recorded the largest number of fatalities in 10 EU countries, 1 EFTA country, and 1 candidate country: Sweden (45.1%), the Netherlands (41.3%), Switzerland (40.4%), Germany (39.7%), Denmark (37.9%), Slovenia (37.8%), Austria (33.9%), Romania (32.3%), Bulgaria (32.0%), Italy (31.0%), Finland (30.4%) and Serbia (29.8%). Among the age group from 18 to 24, Iceland registered the highest share of fatalities, at 23.1%. Cyprus, Luxembourg and Iceland were the only countries where no fatalities were recorded among people aged under 18. === Passengers and drivers of passenger cars accounted for 43.6% of persons killed in 2024, while pedestrians accounted for 17.8% === Drivers and passengers of passenger cars represented the largest category of road traffic deaths in the EU in 2024, with 43.6% of all road traffic fatalities (see Figure 6). Motorcyclists and their passengers (18.5%) was the largest category, followed by pedestrians (17.8%) Cyclists and e-bike riders (motorized cyclists) together accounted for 9.9% of EU road deaths in 2024. It should be noted that cycling deaths are likely to be under-reported as some accidents involving cyclists are not reported to the police. The remaining vehicle categories together accounted for 10.2% of road accident fatalities in the EU in 2024: these include persons killed in accidents involving light- and heavy-goods vehicles, buses and coaches, mopeds and ‘other’ vehicles (agricultural tractors and other motorised vehicles).
Figure 6 In countries where cycling is widespread, such as the Netherlands, it is unsurprising that cyclists account for a larger share of fatalities than in countries where cycling is less common. Table 3 shows that cyclists accounted for 27.0% of all road accident deaths in the Netherlands in 2024, followed by Belgium with 17.9%. It should be noted that there were no road accident deaths involving cyclists were recorded in Luxembourg, Iceland and Malta. [[Image: Road accident fatalities by mode of transport, 2024 (percentage shares)_v1.png|thumb|center|700px|Table 3: Road accident fatalities by mode of transport, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/841afa45-b2fb-432b-856a-1d7a2e2f297e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-14T14:28:02Z tran_sf_roadve])|alt= a table showing road accident fatalities by mode of transport in the year 2024 in the EU, EU Member States, EFTA countries and Serbia. The columns show the different modes of transport. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Luxembourg (50.0%), Greece and Malta (both over 30.0%) had the highest shares of motorcyclists among road fatalities in the EU, ahead of Croatia (28.0%) and Italy (27.4%). The remaining ‘two-wheeled’ category – mopeds – accounted for 6.9% of all road accident fatalities in Denmark, well above the next highest country (the Netherlands with 4.8%). In 2024, the number of pedestrians killed in road accidents remained relatively high: 3 558 pedestrians were killed in the EU, accounting for 17.8% of all fatalities. However, this share varies considerably between EU countries, from 9.7% in the Netherlands to 43.8% in Malta. The share was also around 30% in Romania (32.6%), Latvia (30.4%) and Lithuania (28.2%). === Rural roads accounted for 53.3% of the fatalities in 2024, while urban roads accounted for 38.2% === The road accident fatalities in the EU have also been classified based on the type of road where the accidents occurred. Rural roads accounted for the highest number of fatalities, with 10 619 cases (53.3% of the total), followed by urban roads with 7 618 fatalities (38.2%). Motorways recorded the lowest number of fatalities at 1 691 (8.5%), while fatalities where the road type was unknown were negligible (7 fatalities). Among the EU countries, EFTA and candidate countries, 20 countries recorded 50% or more fatalities on rural roads. The highest shares were registered in Malta (100.0%), Iceland (92.3%), Finland (72.9%), Estonia (72.5%), Luxembourg (72.2%) and Sweden (68.1%).
Figure 7 Shares below 40% of total fatalities for rural roads were recorded in 5 EU countries: Portugal and Slovenia (both over 35%), Croatia (35.1%), Romania (33.4%) and Cyprus (29.4%). Only 8 countries registered shares above 10% of fatalities on motorways, with the highest share in Cyprus (23.5%). No fatalities were registered on motorways in 6 countries (Estonia, Latvia, Malta, Sweden, Iceland and Norway). The final category, representing the shares of fatalities on urban roads, shows considerable variations between the reporting countries, with shares ranging from 0% in Malta to 64.1% in Romania. === Drivers accounted for at least 61.2% of the fatalities over the period from 2014 to 2024 === Among the different types of road users, drivers consistently accounted for the highest number of fatalities in the EU each year (ranging between 61.2% and 67.6%). In 2014, there were 14 775 fatalities among drivers, decreasing to 13 478 in 2024.
Figure 8 Pedestrians recorded the second-highest number of fatalities, with 5 142 in 2014 (21.3% of all fatalities), declining to 3 558 in 2024 (17.8%). Passengers recorded the third-highest number of fatalities, starting at 3 893 in 2014 (16.1% of all fatalities), and decreasing to 2 892 fatalities in 2024 (14.5%).
Figure 9 Drivers accounted for more than 50% of deaths on roads in all reporting countries with the exception of Latvia (47.3%), Romania (46.6%) and Malta (43.8%). Luxembourg and Norway were the only countries which registered more than 80% of fatalities in this category, at 83.3% and 81.6%, respectively. Passengers represented less than 20% of the fatalities recorded in 24 EU countries, 2 EFTA countries, and Serbia, with the smallest shares registered in Luxembourg (no fatalities), Switzerland (8.0%), Belgium (10.0%) and the Netherlands (10.8%). In 3 EU countries, more than 20% of total fatalities were passengers: Romania (20.8%), Slovenia (20.7%) and Latvia (20.5%). Pedestrians accounted for more than 40% of fatalities in Malta (43.8%) and more than 30% in Romania (32.6%) and Latvia (30.4%). At the other end of the scale, pedestrians represented only 9.7% of fatalities in the Netherlands and 13.3% in Finland. === 6 Austrian regions recorded more than 4 000 accidents per million inhabitants === Map 1 presents the number of accidents by NUTS 2 regions and includes only the accidents with at least one casualty (a person injured or killed). Among the regions (at NUTS 2 level) with the highest number of accidents per million inhabitants in 2024 were Liguria (ITC3) in Italy, Salzburg (AT32) and Tirol (AT33) in Austria. These regions recorded 5 275, 5 269 and 5 148 accidents per million inhabitants, respectively. These figures were considerably higher than those observed in other regions. Other regions with notable accident rates include Ciudad de Melilla (ES64) in Spain, Vorarlberg (AT34), Kärnten (AT21), Steiermark (AT22), Oberösterreich (AT31) and Niederösterreich (AT12) in Austria, Schleswig-Holstein (DEF), Hamburg (DE6) and Niedersachsen (DE9) in Germany (data at NUTS 2 level not available) and Toscana (ITI1) in Italy, all recording more than 4 000 accidents per million inhabitants. [[Image: Road accidents by NUTS2 regions, 2024 (number per million inhabitants).png|thumb|center|700px|Map 1: Road accidents by NUTS 2 regions, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f253dfec-03ad-4963-b61e-958f89a4cb17?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-15T08:40:12Z tran_sf_roadnu])|alt= a map showing Road accidents by NUTS 2 regions in the year 2024. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] By contrast, regions with low numbers of accidents per million inhabitants included Dytiki Makedonia (EL53) with 188 accidents per million inhabitants, Kriti (EL43) with 268 and Thessalia (EL61) with 292, all in Greece. These regions recorded relatively lower numbers of accidents compared with other regions. In total, 70 EU NUTS 2 regions (out of 211 – NUTS 1 regions for Germany and Portugal) recorded less than 1 000 accidents per million inhabitants.
Figure 10 Among the 20 NUTS 1 regions with the largest numbers of accidents in 2024, 6 were in Germany, 4 in Italy, 3 in Spain and 1 each in Belgium, Czechia, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Austria and France. Nordrhein-Westfalen (DEA) was the only NUTS 1 region where more than 60 000 accidents were recorded in 2024 (62 741). Eight regions in this list registered less than 20 000 accidents, with Berlin (DE3) registering 13 791 accidents in 2024 and ranking 20th in the list. Among the top 20 NUTS 1 regions, 11 recorded an increase in the number of accidents between 2022 and 2024, with the highest increase observed in Sud (ITF) in Italy (+14.2%). By contrast, Ile-de-France (FR1) in France recorded the largest decrease (-6.1%). === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media: Road_safety_statistics_in_the_EU_2024_v1.xlsx|Road safety statistics in the EU, 2024 – Tables and Figures]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== The data presented in this article come from the Community database on road accidents resulting in death or injury (CARE) database. EU countries have long collected road accident data via their own national systems. EU-wide road accident data have been available via CARE since 1991. The purpose of CARE is to provide a tool that makes it possible to identify and quantify road safety problems throughout Europe, evaluate the efficiency of road safety measures, determine the relevance of EU action and facilitate the exchange of experience in this field. Parts of the national data sets have been incorporated into the CARE database with their original national structure and definitions. However, as existing national accident data collection systems are not always compatible or comparable between countries, the European Commission provides and applies transformation rules for the national data sets, allowing CARE to provide compatible data. Eurostat’s reference database uses CARE data in a number of tables linked to road safety. Various tables are available. It is possible that the two sources differ, as there are regular data updates and updating is not synchronised. Data in this article are limited to the number of persons fatally injured, resulting in death within 30 days of the road accident. Confirmed suicides and natural deaths are not included. Since 2010, all reporting countries apply this rule. Please note that data referring to the French Départements d’Outre-Mer (overseas territories) and the Portuguese autonomous regions of Açores and Madeira are not available. The ‘fatalities per million inhabitants’ ratio takes this into account. For countries with missing breakdowns (by age, type of road, sex and mode of transport) in 2024, the distributions were estimated by applying the percentage shares observed in 2023 to the 2024 total values reported by these countries. As a result, the EU aggregates for these breakdowns combine reported 2024 data with estimated values. The countries concerned are Greece, Cyprus, Malta, Portugal and Slovenia. ===Context=== In response to the growing concern among European citizens over road safety, the European Union made this issue a priority of its common transport policy set out in the 2001 [https://transport.ec.europa.eu/white-paper-european-transport-policy-2010-time-decide_en White Paper on transport: ''European transport policy for 2010: time to decide''] and its mid-term review in 2006 (''Keep Europe moving — Sustainable mobility for our continent''). In the White Paper, the European Commission set the target of halving the number of road fatalities between 2000 and 2010. A variety of measures helped to cut the total road number of deaths by 44% between 2000 and 2010. The target of halving the 2000 number was reached in 2012. Following on from that, the 2011 White Paper [https://transport.ec.europa.eu/white-paper-2011_en Roadmap to a Single European Transport Area — Towards a competitive and resource efficient transport system] set out 40 practical measures for the next decade. On road traffic, the Commission adopted an ambitious road safety programme that aimed to cut road deaths in Europe in half between 2010 and 2020.
