The bars show the years.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:SDG 12 - 2026 edition.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Context === ''' Consumption patterns and green economy ''' The [https://ec.europa.eu/environment/strategy/environment-action-programme-2030_en 8th Environment Action Programme (EAP)] aims to accelerate the transition to a climate-neutral, resource-efficient and regenerative economy. The Green transition pillar of the [https://commission.europa.eu/business-economy-euro/economic-recovery/recovery-and-resilience-facility_en#the-recovery-and-resilience-facility Recovery and Resilience Facility] supports reforms and investments to boost sustainable consumption and production patterns, for example in the areas of sustainable mobility and the circular economy. The 2020 [https://ec.europa.eu/growth/industry/strategy_en EU industrial strategy] and its 2021 update aim to help Europe’s industry lead the twin transitions towards climate neutrality and digital leadership. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52023DC0062&qid=1677776953226 Green Deal Industrial Plan] aims to enhance the competitiveness of Europe’s net-zero industry and support the fast transition to climate neutrality. The 2025 [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/eu-competitiveness/competitiveness-compass_en Competitive Compass] and the [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/eu-competitiveness/clean-industrial-deal_en Clean Industrial Deal] aim to improve competitiveness and support decarbonisation. The 2025 [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_25_635 Automotive Industrial Action Plan] will support the automotive industry's transition to guarantee competitiveness and maintain a strong European production base. EU legislation sets mandatory [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02019R0631-20250101 CO2 emission targets for cars and vans]. The [https://ec.europa.eu/environment/strategy/chemicals-strategy_en Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability] aims to improve the protection of the environment and people’s health from risks posed by chemicals and to support innovation for safe and sustainable chemicals. It includes the [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/chemicals/reach/reach_en.htm REACH] Regulation and the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2008/1272/oj CLP Regulation] on the classification, labelling and packaging of chemical substances and mixtures. The 2021 [https://ec.europa.eu/environment/strategy/zero-pollution-action-plan_en Zero Pollution Action Plan] calls for air, water and soil pollution to be reduced to levels no longer considered harmful to health and ecosystems, respecting planetary boundaries and creating a toxic-free environment. In 2022 the Commission adopted a [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_22_6278 Zero Pollution package] proposing stricter rules for cleaner air and water, including a [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52023PC0416&%3Bqid=1706624227744 soil monitoring law]. '''Waste generation and management''' The [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/waste-and-recycling/waste-framework-directive_en Waste Framework Directive] establishes targets for the EU to prepare to re-use and recycle 60% of municipal waste by weight by 2030 and 65% by 2035. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32025L1892&qid=1760531838376 Revision of the Directive] in 2025 introduced food waste reduction targets of 10% in food processing and manufacturing and of 30% in retail and consumption by 2030. It also introduced mandatory Extended Producer Responsibility schemes for textiles to make producers responsible for the full life cycle of textiles products. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0085 Clean Industrial Deal] from 2025 aims to increase the EU’s circular material use rate to 24% by 2030. The 2025 First [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_25_3151 Circular Economy Package] harmonises rules for secondary plastics materials across the single market. Building on the Action Plan, the planned Circular Economy Act will establish a Single Market for secondary raw materials. It aims to increase the supply of high-quality recycled materials, especially electronics and critical minerals and stimulate demand for these recycled materials within the EU. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2021:801:FIN Council Recommendation on ensuring a fair transition towards climate neutrality] calls for facilitating access to sustainable consumption, especially for people and households in vulnerable situations. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/904/oj Single-Use Plastics Directive] and the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/40/oj Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation] establish targets for a minimum percentage of recycled content. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Sustainable development goals|All articles on sustainable development goals]] *[[Circular economy - material flows|Circular economy - material flows]] *[[Waste statistics|Waste statistics]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/database Sustainable development indicators] ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=sdi}} Sustainable development indicators] ===Methodology=== More detailed information on EU SDG indicators for monitoring of progress towards the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), such as indicator relevance, definitions, methodological notes, background and potential linkages can be found in the [[SDG - Introduction|introduction]] as well as in Annex II of the publication {{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-064|title=’Sustainable development in the European Union — Monitoring report on progress towards the SDGs in an EU context — 2026 edition’}}. ===Publications=== '''Further reading on responsible consumption and production''' *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/preventing-waste-in-europe-progress-and-challenges-with-a-focus-on-food-waste EEA (2025), Preventing waste in Europe - Progress and challenges, with a focus on food waste.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/accelerating-the-circular-economy EEA (2024), Accelerating the circular economy in Europe: State and outlook 2024.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/capturing-the-climate-change-mitigation EEA (2024), Capturing the climate change mitigation benefits of circular economy and waste sector policies and measures.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/topics/in-depth/production-and-consumption?activeAccordion=4268d9b2-6e3b-409b-8b2a-b624c120090d EEA (2024), From data to decisions: material footprints in European policy making.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/many-eu-member-states EEA (2023), Many EU Member States not on track to meet recycling targets for municipal waste and packaging waste.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/pathways-towards-circular-plastics-in/ EEA (2023), Pathways to circular plastics in Europe: Good examples from countries, business and citizens.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/the-european-biomass-puzzle EEA (2023), The European biomass puzzle: Challenges, opportunities and trade-offs around biomass production and use in the EU.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/soer-2020/chapter-09_soer2020-waste-and-resources/view EEA (2019), The European environment — state and outlook 2020. From Legacies to Innovative Solutions: Implementing the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.] ===External links=== '''Further data sources on responsible consumption and production''' *[https://rmis.jrc.ec.europa.eu/ European Commission, Raw Materials Information System (RMIS).] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/explore/all/envir?lang=en&subtheme=env.env_mrp&display=list&sort=category Eurostat, Material flows and resource productivity.] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/circular-economy/monitoring-framework Eurostat, Monitoring Framework for the Circular Economy.] *[https://www.materialflows.net/ Materialflows.net – The Material Flow Analysis Portal]. *[https://www.resourcepanel.org/global-material-flows-database UNEP/IRP, Global Material Flows Database.] === Footnotes === {{Unit|topic=X_Sustainable_development_indicators}} [[Category:EU policy indicators|SDG 12 - Responsible consumption and production]] [[Category:Sustainable development|SDG 12 - Responsible consumption and production]] [[Category:Energy consumption|SDG 12 - Responsible consumption and production]] [[Category:Statistical article|SDG 12 - Responsible consumption and production]] [[Category:Sustainable_development_goals|SDG 12 - Responsible consumption and production]]

title: SDG 11 - Sustainable cities and communities
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of SDG 11 - Sustainable cities and communities. ==Make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable==
Data extracted in April 2026. Planned article update: June 2027. [[Image: SDG 11 tachometer 2026.png|EU trend of SDG 11 on sustainable cities and communities|thumb|center|400px|alt= Goal-level assessment of SDG 11 on Sustainable Cities and Communities showing the EU has made moderate progress during the short-term period.]] This article is a part of a [[Sustainable development in the European Union|set of statistical articles]], which are based on the [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publication {{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-064|title=’Sustainable development in the European Union — Monitoring report on progress towards the SDGs in an EU context — 2026 edition’}}. This report is the tenth edition of Eurostat’s series of monitoring reports on sustainable development, which provide a quantitative assessment of progress of the EU towards the SDGs in an EU context.
SDG 11 aims to renew and plan cities and other human settlements in a way that offers opportunities for all, with access to basic services, energy, housing, transport, waste management, clean air and green public spaces, while reducing resource use and environmental impact.
===Sustainable cities and communities in the EU: overview and key trends=== Three-quarters of the EU population live in urban areas — cities, towns and suburbs — with about 39% residing in cities alone 2024 data. Source: Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d82abad5-c2a0-4fe4-8825-3f12dab8cb18?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-16T10:47:20Z ilc_lvho01]).. With the share of Europe’s urban population projected to rise to more than 80% by 2050  United Nations (2025), [https://www.un.org/development/desa/pd/sites/www.un.org.development.desa.pd/files/undesa_pd_2025_wup2025_summary_of_results.pdf World Urbanization Prospects 2025: Summary of Results], UN DESA/POP/2025/TR/NO. 12. New York: United Nations., it will become increasingly important for cities, towns and suburbs to become more sustainable. Monitoring SDG 11 in an EU context means looking at trends in the quality of life in cities and communities, sustainable mobility and adverse environmental impacts. Overall, the EU has made moderate progress towards SDG 11 over the assessed short-term period. Strong progress has been made towards increasing the quality of life in cities and communities, including in the areas of housing, air quality and safety. Trends in sustainable mobility and regarding impacts on the environment have been mixed. Road traffic deaths and the recycling rate of municipal waste have not improved fast enough to meet their respective 2030 targets, the share of buses and trains in passenger transport has been stagnating, and soil sealing has increased further. At the same time, the share of the population connected to at least secondary wastewater treatment has increased slowly over the past five years. Image: Indicators_measuring_progress_in_SDG_11_2026.png|'''Table 1: Indicators measuring progress towards SDG 11, EU'''|alt=A table showing the indicators measuring progress towards SDG 11 in the EU. Image:Explanation_of_symbols_for_indicating_progress_2026.png|'''Table 2: Explanation of symbols for indicating progress towards SD objectives and targets'''|alt=A table showing the Explanation of symbols for indicating progress towards sustainability objectives and targets. ===Quality of life in cities and communities=== While European cities and communities provide opportunities for employment and other economic and cultural activities, many inhabitants still face considerable social challenges and inequalities. Problems affecting the quality of housing and the wider residential area, such as noise disturbance, crime and vandalism, are some of the most visible challenges that cities and communities can face and which impact quality of life. ''' Quality of housing in the EU has been improving since 2010, but affordability and vulnerability challenges persist ''' Safe and adequate homes are a foundation for living an independent, healthy and fulfilling life. Poor housing conditions, on the other hand, are associated with lower life chances, health inequalities and increased risks of poverty and environmental hazards. The severe housing deprivation rate refers to the share of the total population living in an [[Glossary:Overcrowding_rate|overcrowded]] household while also experiencing types of housing deprivation such as a leaking roof, damp walls, floors or foundations; rot in window frames or floors; lack of sanitary facilities; or a [[Glossary:Dwelling|dwelling]] that is considered too dark. Between 2010 and 2023, the share of EU residents who lived in such conditions fell by 2.1 percentage points, indicating a significant improvement in the perceived quality of EU housing stock. In 2023, 4.0% of the EU population faced severe housing deprivation, compared with 4.3% in 2018 and 6.1% in 2010. Despite these improvements, the housing situation remains precarious for many vulnerable groups, such as people living in low-income households or people with disabilities  European Commission (2025), [https://housing.ec.europa.eu/document/download/2ad4c9f2-602b-43ba-9ed9-ef2ee059cf97_en?filename=0_1.pdf Understanding the housing crisis], SWD(2025) 1053/2, Brussels, p. 133.. At the same time, the EU is facing a growing housing affordability crisis, with house prices rising faster than household incomes. Across the EU, house prices increased by 62% between 2015 and 2025, with some countries experiencing much higher changes. For example, house prices more than tripled in Hungary over this period, while they more than doubled in 11 further countries  Source: Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/73cceaf1-38d0-43c4-9eaa-642f0b321aa7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-27T11:12:52Z prc_hpi_a]).. Rising housing scarcity and declining affordability risk offsetting the gains made in housing quality, with negative implications for health, well-being and future prospects disproportionally affecting vulnerable population groups. '''Perceived safety in residential areas has continued to improve, but noise disturbance levels have stagnated''' Noise disturbance can cause annoyance, stress, sleep deprivation, poor mental health and well-being, as well as harm to the cardiovascular and metabolic system  European Environment Agency (2025), [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/exposure-of-europe-population-to-noise Exposure of Europe’s population to environmental noise].. Likewise, crime and vandalism can also reduce quality of life and housing satisfaction in a residential area. In 2023, 18.1% of the EU population (more than 81 million people) said their household suffered from noise disturbance  Figures on noise disturbance presented here include noise from different sources than those covered by the [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/noise/directive_en.htm Environmental Noise Directive].. While this constitutes a long-term improvement of 2.5 percentage points since 2010, the rate has been stagnating since 2018, only improving by 0.1 percentage points. At the same time, 10.0% of the EU population perceived there had been crime, violence and vandalism in their neighbourhoods in 2023, showing an improvement from 13.1% in 2010. Most of this improvement has occurred since 2013, when the indicator had peaked at 14.1%. The EU’s [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52021DC0400&qid=1623311742827 zero pollution action plan] aims to reduce the share of people chronically disturbed by transport noise by 30% by 2030 compared with 2017. The [https://www.who.int/europe/publications/i/item/9789289053563 WHO guidelines for Europe] recommend that the noise level from road traffic should be below 53 decibels (dB) during the day and below 45 dB at night. While railways and airports represent further significant sources of local noise pollution, their impact on the overall population is much lower. According to European Environment Agency (EEA) estimates on the [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/exposure-of-europe-population-to-noise exposure of Europe’s population to environmental noise], more than 20% of people are exposed to long-term unhealthy levels of transport noise. This figure increases to 30% when considering the more stringent WHO regulations. According to the [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/zero-pollution-monitoring-and-outlook-report Zero pollution monitoring and outlook 2025] report, the EU is unlikely to meet its 2030 target for reducing the number of people chronically disturbed by transport noise by 30%. Its most optimistic scenario estimates a 23% reduction, while its conservative scenario estimates only a 2% decline by 2030. ''' The EU achieved its target of reducing the number of premature death due to PM2.5 exposure in 2023''' Pollutants such as fine [[Glossary:Particulate_matter_-_environment|particulate matter]] (PM2.5) suspended in the air reduce people’s life expectancy and can lead to or aggravate many chronic and acute respiratory and cardiovascular diseases  WHO (‎2021), [https://apps.who.int/iris/handle/10665/345329 WHO global air quality guidelines: particulate matter (‎PM2.5 and PM10)‎, ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide], World Health Organization; European Environment Agency (2023), [https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/harm-to-human-health-from-air-pollution/harm-to-human-health-from Harm to human health from air pollution in Europe: burden of disease 2023], Briefing no. 23/2023.. Exposure to air pollution is of particular concern in cities because the concentration of economic activities and high population densities mean there are many potential emission sources and many people are affected. The EU has successfully managed to reduce fine particulate matter emissions from sources such as residential heating and road transport. As a result, the number of people dying prematurely due to PM2.5 exposure fell by 57% between 2005 and 2023, meaning the EU has met its 2030 target from the zero pollution action plan (a 55% reduction). The downward trend has also continued in the short term, with the number falling by 36% between 2018 and 2023. Nevertheless, in 2023 exposure to fine particulate matter was still responsible for around 182 400 premature deaths. Almost all EU Member States reduced the number of premature deaths attributable to PM2.5 exposure between 2018 and 2023. The biggest declines were observed in Finland (93%), Estonia (80%) and Sweden (77%). In order to reduce exposure to PM2.5and the related premature deaths, the revised [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202402881 Ambient Air Quality Directive] set an annual limit of PM2.5 concentrations of 10 micrograms per cubic metre (μg/m3), to be achieved by 2030  For more information on EU air quality standards see: [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/air/quality/standards.htm http://ec.europa.eu/environment/air/quality/standards.htm].. According to data from the European Environment Agency (EEA), only six EU Member States (Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Luxembourg, Portugal and Sweden) recorded annual PM2.5 concentrations below this limit in 2024 in all their measuring stations. The higher PM2.5 concentrations in central and eastern Europe are mainly due to solid fuel use and an older vehicle fleet  European Environment Agency (2024), [https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/europes-air-quality-status-2024 Europe’s air quality status 2024].. When considering the more stringent WHO air quality guideline of 5 μg/m3, all EU Member States, except for Estonia, reported annual concentration levels that exceeded the limit in at least one or more measuring stations. Additionally, [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/exceedance-of-air-quality-standards EEA estimates] suggest that most of the EU’s population was exposed to key air pollutants above the WHO guideline levels, especially in urban areas. Almost all EU city dwellers (94%) were exposed to PM2.5 concentrations above the WHO guideline level of 5 μg/m3 in 2023. ''' Urban residents in the EU remain the group most affected by noise pollution, crime and high housing costs ''' Statistics on the [[Glossary:Degree_of_urbanisation|degree of urbanisation]] provide an analytical and descriptive lens through which to view urban and rural communities. Eurostat differentiates between three types of area — ‘cities’, ‘towns and suburbs’ and ‘rural areas’ — based on the share of the local population living in urban centres and clusters. In 2023, the perceived occurrence of crime and vandalism in cities (15.3%) was more than three times higher than in rural areas (4.8%) and almost two times higher than the level observed in towns and suburbs (7.8%)  Source: Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4c69d41b-7f16-43c9-87b3-b65e69be0e70?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-16T13:57:43Z ilc_mddw06]).. The perceived level of noise pollution also varies greatly depending on the degree of urbanisation. People living in EU cities were more likely to report noise from neighbours or from the street (24.2%) compared with those living in towns and suburbs (16.9%) or in rural areas (10.5%)  Source: Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cd514953-7516-40ea-bbae-da2994d353d8?lang=en ilc_mddw04]).. People living in cities also faced more problems with their dwelling, with a severe housing deprivation rate of 4.9%, compared with rural areas (3.5%) and towns and suburbs (3.2%)  Source: Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0f2ac789-1721-49c7-9bad-a0af97b48641?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-16T14:05:12Z ilc_mdho06d]).. In addition, city dwellers are more affected by the [[Glossary:Housing_cost_overburden_rate|housing cost overburden rate]], which is defined as the share of the population living in households where the total housing costs (net of housing allowances) represent more than 40% of the total disposable household income. In 2024, 9.8% of the population in cities was overburdened by housing costs, compared with 7.8% in towns and suburbs and 6.3% in rural areas. The situation in cities has improved by 2.0 percentage points since 2019. City dwellers in Greece and Denmark were the most affected, with housing cost overburden rates of 29.1% and 22.7% in 2024, respectively  Source: Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d2c67cb5-ef84-477d-8688-a6c5268e0b0c?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-27T10:46:18Z ilc_lvho07d]).. Moreover, the average housing cost overburden rate hides the potential problem of households living in unsatisfactory conditions but not moving because of high prices both on the rental and real estate markets  European Commission (2025), [https://housing.ec.europa.eu/document/download/2ad4c9f2-602b-43ba-9ed9-ef2ee059cf97_en?filename=0_1.pdf Understanding the housing crisis], SWD(2025) 1053/2, Brussels, p. 48.. ===Sustainable mobility=== A functioning transport system is necessary for people to reach their places of work, education, services and social activities, all of which affect quality of life and equal opportunities for everyone. In addition to availability, the accessibility, affordability, quality and safety of transport systems are also crucial when designing sustainable and inclusive cities and communities. ''' Use of public transport modes improved in 2023 but remained below the pre-pandemic level ''' The EU aims to improve citizens’ quality of life and strengthen the economy by promoting sustainable urban mobility and greater use of clean and energy-efficient vehicles, together with reducing the demand for individual car transport. Public transport networks help to relieve traffic jams, reduce harmful pollution and offer more affordable and sustainable ways to commute to work, access services and travel for leisure. Since 2000, the share of buses and trains in inland passenger transport has stagnated well below 20%, accounting for only 16.9% of passenger-kilometres (pkm) in 2023. The total pkm travelled via these two modes increased by 3.6% between 2000 and 2023, while the pkm travelled by cars grew by 16.7%  European Commission (2025), [https://op.europa.eu/publication-detail/-/publication/52c07e98-a3f4-11f0-97c8-01aa75ed71a1 EU transport in figures — Statistical pocketbook 2025], pp. 48.. The onset of the pandemic in 2020 drastically hit public transport modes, with the share of buses and trains falling by 4.4 percentage points compared with 2019, to 12.8%. The precautionary measures put in place, including domestic and international travel restrictions, quarantine restrictions, introduction of remote-working policies and changing mobility habits had led to a reduction in the use of public transport  Lozzi, G., Ramos, C., Cré, I. (2022), [https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2861/813286 Research for TRAN Committee – Relaunching transport and tourism in the EU after COVID-19 – Part VI: Public Transport], European Parliament, Policy Department for Structural and Cohesion Policies, Brussels. and passengers’ perceptions about safety and comfort. The increase in the share of buses and trains in inland passenger transport in 2023 by 4.1 percentage points relative to 2020 represents a partial recovery since the pandemic. Nonetheless, the shares of public modes of mobility remain below pre-pandemic levels. The figures presented above do not include tram and metro systems, which are common transport modes in — especially larger — cities. According to the [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/457c93e2-98a2-11ee-b164-01aa75ed71a1/language-en 2023 survey on the quality of life in European cities], an average of 43% of respondents used public transport on a typical day, with this figure increasing as cities grow. Overall, the survey reveals that 73% of city residents in the EU are satisfied with their public transport services. Walking, cycling and other active modes of transport are low-cost and emission-free, while offering health benefits associated with an active lifestyle. The survey shows that in 2023, 27% of people walked on a typical day in the city where they live. Between 2019 and 2023, the percentage of people walking increased by 15% (or 3 percentage points). ''' Deaths from road crashes have decreased in recent years, but stronger progress is needed to meet the 2030 target ''' Road traffic injuries are a public health issue and have a huge economic cost. About 100 000 people are estimated to be seriously injured in road accidents in the EU each year  European Commission (2025), [https://road-safety.transport.ec.europa.eu/document/download/545b0348-ed10-4fb8-8f2e-243e554fb393_en?filename=ff_serious_injuries_20260109.pdf Facts & Figures: Serious injuries], European Road Safety Observatory, Brussels, European Commission, Directorate General for Transport.. In 2024, about 55 people a day lost their lives on EU roads. This corresponds to almost 20 000 people for the entire year — a loss equivalent to the size of a medium town. Nevertheless, the EU has made progress in this respect compared with 2009, when road deaths amounted to about 33 000. In recent years, however, the figures have experienced some fluctuations, in part explained by significant changes in traffic volumes because of the COVID-19 pandemic. Since the pandemic-related low in 2020, road traffic deaths have stagnated at around 20 000 each year. Compared with the reference year 2019, road deaths had fallen by 12.4% by 2024, meaning the EU is still far from its [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/d7ee4b58-4bc5-11ea-8aa5-01aa75ed71a1 2030 target of halving road deaths] relative to 2019. The highest share of road-traffic fatalities in 2024 was recorded on rural roads (53%), followed by urban roads (38%) and motorways (8%). Most fatalities on rural roads involve car occupants, light goods vehicles and motorcyclists, while most of the fatalities in urban areas involve vulnerable road users such as pedestrians, cyclists and mopeds. Most (77%) of the fatalities on the European roads in 2024 were men. Data by transport mode show that over the period 2019 to 2024, the reduction in road fatalities was strongest for buses and coaches, by 45%, followed by pedestrians (23%) and mopeds (22%), while fatalities for motorcyclists increased by 3%  European Commission (2026), [https://road-safety.transport.ec.europa.eu/document/download/ed29ad84-b2f1-429e-97ca-2b713e7dc1b1_en?filename=ERSOnext_AnnualReport_20260323.pdf Annual statistical report on road safety in the EU 2026].. According to the European Road Safety Observatory’s [https://road-safety.transport.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2023-10/ERSO-TR-alcohol_drugs_2023.pdf thematic report on alcohol and drugs], around 25% of all road deaths in the EU are alcohol related. It is also estimated that 1.5% to 2% of the kilometres driven in the EU are done by drivers with an illegal blood alcohol content. ===Impacts on the environment=== While cities, towns and suburbs are a focal point for social and economic activity, if not managed sustainably, they risk causing considerable environmental damage. At the same time, large and densely populated cities provide opportunities for effective environmental action, indicating that urbanisation is not necessarily a threat but can act as a transformative force for more sustainable societies UN-Habitat (2016), [https://unhabitat.org/world-cities-report Urbanization and Development: Emerging Futures, World Cities report 2016], pp. 85–100. . EU progress in reducing the environmental impacts of cities and communities is monitored by three indicators on the management of municipal waste, wastewater treatment and artificial land cover. ''' Net land take and soil sealing are increasing slowly but constantly in the EU ''' Offering numerous cultural, educational and job opportunities, an urban lifestyle is attractive to many people. However, growth in the urban population has also come with increased land take. Land take is described as the process of transforming agricultural, forest and other semi-natural and natural areas into artificial areas. To preserve European natural areas and halt ecosystem degradation, the EU aims to achieve [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/soil-health/soil-strategy-2030_en no net land take by 2050]. Between 2018 and 2021, the net land take in cities and their commuting zones, also known as functional urban areas, amounted to 540 square kilometres (km2) annually, which represents an increase of about 32% in the average yearly rate compared with the period 2012 to 2018. Most of the new land take in cities and their commuting zones occurred on arable land, with an annual pace of loss rising from 219 km2 to 270 km2, followed by pastures (from 146 km2 to 184 km2 per year) and forests (from 51 km2 to 63 km2). The increasing net land take is a concern for food security, biodiversity and carbon stocks, and means that the EU is off track to meeting its ‘no net land take by 2050’ target  European Environment Agency (2025), [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/net-land-take-in-cities?activeAccordion= Net land take in cities and commuting zones in Europe].. Between 2018 and 2021, most EU countries increased their annual net land take in cities and commuting zones relative to their total area. The most dramatic increases compared with the period 2012 to 2018 occurred in Croatia, Spain and Latvia (267%, 234%, 202% respectively). In contrast, Luxembourg achieved a 30% decrease in yearly net land take rate, followed by France (15%) and Italy (14%). Soil sealing is the most intense form of land take and is in effect an irreversible process. It destroys or covers soils with layers of partly or completely impermeable artificial material such as asphalt and concrete. Increases in the extent of sealed land can be used to estimate land-use change for human use or intensification. Since 2006, the area of sealed soil in the EU has increased by 6.5 m2 per inhabitant and reached 252.1 m2 per inhabitant in 2021. In absolute terms, this means that between 2006 and 2021, the total EU area covered with impervious materials grew by 5 140 km2 or 4.8%. By 2021, 2.7% of area in the EU was sealed. Across Member States, the area covered with impervious materials ranged from less than 112 m2 per inhabitant in Malta to 467 m2 per inhabitant in Finland. In relation to country area, the share of sealed soil area ranged from below 1% in Sweden and Finland to around 10% in Belgium and the Netherlands, and up to almost 19% in Malta. '''The EU might miss its target for municipal waste recycling as progress slows''' The ‘waste hierarchy’ is the overarching logic that guides EU waste policy. It prioritises waste prevention, followed by [[Glossary:Preparing_for_reuse|preparing for reuse]], [[Glossary:Recycling_of_waste|recycling]], other [[Glossary:Recovery_of_waste|recovery]] and finally disposal, including [[Glossary:Landfill|landfilling]], as the last resort. Waste management activities promote recycling, which reduces the amount of waste going to landfills and leads to higher resource efficiency. Although [[Glossary:Municipal_waste|municipal waste]] accounts for only about 10% of the weight of total waste generated in the EU Eurostat (2026), [[Municipal_waste_statistics|Statistics explained: Municipal waste statistics.]], it is highly visible and closely linked to consumption patterns. Sustainable management of this waste stream reduces the adverse environmental impact of cities and communities, which is why the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2018.150.01.0109.01.ENG&toc=OJ:L:2018:150:TOC EU has set a target] to recycle or prepare for reuse at least 60% of its municipal waste by 2030. In 2024, EU residents generated 232 million tonnes of municipal waste, corresponding to 517 kilograms (kg) of waste per capita per year  Source: Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/32029037-9cbf-4391-897a-68feab3aa6d4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-27T10:22:36Z env_wasmun]).. Between 2019 and 2024, the annual amount of waste generated per capita grew by 12 kg, which represents an increase of 2.4%. Although the EU has not reduced its municipal waste generation, it has clearly shifted to more recycling. Between 2000 and 2021, the recycling rate of municipal waste — covering both recycling and preparing for re-use — increased from 27.3% to 49.7%. However, since 2021 the recycling rate has dropped by 1.6 percentage points, reaching 48.1% in 2024. Over the short-term period from 2019 to 2024, the share of recycled municipal waste thus only increased by 0.9 percentage points. Stronger efforts are therefore needed to put the EU back on track to meet its 2030 recycling targets. ''' Uptake in the connection rate to wastewater treatment in the EU has slowed''' Urban areas also place significant pressure on the water environment through wastewater from households and industry that contains organic matter, nutrients and hazardous substances. The share of the EU population [[Glossary:Population_connected_to_urban_wastewater_treatment|connected to at least secondary waste water treatment plants]], which decompose most of the organic material and retain some of the nutrients, has been steadily growing since 2000 and reached 80.7% in 2023, although the pace has slowed. In six Member States, more than 90% of the population were connected to such services according to the most recent data (which refer to 2022 or 2023, depending on the country). However, it may not be suitable to connect 100% of the population to a sewage collection system, either because it would produce no environmental benefit or would be too costly (see article on [[SDG_6_-_Clean_water_and_sanitation|SDG 6 ‘Clean water and sanitation’]]). ==Main indicators==
===Severe housing deprivation rate===
[[Image: Severe housing deprivation rate_evaluation_2026.png|left|200px|150px|alt= The long-term evaluation of the indicator for severe housing deprivation rate for the period from 2010 to 2023 shows significant progress towards sustainability objectives. The short-term evaluation for the period 2018 to 2023 also shows significant progress towards the SD objectives.]] The severe housing deprivation rate is defined as the percentage of the population living in a [[Glossary:Dwelling|dwelling]] which is considered to be [[Glossary:Overcrowding_rate|overcrowded]], while also exhibiting at least one of the following housing deprivation measures: i) a leaking roof, ii) no bath/shower and no indoor toilet, and iii) considered too dark. The data stem from the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions EU Statistics on Income and Living Conditions] (EU-SILC). [[Image: Severe housing deprivation rate by degree of urbanisation (% of population, EU, 2010, 2018 and 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Severe housing deprivation rate by degree of urbanisation (% of population, EU, 2010, 2018 and 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_11_11}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_mdho06d}})|alt= A vertical bar chart showing severe housing deprivation rate, by degree of urbanisation in the EU, in 2010, 2018 and 2023, as a percentage of the population. The bars represent the figures for total population, cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image: Severe housing deprivation rate (% of population, 2018 and 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Severe housing deprivation rate (% of population, 2018 and 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_11_11}}|alt= A double vertical bar chart showing severe housing deprivation rate as a percentage of the population in 2018 and 2023 in the EU, EU Member States and other European countries. The bars show the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Population living in households suffering from noise===
[[Image: Population living in households considering that they suffer from noise_evaluation_2026.png|left|200px|150px|alt= The long-term evaluation of the indicator for population living in households suffering from noise for the period from 2010 to 2023 shows significant progress towards sustainability objectives. The short-term evaluation for the period 2018 to 2023 shows no progress towards nor movement away from the sustainability objectives.]] This indicator measures the share of the population who declare they are affected either by noise from neighbours or from the street. Because the assessment of noise pollution is subjective, it should be noted that the indicator accounts for both the levels of noise pollution as well as what people consider to be acceptable. Therefore, an increase in the value of the indicator may not necessarily indicate a similar increase in noise pollution levels; it may also indicate a decrease in the levels that European citizens are willing to tolerate and vice versa. In fact, there is empirical evidence that perceived environmental quality by individuals is not always consistent with the actual environmental quality assessed using ‘objective’ indicators, particularly for noise. The data stem from the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions EU Statistics on Income and Living Conditions] (EU-SILC). [[Image: Population living in households considering that they suffer from noise by degree of urbanisation (% of population, EU, 2010, 2018 and 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Population living in households considering that they suffer from noise by degree of urbanisation (% of population, EU, 2010, 2018 and 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_11_20}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_mddw04}})|alt= A vertical bar chart showing population living in households considering that they suffer from noise, by degree of urbanisation in the EU, in 2010, 2018 and 2023, as a percentage of the population. The bars represent the figures for the total population, cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image: Population living in households considering that they suffer from noise (% of population, 2018 and 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Population living in households considering that they suffer from noise (% of population, 2018 and 2023)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_11_20}}|alt= A double vertical bar chart showing population living in households considering that they suffer from noise as a percentage of the population in 2018 and 2023 in the EU, EU Member States and other European countries. The bars show the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Premature deaths due to exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5)===
[[Image: Premature deaths due to exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2_5)_evaluation_2026.png|left|200px|150px|alt= The long-term evaluation of the indicator for premature deaths due to exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) for the period from 2008 to 2023 shows significant progress towards the EU target. The short-term evaluation for the period 2018 to 2023 also shows significant progress towards the EU target.]] The indicator measures the number of premature deaths that can be attributed to exposure to particulate matter. Fine particulates (PM2.5) are particulates whose diameter is less than 2.5 micrometres, meaning they can be carried deep into the lungs where they can cause inflammation and exacerbate the condition of people already suffering from heart and lung diseases. Premature deaths refer to those deaths that occur before the expected age of death. This expected age is typically defined by accounting for the life expectancy in the country, stratified by sex and age. The data stem from the European Environment Agency. [[Image: Premature deaths due to exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2_5) (number, EU, 2005-2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Premature deaths due to exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) (number, EU, 2005-2023)
''Source:'' EEA, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_11_52}}|alt= A line chart with a dot showing the number of premature deaths due to exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5), in the EU from 2005 to 2023. The dot shows the 2030 target. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image: Premature deaths due to exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2_5) (number per 100 000 people, 2018 and 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Premature deaths due to exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) (number per 100 000 people, 2018 and 2023)
''Source:'' EEA, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_11_52}}|alt= A double vertical bar chart showing the number of premature deaths per 100 000 people due to exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) in 2018 and 2023 in the EU, EU Member States and other European countries. The bars show the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Road traffic deaths===
[[Image: Road traffic deaths_evaluation_2026.png|left|200px|150px|alt= The long-term evaluation of the indicator for road traffic deaths for the period from 2009 to 2024 shows moderate progress towards the EU target. The short-term evaluation for the period 2019 to 2024 shows insufficient progress towards the EU target.]] This indicator measures the number of fatalities caused by road crashes, including drivers and passengers of motorised vehicles and pedal cycles, as well as pedestrians. People who die from road crashes up to 30 days after the crash occurred are counted as fatalities. The data come from the CARE database managed by DG Mobility and Transport (DG MOVE). [[Image: Road traffic deaths (number, EU, 2000-2024).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 7: Road traffic deaths (number, EU, 2000-2024)
''Source:'' European Commission services, DG Mobility and Transport, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_11_40}}|alt= A line chart with a dot showing road traffic deaths as the number, in the EU from 2000 to 2024. The dot represents the 2030 target. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image: Road traffic deaths (number per 100 000 people, 2018 and 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 8: Road traffic deaths (number per 100 000 people, 2018 and 2023)
''Source:'' European Commission services, DG Mobility and Transport, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_11_40}}|alt= A double vertical bar chart showing road traffic deaths as the number of killed people per 100000 people in 2019 and 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and other European countries. The bars show the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Soil sealing ===
[[Image: Soil sealing_evaluation_2026.png|left|200px|150px|alt= The long-term evaluation of the indicator for soil sealing for the period from 2006 to 2021 shows moderate movement away from sustainability objectives. The short-term evaluation for the period 2015 to 2021 also shows moderate movement away from sustainability objectives.]] This indicator shows the area of soil per inhabitant that is sealed with impervious materials due to development and construction (such as buildings, constructions and laying of completely or partially impermeable artificial material such as asphalt or glass). The indicator builds on data from the Imperviousness High Resolution Layer (a product of the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service). [[Image: Soil sealing index (m² per inhabitant, EU, 2006-2021).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 9: Soil sealing index (m² per inhabitant, EU, 2006-2021)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_11_32}}|alt= A line chart showing soil sealing in the EU in square metres per inhabitant for the period from 2006 to 2021. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image: Soil sealing (m² per inhabitant, 2015 and 2021).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 10: Soil sealing (m² per inhabitant, 2015 and 2021)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_11_32}}|alt= A double vertical bar chart showing soil sealing in square metres per inhabitant in 2015 and 2021 in the EU, EU Member States and other European countries. The bars show the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Recycling rate of municipal waste===
[[Image: Recycling rate of municipal waste_evaluation_2026.png|left|200px|150px|alt= The long-term evaluation of the indicator for recycling rate of municipal waste for the period from 2009 to 2024 shows moderate progress towards the EU target. The short-term evaluation for the period 2019 to 2024 shows insufficient progress towards the EU target.]] This indicator measures the tonnage recycled or prepared for re-use from municipal waste divided by the total municipal waste generated. Recycling includes material recycling, composting and anaerobic digestion. Municipal waste primarily consists of waste generated by households but it also includes similar types of waste generated by small businesses, offices and public institutions that are collected by or on behalf of municipalities. The specific composition of municipal waste can vary from municipality to municipality and from country to country, depending on the local waste management systems in place. For areas not covered by a municipal waste collection scheme the amount of waste generated is estimated. [[Image: Recycling rate of municipal waste (% of total municipal waste generated, EU, 2000-2024).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 11: Recycling rate of municipal waste (% of total municipal waste generated, EU, 2000-2024)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_11_60}}|alt= A line chart with a dot showing the recycling rate of municipal waste as a percentage of total municipal waste generated, in the EU from 2000 to 2024. The dot shows the EU target. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image: Recycling rate of municipal waste (% of total municipal waste generated, 2019 and 2024).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 12: Recycling rate of municipal waste (% of total municipal waste generated, 2019 and 2024)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_11_60}}|alt= A double vertical bar chart showing the recycling rate of municipal waste as a percentage of total municipal waste generated in 2019 and 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and other European countries. The bars show the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:SDG 11 - 2026 edition.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Context === ''' Quality of life in cities and communities and impacts on the environment''' Under the [https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/policy/what/investment-policy_en EU Cohesion Policy], a minimum of 8% of the European Regional Development Fund of each national envelope is dedicated to supporting sustainable urban development. It is accompanied by the [https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/en/newsroom/news/2019/03/20-03-2019-european-urban-initiative-post-2020-the-commission-proposal European Urban Initiative] supporting innovation, capacity and knowledge building in urban areas. The [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/noise/directive_en.htm Environmental Noise Directive] is the main EU instrument for identifying and combating noise pollution. The EU addresses air pollution through [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/air_en specific legislation on clean air] as well as [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/air/air-pollution-key-sectors_en legislation addressing the key sources of emissions]. The [https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/sectors/automotive-industry/environmental-protection/emissions-automotive-sector_en EU emission standards for road vehicles, for example, will help improve air quality in cities. With the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/urban-environment/green-city-accord_en Green City Accord], European Mayors can commit to improving their cities by addressing five areas of environmental management — air, water, noise, nature and biodiversity and waste. The Action Plan [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52021DC0400&qid=1623311742827 ‘Towards Zero Pollution for Air, Water and Soil’] includes the target of reducing the health impacts due to air pollution by 55% by 2030, compared with 2005, and maximises synergies with relevant EU policies, such as limiting soil sealing and urban sprawl. The 2022 [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_22_6278 Zero Pollution package] proposed stricter rules for cleaner air and water. The revised [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/2881/oj/eng Ambient Air Quality Directive] aligns EU air quality standards more closely with WHO recommendations, and improves air quality monitoring, modelling and plans. In December 2025 the European Commission has adopted the [https://housing.ec.europa.eu/european-affordable-housing-plan_en European Affordable Housing Plan] that aims to support EU Member States, regions and cities to boost the supply of affordable, sustainable and quality housing while also aiming to improve social inclusion, fighting homelessness and housing exclusion. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52021DC0699 EU Soil Strategy for 2030] aims to protect and restore soils and ensure their sustainable use, and sets a goal of no net land take by 2050. The new [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/soil-health/soil-monitoring-law_en Soil Monitoring Law] addresses key soil threats such as erosion, loss of soil organic matter, salinisation, contamination, compaction and sealing, and loss of soil biodiversity. The [https://ec.europa.eu/environment/topics/circular-economy/first-circular-economy-action-plan_en circular economy action plan] supports the transition to a stronger and more circular economy. In 2018, the legally binding [http://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2018/05/22/waste-management-and-recycling-council-adopts-new-rules/ targets] for recycling and reuse of municipal waste [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32018L0851 entered into force]. EU countries will now be required to recycle at least 55% of their municipal waste by 2025, 60% by 2030 and 65% by 2035. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202500040&pk_campaign=todays_OJ&pk_source=EUR-Lex&pk_medium=X&pk_content=Environment&pk_keyword=Regulation Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation] aims to reduce packaging waste and increase recycling. The [https://new-european-bauhaus.europa.eu/about/about-initiative_en New European Bauhaus] initiative brings citizens, experts, businesses and institutions together to reimagine sustainable living in Europe and beyond, incorporating the values of sustainability, aesthetics and inclusion. ''' Sustainable mobility''' The [https://urban-mobility-observatory.transport.ec.europa.eu/sustainable-urban-mobility-plans/sump-guidelines-and-decision-makers-summary_en EU guidelines for sustainable urban mobility planning] and funding for related projects, combined with the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52020DC0789 Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy] adopted in 2020, support the green and digital transformation of the EU transport system. The revised [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:L_202401679 TEN-T Regulation] adopted in 2024 reinforced the link between transport networks and urban mobility. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52018DC0293 Strategic Action Plan on Road Safety] and the [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/d7ee4b58-4bc5-11ea-8aa5-01aa75ed71a1 EU road safety policy framework 2021–2030] set a 50% reduction target for deaths and serious injuries by 2030 compared with 2019 and aims to move close to zero road deaths by 2050. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Sustainable development goals|All articles on sustainable development goals]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/database Sustainable development indicators] ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=sdi}} Sustainable development indicators] ===Methodology=== More detailed information on EU SDG indicators for monitoring of progress towards the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), such as indicator relevance, definitions, methodological notes, background and potential linkages can be found in the [[SDG - Introduction|introduction]] as well as in Annex II of the publication {{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-064|title=’Sustainable development in the European Union — Monitoring report on progress towards the SDGs in an EU context — 2026 edition’}}. ===Publications=== '''Further reading on sustainable cities and communities''' *[https://road-safety.transport.ec.europa.eu/document/download/a7428369-8eaf-4032-806e-ea08b46028c0_en?filename=ERSO-TR-MainCauses.pdf European Commission (2024), Road safety thematic report – Main factors causing fatal crashes, European Road Safety Observatory, Brussels.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/air-quality-status-report-2025 EEA (2025), Air quality status report 2025.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/urban-adaptation-in-europe-what-works EEA (2024), Urban adaptation in Europe: what works? Implementing climate action in European cities.] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/ks-ha-24-001 Eurostat (2024), Eurostat regional yearbook 2024, Publications Office of the European Union, Luxembourg.] *[https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC136039 Joint Research Centre (2024), Atlas of the Human Planet 2024, Publications Office of the European Union, Luxembourg.] *[https://www.housingeurope.eu/resource-1825/the-state-of-the-housing-in-europe-2023 The Housing Europe (2023), The State of Housing in Europe 2023, Housing Europe, the European Federation for Public, Cooperative and Social Housing, Brussels.] *[https://unhabitat.org/wcr/ UN-Habitat (2024), World Cities Report 2024: Cities and Climate Action.] *[https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240086517 WHO (2023), Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023.] *[https://www.who.int/europe/publications/i/item/9789289053563 WHO (2019), Environmental Noise Guidelines for the European Region, WHO Regional Office for Europe, Copenhagen.] ===External links=== '''Further data sources on sustainable cities and communities''' *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/topics/in-depth/air-pollution EEA, Air pollution.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/data-and-maps/indicators/land-take-3/assessment EEA, Land take.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/topics/in-depth/noise EEA, Noise.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/waste-recycling-in-europe EEA, Waste recycling.] *[https://road-safety.transport.ec.europa.eu/european-road-safety-observatory/data-and-analysis_en European Commission, European Road Safety Observatory – Data and analysis.] *[https://urban.jrc.ec.europa.eu/urban?lng=en European Commission, Urban Data Platform.] === Footnotes === {{Unit|topic=X_Sustainable_development_indicators}} [[Category:EU policy indicators|SDG 11 -
