title: SDG 14 - Life below water
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the life below water as a part of the Sustainable Development Goals. ==Conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources for sustainable development==
Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: June 2027 [[Image: SDG 14 tachometer 2026.png|EU trend of SDG 14 on life below water |thumb|centre|400px|alt= Goal-level assessment of SDG 14 on Life below water showing the EU has made slight progress towards sustainability objectives during the short-term period.]] This article is a part of a [[Sustainable development in the European Union|set of statistical articles]], which are based on the [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publication {{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-064|title=’Sustainable development in the European Union — Monitoring report on progress towards the SDGs in an EU context — 2026 edition’}}. This report is the tenth edition of Eurostat’s series of monitoring reports on sustainable development, which provide a quantitative assessment of progress of the EU towards the SDGs in an EU context.
SDG 14 aims to protect and ensure the sustainable use of oceans. This includes reducing marine pollution and ocean acidification, ending overfishing and conserving marine and coastal ecosystems. SDG 14 is strongly related to other SDGs because oceans sustain coastal economies and livelihoods, contribute to food production and function as a carbon sink.
===Life below water in the EU: overview and key trends=== The health and productivity of marine ecosystems are of paramount importance for coastal livelihoods, food security, biodiversity and the regulation of Earth’s climate. At the same time, marine and coastal environments are heavily affected by climate change, habitat destruction, degradation and alteration, biodiversity loss, over-exploitation of marine resources and pollution. Monitoring SDG 14 in an EU context thus involves analysing developments in the areas of ocean health, marine conservation and sustainable fisheries. Over the short-term period, the EU has made only slow progress towards the goal. On the positive side, fish stocks in EU marine waters (especially in the North-East Atlantic) seem to be recovering as a result of more sustainable fishing practices. However, ocean acidification and eutrophication increase continuously. Additionally, the designation of new marine protected areas needs to speed up to achieve the target of protecting at least 30 % of EU seas by 2030. Image: Indicators_measuring_progress_in_SDG_14_2026.png|'''Table 1: Indicators measuring progress towards SDG 14, EU'''|alt=A table showing the indicators measuring progress towards SDG 14 in the EU. Image:Explanation_of_symbols_for_indicating_progress_2026.png|'''Table 2: Explanation of symbols for indicating progress towards SD objectives and targets'''|alt=A table showing the Explanation of symbols for indicating progress towards sustainability objectives and targets. ===Ocean health=== Accomplishing the goal of a clean, healthy and productive ocean requires an integrated approach that addresses multiple pressures on marine ecosystems. To monitor progress towards SDG 14 in the EU context, indicators focus on ocean acidification, eutrophication and bathing water quality. To improve water quality in marine waters and coastal areas across its sea basins, the EU has put in place a range of land-based and marine policies, strengthened its engagement in [https://ec.europa.eu/environment/marine/international-cooperation/regional-sea-conventions/index_en.htm Regional Sea Conventions], sea-basin and macro-regional strategies, and support for its outermost regions. Over the past five years, bathing water quality has largely stabilised at a high level, while eutrophication remains an unsatisfactory pressure in several sea basins. Progress has been made in reducing nutrient inputs contributing to eutrophication and pathogens from point sources, notably through improved urban wastewater treatment. However, ocean acidification has continued due to global climate change. ''' Seawater acidification remains on an upward trajectory ''' Seawater acidification occurs when increased levels of carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere are absorbed by the sea. Dissolved atmospheric CO2 reacts with water molecules and increases the hydrogen ion concentration in the ocean, thus increasing ocean acidity. Data on the global yearly ocean carbon uptake show that the sea has absorbed more carbon as atmospheric concentrations of CO2 have risen  Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (2019), [https://www.ipcc.ch/srocc/download/ IPCC Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate], Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, UK and New York, NY, USA.. While the ocean helps to mitigate atmospheric warming by absorbing this greenhouse gas, its capacity to do so is limited and the added CO2 fundamentally changes the ocean’s chemistry. Acidification reduces calcification and affects biochemical processes such as photosynthesis, with knock-on effects for entire ecosystems. Because cold water absorbs more CO2, polar regions are disproportionately affected by acidification. Research has shown that organisms relying on calcification (for example, mussels, corals and plankton) and photosynthesis (plankton and algae) are particularly vulnerable to increased acidity  European Environment Agency (2017), [https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/climate-change-impacts-and-vulnerability-2016 Climate change, impacts and vulnerability in Europe 2016 — An indicator-based report], EEA Report No 1/2017, Copenhagen.. A decline in the extent of coral reefs not only leads to habitat loss for many species and impacts on the food web, it also increases flood risk due to coastal erosion. The Copernicus Marine Services has been monitoring [https://marine.copernicus.eu/ocean-climate-portal/ocean-acidification ocean acidification] since 1985. Over the whole period from 1985 to 2025, the mean concentration of hydrogen ions in surface seawater in the Northeast Atlantic and the Mediterranean and Black Sea increased by 17.0%, reaching 8.76 nanomoles per litre (nmol/l). This corresponds to a pH value of 8.06, which is considerably below the pre-industrialisation surface seawater pH range of 8.3 to 8.2  European Environment Agency (2025), [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/ocean-acidification Ocean acidification].. Ocean acidification in EU marine areas has risen slightly in recent years, with the hydrogen ion concentration increasing by 8.0% since 2010 and by 3.0% since 2019. Unless CO2 emissions are significantly reduced, ocean acidity measured as hydrogen ion concentration is projected to double or triple by 2100  Canadell, J. G. et al. (2021), “[ https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-5/ Global Carbon and other Biogeochemical Cycles and Feedbacks]”, in: IPCC, Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis.. Mitigating climate change (SDG 13) is thus vital for reaching SDG target 14.3 on minimising seawater acidification. ''' Pollution continues to threaten the marine environment ''' In addition to acidification, Europe’s marine ecosystems are still under threat from organic and chemical pollutants from human activities, as well as marine litter and noise pollution. Excessive nutrient loads from agriculture and municipal [[Glossary:Wastewater|wastewater]] — in particular phosphorus and nitrogen compounds — cause eutrophication, which can lead to problematic algal blooms and oxygen depletion, with severe consequences for the marine ecosystem’s health and biodiversity. The [https://marine.copernicus.eu/ Copernicus Marine Service] monitors all EU sea basins for oxygen depletion and measures anomalies in chlorophyll-a levels as an indicator of eutrophication. The chlorophyll data show strong annual fluctuations in the area of EU marine waters affected. Since 2003, eutrophication has affected between around 2 000 and 50 000 square kilometres (km²) of EU marine waters, corresponding to between 0.04% and 0.9% of the EU’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ). In 2025, about 8 600 km² of EU marine waters were affected by eutrophication, corresponding to 0.15% of the EU’s EEZ. A smoothed four-year moving average for the trend assessment reveals that while the area affected by eutrophication has declined by 26% since 2010, the short-term trend has been unfavourable, showing a 11% increase since 2019. An [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/chlorophyll-in-transitional-coastal-and analysis from the European Environment Agency (EEA)] covering the period 1980 to 2023 shows that while some locations demonstrated a decline in chlorophyll-a levels, indicating an improvement in the water quality, most areas have seen no significant trend. Areas with higher chlorophyll-a concentrations — especially during summer — are located in the Baltic Sea and along coastal areas in the North Sea and Mediterranean Sea. The findings on chlorophyll-a concentrations largely align with trends on [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/nutrients-in-transitional-coastal-and nutrient] and [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/oxygen-concentrations-in-coastal-and oxygen] concentrations in Europe's seas, suggesting that further efforts are necessary to maintain and improve water quality, particularly in problem areas. Chemical pollution from [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/hazardous-substances-in-marine-organisms hazardous substances], marine plastic litter and microplastics is another relevant threat to the marine environment. Chemical pollution stems from land-based and marine sources, including agriculture (through the application of pesticides and veterinary medicines), industry, households and the transport sector. Of particular concern are persistent organic pollutants (POPs), which degrade slowly and can bioaccumulate in the food chain. Marine litter, such as plastic bottles and packaging, can also break down into smaller particles through photodegradation, releasing chemicals such as bisphenol A (BPA) and phthalates into the water. All in all, the transfer of toxic chemicals from the litter into the food web is already taking place on a large scale and ultimately poses combined risks to marine life and human health such as organ failure, reduced fertility and increased cancer  Sameh S. Ali, Mohammed Hussein M. Alsharbaty, Rania Al-Tohamy, Michael Schagerl, Majid Al-Zahrani, Michael Kornaros and Jianzhong Sun (2025), [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2590182624000651?via%3Dihub Microplastics as persistent and vectors of other threats in the marine environment: Toxicological impacts, management and strategical roadmap to end plastic pollution], Environmental Chemistry and Ecotoxicology 7, 229–251.. Estimates of plastic litter entering the ocean are highly tentative, due to a lack of data. However, the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM%3A2018%3A28%3AFIN European Commission estimates] that 150 000 to 500 000 tonnes of plastic enter the EU’s marine waters every year, with most of it being carried to the sea by rivers. Accordingly, 75% of the [https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/european-marine-litter-assessment/from-source-to-sea-the marine areas assessed by the EEA] are classified as polluted. Plastic pollution has many harmful effects on the marine environment, for example it traps and strangles marine animals or is ingested by them. Marine litter can come from both sea- and land-based sources, with the latter accounting for 80%. The top 10 most commonly found single-use plastics account for about 43% of all marine litter on European beaches  European Environment Agency (2025), [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/circularity/sectoral-modules/plastics/litter-found-on-european-beaches Litter found on European sea beaches]. . Noise, caused by ships and offshore activities such as oil and gas exploration, is one of the most widespread human induced pressures in the marine environment  European Environment Agency (2019), [https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/marine-messages-2/ Marine Messages II: navigating the course towards clean, healthy and productive seas through implementation of an ecosystem based approach], EEA Report No 17/2019, Copenhagen.. Noise pollution can negatively affect marine life, causing increased stress and resulting in behavioural changes that can impact animals’ foraging and reproductive abilities. Furthermore, the constant noise frequencies released by ships potentially obscure the sounds that various marine species, such as whales and dolphins, make to communicate, hunt, navigate and protect themselves. According to the [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/maritime-transport-2025 European Maritime Transport Environmental Report 2025], underwater radiated noise from ships in EU waters increased steadily between 2014 and 2019, with a slight decrease in 2020 that was likely due to reduced maritime traffic during the COVID-19 pandemic. Between 2020 and 2023, noise levels rose again, but they have not yet returned to 2019 levels. Human-induced eutrophication, contaminant concentrations, marine litter and noise pollution are common multiple pressures that must be minimised for marine waters to achieve good environmental status under the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD) and good ecological status for coastal waters under the Water Framework Directive (WFD). ''' The share of European coastal bathing waters with excellent quality has stagnated in recent years ''' Coastal water quality is affected by land-based pollution from sewage, agricultural run-off and surface run-off from coastal cities, which can carry pathogens, hazardous chemicals, nutrients, plastic litter and microplastics. This pollution puts significant pressure on aquatic ecosystems and underwater life as well as on blue economy activities and the livelihoods of coastal communities. The quality of the EU’s coastal bathing waters improved between 2011 and 2019, but progress has slowed since then. In 2024, 88.8% of the EU’s coastal bathing waters had ‘excellent’ quality. While this reflects a notable increase compared with 81.3% in 2011, it is only marginally above the share of 88.4% reported in 2019. Across Member States, bathing water quality was highest in Lithuania, Slovenia and Cyprus, with virtually all coastal bathing waters having excellent quality in 2024. ===Marine conservation=== The lives of European citizens depend in many ways on the services marine [[Glossary:Ecosystems_and_their_services|ecosystems]] provide, including climate regulation, fish and seafood provision, coastal protection, cultural value, recreation and [[Glossary:Tourism|tourism]]. Against this backdrop, the European Commission and Member States have taken multiple steps to combat the destruction and degradation of aquatic and coastal [[Glossary:Habitats|habitats]] and [[Glossary:Biodiversity|biodiversity]], which poses a serious threat to human livelihoods, food security and climate stability  European Commission (2021), [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/1625f673-b201-11eb-8aca-01aa75ed71a1/language-en Assessment of the existing EU policy tools in the field of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 14 and other ocean-related Agenda 2030].. A crucial step has been the designation of a network of marine protected areas (MPAs), in which some human activities are subject to stricter regulation. The degree of protection and hence the effectiveness of MPAs depends on the management plan regulating each protected area. Management measures may range from a total ban on fishing, mining or wind power generation, to a more moderate protection regime where economic activity is restricted, for example, allowing only certain types of fishing methods. However, many MPAs still lack comprehensive management plans, or permit some level of commercial or recreational exploitation of fisheries  European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (2025), Mapping of Marine Protected Areas and their associated fishing activities: [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/9029283c-fefa-11ef-9503-01aa75ed71a1 Baltic and North Seas, Atlantic EU Western Waters and Outermost Regions (MAPAFISH)], Final Report, Publications Office of the European Union, Luxembourg; and European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (2025), Mapping of Marine Protected Areas and their associated fishing activities: [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/8f3171d9-edaa-11ef-b5e9-01aa75ed71a1/language-en Mediterranean and Black Seas (MAPAFISH–MED)], Final Report, Publications Office of the European Union, Luxembourg.. One of the commitments made by the international community at the [https://maritime-spatial-planning.ec.europa.eu/news/results-one-ocean-summit-2022 2022 One Ocean summit] and the UN COP15 on Biodiversity was to set a goal for new MPAs to have 30% of marine space under protection, including 10 % under strict protection, by 20230  Strict protection does not necessarily mean the area is not accessible to humans, but it leaves natural processes essentially undisturbed to respect the areas’ ecological requirements.. This goal is also supported by the [https://www.un.org/bbnjagreement/en BBNJ Agreement] and is included in the EU [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A52020DC0380 Biodiversity Strategy for 2030]. With the ambition to accelerate the implementation of SDG 14 globally, the EU and its Member States pledged voluntary commitments amounting to EUR 1 billion at the [https://oceans-and-fisheries.ec.europa.eu/events/eu-3rd-united-nations-ocean-conference-2025-06-09_en third UN Ocean Conference]. Commitments cover a wide range of topics and regions around the world. ''' The extent of marine protected areas has been growing slowly in the EU and remains far below the 2030 target ''' An EU assessment of measures to protect coastal and marine environments from 2025 shows that good environmental status has not been achieved across marine regions, and that marine biodiversity continues to decline while pollution still harms marine life  European Commission (2025), [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM%3A2025%3A3%3AFIN&qid=1738676411960 Assessment of the Member States’ programmes of measures as updated under Article 17 of the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (2008/56/EC)].. A high proportion of marine species and habitats across Europe’s seas are still in ‘unfavourable conservation status’ and the marine ecosystem condition is generally not 'good'  European Environment Agency (2020), [https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/state-of-nature-in-the-eu-2020 State of nature in the EU. Results from reporting under the nature directives 2013–2018], Publications Office of the European Union, Luxembourg.. One approach to protect the state of marine ecosystems is the designation of MPAs and the subsequent implementation of management measures. Between 2012 and 2023, the extent of marine protected areas more than tripled from 216 972 square kilometres (km²) to 689 211 km², with most of this growth taking place between 2012 and 2019. While the designation of additional MPAs has since slowed, between 2022 and 2023 the extent of marine protected areas increased by 9.6%. In 2023, MPAs represented 13.7% of overall EU marine area (with only around 1% strictly protected  European Commission (2020), [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/biodiversity-strategy-2030_en EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030: Bringing nature back into our lives].), meaning efforts will need to accelerate for the EU to meet its 30% target by 2030. In 2023, the highest shares of marine protected areas were reported by Germany (45.5% of national marine area), France (45.4%) and Belgium (38.1%). Since 2019, MPA coverage has increased in most EU Member States that have a sea border, with particularly notable relative increases recorded in Italy (from 5.4% to 10.0%) and Spain (from 12.0% to 18.4%), alongside further gains in France, the Netherlands and Denmark. Growth in the extent of protected areas alone does not necessarily provide a reliable indication of how effectively species and habitats are protected, because the conservation outcomes of MPAs depend largely on the management measures and levels of protection applied. At the EU level, there is still no harmonised overview of the level of protection and implementation of management measures across MPAs in Europe’s regional seas. Recent research assessing the regulation of human activities in EU MPAs indicates that around 86% of MPA areas are subject to low levels of protection  Aminian-Biquet, J., Gorjanc, S., Sletten, J., Vincent, T., Laznya, A., Vaidianu, N., Claudet, J., Young, J., & Horta e Costa, B. (2024), [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2590332224003646 Over 80% of the European Union’s marine protected areas only marginally regulate human activities], One Earth, 7(9): 1614–1629., meaning that potentially harmful activities may still be permitted. This finding is consistent with earlier assessments, including a [https://www.eca.europa.eu/en/publications?did=57066 European Court of Auditors report], which concluded that EU MPAs often provide limited protection in practice. Research suggests that MPAs may help increase fish populations inside their borders. The benefit for nearby fisheries depends on the MPA’s age, local conditions and if it is part of a larger MPA network  European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (2024), [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/5eb36610-68d6-11ef-a8ba-01aa75ed71a1/language-en Assessing spillover from marine protected areas to adjacent fisheries — Baltic and North Seas, Atlantic EU Western Waters and Outermost Regions], Final report, Publications Office of the European Union, Luxembourg.. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A52020DC0380 Biodiversity Strategy for 2030] requires the Commission, in cooperation with Member States and the EEA, to advance [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/publications/criteria-and-guidance-protected-areas-designations-staff-working-document_en criteria and guidelines for the identification and designation of new protected areas], as well as for coherent management planning. In 2023, the European Commission adopted an [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM%3A2023%3A102%3AFIN&qid=1676984139637 action plan for protecting and restoring marine ecosystems for sustainable and resilient fisheries]. This action plan calls on EU Member States to, among other things, improve fishing selectivity and reduce the impact of fishing on sensitive species and the seabed. This objective is flanked by the [https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe/eu-missions-horizon-europe/restore-our-ocean-and-waters_en EU Mission Restore our Ocean and Waters] and the [https://projects.research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/en/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe/eu-missions-horizon-europe/restore-our-ocean-and-waters/eu-blue-parks-community EU Blue Parks Community Initiative]. ===Sustainable fisheries=== Besides pollution, the unsustainable use of living resources is the main threat to marine habitats and species in the EU. An ecosystem-based approach to managing Europe’s fishing fleets is provided for under the EU’s Common Fishing Policy (CFP) and is required for biodiversity conservation. Governance of fisheries in EU waters mainly focuses on fair access and sustainable supply. The CFP aims to ensure that fishing and aquaculture activities are environmentally sustainable in the long term and are managed in a way that achieves economic, social and employment benefits, and contributes to the availability of seafood supplies. The CFP limits the total amount of fish catches and controls who is allowed to fish — including how, when and where — to prevent damage to vulnerable marine ecosystems and preserve fish stocks. Thus, the CFP’s ambition and implementation will directly affect whether SDG 14 is achieved, in particular its aim of ending overfishing, destructive and/or illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing practices, and subsidies that encourage these activities. In addition, unsustainable fisheries are a major threat to marine ecosystems through seabed degradation and the bycatch of non-target species (such as birds and cetaceans). The CFP empowers Members States and the Commission to regulate fisheries so they comply with the obligations of the Birds and Habitats Directives and the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD). ''' Fisheries in EU marine waters have become more sustainable ''' European fisheries affect fish stock productivity and stock size through catches. However, because stock size also varies naturally, managing fisheries is a complex exercise. Controlling fishing mortality is one way of managing fisheries. Fishing mortality (F) reflects the proportion of fish of a given age that is caught during one year. For fisheries to be sustainable, fishing mortality should not exceed the maximum sustainable yield (FMSY), which is the largest catch that can be taken from a fish stock over an indefinite period without harming it. The model-based median value of all F/FMSY stock assessments can be used to estimate fishing pressures on fish stocks. Values above 1.0 mean the current fishing mortality (F) exceeds the estimated maximum sustainable yield (FMSY). The results for EU marine waters show a 38% reduction in fishing pressure, from 1.37 in 2008 to 0.85 in 2023. This overall figure aligns with the fact that fish stocks both in the North-East Atlantic (including the Baltic Sea) and in the Mediterranean and Black Sea were on average fished sustainably (F/FMSY median of 0.78 in 2023 in the North-East Atlantic and F/FMSY median of 0.92 in 2023 in the Mediterranean and Black Sea). These results are complemented by the share of sustainably exploited stocks: while in the North-East Atlantic 71% of fish stocks were exploited sustainably in 2023, this share was 53% in the Mediterranean and Black Sea  Source: Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f196e108-3596-4edd-8bc3-6e0c0f273a51?lang=en env_bio5]).. In this context, it is important to mention the harm that decreased freshwater flow has caused to marine ecosystems in the Mediterranean Sea, affecting the biomass of commercial fish and invertebrate species, with the lowest flows observed in 2022  Macias, D., Bisselink, B., Carmona-Moreno, C., Druon, J.-N., Duteil, O., Garcia-Gorriz, E., Grizzetti, B., Guillen, J., Miladinova, S., Pistocchi, A., Piroddi, C., Polimene, L., Serpetti, N., Stips, A., Trichakis, I., Udias, A., & Vigiak, O. (2025), [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-54979-4#Abs1 The overlooked impacts of freshwater scarcity on oceans as evidenced by the Mediterranean Sea], Nature Communications, 16: 998.. Amid this background and despite an improving trend, the EU needs to further increase efforts in these sea regions to meet its own targets for sustainable fisheries. The EU’s approach to sustainable fisheries is not limited to respecting MSY. The Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSDFD) requires commercially exploited fish and shellfish populations to have a healthy distribution of age and size. The status of stocks and their reproductive capacity can be measured and described by fish stock biomass as well as by spawning stock biomass (SSB). Biomass estimates are, however, associated with high levels of uncertainty due to the high annual variability of stock biomass. Fish stocks can also take time to respond to changes in management measures, and results can be masked by other factors, such as environmental conditions and predation  Measuring the Effect of Catch Shares (2018), [http://www.catchshareindicators.org/northeast/ecological-indicators/biomass/ Has the status of fish stocks changed? Biological indicators: Biomass].. For this reason, analyses of stock biomass trends should always focus on longer term patterns. Model-based estimates show a 22% increase in fish stock biomass in EU marine waters between 2008 and 2023. In the short term, between 2018 and 2023, growth in fish stock biomass amounted to 6%. ==Main indicators== ===Mean surface seawater acidity=== [[Image: Mean surface seawater acidity_evaluation_2026.png|left|200px|alt= The long-term evaluation of the indicator for mean surface seawater acidity for the period from 2010 to 2025 shows moderate movement away from the sustainability objectives. The short-term evaluation for the period 2019 to 2025 also shows moderate movement away from the sustainability objectives.]] This indicator shows the yearly mean concentration of hydrogen ions in surface seawater in the Northeast Atlantic and the Mediterranean and Black Sea, expressed in nanomoles per litre (nmol/l). An increase in the concentration of hydrogen ions corresponds to a decline in pH values and an increase in seawater acidity. This trend is caused by an increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) concentrations, which increases the uptake of CO2 by the ocean. The [https://resources.marine.copernicus.eu/product-detail/GLOBAL_OMI_HEALTH_carbon_ph_area_averaged/INFORMATION Copernicus Marine Service] has reconstructed the trends in global ocean acidification from 1985 onwards. [[Image: Mean surface seawater acidity in the Northeast Atlantic and the Mediterranean and Black Sea (nmol_l, 1985-2025).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Mean surface seawater acidity in the Northeast Atlantic and the Mediterranean and Black Sea (nmol/l, 1985–2025)
''Source:'' Mercator Ocean International, Copernicus Marine Service, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_14_51}}|alt= A line chart showing the mean surface seawater acidity in the Northeast Atlantic and the Mediterranean and Black Sea, from 1985 to 2025, expressed in nanomoles per litre.]] ===Marine waters affected by eutrophication=== [[Image: Marine waters affected by eutrophication_evaluation_2026.png|left|200px|alt= The long-term evaluation of the indicator for marine waters affected by eutrophication for the period from 2010 to 2025 shows significant progress towards sustainability objectives. The short-term evaluation for the period 2019 to 2025 shows significant movement away from the sustainability objectives.]] Eutrophication is the process by which an excess of nutrients — mainly phosphorus and nitrogen — leads to increased growth of plant material, particularly planktonic algae, in an aquatic body, resulting in a decrease in water quality. This can, in turn, cause death by hypoxia of aquatic organisms. Anthropogenic activities, such as farming, agriculture, aquaculture, industry and sewage, are the main source of nutrient input in problem areas. This indicator shows the extent of eutrophic marine waters in the EU's exclusive economic zone (EEZ). An area is classified as eutrophic if chlorophyll-a concentrations, as a proxy, are above the 90th percentile of the 1998 to 2017 reference base line for more than 25% of the observation days in a given year. The Copernicus Marine Service calculates the indicator from satellite imagery. [[Image: Marine waters affected by eutrophication (km², EU, 2000-2025).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Marine waters affected by eutrophication (km², EU, 2000–2025)
''Source:'' Mercator Ocean International, Copernicus Marine Service, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_14_60}}|alt= A line chart with two lines showing the square kilometres of marine waters affected by eutrophication, in the EU from 2000 to 2025. The lines show the annual data and the four-year moving average.]]
[[Image: Marine waters affected by eutrophication (% of exclusive economic zone (EEZ), by country, 2019 and 2025).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Marine waters affected by eutrophication (% of exclusive economic zone (EEZ), 2019 and 2025)
''Source:'' Mercator Ocean International, Copernicus Marine Service, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_14_60}}|alt= A double vertical bar chart showing marine waters affected by eutrophication as a percentage of the exclusive economic zone (EEZ) in 2019 and 2025 in the EU and EU Member States. The bars show the years.]] ===Bathing waters with excellent quality=== [[Image: Bathing waters with excellent quality by location_evaluation_2026.png|left|200px|alt= The long-term evaluation of the indicator for Bathing waters with excellent quality from 2011 to 2024 shows moderate progress towards sustainability objectives for coastal and inland bathing waters. The short-term evaluation for the period 2019 to 2024 shows no progress towards nor movement away from sustainability objectives for coastal waters and moderate movement away from sustainability objectives for inland waters.]] This indicator shows the share of inland and coastal bathing waters with excellent quality in the EU. It is calculated based on the moving average of 16 sampling events in four years to be sure that most weather events are covered. Bathing water quality is assessed according to standards for microbiological parameters (intestinal Enterococci and Escherichia coli). The [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32006L0007 Bathing Water Directive] (BWD) requires Member States to identify and assess the quality of all inland and marine bathing waters and to classify these waters as ‘poor’, ‘sufficient’, ‘good’ or ‘excellent’ depending on the levels of faecal bacteria detected. The data presented in this section stem from the European Environment Agency (EEA) and are based on Member States reporting under the BWD. [[Image: Bathing waters with excellent quality by location (% of bathing sites, EU, 2011-2024).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Bathing waters with excellent quality, by location (% of bathing waters, EU, 2011–2024)
''Source:'' EEA, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_14_40}}|alt= A line chart with two lines showing percentage of bathing waters with excellent quality, by location, in the EU from 2011 to 2023. The lines show percentages for coastal waters and inland waters.]]
[[Image: Bathing waters with excellent quality by location (% of bathing sites, 2024).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Bathing waters with excellent quality, by location (% of bathing waters, 2024)
''Source:'' EEA, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_14_40}}|alt= A double vertical bar chart showing percentage of bathing waters with excellent quality by location in 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and other European countries. The bars represent percentages for coastal waters and inland waters.]] ===Marine protected areas=== [[Image: Marine protected areas_evaluation_2026.png|left|200px|alt= The long-term evaluation of the indicator for marine protected areas for the period 2012 to 2023 shows significant progress towards the EU target. The short-term evaluation for the period 2019 to 2023 shows moderate progress towards the EU target.]] This indicator measures the proportion of EU marine waters designated as marine protected areas (MPAs). MPAs are biodiversity ‘hotspots’ and can serve various objectives including species and habitats protection, biodiversity conservation and restoration, but also resource use within defined ecological boundaries. MPAs may also benefit neighbouring areas. The indicator comprises nationally designated protected areas and Natura 2000 sites. A nationally designated area is an area protected by national legislation. The Natura 2000 network comprises both marine and terrestrial protected areas designated under the EU Habitats and Birds Directives with the goal to maintain or restore a favourable conservation status for habitat types and species of EU interest. The EU biodiversity strategy for 2030 aims to protect at least 30% of land and sea in Europe, including both nationally designated sites and Natura 2000 sites. Data provided by the Member States to the Commission are consolidated by the European Environment Agency and collected by European Commission Directorate-General for the Environment. [[Image: Marine protected areas (% of marine area, EU, 2012-2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Marine protected areas (% of marine area, EU, 2012–2023)
''Source:'' EEA, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_14_10}}|alt= A vertical bar chart with a dot showing the marine protected areas as a percentage of marine areas for the years 2012, 2016, 2019, 2021, 2022 and 2023 in the EU. The dot shows the 2030 target.]]
[[Image: Marine protected areas (% of marine area, 2019 and 2023).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 7: Marine protected areas (% of marine area, 2019 and 2023)
''Source:'' EEA, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_14_10}}|alt= A double vertical bar chart showing the marine protected areas as a percentage of marine areas in 2019 and 2023 in the EU and EU Member States. The bars show the years.]] ===Estimated trends in fish stock biomass=== [[Image: Estimated trends in fish stock biomass_evaluation_2026.png|left|200px|alt= The long-term evaluation of the indicator for estimated trends in fish stock biomass for the period 2008 to 2023 shows significant progress towards sustainability objectives. The short-term evaluation for the period 2018 to 2023 also shows significant progress towards sustainability objectives.]] Fish stock biomass is a function of biological characteristics such as abundance and weight, and can indicate the status of a fish stock when measured against reference values. This is a model-based indicator that is computed using results from single-species quantitative stock assessments. It shows the median value of fish stock biomass relative to 2003. The full time series is updated every year, sometimes including new stocks due to newly available quantitative assessments which can result in small differences from one release year to the next. [[Image: Estimated trends in fish stock biomass by fishing area (index 2003 = 100, 2003-2024).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 8: Estimated trends in fish stock biomass, by fishing area (index 2003 = 100, 2003–2024)
''Source:'' Joint Research Centre (JRC) — Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF), Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_14_21}}|alt= A line chart with three lines showing the estimated trends in fish stock biomass from 2003 to 2024, indexed to 2003. The lines represent the estimated trends for EU total marine waters, Northeast Atlantic (or the FAO area 27) and the Mediterranean and Black Sea (FAO area 37).]] === Estimated trends in fishing pressure=== [[Image: Estimated trends in fishing pressure_evaluation_2026.png|left|200px|alt= The long-term evaluation of the indicator for estimated trends in fishing pressure for the period 2008 to 2023 shows significant progress towards sustainability objectives. The short-term evaluation for the period 2018 to 2023 also shows significant progress towards sustainability objectives.]] The indicator presents the model-based median value of fishing pressure (F/FMSY) in EU marine waters of the North-East Atlantic and adjacent seas (FAO area 27) and the Mediterranean and the Black Sea (FAO area 37), for which current fishing mortality (F) exceeds the estimated fishing mortality consistent with achieving maximum sustainable yield (FMSY). Fishing mortality is a measure for death or removal of fish from a population due to fishing. The fishing mortality rate consistent with achieving maximum sustainable yield is determined by the long-term average stock size that allows fishing at this level. For fisheries to be sustainable, F should not exceed FMSY — the point at which the largest catch can be taken from a fish stock over an indefinite period without harming it. The model-based median value of fishing pressure (F/FMSY) indicates the trend of exploitation: values below 1 indicate sustainable fishing levels (F ≤ FMSY). [[Image: Estimated trends in fishing pressure by fishing area (model-based median value of fishing pressure (F_FMSY), 2003-2024).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 9: Estimated trends in fishing pressure, by fishing area (model-based median value of fishing pressure (F/FMSY), 2003–2024)
''Source:'' Joint Research Centre (JRC) — Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF), Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_14_30}}|alt= A line chart with three lines and a highlighted area showing the estimated trends in fishing pressure as a model-based median value of fishing pressure from 2003 to 2024. The lines represent the estimated trends for EU total marine waters, Northeast Atlantic (or the FAO area 27) and the Mediterranean and Black Sea (FAO area 37); and the highlighted area represents the sustainable fishing level.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media: SDG 14 - 2026 edition.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Context === '''Ocean health and marine conservation''' The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32008L0056 Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD)] aims for good environmental status in EU waters and promotes marine protected areas, while the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32014L0089 Maritime Spatial Planning Directive] (MSPD) supports the integration of ocean health and marine conservation objectives into maritime spatial planning. The [https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe/eu-missions-horizon-europe/restore-our-ocean-and-waters_en EU Mission ‘Restore our Ocean and Waters'], launched in September 2021, aims to protect and restore the health of our ocean and waters by 2030 through research and innovation, citizen engagement, the development of a Digital Twin Ocean, and investments in the sustainable blue economy. The [https://oceans-and-fisheries.ec.europa.eu/european-ocean-pact_en European Ocean Pact] adopted in June 2025 aims at bringing together EU ocean policies under one single and coordinated framework. The [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/water/water-framework-directive_en Water Framework Directive] requires Member States to draw up management plans to ensure good ecological status of coastal waters. The [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32006L0007 EU Bathing Water Directive] lays down provisions for monitoring bathing water quality at designated bathing sites. The [https://www.cbd.int/doc/c/abb5/591f/2e46096d3f0330b08ce87a45/wg2020-03-03-en.pdf UN Biodiversity Conference (COP 15)] in 2022 adopted a global biodiversity framework to protect at least 30% of the global sea areas by 2030. The [https://www.un.org/bbnjagreement/sites/default/files/2024-08/Text%20of%20the%20Agreement%20in%20English.pdf BBNJ Agreement] establishes a global framework for protecting marine biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction. The European Commission has adopted a [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52025PC0173 proposal] to transpose the agreement into Union law in 2025. The 3rd UN Ocean Conference in 2025 [https://www.un.org/pga/wp-content/uploads/sites/109/2025/05/UNOC3-declaration-final.pdf called for ambitious, united and urgent actions] to protect, conserve, sustainably use and restore the ocean and its ecosystems. The EU [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0380 Biodiversity Strategy for 2030] aims to achieve good environmental status for marine ecosystems and introduces the target of protecting at least 30 % of EU seas by 2030. Additionally, the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/nature-and-biodiversity/nature-restoration-law_en Nature Restoration Regulation] sets binding targets to restore European habitats in poor condition, including marine and coastal ecosystems. The EU [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A01992L0043-20130701 Habitats Directive] contributes to the conservation of marine habitat types and species. Making ocean sustainability a reality by 2030 is one of the four pillars of the EU’s updated [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=JOIN:2022:28:FIN International Ocean Governance Agenda]. The EU combats marine pollution through a wide set of legal instruments on [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32008L0098 waste management], [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32019L0883 port reception facilities] and [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/904/oj single-use plastics]. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM%3A2021%3A400%3AFIN&qid=1620981596225 Zero Pollution Action Plan for Air, Water and Soil] sets out key actions to improve water quality by reducing emissions of waste, plastic litter at sea and microplastics. The EU [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/3101/oj/eng Ship-Source Pollution Directive] strengthens measures to prevent and respond to marine pollution caused by illegal discharges from ships. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2021:82:FIN EU strategy on adaptation to climate change] aims to tackle ocean acidification and encourage nature-based solutions for sustaining Europe’s seas. '''Sustainable fisheries''' The [https://oceans-and-fisheries.ec.europa.eu/policy/common-fisheries-policy-cfp_en Common Fisheries Policy] (CFP) aims at ensuring that fishing and aquaculture activities are environmentally and socio-economically sustainable in the long-term. The EU [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2008/1005/oj/eng IUU Regulation] aims to combat illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. The [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM%3A2023%3A102%3AFIN&qid=1676984139637 Action plan on protecting and restoring marine ecosystems for sustainable and resilient fisheries] contributes to the delivery of the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Sustainable development goals|All articles on sustainable development goals]] *[[Fisheries - catches and landings|Fisheries - catches and landings]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/database Sustainable development indicators] ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=sdi}} Sustainable development indicators] ===Methodology=== More detailed information on EU SDG indicators for monitoring of progress towards the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), such as indicator relevance, definitions, methodological notes, background and potential linkages can be found in the [[SDG - Introduction|introduction]] as well as in Annex II of the publication {{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-064|title=’Sustainable development in the European Union — Monitoring report on progress towards the SDGs in an EU context — 2026 edition’}}. ===Publications=== '''Further reading on life below water''' *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/healthy-seas-thriving-fisheries EEA (2024), Healthy seas, thriving fisheries: transitioning to an environmentally sustainable sector.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/how-climate-change-impacts EEA (2024), How climate change impacts marine life.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/european-marine-litter-assessment EEA (2024), From source to sea — The untold story of marine litter.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/european-bathing-water-quality-in-2023 EEA (2024), European bathing water quality in 2023.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/marine-messages-2 EEA (2019), Marine Messages II. Navigating the course towards clean, healthy and productive seas through implementation of an ecosystem-based approach, EEA Report No 17/2019, European Environment Agency, Copenhagen.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/european-bathing-water-quality-in-2023 EEA (2024), European bathing water quality in 2023.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/europes-marine-biodiversity-remains-under-pressure/europes-marine-biodiversity-remains-under-pressure EEA (2021). Europe’s marine biodiversity remains under pressure.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/marine-messages-2 EEA (2019), Marine Messages II. Navigating the course towards clean, healthy and productive seas through implementation of an ecosystem-based approach, EEA Report No 17/2019, European Environment Agency, Copenhagen.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/nutrient-enrichment-and-eutrophication-in EEA (2019), Nutrient enrichment and eutrophication in Europe's seas, EEA Report No 14/2019, European Environment Agency, Copenhagen.] *[https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/06690fd0-d133-424c-9673-1849e414543d FAO (2024), The State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture 2024 – Blue Transformation in action, Rome.] *[https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC137731 Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF) (2024), Monitoring the performance of the Common Fisheries Policy (STECF-Adhoc-24-01).] *[https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000375147 UNESCO (2020), Global Ocean Science Report — Charting Capacity for Ocean Sustainability, K. Isensee et al. (eds), UNESCO Publishing, Paris.] ===External links=== '''Further data sources on life below water''' *[https://ec.europa.eu/maritimeaffairs/atlas/maritime_atlas/ Directorate-General for Maritime Affairs and Fisheries, European Atlas of the Seas.] *[https://marine.copernicus.eu/ European Commission, Copernicus Marine Service] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/marine-protected-areas-in-europes-seas EEA, Marine protected areas in Europe's seas.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/data-and-maps/indicators/nutrients-in-transitional-coastal-and-4/assessment EEA, Nutrients in transitional, coastal and marine waters.] *[https://www.eea.europa.eu/data-and-maps/explore-interactive-maps/state-of-bathing-waters-in-2023 EEA, State of bathing waters in 2023 – interactive map.] *[http://www.emodnet.eu/ European Marine Observation and Data Network (EMODnet).] *[https://www.soest.hawaii.edu/soestwp/research/data/hawaii-ocean-timeseries-hot-database/ School of Ocean and Earth Science and Technology at the University of Hawai'i, Hawaii Ocean Time Series (HOT).] === Footnotes === {{Unit|topic=X_Sustainable_development_indicators}} [[Category:EU policy indicators|SDG 14 - Life below water]] [[Category:Sustainable development|SDG 14 - Life below water]] [[Category:Biodiversity|SDG 14 - Life below water]] [[Category:Statistical article|SDG 14 - Life below water]] [[Category:Sustainable development goals|SDG 14 - Life below water]] [[Category:Water|SDG 14 - Life below water]]

title: Rural development statistics
text:
Data from March 2025. Planned article update: 2030 The number of agricultural holdings receiving rural development support is estimated to have more than doubled between 2010 and 2020. In a majority of EU countries at least one half of agricultural holdings received rural development support. The range was from 97% of all holdings in Finland to 4% of all holdings in Romania. The most common form of support in 2020 was for natural constraints (covered by biophysical criteria concerning the climate, soil and terrain, such as dryness, limited soil drainage and steep slopes).
[[Image:Rural Development Visual 02 1920x1080 REVISION-100.jpg|centre|700px|thumb|''Source'': Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_m_rd}}]]

This article provides information about the agricultural holdings in the EU that received rural development support in 2020, as well as the managers of those holdings. Rural development support is jointly funded by EU and national budgets. Note that it does not look at levels of monetary support; this information is not captured in the agricultural census. The article consists of an overview of data, complemented by all information on [[#Methodology|definitions,]] [[#Methodology|measurement methods]] and [[#Context|context]] needed to interpret them correctly. ===Understanding the common population of agricultural holdings=== There were 9.1 million agricultural holdings in the EU in 2020, of which 6.4 million holdings formed what is called ‘the common population’. The common population represents holdings of a certain size (above one of a number of [[Integrated farm statistics - impact of changes in coverage|thresholds]]); it excludes holdings that have kitchen gardens (no market activity) and many of the holdings clearly producing farming goods only for their own subsistence, without market activity. This subset of holdings is used for comparisons across time and in those cases where data for the full population is unavailable. Most of the agricultural holdings outside the common population in 2020 were in Romania (see Figure 1); 1.9 million holdings were excluded from the overall 2.9 million agricultural holdings in Romania. Note that most of the holdings in Romania (90.3%) were smaller than 5 ha (for more information see [[Farms and farmland in the European Union - statistics|Farms and farmland in the European Union]]). A further 0.3 million holdings in Poland were excluded from the common population in 2020, with half this number also being excluded in Italy. No holdings were excluded from the common populations of 12 EU countries. [[Image:Fig1 27022025 Agricultural holdings in EU countries (2020).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Agricultural holdings in EU countries (2020)
''Source'': Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_m_farmleg}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_m_rd}}|alt= double column chart showing the number of total number of agricultural holdings and the number of holdings in the common population in each EU country, for the year 2020.]] ===Who got support in 2020?=== Data on rural development support for all agricultural holdings are not available for Spain, Lithuania or Slovenia and, as a result, not for the EU as a whole. However, data are available for holdings above the thresholds of the common population for all EU countries and the EU. Almost two-fifths (38.0%) of the holdings that formed the common population in the EU received rural development support in 2020. This means that about 60% of the EU’s agricultural holdings in the common population were not beneficiaries of this [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy/financing-cap/cap-funds_en second pillar] of the EU's [[Glossary:Common_agricultural_policy_(CAP)|common agricultural policy]]. Among EU countries, Romania had the lowest share (4.0%) of all holdings receiving rural development support in 2020. The share of holdings within the common population in Romania that received rural development support was marginally higher at 7.8% higher. Both shares are shown in Figure 2 below. Poland had 1.3 million agricultural holdings in 2020, the second highest number among EU countries. Just under two-thirds (65.7%) of all its holdings received rural development support in 2020. Italy had 1.1 million agricultural holdings in 2020, with just over one-fifth (22.6%) receiving rural development support. The EU countries with the highest proportion of their agricultural holdings receiving rural development support were Finland (97.4%) and Luxembourg (90.4%). By contrast, the shares in Romania (4.0%) and the Netherlands (7.3%) were the lowest.
[[Image:Fig2 27022025 Share of agricultural holdings in each EU country .png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Share of agricultural holdings in each EU country receiving rural development support, 2020
''Source'': Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_m_rd}}|alt= double column chart showing the share of all holdings and the share of all holdings in the common population in each EU country that receive rural development support, for the year 2020. Data for the EU, Spain, Lithuania and Slovenia are unavailable for all holdings.]] ===What kind of support was provided in 2020?=== EU countries could choose from 20 broad measures for [[Glossary:Rural development|rural development]] support. For the purposes of this analysis, these measures were grouped into: * investments * farm and business developments * commitments * area-specific disadvantages * natural constraints * knowledge exchange * cooperation The most common form of rural development support provided in 2020 was for natural constraints (these are covered by biophysical criteria concerning the climate, soil and terrain, such as dryness, limited soil drainage and steep slopes): 1.9 million agricultural holdings in the common population (above threshold) received support in this form, equivalent to 80% of agricultural holdings in the common population receiving some form of rural development support (see Figure 3). Also, 0.9 million agricultural holdings in the common population received support for commitment measures (such as for animal welfare, for organic farming, for the environment and climate, and to support genetic resources); this was equivalent to 37% of agricultural holdings in the common population receiving some form of rural development support. Note that holdings may have received more than one measure of support. By contrast, relatively few agricultural holdings received support in the forms of measures for area-specific disadvantages (habitat and water framework directive), cooperation (quality schemes) or knowledge exchange (farm advisory services). [[Image:Fig3 27022025 Share of agricultural holdings .png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Share of agricultural holdings receiving different measures of rural development in the EU, 2020
''Source'': Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_m_rd}}|alt= bar chart showing the share of agricultural holdings in the EU receiving different measures of rural development, in 2020.]] Among EU countries, there were some noticeable differences in the distribution of rural development support being provided to agricultural holdings in the common population, including: * Almost one half (47%) of agricultural holdings receiving rural development support in Estonia did so for knowledge exchange measures. The proportion was also relatively high in Slovenia (39%). The EU share was 2%. * 30% of agricultural holdings receiving rural development support in Austria did so for cooperation measures. The EU share was 2%. * Between 25% and 30% of agricultural holdings receiving rural development support in Bulgaria, Denmark and Hungary did so for area-specific disadvantage measures. The EU share was 3%. * Slightly more than one quarter (28%) of agricultural holdings receiving rural development support in Romania did so for farm and business development measures. The share was also relatively high in Slovenia (21%). The EU share was 6%. * A majority (59%) of agricultural holdings receiving rural development support in Bulgaria did so for investment measures. The share was also relatively high in the Netherlands (36%). The EU share was 10%. ===What kind of agricultural holdings received rural development support?=== '''Analysis at economic level''' The EU had 3.4 million agricultural holdings that had a standard output below €2 000 per year in 2020. Within the common population, there were 1.0 million agricultural holdings that had a standard output below €2 000 per year in 2020. Of these very small agricultural holdings, 168 000 were beneficiaries of rural development measures in the common population. Whereas these very small agricultural holdings represented 38% of all holdings in the EU in 2020, they only represented 7% of all the holdings in the common population that received some rural development support. By contrast, the EU had 0.7 million agricultural holdings that had a standard output above €100 000 per year in 2020. All these holdings appeared in the common population. Whereas these ‘large’ holdings represented 8% of all the EU’s agricultural holdings in 2020, they represented 17% of all the holdings in the common population that received some rural development support (see Figure 4). Within this standard output range were small agricultural holdings, presented here as having a standard output of between €2 000 and €25 000 per year, and medium-sized holdings with a standard output of between €25 000 per year and €100 000 per year. There were 3.9 million agricultural holdings in the EU that had a standard output of between €2 000 and €25 000 per year in 2020. These small agricultural holdings represented 43% of all the EU’s agricultural holdings, but 52% of all the holdings in the common population that received some rural development support. The remaining 1.0 million holdings in the EU can be considered as medium-sized holdings, with a standard output of between €25 000 per year and €100 000 per year. These medium-sized agricultural holdings represented 11% of all the EU’s agricultural holdings, but 24% of all the holdings in the common population that received some rural development support. Among EU countries, there were some noticeable differences compared with the EU averages: * Almost 40% of all the holdings in the common population receiving rural development support in Latvia were very small holdings with a standard output of less than €2 000 per year. Shares were also relatively high in Cyprus (33%) and Portugal (20%). * Most (90%) of the holdings in the common population (above threshold) receiving rural development support in the Netherlands were large holdings with a standard output above €100 000 per year. Shares were also relatively high in Belgium (66%), France (56%) and Luxembourg (55%). [[Image:Fig4 28022025 Distribution of agricultural holdings receiving rural development support, by economic size class (%, 2020).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Distribution of agricultural holdings receiving rural development support, 2020
''Source'': Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_m_rd}}|alt=A 100% stacked bar graph showing distribution of holdings within the common population receiving rural development support by five economic size classes for each EU country.]] '''Analysis at physical size level''' The agricultural holdings in the EU’s common population (above threshold) farmed 152.4 million hectares of utilised agricultural area (UAA) in 2020 The EU’s total UAA in 2020 was 157.4 million hectares. Outside, the common population, there were 2.7 million holdings that farmed 5.0 million hectares of UAA, underlining the very small nature of these holdings. . Just under two-thirds (about 63%) of this utilised agricultural area was farmed by agricultural holdings in the common population that received rural development support in 2020, a much higher proportion than the corresponding share of holdings receiving support (about 38%). Among EU countries, the range of shares was similar to the shares at holding level: the highest shares of UAA covered were in Finland and Luxembourg (both above 99%), with the lowest shares in Denmark (20%), and Romania and the Netherlands (both 14%). The majority of holdings in the common population that received rural development support were also of a medium-size in terms of hectares of UAA. Holdings of between 5 ha and 29.9 ha represented almost one half (47%) of all holdings in the common population that received rural development support. A further 19% of holdings within this common population had UAA of between 30 ha and 99.9 ha and received rural development support. Holdings of less than 5 ha (the smallest holdings) accounted for one quarter of the holdings that received rural development support. By contrast, the largest holdings with over 100 ha of UAA represented only 9% of the holdings in the common population that received rural development support. '''Analysis at farm type level''' Almost three-fifths (58%) of all agricultural holdings in the EU were crop specialist farms in 2020 (see Figure 5). The proportion of agricultural holdings in the common population receiving rural development support in 2020 that were crop specialist farms was slightly lower at 52%. Conversely, the proportion of agricultural holdings in the common population receiving rural development support in 2020 that were livestock specialists was notably higher than the overall share of specialist livestock farms (32% compared with 22%). [[Image:Fig5 27022025 Specialist holdings (% shares, EU, 2020).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Specialist holdings, EU, 2020
''Source'': Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_farmleg}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_m_rd}}|alt=A double bar graph showing the shares of holdings in the EU that were specialist crop farms, specialist livestock farms and mix farms, both for all agricultural holdings and the agricultural holdings within the common population, in 2020.]] ===What are the characteristics of the farm managers obtaining rural development support?=== Farm managers in the EU have different levels of training: there are those with full agricultural training, those with basic training and those with only practical experience. In 2020, only 1 in every 10 (10.2%) farm managers in the EU had full agricultural training. However, 1 in every 5 (21.4%) of the holdings in the common population that received rural development support had a manager that had full agricultural training (see Figure 6). In 2020, there were 1.6 million agricultural holdings that were managed by someone with only basic agricultural training, the equivalent of 17.5% of all farm managers. Nevertheless, about one quarter (25.5%) of the holdings in the common population that received rural development support had a manager with only basic training. About 6.6 million agricultural holdings in the EU were managed by someone with only practical experience in 2020, the equivalent of 72.4% of all farm managers. However, just over one half (53.1%) of the holdings in the common population that received rural development support were managed by someone with practical experience only. [[Image:Fig6 27022025 Farm managers by educational attainment (% shares, EU, 2020).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Farm managers by educational attainment, EU, 2020
''Source'': Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_mp_training}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_m_rd}}|alt=A double bar graph showing the shares of farm managers in the EU that had either only practical experience, only basic training, or full agricultural training, both for all agricultural holdings and the agricultural holdings within the common population, in 2020.]] Around one third (33.2%) of the farm managers on the EU’s 9.1 million agricultural holdings in 2020 were aged 65 years and over. A much lower proportion of the agricultural holdings in the common population that received rural development support were managed by persons aged 65 years or older (19.0%). The relative proportions of holdings receiving rural development support were all higher in the other age categories of farm managers than for the corresponding shares for all holdings (see Figure 7). [[Image:Fig7 27022025 Farm managers by age (% shares, EU, 2020).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 7: Farm managers by age, EU, 2020
''Source'': Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_mp_training}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_m_rd}}|alt=A double bar graph showing the shares of farm managers in the EU according to six age classes, both for all agricultural holdings and the agricultural holdings within the common population, in 2020.]] In 2020, 68.4% of the EU’s farm managers were male and 31.6% female (see Figure 8). Among the holdings of the common population that received rural development support in 2020, 74.2% of farm managers were male and 25.8% female. [[Image:Fig8 27022025 Farm managers by sex (% shares, EU, 2020).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 8: Farm managers by sex, EU, 2020
''Source'': Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_farmang}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=ef_rd_man}}|alt=A double bar graph showing the shares of farm managers in the EU according to sex, both for all agricultural holdings and the agricultural holdings within the common population, in 2020.]] ===How has support changed over time?=== There were some notable developments in the rural development support provided to agricultural holdings between 2010 and 2020: * despite a sharp decline in the number of EU agricultural holdings in the census basic population between 2010 and 2020 (a loss of about 3.0 million farms), the number of holdings within the common populations receiving rural development support increased from about 1.1 million holdings to 2.4 million holdings. * as a result, the share of holdings within the common populations receiving rural development support increased considerably: the share in 2010 was 14%, rising to 38% in 2020. * the share of utilised agricultural area covered by holdings within the common populations receiving rural development support also rose sharply: from 38% in 2010 to 63% in 2020. * the shares of the smallest holdings receiving rural development support increased slightly between 2010 and 2020. For the very smallest holdings with an economic output below €2 000 per year, the share rose from 5% to 7% of the EU’s agricultural holdings in the common population. For small holdings with a standard output between €2 000 and €24 999 per year receiving rural development support the share increased from 46% to 52%. * the shares of medium-sized and large agricultural holdings receiving rural development support declined slightly between 2010 and 2020. For medium-sized holdings with an economic output between €25 000 and €99 999 per year, the share declined from 29% to 24% of all agricultural holdings in the common population. The share for the largest agricultural holdings (with a standard output above €100 000 per year) declined from 20% to 17%. ===Source data for tables and graphs=== *[[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] [[Media:SE Rural development 28022025.xlsx|Rural development statistics]] ===Data sources=== The tables {{Template:Publication|code=ef_m_rd|title=ef_m_rd}} and {{Template:Publication|code=ef_rd_man|title=ef_rd_man}} contain the population covered by the module rural development sent to Eurostat in 2020 detailed in item 3.6.2 in the metadata file for each country. Virtual entities (common land units without a farm manager) are excluded from the table as they are not agricultural holdings according to the definition set in Art 2(a) of the Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 July 2018. The dimension STATINFO refers to the thresholds laid down in Annex II of the Regulation (EU) 2018/1091. ABVTH (above threshold) corresponds to the agricultural holdings that meet at least one of the physical thresholds listed in Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 with regards to the size of agricultural land or the number of livestock units. BLWTH (below threshold) corresponds to the agricultural holdings that fall below all physical thresholds listed in Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 with regards to the size of agricultural land or the number of livestock units. TOTAL corresponds to all agricultural holdings. For a few countries (namely Spain, Slovenia, and Lithuania), the data of this table do not cover the agricultural holdings accounting for at least 98% of the total utilised agricultural area (without kitchen gardens) and at least 98% of the total livestock units of the country and the data cover only the ABVTH (above threshold) category. While this complies with Regulation (EU) 2018/1091, it limits the comparability across all countries in 2020. Further details about the coverage and limitations in the comparability of the data across and within years can be found in the latest IFS handbook in Section 9.7. === Context === Rural development is the 'second pillar' of the [[Glossary:Common agricultural policy (CAP)|common agricultural policy (CAP)]], reinforcing the ‘first pillar’ of income support and market measures, by strengthening the social, environmental and economic sustainability of rural areas. The main objectives of rural development support measures are to (i) foster the competitiveness of agriculture and forestry, (ii) ensure the sustainable management of natural resources and climate action and (iii) achieve a balanced territorial development of rural economies and communities, including the creation and maintenance of employment. Rural development programs are funded jointly by the European agricultural fund for rural development (EAFRD) and national budgets, and may be prepared on either a national or regional basis. Since the 2023 reform of the CAP, the rural development actions have been included in national CAP strategic plans. Provisions were made in {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32013R1305:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 1305/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council}} to provide €93 billion to EU countries in rural development support measures for agriculture, forestry and environment / natural resources management as well as the sustainable development of the rural economy for the period from 2014 to 2020. '''Policy''' When designing their rural development programmes (RDPs), EU countries may apply funding from the European fund for rural development (EAFRD) through a number of measures. Countries choose from twenty broad measures, which are further broken down into more [https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy/rural-development/measures_en#:~:text=When%20designing%20their%20rural%20development%20programmes%20%28RDPs%29%2C%20EU,are%20further%20broken%20down%20into%20more%20specific%20sub-measures. specific sub-measures]. These measures can be directed towards one or more of the EAFRD’s priority areas. In their RDPs, EU countries must indicate which measures they have used and how they will contribute towards the priorities of the EAFRD. These measures cover: 1. Knowledge transfer and information 2. Advisory services, farm management and relief services 3. Quality schemes for agriproducts and foodstuffs 4. Investments in physical assets 5. Natural disasters: restoring production potential and preventing damage 6. Farm and business development 7. Basic services and village renewal in rural areas 8. Investments in forest area development and improvement of the viability of forests 9. Setting up of producer groups and organisations 10. Agri-environment-climate 11. Organic farming 12. Natura 2000 and Water Framework Directive payments 13. Payments to areas facing natural or other specific constraints 14. Animal welfare 15. Forest-environmental and climate services and forest conservation 16. Cooperation 17. Risk management 18. Complementary direct payments for Croatia 19. Support for LEADER local development (CLLD) 20. Technical assistance ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/database Agriculture (agr)], see: :Farm structure (ef) ::Main farm indicators by NUTS 2 region (ef_mainfarm) :::Main farm indicators by rural development support measures, utilized agricultural area, type and economic size of the farm and NUTS 2 region (ef_m_rd) :Rural development measures (ef_rd) :::Beneficiary of rural development support measures by age, sex and training of farm manager and NUTS 2 region (ef_rd_man) :::Beneficiary of rural development support measures by legal form, economic size and farm type of the agricultural holding and NUTS 2 region (ef_rd_leg) === Dedicated section === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/agriculture/overview Agriculture] === Publications === *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-24-000|title=Key figures on the European food chain – 2024 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-24-024|title=A look at European farms – agricultural census results}} ===Other articles=== *[[Farms_and_farmland_in_the_European_Union_-_statistics|Farms and farmland in the EU]] *[[Agriculture_statistics_-_family_farming_in_the_EU|Family farming in the EU]] *[[Farm_tenure|Farm tenure]] *[[Farmers_and_the_agricultural_labour_force_-_statistics|Farmers and the agricultural labour force]] *[[Integrated farm statistics - methodological articles]] * [[Integrated farm statistics - impact of changes in coverage|Integrated farm statistics - impact of changes in coverage]] (methodological article) === Legislation === *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R1166:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1166/2008}} of the European Parliament and of the Council on farm structure surveys and the survey on agricultural production methods (farm structure survey from 2010 to 2016) * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=legissum:4369111 Summaries of EU Legislation: EU integrated farm statistics] *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32014R0715:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) No 715/2014}} of 26 June 2014 amending Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 1166/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council on farm structure surveys and the survey on agricultural production methods, as regards the list of characteristics to be collected in the farm structure survey 2016 '''Implementing legislation''' *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32009R1200:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EC) No 1200/2009}} implementing Regulation (EC) No 1166/2008 on farm structure surveys and the survey on agricultural production methods (farm structure survey from 2010 to 2016) *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32015R1391:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) 2015/1391}} amending Regulation (EC) No 1200/2009 *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R1874:EN:NOT|title=Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/1874}} of 29 November 2018 on the data to be provided for 2020 under Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 of the European Parliament and of the Council on integrated farm statistics and repealing Regulations (EC) No 1166/2008 and (EU) No 1337/2011, as regards the list of variables and their description (Text with EEA relevance.)
