title: Social protection statistics - family and children benefits
text:
EU statistics concerning expenditure on family/children social benefits. Data extracted in March 2026 Planned article update: April 2027 In 2023, €400 billion was spent on family/children benefits in the EU, amounting to 2.3% of GDP. In 2023, expenditure on family/children benefits in the EU was equivalent to 8.7% of all expenditure on social benefits. EU expenditure on family/children benefits rose by 51.3% in real terms between 2000 and 2023, despite a decline of 8.5% in the number of children aged less than 18 years. [[Glossary:Social_protection_benefits|Social protection benefits]] are transfers, in cash or in kind, made to relieve households and individuals of the burden of one or more social risks or needs. This article presents statistics on social protection benefits intended to address the risks and needs associated with family and children. The data are collected annually through the [[Glossary:European_system_of_integrated_social_protection_statistics_(ESSPROS)|European system of integrated social protection statistics (ESSPROS)]]. These benefits are those classified as family/children benefits in the ESSPROS classification (see Figure 6). Education benefits are generally excluded from social protection. This article provides some facts looking from the perspective of a country’s expenditure on family/children benefits; to look at the impact of these social protection benefits and what they mean for people, other socio-economic aspects would need to be considered. === Family/children expenditure in 2023 === In 2023, expenditure across the [[Glossary:EU enlargements|European Union (EU)]] on family/children benefits was €400 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]], which was equivalent to 2.3% of [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|GDP]]. The level of spending varied between [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU countries]], ranging from a high of 3.5% of GDP in Germany to lows of 0.8% in Malta and 0.9% in Cyprus (see Figure 1). [[Image:Expenditure on family_children benefits, 2023_(% of GDP)_SPS2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Expenditure on family/children benefits, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e97f6503-3df5-4beb-9a12-43c212aca858?lang=en spr_exp_func])|alt=A column chart showing expenditure on family and children benefits relative to GDP. Data are presented in percent for 2023. Data are shown for the EU and for EU, EFTA and candidate countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, expenditure on family/children benefits in the EU amounted to 8.7% of total expenditure on [[Glossary:Social_benefits|social benefits]]. The relative importance of family/children benefits varied between EU countries. The highest share was in Luxembourg, with 14.7% of all expenditure on social benefits; double-digit shares were also recorded in 10 other EU countries. At the other end of the range, 5.0% or less of total expenditure on social benefits was devoted to family/children benefits in Cyprus (4.7%), Greece (4.9%) and the Netherlands (5.0%) – see Figure 2. [[Image:Expenditure on family_children benefits, 2023 (% of expenditure on social benefits)_SPS2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Expenditure on family/children benefits, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/df75ce1e-97a7-479e-86f7-ffee24f853bf?lang=en spr_exp_func])|alt=A column chart showing expenditure on family and children benefits as a share of expenditure on social benefits. Data are presented in percent for 2023. Data are shown for the EU and for EU, EFTA and candidate countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] It should be considered that the proportion of expenditure on social benefits allocated to family/children benefits is impacted by the amounts spent on other areas of social protection, which are in turn affected by a vast array of socioeconomic factors. For example, expenditure on unemployment-related benefits is linked (among other factors) to the state of the labour market, while expenditure on old-age pensions is linked (among other factors) to the demographic structure of the population. In the case of expenditure on family/children benefits, there is likely to be some link with fertility rates and the share of children within the population. A better comparison of expenditure levels for family/children benefits might therefore be to consider expenditure per child; this can be obtained using the average level of expenditure for each person aged less than 18. This comparison may be made in euro (€) terms or alternatively in [[Glossary:Purchasing_power_standard_(PPS)|purchasing power standard (PPS)]] terms (see Figure 3); the latter eliminates price level differences between countries. Note that the demographic data used in this section refer to the number of inhabitants aged less than 18 years. In making this comparison, users need to be aware that the figures for some countries may be overstated because the expenditure also includes amounts paid out with respect to dependent children aged 18 years or over and/or to relatives other than children. [[Image:Expenditure on family children benefits per child, 2023 (EUR and PPS per child)_SPS2026_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Expenditure on family/children benefits per child, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/386dc93e-3851-46b3-af83-1d225beecfae?lang=en spr_exp_func] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2c09d10a-25fa-4dfe-8388-e52ff650f662?lang=en demo_pjan])|alt=A double column chart showing average expenditure on family and children benefits per child. Data are presented in euro and purchasing power standard terms for 2023. Data are shown for the EU and for EU, EFTA and candidate countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] EU expenditure on family/children benefits in 2023 amounted to an average of 5 215 PPS per child but varied considerably across EU countries. The average level of expenditure on family/children benefits was particularly high in Luxembourg, where this ratio was 14 817 PPS per child, with relatively high levels of spending directed to non-means-tested family-related benefits. It should be noted that this figure is likely to overestimate the true level of expenditure per resident child substantially, as a large proportion – over a quarter – of these benefits are provided to families of workers not resident in Luxembourg. Elsewhere in the EU, the level of expenditure on family/children benefits ranged from 10 153 PPS per child in Germany down to 1 810 PPS per child in Cyprus. === Family/children expenditure between 2000 and 2023 === EU (excluding Bulgaria and Croatia) expenditure on family/children benefits (in constant price terms) rose by 51.3% between 2000 and 2023 (see Figure 4), despite a decline of 8.5% in the overall number of children aged less than 18 years during the same period. The increase in the level of expenditure for family/children benefits was broadly the same as the increase recorded for all social benefits (up overall by 51.7%). [[Image:Developments for expenditure on social benefits and family_children benefits, GDP and population aged less than 18 years, EU, 2000–23_(index, 2000 = 100)_SPS2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Developments for expenditure on social benefits and family/children benefits, GDP and population aged less than 18 years, EU, 2000–23
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c48ce652-4c66-4b32-9aa4-fd5fd200da45?lang=en spr_exp_func], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/27036ae9-abe8-42b1-b17c-92f26b6fb9e8?lang=en nama_10_gdp] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ae926ef0-30d3-477b-b836-5eab2a8ae7fd?lang=en demo_pjan])|alt=A line chart with 4 lines showing the development of expenditure on social benefits, the development of expenditure on family and children benefits, the development of GDP, and the development of the population aged less than 18 years. Data are presented for the period 2000 to 2023 in the form of indices based on 2000 equals 100. Data are shown for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The rising level of EU expenditure on family/children benefits was underpinned by increases in all EU countries for which data are available (incomplete data for Bulgaria and Croatia). During the period from 2000 to 2023, the level of expenditure on family/children benefits more than doubled (in constant price terms) in Slovakia, Latvia, Luxembourg, Spain and Cyprus, more than tripled in Lithuania and Estonia, more than quadrupled in Romania, while in Poland it was 7.1 times as high in 2023 as it had been in 2000. EU (excluding Bulgaria and Croatia) expenditure (in constant price terms) on family/children benefits rose every year between 2000 and 2010, increasing overall by 22.0% during this period. There was a modest reduction in the level of expenditure in both 2011 and 2012 (perhaps influenced by the aftermath of the global financial and economic crisis). However, expenditure resumed an upward path in 2013 and this development continued through to 2023 (other than a period of no change in 2021 and 2022). Expenditure on family/children benefits increased by 1.4% in 2023. === Composition of family/children expenditure === '''Distribution by type of benefit''' Periodic cash benefits accounted for 58.8% of expenditure on family/children benefits in the EU in 2023 and benefits in kind for 39.1%, while lump-sum cash benefits accounted for a relatively small share (2.2%) – see Figure 5. [[Image:Expenditure on family_children benefits by type, 2023 (% of total expenditure on family_children benefits)_SPS2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Expenditure on family/children benefits by type, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/50fca00e-9e22-468c-b423-4ecc8ce75efb?lang=en spr_exp_ffa])|alt=A stacked column chart showing the share of expenditure on family and children benefits by type. The stacks for each country sum to 100% and present the shares for periodic cash benefits, lump-sum cash benefits and benefits in kind. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU and for EU, EFTA and candidate countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, periodic cash benefits were the majority of expenditure on family/children benefits in all but 7 EU countries: in Finland, Denmark, Sweden, Spain, Bulgaria and Malta, a higher level of expenditure was recorded for benefits in kind than for periodic cash payments; in Croatia, the share of periodic cash benefits was just less than half, but still larger than for either of the other 2 categories. Lump-sum cash benefits accounted for less than 10.0% of expenditure on family/children benefits in all but 2 EU countries – Cyprus (29.2%) and Greece (20.7%). In Cyprus, around 90% of these lump-sum payments relate to financial assistance for families with limited resources whose children are in education Generally, education-related expenditure is outside the scope of ESSPROS. However, benefits provided exclusively to poverty-stricken families after a means test may be included in the family/children function on the basis that the objective is to redistribute income in favour of people with insufficient resources rather than to provide free access to education.. '''Distribution by detailed benefit type''' Considering expenditure across the detailed benefit classification provides further insight into the composition of expenditure on family/children benefits (see Figure 6). [[Image:Expenditure on family_children benefits by detailed benefit type, EU, 2023 (% of total expenditure on family_children benefits)_SPS2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Expenditure on family/children benefits by detailed benefit type, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/spr_exp_ffa__custom_14036531/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=1adea1db-0949-4857-ba55-3178df8e2de2&c=1733245987898 spr_exp_ffa], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/spr_exp_ffa__custom_14011878/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=a98bf28a-3967-4d9e-bdf3-5a10e57daee1&c=1733145997026 spr_exp_ffa] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/spr_exp_ffa__custom_16274680/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=db4f7866-d3dc-46f4-94d6-1f2b2a53a529&c=1744725173833 spr_exp_ffa])|alt=A bar chart showing the share of total expenditure on family and children benefits by type of disbursement. Detailed data are presented for 11 different benefit types under 3 broad headings: periodic cash benefits, lump-sum cash benefits and benefits in kind. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ESSPROS distinguishes 4 types of periodic cash benefits 1) income maintenance in the event of childbirth 2) parental leave 3) family/child allowances 4) other periodic cash benefits. Family/child allowances were by far the most common type, accounting for 42.8% of EU expenditure on family/children benefits in 2023, thus explaining why the largest form of disbursement is periodic cash benefits. Indeed, family/child allowances were the largest type of benefit in 18 EU countries, with their share of total expenditure peaking in Belgium (65.6% of all expenditure on family/children benefits). Income maintenance in the event of childbirth accounted for 6.8% of EU expenditure on family/children benefits. In Estonia, this was the largest type of benefit, with a 39.7% share. Periodic payments for parental leave accounted for 4.5% of the total in the EU but reached 31.4% in Hungary. Similarly, ESSPROS distinguishes 4 types of benefits in kind 1) child day care 2) accommodation 3) home help 4) other benefits in kind. Child day care, which accounted for 25.2% of EU expenditure on family/children benefits, was the largest type of benefit in kind and the second largest family/children benefit overall (after family/child allowances). Child day care accounted for the largest portion of total expenditure on family/children benefits in 6 EU countries (Finland, Denmark, Sweden, Spain, Slovenia and Croatia). The category of other benefits in kind, including for example access to leisure centres or price reductions for children, was also relatively noteworthy, accounting for 8.7% of total expenditure on family/children benefits in the EU. The share for this category peaked among the EU countries at 41.1% in Bulgaria. Lump-sum cash benefits can be broken down into 3 detailed benefit types 1) birth grants 2) parental leave benefits 3) other lump-sum cash benefits. None of these are particularly large in terms of their contribution to overall EU expenditure on family/children benefits as they each accounted for shares that were less than 2.0% in 2023. '''Distribution by application of means testing''' At EU level, means-tested benefits accounted for just over a quarter (26%) of total expenditure on family/children benefits in 2023 (see Figure 7). Higher shares were observed in a number of EU countries, led by Portugal (68.9%) and Cyprus (64.8%), while in Slovenia (59.2%) and Greece (57.6%) means-tested benefits also represented more than half of total expenditure. By contrast, several countries recorded low but still positive shares, including Latvia (0.2%), Slovakia (0.6%), Lithuania (2.1%) and Hungary (2.6%). No expenditure on means-tested family/children benefits was recorded in Estonia, Finland or Sweden. [[Image:Expenditure on means-tested family_children benefits, 2023 (% of total expenditure on family_children benefits)_SPS2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Expenditure on means-tested family/children benefits, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c115bf8e-62ab-441d-8a35-3589eff0c957?lang=en spr_exp_ffa])|alt=A column chart showing expenditure on means-tested family and children benefits as a share of total expenditure on family and children benefits. Data are presented in percent for 2023. Data are shown for the EU and for EU, EFTA and candidate countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Change in the composition of family/children expenditure between 2000 and 2023 === '''Distribution by type of benefit''' In the EU (excluding Bulgaria and Croatia), expenditure on family/children benefits (in constant price terms) increased for 2 of the 3 forms of disbursement during the period from 2000 to 2023 (see Figure 8). Expenditure rose at a particularly rapid pace for benefits in kind, more than doubling (up 121.7%) overall during the period under consideration, while there was also an increase in the level of expenditure for periodic cash benefits (up 28.7% overall). By contrast, lump-sum cash benefits had some relatively volatile developments – with a notable fall in expenditure between 2009 and 2012 – and fell 23.8% overall between 2000 and 2023. [[Image:Developments for expenditure on family_children benefits at constant prices (2010) by type of disbursement, EU, 2000–23 (index, 2000 = 100)_SPS2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Developments for expenditure on family/children benefits at constant prices (2010) by type of disbursement, EU, 2000–23
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/abd2964e-a43e-48cd-9d38-f52cae849d14?lang=en spr_exp_ffa])|alt=A line chart with 4 lines showing developments for expenditure on family and children benefits at constant prices by type of disbursement. The lines show periodic cash benefits, lump-sum cash benefits, benefits in kind and total expenditure. Data are presented for the period 2000 to 2023 in the form of indices based on 2000 equals 100. Data are shown for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Distribution by detailed benefit type''' Based on information that is available for 25 EU countries (excluding incomplete data for Bulgaria and Croatia), the contribution of benefits in kind to overall expenditure on family/children benefits rose over the period from 2000 to 2023 from 26.7% to 39.0% (based on current price data). By contrast, the relative contribution of periodic cash benefits and lump-sum cash benefits declined (from 68.8% to 58.9% and from 4.5% to 2.1%, respectively). As such, the increased level of expenditure for benefits in kind accounted for 48.0% of the total increase (in current price terms) in expenditure on family/children benefits between 2000 and 2023. In real terms, EU (excluding Bulgaria and Croatia) expenditure increased between 2000 and 2023 for all detailed types of family/children benefits except for lump-sum payments for parental leave (down 74.7%), home help (down 55.3%) Home help reported in the family/children function is limited to support for children. Home help targeting older people and people (including children) with disabilities are reported under assistance in carrying out daily tasks in the old-age and disability functions. and other lump-sum benefits (down 27.7%). Concerning parental leave, it is important to note that periodic parental leave benefits increased 19.0% over the same period, in absolute terms more than compensating for the overall decline in the much smaller expenditure on lump-sum benefits for parental leave (see Table 1). [[Image:Expenditure on family_children benefits by type, EU, 2000–23_SPS2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Expenditure on family/children benefits by type, EU, 2000–23
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/spr_exp_ffa__custom_20721858/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=9fcad550-605c-480e-b1f4-5344fce6616c&c=1774545844075 spr_exp_ffa] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/spr_exp_ffa__custom_20721872/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=5ca3d315-2371-4623-87f9-95ff9654bfa8&c=1774523276413 spr_exp_ffa])|alt=A table showing expenditure on family and children benefits by type. The columns of the table present data in current price terms, constant 2010 price terms and the share of family and children benefits. The rows of the table present expenditure on family and children benefits by type of disbursement, with a total and detailed data under 3 broad headings: periodic cash benefits, lump-sum cash benefits and benefits in kind. Data are shown for 2000 and 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The absolute increase in expenditure on family/children benefits between 2000 and 2023 was primarily driven by higher levels of spending for family/child allowances, child day care, other benefits in kind and income maintenance in the event of childbirth; expenditure on these types of benefit across the EU (excluding Bulgaria and Croatia) rose in current price terms by an amount between €16.5 billion (for income maintenance in the event of childbirth) and €81.4 billion (for family/child allowances) during the period under consideration. The rise in expenditure on child day care is perhaps unsurprising given that EU employment policy has strongly encouraged the importance of affordable childcare in allowing parents to work (if they want to) while raising a family. Indeed, total expenditure on child day care (in current prices) grew in all EU countries for which data are available except in *Czechia, where it fell from €390 000 to €0 *Estonia and Ireland, where there was no expenditure on child day care benefits in either 2000 or 2023. '''Distribution by application of means testing''' In 2023, means-tested benefits across the EU were more than a quarter of total expenditure on family/children benefits (26.0%), while the majority of benefits were non-means-tested (74.0%). Between 2000 and 2023, EU (excluding Bulgaria and Croatia) expenditure on means-tested family/children benefits rose by 45.1% (in real terms), while expenditure on non-means-tested benefits increased by 53.6% (see Figure 9). These similar overall figures hide contrasting developments. *Means-tested benefits tended to increase at a slower pace (than non-means-tested benefits) during the period up to and including 2008, with exceptions in 2004 and 2006. *Thereafter, there was a faster increase in the level of expenditure for means-tested benefits in the EU through to 2017 (apart from a fall in 2010). *During 2018, 2019 and 2020, means-tested benefits tended to increase at a slower pace (than non-means-tested benefits). This situation reversed again in 2021, as means-tested benefits increased 3.0% while non-means-tested benefits decreased 1.1%. *In 2022, means-tested benefits decreased 5.8% while non-means-tested benefits increased 2.3%. The difference between these two rates of change was by far the largest during the period studied. *In 2023, means-tested benefits continued to decrease (down 0.7%) while non-means-tested benefits continued to increase (up 2.2%). *Between 2000 and 2023, expenditure on non-means-tested benefits increased every year except for 3 successive years from 2011 to 2013 as well as in 2021. Means-tested benefits increased every year except for 2005, 2007, 2010, 2022 and 2023. The different developments for means-tested and non-means-tested benefits may reflect the introduction of a range of policies related to the conditionality of family/children benefits, for example in order to reduce government spending or in response to crises such as the global financial and economic crisis or the COVID-19 crisis. [[Image:Developments for expenditure on family_children benefits at constant prices (2010) by application of means testing, EU, 2000–23 (index, 2000 = 100)_SPS2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: Developments for expenditure on family/children benefits at constant prices (2010) by application of means testing, EU, 2000–23
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/spr_exp_ffa__custom_20721882/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=2895f6a3-0bd2-4e89-a527-b73ec2737f1a&c=1774523299507 spr_exp_ffa] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/spr_exp_ffa__custom_16275942/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=b66a5798-aba1-470b-96c8-67f58055b5e8&c=1744728114777 spr_exp_ffa])|alt=A line chart with 3 lines showing developments for expenditure on family and children benefits at constant prices by application of means testing. The lines are for total expenditure, means-tested benefits and non-means-tested benefits. Data are presented for the period 2000 to 2023 in the form of indices based on 2000 equals 100. Data are shown for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=Social protection statistics - family and children benefits_SPS2026_v1.xlsx|title=Social protection statistics – family/children benefits: tables and figures}} === Data sources and availability === All of the data presented in this article are from the European system of integrated social protection statistics (ESSPROS), specifically the core system. These data are compiled by countries (generally, from administrative sources) and then transmitted to Eurostat. {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32007R0458:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 458/2007}} of the European Parliament and of the Council provides the legal basis for the collection of this data and a series of Commission regulations provide further specifications for the implementation of this regulation. '''Methodological issues''' Further methodological issues may need to be taken into account when comparing data on family/children benefits between countries, such as supplements and fiscal benefits. *'''Supplements:''' benefits recorded in other functions of social protection may include supplements for dependent children. In principle, such supplements should be split from the main benefit and reported separately. However, this is often difficult in practice, so the supplements are instead reported along with the main benefit and therefore not in the family/children function. For example, a range of periodic cash benefits related to disability, old age, survivors and unemployment may include supplements for dependent children that are not reported in the expenditure of the family/children function. As a result, countries that implement a universally available family/child allowance and do not use supplements may appear to have a higher level of expenditure than countries which implement a more restricted family/child allowance and rely on supplements to top-up the income levels of families confronted by other risks/needs. *'''Benefits provided through the fiscal system:''' with the exception of [[Glossary:payable tax credits|payable tax credits]], family/children benefits provided through the fiscal system are excluded. For example, non-payable tax credits and higher tax-free allowances provided to people with dependants may reduce taxes paid by recipients but are excluded in the expenditure recorded by the ESSPROS core system. === Context === The organisation and financing of social protection systems is the responsibility of each EU country. Nevertheless, the [[Glossary:European_Commission_(EC)|European Commission]] provides support to help reach a range of targets through flagship initiatives such as the [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1226&langId=en European pillar of social rights]. Furthermore, the European Commission provides guidance to EU countries to modernise their welfare systems through the [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?langId=en&catId=1044&newsId=1807&furtherNews=yes social investment package]. The European pillar of social rights is built upon [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/european-pillar-social-rights-20-principles_en 20 principles], half of which are classified under the heading of ''Social protection and inclusion'', including principle 11 which covers childcare and support to children. === Footnotes === ===Other articles=== *[[Social protection statistics - overview|Social protection statistics – overview]] *[[Social protection statistics - background|Social protection statistics – background]] *[[Social protection statistics - pension expenditure and title: Social protection statistics - unemployment benefits
text:
EU statistics concerning expenditure on unemployment-related social benefits. Data extracted in March 2026 Planned article update: April 2027 In 2023, expenditure on unemployment-related benefits in the EU was €179 billion, which was equivalent to 1.0% of GDP. In 2023, expenditure on unemployment-related benefits in the EU was 3.9% of total expenditure on social benefits. EU expenditure on unemployment-related benefits was 25.9% lower (in constant prices) in 2023 than it had been in 2013, while the total number of unemployed people was 45.1% lower. [[Glossary:Social_protection_benefits|Social protection benefits]] are transfers, in cash or in kind, made to relieve households and individuals of the burden of 1 or more social risks or needs. This article presents statistics on social protection benefits intended to address the risks and needs associated with [[Glossary:Unemployment|unemployment]]. It covers not only unemployment benefits paid to unemployed people but also: *other cash benefits such as partial unemployment benefits, early retirement benefits for labour market reasons, vocational training allowances and redundancy compensation *benefits in kind such as mobility and resettlement benefits, vocational training, placement services and job search assistance. Data on unemployment-related benefits are collected annually through the [[Glossary:European_system_of_integrated_social_protection_statistics_(ESSPROS)|European system of integrated social protection statistics (ESSPROS)]]. Unemployment levels move in a cyclical manner, largely related to the general [[Glossary:Business cycle|business cycle]]. However, other factors such as [[Glossary:Labour market|labour market]] policies and demographic changes may also influence the short and long-term development of unemployment and expenditure on unemployment-related benefits. ===Unemployment-related expenditure in 2023=== In 2023, expenditure across the EU on unemployment-related benefits was €179 [[Glossary:billion|billion]], equivalent to 1.0% of [[Glossary:GDP|GDP]]. The level of spending varied between EU countries, ranging from 1.7% of GDP in France and 1.6% in Finland and Spain to 0.1% in Malta and 0.0% in Romania (see Figure 1). [[Image:Expenditure on unemployment-related benefits, 2023 (%, relative to GDP)_SPS2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Expenditure on unemployment-related benefits, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/09c40006-440d-4d9f-a994-45860649d1e4?lang=en spr_exp_func])|alt=A column chart showing expenditure on unemployment-related benefits relative to GDP. Data are presented in percent for 2023. Data are shown for the EU and for EU, EFTA and candidate countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Expenditure on unemployment-related benefits in the EU amounted to 3.9% of all expenditure on social benefits in 2023, with this share ranging from 6.2% recorded in Spain and also at least 5.0% in France, Finland and Lithuania down to 0.2% in Romania (see Figure 2). [[Image:Expenditure on unemployment-related benefits, 2023 (% of total expenditure on social benefits)_SPS2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Expenditure on unemployment-related benefits, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7f5c1aab-087f-4d50-8f04-dd7b1d93a914?lang=en spr_exp_func])|alt=A column chart showing expenditure on unemployment-related benefits as a share of total expenditure on social benefits. Date are presented in percent for 2023. Data are shown for the EU and for EU, EFTA and candidate countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The proportion of social benefit expenditure allocated to unemployment does not necessarily provide an immediately useful basis for comparison between countries because of differences in the design of social protection systems. Expenditure on unemployment-related benefits is linked not only to the relative generosity of the system in terms of the types of benefits available and the level and duration of benefits provided but also to the way it is targeted and the size of the corresponding target groups. Bearing in mind that expenditure is, at least in part, related to the number of unemployed people, expenditure per unemployed person (according to the ILO definition People who are without work, currently available for work and seeking work; see [[Glossary:Unemployment|unemployment]].) may provide a more meaningful cross-country comparison of expenditure on unemployment-related benefits. This comparison can be made in euro (€) terms or in [[Glossary:Purchasing_power_standard_(PPS)|purchasing power standards (PPS)]] (see Figure 3); the latter eliminates price level differences between countries. [[Image:Average expenditure on unemployment-related benefits, 2023 (EUR and PPS per unemployed person)_SPS2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Average expenditure on unemployment-related benefits, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/688c393d-adc9-4028-ae70-8603bdb07131?lang=en spr_exp_func] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3cb88c4b-4002-4b9d-b70c-5911de421b0f?lang=en une_rt_a])|alt=A double column chart showing average expenditure on unemployment-related benefits. Data are presented in euro per unemployed person and in purchasing power standards per unemployed person for 2023. Data are shown for the EU and for EU, EFTA and candidate countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Average expenditure on unemployment-related benefits in 2023 amounted to about 13 600 PPS per unemployed person across the EU but varied considerably among EU countries. The highest expenditures per unemployed person were recorded in Germany (27 000 PPS) and Austria (22 900 PPS), while by far the lowest was recorded in Romania, at just over 400 PPS. It should be noted that some high ratios may – in part – reflect benefits targeting unemployed people who are not part of the denominator used to measure per person expenditure. For example, this may be because they are non-resident and typically live in neighbouring countries (as is, for example, relatively common for Luxembourg’s expenditure). Another example is people who receive unemployment allowances as a pre-pension but have withdrawn either fully or partially from the labour market (as is, for example, relatively common in Belgium). As such, some care is required when analysing expenditure per unemployed person as the information presented may lack comparability due to differences between subpopulations receiving benefits. Indeed, as mentioned in the introduction, the unemployment function in ESSPROS covers not only unemployment benefits providing income replacement to the unemployed but also a range of other benefits targeted at wider groups, including people that may be employed. An example is partial unemployment benefits, which are paid to employees of enterprises implementing reduced working time or the temporary suspension of work due to economic, climatic or other difficulties; such payments were unusually common in 2020 and to a lesser extent in 2021 due to restrictions put in place during the COVID-19 crisis. The data also cover benefits in kind such as placement services and job search assistance, which are usually made available to anyone seeking work (not just the unemployed), including those who are already employed and/or those who were inactive. ===Developments in unemployment-related expenditure=== EU expenditure on unemployment-related benefits (in constant price terms) was lower in 2023 than in 2013 (see Figure 4). The developments in this period can be split into 2 parts, namely those between 2013 and 2019 and those between 2019 and 2023. Focusing on the period from 2013 to 2019, expenditure on unemployment-related benefits fell 18.7% in the EU; the number of unemployed people also fell, down 39.8%. During the same period, expenditure on all social benefits increased (up 11.8%) as did GDP (up 13.3%). The developments for all 4 of these time series were quite regular between 2013 and 2019: *the number of unemployed people fell steadily *expenditure on unemployment-related benefits also fell steadily from 2013, recording a marginal increase in 2019 *expenditure on social benefits increased every year between 2013 and 2019 *GDP increased every year between 2013 and 2019. The patterns observed up to 2019 were interrupted by the COVID-19 crisis in 2020. *Expenditure on unemployment-related benefits increased by 75.5% in 2020 and then fell by 18.8% in 2021, by 34.2% in 2022 and by 2.6% in 2023. The extraordinary increase in 2020 reflects the impact of the COVID-19 crisis and its related restrictions on labour markets and consequently expenditure on unemployment-related benefits. *During the same years, the number of unemployed people rose by 4.7% (2020) and then fell by 1.0% (2021), by 11.1% (2022) and by 1.0% (2023); these rates of change were considerably smaller than those observed for expenditure on unemployment-related benefits. In more normal times, changes in the total number of unemployed people and in expenditure on unemployment-related benefits may be expected to follow a broadly similar pattern. This is primarily due to the fact that the majority of unemployment-related expenditure relates to benefits that are received by the unemployed. However, there are several reasons why this might not happen. *A substantial part of the differing developments after 2019 can be explained by a major change in the composition of unemployment-related expenditure. Between 2019 and 2020, there was a huge increase in the share of expenditure relating to partial unemployment, a benefit usually granted to people who are still employed. It should be noted that partial unemployment benefits are paid to people who are still in employment and therefore not counted in the number of unemployed people. ===Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=Social_protection_statistics_-_unemployment_benefits_SPS2026.xlsx|title=Social protection statistics – unemployment benefits: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data related to social protection presented in this article are from the European system of integrated social protection statistics (ESSPROS), specifically the core system. These data are collected from national statistical offices and/or ministries of social affairs in each country and are generally compiled from administrative sources. {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32007R0458:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 458/2007}} of the [[Glossary:European_Parliament_(EP)|European Parliament]] and of the [[Glossary:Council|Council]] provides the legal basis for the data collection and a series of Commission regulations provide further specifications for the implementation of this regulation. '''Methodological issues''' Some of the principal methodological issues that need to be considered when comparing data on unemployment-related benefits between countries include the following. *'''Registered unemployment:''' access to certain types of unemployment-related benefit is often conditional on being registered as unemployed with the public employment services (PES). The comparison of expenditure per unemployed person (as shown in Figure 3) is based on data from the EU’s labour force survey (LFS) See http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/lfs/overview. where the number of unemployed people is shown according to the ILO definition, which refers to people who are without work, currently available for work and actively seeking work. The population of unemployed people measured in this way does not necessarily correspond with the count of people registered as unemployed with the PES and who are therefore potentially eligible for unemployment benefits. Some unemployed people following the ILO definition do not register with the PES, while some of those registered may – depending on the rules in each country – have a part-time job or not be immediately available for work and would therefore not be counted as unemployed according to the ILO definition. The extent to which these 2 concepts overlap depends on national (or regional) regulations establishing the criteria for registering as unemployed. As a result, indicators on expenditure can vary considerably depending on the denominator used. *'''Structure of unemployment:''' certain unemployment-related benefits are provided only for a limited duration. For example, the most generous unemployment insurance benefits (in terms of relaxed eligibility criteria and/or levels of income replacement) are usually time limited. After exhausting their entitlement to such benefits, people that remain unemployed are typically transferred to a means-tested unemployment assistance benefit or minimum income allowance, depending on the system in each country. The former would still be recorded in ESSPROS as an unemployment-related benefit but the latter would usually be recorded as expenditure to counter the risk of social exclusion Minimum income allowance is reported in the expenditure on social exclusion in ESSPROS rather than as expenditure on unemployment-related benefits unless specific provisions are made for the unemployed., creating differences between countries when comparing data by function. Furthermore, the time limit for receipt of unemployment-related benefits varies between countries so the expenditure recorded as being unemployment-related (both in absolute terms and per unemployed person) is impacted not only by the design of the benefits system, but also by the structure of unemployment. Paradoxically, a country with a high number of long-term unemployed people could have relatively low expenditure on unemployment-related benefits, particularly when measured on a per unemployed person basis. This issue highlights the need for better data on the numbers of recipients of unemployment-related benefits. *'''Family/children supplements:''' in principle, supplementary unemployment-related benefits that are granted for dependent children should be classified under the family/children function. However, this is often difficult in practice and the value of such supplements may remain as part of the unemployment function. As a result, countries that implement a universally available family allowance and do not use supplements may appear to have a lower level of expenditure on unemployment-related benefits than countries which implement a more restricted family allowance and rely on supplements to top-up the income of families confronted by unemployment. *'''Impact of the fiscal system:''' with the exception of payable tax credits, unemployment-related benefits that are provided through the fiscal system are not included in the data presented. For example, tax exemptions, tax credits and higher tax-free allowances provided to unemployed people may reduce taxes paid by recipients but are not included in the expenditure recorded by the ESSPROS core system. Similarly, taxes and social contributions deducted from unemployment-related benefits and recouped by the government are included in benefits. Therefore, the gross expenditure data do not necessarily reflect the contribution of such benefits to the disposable income of beneficiaries. ===Context === The organisation and financing of social protection systems is the responsibility of each EU country. Nevertheless, the [[Glossary:European_Commission_(EC)|European Commission]] provides support to help reach these targets through flagship initiatives such as the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/economy-works-people/jobs-growth-and-investment/european-pillar-social-rights/european-pillar-social-rights-20-principles_en European pillar of social rights]. The European pillar of social rights is built upon 20 principles, including *principle 4, which seeks to ensure that long-term unemployed people have the right to an in-depth assessment at the latest after 18 months of unemployment *principle 13, which seeks to ensure that unemployed people have the right to adequate activation support from public employment services to (re)integrate into the labour market and adequate unemployment benefits of reasonable duration. On 8 November 2019, the Council adopted the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.C_.2019.387.01.0001.01.ENG&toc=OJ:C:2019:387:TOC Recommendation on access to social protection for workers and the self-employed], a key initiative part of the roll-out of the European pillar of social rights. On May 2021, the European Commission adopted [https://op.europa.eu/webpub/empl/european-pillar-of-social-rights/en/#about The European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan], which sets out specific initiatives to turn the European Pillar of Social Rights into reality, proposing headline targets for the EU by 2030. Furthermore, the European Commission provides guidance to EU countries to modernise their welfare systems through the [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?langId=en&catId=1044&newsId=1807&furtherNews=yes social investment package]. === Footnotes === ===Other articles === *[[Social protection statistics - title: Social protection statistics - social benefits
text:
Data from November 2025 Planned article update: October 2026 In 2023, the total expenditure on social protection benefits in the EU amounted to €4 607 billion, or 26.7% of GDP. In 2023, some 47% of total expenditure on social protection benefits in the EU was for the old age and survivors function, followed by the sickness/health care function with 30%. During the period 2013-2023, expenditure on social protection benefits recorded the most expansion in the housing and social exclusion function, followed by the family/children function. This article presents statistics relating to expenditure on [[Glossary:Social protection benefits|social protection benefits]] in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]], the [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] countries, as well as the [[Glossary:Enlargement_countries|enlargement]] countries. These statistics are collected through the [[Glossary:European system of integrated social protection statistics (ESSPROS)|European system of integrated social protection statistics (ESSPROS)]]. ===Expenditure on social protection benefits by function=== In 2023, the total expenditure on [[Glossary:Social_protection_benefits|social protection benefits]] in the [[Glossary:EU|EU]] amounted to €4 607 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]], which was equivalent to 26.7% of [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]]. An analysis by function reveals that the highest level of expenditure in the EU was recorded for the [[Glossary:Old_age_function|old age]] and [[Glossary:Survivors_function|survivors function]] (largely composed of pensions), which accounted for close to half (46.9%) of the total expenditure on social protection benefits in 2023. The next highest share, accounting for slightly under a third (29.6%) of the EU's expenditure on social protection benefits, was for the [[Glossary:Sickness-health_care_function|sickness/health care function]], while each of the remaining functions (shown in Figure 1) accounted for single-digit shares. Among these, the highest proportion was recorded for the [[Glossary:Family-children_function|family/children function]] (8.7% of total expenditure on social protection benefits), followed by [[Glossary:Disability_function|disability]] (7.1%), [[Glossary:Unemployment_function|unemployment]](3.9%) and [[Glossary:Housing_function|housing]] and [[Glossary:Social_exclusion_not_elsewhere_classified_function|social exclusion]] (3.9%). [[Image:Expenditure on social protection benefits by function (% share of total benefits, EU, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Expenditure on social protection benefits by function, EU,
(%, share on total benefits)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/spr_exp_func__custom_18745486/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=65fd8285-d21a-4aa1-a106-22bd04aad68a&c=1762267413000 (spr_exp_func)]|alt= Pie chart showing expenditure on social protection benefits by function as percentage share of total benefits in the EU for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''In France, the level of expenditure on social protection benefits was about one-third of GDP''''' There were considerable variations between EU Member States with respect to their levels of expenditure on social protection benefits relative to GDP. In 2023, this ratio peaked at 31.5% in France, followed by Finland (31.3%), Austria (29.7%) and Germany (28.7%). At the other end of the range, the ratio of expenditure on social protection benefits relative to GDP was 12.2% in Ireland, 13.0% in Malta, 15.2% in Estonia and 16.3% in Romania; relatively low ratios (below 20%) were also recorded in Lithuania, Hungary, Latvia, Cyprus, Bulgaria, Slovakia and Croatia (see Figure 2). It is important to take into consideration these overall ratios of expenditure in the different EU Member States when analysing the relative shares of different functions in total expenditure. On average, from 2013 to 2023 the share on GDP of expenditure in social benefits decreased in the EU from 27.5% to 26.7%; however, there are large differences among countries: most EU countries showed a reduction in this share (with a maximum of -9.5 pp in Ireland), while 12 countries recorded an increase in this share, the highest being measured for Latvia and Poland (+2.8 pp both). [[Image:Expenditure on social protection benefits (% relative to GDP, 2013 and 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Expenditure on social protection benefits, 2013 and 2023
(% relative to GDP)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/spr_exp_func__custom_18745486/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=65fd8285-d21a-4aa1-a106-22bd04aad68a&c=1762267413000 (spr_exp_func)]|alt= Vertical bar chart showing expenditure on social protection benefits as percentage relative to GDP in the EU, euro area, individual EU Member States, Iceland, Switzerland, Norway, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro and Türkiye. Each country has two columns representing the years 2013 and 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Old age and survivors plus sickness/health care are predominant functions in all countries''''' As noted above, benefits for old age and survivors accounted for the highest share of EU expenditure on social protection benefits in 2023, at 46.9%. This pattern of the old age and survivors' function recording the highest share of total expenditure was repeated in each of the EU Member States except for Ireland where the sickness/health care function was the largest (42.4%). [[Image:Table 1 Expenditure on social protection benefits by function (%, 2023)V1.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: Expenditure on social protection benefits by function, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/spr_exp_func__custom_13681797/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=d4e87267-67f6-4ff6-8041-13bbec9fb432&c=1762268985000 (spr_exp_func)]|alt= Table showing expenditure on social protection benefits by function as percentage in the EU, euro area, individual EU Member States, Iceland, Switzerland, Norway, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro, Albania and Türkiye for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, the second highest level of EU expenditure on social protection benefits was for sickness/health care, which accounted for about a third (29.6%) of total expenditure. This pattern was repeated in all EU countries except Ireland, where the level of expenditure on sickness/health care was higher than that for old age and survivors. The share of sickness/health care in total expenditure on social protection benefits ranged from highs of 42.4% in Ireland and 36.9% in Slovenia down to lows of 22.2% in Denmark and 22.1% Italy. Benefits for family/children averaged 8.7% of total EU expenditure on social protection benefits in 2023. This share ranged from a high of 14.7% in Luxembourg down to a low of 4.7% in Cyprus. In a majority (17) of the EU Member States, family/children accounted for the third highest level of expenditure among the 6 different functions that are shown in Table 1 (behind old age and survivors and sickness/health care). The average share of disability benefits within the total expenditure on social protection benefits was 7.1% across the whole of the EU, while in 9 of the EU Member States the disability function accounted for the third highest level of expenditure among the 6 different functions that are shown in Table 1. The share of EU expenditure on unemployment benefits on total social protection benefits equated to 3.9% in 2023. This share ranged from 6.2% in Spain to less than 1% in Malta and Poland, with a low of 0.2% recorded in Romania. In addition, 3.9% of the EU's expenditure on social protection benefits in 2023 was accounted for by housing and social exclusion. The relative weight of housing and social exclusion in total expenditure on social protection benefits was considerably higher in the Netherlands (7.4%), Ireland (6.8%), Finland (6.4%) and Denmark (6.1%). By contrast, in Bulgaria and Estonia less than 1.5% of total expenditure on social protection benefits was used for housing and social exclusion. Cyprus (with a share of 5.6%) was the only country where this function accounted for the third highest level of expenditure among the 6 different functions that are shown in Table 1. ===Developments for social protection benefits in constant prices=== The development of EU expenditure on social protection benefits in constant prices over the period covering 2013-2023 reveals that total expenditure on social benefits rose in all EU Member States, on average by 1.6% per year. See Table 2, which presents data using constant 2015 prices. In other words, changes in expenditure are presented in real terms. The highest growth rate between 2013 and 2023 was registered in Romania, where expenditure on social protection benefits rose by an average of 5.7% per year in real terms; the next highest rates of change were recorded in Poland (5.2% per year) and Bulgaria (4.8% per year). By contrast, in Greece and Denmark the increase was smaller than 1% per year (0.6% and 0.5% respectively). '''''Between 2012 and 2023, EU expenditure on housing and social exclusion rose by an average of 3.1% per year''''' The various developments observed over time in relation to expenditure on the different social protection functions reflect a range of issues, including: the overall health of each economy, changes in the level of demand for specific benefits, demographic developments, and the focus/aim of political reforms with respect to social protection legislation. Across the whole of the EU, the highest growth rate for expenditure on social protection benefits during the period 2013-2023 was recorded for housing and social exclusion, where expenditure rose, on average, by 3.1% per year. The next highest rates of change were recorded for the family/children function (2.3% per year) and for the sickness/health care function (2.0% per year). By contrast, the unemployment function showed a negative average growth rate (-3.0% per year). The largest increase in expenditure for housing and social exclusion was registered by Greece (22.2% per year), while Poland recorded the highest growth for the family/children function (11.9% per year) and Cyprus for the sickness/health care function (11.3% per year). Belgium and Romania showed the largest decrease for the unemployment function (-10.8% and -10.7% per year respectively). [[Image:Table 2 Average annual growth rate of expenditure on social protection benefits (%, 2013-2023) V1.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 2: Average annual growth rate of expenditure on social protection benefits, 2012-2023
(%)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/spr_exp_func__custom_18746498/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=da11dec8-4e62-4988-9d74-548a1b1e0d4e&c=1762270858000 (spr_exp_func)]|alt= Table showing average annual growth rate of expenditure on social protection benefits by function as percentage in the EU, euro area, individual EU Member States, Iceland, Switzerland, Norway, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro, Albania and Türkiye for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Social protection benefits in cash and in kind=== Expenditure on social protection benefits can take a variety of different forms in terms of its delivery. Payments may be made in cash, paid out either at regular intervals or as lump sums, or alternatively may take the form of benefits in kind. In a similar vein, some governments choose to target certain benefits by making them means-tested (dependent upon different income levels), whereas other payments might be made to the whole of a (sub)population, for example, a winter fuel allowance (for heating) paid to all elderly persons. Figure 3 shows that in 2023 almost two-thirds (64.7%) of the total expenditure on social protection benefits in the EU were made in the form of cash payments. The share of cash benefits in total expenditure on social protection benefits peaked at 76.4% in Italy and at 75.9% in Greece, while cash benefits also accounted for more than 70% of total expenditure in Poland (71.4). At the other end of the range, cash benefits accounted for less than 60% of the total expenditure on social protection benefits in Finland (57.4%), Denmark (56.1%), Malta (55.4%), Ireland (52.7%) and Sweden (51.6%). [[Image:Expenditure on social protection benefits in cash and kind (% of total expenditure on social protection benefits, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Expenditure on social protection benefits in cash and in kind, 2023
(% of total expenditure on social protection benefits)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/spr_exp_ftm__custom_18747890/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=e615061f-bbef-4bc9-a8b7-a8e037a21323&c=1762272346000 (spr_exp_ftm)]|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing expenditure on social protection benefits in cash and kind as percentage of total expenditure on social protection benefits in the EU, euro area, individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Iceland, Norway, Albania, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Türkiye. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has four stacks representing cash benefits not means-tested, cash benefits means-tested, benefits in kind not means-tested and benefits in kind means-tested for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Across the whole of the EU, the ratio between means-tested and non means-tested cash benefits was heavily skewed in favour of the latter. In 2023, the value of cash benefits that were not means-tested was about 8 times as high as that for cash benefits that were means-tested. The general pattern of less means-tested benefits than not means-tested benefits was repeated in all of the EU Member States and was particularly notable among the [[Glossary:Baltic Member States|Baltic Member States]], as well as in Poland, Bulgaria, Czechia, Sweden and Hungary. In 2023, more than one-third (35.3%) of the total expenditure on social protection benefits in the EU was composed of benefits in kind. The vast majority of these were made up of not means-tested benefits in kind (30.4% of total expenditure), leaving 4.9% attributed to means-tested benefits in kind. The level of expenditure on not means-tested benefits in kind was systematically higher than the level of expenditure on means-tested benefits in kind in each of the EU Member States. ===Means-tested benefits=== Across the EU, means-tested benefits accounted for 10.8% of all expenditure on social protection benefits in 2023. A relatively high share of this expenditure was made in relation to the housing and social exclusion function (note that housing benefits are exclusively means-tested). Among the EU Member States, the share of means-tested benefits in total expenditure on social protection benefits reached a high of 36.2% in Denmark, while a relatively high share was also recorded in Ireland (24.8%); their shares were considerably higher than in the remaining Member States, as the third highest share was 15.9%, recorded in the Netherlands. At the other end of the range, means-tested benefits accounted for less than 3.0% of the total expenditure on social protection benefits in 6 Member States, with the lowest shares recorded in Poland (1.5%) and Estonia (0.9%). [[Image:Expenditure on means-tested social protection benefits (% of total expenditure on social protection benefits, 2023).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Expenditure on means-tested social protection benefits, 2023
(% of total expenditure on social protection benefits)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/spr_exp_ftm__custom_18748143/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=c8e83d28-8199-45bc-bc6d-2b20d4a1573d&c=1762274055000 (spr_exp_ftm)]|alt= Vertical bar chart showing expenditure on means-tested social protection benefits as percentage of total expenditure on social protection benefits in the EU, euro area, individual EU Member States, Iceland, Switzerland, Norway, Türkiye, Serbia, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== {{Template:Excel|filename=Social protection statistics - social benefits2023 v2.xlsx|title=Social protection statistics — social benefits: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The statistics presented in this article were collected from national statistical authorities and/or ministries of social affairs. Most of the data were compiled from [[Glossary:Administrative_data|administrative]] sources. For more detailed information, please refer to: *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/social-protection/quality consolidated quality reports on social protection statistics]; *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/social-protection/database/qualitative-information qualitative information]; *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/social-protection/quality national quality reports on the ESSPROS core system]. The [[Glossary:European system of integrated social protection statistics (ESSPROS)|European system of integrated social protection statistics (ESSPROS)]] was jointly developed in the late 1970s by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] and representatives of the EU Member States in response to the need for a specific statistical instrument for the observation of social protection issues. ESSPROS is a common framework which enables international comparisons of administrative data on national social protection systems. It provides a coherent comparison of social protection benefits for households and their financing across European countries. ESSPROS is composed of a core system and a set of modules. The modules contain supplementary statistical information on particular aspects of social protection, essentially they relate to the number of [[Social_protection_statistics_-_pension_expenditure_and_pension_beneficiaries|beneficiaries of social protection pensions]] and to net social protection benefits. On the other hand, the core system contains data that have been collected by Eurostat since 1990, namely: *[[Glossary:Quantitative data|quantitative data]] — social protection expenditure and receipts by [[Glossary:Social protection scheme|scheme]] (a distinct body of rules, supported by one or more institutional units, governing the provision of social protection benefits and their financing); *[[Glossary:Qualitative data|qualitative data]] — metadata for the different schemes and detailed social protection benefits. The receipts for social protection schemes may be classified according to type and origin: *the type gives the nature of, or the reason for, a payment — social contributions, general government contributions, transfers from other schemes, and other receipts; *the origin specifies the institutional sector from which the payment is received — all resident institutional units (corporations, general government, households, non-profit institutions serving households) and the rest of the world. The expenditure of social protection is classified by type, indicating the nature of, or the reason for, the expenditure: *social protection benefits; *administrative costs; *transfers to other schemes; and, *other expenditure. Social protection benefits are transfers to households, in cash or in kind, that are designed/intended to relieve households of the financial burden of a number of different risks/needs that are classified as functions. The following list of functions is identified within ESSPROS: *old age and survivors; *sickness/health care; *disability; *family/children; *unemployment; *housing; *social exclusion. '''Tables in this article use the following notation:''' {| |Value in ''italics''    ||data value is forecasted, provisional or estimated and is therefore likely to change; |- |:||not available, confidential or unreliable value; |} ===Context=== The organisation and financing of social protection systems is the responsibility of each of the EU Member States. The models used in the Member States are therefore somewhat different from each other. The EU institutions play a coordinating role to ensure that people who move across borders continue to receive adequate protection; they seek to promote actions among the Member States to combat poverty and social exclusion as well as to reform social protection systems on the basis of policy exchanges and mutual learning. The main policy framework in the field of EU social protection is the [https://op.europa.eu/webpub/empl/european-pillar-of-social-rights/en/ European pillar of social rights]. The pillar contains 3 main categories for action, one of which concerns social protection and inclusion. ===Other articles=== *[[Disability_statistics|Disability statistics — online publication]]
