title: Stock of vehicles at regional level
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the sock of vehicles at regional level. Data from February 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 In the EU, there was an average rate of 0.57 passenger cars per inhabitant in 2024. At regional level, apart from 2 extreme values, the highest regional rate of passenger cars per inhabitant was 1.9 and the lowest one was 0.1. In the EU, the highest shares of electric passenger cars in 2024 were often registered in northern European regions, such as Flevoland (the Netherlands) which registered 22.1% of electric passenger cars and Stockholm (Sweden) with 14.4%. The region of Bucureşti-Ilfov in Romania recorded the highest number of public transport road vehicles per thousand inhabitants (5.0) followed by the Prov. Namur in Belgium (4.6). [[Image:Motorisation_rate,_by_NUTS_2_regions, 2024.png|thumb|centre|600px|Motorisation rate, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2fae62eb-1752-417b-9a3e-9f23adabbad0?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T09:14:39Z tran_r_vehst])|alt= Map showing motorisation rate by NUTS 2 regions as passenger cars per thousand inhabitants in the EU, EFTA countries, candidate countries and the potential candidate. Each region is labelled based on a range of passenger cars per thousand inhabitants for the year 2024.]] This article presents recent statistics on the number of passenger cars, utility vehicles (lorries, road tractors and special vehicles excluding trailers and semi-trailers), and road public transport (motor coaches, buses and trolleybuses) in the [[Glossary:European_Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], as well as in the [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]], candidate countries and the potential candidate, down to the level of regions ([[Glossary:Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)|NUTS]] 2). === Stock of passenger cars at regional level === '''High motorisation rate in regions of northern Italy''' Figure 1 indicates that, in 2024, 6 out of the 10 EU regions with the highest motorisation rates (number of passenger cars per thousand inhabitants) were located in Italy. The other regions present in the top 10 are capital regions or regions close to major urbanised areas, such as Flevoland, Attiki or Praha. A particular case is the Finnish Åland islands group in the Baltic Sea, also with a particularly high motorisation rate. At the other end, 4 regions out of the 10 with the lowest motorisation rates in 2024 were located in Greece, 2 were located in France, 1 in Belgium, 1 in Germany, 1 in Austria and 1 in Romania. The value for the French overseas region Mayotte was exceptionally low, with 85 passenger cars per thousand inhabitants (see Figure 2). Figure 1
Figure 2 Over the period 2004-2024, at national level, almost all countries recorded a linear increase of the motorisation rate. Romania registered the highest average annual growth rate of passenger cars among the EU countries (5.5%), followed by Slovakia (4.1%) and Poland (3.5%). Türkiye displayed a similar high increase with an average annual growth rate of 4.5%. At the opposite end of the scale, there were Sweden and Luxembourg with 0.15% and 0.14%, respectively. In general, the [[Glossary:Baltic_Member_States|Baltic]], eastern and central EU countries have registered stronger growths over the 2004-2024 period than western European countries (see Figure 3). Figure 3 The motorisation rate registered in the various regions of the European Union is often linked to economic issues. A special case was the Italian region of Valle d'Aosta with a lower taxation on new vehicle registration. Several regions close to larger cities also had high motorisation rates, suggesting a larger number of commuters. Examples of such regions were Flevoland in the Netherlands and Attiki in Greece. Map 1 highlights the significant differences observed between western and eastern EU countries when considering the number of passenger cars per thousand inhabitants in 2024. At national level, eastern European countries registered the lowest numbers of passenger cars per thousand inhabitants. In comparison, western and northern European countries recorded higher rates, but with various countries presenting marked regional disparities. Map 1: Motorisation rate, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4dba1c05-7677-4613-911e-929a9a709258?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T09:17:17Z tran_r_vehst]) [[Image:Motorisation_rate,_by_NUTS_2_regions,_2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Motorisation rate, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4dba1c05-7677-4613-911e-929a9a709258?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T09:17:17Z tran_r_vehst])|alt= Map showing motorisation rate by NUTS 2 regions as passenger cars per thousand inhabitants in the EU, EFTA countries, candidate countries and potential candidates. Each region is labelled based on a range of passenger cars for the year 2024.]] Noticeable disparities are clearly observable for some countries on Map 1. In Greece, for example, strong regional differences could be observed between the highest rate registered in the capital region (903 passenger cars per thousand inhabitants in the Attiki region) and the lower rates observed for other country regions, with the lowest rate (208 passenger cars per thousand inhabitants in the Peloponnisos region). ===Stock of electric passenger cars=== '''The northern regions adopt electric passenger cars faster than other regions.'''

The share of electric passenger cars can be linked to different factors such as governmental incentives (e.g. tax reductions or subsidies), the availability and access to recharging stations, as well as the offer of electric passenger cars and their cost. In the EU, the region Flevoland in the Netherlands and the region Stockholm in Sweden were in 2024 the ones with the highest share of electric passenger cars, 22.1% and 14.4% respectively (Map 2). Five regions in Denmark, 2 in the Netherlands (Including Flevoland), and 1 in Belgium recorded shares of electric passenger cars above 10% in 2024. Norwegian regions had shares of electric passenger cars in 2024 higher than the EU countries, with an average of 20.9% of electric passengers cars, and peaks at 34.7% in Oslo og Viken and 29.1% in Vestlandet regions. Most southern and eastern European regions have shares of electric passenger cars between 0.1% and 1%. The same can be observed for most regions in Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Serbia and most regions in Türkiye. Map 2: Share of electric passenger cars, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6db35459-31e1-427b-bd55-2a0cd85354e7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T09:17:48Z tran_r_elvehst]) [[Image:Share_of_electric_passenger_cars,_by_NUTS_2_regions,_2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 2: Share of electric passenger cars, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6db35459-31e1-427b-bd55-2a0cd85354e7?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T09:17:48Z tran_r_elvehst])|alt= Map showing the share of electric passenger cars in the total passenger cars by NUTS 2 regions in the EU, EFTA countries, candidate countries and potential candidates. Each region is labelled based on a range of the share of electric passenger cars for the year 2024.]] === Stock of utility vehicles (lorries, road tractors and special vehicles)=== '''The economic importance of the regions influences the stock of utility vehicles'''

The picture is quite different when looking at utility vehicles (lorries, road tractors and special vehicles excluding trailers and semi-trailers), where no systematic difference could be observed between western and eastern or northern and southern European regions. The share of utility vehicles in the total number of road vehicles (excluding trailers, semi-trailers and motorcycles) in a region depends on several factors. Among these are the regional transport systems and related infrastructure for different modes of freight transport, such as the capacity of motorways, railway lines, ports and airports. The economic characteristics of a region also play a role, i.e. whether the regional economy is dominated by manufacturing industries or services, and whether the region is located on key European freight corridors. The top 15 EU regions with the lowest shares of utility vehicles in total number of vehicles for which all data are available (excluding trailers, semi-trailers and motorcycles) were in German urbanised areas (ranging between 6.3% and 7.6 %) (Figure 4). Figure 4 Figure 5 indicates that the range of the top 15 EU regions with the highest shares of utility vehicles in the total stock of vehicles in 2024 is between 16.9% and 22%. Valle d’Aosta is the only Italian region in the top 15 regions, and it stands at the top of the list. Included in the list of the top 15 are also 3 regions in Belgium - Prov. West-Vlaanderen (20.5%), Prov. Limburg (17.9%) and Prov. Oost-Vlaanderen (17.8%); 2 regions in Ireland - Northen and Western (20%) and Southern (16.9%); 2 in France – Guyane (20%) and Corse (19%); 4 in Finland - Pohjois- ja Itä-Suomi (19.2%), Länsi-Suomi (19.1%), Åland (19.1%) and Etelä-Suomi (17.2%); 2 in Spain - Canarias (17.2%) and Castilla-La Mancha (17%); and Kýpros (16.9%) which does not have a regional breakdown and itself counts as a NUTS 2 region. Figure 5 === Public transport road vehicles=== '''The eastern regions favour road public transport compared to western regions'''

On Map 3, we observe that the number of public transport road vehicles (motor coaches, buses and trolleybuses) per thousand inhabitants was higher in the eastern European regions, in contrast with the motorisation rate of passenger cars (cars per thousand inhabitants) being higher in western European regions. This underlines the bigger use of road public transport in the eastern regions compared with the western regions where passenger cars were used the most. In 2024, among the EU countries, the region of Bucureşti-Ilfov in Romania recorded the highest number of public transport road vehicles per thousand inhabitants (5.0) followed by the Prov. Namur in Belgium (4.6). At the other end of the scale, 7 regions in the Netherlands reported the lowest numbers of public transport road vehicles per thousand inhabitants with values ranging from 0.2 to 0.6. Türkiye recorded the highest number of motor coaches, buses and trolleybuses per thousand inhabitants in 2024, with numbers ranging from 14.2 to 4.4. Map 3: Stock of road public transport, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024
''Source:'' ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bcf46242-700b-469d-ac09-9cf8b27aee72?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T09:18:52Z tran_r_vehst]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_r_d2jan__custom_20182392/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=b7db51b1-458a-4d33-976d-37d01991b643&c=1771510463000 demo_r_d2jan]) [[Image:Stock_of_road_public_transport_by_NUTS_2_regions,_2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 3: Stock of road public transport, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024
''Source:'' ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/bcf46242-700b-469d-ac09-9cf8b27aee72?lang=en&createdAt=2026-03-05T09:18:52Z tran_r_vehst]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_r_d2jan__custom_20182392/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=b7db51b1-458a-4d33-976d-37d01991b643&c=1771510463000 demo_r_d2jan])|alt= Map showing the stock of road public transport vehicles (motor coaches, buses and trolleybuses) by NUTS 2 regions as road public transport per thousand inhabitants in the EU, EFTA countries, candidate countries and potential candidates. Each region is labelled based on a range of road public transport for the year 2024.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Stock_of_vehicles_at_regional_level_2026.xlsx|title=Stock of vehicles at regional level: maps, tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] collects regional statistics on the infrastructure of road, railways and inland waterways, as well as vehicle stocks and road accidents. The data are provided by the EU Member States, the [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries]], potential candidates and [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] countries on a voluntary basis. The data are collected at [[Glossary:NUTS|NUTS 2]] level. Population data for Bosnia and Herzegovina and for Kosovo* is not available in the dataset: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_r_d2jan$defaultview/default/table?lang=en Population on 1 January by age, sex and NUTS 2 region]. As a result, indicators expressed per thousand inhabitants (such as the rates in Figure 3, Map 1 and Map 3) are not available for these 2 countries. However, the number of the different types of vehicles for the 2 countries can be found in Eurostat’s online database.

''* This designation is without prejudice to positions on status, and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo Declaration of Independence.''

'''Country-specific notes'''
The major events affecting comparability over time and possible discrepancies in the data are described in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/tran_r_esms.htm# Country Specific Notes]. '''Passenger cars'''
Road motor vehicle, other than a moped or a motor cycle, intended for the carriage of passengers and designed to seat no more than nine persons (including the driver). Included are: :*Passenger cars :*Vans designed and used primarily for transport of passengers :*Taxis :*Hire cars :*Ambulances :*Motor homes :*Micro-cars (needing no permit to be driven) Excluded are light goods road vehicles, as well as motor-coaches and buses, and mini-buses/mini-coaches. '''Number of passenger cars per inhabitants'''
For a given year, this indicator is calculated on the basis of the stock of vehicles as of 31st December and the population figures as of 1st January of the following year. '''Electric vehicles'''
Electric vehicles refer to 'pure' electric vehicles (battery-electric vehicles - BEVs). Trolleybuses, as electric vehicles per se, are included. Excluded are the hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), including plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) and the hydrogen-powered vehicles, the majority of which use a fuel-cell to generate electricity. '''Utility vehicles'''
Utility vehicles correspond to the sum of lorries, road tractors and special vehicles. Trailers and semi-trailers are excluded. A lorry corresponds to a rigid road motor vehicle designed, exclusively or primarily, to carry goods. Road tractors are road motor vehicles designed, exclusively or primarily, to haul other road vehicles which are not power-driven (mainly semi-trailers). Agricultural tractors are excluded. Special purpose road motor vehicles are defined as road motor vehicles designed for purposes other than the carriage of passengers or goods. This category includes: :*Fire brigade vehicles :*Mobile cranes :*Self-propelled rollers :*Bulldozers with metallic wheels or track :*Vehicles for recording film, radio and TV broadcasting :*Mobile library vehicles :*Towing vehicles for vehicles in need of repair :*Other special purpose road motor vehicles. '''Public transport road vehicles'''
Public transport road vehicles refer to motor coaches, buses and trolleybuses which are passenger road motor vehicles designed to seat more than nine persons (including the driver). Included are mini-buses and mini-coaches designed to seat more than 9 persons (including the driver). This category includes: :*Motor coaches: passenger road motor vehicles designed to seat 24 or more persons (including the driver) and constructed exclusively for the carriage of seated passengers. :*Buses: passenger road motor vehicles designed to carry more than 24 persons (including the driver), and with provision to carry seated as well as standing passengers. The vehicles may be constructed with areas for standing passengers, to allow frequent passenger movement, or designed to allow the carriage of standing passengers in the gangway. :*Mini-buses / mini-coaches: passenger road motor vehicles designed to carry 10–23 seated or standing persons (including the driver). The vehicles may be constructed exclusively to carry seated passengers or to carry both seated and standing passengers. :*Trolleybuses: passenger road vehicles designed to seat more than nine persons (including the driver), which is connected to electric conductors and which is not rail-borne. This term covers vehicles which may be used either as trolleybuses or as buses, if they have a motor independent of the main electric power supply. '''Regional breakdown'''
The Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics (NUTS) was established by Eurostat more than 30 years ago in order to provide a single uniform breakdown of territorial units for the production of regional statistics for the European Union. From 1 May 2004, the regions in the 10 new EU Member States were added, as well as the regions of Bulgaria and Romania as of 1 January 2007 and the regions of Croatia as of 1 July 2013. The different legal acts stablishing the NUTS codes are listed below. Data used in this article correspond to NUTS 2024 codes. Data used are figures at different levels of NUTS 2024 as defined in the following legal acts: *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32003R1059:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1059/2003}} of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 May 2003 on the establishment of a common classification of territorial units for statistics (NUTS); *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32005R1888:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1888/2005}} of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 October 2005 amending Regulation (EC) No 1059/2003 on the establishment of a common classification of territorial units for statistics (NUTS) by reason of the accession of the Czech Republic, Estonia, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Malta, Poland, Slovenia and Slovakia to the European Union; *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32007R0105:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EC) No 105/2007}} of 1 February 2007 amending the annexes to Regulation (EC) No 1059/2003 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the establishment of a common classification of territorial units for statistics (NUTS) *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008R0176:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 176/2008}} of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 February 2008 amending Regulation (EC) No 1059/2003 on the establishment of a common classification of territorial units for statistics (NUTS) by reason of the accession of Bulgaria and Romania to the European Union. *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0031:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) No 31/2011}} of 17 January 2011 amending annexes to Regulation (EC) No 1059/2003 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the establishment of a common classification of territorial units for statistics (NUTS). *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32013R1319:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) No 1319/2013}} of 9 December 2013 amending annexes to Regulation (EC) No 1059/2003 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the establishment of a common classification of territorial units for statistics (NUTS). *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32014R0868:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) No 868/2014}} of 8 August 2014 amending the annexes to Regulation (EC) No 1059/2003 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the establishment of a common classification of territorial units for statistics (NUTS). *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32016R2066:EN:NOT|title=Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/2066}} of (NUTS). *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R1755:EN:NOT|title=Commission Delegated Regulation 2019/1755}} of 8 August 2019 amending the Annexes to Regulation (EC) No 1059/2003 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the establishment of a common classification of territorial units for statistics (NUTS). *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32023R0674:EN:NOT|title=Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/674 }} of 26 December 2022 amending the Annexes to Regulation (EC) No 1059/2003 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the establishment of a common classification of territorial units for statistics (NUTS). Certain smaller countries are not sub-divided in NUTS regions. This is the case for Estonia (EE), Cyprus (CY), Latvia (LV), Luxembourg (LU), Malta (MT), Iceland (IS), Liechtenstein (LI) and Montenegro (ME). '''For country codes see [[Glossary:Country_codes|here]].''' ===Context=== This article provides basic figures on the regional distribution of the stock of passenger cars, electric passenger cars, road utility vehicles and public transport road vehicles. However, these data are only part of the wider set of regional transport statistics available in Eurostat's databases. Regional transport statistics show patterns of variation across regions, where transport-related variables are often closely related to levels of economic activity. Transport policies are at the very heart of efforts to reduce regional inequality and improve regional cohesion. One of Eurostat's long-term objectives is to expand the current regional transport indicators in order to provide a better understanding of the impact of transport policies on economic growth, transport needs and the environment. ===Other articles=== *[[Road freight transport statistics]] *[[Inland transport infrastructure at regional level]] ===Publications=== title: Structural business statistics overview
text:
Structural business statistics (SBS) describe the structure, main characteristics and performance of economic activities in the EU. Data extracted in September 2026 Planned article update: 30 September 2027 33.1 million enterprises were active in the EU in 2023, employing 162.2 million persons. Of that total, 99.8% were small and medium-sized enterprises, which employed almost two-thirds of the active population in the EU business economy. In 2023, the service sector was the biggest of the EU’s business economy, accounting for nearly two thirds of the enterprises (63%), half of total value added (49%), and employing over half of the workforce (52%). [[Image: Business economy (SBS) sept2025 1920px copy 2.jpg|thumb|centre|700px|alt= Three separate doughnut charts showing number of enterprises, number of persons employed and value added as percentage of sector in total sector economy in absolute values by NACE Rev. 2. Each chart has four segments representing industry, construction, trade and other services for the year 2023.]] This article presents [[Glossary:Structural business statistics (SBS)|structural business statistics (SBS)]] that inform in detail about the structure, economic activity and performance of businesses across the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], its Member States and [[Glossary:EFTA |EFTA ]] countries. SBS statistics support the decision-making and monitoring of the policies related to the business sector in the EU. SBS data is also used by the business and scientific communities, and all information is available to the public. SBS cover the 'business economy' (NACE Rev. 2 sections B to N, P to R as well as division S95 and S96) which includes: industry, construction, distributive trades and services. While the statistics presented in this article are generally analysed at the level of [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] sections, SBS are available at a much more detailed level (for several hundred economic activities). In addition, analysis for different sizes of enterprises is possible, e.g. for Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SMEs).

SBS provide answers to questions on the wealth creation ([[Glossary:Value added at factor cost|value added]]), [[Glossary:Gross investment in tangible goods - SBS|investment]] and labour input of different economic activities. The data can be used to analyse structural shifts, for example between industry and services, country specialisations in particular activities, sectoral [[Glossary:Productivity|productivity]] and [[Glossary:Profitability|profitability]], as well as a range of other topics. Because they are available with an analysis by [[Glossary:Enterprise size|enterprise size]] class, SBS also illustrate the relative role of [[Glossary:Large enterprises|large enterprises]] and [[Glossary:Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)|small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)]], which is of particular use to EU policymakers and analysts wishing to focus on entrepreneurship and the role of SMEs and large enterprises in stimulating economic performance and job creation. Furthermore, SBS provide useful background information for an interpretation of [[Glossary:Short-term business statistics (STS)|short-term statistics]] and the [[Glossary:Business cycle|business cycle]]. ===Sectoral analysis=== Services activities accounted for the largest share of the [[Glossary:Enterprise - SBS|enterprise population]] within the [[Glossary:EU|EU]]'s [[Glossary:Business_economy|business economy]] when analysed at NACE Rev. 2 section level for 2023: just under one-fifth (17.6%) of the 33.1 million enterprises in the EU's business economy were classified to distributive trades (motor trade, wholesale trade and retail trade), while close to one in six (15.6%) were in professional, scientific and technical activities – see Figure 1. Many business services have benefitted from outsourcing, which may explain, in part, the structural shift towards services. Human health and social work activities is ranked third among the services activities, accounting for (7.3%) of the EU's business economy, with 2.4 million enterprises.
Figure 1: Number of enterprises within the business economy, EU, 2024, |alt=An interactive bar chart showing the number of enterprises, absolute values, in the EU, individual EU countries, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
The business economy workforce ([[Glossary:Persons_employed_-_SBS|persons employed]]) reached over 162.2 million in 2023 in the EU, and generated a total of €10 460 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] of value added.
Among the NACE Rev. 2 sections within the business economy, 'Manufacturing' was the largest in terms of value added: about 2.2 million manufacturing enterprises in the EU generated approximately €2 470 billion of value added in 2023, while providing [[Glossary:Employment|employment]] to 30.3 million persons. Distributive trade enterprises had the second largest share of employment: these enterprises provided employment to over 29.8 million persons and generated €1 576 billion of value added. Financial and insurance activities had the third highest value added (€955.7 billion) but only the tenth largest workforce (5.0 million persons). 'Professional, scientific and technical activities' had the fourth highest value added (€779.3 billion) and only the sixth largest workforce (12.4 million persons).
Figure 2: Number of persons employed within the business economy, EU, 2024, |alt=An interactive bar chart showing the number of persons employed, absolute values, in the EU, individual EU countries, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

Figure 3: Value added within the business economy, EU, 2024, |alt=An interactive bar chart showing value added in millions of euro in the EU, individual EU countries, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Figure 2 distinguishes the value added and employment contributions of the various sectors to the business economy totals. The industrial activity of 'manufacturing' contributed more in terms of value added than employment to the overall business economy, indicating an above average [[Glossary:Apparent labour productivity - SBS|apparent labour productivity]]. This was also the case in some of the service activities, namely 'Financial and insurance activities', which had the highest apparent labour productivity overall, as well as 'Real estate activities', as 'Information and communication services', 'Arts, entertainment and recreation' and 'Other personal service activities'. By contrast, the 'Construction sector' and a number of services – notably 'Repair of computers and personal and household goods' as well as 'Accommodation and food services' and 'Administrative and support services' (which includes cleaning and security services, as well as employment services such as the provision of temporary personnel)– reported relatively low levels of apparent labour productivity. 'Transportation and storage' and 'Human health and social work activities' have highest difference in the share between value added and employment. Distributive trade also presents a lower share in value added than employment; however, it represents the second largest contributor after 'Manufacturing' in terms of both value added and employment. It should be noted that the employment data presented are in terms of head counts and not, for example, [[Glossary:Full-time equivalent (FTE)|full-time equivalents]], and there may be a significant proportion of persons working part-time in some of these service activities, which may explain, at least to some degree, their relatively low levels of apparent labour productivity. [[Image: Analysis of value added and employment within the business economy, EU, 2023 (% of value added and employment withing the business economy).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Analysis of value added and employment within the business economy, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code= sbs_sc_ovw }}|alt= Horizontal bar chart showing analysis of value added and employment within the business sector in the EU as percentages. Each business economy sector has two bars representing value added and employment for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Varying rates of part-time work also help explain, in part, the considerable differences in average [[Glossary:Personnel costs - SBS|personnel costs]] within the business economy of the EU, as shown in Table 3. Average personnel costs in the EU was highest in the 'Financial and insurance activities' at €78 350 per employee in 2023 and were slightly lower for the 'Electricity, gas steam and air conditioning supply' sector (€71 300 per employee) and 'Information and communication' (€65 600 per employee). Average personnel costs for the 'Financial and insurance activities' sector were almost 4 times as those recorded for 'Accommodation and food services' (€22 150 per employee) and more than twice those recorded for 'Repair of computers and personal and household goods' (€32 230 per employee), 'Arts, entertainment and recreation' (€35 090 per employee) and 'Distributive trades' (€36 600 per employee). The variation in average personnel costs was even more marked between EU countries: for example, for the 'Information and communication' sector average personnel costs ranged (among those EU countries for which data are available) by a factor of more than 10, from a high of €97 900 per employee in Ireland to a low of €30 500 per employee in Croatia; within the 'Manufacturing' sector average personnel costs ranged by a factor of 7, from a high of €79 250 per employee in Denmark and €78 750 per employee in Belgium to a low of €13 200 per employee in Bulgaria.
Figure 5: Average employee benefits expense within the business economy, EU, 2024, |alt=An interactive bar chart showing average employee benefits expense as thousands of euro per employee in the EU, individual EU countries, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
The influence of part-time employment is largely removed in the [[Glossary:Wage-adjusted labour productivity ratio|wage adjusted labour productivity ratio]], which shows the relation between average value added per person employed and average personnel costs per employee (see Figure 3). This ratio was particularly high (387%) in the EU 'Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply' activities in 2023, as well as in 'Financial and insurance' activities (244%) and in 'Real estate activities' (242%). The wage adjusted labour productivity ratio, for which information is available, fell below 100% in 2 services activities: 'Other personal service activities' and 'Repair of computers, personal and household goods'.
Figure 6: Wage adjusted labour productivity within the business economy, EU, 2024 (%) |alt=An interactive bar chart showing percentage wage adjusted labour productivity within the business economy in the EU for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
The [[Glossary:Gross operating rate - SBS|gross operating rate]] shown in Figure 4 relates the [[Glossary:Gross operating surplus - SBS|gross operating surplus]] (value added less personnel costs) to the level of [[Glossary:Turnover - SBS|turnover]] and in this way indicates the extent to which sales are converted into gross operating profit (before accounting for depreciation or taxes). Due at least in part to the very high level of sales inherent in wholesaling and retailing, the EU distributive trades sector displayed the lowest gross operating rate across NACE sections, at 5.8% in 2023. Capital-intensive activities (such as 'Real estate activities'; 35.5% and 'Financial and insurance activities'; 24.8%) tended to have high gross operating rates as the gross operating surplus by definition does not take account of financial or extraordinary costs related to capital expenditure.
Figure 7: Gross operating rate within the business economy, EU, 2024 (%) |alt=An interactive bar chart showing percentage gross operating rate within the business economy in the EU for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Size class analysis=== Structural business statistics can be analysed by enterprise size class (defined in terms of the number of persons employed). The overwhelming majority (99.8%) of enterprises active within the EU's business economy in 2023 were micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) – some 33.0 million – together they contributed 51.4% of the value added generated within the EU's business economy. More than 9 out of 10 (99.1%) enterprises in the EU were [[Glossary:Micro enterprises|micro enterprises]] (employing less than 10 persons) and their share of value added within the business economy was considerably lower, around one-fifth (19.6%).
Figure 8: Enterprise size class analysis of employment, EU, 2024 |alt=An interactive horizontal queued bar chart showing enterprise size class analysis of employment in the EU. Each business economy sector column has four queues representing micro, small, medium-sized and large enterprises for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Perhaps the most striking phenomenon of SMEs is their contribution to employment. Almost two-thirds (63.5%) of the EU’s business economy workforce was employed in an SME in 2023. Some 19.9 million persons worked in SMEs in the distributive trades sector, 15.4 million in manufacturing and 12.1 million in construction. In 2023, micro enterprises in the EU employed more people than any other enterprise size class in almost half of the service sectors (at the section level of detail). This pattern was particularly pronounced for 'Real estate activities', the 'Repair of computers', 'Personal and household goods' and 'Other personal service activities' where an absolute majority of the workforce worked in micro enterprises. By contrast, for 'Financial and insurance activities' as well as 'Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply' and 'Mining and quarrying', 'Water supply, waste and remediation' and 'Administrative and support service activities', large enterprises employed more than half of the workforce. [[Image: Enterprise size class analysis of value added, EU, 2023 (% of sectoral total).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Enterprise size class analysis of value added, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code= sbs_sc_ovw }}|alt= Horizontal queued bar chart showing enterprise size class analysis of value added as percentage of sectoral total in the EU. Totalling 100 percent, each business economy sector column has four queues representing micro, small, medium-sized and large enterprises for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Time series=== TO BE IMPLEMENTED === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Structural business statistics overview 2025 10 V3.xlsx|title=SBS overview: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== Eurostat's structural business statistics describe the structure, conduct and performance of economic activities, down to the most detailed activity level (several hundred sectors). Without this structural information, short-term data on the economic cycle would lack context and would be more difficult to interpret. ====Coverage, units and classifications==== Structural business statistics cover the 'business economy', which includes industry, construction and many services (NACE Rev. 2 sections B to N, P to R as well as division S95 and S96). Structural business statistics do not cover agriculture, forestry and fishing, nor public administration. Structural business statistics describe the business economy through the observation of units engaged in an economic activity; the unit in structural business statistics is generally the enterprise. An enterprise carries out one or more activities, at one or more locations, and it may comprise one or more legal units. Enterprises that are active in more than one economic activity (plus the value added and turnover they generate, the people they employ, and so on) are classified under the NACE heading corresponding to their principal activity; this is normally the one which generates the largest amount of value added. NACE Rev. 2 was adopted at the end of 2006, and implemented in structural business statistics from the 2008 reference year. Compared with NACE Rev. 1.1, this has enabled a broader and more detailed set of information to be compiled on services, while also updating the classification to identify new areas of activity better. Starting with the reference year 2021, Structural Business Statistics are compiled under the legal basis of the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32019R2152 EU regulation 2019/2152] on European business statistics and its implementing act, [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32020R1197 EU regulation 2020/1197] on technical specifications and arrangements. ====Size class and regional analysis==== Structural business statistics are also available with an analysis by region or by enterprise size class. In structural business statistics, size classes are defined by the number of persons employed, except for specific data series within retail trade activities where turnover size classes are also used. A limited set of the standard structural business statistics variables (for example, the number of enterprises, turnover, value added and persons employed) is analyzed by size class, mostly down to the three-digit (group) level of NACE. For statistical purposes, SMEs are generally defined as those enterprises employing fewer than 250 persons. The number of size classes available varies according to the activity under consideration. However, the main groups used in this article are: *small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs): with less than 250 persons employed, further divided into; *micro enterprises: with less than 10 persons employed; *small enterprises: with 10 to 49 persons employed; *medium-sized enterprises: with 50 to 249 persons employed; *large enterprises: with 250 or more persons employed. Structural business statistics contain a comprehensive set of basic variables describing business demographics and employment characteristics, as well as monetary variables (mainly concerning operating income and expenditure, or investment). In addition, a set of derived indicators has been compiled: for example, ratios of monetary characteristics or per head values. SME Relief Package and aligned to the SME definition regulated by the Recommendation 2003/361/EC. ===Context=== In March 2020, the European Commission presented a new [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52020DC0102 Industrial Strategy for Europe] that laid out a plan for how the EU’s world-leading industry could lead the twin green and digital transitions, drawing on the strength of its traditions, its businesses and its people to enhance its competitiveness. It set in motion a new policy approach to deliver on this, focused on better connecting the needs and support provided to all players within each value chain or industrial ecosystem. To support this, it underlined the fundamentals of industry - innovation, competition and a strong and well-functioning single market - while strengthening EU global competitiveness through open markets and a level playing field.
In May 2021, the Commission [https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/9ab0244c-6ca3-4b11-bef9-422c7eb34f39_en?filename=communication-industrial-strategy-update-2020_en.pdf updated the EU Industrial Strategy] to ensure that its industrial ambition took account of the circumstances following the COVID-19 crisis, while ensuring EU industry could lead the way in transitioning to a green, digital and resilient economy. In particular, it focused on strengthening of the resilience of the Single Market; supporting Europe’s open strategic autonomy through dealing with dependencies; supporting the business case for the twin transitions. The [[Glossary:Single market|internal market]] remains one of the EU's most important priorities. The central principles governing the internal market for services were set out in the [[Glossary:EC Treaty|EC Treaty]]. This guarantees EU enterprises the freedom to establish themselves in other EU countries and the freedom to provide services on the territory of another EU country other than the one in which they are established.
With the [https://commission.europa.eu/funding-tenders/find-funding/eu-funding-programmes/single-market-programme/overview_en Single Market Programme (SMP)] the European Commission helped the single market reach its full potential and ensured Europe’s recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic providing an integrated package over the period of 2021-2027 to support and strengthen its governance.
SMEs are often referred to as the backbone of the European economy, providing a potential source for both jobs and economic growth. In March 2020, the European Commission adopted a Communication on SMEs referred to as [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0103 An SME Strategy for a sustainable and digital Europe]. The objective was to unleash the power of Europe's SMEs of all kinds to lead the twin transitions. It aimed to considerably increase the number of SMEs engaging in sustainable business practices as well as the number of SMEs employing digital technologies. Ultimately, the goal was that Europe became the most attractive place to start a small business, make it grow and scale up in the single market.
In September 2023 the European Commission presented the [https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/document/download/8b64cc33-b9d9-4a73-b470-8fae8a59dba5_en?filename=COM_2023_535_1_EN_ACT_part1_v12.pdf SME Relief Package] that aimed to provide short-term relief, boost long-term SME competitiveness and resilience, and foster a fair and SME-friendly business environment. The actions set up all revolve around the three main operational challenges for SMEs – administrative burden, finance and skills – with the aim to achieve very concrete goals: providing an enabling regulatory framework, reducing reporting requirements, simplifying taxes, fostering liquidity, improving access to finance, providing SMEs with the right skills and supporting them throughout their life cycle. ===Other articles=== *[[Structural business statistics (SBS)]] — theme navigation page *[[Structural business statistics overview]] *[[Structural business statistics at regional level]] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/KS-01-24-007 European Business Statistics Methodological Manual for Structural Business Statistics (2024 edition)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/structural-business-statistics/publications Recent Eurostat publications on SBS] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-key-figures/w/KS-EI-24-001 Key figures on Europe – 2024 edition] – see subchapter on Business *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/KS-HA-24-001 Eurostat’s Regional Yearbook] – see chapter 8. Business *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20241205-1 News Release SBS] – 2022 final data *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/business-demography/publications Recent Eurostat publications on BD] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20241025-2 News Release BD2022 final data] ===Selected Datasets=== title: Structure of government debt
text:
<newarticle pic="Allstars Shutterstock 108661346 RV.jpg"></newarticle>


<metadescription>Statistics on the structure of government debt are presented in the context of the EU Stability and Growth Pact and of the Excessive Deficit Procedure.</metadescription>

<updatedata>
Data extracted on 03 June 2026 

Planned update: 20 November 2026
</updatedata>

<highlight>
<highlight-message>
Government gross debt of euro area largely in euro. </highlight-message>

<highlight-message>
Apparent cost of debt slightly increased or remained stable in most EU countries between 2024 and 2025.</highlight-message>

[[Image:General government gross debt denominated in euro, national currencies other than euro and in other currencies, 2025, % of total.jpg|centre|700px |alt=  an image showing a vertical stacked bar chart with 2025 general government gross debt broken down by currency of issuance for the EU countries and Norway. The stacks show debt denominated in euro, national currencies other than euro and in other currencies. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

This article presents the main results of the latest data collection on the structure of general [[Glossary:Government gross debt|government debt]] and its relationship to [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]], fully or partly completed by the 27 [[Glossary:EU-27|EU]] countries and Norway and collected as part of the ESA 2010 transmission programme (ESA table 28A).
</highlight>
<articlecontent>
<sesection>
=== General government gross (Maastricht) debt as a percentage of GDP  ===

At the end of 2025, 12 out of 27 EU countries reported debt to GDP ratios higher than 60.0%, while 5 EU countries recorded debt to GDP ratios of more than 100.0%: Greece recorded the highest debt to GDP ratio (146.1%), followed by Italy (137.1%), France (115.6%), Belgium (107.9%) and Spain (100.7%). The lowest debt to GDP ratio was registered by Estonia (24.1%), followed by Luxembourg (26.5%), Denmark (27.9%), Bulgaria (29.9%) and Ireland (32.9%).

Between the end of 2024 and the end of 2025, 19 EU countries, as well as Norway, registered an increase in their debt to GDP ratio, and 8 EU countries registered a decrease. The largest increases among the EU countries were recorded in Finland (+6.2pp), Bulgaria (+6.0pp), Poland (+4.8pp), Romania (+4.5pp), Belgium (+3.9pp), France (+2.9pp) and Italy (+2.4pp), while the largest decreases were recorded in Greece (-8.0pp), Cyprus (-7.7pp), Ireland (-5.4pp), Portugal (-3.8pp) and Denmark (-2.6pp).  

[[Image:General_government_gross_debt_as_a_percentage_of_GDP,_2024–2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: General government gross debt as a percentage of GDP, 2024–2025 - Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10dd_edpt1}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10q_ggdebt}}|alt=A  double vertical bar chart showing general government gross debt as a percentage of GDP for 2024 and 2025 in the EU, the euro area 20, EU countries and Norway. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

[[Glossary:Maastricht criteria|Maastricht debt]] followed an upward trend after the 2008 financial crisis. From a high point at the end of 2014 (86.9% of GDP), at EU level, the debt to GDP ratio decreased continuously to 77.5% of GDP at the end of 2019. Then, the ratio increased sharply in 2020 to 89.5% of GDP, mainly due to the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. The 2020 increase represents the steepest increase observed in the time series, and the highest level of general government gross debt as percentage of GDP recorded in the available time series. 

Between the end of 2020 and the end of 2025, the EU general government gross debt decreased by -7.8 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp) to 81.7% of GDP. Compared to the end of 2024, the ratio in 2025 increased by +1.0pp of GDP. In the euro area, the general government gross debt also increased from 87.0% of GDP at the end of 2024 to 87.8% at the end of 2025 (or by +0.8pp). 

[[Image:General government gross debt, EU and euro area, 1995-2025, % of GDP.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: General government gross debt, EU and euro area, 1995-2025, % of GDP - Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10dd_edpt1}}|alt=A  double vertical bar chart showing general government gross debt as a percentage of GDP for years 1995 to 2025 in the EU and the euro area 20. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Breakdown by subsector of general government ===

According to [[Glossary:ESA 2010|ESA 2010]], the [[Glossary:General government sector|general government sector]] (S.13) is divided into 4 subsectors: 

*[[Glossary:Central government|Central government]] (S.1311); 
*[[Glossary:State government|State government]] (S.1312); 
*[[Glossary:Local government|Local government]] (S.1313); 
*[[Glossary:Social security fund|Social security funds]] (S.1314).

Figure 3 gives an overview of the subsector breakdown, as a percentage of total debt for all subsectors, i.e. not [[Glossary:Consolidated accounts|consolidated]] between different levels of government.

[[Image:General_government_gross_debt_by_subsector,_percentage_of_total_gross_debt,_non-consolidated_between_subsectors,_2025.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: General government gross debt by subsector, percentage of total gross debt, non-consolidated between subsectors, 2025 - Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10dd_edpt1}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10q_ggdebt}}|alt=A vertical stacked bar chart showing the general government gross debt by subsector as a percentage of total gross debt, non-consolidated between subsectors in 2025 in the EU, the euro area 20, EU countries and Norway. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

For 24 of the 27 EU countries, the central government represented more than 75% of the general government debt (not consolidated between subsectors) at the end of 2025. Other subsectors of general government had a comparatively large share in Sweden (41%), Denmark (33%) and Germany (31%), as well as in Norway (29%). 

Local government debt (non-consolidated between subsectors) played an important role in Sweden (40%), Denmark (33%), Finland (16%) and Estonia (15%). The share of local government debt was also important in Norway (29%). While for the majority of EU countries, the main creditors of local government were other sectors of the economy, this was not the case for Ireland, Latvia and Austria, where the majority of local government gross debt was held by central government (see table 1)

In Germany (23%), Belgium (18%) and Spain (17%) state governments accounted for a significant share in the total gross debt (not consolidated between subsectors). State government as a subsector of general government exists only in 4 EU countries, namely, Belgium, Germany, Spain and Austria. The debt share of state government was 7% in Austria. For Spain and Austria, the majority of the debt of state government was held by central government (see table 1).

The impact of [[Glossary:Social security fund|social security funds]] on the general government debt continues to be relatively small: contributions of less than 5% were recorded in 24 countries (out of the 26 reporting countries with a social security funds' subsector), with 9 out of the 26 countries for which social security funds is reported as a separate subsector reporting a level of debt at the end of 2025 of zero or less than 1 million of national currency. Only 2 countries had somewhat higher share of debt for social security funds: France (8%) and Spain (7%). For France, at the end of 2025, the creditors of social security funds were nearly all other sectors of the economy rather than other subsectors of general government. For Spain, in contrast, at the end of 2025, social security fund debt was nearly all held by central government. This was also the case for Belgium, Germany, Croatia, Hungary, the Netherlands, Austria and Romania. 

'''Impact of consolidation'''

The general government debt has to be consolidated within each subsector and between subsectors at the level of general government. This implies that the debt issued by one subsector and held by another one should be excluded from the general government debt. When debt of one subsector of general government is held by another subsector, general government gross debt is then lower than the sum of subsector gross debt. Table 1 illustrates this effect in percentage of total general government gross debt (consolidated within subsectors and between subsectors).

[[Image:Impact of consolidation as a percentage of general government gross debt, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Impact of consolidation as a percentage of general government gross debt, 2025 - Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10dd_edpt1}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10q_ggdebt}}|alt=A table showing the Impact of consolidation on general government debt in 2025 in the EU, the euro area 20, the euro area 21, EU countries and Norway. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

For 18 of the 27 EU countries and Norway, at the end of 2025, the consolidation between the subsectors of general government had a limited impact, reducing the general government debt by less than 5%. The most significant consolidation effect was observed in Cyprus (67%, mainly due to deposits of social security funds with the central government). Large effects of consolidation were also observed followed by Latvia (26%, due to deposits of local government and social security funds with central government and local government loan liabilities held by central government), Spain (21%, mainly due to state government and social security funds' debt held by central government), the Netherlands (18%, mainly due to central government deposit liabilities held by social security funds and local government), Ireland (14%, mainly due to social security funds holding central government short-ter debt securities and loans extended by central government to local government units), Portugal and Estonia (both 12%). Significant consolidation effects are often due to central government liabilities in deposits held by local government and social security funds, for example in Estonia, Latvia and Cyprus. The level of consolidation tends to be influenced by the growing prevalence of cash pooling arrangements.

On the other hand, at the end of 2025, 6 countries showed no consolidating amounts between subsectors of general government or consolidating amounts below 1%: Malta, Luxembourg, Slovenia, Croatia and Finland as well as Norway.
</sesection>

=== Breakdown by financial instrument ===

The Maastricht debt is composed of the stock of liabilities at face value in the following financial instruments according to the ESA 2010 classification: 

*currency and deposits (AF.2); 
*debt securities (AF.3); and 
*loans (AF.4).

The breakdown of debt by [[Glossary:financial instruments|financial instrument]] is presented in Figure 4.

[[Image:General_government_gross_debt_by_financial_instrument,_2025.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: General government gross debt by financial instrument, 2024 - Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10dd_ggd}}|alt= A vertical stacked bar chart showing the general government gross debt by financial instrument, in 2025 in the EU, the euro area 20 and EU countries. The stacks show currencies and deposits, debt securities, and loans. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

Data for 2025 show that for the EU, debt securities represented 83.5% of the general government gross debt, loans represented 14.2%, and currency and deposits represented 2.4%. For the euro area, debt securities represented 84.1% of the general government gross debt, loans represented 13.5%, and currency and deposits represented 2.4%.

For 26 of the 27 EU countries, the most used debt instrument remained debt securities at the end of 2025. The share of debt securities in general government gross debt ranged from 27.0% in Greece and 57.7 % in Portugal as well as 30.3% in Norway, to 90.6% in Czechia, 90.5% in Latvia, 90.0% in Denmark, 89.5% in France, 89.4% in Slovakia, and 89.3% in Spain.

Greece (70.9%), Cyprus (41.2%) and Estonia (40.4%), as well as Norway (69.7%) registered high shares of loans. Significant loan to total debt ratios were also recorded for Sweden (33.7%), Poland (26.3%) and Croatia (26.1%). The countries reporting a higher share of loans tended to be those either having a relatively low level of general government gross debt (e.g. Estonia), a relatively high share of debt of subcentral sectors of government (e.g. Sweden) or having benefited in recent years from loans of the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF), the European Stability Mechanism (ESM), the [[Glossary:International_Monetary_Fund_(IMF)|International Monetary Fund (IMF)]] and other international institutional financing (e.g. Greece and Cyprus).

At the end of 2025, currency and deposits represented less than 5% of total debt for 22 countries. In contrast, currency and deposits accounted for 18.3% of total general government gross debt in Portugal (due to saving certificates), 12.0% in Ireland (due to defeasance structures), 7.1% in Bulgaria (mainly due to funds places by entities classified outside general government sector in government suspense accounts), 7.0% in Sweden and 5.5% in Italy (due to saving certificates).

For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

=== Breakdown by sector of debt holder  ===

Figure 5 presents general government gross debt by [[Glossary:Institutional sector|sector]] of the debt holder: non-financial residents (non-financial corporations, households and non-profit institutions serving households), financial residents (financial corporations) and non-residents (rest of the world).

[[Image:General_government_gross_debt_by_sector_of_debt_holder,_2025.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: General government gross debt by sector of debt holder, 2024 - Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10dd_ggd}}|alt= A vertical stacked bar chart showing the general government gross debt by sector of debt holder in 2025 in the EU, the euro area 20 and EU countries. The stacks show resident financial corporations, non-residents, rest of the world, resident non-financial sectors, sector of debt holder not defined. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

At the end of 2025, government debt held by the (resident) financial corporations sector accounted for over half of total debt in 7 EU countries. Its share was the highest in Sweden (69.1%), Czechia (68.9%) and Croatia (61.2%). At the other end of the scale, the smallest proportion of debt held by financial corporations was recorded in Cyprus (11.1%), followed by Estonia (18.2%), Greece (20.4%) Latvia (22.3%) and Lithuania (26.4%). 

The debt share held by non-residents (rest of the world sector) was more than 50% in 16 EU countries and Norway. Among the countries with the highest share of non-resident sector as debt holder were: Cyprus (88.1%), Estonia (77.8%), Greece (70.8%), Latvia (74.2%), Lithuania (72.3%) and Austria (66.2%). In contrast, this proportion was only 21.6% in Malta, 23.0% in Sweden, 24.5% in Czechia and 29.4% in Croatia.

The resident non-financial sectors (non-financial corporations, households and non-profit institutions serving households) played a major role as debt holder in Malta (24.5%), Hungary (22.5%), Portugal (18.5%), Italy (14.5%) and Ireland (12.5%).

=== Breakdown by original/initial maturity  ===

The data collection aims to provide detailed information on the time structure of government debt based on its original [[Glossary:Debt maturity|maturity]]. The maturity is subdivided into several maturity brackets: less than 1 year, one to 5 years, 5 to 10 years, 10 to 30 years, and more than 30 years, as well as the summary category of more than 1 year. For some countries, those that did not provide the complete breakdown, only 2 categories are shown: less than 1 year (short-term) and more than 1 year (long-term). For the other 14 countries, a detailed debt maturity breakdown is available. The debt structure by initial maturity (share of short-term and long-term debt to total debt) is illustrated in Figure 6.

[[Image:General_government_gross_debt_by_initial_maturity,_2025.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: General government gross debt by initial maturity, 2025 - Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10dd_ggd}}|alt= A vertical stacked bar chart general government gross debt by initial maturity in 2025 in the EU, the euro area 20 and EU countries. The stacks show long term and short term initial maturity.]]

General government gross debt classified by initial or original maturity reveals a common pattern for EU countries looking at data reported for the year 2025: between 71.1% (in Sweden) and nearly 100% (in Lithuania and Slovakia of the outstanding debt was incurred on a long-term basis. Low shares of short-term debt were recorded in Slovakia (0.5%) and Lithuania (0.6%) as well as Cyprus (1.4%) and Luxembourg (1.8%).
 
At the end of 2025, the short-term debt ratio was significant in Sweden (28.9%), followed by Portugal (21.5%), Estonia (12.1%), the Netherlands (11.6%) and Italy (10.9%).

For Norway, the outstanding debt was equally distributed between short-term (53%) and long-term (47%) maturities at the end of 2025.

The countries providing a detailed long-term debt breakdown showed very different structures. This is shown in Figure 7. 

[[Image:General_government_gross_debt_by_detailed_initial_maturity,_2025.png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: General government gross debt by detailed initial maturity, 2025 - Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10dd_ggd}}|alt= A vertical stacked bar chart showing general government gross debt by detailed initial maturity in 2025 in the EU, euro area and EU countries. The stacks show short- and long-term maturity breakdowns and 4 detailed long-term maturity groups. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

=== Breakdown by remaining maturity ===

While the initial or original maturity of debt measures the time between issuance date and redemption date, the remaining maturity of debt measures the time left until the redemption date. 

Figure 8 shows the share of general government gross debt with a remaining maturity of less than 1 year, at end 2024 and at end 2025, i.e. the share of the general government debt which was to be redeemed in 2025 and is due to be redeemed during 2026. 

Data is available for 25 out of the 27 EU countries.

At the end of 2025, the highest shares of short-term remaining maturity in total general government debt were reported by Sweden (38.5%), ahead of  Portugal (26.0%), Ireland (25.6%) and Italy (19.2%) as well as Norway (56.7%), while the lowest shares were observed for Slovakia (6.5%) and Greece (6.6%).

The largest reductions in the share of short-term remaining maturity of debt between the end of 2024 and the end of 2025 were observed for Denmark (-5.9pp), Croatia (-3.4pp) and Slovakia (-2.9pp), whereas the largest increases in the shares were noted for Ireland (+3.4pp), Malta (+3.2pp) and Slovenia (+3.1pp).

[[Image:General government gross debt with remaining maturity of less than one year, 2024–2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Share of general government gross debt with remaining maturity of less than one year, 2024-2025 - Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10dd_rmd}}|alt= A vertical double stacked bar chart showing the share of general government gross debt with remaining maturity of less than one year at the end of 2024 and 2025 in EU countries. The bars show the years 2024 and 2025.]]

Figure 9 shows the average remaining maturity of general government gross debt in years, at the end of 2024 and the end of 2025.

Data is available for 25 out of the 27 countries.

At the end of 2025, the longest average remaining maturity of general government gross debt was reported for Greece (18.4 years), ahead of Austria (11.3 years) and Belgium (10.8 years), while the shortest average remaining maturity was observed for Sweden (3.2 years), followed by Bulgaria (4.4 years) and Hungary (5.3 years).

[[Image:Average remaining maturity of general government gross debt, 2024-2025, in years.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: Average remaining maturity of general government gross debt, 2024-2025, in years - Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10dd_rmd}}|alt= A vertical bar chart showing the average remaining maturity of general government gross debt in years at the end of 2024 and 2025 in EU countries. ]]

=== Breakdown by currency of denomination ===

As shown in Figure 10, at the end of 2025, for all euro area (EA20) members, all or almost all (more than 99.5%) of their general government gross debt at face value was denominated in euro. 
 
Similarly, for Czechia and Sweden, over 90% of their general government gross debt was denominated in their national currency.  

Only for 2 EU countries, more than 50% of their general government gross debt was denominated in foreign currencies at the end of 2025: Bulgaria (75%, with 71% of debt denominated in euro) and Romania (53%). Significant shares of foreign currency debt were also noted for Hungary (32%), Poland (26%) and Denmark (24%), as well as Norway (42%).  

The majority of all non-euro area EU countries’ foreign currency debt at the end of 2025 was denominated in euro. For all EU countries, over 90% of general government gross debt was denominated either in euro, or in their national currency for non-euro area EU countries.

[[Image:General_government_gross_debt_by_currency_of_issuance,_%_of_total,_2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 10: General government gross debt by currency of issuance, % of total, 2025 - Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10dd_dcur}}|alt= A vertical stacked bar chart showing General government gross debt by currency of issuance as a percentage of total in 2025 in the EU and the euro area 20 EU countries. All general government debt was denominated in euro or swapped into euro in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, France, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Portugal and Finland. A share higher than 99% of total general government gross debt was denominated in euro in Slovakia, the Netherlands, Croatia, Italy, Spain, Slovenia, Austria, Greece and Germany.  

In contrast, the major issuing currency in most of the non-euro countries were their national currencies: Sweden (96.7% of debt in Swedish krona), Czechia (93.7% of debt in Czech koruna), Denmark (76.5% of debt in Danish krone), Poland (73.8% of debt in Polish zloty), Hungary (67.8% of debt in Hungarian forint) and Norway (58.5%).

The stacks show euro and other currencies. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

=== Apparent cost of government debt  ===

The apparent cost of general government debt (i.e. the ratio of interest expenditure during the year (accrual basis), divided by the average outstanding amount of debt for that same year) shows the past and present conditions countries encounter when accessing the financial markets. In general, as long as debt issued is not indexed on inflation, this measure of the cost of debt depends on interest rates prevailing at the moment of issuance in the past, and it is normally not very sensitive to the most recent market trends, provided that the composition of debt is mainly long-term. 

Based on the data transmissions of 27 EU countries and Norway, the estimates of apparent cost of general government debt are shown in Figure 12.

[[Image:Apparent cost of general government gross debt, 2024-2025, ratio.jpg|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 12: Apparent cost of general government gross debt, 2024-2025 - Source: Eurostat{{Stable link|title=|code=gov_10dd_acd}}|alt= A vertical double stacked bar chart showing apparent cost of general government gross debt in 2024 and 2025 in the euro area 20 and EU countries. The stacks show the years 2024 and 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

In most EU countries for which data was available, the apparent cost of the government debt remained stable or slightly increased between 2024 and 2025, mainly due to new issuances carrying a higher interest than debt redeemed.

For 2025, the highest apparent cost of general government gross debt among countries for which data were available was reported by Romania (5.2%), followed by Poland (4.5%), Czechia (3.1%) and Italy (3.0%). The lowest apparent cost of debt was noted for Ireland (1.4%), followed by Luxembourg (1.5%), the Netherlands (1.7%), Germany (1.8%) as well as France, Finland and Sweden (all +1.9%).

Compared to 2024, the largest increases were observed for Lithuania, Denmark and Romania (all +0.3pp), followed by Poland (+0.2pp). By contrast, the apparent cost of debt decreased in 2025 in 7 EU countries. The highest decreases were noted in Estonia (-0.8 pp), Sweden (-0.3 pp) and Croatia (-0.2 pp).
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Government guarantees as a percentage of GDP  ===

The data collection additionally contains data on guarantees granted by general and central government to non-government units. These guarantees (both 'one-off' and 'standardised') are not part of government gross debt, as they are contingent liabilities, being contingent on the actual call of the guarantee in the case of one-off guarantees and being provisioned for the part expected to be called for standardised guarantees. 

The ratio of government guarantees provided by general government on debt of non-government units as a percentage of GDP is shown in Figure 13. At the end of 2025, the amount of government guarantees exceeded 10% of GDP in 4 countries: Italy (14.7%), Austria (12.0%), France (11.6%) and Sweden (10.5%), out of 20 countries reporting data for 2025. At the end of 2024, for which data is available for 22 EU countries, the ratio of 10%-to-GDP was exceeded in the Netherlands (31.0%), Italy, Germany (13.6%), Austria, France, Sweden and Greece.

At the end of 2025, a ratio to GDP of less than 5% was recorded in 14 of the reporting countries. The lowest ratios to GDP were observed in Ireland (0.1%), Czechia (0.3%), Slovakia (0.4%), and Lithuania and Estonia (both 1.1%).

Between 2024 and 2025, ratio of the stock of guarantees granted by general governments as a percentage of GDP decreased in 14 of the 20 countries for which data is available. The largest decreases were reported by Romania (-1.5pp) and France (-1.0pp), while data for Portugal shows the largest increase (0.4pp).
