title: Structure of multinational enterprise groups in the EU
text:
Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: April 2027
EXPERIMENTAL
 In 2024, more than 51 million people in EU and EFTA countries were employed in multinational enterprise groups. Over 24 000 multinational enterprise groups operating in the EU and EFTA countries were controlled by UK, US or China, reflecting the global integration of the European economy. This article gives an overview of [[Glossary:Multinational_enterprise_(MNE)|multinational enterprise groups]] operating in [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union countries]] and [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|European Free Trade Association (EFTA) countries]] in 2024, according to the data available in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/statistical-business-registers/information-data EuroGroups Register] (EGR). In 2024, according to the EGR * 149 678 multinational enterprise groups operated in EU or EFTA countries. * They employed over 51 million people – around 30% of the people in the European business economy worked for multinational enterprise groups. * Most people employed in multinational enterprise groups worked in groups controlled by an EU country (76%), while 6% worked in groups controlled by an EFTA country. Employment was highly concentrated: the majority of people worked in a small number of large groups employing more than 1 000 persons (84%) carrying out more than 5 economic activities (75%) and operating in more than 6 EU or EFTA countries (65%). The EGR brings together microdata on multinational enterprise groups from the national statistical business registers in EU and EFTA countries, in line with the requirements in {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R2152:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 2152/2019}}, from a commercial data source and complemented by open data sources available online for data outside the EU and EFTA countries. === How many multinational enterprise groups operate in the EU and EFTA countries? === In 2024, the EGR includes * the structure of control of the 149 678 multinational enterprise groups with activities in the EU or EFTA countries; * their main economic characteristics (employment, NACE, net turnover and assets); * their perimeter in terms of [[Glossary:Legal_unit|legal units]] (about 1.6 million) and [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]] (544 500 enterprises inside EU or EFTA countries and 609 500 enterprises outside the EU and EFTA countries). In the EGR, a multinational enterprise group is defined as an enterprise group that operates in at least 2 countries, with one of these being in a EU or EFTA country. Each legal unit in the EGR is identified by a unique identifier (combining a country code and a national identifier), allowing this microdata to be linked with other statistical or administrative data. The EGR is updated annually, and the microdata are provided to national statistical authorities, national central banks and the [[Glossary:European_Central_Bank_(ECB)|European Central Bank]] for statistical purposes only. On average, about 590 statisticians access the EGR online applications each year. The number of multinational enterprise groups in EGR slightly decreased by 1% in 2024 compared with 2023. From a longer perspective, this number increased by 17% in 2021 and by 13% in 2024 compared with 2018 levels (see Figure 1). The trend is highly impacted by the variation of groups of a very small size. The increase in 2021 was also due to the implementation of the EBS Regulation (EU) No 2019/2152, which expanded the coverage of legal units. Figure 1 === Who controls the multinational enterprise groups operating in the EU and EFTA countries? === In 2024, 74% of the multinational enterprise groups operating in the EU or EFTA countries were controlled by an EU country (64%) or an EFTA country (9%). Together, they employed 82% of the total workforce of multinational enterprise groups in the EU and EFTA countries. The remaining 26%, employing 18% of the workforce of these groups, were controlled by countries outside the EU and EFTA area (see Figure 2 and Maps 1 and 2). Figure 2 Between 2018 and 2024, the distribution of multinational enterprise groups operating in EU or EFTA countries by controlling area is relatively stable (see Figure 3). The EU ranked first accounting for 64% to 66% of the multinational enterprise groups, EFTA accounted for 9% to 10%, and the rest of the world for 23% to 27%. Figure 3 The control of a multinational enterprise group in the EGR is assigned to the country of the [[Glossary:Foreign_affiliates_statistics_(FATS)|Ultimate Controlling Institutional]] (UCI) unit. Map 1: Multinational enterprise groups controlled and operating in EU-EFTA, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=egr_mne}} [[Image: SE-MNE-Map1.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 1: Multinational enterprise groups operating in EU-EFTA by country of control, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=egr_mne}}|alt= Bubble map showing multinational enterprise groups operating in EU or EFTA countries by country of control. Each country has a bubble sized within ranges of the number of MNE groups for the year 2024.]] More than 130 countries outside the EU and EFTA areas controlled at least 1 multinational enterprise group operating in the EU or EFTA countries (see Map 2). [[Image: SE-MNE-Map2.png|thumb|center|700px|Map 2: Multinational enterprise groups operating in EU-EFTA controlled by extra-EU-EFTA countries, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat |alt= Bubble map showing multinational enterprise groups operating in EU-EFTA controlled by extra-EU-EFTA countries. Various countries on the world map have a bubble sized within ranges of the number of MNE groups for the year 2024.]] According to the EGR, in 2024, the 3 countries outside the EU and EFTA areas that controlled the most multinational enterprise groups in the EU or EFTA countries were: * the United Kingdom (14 118 multinational enterprise groups) * the United States (8 003 multinational enterprise groups) * China including Hong Kong (2 135 multinational enterprise groups) In 2024, the EGR recorded 376 Russian-controlled multinational enterprise groups operating in EU or -EFTA countries – a 41% decline compared to 2021. These groups employed approximately 18 300 people in EU or EFTA countries, marking a 72% reduction since 2021. Around, 2 9000 multinational enterprise groups operating in EU or EFTA areas maintained at least one legal unit in Russia, reflecting a decrease from a 16% decrease from 2021. Figure 4 provides a breakdown of employment in multinational enterprise groups in the EU and EFTA by controlling area, i.e. with an ultimate institutional controlling unit (UCI) in the same country, in other EU-EFTA countries or in extra-EU-EFTA countries. Figure 4 ===Top sectors of multinational enterprise groups in the EU and EFTA countries=== In 2024, multinational enterprise groups operating in the EU and EFTA countries carried out a large variety of economic activities, covering 21 [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] sections and 87 [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]] divisions, according to the EGR. Figure 5 The 5 economic activities with the largest employment at NACE section level are * manufacturing (33%) * wholesale and retail trade; repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles (17%) * administrative and support service activities (8%) * financial and insurance activities (8%) * transporting and storage (8%) The multinational enterprise groups mainly active in manufacturing employ around 16.5 million people in the EU and EFTA countries. The top 3 activities at NACE division level in terms of employment in EU and EFTA countries (see Figure 5B) are: * manufacture of motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailer (2.5 million); * manufacture of machinery and equipment (2.3 million); * manufacture of food products (1.6 million). Figure 5B Manufacturing is the biggest area of activity, at NACE section level, for multinational enterprise groups active in the EU or EFTA areas. However, at a more detailed level 5NACE section), other industries also stand out. For instance, over 10 000 multinational enterprise groups are mainly active in the following areas (see Figure 5C detailing NACE sections): * wholesale trade, except for motor vehicles and motorcycles; * financial service activities, except insurance and pension funding; * computer programming, consultancy and related activities. Figure 5C === How multinational enterprise groups shape employment in the EU and EFTA counties business economy?=== In 2024 * 6% of the largest multinational enterprise groups (employing more than 1 000 persons) operating in the EU and EFTA countries, accounted for 84% of the employment in the MNE groups (employ 84% of the total number of persons employed in the MNE groups in EU and EFTA countries); * 62% of the smallest multinational enterprise groups (employing fewer than 50 persons), recorded a share of 1% in the total number of persons employed in the multinational enterprise groups in EU and EFTA countries (see Figure 6). Figure 6 According to the EGR, in 2024, multinational enterprise groups employed more than 51 million people in EU and EFTA countries as compared with 42 million in 2018. The multinational enterprise groups increased their employment in EU and EFTA countries by extending their control on attractive enterprises (e.g. via acquisitions), by creating new jobs in their enterprises, or by creating new enterprises. Figure 7 In 2024, 30% of people working in the business economy work in a multinational enterprise group and this share is rather stable (see Figure 8). It accounted for around 31% in 2018 and 2019, 32% in 2020, and a slight drop to 28% could be observed in 2021 and 2022. In 2021, a break in series was recorded caused by the extended scope of the NACE sections used for the total employment (i.e. the denominator). Since 2021, the total employment encompassed the employment in the NACE activity sections B to S (excluding O and S94), while before 2021 only the non-financial business economy was covered (NACE sections from B to N excluding K). Figure 8 Between 2018 and 2024, in the EU and EFTA counties, the percentage of people working in multinational enterprise groups in the total business economy employment remained stable as well, as shown in Figure 8. However, the percent level varies from country to country, ranging from less than 14% in Greece to more than 54% in Luxembourg. Between 2018 and 2024, the concentration of employment in the largest multinational enterprise groups was high and steady (see Figure 9), the largest MNE groups ranked first, gathering 84% of the persons employed by the MNE groups in EU and EFTA countries. Figure 9 In 2024, most multinational enterprise groups recorded in the EGR carried out more than one economic activity (61 %) * 38% carried out only 1 activity (mono-active groups) * 52% carried out 2-4 economic activities * 9% carried out more than 5 economic activities. In the EGR, the diversification of a multinational enterprise group is determined by the number of activities carried out by its enterprises at NACE division level. Most of the employment (75%) was concentrated in the multinational enterprise groups carrying out more than 5 economic activities (see Figure 10). Figure 10 ===Where multinational enterprise groups operate?=== In 2024, 59% of the multinational enterprise groups operating in the EU and EFTA have affiliates only within the borders of the EU-EFTA area, while 41% of them also have affiliates in the rest of the world. In 2024, the EGR recorded that * 4% of multinational enterprise groups active in the EU and EFTA area are present in 6 or more EU and EFTA countries, employing 65% of the people working in multinational enterprise group in the EU and EFTA * 13% of multinational enterprise groups were present in between 3 and 5 EU and EFTA countries, employing 18% of persons employed * 82% of multinational enterprise groups were present in fewer than 3 EU and EFTA countries, employing 17% of persons employed (see Figure 11) Figure 11 In 2024, the EGR recorded around 59 000 multinational enterprise groups controlled by EU or EFTA countries having legal units located in non-EU and non-EFTA countries. Among them * 13 085 multinational enterprise groups had at least 1 legal unit in the United Kingdom * 5 895 had a legal unit in the United States (see Map 3) [[Image: SE-MNE-Map3.png|thumb|thumb|center|700px|Map 3: Worldwide presence of multinational enterprise groups controlled by EU-EFTA countries, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat|alt= Bubble map showing worldwide presence of multinational enterprise groups controlled by EU and EFTA countries. Various countries on the world map have a bubble sized within ranges of the number of MNE groups operating in EU-EFTA for the year 2024.]] ===Feedback=== To help Eurostat improve these experimental statistics, users and researchers are kindly invited to give us their [mailto:ESTAT-EGR@ec.europa.eu?subject=Feedback_on_experimental_statistics feedback by email] ===Data sources=== The EuroGroups register (EGR) database is the source of the above-mentioned multinational enterprise groups data. The EGR is the statistical business register of the EU Member States and EFTA countries for multinational enterprise groups. It produces data in yearly cycles and covers microdata on the groups and their consisting enterprises and legal units. The EGR aims to register all multinational enterprise groups that have enterprises in EU Member States or EFTA countries, including European and non-European groups. EGR does not cover all-resident enterprise groups – those that consist of enterprises only in 1 country, nor independent enterprises. However, the EGR final frame includes additional foreign-controlled units. These are either single legal units or all-resident enterprise groups without an identified foreign-controlling parent, where only the residence country of the foreign parent has been delivered to the EGR. Such additional foreign-controlled units are not included in this article. The EGR microdata help explore the structure and impact of multinational enterprise groups in Europe. We can analyze group size, complexity and employment patterns in European countries, together with their European influence. The EGR makes it possible to present results from 2 sides: from the multinational enterprise group perspective, based on the country of control of the group, and from the national perspective of the country in which the group is located, irrespective of where the UCI is located. The EGR is a statistical business register that serves statistical purposes only. Access to EGR data is restricted to national statistical institutes and national central banks that produce official statistics in the EU Member States and EFTA countries. ===Context=== Globalisation and the increasing complexity of multinational enterprise group activities means it is difficult to produce business statistics and macroeconomic statistics and correctly and consistently reflect MNE group activities in European statistics. To better analyse cross-border transactions of large multinational enterprise groups and correctly record them in statistical business registers, statisticians in the European Statistical System [[Glossary:European statistical system (ESS)| European Statistical System (ESS)]] and European System of Central Banks (ESCB) need to be able to observe the complete and correct economic structures of multinational enterprise groups. ===Other articles=== * [[Employment_in_large-scale_multinational_enterprise_groups|Employment in large-scale multinational enterprise groups]] * [[Employment_in_foreign-controlled_multinational_enterprise_transport_groups|Employment in foreign controlled multinational enterprise transport groups]] * [[EuroGroups_Register_and_industry_concentration|EuroGroups Register and industry concentration]] * [[Economic_indicators_of_enterprises_belonging_to_multinational_enterprise_groups|Economic indicators of enterprises belonging to multinational enterprise groups]] ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/statistical-business-registers/overview Statistical business registers (SBR)] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/globalisation-businesses/overview Globalisation of businesses] ===Methodology=== * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/experimental-statistics/multinational-enterprise-groups Multinational enterprise groups methodological note] * Methodology on enterprise groups and registers is available in the {{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-20-006|title=Business registers Recommendations manual}} * Methodology on the compilation of the EuroGroups Register is available in the {{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-067|title=European business statistics compilers’ manual for EGR}} * EuroGroups Register metadata [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/egr_esms.htm EuroGroups Register metadata] ===Database=== * {{Template:Publication|code=egr_mne|title=Multinational enterprise groups in EU-EFTA countries by controlling country}} * title: Surgical operations and procedures statistics
text:
Statistics on the most common, fastest growing and fastest declining surgical operations and procedures are presented, as part of an online publication on health activities in the EU. Data extracted in February 2026 Planned article update: November 2026 There were 5.01 million cataract surgeries performed in the EU in 2023. Large positive rates of change reported in recent years by most EU countries for keyhole surgery used to perform hysterectomies, repairs of inguinal hernias and appendectomies. In nearly all EU countries, there has been a fall in recent years in the use of in-patient procedures for cataract surgery. This article presents an overview of [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] statistics related to [[Glossary:Surgical_procedure|surgical operations and procedures]]. It provides information for a selection of the most common surgical operations and procedures in addition to details on the fastest growing and fastest declining operations and procedures over the last 10 years. This article is included in a set of statistical articles concerning healthcare activities in the EU which forms part of the online publication on [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union - facts and figures]]. ===Number of surgical operations and procedures=== '''''The most common surgical operation/procedure performed in EU hospitals (for which data are collected) was cataract surgery''''' Tables 1 and 2 indicate how frequently a selection of the most common surgical operations and procedures were conducted in 2023. In both tables, the data are presented relative to the size of the population (per 100 000 inhabitants). For several of these operations and procedures, such as [[Glossary:Repair_of_inguinal_hernia|repair of inguinal hernia]], additional information is given on the frequency with which these are carried out [[Glossary:Laparoscopic/Keyhole_surgery|laparoscopically]]. This approach typically results in less pain, reduced recovery time, and minimal scarring compared with open surgery. It is also known as keyhole surgery. [[Image:Surgical operations and procedures performed in hospitals – top 10 procedures, group 1, 2023 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Surgical operations and procedures performed in hospitals – top 10 procedures, group 1, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f20167fa-339f-47b2-8019-6b2fc1536ac1?lang=en hlth_co_proc3])|alt=A table showing the number per hundred thousand inhabitants of the top five surgical operations and procedures performed in hospitals, as well as data for laparoscopic repair of inguinal hernia. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] [[Glossary:Cataract_surgery|Cataract surgery]] (ICD-9-CM codes 13.1 to 13.8) was conducted 5.01 million times in 2023 across the EU countries, making this the most common surgical surgery or procedure presented in this article. Relative to population size, cataract surgery was performed 1 118 times per 100 000 inhabitants in the EU. In 17 of the EU countries, cataract surgery was performed over 1 000 times per 100 000 inhabitants, peaking at 1 627 times per 100 000 inhabitants in Luxembourg. By contrast, cataract surgery was performed fewer than 400 times per 100 000 inhabitants in Romania. [[Image:Cataract surgery, 2023 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Cataract surgery, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/607ddb5f-ad36-4f6c-8dc5-230ea0363777?lang=en hlth_co_proc3])|alt=A column chart showing the number of people per hundred thousand inhabitants who underwent cataract surgery. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''1.11 million transluminal coronary angioplasties performed in the EU''''' Another common procedure was [[Glossary:Transluminal_coronary_angioplasty|transluminal coronary angioplasties]] (ICD-9-CM codes 36.01, 36.02 and 36.05). In 2023, there were 1.11 million transluminal coronary angioplasties performed in the EU. Over 326 500 transluminal coronary angioplasties were performed in Germany, while the only other EU countries with more than 100 000 procedures were France (205 000) and Italy (137 000). In 2023, transluminal coronary angioplasties were conducted 248.3 times per 100 000 inhabitants in the EU. Relative to population size, these were most commonly conducted in Croatia, Bulgaria and Germany where they were performed on average 545.0, 432.0 and 392.1 times per 100 000 inhabitants, respectively. They were conducted between 141.4 and 374.9 times per 100 000 inhabitants in most of the remaining EU countries for which data are available, with Spain, Portugal and Greece below this range. [[Image:Transluminal coronary angioplasties, 2023 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Transluminal coronary angioplasties, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4f674128-d0e4-470c-aacb-f0609ff33014?lang=en hlth_co_proc3])|alt=A column chart showing the number of transluminal coronary angioplasties per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] [[Glossary:Caesarean_section|Caesarean sections]] (ICD-9-CM codes 74.0 to 74.2, 74.4 and 74.99) were performed 1.10 million times across the EU in 2023. A total of 220 500 caesarean sections were performed in Germany, while between 117 600 and 143 000 caesarean sections were performed in France, Italy and Poland. While the EU average was 246.1 caesarean sections per 100 000 inhabitants in 2023, between 175.8 and 405.6 caesarean sections were performed per 100 000 inhabitants in most (20) of the EU countries. This procedure was more frequent in Cyprus and Romania, with 664.2 and 431.8 caesarean sections performed per 100 000 inhabitants, respectively. It was less frequent in Estonia (165.4 per 100 000 inhabitants), Spain (163.7), Lithuania (161.7), Finland (158.7) and the Netherlands (146.0). [[Glossary:Hip_replacement|Hip replacements ]](ICD-9-CM codes 81.51 to 81.53) were performed 1.06 million times in the EU in 2023; relative to population size, this operation was performed 236.4 times per 100 000 inhabitants. The highest frequencies of this procedure were 350.8 times per 100 000 inhabitants in Germany and between 296.8 and 313.6 times per 100 000 inhabitants in Austria, Denmark and Finland. Fewer than 100.0 hip replacements were performed per 100 000 inhabitants in Romania, Malta and Greece. [[Glossary:Repair_of_inguinal_hernia|Repairs of inguinal hernia]] (ICD-9-CM codes 53.0 and 53.1) were undertaken 931 000 times in the EU in 2023; relative to population size, this was 207.6 times per 100 000 inhabitants. Among the EU countries, such repairs were typically undertaken between 154.8 and 241.9 times per 100 000 inhabitants in 2023, with Cyprus, Austria and Greece reporting higher frequencies (393.9, 287.4 and 284.5 per 100 000 inhabitants, respectively), while Latvia, Romania and Ireland reported lower frequencies (all below 130.0 per 100 000 inhabitants). A majority of these repairs were undertaken laparoscopically in Denmark, Germany, Luxembourg, Belgium, Austria, the Netherlands, Czechia and Slovakia. This share was below 50% in the remaining EU countries for which data are available and was below 10.0% in Sweden (9.6%), Portugal (9.1%) and Italy (6.6%). [[Image:Surgical operations and procedures performed in hospitals – top 10 procedures, group 2, 2023 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Surgical operations and procedures performed in hospitals – top 10 procedures, group 2, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2cae831c-23d4-479c-ae96-1bfbb3b7f385?lang=en hlth_co_proc3])|alt=A table showing the number per hundred thousand inhabitants of five more surgical operations and procedures performed in hospitals, as well as data for laparoscopic cholecystectomy, laparoscopic appendectomy and laparoscopic hysterectomy. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, 914 500 [[Glossary:Cholecystectomy|cholecystectomies]] (ICD-9-CM codes 51.22 and 51.23) were performed in the EU; relative to population size, this was equivalent to 203.9 per 100 000 inhabitants. In general, the frequency of cholecystectomies varied less between the EU countries than did most other procedures presented in Tables 1 and 2. The frequency of cholecystectomies in 2023 was highest in Cyprus, Greece and Lithuania, at 305.7, 286.6 and 280.0 procedures per 100 000 inhabitants, respectively. It was lowest in Bulgaria (103.9 per 100 000 inhabitants) and Malta (65.0). The vast majority of cholecystectomies were performed laparoscopically, their share in 2023 ranging from 79% in Bulgaria to 97% in Malta. [[Glossary:Total_knee_replacement|Knee replacements]] (ICD-9-CM code 81.54) were performed 791 000 times in the EU in 2023, equivalent to 176.4 per 100 000 inhabitants. More than 200.0 knee replacements per 100 000 inhabitants were performed in Germany, Finland, Denmark, Austria, Cyprus, France and Luxembourg compared with fewer than 60.0 per 100 000 inhabitants in Bulgaria and Romania. In 2023, 455 500 [[Glossary:Appendectomy|appendectomies]] (ICD-9-CM codes 47.0 and 47.1) were performed in the EU. Relative to population size, this procedure was performed 101.6 times per 100 000 inhabitants. The frequency of appendectomies, varied between 154.1 per 100 000 inhabitants in Lithuania and 60.4 in Italy. There was more variation in the frequency of laparoscopic appendectomies; with the highest rates in Estonia, Belgium and Lithuania (all in the narrow range of 125.7 to 126.3 per 100 000 inhabitants) and lowest in Bulgaria, where there were fewer than 13.0 laparoscopic appendectomies per 100 000 inhabitants. The share of appendectomies that were performed laparoscopically varied greatly, from 19% of the total number of appendectomies in Bulgaria to more than 90% in France, Malta, Belgium, Denmark, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. Another common procedure performed within the EU was [[Glossary:Hysterectomy|hysterectomies]](ICD-9-CM codes 68.3 to 68.7 and 68.9). Hysterectomies were most frequently performed in 2023 in Czechia and Cyprus (142.6 and 141.6 per 100 000 inhabitants, respectively). In the remaining EU countries, the frequency ranged from 50.8 per 100 000 inhabitants in the Netherlands to 129.2 per 100 000 inhabitants in Bulgaria. More than two thirds of all hysterectomies in Denmark, Finland and Estonia were performed laparoscopically. The share of hysterectomies performed laparoscopically was below one fifth in Malta, Slovenia and Romania, with the latter recording the lowest share, at 8%. A total of 441 400 [[Glossary:Tonsillectomy|tonsillectomies]] (ICD-9-CM codes 28.2 to 28.4) were performed in the EU in 2023, equivalent to 98.4 per 100 000 inhabitants. The frequency of tonsillectomies varied considerably between EU countries in 2023. In Estonia, this procedure was performed 281.8 times per 100 000 inhabitants, while in Bulgaria it was performed 27.3 times per 100 000 inhabitants. The only other countries to report more than 200 tonsillectomies performed per 100 000 inhabitants was in Belgium (211.4) and Cyprus (208.2; note the difference in coverage), and the only other country to report less than 50 tonsillectomies per 100 000 inhabitants was Italy (44.0). ===Increasing and decreasing surgical operations and procedures=== '''''Large increases reported for hysterectomies performed using keyhole surgery''''' A selection of surgical operations and procedures which have generally become more frequent during recent years is presented in Table 3; two of these concern laparoscopic techniques. Data are usually presented for 2013 and 2023: alternative years are presented for some countries – see Table 3 for the precise coverage. [[Image:Selected high growth procedures performed in hospitals, 2013 and 2023 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Selected high growth procedures performed in hospitals, 2013 and 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/125f3edb-2a25-44d2-bcb5-933232bf27e6?lang=en hlth_co_proc3])|alt=A table showing the number per hundred thousand inhabitants of selected high growth procedures performed in hospitals. Data are shown for 2013 and 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Relative to population size, the frequency of laparoscopic hysterectomies increased between 2013 and 2023 in 21 of the 22 EU countries for which data are available. The exception was Slovenia, where there was a very small fall in the rate at which these procedures were performed. There were six EU countries which reported the frequency of this procedure more than doubling during the period under consideration. Excluding Cyprus, Ireland and Hungary, which had breaks in series, the largest relative increase was in Croatia with the frequency some 4.7 times as high in 2023 as it had been in 2013, up from 5.1 to 24.1 procedures per 100 000 inhabitants. Between 2013 and 2023, the frequency of laparoscopic repair of inguinal hernia increased in all 21 EU countries for which data are available. In 11 of these countries, the frequency of this procedure more than trebled during the period under consideration. Leaving aside those countries where there is a break in series, the largest relative increases were observed in Slovenia and Portugal, the frequency being, respectively, 9.2 and 6.1 times as high in 2023 as in 2013. The frequency of total knee replacements (ICD-9-CM code 81.54) increased between 2013 and 2023 in 23 of the 24 EU countries for which data are available. Excluding Cyprus (for which there is a break in series), the largest increase was in Poland, where the frequency in 2023 was 4.0 times as high as in 2013. Malta was the only EU country to report a decrease in frequency, with a fall of 22.5% between 2013 and 2023. The frequency of cataract surgeries – the most common procedure among those shown in Table 3 – increased between 2013 and 2023 in all 26 EU countries for which data are available. Focusing on those EU countries without a break in series, the largest relative increases were in Croatia, Lithuania, Poland and Portugal, where the frequency was 2.0, 1.7, 1.7 and 1.6 times as high in 2023 as in 2013. The frequency of hip replacements also increased between 2013 and 2023 in all 25 of the EU countries for which data are available. The frequency of this procedure more than trebled in Cyprus and more than doubled in Poland, Greece and Ireland; note that Cyprus and Ireland both had breaks in series. '''''Tonsillectomies were performed with a decreasing frequency''''' A selection of surgical operations and procedures which have become less common in recent years is presented in Table 4. For two of these procedures, hysterectomies and appendectomies, the overall frequency declined, despite the relatively fast growth in their performance using laparoscopic techniques. Data are generally presented for 2013 and 2023; alternative years are presented for some countries – see Table 4 for the precise coverage. [[Image:Selected large decline procedures performed in hospitals, 2013 and 2023 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 4: Selected large decline procedures performed in hospitals, 2013 and 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/865d24cf-87db-491a-8f5b-1e4e3b747198?lang=en hlth_co_proc3])|alt=A table showing the number per hundred thousand inhabitants of selected large decline procedures performed in hospitals. Data are shown for 2013 and 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] For [[Glossary:Coronary_artery_bypass_graft|bypass anastomosis for heart revascularisation]](ICD-9-CM code 36.1) 18 of the 24 EU countries for which data are available reported a decline in the frequency between 2013 and 2023. The frequency of carrying out bypass anastomosis for heart revascularisation increased in Cyprus, Ireland, Croatia, Slovakia, Slovenia and Romania; note there is a break in series for Cyprus and Ireland. The frequency decreased by more than 50% in Finland, Malta and Denmark, with the latter reporting the greatest decrease (down 67.2%); note there is a break in series for Finland and Denmark. Among the 25 EU countries for which data are available, 18 recorded a lower frequency of appendectomies in 2023 than in 2013. The frequency of this operation was down by 56.9% in Romania and 39.1% in Bulgaria during the period under consideration. Aside from countries with a break in series, the largest increases in the frequency of this procedure were observed in Croatia (up 12.0%) and Slovenia (up 7.4%). Within the EU, a tonsillectomy remains a relatively common procedure despite a decline in its frequency. In all but 7 of the 25 EU countries for which data are available, the frequency of tonsillectomies fell between 2013 and 2023; the only increases were reported in Cyprus, Denmark, Ireland (all of which reported a break in series), Croatia, Lithuania, Poland and France. The sharpest decline in the frequency of tonsillectomies was recorded in Bulgaria, down 64.3%. A total of 24 EU countries have data available for both 2013 and 2023 for the frequency of hysterectomies. Denmark, Cyprus, Ireland (all of which reported a break in series) and Poland were the only EU countries to report an increase in the frequency of this procedure between 2013 and 2023. The frequency fell by more than 30% in the Netherlands (break in series; down 33.2%), Portugal (down 39.2%) and Malta (down 40.6%). Among 26 EU countries for which data are available, 18 reported decreases in the frequency of caesarean sections between 2013 and 2023. Aside from Cyprus (where there is a break in series), Croatia and Bulgaria recorded the largest increases, up 35.5% and 21.0%, respectively. There were three EU countries where the frequency of carrying out a caesarean section fell by more than a quarter, Italy (down 33.0%), Lithuania (down 30.7%) and Spain (down 28.6%; note that there is a break in series). ===In-patient procedures: cataract surgery=== '''''Widespread fall in the use of in-patient procedures for cataract surgery''''' As already noted, cataract surgery is among the most common procedures conducted in the EU. Several decades ago, this procedure required admission as an in-patient. Figure 3 shows that this is no longer the case in many EU countries. In 2023, only 6.4% of the total procedures for cataract surgery were carried out as in-patient procedures in the EU. Fewer than 10.0% of procedures were carried out as in-patient procedures in 21 of the EU countries. The lowest shares – less than 1.0% – were recorded in Spain, Estonia, Portugal, Slovenia, Denmark, Cyprus and the Netherlands. There were two EU countries where at least half of the procedures for cataract surgery in 2023 were performed on in-patients: Romania (57.0%) and Bulgaria (54.7%). [[Image:Share of in-patient procedures for cataract surgery, 2013 and 2023 (%)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Share of in-patient procedures for cataract surgery, 2013 and 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7e0ee5c8-5a13-4359-a99f-c32753e06daa?lang=en hlth_co_proc3])|alt=A double column chart showing the share of cataract surgeries carried out as in-patient procedures. Data are shown for 2013 and 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Between 2013 and 2023, the share of procedures for cataract surgery carried out on in-patients fell in nearly every EU country for which data are available. The exceptions were Estonia and Finland where low shares had already been recorded in 2013; while the shares increased between 2013 and 2023 in these two countries, they remained lower than in a majority of EU countries. In 17 EU countries, the share of these procedures carried out on in-patients fell by more than half. Aside from Cyprus (where there is a break in series), the largest relative decrease was in Lithuania, where the share of cataract surgery carried out on in-patients fell from 64.9% in 2013 to 3.7% in 2023. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Surgical_operations_and_procedures_statistics_Health2026.xlsx|title=Surgical operations and procedures: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''Key concepts''' Surgical procedures are all types of medical interventions involving an incision with instruments mostly performed in an operating theatre; these normally involve anaesthesia and/or respiratory assistance. Surgical procedures can be performed as in-patient cases, day cases or out-patient cases. Only the main procedure performed on a patient should normally be reported, regardless of whether performed during a hospital stay, as a day case or as out-patient treatment. An in-patient is a patient who is formally admitted (or ‘hospitalised’) to an institution for treatment and/or care and stays for a minimum of one night or more than 24 hours in the hospital or other institution providing in-patient care. An in-patient or day care patient is discharged from hospital when formally released after a procedure or course of treatment (episode of care). A discharge may occur because of the finalisation of treatment, signing out against medical advice, transfer to another healthcare institution or because of death. '''Healthcare resources and activities''' Statistics on healthcare resources and healthcare activities (such as information on surgical operations and procedures) are documented in a background article on the [[Healthcare_non-expenditure_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of healthcare non-expenditure statistics]]. This provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. For surgical operations and procedures,[http://icd9cm.chrisendres.com/ the the International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM] is used: *cataract surgery (13.1 to 13.8) *caesarean section (74.0 to 74.2, 74.4 and 74.99) *transluminal coronary angioplasty (36.01, 36.02 and 36.05) *hip replacement (81.51 to 81.53) *repair of inguinal hernia (53.0 and 53.1) **of which: laparoscopic repair of inguinal hernia (17.1 and 17.2) *cholecystectomy (51.22 and 51.23) **of which: laparoscopic cholecystectomy (51.23) *total knee replacement (81.54) *appendectomy (47.0 and 47.1) **of which: laparoscopic appendectomy (47.01 and 47.11) *hysterectomy (68.3 to 68.7 and 68.9) **of which: laparoscopic hysterectomy (68.31, 68.41, 68.51, 68.61 and 68.71) *partial excision of mammary gland (85.20 to 85.23) *tonsillectomy (28.2 to 28.4) *bypass anastomosis for heart revascularisation (36.1). For country specific notes, please refer to the annexes at the end of the national metadata reports accessible from links at the beginning of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/hlth_res_esms.htm European metadata report]. In particular, note that: *data for Cyprus are generally based on information for public hospitals, but that estimates are made for the private sector (based on the same distribution as for public sector procedures) *data for Malta exclude some small private hospitals *data for Serbia only concern public hospitals. The {{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-028|title=Healthcare non-expenditure statistics manual}} provides an overview of the classifications, both for mandatory variables and variables provided on a voluntary basis. '''Symbols''' In tables, a colon ‘:’ is used to show where data are not available. Data in italics are estimates or provisional. ===Context=== For any particular type of surgical operation or procedure, the extent to which this is performed is influenced by a number of factors, including the size, age, and sex of the population and the prevalence or incidence of the underlying disease or injury among the population. Other factors include differences in medical practices between countries and the availability of financial, technical and human resources. ===Other articles=== '''Online publications''' title: Structural business statistics at regional level
text:
Eurostat regional yearbook; 2026 edition; flagship publication; EU; regional statistics; NUTS; structural business statistics; business; enterprise birth rate; enterprise death rate; employment; high-growth enterprises; regional specialisation; manufacturing; market services; knowledge-intensive; high-technology Data extracted in March 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 This article forms part of the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026]'', an annual [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications flagship publication]. It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the [[Glossary:EU|EU]], [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate]] countries. A [[Regional_yearbook_introduction#A_short_reading_guide|short reading guide]] is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps. In 2023, the EU’s enterprise birth rate was 10.5%, unchanged from 2022. Several regions in the Baltic countries, France, Malta and Portugal recorded considerably higher rates. In 2023, manufacturing activities accounted for over 30.0% of the business economy workforce in 7 NUTS level 1 regions – Czechia, Baden-Württemberg and Thüringen (Germany), Dunántúl and Alföld és Észak (Hungary), Macroregiunea Unu and Macroregiunea Patru (Romania) – well above the EU average of 18.7%.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:Compet_icon_RYB2026_small.png|left]]
[[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH08_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c7789a00-c1db-4662-8c70-c0cf1693805f?lang=en sbs_r_nuts2021] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4e4af5e0-f9e5-47a1-9efe-fdd344f9e866?lang=en sbs_sc_ovw])|alt=An infographic showing the ten EU regions with the highest shares of employment for the manufacture of motor vehicles. Data are shown in percent, based on the share of business economy employment for 2023. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Presented according to the activity classification [[Glossary:NACE|NACE]], this chapter is divided into 2 parts. *The first draws on selected regional [[Glossary:Business demography|business demography]] statistics, including [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprise]] [[Glossary:Birth of enterprise|birth]] and [[Glossary:Enterprise death|death]] rates, and the share of [[Glossary: High-growth_enterprise|high-growth enterprises]]. *The second presents [[Glossary:Structural business statistics (SBS)|structural business statistics]] for the [[Glossary:Business_economy|business economy]], [[Glossary:Manufacturing|manufacturing]] and market services, highlighting regional patterns of specialisation and concentration. As part of the European Commission’s 2024 to 2029 priorities, ''[https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/competitiveness_en A new plan for Europe’s sustainable prosperity and competitiveness]'' outlines a strategic vision to strengthen EU economic resilience while promoting environmental sustainability and social well-being. Key objectives include simplifying business processes, fostering circular and sustainable activities, improving economic resilience, increasing productivity through digital technologies, prioritising research and innovation, boosting investment, and addressing skills and labour gaps. The ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0085 Clean Industrial Deal: A joint roadmap for competitiveness and decarbonisation]'' (COM(2025) 85 final) will mobilise over €100 billion to support clean manufacturing. The European Commission plans a new framework to accelerate the rollout of renewable energy deployment, decarbonise industry and ensure sufficient production capacity for clean technologies. It aims to stimulate demand for EU-made clean products by embedding sustainability, resilience and ‘made in Europe’ criteria into public and private procurement. Recent policy directions highlight innovation, decarbonisation, digitalisation and supply chain resilience. In motor vehicle manufacturing, measures such as carbon dioxide standards, battery value chains, skills development and regulatory alignment aim to improve productivity, cost efficiency and the EU’s global competitiveness. In 2023, motor vehicle manufacturing (NACE Division 29) accounted for 1.5% of employment in the EU’s business economy. There were 3 regions that registered double-digit shares: Braunschweig in Germany, Vest in Romania and Střední Čechy in Czechia (see the '''infographic''' above for details). ===Business demography=== Business demography statistics capture key events in an enterprise’s life cycle, offering an insight into overall business dynamics. New and fast-growing enterprises are often highly agile, helping to boost efficiency and productivity in the economy. The data presented in the section below cover: *the birth of new enterprises *the growth and survival of existing enterprises, with a focus on high-growth enterprises *enterprise deaths.
'''More about the data: business demography statistics''' Business demography statistics are presented for the business economy – defined here as NACE Sections B to N and P to R and Divisions 95 and 96 – covering industry, construction, distributive trades and other market services. Business demography indicators are generally presented for 2023; the latest information for enterprise death rates concerns 2022. For enterprise birth and death rates, data are not available for [[Glossary:Nomenclature_of_territorial_units_for_statistics_(NUTS)|NUTS]] level 2 regions in Belgium, Norway, Albania, Serbia and Türkiye; national data are shown instead. High-growth enterprises are of particular interest to policymakers because they have the potential to boost regional economic performance, create jobs and, if sustained, reshape economic structures. In this publication, high-growth enterprises are defined as those meeting the following criteria: • at least 10 employees in 2020 • average annual employee growth over 10% between 2020 and 2023. High-growth enterprises may create new markets or compete in existing domestic and/or international markets. While their expansion does not always directly translate into economic growth at a national level, it is nevertheless correlated positively with the overall economic performance of a country.
'''Enterprise births and deaths''' '''''In 2023, the EU’s enterprise birth rate was 10.5%''''' The enterprise birth rate measures the number of new enterprises born during a year in relation to the total population of active enterprises in the same year. In 2023, there were 3.5 million enterprise births within the EU’s business economy. When expressed relative to the total number of enterprises (33.2 million), this equated to an enterprise birth rate of 10.5%. In 2023, enterprise birth rates for the business economy across NUTS level 2 regions were unevenly distributed. Some 34.2% of regions (80 out of 234) recorded rates above the EU average, 64.5% were below, and 1.3% had a rate that was identical to the average. This suggests that entrepreneurial activity tends to be geographically concentrated within the EU. '''Map 1''' shows that enterprise birth rates were relatively homogeneous across many EU countries, suggesting that the underlying national business environment, administrative, macro- and socio-economic conditions likely have an important impact. For example, every NUTS level 2 region in Portugal had an enterprise birth rate of at least 14.4%, while all regions in Czechia, Denmark, Greece, Italy, Hungary, Austria, Finland and Sweden recorded rates below the EU average of 10.5% (this was also the case in Belgium, Cyprus and Luxembourg). Predominantly urban regions – especially those in and around capital cities – are often found to record some of the highest enterprise birth rates. In 2023, the capital regions of Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Ireland, Greece, Austria, Poland, Romania, Slovenia and Finland posted the highest rates of enterprise creation in their respective countries. Several factors may drive these high rates of business formation, including the presence of an innovative environment, research clusters, technology hubs, easier market access, modern infrastructure or a concentration of skilled labour. In 2023, 22 NUTS level 2 regions recorded an enterprise birth rate of at least 14.0% within their business economies (see '''Map 1'''). *Some of the highest rates were concentrated in France (8 regions) and Portugal (all 9 regions). **In France, the 5 outermost regions had the highest rates of enterprise creation, peaking at 53.9% in Mayotte – by far the highest rate among EU regions. Outside of its outermost regions, the capital region of Ile-de-France had the highest enterprise birth rate, at 15.9%. **In Portugal, every region recorded a rate of at least 14.0% in 2023, peaking at 20.7% in the southern region of Península de Setúbal; Algarve (18.7%) and the capital region of Grande Lisboa (18.6%) followed with the next highest rates. *This group of 22 regions also included both Lithuanian regions, Bucureşti-Ilfov (the capital region of Romania), as well as Estonia and Malta. Rural and less economically developed regions often register lower enterprise birth rates. This may reflect relatively static local economies, with a lack of factors stimulating new business activity; alternatively, it may indicate barriers to entrepreneurship, such as cultural attitudes toward risk, limited access to capital or shortages of skilled labour. In 2023, 26 NUTS level 2 regions recorded enterprise birth rates for their business economies that were below 7.0%. These regions were concentrated in Austria (all 9 regions) and Germany (6 regions); they were joined by 3 regions from each of Denmark, Spain and Italy, as well as 2 regions in Greece. *In Austria, the lowest enterprise birth rates were observed in the westernmost regions: Vorarlberg (5.3%), Tirol and Salzburg (both 5.7%). *The neighbouring eastern regions of Thüringen and Chemnitz reported the lowest rates in Germany (both 5.3%). *Midtjylland recorded Denmark’s lowest rate (6.5%). *In Spain, 3 northern regions – Comunidad Foral de Navarra, La Rioja and Castilla y León –reported the lowest rates (all 6.8%). *The northern region of Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen had the lowest rate in Italy (6.2%). *In Greece, the island region of Voreio Aigaio recorded the lowest rate (6.5%). Map 1: Enterprise birth rate
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e73a7883-7094-4f34-a33a-f1704b366c0a?lang=en bd_hgnace_r] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/75c0653e-7189-40b0-bea9-9a394d259489?lang=en bd_l_form]) [[Image:Enterprise birth rate (% of enterprise births among active enterprises, by NUTS 2 regions, 2023)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Enterprise birth rate
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e73a7883-7094-4f34-a33a-f1704b366c0a?lang=en bd_hgnace_r] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/75c0653e-7189-40b0-bea9-9a394d259489?lang=en bd_l_form])]] '''Enterprise death rate''' '''''In 2022, the EU’s enterprise death rate was 8.4%''''' In 2022, 2.7 million enterprises definitively ceased activity within the EU’s business economy; expressed relative to the total enterprise population of 32.6 million, this equated to an enterprise death rate of 8.4%. The distribution of enterprise death rates was somewhat skewed: around 3 out of 5 NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available (142 out of 234, or 60.7%) reported rates below the EU average. Regional enterprise death rates across the business economy tended to be within a relatively narrow range in most EU countries. It was relatively common for regions with high enterprise birth rates to also record high enterprise death rates. This is not surprising, as dynamic and innovative enterprises entering a market may be in a position to drive less productive incumbents out of the market (‘creative destruction’). Moreover, a more risk-prone culture might lead to the creation of new enterprises that, however, do not stand the test of time. '''Map 2''' shows a band of relatively high enterprise death rates along the eastern flank of the EU, stretching from the Baltic countries down to Hungary. High death rates were also common across Portugal and in some regions of France. At the top of the distribution: *the French overseas region of Mayotte recorded the highest regional enterprise death rate, at 18.2% (and also had the highest enterprise birth rate) *the next highest rates were in the neighbouring Hungarian regions of Budapest (17.7%) and Pest (17.6%) *17 additional regions reported enterprise death rates of at least 12.0%, including **all 6 remaining Hungarian regions **4 Polish regions **the French capital region, Ile-de-France, along with 2 other outermost regions, Guyane and Guadeloupe **both regions of Lithuania **2 Portuguese regions, including the capital region of Grande Lisboa. At the other end of the spectrum, the lowest enterprise death rates in 2022 were consistently observed in Greece. All 13 Greek regions ranked near the bottom, with rates consistently below 4.0%. The island regions of Kriti (1.5%; 2021 data), Voreio Aigaio (1.9%; 2021 data) and Notio Aigaio (2.4%) recorded the lowest values. Outside Greece, the northern Swedish regions of Mellersta Norrland (3.9%) and Övre Norrland (4.2%), along with the northern Italian region of Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen (4.2%), also reported low enterprise death rates; Belgium (4.2%; national data) had a comparable rate. Map 2: Enterprise death rate
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e73a7883-7094-4f34-a33a-f1704b366c0a?lang=en bd_hgnace_r] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/75c0653e-7189-40b0-bea9-9a394d259489?lang=en bd_l_form]) [[Image:Enterprise death rate (% of enterprise births among active enterprises, by NUTS 2 regions, 2022)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 2: Enterprise death rate
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e73a7883-7094-4f34-a33a-f1704b366c0a?lang=en bd_hgnace_r] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/75c0653e-7189-40b0-bea9-9a394d259489?lang=en bd_l_form])]] '''High-growth enterprises''' '''''In 2023, 10.5% of all enterprises in the EU were high-growth enterprises''''' There were 180 200 high-growth enterprises across the EU in 2023 (see the shaded box above for a definition). High-growth enterprises accounted for 10.5% of the total number of active enterprises with at least 10 employees in the EU’s business economy. There was a relatively even distribution of high-growth enterprises among NUTS level 2 regions: 104 regions out of the 234 for which data are available (or 44.4%) recorded shares that were above the EU average. The presence of high-growth enterprises reflects, at least in part, the underlying structure of each region’s business economy. Several factors tend to support rapid enterprise growth: *relatively small enterprises often grow faster than larger ones – a pattern often referred to as the ‘catch-up’ process *enterprises located in regions specialised in dynamic sectors of the economy such as information and communication technologies, life sciences or knowledge-intensive services typically grow more rapidly *a favourable business environment – such as a well-developed innovation ecosystem, easy access to capital and a skilled workforce. '''Figure 1''' presents information for those regions with the highest and lowest shares of high-growth enterprises in each country. In 2023, Kriti in Greece recorded the highest share of high growth enterprises (23.4%) across NUTS level 2 regions, while the only other regions to record shares of more than 20.0% were all located in Ireland, peaking at 21.5% in the capital region of Eastern and Midland. There were also relatively high shares of high-growth enterprises in the Nordic countries, peaking in the capital regions of Helsinki-Uusimaa, Hovedstaden and Stockholm (all 17.5%). In 2023, a majority of EU countries reported that their capital region had the highest share of high-growth enterprises on their national territory. This pattern likely reflects factors such as a favourable business climate (as mentioned above) alongside a critical mass of potential business and/or household clients. The only exceptions (among multi-regional EU countries) were Greece, Spain, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal and Romania, although: *Ile-de-France had the third highest share in France, behind the outermost regions of Guyane and La Réunion *Noord-Holland had the second highest share in the Netherlands, behind Groningen *Grande Lisboa had the third highest share in Portugal, behind Região Autónoma da Madeira and Algarve. Across the EU, regional shares of high-growth enterprises varied considerably within some EU countries. Greece had the widest range, with the share in Kriti (23.4%) some 13.7 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] higher than in Voreio Aigaio (9.7%). Sweden, France, Germany, Czechia, Italy, Poland and Spain each exhibited ranges of at least 5.0 percentage points between their highest and lowest regions. By contrast, Slovenia and Ireland recorded the narrowest ranges, less than 1.0 percentage points difference between their highest and lowest regions; however, both countries have relatively few regions – just 2 and 3, respectively.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:Compet_icon_RYB2026_small.png|left]]
[[Image:High-growth enterprises (% of active enterprises, by NUTS 2 regions, 2023)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: High-growth enterprises
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/51ef9026-0d00-40c1-8d11-b2b54660b07f?lang=en bd_hgnace_r] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/1596a34b-171d-4d18-b4a3-2990708f65c2?lang=en bd_hg])|alt=A high-low chart showing information on high-growth enterprises, relative to the total number of active enterprises. Data are shown in percent for 2023. Data are shown for the regions in each country with the highest and lowest shares, as well as for the national average. Data are shown for level 2 regions in EU, EFTA and candidate countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
===Regional patterns of employment specialisation and concentration=== '''Manufacturing''' Manufacturing is defined as NACE Section C. It covers activities ranging from craft industries to large-scale industrial production across a wide range of sectors, including the manufacture of food, beverages and tobacco, wood and paper, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, fabricated metal products and transport equipment. It does not include mining and extraction, energy and water supply, nor construction and civil engineering. Manufacturing is considered vital to the EU economy, driving productivity, innovation and exports. It supports millions of jobs, strengthens regional development and underpins strategic autonomy in key products such as pharmaceuticals, machinery and green technologies. In 2023, the EU’s manufacturing sector comprised 2.2 million [[Glossary:Enterprise|enterprises]], [[Glossary:Persons_employed_-_SBS|employing]] 30.3 million people, with total [[Glossary:Wages_and_salaries_-_EBS|wages and salaries]] valued at €1 126 billion. Although accounting for 6.6% of all enterprises within the business economy, manufacturing had a significantly higher share of employment (18.7%). Average earnings in the manufacturing sector were also higher than the business economy average, as indicated by its 24.1% share of total wages and salaries. '''Map 3''' clearly shows the relative weight of the manufacturing sector in the business economy across these 3 indicators.
'''More about the data: structural business statistics''' Structural business statistics (SBS) provide detailed data on economic activities across hundreds of sectors, broken down by enterprise size (micro, small, medium-sized and large enterprises) and by region. They cover issues such as labour input, value added, productivity, profitability and investment. This information can be used to explore (among other issues) structural shifts in an economy, national or regional specialisations, and sectoral patterns of concentration. The legal basis for European business statistics changed with the adoption of ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2019.327.01.0001.01.ENG Regulation (EU) 2019/2152 on European business statistics]'' in November 2019. It created a cross-cutting legal framework for the collection, compilation, transmission and dissemination of statistics, covering the economic activities of market producers within the business economy (as defined by NACE Rev. 2 Sections B to N, P to R and Divisions 95 and 96). The data are based on non-confidential data: some activities are not available for a small number of regions, which may lead to an underestimation of the overall size of the business economy and a corresponding overestimation of the shares attributed to individual activities. It should be noted that the data for the EU aggregate (and some non-EU countries) presented in this section are based on enterprises, while regional statistics are based on local units.
'''''High presence of manufacturing local units across Czechia and Slovakia''''' In 2023, the EU’s manufacturing sector accounted for 6.6% of all enterprises within the business economy. Across EU regions, local units within manufacturing tend to be larger than average (in size), employing more people and accounting for a disproportionately high share of wages and salaries within the overall business economy. Regions in northern and western EU countries tend to have larger, more capital-intensive local units, while regions in southern and eastern EU countries are often characterised by smaller, family-owned or medium-sized local units. This reflects, among others, differences in industrial structure/tradition, investment, access to finance and technological capacity. '''Map 3''' shows the relative importance of the manufacturing sector in terms of its share of local units within the business economy. In 2023, there were 9 out of 90 NUTS level 1 regions for which data are available, where the manufacturing sector accounted for a double-digit share of the total number of local units within the business economy. Other than Nord-Est Italy, all of these regions were located in eastern EU countries. The highest shares were recorded in Czechia (14.6%) and Slovakia (13.5%). At the other end of the scale, manufacturing local units generally represented a very small share of all local units in several capital regions and regions with prominent tourist destinations, both of which are typically dominated by service activities. Luxembourg (1.9%), Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest (2.7%), Berlin (2.9%) and Região Autónoma da Madeira (2.9%) were the only regions across the EU where manufacturing local units accounted for fewer than 3.0% of all local units in the business economy.

In 2023, 18.7% of the EU’s business economy workforce was employed in manufacturing enterprises. This share was considerably higher in several NUTS level 1 regions (based on local units data), peaking at 33.0% in the western Hungarian region of Dunántúl, which hosts industrial clusters in sectors such as motor vehicles, electronics and machinery, with its strong manufacturing specialisation supported by its attractiveness to foreign investors. There were 6 other EU regions where the manufacturing sector accounted for at least 3 out of 10 people within the business economy workforce in 2023: *Macroregiunea Unu and Macroregiunea Patru in Romania (both 31.7%) *Baden-Württemberg (31.5%) and Thüringen (30.5%) in Germany *Alföld és Észak in Hungary (31.2%) *Czechia (30.9%). In absolute terms, the German regions of Bayern (1.6 million people), Baden-Württemberg (1.5 million), and Nordrhein-Westfalen (also 1.5 million) had the largest manufacturing workforces in the EU. Only 3 other NUTS level 1 regions employed more than 1.0 million people in manufacturing: the Italian regions of Nord-Ovest and Nord-Est, and Czechia. '''''Manufacturing accounted for a particularly high share of wages and salaries in the business economies of Dunántúl and Baden-Württemberg''''' The manufacturing sector across the EU generally provides relatively high wages and salaries, reflecting its capital-intensive nature, reliance on skilled labour, a prevalence of high-value and innovation, and productivity gains from advanced technology and automation. This pattern is especially evident in a cluster of regions stretching from northern Italy and southern Germany into eastern Europe, where established industrial clusters and [[Glossary:Foreign direct investment (FDI)|foreign direct investment (FDI)]], supported by supplier networks, sustain relatively well-paid manufacturing employment. In 2023, the level of manufacturing wages and salaries peaked, among NUTS level 1 regions, at €93.6 billion in Baden-Württemberg (south-west Germany). This region is among the EU’s leading manufacturing hubs, renowned for high-value, technology-intensive industries such as the manufacture of motor vehicles, machinery, electronics, pharmaceuticals and medical technology. Its innovative and diversified industrial clusters, skilled workforce and extensive research activities underpin well-paid manufacturing jobs. Wages and salaries were also relatively high – in absolute terms – in 2 other German regions: €90.8 billion in Bayern and €80.7 billion in Nordrhein-Westfalen, underlining Germany’s substantial contribution to the EU’s manufacturing base. The next highest value was observed in Italy’s Nord-Ovest region (€45.9 billion). There were several NUTS level 1 regions within the EU where the manufacturing sector accounted for close to half of all wages and salaries within the business economy (see '''Map 3'''). The highest regional shares in 2023 were recorded in the western Hungarian region of Dunántúl (48.0%) and the German region of Baden-Württemberg (45.1%). There were 3 other regions that recorded shares that were higher than 40.0%, namely, Alföld és Észak in Hungary (44.6%), Nord-Est in Italy (42.6%) and Thüringen in Germany (40.1%). '''''Average number of people employed per local unit''''' '''Map 4''' illustrates the average number of people employed per local unit in the business economies of NUTS level 1 regions. Shown as an index (with the EU average equal to 100.0), the map highlights regional differences in business structures, providing insights into productivity and economic specialisation. Higher values typically reflect capital-intensive operations benefitting from economies of scale, while lower values indicate smaller units generally characterised by more labour-intensive activity. In 2023, an average of 4.9 people were employed per local unit active in the EU’s business economy. Among the EU countries, Germany – and to a lesser degree, Denmark and Romania – were characterised by larger local units in terms of average employment. The highest numbers of people employed per local unit were consistently observed in Germany. In 2023, the average number of people employed peaked at 13.1 per local unit in the northern region of Bremen. In 7 additional German regions – Baden-Württemberg, Hamburg, Niedersachsen, Saarland, Hessen, Nordrhein-Westfalen and Sachsen-Anhalt – each local unit employed, on average, more than twice as many people as the EU average. In 2023, the lowest average number of persons employed per local unit was recorded in the French region of Corse, with 2.2 persons employed per unit. Low averages – fewer than 3.0 people employed per unit – were also observed in several other regions, including: *Régions Ultrapériphériques Françaises and Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur in France *Kentriki Elláda in Greece *Slovakia *West-Nederland and Noord-Nederland in the Netherlands *Isole in Italy *Região Autónoma dos Açores in Portugal *Åland in Finland. Some of the smallest local units were observed in island regions, where economic activity is often concentrated in local businesses, particularly in service-oriented or artisanal sectors. These structures often result in more fragmented production, limited economies of scale and a greater reliance on labour-intensive activities. '''''Average wages and salaries per person employed''''' '''Map 4''' also shows average wages and salaries per person employed in the business economies of NUTS level 1 regions. Presented as an index (with the EU average equal to 100.0), it highlights regional variations in remuneration. Higher values may be associated with more productive, technology-driven or skills-intensive activities, while lower values typically correspond to regions dominated by more labour-intensive activities. Note that the use of the number of persons employed rather than the number of employees understates the calculated average; ratios for those regions with a high incidence of self-employment and/or unpaid family workers will be particularly affected. In 2023, people employed within the EU’s business economy received an average of €28 900 as a wage or salary. Across NUTS level 1 regions, the highest average wages and salaries were observed in Luxembourg (€66 400) and Denmark (€52 800). This may reflect, at least in part, highly productive, capital- and skill-intensive economies, along with labour regulations and wage-setting mechanisms aligned with local living costs. Aside from Luxembourg and Denmark, several other EU regions recorded wages and salaries per person employed at least 25.0% above the EU average: *7 predominantly western regions of Germany *all 3 Austrian regions *2 Belgian regions *both Finnish regions *single regions from France, the Netherlands and Sweden (all including their capitals) *Ireland. Wages and salaries per person employed were considerably below the EU average in most Greek regions and across many eastern parts of the EU in 2023. The lowest averages were recorded in the Greek regions of Kentriki Elláda (€5 900; 20.4% of the EU average), Nisia Aigaiou-Kriti (€7 700; 26.7%) and Voreia Elláda (€8 300; 28.9%). The only other region with wages and salaries per person employed below €10 000 was Severna i Yugoiztochna Bulgaria (€8 400; 29.0%).
