title: Sustainable development goals (SDGs) and EU regions - peace
text:
EU statistics, providing an overview of regional statistics for the EU’s set of sustainable development indicators, covering the topic of peace. Data extracted in February 2026 Planned article update: March 2028 Within the EU in 2022, there were 0.66 deaths due to homicide per 100 000 inhabitants. Some of the highest death rates due to homicide in the EU were recorded in a band of regions running down the easternmost edge of the EU and in a number of the EU’s autonomous and outermost regions. This article looks at [[Glossary:Sustainable development|sustainable development]] indicators from a regional perspective – it covers Goal 16, peace. The information was selected from the 2025 editions of two of Eurostat’s flagship publications: the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/ks-01-25-037 Eurostat Regional Yearbook]'' and ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/ks-05-24-071 Sustainable development in the European Union – Monitoring report on progress towards the SDGs in an EU context]''. All data were re-extracted at the start of February 2026 to ensure that the most up-to-date information is presented, which may explain differences in coverage compared with the original publications. ===Goal 16 – Peace, justice and strong institutions=== [[Image:SDG16.PNG|left|80px|80px]] SDG 16 calls for peaceful and inclusive societies based on respect for human rights, protection of the most vulnerable, the rule of law and good governance at all levels. It also envisions transparent, effective and accountable institutions. Peace, security, democracy, the rule of law and respect for fundamental rights are also founding values of the EU. Across EU regions, SDG 16 tracks the number of deaths due to homicide and injuries inflicted by another person with the intent to injure or kill by any means, as defined by the [[Glossary:International_classification_of_diseases_(ICD)|International Classification of Diseases (ICD)]] codes X85 to Y09 and Y87.1. The data are presented as standardised death rates, meaning they are adjusted to a standard European age distribution to measure death rates independently of the population age structure in individual EU regions; they are expressed as a ratio per 100 000 inhabitants. Within the EU in 2022, there were 0.66 deaths due to homicide per 100 000 inhabitants. Some of the highest rates were recorded in a band of regions running down the easternmost edge of the EU from Sweden and Finland, through the [[Glossary:Baltic_Member_States|Baltic]] countries to Romania, Bulgaria, Greece and Cyprus. There were also very high death rates in a number of the EU’s autonomous and outermost regions, including the Spanish region of Ciudad de Ceuta (5.27 deaths due to homicide per 100 000 inhabitants) and the French regions of Martinique (4.23 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants), Guyane (4.07 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants) and Guadeloupe (3.97 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants); indeed, these 4 regions had the highest rates across the EU among NUTS level 2 regions. They were followed by Åland in Finland (3.58 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants; 2020 data) and Latvia (2.93 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants), while Corse in France, Nord-Est in Romania and Severozapaden in Bulgaria were the only other regions in the EU to report standardised death rates due to homicide of at least 2.00 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants. Map 1: Standardised death rate due to homicide, 2022
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0b55d833-7e3d-46d0-b980-c5095fbba669?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-30T15:46:55Z hlth_cd_asdr2]) [[Image:Standardised death rate due to homicide (per 100 000 inhabitants, by NUTS 2 regions, 2022)_SDG2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Standardised death rate due to homicide
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0b55d833-7e3d-46d0-b980-c5095fbba669?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-30T15:46:55Z hlth_cd_asdr2])]] ===Source data for figures and maps=== {{Template:Excel|filename=Sustainable development goals – indicators for EU regions_2026_peace.xlsx|title=Sustainable development indicators – regional analyses – peace}} ===Data sources=== All of the data presented in this article can be found on Eurostat’s [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database database]. The data presented within this article concern regional statistics for EU and [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|European Free Trade Association (EFTA)]] countries, as well as [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]]. The classification of territorial units for statistics – known as [[Glossary:Nomenclature_of_territorial_units_for_statistics_(NUTS)|NUTS]] – is at the heart of the EU’s regional statistics. This classification is based on a hierarchy, subdividing each EU country into regions. These are classified according to NUTS levels 1, 2 and 3, from larger to smaller regions. The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-gq-23-010 2024 edition of the NUTS classification] provides the basis for classifying regional information in this article. For EFTA and candidate countries, the concept of ‘statistical regions’ is used instead of NUTS. This applies the same principles as those used in the establishment of the NUTS classification but is based on bilateral agreements between the countries concerned and Eurostat. Note that currently there is no agreed list of regions concerning Bosnia and Herzegovina, Moldova or Georgia. For further information concerning metadata and data sources, please refer to the links that are provided at the end of each section in the article above. ===Context=== '''The United Nations framework for sustainable development''' In September 2015, the [https://www.un.org/en/ga/ United Nations General Assembly] adopted the [https://sdgs.un.org/2030agenda 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development]. The 2030 Agenda is a bold and transformative step designed to stimulate action through to 2030, shifting the world onto a sustainable and resilient path with the aim of leaving no one behind. At its core is a list of [https://sdgs.un.org/goals 17 sustainable development goals] and 169 related targets that can be categorised under what are often referred to as the '''five P’s''': *'''people''' – end poverty and hunger *'''planet'''– protect the planet from degradation *'''prosperity''' – ensure that all human beings can enjoy prosperous and fulfilling lives *'''peace''' – foster peaceful, just and inclusive societies *'''partnership''' – mobilise the means required to implement the Agenda. A set of indicators to track progress towards the SDGs was agreed under the supervision of the [https://unstats.un.org/UNSDWebsite/statcom/ UN Statistical Commission]. Comprehensive reviews of this indicator framework were conducted in 2020 and again in 2025. At the time of writing (February 2026), the [https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/indicators/indicators-list/ SDG indicator framework] consists of 234 unique indicators (some of which are repeated under two or three of the different targets). The 2030 Agenda provided the European Commission with a new impetus for achieving sustainable development, as described in the ''[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/sustainable-development-goals/eu-approach-sdgs-implementation_en EU approach to SDGs implementation]''. The EU is fully committed to delivering on the 2030 Agenda, and the SDGs form an intrinsic part of the European Commission’s work programme. Eurostat supports this approach through a quantitative assessment of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/publications EU’s progress towards the SDGs] using a set of 102 [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/database indicators] that have been adapted to the EU context. The EU SDG indicator set is structured according to the 17 SDGs – each goal has six indicators attributed to it (while there are supplementary indicators for other goals that may be used to complement the monitoring of a particular goal). The initial focus of the 2030 Agenda was on supranational and country-based programmes. However, over time there have been efforts to localise SDGs, highlighting the links between local actions and global challenges. Sustainable development strategies have increasingly focused on involving regional, local and civil society stakeholders, while monitoring different territorial typologies has reinforced national efforts, supported regional development strategies and provided a broader picture of developments within countries. Regional statistics, structured by SDG, offer a detailed territorial view of the current socioeconomic situation in areas such as living conditions, health, education, equality, economic growth or climate action. These regional statistics make it possible to pinpoint areas that require targeted interventions, address disparities between regions, and ensure that no one is left behind. '''The EU’s approach to implementing the SDGs''' Several major policy documents have shaped the EU’s approach to implementing the SDGs. A communication, ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2016:739:FIN Next steps for a sustainable European future: European action for sustainability]'' (COM(2016) 739 final) highlighted the integration of the SDGs into the EU’s policy framework. The EU’s approach for implementing the 2030 Agenda is described in detail within ''[https://commission.europa.eu/document/1ae1e765-0a3f-4092-b87e-86ecbd1ec0c7_en Delivering on the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals – A comprehensive approach]''. For a complete overview of the European Commission’s activities, see the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/sustainable-development-goals/eu-whole-government-approach_en EU’s ‘whole of government’ approach to implementing the SDGs]. '''EU policies that help towards the implementation of the 2030 Agenda''' The European Commission’s political priorities for 2024 to 2029 seek to deliver [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/competitiveness_en A new plan for Europe’s sustainable prosperity and competitiveness]. To safeguard and boost Europe’s competitiveness, prosperity and fairness, the EU will seek to: *make business easier and faster *build a new clean industrial deal *work towards a more circular and resilient economy *boost productivity with digital technology diffusion *put research and innovation at the heart of the EU economy *turbo charge investment *tackle skills and labour gaps. The [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en European Green Deal], adopted in December 2019, is the EU’s growth and transformation strategy as it seeks to tie environmental sustainability to competitiveness and job creation. It aims to transform the EU into a climate-neutral society while leaving no one behind, creating a modern, resource-efficient, competitive and fair economy where there are no net emissions of greenhouse gases by 2050 and where economic growth is decoupled from resource use. The European Green Deal is an integral part of the European Commission’s strategy to implement the 2030 Agenda and the SDGs. [https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/policy/what/investment-policy_en Cohesion policy] in the EU is strongly aligned with the SDGs. It contributes to strengthening economic, social and territorial cohesion and correcting imbalances between countries and regions. It delivers on the EU’s political priorities, especially the green and digital transitions. The above information contains three examples of EU policies that highlight the EU’s comprehensive approach to implementing the 2030 Agenda. Below is a non-exhaustive list of some other policies that contribute towards its delivery: *[https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/biodiversity-strategy-2030_en Biodiversity strategy for 2030] *[https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/circular-economy_en EU initiatives for the transition to a circular economy] *[https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/european-climate-law_en European Climate Law] *[https://op.europa.eu/webpub/empl/european-pillar-of-social-rights/en/ European Pillar of Social Rights] *[https://commission.europa.eu/business-economy-euro/european-semester_en European Semester] *[https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/farm-fork-strategy_en Farm to fork strategy] *[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/gender-equality/gender-equality-strategy_en Gender equality strategy] *[https://next-generation-eu.europa.eu/index_en NextGenerationEU: for a stronger, more resilient Europe] *[https://rural-vision.europa.eu/action-plan_en Rural action plan] *[https://www.urbanagenda.urban-initiative.eu/ Urban Agenda for the EU]. ===Other articles=== *[[EU_sustainable_development_indicators_at_regional_level|EU sustainable development indicators at regional level]] *[[Sustainable_development_goals_(SDGs)_and_EU_regions_-_people|Sustainable development goals (SDGs) and EU regions - prosperity]] *[[:Category:Regions and cities|All articles on regions and cities]] *[[:Category:Sustainable development goals|All articles on sustainable development goals]] ===Publications=== '''Paper and PDF publications''' *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-037|title=Eurostat regional yearbook – 2025 edition}} *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-flagship-publications/w/KS-01-24-018 Sustainable development in the European Union – Monitoring report on progress towards the SDGs in an EU context – 2025 edition] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-catalogues/w/KS-01-24-019 Sustainable development in the European Union – Overview of progress towards the SDGs in an EU context – 2025 edition] '''Online publications''' *[[Eurostat_regional_yearbook|Eurostat Regional Yearbook]] *[[Sustainable_development_in_the_European_Union|Sustainable development in the European Union]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/regions/database Regional statistics by NUTS classification (reg)], see: :Regional agriculture statistics (reg_agr) :Regional demographic statistics (reg_dem) :Regional economic accounts (reg_eco10) :Regional education statistics (reg_educ) :Regional science and technology statistics (reg_sct) :Regional structural business statistics (reg_sbs) :Regional business demography (reg_bd) :Regional health statistics (reg_hlth) :Regional tourism statistics (reg_tour) :Regional transport statistics (reg_tran) :Regional labour market statistics (reg_lmk) :Regional labour costs statistics (reg_lcs) :Regional digital economy and society (reg_isoc) :Regional environmental and energy statistics (reg_env) :Regional poverty and social exclusion statistics (reg_ilc) :Regional crime statistics (reg_crim) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/database Sustainable development indicators (sdg)], see: :Goal 1 - title: Sustainable development goals (SDGs) and EU regions - prosperity
text:
EU statistics, providing an overview of regional statistics for the EU’s set of sustainable development indicators, covering the topic of prosperity. Data extracted in February 2026 Planned article update: March 2028 Some of the highest levels of GDP per inhabitant were clustered in western EU countries – with particularly high levels in Ireland, the Benelux countries, Germany and Austria – as well as many of the EU’s capital regions. The Polish and Slovakian capital regions of Warszawski stołeczny and Bratislavský kraj – together with the autonomous Finnish archipelago of Åland – had the highest regional employment rates in the EU. The information was selected from the 2025 editions of 2 of Eurostat’s flagship publications, the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/ks-01-25-037 Eurostat Regional Yearbook]'' and ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/ks-05-24-071 Sustainable development in the European Union – Monitoring report on progress towards the SDGs in an EU context]''. All data were re-extracted at the start of February 2026 to ensure that the most up-to-date information is presented, which may explain differences in coverage compared with the original publications. ===Goal 8 – decent work and economic growth === [[Image:SDG8.PNG|left|80px|80px]] SDG 8 recognises the importance of sustained economic growth and high levels of economic productivity for the creation of well-paid quality jobs and calls for opportunities for full employment and decent work for all. GDP per inhabitant is calculated as the ratio of GDP to the average population in a specific year. These data are expressed in [[Glossary:Purchasing_power_standard_(PPS)|purchasing power standard (PPS)]] terms, which represent a common currency that eliminates differences in price levels between countries to allow meaningful volume comparisons of GDP. In 2024, GDP per inhabitant averaged 39 900 PPS across the EU. Some of the highest levels of GDP per inhabitant were clustered in western EU countries, with particularly high levels in Ireland, the [[Glossary:Benelux|Benelux]] countries, Germany and Austria. There were also relatively high levels recorded in many of the EU’s capital regions (see '''Map 1''') and in northern Italy. The Eastern and Midland region of Ireland recorded the highest level of GDP per inhabitant in 2024, at 107 200 PPS. It was followed by Luxembourg (97 700 PPS), Southern in Ireland (86 500 PPS), Hamburg in Germany (78 300 PPS), the Czech capital region of Praha (76 600 PPS) and the Belgian capital region of Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest (76 000 PPS). Five other regions also reported GDP per inhabitant of at least 65 000 PPS: the capital regions of Denmark, Hungary, the Netherlands and Romania, as well as Oberbayern in southern Germany. For more information on regional disparities in GDP per inhabitant, please refer to SDG 10 below, where the focus is on reducing inequalities within and among countries. Map 1: GDP per inhabitant

Having peaked at 16.1% in 2013, the NEET rate subsequently fell during 6 consecutive years. With the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, it climbed to 13.8% in 2020, after which a downward trend returned. In 2024, the EU’s NEET rate stood at 11.1%. Economic crises tend to hit young people disproportionately hard, as young people are more likely to work with temporary and other forms of precarious contracts that are easier to terminate. The NEET rate can be used to investigate the share of young people who have not transitioned from education/training to employment. It is generally considered a more comprehensive measure than the unemployment rate, insofar as it is more closely linked to young people’s risk of social and labour market exclusion. In 15 out of the 240 NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available, at least 20.0% of all young people aged 15–29 were neither in employment, nor in education or training in 2024, see '''Map 2'''. Some of the highest NEET rates were recorded in predominantly rural regions located in southern and eastern EU countries, as well as some of the outermost regions, including: *all 4 of the French outermost regions (for which data are available; no information for Mayotte), including Guyane, which recorded the highest NEET rate in the EU, as 34.4% of all young people were neither in employment, nor in education or training *4 regions located in southern Italy – Calabria (26.2%), Sicilia (25.7%), Campania (24.9%) and Puglia (21.4%) *4 regions located in Romania – Sud-Est (29.9%), Sud-Vest Oltenia (25.0%), Centru (24.8%) and Sud-Muntenia (20.2%) *2 regions located in Greece – Ionia Nisia (23.5%) and Notio Aigaio (20.0%) *Severozapaden in Bulgaria (24.7%). In 2024, there were 88 NUTS level 2 regions that reported a NEET rate that was already below the EU’s policy target of 9.0% (to be reached by 2030). Among these, there were 7 regions where the NEET rate was less than 5.0%: *the vast majority of these – 6 regions – were located in the Netherlands, including the region of Utrecht that had the lowest NEET rate in the EU, at 4.4% *the Czech capital region of Praha (4.8%) was the only other region to report a rate of less than 5.0%. Capital regions generally recorded lower than (national) average shares of young people who were neither in employment nor in education or training. In 2024, the only exceptions – among multi-regional EU countries – were in Austria, Germany, Belgium and Ireland; the difference in the latter was minimal. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''The employment rate''' The EU’s [[Glossary:Employment_rate|employment rate]] target is to have, by 2030, at least 78% of the population aged 20 to 64 in work. The choice of this age range reflects the growing proportion of young people who remain within education into their late teens (and beyond), potentially restricting their participation in the labour market. Prior to the onset of the COVID-19 crisis, the EU’s employment rate for the core working-age population (20 to 64 years) had increased for 6 consecutive years, reaching 73.1% by 2019. This pattern came to an abrupt end in 2020 as the rate fell 0.9 percentage points. However, all of the losses during the initial stages of the pandemic were recovered in 2021 (up 0.9 percentage points). The EU’s employment rate continued to increase between 2022 and 2024, rising 1.5, 0.7 and 0.5 percentage points, respectively, to stand at a historical high of 75.8% in 2024. '''Map 3''' shows the employment rate for NUTS level 2 regions in 2024. Some 46.5% of EU regions (113 out of the 243 for which data are available) had already reached or surpassed the EU target of 78.0%. These regions were mainly concentrated in Czechia (all 8 regions), Denmark (all 5 regions), Germany (35 out of 38 regions; the exceptions being Berlin, Düsseldorf and Bremen), Ireland (all 3 regions), Hungary (5 out of 8 regions), the Netherlands (all 12 regions), Austria (6 out of 9 regions), Poland (6 out of 17 regions), Portugal (5 out of 9 regions), Slovakia (3 out of 4 regions) and Sweden (all 8 regions). In 2024, the Finnish archipelago of Åland had the highest employment rate among NUTS level 2 regions of the EU, at 86.4%. The second highest rate was recorded in the Polish capital region of Warszawski stołeczny (86.2%), while the third highest rate was in another capital region, namely, Bratislavský kraj in Slovakia (85.4%). Many of the regions with relatively low employment rates were characterised as rural, sparsely-populated, or peripheral regions. This pattern was particularly apparent in southern regions of Spain and Italy, much of Greece, several regions in Romania and the outermost regions of France. These areas typically suffered from limited employment opportunities, especially for individuals with intermediate and high skill levels. Another group of regions characterised by relatively low employment rates are former industrial heartlands that have not adapted economically. Some of these have witnessed the negative impact of globalisation on traditional sectors of their economies (such as coal mining, steel or textiles manufacturing). Examples include a band of regions running from north-east France into the Région wallonne (Belgium). Approximately a tenth (24 out of the 243 regions for which data are available) of all EU regions had an employment rate that was below 67.0% in 2024. This group included the capital region of Belgium, as well as 2 regions in southern Italy where less than half of the core working-age population was employed: Calabria (48.5%) and Campania (49.4%). It also recognises the importance of research and innovation for finding solutions to social, economic and environmental challenges.

'''R&D intensity''' [[Glossary:Gross domestic expenditure on R %26 D (GERD)|Gross domestic expenditure on R&D (GERD)]] includes research expenditure made by businesses, higher education institutions, governments and private non-profit organisations. In 2023, the EU’s GERD was valued at €389.2 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]]; this is the latest year for which regional statistics are available. [[Glossary:R_%26_D_intensity|R&D intensity]] is frequently used as a measure to determine an economy’s creative/innovative capacity; it is the ratio of R&D expenditure to GDP. Despite modest annual increases over the last couple of decades, R&D intensity in the EU remains below a long-established target of 3.00%. Having increased somewhat during the COVID-19 crisis – reflecting a larger downturn in GDP than R&D expenditure – R&D intensity returned to its pre-pandemic levels, with a ratio of 2.26% in 2023. The regional distribution of R&D intensity was heavily skewed: in 2023, some 12.1% (or 28 out of 231) of all regions for which data are available across the EU had an intensity ratio above the EU target of at least 3.00%, see '''Map 4'''. They were concentrated exclusively in western and [[Glossary:Nordic_Member_States|Nordic]] EU countries: Germany (11 regions), Belgium, Austria, Sweden (all with 4 regions), France (2 regions), as well as single regions located in each of Denmark, the Netherlands (NUTS level 1) and Finland. There were 5 capital regions within this group of 28, namely: Hovedstaden in Denmark (4.63%), Wien in Austria (3.95%), Helsinki-Uusimaa in Finland (also 3.95%), Stockholm in Sweden (3.53%) and Berlin in Germany (3.07%). In 2023, the highest ratio of R&D intensity among NUTS level 2 regions was recorded in the Belgian region of Prov. Brabant wallon (9.27%); its research activities are centred on pharmaceuticals, university research, life sciences, medical imagery, computing and telecommunications. The next highest ratios were recorded in 3 German regions: Stuttgart (7.83%), Braunschweig (6.10%) and Karlsruhe (5.90%). Map 4: R&D intensity

It calls for nations to reduce inequalities in income as well as those based on age, sex, disability, race, ethnicity, origin, religion, and economic or other status within a country. The goal also addresses inequalities among countries and calls for support for safe migration and the mobility of people. '''Regional disparities for GDP per inhabitant''' '''Figure 2''' presents information on regional disparities in GDP per inhabitant. The [[Glossary:Coefficient_of_variation|coefficient of variation]] is used as a measure of disparity across regions: a higher number means greater disparity within the EU country being analysed. In 2024, there were considerable regional disparities for GDP per inhabitant across 4 eastern EU countries: Romania, Hungary, Czechia and Bulgaria. They each had coefficients of variation of at least 43.7%. Their coefficients of variation reflected particularly high levels of GDP per inhabitant in capital regions that could be contrasted with the remainder of the territory where GDP per inhabitant was lower than the EU average. By contrast, GDP per inhabitant was much more uniformly distributed across the regions of Austria, Finland, Sweden and the Netherlands, where the coefficient of variation was within the range of 15.8% to 20.1%. During the period 2014 to 2024, regional disparities for GDP per inhabitant fell at a relatively rapid pace in Finland and Poland, where the coefficient of variation was 5.8 percentage points and 2.9 percentage points lower at the end of the period under consideration. By contrast, there were 4 EU countries where the coefficient of variation rose between 2014 and 2024 by a considerable margin (at least 3.9 percentage points). The largest increase was observed in Romania, up 5.9 percentage points from 51.4% to 57.3%, while there was also a relatively large widening of regional disparities in Denmark, Hungary and Bulgaria (generally reflecting faster than average growth in their capital regions). For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Income distribution''' Although GDP per inhabitant has traditionally been used to assess regional divergence/convergence in overall living standards, this measure does not account for income paid/received across national or regional borders, nor does it capture the distribution of income within a population. Consequently, social scientists are increasingly using alternative/broader measures in their quest to gain a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of economic and societal developments. The [[Glossary:Income_quintile_share_ratio|income quintile share ratio (S80/S20)]] is used to measure the inequality of income distribution. In 2024, the EU’s ratio was 4.7 – in other words, the combined income received by the 20% of people with the highest incomes was 4.7 times as high as the combined income received by the 20% with the lowest incomes. Note that the ratio for the EU is not calculated directly across the EU population, but as a population-weighted ratio of national ratios. '''Map 5''' shows the regional distribution of the income quintile share ratio. In 2024, this distribution was skewed: 149 out of 210 regions for which data are available had a ratio that was below the EU average, while there were 61 regions that reported income disparities that were equal to or greater than the EU average. At the top end of the distribution, there were 13 NUTS level 2 regions where the income quintile share ratio was at least 6.0 in 2024. The highest ratios were concentrated in Bulgaria, the autonomous Spanish regions of Ciudad de Melilla and Ciudad de Ceuta, Italy, Latvia and Lithuania. Leaving aside the atypical Spanish autonomous regions, the highest ratios were recorded in the Bulgarian capital region of Yugozapaden and in the southern Italian region of Calabria (where the income of the top 20% of earners was 7.6 times as high as the income of the bottom 20% of earners). In 2024, the lowest income quintile share ratio was recorded in the Slovak capital region of Bratislavský kraj, where the share of total income held by the highest earning 20% of the population was 2.5 times as high as the share held by the lowest earning 20% of the population. Ratios less than 3.0 were also recorded in: *the Dutch regions of Drenthe (2.6) and Zeeland (2.8) *another Slovak region, Západné Slovensko (2.8) *Jihozápad in Czechia (2.9). Within multi-regional EU countries (no regional data for France), the distribution of income often had a different pattern in the capital region when compared with the rest of each territory. In 2024, it was commonplace to find that the capital region had the highest income quintile share ratio. This was the case in Belgium (5.0; NUTS level 1), Bulgaria (7.6), Czechia (4.2), Denmark (5.0), Ireland (3.8), Hungary (4.6), the Netherlands (4.4), Austria (5.9), Poland (4.7), Finland (4.1) and Sweden (5.0). By contrast, this pattern was reversed in Romania, where the lowest income quintile share ratios was recorded in the capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov and in Vest (both 3.5). In 2024, approximately 3 out of 4 people across the EU lived in urban areas – in cities or in towns and suburbs. With the share of Europe’s urban population projected to rise, sustainable cities, towns and suburbs are essential for citizens’ well-being and quality of life. '''Road fatalities''' The EU’s roads are among the safest in the world. The EU has set itself the goal of cutting by half the number of [[Glossary:People killed in road accidents|road fatalities]] and serious injuries by 2030, and committed to reduce the number of fatalities on its roads to almost zero by 2050. Within a statistical context, the number of road fatalities concerns people who were killed immediately in a traffic accident or who died within 30 days as a result of an injury sustained in a road accident. In 2023, there were 46 road fatalities per million inhabitants in the EU. These fatalities were quite evenly distributed insofar as 123 out of 234 NUTS level 2 regions (or 52.6% of all regions) recorded an incidence of road fatalities that was above the EU average, while 104 had a value that was below; there were 7 regions that had the same number of road fatalities per million inhabitants as the EU average. '''Map 6''' confirms that some of the highest incidence rates for road fatalities were recorded in rural regions of the EU. In 2023, there were 7 NUTS level 2 regions with at least 100 road fatalities per million inhabitants. This group was located almost exclusively in the south-eastern part of the EU, although it also included a single outermost region. The highest incidence of road fatalities was recorded in the Bulgarian region of Severozapaden (166 road fatalities per million inhabitants), followed by the Greek island regions of Ionia Nisia (120) and Notio Aigaio (119), and the French outermost region of Guyane (117). By contrast, urban and capital regions tended to report much lower incidences of road fatalities. Among other factors, this may be linked to more extensive public transport networks, lower motorisation rates and lower average speeds – there may be lower speed limits in built-up areas, while motorway networks in and around major conurbations are often congested. There were 26 NUTS level 2 regions where there were fewer than 25 road fatalities per million inhabitants in 2023. A majority of regions in this group were characterised as urban areas, including 11 that were capital regions. Particularly low incidence rates were recorded in the Belgian capital region of Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest (5 deaths per million inhabitants), the Austrian capital region of Wien (6) and the German capital region of Berlin (9). In addition, natural sources of air pollution include volcanic eruptions, desert dust and forest fires. Air pollution remains a major cause of premature death and disease across the EU, with [[Glossary:Particulate_matter_-_environment|fine particulate matter]] identified as having the most serious human health impacts. The definition of fine particulate matter covers particles with a diameter of 2.5 micrometres or less (otherwise referred to as PM2.5). Some of the most common causes of both illness and premature death attributed to air pollution include heart disease, stroke, lung disease, lung cancer and asthma; these illnesses also have an associated economic cost through lost working days and healthcare expenditure. To address this, the [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/zero-pollution-action-plan_en EU’s zero pollution action plan] has set a target to reduce premature deaths caused by fine particulate matter by at least 55% by 2030 (relative to 2005 levels). More broadly, the plan aims to bring air, water and soil pollution down to levels no longer considered harmful to human health and natural ecosystems by 2050. The [[Glossary:European_Environment_Agency_(EEA)|European Environment Agency (EEA)]] estimates that fine particulate matter resulted in 239 100 premature deaths across the EU in 2022, which equated to 78 premature deaths per 100 000 inhabitants aged 30 years or more. Note that all of the information in this section on premature deaths attributable to fine particulate matter concerns a cohort of people aged 30 years or more – sometimes referred to as the ‘affected population’ – since this is the population age range generally considered within epidemiological studies. Unsurprisingly, the highest absolute numbers of premature deaths associated with fine particulate matter occurred in some of the most populous NUTS level 3 regions, primarily in southern and eastern EU countries, particularly in predominantly urban regions. The northern Italian region of Milano (4 486) recorded the highest number of premature deaths attributed to fine particulate matter in 2022. High counts were also observed in Barcelona in Spain (3 357) and the Italian capital region of Roma (2 862). The regional distribution of premature deaths attributed to fine particulate matter was skewed: in 724 out of 1 061 NUTS level 3 regions for which data are available in 2022 – or approximately 2 out of every 3 regions in the EU (68.2%) – the number of premature deaths per 100 000 inhabitants was below the EU average. While the absolute number of premature deaths attributed to exposure to fine particulate matter was highest in some of the most populous NUTS level 3 regions of the EU, the most significant impacts of air pollution (when normalised relative to population size) were generally observed in eastern EU countries. In 2022, there were 79 NUTS level 3 regions within the EU where the number of premature deaths attributable to air pollution was at least 150 per 100 000 inhabitants, see '''Map 7'''. At the top end of the distribution, the Bulgarian capital region of Sofia (stolitsa) had the highest ratio, at 240 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants. There were 5 other regions that reported rates of at least 200 premature deaths per 100 000 inhabitants attributable to air pollution, including: *2 more regions in Bulgaria – Vidin and Plovdiv *the Polish regions of Miasto Kraków and Katowicki *the Croatian region of Brodsko-posavska županija. At the other end of the distribution, there were 11 NUTS level 3 regions in the EU with no premature deaths associated with fine particulate matter in 2022. All of them were located in Sweden, the majority being in the northern part of the country. Note that, as only partial data are currently available for Finland based on the NUTS 2024 classification, national data have been published for this country. Information from an earlier version of the NUTS classification suggests that several regions – particularly in northern Finland – also recorded no premature deaths associated with fine particulate matter. Map 7: Premature deaths attributed to exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5)
'' Source:'' European Environment Agency (EEA) [[Image:Premature deaths attributed to exposure to fine particulate matter (per 100 000 inhabitants, by NUTS 3 regions, 2022)_SDG2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 7: Premature deaths attributed to exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5)
'' Source:'' European Environment Agency (EEA)]] ===Source data for figures and maps=== {{Template:Excel|filename=Sustainable development goals – indicators for EU regions_2026_prosperity.xlsx|title=Sustainable development indicators – regional analyses – prosperity}} ===Data sources=== All of the data presented in this article can be found on Eurostat’s [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database database]. The bulk of the information was collected through the [[Glossary:European_statistical_system_(ESS)|European Statistical System (ESS)]]. However, a number of alternative data sources have been used, including data the European Environment Agency (EEA). Specific details concerning the sources used are provided under each infographic, map or figure. The data presented within this article concern regional statistics for EU and [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|European Free Trade Association (EFTA)]] countries, as well as [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]]. The classification of territorial units for statistics – known as [[Glossary:Nomenclature_of_territorial_units_for_statistics_(NUTS)|NUTS]] – is at the heart of the EU’s regional statistics. This classification is based on a hierarchy, subdividing each EU country into regions. These are classified according to NUTS levels 1, 2 and 3, from larger to smaller regions. The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-gq-23-010 2024 edition of the NUTS classification] provides the basis for classifying regional information in this article. For EFTA and candidate countries, the concept of ‘statistical regions’ is used instead of NUTS. This applies the same principles as those used in the establishment of the NUTS classification but is based on bilateral agreements between the countries concerned and Eurostat. Note that currently there is no agreed list of regions concerning Bosnia and Herzegovina, Moldova or Georgia. For further information concerning metadata and data sources, please refer to the links that are provided at the end of each section in the article above. ===Context=== '''The United Nations framework for sustainable development''' In September 2015, the [https://www.un.org/en/ga/ United Nations General Assembly] adopted the [https://sdgs.un.org/2030agenda 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development]. The 2030 Agenda is a bold and transformative step designed to stimulate action through to 2030, shifting the world onto a sustainable and resilient path with the aim of leaving no one behind. At its core is a list of [https://sdgs.un.org/goals 17 sustainable development goals] and 169 related targets that can be categorised under what are often referred to as the '''five P’s''': *'''people''' – end poverty and hunger *'''planet'''– protect the planet from degradation *'''prosperity''' – ensure that all human beings can enjoy prosperous and fulfilling lives *'''peace''' – foster peaceful, just and inclusive societies *'''partnership''' – mobilise the means required to implement the Agenda. A set of indicators to track progress towards the SDGs was agreed under the supervision of the [https://unstats.un.org/UNSDWebsite/statcom/ UN Statistical Commission]. Comprehensive reviews of this indicator framework were conducted in 2020 and again in 2025. At the time of writing (February 2026), the [https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/indicators/indicators-list/ SDG indicator framework] consists of 234 unique indicators (some of which are repeated under two or three of the different targets). The 2030 Agenda provided the European Commission with a new impetus for achieving sustainable development, as described in the ''[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/sustainable-development-goals/eu-approach-sdgs-implementation_en EU approach to SDGs implementation]''. The EU is fully committed to delivering on the 2030 Agenda, and the SDGs form an intrinsic part of the European Commission’s work programme. Eurostat supports this approach through a quantitative assessment of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/publications EU’s progress towards the SDGs] using a set of 102 [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/database indicators] that have been adapted to the EU context. The EU SDG indicator set is structured according to the 17 SDGs – each goal has six indicators attributed to it (while there are supplementary indicators for other goals that may be used to complement the monitoring of a particular goal). The initial focus of the 2030 Agenda was on supranational and country-based programmes. However, over time there have been efforts to localise SDGs, highlighting the links between local actions and global challenges. Sustainable development strategies have increasingly focused on involving regional, local and civil society stakeholders, while monitoring different territorial typologies has reinforced national efforts, supported regional development strategies and provided a broader picture of developments within countries. Regional statistics, structured by SDG, offer a detailed territorial view of the current socioeconomic situation in areas such as living conditions, health, education, equality, economic growth or climate action. These regional statistics make it possible to pinpoint areas that require targeted interventions, address disparities between regions, and ensure that no one is left behind. '''The EU’s approach to implementing the SDGs''' Several major policy documents have shaped the EU’s approach to implementing the SDGs. A communication, ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2016:739:FIN Next steps for a sustainable European future: European action for sustainability]'' (COM(2016) 739 final) highlighted the integration of the SDGs into the EU’s policy framework. The EU’s approach for implementing the 2030 Agenda is described in detail within ''[https://commission.europa.eu/document/1ae1e765-0a3f-4092-b87e-86ecbd1ec0c7_en Delivering on the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals – A comprehensive approach]''. For a complete overview of the European Commission’s activities, see the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/sustainable-development-goals/eu-whole-government-approach_en EU’s ‘whole of government’ approach to implementing the SDGs]. '''EU policies that help towards the implementation of the 2030 Agenda''' The European Commission’s political priorities for 2024 to 2029 seek to deliver [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/competitiveness_en A new plan for Europe’s sustainable prosperity and competitiveness]. To safeguard and boost Europe’s competitiveness, prosperity and fairness, the EU will seek to: *make business easier and faster *build a new clean industrial deal *work towards a more circular and resilient economy *boost productivity with digital technology diffusion *put research and innovation at the heart of the EU economy *turbo charge investment *tackle skills and labour gaps. The [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en European Green Deal], adopted in December 2019, is the EU’s growth and transformation strategy as it seeks to tie environmental sustainability to competitiveness and job creation. It aims to transform the EU into a climate-neutral society while leaving no one behind, creating a modern, resource-efficient, competitive and fair economy where there are no net emissions of greenhouse gases by 2050 and where economic growth is decoupled from resource use. The European Green Deal is an integral part of the European Commission’s strategy to implement the 2030 Agenda and the SDGs. [https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/policy/what/investment-policy_en Cohesion policy] in the EU is strongly aligned with the SDGs. It contributes to strengthening economic, social and territorial cohesion and correcting imbalances between countries and regions. It delivers on the EU’s political priorities, especially the green and digital transitions. The above information contains three examples of EU policies that highlight the EU’s comprehensive approach to implementing the 2030 Agenda. Below is a non-exhaustive list of some other policies that contribute towards its delivery: *[https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/biodiversity-strategy-2030_en Biodiversity strategy for 2030] *[https://environment.ec.europa.eu/strategy/circular-economy_en EU initiatives for the transition to a circular economy] *[https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/european-climate-law_en European Climate Law] *[https://op.europa.eu/webpub/empl/european-pillar-of-social-rights/en/ European Pillar of Social Rights] *[https://commission.europa.eu/business-economy-euro/european-semester_en European Semester] *[https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/farm-fork-strategy_en Farm to fork strategy] *[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/gender-equality/gender-equality-strategy_en Gender equality strategy] *[https://next-generation-eu.europa.eu/index_en NextGenerationEU: for a stronger, more resilient Europe] *[https://rural-vision.europa.eu/action-plan_en Rural action plan] *[https://www.urbanagenda.urban-initiative.eu/ Urban Agenda for the EU]. '''Global and EU targets for air quality''' In September 2021, the [[Glossary:World_Health_Organization_(WHO)|World Health Organization (WHO)]] issued new global air quality guidelines, emphasising the need to safeguard public health: the long-term guideline level was set as an annual average of 5 µg/m³ for PM2.5. These guidelines reflect growing scientific evidence that even low concentrations of air pollution may pose significant risks to human health. As part of its goal to eliminate pollution by 2050, the European Commission has outlined key targets and initiatives. Among these, an intermediate goal to reduce premature deaths resulting from exposure to air pollution by at least 55% between 2005 and 2030. In December 2024, a revised [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202402881 Directive on ambient air quality and cleaner air for Europe] (Directive (EU) 2024/2881) came into force. Under this directive, the European Commission will review the latest scientific evidence on air pollution and its health impacts by the end of 2030 and every five years thereafter – or more often if new findings warrant it – to ensure the standards continue to be appropriate. The directive sets a new annual limit value for the EU of 10 µg/m³ for PM2.5, to be met by 1 January 2030. The revised directive also aims to strengthen air quality plans and roadmaps for territorial units where pollution exceeds EU standards. It updates air quality limits for 12 pollutants, including fine particulate matter. In addition, it also provides an opportunity for individuals to seek compensation if their health is harmed due to violations of EU air quality rules. ===Other articles=== *[[EU_sustainable_development_indicators_at_regional_level|EU sustainable development indicators at regional level]] *[[Sustainable_development_goals_(SDGs)_and_EU_regions_-_peace|Sustainable development goals (SDGs) and EU regions - title: Sustainable development goals (SDGs) and EU regions - people
text:
EU statistics, providing an overview of regional statistics for the EU’s set of sustainable development indicators, covering the topic of people. Data extracted in February 2026 Planned article update: March 2028 The highest rates of severe material and social deprivation were observed in the south-east of the EU, while the lowest rates were concentrated in northern/central Italy, the Netherlands, Austria and Poland. There were 26 regions across the EU where at least a quarter of all adults aged 25 to 64 participated in education and training, including all Danish and Swedish regions, a majority of regions in the Netherlands and Finland, and the Slovenian capital region. [[Image:Which EU regions had the highest shares of people with tertiary educational attainment_SDG2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a96cbfb9-f4fc-46ea-89e3-7ebbe14b7eb6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-02T13:08:42Z edat_lfse_04])|alt=Bar chart. People aged 25 to 34 with a tertiary level of educational attainment, in percent. Data for NUTS level 2 regions with the highest shares and data for the EU average. Annual data for 2024. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article looks at [[Glossary:Sustainable development|sustainable development]] indicators from a regional perspective – it covers Goal 1 – no poverty, Goal 2 – zero hunger, Goal 4 – quality education and Goal 5 – gender equality. The information was selected from the 2025 editions of two of Eurostat’s flagship publications, the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/ks-01-25-037 Eurostat Regional Yearbook]'' and ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-flagship-publications/w/ks-05-24-071 Sustainable development in the European Union – Monitoring report on progress towards the SDGs in an EU context]''. All data were re-extracted at the start of February 2026 to ensure that the most up-to-date information is presented, which may explain differences in coverage compared with the original publications. ===Goal 1 – no poverty === [[Image:SDG1.PNG|left|80px|80px]] SDG 1 calls for the eradication of poverty in all its manifestations. It envisions shared prosperity, a basic standard of living and social protection benefits for people everywhere, including the poorest and most vulnerable.

'''People at risk of poverty or social exclusion'''
'''More about the data: at risk of poverty or social exclusion''' The indicator for people at risk of poverty or social exclusion is based on measures of relative poverty, severe material and social deprivation, and quasi-joblessness. The number/share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion combines these criteria to cover people who are in at least one of the following situations: *[[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|at risk of poverty]] – people with an [[Glossary:Equivalised disposable income|equivalised disposable income]] (after [[Glossary:Social transfers|social transfers]]) below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold, which is set at 60% of the national [[Glossary:Median|median]] equivalised disposable income *facing [[Glossary:Severe_material_and_social_deprivation_rate_(SMSD)|severe material and social deprivation]] – people unable to afford at least seven out of 13 deprivation items (six related to the individual and seven related to the [[Glossary:Household - social statistics|household]]) that are considered desirable – or even necessary – to have an adequate quality of life *[[Glossary:Persons living in households with very low work intensity|living in a household with very low work intensity]] – where working-age adults (aged 18 to 64, excluding students aged 18 to 24 and those who are retired) worked for 20% or less of their combined potential working time during the previous 12 months.
In 2024, more than 1 in 5 (21.0%) of the EU’s population was at risk of poverty or social exclusion. '''Map 1''' shows the regional distribution of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion across NUTS level 2 regions. The regional distribution of this indicator was somewhat skewed, as close to 40% of all EU regions (97 out of the 243 for which data are available) recorded shares of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion that were equal to or higher than the EU average. The highest risks of poverty or social exclusion were typically observed in southern, eastern and outermost regions of the EU. At the top end of the distribution, there were 25 NUTS level 2 regions that recorded shares of at least 33.0% in 2024. The French outermost region of Guyane (59.5%) had the highest regional share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion; it was the only region to report that more than half of its population faced such a risk. The southern Italian regions of Calabria and Campania (48.8% and 43.5%, respectively), and the Spanish autonomous regions of Ciudad de Melilla and Ciudad de Ceuta (44.5% and 42.2%, respectively) were the only other regions in the EU where the share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion was more than twice as high as the EU average (21.0%). At the other end of the distribution, there were 24 NUTS level 2 regions where less than 12.0% of the population was at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2024. This group included 5 regions that had single-digit shares, including: *the Czech regions of Severovýchod (9.5%) and Jihozápad (8.8%) *the Polish capital region of Warszawski stołeczny (8.9%) *the Slovak capital region of Bratislavský kraj (8.6%) *the northern Italian region of Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen, that had the lowest regional share (6.6%). Map 1: People at risk of poverty or social exclusion
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/09134d89-af4e-4fc6-92ca-fd5fb6022372?lang=en ilc_peps11n]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2353e99b-4aeb-4b9e-b554-e531cf27db80?lang=en ilc_peps01n]) [[Image:People at risk of poverty or social exclusion (%, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024)_SDG2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: People at risk of poverty or social exclusion
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/09134d89-af4e-4fc6-92ca-fd5fb6022372?lang=en ilc_peps11n] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2353e99b-4aeb-4b9e-b554-e531cf27db80?lang=en ilc_peps01n])]] '''Figure 1''' identifies the NUTS level 2 regions that had the biggest changes in their respective shares of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion between 2022 and 2024. There was a modest decrease across the EU, as this share fell 0.6 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] from 21.6% to 21.0%. Among the 236 regions for which data are available, the share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion rose in 99 regions, remained unchanged in 2 regions and fell in 135 regions. The regions with the biggest falls in their respective shares of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion were located in Italy, Portugal and Romania. Between 2022 and 2024, 2 Italian regions reported falls in double-digits: Liguria (down 10.5 percentage points) and Abruzzo (down 10.2 percentage points). There were 9 other regions that reported falls of at least 7.0 percentage points: *6 regions in Romania – Sud-Vest Oltenia (down 9.6 percentage points), Sud-Muntenia (down 8.3 percentage points), Vest (down 8.2 percentage points), the capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov (down 7.2 percentage points), Sud-Est (also down 7.2 percentage points) and Centru (down 7.0 percentage points) *2 regions in Portugal – Região Autónoma da Madeira (down 7.3 percentage points) and Algarve (down 7.0 percentage points) *another Italian region – Molise (down 9.7 percentage points). [[Image:People at risk of poverty or social exclusion (by NUTS 2 regions, 2024)_SDG2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: People at risk of poverty or social exclusion
'' Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/09134d89-af4e-4fc6-92ca-fd5fb6022372?lang=en ilc_peps11n]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2353e99b-4aeb-4b9e-b554-e531cf27db80?lang=en ilc_peps01n])|alt=Two bar charts. People at risk of poverty or social exclusion. First chart: data for EU regions with the highest and lowest rates, in percent. Second chart: data for EU regions with the biggest increases and biggest decreases compared with 2022, in percentage points. Data for NUTS level 2 regions and data for the EU average. Annual data for 2024. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

'''People at risk of poverty''' The [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|at-risk-of-poverty rate]] identifies the proportion of the population who live in a household with an equivalised disposable income that is below 60% of the national median (after social transfers). The at-risk-of-poverty rate before social transfers measures a hypothetical situation where social transfers are absent. Such transfers include, for example, unemployment benefits, sickness and invalidity benefits, housing allowances, social assistance and tax rebates. '''Map 2''' shows the at-risk-of-poverty rate for NUTS level 2 regions. In 2024, the regional distribution of this rate was skewed. There were 94 regions (38.7% of the 243 regions for which data are available) that recorded a rate above the EU average of 16.2%, 1 region with the same rate, while the remaining 148 regions recorded lower than average rates. In 2024, the French outermost region of Guyane recorded the highest at-risk-of-poverty rate among NUTS level 2 regions, at 53.3% (the only region to report a majority of its population experiencing such a risk). There were 6 other regions in the EU where one third or more of the population was at risk of poverty: the Spanish autonomous regions of Ciudad de Melilla and Ciudad de Ceuta, the southern Italian regions of Calabria, Campania and Sicilia, and another French outermost region, Guadeloupe. By contrast, at the other end of the distribution the lowest risk was recorded in the Romanian capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov (3.7%). There was a considerable degree of inter-regional variation among at-risk-of-poverty rates across some EU countries, for example: *the rate in the Belgian capital Région de Bruxelles-Capitale/Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest was 4.6 times as high as that recorded in the northern region of Prov. Oost-Vlaanderen *the rate in the French outermost region of Guyane was 5.0 times as high as that recorded in the western region of Bretagne *the rate in the southern Italian region of Calabria was 6.3 times as high as that recorded in northern region of Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen *the rate in the south-western Romanian region of Sud-Vest Oltenia was 8.1 times as high as that recorded in the capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov. '''Severe material and social deprivation''' The [[Glossary:Severe_material_and_social_deprivation_rate_(SMSD)|severe material and social deprivation rate]] provides information on people experiencing an enforced lack of items that are necessary and desirable to lead an adequate life (individuals who cannot afford a certain good, service or social activity). It is 1 of 3 criteria used to identify people at risk of poverty or social exclusion and is defined as the share of people who are unable to afford at least 7 out of 13 items (6 related to the individual and 7 related to the household) that are considered desirable – or even necessary – to lead an adequate quality of life. In 2024, 27.5 million people in the EU (6.4% of the population) faced severe material and social deprivation. In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, the rate stood at 6.7% in 2022 and increased marginally in 2023 to 6.8%; these relatively high rates may be linked, at least in part, to the cost-of-living crisis. The EU’s severe material and social deprivation rate subsequently fell by 0.4 percentage points in 2024. '''Figure 3''' shows the regional distribution of severe material and social deprivation rates. Many of the highest rates were observed in the south-east of the EU, while the lowest rates tended to be concentrated in northern/central Italy, the Netherlands, Austria and Poland, as well as parts of Czechia, Germany, Croatia, Slovenia, Slovakia and Sweden. In 2024, the highest regional share of people experiencing severe material and social deprivation was recorded in the Greek island region of Ionia Nisia (28.0%). There were 7 other regions in the EU where more than a fifth of the population faced severe material and social deprivation: *Sud-Est (26.4%) and Sud-Muntenia (20.3%) in Romania *Calabria (24.9%) in Italy *Yugoiztochen (22.7%), Yuzhen tsentralen (22.1%) and Severen tsentralen (21.6%) in Bulgaria *Anatoliki Makedonia, Thraki (21.4%) in Greece. At the other end of the distribution, every region in Czechia, Denmark, Ireland, Croatia, the Netherlands, Poland, Slovenia, Finland and Sweden had a severe material and social deprivation rate in 2024 that was below the EU average (6.4%); this was also the case in Estonia, Cyprus, Latvia, Luxembourg and Malta. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Goal 2 – zero hunger === [[Image:SDG2.PNG|left|80px|80px]] SDG 2 seeks to end hunger and malnutrition and ensure access to safe, nutritious and sufficient food. Achieving this goal will largely depend on promoting sustainable production systems and increasing investment in rural infrastructure and agricultural research and development. Farms across the EU play a crucial role in supplying safe, affordable food. Farm managers are increasingly encouraged to manage the countryside for the public good. This shift towards sustainability – alongside a rise in environmentally-conscious consumers – has spurred growth in [[Glossary:Organic_farming|organic farming]]. The infographic below illustrates that organic farming accounted for 6.9% of the EU’s [[Glossary:Utilised agricultural area (UAA)|utilised agricultural area]] in 2023. '''Organic farming''' The EU has set itself a target to have at least 25% of its agricultural land under organic farming and a significant increase in organic aquaculture by 2030. In 2020 (latest reference year available for the EU), organic farming covered 10.6 million hectares (equivalent to 106 000 km²) of land; note these figures refer to agricultural holdings above the survey threshold (and hence, will under-report the area covered). To put this figure into context, the EU’s organic area represented 6.9% of the total utilised agricultural area. The relative size of organic farming shows considerable variations, both across EU countries and among NUTS level 2 regions. For instance, the share of utilised agricultural area that was under organic farming exceeded the EU average of 6.9% (2020 data) in every region of Denmark (2020 data), Austria, Slovenia, Finland and Sweden in 2023; the share was also above the EU average in Estonia and Latvia. Conversely, this share was lower than the EU average in every region of Bulgaria, Ireland, Hungary (incomplete data), Poland and Romania; the share was also below the EU average in Cyprus, Luxembourg and Malta. Among the 240 NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available (for 2020 or 2023), there were 28 regions – predominantly located in Poland and Romania – where less than 1.0% of the utilised agricultural area was given over to organic farming. By contrast, there were 10 regions with more than 27.5% of their utilised agricultural area under organic farming, see '''Map 3'''. The Austrian region of Salzburg recorded the highest regional share in 2023, with over half (51.3%) of its utilised agricultural area under organic farming. There were 4 other NUTS level 2 regions where organic farming accounted for more than a third of the utilised agricultural area: *the Italian regions of Calabria (44.3%) and Toscana (36.5%) *2 more Austrian regions – Burgenland (38.7%) and Wien (38.5%). For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Goal 4 – quality education === [[Image:SDG4.PNG|left|80px|80px]] SDG 4 seeks to ensure access for all to quality education through all stages of life, as well as to increase the number of young people and adults who have the relevant skills for employment, decent jobs and entrepreneurship.

'''Early leavers from education and training''' Within the EU, education policy seeks to ensure that all people in the EU (irrespective of age) have the skills, knowledge and capabilities to develop their careers. The transition from education into work may prove particularly difficult for people with low levels of literacy and numeracy, those who leave education at an early age, and people coming from disadvantaged backgrounds. A particular area of concern is the proportion of [[Glossary:Early leaver from education and training|early leavers from education and training]]. The EU has set a goal to reduce the proportion of early leavers to less than 9% by 2030. Over the last 2 decades, the share of early leavers from education and training (aged 18 to 24) has declined across the EU. From 16.9% in 2002 (start of the time series), this share fell steadily each year, reaching 10.5% by 2017. After remaining unchanged in 2018, it decreased further over the next 4 years, falling to 9.6% by 2022. The proportion of young people with at most a lower secondary level of education who were not engaged in further education or training remained stable in 2023. However, it resumed a downward path in 2024, falling by 0.2 percentage points to 9.4% (which was just 0.4 percentage points above the EU’s 2030 policy target). There is both a spatial and a gender dimension to the issue of early leavers from education and training. *The proportion of early leavers tends to be higher in rural and sparsely populated regions of the EU, as well as in regions characterised as former industrial heartlands. Among other reasons, this pattern may be a reflection of fewer educational opportunities and weak local labour markets, which may discourage people from staying longer in education and also act as a ‘push factor’ to encourage people with higher levels of educational attainment to move away. *For the gender dimension, a higher proportion of young men (compared with young women) tend to be early leavers. Across the EU, the share of early leavers from education and training in 2024 was 11.0% among young men, which was 3.3 percentage points higher than the corresponding share among young women (7.7%). In 2024, the share of early leavers from education and training was already below the 9.0% policy target in approximately half (96 out of 199) of the NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available, see '''Map 4'''. Looking in more detail, the share of early leavers from education and training was less than 9.0% for every region (for which data are available) of Ireland, Croatia and Slovenia, and all but 1 of the regions in Czechia and the Netherlands; shares of less than 9.0% were also recorded in Latvia, Luxembourg, Poland (only national data) and Slovakia (only national data). At the other end of the range, there were 7 NUTS level 2 regions where the share of early leavers from education and training in 2024 was at least 20.0%. This group included sparsely populated, island and/or peripheral regions; it is likely that a disproportionately high share of students from some of these regions have to leave home if they wish to follow a particular course or programme, leaving behind a higher concentration of early leavers.
