title: Technology in European Neighbourhood East countries
text:
This article is part of an online Eurostat publication that provides a statistical overview over the European Neighbourhood Policy-East (ENP-East) countries. The article presents statistics on the access to and use of information and communication technology in Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine and compares these with the EU. Data extracted in January 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 In 2024, over 90% of households in Georgia (91.5%) and Azerbaijan (90.2%) had internet access, approaching the EU average of 94.2%. Frequent internet use was very high in Azerbaijan, where 90.5% of individuals used the internet daily in 2023 (latest data), exceeding the EU level of 88.3% in 2024. In 2024, fewer than 40% of enterprises had their own website in Moldova (38.7%), Georgia (39.7%) and Ukraine (38.2%), compared with 78.3% in the EU. Ukraine recorded the highest gross domestic expenditure on research and development among the ENP-East countries, at 0.32% of GDP in 2023, still far below the EU level of 2.26%. This article is part of an [[European_Neighbourhood_Policy_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]]. It presents information on technology and on research and development for 5 [[Glossary:European Neighbourhood Policy (ENP)|European Neighbourhood Policy-East (ENP-East)]] countries, namely, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine. Information on these 5 countries is compared with developments in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are also [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]]. The European Council granted Moldova and Ukraine candidate status on 23 June 2022 and Georgia on 14 December 2023. This article does not contain any data on Belarus, as statistical cooperation with Belarus has been suspended as of March 2022. Data shown for Georgia exclude the regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia over which the government of Georgia does not exercise control. The data managed by the National Bureau of Statistics of Moldova does not include data from the Transnistrian region over which the government of Moldova does not exercise control. Since 2014, data for Ukraine generally exclude the illegally annexed Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the City of Sevastopol and the territories which are not under control of the Ukrainian government. For Ukraine official statistics for 2022-2025 were not fully produced due to the martial law. It will gradually be produced and disseminated as defined by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine, taking into account the specific conditions of producing statistics during Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. The article presents a range of [[Glossary:Information_and_communication_technology_(ICT)|technology]] and [[Glossary:Research_and_development_(R_%26_D)|research and development (R&D)]] indicators such as the shares of households and enterprises with [[Glossary:Internet_access|internet access]], enterprises’ use of [[Glossary:Information_and_communication_technology_(ICT)|ICT]], individuals’ frequency of internet use, [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_expenditure_on_R_%26_D_(GERD)|gross domestic expenditure on R&D (GERD)]] and [[Glossary:R_%26_D_expenditure_by_source_of_funds|gross domestic expenditure on R&D by source of funds]]. Where a table or graph refers to a single reference year (for example, 2024), or where annual data are unavailable for certain countries, the most recent available data within the preceding five years are used. Where both the start and end years are intended to be shown but the corresponding data series are not available, data from the closest possible years are presented instead (for example, 2023 data instead of 2024). ===Enterprises and households with internet access=== Figure 1 illustrates the continued expansion of internet access among enterprises and households in the EU and the ENP-East countries between 2014 and 2024, showing high overall connectivity but persistent differences between countries and user groups. By 2024, the vast majority of enterprises in the ENP-East countries had internet access, although coverage levels varied across countries. Georgia reported internet access for almost all enterprises (99.3%), slightly exceeding the EU average (99.0%). High levels of enterprise connectivity were also observed in Moldova (92.0%; 2023 data) and Ukraine (93.8%), despite a decline in Ukraine compared with 2014. In contrast, Azerbaijan continued to record lower levels of enterprise internet access, rising only slightly from 71.1% in 2014 to 74.0% in 2024. In Armenia, 77.0% of enterprises had internet access in 2023. Internet access among households also increased across the region. Georgia recorded one of the strongest gains, rising from 44.8% in 2014 to 91.5% in 2024. Azerbaijan saw household access increase from 75.2% to 90.2%, while in Armenia it rose from 53.1% to 80.0% over the same period. In Moldova, household internet access nearly doubled, from 42.7% in 2014 to 74.1% in 2024, although it remained below the levels observed in most other ENP-East countries. In Ukraine, household internet access stood at 47.3% in 2014. At EU level, household internet access increased from 79.6% in 2014 to 94.2% in 2024. Overall, the data points to significant progress in digital connectivity across the ENP-East countries, particularly for households. Nevertheless, gaps remain compared with the EU, especially in Moldova and Armenia, and enterprise connectivity in Azerbaijan continues to trail behind regional peers. [[Image: ENPE26_Enterprises and households with internet access, 2014 and 2024_(%)_v1.png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 1: Enterprises and households with internet access, 2014 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a006e1bf-e7df-4a0a-b98e-f0969f56b215?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T10:09:35Z isoc_ci_in_en2]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b0d31f1c-aea6-4c09-beb4-41d080cba4bf?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T10:10:01Z isoc_ci_in_h]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f917de2d-4f33-4a67-8097-c2b63de0ea2d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-26T13:47:01Z enpe_isco_ci_in_ens]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/92685539-2ac1-426c-89b2-72c95c2f65f0?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T11:07:06Z enpe_isoc_ci_in_h])|alt= Bar chart showing the shares of enterprises and households that had internet access in the EU, Moldova, Georgia, Ukraine, Armenia and Azerbaijan in 2014 and 2024, respectively. The bars show the percentage of enterprises and households having internet access in each reference year for each country. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Frequency of internet use by individuals=== Figure 2 illustrates the increasing importance of the internet in everyday life, as reflected in the share of individuals (aged 16-74) using the internet daily or at least weekly (but not daily) in the EU and ENP-East countries. In Azerbaijan, internet use was very widespread. In 2023 (more recent data not available), 90.5% of individuals used the internet daily (+9.6 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] compared with 2014) and a further 7.6% at least weekly (-9.0 pp compared with 2014), meaning that 98.1% of the population were frequent internet users. This level of use was higher than in the EU, where 88.3% of individuals used the internet daily in 2024 and 3.4% at least weekly. In Georgia, the share of daily internet users increased from 53.3% in 2016 (earlier data not available) to 84.5% in 2024 (+31.2 pp), while an additional 3.8% used the internet at least weekly (-2.7 pp compared with 2016). Despite this strong growth, overall internet use remained slightly below the EU level. For Ukraine, data are only available for 2014, when 61.0% of individuals reported daily internet use and 31.1% used it at least weekly. Overall, the data indicate a strong increase in frequent internet use where time series are available, particularly in Georgia and Azerbaijan. Usage levels in some ENP-East countries match or exceed those observed in the EU. [[Image: ENPE26_Frequency of internet use, 2014 and 2024_(% of population aged 16-74 years old)_v1.png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 2: Persons using the internet by frequency of use, 2014 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ea800df6-99fc-439b-8e6f-75fe4cf5c5ef?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T10:10:43Z isoc_ci_ifp_fu]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/23e8d865-06e0-4d63-aa13-725bda7c0574?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T11:05:18Z enpe_isoc_ci_ifp_fu])|alt=Bar chart showing the share of the population aged 16-74 years old that used the internet in the EU, Moldova, Georgia, Ukraine and Azerbaijan in 2014 and 2024. The bars show the percentages of persons that used the internet daily and weekly but not daily, respectively, for each country and reference year. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Enterprises using information and communication technology=== The use of information and communication technologies (ICT) is an important aspect of business operations, reflecting how enterprises adopt digital tools for communication, information access and online presence. Key indicators include access to the internet and the use of websites, which provide insights into the level of digitalisation among enterprises. In 2024, fewer than two fifths of enterprises had a website in Moldova (38.7%), Georgia (39.7%) and Ukraine (38.2%), well below the EU level (78.3%, 2023 data). Armenia was an exception, with 43.0% of enterprises having an own website (2023 data). Although Azerbaijan showed a clear improvement, with the share of enterprises having a website rising from 10.4% in 2014 to 21.0% in 2024, it remained the lowest among the ENP-East countries shown. Overall, the results point to a clear gap between basic connectivity and more advanced digital engagement among enterprises in the ENP-East countries. While internet access is nearly universal, the relatively low share of enterprises with a website indicates that many businesses have yet to fully exploit digital tools for visibility, communication and commercial activities. Compared with the EU, this highlights a slower uptake of more advanced digital practices. [[Image: ENPE26_Enterprises using ICT, 2014 and 2024_(%)_v1.png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 3: Enterprises using ICT, 2014 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9b75c082-ecee-4d12-bad6-c85fd96e8afd?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T10:11:09Z isoc_ci_in_en2]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ccf761f1-22a1-435c-aa2b-8e02790f2277?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T10:11:25Z isoc_ciweb]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/33f4108f-5054-4ab5-a1a3-23cdfbae60de?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-26T14:03:53Z enpe_isoc_ci_in_ens]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0e2dafc4-ac98-4bd8-8a70-ca8e39c8eea6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-26T14:04:31Z enpe_isoc_ciweb])|alt=Bar chart showing the shares of enterprises that were using information and communication technologies in the EU, Moldova, Georgia, Ukraine, Armenia and Azerbaijan in 2014 and 2024, respectively. The bars show the percentages of enterprises using computers and having a website in each of the 2 reference year for each country. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Use of digital skills by type=== Figure 4 shows the use of selected ICT skills among individuals aged 16–74 in the ENP-East countries and the EU, based on activities carried out in the three months preceding the survey. The indicators cover three types of skills with increasing levels of complexity: using spreadsheet software, creating electronic presentations, and writing code in a programming language. These activities can be regarded as proxies for applied [[Glossary:Digital_skills|digital skills]]. Among the ENP-East countries, Georgia showed relatively low but stable levels of digital skill use. The share of individuals using spreadsheet software increased modestly from 11.7% in 2019 to 12.7% in 2024, while the proportion of creating electronic presentations remained broadly unchanged. Coding skills were marginal and declined slightly over the period. In Ukraine, around one in ten individuals used spreadsheets or created presentations, while just over 1% reported writing code, indicating a comparatively limited diffusion of advanced digital skills (data from 2019). By contrast, Azerbaijan experienced an expansion in the use of all three digital skills. Between 2019 and 2024, the share of individuals using spreadsheet software more than doubled, while the proportion of creating electronic presentations increased more than fivefold. The most striking growth was observed in coding skills, which rose from 1.0% to 10.1%, far exceeding the levels recorded in the other ENP-East countries. Overall, the EU recorded much higher levels of ICT skill use than the ENP-East countries for which data are available. Between 2019 and 2024, the shares of individuals using spreadsheets and creating presentations in the EU rose slightly, while coding skills also increased, from 5.8% to 6.5%. [[Image: ENPE26_Use of ICT skills by type, 2019 and 2024_(%)_v1.png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 4: Use of ICT skills by type, 2019 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7d09831b-7591-424a-a1e7-1633d679de48?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T10:11:56Z isoc_sk_cskl_i21]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/669c1d6f-af05-42fb-bd31-fdab6e4bada6?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T11:03:11Z enps_isoc_sk_skl_i])|alt=Bar chart showing the shares of the population aged 16-74 years old that used different types of ICT skills in the years 2019 and 2024. The chart presents data for Georgia, Ukraine and Azerbaijan on the shares of this age group that used ICT skills to create an electronic presentation, write computer programs, and used spreadsheet software, respectively, in each of the two reference years. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Gross domestic expenditure on research and development (GERD)=== [[Glossary:Gross domestic expenditure on R %26 D (GERD)|Gross domestic expenditure on research and development (GERD)]] measures the total expenditure on research and development activities performed within a country during a given year. It covers [[Glossary:Research_and_development_(R_%26_D)|research and development (R&D)]] carried out by businesses, government, higher education institutions and private non-profit organisations. Expressed as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP), GERD indicates the overall intensity of research and development in an economy and allows comparisons across countries of the relative importance of R&D activities. Among the ENP-East countries with more complete time series, Ukraine recorded the highest R&D intensity at the beginning of the period, at 0.65% of GDP in 2014. However, GERD declined steadily over time, falling to 0.32% by 2023 (more recent data not available), indicating a sustained weakening of R&D effort relative to the size of the economy. In Moldova, R&D expenditure as a share of GDP also followed a downward trend. From 0.31% in 2014-2015, GERD gradually decreased to 0.22% by 2023-2024 (2024 data provisional), pointing to a slow but persistent reduction in R&D intensity. Azerbaijan showed more volatility over the period. GERD fluctuated between 0.18% and 0.22% of GDP, reaching a low of 0.15% in 2022 before recovering to 0.21% in 2024. Despite this recent rebound, R&D intensity remained low in comparison with both the EU and Ukraine. Georgia reported a very low R&D intensity of 0.10% in 2014, while Armenia recorded values around 0.23-0.25% between 2014 and 2016. Overall, R&D intensity in the ENP-East countries remained well below the EU level throughout the period. The EU consistently devoted just over 2% of GDP to R&D, rising gradually from 2.09% in 2014 to 2.24% in 2024, despite some fluctuations in recent years. [[Image: ENPE26_Gross domestic expenditure on research and development (GERD), 2014-2024_(% of GDP)_v1.png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 5: Gross domestic expenditure on research and development, 2014 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/55f34968-8edb-4281-848d-96399fecc3da?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T10:12:15Z rd_e_gerdtot]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5cbb0831-3f55-44e6-8a57-3834faea617b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T11:00:45Z enpe_rd_e_gerdfund)]|alt=Bar chart showing the shares of gross domestic expenditure on research and development from 2014 to 2024. Data are presented for the EU, Ukraine, Moldova, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Armenia. For each country and reference year, the bars show the percentage of total R&D expenditure. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Gross domestic expenditure on R&D by source of funds=== Following the presentation of overall gross domestic expenditure on research and development (GERD), Figure 6 focuses on how this expenditure is financed. It shows the distribution of R&D funding by source in the ENP-East countries and the European Union, distinguishing between the business sector, government sector, higher education sector, private non-profit sector and funds from abroad, with a comparison between 2014 and 2024 (or the closest available year). Overall, in the ENP-East countries for which data are available, R&D funding remained heavily concentrated in the government sector, while the business sector and funding from abroad played more limited roles. By contrast, the EU continued to rely primarily on business-funded R&D, supported by a substantial contribution from the government sector. In Moldova, estimated data are only available for 2024. R&D funding was dominated by the government sector, which accounted for two thirds (66.7%) of gross domestic R&D expenditure. Funds from abroad represented a comparatively large share (23.8%), making them the second most important source, while the business sector contributed just 7.6%. The higher education sector played a minor role (1.9%), and data for the private non-profit sector are not available. The funding structure in Ukraine was more balanced. Between 2014 and 2024, the business sector increased its role as a source of R&D funding, from 35.2% to 40.4%, while the government sector remained broadly stable, at around 43%. Over the same period, the share of funds from abroad declined from 19.8% to 15.9%. Contributions from higher education and the private non-profit sector remained negligible. In Azerbaijan, the government sector strengthened its dominant position in R&D funding. Its share rose from 67.6% in 2014 to 82.6% in 2024. In contrast, the business sector’s contribution fell sharply, from 30.5% to 17.0%. All other funding sources accounted for well below 1% of total R&D expenditure in both years. At EU level, the structure of R&D funding remained relatively stable. The business sector continued to be the main source, accounting for 56.7% of R&D expenditure in 2024, only slightly below its 2014 level. Government funding decreased modestly, from 32.3% to 30.1%, while funding from abroad became more important, rising from 8.7% to 10.9%. The higher education and private non-profit sectors each accounted for around 1% of total R&D funding. [[Image: ENPE26_Gross domestic expenditure on R&D, by source of funds, 2014 and 2024_(%)_v1.png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 6: Gross domestic expenditure on R&D by source of funds, 2014 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/a64081cf-e1f5-4ce4-9366-228d08c1b36a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T10:12:37Z rd_e_gerdfund]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cffa480f-c0ec-4a10-bfb4-7ca90eff52f4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T11:02:19Z enpe_rd_e_gerdsec])|alt=Bar chart showing the shares of gross domestic expenditure on research and development by the different funding sectors, in 2014 and 2024, respectively. Data are presented for the EU, Moldova, Ukraine and Azerbaijan. For each country and reference year, the bars show the percentage of total R&D expenditure stemming from the five funding sectors: business enterprises; government; higher education; private non-profit sector, and abroad. For each country for each reference year, these shares total 100 per cent. For more details, please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs=== *{{Template:Excel|filename=ENPE26_Technology_V3.xlsx|title=Technology in European Neighbourhood East countries: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data for ENP-East countries are supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country on a voluntary basis. The data result from an annual data collection cycle that has been established by [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]. These statistics are available free-of-charge on Eurostat's website, together with a range of different indicators for ENP-East countries covering most socio-economic topics. '''''Information society''''' Eurostat's [[Glossary:EU_survey_on_the_use_of_ICT_in_households_and_by_individuals|survey on ICT usage in households and by individuals]] and [[Glossary:EU_survey_on_ICT_usage_and_e-commerce_in_enterprises|survey on ICT usage in enterprises]] are separate, annual surveys. The enterprise survey generally covers enterprises with at least 10 persons employed; the activity coverage excludes financial and insurance activities ([[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE]] Rev. 2 Section K). While these surveys initially concentrated on access and connectivity issues, their scope has subsequently been extended to cover a range of subjects, for example, [[Glossary:E-government|e-government]], social media or [[Glossary:E-commerce|e-commerce]]. Within the European statistical system, these two surveys are based on two methodological manuals: one for [https://circabc.europa.eu/sd/a/de335f25-b129-4147-8530-93bf7e1bf4c6/Methodological%20manual%202020%20Part%20I%20Enterprise%20survey.zip enterprise statistics] and one for [https://circabc.europa.eu/sd/a/880a4015-3bfb-495c-814c-cea7901c42b5/Methodological%20manual%202020%20Part%20II%20Household%20survey.zip statistics related to households and individuals], both of which are updated annually. The definitions laid down in these manuals form the basis for the methodology the ENP-East countries are requested to follow. '''''Research and development''''' Eurostat data on [[Glossary:Research_and_development_(R_%26_D)|research and development (R&D)]] aim to show a comprehensive picture of the situation in the EU, covering indicators related to expenditure and personnel. The international standards for collecting and reporting data on research and experimental development are specified in the [https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/frascati-manual-2015_9789264239012-en.html Frascati Manual]. The definitions which the ENP countries have been asked to follow when providing data are based on the methodology contained within this manual. [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_expenditure_on_R_%26_D_(GERD)|Gross domestic expenditure on R & D (GERD)]] includes expenditure on R & D by [[Glossary:Business_enterprise_sector_-_R_%26_D|business enterprises]], [[Glossary:Higher_education_sector_-_R_%26_D|higher education institutions]], [[Glossary:Government_sector_-_R_%26_D|government]] and [[Glossary:Private_non-profit_sector_-_R_%26_D|private non-profit organisations]], as well as [[Glossary:Abroad_sector_-_R_%26_D|R&D funding from abroad (including international sources)]]. ===Context=== Information and communication technologies (ICT) affect people's everyday lives in many ways, both at work and at home. The development and expansion of the information society is regarded as critical to improve the [[Glossary:Competitiveness|competitiveness]] of the EU, while EU policymakers also seek to regulate areas such as e-commerce or the protection of individuals’ privacy. In December 2022, European Parliament and Council [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32022D2481&qid=1715866453897 Decision (EU) 2022/2481 established the Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030]. This programme aims to encompass social, moral and economic impacts of digital technologies, to promote and drive the digital transformation toward a sustainable and inclusive path to reach a fair economy. Statisticians are well aware of the challenges posed by rapid change in areas related to web services, artificial intelligence (AI), information and communication technologies, etc. As such, there has been considerable development in this area, with statistical tools adapted to satisfy new demands for data. Statistics within this domain are continuously reassessed to meet user needs and reflect the rapid pace of technological change. On 2 July 2021, the European Commission and the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy presented the [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_21_3367 Eastern Partnership: a Renewed Agenda] for cooperation with the EU's Eastern partners. This agenda is based on the five long-term objectives, with resilience at its core, as defined for the future of the [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/european-neighbourhood-policy/eastern-partnership_en Eastern Partnership (EaP)] in the Joint Communication [https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eeas/joint-communication-eastern-partnership-policy-beyond-2020-reinforcing-resilience-%E2%80%93-eastern_en Eastern Partnership policy beyond 2020: Reinforcing Resilience – an Eastern Partnership that delivers for all] in March 2020. It is further elaborated in the Joint Staff Working Document [https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eastern-partnership/joint-staff-working-document-recovery-resilience-and-reform-post-2020-eastern-partnership-priorities_en Recovery, resilience and reform: post 2020 Eastern Partnership priorities], amongst others defining the 'Top Ten Targets for 2025'. The Eastern Partnership’s agenda for recovery, resilience and reform is underpinned by an 'Economic and Investment Plan for the Eastern Partnership (EaP): Investing in resilient and competitive economies and societies' (Annex I of the Joint Staff Working Document). More detailed overviews are given in a [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/document/download/94735c00-2cfa-4ef7-92a6-41515b8b466d_en Factsheet on the Eastern Partnership Joint Communication], presenting the policy objectives and the specific priorities, as well as in a [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/document/download/d675e1d6-fd68-45fa-a671-80a69a117f1f_en Factsheet on EU-Eastern Neighbourhood flagship projects 2023-2024]. The [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/news/eastern-partnership-summit-joint-declaration-2021-12-15_en Joint Declaration of the Eastern Partnership Summit 'Recovery, Resilience and Reform'] of 15 December 2021 reaffirmed the strong commitment to a strategic, ambitious and forward-looking Eastern Partnership. At the [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/meetings/international-ministerial-meetings/2023/12/11/ Eastern Partnership Foreign Affairs Ministerial meeting of 11 December 2023], the EU, member states and partners declared that they will step up their efforts to implement the Eastern Partnership’s agenda for recovery, resilience and reform, as well as tackling challenges related to the ongoing consequences of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine for the entire region. On 14-15 December 2023, the European Council decided to [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2023/12/14/european-council-conclusions-on-ukraine-enlargement-and-reforms/ open accession negotiations] with Moldova and Ukraine, and granted the status of candidate country to Georgia. In cooperation with its ENP partners, Eurostat has the responsibility to promote and implement the use of European and internationally recognised standards and methodology for the production of statistics, necessary for designing and monitoring policies in various areas. Eurostat manages and coordinates EU efforts to increase the capacity of the ENP countries to develop, produce and disseminate good quality data according to European and international standards. Additional information on the policy context of the ENP is provided on the website of [https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/index_en Directorate-General Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood (ENEST)]. A regional statistical cooperation programme, STAT-East, is in place since January 2026 to strengthen partner countries’ statistical capacity to develop, produce and disseminate high-quality statistics and to reinforce the independence and institutional capacity of national statistical systems. ===Other articles=== *[[:Category:Non-EU_countries|All articles on non-EU countries]] title: Temporary and permanent employment - statistics
text:
EU temporary and permanent employment statistics present the trend in temporary employment and its characteristics. It provides data by sex, age, level of education and occupation among others. It also focuses on agency workers and the impact of presence of children in the household. This article also addresses the level of temporary employment in EU countries. Data from December 2024 Planned article update: December 2026 In 2024, the share of temporary employment in the EU was the lowest observed from 2015 to 2024, at 11.0%. In 2024, 31.1% of employees aged 15 to 29 in the EU had a temporary job, compared with 7.4% among those aged 30 to 54 and 4.6% for those aged 55 to 64. This article presents the latest statistics on [[Glossary:Temporary_employment|temporary employment]] based on data from the [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)|EU Labour Force Survey (EU-LFS)]]. It provides an overview of trends in temporary employment and describes profiles of temporary workers based on various factors such as sex, age, education level, occupation and the presence of children in the household. The results are shown for the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|EU]] and its [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|member countries]], along with data for [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries]] where available. ===Main concept=== The [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)|EU-LFS]] collects information on employment permanency (temporary or permanent) only for an employee's main job. Employees are categorised by their employment status, distinguishing between employees, self-employed with employees (employers), self-employed without employees (own-account workers), and unpaid family workers. On-call or casual workers are classified as either employees or self-employed, based on the specific characteristics of their employment relationship. All forms of employment can be part-time or full-time. Most employed people in the [[Glossary:EU|EU]] are on either permanent or temporary contracts. Temporary employment covers employees with fixed-term or otherwise limited-duration contracts, whereas permanent employment refers to employees whose contracts are of unlimited duration. Employment other than temporary includes all forms except temporary employees, such as permanent employees, self-employed, unpaid family workers and those for whom information was unavailable due to non-response. A job is deemed be temporary if both the employee and the employer agree that its duration is determined by objective criteria, usually set out in a limited-duration work contract. Such criteria might include a set end date, task completion, or the return of another employee who is temporarily absent. Examples include seasonal workers, employees substituting those on maternity leave, workers under project-based contracts, and those with training contracts of specified duration. Reasons for temporary employment (source: Eurostat dataset code [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfsa_etgar/default/table?lang=en lfsa_etgar]) differ across age groups. In 2024, among people aged 15 to 29, the most common reason for having a temporary contract was participation in education or training (30.2% of employees with temporary jobs). This was followed by not finding a permanent job (18.6%) and a job being available only as a temporary contract (16.1%). Another 12.4% of young temporary employees were in a probation period, while 12.0% expressed no desire for a permanent job. For those aged 25 to 64, the most frequent reasons for temporary employment were not finding a permanent job (32.7%) and availability only as a temporary contract (28.1%), together making up 60.8% of employees with temporary jobs. Education or training accounted for 7.3% of temporary employment in this age group, while 12.6% were in a probation period. The share of people not wanting a permanent job was 8.2%. Other reasons and non-response accounted for similar proportions in both age groups: 8.3% and 2.5%, respectively, among those aged 15 to 29, and 8.9% and 2.2% for those aged 25 to 64. ===Trends in temporary employment=== Since 2019, the share of temporary employment has generally declined, with similar developments for men and women (see Figure 1). Between 2019 and 2024, the total share of temporary employment decreased by 2.2 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp), from 13.2% to 11.0%. Over the same period, the share fell from 12.4% to 10.0% among men and from 14.3% to 12.2% among women. After as significant decline in 2020, temporary employment increased slightly in 2021 and stayed relatively stable in 2022 before decreasing again in 2023 and 2024. From 2015 to 2024, the highest levels of temporary employment were recorded in 2017, at 13.8% for all employed, with 12.9% for men and 14.9% for women. Conversely, the lowest figures were observed in 2024, when temporary employment accounted for 11.0% of total employment, corresponding to 10.0% for men and 12.2% for women. The difference between women and men remained stable over the period, at roughly 2 pp, with consistently higher shares among women. [[Image:FIGURE 1 Trend in temporary employment by sex, EU, 2015-2024 (% of total employment, people aged 15 to 64).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Trend in temporary employment by sex, EU, 2015-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfsi_pt_a__custom_19820135/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=fbd3adfa-36f7-444e-96a3-1810071071b1&c=1769513715000 lfsi_pt_a])|alt=Line graph showing the trend in temporary employment in the EU by sex from 2015 to 2024. There are 3 lines, one each for men, women and total. Data is shown as percentage of total employment for those aged 15 to 64. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Annual changes in temporary employment compared with those in non-temporary employment provide insights into how temporary work is evolving relative to other employment types. Between 2015 and 2024, fluctuations in temporary employment were typically more pronounced than those recorded for non-temporary employment (see Figure 2). In this context, non-temporary employment is calculated as total employment (resident population concept - EU-LFS) minus temporary employees; annual changes are expressed as year-on-year percentage changes. A notable difference was observed between 2018 and 2019, with temporary employment decreasing by 2.5% while non-temporary employment increased by 1.6%. The most significant disparity occurred in 2020, when temporary employment fell by 11.3%, compared with a 0.4% decrease in non-temporary employment. After 2020, temporary employment increased in 2021 and 2022 (by 2.5% and 2.6%, respectively), along with increases in non-temporary employment. In the last two years, temporary employment declined by 3.7% in both 2023 and 2024, whereas non-temporary employment continued to grow (by 1.7% and 1.5%, respectively). [[Image:Annual changes in permanency of main job, EU, 2015-2024 v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Annual changes in temporary employment and in employment other than temporary, EU, 2015-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfsi_pt_a}} and{{Stable link|title=|code=lfsi_emp_a}}|alt=A double vertical bar chart showing the annual changes in temporary employment and in employment other than temporary in the EU from 2015 to 2024. Data are shown as percentage change of people aged 15 to 64. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Worker characteristics by type of employment=== In 2024, the share of employees with temporary jobs were considerably higher for those aged 15 to 29 compared with those aged 30 to 64, for both men and women (see Figure 3). Within younger workers, 29.5% of men and 33.0% of women were on temporary contracts, compared with 5.7% of men and 7.9% of women in the 30-64 age group. Among people aged 30 to 64, most were employees with a permanent job, accounting for 76.0% of men and 81.0% of women. Within this age group, non-employees (‘other’) represented 18.2% of men and 11.1% of women. In those aged 15 to 29, the share of non-employees was lower, at 8.4% for men and 5.1% for women. [[Image: Employed persons by age, sex, employment status and permanency of main job, EU, 2024 v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Employed persons by age, sex, employment status and permanency of main job, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, EU-LFS ad hoc extraction|alt=A stacked vertical bar chart showing employed people by age, sex and status in employment with total duration of main job in the EU for the year 2024. For each category there is a column for females and males, and each column shows values for employees with fixed-term jobs, employees with permanent jobs, and others. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The number of employed people varies across education levels in terms of both job permanence distribution and the employed population size (see Figure 4). In absolute terms, the largest numbers of permanent job holders were among those with medium and high levels of education, while significantly fewer were recorded among those with low education levels. In the medium education category, 38.2 million men and 32.0 million women held permanent jobs, compared with 4.7 million men and 4.7 million women on temporary contracts. For high education levels, permanent job holders numbered 27.6 million men and 32.2 million women, while temporary employment figures were 2.8 million men and 4.4 million women. For people with low education levels, there were 12.8 million men and 8.3 million women in permanent jobs, while 3.2 million men and 2.3 million women held temporary contracts. [[Image:Employed persons by education level, sex, employment status and permanency of main job, EU, 2024 v2.png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 4: Employed persons by education level, sex, employment status and permanency of main job, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, EU-LFS ad hoc extraction|alt=A grouped bar chart showing employed people by education level, age, sex and status in employment with total duration of main job in the EU for the year 2024. For each education category there is a column for females and males, and each column shows values in millions for employees with fixed-term jobs, employees with permanent jobs, and others. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Temporary employment by country=== In 2024, temporary employment was most common for young employees aged 15 to 29 across all countries shown (see Figure 5). At the EU level, 31.1% of employees in this age group had temporary jobs, compared with 7.4% in those aged 30 to 54 and 4.6% in those aged 55 to 64. The overall share of temporary employment within the working-age population (people aged 15 to 64) in the EU was 11.0%. In absolute terms, this corresponded to 22.1 million employees with temporary jobs in the EU, with 11.1 million aged 15 to 29, 9.2 million aged 30 to 54 and 1.9 million aged 55 to 64. There are noticeable differences across countries. Among people aged 15 to 29, the highest shares of temporary employment were recorded in the Netherlands (48.8%), Portugal (36.7%), France (35.9%), Sweden (34.4%) and Italy (34.3%). The lowest shares were observed in Lithuania (2.7%), Bulgaria (4.2%) and Romania (4.3%). For the total working-age population, temporary employment ranged from 1.4% in Lithuania and 1.5% in Romania to over one fifth in the Netherlands (22.2%). In terms of population levels, Germany had the largest number of employees with temporary jobs among people aged 15 to 64 (4.3 million), followed by France (3.8 million), Spain (2.9 million), Italy (2.7 million), Poland (2.0 million) and the Netherlands (2.0 million). Thus, the 6 EU countries with the largest numbers of employees in temporary jobs accounted for a combined total of around 17.8 million people, representing about 80% of all temporary employees across the EU. In contrast, the 6 EU countries with the smallest numbers of temporary employees collectively made up around 0.17 million people, representing only about 0.8% of the EU total. [[Image:Temporary employment by age and country, 2024 v2.png|thumb|centre|600px|Figure 5: Temporary employment by age and country, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, EU-LFS ad hoc extraction|alt=A scatter chart showing temporary employment by age and country in 2024 for the EU, the EU Member States, some EFTA and candidate countries. Data are shown as percentage of total employment. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] A form of temporary employment involves work through temporary employment agencies. These workers are employed by an agency and assigned to a company temporarily, with the employment contract typically between the worker and the agency rather than with the company. In 2024, temporary employment agency workers represented 2.3% of total employment in the EU (people aged 15 to 64), with a higher share for men (2.6%) than for women (1.9%) (see Figure 6). Considerable variations were observed across countries. Latvia (7.3%), Ireland (6.0%), Slovakia (5.9%) and Slovenia (5.8%) recorded the highest shares, whereas Greece (0.8%), Lithuania (0.7%), Denmark (0.6%), Italy (0.6%), Hungary (0.5%), Poland (0.5%) and Romania (0.5%) had values below 1%. [[Image: Temporary employment agency workers by sex and country, 2024 v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Temporary employment agency workers by sex and country, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfsa_qoe_4a6r2__custom_19838841/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=766f794d-66d1-4116-9a83-cba7e5e61096&c=1769607496000 lfsa_qoe_4a6r2])|alt=A stock chart showing temporary employment agency workers by sex and country in 2024 for the EU, the EU Member States and some EFTA countries. For each country there is a marker for males, females and total. Data are shown as percentage of total employment. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In most countries, men accounted for a higher share of temporary agency workers than women. This was particularly the situation in the Netherlands (5.3% for men versus 3.6% for women), France (3.4% versus 1.5%), Spain (4.5% versus 3.5%) and Germany (2.9% versus 1.9%). Conversely, a few countries observed higher shares for women, such as Malta (5.6% for women versus 3.2% for men), Ireland (6.8% versus 5.3% for men) and Slovenia (6.3% versus 5.3%). These statistics highlight the differences across countries in both the level and structure of temporary employment, with marked variations for younger workers and for temporary agency work, illustrating the diversity of temporary employment patterns across national labour markets. ===Temporary employment by occupation=== Comparing the distributions of temporary and non-temporary employment across ISCO-08 occupational groups provides insights into the types of occupations where temporary workers are employed relative to other workers. The comparison can be done, for instance, by examining each employment type separately across occupational categories (see Figure 7). In 2024, the largest shares of temporary employment were recorded for professionals (21.6%) and service and sales workers (21.5%). Elementary occupations also accounted for a substantial share of temporary employment (15.3%). By comparison, among non-temporary employment, professionals constituted the largest group (23.2%), followed by technicians and associate professionals (16.6%) and service and sales workers (15.5%). Temporary employment was more concentrated in service and sales occupations and elementary occupations than non-temporary employment. Service and sales workers accounted for 21.5% of temporary employment, compared with 15.5% of non-temporary employment, while elementary occupations represented 15.3% of temporary employment, compared with 7.4% of non-temporary employment. In contrast, managers constituted a much smaller share of temporary employment (1.3%) compared with non-temporary employment (5.8%). Lower shares for temporary employment were also observed for technicians and associate professionals (13.1% versus 16.6%) and for craft and related trades workers (9.9% versus 11.6%). Overall, the distributions (see Figure 7) indicate that the occupational composition of temporary employment differs from that of non-temporary employment, particularly in service and sales occupations, elementary occupations and technicians and associate professionals. [[Image:Permanency of main job by occupational category, EU, 2024 v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Temporary and non-temporary employment by ISCO-08 occupational category, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfsa_etgais}} and {{Stable link|title=|code=lfsa_egais}}|alt=A double vertical bar chart showing temporary employment and employment other than temporary by main ISCO-08 occupational category in the EU in 2024. Data are shown as percentage of total in each type of employment. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Temporary employment by education, sex and presence of children=== In 2024, clear differences in temporary employment were observed by sex, level of education and the presence of children in the household among people aged 25 to 64 (see Figure 8). Across educational levels, women had higher shares of temporary employment than men, both among those with children (9.0% for women compared with 5.4% for men) and those without children (9.3% compared with 8.1%). The share of temporary employment decreased as the level of education increased, for both men and women, regardless the presence of children. Among people with a low level of education, temporary employment ranged from 9.5% (men with children) to 16.1% (women with children), while among those with high education it ranged from 3.9% (men with children) to 10.8% (women without children). The presence of children in the household was associated with lower shares of temporary employment for men at all education levels. For women, however, the pattern varied by education: among those with low or medium education, women with children had higher shares of temporary employment than those without children, whereas for women with high education, lower shares were observed for those with children. [[Image: Employment by level of education, presence of children, sex, employment status and permanency of main job, EU, 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Employment by level of education, presence of children, sex, employment status and permanency of main job, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, EU-LFS ad hoc extraction|alt=A stacked vertical bar chart showing employment by type of contract, sex, level of education and presence of children in the EU in 2024. Data is shown as percentage of total people aged 25 to 64. For each category there is a column for females and males showing fixed-term job, permanent job and other. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In summary, in 2024, temporary employment in the EU showed variations by age, sex, education level, occupation and country. Higher shares of temporary employment were more common among younger age groups than older ones, while women registered slightly higher shares than men across most population categories. Across education levels, temporary employment decreased with higher education levels. County differences were also substantial, both in the proportion of employees in temporary employment and in the distribution of temporary agency work. In addition, the occupational composition of temporary employment differed from that of non-temporary employment, particularly in service, sales and elementary occupations, as well as among technicians and associate professionals. Collectively, these statistics on temporary employment highlight the diversity of temporary employment patterns across the EU in demographic, occupational and national dimensions. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=DATA-2024-UPDATE-2025-SE-TEMPORARY-EMPLOYMENT v4.xlsx|title=Temporary employment 2024 data and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''Methods and definitions''' '''Source:''' The EU-LFS is the largest European household sample survey providing quarterly and annual data on labour participation for people aged 15 years and over, as well as on persons outside the labour force. It covers private households. residents Conscripts in military or community service are not included in the data. The EU-LFS is an important source of information on national and EU labour market situations and trends. Each quarter, around 1.2 million interviews are conducted across participating countries to obtain statistical information for approximately 100 variables. Due to the diversity of information and large sample size, the EU-LFS is also an important source for other European statistics, such as education statistics and regional statistics. '''Reference period:''' Yearly results are obtained as averages of the four quarters in the year. '''Coverage:''' The results from the EU-LFS currently cover all [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union]] countries, the [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] countries Iceland, Norway and Switzerland, as well as the [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]] Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia and Türkiye. For Cyprus, the survey covers only the areas of Cyprus controlled by the Government of the Republic of Cyprus. '''European aggregates:''' EU and EU-27 refer to the sum of the 27 EU countries. If data are unavailable for a country, the corresponding aggregates are calculated using the most recent data available for that country, with such instances noted. '''Country notes''' '''The Netherlands''' collects EU-LFS data using a rolling reference week instead of a fixed one, asking interviewees about the situation of the week before their interview rather than a pre-selected week. '''Definitions and main concepts''' EU-LFS concepts and definitions adhere the resolutions of the International Conference of Labour Statisticians held every 5 years, organised by the [[Glossary:International Labour Organization (ILO)|International Labour Organization (ILO)]]. Key employment characteristics, as per the EU Labour Force Survey, include: *[[Glossary:Employee - LFS|Employees]] are those working for a public or private employer and who receive compensation in the form of wages, salaries, payment by results, or payment in kind; this category includes non-conscript armed forces members; *[[Glossary:Self-employed|Self-employed persons]] work in their businesses, farm or professional practice. They are considered working during the reference week if they meet criteria such as working for profit; spending time on business operations; or establishing a business; *Full-time and part-time work distinction is usually based on respondents’ spontaneous responses, except in the Netherlands and Iceland, where a 35-hour limit is applied, Sweden where a limit is applied to the self-employed, and Norway where those working between 32 and 36 hours are asked whether they have a full- or part-time position; *Indicators for employed persons with a second job refer only to those with multiple jobs simultaneously; those who have changed jobs during the reference week are not counted as having two jobs; *An employee is deemed to have a temporary job if the employer and employee agree that the end of the job is determined by objective conditions, such as a specific date, the completion of an assignment, or the return of a temporarily replaced employee. Typical cases include: people in seasonal employment; people engaged by an agency or employment exchange and hired out to a third party to perform specific tasks (unless there is a written work contract of unlimited duration); people with specific training contracts. Educational attainment refers to the highest level of education completed. *Low level of education corresponds to ISCED levels 0-2 (less than primary, primary and lower secondary education), *Medium level corresponds to ISCED levels 3 and 4 (upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education) and *High level corresponds to ISCED levels 5-8 (tertiary education). '''Time series''' Regulation (EU) 2019/1700 came into force on 1 January 2021 and induced a break in the EU-LFS time series for several EU countries. To track employment and unemployment evolution despite this break, EU countries assessed the break’s impact and calculated impact factors or break-corrected data for certain indicators. Break-corrected data are available on Eurostat’s website for the EU-LFS main indicators. '''Publication of results''' Eurostat provides two sets of indicators linked to the annual employment rate, serving different purposes and sometimes differing: 1) The EU-LFS main indicators, which contain seasonally adjusted series. They include labour market headline indicators used in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/macroeconomic-imbalances-procedure/database Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure Scoreboard] or the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/dashboard/european-statistical-monitor/ European Statistical Monitor], consequently used for policy monitoring. They feature limited breakdowns, typically referring to the age group 20-64 years. 2) The detailed results, which contain non-seasonally adjusted series, with extensive breakdowns, suitable for detailed analysis. For France, only one data series is published, with metropolitan France data until the fourth quarter of 2013, and including French overseas departments from 2014 onwards. ===Context=== Employment statistics serve various analyses, including macroeconomic (labour as a production factor), [[Glossary:Labour productivity|productivity]] or [[Glossary:Competitiveness|competitiveness]] studies. They can also be used to study a range of social and behavioral aspects related to an person's employment situation, such as the social integration of minorities, or employment as [[Glossary:Household - social statistics|household]] income. Employment is both a structural and a short-term indicator. As a structural indicator, it may shed light labour markets and economic systems’ structures, measured through labour supply and demand balance, or the quality of employment. As a short-term indicator, employment follows the [[Glossary:Business cycle|business cycle]] but has limitations, as employment is often seen as a [[Glossary:Lagging indicator|lagging indicator]]. The [https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1226&langId=en European Pillar of Social Rights] was signed by the European Parliament, the Council and the Commission on 17 November 2017. Employment and social policies are the main fields of interest of the European Pillar of Social Rights, aimed at delivering new and more effective rights for citizens. It has 3 main categories: (1) Equal opportunities and access to the labour market, (2) Fair working conditions and (3) Social protection and inclusion. In particular, today's flexible working arrangements provide new job opportunities, especially for the young but may lead to new precariousness and inequalities. Building a fairer Europe and strengthening its social dimension is a Commission priority. The European Pillar of Social Rights is accompanied by a 'social scoreboard' to monitor its implementation, tracking trends and performances across EU Member States in 12 areas, feeding into the European Semester of economic policy coordination. The European Commission’s March 2021 action plan guides the European Pillar of Social Rights implementation, covering employment, skills and social protection. It sets three main targets for the EU by 2030: *An employment rate of at least 78% in the EU; *At least 60% of adults attending training courses every year; *A reduction of at least 15 million in the number of people at risk of social exclusion or poverty. For more information, see [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/meetings/european-council/2021/05/07-08/ commitment to implementing the European Pillar of Social Rights]. All EU countries have identified and submitted [https://ec.europa.eu/social/BlobServlet?docId=25728&langId=en national targets] (final or preliminary) aligning with the EU framework and ambition towards achieving the EU headline target by 2030. title: Territorial typologies
text:
Traditionally, typologies of territory were determined by population size and density of [[Glossary:LAU2|local administrative units]] at level 2 (LAU level 2), such as communes, municipalities or local authorities. The typologies that are described here use a population grid, which goes far beyond the administrative territorial units. The population grid enables comparable results, is stable over the time and is not a result of historical circumstances which the administrative boundaries often are. This article provides a short overview of the typologies, including definitions, terminology and some basic statistical data. These typologies start by classifying grid cells of 1 km² to a typology of clusters according to their similarities in terms of population size and density: each grid cell is classified to one type of cluster only. Areas (LAU level 2) or regions ([[Glossary:NUTS|NUTS]] level 3) can then be classified to area or regional typologies based on the population share in different types of clusters: again, each LAU level 2 area or NUTS level 3 region is classified to one type only. In each of these various typologies (of clusters, areas or regions) the whole geographical territory of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] is covered without any overlaps or omission. The area typology applied to LAU level 2 is primarily used in surveys such as the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|labour force survey (LFS)]] and the [[Glossary:EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)|survey on income and living conditions (SILC)]]; the regional typologies applied to the NUTS level 3 regions are mainly used to monitor rural and urban development, maritime economy and and development in metropolitan regions. However, the metropolitan and the coastal typologies are out of the scope of this article. ===Typologies=== '''Cluster types''' [[Image:Type of clusters Map 14.1.png|thumb|centre|450px|Map 1: Type of clusters (1) - Source: Eurostat, JRC, EFGS, REGIO-GIS]] The typology of clusters classifies 1 km² grid cells (and clusters thereof), splitting them into three types. The criteria used are the population density in the individual grid cells and the combined population level of clusters, where clusters are made up of contiguous cells (in other words, neighbouring or adjoining cells); see later for a more detailed explanation of contiguous cells and the so-called gap-filling technique used for high-density clusters. The three types of grid cells or clusters in the typology are the following. *Urban centres (High-density clusters): clusters of contiguous grid cells of 1 km² with a density of at least 1 500 inhabitants per km² and a minimum population of 50 000 after gap-filling. *Urban clusters: clusters of contiguous grid cells of 1 km²with a density of at least 300 inhabitants per km² and a minimum population of 5 000. *Rural grid cells: grid cells outside high-density clusters and urban clusters.
'''Contiguous cells and filling gaps in the cluster typology''' To determine population size, the grid cells need to be grouped in clusters. The methods presented here use three different rules for contiguity to create clusters. These three rules are explained below. #Contiguous including diagonals — used for urban clusters If the central square (grid cell) in Figure 1 is above the density threshold, it will be grouped with each of the other surrounding eight grid cells that exceed the density threshold. #Contiguous excluding diagonals — used for high-density clusters If the central square in Figure 1 is above the density threshold, it will be grouped with each of the four cells directly above, below or next to the central square that also exceed the density threshold. This means that cells numbered 2, 4, 5 and 7 can be included in the same cluster. Cells with number 1, 3, 6 and 8 cannot as they have a diagonal connection. #The majority rule or gap-filling — used for high-density clusters [[Image:Contiguous_grid_cells.png|thumb|centre|450px|Figure 1: Contiguous grid cells]] The goal for the high-density clusters is to identify urban centres without any gaps. Therefore, enclaves need to be filled. If the central square in Figure 1 is not, in its own right, a part of a high-density cluster, it will be added to a high-density cluster if five or more of the eight surrounding cells (therefore including diagonals) belong to a single high-density cluster. This rule is applied iteratively until no more cells can be added.
'''Degree of urbanisation typology for LAU level 2 areas — an area typology''' [[Image:Degree of urbanisation for LAU level 2 areas Map 2.png|thumb|centre|450px|Map 2: Degree of urbanisation for LAU level 2 areas (1) - Source: Eurostat, JRC and European Commission Directorate-General for Regional Policy]] Depending on the share of the population living in the different types of cluster, LAU level 2 areas are classified into three degrees of urbanisation. Due to some national specificities, the degree of urbanisation classifications of Denmark, Greece and Malta have also been produced at the LAU level. *Cities (Densely populated areas): at least 50 % of the population lives in high-density clusters In addition, each high-density cluster of at least 50 000 inhabitants should have at least 75 % of its population in densely-populated LAU level 2 areas. This also ensures that all high-density clusters are represented by at least one densely-populated LAU level 2, even when this high-density cluster represents less than 50 % of the population of that LAU level 2.. *Towns and suburbs (intermediate density areas): less than 50 % of the population lives in rural grid cells and less than 50 % lives in high-density clusters. *Thinly-populated areas/rural areas: more than 50 % of the population lives in rural grid cells.
'''Urban-rural typology for NUTS level 3 regions — a regional typology''' [[Image:Urban-rural typology for NUTS level 3 regions map3.png |thumb|centre|450px|Map 3: Urban-rural typology for NUTS level 3 regions (1) - Source: Eurostat, JRC and European Commission Directorate-General for Regional Policy]] Depending on the share of the [[Glossary:Urban-rural typology|rural population]] (in other words, the share of the population living in rural grid cells, the NUTS level 3 regions are classified into the following three groups: *Predominantly urban regions/urban regions: the rural population is less than 20 % of the total population. *Intermediate regions: the rural population is between 20 % and 50 % of the total population. *Predominantly rural regions/rural regions: the rural population is 50 % or more of the total population. To resolve the distortion created by extremely small NUTS 3 regions, for classification purposes regions smaller than 500 km² are combined with one or more of their neighbours. In a last step, the size of the cities in the region is considered. *A region classified as predominantly rural by the criteria above becomes intermediate if it contains a city of more than 200 000 inhabitants representing at least 25 % of the regional population.  *A region classified as intermediate by the criteria above becomes predominantly urban if it contains a city of more than 500 000 inhabitants representing at least 25 % of the regional population.
'''Summary table: names and alternative names''' The names of typologies and items may differ according to context, users or means of dissemination. Table 1 gives a summary of the vocabulary used as well as the geographical scale. [[Image:Summary regarding the names of the different typologies and items. final.png|thumb|centre|450px|Table 1: Summary regarding the names of the different typologies and items - Source: Eurostat, JRC, EFGS, REGIO-GIS]] === Share of population by type of territory === Although these typologies classify the same phenomena, the use of different geographical scales result in different shares of the rural population. Thus, as Table 2 shows, around 34 % of the EU-28 population lived in rural grid cells, 24 % in rural areas and 19.5 % in predominantly rural regions. Since a high density cell is also an urban cell, the overlapping populations have been excluded from the urban cell's populations. Moreover, the variability between the figures is more pronounced at the national level than for the EU as a whole. As Table 2 illustrates, 32.7 % of the Bulgarian population lived in high-density clusters, 44.5 % in cities and 17.6 % in predominantly urban regions. Another example for the different sensitivity of the three typologies is Luxembourg (a special case where the only NUTS 3 region is equal to the country level) where 9.7 % of the population lived in high-density clusters, 18.7 % in the city and no one lived in predominantly urban regions since the only Luxembourgish region has been classified as intermediate. The most densely populated EU country was Malta with just 5.7 % of its population living in rural grid cells. [[Image:Share of population using different typologies (% of population) final.png|thumb|centre|450px|Table 2: Share of population using different typologies (1)
(% of population) - Source: Eurostat, JRC, EFGS, REGIO-GIS]] === Share of land area by type of territory === The data produced using these different typologies present a broader range in terms of surface area than in terms of the population. As Table 3 shows, 23.6  % of the EU-28’s land area was covered by urban areas (cities, towns and suburbs) and around 44 % was covered by intermediate and predominantly rural regions (each category). Again, there is greater variability at the national level than for the EU as a whole, as Table 3 clearly shows. The most significant variations are observed in Spain, Cyprus and Luxembourg. [[Image:Share of land area using different typologies (% of land area) update.png|thumb|centre|450px|Table 3: Share of land area using different typologies (1)
(% of land area) - Source: Eurostat, JRC, EFGS, REGIO-GIS]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Focus on territorial typologies update 2016 final.xls|title=Focus on territorial typologies: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== These typologies classify different territories, defined at different geographical scales, namely grid cells, LAU 2 areas or NUTS level 3 regions. However, the analysis of the statistical data using these typologies may be disseminated at a higher geographical level. Hence, the proportion of EU-28 land area classified as being composed of intermediate regions is an indicator for the EU based on a regional typology. A similar indicator could also be disseminated at national ant at NUTS level. However, in some cases statistical data using these typologies can only be calculated and disseminated for the EU as a whole or at the national level. This is mainly to do with representativeness, confidentiality and reliability of the indicator. Some surveys, for example the LFS and EU-SILC, can provide reliable statistics by degree of urbanisation for thinly populated areas as well as for cities, towns and suburbs and by urban-rural typology at the national level, but not at NUTS level 3. Thus the territorial typologies can add great value to the diversity of the data disseminated by Eurostat. ===Context=== The European Commission has introduced typologies based on population size and density to monitor situations and trends in urban and rural areas and regions. [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/JOHtml.do?uri=OJ:C:2010:083:SOM:EN:HTML The Treaty on European Union (also called the Treaty of Maastricht)] specifically mentions that particular attention should be paid to rural areas and rural regions. Harmonised European definitions of territorial typologies are therefore essential. On the other hand, the cities, towns and suburbs together called urban areas are used to design, monitor and assess cohesion policy and its urban dimension. The ‘Pact of Amsterdam’ '[http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/policy/themes/urban-development/agenda/pact-of-amsterdam.pdf. adopted in May 2016 establishes the Urban Agenda for the EU and lays out its key principles. It is expected that economic growth in the EU will come primarily from its towns and cities. Furthermore, the United Nations adopted a set of global goals to be achieved by 2030. Goal number 11 is to make cities inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable. The report '[http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docoffic/official/reports/cohesion6/light_6cr_en.pdf. Investment for jobs and growth — Sixth report on economic, social and territorial cohesion]’ aims to promote development and good governance in EU regions and cities. One of the main issues related to territorial cohesion is the need for data on different territorial levels, particularly for lower geographical levels. The classification of the degree of urbanisation provides a unique insight into trends at the local level, and highlights the differences between urban and rural areas. With this respect, harmonised European definitions of territorial typologies are essential. ===Other articles=== *[[Regions and cities|All articles on regions and cities]] *[[Territorial typologies for European cities and metropolitan regions]] (background article) ===Dedicated section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=degree_urbanisation}} Degree of urbanisation] *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=region_cities}} Regions and cities], see: :City statistics - Urban Audit ===Publications=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docgener/focus/2011_01_typologies.pdf Regional typologies: a compilation] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/35209/35256/Urban_rural_poster_3levels_A1_Aug2013.pdf/06a732d8-b614-4c81-844e-c0a9e330aec0 A system of urban-rural typologies] - overview poster published by DG Regional policy ===Methodology=== *A file with all the classifications can be found [https://circabc.europa.eu/d/d/workspace/SpacesStore/ea154527-d900-431f-b5a8-97fbea6e4b08/regtyp.xls here]. :''Please note that this link may not work with certain versions of Internet Explorer - please try another web browser (e.g. Chrome, Opera or Firefox) if you encounter problems.'' ===Visualisations=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistical-atlas/gis/viewer/?chapter=Typologies Eurostat Statistical Atlas (Territorial typologies)] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RSI/#?vis=typologies.urb_typology Typologies Illustrated] ===External links=== *[http://www.oecd.org/gov/regional-policy/OECD_regional_typology_Nov2012.pdf OECD regional typology] (pdf file, 1.93 Mb) === Notes === {{Unit|topic=X_Regions}} [[Category:General and regional statistics|Territorial typologies]] [[Category:Regions and cities|Territorial typologies]] [[Category:Background_article|Territorial typologies]] [[Category:Regions and cities typologies|Territorial typologies]]
