title: Territorial typologies for European cities and metropolitan regions
text:
Data from February 2013 :{|width="90%" cellpadding="2" cellspacing="0" style="vertical-align:top;background-color:#f5faff" border="1" |'''''Maps can be explored interactively using the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistical-atlas/gis/viewer/?year=2013&chapter=01 Eurostat Statistical Atlas] (see [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/140934/4381601/Eurostat-Statistical-Atlas-Help2014 User's manual]).''''' |} This article describes two linked typologies which have been developed to cover, without any overlaps or omission, the whole geographical territory of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], Iceland, Norway, Switzerland and Croatia at the local and regional level — the typologies cover: *the definition of a city and its commuting zone, and; *a typology of metro regions. As opposed to the typologies presented in the [[Territorial_typologies|territorial typologies]] article (the degree of urbanisation and the urban–rural regional typology) which rely mainly on population density, the two typologies presented in this article add a functional dimension. They are both forms of functional urban areas and are based on the flows of people commuting to work in a city. === Functional urban areas: a city and its commuting zone === '''Definition of a city''' [[Image:Defining_a_city_—_high-density_cells,_urban_centre_and_city_(Graz,_Austria).png|thumb|centre|450px|Figure 1: Defining a city — high-density cells, urban centre and city
(Graz, Austria) - Source: Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy]] The new city definition works in four basic steps and is based on the presence of an 'urban centre', a new spatial concept based on high-density population grid cells. Step 1: all grid cells with a density of 1 500 inhabitants per km² or more are selected (image 1 of Figure 1). Step 2: the contiguous Contiguity for high-density clusters does not include the diagonal (in other words, cells with only the corners touching). high-density cells are then clustered, gaps Gaps in the high-density cluster are filled using the majority rule iteratively. The majority rule means that if at least five out of the eight cells surrounding a cell belong to the same high-density cluster it will be added. This is repeated until no more cells are added. are filled and only the clusters with at least a population of 50 thousand inhabitants (image 2 of Figure 1) are kept as an 'urban centre'. Step 3: all the municipalities (local administrative units level 2 (LAU2)) with at least half their population inside the urban centre are selected as candidates to become part of the city (image 3 of Figure 1). Step 4: the city is defined ensuring that: *there is a link to the political level; *at least 50 % of the population lives in an urban centre, and; *at least 75 % of the population of the urban centre lives in a city (image 4 of Figure 1). In most cases, as for example in Graz (in Austria), the last step is not necessary as the city normally consists of a single municipality that covers the entire urban centre and the vast majority of the city’s residents live in that urban centre. For 33 urban centres stretching far beyond the city, a 'greater city' level was created to improve international comparability (for more detail see the Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy’s publication — [http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docgener/focus/2012_01_city.pdf Regional Focus 01/2012)]. To ensure that the above definition identified all relevant centres, national statistical authorities were consulted and minor adjustments were made where needed and consistent with this approach. '''Identification of a commuting zone''' [[Image:How_to_define_a_city_and_its_commuting_zone_(Genova,_Italy).png|thumb|centre|450px|Figure 2: How to define a city and its commuting zone (Genova, Italy) - Source: Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy]] Once all cities have been defined, a commuting zone can be identified based upon commuting patterns using the following steps: *if 15 % of employed persons living in one city work in another city, these cities are treated as a single city (image 1 of Figure 2); *all municipalities with at least 15 % of their employed residents working in a city are identified (image 2 of Figure 2); *municipalities surrounded Surrounded is defined as sharing 100 % of its land border with the functional area. by a single functional area are included and non-contiguous municipalities are dropped (image 3 of Figure 2). The functional urban area (FUA) consists of the city and its commuting zone. [[Image:Urban_Audit_cities_and_Functional_urban_areas,_2012.png|thumb|centre|450px|Map 1: Urban Audit cities and Functional urban areas (FUAs), 2012 (1) - Source: Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy]] For more details on the sources and reference years for the commuting zones, see [http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docgener/focus/2012_01_city.pdf Regional Focus 01/2012)] : Cities in Europe — The new OECD–EC definition (Lewis Dijkstra and Hugo Poelman). === A typology of metro(politan) regions === [[Image:Typology_of_metro_regions,_2012_(1).png|thumb|centre|450px|Map 2: Typology of metro regions, 2012 (1) - Source: Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy]] Metro regions are NUTS level 3 approximations of the functional urban areas (city and commuting zones) of 250 thousand or more inhabitants following the definition described above. Each metro region consists of one or more NUTS level 3 regions and is named after the principal functional urban area inside its boundaries. The typology distinguishes three types of metro regions: *capital metro regions; *second-tier metro regions; *smaller metro regions. The capital metro region includes the national capital. Second-tier metro regions are the group of largest cities in a country, excluding the capital. For this purpose, a fixed population threshold could not be used. As a result, a natural break served the purpose of distinguishing the second-tier from the smaller metro regions. The regions which do not belong to a metro region are simply called non-metro regions. This typology can be simplified even further by grouping all individual metro regions together into metro regions. The boundaries of a functional urban area do not necessarily coincide with those of NUTS level 3 regions. Therefore, NUTS level 3 regions in which at least 50 % of the regional population lives inside a given functional urban area were selected as the components of the metro region related to that functional urban area. In some cases, the NUTS level 3 approximation of the functional urban area is very good. In others cases, the metro region may be larger or smaller than the functional urban area. Each functional urban area is represented by at least one NUTS level 3 region, even if that NUTS level 3 region has less than 50 % of its population inside the functional urban area. === Links between the definition of a city and its commuting zone and the degree of urbanisation typology === The first building block of the city definition described above is the urban centre and this is identical to the one used in the [[Territorial_typologies#Degree_of_urbanisation_typology_for_LAU_level_2_areas_.E2.80.94_an_area_typology| degree of urbanisation typology]]. As a result, the city (or densely-populated area) as defined in the degree of urbanisation is identical to the city definition described here. The two maps below show the two local typologies for the area of the Polish–Slovakian border. The difference arises in the second building block. The city definition identifies contiguous areas which have strong commuting flows. These are the commuting zones (see Figure 3). [[Image:Cities_and_commuting_zones_compared_with_the_degree_of_urbanisation_on_the_Polish–Slovakian_border.png|thumb|centre|450px|Figure 3: Cities and commuting zones compared with the degree of urbanisation on the Polish–Slovakian border - Source: Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy]] The degree of urbanisation identifies towns and suburbs (or intermediate density areas) and rural areas (or thinly-populated areas) based on population density. As a result, these two categories partially overlap with the commuting zones. The towns and suburbs category will occur both inside commuting zones (in this case they are more likely to be suburbs) and outside (in this case they are towns). Rural areas fall primarily outside commuting zones, but some rural areas have developed a strong commuting relationship with a nearby city and thus can also be found in some commuting zones. === No link between metro regions and the urban–rural regional typology === The two local level typologies have one type in common, namely cities, whereas the two regional typologies each have different types. The typology of metro regions divides NUTS level 3 regions into metro and non-metro regions while the urban–rural typology divides NUTS level 3 regions into predominantly urban, intermediate and predominantly rural regions. Despite the absence of an identical type or class of region, the two regional typologies are quite similar: *most urban regions are metro regions and vice versa; *most rural regions are non-metro and vice versa; *intermediate regions are split between metro and non-metro regions. Figure 4 shows the classification of regions close to the Polish–Slovakian border and contains examples of the most common links between these two regional typologies. The differences arise from three main sources: a different logic, different size thresholds, and; a different number of classes. [[Image:Metro_and_non-metro_regions_compared_with_the_urban–rural_typology_on_the_Polish–Slovakian_border.png|thumb|centre|450px|Figure 4: Metro and non-metro regions compared with the urban–rural typology on the Polish–Slovakian border - Source: Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy]] #The different logic behind the two typologies can be described as morphological and functional. The urban–rural typology depends more on the population size and density, which in turn is determined by urban form. So this is a variant of the morphological definition. The typology of metro regions relies on the presence of an urban centre and of functional economic ties to this centre. #The two typologies use quite different size thresholds. Metro regions are related to cities plus commuting zones of at least 250 thousand inhabitants. Urban regions represent urban centres of 50 thousand or more inhabitants (which also define cities) and/or urban clusters of 5 thousand or more inhabitants (which also define towns and suburbs). #The urban–rural typology has three types of region, while the typology of metro regions has only two. Due to these differences, some urban regions will become non-metro regions because the city and its commuting zone are too small (or does not have a city). Some rural regions can become part of a metro region if they have strong commuting links to a city in that or a neighbouring region. ===Data source=== These two typologies — the definition of a city and its commuting zone and the typology of metro regions — have been developed to benefit from three different data sources: the Urban Audit; survey data using the degree of urbanisation; and NUTS level 3 data. The [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/cities/statistics-illustrated Urban Audit] collects a limited number of key indicators for individual cities and their Functional urban area (FUA) (city plus commuting zone) annually. This new definition ensures high international comparability both within Europe and — through cooperation with the [[Glossary:OECD|OECD]] — outside of Europe. Surveys using the degree of urbanisation can provide data points for all cities in a country. Usually the sample inside cities is sufficient to provide reliable estimates for the headline indicators, in other words the key indicators that refer to the entire population. This source cannot however provide data for the commuting zone and in most cases the sample is also too small to provide figures for individual cities. The main exception is labour force survey data for cities that are also NUTS level 2 regions, such as Inner and Outer London in the United Kingdom, the Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest in Belgium, Wien in Austria or Praha in the Czech Republic. The [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/cities/statistics-illustrated metro regions] allow an analysis of NUTS level 3 data. This is particularly useful to analyse changes in GDP and employment (by sector). This facilitates an assessment of the differences in GDP per inhabitant, labour productivity and employment shares and their changes over time. In addition, several other data collections are available for metro regions including patent data, population change and net migration. ===Context=== The European Commission has introduced typologies based on population size, density and commuting flows to monitor the situation and developments in cities and metro regions. The [http://europa.eu/lisbon_treaty/index_en.htm Lisbon Treaty] included territorial cohesion alongside economic and social cohesion as an objective for the EU. This concept was presented in a Green Paper on {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52008DC0616:EN:NOT|title=territorial cohesion: turning territorial diversity into strength}} (COM(2008) 616) and the background summarised in the [http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docoffic/official/reports/interim6_en.htm sixth progress report on cohesion] (2009). The [http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docoffic/official/reports/cohesion5/index_en.cfm fifth cohesion report] explains the main issues related to territorial cohesion and how these could be incorporated into policy proposals. One of the main issues is the need for data on different territorial levels, particularly for lower (more detailed) geographical levels. The city definition and the typology of metro regions provide new insights into developments at the local and the regional level and improve data availability by linking and simplifying the number of territorial definitions. ===Other articles=== *[[Regions and cities ]] *[[Territorial typologies]] (background article) ===Database=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/metropolitan-regions/data/database Metropolitan regions (met)] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/cities/data/database Urban audit] ===Dedicated section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=degree_urbanisation}} Degree of urbanisation] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/cities/statistics-illustrated Cities] ===Publications=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/4337659/4337763/Degree+of+urbanisation+Poster/19bee117-2e6a-4f7d-9b7f-e1ba05af3df6 Defining urban areas in Europe (PDF)] *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-HA-13-001|title=Eurostat regional yearbook 2013}} - chapter 13 *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/degree-of-urbanisation/overview Defining urban areas in Europe], overview poster published by DG Regional and Urban Policy (PDF file) ===Visualisations=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistical-atlas/gis/viewer/?year=2013&chapter=13 Eurostat Statistical Atlas (Chapter 13)] === Notes === {{Unit|topic=X_Regions}} [[Category:General and regional statistics|Territorial typologies for European cities and metropolitan regions]] [[Category:Regions and cities|Territorial typologies for European cities and metropolitan regions]] [[Category:Background_article|Territorial typologies for European cities and metropolitan regions]] [[Category:Regions and cities typologies|Territorial typologies for European cities and metropolitan regions]]

title: Temporary protection for persons fleeing Ukraine - monthly statistics
text:
On 4 March 2022, the European Council unanimously adopted an implementing decision introducing temporary protection for people fleeing Ukraine as a consequence of Russia's invasion. Data extracted on 4 August 2026 Planned article update: 10 September 2026 On 30 June 2026, 4.41 million non-EU citizens, who fled Ukraine as a consequence of Russia’s war of aggression, were under temporary protection in the EU. In Q2 2026, EU countries issued 138 045 new decisions providing temporary protection, a decline of 16.2% compared to the previous quarter. At the end of June 2026, the ratio of temporary protection beneficiaries from Ukraine relative to the population was the highest in Czechia (35.8 per 1 000 people), ahead of Slovakia (27.2) and Cyprus (26.8). [[Image:Map1_Non-EU_citizens_who_fled_Ukraine_and_were_under_temporary_protection_at_the_end_of_June_2026.jpg|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_asytpsm__custom_19168926/default/table migr_asytpsm]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_asytpspop__custom_19168875/default/table migr_asytpspop]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_gind__custom_19168715/default/table demo_gind)]|alt= Map showing non-EU citizens who fled Ukraine and were under temporary protection in the EU Member States and surrounding countries at the end of June 2026. Each country is classified based on the ratio per thousand people. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] On 4 March 2022, the [[Glossary:European_Council|European Council]] unanimously adopted an implementing decision introducing [[Glossary:Temporary_protection|temporary protection]] for people fleeing Ukraine as a consequence of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine that began on 24 February 2022. On 13 June 2025, the [https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2025/06/13/eu-member-states-agree-to-extend-temporary-protection-for-refugees-from-ukraine/ Council] extended temporary protection until 4 March 2027. Temporary protection is an exceptional measure to provide immediate and temporary protection to displaced people from non-EU countries and those unable to return to their country of origin. It applies when there is a risk that the standard [[Glossary:Asylum|asylum]] system will struggle to cope with demands stemming from a mass inflow, risking a negative impact on the processing of claims. This article presents the main developments for June 2026. === Which EU countries do people fleeing Ukraine go to? === At the end of June 2026, the [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU countries]] hosting the highest number of beneficiaries of temporary protection from Ukraine were Germany (1 286 230 people; 29.2% of the EU total), Poland (961 170; 21.8%), and Czechia (390 810; 8.9%). The number of people under temporary protection relative to the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|EU ]]population was 9.8 per 1 000 people at the end of June 2026. The highest ratios were observed in Czechia (35.8 per 1 000 people), ahead of Slovakia (27.2) and Cyprus (26.8)(Map 1). Compared with the end of May 2026, the number of people from Ukraine under temporary protection at the end of June 2026 increased by 24 380 across the EU (+0.6%). The number of people under temporary protection increased in 24 EU countries and decreased in 3. The largest absolute increases were observed in in Italy (+4 115; +8.8%), Czechia (+3 835; +1.0%), and Germany (+2 960; +0.2%). The decreases were recorded in Poland (-6 335; -0.7%), Belgium (-35; -0.04%), and Ireland (-15; -0.01%). [[Image:Map1_Non-EU_citizens_who_fled_Ukraine_and_were_under_temporary_protection_at_the_end_of_June_2026.jpg|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Non-EU citizens who fled Ukraine and were under temporary protection at the end of June 2026
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_asytpsm__custom_19168926/default/table migr_asytpsm]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_asytpspop__custom_19168875/default/table migr_asytpspop]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_gind__custom_19168715/default/table demo_gind)]|alt= Map showing non-EU citizens who fled Ukraine and were under temporary protection in the EU Member States and surrounding countries at the end of June 2026. Each country is classified based on the ratio per thousand people. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Interactive Figure 1 shows the number of people under temporary protection as well as the ratio per 1 000 people and the share in percentage of the EU total.
Figure 1 === Who are the people fleeing Ukraine and receiving temporary protection? === At the end of June 2026, 98.5% of the people who had fled Ukraine and were under temporary protection in the EU were Ukrainian. Among other non-EU citizens under temporary protection, the main countries of citizenship were Russia (11 840; 0.3%), Nigeria (4 715; 0.1%), and Azerbaijan (4 375; 0.1%). At the end of June 2026, adult women made up 43.4% of the people under temporary protection, 53.8% of them were aged 35 to 64 years. Minors represented almost one third (29.6%), while adult men accounted for slightly more than a quarter (27.0%). The proportions of boys and girls under the age of 18 years were 15.7% and 14.0%, respectively (Figure 2). [[Image:F2_Structure_of_beneficiaries_of_temporary_protection_by_age_and_sex,_EU,_end_of_June_2026_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Structure of beneficiaries of temporary protection by age and sex, end of
June 2026
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_asytpsm__custom_19168926/default/table migr_asytpsm])|alt= Population pyramid as horizontal bar chart showing structure by age and sex of beneficiaries of temporary protection in the EU at the end of June 2026 in percentages. Five bars represent the age groups less than 14 years, 14 to 17 years, 18 to 34 years, 35 to 64 years and 65 years and over. Each bar has two sections for male and female. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] On a quarterly basis, the share of temporary protection decisions for minors (20.7%) and adult women (41.3%) was higher by 0.2 and 2.3 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]], respectively, during Q2 2026 (Figure 3) compared to Q1 2026. In contrast, the share of decisions granted to adult men (38.1%; -2.5 pp) dropped during Q2 2026. The monthly share of adult men (36.7%) among people granted temporary protection decreased in June 2026 by 2.6 pp compared with May 2026. During the same period, the monthly share of adult women (41.9%) remained the same, whereas the share of minors (21.4%) increased by 2.7 pp. [[Image:F3_Quarterly_and_monthly_shares_of_main_population_groups_among_people_granted_temporary_protection,_EU_(%)_edition_August2026_v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Quarterly and monthly shares of main population groups among people granted temporary protection, EU
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_asytpfq__custom_19168987/default/table migr_asytpfq]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_asytpfm__custom_19169020/default/table migr_asytpfm])|alt= Vertical stacked bar chart showing quarterly and monthly shares of main population groups among people granted temporary protection as percentages in the EU from March 2022 to June 2026. Totaling 100 percent, each monthly column has three stacks representing adult men, adult women and minors. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === How many decisions providing temporary protection were issued? === In June 2026, 42 820 new decisions providing temporary protection in the EU were issued, 3 920 more compared with May 2026 (Table 1). Among the EU countries, 9 countries issued fewer decisions in June 2026 compared with May 2026. The 3 largest decreases were observed in Poland (-2 170), Cyprus (-520), and Italy (-165). 18 EU countries issued more decisions in June 2026 than in May 2026, with the largest absolute increases being recorded in Germany (1 825), Czechia (1 470), and Bulgaria (870). On a quarterly basis, EU countries issued 138 045 new decisions providing temporary protection during Q2 2026. Compared with Q1 2026, the number of new decisions decreased by 26 760 (-16.2%). A decline was observed during Q2 2026 in 14 EU countries, with the 3 largest absolute decreases being recorded in Germany (-21 010), Poland (-11 325), and Czechia (-1 200). 13 EU countries issued more decisions providing temporary protection during Q2 2026 than during Q1 2026, with the 3 largest increases recorded in Slovakia (+2 365), Bulgaria (+2 215), and Greece (+1 315). Since the beginning of Russia’s war of aggression in February 2022, EU countries have provided temporary protection to 7.2 million people fleeing Ukraine. Since March 2022, Poland (2 165 500, 30.2% of the EU total), Germany (1 637 505, 22.8%), and Czechia (773 380, 10.8%) have issued nearly two-thirds (63.8%) of those decisions. [[Image:T1n_Number_of_decisions_on_temporary_protection_in_EU_and_EFTA_countries_editionAugust2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Number of decisions on temporary protection in EU and EFTA countries
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_asytpfq__custom_19168987/default/table migr_asytpfq]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_asytpfm__custom_19169020/default/table migr_asytpfm]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_asytpfa__custom_19168956/default/table migr_asytpfa)]|alt= Table showing the number of decisions on temporary protection in the EU, individual EU Member States and EFTA countries from Q1 2022 to June 2026. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Where did unaccompanied minors fleeing Ukraine go? === Among the EU countries for which data are available, Austria (3 770), the Netherlands (2 220), and Denmark (2 045) have granted most of the temporary protection statuses to unaccompanied minors from Ukraine since March 2022 (Table 2). In relative terms, the highest share of unaccompanied minors in the total number of minors granted temporary protection was recorded in Croatia (15.9%), ahead of Denmark (9.6%), and Austria (8.0%) (Figure 4). [[Image:T2n_Number_of_unaccompanied_minors_granted_temporary_protection_editionAugust2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Number of unaccompanied minors granted temporary protection
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_asyumtpfq__custom_19169210/default/table migr_asyumtpfq]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_asyumtpfm__custom_19169193/default/table migr_asyumtpfm]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/migr_asyumtpfa__custom_19169121/default/table migr_asyumtpfa])|alt= Table showing the number of unaccompanied minors granted temporary protection by quarter and by month in individual EU Member States and EFTA countries from March 2022 to June 2026. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:F4n_Share_of_unaccompanied_minors_in_the_total_number_of_minors_granted_temporary_protection_from_March_2022_to_June_2026_(%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Share of unaccompanied minors in the total number of minors granted temporary protection from March 2022 to June 2026

For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Temporary_protection_for_persons_fleeing_Ukraine_edition_August_2026_v2.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === The data used for this publication are provided to [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] by the interior and justice ministries or immigration agencies of the EU Member States and [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA countries]]. Data on temporary protection are collected monthly on a voluntary basis, whereas the quarterly number of decisions providing temporary protection is collected on a mandatory basis. They are based entirely on relevant administrative sources and supplied in accordance with the provisions of Article 4 of [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32007R0862 Regulation (EC) No 862/2007] on community statistics on migration and international protection. Statistics on unaccompanied minors presented in the article refer to the age accepted by the national authorities, and generally before the age assessment procedure was carried out/completed due to the data reporting deadline. Structures by age and by sex have been calculated based on available data while disregarding the unknown category. Some data are unavailable. This is because the monthly data collection is carried out on a voluntary basis, so the completeness of the data may vary: * When renewal of temporary protection status is not automatic, some beneficiaries of temporary protection might be temporarily excluded from the statistics while undergoing renewal. * Deregistration procedure of people under temporary protection varies across countries and can result in large month-to-month decreases in the number of registered beneficiaries if not implemented on a continuous basis. * France: in most cases, minors can stay in France without a permit. Therefore, minors are generally not included in statistics on temporary protection. * France, Italy and Iceland: unaccompanied minors fleeing Ukraine are benefitting from another protection scheme than the European temporary protection status. * Poland: unaccompanied minors arriving in Poland from Ukraine are already into the care of an adult designated by a Polish court before receiving temporary protection and then are considered as accompanied minors. * Spain and Cyprus: the number of unaccompanied minors is assumed to be equal to zero because of the few possible cases and the high level of uncertainty related to the determination of their status. * Hungary: data on temporary protection broken down by age group are not available from March 2022 to December 2024. * Data on the number of people under temporary protection at the end of the month until December 2022 (for the Netherlands), until January 2024 (for Bulgaria), until June 2024 (for Germany) and until May 2025 (Italy) include some people whose temporary protection status was no longer valid and are not comparable with data of the following reference periods. * Iceland: data are not available for May and June 2026. * Italy: break in time series in June 2025 for the number of people under temporary protection at the end of the month. People who did not show up during the renewal procedure introduced in 2025 were removed in June 2025 from the statistics on the number of people under temporary protection. Late renewals are reintroduced in the statistics only at the date of the renewal. Before June 2025, only people, who explicitly informed Italian authorities about leaving the Italian territory or changing residency status, were removed from the statistics. Due to the short timeline for the provision of data, figures presented may be subject to future revisions. === Context === In line with the commitment of the European Statistical System to provide relevant and timely official statistics, Eurostat asked EU countries and EFTA countries to transmit voluntary monthly data within 1 month following the end of a reference period and for the first time by the end of April for the reference month March 2022 for the following data series within the framework of Eurostat data collections in the field of Asylum (Article 4 of [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32007R0862 Regulation (EC) No 862/2007]) * decisions during the reference period granting temporary protection status by age, sex, citizenship and type of minor (flow data) * beneficiaries of temporary protection at the end of the month by age, sex, citizenship and type of minor (stock data) Temporary protection status and conditions of applications are defined by Council Directive 2001/55/EC of 20 July 2001 whereas Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2022/382 of 4 March 2022 establishing the existence of a mass influx of displaced people from Ukraine within the meaning of Article 5 of Directive 2001/55/EC is the first one with the effect of introducing temporary protection. These data are supplied to Eurostat by the national Ministries of Interior and related immigration agencies. Official statistics provided to Eurostat may differ from operational data collected under other collection frameworks in the Commission or by European or international agencies like the European Union Asylum Agency or the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) for various reasons including various definitions used, frequencies, deadlines for provision and quality requirements. ===Other articles=== *[[Asylum applications - annual statistics]] *[[Statistics on countries responsible for asylum applications (Dublin Regulation) ]] *[[Enforcement of immigration legislation statistics]] *[[Residence permits - statistics on first permits issued during the year]] === Database === Temporary protection, see:

title: Territorial typologies for European cities and metropolitan regions/de
text:
1 =Territoriale Typologien für europäische Städte und Metropolregionen= Daten von Februar 2013 Dieser Artikel beschreibt zwei miteinander verbundene Typologien, die entwickelt wurden, um das gesamte geografische Gebiet der [[Glossary:European Union (EU)/de|Europäischen Union (EU)]], Islands, Norwegens, der Schweiz und Kroatiens ohne Überschneidungen oder Auslassungen auf lokaler und regionaler Ebene zu erfassen. Die Typologien umfassen Folgendes: *die Definition einer Stadt und ihres Pendlereinzugsgebiets und *eine Typologie von Metropolregionen. Im Gegensatz zu den Typologien im Artikel „[[Territorial typologies|Territorial typologies]]“ (Typologie des Verstädterungsgrades und regionale Stadt-Land-Typologie), die sich in erster Linie auf die Bevölkerungsdichte stützen, beziehen die beiden im vorliegenden Artikel vorgestellten Typologien eine funktionale Dimension ein. Beide sind Formen funktioneller städtischer Gebiete und basieren auf den Pendlerströmen einer Stadt. === Funktionale städtische Gebiete: eine Stadt und ihr Pendlereinzugsgebiet === '''Definition einer Stadt''' [[Image:Defining_a_city_—_high-density_cells,_urban_centre_and_city_(Graz,_Austria).png|thumb|centre|500px|Abbildung 1: Definition einer Stadt – Rasterzellen mit hoher Bevölkerungsdichte, urbanes Zentrum und Stadt
(Graz, Österreich) – Quelle: Generaldirektion Regionalpolitik und Stadtentwicklung]] Die neue Definition einer Stadt erfolgt in vier grundlegenden Schritten und basiert auf dem Vorhandensein eines „urbanen Zentrums“, eines neuen räumlichen Konzepts auf der Grundlage von Rasterzellen mit hoher Bevölkerungsdichte. Schritt 1: Alle Rasterzellen mit einer Bevölkerungsdichte von 1500 Einwohnern je km² oder mehr werden ausgewählt (Bild 1 in Abbildung 1). Schritt 2: Die sich berührenden Die Kontiguität für Cluster mit hoher Bevölkerungsdichte schließt die Diagonale (d. h. Zellen, die sich nur an den Ecken berühren) nicht ein. Zellen mit hoher Bevölkerungsdichte werden dann zu Clustern zusammengefasst, Lücken Lücken in Clustern mit hoher Bevölkerungsdichte werden iterativ anhand der Mehrheitsregel geschlossen. Die Mehrheitsregel besagt, dass eine Zelle zu einem Cluster mit hoher Bevölkerungsdichte hinzugefügt wird, wenn mindestens fünf der acht sie umgebenden Zellen zu dem gleichen Cluster mit hoher Bevölkerungsdichte gehören. Dies wird wiederholt, bis keine Zellen mehr hinzugefügt werden. werden geschlossen, und nur die Cluster mit einer Bevölkerung von mindestens 50 000 Einwohnern (Bild 2 in Abbildung 1) werden als „urbanes Zentrum“ beibehalten. Schritt 3: Alle Gemeinden (lokale Verwaltungseinheiten der Ebene 2 (LAU2)), bei denen sich mindestens die Hälfte ihrer Bevölkerung in dem urbanen Zentrum befindet, werden als potenzielle künftige Teile einer Stadt ausgewählt (Bild 3 in Abbildung 1). Schritt 4: Die Stadt wird so definiert, dass Folgendes sichergestellt ist: *Es besteht eine Verknüpfung zur politischen Ebene; *mindestens 50 % der Bevölkerung leben in einem urbanen Zentrum; und *mindestens 75 % der Bevölkerung des urbanen Zentrums leben in einer Stadt (Bild 4 in Abbildung 1). In den meisten Fällen — auch im Beispiel Graz (in Österreich) — ist der letzte Schritt nicht erforderlich, da die Stadt normalerweise aus einer einzigen Gemeinde besteht, die das gesamte urbane Zentrum abdeckt, und da die überwiegende Mehrheit der Einwohner der Stadt in diesem urbanen Zentrum lebt. Für 33 urbane Zentren, die sich weit über die Grenzen der Stadt erstrecken, wurde eine Ebene „Greater City“ (Ballungsraum) geschaffen, um die internationale Vergleichbarkeit zu verbessern (zu ausführlicheren Erläuterungen siehe die Veröffentlichung „[http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docgener/focus/2012_01_city.pdf Regional Focus 01/2012)]“ (auf Englisch) der Generaldirektion Regionalpolitik und Stadtentwicklung. Um sicherzustellen, dass die oben erläuterte Definition alle relevanten Zentren erfasst, wurden nationale statistische Behörden konsultiert, und es wurden kleinere Anpassungen vorgenommen, sofern diese erforderlich und mit diesem Ansatz konsistent waren. '''Identifizierung eines Pendlereinzugsgebiets''' [[Image:How_to_define_a_city_and_its_commuting_zone_(Genova,_Italy).png|thumb|centre|500px|Abbildung 2: Wie man eine Stadt und ihr Pendlereinzugsgebiet definiert (Genova, Italien) – Quelle: Generaldirektion Regionalpolitik und Stadtentwicklung]] Sobald alle Städte definiert wurden, kann ein Pendlereinzugsgebiet auf der Grundlage von Pendlerverkehrsmustern anhand der folgenden Schritte bestimmt werden: *Wenn 15 % der Beschäftigten, die in einer Stadt leben, in einer anderen Stadt arbeiten, werden diese beiden Städte als eine einzige Stadt behandelt (Bild 1 in Abbildung 2). *Alle Gemeinden, bei denen mindestens 15 % ihrer erwerbstätigen Einwohner in einer Stadt arbeiten, werden ermittelt (Bild 2 in Abbildung 2). *Gemeinden, die von einem einzigen funktionellen Gebiet umgeben Ein „umgebenes“ Gebiet ist definiert als ein Gebiet, das eine gemeinsame Landgrenze von 100 % mit dem funktionellen Gebiet hat. sind, werden aufgenommen, und nicht angrenzende Gemeinden werden ausgeschlossen (Bild 3 in Abbildung 2). Die funktionales städtisches Gebiet (FUA-"Functional urban area") umfasst die Stadt und das Pendlereinzugsgebiet. [[Image:Urban-Audit-Städte_und_funktionale_städtische_Gebiete,_2012.png|thumb|centre|500px|Karte 1: Urban-Audit-Städte und funktionale städtische Gebiete , 2012 (1) – Quelle: Generaldirektion Regionalpolitik und Stadtentwicklung]] Zu weiteren Einzelheiten über die Quellen und die Bezugsjahre für die Pendlereinzugsgebiete siehe „[http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/information/focus/index_de.cfm Regional Focus 01/2012]: Cities in Europe — The new OECD-EC definition“ (Lewis Dijkstra und Hugo Poelman, auf Englisch). === Typologie von Metropolregionen === [[Image:Typology_of_metro_regions,_2012_(1).png|thumb|centre|500px|Karte 2: Typologie von Metropolregionen, 2012 (1) – Quelle: Generaldirektion Regionalpolitik und Stadtentwicklung]] Metropolregionen sind Annäherungen der funktionale städtische Gebiete (Städte und Pendlereinzugsgebiete) auf NUTS-Ebene 3 mit mindestens 250 000 Einwohnern, die die oben beschriebene Definition erfüllen. Jede Metropolregion umfasst eine oder mehrere NUTS-3-Regionen und ist nach der wichtigsten funktionales städtisches Gebiet innerhalb ihrer Grenzen benannt. Die Typologie unterscheidet drei Arten von Metropolregionen: *Hauptstadt-Metropolregionen, *Metropolregionen der zweiten Kategorie und *kleinere Metropolregionen. Die Hauptstadt-Metropolregion umfasst die Hauptstadt des Staates. Metropolregionen der zweiten Kategorie sind die Gruppe der größten Städte in einem Land mit Ausnahme der Hauptstadt. Für diesen Zweck kann kein fester Grenzwert für die Bevölkerungszahl verwendet werden. Daher wurde ein natürlicher Schwellenwert genutzt, um die Metropolregionen der zweiten Kategorie von den kleineren Metropolregionen abzugrenzen. Die Regionen, die nicht zu einer Metropolregion gehören, werden einfach als Nicht-Metropolregionen bezeichnet. Diese Typologie kann noch weiter vereinfacht werden, indem alle einzelnen Metropolregionen zu übergeordneten Metropolregionen zusammengefasst werden. Die Grenzen einer funktionales städtisches Gebiet stimmen nicht zwangsläufig mit denen der NUTS-3-Regionen überein. Daher wurden NUTS-3-Regionen, in denen mindestens 50 % der regionalen Bevölkerung innerhalb einer bestimmten funktionales städtisches Gebiet leben, als Bestandteile der Metropolregion ausgewählt, die zu dieser funktionales städtisches Gebiet gehört. In einigen Fällen stimmt die Annäherung der NUTS-3-Region weitgehend mit der funktionales städtisches Gebiet überein. In anderen Fällen kann die Metropolregion größer oder kleiner als die funktionales städtisches Gebiet sein. Jede funktionales städtisches Gebiet wird durch mindestens eine NUTS-3-Region repräsentiert, selbst wenn weniger als 50 % der Bevölkerung dieser NUTS-3-Region in der funktionales städtisches Gebiet leben. === Verbindungen zwischen der Definition einer Stadt und ihres Pendlereinzugsgebiets einerseits und der Typologie des Verstädterungsgrades andererseits === [[Image:Cities_and_commuting_zones_compared_with_the_degree_of_urbanisation_on_the_Polish–Slovakian_border.png|thumb|centre|500px|Abbildung 3: Städte und Pendlereinzugsgebiete im Vergleich mit dem Verstädterungsgrad an der polnisch-slowakischen Grenze – Quelle: Generaldirektion Regionalpolitik und Stadtentwicklung]] Der erste Baustein der oben angeführten Definition einer Stadt ist das urbane Zentrum. Dieser Baustein ist identisch mit dem in der [[Territorial_typologies#Degree_of_urbanisation_typology_for_LAU_level_2_areas_.E2.80.94_an_area_typology/de| Typologie des Verstädterungsgrades]] verwendeten Konzept. Die Stadt (oder das dicht besiedelte Gebiet) gemäß der Definition des Verstädterungsgrades ist also identisch mit der in diesem Artikel beschriebenen Definition der Stadt. Die beiden nachstehenden Karten zeigen die zwei lokalen Typologien für das polnisch-slowakische Grenzgebiet. Die Unterschiede werden im zweiten Baustein deutlich. Mit der Definition der Stadt werden sich berührende Gebiete mit starken Pendlerströmen erfasst. Dies sind die Pendlereinzugsgebiete (siehe Abbildung 3). Der Verstädterungsgrad legt Städte und Vororte (oder Gebiete mit mittlerer Bevölkerungsdichte) und ländliche Gebiete (oder dünn besiedelte Gebiete) auf Basis der Bevölkerungsdichte fest. Entsprechend ergeben sich zwischen diesen beiden Kategorien und den Pendlereinzugsgebieten einige Überschneidungen. Die Kategorie der Städte und Vororte kommt innerhalb von Pendlereinzugsgebieten (in diesem Fall eher Vororte) sowie außerhalb von Pendlereinzugsgebieten (in diesem Fall: Städte) vor. Ländliche Gebiete liegen weitgehend außerhalb von Pendlereinzugsgebieten, aber einige ländliche Gebiete haben starke Pendelverbindungen mit einer nahegelegenen Stadt entwickelt und sind daher ebenfalls einigen Pendlereinzugsgebieten zuzurechnen. === Keine Verbindung zwischen Metropolregionen und der regionalen Stadt-Land-Typologie === Die beiden Typologien auf lokaler Ebene haben einen Typ — Städte — gemeinsam, während die beiden regionalen Typologien jeweils unterschiedliche Typen umfassen. Die Typologie der Metropolregionen unterteilt NUTS-3-Regionen in Metropolregionen und Nicht-Metropolregionen, während die Stadt-Land-Typologie NUTS-3-Regionen in überwiegend städtische Regionen, Regionen mit mittlerer Bevölkerungsdichte und überwiegend ländliche Regionen unterteilt. Trotz fehlender identischer Regionstypen oder ­klassen sind die beiden regionalen Typologien recht ähnlich: *die meisten städtischen Regionen sind Metropolregionen und umgekehrt; *die meisten ländlichen Regionen sind Nicht-Metropolregionen und umgekehrt; *Regionen mit mittlerer Bevölkerungsdichte teilen sich zwischen Metropolregionen und Nicht-Metropolregionen auf. Abbildung 4 zeigt die Klassifikation von Regionen in der Nähe der polnisch-slowakischen Grenze und enthält Beispiele für die größten Gemeinsamkeiten zwischen diesen beiden regionalen Typologien. Die Unterschiede sind in erster Linie auf drei Ursachen zurückzuführen: eine unterschiedliche Logik, unterschiedliche Schwellenwerte für die Bevölkerungsgröße und eine unterschiedlichen Zahl von Klassen. [[Image:Metro_and_non-metro_regions_compared_with_the_urban–rural_typology_on_the_Polish–Slovakian_border.png|thumb|centre|500px|Abbildung 4: Metropolregionen und Nicht-Metropolregionen im Vergleich mit der Stadt-Land-Typologie an der polnisch-slowakischen Grenze – Quelle: Generaldirektion Regionalpolitik und Stadtentwicklung]] #Die unterschiedliche Logik, die den beiden Typologien zugrunde liegt, kann als morphologisch bzw. funktionell beschrieben werden. Die Stadt-Land-Typologie stützt sich stärker auf die Bevölkerungsgröße und ­dichte, die wiederum durch die Stadtform bestimmt wird; dies ist also eine Variante einer morphologischen Definition. Die Typologie der Metropolregionen beruht darauf, dass es ein urbanes Zentrum gibt und dass funktionelle wirtschaftliche Verbindungen mit diesem Zentrum bestehen. #Die beiden Typologien verwenden sehr unterschiedliche Schwellenwerte für die Bevölkerungsgröße. Metropolregionen entsprechen Städten, die zusammen mit Pendlereinzugsgebieten mindestens 250 000 Einwohner haben. Städtische Regionen sind urbane Zentren mit mindestens 50 000 Einwohnern. (Dies ist auch die Definition von Städten („cities“)) und/oder städtische Cluster mit mindestens 5000 Einwohnern (dies ist auch die Definition von Städten („towns“) und Vororten.) #Die Stadt-Land-Typologie umfasst drei Regionstypen, während die Typologie der Metropolregionen nur zwei umfasst. Aufgrund dieser Unterschiede werden einige städtische Regionen als Nicht-Metropolregionen eingestuft, da die Stadt und ihr Pendlereinzugsgebiet zu klein sind (oder die Region keine Stadt umfasst). Einige ländliche Regionen können als Teil einer Metropolregion eingestuft werden, wenn sie starke Pendelverbindungen mit einer Stadt in der gleichen oder einer benachbarten Region haben. === Datenquellen === Diese beiden Typologien — die Definition einer Stadt und ihres Pendlereinzugsgebiets und die Typologie der Metropolregionen — wurden so entwickelt, dass sie drei verschiedene Datenquellen nutzen können: das Urban Audit, Erhebungsdaten unter Verwendung des Verstädterungsgrades und Daten zur NUTS-Ebene 3. Das [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/cities/statistics-illustrated Urban Audit] erfasst jährlich eine eingeschränkte Zahl von Schlüsselindikatoren für einzelne Städte und ihre funktionales städtisches Gebiet (FUA). Diese neue Definition stellt eine gute internationale Vergleichbarkeit innerhalb Europas und — durch die Zusammenarbeit mit der [[Glossary:OECD/de|OECD]] — auch außerhalb Europas sicher. Erhebungen unter Verwendung des Verstädterungsgrades können Datenpunkte für alle Städte eines Landes bereitstellen. Normalerweise ist die Stichprobe innerhalb von Städten ausreichend, um zuverlässige Schätzwerte für die Leitindikatoren (d. h. die Schlüsselindikatoren, die sich auf die gesamte Bevölkerung beziehen) bereitzustellen. Diese Quelle kann jedoch keine Daten für das Pendlereinzugsgebiet bereitstellen, und in den meisten Fällen ist die Stichprobe auch zu klein, um Zahlen für individuelle Städte zu ermitteln. Die wichtigste Ausnahme bilden die Daten der Arbeitskräfteerhebung für Städte, die gleichzeitig NUTS-2-Regionen sind, wie z. B. Inner London und Outer London im Vereinigten Königreich, Région de Bruxelles-Capitale/Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest in Belgien, Wien in Österreich oder Praha in der Tschechischen Republik. Die [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/metropolitan-regions/statistics-illustrated Metropolregionen] ermöglichen eine Analyse von Daten der NUTS-Ebene 3. Dies ist besonders nützlich für die Analyse von Änderungen des BIP oder der Beschäftigung (nach Branche) und erleichtert eine Bewertung der Unterschiede des BIP je Einwohner, der Arbeitsproduktivität und des Beschäftigungsanteils sowie der Änderungen im Laufe der Zeit. Darüber hinaus sind mehrere andere Datenerhebungen für Metropolregionen verfügbar, darunter Patentdaten, Bevölkerungsänderungen und Wanderungssaldo. === Kontext === Die Europäische Kommission hat Typologien auf der Grundlage der Bevölkerungsgröße und ­dichte sowie der Pendlerströme eingeführt, um die Lage und die Entwicklung in Städten und Metropolregionen zu beobachten. Im [http://europa.eu/lisbon_treaty/index_de.htm Vertrag von Lissabon] wird der territoriale Zusammenhalt neben dem wirtschaftlichen und sozialen Zusammenhalt als eines der Ziele der EU genannt. Dieses Konzept wurde in einem [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:52008DC0616:DE:NOT Grünbuch zum territorialen Zusammenhalt: Territoriale Vielfalt als Stärke] (KOM(2008) 616) vorgestellt, und der Hintergrund wurde im [http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docoffic/official/reports/interim6_en.htm Sechsten Zwischenbericht über den Zusammenhalt] (2009) zusammengefasst. Im [http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docoffic/official/reports/cohesion5/index_de.cfm Fünften Bericht über den Zusammenhalt] werden die wichtigsten Fragen im Zusammenhang mit dem territorialen Zusammenhalt erläutert, und es wird dargelegt, wie diese in politische Vorschläge einbezogen werden können. Eine der wichtigsten Fragen ist der Bedarf an Daten über unterschiedliche territoriale Ebenen, insbesondere für untergeordnete (detailliertere) geografische Einheiten. Die Definition der Stadt und die Typologie der Metropolregionen bieten neue Einblicke in Entwicklungen auf lokaler und regionaler Ebene und verbessern die Datenverfügbarkeit durch Verknüpfung und Vereinfachung der Zahl territorialer Definitionen. === Weitere Artikel === *[[Regions and cities ]] (auf Englisch) *[[Territorial typologies|Territorial typologies]] (Hintergrundartikel) (auf Englisch) === Datenbank === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/metropolitan-regions/data/database Metropolregionen] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/cities/data/database Urban Audit] === Themenbereich === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/cities/statistics-illustrated Städte] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/degree-of-urbanisation/background Verstädterungsgrad] ===Veröffentlichungen=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-books/-/KS-HA-13-001 Eurostat Jahrbuch der Regionen 2013] - Kapitel 13 (auf Englisch) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/4337659/4337763/Degree+of+urbanisation+Poster/19bee117-2e6a-4f7d-9b7f-e1ba05af3df6 Definition städtischer Gebiete in Europa] Überblicksposter, veröffentlicht von der GD Regionalpolitik und Stadtentwicklung (auf Englisch) ===Datenvisualisierung=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistical-atlas/gis/viewer/?year=2013&chapter=13 Eurostat Statistical Atlas (Kapitel 13)] === Fußnoten === {{Unit|topic=X_Translation}} [[Category:Background_article/de|Territoriale Typologien für europäische Städte und Metropolregionen]] [[Category:Regions_and_cities/de|Territoriale Typologien für europäische Städte und Metropolregionen]]

title: Technology in enlargement countries - digital transformation
text:
This article presents information on access to and use of the internet, use of Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) and digital skills, as well as gross domestic expenditure on research and development (GERD) for the enlargement countries. It presents data for Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Kosovo, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, Türkiye and Ukraine and compares these with the corresponding data for the EU. Data from April 2026 Planned article update July 2027 In 2025, household internet access reached very high levels in several enlargement countries, including Albania and Kosovo''This designation is without prejudice to positions on status and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo Declaration of Independence.''(both 99.3%), exceeding the EU average of 94.7%. Internet use was widespread across the enlargement countries, with 98.0% of individuals in Kosovo using the internet daily in 2025, well above the EU level of 89.5%. In 2025, more than 80% of enterprises in Montenegro (87.3%) and Serbia (84.6%) had a website, both above the EU average of 79.0%, while lower shares were recorded in Türkiye (56.2%) and North Macedonia (48.8%). In 2024, Türkiye recorded the highest research and development intensity among the enlargement countries (1.46% of GDP), still well below the EU level of 2.24%. This article is part of an [[Enlargement_countries_-_statistical_overview|online publication]]. It provides information on [[Glossary:Candidate countries|enlargement countries]] and compares this information with the corresponding data for the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. The data used in this article have all been submitted to and validated by Eurostat's subject matter units, following the same process as for the EU countries. For Moldova, Georgia and Ukraine, data are not yet transmitted according to this process and are therefore not yet available. However, data on Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine are also presented in the [[European Neighbourhood Policy countries - statistical_overview|Statistics Explained articles for European Neighbourhood Policy - East]] countries; these articles are based on annual indicators supplied by and under the responsibility of the national statistical authorities of each country. The article presents a range of [[Glossary:Information_and_communication_technology_(ICT)|technology]] and [[Glossary:Research_and_development_(R_%26_D)|research and development (R&D)]] indicators such as the shares of households and enterprises with [[Glossary:Internet_access|internet access]], individuals’ frequency of [[Glossary:Internet_user|internet use]], shares of enterprises using [[Glossary:Information_and_communication_technology_(ICT)|information and communication technology (ICT)]], individuals’ use of [[Glossary:Digital_skills|digital skills]], [[Glossary:Gross domestic expenditure on R & D (GERD)|gross domestic expenditure on R&D (GERD)]] and [[Glossary:R & D expenditure by source of funds|GERD by source of funds]]. Where a table or graph refers to a single reference year (for example, 2024), or where annual data are unavailable for certain countries, the most recent available data within the preceding five years are used. Where both the start and end years are intended to be shown but the corresponding data series are not available, data from the closest possible years are presented instead (for example, 2023 data instead of 2024). ===Enterprises and households with internet access=== Figure 1 illustrates the continued expansion of internet access among enterprises and households in the enlargement countries and the EU between 2015 and 2025, showing high overall connectivity alongside some remaining cross-country differences. By 2025, internet access among enterprises was nearly universal across the enlargement countries with available data. Full or almost full coverage was reported in Montenegro and Serbia (both 100.0%), as well as in Bosnia and Herzegovina (99.9%) and Albania (99.4%), all above the EU level (99.0%). Slightly lower shares were observed in Türkiye (97.2%) and North Macedonia (96.2%; 2022 data). Internet access among households also increased across the enlargement countries. Albania and Kosovo reported the highest levels, with 99.3% of households having internet access, followed by Türkiye (96.2%) and North Macedonia (91.2%). Serbia (90.1%), Bosnia and Herzegovina (88.2%) and Montenegro (88.1%) also recorded high levels, although still below the EU average (94.7%; break in time series between 2015 and 2025). Overall, the data indicate substantial progress in digital connectivity across the enlargement countries, particularly among households. While enterprise connectivity has reached near-universal levels, household access still shows some gaps compared with the EU in several enlargement countries. [[Image:CPC26_Enterprises and households with internet access, 2015 and 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Enterprises and households with internet access, 2015 and 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6c326bc0-6100-418e-ba2f-9e5ed150c665?lang=en isoc_ci_in_en2] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/51903963-c419-414a-9195-2b4ab96f4ea9?lang=en isoc_ci_in_h])|alt= bar chart showing the shares of households and enterprises with access to the internet in the EU and the enlargement countries in 2015 and 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Frequency of internet use by individuals=== Figure 2 illustrates the increasing importance of the internet in everyday life, as reflected in the share of individuals (aged 16-74) using the internet daily or at least weekly (but not daily) in the EU and enlargement countries. In Kosovo, internet use was almost universal in 2025, with 98.0% of individuals using the internet daily (+22.3 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] compared with 2017 data) and a further 0.3% at least weekly (-6.2 pp), resulting in the highest share of frequent users (98.3%) among the enlargement countries. Montenegro followed, with 92.8% of daily users (+31.2 pp compared with 2017 data) and 1.3% weekly users (-6.1 pp), corresponding to 94.1% of frequent users. High levels of internet use were also recorded in North Macedonia, where 89.2% of individuals used the internet daily (+29.6 pp compared with 2015) and 2.1% at least weekly (-7.1 pp), and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, with 88.2% daily users (+27.0 pp compared with 2018 data) and 1.7% weekly users (-4.8 pp). Slightly lower shares were observed in Serbia and Türkiye, where 87.1% of individuals used the internet daily in 2025 (+32.5 pp and +47.0 pp respectively), with 2.7% and 2.1% using it at least weekly. Albania recorded a similar level of daily use (86.9%; +33.4 pp), while the share of weekly users was particularly low at 0.2% (-8.0 pp). Overall, the data show a strong increase in daily internet use across all enlargement countries, accompanied by a decline in less frequent use. By 2025, usage levels in most enlargement countries were close to those observed in the EU, where 89.5% of individuals used the internet daily and 3.2% at least weekly (break in time series between 2015 and 2025). [[Image:CPC26_Frequency of internet use, 2015 and 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Frequency of internet use, 2015 and 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/72f17b40-900a-44ee-a51e-8f4cca827aad?lang=en isoc_ci_ifp_fu])|alt= bar chart showing the shares of persons using the internet either daily or weekly in the EU and the enlargement countries in 2015 and 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Enterprises using information and communication technology=== The use of information and communication technologies (ICT) is an important aspect of business operations, reflecting how enterprises adopt digital tools for communication, information access and online presence. Key indicators include access to the internet and the use of websites, which provide insights into the level of digitalisation among enterprises. In 2025, internet access among enterprises was nearly universal across the enlargement countries, reaching 100.0% in Montenegro and Serbia (see Figure 3), and 99.9% in Bosnia and Herzegovina. High levels were also observed in Albania (99.4%) and Türkiye (97.2%), while North Macedonia recorded a slightly lower share (96.2%; 2022 data). These figures were broadly in line with the EU average (99.0%). In contrast, the share of enterprises having a website varied more widely. Montenegro (87.3%) and Serbia (84.6%) reported the highest levels in 2025, both exceeding the EU average (79.0%). Bosnia and Herzegovina (68.0%) and Albania (60.6%) recorded more moderate shares, while Türkiye (56.2%; break in time series between 2015 and 2025) and North Macedonia (48.8%; 2021 data) recorded lower shares. Overall, the results suggest that while basic digital connectivity is well established among enterprises in the enlargement countries, the use of websites as a tool for online presence and business activity is less widespread and more uneven. [[Image:CPC26_Enterprises using ICT, 2015 and 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Enterprises using ICT, 2015 and 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5e73daae-9043-4bbd-83d5-67da132c4dbd?lang=en isoc_ci_in_en2] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ee3cfecc-6a7e-4472-946f-3e85140d9ff1?lang=en isoc_ciweb])|alt= bar chart showing the shares of enterprises where the persons employed have access to the internet and the shares of enterprises having a website, in the EU and the enlargement countries in 2015 and 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Use of ICT skills by type=== Figure 4 shows the use of selected ICT skills among individuals aged 16-74 in the enlargement countries and the EU, based on activities carried out in the three months preceding the survey. The indicators cover three types of skills with increasing levels of complexity: using spreadsheet software, creating electronic presentations (with text, images, animations, etc.), and writing code in a programming language, which can be regarded as proxies for applied [[Glossary:Digital_skills|digital skills]]. Among the enlargement countries with available data, Montenegro recorded the highest levels of ICT skill use in 2025. In Montenegro, 39.6% of individuals used spreadsheets and 41.4% created presentations, while 11.4% applied coding skills. Serbia also showed relatively high levels, with 29.9% using spreadsheets, 36.0% creating presentations and 5.4% writing code. At intermediate levels, Bosnia and Herzegovina reported 23.6% of individuals using spreadsheets and 23.7% creating presentations, with 4.4% writing code in 2025. Albania recorded somewhat lower shares. However, they increased rapidly between 2021 and 2025, with the shares of individuals using the respective ICT skills reaching 18.6% for spreadsheets, 27.3% for presentations and 9.7% for coding. Lower levels of ICT skill use were observed in Türkiye and North Macedonia. In Türkiye, 16.2% of individuals used spreadsheets and 15.1% created presentations in 2025, while coding skills remained unchanged at 2.5%. North Macedonia recorded the lowest levels, with 7.4% using spreadsheets and 13.7% creating presentations, although coding skills increased slightly to 4.2%. Overall, most enlargement countries experienced an increase in the use of ICT skills between 2021 and 2025, particularly for more advanced skills such as coding. Nevertheless, the EU continued to record higher levels across all three indicators, with the shares of using the different ICT skills rising to 40.3% for both using spreadsheets and creating presentations and 7.2% for coding in 2025. [[Image: Use of ICT skills by type, 2021 and 2025_(%)_up.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Use of ICT skills by type, 2021 and 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8f5b27c2-4584-48d4-bd57-546e39f1f1fa?lang=en isoc_sk_cskl_i21])|alt= bar chart showing the shares of persons using three different digital skills in the EU and the enlargement countries in 2021 and 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Gross domestic expenditure on research and development=== [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_expenditure_on_R_%26_D_(GERD)|Gross domestic expenditure on research and development (GERD)]] measures the total expenditure on research and development activities performed within a country during a given year. It covers [[Glossary:Research_and_development_(R_%26_D)|research and development (R&D)]] carried out by businesses, government, higher education institutions and private non-profit organisations. Expressed as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP), GERD indicates the overall intensity of research and development in an economy and allows comparisons across countries of the relative importance of R&D activities. Among the enlargement countries, Türkiye recorded the highest R&D intensity throughout the period, rising steadily from 0.85% of GDP in 2014 to 1.46% in 2024 (see figure 5). Serbia followed at a lower level, increasing from 0.69% in 2014 to 0.93% in 2024, despite some fluctuations in recent years. North Macedonia reported comparatively low and stable R&D intensity, ranging from 0.35-0.44% between 2015 and 2023 (2024 data not available). Montenegro showed more variability, peaking at 0.51% in 2018 and 2021 before declining to 0.29% in 2024 (provisional data). Lower levels of R&D intensity were observed in Albania and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Albania, GERD stood at 0.19-0.20% in the most recent years available (2021-2022), while Bosnia and Herzegovina recorded similar levels, ranging between 0.19 and 0.26% over the period, based on limited data. Overall, R&D intensity in the enlargement countries remained well below the EU level. In the EU, GERD stood at 2.24% of GDP in 2024, having gradually increased from 2.09% in 2014, indicating a substantially higher level of investment in research and development compared with the enlargement countries. [[Image:CPC26_Gross domestic expenditure on research and development (GERD), 2014-2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Gross domestic expenditure on research and development (GERD), 2014-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3028ca0c-381c-4be3-a1e9-677e7f070df3?lang=en rd_e_gerdtot])|alt= line chart showing gross domestic expenditure on research and development as share of GDP in the EU and the enlargement countries from 2015 to 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Gross domestic expenditure on R&D by source of funds=== Following the presentation of overall gross domestic expenditure on research and development (GERD), Figure 6 focuses on how this expenditure is financed. It shows the distribution of [[Glossary:R_%26_D_expenditure_by_source_of_funds|R&D funding by source]] in the enlargement countries and the EU, distinguishing between the business sector, government sector, higher education sector, private non-profit sector and funds from abroad, with a comparison between 2013 and 2023 (or the closest available year). Overall, R&D funding structures varied considerably across the enlargement countries. In several cases, the government sector remained the main source of funding, while in others the business sector or funds from abroad played a more prominent role. By contrast, the EU continued to rely primarily on business-funded R&D, supported by a substantial contribution from the government sector. In Türkiye, the business sector was the main source of R&D funding, increasing its share from 48.9% in 2013 to 52.6% in 2023. Government funding also grew, from 26.6% to 33.1%, while the contribution from the higher education sector declined. All other sources remained marginal. In Montenegro, the government sector became overwhelmingly dominant, with its share rising from 31.7% in 2013 to 73.5% in 2023. In contrast, the business sector’s contribution dropped sharply, from 42.3% to 11.8% (2023 data), while funds from abroad also declined. A similar dominance of the government sector was observed in North Macedonia, although with a more balanced structure. Government funding decreased from 52.9% in 2015 to 46.0% in 2022, while the business sector increased its share from 16.8% to 25.9%. The higher education sector remained a significant contributor, accounting for nearly one quarter of R&D funding. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the funding structure changed substantially. The business sector increased its share from 16.4% in 2013 to 38.7% in 2021, while the government sector also grew to 43.1%. At the same time, reliance on funds from abroad fell sharply, from 53.9% to 8.8%. In Serbia, the structure shifted notably towards external funding. The share of funds from abroad rose from 7.8% in 2013 to 30.3% in 2023, while the government sector remained the largest domestic source despite a decline. The contribution of the business sector dropped to a very low level (0.9%), while the higher education sector maintained a relatively strong role. At EU level, the structure of R&D funding remained relatively stable. The business sector continued to be the main source, accounting for 56.7% of R&D expenditure in 2023. Government funding decreased slightly compared with 2013, while funding from abroad became more important. The higher education and private non-profit sectors each accounted for a small share. [[Image:CPC26_Gross domestic expenditure on R&D, by source of funds, 2013 and 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Gross domestic expenditure on R&D, by source of funds, 2013 and 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/80f9d4ac-fd5b-4b2d-a094-86a98b6f437c?lang=en rd_e_gerdfund])|alt= stacked bar chart, showing the shares of gross domestic expenditure on research and development funded by different funding sectors in the EU and the enlargement countries in 2013 and 2023. The stacked bars show the shares of total R&D expenditure funded by each of the five sectors: business enterprises; government; higher education; private non-profit sector; funding from abroad. For each bar, the shares total 100 per cent. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=CPC26_Technology_V3.xlsx|title=Enlargement countries – information and communication technology: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== Eurostat's [[Glossary:EU_survey_on_the_use_of_ICT_in_households_and_by_individuals|survey on the use of ICT in households and by individuals]] and [[Glossary:EU_survey_on_ICT_usage_and_e-commerce_in_enterprises|survey on ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises]] are separate, annual surveys. The enterprise survey generally covers enterprises with at least 10 persons employed; the activity coverage excludes financial and insurance activities ([[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE]] Rev. 2 Section K). While these surveys initially concentrated on access and connectivity issues, their scope has subsequently been extended to cover a range of subjects, for example, [[Glossary:E-government|e-government]], social media or [[Glossary:E-commerce|e-commerce]]. The enlargement countries carry out ICT surveys according to the same specifications as those used by EU Member States. Within the European Statistical System (ESS), these two surveys are based on two methodological manuals: one for [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-25-065 enterprise statistics] and one for [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-25-066 statistics related to households and individuals], both of which are updated annually. The definitions laid down in these manuals form the basis for the methodology the enlargement countries are requested to follow. The enlargement countries provide data directly to Eurostat's unit responsible for innovation and digitalisation, under Eurostat's regular collection of ICT data. These statistics are available on Eurostat's website. Eurostat data on [[Glossary:Research_and_development_(R_%26_D)|research and development (R&D)]] aim to show a comprehensive picture of the situation in the EU, covering indicators related to expenditure and personnel. The international standards for collecting and reporting data on research and experimental development are specified in the [https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/frascati-manual-2015_9789264239012-en.html Frascati Manual]. [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_expenditure_on_R_%26_D_(GERD)|Gross domestic expenditure on R & D (GERD)]] includes expenditure on R & D by [[Glossary:Business_enterprise_sector_-_R_%26_D|business enterprises]], [[Glossary:Higher_education_sector_-_R_%26_D|higher education institutions]], [[Glossary:Government_sector_-_R_%26_D|government]] and [[Glossary:Private_non-profit_sector_-_R_%26_D|private non-profit organisations]], as well as [[Glossary:Abroad_sector_-_R_%26_D|R&D funding from abroad]] (including international sources). While basic principles and institutional frameworks for producing statistics are already in place, the enlargement countries are expected to increase the volume and quality of their data progressively, and to transmit these data to Eurostat in the context of the EU enlargement process. [[Glossary:European statistical system (ESS)|European statistical system (ESS)]] standards in the field of statistics require the existence of a statistical infrastructure based on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/quality/european-quality-standards/european-statistics-code-of-practice principles] such as professional independence, impartiality, relevance, confidentiality of individual data and easy access to official statistics; they cover methodology, classifications and standards for production. Eurostat assesses and supports the alignment of statistical production in the enlargement countries with the EU acquis in the field of statistics. Eurostat supports the national statistical offices and other producers of official statistics through a range of initiatives, such as statistical projects, training courses, traineeships, study visits, workshops and seminars, and participation in meetings within the ESS. The ultimate goal is the provision of harmonised, high-quality data that conforms to European and international standards. ===Context=== Information and communication technologies (ICTs) affect people's everyday lives in many ways, both at work and in the home, for example, through communications with friends and colleagues or buying and ordering goods online. The development and expansion of the information society is regarded as critical to improve the [[Glossary:Competitiveness|competitiveness]] of the EU, while EU policymakers also seek to regulate specific areas, such as e-commerce or the protection of an individual's privacy when using such technologies. In December 2022, European Parliament and Council [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32022D2481&qid=1715866453897 Decision (EU) 2022/2481 established the Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030]. This programme aims to encompass social, moral and economic impacts of digital technologies, to promote and drive the digital transformation toward a sustainable and inclusive path in order to reach a fair economy and investment-oriented approach with the twin objectives of promoting the uptake of artificial intelligence and addressing the risks associated with certain uses of this new technology. Statisticians are well aware of the challenges posed by rapid technological change in areas related to the internet and other new applications of ICTs. As such, there has been a considerable degree of development in this area, with statistical tools being adapted to satisfy new demands for data. Indeed, statistics within this domain are reassessed on an annual basis, in order to meet user needs and reflect the rapid pace of technological change. From 2014 to 2022, the [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/digital-economy-and-society-index-desi-2020 Digital Economy and Society Index (DESI)] summarised indicators on Europe’s digital performance and tracked the progress of EU countries. From 2023, the interactive [https://digital-decade-desi.digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/ DESI dashboard for the Digital Decade] visualises Europe’s performance across the four dimensions of the [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/europes-digital-decade Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030]: digital skills, digital infrastructure, digitalisation of business and digitalisation of public services. DESI is managed by [https://commission.europa.eu/about/departments-and-executive-agencies/communications-networks-content-and-technology_en Directorate-General Communications Networks, Content and Technology (DG CONNECT)]; some of the indicators that form part of DESI are based on Eurostat's Community surveys on ICT usage. Information concerning the current statistical legislation on ICT statistics can be found under [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/digital-economy-and-society/legislation 'Legislation' in the dedicated section on 'Digital economy and society'] on Eurostat's website. Additional information on statistical cooperation with the enlargement countries is provided in the Statistics explained background article [[Enlargement policy and statistical cooperation]]. === Footnotes === ===Other articles=== *[[Enlargement_countries_-_statistical_overview|Enlargement countries – statistical overview]] – online publication *[[International_statistical_cooperation|Statistical cooperation]] – online publication *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Category:Digital_economy_and_society All articles on the information society and use of ICT] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Category:Research_and_development All articles on research and development
