title: Territorial typologies for European cities and metropolitan regions/fr
text:
1 =Typologies territoriales pour les villes et les régions métropolitaines européennes= Données de février 2013 Cet article décrit deux typologies liées qui ont été élaborées afin de couvrir, sans chevauchement ni omission, l’ensemble du territoire de l’[[Glossary:European Union (EU)/fr|Union européenne (UE)]], l’Islande, la Norvège, la Suisse et la Croatie aux niveaux local et régional. Ces typologies couvrent: *la définition d’une ville et de sa «zone de navettage», et *une typologie des régions métropolitaines. Par rapport aux typologies présentées dans l’article relatif aux [[Territorial typologies|Territorial typologies]] (le degré d’urbanisation et la typologie régionale urbaine–rurale) qui s’appuient principalement sur la densité de population, les deux typologies présentées dans cet article ajoutent une dimension fonctionnelle. Ce sont toutes deux des formes de zones urbaines fonctionnelles qui sont basées sur les flux de personnes qui font la navette (d’où le terme de «zone de navettage») pour se rendre au travail dans une ville. === Zones urbaines fonctionelles: une ville et sa zone de navettage === '''Définition d’une ville''' [[Image:Defining_a_city_—_high-density_cells,_urban_centre_and_city_(Graz,_Austria).png|thumb|centre|500px|Graphique 1: Définir une ville - cellules à forte densité, centre urbain et ville
(Graz, Autriche) - Source: direction générale de la politique régionale et urbaine]] La nouvelle définition de la ville suit quatre étapes de base et repose sur la présence d’un «centre urbain», un nouveau concept géographique fondé sur des cellules de grille à forte densité de population. Étape 1: toutes les cellules de grille qui ont une densité de 1 500 habitants par km² ou plus sont sélectionnées (image 1 du graphique 1). Étape 2: les cellules à forte densité contiguës La contiguïté pour les clusters à forte densité n’inclut pas la diagonale (autrement dit, les cellules dont seuls les coins se touchent). sont ensuite regroupées, les trous Les trous dans le cluster à forte densité sont ensuite itérativement comblés à l’aide de la règle de la majorité. La règle de la majorité signifie que si au moins cinq des huit cellules entourant une cellule appartiennent au même cluster à forte densité, celle-ci est ajoutée. Cette manœuvre est répétée jusqu’à ce qu’aucune autre cellule ne soit ajoutée. sont comblés et seuls les clusters avec une population d’au moins 50 000 habitants (image 2 du graphique 1) sont considérés comme un «centre urbain». Étape 3: toutes les communes (unités administratives locales — UAL — de niveau 2) dont au moins la moitié de la population se trouve à l’intérieur du centre urbain sont retenues comme candidates en vue d’être intégrées à la ville (image 3 du graphique 1). Étape 4: la ville est définie en veillant à ce que: *il existe un lien avec le niveau politique; *au moins 50 % de la population vive dans un centre urbain, et *au moins 75 % de la population du centre urbain vive dans une ville (image 4 du graphique 1). Dans la plupart des cas, comme à Graz (en Autriche), la dernière étape n’est pas nécessaire étant donné que la ville se compose normalement d’une seule commune qui couvre la totalité du centre urbain et que la grande majorité des résidents de la ville vivent dans ce centre urbain. Pour 33 centres urbains qui s’étendent bien au-delà de la ville, un niveau «grande ville» a été créé afin d’améliorer la comparabilité internationale (pour plus de détails, voir la publication de la direction générale de la politique régionale et urbaine — [http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docgener/focus/2012_01_city.pdf Focus régional 01/2012 (en anglais)]. Afin de garantir que la définition ci-dessus a recensé tous les centres concernés, les autorités statistiques nationales ont été consultées et des ajustements mineurs ont été apportés lorsqu’ils s’avéraient nécessaires et cadraient avec cette approche. '''Identification d’une zone de navettage''' [[Image:How_to_define_a_city_and_its_commuting_zone_(Genova,_Italy).png|thumb|centre|500px|Graphique 2: Comment définir une ville et sa zone de navettage (Genova, Italie) - Source: direction générale de la politique régionale et urbaine]] Une fois que toutes les villes ont été définies, une zone de navettage peut être identifiée sur la base des habitudes de navettage, en suivant les étapes suivantes: *si 15 % des personnes occupées qui vivent dans une ville travaillent dans une autre ville, ces villes sont traitées comme une seule ville (image 1 du graphique 2); *toutes les communes dont au moins 15 % de la population résidente occupée travaille dans une ville sont recensées (image 2 du graphique 2); *les communes enclavées Par «enclavée», on entend qui partage 100 % de sa frontière terrestre avec la zone fonctionnelle. dans une seule zone fonctionnelle sont incluses dans celle-ci et les communes non contiguës sont laissées de côté (image 3 du graphique 2). La zone urbaine fonctionnelle se compose de la ville et de sa zone de navettage. [[Image:Villes_de_l’audit_urbain_et_zones_urbaines_fonctionnelles,_2012.png|thumb|centre|500px|Carte 1: Villes de l’audit urbain et zones urbaines fonctionnelles, 2012 (1) - Source: direction générale de la politique régionale et urbaine]] Pour plus de détails sur les sources et les années de référence pour les zones de navettage, voir [http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/information/focus/index_fr.cfm Focus régional 01/2012]: Cities in Europe - The new OECD–EC definition (Lewis Dijkstra et Hugo Poelman, en anglais). === Une typologie des régions métropolitaines === [[Image:Typology_of_metro_regions,_2012_(1)-fr.png|thumb|centre|500px|Carte 2: Typologie des régions métropolitaines, 2012 (1) - Source: direction générale de la politique régionale et urbaine]] Les régions métropolitaines sont une approximation de niveau NUTS 3 pour les zones urbaines fonctionnelles (ville et zones de navettage) de 250 000 habitants ou plus suivant la définition décrite ci-dessus. Chaque région métropolitaine se compose d’une ou plusieurs régions de niveau NUTS 3 et est baptisée d’après la zone urbaine fonctionnelle principale située à l’intérieur de ses frontières. La typologie distingue trois types de régions métropolitaines: *les régions métropolitaines capitales; *les régions métropolitaines de niveau 2; *les régions métropolitaines plus petites. La région métropolitaine capitale englobe la capitale nationale. Les régions métropolitaines de niveau 2 se composent des plus grandes villes d’un pays, à l’exclusion de la capitale. À cet effet, il n’a pas été possible d’utiliser un seuil de population fixe. Une séparation naturelle a donc servi à faire la distinction entre les régions métropolitaines de niveau 2 et les régions métropolitaines plus petites. Les régions qui n’appartiennent pas à une région métropolitaine sont simplement appelées «régions non métropolitaines». Cette typologie peut encore être simplifiée en regroupant toutes les régions métropolitaines individuelles en régions métropolitaines. Les frontières d’une zone urbaine fonctionnelle ne coïncident pas nécessairement avec celles des régions de niveau NUTS 3. Les régions de niveau NUTS 3 dans lesquelles au moins 50 % de la population régionale vit dans une zone urbaine fonctionnelle ont donc été sélectionnées comme composantes de la région métropolitaine liée à cette zone urbaine fonctionnelle. Dans certains cas, l’approximation de niveau NUTS 3 de la zone urbaine fonctionnelle est très bonne. Dans d’autres cas, la région métropolitaine peut être plus grande ou plus petite que la zone urbaine fonctionnelle. Chaque zone urbaine fonctionnelle est représentée par au moins une région de niveau NUTS 3, même si moins de 50 % de sa population se trouve à l’intérieur de la zone urbaine fonctionnelle. === Liens entre la définition d’une ville et de sa zone de navettage et la typologie du degré d’urbanisation === Le premier élément constitutif de la définition de la ville donnée ci-dessus est le centre urbain et celui-ci est identique à celui utilisé dans la [[Territorial_typologies#Degree_of_urbanisation_typology_for_LAU_level_2_areas_.E2.80.94_an_area_typology| degré d’urbanisation typologie]]. En conséquence, la ville (ou la zone densément peuplée) telle qu’elle est définie dans le degré d’urbanisation est identique à la définition de la ville donnée ici. Les deux cartes ci-après montrent les deux typologies locales pour la zone frontalière entre la Pologne et la Slovaquie. Les différences apparaissent dans le deuxième élément constitutif. La définition de la ville identifie les zones contiguës qui enregistrent d’importants flux de migration pendulaire («navetteurs»). Il s’agit des zones de navettage (voir graphique 3). [[Image:Cities_and_commuting_zones_compared_with_the_degree_of_urbanisation_on_the_Polish–Slovakian_border.png|thumb|centre|500px|Graphique 3: Villes et zones de navettage comparées au degré d’urbanisation à la frontière entre la Pologne et la Slovaquie - Source: direction générale de la politique régionale et urbaine]] Le degré d’urbanisation identifie les petites villes et les banlieues (ou zones de densité intermédiaire) et les zones rurales (ou zones peu densément peuplées) sur la base de la densité de population. En conséquence, ces deux catégories chevauchent partiellement les zones de navettage. La catégorie des petites villes et des banlieues apparaîtra à la fois à l’intérieur des zones de navettage (dans ce cas, il s’agira plus probablement de banlieues) et à l’extérieur (dans ce cas, il s’agira de petites villes). Les zones rurales se trouvent essentiellement en dehors des zones de navettage, mais certaines zones rurales ont développé une forte relation de navettage avec une ville voisine et peuvent donc aussi se trouver dans certaines zones de navettage. === Absence de lien entre les régions métropolitaines et la typologie régionale urbaine–rurale === Les deux typologies au niveau local ont un type en commun, à savoir les villes, tandis que les deux typologies régionales ont chacune des types différents. La typologie des régions métropolitaines divise les régions de niveau NUTS 3 en régions métropolitaines et non métropolitaines, tandis que la typologie urbaine–rurale divise les régions de niveau NUTS 3 en régions essentiellement urbaines, intermédiaires et essentiellement rurales. Malgré l’absence d’un type ou d’une classe de région identique, les deux typologies régionales sont assez semblables: *la plupart des régions urbaines sont des régions métropolitaines et vice versa; *la plupart des régions rurales sont des régions non métropolitaines et vice versa; *les régions intermédiaires sont réparties entre régions métropolitaines et non métropolitaines. Le graphique 4 présente la classification des régions à proximité de la frontière entre la Pologne et la Slovaquie et contient des exemples des liens les plus courants entre ces deux typologies régionales. Les différences résultent de trois principaux aspects: une logique différente, des seuils de taille différents et un nombre de classes différent. [[Image:Metro_and_non-metro_regions_compared_with_the_urban–rural_typology_on_the_Polish–Slovakian_border.png|thumb|centre|500px|Graphique 4: Régions métropolitaines et non métropolitaines comparées à la typologie urbaine–rurale à la frontière entre la Pologne et la Slovaquie - Source: direction générale de la politique régionale et urbaine]] #La logique différente qui sous-tend les deux typologies peut être décrite comme morphologique et fonctionnelle. La typologie urbaine–rurale dépend davantage de la taille et de la densité de la population, qui sont à leur tour déterminées par la forme urbaine. Il s’agit donc d’une variante de la définition morphologique. La typologie des régions métropolitaines se base sur la présence d’un centre urbain et de liens économiques fonctionnels avec ce centre. #Les deux typologies utilisent des seuils de taille assez différents. Les régions métropolitaines sont liées aux villes + zones de navettage d’au moins 250 000 habitants. Les régions urbaines représentent des centres urbains de 50 000 habitants ou plus (ce qui définit aussi les villes) et/ou des clusters urbains de 5 000 habitants ou plus (ce qui définit aussi les petites villes et les banlieues). #La typologie urbaine–rurale compte trois types de régions, tandis que la typologie des régions métropolitaines n’en compte que deux. En raison de ces différences, certaines régions urbaines deviendront des régions non métropolitaines parce que la ville et sa zone de navettage sont trop petites (ou n’ont pas de ville). Certaines régions rurales peuvent s’intégrer dans une région métropolitaine si elles ont de forts liens de navettage avec une ville située dans cette région ou dans une région voisine. ===Sources des données=== Ces deux typologies (la définition d’une ville et de sa zone de navettage et la typologie des régions métropolitaines) ont été mises au point pour tirer profit de trois sources de données différentes: l’audit urbain, les données d’enquête qui utilisent le degré d’urbanisation et les données disponibles au niveau NUTS 3. L’[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/cities/statistics-illustrated audit urbain] collecte chaque année un nombre limité d’indicateurs pour les différentes villes et leur zone urbaine fonctionnelle (ville + zone de navettage). Cette nouvelle définition assure une grande comparabilité internationale tant en Europe qu’en dehors, grâce à la coopération avec l’[[Glossary:OECD/fr|OCDE]]. Les enquêtes qui utilisent le degré d’urbanisation peuvent fournir des données pour toutes les villes d’un pays. En général, l’échantillon à l’intérieur des villes est suffisant pour donner des estimations fiables pour les indicateurs clés, autrement dit, les principaux indicateurs qui portent sur l’ensemble de la population. Cette source ne peut toutefois pas fournir de données pour la zone de navettage et, dans la plupart des cas, l’échantillon est aussi trop petit pour fournir des chiffres pour les villes prises individuellement. La principale exception concerne les données de l’enquête sur les forces de travail pour les villes qui sont aussi des régions de niveau NUTS 2, telles que l’Inner et l’Outer London au Royaume-Uni, la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest en Belgique, Wien en Autriche ou Praha en République tchèque. Les [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/metropolitan-regions/overview régions métropolitaines] permettent d’analyser les données de niveau NUTS 3. Cela est particulièrement utile pour analyser les évolutions du PIB et de l’emploi (par secteur). Cela facilite l’analyse des différences concernant le PIB par habitant, la productivité de la main-d’œuvre et les taux d’emploi et leur évolution dans le temps. En outre, plusieurs autres collections de données sont disponibles pour les régions métropolitaines, notamment des données sur les brevets, l’évolution démographique et la migration nette. ===Contexte=== La Commission européenne a introduit des typologies basées sur la taille de la population, la densité et les flux de migration pendulaire afin de suivre la situation et l’évolution dans les villes et les régions métropolitaines. Outre la cohésion économique et sociale, le [http://europa.eu/lisbon_treaty/index_fr.htm traité de Lisbonne] prévoyait comme objectif pour l’UE la cohésion territoriale. Ce concept a été présenté dans un livre vert sur [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:52008DC0616:FR:NOT la cohésion territoriale: faire de la diversité territoriale un atout] (COM(2008) 616) et le contexte résumé dans le [http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docoffic/official/reports/interim6_en.htm sixième rapport d’étape sur la cohésion] (2009). Le [http://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/sources/docoffic/official/reports/cohesion5/index_fr.cfm cinquième rapport sur la cohésion] explique les principaux enjeux liés à la cohésion territoriale et comment ceux-ci pourraient être intégrés dans les propositions stratégiques. Un des principaux enjeux est le besoin de données à différents niveaux territoriaux, en particulier pour les niveaux géographiques inférieurs (plus détaillés). La définition de la ville et la typologie des régions métropolitaines permettent de voir l’évolution aux niveaux local et régional sous un jour nouveau et améliorent la disponibilité des données en liant et en simplifiant le nombre de définitions territoriales. ===Autres articles === *[[Regions and cities ]] (en anglais) *[[Territorial typologies|Territorial typologies]] (article de fond, en anglais) === Base de données === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/metropolitan-regions/data/database Régions métropolitaines] *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/cities/data/database Villes (audit urbain)] === Section dédiée === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/cities/statistics-illustrated Villes] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/degree-of-urbanisation/background Degré d'urbanisation] === Publications === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-statistical-books/-/KS-HA-13-001 l'Annuaire régional d'Eurostat 2013] - chapitre 13 (en anglais) *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/4337659/4337763/Degree+of+urbanisation+Poster/19bee117-2e6a-4f7d-9b7f-e1ba05af3df6 Définition d'une zone urbaine en Europe (PDF)] poster récapitulatif publié par la DG Politique régionale et urbaine (en anglais) === Visualisation des données === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistical-atlas/gis/viewer/?year=2013&chapter=13 Eurostat Statistical Atlas (Chapitre 13)] === Références === {{Unit|topic=X_Translation}} [[Category:Background_article/fr|Typologies territoriales pour les villes et les régions métropolitaines]] [[Category:Regions_and_cities/fr|Typologies territoriales pour les villes et les régions métropolitaines]]

title: Territorial typologies manual - acknowledgements
text:
This is the acknowledgements page for Eurostat’s online publication, Methodological manual on territorial typologies: 2024 edition. This ''[[Territorial_typologies_manual|Methodological manual on territorial typologies]]'' provides information that data suppliers concerned with subnational statistics within the European Union (EU) need to ensure coherency and comparability. It also helps end-users understand and interpret the wide range of official statistics that are available at a subnational level for different areas and regions of the EU. The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-gq-18-008 1st edition of the publication] (released in 2018) marked an important milestone as it reflected legislative developments – through an initiative called Tercet – which integrated the most relevant territorial typologies into a consolidated and amended NUTS Regulation at the start of 2018. An update of the manual was carried out during the course of 2024, reflecting changes to the underlying methodology and legislation.
'''Editor''': Máté Farkas (Eurostat, Unit E.4., Regional statistics and geographical information) The editor would like to take the opportunity to thank to those colleagues who were closely involved in the publication’s preparation, namely: Teodora Brandmüller, Jorge Calvo, Joseph Davis, Reka Fodor, Michael Harrop, Oliver Heiden and Jørgen Rasmussen (Eurostat, Unit E.4., Regional statistics and geographical information); Hugo Poelman ([https://commission.europa.eu/about-european-commission/departments-and-executive-agencies/regional-and-urban-policy_en Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy], Unit B.1., Economic analysis). '''Production''': Giovanni Albertone, Simon Allen and Andrew Redpath (Informa s.à r.l.) '''Map production''': Jorge Calvo, Jospeh Davis, Máté Farkas, Michael Harrop and Jørgen Rasmussen (Eurostat, Unit E.4., Regional statistics and geographical information)

title: Territorial typologies manual - border regions
text:
This article on border regions forms part of Eurostat’s online publication, Methodological manual on territorial typologies: 2024 edition. This article forms part of [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]’s ''[[Territorial_typologies_manual|methodology manual on territorial typologies]]''. The [[Glossary:Border_region|border]] typology is applied at the level of [[Glossary:Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)|NUTS]] level 3 regions: it identifies border regions in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] as those regions with a land border, or those regions where more than half of the population lives within 25 km of such a border. ===Classes for the typology and their conditions=== '''Details of the typology''' The border typology is a [[Glossary:Classification|classification]] based on the following 2 categories *border regions *non-border regions (those regions that aren’t defined as border regions). '''Methodology for the typology''' In principle, border regions should ideally be defined as those regions which have part of their territory demarcated by an international border. However, for analytical purposes, border regions are defined as NUTS level 3 regions located along land borders or regions where a majority (> 50%) of the population are living close to a land border. There are 2 main types of border region for analyses *internal border regions, in other words, those regions located on borders between EU countries (this category also includes any particular region that has both a land border with an EU country and with a non-EU country) *external border regions, in other words, those regions located exclusively on borders between an EU country and a non-EU country/countries. As the severity of border effects is likely to diminish as a function of the distance from a border, the definition of border regions is complemented with a population component. As such, border regions also include those regions which, although they don’t have a border, have more than half of their population living within 25 km of a border. Using this broad definition, the following different types of border region may be identified, those with *a land border (internal or external) *more than 50% of the population living within 25 km of a land border (internal or external) *non-border regions. As this typology is based on both the distance and the population distribution between a border and a region, there is a need to use grid-based population data when establishing the typology. Note the border typology isn’t defined/recognised within the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32003R1059 NUTS Regulation], although the NUTS level 3 regions themselves are defined therein. As such, EU legislation on border regions may, for specific reasons, make use of alternative definitions: for example, it may refer to both land and maritime borders or it could refer exclusively to the EU’s external borders. Although not covered here, the following additional types of border region may be considered *a maritime border *a maritime border with more than 50% of the population living within 25 km *a land and a maritime border *a land and a maritime border with more than 50% of the population living within 25 km. ===Links to other spatial concepts/typologies=== There are close links between the border typology and the [[Glossary:Urban-rural typology|urban-rural typology]] (see [[Territorial typologies manual - urban-rural typology|Chapter 5]]) as each border region is classified as a predominantly urban, intermediate or predominantly rural region. Some border regions may also be classified as mountain regions (see [[Territorial typologies manual - mountain regions|Chapter 10]]). ===Results=== Based on the above definitions, there are 393 NUTS 2024 level 3 border regions in the EU and 772 non-border regions. The EU’s border regions include the following classes: 362 regions have a land border (288 have an internal border and 74 have an external border with a non-EU country), while there are 31 additional regions where at least 50% of the population are living within 25 km of a land border. Map 1 provides an overview of the final classification for the border typology showing the different classes described above. [[Image:CH08M01_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Map 1: Border typology
'' Source:'' Eurostat (GISCO) based on census population grid 2021 and NUTS 2024|alt=A categorical map showing the border typology. Areas are shown as regions with land borders, regions with more than 50% of the population living within 25 km of land borders and non-border regions. Data for EU and EFTA countries.]] ===Changes to the typology over time=== The border typology was developed by Eurostat in association with the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission’s]] Directorate-General for [https://commission.europa.eu/about-european-commission/departments-and-executive-agencies/regional-and-urban-policy_en Regional and Urban Policy]. As noted above, the border typology isn’t defined/recognised within the NUTS Regulation and hence EU legislation may, for specific reasons, make use of alternative definitions (over time). For example, the exact definition of border regions within the context of [https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/policy/cooperation/european-territorial/cross-border_en cross-border cooperation] has changed from 1 programming period to the next and currently includes support for regions with maritime borders, as well as external border regions. [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:32021R1059 Regulation (EU) 2021/1059] provides specific provisions for territorial cooperation goals as, for example, border regions often perform less well economically and access to public services (such as hospitals or universities) is generally lower in border regions. The European Commission’s [https://www.interregeurope.eu/ Interreg programme] plays a role in promoting regional development and reducing economic disparities, by addressing regional needs regarding cooperation, governance and more secure borders. For the period from 2021 to 2027, Interreg is focused on addressing several challenges, including: climate change, the digital transformation and social inclusion. The programme covers all of the EU countries, as well as Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Norway, Serbia, Switzerland and Ukraine. The flexible nature of definitions employed for border regions is 1 of the main reasons why a standardised definition of border regions has yet to be integrated into the legislation for territorial typologies. '''''Changes over time that impact on the classification''''' The border regions classification should be updated to reflect any changes to the underlying sources of information that are used in its compilation, in other words, changes to international borders or changes to the boundaries of NUTS level 3 regions and more importantly, changes to population distribution, in other words, the population grid. The NUTS Regulation specifies that the classification of regions should remain stable for a period of at least 3 years; the most recent updates were for NUTS 2016, NUTS 2020 and NUTS 2024. After each revision of the NUTS classification, the distance between each international border and the boundaries of each NUTS level 3 region should be re-assessed in the event that some boundaries have moved closer to (or further away) from an international border; note that when the NUTS classification is revised it is also possible for some regions to be split or merged with other regions. Changes to international borders are far less common (although shouldn’t be entirely ruled out). '''''Future developments''''' The next update of the NUTS classification is planned for 2028. ===Further information=== '''Glossary entry''' [[Glossary:Border_region|Border region]] ===Published indicators=== A variety of different statistical surveys collect data for NUTS level 3 regions and this information may be used to calculate data for border and non-border regions. This process involves aggregating the data for NUTS level 3 regions to compute a total or an average for all border (and non-border) regions within a territory (for example a Member State, or the EU as a whole). '''Visualisation tools''' Eurostat publishes data for the border typology through [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RCI/#?vis=border.typology&lang=en Regions and cities illustrated]. '''Database''' Eurostat’s website provides information for a wide variety of indicators for the border typology. These statistics are available for the following statistical domains: demography, population projections, the labour market, crimes recorded by the police, economic accounts, business demography, intellectual property rights and transport. They are available [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/rural-development/database here]. ===Examples=== [[Rural_Europe|Rural Europe – various statistics on border regions]] [[Urban_Europe|Urban Europe – various statistics on border regions]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/rural-development/database Rural development] ===Dedicated section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/regions-and-cities/overview Regions and cities – overview] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/rural-development/publications Publications on rural development] ===Visualisations=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RCI/#?vis=border.typology&lang=en Border regions] {{Unit|topic=X_Regions}} [[Category:General and regional statistics|Territorial typologies manual – border regions]] [[Category:Regions and cities|Territorial typologies manual – border regions]] [[Category:Background_article|Territorial typologies manual – border regions]] [[Category:Regions and cities typologies|Territorial typologies manual – border regions]]

title: Territorial typologies manual - coastal areas
text:
This article on coastal areas forms part of Eurostat’s online publication, Methodological manual on territorial typologies: 2024 edition. This article forms part of [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]’s ''[[Territorial_typologies_manual|methodology manual on territorial typologies]]''. [[Glossary:Coastal area|Coastal areas]] are [[Glossary:Local administrative unit (LAU)|local administrative units (LAUs)]] that are bordering or close to a coastline. A coastline is defined as the line where land and water surfaces meet (border each other). Due to the existence of several measures (for example, the mean or median tides, high- or low-tides), the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] has adopted the harmonised use of the mean high tide (EC, 1999) in order to delineate EU coastlines. ===Classes for the typology and their conditions=== Coastal areas are a [[Glossary:Classification|classification]] based on the following 2 categories *'''coastal areas''' – LAUs that border the coastline or LAUs that have at least 50% of their surface area within a distance of 10 km from the coastline *'''non-coastal areas''' – LAUs that aren’t ‘coastal areas’; in other words, LAUs that don’t border the coastline and have less than 50% of their surface area within a distance of 10 km from the coastline. The main building blocks for the coastal areas classification are data for LAUs (such as municipalities). Coastal areas and non-coastal areas are classified according to the distance of each LAU to the coastline. The coastal areas typology is therefore atypical, insofar as it is based exclusively on topographical information, while other local typologies are constructed from statistics on [[Glossary:Population grid cell|population grids]]. If an LAU borders the coastline, it is by default coastal. If an LAU doesn’t border the coastline but it has at least 50% of its surface area within a distance of 10 km from the coastline, then it is also considered to be a coastal area. All remaining LAUs are considered as non-coastal areas. An example showing how the methodology is applied to the coastline of Belgium is shown in Map 1. The coastal areas typology is exhaustive, insofar as coastal and non-coastal areas together cover the whole of a territory. Note that among the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] countries, Czechia, Hungary, Luxembourg, Austria and Slovakia are landlocked and therefore don’t have any coastal areas; the same is true for the [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|European Free Trade Association (EFTA)]] countries of Liechtenstein and Switzerland and for the [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries]] of the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia and Serbia. [[Image:CH04M01_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Map 1: Coastal and non-coastal areas in Belgium
'' Source:'' Eurostat (GISCO) based on local administrative units 2021|alt=A map showing the coastal typology. Areas are shown as coastal areas bordering the coastline, other coastal areas with 50% or more of the surface area within 10 kilometres of the coastline, non-coastal areas with some but less than 50% of the surface area within 10 kilometres of the coastline, and non-coastal areas with no surface area within 10 kilometres of the coastline. Data for Belgium.]] '''''Further adjustments''''' There are a small number of special cases where the definition of a ‘coastline’ is treated on a case-by-case basis; for example, how to treat fjords, river estuaries or small islands. These country-specific exceptions to the underlying methodology have been agreed with the national statistical authorities of the EU countries or EFTA countries in question. [[Image:CH04M02_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Map 2: Special cases for the classification of coastal and non-coastal areas
'' Source:'' Eurostat (GISCO) based on local administrative units 2021|alt=Two maps showing special cases for the classifications of coastal and non-coastal areas. Examples are shown for a closed area of inland water separated from the sea by fjords and for an inland maritime port.]] '''Sea or inland water? An example for the Netherlands''' In the Netherlands, the IJsselmeer is a closed area of inland water separated from the sea by a man-made dam (dyke). When applied rigorously the line marking the buffer zone that is 10 km from the coastline should be drawn with reference to this dam (as applied in the classification). An alternative would be to draw the buffer with reference to the inland coastline around the IJsselmeer, whereby the result would be quite different. '''Fjords? An example for Norway''' The municipality of Årdal (shown by the beige line in the first part of Map 2) is located at the end of Sognefjord, which is the deepest and longest fjord in Norway. It is a major tourist destination due to the spectacular scenery along this stretch of water. Årdal, together with other LAUs along the fjord, is considered as a coastal area (despite being approximately 200 km from the open sea). '''Small islands and estuaries? An example for Germany''' In Germany, the city of Hamburg provides an example of an estuary (the Elbe river) and of some small islands. In this case, a relatively strict definition was applied, as a majority of the Elbe estuary is excluded from being classified as a coastal area although the city of Hamburg (shown by the beige line in the second part of Map 2) is considered as a coastal area. This may be attributed to Hamburg’s strong maritime influence (with easy access to its ports). Note in addition, that some small islands off the German coast (Neuwerk, Nigehörn and Scharhörn – also marked with a beige line) are administratively part of the city of Hamburg and, as such, the LAU of Hamburg borders the coastline. ===Links to other spatial concepts/typologies=== Coastal areas are a subgroup of [[Glossary:Coastal region|coastal regions]] (see [[Territorial typologies manual - coastal regions|Chapter 7]]). Within this context, it also worthwhile noting that the EU’s outermost regions – principally islands and archipelagos in the Caribbean, the Western Atlantic and Indian Ocean – are largely composed of coastal areas (except Guyane). ===Results=== Using the above definition, and on the basis of data for reference year 2021, there were 8 947 LAUs in the EU that were considered to be coastal areas (4 932 directly bordering the sea and a further 4 015 that weren't bordering the sea but had at least 50% of their surface area within 10 km of the sea). As such, almost 10% of all LAUs in the EU were coastal areas, a share that ranged – among those EU countries with a coastline – from 0.5% in Romania to 100.0% in Malta (see Figure 1). [[Image:CH04F01_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 1: Distribution of local administrative units between coastal and non-coastal areas
(%)
'' Source:'' Eurostat, based on local administrative units 2021|alt=A stacked column chart showing the distribution of local administrative units between coastal and non-coastal areas. Data are for the EU, EU countries and EFTA countries.]] A correspondence table between coastal/non-coastal areas and LAUs is available on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/nuts/local-administrative-units Eurostat’s thematic page]. Map 3 provides an overview of the final classification of coastal and non-coastal areas for 6 sea basins that border the EU: the Baltic Sea, the North Sea, the North-East Atlantic Ocean, the Mediterranean Sea, the Black Sea and the EU’s outermost regions. [[Image:CH04M03_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Map 3: Coastal areas
'' Source:'' Eurostat (GISCO) based on local administrative units 2021|alt=A categorical map showing coastal and non-coastal areas. Data are for EU and EFTA countries]] ===Changes to the typology over time=== The coastal areas classification should be updated to reflect any changes in LAU boundaries. The list of LAUs is updated on an annual basis *information relating to any changes to the boundaries or structure of LAUs should be communicated by EU countries to the European Commission (Eurostat) within the first 6 months of each calendar year, with reference to 31 December of the previous year *Eurostat publishes a revised list of LAUs before the end of the same year. Once geodata for the new LAU breakdowns become available in late autumn of each year, Eurostat updates the coastal area typology in the LAU list. ===Further information=== '''Glossary entry''' [[Glossary:Coastal area|Coastal area]] '''Detailed methodology''' [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/coastal-island-outermost-regions/methodology Coastal areas – methodology] '''Dedicated section''' [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/coastal-island-outermost-regions/information-data Coastal, island and outermost regions] ===Published indicators=== Tourism statistics for coastal and non-coastal areas have been collected by Eurostat since the 2012 reference year. The legal basis for the collection of this data is [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32011R0692 Regulation (EU) No 692/2011]. '''Database''' Eurostat’s website presents statistics for coastal and non-coastal areas. They are available [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/coastal-island-outermost-regions/database here]. ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/coastal-island-outermost-regions/database Coastal, island and outermost regions (coast)] ===Dedicated section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/coastal-island-outermost-regions/information-data Coastal, island and outermost regions – information on data] ===Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/coastal-island-outermost-regions/methodology Coastal, island and outermost regions – methodology] ===Legislation=== *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32011R0692 Regulation (EU) No 692/2011] – European statistics on tourism {{Unit|topic=X_Regions}} [[Category:Background_article|Territorial typologies manual – coastal areas]] [[Category:Regions_and_cities|Territorial typologies manual – coastal areas]] [[Category:Regions and cities typologies|Territorial typologies manual – coastal areas]]

title: Territorial typologies manual - coastal regions
text:
This article on coastal regions forms part of Eurostat’s online publication, Methodological manual on territorial typologies: 2024 edition. This article forms part of [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]’s ''[[Territorial_typologies_manual|methodology manual on territorial typologies]]''. The [[Glossary:Coastal region|coastal]] typology is applied at [[Glossary:Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (NUTS)|NUTS]] level 3. It identifies coastal regions in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] as having a border with a coastline or having more than half their population within 50 km of the coastline. Additionally, the NUTS level 3 region of Hamburg has been identified as coastal due to its strong maritime influence. ===Classes for the typology and their conditions=== '''Details of the typology''' The basic coastal typology is a [[Glossary:Classification|classification]] with the following 2 categories *coastal regions *non-coastal regions (those regions that aren’t defined as coastal regions). Coastal regions can also be classified according to the sea basin in which they are located. A sea basin is a geographical entity composed of a sea/ocean and the coastal region (land basin) that borders the sea/ocean/coastline. At an aggregated level, the following sea basins may be identified for EU regions *Baltic Sea *North Sea *North-East Atlantic Ocean *Mediterranean Sea *Black Sea *outermost regions. '''Methodology for the typology''' Coastal regions are NUTS level 3 regions in the EU, defined according to 1 of the following 3 criteria *any NUTS level 3 region with a '''sea border''' (coastline) *any NUTS level 3 region that has '''more than half of its population within 50 km of the coastline''', based on population data for 1 km² [[Glossary:Population grid cell|grid cells]] *the NUTS level 3 region for '''Hamburg''' in Germany. ''Case 1: regions with a sea border (coastline)'' The 1st of these criteria is self-explanatory. There are 22 EU countries that have a coastline and therefore also have coastal regions, while Czechia, Luxembourg, Hungary, Austria and Slovakia are landlocked countries and are therefore exclusively composed of non-coastal regions. ''Case 2: regions with more than 50% of their population within 50 km of the coastline'' This criterion requires 2 sources of information *the number of inhabitants living in 1 km² grid cells that are within 50 km of the coastline (A) – more information on population grid statistics is provided in the [[Territorial typologies manual - introduction|introductory chapter]] *the number of inhabitants living in each NUTS level 3 region (B). This information is used to compute the share of the total population in each NUTS level 3 region that lives within 50 km of the coastline ((A/B)*100). All regions that have shares that are greater than 50% are classified as coastal regions. ''Case 3: the region is Hamburg'' Although Hamburg (NUTS level 3 code DE600) is a significant distance from the sea, it is also considered as a coastal region given its strong maritime influence (with easy access for large ships down the river Elbe to its ports) and the fact that some small islands off the German coast – Neuwerk, Nigehörn and Scharhörn – are administratively part of the city of Hamburg and so it may said to border directly onto the sea. [[Image:CH07F01_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 1: Coastal regions typology – an example for Belgium, France and the Netherlands
'' Source:'' Eurostat (GISCO) based on GEOSTAT population grid 2011 and NUTS 2016|alt=A pair of maps comparing population density based on the GEOSTAT population grid and the coastal regions typology. In the first map, data are shown as the number of inhabitants per square kilometre. In the second map, regions are shown as coastal regions bordering the coastline, coastal regions where at least 50% of the population are within 50 kilometres of the coastline, non-coastal regions where some but less than 50% of the population are within 50 kilometres of the coastline and non-coastal regions where none of the population are within 50 kilometres of the coastline. Data for Belgium, France and the Netherlands.]] ===Links to other spatial concepts/typologies=== There is a close link between the typologies for coastal regions and [[Glossary:Coastal area|coastal areas]] (see [[Territorial typologies manual - coastal areas|Chapter 4]]). The latter are considered to be a subgroup of coastal regions: as such, any NUTS level 3 region that is classified as a non-coastal region can’t (by definition) have any coastal areas. ===Results=== Based on the above definitions, there are 341 NUTS 2024 coastal regions in the EU. Of these, 297 regions have a coastline, while 44 regions have no coastline but more than 50% of their population living within 50 km of the sea. For all EU countries, Iceland, Norway, Montenegro, Albania and Turkey, a list of coastal regions is available [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/coastal-island-outermost-regions/methodology here]. Map 1 provides an overview of the final classification for the coastal typology with a division between coastal and non-coastal regions; the former are split between those regions that have a coastline and those which have more than 50% of their population within 50 km of the sea. [[Image:CH07M01_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Map 1: Coastal typology
'' Source:'' Eurostat (GISCO) based on census population grid 2021 and NUTS 2024|alt=A categorical map showing the coastal regions typology. Regions are shown as coastal regions bordering the coastline, coastal regions where at least 50% of the population live within 50 kilometres of the coastline, and non-coastal regions. Data for EU and EFTA countries.]] As noted above, each coastal region can be assigned to a sea basin. Map 2 provides an overview of the main sea basins within the EU, [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate countries]]. [[Image:CH07M02_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Map 2: Coastal typology by sea basin
'' Source:'' Eurostat (GISCO) based on NUTS 2024|alt=A categorical map showing the coastal regions within each sea basin. Regions are shown as coastal regions bordering the coastlines of the Baltic, North, Mediterranean and Black Seas, as well as the North-East Atlantic Ocean and coastal regions of outermost regions. Data for EU, EFTA and candidate countries.]] ===Changes to the typology over time=== The coastal typology was developed by Eurostat in consultation with other services of the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]]. '''''Changes over time that impact on the classification''''' The coastal regions classification should be updated to reflect any changes to the underlying sources of information that are used in its compilation. As such, the classification may be updated to reflect changes to population distributions for 1 km² grid cells or changes in the NUTS classification. The frequency of such updates varies according to the source of information. Changes to the coastal regions classification resulting from a revision of population distributions for 1 km² grid cells are less common and these may be expected every 10 years. The latest major update of the population grid took place for the 2021 reference year. The NUTS Regulation specifies that the classification of regions should remain stable for a period of at least 3 years; the most recent updates were for NUTS 2016, NUTS 2021 and NUTS 2024. After each revision of the NUTS classification, population grid statistics should be re-assessed in order to (re-)compute the share of each NUTS level 3 region living within 50 km of the sea. '''''Recent and future developments''''' A [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2018/1799/oj regulation to implement the population and housing census for 2021] established a statistical action in relation to geocoded data for a 1 km² population grid. As well as information for annual counts of populations, it also envisaged more detailed analyses concerning population disaggregated by sex, population disaggregated by age, number of employed people, population disaggregated by place of birth and population disaggregated by usual place of residence 1 year prior to the census. Eurostat is also discussing post-2021 census developments with national statistical authorities. It is hoped that the [[Glossary:European statistical system (ESS)|European statistical system (ESS)]] will agree to produce – from the mid-2020s onwards – annual counts of populations (based on the usual place of residence) for a 1 km² grid, with data to be made available within 12 months of the reference period, giving the opportunity for more frequent updates. The European Commission’s Directorate-General for Maritime Affairs and Fisheries intends to incorporate a coastal/non-coastal layer into the [https://ec.europa.eu/maritimeaffairs/atlas/maritime_atlas/ European Atlas of the Seas] showing the most important socioeconomic indicators that are related to the blue economy. The next update of the NUTS classification is planned for 2028. ===Further information=== '''Glossary entry''' [[Glossary:Coastal_region|Coastal region]] '''Detailed methodology''' [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/coastal-island-outermost-regions/methodology Coastal, island and outermost regions] '''Correspondence for NUTS regions''' [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/coastal-island-outermost-regions/methodology Correspondence table for coastal, island and outermost regions] ===Published indicators=== A variety of different statistical surveys collect data for NUTS level 3 regions and this information may be used to calculate data for coastal and non-coastal regions. This process involves aggregating the data for NUTS level 3 regions to compute a total or an average for all coastal (and non-coastal) regions within a territory (for example an EU country, or the EU as a whole). '''Visualisation tools''' Eurostat publishes data for the coastal typology through [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RCI/#?vis=maritime.gen&lang=en Regions and cities illustrated]. '''Database''' Eurostat’s website provides information for a wide variety of indicators for the coastal typology. These statistics are available for the following statistical domains: demography, population projections, the labour market, crimes recorded by the police, economic accounts, business demography, intellectual property rights and transport. They are available [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/coastal-island-outermost-regions/database here]. ===Examples=== [[Rural_Europe|Rural Europe – various statistics on coastal regions]] [[Urban_Europe|Urban Europe – various statistics on coastal regions]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/coastal-island-outermost-regions/database Coastal, Island and Outermost Regions] ===Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/coastal-island-outermost-regions/methodology Coastal, island and outermost regions] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/coastal-island-outermost-regions/methodology Correspondence table for coastal, island and outermost regions] ===Visualisations=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RCI/#?vis=maritime.gen&lang=en Regions and cities illustrated] {{Unit|topic=X_Regions}} [[Category:Background_article|Territorial typologies manual – coastal regions]] [[Category:Regions_and_cities|Territorial typologies manual – coastal regions]] [[Category:Regions and cities typologies|Territorial typologies manual – coastal regions]]

title: Territorial typologies manual - cluster types
text:
This article on cluster types forms part of Eurostat’s online publication, Methodological manual on territorial typologies: 2024 edition. This article forms part of [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]’s ''[[Territorial_typologies_manual|methodology manual on territorial typologies]]''. Cluster types are groups of 1 km² [[Glossary:Population grid cell|population grid cells]] that share similar characteristics, based on a combination of their population density and geographical [[Glossary:Contiguous grid cells|contiguity]]. ===Classes for the typology and their conditions=== '''Details of the typology''' The following 3 types of clusters may be identified *[[Glossary:Urban centre|urban centre (high-density cluster)]]: a cluster of contiguous grid cells of 1 km² (excluding diagonals) with a population density of at least 1 500 inhabitants per km² and collectively a minimum population of 50 000 inhabitants after gap-filling *[[Glossary:Urban cluster|urban cluster (moderate-density cluster)]]: a cluster of contiguous grid cells of 1 km² (including diagonals) with a population density of at least 300 inhabitants per km² and a minimum population of 5 000 inhabitants *[[Glossary:Rural grid cell|rural grid cells]]: grid cells that aren’t identified as urban centres or as urban clusters. '''Methodology for the typology''' Cluster types may be identified in relation to the total population living in 1 km² grid cells; note, the [[Territorial typologies manual - introduction|introductory chapter]] provides a more detailed explanation of the population grid. The vast majority of the geographical territory of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] (continental Europe, the Açores, Canarias and Madeira) is covered by the GEOSTAT population grid, while the remaining outermost regions are covered by a [https://ghsl.jrc.ec.europa.eu/datasets.php global population grid] produced by the [https://commission.europa.eu/about-european-commission/departments-and-executive-agencies/joint-research-centre_en Joint Research Centre (JRC)] of the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]]. Each cluster type is identified by classifying 1 km² population grid cells according to characteristics that are based on their total population and population density. Grid cells are classified according to the steps detailed below (note that a cell may belong to an urban centre and an urban cluster as their definitions aren’t mutually exclusive). '''Understanding contiguous cells''' Before looking at the identification of the 3 cluster types, it is necessary to understand the concept of contiguous cells. Figure 1 shows an array of 9 grid cells, with the focus on the central cell which is surrounded by 8 others, numbered 1 to 8. [[Image:CH01F01_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 1: Contiguous grid cells|alt=A diagram of a 3 by 3 statistical grid illustrating the concept of contiguous grid cells.]] 2 types of contiguous grid cells can be identified *a '''narrower definition excluding diagonals''': all cells that touch each other excluding those cells that only touch each other on a diagonal; only cells numbered 2, 4, 5 and 7 are contiguous to the central cell in Figure 1 according to this narrower definition, which is used for identifying urban centres (high-density clusters) *a '''broad definition including diagonals''': all cells that touch each other in any way, including cells that are linked only on a diagonal; all cells numbered 1 to 8 are contiguous to the central cell in Figure 1 according to this broader definition, which is used for identifying urban (moderate-density) clusters. '''''1. Identifying urban centres (high-density clusters)''''' The identification of urban centres (high-density clusters) is done in 2 steps: to begin, all cells with a population density of at least 1 500 inhabitants per km² are plotted (dark blue shading in Figure 2); secondly, groups of contiguous grid cells are identified (groups G1 and G2 in Figure 2). When identifying urban centres diagonal contiguity is excluded. As such, in the example of Figure 2, cells C2 and D3 aren’t considered as contiguous; rather, they are each part of different groups (G1 and G2). [[Image:CH01F02_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 2: Contiguous groups for urban centres|alt=A diagram of a pair of 4 by 6 statistical grids. Each grid cell is one square kilometre. The first grid has aggregated population data for each cell, distinguishing cells with a population greater than or equal to one thousand five hundred inhabitants per square kilometre. Based on the first grid, the second identifies groups of contiguous cells which each have a population greater than or equal to one thousand five hundred inhabitants per square kilometre.]] In a second step, each group of contiguous grid cells is analysed in relation to its total number of inhabitants and only those groups of contiguous cells with 50 000 inhabitants or more are selected (see Figure 3). [[Image:CH01F03_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 3: Identifying urban centres|alt=A diagram of a pair of 4 by 6 statistical grids. Each grid cell is one square kilometre. The first grid has aggregated population data for groups of contiguous cells which each have a population greater than or equal to one thousand five hundred inhabitants per square kilometre. Based on the first grid, the second identifies urban centres.]] The identification of urban centres involves a third step, which is taken to fill gaps and smooth borders. This is done by applying an iterative majority rule: if 5 or more of the (8) cells surrounding a particular cell belong to the same unique urban centre, then that cell is also considered to belong to the same urban centre; this process is repeated (iteratively) until no more cells are added. Note that the criterion for gap-filling includes cells that are linked only on a diagonal. For example, cell B2 on the left-hand side of Figure 3 has 7 of its 8 surrounding cells that belong to the same urban centre. This cell should therefore subsequently be added to the urban centre to smooth borders (as shown on the right-hand side of Figure 3). '''''2. Identifying urban clusters (moderate-density clusters)''''' The method used to identify urban clusters (moderate-density clusters) is similar to that used for urban centres (high-density clusters). Rather than using a threshold of at least 1 500 inhabitants per km², the identification of urban clusters is based on grid cells with a population density of at least 300 inhabitants per km² (see Figure 4). [[Image:CH01F04_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 4: Contiguous groups for urban clusters|alt=A diagram of a pair of 4 by 6 statistical grids. Each grid cell is one square kilometre. The first grid has aggregated population data for each cell, distinguishing cells with a population greater than or equal to 300 inhabitants per square kilometre. Based on the first grid, the second identifies groups of contiguous cells which each have a population greater than or equal to 300 inhabitants per square kilometre.]] The identification of urban clusters is done in 2 steps: to begin, all cells with a population density of at least 300 inhabitants per km² are plotted (light blue shading in Figure 4); secondly, groups of contiguous grid cells are identified (groups G1 and G2 in Figure 4); note that contiguous grid cells may include cells that are linked only on a diagonal – as shown, for example, by cell C2. [[Image:CH01F05_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 5: Identifying urban clusters|alt=A diagram of a pair of 4 by 6 statistical grids. Each grid cell is one square kilometre. The first grid has aggregated population data for groups of contiguous cells which each have a population greater than or equal to 300 inhabitants per square kilometre. Based on the first grid, the second identifies urban clusters.]] Thereafter, each group of contiguous grid cells is analysed in relation to its number of inhabitants and those groups of contiguous cells with 5 000 inhabitants or more are selected; these are urban clusters. Continuing with the same example, Group G1 is considered an urban cluster as it has a population of 7 000 inhabitants, as shown on the right-hand side of Figure 5, while G2 isn’t an urban cluster as its population is only 3 050 inhabitants. [[Image:CH01F06_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 6: Schematic overview identifying urban centres and urban clusters
'' Source:'' Eurostat, JRC and European Commission, Directorate-General Regional and Urban Policy and Directorate-General Agriculture and Regional Development|alt=A set of three maps. the first identifies grid cells (of one square kilometre) which have a population greater than or equal to 300 inhabitants per square kilometre. The second identifies urban clusters and the third identifies urban centres within the urban clusters.]] '''''3. Identifying rural grid cells''''' Rural grid cells are those cells that aren’t identified as urban centres or as urban clusters. The majority of rural grid cells have a population density that is less than 300 inhabitants per km², although this isn’t necessarily the case. Some rural grid cells may have a higher number of inhabitants if they don’t form part of a cluster that meets the criteria for an urban centre or an urban cluster. [[Image:CH01F07_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 7: Identifying rural grid cells|alt=A diagram of a pair of 4 by 6 statistical grids. Each grid cell is one square kilometre. The first grid has aggregated population data for each cell, distinguishing cells with a population greater than or equal to 300 inhabitants per square kilometre. Based on the first grid, the second identifies groups of contiguous cells which each have a population greater than or equal to 300 inhabitants per square kilometre.]] In Figure 7, cells A3, B4 and F1 each meet the population criterion for an urban centre (at least 1 500 inhabitants per km²), while cells B3, C2 and E1 each meet the population criterion for an urban cluster (at least 300 inhabitants per km²). Each group of contiguous grid cells (groups G1 and G2 in the right-hand side of Figure 7) may be analysed in relation to their total number of inhabitants and those groups of contiguous cells with 5 000 inhabitants or more are selected. [[Image:CH01F08_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 8: Identifying rural grid cells|alt=A diagram of a pair of 4 by 6 statistical grids. Each grid cell is one square kilometre. The first grid has aggregated population data for groups of contiguous cells which each have a population greater than or equal to 300 inhabitants per square kilometre. Based on the first grid, the second identifies rural grid cells.]] In Figure 8, neither group G1 with a total population of 3 900 inhabitants, nor group G2 with a total population of 2 650 inhabitants reaches the population threshold for an urban cluster. As such, each cell in these 2 groups is classified as a rural grid cell, as shown on the right-hand side of Figure 8, despite some cells having populations that are higher than the thresholds for urban centres and/or urban clusters. Note also, as mentioned above, that it is possible for grid cells with a population density of less than 300 inhabitants per km² to be classified as part of an urban centre, due to gap-filling. ===Special grid cells=== The identification of different cluster types is generally a relatively simple operation for those cases where grid cells cover the land. However, the population count for a 1 km² cell is more complex if it covers both land and sea (or ocean). In such a case, it is necessary to first identify the proportion of the grid cell that covers land. This can be calculated using the CORINE land cover raster dataset. For example, if a grid cell has a population count of 100, and 50% of that cell covers the sea, then the calculation would be 100/0.5, resulting in a population density of 200 inhabitants per km². In the case that the whole of a cell covers the sea, it isn’t possible to divide by zero and therefore the population density is set to the population count of the cell. These kinds of ‘cell modifications’ are particularly important when the population density of an individual cell can impact the identification of contiguous grid cells. As discussed earlier, if a cell can potentially form part of a group of contiguous grid cells that constitute a high-density cluster, then it has to have a population density of at least 1 500 inhabitants per km² and the group of contiguous cells has to have a total population of at least 50 000 inhabitants. Figure 9 provides an example for a grid cell where 45% of its area covers land and 55% covers the sea. Let’s assume the total number of inhabitants of the cell is 1 200. Generally, this would mean the population density is 1 200 inhabitants per km². However, assuming that all of the inhabitants live on land, then the actual population density can be computed as 1 200/0.45 = 2 667 inhabitants per km². As a result, the grid cell in this example could potentially form part of a group of contiguous grid cells in a high-density cluster (urban centre), as the modification taking into consideration the land and sea areas results in the population density rising above the 1 500 inhabitants per km² threshold. [[Image:CH01F09_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 9: Calculation of the population density for a 1 km² grid cell that covers land and sea|alt=A diagram showing a grid cell of one square kilometre. The grid cell is split into two parts: 45 per cent of its area covers land and 55 per cent covers the sea.]] ===Links to other spatial concepts/typologies=== Cluster types are used as a basis for the following local territorial typologies *the [[Glossary:Degree of urbanisation|degree of urbanisation]] (see [[Territorial typologies manual - degree of urbanisation|Chapter 2]] for more information), to identify cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Commuting flows may then be used to identify *the commuting zones of cities and hence their [[Glossary:Functional urban area|functional urban areas]] (see [[Territorial typologies manual - cities, commuting zones and functional urban areas|Chapter 3]] for more information). Cluster types are used as a basis for the following regional territorial typologies *the [[Glossary:Urban-rural typology|urban-rural typology]] (see [[Territorial typologies manual - urban-rural typology|Chapter 5]]), to identify predominantly urban regions, intermediate regions and predominantly rural regions. Functional urban areas may then be used as a basis for the following regional territorial typology *the [[Glossary:Urban-rural typology|metropolitan typology]] (see [[Territorial typologies manual - metropolitan regions|Chapter 6]]), to identify metropolitan and non-metropolitan regions. ===An example=== Map 1 provides an overview of the final classification of cluster types for a 1 km² population grid (as established in 2021). It shows that some of the largest concentrations of urban centres are located in western Germany and the Benelux countries. The information presented in Map 1 may be compared with Map 11 (in the [[Territorial typologies manual - introduction|introductory chapter]]) which shows the population density of individual 1 km² grid cells. While aggregating information for cluster types (as done for Map 1) allows some of the noise to be removed from the map, thereby highlighting more clearly the main urban centres in the EU, it is also apparent that a considerable amount of information may be lost when aggregating individual grid cells to larger clusters. [[Image:CH01M01_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Map 1: Cluster types based on 1 km² grid cells
'' Source:'' Eurostat (GISCO) based on census population grid 2021|alt=A map showing cluster types. Areas are shown as urban centres, urban clusters or rural grid cells. Data for the EU and EFTA countries. Annual data for 2021.]] ===Further information=== '''Glossary entries''' [[Glossary:Urban centre|Urban centre (high-density cluster)]] [[Glossary:Urban cluster|Urban cluster (moderate-density cluster)]] [[Glossary:Rural grid cell|Rural grid cell]] ===Dedicated section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/gisco/overview GISCO: geographical information and maps] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/gisco/geodata/population-distribution/clusters GISCO: geographical information and maps – clusters] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/gisco/geodata/population-distribution/geostat GISCO: geographical information and maps – GEOSTAT] ===Visualisations=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RCI/#?vis=degurb.gen&lang=en Regions and cities illustrated] *[https://ec.europa.eu/statistical-atlas/viewer/? Statistical atlas] ===External links=== *[http://ghsl.jrc.ec.europa.eu/ghs_pop.php Global population grid] – produced by the Joint Research Centre (JRC) of the European Commission. *[https://commission.europa.eu/about-european-commission/departments-and-executive-agencies/joint-research-centre_en Joint Research Centre (JRC)] of the European Commission {{Unit|topic=X_Regions}} [[Category:Background_article|Territorial typologies manual – cluster types]] [[Category:Regions_and_cities|Territorial typologies manual – cluster types]] [[Category:Regions and cities typologies|Territorial typologies manual – cluster types]]

title: Territorial typologies manual - cities, commuting zones and functional urban areas
text:
This article on cities, commuting zones and functional urban areas forms part of Eurostat’s online publication, Methodological manual on territorial typologies: 2024 edition. This article forms part of [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]’s ''[[Territorial_typologies_manual|methodology manual on territorial typologies]]''. A [[Glossary:City|city]] is a [[Glossary:Local administrative unit (LAU)|local administrative unit (LAU)]] where a majority of the population lives in an [[Glossary:Urban centre|urban centre]] of at least 50 000 inhabitants. A [[Glossary:Commuting zone|commuting zone]] contains the surrounding travel-to-work areas of a city where at least 15% of employed residents are working in the city. A [[Glossary:Functional urban area|functional urban area]] consists of a city and its commuting zone. Functional urban areas therefore consist of a ''densely inhabited city and a less densely populated commuting zone whose labour market is highly integrated with the city'' (OECD, 2012). ===Classes for the typology and their conditions=== '''Details of the typology''' Functional urban areas are a [[Glossary:Classification|classification]] based on the following 2 categories *'''cities''', otherwise referred to as densely populated areas *'''commuting zones'''. Note these 2 categories aren’t exhaustive; they don’t cover the whole territory. '''Methodology for the typology''' The starting point for defining a city and its commuting zone is to consider what features form a city. The definition used builds on the idea of a city as a place with a relatively high spatial concentration of population. The main building blocks are data for 1 km² [[Glossary:Population grid cell|population grid cells]]. Each grid cell has the same shape and surface area, thereby avoiding distortions caused by using units varying in size. This is a considerable advantage when compared with alternative approaches such as those based on the use of administrative data for LAUs (such as municipalities). '''''Step 1: classifying grid cells''''' These 1 km² population grid cells are plotted in relation to their neighbouring cells to identify cluster types; note this is the same process that is used for the [[Glossary:Degree of urbanisation|degree of urbanisation]] typology (see [[Territorial typologies manual - degree of urbanisation|Chapter 2]]). The cluster type used to identify cities is that of *[[Glossary:Urban centre|urban centres]] (or high-density clusters): a cluster of non-diagonal contiguous grid cells (in other words, excluding those cells with only touching corners) having a population density of at least 1 500 inhabitants per km² and collectively at least 50 000 inhabitants after gap-filling. For a more detailed explanation of how densely populated grid cells are classified to urban centres (including the gap-filling process), see [[Territorial typologies manual - cluster types|Chapter 1]]. '''''Step 2: classifying cities''''' The typology for functional urban areas is established at the level of local administrative units (LAUs). Once all grid cells have been classified and urban centres identified, the next step concerns overlaying these results onto LAUs, to identify cities *'''cities''' (densely populated areas) – where at least 50% of the population lives in 1 or more urban centres (note this definition is identical to that used for the degree of urbanisation typology). A city is defined in an identical way to the approach adopted for the degree of urbanisation (see [[Territorial typologies manual - degree of urbanisation|Chapter 2]]) when identifying densely populated areas (and thereafter cities). In both of these typologies, cities are covered by the exact same local administrative units. There is, however, a difference in the coding of the 2 concepts. The degree of urbanisation classifies all local administrative units in 3 groups, which means that all the densely populated areas or all cities get the same code. Each city is assigned an individual code, which allows LAUs for each city to be grouped and classified (by population size). In simple terms, the degree of urbanisation typology results in data that may be analysed at an aggregate level for all of the cities in a specific country, while the functional urban area definition allows data to be analysed at the level of each individual city. In most cases, defining a city is a simple task, insofar as the city consists of a single administrative unit that covers the entire urban centre. However, in some cases the relationship between LAUs and urban centres may be more complex – these are examined below. '''The urban centre is much bigger than the ‘central’ administrative unit''' In some cases, the urban centre may stretch far beyond the boundaries of the ‘central’ LAU (or municipality). This is often the case with large capital cities that have outgrown the small LAU that carries their name. To strictly define the city as the central LAU would create a problem of ‘under-bounding’, in other words the city would be too small relative to its urban centre and a large share of the population living in the urban centre would inhabit areas outside the city. As the methodological definition of a city states that all LAUs with at least 50% of their population in the urban centre are part of the city, the boundaries of the city are extended to include these units (in order to better capture and represent all urban centres). Although, particularly in urbanised areas, morphological definitions typically reflect reality in terms of actual urban characteristics and human activities better than administrative definitions, the latter are often more firmly anchored in people’s minds and are more often used as reference geographies in research, urban planning and policymaking. However, misunderstandings can arise when there is uncertainty about the geographical reference area under consideration. For example, the morphological definition of the city of Paris, based on the degree of urbanisation, includes 295 municipalities with a population of around 10 million inhabitants. However, the administrative and conventional definition of the city of Paris only includes the municipality of Paris with its 20 arrondissements and a population of around 2.2 million inhabitants. In order to draw attention to this discrepancy and to make the spatial references of city statistics published by Eurostat transparent, the attribute (greater city) has been added to all city names for which the morphological definition of the city doesn’t correspond to its conventional, administrative definition. It is important to note that in contrast to the territorial classification used for Urban Audit up until 2017, ‘greater city’ is no longer used as a spatial concept (see the ‘Historical developments’ section below). Rather, a ‘greater city’ is an attribute that is intended to serve the purpose of better understanding geographical references in European city statistics. Eurostat has therefore modified the coding system for city statistics such that the default level of analysis is the harmonised code (‘C’) – composed of greater cities and all other cities (for which no information is available at the level of the greater city). '''The urban centre covers 2 (or more) distinct cities''' Some urban centres cover more than 1 (distinct) city. This can be due to inaccuracies in the population grid or because 2 (or more) cities have almost grown together – but remain functionally distinct. In such cases, a national statistical authority may choose to create multiple cities to cover the single urban centre. Note that when multiple cities are defined as covering a single urban centre, each of the (distinct) cities should have a population of at least 50 000 inhabitants. Ulm in Germany (see Figure 1) provides an example: it has an urban centre that is composed of 2 cities, namely those of Ulm and Neu-Ulm, divided by the river Danube. This single urban centre is considerably larger in size than the administrative boundaries of the city of Ulm. Note: these distinct cities – in this case, Ulm and Neu-Ulm – may belong to the same (single) commuting zone if 1 of the cities has a flow of commuters to the other city that reaches at least 15%. [[Image:CH03F01_TT2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 1: High-density grid cells, urban centres and city boundaries – an example for Ulm
'' Source:'' Eurostat|alt=A series of four maps showing high-density grid cells, urban centres and city boundaries. Data are for Ulm and Neu-Ulm in Germany.]] '''A city includes more than 1 urban centre''' This situation is usually caused by topographical features, such as a wide river/estuary or a mountain ridge that may lead to an urban centre being split into 2 unique parts; this occurs, for example, in Tromsø (Norway). In such a case, the city is defined to cover both urban centres. '''The administrative unit is located between 2 urban centres''' If an LAU has a share of its population in 2 urban centres, the unit should belong to the urban centre that captures the largest share of its population; even if that share is below 50%. For example, if an LAU has 40% of its population in urban centre A and 20% of its population in urban centre B, then it should be classified as part of the city that represents urban centre A. '''Cross-border cities''' The definition used for cross-border cities follows and complies with the definition used for cities as laid out in the degree of urbanisation methodology. In the case of cross-border cities, the urban centre (cross-border cluster) need to extend across national borders. As for cities in general, the building block used to identify a cross-border city is a 1 km² population grid, where each grid cell has the same shape and surface area. A city is composed of small spatial units – local administrative units (LAUs) where a majority of the population lives in an urban centre. An urban centre is a cluster of non-diagonal contiguous grid cells of 1 km² with a population density of at least 1 500 inhabitants per km² and collectively at least 50 000 inhabitants after gap-filling. Adjustments can be made for special cases that concern LAUs that form part of a cross-border city. If for instance, the cross-border urban centre extends to an LAU that isn’t considered part of the city definition, that LAU may nevertheless be excluded from the cross-border city.
