'''''Recent and future developments''''' A [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2018/1799/oj regulation to implement the population and housing census for 2021] established a statistical action in relation to geocoded data for 1 km² population grid. As well as information for annual counts of populations, it also envisaged more detailed analyses concerning population disaggregated by sex, population disaggregated by age, number of employed people, population disaggregated by place of birth and population disaggregated by usual place of residence 1 year prior to the census. Eurostat is also discussing post-2021 census developments with national statistical authorities. It is hoped that the [[Glossary:European statistical system (ESS)|European statistical system (ESS)]] will agree to produce – from the mid-2020s onwards – annual counts of populations (based on the usual place of residence) for a 1 km² grid, with data to be made available within 12 months of the reference period, giving the opportunity for more frequent updates. The next update of the NUTS classification is planned for 2028. ===Further information=== '''Glossary entries''' [[Glossary:Urban-rural typology|Urban-rural_typology]] [[Glossary:Predominantly urban region|Predominantly_urban_region]] [[Glossary:Intermediate region|Intermediate_region]] [[Glossary:Predominantly rural region|Predominantly_rural_region]] '''Detailed methodology''' [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/rural-development/methodology Rural development] '''Correspondence for NUTS regions''' [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/rural-development/methodology Correspondence table for urban-rural typology] ===Published indicators=== A variety of different statistical surveys collect data for NUTS level 3 regions and this information may be used to calculate data for the 3 different categories in the urban-rural typology. This process involves aggregating the data for NUTS level 3 regions to compute a total or an average for all predominantly rural regions, intermediate regions, or predominantly urban regions within a territory (for example an EU country, or the EU as a whole). '''Visualisation tools''' Eurostat publishes data for the urban-rural typology through [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RCI/#?vis=urbanrural.urb_typology&lang=en Regions and cities illustrated]. The urban-rural classification may be viewed through Eurostat’s [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/gisco/gisco-activities/statistical-atlas Statistical atlas]. '''Database''' Eurostat’s website provides information for a wide variety of indicators for the urban-rural typology. These statistics are available for the following statistical domains: demography, population projections, the labour market, crimes recorded by the police, economic accounts, business demography, intellectual property rights and transport. They are available [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/rural-development/database here]. ===Examples=== [[Urban-rural_Europe_-_population_projections|Statistics by urban-rural typology – Rural Europe and Urban Europe – Population projections]] [[Urban-rural_Europe_-_economy|Statistics by urban-rural typology – Rural Europe and Urban Europe – Economy]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/rural-development/database Rural development] ===Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/rural-development/methodology Rural development] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/rural-development/methodology Correspondence table for urban-rural typology] ===Visualisations=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RCI/#?vis=urbanrural.urb_typology&lang=en Regions and cities illustrated] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/gisco/gisco-activities/statistical-atlas Statistical atlas] {{Unit|topic=X_Regions}} [[Category:Background_article|Territorial typologies manual – urban-rural typology]] [[Category:Regions_and_cities|Territorial typologies manual – urban-rural typology]] [[Category:Regions and cities typologies|Territorial typologies manual – urban-rural typology]]

title: Tertiary education statistics
text:
EU statistics are provided on tertiary education: students and graduates analysed by age, sex and fields of education, and teaching staff. Data extracted in May 2026 Planned article update: June 2027 In the EU, there were 19.1 million tertiary education students in 2024, of which 59% were studying for bachelor’s degrees. In 2024, 22% of tertiary education students in the EU were studying business, administration or law. Within the EU, 58% of all tertiary education graduates in 2024 were women. In all EU countries, more women graduated from tertiary education than men. In 2024, the most frequently awarded degrees in the EU were in the field of business, administration and law, accounting for a quarter of the total. This article presents statistics on [[International_Standard_Classification_of_Education_(ISCED)|tertiary education]] (levels 5 to 8 of the [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|International Standard Classification of Education – ISCED]]) in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] and forms part of an [[Education_and_training_in_the_EU_-_facts_and_figures|online publication]] on [[Glossary:Education|education]] and training in the EU. Tertiary education – provided by universities and other tertiary educational institutions – typically follows secondary schooling. It is considered to play an essential role in society, by fostering innovation, driving economic development and growth, and more generally improving the well-being of the population. Some European universities are among the most prestigious in the world. A relatively large number of students in tertiary education are internationally mobile and study abroad: an analysis of this phenomenon is available in a [[Learning_mobility_statistics|separate article]]. ===Participation by level=== [[Image:Number_of_tertiary_education_students_by_sex_and_level_of_education,_2024_(1 000)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Number of tertiary education students by sex and level of education, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7c355076-fa4b-41b6-9227-aa4e88b0532b?lang=en educ_uoe_enrt01])|alt=A table showing the number of tertiary education students by sex and level of education. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 1 presents data on the number of students in each of 4 [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|levels of tertiary education]]. Bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral levels of tertiary education are found in all EU countries, while short-cycle tertiary education, which is typically vocational (occupationally specific) and designed to prepare students for the labour market, is not part of the education system in Bulgaria, Estonia, Greece, Romania or Finland. In several other EU countries – namely Czechia, Germany, Croatia, Lithuania and Poland – short-cycle tertiary education accounts for less than 1.0% of the total number of tertiary students. In the [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU]], there were 19.1 million tertiary education students in 2024 (see Table 1). Germany – the most populous country in the EU – had 3.3 million tertiary education students, which was the highest number in the EU and equivalent to 17.2% of the EU total. France (15.1% of the total), Spain (12.8%) and Italy (12.1%) had the next largest shares of the EU’s tertiary student population. Among the 19.1 million tertiary education students in the EU *7.9% were following short-cycle tertiary courses *59.0% were studying for bachelor’s degrees *29.4% were studying for master’s degrees *3.8% were studying for doctoral degrees. Students of bachelor’s and master’s degrees accounted for 88.3% of the total number of tertiary students in the EU in 2024. The highest shares for these 2 levels of education were reported for Poland (98.5%), Bulgaria, Lithuania (both 97.4%), Croatia (96.9%), Italy (96.3%), Greece (96.1%) and Romania (96.0%). Notably lower shares were recorded for France (80.5%), Austria (79.1%), Latvia (78.3%), Ireland (77.9%), Luxembourg (77.5%) and – most notably – Spain (70.6%). Short-cycle tertiary courses were most common in Spain where they accounted for 25.3% of all tertiary students; they were also relatively common in Ireland, Latvia, France and Austria. Luxembourg, Cyprus, Austria and France were the only EU countries where fewer than 50% of all tertiary students were studying for bachelor’s degrees. Among EU countries, the highest share of tertiary students who were studying for bachelor’s degrees was 84.0% in Greece. Greece had the lowest share of tertiary students studying for master’s degrees in 2024, around an eighth (12.1%) of all tertiary students. This share was also below 20.0% in Ireland and Spain. By contrast, the highest shares were recorded in Cyprus (48.6%) and Croatia (40.5%). By far, the highest share of tertiary students studying for doctoral degrees in 2024 among the EU countries was recorded in Luxembourg (12.6%), with the next highest shares in Germany (6.3%) and Portugal (6.0%). In line with the fact that Germany had the highest total number of tertiary students among the EU countries, it also had, by far, the highest number of students studying for doctoral degrees (204 900) – see Table 1. This was more than twice the number of students studying for a doctoral degree in any of the other EU countries; the next highest counts were recorded in Spain (99 400) and France (69 600). Although France had the second highest total number of tertiary students among the EU countries, at 2.4% the share of students studying for doctoral degrees in France was the third lowest among the EU countries. The lowest shares of doctoral students in the total number of tertiary education students were observed in Poland (1.5%) and Italy (2.1%). ===Participation in tertiary education by sex=== In 2024, women accounted for 54.9% of all tertiary students in the EU. The share of women among tertiary students was *48.5% for those following short-cycle tertiary courses *54.3% for those studying for bachelor’s degrees *58.6% for those studying for master’s degrees *49.7% for those studying for doctoral degrees. As such, the majority of short-cycle tertiary and doctoral students were male, while relatively large majorities of bachelor’s and master’s students were female. In 2024, 60.7% of all tertiary students in Sweden were female, while the share was close to this level in Poland (60.1%) and Estonia (59.9%). Women were also in a majority among tertiary students in all of the other EU countries except for Greece (49.4% were female) and Ireland (49.0%). *For short-cycle courses, 10 of the 22 EU countries in which such courses exist had more female than male students. *For bachelor’s degrees, Greece, Germany and Cyprus were the only EU countries where there were more men than women studying at this educational level. The highest share of female students among those studying for bachelor’s degrees was recorded in Sweden (64.4%). *Among students studying for master’s degrees, women were in the majority in 2024 in all of the EU countries. The highest female shares were recorded in Cyprus and Poland, where women accounted for more than two thirds (69.6% and 68.4%, respectively) of the total number of students. *Women were in a majority among doctoral level students in 16 of the EU countries, despite the fact that men made up a majority (50.3%) of doctoral students in the EU as a whole. The highest share for women was in Latvia (63.7%), while the highest share for men was in Luxembourg (55.7%). ===Participation in tertiary education by field of education=== [[Image:Distribution_of_tertiary_education_students_by_broad_field_and_sex,_EU,_2024_(%)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Distribution of tertiary education students by broad field and sex, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fdea1c6c-48a3-43ed-a4fc-6661d3033e83?lang=en educ_uoe_enrt03])|alt=A double bar chart showing the percentage distribution of tertiary education students in the EU by broad field and sex. The 12 selected broad fields of study each have two bars comparing the shares of male and female students for 2024. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Across the EU, more than a fifth (21.9%) of all students in tertiary education in 2024 were studying business, administration or law. Women accounted for a majority of the total number of students within this [[International_Standard_Classification_of_Education_(ISCED)#ISCED_1997_.28fields.29_and_ISCED-F_2013|field of education]] – see Figure 1. The second and third most common fields of education were health and welfare, and engineering, manufacturing and construction; these each accounted for 14.7% of all tertiary education students. In health and welfare, almost three quarters (72.7%) of all students were female. In engineering, manufacturing or construction, 72.2% of all students were male. The only other field of study to account for a double-digit share of tertiary education students was arts and humanities (11.1%), where women also accounted for a relatively large majority (65.3%) of the total number of tertiary students in this field. Among the remaining fields of study shown in Figure 1, there was a particularly high share of female students among those studying education (78.8%), while there was a relatively high share of female students among those studying social sciences, journalism and information (66.7%). By contrast, there was a relatively high male share (79.1%) of people studying information and communication technologies. ===Participation in tertiary education by type of institution=== [[Image:Distribution of students in tertiary education by type of institution, 2024 (%)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Distribution of students in tertiary education by type of institution, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/96a69889-026b-49a7-8474-1656a94d63b8?lang=en educ_uoe_enrt01])|alt=A stacked column chart showing the percentage distribution of students in tertiary education by type of institution. Each column contains three stacks representing private independent, private dependent and public institutions. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In the EU, the vast majority (73.0%) of tertiary education students in 2024 were taught in public institutions According to the UOE classification, the distinction between public and private is made according to whether a public agency or a private entity has the overall control of the institution and not according to which sector provides the majority of the funding. If a private institution receives the majority of funding from a public agency it is considered to be dependent; if not, it is independent. – see Figure 2. *In 2024, all tertiary education students were studying in public institutions in Greece and Luxembourg; in a further 19 EU countries, a majority of tertiary education students were studying in public institutions. *In Finland, half of tertiary education students were studying in public institutions and half in (government-dependent) private institutions. *In 5 EU countries, a minority of tertiary education students were studying in public institutions **in Belgium, the share was 41.4%, with students in private institutions almost exclusively in government-dependent private institutions **in the Netherlands, the share was 30.6%, with students in private institutions predominantly in government-dependent private institutions, although independent private institutions did account for more than a tenth of all tertiary students **in Cyprus, the share was 25.5%, with students in private institutions exclusively in independent private institutions **in Hungary, the share was 21.6%, with students in private institutions predominantly in independent private institutions **in Latvia, the share was 6.5%, with students in private institutions mainly in government-dependent private institutions, although independent private institutions did account for more than a fifth of all tertiary students. ===Graduates=== [[Image:Ratio of women to men among tertiary education graduates, 2024 (number per 100 men)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Ratio of women to men among tertiary education graduates, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/09299e3a-dd6b-4bc6-a167-98b448490b64?lang=en educ_uoe_grad09] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/563a2cb4-2e50-45fe-8d80-d2dd95b73a5a?lang=en educ_uoe_grad02])|alt=A high-low chart showing the ratio of women per 100 men among tertiary education graduates. Data are shown as markers for bachelor’s or equivalent, master’s or equivalent, short-cycle tertiary and doctoral or equivalent. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, some 4.5 million students graduated from tertiary education in the EU (including 2023 data for Czechia and Ireland). France (885 100) had the largest number of tertiary graduates, some way ahead of Germany (635 300), Spain (590 500), Italy (543 800) and Poland (404 700); all of the remaining EU countries had fewer than 200 000 tertiary graduates. The relatively high number of graduates in France may, at least to some extent, reflect a shorter average course length due to the particularly large number of students enrolled and graduating from short-cycle tertiary and master’s courses. As noted above, the majority of short-cycle tertiary students and doctoral students in 2024 in the EU were men, while the majority of bachelor’s and master’s students were women. This gender difference among tertiary students is reflected, to some extent, in the data for tertiary graduates (EU data include 2023 data for Czechia and Ireland). *Despite men being in the majority among the short-cycle tertiary student population, there were slightly more women than men graduating, with a ratio across the EU of 104 women for every 100 men. *The ratio of women to men among graduates was highest for graduates of bachelor’s and master’s levels: there were 144 women who were graduates from master’s or equivalent courses for every 100 men; for bachelor’s or equivalent courses the ratio was very similar, at 143 women for every 100 men. *The majority of doctoral or equivalent students were men and this was reinforced in terms of the number of graduates. There were 94 women among doctoral or equivalent graduates for every 100 men. Among the EU countries, the highest ratios of women to men among tertiary graduates in 2024 were observed in Latvia (194 women for every 100 men), Poland (190 women for every 100 men), Cyprus (185 women for every 100 men) and Estonia (180 women for every 100 men). In all EU countries, there were more women who graduated from tertiary education than men. The lowest female-to-male ratio was in Germany (106 women for every 100 men) – although women were only in the majority among graduates of master’s or equivalent courses. [[Image:Distribution of tertiary education graduates by broad field of education, 2024 (%)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Distribution of tertiary education graduates by broad field of education, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/09d3ba50-787a-4092-bb25-93c2517632ac?lang=en educ_uoe_grad02])|alt=A table showing the percentage distribution of tertiary education graduates by broad field of education. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, an analysis of the number of graduates in the EU (including 2023 data for Czechia and Ireland) by field of education shows that approximately a quarter (25.1%) of all tertiary students had graduated in business, administration or law. The next 2 largest fields were health and welfare (14.7%) and engineering, manufacturing and construction (13.9%), followed by arts and humanities (9.7%) and social sciences, journalism and information (9.6%). For several fields of education, there was a remarkable variability in the distribution of tertiary graduates in 2024 across the EU countries. *The proportion of graduates in business, administration and law ranged from 15.4% in Sweden to 43.6% in Luxembourg. *The share of all graduates in health and welfare was below 10.0% in 4 EU countries, with Luxembourg recording the lowest share (6.6%). By contrast, Latvia (20.2%), Lithuania (21.0%), Finland (21.4%), Denmark (21.6%), Malta (22.3%) reported shares of more than a fifth, rising to more than a quarter in Belgium, where the highest share was observed (26.1%). *For engineering, manufacturing and construction studies, the share of all graduates was below 10.0% in 6 EU countries, with Malta recording the lowest share (5.0%). By contrast, Germany (21.3%) reported the highest share. *The share of tertiary graduates from the education field was below 5.0% in France (4.0%) and Portugal (4.4%), while the highest share was recorded for Cyprus (23.6%). *Larger gaps (in relative terms) between the highest and lowest shares were observed for some of the smaller fields, most notably for agriculture, forestry, fisheries and veterinary where the 4.1% share in Romania was 13 times as high as the 0.3% share in Cyprus. [[Image:Distribution of tertiary education graduates by broad field and sex, EU, 2024 (%)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Distribution of tertiary education graduates by broad field and sex, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9d4af256-904b-41e0-90d2-8fa86bb411ee?lang=en educ_uoe_grad02])|alt=A double bar chart showing the percentage distribution of tertiary education graduates in the EU by broad field of study and sex. The twelve selected broad fields of study each have two bars comparing the shares of male and female graduates for 2024. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 4 extends the analysis of Table 2 by presenting not only an analysis by broad field of education, but also by the sex of the graduates. The distribution of tertiary education graduates by sex and field of study reflects the distribution of participation numbers in tertiary education as shown in Figure 1. Within the EU, 57.8% of all tertiary education graduates in 2024 (including 2023 data for Czechia and Ireland) were women. *Some 14.5% of all tertiary graduates were women graduating from business, administration and law, while 10.6% were men from the same field. *Around a tenth of all tertiary graduates were women graduating from health and welfare (11.1%), while a similar share were men graduating from engineering, manufacturing and construction (10.0%). *There were more women than men among graduates from all fields except for i) engineering, manufacturing and construction, ii) information and communication technologies and iii) services. *As such, women outnumbered men among graduates from all fields where they also outnumbered men among students. With the exception of agriculture, forestry, fisheries and veterinary, men outnumbered women among graduates from all fields where they also outnumbered women among students. The analysis by sex of students and graduates from different fields varied most for generic programmes and qualifications – compare Figure 1 and Figure 4. In this field, there were 1.7 times as many female as male students, but 2.1 times as many female as male graduates. In all fields, the ratio of women to men was higher among graduates than among students: the smallest differences – where the ratios were almost the same – were the male-dominated fields of engineering, manufacturing and construction (0.4 female students/graduates for every male) as well as information and communication technologies (0.3 female students/graduates for every male). A more detailed analysis of field of study is presented in Figure 5, which shows the number of graduates with a bachelor’s or a master’s degree. While many subjects are offered at both bachelor’s and master’s levels, it is important to note that courses in some fields, for example medicine and law, may be offered in some EU countries principally or exclusively as master’s courses. In these cases, the number of graduates at the bachelor’s level may be small or even zero. In 2024, the most frequently awarded degree – based on detailed fields of education – was for management and administration; across the EU, some 230 900 people in this field graduated with a bachelor’s degree and 147 500 with a master’s degree. Nursing and midwifery was the second most common field for those graduating with a bachelor’s degree (109 000), followed by law (99 100). By contrast, medicine was the second most frequently awarded degree among those graduating with a master’s degree (133 000), followed by law (106 400). [[Image:Number of tertiary education graduates in each detailed field of education, EU, 2024 (1 000)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Number of tertiary education graduates in each detailed field of education, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/37d15ea0-7a0b-46b8-8a4a-8e5a0af35502?lang=en educ_uoe_grad02])|alt=Two bar charts showing the number of tertiary education graduates in each detailed field of education in thousands. The first bar chart shows data for bachelor’s or equivalent graduates and the second data for master’s or equivalent graduates. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] [[Image:Tertiary education graduates in science, mathematics, computing, engineering, manufacturing and construction, 2024 (number per 1 000 inhabitants aged 20–29 years)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Tertiary education graduates in science, mathematics, computing, engineering, manufacturing and construction, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d8d54bbe-5d35-4132-9bb3-8fdea7122b8f?lang=en educ_uoe_grad04])|alt=A high-low chart showing the number of tertiary education graduates in science, mathematics, computing, engineering, manufacturing and construction per thousand inhabitants aged 20 to 29 years. Two markers show the ratios for males and for females. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Relative to the size of the population aged 20 to 29 years, the number of tertiary graduates in science, mathematics, computing, engineering, manufacturing and construction (referred to hereafter as STEM) in the EU increased in recent years. In 2014, the ratio was 18.5 per 1 000 people aged 20 to 29 years while in 2023 it was 22.4 per 1 000. Figure 6 shows this ratio for male and female graduates for the latest year. There were almost twice as many male as female STEM graduates in the EU in 2023: 29.0 men per 1 000 male inhabitants aged 20 to 29 years and 15.5 women per 1 000 female inhabitants aged 20 to 29 years. In relative terms, the gender gap for this field of education in 2024 was most marked in Spain, where the ratio for male graduates was 2.5 times as high as the ratio for female graduates. The narrowest gender gaps for this indicator were observed in Romania and Greece, where the ratios for male graduates were 1.3 times as high as the ratios for female graduates. ===Teaching staff=== [[Image:Teaching staff in tertiary education by sex and level of education, 2024 (%)_ET2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Teaching staff in tertiary education by sex and level of education, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/fb770b0d-30e7-4a5d-8ceb-892de6aa0175?lang=en educ_uoe_perp01])|alt=A double stacked column chart showing the percentage of teaching staff in tertiary education. The columns show two education levels: short-cycle and other tertiary. Each column contains two stacks, one for men and one for women. Data are shown for 2024 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] There were 1.55 million people teaching in tertiary education across the EU in 2024. Close to a third (30.9%) of the tertiary education teaching staff in the EU were teaching in Germany, with more than a tenth in Spain (12.9%). In contrast to the teaching staff in schools, where women were in the majority, in 2024 a higher proportion of tertiary education teaching staff in the EU were men (54.9%). Note that the countries in Figure 7 are ranked on the share of women among the teaching staff for the whole of tertiary education. *The share of men among tertiary education teaching staff exceeded 60.0% in Luxembourg, Greece, Czechia, Malta and Italy. *Women accounted for a majority of the tertiary education teaching staff in Belgium, Croatia, Bulgaria, Finland, Romania and Latvia, with this share peaking at 56.2% in Lithuania. Figure 7 provides information on the relative shares of men and women within tertiary education teaching staff in 2024. An analysis by level of education provides data for short-cycle tertiary education separate from the rest of tertiary education. *For the EU, the share of women within the teaching staff was higher for short-cycle tertiary education (52.0%) than for the rest of tertiary education (44.6%). *A particularly high share of women within the teaching staff for short-cycle tertiary education was observed in Belgium (83.0%). *Among the 16 EU countries for which the analysis by level of education is available (see Figure 7), Germany, Cyprus, Sweden and Denmark were the only ones where the share of women within the teaching staff for short-cycle tertiary education was lower than the equivalent share for the rest of tertiary education. === Source data for tables and graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=Tertiary education statistics ET2026.xlsx|title=Tertiary education statistics: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''Source''' The standards for international statistics on education are set by 3 international organisations *the [[Glossary:United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)|United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)]] institute for statistics (UIS) *the [[Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)]] *[[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]], the statistical office of the EU. The source of data used in this article is a [[Glossary:UOE data collection|joint UNESCO/OECD/Eurostat (UOE) data collection]] on education statistics, and this is the basis for the core components of Eurostat’s database on education statistics. In combination with the joint data collection, Eurostat also collects data on regional enrolments, foreign language learning and tertiary graduates with credit mobility. More information about the joint data collection is available in an article on the [[UNESCO_OECD_Eurostat_(UOE)_joint_data_collection_%E2%80%93_methodology|UOE methodology]]. '''Classification''' The [https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000219109 international standard classification of education (ISCED)] is the basis for international education statistics, describing 9 different [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|levels of education]]. Eurostat data by fields of education are classified according to the [https://www.uis.unesco.org/sites/default/files/medias/fichiers/2025/04/international-standard-classification-of-education-fields-of-education-and-training-2013-detailed-field-descriptions-2015-en.pdf ISCED-F 2013] classification. The fields of education – as classified by ISCED-F 2013 – are broad domains, branches or areas of content covered by an education programme or qualification. The classification has a 3-level hierarchy based on broad fields (the highest level), narrow fields (the second level) and detailed fields (the third level) of education. '''Symbols''' In tables, a colon ‘:’ is used to show where data are not available and a dash ‘–’ when data are not relevant or not applicable; data in italics are estimates or provisional. ===Context=== Tertiary education builds on secondary education, providing learning activities in specialised fields of education. Tertiary education includes not only what is commonly understood as ‘academic’ education, but also advanced vocational or professional education. The content of programmes at tertiary level is more complex and advanced than at lower ISCED levels. A prerequisite of tertiary education is the successful completion of ISCED level 3 programmes that give direct access to first stage tertiary education programmes (access may also be possible from ISCED level 4 programmes). In addition to qualification requirements, entry into education programmes at these levels may depend on subject choice and/or grades achieved. Furthermore, it may be necessary to take and succeed in entrance examinations. There is usually a clear hierarchy between qualifications granted by tertiary education programmes. The transition between programmes at tertiary level is, however, not always clearly distinguished and it may be possible to combine programmes and transfer credits from 1 programme to another. In certain cases, credits received from previously completed education programmes may also be counted towards the completion of a programme at a higher ISCED level. Nevertheless, the successful completion of a master’s or equivalent level programme (ISCED level 7) is usually required for entry into a doctoral or equivalent level programme (ISCED level 8). '''Bologna process and the renewed agenda for higher education''' Since the introduction of the [https://education.ec.europa.eu/education-levels/higher-education/inclusive-and-connected-higher-education/bologna-process Bologna process] (see the article on [[Education_and_training_statistics_introduced|Education and training statistics introduced]]), a major expansion in higher education systems In UOE statistics, the term ‘tertiary education’ is used, and this refers to ISCED levels 5 to 8. The term ‘higher education’ is not used in UOE statistics and does not have a comparable international definition in terms of indicating a specific grouping of ISCED levels. A number of countries do not consider institutions delivering ISCED level 5 programmes to be part of what is nationally defined as ‘higher education’. has taken place, accompanied by significant reforms in degree structures and quality assurance systems. While the Bologna process put in motion a series of reforms to make European higher education more compatible, comparable, competitive and attractive for students, it is only a part of a broader effort concerning higher education. To establish synergies between the Bologna process and the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=LEGISSUM:ef0018 Copenhagen process] (for enhanced European cooperation in [[Glossary:Vocational education and training (VET)|vocational education and training]]), the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] and EU countries have established a [https://europa.eu/europass/en/description-eight-eqf-levels European qualifications framework for lifelong learning (EQF)]. In May 2017, the European Commission adopted a Communication on [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52017DC0247 a renewed EU agenda for higher education] (COM(2017) 247 final), focusing on 4 priority activities: *tackling future skills mismatches and promoting excellence in skills development *building inclusive and connected higher education systems *ensuring higher education institutions contribute to innovation *supporting effective and efficient higher education systems. More information on the communication as well as on other [https://education.ec.europa.eu/education-levels/higher-education/about-higher-education higher education initiatives] is available in the article on [[Education_and_training_statistics_introduced|Education and training statistics introduced]]. In January 2022, the European Commission adopted a Communication on [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52022DC0016 a European strategy for universities] (COM(2022) 16 final), highlighting the unique position of universities at the crossroads of education, research, innovation, serving society and the economy. '''European Education Area''' A [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32021G0226(01) Council Resolution on a strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training towards the European Education Area and beyond], was adopted by the [[Glossary:Council of the European Union|Council]] in February 2021. For monitoring progress, 7 EU-wide targets have been introduced. They define benchmarks against which performance across education and training may be judged and refer to levels of average performance across the EU. These include: *the share of people aged 25 to 34 years with tertiary educational attainment should be at least 45%, by 2030 *at least 47% of people aged 25 to 64 years should have participated in [[Glossary:Lifelong_learning_(LLL)|adult learning]] during the previous 12 months, by 2025. More information on the European Education Area is available in the article on [[Education_and_training_statistics_introduced|Education and training statistics introduced]]. '''Erasmus+''' In 2014, the [[Glossary:Erasmus programme|Erasmus programme]] was superseded by the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/en/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32021R0817 EU’s programme for education, training, young people and sport], referred to as ‘[https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/ Erasmus+]’. The programme currently covers the period 2021 to 2027 and has an overall budget of €26.2 billion. This is nearly double the funding compared with its predecessor programme (2014 to 2020). === Footnotes === ===Other articles=== *[[Education_and_training_in_the_EU_-_facts_and_figures|Education and
