title: Test Migrant integration
text:
Statistics on the demographic characteristics of foreign-born people and their descendants in the EU. Native-born and foreign-born populations. Data extracted on 21 July 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 Between 2021 and 2025, the share of foreign-born people in the EU population aged 15 - 74 increased from 13.0% to 15.2%. The share of native-born people with one foreign-born parent rose from 4.1% to 4.4%, and those with 2 foreign-born parents from 2.9% to 3.3%. The article presents statistics on the migration status of people aged 15 - 74 years usually residing in private households in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. It examines both the main characteristics of people residing in private households in the EU and the household composition according to migration status, focusing on different household types such as single-adult and multi-adult households. Migration status is defined according to individuals’ country of birth and, where relevant, their parents’ country of birth. Individuals are grouped as either native-born or foreign-born. Native-born individuals are further classified based on the birthplace of their parents, in order to reflect on the possible migrant background. As a result, the migration status categories used are: native-born with 2 native-born parents, native-born with one foreign-born parent, native-born with 2 foreign-born parents, and foreign-born persons. Additional analysis by citizenship classifies individuals as either nationals or non-nationals of the country in which they reside. Non-nationals are further divided into 2 groups: those who hold a citizenship of another EU country and those who hold a citizenship of a non-EU country. The types of households have been categorised based on the migration background. For single-adult households, the household migration background reflects the migration background of that person *'''household of native-born with native background''': household where the adult is a native-born person with both parents native-born *'''household of native-born with foreign background''': household where the adult is a native-born with one or both parents born abroad *'''household of foreign-born''': household where the adult is a foreign-born. For multi-adult households, the same three categories apply when all members share the same migration background. However, adults of a household may have different migration backgrounds. Therefore, one additional category is included *'''mixed household''': households where at least 2 adults have different migration backgrounds, including native-born with a native background, native-born with a foreign background, and foreign-born. In addition, there are households where the migration background is not available. These are mostly households where the majority of adults are aged 75 years and over and for whom no information on the migration background of their parents was surveyed. In the following sections, to facilitate the reading of the figures and the comparison between the household migration background, these households where the migration background is not available, were excluded from the analysis. This article forms part of the online publication on [[Migrant_integration_statistics - facts and figures|migrant integration statistics]]. ===Overview=== In 2025, 90.2% of the EU population aged 15–74 were citizens of the country in which they resided (Figure 1), while 6.6% were citizens of non-EU countries and 3.2% were citizens of another EU country. Looking instead at migration background, most of the population (77.0%) were native-born with 2 native-born parents, while 15.2% were foreign-born, 4.4% were native-born with one foreign-born parent and 3.3% were native-born with 2 foreign-born parents. Figure 1 ===Main characteristics of foreign-born people and their descendants=== The distribution of the population by migration background varied considerably across the EU countries (Figure 2). Luxembourg stood out in the EU as the only country where more than half of the population aged 15 - 74 was foreign-born (56.1%). This was far above the EU pattern, where native-born people with native-born parents remained the clear majority. Malta (36.7%) and Cyprus (32.0%) also recorded exceptionally high shares of foreign-born people, placing them well above most other EU countries. On the other hand, in Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia and Poland, foreign-born people accounted for only a small share of the population. Figure 2 Focusing only on people residing in their country of citizenship, the age distribution in 2025 differed markedly by migration status (Figure 3). At EU level, native-born citizens with both parents born abroad were the youngest group, with 44.2% aged 15 - 29 and only 19.8% aged 55 - 74. By contrast, foreign-born citizens were concentrated in the older age groups: only 12.4% were aged 15 - 29, while 50.7% were aged 30 - 54 and 36.8% were aged 55 - 74. The age distribution of native-born citizens with both parents native-born and of native-born citizens with one parent born abroad was more balanced, although in both groups the largest share was aged 30 - 54. Figure 3 In 2025, people aged 15 - 74 with a migrant background in the EU were more concentrated in cities than native-born people with both parents native-born (Figure 4). The share living in cities was 54.5% among native-born people with both parents foreign-born and 53.5% among foreign-born people, compared with 44.9% for those with one parent born abroad and 36.8% for native-born people with both parents native-born. By contrast, rural residence was most common among native-born people with both parents native-born (28.1%), while it was less than half that level among foreign-born people (12.9%) and native-born people with both parents foreign-born (12.3%). The differences were smaller in towns and suburbs, where all groups recorded shares of around one third, ranging from 33.2% to 35.1%. Figure 4 ===Household composition=== Figure 5 shows that, in 2025, households composed of native-born people with a native background remained the largest group in the EU, accounting for 27.3% of single-adult households and 45.8% of multi-adult households. Between 2021 and 2025, their share increased among single-adult households, by 0.6 percentage points, while it declined by 3.1 percentage points among multi-adult households. At the same time, the share of foreign-born households increased steadily in both household types, rising from 5.0% in 2021 to 6.0% in 2025 among single-adult households, and from 5.5% to 6.4% among multi-adult households. The share of households composed of native-born people with a foreign background increased at lower pace among single-adult households, from 2.7% to 3.0%, while it remained stable among multi-adult households, between 1.0% to 1.1%. Mixed households represented around one tenth of multi-adult households over the whole 2021-2025 period. Figure 5 In 2025, at EU level, single-adult households were most commonly composed of native-born people with native-born parents (Figure 6). The share of such households was particularly high in Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Poland, Hungary, Greece and Lithuania, where it exceeded 90.0% in each case. By contrast, Malta (60.9%) and Luxembourg (57.5%) recorded high proportions of single-adult households of foreign-born people, while Latvia and Estonia reported a notable presence of households with native-born people who had one or 2 foreign-born parents. In the case of multi-adult households, the most common group across the EU remained those composed of native-born people with native-born parents. Smaller shares were observed for households composed of foreign-born people, for mixed households, and for native-born people with one or 2 foreign-born parents. Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Poland, and Hungary had a particularly high share of households composed of native-born people with native-born parents, all above 90.0%. Luxembourg, Malta and Cyprus recorded high proportions of households composed of foreign-born people (45.0%, 28.1% and 25.1%, respectively). Mixed households were more frequent in Luxembourg, Latvia, Estonia, Belgium, and France. Figure 6 In 2025, across the EU, among all households, mixed households were the most likely to have children (39.6%), followed by households of foreign-born persons (31.8%), while households of native-born persons with a foreign background were the least likely (15.8%) (Figure 7). Among single-adult households, those with children were least common among native-born persons with a native background (8.9%) and most common among foreign-born people (11.6%). Among multi-adult households, those of foreign-born people were the most likely to have children (50.9%), while the shares were lower among households of native-born people, regardless of whether they had native-born or foreign-born parents. Figure 7
===Source data for graphs=== The data displayed in these visualisations were calculated using data from 3 Eurostat datasets: * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfsa_pganedm/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=7bec084f-4c22-46b0-bb14-dcdc01b27d56&c=1749481086660 Population by sex, age, migration status, citizenship and educational attainment level [lfsa_pganedm]]; * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfst_r_pgaum__custom_17589412/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=75327873-2422-464f-a3df-e512b4474d01&c=1753457699895 Population by sex, age, migration status and degree of urbanisation [lfst_r_pgaum]] * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfst_hhmgscomp/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=824ac8ce-6a05-435a-a22d-128df749da12&c=1753278625311 Number of households by migration status, working status and household composition [lfst_hhmgscomp]] Information on data reliability, series breaks, and differing definitions, flags can be consulted in the online datasets. ===Data sources=== The data presented in this article are from the EU [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)| labour force survey (EU-LFS)]], the largest household sample survey in the EU. The survey covers the resident population in private households. As such, people living in collective households are excluded from the target population. The concept of usual residence is used, which means the place where a person normally spends the daily period of rest, regardless of temporary absences for purposes of recreation, holidays, visits to friends and relatives, business, medical treatment or religious pilgrimage. The data for the EU are aggregated results for the 27 EU countries. For more information on the data sources used, please consult the online publication [[EU_labour_force_survey|EU labour force survey]]. Due to the sampling nature of the survey, some data have low reliability or are not published due to very low reliability or confidentiality. '''Calculation of shares in totals''' All the figures in this article present shares of a total. For some of the analysed breakdowns, e.g. by migration status, citizenship, household composition there is a certain amount of non-response (also called ’not stated’ or ’unknown’). Wherever possible, the calculation of shares in this article is based on a total excluding the number of people classified in the not stated or unknown categories. As such, all exhaustive breakdowns presented in graphs should sum to 100.0% (allowing for rounding errors). ===Context=== The data in this article provide information not only on foreign-born persons living in the EU but also about native-born persons with at least one foreign-born parent. Successful integration may lead to economic and social benefits for migrants and their children, and for the society where they live. More information on the policies and legislation in force in this area can be found in an introductory article: [[Migrant_integration_statistics_introduced|Migrant integration statistics introduced]]. ===See also=== *[[:Category: Migration and asylum |All articles on migration and asylum]] '''Online publications''' *[[Migrant integration statistics - facts and figures]] '''Methodology''' *[[EU_Labour_Force_Survey_-_new_methodology_from_2021_onwards|Labour force survey]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/migrant-integration/database Migrant integration] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/lfs/database Labour force survey] ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/lfs/overview Labour force survey] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/migrant-integration Migrant integration] ===Publications=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/migrant-integration/publications All publications on migrant integration] ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=lfsa_esms|title=LFS series – Detailed annual survey results}} (ESMS metadata file – lfsa_esms) *[[EU labour force survey]] ===Legislation=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/migration-asylum/migrant-integration/legislation All legislation on migrant integration] ===External links=== *[https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/migrant-integration/eu-integration-policy_en#action-plan-on-integration-and-inclusion-2021-2027 Action Plan on integration and inclusion 2021–2027] *[https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/index_en European Commission – Directorate-General for Migration and Home Affairs (DG HOME)], see: **[https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/legal-migration-and-resettlement_en Legal migration and resettlement] **[https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/migrant-integration_en Migrant integration] **[https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/statistics-migration-europe_en Statistics on migration to Europe] *[https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/migrant-integration/migrant-integration-hub_en Migrant integration hub] {{Unit|topic=X_Dissemination}} [[Category:Under construction|Test Migrant integration]]

title: Test Kasia
text:
This article examines the evolution of the number of deaths that occurred each month in the European Union, compared with a 'baseline' of the average number of deaths for a particular month over the 4 years from 2016 to 2019. Data extracted on 13 June 2025 Planned article update: 16 September 2025 As the beginning of 2025, excess mortality across the European Union kept declining, it was 4.4% in January, 1.2% in February and 0.7% in March 2025. By the end of the first quarter in March 2025, excess mortality was negative in 11 out of 26 EU countries. Cyprus, Malta, and Portugal recorded the highest excess mortality rates in March 2025 (24.0%, 21.1%, and 9.3%, respectively), while Latvia, Bulgaria, and Luxembourg recorded the lowest rates (−14.7%, −9.7%, and −7.0%).
|alt= Interactive line chart tool showing monthly excess mortality as percentage of additional deaths compared with average monthly deaths over the years 2016 to 2019. The tool allows the selection of the EU, individual EU countries and EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.
This article presents an overview of the developments of excess mortality across the EU in the first quarter of 2025, based on all-cause mortality data. In this article, [[Glossary:Excess mortality|excess mortality]] refers to the number of deaths from all causes measured during a defined period, above that which was observed in the baseline period. The baseline consists of the average number of deaths that occurred in each month during the period 2016-2019. The higher the value, the higher the number of additional deaths compared with the baseline. A negative indicator shows that fewer deaths occurred in a particular month compared with the baseline period. This indicator, which is part of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/dashboard/european-statistical-monitor/ European Statistical Monitor], provides a comprehensive comparison of additional deaths among the European countries. It provides a general measure of mortality because it includes all deaths regardless of their cause. For more information on the method to calculate the indicator, see below under Data sources. ===Recent data on excess mortality in the EU=== Excess mortality in the EU varied significantly from January 2024 to March 2025, with the highest rates seen between August and October 2024 (Figure 1). In the first quarter of 2025, the EU recorded the highest excess mortality rate in January (4.4%), followed by a decline through February (1.2%) and March (0.7%). Overall, excess mortality in the EU remained higher in early 2025 than in the same period a year earlier. Figure 1 In total, there were 31 915 excess deaths recorded across the EU in the first quarter of 2025 compared to the pre-pandemic average for the same period from 2016 to 2019, distributed as follows: 18 489 in January, 10 024 in February, and 3 403 in March. Figure 2
'''Excess mortality by EU countries''' The excess mortality continued to vary across the EU in the first quarter of 2025 (Figure 2). In January 2025, the excess mortality rate was negative in 10 EU countries. By February, this number increased to 14. In March, 11 countries reported negative excess mortality rates with Latvia recording the lowest at -14.1%, followed by Bulgaria at -9.7%, and Luxembourg at -7.0%. This marks a decrease compared to March 2024 when 19 countries had negative excess mortality rates. Meanwhile, 15 EU countries experienced excess deaths in March 2025. The highest rates were observed in Cyprus at 24.0%, Malta at 21.1%, and in Portugal at 9.3%. Figure 3 ===Recent data on weekly deaths in the EU=== In the first quarter of 2025, weekly deaths in the EU ranged between 108 000 and 111 000 per week in January. Numbers then gradually declined through February, reaching around 99 000 in Week 9 and fell further in March, dropping to approximately 91 000 by Week 13. In total, over 1 340 000 deaths were recorded across all weeks of the first quarter of 2025. *The second week of January was marked by the highest number of weekly deaths across EU countries (111 142). In comparison with the same period of the previous year, the highest number during the first quarter 2024 occurred during the first week of January but was slightly higher, at 111 455 deaths. *The lowest weekly death count in the first quarter of 2024 was observed in week 12, with 89 453 deaths. *In the first quarter of 2025, the data shows a decline in mortality starting from week 8. Figure 4 ===Further releases=== Data for the most recent months are provisional and subject to revision. Starting from the data reference period of January 2025, this article and the related indicator will be updated quarterly, with Q2 2025 scheduled for publication by mid-September 2025. For additional information on the COVID-19 pandemic see [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Deaths_during_the_COVID-19_pandemic Deaths during the COVID-19 pandemic]. ===Data sources=== The excess mortality indicator takes the number of deaths from any cause in a given period and compares it with a historical baseline from previous years in a period that was not affected by the COVID-19 pandemic. In this case, the baseline consists of the average number of deaths that occurred in each month during the period 2016-2019. The European Union (EU) average baseline for 2016-2019 was not adjusted for age-specific mortality rates or increasing life expectancy. The indicator is expressed as the percentage of additional deaths compared with the baseline period (2016-2019). A negative percentage indicates that no additional deaths occurred in a particular month compared with the baseline period. The excess mortality indicator, covering EU and EFTA countries, is based on weekly death data transmitted to Eurostat by EU countries on a voluntary basis. Data are classified by sex, 5-year age groups and NUTS regions, and are continuously updated with more recent weeks of mortality statistics. These weekly data are then attributed pro-rata to months to compute the excess mortality indicator. For the purpose of the excess mortality indicator, the death figures for the latest weeks available in a Member State are corrected for incompleteness. Data remain provisional and subject to revision with the next releases. The excess mortality indicator is based on a data collection for which National Statistical Institutes from the EU and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) have transmitted weekly deaths data to Eurostat on a voluntary basis since April 2020. The weekly deaths dataset that Eurostat publishes regularly is used to compute the monthly excess mortality indicator by mapping the deaths of each week to a full month. 26 EU countries provided weekly mortality data: Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Croatia, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary, Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland, Sweden. Data received from EFTA and EU candidate and neighboring countries are not present in this article. The EU aggregate for the first quarter 2025 was estimated using the most recent available data. The mortality indicator is unavailable for Romania in March. Data for several countries were recalculated from 2021 onwards by applying the new coefficients of data completeness transmitted by the National Statistical Institutes in May 2023. For more information about Methodology, please consult Excess Mortality Metadata [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/demo_mexrt_esms.htm]. The excess mortality indicator does not distinguish between the causes of death and did not differentiate between sex and age class. For more information on causes of death statistics, please see [[Causes of death - monthly statistics]] and [[Causes of death statistics]]. During the COVID-19 pandemic, excess death statistics revealed the mortality burden potentially linked to the pandemic, encompassing not only direct virus-related deaths, but also indirect deaths. This measure included undiagnosed and unreported COVID-19 deaths as well as deaths from other causes influenced by the overall crisis. It also accounted for the reduction in deaths from other causes, such as accidents that did not occur due to restrictions on commuting or travel during lockdown periods. In the post-pandemic period, the indicator captures the effects of heat waves during summer and influenza during winter. ===Context=== The COVID-19 pandemic has triggered tremendous interest in statistics. Hence, in April 2020, in cooperation with the National Statistical Institutes of the European Statistical System, Eurostat set up a special data collection on weekly deaths, to support the policy and research efforts related to the pandemic. The National Statistical Institutes regularly and voluntarily transmit data to Eurostat on weekly deaths up to the latest available week. 'Excess mortality' has been identified as the most useful indicator for assessing additional deaths, complementing the other indicators contained in the European Statistical Monitor. To capture the dynamics of mortality changes in a stable way, the excess mortality indicator is calculated for each month, no later than 45 days after the end of the reference period (depending on data available to Eurostat from the National Statistical Institutes). Eurostat started to publish the excess mortality indicator in relation to the COVID-19 public health emergency announced by the World Health Organisation. While the global COVID-19 crisis is over, the indicator remains relevant and is available to capture possible future factors affecting mortality in the EU. ===Other articles=== *[[Deaths during the COVID-19 pandemic]] *[[Weekly death statistics]] *[[Causes of death statistics]] *[[Causes of death statistics by age group]] *[[Mortality and life expectancy statistics]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/DEMO_MEXRT__custom_1210067/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=fc27a3a9-082b-461d-830b-a4c7b36caf4f Mortality (DEMO_MEXRT)], see: :Excess mortality - monthly data (demo_mexrt) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/demography-population-stock-balance/database?node_code=demomwk Mortality (demomwk)], see: :Weekly deaths - special data collection (demomwk) ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/covid-19/population-health Population and health] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/population-demography/overview Population and Demography overview] ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=demo_mexrt_esms|title=Excess mortality}} (ESMS metadata file — demo_mexrt) ===Visualisations=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_mexrt/default/line?lang=en Data Browser (Excess mortality line chart)] - select geopolitical entity and time *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_mexrt/default/bar?lang=en Data Browser (Excess mortality bar chart)] - select time

text:
'''Pixel testing done on 02/09/2026''' Statistics on inland waterway goods transport are presented for the EU and other countries connected to the EU inland waterways network, focusing on the main type of goods transported. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 In 2025, freight transport on EU inland waterways, measured in tonne-kilometres, decreased by 3.0% compared with 2024. This article presents inland waterway goods transport in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] and other countries connected to the EU inland waterway network. It focuses on the main types of goods transported, based on annual data for 2025 and comparisons with 2024. For an overview of the annual and quarterly inland waterway transport, please refer to the Statistics Explained article [[Inland waterway freight transport - quarterly and annual data]]. === 'Metal ores and other mining and quarrying products' – top type of goods transported === 'Metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium' (NST2007 division 03) was the main type of goods transported on EU inland waterways in 2025, both in terms of tonne-kilometres (Table 1) and tonnes (Table 2). It accounted for nearly a quarter of total tonne-kilometres (22.2%) and slightly more than a quarter of total tonnes transported (26.7%). [[Image: Inland waterway transport by type of goods and type of transport, EU, 2024-2025 (million tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Have written 700px]]
[[Image:Figure 1_Employment in sport - annual rates of change, 2022-2025_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Have written 700px]] 'Coke and refined petroleum products' (NST2007 division 07) constituted the second most significant type of goods transported on EU inland waterways in 2025 in terms of tonne-kilometres, and the third in terms of tonnes. It represented 16.2% of the tonne-kilometres performed and 15.9% of the total tonnes transported. The transported volume in terms of tonnes transported of this type of goods was 40.3% less than the one of 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products; peat; uranium and thorium'. Compared with 2024, transport of 'coke and refined petroleum products' decreased for both tonnes (-4.5%) and tonne-kilometres (-3.6%). [[Image:Inland waterway transport by type of goods and type of transport, EU, 2024-2025 (million tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 2: Have written 800px]]
[[Image:Figure 1_Employment in sport - annual rates of change, 2022-2025_(%).png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 1: Have written 800px]] ===The Netherlands and Germany dominated transport of 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products'=== In 2025, the main country involved in the EU inland waterway transport of 'metal ores and other mining and quarrying products' was the Netherlands, which alone accounted for 43.7% of the tonnes transported and 38.3% of the tonne-kilometres performed (Figure 1). Germany secured second position in both metrics, scoring 22.3% of the tonnes transported and 31.1% of the tonne-kilometres performed. This distribution remained broadly unchanged compared with the previous year and reflects the extensive inland waterway networks in the Netherlands and Germany, which play a significant role in their transport systems. These networks are also connected to major ports such as Rotterdam and Hamburg, which are key hubs for imports to and exports from the EU. [[Image:Inland waterway transport by type of goods and type of transport, EU, 2024-2025 (million tonne-kilometres).png|thumb|centre|500px|Table 3: Have written 500px]]
[[Image:Figure 1_Employment in sport - annual rates of change, 2022-2025_(%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 1: Have written 500px]] ===The Netherlands and Germany were the top transporters of 'coke and refined petroleum products' === In 2025, the main countries involved in the EU inland waterway transport of 'coke and refined petroleum products' were, as in previous years, the Netherlands and Germany (Figure 2). The Netherlands ranked first, with 55.3% of the total tonnes transported and 42.2% of the tonne-kilometres performed. Germany ranks second, with 28.0% of the total tonnes transported and 41.7% of tonne-kilometres performed. These shares reflect the longer distances performed by vessels passing through German inland waterways. In terms of tonnes transported, Belgium ranked third, with a share of 5.5%, followed by France (3.8%) and Romania (2.5%). In terms of tonne-kilometres performed, Romania, with a share of 5.6%, ranked third, followed by France (2.8%) and Belgium (2.6%). [[Image: Inland waterway transport by type of goods and type of transport, EU, 2024-2025 (million tonne-kilometres).png |thumb|centre|Table 5: No px specified]]
[[Image:Figure 1_Employment in sport - annual rates of change, 2022-2025_(%).png|thumb|centre|Figure 1: No px specified]] === Source data for tables and figures (MS Excel)=== {{Template:Excel|filename=SE_article_Goods_2026-09.xlsx|title=Inland waterway transport statistics by type of goods}} === Data sources=== All figures presented in this article have been extracted from the [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] online inland waterways transport database. The related datasets are collected according to {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R0974:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 2018/974}} of the European Parliament and of the Council on statistics of goods transport by inland waterways. === Context=== The content of this statistical article is based on data collected within the framework of {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32018R0974:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2018/974}} of the European Parliament and of the Council on statistics of goods transport by inland waterways. === Other articles === *[[Freight transport statistics - modal split]] *[[Inland waterway freight transport - quarterly and annual data]] *[[Inland waterways - statistics on container transport]] *[[Inland waterway freight transport at regional level]] === Selected Datasets === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/database Transport], see selected datasets under 'Inland waterways transport': :Inland waterways transport (t_iww) ::Goods transport by inland waterways (ttr00007) === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/transport/database Transport], see detailed datasets: :Inland waterways transport (iww) ::Inland waterways transport infrastructure (iww_if) ::Inland waterways transport equipment (iww_eq) ::Inland waterways transport - title: Test Wendy
text:
Eurostat regional yearbook; 2026 edition; flagship publication; EU; regional statistics; NUTS; labour market; employment; focus on young people in the labour market; unemployment; employment rates; gender employment gap; young people neither in employment nor in education and training; NEETs; unemployment rate; long-term unemployment rate Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 This article forms part of the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026]'', an annual [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications flagship publication]. It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the [[Glossary:EU|EU]], [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate]] countries. A [[Regional_yearbook_introduction#A_short_reading_guide|short reading guide]] is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps. All but 1 of the EU regions had an employment rate of at least 50.0% in 2025, with the lowest level recorded in the French outermost region of Mayotte (36.9%). Relatively low rates were recorded in some other outermost regions of France, as well as southern Italy and the Spanish autonomous regions of Ciudades de Ceuta y Melilla. In 2025, NEET rates were below 10.0% in every region of Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Sweden, as well as in Luxembourg and Malta.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:SDG wheel icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:Compet and SDG wheel icons RYB2026_small.png]]
[[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH04_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/194b8ae4-edc2-4b87-a518-a704bd1950c3?lang=en lfst_r_lfe2emprt)]|alt="An infographic showing the ten EU regions with the highest employment rates for people aged 20 to 64. Data are shown in percent for 2025. Data are presented for the EU and selected NUTS level 2 regions with the highest rates. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image."]]
On 4 March 2021, the European Commission set out its ambition to build a stronger, more social EU by focusing on jobs and skills, paving the way for a fair, inclusive and resilient socio-economic recovery from the COVID-19 crisis. ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2021:102:FIN The European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan]'' (COM(2021) 102 final) outlines specific actions and headline targets to improve [[Glossary:Employment|employment]], skills and social protection across the EU. One of its principal targets is to have, by 2030, an EU [[Glossary:Employment rate|employment rate]] of at least 78% among people aged 20 to 64. Employment and social policies offer a broad range of practical benefits for people living in the EU, including employment support, mobility within the labour market, skills development, social protection and inclusion, as well as range of different rights at work. In 2025, there were 259.7 million people aged 20 to 64 in the EU (those considered to be of core working age). Of these, the [[Glossary:Labour force|labour force]] was composed of 209.9 million people, of which 197.7 million were [[Glossary:Employed person - LFS|employed]] and 12.1 million were [[Glossary:Unemployed|unemployed]] (not employed, actively seeking and available for work). There were 49.8 million people [[Glossary:People_outside_the_labour_force|outside the labour force]], for example students, retired people (if under the age of 65), people caring for other family members, volunteers and those unable to work due to a long-term illness or disability. Across NUTS level 2 regions, the Polish capital region of Warszawski stołeczny (86.9%) and the Czech capital region of Praha (86.0%) recorded the highest employment rates in 2025 among people aged 20 to 64. There were 2 other capitals that also ranked among the 10 EU regions with the highest employment rates: Sostinės regionas in Lithuania and Noord-Holland in the Netherlands. This chapter examines employment and unemployment patterns across EU regions, offering a detailed analysis of regional labour markets, with a focus on young people. It highlights key indicators such as employment rates, [[Glossary:Young_people_neither_in_employment_nor_in_education_and_training_(NEET)|young people who are neither in employment nor in education and training (NEET)]] and unemployment rates, providing an insight into regional disparities. [[File:Value of sold production for 1 kg of fresh bread in the EU, 2015-2025 (€ per kg).png|thumb|center|700px|Value of sold production for 1 kg of fresh bread in the EU, 2015-2025 (€ per kg)
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/69faf059-e8f0-4dd3-8a95-0a94be39357b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-26T16:18:35Z DS-059358] [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7e0aab97-cd48-4515-b588-3bd157e45efc?lang=en&createdAt=2026-08-20T12:50:53Z DS-059367]|alt= a line chart showing the Value of sold production for one kilogram of fresh bread in EU from 2015 to 2025 and a vertical bar chart showing the Value of sold production for one kilogram of fresh bread by country in the Member States and some candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]

{| style="background-color: #f5faff; vertical-align: top" class="wikitable" |- ! Header text !! Header text |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |- | Example || Example |} ===Source data for figures and maps=== {{Template:Excel|filename=RYB2026 CH04 Labour market.xlsx|title=Regional labour market statistics}} ===Data sources=== The information presented in this chapter relates to annual averages derived from the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|EU’s labour force survey (EU-LFS)]]. Eurostat compiles and publishes labour market statistics for the EU and individual EU countries, as well as for EU regions. In addition, data are also available for 3 EFTA countries – Iceland, Norway and Switzerland – and several candidate countries – Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Serbia and Türkiye – and their statistical regions. The EU-LFS population generally consists of people aged 15 or over living in private households; definitions are aligned with those provided by the International Labour Organization (ILO). EU-LFS microdata are collected through a survey to obtain information on an individual’s demographic background, labour status, employment characteristics of their main job, hours worked, employment characteristics of their second job (if relevant), time-related underemployment, the search for employment, education and training, previous work experience of people not in employment and their income. These statistics are aggregated by region and are generally published down to NUTS level 2. When evaluating regional information from the EU-LFS, it is important to bear in mind that the information presented relates to the region where the respondent has their permanent residence and that this may be different to the region where their place of work is situated as a result of commuter flows. The collection of EU-LFS data up to and including reference year 2020 was conducted by national statistical authorities in accordance with Council Regulation (EEC) No 577/98. A new legal basis was introduced for EU-LFS data from 2021 onwards: [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32019R1700 Regulation (EU) 2019/1700] establishing a common framework for European statistics relating to persons and households, based on data at individual level collected from samples. Furthermore, [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2019/2240 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2240] specifies the technical items of the dataset, establishing formats for the transmission of information and specifying the detailed arrangements and content of the quality reports on the organisation of the sample survey. This change in legal basis implies a break in series between 2020 and 2021; results obtained before and after 1 January 2021 are consequently not fully comparable. Some countries/regions have other quality concerns that may impact geographical comparability. *Changes in survey methodology led to a break in series for German data in 2020. Therefore, data for Germany from 2020 onwards should not be compared directly with those for previous years. In addition, data collection during 2020 was impacted by technical issues and COVID-19 measures and hence there is a low degree of reliability for some regions. For more information, please refer the online methodological publication for the [[EU_labour_force_survey|EU’s labour force survey]]. ==== Indicator definitions ==== The '''labour force''' includes all people who were either employed or unemployed during the reference week. This aggregate includes people offering their work capacity on the labour market: as such it reflects the supply side. In the context of the EU-LFS, employed people include those aged 15 to 89 who, during the reference week, performed work – even if just for 1 hour – for pay, profit or family gain. Alternatively, the person was not at work, but had a job or business from which they were temporarily absent, for example due to illness, holiday, maternity or paternity leave, job-related training, paid parental leave or working time arrangements. This definition follows guidelines of the [https://www.ilo.org/ International Labour Organization (ILO)]. Within this publication, most labour force indicators are for a narrower definition of core working-age people, namely people aged 20 to 64. '''Employment rate''' The employment rate is the percentage of employed people in relation to the comparable population. The comparison is generally made within the population of core working-age (defined within this publication as people aged 20 to 64). Regional labour market disparities are measured using the population-weighted coefficient of variation. This indicator compares the standard deviation of regional employment rates with the national employment rate, while weighting each region by its population size. The aggregated EU value is calculated using all available regions in EU countries. However, dispersion across countries are only published for countries that have more than 4 NUTS level 2 regions. As a result, data are not presented for Estonia, Ireland, Croatia, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Slovenia or Slovakia; equally, they are not published for Iceland, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia or Serbia. The gender employment gap is defined as the employment rate for men minus the employment rate for women (among people aged 20 to 64). Employment rates may be calculated for other cohorts according to a range of socio-economic criteria, for example, by educational attainment. Within this publication, the employment rate of people with different levels of educational attainment concerns people aged 25 to 64 who had completed: *no more than a lower secondary education (as defined by the [[International_Standard_Classification_of_Education_(ISCED)|international standard classification of education (ISCED)]] levels 0 to 2) *an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (as defined by ISCED levels 3 to 4) *a tertiary level of education (as defined by ISCED levels 5 to 8) – in other words, people who had completed a short-cycle tertiary education, bachelor’s, master’s or doctoral (PhD) degree. '''Young people neither in employment nor in education or training (NEET)''' The share of young people who are neither in employment nor in education and training, abbreviated as NEET, corresponds to the share of the population (of a given age group and sex) that is not employed and not involved in further (formal or non-formal) education or training during the 4 weeks ending with the reference week. The numerator refers to people meeting these 2 conditions, while the denominator is the population (of the same age group and sex), excluding respondents who did not answer the question in the survey about participation in regular (formal) education and training. For the purpose of this publication, the share of young people neither in employment nor in education or training relates to people aged 15 to 29. '''Unemployment''' Eurostat‘s unemployment statistics are based on guidelines provided by the ILO. Unemployed people are those aged 15 to 74 who are without work, but who have actively sought employment in the 4 weeks preceding the survey’s reference week (or have already found a job to start within the subsequent 3 months) and are available to begin work within the following 2 weeks. The unemployment rate is defined as the number of unemployed people expressed as a percentage of the labour force of the same age (defined within this publication as people aged 15 to 74). The youth unemployment rate is defined as the number of unemployed people aged 15 to 29 expressed as a percentage of the labour force of the same age. * Long-term unemployment refers to the number of people aged 15 to 74 who are out of work and have been actively seeking employment for at least a year. * The long-term unemployment ratio is the number of long-term unemployed people expressed as a percentage of the number of unemployed people of the same age. ===Context=== '''Safeguarding jobs and ensuring fair working conditions''' Since 2020, the European Commission has introduced several initiatives to support labour market resilience in line with the European Pillar of Social Rights. *''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:32020R0672 Council Regulation (EU) 2020/672]'' established the [https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/eu-financial-assistance/sure_en European instrument for temporary support to mitigate unemployment risks in an emergency (SURE)] to protect jobs and protect income during the COVID-19 crisis. *The [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/eu-employment-policies/youth-employment-support_en Youth employment support] initiative reinforced the [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/eu-employment-policies/youth-employment-support/reinforced-youth-guarantee_en Youth Guarantee], providing additional support to vocational training, apprenticeships and entrepreneurship opportunities for young people. *The [https://commission.europa.eu/funding-tenders/find-funding/eu-funding-programmes/just-transition-fund_en Just Transition Fund] helps communities manage the socio-economic costs/effects of the shift to a climate-neutral economy. *''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2022/2041/oj Directive (EU) 2022/2041 on adequate minimum wages in the European Union]'' promotes fair minimum wages, strengthens collective bargaining and supports upward social convergence across EU countries. *A ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=oj:JOC_2023_041_R_0001 Council Recommendation on adequate minimum income ensuring active inclusion 2023/C 41/01]'' complements earlier initiatives by addressing income protection for individuals outside employment. *The EU has also addressed emerging forms of employment through ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/2831 Directive (2024/2831) on improving working conditions in platform work]'' – an initiative aimed at strengthening conditions for those working with digital labour platforms (for example, food delivery riders or taxi drivers). *The [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/union-skills_en Union of skills] (COM(2025) 90 final) aims to strengthen lifelong learning, upskilling and reskilling opportunities, support enterprise competitiveness – particularly for SMEs – and improve the transparency and recognition of skills and qualifications across the EU. '''Promoting gender equality in the labour market''' The European Commission adopted [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0097 A Roadmap for Women’s Rights] (COM(2025) 97 final) in March 2025. It addresses emerging gender equality challenges, including technology-facilitated discrimination through a ‘Declaration of principles for a gender-equal society’. Although inequalities still exist, the EU has made significant progress in terms of gender equality over recent decades. The European Commission’s [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/gender-equality/gender-equality-strategy_en Gender equality strategy 2026–30] aims to build on this by countering gender stereotypes, promoting gender mainstreaming (including gender perspectives, for example in policies, to promote equality), closing gender gaps and increasing women’s participation in decision-making. The strategy aims to strengthen action across several policy areas, including: *tackling gender-based cyberviolence *enhancing women’s health (for example, through work addressing the social and economic impacts of the women’s health gap, including conditions such as menopause) *reducing gender gaps in employment and promoting equality in the labour market *ensuring that EU funding is gender-sensitive. '''Investing in people: funding and skills development''' The [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/funding/european-social-fund-plus-esf_en European Social Fund Plus (ESF+)] is the EU’s main financial instrument for investing in people. With a budget of €142.7 billion allocated for 2021 to 2027, it supports employment, social inclusion, poverty reduction and youth investment. The ESF+ is central to advancing the European Pillar of Social Rights and the post-pandemic recovery. To respond to changes in labour markets – especially those driven by the green and digital transitions – the EU has prioritised skills development through initiatives such as the ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0274 European Skills Agenda for sustainable competitiveness, social fairness and resilience]'' (COM(2020) 274 final), the [https://year-of-skills.europa.eu/index_en European Year of Skills] launched in 2023 and extended into 2024, and ''The Union of Skills''. '''Towards a fair and inclusive future labour market''' Labour markets across the EU are adapting to technological progress, demographic change and sustainability goals. Policymakers have introduced measures to improve employment access for underrepresented groups at risk of exclusion – such as young people, older workers and people with disabilities – while, at the same time, supporting regional adaptation to structural change. The growth of platform work and other non-standard forms of employment has also reinforced the need for fair working conditions. A key initiative in this area is the ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52024DC0131 Labour and skills shortages in the EU: an action plan]'' (COM(2024) 131 final) which provides a coordinated policy response to persistent labour market imbalances, focusing on: *increasing labour market participation among underrepresented groups *advancing skills development and training *improving working conditions in critical sectors *facilitating intra-EU mobility *attracting international talent. ===Other articles=== *[[Employment - annual statistics|Employment – annual statistics]] *[[Employment_statistics_-_utilisation_of_job_skills|Employment statistics – utilisation of job skills]] *[[EU labour force survey]] – online publication *[[EU labour force survey statistics]] – online publication *[[Flexibility_at_work_-_statistics|Flexibility at work – statistics]] *[[Gender_statistics|Gender statistics]] *[[Labour market flow statistics in the EU]] *[[Labour market slack - employment supply and demand mismatch|Labour market slack – employment supply and demand mismatch]] *[[Main_place_of_work_and_commuting_time_-_statistics|Main place of work and commuting time – statistics]] *[[Participation of young people in education and the labour market]] *[[Self-employment_statistics|Self-employment statistics]] 1 Data extracted in February 2023 Planned article update: This indicator has retired After nearly 30 years of service, the most productive terminator in Eurostat retires. Between 2011 and 2023, LCN carried out over 23 000 edits in Statistics Explained. [[Image:Achievement levels in main production categories, LCN, 2022 (%) V4.png|centre|750px]] Louise’s first contact with Eurostat was on 6th December 1994, and little did anyone suspect that this la petite Suédoise will in less than 30 years become one of the most respected and, yes, even feared Eurostat forces. Known for her swift decision making, gentle and not so gentle nudges and reminders, coupled with equal measures of kindness and a sympathetic ear, Louise is an inspiration and motivation for her team and colleagues. This background article looks at some of the highlights of Louise’s years in the Statistics Explained and Publications team. === Editing intensity indicator for LCN: highest in Eurostat history === Louise’s Statistics Explained account was created on 22 November 2011 at 8.29:30 o’clock. Until 7 February 2023 eob, Louise has done 23 369 edits, which gives for the structural indicator Editing intensity (Average number of Statistics Explained edits per actual working day) the value 9.9 edits per actual working day (unofficial Eurostat estimate based on the following assumptions on averages per calendar year: 243 working days - 31 days annual leave - 2 days of sick or special leave = 210 actual working days). [[Image:Dissemination products output by LCN, by product type, 2022 (number) V2.png|thumb|centre|750px|Figure 1: Dissemination products output by LCN, by product type, 2022 (number)
''Source:'' Dissemination products team]] === Data sources === A full overview of the career history of Louise Corselli-Nordblad can be found in Sysper2. === See also === * Young Swedish women most likely to marry in 2022 (news item) * Production indicators for Eurostat communication officers * EU statistics on income and living conditions of Swedes in Luxembourg (background article) * Eurostat publishes yet another style guide (news item) === Publications === *Key figures on Louise Corselli-Nordblad, special edition === Legislation === *Regulation (EU) No 1011/1960 {{Unit|topic=}}

Eurostat regional yearbook; 2026 edition; flagship publication; EU; regional statistics; NUTS; labour market; employment; focus on young people in the labour market; unemployment; employment rates; gender employment gap; young people neither in employment nor in education and training; NEETs; unemployment rate; long-term unemployment rate [[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH04 RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|380px|''Source:'' Eurostat]] Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 This article forms part of the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026]'', an annual [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications flagship publication]. It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the [[Glossary:EU|EU]], [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate]] countries. A [[Regional_yearbook_introduction#A_short_reading_guide|short reading guide]] is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps. All but 1 of the EU regions had an employment rate of at least 50.0% in 2025, with the lowest level recorded in the French outermost region of Mayotte (36.9%). Relatively low rates were recorded in some other outermost regions of France, as well as southern Italy and the Spanish autonomous regions of Ciudades de Ceuta y Melilla. In 2025, NEET rates were below 10.0% in every region of Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Sweden, as well as in Luxembourg and Malta.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:SDG wheel icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:Compet and SDG wheel icons RYB2026_small.png]]
[[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH04_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/194b8ae4-edc2-4b87-a518-a704bd1950c3?lang=en lfst_r_lfe2emprt)]|alt="An infographic showing the ten EU regions with the highest employment rates for people aged 20 to 64. Data are shown in percent for 2025. Data are presented for the EU and selected NUTS level 2 regions with the highest rates. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image."]]
On 4 March 2021, the European Commission set out its ambition to build a stronger, more social EU by focusing on jobs and skills, paving the way for a fair, inclusive and resilient socio-economic recovery from the COVID-19 crisis. ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2021:102:FIN The European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan]'' (COM(2021) 102 final) outlines specific actions and headline targets to improve [[Glossary:Employment|employment]], skills and social protection across the EU. One of its principal targets is to have, by 2030, an EU [[Glossary:Employment rate|employment rate]] of at least 78% among people aged 20 to 64. Employment and social policies offer a broad range of practical benefits for people living in the EU, including employment support, mobility within the labour market, skills development, social protection and inclusion, as well as range of different rights at work. In 2025, there were 259.7 million people aged 20 to 64 in the EU (those considered to be of core working age). Of these, the [[Glossary:Labour force|labour force]] was composed of 209.9 million people, of which 197.7 million were [[Glossary:Employed person - LFS|employed]] and 12.1 million were [[Glossary:Unemployed|unemployed]] (not employed, actively seeking and available for work). There were 49.8 million people [[Glossary:People_outside_the_labour_force|outside the labour force]], for example students, retired people (if under the age of 65), people caring for other family members, volunteers and those unable to work due to a long-term illness or disability. Across NUTS level 2 regions, the Polish capital region of Warszawski stołeczny (86.9%) and the Czech capital region of Praha (86.0%) recorded the highest employment rates in 2025 among people aged 20 to 64. There were 2 other capitals that also ranked among the 10 EU regions with the highest employment rates: Sostinės regionas in Lithuania and Noord-Holland in the Netherlands. This chapter examines employment and unemployment patterns across EU regions, offering a detailed analysis of regional labour markets, with a focus on young people. It highlights key indicators such as employment rates, [[Glossary:Young_people_neither_in_employment_nor_in_education_and_training_(NEET)|young people who are neither in employment nor in education and training (NEET)]] and unemployment rates, providing an insight into regional disparities. ===Employment===
'''More about the data: employment rate targets''' One of the EU’s key policy objectives is to increase the number and share of people in work. This goal has been central to [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/eu-employment-policies_en EU employment policies] since the launch of the European employment strategy in 1997 and was subsequently integrated into the Lisbon and Europe 2020 strategies. The employment rate is a key indicator in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/dashboard/social-scoreboard/ social scoreboard], which monitors the implementation of the [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/european-pillar-social-rights-building-fairer-and-more-inclusive-european-union_en European Pillar of Social Rights]. By 2030, the EU has set a target of having an employment rate of at least 78% among its core working-age population (those aged 20 to 64). This age range reflects the growing share of young people who remain within education into their late teens and beyond, potentially limiting early labour market participation, while most EU residents retire by the age of 65. Individual EU countries have different employment rate targets. To achieve the overall EU target of 78% by 2030, individual countries presented and agreed national targets in June 2022. These are generally higher for countries that already had relatively high rates. For example, the target for Hungary has been set at 85.0%, for Malta at 84.6% and for Germany at 83.0%. The employment rate is also included in the EU’s [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/sdi/overview sustainable development goals (SDGs)] indicator set. Goal 8 seeks to promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, through full and productive employment and decent work for all.
'''''In 2025, the EU’s employment rate was 1.9 percentage points below its 2030 target''''' Prior to the COVID-19 crisis, the EU’s employment rate for the core working-age population (people aged 20 to 64) increased steadily for 6 consecutive years, reaching 72.7% by 2019. This upward development was interrupted in 2020 when the pandemic contributed to a fall of 1.0 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]]. However, the employment rate rebounded in 2021, returning to above its pre-pandemic level, and continued to rise in subsequent years, with particularly sharp increases in 2021 (up 1.4 points) and 2022 (up 1.5 points). By 2025, the EU’s employment rate had climbed to an all-time high (time series starts in 2009) of 76.1%, which was 1.9 points below the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan target for 2030. '''Map 1''' shows the employment rate in 2025 for NUTS level 2 regions. Almost half (47.1%) of all EU regions – 115 out of 244 regions – had already reached or surpassed the EU’s target of 78.0% by 2025. These 115 regions were found in clusters, with high concentrations in Czechia (all 8 regions), Denmark (4 out of 5 regions), Germany (34 out of 38 regions; the exceptions being Bremen, Berlin, Düsseldorf and Arnsberg), Ireland (all 3 regions), Hungary (6 out of 8 regions), the Netherlands (all 12 regions), Portugal (7 out of 9 regions), Slovakia (3 out of 4 regions) and Sweden (all 8 regions); this group also included Estonia, Cyprus and Malta. In 2025, a small group of 6 regions recorded the highest employment rates among NUTS level 2 regions, with rates of at least 85.0%: *Warszawski stołeczny, the Polish capital region (86.9%) *Praha, the Czech capital region (86.0%) *the archipelago of Åland in Finland (85.5%) *Utrecht in the Netherlands (85.4%) *the southern German region of Oberbayern (85.1%) *the northern Swedish region of Mellersta Norrland (85.0%). Beyond these 6 regions, a further 23 regions posted employment rates of at least 83.5% in 2025. These regions were concentrated in Germany (9 regions) and the Netherlands (6 regions), while Hungary and Sweden each accounted for 2 regions. The remaining regions in this group of 23 were distributed across Czechia, Lithuania, Malta and Slovakia (with a single region from each). In 2025, all multi-regional northern, eastern and southern EU countries reported that their capital region had a higher employment rate than their national average. For example, Romania’s capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov had an employment rate of 81.1%, which was 12.1 percentage points above the national average of 69.0%. By contrast, this pattern was reversed in 3 western EU countries – Belgium, Germany and Austria – where the capital regions recorded employment rates that were below their respective national averages. Indeed, a closer inspection reveals that Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest (63.9%) and Wien (71.3%) registered the lowest employment rates across all regions of Belgium and Austria, respectively. '''''In 2025, the French outermost regions of Mayotte and Guyane and the southern Italian regions of Calabria, Campania and Sicilia recorded the lowest employment rates''''' Many of the regions with relatively low employment rates were rural, sparsely populated, or regions on the periphery of the EU. This pattern was particularly apparent in southern regions of Spain and Italy, much of Greece, some regions in Romania, and the outermost regions of France. These regions were typically characterised by limited employment opportunities, especially for individuals with intermediate and high skill levels. Former industrial heartlands form another group of regions characterised by relatively low employment rates. Some of these have witnessed the negative impact of globalisation on traditional sectors of their economies (such as coal mining, steel or textiles manufacturing). Examples include a band of regions running from north-east France into the Région wallonne (Belgium). In 2025, approximately a quarter of all EU regions – 64 out of 244 regions – recorded employment rates below 74.0%. Among others, this group comprised: *11 French regions, including all 5 outermost regions; Mayotte and Guyane recorded the lowest employment rates in the EU, at 36.9% and 50.0%, respectively *11 Italian regions, concentrated almost exclusively in central and southern Italy, with the lowest rates observed in Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicilia (51.4%) *11 out of 13 Greek regions, the exceptions being Kriti and Peloponnisos *11 Spanish regions, many of them peripheral, island or predominantly rural regions *7 of the 8 Romanian regions, the exception being the capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov *the capital regions of Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest in Belgium (63.9%), Lazio in Italy (69.3%), Wien in Austria (71.3%) and Attiki in Greece (73.1%); Luxembourg (73.9%) also recorded a relatively low employment rate.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:SDG wheel icon RYB2026.png|50px]]
Map 1: Employment rate
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/194b8ae4-edc2-4b87-a518-a704bd1950c3?lang=en lfst_r_lfe2emprtn]) [[Image:Compet and SDG wheel icons RYB2026_small.png]] [[Image:Employment rate (% of people aged 20–64, by NUTS 2 regions, 2025)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Employment rate
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/194b8ae4-edc2-4b87-a518-a704bd1950c3?lang=en lfst_r_lfe2emprtn])]] '''''In 2025, Italy had the highest regional disparity for employment rates''''' Several EU countries face considerable labour market disparities across their regions, with labour shortages in some regions contrasted against persistently high unemployment in others. A population-weighted coefficient of variation provides a means to analyse these inter-regional disparities. '''Figure 1''' shows that, in 2025, Italy had the highest regional disparities in employment rates, with a coefficient of variation of 15.1%. Broadly, there was a north-south split: for example, the Alpine region of Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen recorded the highest employment rate in Italy (80.0%), while the southern region of Calabria had the lowest (50.3%). Romania (8.0%), Belgium (7.9%) and Spain (6.1%) had the next highest coefficients of variation for regional employment rates in 2025: *in Belgium, the highest regional employment rates were generally recorded in Vlaams Gewest, while lower rates were observed in Région wallonne and particularly in the capital region *in Romania, the highest regional employment rate was in the capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov (81.1%), with notably lower rates observed in all other regions, in particular, Sud-Vest Oltenia (61.7%) and Sud-Est (62.1%) *in Spain, the highest regional employment rates were generally recorded in northern and eastern regions, as well as the capital region; lower rates were observed in peripheral, southern and western regions. At the other end of the range, the lowest regional disparities in employment rates – with a coefficient of variation of 2.0% or less – were recorded in the [[Glossary:Nordic Member States|Nordic EU countries]] of Finland and Sweden, as well as the Netherlands and Portugal. '''Figure 1''' shows that regional employment rates converged to some degree between 2015 and 2025. The coefficient of variation for the EU as a whole fell from 12.5% to 9.2%. In 15 (out of 17) EU countries for which data are available, the disparities between inter-regional employment rates narrowed. The largest falls – in relative terms – occurred in Finland, Portugal and Spain, where the coefficient decreased by at least 40%. By contrast, Denmark and Romania were the only EU countries to report an increase in regional disparities, rising 22.2% and 2.6%, respectively.

'''''The EU’s gender employment gap was 9.7 percentage points in 2025''''' The gender employment gap is included in the EU’s SDGs indicator set. Goal 5 seeks to achieve gender equality by, among other actions, ending all forms of discrimination, violence, and any harmful practices against women and girls, while promoting women’s social and economic empowerment. Long-standing challenges related to female participation in the labour force are reflected in persistent gender gaps in employment and pay. These gaps exist for a variety of reasons, including: *women often bear a disproportionate share of unpaid care and household chores that may limit their availability for paid employment *gender bias and discrimination when hiring, promoting and paying women *fewer women in leadership positions to draw attention to gender-related policies or to mentor more junior female staff *a lack of affordable childcare and support for working parents *disincentives in tax and benefit system that can lead to second earners bearing a higher tax burden when they choose to participate in the labour market *occupational segregation, with women often concentrated in specific activities that are characterised by lower wages and/or fewer opportunities for career development. In 2025, the EU employment rate for men aged 20 to 64 was 80.9%, while the corresponding rate for women of the same age was considerably lower, at 71.2%. This resulted in a gender employment gap – defined here as the difference between male and female employment rates – of 9.7 percentage points. As part of its broader target to increase the overall employment rate to 78% by 2030, the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan also includes a subgoal of halving the gender employment gap. This implies reducing the gap to 5.7 percentage points by 2030, equivalent to an average annual decrease of 0.5 points from 2019 onwards. According to the latest available data, the gender employment gap in the EU fell from 10.0 percentage points in 2024 to 9.7 points in 2025. '''''In 2025, more than a quarter of EU regions already had a gender employment gap below the 2030 target''''' As noted above, regions with relatively narrow gender employment gaps are often characterised by high overall employment rates, which may reflect more inclusive labour markets, higher female participation and greater availability of part-time or flexible working arrangements. In 2025, 65 out of 244 NUTS level 2 regions – corresponding to more than a quarter of all EU regions – recorded a gender employment gap of less than 5.7 percentage points, thereby already surpassing the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan target for 2030 (see '''Map 2'''). These 65 regions were mainly concentrated in France (14 regions), Germany (12 regions), Sweden (7 out of 8 regions), Belgium (5 regions), Portugal (5 regions) and Finland (all 5 regions); among others, they also included all of the Baltic regions, as well as both regions in Slovenia. Some of the lowest gender employment gaps were recorded in Baltic and Nordic regions. In 2025, there were 8 regions where the gap between male and female employment rates was less than 1.0 percentage points. In 5 of these regions, male employment rates remained slightly higher. This group included: *the Finnish regions of Etelä-Suomi, Länsi-Suomi (both 0.1 percentage points) and Åland (0.7 percentage points) *Estonia (0.5 percentage points) *the Lithuanian region of Vidurio ir vakarų Lietuvos regionas (0.7 percentage points). Furthermore, there were 3 regions that reported higher female (than male) employment rates: *the Lithuanian capital region of Sostinės regionas, where the female employment rate was 3.3 points higher than the male rate *the French outermost regions of Martinique and Guadeloupe, where female employment rates exceeded male rates by 5.0 and 1.0 percentage points, respectively. This atypical pattern may reflect a combination of factors, including higher male participation in informal or seasonal activities (such as fishing), alongside higher levels of female employment in the relatively stable public-sector and service-sector occupations. '''''The widest gender employment gaps were recorded in the central Greek region of Sterea Elláda and the southern Italian regions of Puglia, Campania and Sicilia''''' Despite some progress in reducing the gender employment gap, female employment rates continue to lag behind male rates in the vast majority of EU regions. Regions with wider gaps are often characterised by high unemployment, weaker and more informal labour markets, and a higher share of women outside the labour force. Low female employment rates may reflect a combination of constraints: women are more likely to take on unpaid family and caregiving responsibilities, while limited access to affordable childcare and support for older people, alongside persistent expectations around traditional family roles, can further reduce their participation in paid employment. In 2025, 26 NUTS level 2 regions reported gender employment gaps of at least 18.0 percentage points. These regions were concentrated in southern and eastern EU countries: *10 of the 13 regions in Greece (the exceptions being Attiki, Ipeiros and Kriti) *8 regions in Italy, 7 of which were in the south (the exception being Veneto) *5 of the 8 regions in Romania (the exceptions being Bucureşti-Ilfov, Nord-Vest and Vest) *the Spanish autonomous regions of Ciudad de Melilla and Ciudad de Ceuta *the French outermost region of Mayotte. At the very upper end of the distribution, the widest gender employment gaps in the EU were observed in: *the central Greek region of Sterea Elláda, which recorded a gender employment gap of 29.0 percentage points in 2025; this may reflect, at least in part, a high male employment rate (the highest in Greece), with a concentration of jobs in traditionally male-dominated industrial sectors *the southern Italian regions of Puglia (28.7 percentage points), Campania (28.2 points), Sicilia (28.1 points), Calabria (25.4 points) and Basilicata (25.3 points) *Sud-Muntenia in southern Romania (25.1 points), the only other region in the EU with a gap of at least 25.0 percentage points.
