'''More about the data: employment rates by educational attainment''' An individual’s level of educational attainment can play a key role when seeking employment. People with a tertiary level of educational attainment (as defined by the [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|international standard classification of education (ISCED 2011 levels 5 to 8)]]) generally enjoy the most success when trying to find work. They also tend to be better shielded from the risks of unemployment than their peers with lower levels of educational attainment. The data presented in this section concern people aged 25 to 64, as this represents a cohort of individuals who have generally completed their education or training and are most likely to be actively participating in the labour market. As such, it excludes younger individuals who may still be studying, as well as older individuals who may be in retirement.
In 2025, 185.1 million people aged 25 to 64 were employed across the EU. The largest share of this cohort consisted of people with an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (ISCED levels 3 to 4; 44.3%), closely followed by those with a tertiary level of educational attainment (ISCED levels 5 to 8; 41.5%). A relatively small share of the EU workforce had no more than a lower secondary education (ISCED levels 0 to 2; 14.1%). The strong links between educational attainment and employment opportunities are reflected in the latest EU employment rates for 2025: *58.9% for people with no more than a lower secondary education (hereafter referred to as a low level of education) *78.5% for people with an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (a medium level of education) *88.1% for people with a tertiary level of education (a high level of education). '''Map 3''' presents employment rates in 2025 for people aged 25 to 64 according to these 3 different levels of educational attainment. *There were 53 NUTS level 2 regions where fewer than half of all people with a low level of education were in employment. By contrast, employment rates for people with medium or high levels of education exceeded 50.0% in every region of the EU. *There were 83 NUTS level 2 regions where at least 90.0% of all people with a high level of education were in employment. By contrast, employment rates for people with low or medium levels of education remained consistently below 90.0% across every region of the EU. '''''In 2025, the Slovak region of Východné Slovensko recorded an employment rate of 25.6% among people with a low level of education, the smallest share among EU regions''''' The first part of '''Map 3''' shows employment rates for people aged 25 to 64 with a low level of education. In 2025, there were 53 NUTS level 2 regions with employment rates below 50.0% for this cohort. This group included two capital regions: Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest (Belgium) and Grad Zagreb (Croatia). These 53 regions were mainly concentrated in: *eastern EU countries (excluding Czechia, Hungary and Slovenia) *Belgium, particularly in the south *north-eastern France and the outermost regions of France *southern Italy. In 2025, the lowest employment rates for people aged 25 to 64 with a low level of education were recorded in the eastern Slovak region of Východné Slovensko (25.6%) and the French outermost regions of Mayotte (27.0%) and Guyane (28.3%); in other words, around a quarter of people in this cohort were in employment. A further 8 regions reported employment rates below 40.0%: *the Romanian regions of Sud-Est (36.9%), Sud-Vest Oltenia (37.1%) and Centru (38.4%) *Panonska Hrvatska in Croatia (37.6%) *Severozapaden in Bulgaria (38.3%) *the southern Italian regions of Campania (38.6%) and Sicilia (38.8%) *the French outermost region of Guadeloupe (39.2%). '''''Employment rates for people with a medium level of education were generally low across southern Italy, with Calabria recording the lowest rate (56.0% in 2025)''''' The second map shows employment rates for people aged 25 to 64 with a medium level of education. In 2025, there were 10 NUTS level 2 regions that recorded an employment rate of at least 87.0% for this cohort, they included: *4 regions from Czechia (including the capital region of Praha) *3 regions from Portugal *Malta *Åland in Finland *Pest in Hungary. At the lower end of the distribution, there were 3 regions where, in 2025, fewer than 60.0% of people with a medium level of education were in employment: *the southern Italian regions of Calabria (56.0%) and Campania (59.2%) *the Belgian capital region – Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest (58.3%). '''''The highest employment rate among tertiary-educated people was recorded in the Portuguese Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6% in 2025)''''' The third map shows employment rates for people aged 25 to 64 with a high level of education. In 2025, there were 83 NUTS level 2 regions across the EU that recorded employment rates of at least 90.0% for this cohort. These regions were mainly clustered across: *Bulgaria (all 6 regions) *Croatia (3 out of 4 regions) *Lithuania (both regions) *Hungary (all 8 regions) *the Netherlands (8 out of 12 regions) *Poland (16 out of 17 regions) *Portugal (8 out of 9 regions) *Romania (all 8 regions) *Slovenia (both regions) *Slovakia (all 4 regions) *Malta had a similarly high level. The highest proportion of tertiary-educated people in employment was recorded in the Portuguese island region of Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%). Employment rates above 93.0% were also observed in 5 regions located in eastern EU countries: *the capital regions of Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (93.6%), Warszawski stołeczny in Poland (93.5%) and Bratislavský kraj in Slovakia (93.3%) *the Romanian regions of Nord-Est (93.4%) and Centru (93.3%). In 2025, employment rates for people aged 25 to 64 with a tertiary level of education were generally higher in capital regions than their respective national averages. This may reflect the ability of capital regions to attract highly qualified individuals, exerting considerable ‘pull effects’ through the diverse educational, employment and social/lifestyle opportunities that they offer. This pattern was particularly evident in several eastern and southern EU countries, for example: *in Czechia, the employment rate for tertiary-educated people in the capital region of Praha was 2.6 percentage points above the national average *in Spain, the rate in the capital region of Comunidad de Madrid was 2.2 percentage points above the national average. A similar, although less pronounced, situation was observed in Slovakia, Greece, Croatia, Poland, Denmark, Bulgaria and Lithuania, where the gap between these 2 rates also exceeded 1.0 percentage points. By contrast, there were 4 western EU countries where employment rates for tertiary-educated people in the capital region were at least 1.0 percentage points below the national average: *in Belgium, the employment rate for tertiary-educated people in the capital Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest was 6.1 percentage points below the national average *in Austria, the rate in the capital region of Wien was 4.5 percentage points below the national average. A similar, although less pronounced, pattern was observed in Germany and France, where the gap between the capital region and the national rate was 2.9 and 1.0 percentage points, respectively. There were 4 regions across the EU where, in 2025, the employment rate for people aged 25 to 64 with a high level of education was below 78.5%. These regions were predominantly rural, typically characterised by relatively large agricultural sectors and more limited opportunities for highly skilled employment. They were exclusively located in southern EU countries: *3 regions in Italy – Calabria (73.1%, the lowest rate in the EU), Sicilia and Campania *Ionia Nisia (75.8%) in Greece.

'''More about the data: young people neither in employment nor in education and training (NEET)''' The share of young people (aged 15 to 29) who are neither in employment nor in education and training (NEET) provides a useful measure for studying the vulnerability of young people in terms of their labour market participation and social exclusion. The NEET rate is expressed relative to the total population of the same age (15 to 29); the numerator includes not only young people who are unemployed but also young people who are outside the labour force for reasons other than education or training (for example, because they are unable to work for health reasons, caring for family members, volunteering or travelling). Within the framework of the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan, the EU has set a policy target to reduce the NEET rate from 12.6% (in 2019) to 9.0% by 2030. This target forms part of broader efforts to strengthen labour market participation and improve social inclusion among young people. Lowering the share of young people who are neither in employment nor in education and training is also considered important for helping to address skills shortages and supporting the EU’s long-term economic competitiveness. The NEET rate is also included in the EU’s SDG indicator set. Goal 8 seeks to promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all.
'''''In 2025, 11.0% of young people aged 15 to 29 in the EU were neither in employment nor in education and training''''' Economic crises tend to impact young people disproportionately, as they are more likely to work under temporary and other atypical contracts that are easier to terminate. The NEET rate helps assess the share of young people who have not transitioned from education or training to employment. It is generally seen as a more comprehensive measure than the unemployment rate, as it more closely reflects young people’s risk of social and labour market exclusion. Having peaked at 16.1% in 2013, the EU’s NEET rate subsequently fell during 6 consecutive years. The COVID-19 pandemic reversed this trend, pushing the NEET rate up to 13.8% in 2020, after which it resumed its downward trajectory. By 2025, it stood at 11.0%, marking a modest decrease of 0.1 percentage points compared with the previous year. Of the 241 NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available in 2025, 146 regions recorded NEET rates below the EU average of 11.0%. A further 93 regions reported rates above the EU average, while 2 regions – Latvia and Etelä-Suomi in Finland – had the same rate as the EU (see '''Map 4'''). This uneven split suggests a skewed distribution, with relatively few high values pulling the EU average upward. At the upper end of the distribution, 27 regions recorded NEET rates of at least 16.0% among young people aged 15 to 29. The highest rates were generally observed in predominantly rural regions of southern and eastern EU countries, as well as in the French outermost regions. Within this group, 5 regions had NEET rates of at least 25.0%, including: *the French outermost regions of Mayotte (47.2%), Guyane (31.9%) and La Réunion (25.2%), with Mayotte recording the highest NEET rate in the EU *the Romanian regions of Sud-Vest Oltenia (27.9%) and Sud-Est (26.3%) *the Bulgarian region of Severozapaden (25.3%). '''''The lowest NEET rate was in the Hungarian capital region of Budapest, 3.8% in 2025''''' In 2025, 86 NUTS level 2 regions reported a NEET rate of less than 9.0% (the EU’s policy target to be reached by 2030). This group was mainly concentrated in northern Belgium (5 regions, mainly from Vlaams Gewest), Czechia (6 out of 8 regions), Ireland (2 out of 3 regions), northern and central Italy (7 regions), the Netherlands (all 12 regions), Slovenia (both regions), Slovakia (3 out of 4 regions) and Sweden (all 8 regions); it also included Luxembourg and Malta. Looking in more detail at the lower end of the distribution, 24 regions recorded NEET rates below 6.5% in 2025, including: *the capital regions of Hungary, Czechia, Poland, the Netherlands, Bulgaria and Sweden; the Hungarian capital region of Budapest recorded the lowest rate in the EU, at 3.8% *a further 9 regions from the Netherlands (in addition to the capital region of Noord-Holland), with the lowest rate in Utrecht (4.0%); the only Dutch regions to record rates above 9.0% were Drenthe and Friesland *4 regions from Sweden (in addition to the capital region of Stockholm), with the lowest rate observed in Sydsverige (4.6%) *5 other regions with particularly low rates, dispersed across the EU, including Schwaben in southern Germany, Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen in northern Italy, Nyugat-Dunántúl in western Hungary, Prov. West-Vlaanderen in northern Belgium and Centro in Portugal. In 2025, capital regions in the EU generally recorded lower NEET rates than their national averages. There were only 5 exceptions observed among multi-regional EU countries, where the rate in the capital region was higher than the national average: *Berlin in Germany (13.9%), where the share of young people neither in employment nor in education or training was 4.4 percentage points above the national average (9.5%) *Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest in Belgium (12.8%), 3.0 points above the national average (9.8%) *Wien in Austria (12.9%), 2.6 percentage points above the national average (10.3%) *Lazio in Italy (13.7%), slightly above the national average (13.3%) *Eastern and Midland in Ireland (8.3%), marginally above the national average (8.1%).

High levels of youth unemployment can lead to considerable economic and social challenges. Indeed, persistent unemployment among young people is likely to increase the risk of poverty, social exclusion and mental health issues, while reducing lifetime earnings and productivity. It may also contribute to concerns about social cohesion and public confidence in institutions. Youth employment is a key priority, with the EU aiming to reduce youth unemployment and increase the youth employment rate, ensuring young citizens have access to opportunities. The [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/eu-employment-policies/youth-employment-support/reinforced-youth-guarantee_en Youth Guarantee], reinforced in 2020, provides young people with an offer of employment, education, apprenticeship or traineeship within 4 months of becoming unemployed or leaving education. Unemployment rates in the EU vary considerably as a function of age: in 2025, they were highest among young people aged 15 to 29 (11.7%) and lowest among people aged 45 to 54 and aged 55 to 64 (both 4.4%). Subject to data availability, young people systematically faced the highest unemployment rates in every NUTS level 2 region. For example, in the Croatian capital region of Grad Zagreb, the unemployment rate of young people (12.2%) was 4.1 times as high as the overall rate (3.0%), while in the southern Italian region of Sicilia, the unemployment rate of young people (27.2%) was 15.0 percentage points higher than the overall rate (12.2%). '''Map 5''' illustrates the distribution of youth unemployment rates among people aged 15 to 29 across NUTS level 2 regions. In 2025, the highest youth unemployment rates were mainly concentrated in southern EU countries, although several regions in Belgium, France, Romania and Sweden also recorded relatively high rates. By contrast, some of the lowest rates were observed in a band of regions extending from the Netherlands, Germany, northern Italy and Austria through parts of Poland, Czechia and Hungary. In 2025, particularly high youth unemployment rates – of at least 25.0% – were recorded in 11 regions across the EU, including: *the Spanish autonomous regions of Ciudades de Ceuta y Melilla and the western Spanish region of Extremadura *all 5 of the French outermost regions – Mayotte, Martinique, Guadeloupe, Guyane and La Réunion – as well as the French island region of Corse (2024 data) *the southern Italian regions of Campania and Sicilia. At the lower end of the distribution, the lowest youth unemployment rates were generally observed in predominantly urban regions, including several capital regions. In total, there were 9 regions in the EU that recorded rates below 5.0%: *3 capital regions in eastern EU countries – Yugozapaden (Bulgaria), Warszawski stołeczny (Poland) and Praha (Czechia) *2 additional regions in Czechia – Střední Čechy and Jihovýchod *Weser-Ems in north-western Germany *Nyugat-Dunántúl in western Hungary *Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen in northern Italy (2024 data) *Zeeland in the south-west of the Netherlands, which recorded the lowest youth unemployment rate in the EU, at 3.6%. From an economic perspective, unemployment reflects unused labour capacity and can reduce a country’s or region’s productive potential. It also leads to lower tax revenues and higher public spending on social benefits. At the same time, unemployment has significant social impacts. It results in a loss of income for individuals. Beyond these financial effects, it is also associated with a higher risk of poverty, social exclusion, debt and homelessness, and may have adverse effects on (mental) health and overall well-being.
'''More about the data: the unemployment rate''' Within this section, data are presented for people aged 15 to 74; this is the standard age range used by Eurostat and the [[Glossary:International Labour Organization (ILO)|International Labour Organization (ILO)]] for analysing unemployment. The unemployment rate is defined as the share of unemployed people (aged 15 to 74) in the total labour force (in other words, employed and unemployed people) of the same age group. Note that the unemployment rate is not the opposite of the employment rate, as the two indicators use different denominators: the unemployment rate is based on the labour force, while the employment rate is based on the population.
The EU unemployment rate fell from a peak of 11.6% in 2013, declining over 6 consecutive years to 6.8% by 2019. With the onset of the COVID-19 crisis, the rate increased 0.4 percentage points in 2020 and remained almost unchanged in 2021 (down 0.1 points), as the pandemic continued to affect much of the EU economy. Following a marked decline in 2022, unemployment continued to fall in 2023 and 2024 at a more moderate pace, reaching its lowest rate since the start of the time series in 2009. The rate was unchanged in 2025, at 6.0%. In 2025, there were 13.3 million unemployed people aged 15 to 74 across the EU. Compared with 2024, the number of unemployed people in 2025 was 223 000 higher. '''Map 6''' presents unemployment rates (for people aged 15 to 74) across NUTS level 2 regions. In 2025, the distribution of regional unemployment rates was slightly skewed towards lower values: of the 241 NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available, 103 had rates above the EU average of 6.0%, while 137 were below this level; Piemonte (northern Italy) reported an unemployment rate equal to the EU average. The highest regional unemployment rates were generally concentrated in southern EU countries and France’s outermost regions, while the lowest rates were mainly observed across eastern EU countries and parts of southern Germany and northern Italy. In 2025, 23 regions across the EU reported unemployment rates of at least 10.0%, as shown by the darkest shade in '''Map 6'''. At the upper end of the distribution, the Spanish autonomous region of Ciudad de Melilla and the French outermost region of Mayotte recorded the highest rates, both 24.9%, closely followed by Ciudad de Ceuta (24.3%). Leaving these atypical Spanish and French regions aside, the highest unemployment rates – above 12.0% – were observed in: *the north-western Greek region of Dytiki Makedonia *several other Spanish regions – Andalucía, Extremadura, Canarias, Castilla-La Mancha and Región de Murcia *the southern Italian regions of Campania and Sicilia *the Belgian capital region of Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest. '''''The Czech region of Střední Čechy (which surrounds the capital region of Praha) reported the lowest regional unemployment rate in the EU, at 1.5% in 2025''''' At the lower end of the distribution, there were 25 regions with unemployment rates below 3.0% in 2025, as shown by the lightest shade in '''Map 6'''. These regions were mainly concentrated in Czechia (5 regions), Germany and Poland (both 7 regions). There were a number of other regions that recorded rates below this level including Yugozapaden (the Bulgarian capital region), Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen and Provincia Autonoma di Trento (northern Italy), Zeeland (the Netherlands), Bucureşti-Ilfov (the capital region of Romania) and Bratislavský kraj (the capital region of Slovakia). The Czech region of Střední Čechy (which surrounds the capital region of Praha) recorded the lowest unemployment rate in the EU, at 1.5%. Unemployment rates in the capital regions of multi-regional eastern and Baltic EU countries were consistently below their national averages. In 2025, this pattern was particularly pronounced in Romania and Slovakia, where national rates were 3.4 and 2.2 times as high as than those in Bucureşti-Ilfov and Bratislavský kraj, respectively. By contrast, capital regions in most western and Nordic EU countries recorded higher unemployment rates than their national averages. This pattern was observed for Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Ireland, France, Austria, Finland and Sweden. In this group of countries, capital regions often recorded the highest regional unemployment rate; the only exceptions were France and Sweden. The contrast was most evident in Belgium, where Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest recorded an unemployment rate of 12.6%, which was more than twice the national average (6.4%). A comparable, although less pronounced, pattern was observed in the German and Austrian capital regions of Berlin and Wien, as their unemployment rates were 1.7 times as high as their respective national averages. (% of labour force among people aged 15–74, by NUTS 2 regions, 2025)
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cdf944e1-63b2-444a-bb8a-c553e51fdfa3?lang=en lfst_r_lfu3rt]) [[Image:Unemployment rate (% of labour force among people aged 15–74, by NUTS 2 regions, 2025)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 6: Unemployment rate
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cdf944e1-63b2-444a-bb8a-c553e51fdfa3?lang=en lfst_r_lfu3rt])]] '''''In 2025, almost a third of unemployed people in the EU had been jobless for more than a year''''' [[Glossary:Long-term_unemployment|Long-term unemployment]] is a major challenge in the EU, that may impact both individual well-being and social cohesion. High rates often signal structural issues in the labour market, skill mismatches or economic stagnation, leading to income loss, social exclusion and increased pressure on public welfare systems and community well-being. A [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32016H0220(01) Council recommendation on the integration of the long-term unemployed into the labour market (2016/C 67/01)] includes 3 key steps (aimed at supporting vulnerable groups): *encouraging registration with an employment service *providing individual in-depth assessments *offering job integration agreements. In March 2024, the European Commission presented an [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-sets-out-actions-tackle-labour-and-skills-shortages-2024-03-20_en action plan to tackle labour and skills shortages] driven by demographic changes, emerging skill demands and poor working conditions. Building on existing initiatives – including the European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan – it supports training, mobility and attracting talent – one of its key measures is the financing of new projects aimed at achieving zero long-term unemployment. Furthermore, a range of active labour market policies, including job training and upskilling, wage subsidies for hiring long-term unemployed people, public employment programmes, job matching services and school-to-work transition programmes are funded through EU cohesion instruments. In 2025, 4.2 million people across the EU had been unemployed for more than a year. The long-term unemployment ratio – which is defined as the share of unemployed people (aged 15 to 74) that has been unemployed for 12 months or more – stood at 31.6%. '''Map 7''' shows the long-term unemployment ratio (for people aged 15 to 74) across NUTS level 2 regions. Of the 207 regions for which data are available in 2025, 86 recorded ratios above the EU average of 31.6%, while 120 were below and 1 recorded the same rate. The highest ratios were predominantly concentrated in a cluster of regions in Baltic, southern and eastern EU countries, as well as in southern Belgium, eastern Germany and the French outermost regions. There were 27 regions across the EU where the long-term unemployment ratio was at least 50.0% (indicating that at least half of all unemployed people had been without work for at least a year). Such patterns may reflect structural characteristics of regional labour markets, including skills mismatches, limited job creation, and broader economic conditions such as deindustrialisation or economies with a high reliance on agriculture and a limited industrial or service base, often accompanied by outward migration of younger populations. This group of 27 regions included: *all 4 regions in Slovakia (2024 data for Bratislavský kraj), with the easternmost region of Východné Slovensko recording the highest ratio in the EU, with almost three quarters (72.5%) of unemployed people without work for at least a year *8 of the 13 regions in Greece, with the highest ratio observed in Sterea Elláda (66.9%) *9 of the 21 regions in Italy, predominantly in the southern half of the country, with the highest ratio recorded in Molise (70.1%) *the Spanish autonomous regions of Ciudades de Ceuta y Melilla *the northern Bulgarian region of Severen tsentralen *the French outermost regions of Mayotte and Guadeloupe *the Romanian capital region of Bucureşti-Ilfov. In 2025, there were 13 regions across the EU where the long-term unemployment ratio was below 15.0% (as shown by the lightest shade in '''Map 7'''). These regions were concentrated in the Netherlands, with Utrecht recording the lowest ratio in the EU, at 11.0%. The remainder of this group of 13 regions was composed of: *6 additional regions from the Netherlands *3 of the 5 regions in Denmark, including the capital region of Hovedstaden *2 regions in north-west France, Bretagne and Pays de la Loire *Prov. West-Vlaanderen in northern Belgium.

'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d3f0fe1b-01ff-48a1-84fa-e421f73fbae8?lang=en lfst_r_lfu2ltu])]] ===Source data for figures and maps=== {{Template:Excel|filename=RYB2026 CH04 Labour market.xlsx|title=Regional labour market statistics}} ===Data sources=== The information presented in this chapter relates to annual averages derived from the [[Glossary:Labour force survey (LFS)|EU’s labour force survey (EU-LFS)]]. Eurostat compiles and publishes labour market statistics for the EU and individual EU countries, as well as for EU regions. In addition, data are also available for 3 EFTA countries – Iceland, Norway and Switzerland – and several candidate countries – Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Serbia and Türkiye – and their statistical regions. The EU-LFS population generally consists of people aged 15 or over living in private households; definitions are aligned with those provided by the International Labour Organization (ILO). EU-LFS microdata are collected through a survey to obtain information on an individual’s demographic background, labour status, employment characteristics of their main job, hours worked, employment characteristics of their second job (if relevant), time-related underemployment, the search for employment, education and training, previous work experience of people not in employment and their income. These statistics are aggregated by region and are generally published down to NUTS level 2. When evaluating regional information from the EU-LFS, it is important to bear in mind that the information presented relates to the region where the respondent has their permanent residence and that this may be different to the region where their place of work is situated as a result of commuter flows. The collection of EU-LFS data up to and including reference year 2020 was conducted by national statistical authorities in accordance with Council Regulation (EEC) No 577/98. A new legal basis was introduced for EU-LFS data from 2021 onwards: [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32019R1700 Regulation (EU) 2019/1700] establishing a common framework for European statistics relating to persons and households, based on data at individual level collected from samples. Furthermore, [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2019/2240 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2240] specifies the technical items of the dataset, establishing formats for the transmission of information and specifying the detailed arrangements and content of the quality reports on the organisation of the sample survey. This change in legal basis implies a break in series between 2020 and 2021; results obtained before and after 1 January 2021 are consequently not fully comparable. Some countries/regions have other quality concerns that may impact geographical comparability. *Changes in survey methodology led to a break in series for German data in 2020. Therefore, data for Germany from 2020 onwards should not be compared directly with those for previous years. In addition, data collection during 2020 was impacted by technical issues and COVID-19 measures and hence there is a low degree of reliability for some regions. For more information, please refer the online methodological publication for the [[EU_labour_force_survey|EU’s labour force survey]]. ==== Indicator definitions ==== The '''labour force''' includes all people who were either employed or unemployed during the reference week. This aggregate includes people offering their work capacity on the labour market: as such it reflects the supply side. In the context of the EU-LFS, employed people include those aged 15 to 89 who, during the reference week, performed work – even if just for 1 hour – for pay, profit or family gain. Alternatively, the person was not at work, but had a job or business from which they were temporarily absent, for example due to illness, holiday, maternity or paternity leave, job-related training, paid parental leave or working time arrangements. This definition follows guidelines of the [https://www.ilo.org/ International Labour Organization (ILO)]. Within this publication, most labour force indicators are for a narrower definition of core working-age people, namely people aged 20 to 64. '''Employment rate''' The employment rate is the percentage of employed people in relation to the comparable population. The comparison is generally made within the population of core working-age (defined within this publication as people aged 20 to 64). Regional labour market disparities are measured using the population-weighted coefficient of variation. This indicator compares the standard deviation of regional employment rates with the national employment rate, while weighting each region by its population size. The aggregated EU value is calculated using all available regions in EU countries. However, dispersion across countries are only published for countries that have more than 4 NUTS level 2 regions. As a result, data are not presented for Estonia, Ireland, Croatia, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Slovenia or Slovakia; equally, they are not published for Iceland, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia or Serbia. The gender employment gap is defined as the employment rate for men minus the employment rate for women (among people aged 20 to 64). Employment rates may be calculated for other cohorts according to a range of socio-economic criteria, for example, by educational attainment. Within this publication, the employment rate of people with different levels of educational attainment concerns people aged 25 to 64 who had completed: *no more than a lower secondary education (as defined by the [[International_Standard_Classification_of_Education_(ISCED)|international standard classification of education (ISCED)]] levels 0 to 2) *an upper secondary or post-secondary non-tertiary education (as defined by ISCED levels 3 to 4) *a tertiary level of education (as defined by ISCED levels 5 to 8) – in other words, people who had completed a short-cycle tertiary education, bachelor’s, master’s or doctoral (PhD) degree. '''Young people neither in employment nor in education or training (NEET)''' The share of young people who are neither in employment nor in education and training, abbreviated as NEET, corresponds to the share of the population (of a given age group and sex) that is not employed and not involved in further (formal or non-formal) education or training during the 4 weeks ending with the reference week. The numerator refers to people meeting these 2 conditions, while the denominator is the population (of the same age group and sex), excluding respondents who did not answer the question in the survey about participation in regular (formal) education and training. For the purpose of this publication, the share of young people neither in employment nor in education or training relates to people aged 15 to 29. '''Unemployment''' Eurostat‘s unemployment statistics are based on guidelines provided by the ILO. Unemployed people are those aged 15 to 74 who are without work, but who have actively sought employment in the 4 weeks preceding the survey’s reference week (or have already found a job to start within the subsequent 3 months) and are available to begin work within the following 2 weeks. The unemployment rate is defined as the number of unemployed people expressed as a percentage of the labour force of the same age (defined within this publication as people aged 15 to 74). The youth unemployment rate is defined as the number of unemployed people aged 15 to 29 expressed as a percentage of the labour force of the same age. Long-term unemployment refers to the number of people aged 15 to 74 who are out of work and have been actively seeking employment for at least a year. The long-term unemployment ratio is the number of long-term unemployed people expressed as a percentage of the number of unemployed people of the same age. ===Context=== '''Safeguarding jobs and ensuring fair working conditions''' Since 2020, the European Commission has introduced several initiatives to support labour market resilience in line with the European Pillar of Social Rights. *''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:32020R0672 Council Regulation (EU) 2020/672]'' established the [https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/eu-financial-assistance/sure_en European instrument for temporary support to mitigate unemployment risks in an emergency (SURE)] to protect jobs and protect income during the COVID-19 crisis. *The [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/eu-employment-policies/youth-employment-support_en Youth employment support] initiative reinforced the [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/eu-employment-policies/youth-employment-support/reinforced-youth-guarantee_en Youth Guarantee], providing additional support to vocational training, apprenticeships and entrepreneurship opportunities for young people. *The [https://commission.europa.eu/funding-tenders/find-funding/eu-funding-programmes/just-transition-fund_en Just Transition Fund] helps communities manage the socio-economic costs/effects of the shift to a climate-neutral economy. *''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2022/2041/oj Directive (EU) 2022/2041 on adequate minimum wages in the European Union]'' promotes fair minimum wages, strengthens collective bargaining and supports upward social convergence across EU countries. *A ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=oj:JOC_2023_041_R_0001 Council Recommendation on adequate minimum income ensuring active inclusion 2023/C 41/01]'' complements earlier initiatives by addressing income protection for individuals outside employment. *The EU has also addressed emerging forms of employment through ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/2831 Directive (2024/2831) on improving working conditions in platform work]'' – an initiative aimed at strengthening conditions for those working with digital labour platforms (for example, food delivery riders or taxi drivers). *The [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/competitiveness/union-skills_en Union of skills] (COM(2025) 90 final) aims to strengthen lifelong learning, upskilling and reskilling opportunities, support enterprise competitiveness – particularly for SMEs – and improve the transparency and recognition of skills and qualifications across the EU. '''Promoting gender equality in the labour market''' The European Commission adopted [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0097 A Roadmap for Women’s Rights] (COM(2025) 97 final) in March 2025. It addresses emerging gender equality challenges, including technology-facilitated discrimination through a ‘Declaration of principles for a gender-equal society’. Although inequalities still exist, the EU has made significant progress in terms of gender equality over recent decades. The European Commission’s [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/gender-equality/gender-equality-strategy_en Gender equality strategy 2026–30] aims to build on this by countering gender stereotypes, promoting gender mainstreaming (including gender perspectives, for example in policies, to promote equality), closing gender gaps and increasing women’s participation in decision-making. The strategy aims to strengthen action across several policy areas, including: *tackling gender-based cyberviolence *enhancing women’s health (for example, through work addressing the social and economic impacts of the women’s health gap, including conditions such as menopause) *reducing gender gaps in employment and promoting equality in the labour market *ensuring that EU funding is gender-sensitive. '''Investing in people: funding and skills development''' The [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/funding/european-social-fund-plus-esf_en European Social Fund Plus (ESF+)] is the EU’s main financial instrument for investing in people. With a budget of €142.7 billion allocated for 2021 to 2027, it supports employment, social inclusion, poverty reduction and youth investment. The ESF+ is central to advancing the European Pillar of Social Rights and the post-pandemic recovery. To respond to changes in labour markets – especially those driven by the green and digital transitions – the EU has prioritised skills development through initiatives such as the ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0274 European Skills Agenda for sustainable competitiveness, social fairness and resilience]'' (COM(2020) 274 final), the [https://year-of-skills.europa.eu/index_en European Year of Skills] launched in 2023 and extended into 2024, and ''The Union of Skills''. '''Towards a fair and inclusive future labour market''' Labour markets across the EU are adapting to technological progress, demographic change and sustainability goals. Policymakers have introduced measures to improve employment access for underrepresented groups at risk of exclusion – such as young people, older workers and people with disabilities – while, at the same time, supporting regional adaptation to structural change. The growth of platform work and other non-standard forms of employment has also reinforced the need for fair working conditions. A key initiative in this area is the ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52024DC0131 Labour and skills shortages in the EU: an action plan]'' (COM(2024) 131 final) which provides a coordinated policy response to persistent labour market imbalances, focusing on: *increasing labour market participation among underrepresented groups *advancing skills development and training *improving working conditions in critical sectors *facilitating intra-EU mobility *attracting international talent. ===Other articles=== *[[Employment - annual statistics|Employment – annual statistics]] *[[Employment_statistics_-_utilisation_of_job_skills|Employment statistics – utilisation of job skills]] *[[EU labour force survey]] – online publication *[[EU labour force survey title: The EU in the world - research and information society
text:
Data extracted in April 2018. No planned article update. The highest research and development intensity in 2015 among the G20 members was in South Korea. By 2016, all G20 members registered at least 80 mobile telephone subscriptions per 100 inhabitants. [[Image:Gross domestic expenditure on research and development, 2005 and 2015 (% of GDP)_world18.png|thumb|centre|500px|Gross domestic expenditure on research and development, 2005 and 2015
(% of GDP)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=rd_e_gerdtot}} and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UIS: Science & Technology)| alt= A bar chart showing the gross domestic expenditure on research and development in 2005 and 2015 in the EU, world and multiple other countries. The vertical axis displays the percentage of the GDP, while the horizontal axis displays the countries and regions. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article is part of a [[The_EU_in_the_world|set of statistical articles]] based on [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat’s]] publication ''{{Template:Publication|code=KS-EX-18-001|title=The EU in the world 2018}}''. This article focuses on science and technology and the digital society in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] and the 15 non-EU members of the [[Glossary:Group of Twenty (G20)|Group of Twenty (G20)]]. It covers a range of statistics on [[Glossary:Research and development (R %26 D)|research and development (R & D)]] [[Glossary:R %26 D expenditure|expenditure]] and [[Glossary:Research and development (R & D) personnel and researchers|personnel]], and the use of information and communication technologies. It gives an insight into the EU’s economy in comparison with the major economies across the rest of the world, such as the EU’s counterparts in the so-called [[Glossary:Triad|Triad]] — Japan and the United States — and the [[Glossary:BRICS|BRICS]] composed of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. ===R & D expenditure=== Research and development (R & D) includes creative work carried out on a systematic basis in order to increase the stock of knowledge of man, culture and society, and the use of this knowledge to devise new applications. [[Glossary:Gross domestic expenditure on R %26 D (GERD)|Gross domestic expenditure on research and development (GERD)]] is a key measure of the level of R & D activity performed in an economy. It includes R & D that is funded from [[Glossary:Abroad sector - R %26 D|abroad]], but excludes payments made abroad. '''''The highest R & D intensity in 2015 among the G20 members was in South Korea''''' GERD in the [[Glossary:EU-27|EU-28]] was just over [[Glossary:Euro|EUR]] 300 billion in 2015. The relation between the level of GERD and [[Glossary:Gross domestic product (GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]] is known as R & D intensity (see Figure 1), and in 2015 it stood at 2.04 % in the EU-28. By far the highest R & D intensity among the G20 members was in South Korea, where GERD was equivalent to 4.23 % of GDP in 2015. The latest data for Japan, the United States, Australia (2013 data) and China show that they also recorded relatively high R & D intensities, all above the EU-28 average and between 2.0 and 3.5 %. Indonesia recorded by far the lowest R & D intensity among the G20 members, with GERD equivalent to less than 0.10 % (2013 data) of GDP.[[Image:Gross domestic expenditure on research and development, 2005 and 2015 (% of GDP)_world18.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 1: Gross domestic expenditure on research and development, 2005 and 2015
(% of GDP)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=rd_e_gerdtot}} and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UIS: Science & Technology)| alt= A bar chart showing the gross domestic expenditure on research and development in 2005 and 2015 in the EU, World and multiple other countries. The vertical axis displays the percentage of the GDP, while the horizontal axis displays the countries and regions. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Between 2005 and 2015, R & D intensity increased worldwide by 0.16 % of GDP and in the EU-28 by 0.30 %. The largest increases among the G20 members were observed for South Korea (1.22 %; 2007-2015), Saudi Arabia (0.78 %; 2005-2013; based on the R & D budget rather than actual expenditure) and China (0.76 %; note that there is a break in series). The only declines shown in Figure 1 were in South Africa, India and Canada; note that there is a break in series for Canada. An alternative calculation based on R & D expenditure can be seen in Figure 2, namely the level of GERD relative to population size. For this indicator GERD is presented in a common currency (United States dollars) using [[Glossary:Purchasing power parities (PPPs)|purchasing power parities (PPPs)]] rather than market exchange rates: PPPs are indicators of price level differences across countries. The resulting ratio per inhabitant provides a very clear distinction between G20 members. The United States, South Korea and Japan stand out with GERD per inhabitant in excess of USD 1 300. Australia (2013 data), the EU-28 and Canada (2014 data) completed the group of G20 members with relatively high GERD per inhabitant, all in the range of USD 700-1 000. Among the other G20 members, only Saudi Arabia (2013 data), China and Russia recorded GERD in excess of USD 200 per inhabitant, while this indicator was below USD 10 per inhabitant in Indonesia (2013 data).[[Image:Gross domestic expenditure on research and development, 2005 and 2015 (international USD per inhabitant)_world18.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 2: Gross domestic expenditure on research and development, 2005 and 2015
(international USD per inhabitant)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=rd_e_gerdtot}} and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UIS: Science & Technology)| alt= A bar chart showing the gross domestic expenditure on research and development in 2005 and 2015 in the EU and multiple other countries. The vertical axis displays the international USD per inhabitant, while the horizontal axis displays the countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===R & D personnel=== '''''The number of people working in R & D in the EU-28 in 2015 was 2.9 million full-time equivalents''''' R & D personnel include all individuals employed directly in the field of R & D, covering not only [[Glossary:Research and development (R & D) personnel and researchers|researchers]], but also technicians and equivalent staff as well as supporting staff (such as managers, administrators and clerical staff). Among the G20 members shown in Figure 3, China had the largest R & D workforce, numbering 3.8 million [[Glossary:Full-time equivalent (FTE)|full-time equivalents]] in 2015, followed by the EU-28 with an R & D workforce of 2.9 million; note that the United States is among the G20 members for which data are not available. The third and fourth largest R & D workforces were in Japan and Russia, each less than a quarter of the size of the workforce in China and less than a third of that in the EU-28. A full-time equivalent is a unit to measure employed persons or students in a way that makes them comparable although they may work or study a different number of hours per week. The unit is obtained by comparing the number of hours worked or studied by a person with the average number of hours of a full-time worker or student. A full-time person is therefore counted as one unit, while a part-time person gets a score in proportion to the hours they work or study.[[Image:Research and development personnel, 2005 and 2015 (thousand full-time equivalents)_world18.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 3: Research and development personnel, 2005 and 2015
(thousand full-time equivalents)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=rd_p_persocc}} and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UIS: Science & Technology)| alt= A bar chart showing the research and development personnel in 2005 and 2015 in the EU and multiple other countries. The vertical axis displays the thousand full-time equivalents, while the horizontal axis displays the countries and regions. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The number of R & D personnel in China nearly trebled between 2005 and 2015, although a break in series should be noted, while the R & D workforces of Turkey and South Korea (also a break in series) also more than doubled; in the EU-28 the number of R & D personnel increased by 31 %. Japan, Russia and Mexico (2005-2013) were the only G20 members to record a fall in their number of R & D personnel during the period under consideration. R & D personnel can be classified to the following sectors: [[Glossary:Business enterprise sector - R %26 D|business]], [[Glossary:Government sector - R %26 D|government]], [[Glossary:Higher education sector - R %26 D|higher education institutions]], and [[Glossary:Private non-profit sector - R %26 D|private non-profit making organisations]]. More than half (55 %) of all R & D personnel in the EU-28 were employed in the business enterprise sector in 2015, around one third (32 %) in higher education and most of the remainder in the government sector (13 %) — see Figure 4. The share of R & D personnel in the business enterprise sector peaked at 77 % in China and was around 70 % in South Korea and Japan. By contrast, less than one third of R & D personnel were in the business enterprise sector in South Africa (2013 data), India, Brazil (2010 data) and Argentina (2014 data). In Brazil, the higher education sector was the dominant employer, with 73 % of the total; South Africa was the only other G20 member where the share of R & D personnel in this sector exceeded two fifths. In India and Argentina, the government sector employed around half of all R & D personnel. The share of R & D personnel in the private non-profit making sector was generally small, peaking at 5 % in India.[[Image:Research and development personnel by sector of performance, 2015 (%, based on full-time equivalents)_world18.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 4: Research and development personnel by sector of performance, 2015
(%, based on full-time equivalents)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=rd_p_persocc}} and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UIS: Science & Technology)| alt= A bar chart showing the research and development personnel by sector of performance in 2005 and 2015 in the EU and multiple other countries. The vertical axis displays the percentage based on full-time equivalents, while the horizontal axis displays the countries and regions. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Telecommunications=== Telecommunication networks and services are the backbone of the digital society. Individuals, enterprises and public organisations alike depend increasingly on convenient, reliable and high-speed telecommunication networks and services. A shift in the importance of various services can be noted, from wired to wireless networks and from voice to data services. The number of fixed telephone subscriptions relative to the size of the population increased between 2006 and 2016 in just two of the G20 members (see Figure 5), up by 20 % in South Korea and by 15 % in Japan. Elsewhere, the decreases ranged from less than 20 % in Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, the EU-28 and South Africa, through the world average of 29 %, to closer to 50 % in China, India (both 47 %) and Turkey (49 %).[[Image:Telephone subscriptions, 2006 and 2016 (per 100 inhabitants)_world18.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 5: Telephone subscriptions, 2006 and 2016
(per 100 inhabitants)
''Source:'' the International Telecommunication Union| alt= A horizontal bar chart showing the telephone subscriptions in 2005 and 2015 in the EU and multiple other countries. The vertical axis displays the countries and regions, while the horizontal axis displays the unit per 100 inhabitants. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''By 2016, all of the G20 members registered at least 80 mobile telephone subscriptions per 100 inhabitants''''' A mobile phone subscription refers to the use of public mobile telecommunication systems (also called mobiles or cellphones) using cellular technology. Active pre-paid cards are treated as subscriptions and people may have more than one subscription. In all G20 members, the number of mobile subscriptions relative to population size increased between 2006 and 2016 (see Figure 6). Indonesia experienced by far the strongest absolute growth, from 28 mobile subscriptions per 100 inhabitants in 2006 to 148 per 100 inhabitants in 2016, an increase of 120 per 100 inhabitants, which was double the average for the world as a whole, (up from 42 to 102 per 100 inhabitants). India reported the second largest increase in absolute terms, up 71 per 100 inhabitants to reach 85 mobile subscriptions per 100 inhabitants in 2016, moving it from last place in the rankings in 2006 to second last in 2016, overtaking Canada (also 85 per 100 inhabitants in 2016). As such, all of the G20 members registered at least 80 mobile subscriptions per 100 inhabitants in 2016, with Mexico, Turkey and China the only other G20 members alongside Canada and India where there were fewer mobile subscriptions than inhabitants.[[Image:Fixed broadband subscriptions, 2006 and 2016 (per 100 inhabitants)_world18.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 6: Fixed broadband subscriptions, 2006 and 2016
(per 100 inhabitants)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=isoc_tc_fbsupe}} and the International Telecommunication Union| alt= A bar chart showing the fixed broadband subscriptions in 2006 and 2016 in the EU and multiple other countries. The vertical axis displays the per 100 inhabitants, while the horizontal axis displays the countries and regions. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Broadband refers to telecommunications in which a wide band of frequencies is available to send data. Broadband telecommunication lines or connections transport data at high speeds. The technologies most widely used for fixed broadband internet access are digital subscriber line (DSL) and its variations (xDSL), or cable modem (connection to a local television line). Like the number of fixed telephone lines in general, relative to population size the number of fixed [[Glossary:Broadband|broadband]] subscriptions among the G20 members was much more diverse than was the case for mobile subscriptions. South Korea had 40 subscriptions per 100 inhabitants in 2016 while several other G20 members — Canada, the United States, Japan, Australia and the EU-28 (2013 data) — reported between 30 and 37 subscriptions per 100 inhabitants. At the other end of the ranking, Saudi Arabia (10 subscriptions per 100 inhabitants) had a fixed broadband subscription rate that was below the world average (12 per 100 inhabitants) while South Africa, Indonesia and India had 1 or 2 subscriptions per 100 inhabitants. Between 2006 and 2016, all G20 members reported growth in fixed broadband subscriptions relative to population size, with the strongest growth in absolute terms reported for China (an extra 19 subscriptions per 100 inhabitants) and Russia (17 subscriptions per 100 inhabitants more). === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Ch10 Research and development and the digital society EU_world18.xlsx|title=Research and development and the digital society: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The statistical data in this article were extracted during April 2018. The indicators are often compiled according to international — sometimes worldwide — standards. Although most data are based on international concepts and definitions there may be certain discrepancies in the methods used to compile the data. '''EU data'''
All of the indicators presented for the EU have been drawn from Eurobase, Eurostat’s online database. Eurobase is updated regularly, so there may be differences between data appearing in this article and data that is subsequently downloaded. '''G20 members from the rest of the world'''
For the 15 non-EU G20 members, the data presented have been compiled by the [http://www.itu.int/en/Pages/default.aspx International Telecommunication Union] and the [[Glossary:United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)|United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO)]], supplemented by data from the [[Glossary:World Bank|World Bank]]. For some of the indicators shown a range of international statistical sources are available, each with their own policies and practices concerning data management (for example, concerning data validation, correction of errors, estimation of missing data, and frequency of updating). In general, attempts have been made to use only one source for each indicator in order to provide a comparable dataset for the members. ===Context=== Practical applications of science are integrated in almost every moment of our lives, for example, in household appliances, medicine and healthcare, transport, communications and entertainment. R & D and [[Glossary:Innovation|innovation]] underlie such applications and are often considered as some of the primary driving forces behind competitiveness, economic growth and job creation. ===Other articles=== *[[Articles by theme#Science, technology, and digital society|All articles on science, technology and digital society]] *[[International cooperation|All articles on International cooperation]] *[[The EU in the world|Other articles from ''The EU in the world'']] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-EX-18-001|title=The EU in the world 2018}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-FQ-17-001|title=The European Union and the African Union — A statistical portrait — 2018 edition}}; *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-04-17-780|title=Sustainable Development in the European Union — Monitoring report on progress towards the SDGs in an EU context}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-EZ-17-001|title=Smarter, greener, more inclusive ? Indicators to support the Europe 2020 strategy — 2017 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-06-17-380|title=Globalisation patterns in EU trade and investment}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-17-424|title=40 years of EU-ASEAN cooperation — 2017 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GO-16-001|title=Key figures on the enlargement countries — 2017 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-02-16-356|title=Asia-Europe Meeting (ASEM) — A statistical portrait — 2016 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GR-15-001|title=Euro-Mediterranean statistics — 2015 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-31-11-414|title=The European Union and the BRIC countries}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-32-11-816|title=The European Union and the Republic of Korea — 2012}} *{{Template:Publication|code=978-92-9201-242-7|title=Key data on education in Europe 2012}} ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/science-technology-innovation/database Science and technology (scitech)], see: :Research and development (research) ::Statistics on research and development (rd) :::R&D expenditure at national and regional level (rd_e) ::::Intramural R&D expenditure (GERD) by sectors of performance (rd_e_gerdtot) :::R&D personnel at national and regional level (rd_p) ::::Total R&D personnel by sectors of performance, occupation and sex (rd_p_persocc) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/digital-economy-and-society/database Digital economy and society (isoc)], see: :Digital economy and society - title: The Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure (MIP) introduced
text:
EU statistics provide an introduction of the Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure. Data extracted on 31 October 2025 Planned article update: November 2026 This article provides information on the Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure (MIP), as well as on indicators and statistical data used in this context. The MIP is part of the European Semester, which is an annual cycle enabling the [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|European Union Member States]] to coordinate their economic and social policies throughout the year. The MIP aims to identify potential macroeconomic risks early on, preventing the emergence of harmful macroeconomic imbalances and allowing the correction of existing imbalances. ===Background=== [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?qid=1407944142061&uri=CELEX%3A32011R1176 Regulation (EU) No 1176/2011] defines a '''macroeconomic imbalance''' as: :''any trend giving rise to macroeconomic developments which are adversely affecting, or have the potential to adversely affect, the proper functioning of the economy of a Member State or of the economic and monetary union, or of the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|Union]] as a whole''. While '''excessive imbalances''' are defined in the same legal act as: :''severe imbalances, including imbalances that jeopardise or risk jeopardising the proper functioning of the economic and monetary union''. As defined in the [https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/document/download/6216cc55-c9fc-40ed-9046-9136dd753458_en?filename=2016-european-semester-country-reports-comm-en.pdf 2016 Communication on Country Reports], the macroeconomic imbalances categories are the following: no imbalance, imbalances, excessive imbalances, and excessive imbalances with corrective action ([https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/economic-and-fiscal-governance/macroeconomic-imbalance-procedure/excessive-imbalance-procedure_en#:~:text=The%20excessive%20imbalance%20procedure%20(EIP)%20is%20an%20enhanced%20surveillance%20mechanism,countries%20identified%20with%20excessive%20imbalances. Excessive Imbalance Procedure, EIP]). The MIP covers a number of sequential steps, having the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/macroeconomic-imbalances-procedure/publications Alert Mechanism Report (AMR) and its Statistical Annex (SA)] as a starting point. The AMR comprises an economic and financial assessment based on an economic reading of a set of macroeconomic indicators (the MIP scoreboard). It screens all Member States to identify those that may be affected, or may be at risk of being affected, by economic imbalances, and selects Member States for which an in-depth review (IDR) will be prepared. Eurostat is in charge of producing the SA, a document presenting the MIP indicators for a 10-year period for each Member State and, since 2023, for the European Union and the euro area. The SA and the AMR are published at the same time, where the AMR is based on the data in the SA, as well as more recent available data of higher frequency. The AMR for year t is published in year t - 1, with scoreboard data up until year t - 2 (e.g. the 2026 AMR and SA are published in November 2025 with scoreboard data up to 2024). Table 1 below shows the MIP scoreboard indicators values used within the latest AMR. [[Image:Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure (MIP) Scoreboard 2024.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: MIP scoreboard, year 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat, [https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/327cb335-0aa7-4ca2-b888-12516a2243a5_en?filename=SWD_2025_900_2_EN_0.pdf Statistical Annex of 2026 Alert Mechanism Report]|alt= Table showing the Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure scoreboard in the EU, euro area, and individual Member States for the year 2024.]] In 2024, both the scoreboard and the auxiliary indicators were streamlined as part of the regular review process set out in the MIP regulation (Art. 4(7) of Regulation 1176/2011). For more information, see [https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/89023048-a1fc-4970-abad-42c9dad347c6_en?filename=SWD_2024_702_3_EN.pdf The MIP indicators Commission Staff Working Document - On the changes in the scoreboard of the Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure]. Following the [https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2023-04/COM_2023_240_1_EN.pdf Commission proposal for a regulation on the effective coordination of economic policies] of 26 April 2023, the MIP takes a reinforced forward-looking perspective to identify emerging risks sufficiently early on and to better gauge the prospects for the evolution of imbalances. At the same time, great attention is given to systemic challenges and to developments in the European Union and euro area. EU and euro area aggregates are therefore presented in the SA. === The Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure (MIP) in the context of the European Semester === Since 2010, the European Union is running an annual cycle of economic and social policy coordination called the [https://ec.europa.eu/info/business-economy-euro/economic-and-fiscal-policy-coordination/eu-economic-governance-monitoring-prevention-correction/european-semester_en European Semester]. By achieving stronger economic and social coordination of Member States' policies, the European Semester aims to ensure sustainable economic growth, job creation, macroeconomic stability and sound public finances across the EU. On 30 April 2024, the European Semester was revised as part of the [https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/economic-and-fiscal-governance/evolution-eu-economic-governance/new-economic-governance-framework_en Economic Governance Review (EGR)], which seeks to ensure a simpler, more transparent and effective framework with greater national ownership and better enforcement. The European Semester's specific annual cycle begins in autumn with the publication of a policy package known as the Autumn Package, which the AMR is a part of. The [https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/56f83799-0eb9-4955-8550-728dc4ebbaf2_en?filename=COM_2025_956_1_EN_0.pdf communication on the AMR] lays out the list of Member States for which the Commission will prepare country-specific [https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/economic-and-fiscal-governance/macroeconomic-imbalance-procedure/depth-reviews_en in-depth reviews (IDR)], that encompass a thorough assessment of imbalances in the Member State under review, taking into account country-specific economic conditions. The IDRs then provide a comprehensive assessment of imbalances based on a wider set of data, also assessing the risks of spillovers of macroeconomic imbalances to other Member States. Based on IDRs, the Commission concludes whether imbalances or potentially excessive imbalances exist. The conclusions of the IDRs serve as input for the Commission's proposal of country-specific recommendations on economic and social policy addressed to each Member States in spring. In summer, the Council agrees on the final version of the country-specific recommendations, highlighting areas where Member States need to take further actions to boost growth, job creation, training and education opportunities, research and innovation. The country-specific recommendations for the Member States identified with imbalances or excessive imbalances under the MIP should include calls for policy action to tackle them. The Member States are then invited to address these recommendations. '''Outcome of the 2026 AMR''' The [https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/6ab4287c-c7cf-4b10-845f-9d35b0ea6ef6_en?filename=SWD_2025_956_1_EN_0.pdf 2026 AMR] was published on 25 November 2025. The economic reading of the MIP scoreboard considers outcomes for 2024 and is interpreted in light of available in-year data for 2025 and the Commission’s 2025 autumn forecast. The conclusion of the 2026 AMR states that IDRs will be prepared for the seven Member States that were identified as experiencing imbalances or excessive imbalances in the previous annual round of MIP surveillance : Greece, Italy, Hungary, the Netherlands, Romania, Slovakia, and Sweden. === The MIP indicators === MIP scoreboard and auxiliary indicators cover external and internal imbalances, competitiveness positions, labour market and social developments. They are calculated from several statistical areas, including National Accounts (NA), Balance of Payments (BoP) and International Investment Position (IIP) statistics, Price statistics, Excessive Deficit Procedure (EDP) statistics, Labour Market and Living Conditions statistics. Indicators stemming from the NA, BoP/IIP domains are computed following the European System of Accounts 2010 (ESA 2010) and the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual, 6th edition (BPM6) that guarantee a high level of comparability and internal consistency across Member States. The MIP scoreboard is a tool to support the early identification and monitoring of imbalances, which in the 2026 AMR consisted of 13 scoreboard indicators (see Table 2). Each scoreboard indicator has indicative thresholds serving as alert levels. However, as in the relevant legal provisions of the MIP, the MIP scoreboard should not be interpreted mechanically. Moreover, the economic reading of the scoreboard indicators is complemented by the analysis of a wider set of 23 auxiliary indicators (see Table 3) that do not have any associated thresholds, but which provide additional information on aspects linked to the general macroeconomic situation. ''Source:'' [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/macroeconomic-imbalances-procedure/information-data Eurostat thematic section for MIP]. |} A 3-level quality assurance framework ensures the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/macroeconomic-imbalances-procedure/quality quality] of the MIP indicators. The first level assesses the reliability and comparability of indicators underlying statistics and addresses relevant quality issues; it enhances the communication on quality assurance of MIP statistics towards the European Parliament and Council, policy makers and the public at large by the annual publication of a quality report. This report draws on the information gathered in levels 2 (domain-specific quality reports produced by Eurostat and the ECB) and 3 (national quality reports/self-assessments produced by the institutions compiling the national statistics). The main source for the MIP scoreboard and auxiliary indicators is Eurostat, using data transmitted by EU countries, following European legislation, although some data are produced by the Commission's Directorate General for Economic and Financial Affairs (DG ECFIN), the [[Glossary:Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development_(OECD)|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)]] for the denominator of one scoreboard indicator, the [[Glossary:European_Central_Bank_(ECB)|European Central Bank (ECB)]] for 3 auxiliary indicators based on banking data as well as data for certain components used in the computation of one scoreboard indicator, and the [[Glossary:International_Monetary_Fund_(IMF)|International Monetary Fund (IMF)]] for the denominator of one auxiliary indicator. The list of the indicators is regularly reviewed and it may evolve over time in order to reflect new developments or needs. === Recent statistical improvements === Looking at data quality, and in particular to cross-domain consistency, Eurostat continues to work on the reconciliation of the balance of payments and the rest of the world (RoW) account at national level, and regularly assesses the state of consistency between BoP and NA statistics. Moreover, Eurostat and the ECB follow several initiatives to improve consistency and reduce asymmetries. In view of regular data comparisons, Eurostat conducts regular comparisons of quarterly BoP and quarterly/annual sector accounts for the Rest of the World (RoW) sector. The harmonisation of methodological standards (ESA2010 and BPM6) has helped to eliminate some previous discrepancies. The implementation of the [https://circabc.europa.eu/sd/a/1ee1d421-80e3-4e2b-852e-0a493e799e8d/2012-07%20-%20The%20CMFB%20revision%20policy%20for%20bop_iip%20and%20national%20accounts.pdf harmonised European revision policy (HERP) for NA and BoP statistics], covering benchmark and routine revisions, is progressing on a voluntary basis. In the '''National Accounts''' domain, Member States – with the exception of one country - carried out a benchmark revision of their NA estimates in 2024, following recommendations of the HERP. The purpose of this benchmark revision was to implement changes introduced by the amended ESA 2010 regulation, and to incorporate new data sources and other methodological improvements. All revisions were closely monitored and validated by Eurostat. The main changes, dates and overviews of national releases were published on Eurostat’s [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/esa-2010/data-revision ESA 2010 data revision web page]. In the '''Balance of Payments''' domain, progress has been made on addressing the asymmetries in statistics for trade in goods and services and foreign direct investment (FDI). Eurostat continued activities to further reduce asymmetries, in particular the follow up of some of the recommendations resulting from the previous International Trade in Services Statistics (ITSS) Asymmetry Resolution Mechanism (ARM). It is an ongoing initiative to obtain the Member States’ VAT Information Exchange System (VIES) data for the intra-EU exports side, and the development of a flexible tool to exchange on a bilateral basis information on compensation of employees. In addition, an ARM is managed by ECB and Eurostat in the context of quarterly BoP production. The purpose of this ARM is to facilitate bilateral and/or multilateral reconciliation exercises to reduce asymmetries in FDI. Eurostat has also been working to provide further guidance on the treatment of non-resident VAT traders in BoP statistics. Eurostat hosted a workshop on non-resident VAT traders in April 2024. Based on these findings, Eurostat published in February 2025 a ESA 2010 Methodological Note “Foreign trade reported by non-resident VAT traders (NR-VATT), 2025 edition”, providing BoP/IIP compilers with harmonised recommendations consistent with the change-of-economic-ownership principle in BPM6/ESA 2010. In the domain of '''Financial Accounts''', some ongoing initiatives will be beneficial for the quality of MIP indicators: the recording of other equity, of derivatives, of loans between non-financial corporations, of foreign-controlled corporations and special purpose entities, and the analysis of the vertical discrepancy with Non-Financial Sector Accounts. On the latter, Eurostat and the ECB published a report with recommendations with the aim of improving vertical consistency across institutional sectors in order to enhance cross-country comparability. Concerning the '''Labour Force Survey (LFS)''', in 2021, the EU regulation 2019/1700 (Integrated European Social Statistics Framework regulation, IESS FR) entered into force, together with its LFS implementing regulation (the EU regulation 2019/2240). The innovations introduced concern all aspects of the survey, in order to harmonise the fundamental survey features among Member States. Together with the IESS regulation, several Member States introduced national specific innovations. Consistency in MIP scoreboard indicators stemming from the LFS has been ensured thanks to back-calculation, as required by the new regulation. Although labour market indicators in the MIP scoreboard may show different figures than in the past, including in the initial part of the series, series are consistent over time and multi-annual indicators are calculated with consistent figures. In the '''House Prices''' domain, the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1470, which establishes the methodological and technical specifications for the house price index and the owner-occupied housing price index, was adopted in 2023. This regulation has been applied to all data transmissions since 1 January 2024, and previously transmitted data have, where necessary, been revised where data sources are available. In consultation with several Member States, Eurostat has complemented most of the cases of missing data for the auxiliary indicator “Standardised house price-to-income ratio” in the early years of the back series with appropriate estimates. '''General Government Gross Debt''' data notified for the years 2021 to 2024 were released on 21 October 2025 within the EDP notification. For more information on the main revisions between April 2025 and October 2025 notifications, please see the latest [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-euro-indicators/w/2-21102025-ap EDP news release]. Timeliness and availability of General Government Gross Debt data remained excellent. In February 2023, Eurostat published an updated version of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-gq-23-002 Manual on Government Deficit and Debt]. === Published AMRs === The complete list of the AMRs, SAs and Eurostat's news items are published on the [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/macroeconomic-imbalances-procedure/publications MIP dedicated web section]. Table 4 shows the publication dates of the different editions of the AMRs.
