title: Tourism statistics - impact of Covid-19 on trips of Europeans
text:
4 Impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on the volume of trips made by Europeans and how the characteristics of those trips, for instance destination or type of accommodation, were affected, focusing on the first year of the pandemic (2020) Data extracted in June 2022 No update planned for this article. [[Image:Trips of EU residents, 2019 and 2020 (million).png|thumb|centre|500px|Trips of EU residents, 2019 and 2020 (million)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tttot}}]] Tourism is one of the sectors most affected by the Covid-19 pandemic. In 2020, the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation establishments in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] decreased by 51 % compared with 2019. The accommodation sector in the EU started recovering in 2021, with 28 % more nights spent compared with 2020, reaching nearly two thirds of the pre-pandemic 2019 levels (see [[Tourism_statistics_-_nights_spent_at_tourist_accommodation_establishments|article on Nights spent at tourist accommodation establishments]]). In 2020, 51 million fewer residents of the European Union made tourism trips (for personal purposes). While in the year before the pandemic 243 million Europeans made at least one tourism trip with overnights stays in the course of the year, this number dropped by 21% to 193 million in the year 2020 (see [[Tourism_statistics_-_participation_in_tourism|article on Participation in tourism]]). Expressed as a share of the population (aged 15 or over), 52 % participated in tourism in 2020, down from 65 % in 2019. This article looks at the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on the volume of trips made by Europeans and how the characteristics of those trips, for instance destination or type of accommodation, were affected, focusing on the first year of the pandemic (2020). === Trips and tourism nights spent by Europeans dropped by 37 % in 2020 === In 2020, EU residents aged 15 and over made 713 million tourism trips where they spent 3.6 billion nights (see Table 1). [[Image:Trips, nights spent and average length of trips made by EU residents by destination, 2020.png|thumb|centre|500px|Table 1: Trips, nights spent and average length of trips made by EU residents by destination, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tttot}} {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tntot}}]] Compared with pre-pandemic levels, both the number of trips and the number of nights spent decreased by 37 % (see Figure 1 and Figure 2). Looking at the data broken down by destination, duration or purpose, the drops were more pronounced for outbound trips (-67 % vs -26 % for domestic), long trips (-40 % versus -35 % for short trips) and professional trips (-51 % versus -36 % for personal trips). In other words, Europeans made relatively fewer outbound trips, fewer long trips and fewer professional trips. The pattern was similar in terms of nights spent. However, the number of nights spent on domestic trips dropped less significantly than the number of domestic trips, meaning that domestic trips were, on average, a bit longer than before the pandemic. This could indicate that domestic trips became more important as a destination for the main holiday in the year. [[Image:Trips of EU residents, 2019 and 2020 (million).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 1: Trips of EU residents, 2019 and 2020 (million)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tttot}}]]
[[Image:Tourism nights spent by EU residents, 2019 and 2020 (million).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 2: Tourism nights spent by EU residents, 2019 and 2020 (million)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tntot}}]] === In 2020 EU residents spent more than 8 out of 10 of their tourism trips inside their own country === The findings in the previous section are confirmed in Figure 3 and Figure 4, showing the distribution of trips by duration and destination in 2019 and in 2020. The share of domestic trips increased in 2020 from 73 % to 85 %, including a big increase in the share of long domestic trips (trips of at least 4 nights). More than half (54 %) of all trips were short domestic trips (1 to 3 nights), while the share of trips abroad shrank to 5 % for short outbound and to 10 % for long outbound trips. As mentioned above, the number of domestic trips dropped by 26 %, from 827 million trips in 2019 to 608 million in 2020. The number of outbound trips was cut by 2 thirds, decreasing from 311 million trips to 104 million trips. Image:Trips of EU residents by destination and duration, 2020 (% of all trips).png|'''Figure 3 - ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tttot}}''' Image:Trips of EU residents by destination and duration, 2019 (% of all trips).png|'''Figure 4 - ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tttot}}''' The same distribution in terms of nights spent is shown in Figure 5 and Figure 6. While in 2019 the nights spent on long outbound trips accounted for more or less the same share in total nights spent as long domestic trips (39 % and 40 % respectively), long outbound trips accounted for only 22 % of nights spent in 2020, as compared with the share of long domestic trips increasing to 56 %. Image:Tourism nights of EU residents by destination and duration, 2020 (% of all nights).png|'''Figure 5 - ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tntot}}''' Image:Tourism nights of EU residents by destination and duration, 2019 (% of all nights).png|'''Figure 6 - ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tntot}}''' The impact of Covid-19 at country level is shown in Figure 7, comparing the number of trips made in 2019 and 2020. The biggest drops were observed for residents of Slovakia, Latvia, Ireland and Slovenia, with less than half as many trips in 2020. On the other hand, in Sweden the impact was minimal with only 2 % fewer trips made by its residents, mainly because of a significant increase of 35 % in the number of domestic trips. Sharp increases in domestic trips were also recorded in Malta (+52%) and Luxembourg (four times higher, but still relatively unimportant compared with the volume of outbound trips). The pattern in Figure 7 shows that, across all countries, the impact of the pandemic on tourism trips was much heavier for outbound tourism than for domestic tourism. [[Image:Trips of EU residents by destination, 2020 compared with 2019 (%).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 7: Trips of EU residents by destination, 2020 compared with 2019 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tttot}}]] === Over half of all overnight stays in 2020 were in non-rented accommodation === EU residents made a total of 3.6 billion overnight stays during tourism trips in 2020. More than half of these nights (54 %) were spent in non-rented accommodation, which was an unusually high share compared to pre-pandemic levels (44 % in 2019). Figure 8 and Figure 9 look at the distribution of the tourism nights by choice of accommodation in 2019 and in 2020. At EU level, in 2020 the biggest share of nights (35 % vs 28 % in 2019) were spent in accommodation provided by relatives or friends. Nights spent in own holiday homes also went up from 13 % to 17 %. This can indicate that tourists preferred accommodation options with people they know or with fewer people around. This observation is supported by the drop in the share of nights spent in hotels or similar accommodation (from 32 % in 2019 to 20 % in 2020). Image:Tourism nights spent by EU residents by mode of accommodation, 2020 (%).png|'''Figure 8 - ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tnac}}''' Image:Tourism nights spent by EU residents by mode of accommodation, 2019 (%).png|'''Figure 9 - ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tnac}}''' === 71 % or 129 million fewer trips made by air plane in 2020 than in 2019 === Motor vehicles (private or rented) were the main means of transport for 75 % of all trips in 2020 (see Figure 10). This share increased by 10 percentage points compared with 2019 (65 %), while the share of trips by airplane dropped from 16 % in 2019 to 7 % in 2020. This loss signifies 71 % or 129 million fewer trips made by airplane in 2020 than in 2019. [[Image:Trips of EU residents by mode of transport, 2020 and 2019 (% of all trips).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 10: Trips of EU residents by mode of transport, 2020 and 2019 (% of all trips)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tttra}}]] The shift to travelling by car instead of airplane was even more significant in the segment of long trips (see Figure 11); in 2020, 73 % of long trips were made by car while this share was 55 % in 2019. The shift towards destinations closer to home, for instance domestic trips rather than outbound trips, most likely explains the drop in air travel, jointly with concerns about distancing rules in shared modes of transport. [[Image:Long trips of EU residents by mode of transport, 2020 and 2019 (% of all long trips).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 11: Long trips of EU residents by mode of transport, 2020 and 2019 (% of all long trips)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tttra}}]] === In terms of number of trips, Austria was the top foreign destination for EU residents in 2020, while in terms of nights spent, Spain was on top === As discussed above, Europeans turned to domestic tourism in 2020. Figures 12 and 13 show that the shares of trips to all destinations abroad decreased compared with 2019. On average for the EU, 15 % of all trips were made in a foreign country: more than 11 % in another EU Member State and just over 3 % outside the EU. One year earlier, this was 20 % and 8 % respectively. Image:Trips of EU residents by destination, 2020 (% of all trips).png|'''Figure 12 - ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_ttw}}''' Image:Trips of EU residents by destination, 2019 (% of all trips).png|'''Figure 13 - ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_ttw}}''' In terms of number of trips, Austria was the number one foreign destination for EU residents (10.6 million trips, see Table 2), possibly because of the winter season at the beginning of 2020, just before tourism came to a stop in March 2020. In terms of number of nights spent, Spain was on top (92.2 million nights spent). 10 % of all outbound trips made by Europeans were spent in Austria, followed by Italy and Germany (8 % each), while 11 % of tourism nights were spent in Spain, followed by France (9 %) and Austria (8%). A neighbouring or nearby country has always been a popular foreign destination for trips of nearly all European tourists. However, in 2020, the proximity of the destination became more important (see Table 3 in the excel file). [[Image:Trips and nights spent by EU residents - Domestic, outbound and top 3 outbound destinations, 2020.png|thumb|centre|500px|Table 2: Trips and nights spent by EU residents - Domestic, outbound and top 3 outbound destinations, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_ttw}} {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tnw}}]] === In 2020, Europeans spent less than half of what they had spent on their trips in 2019 === These closing paragraphs look at tourism spending by EU residents living in the [[Glossary:Euro-area|euro area]]. Tourists from those 19 Member States spent €215 billion less on tourism trips, with tourism expenditure down from €396 billion in 2019 to €181 billion in 2020. When taking into account the fact that the number of trips and nights dropped significantly in 2020, tourists still spent, on average, less per trip and per night than one year earlier. The average spending per trip dropped by 25 % from €442 per trip to €333 per trip (see Figure 14). While the average spending per trip stayed relatively stable for domestic trips, the impact was more pronounced for trips abroad. [[Image:Average_tourism_expenditure_per_trip_of_residents_of_the_Euro_area,_by_destination_(domestic_outbound),_2019_and_2020,_(EUR).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 14: Average tourism expenditure per trip of residents of the Euro area, by destination (domestic/outbound), 2019 and 2020, (EUR)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_extot}}]] Tourists from euro area countries spent relatively more in their own economies in 2020 compared with 2019, with domestic tourism accounting for 65 % of all tourism expenditure (up from 44 % - see Figure 15 and Figure 16). Notwithstanding this comparative advantage, total expenditure on domestic tourism decreased in 2020 (-29 % for accommodation, -35 % for transport, -31 % for other expenditure), but less dramatically than the absolute values for expenditure on outbound trips (respectively -72 %, -73 % and -70 % - see Figure 17). Image:Tourism expenditure of residents of Euro area by type of expenditure, 2020 (% of total expenditure).png|'''Figure 15 - ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_exexp}}''' Image:Tourism expenditure of residents of Euro area by type of expenditure, 2019 (% of total expenditure).png|'''Figure 16 - ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_exexp}}''' [[Image:Tourism expenditure of residents of Euro area by type of expenditure, 2019 and 2020 (in million euro).png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 17: Tourism expenditure of residents of Euro area by type of expenditure, 2019 and 2020 (in million euro)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_exexp}}]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Impact of Covid19 on trips 27-06-2022.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === '''Collection of annual data on trips of EU residents''' The collection consists of harmonised data collected by the Member States in the frame of the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0692:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 692/2011}} of the European Parliament and of the Council concerning European statistics on [[Glossary:European_statistics_on_tourism|tourism]]. The scope of observation for data on tourism trips are all tourism trips with at least one overnight stay, made by the [[Glossary:Resident|resident population]] aged 15 and over. It includes trips made for private or professional purpose, outside the usual environment. === Context === The EU is a major tourist destination, with four Member States among the world’s top ten destinations for holidaymakers, according to [https://www.e-unwto.org/doi/book/10.18111/9789284421152 UNWTO] data. Tourism is an important activity in the EU which has the potential to contribute towards employment and economic growth, as well as to development in rural, peripheral or less-developed areas. These characteristics drive the demand for reliable and harmonised statistics within this field, as well as within the wider context of regional policy and sustainable development policy areas. === See also === *[[Tourism|All articles on tourism statistics]] === Main tables === *Tourism [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database?node_code=t_tour (t_tour)], see: :Annual data on trips of EU residents (t_tour_dem) === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/tourism/database Tourism (tour)], see: :Annual data on trips of EU residents (tour_dem) === Dedicated section === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=tourism}} Tourism statistics] === Publications === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/tourism/publications Recent Eurostat publications on tourism] === Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=tour_dem_esms|title=Annual data on trips of EU residents}} (ESMS metadata file — tour_dem_esms) *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-GQ-13-007|title=Methodological manual for tourism statistics}} === Legislation === *'''Use Eur-Lex icon on the ribbon tool at the top of the statistical article to enter the year and reference of your regulation or directive.''' *'''See example of what should be issued hereafter''' *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32016R1013:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 1013/2016}} === Visualisations === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RSI Regional Statistics Illustrated] - title: Tourism statistics - intra-EU tourism flows
text:
Data extracted in November 2025. Planned article update: November 2026. Greece and Romania recorded the longest stays by visitors from other EU countries in 2024 (around 9 nights on average), the average for EU destinations was 7 nights. In 2024 the highest average expenditure was observed for trips to Cyprus and Greece, 2 countries that are mainly reached by air travel. Most countries are predominantly reached by car, but more than one-third of the destination countries is most frequently visited by airplane (mainly island destinations and more remote countries in the EU). This article is part of the [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] online publication '''[[Tourism trips of Europeans]]''', providing recent statistics on tourism [[Glossary:Demand side tourism statistics|demand]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] and [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] countries. Three types of [[Glossary:Tourism|tourism]] flows can be distinguished: domestic tourism (persons making tourism trips within their country of residence), outbound tourism and inbound tourism. Until recently, the main source for European statistics on inbound tourism was statistics on [[Glossary:Arrival_of_tourist_at_a_tourist_accommodation_establishment|arrivals]] and [[Glossary:Nights_spent|nights spent]] by non-residents at [[Glossary:Tourist_accommodation_establishment|tourist accommodation establishments]]. This article tries to fill the data gap on inbound tourism by, at least for trips within the EU, re-using the outbound flows reported by countries to a range of destination countries as an estimate of the inbound flows from the point of view of those destination countries. The methodological approach is based on the simple fact that an outbound flow for 1 country represents an inbound flow for the country visited. When all outbound trips made by Europeans to a given country (as their main destination) are combined, an estimate of the intra-EU inbound tourism flows into this country can be obtained. The aim of this last article in the online publication Tourism trips of Europeans is mainly to briefly outline the potential offered by using partner countries' data to produce otherwise unavailable information, rather than to draw a comprehensive picture of inbound tourism. Note that for the segment of trips spent at rented accommodation, statistics on nights spent and arrivals by non-residents do exist (see the article on [[Tourism statistics - annual results for the accommodation sector| Tourism statistics - annual results for the accommodation sector]]). ===Europeans stay around 1 week on average when visiting other EU countries=== In 2024, tourism trips made by EU residents to another EU countries had an average duration of almost 1 week (6.8 nights), ranging from 3.1 nights for trips to Estonia and 3.6 nights in Belgium to over 8 nights for trips to Greece, Romania, Bulgaria, Spain and Cyprus (see Figure 1). [[Image: F1_Trips made by EU residents to other EU countries - Average duration by destination country, 2024 (Nights).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Trips made by EU residents to other EU countries - Average duration by destination country, 2024 ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_ttw}} {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tnw}}|alt= A vertical bar chart showing the trips made by EU residents to other EU countries by average duration by destination country in 2024. The bars show the number of Nights spent in the EU, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Differences in the duration of trips across Europe are often associated with accessibility in terms of transport and the proximity of the main generating markets. For instance, the relative price (and distance) to reach Greece, Spain or Cyprus and the fact that they are top holidays destinations will motivate tourists to stay longer, while the proximity and accessibility of Belgium to its main generating market (the Netherlands, followed by France) will make short breaks of a few days the more likely way of visiting this country. This also applied to Luxembourg, whose main generating market was the nearby Germany, followed by the Netherlands. ===Average expenditure on trips to another EU country is €851=== Inbound visitors coming from other EU countries spent on average €851 (see Figure 2), ranging from €344 in Slovakia (a country seeing many tourists from neighbouring countries on a short trip – see also Figure 1) to €1 476 in Cyprus, followed by Greece (€1 370), Ireland (€1 231) and Spain (€1 120). These 4 destinations have relatively long stays of around 8 nights or more on average and a prevalence (78% of trips or more) of air travel to reach the country (see Table 1). Per night, visitors from the EU to other EU countries spent on average €125 (see Figure 3), ranging from €72 for trips to Romania, €78 to Slovakia and €94 to Bulgaria or Luxembourg, to over €170 per night for trips to Finland, Cyprus and Estonia. For 3 EFTA countries, the average expenditure per night of EU visitors was higher than the EU average, peaking in Iceland at €169. [[Image:F2_Trips made by EU residents to other EU countries - Average expenditure per trip, by destination country, 2024 (€).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Trips made by EU residents to other EU countries - Average expenditure per trip, by destination country, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_extotw}}|alt= A vertical bar chart showing the average expenditure per trip made by EU residents to other EU countries, by destination country in 2024 in Euro, in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:F3_Trips made by EU residents to other EU countries - Average expenditure per night by destination country, 2024 (€).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Trips made by EU residents to other EU countries - Average expenditure per night by destination country, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_extotw}}|alt= A vertical bar chart showing the average expenditure per night spent by EU residents to other EU countries by destination country in 2024 in Euro, in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===For intra-EU trips, car is the dominant means of transport=== Residents of the EU made 250 million tourism trips of at least 1 overnight stay to destinations in another EU countries in 2024. For 44% of those trips, rented or private motor vehicles were the main means of transport (see Table 1), followed by airplane (41%). Train (7%), bus (5%) and transport using waterways (2%) were far less significant. [[Image:T1_Trips made by EU residents to other EU countries - Share of means of transport by destination country, 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 1: Trips made by EU residents to other EU countries - Share of means of transport by destination country, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_ttw}} {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tttr}}|alt= A table showing the trips made by EU residents to other EU countries as a percentage share of means of transport by destination country in 2024 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries. The columns show air, waterway, railway, bus, motor vehicle and other. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] When looking at the countries visited, air transport accounted for at least 3 out of 4 intra-EU inbound flows in Cyprus and Malta (96% each), Ireland (88%), Greece (85%) and Spain (78%). Note that all these destinations are islands or have an important part of their destinations situated on islands (Greek Islands, Canary or Balearic Islands etc.). In 5 countries, the share of inbound trips made by motor vehicle was 60% or more: Slovakia (75%), Austria (72%), Croatia (69%), Slovenia (66%) and the Netherlands (62%). Only in Estonia was waterway the dominant means of transport for inbound visitors (65% of all intra-EU trips) most likely because of the popular ferry connection between Tallinn and Helsinki. The share of waterway was particularly high also for intra-EU trips to Finland (29%) and Sweden (21%). Railway was relatively significant for visitors to Luxembourg (34% of intra-EU inbound trips), probably due to the free public transport inside the country, as well as to Belgium (18%), Czechia (15%), Germany (13%), Denmark, Poland, Slovakia (11% each), while buses were relatively significant (at least 10%) for intra-EU trips to Lithuania, Slovenia, Latvia and Hungary. === Over 2 out of 3 intra-EU tourism nights are spent in rented tourist accommodation=== In 2024, EU residents spent 1.7 [[Glossary:Billion|billion]] tourism nights during their trips to other EU countries. 75.4% of those nights were spent in [[Glossary:Tourist_accommodation|rented tourist accommodation establishments]] (see Figure 4). Hotels or similar accommodation providing services such as daily cleaning and bed-making came on top with 39%, while 25% of all intra-EU tourism nights were spent at a house, villa or apartment and 7% in campsites (including caravan or trailer parks). The remaining 3% were spent in other types of rented accommodation (e.g. youth hostel, mountain hut). Looking at non-rented accommodation, own holiday homes accounted for 8% of all intra-EU tourism nights and accommodation provided for free by friends or relatives for 14%. [[Image:F4_Tourism nights spent by EU residents to other EU countries - Share by type of accommodation, 2024 (%).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Tourism nights spent by EU residents to other EU countries - Share by type of accommodation, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tnw}} {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tnac}}|alt= A pie chart showing the Tourism nights spent by EU residents to other EU countries, share by type of accommodation in 2024. The segments show rented hotels and similar, rented campsites, rented house, villa or apartment, rented other, non-rented own holiday homes, non-rented by relatives or friends and non-rented other. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Across the EU, the significance of rented and non-rented accommodation for inbound visitors was quite contrasting. The share of rented accommodation ranged from 93% of all EU residents' tourism nights in Cyprus and Malta to 29% of those spent in Romania, where a big amount of tourist trips are done by Romanians living abroad visiting friends and family (see Figure 5). [[Image:F5_Tourism nights spent by EU residents to other EU countries - Share by type of accommodation, by destination country, 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Tourism nights spent by EU residents to other EU countries - Share by type of accommodation, by destination country, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tnw}} {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tnac}}|alt= A vertical stacked bar chart showing Tourism nights spent by EU residents to other EU countries - Share by type of accommodation, by destination country, 2024 in percentage, in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries. The stacks show rented accommodation and non-rented accommodation. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Around 1 in 4 intra-EU trips are made in July and August === Looking at the breakdown by month of departure of trips, August (12.8%) and July (11.7%) accounted for almost 1 out of 4 trips, while January represented only 4.5% of intra-EU trips in 2024 (see Table 2). [[Image:T2_Trips made by EU residents to other EU countries - Distribution over the year, by destination country, 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 2: Trips made by EU residents to other EU countries - Distribution over the year, by destination country, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_ttw}}|alt= A table showing Trips made by EU residents to other EU countries as a distribution over the year, by destination country, in 2024, in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries. The columns show the share of each month. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Seasonality of inbound trips by visitors coming from other EU countries was particularly high in Croatia, where a little less than half of all inbound trips (44.1%) took place during the 2 core summer months, July and August. In Greece the share of these 2 months was 34.9%, followed by Bulgaria (34.6%) (see Figure 6). [[Image:F6_Distribution over the year of EU residents' trips to Bulgaria, Greece and Croatia, 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Distribution over the year of EU residents' trips to Bulgaria, Greece and Croatia, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_ttw}}|alt= A line chart with four lines showing the distribution over the year of EU residents' trips to Bulgaria, Greece and Croatia in 2024. The lines show the EU, Bulgaria, Greece and Croatia. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
In Cyprus, the number of trips made by EU visitors in the peak month was 32 times higher than the lowest month, while this ratio was 25 to one for Greece and 24 to one for Croatia. The lowest seasonality was recorded in Belgium and Germany; in these countries the number of intra-EU inbound trips during the peak month was less than 2.5 times higher compared with the lowest month (see Figure 7). [[Image: F7_Ratio of the peak month by the weakest month for EU residents' trips to other EU countries, by destination country, 2024.png|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 7: Trips made by EU residents to other EU countries - Ratio of the peak month by the lowest month, by destination country, 2024 - Source: Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_ttw}}|alt= A vertical bar chart showing the Trips made by EU residents to other EU countries - Ratio of the peak month by the lowest month, by destination country, in 2024, in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries.]] === Source data for tables and graphs=== *[[Media:Tourism IntraEU_2024data.xlsx |Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== '''Collection of annual data on trips of EU residents''' The collection consists of harmonised data collected by the Member States in the frame of the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0692:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 692/2011}} of the European Parliament and of the Council concerning European statistics on [[Glossary:European_statistics_on_tourism|tourism]]. The scope of observation for data on tourism trips are all tourism trips with at least 1 overnight stay, made by the [[Glossary:Resident|resident population]] aged 15 and over. It includes trips made for private or professional purpose, outside the usual environment. Data on type of destination is sent to Eurostat every 3 years. This article includes data for the reference year 2022. Next transmission will take place in 2026 for the reference year 2025. For this variable, multiple answer possibilities are allowed. In case of a trip involving several destinations, it should refer to the entire trip and not only to the main destination of the trip. ===Context=== The EU is a major tourist destination, with 6 EU countries among the world's top 10 destinations for holidaymakers, according to UN Tourism[https://www.e-unwto.org/toc/wtobarometereng/22/3 UN Tourism] data. Tourism is an important activity in the EU which contributes to employment and economic growth, as well as to the development of rural, peripheral or less-developed areas. Tourism is estimated to account for 4.5% to the EU's gross value added. These characteristics drive the demand for reliable and harmonised statistics on this activity, as well as within the wider context of regional policy and sustainable development policy areas. ===Other articles=== *[[Tourism trips of Europeans]] (online publication) *[[:Category:Tourism|All articles on tourism statistics]] ===Publications=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/tourism/publications Recent Eurostat publications on tourism] ===Selected datasets=== *Tourism [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database?node_code=t_tour (t_tour)], see: :{{Template:Publication|code=tin00190|title= Trips by detailed country/world region of main destination (tin00190)}} :{{Template:Publication|code=tin00193|title= Nights spent by detailed country/world region of the main destination (tin00193)}} ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/tourism/database Tourism (tour)], see "Trips of EU residents - annual data": :Tourism trips (tour_dem_tt) :Tourism nights (tour_dem_tn) :Expenditure on tourism trips (tour_dem_ex) ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=tourism}} Tourism statistics] ===Data visualisations=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/RSI/#?vis=nuts2.tourism Regional Statistics Illustrated] - Tourism ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=tour_dem_esms|title=Trips of EU residents - annual data}} (ESMS metadata file — tour_dem_esms) ===Legislation=== *With 2012 as reference year: :*{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0692:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 692/2011}} of 6 July 2011 concerning European statistics on tourism and repealing Council Directive 95/57/EC. title: Tourism statistics - participation in tourism
text:
Statistics on the participation in tourism in the EU. Data extracted in October 2025 Planned article update: November 2026 In 2024 compared with 2023, 2.3% or 5.7 million more Europeans made tourism trips. 65% of Europeans participated in tourism in 2024. In 2024, around half of the European tourists only made domestic trips. This article is part of the [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] online publication '''[[Tourism trips of Europeans]]''', which provides statistics on tourism [[Glossary:Demand side tourism statistics|demand]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] and [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] countries. The article analyses participation in [[Glossary:Tourism|tourism]] (sometimes called 'tourism propensity'), defined as the proportion of a given population that makes at least one tourism trip of a specified minimum duration in a given reference period. In this article, the reference period is one calendar year (2024) and the scope is all tourism trips taken for personal purposes (excluding trips for professional purposes) of at least one overnight stay. These statistics show how many Europeans participate in tourism in the context of policy initiatives promoting "tourism for all". However, not all "non-tourists" should be considered excluded — some population groups are simply not interested in making tourism trips (as opposed to others whose reasons for not travelling are linked to constraints such as their financial situation, physical disabilities or lack of time due to family and/or work commitments). Already since 2022, there have been no travel restrictions due to the COVID-19 pandemic anymore. The tourism sector started to recover already in 2021, getting closer to the levels of 2019, pre-pandemic year, and this recovery continued also in 2022, 2023 and 2024. === 5.7 million more Europeans made tourism trips in 2024 compared with 2023 === In recent decades, tourism trips have become an important aspect of the lives of many Europeans. Tourism gives people the opportunity to break out from their usual environment and discover other parts of their own country, other countries in Europe or other regions of the world. Tourism thus helps to bring people from different cultures together and fosters mutual respect between different communities within and across countries or continents. In 2020, the outbreak of COVID-19 had an unprecedented impact on travel behaviour of people all around the world due to the related measures put in place in all countries worldwide and the perceived health risk and uncertainty of people to travel. In 2021, many of the restrictions were lifted, allowing the tourism sector to start recovering. Nearly 249 million Europeans (aged 15 or over) participated in tourism in 2024, making at least 1 tourism trip for personal purposes (see Table 1). This represents an increase of 2.3% (or 5.7 million more tourists) compared with 2023, while compared to 2019, there were 5.5 million more tourists. 22 countries exceeded 2023 levels, the highest increases being registered in Romania (30.5%), Sweden (16.6%) and Lithuania (13.5%). The 5 countries which registered lower values in tourism participation in 2024 compared to the previous year are Poland, Portugal, Italy, France, Denmark and Bulgaria, as seen in Figure 1. [[Image: T1_Change in the number of EU residents (aged 15 and over) participating in tourism by destination, 2024 compared with 2023 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Change in the number of EU residents (aged 15 and over) participating in tourism by destination, 2024 compared with 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_totot}}|alt=A table showing the change in the number of EU residents aged 15 and over participating in tourism by destination, comparing 2023 with 2024. Data are shown in percentages for the EU, the EU Member States and one of the EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image: F1_Change in the number of EU residents (aged 15 or over) participating in tourism, 2024 compared with 2023 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Change in the number of EU residents (aged 15 or over) participating in tourism, 2024 compared with 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_totot}}|alt=A vertical bar chart showing the change in the number of EU residents aged 15 and over participating in tourism, comparing 2023 with 2024. Data are shown in percentages for the EU, the EU Member States and one of the EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Looking closer at the destination of the trip, 6.8% more Europeans travelled abroad in 2024 compared with the previous year. This increase at EU level reflects increases in 23 of the EU countries, as seen in Table 1. The biggest increases were in Sweden (75.3%), Romania (62.2%), Slovakia (19.4%) and Spain (14.3%), while decreases were registered in Bulgaria (-14.1%), Denmark (-8.5%), Italy (-2.2%) and Finland (-0.2%). In domestic tourism, a similar trend is observed, though the changes have been more moderate. In 2024, there was a 2.5% increase in the number of Europeans engaging in tourism compared to 2023. Notably, Sweden, Romania and Cyprus experienced the highest growth, each recording an increase of over 20%. === More than 6 in 10 EU residents made tourism trips in 2024 === This subpopulation of tourists (not including business trips) of nearly 249 million Europeans who made at least 1 tourism trip for personal purposes in 2024 corresponds to nearly two thirds (65%) of the EU population (aged 15 or over). Around one third (31%) of Europeans made at least 1 domestic tourism trip with at least 1 overnight stay and no trips abroad, while only 10% made at least 1 trip abroad and no domestic trips. However, one quarter of the Europeans made domestic trips as well as foreign trips (see Figure 2). When only trips of at least 4 overnight stays are taken into account – thus excluding tourists whose trips lasted no more than 3 nights – the participation rate drops to 52% (see pie chart on the right of Figure 2). [[Image:F2_Share of the EU population (aged 15 and over) participating to personal trips, 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Share of the EU population (aged 15 and over) participating to personal trips, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_totot}}|alt=A double pie chart showing the share of the EU population aged 15 and over participating to personal trips for the year 2024. Date are shown in percentages by length of trip. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 3 shows the change in the shares of participation in tourism in 2024 compared with 2023. The share of the EU population participating in tourism, regardless of the destination, increased by 0.5 percentage points for trips with at least 1 overnight stay and by 1.3 percentage points for long trips of at least 4 overnight stays. The analysis in the first chapter shows an increase in the number of domestic tourists, those who made at least 1 trip inside their own country, independently of whether they also travelled abroad or not. Looking closer at Europeans who made only domestic and no foreign trips, the share of participation was slightly lower in 2024 compared with 2023 both for all trips and for the segment of long trips. Almost a third of the European tourists made only domestic trips in 2024. However, compared with 2023, the share of participation only in domestic trips dropped by 1.2% for all trips and by 0.6% for the segment of long trips, while the share increased for people having participated in both domestic and international trips or in international trips only. [[Image: F3_Change in the share of the EU population (aged 15 and over) participating to personal trips, 2024 compared with 2023 (percentage points).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Change in the share of the EU population (aged 15 and over) participating to personal trips, 2024 compared with 2023''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_totot}}|alt=A double vertical bar chart showing the change in the share of the EU population aged 15 and over participating to personal trips by type of trip. Data are shown in percentage points, comparing 2023 with 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === In 2024, participation of Europeans in tourism ranged from 84% in the Netherlands to 28% in Romania=== In 9 countries, at least 7 out of 10 residents made at least 1 tourism trip for personal purposes in 2024: the Netherlands (84%), Luxembourg, Finland and Sweden (83% each), France (81%), Germany (80%), Ireland (79%), Austria and Czechia (76% each) (see Table 2 and Figure 4). At the other end, 3 out of 10 residents of Bulgaria (32%) and less than 3 out of 10 residents of Romania (28%) participated in tourism. In 2023, the share of persons participating in tourism ranged from 27% in Romania to 85% in France. [[Image:T2_Participation in tourism of EU residents (aged 15 and over), 2024 and 2023.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 2: Participation in tourism of EU residents (aged 15 years and over), 2024 and 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_totot}}|alt= Table showing participation in tourism of EU residents aged 15 years and over in the EU, individual EU Member States and Norway for the years 2024 and 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:F4_Share of EU population (aged 15 and over) participating in tourism by destination, 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Share of EU population (aged 15 years and over) participating in tourism by destination, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_totot}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage share of EU population in the EU, individual EU Member States and Norway aged 15 years and over participating in tourism by destination. Each country column has three stacks representing domestic only, domestic and foreign and foreign only for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In the 2 largest countries, Germany and France, in terms of population, the participation rate was higher than the EU average (80% and 81%, respectively); together they accounted for 4 out of 10 European tourists. Countries with the highest participation rates in domestic tourism (namely 'domestic trips only' plus 'domestic and foreign trips' were Sweden (77%), France and Finland (76% each), Czechia (69%), Germany (66%) and Spain (64%). As regards foreign tourism, the highest participation rates were observed among residents of Luxembourg (83%), followed at some distance by Ireland (68%), the Netherlands (67%), Austria (62%), Germany and Belgium (61% each). Countries whose populations made the highest proportion of domestic trips only (and no foreign trips) during 2024 were France (51%), Poland and Spain (43% each). === Almost half of the Europeans aged 65 years and over did not make any trips in 2024 === On average, 65% of the EU population made tourism trips for personal purposes in the course of 2024. The participation rate ranged between 65% and 74% in all age groups except for those aged 65 years and over, where it dropped to 51% (see Figure 5). While persons aged 65 years and over represented 25% of the EU population aged 15 years and over, they accounted for only 20% of EU tourists (see Figure 6). However, even with a low share of participation in tourism, this age group of 65 years and over represented nearly 49 million tourists. [[Image:F5_Share of EU population participating in tourism by age group, 2024 (%)_v1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Share of EU population participating in tourism by age group, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_toage}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing percentage share of EU population participating in tourism by age group. Seven columns represent age groups. Totalling 100 percent, each column has two stacks representing participating in tourism and not participating in tourism for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image: F6_Share of each age group in EU population and in EU tourist population, 2024 (%)_1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Share of each age group in EU population and in EU tourist population, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_toage}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_pjangroup}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing percentage share of each age group in EU population and in EU tourist population. Six sections represent age groups. Each section has two columns representing share of the age group in EU population aged 15 years and over and share of the age group in in EU population aged 15 years and over participating in tourism for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Compared with 2023, participation in tourism increased for all age groups in 2024 but one, ranging from 0.9% for Europeans aged 35 to 44 years to 6.0% for those aged 65 years and over. The only exceptions corresponded to Europeans aged 25 to 34 years, who recorded an drop of -3.6% compared to 2023 (see Figure 7). [[Image:F7_Change in the number of Europeans participating in tourism by age group, EU, 2024 compared with 2023 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Change in the number of Europeans participating in tourism by age group, EU, 2024 compared with 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_toage}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing percentage change in the number of Europeans participating in tourism by age group in the EU for the year 2024 compared with 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === In 2024, 47% of the European tourists made only domestic trips === This section looks closer at the segment of the EU population who made tourism trips and the breakdown by destination of those trips. More than a third of the EU tourists made, during 2024, both domestic and foreign trips (38%), an increase compared with 2023 when this share was 36% (see Figure 8). Almost half (47%) of the EU tourists made only domestic trips in 2024 and considering tourists who made both domestic and foreign trips, 85% of EU tourists made at least 1 domestic trip in 2024. The pattern was fairly stable across all age groups for domestic trips. 45% of tourists aged 65 years and over made foreign trips while for the other age groups this share ranged from 53% to 59% of their tourist population (see Figure 9). [[Image:F8_EU tourists by destination, 2024 and 2023 (% of tourist population).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: EU tourists by destination, 2024 and 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code= tour_dem_totot}}|alt= Two separate pie charts showing EU tourists by destination as percentage of tourist EU population. One pie chart shows the year 2024 and the other 2023. The segments include domestic only, domestic and foreign and foreign only. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:F9_Destinations of European tourists by age group of the tourist, 2024 (% of tourist population)_1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: Destinations of European tourists by age group of the tourist, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_toage}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing destinations of European tourists by age group of the tourist as percentage of tourist population. Seven columns represent age groups. Totalling 100 percent, each column has three stacks representing domestic trips only, domestic and foreign trips and foreign trips only for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === In 2024, nearly 3 out of 10 Europeans could not afford to pay for 1 week of holidays === The collection of data on reasons for not participating in tourism started in 2014 with 2013 as first reference year. This data is sent to Eurostat every 3 years. In 2013, 20% of all EU residents aged 15 years and over reported financial issues as 1 of the main reasons for not participating in tourism. This share dropped to 18% in 2016 and decreased further to 16% in 2019, reaching 15% in 2022. The statistics on [[Quality of life indicators|income and living conditions]], however, include an indicator related to tourism which gives the proportion of the population that cannot afford to pay for 1 week of annual holiday away from home during the reference year (see Figure 10 and Figure 11). After a peak of 40.5% in 2012 due to the economic crisis, this proportion started decreasing in 2013 and reached 28.0% in 2019. In 2020, the share of Europeans who could not afford 1 week of annual holidays increased again to 28.7% and then decreased to 27.7% in 2021. In 2024 it was 27.0%, ranging from 9% in Luxembourg to more than 40% in Romania, Greece and Bulgaria. The data on participation in tourism shows that the share of EU residents aged 15 years and over that did not participate in any trips of at least four overnight stays remained more or less stable during the 10-year period 2010-2019, ranging from 48.8% in 2019 to 52.9% in 2014, but increased sharply to 61.9% in 2020. A decrease followed in 2021, reaching 57.8% and continued further in 2022 (51.6%), 2023 (48.9%) and 2024 (47.6%), the lowest level in the past 15 years. This data looks at Europeans who did not make any long trips, independently of the reason for not travelling; it reflects, however, the impact of COVID-19 in 2020 and the slow recovery in 2021. Given the relatively stable share of the population that cannot afford to pay for 1 week of annual holiday away from home in 2020 and 2021, the lower participation during these years tends to be mainly due to other reasons than financial ones (for example, health reasons, COVID-19 restrictions, no motivation to travel, etc.). [[Image: F10_Share of EU population unable to afford paying for one week annual holiday and share of EU population not participating in tourism, 2010-2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 10: Share of EU population unable to afford paying for one week annual holiday and share of EU population not participating in tourism, 2010-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_mdes02}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_totot}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_npsex}}|alt= Line chart showing percentage share of EU population over the years 2010 to 2024. Three lines represent, firstly, unable to afford paying for one week holiday. Secondly, not participating in trips of four nights or more. Thirdly, not participating in tourism for financial reasons. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:F11_Share of the EU population unable to afford paying for one week annual holiday, 2024 (%)_1.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 11: Share of the EU population unable to afford paying for one week annual holiday, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_mdes02}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing percentage share of the EU population unable to afford paying for 1 week annual holiday in the EU, individual EU Member States and Norway for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs=== *[[Media:Participation in tourism_2024 data.xlsx|Download Excel file - Tables and figures on Participation in tourism]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== '''Collection of annual data on trips of EU residents''' The collection consists of harmonised data collected by the Member States in the frame of the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0692:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 692/2011}} of the European Parliament and of the Council concerning European statistics on [[Glossary:European_statistics_on_tourism|tourism]]. The scope of observation for the data on participation in tourism are the residents of the country, aged 15 years and over, and refers only to tourism for personal purposes, excluding trips made for professional reasons. The scope of observation for the data on quality of life, in particular the inability to afford to pay for 1-week annual holiday away from home, are all persons living in private households, excluding in general the persons living in collective households and in institutions from the target population. ===Context=== The EU is a major tourist destination, with 6 EU countries among the world's top 10 destinations for holidaymakers, according to UN Tourism[ https://www.e-unwto.org/toc/wtobarometereng/22/3] data. Tourism is an important activity in the EU which contributes to employment and economic growth, as well as to the development of rural, peripheral or less-developed areas. Tourism is estimated to account for 4.5% to the EU's gross value added. These characteristics drive the demand for reliable and harmonised statistics on this activity, as well as within the wider context of regional policy and sustainable development policy areas. ===Other articles=== *[[Tourism trips of Europeans]] (online publication) *[[Tourism|All articles on tourism statistics]] ===Publications=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/tourism/publications Recent Eurostat publications on tourism] ===Selected Datasets=== *Tourism [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database?node_code=t_tour (t_tour)], see "Annual data on trips of EU residents": :{{Template:Publication|code=tin00185|title=Persons participating in tourism for personal purposes - number of tourists (tin00185)}} :{{Template:Publication|code=tin00186|title=Participation in tourism for personal purposes - % of total population (tin00186)}} ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/tourism/database Tourism (tour)], see "Trips of EU residents - title: Tourism statistics - seasonality at regional level
text:
The tourist accommodation sector in the EU is described as seasonal aspects of nights spent at tourist accommodation establishments, at NUTS 2 regional level Data extracted in November 2025 Planned article update: November 2026 In 1 in 6 EU NUTS 2 regions, more than 40% of the annual tourism nights are focused in the top 2 months in 2024 Coastal regions tend to be highly seasonal, while capital regions seem less affected by seasonality in tourism. Share of the top 2 months in total annual nights spent in the region, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/tour_occ_nin2m/default/table?lang=en tour_occ_nin2m])
This article focuses on the [[Glossary:Tourist accommodation establishment|tourist accommodation]] sector in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] Member States, [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate countries]] and [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] countries, and looks at the seasonality of [[Glossary:Nights spent|nights spent]] in accommodation establishments at regional [[Glossary:Nomenclature_of_territorial_units_for_statistics_(NUTS)|NUTS 2]] level. The article [[Seasonality in the tourist accommodation sector|Seasonality in the tourist accommodation sector]] examines the seasonality at national level, based on short-term data that Eurostat receives monthly from the Member States. This article gives information on seasonality looking deeper at regional NUTS 2 level across the EU, based on a breakdown by month of the regional data that Member States send to Eurostat once per year (since the entry into force of [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32019R1681 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/1681] in 2020). This article complements the article [[Tourism statistics at regional level|Tourism statistics at regional level]] (most recent update March 2025, with 2023 data). A more comprehensive discussion of accommodation statistics is available in the article [[Tourism_statistics_-_annual results for the accommodation sector|Tourism statistics - annual results for the accommodation sector]] (most recent update September 2025, with 2024 data). === Introduction === Seasonality is a key tourism policy issue. The impact of seasonality varies across EU destinations, as discussed in the following sections of this article. The concentration of tourism demand in a limited number of months – often July and August – can impact on the environment (e.g. waste production, water and energy use), but also on the labour market conditions and quality of service provided or support for tourism by local communities. Seasonality can also affect the economic performance of the tourism industries, as infrastructure and workforce are used only for part of the year, leading to higher costs and lower profitability. Policy needs for tourism data are often at regional level, as highlighted in the 2022 Commission report [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/404a8144-8892-11ec-8c40-01aa75ed71a1 Transition Pathway for Tourism]. For instance, according to the report, the 2040 vision for rural areas highlights their potential and their importance for European identity. Rural areas can offer unique natural and cultural experiences to visitors, but they can also face problems of limited transport or digital connectivity. The most remote parts of the EU – the outermost regions - are highly dependent on tourism as it accounts for a particularly high share of their economy. They suffer from seasonal fluctuations and are fully dependent on (limited) air connections. Our data enables the analysis of seasonality at a subnational level in this article, complementing and deepening the article on [[Seasonality_in_the_tourist_accommodation_sector|Seasonality in the tourist accommodation sector]] that focuses on the country level. Different measures of seasonality can be used, ranging from inequality indices, such as the Gini coefficient or dispersion measures such as the coefficient of variation for 12 monthly values, to more transparent or clear measures comparing top and bottom observations or indicating the share of the top months in the annual total. While the first group might better capture the skewness of the distribution of the 12 monthly observations and better absorb the effect of outliers, the latter approach is used in this publication, for reasons of clarity and simplicity of interpretation for non-expert users. Unless mentioned differently, this article looks mainly at the share of the top 2 months in the annual number of nights spent in rented accommodation. === The regions with the highest seasonality are coastal regions === Map 1 shows for each EU region the share in the annual total of the top 2 months in terms of nights spent at tourist accommodation establishments, Table 1 shows the data for the 20 regions with the highest seasonality. The map reveals a very dispersed pattern across Europe but also within most of the countries, underlining the relevance of analysing seasonal patterns at a subnational level. In 9 EU regions located in Bulgaria, France, Italy, Croatia and Romania, more than half of tourist nights are spent in July or August, the two busiest months in these regions. Also the Albanian region of Veri records more tourist nights in July and August than in the rest of the year. All these regions are coastal regions. The remaining 11 regions in Table 1, recording between 47% and 50% of annual nights spent in the top 2 months, all but one are coastal regions. The exception is the Dél-Dunántúl region of Hungary, on the shores of Lake Balaton. [[Image: Map1new2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Share of the top 2 months in total annual nights spent in the region, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_occ_nin2m}}|alt= Map showing seasonality in tourist accommodation by EU NUTS 2 regions as percentage share of the top 2 months in total annual nights spent in the region. Each region is colour-coded based on percentage ranges for the year 2024.]]
[[Image: T1 Seasonality in tourism V4.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Seasonality in tourism - Top 20 NUTS 2 regions in terms of nights spent in tourist accommodation, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/tour_occ_nin2m__custom_18882606/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=83c48518-96b8-43cf-8ce5-f37869ea6fb8&c=1765821247000 tour_occ_nin2m])|alt= Table showing seasonality in tourism of the top 20 EU NUTS 2 regions in terms of nights spent in tourist accommodation, percentage share of the 2 highest months and percentage share of the nights spent by domestic tourists for the year 2024.]] The EU region with the highest level of seasonality is Sud-Est, in Romania, with 66.0% of all nights concentrated in August and July. The 5 regions with the highest seasonality in 2024 further include the 2 main tourism regions in Bulgaria jointly accounting for 63% of all nights spent in the country in 2024, namely Yugoiztochen (60.1% of all nights concentrated in July and August) and Severoiztochen (56.9%), the coastal region of Italy, Calabria (58,8%) and the Croatian region Jadranska Hrvatska (57.7%), which is also the third EU region in terms of number of nights spent in the entire year. In 1 out of 6 regions for which data is available (39 out of 244 regions), more than 40% of the annual nights are spent in the top 2 months (in all cases it concerns the tandem July and August, except the Finnish region Åland where July and June are the dominant months). The 20 most seasonal regions listed in Table 1 jointly record 170 million nights spent during their 2 peak months (52.6% of the nights spent in these regions in 2024). === August remains the most popular tourist month in most EU regions === Map 2 shows for each EU region the month with the highest number of nights spent in tourist accommodation throughout 2024. In the majority EU regions (174 out of the 244 EU regions with available data), August is the month with the highest concentration in the number of nights spent. July is the dominant month in 48 EU regions, mainly covering most of northern Europe and parts of Belgium, Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Germany. [[Image: Map2new6.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 2: Seasonality in tourism by NUTS2 region - Top month in terms of nights spent, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_occ_nin2m}}|alt= Map showing seasonality in EU tourist accommodation by NUTS 2 region based on top month in terms of nights spent. The months January or February, May, June, July, August, September or October and December and data not available each have a colour and the regions are colour-coded according to the top month for the year 2024.]] October is the busiest month in only 6 EU regions, with the French Ile de France, the capital of Paris and the Spanish Comunidad de Madrid standing out. The Romanian capital region, Bucharest-Ilfov, the French island of La Réunion and the Greek region of Dytiki Makedonia also registered the most guest nights in October. February is the busiest month in 5 EU regions, with the most guest nights recorded in the Austrian regions of Tyrol, Salzburg and Voralberg. This group also includes the French island of Guadeloupe and the Bulgarian region of Yugozapaden. In none of the regions, March, April and November is the top month. For all 22 regions where neither July nor August are the top month, these regions have a relatively weak seasonality, far below the EU average (which is 31% of annual nights spent in the top 2 months). === Seasonal shifts are less significant in most capital regions=== Table 2 breaks down the data by country, showing for each the region with the highest seasonality and the region with the lowest seasonality. The 3 countries that include the most seasonal regions (see above) have also the widest spread within the country: in Romania, the most seasonal region records 66% of all tourism nights during July or August, while in the least seasonal region, Bucureşti-Ilfov, the top 2 months account for only 19% of all tourism nights. Similarly, in Bulgaria the least seasonal region only records 21% of annual tourism nights in the top 2 months (February and January, for the region of Yugozapaden), compared with 60% for the most seasonal region. In Italy, the most seasonal region records 59% of all tourism nights during July or August, while the least seasonal region, Lazio, accounts for only 21% of annual tourism nights in the top 2 months. [[Image: T2 Seasonality in tourism V4.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 2: Seasonality in tourism - NUTS 2 regions with highest and lowest seasonality, by country, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/tour_occ_nin2m__custom_18882606/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=83c48518-96b8-43cf-8ce5-f37869ea6fb8&c=1765821247000 tour_occ_nin2m])|alt= Table showing seasonality in tourism of the NUTS 2 regions with highest and lowest seasonality in the EU, individual EU Member States, EFTA countries, North Macedonia, Albania and Serbia for the year 2024.]] Generally speaking, regions that include capital cities tend to attract tourists all year round, be it for private or professional reasons, and show a less pronounced seasonal pattern. In 18 out of 21 countries that have regional subdivisions and where data for all regions is available, the capital region is the least seasonal region. This is the case for the regions comprising Brussels, Sofia, Prague, Copenhagen, Berlin, Dublin, Athen, Paris, Zagreb, Rome, Vilnius, Budapest, Vienna, Warsaw, Bucharest, Bratislava, Helsinki and Stockholm. === 40% of EU regions have the same seasonal peak period for domestic and international guests=== Tables 3 and 4 look at the seasonal pattern in tourism flows, broken down by domestic guests and international guests respectively. Among the top 10 regions that have the highest seasonality when considering the segment of domestic tourists, four are located in Italy. These Italian regions - Calabria, Puglia, Sardegna and Molise - attract predominantly domestic tourists all year round. [[Image: T3 Seasonality in domestic tourism V4.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Seasonality in domestic tourism, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/tour_occ_nin2m__custom_18882606/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=83c48518-96b8-43cf-8ce5-f37869ea6fb8&c=1765821247000 tour_occ_nin2m])|alt= Table showing seasonality in tourism of the top 20 EU NUTS 2 regions in terms of nights spent by domestic tourists, percentage share of the 2 highest months and percentage share of the nights spent by domestic tourists for the year 2024.]] Alternatively, when looking at the top 10 regions that have the highest seasonality when considering the segment of international tourists, 5 are located in France. However, the significance of international tourism is relatively low in these regions. In 99 out of 244 regions, the top 2 months for domestic tourists are the same as the top 2 months for international tourists. [[Image: T4 Seasonality in international tourism V4.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 4: Seasonality in international tourism, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/tour_occ_nin2m__custom_18882606/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=83c48518-96b8-43cf-8ce5-f37869ea6fb8&c=1765821247000 tour_occ_nin2m])|alt= Table showing seasonality in tourism of the top 20 EU NUTS 2 regions in terms of nights spent by international tourists, percentage share of the 2 highest months and percentage share of the nights spent by international tourists for the year 2024.]] === Three Greek regions are among the top 5 areas with the highest tourism intensity (tourists per local resident) during the peak season === Seasonality can negatively impact on perceived tourism pressure at tourism destinations. This section puts the nights spent by tourists in relation to the size of the local population or the area (in km2) of the regions. Map 3 shows for each region the tourism intensity during the peak month, defined as the number of nights spent at tourist accommodation establishments on an average day in the peak month, per 1000 inhabitants. In 11 EU regions, this ratio exceeds 200. The highest ratio is observed in the island region Notio Aigaio in Greece (which includes popular islands like Rhodes, Kos, Mykonos), where during the peak month (August) 896 overnight stays by tourists are recorded per 1000 inhabitants. It should be noted that the data is an underestimation of the real tourism pressure as the nominator of the ratio doesn’t include same-day visitors or tourists staying in non-rented accommodation, such as second homes or stays with friends or relatives. Other regions with a high tourism intensity are the region bordering the island regions in Greece (Ionia Nisia, Kriti), the Adriatic coast in Croatia (Jadranska Hrvatska), the Austrian and Italian alpine areas, Spain (Illes Balears) and France (Corse), and Algarve in Portugal. [[Image: Map3new2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 3: Tourism intensity during the busiest month of the year, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_occ_nin2m}}|alt= Map showing seasonality in EU tourist accommodation by NUTS 2 region as average overnight stays per day during the busiest month of the year, per thousand inhabitants. Each region is colour-coded based on overnight stays ranges for the year 2024.]] When considering the number of tourism nights per square kilometre during the peak month (Map 4), the regions with the highest tourism density are generally smaller regions that comprise a major city. This is the case for regions that comprise Vienna (on average 156 tourists per night per km2 in the peak month), Brussels (144), Prague (125), Berlin (110), Budapest (71) and Hamburg (70). In these 6 cities, the peak month is July, August or, for Vienna, December. With 139 overnights stays on average per square kilometer, the tourism density was also high in the peak month for Malta (August), while in Illes Balears in Spain, it reached 91 overnights stays on average per square kilometer. [[Image: Map4new2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 4: Tourism density during the busiest month of the year, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_occ_nin2m}}|alt= Map showing seasonality in EU tourist accommodation by NUTS 2 region as average overnight stays per day during the busiest month of the year, per square kilometre. Each region is colour-coded based on overnight stays ranges for the year 2024.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media: Tourism_seasonality_regional_2024 V5.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0692:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 692/2011}} concerning European statistics on tourism, organises the [[Glossary:European statistical system (ESS)|European statistical system]] of tourism statistics. This system consists of two main components: statistics on capacity and occupancy of tourist accommodation and statistics on tourism demand. The former are generally collected in most Member States via surveys filled in by accommodation establishments, while the latter are mostly collected by means of traveller surveys at the border or via traditional household surveys. Statistics on the occupancy of tourist accommodation refer to the number of arrivals (at accommodation establishments) and the number of nights spent by residents and non-residents, broken down by type of establishment or by region. Both annual and monthly series are available. Statistics on the use of bed places and bedrooms ([[Glossary:Net occupancy rate|occupancy rates]]) are also compiled. This article uses data on monthly nights spent at NUTS 2 regional level, transmitted once per year to Eurostat by the statistical offices of the Member States. Statistics on the demand for tourism look at participation, i.e. the number of residents that make at least one trip of at least one overnight stay during the reference period. They also look at the number of tourism trips made (and the number of nights spent on those trips), broken down by tourism-related variables such as country of destination, month of departure, length of stay, type of organisation of the trip, mode of transport, type of accommodation or expenditure, and by socio-demographic variables, such as age or gender. === Context === In June 2010, the European Commission released a Communication entitled [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52010DC0352 Europe, the world's No. 1 tourist destination - a new political framework for tourism in Europe]. One of the challenges and opportunities facing the European tourism industry is the seasonal distribution of demand for tourism. Better use of existing tourist infrastructure and staff in the low season could help businesses improve their productivity and benefit from a more stable and motivated workforce. Extending the tourism season or spreading tourism activities more evenly throughout the year can significantly boost the [[Glossary:Sustainable development|sustainability]] and [[Glossary:Competitiveness|competitiveness]] of European tourist destinations. === Other Articles === *[[:Tourism|Tourism entry page in Statistics Explained]] === Selected Datasetss === *Tourism [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database?node_code=t_tour (t_tour)] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/tourism/database Tourism (tour)] === Thematic section === *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=tourism}} Tourism statistics] === Publications === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/tourism/publications Recent Eurostat publications on tourism] === Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=tour_occ_esms|title=Capacity and occupancy of tourist accommodation establishments}} (ESMS metadata file — tour_occ_esms) === Legislation === *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0692:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 692/2011}} of the European Parliament and of the Council of 6 July 2011 concerning European statistics on tourism and repealing Council Directive 95/57/EC.
