title: Towards Digital Decade targets for Europe
text:
Towards Digital Decade targets for Europe [[Image:Digital-Compass-Revisited-Visual-01-1200x630-V7.jpg|thumb|centre|380px]] Data extracted in June 2026 Planned article update: June 2027 In 2025, 60% of EU citizens aged 16-74 years had at least basic overall digital skills, 20 percentage points below the 2030 target set in the Digital Decade. In 2025, 10.4 million people were employed in ICT specialist occupations in the EU, over 9.6 million short of the 2030 goal set in the Digital Decade. In 2025, 72% of EU small and medium-sized enterprises reached at least basic digital intensity, 18 percentage points shy of the ambition set in the Digital Decade for 2030. Digital technologies have pervaded almost all spheres of people's lives. They transform business models, jobs and production, and stimulate growth and innovation. The fast progressing digital transformation is increasingly highlighting its potential for society and the economy: supporting employment, health and education, improving the economic resilience of businesses, and contributing to sustainability. Digital transformation is high on the European policy agenda, being one of the [[Glossary:European_Commission|European Commission]]'s main political priorities for the coming years. On 9 March 2021, the Commission presented the [https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/priorities-2019-2024/europe-fit-digital-age/europes-digital-decade-digital-targets-2030_en Digital Decade] Communication, which sets a vision and targets for a successful digital transformation of Europe by 2030. The Digital Decade policy programme sets out concrete targets for achieving the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|EU]]'s digital ambitions, evolving around four cardinal points: skills, digital transformation of businesses, secure and sustainable digital infrastructures and digitalisation of public services. Progress towards these 2030 targets is monitored in the [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/2024-state-digital-decade-package State of the Digital Decade report]. This article presents the results drawn primarily from two surveys on information and communication technologies (IoT):, one on ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises and one on the use of ICT in households and by individuals. These surveys provide data essential for the State of the Digital Decade report. Additionally, data on ICT specialists in employment are source the Labour Force Survey, while data on broadband internet coverage is derived from the Broadband Coverage in Europe study, which is based on a survey of national regulatory authorities and operators. === Digitally skilled citizens and professionals=== The ambitions set for the area of skills in the Digital Decade are that, by 2030, at least 80% of all adults should have at least basic digital skills, and that there should be 20 million employed ICT specialists in the EU, with increased women's participation. '''In 2025, 60% of EU citizens aged 16-74 years had at least basic overall digital skills.''' Digital literacy is crucial for people to benefit from the ongoing digital transformation and the vast variety of services available online, thus preventing them from being digitally excluded. Having digital skills is also critical to protect oneself from cyber threats stemming from the increasingly digitalised world. The digital skills indicator (DSI) is a composite indicator covering five areas: information and data literacy skills; communication and collaboration skills; digital content creation skills; safety skills; and problem-solving skills. These reflect the five competence areas of the revised [https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/digcomp/digital-competence-framework_en Digital Competence Framework] (DigComp 2.0). It is assumed that individuals who have performed certain activities have the corresponding skills, hence the indicator can be considered as a proxy of individuals' digital skills. To have at least basic overall digital skills (derived as a sum of basic and above basic levels), people must know how to perform at least one activity related to each area. For more information on DSI levels and the types of activities related to each skill, consult the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/isoc_sk_dskl_i21_esmsip2.htm metadata file]. In 2025, 60% of people aged 16-74 years in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|EU ]] had at least basic overall digital skills, 20 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp) below the 2030 target set in the Digital Decade. The highest proportions of people aged 16-74 years who had at least basic overall digital skills were found in the Netherlands (84%) and Ireland (83%), followed by Denmark and Finland (both 81%). On the other hand, the lowest were recorded in Romania (32%) and Bulgaria (38%). In most EU countries, the shares of people with at least basic digital skills were higher among men than among women, with Germany and Croatia recording the highest difference of 6 pp and 5 pp respectively. In 8 EU countries, the situation was reversed, with higher shares of women with at least basic digital skills, with the largest difference in Finland (4 pp) (Figure 1). [[Image:Fig1 Individuals with at least basic overall digital skills, by sex.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Individuals with at least basic overall digital skills, by sex, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e120eb07-b7c0-4c26-8d5d-32a6e1222729?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T15:14:15Z isoc_sk_dskl_i21]) |alt= a double bar chart with a marker showing individuals with at least basic overall digital skills, by sex, 2025 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries, potential candidates. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] In 2025, in the EU, 59% of women and 62% of men demonstrated at least basic digital skills. The level of digital skills varies not only by gender, but also among different age groups. The highest shares of people with at least basic digital skills were recorded in younger age groups for both women and men. In particular among 16-24-year-olds, with 76% of women and 73% of men of this age having at least basic digital skills and among 25-34-year-olds, where 75% of women and 74% of men demonstrated basic or above basic digital skills. The lowest shares were observed among 65–74-year-olds, where 38% of men and 29% of women had at least basic digital skills. Interestingly, in the younger age groups – below 45 years of age – the proportions of people with at least basic digital skills were higher among women than among men. Among people aged 45 years and over, the situation is reversed and the shares are higher among men. The largest difference is visible in the older age group, where among those aged 65-74 years the share of women with at least basic digital skills was 9 points lower than among men in this age group. A relatively large gender gap was noticeable also in the youngest age group of 16-24 (3 pp higher for women than for men), similar to the one among people aged 55-64 years (4 pp higher for men than for women). Looking even more in detail at the level of digital skills, there are also some differences in the proportions of people with basic or above basic digital skills. Among women aged less than 34 years, more than half of those with at least basic digital skills had above basic digital skills, with the highest share of women in the youngest age group – 45%. Among men, the share of people with above basic digital skills was higher than the share of people with basic digital skills in age groups younger than 55 years. The highest share of men with above basic digital skills was in the age group 25-34 years (Figure 2). [[Image:Fig2 Individuals with at least basic overall digital skills, by age and sex, EU.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Individuals with at least basic overall digital skills, by age and sex, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5a87e943-20fc-4839-bf82-3c5d168ab28a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-03T12:48:00Z isoc_sk_dskl_i21])|alt= a horizontal stacked bar chart showing individuals with at least basic overall digital skills, by age and sex, EU, 2025, the bars show age and sex, male and female. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] In 2025, 60% of EU citizens had at least basic digital skills, with 31% of people aged 16-74 years having basic overall digital skills and 29% demonstrating above basic overall digital skills. Among people with different levels of education, the higher the level of education attained, the higher the share of people with at least basic overall digital skills. The highest share was among individuals with higher education (82%), with 30% having basic and 50% having above basic overall digital skills. The proportions of people with at least basic overall digital skills also varied quite significantly depending on their status in the labour market. Students and working people (employees, self-employed, family workers) were the groups with the highest shares (80% and 69% respectively). Among unemployed people, and those retired or not active in the labour force (excluding students), the shares of people with at least basic digital skills were lower (54% and 37% respectively) (Figure 3). [[Image:Fig3 Individuals with at least basic overall digital skills.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Individuals with at least basic overall digital skills, by education attainment level and by status in labour market, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/be2f8f36-3f2a-4fd5-b204-62ff5d76584d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T16:02:15Z isoc_sk_dskl_i21])|alt=a horizontal bar chart showing individuals with at least basic overall digital skills, by education attainment level and by status in labour market in the EU in 2025. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] '''In 2025, over 10.4 million people worked as ICT specialists across the EU.''' The number of people employed as ICT specialists in the EU has been steadily increasing over recent years, with their share in total employment growing as well. In 2025, 10.4 million people were employed in ICT specialist occupations in the EU, a little over 9.6 million below the 2030 goal set for the EU in the Digital Decade. In 2025, ICT specialists constituted 5% of the EU's total employed (Figure 4). [[Image:Fig4 ICT specialists in employment, EU.png|thumb|centre|700px| Figure 4: ICT specialists in employment, EU, 2016-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3bb3da54-b9eb-49de-a7f6-6130b7b2389e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T16:32:33Z isoc_sks_itspt])|alt=a line chart with tow lines showing ICT specialists in employment in the EU from 2016 to 2025, the lines show the number of persons employed and share of total employment as a percentage. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] In 2025, most people employed as ICT specialists in the EU were men, with women accounting for only 19.5% of ICT employment. The highest shares of women in total ICT employment were recorded in Romania (27.8%), Latvia (25.9%) and Bulgaria (25.0%). With 12.9%, Czechia had the lowest share of women among people employed in ICT occupations (Figure 5). [[Image:Fig5 Distribution of ICT specialists by sex, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Distribution of ICT specialists by sex, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9b40ce86-554a-4f74-8756-6f06992940c1?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T17:13:15Z isoc_sks_itsps])|alt= a vertical stacked bar char showing the distribution of ICT specialists by sex in 2025 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] In 2025, the highest share in the EU of employed ICT specialists in the total employment was recorded in Sweden (9.4%), followed by Luxembourg (8.8%) and Finland (8.1%). The lowest proportions of people employed in ICT occupations in total employment were in Greece (2.6%) and Romania (2.7%). The lowest proportions of people employed in ICT occupations in total employment were in Greece (2.6%) and Romania (2.7%). The share of employment in ICT occupations in the total employment was much lower in the EU among women (2.2%) than among men (7.8%). There are significant disparities in male and female ICT specialists’ participation in the total employment across all the EU. The largest differences between the shares of men and women employed in ICT occupations were in Luxembourg (9.5 pp), Sweden (8.8 pp) and the Netherlands (8.5 pp). The smallest differences in the shares of male and female ICT specialists in employment were in Romania (1.6 pp), Greece (2.9 pp), Italy (4.2 pp), Bulgaria (4.4 pp) and Latvia(4.7 pp) (Figure 6). (Figure 6). [[Image:Fig6 ICT specialists in employment, by sex.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: ICT specialists in employment, by sex, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/84c6b3f7-77a2-4c50-a83e-4042391db4a5?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T16:56:28Z isoc_sks_itspt]), ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/04d067d7-edcd-41bf-94eb-fa84d11a6fa9?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T16:59:14Z isoc_sks_itsps]) and ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/90ee4564-204a-4065-95bb-0babac1f934b?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-22T17:08:48Z lfsa_egan])|alt= a double vertical bar char with a marker showing ICT specialists in employment, by sex in 2025 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] === Digital transformation of businesses=== The Digital Decade sets goals for the EU's digital transformation of businesses. By 2030, 3 out of 4 EU companies should use cloud computing services, big data or artificial intelligence, and more than 90% of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) should reach at least a basic level of digital intensity. '''In 2025, 47% of EU businesses used sophisticated or intermediate cloud computing services.''' Cloud computing gives businesses an opportunity to access computing resources hosted by third parties on the internet (the cloud), instead of building or expanding their own IT infrastructure, which would include hardware and involve developing and maintaining software applications and databases. In technological terms, cloud computing is a model for providing businesses with ubiquitous, flexible, on-demand access over the internet to a pool of configurable computing resources, including servers, databases, software applications, storage capacity and computing power. In 2025, 47% of enterprises in the EU reported that they bought sophisticated or intermediate cloud computing services (i.e. at least one of the following: finance or accounting software applications; enterprise resource planning (ERP) software applications; customer relationship management (CRM) software applications; security software applications; hosting the enterprise's database(s); computing platform providing a hosted environment for application development, testing or deployment). The highest shares of sophisticated or intermediate cloud services users among businesses were in Finland (73%), followed by Italy, Denmark and Sweden (all 68%). In 11 EU countries, the shares of enterprises using sophisticated or intermediate cloud computing were below the EU average, with the lowest proportions recorded in Bulgaria (16%), Greece (21%) and Romania (22%) (Figure 7). [[Image:Fig7 Enterprises using sophisticated or intermediate cloud computing services.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Enterprises using sophisticated or intermediate cloud computing services, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/12fdab9a-da13-4be8-9763-b9c2557a26f4?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-01T08:26:50Z isoc_cicce_use])|alt=a vertical bar chart showing enterprises using sophisticated or intermediate cloud computing services in 2025 in the EU, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries, potential candidates. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] The uptake of cloud computing services varies significantly among different economic activities, to a large extent determined by their need of such technologies. Information and communication stood out with the highest uptake of sophisticated or intermediate cloud services, with 78% of the EU businesses active in this economic activity using them in 2025, followed by businesses in professional, scientific and technical activities (61%). The lowest uptake of the sophisticated or intermediate cloud services was understandably among enterprises active in retail trade (38%)%), construction (42%) and transport and storage (41%) (Figure 8). [[Image:Fig8 Enterprises using sophisticated or intermediate cloud computing services, by economic activity.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Enterprises using sophisticated or intermediate cloud computing services, by economic activity, EU, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/93c00bce-9499-4880-8a12-a052c8594a30?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-01T08:47:05Z isoc_cicce_usen2])|alt= a horizontal bar chart showing enterprises using sophisticated or intermediate cloud computing services, by economic activity in the EU in 2025. For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] '''In 2025, 20% of EU enterprises used artificial intelligence technologies.''' Artificial intelligence (AI) can bring many benefits to businesses, such as improved decision-making, productivity or efficiency gains, and optimised and more sustainable energy or resource management. AI systems can be software-based (e.g. image recognition software, virtual assistants, speech and face recognition systems) or embedded in devices (e.g. autonomous robots, self-driving vehicles, drones). In 2025, 20% of EU enterprises used at least one AI technology - text mining, speech recognition, natural language generation, image recognition or processing, machine learning (incl. deep learning) for data analysis, technologies automating different workflows or assisting in decision-making (AI based software robotic process automation), technologies enabling machines to physically move by observing their surroundings and taking autonomous decisions. With the boom of various applications of AI technologies, this share was notably higher compared to the previous year (13%). The highest share of enterprises using AI was recorded in Denmark (42%), Finland (38%) and Sweden and Belgium (both 35%). The lowest shares were recorded in Romania (5%), Poland (8%) and Bulgaria, Greece and Cyprus (all 9%) (Figure 9). [[Image:Fig9 Enterprises using AI technologies.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: Enterprises using AI technologies, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f9248a21-ceb8-4690-aaea-19e536f0574a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-03T14:12:08Z isoc_eb_ai])|alt=a vertical bar chart showing the enterprises using AI technologies in 2025 in the EU, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries, potential candidates. The highest share of AI users was recorded among large enterprises (55%), followed by medium-sized enterprises (30%) and small enterprises (17%). In 2025, the most commonly used AI technologies were technologies analysing written language (i.e. text mining) – used by 12% of EU enterprises, as well as AI technologies identifying objects or persons based on images (image recognition, image processing) and AI technologies enabling machines to physically move by observing their surroundings and taking autonomous decisions (e.g. self-driving vehicles) – both used by 9% of enterprises. For AI technologies identifying objects or persons based on images (image recognition, image processing) the percentage was 7%. AI technologies automating various workflows or assisting in decision-making (AI-based software robotic process automation) and machine learning for data analysis were used by 5% of enterprises. AI technologies converting spoken language into a machine-readable format (speech recognition) were used by 4% of enterprises and AI technologies generating written or spoken language (natural language generation) by 1% of businesses. The uptake of these various AI technologies was much higher among large enterprises rather than medium-sized or small enterprises (Figure 10). For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] '''In 2025, 33% of EU enterprises used data analytics.''' Big data analysis uptake, alongside cloud computing services and artificial intelligence, is one of the components of the Digital Decade target for 75% of the EU businesses to adopt advanced technologies. The technological developments and the pervasive use of digital tools and services by people and businesses have increased the amount of data being created constantly. The data-intensive environment has prompted businesses to capitalise on the available information by analysing the vast data resources existing in either their own systems or other data sources, for instance by gaining better customer insights, improving business operations, strengthening their supply chain management or increasing innovation. Following these developments, European countries are measuring the data analytics uptake by enterprises, shifting the focus from big data to the wider concept of data analytics. The indicator, will be used as a proxy of the big data indicator for monitoring the 2030 EU target. In 2025, 40% of enterprises in the EU performed data analytics or had another enterprise or organisation perform data analytics for them. The highest shares of businesses trying to benefit from data analytics were recorded in Denmark (60%), Estonia and the Netherlands (both 56%), Lithuania (54%) and Belgium (52%). The lowest proportions of businesses performing data analytics internally or externally were in Poland (25%), Austria (26%) and Bulgaria (27%). Among EU enterprises, 33% used data analytics performed by their own employees. The highest shares of enterprises with data analytics conducted internally were in Denmark (50%), followed by the Estonia and Lithuania (both49%). The lowest percentages were recorded in Austria (18%), Bulgaria (22%), Poland and Hungary (both 23%). The highest share of enterprises which relied on external providers to conduct data analytics for them was in Denmark (25%) the Netherland (24%), Belgium and Finland (23%) (Figure 11). (Figure 11). [[Image:Fig11 Enterprises using data analytics performed by own employees or an external provider.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 11: Enterprises using data analytics performed by own employees or an external provider, 2025

For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] In 2025, the most used data sources for performing data analytics by businesses in the EU were data from transaction records such as sale details, payments records (26%) and data about customers such as purchasing information, location, preferences, customer reviews, searches (e.g. from Customer Relationship Management system (CRM) or own website) (18%), followed by data from social media including from enterprises' own social media profiles and web data (e.g. search engine trends, web scraping data), both of which were used by 11% of EU businesses. Less used data sources were location data from the use of portable devices or vehicles, and government authorities' open data (both 7%), data from smart devices or sensors (6%) and satellite data (e.g. satellite imagery, navigation signals, position signals) (4%). The data from transaction records such as sale details, payments records was most often analysed by enterprises in the Denmark (41%), Czechia (40%), Estonia (38%) and Belgium (37%). The highest shares of businesses analysing data about customers such as purchasing information, location, preferences, customer reviews, searches were recorded in the Estonia and Denmark (both 31%) (Table 1). In 2025, 63% of EU businesses adopted at least one of the more advanced technologies: AI or sophisticated or intermediate cloud computing services or performed data analytics (by own employees or an external provider), 12 pp below the target set for 2030. Five countries already surpassed this target for the EU –Denmark (82%) and Finland, 81%, the Netherlands (80%), Italy (78%) and Sweden (77%).. The lowest shares of businesses using at least one of the three technologies were recorded in Bulgaria (35%) and Greece (41%) (Figure 12). For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] '''In 2025, 71% of small and medium-sized enterprises reached at least basic digital intensity.''' The uptake of digital technologies by businesses has the potential to improve services and products, and to increase competitiveness. The crisis caused by COVID-19 has also shown that digitalisation is crucial for improving the economic resilience of businesses. The level of digitalisation of EU businesses is measured by the Digital Intensity Index (DII). The DII measures the use of different digital technologies by businesses. Its score (0-12) is determined by how many of the [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/89577311-0f9b-4fc0-b8c2-2aaa7d3ccb91/library/84b390d2-6a83-4dae-8aba-37c18557eb5b/details 12 selected digital technologies] are used by businesses. The higher the score, the higher the digital intensity of the business, ranging from very low (0-3 technologies used), through low (4-6), high (7-9) to very high (10-12). According to one of the targets of the EU's vision for the decade of the digital transformation, more than 90% of EU small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) should reach at least a basic level of digital intensity by 2030. Basic level entails the use of at least four of the selected technologies, which means it includes businesses with low, high and very high DII. In 2025, 71% of EU SMEs reached at least basic level of digital intensity, 19 pp shy of the ambition set in the Digital Decade for 2030. The majority of SMEs had a low level of digitalisation, with 29% scoring a very low level of DII and 35% a low level of DII. Among all EU businesses, 72% reached at least a basic level of digital intensity. The level of DII varied significantly among enterprises of different size classes, with 96% of large enterprises reaching at least basic digital intensity, compared with 87% of medium-sized and 69% of small enterprises. Large enterprises stood out with the highest share in the very high digital intensity category (43%) compared with enterprises in other size classes – 20% of medium-sized enterprises and 7% of small enterprises. Consequently, large enterprises also had had the smallest share of businesses with the very low level of digital intensity (4%) (Figure 13). [[Image:Fig13 Digital intensity of enterprises, by size class, EU.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 13: Digital intensity of enterprises, by size class, EU, 2025

For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] In 2025, only 9% of SMEs reached a very high DII level, while 27% reached a high level. Most businesses in small and medium size class recorded low (35%) or very low (29%) levels of DII. The highest proportions of SMEs reaching a very high DII level were in Denmark (26%) and Finland (24%),. Bulgaria and Romania were lagging behind with the lowest shares of SMEs reaching a very high digital intensity (2%). The levels of digital intensity among SMEs did not differ much from the levels of digital intensity among enterprises of all size classes, both at EU level and national level (Figure 14). Apart from information and communication, six other sectors had the shares of enterprises with a basic digital intensity at or above the EU average of 72%. These sectors were accommodation (89%), professional, scientific and technical activities (88%), real estate activities (80%), wholesale and retail trade; repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles (78%) and electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply; water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities (77%) and manufacturing (72%). For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] ===Digitalisation of public services=== The Digital Decade targets for digitalisation of public services are that, by 2030, all key public services should be available online, all citizens will have access to their e-medical recordsThe targets refer to the availability of public services. The data presented below do not refer directly to those targets, as they present the level of use, not availability of the service., and 80% of citizens should use an eID solution. In 2025, 58% of people aged 16-74 years in the EU, in the 12 months prior to the survey on ICT usage in households and by individuals, contacted or interacted over the internet with public authorities or public services for private purposes. The highest rates of individuals using e-government (incl. websites concerning citizen obligations (e.g. tax declaration, notification of moving), rights (e.g. social benefits), official documents (e.g. ID card, birth certificate), public educational services (e.g. public libraries, information on enrolment in schools or universities), public health services (e.g. services of public hospitals)) were recorded in Finland and Denmark (both 91%), the Netherlands (85%), Sweden (84%) and Estonia (83%). The lowest use of e-government was in Romania (17%) and Bulgaria (27%) (Figure 16). For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] ===Secure, performant and sustainable digital infrastructures=== Some of the ambitions set in the Digital Decade for the secure, performant and sustainable digital infrastructures are that, by 2030, all EU households should have gigabit connectivity and all populated areas should be covered by 5G. In 2025, most EU households (98% of the total number of households), including households in rural areas (93%), were covered by fixed broadband internet technologies. Among these technologies, DSL covered 70% of households, FWA was accessible to 76% of households, FTTP to 74%, and cable modem DOCSIS 3.0 covered 40% of households. Next generation access (NGA) technologies (comprising VDSL, VDSL2 vectoring, FTTP, DOCSIS 3.0, DOCSIS 3.1), capable of delivering download speeds of at least 30 Mbps, covered 95% of households, including 86% of households in rural areas. Fixed very high capacity networks (fixed VHCN, which include FTTP and cable network upgrades to DOCSIS 3.1), having the capabilities of offering gigabit connectivity, were accessible to 86% of EU households and 67% of households in rural areas. Of the mobile technologies, 5G covered 97% (89% in rural areas) and satellite coverage reached almost 100% (Figure 18). [[Image:Fig18 Total broadband internet coverage by technology, EU.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 18:Total broadband internet coverage by technology, EU, 2025

For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] While all households in the EU were covered by broadband technologies, the internet take-up among EU households was below 100%. In 2025, 95% of EU households had access to the internet at home. The highest shares of households having internet at home were recorded in the Netherlands and Luxembourg (both 99%), followed by Malta and Finland (both 98%). The lowest percentages of households having internet access at home were in Croatia (88%) and Greece and Lithuania (both 89%) (Figure 19). For more details, see the link to the dataset below.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=DD_targets_graphs_tables_2026_final.xlsx|title=Digital Decade targets - graphs and tables}} === Data sources === The data presented in this article are based on the results of the [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] [[Glossary:EU survey on the use of ICT in households and by individuals|survey on ICT usage in households and by individuals]] and the [[Glossary:EU survey on ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises|survey on ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises]]. Secondary statistics on ICT specialists, covering people working as ICT specialists in all parts of the economy, derived from the [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)|Labour Force Survey (LFS)]], have also been used. Additionally, some results come from the Grant Thornton Advisory and LS telcom studies Broadband Coverage in Europe. The two annual surveys on ICT usage are revised every year to accommodate various data needs and to maintain their relevance, taking into account developments in technologies, their uptake and their impact. Therefore, some data may not be available every year, and are presented for the last available period. The reference period for the survey on ICT usage in households and by individuals is in most cases the first quarter of each year; in most countries, the survey is conducted in the second quarter of each year. The household ICT survey covers those households having at least one member in the age group 16-74. Internet access of households refers to the percentage of households that have an internet access, so that anyone in the household could use the internet at home, if desired. The survey on ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises is conducted by national statistical authorities in the first months of the year. The reference period is the current situation of the survey period or, for selected questions, the preceding calendar year. In 2025, 157 000 enterprises, with 10 or more employees or self-employed persons, out of 1.53 million in EU were surveyed. Out of these 1.53 million enterprises, approximately 83% were small enterprises (with 10-49 employees or self-employed persons), 14% medium (50-249) and 3% large enterprises (250 or more). The observation statistical unit is the enterprise, as defined in [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A31993R0696 Regulation (EC) No 696/1993] of 15 March 1993. The survey covered enterprises with at least 10 employees and self-employed persons. Economic activities correspond to the classification [[Glossary:Statistical_classification_of_economic_activities_in_the_European_Community_(NACE)|NACE ]] Revision 2. The sectors covered are: manufacturing; electricity, gas and steam; water supply; construction; wholesale and retail trades; repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles; transportation and storage; accommodation and food service activities; information and communication; real estate; professional, scientific and technical activities; administrative and support activities; and repair of computers and communication equipment. Source data shown as ':' refer to data that are unavailable, unreliable, confidential or not applicable. Unreliable data are included in the calculation of European aggregates. Data presented in this article may differ from the data in the database on account of updates made after the data extractions used for this article. Data in the database are organised according to the survey year. The secondary statistics on ICT specialists are derived from the Labour Force Survey (LFS). Regulation (EU) 2019/1700, which came into force on 1 January 2021, made a break in the LFS time series (the source data) for all EU Member States. More information on the source data can be found in the online publication [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey EU Labour Force Survey], which includes articles on technical and methodological aspects of the survey. The EU-LFS methodology in force from the 2021 data collection onwards is described in [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_Labour_Force_Survey_-_new_methodology_from_2021_onwards ''Methodology from 2021 onwards'']. Statistics on ICT specialists, defined as persons who have the ability to develop, operate and maintain ICT systems and for whom ICTs constitute the main part of their job, are compiled based on the OECD definition ([https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/information-technology-outlook-2004_it_outlook-2004-en.html OECD, 2004]), which is built on the [https://ilostat.ilo.org/methods/concepts-and-definitions/classification-occupation/ International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO)]. For data up until 2010, the definition was based on [https://ilostat.ilo.org/methods/concepts-and-definitions/classification-occupation/#the-history-of-isco ISCO-88], whereas the data from 2011 onwards are based on ISCO-08; as such, there is a break in series in 2011. Under ISCO-08, Eurostat and the OECD define ICT specialists as people with the following occupations: ICT service managers; information and communications technology professionals (software and multimedia developers and analysts, and database specialists and systems administrators); information and communications technicians (ICT operations and user support technicians, and communications technicians); electronic engineers; telecommunication engineers; graphic and multimedia designers; information technology trainers; ICT sales professionals; electronics engineering technicians; electronics mechanics and servicers; and ICT installers and servicers. === Context === In 2019, the European Commission President outlined the vision for the EU to grasp the opportunities presented by the digital age. Such a digital transformation is based on the premise that digital technologies and solutions should: open up new opportunities for businesses; boost the development of trustworthy technology; foster an open and democratic society; enable a vibrant and sustainable economy; and help fight climate change. One of the six Commission priorities for the period 2019-2024 is [https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/priorities-2019-2024/europe-fit-digital-age_en A Europe fit for the digital age]. The strategy is built on 3 pillars: (1) technology that works for the people; (2) a fair and competitive digital economy; and (3) an open, democratic and sustainable society. Furthermore, a very concrete vision of the EU's digital transformation and targets for 2030 were set by the [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/europes-digital-decade Digital Decade policy programme], evolving around four cardinal points: skills, digital transformation of businesses, secure and sustainable digital infrastructures, and digitalisation of public services. === Other title: Tourism trips - introduction and key figures
text:
Eurostat's online publication on tourism deals with characteristics of trips, participation, destinations, seasonality, expenditure, and inbound and outbound travel. Data extracted in November 2025. Planned article update: November 2026. The average length of a trip for an EU resident in 2024 was 5 nights, on average 4 nights for domestic trips and 8 nights for trips abroad. Nearly 3 out of 4 trips made by EU residents in 2024 were within their own country of residence. EU residents spent €618 billion on tourism trips in 2024, on average €518 per person per trip. '''[[Tourism trips of Europeans]]''' is a [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] online publication consisting of seven articles providing recent statistics on tourism [[Glossary:Demand side tourism statistics|demand]] in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] and [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] countries. It discusses [[Glossary:Resident|residents']] patterns of [[Glossary:Tourism|tourism]] and the trips they made, and takes a close look at [[Glossary:Tourist|tourists']] socio-demographic characteristics (such as age and gender) and characteristics of the trips, such as destination, means of transport and accommodation, purpose and expenditure. ===On line publication=== {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0692:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 692/2011}} of 6 July 2011 concerning European statistics on tourism aims at harmonising these statistics in order to compile comparable data for the European Union. The national statistical authorities collect – usually via sample surveys – a wide range of information on domestic and foreign trips made by residents of their country. Different aspects of tourism demand are dealt with in a set of detailed articles: * [[Tourism statistics - characteristics of tourism trips|Characteristics of tourism trips]] - ''How and for what purpose do Europeans travel?'' * [[Tourism statistics - participation in tourism|Participation in tourism]] - ''What proportion of the population makes tourism trips throughout the year?'' * [[Tourism statistics - top destinations|Top destinations]] - ''Where do Europeans travel?'' * [[Seasonality in tourism demand|Seasonality]] - ''When do Europeans travel?'' * [[Tourism statistics - expenditure|Expenditure]] - ''How much do Europeans spend on their tourism trips?'' * [[Tourism statistics - intra-EU tourism flows|Intra-EU tourism flows]] - ''What is the size of inbound and outbound flows within the EU?'' ==Main findings== In 2024, EU residents aged 15 years and over made nearly 1.2 billion tourism trips (see Table 1) with an average length of 5.0 overnight stays per trip. In all, 56.3% of these trips were short trips of 1 to 3 overnight stays, while 43.7% were trips of 4 nights or more. Europeans tend to prefer trips inside the country where they live. Nearly 3 out of 4 trips were domestic, where they spent on average 4 nights. For foreign trips, the length of stay was longer (8 nights on average). In terms of expenditure, long foreign trips take up the biggest share (50.5%) of the estimated €617 914 million expenditure on tourism trips. Expenditure (per individual) on a tourism trip was on average €518, while expenditure per night was €104 (ranging from €78 per night on long domestic trips to €224 per night on short foreign trips). Of course, these figures for the European Union at aggregate level do not show the different patterns observed across countries. The diversity of tourism by Europeans is more closely analysed in the detailed articles mentioned above. [[Image:T1_Key figures of trips of EU residents aged 15 and over, 2024.png|thumb|center|800px|Table 1: Key figures of trips of EU residents aged 15 years and over, 2024
''Source'': Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tttot}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_tntot}}, {{Stable link|title=|code=tour_dem_extot}}|alt= Table showing key figures of trips of EU residents aged 15 years and over for the year 2024. The key figures include the number of trips, nights spent and expenditure in euros. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Data sources=== '''Collection of annual data on trips of EU residents''' The collection consists of harmonised data collected by the Member States in the frame of the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0692:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 692/2011}} of the European Parliament and of the Council concerning European statistics on [[Glossary:European_statistics_on_tourism|tourism]]. The scope of observation for data on tourism trips are all tourism trips with at least 1 overnight stay, made by the [[Glossary:Resident|resident population]] aged 15 years and over. It includes trips made for private or professional purpose, outside the usual environment. The scope of observation for the data on participation in tourism are the residents of the country, aged 15 years and over, and refers only to tourism for personal purposes, excluding trips made for professional reasons. ===Context=== The EU is a major tourist destination, with 6 EU countries among the world's top 10 destinations for holidaymakers, according to [https://www.e-unwto.org/toc/wtobarometereng/22/3 UN Tourism] data. Tourism is an important activity in the EU which contributes to employment and economic growth, as well as to the development of rural, peripheral or less-developed areas. Tourism is estimated to account for 4.5% to the EU's gross value added. These characteristics drive the demand for reliable and harmonised statistics on this activity, as well as within the wider context of regional policy and sustainable development policy areas. ===Other articles=== *[[Tourism|All articles on tourism statistics]] ===Publications=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/tourism/publications Recent Eurostat publications on tourism] ===Selected Datasets=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/tourism/database Tourism (tour)], see: :Annual data on trips of EU residents (t_tour_dem) ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/tourism/database Tourism (tour)], see: :Trips of EU residents - annual data (tour_dem) ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=tourism}} Tourism statistics] ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=tour_dem_esms|title=Trips of EU residents - annual data}} (ESMS metadata file — tour_dem_esms) {{Unit|topic=X_Tourism}} [[Category:Industry, trade, and services|Tourism trips - introduction and key figures]] [[Category:Tourism|Tourism trips - introduction and key figures]] [[Category:Statistical article|Tourism trips - introduction and key figures]] [[Category:Residents' trips and destinations|Tourism trips - introduction and key figures]] [[Category:November2026|Tourism trips - introduction and key figures]]

title: Tourism statistics - summer season occupancy
text:
4 Data extracted in March 2019. Planned article update: No planned update. 7.5 million (0.8 %) more nights were spent in hotels and similar accommodation of the EU in the summer season 2018 compared with 2017. Spain, Italy and Greece were the most popular EU destinations for people travelling outside their own country in summer 2018. Compared with the same period in 2017, the net occupancy rates of bed places in the European Union increased by 0.8 % during the 2018 summer season, ranging from 31.4 % in Luxembourg, to 97.3 % in Croatia. This article analyses the [[Glossary:Tourism|tourism]] trends of the 2018 summer season (June to September) in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] Member States, [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate]] and [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] countries. Tourism recorded positive growth rates in most countries, compared with the same period in 2017. This trend is confirmed both by the number of [[Glossary:Nights spent|nights spent]] at [[Glossary:Hotels_and_similar_accommodation|hotels and similar accommodation establishments]], and by their net [[Glossary:Net occupancy_rate|occupancy rates]]. === Summer season tourism trends in 2018 === Comparing the monthly figures for the 2018 summer season with the previous year, 7.5 million more nights (+0.8 %) were spent in hotels and similar accommodation in the European Union. Positive growth rates were recorded in 19 out of 27 Member States where data is available. The highest increase was observed in Latvia (+8.1 %) followed by Lithuania (+7.6 %), while Ireland, Luxembourg, Portugal, the United Kingdom, Spain, Austria, Finland and Croatia reported decreases (see Figure 1). [[Image:Percentage change in number of nights spent at hotels and similar accommodation establishments, June-September 2018 compared with the same period in 2017 (%).png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 1: Percentage change in number of nights spent at hotels and similar accommodation establishments, June-September 2018 compared with the same period in 2017 (%)
Source: {{Stable link|title=Eurostat|code=tour_occ_nim}}]] Two out of three nights in hotels and similar accommodation in the EU-28 were spent in five countries: Spain (17.5 %), Italy (16.4 %), Germany (12.7 %), France (9.8 %) and the United Kingdom (9.6 %). The most popular destinations for [[Glossary:Non-resident|non-residents]] were Spain, Italy and Greece, together accounting for nearly half of all nights spent by non-residents in the EU-28 in summer 2018(see Table 1). [[Image:Nights spent at hotels and similar accommodation establishments, non-residents and residents, June-September 2018 compared with the same period in 2017 (Thousand nights).png|thumb|center|500px|Table 1: Nights spent at hotels and similar accommodation establishments, non-residents and residents, June-September 2018 compared with the same period in 2017 (Thousand nights)
Source: {{Stable link|title=Eurostat|code=tour_occ_nim}}]] === Nights spent by residents and non-residents === In the European Union, the number of nights spent by non-residents at hotels and similar accommodation increased by 0.2 % in summer 2018 compared with the same period of 2017. Positive growths were observed in most Member States where data is available, while Lithuania, Latvia and the Netherlands reported increases above 7 %. However drops were recorded in 11 Member States (see Table 1). The share of non-residents was more than 90 % in Malta (96.7 %), Cyprus (94.9 %), Croatia (93.4 %) and Luxembourg (90.4 %), while it was particularly low in Romania (17.2 %) and in Germany (24.4 %). In terms of nights spent by [[Glossary:Resident|residents]] staying at hotels and similar accommodation, domestic tourism increased during the 2018 summer season in all Member States where data is available with the exception of Greece (-6.8 %), Luxembourg (-3.4 %), the United Kingdom (-1.7 %) and France (-0.7 %). === Net occupancy rates of bed places === Compared with the same period of the previous year, [[Glossary:Net occupancy_rate|net occupancy rates]] of bed places in the European Union increased by 0.8 percentage points during the 2018 summer season. These rates ranged from 31.4 % in Luxembourg (August), to 97.3 % in Croatia (August) (see Table 2). [[Image:Net occupancy rates of bed places in hotels and similar accommodation establishments, June - September 2018 compared with the same period in 2017 (%).png|thumb|center|500px|Table 2: Net occupancy rates of bed places in hotels and similar accommodation establishments, June - September 2018 compared with the same period in 2017 (%)
Source: {{Stable link|title=Eurostat|code=tour_occ_mnor}}]] August was the month with the highest occupancy rates for most Member States. In Bulgaria, Denmark, Estonia, Cyprus, Finland and Sweden the peak month was July, while in Luxembourg it was September. With more than nine out of ten available bed places having been in use, Croatia and Cyprus were the EU countries with the highest net occupancy rates during their peak summer month (see Figure 2). [[Image:Net occupancy rates of bed places in hotels and similar accommodation establishments in the peak month, summer season 2018 (%).png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 2: Net occupancy rates of bed places in hotels and similar accommodation establishments in the peak month, summer season 2018 (%)
Source: {{Stable link|title=Eurostat|code=tour_occ_mnor}}]] Figure 3 shows the occupancy rates in the 2018 summer season compared with the estimated occupancy rates in the entire year 2018. The differences between these two figures for each country can be less significant than one would expect on the basis of the seasonality of nights spent (see article [[Seasonality in the tourist accommodation sector]]). This can be partly explained by the fact that the net occupancy only takes into account available bed places, in other words some rooms that may be closed during the lower season do not affect the occupancy rate downwards. [[Image:Net occupancy rates of bed places in hotels and similar accommodation establishments, summer season 2018 and entire year 2018 (%).png|thumb|center|500px|Figure 3: Net occupancy rates of bed places in hotels and similar accommodation establishments, summer season 2018 and entire year 2018 (%)
Source: {{Stable link|title=Eurostat|code=tour_occ_mnor}}]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Summer tourism trends 2018 update.xlsx |Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Context=== The EU is a major tourist destination, with five Member States among the world’s top ten destinations for holidaymakers, according to UNWTO[http://mkt.unwto.org/en/highlights UNWTO Tourism Highlights] data. Tourism is an important activity in the EU which has the potential to contribute towards employment and economic growth, as well as to development in rural, peripheral or less-developed areas. These characteristics drive the demand for reliable and harmonised statistics within this field, as well as within the wider context of regional policy and sustainable development policy areas. ===Other articles=== *[[Seasonality in the tourist accommodation sector]] *[[Seasonality in tourism demand]] *[[Tourism|All articles on tourism statistics]] ===Selected Datasets=== *Tourism [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/data/database?node_code=t_tour (t_tour)] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/tourism/database Tourism (tour)] ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=tourism}} Tourism] ===Publications=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/tourism/publications Recent Eurostat publications on tourism] ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=tour_occ_esms|title=Occupancy of tourist accommodation establishments}} (ESMS metadata file — tour_occ_esms) *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-RA-10-010|title=Tourism statistics in the European Statistical System - 2008 data}} ===Legislation=== '''With 2012 as reference year''' :{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32011R0692:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) No 692/2011}} of 6 July 2011 concerning European statistics on tourism and repealing Council Directive 95/57/EC. title: Trade and production of chemicals and related products
text:
EU statistics on the production and trade in chemical products. Data from September 2025 Planned update: October 2026 In 2024 compared to 2023, EU imports of chemicals and related products decreased by 1.1%, while exports increased by 7.0%. The United States, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and China were the 4 largest partners of the EU for exports and imports of chemicals and related products in 2024. Sold production of chemicals and related products grew from €790 billion in 2023 to €830 billion in 2024. This article presents statistics on the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union’s (EU)]] sold production and trade in [[Trade and production of chemicals and related products#Context|chemical products]]. It focuses on the EU [[Glossary:Imports_-_NA|imports ]] and [[Glossary:Exports_-_NA|exports ]] of chemicals and related products with the rest of the world, as well as on how they are related to the total EU sold production of chemicals and related products. This article is part of an [[International trade in goods - a statistical picture|online publication]] providing recent statistics on international trade in goods, covering information on the EU's main partners, main products traded, specific characteristics of trade as well as background information. ===Growing trade surplus in chemicals and related products in 2024=== In 2024 compared to 2023, EU imports of chemicals and related products decreased by 1.1%, while exports increased by 7.0%. Consequently, the trade surplus grew by €40 billion. Over a longer period, between 2014 and 2024, EU imports of chemicals and related products grew from €185 billion to €322 billion in 2024, equivalent to an average annual growth of 5.7%. In the same period exports grew from €303 billion to €560 billion equivalent to an average annual growth of 6.3%. The EU had a growing trade surplus in chemicals and related products throughout the 2014–2024 period. The surplus grew from €119 billion in 2014 to €238 billion in 2024. Figure 1 The share of chemicals and related products in total (imports + exports) extra-EU trade increased from 14.3% in 2014 to 17.6% in 2024, an increase of 3.3 percentage points (pp). The share of imports grew by 1.9 pp while exports grew by 4.8 pp (Figure 2). Figure 2 ===Trade of chemicals by product=== In 2024, the largest product group in extra-EU imports of chemicals and related products was 'Medical and pharmaceutical products' followed by 'Organic chemicals' (see Figure 3). Figure 3 In 2024, the largest product group in extra-EU exports of chemicals and related products also was 'Medical and pharmaceutical products' (see Figure 4). Figure 4 ===Main extra-EU partners for trade in chemicals and related products=== In 2024, for imports (see Figure 5), the United States (€78 billion) was the largest partner, followed by Switzerland (€ 64 billion), China (€ 644 billion) and the United Kingdom (€28 billion). Figure 5 In 2024, the United States (€170 billion) was also the largest export destination (see Figure 6), followed by Switzerland (€ 64 billion), the United Kingdom (€46 billion) and China (€36 billion). Figure 6 Figure 7 and 8 show EU trade with the United States by product group in 2024. The largest group in both imports (59%) and exports (70%) was medicine & pharmaceutical products. No other product group had a share above 15%. Figure 7 Figure 8 Figure 9 and 10 show EU trade with Switzerland by product group in 2024. The largest group in both imports (62%) and exports (80%) was medicine & pharmaceutical products. Organic chemicals had a share of 27% in imports but only 6% in exports. Figure 9 Figure 10 Figure 11 and 12 show EU trade with the United Kingdom by product group in 2023. The largest group in both imports (31%) and exports (39%) was medicine & pharmaceutical products but with much smaller shares than the United States and Switzerland. Trade was more evenly spread over the different groups; essential oils and related materials and chemical materials and products had shares above 10% in both imports and exports as did organic chemicals but only for imports. Figure 11 Figure 12 Figure 13 and 14 show EU trade with China by product group in 2023. The largest group in exports was medicine & pharmaceutical products (47%). In imports medicine & pharmaceutical products (10%) was preceded by organic chemicals (55%) and chemical materials and products (12%). Figure 13 Figure 14 ===EU is the largest exporter of chemical products=== Looking at the major international players in trade of chemicals and related products, the EU headed the list in 2024 with a total trade of €882 billion, which consisted of €560 billion of exports and €322 billion of imports, thus recording the highest trade surplus (€238 billion) as shown in Figure 15. The United States was the largest importer (€380 billion) and second largest exporter (€283 billion) and had the largest trade deficit (€97 billion). China was both the third largest importer (€231 billion) and exporter (€278 billion). Figure 15 ===Sold production of chemicals === The total sold production of chemicals and related products in terms of value increased from €663 billion to €830 billion between 2014 and 2024 (see Figure 16) despite falling 10.0% in 2023. Growth was especially strong between 2020 and 2022. Figure 16 Figure 17 shows that sold production between 2014 and 2024, grew in all groups of chemicals and related products with the exception of organic chemicals which had an average annual growth rate of -0.9%. The largest increases were for medical & pharmaceutical products (4.3%), inorganic chemicals (4.2) and chemical materials and products (3.7%). Figure 17 Table 1 shows the level of the sold production for the top 20 of chemicals and related products in the EU. 'Other medicaments of mixed or unmixed products' topped the list of the most sold chemical products in the EU in value terms in 2024 with an estimated value of €78 billion, followed by 'Antisera, other immunological products which are directly involved in the regulation of immunological processes and other blood fractions' (€48 billion). No other products had a sold production above €25 billion. [[Image:EU sold production of top 20 chemicals and related products, 2024 (€ million).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: EU sold production of top 20 of chemicals and related products products, 2024
[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d0bc4751-190b-4f97-bf6b-8677c9ac8097?lang=en&createdAt=2026-01-27T14:48:48Z ''Source:'' Eurostat ds-059358] |alt=A table showing the EU sold production of the top 20 of chemicals and related products for the year 2024 in euro million. The table shows the prodcom code and the product description. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Chemicals update september 2025.xlsx|title=Graphs and tables}} ===Data sources=== '''International trade in goods''' EU data is taken from [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat's]] [[Glossary:COMEXT|COMEXT]] database. COMEXT is the reference database for international trade in goods. It provides access not only to both recent and historical data from the EU Member States but also to statistics of a significant number of third countries. International trade aggregated and detailed statistics disseminated via the Eurostat website are compiled from COMEXT data according to a monthly process. Data are collected by the competent national authorities of the Member States and compiled according to a harmonised methodology established by EU regulations before transmission to Eurostat. For extra-EU trade, the statistical information is mainly provided by the traders on the basis of customs declarations. EU data are compiled according to Community guidelines and may, therefore, differ from national data published by the Member States. Statistics on extra-EU trade are calculated as the sum of trade of each of the 27 EU Member States with countries outside the EU. In other words, the EU is considered as a single trading entity and trade flows are measured into and out of the area, but not within it. The United Kingdom is considered as an extra-EU partner country for the EU for the whole period covered by this article. However, the United Kingdom was still part of the internal market until the end of the transitory period (31 December 2020), meaning that data on trade with the United Kingdom are still based on statistical concepts applicable to trade between the EU Member States. Consequently, while imports from any other extra-EU trade partner are grouped by country of origin, the United Kingdom data reflect the country of consignment. In practice this means that the goods imported by the EU from the United Kingdom were physically transported from the United Kingdom but part of these goods could have been of other origin than the United Kingdom. For this reason, data on trade with the United Kingdom are not fully comparable with data on trade with other extra-EU trade partners. '''Production of chemicals''' Industrial production data comes from [[Glossary:PRODCOM|PRODCOM]]. Prodcom provides statistics on the production of manufactured goods. Prodcom data includes * the physical volume of production sold during the survey period * the value of production sold during the survey period * for some products, the volume of total production during the survey period Prodcom data is obtained by the National Statistical Institutes (NSIs) who conduct a survey of enterprises. Eurostat calculates EU totals at EU level from the national data. '''International trade in chemicals''' Trade in goods data comes from [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat's]] [[Glossary:COMEXT|COMEXT]] database. COMEXT is the Eurostat reference database for international trade in goods. It provides access not only to both recent and historical data from the [[Glossary:EU_Member_States|EU Member States]], but also to statistics of a significant number of non-EU countries. Because COMEXT is updated on a daily basis, data published on the website may differ from data stored in COMEXT in case of recent revisions. Chemical products are classified according to the [[Glossary:Standard_international_trade_classification_(SITC)|Standard International Trade Classification (SITC)]] of the United Nations. Section 5 ‘Chemicals and related products, N.E.S.’ of SITC Rev. 4 is made up of the following divisions *51 Organic chemicals *52 Inorganic chemicals *53 Dyeing, tanning and colouring materials *54 Medicinal and pharmaceutical products *55 Essential oils and resinoids and perfume materials *56 Fertilizers (other than those of group 272) *57 Plastics in primary forms *58 Plastics in non-primary forms *59 Chemical materials and products, N.E.S ===Context=== Through the seventh [https://ec.europa.eu/environment/action-programme/ Environment Action Programme to 2020 (7th EAP)] the EU sets policies on chemicals management, of which [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/chemicals/reach/reach_en.htm REACH] (the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals) is the central element. The main aim of REACH is to ensure a high level of protection of human health and the environment from the risks that can be posed by chemicals. This includes promoting alternative methods to assess the hazards of substances, the free circulation of substances on the internal market, and the enhancement of competitiveness and innovation in the EU chemical industry. By providing knowledge about hazardous properties of chemicals and appropriate safety information, REACH is expected to enhance the communication and implementation of conditions of safe use in supply chains and the substitution of dangerous substances by less dangerous ones. In addition, through different types of measures on highly dangerous substances, EU policies aim to reduce the risks to human health and to ecosystems at EU level. ===Other articles=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=International_trade_-_goods International trade in goods -
