title: Tutorial:AI guidelines
text:
__toc__ === Introduction === Using AI tools can facilitate authors' writing tasks in the ways mentioned below. Please keep in mind that technology is changing rapidly and guidelines are being regularly updated. Join the following Teams channel to stay up to date with changes: [https://teams.microsoft.com/l/channel/19%3AK6XwF8zVDwzBN-1rEm4TADhMOfjfESynJQvnACbv1BI1%40thread.tacv2/ESTAT-AI%20community%20of%20practice?groupId=74a1847a-25ca-4808-8754-1f98909c0304&tenantId=b24c8b06-522c-46fe-9080-70926f8dddb1 ESTAT-AI community of practice | GRP-ESTAT-SE authors | Microsoft Teams] === AI best practices === Several prompts have been developed to assist with writing and updating Statistics Explained articles using AI, available in both the AI Lab and GPT@EC. ==== AI Lab (creating new articles and updating existing articles) ==== The [https://language-tools.ec.europa.eu/eDraftingLabServices/Default AI Lab] is a testing environment for new prompts, such as '[https://language-tools.ec.europa.eu/eDraftingLabServices/EditingStatisticsExplained Statistics Explained]' and '[https://language-tools.ec.europa.eu/eDraftingLabServices/SummaryImages Images]' which are accessible only to Eurostat accounts. * '''Statistics Explained prompt'''- it reads and interprets data from multiple formats, including Excel files. It assists in drafting new articles or updating (rewriting) existing ones. It is important to remember that the results should always be double-checked by the writer and adapted to the guidelines, as the tool might make errors * '''Images prompt'''- it extracts information from images and converts it into text. The prompt is able to analyse various types of images, including graphs and tables, and can be also used in drafting the alternative text. Like Statistics Explained prompt, the data produced needs to be double-checked and adapted accordingly [[Image:Statistics Explained promp ai lab.png|thumb|right|800px]]
More information about the AI Lab and available prompts can be found in the [https://eceuropaeu.sharepoint.com/:b:/r/teams/GRP-GRP-ESTAT-AITestingSE/Shared%20Documents/ESTAT-AI%20community%20of%20practice/DGT%20AI%20Lab%20functionalities.pdf?csf=1&web=1&e=2fLaQX AI Lab presentation]. ==== GPT@EC (rewriting existing articles) ==== Below, you can find the best practices for rewriting existing Statistics Explained articles: * make sure to follow the Commission AI guidelines: [https://eceuropaeu.sharepoint.com/sites/KNB-AIEC/SitePages/GUIDELINES-FOR-STAFF-ON-THE-USE-OF-ONLINE-AVAILABLE-GENERATIVE-ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE-TOOLS.aspx Guidelines for staff on the use of AI] * feel free to use the built-in prompts for writing and updating new articles: [https://gpt.tech.ec.europa.eu/prompts-library GPT@EC] [[Image:Clear_writing_prompt_library.png|thumb|right|350px]] and [https://language-tools.ec.europa.eu/EBriefingServices/WebText Digital Europe - WebText] [[Image:Web_writing_prompt.png|thumb|right|350px]] If you want to learn more about both tools, please refer to the [https://eceuropaeu.sharepoint.com/:p:/r/teams/GRP-ESTAT.B.4/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B74608DD9-97E5-4437-B57D-8F93F68B4D5B%7D&file=AI%20tools%20presentation.pptx&action=edit&mobileredirect=true AI tools presentation] * ensure that you do not upload confidential data to the tool * if you wish to use your own personalised prompt, please refer to the bullet points below and/or the presentation that demonstrates prompt testing and the differences between the commercial ChatGPT and GPT@EC: [https://eceuropaeu-my.sharepoint.com/:p:/g/personal/karina-joanna_karpinska_ext_ec_europa_eu/Ecqc9DcA7_5KnPohrg2n8LoBnym6MqeZcRqsc3AIqPOGew?e=NNQcQO 2nd AI tools workshop] === What to keep in mind when creating/ updating text using GPT@EC based on the most common mistakes made by this tool? === * ensure sources are accurate * use digits instead of words for numbers (e.g. 17 instead of seventeen) * include internal links, especially to glossaries * text in British English * correct bullet points structure and dashes * follow proper number formatting (e.g. 110 000 instead of 110,000) * consider the appropriate use of jargon * ensure no critical information is missing * when replacing old text with new text, make sure to add the new data in the prompt as the Commission AI tool doesn’t read the changes from the Word file * GPT@EC works better on its own; try not to ask for a specific article to be updated with new information. Instead, it’s better to create a new article or analyse the data === Advice to create your own prompt === * be as detailed as possible * make sure to double-check the text * focus on the "What to keep in mind" section specifically, as these are the most common mistakes made by AI tools * good tips: [https://eceuropaeu.sharepoint.com/teams/GRP-GPTEC2/SitePages/7-Ingredients-for-a-good-prompt.aspx 7 Ingredients for a good prompt] ===See also=== {{Unit|topic=}} [[Category:Tutorial|AI guidelines]]

title: Tutorial:Access and rights
text:
Contributing to [[:Statistics Explained:About|Statistics Explained]] is normally reserved for [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] staff only. However, the right to create, insert or modify content can also be granted to three categories of externals:
*staff from other [[Glossary:European_Commission_(EC)|European Commission]] directorates and agencies
*staff from NSIs
*external contractors

The short and simple procedure to obtain editing rights is explained below. 

=== General principles ===

Statistics Explained uses the '''European Commission's user authentication service''' (or '''EU Login'''), to control access. European Commission staff (including Eurostat employees) have a 7-letter username and a corresponding password also used for SYSPER and other Commission applications.

All staff can use this EU Login username and password to log in to Statistics Explained and thereby create a '''Statistics Explained username'''.

Having a username and using this to log in, however, '''does not automatically confer editing rights''' in Statistics Explained. One further step is needed: a Statistics Explained administrator has to add the username to the user group 'alloweduser'. 

Below is the procedure to register in Statistics Explained, via logging in, and then obtaining editing rights, first for Eurostat staff, and then for the three categories of externals (non-Eurostat European Commission personnel, NSI staff and external contractors). 

'''Please note that all staff changes must be reported to the SE team so that access rights can be removed.'''

=== Eurostat staff ===

Request editing rights: 

*click button 'log in' on the top right of any Statistics Explained page 
*enter your EU Login username and password
*send an e-mail to the SE team [mailto:estat-statistics-explained@ec.europa.eu estat-statistics-explained@ec.europa.eu] requesting access rights 
*once granted, you will receive a notification e-mail and will be able to view and edit draft Statistics Explained articles

'''Staff leaving Eurostat must inform the SE team so that access rights can be removed'''

=== European Commission staff (outside Eurostat) ===

Non-Eurostat European Commission staff can register in Statistics Explained in the same way as Eurostat staff, but are blocked from editing (staff leaving Eurostat for another part of the Commission must inform the SE team so that access rights can be removed). 

A Commission staff member needing to edit in Statistics Explained, can obtain the right to do so by submitting a motivated request to estat-statistics-explained@ec.europa.eu (also informing the Eurostat unit responsible for the page(s) to be edited - and expected to be involved in this editing).

=== NSI staff ===

NSI staff can obtain editing rights in Statistics Explained, in the context of a common project such as the [[Tutorial:ESS glossary|ESS glossary]] following this procedure: 

*click button 'log in' on the top right of any Statistics Explained page
*you will be redirected to the 'European Commission's user authentication service', EU Login for short; enter EU Login username and password if you already have one; if not: 
*to register in EU Login, go to [https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/cas EU Login] and complete the form

::Please note that EU Login only allows '''one''' username to be associated with a given e-mail address, so you cannot create a username if you already have one linked to your e-mail address, so you have to use the existing one to log in.
 
:*choose a password;

*complete the log in procedure to Statistics Explained using the EU Login username and password
*inform the Statistics Explained team ([mailto:estat-statistics-explained@ec.europa.eu estat-statistics-explained@ec.europa.eu]) that you have registered in Statistics Explained and confirm your username, so we can assign the necessary editing rights 
*next time you log in to Statistics Explained via redirect to EU Login (https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/cas/login EU Login) and EU Login username and password, you will be able to edit in Statistics Explained

'''Once the project has concluded, the SE team must be informed so that access rights can be removed'''

=== External contractors ===

External contractors can obtain editing rights in Statistics Explained, temporarily for the time of the contract, following this procedure: 

*click button 'log in' on the top right of any Statistics Explained page 
*you will be redirected to the 'European Commission's user authentication service', EU Login for short; enter EU Login username and password if you already have one; if not: 
*to register, go to  [https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/cas EU Login] and complete the form

::Please note that EU Login only allows '''one''' username to be associated with a given e-mail address, so you cannot create a username if you already have one linked to your e-mail address, so you have to use the existing one to log in.
 
:*choose a password;

*complete the logging in to Statistics Explained using the EU Login username and password
*inform the Statistics Explained team ([mailto:estat-statistics-explained@ec.europa.eu estat-statistics-explained@ec.europa.eu]) that you have registered in Statistics Explained and confirm your username, so we can assign the necessary editing rights 
*next time you log in to Statistics Explained via redirect to (https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/cas/login EU Login) with username and password, you will be able to edit in Statistics Explained

'''Once the contract has terminated, the Eurostat author unit is responsible for informing the SE team so that access rights can be removed'''

===See also===

title: Transport statistics at regional level
text:
Eurostat regional yearbook; 2026 edition; flagship publication; EU; regional statistics; NUTS; transport; road transport; maritime transport; rail transport; air passengers; passenger cars; electric vehicles; road fatalities; maritime freight handled; maritime passengers carried; electrified railway lines [[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH11 RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|380px|''Source:'' Eurostat]] Data extracted in April 2026 Planned article update: September 2027 This article forms part of the ''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Eurostat_regional_yearbook Eurostat regional yearbook – 2026]'', an annual [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/main/publications/flagship-publications flagship publication]. It provides a detailed picture relating to a broad range of statistical topics across the regions of the [[Glossary:EU|EU]], [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate]] countries. A [[Regional_yearbook_introduction#A_short_reading_guide|short reading guide]] is provided in the introductory chapter, including an explanation of how to interpret the maps. Paris-Charles de Gaulle was the EU’s busiest airport in 2024 in terms of passenger numbers (70.3 million), followed by Amsterdam Schiphol and Adolfo Suárez Madrid Barajas. Around 20 000 people died on EU roads in 2024, with the highest number of road deaths recorded in Lombardia, Andalucía and Rhône-Alpes. [[Image:RYB-Infographics-CH11_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/6bd139a6-be62-4a70-bf83-207f36fd8c39?lang=en avia_paoa])|alt=An infographic showing the ten main airports in the EU with the highest numbers of passengers. Data are shown in millions for 2024. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Transport is vital to the EU economy, supporting global supply chains and daily life by enabling the free movement of people and goods within the EU’s [[Glossary:Single market|single market]]. However, it also generates considerable societal, environmental and economic costs, including greenhouse gas emissions, air pollution, noise, congestion and injuries/fatalities caused by accidents. Accounting for around a quarter of greenhouse gas emissions, the EU’s transport policy prioritises safer, more efficient and environmentally sustainable mobility through integrated networks. The EU’s ''[https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/mobility-strategy_en Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy]'' (COM(2020) 789 final) part of ''[https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en The European Green Deal]'' sets out policy initiatives to achieve a greener and more resilient transport system that remains accessible, affordable and inclusive, while promoting high levels of safety and security across all modes of transport. Within the strategy, there are several key milestones, including: *30 million zero-emission cars in use by 2030 *a doubling of high-speed rail traffic by 2030 *nearly all new cars, vans, buses and heavy-duty vehicles to be zero-emission by 2050 *cutting transport emissions by 90% by 2050 *a fully operational, multimodal [https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/infrastructure-and-investment/trans-european-transport-network-ten-t_en Trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T)] connecting Europe sustainably by 2050 *zero-emission large aircraft ready for market by 2050. In 2024, EU airports carried 1.05 billion passengers. Over recent decades, liberalisation measures have supported the rapid expansion of low-cost airlines and the development of smaller regional airports, which are often less congested and charge lower landing fees than major international hubs. There were 42 airports in the EU that carried at least 10.0 million air passengers. These airports were typically located close to capital cities, major economic centres and popular holiday destinations. Paris-Charles de Gaulle (France) recorded the highest passenger numbers (70.3 million), followed by Amsterdam Schiphol (the Netherlands; 66.8 million) and Adolfo Suárez Madrid Barajas (Spain; 66.1 million). Frankfurt (Germany) and Barcelona El Prat (Spain) were the only other airports to exceed 50 million passengers. The selection of information presented for regional transport statistics within the ''Eurostat regional yearbook'' changes on an annual basis (covering different modes of transport and focusing on different passenger/freight indicators). Previous editions of the publication can be found at the bottom of this [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-flagship-publications/w/KS-01-26-039 webpage]. ===Road transport – passenger cars=== Roads are the most commonly used transport mode in the EU for both passengers and inland freight. The EU’s ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0789 Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy – putting European transport on track for the future]'' (COM(2020) 789 final) highlights that, while road mobility brings significant economic and social benefits, it also generates substantial external costs, including greenhouse gas emissions, air pollution, congestion and road accidents. The strategy sets out 10 flagship areas and a series of milestones for 2030 and 2040 in support of the objective of making Europe the first climate-neutral continent by 2050, including an indicative target of at least 30 million zero-emission vehicles on the EU’s roads by 2030. More broadly, EU road transport policy objectives include, among others, to improve mobility on increasingly congested networks, reduce fatalities, cut emissions and air pollution, lower dependence on fossil fuel through electrification and improve working conditions for professional drivers. The passenger car transformed personal mobility, offering freedom and flexibility while contributing to economic development. It also has cultural significance, symbolising status and progress for some, while others opt not to make use of a car. As the EU transitions towards greener technologies, the passenger car remains central to debates on sustainability and innovation.
'''More about the data: road transport statistics''' Passenger cars are defined as road motor vehicles intended for the carriage of passengers and designed to seat no more than 9 persons (including the driver). This category includes passenger cars, vans designed primarily for transporting passengers, taxis, hire cars, ambulances, police cars, firefighter cars, motor homes and micro cars (not requiring a driving permit), provided they have fewer than 10 seats. Excluded are light goods vehicles, as well as motor coaches, buses, mini-buses and mini-coaches. For France, passenger car statistics refer to NUTS level 1 regions, while only national data are available for Portugal. Electric vehicles refer to battery electric vehicles (BEVs; also known as fully electric vehicles). Hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), including plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), as well as hydrogen-powered vehicles, are excluded. *For statistics on electric passenger cars, the data for France refer to NUTS level 1 regions, while only national data are available for Bulgaria and Portugal. The latest data for Greece and Slovakia refer to 2023. *For statistics on electric vehicles and recharging points, the data for France refer to NUTS level 1 regions, while only national data are available for Bulgaria, Denmark, Greece, Portugal and Slovakia. No data are available for the outermost regions of France (RUP FR – Régions Ultrapériphériques Françaises (FRY)), which are therefore excluded from both the French national total and the EU aggregate.
In 2024, there were 260 million registered passenger cars in the EU, accounting for around 4 out of every 5 motor vehicles. At regional level (NUTS level 2), the highest count was recorded in Lombardia in northern Italy (6.4 million passenger cars). It was followed by the French capital region of Ile-de-France (5.4 million) and the south-eastern French region of Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes (5.1 million), while there were 6.1 million passenger cars across the whole of Portugal (national data). A further 4 regions recorded between 4.0 and 4.6 million cars: Andalucía and Comunidad de Madrid in Spain, Nouvelle-Aquitaine in south-west France and the Italian capital region of Lazio. The EU’s motorisation rate – defined as the number of passenger cars per 1 000 inhabitants – stood at 578 in 2024 (see '''Map 1'''). Car ownership is typically lower in regions characterised by extensive and efficient public transport networks offering frequent services. In these regions, people may be less likely to own a vehicle (or multiple vehicles per household), especially in regions impacted by congestion and limited parking availability. This pattern was particularly apparent in capital regions and predominantly urban regions of western and Nordic EU countries. By contrast, in several eastern and southern EU countries, the highest motorisation rates were often recorded in capital regions. Relatively high rates were also observed in some tourist-intensive regions, which may partly reflect the presence of rental vehicle fleets. Berlin – the capital region of Germany – had one of the lowest motorisation rates in the EU, at 334 passenger cars per 1 000 inhabitants in 2024. Car ownership in Berlin was considerably lower than in any other part of Germany, with the next lowest motorisation rates being recorded in Bremen and Hamburg (427 and 435 passenger cars per 1 000 inhabitants, respectively). Other capital regions to report relatively low motorisation rates – less than 400 passenger cars per 1 000 inhabitants – were those of Austria, Belgium and Sweden. By contrast, higher motorisation rates are often found in suburban, rural and peripheral regions, possibly reflecting a lack of alternative modes of inland passenger transport. The highest motorisation rates in the EU – at least 700 passenger cars per 1 000 inhabitants in 2024, as shown by the darkest shade in '''Map 1''' – were recorded in 22 regions, predominantly in Italy (14 regions, including the capital region of Lazio) and Finland (4 regions). This group also included Praha and Attiki, the capital regions of Czechia and Greece, as well as Prov. Vlaams-Brabant and Flevoland, both of which are located within commuting distance of the Belgian and Dutch capital regions, respectively. '''''The motorisation rate in Valle d’Aosta/Vallee d’Aoste (Italy) was 9.3 times as high as that recorded in Peloponnisos (Greece)''''' Some of the highest motorisation rates across NUTS level 2 regions were recorded in northern Italy, notably Valle d’Aosta/Vallée d’Aoste (1 936 passenger cars per 1 000 inhabitants in 2024) and Provincia Autonoma di Trento (1 610). These exceptionally high values may reflect specific regional circumstances: for example, in Valle d’Aosta/Vallee d’Aoste, the high rate is, at least in part, influenced by lower taxation on new vehicle registrations. There were also relatively high rates reported in the Dutch region of Flevoland (910 passenger cars per 1 000 inhabitants), the Greek capital region of Attiki (903) and the Finnish archipelago of Åland (867). These 5 regions were the only ones in the EU to report an average of more than 800 passenger cars per 1 000 inhabitants. The lowest motorisation rates were recorded in the Greek region of Peloponnisos (208 passenger cars per 1 000 inhabitants in 2024) and Sterea Elláda (278). Voreio Aigaio and Dytiki Elláda in Greece, Berlin in Germany and Nord-Est in Romania were the only others in the EU with fewer than 350 passenger cars per 1 000 inhabitants. Overall, 21 regions reported motorisation rates below 425 (shown by the lightest shade in '''Map 1'''). These were concentrated mainly in eastern and southern EU countries, particularly Greece (8 regions) and Romania (3 regions), but also included several capital regions in western or northern EU countries, as well as Latvia. Map 1: Passenger cars
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4d1af1a0-9d16-4469-ac2e-ae812e3f4e01?lang=en tran_r_vehst] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/99e703e9-1f64-42ac-b3fa-f11bb1e049e7?lang=en road_eqs_carhab]) [[Image:Passenger cars (per 1 000 inhabitants, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Passenger cars
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4d1af1a0-9d16-4469-ac2e-ae812e3f4e01?lang=en tran_r_vehst] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/99e703e9-1f64-42ac-b3fa-f11bb1e049e7?lang=en road_eqs_carhab])]] '''Electric passenger cars''' The uptake of electric passenger cars reflects, among other factors, income levels, price differentials between electric and other vehicles, subsidies and incentives, infrastructure investment, battery technology, fuel prices, urban policies, the availability and cost of public transport, and environmental consciousness. Over the most recent decade for which data are available, the number of electric cars in the EU has grown rapidly, with the total stock surpassing 1.0 million in 2020 and continuing to expand strongly thereafter, exceeding 3.0 million in 2022 and reaching 5.8 million by 2024. While the overall trend remains strongly upward, the pace of growth has shown signs of moderating, with the number of electric passenger cars increasing by 30.2% in 2024 (a lower rate than in previous years). In absolute terms, the largest annual increase was recorded in 2023, when the stock rose by 1.4 million vehicles, followed by a similar increase in 2024, when it grew by a further 1.3 million. The stock of electric passenger cars in the EU stood at 5.8 million in 2024, equivalent to 2.2% of all passenger cars. The share of electric passenger cars was highest in the Nordic and Benelux EU countries, as well as Austria and Germany. By contrast, electric passenger cars made up smaller shares of the total stock of cars in most southern and eastern regions of the EU. In 2024, the regional distribution of the share of electric passenger cars among all passenger cars was slightly skewed, with 123 out of the 218 regions (56.4%) recording a share below the EU average. Within most EU countries, the share of electric passenger cars was relatively homogeneous across regions, suggesting that national circumstances (such as the availability of recharging infrastructure) and national policies (such as subsidies and incentives) play an important role in shaping patterns of uptake for these vehicles. For example, all regions in Vlaams Gewest (northern Belgium), Denmark, the Netherlands, Austria and Sweden recorded shares above the EU average, as did Luxembourg and Portugal. By contrast, the Hungarian capital region of Budapest was the only region in the eastern EU countries to record a share that exceeded the EU average. '''Figure 1''' shows EU regions with the highest and lowest shares of electric cars in the total number of passenger cars. In 2024, there were 9 regions across the EU that reported double-digit shares. The highest value was recorded in Flevoland (the Netherlands), where more than 1 in 5 passenger cars were electric (22.1%). This unusually high figure may reflect the presence of vehicle leasing companies based in the region, which register large fleets of electric vehicles and thereby inflate the number of registrations relative to the size of the regional population. High shares of electric cars were also observed in the Nordic capital regions of Stockholm (14.4%; Sweden) and Hovedstaden (13.3%; Denmark). This group of 9 regions with double-digit shares also included the other 4 regions in Denmark, where regional shares ranged from 10.2% to 12.6%, as well as Prov. Vlaams-Brabant (Belgium) and Utrecht (the Netherlands). At the lower end of the distribution, 32 regions reported that electric cars accounted for fewer than 0.25% of all passenger cars in 2024. This group was concentrated in eastern and southern EU countries, particularly Greece (11 of 13 regions; 2023 data), Poland (13 of 17) and Slovakia (3 of 4; 2023 data). Among the 10 regions with the lowest overall shares, 8 were located in Greece and the remaining 2 in Poland. The lowest shares in the EU were recorded in the Greek regions of Thessalia and Anatoliki Makedonia, Thraki, both at 0.07%.
[[Image:Compet icon RYB2026.png|50px]] [[Image:Compet_icon_RYB2026_small.png|left]]
[[Image:Electric passenger cars (% of all passenger cars, by NUTS 2 regions, 2024)_RYB2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Electric passenger cars
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/cf890cec-06f1-482d-9750-805f0492cca8?lang=en tran_r_elvehst], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/832bf25b-2833-4253-89e2-1ff9ac872798?lang=en tran_r_vehst] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9361ca6a-e19b-440f-aa0f-d1e44fb17ab7?lang=en road_eqs_carpda])|alt=A bar chart showing the ten regions with the highest and lowest shares of electric passenger cars in all passenger cars, together with data for the EU aggregate. Data are presented in percent. Data are shown for NUTS level 2 regions in the EU for 2024. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''Electric recharging points''' The majority of recharging points for electric vehicles in the EU are concentrated in predominantly urban regions, leaving rural areas and inter-city routes less well-served. Furthermore, cross-border travel by electric car may be hindered by fragmented payment systems and varying standards, although ongoing efforts aim to improve the interoperability of the EU’s charging network. ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1804 Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 on the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure]'' aims to support the EU’s climate goals by ensuring the coordinated roll-out of alternative fuels infrastructure and a smooth transition to renewable (‘zero-carbon’) fuels. The regulation emphasises the need to increase the capacity of public recharging points for electric vehicles, alongside stimulating the deployment of fast charging stations and dedicated infrastructure for heavy-duty vehicles. It sets binding targets for EU countries, including minimum fast-charging densities on some of the EU’s principal routes along the [https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/infrastructure-and-investment/trans-european-transport-network-ten-t_en TEN-T] road network, alongside broader objectives to expand the network to around 3.5 million semi-public or public charging units by 2030. In 2024, there were 896 700 semi-public and public electric recharging points across the EU. These data are provided by Eco-Movement through the European Alternative Fuels Observatory (EAFO) that is funded by the European Commission’s [https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/tentec-maps/web/public/screen/home Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport]. It is important to note that the main modes of recharging in the EU are private charging at home, followed by workplace charging, while semi-public and public recharging points are generally used less frequently. Home and workplace charging typically rely on lower-power outlets, resulting in longer charging times but lower costs compared with faster, more expensive public charging points. Semi-public and public electric charging infrastructure is unevenly distributed across the EU. In urban areas of several western EU countries – such as Germany, France and the Netherlands – the network of charging points is relatively dense, reflecting both higher electric vehicle uptake and a greater concentration of the population. This pattern is also evident in regions across northern Belgium and northern Italy. By contrast, eastern EU countries generally have fewer charging points, although these often provide higher recharging capacity. In 2024, the Netherlands recorded 184 000 semi-public or public recharging points, representing slightly more than a fifth (20.5%) of the EU total. Germany and France followed with shares of 18.2% and 16.2%, respectively, while no other EU country recorded a double-digit share. Looking in more detail at NUTS level 2 regions, Zuid-Holland in the Netherlands had the highest count of semi-public and public recharging points in 2024, at 47 400. The next highest numbers of recharging points were also recorded in the Netherlands, namely, in the capital region of Noord-Holland (34 000 points) and the southern region of Noord-Brabant (27 500). Outside of the Netherlands, the highest count of semi-public and public recharging points was in the French capital region of Ile-de-France (25 700). '''Map 2''' shows the number of electric vehicles (passenger cars, buses and goods vehicles less than or equal to 3.5 tonnes) per semi-public and public recharging point. In 2024, there were, on average, 6.8 electric vehicles per recharging point across the whole of the EU. The distribution across regions was quite even, insofar as there were 98 regions recording a ratio below the EU average and 98 regions above it, while 2 regions had the same ratio as the EU. At the upper end of the distribution, there were 11 regions in the EU with an average of at least 15.0 electric vehicles per recharging point in 2024: this may simply reflect potentially high pressure on the charging infrastructure (through a high number of electric vehicles relative to a more limited availability of recharging points), low average use of vehicles (and therefore less frequent need for recharging) or other factors, such as a high proportion of the vehicles registered in a region recharging in other regions (for example because of commuting flows or because vehicle fleets are used in regions other than where they are registered). This group included 2 western German regions (Köln and Detmold), 2 of the 3 Irish regions (Eastern and Midland, and Southern) and 2 neighbouring regions from Hungary (Budapest and Pest). It also included the northern Italian region of Provincia Autonoma di Trento, Malta, Flevoland in the Netherlands, as well as the Polish and Romanian capital regions of Warszawski stołeczny and Bucureşti-Ilfov. At the lower end of the distribution, there were 16 regions across the EU with fewer than 2.5 electric vehicles per recharging point in 2024, indicating a comparatively high provision of charging infrastructure relative to electric vehicle uptake and therefore potentially lower pressure on recharging points. This group included 6 predominantly rural regions in Spain, where – excluding the atypical region of Ciudad de Ceuta (incomplete data) – the lowest ratio was recorded in Castilla y León (1.5 electric vehicles per recharging point). It also included 4 regions in the Netherlands, with the lowest ratio observed in Zeeland (1.7 electric vehicles per recharging point), and 3 regions in Belgium, where the lowest ratio was recorded in Prov. Luxembourg (also 1.7). This group of 16 regions also comprised 2 regions in Italy, with Liguria recording a ratio of 2.3 and Sardegna a ratio of 2.4, while the final region was the north-western Polish region of Zachodniopomorskie (also 2.4).

'''More about the data: road fatalities''' The EU’s road safety policy is guided by a European Parliament resolution on the ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52021IP0407 EU Road Safety Policy Framework 2021–2030 – Recommendations on next steps towards ‘Vision Zero’]'' (2021/2014), which aims to halve road deaths by 2030 and reduce them to near zero by 2050. A recent European Commission [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2026:77:FIN communication] (COM(2026) 77 final) indicates that, while progress has been made in reducing the number of road fatalities, the current pace is insufficient to meet either of the targets. In a statistical context, the number of [[Glossary:People killed in road accidents|road fatalities]] refers to people who died immediately in a road traffic accident or within 30 days as a result of injuries sustained in a road traffic accident. Statistics on road fatalities are available for all NUTS level 2 regions. The latest data for Greece refer to 2023. Road accident statistics include fatalities for vehicles which are in transit through a region as well as fatalities and injuries of non-residents staying in a region on holiday, for business or another reason. As such, and other things being equal, regions that have transit corridors or regions with high numbers of visitors may well experience a higher incidence of fatalities.
'''''The northern Italian region of Lombardia had the highest number of road fatalities – 383 in 2024 …''''' The EU’s roads are among the safest in the world. In 2024, there were 20 210 road fatalities across the EU’s territory, equivalent to 45 per million inhabitants. The northern Italian region of Lombardia recorded the highest number of road fatalities in 2024, with 383 fatalities; this was 6 more than in 2023. The only other regions in the EU where the number of road fatalities reached at least 300 were: *Andalucía in southern Spain (358 fatalities; 48 more than in 2023) *Rhône-Alpes in southern France (325 fatalities; 17 more than in 2023) *Lazio, the Italian capital region (319 fatalities; 27 fewer than in 2023). At the other end of the range, there were 6 NUTS level 2 regions that recorded fewer than 10 road fatalities in 2024. The sparsely populated Åland archipelago in Finland was the only region in the EU to report no road fatalities – its third consecutive year without any such fatalities. The other regions with fewer than 10 fatalities included: *the Spanish autonomous regions of Ciudad de Ceuta and Ciudad de Melilla (both recorded a single fatality) *the northern Italian region of Valle d’Aosta/Vallée d’Aoste (7 fatalities) *the westernmost region of Austria, Vorarlberg (also 7 fatalities) *the French outermost region of Mayotte (8 fatalities). '''''… while the north-western Bulgarian region of Severozapaden had the highest incidence rate – 148 road fatalities per million inhabitants''''' Across the EU, there were 45 road fatalities per million inhabitants in 2024. The regional distribution was relatively even, with 129 of the 244 NUTS level 2 regions for which data are available recording a rate above the EU average, 113 below it, and 2 recording the same value. '''Map 3''' highlights that several rural and peripheral regions of the EU reported some of the highest road fatality rates. In 2024, 22 regions recorded at least 80 fatalities per million inhabitants (as shown by the darkest shade on the map). These regions were concentrated in southern and eastern EU countries, as well as in France and southern Belgium. The highest rates, exceeding 100 fatalities per million inhabitants, were observed in: *Severozapaden (north-western Bulgaria), which recorded the highest rate in the EU, at 148 fatalities per million inhabitants *the southern Portuguese region of Alentejo (137 fatalities per million inhabitants) *the French outermost regions of Guadeloupe (131 fatalities per million inhabitants) and Guyane (114 fatalities per million inhabitants), as well as the island region of Corse (113 fatalities per million inhabitants) *the Greek island regions of Ionia Nisia (120 fatalities per million inhabitants; 2023 data) and Notio Aigaio (119 fatalities per million inhabitants; 2023 data) *the south-western Romanian region of Sud-Vest Oltenia (111 fatalities per million inhabitants). By contrast, urban and capital regions tended to report much lower incidences of road fatalities. This may reflect factors such as more extensive public transport networks, lower motorisation rates and lower average speeds – for example, due to stricter speed limits in built-up areas or frequent congestion on urban motorway networks. In 2024, 15 regions recorded fewer than 20 deaths per million inhabitants (they are presented in the lightest shade in '''Map 3'''). Ciudad de Ceuta, Ciudad de Melilla and Comunidad de Madrid (all Spain) were the only southern regions, while the Czech capital region (Praha) was the only eastern region. Apart from the atypical cases of Åland (Finland; no fatalities) and the two Spanish autonomous cities (both a single fatality), most of these regions were predominantly urban, with 8 of them being capital regions. Among those with the lowest incidence rates were: *Région de Bruxelles-Capitale / Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest in Belgium (9 road fatalities per million inhabitants) *Stockholm in Sweden (10 fatalities per million inhabitants) *Wien in Austria (also 10 fatalities per million inhabitants).

For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Maritime transport=== The quality of life on many European islands and in peripheral maritime regions depends to a great extent on the availability, reliability and efficiency of maritime transport services. These connections are often the primary link between island communities and the mainland, enabling the movement of passengers, goods, medical supplies and other essential services. Without regular and affordable ferry and shipping routes, residents may face increased isolation, limited access to healthcare and education, as well as higher costs for everyday products. Maritime transport plays a vital role in supporting local economies, facilitating trade and sustaining tourism, which is a key source of income for many island regions. In this context, strong maritime connections are essential not only for mobility, but also for economic resilience and the broader integration of peripheral regions within the EU. '''Maritime freight''' Maritime freight services facilitate trade within the EU and between the EU and the rest of the world. Along with other products, they contribute towards the security of supply of energy and food, while providing EU exporters with a means of reaching international markets and non-EU exporters with a means of reaching EU markets; indeed, the vast majority (in tonnage) of the EU’s international freight is transported by sea. The distribution of ports around the EU’s coastline reflects a range of influences including (among others) historical trade routes, geographic features, resource endowment, economic activities and political considerations. A large number of the EU’s main ports are concentrated along North Sea coastlines, close to some of the most densely populated regions of the EU that are served by an extensive network of motorways, railways, rivers and canals. '''''Rotterdam in the Netherlands was the largest port in the EU with almost 400 million tonnes of freight handled in 2024''''' In 2024, the gross weight of goods handled in all EU ports was 3.36 billion tonnes. Of this total, 2.08 billion tonnes, or 61.9%, flowed inwards towards the EU. This apparent imbalance may be explained, at least in part, by the nature of EU imports, with a relatively high share of the inward flows made-up of bulk commodities such as raw materials and energy resources. By contrast, when ships leave EU ports they are laden with different types of freight that may be less bulky / of lower weight, for example higher-value manufactured goods. '''Map 4''' shows information for the EU’s main ports in 2024, covering only ports handling at least 2.0 million tonnes of freight (inward and outward combined); note that Estonian ports are excluded for confidentiality reasons. The largest freight port in the EU was Rotterdam in the Netherlands. With 397.3 million tonnes of maritime freight handled in 2024, it accounted for 11.8% of all goods handled in EU ports. Inward flows into Rotterdam were particularly significant, standing at 288.0 million tonnes (13.9% of the EU’s inward flows), compared with 109.3 million tonnes of outward flows (8.6%). The second largest port in the EU was Antwerp-Bruges in Belgium, which combines the ports of Antwerp and Zeebrugge under a single port authority following a 2022 merger. In 2024, it handled 244.2 million tonnes of maritime freight, equivalent to 7.3% of the EU total and around three fifths of the quantity handled in Rotterdam. Unlike Rotterdam, trade in Antwerp-Bruges was relatively balanced, with inward flows of 123.7 million tonnes (6.0% of the EU’s inward flows) and outward flows of 120.6 million tonnes (9.4%). Several of the next largest freight ports in the EU were also located in the North Sea, within relatively close proximity of Rotterdam and Antwerp-Bruges: the German port of Hamburg (97.0 million tonnes), the Dutch capital of Amsterdam (78.8 million tonnes) and the French channel and river ports of HAROPA (Le Havre, Rouen and Paris; 76.7 million tonnes). Outside the North Sea basin, several relatively large freight ports were located in the Mediterranean: the Spanish ports of Algeciras (81.5 million tonnes), Valencia (64.5 million tonnes) and Barcelona (55.5 million tonnes), the French port of Marseille (66.0 million tonnes) and the Italian port of Trieste (53.5 million tonnes). There were also 2 other EU ports handling more than 50.0 million tonnes of goods in 2024: the Baltic port of Gdańsk in Poland (71.0 million tonnes) and the Black Sea port of Constanța in Romania (57.6 million tonnes). Most of the EU’s principal ports have higher levels of inward (rather than outward) flows of maritime freight when measured in tonnes (see '''Map 4'''). For example, in the EU’s principal port of Rotterdam, inward flows were 2.6 times as high as outward flows. Higher ratios were recorded in several other leading ports in the EU: Trieste in Italy (where inward flows were 9.1 times as high as outward flows), Gdańsk in Poland (3.9 times), as well as the French ports of Dunkerque (3.1) and Marseille (3.0). The overall level of maritime freight handled in EU ports decreased 0.2% between 2023 and 2024, with some of the EU’s principal ports experiencing much larger falls in the quantity of freight handled (inward and outward combined). The largest decreases – among the top 20 EU ports in 2024 – were recorded in Constanţa (-14.3%) and Gdańsk (-11.0%), with 6 other ports also reporting declines, including Rotterdam (-1.1%). By contrast, the fastest growth rate among the top 20 EU ports was recorded at the Atlantic port of Sines in Portugal, where the quantity of freight handled rose 10.7%. The North Sea port of Göteborg in Sweden was the only other port among the top 20 to record a double-digit increase (up 10.1%).

'''Map 5''' shows information on the principal EU ports for maritime passengers, covering only ports with at least 100 000 passengers carried (total of embarked and disembarked); note that Estonian ports are excluded for confidentiality reasons (Tallinn is among the EU’s top ports for passenger traffic). '''''Messina on the Italian island of Sicilia was the largest port in the EU for maritime passengers, with 11.4 million embarked and disembarked in 2024''''' Some of the EU’s most frequented maritime passenger routes are concentrated in the Mediterranean Sea. In 2024, the Italian port of Messina (Sicilia) remained the largest passenger port in the EU, with 11.4 million passengers embarked and disembarked, followed by Reggio di Calabria in southern Italy (11.2 million passengers) that acts as the main port linking the Italian mainland to Sicilia. There were 2 other Mediterranean ports with at least 10.0 million maritime passengers: *the southern Italian port of Napoli (11.0 million passengers), that is used as a gateway to nearby islands and coastal towns, as well as for longer domestic ferry routes and cruise departures *the Greek port of Peiraiás (10.0 million passengers), located close to the capital city of Athens, which is used as a hub for departures to the Greek islands. In 2024, among the main EU ports for maritime passengers, the following ports recorded the highest numbers of embarked and disembarked passengers in each EU country (excluding Italy and Greece (which are already mentioned above), and Estonia (no data available for ports)): *Helsinki, Finland (9.3 million passengers) *Palma de Mallorca, Spain (8.3 million passengers) *Calais, France (7.6 million passengers) *Stockholm, Sweden (6.9 million passengers) *Mġarr (Gozo), Malta (6.9 million passengers) *Helsingør (Elsinore), Denmark (6.4 million passengers) *Split, Croatia (5.0 million passengers). The overall level of maritime passenger transport in EU ports increased by 6.2% between 2023 and 2024, with most of the EU’s principal ports also experiencing growth in their number of embarked and disembarked passengers. The highest annual increases in passenger numbers were recorded in the Italian ports of Napoli (up 26.1%) and Capri (up 21.7%), which are connected by frequent ferry and hydrofoil services. Double-digit increases were also observed in the Greek ports of Perama and Paloukia (both up 13.8%), which are linked by a ferry that connects the Greek capital and its surrounding areas with the nearby island of Salamina. Among the top 20 EU ports for maritime passengers in 2024, there were only 3 that recorded a fall in passenger numbers: the German port of Burgstaaken/Fehmarn (-2.0%), the Swedish port of Stockholm (-1.9%) and the Spanish island port of Santa Cruz de Tenerife (-0.1%).

It aims to link major cities, ports, airports and freight terminals, providing a coherent, efficient, multimodal and high-quality transport infrastructure to support the movement of people and goods. According to current planning within the EU, the core network is expected to be completed by 2030, the extended core network by 2040, and the comprehensive network – designed to connect all regions – by 2050. The TEN-T policy framework is designed to make the EU’s transport system greener, more efficient and more resilient. Within rail transport, there are still several challenges for cross-border services, many of which can be linked to differing national standards in electrification, signalling and track gauge. For example, Ireland, Finland and the Baltic countries use broader track gauges than the standard used in most other EU countries, while Spain and Portugal retain Iberian gauge on conventional lines (although high-speed networks use standard gauge). To address interoperability issues, the [https://www.era.europa.eu/domains/infrastructure/european-rail-traffic-management-system-ertms_en European Railway Traffic Management System (ERTMS)] has been developed as a single European standard for train control and command. It is intended to replace more than 20 incompatible national systems, improving cross-border operability, safety and efficiency across the EU’s rail network. In May 2026, the European Commission made [https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1056 3 proposals] for new legislation covering rules to protect rail passengers better, while simplifying the planning and booking of regional, long-distance and cross-border travel, in particular, for rail journeys involving multiple operators. These included: *putting in place new protection for rail passengers’ rights, including assistance, rerouting, reimbursement and compensation *enabling single-ticket bookings across multiple rail operators, which can be bought in a single transaction through a ticketing platform of their choice *introducing new obligations for ticketing platforms and operators to ensure fair access to selling tickets and the neutral presentation of travel options. '''''In 2024, more than half of the EU’s railway lines were electrified''''' In 2024, there were around 202 000 km of railway lines across the EU and 332 000 km of tracks; – a line is made up of 1 or more tracks forming a route between 2 points. Note that there are no railways in Cyprus and Malta nor in 15 other EU regions in the EU; there are also no railways in Iceland nor in 1 Norwegian and 1 Turkish region. More than half (57.6%) of the EU’s railway lines were electrified. Electrified railway lines offer a number of benefits over diesel-powered trains running on non-electrified lines: they generally have lower operating costs, improved performance, higher energy efficiency, reduced emissions (especially if powered by renewable energy sources) and they tend to be quieter. Within the EU, there were 7 NUTS level 2 regions where practically all (100.0%) of the railway lines were electrified in 2024. This was the case in: *the Spanish regions of Comunidad Foral de Navarra, La Rioja and Illes Balears *the Croatian capital region of Grad Zagreb *the Dutch regions of Drenthe and Flevoland *the Portuguese region of Península de Setúbal. Alongside these 7 regions, there were a further 8 regions where the share of electrified railway lines was at least 95.0%. Together, these 2 groups are shown in the darkest shade in '''Map 6'''. This group of 8 regions – where at least 95.0% (but not 100.0%) of all railway lines were electrified – composed the capital regions of France, Poland and Sweden, as well as Liguria and Umbria in Italy, the eastern Bulgarian region of Yugoiztochen, Luxembourg and the Dutch region of Utrecht. At the other end of the range, there were 16 regions where fewer than 20.0% of all railway lines were electrified in 2024. This group was widely distributed across the EU and contained all 3 Baltic countries (for which only national data are available): a major infrastructure project – Rail Baltica – is underway, aiming to develop a double-track electrified railway linking the capital cities of the Baltic countries with Poland. Within this group, there were 8 regions where none of the railway lines were electrified: *the Irish regions of Northern and Western; Southern *the Greek regions of Anatoliki Makedonia, Thraki; Dytiki Makedonia; Dytiki Elláda *the French island region of Corse *the Italian regions of Valle d’Aosta/Vallée d’Aoste; Sardegna.

They cover a broad range of indicators, for example, transport infrastructure (the length or density of transport networks) or equipment rates (the number of vehicles per inhabitant). The other main area of regional transport statistics concerns flows of passenger and freight traffic between, within and through regions for maritime transport and for air transport. Differences between regions are often closely related to the level and structure of their economic activity, their number of inhabitants, or their geographical location in relation to key transport infrastructure such as road and rail networks, ports, airports, other hubs and terminals. The legal bases for the transport statistics presented in this chapter are: *road transport statistics – ''[http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX%3A32012R0070 Regulation (EU) No 70/2012] on statistical returns in respect of the carriage of goods by road'' *maritime statistics – ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32009L0042 Directive 2009/42/EC] on statistical returns in respect of carriage of goods and passengers by sea'' and ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2018.180.01.0029.01.ENG European Commission Delegated Decision (EU) 2018/1007] supplementing Directive 2009/42/EC as regards the list of ports'' *air statistics – ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003R0437 Regulation (EC) 437/2003] on statistical returns in respect of the carriage of passengers, freight and mail by air'' and ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003R1358 Commission Regulation (EC) No 1358/2003] implementing Regulation (EC) No 437/2003 on statistical returns in respect of the carriage of passengers, freight, and mail by air''. '''Indicator definitions''' '''Air passengers carried''' An air passenger is any person, excluding on-duty members of the flight and cabin crews, who makes a journey by air; infants in arms are included. The number of air passengers carried refers to all passengers on a particular flight (with a single flight number), counted only once – not repeatedly for each stage of a flight. It includes both revenue and non-revenue passengers whose journey begins or terminates at the reporting airport, as well as transfer passengers joining or leaving the flight at the reporting airport; it excludes direct transit passengers. '''Electric passenger cars''' The principal type of motor energy used by a vehicle is that certified by the competent authority of the country of registration. Battery electric passenger cars are vehicles that only use batteries to feed an electric motor for propulsion. '''Electric recharging points''' The data on electric recharging points come from [https://www.eco-movement.com/ Eco-Movement through the European Alternative Fuels Observatory (EAFO) financed by the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport], which collects detailed information on semi-public and publicly accessible charging points. This includes data on their location, connector types and power output. The data on electric charging points are aggregated to NUTS level 2 regions and subsequently combined with Eurostat statistics on the stock of electric vehicles. This allows the calculation of a derived indicator on the number of electric vehicles per recharging point. '''Electric vehicles''' Within this publication, the aggregate for electric vehicles (as used in Map 2) is composed of passenger cars, buses and goods vehicles less than or equal to 3.5 tonnes. '''Motorisation rate''' This rate is the number of passenger cars registered per 1 000 inhabitants. A passenger car is a road motor vehicle, other than a moped or a motorcycle, intended for the carriage of passengers and designed to seat no more than 9 persons (including the driver). It includes microcars, taxis, hired passenger cars and vans designed primarily for passenger transport. It may also include special-purpose passenger vehicles such as ambulances, police cars and motor homes. Excluded are light goods road vehicles, motor coaches and minibuses. '''Road accidents''' A fatal road transport accident involves at least 1 road vehicle in motion on a public road (or a private road to which the public have a right of access), resulting in at least 1 killed person. Road fatalities include people who are killed immediately in a traffic accident or who die within 30 days as a result of an injury sustained in a road accident; these statistics exclude suicides. A road crash – alternatively referred to as a road traffic accident – is defined as a crash involving at least 1 vehicle on a public road. Damage-only accidents – where there are no fatalities or injuries – are excluded from the information collected. '''Maritime freight''' Maritime freight statistics refer to the carriage of goods by sea between ports, measured in tonnes of goods loaded and unloaded. The data include all goods transported by seagoing vessels, including containerised and non-containerised goods, bulk goods (such as oil, coal and grain), and roll-on/roll-off freight (such as trucks and trailers). Excluded are bunkers (fuel for a ship’s own propulsion), ship’s stores and supplies for own use. '''Maritime passengers''' Maritime passengers generally refer to people who make a journey by sea on a seagoing vessel, excluding the vessel’s crew. As such, they include ferry passengers, cruise passengers or any other paying or non-paying passengers travelling by sea, other than crew members and people who do not actually travel (for example, those who only visit a terminal). Eurostat typically counts maritime passengers in terms of those who are embarked/disembarked. '''Port''' A port is a place having facilities for merchant ships to moor and to load or unload cargo or to disembark or embark passengers to or from vessels, usually directly to a pier. Main ports are ports that handle more than a million tonnes of goods or 200 000 passengers annually. A statistical port consists of 1 or more ports, normally controlled by a single port authority, able to record ship and cargo movements. '''Rail infrastructure''' A railway line is a continuous section of rail infrastructure within a railway network, composed of 1 or more running tracks, used for the movement of railway vehicles. A track is a physical rail installation consisting of 2 rails and supporting infrastructure enabling train operation. Railway lines may be classified by electrification status: electrified railway lines are those equipped with fixed infrastructure for electric traction supply (for example, overhead contact lines or third rail systems), enabling the operation of electric rolling stock. Non-electrified lines lack such infrastructure and are typically operated using diesel or other non-electric traction modes. Electrified line length is recorded as a subset of total railway line length. ===Context=== '''Transport policy''' The European Commission’s [https://ec.europa.eu/info/departments/mobility-and-transport_en Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport] is responsible for developing [https://commission.europa.eu/topics/transport_en transport policy] within the EU. Its remit is to ensure mobility in a single European transport area, integrating the needs of the population and the economy at large, while minimising adverse environmental effects. The promotion of more efficient and interconnected transport networks in the EU aims to bring about several benefits, including advanced mobility, reductions in emissions, improved competitiveness and productivity gains. Since 2020, the EU’s transport policies have been shaped largely by [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/european-green-deal_en The European Green Deal], the Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy and related legislative packages. Policy initiatives within the transport domain touch on everyday lives; for example, the European Commission has proposed legislation about: *the protection of [https://europa.eu/youreurope/citizens/travel/passenger-rights/index_en.htm passenger rights] for air, rail, bus and coach, and maritime passengers *security measures, such as a [https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/eu-air-safety-list_en list of airlines banned from EU skies] *[https://road-safety.transport.ec.europa.eu/eu-road-safety-policy_en road safety] measures to reduce road fatalities and serious road accidents *funding to deliver a modern [https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/infrastructure-and-investment/trans-european-transport-network-ten-t_en trans-European transport network (TEN-T)] with multimodal management systems that facilitate the mobility of goods and passengers across the EU *a range of policies designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by delivering [https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/sustainable-transport_en sustainable transport] and [https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/urban-transport/sustainable-urban-mobility_en sustainable urban mobility]. '''Sustainable and smart mobility''' In December 2020, the European Commission adopted the ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52020DC0789 Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy – putting European transport on track for the future]'' (COM(2020) 789 final). The strategy lays the foundations for a fundamental transformation of the EU’s transport system, supporting both the green and digital transitions, while increasing resilience to future crises. It presents a roadmap structured around 3 key dimensions of mobility and 10 flagship initiatives. *Sustainable mobility **boosting the uptake of zero-emission vehicles, renewables and low-carbon fuels and related infrastructure **creating zero-emission airports and ports **making inter-urban and urban mobility more sustainable and healthier **greening freight transport **pricing carbon and providing better incentives for users. *Smart mobility **making connected and automated multimodal mobility a reality **innovation, data and artificial intelligence for smart mobility. *Resilient mobility **reinforcing the single market **making mobility fair and just for all **enhancing transport safety and security. The strategy is a wide-ranging plan built upon a set of key milestones, including, among others, the following targets: *at least 30 million zero-emission cars should be in operation by 2030, while nearly all cars, vans, buses and heavy-duty vehicles should be zero-emission vehicles by 2050 *traffic on high-speed rail should double by 2030 (compared with 2015) *rail freight traffic should double by 2050 (compared with 2015) *a multimodal trans-European transport network (TEN-T), equipped for sustainable and smart transport with high-speed connectivity, should be fully operational by 2050. '''TEN-T (Trans-European Transport Networks)''' The EU’s TEN-T policy, governed by ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02024R1679-20240628 Regulation (EU) 2024/1679 on Union guidelines for the development of the trans-European transport network]'', aims to create a high-quality, multimodal transport infrastructure across the EU. It integrates rail, road, inland waterways, short sea shipping, ports, airports and terminals to ensure seamless connectivity and efficient transport of people and goods. The revised regulation supports economic, social and territorial cohesion, while focusing on environmental sustainability, safety and resilience. It also introduces tighter deadlines – for example, completing work on core corridors by 2030. Some key initiatives to be achieved by 2040 include: *passenger trains on core and extended networks must travel at 160 km per hour or more *the deployment of the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) to enhance rail safety and efficiency, with national signalling systems phased out *major airports with over 12 million annual passengers must be connected by long-distance rail, thereby offering a competitive alternative to domestic flights *an expansion of freight terminals to support increased capacity and multimodal transport. '''Alternative fuels and clean vehicles''' ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1804/oj/eng Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 on the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure]'' became effective across the EU on April 13, 2024. It aims to support the EU’s climate goals by ensuring the coordinated roll-out of alternative fuels infrastructure, forming part of broader efforts to decarbonise transport and reinforce the clean vehicles’ value chain. The regulation on alternative fuels infrastructure sets binding targets for charging infrastructure. For example, there should be at least 1.3 kilowatts (kW) of publicly accessible charging power available for every registered electric vehicle, while fast charging stations (at least 150 kW) should be available every 60 km along major transport routes (the TEN-T core network) by 2025. Hydrogen refuelling stations must be available every 200 km and in principal urban conurbations by 2030. The regulation sets out requirements for full technical interoperability, real-time consumer information, transparent pricing and accessible payment options that offer alternatives to subscription-based models. EU countries must develop national frameworks and report on progress to ensure compliance. '''Automotive package''' The European Commission presented an [https://transport.ec.europa.eu/transport-themes/action-plan-future-automotive-sector/automotive-package_en automotive package] to support the EU automotives sector’s transition to clean mobility, aiming to balance climate neutrality by 2050 with industrial competitiveness and greater flexibility for manufacturers. It maintains a strong push for zero-emission vehicles while simplifying rules, reducing administrative costs and supporting EU-made vehicles and batteries. The package revises carbon dioxide standards for cars, vans and heavy-duty vehicles while introducing measures to increase uptake of low- and zero-emission corporate fleets, including incentives for small EU-made electric cars. From 2035, manufacturers must achieve a 90% reduction in tailpipe emissions, with the remaining 10% covered through low-carbon steel, e-fuels or biofuels, allowing continued use of hybrids and combustion-engine vehicles alongside electric and hydrogen technologies, while additional flexibility is provided for heavy-duty vehicles to ease compliance with 2030 targets. '''Road safety''' The EU has a long-term strategic goal for road safety: Vision Zero. In October 2021, the European Parliament adopted a resolution on the ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52021IP0407 EU road safety policy framework 2021–2030 – Recommendations on next steps towards ‘Vision Zero’]'' (2021/2014(INI)). The framework aims to halve the number of fatalities and serious injuries on EU roads by 2030 and commits to bringing the number of road deaths close to zero by 2050. To achieve these targets, it will monitor indicators such as vehicle safety, seat belt usage, speed compliance and post-crash care. In order to better understand the factors influencing road safety performance, the European Commission has developed a set of key road safety performance indicators (KPIs). A [https://road-safety.transport.ec.europa.eu/european-road-safety-observatory/data-and-analysis/key-performance-indicators-kpis_en report] was published at the end of 2025, highlighted significant gaps in compliance with basic safety measures, including widespread non-compliance with speed limits in urban areas, where pedestrians, cyclists and other vulnerable road users are most at risk. '''Ports and maritime strategy''' In March 2026, the European Commission adopted 2 strategies to drive competitiveness, sustainability, security and resilience within the EU’s maritime sector. The strategies focus on ports, shipping and shipbuilding. The ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026DC0112 EU ports strategy]'' (COM(2026) 112 final) aims to strengthen the competitiveness, resilience and sustainability of EU ports through coordinated investment, innovation and security measures. The European Commission plans to introduce clearer criteria for EU funding and foreign ownership in strategic ports, while supporting digitalisation, green technologies and the uptake of innovative solutions. It will accelerate approvals for energy and environmental projects, promote port electrification and clean energy partnerships, and improve access to financing and advisory support. At the same time, the strategy focuses on enhancing port security by addressing cybersecurity risks, drug trafficking and emerging threats through updated guidance, stronger customs coordination and international cooperation. Finally, it emphasises social cohesion and workforce development by supporting skills training, reskilling and safer working practices across the ports and blue economy sectors. The ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52026DC0111 EU industrial maritime strategy]'' (COM(2026) 111 final) aims to strengthen Europe’s shipbuilding and shipping industries to safeguard strategic autonomy, trade, defence and maritime security amid rising global competition. It focuses on 3 pillars: reinforcing Europe’s maritime manufacturing and repair capabilities through innovation, digitalisation and industrial cooperation; improving the competitiveness, sustainability and global influence of maritime transport through simpler regulations, green transition measures and stronger international engagement; and enhancing maritime security, naval production and military mobility capabilities. The strategy is further supported by investments in research, innovation, skills development and workforce training, alongside efforts to mobilise EU, national and private funding for decarbonisation, technological leadership and defence-related maritime projects. '''Rail transport''' In November 2025, the European Commission unveiled a comprehensive plan to accelerate the development of high-speed rail across the EU: ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025DC0903 Connecting Europe through High-Speed Rail]'' (COM(2025) 903 final). It outlines concrete actions to connect the EU better through fast, comfortable, safe and reliable rail services, considerably shortening travel times. For example: *by 2030, passengers should be able to travel between Berlin and Copenhagen in 4 hours, instead of the 7 hours required today *by 2035, new connections should make it possible to travel by train from Paris to Lisbon (via Madrid). ===Other articles=== *[[Air passenger transport statistics]] *[[Characteristics of the railway network in Europe]] *[[Inland transport infrastructure at
