title: Tutorial:Assigning an article to a unit or a category
text:
==Assigning an article to a unit==

All statistical and methodological articles in [[:Statistics Explained:About|Statistics Explained]] are 'owned' by a unit of [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] who takes responsability for its content. Glossary pages, however, are not owned individually; [[Thematic glossaries|thematic glossaries]] (for instance the [[:Category:Transport glossary|Transport glossary]]) are assigned to the most appropriate unit and as a result responsability is more diffuse  -  pages are assigned to a Unit, which is responsible for their content. This is done by placing every page into a topic category. Topic categories, starting with X_, are internal categories, hidden from outside users. They are only shown in edit mode. Each page must have exactly one topic category. 

In order to assign your article to a Unit, replace <X_topic> with the appropriate topic in ''<nowiki>{{Unit|topic=<X_topic>}}</nowiki>''; all topics are linked automatically to the responsible Unit (see [[Tutorial:Topics_and_Units|list of all topics and their corresponding Unit]]), and will be re-allocated automatically in case of a reorgaisation.

==Categories==
 
To allow users to find similar articles easily, each article must be put into one or several categories (see the [[Special:Categories|list of current categories)]]. Categories are user-oriented ad hoc groupings of similar articles. They serve as a navigation aid for users and make it possible to find other articles possibly of interest.
Category pages have no text except a short description of their content and maybe some links, for instance:
 
Statistical articles can be put in three different types of categories; the first two are mandatory, the third one is to be avoided if possible:

*1.theme/subtheme: the hierarchy of themes and subthemes is the producer-oriented nomenclature of Eurostat dissemination products, but the items, preferably at the level of the subtheme, are also used as categories; statistical articles are to be added to one or sometimes several subthemes (see list of statistical themes and subthemes for the exact names);
*2.type of article: in this case Statistical article (the alternative for articles is Background article);
*3.ad hoc category: to be used very sparingly and only if it adds value for users: at the moment only 1 ad hoc category for statistical articles is in use: Prices.
 
===Number and ordering of categories===
Categories are always in alphabetical order. The number of categories has no limit in theory, but categories should only be added if they offer a real service to users for finding similar articles.
 
[[Category:<Subtheme category name(s)>|Name of the statistical article]] [[Category:<Statistical article>|Name of the statistical article]]
 
===Assigning an article to a category===
*Remove, at the very end of the page, < > in [[Category:<Under construction>|Name of the statistical article]], thus putting the new article in the category 'Under construction';
*When the article has been sighted and validated to a stable page, this category must be removed: remove < and > and replace '<Category name(s)>' (do not forget to remove the comment markup < > as well!!!) in [[Category:<Category name(s)>|xxx]] with the name of the appropriate theme or subtheme (capital letter at the beginning!). If you want to put the article in additonal categories, copy and paste [[Category:<Category name(s)>|xxx]] after the first one, separated by a blank, and change it accordingly.
 
A category which does not yet exist, appears in red in 'page' view. To create it, click on it, add a very brief description of one sentence only in the text frame and then save it. 

A category with only one article is not a problem if it is likely to contain more in the future.
 
When saving an article the name of the article is automatically added at the end of the category link (if no text is yet present there, after the '|'), to be displayed on the category page; in this instance 'Transport infrastructure'.

===See also===

*[[Tutorial:Topics and Units |Topics and Units ]]

title: Tutorial:Accessibility guidelines
text:
'''This page and the related guidance is being revised in 2025; please consult the Statistics Explained team in case of any questions.''' This page provides guidance and instructions for ensuring that Statistics Explained articles are compliant with the web accessibility rules and guidelines set out in the Web Accessibility Directive. ===Alternative text=== Alternative text (alt text) is descriptive text embedded in a webpage's code that explains an image's meaning or function, primarily for users who rely on screen readers, but also for search engines. Alternative text is important as it allows people with visual impairments to understand the content of images through screen readers. Every PNG image of a graph or table that is included in a Statistics Explained article must have alternative text added to the wikitext tags, following these guidelines: *The tag for alternative text is '''alt='''
Example:
[[Image:Annual-number-of-transacted dwellings-Annual-average-rate-of-change-2023-and-2024(%)-v2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Annual number of transacted dwellings
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=prc_hpi_hsna}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing percentage annual average rate of change of annual number of transacted dwellings in 17 EU Member States. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] *Alternative text should not be too detailed; it should briefly describe what is depicted in the image, without detailing individual countries or results *This text should be included in the alternative text: “For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.” (just make sure that there actually is a link to the source dataset and adapt if there are several datasets) *Vistool graphs do not need alternative text as they have a table view option which is machine readable ===Accessibility for graphs and tables=== * Excel add-in Every Statistics Explained article that includes PNG images of tables or graphs that have been created using the Excel add-in must also include the excel file with the corresponding information to enable the use of screen readers. Ensure that a bookmark leading to the exact dataset (not the default dataset) is included in the excel file for each graph or table, written as follows: :Bookmark: :hlth_rs_prs2 https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/65709a40-8efe-44d7-9bcc-9898c08675bf?lang=en :Example:[[Media:Example excel file with bookmarks.xlsx|Excel file with bookmarks]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] * Vistool The Vistool has been developed to already include the necessary requirements for accessibility compliance.
By clicking on '''View table view''' from the chart context menu, a machine readable table version of the data is displayed.
Example: [[Image:Vistool graph- accessibility.png|thumb|none|600px]]
[[Image:Vistool graph- accessibility 2.png|thumb|none|600px]] ===General accessibility rules=== *No reference should be made to colours or shading; reference to the graph or map is enough *Links should not show the complete URL address, eg https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/earn_minw_esms.htm :to prevent this, insert links like this:
[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/earn_minw_esms.htm NAME OF LINK]
:leaving a space after the URL and then adding the name of the link *Links should be clearly named and not simply be directed with vague terms, eg "here"
Example of incorrect link naming:
:The data can be found [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/earn_minw_esms.htm here]. ===See also=== *[[Statistics Explained:Accessibility|SE accessibility statement]] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/0o.o0o.documentation.o0o.o0/accessibility Eurostat website - accessibility] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/4443939/14379268/Eurostat+Web+Accessibility+Action+Plan+2023_DM.pdf/9bb05a94-50e1-2ac4-a16c-09dad8a29440?t=1684912819107 Eurostat Web Accessibility Action Plan 2023] *EC webguide: [https://commission.europa.eu/resources/europa-web-guide/design-content-and-development/accessibility_en Accessibility overview] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/4443939/14379268/Guidelines+for+the+accessibility+of+content+produced+by+Eurostat_DM.pdf/45c8d447-75b9-b91a-19ad-2ad0748f3162?t=1684912818415 Guidelines for the accessibility of content produced by Eurostat] *[https://op.europa.eu/en/web/accessibility/accessibility OP guides on accessibility] and [https://op.europa.eu/en/web/accessibility/accessibility-tips Accessibility tips] [[Category:Tutorial| Accessibility guidelines]]

title: Tutorial:Checklist for publishing
text:
===Checklist=== ====Text==== *Is the '''introduction short''' and does it inform the reader about the content of the article? *No mandatory '''section missing'''? (Main statistical findings, Excel file, Data sources, Context, See also, Footnotes, Explore further)? ''Not applicable for background articles.'' *Did you add corresponding '''categories''' within the article: [[Articles_by_theme|Articles by theme]]? *Are all '''acronyms explained''' the first time they appear? *Are all statistical and technical terms linked to the corresponding '''glossary page''' when they first appear? *Do the '''figures in the text correspond''' to the figures in the tables/graphs? *Is the '''ranking of Member States''' in the text in the right order? *Are the '''references to the tables and graphs''' correct? *No '''spelling''' mistakes? ====Tables and graphs==== *Do the tables and graphs follow the '''Eurostat layout''' (are the same '''theme colours''' used throughout the article)? *Are graphs, tables and maps '''positioned optimally''' with regard to the related text? *Do the titles include unit and period? *Do the tables and graphs include the '''data sources'''? *Are the tables and graphs easily readable when clicked on? *Are possible footnotes included below the image? *Are tables and graphs the correct size (700 px)? *Is alternative text included, with a reference to the link to the dataset? *Is the Eurostat logo added (and ribbon for maps)? *Is a disclaimer added if the y-axis doesn’t start at 0? ====Maps==== *Has the map been approved by the GISCO team - send to the following Teams group: [https://teams.microsoft.com/l/channel/19%3auuO3L9aRtP0qTF8u0goOzLSLVxgA0S07wbUqNs9opcY1%40thread.tacv2/General?groupId=d43cf916-f6e8-4078-8642-c61e0354637c&tenantId=b24c8b06-522c-46fe-9080-70926f8dddb1 GRP-ESTAT GISCO MAP CHECKING] ====Links==== *Do all '''links work'''? *Are Regulations, Directives, Commission documents mentioned in text '''linked to EUR-Lex''' product page? (using the EUR-Lex template) *Is the '''Excel file''' with the source data for tables, figures and maps present? *Are all technical terms linked to glossaries? *Are Eurostat publications mentioned linked to the publication product page? *Are there links to Eurostat data? ====Language==== *'''Important: has a native English speaker read and corrected the article?'''
All articles must be first proofread by a native speaker (within your unit or Directorate if available) or sent for '''proofreading to DGT via Poetry''' (the author is responsible for requesting the proofreading). *'''Is the style adapted to a non-specialist audience?''' *Is the text written in '''British English'''? ===Approval procedure=== ====Updated articles==== If your article updates an existing one, the '''editor''' (see the [[Tutorial:Statistics Explained - Editor|list of editors]]) appointed by the head of unit must approve it in the system. The Statistics Explained team is notified automatically and checks the layout and consistency of tables and text before publishing. ====New articles / Major updates==== For a new article or major update, obtain approval from your Head of Unit and Director, after which the '''editor''' can approve it in the system. The Statistics Explained team receives automatic notification, checks layout and consistency, and sends the article for approval from Director B before publishing. Please pay attention to the following time requirements: *final draft, including unit Director approval, should be sent to the SE team '''at least 5 working days''' before the scheduled publishing date *if the draft is not ready by Thursday CoB in the week prior to the publishing date, and also allowing for the 5-working day timeframe, then it will not be included in the release calendar
In exceptional cases where approval by the Dirctor General is required: *the unit will send their article to the SE team, fully approved by their Director, at least '''3 extra working days''' in advance (ie 8 working days) to accommodate this additional approval step *the unit will wait for Director B approval before submission to the Director General *if a delay is likely, the unit will ask the SE team, well in advance (by Thursday CoB in the week prior to the publishing date), to remove the article from the release calendar (before the calendar is released to users and journalists) ====Approving an article==== *Go to the ''''Review this revision'''' pane at the bottom of the draft page (only the first line, Director/Editor approval button is visible to a person with 'editor' rights) [[Image:Review this revision pane.png|center|450px]] *Next to 'Director/Editor approval', tick the box ''''Approved'''' *Click ''''Submit approvals'''' *Article is checked and published by SE team and put on the homepage
====Publishing date==== *The date for publishing the Statistics Explained article is agreed in advance between the author unit and the Statistics Explained team and entered as preliminary in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/main/news/release-calendar Eurostat release calendar] *Reminders are sent to the author units one month in advance and the date is confirmed in the release calendar *Any changes must be requested before the release calendar is published (every Friday at 11:00); any changes after this must be approved by the Director of the corresponding unit. *An article can be linked to a '''news release''' (this must be requested in advance) and '''data release'''. ===See also=== *[[tutorial:Statistics Explained - Editor| List of editors]] [[Category:Tutorial|Checklist for publishing]]

title: Tuberculosis, viral hepatitis and HIV statistics
text:
EU statistics present an overview of tuberculosis, viral hepatitis and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) disease. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: August 2027 0.06% of all deaths in the EU in 2023 resulted from tuberculosis, 0.07% from viral hepatitis and 0.04% from HIV. In 2023, there were 51 200 resident in-patients with tuberculosis who were discharged from hospitals across the EU, along with 2 800 discharges of day cases (excluding Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia and Malta). In 2023, the average length of stay for resident in-patients treated for tuberculosis ranged from 10 days in Cyprus to 54 days in Czechia and Poland and 122 days in Lithuania. |alt=Dynamic interactive line chart showing the deaths from tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis of residents, as standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2011 to 2023 for the EU. This article presents an overview of [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] statistics related to tuberculosis, human immunodeficiency virus disease (hereafter referred to as HIV) and viral hepatitis. *Tuberculosis is a contagious bacterial disease, initially affecting the lungs. It is typically transmitted between people through the air, for example when an infected person coughs, sneezes or spits. *HIV is a retrovirus which, if untreated, progresses to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); treatment can slow or prevent HIV from advancing to AIDS. HIV attacks and destroys the body’s white blood cells, weakening the immune system. It is commonly transmitted through bodily fluids during unprotected sexual activity; among other means of transmission, it may result from injecting drugs or may be passed from an infected mother to a child during pregnancy. *Viral hepatitis is an inflammation of the liver, typically caused by an infection through a hepatotropic virus. It is typically transmitted through food, water, blood or bodily fluids. This article covers deaths among residents from these 3 diseases, as well as healthcare activities assessed in terms of the number of hospital discharges and average lengths of stay. This article is included in a set of statistical articles concerning specific health conditions in the EU which forms part of the online publication [[Health_in_the_European_Union_-_facts_and_figures|Health in the European Union – facts and figures]]. ===Development of deaths from tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis in the EU=== In 2023, there were 7 802 deaths in the EU resulting from tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis, equivalent to 0.16% of all deaths. Relative to the population size, there were 1.62 deaths from tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis per 100 000 inhabitants. '''''Death rates for tuberculosis and HIV in the EU fell almost every year since 2002''''' Figures 1 and 2 show the development of the [[Glossary:Standardised_death_rate_(SDR)|standardised death rate]] for these 3 diseases from 2002 to 2023. The time series are shown in 2 periods, the first (up to 2010) coded according to the [https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/classification-of-diseases International Classification of Diseases (ICD)] version 9 (ICD-9) and the second (from 2011) coded according to ICD-10. *During the first period, from 2002 to 2010, EU standardised death rates were relatively stable for viral hepatitis but showed a clear decline for the other 2 diseases. **Among the 3 diseases, viral hepatitis recorded the smallest fall during this period. The rate fluctuated between 1.6 and 1.8 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants each year, starting at 1.7 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2002 and finishing at 1.6 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2010. **The rate for tuberculosis almost halved, down from 2.2 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2002 to 1.2 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants by 2010, falling almost every year. **The number of deaths per 100 000 inhabitants for HIV initially rose from 1.3 in 2002 to 1.4 in 2003 before declining to 0.9 in 2010. *During the second period, from 2011 to 2023, all 3 death rates fell. **The rate for viral hepatitis initially increased, up from 1.38 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2011 to 1.56 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2013; thereafter it declined every year, reaching 0.64 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2023. **The rate for tuberculosis continued its downward path from the first period, interrupted only by an increase in 2013. Overall, it fell from 0.93 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2011 to 0.58 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2023. **The rate for HIV also continued its downward path, falling from 0.87 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2011 to 0.40 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2021; it then stabilised at this level in 2022 and 2023. [[Image:Standardised death rates for tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis, EU, 2002–10 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Standardised death rates for tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis, EU, 2002–10
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/190f2c4b-cc39-4ca8-b520-2186ece246d2?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr])|alt=A line chart showing the deaths from tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis of residents, as standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2002 to 2010 for the EU. The complete data of the figure are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] [[Image:Standardised death rates for tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis, EU, 2011–23 (per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Standardised death rates for tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis, EU, 2011–23
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e798de00-3454-4a7b-a241-f7f5c71d8284?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A line chart showing the deaths from tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis of residents, as standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants. Data are shown for 2011 to 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the figure are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Developments of potential years of life lost in the EU=== '''''5 235 people died before the age of 75 years from tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis in 2023, resulting in the loss of 23.5 potential years of life per 100 000 inhabitants''''' As noted earlier, there were 7 802 deaths in the EU resulting from tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis in 2023. Of these, 5 235 were deaths before the age of 75 years, equivalent to 0.34% of all deaths within this age range. Tuberculosis is considered to be both a preventable and a treatable disease, while HIV and viral hepatitis are considered to be preventable. Over the course of 2023, a total of 23.5 [[Glossary:Potential years of life lost|potential years of life were lost]] per 100 000 inhabitants through the deaths of EU residents aged less than 75 years from these 3 causes. This rate is calculated by summing the number of years between the age at death and 75 years for each premature death from these causes and then expressing this total relative to the size of the age-standardised population aged less than 75 years. The number of potential years of life lost in 2023 per 100 000 inhabitants was 9.1 for HIV, 8.2 for tuberculosis and 6.2 for hepatitis. As the death rates from these 3 diseases fell in recent years, so have the numbers of potential years of life lost, as can be seen from the similar developments shown in Figures 2 and 3. Relative to population size, the number of years lost per 100 000 inhabitants fell among all 3 diseases between 2011 and 2023: *from 25.5 to 9.1 years per 100 000 inhabitants for HIV *from 14.6 to 8.2 years per 100 000 inhabitants for tuberculosis *from 14.2 to 6.2 years per 100 000 inhabitants for viral hepatitis. [[Image:Potential years of life lost from tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis, people younger than 75 years, EU, 2011–23_(years per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Potential years of life lost from tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis, people younger than 75 years, EU, 2011–23
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9226d251-d5c8-47a0-b7f7-36c91cea1d82?lang=en hlth_cd_apyll])|alt=A line chart showing the number of potential years of life lost per hundred thousand inhabitants through deaths among people aged less than 75 years. The lines show data for tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis. Data are shown for 2011 to 2023 for the EU. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Deaths from tuberculosis, HIV and viral hepatitis in 2023 === '''''More than two thirds of deaths from tuberculosis in the EU in 2023 were among males''''' In 2023, there were 2 782 deaths in the EU resulting from tuberculosis. More than two thirds (71.3%) of these were among males, while a small majority (53.8%) were among people aged 65 years or over. The standardised death rate for tuberculosis in the EU was 0.58 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2023, with this rate notably higher for males (0.91 per 100 000 male inhabitants) than for females (0.28 per 100 000 female inhabitants). The rate for older people (1.53 per 100 000 people aged 65 years or over) was 4.4 times as high as the rate for people younger than 65 years (0.35 per 100 000 younger inhabitants). Across the EU countries, the highest standardised death rates for tuberculosis in 2023 were recorded for Romania (3.62 per 100 000 inhabitants) and Lithuania (3.02 per 100 000 inhabitants), followed at some distance by Latvia (1.98 per 100 000 inhabitants). Rates of at least 1.00 per 100 000 inhabitants were also recorded in Poland, Portugal and Bulgaria. Elsewhere the rates were at most 0.61 per 100 000 inhabitants. The lowest rates were observed in Luxembourg (0.00 per 100 000 inhabitants, as there were no cases), Slovenia (0.09 per 100 000 inhabitants) and the Netherlands (0.10 per 100 000 inhabitants). In all EU countries except for Sweden, the standardised death rate for tuberculosis in 2023 was higher for males than for females. Luxembourg, Malta and Slovenia all had rates of 0.00 per 100 000 female inhabitants (as there were no cases); leaving these aside, the largest relative difference was in Slovakia, where the rate for males was 5.1 times as high as the rate for females. The largest absolute difference was recorded in Romania, where the rate for males was 6.24 per 100 000 male inhabitants and the rate for females was 1.35 per 100 000 female inhabitants. In all EU countries except for Cyprus, the standardised death rate for tuberculosis in 2023 was higher for people aged 65 years or over than for younger people. Luxembourg, Malta and Finland all had rates of 0.00 per 100 000 younger inhabitants (as there were no cases); leaving these aside, the largest relative difference was in Ireland, where the rate for older people was 58.7 times as high as the rate for younger people. The largest absolute difference was recorded in Lithuania, where the rate for older people was 6.71 per 100 000 older inhabitants and the rate for younger people was 2.13 per 100 000 younger inhabitants. [[Image:Deaths from tuberculosis, 2023_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Deaths from tuberculosis, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3d0a88e0-5a77-4f50-9f97-97081344eece?lang=en hlth_cd_aro] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/16e46af1-72d4-4263-bdf8-f4f2af4bdf5e?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A table showing the number of deaths and the standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for tuberculosis. Data are analysed by sex and age group. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, there were 1 848 deaths in the EU resulting from HIV. More than three quarters (76.5%) of these were among males, and more than three quarters (76.9%) were among people younger than 65 years. The standardised death rate for HIV in the EU was 0.40 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2023, with this rate notably higher for males (0.62 per 100 000 male inhabitants) than for females (0.18 per 100 000 female inhabitants). The rate for older people (0.45 per 100 000 older inhabitants) was 1.2 times as high as the rate for people younger than 65 years (0.38 per 100 000 younger inhabitants). Across the EU countries, the highest standardised death rates for HIV in 2023 were recorded for Latvia (2.88 per 100 000 inhabitants) and Estonia (2.29 per 100 000 inhabitants), followed at some distance by Portugal (1.33 per 100 000 inhabitants) and Lithuania (1.08 per 100 000 inhabitants). Elsewhere the rates were at most 0.55 per 100 000 inhabitants. The lowest rate was observed in Slovenia (0.00 per 100 000 inhabitants, as there were no cases). In all EU countries, the standardised death rate for HIV in 2023 was higher for males than for females. Cyprus, Luxembourg, Hungary, Slovenia and Finland all had rates of 0.00 per 100 000 female inhabitants (as none had any cases); leaving these aside, the largest relative difference was in the Netherlands, where the rate for males was 8.3 times as high as the rate for females. The largest absolute difference was recorded in Latvia, where the rate for males was 4.53 per 100 000 male inhabitants and the rate for females was 1.39 per 100 000 female inhabitants. Portugal and Estonia were the only other EU countries where the difference was greater than 0.66 per 100 000 male/female inhabitants. Despite the standardised death rate for HIV in 2023 being higher for people aged 65 years or over than for younger people in the EU as a whole, this situation was observed in a minority of EU countries (10 of 27). Slovenia had a rate of 0.00 per 100 000 younger inhabitants for younger people (and also for older people), as there were no cases; leaving this aside, the largest relative difference was in Denmark, where the rate for older people was 10.8 times as high as the rate for younger people. The largest absolute differences were recorded in the [[Glossary:Baltic_Member_States|Baltic EU countries]], all with higher rates for younger people. Most notably, in Estonia the rate for younger people was 2.69 per 100 000 younger inhabitants and the rate for older people was 0.65 per 100 000 older inhabitants. [[Image:Deaths from HIV, 2023_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Deaths from HIV, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c99721e2-7e66-4b4c-94e6-c423b8eadd19?lang=en hlth_cd_aro] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c4908d62-df09-4f8a-8d9f-0124fd3f0946?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A table showing the number of deaths and the standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for HIV. Data are analysed by sex and age group. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, there were 3 172 deaths in the EU resulting from viral hepatitis. A majority (58.3%) of these were among males, while close to two thirds (64.3%) were among people aged 65 years or over. The standardised death rate for viral hepatitis in the EU was 0.64 deaths per 100 000 inhabitants in 2023, with this rate more balanced between the sexes than for tuberculosis and HIV: 0.84 per 100 000 male inhabitants compared with 0.45 per 100 000 female inhabitants. By contrast, the rate for viral hepatitis was more unbalanced when analysed by age: the rate for older people (2.05 per 100 000 older inhabitants) was 6.8 times as high as the rate for people younger than 65 years (0.30 per 100 000 younger inhabitants). Across the EU countries, the highest standardised death rates for viral hepatitis in 2023 were recorded for Italy (1.62 per 100 000 inhabitants) and Latvia (1.54 per 100 000 inhabitants), followed at some distance by Austria (1.02 per 100 000 inhabitants). Elsewhere the rates were at most 0.84 per 100 000 inhabitants. The lowest rates were observed in Luxembourg (0.00 per 100 000 inhabitants, as there were no cases) and Finland (0.07 per 100 000 inhabitants). In all EU countries except for Slovenia and Finland, the standardised death rate for viral hepatitis in 2023 was higher for males than for females; in Finland it was the same for both sexes while in Slovenia it was lower for males. Luxembourg and Slovenia both had rates of 0.00 per 100 000 male inhabitants (as neither had any cases), while Luxembourg and Malta both had rates of 0.00 per 100 000 female inhabitants (as neither had any cases); leaving these aside, the largest relative difference was in Portugal, where the rate for males was 3.7 times as high as the rate for females. The largest absolute difference was recorded in Latvia, where the rate for males was 2.38 per 100 000 male inhabitants and the rate for females was 0.83 per 100 000 female inhabitants. In all EU countries except for Luxembourg, Malta and Finland, the standardised death rate for viral hepatitis in 2023 was higher for people aged 65 years or over than for younger people; in Luxembourg and Finland it was the same for both age groups while in Malta it was lower for older people. Luxembourg and Slovenia both had rates of 0.00 per 100 000 younger inhabitants (as neither had any cases), while Luxembourg and Malta both had rates of 0.00 per 100 000 older inhabitants (as neither had any cases); leaving these aside, the largest relative difference was in Italy, where the rate for older people was 11.0 times as high as the rate for younger people. The largest absolute difference was also recorded in Italy, where the rate for older people was 6.04 per 100 000 older inhabitants and the rate for younger people was 0.55 per 100 000 younger inhabitants. [[Image:Deaths from viral hepatitis, 2023_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Deaths from viral hepatitis, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0ef86c5b-6f00-4061-b206-1192fbc2279e?lang=en hlth_cd_aro] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/deecbeb1-bb20-46aa-9b8e-f789912646b2?lang=en hlth_cd_asdr2])|alt=A table showing the number of deaths and the standardised death rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for viral hepatitis. Data are analysed by sex and age group. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Healthcare for tuberculosis and HIV=== In 2023, there were 51 200 resident [[Glossary:In-patient|in-patients]] with tuberculosis who were [[Glossary:Hospital_discharge|discharged]] from hospitals in the EU. In Romania, there were 18 300 resident in-patient discharges among people treated for tuberculosis in 2023. There were 3 other EU countries which recorded in excess of 5 000 resident in-patient discharges: Germany (6 000), France (5 800) and Poland (5 500). This disease accounted for fewer than 100 resident in-patient discharges in Malta, Luxembourg, Cyprus, Denmark and Slovenia. In addition, there were 2 800 day case discharges in the EU in 2023, excluding Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia and Malta. Relative to population size, Romania recorded the highest number of in-patient discharges for tuberculosis in 2023, with 95.8 discharges per 100 000 inhabitants. Latvia, Bulgaria, Lithuania and Estonia also recorded more than 20.0 in-patient discharges for tuberculosis per 100 000 inhabitants. The ratio in Romania was 59 times as high as the equivalent ratio for Denmark, where the lowest rate was recorded (1.6 in-patient discharges per 100 000 inhabitants). In the other EU countries for which data are available, there were between 2.2 and 15.0 in-patient discharges for tuberculosis per 100 000 inhabitants. '''''Croatia had the highest discharge rate for day cases concerning tuberculosis''''' Day case discharges for tuberculosis in 2023 relative to population size were highest, by far, in Croatia, at 9.1 discharges per 100 000 inhabitants. Luxembourg recorded 3.0 day case discharges per 100 000 inhabitants and Ireland 1.9 per 100 000 inhabitants. Elsewhere the ratio was no greater than 1.02 per 100 000 inhabitants, with the lowest rates in Slovakia and Sweden (both below 0.05 per 100 000 inhabitants). In 2023, there were 18 100 resident [[Glossary:In-patient|in-patients]] with HIV who were [[Glossary:Hospital_discharge|discharged]] from hospitals in the EU (including 2022 data for Cyprus and Malta). In Romania, there were 7 700 resident in-patient discharges among people treated for HIV in 2023. There were 4 other EU countries which recorded in excess of 1 000 resident in-patient discharges: Poland (2 400), Italy (2 100), Spain (1 400) and France (1 200). This disease accounted for fewer than 10 resident in-patient discharges in Cyprus and Malta in 2022 and Slovenia in 2023. In addition, there were 123 200 day case discharges in the EU in 2023, excluding Czechia, Denmark, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Slovenia and Slovakia. The vast majority of these were in Romania (111 200), with most of the rest in Italy (7 100), Spain (2 300), France (1 200) or Poland (1 000). In each of the other EU countries for which data are available, the number of day case discharges for HIV was below 100. '''''Romania had the highest discharge rates concerning HIV both for in-patients and for day cases''''' Relative to population size, Romania recorded the highest number of in-patient discharges for HIV in 2023, with 40.5 discharges per 100 000 inhabitants. Latvia (18.0 per 100 000 inhabitants) was the only other EU country to record more than 10.0 in-patient discharges for HIV per 100 000 inhabitants. The ratio in Romania was 213 times as high as the equivalent ratio for Slovenia, where the lowest rate was recorded (0.2 in-patient discharges per 100 000 inhabitants). Day case discharges for HIV in 2023 relative to population size were also highest in Romania, at 583 discharges per 100 000 inhabitants. Italy recorded the next highest rate, at 12.1 day case discharges per 100 000 inhabitants, followed by Luxembourg (6.3 per 100 000 inhabitants) and Spain (4.7 per 100 000 inhabitants). Elsewhere the ratio was no greater than 2.6 per 100 000 inhabitants, with the lowest rates in Germany (0.00 per 100 000 inhabitants), Sweden and Hungary (both 0.01 per 100 000 inhabitants). [[Image:Hospital discharge rates for residents with tuberculosis or HIV, 2023_(per 100 000 inhabitants)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 4: Hospital discharge rates for residents with tuberculosis or HIV, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/62865254-c813-4d05-a1eb-6c469354c6a8?lang=en hlth_rinpat2] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/39f39a55-eed1-49ff-bd9c-63f236683ce9?lang=en hlth_rdc2])|alt=A table showing hospital discharge rates per hundred thousand inhabitants for in-patients and day cases for tuberculosis and HIV. Data are shown for 2023 for the EU as well as EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Long average length of stay for resident in-patients with tuberculosis''''' Figure 4 presents an analysis of the average length of hospital stays for resident in-patients treated for tuberculosis and for HIV in 2023. Among the EU countries, the average length of stay for in-patients generally ranged: *from 10.0 to 54.0 days for in-patients treated for tuberculosis, with Lithuania (122.1 days) above this range *from 5.8 to 25.5 days for in-patients treated for HIV, with Sweden (56.6 days) and Austria (49.5 days) above this range. In most EU countries, the average length of hospital stays for resident in-patients in 2023 was longer for patients treated for tuberculosis than for those treated for HIV. The most notable exceptions were Sweden and Austria, which had the 2 longest average lengths of stay for HIV; the other exceptions, with smaller differences, were Luxembourg and Malta (note that the data for HIV are for 2022). [[Image:Resident in-patient average length of stay for tuberculosis and HIV, 2023 (days)_Health2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Resident in-patient average length of stay for tuberculosis and HIV, 2023
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ee818460-e3cd-4339-aa8b-04ce0acd49ed?lang=en hlth_ralos1])|alt=A double column chart showing in-patient average length of stays in days. Data are analysed comparing the average stay for tuberculosis and HIV. Data are shown for 2023 for EU, EFTA and enlargement countries. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Tuberculosis viral hepatitis and HIV statistics_Health2026.xlsx|title=Tuberculosis, viral hepatitis and HIV statistics: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== '''Causes of death''' Statistics on causes of death provide information on [[Glossary:Mortality|mortality]] patterns, supplying information on developments over time in the underlying causes of death. This source is documented in more detail in a background article on the [[Causes_of_death_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of causes of death statistics]]. This provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis and the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. Statistics on causes of death are based on death certificates established by medical experts assessing the underlying cause of death. Note there is a difference in the coding of cases where the mental and behavioural disorder was the established underlying cause of death, as distinguished from cases where a death occurred for someone who was suffering from a mental and behavioural disorder at the time of death. Causes of death are currently classified according to the 86 causes in the [[Glossary:European_shortlist_of_causes_of_death|European shortlist]], which is based on the [[Glossary:International classification of diseases (ICD)|International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD)]] 10th revision. Chapter I (A00-B99) of the ICD covers certain infectious and parasitic diseases. For this article, the following ICD-10 codes were used for the described causes of death: *A15 to A19 for tuberculosis *B15 to B19 for viral hepatitis and B94.2 for sequelae of viral hepatitis *B20 to B24 for HIV. Previously, causes of death were classified based on the ICD ninth revision (ICD-9). Chapter I of ICD-9 covered infectious and parasitic diseases (001-139). For this article, the following ICD-9 detailed list numbers and diseases were used for the described causes of death: *010 to 018 for tuberculosis *042 to 044 for HIV (not originally included in ICD-9) *070 for viral hepatitis. A [[Glossary:Death|crude death rate]] can be calculated from the number of deaths from a particular cause of death expressed relative to the size of the population. A [[Glossary:Standardised_death_rate_(SDR)|standardised death rate (SDR)]] can be compiled which is independent of the age and sex structure of a population. This is done as most causes of death vary significantly by age and by sex; the standardisation facilitates comparisons of rates over time and between countries Standard population report: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/en/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/-/ks-ra-13-028.. For country-specific notes on causes of death, please refer to the national metadata reports, which can be accessed through the links at the beginning of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/hlth_cdeath_sims.htm European metadata report]. The Eurostat {{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-020|title=Causes of death statistics manual – 2025 edition}} provides an overview of the statistical processing of causes of death data, including the transmission, validation, metadata and quality reporting. '''Healthcare resources and activities''' Statistics on healthcare resources (such as beds and personnel) and healthcare activities (such as information on hospital discharges) are documented in a background article on the [[Healthcare_non-expenditure_statistics_-_methodology|methodology of healthcare non-expenditure statistics]]. This provides information on the scope of the data, its legal basis, the methodology employed, as well as related concepts and definitions. An [[Glossary:In-patient|in-patient]] is a patient who is formally admitted (or ‘hospitalised’) to an institution for treatment and/or care and stays for a minimum of 1 night or more than 24 hours in the hospital or other institution providing in-patient care. An in-patient or day care patient is discharged from hospital when formally released after a procedure or course of treatment (episode of care). A discharge may occur because of the finalisation of treatment, signing out against medical advice, transfer to another healthcare institution, or because of death. For hospital discharges and the length of stay in hospitals, the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/Annexes/hlth_res_esms_an_2.pdf International Shortlist for Hospital Morbidity Tabulation] (ISHMT) is used to classify data from 2000 onwards; Chapter I covers certain infectious and parasitic diseases: *tuberculosis (0103) *HIV (0105). For country-specific notes, please refer to the annexes at the end of the national metadata reports, which can be accessed through the links at the beginning of the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/hlth_res_esms.htm European metadata report]. The Eurostat {{Template:Publication|code=ks-01-25-028|title=Healthcare non-expenditure statistics manual}} provides an overview of the classifications, both for mandatory variables and variables provided on a voluntary basis. '''Symbols''' In tables, a colon ‘:’ is used to show where data are not available and a dash ‘–‘ is used to show where data are not relevant or applicable. ===Context=== '''United Nations sustainable development goals''' The [https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/sustainable-development-goals/ sustainable development goals (SDGs)] of the [[Glossary:United Nations|United Nations]] are the blueprint to achieve a better and more sustainable future for all. Goal 3 concerns [https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/health/ good health and well-being]. Within this goal, target 3.3 is: ''By 2030, end the epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria and neglected tropical diseases and combat hepatitis, water-borne diseases and other communicable diseases.'' '''EU’s commitment to the SDGs''' The EU expressed its political commitment to support EU countries in reaching the SDG’s targets through the 2016 [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52016DC0739 Communication on Next steps for a sustainable European future – European action for sustainability]. In 2017, the EU adopted the [https://international-partnerships.ec.europa.eu/policies/european-development-policy/european-consensus-development_en European Consensus on Development] as part of its response to the UN’s 2030 SDGs. Within the EU’s monitoring of progress towards the SDGs in an EU context, avoidable mortality is one of the [[SDG_3_-_Good_health_and_well-being#Standardised_avoidable_mortality|indicators for Goal 3]]. '''EU policies on HIV/AIDS''' In 2005, the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52005DC0654 Communication on combating HIV/AIDS] was the first EU-wide policy on this subject and was the basis for EU action from 2006 to 2009. A [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52009DC0569 second communication] was adopted in 2009, accompanied by 2 action plans (for [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52009SC1403 2009–13] and [https://health.ec.europa.eu/document/download/c86cb06c-d22e-469c-8d9f-9ca7dc126341_en?filename=ec_hiv_actionplan_2014_en.pdf 2014–16]). '''EU4Health''' ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2021.107.01.0001.01.ENG Regulation (EU) 2021/522 establishing a Programme for the Union’s action in the field of health (‘EU4health programme’) for the period 2021 to 2027]'' provides funding to EU countries, health organisations and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and is designed, among other objectives, to boost the EU’s preparedness for major cross-border health threats. EU4Health has a budget of €5.8 billion for the period 2021 to 2027 and aims to improve health outcomes by supporting efficient and inclusive health systems. The actions funded through the health programme help the development and implementation of good practices to attain international commitments to end AIDS and tuberculosis and reduce viral hepatitis. Their main themes and focus relate to: *promoting early diagnosis for HIV, hepatitis and tuberculosis *integrating treatment and care, ensuring access, integrated diagnosis and case management, bridging health services in the community and health services, including prison health care *enhancing access to community-based services to hard-to-reach populations *supporting civil society for their actions against the diseases. The [https://hadea.ec.europa.eu/index_en European Health and Digital Executive Agency (HaDEA)] manages these actions. '''The European Health Union''' In May 2024, the European Commission summarised the work done and the progress made within the health domain through a communication ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52024DC0206 The European Health Union: acting together for people’s health]'' (COM(2024) 206 final). It highlights a range of actions designed to make people’s lives safer and healthier. === Footnotes === ===Other articles=== '''Online publications''' *[[Health in the European Union - facts and title: Tutorial:Article analytics
text:
=== Europa Analytics === Europa Analytics is the corporate web analytics service of the European Commission. Using this, you can track, analyse and understand better your website audience. It is available for the Eurostat website and related tools, such as Statistics Explained. For details, please consult the following corporate resources: *[https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/fpfis/wikis/display/EuropaAnalyticsWiki/FAQ#FAQ-WhatisthecurrentEuropaAnalyticsreportingtoolandhowtoaccessit? FAQs on Europa Analytics] *[https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/fpfis/wikis/display/EuropaAnalyticsWiki/Training+material Training material] (including video tutorials) === Access === Use this URL: [https://www.webanalytics.europa.eu/analytics/#/a441974e-4574-4f0a-9ed2-f90fb8547bb7/dashboards/59fdd738-4202-462d-9d6e-4a003f87b5c0/] (EU Login required) === Set-up === In the upper right hand corner, select ‘Eurostat’ as the site [[Image:Article analytics - Picture1.png|thumb|centre|700px]] === Checking analytics for webpages (Statistics Explained) === [[Image:SE dashboard.png|thumb|centre|500px]] This way, you will find analytics related to Statistics Explained only which can be useful for more personalised reports, such as: * '''page analytics'''- page statistics give you a snapshot of how people interact with your website, including the number of unique visitors, the times they engage in sessions, the pages they view, and the percentage of those who come back, helping you understand overall visitor behavior and website effectiveness [[Image:Page analytics.png|thumb|centre|500px]] * '''audience'''- on a given day, the audience overview highlights how frequently visitors engage in sessions, how many pages they explore, and the percentage who return, offering insights into daily usage patterns and visitor loyalty [[Image:Audience overview.png|thumb|centre|500px]] * '''location'''- the location-based audience overview reveals the countries your visitors come from, helping you understand the geographical origins of your user base [[Image:Location overview.png|thumb|centre|500px]] * '''channel'''- the channel overview shows how users find their way to your site, whether through AI referrals, campaigns, direct entries, search engines, social media, or websites, providing a clear picture of traffic sources [[Image:Channel overview.png|thumb|centre|500px]] * '''devices'''- the devices overview highlights how visitors access your site, whether through smartphones, desktops, tablets, or other devices, helping you understand user preferences and optimize the experience across different platforms [[Image:Devices.png|thumb|centre|500px]] * '''outlinks'''- the outlinks overview shows which external links users click on from your site, providing insights into their interactions beyond your content [[Image:Outlinks.png|thumb|centre|500px]] === Checking analytics for webpages (Eurostat general) === 1. Select from the top panel ‘REPORTS’ and then from the left side menu ‘PAGES’ [[Image:Article analytics - Picture2.png|thumb|centre|700px]] 2. Copy in the webpage URL and set the time period for which you wish to obtain the information [[Image:Article analytics - Picture3.png|thumb|centre|700px]] 3. Select / look at the metrics you are interested in; usually the most interesting are page views or unique page views [[Image:Article analytics - Picture4.png|thumb|centre|700px]] * Page views: the number of times a page was visited. * Unique page views: the number of times a page was uniquely visited. If a visitor views a page several times during one session, it will be counted only once. * Entries: the number of page views for a page that was first during a session. * Page bounce rate: an accurate bounce rate for a page URL or page title. The percentage of sessions during which visitors viewed only that page and didn’t continue to another page view, goal conversion, or ecommerce conversion.
:Page bounce rate = (Bounces / Entries) * 100% * Exit rate: The percentage of sessions that finished on a selected page.
:Exit rate = Exits / Sessions * 100% === Checking analytics for documents / downloads === 1. Select from the top panel ‘REPORTS’ and then from the left side menu ‘DOWNLOADS’
2. Copy in the document URL and set the time period for which you wish to obtain the information [[Image:Article analytics - Picture5.png|thumb|centre|700px]] ===See also=== [[Category:Tutorial|Article analytics]]

title: Tutorial:Country codes and protocol order
text:
This page describes the rules for the abbreviations, codes and protocol order to use for countries.

These rules were taken from the [http://publications.europa.eu/code/en/en-000300.htm Interinstitutional style guide] and should be applied to all publications, namely Statistics Explained articles, statistical books and statistical working papers.

''Please note that different rules apply to the reference database, especially concerning the codes for the EU aggregates. Some examples are provided in the table below; see also the complete [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/metadata/code-lists code lists].''


=== EU and euro area aggregates  ===

In Statistics Explained articles, when referring to aggregates, use the simple abbreviation without the Member State count, i.e [[Glossary:EU enlargements|'EU']] and not 'EU-27'; the 'euro area' should be written in full, unless in graphs and tables, where it can also be abbreviated as [[Glossary:Euro area enlargements|'EA']], but not 'EA-20'.

Use the term "EU countries" within the article text and "EU Member States" in methodological sections.

=== Protocol order of countries  ===

'''In tables'''

'''Tables''' must always respect the protocol order of countries. The following protocol order is to be applied with an appropriate divider between each group: 

#EU and EA aggregates; 
#EU Member States in alphabetical order of their official name (see list above)
#EFTA countries in alphabetical order of their official name (IS, LI, NO, CH)
#Candidate countries in alphabetical order of their official name (see list above)
#Potential candidates in alphabetical order of their official name 
#Other countries outside the EU (Japan, the United States for example)



In country tables, all EU countries should be present. Other countries (EFTA, candidate, potential candidate) should only be added if data are available. It is also advised to use the full country names instead of the country codes whenever possible.

'''In graphs'''

As for tables, it is advised to use the full country names instead of the country codes.

'''Graphs sorted by value'''

'''It is recommended''' in graphs to display the countries sorted by value in ascending or descending order. It is also recommended to  group the countries as it is done in tables in the following order:

*EU and EA (if relevant) aggregates, followed by a blank space
*Member States, followed by a blank space
*EFTA countries, followed by a blank space
*Candidate countries, followed by a blank space
*Potential candidates, followed by a blank space
*Other countries



'''Graphs not sorted by value'''

If, '''as an exception to the rule''', the graphs are '''not''' sorted by value,  the protocol order should be used (see example 3):
* EU and EA (if relevant) aggregates, followed by a blank space
* EU Member states, followed by a blank space,
* EFTA countries, followed by a blank space
* Candidate countries, followed by a blank space
* Potential candidates, followed by a blank space
* Other countries.


In country graphs, all '''available''' EU and EFTA countries should be present. Missing countries should be mentioned in a ‘Note’ under the chart e.g.: Note: xx not available / or not applicable’. Other countries (candidate, potential candidate, other) should only be added if relevant and if data are available. 

It is also advised to use the full country names instead of the country codes whenever possible.

'''In text'''

Lists of country or region names in '''text''' should however ''not'' follow the protocol order, for reasons of user-friendliness: they should be in the alphabetical order of the language of the text (the same rule is also applied in [[Tutorials|tutorials]] and glossary pages, for instance in the many language versions of [[Glossary:European Union (EU)]]). Another option is to mention the countries by statistical order (ranking).



===See also===

*[[Glossary:Country codes|Country codes]] (glossary, more extensive)

title: Tutorial:Creating PDF version
text:
A [[:Statistics Explained:About|Statistics Explained]] article can be printed as a '''PDF''' by using the print function at the top right of each page. The print function has been developed with optimal sizing and positioning of PNG images to automatically produce a correctly layouted document.
This tutorial includes special print tags for use should custom sizing and positioning of images be necessary, and for displaying or hiding additional text blocks or images that are suitable for either only a PDF version or only a web version. ==Selectively displaying text in web version or PDF version== Via the tags '''noprint''' and '''onlyprint''' it is possible to have a selected part of an article only displayed in the web version and not in the PDF version for printing; or the opposite, only in the PDF version for printing and not in the web page view.
For example, an interactive map that has been used in the web version can be replaced in the PDF version by a static PNG image that should not be visible online. *Text available in web version but not in PDF: :'''''': content between tags is not converted into PDF *Text available in PDF but not in web version: :'''''': content between tags is converted into PDF but not displayed on the web page == Page layout== The additional tags '''pdfpagebreak''' and '''pdflinebreak''' are available to optimise the page layout in the PDF version: '''''' creates a page break in the PDF where it is added; '''''' creates a hyphenation (splitting a word) in the word where it is added. ===Positioning=== '''Please note that positioning is automated for PDF versions; the following codes/tags only need to be used in exceptional cases''' To position a specific image in a PDF it first has to be uniquely identified (tag '''''' with parameter '''imgid''') and then the location must be indicated at which it will be displayed in the PDF, in relation to the text (tag ''''''): *the ''image tag'' '''''' encapsulates an image link of an article, to which parameters for identification and display can be added; *with the ''image identification parameter'' '''imgid='image identifier'''' a unique name ''image identifier'' (e.g. ''figure1'') is assigned to a particular image; '''it is recommended to use as name simply 'table1', 'figure2', 'map3' etc., in line with the caption below the image''' (nothing more is needed, because the name only has to be unique within a particular article and PDF generation); *the ''image location tag'' '''''' can then be used in combination with the imgid identifier to display this particular image at any chosen location within the generated PDF (possibly requiring some trial and error in the final layouting stage, see below); in wikitext this looks like , with the first part between < > specifying the 'beginning' of the location for table1, and the second one between the closing 'end' of this location. Note that no extra break tags or empty lines should be added before or after the line with this image location tag which in itself already a 'blank' line creating a new paragraph; this would result in extra empty lines in the page view, to be avoided. '''Examples''' *identifier (''combined with other parameters, see further down''): :[[Image:ENPS_Youth_Population by age class.PNG|thumb|right|350px|Table 1: Population by age class (1 000 persons) - ''Source:'' for the EU-28, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=demo_pjan}}; for the MED countries, Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=med_ps112}}]] *positioning: : ===Size and orientation=== The size and the orientation of an image at a specific location in a PDF has been automated. However, it can be customised via another set of parameters ('''fullwidth''', '''zoom''', '''fullpage''' and '''rotation'''), to be inserted within the ''image tag'', right after the identifier tag imgid, separated by a blank: *'''fullwidth='on'''' displays the image at the maximum width, using the full width of the page (but without automatically rotating it, no auto rotation); *'''zoom='n'''' ( 0 > n > 100 ) zooms the picture to n % of the page width (see example above, with display at 80 %); *'''fullpage='on'''' displays the image on one full page, rotating it automatically if necessary to better fit the page; *'''rotation='on'''' displays the image rotated by 90°. '''Examples''' * [[Image:Resource_productivity_2000-2007.jpg|thumb|right|350px|Figure 1: Resource productivity]] ::displays Figure 1 on a full page in the PDF, non-rotated *[[Image:Resource_productivity_2000-2007.jpg|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Resource productivity]] ::displays Figure 1 with a size reduced to 80 % [[Category:Tutorial|Creating PDF version]]
