title: Urban-rural Europe - income and living conditions
text:
This article forms part of Eurostat’s twin publications, Rural Europe and Urban Europe: 2026 editions. It focuses on income and living conditions statistics. Data extracted: June 2026. Planned article update: September 2027. By global standards, most people living in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] are prosperous: they have relatively high income/wealth and a positive sense of well-being, while there are established social protection systems that provide a safety net for people who are less well off. Indeed, the European social model is based on offering protection to people who are most in need. Regardless of national differences, the implementation of social protection in EU countries is designed to provide people with some protection against, among other issues, the costs of bringing up a family or housing, the risks related to unemployment, poor health, poverty or social exclusion, and the consequences of old age. Nevertheless, 92.7 million people in the EU’s population, were [[Glossary:At_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_(AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion]] in 2025 (see Infographic 1); this equated to around 1 in 5 (20.9%) people. The COVID-19 crisis underlined systemic inequalities in living conditions both between and within individual EU countries. While some people were fortunate enough to continue working full-time from home (and in some cases were even able to save more of their income than usual), many people in precarious employment or working in sectors/businesses particularly impacted by successive lockdowns faced reduced earnings, short-time work and unemployment. As the impact of the pandemic abated, concern shifted – from early 2022 onwards – to the cost-of-living crisis. This led several EU governments to introduce a range of support schemes, such as energy price caps, rebates for fuel prices or additional support for low income [[Glossary:Household - social statistics|households]] / pensioners (who typically spend a disproportionate amount of their income on essential purchases such as housing, food and energy). This article forms part of [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]’s twin publications on ''[[Rural_Europe|Rural Europe]]'' and ''[[Urban_Europe|Urban Europe]]''. [[Image:How many people in the EU were at risk of poverty or social exclusion (million, 2025)_URE2026.jpg|thumb|centre|700px|Infographic 1: How many people in the EU were at risk of poverty or social exclusion?
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d39dfdf1-65cb-4fc7-9479-cd65297734c7?lang=en ilc_pees01n], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/374c5bb6-238e-4598-b689-ad601b845e78?lang=en ilc_pees01n], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/72e03cef-a3c4-424c-932f-a495867ecdf7?lang=en ilc_li43], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e4e9245d-06c8-43d9-8dfe-be994e28b80d?lang=en ilc_mdsd19], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4b3e384a-1434-478d-9d32-0d3e891b6ba6?lang=en ilc_lvhl23n] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2ad41a0e-55a7-4db8-93bc-b60bbbddfb71?lang=en ilc_lvho01]))|alt=An infographic in the form of a Venn diagram showing the number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion. Data are presented for people at risk of poverty, severely materially and socially deprived people, and people living in a household with very low work intensity. Data are also shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented in numbers for millions of people. Data are shown for the EU. Annual data are presented for 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ''Due to rolling updates, some temporary inconsistencies may appear between the colour schemes used for maps and figures in different chapters of Urban Europe and Rural Europe.'' ===People at risk of poverty or social exclusion=== The number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion is a headline indicator for social protection and inclusion within the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/european-pillar-of-social-rights European pillar of social rights]. This indicator monitors the progress towards 1 of the EU’s headline 2030 targets, namely, to reduce the number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion by at least 15 million (when compared with 2019).
'''More about the data: people at risk of poverty or social exclusion''' The risk of poverty and social exclusion is not dependent solely on a household’s level of income, as it may also reflect joblessness, very low work intensity, working status, or a range of other socioeconomic characteristics. To calculate the number or share of people who are at risk of poverty or social exclusion, 3 separate criteria are combined (see the infographic at the start of this article), covering people who are in at least 1 of the following situations: *[[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|at risk of poverty]] – people with an [[Glossary:Equivalised disposable income|equivalised disposable income]] (after [[Glossary:Social transfers|social transfers]]) below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold, which is set at 60% of the national [[Glossary:Median|median]] equivalised disposable income *facing [[Glossary:Severe_material_and_social_deprivation_rate_(SMSD)|severe material and social deprivation]] – people unable to afford at least 7 out of 13 deprivation items (6 related to individuals and 7 related to their household) that are considered desirable – or even necessary – to lead an adequate quality of life *[[Glossary:Persons living in households with very low work intensity|living in a household with very low work intensity]] – as measured by the share of people aged less than 65 years living in households where the adults (aged 18 to 64 years; excluding students aged 18 to 24 years and retired people) worked for 20% or less of their combined potential working time during the previous 12 months.
Across the EU, the share of people who were at risk of poverty or social exclusion declined for 4 consecutive years between 2015 (the first reference year for which data are available) and 2019. This pattern was largely repeated when analysed by [[Glossary: Degree of urbanisation|degree of urbanisation]] (see Figure 1); the only exception was for people living in [[Glossary:City|cities]], where there was no change in the share of people who were at risk of poverty or social exclusion between 2018 and 2019. With the onset of the COVID-19 crisis, the share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in the EU increased in 2020 across all degrees of urbanisation: by 0.5 percentage points among people living in cities, and by 0.4 points among people living in [[Glossary:Town or suburb|towns and suburbs]] and [[Glossary:Rural area|rural areas]]. Developments in 2021 were more mixed. The share continued to increase among people living in towns and suburbs (up 1.3 points), remained unchanged among city dwellers and declined among those living in rural areas (down 0.8 points), for the latter falling below its pre-pandemic level. In 2022, the share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in towns and suburbs continued to rise, although at a slower pace (up 0.2 points). This was followed by declines in 2023 and 2024, before a marginal increase in 2025. By contrast, the share fell consistently between 2022 and 2025 among people living in cities, and between 2021 and 2024 among those living in rural areas (before a modest increase in 2025). Overall, the share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion fell 0.1 percentage points in 2025. This reflected a decline of 0.3 points among people living in cities, while marginal increases of 0.1 points were recorded among those living in towns and suburbs and in rural areas. In 2025, the latest available data show the share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion was: *21.4% for people living in rural areas *21.0% for people living in cities *20.4% for people living in towns and suburbs. As a result of the changes described above, the at risk of poverty or social exclusion rates for the 3 degrees of urbanisation generally converged over time, with the widest ranges recorded during 2016 to 2018 and the narrowest during the period 2022 to 2025; see Figure 1. [[Image:At risk of poverty or social exclusion rate, by degree of urbanisation, EU, 2015–25 (%)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: At risk of poverty or social exclusion, by degree of urbanisation, EU, 2015–25
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/144f6ecd-8e77-4e87-bcb3-beea9a8c6d31?lang=en ilc_peps13n)]|alt=A line chart showing the development of the at risk of poverty or social exclusion rate. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented in percent. Data are shown for the EU. Annual data are presented for the period 2015 to 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2025, the EU’s at-risk-of-poverty or social exclusion rate was highest for people living in rural areas, followed by those living in cities, with the lowest rates recorded for people living in towns and suburbs. Although the latest rates for the EU were within a relatively narrow range, there was a much wider variation observed in several EU countries. This was particularly notable in Romania, where the risk of poverty or social exclusion was faced by approximately two fifths (39.8%) of the rural population, some 26.1 percentage points higher than the rate for people living in cities (13.7%). A similar pattern was repeated in: *Bulgaria, where a peak of 40.8% was recorded among people living in rural areas, some 19.9 points higher than the rate for those living in cities (20.9%) *Lithuania, where a peak of 34.8% was recorded among people living in rural areas, some 18.0 points higher than the rate for those living in cities (16.8%). In 2025, some of the highest shares of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion were recorded in rural areas of principally eastern, Baltic and southern EU countries. These included the shares mentioned above for Bulgaria (40.8%), Romania (39.8%) and Lithuania (34.8%), while rural areas also recorded the highest at risk of poverty or social exclusion rates with more than a quarter of the rural population facing such a risk in Greece (33.7%), Latvia (28.9%), Hungary (27.1%) and Croatia (25.7%). In 3 EU countries, the situation was atypical insofar as the highest share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025 was recorded among people living in towns and suburbs: Spain (29.2%), Estonia (22.9%)and Slovenia (16.0%). By contrast, the highest risk of poverty or social exclusion was recorded among people living in cities in all Nordic countries (peaking at 22.2% in Denmark), as well as in several western EU countries, with relatively high shares recorded in: *Austria (27.1% of the population living in cities) *Belgium (25.4%) *Germany (24.9%) *France (24.7%).

An interactive dot plot showing poverty and social exclusion indicators: the at risk of poverty or social exclusion rate; the at-risk-of-poverty rate; the severe material and social deprivation rate; the share of people living in households with very low work intensity. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented in percent. Data are shown for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. Annual data are presented for 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.

Figure 2
[[Image:At risk of poverty or social exclusion rate, by degree of urbanisation, 2025 (%)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2A: At risk of poverty or social exclusion rate, by degree of urbanisation, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ceed83e9-b02d-4c01-bc8f-8ea90cb12746?lang=en ilc_peps13n])]] ====At-risk-of-poverty rate==== The at-risk-of-poverty rate (after social transfers) is 1 of the 3 criteria used to identify people at risk of poverty or social exclusion. It identifies the proportion of the population which lives in a household with an annual equivalised disposable income that is below 60% of the national median (a threshold which is set separately for each EU country). As such, this indicator provides a measure of relatively low income compared with other residents of the same country; it does not necessarily imply a low overall standard of living. In 2016, the EU’s at-risk-of-poverty rate by degree of urbanisation peaked at 20.4% among people living in rural areas; the lowest rate in that year was recorded among people living in towns and suburbs (15.9%), a gap of 4.5 percentage points; see Figure 3. During the 7 years that followed, there was initially a step-like decrease followed by a continuous fall in the risk of poverty for people living in rural areas, whereas for people living in cities there was almost no change. Recent developments for people living in towns and suburbs were different: a clear fall was observed between 2017 and 2019 and a notable increase in 2021. In 2025, the gap between the highest and lowest at-risk-of-poverty rates was 1.2 points, with a peak of 17.2% for people living in rural areas and lows of 16.0% among people living in towns and suburbs and people living in cities. [[Image:At risk of poverty rate, by degree of urbanisation, EU, 2015–25 (%)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: At risk of poverty rate, by degree of urbanisation, EU, 2015–25
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d66b0039-0010-4669-9f9b-d8cf332b3126?lang=en ilc_li43])|alt=A line chart showing the development of the at risk of poverty rate. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented in percent. Data are shown for the EU. Annual data are presented for the period 2015 to 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2025, the highest risks of poverty for people living in cities were recorded in Austria (23.7%), France (19.7%), Estonia (19.4%), Germany (19.2%) and Latvia (18.2%). At the other end of the scale, fewer than 1 in 10 people living in the cities of Romania (5.1%), Slovakia (6.7%), Hungary (8.3%), Poland (9.0%), Ireland (9.4%) and Czechia (9.7%) faced the risk of monetary poverty. There were 5 EU countries where more than a quarter of the rural population was at risk of poverty in 2025, with the 2 highest shares recorded in Bulgaria (31.4%) and Romania (30.7%). By contrast, there were 4 EU countries where fewer than 1 in 10 of the rural population was at risk of poverty: the Netherlands (8.5%), Belgium (8.8%), Czechia (8.9%) and Denmark (9.8%). Data by EU country for the at-risk-of-poverty rate are presented above as part of Figure 2 (use the dropdown list to select the indicator). [[Image:At risk of poverty rate, by degree of urbanisation, 2025 (%)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2B: At risk of poverty rate, by degree of urbanisation, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/f8f44fac-7cb5-4c3d-a062-87840c7f5b42?lang=en ilc_li43])]] ====Severe material and social deprivation rate==== The severe material and social deprivation rate is also 1 of the 3 criteria used to identify people at risk of poverty or social exclusion. It provides information on the share of the population who could not afford (rather than did not want or did not need) at least 7 out of 13 surveyed items. In 2025, the EU’s severe material and social deprivation rate was 6.3%, which was 0.1 percentage points lower than the year before. During the period 2019 to 2025, there was an initial period of convergence in the EU’s severe material and social deprivation rates when analysed by degree of urbanisation (see Figure 4) through to 2023, when there was 0.3 percentage points difference between the 3 rates. From 2023 to 2025, severe material and social deprivation rates fell for all 3 degrees of urbanisation. In 2025, the latest rates were: *6.5% among people living in cities *6.4% among people living in rural areas *5.9% among people living in towns and suburbs. [[Image:Severe material and social deprivation rate, by degree of urbanisation, EU, 2019–25 (%)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Severe material and social deprivation rate, by degree of urbanisation, EU, 2019–25
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/aea5fd35-14a6-4929-9807-781fd1edc7cc?lang=en ilc_mdsd19])|alt=A line chart showing the development of the severe material and social deprivation rate. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented in percent. Data are shown for the EU. Annual data are presented for the period 2019 to 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 2 above (use the dropdown list to select the severe material and social deprivation rate) shows that most EU countries had severe material and social deprivation rates in 2025 that were below 10.0%. This pattern was generally repeated across all 3 degrees of urbanisation, as the only exceptions were: *Bulgaria and Romania, where double-digit rates were recorded for all 3 degrees of urbanisation, with by far the highest rates among people living in rural areas – 23.3% in Romania and 21.5% in Bulgaria *Greece, where broadly similar rates were recorded for all 3 degrees of urbanisation (in the range of 14.1% to 16.9%) *Hungary, where a double-digit rate was recorded exclusively for people living in rural areas (12.2%). Following a geographic split, there were some common patterns observed across the EU countries for severe material and social deprivation rates: the highest rates were often recorded among people living in: *rural areas in eastern EU countries – this was the case in Bulgaria, Croatia, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Slovakia *cities in several western and southern EU countries – this was the case in Belgium, Germany, Spain, France, Italy, Malta, the Netherlands, Austria and Portugal *towns and suburbs in 2 of the 3 Baltic countries – Estonia and Latvia. [[Image:Severe material and social deprivation rate, by degree of urbanisation, 2025 (%)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2C: Severe material and social deprivation rate, by degree of urbanisation, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/2857fe86-9d13-4680-9b98-887bc616a88a?lang=en ilc_mdsd19])]] ====People living in households with very low work intensity==== The final criteria used to identify people at risk of poverty or social exclusion is the share of people aged less than 65 years living in households where the adults (aged 18 to 64 years; excluding students aged 18 to 24 years and retired people) worked no more than 20% of their total potential during the previous 12 months. Within the EU, there were 26.1 million people who were in this situation in 2025, equivalent to 7.9% of all people aged less than 65 years. The share of people living in households with very low work intensity was higher for people living in cities (8.7%) than it was for people living in towns and suburbs (8.0%) or in rural areas (6.5%). During the period 2015 to 2025 (see Figure 5), the share of people aged less than 65 living in EU households with very low work intensity generally followed a downward trend from 2015 to 2019 across all 3 degrees of urbanisation, but thereafter, developments diverged. *For people living in cities and in towns and suburbs, the share increased in both 2020 and 2021, before declining again from 2022 to 2024. In 2025, it continued to decrease among people living in cities but increased among people living in towns and suburbs. *For people living in rural areas, the share continued to fall through to 2022 – interrupted by a small increase in 2021; it then remained stable in 2023 and 2024 and increased slightly in 2025. The difference in the share of people living in households with very low work intensity by degree of urbanisation widened to 3.8 percentage points in 2021, with the highest share recorded among people living in cities and the lowest share among people living in rural areas. The difference between these 2 shares narrowed in each of the 4 subsequent years, with a gap of 2.2 points by 2025. [[Image:Share of people (0–64 years) living in households with very low work intensity, by degree of urbanisation, EU, 2015–25 (%)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Share of people (0–64 years) living in households with very low work intensity, by degree of urbanisation, EU, 2015–25
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/0232040a-4376-4488-bc83-340ad6bc2485?lang=en ilc_lvhl23n])|alt=A line chart showing the development of the share of people aged 0 to 64 years living in households with very low work intensity. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented in percent. Data are shown for the EU. Annual data are presented for the period 2015 to 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In keeping with the other criteria that compose the at-risk-of-poverty or social exclusion rate, there was some evidence of a geographic split when analysing the share of people aged less than 65 years living in households with very low work intensity. In 2025, several western and all of the Nordic EU countries recorded their highest shares for people living in cities, whereas in most of the eastern and all of the [[Glossary:Baltic_Member_States|Baltic]] EU countries people living in rural areas recorded the highest shares. *In Belgium, Germany, Finland, Denmark, Austria and France, the share of city dwellers living in households with very low work intensity was in double-digits; this share was more than 6.0 percentage points higher for people living in cities than it was for people living in rural areas in Belgium, Austria, Germany and Finland. *By contrast, within rural areas the share of people living in households with very low work intensity was in double digits in Lithuania, Bulgaria and Ireland. Rates recorded in rural areas were considerably higher than those for people living in cities in Lithuania (10.9 percentage points difference) and in Bulgaria (7.1 points), with a smaller gap in Ireland (2.6 points). Data for people living in households with very low work intensity are presented above as part of Figure 2 (use the dropdown list to select the indicator). [[Image:Share of people (0–64 years) living in households with very low work intensity, by degree of urbanisation, 2025 (%)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2D: Share of people (0–64 years) living in households with very low work intensity, by degree of urbanisation, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d8349558-3b7e-47fd-833f-299e4dfb77bd?lang=en ilc_lvhl23n])]] ===Housing=== Demographic changes have led, in some cases, to a mismatch between the demand for and supply of housing. Some people face overcrowded conditions. A growing proportion of people in the EU are living alone, with some older people living in houses or flats that they previously occupied with a larger family. In 2025, 33.4% of the EU’s population lived in an [[Glossary:Under-occupied_dwelling|under-occupied dwelling]]. This share was considerably higher among those living in rural areas, where living space tends to be more abundant. Indeed, 41.3% of the EU’s rural population lived in an under-occupied dwelling, compared with 35.6% for those living in towns and suburbs and 26.2% for people living in cities; see Figure 6.

An interactive dot plot showing housing indicators: the share of people living in under-occupied dwellings; the overcrowding rate. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented in percent. Data are shown for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. Annual data are presented for 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.

Figure 6
[[Image:Share of people living in under-occupied dwellings, by degree of urbanisation, 2025 (%)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6A: Share of people living in under-occupied dwellings, by degree of urbanisation, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/90d7e42f-f641-455c-9c7e-6e64058065a1?lang=en ilc_lvho50d])]] Across most EU countries, it was also generally the case that the highest proportion of people living in under-occupied dwellings was recorded for those living in rural areas. In 2025, this was the situation in 26 out of the 27 EU countries; the only exception was Hungary, where a higher share of people living in cities were living in under-occupied dwellings. In 2025, there were 12 EU countries where more than half of the rural population was living in an under-occupied dwelling. Cyprus, Ireland and Belgium had shares from 71.1% to 72.8%, while a peak of 73.3% was recorded in the Netherlands. There was no distinct pattern concerning the change in the share of people living in under-occupied dwellings between 2024 and 2025, as 15 EU countries reported a mix of positive and negative rates of change for the 3 categories within the degree of urbanisation classification. In France, Italy, Hungary, Austria, Romania, Slovakia and Sweden, the share of people living in under-occupied dwellings increased for all 3 categories; in Belgium, Spain, Luxembourg and Portugal, it fell in all categories; in Germany, the share increased in 2 categories and was unchanged for people living in towns and suburbs. *For people living in cities, the highest increase was in Hungary (up 2.5 percentage points) and the largest fall was in Luxembourg (down 3.4 points). *For people living in towns and suburbs, the highest increase was in Slovakia (up 3.1 percentage points) and the largest falls were in Luxembourg and Portugal (both down 3.8 points). *For people living in rural areas, the highest increase was in Austria (up 3.2 percentage points) and the largest fall was (again) in Luxembourg (down 8.9 points). [[Image:Annual change in the share of people living in under-occupied dwellings, by degree of urbanisation, 2025 (percentage points)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Annual change in the share of people living in under-occupied dwellings, by degree of urbanisation, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/57f2007d-0daa-4a19-9922-556598449a29?lang=en ilc_lvho50d])|alt=A hi-lo chart showing the annual change in the share of people living in under-occupied dwellings. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented in percentage points. Data are shown for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. Annual data are presented for 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] While a relatively high share of the EU’s population live in under-occupied dwellings, it is also the case that a considerable proportion live in overcrowded accommodation (which lacks a minimum number of rooms in relation to the number and type of relationships of occupants). In 2025, the [[Glossary:Overcrowding_rate|overcrowding rate]] across the EU was 16.8%. By degree of urbanisation, the highest overcrowding rate was recorded among people living in cities (20.4%), with considerably lower shares for those living in towns and suburbs (14.8%) and in rural areas (14.2%). National data for the overcrowding rate are presented above as part of Figure 6 (use the dropdown list to select the indicator). [[Image:Overcrowding rate, by degree of urbanisation, 2025 (%)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6B: Overcrowding rate, by degree of urbanisation, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/9e963bdd-22e1-497c-b718-5041f9461633?lang=en ilc_lvho05d])]] Across most EU countries, it was also generally the case that the highest overcrowding rate was recorded for people living in cities. In 2025, this was the situation in 24 out of the 27 EU countries. The only exceptions were: *Greece and Cyprus, where the overcrowding rate was highest for people living in towns and suburbs and the lowest rate was recorded among people living in rural areas *Hungary, where the overcrowding rate was highest for people living in rural areas and lowest for people living in cities. In 2025, there were 3 EU countries where at least 40.0% of the people living in cities occupied an overcrowded dwelling: the highest shares were in Latvia (45.0%), Romania (43.6%) and Bulgaria (40.0%). There was also no distinct pattern concerning the change in the share of people living in overcrowded dwellings between 2024 and 2025, as 16 EU countries reported a mix of positive and negative rates of change for the 3 categories within the degree of urbanisation classification. In Greece, Spain, Lithuania, Luxembourg and Portugal, the share of people living in an overcrowded dwelling increased for all 3 categories, while in Bulgaria, the Netherlands, Poland, Slovakia and Sweden it fell for all 3 categories; in Malta, the share increased in 2 categories and was unchanged in rural areas. *For people living in cities, the highest increase was in Luxembourg (up 4.9 percentage points) and the largest fall was in Poland (down 2.9 points). *For people living in towns and suburbs, the highest increase was in Portugal (up 3.2 percentage points) and the largest fall was in Poland (down 2.6 points). *For people living in rural areas, the highest increase was in Spain (up 1.5 percentage points) and the largest fall was in Slovakia (down 3.0 points). [[Image:Annual change in the overcrowding rate, by degree of urbanisation, 2025 (percentage points)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Annual change in the overcrowding rate, by degree of urbanisation, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e25d6514-bc1f-46bc-b85c-d53bd56bdd8e?lang=en ilc_lvho05d])|alt=A hi-lo chart showing the annual change in the overcrowding rate. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented in percentage points. Data are shown for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. Annual data are presented for 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Income=== The issue of inequality has gained increasing importance in political and socioeconomic discourse *in the aftermath of the global financial and economic crisis *in the context of people and specific geographical territories being ‘left behind’ *in relation to the cost-of-living crisis. [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|GDP]] per inhabitant has traditionally been used to assess divergence/convergence in mean living standards between countries. However, it does not capture the distribution of income within a population and thereby does little to reflect economic inequalities. [[Glossary:Equivalised_disposable_income|Equivalised disposable income]] is the total income of a household, after tax and other deductions, that is available for spending or saving, divided by the number of household members, where the number has been converted into equivalent adults; household members are made equivalent by weighting each according to their age, using the so-called modified [[Glossary:Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development_(OECD)|OECD]] equivalence scale. In 2025, [[Glossary:Median|median]] equivalised net income in the EU was €22 939 per year. Figure 9 shows that people living in cities and in towns and suburbs generally had a higher level of income than those living in rural areas. Incomes grew at a relatively steady pace across the EU between 2013 and 2020. In 2021, there was a slowdown or a reversal of the development, which may be linked (at least in part) to the COVID-19 crisis. This was followed by renewed income growth across all 3 degrees of urbanisation from 2022 to 2025. In 2025, median equivalised net income in the EU ranged from €20 994 per year among people living in rural areas up to €23 722 per year for people living in cities; the income for people living in towns and suburbs was almost as high, at €23 524 per year. As such, the median equivalised net income of people living in cities was 1.13 times as high as that for people living in rural areas. [[Image:Median equivalised net income, by degree of urbanisation, EU, 2015–25 (EUR)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: Median equivalised net income, by degree of urbanisation, EU, 2015–25
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e3a216af-dc89-4b48-b739-ace5f1ed2a2e?lang=en ilc_di17])|alt=A line chart showing the development of median equivalised net income. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented in euros. Data are shown for the EU. Annual data are presented for the period 2015 to 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 10 shows that income levels varied considerably between EU countries. These wide variations exist even though the information presented is shown in [[Glossary:Purchasing_power_standard_(PPS)|purchasing power standards (PPS)]]. PPS is a unit that takes account of price-level differences between countries; comparisons based on PPS usually result in narrower ranges between countries than when values are compared in euro. The median equivalised net income of people living in cities was generally higher than that recorded for people living in towns and suburbs or rural areas. This pattern was exhibited in 20 out of 27 EU countries in 2025; the only exceptions were: *Belgium, Denmark, Germany and Austria, where people living in towns and suburbs had the highest median levels of net income *France, Malta and the Netherlands, where people living in rural areas had the highest median levels of net income. Looking in more detail at income levels for people living in cities, the highest median equivalised net income in 2025 was recorded in Luxembourg (45 660 PPS). This was followed at some considerable distance by the Netherlands (29 710 PPS) and Austria (29 648 PPS). By contrast, people living in the cities of Hungary and Greece had the lowest levels of net income – less than 15 000 PPS. In 2025, the median equivalised net income in PPS terms of people living in rural areas of the EU was 88.5% of the average recorded for people living in cities. The median equivalised net income of people living in rural areas of Romania (10 279 PPS) was 65.2% of that recorded for people living in cities (15 760 PPS). There was a similar pattern in Bulgaria, which was the only other EU country where the median equivalised net income of people living in rural areas was less than 70% of the average recorded for people living in cities.

An interactive dot plot showing the median equivalised net income. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented in purchasing power standards (PPS). Data are shown for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. Annual data are presented for 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.

Figure 10
[[Image:Median equivalised net income, by degree of urbanisation, 2025 (PPS)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 10: Median equivalised net income, by degree of urbanisation, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e81c05c2-6d6d-40e0-bd1a-45b77b884861?lang=en ilc_di17])]] Across the EU, median equivalised net income for males was €23 486 in 2025; this was slightly more than €1 000 higher than the median value for females (€22 410). These equivalised income figures present an average that covers the whole population (including people who are not in work); they are also equivalised incomes for households. Figure 11 shows that – when analysed by degree of urbanisation – the EU gender gap for median equivalised net income was often situated within a relatively narrow range during the last decade. In 2025, the difference between male and female incomes was 5.2% of male incomes among people living in cities and in towns and suburbs, while a smaller difference was recorded for people living in rural areas (3.1%). [[Image:Gender gap for median equivalised net income, by degree of urbanisation, EU, 2015–25_(%)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 11: Gender gap for median equivalised net income, by degree of urbanisation, EU, 2015–25
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7af0ea19-6ad9-4cc2-a4ea-97798782fb5c?lang=en ilc_di17])|alt=A line chart showing the development of the gender gap for median equivalised net income. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented as the difference between male and female incomes as a percentage of male incomes. Data are shown for the EU. Annual data are presented for the period 2015 to 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In all EU countries, median equivalised net incomes for males were higher than those for females. This was also observed for nearly all EU countries in each of the 3 degrees of urbanisation. There were only 2 exceptions, both in Malta: the median equivalised net income was €593 higher for females than for males for people living in towns and suburbs; the medians were the same for both sexes in rural areas. In absolute terms, the largest gender gaps were recorded among people living in the rural areas of Luxembourg and the Netherlands, in the towns and suburbs of Denmark and Austria, as well as in the cities of Lithuania and Latvia. In relative terms (as shown in Figure 12), some of the widest gender gaps were recorded in the Baltic EU countries, where the median equivalised net incomes of males were more than 10.0% higher than those of females: *among people living in the cities of Lithuania *among people living in the cities and in the towns and suburbs of Latvia.

An interactive dot plot showing the gender gap for median equivalised net income. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented as the difference between male and female incomes as a percentage of male incomes. Data are shown for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. Annual data are presented for 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.

Figure 12
[[Image:Gender gap for median equivalised net income, by degree of urbanisation, 2025 (%)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 12: Gender gap for median equivalised net income, by degree of urbanisation, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/09c1ca3f-2a06-4e15-a826-60d9f0cf4bbf?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-24T09:01:01Z ilc_di17])]] The unequal distribution of income can, among other consequences, lead to economic inequalities that manifest themselves in various forms of poverty or social exclusion. In 2025, almost 1 in 5 (18.9%) of the EU’s population had a level of income that was at least 150% of the median income. By this measure, the distribution of income was less equitable across those living in cities, where almost 1 in 4 (23.5%) of the population had a level of income that was at least 150% of the median income, with lower shares recorded among those living in towns and suburbs (17.5%) and, most notably, rural areas (13.6%). Figure 13 shows that income inequalities (as measured by the share of people having an income at least 150% of the median) were generally concentrated in cities. In 2025, this was particularly the case in Bulgaria, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary, Latvia and Romania where 30.0% or more of the population living in cities had an income that was at least 150% of the median. There were 2 EU countries where the highest share was not observed for cities: in Malta, a higher share of the people living in rural areas (32.1%) had a level of income that was at least 150% of the median income, while in Belgium the highest share was recorded among people living in towns and suburbs (14.4%).

An interactive dot plot showing the share of people having an income that was at least 150% of the median income. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas. Information is presented in percent. Data are shown for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. Annual data are presented for 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.

Figure 13
[[Image:Share of people having an income that was at least 150% of the median income, by degree of urbanisation, 2025 (%)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 13: Share of people having an income that was at least 150% of the median income, by degree of urbanisation, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/085539cd-dad3-4a65-9ba3-c266e729c552?lang=en ilc_di23])]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Income and living conditions_URE2026.xlsx|title=Income and living conditions: tables and figures}} ===Context=== On 4 March 2021, the [[Glossary:European Commission_(EC)|European Commission]] set out its ambition for a stronger social EU to focus on education, skills and jobs, aiming for a fair, inclusive and resilient socioeconomic recovery from the COVID-19 crisis, while fighting discrimination, tackling poverty and alleviating the risk of exclusion for vulnerable groups. The ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2021:102:FIN European pillar of social rights action plan]'' (COM(2021) 102 final) outlines a set of specific actions and headline targets for employment, skills and social protection in the EU. It includes a benchmark target for reducing the number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion by at least 15 million people between 2019 and 2030 (of which, at least 5 million should be title: Urban-rural Europe - labour market
text:
This article forms part of Eurostat’s twin publications, Rural Europe and Urban Europe: 2026 editions, it focuses on labour market statistics. Data extracted: June 2026. Planned article update: September 2027. In 2025, the working-age population (defined here as people aged 20 to 64 years) of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] numbered 259.7 million. The [[Glossary:Labour force|labour force]] within this age range was composed of 209.9 million people, while 49.8 million were outside the labour force, in other words they were economically [[Glossary:Inactive|inactive]]. This latter cohort is largely composed of students, pensioners, people caring for other family members, as well as volunteers and those unable to work because of long-term sickness or disability. The EU labour force aged 20 to 64 years was composed of 197.7 million [[Glossary:Employed person - LFS|employed people]] and 12.1 million [[Glossary:Unemployed|unemployed people]] (people who were not employed, but actively seeking and available for work). In the EU, more than 4 out of every 5 men aged 20 to 64 who were living in [[Glossary:Rural area|rural areas]] (81.4%), in [[Glossary:Town or suburb|towns and suburbs]] (81.3%) and in [[Glossary:City|cities]] (80.3%) were employed in 2025. For each [[Glossary:Degree of urbanisation|degree of urbanisation]], the proportion of men in employment was consistently higher than the proportion of women in employment. In contrast to the pattern observed for men, the highest proportion of women in employment was recorded among those living in cities (72.2%). For both men and women, the lowest shares of people outside the labour force were observed among those living in cities (14.1% for men and 22.7% for women). This article forms part of [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]]’s twin publications on ''[[Rural_Europe|Rural Europe]]'' and ''[[Urban_Europe|Urban Europe]]''. The statistics presented are sourced from the [[Glossary: Labour force survey (LFS)|European labour force survey]] (EU-LFS). The [[Glossary:Activity_rate|activity rate]] is the number of people in the labour force (within a specified age range) as a percentage of the population (of the same age). The activity rate is a secondary indicator for measuring fair working conditions within the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/european-pillar-of-social-rights European pillar of social rights]. In 2025, the EU’s activity rate for working-age people (20 to 64 years) was 80.8%. The highest activity rate among people of this age was recorded for those living in cities (81.5%), with rates for rural areas (80.4%) and towns and suburbs (80.2%) slightly lower than the average for the whole of the EU territory; see Figure 1. During the period 2015 to 2025, there was a general upward development for the EU’s activity rate for working-age people, punctuated by the COVID-19 crisis in 2020; note also that, due to a break in series, data for 2021 and onwards are not fully comparable with previous years. Except in 2020, the EU’s activity rate increased every year for all 3 degrees of urbanisation; the most rapid annual increases were recorded when rates rebounded after 2020. Over the latest decade for which information is available, the EU’s activity rate for working-age people increased 4.4 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] among those living in cities, 4.1 points for those living in rural areas, and 3.9 points for those living in towns and suburbs. A more detailed analysis reveals that the highest activity rates for all working-age people (both sexes) were generally recorded among those living in cities; this was the case in 16 out of 27 EU countries; see Figure 2. ''Source:'' Eurostat (GISCO)]] The [[Glossary:Employment rate|employment rate]] is the number of employed people (within a specified age range) as a percentage of the population (of the same age). The employment rate is a headline indicator for fair working conditions within the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/european-pillar-of-social-rights European pillar of social rights]. The EU employment rate for working-age people (20 to 64 years) is cyclical, with rates generally rising in the second and third quarters of each year and falling in the fourth and first quarters; this pattern is particularly pronounced in rural areas (see Figure 5). Between 2015 and 2019, employment rates by degree of urbanisation followed an upward development. However, the COVID-19 crisis had a considerable impact on labour markets in 2020: some people were placed on furlough schemes Also known by other names, such as temporary lay-off or technical unemployment. In a furlough scheme, for a fixed or open-ended period of time employees are not required to work but are not made unemployed. Depending on the details of specific schemes: workers receive full, reduced or no pay; employers receive full, partial or no financial support from public authorities. Furlough schemes help employers to retain employees during economically difficult times, with the intention that employees return to work for the same employer at the end of the scheme., others were made unemployed, and some self-employed people lost their income (in part or full). The initial impact of the COVID-19 pandemic resulted in the EU employment rate for cities falling at a faster pace (than that for towns and suburbs or for rural areas). The asymmetric nature of the crisis was also apparent insofar as it impacted particular groups, for example, younger people, temporary employees, those in precarious employment, or those working in leisure, hospitality and transport-related activities. From the second quarter of 2021, there was a recovery in EU employment rates for each degree of urbanisation, as rates rose above their pre-crisis levels; note that due to a break in series, data for 2021 and onwards are not fully comparable with previous years. Having remained relatively unchanged in 2022, EU employment rates continued to grow – albeit at a relatively modest pace – from 2023. There were relatively small differences in employment rates by degree of urbanisation, with a peak of 76.4% recorded for people living in rural areas, while the lowest rate was 75.9% for people living in towns and suburbs; see Figure 6. An analysis by sex and degree of urbanisation reveals that the highest male employment rate was recorded for men living in rural areas (81.4% across the EU), while the lowest rate was registered for those living in cities (80.3%). A different pattern existed for women, insofar as the highest employment rate was recorded for women living in cities (72.2%) and the lowest for those living in towns and suburbs (70.4%). Across the EU countries, the highest employment rates for working-age people (both sexes) living in cities were recorded in Czechia (83.9%), followed by Hungary (83.6%), Lithuania (83.4%) and Malta (83.2%). By contrast the lowest employment rates for people living in cities were observed in Belgium (66.0%) and Italy (67.4%). The range between the highest and lowest employment rates was similar for people living in towns and suburbs but notably wider for people living in rural areas. The employment rate for people living in towns and suburbs peaked in the Netherlands at 85.1%, some 17.7 percentage points higher than the rate observed in Italy (67.4%). The Netherlands also recorded the highest employment rate for people living in rural areas (85.6%), which was 24.9 points higher than the rate recorded in Romania (60.7%).

Across the EU, the lowest employment rates tended to be recorded for people aged 15 to 24 years (see Figure 8), many of whom continue to pursue full-time education. Rates generally peaked for people aged 25 to 54 years before tailing off among those aged 55 to 64 years (when, among other factors, early retirement, ill health and caring responsibilities may result in people leaving the labour market); see Figure 9. The EU employment rate for young people aged 15 to 24 years was 34.5% in 2025. For young males, the employment rate was higher for people living in rural areas (38.8%) than it was for people living in towns and suburbs (37.5%) or in cities (34.5%). This pattern was reversed for young females, insofar as the highest EU employment rate was recorded for people living in cities (33.3%), with lower rates for people living in towns and suburbs (32.4%) and in rural areas (30.6%). As a result, the EU gender employment gap for young people (with higher rates for young males) ranged from a difference of 1.2 percentage points for people living in cities, through 5.1 points difference for people living in towns and suburbs, to 8.2 points for people living in rural areas. In 2025, a majority of EU countries (18 out of 25; no data for Luxembourg and incomplete data for Malta) reported their highest employment rates for young males among those living in rural areas. There was considerable variation between countries, with the employment rate of young males living in rural areas peaking at 81.9% in the Netherlands, while the lowest rate was recorded in Bulgaria (24.0%). A majority of EU countries (14 out of the same 25) posted their highest employment rates for young females among those living in cities. There was again considerable variation between countries, with the employment rate of young females living in cities peaking at 72.8% in the Netherlands, while the lowest rate was recorded in Croatia (11.7%). Between 2015 and 2025, the EU employment rate for working-age people rose 7.1 percentage points; it stood at 76.1% at the end of the period under consideration. Note that due to a break in series, data for 2021 and onwards are not fully comparable with previous years. EU employment rates for working-age people increased for each degree of urbanisation between 2015 and 2025. Similar increases were recorded for people living in cities (where rates were up 7.3 percentage points) and people living in rural areas (up 7.2 points), while increases were somewhat smaller for towns and suburbs (up 6.9 points); see Figure 10. This pattern of increasing employment rates was repeated in every EU country and for all 3 degrees of urbanisation, with a single exception. The employment rate of working-age people living in rural areas of Romania was 4.8 percentage points lower in 2025 than it had been in 2015. Note, however, that due to changes in survey methodology that came into force in 2021, there is a break in the time series. In Romania, the most notable change concerned the exclusion of employed people producing agricultural goods intended exclusively for self-consumption; this may, at least in part, explain the considerable changes observed, in particular for employment in rural areas. In 2025, around three fifths (60.3%) of the EU’s working-age population (20 to 64 years) who were employed had been in their current job for at least 5 years (at least 60 months). This figure was higher among people living in rural areas (64.1%) and towns and suburbs (62.1%), than it was among people living in cities (56.6%). By contrast, working-age people living in cities were more likely (than those living in other areas) to have been in their job for less time; some 13.3% of people in cities who were employed had been in their current job for less than 12 months, compared with 10.3% in rural areas. In 2025, the share of people employed in their current job for at least 5 years was higher for working-age people living in rural areas (compared with those living in cities) in most EU countries (22 out of 27). The exceptions were eastern EU countries: Bulgaria, Croatia, Hungary, Romania and Slovakia. In Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Luxembourg, Malta, Austria, Finland and Sweden, the share of working-age employed people living in rural areas who had been in their current job for at least 5 years was more than 10.0 percentage points higher than the corresponding share for people living in cities. The gender gap in part-time employment is a secondary indicator for equal opportunities within the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/european-pillar-of-social-rights European pillar of social rights]. There were 33.7 million working-age people (20 to 64 years) employed on a part-time basis within the EU in 2025; just over three quarters of all people working on a part-time basis were women (25.4 million, or 75.5% of the total). Within the EU, more than 1 in 6 people (17.0%) aged 20 to 64 years were employed on a part-time basis in 2025. The relative importance of part-time work was considerably higher among women (27.5% of those employed) than it was among men (7.8%). Part-time employment rates (both sexes combined) were higher for those living in towns and suburbs (18.0%) and cities (17.4%) than they were for people living in rural areas (15.1%). Across the EU countries, it was relatively common to find that female part-time employment rates were higher in rural areas (than they were in cities), whereas male part-time employment rates tended to be higher in cities (than they were in rural areas). [[Image:Employment characteristics (20–64 years), by degree of urbanisation, 2025 (% share of total employment)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 12: Employment characteristics (20–64 years), by degree of urbanisation, 2025
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data codes: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/5de729ef-b15f-4ec2-a143-1a4c84d0bd5d?lang=en lfst_r_egadu] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/905d40c0-36b5-493f-b8bd-c4a7d2133931?lang=en lfst_r_e2pgaedcu])|alt=A heat map showing the employment characteristics of working-age people aged 20 to 64 years. Data are presented for job tenure broken down by time (for 0 to 11 months and for greater than or equal to 60 months) and for part-time employment broken down by sex (for men and for women). Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities and for rural areas. Information is presented in percent, as a share of total employment. Data are shown for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. Annual data are presented for 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2025, there were 19.6 million fixed-term employees of working age (20 to 64 years) in the EU; this subpopulation is sometimes referred to as temporary employees. These 19.6 million fixed-term employees equated to 11.5% of the EU’s total number of employees. The share of fixed-term employees within the total number of employees was higher among people with a relatively low level of educational attainment, in other words, people with no more than a lower secondary level of attainment (as defined by the [[Glossary:International standard classification of education (ISCED)|international standard classification of education (ISCED)]] levels 0 to 2). In the EU, close to a sixth (15.7%) of all employees with a relatively low level of educational attainment were fixed-term employees; this share was considerably lower (10.5%) among employees with a tertiary level of educational attainment (as defined by ISCED levels 5 to 8). In the EU, the share of fixed-term employees in the total number of employees was broadly similar for people with a low level of educational attainment in 2025, irrespective of whether they lived in cities (15.7%) or rural areas (15.9%). By contrast, the share of fixed-term employees with a tertiary level of educational attainment was higher among those living in cities (11.7%) than it was for those living in rural areas (8.7%). In 2025, some of the highest shares of fixed-term employees – for all education levels combined – were recorded in the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Portugal and Cyprus; they each recorded a share of more than 14.0%. Looking in more detail (and subject to data availability – see Figure 13 for data coverage), fixed-term employees accounted for at least a fifth of all employees: *with a low level of educational attainment living in the cities of Poland, Cyprus, the Netherlands, Sweden and Denmark; *with a low level of educational attainment living in the rural areas of Poland, Greece, Hungary, Cyprus and the Netherlands; *with a tertiary level of educational attainment living in the cities of the Netherlands. [[Image:Fixed-term employees (20–64 years), by educational attainment and degree of urbanisation, 2025 (% share of total employees)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 13: Fixed-term employees (20–64 years), by educational attainment and degree of urbanisation, 2025
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3969fe93-0647-4889-8ba8-f30bb162e33e?lang=en lfst_r_e2tgaedcu])|alt=A pyramid distribution plot showing the employment rate of working-age people aged 20 to 64 years. Data are shown by educational attainment for people with no more than a lower secondary level of education and for people with a tertiary level of education; the left-hand side of the chart shows data for cities and the right-hand side shows data for rural areas. Information is presented in percent, as a share of total employees. Data are shown for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. Annual data are presented for 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Unemployment=== Unemployment can have a bearing not just on the macroeconomic performance of a country (lowering productive capacity) but also on the well-being of individuals without work and their families. The personal and social costs of unemployment are varied and include a higher risk of poverty and social exclusion, debt or homelessness, while the stigma of being unemployed may have a potentially detrimental impact on (mental) health. The [[Glossary:Unemployment|unemployment rate]] is a headline indicator for fair working conditions within the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/european-pillar-of-social-rights European pillar of social rights]. The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people, expressed as a proportion of the labour force (the sum of employed and unemployed people); in other words, the denominator does not include people who are outside of the labour force, for example, full-time students, those who do not want to or cannot work, or retired people. In 2025, the EU’s unemployment rate for people aged 15 to 74 years stood at 6.0%. While the rate had risen during the COVID-19 crisis, by 2022 it had fallen back to a level that was below that recorded prior to the pandemic (6.7% in 2019); note that due to a break in series, data for 2021 onwards are not fully comparable with previous years. By degree of urbanisation, the lowest unemployment rates in the EU in 2025 were recorded for people living in rural areas (5.3%), with somewhat higher rates for those living in towns and suburbs (5.6%) and cities (6.8%). This pattern – the lowest unemployment rate for rural areas and the highest for cities – was repeated for both sexes, with female unemployment rates at a somewhat higher level (than male rates) for each degree of urbanisation. In 2025, the unemployment rate for people living in cities peaked among the EU countries at 11.5% and 10.1%, respectively, in Finland and Spain. For people living in towns and suburbs, the highest unemployment rates were recorded in Spain, Greece and Finland, while the highest rates for people living in rural areas were observed in Spain and Romania. At the other end of the range, the lowest unemployment rates for people living in cities were recorded in Romania (2.1%) and Bulgaria (2.3%). The Netherlands had the lowest unemployment rate (2.9%) for people living in towns and suburbs, while the lowest rates for people living in rural areas were recorded in Germany (2.4%), Czechia and the Netherlands (both 2.5%). In approximately half of the EU countries (incomplete data for Luxembourg), the highest unemployment rate by degree of urbanisation in 2025, was most often recorded for people living in cities. There were however several exceptions: *in Czechia, Estonia, Ireland and Spain, the highest unemployment rate was recorded for people living in towns and suburbs; *in Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Poland, Romania and Slovakia, the highest unemployment rate was recorded for people living in rural areas.

An interactive dot plot showing unemployment rates for people aged 15 to 74 years. Data are shown by degree of urbanisation for cities, towns and suburbs, and rural areas; data are also shown by sex for the total (both sexes), males and females. Information is presented in percent, as a share of the labour force. Data are shown for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. Annual data are presented for 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.

Figure 14
[[Image:Unemployment rate (15–74 years), by sex and degree of urbanisation, 2025 (% share of labour force)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 14: Unemployment rate (15–74 years), by sex and degree of urbanisation, 2025
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/422521d7-e18d-45b4-b6a8-56c3a2b16959?lang=en lfst_r_urgau])]] Figure 15 shows changes in unemployment rates between 2015 and 2025. Note that unemployment rates were relatively high in 2015 (in the aftermath of the global financial and economic crisis and the sovereign debt crisis) and that due to a break in series, data for 2021 and onwards are not fully comparable with previous years. During the period under consideration, the EU’s unemployment rate fell by 4.1 percentage points. The unemployment rate fell overall by similar amounts across the 3 different degrees of urbanisation: among people living in cities and people living in rural areas it was down 4.1 points, while for people living in towns and suburbs it was 4.0 points lower. Unemployment rates fell in the vast majority of EU countries between 2015 and 2025 for each degree of urbanisation; this was particularly noticeable in the economies most severely impacted by the earlier crises. There were, however, a few exceptions, as unemployment rates: *rose for people living in the cities of Estonia, Sweden, Finland and Denmark *rose for people living in the towns and suburbs of Estonia, Sweden and Denmark; *rose for people living in the rural areas of Romania (note there is a break in the time series which is likely to have had a considerable impact on the unemployment rate in rural areas) and Sweden; *remained unchanged for people living in rural areas of Luxembourg. [[Image:Unemployment rate (15–74 years), by degree of urbanisation, 2015 and 2025 (% share of labour force)_URE2026.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 15: Unemployment rate (15–74 years), by degree of urbanisation, 2015 and 2025
'' Source:'' Eurostat (online data code: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8aefad29-1ae9-4759-9645-f8834148818f?lang=en lfst_r_urgau])|alt=Three double bar charts showing the unemployment rate for people aged 15 to 74 years. There is a separate chart for each degree of urbanisation: with a chart for cities, for towns and suburbs, and for rural areas. Information is presented in percent, as a share of the labour force. Data are shown for the EU as well as EU and EFTA countries. Annual data are presented for 2015 and 2025. The complete data of the visualisation are available in the Excel file at the end of the article. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The [[Glossary:Youth_unemployment|youth unemployment]] rate in the EU has traditionally been somewhat more than twice as high as the overall unemployment rate. This rate is a secondary indicator for fair working conditions within the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/european-pillar-of-social-rights European pillar of social rights]. In 2025, the EU’s youth unemployment rate (covering young people aged 15 to 24 years) was 15.2%, while the overall unemployment rate for people aged 15 to 74 years was 6.0%. Youth unemployment in the EU was particularly concentrated in cities, where the unemployment rate stood at 16.4%, compared with 14.8% for rural areas and 14.1% for towns and suburbs. This pattern of the highest youth unemployment rates being among people living in cities was repeated in 11 out of 22 EU countries (see Figure 16 for data coverage). By contrast, the highest youth unemployment rates in Czechia, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain and Sweden were recorded in towns and suburbs, while young people living in rural areas experienced the highest rates in Bulgaria, Cyprus, Hungary, Poland and Romania. In 2025, youth unemployment covered more than a quarter of the labour force aged 15 to 24 years in: *the towns and suburbs, and rural areas of Spain and Romania *the cities of Italy *the towns and suburbs of Estonia and Sweden. An analysis by sex reveals that in 2025 the male youth unemployment rate was higher than the female rate for each degree of urbanisation in Germany, whereas the female youth unemployment rate was higher than the male rate for each degree of urbanisation in Spain and Italy. *The male youth unemployment rate for people living in the cities of Croatia was 6.4 percentage points higher than the corresponding rate for females. *The female youth unemployment rate for people living in the cities of Italy was 2.9 percentage points higher than the corresponding rate for males. *The male youth unemployment rate for people living in the towns and suburbs of Belgium was 4.1 percentage points higher than the corresponding rate for females. *The female youth unemployment rate for people living in the towns and suburbs of Portugal was 7.1 percentage points higher than the corresponding rate for males. *The male youth unemployment rate for people living in the rural areas of Lithuania was 14.7 percentage points higher than the corresponding rate for females. *The female youth unemployment rate for people living in the rural areas of Greece was 14.7 percentage points higher than the corresponding rate for males.

Figure 17 shows the largest reduction in youth unemployment rates by degree of urbanisation was for young people living in towns and suburbs, down 6.9 percentage points during the period under consideration. Youth unemployment rates also fell in cities (down 6.6 points) and in rural areas (down 6.4 points). Between 2015 and 2025, youth unemployment rates fell across all 3 degrees of urbanisation in most EU countries. The only exceptions were: *the Baltic and Nordic EU countries, as well as Austria, where the youth unemployment rate rose in cities *Sweden, Romania, Denmark, Malta and Austria, where the youth unemployment rate rose in towns and suburbs *Romania (note there is a break in the time series which is likely to have had a considerable impact on the youth unemployment rate in rural areas), Estonia and Sweden, where the youth unemployment rate rose in rural areas. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Labour market_URE2026.xlsx|title=Labour market: tables and figures}} ===Context=== The [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] has set [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029_en 7 key priorities for the period 2024 to 2029], including initiatives such as [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/competitiveness_en a new plan for Europe’s sustainable prosperity and competitiveness] and [https://commission.europa.eu/priorities-2024-2029/european-social-fairness_en supporting people, strengthening our societies and our social model], whereby the EU seeks to create a more attractive investment environment and growth that creates quality jobs, especially for young people and small businesses. Some of the principal challenges outlined by the President of the European Commission include fully implementing the European pillar of social rights; tackling the cost of living; ensuring that workers have at least a fair minimum wage; promoting a better work-life balance; tackling gender pay gaps and other forms of workplace discrimination; getting more disabled people into work; and protecting people who are unemployed. On 4 March 2021, the European Commission set out its ambition for a stronger social EU to focus on jobs and skills, to lead to a fair, inclusive and resilient socioeconomic recovery from the COVID-19 crisis. The ''[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=COM:2021:102:FIN European pillar of social rights action plan]'' (COM(2021) 102 final) outlines a set of specific actions and headline targets for employment, skills and social protection in the EU. It includes a benchmark for the [[Glossary:Employment rate|employment rate]], namely that – by 2030 – at least 78% of people aged 20 to 64 years should be in employment. Within the EU’s labour market, particular attention has been given over to reducing the number of young people who do not participate in the labour force or who are unemployed, including young people who are not in employment, education or training (NEET). The European pillar of social rights action plan includes an objective to reduce the NEET rate from 12.6% in 2019 to no more than 9.0% by 2030. The youth guarantee was created in 2013 and [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/eu-employment-policies/youth-employment-support/reinforced-youth-guarantee_en reinforced in 2020]. It is the EU’s reference policy framework to fight youth unemployment and inactivity, helping 15 to 29 year-olds to receive an offer of employment, education, apprenticeship or traineeship within 4 months of becoming unemployed or leaving education; it has helped around 50 million young people. === Notes === ===See also=== '''Online publications''' *[[Eurostat_regional_yearbook|Eurostat regional
