title: Waste statistics - electrical and electronic equipment
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the waste - electrical and electronic equipment. Data from: October 2025 Planned update: 14 October 2026 In 2023, 11.6 kg of electrical and electronic equipment waste were collected per inhabitant in the EU. In 2023, Bulgaria, Latvia and Slovakia achieved the target of collecting 65% of waste electrical and electronic equipment, based on the amount of such equipment put on the market in the 3 previous years. In 2023, Poland achieved the target of collecting 85% of waste electrical and electronic equipment, based on the amount of such equipment generated in the same year. |alt= Interactive vertical bar chart showing kilograms per inhabitant of waste electrical and electronic equipment collected in the EU, individual EU countries, Norway and Liechtenstein for the year 2022. This article provides an overview of processed amounts of [[Glossary:Waste_electrical_and_electronic_equipment_(WEEE)|waste electrical and electronic equipment]] (WEEE) in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]] and in the [[Glossary:European_Free_Trade_Association_(EFTA)|EFTA countries]]. It is based on data collected within the framework of {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX::02012L0019-20180704:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2012/19/EU}} on waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE Directive). The objective of the WEEE Directive is to promote collection of waste electrical and electronic equipment and recovery, recycling and preparation for reuse of this waste, in order to reduce the quantity disposed. In 2023, the collection rate of WEEE in the European Union was 37.5% (measured as the weight of WEEE collected relative to the average weight of electronic equipment put on the market in the 3 preceding years, i.e. 2020-2022). === Electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) put on the market and WEEE processed in the EU=== Figure 1 shows the trends in the amount of electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) put on the market and in WEEE collected, treated, recovered, recycled and prepared for reuse in the EU in the years from 2012 to 2023. Missing data for some EU countries have been estimated in order to show the developments for the EU as a whole. Information on the lifespan of EEE products from the year they are put on the market to the year when they become waste is currently not available in the data collected for monitoring the WEEE collection target. This collection target changed in connection with the revised monitoring introduced from the reference year 2016 onwards (see the Context section below for more details). The amount of electrical and electronic equipment put on the market in the EU evolved from 7.6 million tonnes in 2012 to a peak of 14.4 million tonnes in 2022 and 2023. Within this period, the lowest level was recorded in 2013, with 7.3 million tonnes. Over the period 2012-2023 as a whole, the amount of EEE put on the market grew by 89%. The total collected WEEE increased from 3.0 million tonnes in 2012 to 5.2 million tonnes in 2023 (+75%), while the total treated WEEE grew from 3.1 to 5.2 million tonnes (+66%) over the same period. Recovered WEEE developed from 2.6 to 4.8 million tonnes (+83%), and WEEE recycled and prepared for reuse grew from 2.4 to 4.3 million tonnes (+77%) from 2012 to 2023. [[Image:WEEE_Figure1_RY2023.png|thumb|centre|800px|Figure 1: Electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) put on the market and waste EEE collected, treated, recovered, recycled and prepared for reuse, EU, 2012-2023
''Sources'': {{Stable link|title=Eurostat|code=env_waseleeos}} and {{Stable link|title=Eurostat|code=env_waselee}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing thousand tonnes of electrical and electronic equipment. Five sections represent total put on market, total collected, total treatment, total recovered and total reused and recycled. Each section has 11 columns representing each year from 2012 to 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
 === Electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) put on the market and WEEE collected by country === The recast of the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02012L0019-20240408:EN:NOT|title=WEEE Directive (2012/19/EU)}}, which entered into force on 13 August 2012, introduced an increase in the collection targets step by step, taking effect from reference years 2016 and 2019, respectively. From 2016 onwards, the annual collection target for WEEE is defined as the ratio between the amount of WEEE collected in the reference year and the average weight of EEE put on the market in the 3 preceding years. The collection target was set at 45% from 2016, rising to 65% from 2019 onwards.From reference year 2019 onwards, the collection rate may also be calculated on the basis of WEEE generated in the same year, instead of on the basis of the average weight of EEE put on the market in the 3 preceding years. The EU countries choose which of these two methods shall be applied for assessing progress towards and achievement of the collection rate target. For 2023, Denmark, Luxembourg, Poland and Hungary have chosen to calculate the collection rate on the basis of WEEE generated in the same year. This calculation methodology is defined in Annex II of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/699 as the sum, for each EEE product category, of the amount of EEE placed on the market and the estimation of the lifespan of the corresponding products. For countries applying this methodology, the collection target is set at 85% from 2019 onwards. In addition to these 4 EU countries, several other countries voluntarily provide data on WEEE generated and WEEE collection rate calculated on this basis. According to the derogation set out in Article 7 Point 3 of the WEEE Directive, the following EU countries could decide to postpone the achievement of the collection target until 14 August 2021: Bulgaria, Czechia, Latvia, Lithuania, Hungary, Malta, Poland, Romania, Slovenia and Slovakia. In Figure 2a, WEEE collected is shown as the share of the EEE put on the market. The share is calculated as the ratio of the amount of collected WEEE in 2023 in relation to the average amount of EEE put on the market in the 3 preceding years, i.e. 2020-2022. These ratios provide an overview of the EU countries’ performance towards the collection targets of 45% and 65%, respectively. In 2023, 9 EU countries surpassed the 45% WEEE collection target. In addition, 3 EU countries reported a rate close to this target, at 44.2% (France), 43.9% (Croatia), and 43.6% (Ireland). 3 EU countries (Bulgaria, Slovakia, and Latvia) achieved the more ambitious target of a 65% collection rate in 2023. Czechia reported a rate close to this more ambitious target in 2023, reporting a WEEE collection rate of 61.7%. Figure 2b shows the collection rate calculated as the amount of collected WEEE in relation to the amount of WEEE generated in the same year. 4 EU countries (Denmark, Hungary, Luxembourg, and Poland) have chosen this methodology to calculate the collection rate. For this calculation method, the WEEE Directive sets a collection target of 85% from reference year 2019 onwards. Only Poland, achieved this target. [[Image:WEEE_Figure2a_RY2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2a: Total collection rate for waste electrical and electronic equipment, 2023
''Source'': {{Stable link|title=Eurostat|code=env_waseleeos}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing total collection rate for waste electrical and electronic equipment as the year 2023 percentage share of WEEE collected based on average weight of EEE put on the market in the 3 preceding years in the EU, individual EU countries, Norway and Iceland. Two lines across all countries represent the 45 percent target and 65 percent target. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
[[Image:WEEE_Figure2b_RY2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2b: Total collection rate for waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) as a share of generated WEEE, 2023
''Source'': {{Stable link|title=Eurostat|code=env_waseleeos}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing total collection rate for waste electrical and electronic equipment as the year 2023 percentage share of WEEE collected based on average weight of WEEE generated in the same year in Poland, Luxembourg, Denmark, and Hungary. A line across all countries represents the 85 percent target. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
Figure 3 shows the amount of WEEE collected in 2023, in comparison with the EEE put on the market in the 3 preceding years (2020-2022) and the WEEE generated in 2023, respectively. These are all expressed in kilograms per inhabitant (based on the average number of inhabitants in 2023). In the EU, the WEEE collected in 2023 was estimated at 11.6 kilograms per inhabitant, while the average EEE put on the market over the period 2020-2022 was estimated at 30.2 kilograms per inhabitant. The variation in the collected amounts reflects differences in EEE consumption level between countries, as well as differences in the performance of their respective waste collection schemes. Due to the transition from the previous methodology that used 10 product categories for EEE to the new methodology using 6 product categories, taking effect from reference year 2019, countries have calculated the collection rate based on the average weight of EEE placed on the market in the three preceding years by estimating the amounts for 2020-2022 according to this methodology (these amounts are not published). The average of the three preceding years according to the 6 categories methodology has been calculated as WEEE collected divided by WEEE collection rate. (See the 'Context' section for more details on the EEE product categories.) [[Image:WEEE_Figure3_RY2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Electrical and electronic equipment put on the market in the three preceding years, waste EEE generated and collected, 2023
''Source'': {{Stable link|title=Eurostat|code=env_waseleeos}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing kilograms per inhabitant of electrical and electronic equipment in the EU, individual EU countries, Norway and Liechtenstein. Each country has three columns representing EEE put on the market in the three preceding years, WEEE generated and WEEE collected for the year 2023. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Source data for tables and graphs=== *[[Media:Waste_electrical_and_electronic_equipment_RY2023.xlsx|Waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) - Excel file – October 2025]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== Data on WEEE are reported by the EU countries according to {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32005D0369:EN:NOT|title=Decision 2005/396/EC}} laying down rules for monitoring compliance of EU countries and establishing data formats for the purposes of {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02012L0019-20180704:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2012/19/EU}} of the European Parliament and of the Council on waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE Directive). EU countries have the obligation to report to the Commission within 18 months of the end of the reference year on the achievement of the targets for WEEE collection, reuse, recycling and / or recovery on the basis of Decision 2005/369/EC. This Commission Decision remained valid after {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32002L0096:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2002/96/EC}} was repealed and replaced by Directive 2012/19/EU (article 25). The reported data become available in the Eurostat database approximately 3 months after the reporting deadline. Data are available from reference year 2005 onwards. ===Context=== Unless properly managed, materials and components arising from waste electrical and electronic equipment can cause major environmental and health problems due to hazardous content. Moreover, production of modern electrical and electronic equipment requires the use of rare and expensive resources. The amelioration of collection, treatment and recycling of WEEE is essential to improve its environmental management, its contribution to a circular economy and enhance resource recycling efficiency. The management of WEEE is regulated by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02012L0019-20180704:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2012/19/EU}} of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 July 2012 on waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE Directive). The first WEEE Directive ({{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32002L0096:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2002/96/EC}}) entered into force in February 2003. The Directive provided for the creation of collection schemes where consumers return their WEEE free of charge. These schemes aim to increase the recycling and / or re-use of WEEE. Directive 2002/96/EC was repealed on 15 February 2014 and replaced by Directive 2012/19/EU on waste electrical and electronic equipment, which introduced a stepped increase in collection targets with effect from reference years 2016 and 2019, respectively. Furthermore, from 15 August 2018 onwards, the scope of the WEEE Directive was extended to all categories of EEE (excluding EEE described in paragraphs 3 and 4 of Article 2 of Directive 2012/19/EU). Consequently, the definition and number of the categories is different and the reporting obligation applies as described here below: (a) until reference year 2018, to EEE falling within the 10 product categories set out in Annex I to Directive 2012/19/EU : # Large household appliances # Small household appliances # IT and telecommunications equipment # Consumer equipment and photovoltaic panels # Lighting equipment # Electrical and electronic tools (with the exception of large-scale stationary industrial tools) # Toys, leisure and sports equipment # Medical devices (with the exception of all implanted and infected products) # Monitoring and control instruments # Automatic dispensers Annex II contains an indicative list of products falling under the categories in Annex I. (b) from reference year 2019 onwards, all EEE shall be classified within 6 product categories set out in Annex III as classified here below, with exclusion of the EEE described in paragraphs 3 and 4 of article 2 of Directive 2012/19/EU # Temperature exchange equipment # Screens, monitors and equipment containing screens having a surface greater than 100 cm2 # Lamps # Large equipment (any external dimension more than 50 cm) including, but not limited to: Household appliances; IT and telecommunication equipment; consumer equipment; luminaires; equipment reproducing sound or images, musical equipment; electrical and electronic tools; toys, leisure and sports equipment; medical devices; monitoring and control instruments; automatic dispensers; equipment for the generation of electric currents. This category does not include equipment included in categories 1 to 3. # Small equipment (no external dimension more than 50 cm) including, but not limited to: Household appliances; consumer equipment; luminaires; equipment reproducing sound or images, musical equipment; electrical and electronic tools; toys, leisure and sports equipment; medical devices; monitoring and control instruments; automatic dispensers; equipment for the generation of electric currents. This category does not include equipment included in categories 1 to 3 and 6. # Small IT and telecommunication equipment (no external dimension more than 50 cm) Annex IV contains a non-exhaustive list of EEE which falls within the categories set out in Annex III (open scope). ===Other articles=== *[[Waste statistics]] *[[End-of-life vehicle statistics]] *[[Food waste and food waste prevention - title: Waste statistics
text:
EU statistics on development of waste management. Data extracted in September 2024 Planned article update: October 2026 In 2022, 5.0 tonnes of waste were generated per EU inhabitant. In 2022, 40.8% of waste were recycled and 30.2% landfilled in the EU. |alt= Interactive vertical bar chart showing waste generation as kg per capita for the EU, individual EU Member States, Liechtenstein, Iceland, Norway, Serbia, Montenegro, Türkiye, North Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo for the year 2022. This article gives an overview on [[Glossary:Waste|waste]] generation and treatment in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] and several non-EU countries. It draws exclusively on data collected in accordance with {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32002R2150:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 2150/2002}} of the [[Glossary:European Parliament (EP)|European Parliament]] and [[Glossary:Council of the European Union|Council]] on waste statistics. Waste, defined by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008L0098:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2008/98/EC}} Article 3(1) as 'any substance or object which the holder discards or intends or is required to discard', potentially represents an enormous loss of resources in the form of both materials and energy. In addition, the management and disposal of waste can have serious environmental impacts. [[Glossary:Landfill|Landfill]], for example, takes up land space and may cause air, water and soil pollution, while [[Glossary:Incineration|incineration]] may result in emissions of air pollutants. EU waste management policies therefore aim to reduce the environmental and health impacts of waste and to improve the EU's [[Glossary:Resource productivity|resource efficiency]]. The long-term aim of these policies is to reduce the amount of waste generated and when waste generation is unavoidable to promote it as a resource and achieve higher levels of [[Glossary:Recycling of waste|recycling]] and the safe [[Glossary:Waste|disposal of waste]]. ===Total waste generation=== In 2022, the total waste generated in the [[Glossary:EU enlargements|EU]] by all economic activities and households amounted to 2 233 million tonnes or 4 991 kg per capita. [[Image: T1 Waste generation by economic activities and households, 2022 (% share of total waste ).png|thumb|center|800px|Table 1: Waste generation by economic activities and households, 2022
(% share of total waste)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_wasgen}}|alt= Table showing waste generation by economic activities and households as percentage share of total waste in the EU, individual EU Member States, Liechtenstein, Iceland, Norway, Serbia, Montenegro, Türkiye, North Macedonia, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo for the year 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The share of different economic activities and of households in total waste generation in 2022 is presented in Figure 1. In the EU, construction contributed 38.4% of the total in 2022 and was followed by mining and quarrying (22.7%), waste and water services (10.5%), manufacturing (10.4%) and households (8.9%); the remaining 9.2% was waste generated from other economic activities, mainly services (5.2%) and energy (3.0%). [[Image:Waste generation by economic activities and households, EU, 2022_(% share of total waste).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Waste generation by economic activities and households, EU, 2022
(% share of total waste)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_wasgen}}|alt= Pie chart showing waste generation by economic activities and households as percentage share of total waste in the EU for the year 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 2 shows an analysis of the amount of waste generated in a standardised form, in relation to population size. The high levels of total waste generated in some of the smaller EU countries can be clearly seen, with particularly high values recorded for Finland where on average almost 20 tonnes of waste were generated per inhabitant in 2022, 4 times the EU average of 5.0 tonnes per inhabitant. Several of the EU countries with particularly high levels of waste generated per inhabitant reported very high shares of waste from mining and quarrying, while elsewhere construction and demolition often contributed to the high shares. A lot of the waste from mining and quarrying and from construction and demolition is classified as major mineral waste: the analysis presented in Figure 2 distinguishes major mineral waste from all other wastes. Of the total waste generated in the EU in 2022, 64% (3.2 tonnes) per inhabitant was major mineral waste. The relative share of major mineral waste in the total waste generated varied considerably between EU countries, which may reflect, at least to some degree, different economic structures. In general, those EU countries that had higher shares of major mineral waste were those that were characterised as having relatively sizeable mining and quarrying activities, such as Finland, Romania and Sweden, and/or construction and demolition activities, such as Luxembourg; in these countries, major mineral waste accounted for between 82% and 91% of all waste generated. [[Image:F2 Waste generation, 2022 (kg per capita) V2.png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Waste generation, 2022
(kg per capita)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_wasgen}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing waste generation as kg per capita for the EU, individual EU countries, Liechtenstein, Iceland, Norway, Serbia, Montenegro, Türkiye, North Macedonia, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo. Each country column has two stacks representing waste excluding major mineral waste and major mineral waste for the year 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Waste generation excluding major mineral waste=== In the EU, 795 million tonnes of waste excluding major mineral waste were generated in 2022, equivalent to 36% of the total waste generated. When expressed in relation to population size, the EU generated, on average, 1.8 tonnes per inhabitant of waste excluding major mineral waste in 2022 (Figure 3). Across the EU countries, waste generation excluding major mineral waste ranged from an average of 7.5 tonnes per inhabitant in Estonia to 1.1 tonnes per inhabitant in Romania, Latvia and Malta in 2022. The large quantity of waste generated in Estonia is related to energy production based on oil shale. [[Image:Waste generation, excluding major mineral waste, 2010 and 2022 (kg per capita)v4.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Waste generation, excluding major mineral waste, 2010 and 2022
(kg per capita)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_wasgen}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing waste generation excluding major mineral waste in as kg per capita for the EU, individual EU Member States, Liechtenstein, Iceland, Norway, Serbia, Montenegro, Türkiye, North Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo. Each country has two columns representing the years 2010 and 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 2 shows the development of EU waste generation excluding major mineral waste analysed by economic activity. In 2022, the highest levels of waste generation were recorded for waste and water services (216 million tonnes), for households (193 million tonnes) and for manufacturing activities (166 million tonnes). Their developments followed different patterns over time: between 2004 and 2022, waste generation (excluding major mineral waste) by waste and water services and by households increased by 187.2% and 10.6 %, respectively, while generation by manufacturing activities diminished quite considerably, down by 30.7%. [[Image:Waste generation, excluding major mineral waste, EU, 2004-2022 (million tonnes).png|thumb|center|800px|Table 2: Waste generation, excluding major mineral waste, EU, 2004-2022
(million tonnes)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_wasgen}}|alt= Table showing waste generation excluding major mineral waste by economic activities and households in million tonnes for selected years between 2004 and 2022. A table column also shows the percentage change between 2022 and 2004. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Hazardous waste generation=== Hazardous waste may pose an elevated risk to human health and to the environment if not managed and disposed of safely. Among the waste generated in the EU in 2022, 119.0 million tonnes (5.3% of the total) were classified as hazardous waste. Compared with 2010, 31.1% more hazardous waste was generated in 2022 in the EU. This is an increase in quantity terms from 90.8 to 119.0 million tonnes. A substantial increase was observed between 2020 and 2022 (25%), largely attributed to an almost eightfold rise in the volume of hazardous waste in Finland during this period. In 2022, the share of hazardous waste in total waste generation was between 0.7% in Romania and 24.6% in Finland. Among the non-EU countries shown in Figure 4, Türkiye recorded the highest share of hazardous waste in total waste generation (24.8%) and was followed by Montenegro (23.3%), North Macedonia (21.6%), Serbia (16.9%) and Norway (13.5%). [[Image:Figure 4 Hazardous waste generated, 2010 and 2022 (% share of total waste)V1.png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Hazardous waste generated, 2010 and 2022
(% share of total waste )
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_wasgen}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing hazardous waste generated as percentage share of total waste for the EU, individual EU Member States, Liechtenstein, Iceland, Norway, Montenegro, Türkiye, North Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Each country has two columns representing the years 2010 and 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Waste treatment=== In 2022, some 1 992 million tonnes of waste were treated in the EU. This does not include exported waste but includes the treatment of waste imported into the EU. The reported amounts are therefore not directly comparable with those on waste generation. Figure 5 shows the development of total waste treatment in the EU, as well as for the two main treatment categories – recovery and disposal – during the period 2004-2022. The quantity of waste [[Glossary:Recovery of waste|recovered]], in other words recycled, used for backfilling (the use of waste in excavated areas for the purpose of slope reclamation or safety or for engineering purposes in landscaping) or incinerated with energy recovery, increased by 40.6% from 870 million tonnes in 2004 to 1 223 million tonnes in 2022; as a result, the share of such recovery in total waste treatment rose from 45.9% in 2004 to 61.4% in 2022. The quantity of waste subject to disposal decreased from 1 027 million tonnes in 2004 to 769 million tonnes in 2022, which was a decrease of 25.1%. The share of disposal in total waste treatment decreased from 54.1% in 2004 to 38.6% in 2022. [[Image:Figure5 Waste treatment, EU, 2004-2022 (Index 2004 = 100).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Waste treatment, EU, 2004-2022
(Index 2004 = 100)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_wastrt}}|alt= Line chart showing waste treatment with the year 2004 indexed at 100 for the EU. Three lines represent recovery, total and disposal over the years 2004 to 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] As stated above, in the EU in 2022, more than a half (61.4%) of the waste was treated in recovery operations: recycling (40.8% of the total treated waste), backfilling (14.2%) or energy recovery (6.4%). The remaining 38.6% was either landfilled (30.2%), incinerated without energy recovery (0.4%) or disposed of otherwise (8.0%). Significant differences could be observed among the EU countries regarding the use they made of these various treatment methods. For instance, some countries had very high recycling rates (Italy, Belgium, Slovakia and Latvia), in others landfill is the prevailing treatment category (Romania, Bulgaria, Finland, see Figure 6). [[Image:F6 Waste treatment by type of recovery and disposal, 2022 (% of total treatment).png |thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Waste treatment by type of recovery and disposal, 2022
(% of total treatment)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_wastrt}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing waste treatment by type of recovery and disposal as percentage of total treatment for the EU, individual EU countries, Iceland, Norway, Serbia, Montenegro, Türkiye, North Macedonia and Kosovo. Totalling 100 %, each country column has five stacks representing recovery - recycling, energy recovery, recovery - backfilling, disposal - landfill and other, and disposal - incineration without energy recovery for the year 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Hazardous waste treatment=== In total, 99.6 million tonnes of hazardous waste were treated in the EU in 2022, with more than 70% of this treated in just four EU countries, Finland (29.3 million tonnes or 29.5% of EU total),Germany (21.4 million tonnes or 21.5% o), Bulgaria (13.7 million tonnes or 13.7%), and France (7.5 million tonnes or 7.5%) see Figure 7. [[Image:Figure 7 Hazardous waste treatment, 2022 (million tonnes).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 7: Hazardous waste treatment, 2022
(million tonnes)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_wastrt}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing hazardous waste treatment in million tonnes for individual EU Member States, Iceland, Norway, Serbia, Montenegro, Türkiye and North Macedonia for the year 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2022, 36.4% of the hazardous waste treated in the EU was recovered: 30.0% by recycling or backfilling (67 kg per inhabitant) and 6.4% by energy recovery (14 kg per inhabitant, see Figure 8). The remaining 63.6% were incinerated without energy recovery (4.1% or 9 kg per inhabitant), landfilled, in other words deposited into or onto land or through land treatment (41% or 91 kg per inhabitant) or disposed of by other way (18.5% or 41 kg per inhabitant). [[Image:Figure 8 Hazardous wase treatmentV3.png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 8: Hazardous waste treatment, 2022
(kg per capita)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=env_wastrt}}|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing hazardous waste treatment in kg per capita for the EU, individual EU Member States, Iceland, Norway, Serbia, Montenegro and Türkiye. Each country column has five stacks representing recovery - recycling, recovery - backfilling, recovery - energy recovery, disposal - landfill and other, and disposal - incineration without energy recovery for the year 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Waste statistics 30 09 2024cor.xlsx|title=Waste statistics: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== In order to monitor the implementation of waste policy, in particular compliance with the principles of recovery and safe disposal, reliable statistics on the production and management of waste from businesses and private households are required. In 2002, {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32002R2150:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 2150/2002}} on waste statistics was adopted, creating a framework for harmonised Community statistics in this field. Starting with reference year 2004, the Regulation requires EU Member States to provide data on the generation, recovery and disposal of waste every 2 years. Data on waste generation and treatment are currently available for even reference years from 2004 to 2022. ===Context=== EU waste management policies aim to reduce the environmental and health impacts of waste and improve Europe's resource efficiency by extracting high-quality resources from waste as much as possible. The European Green Deal aims to promote growth by transitioning to a modern, resource-efficient and competitive economy. For more information see: [https://ec.europa.eu/environment/topics/waste-and-recycling_en Waste and recycling]. The Waste Framework Directive ({{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32008L0098:EN:NOT|title=Directive 98/2008/EC}} article 4) introduced a five-step waste hierarchy where prevention is the best option, followed by re-use, recycling and other forms of recovery, with disposal such as landfill as the last resort: *reduce the amount of waste generated; *maximise recycling and re-use; *limit incineration to non-recyclable materials; *phase out landfilling to non-recyclable and non-recoverable waste; *ensure full implementation of the waste policy targets in all EU Member States. ===Other articles=== *[[End-of-life vehicle statistics]] *[[Environmental economy – statistics on employment and growth|Environmental economy – statistics on employment and growth]] *[[Municipal waste statistics]] *[[Packaging waste statistics]] *[[Recycling – secondary material price indicator|Recycling — secondary material price indicator]] *[[Waste shipment statistics]] *[[Waste statistics - electrical and electronic equipment|Waste statistics — electrical and electronic equipment]] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-DK-20-001|title=Energy, transport and environment statistics}} — 2022 edition *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-32-10-283|title=Environmental statistics and accounts in Europe}} (2010) ===Database=== *https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/waste/database (env_was), see: :Waste generation and treatment (env_wasgt) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/waste/database Waste] (t_env_was), see: :Waste generation and treatment (t_env_wasgt) ===Thematic section=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/waste/overview Waste] ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-RA-13-015|title=Manual on waste statistics}} *{{Template:Esms|code=env_wasgt_esms|title=Waste generation and treatment}} (ESMS metadata file — env_wasgt_esms) ===Legislation=== *[http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:02002R2150-20090420:EN:NOT Regulation (EC) No 2150/2002] of 25 November 2002 on waste statistics *[http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32010R0849 Regulation (EU) No 849/2010] of 27 September 2010 amending Regulation (EC) No 2150/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council on waste statistics ===External links=== *[http://ec.europa.eu/environment/waste/index.htm European Commission — DG Environment — Waste in the EU] *[http://www.eea.europa.eu/themes/waste European Environment Agency — Waste and material resources] *[http://ec.europa.eu/environment/waste/strategy.htm Thematic strategy on the prevention and recycling of waste] {{Unit|topic=X_Environment}} [[Category:Environment and energy|Waste statistics]] [[Category:Waste|Waste statistics]] [[Category:Statistical_article|Waste statistics]] [[Category:October2026|Waste statistics]]

title: Waste shipment statistics
text:
EU statistics provide an analysis of the waste shipment. Data extracted in October 2025 Planned article update: December 2026 Between 2010 and 2021, exports of hazardous waste from EU countries increased substantially, from 6.1 million tonnes to 9.6 million tonnes. In 2023, exports of hazardous waste from EU countries fell to 7.0 million tonnes. In 2023, 72.1% of the hazardous waste exported by EU countries was treated through recovery processes, 27.8% by disposal. [[Image: WasteShip_IntroFig_RY2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Treatment of hazardous waste exported by EU countries, 2010-2023
''Source: '' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_wasship__custom_18860697/default/table env_wasship])| alt= A bar chart showing the treatment of hazardous waste exported by EU countries between 2010 and 2023. The vertical axis displays the values in millions tonnes, while the horizontal axis displays the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article reports the hazardous and non-hazardous waste exported by EU countries to other EU countries and to countries outside the EU. The data are analysed by the type of waste, the main destinations, waste treatments in the destination, as well as the EU country with the highest exported quantity for each waste category. There is also a special section analysing exports of [[Glossary:Waste_electrical_and_electronic_equipment_(WEEE)|waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE)]] (also known as ‘e-waste’). * The largest share of hazardous waste exported by the EU countries is waste stemming from construction, civil engineering and demolition activities. * Exports of hazardous waste from EU countries increased steadily from 6.1 million tonnes in 2010 to 9.6 million tonnes in 2021. Since 2021, the tonnage of exports has decreased, falling to 9.0 million tonnes in 2022 and fell again in 2023, when 7.0 million tonnes was exported. * [[Glossary:Landfilling|Landfilling]] (D1) of hazardous waste exported by EU countries initially peaked at 698 000 tonnes in 2017, before falling to 421 000 tonnes in 2020. Since then, it has risen above the 2017 peak, reaching 727 000 tonnes in 2023. * ''R4: [[Glossary:Recycling_of_waste|Recycling]]/[[Glossary:Recovery_of_waste|reclamation]] of metals and metal compounds'', ''R5: Recycling/reclamation of other inorganic compounds'', and ''R1: Use as a fuel (other than in direct incineration) or other means to generate energy'' dominate the treatment of exported hazardous waste dominate the treatment of exported hazardous waste. In particular, ''R5: Recycling/reclamation of other inorganic compounds'' increased from 0.6 million tonnes in 2010 to 1.5 million tonnes in 2023 (peaking at 1.8 million in 2021 and 2022). * EU countries primarily export their hazardous waste to other EU countries; between 2014 and 2023, this share has fluctuated between 89% and 91%. Since 2010, small tonnages of exports of hazardous waste to non-OECD countries have been registered (<5% of total hazardous waste exports in each year). * In 2023, EU countries exported 136 930 tonnes of ‘Waste electrical and electronic equipment’ (WEEE) containing hazardous substances, but only 20 963 tonnes of non-hazardous WEEE. === Exports of hazardous waste – total quantities and per capita === Hazardous waste is waste which is harmful to humans or to the environment. Annex III of the Waste Framework Directive ({{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02008L0098-20180705:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2008/98/EC}} on waste) provides a list of properties which renders waste hazardous. This list includes properties such as the waste being explosive, oxidizing, flammable, irritant, harmful, toxic or releasing toxic gases when in contact with eater, air or an acid, corrosive, infectious, as well as waste which is capable of causing a hypersensitization reaction or may induce cancer, congenital malformations or hereditary genetic defects. It also includes waste that may present risks for one or more sectors of the environment. Between 2010 and 2023, the amount of hazardous waste exported from EU countries increased from 6.1 million tonnes in 2010 to 7.0 million tonnes in 2023 (see Table 1). There was a sharp upturn in exports from 2016 to 2017, increasing by more than one fifth from 6.1 to 7.4 million tonnes (+22%), followed by a steady increase to 2020 where exports reached 8.2 million tonnes. The tonnage of hazardous waste exports then rose sharply and peaked at 9.6 million tonnes in 2021 before steadily decreasing to 7.0 million in 2023. In 2023, the EU countries accounting for the highest quantities of exported hazardous waste were Italy (1.6 million tonnes), Germany and the Netherlands (both 0.9 million tonnes). France’s hazardous waste exports reduced from 2.4 million in 2022 (the highest quantity of exported hazardous waste in that year) to 0.6 million tonnes in 2023. [[Image:Exports of hazardous waste, 2010-2023 (thousand tonnes) V2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Exports of hazardous waste, 2010-2023
''Source: '' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_wasship__custom_18860964/default/table env_wasship])| alt= A table showing the exports of hazardous waste between 2010 and 2023 in thousands tonnes in the EU, EU countries and some EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Overall, the EU exported 15.6 kg of hazardous waste per inhabitant in 2023, down from 20.2 kg per capita recorded in 2022. Luxembourg exported 624.8 kg of hazardous waste per inhabitant. Other EU countries with notable exports of hazardous waste were Malta (77.5 kg), Denmark (56.5 kg), Belgium (53.8 kg), Netherlands (51.8 kg), and Ireland (42.1 kg) (see Table 2). In 2023, 14 of the EU countries who reported data exported less than 10 kg of hazardous waste per inhabitant. [[Image:Exports of hazardous waste, 2010-2023 (kilogrammes per capita) V2.png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Exports of hazardous waste, 2010-2023
''Source: '' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_wasship__custom_18861265/default/table env_wasship])| alt= A table showing the exports of hazardous waste between 2010 and 2023 in kilogrammes per capita in the EU, EU countries and some EFTA countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Exports of hazardous waste between EU countries and out of the EU === In 2023, 7.0 million tonnes of hazardous waste were exported from an EU country to another (see Table 3), corresponding to approximately 91.4% of the exports of hazardous waste. [[Image:Destinations of hazardous waste exported by EU Member States, 2010-2023 (thousand tonnes) V2.png|thumb|centre|500px|Table 3: Destinations of hazardous waste exported by EU countries, 2010-2023
''Source: '' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_wasship__custom_18861419/default/table env_wasship])| alt= A table showing the destinations of hazardous waste exported by EU countries between 2010 and 2023 in kilogrammes per capita in other EU countries, some EFTA countries and OECD (non-EFTA) countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The exports of hazardous waste from EU to [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA]] countries, chiefly Switzerland and Norway, declined to 426 thousand tonnes in 2023. This corresponded to 6.1% of the total export of such waste. The exports to other [[Glossary:Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development_(OECD)|OECD]] countries, outside the EU and EFTA, amounted to 174 thousand tonnes in 2023. This constituted 2.5% of the total. The main destinations among these countries were the United Kingdom (71.3%) and Turkey (27.7%). === Treatment of exported hazardous waste === The amount of hazardous waste exported from EU countries for disposal was 1.9 million tonnes in 2023, an increase from 1.8 million tonnes in 2022. The amount exported for recovery remained between 4.3 – 4.5 million between 2010 and 2016. Between 2016 and 2021, however, there was a sharp increase from 4.3 million to 7.9 million tonnes. The tonnage exported for recovery then fell in 2022 to 7.2 million tonnes and again decreased to 5.0 million tonnes in 2023. Figure 1 shows the shares of the hazardous waste exported by EU countries for recovery or disposal in the destination countries. In general, as a percentage of the total shipments, the share for recovery increased from 71.8% in 2010 to a peak of 82.4% in 2021. It then decreased slightly to 80.0% in 2022, and again to 72.1% in 2023. Correspondingly, the share for disposal has followed a decreasing trend over the same period from 28.1% in 2010 to 17.6% in 2021. However, the percentage exported for disposal rose to 19.9% in 2022 and then to 27.8% in 2023. The treatment is unknown or is a mix of recovery and disposal for only a fractional share of the exported hazardous waste, with a share well below 1% in most years; it only exceeded 1% in 2016 (1.2%). [[Image:WasteShip_Fig1_RY2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Treatment of hazardous waste exported by EU countries, 2010-2023
''Source: '' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_wasship__custom_18860697/default/table env_wasship])| alt= A bar chart showing the treatment of hazardous waste exported by EU countries between 2010 and 2023. The vertical axis displays the percentage, while the horizontal axis displays the years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, the main treatment categories for exported hazardous waste were ''R5: recycling/reclamation of other inorganic materials'' (1.5 million tonnes) and ''R4: recycling/reclamation of metals and metal compounds'' (1.3 million tonnes) (see Figure 2). [[Image:WasteShip_Fig2_RY2023.png|thumb|centre|650px|Figure 2: Main treatments of hazardous waste exported by EU countries, 2013 and 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat (detailed Excel data file available on [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/b01d2930-990e-44fb-9121-a9a6b00a1283/library/06c7f542-5d74-4379-8b15-fbca2113f0ae/details EU Commission web-based open-source application])| alt= A horizontal bar chart showing the main treatments of hazardous waste exported by EU countries between 2012 and 2023 in thousand tonnes. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2023, around 861 000 million tonnes of exported hazardous waste were ''[[Glossary:Incineration|incinerated]]'' with energy recovery (''R1: Use as fuel'') and 590 000 tonnes without energy (''D10:Incineration on land''), together accounting for more than one fifth (20.8%) of the total treatment of exported hazardous waste. Among the disposal activities, ''D1: Deposit into or onto land (landfilling)'' of exported hazardous waste increased from 657 000 tonnes in 2022 to 727 000 tonnes in 2023 (the highest amount since 2010). From 2013 to 2017, landfilling grew continuously, rising from 417 000 tonnes in 2013 to 698 000 tonnes in 2017, when it reached a peak. Between 2017 and 2020, the tonnage landfilled has decreased and in 2020 421 000 tonnes were treated by landfill. Since 2020, landfilling has increased again, reaching a new peak (727 000 tonnes) in 2023. Exports of hazardous waste for ''R5: Recycling/reclamation of other inorganic materials'' also increased since 2011. The amount of ''R5: Recycling/reclamation of other inorganic materials'' was 0.5 million tonnes in 2011 and has risen to 1.5 million tonnes in 2023, peaking to 1.8 million tonnes in 2021. ''R4: Recycling and reclamation of metals'', however, has remained fairly constant, hovering around 1.3 million tonnes between 2010 and 2023, apart from small peaks in 2014 (1.5 million) and 2021 (1.6 million). === Waste shipment based on the European List of Waste (LoW) codes === A more detailed understanding of exports (‘transboundary waste shipments’) is possible by supplementing the information based on reporting under the Basel Convention presented above with the codes of the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02000D0532-20150601:EN:NOT|title=European List of Waste (LoW)}} classification about the types of waste crossing the borders. It is possible to link waste identified by a European LoW code to the most common treatment for the waste exported, to identify the main EU countries exporting the different waste categories and the main destination countries for these exports. === Hazardous waste — main treatment, exporting EU country and destination === [[Image:Top 10 hazardous wastes exported, by European List of Waste (LoW) code, main treatments, exporting EU Member States and destination countries, 2023 (tonnes).png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 4: Top 10 hazardous wastes exported, by European List of Waste (LoW) code, main treatments, exporting EU coutries and destination countries, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat (detailed Excel data file available on [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/b01d2930-990e-44fb-9121-a9a6b00a1283/library/06c7f542-5d74-4379-8b15-fbca2113f0ae/details EU Commission web-based open-source application])| alt= A table showing the top 10 hazardous wastes exported, by European List of Waste (LoW) code, main treatments, exporting EU countries and destination countries in 2023 in tonnes. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Table 4 shows that a large part of the exported hazardous waste comes from construction and demolition activities (LoW chapter 17) such as ''Bituminous mixtures containing coal tar'' (17 03 01*) and ''Soil and stones containing dangerous substances'' (17 05 03*). ''Bituminous mixtures containing coal tar'' (17 03 01*) covers construction and demolition wastes, more specifically excavated roads, parking spaces and other tarred surfaces, etc. This is mainly treated through ''R5: Recycling/reclamation of other inorganic materials'' (87% of the total exports of this waste category). The main source for export of this waste among EU countries was Germany, which accounted for 66% of the total exported amount from EU countries in 2023. The waste was primarily transported to the Netherlands, which treated 87% of the exported total. In 2023, 43% of the exported ''Soil and stones containing dangerous substances'' (17 05 03*) were mainly treated by ''D1: Deposit into or onto land, (e.g., landfill, etc.)''. Italy, with 303 988 tonnes (49% of the total), was the main exporting EU country. Germany was the main destination, receiving 268 697 tonnes of the exports from EU countries (44% of the total). Waste from waste management facilities (LoW codes starting with 19) is also exported in high quantities. A large part of the waste residues from waste treatment (Basel code Y-18) comes from mechanical waste treatment (sorting, crushing etc.), including waste from LoW subchapter 19 12 which includes ''Other wastes (including mixtures of materials) from mechanical treatment of waste containing dangerous substances'' (19 12 11*) and ''Wood containing dangerous substances'' (19 12 06*). Other important waste types from waste treatment facilities include ''Wastes from physico/chemical treatments'' (LoW subchapter 19 02), including ''Premixed wastes composed of at least one hazardous substance'' (19 02 04*) featured in the top 10 of hazardous wastes exported from EU countries in 2023, as well as ''Fly ash containing dangerous substances'' (19 01 13*). ''Solid wastes from gas treatment containing dangerous substances'' (10 02 07*) also appeared in the top 10 list in 2023. It refers primarily to the treatment of bottom ash from the iron and steel industry. This is almost exclusively treated in recycling operations for the ''R4: Recycling/reclamation of metals and metal compounds'' (89% of the total exports of this waste category) found in this ash. The main source in the EU for this waste was Austria, accounting for 18% of the total exported amount. The waste was primarily sent to Germany, which treated 33% of the total. Other hazardous waste categories also exported in high quantities are ''Lead batteries'' (16 06 01*), which are the third highest exported waste type, ''Track ballast containing dangerous substances'' (17 05 07*), and ''Mineral-based non-chlorinated engine, gear and lubricating oils'' (13 02 05*). === Non-hazardous waste – main treatment, exporting EU country and destination === [[Image:WasteShip_Table5_RY2023.png|thumb|centre|800px|Table 5: Top 10 non-hazardous wastes exported, by European List of Waste (LoW) code, main treatments, exporting EU countries and destination countries, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat (detailed Excel data file available on [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/b01d2930-990e-44fb-9121-a9a6b00a1283/library/06c7f542-5d74-4379-8b15-fbca2113f0ae/details EU Commission web-based open-source application])| alt= A table showing the top 10 non-hazardous wastes exported, by European List of Waste (LoW) code, main treatments, exporting EU countries and destination countries in 2023 in tonnes. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] EU countries exported 18.8 million tonnes of non-hazardous wastes in 2023.Non-hazardous waste exported by European List of Waste (LoW) codes; mixed codes are not included Table 5 shows the top 10 non-hazardous waste types according to the European LoW. These 10 most exported waste categories added up to 16.5 million tonnes, corresponding to 88% of the total exports of non-hazardous waste from EU countries in 2023. Construction and demolition activities (LoW chapter 17) accounted for a large share of the exports of non-hazardous waste (approximately 7.0 million tonnes, or 37% of the total), with ''Soil and stones other than those containing hazardous substances'' (17 05 04) as the largest category in the list. This waste was primarily exported for ''R5: Recycling and reclamation of other inorganic materials'', with a share of 96% of the total exported quantity of this category. Belgium accounted for 33% of the total exports of this waste category in 2023. France was the main destination, with 2.2 million tonnes (36%). Waste from waste treatment (LoW chapter 19) made up three of the four most exported waste categories at the top of the list in 2023. Almost 3.3 million tonnes of ''Other wastes (including mixtures of materials) from mechanical treatment of wastes, other than those containing hazardous substances'' (19 12 12) were exported from EU countries in 2023. The main exporting country was Italy (45% of the total), while the main destination was the Germany (21% of the total). The main treatment, covering 70% of the exported quantity, was ''R1: Use as fuel or to generate energy''. Of the 2.8 million tonnes of waste of ''Wood not containing hazardous substances'' (19 12 07), 56% was for ''R3: Recycling or reclamation of organic substances''. France was the main exporting country of this category (39% of the total). The main destination for these exports of wood waste was Germany (19% of the total). === Waste of electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE)=== In 2023, EU countries exported 136 930 tonnes of ''Waste of electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE)'' containing hazardous substances and 20 963 tonnes of non-hazardous WEEE. Table 6 shows the quantities of different types of hazardous and non-hazardous notified waste of electrical and electronic equipment exported in 2023. [[Image:Waste of electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) exported, by European List of Waste (LoW) codes, EU, 2023.png|thumb|centre|500px|Table 6: Waste of electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) exported, by European List of Waste (LoW) codes, EU, 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat (detailed Excel data file available on [https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/b01d2930-990e-44fb-9121-a9a6b00a1283/library/06c7f542-5d74-4379-8b15-fbca2113f0ae/details EU Commission web-based open-source application])| alt= A table showing the waste of electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) exported, by European List of Waste (LoW) codes in the EU in 2023 in tonnes. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] WEEE exported from EU countries is mostly recovered, with 87% of the total recovered. 19% of all exported WEEE is classified as ''R4: Recycling/reclamation of metals and metal compounds'', 17% as ''R3: Recycling/reclamation of organic substances which are not used as solvents'', 13% as ''R1: Use as a fuel'', and 6% as ''R5: Recycling/reclamation of other inorganic materials are the primary recovery operations''. === Source data for tables and graphs === * [[Media:WasteShipments 2025-10 RY2023 V2.xlsx|Waste shipment statistics – reference year 2023]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]]
'''''[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_wasship/default/table?lang=en&category=env.env_was.env_wasst/ Data from 2010 to the most recent reference year available] can be found on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/explore/all/envir?sort=category&lang=en&subtheme=env.env_was&display=list Eurostat Database dedicated section on Waste (env_was)]'''''
=== Data sources === The main source for this article is the data reported by EU countries according to the '''Waste Shipment Regulation'''. In the EU, exports of waste are regulated by {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02006R1013-20130410:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1013/2006}} on shipments of waste, commonly referred to as the Waste Shipment Regulation (WShipR). It implements the [http://www.basel.int/ Basel Convention], which bans exports of hazardous waste from [[Glossary:Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)|OECD]] countries to non-OECD countries. According to the WShipR, all hazardous waste as well as some problematic waste streams and other wastes defined in the WShipR, must be notified to the authorities before being shipped across borders. EU countries must report the precise treatment of the hazardous waste. The treatment of waste is broken down by recovery and disposal operations, as listed in Annexes I and II to the Waste Framework Directive ({{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02008L0098-20180705:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2008/98/EC}} on waste). Information about notified shipped waste can be greatly enhanced when countries also indicate the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02000D0532-20150601:EN:NOT|title=European List of Waste (LoW)}} in addition to the Basel codes. The main extra information relates to: * the type of waste shipped across borders; * the processes behind the generation of the wastes; * special hazardousness or hazardous substances contained in the waste; * possibilities for assessing required waste treatment capacities. The shipment notification application form used in the EU is included as Annex VII of the WShipR. It asks for information on: * Basel Y-codes according to Annexes I and II of the Basel Convention (47 different code numbers are available, 45 of which concern hazardous waste); * detailed Basel codes according to Annexes VIII and IX of the Convention (120 code numbers are available, 60 of which concern hazardous waste); * OECD codes (150 different code numbers are available, 60 of which concern hazardous waste); * European List of Waste codes (842 code numbers are available, 408 of which concern hazardous waste). The submitted data regarding transboundary shipments of waste covers both waste shipped out of and into EU countries. '''Definitions''' The term '[[Glossary:Export|exports]]' is used for transboundary waste movements (‘shipments’) both within the EU and in particular for movements of waste to other OECD countries. Detailed information on exports of waste based on the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02000D0532-20150601:EN:NOT|title=European List of Waste (LoW)}} classification is also provided. The recovery (R) and disposal (D) codes refer to the operations included in Annex IA of the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02006R1013-20210111:EN:NOT|title=Waste Shipment Regulation (WShipR) (Regulation (EC) No 1013/2006)}} and Annexes I and II of the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02008L0098-20180705:EN:NOT|title=Waste Framework Directive (WFD) (Directive 2008/98/EC)}}. Hazardous waste is waste which is harmful to humans or to the environment. Annex III of the Waste Framework Directive ({{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02008L0098-20180705:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2008/98/EC}} on waste) provides a list of properties which renders waste hazardous. Waste from electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) includes a large range of devices such as computers, fridges and mobile phones at the end of their life. This type of waste contains a complex mixture of materials, some of which are hazardous. These can cause major environmental and health problems if the discarded devices are not managed properly. In addition, modern electronics contain rare and expensive resources, which can be recycled and re-used if the waste is effectively managed. Shipments of WEEE cannot be identified under the Basel Y-codes, but different types of WEEE can be distinguished using the LoW codes, including hazardous WEEE and non-hazardous notified WEEE exports. '''Context''' According to the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02006R1013-20210111:EN:NOT|title=Waste Shipment Regulation (WShipR) (Regulation (EC) No 1013/2006)}}, all hazardous waste as well as some problematic waste streams and other wastes defined by the WShipR, must be notified to the authorities before it is allowed to be shipped across national borders. Article 51(1) of the WShipR states that, before the end of each calendar year, each EU country shall send to the [[Glossary:European Commission (EC)|European Commission]] a copy of the report for the previous calendar year on the quantities of notified transboundary shipped waste and the quantity of hazardous waste generated which, in accordance with Article 13(3) of the Basel Convention, it has drawn up and submitted to the Convention Secretariat. In November 2021, the European Commission presented a {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52021PC0709:EN:NOT|title=Proposal for a new Regulation on Shipments of Waste}}. In January 2023, the European Parliament adopted [https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-9-2023-0003_EN.pdf amendments on the Commission’s proposal]. In line with the objectives set out in the European Green Deal, the Circular Economy Action Plan and the review clauses in the Waste Framework Directive (WFD), in February 2022 launched an [https://environment.ec.europa.eu/news/waste-framework-directive-revision-2022-02-14_en open consultation for revision of the Waste Framework Directive (WFD)]. The aim was to gather evidence to improve the overall environmental outcome of waste management in line with the waste hierarchy and the implementation of the polluter pays principle. [[Glossary:Eurostat|Eurostat]] publishes data and analysis on transboundary [[Glossary:Waste|waste]] shipments in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]] since 2011. The data and analysis cover various aspects of waste shipments, generally on an aggregated level. The quantity of [[Glossary:Waste_electrical_and_electronic_equipment_(WEEE)|waste electrical and electronic equipment]] (widely known as WEEE or e-waste) generated every year in the EU is increasing rapidly. It is now one of the fastest growing waste streams. The EU has introduced the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02012L0019-20180704:EN:NOT|title=Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Directive (WEEE Directive)}} and the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02011L0065-20160715:EN:NOT|title=Restriction of the use of certain Hazardous Substances in Electrical and Electronic Equipment Directive (RoHS Directive)}} to tackle the issue of the growing amount of WEEE. === Other articles === * [[Waste statistics]] * [[Municipal waste statistics]] * [[Packaging waste statistics]] * [[End-of-life vehicle statistics]] * [[Waste statistics - electrical and electronic equipment]] * [[Recycling – secondary material price indicator]] === Selected Datasets === * [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=t_env_was Waste], see: :Waste streams (t_env_wasst) === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/explore/all/envir?sort=category&lang=en&subtheme=env.env_was&display=list Waste], see: ::Waste streams [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/explore/all/envir?sort=category&lang=en&subtheme=env.env_was&display=list Waste stream (env_wasst)] :::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_wasship/default/table?lang=en&category=env.env_was.env_wasst Transboundary shipments of notified waste by partner, hazardousness and waste management operations (env_wasship)] === Thematic section === * [{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=waste}} Eurostat´s dedicated website on Waste] === Publications === * {{Template:Publication|code=KS-DK-20-001|title=Energy, transport and environment indicators – 2020 edition}} * {{Template:Publication|code=KS-RA-13-015|title=Manual on waste statistics}} ‎ ===Legislation === * {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02008L0098-20180705:EN:NOT|title=Directive 2008/98/EC Waste Framework Directive (WFD)}} * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/LSU/?uri=CELEX:32008L0098 Summaries of EU legislation: EU waste management law] * {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:02006R1013-20130410:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EC) No 1013/2006 Waste Shipment Regulation (WShipR)}} * [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/LSU/?uri=CELEX:32006R1013 Summaries of EU legislation: Safe waste shipments within the EU and with non-EU countries] === External links === * European Commission - title: Water statistics
text:
EU statistics on fresh water resources, water abstraction, water use and waste water show how the EU concentrates on this resource. Data extracted in July 2026 Planned article update: July 2027 Among the EU countries, Croatia recorded the highest renewable freshwater resources (with a long-term average of 30 600 m³ per inhabitant), followed by Finland (19 600 m³), Estonia (18 700 m³), Sweden (18 200 m³) and Latvia (18 000 m³). Water resources have remained stable compared to last year. Over the last few decades, an increasing share of the population has been connected to wastewater treatment.
Water is essential for life, and an indispensable resource for the economy. It also plays a fundamental role in the climate regulation cycle. The management and protection of water resources including fresh and salt water ecosystems and the water we drink and bathe in is therefore one of the cornerstones of environmental protection in the EU. This article presents water statistics in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. It is based on data on [[Glossary:Freshwater resources|freshwater resources]], [[Glossary:Water abstraction|water abstraction]], [[Glossary:Water use|water use]] and [[Glossary:Wastewater|wastewater]] treatment and disposal. ===Water as a resource=== Water resources refer to the freshwater available for use in a country and include [[Glossary:Surface water|surface waters]] (lakes, rivers and streams) and [[Glossary:Groundwater|groundwater]]. Renewable water resources are calculated as the sum of [[Glossary:Internal flow|internal flow]] (which is [[Glossary:Precipitation|precipitation]] minus actual [[Glossary:Evapotranspiration|evapotranspiration]]) and [[Glossary:External inflow|external inflow]]. Freshwater availability in a country is primarily determined by climate conditions and transboundary water flows (in other words, external inflows), while for total amounts, the size of the country matters. Freshwater resources per inhabitant are considered an important indicator for measuring the sustainability of water resources. For EU countries, average water resources are about 8-9 thousand m³ per inhabitant. In water-rich countries an inhabitant's share can be as high as around 30 thousand m³ (Croatia) or close to 67 thousand m³(Norway). According to the World water development report of the United Nations, a country experiences 'water stress' when its annual water resources are below 1700 m³ per inhabitant; among the EU countries, this is the case in Poland, Czechia, Cyprus and Malta. [[Image:Table 1 Renewable freshwater resources - long-term annual average (million m³).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Renewable freshwater resources - long-term annual average
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_wat_ltaa__custom_22250775/default/table (env_wat_ltaa)] and [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/01fb1faf-75e4-4179-bc3f-a1656bd6474a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-29T08:35:00Z (demo_gind)]|alt= Table showing renewable freshwater resources long-term annual average over 30 years in million cubic metres in individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Norway, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Türkiye and Kosovo. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Many countries receive a significant proportion of their renewable freshwater resources as external inflow (see Figure 1). Within the EU, four countries — Hungary (95.1%), the Netherlands (89.0%), Bulgaria (83.5%) and Slovakia (82.4%) — obtain more than 80% of their renewable freshwater resources from external sources, making them highly dependent on transboundary water resources. [[Image:Share of external inflow from neighbouring territories in renewable freshwater resources - long-term average_(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Share of external inflow from neighbouring territories in renewable freshwater resources - long-term average
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/env_wat_ltaa__custom_22250775/default/table (env_wat_ltaa)]|alt= Vertical bar chart showing percentage share of external inflow from neighbouring territories in renewable freshwater resources as a long term average over 30 years in individual EU Member States, Switzerland, Norway, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Türkiye and Kosovo. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Water uses=== The overall use of water resources can be considered sustainable in the long-term in most of Europe. However, specific regions may face problems associated with water scarcity; this is the case particularly in parts of southern Europe, where it is likely that efficiency gains in agricultural water use (as well as other uses) will need to be achieved in order to prevent seasonal water shortages. Regions associated with low rainfall, high population density, or intensive agricultural or industrial activity may also face sustainability issues in the coming years, which could be exacerbated by climate change impacts on water availability and water management practices. Water is provided either by public water supply (public or private systems with public access) or is self-supplied (for example, private wells). While the share of the public water supply sector in total water abstraction depends on the economic structure of a given country and can be relatively small, it is nevertheless often the focus of public interest, as it comprises the water volumes that are directly used by the population. Table 2 presents households' water use from public supply. It varies across European countries - the median is around 40-50 cubic metres per inhabitant and has been decreasing slightly over the last few decades. [[Image:Household water use from public water supply, 1990-2024 (m³ per inhabitant).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 2: Household water use from public water supply, 1990-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8b144885-1192-4f86-8f45-72d9a8687d46?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-29T09:40:46Z (env_wat_cat)], [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/01fb1faf-75e4-4179-bc3f-a1656bd6474a?lang=en&createdAt=2026-07-29T08:35:00Z (demo_gind)]|alt= Table showing household water use from public water supply in cubic metres per inhabitant in individual EU Member States, Iceland, Switzerland, Norway, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Albania, Türkiye and Kosovo for the years 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020 and 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Wastewater treatment and disposal=== Overall, there is a development towards a higher proportion of the population being connected to wastewater treatment. Table 3 presents information on the proportion of the population connected to at least secondary wastewater treatment plants, which typically is an acceptable level of environmental protection unless the receiving waters are in a sensitive area. This share has been generally increasing over the past decades and was above 80% in half of the EU countries for which recent data are available (mixed reference years). The share of the population connected to at least secondary wastewater treatment plant even rose to 95% and above in 6 countries (Denmark, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Austria and Sweden), as well as in Switzerland. At the other end of the range, only in Croatia less than 1 in 2 households were connected to at least secondary urban wastewater treatment plants, while the same was also true in Albania, Serbia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina. For several countries, recent data were missing. [[Image:Share of the population connected to at least secondary urban wastewater treatment, 2000-2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 3: Share of the population connected to at least secondary urban wastewater treatment, 2000-2024
(%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sdg_06_20}}|alt= Table showing percentage share of the population connected to at least secondary urban wastewater treatment in the EU, individual EU Member States, Iceland, Switzerland, Norway, United Kingdom, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Albania and Türkiye for the years 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2023 and 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:SE-Water-statistics-2026.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== Water statistics are collected through the joint OECD/Eurostat questionnaire on inland waters, which is an established data collection yielding long time series. However, data collection is on a voluntary basis, which leads to considerable data gaps. The joint questionnaire on inland waters includes the following characteristics: *freshwater resources in groundwater and surface water — these can be replenished by precipitation and external inflow (water flowing into a country from other territories); *water abstraction — a major pressure on resources, although a large part of the water abstracted for domestic, industrial (including energy production) or agricultural use may be returned to the environment and its water bodies (although often as wastewater with impaired quality); *water use — analysed by supply category and by industrial activities; *the share of the population connected to wastewater treatment plants — which gives an overview of the development status of the infrastructure, in terms of quantity and quality, that is available for the protection of the environment from pollution by wastewater; *sewage sludge production and disposal — an inevitable product of wastewater treatment processes, its impact on the environment depends on the methods chosen for its processing and disposal; *generation and discharge of wastewater — pollutants present in wastewater have different source profiles and, similarly, the efficiency of treatment of any pollutant varies according to the method applied  Discharges from cooling water are not regarded as wastewater in water statistics.. In general, Eurostat collects national data. Some of the characteristics above are also collected at the level of river basin districts by means of a regional questionnaire. A large amount of data and other information on water is accessible via [http://water.europa.eu/ WISE], the water information system for Europe, which is hosted by the [http://www.eea.europa.eu/ European Environment Agency (EEA)] in Copenhagen. ===Context=== '''Water policies: floods, droughts and other challenges''' The EU's water policy over the past 30 years has been focused on the protection of water resources, ensuring that good quality water, in sufficient quantity, is available for all legitimate uses. The central element of European water policy is a Directive for '{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32000L0060:EN:NOT|title=Community action in the field of water policy}}' (2000/60/EC) — often referred to as the Water Framework Directive (WFD) — which aims to achieve a good ecological and chemical status of European waters. Together with its daughter legislation ({{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32006L0118:EN:NOT|title=Directive 0118/2006}} and {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32007L0060:EN:NOT|title=Directive 0060/2007}}), the WFD focused on water management at the level of (in most cases transboundary) hydrological catchments (river basins). An important step in the course of its implementation involved establishing river basin management plans. The state of play is described by the {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52025DC0002:EN:NOT|title=sixth implementation report}} (2025). In a Communication '{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52025DC0280:EN:NOT|title=European Water Resilience Strategy}}' (COM(2025) 280 final), the European Commission aims to help the EU improve the way we manage water while making our businesses more competitive and innovative. The Commission will work towards water resilience by restoring and protecting the water cycle, thereby ensuring access to clean and affordable water for all, and at the same time by building a water-smart economy. In a [https://ec.europa.eu/environment/water/fitness_check_of_the_eu_water_legislation/documents/Water%20Fitness%20Check%20-%20SWD(2019)439%20-%20web.pdf Fitness check of the EU Water Framework Directive and related legislation (2019)], the Commission identified strengths and weaknesses of the existing legislation and explored the need for possible amendments. '''Wastewater''' In an effort to reduce pollutants discharged into the environment with wastewater, the EU has implemented legislation on {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:31991L0271:EN:NOT|title=urban wastewater treatment}} (Directive 1991/271/EC). The pollution of rivers, lakes and groundwater and water quality is affected by human activities such as industrial production, household discharges, or arable farming; a report on {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52007DC0120:EN:NOT|title=the protection of waters against pollution by nitrates from agricultural sources}} (COM(2007) 120 final) was released in March 2007. Another aspect of water quality relates to coastal bathing waters. The European Commission and the EEA present an [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/water/water-bathing/index_en.html annual bathing water report]. The latest of these always covers information of the preceding year and shows that more than 95% of the EU's bathing waters met the minimum water quality standards. '''Blueprint to safeguard Europe's water resources''' These policy perspectives up to 2050 were developed in the '{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52012DC0673:EN:NOT|title=Blueprint to safeguard Europe's water resources}}' (COM/2012/0673) which integrates the results of a policy review concerning: water scarcity and droughts; an analysis of the implementation of river basin management under the WFD; a review of the vulnerability of environmental resources (such as water, biodiversity and soil) to climate change impacts and man-made pressures; and a review of the whole of the EU's water policy framework in the light of the European Commission's 'better regulation' approach. The blueprint is closely related to the [http://ec.europa.eu/environment/resource_efficiency/about/roadmap/index_en.htm Resource efficiency roadmap] (COM(2011) 571). However, the blueprint covers a longer time span, through to 2050, and is expected to drive EU water policy over the long term. As part of the blueprint there are a number of policy reviews assessing implementation. ===Other articles=== *[[Agri-environmental indicator - irrigation]] *[[Waste statistics]] === Database ===
