title: Young people - digital world
text:
These statistics present the situation of children and young people across the European Union (EU) and how they interact with the digital world. Data extracted in a March 2026 Planned article update: March 2027 In 2025 in the EU, 98 % of young people used the internet daily, compared with 90 % of all individuals. In 2025, 76 % of young women and 73 % of young men in the EU had at least basic digital skills. In 2025, 41% of young people and 31% of all individuals in the EU who used the internet verified the information or content they found online. In 2025, 60% of young people and 33% of all individuals in the EU used generative AI in the 3 months before surveying. [[Glossary:Information and communication technology (ICT)|Information and communication technologies (ICT)]] have become an integral part of people’s everyday lives. A large proportion of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|EU]] population uses the internet for work, education, leisure, dealing with public administrations, and many other activities. In 2025, a high proportion of young people in the EU continued to make use of the internet for a range of activities that take up an increasing share of their daily lives. ===A digital age gap=== '''''98% of young people in the EU use the internet daily ''''' In 2025, 98% of young people aged 16-29 years in the EU used the internet every day, compared with 90% of the total population. In every EU country, between 95% and 100% of young people were daily internet users. Daily internet use is consistently high among young people in all countries, but Figure 1 shows much greater variation for the total population. On average in the EU, the gap between young people and the total population using the internet every day was 8 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]]. This gap is narrowing: it was 15 pp in 2021 and 11 pp in 2023. This age gap in daily internet use was largest in Croatia (16 pp), followed by Bulgaria (15 pp), Poland and Lithuania (both 14 pp). In Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands and Sweden there was almost no difference between young people and the total population. [[File:People who used the internet on a daily basis, 2025 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: People who used the internet on a daily basis, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/095f80ac-7b3d-4757-a0bc-4090eb046290?lang=en isoc_ci_ifp_fu]|alt= a line chart showing the percentage of people aged 16-29 who used the internet on a daily basis compared to the percentage of the total population who used the internet on a daily basis in 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Youth online: a way of life''''' Of all the internet activities analysed, participation in social networks was the most common among young people in 2025. Creating a user profile and posting messages or other content was routine for at least 80% of young people (in Italy), and up to 98% (in Cyprus), with an EU average of 89%. Figure 2 gives country-level detail on online social networking in 2025. In 20 EU countries, at least 90% of young people used social networking sites. Among the total population, participation ranged from 56% (in Italy) to 90% (in Denmark). Across the EU, young people were far more likely than the total population to use online social networks. At EU level the difference was 22 pp. In individual EU countries, the gap reached 29 pp in Croatia, 28 pp in Austria and 27 pp in Poland, Czechia and Slovakia. [[File:People who participated in social networks, 2025(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: People who participated in social networks, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4fe2f317-b63f-4a0a-a638-c07d603da8b4?lang=en isoc_ci_ac_i]|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing People who participated on social networking sites, in 2025, in the EU, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries, The bars show young people aged 16-29 years and adult population. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Differences between EU countries in online civic or political participation''''' In 2025, young people aged 16 to 29 years were on average more likely than the total population to express their opinion or take part in online voting on civic or political issues. The gap was 4 pp. By comparison, the gap in social network participation between young people and the total population was 22 pp. Young people are generally more likely not to engage in active citizenship because of lack of interest, but the difference was 5 pp on average in the EU and does not fully account for the digital gap (see Eurostat dataset [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7332cc28-ef62-4a69-83d0-c4c52bf88a17?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-08T12:12:41Z Persons not participating in active citizenship by sex, age and level of disability (activity limitation) [ilc_scp40__custom_20229844]], latest data from 2022). In 2025, online civic or political participation among young people was highest in Slovenia (49% of 16 29-year-olds expressed an opinion or took part in an online civic or political activity), followed by Latvia (33 %), the Netherlands and Italy (both 31%). The lowest shares were in Belgium (12%) and Czechia (14%). In most EU countries, young people were more likely than the total population to use the internet for civic or political participation. The largest gaps were recorded in Slovenia (16 pp), Latvia (9 pp) and Italy (7 pp). In Finland and Cyprus, the total population participated slightly more than young people, and in 4 countries (Luxembourg, Ireland, Croatia, Malta) there was no age difference. [[File:People who used the internet for civic or political participation,2025(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: People who used the internet for civic or political participation, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/d1b26c63-6a7c-4b83-a56a-d62f3e8cf982?lang=en isoc_ci_ac_i]|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing people who used the internet for civic or political participation, in 2025, in the EU, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries, the bars show young people aged 16-29 years and adult population. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Online education declining from the 2021 peak''''' The shift of education activities online, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic, clearly shows how the internet and digital skills affect everyday life. This shift is now receding. In 2021, 35% of young people followed an online course; by 2025 this had fallen to 22%. Nevertheless, more than half (54%) of young people aged 16-29 in Finland used the internet to follow an educational course, followed by 43% in Hungary and Greece. The lowest shares were 6% in Romania, 11% in Denmark and 12% in Germany. On average in the EU, 22% of young people and 16% of the total population followed an online course (see Figure 4). In almost all EU countries, young people were more likely than the rest of the population to take an online course. The gaps were as wide as 25 pp in Finland, 21 pp in Greece and 19 pp in Hungary. There were 3 exceptions where the total population was more likely to use the internet for an online course: Ireland (-7 pp), Denmark (-3 pp) and Luxembourg (-2 pp). [[File:People who used the internet for doing an online course,2025(%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: People who used the internet for doing an online course, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/13ab97cf-c12e-4c99-ab0a-653c0cbd9da9?lang=en isoc_ci_ac_i]|alt= a line chart showing the share of 16-29 year olds who used the internet for doing an online course compared to the share of the total population who used the internet for doing an online course, in 2025, in the EU. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Verifying sources''''' The internet allows people to share experiences and exchange views, but it also carries risks. The data indicate growing awareness of online safety and of the need for young people to analyse, compare and critically evaluate the credibility and reliability of online data, information and digital content. At EU level, 41% of young internet users undertook activities related to checking the accuracy of online information and its sources. In Ireland, 78% of young people reported checking their internet sources, followed by the Netherlands (63%), Luxembourg and Sweden (both 57%). The lowest shares were in Greece (12%), Cyprus (17%), and Bulgaria and Romania (both 26%). Even in these countries, however, the share of young people fact checking internet sources increased by double digits compared with 2023. Young internet users are more likely than the total population to fact-check online information. In 2025, the EU-level gap was 10 pp (up from 9 pp in 2023). The gap reached 16 pp in Croatia, 15 pp in Estonia and 14 pp in Ireland. Cyprus was the only country where the pattern was reversed: 3 pp fewer young people fact checked their sources compared with the total population (see Figure 5). [[File:Percentage of individuals who have verified the information or content found on the internet, 2025 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: People who used the internet for doing an online course, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/13ab97cf-c12e-4c99-ab0a-653c0cbd9da9?lang=en isoc_ci_ac_i]|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing People who used the internet for doing an online course, in 2025, in the EU, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries, The bars show young people aged 16-29 years and adult population. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''''Internet use dynamics over time''''' How has internet use for everyday activities changed over time? In 2025, 89% of young people aged 16-29 in the EU used the internet to participate in social media networks. After remaining at around 83% for almost a decade, young people’s social media use rose to 88% in 2024 and 89% in 2025. During the COVID-19 pandemic, most online activities increased, especially in online courses, which rose from 8% in 2015 to 35% in 2021. This was followed by a decline: in 2022, the share of young people taking online courses fell to 28% (-7 pp), and then further to 22% in 2025. Use of the internet for banking has risen steadily, from 46% of young people in 2015 to 73% in 2025. Reading news online peaked in 2020 (73%), then declined: in 2025, 65% of young people read news online. In 2025, 24% of young people used the internet for civic or political participation, 5 pp higher than in 2015. [[File:Young people's internet use in the EU, selected activity indicators 2015-2025 (%) .png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Young people's internet use in the EU, selected activiy indicators 2015-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/13ab97cf-c12e-4c99-ab0a-653c0cbd9da9?lang=en isoc_ci_ac_i]|alt= a line chart showing how the share of people aged between 16 and 29 changed for various selected online activities between 2015 and 2025, in the EU. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Digital skills === [[Glossary:Digital skills|ICT skills]] are regarded as essential both to benefit from and to contribute to a knowledge-based economy and society. By the time young people in the EU complete compulsory education, most have regularly used computers and the internet for many different purposes. It is therefore important that they become confident and responsible digital users with appropriate digital skills. Map 1 shows the share of young people aged 16-29 reporting basic or above basic overall digital skills in 2025. National shares range from 91% in Czechia, 90% in Denmark and Finland, and 88% in the Netherlands, down to 52% in Romania and 54% in Bulgaria. The EU average is 75%. [[File:Map1 digital skills.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Digital skills of young Europeans in 2025: Share of young people (16-29) with basic or above digital skills
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/77a30c9b-9697-4566-8482-b2472b6ac440?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-10T16:29:38Z isoc_sk_dskl_i21] |alt= a map showing the digital skills of young Europeans as a Share of young people aged 16-29 with basic or above digital skills in 2025 in the EU, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2025, at EU level, a higher share of young women (76%) than young men (73%) reported having basic digital skills. This pattern appears in most countries. The largest gaps in favour of young women were in Slovenia and Cyprus, where they were 12 pp more likely than young men to have at least basic digital skills. The opposite pattern appears in 3 EU countries, where young men are slightly more likely than young women to have at least basic digital skills (Hungary, Slovakia, Romania). For writing code in a programming language (digital content creation) the gender pattern reverses. [[File:Young people with at least basic digital skills by sex, 2025 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Young people with at least basic digital skills by gender, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3f063691-6ebe-4087-ba55-676cb2baf2b0?lang=en isoc_sk_dskl_i21]|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing Young people with at least basic digital skills by gender, in 2025 in the EU, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries. The bars show young males and young females. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Digital skills refer to 5 areas: :* information and data literacy skills :* communication and collaboration skills :* content creation skills :* safety skills and problem-solving skills To be classified as having basic overall digital skills, people must have carried out at least one activity in each area in the 3 months preceding the survey. Some of the activities used to measure digital skills were analysed in more detail (further information on the activities related to each skill is available in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/isoc_sk_dskl_i21_esmsip2.htm metadata file]). These include: :* Participating in social networks (communication and collaboration) :* Using the internet for civic or political participation (communication and collaboration) :* Using the internet for an online course (problem solving) :* Fact checking :* Writing code (digital content creation) The share of young people who had written computer-programming code was twice as high as that of the total population. In 2025, almost four fifths (77%) of all young people aged 16-29 in the EU reported that they had at some point carried out basic computer tasks such as copying or moving a file or folder. Slightly fewer (75%) had downloaded or installed software or applications. More advanced skills, such as writing code in a programming language, were far less common. Only 14% of young people in the EU reported writing code in the 3 months preceding the survey, but this was still more than double the 7% recorded for the total population. Figure 8 shows the differences between men and women. At EU level, 19% of young men and 9% of young women had written code in a programming language. Among young women, the Netherlands recorded the highest share (14%), followed by France and Portugal (both 13%). The lowest shares of female code writers were in Greece (1%), Romania (2%) and Bulgaria (4%). Among young men, the highest shares were in Ireland (31%), Portugal (30%) and Finland (28%). Four countries recorded less than 10% of young men writing code: Romania (5%), Bulgaria (6%), Greece (8%) and Cyprus (9%). [[File:Individuals who wrote code in a programming language by sex, 2025 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Young people who wrote code in a programming language by gender, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3f063691-6ebe-4087-ba55-676cb2baf2b0?lang=en isoc_sk_dskl_i21]|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing people aged between 16 and 29 who wrote code in a programming language, by gender, in 2025 in the EU, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries. The bars show young males and young females. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Use of generative AI tools=== In 2025, young people were twice as likely to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools as the total population. Generative AI refers to systems that can create new content — such as text, images, audio or code — by learning patterns from existing data. These systems include tools that generate written answers, produce images from short descriptions or assist with coding tasks. Across the EU in 2025, 60% of young people aged 16-29 used generative AI tools in the 3 months prior the survey. This was almost twice the share recorded for the total population. Use of AI tools among young people was highest in Greece, where 82% reported using AI in the 3 months prior to the survey, followed by 79% in Estonia and 74% in Portugal. However, usage varied considerably between EU countries. In Romania (38%), Italy (43%) and Bulgaria (45%), the shares were around half these levels and were the lowest recorded in the EU (see Map 2). [[File:Map2 use of AI.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 2: Use of generative AI tools among young Europeans in 2025: Share of young people (16-29) using generative AI
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/65d017ce-5a1b-4e72-803d-3e1084f4ec24?lang=en&createdAt=2026-04-10T16:33:12Z isoc_ai_iaiu]|alt= a map showing the share of young Europeans aged 16-29 who used AI in the 3 months prior to being surveyed in the EU, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries for 2025. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The age gap between the use of AI of people aged 16-29 and the total population was also significant across EU countries (see Figure 9). At EU level, young people used AI on average almost twice as much as the general population. The age gap was most significant in Greece (38 pp), Czechia (37 pp), France and Latvia (36 pp for both). The smallest difference was seen in Ireland (but it was still 20 pp), as well as in Romania, Finland and Germany (21 pp in each). In relative terms, in 8 EU countries the share of young people using AI was more than double this share for the total population, and even in Ireland, where the age gap was the smallest, the share of young people using AI was 1.5 times more than the average. [[File:People who used generative AI tools, 2025 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 9: People using generative AI by age group, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/3f063691-6ebe-4087-ba55-676cb2baf2b0?lang=en isoc_sk_dskl_i21]|alt= a double vertical bar chart comparing the share of Young people using AI in the 3 months prior to survey with the same share for the total population, in 2025 in the EU, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries, candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Conclusions: what future for young people in the digital world?=== The data show that ICT use among young people is widespread and, in some areas, reaching saturation. Young people use the internet more often than the total population, and this is likely to remain the case. The key task for policymakers is to ensure that the social and economic benefits from ICT go hand in hand with safe use of digital media, in particular for more vulnerable groups. === Source data for tables and graphs=== {{Template:Excel|filename=Youth in the digital world 2026.xlsx|title=Being young in Europe today - digital world: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data presented in this article come from Eurostat’s [[Glossary:EU survey on the use of ICT in households and by individuals|survey on ICT usage in households and by individuals]], which is updated annually to keep the data relevant. While some questions change each year to reflect current ICT use, a core part of the survey remains stable to allow time series for key indicators. The surveys initially focused on access and connectivity, but now cover a wide range of topics, including internet security and the use of social media and cloud services. The results can be broken down by various socioeconomic characteristics, such as sex, age, level of education and the presence of children in the household. In most EU countries, the surveys are carried out in the second quarter of each year and ask about activities in the first quarter; some questions (for example, on e-commerce or e-government) refer to activities in the previous 12 months. ICT surveys cover households with at least one member aged 16-74 years. Households with children are those with at least one member under 16 years. In this article, ‘total population’ refers to people aged 16-74 years, while ‘young people’ refers to those aged 16-29 years. ===Context=== '''A Europe fit for the digital age''' In her agenda for Europe, the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, set out priorities for 2019-2024. In February 2020, the European Commission adopted a Communication on [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en Shaping Europe’s digital future], which highlights the opportunities offered by new technologies such as artificial intelligence and 5G networks, or by exploiting big data. Alongside promoting these technologies, the strategy aims to ensure that developments are trustworthy and support an open and democratic society, a vibrant and sustainable economy, and action on climate change and the green transition. Digital skills indicators are among the key performance indicators for the [https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/europes-digital-decade Digital Decade], the EU’s vision for digital transformation. The [https://transition-pathways.europa.eu/retail/policy/2030-digital-compass-european-way-digital-decade Digital Compass] sets a target for 80% of EU citizens aged 16-74 years old to have basic digital skills by 2030.
'''Better internet for our children''' The internet offers opportunities for work, study, leisure activities and social interaction, but it also poses risks. The European Commission’s [https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/betterinternet/items/750544/en Digital Decade Better Internet for kids strategy] aims to protect children and young people, raise their awareness of online risks and promote digital literacy so that they can benefit from being online in a safe and informed way. Adopted in May 2012, the strategy is build on four pillars: promoting high-quality online content for young people; increasing awareness and empowerment; creating a safer online environment for children; and combating child sexual abuse and exploitation. '''Insafe, Inhope and safer internet''' [https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/about/insafe-inhope Insafe and Inhope] are European networks, co-funded by the EU, made up of national Safer Internet Centres. These centres run awareness and educational campaigns, operate helplines and work closely with young people to ensure an evidence-based, multi-stakeholder approach to creating a better internet. On 6 February 2018, the EU launched a range of new initiatives under the heading of [https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/saferinternetday Safer internet day]. They were designed to ensure that children, young people, parents, teachers and other EU citizens become empowered and responsible digital users. The [https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en Better internet for kids] web portal provides extensive information, including an online course on child safety and teaching resources for topics such as fake news, cyberbullying and radicalisation. ===Other articles=== *[[Digital economy and society statistics - households and individuals]] ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/digital-economy-and-society/database Digital economy and society (isoc)], see: :ICT usage in households and by individuals (isoc_i) :Digital skills (isoc_sk) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/digital-economy-and-society/database Digital economy and society (t_isoc)], see: :ICT usage in households and by individuals (t_isoc_i) :Digital skills (t_isoc_sk) ===Thematic section=== *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=digital_economy_and_society}} Digital economy and society] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-04-18-130|title=Digital economy & society in the EU - a browse through our online world in figures}} - 2018 edition; online publication ===Methodology=== *{{Template:Esms|code=isoc_i_esms|title=ICT usage in households and by individuals (isoc_i)}} (ESMS metadata file - isoc_i) ===Legislation=== *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52010DC0245:EN:NOT|title=European Commission Communication (COM(2010) 245 final)}}, of 19 May 2010 on a Digital Agenda for Europe *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52020DC0067:EN:NOT|title=European Commission Communication (COM(2020) 67 final)}}, of 19 February 2020 Shaping Europe’s digital future *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:52012AE1518:EN:NOT|title=Opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee (COM(2012) 196 final)}}, of 2 May 2012 on a European Strategy for a Better Internet for Children ===External links=== *[https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en Better Internet for Kids] *[https://ec.europa.eu/digital-single-market/en/policies/better-internet-kids Creating a better internet for kids] *[https://digital-agenda-data.eu/ Digital scoreboard - data and indicators] *[https://ec.europa.eu/digital-single-market/ Shaping Europe’s digital future] *[https://ec.europa.eu/digital-single-market/en/desi The digital economy and society index (DESI)] {{Unit|topic=X_Dissemination}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Young people - digital world]] [[Category:Children and youth|Young people - digital world]] [[Category:Digital economy and society|Young people - digital world]] [[Category:Digital economy and society - households|Young people - digital world]] [[Category:Digital economy and society - young people|Young people - digital world]] [[Category:Statistical article|Young people - digital world]] [[Category:March2027|Young people - digital world]]

title: Young people - family and society
text:
These statistics present the situation of children and young people in families and society across the European Union (EU). Data extracted in November 2025. Planned article update: December 2026. In 2022, 70.8% of people living in households with children in the EU reported to feeling happy all or most of the time, compared to 59.8% in households without children. In 2024, slightly just under a quarter, 23.5%, of households in the EU included children. In 2024, over half, 63.5%, of households with children in the EU were couples with children, while single-parent households made up 12.7%. ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|ilc_pw09}}|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the percentage of people who reported to be happy all or most of the time, comparing those living in households with children to people living in households without children in the EU and individual EU countries in 2022.> This article presents data about household composition and its link to happiness across the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|EU]]. Family structures in EU countries vary, reflecting cultural and normative differences and other factors. Children most commonly grow up in households with 2 adults, though multigenerational and single-parent households are also prevalent. === Share of households with children === Nearly a quarter of households in the EU included children in 2024, a proportion that has been gradually decreasing over the last 15 years –from 26.9% in 2010 to 26.4% in 2014, and down to 23.5% in 2024 (see Figure 1). [[File:Proportion of households with dependent children, EU, 2010-2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Proportion of households with dependent children in the EU, 2010-2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfst_hhnhtych__custom_18586775/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=9e69096e-eb9b-4e8d-9b85-235428c79ffa&c=1761225623000 lfst_hhnhtych])|alt= Line chart showing the percentage of private households in the EU wit dependent children, between the years 2010 and 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Conversely, the share of single-adult households increased by 6.4 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp) between 2010 and 2024 (Figure 2). All household types with children saw a decline in their overall proportion compared to 15 years ago, except for single-parent households, which experienced a slight rise. Specifically, the proportion of couples with children fell from 17.1% to 15.0%, and other household types with children dropped from 6.9% to 5.6%. [[File:Composition of private households, EU, 2010 and 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Composition of private households, EU, 2010 and 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfst_hhnhtych__custom_18587034/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=c1304a8b-a96a-4ab4-b0a8-149518a363aa&c=1761575211000 lfst_hhnhtych])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing private households as percentages in the EU, comparing the years 2010 and 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Figure 3 shows how household structures vary across EU countries. In 2024, over half of households in Lithuania and Estonia were single-adult households without children. In 12 other EU countries, more than a third of households were single-adult households without children. By contrast, only 1 in 10 households in Slovakia consisted of a single adult. [[File:Composition of private households, 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Composition of private households, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfst_hhnhtych__custom_18629023/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=8fb26efe-fc1a-4277-bf80-aa4835123800&c=1761575055000 lfst_hhnhtych])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing private households as percentages in the EU and individual EU countries. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has six stacks representing couple with children, single adult with children, other types of households with children, couple without children, single adult without children, and other types of households without children for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The second most common household type in the EU in 2024 was couples without children, making up 28.6% of households in Sweden and Finland, 27.7% in Germany, and 26.6% in the Netherlands. Conversely, these households constituted 13.4% in Lithuania, 14.7% in Latvia and 16.4% in Estonia. These patterns have remained stable over time, suggesting cultural influences on trends like couples without children. Overall, highest shares of households without children are found in Finland (82.0%), Lithuania (80.4%) and Germany (80.0%), with lowest in Slovakia (64.4%), Ireland (69%) and Cyprus (71.4%). ===Composition of households with children=== Looking closely at households with children (Figure 4), which represent 23.5% of all households, most consisted of couples with children, accounting for 63.5% at the EU level. Other household types with children, such as multigenerational families, accounted for 23.7% and single-parent families 12.7%. The EU countries with the highest proportion of couples with children among households with children are Sweden, Greece and the Netherlands (74.5%, 73.1% and 71.6% respectively). In other EU countries, this proportion is around half or less (50.5% in Estonia, 46.4% in Latvia and 45.9% in Denmark). [[File:Households with children, 2024 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Households with dependent children, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/lfst_hhnhtych__custom_18660730/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=cac803b3-b8af-4e49-b4db-73adb7eab36d&c=1761736196000 lfst_hhnhtych])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing the composition of households with dependent children as percentages in the EU and individual EU countries. Totalling 100 percent, each country column has three stacks representing couple with children, single adult with children, other types of households with children for the year 2024. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In 2024, Estonia had the highest share of single-parent households, at 36.7%, followed by Lithuania at 29.5% and Latvia at 24.9%. Slovakia (2.7%), Greece (3.4%), Slovenia (4.2%), and Croatia (5.2%) had the lowest shares of single-parent households. However, Slovakia and Croatia had the highest proportion of households classified under the ‘other type’ category of households with children, with 41.1% in Slovakia and 36.9% in Croatia being neither single-parent households nor households with couples. These households, where several generations may live together are also common in Romania (36.5% of households with children), Bulgaria (35.7%) and Spain (34.5%). Estonia and Lithuania, which have the highest share of single-parent families, also have the lowest share of ‘other type’ households with children: 12.8% and 15.2%, respectively. Finland also has a low share at 13.3%. ===Happiness and household composition=== The latest data from 2022 on subjective happiness related to household composition in the EU shows that 70.8% of people living in households with dependent children reported being happy all or most of the time over the past 4 weeks, compared to 59.8% of those living in households without dependent children. Among households without children, 65.4% of individuals in two-adult households reported feeling happy all or most of the time, followed by 63.1% in households with 3 or more adults. In single-adult households, 50.3% reported being happy all or most of the time in the past 4 weeks, 30.8% felt happy some of the time, and 15.2% experienced happiness little or none of the time (Figure 5). [[File:How often people were happy during the 4 weeks prior to the survey2, by household composition, EU, 2022 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: How often people declared to be happy in the 4 weeks prior to the survey, by household composition, EU, 2022
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_pw09__custom_13777967/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=fadf70fa-7f9c-42ea-a337-efccafd85537&c=1731676361461 ilc_pw09])|alt= Stacked vertical bar chart showing how often people reported to be happy in the 4 weeks prior to the survey, in the EU. Totalling 100 percent, each column has four stacks representing a little/none of the time, some of the time, all/most of the time and unknown, for the year 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] In nearly every EU country, a high percentage of people living in households with dependent children reported being happy all or most of the time (Figure 6). The gap between happiness levels in households with and without dependent children can be considerable: 23 pp in Croatia, 19.9 pp in Bulgaria, and 18.7 pp in Lithuania. However, there was minimal difference in Luxembourg (-0.1 pp), with small differences in Malta (2.7 pp) and Ireland (3.2 pp). [[File:People reporting to be happy all or most of the time, by household composition, 2022 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: People reporting to be happy all or most of the time, by household composition, 2022
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_pw09__custom_13774931/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=7fd67bea-c263-422c-9c75-da2990f48a55&c=1731676234927 ilc_pw09])|alt= Vertical bar chart showing the percentage of people who reported to be happy all or most of the time, comparing those living in households with children to people living in households without children in the EU and individual EU countries in 2022. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for graphs === {{Template:Excel|filename=Family composition and happiness V2 (1).xlsx|title=Family and society: tables and figures}} === Data sources=== This article’s data comes from the [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)|EU labour force survey (EU-LFS)]] and the [[Glossary:EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]]. The EU-LFS provides statistics on household numbers, characteristics and types. Moreover, under its specific topic, it details household composition, numbers and sizes, and the estimated age at which young people leave the parental home. ‘Other types of households’ may refer to households with 2 adults not forming a couple or households with 3 or more adults (e.g., parents with a child aged over 18, multigenerational households, or siblings living together). The survey only includes individuals in private households excluding those in collective or institutional households. Figures on subjective well-being come from the EU-SILC, specifically the 6-yearly rotating module on well-being, first collected in 2022. The ‘being happy’ variable denotes a general state of well-being, implying a more sustained happiness over time. It was also collected in the EU-SILC ad hoc modules on well-being in 2010 and 2018. It is noteworthy that households with [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Dependent_children dependent children] in the EU-SILC include those with children aged 18-24 years who are inactive and living with at least one parent. ===Context=== '''''EU policies targeting children ''''' In 2021, the [https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/rights-child/eu-strategy-rights-child-and-european-child-guarantee_en European Commission Strategy on Children’s rights and the EU Child’s guarantee] was adopted. This policy framework aims to protect children’s rights and ensure vulnerable children can access basic services. The Commission has implemented various measures to safeguard children, help them fulfil their rights, and place at the centre of EU policymaking. Many of these measures are already in place. '''''EU policies targeting subjective well-being''''' Promoting well-being is a key EU aim, as outlined in the [[Glossary:Treaty_on_European_Union|Treaty on European Union]]. The EU considers a wide range of outcomes when assessing social and economic policy goals, including subjective life quality measures. Many international, EU, and national bodies report on subjective well-being, issuing reports that extend going beyond [[Glossary:Gross_domestic_product_(GDP)|gross domestic product (GDP)]] as a societal performance measure. === Other articles=== *[[Living conditions in Europe - title: Wood products - production and trade
text:
EU statistics are provided on the production of wood, wood-related employment and international trade. Data extracted in October 2023. No planned article update. EU has been a net exporter of roundwood in the past four years, exports to non-EU countries surpassing imports by 12.5 million m3 in 2022. 25% of the EU’s roundwood production in 2022 was used as fuelwood; the rest was used for sawnwood and veneers, pulp and paper production. This article is part of a set of statistical articles that the Eurostat [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agriculture,_forestry_and_fishery_statistics&stable=0&redirect=no online publication "Agriculture, forestry and fishery statistics"] is based on. It presents statistics on production and trade in wood products in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]]. The EU accounts for approximately 5 % of the world's [[Glossary:Forest|forests]]. Apart from the forests' ecological value, their role as an essential element in the European landscape and their importance for some non-economic uses, such as recreation, forests are also an economic resource. This article presents indicators on the volume of [[Glossary:Roundwood_production|roundwood ]] production, production of selected primary and secondary wood products, as well as on the performance and employment of the EU's wood-based industries. === Roundwood production === After the temporary decrease in 2020, roundwood production increased by 3.8 % in 2021 and stabilised in 2022 (0.04 % increase). In 2022, it reached an estimated 510 million m3. This is 26 % more than at the beginning of the millennium. With the exception of four Member States where roundwood production decreased and further four Member States where data are unavailable, all EU countries recorded an increase in roundwood production in the period of 2000–2022. The largest relative increase during the two decades in the amount of harvested wood took place in the Netherlands (190 %), Czechia (126 %), Slovenia and Poland (85 and 76 % respectively). Just as last year, in 2022 Germany was still the largest producer of roundwood in the European Union (79 million m3), followed by Sweden and Finland (each producing between ca 66 and 77 million m3) (Table 1 and Figure 1). [[Image:Roundwood production 2022.jpg|thumb|center|800px|Table 1: Roundwood production 2022
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=for_remov}}|alt=A table showing the roundwood production in the EU for the year 2022. Data present the total production, fuelwood and industrial roundwood in thousand metres cubed under bark for the EU, the EU Member States and the EFTA countries.]]
[[Image:Change in roundwood production in the EU and EFTA, 2000–2022 (%).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 1: Change in roundwood production in the EU, 2000–2022 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=for_remov}}|alt=A vertical bar chart showing the change in roudwood production in the EU and some of the EFTA countries between 2000 and 2022. Data are shown as percentages.]] Traditionally, the output of roundwood in the EU has been dominated by coniferous trees. Their share in 2022 accounted for 69 % of all roundwood harvested in the forests of EU countries. Although the output of coniferous roundwood shows minor fluctuations, the output of non-coniferous roundwood has been steady over the past 20 years. Overall, the share of coniferous roundwood has remained stable during the period 2000–2022 (Figure 2). [[Image:Annual production of roundwood, EU, 2000–2022_(1000 m³).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 2: Annual production of roundwood, EU, 2000–2022
(1 000 m3)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=for_remov}}|alt=An area chart showing the annual production of roundwood in the EU between 2000 and 2022. Data are shown for coniferous and non-coniferous roundwood in thousand cubic metres.]] === Primary wood products === Wood has been increasingly used as a source of renewable energy. Almost a quarter (24 %) of the EU's [[Glossary:Roundwood production|roundwood production]] in 2022 was used as fuelwood, while the remainder was industrial roundwood mostly used for [[Glossary:Sawnwood|sawnwood]] and veneers or for pulp and paper production. Fuelwood production has slightly increased in 2022 (3.6 %), and industrial roundwood production has decreased by 1%. Their ratio has been stable around 24:76. This represents an increase of 7 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp) compared with 2000, when fuelwood accounted for 17 % of the total roundwood production. In some EU Member States, specifically Cyprus, fuelwood represented the majority of roundwood production (more than 80 %) in 2022. On the other hand, Slovakia and Sweden reported that over 90 % of their total roundwood production was industrial roundwood (Table 1). While the share of fuelwood in roundwood production differs across EU countries, most Member States reported its increase since 2000. The largest increase was recorded for the Netherlands and Cyprus (63 % and 55 % respectively) as shown in Figure 3. [[Image: Change in the share of fuelwood in total roundwood production in the EU and EFTA, 2000–2022 (%).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 3: Change in the share of fuelwood in total roundwood production in the EU, 2000–2022 (%)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=for_remov}}|alt=A vertical scatter chart showing the change in the share of fuelwood in total roundwood production between 2000 and 2022. Data are shown for the EU, the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries in percentage.]] In 2022 Germany and Sweden were the EU's leading sawnwood producers, accounting for approximately 24 % and 18 % of the EU total sawnwood output, respectively (Figure 4). For both countries, their share has increased during last year by 1 %. [[Image: Sawnwood production, 2000 and 2022 (1000 m3).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 4: Sawnwood production, 2000 and 2022
(1 000 m3)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=for_swpan}}|alt=A double vertical bar chart showing the sawnwood production in the EU for the years 2000 and 2022. Data are shown for the EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries in thousand cubic metres.]] === Secondary wood products === Secondary products include further processed wood and paper products (e.g. further processed sawnwood, wooden wrapping and packaging material, wooden furniture, etc.). As a new item, Eurostat and its partner institutions have started to collect data on the production of glue-laminated timber, cross-laminated timber and I-beam. Only 13 countries reported provisional production data for 2022. Austria and Germany are the main producers of these two items in Europe, reaching a total of 2.5 and 2.1 million m3 in 2022. [[Image: Cross-laminated and glue-laminated timber production in 2022 (1000m3).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 5: Cross-laminated and glue-laminated timber production in 2022
(1 000 m3)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=for_swpan}}|alt=A double vertical bar chart showing the cross-laminated and glue-laminated timber production in the EU for the year 2022. Data are shown for some of the EU Member States in thousand cubic metres.]] === Trade in roundwood and fuelwood === Trade of roundwood presents for the EU in 2022 a net balance of 12 billion m3 (Figure 6). Total exports have steadily increased since 2015 by 77% over the seven years, while total imports have declined since 2018 by 7.4%. The net balance is driven by the extra-EU trade of roundwood and represents 12.5 million m3. 31% of all roundwood exports go outside the EU, whereas 16% of roundwood imports come from outside the EU. [[Image: Trade in roundwood 2015-2022 (1000m3).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 6: Trade in roundwood 2015-2022
(1 000 m3)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=for_swpan}}|alt=A line chart showing the trade in roundwood in the EU between 2015 and 2022. Data are show in thousand cubic metres.]] Trade of fuelwood shows a different picture (see Figure 7). Total imports have been declining since 2015 reaching 2.9 million m3 in 2022, whereas imports coming from non-EU states reached slightly more than 1 million m3. The rise in fuelwood export however is mild over the past three years, still not reaching the 2015 level. In 2022, exports of fuelwood account for 4.6 million m3 including exports to non-EU countries of 481 thousand m3. During the past 7 years the EU imported more fuelwood from non-EU states than exported outside the EU. The trade balance has been narrowing, but imports are still twice as high as exports. [[Image: Trade in fuelwood 2015-2022 (1000m3).png|thumb|center|700px|Figure 7: Trade in fuelwood 2015-2022
(1 000 m3)
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=for_swpan}}|alt=A line chart showing trade in fuelwood in the EU between 2015 and 2022. Data are shown in thousand cubic metres.]] === Wood-based industries === The EU's wood-based industries cover a range of downstream activities, including woodworking industries, large parts of the furniture industry, pulp and paper manufacturing and converting industries and the printing industry. Together, some 393 000 enterprises were active in wood-based industries across the EU in 2020; they represented one in five (19 %) manufacturing enterprises across the EU, highlighting that - with the exception of pulp and paper manufacturing that is characterised by economies of scale - many wood-based industries had a relatively high number of small or medium-sized enterprises. The economic importance of an industry can be measured by the share of its gross value added (GVA) in the economy. In 2020, the GVA of wood-based industries in the EU was €136 billion or 7.2 % of the total manufacturing industry. The distribution of GVA across each of the four wood-based activities in 2020 is presented in Table 2. Within the EU's wood-based industries, the largest GVA was recorded for pulp, paper and paper products manufacturing (34 % or €46 billion). With regard to the other three sectors, printing and service activities related to printing amounted to 16 % of the GVA of wood based industries, while the manufacture of furniture and manufacturing of wood and wood products each made up between 23 % and 27 %. [[Image:Main economic indicators for wood-based industries, EU-27, 2020.png|thumb|center|800px|Table 2: Main economic indicators for wood-based industries, EU, 2020
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=sbs_na_ind_r2}}|alt=A table showing the main economic indicators for wood-based industries in the EU for the year 2020. Data presented show the number of enterprises in thousands, gross value added at factor cost in billion euros and the number of persons employed in thousands.]] The wood-based industries employed 3.1 million persons across the EU in 2020 or 10.5 % of the manufacturing total. There were more than 900 000 persons employed within both the manufacture of wood and wood products and the manufacture of furniture, whereas an employment of 555 000 persons was recorded for printing and service activities related to printing, representing the lowest employment of the four activities (Table 2). === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=SE Wood products production and trade 16 10 2023.xlsx |title= Wood products - production and trade - tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== Eurostat, the [http://www.unece.org/forests/welcome.html Timber Committee] of the [[Glossary:United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE)|United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE)]], [http://www.fao.org/forestry/en/ Forestry Section] of the United Nations [[Glossary:Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)|Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO)]] and the [http://www.itto.int/ International Tropical Timber Organisation (ITTO)] collect and collate statistics on the production and trade of wood through their [[Glossary:Joint forest sector questionnaire (JFSQ)|Joint Forest Sector Questionnaire]]. Each partner collects data from a different part of the world, Eurostat is responsible for the data collection exercise pertaining to the EU Member States and [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA countries]]. Eurostat produces annual data on forestry using two questionnaires: *The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/forestry/methodology Joint Forest Sector Questionnaire (JFSQ)] on production and trade in wood and wood products; *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/forestry/methodology European Forest Accounts (EFA)], forming part of the environmental satellite accounts initiative that started in the late 1990s. The JFSQ provides data for supply balances of timber used for wood products and for energy and for estimating the carbon contained in harvested wood products.) === Context === A broad array of EU policies and initiatives has a bearing on forests. For several decades, environmental forest functions have attracted increasing attention — for example, in relation to the protection of [[Glossary:Biodiversity|biodiversity]] and, more recently, in the context of [[Glossary:Climate change|climate change]] impacts and energy policies. Apart from the traditional production of wood and other forest-based products, forests are increasingly valued for their environmental role and as a public amenity. The EU promotes sustainable forest management, aiming to * create and preserve jobs and otherwise contribute to rural livelihoods; * protect the environment by preserving the soil, minimising erosion, purifying water, protecting aquifers, improving air quality, absorbing carbon, mitigating climate change and preserving biodiversity; * monitor the state of forests to meet environmental agreements; * improve the competitiveness of forest-based industries in the internal market; * promote the use of wood and other forest products as environmentally friendly products; * reduce poverty in developing countries by furthering forest law enforcement, fair trade conditions and halting deforestation and illegal logging. The European Community and its Member States have been members of the International Tropical Timber Agreement (ITTA) since 1994. A new ITTA was concluded in 2006 and signed by the European Community, see [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2007.262.01.0006.01.ENG 2007/648/EC: Council Decision of 26 September 2007]. Annex 1 is a list of ITTA's members that produce tropical wood, comprising both FLEGT and non-FLEGT countries. Annex 2 is a list of ITTA's members that are consumers of tropical wood. All EU Member States are presently [http://www.itto.int/itto_members/ members of ITTA]. Article 27 on statistics, studies and information states: :''1. The Council shall authorise the Executive Director to establish and maintain close relationships with relevant intergovernmental, governmental and non-governmental organisations in order to help ensure the availability of recent and reliable data and information, including on production and trade in tropical timber, trends and data discrepancies, as well as relevant information on non-tropical timber and on the management of timber producing forests. As deemed necessary for the operation of this Agreement, the Organisation, in cooperation with such organisations, shall compile, collate, analyse and publish such information.'' :''2. The Organisation shall contribute to efforts to standardise and harmonise international reporting on forest-related matters, avoiding overlapping and duplication in data collection from different organisations.'' The European Commission presented a new [http://ec.europa.eu/agriculture/forest/strategy/index_en.htm EU forest strategy] (COM(2013) 659) for forests and the forest-based sector in 2013 in response to the increasing demands put on forests and to significant societal and political changes that have affected forests over the last decades. The strategy is a framework for forest-related measures and is used to coordinate EU initiatives with the forest policies of the EU Member States. A new forest strategy is under preparation as of 2020 with a view for its adoption in 2021. In March 2010, the European Commission adopted a Green paper on forest protection and information in the EU: preparing forests for climate change [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:52010DC0066:EN:NOT (COM(2010) 66 final)]. The paper aimed to stimulate debate concerning the way climate change modifies the terms of forest management and protection and how EU policy should develop as a consequence. ===Other articles=== title: Young people - health
text:
These statistics present the situation of young people across the European Union (EU) in terms of their health. Data extracted in June 2026. Planned article update: June 2027 In 2025 in the EU, 9 in 10 young people aged 16-29 considered their health as very good or good. Long-standing illness is more common among young women: in the EU in 2025, 15.0% of men and 19.6% of women aged 16-29 reported suffering from a long-standing illness or health problem. In 2025, young people in the lowest income quintile were twice as likely to report disability (activity limitations) as those in the highest income quintile (11.2% compared to 5.6%). |alt= Dynamic. vertical multibar chart showing the share of young people and the total population who perceive themselves to be in good or very good health, 2024. Health is a key aspect of quality of life – and a priority for both EU residents and policymakers. According to the [[Glossary:Treaty_on_the_Functioning_of_the_European_Union_(TFEU)|Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union]](Article 168), public health should be considered in all EU policies. Eurostat data offers detailed information on physical activity, mental health, diet and nutrition, substance use, overweight rates, access to healthcare, health education and awareness, among other aspects related to young people’s health. This article presents a range of health indicators for young people in the EU. The analysis looks at how age, sex and level of income affect: * health status * [[Glossary:Cause_of_death|causes of death]] among people aged 16-29 years (15-29 years in some cases). === Health status === The [[Glossary:World_Health_Organization_(WHO)|World Health Organisation (WHO)]] defines health as ‘a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity’. This definition implies different ways of measuring health, such as collecting objective data from health care providers and subjective data on physical functioning, emotional well-being, pain or discomfort, and overall perception of health from survey respondents. This section focuses on 3 key indicators of health status: * self-perceived health * long-standing illnesses or health problems and * disability (activity limitations). '''Self-perceived health – high among young people, but income remains a key disparity''' [[Glossary:Self-perceived_health|Self-perceived health]] is the respondent’s overall rating of their own health in general. It is inherently subjective and is expected to reflect different aspects of health, including psychological and physical symptoms. Young people report better health and see themselves to be healthier than the population as a whole. The percentage of young people who perceive their health as good or very good has remained relatively stable over time, with a slight decrease from 92.0% in 2010 to 89.7% in 2025. This is significantly higher than the same share in the total population over 16 years of age (67.9%). Self-perceived health status varies among EU countries (see Figure 1). In 2025, the lowest shares of young people aged 16-29 who declared themselves to be in good or very good health were registered in Sweden, the Netherlands and Finland (74.4%, 79.8% and 81.4%, respectively). By contrast, the share in Romania reached 98.2%, with similarly high levels in Greece (98.1%) and Croatia (95.9%). In 14 EU countries, more than 90% of 16-29-year-olds considered their health good or very good. [[File:People who perceive themselves to be in good or very good health, 2025 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Share of young people and the total population who perceive themselves to be in good or very good health, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hlth_silc_10__custom_21899398/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=ff63148d-b9a5-40a4-b581-71d343ad1b45&c=1782071951000 hlth_silc_01])|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing the share of young people aged 16-29 years who perceive themselves to be in good or very good health in the year 2025, in the EU, EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries, the bars show the age groups, 16 years to 29 years and 16 years or over. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] The largest differences in the shares of young people and the total population in reporting very good or good health were in Lithuania (a difference of 38.1 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp)) and Latvia (37.1 pp difference). These cross-country differences in self-perceived health may reflect overall health conditions in EU countries, as well as social and cultural factors, such as how people evaluate their own health and how willing they are to disclose health problems in surveys. The link between self-perceived health and income (Figure 2) is clear in almost all EU countries: higher income is associated with better perceived health. In the EU, 85.6% of young people aged 16-29 in the 1st income quintile rated their health as good or very good in 2025, compared with 93.7% in the 5th income quintile. An income-related gap in the self-perceived health status was observed in all but 2 EU countries: in Malta and Bulgaria, the share of people in the 1st (lowest) income quintile reporting good or very good health was slightly higher than in the 5th quintile (by 0.4 pp and 0.1 pp respectively). In all other EU countries, the share of people reporting good or very good health increased with income. The largest difference between the highest and lowest income quintiles in the share of young people reporting very good or good health were observed in Finland (23.4 pp), Denmark (17.7 pp) and Estonia (15.0 pp). The smallest differences were seen in Greece (0.3 pp), Italy (1.2 pp) and Belgium (2.7 pp).
'''Understanding income quintiles''' Income [[Glossary:Quintile|quintiles]] classify households according to their income. When we refer to [[Glossary:Equivalised_disposable_income|equivalised disposable income]], we mean a household's total income after taxes and deductions, adjusted for the number of people living in the household. This adjustment takes account of the ages of household members to allow a fair comparison between households. Here is how we break it down: 1. Total household income – the amount of money available for spending or saving after taxes and other deductions have been paid. 2. Equivalised household members – each household member is assigned a specific weight based on age. For example: * the 1st adult is given a weight of 1.0 * each person aged 14 and over is given a weight of 0.5 * children under 14 are given a weight of 0.3 We use these weights to calculate each household's ‘equivalised’ income. We then rank all households by equivalised income from lowest to highest. After that, we divide them into 5 equal groups, or quintiles, each containing 20% of the population. * the 1st quintile – the lowest 20% of the population by income. * the 2nd to 4th quintiles – middle groups. * the 5th quintile – the top 20%, representing the highest income group. This approach provides a clear basis for analysing and comparing how income is distributed across households in a given area.
[[File:Young people aged 16-29 who perceive themselves to be in good or very good health, by income quintile, 2025 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Young people aged 16-29 who perceive themselves to be in good or very good health, by income quintile, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4a50e5ed-f6e1-4f65-8361-a54ce8fa6539?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-27T13:18:16Z hlth_silc_10])|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing young people aged 16-29 years who perceive themselves to be in good or very good health, by income quintile in the year 2025, in the EU, EU Member State, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries, the bars show the first and fifth quintile. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Long-term or chronic illness – not just an adult issue''' According to the WHO, long-standing health problems or chronic illnesses, such as heart disease, stroke, cancer, chronic respiratory diseases and diabetes, are the leading cause of mortality and disability worldwide. Chronic health conditions affect a substantial share of young people in the EU and have consequences for their well-being and everyday life. In 2025, 17.2% of people aged 16-29 reported that they were living with a long-standing health problem. The lowest prevalence of long-standing health problems in this age group were observed in Romania, Greece, Bulgaria and Italy (all at or below 5.0%). The highest shares of young people reporting long-standing health problems were recorded in Finland (39.9%), Sweden (25.1%) and Estonia (24.2%). These differences between EU countries may reflect cultural variation in self-perception and in approaches to diagnosing, managing and treating long-standing health problems. Figure 3 compares the prevalence of self-reported long-standing illnesses between young women and young men. In 2025, 15.0% of men aged 16-29 in the EU reported that they had a long-standing illness or health problem; this was 4.6 pp lower than the corresponding share for young women in the same age group (19.6%). This pattern – a higher share of young women than young men reporting a long-standing illness or health problem – was seen in most EU countries (20 of them). The gap is widest in Finland, where young women's reports of long-term health problems exceed those of men by 11.7 pp, followed by the Netherlands (9.5 pp) and Sweden (8.3 pp). [[File:Young people aged 16-29 reporting a long-standing illness or health problem, by sex, 2025 (%) v3.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Young people aged 16-29 years suffering from a long-standing illness or health problem, by sex, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hlth_silc_04__custom_21899550/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=db6ab485-d213-4cfd-b387-88e5aff2f86c&c=1782075595000 hlth_silc_04])|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing young people aged 16-29 years suffering from a long-standing illness or health problem, by sex in the year 2025, in the EU, EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries, the bars show young men and young women. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] '''Disability – everyday limitations''' People with long-standing health problems may find everyday activities difficult, which in turn affects their quality of life. Data on the degree of limitation in usual activities due to health problems are used as a proxy measure for disability. In 2025, 8.1% of people aged 16-29 in the EU reported a disability (long-standing limitations in usual activities). This was slightly higher than the 7.5% recorded 15 years earlier and the 7.6% recorded 10 years earlier. Figure 4 shows that for both men and women, the proportions of people with some or severe disability have remained relatively stable over the past 15 years and are considerably higher in the total population than among young people. The gender gap is also more significant in the total population than in the 16-29 age group. [[File:Disability prevalence among young people and adults, by sex, EU, 2010-2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Disability prevalence among young people and adults, by sex, EU, 2010-2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hlth_silc_12__custom_10558567/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=cb8c656f-2de9-4674-9659-ad2803df8e9b&c=1711376237229 hlth_silc_12])|alt=a line chart with four lines showing disability prevalence among young people and adults, by sex in the EU from the year 2010 to the year 2025, the lines show males, 16 years to 29 years, males 16 years or older, females 16 years to 29 years, females 16 years or older. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] Lower income levels were linked to higher disability rates in almost all EU countries (see Figure 5). At EU level in 2025, the prevalence of moderate or severe disability among young people in the 1st income quintile was twice that observed in the 5th (11.2% compared to 5.6%). This income-related gap varied considerably between EU countries. The largest difference between the 1st and the 5th quintiles was registered in Ireland, where the share of young people with a disability in the 1st income quintile was 16.3 pp higher than in the 5th income quintile, followed by Finland (15.2 pp) and Estonia (14.2 pp). In Italy and Lithuania, the share of young people with a disability in the 1st income quintile was lower than the corresponding share in the 5th income quintile, with differences of 1.0 pp and 0.4 pp, respectively. [[File:Prevalence of moderate or severe disability among young people aged 16-29, by income quintile, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Prevalence of moderate or severe disability among young people aged 16-29 years, by income quintile, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hlth_silc_12__custom_21899603/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=799a6c23-cfb9-47c8-9b8c-0462bb9336e9&c=1782076822000 hlth_silc_12])|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing the prevalence of moderate or severe disability among young people aged 16-29 years, by income quintile in the year 2025, in the EU, EU Member States, some EFTA countries and some candidate countries, the bars show, first quintile and fifth quintile. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Causes of death === '''External factors are the main cause of young people’s death''' Causes of death vary substantially between age groups. In 2023, more than half (57.8%) of the 4.85 million deaths occurred in the EU were caused by circulatory diseases and cancer ([[Glossary:Neoplasm|neoplasms]]). For young people aged 15-29, external causes are more prevalent: almost half (48.3%) of the 0.03 million deaths in 2023 were related to accidents and intentional self-harm (see Figure 6). COVID-19, which was monitored separately in recent years, had decreased substantially as a cause of death by 2023. [[File:Causes of death by age group, EU, 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 6: Causes of death by age group, EU, 2022
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hlth_cd_aro__custom_21936056/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=4f0174eb-f2c8-4a15-b559-c1cc0f54e7f4&c=1782305040000 hlth_cd_aro])|alt= a stacked vertical bar chart showing causes of death by age group in the EU in the year 2022, the stacks show the causes of death, Circulatory system, Neoplasms, COVID-19, Respiratory system, Digestive system, Nervous system, Mental and behavioural, Endocrine Infectious and parasitic, Congenital malformations, Accidents, Intentional self-harm, Other causes. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]]
'''Intentional self-harm''' refers to deliberately self-inflicted poisoning or injury and suicide or attempted suicide. '''Suicide''' is the act of deliberately ending one’s life. Risk factors for suicide include mental disorders (such as depression, personality disorder, alcohol or drug dependence or schizophrenia), and certain physical illnesses, including neurological disorders, cancer and HIV infection. ''Source:'' World Health Organization - International Classification of Diseases Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision (ICD-10)
Among people aged 15-29 in the EU in 2023, almost 1 in 5 deaths were classified as intentional self-harm, whereas in the total population self-harm accounted for around 1 in 100 deaths. It was the second most common cause of death for young people, after accidents. In absolute terms, 4 842 young people aged 15-29 years in the EU died as a result of intentional self-harm in 2023. This represents a decrease compared with 10 years earlier, when 5 815 young people died due to self-harm in 2014 (see Figure 7). [[File:Deaths of young people caused by intentional self-harm, by age group, EU, 2014-2023 (number of deaths).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 7: Deaths of young people caused by intentional self-harm, by age group, EU, 2011-2022
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hlth_cd_aro__custom_21936311/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=9039787b-0a10-4593-8c87-b1a0a80bf2c4&c=1782305757000 hlth_cd_aro])|alt=a line chart with three lines showing the deaths of young people caused by intentional self-harm from the year 2011 until the year 2022, the lines show the ages, 16-19 years, 20-24 years, 25-29years. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] As shown in Figure 8, the highest crude death rates attributed to self-harm among young people were recorded for men aged 25-29 years. Young women were substantially less likely to die from suicide or intentional self-harm, with crude death rates for young men in the 5-year age groups between 15 and 29 years being between 1.7 to 3.8 times higher than those for young women in the EU. Over the past 10 years, crude death rates from intentional self-harm among men have generally decreased, while rates for young women have remained stable or shown a slight increase. [[File:Crude death rates from intentional self-harm, by age group and sex, EU, 2014 and 2023.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 8: Crude death rates from intentional self-harm, by age, group, and sex, EU, 2014 and 2023
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/hlth_cd_acdr2__custom_21944160/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=07e3014f-3796-44d5-b44e-5854c62d71b2&c=1782394130000 hlth_cd_acdr2])|alt= a vertical bar chart with two bars and two sets of markers shwoing crude death rates from intentional self-harm, by age group and sex in the EU in the years 2012 and 2022, the bars show males in the year 2022 and females in the year 2022, the markers show males in the year 2012, females in the year 2012. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] People in their twenties were more likely to die from intentional self-harm than in younger age groups. The crude death rate associated with intentional self-harm is higher for the total population than for young people, even though self-harm represent a smaller share of overall deaths in the total population. === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Youth health 26 v2.xlsx|title=Health: tables and figures}} === Data sources=== A wide range of statistics are gathered to describe health and living conditions across the EU. These include data on healthcare systems, health-related behaviour, diseases, and causes of death and a common set of EU health indicators. Through the [https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/glossary/open-method-of-coordination.html open method of coordination] on health issues, EU countries have agreed common definitions and approached to data collection and use. Key data sources include health interview surveys and modules, which provide information on the health status and the health-related behaviours of EU residents. Three main indicators on health status are collected every year, while additional information, including health determinants, is gathered every 3 years in the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)_methodology EU statistics on income and living conditions]. More detailed health indicators are collected every 6 years through the [[Glossary:European_health_interview_survey|European Health Interview Survey (EHIS)]]. Self-reported data have limitations, as they are subjective and influenced by respondents’ personal perceptions and cultural context. Nonetheless, these indicators are essential for assessing population health, anticipating healthcare needs and monitoring socio-economic disparities. Statistics on causes of [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Death death] are among the longest-established medical statistics. They provide evidence on trends over time and differences in causes of death between countries. Statistics on causes of death are based on the medical information recorded on [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Medical_certification death certificate]. These statistics play a key role in the general information system on health in the EU and can be used to determine which preventive and curative measures or research investment may help to increase life expectancy. [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:European_shortlist_of_causes_of_death European shortlist of causes of death] classifies deaths by 86 causes based on the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:International_classification_of_diseases_(ICD) International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD)]. ===Context=== '''WHAT IS THE ‘HEALTH PROGRAMME’?''' The [https://health.ec.europa.eu/funding/eu4health-programme-2021-2027-vision-healthier-european-union_en EU4Health programme] is main instrument for implementing the EU’s public health strategy and provides funding projects on health promotion, health security and health information. The programme was introduced in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and is designed to strengthen crisis preparedness in the EU. It has 4 overarching objectives: * improve and foster health * protect people * access to medicinal products, medical devices and crisis-relevant products * strengthen health systems. Among other priorities, a comprehensive, prevention-oriented and multi-stakeholder approach to [https://health.ec.europa.eu/non-communicable-diseases/mental-health_en mental health] has been developed after extensive consultation with Member States, stakeholders and citizens, and set out in the [https://health.ec.europa.eu/publications/comprehensive-approach-mental-health_en 2023 Communication on mental health]. If you or somebody you know is struggling with the issues mentioned in this article, you can find a support service in your country on the following page: [https://ifightdepression.com/en/get-help Get Help - iFightDepression]. === Other articles=== *[[Health|All articles on Health]] [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Self-perceived_health_statistics#SE_MAIN_TT Self-perceived health statistics] [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Causes_of_death_statistics Causes of death statistics] === Database ===
