title: Young people - qualifications, skills and job alignment
text:
Insert short description for search engines Data extracted in December 2025 Planned article update: No update planned In the EU, 70.0% of young people aged 15-34 reported that their educational attainment level matched their job requirements, while 21.7% had a higher educational level than their job required. Over half of young people (56.4%) with a medium or high level of education reported a very high or high match between their field of education and their current or previous job. 76.3% of young people in the EU reported that their skills matched their job requirements, 18.7% reporting that their skills were higher than required, and 5.0% reporting that their skills were lower than required.
This article explores the relationship between education, skills and job requirements, with a focus on the experiences of young people in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union]] (EU). The article looks at young people aged 15-34 and examines the match between their: * educational attainment and job requirements * field of education and job requirements * skills and job requirements It also highlights the challenges faced by foreign-born young people in finding employment that matches their education and skills. For an overview of young people dropping out of formal education, see the Statistics Explained article [[Young_people_dropping_out_of_education_and_labour_market_participation|Young people dropping out of education and labour market participation]]. === Education level and job requirements === This measure captures the self-reported match between a person’s educational attainment level (the highest level of formal education successfully completed) and the requirements of their current or last main job. The requirements of the current or last main job are not understood as the legal requirements for the job position, but rather as job demands needed to perform the role. In the EU, 70.0% of young people reported that their educational attainment level matched their job requirements (see Figure 1); 21.7% had a higher level of education than their job required and 8.2% had a lower level than required. The match varied slightly according to educational attainment level. The best match was found among young people with a high level of education (73.6%), whereas the lowest match was recorded among those with a medium level of education with a general orientation (58.4%). The high match among young people with a low level of education can be explained by the fact that they mainly worked in low-skilled jobs. Figure 1 ====== Educational level and job demands match across the EU ====== The highest matches, exceeding 80.0%, were reported in Lithuania, Latvia, Slovenia, Bulgaria and Romania (see Figure 1). Except for Romania, all these countries had a small gap of less than 10 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]] (pp) between the highest and lowest match by education level. The lowest matches, below 63.0%, were reported in the Netherlands, Hungary, Cyprus and Luxembourg. In Spain, Cyprus, Greece and Luxembourg, more than a quarter of young people with a high level of education worked in jobs that did not require a high level of education, indicating that they were unable to fully exploit their potential. In contrast, the potential of young people with high education was better exploited in Latvia, Romania, Lithuania and Denmark, where less than 15.0% of young people worked in jobs requiring a lower level of education than their own. In 13 EU countries, young people with a high level of education reported the highest match compared to those with a low or medium level of education. In 10 EU countries, the best match was declared by people with a low level of education, and in 4 countries by those with a medium level of education with a vocational orientation. In most EU countries, people with a medium level of education with a general orientation (20 countries) or a low level of education (6 countries) reported the lowest match. Greece was an exception, where individuals with a high level of education reported the lowest match. ====== Educational level and job demands match by occupation ====== Figure 2 shows that the highest match between educational level and job was found among people in professional occupations (84.0%). This group of occupations includes, for example, doctors, teachers, engineers and financial analysts. The lowest match was recorded for elementary occupations (51.0%). This group of occupations includes, for example office cleaners, farm labourers, sweepers, hand dishwashers and hotel porters. Skilled agricultural, forestry and fishery workers reported the highest match among young people with a low level of education (75.0%). Young people in armed forces occupations reported the best match among those with a medium level of education with a general orientation (80.0%). Craft and related trades workers and technicians and associate professionals reported the highest match among young people with a medium level of vocational education (79.0%). Professionals had the highest match among young people with a high level of education (86.0%). Figure 2 ====== Education level match and over-qualification rate ====== Figure 3 illustrates the relationship between the self-estimated educational attainment level being higher than job requirements and the over-qualification rate, revealing a moderate correlation between these 2 indicators ([[Glossary:Correlation_coefficient|correlation coefficient]] 0.45). This suggests that, in countries with higher over-qualification rates, a larger proportion of young people with a high level of education estimated that their education level was higher than their job requirements. Over-qualification occurs when people with a high level of education work in jobs that do not require their level of educational attainment. This phenomenon may indicate a mismatch between the skills and qualifications of young people and the demands of the labour market. Figure 3 Greece, Spain and Cyprus had an over-qualification rate above 30.0% and at the same time around 30.0% of young people in these countries estimated that their education level was higher than their job requirements. In contrast, Luxembourg stood out as an exception, with the lowest over-qualification rate in the EU. However, in spite of this, a high proportion of young people in Luxembourg estimated that their education level was higher than the requirements of their job. === Field of education and job requirements === The alignment between the field of a person’s highest level of formal education successfully completed and the requirements of their current or last main job was self-reported on the scale: very high, high, moderate, low or none. In the EU, more than half of young people with a medium or high level of education reported a very high or high match between their field of education and their current or previous job in 2024 (32.5% and 23.9%, respectively). Around 20.0% of young people stated that there was no match or that there were no job requirements (see Figure 4). The match was closer for young people with a high level of education (41.1% very high and 27.1% high match) than those with a medium level of education (24.9% very high and 21.2% high match). Work experience during studies played a significant role in field matching. In 2024, 57.6% of young people with a medium level of education who had at least 1 month of work experience during their studies reported a very high or high field match. In contrast, only 36.8% of young people without work experience during their studies reported a very high or high match. This suggests that having some work experience during studies improved young people's chances of finding a relevant job after completing their studies. However, the impact of work experience during studies on field matching was negligible for young people with a high level of education. Figure 4 ====== Match by field and level of education ====== Figure 5 illustrates the very high or high field match by 10 broad fields of education. The match was closer for all fields of education of young people with a high level of education than those with a medium level of education, with a 22 pp gap in the match between a high level and a medium level of education. The largest gaps between education levels were observed for the fields of natural sciences, mathematics and statistics (33 pp), and information and communication technologies (32 pp). The best match was found in the field of health and welfare, where 71.0% of young people with a medium level of education and 81.0% of those with a high level of education worked very closely to their attained field of education. The gap between a medium level and a high level of education was also the smallest for this field. The next best matches were reported by young people with a high level of education in the field of information and communication technologies (77.0%) and young people with a medium level of education in the field of education (58.0%). In contrast, young people who had graduated in the arts and humanities had most difficulties finding a relevant job. The very high or high match was reported by only half of young people with a high level of education (52.0%) and one third of those with a medium level of education (34.0%). Figure 5 ====== Education field and job demands match across the EU ====== The highest matches, above 75.0%, were reported in Latvia, Lithuania and Germany, where most young people’s jobs were closely related to their field of education. In contrast, young people in Italy, Slovakia, Denmark, Ireland, Estonia and Poland had the highest problems finding a job relevant to their education, with less than half of them reporting a very high or high match with their field of education. In 16 EU countries, young people with a health and welfare field of education reported the best match, while the education field had the best match in 5 EU countries. === Skills and job requirements === The self-reported match between a person’s skills and the requirements of their current or last main job showed whether the skills of young people met, exceeded or fell short of the job requirements. The term ‘skills’ refers to all the knowledge, abilities, competences and experience that a person had gained as part of their education, training, learning, internships and working activities. In 2024, over 3 quarters (76.3%) of young people aged 15-34 in the EU reported that their skills matched their job requirements, while 18.7% stated that their skills were higher and 5.0% reported that their skills were lower than the job requirements (see Map 1). This means that almost one fifth (23.7%) of young people were unable to find a job that was relevant to their skills. The best matches between skills and job requirements were found in Latvia, Lithuania, Slovenia and Hungary, where over 85.0% of young people reported a match between their skills and job requirements. In contrast, the lowest shares, below 70.0%, were reported in Luxembourg, Italy, the Netherlands and Ireland. [[Image:MAP skill match.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Young people with a match between skills and job, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b23fe51c-e75b-45f3-b22c-8d59559ffa14?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-12T13:21:41Z (lfso_24match10)]]] Map 1: Young people with a match between skills and current or previous job, 2024,
''Source:'' Eurostat [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/b23fe51c-e75b-45f3-b22c-8d59559ffa14?lang=en&createdAt=2026-02-12T13:21:41Z (lfso_24match10)] The highest share of young people with a match was found among young people with a high level of education (79.0%), followed by those with a low level of education (77.6%) and a medium level of education (73.6%). Figure 6 shows that the match generally increased with job tenure. In 2024, 75.0% of young people who had held a job with their current employer for less than 1 year reported a match between their skills and job requirements, while 83.1% of young people who had held their job for over 10 years had a match. Figure 6 In 18 EU countries, the highest match was reported by young people who had held a job for more than 10 years, while in 8 countries, the highest match was found among young people who had held a job for 5-9 years. Only in Finland did young people who had held a job for 1-4 years report a higher match than those who had held a job for less than 1 year or for 5 years or more. === Education and skills match of foreign-born people === Figure 7 illustrates the match between education level, the field of education, and skills with the current or previous job, comparing foreign-born young people with those born in the reporting country. In general, in the EU in 2024, foreign-born young people faced more difficulties finding a job relevant to their education and skills. The gap between foreign-born and native-born young people was: * 8.5 pp for the match between education level and job * 7.3 pp for a very high or high match between the field of education and job * 6.4 pp for the match between skills and job requirements. Figure 7 The highest gap in the match between education level and job was observed in Estonia, where only 62.0% of foreign-born young people reported a match between their education level and job, compared to 80.0% of native-born young people. Large gaps were also reported in Malta (15.5 pp), Austria and Czechia (both 14.9 pp). In Estonia, Malta and Czechia the large gap was mainly due to young people born in non-EU countries. In contrast, foreign-born young people had a higher match than their native-born counterparts regarding education level match in Greece, Luxembourg and Latvia, where the gap was negative. The match between the field of education and job varied a lot between countries. In 15 EU countries, foreign-born young people had a significantly lower match with a gap of mostly over 10 pp In 8 EU countries, foreign-born young people had a higher match than their native-born counterparts, while in 1 country, the gap was negligible (below 1 pp). The gap was not available for 3 countries due to the low reliability of data for foreign-born young people. The highest gaps in skills match between foreign-born and native-born young people were observed in Malta, Austria and Czechia, where the skills match was over 10 pp lower for foreign-born young people than for native-born young people. However, foreign-born young people reported higher matches than native-born young people in Slovakia, Greece, Finland and Romania, where the gap was negative. Overall, considering all 3 indicators, foreign-born young people reported more of a mismatch than native-born young people in Malta, Austria, Czechia and Estonia. In contrast, foreign-born young people had a lower or the same mismatch as native-born young people in Luxembourg, Greece, Slovakia and Finland. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Figure_1.xlsx|Download Figure 1]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] *[[Media:Figure_2.xlsx|Download Figure 2]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] *[[Media:Figure_3.xlsx|Download Figure 3]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] *[[Media:Figure_4.xlsx|Download Figure 4]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] *[[Media:Figure_5.xlsx|Download Figure 5]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] *[[Media:Figure_6.xlsx|Download Figure 6]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] *[[Media:Figure_7.xlsx|Download Figure 7]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] === Data sources === The [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(EU-LFS)|EU-LFS]] is the largest European household sample survey providing quarterly and annual results on labour market characteristics of people. The EU-LFS covers the resident population, defined as all people usually residing in private households. Since 1999, modules have been an integral part of the EU-LFS. These were called ‘ad hoc modules’ until 2020. From 2021 onwards, they have been called either ‘8-yearly modules’ for variables with an 8-year cycle or ‘modules on an ad hoc subject’ for variables not included in the 8-year datasets. In 2024, the EU-LFS included an 8-yearly module on young people in the labour market. The next 8-yearly module on ‘Young people on the labour market’ will be carried out in 2032. Similar ad hoc modules were conducted in 2000, 2009 and 2016. For further information on the EU-LFS modules, please refer to the article [[EU_labour_force_survey_-_modules|EU labour force survey - modules]]. '''Coverage.''' The 2024 EU-LFS module on young people in the labour market covers all [[Glossary:EU|EU]] countries, 1 [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] country and 1 [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate country]]. For Cyprus, the survey covers only the areas of Cyprus controlled by the Government of the Republic of Cyprus. Only people aged 15-34 were covered by the module. '''European aggregates.''' EU aggregates in absolute values are calculated by aggregating the estimated values (i.e. weighted population totals) of the respective EU countries. For EU aggregates expressed as rates or ratios, the absolute values are first calculated for both the numerator and the denominator, and then the rates or ratios are derived from those results. '''Calculation of percentages.''' All the figures in this article are percentages of a total. The calculation of percentages used in this article is based on a total excluding the number of people classified in the non-response category. As such, all exhaustive breakdowns presented in the figures should amount to 100% (allowing for rounding errors). ====Definitions==== '''The level of the formal education or training activity''' is defined according to the [http://uis.unesco.org/en/topic/international-standard-classification-education-isced International Standard Classification of Education 2011] (ISCED 2011, ISCED-P for education programmes). '''Levels of education:''' *Low level of education – less than primary, primary and lower secondary education (ISCED levels 0-2) *Medium level of education – upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education (ISCED levels 3 and 4) *High level of education – tertiary education (ISCED levels 5-8) '''The over-qualification rate''' is calculated for employed people with a high level of educational attainment ([[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|ISCED]] levels 5-8). It indicates the proportion of people in that group who are employed in occupations that do not require a tertiary level of education (equivalent to [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_occupations_(ISCO)|ISCO]] major groups 4-9). '''The field of the highest level of education''' successfully completed is defined according to the ‘ISCED Fields of Education and Training’ (ISCED-F 2013). A field of education is the ‘Broad domain, branch or area of content covered by an education programme, course or module’. '''Skills''' are defined as all of the knowledge, abilities, competences and experience that a person has gained as part of all their education, training, learning, internships and working activities. The match is defined against all of the knowledge, abilities, competences and experience that are required for the current or last main job. For employed people, '''the match''' referred to the requirements currently needed to do the job (as self-perceived by the respondent); it did not refer to the requirements at the time of recruitment. For unemployed people or people outside the labour force, the variable referred to requirements needed to do the last main job at the time the person was performing it (as self-perceived by the respondent). '''Employed person''' is a person who, during the reference week, was in one of the following categories: * people who, during the reference week, worked for at least 1 hour for pay or profit, including contributing family workers * people with a job or business who were temporarily not at work during the reference week but had an attachment to their job. === Context === The [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/european-pillar-social-rights-building-fairer-and-more-inclusive-european-union/european-pillar-social-rights-20-principles_en European Pillar of Social Rights] sets out 20 key principles and rights essential for fair and well-functioning labour markets and welfare systems. The [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/european-pillar-social-rights-building-fairer-and-more-inclusive-european-union/european-pillar-social-rights-action-plan_en action plan] of the European Pillar of Social Rights sets out concrete initiatives to turn the European Pillar of Social Rights into reality. The initiative [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/european-pillar-social-rights-building-fairer-and-more-inclusive-european-union/european-pillar-social-rights-action-plan/skills-and-equality_en skills and equality] aims to ensure that people have the right skills for the jobs of today and tomorrow, and equal opportunities. === Other articles === *[[Labour market (incl. labour force survey)|All articles on the labour market]] *[[Young_people_dropping_out_of_education_and_labour_market_participation|Young people dropping out of education and labour market participation]] *[[Participation of young people in education and the labour market]] *[[Statistics on young people neither in employment nor in education or training]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/lfs/database Employment and unemployment (Labour Force Survey) (employ)], see: :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=lfso LFS ad-hoc modules (lfso)] ::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=lfso_24 2024. title: Young people - housing conditions
text:
Housing conditions of young people in the EU, looking at the age of leaving the parental home, overcrowded households and housing cost overburden Data extracted in August 2025 Planned article update: 29 September 2026 In 2024, young people across the EU left their parental home on average at the age of 26.2 years, ranging from 31.3 years in Croatia to 21.4 years in Finland. In 2024, 26.5% of young people (aged 15-29 years) in the EU lived in overcrowded dwellings, compared with 16.9% of the overall population. In 2024, 9.7% of people aged 15-29 in the EU lived in households that spent 40% or more of their disposable income on housing – this share is 8.2% in the overall population. [[Image:Map_1_Estimated_average_age_of_people_leaving_their_parental_home,_2024_.png |thumb|center|700px|''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=yth_demo_030}}|alt=a map showing the average age of leaving the parental home for EU countries.]] Young people’s approach to moving out of the family home varies across the EU: in some parts of the EU, it is typical to stay with the parental family for longer, hence increasing the probability of overcrowding. In other parts of the EU [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|European Union (EU)]], young people prefer to move out sooner and face a higher risk of housing cost overburden. Several factors can influence this decision: being in a relationship, the situation in the job market, cultural habits, and financial aspects related to housing costs and the cost of living in general. This article presents an analysis of the age when young people in the EU typically take this decision. It also presents 2 closely related indicators that can describe young people’s housing conditions: the [[Glossary:Overcrowded|overcrowding rate]] and the [[Glossary:Housing cost overburden rate|housing cost overburden rate]]. Further analysis related to this topic can be found in the following Statistics Explained articles * [[Living conditions in Europe - housing#Key findings|Living conditions in Europe - housing - Chapter: Key findings]] , which analyses the housing situation for the population overall * [[Young people - family and society]], which discusses the family situation for young Europeans According to the latest Eurostat data, the average age of leaving the parental household was 26.2 years across the EU in 2024, with particularly high values in the south and east of the EU. At the same time, both the burden of housing costs and the overcrowding rates remain disproportionately high for young adults. ===Leaving the parental home=== In 2024, across the EU, the average age of young people who left their parental home – the age at which 50% of the population no longer live in a household with their parent(s) – was 26.2. However, this average varied among EU countries. The highest average ages, at 30 or over, were recorded in Croatia (31.3), Slovakia (30.9), Greece (30.7), Italy (30.1) and Spain (30.0). In contrast, the lowest average ages, all under 23, were registered in Finland (21.4), Denmark (21.7), Sweden (21.9) and Estonia (22.4). The situation in countries on both ends of the spectrum tends to be stable over time, pointing to different practices concerning co-residence of generations among EU countries. [[Image:Map_1_Estimated_average_age_of_people_leaving_their_parental_home,_2024_.png |thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Estimated average age of people leaving their parental home, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=yth_demo_030}}|alt=a map showing the average age of leaving the parental home for EU countries.]] Looking at this from a different angle, with regard to the relationship with the parental household, several patterns emerge when we break down young people into smaller age groups (16-19-, 20-24- and 25-29-year-olds – see Figure 1). In Croatia, Slovakia, Italy, Spain, Poland, Greece and Ireland, most young people (more than 80% of 16-29-year-olds) live with their parents or contribute to / benefit from the household income. This corresponds to more than 95% of those aged 16-19, more than 85% of those aged 20-24, and more than 60% (59.2% in the case of Ireland) of those aged 25-29. However, on the other end of the spectrum, in Sweden, Denmark and Finland, less than 93% of 16 19-year-olds live with their parents. Furthermore, in the group of 20-24-year-olds, fewer than 40% live with their parents, and for the age group 25-29, these countries have the lowest shares in the EU: 4.3% live with their parents in Denmark, 6.4% in Finland and 12.1% in Sweden. [[Image:Fig_1_Young_people_living_with_their_parents_or_contributing_to_or_benefiting_from_the_household_income,_2024_(_).png |thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Young people living with their parents or contributing to/benefiting from the household income, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_lvps08}}|alt=a stock graph showing the share of young people in different age groups living in, contributing to or benefiting from the parental household for each EU country and the EU as a whole. The points on the graph show ages 15-19 years, 20-24 years and 25-29 years.]] ===Overcrowding rate=== In 2024, 26.5% of young people (aged 15-29 years) in the EU lived in overcrowded dwellings.
The overcrowding rate is defined as the percentage of the population living in an overcrowded household. A person is considered as living in an overcrowded household if it does not have at a minimum number of rooms available that is equal to the sum of *one room for the household *one room per couple in the household *one room per single person aged 18 or over *one room per pair of single people of the same gender between 12 and 17 *one room per single person between 12 and 17 and not included in the previous category *one room per pair of children under 12
In 2024, the overcrowding rate for young people aged 15-29 years stood at 26.5%, 0.5 percentage points (pp) higher than in 2023. Across all EU countries, young people were more likely than the population overall to live in overcrowded households. The overcrowding rate for young people was 9.6 pp higher than the overcrowding rate for the total population (16.9%). There are considerable differences in overcrowding rates between EU countries. In 2024, in Cyprus, 4.1% of young people lived in an overcrowded household, while in Romania, the rate reached 58.3%. More than half of young people also lived in overcrowded households in Latvia and Bulgaria, and more than a third in Lithuania, Italy, Slovakia, Poland, Croatia and Greece (see Figure 2). [[Image: Fig 2 Overcrowding rate, 2024 ( ).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Overcrowding rate, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_lvho05a}}|alt=a double vertical bar chart showing the Overcrowding rate in 2024 in the EU and EU Member States. The bars show persons of all ages and persons aged 15-29 years.]] The highest difference between the rates for young people and those for the total population were seen in Bulgaria (19.4 pp difference), Greece (18.5 pp difference) and Romania (17.6 pp difference). In relative terms, the difference between the overcrowding rate for young people and that for the general population were highest in Denmark, the Netherlands and Finland, where young people were twice more likely to live in an overcrowded dwelling than the general population. Figure 3 presents the overcrowding rate for young people broken down by smaller age groups (15 19-, 20-24- and 25-29-year-olds). Generally, in countries where the overcrowding rate for young people is high, 15-19 is the most affected age group. In Romania, Latvia, Bulgaria and Croatia, more than half of 15-19-year-olds live in overcrowded households (ranging from 65.5% in Romania to 50.6% in Croatia). In most countries the overcrowding rate reduces with age. The biggest difference between 15-19- and 25–29-year-olds is seen in Latvia (21.8 pp difference) followed by Lithuania and Czechia (both at 17.99 pp) and Romania (14.8 pp). By contrast, in Denmark, Finland, Sweden and the Netherlands, overcrowding rates are highest for 20-24-year-olds. The difference between this age group and those aged 15-19 is 15.4 pp in Finland, 13.9 pp in Denmark and 13.5 pp in Sweden. In Finland and Sweden, the overcrowding rate for 20-24-year-olds is more than twice as high as that for 15-19-year-olds. In other countries where the overcrowding rates are lower, the differences among age groups are smaller as well. [[Image:Fig 3 Overcrowding rate for young people (aged 15-29 years), by age group, 2024 ( ).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Overcrowding rate for young people by age group, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_lvho05a}}|alt=a stock graph showing the overcrowding rate of young people by age group in 2024 in the EU and EU Member States. The points on the graph show ages 15-19 years, 20-24 years and 25-29 years.]] ===Housing cost overburden rate=== In 2024, 9.7% of young people (aged 15-29) in the EU lived in households that spent 40% or more of their disposable income on housing. This figure is 1.5 pp higher than for the total population.
The indicator [[Glossary:Housing cost overburden rate|housing cost overburden rate ]]shows the percentage of the population living in households where housing costs equate to more than 40 % of a household’s disposable income.
In 2024, 8.2% of the EU’s population lived in households that spent 40% or more of their disposable income on housing (see Figure 4). For young people, the share was 1.5 pp higher, at 9.7%. However, there are considerable differences between EU countries. Croatia (2.1%), Cyprus (2.8%) and Slovenia (3.0%) had the lowest housing cost overburden rate for young people, while Greece (30.3%) and Denmark (28.9%) had by far the highest. Eight countries had rates above the EU average. [[Image:Fig 4 Housing cost overburden rate, 2024 s( ).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Housing cost overburden rate, EU, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_lvho07a}}|alt=a double vertical bar chart showing the housing cost overburden rate in 2024 in the EU and EU Member States. The bars show persons of all ages and persons aged 15-29 years.]] In 2024, in 16 EU countries, the housing cost overburden rate was higher among those aged 15-29 than for the population overall. The biggest difference between both groups was 14.3 pp in Denmark, followed by the Netherlands with 8.4 pp. In relative terms, the biggest difference was in the Netherlands, as well as in Finland and Denmark, where the rate for young people was more than 1.9 times higher than that for the population overall. Unlike the overcrowding rate, 11 EU countries recorded (slightly) higher housing cost overburden rates for the population overall than for young people. Among these, Croatia had the biggest difference (-1.6 pp). Figure 5 provides a more detailed analysis of the situation, breaking the group down further into smaller groups (15-19, 20-24 and 25-29). Among these groups, the housing cost overburden rate was highest for 20-24-year-olds (11.7%) and lowest for 15-19-year-olds (7.2%). This was the case in most EU countries. [[Image:Fig 5 Housing cost overburden rate for young people (aged 15-29 years), by age group, 2024 ( ).png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 5: Housing cost overburden rate for young people (aged 15-29 years), by age group, 2024 ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=ilc_lvho07a}}|alt= a stock graph showing the housing cost overburden rate of young people, by age group in 2024 in the EU and EU Member States. The points on the graph show ages 15-19 years, 20-24 years and 25-29 years.]] In some of the countries where young people tend to move out of the parental home sooner, such as Denmark, the Netherlands, Sweden, Germany and Finland (see Map 1), the housing cost overburden for young people is higher. Countries where young people move out of the parental home later, like Cyprus, Croatia and Italy, tend to report lower levels of housing cost overburden. However, in Greece and Bulgaria, despite the higher average age of people leaving the family home, the housing cost overburden for young people remains high. === Source data for tables and graphs === *[[Media:Youth_housing_2025_.xlsx|Download Excel file]] [[Image:Microsoft_Excel_2010_Logo.png|20px|link=]] ===Data sources=== The data used in this article are derived from the [[Glossary:EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]] and the [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_labour_force_survey European Union Labour Force Survey (EU-LFS)]. EU-SILC is the main European source of information for statistics related to income, living conditions and social inclusion. The legal basis for these data is {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R1700:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2019/1700}} establishing a common framework for European statistics related to people and households, based on data at individual level collected from samples. In the survey a person is included in the parental household if they are • living with their parents • working away from the family home during the week, but usually return to the family home at the weekends • primary and secondary school pupils away from the family home during the school term • living outside the family home for an extended period of time for work reasons, but are significantly contributing to the household income and are not usual residents of another private household • students in higher education who are away from their family home while at college or university but benefit from the household income and are not usual residents of another private household The EU-LFS is the largest European household sample survey providing quarterly and annual results on labour participation of people aged 15 and above. The EU-LFS is based on the same target populations and uses the same definitions in all countries, meaning that the results are comparable between countries. Yearly results are obtained as averages of the four quarters in the year. The EU aggregate is a population-weighted average of individual national figures. The reference population covered by these data comprises all private households and their current members residing in EU Member States, EFTA countries and EU candidate countries at the time of data collection. Persons living in [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Household_-_social_statistics collective households] and in institutions are excluded from the target population. ===Context=== In 2024, there were 73.4 million people aged between 15 and 29 in the EU According to Eurostat’s demographic data: [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/YTH_DEMO_010__custom_2164673/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=ba5b0ab1-bc92-47e6-8d27-e2fdd622d0ca Child and youth population on 1 January by sex and age] [YTH_DEMO_010__custom_2164673], and, as in many other aspects in life, they can face challenges with housing. Housing conditions are a fundamental aspect of living standards and social integration for individuals. For young people starting life away from the family home, finding and sustaining accommodation can be a major challenge. In the EU’s [https://ec.europa.eu/info/strategy/priorities-2019-2024/economy-works-people/jobs-growth-and-investment/european-pillar-social-rights/european-pillar-social-rights-action-plan_en European Pillar for Social Rights action plan], one of the headline targets is: ‘lifting at least 15 million people out of the risk of poverty and social exclusion by 2030’. For each target, a group of indicators was developed to monitor and support the strategy. Housing conditions are included within the indicators related to material deprivation. Housing issues are also addressed in the [https://europa.eu/youth/strategy_en EU youth strategy] adopted for the 2019-2027 period. ===Other articles=== '''''Theme entry page''''' *[[Children and
