title: Young people - social inclusion
text:
Data extracted in June 2026 Planned article update: June 2027 In 2025, 24.2% of young people aged 15-29 in the EU (17.3 million people) were at risk of poverty or social exclusion. In 2025, the at-risk-of-poverty rate of young people aged 15-29 was 3.3 percentage points higher than that of the total population. In 2025, 8.2% of people aged 15-29 in the EU lived in households with very low work intensity. [[File:Young people AROPE.png|thumb|centre|700px|Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e1ede009-32d2-4459-a170-95c04e03b06e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-16T15:39:24Z ilc_peps01n])|alt= a map showing the share of young people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025 as a percentage for ages 15 to 29 in the EU, the euro area, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries and candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] This article presents statistics on the risk of poverty or social exclusion of young people aged 15-29 years in the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|EU]] and in selected [[Glossary:European Free Trade Association (EFTA)|EFTA]] and [[Glossary:Candidate countries|candidate]] countries. Several factors determine the living conditions of young Europeans, and these are examined in a series of Statistics Explained articles. While young people are often associated with education, mobility and opportunity, many experience economic vulnerability during the transition to adulthood. This article analyses the [[Glossary:At risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)|risk of poverty or social exclusion]] among young people and its 3 components – the [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|at-risk-of-poverty rate]], the [[Glossary:Severe material and social deprivation rate (SMSD)|severe material and social deprivation rate]] and the share of people living in [[Glossary:Persons living in households with very low work intensity|households with very low work intensity]]. ===Young people at risk of poverty or social exclusion=== ''In 2025, nearly 1 in 4 young people aged 15-29 in the EU were at risk of poverty or social exclusion.'' An estimated 24.2% of the [[Glossary:European Union (EU)|EU's]] young people (aged 15-29 years) – [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ilc_peps01n__custom_16882529/bookmark/table?lang=en&bookmarkId=42e65134-fe93-40c6-bc90-a82bea4ffb8c&page=time:2024 17.3 million young people] – were [[Glossary:At risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion]] in 2025. This rate is 3.3 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points (pp)]] higher than that of the total population, which was 20.9%. The share varied from around 1 in 10 young people (10.6%) in Slovenia to almost 1 in 3 (30.8%) in Romania.
The [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:At_risk_of_poverty_or_social_exclusion_(AROPE) at risk of poverty or social exclusion (‘AROPE’)] refers to the total number of people who are either [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|at risk of poverty]], [[Glossary:Severe material and social deprivation rate (SMSD)|severely materially and socially deprived]], or living in a [[Glossary:Persons living in households with very low work intensity|household with very low work intensity]]. The AROPE rate is the share of the total population at risk of poverty or social exclusion. It covers people who are in at least one of these 3 situations: • people who are [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|at-risk-of-poverty]], that is, those with an equivalised disposable income below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold (60% of median income after social transfers) • people who suffer from [[Glossary:Severe material and social deprivation rate (SMSD)|severe material and social deprivation]], that is, those who cannot afford at least 7 of the 13 deprivation items (6 related to the individual and 7 to the household) that are considered desirable or even necessary for an adequate quality of life • people below the age of 65 living in [[Glossary:Persons living in households with very low work intensity|households with very low work intensity]] (also referred to as jobless or quasi-jobless households), that is, those living in households where adults worked 20% or less of their total combined work-time potential during the previous 12 months.
Considering the 3 components of the risk of poverty and social exclusion separately, in 2025: - the at-risk-of-poverty rate for people aged 15-29 in the EU was 19.6% ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/284dc9ab-1a94-4874-8ece-5cd4e6902fec?lang=en&page=time:2025 14 million] young people) - the rate of severe material and social deprivation was 5.8% ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/7884d4fb-2837-48aa-8566-3ddc68edd704?lang=en&page=time:2025 4 million] young people) - the share of people who lived in very low work intensity households stood at 8.2% ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/c99a4536-1f5c-4a6f-bb63-12a87e972419?lang=en&page=time:2024 5.6 million] young people). Some people may fall within more than one of these categories. Analysed by age group and component, the youngest age group (those aged 15-19 years) were the most vulnerable for both the risk of poverty and deprivation components, while 25-29-year-olds were more often living in households with very low work intensity than the youngest group (see Table 1). [[File:Poverty and social exclusion of youth by component and age group, 2025 (%).png|thumb|centre|700px|Table 1: Poverty and social exclusion of youth by components and age group, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/64c6206b-6c68-4f29-913a-0d69727ae098?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-16T15:49:02Z ilc_peps01n]) ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/650e16c7-b045-46c4-a480-a5131b6335bc?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-16T15:52:46Z ilc_li02]) ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ae642565-f240-46da-9193-eb7b1b572db2?lang=en&createdAt=2026-05-10T19:23:58Z ilc_mdsd11]) ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/4988fc29-9b6d-4fe3-8097-09b0da1684b8?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-16T15:47:57Z ilc_lvhl11]) ]] In 2025, the EU countries with the highest levels of young people (aged 15-29) at risk of poverty or social exclusion were Romania (30.8%), Denmark and Finland (both 30.7%) and Greece (30.0%), while the lowest rates were found in Slovenia (10.6%). [[File:Young people AROPE.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Young Europeans at risk of poverty or social exclusion, 2025
Source: Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/e1ede009-32d2-4459-a170-95c04e03b06e?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-16T15:39:24Z ilc_peps01n])|alt= a map showing the share of young people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025 as a percentage for ages 15 to 29 in the EU, the euro area, EU Member States and some of the EFTA countries and candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] At EU level, a smaller share of people aged 25-29 (an estimated 20.2% in 2025) were at risk of poverty or social exclusion than those aged 15-19 and 20-24 (26.3% and 26.0%, respectively). In 18 EU countries, the 15-19 age category faced the highest risk of poverty or social exclusion. By contrast, in several Nordic countries the risk increased sharply after age 20, likely because young people in those countries tend to move out and live independently earlier (see [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20250923-1 Eurostat data] dataset [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/ce0cdf00-f4ba-4932-a01a-1de1a876d74d?lang=en&createdAt=2026-06-08T12:53:44Z yth_demo_030]). In Denmark and Finland, for example, those aged 15-19 were by far the least exposed, with relatively high difference of 27.9pp and 25.2 pp, respectively, compared to those aged 20-24. [[File:People at risk of poverty or social exclusion, aged 15-29 years, by detailed age groups, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 1: Share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, aged 15-29 years, by detailed age group, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/8c56d107-1bf0-4a63-852c-a71c069b3579?lang=en ilc_peps01n]) |alt=a scatter chart showing the share of young people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, from age 15 to 29 in 2025 by percentage, in the EU, the euro area, EU countries and some of the EFTA countries and candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===At-risk-of-poverty rate for young people=== ''Nearly 14 million young people in the EU were at risk of poverty in 2025.'' The [[Glossary:At-risk-of-poverty rate|at-risk-of-poverty rate]], a component of the [[Glossary:At risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion rate]] measures poverty in relative terms. In 2025, the at-risk-of-poverty rate for those aged 15-29 was 19.6% (see Figure 2). At EU level, the risk faced by young people was 3.3 pp higher than that of the total population (16.3%). This was the case in 19 EU countries, with the largest gaps between young people (aged 15-29) and the total population recorded in Finland (13.4% of the total population at risk of poverty compared with 27.3% of young people) and Denmark (11.8% compared with 23.3%). However, in 8 EU countries young people were less likely to be at risk of poverty than the population as a whole. The biggest differences were in Croatia (19.5% for the total population compared with 11.1% for young people), Lithuania (22.6% compared with 17.1%) and Latvia (22.0% compared with 16.6%). [[File:People at risk of poverty, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 2: Share of people at risk of poverty, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/abedb6ec-e365-4968-894b-2ed15377a4c4?lang=en ilc_li02])|alt= a double vertical bar chart showing the share of young people at risk of poverty, for ages 15 to 29, next to the share of the total population at risk of poverty, in 2025, as a percentage in the EU, some of the EU countries, some of the EFTA countries and candidate countries. The bars show young people aged 15-29 and total population. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Severe material and social deprivation of young people=== The [[Glossary:Severe_material_and_social_deprivation_rate_(SMSD)|severe material and social deprivation rate]] complements the relative, income-based poverty indicator by capturing non-monetary aspects, such as being able to keep the home adequately warm, meet unexpected expenses and participate in regular leisure activities. It is an absolute measure of poverty and reflects the differences in living standards between EU countries. Countries such as Finland, Denmark, Luxembourg, Sweden and the Netherlands recorded relatively high at-risk-of-poverty rates but low severe material deprivation rates. This indicates that, although a larger share of young people had incomes below the national poverty threshold, fewer of them experienced severe material hardship. This comparison illustrates that income poverty and material deprivation reflect different dimensions of living conditions. In 2025, the severe material and social deprivation rate for young people aged 15-29 in the EU was 5.8%, compared with 6.3% for the total population. The share of young people was lower than that of the total population in almost all EU countries. Denmark, Sweden and Malta were exceptions, though the difference was small. The highest proportions of young people aged 15-29 who were severely materially deprived were in Romania (15.1%), Greece (14.7%) and Bulgaria (14.0%). In 10 EU countries, less than 3.0% of young people were severely materially or socially deprived. The lowest shares were in Slovenia and Croatia (0.8% in both) and Poland (1.5%) – see Figure 3. [[File:Severe material and social deprivation rate, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 3: Severe material and social deprivation rate, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/55b4464a-dc15-4a2c-be7e-31b2b5fc128e?lang=en ilc_mdsd11])|alt= a vertical bar chart showing severe material and social deprivation rate for people aged 15-29 years, and for the total population, for 2025, as a percentage. In the EU, EU countries, some of the EFTA countries and some candidate countries. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] ===Young people living in households with very low work intensity=== Another component of the [[Glossary:At risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)|at risk of poverty or social exclusion rate]] is the share of people living in [[Glossary:Work intensity|households with very low work intensity]].This indicator covers households where adults did little or no work during most of the previous year, a situation often linked to long-term exclusion from labour market. In 2025, 5.7 million people aged 15-29 in the EU lived in households with very low work intensity, equivalent to 8.2% of the population in this age group – see Figure 4. Among EU countries, Finland (14.8%), Denmark (14.3%), Germany (10.9%), Lithuania (10.8%) and Belgium (10.2%) recorded the highest proportions of people aged 15-29 living in such households. The lowest proportions were in Slovenia (3.0%), Poland and Croatia (both 3.3%) and Cyprus (3.4%). Slovenia’s shares were consistently among the lowest across all 3 components examined in this article. [[File:Share of people living in households with very low work intensity for population aged 15-29 years, 2025.png|thumb|centre|700px|Figure 4: Share of people living in households with very low work intensity for population aged 15-29 years, 2025
''Source:'' Eurostat ([https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/bookmark/116acd18-38cd-46e7-9e69-9fde424cd193?lang=en ilc_lvhl11n])|alt=a vertical bar chart showing the share of young people aged 15-29 years living in households with very low work intensity in 2022 as a percentage. In the EU, the euro area, EU Member States some of the EFTA countries some candidate countries, and some potential candidates. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Source data for tables and graphs === *{{Template:Excel|filename=Young people - inclusionRev.xlsx|title=Social inclusion — young people: tables and figures}} ===Data sources=== The data used in this article come from the [[Glossary:EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)|EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC)]]. EU-SILC data are compiled annually and are the main source of statistics on income and living conditions in Europe. They are also the main source for linking different aspects of the quality of life of [https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Glossary:Household households] and individuals. The reference population for this article covers all private households and their current members living in the territory of an EU country (or non-EU country) at the time of data collection. People living in collective households and institutions are generally excluded from the target population. The EU figures are population-weighted averages of national data. The legal basis for these data is {{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32003R1177:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2019/1700}}, which establishes a common framework for European statistics on persons and households, based on individual-level data collected from samples. ===Context=== The headline EU2030 target on poverty and social inclusion, set out in the [[Glossary:The European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan (EU 2030 targets)|European Pillar of Social Rights]] action plan, is to reduce the number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion by at least 15 million by 2030. Progress towards this target is monitored using the AROPE rate, published by Eurostat. The AROPE indicator was modified in 2021. The severe material deprivation rate was replaced by a new severe material and social deprivation rate (SMSD), based on a revised list of items, and the indicator on ‘people living in very low work intensity households’ was redefined. The revised AROPE indicator is used to monitor the headline target on poverty and social inclusion set out in the European Pillar of Social Rights action plan. Social inclusion was one of the 8 fields of action in the EU youth strategy, which ran from 2010 to 2018. In May 2018, the European Commission proposed a [https://youth.europa.eu/strategy_en new EU youth strategy] for 2019-2027, with 'Inclusive society' as one of 11 goals. The new strategy was adopted in 2021. ===Other articles=== '''''Theme entry page''''' *[[Children and youth]] '''''Online publications''''' *[[Quality of life indicators|Quality of life indicators]] '''''Statistical articles''''' *[[Children at risk of poverty or social exclusion]] *[[Living conditions in Europe - material deprivation and economic strain|Living conditions in Europe — material deprivation and economic strain]] *[[Material deprivation statistics - early results|Material deprivation statistics — early results]] *[[Living conditions in Europe - poverty and social exclusion]] ===Publications=== *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-032|title=Key figures on European living conditions – 2025 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-05-14-031|title=Being young in Europe today — 2015 edition}} ===Database=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/children-youth/database Youth (yth)], see: :Youth social inclusion (yth_incl) *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/income-and-living-conditions/database Income and living conditions (ilc)], see: :People at risk of poverty or social exclusion (Europe 2020 strategy) (ilc_pe) ::Main indicator - Europe 2020 target on poverty and social exclusion (ilc_peps) :Income distribution and monetary poverty (ilc_ip) ::Monetary poverty (ilc_li) :Living conditions (ilc_lv) ::Population structure (ilc_lvps) ::Health and labour conditions (ilc_lvhl) :Material deprivation (ilc_md) ::Material deprivation by dimension (ilc_mddd) *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=youth}} Youth] *[{{Template:Dedicated section|dedicated_section=income_social_inclusion_living_conditions}} Income, social inclusion and living conditions] ===Methodology=== *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=EU_statistics_on_income_and_living_conditions_(EU-SILC)_methodology EU-SILC methodology] ===Legislation=== *[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/social-protection-social-inclusion/social-protection-committee/indicators-sub-group_en European Commission — Directorate General for Employment, Social Affairs & Inclusion: Indicators’ Sub-Group of the Social Protection Committee] *[https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/index_en European Commission — Directorate General for Employment, Social Affairs & Inclusion: Employment and social analysis] ===External links=== *[https://youth.europa.eu/strategy_en EU youth strategy] *[https://europa.eu/youth/EU_en European youth portal] *[https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A52021DC0102 European Pillar of Social Rights Action Plan] *[https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/8648b964-5997-11ed-92ed-01aa75ed71a1/language-en Social Protection Committee Annual Report 2022] === Notes === 1. Households composed only of children, of students aged less than 25 years and/or by people aged 64 years or more are excluded from the computation of this indicator (for both the numerator and denominator). Students aged 18-24 years who live with at least one other person of working age who is not a student are excluded from the computation of the household work intensity, but they are given the household work intensity computed on the basis of the other household members. The same rule applies for children. {{Unit|topic=X_Modernisation_of_social_statistics}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Young people — social inclusion]] [[Category: Income and living conditions|Young people — social inclusion]] [[Category:Children and youth|Young people — social inclusion]] [[Category:Statistical article|Young people — social inclusion]] [[Category:June2027|Young people — social inclusion]]

title: Young people dropping out of education and labour market participation
text:
This article explores the phenomenon of young people dropping out of formal education in the European Union (EU), examining its prevalence, reasons and consequences. Data extracted in November 2025 Planned article update: No update planned 14.2% of young people aged 15-34 in the EU left formal education or training at least once in their lifetime, with men tending to leave at a slightly higher rate (15.2%) than women (13.1%). 42.6% of young people who left education did so due to reasons related to their education programme, such as the courses not meeting their expectations, being too difficult or not aligning with their interests. The rate of young people aged 15-34 not in employment, education or training (NEET rate) in 2024 was higher among those who had left formal education at least once (17.3%) compared to those who had not (11.2%).
This article explores the phenomenon of young people dropping out of formal education in the [[Glossary:European_Union_(EU)|European Union (EU)]], examining its prevalence, reasons and consequences. It delves into the demographic and geographic disparities in education dropout rates and the main reasons why people leave their formal education. The article also investigates the outcomes of dropping out of education, including the likelihood of returning to education and the risk of becoming not in employment, education or training ([[Glossary:Young_people_neither_in_employment_nor_in_education_and_training_(NEET)|NEET]]). === Education dropout rates and levels === In the EU, a significant proportion of young people have dropped out of formal education or training at some point. 14.2% of people aged 15-34 left formal education or training at least once in their lifetime (12.5% left once and 1.7% left several times) (see Figure 1). This phenomenon affected both young men and women, although men were slightly more likely to leave education, with 15.2% (13.2% once and 2.0% several times) compared to 13.1% of women (11.7% once and 1.4% several times). Given the relatively small proportion of people dropping out several times, these 2 groups are considered together in this article. Figure 1 There were significant differences in education dropout rates across EU countries. As illustrated in Map 1, over 20% of young people left formal education at least once in their lifetime in countries such as the Netherlands (32.2%), Denmark (27.1%), Luxembourg (24.8%), Estonia (24.4%), Austria (22.3%), Finland (22.0%) and Belgium (21.1%). By contrast, less than 5% of young people reported dropping out in Bulgaria (3.5%), Greece (2.2%) and Romania (1.5%). Map 1: Share of people aged 15-34 who dropped out of formal education or training, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_24eab01}} [[Image:MAP1 dropped out formal education 2024.png|thumb|centre|700px|Map 1: Share of people aged 15-34 who dropped out of formal education or training, 2024
''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_24eab01}}|alt=A map of Europe showing the percentage of people aged 15-34 who dropped out of formal education or training in 2024, with percentages categorised into ranges and represented by varying shades of pink. Data are shown as percentage for the EU member countries, Norway and North Macedonia. For more details please use the link to the source dataset code below the image.]] === Dropout rates by education level === Figure 2 gives an insight into the education levels at which young people most often dropped out in their lifetime. The level of the formal education or training activity refers to the programme that the student or apprentice started but did not successfully complete. The level of the formal education or training activity is defined according to the [[Glossary:International_standard_classification_of_education_(ISCED)|International Standard Classification of Education 2011]] (ISCED 2011). The data show that around one third of young people who left education in the EU dropped out of upper secondary education (36.2%) and around another third dropped out of bachelor or equivalent education (35.0%). The cumulative dropout rate at all other levels was less than 30%. For those who left education more than once, only the highest level is considered. Figure 2 This article looks at the 3 broader groups of education levels: * low education level: primary and lower secondary education (ISCED levels 1-2) * medium education level: upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education (ISCED levels 3 and 4) * high education level: tertiary education (levels 5-8) Medium education level is divided into 2 groups: programmes with the general orientation (general path) and programmes with the vocational orientation (vocational path). The data reveal that dropouts were distributed as follows: 8.2% at the low education level, 10.2% on the general path of medium education level (including unknown programme orientation), 29.9% on the vocational path of medium education and 51.7% at the high education level. An examination of country-specific trends reveals 2 distinct patterns described below. *In 9 EU countries, medium education was the level at which most young people dropped out, with Hungary (65.0%), Finland (54.8%), Denmark (53.5%), and Malta (53.2%) having the highest rates. *In 18 EU countries, high education was the level at which most young people dropped out, with Cyprus (74.8%) and Croatia (73.7%) having the highest rates. Figure 3 === Main reasons for dropping out === Dropping out of education is a complex issue, and understanding the underlying reasons is crucial for developing effective policies to support young people in completing their formal education or training. The most common reason in the EU for leaving formal education was related to the education programme itself (42.6% of all people who left formal education or training). This includes situations where the courses did not meet expectations or were too difficult; the studies did not align with the person’s interests; the perceived quality of teaching was low; and the expected outcomes were not met both in terms of educational content and expected labour market opportunities. Other reasons include perceiving the studies as too difficult, failing exams and deciding that another course was more suitable. Personal or family reasons also played a significant role (26.3%): 7.8% of people left education due to their own illness or disability, and 18.5% due to other family or personal reasons. These include care responsibilities for children or disabled relatives, pregnancy, marriage and the desire to spend more time with family. In addition, other factors are influential, such as family disapproval of educational choices, the need to relocate for personal relationships, conflicts with faculty or peers, and a general lack of motivation or interest in the programme. A significant portion of young people left education because they preferred to work (13.8%). This decision often hinges more on personal fulfilment rather than financial need, as people either found a job or wanted to look for one. Financial challenges also contributed to dropping out of education (5.3%). This broad category encompasses issues with fees, learning materials, living costs and a general lack of financial resources. ======Differences by education level and sex====== Reasons related to the education programme itself varied across different education levels: they accounted for 28.7% at the low education level, 35.9% at the medium level and a significant 50.2% at the high level. Personal or family reasons, however, were more prominent at lower educational levels and became less significant as education levels increased. Differences by sex were negligible for most of the reasons, except for the preference to work and other family or personal reasons. Young men more frequently reported a preference to work as their main reason for leaving education (16.5% for men and 10.6% for women). By contrast, young women reported other family or personal reasons more than men (20.3% and 16.9% respectively). Figure 4 ======Country-specific trends====== For country-level analysis, some reasons are combined: financial reasons with the preference to work, and own illness or disability with other family or personal reasons (see Figure 5). In Belgium, France, Austria, Denmark and Slovakia, over 50% of people reported leaving education due to issues with the education programme. Except for Slovakia, these countries had high overall education dropout rates. In Lithuania, Latvia, Finland, Cyprus, Poland and Germany, family or personal reasons were the most prevalent causes for dropping out. In Bulgaria, Romania, Greece, Hungary and Italy, over one third of people reported a preference to work or financial reasons. Interestingly, these countries had a lower overall education dropout rate. Figure 5 === Returning to education after dropping out === Although leaving education can have significant consequences, it is encouraging to note that many young people who initially left education were able to continue their educational journey later: about one third of young people who left education were able to attain the same or even higher levels of education. 37.7% of people aged 15-34 who dropped out of primary or lower secondary education later attained medium or high education levels. Among those who left upper secondary education, 35.5% reached medium education, while 5.6% progressed to high education. Around 29.2% of those who dropped out at bachelor level eventually completed a bachelor’s, master’s or PhD. These findings suggest that leaving education is not always a permanent setback as many young people are able to overcome initial obstacles and achieve their educational goals. ======Dropping out of education and NEET rates====== Leaving education is also closely linked to NEET rates, which measure the share of young people not in employment, education or training. The NEET rate was higher among those who left formal education at least once - 17.3% compared to 11.2% for those who did not (see Figure 6). Particularly high NEET rates were seen among those who dropped out at a low education level (32.4%) and a medium level (23.1%). Dropping out at a high education level did not significantly impact NEET rates, with figures remaining low at 10.5%. The data also reveal significant differences in NEET rates among countries. * Romania, Slovakia and Hungary showed significant gaps in NEET rates between people who left education and those who did not, with gaps of 25.5, 21.3 and 20.5 [[Glossary:Percentage_point|percentage points]], respectively. * By contrast, dropping out of education had little influence on NEET rates in Greece, Malta and Slovenia, which all had gaps below 3 percentage points. Figure 6 ======Impact of simultaneous participation in formal education and the labour force===== The data also suggest that participating in the labour force and formal education or training at the same time can hinder successful educational attainment. Across the EU, the [[Glossary:Correlation_coefficient|correlation coefficient]] between the education dropout rate and the rate of simultaneous participation in formal education and the labour force is 0.77, indicating a strong positive link. This means that countries with higher rate of simultaneous participation in formal education and the labour force tend to also have higher education dropout rates, and vice versa. Countries with a high number of people in both education and the labour force also reported high dropout rates. In the Netherlands (36.4% simultaneous participation rate), Denmark (28.1%) and Finland (25.4%), education dropout rates were particularly high at 32.2%, 27.1%, and 22.0% respectively. By contrast, countries with simultaneous participation rates below 4% had low dropout rates, generally under 10%. The overlaps between participation in education and the labour force reflect a wide range of situations. For some young people, employment plays a secondary role to education, for example, students who work just a few hours a week, such as at weekends or in the evenings after classes. Others combine work and formal education at the same time. In some cases, education is secondary to employment, for example, when people take classes after work to obtain a qualification. There are also situations where the same activity counts as both education and employment, e.g. apprenticeships, paid traineeships (when part of a formal education programme) or specific vocational training phases integrated into some higher education study programmes. In line with the EU-LFS definitions, paid trainees are classified as employed, but unpaid trainees are not. Figure 7 === Grouping countries by dropout indicators === A cluster analysis was conducted to group countries based on their dropout indicators. The analysis looked at several characteristics, including: * the education dropout rate * the education level at which people dropped out * the reason for dropping out * the NEET rate among people who left education and those who did not , * the rate of simultaneous participation in education and the labour force. The analysis revealed 5 distinct groups of countries (Figure 7), each with unique characteristics. '''Group 1: Hungary and Romania''' These 2 countries had the lowest share of people who left formal education or training. More than two thirds of those who left dropped out at low or medium education levels. This group reported the lowest percentage of people citing the programme not meeting expectations or being too difficult as the main reason for leaving. The NEET rate was the highest in this group for both those who left education and those who did not. The average rate of people in both education and the labour force was the lowest in this group. '''Group 2: Bulgaria, Greece, Croatia, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland''' This group of countries had a low share of people who dropped out of formal education or training. About two thirds of people in this group dropped out of high education, except Italy and Bulgaria. The NEET rate in this group was above average for both those who left formal education and those who did not. The rate of people in both education and the labour force was relatively low in this group. '''Group 3: Belgium, Ireland, France, Luxembourg, Slovenia, Slovakia and Sweden''' This group of countries had the highest share of people who dropped out of high education. The main reason for leaving was problems related to the programme: it was too difficult or did not meet expectations. The rate of people citing financial reasons or preferring to work was low. The NEET rate of those who left education and those who did not is below the EU average, except France and Slovakia. '''Group 4: Czechia, Germany, Estonia, Spain, Malta, Austria and Portugal''' This group of countries had a higher share of people who left formal education or training than EU average, except Czechia and Germany. The NEET rate in this group was lower than the EU average for both those who left formal education and those who did not. '''Group 5: Denmark, the Netherlands and Finland''' This group of countries had the highest share of people who left formal education or training. The shares of people who dropped out of medium and high education were similar. The rate of people citing preferring to work or financial reasons was the lowest rate among all groups. The NEET rate in this group was low among both those who left formal education and those who did not. The rate of people in both education and the labour force was the highest in this group. === Data sources === The [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(EU-LFS)|EU-LFS]] is the largest European household sample survey providing quarterly and annual results on labour market characteristics of people. The EU-LFS covers the resident population, defined as all people usually residing in private households. Since 1999, modules have been an integral part of the EU-LFS. These were called ‘ad hoc modules’ until 2020. From 2021 onwards, they are called either ‘8-yearly modules’ for variables with an 8-year cycle or ‘modules on an ad hoc subject’ for variables not included in the 8-year datasets. In 2024, the EU-LFS included an 8-yearly module on young people in the labour market. Similar ad hoc modules were conducted in 2000, 2009 and 2016. The next time the same 8-yearly module will be carried out will be in 2032. For further information on the EU-LFS modules, please refer to the article [[EU_labour_force_survey_-_modules|EU labour force survey - modules]]. '''Coverage.''' The 2024 EU-LFS module on young people in the labour market covers all [[Glossary:EU|EU]] countries, 1 [[Glossary:EFTA|EFTA]] country and 1 [[Glossary:Candidate_countries|candidate country]]. For Cyprus, the survey covers only the areas of Cyprus controlled by the Government of the Republic of Cyprus. Only people aged 15-34 were covered by the module. '''European aggregates.''' EU aggregates in absolute values are calculated by aggregating the estimated values (i.e. weighted population totals) of the respective EU countries. For EU aggregates expressed as rates or ratios, the absolute values are first calculated for both the numerator and the denominator, and then the rates or ratios are derived from those results. '''Calculation of percentages.''' All the figures in this article are percentages of a total. The calculation of percentages used in this article is based on a total excluding the number of people classified in the non-response category. As such, all exhaustive breakdowns presented in the figures should amount to 100% (allowing for rounding errors). ====Definitions==== '''Formal education and training''' Formal education and training is defined according to the International Standard Classification of Education 2011 (ISCED 2011) as ‘education that is institutionalised, intentional and planned through public organizations and recognised private bodies and - in their totality - constitute the formal education system of a country. Formal education programmes are thus recognised as such by the relevant national education authorities or equivalent authorities, e.g. any other institution in cooperation with the national or sub-national education authorities. Formal education consists mostly of initial education. Vocational education, special needs education and some parts of adult education are often recognised as being part of the formal education system.’ (ISCED 2011 glossary). The ISCED definition of (formal) education includes (formal) training. '''Dropping out of (or ‘abandoning’) formal education or training''' means that a person has started a formal education programme but has not successfully completed it. According to the ISCED 2011, ‘a common characteristic of an education programme is that, upon fulfilment of learning objectives or educational tasks, successful completion is certified.’ Accordingly, dropping out of formal education is defined as leaving formal education without certification or without obtaining the final credential associated with this formal education. The variable covers all formal education activities abandoned during the life of the person. '''Education levels'''
'''The level of the formal education or training activity''' is defined according to the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED 2011). Data on dropout levels are presented in 3 aggregates: * low education - primary and lower secondary education (ISCED levels 1-2) * medium education - upper secondary and post-secondary non-tertiary education (ISCED levels 3 and 4) * high education - tertiary education (ISCED levels 5-8). The indicator on '''young people neither in employment nor in education and training''' ([[Glossary:Young_people_neither_in_employment_nor_in_education_and_training_(NEET)|NEET]]) corresponds to the percentage of the population of a given age group and sex that is not employed and not involved in education or training. NEET rates estimated based on the EU-LFS module differ slightly from the NEET rates available in the dataset 'Young persons neither in employment nor in education and training by citizenship (NEET rates) {{Template:Publication|code=edat_lfse_23|title=(edat_lfse_23)}}' due to sub-sampling for the module. '''Employed person''' is a person who, during the reference week, was in one of the following categories: * people who, during the reference week, worked for at least 1 hour for pay or profit, including contributing family workers * people with a job or business who were temporarily not at work during the reference week but had an attachment to their job. '''Unemployed person''' is a person who, during the reference week, were in all 3 of the following categories: * not employed during the reference week according to the definition of employed above * currently available for work, i.e. available to start working for paid employment or self-employment before the end of the 2 weeks following the reference week *actively seeking work, i.e. had either carried out activities in the 4-week period ending with the reference week to find paid employment or self-employment, or already found a job expected to start within a period of at most 3 months from the end of the reference week. '''Labour force''' comprises people who were either employed or unemployed during the reference week. === Context === The [https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/european-pillar-social-rights-building-fairer-and-more-inclusive-european-union_en European Pillar of Social Rights] sets out 20 key principles and rights essential for fair and well-functioning labour markets and welfare systems. Principle 4 (‘Active support to employment’) states that ‘young people have the right to continued education, apprenticeship, traineeship or a job offer of good standing within 4 months of becoming unemployed or leaving education’. An overall commitment to an inclusive high employment rate is made by setting an [https://op.europa.eu/webpub/empl/european-pillar-of-social-rights/en/ EU-level target]: the overall goal is that at least 78% of the EU population aged 20-64 should be in employment by 2030. To reach this goal, the target is to improve employment prospects for people aged 15-29 and so reduce the share of this group who are not in employment, education or training to 9%. In 2020, all EU countries committed to implementing the improved [http://eur-lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:32020H1104(01):EN:NOT Youth guarantee in a Council Recommendation] which steps up the comprehensive job support available to young people across the EU and makes it more targeted and inclusive. In 2022, the ministers of education of the EU adopted a [https://education.ec.europa.eu/education-levels/school-education/pathways-to-school-success Council Recommendation on pathways to school success]. The Recommendation aims to promote better educational outcomes for all learners, by improving basic skills performance, reducing early leaving from education and training and promoting well-being at school. Key recommendations include the following described below. * Systemic approach. Simultaneously address underachievement in basic skills and early leaving from education and training, take action to promote students’ and teachers’ well-being, prevent bullying and favour a positive learning climate. * Integrated and comprehensive strategies. Develop or strengthen strategies that include prevention, intervention and compensation measures (but with a stronger emphasis on preventative actions) through all levels of school education. * Attention for groups at risk. Complement universal action with targeted and tailored support for learners requiring extra help in inclusive settings. * Data collection. Develop or improve data collection and monitoring systems at national, regional and local levels. === Other articles === *[[Labour market (incl. labour force survey)|All articles on the labour market]] *[[Participation of young people in education and the labour market]] *[[Statistics on young people neither in employment nor in education or training]] === Database === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/lfs/database Employment and unemployment (Labour Force Survey) (employ)], see: :[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=lfso LFS ad-hoc modules (lfso)] ::[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database?node_code=lfso_24 2024. Young people on the labour market (lfso_24)] === Thematic section === *[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/lfs/overview Labour Force Survey] === Publications === *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/lfs/publications EU labour force survey publications] *[[EU labour force survey|EU labour force survey - online publication]] === Methodology=== *[[EU labour force survey|EU labour force survey - online publication]] *[https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/lfs/methodology Labour force survey (LFS) - Main concepts] *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-01-25-051|title=Quality report of the European Union Labour Force Survey 2021 & 2022 - 2025 edition}} *{{Template:Publication|code=KS-FT-24-003|title=Labour force survey in the EU, EFTA and candidate countries - Main characteristics of national surveys, 2021 - 2024 edition}} '''ESMS metadata files and EU-LFS methodology ''' *{{Template:Esms|code=employ_esms|title=Employment and unemployment (Labour Force Survey)}} (ESMS metadata file - employ_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=lfso_esms|title=LFS ad-hoc modules}} (ESMS metadata file - lfso_esms) *{{Template:Esms|code=lfso_24_esms|title=Young people on the labour market}} (ESMS metadata file - lfso_24_esms) === Legislation === *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32019R1700:EN:NOT|title=Regulation (EU) 2019/1700 of the European Parliament and of the Council}} *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32020R0256:EN:NOT|title=Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/256}} *{{Template:EurLex|code=CELEX:32022R2312:EN:NOT|title=Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/2312}} === External links === *[https://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1&langId=en European Commission, Directorate-General for Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion - Policies and activities] ''View this article online at http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Young_people_dropping_out_of_education_and_labour_market_participation'' {{Unit|topic=X_Labour_market}} [[Category:Population and social conditions|Young people dropping out of education and labour market participation]] [[Category:Labour market (incl. labour force survey)|Young people dropping out of education and labour market participation]] [[Category:Employment|Young people dropping out of education and labour market participation]] [[Category:Vistool|Young people dropping out of education and labour market participation]] [[Category:Statistical article|Young people dropping out of education and labour market participation]] [[Category:No update|Young people dropping out of education and labour market participation]]

title: Young people on the labour market - statistics
text:
<pdftheme>3</pdftheme>
<updatedata>
Data extracted in January 2018

No planned article update
</updatedata>

<highlight>
<tweet>
In 2016, 77 % of young people in the EU did not change or were not willing to change their place of residence for a job.
</tweet>
<tweet>
In 2016,  54 % of young people in the EU did not work while studying for their highest completed qualification, with the largest rate of non-working students in Romania (91 %) and the smallest in Finland (8 %).
</tweet>
<tweet>
In 2016, 16 % of employed persons in the EU aged 15-34 reported that their current main job did not correspond to their level of education. 
</tweet>

<noprint>[[Image:Proportion of people aged 15-34 with some form of education who did not work during their studies in 2009 and 2016 .png|500px|thumb|centre|People aged 15-34 who did not work while studying for their highest qualification, 2009 and 2016 (% of people aged 15-34 who had completed any formal education). ''Source:'' Eurostat customized data extraction]]</noprint>

This article presents some findings from a survey on the situation of young people in the labour market<ref>The European [[Glossary:Labour_force_survey_(LFS)|Labour Force Survey]] is a large sample survey among private households in Europe and an important source for European statistics about the situation and trends in the EU [[Glossary:Labour_market|labour market]]. In addition to the [[EU labour force survey - methodology|core survey]] which is unchanged from year to year, there is also a supplementary, or [[EU_labour_force_survey_-_modules|ad hoc]], module, each year. The topic of the 2016 ad hoc module was ''young people on the labour market''. A similar topic was part of the EU-LFS in 2000 and 2009.</ref>. The survey has a special focus on [http://ec.europa.eu/dgs/education_culture/repository/education/policy/vocational-policy/doc/alliance/work-based-learning-in-europe_en.pdf work based education], finding out in detail how different types of education correlate with, for instance, the [[Glossary:Employment_rate|employment rate]] and with [http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/labour-market/quality-of-employment quality of employment]. Other topics which are covered are education/job mismatch, reasons for not completing qualifications or not continuing education, methods for finding a job, and being ready either to commute or to move residence in order to have or to find a job.
</highlight>

<articlecontent>
<sesection>
=== Key messages===

* The most common reasons respondents give for not completing their education or training courses, is their wish to start working or their lack of interest in the chosen course

* Only 15 % of those who recently started to work received any help from the public employment office to find work

* The most common method of finding a job is to ask friends or relatives

* About one quarter (23 %) of young persons are either willing to move residence or have done so in order to find or have a job

* Having work experience while in education correlates with higher employment rates, but not with higher job quality
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Survey population ===

The Labour Force Survey ad hoc module 2016 targeted persons aged 15 to 34 years. This article will therefore exclusively analyse this age group.
Figure 1 shows that important changes take place in this age span. Almost all 15 year olds are in education but outside the labour force (so neither having a job nor looking for or being available for one), whereas a very large majority of the 34 year olds are in employment and not in education. It also shows that the peak age for being both in education and having a job at the same time is 18 - 21, and that the number of unemployed persons is rather stable between the ages of 20 - 34.<ref>Percentage calculations exclude item non-response.</ref>

<image imgid='figure1' zoom='95'>[[Image:Labour force survey ad hoc module 2016 target population.jpg|thumb|centre|500px|Figure 1:  Survey population of the Labour Force Survey ad hoc module 2016 by age, labour force status and status in education. Millions of persons. ''Source:'' Eurostat customized data extraction]]</image>  
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Few move house or commute to find or to have a job ===

In the EU-28 in 2016, 77 % of young people did not change or would not be willing to change their place of residence for a job. Figure 2 shows that the willingness to move residence correlates somewhat with education level and strongly with status in employment (i.e. employed or unemployed). Among those who had a job at the time of the survey, 90 % had not changed their place of residence in order to get their current job. This 'did not move for the job' rate decreases with increased education level (93.2 % for low education, 84.6 % for high education) that is, persons with high education move residence for professional reasons more often than others. Among those who were unemployed at the time of the survey, 23 % of those with high education would change residence inside the country and 16 % would change residence inside the EU to get a job. The corresponding numbers for persons with medium level education and low level education were a bit lower, at 21.3 % (low education) and 20.4 % (medium education) for moving inside the country and at 11.3 % (medium education) and 10.2 % (low education) for moving to another EU country. People are more willing to change residence inside their countries than to move to another EU country for work purposes. 

<image imgid='figure2' zoom='95'>[[Image:Willingness to move to find a job by education level and employment status, EU-28, 2016 ( % of concerned employment status and education level).png|500px|thumb|centre|Figure 2 : People aged 20-34 by readiness to move residence in order to find or have a job,  education level and labour market status, EU-28, 2016 (% of concerned labour market status and education level). ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_16move4j}})]]</image> 

Regarding commuting, 76 % of young people in the EU-28 are not currently commuting or would not be willing to commute for longer than one hour each way between home and work. Among the EU Member States this rate was highest in the Netherlands (93%) and lowest in Italy (61%). Among all the countries covered by the survey the lowest rate was in Turkey (6%), meaning that practically all young people in Turkey are willing to travel at least one hour each way between home and work every day.

<image imgid='figure3' zoom='95'>[[Image:People not having or not willing to have more than one hour travel time each way to work, 2016 ( % of people aged 15-34 ).png |500px|thumb|centre|Figure 3 : People not having or not willing to have more than one hour travel time each way to work, 2016 ( % of people aged 15-34 ). ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_16cmt4j}})]]</image> 

</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Half worked while studying  ===
<section begin="new" />In 2016,  54 % of young people in the EU-28 did not work at all while studying for their highest completed qualification, neither paid nor unpaid. The largest rate of non-working students was in Romania (91 %) followed by Greece (78 %), Bulgaria (77 %) and Spain (74 %), while the smallest rates were in Finland (8 %) and Sweden (17 %).<section end="new" />
The 2009 and 2016 rates are not fully comparable due to slightly different definitions, <ref>Variable WORKEDUC in 2009 No work or work less than 1 month per year. Variable WORKEXP in 2016 Persons not working at all during studies. </ref> but it can be reasonably concluded that working while studying has become more widespread over time (Figure 4). In the EU the rate of young people not working while studying for their highest completed qualification decreased from 65 % (EU-27) in 2009 to 54 % (EU-28) in 2016.

<image imgid='figure4' zoom='95'>[[Image:Proportion of people aged 15-34 with some form of education who did not work during their studies in 2009 and 2016 .png|500px|thumb|centre|Figure 4 : People aged 15-34 who did not work while studying for their highest qualification, 2009 and 2016 (% of people aged 15-34 who had completed any formal education). ''Source:'' Eurostat customized data extraction]]</image>

Close to a third of the respondents had paid work experience while studying (Figure 5) with the highest rates in Sweden (71 %), the Netherlands (68 %) and Finland (65 %) as well as in Iceland (87 %) and Switzerland (71 %). Among the Member States, Austria is the country with the highest rate of young people with only paid work experience (49 %) while studying. Lithuania, Hungary and Romania are the only countries where the percentage of people with unpaid work experience is higher than the percentage of people with paid work experience. Looking at the share of people with only unpaid work experience, the rate is lower than 15 % in a large majority of the countries (21 of 32 countries). The countries with a high rate of people with only unpaid work experience are France and Hungary (both 31 %).

<image imgid='figure5' zoom='95'>[[Image:Distribution of people aged 15-34 by work experience during studies, 2016 (% of people aged 15-34 who had any form of completed formal education)_.png|500px|thumb|centre|Figure 5 : Young people by work experience while studying, 2016 (% of people aged 15-34 who had completed any formal education). ''Source:'' Eurostat  {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_16workexp}}]]</image>
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Labour market outcomes by type of education  ===

'''High education means high employment rate''' 

The employment rate was lower for people who did not work at all while studying for their highest completed qualification than for those who did (Figure 6).

<image imgid='figure6' zoom='95'>[[Image:Employment rate by education type and by work experience during studies , EU-28, 2016 (% of people aged 15-34 who had any form of completed formal education).png|500px|thumb|centre|Figure 6 : Employment rate of people aged 15-34 by education type and work experience while studying , EU-28, 2016. ''Source:'' Eurostat  {{Stable link|title=|code= lfso_16emprt}}]]</image>

Perhaps surprisingly, work-based learning (work as a structured part of the education) correlates with a lower employment rate than work experience outside the curriculum does, no matter the education level. 

Furthermore it can be observed that education level and type matters greatly: the employment rate of those with a high education is always highest, followed by those with a medium level vocational education, then by those with a medium level general education, and the low level education at the bottom. The impact of the education level on the employment rate is however less pronounced for people having worked only outside the curriculum while studying.

'''Low education means low job quality''' 

[http://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/labour-market/quality-of-employment Quality of employment] can be measured in many ways, three of which are presented in this article.

Figure 7 shows that persons with medium level vocational training are least subjected to short job tenures (defined here as less than one year), and furthermore that among these persons it is those with no work experience while in school that are in the best position, followed by those who had work based learning (i.e. work as a structured part of the curriculum). Persons with medium level general education are worst off on this indicator of short job tenures. It can therefore be reasonably concluded that the orientation of the education (general vs vocational) is more important than the length of the education (low vs medium vs high). There is no clear pattern coming from having had work experience or not.

<image imgid='figure7' zoom='95'>[[Image:Employed persons with job tenure less than one year by education level and work while studying, persons aged 20-34, EU-28, 2016.jpg|500px|thumb|centre|Figure 7 : Employed persons with job tenure less than one year by education level and work while studying, persons aged 20-34, EU-28, 2016 (% of total employed persons). ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_16jobten}})]]</image>

In Figure 8, which shows how many persons work during weekends, it can be seen that the length of the education is the best predictor for the indicator: those with low education are twice as likely to work during weekends as those with high education, and the persons with medium level education are in the middle. Having had work experience only outside the curriculum has some correlation with more weekend work, but the effect is not strong.

<image imgid='figure8' zoom='95'>[[Image:Employed persons working on weekends by education level and work while studying, persons aged 20-34, EU-28, 2016.jpg|500px|thumb|centre|Figure 8 : Employed persons working on weekends by education level and work while studying, persons aged 20-34, EU-28, 2016 (% of total employed persons). ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_16wkendw}})]]</image>

Clear education level effects are also found in Figure 9: precarious work (defined here as work contracts of maximum three months' duration) is much more common among persons with low education than among those with high education. Again, persons with medium level vocational education are better off than those with medium level general education. Work based learning correlates with more precarity for all education levels.

<image imgid='figure9' zoom='95'>[[Image:Labour_force_survey_ad_hoc_module_2016_precarious_work.jpg|500px|thumb|centre|Figure 9 : Precarious work by education level and work while studying, persons aged 20-34, EU-28, 2016 ( % of employees). ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_16precemp}})]]</image>

'''One in six work in jobs that do not fit their qualification level''' 

Figure 10 presents education/job mismatch. At EU-level, 16 % of employed persons aged 15-34 reported in 2016 that their current main job does not correspond at all to their level of education. The mismatch between the current job and the education level was highest in Denmark (32 %) and Slovakia (27 %), followed by France (24 %), Spain and Poland (both 23 %). As regards the non-EU Member States, one out of two persons in Turkey also had this problem. On the other hand, the job mismatch levels were the lowest in the Netherlands and Germany (both 6 %), Romania, Hungary and Switzerland (all 7 %).

<image imgid='figure10' zoom='95'>[[Image:Incidence of job mismatch by country, 2016 (% of people aged 15-34 reporting that their current main job does not correspond at all to their level of education)_.png|500px|thumb|centre|Figure 10 : Education/job mismatch by country, 2016 (% of total employed persons). ''Source:'' Eurostat  {{Stable link|title=|code= lfso_16oklev}} ]]</image>

'''Working while studying increases the chance of finding a job later''' 

In the EU-28, the unemployment rate among young people without work experience during their education was 15.7 % while it was 8.1 % for persons with work experience outside the curriculum  (Table 1). The unemployment rates ranged from 3.2 % (Germany, work based learning and work outside curriculum) to 37.2 % (Greece, no work experience). The results vary greatly among the countries, with the highest unemployment rates for young people with no work experience at all in Greece (37.2 %) and Spain (31.7 %). On the other hand, the lowest unemployment rates were for people with work experience: Germany (3.2 %), Poland (3.5 %, work only outside curriculum) and the United Kingdom (4.6 %, work based learning).

<image imgid='table1' zoom='95'>[[Image:Unemployment rate by education level, type and by work experience during studies , EU-28, 2016 (% of people aged 15-34 who had any form of completed formal education).png|500px|thumb|centre|Table 1 : Unemployment rate of people aged 15-34 rate by work while studying , EU-28, 2016. ''Source:'' Eurostat  {{Stable link|title=|code= lfso_16unert}} ]]</image>
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== Highest dropout rate from tertiary education among those who had work based learning in secondary education  ===

Figure 11 shows persons with completed medium level education and who had not (yet) completed tertiary education. Their decision on whether or not to continue their education is presented according to their previous work experience.

Among those who had work based learning during their secondary education, typically associated with vocational education, more than three quarters (77 %) never started tertiary education. Furthermore, 8 % started but dropped out, and 14 % were in tertiary education at the time of the survey. This means that about one third of those who started tertiary education did not complete their studies. The corresponding number for those who worked only outside the curriculum was one quarter, and for those who did not work at all it was one sixth.

<image imgid='figure11' zoom='95'>[[Image:Tertiary education decisions by work experience while in secondary education.jpg|500px|thumb|centre|Figure 11 : Tertiary education decisions by work experience while in secondary education, people aged 15-34 (% of work experience type). ''Source:'' Eurostat  {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_16ymghied}}) and {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_16ymgnedns}})] and {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_16ymgnednc}})]]</image>
</sesection>

<sesection>
=== One in five are content with the Public Employment Services  ===

Although there are notable differences in the way persons found their current job, three methods are much more common than the other methods (Figure 12). No matter the education level, asking relatives, friends or acquaintances, contacting employers directly and using advertisements vastly outnumber the other methods.

The most used method for persons with low or medium level of education was clearly to ask relatives, friends or acquaintances. On the other hand, the most used methods among persons with high education was to read or place advertisements. Contacting employers directly is almost equally used across all education groups.

<image imgid='figure12' zoom='95'>[[Image:Labour_force_survey_ad_hoc_module_2016_methods_used_to_find_the_current_job.jpg|500px|thumb|centre|Figure 12 : Methods used to find the current job, people aged 15-34 by education level, 2016 (% of people aged 15-34 who stated which method they used). ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_16findmet}})]]</image>

Figure 13 also shows that the use of public employment services are low. About 20 % of persons aged 15-34 say they have received helpful support to find a job this way. Those who are unemployed are happier with the received support than those who are in employment. The education level does not influence this result to any noticeable degree.

<image imgid='figure13' zoom='95'>[[Image:Labour_force_survey_ad_hoc_module_2016_support_for_finding_a_job.jpg|500px|thumb|centre|Figure 13 : Support for finding a job, people aged 15-34 by education level and status in employment, 2016 (% of people aged 15-34 who stated their level of received help). ''Source:'' Eurostat {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_16supemp}}) and {{Stable link|title=|code=lfso_16supnemp}})]]</image>
</sesection>

<datadetails>
=== Data sources===

The data source for this article is the European Labour Force Survey ad hoc module 2016, covering all Member States, as well as Iceland, Norway, Switzerland and Turkey.
</datadetails>

<context>
=== Context ===

The [https://ec.europa.eu/info/business-economy-euro/economic-and-fiscal-policy-coordination/eu-economic-governance-monitoring-prevention-correction/european-semester/framework/europe-2020-strategy_en European Commission's EU2020 Strategy] has several goals for education and labour market participation for young people:

* at least 40% of young people should have a tertiary education
* the employment rate of people aged 20-34 within 3 years after their graduation should be at least 82%
* no more than 10% of early leavers from education and training.

The [http://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1079 Youth Guarantee] is a commitment by all Member States to ensure that all young people under the age of 25 years receive a good quality offer of employment, continued education, apprenticeship or traineeship within a period of four months of becoming unemployed or leaving formal education. 

The [http://www.cedefop.europa.eu/en European Centre for the Development of Vocational Training] is working to increase the quality of vocational training in Europe by making it more accessible and relevant to the needs of the labour market. This is a key component in reducing the number of early leavers from education and training. The [http://www.cedefop.europa.eu/en/news-and-press/news/bruges-communiqu-enhanced-european-cooperation-vocational-education-and-training Bruges communiqué], as part of  the [https://www.eqavet.eu/What-We-Do/European-Policy/Copenhagen-Process Copenhagen Process for European co-operation on vocational education and training], underlines the need for apprenticeships to provide labour market skills.

The European Council is promoting [http://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/policies/youth-employment/labour-mobility/ cross-border EU labour mobility] through the Your first EURES job programme and the Programme for employment and social innovation.
</context>
